## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully compared with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of any importance; embellished with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority and influence in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture and in which passages of their works they did so.*

*An edition of the greatest accuracy, easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reissued works, the exceedingly convenient format of the volumes, consistently uniform throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection—single, systematic, and chronological—which for the first time in our library brings together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.*

### Second Series

The second series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold for 1,200 French francs; the Greek-Latin edition for 1,300. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

## The Complete Works of Saint Paschasius Radbertus

### Prolegomena to the Works of Saint Paschasius Radbertus

[Col. 0009]

## Historical Eulogy of Saint Paschasius Radbertus

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, vol. II.)*

### Chapter I. Radbertus’s Life, Native Place, and Education

[Col. 0009A]

**1.** Such was the esteem in which Paschasius Radbertus was held by the people of his time that Engelmodus, bishop of Soissons, composed a poem in his praise and dedicated it to him while he was still alive. Apart from Engelmodus, the most devout abbot had many admirers, as I shall say below; but no one accurately committed to writing the deeds he had accomplished. For he was a man of singular modesty, and, sensing that his death was near, he summoned the brothers and, bidding them a final farewell, is said to have forbidden them to write anything about his life. Antonio de Caulincurte bears witness to this in the manuscript *Chronicle of Corbie*, composed at the beginning of the previous century.

Engelmodus’s little poem on Radbertus, utterly rough and obscure, which Sirmond placed before Radbertus’s works, did not seem important enough to reprint here. I have thought it sufficient to excerpt from it in this eulogy whatever contributes to illuminating the deeds of the holy man.

[Col. 0009B]

**2.** Radbertus was born in the district of Soissons, or perhaps in the city itself, of unknown parents. Since he was consecrated to God as a boy in the monastery of the Blessed Mary in that city, this suggests that he was a native of Soissons. At one time I suspected that the holy man had been born at Basoches, a small town in the district of Soissons, because, at the request of the inhabitants of that place, he polished the book on the *Life and Passion of Saints Rufinus and Valerius*.

The previously praised Corbie chronicler is certainly mistaken when he says that Paschasius Radbertus was Roman by birth, seventh in the order of deacons, and was brought into Gaul by Blessed Adalhard. Our Menard also fell into the same error, as did several others. The occasion for the mistake seems to me to have arisen from the shared name and rank of Paschasius, deacon of the Holy Roman Church in the time of Pope Symmachus, who nevertheless lived three hundred years before our Paschasius.

Whatever the case, Radbertus was his proper name [Col. 0009C], the name under which he subscribed the Council of Paris. Lupus writes to him under that name; “Paschasius” was an additional name, which he himself usually placed before his proper name, as in the letter to Charles the Bald cited below.

**3.** From his earliest years he was educated in the Benedictine nunnery at Soissons, dedicated to the Blessed Mary. The history of this convent has recently been composed by our Michael Germanus, my companion and assistant in my studies.

Paschasius mentions this favor more than once in his writings, namely in his exposition of Psalm 44 and in his short work *On the Virginity of the Blessed Mary*. He dedicated both works to the aforesaid nuns as a memorial of his gratitude. In these passages, and especially in the dedicatory letters, he professes himself their pupil. Engelmodus also gives testimony in his poem, where he speaks of these virgins as follows:

[Col. 0010A]

“For to these, provident Creator, you entrusted him to be nourished,

You who hold all things by your command,

Who by eternal reason govern what you yourself created,

When, while still a tender infant, the first gifts of his mother,

Who had given birth to him, were covered with the black coverings,

And the devouring image of death surrounded the exposed child.”

From these verses we obscurely understand that Radbertus, a little boy deprived of his mother, fell into danger of death; and therefore, according to the custom of those times, was exposed as though abandoned to his fate—or at least that, after being brought into the church of the Virgin Mother of God, he recovered his health and was entrusted from heaven to the care of the nuns.

### Chapter II. His Tonsure and His Secular and Monastic Life

**4.** While Radbertus was living in that convent, he received the clerical tonsure, as he himself admits at the beginning of the third book of his *Exposition of Psalm 44*, while Engelmodus sang these verses after those quoted above:

[Col. 0010B]

“Born from the heavenly offspring of divine blood,

And enrolled among the flocks endowed with the gift of the angelic choir,

They rightly fitted you, seized away above the heights,

As a fellow citizen of heaven, for the ministries of the Almighty.”

The Saint himself should be heard in the passage soon to be cited, addressing the nuns of Soissons:

“Therefore, dearest ones, while I consider your excellence, while I contemplate the laws and praises of your espousal, everywhere divine, I fear to speak, lest I offend precisely where I desire to please, if I fail to show the reverence due to you in all my writings. For I understand you to be honored in heaven, where you have given your names, so that you are not only brides, but also flowers of the Church and the adornment of the Bridegroom.

“When I behold you at the right hand of our most kind God and Savior Christ, adorned with manifold variety, I grieve deeply because I lost, through a long exile in the world, the crown which I had received as a boy before the holy altar of the Mother of God, with your prayers and with the ministry of praise by which your hearts and heads are consecrated [Col. 0010C] to God, your Bridegroom, the immortal King; I lost it after being defiled by many worldly acts.”

**5.** In this humble and modest confession the holy man teaches us that he departed from that monastery into the world, where he devoted himself to worldly activities—whether in clerical or lay life is uncertain—and that he spent a considerable time in this manner of life.

For this reason he adds:

“Therefore, wounded as I am, while you lift your hearts upward, I ask that, remembering me, you pray before the divine grace already granted to you, so that, through the intervention of your merits, the most merciful Judge may remove from me the punishments I deserve and, in his goodness, restore the crown I lost.”

**6.** Later Radbertus, weary of secular life, withdrew to the monastery of Corbie. There he was admitted, as the monk Gualdo testifies in the prologue to the short work *On the Life of Saint Anscharius*, by Saint Adalhard, whom he repeatedly calls his own master and teacher.

[Col. 0011A] There he cultivated letters with such industry, diligence, and piety that he was afterward acknowledged by his associates as their teacher and earned great esteem among everyone.

“Sirmond writes that, although many things adorned Corbie in Radbertus’s time, I do not know whether anything was more illustrious than Radbertus himself—a man outstanding in learning, integrity, and every mark of a most religious and holy life. Through his wisdom the others became more learned; through his example, holier; and through his zeal and vigilance, they became more diligent, since he presided over them all.”

### Chapter III. His Office as Teacher, His Exercises, Pupils, and Missions

**7.** Radbertus had not merely touched upon humane letters, as is clear to anyone who reads his writings, in which he occasionally brings pagan authors forward. Nor do I doubt that he instructed others in similar disciplines. He learned these disciplines to the extent necessary [Col. 0011B] for the formation of his own mind and that of others; but his principal study was reading and meditating upon Sacred Scripture and the holy Fathers.

Hence, before he was abbot, he expounded the Gospel before his fellow monks on feast days. The prologue to Matthew, addressed to the monk Guntland, confirms this. He writes:

“While, in obedience to my sacred profession, the Gospel was being treated before the brothers on feast days, as is customary, for the purpose of exhortation, although in an unpolished manner of speaking, some of them, fervent in religion, began repeatedly to ask with insistent devotion that I explain in order the text of the narrative of blessed Matthew the Evangelist—though they did not consider whether I was able to do so.”

**8.** In all his studies and writings the holy man did not neglect any duty of monastic life. Rather, as he says in the aforementioned prologue, because under this discipline he had no other free time, he performed the labor of writing during stolen hours.

For it seemed to him [Col. 0011C] that “no activity at present is more blessed or more genuine than taking part in the ministries of the angels, mingling with divine conversations, and presenting oneself before the divine presence.” These are his words at the beginning of the prologue to his exposition of Psalm 44.

Above all, he detested idleness, believing that monks were granted leisure and the opportunity for solitude “not so that we might languish in sloth, but so that we might meditate on the commandments of God, on divine praises and contemplation, on the Sacred Scriptures, on the Law and the Prophets, on the Gospel and the teaching of the apostles, and on the traditions of the holy Fathers, so that somehow we might present to Christ what we know.”

He directed virtually all his studies and all his nocturnal labors toward this end: namely, avoiding sluggish idleness, as will be explained more fully below.

**9.** Radbertus had many disciples in the school of Corbie. Among the more distinguished were Adalhard the Younger, the senior Adalhard’s disciple and deputy in governing the monastery; Saint Anscharius, apostle of the northern peoples [Col. 0011D]; Hildemannus; and Odo, each successively bishop of Beauvais, with Hermenfridus between them; Warinus, later abbot of New Corbie; and many others.

**10.** During this period he undertook various missions and journeys.

In the year 822, he went to Saxony on account of the new monastery—as he himself says in Book I of *The Life of Wala*, chapter 7—in order that the establishment of New Corbie might be completed. He went together with Antonius and Arsenius, that is, Abbot Adalhard and his brother Wala. According to chapter 14 of the same book, Radbertus was Wala’s constant companion in everything, almost a third member of their party in every matter.

Then, in 826, after Adalhard, abbot of French Corbie, had died and the monks had given their votes to Wala, Radbertus was sent to Louis Augustus to obtain his confirmation of the election.

“After Antonius had died,” Radbertus says in chapter 11 of the book already mentioned, “an outstanding shepherd was soon appointed in his place. On account of this election I myself was sent by the brothers, and I promptly obtained from the Emperor what everyone had long desired.”

When one of the nobles asked him why they had chosen so severe a man, Paschasius replied, among other things, that the one who should be preferred was not the man who followed behind, but rather the one who went ahead.

He was employed in public affairs not only by his own people but also by Louis Augustus himself. In the year 831 he was sent by Louis to Saxony as an envoy on account, as I think, of the holy expedition then being undertaken through Anscharius among the northern peoples under the Emperor’s direction. According to chapter 8 of the same book, while returning from there and coming to Agrippina, he learned that Wala had suffered exile as his punishment.

Finally, while Wala was in exile near Lake Limagne, Radbertus was sent by the same Emperor to deal with ecclesiastical and monastic affairs, as stated in Book II, chapter 10. The esteem in which Wala held him, and the value he placed on his counsel, are clear from the fact that he scarcely ever traveled or conducted business without him.

Radbertus was Wala’s companion both at the assembly of the kingdom convened on Judith’s account [Col. 0012B], according to chapters 9 and 10 of the same book, and on his journey to Pope Gregory IV, according to chapters 15 and 16.

In my judgment, however, nothing more strongly commends Wala’s love for Paschasius or more clearly attests the esteem in which he held him than Wala’s final words as he lay dying. Paschasius reports them in Book I, chapter 5, of the *Epitaph*, as follows:

“Most unhappy am I, that I received the final admonitions of your words while so far away! For you say—as our Chremes reported to me—and you say: ‘Yes, my son, do whatever good you know how to do, if possible, lest I be found inferior to you.’ These, my Father, are your final words to me; these are the commands arising from your esteem. It was not because you knew that I was perfect, but you took diligent care that I might advance through knowledge.”

Nothing is more tender than these words of Wala, and nothing more modest than this judgment of Paschasius.

### Chapter IV. His Levitical Rank, Abbatial Dignity, and Deeds

[Col. 0012C]

**11.** Although the holy man was held in such high esteem by everyone, he always thought of himself so modestly that he was content with the levitical rank and could never be persuaded to receive the priesthood.

Hence this familiar subscription belonged to him:

“Paschasius Radbertus, Levite, the refuse of all monks.”

He proved the meaning of this expression of modesty more by his actions than by his words.

**12.** Yet this lower rank did not prevent him from receiving the dignity of abbot, which he was compelled to assume after Isaac, abbot of Corbie, died.

“He was the thirteenth from the first, but the fourth from him

“Who gave laws and established a covenant in the Ausonian fields,”

writes the monk Gualdo at the beginning of his poem on the *Life of Saint Anscharius*.

Radbertus was the fourth abbot of Corbie after Saint Adalhard, who governed Italy during the minority of Pepin. For after the elder Adalhard, his younger namesake, Wala his brother, Heddo, and Isaac, Radbertus’s predecessor, had succeeded one another.

The manuscript *Chronicle of Corbie* assigns the beginning of Paschasius’s government to the year 844 [Col. 0012D].

**13.** Two years later he attended the Council of Paris and obtained from the Fathers letters confirming Corbie’s immunity. The monk Gualdo discusses this immunity in the prologue to the *Life of Saint Anscharius*, mentioned above.

Paschasius also attended the Synod of Quierzy, convened in 849 against Gottschalk. He undoubtedly had him in mind when he said in Book VIII on Matthew:

“Therefore we must know with certainty that whenever someone perishes, he does not perish through God’s predestination, as some wrongly think, nor does he perish through the Father’s will, but through his own sin and God’s just judgment.”

**14.** Burdened by various cares in this office, he was compelled to interrupt his studies. Thus he speaks on this subject both at the beginning of his exposition of Psalm 44 and at the beginning of Book V on Matthew, where we read:

“Having once begun the exposition of Matthew, dearest ones, so that in this office I might, according to my wish, discharge among the brothers the duty of my service, I was finally hindered, after undertaking the position of governance, by the cares of many anxieties and entangled in various affairs of secular business. I was drawn as far away from it as I was removed from the study of letters. Not only did I leave unfinished what I had begun, but, abandoning the benefit of quiet, I almost gave myself over to shipwreck, buffeted by the impulses of many winds. But because God, as that prophet says, has by his providence made these times of leisure for us …”

**15.** From this passage we understand that Paschasius endured some disturbances, so that he was compelled to leave his position. He indicates this more clearly shortly afterward, when he says that he had been received by the people of Centula in adverse circumstances:

“Because you have deigned to receive and refresh me, present among all and in all things, with the most welcome affection in Christ, to entrust me to God in your prayers, especially at the time when, according to the ancient proverb, a friend and a physician are proved in need—this is why, dearest ones, I have so often resolved with great eagerness to come to you on a visit, desiring to see you and to correct in myself what I had long neglected too carelessly. You consoled me amid every adversity through the affection of your love and your prayers.”

The cause of this disturbance must be investigated briefly and carefully.

**16.** In the first place, the trouble may perhaps have originated in certain disagreements that arose between Paschasius and Ratramnus, concerning both the birth of the Blessed Virgin and, as most people think, Eucharistic matters, as well as the twofold predestination. In this matter Ratramnus favored Gottschalk, while Paschasius opposed him, as we saw above in section 13.

For it often happens that, amid such literary disputes, when people are carried away and inflamed by partisan zeal, some withdraw from others. This indeed happened in Paschasius’s case. For the monk Ivo, whom I shall mention below, and a certain Chremes, one of the interlocutors introduced by Paschasius in Book I of the [Col. 0013C] *Epitaph of Wala*, are said to have departed during those troubles, as is stated at the beginning of Book II.

Whether Ratramnus also departed is unclear to me. Certainly he was still residing in the same place toward the end of the year 849, when Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, sent him Letter 79 concerning the confirmation of Hilmerad, bishop of Amiens. The letter is addressed to “his dearest Rotramnus,” and entrusts him with certain recommendations to be made on behalf of Hilmerad, the newly elected bishop.

This indicates that he was then living in the nearby monastery of Amiens, namely Corbie, or at least at Centula.

**17.** The confinement of Prince Charles in the monastery of Corbie may also have supplied material for these disturbances. In the year 849 Charles, son of Pepin, king of Aquitaine, and brother of the other Pepin, was tonsured and confined there, as the chronicler of Fontenelle reports in Chesne’s second volume.

The *Annals of Fulda*, however, assign Charles’s tonsure and confinement to the year 851, the year in which Paschasius relinquished his dignity. Perhaps Charles supported the factional parties. I later find that he escaped from there in the *Annals of Saint-Bertin*, where the following is recorded under the year 854:

“Charles, brother of Pepin, already ordained a deacon, withdrew from the monastery of Corbie”—namely, to Louis, king of Germany.

Henschenius proves this from manuscript annals in his preliminary commentary on the *Life of Rabanus, Archbishop of Mainz*. There it is said that Charles, son of King Pepin, who had escaped from confinement in the monastery of Corbie and defected to his uncle Louis, king of Germany, succeeded him in the bishopric on the eighth day before the Ides of March, not only by the king’s will but also by the consent and election of the people.

I infer from the words of Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, that Carloman, son of Charles the Bald, likewise a deacon and abbot of many monasteries, also fled from the same monastery. In the council in which he proposed a penance for the former king Pepin of Aquitaine, Hincmar says that it must not be forgotten what happened to him—Pepin—in the monastery of Saint Medard, and what happened to Carloman at Corbie [Col. 0014A]. “For,” he says, “what happened then can still happen.”

Pepin, son of Pepin, king of Aquitaine, had been confined and tonsured in the monastery of Saint Medard and was then removed from it through the agency of two monks, as the Acts of the Council of Saint Medard in 853 attest.

It is plausible that these various movements of princes also produced various disturbances among the monks of Corbie. Since Paschasius had fruitlessly devoted his efforts to calming them, he finally resigned the abbacy.

**18.** A third cause, related to these two, arose from his rebuke of certain monks who lived too laxly. Unable to endure Paschasius’s just censure, they left the monastery of Corbie.

Although monastic discipline flourished at Corbie in Paschasius’s time to such a degree that, according even to the testimony of the Council of Paris, the monks seemed not merely to equal their predecessors and founders but to surpass and excel them, there were nevertheless some—since no society is so holy that it contains no wicked members—who fell into more relaxed ways of life.

Paschasius himself discloses the origin of this evil in the *Epitaph of Wala*. He is said to have restrained the negligence of the careless and the obstinacy of the vicious, sometimes by threats, sometimes by blows, sometimes by benefits, and sometimes by gentle persuasion, as reported in Book I, chapter 23. For this reason they called him severe and harsh.

After Wala’s death, since the authority of his successors, Heddo and Isaac, was not as great, the license of the vicious advanced so far that they overturned right and justice, as Paschasius reports in Book I of the *Life of Wala*, chapter 10. According to chapter 21, they more readily indulged in idle leisure, sleep, and pleasures.

One of their number was Ivo, a monk of that place and a relative of Abbot Lupus. After being expelled from Corbie—or perhaps escaping by flight—he was preparing to return there, armed with the protection, namely a letter, of King Charles, so that he might obtain security from punishment for his wrongdoing.

Therefore Radbertus sought Lupus’s influence with Charles and obtained it, so that Ivo would find no refuge with the king, as we understand from Letter 56 of Lupus [Col. 0014C].

In the following letter, addressed to “the most beloved Abbot Radbertus,” Lupus sufficiently implies that some very powerful man had favored Ivo, his relative, and that Lupus eventually induced him to promise “that Radbertus would not merely do no harm, but would also do a great deal of good, if he proved kind toward the relative who had departed during the time of the disturbance and returned once peace had been restored.”

Lupus identifies that disturbance, its authors, and its supporter more clearly afterward:

“I confidently promised that you would gladly do this and obey in everything he might deem fit to command, so long as you enjoyed his favor. I pressed the matter until he firmly promised that he would do you no injury without first discussing the case with me. I therefore brought my request to this conclusion: if at any time rebels should ask that their complaints be supported by his favor, he should not consent indiscriminately, but should reserve only matters worthy of your conscience.”

Paschasius therefore had to endure some rebels among his monks, who perhaps could not bear his stricter discipline [Col. 0014D].

Lupus adds:

“I have discovered certain other matters that must be revealed with such caution that I have not thought it safe to commit them to writing, yet they are so necessary to know that you should come to meet with me as quickly as you can, putting aside every other advantage. Otherwise, if it is not already burdensome, send word to me as I am about to travel with the king, God willing, to Silvacum, so that, when I begin to give thanks, I may not lack an abundance of opportunity for speaking, though I am vainly attempting to say many things.”

Thus, I think, that faction of rebels was finally quieted through the counsel and authority of Lupus. Another letter from him to Radbertus follows immediately; in it he likewise promises that he will lay a friend’s case before the king.

Such was the intimacy between the two abbots, and such was Lupus’s influence with the king!

Throughout all these storms Radbertus always displayed such moderation and gentleness that, although his writings frequently mention his own resignation, the bitterness of his rivals never extracted from his pen a single word of anger. He never expressed or identified them anywhere, not even by name.

### Chapter V. Resignation of His Office, Return to Study, and Death

**19.** After these events Radbertus began to consider resigning his office. The idea took root in his mind both because of his exceptional modesty, because of his reflection on the disturbances just described, and because of his desire to resume the studies he had interrupted.

At first his former pupils resisted this plan; but at last, with God’s approval, he obtained what he desired. The preface to Book IX on Matthew explains what happened:

“After innumerable worldly activities and the troublesome labors of life, after the anxieties of so great a government and the long losses of the present life, God at last granted a prudent man a sufficiently desirable leisure. Thus those who were contriving something else achieved nothing, and imposed upon a son who was then especially dear to me, scarcely having completed his novitiate, a very burdensome yoke, because he was vigorous in mind and body, and, as I hope, worthy in holiness.”

He is referring to Odo, later bishop of Beauvais, who succeeded his master in 851, the year in which Radbertus is wrongly said to have died. Two letters of Abbot Lupus to Odo the abbot survive, namely Letters 111 and 112. This Odo attended the Council of Soissons at the monastery of Saint Medard in 853.

**20.** Once the holy man had been released from the stormy business of the prelacy, he immediately returned to the studies of Sacred Scripture he desired, through which he tempered and soothed the burdens of old age.

He testifies to this more than once with great joy of heart, especially at the beginning of the preface already mentioned. These are his words:

“Philosophy, dearest brothers, can never be praised adequately enough. Whoever obeys it can pass through every period of his life in some manner without distress, because it does not abandon those whom it has nurtured from childhood even in old age.

“This is why, although I abandoned it, it did not allow me at this age to wander farther from it for long. Rather, as soon as I returned to it, after having been sorely afflicted for a long time by the cares of worldly affairs, I recognized that the path of my former life was not the true one. It began to nurse me like a child and restore me with its breasts.

“Therefore, rightly, since the condition of children and old men is almost the same, and their death seems to me to be equalized, the mind of both must always be nourished with the milk of the divine Scriptures: the child, so that he may grow; the old man, so that he may not fail; indeed, both, so that they may advance toward what is better and live, nourished by divine breasts.”

You can see how, in the joy of his restored leisure, the retired old man can scarcely restrain himself, so wholly did he burn with love for sacred studies.

Book I on Psalm 44 should also be read. At the beginning of that book he says:

“When at last I had been released, by divine providence, from the anxiety of pastoral office, the cares of government, and the business of active duties, I returned to those studies which, although retained in my mind, I had set aside during the intervals of time and abandoned amid the various winding paths of secular affairs; and thus I recalled what had been interrupted for a long period.”

He expresses the same sentiment at the beginning of Book II of the *Epitaph of Wala*.

**21.** In these studies the most devout man grew old and eventually declined, though it is not certainly known in what year this occurred. His surviving writings prove, nevertheless, that he lived for a considerable time after resigning his office.

For Book II of the *Epitaph of Wala*, the last four books of the exposition on Matthew, the three books on Psalm 44, and also, as it seems to me, the five books on the Lamentations of Jeremiah—that is, nearly half of his works—were all composed after he resigned his office.

From this it may be inferred that he did not die before the year 860.

Certainly, in Book IV of his exposition of the Lamentations, he mentions the burning of Paris under the letter *Lamed*:

“Who would ever have believed, or who could ever have imagined, that something of this kind could happen in our regions—something which, after time had passed, we all saw happen, grieved over, mourned, and greatly feared, and which we still fear no less today? Namely, that pirates, gathered from very diverse families, should reach the borders of Paris and burn the churches of Christ here and there with fire along the shore.”

And below:

“For I confess, as I think, that not long ago none of the kings of the earth would have imagined such a thing, nor could any inhabitant of our world have heard that an enemy would enter our Paris.”

The Northmen attacked Paris as many as four times: first in 846, according to Aimoinus in Book I of *The Miracles of Saint Germanus*; then in 857; then four years later, according to the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* and others; and finally in 886.

They are said to have found the city and its suburbs deserted on the first occasion, and to have burned it on the second and third.

Perhaps someone will explain the passage of Radbertus quoted above by reference to the first occasion, since he says that the Northmen entered Paris, whereas Aimoinus says that they found the city deserted at that time. But it must certainly be understood of the second incursion of the Northmen, when they invaded Paris and consigned it to the flames together with many churches. In the first incursion there was no devastation, or almost none, and no fires.

The day on which Radbertus died is indicated by the old Corbie charters as the sixth day before the Kalends of May. On that day the manuscript *Martyrology of Nevelon* records:

“At the monastery of Corbie, the passing of Saint Radbertus, abbot and confessor.”

He was buried in the church of Saint John the Evangelist, in the middle of the church before the entrance to the presbytery, as we read in the manuscript *Chronicle of Corbie*, where his cenotaph can still be seen.

In the very old register of the meals of his monastery it is written:

“On the sixth day before the Kalends of May Abbot Radbertus died; for him the chamberlain is to provide the brothers with a service.”

At what time he was entered in the sacred calendar we shall say in what follows. For now, some account must first be given of his virtues, admonitions, and writings.

### Chapter VI. His Virtues, Especially His Avoidance of Leisure, and His Sacred Studies

[Col. 0016C]

**22.** The chief virtue that shone forth in Radbertus was humility. It caused him repeatedly to call himself the refuse of all monks, never to wish to ascend to the priestly rank, and to forbid anyone to commit the deeds of his own dead life to writing.

Evidence of this virtue is scattered throughout all his writings. Engelmodus, the bishop, especially commended this virtue of Radbertus, testifying that although kings and princes bowed before the holy man because of the esteem in which his merits were held, he nevertheless remained simple and humble after blowing away the empty praises of the wind.

Closely allied to this virtue was his sincere love of truth. “What we do not read in the Sacred Scriptures,” he says in Book II on Matthew, “we believe it better to remain ignorant of than rashly to define.”

For this reason, although he understood that certain Fathers had excused the apostle Peter’s denial [Col. 0016D], he nevertheless proves in Book XII, on Matthew chapters 26 and 28, that those who asserted this should not be heeded.

Thus he speaks in the first passage:

“Pious defenders of Peter, who try to defend him in such a way as to prove that the Lord lied.”

It was because of this sincere love that, in explaining Matthew, he did not follow “the tropological interpretations of the Gospel or the mystical understandings of its statements, but explained only the simple sense, as was fitting,” as he writes at the end of Book IV.

23. He was also wholly devoted to tears, and for that reason undertook to explain the Lamentations of Jeremiah, as appears from the preface addressed to Odilmannus, a monk of Corbie. “For,” he says in the prologue to Book II, “since we are growing old, it has always been established that this long life of ours should be devoted to prayer, occupied with lamentation, and spent in mourning either our own offenses or those of others.” This virtue he pursued above all in old age.

24. Throughout his life he especially detested [Col. 0017A] idle leisure, and strove to consecrate all the spare hours of his life—which he himself calls “stolen” hours in the preface to Book I on Matthew—namely, those remaining after the obligations of regular discipline, to literary study. Hear how he speaks at the beginning of his commentary on Matthew:

“Therefore, I ask, let no one be angry with me if at last, trusting in God’s grace, I have chosen to dedicate to the Lord that diligence which heavenly providence seasoned within me with the salt of learning, rather than to grow torpid in the leisure of an empty life while neglecting study. For although I believed that this would benefit not many, I nonetheless believed it would benefit me and my own, if I occasionally turned my mind to this task and committed to writing the fleeting insights of learning acquired through long labor, so that by this means I might be better equipped for thought and more prepared for discussion.”

His exhortation to the monks in the prologue to Book XI is outstanding in this regard:

“Amid the profound silences of the heart and the intensely busy leisure of monastic discipline, we who are bound by divine vows ought to desire greatly—lest we be found idle without the fruit of eternal contemplation—that example of Cato, especially I who am an old man, if perhaps I may ever truly say what he himself wrote about it when already old: that he was accustomed to say that he was never less at leisure than when he was at leisure, nor less alone than when he was alone.

“This is certainly a magnificent saying, my brothers, and worthy of a great and wise man; but it is fitting and absolutely necessary for no one more than for us monks. It shows that such a great man both thought about the affairs of the good life in his leisure and was accustomed to speak useful things with himself in solitude; nor did he ever cease thinking about good and necessary matters.

“How much more ought we, dearest ones, never to cease thinking of divine things in our leisure, since we are devoted to heavenly disciplines; never to be alone in solitude, since we always and everywhere live before God, in whom we live, move, and exist; and before the entire multitude of the citizens above—lest perhaps our enemies mock our Sabbaths if at some hour we are not only useless to ourselves [Col. 0017C] but are even found, as we must often lament has happened, harmful to others.”

I have reported this at greater length so that a judgment of such importance might sink more deeply into the minds of our companions, for whom almost the only danger to be feared is idleness.

25. The most diligent abbot took care to avoid this vice not only while he was in full vigor but especially in declining age. His words at the end of Book IV on Matthew point to this:

“Therefore, dearest ones, my old age ought not to have been either weak in regard to you and my brothers, whom I was obliged to exhort when I presided over you, or idle; indeed, it ought not to have been idle even in leisure, but active, always doing and undertaking something by which both the life of those now living might be formed and an example provided for those to come—lest the sacrament of salt, which as a little boy I once received upon my lips, be emptied of its power either in old age or in advanced age.”

The holy man understood that any monk who abandoned spiritual exercise even in old age was entirely foolish and devoid of heavenly discipline. He did not undertake this task only while he presided over others, but also after resigning his office, as is clear from the preface to Book IX:

“Therefore there should be no idle period of old age that is not beneficial; especially since we remember that studies of Scripture make progress in others, while I at least scatter among the young the seeds of the divine word.”

Let the beginning of Book I on Psalm XLIV also be read.

26. This, then, was the holy man’s chief occupation of mind: not to remain idle, but always, whenever time allowed, to occupy his spirit with pious studies and reflections. He was wholly devoted to reading the sacred Scriptures and the orthodox Fathers, especially Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory the Great, John Chrysostom, and Bede the Venerable, whom he himself praises in the preface to Book I on Matthew. To these he added Tertullian, whom he praises and cites among the foremost Gallican writers of his age in the Life of Adalhard. With these studies, I say, the diligent man refreshed his spirit.

For he did not approve the diligence of certain men of his time in meditating upon and explaining the writings of profane authors. There is an excellent passage on this subject in the preface to Book III on Matthew, where he reproves “the lovers of secular literature, who seek various and different interpreters so that by understanding they may reach the splendid falsehoods of abominable matters; who pass over neither—I do not say a page—nor even a syllable, without examining it more closely with the utmost vigilance and labor,” while they neglect the divine books most shamefully.

“Therefore,” he says, “I greatly wonder what offense the divine utterances have given to the dispositions of certain people, that they are unwilling to investigate the mystical mysteries of God with the diligence with which they desire, sweating with labor, to explore the wailings of tragedies and the fictions of poets. No one can doubt that their zealous labor is fruitless when the matter in question plainly lacks profit and yields no reward.”

Although this is unbecoming in all Christians and ecclesiastical men, it is certainly far more shameful in monks, whose particular occupation ought to be, having rejected every secular thought, to cling to God and occupy their minds with heavenly things. Our author expresses this beautifully in the prologue to Book III on the Lamentations of Jeremiah:

“It is not our task, brother and fellow old man”—he is addressing Odilmannus—“to turn over again the false fables of poets, or Milesian tales, since our way of life demands other conduct; nor to examine the books of philosophers, since in the one case there is play and entertainment, while in the other there is difficulty and labor mingled with toil. Rather, it is more fitting for us to devote ourselves unceasingly to Lamentations and Mourning,” and so forth.

27. Why, in explaining the sacred Scriptures, he employed the holy Fathers, he explains in the preface to Book VI on Matthew:

“My exposition, beloved ones, belongs to many highly learned teachers whom an earlier age produced and whose authority the truth established; but its novelty, commended by my own style, makes it mine, so that the treatise gathered from all of them appears to be one and also specifically mine. For I have made the common understandings of several teachers my own through the faith and understanding of Catholics. I have not considered it right to explain the mysteries of divine understanding or the sayings of God the Savior solely by my own efforts, as many have done who refused to understand what the sacred, divinely inspired Scripture inwardly understands, but applied it perversely to their own errors in many respects,” and so forth.

For this reason he rebukes certain interpreters who indulge too much in clever quibbles in Book VIII on Matthew, chapter 17, since although there may be exercise in such matters, he does not know whether they can yield any fruit of understanding. There is also a passage on the same subject in Book VI on Matthew, chapter 2, p. 527.

Engelmodus therefore rightly applied these verses to him:

> No feigned simulation, deceiving faith by criminal deceit,  
>   
> Nor the barking quarrels of foaming strife,  
>   
> Polluted him by the muddy act of sordid stain,  
>   
> Nor darkened the timely clarity of his mind;  
>   
> But pious simplicity, virtue, and the conscience of what is right.

## CHAPTER VII. The Customs of His Age, and Various Admonitions to Different People

28. In many passages the holy man deplores the customs of his age: ambition, simony, avarice, errors, heresies, and other plagues of his time. He attacks the ambitious in Book II on Matthew, chapter 7:

“Most unhappy is the age of our time, when someone who possesses the form of the Gospel in his way of life is found only rarely; but everyone pursues the honors of present affairs, so that by right and wrong alike they may be more able to rule than to benefit others. Yet everyone proclaims those things which scarcely anyone is willing to hold in conduct and life; for while they commend poverty, all desire to reign.”

29. In more than one passage he attacks the simoniacs. Thus, in Book IX on Matthew, chapter 21:

“Moreover, the holy Fathers have discussed the sale of doves sufficiently and abundantly in many places, especially against the simoniacal heresy, which has often been attacked in Gaul but never conquered; for both those who buy what properly belongs to the Church and those who sell it have become robbers. Although this heresy could be condemned, it has therefore not yet been conquered, because just as a robber is so called from hiding, so these men often act secretly—or at least so boldly, though shamelessly, that no one dares oppose them. What has happened today, to speak frankly, all Gaul feels and mourns.”

It is worthy of observation here that he calls not only those who sell ecclesiastical benefices simoniacs, but also those who confer them upon the unworthy. For shortly after the passage quoted above he adds:

“For I do not mean that in the present time those who occupy the chairs of the churches sell doves; rather, I mean that churches are entrusted to those to whom they ought not to be entrusted—not for the profit of souls, but for luxury and their own desires. I therefore think that great care must be taken lest they be found to sell doves who tyrannically hand over churches consecrated to Christ the Lord [Col. 0019B] to disgraceful and avaricious men, to whom they ought not to be entrusted, men who are undisciplined and irreligious,” and so forth.

Who those men are whom he marks out here may perhaps be understood from Book II, On the Epitaph of Wala, chapter 5.

Finally, he again assails simoniacs in Book XII on Matthew, chapter 26:

“Such priests, therefore, must always be feared—whoever pursue the honors of the churches for a price and not through the grace of the Holy Spirit. With them a false council is always assembled and false witnesses sought; with them not truth, not religion, but an unjust authority is always preferred in legal cases.”

30. Against avaricious priests he cites this verse from Book V on the Lamentations of Jeremiah: “We drink our water for money,” and so forth. After explaining the verse, he adds:

“This meaning applies against greedy priests of God’s temples, who make the house of God a house of commerce; for on account of baptism and the teaching of their preaching, or on account of the gifts and graces of God, they pursue profits and seek more costly gains for themselves. Against them the people of Christ rightly complains and laments.”

31. With the same zeal he rebukes ecclesiastical men who “stir up lawsuits and quarrels over monetary matters,” in Book V on Matthew, chapter 5. In Book IV on the Lamentations of Jeremiah he laments clergy and monks devoted to secular affairs in these words:

“Behold, now scarcely any activity of secular life remains which the priests of Christ do not administer; no business of the world in which the ministers of the altar do not occupy themselves; no wickedness of affairs in which the monastic order does not entangle itself; scarcely any allurements of life with which the chastity of nuns does not defile itself.”

And below:

“They seek one thing from the honor of the religion they have assumed, and display another through the duties of their activity, and daily perish through many wickednesses. Intent upon secular cares and vices, they become all the more insensitive the more eagerly they are found to pursue external things and the desires of the flesh.”

32. In Book VIII on Matthew, chapter 16, he warns bishops not to abuse the power of binding and loosing that Christ has granted them by excommunicating with excessive ease. There he also gives excellent admonitions concerning subjects, even those bound unjustly. Then he adds:

“Let it therefore be far from that senate of heaven that, according to the impulse of the mind of anyone who is proud or angry, they too should unjustly bind or loose before the eyes of the supreme Judge, who sees all things.”

Conversely, he complains of pastors’ excessive readiness to absolve sinners:

“For this is why today the indulgence of penance is so often trampled underfoot and security promised, so that at times it becomes more a mockery than a remedy for those covered with defilement; for when it is granted easily, it is held in lower esteem and guarded more negligently, and the sin committed is sometimes repeated more boldly in the hope of pardon.

“I have not said these things,” he says, “in order to teach that I am a cruel teacher, but to bring the unwary back to caution. For just as it must not be denied to those who seek it with the faith of love, so it must not immediately be granted to deceivers and the faithless. This is why the sacred canons often do not readily admit those who repeatedly return to penance. We too ought not to transgress these limits indiscriminately, but weigh everything with discernment.”

Finally, in Book VII on Matthew, chapter 14, he notes the pusillanimity of certain bishops who said that princes ought not to be reproved. Theodore the Studite also refuted this position in his letter to Stephen, secretary of the emperor Constantine, cited by Baronius under the year 795.

33. Radbertus attacks various errors that arose in his time: the perverse doctrine of Felix, bishop of Urgel, concerning Christ’s adoption, in various passages in his books on Matthew and in his commentary on Psalm XLIV; and the teaching of Claudius, bishop of Turin, who attempted to diminish the veneration of sacred relics and pilgrimages, in Book XI on Matthew, chapter 24.

He also argues against certain recent proclaimers of falsehood who maintained that there were no other kinds of punishments and no places of torment apart from the consciences of human beings, in the same book, on chapter 25. I have no doubt that this criticism applies to John Scotus, an advocate of that error.

Finally, in the letter addressed to Frudegardus he notes certain people who held incorrect views about the Eucharist; they are discussed in the preface.

## CHAPTER VIII. Judgment Concerning His Writings

34. The first of his works that have come down to us is the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, written in the year 831, during the exile of Wala, abbot of Corbie, whom he calls the Arsenius and Jeremiah of his time, as I explained in the preface to this volume.

35. He later wrote twelve books on Matthew: four while still a monk, addressed to Guntlandus, a monk of Centula; four subsequent books when he was already abbot, dedicated to all the monks of that same monastery, whose learning, wisdom, and religious devotion he praises; and the remaining books after resigning his office. The letter to Frudegardus, which is appended to the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, was written after the commentaries on Matthew.

36. He wrote the Life of Saint Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, around the year 830. He published the *Epitaph*—as he calls it—of Wala, likewise abbot and the brother and successor of Adalhard, in two books. He composed the first in the year 836 and the second after resigning his office, that is, after the year 851.

In both works, which I presented above, Paschasius records outstanding material for illuminating both Frankish and monastic affairs, especially in the *Epitaph* of Wala. In Book II of that work he reports the secret history of the deposition of Louis the Pious [Col. 0020D] with great accuracy, as a witness who was himself very much an eyewitness; and he admirably depicts the condition of the Gallican Church as it then was.

The first book was written immediately after Wala’s death; the second only after Paschasius had resigned his office, as appears from the beginning of that book—and indeed after the death of Empress Ermengard, wife of Lothair Augustus, according to chapter 24, that is, after the year 851. Indeed, it was written after the year 857, if Severus, one of the interlocutors in the first book, is the same as Odilmannus Severus, to whom Paschasius dedicated his explanation of the Lamentations after that year.

It was written before the agreement reached between Charles and Louis, according to chapter 19, and therefore before the year 860, to which the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* assign that agreement.

I do not know whether Antonius de Caulincurte had seen this work of Paschasius, since in his *Chronicle* Paschasius is said to have published the Life of Wala. More on this *Epitaph* below.

37. He entitled the book *On the Birth of the Blessed Virgin Mary* to the Venerable Matron of Christ, namely Theodrada, abbess and sister of Saint Adalhard, together with the holy virgins living at Vesona; Paschasius Radbertus, the contemptible refuse of all monks. The beginning of the preface is as follows:

“Dearest women, I have recently resolved to answer for you the question about the birth of the blessed Virgin Mary that was brought to me,” and so forth.

Before the twelfth edition of the *Spicilegium*, this preface was missing from the printed books, in which the little work had been printed corruptly and wrongly attributed to Hildefonsus, bishop of Toledo. It has now finally been restored to its author.

Radbertus composed it on the occasion of a book published by Ratramnus *On the Nativity of Christ*. The name Vesona, however, is not the proper name of the convent at Soissons, but of the city itself, which Radbertus variously calls Vesona and Suessio. Nor is it probable that Vesona was written for Suessona through a copyist’s error. For, apart from the fact that Vesona is read in two manuscript codices containing this work, the same word is also repeated in three places in the *Exposition of Psalm XLIV*, and is there joined to the word Suession.

From the context itself it is perfectly clear that by this name the city of Soissons is meant, not the monastery of the virgins. Thus we read in Book III of the aforementioned *Exposition*:

“Among them also is Vesona, which you inhabit. Once she played the harlot after the idols of fornication; then she came with gifts and became faithful—she who had been the daughter of the most powerful devil. And, as you can see, just as Isaiah said, her wages have now been sanctified to the Lord, because she shines, filled throughout with churches, and has become the possession of the most merciful Savior—she who had been the daughter of perdition and the prey of the destroyer.

“For to the east she now has the camp of monks, with their holy confessors and martyrs; to the west, as though behind you, the trumpet of the holy Gospel resounds in the voice of one admonishing. Thus it comes about that the place in which you are is deprived of no heavenly gifts. But you, established as though in the middle, have chosen only one corner of narrow Soissons.”

And a little farther on:

“These, then, are the gifts . . . that Vesona, once dedicated to demons and now consecrated to God, sends to Christ.”

And at the end of the aforementioned book:

“To this corner of Vesona you have hastened.”

From these passages it is clear that Vesona is the city itself, which has the monastery of Saint Medard to the east, the cathedral church to the west, and between the two the convent of the blessed Mary, situated in a corner of the city.

Certainly Ptolemy calls the Suessiones *Vesones*, and Strabo calls them *Vesiones*.

As for the subject of this work, at that time a dispute arose over whether Christ had come into the light by the ordinary way of other human beings—that is, with the virginal barriers widened—or from a closed womb. This question first began to be debated in Germany, perhaps at the school of Fulda under the teacher Rabanus, and from there was brought into Gaul at approximately the time when Lupus, then a monk of Ferrières, returned home from the schools of Fulda.

Almost everyone supported the later position in this controversy; the earlier position was held by Ratramnus, a monk of French Corbie, who published a little book *On the Nativity of Christ*. He believed that, if Christ had not proceeded from his mother by the ordinary way, he ought not to be said to have truly been born or generated, but rather to have emerged violently.

Paschasius refuted Ratramnus and his followers, asserting that Christ was not born according to the ordinary law of nature, since he had been generated from the flesh of the Virgin in the womb not according to nature’s customary process.

Thus he attempted, in one book, to restrain what he calls the shameless rashness of certain brothers. But when they still did not abandon their opinion and continued to defend it either in writing or orally, he added a second book and dedicated the entire work to the Venerable Matron of Christ, together with the virgins of Christ living a monastic life at Vesona.

This matron of Christ was Theodrada, abbess of the convent of the blessed Mary at Soissons, so called because she had been married in the world. For in his explanation of Psalm XLIV Paschasius calls Imma, Theodrada’s daughter and successor in the governance of the monastery, a perpetual virgin of Christ and her daughter.

Accordingly, Paschasius wrote at least the first book of this work *On the Nativity of Christ* before the year 846, when Theodrada died. He wrote it, as he himself testifies in the preface, after he had already been worn down by great old age—that is, when he was more than sixty. From this it can be understood that he lived to nearly eighty years of age, since he reached or perhaps passed the year 860 of the Christian era. Certainly he had been born and reached adulthood in the eighth century, as may be inferred from Book I of the *Epitaph of Wala*, chapter 3.

38. The abbot composed a little book *On the Passion of Saints Rufinus and Valerius* at the request of the inhabitants of the town dedicated to them, which they call Basilicas [Basoches], in the district of Soissons.

39. After resigning the governance of the monastery, he dedicated his three-book *Exposition of Psalm XLIV*, although without explicitly naming her, to Imma, abbess of the convent at Soissons after Theodrada, and to the virgins of the convent at Soissons, whom he especially praises in Books II and III. In Book I he advises them to regard cohabitation as sufficient for the needs of nature, together with a small income.

In Book III he notes three features of the discipline of that monastery preserved at that time: the customary offering of the virgins by their parents, their perpetual enclosure, and the vows of the nuns, both virgins and widows. Of these vows, he says, “one is the vow of obedience; let there be one conversion of conduct, one stability of place.” These words express the rite of Benedictine profession, by which those making profession promise obedience, conversion of conduct, and stability in the congregation.

40. Last in order comes the explanation of the Lamentations of Jeremiah, dedicated to the aged Odilmannus Severus. Antonius de Caulincurte, in his *Chronicle of Corbie*, believes that this was Radbertus’s final work. This may be the Odilmannus Severus who is one of the interlocutors in Book I of the *Epitaph of Wala*, where he is called Severus.

Therefore he is not Abbot Heddo, Wala’s successor, as I suspected in the note to chapter 21 of that same book. If this is so, Book II of the *Epitaph of Wala*, which is known from its beginning to have been written after Severus’s death, was composed after the explanation of the Lamentations.

Paschasius undertook that work when he was worn out by the long tedium of a much-extended life, and indeed after the year 857, according to the preceding section, no. 18. In all these writings it is evident that the author was learned in Greek and Hebrew.

41. Besides these short works, he also wrote various letters to Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, and to others, whose loss we regret.

Trithemius attributes to Paschasius the book *On the Lives of the Fathers Translated from Greek into Latin*, but it is established that these lives are three hundred years older than Paschasius the deacon.

Some claim that the Life of Saint Richarius, abbot of Centula, was polished and enlarged by our Paschasius, but wrongly, as has been proved in the second volume on the Life of Saint Richarius.

The same judgment should be made concerning the poem that Nicolaus Mameranus published at Cologne in 1550 after the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, attributing it to Paschasius by mere conjecture because in the same codex the poem was bound together with Paschasius’s book on the Eucharist without the author’s name.

In the manuscript codex of Le Puy, the poem is entitled as follows: *Verses on the Day of Judgment, by Bede*, although it does not seem to me to attain even Bede’s vein of composition. Nevertheless, this title is more probable than that of the printed book, *On Solitary Conversation*.

Mameranus is also mistaken in inferring from the final couplet that the author of the poem had a daughter, since the passage concerns a spiritual daughter.

Finally, the conjecture of an anonymous writer is worthless: he attributes to Paschasius Radbertus in the preface, though with hesitation, the book *On the Roman Pontiffs*, which he assigns at its beginning to Liutprand, since neither its date nor the quality of its style suits Radbertus.

## CHAPTER IX. Various Eulogies of Him and His Canonization

42. Various eulogies of Radbertus are found both among authors of his own time and among later writers. The Fathers of the Council of Paris, in the privilege granted to him, praise “the venerable brother Radbertus, abbot,” and call his disciples “splendid and precious members of the eternal King.” This praise reflects back upon their teacher and leader.

Lupus said in the aforementioned letter that he ought to be embraced by all good men. Engelmodus, as stated above, commended him in heroic verse while he was still living.

It is established that Engelmodus was bishop of the Church of Soissons from the privilege that the Gallican bishops, assembled at Soissons at Pistis, granted to the monks of Dionysius in the year 862. I saw this privilege in the original and took care to compare it with the printed versions. Engelmodus subscribed it as “Angilmodus, unworthy bishop of the Church of Soissons,” in Dublet, p. 798. He may have been appointed in place of Rothadus, who was deposed at that assembly, or he may have held the office of chorepiscopus under Rothadus.

Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, praises Radbertus’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* exceptionally highly in Book II of the *Collations*, chapters 30 and the following two. For this reason Durandus, abbot of Troarn, calls him in his book on the Eucharist “the most diligent investigator and Catholic examiner of the divine sacrament”; before him, Herigerus, abbot of Lobbes, did the same in his letter or little book on the Eucharist, which has until now been published under the name of the anonymous Cellotian.

To these may be added Antonius de Caulincurte, a monk of the previous century, in his manuscript *Chronicle of Corbie*, which ends in the year 1529. Our Paulus de Bonofonte pursues the same subject more fully and accurately in his unpublished *History of Corbie*.

43. Finally, under Falco, the thirtieth abbot of Corbie and the first of that name, “so great a multitude of signs was performed by God’s grace at the tomb of Saint Radbertus, and such evident miracles of healing shone forth through his merits upon those who were ill, that by the authority of the Apostolic See his body was lifted from the tomb on the fourth Ides of July and, in the presence of and amid the worship of countless crowds, was honorably transferred with the others to the major church of Saint Peter in the year of salvation 1073.”

Thus far the ancient catalogue of the abbots of Corbie. From it you should correct the *Gallican Martyrology*, in which this event is said to have occurred in the year 1060, and indeed to have been carried out by Guido, bishop of Amiens, who in the more recent catalogue of the abbots is said to have been its author.

The relics of this saint are preserved to the present day in the church of Corbie. At the site of his original tomb, namely in the church of Saint John, his image can be seen carved in stone in a crude and relatively recent work, with the characteristic crozier of an abbot.

Our Corbie community celebrates his feast day with a double rite on the sixth day before the Kalends of May [26 April]. On that same day he is called a saint in the ancient Martyrology of Corbie, and likewise in another manuscript written by hand five hundred years ago, which contains the four later books on Matthew and the *Exposition of Psalm XLIV;* there, at the beginning of the aforementioned *Exposition*, he is depicted with a halo around his head.

## CHAPTER X. The Two Books on the Life of Wala Vindicated for Paschasius

44. There is such similarity of style between the *Epitaph of Arsenius*, or *Acts of Wala*, and the *Life of Adalhard his Brother* that, although the manuscript codex I used in editing the *Epitaph* bears no author’s name, I nevertheless confidently assert that it belongs to Paschasius Radbertus. I do so both because certain catalogues and authors attribute this work to Radbertus and because Paschasius is one of the interlocutors and appears to be, as it were, the chorus-leader of the scene.

That this interlocutor Paschasius is none other than Radbertus is clear from the beginning of Book II, where mention is made of the resignation of pastoral governance and the return to studies that had been interrupted. Radbertus repeatedly mentions both matters in his authentic writings.

But since a learned man has recently adopted the opposite opinion, other arguments must be brought forward—arguments that will persuade anyone comparing the *Acts of Adalhard and Wala* that they have one and the same author.

1. The title *Epitaph of Arsenius*, prefixed to the Life of Wala, corresponds to Radbertus’s words in the Life of Adalhard, where he praises Ambrose and Jerome, who composed epitaphs for their beloved ones with great eloquence.

2. The manner of treating mournful and funeral matters agrees in both *Acts*. In each, Wala, like Adalhard, is praised above all for the grace of his tears, as is clear to anyone comparing no. 25 of the Life of Adalhard with the beginning of the *Epitaph of Wala*.

3. In describing Adalhard’s education in no. 7, Radbertus says that he was instructed in all worldly prudence amid the training of the palace. Concerning Wala he says, “From childhood he was devoted to liberal studies amid the training of the palace,” in Book I, chapter 6.

4. In both works he repeatedly calls Adalhard “the Old Man” and “Antony.”

5. In his Life, Radbertus compares Adalhard, on account of his fearless zeal for justice, to John; likewise the author of the *Epitaph* does so in Book II, chapter 12.

6. In several passages—nos. 13, 23, 59, and especially 68 of his Life—he praises Adalhard’s devotion to poverty at great length. The *Epitaph of Wala* does the same in almost the same words, in Book I, chapters 18 and 19.

For in no. 68 of the Life of Adalhard he introduces Adalhard exhorting his own monks—that is, the monks of New Corbie—to pursue poverty, “and commending to them above all things that they should not be desirous of any earthly possessions, nor wish to accept anything by which others would be burdened.” He also has him say “that many not only of those who govern churches, but even those themselves who live there devoted to God and seem to have renounced the world, were deceived for this reason: that they abounded in excessive possessions.”

The interlocutor Paschasius conveys the same account of Adalhard and Wala in Book I, chapter 18:

“For when these two distinguished men were laying foundations among the peoples to the north of the city . . . they gave these three admonitions above all: that they should not rejoice in becoming very rich in possessions, nor desire the riches of the world so as to set their hearts upon them; but that they should altogether flee delights and pleasures as though they were poisons. Finally, they warned that they should not be delighted by honors and the pomp of pride, as though these were required by religion, lest they should utterly wither and perish in vain. For in Gaul we see many churches, once well founded in religion, to have perished.”

7. The *Life of Adalhard* applies to him this eulogy from Horace:

> Strong, and wholly complete in himself, smooth and rounded.

The *Epitaph of Arsenius* likewise attributes it to Wala in Book I, chapter 9.

8. The Life of Adalhard introduces the example of the painter Zeuxis in no. 20, and the *Epitaph of Wala* does the same immediately at its beginning.

9. The *Acts of Adalhard* praise Wala’s justice in no. 32, where he is called “the guardian of justice and the honor of righteousness,” and even “the just oppressor of the oppressed.” In the *Epitaph*, his fervor for justice is praised in Book I, chapter 12.

10. What is read concerning the foundation of New Corbie in nos. 66, 67, and 68 of the first work corresponds entirely to what is reported in chapter 14 and the following chapters of the second.

11. Finally, to pass over the rest, the same features appear in both works: the same genius, the same style, and often the same words, including unusual ones. One example is *interdum* used in place of *interim*, which occurs with this meaning in no. 71 of the *Acts of Adalhard*, in Book I, chapter 11 of the *Epitaph*, and elsewhere.

[Col. 0025]

# VERSES OF BISHOP ENGELMODUS TO RADBERTUS THE ABBOT

[Col. 0025A]

The powers of talent and the apt skill of eloquent speech of noble teachers, their wish fulfilled, will be able to weave for you, holy Father, a mitre flourishing with the ornament of speech, and to polish a diadem gleaming with little plates of gold—wherewith sweet devotion adorns you—those teachers who, duly nourished by you, their fruitful master, with the banquets of learning, pour forth leaping waves of doctrine and abundant showers of ingenious song.

But we, plucking from barren turf a small blade of grass as a devoted gift of love for you, profane clear odes with foul-tongued games, and the verdant subject withers beneath an idle pen.

It would therefore have been better to have kept shut the little instrument of my sluggish lip, checking the din of a strained voice, lest your ears should receive anything rancid amid pleasing sweetness, or bitterness disturb the nectar of the honeycomb.

Yet the little fire of ardor in my devoted breast—the dear love with which I embrace you in tranquil honor—was not content merely to hold the reins of a bridle drawn back, but broke through the very hard barriers of the enclosure.

[Col. 0025B] For when it then commits itself to the open field and, with unbridled mane, challenges the blasts of the winds, it does not feel itself, released from its stalls, borne through the empty air, but playfully tramples the opposing sedges underfoot.

Therefore, blessed Father, glory and golden light of the world, pillar of the Church, greatest cedar of paradise, summit of religion, strongest shield of faith, therefore I pray that I, a rustic, may be allowed hastily to applaud you with the trifles of uncultivated talent, while hoarse Thalia resounds, and to unfold festive sport and a simple song.

For it is fitting to bring you proclamations of praise and reverently make public the wondrous glory of your life—you who, by the lamp of justice, show all the lofty way leading toward the courts of life, and by which, now blessed, you have deserved to be inscribed in the Father’s register and joined to the blessed citizens of heaven.

Glory shows you great through the splendor of illustrious honor, whereby all whom the broad world contains desire, rejoice, strive, wish, and labor to render you dutiful service and suppliant prayer.

But grace rises higher than the summit of virtues, and the radiance of faith, shining like the sun, penetrates the lofty tribunal of the heavenly throne.

He, flourishing in merits and shining with the probity of his conduct,

Strong in intellect and rejoicing in the governance of his understanding,

Fervent in service and burning with the fires of devotion,

You are proved gentle, tranquil, prudent, just, and kind,

Devout, humble, mild, and gracious.

Neither savage anger, nor the furrowed swelling of a darkened pride,

Nor the venom of hatred, nor, finally, the plague of envy,

Nor lustful love, nor the foul passion of possessing,

Nor a pretended simulation of faith deceiving through guilt,

Nor the barking quarrels of foaming strife

Has polluted you with the filthy act of sordid stain,

Or darkened the timely acumen of your mind.

Rather, pious simplicity, virtue, and a conscience aware of what is right—

With whose sacred milk you were nourished from your earliest years,

And with whose virginal caresses you were duly comforted—

[Col. 0025D] Even as they say the cuckoo grows in nests that have been broken open,

While the nightingale (*luscinia*, apparently misread as “lucina”) sounds its melody in nocturnal hymns,

Among the flower-bearing gardens of divine teaching,

You grew until you reached the full maturity of your age.

The shining droplets of galbanum, breathing forth nectar,

Taught you to rejoice in perpetual serenity,

And, through their sweet goodness, to please the hearts of all.

[Col. 0026A] For in these things the provident Creator ordained that you should be strengthened—

He who, holding all things in his power, governs what he himself created,

The highest and the lowest, by eternal reason—

When, as a tender infant, your mother, who had given birth to you,

Was binding the coverings of dark cloth around your first infant ornaments (*crepundia*),

And the ravenous image of death was circling the abandoned child.

Those who sprang from a heavenly stock,

Endowed with the gathered gifts of the angelic choir,

Properly fitted you also, snatched aloft beyond the heights of heaven,

To serve the All-Powerful.

Nor is this an uncertain faith or a fabricated little tale,

Such as learned antiquity, once pre-eminent in its studies,

Vomiting forth monstrous teachings from a diseased mind,

Set up among the stars lascivious beds and the soft embraces of Camillus,

And assigned the honors of the abducted Ganymede,

Thus venerating the Saturnian god with fitting ceremony

And staining Olympus, the sanctuary of the gods, with its debaucheries.

Rather, in accordance with the merits of a religion worthy of imitation,

By which you serve Christ the Lord with unceasing vows,

We dedicate these praises to you with the honor due to a worshiper of Christ.

[Col. 0026B] O simple and holy mind of a venerable man,

Disciplined by goods worthy of reverence and always intent upon heavenly things!

Joined with the angelic choirs, it exults in the stars;

Happy, it rejoices in fellowship with the apostolic companies;

It sees the ranks adorned with the blood of martyrdom;

It walks with the white-robed flock of virginity;

It rests rejoicing upon the throne of the patriarchs;

It addresses the watchful prophets in a crowded discourse;

Passing through the mysteries, it feasts upon the teachings of life;

And upon these banquets it reclines, to be satisfied by unceasing devotion.

And just as, when the frosts have been removed by the breathing west wind,

The flowering earth brings forth swelling grasses,

And in the new spring paints the fields with varied colors,

The young bees are exercised, dispersed across the meadows,

Fearing the harsh labors shaken out by the preceding winter;

They gather purple flowers and sip the streams.

Nor is there delay or rest, until they either enclose the liquid honey

In slender cells compacted with nectar,

Or build the hard foundations of the honeycombs

With slowly flowing glue,

[Col. 0026C] Or arrange the saffron-colored waxes in orderly rows.

Their constant care seethes; the purest honey gives off fragrance.

So you, sweet glory, captivated by divine love,

While you gaze upon heavenly things alone in the mirror of your heart,

Freely stationed in the lofty outpost of the spirit,

Fly through the groves and pleasant green places of sacred speech,

Which, watered by the clear spring of life,

Put forth joyful leaves and everlasting flowers.

Their inward parts gently swollen with pious dew,

And your arms newly laden with the juice you have received,

Impatient to refresh your spirit with the repose of sleep,

You either pour back the nectar of teachings by letting it drip,

Or construct the honeycombs of books through laborious activity.

And when, already rich in such great merits, you have raised your head among the stars,

Your temples crowned with a golden wreath,

So that the proud fasces of the devoted imperial power

And the shining glory of the kingdom may venerate you with praise,

And the populous theaters may resound with your applause,

You have never been flattered by the empty bag of boastful favor;

[Col. 0026D] Rather, suppliant and humble, you are blessed with a fortunate title.

Whenever someone approached you, sad in his clouded heart,

Mourning that the heap of his exhausted grain had failed,

Or complaining in querulous words that unjust fortune

Had weighed him down and made his life pitiable,

Immediately revived by the generous gift of your bounty,

Or relying upon the gentle solace of prudent counsel,

[Col. 0027A] He returned home rejoicing and cheerful.

And what amazes me even more: nourished by marvelous sweetness,

The insignia of your mind shine forth in the bearing of your body,

And the adornments of your face signify the secret of your spirit.

For your hair, shining with snowy whiteness,

Reveals that virginal modesty dwells in your heart.

Your face, resembling roses, beautiful and flushed,

Names the trophy of the warrior who has conquered the serpent,

Or, in its own ardor, imitates the flames of love.

For your smiling eyes and honorable delight are alike,

So that I might believe the Dioscuri [Castor and Pollux] shine with joyful brightness;

Your conduct depicts the fellowship that bears the palm of faith,

Or recalls the joys of the heavenly kingdom already tasted.

Your neck, encircled by the gentle curve of your hair,

Conceals itself, as is fitting for hope, enclosed beneath a covering of virtues.

The grace upon your lips and the beauty in your mouth

Cannot be contained by your intellect, nor can the abundance of speech convey it—

A more generous stream flows from the leaping vein of wisdom,

Pouring forth lofty channels of eloquence;

It scatters golden clods of the word

And green jewels of meaning upon shining sands.

[Col. 0027B] Armed in due fashion with the lightning of these things,

And burdened with the twisted lash of a Balearic sling,

You easily bring down, by slaughter, the half-beastly Goliath,

[Col. 0028A] Likewise rending the monstrous forms of the hostile battle-line.

Holy Father, you delight to labor in this arena,

For the sacrificial flock, for the chaste ones of the All-Powerful,

To lighten their hard labors through these exercises,

While the vital breath remains and you feed upon the air,

Destined to bear blessed rewards in manifold fruit.

When the King enthroned on high has separated the world by the urn of judgment,

And repaid all according to their deeds,

Then, I trust, exalted and glorified,

The lofty glory of the kingdom will receive you into its flower-bearing embrace.

Then you will rejoice, joined to the companies of the blessed,

And, happy, enjoy everlasting light.

But as for me—alas, I bear this tearfully and tremble as I recount it—

My neck bound in chains beneath the weight of sin,
