Perhaps then the anger of the excessively cruel Judge

Will condemn me, miserably surrendered to dark torturers,

And the devouring flame of Gehenna will consume me when I am seized.

But you, holy one, I beg you, place yourself between me and these dangers;

Defend the wretched man with the pious dew of your aid,

And gently restrain the smoke-producing vapors of punishment.

[Col. 0028B] And now the time has come to fasten the rope to the ship,

And to steady its light course with the bite of ballast,

Lest, while we entrust the vessel too freely to the south winds,

We should later be carried back to the shores after striking the rocks.

[Col. 0027B]

## PRIVILEGE OF THE MONASTERY OF CORBIE, GRANTED TO ABBOT RADBERT BY THE SYNOD OF PARIS IN THE YEAR 866

[Col. 0027B] In the year 846 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the tenth indiction, while the most glorious and serene prince Charles was reigning throughout the provinces of Gaul, after the division of the kingdom and the peace with his brothers—namely, Kings Lothair and Louis—had already been confirmed, we bishops of Gaul assembled at Paris by royal command, so that we might inquire into those matters which, in the churches of God, because of the violence that had passed during the civil war as well as the inactivity of prelates and subjects, were already being conducted very differently from what was proper; and also into the reason why pestilence and disease had so long been raging among the people; into what the order and condition of the holy churches ought to be according to the institution of the Fathers; and into which privileges handed down from ancient times ought to be preserved.

Among other matters, our venerable brother Radbert, abbot of the monastery of Corbie, presented to us sacred letters of the most pious princes—namely, of the pious Emperor Louis, of blessed memory, and of his son Lothair—in which provision had been made that the monastery itself, preserved according to the ancient custom observed from its beginning, should possess the privilege of election and freedom in the administration of its property, in complete integrity, both in our time and in times to come.

Moreover, he produced the authority and consent of the most distinguished and noble King Charles. With the favor of the Lord, from the beginning of his reign he had received this same monastery, according to the custom of his predecessors, into his familiarity and protection, as though by hereditary right; and, as a gift truly most pleasing to God, he had most devoutly offered it to God amid the various storms of legal disputes, so that it might especially enjoy the tranquility appropriate to that order. He had also proclaimed this in his most sacred letters.

He therefore requested that what had been confirmed by the sacred letters of the most pious princes should also, by our authority and at the prince’s wish, be confirmed by us. We judged this both just and worthy of our office: first, out of reverence for God, who protects and advances that place; also because we have undertaken the pastoral office of Christ’s flock; and likewise because of our love for those who have hitherto served the Lord commendably in that place.

For, as we have learned, that venerable place was founded by holy men, Queen Bathilde having obtained it from her son Chlothar (*Clotario*); and it thereafter preserved inviolate the rule of sacred religion that it had received at the beginning, to such an extent that it not only equaled but almost surpassed those who had founded it.

[Col. 0028C] For this reason noble men also willingly gathered in that place for the service of God, and adorned it both with their nobility and with the merit of their lives. Hence it came about that the place became more intimate to the lords of worldly affairs, so that kings and queens received it under their protection.

But because in our times almost everything had been corrupted, the religious men of that place, seeing the rights of election disregarded in many places and fearing that they might suffer the same fate, sought sacred letters from the most merciful princes confirming for them election and the free disposition of their property according to the institution of divine law. Nor did they consider these sufficient; at the command of the most noble and eminent king, they requested that the same things be confirmed to them also by our authority.

This we granted not without good reason. First, because we ought to be fathers and defenders of the Church; next, because we fear that, unless we keep watch over such matters, we shall be guilty before the sight of the divine majesty.

Therefore we admonish and exhort our most pious sons and lords, the princes of our own and of future times, since this is being confused in almost every place, at least for the love and reverence of God and for the due love of his servants, and also for the prosperity and increase of their kingdom, to strive to preserve for that place the privilege of election and the free disposition of its resources.

May the privilege of election always exist in that monastery, just as election was preserved in the churches of ancient times—not imposed or substituted, but free, according to canonical authority and the rule of Saint Benedict.

If it should ever happen that some rector in that place does not live worthily before God, or perhaps is less dutiful toward the prince, we establish that, if he is deposed because of his negligence, their election shall remain inviolate: namely, they shall choose another whom they find suitable for that office according to monastic discipline.

For it is not just that the fault of one should redound upon all; nor can it by any means be right that, when one sins, vengeance should rise against everyone, or that because of one person’s cause the Church of Christ should lose its privileges. Rather, one person’s fault must be cut away in such a manner that provision is made for all who are and who will be in that place.

In the election itself, moreover, let regular authority be preserved. That is, let the man be placed over the holy congregation whom election by the majority has not commended, but whom the brothers of sounder counsel, though fewer in number, have chosen, and whom the merit of his life and the dignity of his wisdom have rendered worthy of approval.

But if it should ever happen that some usurper—indeed, a wolf of the Lord’s fold—or someone using money, after the manner of Simon, or any other favor among the lords of worldly affairs, should wish to obtain that monastery, then, first, according to canonical authority, because he has wished to acquire the Church of God through secular power, we anathematize him together with all the holy Fathers who promulgated the sacred canons. By this action our authority, granted to us by the most merciful grace of God, is no less bound than that of all the preceding Fathers who issued such decrees for the stability of God’s holy Church.

Next we declare that, because he wished to disturb the fellowship of God’s servants, he is to be expelled from the land of the living like Achan (Joshua 7)—provided that he does not quickly repent. But if he has obtained it, let him have no fellowship, either here or in the future, with the holy Church of God, which he has polluted by a sufficiently infamous example.

Indeed, let the chorus of all the churches cry out incessantly against him who said: “I shall possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance. My God, make him like a wheel, like stubble before the face of the wind, like the fire that burns the forest, like the flame that burns the mountains” (Psalm 82:13–15), and the rest that follows.

And because, driven by greed, he also wished to seize and carry away the money and property of God’s servants and the poor of Christ, together with Judas, the squanderer of sacred money and betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, let him receive those curses that were pronounced against him, as an invader of Christ’s flock and a murderer of the poor.

Furthermore, if our sons, the lords of worldly affairs, should assist those who are now perhaps contriving such things or who may at some time attempt them, and, after being admonished once, twice, three times, or even more, should fail to correct themselves, let a sentence of similar condemnation bind them both here and in the future—unless they amend themselves through true satisfaction before him who is King of kings and Lord of lords.

And, so that these sons and lords of ours may fear to do what is contrary to God’s and the Church’s decree, we append what canonical authority establishes concerning these matters in one and in several chapters. Thus it has been decreed (Gangra, canon 8; Book I, canon 47): “If anyone, apart from a bishop or one appointed by him to distribute mercy to the poor, gives or receives offerings, let both the giver and the receiver be anathema.”

We have therefore pursued these matters so that our sons and lords may do what they ought to do and resist those who do not fear to violate the authority of the Fathers, lest they impose perpetual condemnation upon themselves or generate the scandal of offense among their subjects.

For it is evident that whoever yields to one making an evil request both brings upon himself the weight of divine punishment and imposes the anger of the just and perpetual Judge upon the one toward whom he is indulgent [source: “conibet,” corrected in the margin to “connivet”].

To prevent this, we admonish, exhort, and entreat that our sons and lords preserve inviolate what we have established, both now and in the future, and give neither now nor later their consent to anyone wishing to profane the Church of God for worldly use. Thus they may not only escape the anger of the stern Judge but also obtain the crown of everlasting life and the glory of that most blessed and eternal Davidic kingdom.

We also admonish those for whose sake we speak and act in all these matters—namely, the illustrious and most precious members of the eternal King and Savior of all—that they apply continual devotion to their religion with the same affection with which we provide for their welfare and serve their future tranquility in this matter.

That is, let them strive to be before the eyes of the Judge who sees all things what they appear and are believed to be in the eyes of men; so that they may commend us, occupied with ecclesiastical affairs, to God through their prayer and merit, and may obtain the favor of almighty God for our lords and sons.

Thus not only may perpetual authority over their resources and the privilege of election remain with them, but the triumph of everlasting glory may also receive them after the completion of the present life.

And so that what we have decreed may remain inviolate in the present and future time, we have strengthened by the subscription of our hand the provisions set forth above.

We also admonish and beseech our successors that, for the love of Christ and inflamed by zeal for God, they keep watch against the plotters and thieves of the Lord’s fold and drive them away; and that they themselves confirm everything we have established, both by the authority of the sacred Gospel and of the holy Fathers, and by the most merciful favor granted to them by the Savior of all.

Just as we, loving the tranquility and advancement of that place, anathematize according to the institution of the canons anyone who attempts to violate this privilege, [Col. 0030B] and separate him from all fellowship with the saints—provided that he does not repent and correct himself through true satisfaction.

We also beseech our brothers and fellow bishops, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and by our congregation’s gathering in him; and we likewise beseech the religious abbots who did not attend this holy and blessed synod, into whose hands the document of this privilege, issued and confirmed by us, shall come, not to delay confirming it by their own authority and subscription.

Hincmar, bishop of the holy metropolitan Church of Reims, declaring this privilege ratified by episcopal authority, confirmed it in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Erpuin, unworthy bishop of Senlis, subscribed to this privilege, established by episcopal authority, in the name of the Holy Trinity.

Guntbold, bishop of the holy metropolitan Church of Rouen, reread this privilege and, declaring it ratified by episcopal authority, confirmed it in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Simeon, bishop of the holy Church of Laon, assenting to this privilege by episcopal authority, subscribed in the name of the Holy Trinity.

Rothad, prelate of the holy Church of Soissons, assenting to this privilege by pontifical authority, subscribed.

Theoderic, bishop of the holy Church of Cambrai, assenting to this privilege by episcopal authority, subscribed in the name of the Holy Trinity.

Irminfrid, bishop of the holy Church of Beauvais, assenting to this privilege by episcopal authority, subscribed in the name of the Holy Trinity.

Wenilo, bishop of the holy metropolitan Church of Sens, reread this privilege and, declaring it ratified by episcopal authority, subscribed in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0030D] Fulcoin, unworthy bishop of the Church of Thérouanne, assenting to this privilege by episcopal authority, subscribed in the name of the Holy Trinity.

Helias, bishop of Chartres, reread this privilege and judged it worthy to be made ratified.

Raginar, bishop of the holy Church of Amiens, assenting to this privilege by pontifical authority, subscribed.

Prudentius, unworthy bishop of Troyes, assenting to this privilege by episcopal authority, subscribed in the name of the Holy Trinity.

Aldric, bishop of Le Mans.

Agius, unworthy bishop of the Church of Orléans, subscribed to this privilege, established by episcopal authority, in the name of the Holy Trinity.

Erchenrad, bishop of the Church of Paris, subscribed to this privilege, established by episcopal authority.

[Col. 0031A] Freculf, bishop of the Church of Lisieux, declaring it ratified by episcopal authority, subscribed in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Saxobodus, bishop of the Church of Sées, assented to and subscribed this decree.

Immo, unworthy bishop of the Church of Noyon, assented to and subscribed this privilege.

[Col. 0032A] Erluin, by the grace of God bishop of Coutances, assented to this privilege.

Louis, abbot of the monastery of the most precious martyrs of Christ, Denis and his companions, reread this privilege and, declaring it ratified, subscribed.

Radbert, abbot of that monastery, reread this privilege and, declaring it ratified, subscribed.

[Col. 0031A]

## EXPOSITION OF PASCHASIUS RADBERT, ABBOT OF CORBIE, ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW

*(According to the edition of Sirmond.)*

## PROLOGUE TO GUNTLAND, A MONK OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT RICHARIUS THE CONFESSOR
[Col. 0031B] 1–2. When, in obedience to my sacred profession, I was expounding the Gospel before the brothers on solemn days, as is customary—although my manner of speaking was unpolished, more for exhortation than for instruction—some of them, fervent in religion, began repeatedly and earnestly to request (without considering whether I could do so) that I explain in order the continuous text of the narrative of the blessed evangelist Matthew, so that the streams of the whole doctrine committed to writing might flow more abundantly to very many.

At once, having entered into myself, I placed before my eyes, newly moved by their manner of address, the stained life of my frailty and the crimes in which I was enmeshed. And I began to examine the native capacity of my thorny breast, which indulgence—the generosity of the Giver—had granted me, and to search out the depth of so great a mystery: whether, perhaps, divine power might wish to water with the springs of doctrine the dry rock of my heart, and, through the pen of my labor, to adapt the perceptions of the holy Fathers to readers in a single, unified expression.

[Col. 0031C] I wished this to be done in such a way that neither eloquence, stitched together with various and offensively ornate embroideries of sentences, would offend the reader’s mind, nor the different paths through the fissures confuse the brightness of understanding. But while I was considering these matters, long and deeply restrained by shame, the pardon of the author and the grace through which he merited the apostolate from God immediately shone before my eyes.

It also occurred to me that he had not been ashamed to confess himself a publican, and that he had plainly wished the manner in which he was called from the tax office to be proclaimed to everyone in the evangelical voice. As though clearly forewarned by these considerations, I began no longer to doubt pardon, nor to hesitate that, assisted by his support, I ought to be admitted to the banquet of doctrine—by whose hospitality, indeed, before the infusion of the Spirit, the Lord already deigned to dine with sinners and publicans.

[Col. 0031D] If we look carefully at him throughout the entire text of the Gospel, he exercises special care for sinners; hence he also establishes rules of conduct and openly displays everywhere the fountain of true conversion. For this reason, although I understand that I am a sinner, I did not believe myself to be excluded from this grace, especially since I read that the same evangelist preached among the Ethiopians and had poured out the grace of the Holy Spirit in the office of preaching the Gospel. Thus those who had been blackened more deeply than pitch by the soot of sin might be formed by his example toward the grace by which this man, from a publican, was made an evangelist from heaven.

[Col. 0032B] Therefore, I ask that no one be angry with me if, trusting at last in God’s grace, I have chosen to dedicate to the Lord the skill which heavenly Providence has seasoned in me with the salt of learning, rather than grow sluggish in the idleness of an empty life while neglecting study. For although I believed it would benefit not many, I nevertheless believed it would benefit myself and my own, to turn my mind toward this from time to time and bind in writing the fleeting insights of doctrine acquired through long labor, so that through this I might be better equipped for thinking and more prepared for discussion.

[Col. 0032C] Therefore let everyone run with me together to the fountain of pardon; even if they bring no price, let them receive wine and milk freely, without any exchange. If it pleases you, let them approach this publican with me; let them drink from his streams with me. For it is better to follow the mystical teaching of this man, even though it has been unlocked with a ploughman's pen, than to gather flowers through the Elysian fields and drink by continually lapping the golden waves from the fountain of Tantalus.

And if others perhaps draw fuller streams from this source and prepare dishes of riches, at least I do not think they would disdain to receive our pure draughts—those who, in speaking, so often willingly hear the voice of doctrine at their father’s command.

[Col. 0032D] Indeed, because I have chosen to write for no others than those whose studies flourish in such matters, whose devotion burns, and whose charity invites them to receive what belongs to sound doctrine, I set aside as plagues the sluggish and those who, out of envy, maliciously criticize this pious work—at least so that I may benefit my own people, who, burning with goodwill, have advanced me in divine studies.

[Col. 0033A] But if someone should attempt, in opposition, to raise the objection of the envious in the present time: “After the authority of the earlier Fathers, why have you undertaken to expound the Gospel?”—let him know that I have chosen this in advance not through presumption, but through love of religion, desiring, sprinkled with the grace of Christ, to fulfill my father's wishes.

Certainly, none of the learned has prescribed a limit to the gift of the Holy Spirit or to the effectiveness of the mind regarding future things; no one has forbidden obedience to heavenly disciplines. But the laziness of deceitful people has always been more ready, with the audacity of rashness, to slander the fruitful efforts of the Fathers whom we now venerate than to devote itself to knowledge of the truth.

[Col. 0033B] The greatest philosophers endured this; renowned poets endured it; and our teachers, as I have said, endured it. Yet all of them, following the studies of their predecessors, fashioned from their insights things more excellent for those who came after them.

Therefore, if the authority of our writers is to be preferred above all others, let them know that the truth of doctrine commends these authors; it does not, in fact, commend the truth itself through them. For truth is not supported by a disputation resting upon a teacher's ingenuity; rather, truth is sought through disputation. Truth is solid in itself, whereas disputation serves the speaker, so that through it truth, veiled in obscurity, may be disclosed.

[Col. 0033C] Moreover, truth once disclosed and faithfully grasped in writing makes those authors worthy of commendation to readers, as we follow in their footsteps without hesitation—provided that, with God as our guide, they prove that we have suffered no shipwreck of faith in these matters.

If anyone after this wishes, with blinded eyes, to discredit the undertaking of this work, let him consider in whose disciplines we have been instructed, and how the songs of the Sirens have warned us to pass by with deaf ears. For they themselves taught, in their own time, that they had endured such monsters of language.

[Col. 0033D] Let them see whether what we offer displeases those for whom we offer it and who do not disdain it; for we ought not on that account to have remained silent, since the authors of their Churches have demonstrated in their response, more clearly than light, that it is useful for many books to be produced by many people, in different styles but not in different faiths, so that one and the same doctrine of the Holy Spirit, proclaimed in one way to some and in another way to others, may reach very many.

Nor should it be thought that in our own time no one is granted the grace of understanding, since the prophetic statement is plainly fulfilled: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. XII, 4).

A similar privilege is also shown to have been granted to the philosophers of the world, after the labors of their predecessors, by the exercise of reason: the younger their teachers were, the more perceptive they were.

[Col. 0034A] Nevertheless, although I speak in this way, I do not love the boastfulness of arrogance so much as to claim that I have reached their knowledge or merits. Rather, I rejoice that, having been nourished by their teaching, I have grasped the faith which they taught and apprehended the truth.

Therefore, gathering many things here and there from their books, I have composed this work devoutly for the brothers to read—at least so that the boys whom secular instruction had trained in the liberal disciplines from their earliest age might have something fresh, by whose encouragement they could learn to run more eagerly in the field of the holy Scriptures and labor more diligently in it, expanding more broadly and abundantly the small nourishment of kindling which could arise from me.

[Col. 0034B] Especially since I myself, prompted to this undertaking, rejoice that I have made much progress—not, I say, in doctrine, but in life. For when, by way of exhortation to others, I penetrate by unfolding the profound mysteries of God’s words, if I ever repel the vices of human weakness, forewarned by the words of my own assertion, I rebuke myself.

Nor do I doubt that those who follow, under more recent disciplines, will be encouraged to meditate more earnestly on the principal works of Scripture.

But perhaps those whom the more eminent discipline of Christ enlightens, and who possess a higher level of knowledge, will regard this explanation as superfluous and excessively long. Especially since Saint Hilary, a foremost disputant on the faith, and the blessed Jerome, an outstanding interpreter and teacher of the divine law, wished to unlock the streams of this Gospel only through brief and, as it were, elementary commentaries.

[Col. 0034C] In the meantime, let Jerome himself speak about himself better than I can, explaining why he confined an immense subject for exposition to only four little books and a few brief observations. For he says as follows in the Prologue to Matthew:

> “I marvel, most beloved Eusebius, why, being about to sail suddenly to Rome, you wished this, as it were, travelling provision to be given to you by me, so that, explaining Matthew briefly, I might compress the words and expand the meanings. If you had remembered,” he says, “my reply, you would never, in a few days, have demanded a work of years.”

Behold how highly this foremost of men judged the undertaking of this work.

But do you suppose, I ask, that within two weeks, with Easter already approaching, he could have searched out all the secrets of this Gospel and carefully explained everything through the work of a writer? Indeed, he himself confirms through many indications that this was impossible.

[Col. 0034D] For this reason he promises that he will complete what remains, so that it may be understood, as he himself says, how great a difference there is between the rustic boldness of dictation and the painstaking, laboriously polished diligence of writing.

For the rest, let our people consider how many and what kind of Greek authors the eloquence of the Greeks possesses on this same work. Then they will be able to discern how greatly Latin poverty lacks instruction, since scarcely a few commentaries by our predecessors have come into our hands.

Although Fortunatianus and Victorinus are said to have published small works on it, we have not yet been able to find them.

[Col. 0035A] Moved to this undertaking, therefore, by such reasons and others of this kind, I acted willingly, with the Father’s consent, so that I might benefit many; I was also stirred, as I stated above, by the exhortations of the elders, and by the wish of the aforementioned teacher Jerome, who led me toward longer discussions in his desire for greater exposition. I wished, for those asking for a small work, to fulfill his promised act of devotion through my own service.

Thus, just as he is now rewarded for fulfilling his wishes, so may I at last deserve to be refreshed by the benefit of indulgence through his intercessions; and, as a publican, may I at least dine with the Lord as the last guest at this banquet of the blessed Matthew, and be defended against all adversaries by his merits.

Indeed, in place of the boldness of so great a man’s rough dictation, I wished to fulfill, at least in stolen hours—for under this discipline no other time is available—the painstaking diligence of writing which he had promised.

[Col. 0035B] This is not because I am perhaps capable of completing through my own labor what he, with his incomparable knowledge of the divine Scriptures, accomplished through his sweat, as he had promised. Rather, I chose from among all sources what I might use to shape this work while following his wishes.

Nor should I therefore be called a compiler of the ancients, since, as Tullius himself reports—the very king of eloquence—he imitated a certain Zeuxis, who selected the five most beautiful girls from all the virgins of Croton. He set them before his eyes while painting for those who requested it a marvelous image of Helen, so that whatever beauty was lacking in one of them, and whatever each separately displayed more beautifully in herself, he might contribute in its entirety to the colors of his painting.

[Col. 0035C] In the same way, that distinguished orator, as he attests in his own work, selected from all the philosophers who had preceded him what he could use to form a marvelous model of rhetorical art, setting them before him—a model praised by everyone to this day and useful to those who pursue his expertise.

Thus many other philosophers acted; so did poets; and so did the most skilled expositors of our own literature. Among them is the one whom we follow: the interpreter of the divine law and marvelous unraveler of the holy Scriptures, who composed almost all his shorter works from things scattered throughout the writings of those who preceded him. He himself does not blush to confess this in each case, judging it safer for him to follow the teaching of those who had earlier treated the divine Scriptures by the straight path of catholic faith in this Church of Christ.

Yet he acted as an arbiter concerning each source, whereas we, as followers, selected what was suitable. If one wishes to criticize this practice, one will find scarcely any teacher exempt from it. All preferred to follow the footsteps of their catholic predecessors and continually enlarge the streams of Christ’s doctrine through their own intellects, so that what is necessary but hidden in the divine writings might, with God’s grace unlocking it, be revealed more abundantly for the benefit of others.

[Col. 0035D] Following these writers, therefore, I chose the distinguished Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, and the blessed Gregory, as well as John, bishop of Constantinople, and finally Bede the presbyter. Clinging to their footsteps, I believe that I have deviated in no respect from their understanding, although I have occasionally inserted certain things from other sources that agree with the truth.

Nevertheless, I first compared these additions, so that I would admit nothing unless either the aforementioned writers had said it or the truth elsewhere agreed with the evidence.

[Col. 0036A] For this reason I carefully arranged to place the initial letters of these authors' names in the margin of this work, so that from them the reader might proceed securely and immediately recognize opposite each passage whose footsteps I follow.

I have therefore omitted the topics which teachers often explain externally, before the words of the holy Gospel are presented according to established practice. From the same canons, which Ammonius of Alexandria first arranged for the agreement of the Evangelists and which the aforementioned Jerome subsequently took care to affix at each passage so that the correspondences of the individual Evangelists might be grasped sentence by sentence, I wished to recall only the ways in which their agreement is correctly understood.

For we see in very many places that, although they are said to agree through the same numbers, what one is marked as saying in the same sense has no connection with the meaning of the other. For example, Matthew, Mark, and Luke are marked as agreeing concerning the paralytic who was carried by four men; but John is marked as agreeing with them from the passage where he is said to speak of the man who, having been ill for thirty-eight years, lay beside the pool which was stirred once a year by an angel.

[Col. 0036B] Clearly, without my saying anything, all readers can see that this passage does not belong to the same place where the paralytic is narrated. You will be able to verify the same thing, reader, in very many places.

But what they understood from this is that either the Evangelists said the same things together, or neighboring things, or certainly each said what belonged to himself.

They say the same things in two ways: either when they write the same thing in both sense and outward wording, or in sense alone, or when the things are regarded as the same in outward wording alone.

They agree in sense and outward wording in the statement: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Matt. XIII, 57; Mark VI, 4; Luke IV, 24; John IV, 44). If you examine it, the words and sense are the same in each Evangelist.

[Col. 0036C] On the other hand, things may be the same in sense, though not in outward wording, as in Luke, where the Lord says to Peter: “And you, once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII, 32). Then in John, where the Lord says to Peter: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John XXI, 17).

These statements are certainly the same in sense, as are also the passages concerning the paralytic and the man who lay waiting for the movement of the water; but they do not appear to be joined in outward wording.

Things that are neighboring are likewise said to be so in two ways: either they are joined in sense but not in outward wording, or they are joined in outward wording but not in sense.

[Col. 0036D] An example of the latter is found in Luke, where he says: “But they offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb. And when he had eaten before them, he took the leftovers and gave them to them” (Luke XXIV, 42).

In John, on the other hand: “Jesus came and took bread and gave it to them, and likewise fish” (John XXI, 13).

8. These passages are similar only in the outward wording of their words, but dissimilar in meaning. For the story is not the same, nor did the events take place at the same time, although there is some proximity between them and not a great difference.

Similarly, things may be joined in sense but not in outward wording, as in this Gospel: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ,” down to “the husband of Mary, from whom Christ was born” (Matt. I, 1). So too in what John says: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being”; or the statement: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I, 9).

For in these passages a certain proximity of meanings is discerned, although they cannot be the same in every respect.

They also say that some proximity is gathered in both sense and outward wording, as with this genealogy in the present passage and the one in Luke, although they differ in many respects, because in each a single genealogy is woven from the same family of the Savior.

I have said this so that the fruitful labor of such great men might not be lost through being misunderstood. Indeed, I beg the prudent reader, once these matters have been set forth, diligently to seek all those things that are taught externally for the understanding of the holy Gospel, so that he may approach with greater capacity the things that lie within.

## PREFACE: Against Those Who Say That Christ’s Genealogy Does Not Belong to the Gospel

[Col. 0037]

[Col. 0037A] The power of the Holy Scriptures has not been so obscured by mysteries that the simple cannot understand it, nor is it so open that anyone, while living here, can penetrate it completely. Rather, it stands out with such great dignity that it does not permit those who approach it willingly to come close unless they do so with piety and devotion; instead, it sometimes leaves them empty, enclosed below its darkness by the fault of their own error. For although the light shines in the darkness, the darkness did not comprehend it; indeed, if the darkness had comprehended it, the darkness would certainly no longer remain. Sometimes it may even happen that it not only leaves people empty, but also, because divine power lies hidden within these things, condemns those who undertake to handle them impurely.

Accordingly, Demetrius, when explaining the force of the divine law to King Antiochus, said—as Josephus bears witness—that there had been a certain man named Theopompus who, wishing to incorporate something from the divine writings into his own history, immediately became mentally disturbed for somewhat more than thirty days, until he scarcely obtained pardon through his prayers. Afterwards, he is said to have learned through a vision from heaven that this had happened to him because he had searched into divine matters irreverently and wished to present them to impure people. When he ceased writing these things, he is said soon to have recovered his mind.

He also reported concerning Theodectes, the poet of tragedies, that he had attempted to insert into some kind of dramatic composition things contained in the divine writings, and therefore, when his eyes were darkened, he suddenly suffered blindness. From this event, then, we learn that Faustus the Manichaean suddenly lost the eyes of his mind. When he approached the interpretation of the Gospel rashly rather than devoutly, and had ultimately become ill-fated to himself through opposition, as soon as he touched the beginning of blessed Matthew, he seemed to be struck back by a heavenly light, began to whirl as though from dizziness, and withdrew more deeply beneath his own darkness. Unable to extricate himself from that darkness, he undoubtedly brought upon himself a greater gloom.

For he says to himself—I do not know under what dialogue—questioning himself as though in the person of a certain Christian:

“Do you accept the Gospel?”

“Most certainly,” he replies.

Then the other says: “Therefore accept Christ as having been born.”

“Not so,” he replies. “For it does not follow that, if I accept the Gospel, I must consequently accept Christ as having been born. The Gospel both began from the preaching of Christ and takes its name from it. Yet nowhere in this Gospel did he say that he had been born from human beings.”

But the genealogy is so far from being the Gospel that its author himself did not dare to call it the Gospel. What did he write? “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David.”

“Therefore,” he says, “it is not the Gospel, but the book of the generation.” Indeed, a star is introduced there which confirms the *genesis*, so that it can properly be called a *Genesidium* rather than the Gospel. For after John had been confined [Col. 0037B] in prison, Jesus is first read to have begun preaching the Gospel of the kingdom. Therefore, whatever was narrated before this is clearly genealogy, not the Gospel. Otherwise, what prevented Matthew too from writing “The Gospel of Jesus Christ, Son of God,” just as we see Mark did, except that he considered it improper to call the genealogy the Gospel?”

O insane mind! Do we not plainly conclude that this man, since he belonged to the race of darkness that all Manichaeans proclaim, was unable from the beginning to bear the light of truth, and therefore spewed out such things? Especially since this entire passage is directed against those same people, who neither accept the Old Testament nor affirm that Christ was truly human, or that he could have been born of the Virgin Mary.

Therefore, we who hold the catholic faith assert that, according to Matthew, he is declared through the genealogy, and that, in accordance with the statement “the Word became flesh,” he was born of the Virgin Mary. We also recognize that he existed as true man and true God, and that this was proclaimed not only by these evangelists but also by the angel.

What, then? Could or should the book of the Gospel not rightly be called so, as this Faustus attempts to assert—especially since the apostle Paul cries out that he was set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had previously promised in the Holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh? If Faustus had understood this word “Gospel,” he would never have denied altogether that Christ came according to the flesh from the seed of David through this genealogy.

For “Gospel” is said in Greek to mean what in Latin is fully proclaimed as “good news” or “good announcement.” Although this term can always be used whenever something good is announced, it properly ought to designate that announcement of the Savior in the flesh which brought us every good thing—even though Matthew, following ancestral custom, gave the book its name from its beginning and called it “The book of the generation.”

For we also read that, at the Savior’s birth, the angel sang to the shepherds: “Behold,” he said, “I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born for you” (Luke II, 10). And what does it mean that he announces the Gospel, except that, according to the proper meaning of the Latin language, he announces good news to us—namely, that Christ has been born? “Which will be,” he says, “joy for all the people.” Thus it is perfectly clear that the angel says: “I announce good news to you, which will be joy for all the people, because today a Savior has been born for you in the city of David, from whose stock he had formerly been promised to us.”

For Faustus the Manichaean certainly lies when he says that Matthew did not dare to call Christ’s generation or birth the Gospel, but that it rather ought to have been called a *Genesidium*. He plainly does not know the ways in which “Gospel” is rightly said.

“Gospel” is principally said in seven ways, because it first announces to us, concerning Christ, the good of the Incarnation. Second, it shows that he himself was baptized in order to sanctify our baptism. Third, it plainly declares that he suffered for us. Fourth, it proclaims that, having been buried and descending to the underworld, he broke the rights of the enemy. Fifth, it announces to us the good that on the third day he rose victorious from the dead; thereafter, to confirm the faith of the apostles, he is shown to have lived on earth for forty days. Sixth, it announces that on the fortieth day he went to heaven in the flesh before his disciples, and that on the fiftieth day after the resurrection he mercifully poured out from heaven the Holy Spirit previously promised. Seventh, it still announces and promises to us the good that will occur when he comes for judgment to repay each person according to what he has done. For he will say to the saints: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV, 34).

From these things, therefore, we infer that these are the seven seals by which the book is shown sealed in the Apocalypse (Revelation V, 1). In that book, we prove that whatever things have been fulfilled in Christ were written mystically. Hence he reproaches the two who were speaking about him on the road, saying: “O slow of heart to believe all the things that the Scriptures have spoken! And beginning with Moses and the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things written about him” (Luke XXIV, 25).

What he interpreted was nothing other than the Gospel—that is, himself, whom he was explaining. God had long before promised him in the Holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh.

No one, therefore, can rightly doubt that those seven seals were opened in Christ, since the divine response says: “Behold, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has prevailed to open the book and to loose its seven seals” (Revelation V, 5). Those seals are plainly proved to have been opened when all these mysteries were fulfilled in Christ.

Indeed, in those same seals the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit were revealed to all. For when he willed to be born according to the flesh, what else was then first made known on earth than the wisdom of God the Father? Previously he had always been hidden, concerning whom the prophet says: “You are a hidden God, and we did not know you” (Isaiah XLV, 15). Therefore, when by being born he shone forth more manifestly upon the world, what else did he do than open the first seal? In this way, the world received through faith the gift of wisdom, which it had previously not known.

When the time came for baptism, he opened, as it were, the second seal of our salvation. There, by opening the heavens, he graciously disclosed to us the spirit of understanding. For it is exceedingly profound to understand what we were and what, by the grace of the Redeemer, we have now become. There is also the voice of the Father, which thundered from above while revealing the Son: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew III, 17, and XVII, 5). The Holy Spirit also, in the form of a dove, there clearly indicated what had not yet been openly preached: that God is Trinity. From this we understand the mystery that had not yet been revealed to the ages and generations.

Meanwhile, the Savior’s Passion follows. Through it was disclosed the plan that had been entrusted neither to the angels nor fully demonstrated on earth. “For if they had known it,” says the Apostle, “they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Corinthians II, 8). Hence, through Isaiah, he is likewise called the angel of the great plan. It is therefore clear that, in his eternal plan, this sacrament of the mystery had always been hidden and was revealed to all in the last times.

The sum of our purpose, moreover, is gathered from this: that we may die with Christ to the world, so that somehow we may live with him who rose from the dead.

[Col. 0038A] But the fact that, once buried, he descended to the underworld—what else was it than the power of fortitude? Concerning this the Psalmist sings, as though proclaiming it on behalf of the heavenly angels: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Psalm XXIII, 7). The hostile powers answered them: “And who is this King of glory?” Then the holy angels replied: “The Lord, strong and powerful; the Lord, powerful in battle.”

Indeed, unless he had first bound the strong one and taken away his weapons, he would never have said with power, distributing the enemy’s spoils to the Church by his right, that the gates of hell would not prevail against her (Matthew XVI, 73). Hence he still cries from heaven to his soldiers, saying: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John XVI, 33). It is as though he said: “Be strong against every hostile force, because in my strength your victory will assuredly lie.”

He therefore opened to us the spirit of knowledge in the fifth seal of his revelation, when he, rising victorious from the dead, more firmly confirmed for us the hope of rising again. For this reason the Apostle, admonishing his beloved son, says: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel” (II Timothy II, 8).

Great, therefore, is the knowledge of the mystery of the resurrection, in which Christ’s love is confirmed in us. Hence the same Apostle desires us to know “the surpassing love of Christ” (Ephesians III, 19).

When he also displayed the sixth seal to us—namely, his Ascension—in the flesh, then, plainly in accordance with the mystery of his piety, he opened for us the heavenly way and showed us the great sacrament of reconciliation, so that we, who were not worthy to remain longer below the earthly paradise, might, united in his body, be transferred to heavenly things, restored for the better.

Finally, the spirit of fear is manifested when he is promised as one who will come for judgment. Therefore, while we live in the meantime, let us conduct ourselves in fear and trembling. Hence Solomon says at the end of his book: “Fear God and observe his commandments; for this,” he says, “is every human being” (Ecclesiastes XII, 13). David likewise says: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Psalm XVIII, 10).

When these seven mysteries of the heavenly sacraments have thus been opened in Christ, the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled, where he says: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him—the spirit,” he says, “of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isaiah XI, 2).

Why, then, I ask, is one Spirit said to have rested upon him, when he is immediately distinguished as seven spirits? It was surely to show that the grace which was present in him all at once, fulfilling everything, distributed these gifts to us at intervals.

Hence John, in his Apocalypse (Revelation V, 6), introduces a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns—by which he conquered death—and seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God sent into all the earth. For what does it mean for the Lamb, in the midst of the throne and of the living creatures and elders, to have seven horns and seven eyes, except that, through the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit, Christ reigns everywhere throughout the world in his Church, with death conquered?

By these seven horns, through the power of the Holy Spirit, the Church, raised up into the strength of a kingdom, breaks all the horns of sinners. Enlightened by these eyes, she is illumined by signs and powers. By these same columns the house that Wisdom is said to have built for herself is supported and strengthened. This house is proved to be the holy Church of God, which Christ—the power of God and the wisdom of God the Father—dedicated for himself through this sevenfold work of virtues.

These, moreover, are the seven shining lampstands before the Lord, because in Christ, for our illumination and redemption, these things were fulfilled; and now, together with his entire work, he continually intercedes for us before God the Father.

Therefore these seven spirits are said to stand before the Ruler, because whatever we are, all of it consists in the operation of him who, sacrificed for us, is offered daily before the eyes of the divine majesty.

In this wisdom of God the Father, then, we learn to trample the world together with its wisdom, because God chose the foolish things of the world so that, trampling upon all that is strong, we might act in such a way as to be found wise before God.

Moreover, if by this understanding we grasp anything, we understand it wholly so that, reborn in Christ, we may obey the voice of the Father thundering from above: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew XVII, 5). Such a voice, I say, was heard nowhere except over the only-begotten Son of God.

Let us therefore obey his commands, if somehow we can say with the Prophet: “From your commandments I have gained understanding; therefore I have hated every path of iniquity” (Psalm CXVIII, 103).

Our saving and sole counsel is that we should die with Christ, because, if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him. And what can our strength be except his victory, when the Apostle plainly cries out: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans IX, 16)? Hence the Prophet says: “The Lord is the strength of his people” (Psalm XXVII, 11).

Next comes the great gift of piety: united in Christ’s body, we now hope to enter heaven. Finally, we rightly receive the spirit of fear if, according to Peter’s words, we ultimately work out our salvation with fear and trembling.

These, then, are the spirits mystically prefigured in Job’s seven sons—Job, that is, who mercifully suffered and grieved for us. Each of these sons, celebrating banquets in his own house according to the passing of the days, sends for and summons his three sisters. For faith, hope, and love properly feast at no other banquet than where these seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are most worthily shared together in Christ.

Otherwise our faith is empty, and we are lifted up by an empty hope if we glory vainly in some other thing—or perhaps as though in ourselves. For when each person is puffed up by himself, promising himself I know not what else, he is driven away like chaff, a stranger to participation in the kingdom.

But as we wish to explain these things, we become entangled in our own words: how the mystery that is now revealed to us in time was hidden from the ages and generations.

Was the dispensation of the coming Redeemer hidden, then, from either the angelic spirits of the heavenly homeland or from holy human beings, whether living in the flesh or dead, so that they could not even behold it from afar with spiritual eyes? Who could say this, when Isaiah, speaking as though the event were present, says: “Why is your garment red?” (Isaiah LXIII, 2). It is as though he said: “What is this—that you wished to die in the flesh, when you drew no sin from the flesh?”

[Col. 0038B] To him the Lord replied: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me.” He trod the winepress alone, certainly, because he alone overcame the death that he endured.

Hence John also testifies that he saw a strong angel proclaiming in a loud voice: “Who is worthy to open the book and to loose its seven seals?” Immediately it follows: “And no one was able, either in heaven or on earth or under the earth, to open the book or to look upon it” (Revelation V, 2–3).

That is, no one in heaven, because no angel could accomplish the dispensation of human salvation. Hence Isaiah says: “It was not an angel or a messenger; the Lord himself will save them.” No one on earth, because no living human being in the body could do so, since the human being who needed redemption required the help of God the Creator alone. Nor anyone under the earth, because not even a soul separated from the body could do so.

For if a living human being in the body—who certainly can die as a victim—could not accomplish this, how much less could a soul, which, without a body, is no longer essentially capable of dying?

But what does he mean when he says: “Because no one was able to look upon it”? Had not the very same person seen it who shortly before confessed: “Because I saw a book in the right hand of the one seated on the throne, written within and on the outside”? Where, I ask, was it? Or perhaps it was not in heaven, on earth, or under the earth when he saw it?

It therefore seems to me that in this passage he used “to look upon” in the sense of “to comprehend.” For who can comprehend how God became incarnate without seed, how he came forth from a closed womb, how the Lord of glory was crucified, when only a human being dies—and all the other ineffable things that are told concerning Christ?

Hence the Apostle says that he preaches to the Gentiles “the incomprehensible riches of Christ” (Ephesians III, 8). From this it is clear that not only could no angel or human being open the book, but neither could anyone look upon it in the sense that all things were completed in the Son of God.

For although they could foresee from afar the dispensation of Christ that was to be revealed, none of them could behold it fully, as it was afterwards fulfilled.

But since we have recalled that these things were fulfilled in Christ, upon whom we know that the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of fear rested, let us likewise have no doubt that they rested in the Church, as though in one body—namely, in bridegroom and bride, in husband and wife.

We know, however, that they shone more excellently in the head than in the members. These gifts are in us through him. But are they as abundant as they appeared in the Lord? It is certainly established that we received them from him, by whose favor we freely make progress. We must explain these matters elsewhere.

For now, let us rejoice more abundantly that Christ brought the supreme good by being born and completed it by fulfilling the rest. For this reason the holy Church of God believes that he alone is sufficient for her salvation and openly proclaims to all that this is the supreme Gospel. The hope of all Christians depends upon these gifts, and love is broadened and grows, if somehow we love him who first loved us.

If Faustus the Manichaean had been able to know these things, he would never have called the Genealogy of Christ a *Genesidium*, nor denied Christ’s birth altogether.

Hence the Lord says to the Father in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew XI, 25). Again he says to the apostles: “To you it has been given to know the mystery, but to the others in parables” (Luke VIII, 10).

If knowledge of this had been granted to that man, would he ever, so drunk, have spewed out such things? The wretched man did not know that the revelation of the Gospel was granted not to Manichaeus but to Jesus Christ, whom God gave the task of making it known—not to philosophers, nor to those devoted to human wisdom, nor to Jews who glory in the law, nor to those occupied with varied errors of doctrine, nor to those who belonged to the race of darkness, but to his servants and to those subject to divine grace.

To these the heavenly revelation of the Gospel is more clearly disclosed—so that, seeing, they may not see, and understanding, they may not understand, while those who were humble may be rescued from darkness.

Let what has been said suffice for this purpose: that the Genealogy of Christ is truly the beginning of the Gospel.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0043]

[Col. 0043B] CHAPTER I. “The book,” says Matthew, “of the generation of Jesus [Col. 0043C] Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.”

We believe that he did not begin with such a prologue without good reason. Perhaps he knew that this Faustus would arise, one who would not accept the Old Testament; and therefore he used such an opening so that it might immediately strike back at and condemn him.

For the book of the beginning of the Old Testament is ultimately called Genesis from the beginning of the volume, because in it we read, according to our interpretation: “This is the book of the generation of Adam” (Genesis V, 1), and: “These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created” (Genesis II, 4). From this it is clear that, in whatever manner, because the generation of heaven and earth is written there at the beginning, it is called Genesis from that fact.

Therefore it was entirely fitting that the beginning of the New Testament should, as far as possible, be prefigured in a similar manner, so that by proclaiming this in such a way the Evangelist might show that the same God is the author of both the New and the Old Testament.

This is especially so because Matthew wrote in Hebrew for those who had believed from among the Hebrews, so that they might recognize more clearly what they had already received from the law and might prove that the Gospel of Christ truly has its testimony from the law and the prophets, as will subsequently be demonstrated in many passages.

There is no doubt that he wished to indicate this also: that both pages designate one and the same God, through whom all things were created and redeemed. Otherwise, although it is the custom of the Hebrews to give books their names from their beginnings, it seems exceedingly appropriate that the beginning of both Testaments should be called by one name.

It should also be noted that, just as the former is presented according to the letter to carnal Israel, so the latter is more abundantly assigned in Christ to spiritual Israel. For among the Greeks, both books are prefaced by the title “Book of Genesis” (*Biblos Geneseos* [βίβλος γενέσεως]).

Here too, however, the generation of heaven and earth can appropriately be understood, because, since Christ is God and man, both natures are truly contained in him.

Therefore the title is suitably inscribed under the two names “Jesus Christ,” so that through the royal and priestly person the nature of God and of man may at once be designated, as it were, upon the forehead.

The name Jesus had already preceded under the figure of another person. But what was called typologically in that earlier figure is here finally designated substantially.

“Christ,” moreover, is the name of an office, not of a nature, because he was anointed above his companions for the priesthood, to make expiation for us.

In the Old Testament also, because these two functions could not be fulfilled in one and the same person, there came the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus; and he became for us both kingdom and priesthood, so that he might lead his children into the land long and greatly promised to the fathers.

Thus, according to the proper meaning of the name Jesus, he is God powerful to save believers; but according to the dignity of his office, Christ daily intercedes for us.

The wording of the text should also be noted at this point. According to the customary manner of human speech, it appears to be lacking something. The fuller sense would be expressed if the particles of two clauses—namely, the pronoun and the verb—were supplied, so that it would read: “This is the book of the generation.”

But it is a very frequent practice of the divine Scriptures not to place these previously mentioned parts of speech before the beginnings of books. Thus Mark does not say, “This is the beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, Son of God,” but only: “The beginning of the Gospel.”

Isaiah followed this practice, not adding, “This is the vision of Isaiah,” but simply beginning: “The vision of Isaiah.” Solomon used it in two of his books; Jeremiah likewise; and so did those who prefixed titles to the Psalms. John also begins his Apocalypse in this way: “The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ,” without adding, “This is.”

By doing this, they taught that such sentences can have an implied meaning not only according to the idiom of the divine writings but also according to secular custom, in their concern for brevity.

For example, when we read “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ,” we should supply more fully: “This is the book of the generation of Jesus Christ.”

But why is “book of the generation” marked by the singular number, when forty generations are recited in sequence? No one can doubt that the generation of Jesus Christ alone is being sought; the others are brought forward in order to make this one known.

And not only at the beginning, but all the way to the end of the book, the whole work concerns this one generation, so that the one who was born for us may be understood as God and man.

It may also be asked—and it appears to be a very profound question—why Matthew publicly said, “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ,” when Isaiah cries out and says: “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isaiah LIII, 8).

If “who” there is understood as referring to impossibility, how did this man here judge that it was possible for him to recount his generation? Unless we think that there it was spoken of the generation according to Divinity, while here it concerns the generation that he assumed for us according to humanity, although this too is believed to be in large part beyond description.

Nevertheless, the generation by which he was begotten from eternity is proved to be wholly ineffable and incomprehensible.

Unless the statement of John presents an objection: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). Therefore, when he says, “In the beginning was the Word,” he has recounted something; and when he adds what this Word was, and that he was with God the Father, he has now said not merely something about him but many things.

Thus it is not unfittingly asked how something can rightly be called ineffable if it can be spoken, or, if it cannot be spoken, how—as we affirm—anything can be recounted about it.

The holy Church of God, gathering its teaching from the authority of all the divine Scriptures, likewise confesses many things catholicly concerning this divine birth.

Perhaps, then, when it was said, “Who shall recount his generation?” this did not indicate impossibility but the rarity of recounting it, as is also read in other passages of Scripture.

For example, in the Psalm you have: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle? Or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” (Psalm XIV, 1). It does not say that no one will dwell there, or that no one will rest there, but that the inhabitant will be rare and none other than the elect.

And, so that you may know this to be true, it immediately defines what kind of inhabitant that place must have.

In another Psalm: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who shall stand in his holy place?” (Psalm XXIII, 3). The sense is: not just anyone from the common crowd or populace, but one of outstanding life and singular merit.

Whenever “who” is used in the divine writings, it sometimes signifies not “no one” but “someone.” At other times it indicates impossibility, as in: “Who has ever heard of such a thing, or who has seen anything like this?” And perhaps this is the sense in the present passage.

Elsewhere: “In the underworld, who will confess to you?” (Psalm VI, 5).

But when it says: “Who is wise and understands these things?” (Hosea XIV, 10), and: “Who is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord will set over his household?” (Luke XII, 42), and also: “But if a human being sins against God, who will pray for him?” (I Kings II, 25), in these passages a suitable intercessor, or certainly a wise person, is sought. No one is excluded; someone is being sought.

If “who” in the present passage referred to rarity, the question would in some way appear to be resolved. But since here “who” indicates impossibility, as I more truly think, we must acknowledge that it can genuinely be said that the Son of God was begotten from the eternal Father, yet in such a way that the Father is never understood to have existed without him.

Everything that the catholic faith confesses concerning the Son of God can indeed be spoken. But how this occurred, or in what manner the eternal Son was begotten, is surely the mystery of a sacred birth. No apostle learned it, no prophet discovered it, no angel knew it, and no creature understood it.

Therefore consider whether, if the prophet could not recount his birth, anyone can rightly claim to know how the Son could be begotten by the Father.

We therefore speak about him and confess most truly that the Son is coeternal with the Father, but how this is so we utterly do not know.

Hence the statement in the Book of Job: “Where will you find the wisdom of God the Father? For it is hidden from the eyes of human beings and concealed from the birds of heaven” (Job XXVIII, 20)—that is, even from the angels.

And elsewhere: “To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed?” (Ecclesiasticus I, 6). This refers to the origin of the Son of God, because it lies even beyond the understanding and knowledge of the angels.

Thus his generation according to Divinity is proved to be altogether ineffable. Let us therefore, with the Lord’s favor, come to that generation which is according to the flesh, although it too is partly beyond description.

Sons of David, son of Abraham.

It is not believed to have happened without reason that, from the entire lineage of the Old Testament, he placed only these two fathers, whose son Christ is said to be according to the flesh alone. From this it is indeed clear that, since he was writing for those who knew from the Law that Christ had been promised, he wished to disclose more brightly than daylight that he was the one who had long before been promised to those same people. For to these two alone, among all the others, the promise is read as having been made in the Old Testament, so that those who knew that the Savior was to come from their offspring might receive him more readily when they saw all the prophecies of the Law and the Prophets fulfilled in him with one harmonious voice.

For God himself swore to Abraham, when he offered his Son, saying: “By myself I have sworn, because you have done this thing and have not spared your son, I will bless you and multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore. And your offspring shall possess the gates of their enemies; and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your offspring, because you obeyed my voice” (Gen. XXII, 16).

The apostle Paul expounds this passage as follows: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. He does not say, ‘and to offspring,’” he says, “as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: ‘and to your offspring,’ which is Christ” (Gal. V, 16). In this offspring, namely in Christ, all the nations will be blessed, so that Abraham himself, through the alteration of his name—from “Exalted Father”—might become “father of many nations.” This is not because the interpretation of the name contains all of this; rather, because the Holy Spirit, through Moses, wished the addition concerning the nations to be understood implicitly.

He became father of many nations through no other than Christ, concerning whom David sings in accordance with the promise of this passage: “And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all the nations shall magnify him” (Ps. LXXI, 18). You see with what harmonious voice the Holy Spirit, again through the Prophet, promises the blessing of all in Christ, whom he had earlier called Abraham’s offspring.

Therefore the present Evangelist proves in every way that he is Abraham’s son, so that not only the Jews, to whom the promise belonged, but also all the nations, or all the tribes of the earth, might joyfully receive him as having already come from his offspring, through whom Abraham would also become father of many nations.

But since there were two promises concerning his offspring—one, evidently, concerning the flesh, and the other concerning the spirit—it was first said: “Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth.” Then, although those who are promised in the second promise are also raised from the dust, they are nevertheless promised to be like the stars of heaven—not by nature, but by grace. Yet this final blessing embraces both kinds of blessing, since those born anew in Christ are found to be Abraham’s sons in a certain sense both fleshly and spiritual: some are counted among the offspring in name only, others according to the grace of election.

For we read that this same promise concerning the offspring—that all the nations would be blessed in it—was repeated much later through the prophet Isaiah, so that it might become clearer that it should be understood neither of Isaac, who was already dead, nor of anyone other than Christ. For through that same Isaiah God says: “I will bring forth offspring from Jacob,” he says, “and from Judah one who shall possess my holy mountains” (Isa. LXV, 8). We plainly know that both of these, from whom the one here promised to come would arise, belonged to Abraham’s stock.

Therefore let the fellowship pleasing to God confidently preserve the holy community, the true beehive of monks, just as in the catholic faith we have been nourished not only with milk but also with solid food. For although it is said, “Seek the Lord; seek his face always” (Ps. CIV, 4), one must not seek another from God, since he is one; rather, one must ardently investigate the one and the same God, since he is infinite.

Hence let our faith hold fast to him, so that, if the Son of Man should come, he may at least find faith upon the earth. Meanwhile, if Zachariah is sought as a witness—and he is certainly proved righteous from the Gospel—because the Jews contradict the Gospel, we clearly gather that this is the offspring of Abraham of whom he says: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished the redemption of his people; as he spoke,” he says, “through the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been from the beginning” (Luke I, 68).

Then, so that this may be understood, he adds: “The oath which he swore to Abraham our father, that he would grant us” (Luke I, 54). Likewise the blessed Virgin Mary sings: “Remembering his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers,” namely to Abraham “and to his offspring, forever.”

We therefore rightly believe that the Son of this man is Christ, concerning whom the words of the holy Scriptures also resound in very many places. We ought not, therefore, admit any further doubt concerning him; rather, let us see according to the holy Scriptures how he was promised as being from David’s offspring.

“The Lord swore truth to David,” the Holy Spirit says, “and he will not disappoint him” (Ps. CXXXI, 1). What, then, did he swear? He swore to him: “I will place upon my throne one from the fruit of your womb.”

For this reason the blessed apostle Paul says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “The end of every dispute is an oath” (Heb. VI, 16). And because human beings swear by those greater than themselves, whereas God, having no one greater than himself by whom he could swear, swore by himself, saying, “By myself I have sworn” (Gen. XXII, 16), as I showed above, we prove that it was said again to David: “The Lord swore truth to David.”

Therefore, whoever hears God’s oath, even if he is an unbeliever, ought to be softened, so that by faith he may recognize Christ as born from these offspring. Hence we read in another psalm: “Once I have sworn by my holiness” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 35). And what is “by my holiness” except by his only Son, equal and beloved to him, who alone is called Holy and Truth?

What he swore is immediately added: “If I lie to David”—or, instead of “I lie,” “I shall not lie”—“his offspring shall remain forever. And his throne shall be like the sun in my sight; and like the perfect moon forever, and like a faithful witness in heaven.”

Therefore, those who wish to understand this as having been said of Solomon should consider how his throne could have been like the sun in the sight of the Father, when holy Scripture says that his heart was turned aside because of the desires of women, and that he worshiped Astarte and Chemosh, the god of the Sidonians, along with the other monstrosities of the nations (III Kings XI). In the end it adds that God was not with Solomon.

If, then, God was not with Solomon, how did his throne shine like the sun in the sight of God the Father? Especially since Solomon is also said to have been defiled by every impurity of lust and condemned because of idolatry. Or how could he be like the perfect moon forever, when he suddenly fell like a criminal into ruin? Indeed, even if he had been perfect—which is in no way proved—how could he have been a faithful witness in heaven, when he had never penetrated the heavens? Or how could he be a faithful witness in heaven who, while on earth, was found to be a false witness by venerating idols?

“For they become like them,” Scripture says, “those who make them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. CXIII, 8). Since this cannot in any way be understood of Solomon, it is necessary—whether the enemy wishes it or not—to interpret it concerning Christ, so that he may be the offspring of David whose throne continually shines in the sight of God the Father.

Hence, on the mountain, when he was transfigured before his disciples, his face shone like the sun when it radiates in its strength. The Prophet also says concerning him: “For you who fear God, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. IV, 2).

Holy Scripture declares in many places that this throne is the Church, in which God presides like a king upon his throne. Since Christ is its head, the Church is said to shine like the sun in the sight of the Father and to remain like the perfect moon forever. It is called “moon” because of the decline belonging to the present life; “perfect,” however, because it already clings to its head, from whom it is proclaimed immortal and eternal in every respect.

It should also be noted that this throne of the promised offspring consists as one with its head and with the members of its entire body. Thus our head is understood to be united to the body because of the sharing of nature; and because he is God, he is rightly declared to preside divinely in his throne, that is, in his Church.

Let us also set forth another testimony, which announces that the same one was to come from David’s offspring. “And it happened,” it says in the Book of Chronicles, “that the word of the Lord came to Nathan the prophet, saying: Go and say to my servant David: Thus says the Lord. I announce to you that the Lord will build a house for you. And when your days are fulfilled, so that you go to your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall be from your sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He himself shall build me a house, and I will establish his throne forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son; and I will not take my mercy away from him, as I took it away from the one who was before you. I will establish him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne shall be most firmly established forever” (I Chron. XVII).

Whoever thinks that all these things were fulfilled in Solomon seems greatly to err. For how should we understand what was said: “After you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall be from your sons, and I will establish his kingdom”? Should we believe that this was prophesied concerning that Solomon? Certainly not. He began to reign while his father was still alive. Here, however, it is said: “When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring.”

From this it is truly understood that another was promised, who was to be raised up not before David’s death but after his death. Concerning him Jeremiah says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch; and a king shall reign, and he shall be wise, and he shall execute judgment and righteousness upon the earth. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely; and this is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our righteous one” (Jer. XXIII, 5).

Does Jeremiah, who is proved to have lived long after Solomon, promise something concerning him again when he says, “I will raise up for David a righteous branch”? It is more plainly understood as referring to Christ, who is called not only the wise King but also the Wisdom of the Father. Truly, in whose days the true Judah was saved—namely, the one who confesses that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.

All the rest, as John testifies, are not Jews—though they themselves falsely claim to be—but are synagogues of Satan.

By such indications and by others of the same kind from the Scriptures, we hold it certain that Matthew placed these two men alone, whose son Christ is, for this reason: so that those who wished to enter the temple—that is, the Church—through the door might look upon these two columns, set before them on either side, from whose midst Christ had sprung forth.

For he himself speaks concerning himself: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John X, 9). They were placed before the temple doors like columns, because each of them still dwelt in the Law, as in the vestibule of a house.

“And the columns,” Scripture says, “were eighteen cubits high” (III Kings VII, 15), towering above the summit of the New and Old Testament, so that, strengthening both peoples in faith according to the strength of columns, they might show that the door was none other than this Jesus Christ, propagated from their offspring, and that he would be the entrance into the temple, as the one who dwelt intimately between them.

For this reason, in the name of Jesus according to the Greeks, [ΙΗΣΟΥΣ,] the first letter that is written signifies ten, while the second signifies eight.
