Thus, from both offspring, according to the promises of the Scriptures, one is raised up as a standard; and in his name both peoples, united, may strive upward toward heavenly things according to the measure of the fullness of Christ and the firmness of faith.

This is why a cord twelve cubits long surrounds both of them: that is, the faith of the apostles embraces only those fathers in the genealogy from whose midst it proclaims that the door, Jesus Christ, is opened daily to believers, while to unbelievers it wished the entrance into the heavenly homeland to be entirely denied.

But since we wished to strengthen these points with certain testimonies from the holy Scriptures, we have advanced very far. Let us now at last return gradually to the order of the exposition. Here, too, many people sometimes ask, not unreasonably, why David is placed first, although he is found to be much later in age.

The answer is that the necessity of speech demanded this, and the order was reversed—appropriately altered, to be sure. For if he had first called him Abraham’s son and then added David, Abraham would have had to be mentioned again in order to show that David’s origin was from his offspring, and the construction of the words would have become inelegant, at least with respect to eloquence.

“Abraham,” he says, “begot Isaac.”

Thus the genealogy of Christ is rightly reckoned from the beginning of faith, so that the one in whom the promise concerning him is first read as having been made might also become the beginning of the succession, until it reached the one who at that time had been divinely promised from heaven.

For who could more suitably be placed at the beginning of Christ’s genealogy than the one from whose offspring the blessing of all the nations is propagated? We believe this was done so that all the nations, no less than the Jews, might hasten to him whose origin is declared with a clarity brighter than daylight by the oracles of the divine Scriptures.

Thus, in the first father, they might learn what sort of people those must be who wish to receive the blessing of the inheritance in the offspring. For, as the same Lord testifies to the Jews, “if you were Abraham’s children, you would truly do the works of Abraham yourselves” (John VIII, 39), and you would imitate such a great father so that you would not be degenerate.

For Abraham first believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Gen. XV, 6). Then he went farther, advancing and growing, as Scripture relates, and reached Bethel; and he proceeded toward the south (Gen. XII, 8–9), where the bridegroom lies in the Song of Songs (Song I, 6) and feeds among the lilies (Song VI, 2).

After these distinguished acts of virtue, he was tested and found faithful and righteous. Against hope, he believed in hope, and, perfected in every obedience, he is proclaimed by the divine voice as the future father of all nations.

From him, therefore, the cord of the genealogy is rightly woven, so that at its summit the hook, covered with flesh, might be more obscurely fastened for catching the sea-monster of the world—that is, the devil—and piercing his jaw.

From this comes what follows:

> Isaac begot Jacob, and Jacob begot Judah and his brothers.

Moreover, where Matthew says here *begot*, Luke, who says “was,” uses that expression throughout the entire sequence of succession. For Matthew counts only sons according to nature, whereas Luke introduces sons in certain places according to the Law or through adoption.

It should also be noted that Matthew said *begot* and not *generated*. Perhaps this was so that you might recognize the one who was shown at the end, concerning whom the Father said: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II, 7). This word, as though proper and most familiar to him, is therefore placed everywhere concerning him.

Why, then, did he say, “Jacob begot Judah and his brothers”? This is not unreasonably asked. Yet since Abraham begot several sons, and Isaac had Jacob as a brother, why is it that the Evangelist omits all these and mentions only Judah’s brothers?

The answer is that the former, as though alien to the people of God, are deservedly rejected, as Scripture testifies; these latter, however, as heirs, are collectively inscribed in the book of life. And because they are, as it were, the patriarchs of the twelve tribes and were not excluded from the people of God, they do not deserve to be excluded from the generation of Christ either.

This is especially so since the number and pattern of the apostles are signified in them; in their fellowship all the tribes of the earth, united through faith, are divinely consecrated. But they are not expressly named, lest the genealogy be multiplied beyond the predetermined number of the mystical sacrament.

Nor is it without a great and profound mystery that, with three brothers omitted—namely Reuben, Simeon the firstborn, and Levi, the elder brothers—the Holy Spirit chose Judah alone, through whom he would weave the sequence of the birth down to Christ.

Since he is chosen as the fourth, the fourfold number of the Gospel is thereby consecrated. Moreover, what is greater, he alone among all twelve patriarchs is expressly named, so that you might recognize more clearly, without any scruple of mind, the one who had once been promised by the Holy Spirit as arising from his stock.

For Jacob says thus: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. XLIX, 10). To make it clearer who this one would be, he significantly adds: “And he himself,” he says, “shall be the expectation of the nations.”

In view of this, let false Jews see whom they are to receive: the long-desired expectation of the nations embraces, adores, venerates, and worships him. Hence it is plainly established that the whole multitude of the nations, from east to west, has already received in faith, by awaiting him, the one who was to be sent; by receiving him, it confesses and worships him; and by worshiping him, it is daily escorted toward the heavenly homeland.

Thus the whole Church still struggles tirelessly on earth, because those who have confessed him depart from here through death and reign with Christ. Their teaching flourishes, their miracles flash forth, and their virtues are proclaimed everywhere.

But since we have mentioned Judah in this chapter, I think it necessary for the moment to treat the matter at greater length, because of the hardness or blindness of heart of certain people who think that all this must be interpreted concerning Judah in such a way that nothing in it ought to pertain to Christ.

We, however, understanding it correctly, say that some of these things, although they can be fitted to Judah, can nevertheless also suit Christ according to their mystical meanings. Nor do we altogether deny that certain passages pertain to Judah alone; just as we say that some things which we see surpass him pertain to Christ alone.

For when it says, “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins,” we are compelled to understand this concerning Judah, or concerning the tribe itself which was eventually called Judah. But what follows—“until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations”—we know to pertain to Christ alone.

For we do not understand that Judah as Christ, from whose offspring a ruler did not wholly fail until Christ came in the flesh. Rather, we understand the one who had been promised and who, immediately upon arriving, was received by the nations.

A ruler and leader from his loins remained in Judah until that time; thereafter Herod, a foreigner, assumed the kingdom, as we shall later show through many indications from the Scriptures. This was above all an indication that the one had arrived to whom the kingdom had been reserved [“kingdom” is understood]; or, as we read in our translation, that he had come who was to be sent by the Father, since the nations immediately received him.

Meanwhile, the statement addressed to Judah, “Your brothers shall praise you,” can in any historical sense be referred to that Judah, so that his hands may be upon the necks of his enemies in battle. But it is better understood in Christ, whom all who are born anew publicly praise and confess as their brother in the Church.

His hands, therefore, triumph over the necks of his enemies, so that afterward the children of the Father, made such by adoption and formerly his enemies, may adore him.

It follows:

> You have gone up to the prey, my son;

or, as another interpretation has it:

> You have gone up from the germ, reclining you have slept; and like a lion’s cub, who shall rouse him?

In these verses the Jews are not merely refuted; they are utterly excluded. Therefore it must not be admitted that this can in any way be understood of Judah, since we plainly recognize it as spoken of Christ.

For if we take the lion’s cub to be Judah because of his strength in warfare, how is he said to have gone up as a son from the germ? Here *germ* is translated from the Greek, more properly “shoot” or “branch,” as some assert. Judah is said to have arisen from this shoot. But since this does not fit him, a mystical exposition is much more appropriately applied to the passage.

Christ therefore ascended from the germ when he was born from the Virgin without seed. “From the germ,” he says, that is, without the intercourse of a man and without seed, like a shoot being born. Or, as a flower from its root, that is, from the Virgin, the Truth of the flesh is proved to have arisen.

But if it is to be read in this way:

> You have gone up to the prey, my son,

it can be referred both to Judah and to Christ. But that he slept reclining like a lion, or like a lion’s cub, suits no one other than Christ, so that what natural philosophers relate about a lion’s cub may be mystically proclaimed in Christ.

For they say that, when it is born, it sleeps for three days and nights; then it is roused by the roar of its father. In the same way Christ, buried in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, completed the sleep of death and, like a cub, was raised on the third day and rose again.

Hence John says in his Apocalypse: “Behold, the Lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. V, 5). He conquered when he reclined, because by dying he then shattered death.

For all the prey that the opposing lion had seized after humanity had been cast down and defeated, this Lion of ours restored; and by rising again he reformed everything for the better, leading our captivity captive by his power.

In this way the conquering lion was indeed triumphant; and, raised more swiftly on the third day, he showed himself to have been the lion’s cub.

Hence what follows: “And who shall rouse him?” The Prophet, truly contemplating the person of God and of man and wondering that Christ had reclined in death, says: “And who shall rouse him?” It is as though he were saying: “I behold the Son of God the Father, who, when the Word deigned to become flesh, has in a certain way—the Immortal—reclined through death. Who will raise him? Himself? Or God the Father? Or, what is most true, both he himself and God the Father raised him.”

Hence the Apostle cries out and says: “God raised him from the dead.” And, “He who raised Christ from the dead,” he says, “will also raise your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in us” (Rom. VIII, 11).

That he himself also raised it, he says in the Gospel of John: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II, 19). To this the Evangelist adds: “But he was speaking of the temple of his body.”

Since the Prophet saw these things from afar, he rightly says, struck with astonishment at the great unity of the Father and the Son: “And who shall rouse him?”

It follows, as we already stated a little earlier:

> A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent.

Here he plainly declares that one is the person from whom rulers were to come, and another is the one who, as unique and special, was to be sent, whom he announces that the nations had awaited.

But how the blessings mentioned above suit Christ, when up to this point the Father’s speech seems directed solely to Judah and, through Judah, blesses the entire tribe, appears obscure. From this point onward, however, no one doubts that, as though contemplating what he would be like, he plainly demonstrates him by the spirit of prophecy.

Since Christ was still in Judah’s loins—to whom, as many manuscripts have it, the kingdom had been reserved— he directs to him, as to the root or grain of the seed, the blessing promised to the Jews and the nations, and in him exalts the one who was to germinate like fruit from a root.

This is why the obscurity of the blessing is so great that, unless it is examined carefully, it can scarcely be discerned what suits Judah and what suits Christ alone. For that seed of Abraham, already promised in the past, was still in him, and in that seed the blessing of all the nations had been promised. Therefore he says here that he himself is the expectation of the nations.

He was awaited as one who had been promised; he is received as soon as he arrives, as one whose promise has been fulfilled.

His eyes were more beautiful than wine—that is, the apostles and all holy preachers—because they intoxicated the minds of believers with the new wine of the Holy Spirit. And his teeth were whiter than milk, through which he drew all the nations, like the flesh of animals, into his own body, so that, united in him—that is, transferred into the body of Christ—all the nations might be blessed in one offspring.

Hence we read elsewhere: “You are the offspring whom the Lord has blessed” (Isa. LXI, 9). It says *offspring*, not *offsprings*, because we have all become one offspring in Christ.

One grain of wheat, therefore, falling into the earth, was dead alone, but produced many crops from itself. And so whoever wishes to enter the Lord’s granary should see whether he himself has come forth from this root.

It follows:

> “Binding,” he says, “his she-ass to the vine, and his colt to the vine.”

Here the colt signifies the Gentile people, whom he bound to the vine, concerning which he says: “I am the true vine, and you are the branches” (John XV, 5). What is said here to have been bound by him is elsewhere shown to have been grafted in, so that, as a branch remains in the vine, this little ass, united to the body of Christ, might display the perfect vine—namely, the holy Church of God, without spot or wrinkle—composed of all its members who see themselves in it.

For no bond is greater than the bond of unity. Unity does not admit division or endure being cut apart; yet the unity of the body is often broken up through its own parts in such a way that what is one is brought about.

Therefore the wildness of the Gentiles is said to have been grafted into Christ’s body, as though tied to the vine, since it has been united to him by the bonds of faith through grace.

“And to the vine his she-ass.” He is said to have bound his she-ass to the vine when he joined the synagogue to the Church by the bonds of faith. For Christ advanced the synagogue into the Church; he did not again change the Church into the synagogue.

But since we have extended the blessing at such length, so that we might know that he was not without reason placed here in the genealogy by name—or rather, so that the mind might immediately return through him to the prophecy of so great a prophet and believe that the one whom the nations received in their expectation had already come; and so that, since a leader from Judah had failed and no ruler from his loins was found, the hardness of heart might at least be softened by these assembled testimonies and all might receive with holy joy the one whom they had long known the prophets to have foretold as certainly destined to come at that time—let us now gradually proceed to another mystery of the narrative and open somewhat more clearly the sacrament of faith hidden there.

Judas begot Perez and Zerah by Tamar. Behold, here two twin brothers are called by name in Christ’s genealogy, and they are said to have been born from Tamar. Is it without significance that the Evangelist passes over Esau, likewise a twin, and does not name Rebekah, his lawful wife, or the other legitimate women? I would by no means say so: surely so great an Evangelist—or rather, the Holy Spirit through him—did not introduce four female figures into this sequence of the narrative without a great and profound mystery, women who are judged blameworthy according to the Old Testament no less than according to the New.

Tamar, although she is called more righteous than Judah, is nevertheless not excluded from guilt (Gen. XXXVIII). Indeed, Judah is found to be the more culpable through his lack of self-control, as Scripture testifies, since sons were begotten by every means from an illicit intercourse. From this deed a certain kind of parable is introduced, through which the mystical mysteries of prophecy are woven not only here but in very many passages of Scripture. For the Apostle teaches that all the events of that time, which took place among that same people, were prophecy of things to come, saying: “All these things happened to them as a figure” (I Cor. X, 11). And elsewhere: “In many and various ways God spoke of old to the fathers in the prophets” (Heb. I, 1).

When he says that God spoke in the prophets “in many ways,” he shows that they prophesied in words. When he says “in various ways,” he indicates that through events they foreshadowed the future mysteries of God. Among these ways, we now have in our hands one through which God spoke to us in the patriarch, and, as we said, when it is examined, many obscurities of the divine writings are truly disclosed through it.

This method sometimes occurs in parables of events; and even from the sins of human beings and the transgressions of adulterers it intimates a prophecy of future deeds. Such is the public sin of King David, which will shortly be discussed in its proper place; and likewise what is said of Lot, and the deed of Hosea, and many other things in many passages, filled with divine mysteries. Although, according to the truth of the events, these things are proved to be utterly abominable and are condemned by divine authority as criminal, nevertheless divine power, in whatever manner, either prepared through them the effect of the dispensation of the incarnate Word or foresaw some other future deed. On the outside, sins appeared; within, mysteries were also hidden.

But since we have begun to speak of Tamar, let us briefly investigate why the Evangelist placed her here, what he intended to recall through this illicit union, and what mystical reality he signified by it. For the lives of those men were prophetic not only in their speech but also in their conduct; and not merely the lives of certain individuals among them, but that entire kingdom of the Hebrew people was not only, as I have said, a prophecy, but also a kind of great prophet, because by its events and deeds it fulfilled many prophecies concerning Christ and the Church.

To make what is said evident from this passage, let us at last come to the history itself, in which Judah is said to have begotten three sons. The first was called Er, that is, “leathern”; the second was named Onan, which is interpreted as “their sorrow”; and the third, Shelah, was called “dismissal.” From this we understand Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, as the people of the kingdom of the Jews, to whom kings from the tribe of Judah were given as husbands. Her name is therefore interpreted as “bitterness,” because she gave the Lord a cup of gall to drink.

In these two sons of Judah, whom she is read to have received as husbands, two kinds of rulers who did not act rightly among the people are understood: one kind consisting of those who did great harm, the other of those who did no good. One of them is said to have been evil before the Lord; the other spilled his seed upon the ground so that it would not produce fruit. These are two exceedingly useless kinds: one consisting of those who do harm, the other of those unwilling to provide benefit.

One is called “leathern,” like the tunics with which the first human beings were clothed after, as punishment for their condemnation, they were expelled from paradise. The other is called “their sorrow”—whose sorrow, unless it is that of those to whom nothing is of benefit, although they possess the means to be beneficial, and who cast that very means upon the ground? God is nevertheless said to have killed both, by which is signified that he took the kingdom away from such men.

The third son of Judah, because he is not joined to that woman, signifies the time from which the kings of the Jewish people began no longer to come from the tribe of Judah. He was indeed Judah’s son, but Tamar did not receive him as a husband: he belonged to the same tribe of Judah, but from that point no one ruled the people. Hence Shelah is also interpreted as “his dismissal.” Whose dismissal, unless Tamar’s? For, as we have said, Tamar signifies the tribe of Judah, from which tribe kings had already ceased to exist at the time when Christ came.

Therefore, because at that time the kingdom had departed from the tribe of Judah, Christ was about to come—one who would not do harm but would do great good. For it had been foretold:

> “The prince shall not fail from Judah,  
> nor the ruler from his loins,  
> until he comes to whom it has been promised.”

For Herod, who at that time appeared to reign in Judaea, seemed to have been Tamar’s husband; but he was a foreigner and was not joined to her by the covenant of mystical anointing as by a marital bond. Rather, he ruled as an outsider, having received that power from the Romans some time before.

Since he was not from the tribe of Judah and was not proved to have come from his loins, it remains that he must receive the one for whom it had been reserved. Herod was so little counted as king in that mystical kingdom that the Jews publicly cried: “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX, 15), although they said this also in flattery, since Caesar was not properly the king of the Jews, but they spoke thus in order to deny Christ.

Moreover, Herod, who had seized power through ambition for the kingdom, did not belong to them, because ruler and prince had failed from the seed of Judah, since the one who was to be sent had arrived, the one whom the nations and peoples were awaiting.

But the Jews most shamelessly say, lying that this time has not yet been fulfilled, that some king, as though from the loins of Judah, still holds a kingdom in the farthest regions of the East. In their misery, blinded by their dissimulation, they do not notice that, just as no temple, altar, or sacrifice remains for them, so no king or priest has remained for them any longer.

Nor could the prophet Hosea have lied when he said:

> “The children of Israel shall sit without king, without prince, without sacrifice, without altar, and without priesthood. Therefore, without any manifestations”  
> (Hos. III, 4).

All these things, whether the Jews wish it or not, we ourselves see fulfilled among them. They therefore have no room left for lying that they now possess a king from the tribe of Judah somewhere in the world. For just as the prophet promised, “The children of Israel shall sit without altar and without sacrifice,” so he declared that they would be without king and without prince.

Let them therefore show us the temple and the sacrifice, or the altar; then we shall in some fashion be able to believe them when they say that perhaps they have a king. Otherwise, through the obstinacy of their minds, they draw over themselves the darkness of blindness. Especially since, if a king from the tribe of Judah now existed, as they themselves pretend, they cannot deny that the ruler had already failed when Herod, a foreigner, and after him his sons, the tetrarchs, had reigned over Judea.

Not only the Gospel but also all the histories of the Gentiles, and Josephus himself, a historian of that people, publicly testify that Herod, a foreigner, reigned in Judaea, and that at that time no prince from Judah was in power.

But Jacob clearly said: “He shall not fail until he comes to whom it has been promised.” And because it was then proved that the ruler had failed, and that everything had been completed as stated above—even if, as they say, someone from their people is now found somewhere holding a kingdom, which is not at all proved—it is plainly evident that the ruler failed from Judah so that, as Daniel says, “the Holy of holies might be anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions” (Dan. IX, 24).

To demonstrate that he has already come, we introduced Tamar. I do not think it irrelevant to continue with Judah’s deed, so that from it the reason why he was placed in Christ’s genealogy may be more clearly revealed.

We read that he went to shear his sheep at Timnah (Gen. XXXVIII, 13), which is interpreted as “failing.” For by then the ruler had already failed from Judah, and all the anointing of the Jews had ceased; and the one who had been promised had at last come to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

He came with his shepherd, the Adullamite, whose name is interpreted as “having testimony in water.” The Lord plainly came with this testimony, possessing testimony greater than John’s, yet, because of the weak sheep, he used this testimony in water.

The shepherd’s own name was Iras, which, according to its interpretation, means “the vision of my brother.” He certainly saw his brother John, whether according to descent from Abraham or according to the kinship of Mary his mother and Elizabeth. He saw him, and therefore no one born of women arose greater than he.

The Lord came to shear the sheep—that is, to relieve sinners of their burdens. Concerning them it is said to the Church in the Song of Songs:

> “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep  
> that have come up from the washing”  
> (Song IV, 2).

Now let Tamar change her appearance—she is also interpreted as “she who changes”—but let the name of bitterness remain in her, not the bitterness by which she gave the Lord gall to drink, but that by which Peter wept bitterly.

Judas is also called “confession” in Latin. Let bitterness, then, be joined to confession, so that true repentance may be signified. Through this repentance the Church is made fruitful among all the nations. For Christ had to suffer and rise again, and repentance and the forgiveness of sins had to be preached in his name among all the nations.

Moreover, the appearance of a prostitute itself is a confession of sins. Tamar bears the type of the Church called from the nations, sitting at the crossroads of the city. There she is impregnated by one who does not recognize her, as it is written:

> “A people whom I did not know served me”  
> (Ps. XVII, 48).

She therefore first received a ring, which is called the sacrament of faith; then a bracelet of virtue, by which she would be justified; and a staff, through which she is glorified more exaltedly. For “those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.”

The promised kid is sent to the prostitute through that same Adullamite—that is, through the rebuke of sin—for John says: “Brood of vipers” (Matt. III, 7). But the reproach of sin did not find her, for the bitterness of confession had happily changed her.

Now let us produce the ring, the bracelet, and the staff as witnesses, and convict the Jews who judge rashly, saying that we have received Christ. When the proofs from the events of Scripture have been brought forth, perhaps they will judge that we, rather than they, have been justified.

If we consider this carefully, those people intended one thing when they did it, while God intended another, permitting it to happen in this way so that, through God’s providence, it might also signify something that would come to pass. Therefore, when that deed is narrated in Holy Scripture, it is prophecy; but when it is considered in their conduct, it is blameworthy.

God, however, who always makes good use of our evils, wove a sacrament from guilt, displayed for himself a great mystery of prophecy from those very ancestors, and gave us a lesson in doctrine not only by speaking but also by choosing to be born in such a manner from those very people. His faithful, who were to come from every nation, had to learn even from the example of his flesh that the iniquities of their parents could not harm them.

Therefore the bridegroom himself, in keeping with those whom he invited—the one who was to call good and bad alike to the wedding—willed to be born no less from the good than from the wicked. Hence the lamb commanded to be sacrificed at Passover was, according to a certain interpretation, ordered to be taken from sheep and goats, as from the righteous and sinners, in order to prefigure him.

Thus he would not despise good and wicked parents because of the likeness of their humanity; rather, he would become a lamb for the righteous and a kid for sinners. In this way, through his grace, he would unite both in his body so that they might become one. It was just that the one who had come for sinners should also deign to be born from sinners.

For this reason the Evangelist Matthew counted no holy women in Christ’s genealogy, but only those whom the authority of Scripture reproves. Through these four women he wished most clearly to demonstrate that Christ’s Church would be gathered from sinners. Their likeness is compared with it in every respect.

Since we have already touched in large part on the venerable mysteries in Tamar, it remains for the discourse to proceed to investigate what follows, so that the depth of the sacrament may appear in its entirety: if in any way Christ had long before been foreshadowed through this lineage, his Church might be revealed as prefigured in these women.

Since the Church was to be united in his body, it was rightly arranged that he should also be born from those in whom the mystery of godliness was hidden, so that the species might through the sacrament pass into the genus, and through the species what was to come might already shine forth in the genus. For even then the genus was present in the species.

For this reason Scripture recalls only the histories of those women whose deed, kind, order, and number commend the whole future Church of God through mystical gifts.

Their deed does so, so that from the action of the event you might recognize the future gift of God in the image. Their kind and order do so because the first and the last of them are evidently from the stock of the Jews, while the two in the middle came from the nations. This signifies that the future Church of Christ is first gathered from the Jews through the apostles and is thereafter united from the nations, as though from two groups—those who preceded and those who followed.

The final woman who remains, “the well of fullness,” is inscribed once again as being from the Jews. For “when the fullness of the nations has come, then all Israel will be saved.”

In these women the fourfold number of the Evangelists is clearly marked: the first and the last were from the Jews, while the two who, as though from the nations, did not see the Lord in the flesh are placed in the middle like sons to be embraced. Four are chosen from among all, so that in them the four-square Church of God may be more firmly established in mercy.

Finally, let us return to Perez and Zerah and see why they were placed together in the genealogy. When Zerah put out his hand from the womb, the midwife tied it with scarlet thread, saying: “This one shall come out first” (Gen. XXXVIII, 28). But when he drew his hand back into the mother’s womb, the other came out, and the midwife said to him: “Why has the wall been divided because of you?” Hence she called his name Perez, that is, “division.”

After him his brother came out—the one who had first put his hand out from the womb, which the midwife had also tied with scarlet thread. She called his name Zerah, which in interpretation means “rising.”

Who would not see how many riddles of mysteries are disclosed here? What, then, is described in these two twins except the twofold life of peoples—one according to faith, the other according to the law?

And who else is represented in Zerah, who first put his hand out from the womb but was born later, except the people of faith, the people of grace? Zerah therefore put his hand out from the womb because the people of faith—that is, of grace—began to work the righteousness of faith and grace in the patriarchs.

This occurred in Abel and Seth, Enoch, Melchizedek, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and Job, and in others who were able to imitate their examples. These first freely brought forward in this world, through grace, the conduct of their life, which is figured by the hand.

In their hand, moreover, our own deeds also appeared in figure, as though they were the deeds of a complete body, while we were still being held in some manner in the womb of her who bore us. Hence the hand itself drew back with it into the womb the scarlet thread—the signs, namely, of Christ’s Passion, whose outpouring of blood illuminated Christian conduct.

For this reason Zerah also received his name. Zerah is called “rising,” as though indicating the people of the rising Redeemer, concerning whom the prophet Zechariah says: “The rising from on high has visited us” (Luke I, 78).

Although this people was born later, it nevertheless received primacy through the mystical voice of the midwife, who said: “This one shall come out first.” It is no wonder that the one who followed later holds primacy, since he first put out his hand to the work of grace.

Would that, when he extended his hand to this work, he had come forth perfectly born, and that, when he drew back his hand, the other had not divided the wall!

And what do we understand the wall to signify except the work of faith, the building of grace, and the mystery of the Gospel? But when Zerah drew his hand back into the womb, Perez came out and divided the wall. For when the work of faith and grace ceased among the patriarchs, then the law of Moses appeared like a certain wall and inserted itself between them, dividing, in a certain sense, the life of the patriarchs from that of Christians.

But when the Lord came, he removed the wall of the law from the middle, joined together the divided wall, and made the two into one, as Paul testifies when he says:

> “He himself is our peace, who made both one and, breaking down the middle wall of the partition, the enmity in his flesh, abolished the law of commandments in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace”  
> (Eph. II, 14).

Here it should be noted that the Apostle calls the very wall that divided the partition “enmity.” The observance of the law was like a kind of divorce between the simple life of the patriarchs and the subsequent life of Christians, until they were joined to Christ Jesus, the one cornerstone.

For this reason Christ was already then setting forth in his genealogy the mystery through which he prophetically signified the future event. This was especially so because Christ was already then present in the seed, although not yet revealed, drawing to himself through the figures of events the faith of those to come, so that when he was present the faith of believers might more readily recognize him—the one who had displayed future things through the succession of the fathers who preceded him.

Thus Matthew, wishing to designate him more clearly, reckoned Perez and Zerah together as sons of Tamar, so that, with the line of generation traced through them, he might show that Christ had long before mystically dedicated the Church to himself, and that through the prophecy of events he had foreshadowed its future in his own time.

Perez begot Hezron. Hezron begot Aram. Aram begot Amminadab. Amminadab begot Nahshon. Nahshon begot Salmon. Salmon begot Boaz by Rahab.

As we learn from the reading, this Perez entered Egypt together with his father Judah. Thereafter nothing mystical concerning these figures is related for some time, until [Nahshon], Salmon, as we read in Numbers (I, 7; II, 3), is identified as prince of the tribe of Judah when Israel went out from Egypt. No one can doubt that Christ, as the one who had been promised, entered Egypt in the seed of these men.

Therefore, as though through a foreboding, the people were already then being oppressed. Perhaps the enemy perceived that one from this same seed would come who would shatter his rights, and therefore he desired to kill not females but males alone, so that in this way he might destroy the one whom he was plotting against.

Afterward that same enemy employed this strategy through Herod as well, killing many in order to destroy Christ alone. Josephus recalls this foreboding in the second book of the history of the *Antiquities*, saying that there was in Egypt a certain scribe of the sacred rites who, since such men had experience in speaking the truth about future events, announced to the king that at that time someone would be born among the Israelites who would indeed humble the rule of Egypt, but would increase the race of the Israelites through his growth, surpass everyone in virtue, and possess glory memorable forever.

As a result of this counsel, it was decided that every male child born among the Israelites should be drowned in the waters of Egypt. But God averted that outcome; afterward the seas and rivers obeyed him wondrously when he commanded them.

Finally, it is said that, by his own divination, a priest later saw the infant Moses tear the crown from Pharaoh’s head and suspected that he was the one through whom the kingdom of Memphis would perish. And not without reason, since through Moses’ subsequent accomplishment all Egypt was overturned.

Yet another, greater than he, was being indicated: through him the whole world—of which Egypt is a figure—and the true Pharaoh, the Devil, would be drowned in the waves of the abyss.

Salmon, whom we previously wove into the end of the line, is proved, as we said, to have been a prince from the tribe of Judah at the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt. He took Rahab, whom elsewhere in the Old Testament we read to have been a prostitute called Raab.

Here she is written *Rachab* according to the Greek copies, with *CH* because of the Greek letter χ; there, according to the Hebrew, she is pronounced *Raab* without aspiration, since the Hebrews do not have the Greek χ.

Through this Rahab, once again, the sacrament of the Church is recalled to memory, so that the same promised one may always be indicated through figures and riddles. Already through the patriarchs—from whose flesh he was to come—he was most mercifully joining to himself a Church not only from the Jews but also from the nations.

For he was the true patriarch in the patriarchs, and the true prophet in the prophets. Finally, he was the Judge in the judges, just as he is often called the Angel in the angels.

Hence it is clear that Salmon already then represented the leader of true confession, and that he led out of Egypt the tribe from which he had been promised, because only true confessors follow Christ.

Finally, he joined Rahab—that is, the Church from the nations—to himself in marriage after the walls of Jericho had been overthrown (Josh. VI, 25). Nothing from that entire city is saved except the house of Rahab and everything proved to have been in it.

For outside the holy Church of God everything is struck with the ban; and if anything therefrom is preferred to God in love, it is exacted by the harsher punishment of death. For whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is certainly constituted an enemy of God.

Jericho signifies the present world, surrounded by the walls of the seven vices. It is continually encompassed through the cycle of seven days while the trumpets of God’s teachings sound, until at the last trumpet all the walls of vices fall and the last death is destroyed, since it has already been swallowed up in victory.

At times Rahab alone is saved—that is, Christ’s Church, reddened by his blood—because she alone received the messengers of the true Jesus. Therefore she is not merely numbered among the Israel of God; she is also joined to the prince from Judah, namely Christ, like a most beautiful matron who had previously been stained by vices.

Christ was not ashamed to be born from her blood, so that he who had come to seek sinners on earth might also draw his flesh from sinners, in order that, once united to his body through the sacrament of faith, they might no longer be sinners.

Matthew, understanding this sacrament well—for he too had been made an evangelist from a tax collector—invites both sinful women and notorious offenders to repentance by recalling them all.

Boaz begot Obed by Ruth. Concerning her, Isaiah prophesies in supplication, saying:

> “Send forth, O Lord, the Lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion”  
> (Isa. XVI, 1).

When the Evangelist introduces her into this lineage, he plainly testifies that the prophecy of so great a prophet was to be fulfilled, since through her the origin of Abraham’s seed is led in a direct line all the way to Christ.

Through the same woman the future Church from the nations—that is, from Moab—is also prefigured. Moab is interpreted as “from the father.” And what is “from the father” except what the Lord says: “But you are from your father the Devil” (John VIII, 44)?

Scripture plainly testifies that the whole Church, before it passed to Boaz—who is interpreted as “strong,” that is, to Christ—was from the father, the Devil.

Hence the Psalmist sings to the bride in the epithalamium:

> “Hear, O daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house”  
> (Ps. XLIV, 11).

Having therefore forgotten her father’s house—that is, the Devil’s—and passing over to Israel, she is notably called a woman of virtue. Hence Boaz addresses her, saying:

> “All who are within the gates of the city know that you are a woman of virtue”  
> (Ruth III, 11).

And not without reason. For, despising her own people and entering the people of God by the right of widowhood, she confesses to her mother-in-law:

> “Your people shall be my people, and your God my God; the land which receives you when you die, in it I shall die, and there I shall receive a place of burial”  
> (Ruth I, 16).

Are these words not most clearly those of Christ’s Church, which is gathered from the nations into the worship of the one God? Is not the one God of the Old and New Testaments expressed in this figure?

For the Church of Christ says—although not in words, yet in the effect of its works and faith—to those who first believed in Christ from the Synagogue: “Your God is my God, and your people shall be my people,” because Christ is our peace, who made the two one.

The daughter-in-law of the Synagogue is rightly understood as the Church, which deserved to be called the bride. For the fathers through whom Christ deigned to be born also came from the Synagogue. Therefore he is rightly called the son of that same Synagogue.

Thus this Boaz held the figure of Christ in this passage. He is therefore interpreted as “strong,” because he alone was powerful enough to raise up the seed of his brother, namely Moses, who departed from this life as though without children, since the law brought no one to perfection.

This is why John also confesses that he is not worthy to untie his sandal strap: he is the one to whom the bride is properly owed. Hence, standing like the friend of the bridegroom, he rejoices because of his voice, so that at least late he may come to the wedding—the one whom the entire order of the prophets had long awaited with the greatest desire.

But when he came, born at Bethlehem, he bought the field together with that same bride by right of kinship, as though Moses had in some manner removed his sandal. In that field a treasure is hidden, which believers purchase daily after selling everything.

This is, I say, the field that the Lord blessed, in which all beauty is reserved for believers. Whoever finds it rightly leaves everything behind so that he may possess it.

But since it would be too long to explain typologically all the sacramental meanings of this mystery, it is enough to have shown that the Evangelist brought Ruth forward because of the prophecy concerning her. He did so not only for that reason, but also because of the mystical figures through which, as we have said, the Church was already then being founded in Christ’s body.

To this genealogy the utterances of the prophets harmonize. To it the riddles of various events flow together from every side. To it very many obscurities of figures are referred. And all of them make clear in a direct line that he is the one through whom salvation is promised to the nations.

He is, I say, the Lamb long desired from the rock, who, often sacrificed formerly in the law, promised his coming, through which all sins would be completely forgiven.

This is indeed the rock of the desert, according to the interpretation set forth a little earlier, from which God is able to raise up children for Abraham, so that they may no longer be the rock of the desert on account of idolatry, but precious stones, which, being living stones, are rolled and held upon the earth.

See, diligent reader, how frequently the Holy Spirit turns over various and profound figures of the promises concerning this lineage of Christ. See how persistently his goodness brings forth oracles. It does not know how to remain silent or conceal the treasure until the one arrives in whom all the promises of the Father are fulfilled and every obscurity is made manifest more clearly than light. Hence it follows:

Obed, it says, begot Jesse, and Jesse begot David. I would say that it was not without reason that it says “Jesse begot David,” although he is the son of Isai. This is especially so since throughout the entire text of the Book of Kings his father is plainly read as Isai, while Jesse is found only in a few places. Hence it is clearly established that he had two names [*biganorum*; perhaps *binomium*, “a double name”].

But why is he here, as a son, inscribed rather as Jesse? It is a foreshadowing of the Holy Spirit, so that you might now receive as having come the one who, long before, with the same Holy Spirit bearing witness through the prophet Isaiah, was announced as destined to come from his seed:

> “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse,  
> and a flower shall rise from his root;  
> and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him:  
> the spirit of wisdom and understanding,  
> the spirit of counsel and strength,  
> the spirit of knowledge and godliness;  
> and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him”  
> (Isa. XI, 1).

Hence John also saw the Holy Spirit descending upon him in the form of a dove in the water and remaining there (John I, 32). For, as the Apostle says, “in him dwells all the fullness of divinity” (Col. II, 9).

He is the one who will not judge according to the sight of the eyes or according to the hearing of the ears, because a human being sees only the face, whereas God perceives all the hidden things of the heart. Therefore he is rightly understood as God, who is described as destined to come from the root of Jesse.

The root of Jesse is the virgin Mary, born from the stock of David; from her root Christ, the flower, rose. That flower speaks of himself in the Song of Songs:

> “I am the flower of the field  
> and the lily of the valleys”  
> (Song II, 1).

Isaac, smelling this flower from afar for a long time in his son, said:

> “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field which the Lord has blessed”  
> (Gen. XXVII, 27).

He says “of a full field,” because the Holy Spirit had filled him most abundantly, and the fullness of divinity is proved to have dwelt bodily in him.

Again, Isaiah repeats that he was to come from the seed of Jesse, saying:

> “On that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples, him the nations shall beseech, and his tomb shall be glorious”  
> (Isa. XI, 10).

“The nations shall beseech him,” he says, as though he were saying: he is the seed in whom Abraham is promised to become the father of many nations; he is also the one whom Jacob foretells as the expectation of the nations from Judah.

Therefore, hard-hearted ones, when you see all these things fulfilled in him, accept at least belatedly the one whom, as was promised, the nations would beseech—the one whom you, who should have come first to adore him even without being invited by miracles, ought to have approached.

For the riddles of the law and the prophets are open concerning him, and all have now been fulfilled in him. The nations, who had long desired him as he had been foretold, received him with joy and, having received him, venerate and worship him everywhere. But you judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life.

It follows:

“Jesse,” it says, “begot David the king.” It calls him king, not because he alone is proved to have been a king in this genealogy—since all those placed between him and the deportation to Babylon are known to have been kings—but because David was the first king from the tribe of Judah, through which tribe the order of the genealogy clearly runs down to Christ.

It does not mean that he alone was king, but that he was the first and the beginning of the kings. Hence, not without reason, he alone is named king above all the others.

Especially since, according to the testimony of Scripture, nearly all the others are preserved as having been placed upon the royal throne for his sake; and no one among them—even, so to speak, the most righteous king Uzziah himself—was found capable of attaining the dignity of his merit.

Others say that he was more truly called king to distinguish him from another David, whom they think was not a king but a soldier, who in the Book of Kings and Chronicles is doubtfully numbered among the three mighty men, stronger than the thirty (II Kings XXIII, 8). Whether this should be accepted as so or not, let the prudent reader understand.

We, however, believe rather that he was called king for this reason: so that you might recall what had been promised to him and recognize that this was the one whose lineage was being declared, the one who was to be placed as king upon the throne of his father David.

Concerning him that same David prays as a prophet of the future:

> “O God, give your judgment to the king,  
> and your righteousness to the king’s son”  
> (Ps. LXXI, 1).

He says “the king’s son,” because the Son of the eternal Father was also made the son of David, so that this might be fulfilled:

> “He shall sit upon the throne of David  
> and upon his kingdom forever”  
> (Isa. IX, 7).

And who is the one who sits as king upon David’s throne forever except the Son of David? According to the fact that in the beginning he was the Word, he is coeternal with the Father, and his kingdom will have no end; thus he can truly sit as King forever.

Otherwise, it is by no means evident that this was foretold of Solomon, whose kingdom nearly collapsed together with him. And the entire race of the Jews, because it did not believe that this one had come and been placed at the right hand of the Father, upon a great throne, has now perished, scattered here and there from its own dwelling places.

It follows:

David the king begot Solomon by her who had been the wife of Uriah. It is therefore asked, and not without reason, since the three remaining women in this genealogical sequence have already been given under their own names, why Bersabea alone is not here expressed by her name, but is merely indicated as having been Uriah’s wife. To this it is reasonably believed that the answer must be admitted: the three women mentioned above, through whom the notable works of Christ’s mercy are typologically foreshadowed, deserved rightly not only to be blamed but also to be praised. Hence they are listed in this genealogy without any shame attached to their names, as though they possessed outstanding virtue. This woman, however, stained by adultery and at the same time bloodied by the murder of her husband, seems deservedly to have been passed over—at least so that, by the silence concerning her name, she might conceal through silence what could not be concealed by speech and appeared wholly shameful. Thus her husband’s name, Urias, is also inserted, as though that of a righteous man, so that the enormity of the crime might thereby be recalled with greater modesty, since the very man on whose account he was killed is brought forward again.

This does not mean that the sin had not already been forgiven by the Lord for David, who had repented; rather, even while speaking chastely in every respect, he wished to show that God sometimes makes good use of our evils and, even through deeds wickedly performed, foreshadows the greatest benefits of his mercies. It should also be noted that David is read to have received not only forgiveness of his crime but also to have made satisfaction for it. Bersabea, however, just as she is not principally blamed for the crime, so too is she not said to have expiated her own offense through repentance for having consented to the king’s adultery. Therefore, chiefly on account of the mystical sacrament of the Church—which, after the devil has been slain, is mercifully taken into marriage by the true King—she is here mentioned only as “the wife of Uriah”; but, as I infer, because her own guilt still remained unerased, she is entirely withheld from mention by name.

For if we consider this public sin of King David, we recognize that something great and good for the future was prophetically signified through the evil deed itself. David is interpreted as “strong of hand”; Urias as “my light is God”; Ethaeus as “cut off”; and Bersabee as “well of satiety,” or “seventh well.” Whose figure, then, is David the strong-handed believed to have represented in that place, if not that of the Lord [Col. 0066A] Jesus Christ? Of him the Psalmist says: “The Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.” And whom does Urias signify—he whose name, interpreted as “my light is God,” has this meaning—if not the ancient adversary, who, puffed up with the swelling of pride, said: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14)? Since he desired to make himself like the creative and eternal Light that had arisen in time, he lost the very thing by which he shone forth from the Creator. And because he did not stand in the truth, he was also excluded, through the merit of his pride, from his own light—which he had received from the Creator as brighter than that of all other creatures—as though from a dreadful darkness. Thus it rightly suits him that he is called Ethaeus, that is, “cut off.” Having fallen and lost true strength, he now also transforms himself into an angel of light, still daring to say, “The light of God is mine.” And what wonder is it if he calls God’s light his own, when the Apostle cries out concerning him: “He opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called or worshiped as God” (II Thess. II, 4)?

Whose figure, then, did Bersabee express—she whose name is rendered in Latin as “well of satiety,” or “seventh well”—if not that of the Church? The Church of the saints is rightly called the well of satiety, or the seventh well, because that sevenfold teaching of the Spirit is seen to overflow in his elect, and in the divine books it is often most plainly compared with streams of water. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII, 37). The Evangelist who followed explained what this drinking was, saying: “Now he said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive.” Hence, to the Samaritan woman, who bore the type of the Church, he says at the well: “Whoever drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst; rather, the water that I shall give him will become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life” (John IV, 13).

While Bersabee was washing on the roof of the house, therefore, David the king, the strong-handed one, saw her with a lustful eye, desired her, and took her. For our Redeemer, God and Lord Jesus Christ, providentially saw the Church—which he acquired from the nations, cleansed by the washing of water in the word, trampling earthly things beneath her feet and longing for heavenly things—predestined; the Bridegroom loved her when she had been called, so that, once justified, he might unite her to himself in spiritual marriage as her lawful husband. But for Bersabee to be joined to David, her husband Uriah is killed; for the righteous Church to cling to her heavenly Bridegroom, the power of the ancient enemy is shattered, and, once shattered, he is cast down to be trampled under the feet of the elect. Hence the Lord says to them through the Gospel: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon every power of the enemy” (Luke X, 19).

If we attend to what happened according to the literal sense, what could ever be found more criminal? But if we consider in the deed itself the mystery of what was being prefigured, what could ever be found more beneficial? There is still another matter in this deed that is represented even more clearly. David, then, walking on the roof, expresses the type of the Redeemer. Appropriately on a roof, because “he has set his tent in the sun.” The roof received its name not only because it has a level surface like the earth, but also because it is placed in the sun more prominently than the other houses. For the Jewish people, unlike us, do not have a roof over their roofs, as Scripture demonstrates in the account of Absalom, saying: “When he went in to his father’s concubines, his servants had spread a tent for him on the roof” (II Reg. XVI, 22). Thus, as Scripture testifies, he was able to go in to those concubines in full view of everyone.

What, then, is David’s bringing Bersabee to himself except joining to himself, in a spiritual understanding, the lawgiver together with the law joined to the carnal people? Bersabee, as we have said, is called “the seventh well,” because through knowledge of the law the perfect wisdom of the infusion of spiritual grace is shown to us. Whom does Uriah signify, then, if not the Jewish people, whose name, as we said, means “my light is God”? The Jewish people, because it exalts itself over the knowledge of the law it has received, boasts as though over the light of God. But David took this Uriah’s wife from him and joined her to himself, because the Redeemer, appearing in the flesh, made known that the law spoke spiritually about him; and by this he showed that she was a stranger to the Jewish people and joined her to himself, because he declared that he was preached through her.

Therefore, while the carnal people retain the commandments of the law and strive to fulfill them, they themselves bring forward the indictment, as though through the Epistles, by which they are condemned. Perhaps the Evangelist, wishing to set the deed before believers as a confirmation of their faith, brought forward this event, by which carnal [Col. 0067C] Israel might be marked as liable to death, while the spiritual Israel, joined to Christ in his body, might receive in faith the true firmness of the King’s marriage. For it is clearly shown in these four women that the Church, to be gathered from the nations, was being manifested; and through them the most direct line of the genealogy is extended, in promising what was to come, all the way to Christ. Hence it follows:

“Solomon begot Roboam, and Roboam begot Abiam. Abia, however, Asa; Asa begot Josaphat; and Josaphat begot Joram.”

What, then, is the meaning of what we read in the Book of Kings? “I will take away,” says the Lord to Jeroboam, king of Samaria, “the kingdom from the hand of Roboam, son of David, and I will give you ten tribes. But to his son”—that is, to Roboam himself—“I will give one tribe, so that a lamp may remain for David my servant all his days before me in Jerusalem, the city that I have chosen, that my name might be there” (III Reg. XI, 35). And to Abia also (III Reg. XV, 4), because of his father David, the Lord God gave a lamp in Jerusalem, to raise up his son.

Although these words may seem capable of being understood according to the letter, I would not say that they should be understood simply; rather, the present history is enveloped in the mystical sacraments of the promises. For when he says, “So that a lamp may remain for David my servant all his days before me in Jerusalem,” it is plainly evident that this cannot stand according to the Jewish interpretation. Jerusalem itself did not deserve to stand for all days, since “not one stone was left upon another” in it. Nor, after the Redeemer’s coming, is any leader from the seed of King David found throughout all Judea upon his throne.

Therefore let the deceitful Jews understand—those who, as I said above, applaud themselves because someone from David’s stock supposedly rules the people in some unknown region of the earth—that no one can be found either in Judah, as Jacob promises, or in Jerusalem, as this divine word declares, who is a lamp in the people upon the throne of the kingdom. Consequently, it is necessary that the divine promise not be weakened, but that we seek another meaning and contemplate in it the higher benefits of God’s mysteries.

What is the lamp that shines before God in Jerusalem for all days, and what is this Jerusalem in which a shining lamp from David’s seed is promised to remain for all days because of him? The Apocalypse of John makes this clear, saying: “And he led me in the spirit to a high and great mountain, and I saw Jerusalem descending from heaven, adorned with its jewels, and its light was like a chrysolite stone” (Apoc. XXI, 10). A little later, after introducing into it the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel, he says: “And I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb. And the city does not need the sun or the moon to shine upon it, because the glory of God illuminates it, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Apoc. XXI, 22, 23).

From this it is perfectly clear that this is that Jerusalem which the Lord chose, so that his name might be there, and that the King from his seed might sit there upon the throne of David forever—not the Jerusalem that we see utterly razed to the ground and still subject to many curses. If it had been chosen according to the election of grace, it would never have collapsed so suddenly, together with the people, after so many promises.

If you object to me as a clever evader that this happened because of its sins, we entirely agree that what you say is true. But the omnipotent God, foreknowing the future—as the prophet testifies, he who beholds all ages (Eccli. XXXVI, 19)—would never bind himself by such promises if this were the Jerusalem of which the utterances of the prophets resounded typologically, and which, according to the election of grace, there is no doubt he had chosen from ancient times.

This earthly Jerusalem, however, which you mention, he chose for a time, so that it might bear the figure of the heavenly Jerusalem until the one from David’s seed should come who would sit in it as King forever. Therefore, because the Lord had sworn truth to him, “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne” (Ps. CXXXI, 11), and elsewhere says, “I will establish his kingdom, and his throne will be made exceedingly firm forever” (I Par. XVII, 11, 14), although his sons were sinners, the succession of the seed is nevertheless always preserved, and Jerusalem is not utterly destroyed until the seed should come to whom it was promised that he would sit forever.

This is what is said here: “I will not do it for the sake of David my servant, but I will give one tribe to his son, so that a lamp may remain for him all his days before me in Jerusalem” (III Reg. XI, 35). What, then, does it mean to say, “I will not do it for the sake of David my servant,” except: I will not do it for the sake of the oath that I swore to him, so that I would not remove his seed from my sight, but would give him a lamp that would shine before me in Jerusalem for all the days of eternity?

Placing this lamp, as it were, before his eyes, David himself said: “Your word is a lamp for my feet, and a light for my paths” (Ps. CXVIII, 104). Clearly this is the lamp of which it was said: “So that a lamp may remain for David my servant before me all his days in Jerusalem.” For if the succession of sons from his seed had been interrupted before Christ, it might perhaps have come about through some chance event; but, according to what had first been sworn to Abraham and afterward to David, the whole promise would have been rendered void.

Yet even then there should have been no doubt that what had been promised would be fulfilled, because it is God who had promised this future reality without change. Therefore, since we hold without ambiguity the entire genealogy through succession from David’s stock down to Christ, and believe that he will sit forever upon his throne and over his kingdom, let us expect no other who is yet to come, lest—God forbid—we receive in his place the Antichrist who is to come into the world.

And if anyone is troubled by how he is said to sit upon the throne and kingdom of David, since David himself did not sit as king upon the throne and kingdom of that heavenly Jerusalem, nor is Christ read to have sat as king over this earthly Jerusalem—especially since he himself says to Pilate, “My kingdom is not of this world; for if my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly fight so that I would not be delivered to the Jews” (John XVIII, 36—we answer that this city of Jerusalem possessed the figure of the heavenly one, and that this kingdom bore its likeness. Accordingly, that other kingdom was already present in this kingdom through a figure, just as the heavenly kingdom may be said in some manner to have been present in this earthly one through a shadow.

But the shadow is now seen to have been emptied, so that the true light might take its place; and the figure flourished for a time so that the truth might meanwhile remain concealed, until the fullness of time should come. Therefore we rightly say that Christ sat upon David’s throne, because in that throne of David the kingdom of Christ was already present in figure, and no one who thinks rightly doubts that David then sat upon that throne.

When Christ came into that kingdom, he assumed flesh from David’s seed, emptied the shadows of future things, and sat upon the glory of the light that had then lain hidden within the kingdom. Accordingly, that city does not need the sun or the moon, because the lamp long promised from David’s seed now shines in it; and that light is the Lamb himself, long sacrificed in figure for the people.

For this reason it is also rightly said concerning Joram and the others who had provoked God by their evil deeds that he preserved the lamp of succession before the Lord for all days, for David’s sake and for Jerusalem’s sake. For neither their sins alone nor all the crimes that the world had accumulated piecemeal could provoke him to such a degree that he would annul the oath of his mercy. Thus, even if some of them did not deserve to be entered in this genealogy, no one was found down to Christ to whom a son would be denied in the succession. This is demonstrated still more clearly in what follows.

“Joram,” he says, “begot Oziam. And Ozias begot Joathan.”

In the Fourth Book of Kings, then, we read that Joram begot Ochozias, and that Joas was begotten from Ochozias; afterward, since Joas begot Amasias, this Ozias succeeded him in the kingdom. Yet he is inscribed here by the Evangelist as Joram’s son (IV Reg. VIII, 24; XI, 2; XII, 21; XV, 1).

This is rightly believed not to be without reason if Matthew’s intention—or rather, the intention of the Holy Spirit through him—is carefully considered. His purpose was to arrange three groups of fourteen in distinct stages and thus to ensure that the mystical number of the sacraments would rise to forty-two. For this reason he is seen to have removed these three from the middle. And he did so not only to complete this mystery, but also to instruct us according to the law and to grant us a great lesson.

Joram had joined himself to the most impious Jezebel. Therefore his memory is rightly removed from the order of the holy nativity down to the third generation. God had earlier said the same in the law through Moses: “I am the Lord, the mighty and jealous God, visiting the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy to many thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments” (Exod. XXX, 5).

Here it should be noted that this is said concerning that offspring which persisted in the sins of its fathers and in hatred of virtue; likewise, mercy is shown in those who have remained constant in love of the Lord. A good man, even if born of evil parents, becomes worthy of mercy; conversely, any wicked person born of a good one is punished and, by God’s judgment, most rightly condemned.

The divine history reveals what sort of man Joram was, for God said to him: “Because you did not walk in the ways of Josaphat your father and in the ways of Asa king of Judah, but walked in the way of the kings of Israel, and caused Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to commit fornication, imitating the fornication of the house of Ahab; moreover, you killed your brothers, the house of your father, who were better than you; behold, the Lord will strike you with a great plague, together with your people, your sons, and your wives, and all your substance. You yourself will suffer from a very grievous disease of the womb, until your entrails gradually come forth day by day” (II Par. XXI, 12).

And so, we read, it happened. He was so consumed by wasting disease that he even discharged his entrails; he lost both his health and his life. He died of a most grievous illness, and the people did not perform for him the customary funeral burning as they had done for his ancestors, nor did they bury him in the tombs of the kings.

His son Ochozias also followed him. Scripture testifies: “He walked in the ways of the house of Ahab. For they were also his counselors after his father’s death, to his destruction” (II Par. XXII, 3).

But this troubles us greatly, because in the Book of Paralipomenon (I, XXII, 2) we read that he was forty-two years old when he began to reign. How can this be, when his father Joram is read to have been thirty-two years old when he began to reign and to have reigned for eight years—together, forty years (II Par. XXI, 20)? This cannot at all be correct. For if Ochozias was forty-two years old when he began to reign after his father, he had evidently been born two years before his father, which nature itself wholly forbids.

Therefore it is clear that the reading we find in the Book of Kings is more correct: that he was twenty-two years old when he began to reign (IV Reg. VIII, 26). The other reading found in many books of Paralipomenon has been corrupted through the fault of the copyists, as has happened in very many other places.

As for Joas, the son of Ochozias, Scripture testifies to what he was like after the priest Joiada died, saying: “The princes of Judah entered and worshiped the king, who, having been flattered by their services, consented to them. And they abandoned the temple of the Lord, the God of their fathers, and served groves and carved images; and the wrath of the Lord came against Judah and Jerusalem because of this sin” (II Par. XXIV, 17, 18).

He also killed the prophet Zacharias, said to have been the son of the priest Joiada, who had raised him in the temple of the Lord and established him as king. Zacharias was his foster-brother and cousin. The Spirit of the Lord clothed him, and he stood before the people and said to him: “Thus says the Lord: Why do you transgress the commandment of the Lord, which will not benefit you, and abandon the Lord, so that he may abandon you?”

They gathered against him and, at the king’s command, threw stones at him in the court of the house of the Lord. King Joas did not remember the mercy that Joiada his father had shown him, but killed his son. As he was dying, Zacharias said: “May the Lord see and avenge” (ibid., 20–22).

The Lord later testified to this, saying: “All the blood that has been shed will be required, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zacharias, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matt. XXIII, 35).

After King Joas died, therefore, his son Amasias succeeded to the kingdom. After the slaughter of the Idumaeans, he brought back the gods of the sons of Seir, set them up as his gods, and worshiped them, burning incense to them. Therefore, in anger, the Lord sent a prophet to him, who said: “Why have you worshiped gods who did not deliver their people?” He replied: “Are you the king’s counselor? Be quiet, lest I kill you” (II Par. XXV, 15, 16).

I have set all these matters down here for the present so that you might observe that these three, following their father Joram in every impiety and maintaining continual hatred toward God, are rightly excluded above all others from Christ’s genealogy. The other kings, although they were bad and impious, wherever they are placed in the genealogy are either born entirely from good men or themselves beget good men: that is, either one is the son of a good father or is at least the father of some good son.

Joram, then, was the son of Josaphat, a righteous man, and left behind him a son who was heir both to his kingdom and to his impiety. All those who followed him entered by the same line upon the path of wickedness, until they reached Ozias.

Ozias did what was right before the Lord in almost everything, except that he wished to burn incense upon the altar of incense in the temple. Nevertheless, since he was not an idolater, the impious men having been omitted from the middle, the very straight order of the genealogy continues through him. Thus divine vengeance would not appear to exceed the law, nor would one who refused to imitate the impiety of his fathers appear himself to be entangled in their sins.

Here, as in very many other places, it is proved that each person must die in his own sin; and that, if he follows the conduct of his earlier fathers, whether good or evil, punishments or rewards of blessing are accumulated for him. Thus these men too are entirely removed from the middle here in silence, clearly on account of the punishment of sin; yet they are not deprived of the fruit of blessing in the seed, because of the promises made by their preceding fathers.

For this reason it is also rightly said concerning Joram that the Lord did not wish to destroy the house of David because of the covenant he had made with him, since he had promised to give him a lamp and to his sons at all times (II Par. XXI, 7). It is entirely clear that no sinners’ crimes could extinguish this lamp because of the oath. Yet the wretched Jews, because of their blindness, are still daily darkened by the darkness of their own sins.

Ozias, who is also Azarias, begot Joathan. Joathan begot Achaz. Achaz, however, Ezechias.

Under these four kings, therefore, the prophet Isaiah composed not so much a prophecy concerning Christ—that he would come from the house of David—as he preached the Gospel to everyone. Thus, when he said to Achaz, because he worshiped idols: “Ask for yourself a sign from God, either from heaven or from the depths of hell” (Isa. VII, 11), and Achaz, unwilling, said: “I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord” (ibid., 12), he turned to the whole house of David and said: “Hear now, house of David. Is it not enough for you to be troublesome to men, that you are also troublesome to my God? Therefore,” he said, “the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel” (ibid., 13, 14).

And finally: “Unless you believe,” he says, “you will not understand.” With God’s approval, we shall discuss this testimony in its proper place.

As for Ezechias, while he was still childless, because he had heard from the Lord through the Prophet, “Set your house in order, for you will die and not live” (IV Reg. XX, 1), he is said immediately to have turned toward the wall and said: “I beseech you, Lord; remember, I pray, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your eyes.”

Ezechias then wept with great weeping. He did not weep, I say, because of a very long span of life, since he certainly knew that Solomon had pleased God precisely because he had not asked for additional years of life. Rather, as he was about to depart from this life, he wept with great weeping because of the Lord’s promise to David, which he saw would then perish entirely with his own death. At that time Ezechias had no children.

Therefore he wept bitterly, lest on his account the lamp long promised to the fathers should be extinguished before the fullness of time arrived. For he knew with certainty that he had been born from David’s stock, through whom the one whom he and many others greatly desired to come was necessarily to arrive according to the succession of the flesh.

Thus, amid his lamentation and grief, he said: “I sought the remainder of my years; I said, I shall not see the Lord God in the land of the living” (Isa. XXXVIII, 10). For this the Septuagint said: “Never again shall I see the salvation of God in the land of the living.” Concerning this it is also written elsewhere: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. CXIV, 9).

This, then, is all that Ezechias feared here: that he would not be worthy to behold the salvation of God—that is, Jesus—when he had been led down to the underworld. Hence what follows says: “I shall not look upon man any more, nor an inhabitant.”

He greatly feared, therefore, that he would not see the Lord in the land of the living; that his offspring would suddenly be dissolved like a tent; that it would be cut off, like the threads of a web, at the very beginning of the light; and that Christ would not arise from his seed.

But the merciful Lord was quickly moved to clemency and stirred to mercy. He immediately changed the sentence that he had pronounced according to his foreknowledge, as a test of Ezechias’s faith, and granted him time to beget a child, in whom the mystical sacraments of future events might also be displayed.
