Thus, after the third year of the life granted to him, Manasses was born through whom Christ’s origin would be traced, since he is read to have begun to reign at the age of twelve after his father’s death. Consequently, whatever had previously been despaired of was afterward restored in him through the succession from his father, although he was a wicked man.

All this, then, was the cause of his weeping: he despaired that Christ would be born from his seed, although he knew that Christ had been promised through many divine oracles and heard him prophesied daily in Isaiah’s many words, set before him.

But, to speak more accurately, he believed and doubted; and for that reason he wept so bitterly. He wept because it had been said to him, while he was childless, “Set your house in order, for you will die and not live”; yet he believed because God, who had made the promise, does not lie. Faith therefore overcame fear.

For this reason, under the hope of life, as the divine account relates, he is suddenly consoled. Let us therefore also believe in the one whom, after so many promises of the Fathers, we have joyfully received; and, with him as our guide, let us remain firm until we reach him himself along that very line of succession.

Manasses, then, begot Amon. Amon begot Josias. Josias begot Jechonias and his brothers at the transmigration of Babylon.

This Josias is the most righteous king, who, before he was born, was promised by the prophecy of the Holy Spirit under his own name, because he was destined to come. Yet his righteousness is not found in the sons whom he is said to have begotten at the transmigration of Babylon.

This does not mean that Josias begot his sons during the transmigration, since he is nowhere read to have been carried into exile; rather, because his sons did not follow him, they are said, as it were by God’s predestination, to have been born for transmigration. Not, I say, “in transmigration,” but “for transmigration,” that is, certainly, in order to be carried into exile.

He places Jechonias and his brothers together for this reason: since they shared a common impiety and equal infamy, their shared punishment and misery might likewise be remembered together.

For when Josias had been wounded in battle against Nechao, king of Egypt, and had died, his son Joachaz, also called Sellum, succeeded to the kingdom and reigned for three months in Jerusalem; afterward he was transferred to Egypt. The king of Egypt appointed in his place his brother Eliachim as king, who was also called Joachim by another name.

After eleven years, King Nabuchodonosor brought him bound in chains to Babylon. His son Joachim reigned in his place; he was also called Jechonias. He too reigned for three months. Nabuchodonosor later sent for him, took him bound away to Babylon, and appointed his uncle Sedechias, the son of Josias and brother of Joachim, in his place.

That same king later blinded Sedechias and brought him to Babylon, shut up like a wild beast in a cage. Thus, since their impiety was equal, their punishment might also be equal, and the Evangelist might preserve a shared memory of their unhappiness.

It is rightly asked why Matthew says that Jechonias and his brothers were begotten by Josias, when it is plainly proved that Jechonias, who was also Joachim, was not Josias’s son but his grandson—that is, the son of Joachim—as the entire text of the Old Testament makes clear.

Furthermore, if we place Jechonias at the end of the second group of fourteen, there will not be fourteen in the third group, but only thirteen will be found.

It remains, therefore, for us to understand that the first Jechonias, whom he says was begotten by Josias, is Joachim himself, the father of Jechonias and son of Josias, who is written of at the beginning of Daniel; while the second Jechonias, whom the Evangelist writes begot Salathiel after the transmigration, is to be understood as Joachim the son of Joachim—that is, the son of the first Jechonias and grandson of Josias—who is also mentioned at the beginning of Ezekiel.

The one Joachim is written among the Greeks with κ and μ, while the other is written with χ and ν. Among the Greeks and Latins, however, this name has become confused, so that some of them regard one and the same person as appearing at the beginnings of the two prophets.

We read nowhere else than in this passage of the Gospel that Joachim, the father of Jechonias, was called Jechonias. If this is indeed how he wished it to be understood, no sound reason of faith contradicts the Evangelist’s authority: either he was formerly called by this name, although divine Scripture now keeps silent about it, or the Evangelist alone calls him by the same name because Jechonias is interpreted as “the preparation of the Lord.”

He is rightly called a preparation because the Lord had long prepared him, as well as his son Jechonias, for transmigration. Therefore, as we said above, Josias is said to have begotten them not in transmigration but for transmigration. They are spoken of as though born for this purpose—namely, because the Lord, foreknowing that they would be taken captive for their own sins and those of the people, knew that they would go into transmigration.

Let the prudent reader know that, in what we have just said concerning the distinction between the names of the two men, we followed the truth of the history, so that we might place one at the end of the preceding group of fourteen and the other at the beginning of the following group, in order that each group might complete the number fourteen.

According to the mystical sense, however, there is one and the same Jechonias, counted twice, as it were, at a corner. For when he had divided the fourteen generations into three sections, saying that there were fourteen generations from Abraham to David, fourteen from David to the transmigration of Babylon, and as many again from the transmigration to Christ, he did not nevertheless add them together by saying, “Thus there are forty-two in all.”

One of the ancestors is counted twice: Jechonias, namely, at whom a certain deviation into foreign nations began when he migrated to Babylon. Wherever the order bends away from the straight line and turns toward a different direction, it forms, as it were, a corner; and the thing situated at the corner is counted twice—at the end of the preceding order and at the beginning of the very deviation.

This already prefigured Christ as migrating, in a certain sense, from circumcision to the uncircumcised, as from Jerusalem to Babylon, and as being present in the midst of believers from both sides, like a cornerstone.

These things God was then preparing in figure, while the realities destined to come were to appear in truth. Jechonias himself, at the place where this corner was prefigured, is interpreted as “the preparation of God.”

Accordingly, there are not now forty-two generations, which would be three times fourteen, but forty-one, because one is counted twice. With the Lord’s help, we shall speak more fully about this afterward in its proper place.

Moreover, according to the understanding of that same teacher, it is not sufficiently clear why Joachim, the father of Jechonias, was omitted; that notable investigator of hidden questions kept silent about it. Unless perhaps we should accept that the Evangelist wished Jechonias to be counted twice in order to make him a type of Christ, and decided to omit Joachim so that the number would not be increased.

Jechonias, after the transmigration of Babylon, begot Salathiel. Salathiel begot Zorobabel. That Zorobabel was Salathiel’s son is found without ambiguity in many places in the sacred Scriptures. But in Paralipomenon [57] it is presented very differently.

Thus we read there that Jeconiah had sons named Asir, Shealtiel, Melchiah, and Pedaiah. From Pedaiah were descended Zerubbabel and Shimei. But it is not easy to discover what we should say about this intermediate matter. If we were to say that these two brothers, at different times, each took the same woman as wife, and that one of them begot a son who was adopted by the other according to the law, the very words of Scripture refute this: Matthew says that Shealtiel begot Zerubbabel. Moreover, the book of Chronicles states that from Pedaiah were descended [Col. 0075D] Zerubbabel and Shimei. For “begot” cannot here be understood in any other sense than that he begot him from his own seed; nor can “were descended” mean anything other than that they were born from that man’s flesh. Yet it is absurd to understand them as born simultaneously from the seed of both men, since nature itself forbids this.

Hence, as the Hebrews relate, it is true that he had three names—namely, Asir, Shealtiel, and Pedaiah. Asir is interpreted as “blinded,” Shealtiel as “shrub of God,” and Pedaiah as “redeemed of the Lord.” Or perhaps the matter should be understood in this way: Shealtiel and Pedaiah were two brothers, and each of them gave the son whom he begot the name Zerubbabel, so that there were two men of that name. I do not approve this explanation, especially since the evangelist says that this Zerubbabel also begot Abiud. The book of Chronicles, [Col. 0076A] however, says that Zerubbabel begot Meshullam, Hananiah, and the others, among whom Abiud is nowhere numbered.

Therefore the matter must be handled in this way, or by some other solution, so that divine authority may not appear to disagree with itself. Otherwise, we must believe that the evangelist gave the more accurate account; and divine authority agrees with him in very many other places as well—provided, nevertheless, that some doubt can be raised concerning the point under discussion. For especially in this book, as also in Ezra, because of scribal corruptions, very many genealogical questions arise that cannot be brought to an end. Hence the Apostle says: “Avoid useless and interminable genealogical questions” (Titus 3:9).

From that point onward, concerning those whose names are recorded down to Christ, we find no mention in the records of the sacred Scriptures. [Col. 0076B] Yet credence must be given to the apostle and the evangelist. Even if this information could have been found nearby in the Jewish archives, he could have learned it and committed it to writing through the diligence of his relatives, since it was known to all Jews that Christ was to come from the flesh of David. For this reason the whole lineage was preserved with particular care in memory. 58

This is why Africanus, writing about the agreement of the evangelists, asks how it is that Matthew says Joseph was the son of Jacob, while Luke records him as the son of Heli. Africanus further demonstrates that Heli was the son of Matthat, and Matthew the evangelist demonstrates that Jacob was the son of Matthan. He says:

“Matthat and Matthan lived at different times, and each of them fathered a son by one and the same woman, named Estha. [Col. 0076C] For Matthan, who was descended through Solomon, had first taken her as his wife and, leaving one son named Jacob, died. After his death, since the law does not forbid a widow to marry another man, Matthat, who traced his lineage through Nathan, being of the same tribe but not of the same family, took the widow Estha as his wife. From her he too received a son named Heli. Thus Jacob and Heli became uterine brothers, though they belonged to different paternal families.

“Of these two, Jacob—having taken, in obedience to the law, the wife of his brother Heli, who had died childless, and having begotten Joseph—was indeed his son by natural descent; and therefore it is written: ‘Jacob begot Joseph.’ But according to the commandment of the law, Joseph became Heli’s son, since Jacob, being his brother, had taken Heli’s wife in order to raise up offspring for his brother. Thus the genealogy is found to be both valid and complete.

[Col. 0076D] “Africanus says that these matters were not suddenly discovered by us or devised without any authorities. Rather, the Savior’s own relatives according to the flesh handed them down—either out of eagerness to demonstrate the greatness of such a lineage, or in order to teach what had actually taken place. For if this historian took such care to investigate the truth of the matter, how much more did the evangelist, who lived with the Lord in the flesh and spent every day among his relatives?”

Nevertheless, when some among us also say that Joseph was the son of Heli—not by natural descent but according to the law, because Jacob took his deceased brother’s wife in order to raise up offspring for him, as the law prescribes, since Heli had died childless—this solution to the question appears weakened. [Col. 0077A] The deceased brother’s name ought to have been retained, so that his father’s name might be raised up in him, as the law seems to require, unless some other reasonable explanation can be found by which the foregoing opinion may be shown to stand.

This is especially so since, in the case of Judah and his daughter-in-law Tamar, although Judah unknowingly raised up offspring for his deceased son, neither of those born from that single union is recorded as having been called Er, the name of the deceased. Rather, one was certainly called Perez and the other Zerah. 59 Therefore it is shown not to contradict the authority of the Old Testament that Joseph here is known by the name Joseph, and not Eli, although he is Heli’s son according to the law.

Likewise, when Boaz took Ruth in accordance with the law, [Col. 0077B] it pleased those concerned that the son born from her should be called Obed, not Abimelech—the name in which the deceased’s offspring was being raised up. Thus, if the law had commanded that the offspring of the deceased could not be called by any name other than that of the man whose offspring was being raised up, we could hardly believe that men and women of virtue would have wished to act against the law. It is therefore plainly established that this question remains firmly resolved, just as it is seen to have been explained and committed to writing by our predecessors.

Furthermore, by consistently saying “Matthew: this man begot that man,” Matthew shows that he has listed only sons of the flesh, descended from the seed of each individual. Luke, however, because he says, “who was the son of Heli, who was the son of Matthat,” and proceeds in the same way with the rest, shows that in this genealogy too he has included sons who were not sons of the flesh.

Hence blessed Augustine, in his book *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, says:

“Those who are troubled by the fact that Matthew enumerates different ancestors [Col. 0077C] as he descends from David to Joseph, while Luke names different ones as he ascends from Joseph to David, should easily understand that Joseph could have had two fathers: one from whom he was begotten, and another by whom he was adopted. For the custom of adoption is ancient, even among that people of God, so that they made their own sons whom they themselves had not begotten. For, apart from the fact that Pharaoh’s daughter adopted Moses—for she was a foreigner—Jacob himself, in unmistakable words, adopted the grandsons born to Joseph, saying: ‘Now therefore your two sons, who were born to you in Egypt before I came to you, are mine: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, like Reuben and Simeon; but the children whom you father afterward shall be yours’ (Genesis 48:5). Thus it came about that there were twelve tribes of Israel [Col. 0077D], apart from the tribe of Levi, which served the temple.”

From this it is understood that Luke accepted in his Gospel as Joseph’s father not the man from whom Joseph was begotten, but the man by whom he had been adopted; and Luke recalled that man’s ancestors in ascending order until he reached David. Who, then, more probably preserved the lineage of the adoptive father than the one who refused to say that Joseph had been begotten by the man whom he reported as Joseph’s father?

[Col. 0078A] For it is more appropriately said that he was the son of the man by whom he had been adopted than that he had been begotten by one from whose flesh he had not been born. Matthew, however, saying, “Abraham begot 60 Isaac,” and continuing throughout with the expression “begot,” until at the end he says, “Jacob begot Joseph,” clearly showed that he always traced the succession of begetters to the father from whom Joseph was not adopted but begotten.

Even if Luke had said that Joseph was begotten by Heli, this expression ought not to disturb us so as to make us believe anything other than that one of the two fathers was being presented as the begetter and the other as the adopter. For one may without absurdity be said to have begotten, not by the flesh but by affection, a son whom one has adopted.

Thus God too, to those whom he gave the power to become children of God, did not give birth by nature and substance as he did to the only Son; rather, he adopted them through love, so that, as the Apostle says, “we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:5). Yet we are said, having received this power, to have been born from God so that we might become his children, although we were already human beings. We therefore become sons by grace, not by nature. For if we were sons by nature, we would never have been anything else.

[Col. 0078B] Nevertheless, since we are said to have been born from God through adoption, it would not be contrary to the truth if Luke too said that Joseph had been begotten by the man by whom he had been adopted. For that man begot Joseph not so that he would be a human being, but so that he would be a son, just as God begot us so that we might be his sons, although he had previously made us human beings.

He begot the only Son not merely so that he might be a Son—which the Father is not—but also so that he might be God—which the Father likewise is. But if Luke had used the expression “begot,” it would remain uncertain which of the two fathers he had identified as the adopter and which as the begetter according to the flesh.

For the rest, it is useless to dispute which of these explanations should be followed—whether Heli’s son was so according to the law or through some form of adoption—so long as we prove that both evangelists spoke the truth.

[Col. 0078C] The statement that follows—that Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Christ was born—naturally creates a very difficult question for unbelievers: what relevance does a genealogy traced from David down to Joseph have to Christ, when, according to divine Scripture, we all confess in catholic faith that Christ was not born from Joseph’s seed, but was conceived from the Holy Spirit and born from the Virgin Mary, as we confess in the Creed?

To them the first and easiest answer is that it is not the custom of the sacred Scriptures to set out the line of women in genealogies, as we can prove from all the books of the divine law. 61 [Col. 0078D] Therefore the succession of the genealogy is introduced not through Mary but through Joseph, so that the idiom of the Scriptures may not at the outset be violated.

In addition, we prove that Joseph and Mary were from one tribe. Consequently Joseph was compelled by the commandment of the law to take her as a near relative, lest he mingle one tribe with another, but so that each man might lawfully take a wife from his own tribe. Therefore, when the first census of the Roman Empire was being conducted so that each person might register in his own city, Joseph and Mary were enrolled together at Bethlehem, not only as belonging to one tribe but also as descended from one family.

For otherwise it would not have been said: “Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, [Col. 0079A] to register with Mary, his betrothed wife” (Luke 2:4). For, as we read, each person went to register in his own city. And if each person did so, Mary too at that time certainly went up to her own city, so that Joseph, who was her betrothed, might register there with her.

Moreover, above we demonstrated sufficiently from the oracles of the prophets that Christ was to come from the seed of David. From this we prove clearly that Mary descended from his lineage. Hence the prophet addresses the house of David more particularly: “Hear now, house of David: Is it not enough for you to weary men, that you weary my God also? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isaiah 7:13).

It is as though he were saying: “This will certainly be given to you, because he will be from you, among you, and for you.” [Col. 0079B] Here it should be noted that he expressly declares her to be a virgin, lest perhaps, when we hear the word “man” or “husband” (*virum*), we should suppose, as certain heretics do, that Christ was generated from Joseph’s seed.

Why he called Joseph Mary’s husband will be shown more clearly shortly. For it was not right to think that Joseph should on this account be separated from Mary’s marriage, because the Virgin bore Christ not from intercourse with him. This example most splendidly teaches married believers that, even when continence is preserved by mutual consent, a marriage can remain and be called a marriage—not through bodily intercourse, but through the preservation of the affection of the mind.

Nor should Joseph for that reason not have been called Christ’s father, because he did not beget him by intercourse, since he would rightly have been the father even of one whom he had adopted from elsewhere as his son, though he had not begotten him from his own wife.

[Col. 0079C] But now, 62 because he is born from Joseph’s betrothed—the one whom everyone regarded as his son—Joseph is rightly called the husband of his wife and the father of his son. Christ was indeed regarded as Joseph’s son, as though he had been born from Joseph’s flesh, but only by those to whom Mary’s virginity was hidden.

For Luke says: “And Jesus himself, when he began, was about thirty years of age, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph” (Luke 3:23). And elsewhere he says: “His father and mother were marveling at what was said about him” (Luke 2:33).

Since, therefore, Joseph is rightly called Christ’s putative father, what is surprising if we say that he was rightly called Mary’s husband without bodily intercourse? Indeed, he is called Christ’s father much more closely because Christ was born from his wife than if Joseph had adopted him as a son from elsewhere.

Therefore, when the evangelist says that Christ “was regarded as the son of Joseph,” it is clear that he said this with reference to those who supposed that Christ had been born from Joseph in the same way that other human beings are born. [Col. 0079D]

Accordingly, I say, if anyone could demonstrate—and certainly no one can—that Mary derived no consanguineous lineage from David, it would still be sufficient, according to this reasoning, to understand Christ as the son of David, since we rightly understand Joseph to be Mary’s husband and the Savior’s father, as stated above.

How much more, then, now that the prophetic utterances and the Gospel affirm in many places that he was born from David together with his lineage? Hence the Apostle Paul says that he was set apart for the Gospel of God, “which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:1–3).

For this reason we must not doubt at all that Mary derived her consanguineous lineage from the family of David. [Col. 0080A] Nor is her priestly descent left unmentioned by Luke, who indicates that Elizabeth was her relative and says that Elizabeth was from the daughters of Aaron. Therefore we have no doubt that Christ’s flesh was propagated from both lines—namely, that of kings and that of priests.

Among the persons of that Hebrew people, the mystical anointing of Christ was also prefigured: he was destined to be the one in whom the royal and priestly orders would together be more fittingly fulfilled through one and the same mediator between God and human beings.

“Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Christ was born.” It is beautifully said “from whom he was born,” and not “from whom they were born,” because everywhere he is proclaimed to have been generated from Mary without the intercourse of a man.

After these matters have been traversed, the evangelist once again concludes by recapitulating the entire genealogy mystically under a numerical pattern.

[Col. 0080B] “From Abraham,” he says, “to David, fourteen generations; and from David to the deportation to Babylon, fourteen generations; and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ, fourteen generations.” In this division, three periods are evidently shown to converge upon Christ: namely, before the Law, during which Abraham lived, naturally observing the commandment out of devotion; after the Law, when the Jews, transgressing, were led into captivity; and after grace, through which all are released from that same miserable captivity of Babylon.

And throughout all these periods, those who come to Christ are shown to be designated more clearly: some are justified at the beginning, in one way, by faith alone after being reborn; others according to the grace of election, those who from David are sent into Babylon—that is, into temptation; and they, in turn, having been tested in that very temptation, ascend to Christ after their struggles, like victors, to be crowned.

This division is distributed in an equal number, so that in each part fourteen are found, that is, twice seven. For the grace of the Holy Spirit in a human being is doubled on account of both substances, inward and outward. Indeed, if he does not possess both parts, we cannot rightly say with the prophet: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Psalm LXXXIII, 2). That person rejoices wholly in God whom the grace of the Holy Spirit fills completely.

Thus each person is sometimes filled to completeness when soul and flesh alike are nourished with the richness of Christ’s sacred anointing. But the fact that three groups of fourteen are counted [Col. 0080D] dedicates the true worship of religion to him who hastens toward Christ. For what else do four and ten signify than the Old and New Testaments of the Law? The way that invites believers to Christ is proclaimed through the ten words of the Law and the four Gospels of the heavenly kingdom. This is so, however, only if we consecrate to the Trinity, which is God, everything written in those same lines, as though tripling it within us. Otherwise, the perfection of the commandments would not be fulfilled if anyone were deficient in some respect in this number of worshiping God.

And so that it may become more evident that this is the way of reaching the homeland, let the whole number be gathered into a sum, and there result forty-two generations. [Col. 0081A] By this number of stages the true Hebrew departs from Egypt, so that at last, after the labor of the journey, he may enter the homeland. We understand this homeland to be Christ, long promised to the fathers without exception, because he himself is that land of the living in which the Prophet believes that he will see the Lord’s goodness (Psalm XXVI, 19), since all the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge are in him.

Through these stages, therefore, the generations of Christ, as we have said, the true Hebrew runs—the one who hastens to cross from earth to heaven and, abandoning the Egypt of the world, enters the promised land. Nor is it surprising that by the sacramental meaning of that number we arrive at the kingdoms of heaven, under which the Lord and Savior proceeded from the first patriarch, to whom he had been promised, as far as the Virgin, like the Jordan, which, flowing with a full torrent, [Col. 0081B] overflowed with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

For Matthew began the genealogy from Abraham, as though weaving the stages of the heavenly homeland, and counted forty-two generations, omitting whatever generations were passed over. To make them equal in number, he counted Christ at the end, since he is the completion of the entire journey and the dwelling-place of everlasting life, prepared for believers before the ages of the world.

God separated Abraham—for in him the Hebrew nation was first distinguished from the other nations—from his land and from his kindred, so that it might more distinctly serve the task of prophesying and especially foretelling Christ, since it was being promised from which nation he would come. In him faith is first reckoned as righteousness; and therefore, as though the beginning of the road to Paradise, the journey is directed from him to Christ through forty-two generations.

Indeed, the present time of the holy Church is signified by this number, since the Lord works inwardly with us when we do anything that is right. Seven times six makes forty-two. Few, surely, would doubt that six pertains to works, while seven signifies the rest of the life to come. Hence that people, saved from the land of Egypt because they are under the hope of entering into rest, and corrected by the rod of God’s discipline, encamps through seven sixes—that is, through forty-two stages—along the narrowest road to the homeland.

In the last of these, when it received Jesus as its leader, the Jordan was immediately opened, its enemies were defeated, and it entered the rest promised long ago and obtained the inheritance of its own kingdom.

[Col. 0081D] Thus our Lord Jesus, coming in the flesh in the forty-second generation, after the world had left behind the darkness of its ancient blindness and Abraham had left behind the fires of the Chaldeans when he believed, opened for us the baths of baptism and the gates of heaven. Therefore, by the course of the virtues, under the sacramental meaning of that same number, we strive toward what we do not yet see; but in hope we patiently await it, until what we have joyfully received in Christ arrives, and, already tasting it daily in advance, we enjoy the savor of heavenly mysteries.

Therefore, so that, with the Holy Spirit shedding light from above, we may better pass along this road of such a narrow journey, let us turn back briefly to the passage, so that, morally encamping through each of the Fathers along the path of virtue, we may cross the vast wilderness of vices and, with divine grace assisting, reach Christ more quickly.

Through these Fathers, then, Christ was coming into the world for our salvation, and in himself he bore the office of them all, so that through the interpretation of their names he might signify our salvation. As we rightly seek this salvation, let us first take care to depart with Abraham from the fire of vices and advance toward the homeland of virtues that God has shown us through himself.

There faith must first intervene—the faith that works through love—so that through that same faith, since we cannot do so through the flesh, we may be children of Abraham and thereafter be able to become his coheirs. For we read that it is written: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Genesis XV, 6).

Let us therefore also believe that these things were written for us, and let us depart from the land of our flesh, journeying farther toward the south, where Christ feeds and reclines in the fullness of charity. Then each person is rightly called “exalted father” when he is raised up by such great strength of faith that he begets Christ more by faith than by flesh from himself.

For Abraham is first justified only through faith, and therefore, having become obedient, he deserved to hear that all nations would be blessed in his seed. Therefore, if you wish to become an exalted father, imitate that patriarch; for we are true children of Abraham, as the Lord says, if we do his works (John VIII, 39).

Abraham is later changed into “father of many nations,” because through grace each person becomes the father of many [Col. 0082C] virtues. For faith joined to the grace of Christ generates within us an abundance of many virtues and sometimes makes us depart obediently, through contemplation, for the place that we shall later receive as an inheritance.

He departed, not knowing where he was going; and we, walking by faith, are enveloped in the darkness of obscurity, because we do not yet walk by sight. This, I say, is—as the Apostle says—“the victory that conquers the world, our faith” (John V, 4).

And therefore, if we desire to be coheirs of so great a father, let us hold fast everywhere to faith, which works through love, because without faith we cannot possibly please God. This is the first stage, in which the true Hebrew, fleeing Egypt, encamps most firmly upon the rock that is Christ.

From this faith, which is the initiator of many virtues, the true Isaac is certainly born. Isaac is interpreted as “laughter” or “joy,” since we truly rejoice when, joined to the Lord through faith, we fulfill works of virtue. Hence the Apostle cries out, saying: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Philippians IV, 4).

True joy, therefore, is generated only from the substance of faith and works of virtue; and the Apostle calls that same faith “the substance of things hoped for” (Hebrews XI, 1). Therefore, concerning God, we should not understand anything through faith other than what those who still hope await in the future through Christ.

The substance of things hoped for is sometimes called faith for this reason: whatever God is must dwell by faith in our hearts—whether by understanding or, certainly, by believing—while we are still on the road. Therefore, what heaven and earth cannot contain must be embraced in the bosom of faith; we must conceive of God as he is and, in everything that appears incomprehensible, comprehend all things through faith according to the truth of the matter.

Otherwise it should be called error rather than faith if something other than what God is is conceived by faith, and other than what God the Holy Spirit revealed about himself to believers so that they might believe. For faith surpasses all understanding while we are here on the road. Whatever we are unable to understand, we believe by faith, because God, who is truth, does not lie; and in faith, through its substance, we already hold whatever that reality is.

We therefore encamp in Isaac, whose name is interpreted as “laughter,” possessing fully the substance of things hoped for—not knowing exactly how it is, but believing most fully that it is. Although we do not yet rejoice in the reality itself, we certainly rejoice in hope. Isaac, conceived through faith because he was promised, born through grace, generated joy for his parents, being wholly a matter of hope.

So too the Apostle himself wished us to rejoice, because from the hope of a good conscience that we possess in Christ through faith, which works through love, laughter is generated for us by grace.

[67] Hence we strive with virtue so that, like Isaac, we may receive a hundredfold in hope, sowing in the same year—that is, in the present life—and may possess eternal life in the future. But because in Isaac the hope of life is represented, we must take Rebecca, who is interpreted as “patience,” in marriage, lest hope quickly be broken without patience.

But, as the Apostle says: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Romans XII, 12). Hence Rebecca is said to have been born in Mesopotamia, since Mesopotamia is surrounded by rivers, so that, having been schooled amid temptations and storms of tribulation and trained by many injuries of hardship, she may know how to bear children for God from the conception of hope, and reverently meet meditating Isaac in the field, covered with the mantle of virtues.

Isaac—that is, the hope of God’s promises—meditates in the field where he knows that the treasure has been hidden; and patience, his wife, meets him, arranging everything through her embrace, so that through labors and struggles he may be able to dig out the treasure and at last happily reach the promised hope. It was on account of this hope that the blessed Apostle warned his hearers: “Let us live justly and piously in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the Lord” (Titus II, 13).

This is the hope that has advanced even within Christ’s veil; and, like the dawn when it is struck by waves, because it is joined with patience, it remains so great and immovable and is endangered by no difficulties. We rightly introduce this patience into Sarah’s tent when, however much we are wearied by labors, we entrust everything with the greatest patience to the grace of the Redeemer.

And from such parents what else is generated than charity? Since hope promises us things such as “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered in any way into the human heart,” we surely cannot fail to love. Hence charity, once begotten, continually burns more intensely and, fighting against all carnal vices, overthrows them.

But why should I say that charity is signified by Jacob? If we carefully observe, we shall be able to see it very easily, especially if we bring forward only his two wives, Leah and Rachel. Leah is interpreted as “laboring,” while Rachel is said to mean “the beginning of sight.” When charity first rightly desires her in marriage, she ardently endures the labors of the present life. Whatever exceptional danger there is, she overcomes it without ceasing, struggling through patience all the way to death.

So much so that the labor seems little to her if she can perhaps reach the one whom she loves. Hence it is written: “You have desired wisdom; keep the commandments, and the Lord will provide it for you” (Ecclesiasticus I, 33).

But Leah—that is, the active life—is given first in marriage at night, while here we are commanded meanwhile to love our neighbors through charity. For if we do not first love the neighbor whom we see, we cannot love the Lord whom we do not see as we ought.

The same patriarch is rightly called first Jacob and then Israel. For that same charity first embraces the practical life by overthrowing vices through labors; afterward, through contemplation, it most certainly enjoys God face to face, as he is.

Hence the Apostle says: “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity; but the greater of these is charity” (1 Corinthians XIII, 13). And why is it greater? Because when what is partial has come to an end, we shall enjoy charity alone and contemplate what is perfect, that wisdom which is God; and thus, living blessedly with it and through it, we too shall be blessed.

For its sake every religious person serves and labors strenuously in the struggle, desiring its immense beauty, if he may someday deserve to reach that beginning of sight and happily delight in it. No one turns to serve righteousness through charity for any other reason than to live in peace in the Word, through whom the beginning—that is, God—is seen, and to rest immediately after labor.

Who would ever have loved to toil at works of righteousness, to undergo the labor of suffering, not for Rachel, but rather for Leah? Who ever sought that life for its own sake, or sought through death the life that all abandon by dying?

Hence charity loves God with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all the strength for no other reason than for his own sake; but it intends to love the neighbor not for the neighbor’s own sake, but for God’s sake, and strives to serve him through charity.

Nevertheless, although for the sake of that same Rachel—that is, for the sake of the beginning of the vision of eternal life—we perform all works of virtue with complete devotion, Leah is first placed beneath us at night, because the laborious life could not be loved for its own sake, so that through it, generating children of virtue for God, we may at last reach the sweet embraces of heavenly life.

This one is endured so that the other may be enjoyed. While the other is sought, this one is placed beneath us, so that after this one we may reach the other. We serve first, when Leah is loved by us, for seven years—that is, observing the seven commandments of the Law that pertain to love of neighbor. Then we take up another seven years according to the perfection of life, if somehow we may ardently enter upon the one we desire.

Hence it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” And: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” Also: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” And: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for theirs is the fullness of eternal life.” And: “Blessed are the merciful and the peacemakers, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew V, 3–7).

Happy, therefore, are the monks whose incentives to virtue are such as these. For if they truly are what they are called, these increases of virtue prepare the blessedness of the kingdom in their life. Although they do not yet possess it in reality, they are crowned daily with such things in hope.

They would wish, if it were possible, to reach immediately the delights of beautiful and perfect wisdom without enduring the labor that embraces action and work. But this cannot happen here, while one lives on the earth of the dying. This may also be signified by what was said to Jacob: “It is not customary in our place for the younger to marry before the elder” (Genesis XXIX, 26).

She is rightly called “elder” because she is earlier in time, on account of the instruction of the divine will, although the other surpasses her deservedly on account of the vision of divine beauty. This, I say, is charity, designated by the two names Jacob and Israel. When it has been wearied by struggles all the way to the dawn of morning light, it will be called Israel alone, because thereafter, as I have said, charity will contemplate God face to face and rejoice without end in the embraces of everlasting light.

Whoever wishes to be blessed in the seed of Abraham and counted among his children must first enter these three stages of virtue, and then encamp daily, advancing, toward the remaining ones. For without these, no works of virtue lead us by the road that is Christ to the homeland.

Hence I rightly infer that God is called the God of these three only so that through them he might demonstrate those who, according to the inner person, are propagated in these three virtues and devoted to divine worship—those whose God he is not ashamed to be called.

He dedicated all these to himself, according to the grace of election, as servants. For what else does it mean to say, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus III, 6), [70] than openly to show that he is the God only of those who are gathered into the merit of these three virtues?

Or, to put it more suitably, what else is proved in anyone than these three mystical gifts of virtue? Through them the divine word passes from the particular to the general, and God is called the God of Abraham—that is, of those who are justified with him through faith and become fathers of many virtues, so that, according to the promise of the seed, all may be found united in the same one.

God is rightly understood as the God of Isaac—that is, of those who, rejoicing in hope, suffer tribulations; their voice is that of the Apostle: “For he made us sit in the heavenly places” (Ephesians II, 6). They glory most fully, not yet in reality but in hope, and are weakened by no promises of eternal life.

Hence the Apostle divinely exhorts believers: “Therefore, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in the heavens” (Colossians III, 1).

Hope makes us such people rejoice and causes us to be dedicated under the name Isaac, because, living justly and piously in the present life, desiring nothing other than the blessed hope, we await the coming of the Lord. Since God is found to be their portion and inheritance, he is rightly called the God of Isaac—that is, of those who rejoice in hope.

But because for the present God is attributed to Jacob rather than to Israel, this designates that charity which here works through love of neighbor together with faith and conducts the business of the active life in hope. For while one lives with these, no one here enjoys the vision of God as he is.

Therefore, in the meantime, he is rightly called the God of Jacob rather than Israel, lest what does not yet exist be nominally granted as a gift to those who are still in the struggle, without the grace of fruition.

Nor should you be surprised that I said that through these three the universality of the elect is designated, as it were, through particular examples, when elsewhere Noah, Job, and Daniel are taken to represent all those who alone will be delivered by their righteousness at the end. “Their own,” I say, because, freely justified through faith, by adhering to the works of those fathers whose names he foreshadowed, and preserving the righteousness of God, they acquired their own salvation through their merits.

Similarly, in these cases, God is understood as the God of those who are joined to the fathers through faith, hope, and love and serve divine worship. For, as is plainly evident, no one approaches God without these three virtues, nor is God called the God of those whose life’s work does not display these virtues as the virtues of all virtues.

Having therefore encamped in these stages, we shall travel more easily under Christ’s leadership through the remaining ones, piling the works of the other virtues upon these. For these are perfected only through the works of all the virtues, so that the true Hebrew may at last reach the land that is Christ, long promised to the fathers.

There, immediately before the others and more significantly after those whom the evangelist listed earlier, Judah first appears. His name is rightly interpreted as “confession,” because, after we have entered upon the Christian journey through these three steps of virtue, we must at once prepare ourselves for confession of faith, so that before kings and governors—or, certainly, whenever we are released for a time from temptation—we may hold confession no less in heart than in mouth, lest through the weakness of the flesh we suddenly abandon the virtues we have received.

If Peter had preserved this confession altogether during the Passion, he would not have incurred the danger of denial. But because he feared to confess Christ, he suddenly set aside the ardor of faith and charity and did not escape the snare of denial.

Yet, so that he might not remain longer in the abyss of despair, divine mercy immediately looked upon him, and what he had done wrong through the instability of faith he afterward cleansed more bitterly through confession.

Confession is said to be twofold: one kind is confessing God through faith and steadfastly retaining this confession, with the ardor of charity, to the end of life amid every torment; the other is being cleansed through confession of sin after we have fallen, when conscience accuses us.

Both virtues are nevertheless proclaimed. The former is wondrous because of the virtue of martyrdom; the latter is praiseworthy in a certain sense because of confession and the remedy of sin. The former is crowned by martyrdom; the latter at least merits pardon after guilt.

Of the former it is said: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew X, 32). Of the latter: “There is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke XV, 7).

Nor is it without reason that Judah is placed in the fourth position, because God the Trinity, although he must be worshiped everywhere through the three virtues already mentioned, is proclaimed to human beings through the fourth alone, namely confession.

Thus we read: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans X, 10). Therefore, whoever you are, Christian, if you wish these three virtues to advance you toward salvation, clothe yourself with confession, so that you may be able to emerge victorious against all adversities.

For the devil sought to have them all, to sift them as wheat. But you will either preserve completely, through confession, the treasure of faith entrusted to you, so that against the vices of temptation you may prove yourself a Christian; or, after guilt, you will be cleansed by repentance through confession alone.

Otherwise, whoever you are, you will not escape if you fail to hold fast to one of these virtues.

Perhaps, therefore, Christ wished to be born from Judah, who is fourth from Abraham, and chose him—passing over three brothers—from whom he would come according to the flesh, so that, once we have received the grace of faith, hope, and charity, Christ might be born from our confession, when we truly profess him in conduct and voice. Thus, being divinely united to him in the seed that is himself, we may enjoy blessing, even if we fall after baptism.

Therefore, because the wise men of the world have said that there are three movements of the soul, we must immediately be restored through confession, which follows in fourth place. Thus Christ, who is slain within us by desire, anger, and human reason, may immediately rise again and be renewed through true confession of sin for his former work of charity.

Reuben, who is said to be “poured out like water,” denotes desire. Simeon is assigned to the vice of anger, since his persistent fury is reproved as criminal. Levi, moreover, bears the form of reason, and the keeping of the Law is entrusted to him.

But because human reason does not prevail against the divine judgment, whatever is negligently contracted through these three movements must be erased by confession.

Of this confession the Prophet beautifully says: “You have put on confession and beauty” (Psalm CIII, 2), namely, adorning Christ in everything through faith and conduct, so that we may not be found naked. Rather, through this confession—because the beauty of virtue and the confession of faith are always present in his sight—we present ourselves everywhere before the Lord and are found clean and undefiled.

Whoever, therefore, is reckoned by the Christian name should not glory merely in being called one rather than in being one. For this is the four-sidedness of the virtues that makes a perfect Christian, firm on every side with complete solidity. Upon it the structure of the remaining virtues is more solidly established, since without these no virtue can subsist and no one can be a Christian.

But because we have lingered long at the foundation, taking the royal road, it remains for us to come more quickly to Phares and Zara.

Phares is interpreted as “divided” in our language; Zara seems to signify “rising.” He is rightly called Phares whom the torrent of tribulation divides from the midst of Babylon together with the people on pilgrimage.

Hence the Prophet cries out—or rather, the Lord through the Prophet: “Come out, my people, from the midst of Babylon; come out, you who bear the vessels of the Lord, and do not touch what is polluted” (Isaiah LII, 11).

He had rightly separated himself from the people, that is, from earthly things, who said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians II, 20). David also says: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Psalm XLII, 1).

As the holy people of God advanced through such increases of virtue, they went rejoicing toward the homeland of Paradise and continually stretched themselves forward toward what lies ahead. Hence, in Zara, as they contemplated the morning dawn of God, the sun of righteousness shone everywhere in them, and the true Lucifer rose in their hearts.

In Esrom, moreover, as though drawn up in battle formation, we direct the arrows with which Christian warfare is armed against the enemy. Of these arrows it is said: “Your arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath you” (Psalm XLIV, 7).

Holding these arrows, the sons of the “shaken-out” ones (excussorum)—that is, the apostles—went everywhere flashing like lightning and bringing every height into captivity. It will come to pass that the whole world will be subjected to God.

Each person then places these arrows of virtue against his heart when he receives the compunction of the divine Spirit and devoutly applies, as destroying agents against every chill of sin, the coals taken up with tongs from God’s altar.

And thus it comes about that at last we reach Aram, which is interpreted as “chosen” or “exalted,” because those who have been nourished by these virtues are found to be a chosen race, according to the grace by which each person is favored.

Happy, therefore, is the one who, according to God’s election, has been called exalted through the intervention of merits and has deserved to be approved as chosen at the final examination by God.

While such a person lives here on the road, he is suitably called a “willing people,” which is Aminadab. For he voluntarily sacrifices himself to God each day and freely offers himself in all the commandments and judgments of the Lord, which are the instruments of good works, continually meditating upon them.

Otherwise the offering of a work will not be acceptable to God if it has not been dedicated willingly, from the abundance of good will. Hence, in the Law, those who offer gifts are expressly required to be voluntary, so that what each person has may become acceptable—not what someone does not possess in his will.

Nothing, therefore, is richer than good will. It then truly becomes devout if it always looks toward the future dwelling-place and directs its attention unceasingly to eternal goods.

Now Naason is perhaps interpreted as “augury.” And what is “augury,” if not right faith, through which, contemplating divine things, we regard as of little worth the promised riches of human things?

Everything earthly becomes worthless if those things that are promised to us in heaven are rightly considered, as though through augury. Perhaps Joseph therefore boasted that he had been instructed by such augury, and for that reason said to his brothers: “Do you not know that there is no one like me in augury?” (Genesis XLIV, 15.)

The augury of the saints, which consists in confidence of receiving what is promised, gives great firmness to what it promises; unlike the error of the gentiles, in which there is nothing except the false invention of demons.

But because the true observer of divine things, always contemplating, longs for what is above, he must at some point render himself perceptive and understand the mysteries of God’s commandments. Instructed by these sacramental meanings, the Prophet said: “From your commandments I have gained understanding; therefore I have hated every way of iniquity” (Psalm CXVIII, 103).

And the Apostle says: “Think of the Lord in goodness and in simplicity of heart” (Wisdom I, 1). What, then, is it to think of the Lord in goodness, if not to perceive him sweetly in some manner and, with a kind of palate of the heart, taste beforehand how sweet the Lord is?

Such a righteous person rejects every desire of the flesh, if it is in us, and by refreshing us strengthens and consolidates us amid present miseries. Meanwhile, whoever thus perceives the Lord cannot perceive the anxieties and pleasures of the present life, because the Lord’s greatest strength is in him.

Nourished by such a sense of sweetness, Booz—whose name signifies “in him is strength”—is most suitably called “strengthened” by this taste. Thus, when Elijah had received food from the hand of the angel, refreshed by its taste, he walked in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights as far as Mount Horeb, the mountain of God.

We do not doubt that this mountain signifies Christ, toward whom each faithful person hastens daily through these increases of virtue, destined eventually to reach him.

Therefore, when the holy soul of a man has tasted for a little while how sweet the Lord is, immediately, ignorant of the world, it burns with the fires of love and becomes strong, so that it does not seem impossible to it to reach what it is striving toward.

Having become stronger in battle, it leaps over and despises everything adverse that confronts it. If it begins to grow weary, immediately, sensing God present everywhere as its strongest defender, strengthened by his arm, it does not falter.

Therefore, aided by the Lord’s consolation, the true athlete of Christ, always carrying the weapons of obedience, becomes Obed. For Obed is called “serving” in our language.

So that this service may be perpetual, it is rightly generated from nothing other than strength and the swiftness of the fear of God. Hence Ruth, from whom he is born here, is interpreted as “hastening,” so that the meaning may be that the warfare of the heavenly life arises from such parents and generates Jesse, whose name is said to mean “incensed.”

That is the incense which, within the Holy of Holies, where Jesus the high priest entered, is offered upon the altar as a most sweet fragrance to the Lord morning and evening. For to serve in this way is to give off the fragrance of good incense and to be happily consumed as a burnt offering to God in the fire of charity.

[Col. 0090A] Of this sacrifice of virtues it is indeed said in the Pentateuch: “And the Lord smelled the fragrance of sweetness” (Genesis VIII, 21). Otherwise, the burning of fleshly sacrifices produces a stench rather than a sweet fragrance for the Lord.

Or does God appear rightly to delight in such things, in which not even human sense, though at times nourished by them, delights when behaving more honorably? The fragrances of heavenly virtues are not like that. According to the Apocalypse of John, they are the prayers of the saints (Revelation V, 8).

Hence David said: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm CXL, 2). Because this incense is composed of many kinds of good works, it is directed into God’s sight with the greatest confidence of devotion, so that from it David—whose name is interpreted as “strong of hand”—may, as it were, be born from the merit of the virtues.

Nevertheless, although Booz is understood as “in him is strength,” the greater person is rightly judged to be the one who now attempts to do with his own hand what is in him and, together with God’s grace, is able by his strength to break the arms of bears and the jaws of lions, rather than the one who has hitherto been unwilling or unable to fulfill in works the strength that is in him.

By whatever strength a person has cast down the hostile powers, it is enough for him afterward to be regarded as Solomon—that is, “peaceful.” For no one here appears to fight more than for the sake of peace. And therefore, once vices have been overthrown and enemies subjected, it is fitting for each person to live thereafter tranquil and at rest, so that he may already begin to be what he is believed destined to become.

For “blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew V, 9).

What, then, is more blessed in this life, where nothing but quarrels and scandals flourish, than to be peaceful among those who hate peace? Or what is more difficult than, amid seditions and the machinations of vices, amid the frauds and snares of the enemy, to remain free from them and continually practice the things that belong to peace?

This is the seventh among the eight beatitudes, which is promised more fully in the future, when the adoption of the sons of God has been manifested; through it the supreme rest of the saints is signified. For in Genesis the seventh day is sanctified, and God is read to have rested on it. Through this day that eternal peace, which surpasses all understanding, is consecrated from the beginning by the grace of the Holy Spirit, as a foretoken of future things.

And if, beginning from the origin of faith—that is, from Abraham, who, having been justified by faith, first received the promise concerning Christ—you count all the generations together up to Solomon, fifteen are gathered, the steps by which one formerly ascended to the temple; and under that same number also
The songs of fifteen psalms are prefaced by headings. This number, certainly, consists of seven and eight, so that by these same steps of virtue it may make us sufficiently peaceful for the adoption as sons of God, and by the growth of our works may lead us upward to the summit of peace. We therefore refer the seven to the Sabbath and pursue the observances prescribed for life by the Law; but the eight we carry out on account of the glory of the resurrection, so that, tasting more fully and swiftly what the peace of the heavenly homeland is, we may become worthy to attain it.

He, therefore, has climbed no small height in this life—whoever, by the dispensation of the Lord’s grace, is now rightly called peaceful. What indeed remains for such a person except that, enlarged and established in charity through the progress of others, he should spread everywhere? For “Roboam” is interpreted as “breadth of the people.” 77 What, however, is the breadth of the people except charity? Of it, indeed, it is said: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Psalm 118:96). And again: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (ibid., 32). That person is rightly believed to be the breadth of the people who, with an enlarged heart, is shown to fulfill the way of God’s commandments by his works; for what is hidden and what is manifest seem to embrace everything within, while he devoutly carries charity in his conduct. No one is excluded from his embrace, because he desires that all should remain in Christ no less than reach him; and with chaste affections he rejoices and strives to love God for his own sake, and his neighbor for God’s sake.

Next comes Abia, whose name is interpreted as “the Father is Lord.” He is already encamped far away from Egypt, since, through the breadth of charity, having already become a son of God, he truly cherishes, honors, and loves all the brethren in Christ in the bosom of love. Such a person no longer sighs for pots of meat; but, as an heir of God and fellow-heir of Christ, he now savors, meditates upon, and attends only to heavenly things.

Furthermore, Asa, his son, is rightly called “one who raises up.” For whoever has reached this summit of holiness must always raise and lift himself toward higher things, so that, through the growth of virtues, he may swiftly ascend from this valley of tears. “He has set ascents in his heart.” And therefore he more quickly attained the name Josaphat. Josaphat thus means “he himself judging,” or signifies “the judgment of God.” For if the blessed soul raises itself daily so as to become spiritual, it is rightly interpreted as “he himself judging.” As the Apostle says, “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Corinthians 2:15). Yet he deals daily with himself by considering God’s judgment, lest, while examining everything, he himself be found reprobate in some respect.

This person, therefore, dwelling in the heights, considers all things from above and rightly rejoices that he has reached the heights of virtue. And so Joram, who follows, is appropriately called “the exalted,” according to the path we are traveling, so that the traveler on this road may learn to say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

Furthermore, Amasias means “an elevated people,” and Ozias “the strong one of the Lord,” so that this prophetic saying may cling to them both: “Rise up, rise up, O Jerusalem; put on strength, O arm of the Lord” (Isaiah 51:9, 17). The faithful person rightly raises himself toward higher things when he clothes himself not in his own strength but takes for himself the help of the Lord’s arm. 78

Next, Joathan is rightly understood as “progress,” because the mind of a holy man, while he lives in this life, continually makes progress and goes constantly from virtue to virtue, so that he may lay hold of the God of gods in Zion. Hence Achaz, who follows, is appropriately interpreted as “laying hold.” For the mind of the perfect man meditates with the Apostle (Philippians 3:12) on laying hold of that by which, through the divine dispensation of mercy, he has already been laid hold of. Therefore, after progress in works, the order of virtues follows, so that he may be understood as “laying hold.”

Next comes Ezechias, “the Lord is strong,” because such a person no longer lives for himself, but the highest virtue of Christ lives in him. And therefore it is not he himself but “the Lord is strong” who is more happily than arrogantly proclaimed in him. Consequently, because he is no longer himself in the effectiveness of his mind, although through the substance of the flesh he still dwells among the weakness of the world, “forgetful” is rightly joined immediately to him.

Thus Manasse is called “forgetfulness” in our language. Hence Paul, that outstanding preacher, “forgetting what lies behind,” pressed forward as quickly as possible toward what lies ahead (Philippians 3:13), so that he might be found faithful in Ammon; and through Josias, “the salvation of the Lord,” having been found as his companion, he himself might, after the end of life, gloriously sing with the angels: “Salvation belongs to our God who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb” (Revelation 7:10).

Now that our true Hebrew has passed through these successive dwelling-places, it remains for him to prepare himself according to Jechonias—not indeed for captivity, but from this place for migration, since blessed are those who are prepared to meet Christ. Hence we read elsewhere: “Those who were ready went in with him to the wedding” (Matthew 25:10). And likewise, the voice of the Redeemer says to the watchful servants: “You also must be ready.” Through this Jechonias, therefore, those are rightly understood in whom there is only preparation for the Lord, and who meanwhile await his coming until their petition is fulfilled. For Jechonias is shown by every circumstance to mean “prepared for the Lord.”

From him, then, Salathiel is begotten, whose name is interpreted as “God is my petition.” He designates the person of those who seek nothing on earth but say with the prophet: “One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek” (Psalm 26:4). God is found to be their portion and inheritance, and their continual prayer is that God may be all things in all things to them, so that one day they themselves may also be found to be one with him. 79

Zorobabel succeeds him and is called “teacher” in our language, so that he may display the teaching of truth to those who know how to refute, amid the darkness of obscurities, the confusions of those who dwell in Babylon and are still held captive, entangled in the snares of their sins. Such teaching is established in the Church so that, together with Jesus the great high priest, teachers may proclaim by the straight road liberation from captivity to those in Jerusalem who had been caught in the snares of error, and may make them understand what Abiu appears to signify.

For Abiu is interpreted as “my father is this one.” They are then rightly proved to confess him if, freed from the bonds of sins, they adore, honor, and worship no other than the one and same God who possessed, made, and created them.

From that region, then, let us now proceed for a while to Eliachim, who is called “the resurrection of God.” Let us rise in such a way that thereafter we may walk in newness of life and, aided by God’s help, conquer the enemies of our salvation, if at last we may deserve to be justified in Sadoch by him who justifies the ungodly and makes the pious out of sinners. For Azur is interpreted as “helped,” and Sadoch as “justified.” No one is justified before, aided by God’s mercy, he has been subjected to God’s justice, so that through him God’s help may be invoked.

Meanwhile, concerning Joachim, whose name means “my brother,” what else can we understand than what the Lord himself says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matthew 12:50)? Hence, in the Lord’s Prayer, we daily pray that his will may be done in us on earth as it is done by the angels in heaven. Such a will makes us one with God and joins and unites us with the truth above.

Here the prudent mind should carefully attend to the fact that we have not expressed their qualities or actions according to their mortality, but have shown, through the interpretations of their names alone, spiritual things by comparison with spiritual things, and the progress of virtues and the stages of the true way. For all the instruments of good works cling to one another, and everything is so interconnected that whoever lacks any one of them lacks them all.

And lest a fastidious listener say that the evangelist did not wish, in these names, to set forth an ethical teaching for those desiring to go to their homeland, let him consider why the names of some persons in the genealogical catalogue were omitted, while others were recorded in such a way that they both satisfied the number and evidently corresponded to the growth of virtues. If that Hebrew people, ascending through the desert, is said by catholic teachers to have climbed the path of virtues according to the interpretations of the stopping-places, how much more rightly is the way of life understood in those through whom Christ, according to God’s promises, is shown to have come to us in the form of a servant?

It is therefore fitting that we strive to approach him by the same line of holiness through which he deigned to show that he had descended to us. For he came as the Mediator of God and human beings so that there might be one firm descent of God’s goodness and mercies, and through him our daily ascent in virtues. Therefore I admonish my reader not to disdain, according to these interpretations of the names, to ascend the way of virtues through those by whom the Author of life did not disdain, according to the promises formerly made, to descend to us.

His descent, seen from afar, the bride in the Song of Songs perceived and said: “Behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills” (Song of Songs 2:8). What does it mean to say, “Behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains”? “Behold” belongs to one who points something out. How, then, is he shown as though present, when Scripture testifies that he is to come only after a long interval? It is because in all these things he was seen as though already placed before us in the seed, according to the promise. He was seen leaping over the mountains or bounding over the hills—not making his way through level ground or cultivated land, but traveling through wildernesses, over mountain peaks, and through the desolate places of the hills.

Therefore we have not inappropriately shown through these persons the moral way for him who wishes to ascend swiftly to the homeland promised for so long. Through them, and in them, we rejoice that Christ came down to us as one walking, like a roe-deer and a fawn of the stags. For he, exulting and playing, feared none of the hunters’ ambushes toward the mountains of Bethel, where we read that these men dwelt; he dreaded neither traps nor snares. Therefore, in a certain sense, he taught us to go by this way over the mountains of Bethel, by which Scripture showed that he had descended to us.

81 The journey to God is without stumbling if we pass from virtue to virtue and look before our eyes at nothing other than God, turning neither to the right nor to the left. Hence Eliud is interpreted as “my God.” Eleazar, however, appears to mean “my God is helper.” For God alone is recognized as theirs, and those alone walk this road with God’s help who advance to the point of possessing nothing else on earth except God, whom they desire to have in heaven as their highest and everlasting gift.

Accordingly, Mathan, whose name means “gift,” is immediately added, so that, while eagerly pressing toward that one eternal gift, we may meanwhile trample down our vices. Jacob, who follows, indicates that this must indeed be done, for he is interpreted as “supplanter.” For although above the supplanting of vices was introduced through Jacob, it is again recalled at the end through this same name, so that we may regard it as necessary to maintain a struggle against vices until the very end of life, until, added to our fathers, we are increased in eternal virtues in Christ.

Joseph aptly demonstrates this, for his name is understood in the conclusion as “added” or “increased.” Each person is then heaped with virtues when he has been added to the holy Fathers and has entered the city of virtues, where he will dwell forever.

For this to happen, Mary, the “star of the sea,” or “the illuminator,” must be followed in faith and conduct amid the wave-tossed waters of the sea, lest we be submerged by the floodwaters. Rather, through her may we be illuminated, so that we may believe Christ, born from her for the salvation of the whole world.

This, then, is that land which was promised to the Fathers in figure and in riddle. This land, I say, is the one of which David sings with longing: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 29:19). For this is the land inhabited only by the meek, of whom it is said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matthew 5:4).

Through these patriarchs Christ was coming into the world for our salvation. In himself he carried out the office of them all, and through the interpretation of their names he signified our salvation. Therefore the prudent investigator should carefully examine what Scripture, speaking here and there about those Fathers, and about matters pertaining to them, conveys to us. He will immediately find that everywhere Christ, as though looking through windows and gazing through lattices, declares to his bride, namely his Church, that he will soon come in the flesh.

For love of him, every soul must be stripped of vices, turn toward him who comes to it, contemplate his approaching arrival, and say to those who do not see: “Behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains” (Song of Songs 2:8). Over the mountains, certainly, so that they may first receive peace; then bounding over the hills, so that these too may be able to receive the righteousness that is in Christ.

You too, if you are a mountain, if the word of God leaps into you, if you pass from virtue to virtue, will receive peace. But if you are the second after the mountain—that is, a hill—Christ bounds over you. Yet this is so only if you are great enough to receive righteousness and complete works of virtue, so that through faith you may come to Christ.

But since up to this point we have heard Christ speaking to his Church behind our wall, amid riddles and mystical figures of obscurities, it was also necessary to enter the bridal chamber in which the Holy Spirit has prepared all the gifts of grace. But since Faustus, like a scorpion, spreads his poison at the end of this genealogy, we beseech the reader not to grow weary or look displeased at what we do by repeating ourselves, lest he entangle the simpler among us in his snares of error.

Therefore the matter must still be set forth, lest at the end of this genealogy he lie in wait for our heel like a serpent. For he labors to prevent us from entering by the straight path of faith to Christ, who was promised long ago to the Fathers. And he desires to abolish the belief that Christ arose from the stock of David.

Thus the crafty persuader speaks to himself, as though weaving a dialogue capable of ensnaring the simpler:

“What did Matthew write? ‘The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.’ I had thought,” he says, “that he would say, ‘The book of the generations of Jesus Christ, Son of God.’ But now, since Matthew here does not admit that he is writing the generation of the Son of God, but of David, he will meanwhile be born to me from Mary; so that, concerning the Son of God, you may observe only that no mention of generation is made in this text until the baptism is reached.

“But you,” he says, “bring this accusation against the writer in vain, as though he had confined the Son of God in a woman’s womb. If, especially, you consider the evangelist’s purpose, he rather wishes us to accept that he was made so at the waters of the Jordan through baptism than that he was born from the Virgin Mary. For there he says that the one baptized by John—the one whom he had designated from the beginning as David’s son—was at some point made the Son of God, only after about thirty years, according to Luke’s account. Then for the first time a divine voice descended upon him and said: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’

“You see, therefore,” he says, “that what was born thirty years ago, as it seems to this writer, from Mary, is not itself the Son of God, but that which was later made through baptism: namely, a new human being, whom we seem to believe was converted from the error of paganism to God. Yet I do not know whether this agrees sufficiently with the faith which you call catholic.

“Thus,” he says, “this is how it seems to Matthew, if these words are his. For at Mary’s childbirth it is not read that God said, ‘You are my Son,’ or, ‘This is my beloved Son.’”

Behold how madly and senselessly he speaks about Christ, so that we need no testimonies from Scripture to refute him—especially since the entire sequence of the New Testament, namely the teaching of the evangelists and apostles, clearly affirms everywhere that the Lord and Savior is one and the same Son of God according to his divinity and son of David according to the flesh, not by the opinion of a single author or the assertion of a single book.

We prove this from the Gospels and apostolic writings in such a way that no one can contradict it without contradicting those writings themselves. It is not as Faustus proposed to himself: that some unknown person spoke a few words, and that afterward no testimonies were brought forward against the cunning of the same trickster. Whenever anyone chooses to act in this way, nothing remains for the opponent to answer except that by which he tries even more clearly to mock and nullify the force of the most evident truth in the divine writings—answering as though falsehood had been introduced into the sacred Scriptures, and wishing in his madness to assert everywhere whatever sounds against him.

But since, by the dispensation of the Lord’s grace, the truth of the Gospel now prevails everywhere, and all the books, in every nation and amid every variety of languages, harmonize according to the catholic and apostolic faith, we must consider how far from the profession of blessed Matthew this man has strayed. Matthew commends one and the same Christ, Son of God and of man, from the beginning of his Gospel to its end.

He therefore differs from catholic teaching as greatly as, while we remain silent, he is shown everywhere by divine Scripture to differ from the truth.
