Whoever wishes to know how Matthew leads the one whom he calls the son of David through his narrative all the way to the passion and resurrection, continually designating him as the one and same Son of God and of man to the end, should read attentively. He will find that this wretched man raved and scattered the clouds of his empty words before the simple.

For although the blessed evangelist did not say at the beginning, “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom the Son of God was born,” but simply, without addition, “from whom Christ was born,” it is nevertheless sufficiently clear that he wished to identify the one whom the Apostle elsewhere testifies to have risen from the dead from the seed of David. And immediately he makes it as clear as daylight that this same one was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born from the Virgin Mary. To this he adds the testimony of the prophet: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted as “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14).

But here blessed Matthew—or rather, through him, the Holy Spirit—is seen to have proposed him not only without an addition, but even without the name Jesus, which he was accustomed to join everywhere. This was because the name had immediately to be introduced through the angel, so that shortly afterward it might sound more gloriously, and he might receive a name divinely bestowed—almost as a foreshadowing—for he alone had been prophetically announced from of old as the Savior in his very substance.

What, then, is greater, as this man asserted: that he was made the Son of God through baptism, when it was said, “This is my beloved Son,” or that the same Apostle brought forward divine testimony from the prophet, where, through the angel, the Virgin’s child is called “God with us”?

For although from heaven at the baptism, or certainly on the mountain, the voice sounded, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), he was nevertheless already the Son of God. For from the Virgin’s womb he received the form of a servant—the one who, existing in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized.

Finally, the Apostle Paul says most openly of him: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the Law.” Almost the whole of the New Testament declares that he was made of a woman, not from baptism, as this man falsely claimed.

And therefore, whoever wishes to oppose blessed Matthew in the way this man attempts, or wishes to deny that he was the author of this Gospel, must contradict the whole authority of the Church and struggle against all the streams of the divinely inspired Scriptures. For every page of the writings is shown to assert this with harmonious voice, and the faith of all people and the knowledge of every language are known to believe and confess nothing other than Christ, Son of God and of man, born from Mary and from the seed of David.

Therefore, because this madman dared by lying to oppose the summit of such authority, he was rightly expelled from the Church with all his followers and condemned by anathema, so that no memory of them should be found on earth except that they committed their nonsensical error to writing. 85

And lest, as I have said, the darkness spread elsewhere in any direction disturb a simple reader, we have taken care, as the place required, to note prudently the cunning of this deceit, lest through inexperience it entangle those of slower understanding and obscure the truth with lies.

Among other things, he still says through the deception of his poison:

“Nor can Christ himself, whom Mary bore—if indeed there was such a person—rightly be called David’s son unless it is established that he was wholly born from Joseph’s seed. Since you deny this,” he says, “you must also admit that he is not David’s son. For the generation which is traced from Abraham to David and from David to Joseph, and which is directed through all the Hebrew Fathers to him, is immediately denied to belong to Christ. Since Jesus was not conceived from that line, as is written, he is not found to be David’s son, as you assert.

“For the origin of the Virgin herself is not shown to have been from this tribe, from which David is known to have arisen, but from the tribe of Levi, from which priests altogether came. This is clear from the fact that she had as her father a certain priest named Joachim. How, then, is Mary said to belong to the lineage of David, when you see that she had neither a father nor a husband from that line?”

Rightly, then, this man—who contradicts the truth of the Gospel—claims authority for his falsehood from I know not what apocryphal book. But since, as we have said, we have already spoken about this as much as should suffice for the faith, we must now treat it more briefly, so that the truth may become more evident and we may not weary the reader.

Especially since this controversy of the Manichaeans has been so thoroughly stifled by the eternal anathema of all the holy Fathers and buried in the sleep of silence that it is not believed ever to rise again or to sprout further in any place.

Nor was Joseph not a husband because he had not united with her in intercourse. The holy evangelist himself immediately reports that the angel called Mary his wife; he also reports that she conceived not from intercourse with him but from the Holy Spirit.

If Matthew did not write these true things, but some other person, as has been supposed, composed falsehoods under his name, would he himself speak contradictions in matters so plain and so closely connected? Would he, while calling Christ David’s son and saying that he was born from the Virgin Mary without intercourse with any man, proceed by counting his parents step by step all the way to the very man whom he himself had said was not united with Mary?

But we are neither so foolish as to suspect such things about Matthew nor so foolish as to believe that these words belong to anyone other than Matthew. Therefore Joseph is rightly called Mary’s husband: he had her as his wife in continence, not through intercourse but through affection; not through the joining of bodies but through the union—which is dearer—of souls.

And therefore we firmly reject the claim that the Virgin’s husband ought to have been separated from the series of Christ’s ancestors, since through him, as we said above, Mary’s origin was shown. Moreover, since by the Law he was compelled to take her as a kinswoman, it is more clearly established that she came from the stock of David, from whose lineage no one doubts that Joseph descended.

By such indications, and by very many others, it is shown that Mary derived some descent of flesh and blood from David, so that the flesh of Christ, although born from a Virgin, would likewise unquestionably be proved to have originated from the seed of David.

What, then, appears contrary to the faith, when one and the same narrator says and commends both: Joseph as Mary’s husband, the Virgin as Christ’s mother, Christ as being from the seed of David, and Joseph, in the genealogical succession, as Christ’s ancestor from David’s line? Is it not more fitting to believe the Gospel than the fables of heretics?

Therefore, because we believe the sacred Scriptures, which say both that Christ is from the seed of David according to the flesh and that his mother Mary bore him as a virgin, not through intercourse, we also gather, no less certainly, examples from the divine Scriptures by which what the universal faith of the Church everywhere confesses and believes can be established more clearly.

The oracles of the prophets sing this; the Old Testament attests it through many enigmas of figures; the teaching of all the apostles confirms it; the voices of the angels also proclaim it; all the elements bear witness to it; and these four evangelists, filled everywhere with the Holy Spirit, preach it.

Among their proclamations of virtues, very many people from the common multitude are also reported to have held this view. For at that time it was manifest to everyone that Mary had descended from David’s origin.

As for what this man asserted—that her father was a certain priest named Joachim from the tribe of Levi—we do not accept it, because it is not canonical, nor can it move us, since according to catholic discipline that writing possesses no weight of authority.

But even if we believed it, we would rather say that Joachim himself somehow belonged to David’s blood: that he, or one of his ancestors, somehow belonged to the tribe of Judah and had been adopted into the tribe of Levi; or certainly that, though born in the tribe of Levi, he had some blood relationship deriving from David’s stock.

It could thus have happened, as the same false accuser admits, that Mary was of the tribe of Levi, yet was given in marriage to a man who was of David’s stock, that is, of the tribe of Judah; and we say that Christ could in this way also be received as David’s son.

For even if Joachim’s mother—Joachim being the man whom he mentions as Mary’s father—belonged to the tribe of Judah and David’s race, and married into the tribe of Levi, Joachim, Mary, and Mary’s son may nevertheless rightly be said to be from David’s seed.

This, or something similar, ought rather to have been believed if we were constrained by the authority of that apocryphal writing in which Joachim is read to be Mary’s father, rather than to make the Gospel a lie, in which it is written that Jesus Christ our Savior was begotten according to the flesh from David’s seed.

From this it is plainly evident that falsehood does not seek truth as a witness. Rather, it seeks what is doubtful or certainly false to itself in order to fortify its error; for when truth is present, falsehood is immediately overcome. Otherwise, unless it evades the truth, it cannot find room to lie.

And so Faustus, deceived by the one who does not stand in the truth and unable to bear the light of truth, fabricated a gospel of truth for himself—as though the true Gospel were false and apocryphal—and adopted it as a true witness. Thus the doubtful would be confirmed by doubt into uncertainty, and the false, proceeding from falsehood, would, as though punished for the penalty of sin, be chastised more severely in its lying.

There is no fellowship between light and darkness. Therefore blindness, as it becomes more deeply entangled in its own darkness, cannot behold the light of truth. For if it saw the truth as it is, it would no longer be blindness.

Although the obstinacy of the mind, with a conscience seemingly unaware, often struggles against the truth, it nevertheless bears witness against itself: the person who carries the darkness of falsehood within refuses to come out into the light.

Indeed, each person is blinded by his own light, when he does not fail to recognize the truth yet is not afraid, by lying, to deceive someone with the shadow of falsehood.

This is why Faustus, and nearly the whole school of heretics, attempted to violate and corrupt not only the evangelists but also the apostles and all catholic teachers. They scattered the Gospels and corrupted the Epistles of the apostles, making them their own rather than Christ’s. Whatever in them sounded contrary to their doctrine, they erased entirely.

Then, corrupting them still more boldly, they dared to say: “This part belongs to the Gospel of Matthew, or of Luke, or of another evangelist; but this part belongs neither to him nor to the catholic faith.” They made everything doubtful to themselves, so that they might never attain knowledge of the truth.

Thus it is evident that they were not enlightened by the Holy Spirit, nor illumined. For this reason they remained outside, wandering beneath their own darkness.

But the holy Church of God, because from the beginning it received the Spirit of God, is never moved by errors, deceived by frauds, or deprived of promises. Truth was believed while promising truth, and therefore it is obscured by no errors.

For he says: “I will send the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, and he will teach you all truth” (John 16:13). Nothing, therefore, lies outside the whole truth except falsehood alone. And so, apart from the Holy Spirit, we now receive no other teacher, admit no lie, and are seduced by no falsehood. Rather, we believe and confess what the universal Church believes—the Church that rejoices to have come everywhere into the whole truth and to preserve the path of pure faith without deviation to the end.

The Scriptures, therefore, which say that Christ was from the seed of David, and which we believe, would have sufficed for us; they can never be convicted of falsehood by their enemies, even if we had been less able to show that what we assert is expressed more explicitly in those same writings.

But now, because the divine Scripture itself everywhere testifies that Christ was to be born from David’s seed, and because in those same writings we find this expressed more clearly through indications in their wording, let us hold to the clearest and strongest testimony designating the same one whom we read was everywhere and most firmly promised in the Old Testament: that he would come from a virgin, when he would come in time, and where he would come in time.

Not, as this man slanders, enclosed in a woman’s womb, as though the one whom heaven and earth cannot contain were absent from beyond it; but, remaining in himself, reigning with the Father, and governing the whole creation, he reaches powerfully from end to end and orders all things sweetly.

In his ordering of all things, it was wondrous that he created a mother for himself on earth, through whom and from whom he might receive the form of a servant, so that through her he might free servants and, having conquered death, redeem us.

But because, with the breeze of the Spirit blowing, we have leapt farther than the expositor’s office in the conclusion of this book, as though into the middle doorway of a house, we now proceed to the following verse, looking back and forth from this point.

Christ’s generation, however, was as follows. It is as though he were saying: The generation by which Christ deigned to come was such that he might be shown to have taken flesh through Joseph from David’s stock, while he is believed to have been conceived not through that same Joseph, but of the Holy Spirit. What, then, does a generation traced from David have to do with Christ, if Mary’s origin is not believed to have descended through Joseph? Wishing to express this more clearly, the evangelist says, “Christ’s generation was as follows.” It was as follows, I say: Mary’s origin was to become clear through Joseph, while Christ was to be conceived and certainly born not from Joseph’s seed but from a virgin, of the Holy Spirit, just as had been promised.

He is born both God and man. Therefore the statement concerning his generation refers to both natures: through that part in which the sequence of generation is described according to the flesh, he is shown to have been human; but through that by which he is conceived of the Holy Spirit from a virgin, he is most manifestly declared to be God. It should also be noted that he did not, as Faustus asserts, become the Son of God through the regeneration of the Holy Spirit in baptism. Rather, already when he is conceived, he is wholly and identically the one who is generated from the Holy Spirit. Thus he does not become so in baptism; instead, the Word, made flesh, is born from the Virgin’s womb. Because he is the Word, we believe him to have been born before the ages from the Father as the Son of God; but because he was made flesh, we fully confess that he was born today in time from the Virgin.

It is believed that here he placed only the name “Christ,” without the addition of “Jesus,” as we have said, [Col. 0101A] so that you might understand him to be the one of whom the Prophet had said, “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:9). The name “Jesus,” which was substantially inherent in him, he reserved for the angel to pronounce, so that the one who was shortly afterward going to say that he had been conceived of the Holy Spirit might himself divinely declare his consubstantial name—as though it were a proper name—and, in accordance with the office of salvation promised in the prophets, might make it known in a more exalted manner to all who desired to understand.

Moreover, at times the evangelist—or rather, through him, the Holy Spirit who had led him into all truth—says, as though pointing inward from both sides, “Christ’s generation was as follows.” It was as follows, I say, in the manner prescribed; certainly as it was immediately commended in writing, just as afterward it was more manifestly displayed through signs and wonders.

“Christ’s generation was as follows.” [Col. 0101B] Therefore whoever wishes to understand it must believe it as it is prescribed and signified. Otherwise Isaiah confesses, saying: “If you do not believe, you will not understand.” Certainly you will not understand that a virgin will conceive and bear a son, nor will you remain in him—that is, in Christ, as other codices have it. For you will in no way be able to call him Emmanuel, which means “God with us.” Since, then, belief must come first if we wish to understand the divine words that are spoken, let us by every means avoid weighing them by human standards. Human understanding must be laid aside wherever everything that is said is divine.

For what is born as God from a virgin is not custom but mystery; it is not nature but power and condescension; it is not an ordinary sequence but authority. What, then, will worldly wisdom grasp here, and what will the understanding of the flesh seek, where everything narrated is divine and ineffable? [Col. 0102A]

“Christ’s generation,” he says, “was as follows.” Therefore, to speak more profoundly, he did not say, “It was made thus,” but “It was thus,” because Christ’s generation was with the Father when, through this genealogy set forth above, he was being generated from his mother. But whatever was, certainly always was. Therefore he always was—the one who “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). Consequently, unless you first believe that Christ’s generation was as follows, you will be wholly unable to understand that it is divine and therefore cannot be explained by words.

If he was on earth because he deigned to be, as we have heard, so also he is in heaven—something we have come to know nowhere except through him. Since, by the Lord’s grace ordering these matters, we have been granted to know much about this generation on earth, if anything remains hidden, let us believe with the whole devotion of our minds that Christ’s generation was as the evangelist testifies: beginning from Abraham and descending through David all the way to Christ. Beginning, indeed, from faith and commending faith also at the end, so that through faith he may eventually lead each of his hearers to contemplate the vision of his glory.

Therefore, after this sequence of the reading has been unfolded at length, let us too, with our senses restored in Christ, rest for a little while; so that, returning at the beginning of another book, and for a time revived more keenly by the sight of his light, we may be able to behold more sublimely and attentively, through contemplation, the mysteries of his generation already in the womb, as proclaimed by the angel.

## PROLOGUE TO THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0101]

[Col. 0101C] Since we now have in our hands the figures of past events and the predictions of all the prophets, by which Christ, who was once to come in the flesh, is foreshadowed, the Holy Spirit must be invoked with the utmost devotion of mind. He once promised us the Savior’s coming through the mouth of all the prophets. He must indeed be invoked so that he himself may open the eyes of our hearts, lest, because we are less capable on account of the veil of the flesh, we fail to understand sufficiently the one whom they, seeing from afar with their own visible eyes, discerned and, as though standing before them, pointed out with a finger—the one whom they truly and faithfully knew would come.

Hence it is that everywhere they say, “Behold, he comes.” For what else does it mean to say so frequently, “Behold, he comes,” as though presenting before our eyes one who did not yet exist, except to promise visibly to everyone the one whom they perceived everywhere as God present? They perceived him in the Spirit. Therefore the one whom they saw without time—before whom past and future are present—even though the fulfillment still had to occur, they indicated as present. For he is, as the Prophet says, “the beholder of all the ages” (Sirach 36:19).

Thus they too, carried beyond themselves in the Spirit, gazed in the present upon whatever the divine Spirit revealed to them as future. For eternity, since it exceeds all time, certainly comprehends at once everything that takes place in time. Hence the wise men of this age, wishing also to show eternity to us, said: “Eternity is the complete and perfect possession, all at once, of interminable life”—which becomes clearer by comparison with temporal things.

To this eternity the prophets, carried in the Spirit beyond themselves and beyond everything bodily that exists within time, saw as present that which was already present in him before time. For there always exists, present all at once, the boundless possession of things, together with the fullness of events and the totality of causes. Because the sluggishness of all the heretics could not reach this point in order to see it, they were surrounded by the darkness of blindness and did not recognize him as present in the Virgin’s womb, as was fitting, nor as begotten from the Father at the beginning, creating all things, as was necessary. [Col. 0102D]

Therefore we must earnestly implore that our mind be illumined by the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that by his divine inspiration we may sometimes understand in accordance with the truth of the matter; but at other times, where it surpasses our understanding, may submit ourselves to divine things in such a way that eventually, through humble devotion, we may be raised by the Lord’s grace to the summit of supreme understanding. Then reason, illumined from heaven, will see most rightly what it could not initially perceive by itself.

For in human matters, whatever is known is known not from its own nature but from the nature of those who comprehend it. If human reason proves insufficient to discern the matter under discussion, nevertheless whatever it is will remain what it is in its subsistence. We, however, will either be cleansed of ignorance by simplicity or be deceived by the rashness of falsehood.

Therefore, if anyone wishes to understand the truth of the divine majesty and to know the purity of the Son of humanity born from a mother without a father, let him not speak from himself alone, but, irradiated by the divine Spirit, let him say something about it as it is by knowing it from that Spirit. For unless each person is enlightened concerning God as is fitting, he understands nothing at all.

Hence it is that wicked people, not yet enlightened, while attempting to fashion God for themselves from their own resources, are not only wrapped in ignorance but also lose through error the simple faith they could have possessed. And therefore, from the depths of my heart, O God our Trinity, I earnestly invoke and beseech your majesty: grant that I may explain more clearly the mysteries of this holy Gospel, following in every respect the footsteps of the holy Fathers, with the same Spirit by whom these mysteries were divinely watered for the advancement of all.

I implore you: in your mercy rule my understanding, lest, presuming anything about myself, I stray from the path of truth. Supported by your grace, may I perceive from you everything that must be narrated in it; and whatever is lesser because I do not yet grasp it, may I more suitably leave to another—the Holy Spirit—to disclose, so that by every means, through devout dedication, I may avoid falling into the audacity of rashness. [Col. 0104A]

Grant, I ask, most gracious Ruler, by your ordering grace, that what I cannot yet understand I may at least grasp through complete faith; and whatever is proclaimed in these same writings, may I hold wholly by believing it. May neither my life nor my conduct contradict the understanding of truth. Truly, it is a great sacrament of divine assistance granted to us who meanwhile walk by faith, if we are not corrupted by the darkness of sin.

I know, therefore, most holy Creator, that no one who thinks rightly confines you wholly within the judgment of understanding, nor determines that you remain outside the understanding of perception. Thus I do not presume that everything belonging to faith can sometimes be comprehended by reason alone. Rather, by diligently following the way of truth, I ask that I may never, contrary to faith, form an opinion about faith without faith.

For this reason even the greatest men are often shown to have fallen. Whatever differs from the understanding of the Holy Spirit, who uttered the words read in the holy Scriptures, must be attributed to ignorance—or rather to error—rather than to virtue. Since they were stubborn in following their own judgment and barked against the divine Spirit, they could not receive its true understanding.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0103]

[Col. 0103C] “When Jesus’ mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph.” Here the first proper question is why Isaiah promises only a virgin, saying, “Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son” (Isaiah 7:14), whereas the blessed evangelist calls her betrothed, while with equal agreement he also confesses her to be a virgin.

It is by no means without purpose, in the work of divine providence, that Wisdom, which reaches from end to end and orders all things gently, preferred to be born from a betrothed woman rather than from a merely virgin woman. Unless, perhaps, we must admit that Isaiah foretold this to those who did not yet believe, using a designation that would become a miracle to everyone; whereas the evangelist, revealing the truth of the matter, indicates what is also a mystery for us.

For although the Gospel is no longer shadow but truth, nevertheless, on account of the mystical words of its teachings, no point, letter, syllable, word, name, or person in it is empty of divine figures. Hence the reason for the matter is that a bride is sought here, so that through her the future universal Church of Christ might already then be signified as destined for betrothal, and the whole might be gathered in the particular, in accordance with what the prophet Hosea declares:

“I will betroth you to myself in mercy and compassion,  
and I will betroth you to myself in faith” (Hosea 2:19–20).

For what else does “I will betroth you to myself in faith” mean except to show that Mary conceived Christ from the Holy Spirit through faith? Here the universal Church is prefigured as ultimately to be filled with the Holy Spirit, through whom she too daily gives birth to Christ in the hearts of believers—not only because she is mother and virgin, but also because she is called bride in every respect.

Hence John says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29). And blessed Paul says: “I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). Truly she is a bride who, through a virginal birth, brings forth Christ’s new infancy.

Therefore, as we have said, the mother-bride is first prepared here in the particular, so that afterward, through this union of flesh, the Church may be gathered in the universal. For because of the fact that the Word was made flesh, the whole Church is gathered into the body like its members; and, united to Christ by grace, the bride is already then prepared for Christ in the bridal chamber.

Wishing, therefore, for the blessed evangelist to prefigure the grace of election in Mary, he first commends her as bride, whom afterward he confesses to be wholly a virgin. In this way, as I have said, he establishes in the particular all at once what was still to be accomplished in the universal.

For this reason too he wished Christ to be born from a betrothed woman rather than from a merely virgin woman, so that Christ’s genealogy might be woven not through a woman, contrary to the custom of Scripture, but through a man, as was customary. Another plausible reason is also offered: so that she would not be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress. Who at that time would have believed that a virgin had conceived from the Holy Spirit rather than condemning her as an adulteress?

And lest someone perhaps say that the divinity of Christ could have assisted him by other means, lest anything unworthy of a man occur, let him know clearly that God’s plan—unknown to the ages and generations—was concealed beneath flesh for the work of healing. Therefore, for the time being, it was necessary that the cradle be concealed by the weakness of his parents, so that God hidden in the human being might gradually be disclosed to believers through other indications of power.

Otherwise it would not have been something new—unless it were contrary to nature, or rather beyond nature—for a virgin to bear God and man without intercourse. Joseph is also taken as her betrothed for another reason, as a suitable witness: not only to preserve her unharmed, with the modesty of her virginity protected from suspicion, but also so that virgins would not be given a pretext for excuse, because the Lord’s mother had been disgraced by accusations.

Hence a witness to chastity is chosen and provided as a husband who could refute every reproach against her virginity and, by concealing the birth, protect it, even if he did not recognize the mystery. For childbirth is the reward of marriage among women. Thus no opportunity for deception was left to anyone, since a betrothed virgin could not be accused of having covered herself with a lie when a witness to her chastity had been appointed, while the sayings of the prophets resounded over him, the ministries of angels were active, and their proclamations confirmed that God had been born as a child.

While the star served as guide, the gifts of the Magi testified to this same event; and, as had been foretold, the shepherds’ hearts confirmed it. Through such reasons and others of this kind, divine providence arranged that the Father’s Wisdom should be born from a betrothed woman. In her, as he testifies through Solomon, “he built himself a house and hewed out seven pillars” (Proverbs 9:1).

By these pillars the whole house that he built for himself—namely, the holy Church of God—is sustained, supported, and governed throughout the entire world. It should also be noted that the one who is conceived from the Holy Spirit first builds a house for himself and hews out seven pillars: that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, from whom he is conceived, and through whom he confirms, strengthens, and makes everlasting those who believe in him.

He would certainly not do this at all unless the one who is conceived possessed the same authority as the Father and the Holy Spirit. Therefore he is rightly said to have hewn out the pillars for himself: while remaining eternal with the Father in the same authority, he consecrated Mary and through her united the Church to himself, distributing to her the seven principal gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Otherwise they would not only have condemned her to death as an adulteress, as in the case of Susanna; they would also have falsely claimed that they had justly killed Christ as one born from adultery. Hence it is that meanwhile Joseph was believed by almost everyone to be the father, to such an extent that the evangelists, following popular opinion and in accordance with the law of historical writing, expressed him as the Savior’s father.

When he fled into Egypt, he also provided support as a foster father, lest the Virgin, deprived of strength, be broken by the troubles of her circumstances. Through this too, as some say, the Virgin’s childbirth was concealed from the devil, while he saw the betrothed man, with devoted affection, serve marriage in chastity; for perhaps he could not clearly discern whether the child had been born without seed or simply from the Virgin.

Therefore the succeeding evangelist adds:

“Before they came together, she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit.” [Col. 0106A]

Hence it is that he is conceived and that he is generated. He does not say, “Before they came together,” in such a way as to imply that they came together immediately after the birth, as we grieve that a certain foolish man misunderstood it. Rather, simply wishing to indicate the time immediately preceding the marriage, he shows that before they came together the effect of coming together had already occurred in the womb, without intercourse, so that she who had previously been a betrothed woman began to be a wife without the work of a man.

It is as though he had said: Before they mingled kisses and embraces, before they performed the act of marriage, she was found to have in her womb something greater than a work of nature, because what is born is from the Holy Spirit and is called the Son of the Most High according to the angel’s testimony.

The wretched man of whom I spoke—the most foolish of men—did not understand that this form of expression occurs frequently, not only in the sacred Scriptures but also in secular writings. For example, let us say: “Matthew, before he died, never strayed from the truth”; and: “Some other person, whoever he may be, was overtaken by death before he had done penance.” It does not therefore follow that the former strayed from the truth after death—when he then entered into all truth—or that the latter did penance after he died, which he had not done before.

Therefore it plainly does not follow that Mary had intercourse after the birth, since it is entirely clear that she did not do so before the conception. And if this kind of expression necessarily implied such a conclusion, many testimonies of Scripture would contradict it.

Accordingly, rightly warned by such language, let us say that every faithful person ought to die before believing that anyone had intercourse with Mary after the birth. And if persecution arises from this, what cannot be confessed after death must not be admitted before death.

That dull-witted yet crafty disputant did not understand that this was said specifically of her in the Song of Songs, although we understand it to be signified generally of the Church. For whatever is narrated in it in a particular form is marked out more explicitly in the universal.

The Bridegroom says:

“A garden enclosed is my sister,  
a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Song of Songs 4:12).

Thus she is a garden enclosed, because the Virgin’s womb was wholly intact and incorrupt in every respect. It is called a garden because all the delights of paradise blossomed in it; and the womb of modesty is sealed, where the fountain of our redemption sprang forth.

It was sealed, I say, because the blood from which the stream of liquid flowed remained uncontaminated and incorrupt. Therefore, because it was sealed with the seal of modesty, she was found by the bridegroom to have a child in her womb—not from anywhere else, but from the Holy Spirit—so that this same investigator of the mystery might also become a witness to her chastity.

“She had in her womb,” he says—not “receiving from elsewhere”—so that, in some manner, the prophecy of Jeremiah might be fulfilled: “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth, and a woman will encompass a man” (Jeremiah 31:22). She will encompass him by giving birth from herself and nowhere else, so that it might be something new and unheard of throughout the ages: that a virgin should conceive and afterward remain incorrupt.

Otherwise it would not be something new—unless it were contrary to nature, or rather beyond nature—for a virgin to bear God and man without intercourse.

It should also be noted that Jeremiah calls her a woman, while Isaiah, in order to proclaim the matter more wondrously, designated her a virgin. The former calls her a woman to display her sex, and both indicates and introduces the word “new” to explain that she was a virgin. The latter, in order to soften unbelievers toward faith, more plainly prefigured a virgin who would give birth as a miracle.

Meanwhile, as we have said, she was found by Joseph to have a child from the Holy Spirit. It is not absurd to ask why afterward he deliberates with himself, as though uncertain, and decides to dismiss her. It is plainly evident from this that she was found by him to be pregnant, but that he was completely ignorant whether it was from the Holy Spirit or from some other act.

He knew that he had taken her as a virgin and had kept her untouched; nevertheless, uncertain about her, he chose a middle course by which he might escape appearing to conceal what he did not know, and might not hand over for punishment as guilty the woman whom he knew beyond doubt to be innocent.

The addition, “having a child from the Holy Spirit,” appears to have been added in advance by Matthew out of ardent love, before the angel explained it—especially so that the reader’s mind might not immediately be seized by a suspicion that would afterward need to be cleansed by the angel’s words.

Although Joseph knew that she was pregnant not through carnal intercourse, he did not know that the child was from the Holy Spirit. Therefore, uncertain between the two possibilities, he chose, as I have said, a middle way of escape: he would dismiss her secretly, because up to that point he certainly did not know from what or what sort of thing was within her.

Concerning the statement that she was found to have the child “from the Holy Spirit”—or, as it is in Greek, *ek pneumatos hagiou*, “from the Holy Spirit”—it should be understood that whatever is from another is either from that other’s substance or from that other’s power. It is from God’s power, for example, when it is said that all things are from him; but from substance when the same Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Here, therefore, it must be understood as referring to power rather than substance. Nor should the Spirit be understood to have become incarnate, even though the Son and the Holy Spirit are of one substance.

Joseph, her husband, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her. [Col. 0107D]

Here, as in any other place, we must understand “husband” to mean nothing other than “betrothed,” according to the usage of the divine Scriptures, just as we understand “wife” to mean nothing other than “betrothed woman.” It is the custom of the holy Scriptures to call betrothed men husbands and betrothed women wives.

A few testimonies among many should therefore be drawn from Deuteronomy, so that what we are saying may become clear:

“If anyone,” he says, “finds a virgin betrothed to a man in the countryside, and, using force, lies with her, let them both die, because he humbled the wife of his neighbor” (Deuteronomy 22:25).

And in another place:

“Who is the man who has betrothed a wife but has not yet taken her? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in battle and another take her” (Deuteronomy 20:7).

And elsewhere:

“But if a young woman is betrothed to a man, and a man finds her and humiliates her, let them both die: the young woman because she did not cry out, and the man because he humiliated the wife of his neighbor” (Deuteronomy 22:23).

From these and other passages of Scripture it is therefore evident that betrothed men are called husbands. For this reason we rightly understand him here as a husband, especially since the affection of love is preserved in him, which is true marriage, and in her the fruit of marriage was found without intercourse.

I see no obstacle, then, to Joseph rightly being called husband and Mary wife, except that sexual desire alone could not intervene where virginity was being preserved for the formation of a life of perpetual chastity.

But what does it mean that Joseph is rightly called righteous? He is not inflamed with zeal for chastity, nor does he even investigate the cause. Yet this itself is testimony to Mary’s modesty: he knew her to be innocent, so that by preserving her he could rightly be called righteous.

Nevertheless, the action seems more appropriate to a compassionate man than to a righteous one, since he did not wish to hand a pregnant woman over to death. But the virtue of each is true according to divine judgment only when compassion is not found without justice, nor justice without compassion. If separated from one another, they collapse, so that justice without compassion is called cruelty. Thus everyone is rightly called righteous because he is compassionate.

The holy evangelist, however, commends him more as righteous, so that through this he might be a witness to Mary’s chastity. He demonstrates him to be compassionate when he says that he did not wish to expose her.

The word “expose” (*traducere*) seems capable of referring to both possibilities: either that he delayed taking into marriage the woman whom he had received as betrothed, or that he did not wish to expose her to punishment, in which he knew there was no disgrace of betrayal. But the word “expose” is found in Scripture more often used to signify guilt than any other cause.

Since, therefore, she had not been conceived from the root of original sin, it was just that he himself should not expose her, because he was conscious of her chastity; and because of that justice he himself is deservedly called righteous. Through fear he was found to be compassionate; but through the knowledge of her chastity that he possessed, because he did not wish to expose her, he is certainly approved as righteous.

Some say, indeed, that this word is expressed more significantly in Greek as *paradeigmatisai* (παραδειγματίσαι), which is interpreted as “to make public” or “to expose openly.” The sense would then be that he did not wish to make her conception known to everyone.

But, following the authority of our translator, we judge more truly that what we drink has been translated from the Hebrew fountain, since we have no doubt that this Gospel was first written in that language.

“He wished,” it says, “to dismiss her secretly.” Why secretly? So that, if it became public, she would be punished altogether as an adulteress; or else, if he kept her with him while ignorant of the outcome, he would make himself guilty before the Lord as one conscious of sin.

Let the rash hear this and learn, amid uncertainty about causes, to deliberate for a long time within themselves out of reverence and fear of God, lest, driven by the danger of frivolity, they fall into something worse.

As he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream. [Col. 0109A]

What, then, does “as he was considering these things” mean, except what the evangelist introduced beforehand by anticipation? The sense should plainly be rendered as though he had said: While, before reaching a decision, he was considering in his distress what he should do—whether he should dismiss her secretly or should expose her—and while he had begun to deliberate with himself about these things, wishing to dismiss her secretly, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying:

“Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife.”

When the holy man’s mind was distressed and shaken by the novelty of the matter, and when, amid the darkness of ignorance, he had chosen compassion lest, under the guise of justice, he incur cruelty, he was suddenly consoled in sleep by the angel’s affection and assured concerning the conception.

It is therefore evident that during the delay he was committing everything to God, not knowing what he should do. For this reason he soon deserved consolation, lest he incur guilt.

And we too, brothers, whenever the darkness of uncertainty troubles us, whenever the appearance of things deceives us and the surface of circumstances sometimes makes us ignorant of their inner truth, let us withdraw from an immediate judgment, hold back our decision, and flee danger. Let us entrust everything to God, lest, while rashly attempting to determine a judgment, we prepare ruin for ourselves through another person’s peril.

The fact that the angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, rather than through some other and clearer revelation, signifies the uncertainty of his mind. While he was doubtful and anxious amid his distress, as though oppressed by the sleep of unbelief, he did not deserve to see the angel in a visible manifestation. Yet because, through fear and devotion, he appeared righteous in his compassion, at least through sleep he was able to see the vision, lest the guilt of uncertainty weigh longer upon one whom the justice of equity commended.

It should also be noted that the angel is said to have appeared to him not “in sleep” but “in dreams.” Perhaps he was shown through many visions until his faith was sufficient; sleep concealed him for a time because Joseph was surrounded by darkness.

Yet I think we should inquire, according to the proper meaning of the word, whether the divine speech may wish to signify something more precise by “in dreams” than if it had said “in visions.” For sleep is the repose itself of those who sleep, whereas a dream is sometimes the deception of the sleeper.

Hence it is said that the angel appeared, because an extraordinary reality was disclosed beyond the phantasms of dreams. It was not Joseph’s nature to see the angel whenever he wished, but it was in the power of the one appearing when and how he would present himself.

For divine Scripture, frequently using this word and this kind of expression, always signifies the power of the one who appears, raising us to consider more deeply the circumstances of events, to which the manifestation of the one who reveals himself almost always conforms.

Thus, because Joseph, uncertain in anguish, was weighed down by that sleep in which the eyes of the apostles were pressed down during the Passion—not, however, because his uncertainty arose from hardness of heart, but from astonishment at the greatness of the event—he was at least instructed in dreams, so that what he carried within his heart might be revealed.

Significantly, it is also added, “the angel of the Lord,” to distinguish him from another angel and prevent the appearance from being thought a chance deception. Since compassion and justice seemed to contend in Joseph, his uncertainty was immediately dispelled and the mystery revealed.

What had first been shown through the angel to Mary was plainly disclosed, and immediately became a mystery. It seems quite extraordinary if Joseph could not learn through Mary what had once been told to her. But because, for the sake of certain wearisome people who favor brevity, we omitted from our inquiry matters that are even more profound in the mystery, let us turn to the remaining commentary that follows.

“Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife.”

These words, spoken with the affection of one who consoles, designate him as especially familiar and known to the speaker, whose name and lineage the angel expressly declares. This is surely done so that he may recognize the words once spoken to David:

“The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not frustrate him: ‘From the fruit of your womb I will set upon my throne’” (Psalm 131:11).

Joseph knew that he had descended from David’s stock, and therefore he had to be reminded to recall from the Prophet what he already saw being fulfilled in himself and in Mary.

Indeed, when he is called “son of David” here, Mary is understood, since he had recognized that she had descended from the same stock from which he himself, the son of David, was called by the angel. Wishing to show this, the angel says, “Joseph, son of David,” as though he were saying plainly:

“Recognize what was said to the house of David, because what was promised there in prophecy has now truly been fulfilled through Mary. Therefore do not fear to take Mary as your wife. For although the one who will be born will not be born from your intercourse, a son is generated for you through her, because he derives the kinship of flesh from you.”

And lest you suspect that he was begotten by another, know that he is from the Holy Spirit, so that you may grasp in the mystery the whole of what you once possessed in the promise.

Just as you hear me call you by lineage in your own person and reiterate the whole genealogy in you, so that you are said to be born as the son of David in the thirty-eighth generation, understand more closely that Mary is, in a reciprocal manner, derived in some way from your flesh. I warn you to accept a son without intercourse and to possess her as your wife with the fullest affection of love.

“For this reason,” he says, “do not fear.”

It is as though he were saying: “Do not fear guilt; rather, embrace your wife in the service of love, because love casts out all fear.”

Why he called her “wife” has already been explained above, including the fact that nothing belonging to the work of marriage was lacking except the mingling of sexual desire. To such an extent does Christ’s birth according to the flesh pertain to Joseph that, in some manner, he can be called the Savior’s father.

“For what has been born in her,” he says, “is from the Holy Spirit.” [Col. 0110D]

Here too a very subtle understanding seems to arise, lest what has been born in her be absurdly understood as the son of that same Spirit from whom he was conceived, in accordance with what we ourselves confess in the Creed. For we say that he was conceived from the Holy Spirit and from the Virgin Mary.

If we understand this in such a way that we call him the son of the Holy Spirit according to his humanity, we clearly introduce two fathers into the holy Trinity: one as the propagator of his divinity, and another—the Holy Spirit—as the propagator of his humanity. But who would dare say this?

Therefore it is understood otherwise, and it must be asked whether he is called born from the Holy Spirit for this reason: because the Spirit caused him to be born from the Virgin. For this wondrous work was accomplished entirely as a gift of God, and the gift of God is properly called the Holy Spirit.

Moreover, the Spirit himself is everywhere proclaimed by catholic teaching to be the love of the Father and the Son. It was this love alone that brought him to become incarnate. Therefore, because he was born from the Virgin Mary, it is rightly interpreted that he was born from the Holy Spirit, since love alone was the cause of his birth.

Nor is it permissible to say that, because God made this world, he is therefore called the Son of God or in any way proclaimed to have been born from God. Rather, it can rightly be said to have been made, created, instituted, or founded by him—or whatever similar term may be appropriate.

Nor should it be conceded that whatever is born from something else must immediately be proclaimed the son of that same thing. I shall set forth a few examples among many.

Certainly all who are reckoned under the Christian name are born from water and the Holy Spirit, since they cannot be Christians in any other way. But would anyone rightly call them sons of water or sons of the Holy Spirit? Rather, they are called sons of God the Father and of the holy mother Church.

Thus, although the Son of God is said to have been born from the Holy Spirit in a very different sense, he must in no way be called the son of that same Holy Spirit.

It also seems that the angel’s statement, “What has been born in her,” is intended to instruct certain people further. For it is not our custom to call someone “born” before he comes into the light of this world, since that birth has not yet been completed. But perhaps we should understand the expression according to the customary manner of speech in the holy Scriptures, where what is known to be future is often narrated as already past.

Or certainly, according to the foreknowledge that the angel possessed from God—for whom what is future is already like what is past—he is rightly understood to have been born.

And she will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. Elsewhere, according to Luke, the same thing is read as having been said to Mary [103]: “Do not be afraid, Mary,” he says, “for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great, and he will be called Son of the Most High; and the Lord will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:30–33). I have said all this so that at least the angel’s voice may be believed to establish that Mary came from the stock of David, something Faustus had contradicted above; and so that the faithful hearer may understand that all the promises of the patriarchs [Col. 0111D] and all the utterances of the prophets harmonize with this promise: the one who is promised must reign forever. Moreover, since the angel says to her, “you shall call,” the same words which he had previously spoken to Mary, we ought to observe that the same angel remains consistent in his judgment, commanding each of them, so that divine Scripture—which in many places promised Jesus by name, namely as “Savior” or “salvation”—might represent him as having already come through the voice.

For he himself will save his people from their sins. Wishing, then, to interpret his name, the angel added: “He will save his people.” For the sickness of our vices could not otherwise have been healed unless the salvation of believers had arrived. [Col. 0112A] Although there had been many people named Jesus in former times, this one was substantially called “salvation.” And we must note that he is not coming, as the Jews mistakenly suppose, to save an earthly Jerusalem; rather, he came to save his people from their sins. “His people,” he says, because, although we had been sold under sin, we nevertheless belonged to him by the laws of nature. Hence Zechariah says: “And he has accomplished the redemption of his people in the house of David his servant” (Luke 1:68). Therefore, the people whom he foreknew as his own he undoubtedly came to save; all the rest he left, by his hidden judgment, in the mass of damnation. It follows:

Now all this took place so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, when he said. What, then, is this “all this” that took place, or which of them said it? [Col. 0112B] For if we say that these are the angel’s words, there nevertheless remains the question of how it can be said, “All this took place,” since Jesus had not yet been born, had not yet been named according to the law of circumcision, and had not yet saved by his passion those for whom he had come to redeem. Although this might seem capable of being resolved by saying that all things which have not yet happened are already present before God, we think it more likely that the Evangelist added this afterward [104], when all these things had unquestionably been completed in fact. It is as though he were saying: All this—that before they came together Mary was found to have conceived from the Holy Spirit; that the virgin bore a son; that he was called Jesus; and that he saves his people from their sins—took place so that what had been spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled; [Col. 0112C] for the fulfillment of this one event also completes many mystical sacraments.

But another question is again raised here: how are we to understand the statement, “All this took place so that what had been spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled”? For if all this took place so that Christ might be born of a virgin, because the prophet, foreknowing that it would happen, foretold it, then it seems to follow that the sole reason Christ came in the flesh was the prophetic prediction. If we reply that the prophet’s word depended on the foreknowledge of God, who spoke future things through the prophet’s mouth, it follows that the utterances of the prophets necessarily had to be fulfilled precisely as they had been foretold, and that everything future was bound by necessity. For it seems plausible that God foreknows all things and cannot in any way be deceived, so that whatever his foreknowledge saw as future must immediately come to pass. Therefore, if—as they say—he foreknows not only the deeds but also the plans and wills of individuals, there will be no freedom of choice. For nothing other than what had been foretold through the foreknowledge of the prophets could have existed in the deed itself. Thus, because the matter could not have happened otherwise, those who are pressed by the necessity of foreknowledge seem not to be held guilty of crimes, since the prophetic utterances prescribed those acts for them, so that nothing else could occur until everything had been fulfilled that had been proclaimed about them by divine speech before they were born. [Col. 0112D]

Our own teachers, disentangling this question, have said: Things do not happen because divine providence foresaw that they would happen; rather, conversely, divine providence cannot fail to know what was going to happen. Yet it seems sufficiently backward to say that the events of temporal things are the cause of eternal foreknowledge. For what else is it to suppose that future things are foreseen with complete clarity because they are going to happen, than to think that things which once happened were the cause of that supreme divine providence? [Col. 0113A] Or perhaps [105] should we say that what is foreseen does not necessarily occur, but that what is going to happen must necessarily be foreseen? Yet this interpretation sounds quite contrary to the statement: “All this took place so that what had been spoken by the Lord might be fulfilled.” Here we must admit that this one and singular event, because it rises above every exercise of free choice [Col. 0113B] and surpasses every human merit, perhaps took place for that reason—not as though it had been sought through our free choice, but so that what had already been not only foretold but also foreknown by the Lord might be fulfilled. For we do not say that anything is fulfilled unless it is already capable of fullness. Therefore, since it was already in the predestination and foreknowledge of God that it should receive fulfillment, what did not yet exist before it occurred already existed in a certain manner; and thus what was already there is fulfilled. It existed, I say, in God’s eternity, though it was to be brought about in time. Consequently, nothing other than what already existed was done, so that what had been foretold and predestined might be fulfilled for us; for it was already entirely capable of occurring then in precisely the manner in which it occurred.

Hence the Apostle says: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law” (Gal. 4:4). [Col. 0113C] Therefore, when the fullness of time came—when it had been predestined in God’s eternity, before the ages of the world, that he should come—God sent his Son, made flesh from a woman. Thus there was no new will in God and no necessity of coming arising, as it were, from prophetic speech, but only the presentation of the truth. The Prophet, looking toward the future, said: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84:12). What, then, does it mean to say, “Truth has sprung up from the earth,” except openly to show Christ arising from Mary like a shoot from the earth? For it was right that, from the fullness of God’s foreknowledge, the fullness of his promises should be fulfilled in the fullness of time. Otherwise all the utterances of the prophets would remain empty. [Col. 0113D] But because the prophets’ predictions had been drawn in truth from the fountain of truth, nothing else could come to pass except that what they had promised should be presented.

Moreover, since above we said, according to certain people, that freedom of choice appears to be taken away, so that not even just punishment follows—for, as they say, prophecy prescribed sinners for guilt—we must understand that prophecy does not impose the necessity of sinning, nor does it prescribe anyone in such a way that, because things were foreknown, it compels people to fall into ruin. Rather, these things were foretold so that they might be signs of God’s presence, bringing healing to believers. For no sign brings about the thing it signifies; it is only the sign of the thing it displays. [Col. 0114A] Therefore prophecy does not create the necessity of the things it foretells; it is a sign of God’s foreknowledge and a remedy for our weakness. Thus the person who does not doubt that God knows all things may infer from prophecy that the one who foretells future things before they occur cannot be wholly ignorant of present things.

Things foreknown are foretold so that a hard and unbelieving mind may not be able to resist when the event arrives, lest it refuse to believe what had once been announced and foreknown before it occurred. Rather, it should submit more fully to God and obey the divine will, lest through arrogance it resist or suppose that God certainly does not care about mortal affairs. If someone says that, because things were foreknown, they cannot happen otherwise—since they cannot be foreknown unless they are certain, and, more firmly still, since foreknowledge belongs to God alone as an act of willing, so that whatever he foreknows cannot fail to happen—I will admit that, insofar as it is referred to divine knowledge, this future event is altogether necessary; but when it is considered in its own nature, or in relation to the will of the agent, some things happen entirely through free choice. [Col. 0114B]

Two kinds of necessity seem to arise in this argument. One is the necessity by which all human beings must be mortal; the other is conditional necessity, as when, if I see someone walking, he must be walking. The necessity involved in walking seems to belong to free choice, while that involved in mortality is the punishment of sin. The one who walks is in some manner made to walk by his own will or desire; the mortal person, however, is made by the punishment of sin to return to the earth even against his will. [Col. 0114C] Thus all things that God’s providence observes in contemplation occur necessarily when referred to the divine gaze; but when considered in themselves, they occur either through their own freedom—although, because of the punishment of sin, they are carried into vice—or, once freedom has been restored, they surrender their own will to God’s grace for merit.

For this reason, although things come to pass in their existence through a gift, they nevertheless possess the reward of recompense because of labor; or else they do not escape the proper vengeance of sin on account of their offense, since before they occurred they could, in a certain sense, also have failed to occur. Therefore, if you pay careful attention, you will find many predictions in prophecy that were not fulfilled in deeds in the manner in which they had been foretold [107], because they were either rendered void by grace forestalling sins, or else, through free choice together with God’s grace, granted to penitents for pardon. [Col. 0114D]

From this we can clearly establish that one kind of prophecy arises from God’s predestination, and must occur in every respect: truth, which already exists in God’s eternal will, is fulfilled temporally in the course of events, sometimes without the exercise of our free choice, as in the matter now before us. Another kind arises from God’s foreknowledge, in which our free choice is involved; and, with God’s grace cooperating, we either attain a reward or, when he justly abandons us, are dragged toward punishment. One of these comes from predestination; the other remains only in foreknowledge.

There is also another kind of prophecy, properly called a threat. It is made rather as a sign of divine retribution than as a terror arising from foreknowledge, because the thing foretold is foreknown in a very different manner from the way in which it is threatened as coming. A sign is made so that those who behold it may flee from the face of the bow and the elect may be delivered, while those who resist may be seen to be justly punished in suffering. [Col. 0115A] It would be pointless to gather examples of these matters, since they are evident even to those who do not seek them.

But because we have gone on at greater length on account of the objections of certain people, although I have not said enough to avoid burdening the reader, let us once more fix the eye of our mind where eternal—not, as we understand it, merely foreknowledge, but the true knowledge of God—surpasses all temporal movement. Let us see, as far as we can, how the prophet, carried away into the divine knowledge of truth and predestination, said, as though pointing with his finger: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive” (Isa. 7:14). For in the word “behold” there is a showing of present things [Col. 0115B]; but in “she shall conceive” there was a foreknowledge of future things. Yet when the Evangelist again takes up the same statement as testimony and says, “All this took place so that what had been spoken by the Lord might be fulfilled,” there is no doubt that this is the temporal manifestation of God’s foreknowledge and predestination, and, in accordance with what the speaker saw, the fulfillment of the promises in the present display of truth.

Therefore, if we wish to weigh foreknowledge correctly—the knowledge by which God recognizes all things—we shall more properly call it not foreknowledge but the knowledge of an ever-unfailing presence [108]. In our usage, “prevision” seems a legitimate term, but, insofar as it comes from God, it is more properly called “providence.” It is called providence because, established far above events, it sees all things as if from the lofty summit of the world. [Col. 0115C] Hence, if we do not wish to conceal the truth from ourselves, a great obligation of moral integrity rests upon us: we must always be vigilant, because we too are continually seen before the eyes of the judging God, and all our intention is constantly present before him.

“Behold,” he says, “the virgin will have a child in her womb, and she will bear a son.” To this the Jews, always ready to slander, reply that the Hebrew text does not have “Behold, the virgin shall conceive,” but “a young woman,” wishing by this term to signify the nature of age rather than integrity, so that through this the mystery of our faith might more easily be emptied of meaning. [Col. 0115D]

But first let us ask them how something can be called a sign if a young woman, and not a virgin, has given birth. For the prophet says: “The Lord himself will give you a sign.” If, therefore, it was a sign, there is no doubt that it occurred outside ordinary human experience. Hence Jeremiah also says: “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth: a woman will encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22). For it would not be a sign, nor could it be considered anything new, unless a virgin could conceive and bear a son without sexual intercourse.

Nor are we deceived as though, according to Isaiah, the Hebrew text contained *Betula*, which means “virgin.” Instead, *Alma* is placed for this word, which, apart from the Septuagint, all translators rendered “young woman.” Now *Alma* is an ambiguous word among them. It means both “young woman” and “hidden woman.” But the Septuagint translated *Alma* as “hidden” in nearly every place where it occurs. [Col. 0116A] Aquila, following them, also frequently interpreted this word in the same way. From this it is understood that it signifies not only a girl or virgin but also, as though by an epithet—for why should a word that is fixed as a name not often perform an adjectival function among us?—a virgin who is deeply secluded and most secret, one who had never been exposed to the gaze of men but had been carefully guarded by her parents.

In the Punic language too, which derives from Hebrew sources, a virgin is properly called *Alma*. Therefore, since the Hebrews make use of words from nearly all languages, perhaps the prophet adopted this term into his utterance so that it might portray what she was destined to be, because *Alma* in our language is understood as “holy.” [109] [Col. 0116B] That they themselves also use words from other languages is shown by the Greek word φορεῖον (*phoreion*, “litter”) in the Song of Songs, where we write: “King Solomon made a litter” (Song 3:9); the same word is also read in the Hebrew text. There are many other words from foreign languages which they have adopted into their own speech. And, as the expertise of the holy Fathers teaches—those who proved themselves highly accomplished interpreters from that same language—they unanimously testify that they have never read *Alma* of a married woman, but always of one who was a virgin.

From this it is also understood that Mary was not only a virgin but also a girl of youthful age. Indeed, it is a designation of greater praise than “girl” or “virgin,” for one who might perhaps barely have reached the marriageable years of adolescence and still have had no knowledge of a man. Hence in Deuteronomy also a virgin is designated under the name of “girl” or “young woman.” “If a man,” it says, “finds a betrothed girl in the field, and, using force, lies with her, you shall kill the man who lay with her, but you shall do nothing to the girl,” and so forth (Deut. 22:25). [Col. 0116C] Here “girl” plainly indicates nothing other than a virgin.

Likewise, in the Book of Kings we read that they sought a young virgin and brought her to the king. “And,” says Scripture, “the girl was exceedingly beautiful, and she ministered to him, but the king did not know her” (1 Kings 1:4). If the Jews object that, in this passage of Isaiah, the Hebrew text does not have “virgin,” let them understand the idiom of the divine Scriptures, and it will become clear that girls are very often called virgins. And, as some explain more precisely, a virgin among the Hebrews has three names: *Alma*, *Betula*, and *Nara*. But in this passage only *Alma* ought to have been used, because it signified all these things together: a girl, an adolescent, a hidden woman, and one made worthy by virginity; hidden through the care of her parents and adolescent because of her youthful age. [Col. 0116D] For *Nara*, they say, designates a little child who, because she is not yet grown, does not yet understand what feminine modesty is.

Meanwhile, what follows is:

And they will call his name Emmanuel. In the Hebrew text, according to the prophet Isaiah, it does not say “they will call,” but “you will call.” For there he was speaking specifically and particularly to the house of David; here, however, he speaks generally of the whole human race: “they will call.” Nevertheless, in Isaiah the word *Karathim*, which all translators rendered, can be interpreted as either “you will call” or “he will call,” so that the sense may be that the virgin Mary herself ought also to call him Emmanuel. [110]

From this we must note that the Evangelist did not follow the order of the words but their meaning, when he said “she will have a child in her womb” instead of “she will conceive,” and announced “they will call” instead of “you will call.” [Col. 0117A] For it is one thing to conceive in some manner from elsewhere, but another not to receive something from elsewhere and instead to have it from oneself; for whoever already has something will not receive it.

By these words, then, his birth from the Holy Spirit and from the substance of the flesh is clearly indicated. For by saying “she will conceive,” he wished it to be understood that what the virgin did not possess from herself in order to bear a son would come from the Holy Spirit. But the statement here, “she will have a child,” makes clear that she would have within herself, from the substance of her own flesh, what she had not conceived from elsewhere through intercourse. Thus Jeremiah’s prophetic saying appears: that the Lord, doing a new thing, would cause a woman, with her womb closed, to encompass a man.

“And they will call,” he says, [Col. 0117B] “his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us.” It is therefore rightly asked who said this phrase, “which is interpreted ‘God with us’”: the prophet, or Matthew? But since it is not found in the book of that prophet, we judge that the Evangelist rather than the angel or Jerome is the interpreter of this expression. For we do not believe that he added anything of his own as interpreter; indeed, we have no doubt that he translated everything word for word or sense for sense.

Yet another question arises here: since Matthew wrote his Gospel in the Hebrew language and used a Hebrew word, he seems to have had less need to interpret it in that same language. To this we must reply that, although Emmanuel is a Hebrew word, it is nevertheless exceedingly obscure among them, just as many words among us are obscure. [Col. 0117C] It was therefore necessary to explain it more clearly, so that such a great promise would not be obscure in any wording, but would become more evident to everyone through this explicit restatement.

For Emmanuel is a proper name, just as Jesus is, a name he was called by evangelical command. Thus, through these two names, it is proclaimed that the one who appeared as God and man in our flesh would be not only our Creator and Restorer, but also our Governor and the Providence who cares for all things. For when the angel calls him Jesus, he more fittingly identifies him as the Savior of those who had perished. [111] But when the prophet calls him Emmanuel, he indicates that he himself, as he promised, remains daily with those whom he has once saved, healing and helping them continually. [Col. 0117D]

The Evangelist John explains what it means to say “God with us”: “The Word,” he says, “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Thus the prophecy of Baruch is fulfilled: that he appeared on earth and lived among human beings (Bar. 3:38). For this same Emmanuel is commended as God and man together, understood as one and the same person.

This is plainly why we now confess with the Catholic orthodox not merely that Mary is the mother of a man, but also that she is θεοτόκον, that is, “Mother of God.” We therefore devoutly believe that this God-with-us is present, as it was marked out in prophecy and disclosed by the Evangelist through the same testimonies. We confess that he dwells with us because, except for sin, he graciously became everything that we are, coming clothed in our flesh. [Col. 0118A] Therefore, because he was from us and for us, he is rightly called Emmanuel, God with us, so that through this we too may be one in him.

The Evangelist appears to establish those things from the Old Testament which he sets forth in the Gospel for three effective purposes: first, as a testimony to the mystery of the New Testament, so that it may have, according to the Apostle Paul (Rom. 3:21), testimony from the Law and the Prophets; second, for the firm confirmation of our faith, so that these things may more easily be believed when we see fulfilled what had been divinely not only foreknown and predestined but also proclaimed by mortals before it occurred; and third, for the joining of the Old and New Testaments, so that what Ezekiel saw might be displayed—“a wheel within a wheel” (Ezek. 1:16), namely, the New Testament prefigured in the Old—and so that people might be encouraged toward their spiritual understanding when they saw that the spirit of life was the entrance. [Col. 0118B]

But Joseph, rising from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him. Here the perfect obedience of the righteous man is clearly described, when it says: “He did as the angel of the Lord commanded him.” For unless one does precisely what is commanded, does nothing other than what is commanded, and does it when and where it is commanded [112], there can be no true obedience. [Col. 0118C]

Here we must take care lest, misunderstanding the statement, “He did as the angel of the Lord commanded him,” because the angel had said to him, “Do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife,” we should be shipwrecked in faith, as though, because he commanded him to take her as a wife, we should say that Joseph practiced the acts of marriage in obedience. Helvidius, wishing to assert this, was overcome by the sluggishness of his own mind and crushed beneath the weight of the divine Scriptures; at last he learned that he had not known even what he had long been completely ignorant of.

Therefore, as we said shortly before, recalling the same matter, we acknowledge that, although she had been betrothed to Joseph, she rightly passed into the status of wife; for in their relationship, apart from sexual intercourse, there is found not only affection but also the fruit of marriage, with virginity preserved. Since she displayed the whole affection of service and love by following obedience, she is rightly said to have done everything that had been commanded her by the angel. [Col. 0118D]

Here we must note that the designation “angel of the Lord” is added so that he may not be thought to have been some evil angel, and so that no opportunity for deception may appear in a matter through which divine mysteries are accomplished and the highest devotion of angels is celebrated.

“And he took,” it says, “his wife, and did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son.” Behold, the aforementioned adversary of Christ labors in vain, asserting that the word “knew” refers more to intercourse than to knowledge. It is as though any one of us would deny this, so that from it he might construct the argument that “until” signifies a definite period. Since Joseph did not know her until she bore her firstborn son, he would conclude that, once this period had been completed, she immediately became known to him, and that only the birth of the son had prevented him from having intercourse with her beforehand. [Col. 0119A]

In answer to this, we briefly profess that in the holy Scriptures we understand the word “knew” in two ways. It often refers to knowledge, as when the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem and his parents did not know it. It also refers to intercourse, as this person tries, without hesitation, to establish in the present passage.

Nevertheless, a tradition held by some says that Joseph was unable to look upon her face, because the Holy Spirit had completely filled her so that she might conceive, and the power of the Most High divinely overshadowed him, lest he suffer the heat of lust.
