[113] Therefore, according to their account, he did not know even the face of the virgin to whom he had been betrothed until her womb had been emptied, because out of excessive reverence he could not behold her with a direct gaze. This is a religious assertion, full of the piety of tradition. [Col. 0119B]

But we do not hesitate to understand the statement about intercourse as saying that he did not have intercourse with her until she bore her firstborn son. For “until” or “up to” in the holy Scriptures sometimes signifies a definite period and often an indefinite one. Hence God says through the prophet: “I am, I am, and until you grow old I am.” What does he mean by “until you grow old I am”? Will God, who is eternal, cease to exist after they have grown old?

The Savior likewise says in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you every day until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). Therefore, after the consummation of the age, will God no longer be with his apostles or with his saints, when God will be all in all? [Col. 0119C] And the Apostle says, speaking in the person of the Son: “For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Cor. 15:25). Will he reign only until his enemies are subjected to him? Or will he cease to reign after they have been subjected?

Using this manner of expression, then, the Evangelist certainly intended to indicate that Mary was not known by her husband until the birth. For during that period there could more readily arise a scandal even among believers, since the fruit of intercourse with a bride was visibly seen in the child. But since Joseph truly abstained at the time when there could still have been doubt about the command, it must be understood all the more that he did not know her after the birth, when, through many signs of divine matters, the same God who was being born and the Son of God in human form had been revealed. [Col. 0119D]

If we ask why Joseph abstained from intercourse until the day of the birth, there is no doubt that he had heard the angel say that what had been conceived in her was from the Holy Spirit. But together with this statement he had also received the command: “Do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife.” Therefore, when he was forbidden to abandon her or to consider her an adulteress, do you suppose that he was separated from marital relations, when he was rather admonished not to separate from her?

A man who believed her to be so holy that, although he was her husband, he dared not touch her, and who heard that the Son of God was in her womb—could he have thought of intercourse with the Virgin? [Col. 0120A] For he had heard the shepherds, and the angel of God announcing to them the great joy that would be for all the people [114]: “For today,” he says, “a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke 2:11); and he had also heard the praises of the heavenly host joining with the angel: “Glory to God in the highest,” and the rest that follows.

He had also heard Simeon, while embracing the child, proclaiming: “Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace, according to your word, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (ibid., 29). He had heard the prophetess Anna; he had seen the magi and the star. Or had he not heard that Herod was disturbed by them? Had he not learned from the prophecy that Bethlehem had been designated by the chief priests as the place where Christ would be born?

If he is shamelessly said to have been ignorant of all these things, what does Luke mean when he reports that “his father and mother were amazed at the things that were being said about him” (ibid., 33)? [Col. 0120B] How could they be amazed if they did not know them? They certainly did know them; and therefore it is impious to believe that he dared to violate the temple of God, the seat of the Holy Spirit, and the mother of the Lord.

Especially since Luke says that Mary “kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:19), so that she might see how all the mysteries of the divine law corresponded to this sacrament. For it is sufficiently impious to imagine that she could ever have been stained by the pollution of intercourse.

Even if “until” everywhere and always signified a fixed period, reason, with the divine law forbidding it, would in no way permit us to understand it as fixed here. Otherwise, if someone supposes that Joseph knew her immediately after the birth, with no intervening period of purification, where would be the requirement that she remain unclean for seven days according to the law concerning menstrual separation, and remain in the blood of purification for thirty-three days, touching nothing holy during that time? [Col. 0120C]

Or did Joseph immediately assail her amid the proclamations of the angels, when there was no room in the lodging? It is established in every respect that there was no opportunity for marital relations amid the cramped manger and the animals. Nor would he rightly be called just in the Gospel if he were so madly inflamed by desire that he sought to violate even the woman whom he had read, through many figures of Scripture, was destined to remain a virgin forever. [Col. 0120D]

“And she bore,” it says, “her firstborn son.” By “firstborn,” he does not mean one followed by brothers, but one whom no one preceded. Therefore it might seem that he ought rather to have said “only-begotten” than “firstborn,” according to what secular writings indicate: that “firstborn” should be said of one whom brothers follow [115]. Yet the idiom of the holy Scriptures calls those consecrated to the Lord, or everything that opens the womb, “firstborn.” For this reason, preserving the wording of the Gospel, he preferred to say “firstborn” rather than “only-begotten.”

Elsewhere also he himself is called “firstborn among many brothers” in the resurrection (Rom. 8:29). Since the general is contained in the particular, although by nature he is only-begotten, he ought here also to be called firstborn, so that it might be an indication that many other brothers were already being gathered in him through grace. [Col. 0121A]

In the Old Testament too, firstborn are granted to those who are chosen beforehand by the grace of God; their dignity is not advanced by nature but by the merit of grace. Thus we say that “firstborn” is written here with greater significance, so that through him all who are gathered together by grace may immediately possess the status of firstborn in heaven.

All those firstborn consecrated to the Lord under the law bore this figure. Hence we read that the Lord established the following judgment concerning them for Aaron: “Everything that opens the womb, of all flesh that is offered to the Lord, from human beings to cattle, shall be mine; but the firstborn of unclean animals shall be redeemed for a price” (Exod. 34:19).

Behold, the divine word has defined what “firstborn” means: “Everything,” it says, “that opens the womb.” Otherwise firstborn would not be owed among the priests so long as it was believed that others of every kind could still be born, lest perhaps not firstborn but only-begotten children be consecrated to the Lord. [Col. 0121B] For if the term were to be understood only of one followed by brothers, the priests could have offered the following excuse: “Why do you constrain me, at the appointed time of one month, to offer under the law a firstborn whose brothers have not followed? Wait a little until a second is born, because meanwhile I owe nothing to the priest unless one has been born through whom the one already born may begin to be firstborn.”

For it is written concerning Mary: “When the days of her purification according to the law of Moses had been fulfilled, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law: Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord; and to offer sacrifices according to what is said in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (Luke 2:22). [Col. 0121C]

Therefore, if those who follow make someone a firstborn, and this law seems to apply only to firstborn children, he should not have been counted under the law as a firstborn, since no brothers had yet succeeded him. But he is rightly held to be firstborn because all only-begotten children can be firstborn, whereas not all firstborn can rightly be called only-begotten.

From this it follows in summary that the one who opens the womb and before whom no one came should be called firstborn—not only the one whom brothers follow. Christ is therefore rightly called firstborn from the virgin, because from the beginning he is the firstborn of all creation. He is also rightly called the firstborn of the faithful in baptism, and he is said to have risen as the firstborn from the dead in the resurrection. [Col. 0121D]

He is sometimes called only-begotten because he alone is the unique and proper Son of God. Hence the same one is appropriately proved to be only-begotten from Mary, although he is called firstborn. For he is only-begotten because he alone, as the Son, was born from the substance of the Father; likewise, from Mary he is the unique and proper son of a human being.

But because through this he became the mediator between God and human beings, he is rightly called firstborn among many, so that through grace he might have many brothers and hold primacy over them everywhere. For according to the proper character of nature, the title “Only-begotten” is more significantly proclaimed in both substances. [Col. 0122A]

## Chapter II

“Now when Jesus had been born in Bethlehem in the days of King Herod.”

Here four foundations are surely laid, strengthened by the predictions of the prophets, so that the house founded upon the rock may not waver before any human reasoning. His birth is described, concerning which it had been said: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6). His person is also declared by his name, already foretold in many places. The place, too, is shown by the prophecy, and the time of his birth is indicated by the period that had elapsed under Herod.

Yet it is not unreasonable to ask why his birth—which was to be proclaimed throughout the whole world—is measured by Herod according to the practice of chronographers. [Col. 0122B] Especially since the year of Herod’s reign is not specified by an exact number, as historians customarily indicate when Christ was born. Moreover, the evangelist might perhaps seem to have acted more appropriately by introducing Octavian Augustus to mark the time of Christ’s birth. His power had extended to the ends of the earth and, among the other kingdoms of the world, enclosed this Herod and the whole province of Palestine within his empire. For in the fortieth year of Augustus’s reign, when Jesus was born, by divine ordering the firmest peace first served mortals throughout every part of the earth. [Col. 0122C] It was then, surely, that the angels sang while human beings listened: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 1:14).

From this it is plainly established that this peace was brought about not by Caesar’s power but by Christ’s grace. So much so that Augustus himself, toward whom supreme authority in affairs had converged, did not permit himself to be called lord in the assembly. Indeed, he did not dare to do so because of divine displeasure, since the true Lord of the whole human race was being born among human beings.

In that same year, people everywhere in the individual provinces were registered by name, and each made his declaration in his own locality, so that a slave who had not returned to his own master was legally punished with death. The whole world was registered, as Luke records, and that famous enrollment of all human beings designated Caesar as ruler of them all. Among them Christ—the one who founded the whole human race—willed to be found and registered as a human being among human beings, subject to human laws, so that through this he might enroll his own citizens in the eternity of their heavenly homeland, by submitting to human authority.

Nothing of the kind had ever occurred from the beginning of any kingdom: that someone should possess authority over the whole world. Hence it is most clearly evident to the scrutiny of our faith that, when our Lord Jesus Christ came, he restored peace to the world above all so that his preachers might have a free path for entering throughout the earth, and so that, once peace had been received, the tranquil world might attend to the word of preaching. Thus it is written that the apostles’ sound went out into all the earth (Rom. 10:18), and it is shown that the word of preaching ran to the ends of the world.

Moreover, it is shown that this happened above all so that the arrival of the one who had come might be confirmed more firmly—the one of whom a certain great poet [Virgil] had sung:

> He rules the pacified world by the virtues of his fathers.

> He will receive the life of a god and will see heroes  
> mingled with the gods, and he himself will be seen among them;

and:

> With you as guide, if any traces of our crime remain,  
> they will free the earth from perpetual fear.

Then indeed the earth was freed from the fear of all wars, just as the same poet testifies, when he says:

> Now a new generation is sent down from high heaven;

and:

> The great order of the ages is born again from the beginning;

and:

> Throughout the whole world the golden race arises.

[Col. 0123B] This supreme poet, writing these things to Prince Octavian, because a light breath of air had touched him, unknowingly displayed something divine within him through his Sibylline song and foretold it in his own eloquence. Thus he says:

> The final age of the Cumaean song has now come—

that is, whatever the Sibyls had once foretold, all of which was to be fulfilled at that time. For, as will be shown in its proper place, the divine Spirit used him wonderfully, as though he were an instrument, so that almost everything concerning Christ that was fulfilled might be marked out long beforehand in his song.

Since, as we have said, the Roman Empire had reached the height of its power, the evangelist might seem to have acted more appropriately if he had assigned the Savior’s birth to that empire, since it was to be proclaimed throughout the world and was known to all peoples under the four regions of heaven. But if we consider the matter attentively, it will immediately become clear that he did not mention Herod merely in order to describe the time of the birth in human fashion. Rather, he did so to show more significantly that the prophecy of the patriarch Jacob had finally been fulfilled.

Let us therefore read the histories of Africanus and of the others, and we shall certainly find that this Herod, who is said to have ruled in Judaea at that time, was not of Jewish stock, nor had he derived any bodily origin from them, by reason of which he ought rightly to have ruled over them. Instead, born of foreigners, through the authority of Caesar Augustus and by the just judgment of God, he unjustly possessed the kingdom of the Jews.

For it had been said: “The prince shall not fail from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs, until he comes to whom it has been reserved” (Gen. 49:10). Therefore, wishing to indicate that the one to whom it had been reserved had now certainly come, [Col. 0123D] the evangelist preferred to insert Herod for the sequence of the time rather than Augustus, so that by this he might explain more firmly, from the prophecy, the fullness of Christ’s advent. For unless this were the one to whom it had been reserved, the prince from Judah and the ruler from his thighs would not have failed at all.

Indeed, up to this point—that is, up to Christ and the Temple—priests from both Jewish tribes had jointly governed the people. Their last representatives were Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, sons of Alexander the priest, who became high priests. Inflamed by the torches of ambition and seeking royal dignity, they fought against one another. In this way they provided the Romans with an opportunity to invade Judaea as enemies.

Pompey was the first of them. After capturing the city and opening the Temple, he approached even the Holy of Holies like a tyrant. He also carried Aristobulus away in chains and handed the high priesthood over to Hyrcanus. Then he made Antipater—the son of a certain man of Ascalon who had formerly been, they say, a temple-warden of the temple at Ascalon—governor of the province of Palestine.

Thus this Herod, under whom Christ was born, the son of that Antipater, was sent by Hyrcanus to Rome and came to the attention of Octavian Augustus and the Senate. But after Hyrcanus had died and the high priesthood had been abolished, Herod—who had no claim to it, being the son of Antipater the Ascalonite and of his Arab mother Cypros—received from the Romans, in the eleventh year of Augustus’s reign, the rule of the Jews as a foreigner.

His descendants, as the Scriptures relate, held that same kingdom for a time through successive generations. No one succeeded to the priesthood in the Temple according to the law until the city and Temple were utterly destroyed to their foundations and the people were wiped out with them.

At that time, in accordance with Daniel, the sacrifice and offering began to cease, and the abomination of desolation came to be in the Temple (Dan. 9:27). Thereafter, until the consummation and until the end, desolation continues, according to the same prophet, to such a degree that, in the place where the Temple and religious worship formerly existed, the Saracens possess a shrine of their worship, constructed in the manner of a holy temple for the profanation of the sanctuary, which in their language, they say, they call *Mischida* [mosque].

From this point judgments come against the Jews from every side. Although they possess a heart of stone, the authority of the sacred Scriptures and the pages of secular literature cry out no less against them and refute them because they oppose the truth with a stubbornly blind mind.

The arguments of orators concerning matters—arguments found no less in the Gospel than in the prophets—are numerous. From these I have gradually inserted seven concerning Christ here and there for the sake of faith. All the writers on the arts have treated these together and left them embedded in their precepts; through them every assertion about matters is established and completed.

For in every kind of case it is asked who and what the matter concerns, why, where, and when, in what manner, and by what supports the matter is upheld. Scripture has given these things to us in Christ, each separately and distinctly—and, what is more, strengthened by the sayings of the prophets and declared by the voices of angels—so that neither miracles would be lacking for the Jews as an aid to faith, nor matters requiring belief concerning this sacred birth would be lacking for the wise Greeks as an aid to persuasion.

But who is the one who was born? Let the prophet Isaiah be asked first, and let him say that the one who was born is the angel of great counsel, and that he is called Strong, Ruler, Father of the age to come, and Prince of Peace (Isa. 9:6). This is Jesus, whom the angel expressly announces as the Son of the Most High, and whom the sayings of the prophets name as the future Savior.

What he is, the evangelist John also plainly indicates when he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Then he adds that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 1:14). Here, indeed, the matter is shown clearly and unmistakably.

Why he came, the angel indicates: namely, to save his people from their sins and, as it is said elsewhere, “to show an opening to those shut in” (Isa. 61:1).

Where he came, let John say: he came to what was his own. The prophet describes it, saying: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are not the least among the rulers of Judah; for from you will come forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel” (Mic. 5:2). I mean the ruler to whom it had been reserved, whom Daniel had foreseen as destined to come.

When he came was when the ruler from Judah and the prince from his thighs began to fail—when the fullness of time came: namely, in the days of King Herod, who, already a foreigner, was ruling in Judaea against the law.

How he was born is clear: ineffably, from a Virgin. For this manner of birth was not an expression of the frailty of human nature but a condescension of divine majesty. [Col. 0125B] By what means it happened, the angel declares to Mary when he says: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” And again: “The child conceived in her was from the Holy Spirit.”

Because these principles of the philosophers seem suitable for persuading unbelievers, we have added them so that it may become evident on every side how richly the divine word is fragrant with mysteries, how greatly it surpasses in signs, and how much it excels the utterances of secular literature. It is more steadfast in speech, richer in eloquence, deeper in meaning, loftier in understanding, brighter in vision, sweeter in taste, more certain in promise, and more fruitful in result. Whoever digs more deeply into it acquires greater treasures for himself and suddenly discovers there, through the grace of the Spirit, things that are unspeakable to mortals.

Bethlehem of Judah is so called to distinguish it from another Bethlehem, which is in Galilee, in the tribe of Zebulun, although in older copies “of Judaea” is found. For “Judaea” properly signifies that whole region of the ten tribes, whereas “Judah” more clearly designates that one tribe of David.

Both of these places are in Judaea. Therefore “of Judah” should be read here, so that the city of David in the tribe of Judah may be expressed more significantly—the city from which Christ, long promised prophetically, was expected.

This, I say, is the city of David, situated in the territory of the tribe of Judah, about six miles from Aelia, toward the southern region, beside the road that leads to Hebron. [Col. 0125D] Even today the tomb of Jesse and David is shown there, although elsewhere it is also recorded that he was buried in Jerusalem.

Bethlehem is interpreted as “house of bread.” From this an anticipation of future things is introduced: that there the living bread, which came down from heaven for the nourishment of those who were to believe, would one day be born. Previously it was called Ephrathah, but afterward, when its name was changed, it was more significantly called Bethlehem.

It represents the whole Church, which is appropriately called the house of bread. In it believers are daily nourished by heavenly sweetness with that angelic food, and are fattened as they taste beforehand the flesh and blood of the Redeemer. “My flesh,” he says, “is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:55).

Thus he is born in Bethlehem because the true house of bread is shown to be the Christian Church alone, outside which that heavenly bread is not found. For this reason he is placed in a manger, as an abundant food for pious animals, so that if he found any who lacked reason, he might restore them, refreshed by spiritual nourishment, to the higher dignity of angels. The significance of this place of birth will be explained more fully shortly.

“Behold,” he says, “magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?’”

In these magi, therefore, the faith of the nations is already consecrated to the Lord like firstfruits. Through faith they saw the star in the East and happily followed the morning star, which is Christ. For unless the morning-bringing light first rose in their hearts, they would never have sought the king of the Jews so steadfastly with the star going before them.

They were, as they say, of the race of Balaam and successors to his teachings. Therefore, from his prophecy they recognized more clearly what, diligently recalling it in their study of his teaching, they were considering testing according to the discipline of that art.

The magi are the same people who were later called mathematicians. Their task is to examine the nativities of those born under the stars and to infer the outcomes of events from astrology (*mathesis*). But concerning these magi it should rather be confessed that they believed because of prophecy, or certainly because the Holy Spirit stirred them, than that they were introduced to the faith through some deception of the enemy—especially since the prophecy of their teacher was destined to be a sign of the promised future for all.

“From Jacob,” he says, “a star shall arise, and a man or scepter shall rise from Israel; he shall strike the leaders of Moab, lay waste all the sons of Seth, and Edom shall be his possession” (Num. 24:17–18). And shortly afterward: “From Judah,” he says, “there shall be one who rules and destroys the survivors of the city” (ibid., 24:19).

No one doubts that these things are to be understood of Christ. Therefore these men, taught by such a proclamation and inspired by divine grace, announced the birth of the supreme ruler, although they did not yet know the place where he would be born.

They knew what they had learned from the prophecy of the teacher whom they followed, but they were entirely ignorant of the place that the Holy Spirit elsewhere declared through the prophet. Hence a marvelous exchange of teachings takes place between Jews and Gentiles. The Jews indicate the place, although they do not recognize the time of the Lord’s coming.

For it is written that “the kite, the swallow, and the stork observe their appointed time, but my people have not observed the judgment of their God, nor recognized the time of their visitation” (Jer. 8:7). These men, on the other hand, proclaim the time, although by the discipline of their art they cannot comprehend the place of his birth.

They come from the East to Jerusalem because that city of the Most High God shone throughout the whole world, so that there they might be instructed by divine laws in what they had been taught less fully.

But how they came from the East, traversing such immense distances in so short a time, is not sufficiently clear, unless perhaps they are believed, as some wish, to have come after a year. That view cannot stand at all. For if they had come after a year, they would not have found him in the manger, as the Gospel relates, but would have found him already carried away into Egypt.

From this it is clear that they came on the twelfth day and that, at that point in the calendar, he was worshiped by the magi in the manger—the same one who afterward, in the Jordan, was anointed by the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove and was attested from heaven by the Father’s voice: “This is my beloved Son.”

It is appropriately believed that they could have arrived on the twelfth day because the whole region lying before Jerusalem is rightly called “the East,” as ordinary speech itself teaches and as the authority of the divine Scriptures proves in many places that it should be understood.

Thus Habakkuk, rejoicing over this very birth, sings: “God has come from the South.”

Because Bethlehem, where Christ was born, lies about six miles from Jerusalem toward the southern region, they are therefore rightly said to have come from that part of the country.

These men were, as tradition relates, from the land of the Persians, as our Juvencus sings:

> Then he commands the Persians to extend their steps,

but they are believed to have lived especially in Evilat, where the finest gold abounds.

Concerning them Isaiah says: “At that time a gift will be brought to the Lord of hosts from a people scattered and torn apart, from a people terrible beyond any other” (Isa. 18:7). He says this hyperbolically because of the exceptionally strong Persian nation, since no people in those regions at that time could be compared with its power.

From that nation the magi came and, by God’s direction, brought gifts to Christ. Again Isaiah himself acknowledges this when he says: “All those from Sheba shall come, bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praise of the Lord” (Isa. 60:6).

For in those parts of Persia the river Saba flows, and the whole region is called by its name. Arabia lies beside it and borders that region. Hence David also says: “He shall live, and gold from Arabia shall be given to him.” Shortly afterward: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabs and of Sheba shall bring presents” (Ps. 71:10, 15).

No one who has read the histories of the Gentiles is unaware that, in these regions toward the eastern side of Jerusalem, the magi were kings; for this reason we judge them to have been kings. Although they are said to have brought three kinds of gifts, it is not for that reason immediately proved from the Gospel that there were no more than three of them.

Rather, this comes from the tradition of the elders, so that through them the multitude of the nations, which springs from the three sons of Noah, might be prefigured as destined to come to the faith of Christ. Since many people also individually specify their names, it is possible that there were that many rulers of religion and power on such a journey, with many others in their company as attendants, as is customary among the great.

Otherwise it seems difficult that only three men should have undertaken such an enterprise through foreign provinces and should have stirred the whole of Jerusalem by their announcement.

But whether the star they had seen rose in the East, or whether, while they were located there, they saw it born in the West, seems uncertain—especially since the evangelist says that, as they were leaving Jerusalem, “behold, the star that they had seen in the East went before them.”

He does not make clear whether the star itself had led them to Jerusalem and abandoned them when they entered the royal city, or whether only after they had left Jerusalem did that same star, which they had seen while they were in the East, begin to be their guide and companion on the journey.

It may indeed fit what many teachers relate: that it led them from the East to Jerusalem. But when they sought human assistance, as though required by the law, they were immediately deprived of divine assistance.

Yet if the Gospel’s truth is examined more carefully, it does not seem at all to establish that the star led them to Judaea. Rather, it acknowledges only that they saw the star in the East, and from it understood that the one of whom Balaam had prophesied had been born in Judaea.

Therefore, as soon as they saw it, they set out for Judaea and came to the royal city, where they believed from the prophetic oracles that they would learn of his birth. When they discovered from the testimony of the prophets that he had been born in Bethlehem, they immediately began their journey there. Then, behold, they recognized the star they had seen in the East going before them.

This is how the Gospel has it when the magi say: “We saw his star in the East.” They do not admit that it led them from the East to that place, but say only: “We saw his star in the East.” After they had heard of the king, the text continues: “They went away, and behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them.”

It is not written that they had seen it elsewhere, nor that it was their companion on the journey. Nevertheless, even if the matter can be explained and clarified in this way, the earlier opinion of the majority should not immediately be rejected. For even if the star did not visibly go before them along the course of their journey, it was inwardly their companion through the illumination of faith.

That it did not follow celestial paths is shown by the report that it stood above the place where the child was. If it had been situated among the other stars at the highest point of heaven, it would have seemed to stand above the head of every house in the whole city. Thus it clearly indicates that it stood very near the house where the child was.

Moreover, if it had shone from the center of heaven, as we can establish concerning other signs, it would neither have shown the travelers their route nor singled out the house in which the child was.

In this work, four things seem to fit together at once: a sign, a prophecy, a demonstration, and a symbolic entry into the heavenly Jerusalem, with the new faith going before it.

It was a sign of this mystery: that fiery pillar which went before the people of God as they journeyed toward Jerusalem. Through it the Holy Spirit is designated as the guide of those who come to Christ.

For this reason some assert that the Holy Spirit was seen through the star in the form of a dove. The Gospel says nothing of this, however, and it does not seem probable or plausible, although the star itself did bear the figure of the Holy Spirit, through whom faith shines in the hearts of believers.

It was the fulfillment of prophecy, as we have already indicated, because it had been said: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise in Israel.” Although “A star shall arise from Jacob” can be understood simply of Christ, because the star is suggested to have appeared as though from heaven, we nevertheless admit that the saying can be referred to both: Christ, according to John’s statement in the Apocalypse (22:16), was a star, and in the star that appeared Christ was most clearly shown.

No sign, therefore, could have appeared more appropriately for inviting people than one through which the faith of believers would shine in a miracle and the true star from Jacob, who is Christ, would be foretold by the oracle.

Those who serve Christ in true faith, being conformed to him, would thereby already shine like the stars of heaven in eternal perpetuity and, through the power of hope, reign in heavenly places. For what could be more fitting than for faith—the way by which one travels to the star—to be displayed through a star, so that, illuminated by it, we may shine in perpetual eternity, since we possess no light of our own?

The demonstration of Christ was certainly in the star. Otherwise they would not have said: “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and have come to worship him.”

To whoever reaches him and enters that heavenly Jerusalem, Christ, the morning star, will immediately be shown according to John’s promise. He is therefore rightly said to have stood above the child, because he is recognized as the glory of the saints. Whoever sees that glory will rejoice with exceedingly great joy and will not cease to worship before the sight of God. For once he has entered the house, he enjoys Christ joyfully in eternal satisfaction.

But why did those same magi enter Jerusalem, with such a great light going before them? I believe it was not without purpose.

First, so that the Jews, who did not believe that Christ had been born, might learn from magi who had come from far away. If they refused to believe, they would remain altogether without excuse, convicted by the sayings of the prophets.

Second, so that the priests, scribes, and Pharisees, who indicated the place of the birth from prophecy, might be condemned appropriately—not because of ignorance but because of the hardness of their hearts and their refusal to believe—as immovable milestones standing by the road.

Third, so that Christ, who is called our peace, might be proclaimed more clearly from Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” as Isaiah says: “For the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3), as though he were saying: “It shall be preached.”

Thus the angel announces Christ to the Jewish shepherds, who were more prepared to receive a rational message as people instructed by the law. To these magi, however, as unbelievers, God speaks through signs, because, as the Apostle says, signs were given not to believers but to unbelievers (1 Cor. 14:22).

To both groups, nevertheless, heaven is opened, so that, by believing the heavenly signs, those who were already heavenly might be invited more firmly to heavenly realities.

As I have said, it is reported that this star did not follow celestial paths. It moved somewhat lower, although it appeared higher than the flight of birds, because it pointed out on the journey the one who, in the flesh, was made a little lower than the angels but nevertheless surpassed all the saints in nature and grace.

Thus that star, according to the mathematicians—or the Priscillianists—which the magi saw did not exercise dominion over Christ according to the flesh by a decree derived from mathematical calculation. Rather, as his creature, it served him as a witness. It did not subject him to its authority but indicated him in dutiful service.

Accordingly, it is clear that it was not one of those stars that maintained their appointed course from the beginning. A new star appeared with the Virgin’s new birth. It performed its office of service even for the magi who were seeking Christ, going before their faces until, by leading them ahead, it brought them to the very place where the Word of God was an infant.

Let the astrologers, then, who have established the fate of human beings under the stars, produce some star that, when a particular person was born, abandoned the course of its own movement and proceeded toward the one who had been born. For they believe that the destiny of the one being born is bound by the order of the stars, not that the order of the stars can be changed by the day on which a human being is born.

Therefore, if that star was one of those that carry out their course in heaven, how could it determine what Christ, once born, would do, when, after Christ was born, it was compelled by divine command to abandon what it was doing?

But if, as is more plausibly believed, it arose because it was not previously present in order to demonstrate Christ, then Christ was not born because it appeared; rather, it appeared because Christ was born. He gave it, not it to him, the cause of its appearing.

Nor should something be called new merely because God ceased, at the beginning, to create a new creature thereafter. Although the thing that was suddenly made did not previously exist, the other stars had nevertheless already been created individually, and among them this one was assigned, through a new rising, to the service of manifestation.

The angels show Christ to the shepherds, but the star shows him to the magi. To both, however, the heavens speak with their own language—the language in which the prophets had now ceased to speak. Thus, through both, the heavens declare the glory of God, so that those who were near and those who were far away might together become citizens of heaven.

What, then, is the reason that, although so many kings had previously been born in Judaea, no one had ever been sought for worship by foreigners—especially since the magi did not worship Herod, whom they approached?

Because, although they found Herod reigning, they understood that another king of the Jews had already been born, since the ruler from Judah had failed.

“And we have come,” they say, “to worship him.”

They understand him to be God, since the star serves him. Otherwise they ought first to have worshiped Herod, whom they saw arrogantly displaying royal authority.

But because they were divinely moved to seek for worship the hidden God lying in swaddling clothes or crying among the mangers, they neither regard Herod as king, nor honor him, nor consider him to be anything.

I would say that the same impulse of inspiration brought about what I mentioned earlier concerning Octavian Augustus. At the time when he perceived that the whole world was subject and subordinate to him, and when the entire people in an assembly wished to acclaim him lord of the whole earth, he by no means permitted it. He prohibited it by law, something no king before him is ever recorded to have done.

From this it is entirely clear that the divine power which inwardly moved these men with an impulse of devotion itself restrained this ruler, so that he would not improperly accept applause for himself, since the whole world under heaven was being subjected to the monarchy of the Roman Empire by the power of another.

But Herod, like a frenzied Corybant, is said to have been troubled when he heard that someone other than himself was being sought as king of the Jews, and all Jerusalem with him.

For, although he was a foreigner and ignoble by birth, he was striving to appear to be the legitimate king of the Jews. Therefore, according to Josephus, he had burned all the records in which the genealogy of the Jews was set out, so that they would not expose his ignoble origin by keeping silent about it, nor commend the distinguished order of descent from the tribe of Judah.

He therefore thought that he could appear noble if he were not pressed down by the authority of the sacred Scriptures.

Thus what Africanus intimates is certainly true: there were diligent men among the Jews called *Heriles*, evidently because of their kinship with Christ’s family. They were Nazoreans who traveled throughout the entire region. Partly from memory, partly from the Books of Chronicles—which they had at home, taken from the Temple archives when those records were being burned—and partly from what their grandfathers and great-grandfathers had related, they preserved the order of Christ’s genealogy and committed it to writing in its proper sequence.

After all these things had been investigated, especially those preserved in the same archives or elsewhere in inaccessible and hidden places, the authority of our divine books is derived from them here and there, so that the truth of the Gospels may be declared more clearly.

He calls Herod “king,” although he could not rightly be called king, since he did not know how to rule the movements of his own mind. By comparison with the king of the Jews, whom the magi sought in order to worship, Herod is understood to be an outsider, because their own ruler had already failed.

It should also be noted that anyone who, through insolence, claims an authority he does not possess, and is troubled by many suspicions, so that by wicked schemes and crooked arguments he attempts to obstruct every affair and refuses to yield the place of rule to someone more worthy, though he is proved unworthy to hold it himself, is like this criminal Herod. Through the deceitful schemes of his desires, Herod tried to oppose the divine decree by sinning through the slaughter of many children.

Therefore, as soon as he was troubled, he is said to have had many of his own people as accomplices, so much so that, in the manner of the mob, the former people of God are said to have been troubled by favor toward him, grieving that the one promised from heaven had already arrived.

O miserable condition of human frailty, which often favors unjustly those whom God in his just judgment permits to be cruel oppressors, and is not afraid to flatter those whom it sees daily resisting God’s will within themselves!

Hence Solomon’s statement is proved true: “An unjust king will have all his ministers as wicked men” (Prov. 29:12).

Herod is perhaps said to have been troubled for two reasons: either because he feared the destruction of his kingdom, and therefore the earthly king was troubled when the King of heaven was born; or because Caesar Augustus and the Senate had decreed that no one should be called king or god without their consent.

For this reason, perhaps, when he heard the word “king,” he was moved to fury, fearing that, if it became known that he had violated the decrees of the Senate, a sentence of danger would fall upon him.

“Gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born.”

He displays the diligence of one making inquiry, so that, if he found the child, he might do what he later indicates that he wished to do. But if the matter should eventually be reported to Caesar Augustus or the Senate, his diligence would excuse him, since he could claim to have done everything he could out of zeal for Roman authority.

Alternatively, he may have done this because of his knowledge of the law, so that he could investigate them more carefully and discover whether the king promised to their nation by the law would make them sorrowful or joyful.

He calls him “Christ” because he had learned that, according to the custom of the Jewish nation, all kings were called *christs*—that is, “anointed ones”—from their anointing.

But they said: “In Bethlehem of Judah”; for thus it is written through the prophet: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for from you will come forth a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.”

That this testimony agrees neither with the Hebrew nor with the Septuagint translators is demonstrated, even without our saying so, by [Col. 0132B] the text itself. Hence certain slanderers say that in almost all the testimonies taken from the Old Testament an error of this kind resounds: either the order of the words or that of the meanings is changed, so much so that the sense sometimes appears different. “The apostles,” they say, “or the evangelists did not extract their testimonies from the books, but, trusting memory—which is sometimes mistaken, they occasionally produced contradictory statements.” As though they had spoken merely from their own skill and not, rather, by divine grace inspiring them through the Spirit by whom the Scriptures were formerly produced; and as though they had not disclosed the testimonies of God’s utterances, inserting mysteries not contrary to them but according to what was appropriate.

Here, however, we think that the blessed evangelist is reproving the sluggishness of the scribes and Pharisees and [Col. 0132C] noting their negligence toward the divine Scriptures, and therefore he set it down as they themselves had said it. Although they are reproved for their dullness, they nevertheless restore the sense to something like the truth. For in Hebrew it reads: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, are little among the thousands of Judah; from you there will come forth for me one who shall be ruler in Israel; and his coming forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. V, 2).

The meaning is this: “You, Bethlehem—that is, Ephrata—are by no means least in size or number among all the cities of Judah, though, compared with so many thousands of cities, you are scarcely a small village.” It is as though he were saying: “You are by no means least, because from you the great Christ will come forth, and he will indeed be ruler in Israel.” Nor should you suppose that he is merely of David’s line, to whom I promised, saying: “From the fruit of your womb I will place upon my throne”; for the assumption of flesh does not impede divinity. His coming forth is indeed from my substance, born from the days of eternity, according to the words: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.” For the Creator of times is not held beneath time, although God, having become human, is born within time.

See how clear this testimony is, not only against the Jews but also against those who say that Christ in the flesh was merely a human being. Moreover, the fact that in Hebrew it is written “And you, Bethlehem Ephrata,” and not “Judah,” is believed to have been altered later through the malice of the Jews, so that Christ might not appear to have arisen from the tribe of Judah. But when they had not yet been stirred by envy against Christ, they themselves plainly pronounced, “And you, Bethlehem Judah,” although in other respects they are reproved for negligence, since the phrase is afterwards scarcely found in their manuscripts.

For it is clear that “Ephrata” was added by the Septuagint for another significance, as we read that they did this in many places. Nevertheless, in the meantime we can rightly prove from divine authority that Bethlehem is entirely in the tribe of Judah. For it is read in the Book of Judges (XVII, 7) that there was a Levite living on the slopes of Mount Ephraim, and that he took for himself a concubine from Bethlehem of Judah; and the same name is repeatedly used thereafter. Indeed, according to the Septuagint, although here they said, “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrata,” nevertheless in Jesus Nave, where the cities and towns of the tribe of Judah are described, we also read this inscription: “Teko and Ephrata,” it says, “that is, Bethlehem, Phagor” (Josh. XV), along with the eleven cities that follow. This is found absolutely neither in the Hebrew nor in any other translator.

Moreover, no one can doubt that the entire family of the house of [Col. 0133B] David held this inheritance by lot. All the pages of the divine distribution speak of that house as belonging to the tribe of Judah and as having received within it the allotted boundary of its possession.

As for the fact that the Septuagint says, “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrata,” this accords with the truth of the matter according to the Book of Genesis, because it is Bethlehem where Rachel is said to have died and been buried on the road to Ephrata, which, it says, is Bethlehem. Ephrata was its older name, and afterwards it was changed to a more significant one because of the mystical sacrament of its meaning. For Ephrata is interpreted as “she saw fury.” [Col. 0133C] This plainly prefigures Herod’s madness, because when he sought to destroy Christ, he was deceived by the Magi; hence, greatly enraged, he sent and killed all the boys in Bethlehem. For this reason it was rightly called of old “seeing fury.”

But now let no one fear, let no one doubt, let no one despair, because that rest which David sought was heard of in Ephrata and found in the fields of the forest, and the house that saw fury became the house of bread. Hence Rachel, bearing the figure of the Church, is read to have been buried there, so that her complete rest might be signified in the same place where Christ, the living bread who came down from heaven, is daily present in a new coming forth without exhaustion.

The pains of a woman in labor therefore seized him before Christ was born, and for this reason it is aptly called beforehand “seeing fury.” It saw fury, then, because it was giving birth to iniquity, continually conceiving pains and bringing forth injustices in abundance. For there is no pain greater than the wound of sin, where nothing in the conscience is strong, nothing sound, but everything abounds in grief and torments the unhappy soul beneath the weight of sins. Hence David, shuddering at the terrible wounds of his miseries, says: “My eye is troubled because of fury; I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. VI, 8).

All the nations, indeed the entire human race, were subject to this fury of blindness, because we were all children of wrath. But let us give thanks to our Benefactor, because, as I have said, behold: where the house of the one seeing fury was, there the house of bread has been made; where there was cruelty, there is mercy; where wrath, there is compassion; where a heavy yoke lay upon the sons of Adam from the day of their birth, there is Christ’s easy burden and gentle yoke. What was Ephrata is itself Bethlehem.

Christ was therefore born in the house of fury; and for that reason it is now called not the house of fury but the house of bread, because it received the bread coming from heaven, and is called so more happily. Yet Ephrata also seems to signify the same meaning, for Ephrata is said to mean “fruitful”: because in the present life the one cultivating the field where Christ blossomed strives continually to carry the fruits of life into the granary.

Indeed, it is fruitful here, so that there, when Christ’s glory has been revealed, it may be satisfied with the richness of grain and filled with every perpetual happiness. Perhaps it should also be noted that these two interpretations of one name suit that meaning very well, [Col. 0134B] since the Prophet, singing beautifully, says: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy; going forth, they went and wept, bearing their seeds” (Ps. CXXV, 6).

The Church of God therefore does not cease to weep while it is on the way, even though it is said to be buried beneath the allurements of the world, because it sees the fury of the coming Judge. Hence it cries out: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury” (Ps. VI, 1). When he says, “Those who sow in tears,” he teaches that it is rightly called fruitful because of its own labor. For every day it gathers and stores within the threshing floor—which Christ will thoroughly cleanse with his winnowing fan—all the works of virtue.

It was therefore fitting that Christ should be born in a place bearing the figure of the whole Church and that, through its name, it should signify to all believers that Christ would be present there as nourishment, since outside the Church of God the hunger of impiety cruelly lays waste the sons of this kingdom with the famine of death.

Then Herod secretly summoned the Magi and carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared.

His diligence was the diligence of deceit and fraud: he wished to investigate because he had learned from the prophecy the place where he would be born. Therefore he promised to worship, so that no one would notice what he was concealing in his heart, which is afterwards inferred from the circumstances. By secretly summoning the Magi, he conferred with them lest the scribes and Pharisees, as though they were concealing a promise from God’s oracle, should detect from some sign that he intended to destroy him.

For he could not suppose that they would rage with such hatred against God’s promises that they would refuse to receive him who had been promised by the voices of the prophets as arising from their own race. Hence, secretly summoning the Magi, he carefully learned from them the time of the star.

But in truth it is not sufficiently clear from their answers what he learned about it, or when, where, or how it appeared. Thus, whether they wished it or not, those who invented various explanations left everything that seemed exceedingly difficult to human beings to the possibility of God.

Meanwhile, sending them to Bethlehem, he said: “Go and inquire carefully about the child, and report back to me, so that I too may come and worship him.” He pretends that he will worship the one whom he intends to kill, in order to persuade them, without any suspicion of fraud, to report to him out of goodwill.

And behold, the star that they had seen in the East went before them until it came above where the child was.

After they had entered Judea, they were deprived of the star’s guidance so that they might be compelled, on account of the mysteries of faith contained in the Law, to inquire more diligently about the birth of so great a king. Thus, when the priests themselves were questioned by the Magi about where Christ would be born, they would be inexcusable concerning his coming.

Since they were weighed down by sluggishness and failed to attend to the prophecies, they were forewarned by the Gentiles, so that at least, invited by examples to render the service of veneration that was owed, they might believe in him whom, as the first to do so according to the prophecy, they ought to have come more quickly to worship.

For they are provoked to faith, as it is written, by those who were not of the people of God, and they are incited to emulation by a foolish nation, so that, convicted on both counts, they might be inexcusable. But they, like Jacob blessing his sons, were blinded by eyes darkened with obscurity, because they did not behold the present light, although from the prophecy, as though pointing with a finger from afar, they indicated the very place of his birth.

In another sense, the Magi are abandoned while traveling by divine assistance when they seek human help, so that it may be evident from this that we, whom faith and the grace of Christ enlighten, ought not, with doubtful minds, to seek human aid for instruction.

For the sign of the miracle, shown to the Magi as though they were unbelievers, ought not to have appeared to those teachers of the Law, whom the utterances of the prophets, the predictions of the patriarchs, and the enigmas of the figures, as members of the household, had prepared not only for faith but also for a thorough knowledge of the promises.

Therefore there is reason to fear concerning the things contained in the divine writings if the mind is badly disposed—unbelieving through the knot of infidelity, or deceitful through the test of evasion—lest it should ever be capable of being summoned by any prodigies of signs. For “if they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.”

At last the Magi, with the star accompanying them, arrived at the place; and the star served them from above, standing over the place where the child was, to which it had led them from the East.

“They rejoiced with very great joy.”

The usage of Scripture seems frequently to call him “child” for this reason: so that you may recognize the one of whom the prophet sings: “A child is born for us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. IX, 6). But if nothing in the divine writings is believed to be superfluous, and not even one stroke or iota is empty of mystery, this passage of Scripture seems to raise a question: no one can rejoice except in joy, just as no one can live except in life or die except in death—especially since it is not simply noted that “they rejoiced with joy,” but “very great” is also added and heaped upon it.

For we read in Genesis that the Lord said to Adam: “On whatever day you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you will die by death” (Gen. II, 17). And through Ezekiel: “If the wicked person repents of all his sins that he has committed and does judgment and righteousness, he will live by life and will not die” (Ezek. XVIII, 28).

I would therefore never say that expressions of this kind in the Holy Scriptures are superfluous. For just as one often lives toward death and dies toward life, as the usage of Scripture demonstrates, so someone certainly rejoices with joy when, for God’s sake—which is true joy—he rejoices.

For what else is “to live by life” than to live in virtues and, while still in the life of this body, to possess the actions of blessed life? Conversely, what else is “to die by death” than to be punished with death for vices and sins? Thus the one who, if he had wished, could not only have avoided death but also, through obedience, eventually have been regarded by God as immortal, became mortal by dying in sins and, if he were not redeemed, would thereafter, after the death of the flesh, live forever in death because of the death of the soul.

From this it is entirely clear that nothing in the divine writings is superfluous; rather, through a marvelous distinction of words, everything is filled with mysteries and varied with wondrous beauty of meaning. Therefore the blessed evangelist, wishing to intimate to believers that unique and marvelous joy, first mentioned their instruction in rejoicing and the gift of gladness, poured out from heaven in the heart of those who eagerly sought it with faith and grace.

He says not only that they rejoiced with joy, but with great joy—than which none is greater—and that within that great joy they rejoiced very greatly. For within one and the same great joy one person can rejoice more and another less.

These men, whose appearance prefigured the Gentile race of believers, rejoiced from that great joy: assured of its attainment, faithful in its outcome, devoted in affection, and inwardly burning through inspiration. Yet “great joy” may also be said by distinction from another kind of joy, since there is a lower joy in which we are properly said to exult more, although it may, by an improper usage, rightly be called joy.

Hence Solomon says, according to the Septuagint: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. II, 14). There is also an intermediate joy of life, whenever a people is said to rejoice in the temporal goods of the Lord. For if it is referred to those goods themselves, it is proved to be the lowest kind; but if it is referred to God, who gave them, it is recognized as having at least some value, since through rejoicing in those things the mind is raised toward that highest and unchangeable good, even if it is not yet worshiped for its own sake.

But great joy is rightly understood to be found nowhere except in God for his own sake. Because these Magi were the first fruits of the Gentiles, suffused with the vision of humility and having received faith, they devotedly worshiped God and, religiously fulfilling their vow, faithfully offered gifts to the Lord.

With this joy the blessed John, the friend of the bridegroom, declares that he rejoices: “The friend stands and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice, for he is his friend” (John III, 29).

So these men, justified by faith, rejoice with great joy, glad and rejoicing because of the ardor of charity, since they understand that they have been made friends rather than enemies through reconciliation. Hence Scripture testifies that they opened their treasures, offered him gifts, and, falling down, devotedly worshiped him.

By this deed the great mystery of our religion is revealed: with faith going before us, we should not disclose our treasures on the way, until, having passed beyond the ambushes of enemies and grace enlightening us, we devote ourselves to the Lord alone and offer gifts from the hidden treasures of our secret hearts.

Concerning this treasure it is rightly said elsewhere: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise.” Because Hezekiah carelessly revealed all his treasures to foreigners, he was struck by the divine sentence and condemned in his descendants by God’s just judgment.

It is an ancient tradition that none of the kings of the Parthians and Persians worshiped without gifts. For this reason they say that these men, accustomed to gifts through the proximity of their fellow citizens, offered gifts. But, from divine inspiration, we assert rather that it happened so that in the figure of the entire race a heavenly instruction might shine forth; and for this reason we believe it was deliberately related that they offered three gifts.

Namely, gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

By gold, which is especially the ornament of kings, they declared the insignia of a king. By frankincense, because it was formerly placed in sacrifices, they acknowledged that he was God by venerating him. By myrrh, with which the bodies of the dead were commonly embalmed, they testified, as though by a foreshadowing, that he would die as a human being. From this, if he had then spoken aloud, he could have said—as he himself admits elsewhere—that they had made it for his burial.

It is rightly asked, therefore, whether each person offered one gift, or whether all together offered these three; or, what must be acknowledged as more fitting, whether each one of them perhaps offered all three gifts together. For this accords better with the mystery. No one is rightly called a Christian unless he confesses that Christ reigns as God everywhere and unequivocally acknowledges that, for the salvation of the human race, God became human and died.

These men steadfastly seek the King of the Jews among those very Jews and in the presence of Herod himself, who was king; and therefore, as had been foretold, they faithfully bring him gold in the spirit. They knew that he was truly to be proclaimed everywhere to all as God, without fear of human terror. Therefore, in worshiping him, they say: “We have come to adore him.”

They also bring the incense of frankincense, which alone was completely burned for him every day, morning and evening, within the Holy of Holies according to the commandment. Enlightened from heaven, they understand that he who had become human was God, and they also rightly understand that he would die. Therefore they eagerly ask: “Where is he who has been born?” And in faith they devoutly offer him myrrh as a gift for burial, as a sign of mortification.

For each person rightly prepares Christ for burial when, having been mortified in himself, he truly confesses that Christ suffered in the flesh. Hence the Apostle says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with God in heaven” (Col. III, 3).

Our gifts must therefore continually be offered to the Savior: in gold, the purest knowledge of divine things; in frankincense, unceasing prayer or rightly directed compunction; and in myrrh, as we have indicated, the renunciation of both desires and vices, together with the true mortification of the flesh, is signified as something to be offered beforehand to God.

These gifts are rightly brought forth from the hidden treasures of the soul when one believes with the heart unto righteousness, but confesses with the mouth unto salvation.

And having received an answer in a dream, they returned to their own country by another way, so that they would not go back to Herod.

“He received an answer,” he says, although we read that he questioned them to no purpose. But the indication of the truth is clear: while they were considering whether or not they ought to return to Herod, they received an answer concerning their thoughts before they had deliberated.

Here the sober care of their concern is signified, and it is clearly suggested to us that God, always present everywhere, is present to our heart. Yet, just as Moses cried out to God in his mind without saying anything, so these men, remaining silent, anxiously asked through a pious devotion of affection what the divine will commanded, lest through the negligence of their own rashness they should deviate in anything from the balance of almighty God.

A pattern is therefore impressed upon all believers in this figure: they should come devotedly to God and, after they have come, attend to what God commands. That is, they should not return to the one whom they have renounced, nor retrace the paths of vice, but by following another way—the paths of virtues—hasten back to the homeland of paradise, so that we who fell through contempt may grasp the ways of life through obedience and abstinence.

It should also be noted that this answer is not said to have been given through an angel, as it was to Joseph. Rather, the tradition of the holy Fathers is that they were divinely instructed by the Lord himself, because no one else is known ever to have established the way of return to the homeland except the one who offered himself as the way to be imitated, so that, journeying through him toward himself, we might eventually return to our homeland.

Hence he himself says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). By walking along this way, each person proceeds without error, so that he may enter swiftly into life by following the truth.

The child lying in the manger does not address them in a human voice, since he is not yet grown, lest by acting contrary to the nature of our humanity he should reveal himself openly. Rather, he regulates everything in such a way that his hidden divinity may be discerned through faith in that man, lest it be imprudently revealed to anyone before the proper time.

For faith had to be nourished for the reward, and the way of his teachings had to be laid down everywhere for those who followed him to walk upon. Otherwise he would not truly have assumed our weakness if he had not grown through every age by the human process of development and had not exhibited in himself the capacities of our nature, apart from those things he performed more wondrously by divine power.

Hence the evangelist Luke rightly testifies that “the child Jesus advanced in age and wisdom before God and human beings” (Luke II, 52), in order to indicate every development both of body and of soul and to show that the fullness of humanity was in him.

Therefore throughout the whole period of his childhood he had to observe the condition proper to childhood, in which the fragility of the assumed flesh is most fully expressed and the humility of his long-suffering is commended by its indications.

There was therefore complete humanity in him, just as there was complete grace and complete truth. Hence the evangelist John says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I, 14).

Because the Word became flesh, he was full of truth. For the only-begotten Son of God himself is truth—not by grace but by nature. Grace assumed humanity when he was conceived of the Holy Spirit. The unity of person was so great that the very one who is proclaimed the Son of humanity is also the one and only, indeed the only-begotten, Son of God.

In this one God and human being, the fullness of the grace of humanity and the fullness of the truth of divinity are rightly proclaimed and worshiped according to catholic faith. This fullness of divinity in itself possesses the fullness of grace, which is the whole of humanity in his divinity; and the fullness of grace in itself possesses the whole fullness of truth, which is the whole of divinity in his humanity.

Thus the fullness of truth perfectly contains within itself the fullness of grace, and the fullness of grace contains within itself the fullness of truth. The fullness of humanity was therefore assumed from divinity in such a way that in his humanity the whole fullness of divinity is rightly believed to have dwelt bodily, as the Apostle says (Col. II, 9).

Accordingly, all the developments of humanity, both of body and of soul, had to be exhibited for believers. Likewise, his full divinity, together with grace from the beginning of his conception, had gradually to be revealed to all through signs and virtues, so that faith, through the grace of free choice, might be more exaltedly nourished for the attainment of rewards.

As these men were returning,

“Behold, an angel of the Lord appeared again to Joseph in a dream, saying: ‘Rise, take the child and his mother, flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you.’”

O what an unheard-of message, and what a profound matter of humility! He of whom the faithful Prophet had shortly before sung, “Lord, you have become our refuge” (Ps. LXXXIX, 1), and “Our God is refuge and strength” (Ps. XLV, 1), entered Egypt himself, carried there by flight.

It is by no means without mystery, then, that the refuge seeks Egypt by fleeing; that strength, as though struck by fear, appears to be weakened; and that the protection of all, having escaped by flight, migrates to foreigners. Perhaps, just as he was born in order to restore corrupted nature, so too he fled in order to recall fugitives by his examples.

For he was going to command: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. X, 23). Therefore, if strength preserves itself by delaying for more important struggles of virtue, and the defense of all withdraws from danger by taking refuge among foreigners, human frailty should not presumptuously and rashly presume upon its own strength, but should always consider most diligently in everything what is more fruitful.

For God’s fleeing from human beings was a matter of sacrament, not of fear. No one who wishes to entrust his triumph to the ages and leave an example of fighting to posterity enters into a hidden conflict. For he did not flee death who had come to die. Nor did he fear human ambushes who had come to expose and more powerfully overcome all the devil’s cunning and fraud.

For it was written: “You shall not kill a lamb in its mother’s milk” (Exod. XXIII, 19). Therefore provision was made lest what had long been proclaimed, though secretly, in the mystery should be carried out upon one still untried.

For the crafty persuader was plotting to forestall Christ’s assumed infancy and anticipate the signs of his power. Perhaps he had already perceived that certain prophecies were being fulfilled in him. Without doubt he had understood, in accordance with the prophet’s statement, that before the child knew how to call his father or mother—according to the infancy of his humanity—he had received the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria [Col. 0140A] (Isa. VIII, 4).

Isaiah had also foretold this flight, saying: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud,” that is, clothed in flesh without sin, “and he will enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will be shaken before his face” (Isa. XIX, 1). This is confirmed by the traditions of many, so that in a certain city all the idols of Frondosius the commander are said to have fallen entirely to the ground.

And of the five cities speaking the language of Canaan, one was then called the City of the Sun, in which he is said to have dwelt for a longer time. For, as some calculate, from his entry into Egypt until the beginning of Archelaus’s reign there were seven years, during which Christ is believed to have remained hidden in Egypt.

Blessed, I say, is the region which, for so long a period, the Sun of righteousness enlightened by his presence, so that what had been polluted by such filth of idols might at last become like a watered garden through Christ’s teaching and like the paradise of the Lord, gently enriched with heavenly discipline.

Hence it is clear that afterwards almost the whole of that region became a land of monks, both cenobitic and eremitical, a heavenly habitation fashioned in some way after the likeness of paradise. Whoever wishes to know about it should read the Lives of the Fathers and their Conferences. It will become sufficiently and abundantly clear that Christ did not descend into Egypt without reason; indeed, he heard the groaning of those who were afflicted by earthly labors, and he descended to free them, so that, Pharaoh having been drowned, those who had been oppressed by such tribulations and hardships might be released from the yoke of slavery.

“For it will happen,” says the evangelist, “that Herod will seek the child in order to destroy him.”

The angel of the Lord reveals that Herod, while deceitfully lying in wait, had promised that he would worship him, and he warns that the one whom Herod was fraudulently preparing to kill must be carried away according to divine counsel. From this it is entirely clear that frauds, hostilities, and every kind of deceit never escape the eyes of the divine majesty.

For this reason the Lord everywhere abhors a man of blood and deceit and binds him within the bundle of divine vengeance: “Take the child and his mother.” Hence Joseph is taken along not as a husband but as the foster-father and guardian of the Savior’s infancy, and the preservation of virginity is entrusted to him.

He is taken up at night so that this might signify how great and what kind of darkness of unbelief had overshadowed the land of Judea. For the hearts of the Jews were oppressed by nothing other than the night of blindness. He therefore departed at night because, secretly, he descended by flight to enlighten Egypt. But when he came back up from there, neither night nor day is mentioned.

“This was to fulfill,” he says, “what had been spoken by the Lord: ‘Out of Egypt I called my son.’”

We have already discussed above the fulfillment of the prophets. But now also we say that he fled so that the truth of the Law might stand, faith in the prophecy might be confirmed, and the testimony of the Psalter might be strengthened, when the true David fled from the face of King Saul. Hence the Lord also says: “It was necessary that what was written about me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV, 44).

Where this is written, our most distinguished and learned interpreter of all interpreters frequently testifies: according to the Hebrew truth, it is written in Hosea. Some, however, as he himself does not deny, assert that it was taken from the Book of Numbers, from the words of Balaam.

Indeed, in some manuscripts one often finds: “Out of Egypt I called my sons,” which more appropriately applies altogether to the sons of Israel coming out of captivity. But we follow the blessed evangelist and the Hebrew truth, fully confessing that the statement may rightly be understood as concerning Christ, even if it signifies something else, through the foreshadowing of the prophets.

Nevertheless, it appears to have been taken from Numbers, and it seems possible to maintain that it reads as spoken by the Lord. For if, as they say, it had been uttered by one of the holy prophets in Matthew’s words, it would more properly have been said, “as spoken through the Prophet.” But because it perhaps appears to have been inserted here from the words of Balaam the soothsayer, God, the author of this prophecy, who spoke through him, rightly confirms it.

But we do not seek to provoke controversy by objecting as to which of these is more accurate. For even if the statement is understood to have been spoken about Christ in both places, the assertion is thereby made still more secure. For “every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.”

It should also be noted that he says: “Out of Egypt I called my son.” “My,” he says, because the Word became flesh and, according to the unity of person, the one and same person is called both the Son of humanity and properly the Son of God.

Then Herod, seeing that he had been deceived by the Magi, became very angry. And sending out, he killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in all its districts, from two years old and under, according to the time that he had carefully learned from the Magi.

This statement—that he was deceived by the Magi—clings to the preceding words, where it says that they returned to their own country by another way. He is therefore said to have become very angry because, having first been disturbed by rage over Christ’s birth, he was afterwards deceived, and his anger, inflamed by the stimulus of fury, accumulated into a great blaze.

He is said to have killed them because he gave the command by word; for he used his tongue in place of a sword. Hence it is written: “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI, 6).

He killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem so that the one who was recently said to have been born there might not escape. And he did not kill only those found in the city itself; he also slaughtered throughout all its surrounding districts the tender offspring of mothers, from two years old and under, according to the time that he had learned from the Magi.

The time he had learned, then, was reckoned from the rising of the star at its appearance. It does not seem likely that he would have waited for them to return to him from nearby after two years had been completed. For “two years old” in Greek signifies two years.

Hence some suppose that the Magi came after a complete year from Christ’s birth; then, when another year had passed, Herod, seeing that he had been deceived, slaughtered the boys, driven by the goad of fury. Accordingly, it is rightly related that he sought out a period of two years and under from them.
