Nevertheless, I think it should rather be acknowledged that he suppressed the poison of his fraud for so long a time, whatever the reason, until at some point he detected more carefully that the child might slip from his hands. Thus it is established that he waited two years, perhaps lest the child should remain hidden from him by any means. Or perhaps those who had been sent eventually reported back after the reasons for their delay had been resolved.

But when he became certain that he had been deceived, he killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in all its districts, from two years old and under. That is, from the time when the star was known to have appeared until the child of one night old.

Whatever infant age had been enclosed within this period, he therefore ordered to be slaughtered, so that, if there were a child endowed with any grace, he should not escape: if he could not be identified in every way within this span, at least he would be killed among the many.

He therefore killed all, so that not one might escape. But how many there were is not easily discovered, although the tradition of some says, in accordance with the Apocalypse of John, that there were 144,000 (Rev. VII, 5). For there twelve thousand from every tribe are recorded there; here, however, all are said to have been killed only from Bethlehem and its districts.

Others again assert that two thousand infants were killed across a span of twenty localities, so that one hundred were slain in each place. We do not affirm this, because we believe that what we do not read in the Holy Scriptures is better left unknown than rashly defined.

For the present we acknowledge only this: they are not hidden from God, to whom all live, those who for the Lord endured the loss of life.

The cruel command of the king, moreover, anticipated all the districts of that same city, just as it also anticipated the entire period that he had previously learned from the Magi, so that the one who, while remaining with the Father without place or time, was born within time and place as one possessing locality, might be concealed neither by place nor by time.

Hence some more truly think that he killed the boys after the completion of a year from the birth; but he ordered them killed from two years old and under so that, just as he had anticipated the city’s surrounding districts, he likewise anticipated beyond a complete year an equal span of time, extending backward through the whole preceding age up to the limit of the child who was one night old.

The exceedingly crafty enemy therefore knew that the child who was divine could suddenly appear before his eyes as though two years old or one night old, in order to conceal the age proper to his time. For this reason, under this condition, he anticipated all the divisions of time and place on either side, so that without any ambiguity he might enclose for death the one whom he sought.

[Col. 0142D] Then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah, who said:

> “A voice was heard in Rama, lamentation and great wailing: Rachel weeping for her children.”

Here he perhaps recalls the ancient history (Judges 19–20), where, on account of the Levite’s wife, who had been killed after being violated and divided into twelve parts according to the number of the twelve tribes, all Israel destroyed the tribe of Benjamin almost to extinction, except for three hundred men. The wailing and great cry of those who survived them is said to have been heard as far as Rama, nearly twelve miles from Bethlehem, and is magnified to such an extent that Rachel, already dead, is poetically said to weep for her children in the grief of one who mourns.

Thus, by this passage, a history concerning the Chaldeans is woven: the future devastation of the Jewish people would be like that earlier disaster. But more truly, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, the blessed Evangelist understands the prophecy of the killing of the children, who were slain for Christ, although it does not seem inappropriate to refer it to both events, in the manner of prophecy.

Therefore it is rightly said that then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah, who said, “A voice was heard in Rama.” For although the prophetic utterance looks toward the impending captivity of the Jews, nevertheless, as though from a shadow, the reality of the body—namely, the future slaughter of the infants—is announced in it. And it is said to have been fulfilled because, until it happened, it lay before its readers as though only half-complete: what then seemed to resound in the literal account of the event was secretly promising something quite different in the distant future.

For Rama, where the voice of lamentation and wailing is said to have resounded, we should not think to be the name of the place situated near Gaba, almost twelve miles, as I have said, from Bethlehem. Rather, we often establish from the statements of the teachers that *Rama* means “the lofty place.” Therefore, “A voice was heard in Rama,” that is, in the heights. For the lament of the mourners, resounding far and wide in its intensity, reached God in heaven.

In various places in the holy Scriptures, the voice of a cry is said to reach the heights—that is, the ears of the most high God—such as the cry of sin, which continually cries out before God against sinners. Concerning this the Lord says:

> “The cry of Sodom has come to me” (Genesis 18:20).

And elsewhere the prophet, after recalling the sins of the people, says:

> “Are not all these things in the ears of the Lord of hosts?” (Isaiah 5:9.)

There is also the cry of those who, oppressed by poverty, are cruelly afflicted by exactors; or certainly that of widows and orphans whenever they are unjustly oppressed. Hence the Lord says:

> “They will cry out to me in due time, and I will hear their cry” (Exodus 22:23).

There is also, beneath the altar of God, the cry of the holy dead who were killed for the word of God and for the testimony they possess, whose blood was poured out upon the earth. Concerning them the blessed John says in his Apocalypse (6:10):

> “And they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, O holy and true one, will you not judge our blood against those who dwell on the earth?’”

The voice of Abel’s blood is likewise said to cry out from the earth against Cain. Therefore the Lord says:

> “That all righteous blood which has been shed upon the earth may come upon you, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Luke 6:51).

Among these, the voice of the children is said to have been heard in Rama—that is, in the heights—all the more clearly because the innocent life of the whole multitude was slaughtered with such cruelty for the sake of the one Redeemer of all.

If this voice of the infants, as though foreknown, sounded clearly from the heights when the prophet saw these things in the Spirit, it resounded far more powerfully when many thousands already filled the air everywhere with their groans; when that glorious multitude of infants, in the simplicity of their purity, fell in death for Christ; when all their mothers, their faces covered, tore at the hair upon their heads and beat their bared breasts; when they watered their cheeks with tearful showers and wounded their entire bodies with their fingernails; when fathers and mothers no less than all their relatives stretched out their hands and raised cries of lament to heaven.

Could not such a great cry from them all, and such a cruel persecution of Christ, have reached heaven from everyone? Could the voice of the blood of so many have been silent upon the earth, when the voice of Abel’s blood cries from the earth to God in heaven?

A voice was therefore rightly heard in Rama, because in their likeness the race of all who were to suffer for Christ was represented. Hence, while they are initiated beneath God’s altar to remain there with the others, we rightly say that, in their voices also, the voices of all the holy martyrs are already heard in Rama, that is, in the heavenly realms.

It was therefore no small matter for the prophet to prefigure carefully, though obscurely, the mysteries of so great a secret: just as in them the race of all martyrs for Christ was already signified, so in Rachel the figure of the whole Church, weeping in this valley of tears for her slain children, was displayed more explicitly.

Therefore, as soon as Christ appeared to the world, brought forth by the Virgin, he began to suffer; for while he himself endured persecution, the persecution of all the saints was represented in him, as it were, by way of foreshadowing. Upon him these children are first consecrated by their own blood as a sacrifice, so that infancy, still tender and suckling, might offer a more meaningful beginning, until all the members of the perfected man are gathered into one.[Col. 0144C]

Thus the infants are killed while the infant Christ is sought. In these same infants the form of martyrdom is born, where the infancy of the whole Church is more wonderfully consecrated. From this point onward the members of the body are gradually prepared in conformity with Christ, until, regenerated for eternity into a perfect man according to the measure of his fullness, we all hasten to meet him.

Therefore Rachel, who is called “the sheep of God”—that is, the Church of Christ—rightly mourns her tender lambs slain by death. She does not wish to be consoled at present, because they are not here; rather, she transfers all her hope and the joy of consolation to eternal life, so that there she may receive, clothed in blessed immortality, those whom here she lost, stripped of a life that was all too brief.

The reading of Genesis teaches us about Rachel (48:7), where it says that she died and was buried in the springtime on the road to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. She was buried on the road because she was a type of the Church, which is not yet in the homeland but on the road, which is Christ; those who pass along it go forward weeping and carrying their seeds.

No one of sound judgment can doubt that their voice rises to the heights and that, through their weeping, the ears of God are daily struck. She is also buried on the road in springtime because, while we are here in Christ, we are continually put to death by giving birth to him, and our life is hidden until the cold of unbelief has passed away. Then, when Christ appears, who is our way, truth, and life, we too shall appear with him in glory.

Meanwhile, the voice of the cry grows louder each day, and the weeping and mourning increase, because we are not of this world. For if we were of the world, the world would love what belonged to it. But our Rachel, while giving birth on the road, is sorrowful, since it was said to her:

> “You will weep and mourn, but the world will rejoice.”

Then consolation is immediately added:

> “But your sorrow will be turned into joy.”

Therefore she does not wish to be consoled here, because her children are not of this world. Rather, with all her children she transfers herself to the place where she sent Christ—born, suffering, and raised again—as the food of her satisfaction, before her, in the house of bread.

Since we have touched only briefly upon this matter in proportion to its size, it remains to ask, according to the historical account, how Rachel could mourn the children of Judah, that is, of Bethlehem, as though they were her own, when Benjamin was born from her, while the city of Bethlehem is in no way found within his tribe.

Perhaps the matter can be explained more briefly by the fact that she is read to have been buried there, near Bethlehem, on the road, so that from the eternal lodging of her little body she received the name of mother. Alternatively, she is perhaps said to weep for this reason: Judah and Benjamin were two tribes joined together. Herod, however, had ordered not only the children in Bethlehem to be killed but also those in all the surrounding territory. Since the king’s order occasioned such a slaughter, we understand that many from Benjamin too were put to death.

Rachel mourns these as her children and receives no consolation, according to the twofold understanding of some. Either she thought them dead forever, or she refused to be consoled here concerning those whom she knew would live forever.

More truly, however, as we have said, the figure of the whole Church is expressed in Rachel. Therefore both interpretations suit her from either side: either she grieves not only those who were killed but is also shown to mourn those whom she wished to retain after they had first been born, or whom she wished to give birth to though they had not yet been born. She receives no consolation concerning them because they have been destroyed by eternal death, since they are not destined to remain in eternal stability.

Or she refused consolation because those whom she mourned as lost did not remain; for those who seemed to have died had been transferred through martyrdom into the perfection of eternity. Consolation is rightly sought and afforded for something lost, not for something held or possessed. For from increased happiness the joy of eternal life is surely generated more abundantly in the future.

Nevertheless, whatever understanding of these meanings one may accept, one must not refuse to acknowledge that a figurative expression intervenes. Accordingly, even if the voice of lamentation is said, according to the letter, to have reached as far as Rama from Rachel’s tomb, this does not depart from the truth; just as she is fittingly shown to have mourned her children—not fabulously, but in the manner of transformed speech—even though she was dead.

It is better, however, for the mystical figure of the mystery to be introduced through Rachel than if the city of Bethlehem were said to have mourned, because through her the pattern of the Church of Christ is more clearly commended to all who read.

The Church of Christ is commended through Rachel, together with its head, as mourning both those transferred from this life by death and those killed by punishment, just as the devil, together with his members, is completely represented through Herod.

Thus Herod learned where and when Christ had come, yet he did not venerate him as Christ, nor did he understand where he was from, or for what purpose or in what manner he had come; he did not inquire into these things at all. So too all the wicked, who are the members of the enemy, although they falsely name Christ, neither understand him nor venerate him rightly nor seek him; rather, they persecute him in his members, and by living perversely they withdraw far away and turn aside.

After Herod had died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying:

> “Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel.”

Here we must not understand this Herod to be the one whom we later read had John beheaded, but the one whom we have already discussed above, whose son and successor he unquestionably was.[Col. 0146B]

“Take,” he says, “the child and his mother”—the child, certainly, and not “his son”; the child’s mother, and not “his wife.” Moreover, he is commanded in a dream to return, just as he had earlier been warned in a dream to descend into Egypt, because it had not yet been publicly revealed whom the angel was serving in devoted obedience.

“For those who sought the child’s life have died,” he says. Here it is rightly implied that, when the cruel king had died, his accomplices immediately perished as well—those who had together plotted Christ’s death out of envy, fear, or flattery.

It is therefore surprising how it can be said, “Those who sought the child’s life have died,” when the Lord says:

> “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28).

For if the soul, invisible and intangible, cannot be killed by these bodily weapons, how can it rightly be sought for destruction, especially since it is immortal even after its departure from the flesh?

Here, then, he either simply used “soul” for the flesh alone, or—and this is what I think more likely—for the present life, since in Scripture “soul” is sometimes understood as this temporal life. Accordingly, the one who sought the child’s soul is rightly understood to be the one who was attempting to extinguish his present life.

It should also be noted that Christ possessed a soul, something the Apollinarians attempt to deny. They may perhaps be called “those who sought” in the plural so that by this means Herod’s savagery might be represented as still more atrocious.

For it is reported that, before he died, he ordered all the nobles of the Jews to be killed at his funeral, at least so that the Jews would thereby be compelled to weep as though for his own death. Perhaps the angel wished to allude to this when he said:

> “Those who sought the child’s life have died.”

By synecdoche, many can also be more significantly called dead in place of one, so that it might be shown more clearly that the entire order of persecutors had ceased to persecute.

When he had died, the holy Church of God, living in Christ, was daily invited more fully and perfectly to the heavenly Jerusalem.

We rightly placed the type of the Church first in this passage, since not only is heard the voice of lamentation belonging to that woman who, being already dead, felt no grief over lost children, but through her is also signified, in a higher sense, the voice of this Church, which had long been barren and is now fruitful.

This is not because there are none who were thought to have died through martyrdom, especially since they are believed to have been carried again and again into glory through the increase of eternity. Rather, it is because she was unable to retain all whom she brought forth, or to persuade to the faith from tyranny those whom she continually invited to the rewards of a better life.

For, as we have said, consolation is needed for what is lost, not for what has been increased; what has been happily transformed for the better brings joy rather than sorrow and heaps gladness upon those who enjoy it.

Therefore the blessed Evangelist, wishing to confirm this figure, added what follows, saying:

> “He rose, took the child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel. But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judaea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. And being warned in a dream, he withdrew into the regions of Galilee. And he came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth.”

We have rightly said that the typological form of the narrative is preserved, because Joseph represents the apostles, through whose ministry Christ was to be carried everywhere throughout this Egypt of sorrow and tribulation.

When Herod had died—that is, when the Jewish people, under his rule, had been struck down through the fault of unbelief in the Lord’s passion—the apostles were sent to preach to the Jews, to whom the Lord had been sent as to lost sheep. But while the hereditary dominion of unbelief remained, they were afraid and withdrew, warned through a vision of the Holy Spirit. Observing the gift of grace among the Gentiles, they transferred to them Christ, who had formerly been sent to the Jews.

Otherwise, how could Joseph, hearing that Archelaus was reigning in Judaea in place of his father Herod, have been afraid to go there, if he was being urged by an angel to go up? Should a righteous man have feared what was commanded through an angel? Or, if it was his weakness to fear on account of unbelief, how is he again instructed by an angel, without any reproach, to go over into Galilee?

He is therefore commanded to return to Judaea and is afraid, but when warned to cross into Galilee, the region of the Gentiles, he does not refuse at all. Either he ought not to have been afraid in this way, if it had truly been commanded, or else a command immediately to be changed ought not to have been delivered by the angel.

It is therefore plainly evident that a typological meaning has been preserved here.

Or perhaps we should understand it in this way: when Joseph heard, “Go into the land of Israel,” he understood that he was first commanded to go into Judaea, since he undoubtedly thought Judaea itself to be the land of Israel. But after he learned that Archelaus reigned there, he did not wish to expose himself to danger, especially because he had judged that Christ and his followers—about whom the angelic responses had given such warnings—ought to dwell nowhere other than Jerusalem, where God’s temple and the gathering-place of all the prophets were.

He would certainly have gone there if Archelaus had not already been wielding the royal scepter there in his father’s place.

Nevertheless, when the angel said, “Go into the land of Israel,” he intended not Judaea but Galilee, which the Jewish people also inhabited and in which Nazareth was certainly located. Galilee was in fact the metropolitan city to which Nazareth is shown to have belonged, as a part belongs to the whole.

When the angel saw that the error had arisen from piety, and the fear as though from prudence, he instructed him to go into Galilee, to the city of Nazareth—not changing the command of the vision, but correcting more clearly the error born of piety.

Therefore the Evangelist immediately added, in order to make it clearer that this had been predestined:

> “So that what was written through the prophets might be fulfilled: ‘He will be called a Nazaraean.’”

From this it is gathered that the angel had in no way first commanded anything other than what had been predestined from every side. The sequence did not follow the outcome of events; rather, the outcome of events everywhere followed the predestined sequence.

The sequence, as I think, is not simply transformed in some respect according to any kind of cause. Rather, the truth of predestination is fulfilled in all things to such a degree that the order of events performed typologically brings forth, in almost every case, the mysteries of the realities represented.

Thus the little children are first slaughtered because their only cause was innocence, so that everyone may understand that martyrdom arises neither from the guilt of sin nor from merit or any choice, but from the grace of God.

Indeed, everything is woven together in such a way that the truth is disclosed and the typological utterances of the mysteries lend their support.

At this point some are still troubled because Luke reports that Herod’s monarchy was divided into four parts. How, then, can it be true that Joseph, hearing that Archelaus reigned in Judaea, was afraid to go there, and not rather into Galilee, where, according to the Gospel, another Herod is said to have reigned?

Josephus and many others resolve this question by saying that Archelaus first assumed the monarchy of the entire kingdom after his father, and that, when he grew arrogant, he was deposed by Tiberius from his father’s throne and the kingdom was divided among four tetrarchs.

One of these, namely Galilee, he assigned to Archelaus’s brother Herod. Herod had not yet received it when Archelaus was still oppressing the whole monarchy of the kingdom with his cruel rule; but afterward, by the just judgment of God, Archelaus was transported into exile at Lugdunum, which is a city of Gaul.

This is why Joseph, foreseeing in him an heir of cruelty, had previously feared him.

> “So that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: ‘He will be called a Nazaraean.’”

For if one of the prophets had provided a sufficiently explicit testimony in the Scriptures, he would not have said, as he does here, “through the prophets,” in a manner that leaves the matter uncertain.

Nevertheless, I think he drew the meaning from the very passages of Scripture and thereby fulfilled the truth of his assertion, since here Christ is rightly called a Nazaraean, as though he were the Holy of Holies.

For according to the Hebrew truth, we read in Isaiah:

> “A shoot will go out from the root of Jesse, and a Nazaraean will rise from the root” (Isaiah 11:1).

Therefore Nazareth is interpreted no less as a new shoot than as a flower of the field. From the root of this shoot, the Holy of Holies—that is, the one called the Nazaraean—is, as I think, read to have risen, signifying the substance of his eternity.

Where could he be more suitably nurtured than in Nazareth, from which he would receive a name indicating that, essentially, he himself is holiness, nurtured in holiness, and therefore rightly called the Holy of Holies?

From this it is plainly clear that, just as he chose the time at which he would be born and the place in which he would be born, so too he is rightly said to have chosen the city in which he would grow up, in order to explain more meaningfully the mysteries of his incarnation.

There is, even today, in Galilee, a village facing the region on its eastern side, about fifteen miles away, near Mount Tabor, called Nazara. Many think that this was formerly the same place as Nazareth, but that, gradually declining, it was changed from a city into a village.

The Lord was nurtured there so that, through it, the one who was to be called by that name might be more fully recognized as coming from it.

For *Nazaraean* is understood in various ways in the sacred Scriptures. Under the Law there were Nazaraeans whose vow lasted for a time; or, from the beginning to the end, they became Nazaraeans for the sake of their consecration.

But those who belonged to this city, perhaps by the law of their ancestral land, were likewise called Nazaraeans, or at least Nazarenes, for the sake of distinction.

Among them the Savior wished to be called a Nazaraean, so that he might be recognized as the same one who, through Daniel, was proclaimed to be the Holy of Holies.

The disciples too were first called Nazaraeans, but afterward they received the name “Christians” from Christ, and all Christians have been so called ever since. Concerning them it is rightly sung:

> “They became white as his Nazaraeans” (Lamentations 4:7);

they gave splendor to God because they were clothed in the wedding garment.

Some heretics, moreover, were called Nazarenes because they believed in Christ, but in such a way that they attempted to observe all the institutions of the Old Testament. Thus they preach that Christ must be received in order not to appear to omit the shadow of the Law.

Because their schism chose a distinctive way of life, they found for themselves, I do not know from what author, a distinctive Gospel, properly called the Gospel of the Nazarenes. As though boasting of their religion, they gave themselves the name of holiness, but proved themselves guilty because they did not believe that Christ was sufficient for everyone’s justification.

Thus, in their superstition, attempting to sew new things onto old, they produced a worse division, and became without God, since they were found without faith.

When the Gospel had said that he came and dwelt in the city called Nazareth, so that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled, “He will be called a Nazaraean,” it immediately added:

**(CHAP. III.)** “In those days John the Baptist came, preaching in the wilderness of Judaea, saying: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’”

From this a considerable question appears to arise between the two Evangelists. For as soon as Matthew mentions that the infant or child was brought back from Egypt, he immediately confirms that John the Baptist came “in those days,” as though the events were continuous.

Luke, however, more clearly declares that in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governing Judaea, Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, Philip his brother tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, Lysanius tetrarch of Abilene, and Annas and Caiaphas were chief priests, the word of the Lord came to John, son of Zechariah, in the wilderness. He also indicates that Jesus was then nearly thirty years old, when he is soon afterward shown to have been baptized by John.

We must therefore understand that these were different “days” of time: one period when, according to the testimony of Scripture, Archelaus was still ruling Judaea; another when Luke, in the manner of historians, more explicitly declares through the earthly powers that the herald of Christ came to preach.

At that time Christ, as may be inferred, was not yet eight years old; now he was already approaching thirty. The times themselves had changed so greatly that Pilate was then governing Judaea, and the kingdom was recorded as divided into tetrarchies under the chief priests Annas and Caiaphas.

It is therefore clear that by saying, “In those days,” Matthew intended to indicate not merely the period of childhood, but all the days during which Christ had begun to dwell in Nazareth, until he too came up from Galilee to be baptized by John, and wished to present them as continuous.

During those days, while he still dwelt in Nazareth subject to his parents, John came preaching the baptism of repentance in the wilderness.

Luke also indicates this when he says:

> “The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was with him. His parents went every year to Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover” (Luke 2:40).

And afterward:

> “When he was twelve years old, and they had gone up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the festival day, after the days had been completed, as they were returning, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem. When they searched for him, they found him in the midst of the teachers” (ibid. 2:42).

Then it is written that he went down with them, came to Nazareth, and was subject to them (ibid. 2:51).

From this it is understood that, during those same days when he first began to dwell in Nazareth, while he was still living there, John came into the wilderness to prepare the way for his coming. He preached repentance and announced that the kingdom of heaven had drawn near.

The herald of truth first announces the same things that Truth himself later preaches by his own authority for the salvation of humanity and commends. Since the voice went before the Word, it was right that it should first announce what afterward would sound in harmony from the same Word:

> “Preaching in the wilderness of Judaea and saying: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’”

The word “saying” refers to the command, “Repent”; “preaching” refers to what he had said: “For the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

For the two words could not have been repeated together without meaning, since not even a letter or a jot is without mystery.

To repent, therefore, is to punish within oneself the errors of one’s former life; then, through hope in the promises of the heavenly kingdom, to lift one’s mind toward higher things and urge oneself toward the practices of a better life.

Nothing can have greater power to persuade the minds of hearers than the hope of eternal promise, the fear of punishments, and the threat of divine majesty.

Divine providence, seeing that these things were especially suited to persuasion, wished by saying, “Repent,” to show that the first virtue of the wretched is that, through repentance, they learn to put the old self to death within themselves and hate their vices. Unless each person does this, he will be unable not only to grasp the virtues but even to escape the destruction of punishments.

The virtue of repentance is also conceived through fear; but fear itself, under the inspiration of divine grace, is in turn generated by wisdom. Hence it is written:

> “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Sirach 1:16).

Repentance is rightly believed to derive its name from punishment, because through it each person punishes what he knows he has unlawfully committed. No one can worthily do this unless, enlightened by wisdom, he has begun to distinguish between good and evil.

But when someone is moved by fear and struggles courageously against evils by punishing them within himself, it is necessary that he be lifted up by the hope of grace. Through this hope he becomes accustomed to long for what is worthy.

No one can rightly become accustomed to pursuing what ought to be followed unless he first ceases to pursue what is judged contrary and destroys the efforts of virtue.

Therefore, under this deliberation, whoever wishes to practice repentance for his salvation should always set before his eyes the fear of divine judgment and dread of punishments.

Then, veiled in shame and continually standing before God, covered with modesty, let him temper the sorrow of his heart with tears; for without pain there can be no wounds, unless the vital parts of the limbs have been partly deadened.

If, then, the wound of the heart feels no pain, it is dead, and is all the more incurable because it neither feels itself nor, by feeling, is able to receive the medicine that comes upon it.

If it begins to feel, this will be the work of divine grace, which has first restored to it the freedom to feel. Then freedom, together with grace, must persevere tirelessly, so that by applying the medicine daily the sick soul may receive its former health from the physician.

Thus the herald of truth offers such an antidote of salvation to the sick:

> “Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

It is as though he were saying openly: Let each person punish the evil deeds of his former life, and let him cut away the rotten wounds of his inner organs with the cautery of repentance, because the health we lost has drawn near, and the opportunity of hope has come, so that we may return from where we fell.

“For the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” If it had not drawn near, none of us could have returned to it, since, deprived of the use of our feet and blinded in our sight, we had lost even the way, which is Christ, while we were spiritually unsound.

John came to prepare this way and first proposes the steps of repentance by which one may reach it. Whoever rejects this loses not only what it promises but also falls more deeply on account of his contempt.

Hence Paul also says:

> “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? According to your hardness,” he says, “you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Romans 2:4).

Therefore let no one despise the first voice of the herald in his preaching; let no one neglect the beginning of salvation; let no one scorn the Savior’s first teachings; let no one consider lightly the fruit of repentance, after whose proclamation the kingdom of heaven is announced to be near.

This voice had never before been heard anywhere, and for that reason it ought to be honored greatly.

John was the first, before the others, to preach that the kingdom of heaven was near. Repentance, through which he graciously invites us to come to it, must not be despised.

Thus he announces either that the present Christ, through whom the saints reign in the heavenly realms, has already drawn near by being born; or certainly that the Gospel of the kingdom, through which all are invited to the heavens, has come.

Its first voice is, “Repent,” and therefore it rightly immediately adds that the kingdom has drawn near.

For this is the one of whom it was spoken through the prophet Isaiah:

> “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.”

This testimony appears to have been placed ambiguously. It is not sufficiently clear whether the Evangelist, affirming this about John, continues his account, or whether John himself speaks figuratively about himself as about another, according to the custom of the Scriptures.

If we understand John to have said this about himself—“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. This is the one who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah,” and the rest that follows—the meaning is as though he were saying, “I am the one who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah.”

Such a manner of speech occurs very frequently in the Scriptures. Thus Matthew says:

> “Jesus found a man sitting at the tax booth” (Matthew 9:9),

and he did not say, “He found me sitting,” lest he appear to speak boastfully about himself.

Likewise Moses, throughout the entire text of the divine Law, speaks in this way about himself or another:

> “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying.”

He did not consider it appropriate to write, “The Lord spoke to me,” in order to express himself.

Nor is this surprising, since the Lord himself very often says of himself, “the Son of Man” or “the Son of God,” rather than saying “I,” especially since he wishes to proclaim the Father no less through himself than himself as God.

Thus he says:

> “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day.”

He does not say, “It was necessary for me to suffer.”

In the same way, when John had said, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near,” he preferred to append what follows about himself more obscurely:

> “For this is the one who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah.”

The Evangelist immediately appears to demonstrate this by connecting his narrative in the following manner:

> “Now John himself had clothing made of camel’s hair.”

It should not at all seem contradictory that elsewhere, when questioned about himself, the same John again says:

> “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness,”

although he had already said the same thing earlier, as we have related, when he said, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

He called himself a voice because the prophet, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, had first called him by that name—not by his own assumption, but by the assertion of truth.

No word is heard without a voice, nor can a voice signify anything without the understanding of a word. A kind of proclamation of the word is therefore formed in the voice, so that when the voice has passed away, the inner word, which remains alive, may be perceived.

John too is divinely sent before the Word, so that through his proclamation the Word who was in the beginning with God might be more fully understood.

John was rightly called a voice because he was the herald of the Word. Therefore he confessed about himself what he knew he had long ago been called, and fulfilled the office of a voice, so that the Word who was in the beginning might be rightly understood.

> “Prepare,” he says, “the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.”

It is as though he were saying openly: Since the Word who was in the beginning has come to enlighten the hearts of believers, cleanse your mind and correct your conduct, so that by believing you may be able worthily to receive him within yourselves.

You know, therefore, that the way of the Word is directed toward the heart. Prepare faith, then, so that through it Christ may enter your heart.

Direct your conduct in righteousness, so that through it he may set the steps of salvation within you, as though along the paths of justice.

> “I will dwell,” he says, “in their hearts through faith.”

And the Apostle says:

> “For we walk by faith, and not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7).

Therefore, when faith is rightly held within us, the way of the Lord is directed toward the heart; and when our conduct is changed for the better, we prepare within ourselves the straight paths of God.

But John himself had a garment made of camel hair and a leather belt around his loins. From this, surely, we ought to understand his dress, manner of life, and food in such a way that we remember that the preacher of repentance both presented in his own person the reality of his deeds and offered a model through the practices of those who repent. For the place of his way of life is described not as a gathering of people but as the desert. His clothing, too, is shown to have been not soft and delicate, such as might nourish the flow of lust, but stiff and rough, made of camel hair. Scripture then reveals, even without our saying anything, how meager and unusual his food was. Indeed, nature urges us to confess that life can be preserved in him only by grace, although it does not dare to imitate him.

It was therefore fitting that the one to whom the privileges of first proclaiming the kingdom of heaven were entrusted should, insofar as is permitted to mortals, imitate the angelic life and strip himself of the world’s possessions, so that through him his hearers might learn to fulfill by their deeds what he was urging in words. First, therefore, he sets repentance before his hearers—the return from error, the retreat from crime, the abolition of sin, and progress toward paradise. Then, by living, he displays what he teaches, so that he may instruct all teachers that they must first condemn in themselves the things from which they restrain others, and by their deeds make possible whatever they urge should be done.

Unhappy indeed is the age of our own time, when scarcely anyone is found who possesses by his manner of life the evangelical form, but all pursue the honors of present things, so that by fair means and foul they may rule rather than benefit. Yet all preach things which scarcely even a few would wish to maintain in conduct and life: for while they persuade others to poverty, everyone desires to reign. They have become supporters of the very blessedness which, even if they could—and especially since they ought to—fulfill in deed, they do not wish to move even a finger toward. John, however, because he transforms in himself the form of one who despises the present life, not only desires to endure the world’s evils but also adopts such clothing and food that, as blessed Hilary relates, he bears the figure of all those whom, by the example of his teaching, he figuratively chews and passes through within his body. Thus what he does inwardly is more fully shown by what he displays outwardly.

For by the desert, where he first cries out, “Repent,” he signifies those whom the grace of the Holy Spirit had abandoned, so that this teaches not only what a suitable place for repentance is, but also what those people are among whom, as among deaf hearers, he proclaims that the kingdom of heaven has arrived, if only they have emptied themselves of vices. The haircloth woven from camel hair is a sufficiently clear indication of an austere life, by which the incentives of desire are restrained; and it represents those who, weighed down by the honors of earthly things, come to the faith, especially those gathered from the Gentiles. Hence the prophet, speaking to the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, to the Church—promises: “The multitude of camels shall cover you” (Isa. 60:6).

When John invites these people to the faith of Christ, persuading them here to repent, what else is he doing than sending to Christ, clothed in it, a garment made from camels? Thus on every side the divine mysteries of the teachings give off their fragrance, so that it may be shown that those belong to the adornment of Christ’s garment who, through repentance, lead an austere life and lay down upon Christ the burden of their sin.

The leather belt around his loins, by which the mortification of the flesh is expressed, signifies those who, receiving the faith, have clung to Christ’s loins; through this they are found to be descendants from his seed, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ. Furthermore, the Jews—fugitives from the truth—are not improperly signified by the locusts. Through the law they seemed to bear the wings of virtues, and hence, as though by certain leaps of their bodies, they were lifted higher from the earth. But because they followed the letter without the spirit, they gnawed with their teeth at the harvest of the law, devouring it through their faulty interpretations. They were wanderers, driven by the wind of desire; barren in deeds, querulous in words, and carried about by every wind of doctrine.

Later, however, many of them become food for the saints, together with wild honey, and nourishment for the prophets. Honey is tasted as food not from the law’s beehives but from the trunks of wild trees, so that this may more plainly declare how sweet the Gentile people, called to grace, are when joined to Christ’s body. Hence David sang: “We found it in the fields of the forest” (Ps. 131:6), among which John, nourished by its sweetness, is pleasantly fed. Perhaps Jonathan, the son of Saul, had also come into this forest, where this honey flowed upon the surface of the earth (1 Sam. 14:27). After tasting a little of it, he is read to have been enlightened, so that this might more clearly signify that the grace of the Redeemer had flowed into the Church from the Gentiles. Whoever touches it is not only enlightened but also inwardly refreshed and strengthened.

Then Jerusalem and all Judea and the entire region around the Jordan went out to him, and they were baptized while confessing their sins.

Here it should be noted that they confess their sins in order to become worthy of the grace of baptism, in accordance with what they had heard: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” Hence it is evident that no one can repent rightly unless he first confesses his sins and condemns the errors of his former life, so that he may be made fit to receive grace and then, at last, be consecrated in the body of Christ through the sacred mysteries of the divine sacraments.

[159] Moreover, from what the Apostle says—“For the gifts and the calling are without repentance” (Rom. 11:29)—a question not unfittingly arises for readers. For if the gifts of the mystery are without repentance, and the remission of sins is bestowed upon us in baptism, it seems that repentance is preached to those who hasten to it as though it were unworthy. But repentance is understood in three ways. One is the complete condemnation, through repentance, of the errors of vice and of all the works of the devil before the washing of the font. Another is falling into sin after the font of remission and being renewed again through repentance. There is also the repentance by which the saints are daily cleansed from such offenses, without which our human mortality can scarcely, or certainly cannot, live.

The first kind of repentance is preached so that a person who, by turning aside after vain things, had despised God his Creator and had become a child of wrath through guilt might finally return to himself and utterly condemn the errors of his former life as the beginning of faith. For it was not lawful to serve two masters. Rather, when the rightful master came, it was proper that he should abandon what he had previously held wickedly and punish in himself whatever had lived badly within him, so that by this means he might become capable of divine grace.

Yet his doing these things was not the work of his own freedom, since he was subject to slavery, but of the grace of the One who called him. This grace not only freely forgave the guilty their sins but also gave them the ability to do what it commanded; afterward, it more fully bestowed the merit by which each person might receive what had been promised. And therefore the Apostle rightly proclaims that the gifts and calling are without repentance, especially since everything is given freely, to such an extent that repentance itself is rightly called God’s gift.

Can any repentance belonging to religion, then, be seen without God’s grace, especially when the prophet asks: “Convert me, Lord, and I shall be converted to you” (Jer. 31:18)? “After you, Lord, converted me, I repented; after you showed me, I struck my thigh.” It is as though he were plainly saying: “Unless you had converted me, I certainly would not have repented by my own power.” Hence it is clearly established that repentance is God’s gift.

Nevertheless, the Apostle declares that the grace of baptism and the remission of sins are given without that repentance which is imposed in the Church upon those who sin publicly. Nor are Christ and John at all silent about the repentance by which a person renounces the devil and all his works. In the former, little bodily satisfaction is required; in the latter, time is spent more extensively, in proportion to the gravity of the offense and to the fruit of the repentance of one who laments his errors. This is not so that converts should despair of pardon in one and the same moment, but so that the guilty person, by making satisfaction, may merit to receive a measured draught of tears.

Concerning those who before receiving the gift had pursued vain practices, the Apostle says: “What fruit did you have then, in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21). Concerning these people, elsewhere the divine voice speaks through John: “Remember from where you have fallen, and do repentance, and do your former works” (Rev. 2:5)—namely, the works which you ought first to have performed through charity.

But the Apostle Paul, speaking to the Hebrews, not only denies that this repentance, which we have mentioned, is to be performed before baptism; he even calls baptism itself repentance. He says: “It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, who have likewise tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt” (Heb. 6:4–6).

What, then, does he mean when he says that it is impossible for the enlightened to be renewed again to repentance? Does he deny this second repentance, which we have said occurs after grace? Far from it. He cannot deny the repentance which he himself is repeatedly shown to have preached. But when he says “to be renewed again to repentance,” it is as though he were saying: “It is impossible for them to repeat baptism.” At this point, therefore, he calls baptism repentance, and for that reason rightly denies that they can be renewed again to repentance. For just as Christ died once for our sins, so it is necessary for us also to die once with him through baptism.

In this baptism, gifts and remission are bestowed without repentance, because through baptism that by which we are reborn to become children of God is freely granted to all. But whoever sins after this unto death, although all his sins are consigned to oblivion on whatever day he may be converted, nevertheless cannot be expiated free from repentance without some satisfaction proportionate to the offense.

Perhaps Paul wished to affirm this when he said that the gifts of remission and the calling are without repentance, although we believe that if someone falls afterward, it is necessary for him to fulfill repentance again. But concerning those who do not sin so greatly, and nevertheless punish themselves daily by purifying themselves through the lamentation of strict discipline, we understand the saying: “The just man falls seven times and rises again.” He falls through various excesses of sin, without which our mortality does not subsist; but he rises immediately through humble confession, firm in his purpose even if he is found weak in his failure.

Otherwise he would not be considered just in the interval when he fell into guilt, if, once justified, he did not immediately take up forgiveness again through pardon. Therefore no one at all is found who does not need confession, since truth exposes this need. Let no one excuse himself, so that while the opportunity remains he may not fail to seek mercy. Let him not be ashamed to confess to the physician who has already been sacrificed for all what those people were not ashamed formerly to make known to John, when only a small amount of the antidote of salvation had yet been disclosed to them.

If, then, those who went out to him from every side confessed their sins before they had yet received the truth, what do you think ought to be done by those who, after receiving pardon, are still wrapped in the darkness of sins? Unless they come to the light of confession, they remain surrounded by the gloom of darkness and in death. For everyone who remains in death is still in darkness and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes.

To remain in death, then, is to be confined until now within the gates of sin. No one escapes from those gates unless he is aided by the One to whom David said: “You who lift me up from the gates of death” (Ps. 9:14). Understanding this, John said:

When he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?”

It is as though he were plainly saying: “No one except the only Son of God, whom I announce to you as the One who is to come and whom, by a brief manifestation, I shall point out to you more clearly than light.”

He calls them a brood of vipers because, having been born from poisonous parents, they first ought, by confessing, to lay aside the poisons of their ancient deceit and then, clothed in faith in Christ, enter the font of their cleansing. He appropriately devised this comparison from the nature of vipers, according to the natural philosophers. For they say that the nature of vipers is such that, when the female conceives, she caresses the male’s head with her mouth and, in the excessive heat of lust, draws out his venom; once this has been consumed, the male immediately perishes in death. When the time of giving birth arrives, however, the female herself is killed by the weight of the offspring: for the young tear open their mother’s womb with their claws and are expelled together with her life and her scattered entrails.

[162] So also the Jews, killing with a hostile mouth the head of the man, who is Christ, killed their mother—namely, the synagogue of the prophets, or of those [reading uncertain] from whom they ought to have been born—with bloody hands. Perhaps the Holy Spirit, observing that they still concealed the poisons of their deceit inwardly under his scrutiny, rightly rebukes them with the judgment of severity, asking why they had not first vomited out the cunning devices of their deceit and only then entered the font, where the dove, silvered without the gall of bitterness, is daily whitened in the pallor of gold by the grace of the Holy Spirit; afterward, walking with Christ on earth without wrinkle or spot, she tramples every kind of serpent under her feet and drives away unbelievers.

“Therefore,” he says, “produce fruits worthy of repentance.”

It is as though he were openly saying: “Do not mock what I am doing. Rather, fulfill in pious works what I say, and produce fruits worthy of the repentance that I proclaim. For none of you is justified by his own works or those of his fathers; all of you have become children of wrath through guilt.”

John, therefore, having become the teacher of perfect repentance, not only displayed in himself the person of one who repents but also plainly indicated what its proper measure ought to be when he added: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance.” Otherwise the washing of baptism is judged not the abolition of sin but a deception.

The worthy fruit of repentance, then, is the mortification of the flesh and of all vices, so that the seeds of virtues sown through faith may accumulate a more abundant harvest of good works. Enriched by these, and with grace lending its support, they may repay by their merits the harm they had inflicted upon themselves.

But when the herald of truth struck them with such rebukes, he saw that their minds were inwardly swollen with the arrogance of pride because of the prerogative of their ancestors. He anticipated their thoughts, as though they were saying: “We are not a brood of vipers; we are reckoned children of Abraham, the most holy patriarch.” To those who applauded themselves with such claims, he said:

“Do not say within yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’”

For those who are counted among the seed are not children of the flesh but of grace. Abraham did not have as heir what he received according to the flesh, but what he received according to faith. Therefore, if you wish to belong to the seed, imitate his faith, because he was not justified by works of the law, but because “he believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” You also, therefore, prove the works of faith, through which you may be children according to the inner person.

Otherwise, do not call yourselves children merely because you are children according to the flesh, since Ishmael is by no means counted among the seed. Therefore, produce fruits worthy of repentance—namely, the fruits of baptism—if you wish, through the regeneration of faith, to become heirs of the kingdom.

Otherwise, you are from the father, the devil; for if you were children of Abraham, you would certainly do the works of your father. For this reason, do not glory in being children according to the flesh alone, especially since by imitation you belong to another. Hence those are proved to be children more truly who are propagated in the seed through faith.

Therefore:

“God,” he says, “is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.”

Here the power of God, for whom everything he wills is possible, is not proclaimed as extraordinary merely so that it may be admired as praiseworthy, but also so that their rashness may be broken by this statement and they may begin to consider the works of God’s predestination. For just as nothing is predestined by him that he cannot accomplish, so whatever has been predestined will be brought to completion only when justice directs it—or certainly when mercy provides its support.

The first beginnings of faith are certainly to believe that God can do whatever he wills. Next, one must understand with greater confidence that the provident and merciful Dispenser orders and arranges all things justly and kindly. For this reason, I think that the simple reader will be greatly helped if he firmly believes that God, who created all things from nothing, is able to form children for Abraham from stones and, as though from a lineage promised to him, raise up heirs even from any dust. Otherwise he has not yet grasped the beginnings of faith.

If Greece, poorly instructed by its own monstrous deceptions, attempted to assert that Deucalion scattered stones from which human beings were created for the world, what do you think? Is it more reasonable to confess that the true and living God simply cannot create children for Abraham from stones?

Hence Virgil Maro:

> Immediately Nature imposed these laws  
> and everlasting covenants upon fixed places;  
> at the time when Deucalion first cast stones  
> over the empty world.  
> From them was born the hard race of human beings.

By this he wished to signify the eight hundred and tenth year before the founding of Rome, when, as they say, Amphion, the third ruler after Cecrops, was reigning at Athens. In his time a flood of waters destroyed most of the population of Thessaly, with a few survivors escaping through mountain refuges. Hence he also introduced the story.

At that time, therefore, many people were transported to Mount Parnassus, around which Deucalion held mortal sovereignty. Receiving them as they fled to him in boats, he sheltered, nourished, and preserved them for a time between the mountain’s twin peaks. At last, sending them back into the world, he is said to have restored the human race, as though those who were then born had come from stones laid bare by the flood.

But if the wise men of the world invented such stories about these things in order to blind very many people with their own darkness, how much more religious is it now to believe what is proclaimed to everyone more clearly than light?

Nevertheless, the fact that John expressly said “from these stones,” as though he were pointing out certain stones placed beneath them, is not without a mystery. He undoubtedly wished to reveal the figure of one of these things, or certainly of both. For, mystically—as they say—this was taking place in the very place where Jesus the son of Nun had ordered twelve stones to be carried from the middle of the Jordan onto the land, and other stones to be restored from the land into the same riverbed (Josh. 4:8).

Perhaps then, extending his finger toward those stones, he was saying: “God is able from these stones—by which the killing of the Jews and the transformation of the Gentiles into the appearance of light are prefigured—to raise up children for Abraham, as was promised.”

Indeed, because in those stones there was, if not by nature, nevertheless by figure, the reality of the Gentiles, it is not without reason written that they would be raised up from those same flints in which the grace of their salvation had already long before been foreshadowed.

It is as though he were plainly saying: “Do not say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For God is able from these stones—that is, through the grace shown to be prefigured in them—to raise up children for Abraham from death to life, from darkness to light, and from no nation into a nation, so that they too, reborn through faith, may eventually be found heirs of so great a father.”

Elsewhere, however, he calls the Gentiles “stones” because of the hardness of their hearts, or certainly because idolaters worshiped stones. Hence, according to the Psalmist: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 113:16). Elsewhere, because they themselves were stony, the Lord says through the prophet: “I will take from you the stony heart and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 11:19).

According to the effect of their conduct, therefore, and not according to their substance, the Gentiles are called stones. For by nature they were created good and undefiled; but by corrupting themselves through various activities they became as though they were not, and thus they are not improperly called stones.

From these stones God is able—not merely to raise up children for Abraham as though from something already existing, but altogether to raise them up as though from nothing. For although they existed through God, they corrupted themselves and made themselves as though they did not exist. Scripture bears witness that all nations before God are “as though they were not” and are regarded as nothing.

Therefore those who had been stones because of the hardness and roughness of sin, unfit for any use, by the power of God became living stones. They are rolled across the earth and are finally counted most precious in God’s sanctuary. That heavenly Jerusalem is built from them, and all its walls around are constructed together from them in Christ.

For this reason it might perhaps seem more appropriate for the evangelist to have said: “God is able from these stones to prepare squared stones with which that heavenly city, Jerusalem, may be built,” especially since the word would then have been transferred from one and the same substance. But because he is taught by the Holy Spirit in a far higher and more perfect way, he did not follow the sound of the words; rather, he searched more fully into the depth of their meaning and spoke with complete appropriateness.

Earlier he had said, “Brood of vipers,” not because they existed according to the nature of vipers, but because, through the poison of their teaching and the vice of unbelief, they had been transferred into that lineage. Therefore, lest they glory in the seed of the flesh, he turns the argument toward the Gentiles, so that only those may be regarded as children who have been raised up according to the inner person through grace.

They are “raised up,” I say, because when Christ came, he took the wife of his deceased brother—namely, of the patriarch Abraham. For through Sarah, the mother of us all, the Church is signified; and from her Christ raised up children through grace, through which Abraham had once begotten a son as a foreshadowing.

According to the law, therefore, all who are of faith are counted by the right of a father as heirs of the deceased, no less than sons. For this reason he deliberately inserted the word “raise up,” so that you might recognize that in Christ, whom he proclaims, what Moses had long ago commanded according to the law is fulfilled (Deut. 25:5).

Therefore, if a brother should die without children, Moses commanded that his surviving brother take the dead man’s wife and raise up offspring for his brother. When a son was born to him, he would be the heir of the deceased and would be counted among the heirs of his inheritance.

Because of the sacramental mystery of this practice, when Christ came, Abraham was shown to be dead without children in the matter of faith, since all those descended from his flesh had degenerated. Christ is therefore declared able to raise up his children, in accordance with what had been promised to him, so that so great a patriarch might not be deprived of the divine promises.

Meanwhile, lest they also seem free from blame if they utterly rejected such sacramental gifts, he immediately threatens them, drawing examples from agriculture.

“Already,” he says, “the axe is laid at the root of the trees. Therefore every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

No one who has read the Holy Scriptures can doubt that the trees signify the condition of souls, since Scripture very frequently expresses through them the qualities of good and evil people.

The human race therefore has its own agriculture. When Christ came to cultivate it, he found it extremely unproductive through the excess of unbelief; but after restoring to all, through grace, the freedom of the will, he gave them thereafter the ability to bear fruit. Hence, by the just judgment of God, he threatens that the axe has already been laid at the roots of the trees, so that, if they do not bring forth the fruit of piety through faith, they may be cut off either from the present life or, certainly, from the land of the living, where the saints will reign with the Lord.

Some count four kinds of trees according to their qualities. Some have good greenness and bear good fruit in their seasons. Others are badly green and bear bad fruit. Others are green only in their vigor but remain fruitless and, because they are barren, never bear fruit. Still others are already exhausted of all their greenness, although they are still raised above the earth by their roots; because they have not yet been cut down or, through some force, fallen, they are kept for no other purpose than the uses of fire.

If anyone wishes to observe the examples of all these more carefully, he will be able to consider them in the agriculture of the whole Church. There are heretics who have already dried up inwardly from the greenness of faith and been stripped of the grace of verdure, though they are still in the flesh. There are also some who hide under hypocrisy within the Church, whose fruit is found to be more bitter than any gall because of the contagion of sin. Whoever eats of their fruits is immediately killed by the poison of iniquity and deprived of his own salvation, which comes from Christ.

There are also trees of good works, hot with the fervor of faith, which bear abundant fruit sweetened by every kind of goodness. Concerning these the Lord says: “A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit. You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:18, 20).

There are still others who possess only the greenness of faith; but because they do not have the fruit of faith, they occupy the ground as barren trees. Hence the axe is rightly said to be laid at the roots of the trees, so that those who refuse to bear the better fruit of life may be cut down and, prepared for eternal fires, be burned with greater severity.

Wishing shortly before to indicate how we should flee this fate, he said: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance.” In these words it must be carefully noted that he does not merely command and urge the production of fruits of repentance, but of fruits worthy of repentance.

It is one thing to produce fruit; it is another to fulfill by one’s deeds a fruit worthy of repentance. The fruit of the good work of one who has sinned less ought not to be equal to that of one who has sinned more; nor should the fruit of one who has fallen into no crimes equal that of one who has perhaps fallen into certain grave offenses.

Therefore, by saying “Produce fruits worthy of repentance,” he summons each person’s conscience to seek such profits of good works through repentance as correspond to the greater losses he has inflicted upon himself through guilt. Otherwise, the axe has already been laid at the roots of the trees, so that each unfruitful person may be cut down immediately if, after the manure of repentance, he does not bear worthy fruits.

The axe is Christ incarnate, united from two substances. Through his humanity he is held, as it were, by the hand of our apprehension; through his divinity he is inwardly placed at the roots of our conscience, so that any who are unfruitful there may be cut away more vigorously. For although he sometimes awaits us patiently, through his divinity he examines and determines when, and to what extent, he should strike each person according to the quality of his offense.

“For the word of God is effective and more penetrating not only than an axe but than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts.” These thoughts are not improperly called the roots of the trees, because just as fruit-bearing trees are fixed in the earth through their roots, so we too are lifted through them into heaven as we bear fruit for God—or else, planted in the earth and rooting carnally downward, we are already destined for the underworld.

It should also be noted that the axe is said to be placed not merely beside the root but expressly at the root, so that everyone who understands may perceive that the scrutiny of judgment and the presence of majesty reach even to the division of the soul. Therefore the faithful soul ought to watch itself at every hour and every moment, lest it be struck, and ought to live as though it must always be brought before that fearful tribunal.

For who could be secure when it is said: “Behold, the axe has already been laid at the roots of the trees”? If someone does not see it, at least he will feel it. And if someone can neither sometimes feel nor see it, there is great reason to fear that, already dried up and lulled into death, he may be led unknowingly to Tartarus.

For this reason, we must be exceedingly watchful, lest while we live any one of us be found without the worthy fruit of repentance. No one is excluded, but every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire. “Every,” he says. Since no one is excluded, it is sufficiently terrifying that anyone should suppose himself free from the work required.

Especially since he does not say, “If it produces bad fruit,” but rather: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit,” he says, “will be cut down and thrown into the fire.” But lest he seem to threaten those who despise him merely on his own authority, he next begins to reveal how great is the authority of the one whose presence he threatens them with, and by whose benefits they ought rightly to be persuaded to faith.

[Col. 0162C] “I indeed baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is to come after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.”

Luke seems sufficiently to differ in wording at this point, although he does not depart from the same meaning. For when he had said, as though in response to their thoughts, “I baptize you with water,” he did not at all add “for repentance.” Then he says: “One mightier than I is coming, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie.” But there is no need for anyone to be troubled by this, if he prudently understands that the very statements necessary for knowing the truth remain necessary, however they may be expressed in words. The fact that one writer preserves one sequence of words and another a different one is certainly not contradictory; nor is it contradictory if one says what another omits, [Col. 0162D] since it is not permissible to believe that any of the evangelists lied.

And even if it appears that “to carry sandals” is one thing, while “to untie the sandal strap” is another—not merely in words, the order of words, or some other manner of expression, but in the actual matter itself—we must not immediately suppose that they wrote contradictory accounts, as though through ignorance. Hence it is rightly asked which of these John said: that he was not worthy to carry sandals, or to untie the strap of the sandals. For he alone seems to have narrated the truth who reported what it is certain that John first announced to his hearers.

But if it is relevant to understand something else from the fact that they certainly published these differing forms, what else can we rightly judge than that John said both things, whether at different times or consecutively? It would be as though he had said: “Whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie, nor am I worthy to carry his sandals.” From this, one of them took one statement, while another—as did the other two—took the other; yet we can demonstrate more clearly than daylight that all of them narrated what is true.

Therefore, as we have already said, they should be interpreted in such a way that they are believed to have deviated from the truth in no respect and not to have stated things contrary to one another. But meanwhile let us return to the order of the exposition and see why John baptizes with water for repentance, when he does not remit sins. For it was not permissible for a servant to remit another person’s sins, even if, according to the Lord’s saying, he may rightly be called greater than all others. I do not know, however, whether he was able to avoid the contagion of every sin to the end, although he had been sanctified in his mother’s womb. Even if he was able to do so, if it is permissible to say this, we firmly believe that he avoided it not by his own power but by the grace through which he is said to have been dedicated to the office of herald.

He baptized in order that, by his office of herald, he might precede Christ, lest Christ appear to do anything new against the commandments of the Law. He invited everyone to repentance, so that when the Pontiff appointed for us came, he might already, as Lord, remit the sins of those seeking forgiveness. John makes catechumens and urges everyone toward the wedding, so that, when Christ proceeds as Pontiff of pontiffs to the fonts, the sons, already instructed, may immediately be reborn and, entering the bridal chamber with the Bridegroom, may celebrate the wedding sacramentally through these very things.

Elsewhere, however, he indicates in the Gospel according to John why he himself came. When he was speaking of Christ, he says: “And I did not know him; but in order that he might be manifested in Israel, for this reason I came baptizing with water” (John 1:31). Moreover, there can be no greater reason why he came baptizing. Otherwise that same baptism would have remained thereafter. But because it was useful for no other purpose, when Christ came it ceased, as though its ministry had been completed.

When he says, “One mightier than I is coming,” he does not wish to compare a creature with the Creator; rather, he indicates the strong one without whom there is no strength. Of him the prophet Isaiah says: “Mighty God, Father of the age to come” (Isaiah 9:6). Nevertheless, John did not call him mightier because he himself was strong in comparison with Christ, but because he was thought to be something significant, so that Christ might have been believed to be that person. Therefore he moderated his speech, so that, little by little, through his own works, he might commend more fully how great Christ was.

He was to come after John—not insofar as he is eternal from the Father, but in the birth of his flesh, in the manifestation of his appearance before the people, in his Passion, and in his descent into hell. “Whose,” he says, “sandals I am not worthy to carry.” In accordance with the simple understanding, he humbles himself suitably, lest he appear to have compared himself with the one whose sandals he judges himself unworthy to carry.

But if we look a little higher, the greatness of the mystery surpasses us in the sandals. For by the sandals are signified no less the incarnation of the Word than all the sacraments of the Gospel, which blessed John was in no way worthy to carry. For each person’s meritorious service on behalf of Christ existed in its own appointed time. The feet of the apostles were clothed with these sandals, and they are said to be beautiful for evangelizing. Through them the Church of Christ thereafter confesses: “I will extend my sandal over Edom” (Psalm 107:10), because the proclamation of the Gospel ran as far as those who lead an earthly life.

When blessed John saw that this preaching had been assigned to the apostles’ ministry, he left to them the glory of carrying the proclamation, since it belonged to them, with beautiful feet, to announce peace to the nations. Their feet are rightly said to be shod for the preparation of the Gospel of peace, because through him they were made fit for what they had put on and were shod with the sandal of salvation.

When Moses wished to approach the contemplation of the vision of almighty God, he had not yet been shod with these sandals. Therefore it was said to him: “Remove the sandal from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5). Those sandals of the feet were by no means holy; for this reason, while he was still wearing them, he was not worthy to touch holy ground, nor could he approach the vision of almighty God while shod with them. Nor would the angel later have ordered Joshua to remove the same kind of sandal (Joshua 5:15), if it had been permissible for him still, while wearing such a sandal, to tread upon holy ground.

Since that ancient condition had not yet been removed, although the same herald of truth had been sanctified, perhaps for this reason he truly declares that he is unworthy to carry the sandals. Otherwise, the apostles themselves would not have been worthy to carry them unless they had been stripped of the old condition through Christ’s death (Deuteronomy 25:9).

Among the ancients, moreover, it was customary that, if someone did not wish to take as his wife the woman who was suited to him, the man who would come to her as bridegroom by right of kinship would remove that man’s sandal. What, then, did Christ, clothed in flesh, appear among human beings to be, except the Bridegroom of his holy Church? Concerning him John rightly says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29).
