But because people thought that he was the Christ—a claim that John himself steadfastly denied by confessing the truth—he rightly declares, pressed by humility, that he is unworthy not only, as Luke more significantly relates, to untie the strap of his sandals, but also to carry those same mysteries of betrothal.

This is why Moses and Joshua were not bridegrooms, nor was John himself one; therefore Moses and Joshua are rightly commanded to remove their sandals. Yet John truly asserts that he is unworthy to carry out or undo the same rights of betrothal, which he had learned through the spirit of prophecy were to be fulfilled in Christ.

“He himself,” he says, “will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire”—that is, with the purification of sanctification and, thereafter, for the nourishment of charity, with the testing of tribulation. “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” Therefore, if we are first sanctified through him, what else does this mean than that we are washed in him? And thereafter, if through charity we reach Christ, what else does this mean than that through it we are reborn in Christ?

Through this washing of the Holy Spirit we are reborn in hope of life. Through charity, however, by that regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the seat of his majesty, we shall be clothed more perfectly, by being reborn, with immortality. It is not unfitting that this same charity should be called fire, since it makes the minds of human beings burn.

The apostles, too, although they were first sanctified by receiving the Holy Spirit, were not yet burning to such a degree. But when, on the day of Pentecost, the same Spirit poured charity into them more fully, he made them burn exceedingly. For once reborn through charity, they could not be separated from it by any kind of torment. Hence Paul also constantly said: “I am certain that neither death nor life, neither things present nor things to come, nor any creature will be able to separate us from the love of Christ” (Romans 8:38).

For it was wholly the effect of charity through grace; therefore it could be nothing other than what it had become. Since only a few possess such complete charity in the present life, but in the future all who are reborn through it will possess it in such a way that they remain in it forever, they will all attain complete immortality.

Accordingly, we believe that the saying means: “He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit”—in the present life, for eternal sanctification—“and thereafter with fire,” namely, with charity, after many tribulations, in the regeneration when the Son of Man sits on the seat of his majesty, for the renewal of blessed immortality. For just as all sins are forgiven here, so there also those sins without which our mortality cannot exist will be completely and fully remitted, if a suitable conversion has preceded.

In the Acts of the Apostles, too, the Holy Spirit is said to have appeared in fire so that it might be a sign that he had made those whom he filled burn. And from where did they burn, except from the fire that he had infused? Thus charity itself was fire. Therefore the statement rightly seems to have been made: “He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit,” first according to its signification, and then “with fire,” that is, with perfected charity, when no one will be able to separate you from the love of Christ, when nothing other than the fire of divine love will burn within you.

Unless perhaps it should be understood in this way: “He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire,” as some wish, as though the Holy Spirit himself were fire. We entirely confess this, because “God is a consuming fire.” But since a conjunction is placed between the two, it appears that the conjunction does not join one and the same thing.

Therefore some, avoiding this interpretation, wish the fire of purgatory to be signified—as though he washes us with the Holy Spirit in the present, and thereafter, if some stain of sin should creep in, burns it away completely through the fire of conflagration. But if this is so, it must also be believed concerning lighter and very small sins, since what nearly everyone discusses as a possible opinion is in no way contrary to the truth.

Hence the Apostle also says: “The fire will test what sort each person’s work is” (1 Corinthians 3:13). In Leviticus, too, that fire sent from heaven always burned upon the altar, consuming all the burnt offerings and burning the fat of all the sacrifices. It signified those who, upon Christ, as a sacrifice or burnt offering to the Lord for a pleasing fragrance, are daily burned like victims by the fire of divine love.

By this fire, what else are believers doing except being baptized again? Jesus came to cast this fire upon the earth, and what does he wish except that it burn and consume all the vices of the flesh, so that the elect may be reborn in it each day into a new life?

For this reason, perpetual fire is commanded, fire that will never fail from the altar, so that all who are offered in Christ—that is, upon the altar—may be purified and renewed more gloriously by it. Thus, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the seat of his majesty, they may receive more fully the adoption of the sons of God and be granted the immortality of eternal life.

“Whose winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor, and he will gather the wheat into his granary, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.”

By the winnowing fork the examination of divine judgment is signified. For just as, by a winnowing fork on a threshing floor, the chaff is separated from the wheat, so by divine examination those who are light and empty of the fruit of good works are separated from the company of the saints.

This wheat is seen to have grown from the grain of wheat that, falling into the earth through the Passion of the cross, is said elsewhere to have died. Through faith, therefore, those who spring from it become one in Christ. Having thus been made heirs of God and coheirs of Christ—not by nature but by grace—they are gathered daily, one by one, from the single grain into the granary of paradise, while the chaff is rejected into the fire.

The chaff is handed over to the flames, although it has come forth from the root of the seed—not because it does not come from it, but because it has degenerated from the richness of its fruit. So too sinners, although they are reborn from faith in Christ, are assigned to burn in punishments if they have not possessed the fruit of faith. They are not condemned because they are not in the faith, but because in the divine examination they are judged empty and degenerate from the fruit of faith.

Those others who do not believe are not removed from the wheat by this winnowing fork; rather, because they have already been judged, they are led by the road appointed for them to hell.

When he threatens that the winnowing fork is placed in his hand, judicial authority is expressed, because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” He gave him, on account of the form of his humanity, what he himself had always possessed with the Father on account of the equal majesty of his divinity.

“And he will thoroughly cleanse,” he says, “his threshing floor”—that is, from the chaff, while the good are separated from the evil. By the threshing floor, on which grain is thoroughly threshed, the present Church of God is signified, in which the saints are driven about by various distresses and pressures.

Those who are grains, having been made firm in Christ through endurance, will not be carried here and there. For when Christ has been sown through faith in the hearts of believers, as in good soil they produce abundant fruit through endurance, without which no one bears fruit for God. Since the grains of the seed are united in this firmness and belong to him, they cannot be separated from Christ.

The threshing floor does not signify one thing and the wheat gathered upon it another. Rather, by expressing both as one, he has formed from agriculture a most fitting allegorical figure. For when he says, “He will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor,” it is as though he were plainly saying that each day, driving away the various kinds of temptations, he will purify his wheat and, once it has been approved through endurance, gather it into his granary. But the light chaff, fleeing from every wind of temptation, he will send into unquenchable fire.

He calls it unquenchable not because, as some rave, those who are to be burned will eventually, after judgment has been completed, be recalled to forgiveness from that fire, but because the hay, chaff, and straw will remain as fuel for the fire. Otherwise the fire might rightly be considered unquenchable if it were not continually supplied for eternal torments by the nourishment of those whose burning it is.

For these are made of the same material so that the fire may always be unquenchable: those whose portion is assigned with the devil, so that, having become his members by following him, they may also become participants in the burning of eternal fire. For although the fire is rightly believed to be everlasting, it would not properly be called unquenchable without fuel if these were not enduring forever for the punishments of torment.

Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him.

When he says “then,” he refers to that time when the others were being baptized in the Jordan by John while confessing their sins. He is said to have come from Galilee because Nazareth, where he had until then lived, was, as we have already said, a metropolis in that region. From there he is rightly said to have come in order to be made manifest to human beings, since previously his nature and greatness were hidden.

According to Luke himself, we learn that he was about thirty years old when he came. Meanwhile, this event occurred so that a pattern might be given to those who would succeed in preaching the Gospel: they, too, should undertake the work of piety at that age and display the perfection of life more abundantly in all things.

At this age, therefore, the integrity of a perfect life is most rightly signified as already mature. Hence the universal Church of Christ customarily instructs those whom it advances to the office of the presbyterate, until they reach this age, with more diligent examination and for the sake of their formation under Christ’s discipline, and afterward promotes them more carefully to the priesthood.

It was right that Christ, who wished to present himself as the way to believers, should also show teachers when they ought to undertake the office of preaching and consecrating.

Hence some hold the plausible opinion that all people, having been brought to the perfect human state for immortality, should rise again at approximately this age. I consider it sufficiently pious to believe this and to hope for it with greater confidence from divine power.

Jesus came, then, the Creator of the waters, to be baptized by John in the water of the Jordan, so that he might first display in himself the mystery of a second birth through water and the Spirit, which believers should seek, and might indicate that unless they were reborn through this, they could in no way be regarded as sons of God and his brothers by adoption.

He did not need to be washed by John’s baptism, since he was clean from every stain; but he came to provide a way for us, who had been born in sins, to wash away the crimes of our offenses. Thus, being reborn with him, we might rightly be called his brothers and be his coheirs.

In him we are not only his brothers; through the very purification of sins, the Church of all the reborn is also consecrated as his bride. Therefore it was fitting that he himself should first descend into the font, not for himself but for us, so that through this he might join us to himself more truly in one body and commend the mystery of baptism as something to be desired more gloriously through his descent.

For through this act not he himself but all the streams of water are purified for the ministry of our washing, and the teaching of humility is more fully demonstrated, so that no one, as though superior in life, may disdain to come even to the lowest one whose office it is to baptize.

He came to baptism, especially, as John indicates, to manifest that he is the one who baptizes in the Spirit. For he had received this statement from God: “The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is the one who baptizes” (John 1:33).

In this vision, a great sacrament of faith has been poured out for us, through which we understand very clearly that, whatever the office of the minister may be, this one alone is the one who baptizes.

He has granted this power to none of his servants, but, retaining it in himself, he has made us more secure, so that no one may distrust any minister, nor may any minister presume in baptizing that what he gives comes from himself. Rather, “whoever glories”—both the one who receives and the one who gives—should glory in the Lord, because it is altogether this one who baptizes, and not the person through whose outward ministry what we see is accomplished.

For this reason, among others, we believe that he came: to show that in him the Holy Spirit, remaining in bodily form, is distributed among individuals, and that from this the whole Church is formed into one wondrous body.

And just as all the members of the body are animated by one and the same spirit, so the whole company of those reborn in Christ is given life by one Holy Spirit and sanctified from every stain of vices. Hence the Apostle says: “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8:14).

Nevertheless, we do not think it was without reason that this mystery was celebrated in the Jordan and not in some other river, especially since the Jewish people, circumcised a second time in a mystical sense by Joshua the son of Nun, perhaps entered the promised land through this very place. Concerning it David says, because of the mystery of its greatness: “And you, Jordan, why did you turn backward?” (Psalm 113:5).

It was right that he should be baptized in the river in which the figure of baptism had already preceded him, and whose name more openly indicated what had taken place in it. For Jordan is said to mean “their descent.” Whose descent? Surely that of those who descend from the pride of arrogance to the humility of Christ and are washed there from their sins.

Thus, through the name Jordan, the operation of the whole of baptism is sufficiently and wisely proclaimed. For this reason Christ was fittingly baptized in it, so that on every side the whole matter might correspond to the divine mysteries.

The Jordan, as they say, consists of two rivers, namely Jor and Dan, which, joined together, form the Jordan. Christ is mystically baptized in it, among other reasons, for a reason obscured by a corrupt reading in the supplied text (“here”). The following clause is also syntactically uncertain: “But God-man, because he deigned to teach the two laws joined together to himself.”

Meanwhile, what is celebrated through visible water was done so that he might lead not only the Gentiles to faith but also the Jews, if they might believe that the remission of sins takes place through a visible thing, as they had previously been accustomed to believe through sacrifices. For certainly, if they had not seen bodies being washed, they might perhaps have believed less readily that souls are cleansed.

Now:

John tried to prevent him, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?”

He was alarmed that the one in whom there was no need for baptism had come to him, since he himself took away the sins of the world, as John had already testified. He did not understand, of course, that unless the physician had first come to the sick person who was languishing, the sick person would not seek the physician.

To him the Lord said:

[Col. 0169B] “Allow it for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.”

It was as though he were saying plainly: “Allow that for which I have come to be fulfilled.” For some, wishing to establish their own righteousness, became guilty and did not reach the boundaries of righteousness.

But since all have fallen away through pride, it is fitting for us to restore them to life through the example of humility and to show that no one can be perfectly righteous without the water of baptism.

It was as though he were saying openly: “If I, the Lord, conceived and born of a Virgin through the work of the Holy Spirit, without the contagion of sin, do not disdain to undergo the washing of a second birth, how much more necessary is it for all—even those living innocently and justly—that none of them despise, following my example, being baptized as though by the lowest and humblest?”

For this reason it is fitting for us first to fulfill all righteousness: namely, the righteousness through which the whole sum of righteousness is thereafter fulfilled by everyone. Let all therefore glory not in works or in the choice of free will, but, acknowledging themselves guilty, let them be subject to the righteousness of God and be justified by grace, without which no one is ever perfected through works.

Therefore, when anyone is reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, he is rightly called just through faith, without impropriety, because by believing he fulfilled that through which all the righteousness of God would be fulfilled by grace.

It was especially fitting that Christ should first fulfill this righteousness, not as though from need, but as a teacher, so that the Son of God, reborn in this way, might gather all who are reborn into himself as brothers, and, joined to him by the grace of adoption, might make them sons of God.

[Col. 0169D] When John learned these things, which until then he had not known, he admitted him. Although he knew how great and what kind of person he was, he learned in that moment many things that he had previously not known.

The Holy Spirit, who remained upon him in the form of a dove, taught him and led him into all truth. Therefore what he had previously feared in humility, he afterward, made confident, allowed to be fulfilled in devotion.

Thus John’s humility indicates how the higher works of virtue ought to be sought: he timidly withdraws through awareness of his own weakness, but obeys confidently through divine instruction. For where God cooperates wholly through his gift, mortality has nothing to fear on the basis of merit.

After Jesus had been baptized, he immediately came up from the water. Behold, the heavens were opened.

We must not believe that the heavenly mysteries had become accessible to him for the first time then, since right faith holds that he always remained equal to the Father, wholly present everywhere with him.

Rather, this is a clear indication of the sacrament: through the mystery of holy baptism, the entrance to the heavenly homeland is immediately opened to all who are reborn in Christ.

Nor should we believe that he first received the gifts of the Holy Spirit in the thirtieth year of his life, when he was baptized, since he had been conceived by the same Holy Spirit and had always been full of him.

Thus it is clearly shown that he was baptized for us; that the same Holy Spirit appeared above in visible form was for us. The Father also cried out to us from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 17:5).

All these things were certainly celebrated for us as mysteries of salvation, through which the way into heaven is opened and the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured out more fully everywhere upon all.

When he says, “Then he came up from the water,” it is clearly understood that all who descend from the pride of vanity to be washed in baptism ought daily, by growing, to ascend again to the heights of virtue and hasten back to the homeland from which they had fallen.

It is rightly asked why baptism was established in water and in the Holy Spirit, dedicated to a visible and an invisible substance. When one considers this, the answer immediately presents itself: just as a human being consists of two natures, namely body and soul, so he is reborn to salvation through two substances.

Through water he is buried with Christ; through the Holy Spirit he is likewise wholly sanctified to God. No element, therefore, is found more suitable for burying us with Christ than water, which is also mentioned together with the name of earth in Genesis: “The earth was formless and empty” (Genesis 1:2). There, too, all the waters are included under an unspoken name.

Through water the filth of bodies is cleansed. By this function, what takes place inwardly and divinely in secret is openly prefigured. Through these two elements, water and fire, everything that needs cleansing for human use is purified.

Water cleanses the softer things, while fire purifies the harder metals of material things to a liquid state. So too divine providence has fulfilled in us the work of causing all the crimes of sin within us to be boiled away through water and the fire of the Holy Spirit.

Thus, by water, dying to the world, we are buried with Christ; and by the fire of the Holy Spirit, rising from the font and burning toward what is better, we are carried in mind toward heaven.

For this reason the heavens are opened—not by the opening of the elements, but by a spiritual opening—so that, having already become spiritual, we may immediately be invited spiritually to spiritual things.

Concerning this opening someone says: “The little ear of the sevenfold ether of heaven is split open.”

Ezekiel, too, very fittingly announces the future opening from the beginning of his vision through what he sees as present, saying: “In the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, when I was in the midst of the captives beside the river Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw a vision of God” (Ezekiel 1:1).

No one should doubt that Christ was in Ezekiel, since it is written: “He was represented in the hands of the prophets” (Hosea 12:10). In the thirtieth year of his life Ezekiel also came beside the river Chebar, at the age at which Christ is shown to have come to the Jordan.

Chebar is interpreted as “heaviness” or “gravity.” What, then, is suitably signified by the river Chebar except the human race? It flows from birth into death and is burdensome to itself because of the sins it continually commits and carries.

For it is written: “He sits upon a talent of lead” (Zechariah 5:7). Every sin is heavy, because it does not permit the soul to be lifted to higher things. Hence the Psalmist says: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4:3).

It is therefore written concerning the Lord that he is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). Ezekiel came beside the river Chebar because the strength of God, through the mystery of his incarnation, deigned to draw near to the human race, which bears the weight of its sins.

These weights descended into the depths like a stone; therefore Jordan is rightly interpreted as “their descent.” The Spirit of God blew from above, and all the vices of sins were submerged, together with their prince, like lead in mighty waters.

Then, as I have said, the heavens were opened—not by the opening of the elements, but because the way was opened for us and the hope of returning to higher things was restored.

The heavens were not opened for him but for us, just as he was not baptized for himself; nor did he suffer for himself, but everything was done for us, so that he might restore and raise up to higher things those whom he had made.

Otherwise, he never abandoned the heavens, but, coming here, he was always with the Father. At that time, therefore, the flaming sword that stood before the gates of paradise was extinguished in the waters of baptism.

For this reason the heavens are not inappropriately said to have been opened above him: above him, indeed, because they are opened on account of him and through him, whereas from the beginning they had been closed to all through the first Adam.

### 180

“And he saw the Spirit descending like a dove and coming upon him.”

There is no doubt that Jesus himself saw the Holy Spirit coming upon him. Moreover, according to what is written by John the Evangelist, John also bore witness, saying: “For I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained upon him” (John 1:32). From this it is plainly evident that both of them saw him descending—namely, Christ and John—but not upon both of them: they saw him coming in bodily form only upon Christ.

From this it is reasonably asked whether the body of a true dove was present, in whose form the Spirit appeared, or whether it was perhaps a phantom. It is a sufficiently frivolous thought that anything other than the Truth appeared there. Since Christ, upon whom he had come, was not a phantom but a true man and true God, it seems quite fitting to us that he assumed a true body, formed for the moment in the likeness of a dove, for the sake of teaching the mystery; coming upon Christ’s true flesh, it would outwardly declare what had taken place within. Otherwise, the Holy Spirit could not have appeared to mortal eyes except in bodily form.

We think, moreover, that this body was more probably formed from air or water than generated from any other [Col. 0172A] kind of body. For the time being, therefore, we say that he appeared for the sake of a mystery, and afterward, since he himself willed it, it may be conjectured that what had truly been formed ceased to exist. But why did he descend in bodily form except, as we have already said, so that you might see him and also recognize him?

There is no one who doubts that the dove which Noah sent out from the ark was a figure of this dove; and therefore through it we recognize the type of the sacrament. Perhaps someone will say that since the dove which was sent forth was a real dove, here he is said to have descended like a dove: how, then, do we say that there the figure existed, while here there was the reality? The answer is that the former was an ancient event, and the deed accomplished through it was a prophecy of this sacrament.

Furthermore, concerning the adverb of likeness placed here—“like”—it should be known that, according to the Greek copies, “in the form of a dove” is written in very many exemplars, as it is also said to be written in Luke. Otherwise, what is as true as the divinity that remains forever? A creature cannot be the truth, although no one rightly doubts that a form may be understood in place of the reality. It is therefore clear that it was a true dove; but the word of likeness, “like,” is added so that it may be understood that the same Holy Spirit appeared bodily in a dove, yet that he himself did not appear as a body.

He appeared in a dove so that through it he might explain what those who would attain the grace of that same Spirit were to be like. Since a dove has no gall, this plainly indicates that whoever devoutly desires to come to this grace must not be possessed by the gall of bitterness. Rather, he must retain in his mind and conduct the simplicity and innocence that he displays to those who see him, and represent the simplicity of his life to those who look him in the face.

For many privileges of doves are recounted: this bird, sitting beside flowing waters, attentively watches the shadows of those lying in wait for it and, with exceedingly vigilant suspicion, swiftly escapes the snares laid from them. It is also said to possess such great natural gentleness that it receives the young of all birds as though they were its own and nourishes them by its own labors. It is therefore extremely mild, so much so that it does not wish to tear anyone with its beak or claws. It is said not to eat even the smallest insects or worms, by which the smaller birds scarcely of all birds nourish themselves and their young. They are also known to have a moan instead of a song.

Thus someone, in the spirit of devotion, says: “My tears were my bread day and night, while they say to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’” (Psalm 41:4). By such a feeling of meditation he expresses the character of the whole Church in mourning, and plainly indicates through this what the Holy Spirit accomplishes in us: for he pleads for us with unspeakable groanings, and in this way teaches us to groan. Therefore he rightly appeared in a dove, so that through it he might teach us what he himself accomplishes in us, or what kind of people we ourselves ought to be in him.

A dove usually builds its nest in holes in a rock or in a cavity of a wall—the place where Moses is said to have been placed and to have seen the back parts of God. The rock, however, is Christ, in the opening of whose side the whole Church builds its nest, when it is consecrated by the price of his blood. Hence also, in the Song of Songs, it says: “Arise, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come, my dove, in the holes of the rock, in the cavities of the wall; show me your face, let your voice sound in my ears” (Song of Songs 2:13).

From this it is plainly evident that it is called this through its efficacy, and not by nature. It was therefore right that the one effecting this should appear in the form to which, through grace, he wished to lead us inwardly. Also, as we stated a little earlier, according to the character of the figure, nothing was more suitable than that the one who had been figured through the dove in the Flood should be presented through a dove according to the truth.

For this reason the universal Church of Christ is most appropriately called a dove: “My dove is one” (Song of Songs 6:8), because through this grace of the Holy Spirit the whole Church is seen to be consecrated and united in that same form in which he was shown. It was therefore especially fitting that the Holy Spirit should appear through the one after whose ancient form the Church already bore its name, so that through the very gift he might transfer us to the things understood by the mind, and, after we had passed through the stages of the sacraments, we might at last happily arrive there.

If it is asked why the Son appeared in human form and the Holy Spirit in a dove, we answer appropriately that the former came so that God made man might present to man an example of living, and, united to him through flesh, redeem him by death. The latter appeared so that it might more clearly signify the very gift by which one arrives, through grace, at living well. Both, however, were made visible for the sake of carnal people, so that through the things they see with bodily eyes they might, as I have said, be transferred as quickly as possible to the things understood by the mind, after passing through the stages of the sacraments.

That dove is by no means believed to have suffered, nor is the Holy Spirit through it said to have suffered in the way that God-man is said to have suffered in the flesh. For he did not come to redeem doves, as it is established that Christ Jesus our Lord redeemed us human beings; nor was he assumed into God as Christ Jesus is believed to have been; nor was he received in any manner into the seat of majesty. Rather, just as all those forms in which God the Holy Spirit—or certainly the Son—once appeared visibly to the Fathers were dissolved after the service of their appearance had been completed, so we must acknowledge that this form returned to its proper element, as we have said, by the operation of divine power.

He came to instruct human beings. For their sake not only Christ but also that visible form appeared, so that he might teach true innocence. Once this has been explained, just as a word sounds and passes away—although the things signified by a word do not pass away at the same time when something divine and eternal is expounded by speech—so also that which appeared for the moment disappeared at once, whenever and wherever he willed, while the Holy Spirit remained unchangeably according to his command.

Here, if we have sound understanding, we have received instruction from him; otherwise, what we still do not grasp from the sacrifice we send back to be consumed by the fire of the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, we firmly believe whatever the dove of truth taught the dove concerning truth. We also give thanks to the giver, who gradually trained for himself a sanctified dove from among ravens.

That dove of Noah therefore truly bore the type, through which such a mystery was prefigured. It carried an olive branch to the ark, prefiguring the one who was to bring the joy of peace to the world and anoint it with the oil of his richness. Concerning this oil it is said to Christ: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:8).

The whole Church of Christians has certainly been anointed with the oil of this anointing. Although the name “Christian” is derived from Christ, they are nevertheless called Christians because those who constitute the Church have themselves been anointed. Hence blessed Peter the Apostle, writing to those reborn in Christ, calls them a royal race, or a holy priesthood (1 Peter 4:9). For all who are reborn in Christ are anointed inwardly no less with the oil of the Holy Spirit than we are outwardly, in the sacrament, with material oil.

Through this visible outward sign, what is accomplished inwardly through the same Spirit is indicated. Likewise, through the water with which we are washed, we are taught that we have received it for cleansing. Concerning this Jesus cried out on the last day of the feast, saying: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” The Evangelist adds: “He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive” (John 7:38).

In very many places in Scripture the same Holy Spirit is likewise signified by water. Hence there is no doubt that he appeared above the waters, over which he once moved in the beginning, to teach that he had come in the waters to cherish his rational creature, through which waters he prefigured that he would one day accomplish the mysteries of his mercy.

This Hebrew word also declares the matter more explicitly in that passage. For where our translator placed “was moving,” among the Hebrews *merefeth* is read, as the same authority testified. “We can call it,” he says, “brooding or cherishing,” like a bird animating its eggs with warmth. This can rightly be understood only of the Holy Spirit, who therefore appeared over Christ in the form of a dove, to show that through himself we are brooded over and warmed by his heat unto life. Otherwise, whence would there be such great heat by which one so cold could awaken from death?

From this it is plainly evident that the holy Church of God is rightly called a dove. Animated and given life by its brooding and warmth, it bears the name of the one whose Spirit it possesses and whose appearance it shares. Hence Isaiah, admiring the flight of the saints, said: “Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?” (Isaiah 60:8).

How rightly, then, are the saints individually called doves, since they have all been generated from this one and the same dove that appeared in Christ. Hence David also says: “You send forth your Spirit, and they are created, and you renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 103:30).

The provident dispensation of God is therefore plainly displayed everywhere. It once opened these mysteries of the sacraments so fittingly and distinctly to the Fathers, so that when they began to be fulfilled in the hearts of believers, they might marvel rather than doubt in any respect. Therefore, whoever wishes to be more happily united to the dove “whose wings are silvered” (Psalm 67:14), should manifest in his conduct what the dove taught and retain the warmth of the Spirit until he is wholly consumed as a holocaust for the Lord.

Concerning this fire Paul said to his hearers: “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (1 Thessalonians 5:19). For wherever that Spirit is, he makes a person ardent, advances and strengthens the one he has enlightened toward every impulse to virtue. Nevertheless, if we remain united to Christ Jesus our head, clinging to him like members, and if we are inwardly given life by his Spirit in his body according to the inner person, then we are rightly called and are doves because of the simplicity of our life.

Otherwise we boast vainly of ourselves in the hope of glory if we do not take care to be conformed to the one whose members we are said to be. Thus, recreated by the Holy Spirit through him and in him, we may be happily conformed and transferred into the form of blessed immortality. But in order that we may cling to him more firmly, we ought to listen more attentively to the voice of the Father thundering from above.

### “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

The other two Evangelists, namely Mark (1:11) and Luke (3:22), likewise reported this, except that they differ in the wording while preserving the same understanding of the events in both accounts. For since Matthew says, “This is my Son,” while the other two say, “You are my beloved Son,” both expressions serve to convey the same meaning. As we have already demonstrated above and in other passages that seem to disagree, they are shown by harmonious understanding to express one and the same sense.

The voice of God the Father from heaven said one of these forms, but the Evangelist wished to show that the words spoken amounted to “This is my Son,” so that it might be clearly indicated to those who were listening that he himself was the Son of God. Therefore he wished to report what had sounded—“You are my beloved Son”—as though it had been said to those who were present, with the purpose of pointing him out: “This is my beloved Son.” For this was not being made known to Christ, who already knew it about himself, but to those for whose sake, and to whom, the voice itself came divinely from heaven.

Now, if one Evangelist says, “In whom I am well pleased,” another, “In you I am well pleased,” and another, “In you I have been well pleased,” if you ask which of these sounded in that voice, devoutly accept whichever you wish, provided that you understand that, although they used different words, they reported one and the same meaning. For even if one of them preserved the very words of the voice that sounded, another may reasonably be understood to have varied the wording in order to explain the same meaning more familiarly.

The sense should simply be understood by all as though it had been said: “In you I have established my good pleasure.” That is: “In you I have willed to act, because in the first Adam I was displeased, and through him all, as though made into one mass, became children of wrath, so that through you all whom I have predestined to life may please me.”

Thus, just as at the beginning it was said, “I regret that I made man” (Genesis 6:7), so also: “In you I have been well pleased,” so that through you those who were foreknown may please me. For anyone who corrects through repentance something he has done, by the very fact that he is shown to repent he indicates that it displeased him, since he recalls what he has done for the purpose of correction.

Thus the omnipotent God the Father, speaking long ago in Genesis according to the human manner of speaking, says, “I regret that I made man upon the earth,” plainly indicating there what had displeased him in the sinners whom he had created. But that he was well pleased in the one and only Son, the Lord Jesus Christ—whom he had made man among human beings for the sake of those same people—he declares with an open voice from heaven, so that they among whom and for whom he had come might recognize it.

There was no sin in him. Therefore God not only did not regret him, but established his good pleasure in him. Concerning this the Psalmist sings: “The Lord has sworn and will not regret it: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:5). In this he rightly testifies that God was well pleased with him, whom he had begotten as his one, coeternal, consubstantial Son from his own substance.

Sent for us to become incarnate, he became the Word made flesh and dwelt among us. Therefore God was truly well pleased in him, since he was consubstantial with the one from whom he proceeded, and, from what was ours, became one and the same Son. In all things he did not his own will, but the will of the one who sent him.

Therefore whoever desires to please God the Father should not please himself in himself or as though by his own deeds. Rather, he should be displeased with himself in himself, so that, wholly transferred through faith and love into the one in whom the Father was well pleased, he may please the Father and, reconciled through him from being a child of wrath, become by adoption a son of God.

Otherwise, whoever applauds himself in himself, as though acting from himself, is shown still to be guilty, insofar as he is not united to the will of that one, and not yet pleasing to the Father as he ought. For this reason we also say in prayer: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth” (Luke 11:2), so that all that is earthly in us, by clinging to him, may become heavenly, and may be what he himself says concerning us to the Father: “Father, I will that, just as you and I are one, so they too may be one in us” (John 17:21).

What else could this mean except that, just as the Father and the Son are one in substance, so we too may be one in them through grace? And all this will happen because he established his good pleasure in him, so that through him we may please the Father in him.

It should also be noted that the mystery of the Trinity is most openly proclaimed in this baptism. Not only is the Trinity of the entire majesty most clearly made intelligible, but it is also made perceptible in a certain way, although incomprehensible, as though distinguished to bodily senses and presented with the greatest clarity for understanding.

The Father, clearly, cries out to the Son in a voice; the same Son, truly born as man in the flesh, is more fully proclaimed by the Father; and the Holy Spirit is shown in the dove upon him. Through it also many things that John still did not know about Christ are divinely taught, and there is fulfilled there that prophetic passage: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of majesty has thundered; the Lord is over many waters” (Psalm 28:3).

The Son is therefore proclaimed by the Father; he is proclaimed by the Holy Spirit; and he is also proclaimed by himself when he makes the Father known and testifies that he and the Father are one: “I and the Father,” he says, “are one” (John 10:30).

What further doubt, then, could a mind reborn through such a sacrament have concerning the faith, when at one and the same moment the voice of the Father, descending to us, proclaims the Son visibly appearing in the waters, and the Holy Spirit from above, in the dove, teaches more clearly what should be understood about him?

If every word is established by the testimony of two or three witnesses, then the testimony concerning himself given by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is received with far greater firmness. In this faith we have been reborn. What need have we to reconsider the faith any further, as though we were uncertain?

The apostles were therefore given this command: “Go; teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). When he said “in the name,” he showed that they are one, while he distinguished them with three names sufficiently and admirably to make the Trinity understood.

Therefore all who have been rightly baptized according to the catholic faith have truly been reborn, and through this faith Mother Church has received them into herself. Here, in accordance with Daniel’s prophecy, the Holy of Holies is anointed (Daniel 9:24). From that time onward the perpetual sacrifice of the Jews and all legal anointing ceased, so completely that in the fortieth year after Christ’s ascension into heaven Jerusalem was destroyed, the temple overturned, and the whole people ravaged in an incredible slaughter; their entire religion and priesthood perished together.

Let the hard-hearted Jews therefore either show us the perpetual sacrifice of the Law, the anointings, and the temple, or else, according to Daniel’s prophecy, since all those things ceased long ago, let them hear and understand, even unwillingly, that Christ the Son of God—who is truly the Holy of Holies—has already been anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit above his companions, and let them begin not to blaspheme.

He is said to have been anointed above his companions because the Holy Spirit remained wholly in him. For, as the Apostle says: “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” (Colossians 2:9). No one who understands correctly doubts, however, that the saints and all Christians who are rightly understood to share in him have received the same Spirit according to the measure of faith, through the grace of Christ’s gift.

Therefore, “if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.” Concerning this the Apostle says: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God” (1 Corinthians 2:12). “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Romans 8:16), because we have received him as the pledge of our promised inheritance and as a kind of document of eternal salvation.

This Spirit makes us the temple of God and intercedes for us with unspeakable groanings, fulfilling the duty of his advocacy. He accustoms us daily, through heavenly power, to be joined to spiritual things and associated with eternal life. Through him and by him our bodies, if we belong to him, are trained to advance toward immortality, as they learn to restrain themselves moderately in all things according to his decrees.

He is the one who restrains our insatiable desires within us, breaks our immoderate lusts, extinguishes unlawful passions, conquers our burning impulses, represses drunkenness, drives away greed, and banishes all the pleasures of the world. He binds charity among all, orders the affections of conduct, makes the rule of truth effective everywhere, refutes heretics, and drives out the wicked.

Concerning this the Apostle plainly says: “In the last times some will depart from the faith, attending to deceiving spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy and having their conscience seared” (1 Timothy 4:1). If they truly had the Spirit of God, they would never afterward have believed a deceiving spirit, because no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, “Anathema to Jesus.”

Since all were marked from the beginning with the sign of faith in Christ, it is astonishing that so many afterward, choosing something else, became heretics. And for what other reason, except that they made their first faith void and, as though seeking a new faith, became exiles from the faith?

“They went astray from the womb”; that is, they departed from the faith of the Churches of God. “From the womb they spoke falsehood,” for they were not from us, and therefore they departed from us. For if they had been from us, they would have had the anointing from the Holy Spirit together with us, and they would have remained with us.

There will still be many more who are shipwrecked concerning the faith before the end comes. Nevertheless, those who are chosen will not then pursue another faith; rather, they will preserve in every respect, with no unbelief of mind, the faith in which they were reborn.

It is therefore most absurd to deviate from the faith because many are endangered, especially since the faith of believers ought thereby to become stronger and more robust, because, just as it was foretold through the foreknowledge of God, so it is fulfilled in them.

For we who now exist believe that what we do not yet clearly see will come in the future—except that in very many the ministry of iniquity has already grown long ago, as had been marked out concerning them, although they may also suddenly be crushed and consigned to the underworld. How much firmer, then, ought those to be in the faith upon whom all these things—even the few that remain—will yet be more fully fulfilled?

For the present fulfillment of past promises will be a certainty, if there remain certain future things; when these come, they ought rather to strengthen faith, since God assigned to their proper times the things he had foretold, even those that did not yet exist.

Those who possess that faith in which they were reborn, through which they have also been incorporated among the members of the Church—the substance of things hoped for—do not seek another faith, even though it is said: “Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face continually” (Psalm 102:3); and also the following:

189. “Seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.” For although one ought to seek, one must seek no other than the one God in three persons, by whose name of the Trinity we have been marked. Under this faith, having been stripped bare of the affairs of the world, we entered naked into the spring. For whoever among us has been baptized in Christ in this spring has been baptized into his death: “For we were buried with him through baptism into death.” Therefore, we must no longer reconsider anything concerning the faith, but guard by every means what we have believed and, by believing, have freely received from God.

We must believe absolutely that there is nothing else to be believed; hence it is not to be sought, since we have believed that it has already been found. Therefore we seek nothing else, because he himself does not command us to seek anything else, since he is one; and we know that, apart from this one thing, nothing else is necessary. We embrace him because he is one. And certainly, as we advance in the same and one faith with the affection of devotion, hoping and loving—for he is infinite—we always seek him, still in an enigma and not yet in his visible form. Holding him fast, we search for him daily with the most ardent love.

But when the enigmas of present realities have been removed, we are also certain that no other God than the one and the same Trinity will appear to those who believe in him, as we have now grasped him through faith. Through this faith, therefore, the light of God’s countenance has been marked upon us; and for that reason we must not look toward the unbelief of certain people or toward the darkness of errors.

Trusting, then, in the proof that times of danger are foretold as coming, we wish to warn certain people in advance that they should seek nothing further than what they received by believing in baptism, and that this, and nothing else, is what they should meanwhile seek. The method of seeking appears to consist in three aspects of reality: the matter itself, the time, and the manner. In the matter, so that we may consider what is to be sought; in the time, so that we may know when—lest perhaps we seek when we ought not, or fail to find adequately either something else or the thing we seek; and in the manner, so that we may determine how far the search should extend.

Therefore, we must examine what Christ instituted, and hold fast to him whom we rejoice to have found. For you could not have believed unless you had first found him. You sought, then, in order to find; but you found in order to believe. In this faith, by believing, you fixed the whole proof of your seeking and finding, when, stripped of the world, you buried yourself with Christ in death through the tomb of the spring.

But if you truly died, and your life has been hidden with God in heaven, why do you still dispute concerning the faith with those who live for themselves and not for God, as though you were doubtful? Or why, while a persecutor rages, do you fear death—you who, already dead, are held with Christ in the tomb of the spring, and perfectly believe that your life has been laid up in heaven? There is no doubt that, if you receive your former life on earth, you have lost the new life that you had hidden in heaven with Christ.

Into such a tomb he confined you, since he does not want you henceforth to believe anything other than what he instituted. Therefore you too must certainly seek nothing else, nor, when handed over to torments, confess anything else as though unwillingly.

Finally, I judge it better to advise someone to remain ignorant of what lies outside the sacrament of baptism, and not learn what he ought not to know, than to be seized by some deceitful curiosity and led away captive beyond it. “Your faith,” he says, “has saved you” (Matthew 9:22). Therefore let the Christian remain within the spring of faith, from which he was reborn to salvation. And if he should hesitate about anything for a moment, let him touch Christ, who is still in the spring, with the hand of faith—the Christ into whom the Word, having become flesh, descended and was baptized for us.

Then, through the outer ear, let him hear with the hearing of the inner ear the voice of the Father sounding from above to instruct us: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” This voice, as a means of making him known—or rather, because it was a true body perceptible to the ears—was therefore rightly said to have become perceptible to the ears in some way, although the Father, who is incomprehensible, sounded through it without being enclosed within a voice. Likewise, the Holy Spirit is declared to have appeared visibly through the form assumed by him.

Nevertheless, according to the proper character of his nature, because God is Trinity and is rightly believed to be wholly present everywhere, he is not seen in a place, since he is proved to be incorporeal, without place, and invisible. He is neither bounded by sight nor grasped by touch, neither heard through speech nor perceived by movement. Hence it is also said: “No one has ever seen God, but the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself declared him to us” (John 1:18).

This should not, however, be understood as though he ought to resound audibly in our ears. Rather, because he is the Word and image of the Father, when he makes himself known to our minds, he declares and clearly reveals the Father through ineffable light, in accordance with his own testimony: “Whoever sees me sees my Father also” (John 14:9). This vision is not apprehended by bodily senses, but as it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

The Father therefore proclaims the Son through the perceptible sound of a voice; and the Son, when he presents himself visibly, because he is the Father’s Word, reveals in himself no other than the one whose Son he is. The Holy Spirit, moreover, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son, also appeared in the form of a dove—not divided in the nature of the substance or majesty, but distinct in persons, so that God the Trinity might be disclosed to human beings.

Yet for that reason he is not confined by sight, just as the Father is not here or elsewhere heard through speech. Nor, when he walked in paradise, could he be perceived through movement. Otherwise, whenever he displayed himself to the Fathers through an assumed form, he could be regarded as having been perceptible—which it is absurd to believe. But because he is invisible, he was seen as he willed: not as he is, but in whatever form he was pleased to appear.

Indeed, here he was heard in one way—not only by John, but elsewhere also by others inwardly—and in another way by the crowd, here or elsewhere; the crowd said in one place that it had become thunder. Thus it is not surprising if many do not obey the preacher’s voice, since many also heard this voice and are shown to have gained nothing from it. For it is God who gives the increase inwardly, without a voice.

Concerning this blessed Ambrose says: “When he is thought to be absent, he is seen; and when he is present, he is not seen.” He did not say, “when he is absent,” but “when he is thought to be absent.” For he is never absent, since he fills heaven and earth and all things; he is not enclosed within small spaces or extended through great ones, but is wholly everywhere and contained in no place. Whoever understands this with a mind that has risen beyond ordinary things sees God, even when he is thought to be absent.

Such a person understands that, although God the Trinity appeared distinct in baptism—Trinity in persons—he is everywhere wholly inseparable, because of the unity of his substance. The Father is wholly in the Son, and the Son wholly in the Father—not in a place—and the Holy Spirit remains wholly and together in the Father and the Son, and God remains coeternal.

For whatever the Father is, this also the Son and the Holy Spirit are; and whatever the Son is, this also the Father and the Holy Spirit are; likewise, whatever the Holy Spirit is, this wholly the Father and the Son are. Yet the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another: another, I say, not another thing. For he who is the Father is not the Son, nor the Holy Spirit; likewise, he who is the Son is in no way the Father or the Holy Spirit. Nor is the same Spirit the Father or the Son.

Because God the Trinity wished to reveal this even more clearly to those still immature in faith—people who did not yet know how to conceive anything with their minds except bodily things—he, who is one, shone forth distinctly for recognition in the threefold number of a particular manifestation. Thus those still nursing in faith might carry the first principles of faith inwardly into themselves through these three senses—sight, hearing, and touch—with the help of him who was perceived outwardly, so that afterward perfect faith might be more fully nourished by the rich breasts of Scripture.

For those who were still carnal could not yet fully grasp spiritual things. Therefore it was necessary that the tender infancy of believers receive faith through outward sensation; and, returning inward from the sense of the flesh, the whole person, turned toward God, might become spiritual by seeing invisible things through faith and might rise higher through faith, nourished by the milk of doctrine toward spiritual realities.

Hence many of the saints advanced spiritually so far that, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things, they saw that such realities were more truly perceived by the mind than experienced through bodily sensation. Although he was seen or heard by many, as is read in the divine authority concerning this passage, he was seen either without any change in himself through a body, or certainly through certain bodily images—which God’s will chose, not nature’s formation.

God made these things for whomever he wished, whenever he wished, and in whatever manner he wished, while his own substance remained hidden within them, immutable, and filling all things without any intervals of place or time. Thus he is neither less in a part than in the whole, nor greater in the whole than he is in a part.

Nevertheless, he appeared in places and at times as he wished and as often as he wished, in order to draw those who were themselves subject to places and times toward belief in invisible things, so that they might set aside the things to which they were bound and which they saw daily being undermined by their own deficiencies.

Hence it is certain, as we stated above, that in the baptismal spring the entire divinity of the majesty of the Trinity poured itself, in a manner of speaking, into bodily senses as something perceptible, lest those reborn through faith should afterward embrace another faith than that by which each person is joined to God and, deceived by carnal perception, perish.

This spring has been sealed with the ring of faith, and therefore it must never admit any thief. From its irrigation, the garden of delights—that is, God’s universal Church—blooms and flourishes, sufficiently fortified and enclosed on every side, because it rejoices that Christ has been not only buried in it but also risen.

In these first principles of faith, the soul of every believer rests securely. In this faith it blooms daily through works of virtue and sets itself against every assault of affliction like a shield of protection. Finally, surrounded by the mighty strength of such security, it confidently sings what is written in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2).

It sleeps, lulled by the certainty of its hope; but it remains awake through vigilant diligence, lest what has been sealed with the ring of faith be corrupted by deceit. It no longer knows how to doubt concerning the faith. For although it still dwells on earth, it has been placed in heaven through faith; and although not yet in reality, it reigns with Christ already in hope.

There is therefore a lesser faith in some people, and a greater faith in others. Hence to one it is said: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matthew 14:31). To another: “Great is your faith; let it be done for you as you have asked.” For the gifts of virtues are bestowed by the Holy Spirit upon each person according to the measure of faith.

Moreover, through this faith the saints conquered kingdoms, practiced justice, and obtained promises. Through this one and the same faith we too conquer, because “this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith.” The Apostle also greatly rejoices that he preserved it, saying: “I have kept the faith, I have finished the course; henceforth,” he says, “there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award me on that day” (2 Timothy 4:8).

Therefore, preserving this one and same Catholic faith whole and entire—the faith that we received from the Creed while we were still nourished on milk—let us press onward to the end, continually clinging to good works, because “whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.” Running toward that end ourselves, let us here establish the end of the book under this faith, resting for a little while as though in the safest harbor of peace. Thus, supported by that same faith and carried forward by certain hope, perfected in perfect love, may we happily bring the end of our life to completion in Christ.

## PREFACE TO THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0181]

[Col. 0181D] Lovers of secular literature are accustomed, with excessive shamelessness, to boast of themselves through the teachings of their instructors and to display their eloquence by teaching what they have brought forth without wisdom. Since some of our own people are unable to understand these teachings adequately, they seek various and different interpreters, so that through understanding they may manage to reach the polished falsehoods of their unspeakable subjects.

Although the eloquence of those whose teachings they desire to serve may be polished in its vanity, the speech of their interpreters is often sufficiently unrefined and close to rusticity. Although they are full of the filth of vices, still, because understanding is necessary, they do not pass over—not merely a page, but not even a syllable—without examining it with the greatest vigilance and labor.

I therefore wonder greatly what offense the divine utterances have given to certain people, that they do not wish to scrutinize the mysteries of God with the same diligence with which, laboring and sweating, they desire to investigate the lamentations of tragedies and the inventions of poets; and whether, through the theatrical applause of actors, they may arouse the approval of the crowds.

No one who reflects on the matter can fail to see the ineffectual zeal of their labor, since their subject plainly lacks fruit and is found to be without reward. Although they may have elevated the Academic rhetorician through this empty eloquence of vanity to the living circle of the heavens and made the sleeping Scipio a citizen of heaven, all these things are woven from old-womanish tales rather than supported by any truth.

Therefore I advise the reader to devote himself more earnestly to the utterances of the divine Scriptures, as I have already urged sufficiently above. Let him not disdain the truth in reading because of the insignificance of the person, but accept the person as commended to him on account of the truth, and let him read that same truth devoutly for no other reason than for its own sake.

For we are not treating of Maro’s “arms and the man,” with the savor of Greek mythological seasoning; rather, searching out the interpretations of the Catholic Fathers from the fountain of the Holy Spirit, with Christ’s cooperation we wish to explain to the ears of our people what we understand in the divine writings.

We neither intend to charm the reader with tragic sentiment nor wish to burden him with comic costume; instead, we disclose in simple speech, according to the capacity of our understanding, what in those works gives off a divine fragrance.

Therefore, even if some of our people enjoy the works of Maro—interpreting “arms” as virtue and “the man” as wisdom, and likewise the other things that follow—still, they ought to prefer what we now intend to discuss: the unconquerable virtue and wisdom of God the Father, who, in order to establish the warfare of Christians against the aerial powers, immediately came from the baptismal spring to the desert, like a commander about to enter battle.

## THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0183]

### (CHAPTER IV)

“Jesus,” he says, “was led by the Spirit into the desert, to be tempted by the devil.” Therefore, after baptism, the Wisdom of God could have prudently chosen nothing else as a first action than that by which he would instruct all the soldiers of his kingdom concerning what they too had to do against demons as soon as they had been reborn through the spring.

It was therefore a most ancient custom—not only among the Romans but also among other peoples—that if someone, after long exercises as a recruit, became fit to pass into military service, he should, of his own will, give his name to be entered in the public records; thereafter, when his name had been called out in the king’s army, he was enrolled.

This is what individual Christians do before they enter the baptismal spring. Questioned one by one, they renounce the enemy and all his weapons, and put on the armor of Christ, strong in faith, so that they may be able to stand against the devil’s snares and fight daily against the legions of demons.

Their names, indeed, are inscribed not on tablets but in heaven, so that if they have acted worthily in battle they may be crowned; but if they have fallen, marked with the sign of death as those who were not worthy of heaven, they will be completely erased from the book of life.

To prevent this, Christ, the God-man, went ahead of them. As soon as he came forth from the spring, he showed his army how and with what weapons it ought to fight, and against which enemy. Therefore the blessed Evangelist, wishing no interval of time to intervene, says: “Then Jesus was led into the desert.”

No interval, then, is rightly believed to have intervened, because after the grace of baptism no delay is left to believers before temptation, so that they may be secure. Hence we also read: “My son, when you come to serve God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclesiasticus 2:1). And in Job: “The life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7:1).

A Christian must therefore never lay down the weapons of virtue. The Apostle Paul, understanding this well, urged it in these words: “Put on the armor of God”; for, as he says elsewhere, “our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, and against the rulers of the world of darkness” (Ephesians 6:11–12).

Christians have therefore been placed in the midst of a great spectacle in the world. Against them not only the whole world, the princes of darkness, and every spiritual wickedness wage war, but the human being, divided within himself, also fights and struggles against himself. For this reason the Apostle, bringing his own people back to vigilance, says: “We have become a spectacle to the world and to angels” (1 Corinthians 4:9).

He would not impress this so frequently upon his hearers by admonition if he did not know that we are besieged on every side by deceitful enemies and that our journey to heaven is impeded daily by their contrivances and distractions.

The Lord is therefore led into the desert to complete single combat against the devil, so that the whole army of Christians might observe him. They should learn to conquer by despising visible things and to restrain themselves by trampling down both gluttony and vainglory.

But it is not without reason that the same person is led into the desert to be tempted, especially since the whole world is everywhere full of the snares of temptations. The reason may be that wherever there is greater quiet for serving God, there it is necessarily shown that there is a greater struggle of strength, because even there the persuasive deceit of distractions will never be absent.

By the desert, then, a life more removed from the pressures and disturbances of the world is signified, so that all may learn to desire quiet, devote themselves to God alone, and do so even if they appear to live among human beings.

Otherwise, the Song of Songs would not ask concerning the Church: “Who is this that comes up through the desert, rising like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army set in battle array?” (Song of Songs 3:6).

She is described as ascending like an army set in battle array against enemies because they blockade the road by which she goes to heaven, so that she may not be broken by any assault. She is raised up through the desert of this world because, although she lives amid human disturbances, separated from the world’s commotion, she carries solitude with God everywhere within herself.

In her figure, that army of God is believed to have gone up from Egypt through the desert, so that, walking with God under the guidance of God alone, it might return to its homeland.

It should also be noted that she is proclaimed beautiful as the moon and chosen as the sun because the body and the head advance together: the Church, expressed through the moon, and Christ the head, signified through the sun, ascending with his bride.

Therefore Christ is led into the desert to fight, so that his army might recognize and follow him in some manner and, aided by his support, continue what it sees him doing.

The Prophet likewise, when he saw himself increasingly oppressed by the pressures of worldly affairs, grieved in his struggle and was troubled by the enemy’s voice because iniquities had turned against him, together with the other things that follow, and immediately cried out: “Who will give me wings like a dove? I will fly away and rest. Behold,” he says, “I have gone far off, fleeing, and remained in solitude,” awaiting him who would save him “from faintness of spirit and tempest” (Psalm 54:6–8).

From this it is plainly shown that he sought solitude so that he would not be oppressed by the world’s troubles; yet, while he still asks to be delivered, he does not yet understand himself to be free from danger even in solitude.

For the enemy did not first rise up for battle until he wished to leave the world. Therefore, while anyone still lives in the world, the prince of the world can rise up against him, because he holds him captive under his laws within the boundaries of his kingdom.

Thus Jesus, wishing to summon his army to battle, went first into the desert and established the contest, so that his followers might worthily imitate him. Otherwise, unless each person becomes outside himself and outside the world while still in the world, he cannot fight lawfully, because he remains subject to the laws of the one in whose kingdom his life and conduct have been planted.

John wished to demonstrate this through the duty of his forerunning office. From the beginning of his birth he dwelt in the wilderness, so that he might already be found a soldier of Christ where the rest of the army was going to fight under its head.

The ranks of all monks also hasten to leave the midst of the crowd physically naked, so that it is now scarcely possible to find any desert unoccupied. They do this so that, naked with the Naked One, they may struggle more firmly and steadily, and by struggling conquer.

From this it is rightly believed that the following was said: “Each man’s sword is upon his thigh because of nighttime fears” (Song of Songs 3:8). Otherwise, coming to the desert is useless if one has not been clothed with the whole armor of virtues with a vigilant mind.

For this reason each person leaves the crowd of the world with Christ for solitude—not to grow sluggish in idleness, but to be tempted with him; and, once tempted, to conquer; and, as victor, to be crowned.

Everyone provokes the adversary’s greater fury against himself when he begins to resist his laws more fiercely. John makes this sufficiently clear in his Apocalypse (12:13), when he speaks of the woman who had given birth to a son. He wished to show the holy Church of God, which daily conceives Christ by believing and gives birth to him by clinging to good works.

When two wings were given to her—namely, the love of God and of neighbor—so that she might fly into the desert, where she would be nourished for “a time, and times, and half a time,” away from the face of the serpent, because it desired to devour her son, that is, to destroy Christ in us, the serpent is immediately said to have sent water from its mouth after the woman like a river, so that it might cause her to be swept away by the river.

A little later it is written: “The dragon was angry with the woman and went away to make war with the rest of her offspring, who keep the commandments of God and hold the testimony of Jesus” (ibid. 12:17).

Although these words may seem to refer to the future, no one can doubt that even now all these things advance in this way against those who resist them.

Therefore those who are called by the Christian name must beware lest they imagine themselves to be participants in Christ before they leave the world, or think that anything will profit them after they have left it unless Christ’s soldiers have carried their warfare through to the end.

The fact that Christ is led into the desert is otherwise a lesson concerning military service itself. Because Adam, luxuriating in the delights of paradise, was defeated by the serpent through the pleasure of desire, Christ’s soldiers, seized by the harshness of the desert, were to learn with their head to restrain all the desires of the flesh through self-control.

For just as delights invite one to gluttony, so the barrenness and desolation of the desert soothe the mind toward continence.

Some people therefore maintain, according to the literal sense—although certain others understand it differently—that this was said of the desert encountered on the road by those descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, because of the parable that the Lord proposed elsewhere, where he says: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among thieves” (Matthew 10:30).

That thieves formerly lay in wait for him is proved by the place there, which is still called Domim today [the place-name is uncertain in the supplied text]. Domim is interpreted as “blood,” on account of the shedding of blood that once took place there. Accordingly, the Lord appears to have woven that parable there according to the custom of robbers.

From this it should not seem incredible that the Lord, by fasting in that place, provoked the devil to temptation, so that he might be defeated there in reality according to history, where Adam was first figured as having conquered according to allegory.

For our Samaritan, Christ, descended along the same road on which the wounded man had fallen—not by sinning, but, clothed in flesh, he deigned to descend to the same temptations to which that man had succumbed—so that, having cast down the enemy, he might provide his own people with an example of conquering, since he himself first emerged victorious.

Nevertheless, it is not without reason that the question is asked by what spirit he was led into the desert, especially since the Holy Spirit is very rarely found in the holy Scriptures without an additional qualification.

It is therefore not contrary to truth that the one who endured crucifixion at the hands of the devil’s members also allowed himself to be led by the devil himself for the sake of being tempted. But the meaning is more fitting if we understand that the Holy Spirit, who remained upon him at his baptism, immediately offered for temptation the human being whom he had created from the Virgin and whom he had reborn from the spring where adoption is granted to us.

He did this so that all who are reborn from Baptism might learn that they must immediately fight through continence, since the crafty persuader at once stands against them, ready to engage them with his deceits.

It was therefore entirely fitting that the Holy Spirit, who had remained fully upon Jesus, should rouse him as a king to military service against the enemy, as the forerunner of his army.

By the very means through which he had first defeated Adam in the paradise of delights, he was cast down by the second Adam in the desert of desolation; and thereafter the whole army, with the Spirit of God acting within it, could fight more securely and more carefully while living in this desert.

For the Holy Spirit does not know how to leave ineffective and unready those whom he possesses. Rather, he advances them to battle, so that after victory all who are led by him may, through him and conformed to Christ, rest more happily.

Hence the Apostle also says: “Those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8:14).

When, at the beginning, the Spirit came down from heaven upon the apostles and those who were shut in with them because of fear of the Jews, he immediately drove them out into the midst of the ranks of their persecutors and made them fight without fear—those who had previously been held shut in like timid people.

All the martyrs, inflamed by that Spirit, also ran through the world like sparks in a thicket of reeds and, by fighting bravely, subjected to their feet everything that opposed them.

For, as I said, this Spirit leaves no one here inactive. It must therefore be thought all the more that he himself led Jesus into the desert, so that he might teach in the head what had to be done in the members, if only all the members would tirelessly follow the head through him.

Otherwise, whoever approaches the military service of Christianity without the Spirit of God is suddenly struck down by the force of the storm with which he is attacked.

Hence the Apostle says: “Test the spirits, whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1).
