For unless a person has been inwardly animated by him, he is easily scattered by the wind of temptation, and, fleeing from the one from whom he seemed to have withdrawn, he is carried here and there empty, like chaff.

For this reason the Apostle gives the command: “Stand, beloved, with the loins of your mind girded in truth, and with your feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace; in all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one, and the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:14).

With these weapons, therefore, as inseparable arms, he wanted his followers to be armed with complete invincibility. He knew that all had been called to military service, and therefore he equipped them to remain unconquered as the strongest soldiers of Christ. He showed them with what weapons they should be girded in order to fight more powerfully.

Their loins were to be girded with the belt of chastity and their feet shod with the protection of peace. For an ungirded soldier is quickly defeated by the inciter of immodesty, and one without shoes is easily bitten by a serpent.

For this reason, great care must be taken that no one live carelessly, since no one walks anywhere except among enemies. Whom, then, would he not dare to tempt, when he did not refrain from attempting his deceit even against the Lord Jesus Christ himself?

Wishing to make this clear to his soldiers as a warning, Christ immediately after the baptismal spring went forth first into battle. By fasting he began to overcome gluttony—the means by which the fuel of desires is nourished and the incentives of lust are inflamed more fiercely in us—just as the first man was defeated in paradise.

For the desire of the flesh, which each person unwillingly feels within himself resisting the law of his mind and taking him captive without his consent, is the punishment of sin. Therefore it is nourished by nothing more than gluttony, against which the flesh is hostile as its punishment.

Those who have written more particularly about vices therefore place first among them all *gastrimargia*, that is, the greed of the belly. This makes it clearer that anyone labors in vain if, having been defeated not by the enemy but still only by the flesh, he does not soberly restrain the source of nourishment for the remaining vices.

Then follows:

“And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry.”

If this number of sacred abstinence is carefully considered, it is an evident sacrament of the present age. For, as we have already shown briefly above, through it is signified the whole of the present life, in which Christ himself fights victoriously in his members both against the vices of the flesh and against the aerial powers.

For this reason, as an example, he wisely sanctified this number of days and nights by fasting, so that he might teach that, until the consummation of the age, he would be tempted and would be victorious in his soldiers through this warfare of abstinence.

The number forty is frequently shown to signify the present age. The period during which Jesus lived with his disciples after the resurrection also declares this. Hence he says in one place: “I am with you all the days until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

The entire present age is made up of the four elements, while the world is said to have been perfected in six days. From these numbers, the sum of ten is formed: four and six make ten.

In the reckoning of this perfection, God gave human beings ten commandments to preserve—human beings for whom the world is understood to have been made. The three commandments that pertain to God commend that love by which God is worshiped: with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength.

The remaining seven explain love of neighbor, which operates through the grace of the Holy Spirit. In these ten commandments, the words of the Law and the Prophets hang, so that the Gospel may be fulfilled.

God is the Creator, from whom all things are, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are. Therefore God the Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is rightly understood, with respect to the inner and invisible human being, through the invisible threefold number of the commandments. The creature for whom invisible things were made is commanded to love him with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength.

The invisible threefold number is assigned to the spirit, so that the fourfold number, which constitutes our outward human being, may be assigned to the body: hot and cold, moist and dry. Thus our entire inner and outer human being is consecrated by this sevenfold number of commandments.

And because the Creator, God the Trinity, is rightly to be worshiped by the creature, the whole human being, referred to God, is completed in the sum of ten.

Therefore every discipline that knows and distinguishes the Creator and the creature is rightly indicated by this number ten. This discipline of God’s commandments is ordered to be fulfilled in time through devotion. It consists in faith and in the work of love expressed through deeds, until those who are sometimes nourished as little children on milk become fit for divine contemplation.

But because this discipline of the ten commandments is often not fulfilled as it ought to be through our sluggish negligence, the number ten—which expresses the perfection of the whole discipline of this religion—is multiplied by the square number assigned to the body. Since the love of God and neighbor is violated in us through the movement of the flesh, it rises to a period of forty for the washing away of the stains of sins.

Accordingly, as long as we are in this life, it is always necessary for us, by resisting vices vigorously, to weep more abundantly over the impurities of our offenses, because the present period of life is rightly signified by this number.

Hence, in Leviticus, the woman through whom, as some maintain, the present Church is signified—the woman who has given birth to a male child, namely, conceiving Christ through faith—is told: “She shall sit for seven days in her uncleanness and for thirty-three days in the blood of her purification, until she comes to the temple” (Leviticus 12:2), where Christ the high priest entered. These numbers together make forty, through which the present age and the future purification of the woman who gives birth are perhaps not improperly figured.

For all our righteousness, when compared with the purity of that life, appears to be nothing other than, as the Prophet testifies, “like a menstrual cloth” (Isaiah 64:6).

Hence it also happened that the universal holy Church of God, following the teaching of the Holy Spirit, established for itself annually, under this number forty, a general period of penitence. Through it, by fasting in imitation of Christ under this sacred number, it might wash away more abundantly the stains that it continually contracts through various excesses and might more tightly restore the battle line that had fallen apart in its several parts.

But it may be asked: since, after the day of the Epiphany had passed—the day on which, according to the traditions of the Catholic Fathers, he is believed to have been baptized—he immediately sought the desert and began to fast, why did the universal Church wish to defer this fast and extend it to the time of the Passion? What more fitting answer could be given than that, in preparation for the paschal mysteries, when Christ rose victorious from the dead—as though for the day of his immortality at the end—the Holy Spirit taught them that they must strive with greater earnestness, so that through this the victorious Church of God, with minds purified and sanctified, might more happily be able to enter heaven? Therefore, if Moses and Elijah fasted figuratively under this number, and Christ, in whom there was no cause of sin, instituted fasting for us, how much more ought all of us, who are bound by such great cords of vices, even if not as they did, at least sustained by daily frugality until evening, to fast for successive days and thereby to be increasingly and more abundantly satisfied, according to the inner person, with divine nourishment.

For Moses and Elijah did not fast by their own strength as Christ did—especially since Moses is said to have been sustained by conversation with the enjoyment of God, and Scripture testifies that Elijah, strengthened by the food which he had received through the angel’s bringing it, walked fasting for forty days and forty nights (III Kings 19:8). Christ, however, is believed to have fasted continuously for forty days and nights, sustained neither by conversation with anyone greater nor by the strength of any food. Days are joined to nights so that no one might have an opportunity to lie by saying that he had at least eaten during the nights, and so that no one might anywhere doubt concerning God what we cannot do of ourselves. That he fasted for so long was the power of his divinity; that he became hungry demonstrates the manifestation of the nature of his true humanity.

In this number of days he showed that, through abstinence, two laws were to be fulfilled in the one new man, Christ Jesus: namely, that in forty nothing other than the sum of the commandments of the Decalogue and of the four Gospels resounds, so that neither the four are recited without the ten, nor the ten without the four. Moreover, another rule of perfection is again gathered in the number ten, if every number preceding it, up to the first square number, four, is joined into one. For one and two—in which the unity of the Godhead, the Creator and the creature, are equally proclaimed—and likewise three and four—in which God the Trinity is displayed, and the creature is declared to subsist in four kinds of elements—when gradually joined together, make ten; and these, doubled through the same four, rise to forty.

Therefore, as I have said, it was divinely ordained that under this number of prefiguration we should fight more earnestly, so that by the number through which, in the Flood, all flesh was killed by the waters except what the ark contained, the sins of our flesh might be killed through the figure of that same number, so that none of us might perish, whom Christ’s Church is proved to enclose.

Nevertheless, although Christ had fasted for the entire period, he permitted the manhood of his nature to become hungry, because, unless he had become hungry, the tempter would by no means have approached him with the audacity of attempting him, having found no trace of weakness. Accordingly, when he had received the hunger of our weakness, the devil rejoiced that he had found in him a sign of a passible and mortal nature. Therefore he immediately attacked him and attempted to overcome him. Otherwise he would have found no occasion for tempting him, because there was in him no law of sin to which the adversary could approach—as he does in us—in order to stir up the desires of the flesh as though approaching his own law.

For the cause of sin remains in us, that is, in our flesh; and this cause arose as punishment for sin. Therefore the devil has access to us for tempting us through the rights of his law. But because he found nothing of this kind in Christ, that whole temptation was external, not internal, as it usually is in us. Thus he approached, not a desire which Christ did not possess, but the weakness of the flesh, which he undertook to receive in himself so that the devil might dare to attack him. And rightly was he overcome through the weakness of the flesh who had cast the substance of our humanity, stripped of its powers, into the weakness of death.

“If you are the Son of God,” he said, “tell these stones to become loaves of bread.” It should be observed, then, that the enemy first used a question, to see whether he could discover what he greatly feared, suspecting it strongly. For he was thinking that Christ was the Son of God, just as demons confess elsewhere—although the impious Jews denied it. For this reason it is greatly to be feared what will become of us wretched people, whose life is nothing other than temptation, if he did not hold himself back from the One whom he indeed feared as the Son of God.

The devil could not know, then, that Christ was hungrier for the salvation of souls in the figure of the whole of life—for whose sake he was doing everything—than for bodily food. Yet he orders everything in such a way that, in the order in which he had first overthrown Adam, he might conversely be conquered by Christ in spirit through the flesh.

For he began with gluttony, through which the first man had cast himself and all others into death; through which Esau lost the birthright of his firstborn status; through which the fraudulent persuader of vices confronted the Jews after they had crossed the sea, and through the desire for drink broke the tender beginnings of their virtues.

“Tell these stones,” he said, “to become loaves of bread.” The blind examiner of the Scriptures knew, therefore, that at the beginning God had said, “Let it be,” and had thus made all things from nothing. Yet he had not understood that this was the Word through which the Father had created all things. For the “Let it be” that Moses introduced to carnal hearers was not uttered by God the Father as a sound of the voice; rather, through that temporal word he wished to indicate to his readers that God had created all things together through his coeternal Word.

Nevertheless, wishing to examine this more fearfully, the devil persuaded Christ that he should say that the stones should become loaves, according to the manner in which he had learned Moses to have committed to writing that God had created the universe. For he is not mistaken in this respect: if Christ had commanded it, it would certainly have happened, since every creature perceives and obeys its Creator. But because the matter is conducted through fraudulent cunning, the devil neither ought nor deserves to arrive at knowledge of the truth.

For it is no greater thing to transform one thing and make another from it than to create all things from nothing. Yet the command of the one commanding is restrained by the authority of Scripture, so that the members of Christ’s body might learn to fight more by the teaching of both Testaments than by the miracles of his divinity.

If the first man had known how to repel him by the divine oracle of command, he would never have stumbled into death; rather, blessed after the triumph of his obedience, he would have been transferred into a better state.

The devil turned to the stones as an experiment of his fraud, to test whether Christ was the One by whose command Moses had brought water from the rock for the people. He therefore urges him to relieve the hunger of his condition by producing bread from stones—not because he cared about his salvation, but so that, from the transformation of stones into loaves, he might recognize the power of his miracle; and, if Christ were merely a human being, so that he might mock his patient endurance of hunger with the delight of bread—not bread from the earth or from some germ of seed, as though that were not miraculous, since he creates bread from the earth every day.

Rather, he appropriately chose to demand loaves from stones, so that by such an example the hardness of the speaker might be marked. But because it is harder for Christ to soften toward compassion than for stones, if commanded, to be changed into loaves—a thing sufficiently possible—he teaches that nothing is to be done according to the devil’s will.

For one aspect of this was examination, another temptation: he appeared to confess God with a blind confession, while attempting to mock the human being. Thus he tempts in order to examine what he fears; and he examines in such a way that, by tempting, he may deceive and accomplish what he is contriving. But the Lord deceives him in such a way as to leave him an uncertain, though defeated, adversary; and he conquers him in such a way that, though tempted, he still outwits his frauds.

“For it is written,” he said, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” Here he does not use his power as God, but, as a human being, employs the authority of Scripture so that human beings might learn how to fight.

He teaches that one part belongs to heaven and another to earth. Therefore, a human being does not live by bread alone, through which only the outward person lives in common with the animals, but by every word through which the inner person is made equal to the angels. For every word is rightly understood as God’s love, in which all the words of the Law and the Prophets depend, without which no one ever lives in God or with God (Romans 3:9).

Paul aptly intimates this: “And if there is any other commandment,” he says, “it is summed up in this word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” As if he were saying: Even if there is another food by which the inner person is nourished, let someone possess love, and he will abound in every good, because he enjoys that word toward which all things converge.

For in Christ Jesus there was God and man. Whoever uses that word is nourished by the love of God and of humanity, because he loves and venerates all who are in Christ as members of Christ; and those who are not yet in Christ he cares to bring to him, so that all the members of Christ may be completed.

Otherwise, if someone possesses all the words of things and even completes the other works as though they were virtues, he has become guilty of everything if he has not lived by this whole word. This word is the general word of all words, upon which all words depend—not just any words, but those that proceed from the mouth of God.

The words of heretics, poets, and philosophers, however, are outside this word, because they are not in love and do not enjoy Christ, namely the Word of the Father; therefore they cannot love at all the things that are in Christ.

Intent upon this word, Moses could not desire bread; and nourished by it, Elijah did not feel the hunger of his prolonged abstinence. For one who feeds on this word does not seek earthly bread, being satisfied with the delights of the angels.

Moreover, all the words of the Holy Scriptures, by whatever ministry they are uttered, should be received as though they come from the mouth of God, because they do not belong to the one by whom they are properly narrated in a ministerial capacity, but to God, from whose mouth they proceed.

If a teacher should wish to insert anything different from what is found in this whole word, then, because it is not spoken from the mouth of God and does not subsist in love, it should be rejected like poison, like deadly venom. For divine things are not ministered through human offices; rather, hostile and fraudulent things are suggested through diabolical offices.

It should also be noted that he says, “Man shall not live by bread alone.” From this an indication is given that it is not the divinity but the humanity that is being tempted, so that, as I have already said, this entire temptation may be understood to have taken place externally.

Since words spoken back and forth are read there, it is more plausible that the enemy appeared in the likeness of a man, although the same Christ was everywhere visibly present according to his divinity.

Everyone is tempted in three ways, by which, after being drawn away and enticed, he is sometimes overcome: suggestion, delight, and consent. But Christ yielded to none of these. He neither admitted the desire that he did not possess through suggestion, nor gave consent, since there was no desire in him.

In us, the tinder of pleasurable desire, arising from the law of sin, struggles against the law of the mind. In him, however, the devil had nothing of the law of sin to which he could approach, from which he might at least arouse desires in him.

But in us, because the law of sin is present, the devil approaches it as though it were his own law and stirs up desires so that he may draw us toward delight. Therefore, even if nothing else, at least the poison of desires that is in us, by suggesting more of it, he inflames—although God’s mercy regulates him—in order both to exercise us and to make us victorious once we have been exercised.

For it is God who does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can endure. Otherwise no virtue would be sufficient to resist, if Christ’s grace did not help us, lest we be taken captive, oppressed by the weight of the flesh, into the law of sin.

Each person is tempted by his own desire. But he is then harassed more grievously when the crafty champion stirs up in us that same desire and adds frauds to entice us—frauds by which he wished to overthrow the Lord according to the order in which he had first overthrown the human being.

Again, he took him into the holy city and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple. We understand that city to be none other than Jerusalem, which at that time alone in the whole world was rightly called holy because of divine worship and the religion of the true God.

Therefore, at the Passion, many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep are said to have risen, come into the holy city, and appeared to many. It was called holy so long as justice and judgment dwelt in it; but afterward, when it had been filled with iniquity, it is proclaimed more wicked than Sodom, although up to that point it is called holy by the Evangelist from the name of its ancient peace.

Meanwhile, it must be asked how Christ is said to have fasted in the desert in order to be tempted, while here he is taken up in the holy city to engage in temptation—especially since Mark says more explicitly that he was in the desert for forty days and forty nights in order to be tempted by the devil (Mark 1:13). Was he tempted in the desert, or, after completing his fast and returning to Jerusalem, was what is read about the encounter of the battle accomplished there?

Some attempt to evade this question by asserting that Jerusalem and the entire region, because they had lost the knowledge of God, were rightly called a desert. But others, more correctly in my judgment, think that the first and the last temptation were carried out in the desert, while the middle one—which according to the historical sequence is believed to be the last—was completed in Jerusalem after Christ had returned from the desert.

For Matthew pursues the account of what happened not according to the historical sequence but according to the order of Adam’s temptation. Hence it is clear that one of them explained the matter according to the way it happened, while the other, changing the order of the temptations, taught it so that a figurative teaching might be woven into it.

Some, moreover, hold the opinion that, while Christ’s body remained in one and the same place, these things were shown to his mind in various places. This cannot be sufficiently approved, since all the events that took place are interwoven as having been made clear to bodily senses.

Nor is it surprising if he allowed himself to be carried bodily here and there, if perhaps the word “taken up” is to be understood in this way—he who allowed himself to be crucified by the members of that same devil.

But from this it is even more dreadful that neither the virtue that had been fulfilled, nor the holiness that had been demonstrated, nor the place dedicated to the Lord restrained the shameless enemy from engaging in battle. Rather, he arms himself again with greater terror in his powers, while being defeated by the frequent insignia of Christ’s virtues.

From here also he leads him to higher places and even to the summit of the temple, so that through this an indication might be given of how high he elevates each person whom he desires to hurl downward.

Boastfulness raises the mind above every height; by it, while people think that they are climbing to higher things through their own assumption of lofty deeds, they are thrust downward, already fallen. Who, then, among the human race, does not desire rather to preside and appear higher than to be subject and humbled?

For elevation draws almost everyone away, and all are lifted toward higher things by the devil’s pride. Therefore, wishing to display the teacher of virtues more clearly, he permits himself to be taken up to the pinnacle of the temple, which was the seat of the teachers. There, indeed, whoever is placed is tempted by empty glory and is often enticed into error concerning the Scriptures.

In Palestine there is a customary feature of architecture—which is also proved to have existed in Solomon’s temple—that the upper surface is flat throughout and around its circumference, in accordance with the law’s prescription of a surrounding railing, lest someone accidentally fall from it.

Among these structures, the seat of the teachers was raised upon the pinnacle of the temple, so that from there the teacher, placed as though in a more elevated position, might speak to the people. Yet what was provided for the usefulness of the entire office, the crafty persuader very often uses for the ruin of those who are preferred to others.

Some he raises even to undeserved honors in the breeze of their own inflation. Others, though rightly placed in authority, he tirelessly urges to fall and plunge themselves into vices. Yet although he can persuade, he cannot altogether make them fall.

No vice, therefore, devastates more those whom the honor of teaching raises to a higher position for instruction than empty glory. Through it he makes them inflated even by a good work of virtue, while, seeking not God’s glory but their own, they become empty.

Therefore the outstanding teacher is taken up to the pinnacle of the temple for temptation by a prudent dispensation, so that by this he might teach those who are established in a lofty position what they ought especially to avoid: namely, doing anything through empty glory, lest they incur the vice from which even those who appear sound often suffer most grievously.

The Prophet wisely guarded against this: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Psalm 113:9).

But those who applaud themselves and desire the favor of the crowd to be aroused toward them do not think about the gains of souls. They do everything for the sake of their own praise, and sometimes seek even what is above them, being carried about by every wind of boastfulness. They are not ashamed to appear as what they are not, nor to have proclaimed about them what does not at all belong to them. Thus, through the usurpation of lofty deeds, they fall into lower things.

“If you are the Son of God,” he said, “throw yourself down.” In every respect he wished to test whether Christ was the Son of God. He did not consider why Christ ought to throw himself down, except that he might entangle him in the bonds of boastfulness and thereby learn, at least by conjecture, what he feared—that he was the Son of God.

This voice is entirely fitting for one who strives to hurl everyone downward from a higher degree of merit. For what is more characteristic of him than to send everyone downward by persuasion from the lofty state of the mind? In this he sufficiently demonstrates his weakness to us and marks out his malice: the wretched man can harm no one unless that person has first cast himself downward.

“For it is written,” he said, “He has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways,” and so forth, until the passage reaches the place where he himself is shown to be trampled underfoot and all his magical arts are figuratively proclaimed to be utterly trampled by the power of the saints.

Like a crafty evader, he refuses to speak of his own fraud and trampling, but, speaking as though to a weak person, he earnestly promises the assistance of angels—not to strengthen him toward what is better, but to overthrow him toward what is worse. For he uses the Scriptures for this purpose, not to establish virtues but to introduce errors.

All who frequently adulterate the testimonies of Scripture and bend them to their own interpretations imitate him—not truly to favor the truth, but shamelessly to assert their reckless attempts to carry out their own will.

He was also the first to establish heresy in the New Testament by fraudulently altering such passages from the Old Testament, and he introduced idolatry, persuading people to worship him whom deceived worshipers of false gods also worship wrongly in images. In the Old Testament, when he spoke, he had already deceived the first Adam by overturning God’s judgment.

“Why,” he said, “did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” (Genesis 3:1). It is entirely clear that God had not said this. But, in order to undermine the mind, the devil exaggerates the weight of the command by lying.

Then, after the uncertain answers of unbelief, he alters God’s sentence of severity: “You shall not surely die. For God knows that on whatever day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

Thus the devil always uses examples from Scripture, not to correct but to deceive, even by falsely making grand promises. Hence comes, “All these things I will give you,” and also, “Your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

Therefore it is clearly established, as I have said, that all who fraudulently force the meanings of Scripture into conformity with their own purposes, who deceitfully weaken God’s severe commandments by flattering them away, and who make grand promises to sinners in order to soothe them into evil, are driven by that spirit which, by interpreting wrongly and weakening God’s sentence, delivered the first Adam over to death and desired to overthrow the last Adam by the same art of cunning, treating the Scriptures wrongly as though with divine authority.

Jesus said to him in reply: “Again it is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God.”

This command is often transgressed carelessly by many people of divided hearts: they offend God precisely by trying to test him. It should also be noted that the devil is said to tempt when he tries to persuade people from the Scriptures to accept something other than what is beneficial.

For, just as the Spirit is life in the divine Scriptures when they are rightly understood, so in those who cunningly apply them to their own interests there is immediately found a snare of error, a temptation, and the overthrow of the simple. Their speech, as the Apostle says, spreads like gangrene.

Then the Lord’s response is inflicted with sufficient force against the understanding of those who set snares and against the devil’s insolence: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God.”

By this he declares that no one ought to tempt the Lord as man, nor God according to his divinity, but that in temptations one should do whatever the effort of the human mind is able to do according to him. For the rest, if anything overwhelming threatens, it should be entrusted to God alone, almighty and for whom all things are possible—not by tempting him, but devotedly and confidently.

When Christ testifies that he is “the Lord his God,” this does not mean, as the Manichaeans deliriously claim, that one God belongs to darkness and another to light. Rather, it proves that there is one and the same God of darkness and of light, who, as Christ’s own testimony confirms, also rules over the one who is the abyss of all darkness.

But why is Christ tempted, if he ought not to be tempted by the devil? Clearly, it was because of the tempter’s presumption. And after the devil had cast down the first human being through his temptation, it was entirely just that Christ should not only be tempted but be tempted through those same passions, possessing the incorrupt image and likeness of God, through which Adam the first had also been tempted while he still remained in that inviolate image of God, namely through gluttony (*gastrimargia*), empty glory (*cenodoxia*), and pride.

Christ was not tempted through those things by which Adam was condemned after the transgression of the commandment and thereafter fell into his vice. Rather, he was tempted through the things by which Adam is read to have been tempted and overcome beforehand.

He was tempted by the vice of *gastrimargia*—gluttony—when Adam presumed to eat the forbidden tree’s fruit. He was tempted by *cenodoxia*—empty glory—when it was said to him, “Your eyes will be opened.” Finally, he was cast down by pride when it was said to him, “You will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

In these three vices, therefore, we read that the Lord and Savior was also tempted: by *gastrimargia*, when the devil persuaded him, “Tell these stones to become loaves of bread”; by *cenodoxia*, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down”; and by pride, when the devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory and promised, “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me.”

He was tempted by the same lines of temptation by which Adam had been attacked, and by his example he thoroughly taught us how we ought to conquer the tempter.

Therefore the one Adam and the other are both called Adam: the first, indeed, for ruin and death; the latter, the first for resurrection and life. And if you wish to examine everything carefully, you will find, as the Apostle says, that the first Adam was a figure of the one to come. Yet while the former slipped into ruin, the latter, coming in the likeness of sinful flesh, restored all things for the better through the same lines of temptation.

Thus the devil tempts Christ only through the same vices by which he had deceived the first Adam, supposing that this one too, being simply a human being, could be mocked in other respects if he perceived him overcome in the same matters through which he had cast down the earlier one.

That Luke transposes this order, then, is not due to ignorance but to a mystery. In both accounts, the truth of what happened is made evident, as is the order of Adam’s temptation; and, in addition, the arrangement is adapted morally to the remaining circumstances of the present time.

This is why Luke places avarice in the middle and pride last: because even to the end of life, after all triumphs of virtue, it does not cease to rage. In the statement that the devil showed Christ all the kingdoms of the world in a moment, the passion of *philargyria*—the love of money—is appropriately understood. In the statement, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down,” the persuasion of pride is rightly understood according to this passage.

Therefore, when *gastrimargia* could not overcome Christ, the devil omitted lust and the things that arise from gluttony and moved on to *philargyria*, which he certainly knew to be the root of all evils. Immediately defeated in this, he did not dare to impose upon him any of the vices that followed from it; instead, he passed to the final passion of pride, by which he knew that even the perfect could be assaulted.

In these three vices all the vices joined to one another lie slain. Therefore, seeing himself overcome at each stage of his temptation, the devil increases his frauds and sharpens his devices.

First he places stones before the hungry man, to test his power and break his self-restraint. Second, he prepares snares even from the divine writings, persuading as though from divine authority, in order to beguile. Third, as though defeated in himself, he lays all the assaults of vice and the weapons of his power and craft before Christ’s eyes, so that, if any evil should still be lacking in him, his mind, caught in the snares of blandishments, might be captured by an evil desire for worldly delights.

Here we must consider what we wretched people are going to do, in whom the poison of desire exists and the law of sin rules over all the members, so that each person is tempted when drawn away and enticed by his own desire.

Or what shall we do when the devil himself begins to inflame more fiercely the desires implanted in the flesh and—what is more serious—to blandish and seduce the mind more cruelly, as though with the authority of the divine Scriptures, in order to deceive it?

And what is still more disastrous is now understood: that he uses all the things in the world against us as his weapons. What, then, will the soul do amid such dangers? For there is nothing in the world except the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life. In these three expressions the Apostle comprehends every kind of temptation (1 John 2:16).

Therefore the Lord undertook to conquer all these things in himself without the contagion of sin, so that the soldier might learn what he should continually do together with the grace of God, and which recurring vices he ought to overcome in himself.

He is said to have taken him up onto a mountain so that, from that place, the mountain of Tyre, wounded by the mountain of God, might be signified more clearly—the mountain upon which every avaricious person is raised.

This does not mean that Jesus, inflated by the spirit of pride, was lifted to the place from which the devil himself had fallen. Rather, he is taken up above any mountain of the earth, so that it might be shown more clearly to what height the person is transported who is inflated by the heat of avarice.

Otherwise, he will by no means possess all the kingdoms of the world and their glory more richly unless he has been transplanted above the foundation of pride. For the truly humble glory only in the Lord.

The devil is said to have shown him all the kingdoms of the world—that is, all the things in the world that can be desired, in which the lovers of the world reign. Or the statement may be understood simply, as some wish, that, at the devil’s suggestion, the whole world was said to have been shown to Christ in a moment.

Nor is this surprising, since it is also said that the eminent man Benedict was suddenly shown the world in a sphere before he departed from the body. How much more could the entire world have been seen in a moment by the Lord Christ himself, who always sees all things together?

And rightly “in a moment,” according to what another Evangelist recounts, because everything that exists in the world is proved to be brief and momentary.

Yet it is not absurd to ask with what eye of vision the Savior looked upon their glory, lest—God forbid!—he be understood to have gazed upon it with the eye of desire, by which we, with the mind’s distorted vision, embrace whatever things are desirable.

But if this display of things took place in the mind, then it was certainly an aspect according to his humanity, like that by which physicians are accustomed to observe every kind of disease without any wound of injury, so that by this means they may heal their patients from those diseases and provide more diligently for the salvation of those who are not yet corrupted.

But the statement, “I will give you all these things,” descended from arrogance. The devil did not possess power over the whole world so that he could give all the kingdoms of the world; rather, he spoke in order to persuade Christ first to worship him, and thereby to make him fall before he hastened toward the avarice of riches.

The Apostle also calls avarice the service of idols (Colossians 3:5), because every avaricious person, wrongly persuaded, lies bent beneath the devil’s feet.

He answered him, saying, “Go back, Satan.” Thus Christ’s response gave the devil an appropriate outcome for his audacity. The devil immediately heard his fraud, by which he had been plotting against Christ, struck back in the name “Satan,” and, rightly defeated, deserved to be told to go behind him.

But “go behind” does not mean what was said to Peter, “Go behind me” (Matthew 16:23)—that is, “You are still opposed to my will; follow my examples.” Rather, it means: Go back, plunged by the perversity of your blindness into the abyss, from which you will never be able to extricate yourself; you who attempt by every means, through your frauds, to obscure the light will henceforth be unable to seek the things that belong to the light.

For it is written, he says, “You shall worship the Lord your God.” Here he clearly shows that Christ the man, as God and Lord, is to be worshiped, so that, setting aside all glory of human power and trampling worldly ambition underfoot, we ought to worship God alone—Christ the Lord—with the greatest earnestness. For every worldly honor not referred to God is proved to be the devil’s business. [Col. 0199B]

But where this statement occurs—“You shall worship the Lord your God”—is clear to all readers: it is in the Pentateuch. Through it, that strong-handed God is fittingly signified as about to fight against the monstrous enemy. He placed five stones—that is, the five books of the divine Law—in his shepherd’s bag; with one of them, namely Deuteronomy, through which the New Law is figured, he struck back at his adversary, and, when the enemy had been slain, brought victory to us all: “You shall worship the Lord your God,” he says, “and him alone you shall serve” (Deut. VI, 13).

It is as though he were saying: “You, therefore, are not to be worshiped, although you have already deceived many by the false snare of error; rather, you ought rightly to worship the Lord—the Son, God the Father, and the Holy Spirit alone, who is the one God—and, though deceived in whatever way, serve him alone.” From this it is plainly gathered that, whether he wishes it or not, he obeys the same commands and serves, although unwillingly compelled. God makes just use of this forced service of his wickedness, so that all things serve the writings of the one God and nothing escapes—even what is wickedly lost to itself under the ruler’s command. [Col. 0199C]

For when he says, “You shall serve him alone,” that service belonging exclusively to God alone is rightly expressed—the service owed to no one other than God, which the Greeks call λατρείαν (*latreian*). Hence also the term “idolatry,” since the worship owed to God alone is offered to the devil through images. But that service which signifies ordinary service is more distinctly called δουλεία (*douleia*) in the same language. [Col. 0199D]

It is therefore rightly understood that he likewise spoke of that worship when he said, “You shall worship the Lord God,” which is owed to the Lord alone. For although we read that human beings and angels were worshiped by holy Fathers, we must not suppose that this was the worship by which it is right to worship the one and unique God. Therefore we must take the greatest care lest either this worship be diminished in the heart or, through it, the devotion of one who serves and worships God be altered—so far, that is, that the reverence shown to angels and human beings in common service should exceed what is fitting.

It is certainly proper to pray to God for his own sake, as God, and to serve him as Creator by his creature. But an angel or a human being is to be revered, as is fitting, not for that person’s own sake but for God’s sake, so that God may be revered in them, since they themselves are believed to have been made worthy of reverence by him. Otherwise they are not to be worshiped at all, insofar as they are not true gods. They are indeed to be included in prayers; nevertheless, they are not to be worshiped as though they themselves were adored as God. They have been made worthy of reverence on account of God. Let the Lord simply be loved in them, for whose sake they too, being loved by us, are most devoutly venerated. [Col. 0200A]

But if anyone in any respect falls away from this rule of the Catholic faith—whether by despising the saints and failing to pay them their due reverence, or by preferring them to God and setting them up as gods, although they are not what God is—he will wander exceedingly far from the religion of the true faith. The Apostle also urges us to serve one another through charity, according to that common service of the love of Christ (Gal. V, 13). Elsewhere he likewise admonishes servants not to please their masters merely outwardly, but to serve as servants of the Lord (Eph. VI, 6). And, as the blessed Apostle Peter says, servants ought to serve with all fear not only the good and gentle but also the difficult (*dyscoli*) (I Pet. II, 18), so that Christian religion may in every respect be shown to be devoted to God in all things and blameless. [Col. 0200B]

How exceedingly wretched, too, is mortal humanity, which is obscured by such great darknesses of vice and, walking along a deviating path far from the fairest rule of holy religion, is assailed on every side by sins. Thus those who rule do not fear to harass their subjects with tyrannical force, nor can those who are compelled by their condition to be subject obey their superiors without fear of punishment. Since neither group regards God as the one who stands between them, both depart from the true justice of faith through the wickedness of their conduct. [Col. 0200C]

For true justice is to show each person, as is fitting, the honor due to that person’s right, whether in hardship or despite the wickedness of character. Therefore, when it is said to the devil, “You shall worship the Lord your God,” the command is not superfluous. Christ knew well that the devil would not fulfill this duty of devotion; nevertheless, he speaks according to the sentence of due reciprocity, in order to show, by contrast with what the devil was plotting, what he himself more rightly ought to do, since his own perversity has made him savage toward every work of holiness. It is not unjust to command anyone to render what it is just for that person to offer.

And so, although the devil has been deceived by his own vice of pride, nevertheless, through the words “You shall worship the Lord your God,” it becomes clear that he is subject to the dominion of his Creator. But one may ask whether such words ought to have been brought against him from the authority of the Scriptures—Scriptures given through Moses solely for human instruction and the teaching of right conduct—as though they were commandments addressed both to him and to the other spirits. Was it written for his instruction: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God,” and “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve,” especially since through Moses the teaching of instruction was given not to him but to the people? [Col. 0200D]

It therefore seems more probable that, contrary to what some suppose, the devil was not shown by divine authority that the Lord ought to be worshiped. Rather, the Lord, having assumed the form of humility, set out the way for those returning to their homeland and opposed the adversary’s arrows with the shield of the commandments, so that his followers might learn what they themselves should wisely do in their temptations. For if the Lord’s lucid command is brought against the clouds of temptation, then all the darkness of shadows must immediately be scattered like smoke. [Col. 0201A]

Thus, just as the Savior recalls the saying addressed to him, “Man does not live by bread alone,” so that, in his humanity, he might be illumined by the divine commandments and thereby instruct his own warriors, so also, “You shall not tempt the Lord your God,” and “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve,” are commandments suggested not to the devil but to himself, so that by these bundles of commandments he might drive away the darkness of snares; and, once repelled, the same snares might vanish from afar into nothingness. [Col. 0201B]

Then the devil left him. And behold, angels approached and ministered to him.

He left him when the temptation had been completed—not as though he would not attack him again, but, as the blessed Evangelist Mark says, “for a time,” later to assault him openly through death, by means of the hatred of the Jews. We said that the temptation was completed, not as though the devil had completed what he attempted in order to overthrow Christ, but because, having exhausted every art of tempting against him and finding nothing further to do, he abandoned him.

For the activity of any art is completed when whatever that art, according to the capacity of the matter, has prescribed for carrying out has been completed, even if the practitioner does not attain what he intended. For example, an orator or one of the physicians does not complete the work of his office only when the one persuades or the other heals; rather, the work is rightly said to be completed even when the circumstances of the matter or of the persons do not allow completion, provided that whatever the art itself was able to contribute has been carefully applied to the situations and persons involved. [Col. 0201C]

Thus, when the devil perceived in himself that the expertise of his art had been exhausted, he is said immediately to have left Christ, because he had absolutely nothing further to do. For first he had tempted him through the desire of the stomach, which is the root of all evils; then through empty glory, which is the characteristic of the proud. According to the testimony of the Apostle, pride is proved to be the beginning of every sin, and that form—vain glory—is plainly and unmistakably recognized as one of its species.

Therefore, if desire is the root of all evils and pride the beginning of every sin, the temptation is rightly said to have been completed when the origin of all evils and the beginning of sin were entirely overcome and crushed. For the world too, which is condemned by the Lord as lying in the evil one, has no other temptations than those he set before Christ: the desire of the flesh, which is in our members; the desire of the eyes, which is continually generated outwardly; and the pride of life, which grows through its arrogance both inwardly and outwardly. [Col. 0201D]

The temptation is therefore rightly said to have been completed when, through the authority of the Scriptures, every kind of temptation had been repelled and the defeated enemy had finally succumbed. “And behold,” he says, “angels approached and ministered to him.” [218]

They approached, certainly, not as though they were coming to him for the first time, but as though they had long watched from afar the contest of their Creator, in the assumed form of a human being, against the enemy of the human race. If we, as the Apostle says, have become a spectacle to the world and its angels (I Cor. IV, 9), then they watched with far greater reverence that contest in which God, as man, fought for all. In him we too conquered, because we too were in him, for whom he became man. [Col. 0202A]

The angels stood at a distance so that Christ would not appear to have conquered with their protection, or at least to have needed their assistance. But once that enemy had been defeated and departed through the power of Christ’s single combat, the army of angels—like servants prepared for the service of a king, who had long contemplated his triumph from afar—approached devotedly and ministered in attendance.

Now, the fact that he fought signifies the assumption of our humanity; but the fact that they ministered to him proclaims the privileges of divinity in him. Yet in both there is one Christ, and the examples of instruction are more fully commended in him. For just as the warfare of our entire religion is set forth in this contest, so in the service of the angels the more glorious reward of our service in the future is taught. [Col. 0202B]

For after the triumphs, through this ministry of eternal life the true refreshment of the blessed is signified, where not only the angels, whose love burns without weariness, but also the Lord himself, passing among the saints, is proclaimed to minister to them with the clarity of light. Therefore, whoever wishes later to be refreshed with him by service of such great honor must first, while stationed in the warfare, learn—strengthened by his help—to carry his contest through to the end. For no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully. [Col. 0202C]

When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee. And leaving the city of Nazareth, he came and lived in seaside Capernaum, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali. “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations,” and what follows.

John also reports that Jesus, when invited with his disciples to a wedding at Cana of Galilee, performed a sign of his divinity by turning water into wine: “This,” he says, “Jesus did as the beginning of signs in Cana of Galilee, and he manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him” (John II, 11).

But why, when he heard that John had been handed over to prison, did he withdraw into Galilee? This is very easily understood if the truth of the matter is carefully considered. John incurred the danger of death only because of the Gospel of the kingdom and the justice that comes from the Gospel, which he preached. Christ, however, who was about to preach the justice of the truth more fully and perfectly, necessarily withdrew for a time, lest, before the time of his Passion arrived, the Jews—always friends of unbelief—should add murder to murder and thereby expressly deny the martyrs a refuge for fleeing for a time during the period of persecution. [219] [Col. 0202D]

He withdrew for a time so that his followers might be given an opportunity to flee during persecution, according to the saying: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. X, 23). This was not because of fear, but so that he might become an example and instruction to believers.

Before he went into Galilee, several events connected with John are inserted which the other Evangelists omitted. From this it is understood that some days intervened during which the events he inserts took place. For ecclesiastical tradition maintains—although some have said that the Lord was baptized on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, so that he might be believed to have been reborn on the same day on which he was born, and others assert that the spiritual circumcision was celebrated on the very day on which the bodily circumcision had been fulfilled—that he underwent baptism on the eighth day before the Ides, when it is now celebrated. From there, as John had already related, he was led into the desert. [Col. 0203A]

After that period had been completed, and after some days had intervened, while John had already been shut up in prison, Jesus withdrew into Galilee and then came to live in seaside Capernaum. There, when he began to preach the Gospel amid dazzling miracles, John, still in prison, heard of Christ’s works and sent two of his disciples. They were told that miracles were already being performed and that the Gospel was being preached to the poor. Catholic teachers of Christ hand down that this preaching began on the Kalends of May. [Col. 0203B]

From this it is plainly established that Jesus did not, as some wish, fast and then begin to preach after a year; rather, in one and the same year he was baptized, fasted, and then, after an interval, began to preach.

From that time, after Jesus came to Capernaum, he began to preach that the Gospel of the kingdom had drawn near, so that what had been spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled:

“Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali,  
way of the sea, beyond the Jordan,  
Galilee of the nations:  
the people who sat in darkness saw a great light;  
and for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death,  
light has risen” (Isa. IX, 1–2).

Therefore the Seventy rendered this passage: “Drink this first; act quickly.” For the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali were the first to see Christ’s miracles, so that they might be the first to drink the potion of faith, since they were the first to see the Lord performing miracles.

Accordingly, Matthew, setting down this testimony according to the Hebrew text, says: “At the first time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened of the burden of sins,” because the Savior first preached the Gospel in the regions of these two tribes.

Hence also in the Psalm: “Bless God the Lord from the fountains of Israel” (Ps. LXVII, 28). There is Benjamin, the young man—namely the Apostle Paul—in an ecstasy of mind. Thus he says elsewhere: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God” (II Cor. V, 13).

“The princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali,” because in these tribes there were villages from which the holy leaders, the Apostles, arose. And finally, “the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations, was burdened.” [Col. 0203C]

Galilee of the nations is so called because it is proved to have consisted of two regions. One borders upon and lies near the Tyrians; this is now called Galilee of the nations. There Solomon gave Hiram, king of Tyre, twenty cities in the allotment of the tribe of Naphtali. The other is said to lie around Tiberias and the lake of Gennesaret, in the tribe of Zebulun. That the Lord dwelt in both regions is proved by the proximity of their cities.

Here, however, because of the figure of those who were to be called from the nations, the region that is called Galilee of the nations is rightly mentioned. The Evangelist also omitted the words that occur at the beginning of the prophecy, just as in the middle he omitted the statement that the way of the sea would finally be burdened. For there it belonged to the prophecy also to lay the foundations of the history close beside it; here, however, it was enough to suggest that from the history itself the Lord’s coming and the beginning of his preaching would be revealed with the clarity of light.

“The people,” he says, who walked in darkness—that is, in the gloom of error and the blindness of ignorance—“saw the light” of Christ preaching. And not just any light, but that great light which says in the Gospel: “I am the light of the world.”

How carefully God’s mercy is displayed: those were first lifted from the yoke of the slavery of sin who, as the Hebrews relate, were first captured by the Assyrians and led from the whole people of the Jews into hostile land. Afterwards, not only the two tribes but also the remaining tribes who lived beyond the Jordan and in Samaria were led into captivity. [Col. 0203D]

This is what Scripture now says: the people who were first led into captivity and who lived in the darkness of vices themselves, through God’s mercy, were the first to see the light of the Savior’s preaching; and afterward the Gospel of salvation was spread among all the nations. [221] [Col. 0204A]

Hence it follows:

“For those dwelling in darkness and the shadow of death, light has risen.” They thought that the difference between death and the shadow of death was this: death belongs to those who, together with the works of death, are buried in hell, overcome by death. But the shadow of death belongs to those who sin but have not yet been entirely expelled from this life; rather, they are awaited by the divine judgment so that they may be converted to what is better. [Col. 0204B]

Therefore, if they wish, they can practice repentance and, with the Lord’s grace assisting them, reach the true light as quickly as possible, so that thereafter they may not remain in darkness. For this reason they are given respite: so that they may not reach the true darknesses, which elsewhere are called the outer darkness, but, having emerged from the inner darknesses of sin, may be light in the Lord.

For the darkness of sins is proved to have no other body than perpetual death. Consequently, they are sometimes called the shadows of death: just as shadows never exist without a body, so sins never exist without death. Hence it is written: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII).

Therefore, whoever wishes to escape death must, insofar as is permitted, have no shadow of death within himself. For this reason let him cease from sin and cling wholly to God, so that he may be light in God. For if he clings to the light, he is enveloped by no darkness of sins; just as, where this visible light is present, no place is darkened by gloom, but everything, illumined for the better, shines in the light and is restored to the beauty of its splendor. [Col. 0204C]

From that time Jesus began to preach and say: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” [Col. 0204D]

The Judge therefore proclaims the same message that the herald of truth had proclaimed earlier, and does so most fittingly at once, so that it may be shown that he is none other than the one who had formerly sounded forth in John’s voice. Thus John himself says: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John I, 23).

And what does “I am the voice of one crying” mean except: “I am the voice of him who cries out in me—Christ”? For although he sounded outwardly through a voice, inwardly it was Christ, the Word, crying out. John is rightly understood as the voice of this one who cries, since he is shown to be the instrument of the Holy Spirit, through whose inspiration the Word who was in the beginning with God is revealed to the faithful by John’s voice. [222] [Col. 0205A]

John did not speak anything from himself; rather, the one who moved him to speak was speaking everything within him. Therefore he appropriately declares himself to be Christ’s voice. Yet he confesses himself to be the voice of one crying rather than of one speaking, so that Wisdom herself may be understood to cry out in him—the Wisdom of whom it is said in Solomon: “Wisdom cries aloud outside; she gives her voice in the streets” (Prov. I, 20).

She stands upon the highest and lofty summits above the roads, in the midst of the paths, beside the gates of the city, so that she may be heard everywhere and none of the foolish may excuse himself on the grounds of ignorance. At those very gates she speaks, saying: “O men, I call to you, and my voice is to the sons of men.” [Col. 0205B]

This voice was John, in whom the Wisdom of God the Father, crying out, said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” And so that it might become clearer that he himself was the one who had formerly cried out through John, Christ also had to repeat at the beginning of his own preaching the message that John had proclaimed in the office of herald, so that by his works he himself might shine forth more clearly—the one who had previously cried out through John’s voice.

And if we pay careful attention, Christ was not only in John; in all who, from the beginning, spoke anything by divine inspiration, the very Wisdom of God was a cry. Nevertheless, although Christ cried out in others too, John alone obtained, by the privilege of his merits, the special character of the voice, so that through him the present Word might be recognized—the Word that others had announced long before. [Col. 0205C]

There can be nothing intermediate between voice and word: as soon as the voice has sounded, the present word is perceived. So also no other intermediary is admitted between John and Christ. As soon as John is shut away in prison, Christ is proclaimed in the world through mighty works.

Thus, when the voice began to cease, the Word that was substantial to all, remaining inwardly in the mind for understanding without the noise of a voice, began to grow clear and to explain himself more fully. John, when he had completed the office of the voice, ceased to be heard any longer in the world; Christ, the Word, once received in the heart of each person, remained more firmly.

Therefore the first thing heard from the Word ought to have been nothing other than what the herald had previously announced in the office of the voice, so that whatever faith had conceived through the experience of hearing the voice might resound in its entirety in the Word. [Col. 0205D]

John also held the figure of the Law and the Prophets. When these ceased, the Gospel of Christ was consequently announced. And if you examine the matter more closely, you will perceive that the whole Scripture of the Old Testament was nothing other than the voice of one crying. Therefore, whoever does not obediently attend to the holy Scriptures, or at least to their teachers, insolently despises not them but the one crying out in them.

Knowing that he bore their figure, John said, “I am the voice of one crying,” because in a certain sense he was the fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets. The Law and the Prophets continued until John; in John, however, the voices of all were brought to completion. Thereafter, once the voice had been emptied, only the Word that had sounded inwardly from the beginning of the Law and the Prophets was rightly perceived without uncertainty, by itself. [Col. 0206A]

But if the Savior proclaims the same things that John had previously proclaimed in the spirit of prophecy, he shows himself to be the one whose voice John confessed himself to be, and the one whom the entire order of the Law and the Prophets, running on until John, had long ago announced as coming into the world.

“Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” The kingdom of heaven is rightly understood here as the Gospel, or certainly as Christ himself, the salvation of the world. Formerly he threatened sinners from afar; now he is said to have drawn near through the reconciliation of those who were about to believe. [Col. 0206B]

For how could he have been made nearer to the human race than by deigning to become, without sin, what we ourselves were? “The Word,” says the Evangelist, “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14). That is, he became what we ourselves were and dwelt with us.

The kingdom is rightly called the kingdom of heaven because he himself is that kingdom through which and in which all the saints, destined to reign eternally in the heavenly places, are already gathered here each day through faith into his body.

As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea. They were fishermen. And he said to them: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men.” [Col. 0206C]

This appears to sound very much at variance among the Evangelists. For Matthew relates that Jesus came and lived in seaside Capernaum, and afterward, while the disciples were fishing, called them from the boat to follow him. John, however, gives a quite different account: after the miracle of the water changed into wine, Jesus descended into Capernaum, together with his mother, his brothers, and his disciples; and there, he says, “they remained not many days” (John II, 2). [224] [Col. 0206D]

It is genuinely uncertain whether Peter and Andrew and the two sons of Zebedee had already attached themselves to him, so that the Evangelist is speaking here by recapitulation, as though this had happened in some way before Jesus descended to Capernaum to live there. Or whether his disciples are said to have descended with him into Capernaum in the same sense in which they are already read to have been called disciples when they went with him to the wedding at Cana of Galilee.

They were not already disciples at the time when they are said to have believed in him because of the miracle that took place; rather, they are called disciples in view of what they were destined to become. For even before Christ came to Cana of Galilee, Andrew is said, according to John, to have brought his brother Peter to him and to have stayed with him for a single day. This was not yet so that they might cling to him as disciples, but so that, through experiencing such great sweetness, they might more eagerly taste the nourishment of life from the beginning. [Col. 0207A]

For this reason I think that Matthew spoke by recapitulation, especially since he did not insert his customary expressions—“then,” “afterward,” “later,” or anything of that kind to indicate continuity—but simply said: “As he was walking beside the Sea of Galilee.”

Nevertheless, whichever of these possibilities is considered more likely makes no difference to the faith, provided that the event is believed to have happened in every respect as the Gospel narrates it.

The Sea of Galilee is more expressly called this because of its proximity to the same city, just as this same sea is elsewhere called by many names according to the surrounding lands: the lake of Gennesaret, or the pool, or that of Tiberias, or the lake of the Saltworks.

“He saw,” he says, “two brothers.” This was done with sufficient providence. Just as in the Old Testament Moses and Aaron were called to liberate the people from Egypt through signs of faith, so Peter and Andrew were brought forward by grace to transfer souls by fishing from the world to the heavenly Jerusalem. [Col. 0207B]

Their brotherhood according to the flesh ought to suggest to us that all who are in Christ, according to the regeneration of life, should be true brothers to one another through faith and be called brothers by name.

Thus the text says plainly: “He saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter, and Andrew.” Peter was not first called by this name here, but afterward, when he confessed Christ as the Son of the living God. Then, I say, it was said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church” (Matt. XVI, 18).

Here, then, the Evangelist certainly called him by anticipation, especially since, by the time this Gospel was written, this name had already been given to him from the rock. Some, however, assert that he was called by this name earlier, when Andrew brought him to Jesus, before Jesus went into Galilee, when Jesus said to him: “You shall be called Cephas,” which is translated “Peter” (John I, 42). [225] [Col. 0207C]

But here it seems to be signified, through another obscure designation, as though by a promise, what was to come; nevertheless he had not yet been openly called by this name, as afterward he deserved to be called through faith. For it is one thing to promise, through foreknowledge, what is to come, and another to fulfill by grace what was foreknown.

Christ is rightly said first to have called Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew, from among all the others, to the grace of his discipleship. Simon is interpreted as “obedient,” while Andrew is said to mean “strong” or “manly.” From this it is clear that whoever wishes to pass over to the discipline of Christ must first cultivate the virtue of obedience and then persevere manfully, strong in courage, to the very end. [Col. 0207D]

For no one can worthily enter this warfare of Christ without obedience. If a manly spirit and the virtue of strength are lacking there, no one can endure the contest even unto the death of the cross. Therefore divine providence first called these two brothers to the faith. For these two virtues are true brothers to one another, and through them each person appears to cultivate and fulfill Christ’s contest.

Since the first human being was disobedient in paradise, it was fitting that Simon, whose name means “obedient,” should first take up the journey again on the path of return. The divine word immediately and sufficiently suggests through this example how obedient a person ought to be, saying: “He saw two brothers casting their nets into the sea.” [Col. 0208A]

By saying “casting their nets,” it indicates that they were occupied with the affairs of the present life. But when it immediately adds that they left their nets and followed him, it signifies their perfect obedience. Through this, true imitators of Christ may learn to leave behind whatever is imperfect in themselves, to follow with the swift step of obedience the voice of the one commanding, and to follow him who says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John VI, 8).

“And he called them,” he says. God’s calling, however, is not always in the divine Scriptures according to the election of grace, nor is there one calling common to all. Nevertheless, whoever is called by God through whatever calling must remain in that calling. Otherwise it is believed to do more harm, because the person has made himself unworthy of his calling by beginning, like Judas, to become an apostate.

Judas too was called an apostle, not according to the predestination of life, but according to that saying: “Many are called, but few are chosen.” For more are called, but few are chosen. Sometimes even those come to the faith who do not attain the number of the elect; although here they are mingled with the faithful through their confession, they do not deserve to be counted among the faithful because of their reprobate life. [Col. 0208B]

Those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, these he also called. And those whom he called according to this calling, these he also justified. He first foreknew them, then predestined them; and those whom he predestined, he also called according to the election of grace. Therefore, after they have been justified, they are glorified, as they had been foreknown, through the gift of perseverance, and afterward, for this reason, they are crowned forever. [Col. 0208C]

No one, then, who looks back from his calling is fit for the kingdom of God. No one who lives sluggishly within it can persevere with the fruit of reward unless he is restored again to good works. Otherwise the reference is not to the calling according to which the elect are called, but altogether to that calling by which Judas was called, and by which many come daily, very many of whom do not remain; only a few, of course, are chosen.

The few are counted and chosen, while the many are multiplied upon the sand and cast outside, because they are under a curse and are judged reprobate. “I will multiply,” God says to the woman, “your conceptions and your sorrows” (Gen. III, 16); this multiplication comes from the curse.

Otherwise, if it did not come from the curse, those who are called would not have been multiplied upon the sand, but would have been counted like the stars of heaven, and each would praise the Lord in life and conduct according to the calling by which he had been called. [Col. 0208D]

These two brothers are certainly affected by that calling, and therefore are later crowned through the gift of perseverance. I have said this so that each person may become accustomed, according to the particular character of his calling, to pursue works worthy of it. For those who are called according to the election of grace are not found worthy without the fervor of faith that works through love; nor are those who are not sufficiently chosen rejected except because of the sluggishness of their apathy and the merits of their vices. [227] [Col. 0209A]

Therefore it follows that an apostle must possess the works of a true apostle, and a martyr must be sustained by the love of a martyr. A bishop or presbyter, and then the other ministers of Christ, must each, in his own degree, fulfill his calling through works of faith.

Let none of them measure himself against one who is below him; rather, let him devote himself faithfully to his own calling, lest he either fall from it as unworthy or, growing sluggish through the disease of vice, be lulled into death by lethargic sleep.

Moreover, no virgin, unless she possesses the works of virginity, and no widow or married woman, unless she has adorned herself with the works of her calling, will escape being cast down to the lowest place among the foolish. Unless perhaps they quickly awaken and, according to the saying of the Apocalypse (II, 3), see from where they have fallen and restore their former works—that is, the works they ought previously to have done—by supplying what was lacking through divinely restored repentance. [Col. 0209B]

Therefore let no one applaud himself—not a cleric, not a monk, not any person called holy. Unless they possess the works of their calling, all are assigned either among apostates or certainly among hypocrites.

In these two men whom Christ first calls to the faith there is a figure of all those who, casting their nets from the depths of carnal affairs, are daily called back. Thus, while casting their nets into the sea, all are occupied simultaneously with their own affairs, as each person spreads the net of his desires after the empty profits of the world, like an eager fisherman. No one now lives free from worldly gain and alien to the nets of desire.

Perhaps the two are called together because the whole human race consists of soul and flesh. Thus the soul, the manly portion, is the first to recognize God and leads the flesh, obedient to itself, to Christ; and together they follow until each person is found worthy of his own calling. [Col. 0209C]

“Come after me,” he said, “and I will make you fishers of human beings.” This calling appears in a certain sense to be general, since whoever has been called by any vocation is still advanced so that he may hasten after him who is the way. For whoever is called by any circumstance is urged to come to Christ, without whom no one reaches the homeland. Yet while a general command is given to them, a particular gift is promised: “I will make you,” he says, “fishers of human beings.” The purpose of the occupation is changed, not the function of fishing. The nets are changed into teaching, and desire into love of souls.

The sea is the world; the ship is the Church; the fish are good and wicked human beings, tossed about in the waves of the world. Concerning this sea David, singing, says: [Col. 0209D] “This sea, great and wide, with its spacious reaches; there are creeping things without number” (Psalm 103:26). These creeping things are indeed offered on the sheet lowered before blessed Peter from the four beginnings [or four corners] (Acts 10:11). They are offered so that Peter may learn, without distinction, to draw all people out through the four beginnings of the Gospels, and to transfer them from the waves of this world into his own body, dead to the world. And it is lowered from heaven for this reason: so that he may understand that what will be his work by office has been granted to him from heaven by the grace of God. Hence it is expressly said: “I will make you become fishers of human beings.” Otherwise, one of the teachers labors in vain if he has not been made by God to be effective; for “neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth.”

[Col. 0210A] But they immediately left their nets and followed him. They followed him not only in the affection of their character and in imitation of his teaching, but also in the movement of their feet and in obedience born of love. In them, indeed, the pattern of all believers is given: if anyone wishes to be Christ’s disciple, let him renounce everything that he possesses, and even leave himself behind; then let him take up his cross and follow him. For whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked.
