But how Peter left the boat, which afterward is called Simon’s own and is later taken up again by him for fishing, is rightly asked—unless the meaning is very simple: what had previously been said was no longer understood as arising from a desire to possess it and resume it for his own use, but rather from the duty of obedience and the right of companionship, [Col. 0210B] so that through this sacrament the mystery of the divine work might be woven. Nothing is possessed without being preserved with desire and carnal attachment. Hence, when he had left something outside Christ to love, or thereafter desired anything within the world, he gloried in saying: “We have left everything and followed you; what then will there be for us?” (Matthew 19:27.) He rightly leaves everything who does not even reserve himself for himself, but spends himself entirely for the love of Christ.

It follows that, proceeding from there:

“He saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, with Zebedee their father, mending their nets.” From the choice of these men also the future work of their office is revealed, and the entire integrity of the four-sided structure [Col. 0210C] of the holy preachers is most fully represented by these four fishermen. Beyond the historical truth—for this also happened in their case—the number of future Evangelists is prefigured by them. Through their skill in teaching, by means of the rudiments of the four Gospels, the souls of the reborn are drawn from the waves of the world into the light of heavenly life.

God’s provident dispensation also foresaw this order of the holy calling in such a way that through them it prefigured in a particular instance what was to happen universally. Thus four fishermen are rightly said to have been chosen at the beginning, because the sheet lowered from heaven by its four beginnings [or corners], in which were all kinds of creeping things and four-footed animals, prefigured the net of the four Gospels, which was expressly to be lowered from heaven before the holy preachers. And therefore [Col. 0210D] four men are gathered, in whose number the remaining order of teachers would be symbolized, so that the four beginnings of the one net of the holy Gospel might, for fishing out the nations throughout the four-square seas of the world, be drawn safely by their four hands all the way to the shore of paradise.

How manifold and subtle, therefore, is God’s dispensation, which wisely orders everything in such a way that the truth of events is demonstrated by the narrative, while the mystical mysteries of doctrine are everywhere fulfilled in action. The holy teachers, contemplating these things conspicuously in the Holy Spirit, supply each detail by speaking wonderfully, so that the truth of the event may be disclosed in the discourse, and the deepest things, secretly hidden within the work, may shine forth.

Hence these four are chosen two by two, in [Col. 0211A] whose number the entire order of preachers is suggested. For charity, without which even martyrdom counts for nothing, is twofold; it is not granted to be possessed by anyone anywhere except in relation to another. For this reason not only the twelve, but also the seventy who were later sent, are likewise associated in preaching two by two, so that they might spread more abundantly the love of God and neighbor from the ancient and new sources of Scripture, both in the hearts of those who believed from the nations and in those who were reborn in Christ from the Jews, and might join earthly people to heavenly realities through grace.

These men alone are made four-sided by the mystery; the others, however, are joined with them by office, so that in God’s agriculture, each person, joined to the others under the yoke of twofold charity, might sow abundantly among the peoples by the plow of the word the seed of love for [Col. 0211B] God and neighbor, and so that all, prefigured by the four-sided net of God’s commandments, might together draw it to the shore in these men.

These four alone, therefore, are read as fishermen, so that, drawing the net of the commandments from the four parts of the world, they might transfer everyone together from the waves of darkness to the light that is Christ. Here, indeed, a marvelous exchange in the order of things takes place: those who formerly enclosed fish from life into death now bring back from death to life those who have been put to death in the flesh, through the waters. For they themselves could not have left what they were pursuing or abandoned their father Zebedee unless they had first died to the world.

Zebedee, indeed, is said to be interpreted as “fugitive.” Through him is rightly understood the person who, driven away from the light of truth by his own darkness, will [Col. 0211C] thereafter be unable to approach that conspicuous light of majesty, so as finally to recover from his evils. Wishing to persuade every badly formed soul to flee from such a father, the divine Spirit sings in the Psalm: “Hear, O daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 44:11).

James and John, therefore, leaving behind this father, together with the nets of desires—which they had been mending each day with various wicked longings—became sons of thunder, although until then, together with their father, they had been most fugitive servants. Hence one of them, James, is rightly interpreted as “supplanter,” because by the feet of the virtues he had crushed and overthrown the snares of vices, against which all who wish to escape the torments of death and grasp the life of faith through works [Col. 0211D] struggle.

To enable them to do this, they are first consoled by the grace of God, as by fraternal assistance. Hence the name John likewise appropriately sounds in Latin, from the Greek, as “grace of God.” For every supplanter of vices, placed in the contest, can overthrow the enemy from the opposing ranks only through grace, as through a brother’s aid. Therefore that fellowship must necessarily accompany our actions everywhere, unremoved, with the service of kinship.

Hence Paul also says: “It is not I who work, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10). For just as the virtue of obedience, expressed by Peter, cannot be brought to completion without the strength or manly courage of mind signified by Andrew, so vices, together with the author of their plague, cannot be overcome in combat without the grace of God.

[Col. 0212A] For this reason this square number of men properly consolidates the four-sided foundation of the holy Gospel, so that those who wish to draw the nets of the commandments throughout the world may possess these four virtues, without which no one who puts his hand to the plow can ever reach the crown of victory.

And to show how constant they must be in teaching, the blessed Evangelist immediately adds:

“Jesus went around all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and preaching the Gospel of the kingdom.” By this he clearly teaches how diligent a teacher must be in teaching. For laziness is wholly unsuitable to preachers; they must go around not merely part of the people over whom they are seen to preside, but the whole of them. Nor must they be preoccupied with worldly business. They must teach the doctrine of the present [Col. 0212B] commandments to those subject to the active life, and preach concerning the future to those perfected in the contemplative life, so that some may presently be trained in character, while others may be strengthened by hope of the future through greater instruction.

For contemplation is not climbed from childhood without the works of the active life, nor is the active life brought to fuller perfection without hope in God’s promises. Perhaps, therefore, Jesus is said to have gone around teaching and preaching because he opened both lives to believers by example no less than by speech, so that he might not benefit only a few, but might pour out abundantly upon everyone, without respect of persons, the grace of his calling.

He taught not just any monstrous tales, but things supreme and divine, lest he appear to be introducing the false fictions of the ancients into his own [Col. 0212C] teaching. Hence it is immediately and expressly added that he taught the Gospel of the kingdom. It is called the Gospel of the kingdom because he now permits those who belong to him to reign in hope, and in the future makes them both kings and a kingdom for God once they have obtained the realities promised. Whatever he now promises believers in the hope of forgiveness, he will fulfill through the gifts of grace.

“And healing,” he says, “every disease [Col. 0212D] and every infirmity among the people.” In these two terms he comprehensively includes every kind of illness. For what he here called “every disease and infirmity” he later divided into its individual species, one by one. Indeed, by restoring very many things in their proper places, and also by what he says here, he indicated that we should understand even those miracles of the Savior that have not been committed to writing, and permitted us to believe them by faith.

Some distinguish “disease” and “infirmity” in this passage by saying that disease pertains to the soul, while infirmity should be assigned to bodies. Or they say that disease refers to what the devil, having received power, had inflicted, while infirmity refers only to what a nature badly wounded through lack of balance had brought upon itself.

“And his fame,” he says, “spread throughout all Syria.” The fame that the Jews darkened by the envy of their blindness was gradually illuminating the nations and scattering the fragrance of his virtues through the whole province of Syria, which is not far distant from Galilee. Therefore they brought to him all who were ill in various ways.

It was fitting that the teacher of the high priests should be such that he also received an outstanding testimony [Col. 0213A] of praise from those who were outside. For the illnesses of character are reported more freely to a priest, and wounds are disclosed, when the reputation of his life and a salutary cure are proclaimed among the people.

Syria is interpreted as “sublimity.” The fame of virtues rightly reaches as far as Syria when the life of one’s merits is raised daily, through the growth of good works, to the higher summit of true praise. Thus our physician bore in the flesh the form of teachers; and therefore he heals inwardly all those afflicted by diseases and torments, casts out demons, and cures the lunatic and the paralytic. Through these benefits of his deeds, his reputation is spread even to those who are outside.

For fame does not profit without works of true praise, nor do works of salvation shine sufficiently before their hearers without a reputation [Col. 0213B] for good fragrance. Paul rightly exhorts this when he says: “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are holy, whatever things are just, whatever things are chaste, whatever things are of good report—if there is any virtue, if there is any praise—think on these things,” he says, “which you have learned and heard and seen in me” (Philippians 4:8).

In two words, I say, he summed up everything: “if there is any virtue, if there is any praise.” A good conscience belongs to virtue, while the reputation of one’s life contributes to praise. Without these, the form of a true priest is not commended.

The Lord heals not only souls inwardly, for whose sake he had come, but first also bodies outwardly through a visible benefit, so that they might approach the invisible realities of salvation more readily through faith. Otherwise, since bodies were soon to die, it would have been of little value to bestow salvation upon them [Col. 0213C] unless the power of faith were strengthened through the things performed outwardly. This was done so that they might recognize inwardly the one working before the eyes of their hearts, and, understanding by faith the human being whom they saw outwardly, seek within him the God whom they could not see.

The Savior’s preaching is therefore commended by many benefits, and faith is strengthened by mighty signs, so that the same person may be believed to be God and human. What extraordinary madness in the heretics, who either deny that he was truly human or, conversely, deny that he is one and the same God united from two substances! The flesh is continually shown to be both visible and capable of suffering, while God is openly declared in him through signs and mighty works.

Therefore he healed visibly outwardly and cherished invisibly within: showing himself to be God through miracles [Col. 0213D] and training character through discipline. He thus healed all the diseases of vices, sprinkling the sick with the teaching of wisdom and releasing those seized by torments through the medicine of faith, restoring them to health.

The epileptic and the paralytic are rightly understood as those whom idolatry bloodied at monthly intervals, and whom the disease of discord dissolved from every bond of charity. “Paralysis” in Greek means “dissolution.” Thus those are signified who suffer from the vice of being united with no fellowship of members in Christ’s body, and who, through the disorder of the body, are dissolved from all firmness of love. Although they may appear to live, they perceive almost nothing when they have been healthfully comforted by the hand of the tongue.

The lunatics, however, are so called according to popular opinion, not because they truly were moon-struck, but because, when the cunning enemy tormented them at one or another increase of the moon, [Col. 0214A] they were thought to be moon-struck, as though they were afflicted by the moon’s own impulse. Through its deceit it had brought this about: that God’s creature, being more atrociously defamed, might cause blasphemies to rebound upon the Creator.

“But he healed them all,” he says—that is, all those who had been brought to him from various places. From this it should be noted that he did not entirely omit the many miracles whose powers the other Evangelists reported more fully in other places by narrating them individually. Here, rather, we read in a brief summary that all were healed. Among them were certainly some of those whom Mark or Luke, inserting them in their sequence, described more fully elsewhere for another reason.

Jesus therefore went around all Galilee—that is, all the turning wheel [Col. 0214B] of the world, since Galilee is interpreted as “wheel.” Hence his fame reached as far as Syria, which signifies arriving at the sublimity of the faith of believers. Therefore they followed from Galilee, namely those who by the law of faith had migrated from vices to the beginnings of virtues.

They also came from the Decapolis, truly those who by faith had begun to fulfill the ten commandments. Hence these ten cities are placed together everywhere, because no one comes to Christ from only one of them unless he has kept the ten commandments of the Law together. If anyone offends against one of them, he has become guilty of all.

They also followed from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan: those, clearly, whom the vision of peace had illuminated and who had already learned to confess God with the confession of faith. They are rightly said to have come from beyond the Jordan because, [Col. 0214C] having crossed over through baptism, and entering the land of true promise as though from another region, they were already following Christ step by step in faith.

Hence:

**(Chapter V.)** “When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up onto the mountain.” The Son of God the Father, exalted, ascended above the high mountain so that he might teach them to seek the loftier heights of virtue. By the place he also signified not only the higher mysteries of moral life, but also that the holy Church of God should be raised to a higher level. Above this Church he himself presides as king and priest, not merely issuing judgments, but establishing everyone through his teaching.

For we read that it was written: “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his commandment” (Psalm 2:6). You hear, then, whoever you are who are present, Christ the high priest preaching above [Col. 0214D] Mount Zion. Consider him also as king, because from one and the same seat he teaches and judges, according to the institutions of his teaching, what profit each person brings from his talent and how much he advances through his work, so that at the judgment he may repay rewards to the obedient and punishments to the negligent.

Since he had come to teach believers the salutary commandments of life, it was fitting that he should ascend the mountain, so that he might show that from this same knowledge he would fully instruct, until the end of the world, the Church over which he presided—the Church that is called a mountain.

The order of the figures demanded that the power of teaching be commended mystically through events and times; supported by typological mysteries, it would be revealed more abundantly and invite those whom it had already raised [Col. 0215A] toward contemplation, through figures that taught universally, to ascend still higher.

The righteousness that he handed down to the perfected according to the arrangement of the times was indeed greater than that of the Pharisees, because he fulfilled the Law in all its parts. It was not human but divine righteousness, concerning which we read: “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God; your judgments are a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7).

For this reason it was fitting that he give it nowhere other than above the mountain, so that the height of the Churches—above which Christ, the teacher of truth, sat teaching—might raise itself to sublime things, and the streams flowing from the summit might more abundantly water the whole body.

Christ, therefore, is the true mountain, raised above all hills so that all nations may flow to him. Thus he takes the disciples away with him to a higher place, so that the mountains [Col. 0215B] themselves might first receive peace from the one who was higher, and then the hills from which the whole world is gathered might receive righteousness. That righteousness is indeed “like the mountains of God.”

It should be observed how everywhere the mysteries of doctrine overflow with mystical meaning. The crowd that followed him did not first reach the heights. For this reason, according to Luke, the Lord is rightly thought to have delivered another sermon with them in the plain (Luke 6:17), about which Matthew may have been silent.

Yet it can also be understood in this way: that he first ascended more prominently onto the mountain with the disciples, as though for the sake of prayer; then he descended and, at some elevation of the mountain resembling a plain, where the crowds could be present, delivered one and the same sermon that Matthew and Luke alike [Col. 0215C] recount.

But I think it more truthful to understand it as we have explained, since the Gospel also seems to sound more strongly in that direction. Hence the mystical meaning is more clearly displayed. For the one who examines the hearts of individuals undoubtedly knows to whom he should teach higher things more sublimely, and to whom lesser things more humbly, in particular places and times. Not everyone is capable of everything. Therefore the commandments are not established equally for everyone, although the eternity of life is one. For neither is the desire of all individuals one, nor is the reward equal for everyone according to their merits.

“And when he had sat down,” he says, “his disciples came to him, and opening his mouth he taught them, saying.” The disciples approach him because, already clinging to him in spirit, they drew near inwardly through faith. And he, opening his mouth, taught them.

The opening of the mouth [Col. 0215D] signifies the depth of the mystery. He therefore opens the door of his mouth so that he may pour forth the streams of the abyss. He opens the door of the treasuries so that he may distribute gifts to everyone. He himself had first opened the mouths of the prophets and filled them. He also opened his own mouth because grace came from him—the grace that had formerly poured over them.

Otherwise, if he had not opened the door of his mouth here, their utterances would have been marked as lies, because whatever had been promised throughout the ages was enclosed in him as though in a seal. Therefore, when he unlocked the mystical teachings of wisdom, he is rightly said to have opened his mouth, so that a river might flow from him as from one paradise, watering and renewing not only the Apostles but the whole Church throughout the ages.

“Blessed are the poor in spirit.” Here, then, is a new reality and an [Col. 0216A] ineffable proclamation. Nothing seems more contradictory than poverty and heavenly blessedness. Poverty, after all, is more commonly a condition of misery and the pressure of calamity. And mourning and persecution—what are they other than a kind of painful destruction in the present life?

We must therefore understand to whom blessedness is granted: to those who no longer live in this world. For to those living according to the world, these things are nothing other than the hardship of misery. It is therefore clear that they are called blessed according to that life in which they already live in faith, hope, and charity; although they do not yet possess it in reality, they are rightly regarded as blessed through the hope of attaining it.

Can someone to whom heavenly rewards are promised fail to be blessed in hope? The cause of this blessedness, therefore, is possession of the kingdom of heaven. The Lord ascended the mountain for this reason: so that, as though placed on high, he might give the commandments of heavenly law and divinely bestow the gifts of sacred blessing upon the disciples who were already leaving earthly things [Col. 0216B] and seeking heavenly ones, according to David’s song: “For the lawgiver will give blessings” (Psalm 83:7).

And to designate the grace of the Apostles more clearly, he adds: “They will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion.” It is plainly evident that on this mountain he gave blessings to the Apostles and laid out for them certain firm steps made of precious stones—he who long ago gave the Law to Moses on Mount Sinai.

There he wrote it on tablets of stone; here, however, [Col. 0216C] he wrote the New Testament, according to Jeremiah, concerning which he says: “I will write my laws in their hearts, and I will write them in their understanding” (Jeremiah 31:33). There he addresses them as servants; here, as sons. Hence he uses a wondrous beginning: there he begins with terror, here with blessedness. There he inflicts punishments; here he kindles desire, presents gifts, and promises rewards.

“Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” It should be noted that he does not say simply, without qualification, “Blessed are the poor.” We know that many lack possessions, but they cannot therefore immediately be blessed merely because they are poor. For it is not the necessity of poverty that makes someone blessed, but holy faith and the devotion of poverty.

He rightly signifies as blessed those poor who, despising the things of the world, die to this age in order to live for God, and are regarded as rich and wealthy before him. Concerning this poverty it is said in the Apocalypse [Col. 0216D] to the angel of the church of Smyrna: “Thus says the First and the Last, who was dead and lives: I know your tribulation and your poverty—but you are rich” (Revelation 2:8).

We must therefore understand poverty in every sense, since one of the Evangelists says simply, “Blessed are the poor.” This poverty clearly consists of two parts: the renunciation of earthly possessions and contrition of spirit.

Few are found to possess the one kind of poverty, which consists in renouncing earthly things. The other, which consists in contrition of spirit, can be possessed by all the elect. Through it, even those who appear to use earthly resources are believed to have renounced them, because they use them not for the enticements of the flesh but for necessary works of [Col. 0217A] piety.

Although some of the elect possess much money, they are nevertheless unquestionably shown to be poor because, as we said, they possess it not from carnal desire but from a purpose of piety and the prompting of necessity. Are those not poor who distribute all earthly things, not as their own but as another’s? Yet from this very poverty they become rich. For from the place where they distribute temporal money to the needy on earth, they gather eternal riches for themselves in heaven.

Paul’s saying can be applied to both kinds of people: “As having nothing and possessing everything” (2 Corinthians 6:10). Those who utterly reject earthly riches already possess everything, as though possessing nothing, because they hold heavenly riches through faith. Those who retain earthly riches for use or works of mercy [Col. 0217B] likewise possess everything, as though possessing nothing, because they hope one day to have the heavenly riches for their enjoyment.

Or, to speak of the latter group in particular, they possess everything, as though possessing nothing, insofar as they do not recognize perishable things as belonging to them for their unlawful desires, yet regard them as entirely their own for every useful purpose.

Let this suffice briefly concerning one kind of poverty among the elect; now let us speak of the other, which is indeed full of riches. He says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” They are poor not in clothing but in spirit.

The poor in spirit is the one who, even when doing good, always considers himself unprofitable. The poor in spirit is the one who, although he surpasses many in virtue and holiness, judges himself inferior to all in merit. His voice resounds in the [Col. 0217C] Psalms: “I am needy and poor” (Psalm 69:6). And again: “I am needy and in labors from my youth” (Psalm 87:16).

Such poverty is already richly rewarded with the kingdom, because God is believed to be its portion and inheritance. “Blessed,” says the Prophet, “is the people whose Lord is their God” (Psalm 143:18). Therefore, although those to whom worldly goods overflow are called blessed, by God’s judgment the poor in spirit are proclaimed blessed.

The poor in spirit are understood to be the humble and those who fear God. Just as the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, so poverty of spirit is placed as the first blessedness. For God does not despise a contrite and humbled spirit.

But those whom presumption of spirit inflates and pride stretches out [Col. 0217D] like wind are already, by the judgment of fear, painfully laid waste in this life. Those who are poor in possessions are also rightly regarded as blessed, because they neither desire to possess what they should not possess nor disdain to possess what they do have; or else, afflicting themselves, they give away what they possess to others as though they had nothing.

Whichever kind of poverty you understand, the Lord rightly promised the beginning of blessedness to those who are humble in understanding: they desire nothing except what common nature teaches, and they do not wish to raise themselves to any insolent height. Rather, they continually cultivate only the things that belong to fear and true humility.

Concerning such people the Prophet says in the person of the Savior: “The Lord has anointed me; therefore he has sent me to evangelize the poor” (Luke 4:18; Isaiah 61:1). And appropriately, as though according to his [Col. 0218A] office, he first promises these same people the reward of blessedness, because nothing was more fitting to their merit than to promise the kingdom of heaven to the poor of the present life. Thus those who have decided to follow Christ in poverty and submit to the yoke of servitude may happily possess the rich kingdoms of the future.

It follows:

“Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” Between “mild,” “gentle,” and “modest,” there appears to be no difference except in the words. Although each term is used as though it were proper to particular places, none of them is perfected without the others. Some, however, wish to distinguish them in this way: the gentle person harms no one; the modest person, though harmed, does not repay another in kind; the mild person bears all these things humbly and with equanimity.

But more truly, one and the same virtue is proclaimed not only by these three names; gentleness, sweetness, and other virtues of this kind build up this single quality, so that anyone may rightly be called meek according to the laws of virtue.

The meek person is not afflicted or wearied by anger, quarrels, contention, resentment, harshness of mind, bitterness of gall, or the envy [Col. 0218B] of desires. Rather, the simplicity of faith trains him through the Gospel commandments to endure every injury patiently.

This is a consummate virtue and a perfected possession of character. Concerning it the Savior says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew 11:29). If this were not the path of the highest perfection, the teacher of truth would never have commanded that it be learned especially from him.

Hence the Prophet, relying upon it, confidently says: “Remember, Lord, David, [Col. 0218C] and all his gentleness” (Psalm 131:1). Moses likewise had great grace with God from long ago precisely because he was meek. For the praise of his perfection it is said: “Moses was the meekest of all who dwelt on the earth” (Numbers 12:3).

Truly blessed is the virtue for which, on behalf of believers, not the earth subject to curses—which no human being possesses through meekness—but the earth of the living is granted as an inheritance. To the first human being it was said as a punishment: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19). But to the meek it is said that “they shall inherit the earth and delight in the abundance of peace” (Psalm 36:11).

I have therefore not spoken inappropriately in saying that this virtue consists of many parts, since great kinship of character reigns among the gentle, the meek, the humble, and the kind, whose life is rightly shown to be suited to the fellowship of good people.

This should not be considered insignificant, since Christ, chosen as the model of this teaching, offered himself as a teacher through outstanding virtue and declared it preeminent by the praises of his life. The spirit of piety is rightly joined to it, because piety toward the holy Scriptures [Col. 0218D] believes all their words. The meek person does not resist or dare to contradict whatever is announced in them. Rather, he yields to wickedness and steadfastly conquers evil with good.

How blessed is this ascent, and how orderly this dispensation of virtues! The first blessedness is contempt for the world, to which eternal things are rightly given if someone has first rightly despised worldly things. No one can attain the reward [Col. 0219A] of the heavenly kingdom if, pressed down by desire for the world, he has no freedom to breathe toward sublime things.

The order of merits is therefore proper: first, blessed poverty strips its followers inwardly of every stain of sin and the arrogance of pride. Then it frees them outwardly from every desire of the world, so that they may lay aside on every side the tunic of the first parent. Meekness also tempers their character, and the mind becomes gentle.

Otherwise, upon whom, Christ says, shall I rest “if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2.)

But no one can come to the heights of virtue who is not yet able to follow Christ when commanded at the first footsteps. It is impossible to ascend to the second step outside the proper order unless one has first grasped the first; and you will never be meek unless [Col. 0219B] you have first become poor in spirit.

How, when placed amid riches, cares and anxieties, quarrels and contentions—from which anger, strife, and hatred arise without interruption—can the mind be meek and gentle unless you have first cut off every occasion of discord? Yet the fuel of this fire is scarcely removed completely, and therefore this meekness is so often corrupted in us.

Hence how well—”

Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted—this is consecrated in the third place. For although we have cast away the things of the world and its corrupt ways, and, already following the glorious footsteps of Christ, have clothed ourselves in upright conduct, it remains for us to cleanse the accumulation of cracks through daily tears.

Blessed mourning is not always understood in one and the same way; and therefore future consolation does not arise from every kind of mourning—indeed, offense may arise instead. That mourning alone, therefore, is supported by blessedness through which, in all its parts, we meditate perfectly upon heavenly things. Its final part is to lament the stains of past sins; its middle part is to grieve keenly, through the affection of charity, over present failings and the miseries in which we are involved, as well as over the falls and calamities of others, and sometimes to mourn the dead as dead.

For it is certainly rare to find anyone who has no dead persons to lament—namely, his own sins or those of others. David shows from his own example how we ought to weep over the crimes of our sins, saying: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will drench my couch with my tears” (Psalm 6:7). Jeremiah, moreover, mourns the sins of others as his own in the Lamentations. Hence he says: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” (Jeremiah 9:1.) From this it is clear that, if we are members of one body, we ought to care for the wounds of others as though they were our own.

Samuel, moreover, mourned Saul, and Paul mourned many of those who had sinned previously and had not done penance. Daniel too is afflicted with excessive mourning on account of the sins of others. Therefore, in this valley of tears, among snares and enemies of ruin—since no one is free from misery—no one ought to be a stranger to weeping and the lamentation of the heart, if he does not wish thereafter to be without any effect of consolation.

Nevertheless, this mourning, still belonging to the lower of its two parts, arises from the lower waters, although no one who thinks rightly doubts that it somehow pertains to blessedness. Thus, by God’s gift, the grace of piety is bestowed, by which we can lament sins, mourn eagerly over the afflictions of the present, and, through the love of charity, make the miseries of others our own.

But that flood of tears which arises from the upper waters comes rather from desire for the heavenly homeland, when we remember that blessedness and, by a kind of understanding, inwardly experience the sweetness of its delight. Amid such lamentations this world is regarded as nothing but a prison, and the things that blaze within it with the splendor of beauty are judged to be nothing other than snares of the flesh. Hence the soul of the holy man refused to be consoled, and the delight of joy became the remembrance of God alone.

Yet one who is meanwhile refreshed by such tears rests upon Christ through hope alone, until at last he enjoys him by sight in the homeland. Thus, when this beatitude has been completed in its several parts, it either washes away the present filth of vices or kindles more ardently those who love the life to come. Since this virtue belongs to the third place because God the Trinity forgives sins, it is rightly consecrated there, so that vices may be released through the affection of love for him, and the contemplation of the future may be granted to those who knock after their tears.

The blessed are not called blessed because they weep and mourn amid miseries, but because, stripped of evils, they will be comforted with eternal joys, already satisfied with perpetual happiness. The cause of these beatitudes, therefore, is not the fruit of present things, so that we should be called blessed according to them, but the promise of future things, by which each person is made blessed by Christ. Indeed, the cause of so great a blessedness is Christ’s grace alone, together with the earnest struggle of labor.

## Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.

In this place the hunger for righteousness rightly follows, because the person who laid aside sins out of fear of God, corrected his conduct through an affection for gentleness, and also strove to weep over his offenses, mourning through desire and inflamed by love of the heavenly homeland, can no longer fail to hunger and thirst for righteousness.

Previously, while he was still oppressed by a serious illness, he could not hunger, because disgust with the good life drove away his thirst and hunger for righteousness. Righteousness is made complete through the virtues of many parts. It is, as it were, the genus of the other virtues, by which it appears to consist.

Righteousness, then, is to give each person his due. From this it is evident that it acts not only for itself but also gladly assists others; it prepares itself to be restored to God and to live in a common service with its neighbors. This virtue, moreover, is never fulfilled without the spirit of fortitude.

Therefore, prudent reader, observe carefully: each of these beatitudes, in order to be fulfilled, requires the assistance of an equal number of gifts. And in order to receive these gifts, we are taught by the Master of truth to ask for them in the Lord’s Prayer through seven petitions.

For when we pray, “Deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13), we say nothing other than that, through the spirit of fear of God, all inward swelling of self-exaltation and inflation of pride, as well as every harmful attachment to outward things, may be driven away, so that we may live blessedly under the spirit of poverty.

Thus the Wisdom of God the Father arranged everything, so that the virtue of blessedness might be received from the gift, and the gift of the Holy Spirit might be obtained through the prayer composed by him. No one, therefore, is gentle unless the spirit of piety has sprinkled him; and, so that this virtue may be preserved continually, we ask him: “And lead us not into temptation.”

Next, those who mourn are enlightened by the spirit of knowledge, so that we may know in what evils we are entangled and toward what homeland we ought to hasten as quickly as possible, sighing and mourning. But so that tears may benefit those who mourn, we ask that our debts be forgiven—the debts by which we are held—so that, having recovered our freedom, we may return to the Father securely and as quickly as possible.

But when hunger and thirst for righteousness are eventually to reach satisfaction, they must be supported by the spirit of fortitude, lest they grow weary on the way. We must continually ask for this; and, once supported, so that hunger may be nourished amid various weaknesses and satisfied in the homeland, we must pray: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 11:3).

Refreshed by such bread, we do not thirst for a harmful drunkenness, but for those things with which we are abundantly filled from the breasts of the Scriptures and by which, divinely inspired, we are refreshed through the sacrament of the body and blood. Yet these things too are not tasted without the grace of the Holy Spirit. For just as they are not understood without his grace, so neither are they worthily received without it.

Therefore the spirit of fortitude must be entreated, so that through it we may one day come, by hungering, to satisfaction. Otherwise, when we are satisfied in ourselves—or as though from ourselves—whether inwardly in the mind or outwardly in possessions, we must beware lest we be abandoned. For Christ “filled the hungry with good things, but sent the rich away empty” (Luke 1:53). I say, the hungry—not those who are sluggish, nor those who overflow in themselves or in any of their possessions.

Righteousness, moreover, is fulfilled in no fewer than three ways: when, under divine law, we preserve the rights belonging to our nature; when, in relation to our brothers, we offer ourselves in turn, opposing to them what we do not wish done to us, so that, in matters where we are able, they may not suffer harm; and when, in relation to God, we render with ardent spirit the things that belong to God.

Hence he himself says: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:22). This summit of righteousness will never be completed in us until God is all in all and we are wholly subject to him. For this reason we can hunger here, but we cannot be satisfied, because, resisting the world, we are not yet able to restore ourselves to God as we ought.

But since we cannot be satisfied here, it is exceedingly necessary that, by growing sluggish through disgust, we not die of perpetual hunger.

## Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.

Mercy arises only from the preceding steps. There is no full and true compassion for the wretched unless true humility and fellowship in nature have preceded it; then the mind must become gentle in always submitting to the divine laws, and must begin, through compassion, to mourn its own falls and miseries and those of others; afterward, once purified, it must hunger for righteousness for a while.

From the attainment of these things true mercy is generated. Whoever possesses them will take care to make the miseries of human beings his own and will assist them with all the strength he possesses. If he lacks the means to help, compassion for their miseries will nevertheless not be lacking. Mercy is so called because, in our heart, we make the miseries of others our own.

Although God is also called merciful, no suffering falls upon him; rather, he benevolently assists our miseries. Concerning this mercy the Lord rightly says elsewhere: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36). It is as though he said: Show mercy to your neighbors for the purpose and in the ways in which the Father shows mercy—namely, so that goodness may overflow in all things. He shows mercy to the wicked and grants benefits to them so that at last they may be overcome by goodness and converted to him, and so that he may bestow upon them the things he reserves for the good.

It should be noted that, in the work of this virtue, righteousness comes first and mercy is brought to completion afterward—and rightly so, because no one is righteous without mercy, just as, conversely, no one is merciful without righteousness. Thus mercy is the light of righteousness, just as righteousness is considered the virtue of mercy.

Nevertheless, toward those whose case is not subject to our judgment, our mercy ought also to be enlarged, and the affection of the mind ought to grow, so that the truth of righteousness may be commended more clearly. But in the cases of those whose causes we justly examine, we should not show mercy in the judgment itself; after the sentence, however, insofar as it lies within our power, we should show mercy with discretion.

Certainly the virtue of mercy has many fields of action. None is greater, however, than that by which souls are rescued from the imminent danger of death and future pardon is secured for the brothers. So that this mercy may increase daily on every side through good works, it requires the spirit of counsel, without which no one wisely shows mercy to another in the legal consultation of pardon.

Therefore we must pray without ceasing that God’s will may be done “on earth as it is in heaven,” because “there is no wisdom, there is no counsel against the Lord.” Accordingly, while seeking the Lord’s will, we must act toward one another with mercy, so that we may be freed from every evil.

The order of mercy, however, is that each person begin with himself, as it is written: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclesiasticus 30:24).

Christ himself indicates the goal. Moved by such great mercy, he came even to desire to die for sinners. Those whom he found wounded he healed with his own bruising, and, with the medicine of his blood, restored them to the homeland, mended and carried upon his own shoulders. Therefore, because he displayed such great mercy by his example, those who imitate him are rightly called blessed.

But, conversely, judgment without mercy awaits those who do not wish to show mercy to the needy in this world.

## Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.

How beautifully purity of heart is placed in the sixth position, so that a human being—created on the sixth day—may through it gradually return to the image of the Creator. That image was obliterated by nothing other than the darkness of vices. Once these have been driven away, however, we rightly carry out the commandments of salvation, so that, illuminated again, we may be able to see God.

“The commandment of the Lord,” says the Prophet, is “bright, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm 18:9). The light of the commandments cannot shine in a house of darkness. Therefore let vices be driven from our hearts, so that we may be illuminated by the light of God’s commandments.

But perhaps someone wishes to perform many virtuous works while still retaining in his breast some darkness of vice, which he is not yet willing to have driven away by the light of truth. To such a person that law applies which concerns a wife redeemed by a song, whose husband is given the law that, while he has left Tartarus, he may not be permitted to turn his eyes toward her.

Hence a certain writer says:

“Whoever seeks to lead his mind toward the day above,  
yet, overcome, turns his eyes toward the Tartarean cave,  
loses whatever outstanding light he draws from it  
while he looks upon the realms below.”

Therefore, after the five preceding steps, the eye of the mind must be purified, lest the mind, offended by one of the commandments, become guilty of all. For this reason the lover of true blessedness must withdraw himself from every pleasure of passing things and, turning away from them, turn toward the love of eternal things.

By desire he must contemplate the immutable and immense unity of God and comprehend, through the understanding of faith, that same Trinity of the Godhead, which cannot be contained. For love of it, once he has completed the steps, he must make himself a stranger to every tumult of worldly things and every appetite of desire, so far as he can see God—so far, that is, as those who die to this world are able.

Each person sees him to the extent that he dies to the world. He sees, I say, “through a mirror and in an enigma,” somehow with greater certainty, because the appearance of the light begins to appear more delightfully to him. In the future, however, those who have reached this step will see God, pure in heart, with the eye of the mind as he is.

Therefore the spirit of understanding is rightly assigned to this step, because understanding is the eye of the mind. The fulfillment of God’s commandments opens understanding, as the Prophet sings: “From your commandments I gained understanding.” Hence it is clear that the heart must be cleansed and life illuminated by virtues, so that we may be light in the Lord.

When we are filled with such desires, let everything shine brightly for us in the light, and let all things follow after our affections. Such a heart is rightly called the kingdom of God; and therefore we pray that it may come to be in us: “Your kingdom come.”

The kingdom of God is therefore a pure possession, and is so much more complete the fuller it is in virtues and the more cleansed it is of vices. For, as I have said, as long as the darkness of vices and the blindness of sluggishness darken the mind, I doubt not only that it is light, but even that we are able to see the light.

Nor will God the Trinity be seen by any other eyes than those of the mind. There is no doubt that those are called pure in heart whose minds are illuminated by the exercises of the preceding beatitudes and whose purity directs the heart toward Christ.

Exceedingly wretched and unhappy are those whose attention is still blinded by vices. For just as those who are disgusted with hunger do not receive the hunger for righteousness in a life-giving manner, so those blinded by the darkness of sin cannot see the light, even when it shines brightly.

## Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.

The blessedness of the peacemakers is therefore the reward of adoption, through which we await becoming sons—though already called such in hope. Nothing greater or more perfect, then, is promised to us. This is therefore the highest step, toward which every purified person continually strives and toward which the illuminated person is directed.

The person who reaches it does not compromise the truth, either for himself or for the one whom he loves as himself. He is not broken or deterred from the truth either by the desire to please, by the gain of any advantage or pleasure, or even by the danger of adversity.

Such a person reaches this state, and the wisdom of the Spirit—which is the greatest of the gifts—in an orderly way, so that, at peace with God and tranquil, he may enjoy blessed adoption.

This must first begin properly with us, because, as long as the law of the flesh opposes the law of the mind, we cannot be at peace—not only with another, but even with ourselves. Sometimes we cannot bring healing to others without offense, because, divided within ourselves, we are devastated by civil war.

Therefore all the movements of the mind must first be quieted and the flesh restrained. Then we must compose them by subjecting them to the spirit, the mind, and reason, mastering and trampling down every fissure of desire, so that whatever is more excellent may rule in us and our whole humanity may obey the disciplines of the Holy Spirit.

Then the fountain of peace is rightly conveyed to others, when it has flowed within us and occupied and held all the parts of soul and body. Therefore, insofar as it depends upon us, we ought to have peace with all human beings.

Then we must restore those who disagree among themselves and within themselves—each one inwardly and with all others—to peace, by exhorting, moving, and acting upon them in the affection of righteousness. True peace exists where nothing resists.

Therefore, even if we are at peace with ourselves, let us carefully consider whether in any respect we differ from the sanctification of God’s name. Let the Father’s name, consecrated in his sons, be displayed in life and conduct. Hence we pray: “Hallowed be your name”—truly, so that we too may be holy.

This peace is nourished only by good will, as the angels rightly sang at the Savior’s birth: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). The world cannot give this peace. Jesus left it to his heirs as an inheritance and testament of adoption: “I give you peace; I leave you peace” (John 14:27).

What a great exchange of inheritance, by which we are made sons of the Father and receive an eternal kingdom!

But we must ask whether the peace that he distributed to his disciples is the peace of which the Apostle says: “The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding” (Philippians 4:2). If it surpasses all understanding, then how can it be surpassed by the understanding of the apostles? Or how can we be peacemakers according to a peace that we cannot comprehend?

Whatever is surpassed does not even reach what surpasses it, because, pressed down by its weakness, it lies far below. Therefore, if the peace of God surpasses all understanding, the human understanding lies defeated at a distance within itself.

Perhaps, then, it cannot comprehend that peace which surpasses it—indeed, cannot even reach it, insofar as it depends upon itself. From this it follows that, if understanding cannot comprehend the peace that surpasses it, it also cannot receive it; and, if it cannot receive it, perhaps it cannot be given.

Yet because it is given, we must consider most carefully how it can be received. For what Truth has promised is not changed. Peace was left to the apostles not merely so that they themselves might be peacemakers, but so that nearly the whole world might, through them, be reconciled and brought to peace with the peace of God.

Therefore either the statement that understanding does not comprehend it must be understood to mean that, through mercy, the apostles are themselves received by it so that they may be adopted; or else, because of its greatness, it surpasses understanding and cannot be received as it is, although it can indeed be received according to the capacity of rational understanding.

I mean, not as great as it is, but insofar as it suffices for reconciliation in adoption. No one, therefore, doubts that the infinity of eternal peace exceeds the capacity of our understanding.

For this reason the peace of God surpasses our understanding in these ways: peace is freely sent from heaven to the sons of wrath, and, reconciled by the peace of Christ, they do not first comprehend it; rather, they themselves are comprehended by it. This peace therefore rightly surpasses all understanding.

What, then? Do you know how peace is fitting for the sons of wrath? Or do you know how God, dwelling tranquilly in peace and yet appearing severe, judges all things? And, what is more wondrous, who has understood how great and what kind is the peace of the whole Trinity?

There one power and one Godhead are proclaimed: one virtue, one operation, and an undivided will. I think that unless such a great and such a peace is somehow grasped by the sense and understanding of faith, the mind is not illuminated by that same peace.

But once illuminated, if it presumes that it has comprehended this infinite height, it is emptied of the very understanding by which it is deprived of the light of truth and weighed down by the error of presumption.

Perhaps this is why the height of so great a peace eludes and surpasses every understanding. Yet it does not leave understanding without the substance of faith or the illumination of understanding concerning what that peace is, and how great and of what kind it is, as it is proclaimed in the sacred Scriptures. Rather, understanding rejoices to perceive and be illuminated, and continually, through grace, to be reconciled to that same peace.

Therefore it withdraws itself from everything that disagrees with it, so that it may possess the gift brought to it from heaven.

Once a person has been inwardly possessed on every side by the peace of Christ, then the blessedness of adoption will certainly be bestowed, because in no respect the sanctification owed to sons is diminished in him. In no respect, therefore, does he rebel against the kingdom of the whole Trinity; in no respect does he contradict the will of God.

Yet, as long as we are burdened by the flesh, such a great and complete peace is scarcely, or perhaps never, preserved without interruption. For how often we ourselves resist within ourselves!

Nevertheless, the peaceful person, guarding inwardly the covenants of peace, subdues, restrains, and composes whatever resists outwardly. Yet, because he keeps the faith he has promised, although he wages war against vices, he does not in any respect break the peace that God has granted.

Hence it is written: “Great peace have those who love your law, O Lord, and there is no scandal for them” (Psalm 118:165). Otherwise, as long as we are separated from this peace, we must fear that we may be counted among the sons of wrath rather than among the sons of adoption.

Yet God, who observes our weakness, has taught us many remedies of reconciliation, so that, because we offend daily, we may seek peace daily and obey the teachings of life.

Thus far I have examined the growth of the virtues. It remains for us to consider how great the rewards are through their growth. For although I understand less, just as there are increases of virtues, so increases of rewards have also been promised.

Nor is a uniform proportion of rewards rightly promised where the preceding virtue has not been one and the same in all. Rather, divine speech has established different measures of recompense for different labors.

Thus, although those whose kingdom is the kingdom of heaven are called blessed, and those who will possess the earth are called blessed, along with the other blessings that follow, we nevertheless believe that there is a great difference between receiving consolation and possessing the fullness of satisfaction in righteousness; and a great distance between those who will obtain mercy and those who will have merited the most glorious vision of God.

One brightness, therefore, belongs to the sun, another to the moon, and another to the stars. Star differs from star in brightness, and so also is the resurrection of the dead.

The kingdom of heaven is common to all who have been reconciled to God, wherever they may be; within it, however, the various merits of rewards are distinguished. Yet it is something greater to possess, by right, some particular dignity within that kingdom.

There are therefore many dwelling places there, and thus consolation arises from the possession of so great a happiness. To be satisfied with righteousness is something greater than to be comforted from mourning; and, finally, to be a son of God is greater than to obtain mercy’s pardon for guilt.

Nevertheless, within the palace of the supreme King there are many steps. One person is already distinguished in rank if he is permitted to see ever more fully the brightness and face of the eternal King; another is higher, having gloriously received the final adoption that I mentioned above.

It should be noted that, generally, one kingdom of heaven is spoken of for all, even though distinctions among merits are counted. For although it can rightly be said to belong to the one who will be last in it, the dignity of all will be held in common, since, through charity, even the last will possess each individual good in common.

Therefore, although they differ in brightness and are distinguished from one another, all will be blessed in it fully and abundantly, possessing everything through love.

As has been said, the blessed person is rightly understood to be one who wishes nothing evil and has everything whatsoever that he wishes. Therefore, although the one who is last in that kingdom is rightly called blessed—because he desires nothing beyond the merit of grace and wishes for nothing more, since he wishes nothing unjustly—nevertheless, enriched by the grace of blessedness, he possesses through charity, as though granted to himself, the brightness and glory attributed to others.

Hence all are believed blessed through faith, even though the brightness of their merits differs within that realm.

But why did I say that there are eight, when rewards for laborers are promised in only seven gifts? The promise of the eighth is none other than the first repeated in words: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” And:

“Blessed,” he says, “are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

From this it is plainly evident that whatever is repeated in the promise has a mystical significance in its number. Within the seven, the first has the same sound; yet it is counted outside the seven, so that the glory of the sacred resurrection in Christ may be consecrated through these eight degrees of reward.

For the eighth day of resurrection is the same as the first. On it, at the beginning, light is read to have been created; on that same day, once created, it is finally illuminated by the glory of a more abundant life.

Meanwhile, although the promise of the reward appears to be the same, it nevertheless stands out with greater dignity, because I would never say that beginners and the perfect will receive an equal reward.

Here we are perhaps taught mystically that the first kingdom of heaven is to be dissolved and to be with Christ, when the saints are caught up in the clouds into the air to meet Christ. Then many of those who sleep will rise: some to eternal life, others to reproach.

The first kingdom is proposed, namely, in the liberation of the body—or rather, first, in its liberation from every desire of the world and every enticement of the flesh. Then, once possessed by the spirit of poverty and already carried upward by hope into heavenly things, the mind begins to dwell there.

The evangelist otherwise indicates this quite clearly when he promises it not as something future but as something present, saying: “For theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” By this he asserts that they already reign there in the present, so that meanwhile hope may be strengthened amid pressures and the various events of life.

The capacity to reign is already supplied through the exceedingly rich gifts, so that they may cling more firmly to future things and desire and guard more earnestly the kingdom they have received.

The true poverty of Christ is rightly promised to reign already, because, inwardly in the mind more than outwardly in the flesh, it is alienated from every pleasure of the world and every enticement of desire. With the favor of the Holy Spirit’s grace, it rests wholly upon the joys of the life to come and delights in the things of God alone.

This virtue arises from fear of God, just as the other six beatitudes are each generated from one of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Prophet says: “The spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety” (Isaiah 11:2).

Finally, as something more particular—like a special district separated from every stain of sin—he adds: “And the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him” (ibid., 3). For the fullness of fear does not permit anyone whom it has filled to be capable of another thing.

Therefore, although this virtue is an imitator of wisdom, as is the poverty of the beatitudes, it must not be considered insignificant. For although the riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge, the Prophet rightly proves that the fear of the Lord itself is his treasure.

This dwelling of poverty has many stages of progress, as do the other dwellings; for that reason it must not be considered superficially, especially since it already reigns richly in heavenly things—not through a hope of the future, but through a hope that brings the future into the present.

After the resurrection of the flesh, however, it is appropriately understood as a second kingdom of the perfect, in which the advancement of the dwelling places and the various rewards of merits are counted.

But to the martyrs who suffer for righteousness that kingdom is rightly granted in its fullness at once. For when they have raised themselves through the degrees of the virtues to higher things, receiving what is more sublime, the lower dignity is not immediately denied them.

The reward of the former life is not annulled when the greater glory of merits is increased through virtues. Therefore, as I said, the final promise of blessedness is mystically arranged so that it is both one of the seven and, repeated in the same words, stands above the seven outside them.

From this it is plainly evident that the whole kingdom begins in blessedness, while within it the brightness of merits is illuminated through the same degrees.

The end and the beginning are rightly concluded as nothing other than one kingdom of heaven. Although it has been opened to believers through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, long sought through the seven petitions mentioned above, and eagerly pursued through the corresponding virtues of these beatitudes, its rewards will nevertheless not be obtained without Christ’s resurrection on the eighth day.

To this, reader, I would have you raise your mind a little higher and see how harmonious and mystical the sacraments of God reveal themselves on every side.

There is no doubt that, just as all the gifts of the virtues are bestowed through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, so through the same seven petitions, by God’s authority, all the things beneficial to present and eternal life are daily requested.

And when what we pray for has been granted, the heavenly gifts are counted among those predestined to life according to the works of each, through Christ’s resurrection on the eighth day and through the corresponding virtues of these beatitudes.

For, in accordance with the testimony of the Apocalypse (chapter 1), the sevenfold spirits, sent throughout the world, traversing the sevenfold Church of Christ and working through the authority of their power, daily adorn the works of the virtues—as though they were seven lampstands shining before the Ruler—and kindle them in the richness of charity, so that they may shine more and more.

Source preparation: Supplied local source; translated as part of this section.

I beseech you, Lord Jesus, that I too may be a candelabrum of upright action, shining among these lamps of the beatitudes; and may it not be moved until it is established by your firm acceptance, so that it may shine before you forever. Come, then, I ask, and teach me the discipline of these your teachings.

Surely, therefore, it was not without the profound mystery already mentioned that your holy evangelist placed first, under the sacramental meaning of this reckoning, the merits of all the predestined, gathered together so that they might shine; nor was it without significance that he said that, while seated, you opened your mouth [Source p. 252]. This means, of course, that you opened the treasures of wisdom and knowledge [Col. 0228C], and poured forth the deep mysteries of your grace, hidden from ages and generations. Thus your thoroughly instructed Apostle, in accordance with such teaching, asks for prayer (Eph. VI, 19), that speech may be given him in the opening of his mouth. Therefore I too implore that the mouth of knowledge be opened for me with its key, because your word, proceeding from you, is the key of the mouth. Whenever speech is required, I ask that, once the chains of silence have been loosened, the utterances of your understandings may be opened to me.

For I shall understand that there are seven gifts, but one Spirit; seven prayers, but one petition. Hence the Prophet says: “One thing have I asked of the Lord, this will I seek” (Ps. XXVI, 4). There are seven beatitudes of the virtues, but one charity, which even now, as though by its own members, is supported and strengthened by them; seven increases of merits, but one power arising from Christ’s resurrection [Col. 0228D], which is the eighth, from which the kingdom of heaven is promised to those who suffer for righteousness.

Indeed, the blessed evangelist reserved this beatitude under a mystical number for that reason: many psalms are also inscribed “for the eighth.” For just as the immortality of Christ, in the eighth, shone forth supremely among the virtues, so the reward of the predestined in this eighth beatitude will be. Likewise Solomon says: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Eccl. XI, 2). Perhaps this is because we are commanded to devote our works to the number of the virtues mentioned above, and yet to assign wholly, in their entirety, the progress of our merits and the benefits of the Giver to the hope of our eighth, which is Christ.

Otherwise, who is capable of these things by himself? Indeed, in order that we might be capable, the seven Spirits of God were sent into the world [Col. 0229A], from whom all the gifts of the virtues flow. Under their protection, Christ taught the prayers of petitions in the prayer he gave us. In them all the fragrances of life are suspended, although, as the Apostle testifies (Rom. VIII, 26), we do not yet know how we ought sometimes to pray. The anointing of the Spirit teaches us about all these things. Otherwise, we can neither live according to his gifts, nor implore them salutarily in our prayers, nor happily attain the promises of the beatitudes.

Therefore gifts are first freely bestowed for the undertakings; then exercises in the virtues are required with profit, according to the talents of the gifts; and afterward, once the struggles of life are over, the rewards are repaid according to the burden of service. For this reason our Savior taught an equal number of prayers, so that the gifts might be sought more abundantly [Col. 0229B] and, once received, might be enriched most dutifully through the virtues. Their reward, increased still more happily in the heavenly places, may thus be granted to us who labor [Source p. 253].

Yet nothing more severely is commanded to believers in this life than to suffer for righteousness. For true hunger for righteousness is proved when someone would rather die for it than allow the faith by which he has been justified to be violated by the falsehood of a lie. Nevertheless, this final and principal beatitude of the way, supplied with the gifts of the seven preceding ones, is rightly made more glorious when, through the final suffering of martyrdom, it preserves what it has received.

Otherwise, to go to suffering without these things is a feeble attempt, since mortal weakness is quickly overcome by the bitterness of punishments. Therefore Christ’s soldier must be fortified with the weapons of the virtues in time of peace, without which no one engages in glorious battles [Col. 0229C]. These virtues, if persecution is absent, can more readily obtain the palm of the campaign through Christ’s gift without the shedding of blood; but the latter, if the time of suffering arrives, can never be salutarily crowned by boldness in death alone, without these virtues.

No one, therefore, suffers for righteousness without Christ’s peace, without purity of heart, or without mercy. Who, indeed, would ever say that someone could rightly endure tortures without love of righteousness? No one, I say, willingly submits to death for it without compunction of heart and desire for the future homeland. No one does so without Christ’s gentleness, or without an affection for poverty—especially since the true athlete of God does not wish to preserve himself for himself, but prefers, even at the cost of his life, to become gain for the Creator, or chooses to be sacrificed sooner for righteousness [Col. 0229D].

But whoever suffers worthily for some other cause, not devoutly for righteousness, but because his sins demand it, accumulates not beatitude but the punishment of sin, according to God’s just judgment. Let what has been said about these matters suffice.

As for the forms of these virtues, let the reader’s diligence discern them more carefully. The legislator Moses first proposed the Ten Commandments generally on the mountain, then explained the same commandments in their several parts; and, by repeating the substance of the commandments for various reasons, divided it again into its individual forms. So too Christ, wishing to show that he had taught those things through the Holy Spirit, now proposed, in a similar manner, as it were the genera of the virtues, the words of the eight beatitudes. From them, if I am not mistaken, everything he taught on that same mountain depends.

But because he had compressed many things into a few words in a rather obscure manner [Col. 0230A], he then explains them more fully, in ways appropriate to the persons and matters involved, elaborating and fitting each portion of the sayings to its corresponding subject. First, in the utterance of both laws, he proposes the genera of the sayings, compressed into a few words [Source p. 254]—obviously because the particular form of things often diminishes the force of the genus. Then he wisely divides them into parts, since division is of great value for grasping matters of the greatest difficulty.

Therefore the prudent and devoted hearer should consider that what has been gathered together at once in a few words possesses greater force and wonder. Then let him understand the greater number of things attributed more specifically to each matter in scattered form; and whatever he sees to correspond to his purpose in one part, let him faithfully receive as applying to the whole, as though it had been opened more clearly for him. This is so that neither the variety of the forms should weaken the force and sum of the beatitudes, nor the obscurity of perception confuse the moral understanding composed as a whole [Col. 0230B].

For this reason, then, he seems first to have enumerated these eight in order, and afterward to have significantly resumed the forms represented by figures. Hence, according to the ancient translation:

> “Blessed are you,” he says, “when all people hate you, and say every evil thing against you, and expel you.”

These words plainly reveal what I am saying: nothing other than the virtue of the eighth beatitude is recapitulated at greater length here, and the various aspects of persecutions for righteousness are more fully explained. For above these things are spoken generally and absolutely to everyone; here, however, it is declared more explicitly that the apostles and their successors will suffer for righteousness. Nevertheless, both that passage and this one apply to the apostles and to all who suffer for Christ [Col. 0230C].

In this saying, in which the oppression of the churches is continued as one, three kinds of persecution are indicated: the wicked either persecute the good with hatred of heart, or tear them apart with slanderous words, or—what is more criminal—drive them out through evil deeds. In these degrees of criminality the whole cruelty of hostile people is represented.

Yet each of these parts has, in turn, its own members by which its deceit is carried out. Thus expulsion is rightly understood in two ways: either when someone is sometimes separated with injury from the company of citizens, or when the present life, driven from its dwelling, is ended by the death of the flesh. In that event, however, no one doubts that, if it is for righteousness, what has died lives the better.

Conversely, those who slander are rightly said to lie if we, pursuing righteousness, devoutly suffer for Christ [Col. 0230D]. Otherwise, whoever is condemned because his sins demand it pays the penalty for his guilt. This is why he urges those who suffer to rejoice and exult for righteousness, because a conscience that bears witness and faithful devotion require nothing other than the summit of righteousness.

Hence, whereas above the kingdom of heaven is mentioned, here a plentiful reward in the heavenly places is signified as future [Source p. 255]. But lest what he says be heard as too harsh, he first moderates the severity of suffering by an example, so that they may endure what he threatens all the more easily, the more happily they recognize that through these things they will reach the eternal joys he promises.

> “For so,” he says, “they persecuted the prophets who were before you.”

It is as though he were openly saying: “Their examples invite you. For, as is true, those who proclaimed my coming were put to death for righteousness [Col. 0231A].” Therefore you can have no doubt that you must follow me through labors to glory, since you see those whose prophecies you recognize as fulfilled in me, before the triumph of the passion, devout and faithful, without precedent, falling into death.

Let these things be said according to the earlier exemplars. Our own interpretation, however, is as follows:

> “Blessed are you,” he says, “when they curse you, persecute you, and say every evil thing against you, lying because of me.”

In these words the same things seem to be signified, especially since curses arise from hatred of the heart, and persecution, together with various punishments, drives life from the body. Yet he commands them then rightly to rejoice and exult if they patiently endure all these things outwardly for Christ, who is commended as the true righteousness [Col. 0231B]; inwardly, however, the beatitude of hope, conscious of the truth, possesses greater strength.

Of such things the Prophet says: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. XLIV, 14). Therefore, although persecutions and every other form of violence rage outwardly, it is nevertheless fitting for us to rejoice, since a plentiful reward is preserved for us in the heavenly places. We are commanded not only to rejoice but also to exult, because the reward will be all the greater insofar as faith has been more devoted to Christ, with joy and exultation, amid tribulations.

By “the heavenly places,” I do not think that the higher regions of the world are meant, nor things subject to change, but spiritual firmaments in which no corruption rules. Concerning these heavens Paul said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20) [Col. 0231C]. To rejoice, therefore, in spiritual goods and always pursue gain from them is not merely to store up treasure in them but already to live there, because “where your treasure is, there also your heart will be.”

> “You are the salt of the earth.”

Salt, of course, is figuratively understood as wisdom. Concerning this Paul says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (I Cor. II, 6). He says that we speak not the wisdom of this world, nor of the rulers of this world, who are being destroyed, but God’s wisdom, hidden in a mystery, which he predestined before the ages for our glory [Source p. 256].

It is therefore not surprising that he wished to call them wisdom, since they have also been called gods and light—not substantially, certainly, but exalted by grace through many such names. When he says “the salt of the earth,” that is, wisdom, he means them because of the gift of the Holy Spirit, through which they have become participants in true wisdom [Col. 0231D].

And if the proper meaning of the words is to be sought, the elements of water and fire, from which salt is made, should be considered. Hence the Psalm says: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Ps. LXV, 12). It is as though he were plainly saying: “You are the salt of the earth because, from the water of the Holy Spirit that I gave you and from the fire of tribulation, you have been formed into one savor of wisdom.”

Or certainly, reborn through the water of baptism and the fire of charity, you have been given as seasoning for earthly minds. For the foolishness of earthly minds, because they pursue the earth, stains souls. Therefore the apostles’ teaching was given the task of salting them, like salt. Whatever is seasoned with salt, when it is prepared [Col. 0232A], is free from blood and cleanses putrefaction. When the corruption of sin is dried out by the salt of wisdom, worms do not destroy it, nor does its flavor become insipid.

Therefore, just as food is not fit to eat unless it is seasoned with salt, so speech will not be useful for instruction if it does not possess the teaching of apostolic wisdom.
