Hence it is said in Leviticus: “You shall not remove the salt of the covenant of your God from any sacrifice of yours; and in every sacrifice you shall offer salt” (Lev. II, 13). That is, in every gift, whatever you teach or correct, and whatever purpose you pursue, always possess apostolic wisdom and imitate it.

As far as the eloquence of Latin is concerned, these concluding clauses of the sayings seem to depend on the passage where he says, so that the sentence may be complete [Col. 0232B]: “He was teaching them, saying.” He was teaching them, I say, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” and the rest that follows. Likewise: “You are the salt of the earth and the light of the world”; or, for the instruction of those who were going to believe: “You will be blessed when they persecute you and say every evil thing.” Thus, when he says “every evil thing,” he embraces together every kind of word spoken by the wicked.

> “But if the salt has lost its savor, with what will it be salted?”

It is as though he were openly saying: “If the teacher has erred, by what teacher will he be corrected?” He says: “You are the salt of the earth.” But if, through fear of temporal things or through the impulse of desire, you abandon the savor of wisdom, who will be the means by which the foolishness of your folly and the error of your vices are removed [Col. 0232C] [Source p. 257]?

It should be noted that the proposition of this saying is directed, as it were, solely to the apostles; the following assumption, however, is pronounced concerning all who are counted by the name of teachers, and at the end it is concluded concerning everyone. There is no doubt that those who have undertaken the office of salting, in order to season the minds of the faithful and preserve bodies for eternal life through the word of instruction, are called “the salt of the earth” by virtue of their teaching.

Therefore the reckless must hear, without any advantage gained through falsehood, how terrifying is the judgment concluded in this passage against those who lose the savor of their sacred office in teaching.

> “It is good for nothing thereafter,” he says, “except to be thrown outside and trampled by people.”

By “outside,” he signifies that it is to be thrown outside the Church, or perhaps outside the office of teaching, because it has not retained the savor of grace. For if the comparison with salt is weighed according to the nature of its kind, without considering the rigor of softening [Col. 0232D], no argument remains: once it has lost its flavor, it is proved to be no longer suitable for any use.

Whether this is said about the teacher’s life, or only about his teaching, or about both together, I do not think should be judged rashly. Especially since it is said elsewhere: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore,” he says, “whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works” (Matt. XXIII, 2).

Behold, in this passage he commends the soundness of their teaching. Who, then, denies that it benefits those who act, when the teacher of truth commands that what is prescribed be observed? Nevertheless, he commands that their works not be imitated, but that their teaching be followed. There is no doubt that, by the example of those he condemns, he warns the teachers of the truth of the New Testament [Col. 0233A], just as he gradually concluded the matter concerning the righteousness of the Pharisees: they must not oppose in their conduct what they have taught in their words.

Otherwise, even if someone possesses the seasoning of sound doctrine and the savor of true wisdom, he presumes dangerously to teach if, having become insipid in himself, he corrupts others with the stench of his vices. Even if he is not thrown outside, he is already trampled by everyone when his life is despised. It is rightly despised if he is such that he is thereafter good for nothing. Indeed, having lost the flavor by which he salts, so that he cannot season what is corrupt, he is crushed beneath the feet of his subjects.

But the holy and true minister of Christ, although he suffers many things on earth and the wicked mock him, cannot be trampled down, because, fixed in mind upon heaven, he remains there. Hence the Truth expressly instructs the apostles not to empty the wisdom they have received within themselves [Col. 0233B] [Source p. 258] for the sake of, or through fear of, desire for, or sluggishness concerning, anything; rather, they must remain in the solidity of salt, always remembering what its nature is and what they received from its Maker.

> “You are the light of the world.”

They are called light because, receiving the light of truth, they have been assumed by grace into the body of Christ. Hence the Apostle also says: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8).

It is the nature of light, wherever it is brought, to drive out darkness. So too the apostles, having become light in the Lord, were placed here so that, since the world, set outside the knowledge of God, was blinded by the darkness of ignorance, all might be enlightened through them.

Hence the prophet, speaking of Christ or significantly in the person of anyone, says: “I have set you as a light for the nations [Col. 0233C], that my salvation may reach the end of the earth” (Isa. XLIX, 6). They are light when they are directed toward the illumination of faith, but salvation when they are directed toward healing. Therefore he previously mentioned that they are salt, so that the corrupt might be healed through their wisdom.

Indeed, they are called light through the illumination of grace, so that darkness may be driven from human hearts by their enlightenment. The Prophet says the same concerning the Lord: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation” (Ps. XXVI, 1). Through these two sayings the integrity of our salvation is invoked.

Therefore the apostles, so that they might be understood as gods according to grace, have been called not only wisdom for salvation but also light for the illumination of this world. Hence in certain manuscripts, to distinguish the other age, the demonstrative word “this” is added [Col. 0233D]. It is as though he were plainly saying: “You are the light of this world by your office, and the salt of the earth through your ministry. But because I am the true Light, I shall be eternal light for everyone.”

By “the world” either the universality of the human race is designated, or only those who are received by Christ, chosen out of this world set in evil. If they are understood universally as the light of the world, perhaps this is because they were directed toward everyone for the reception of faith. But if they are called light according to the predestination of these people, they are rightly called light because through them others are enlightened for life.

Although the light shines in darkness, the darkness did not comprehend them—or rather, Christ through them. For if it had apprehended them, darkness would certainly no longer have remained. Moreover, the apostles, when they had been sons of darkness, became, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, light in the Lord [Col. 0234A]. They did not become this by nature, but through the effect of the gift, according to what is written: “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17) [Source p. 259].

It should also be noted that this is the same grace in the apostles by which, above, those pure in heart are made blessed, their hearts being cleansed by faith and understanding. By this light God is rightly believed to be seen. Through it the apostles, divinely illuminated and clinging to the light, are rightly called “the light of the world,” by reason of their share in the greater grace.

Their being called salt above also accords with those who make peace, because without wisdom the seasoning of peace cannot be maintained. Hence Mark says: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX, 50). For the salt of discernment and wisdom is of no use without the peace of Christ; and, conversely, peace does not cling to God without wisdom [Col. 0234B].

Through these gifts, the perfection of the apostles is signified. Therefore these three chief and principal things among the eight are specially assigned to them, so that you might understand more fully that they had attained the others as well. Hence it follows:

> “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.”

In these words that city is the heavenly Jerusalem, and it is as though it were dedicated upon Christ, who has truly been called the mountain, with the splendor of twelve precious stones. The place where he was teaching them demonstrates this well, as though he were openly saying: “Look at the place where you have been set, for the place indicates the mountain upon which you, in whom the heavenly city is founded, have been built.”

You are the foundations of that city, which is founded upon the holy mountains; therefore, already from its foundation, you are openly called a city [Col. 0234C]. A city set upon a prominent mountain cannot hide itself, lest what it does, whether well or badly, become known; nor can it conceal itself through fear, lest it be found by enemies.

Therefore dedicate in the foundation what is to remain at the summit. Prepare the city’s armor, because, placed upon the mountain, you will have no possibility of escaping below or of doing anything secretly. The mountain of righteousness is exalted, and you are exposed upon it even if you wish to hide yourselves. Therefore fortify yourselves instead with the weapons of the virtues, since you have been placed in the light for the defeat of the world’s adversaries.

Providence is watchful in all things. For above he specially assigned three things to the apostles, but the city set upon a mountain, which cannot be hidden, he indicated absolutely concerning everyone [Col. 0234D]. For the heavenly Jerusalem, which on earth is still being polished from living stones from the beginning to the end of the age, is shown to be the order of the predestined. Thus what was going to occur scattered among particular forms is now gathered together in general [Source p. 260].

It is said in the Song of Songs: “Your neck is like the tower of David, built with its defenses; a thousand shields hang upon it, all the armor of the mighty” (Song IV, 4).

Moreover, because this city, or tower, is set on high and possesses immense and ineffable riches of treasures, the hostile powers rage against it. Hence sixty mighty men, the strongest of Israel, surround Solomon’s bed—namely, Christ’s passion and the glory of his resurrection—all holding swords and thoroughly trained for war. “Each man’s sword,” it says, “is upon his thigh, because of night terrors.” [Col. 0235A]

The teacher of truth, anticipating these terrors, warns those in whom this city is dedicated from the beginning, and through them all the members of his body, to clothe themselves with the weapons of the virtues. For, placed openly before all their enemies, they will have no place in which to hide unless they defend themselves with heavenly fortifications.

And wondrous is God’s predestination. Although it has not yet been built even upon its foundations, it is dedicated as though it were already complete. Justice is proposed and future things are foretold. The king and craftsman of the city, who is going to depart far away, forbids its citizens to rely on concealment, so that they may surround themselves with stronger weapons of the virtues.

If you consider the order of the gifts [Col. 0235B], you will see that these things belong to the spirit of counsel and fortitude: inwardly, they are to govern their inhabitants mercifully through counsel; outwardly, by the power of the Spirit, they are to defeat their adversaries while fighting for righteousness with the whole equipment of faith.

> “Nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel.”

If he is speaking figuratively of himself, the meaning is that he should not be placed under the obscurity of the Law, as some wish, or under the bushel of the flesh. Then the candlestick rightly signifies the cross of the passion upon which he was to be lifted, and the lamp shining inwardly signifies the divinity revealed in the flesh.

Nevertheless, considering the context more closely, we think that the apostles and apostolic men are lamps, although above they were more gloriously called light. For although, clinging to the light, they had deserved to be light, they were nevertheless kindled by another’s light; and just as a lamp is nourished by another’s gifts, so they ought not to lie hidden under the bushel of fear, or certainly under the convenience of the present life [Col. 0235C].

Kindled by the light of truth, they were to be placed upon the candlestick, upon which the seven lamps mystically placed in the Temple were continually nourished with oil, that is, with the grace of the Holy Spirit. Why the lamp of faith and good works ought to shine with greater prominence [Source p. 261], he plainly indicates when he adds:

> “So that it may shine,” he says, “for all who are in the house.”

That is, in the Church, which is proclaimed to be one and perfect house. Or perhaps it means that it should shine for everyone in the house of this world, which, under one heaven, is enclosed as though in a chamber. This is especially so since above they were generally called the light of the whole world.

> “So let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” [Col. 0235D]

It is as though he were openly saying: “Let it shine in the way I prescribe, precisely in the way I teach. I teach you not to place it under a bushel but upon a candlestick. I explain the reason: let your light shine for all who are in the house, and when they see your good works, let them glorify not you but your Father who is in heaven.”

For I require works to be seen so that your teaching may be confirmed. Yet the end of the work must be placed nowhere else except in this: through them God the Father is glorified, he who poured true light into you and, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, gave you the power to act.

Otherwise there is empty labor and vain presumption if the teacher’s life and the office of his tongue are not most devoutly directed toward the glory and praise of God [Col. 0236A]. To gather everything together: up to this point, while specially instructing them fully concerning what he had previously taught generally about everyone, he taught lofty and supreme things—so that they might season souls for incorruption through the office of salt; illuminate them for understanding the truth; defend those whom they had acquired against hostile assault; and, once defended, kindle them toward the love of divinity.

Now, as a heavenly orator, perhaps because they might suppose that he wished to weaken and completely abolish the authority of the ancient commandments, he anticipates their unspoken question:

> “Do not think,” he says, “that I have come to abolish the Law or the prophets.”

He would indeed have abolished the Law if he had forbidden believers to turn their minds toward it and to fulfill spiritually the things that had been spoken. “I have not come,” he says, “to abolish, but to fulfill.” [Col. 0236B]

For he fulfilled everything in the Law and the prophets that had been set forth for the beginning of a life to be practiced or signified, both by adding many things for the perfection of the moral commandments and by declaring completed in himself everything that had been spoken about him or about the Church, which had formerly been hidden under signs in those writings.

Christ is the power of the Law and the prophets. For if he himself had not fulfilled the things foretold and prefigured concerning him, all the riddles of the words would have remained incomplete and empty [Source p. 262]. He fulfilled them by acting; he also fulfilled them for those who were more perfect by adding what was lacking in the practice of life. He fulfilled as well the mysteries of the things signified, or the mystical sacraments of the prophets, by manifesting plainly whatever had been foretold, so that everything might remain true and trustworthy [Col. 0236C].

For in all these matters, the manifestation of past things enacted in the Law, or received through belief in the Law, is the perfect fulfillment of the truth of future things. Therefore you must not question the ancient commandments, marvel at the new promises, or be terrified by the various anxieties of afflictions, because all these things are accumulated so that what has already been marked out in words or deeds may be completed.

> “Amen, indeed, I say to you: until heaven and earth pass away, one iota or one apex will not pass away from the Law until all things come to pass.”

Here, to be sure, “Amen” is used as an affirmation, a usage that is not otherwise doubled anywhere in Matthew. By heaven and earth passing away he may perhaps mean their passing into a better form, since new heavens and a new earth are promised to us. Hence elsewhere he says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. XXIV, 35) [Col. 0236D].

There, then, the same words seem to signify what “iota” signifies here, so that the sense is this: just as the words will not pass away unless they are fulfilled, so not one iota—or, what is smallest, not one apex—will pass away from the Law until all things come to pass, including those things in the Law that are considered least.

I do not say that they will pass away so as no longer to exist, but that they will pass away into something better. Not one iota will pass away unless it is fulfilled through works. For we said that Christ fulfilled the Law principally in two matters: in the commandments concerning the life to be practiced, which is sufficiently represented figuratively by the single iota; and in the life to be signified, which is expressed more clearly through the apex.

Among the Greeks, iota is tenth in the order of the alphabet, and it therefore signifies ten in their numerical system [Col. 0237A]. Hence the sum of the Ten Commandments concerning the life to be practiced is clearly gathered. This shows that Christ did not come to abolish any of them, but to fulfill them all more perfectly by prescribing what is more excellent to those who are more perfect.

Then understand that by “one apex” of the letters he means every smallest detail of the commandments concerning the life to be signified. But by the apex of things and of all the commandments he means himself, namely the one who comes from the Law and the prophets, restoring each thing more perfectly and completely so that they might be fulfilled in truth.

Otherwise, I do not see why the evangelist, writing these things in the Hebrew language, would not have used *Ioth*, according to the proper character of that language, as a figure [Source p. 263], rather than *iota* from another language, from which ten is everywhere displayed in numerical form. *Ioth* is interpreted as “confusion” or “desolation,” [Col. 0237B] and therefore it was not suitable to use it in that place; rather, he used the letter through which the mystical number of the deeds is signified.

When he says, “Until heaven and earth pass away, one iota or one apex will not pass away from the Law,” it is as though he were saying: nothing of either part will pass away unless those things are always more perfectly practiced in works, and these things signifying me are completed in truth, with a light clearer than day.

Meanwhile, however, until heaven and earth pass away, if any small matters remain that have not yet been shown figuratively through enigmas, nothing of them will pass away prematurely into a form of corruption; rather, all things will gradually continue until they are completed.

Having said these things, I do not prescribe the simpler explanation of every matter; I leave it to the reader to disclose and determine whether something more suitable can be found that agrees with the truth [Col. 0237C]. Let him understand in every way that those things in the Law that are considered least are all full of sacraments. In the Gospel too, everything is recapitulated, and, until the elements of the world pass away, the things not yet restored are to be completed through works and figures.

> “Therefore whoever loosens one of these commandments will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.”

He speaks with sufficient significance of “these commandments,” which above he prefigured more expressly for perfection through the iota and the apex. Although they may seem small, if someone loosens them—those by not doing them, these by not believing them—and teaches people to do so, he will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. This is certainly not because he taught, but because he loosened them and thus taught [Col. 0237D].

I say, not according to what he found and read, but according to what he did not practice or did not rightly believe. To loosen one of them is either not to do what he understands rightly, or not to understand rightly what he has corrupted through his own tradition; or perhaps to diminish whatever has flowed from the Gospel toward the integrity of perfection.

Thus, in whatever manner someone loosens one iota or one apex from these least commandments and teaches people to do so, he will be called least—not because he taught, indeed, but because he loosened wrongly and thus taught. Here I would have the prudent reader attend to how dangerous it is for teachers of the churches to be subject even to the smallest sins. What benefit is there in teaching righteousness when a minimal fault destroys the teacher and a light presumption casts him down from the highest rank [Col. 0238A] [Source p. 264]?

In this passage he reproves the scribes and Pharisees, who, despising God’s commandments, established traditions of their own; Christians too must beware of this. Moreover, he is said to be called least in the kingdom of heaven because he will be unworthy of it. In that kingdom there will be no one least, but all will be great. For even if the small are blessed first, they will be worthy of that very blessing, because amid the highest joys of paradise they will then be great.

This is well signified by that catch of fish in which a full net of large fish—one hundred and fifty-three, namely—is drawn to shore.

It can also be interpreted otherwise: “He will be called least in the kingdom of heaven,” that is, in the present Church of Christ, which in many passages is already called the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0238B]. Such a person, when it becomes clear what he is, will be called least in the Church, because he will be despised. Therefore he will certainly not be in that kingdom in which only the great will be, because, while he was in this present kingdom, he was unworthy of the rank of authority.

Hence it follows:

> “But whoever does and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

Perhaps, then, because he was humble and perfect in the Church, even if he was rejected, he will rightly be great in that kingdom. But, conversely, the other man, because he was unworthily promoted and was contemptuous, will not merely fail to be great in that kingdom; even in the present kingdom of the churches of God, he will already be called least and will be contemptible in the judgment of God and human beings.

I say to you: unless your righteousness surpasses that of the scribes and Pharisees by a greater measure, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

Certainly, when he says, “I say [Col. 0238C] to you,” he has struck the reader’s mind with great force and a profound insight for reflection. For it is not just anyone, but the divine Majesty and the boundless Almighty himself who says, “I say to you.” He, I say, is the one who in his own time gave those earlier commands to the less perfect through the ministers of the law and the prophets; and now, through himself, he has added to us, who are already more instructed, greater things pertaining to salvation. For he added them, and did not abolish what he had previously commanded.

Therefore he says, “Unless your righteousness surpasses”—and by “their righteousness” he means all those things actually commanded for divine worship, or those mystical matters of the figures, nevertheless established according to the letter, by the completion of all of which the righteousness of the scribes was applauded. But because Christ added what was lacking for the conduct of life, and filled with the truth and perfection of himself what had been foreshadowed by promises of the life to be signified, [265] he rightly says to his now more perfect disciples, or to all Christians, “Unless your righteousness surpasses that of the Pharisees,” and so forth. For it surpasses theirs when they hate their enemies but we love them; when they merely refrain from adultery but we do not look upon a woman in order to desire her; when they do not kill but we do not even become angry. Such things, and others of this kind that have been added by Christ, commend our righteousness to God as the superior one—the righteousness by which everyone who lives by faith is justified.

For the righteousness of Christians is not something other than true faith, brought to completion in the Gospel through perfected works derived from the law. But because the scribes and Pharisees in no way believed that he had come from the law, they therefore refused to accept those things [Col. 0239A] that belong to the completion of the commandments. If, in all these matters, the righteousness of Christians does not surpass theirs, they will not be able—truth itself bearing witness—to enter the kingdom of heaven.

But some ask: since he said above, “Whoever annuls one of these least commandments,” and then, “Whoever does and teaches thus,” with reference to which commandments should this be understood? For if it concerns the legal commandments, how can he now say, “Unless your righteousness surpasses that of the scribes, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” when the one who does and teaches those things in this way is said to be great in the kingdom of heaven? Or what need was there to add anything to those same least commandments, since whoever fulfilled and taught them would become great?

Hence, as I have said, it is plainly evident that the statement was made with reference to both parts: whoever does not annul one iota or one stroke—that is, the least of the commandments added to the law—will bring all the commandments of the law and the Gospel to completion. For while the things added for perfection are being done, those also that were given beforehand for initiation are performed far more fully. Whoever does not look upon a woman in order to desire her does not commit fornication either; and if he does not become angry, he will be much farther removed from homicide.

It should be noted, as I have already mentioned above, that the righteousness of faith consists in the several parts of the virtues. And the order of perfection is exceedingly beautiful: through it the true Christian begins to surpass the work of the law, and by progress in that more abundant righteousness surpasses the righteousness of the Pharisees. Thus it follows:

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.”

Here the outstanding Teacher begins to explain more clearly the perfection he came to fulfill, so that the true righteousness of the disciples may be declared more worthy. [266] But I think we should ask why he said, “He shall be liable to judgment.” The reason is that it was written in the law: “If anyone kills a man, moved by the anger of resentment, he himself shall again be condemned to death as liable according to the judgment of the law” (Exod. XXI, 12).

“But I say to you, everyone who is angry with his brother without cause,” and what follows. Therefore I think that “without cause” ought to be removed, because it is established that it is not found in certain Hebrew codices, although nearly all the Greek copies possess it, as do the more ancient Latin ones.

Nevertheless, one must consider why the apostle Paul, writing to the Galatians, calls them “foolish and senseless” (Gal. III, 1), while, admonishing them in order to correct them, he nevertheless calls them brothers—especially since he also commends them with many praises. For this and other such reasons, perhaps some authorities decreed that this phrase should not merely be written once, but should also be understood in the other two clauses: so that, with it included, the first complete sentence would read, “Whoever is angry with his brother without cause”; then, in the second, “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’” with “without cause” understood; and third, “Whoever says, ‘Fool,’” so that the fuller sense would be, “to his brother, without cause,” as though the abbreviated sentence were understood.

Indeed, those who considered this carefully and prudently yielded to human weakness, since they say that it is natural to become angry, provided that it does not happen without cause. Certainly that prophetic saying seems rightly to be applied to this interpretation: “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. IV, 5), except that every occasion for anger is removed when we are commanded to love our enemies and to offer the other cheek to the one who strikes us.

Nevertheless, we must first ask what difference there is between one who is angry with his brother, one who says “Raca,” and one who insults his brother by calling him “fool”; and likewise how, on account of these offenses, degrees of punishment are imposed, from lesser to greater, until they extend even to the gehenna of fire. The vengeance for offenses would not have various limits of condemnation if the acts committed were not also different before the divine judgment.

Anger is the fuel of quarrels and the weapon of homicides. While it is still concealed in the mind and has not yet been stirred into greater violence, it is evidently lighter than when, through the feeling of the angry person’s voice, it bursts forth externally. For anger is nothing other than a movement of the mind stirred against someone by the bitterness of gall. [Col. 0240B]

“Raca,” however, is anger accompanied by the voice of the angry person. Yet “raca” is shown to be Hebrew, signifying the movement of an indignant mind—what grammarians call the parts of speech known as interjections, as when in Latin a grieving person says “heu!” and an angry person says “hem!” These expressions can scarcely be transferred into another language; hence this one also could not be translated, but it preserved the force of its meaning in Latin together with the sound. [267]

But whoever says “Fool” with an intention to curse is certainly more liable to the offense, inasmuch as a definite reproach is intensified against the person to whom it is directed. For it is no slight fury to violate the gravity of virtue and patience, to assail with the insult of foolishness one whom God has seasoned with the salt of his wisdom, and even impiously, by the word “fool,” to disparage God inwardly—him who works and seasons with salt. [Col. 0240C]

Therefore the Teacher of truth, wishing to show the perfection of his teaching to the more perfect, added an iota or a stroke—not merely to remove homicides from our midst, but also curses and words of anger, and even to take entirely from the heart the fuel of anger. Let the devout mind therefore understand how terrible it is to become angry, even though anger is human.

For what was said to the ancients—“If anyone kills, he shall be liable to judgment”—is also said to those who become angry, so that the difference between the righteousness of the Pharisees and that of Christians may be apparent; the latter is proclaimed to be true and perfect righteousness. But who could explain the ways in which divine discernment determines these matters? For what is charged in the law concerning homicide is charged in the Gospel concerning anger.

Thus whoever truly fears becoming liable to judgment will be watchful concerning anger and will never inflict upon his brothers the more atrocious crimes of insult. Yet it must be understood that although one is judged liable before God’s judgment on account of anger as though on account of homicide, those who are liable to the fires of gehenna are nevertheless punished differently for various reasons. [Col. 0240D]

There seems to be this difference between being liable to judgment, being liable to the council, and being liable to the fire of gehenna: in judgment, there is still a place for defense. For the matter is first rightly examined in the case, whether the accused is guilty; because in that legal condition in which matters are often deliberated before judges, many defenses arising from circumstances frequently provide assistance. By these the accused is either cleared of the offense, or, if convicted, pleads for mercy, accusing himself of having sinned through the provocation of zeal, through the surprise of error, through the impulse of chance, through the constraint of necessity, or through the guilt of forgetfulness. [Col. 0241A]

By such arguments, and by very many others of this kind, before guilt is judged in the council, the accused are often, as I have said, either cleared of the offense or obtain pardon for it through supplication.

In the council, however, although “judgment” and “council” are often used indiscriminately in the Scriptures, the question is no longer whether that same accused person should be condemned for the offense. Rather, the judges decide and confer among themselves what punishment should be inflicted on the accused, who is known to be altogether deserving of condemnation. In that council, no reasoning or defense can sometimes help him at all until he receives the sentence for his guilt. [268]

Therefore we ought first to deliberate in our mind, while the matter is still being suggested in thought through the emotion of persuasion, whether what is urged should be brought forth in speech. For just as guilt is more serious when expressed, so in the council the sentence concerning the offense is more dangerous.

Finally, concerning the deed committed—or, in what may be felt to be a lesser matter, concerning the insult against a brother—there is no need to explain in many words how terrible a conclusion follows: those whom the fire of gehenna consumes pay the penalty of their condemned guilt.

Whoever does not carefully guard himself against these degrees of offense will experience the judgment of condemnation for what he has committed, and the fire of gehenna because of the impenitence and guilt of his heart. It is certain that, just as nothing is happier in this life than a good Christian, so nothing is more worthy of condemnation than the one who, even after falling, refuses, while he has the opportunity, to think about pardon through repentance, and who, though vicious, refuses to cease from guilt by clinging to good works.

But when we despise these things as though they were insignificant, we are released for the punitive commission of more unspeakable crimes, already condemned as the cause of sin, as the Apostle teaches. [Col. 0241C]

“If, therefore, you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you,” and what follows.

He now explains the greater righteousness of Christians that he had begun to expound. Concerning the brother of whom he had said that one must not be angry, or say “Raca” or “Fool,” he teaches that it is much less permissible to retain inwardly anything that could be turned into hatred.

Indeed, it is fitting to recall Cain and his gifts. When he offered, the Lord did not look upon him or upon his gifts, plainly because he harbored envy and indignation in his heart against his brother. Hence it is said: “If you offer rightly, but do not rightly divide, you have sinned; be still.” [Col. 0241D]

What does “You have sinned; be still” mean, except: You have sinned by becoming angry or envious, or by contriving in some way something against your neighbor; cease from this foolishness; stop being angry or envious; otherwise I will not accept a gift from your hand?

Here [269] we recall both a commandment and an example. Let no one favor himself; let no one deceive himself. For if we harbor anything evil in our mind against our neighbor, we cannot offer God a gift that pleases him.

But if, conversely, our neighbor has something against us—not anger, I say, but any injury in which we have harmed him and which we remember—even at the moment of sacred offering we cannot offer what is acceptable until we have been reconciled with the one whom we offended.

What if he is absent, or is far away beyond the sea or outside the region, and something of this kind comes to mind? Must what we are offering then be abandoned, and must we search for him on foot when perhaps we cannot find him? [Col. 0242A]

The meaning is entirely clear: if the person in question is present, we ought to appease him and make satisfaction by pleading with him. But if we are completely unable to reach him, it is more fitting to go to him through the movements of the mind, with humble affection and the devotion of a loving heart; and, prostrating ourselves before the sight of the one whose gift we are offering, to entreat pardon from our brother, bound to him by the kindness of the heart.

No one doubts that, as far as depends on us, we ought to have peace with everyone, because by peace alone we are reconciled to God.

Behold, the Teacher of truth gave a command concerning remembrance before the face of the altar. What if elsewhere we offer a gift of praise, or the sacrifice of a religious life, or alms, or any sacrifice of a good work? If we remember something of this kind, should we think that it can please God merely because we are not physically before an altar? Or where will the gift be left if we are not with the person with whom we are commanded to leave it? Or if it is something that we cannot locally leave behind without ourselves, what then should be done? [Col. 0242B]

It is therefore evident that all these things do not belong to sacred religion according to the letter, but are to be understood spiritually. Nevertheless, even when fulfilled according to the historical sense concerning religious worship, they are not incompatible with it, so that faith may be understood as the temple and Christ as the altar, before whom we devotedly offer the offerings of our faith.

For he is that lofty altar of heaven before the face of the Father, beneath which the souls of the saints rest. On this altar the vows of the faithful and the gifts of holocausts are offered to the Lord. No one therefore brings the vows of the virtues sufficiently as a holocaust unless he reaches it by the steps of faith. [Col. 0242C]

If, among the multitude of the saints, we remember that someone has something against us, we ought to leave the gift of our devotion before him, return inwardly beneath the conscience of our conduct, and there, if the one whom we injured is absent, make satisfaction until, once reconciled, we may offer the gift with a pure conscience, as far as depends on us. [270]

For we are not commanded without reason to leave the gift before the altar, because whatever is rightly offered before God cannot remain unaltered. Rather, the defect of the perverse mind must be corrected, and the love that one owes first restored to the brother. [Col. 0242D]

Then he should return as quickly as possible to the one before whom he has set down the gift. Meanwhile, he also wished this to be a bond of indebtedness (*chirographum*). Therefore he said, “Do not bring back your gift, but leave it,” until, with a conscience made fit for peace, you can offer more acceptably what you vowed.

He did not reject the gift at all; rather, he sought love of neighbor, without which no one reaches the love of God. Therefore the debtor of charity’s interest must first discharge it if he wishes to please God with a gift of lawful service. For if he has not been established in his heart by the spirit of humility, he will scarcely be able to fulfill what he is commanded.

Those puffed up with pride not only disdain making satisfaction for offenses, but also do not fear injuring their brothers even more. Thus far he has spoken about repaying the debt owed to one’s neighbor; now he also commands us to have the goodwill of peace with an adversary. [Col. 0243A]

“Agree,” he says, “with your adversary while you are on the way with him.”

Here we must ask who our adversary is, with whom we are commanded to agree on the way. If we understand the statement as referring to the devil, as some think—since our adversary the devil rages against us like a lion—the whole context of the reading is overturned, and the perfection of the legal commandments is no longer immediately continued from the Gospel.

It seems a forced interpretation that we ought to be well disposed toward him, since we do not obey his deceits, lest he be tormented by eternal punishments on our account. What kind of perfection would it be to abandon vices not for the love of God, but for the sake of the one whom we determined in baptism to hate, against whom we declared war? Or how are we on the way with him, when he has never stood on the way, and, if we think rightly, we have never been with him in mind or will? [Col. 0243B]

Therefore it is better to understand the statement as referring to any brother who opposes us, or certainly to the precepts of the Gospel, so that we preserve both the continuous text of the reading and the agreement of the meanings of Scripture everywhere.

We are therefore commanded to agree with the one who opposes us on the way, showing him kindness. [271] This seems to be expressed more clearly in the Greek word εὐνοῶν (*eunōn*), that is, “being well disposed.” The meaning is:

“Since I have taught you to be reconciled with your brother if he has been injured by you, I now carry out what is greater. Even if he becomes an adversary, be well disposed toward him while you are with him on the way, with a conciliatory affection; and agree with him so that you may pursue better things pertaining to salvation through the word of the Gospel, which also opposes you while you are on the way with him.” [Col. 0243C]

For the Gospel commands us to love enemies, father and mother, brothers and sisters; indeed, it even commands us to hate one’s own life, which is sufficiently contrary to the flesh.

From these two adversaries, perhaps one is formed: at times a brother unjustly becomes an adversary, against whom the prudence of the flesh and the bitterness of gall are aroused; while, conversely, the divine word commands us not to resist evil, but to overcome evil with good.

Therefore, since the Greek has “well disposed,” while our interpretation has “consenting,” it is as though by one word we are made well disposed toward brothers, even when they oppose us for legitimate reasons, and consenting to the Gospel in which it is said, “Do not resist evil.”

No adversary is greater than the one who attacks on many fronts and grants no possibility of resistance without more serious loss. For this reason we are compelled to retain this meaning, because it agrees better with the surrounding teachings, without nevertheless refuting those who bring forward arguments on either side in defense of the Catholic interpretation. [Col. 0243D]

The sense we have fashioned, as though from two metals, is explained by what follows: he commands us to offer the other cheek to the one who strikes us, to leave the cloak to the one who takes the tunic, to yield to the one who compels us, and to go with him another thousand paces. All these things mean nothing other than favoring the adversary in his presence.

Nevertheless, we must tolerate such things in accordance with what follows, so that benevolence may accompany everything, as far as depends on us, toward the one who opposes us, with affection, while the divine oracle is always obeyed without guilt. [Col. 0244A]

No one consents better to both adversaries than the one who loves and, without sin, suffers on behalf of the one whom he loves.

We are therefore with him on the way, because the divine word itself is nothing other than the way for us. Hence David also says: “I have run the way of your commandments, for you have enlarged my heart” (Ps. CXVIII, 32).

Christ is the way, through whom and in whom we rightly walk with the adversary of our vices, namely, by the word of the Gospel. Thus, while we obey his commands, we may eventually come to life without offending the Judge. [272]

Like a traveler, the word of the Gospel walks with us temporarily, as a companion on the way; but toward the perfection of life, the word will henceforth be eternal. Thus John says in his Apocalypse that he saw, in the person of Christ, an angel who possessed an eternal Gospel. [Col. 0244B]

It will perhaps be eternal because thereafter there will be no active life, which is proclaimed by many divine Gospel sayings.

But it is not absurd to ask how our adversary walks with us on the way. For if he were walking with us on the way that is Christ, he would certainly not be an adversary. It is therefore plainly evident that the statement is rather about the way of the present age, through which we all pass together by being born, living, and dying.

There, while the adversary is still journeying with us during the time in which we live, we ought to be patient and well disposed toward him for the sake of love—not so that he may remain an adversary, but so that he may become a friend on the way of God.

But perhaps someone will ask: if the adversary remains, and he too is judged before the Judge as liable at least for the crimes of enmity, how can he, bound by guilt, hand over the guilty person to the Judge? [Col. 0244C]

He will hand us over, therefore, even though he himself is guilty, because the anger of our mutual hostility remains in him; and, since we do not wish to appease him by seeking to soothe him, it accuses us before the Judge on account of our impenitence.

To speak more plainly: the one who wounded me with a mortal wound handed me over to the hands of physicians. So, because adversity overcame me, so that I did not foster him with goodwill and consent to the word of the Gospel, he handed me over to the Judge, bound by the guilt of the bloody malice of the wound; and no further excuse benefits one who did not consent to the adversary [the text reads *noluit*, perhaps for *nolui*, “I did not consent”]. [Col. 0244D]

The meaning is therefore clear: the divine word opposes the enticements of our desires. Unless the mind consents to it, it is handed over by the one whom it has violated to the Judge, to be punished by everlasting death.

But if someone asks how the matter should be understood if the human adversary is suddenly killed, as often happens, is the opportunity for repentance removed because, in the present way, consent and the goodwill of reconciliation are no longer possible?

If, as must be admitted, pardon is granted to the guilty upon repentance, it must nevertheless be asked how one can be handed over by the person whom he killed, unless the Savior tempered the sentence in such a way that the guilty person is without doubt shown to be handed over for the punishment of sin, while pardon is not denied to those who repent.

Therefore, without specifying the manner:

“Lest he hand you over,” he says, “to the Judge.” [273]

Thus he tempered the word of uncertainty so as not to remove the opportunity for repentance. There is no doubt that the Savior himself has been established as the Judge of the living and the dead, since “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” [Col. 0245A]

The ministers to whom the person is handed over by the Judge are angels, of whom it is said: “Angels came and ministered to him.” For he is also read to come to judgment with the angels, who will separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous and cast them into the furnace of fire, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

But where he calls it the “furnace of fire,” here he figuratively called it a “prison,” which is the custody of the guilty. Yet a very terrible sentence is imposed.

“Amen, I say to you,” he says, “you will not come out from there until you repay the last quadrans.”

Let each person reflect within himself and regard this as having been specially foretold to him. For the one who speaks is truth and does not lie. What has been said to each individual, let each individual hear; and let no one presume on boldness, because he will not come out from there until he has paid every least sin. This is apparently what he signified by the quadrans. [Col. 0245B]

It must not be judged, as some have said, that “until” means that when the period has been completed, it will at some time be permitted to leave the prison, as though after the punishments have been completed. They join to this the statement of Isaiah: “The wicked shall be shut up in prison, and after a thousand years they shall be visited” (Isa. XXIV, 22).

Especially since the latter statement says simply “they shall be visited,” which can also be understood as referring to vengeance; and many plainly interpret it as referring to the day of the future age, when the wicked will receive their bodies and undergo a heavier sentence of condemnation.

Therefore, in this passage, “until” is used in an infinite sense. Wicked people, unwilling to consider this, wished not to apply their own meanings to the divine Scriptures, but to apply the Scriptures to their wicked meanings. Unwilling to attend to any of the forms of expression, or to the Holy Spirit speaking with his own authority, they fashioned for themselves a false wisdom from eloquence. [Col. 0245C]

But those who think soundly have understood that the words and eloquence of matters always serve divine wisdom like a handmaid, according to the will of those who use them in speaking.

This expression, on which they build their false argument, because it is like a boundary of time, seems sometimes to determine one matter by denying another, and sometimes to grant one by implication. This occurs in three different ways.

It happens either when both terms are completed at the same time and the sentence concerning both parts comes to an end; or, conversely, when in ordinary speech time and an action are joined together in a manner that treats both as indefinite; or when one portion of the two is finite, while the other, although joined with it, is nevertheless understood as infinite. [274]

For example, in the Psalm: “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they fail” (Ps. XVII, 38). It is as though he says: when they fail, I will immediately turn back and rest.

Likewise: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV, 49). Once they had received that power, they immediately went out from the city to preach.

Heretics, wishing to apply this principle to every occurrence of the word “until,” so that both consequences would end simultaneously, have gone astray in many places.

Nevertheless, one of the two parts is very often understood as infinite, while the other is clearly shown to be quite finite, as in the same work about which I spoke: “He did not know her until she had brought forth her firstborn son.” [Col. 0246A]

The statement is finite in the part that says, “until she had brought forth her firstborn son”; but according to the Catholic faith it is infinite in the part that says that he “did not know her,” not merely until she gave birth, but, as is established, that he never knew her. For her virginity remained undefiled. Enough has already been said about this.

The third kind of expression is when both parts of the same statement are understood as infinite, as the present passage shows: “You will not come out from there,” he says, “until you repay the last quadrans.”

Therefore both of these terms will be infinite: neither will the name of the debt ever be removed from the debt, nor will anyone bound by guilt leave that prison, after the judgment has been completed, set free.

The end of each part of this sentence must therefore be understood as without end, so that neither will the condemned person be able to escape the debt there, nor will the one shut in the prison ever remove himself from the chains of his guilt. [Col. 0246B]

In this manner of speaking it is said: “Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies beneath your feet” (Ps. CIX, 2); and likewise: “He must reign until he places his enemies beneath his feet” (1 Cor. XV, 25)—that is, until he subjects to himself all those who contradict him.

Will he not reign afterward, when his enemies have been subjected to him and placed under his power? Certainly he will reign without end, and they themselves will be subject to him without end.

For [275] it does not follow that, when his enemies have been subjected to him, he will then cease to reign; nor, because he will continue to reign forever, will those whom he has subjugated thereafter cease to be subject to him.

We also frequently use this manner of speaking. For example, I might say: “The truth of this meaning maintains its force, and that meaning will never be weakened until the truth lies.” This is plainly understood in an infinite sense: just as truth never lies, so, while truth remains, this meaning will never be emptied of its force. [Col. 0246C]

But it is asked: since a human being sinned within time by failing to repay the debt of love to his neighbor, how is it just that he should be condemned without end by a just Judge?

The meaning is very easily evident from Paul’s statement (Rom. II, 5): “According to the hardness and impenitence of his heart, he is storing up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God.” Rightly, therefore, he pays without end the treasury of wrath—he who, through the hardness and impenitence of his heart, determined to sin without end.

He did not wish to repay the debt of love to his brother; whether he wishes it or not, he will repay the punishment of wrath that he stored up for himself. [Col. 0246D]

He preserves throughout the metaphor, as though drawn from the public and judicial exaction exercised by worldly authority. The adversary, to whom love is justly owed, is introduced; the Judge, to whom the guilty person is handed over by that adversary because he did not repay the interest of affection, is introduced; then the minister who diligently exacts the entire payment; afterward the prison in which the guilty person is confined; and finally the sentence that extends to the last quadrans of the coin, since he cannot leave the prison of punishment before he has paid every least debt.

The quadrans is therefore exacted, but the punishment of sin is paid. Hence some, because the whole world consists mystically of four elements, have wished to interpret the quadrans mystically. The final portion of these is shown to be earth; and therefore, through earth, the offenses of every earthly action and the preoccupation of the flesh are exacted in punishment by the fire, as though they were the last quadrans. [Col. 0247A]

According to this interpretation, the first quadrans is rightly said to be fire, because it comes from the heavenly realm and signifies love; the second is air, which we continually breathe and through which our life is signified; the third is water, through which we are reborn in the Holy Spirit; and finally the last quadrans is counted as earth, through which the carnal life and the sins of earthly contamination are represented.

Hence we also read that it was said to the first human being: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19). It is as though he said: “You will repay what you chose to be, even to the last quadrans,” because none of your sins will remain unpunished. [276]

Therefore let the prudent mind recall—even if, wherever I may have omitted mentioning what I proposed above—that all these things are viewed as a kind of genus through those eight beatitudes. [Col. 0247B]

This is why the prayer of faith here implores that we be delivered from evil, that is, from the adversary, through the spirit of piety, so that the mind may become gentle and be able to endure everything. Otherwise, if it has not become gentle, how can it consent with the adversary on the way?

Yet even if the statement is to be referred to the Gospel, how will anyone consent to its commands unless he has been filled with the spirit of piety? The one who consents is the one who hears and understands it devoutly.

Then, whatever he has understood—even if it sounds contrary to his own will—he does not oppose it, but loves it all the more by obeying and rejoices to fulfill it, even if it conflicts with his own habits.

He does not twist it to suit his own will; rather, he humbly directs his habits and the whole intention of his heart toward what is said.

You have heard that it was said to the ancients: “You shall not commit adultery.” But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

This sentence therefore depends upon what he says elsewhere: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it.” He fulfills it in what he says: “Whoever looks at a woman.” Yet he does not abolish the law when he removes adultery from the heart and commands chastity to be preserved in the flesh. For he does not release that command, but fulfills in the Gospel what was lacking in the law, so that the righteousness of Christians may be greater than that of the scribes and Pharisees.

Here it must be considered that he did not say, “Everyone who desires a woman,” but “whoever looks at her in order to desire her”—that is, with the purpose and intention of desiring her, consenting to lust, if the opportunity for its fulfillment should arise. The Greeks explain this passage more significantly with two words, πάθος and προπάθειαν—that is, “passion” and “pre-passion.” They call passion what is reckoned as a fault of the soul; pre-passion, although it has the beginning of fault, is nevertheless not held as a crime.

For προπάθεια is a temporary or sudden movement of the soul, such as when someone becomes angry or falls in love with something; πάθος, or ἦθος, as some say, is a certain disposition or deliberation of the soul arising from consent, almost like a natural habit of the mind—as when we call someone irascible or a lover of something. For πάθος is said not only of anyone who is angry or in love, but also of one who harbors anger against another, or mercy, or desire, or love.

Hence, earlier, after saying, “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not kill,’” he fulfilled what was lacking and added that “everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment.” Thus he does not simply say “everyone who is angry,” but adds “with his brother.” David aptly explains the same sense in two words: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Psalm 4:5). It is as if he said: If you become angry, since you are prone to anger, do not sin by becoming angry with your brothers.

There is no doubt that, just as προπάθεια is an incidental movement without deliberation toward either a good or an evil deed, so πάθος is an affection of the deliberating soul, if opportunity for carrying it out is present. Hence it should perhaps not be doubted that, just as, in their consummation, anger against one’s brother makes persons liable to judgment as murder does, so desire for a woman, or the wicked deliberation of the mind concerning any illicit intercourse, makes persons adulterers and liable to death according to the law.

For “adultery” is understood there in general as every illicit intercourse, because when he said, “You shall not commit adultery,” he prohibited every crime of lust. Moses later distributed these among various kinds of offenses and condemned each by its own judgment. Otherwise, in those ten words of the law, neither fornication, nor intercourse between males, nor the other monstrous forms of lust are seen to be expressly prohibited. It is therefore clear that, although adultery properly refers to intercourse with another man’s wife, it is nevertheless prohibited in general as every incestuous act of lust, as I have admitted.

In the same way here, when the desire for a woman—which is removed from the heart as though it were natural—must be removed so that a Christian may not be an adulterer, it immediately becomes clear that he has commanded the desire for males, or the flame of any lust—which are more properly called monstrosities of depravity than vices—to be utterly removed from the heart. For just as the righteousness of chastity is demanded more strictly in the Gospel, so conversely a harsher punishment is imposed upon the guilty.

Therefore, if we are stirred by some pre-passion, we must take the eyes of the mind away from contemplating the deed, lest a slight suggestion pass into pleasure and the affection of the heart, and lest we be condemned as guilty on account of a passion deliberately embraced by the soul. What do you think? When we are absent from women, if we look upon a female in our heart—or, what is more criminal, upon some other object—in such a way that, if the opportunity existed, we would already have made a fixed decision within ourselves, and if in our consciousness we repeatedly turn over some person in meditation for this purpose, is the heart not committing adultery where such deliberation is present, even if the outward appearance that might be desired is absent from the eyes of the body?

Indeed, we then commit adultery in the heart when those eyes are opened which, because of the punishment for sin, we read were wrongly opened in our first parents in paradise, and when the incentives of the flesh affect them. Then the reins of desire are loosened toward the affection of lust; an image is present before the eyes of the mind, where only the opportunity for sinning is lacking, not the will. This intention is called not προπάθεια but πάθος, because the mind, wrongly enticed, has passed into the passion of consent.

Rightly, therefore, according to the Gospel, such deliberation in every undertaking of vice is reckoned as a deed before the eyes of the Judge who is meanwhile observing us, since each person is judged according to what he is or what he carries in his heart. For no one can doubt or question that a good will alone, and the mind’s ready devotion, when the ability to act is lacking, is acceptable to the merciful rewarder on account of the affection of charity.

It is therefore pleasing that “peace on earth to people of good will,” and “glory to God in the highest,” are proclaimed by the angels. So, indeed, by contrast, those whose will is corrupted and is enticed by anger or hatred toward a brother, or by desire for incest or shameful conduct, and is nourished by luxury, by any inclinations of malice, and by deliberation upon vices, are justly threatened with the punishment of guilt. For on the day when God judges the hidden things of human beings, a person is accused or defended not according to what he was unable to do or was not permitted to do, but according to what he was and intended in his conscience.

It follows:

> “And if your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you.”

This sentence is attached to the preceding words, where he says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her.” From this it is clear that the right eye must be understood as whatever is inwardly desired with the mind’s delight. For when that interior eye is opened for desire, we are immediately more violently scandalized by the disturbed movement of lust.

It is appropriately called “right” because it belongs to the better part of the mind. Just as the superior part of the body is called the right side, so that sight from within, because it sees more excellently, is rightly called “right.” It causes us to stumble when it is opened for desire and the mind is led captive through various and unlawful forms of thought, away from the state of purity and righteousness.

That right eye, when it is drawn away by enticement toward desire, must both be torn out and thrown away from us, lest through it we seize what is harmful. It must be torn out before it slips into vice, lest what is best in us quickly be bent toward guilt. For what can cause us to stumble more than what calls us back from our purpose and removes us from the way of righteousness?

Therefore, if this eye had not caused our first parent to stumble, he would never, oppressed by fear and shame before the face of God, have hidden himself while placed in paradise. If, before wantonness defiled it, he had recalled it from looking at what was forbidden, he would never have suffered the stumbling block of error.

And for that reason such a gaze must immediately be thrown away before the mind slips into vice—not because it is right, but because it causes us to stumble by desiring wrongly, even though it has been well placed within the law of God’s commandments. Otherwise, as long as it is fixed upon charity, it must be continued and preserved in contemplation, because “great peace” is believed to belong to those who love the law of God, and no stumbling block can come upon them.

But if it begins to cause us to stumble through the enticement of pleasure, the sight of our thoughts must immediately be torn out, lest it look upon a woman in order to desire her. It must therefore be cast away, lest it spread outward toward the things of the flesh; rather, cleansed by heavenly disciplines, it should always guard itself by returning, like a cherubim, around the altar and toward the mercy seat.

Concerning this eye of contemplation, the bridegroom sings in the Song of Songs to the Church:

> “You have wounded my heart, my sister; you have wounded my heart with one lock of your neck” (Song of Songs 4:9).

For she wounded the bridegroom’s heart in one of her eyes with the sword of charity, because, stained by no wantonness of the flesh, she was accustomed to look nowhere but toward that same mercy seat. Filled with an immense love for it, she also said of herself:

> “I am wounded by love.”

Such an eye is called the eye of doves, which dwell by their windows. Therefore, bringing not scandal but peace, it draws nothing outward toward desire; rather, whatever belongs to salvation is kept pure within.

Because of the context of the reading, since the subject of a woman is mentioned on both sides, we have more appropriately referred the middle portion between the two sections to this interpretation, so that the divine discourse might continue coherently. Above, he declares that whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her is an adulterer in his heart. Now again, before he reaches that point, he commands the same eye of the heart to be torn out and thrown away, lest it look upon what will cause a deceived person to perish.

And it must be noted: if the things that are right in us—namely, the eye or the hand—sometimes cause us to stumble, how much more do the things that are left? For if the soul slips inwardly, the body, which is more inclined toward sinning, does so much more readily.

And therefore that superior eye must be cleansed, and the unlawful gaze torn out. For while it is continually directed without scandal from a perverse vision toward the mercy seat, the left and exterior eye, restrained by the law of that other eye, is daily guarded from every stain of vice.

Nevertheless, although I have spoken in this way, I do not claim to have exhausted the various interpretations of the senses. For in the right eye or right hand may be indicated the affection of brothers, a wife, children, dear friends, or any relatives, since we love them no less than our eyes. Those who wish to show that they love someone greatly commonly say: “I love him as my own eyes.”

Perhaps, therefore, the phrase “if your right eye or right hand causes you to stumble” was added to heighten the force of love, so that, if it becomes an impediment to contemplating the true light, you should cut it off, and utterly sever whatever may be the object of your most special love, lest it obstruct you.

Care must therefore be taken lest, while we wish to win others, we ourselves perish forever. Hence in Leviticus it is said of the high priest, whose soul is dedicated to the worship of God, that he must not be defiled on account of his father, mother, or children—that is, he must recognize no affection except for the one whose worship he has been dedicated to (Leviticus 21:11).

Nevertheless, although the hand and the eye are the principal parts of one body, because they do not perform the same action, I would never say that they signify one and the same thing. Therefore, while retaining the interpretation I preferred above, the eye may be understood as any one of the teachers whose office is to foresee the conduct and life of their subjects, or perhaps as some friend whose counsel you use in examining your actions and meditating upon heavenly things.

If such a person causes you to stumble, he must be cast away, lest you perish, enticed by his evil example, or rush into death, corrupted by his error.

The hand, on the other hand, may signify, according to the preceding interpretation, some affluent or prosperous activity of the active life; according to the interpretation we have just offered, perhaps any energetic helper amid the affairs of life, through whose assistance our life in this world may also prosper through successful results.

When such a person begins to oppose us and becomes a stumbling block in the law of God’s commandments, it is better, after cutting him off, to be saved without his help than for our whole body to perish with him in Gehenna.

The right hand may also signify the active life itself, under which Martha is occupied with various tasks and responsibilities. In the same way, the eye may express the contemplative life, by which the weak are often scandalized because they are unable to contemplate with complete purity.

The former are scandalized because of excessive sloth in life and the idleness of torpor; the latter because of the manifold bustle of the world and the weariness of their many occupations. Therefore, whatever eye or hand of such people suffers the stumbling block, if one of the two ways of life cannot sometimes be followed, it is better to retain only the other than to perish through the scandal caused by the excessive weakness of both.

The greatest care must therefore be taken lest someone who cannot enjoy the contemplative life grow sluggish in idleness while neglecting the active life, or lest someone who is occupied with the practical affairs of business wither away from inward sweetness, when he might make better progress in contemplation.

Now, since we are commanded to cut off or throw away from us the right eye or hand if they should cause us to stumble, there can be no doubt concerning the left ones, where whatever is more excellent in the body is cut away.

If someone wishes to take this literally, although his affection may arise from piety, he should not be heeded as though the cutting off of bodily members were being preached. Rather, the wickedness of conduct and the perversity of actions are to be cut away.

Therefore, whatever inwardly in the eye of the mind wishes to overthrow us from the way of injustice and upright conduct must immediately be torn out by us. And whatever outwardly drives us away from the practice of the virtues, even if it appears to be the right hand or eye, must be driven far from the body of our fellowship as a stumbling block to our salvation, lest—God forbid—the whole body perish in Gehenna, corrupted by its disease.

It was also said:

> “Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.”  
> “But I say to you: Whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.”

Our Lord and Savior explains this passage more fully a little later: Moses commanded this because of the hardness of their hearts—not because he wished divorce, but because he removed the danger of murder. For it was much milder, even if a grievous separation should occur, than that blood should be shed through hatred and persecution of one’s wife.

The Lord, who loves peace, had not commanded this. Moses granted it on his own authority, for the sake of preventing something worse. Therefore the author of love and teacher of truth restored to those who were more perfect what was lacking, and rejected the divorce that arises from hostility, which had been granted to the hard-hearted and not to the devout and gentle.

Christ therefore took nothing away from the law in this passage or elsewhere; rather, he added many things. Thus, when the law had commanded that freedom be granted by authority of a certificate of divorce, it nevertheless, through reflection upon grace and avoidance of guilt in a worse crime, imposed—let me not say a desire for peace, but—the adultery of the hated wife upon the husband, when she commits adultery after being dismissed.

He says: “Whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication,” as if he were saying: Whoever rejects the marriage bond on account of some matter, or because of the ugliness of morals or bodies, and, overcome by injuries, separates what God has joined, compels the weaker party to commit fornication with another; and he himself becomes the cause of her guilt, since by dismissing her he makes her commit adultery.

This is especially so because formerly there were many reasons for putting away wives—for example, if she were a leper, barren, hateful, adulterous, and so forth. Christ, however, granted permission to abandon her only on account of fornication.

Rightly, therefore, since that alone is the vice by which the fidelity of chastity and the marriage bond are first broken, he does not make her commit adultery; rather, she herself is the cause of her guilt and of the dissolution of the bond.

In all other cases she must be loved and retained, so that the superior righteousness of Christians may be commended and the stronger charity of marriage preserved until death.

In this commandment concerning chastity, many questions arise here and there because of the brevity of the treatment. I have decided to touch only upon those demanded by necessity. Since it has been sufficiently expressed what a husband may do if his wife has committed fornication, it must therefore be asked, conversely, what the wife should do if the husband has committed fornication.

Paul says that neither of them has authority over his own body (1 Corinthians 7:4), and the Lord, excepting only the cause of fornication, did not say whose cause he meant—whether the man’s or the woman’s. For this reason the two parties appear to be joined together under one law, lest one of them do what is not permitted to the other, even if the husband has authority over the woman.

Authority is given to him because he is superior by nature and because the woman is read to have been made from the man, not because he is his wife’s servant; and he is commanded not to seek a dissolution.

Otherwise the Apostle’s statement applies: “In whatever you judge another, you condemn yourself, for you do the same things that you judge” (Romans 2:1). Therefore whoever wishes to dismiss his wife on the charge of fornication must himself also be free from fornication, since nothing is more unjust than to cast away one’s wife on account of fornication while failing to guard oneself from the same vice.

It follows:

> “And whoever marries the woman released from her husband commits adultery.”

He commits adultery because, according to the Apostle, she must remain unmarried or perhaps be reconciled to her husband (1 Corinthians 7:11). From this it appears that the husband who dismissed her cannot, while she is still alive, take another woman in marriage, as the Apostle makes clear.

But some ask whether the woman also commits adultery when she causes the man with whom she has had intercourse to commit adultery. From what is said here and elsewhere, whether in the Gospel or by the Apostle, it is sufficiently clear that even if she has left her husband on account of fornication, she is not permitted to join herself to another man—how much less if she has been dismissed by her husband.

It may happen either that she leaves or that the husband dismisses her against her will. But whichever of these occurs, neither of them may, while the other remains alive, be joined to anyone else. For although separation may take place on either side on account of fornication, it is granted not by command but by rightful indulgence.

Thus, because the will of one has forbidden marital intercourse and the guilt of the other has compelled it, there is no doubt that both must remain without intercourse unless they are reconciled to one another—those who previously, if they wished, were permitted not to separate.

And this is so because the situation arose not from a vow but from a separation. Therefore either they should return together or they should practice continence together, so that fornication may not have greater force in the matter than the marriage bond.

But where the vows of both agree, since God is involved in the matter, the marriage of the flesh may not be revoked, because it was not man but God who joined them. For it is written: “What God has joined, let no man separate” (Matthew 19:6).

Man therefore does not separate them; rather, God joins more perfectly to himself those whom the charity of Christ, through a blessed vow, invites to the freedom of life.

But since, as I said, very many questions boil up all around this subject, let these simple remarks about them suffice, although brevity has not allowed me to set them out beforehand or to confirm everything with testimonies from Scripture.

Again, he says, you have heard that it was said to the ancients: “You shall not swear falsely, but you shall fulfill your oath to the Lord your God.”

Here, as everywhere in these matters, the accumulation of righteousness is restored. For by whatever a person swears, he either reverences, loves, or fears it. Therefore it was lawful under the law for the carnal people to swear by God.

This was granted to them as to little children: just as they sacrificed victims to God rather than offering them to idols, so they were permitted to swear by God—not because they were doing this rightly, but because it was better to offer it to God than to demons.

Yet they always maintained the worst habit of swearing by the elements, as they are often reproved by the prophets. They swore by angels; they swore by the city of Jerusalem and by the temple. They also revered creatures and bodily things with the service and honor due to God.

Therefore he condemns the superstition of their old obstinacy and removes the religious practice of swearing by heaven, earth, or one’s head, because they referred the veneration of the oath to an insult against God.
