The Jews, moreover, did some things from the law, others from the tradition and superstition of the Pharisees, and others because they had been deceived by the error of falsehood. Removing all these things, the Teacher of truth fulfilled what was lacking in the law.

Hence he also says: “But I say to you, do not swear at all by heaven,” and he adds, “because it is the throne of God.” It is indeed God’s throne, and not God himself, because it is proved to be a creature.

In the law, however, he says: “You shall fulfill your oath to the Lord your God.” But they, by contrast, either supposed that heaven was something greater, or perhaps believed that if they swore by it they would not be bound by their oath.

Therefore the provident arbiter so regulates the sentence that heaven is believed to be God’s creature and yet, because according to spiritual understanding it is God’s throne, he asserts that whoever swears by it is bound by his oath.

The same must be understood about the earth, by which he altogether forbids swearing, because it is the footstool of his feet. This does not mean that heaven presides by reason of the enormous size of its limbs and encloses this vast expanse of air between its legs, as the Anthropomorphites suppose, so that it may touch the earth as a footstool with its feet.

Rather, the holy Church of God is signified by the earth. It is rightly called the footstool of his feet because, subject to the Creator and prostrate beneath his steps, it submits itself in faithful devotion.

Hence also in the Psalm: “Until I place your enemies as the footstool of your feet” (Psalm 109:2). The enemies become a footstool when, reconciled to God, they bow devotedly under his dominion.

This is the land of the living, founded upon Christ’s solidity over the waters. In another sacramental vision, it is seen by Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, together with the seventy elders, beneath the feet of the God of Israel, as though it were a work of sapphire, and as though heaven were clear.

Do not be surprised, meanwhile, if the holy Church of God is now called earth, now his footstool, and at another time is seen beneath his feet as heaven when it is clear. One and the same reality is disclosed with a light clearer than day through various figurative enigmas, on account of the efficacy of its merits and the significance of its causes.

For this reason he forbade anyone to swear by the earth, which is his footstool and, as clear heaven beneath his feet, is established in enduring solidity—that is, the holy Church of God.

Therefore, if someone thinks that earth, heaven, or Jerusalem is something more than a creature, he is in error. But if someone thinks that he is not bound by an oath because these things are seen to be creatures, let him consider that greater mysteries are contained and shadowed forth in all of them.

Who does not know that the earthly Jerusalem bears the image of that heavenly Jerusalem? Therefore whoever swears by it owes the oath to the one whose city it is, and it is rightly thought that it should be rendered to no one else.

But, to speak more simply, they argued that they were not bound by an oath if they had sworn by these things only according to the letter, because it had been said: “You shall fulfill your oath to the Lord your God.”

Therefore he teaches that nothing among God’s creatures is so insignificant that anyone should swear falsely by it, since all created things, from the highest to the lowest, are governed by divine Providence.

Hence he begins with God’s throne, which is the highest, and reaches down to the white or black hair, which is the lowest. He indicates that we should not even swear by our head, although nothing seems to belong more closely to us.

But how is it ours, when we have no power to make or change the color from black to white or from white to black? Therefore the one who holds all things ineffably and is present everywhere is owed the oath of truth.

Whoever swears by his head owes the oath to the one who has authority over the head and whose figure the head bears. For Christ is our head, and God is Christ’s head. Therefore whoever swears by his head owes his oath to the one whose figure and authority remain in it.

Nevertheless, since these practices arose from the superstition or error of the Jews, he cuts away what was harmful and superfluous and brings the matter to perfection by removing the opportunity for swearing, which had been lacking.

Yet, because the Apostle appears to have sworn frequently, and because among Christians oaths concerning the truth are more often allowed for the sake of satisfying another—although they arise from evil—it is clear that Christ did not altogether prohibit swearing. Rather, on account of the opportunity for perjury, he taught what is more perfect and showed that whatever is done beyond this, even if permitted for the sake of truth, arises from evil, when someone is compelled to swear in order to convince another who does not believe.

[Note: “Here this should be inserted, or at least understood”; a word which authors of that age, in their customary use of ellipsis, omit in this and similar constructions of phrases.]

This is why the Apostle often swears, in order to persuade the weak to believe. This is why the Church frequently allows her members to swear for the sake of the bond of peace and the assent of faith.

But the Lord taught what is more perfect, permitted what belongs to weakness, and cut away what was superstitious and harmful. For just as someone who does not speak cannot lie, so someone who never swears cannot commit perjury.

Therefore no one should seek an oath as a good thing. Rather, on account of another’s weakness—which arises from evil, since weakness is evil—one should use an oath as an aid to truth, trusting in it in order to persuade someone whom one rightly sees to be wavering in necessary faith.

Otherwise:

> “Let your speech,” he says, “be: Yes, yes; No, no.”

For evangelical truth altogether does not admit an oath. Another person’s weakness compels it, when someone cannot accept simple truth.

Yet every faithful statement is rightly accepted in place of an oath, and therefore in affirmation it must always contain “yes, yes,” and in denial “no, no.” It is enough for the mouth to say “that is” concerning what is in the heart; and for the mouth to say “that is not” concerning what is not in the heart.

Whatever is otherwise beyond this rule arises either from falsehood or from another’s weakness, even if what is sworn is true. Therefore he does not say, “Whatever is more than this is evil,” but moderates the sentence and says, “It is from evil.” For if anything more or less slips in, it is proved to arise from evil.

Accordingly, what is in the heart must also be in the mouth; what is not in the heart must by no means be there, because it ought not to be in the mouth. Therefore, if anyone takes care to speak the truth, he must first dip the pen of his tongue inwardly in truth, and then bring forth from that same truth the truth outwardly in his mouth.

Every truth is truth from Truth, and everything that exists has its being because it is from the one who is. Thus every truth receives from the True One what makes it altogether truth. Therefore it is not said simply but twice: “Let all your speech be: Yes, yes; No, no.”

For it is not permissible to confuse these in reverse order, so that “yes” and “no” coexist in the same statement, which the Apostle rejects. Rather, in the essence of truth that we carry in our hearts, what we utter with our mouths must be “yes” or “no.”

Truth, however, is God, and whoever speaks the truth speaks from him. For just as everything that exists has its being from the one who is essentially being, so from him who is God, the Truth in us and in our faith, what is true must be spoken by the mouth.

Otherwise, even if something appears to be true, unless it receives its being from him, it is not truly so. For being belongs substantially to God; to us, to created things, and to all affairs, it belongs accidentally.

Therefore whatever we are, whatever exists in us or from us, and whatever exists around us, has its being from him who is. But if it has not received being from him, then it does not exist.

For this reason the marvelous ordering of things shows that everything which is not, because it does not have being from him who is, is no less truly “not” than what exists is truly “is”; while what exists shares in being from him who is.

From this it follows that in the mouth of a Christian truth must always be present no less in denial than in affirmation. Yet no one can guard such things, which are so arduous and difficult, without the spirit of fortitude; and no one will fulfill the more perfect parts of life and the completed righteousness of the heavenly kingdom unless he hungers and thirsts for righteousness.

You have heard that it was written: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.” “He shall repay” must be understood, so that the undeveloped age of human life might be prepared, as it were, with the beginning of righteousness.

But Christ, revealing the righteousness of a perfected life, added what was lacking. Hence, here as in the other passages, it is clear that the things belonging to the law lie between the prudence of the flesh and the completed righteousness of the Gospel.

Two boundaries therefore remain on either side: one that draws downward toward guilt, and the other that more perfectly fulfills the righteousness of the kingdom. The middle between these still sets forth the discipline of the law for the untrained.

It is certainly no small degree of righteousness not to repay someone who has inflicted harm with more harm than he has caused. For the prudence of the flesh, which the Apostle calls death (Romans 8:6), consists in taking revenge, plotting, desiring, cleverly pursuing the things of the flesh, and other matters of this kind.

The righteousness of the law separates us from these things and begins to instruct its still earthly pupils in the beginning of the perfect life. Then the righteousness of Christ, through which the kingdom of heaven is worthily sought, teaches us not to resist evil at all.

The righteousness of the Gospel would indeed be greater if it commanded each person to return less injury to the one who inflicted harm than he had received. But now it far surpasses that standard, since it commands us not to resist evil.

Therefore the righteousness of the Pharisees possesses something more than the prudence of the flesh, yet it lies far below the righteousness of the kingdom. Hence it is rightly said to Christians: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

But no one will complete this righteousness worthily without the spirit of counsel and the grace of mercy. Such people must be endured in the spirit of gentleness as though they were frenzied and out of their minds, so that at some point they may recover their senses and those who were previously persecutors may become enduring friends.

For a disciple of Christ, therefore, it is little, in this respect, for the perfection of righteousness merely not to inflict on the one who has caused harm more than he has received according to the law. Even if he returns less, or nothing at all, that is the integrity of this perfection, according to the Lord’s command—not to resist evil.

For this reason let us establish the boundaries of righteousness, so that we may carefully contemplate their middle points according to their proportion.

The beginning of righteousness is not to repay more, but to exact from the one who has caused harm an equal repayment according to the law. Its perfection, however, is not to resist evil, but to be prepared to endure everything with the greatest patience.

The middle points between these are: to return much less than one has suffered, or to return nothing at all.

The first boundary—“a tooth for a tooth, an eye for an eye,” or at least demanding loss for loss in equal measure—although it is contained within the limits of righteousness, is nevertheless nourished by the prudence of the flesh. Because of its proximity to that prudence, it is obscured, even though it holds a degree of righteousness.

But to be prepared to endure everything for Christ and not to resist evil is proclaimed as the integrity of life and the completed virtue of righteousness.

The middle between these—demanding much less than one has suffered—still clings to the beginning and is frequently disturbed by some prudence of the flesh. To return no evil at all already clings to perfection; and if it arises from love of Christ, it persists in the spirit of gentleness.

When the spirit of fortitude is present for enduring everything, so that one does not resist evil even when one has the power to do so, complete righteousness is possessed in the patience of Christ.

Nevertheless, we must consider what he says: “Do not resist evil.” Are vices and sins not evil, against which we struggle with every effort of the mind? Or is our adversary, the devil, not evil, of whom the Apostle says, “Resist him, strong in faith” (1 Peter 5:9)?

These things are certainly evil, but the divine discourse is not speaking of those evils. There are evils that wound the soul and by which we are punished with eternal death; and there are temporal evils by which we are afflicted in the present so that we may be tested. Once tested, we are not put to shame, but await the crown of the contest.

It is these temporal evils that he commands us not to resist, because through patience they cooperate with us for good. But the evil of sin remains to be guarded against and driven away, lest it corrupt the integrity of the soul, since, when it finds allies, it cooperates toward death.

Therefore, if such evils are suggested to us inwardly or outwardly, they must certainly be resisted and avoided. But if they are temporal evils, even though they are inflicted by the devil or by some human being, they must not be resisted; they must be endured with the greatest patience.

Job, the true athlete, confirms this by his example, having foreseen it well. Struck by many evils, he does not resist; yet, when tested inwardly, he does not wrongly admit sin.

I have said this so that the diligent reader may observe the freedom of Scripture in its manner of speaking, because it does not always fear the slanders of heretics, but leaves us to understand the rules of Catholic truth through the effectiveness of its expressions.

Therefore it did not say, “Do not resist this or that evil,” but absolutely: “Do not resist evil.” Yet it immediately explains more fully, part by part, what evil it means.

It follows:

If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also.

By the right cheek, our conscience—which we possess according to God—is rightly understood. If someone strikes us there by blaming what is most conspicuous and prominent in us, let us willingly offer our whole body to be afflicted, lest, unable to bear reproaches concerning what is most important, we lose it. By these three kinds of injury every evil of the present life is distinguished. For everything we suffer either afflicts us with tortures in our body, or troubles us externally through the loss of possessions, or certainly harasses us through the various activities of our affairs. But in all these things we must be ready to endure and patient. Hence the Prophet says: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready. I will sing and play music in my glory” (Psalm 107:1).

The heart of that person is ready who is inwardly prepared to suffer for Christ and who, though outwardly engaged in compulsory service, is devoted to enduring with the greatest patience whatever may be inflicted. Therefore, on account of these two cheeks, the prophetic statement is repeated. It is as though he said: “My heart is ready, O God, to endure inwardly all the reproaches of the wicked; it is also ready outwardly, for your sake, willingly to endure whatever can torment me.” For this reason I will joyfully sing and play music in my glory. “In my glory,” I say, because, secure in a good conscience, I am put to shame by none of the things I suffer. “Our glory,” the Apostle says, “is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12). By these words it is plainly evident that whenever a Christian is struck on one cheek, he must always be ready devotedly to offer the other to be struck.

Accordingly, it is deliberately said: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also.” He said “the other,” not “the left,” as though he were saying: “Offer him the other right cheek.” For according to this interpretation the righteous person is wholly right-handed; and, like Ehud in the Book of Judges, he uses both hands as right hands (Judges 3:15), while the human being’s outward and inward virtue is sacrificed as a holocaust to the Lord. This is more correctly understood than taking the words literally, as though the left cheek were to be presented when the right had been struck.

Otherwise Christ, during his Passion, did not fulfill what he taught his disciples: although prepared to suffer, he did not offer the other cheek to the one who struck him. Paul likewise did not fulfill it when he was struck in the face. He said to the high priest: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall!” (Acts 23:3); and, “If I have spoken wrongly, testify about the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23).

What do you think? Is Christ contrary to his own commandments? Or did Paul, the disciple of truth, forget what had been commanded him in the Gospel? Certainly not. For Christ not only offered the other cheek, but mercifully offered his whole body and soul for us upon the cross. And Paul’s readiness to die for Christ was afterward proved by his suffering. Therefore Christ taught what he displayed in his deeds, not what some delirious person might frivolously devise for himself from the words of the Gospel.

For it is of no benefit to offer the flesh of the other cheek to the one who strikes, if the devoted cheek of the mind is not offered with it also. This is what Christ taught when he said: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29). What sort of humility ought to be, he showed from his own example: he portrayed the evangelical man. Therefore whoever serves in the Gospel must be prepared to suffer for the Gospel if necessity arises.

Jeremiah likewise says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth; he shall give his cheek to the one who strikes him, he shall be filled with reproaches” (Lamentations 3:27, 30). When he is filled with reproaches, he is inwardly struck on the right cheek; when he is commanded to offer the other cheek outwardly—that is, the right one—he is commanded to offer his whole body to be struck for the Gospel.

Thus we must keep offering successive right cheeks to the adversary who beats us, until either the enemy’s anger is changed into the harmony of peace and true love, or the whole right-sided person, afflicted by blows and sufferings, becomes a holocaust. Behold, it is plainly evident how far the summit of perfection stands above the narrowness of the Law. The Law restrained the carnal people through fear of punishment and moderated their raging minds by the harsh retaliation of vengeance. But the Lord, wishing to prove by deeds themselves our faith, which works through love, not only forbids each person to become the avenger of an injury inflicted upon him; he also commands him, with the insult he has endured set aside, to offer the other cheek, and thereafter freely to suffer for the Lord as a freeborn man.

“And to the one,” he says, “who wishes to go to court with you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak also.”

By this statement he commands us not only to endure, in perishable possessions, the violent judgments of human courts by which those who seize our goods strip us, but also, willingly and freely, if someone wishes by a violent legal judgment to take our tunic, to let him have our cloak as well, and not to resist evil.

By the tunic we rightly understand whatever is more necessary to us from our substance; by the cloak, we may appropriately understand whatever is externally added from what is superfluous. Through these two things all those possessions are signified concerning which someone may contend with us in court, so that we may gladly transfer them from our right into his, voluntarily and without any legal dispute.

Hence Paul praises his hearers: “You received with joy the seizure of your possessions” (Hebrews 10:34). If this is understood of the necessary clothing of life, how much more ought we to despise what is superfluous? Through these two categories, therefore, it is shown generally that every form of money and property ought to be despised.

Accordingly, some interpreters have translated “cloak” as “garment.” Luke, reversing the order, first mentions “garment” and then says not to withhold the tunic (Luke 6:29). From this it is clear that necessary things are to be understood by “tunic,” while by “garment” all that remains over is meant—as though he were saying: “If anyone wishes to take from you those things that presently abound for you, give him also whatever necessity of life you possess.”

A garment is an item of human clothing; but “garment,” among philosophers also, denotes the whole equipment of one’s possessions. Every tunic is therefore a garment, but not every garment is called a tunic. Thus what is less necessary is called a garment; or, rather, whatever belongs to an abundance of great possessions is shown, not without reason, to be something that ought to be despised.

A Christian must therefore despise worldly wealth, so that he may generously rebuke the empty desire of fools and the vanity of insatiable greed, and show that he is already rich in Christ through hope in future goods. But the unbelief of many now ravages their minds with terrible force. Hence disputes and quarrels over financial matters sometimes rage even among churchmen. Brother fights brother in court, and now there are few who either by action or by teaching lay a hand to remedy this.

Nevertheless, the sentence remains in force: “Whoever loosens one of these commandments and teaches others to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.” And also: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” Therefore each faithful hearer should reflect within himself and not follow the great mass of the crowd. Rather, let him hold fast the examples of the commandments and of the few who are perfected. Even if what is commanded is difficult, an abundant reward is promised to them in heaven.

Some, however, transmit a higher interpretation of this passage: the tunic is understood as the soul, while the cloak is the external body; thus, if someone wishes to destroy your soul, you should surrender your body also in martyrdom. In a similar way they give another interpretation of the cheek: if someone among the heretics strikes you with one testimony of Scripture, offer him another, until, conquered by the truth, he finally comes to his senses.

“And whoever,” he says, “forces you to go one mile, go with him two.”

Therefore, give him not only your clothing without judicial contention, but yourself also. He has spoken according to the custom of the ancients. Accordingly, not only Jesus but also Simon of Cyrene was compelled to carry the cross after him.

Whoever bears the cross under compulsion carries it when, necessity having been imposed upon him, he devotedly endures not merely the burden of preaching the Gospel, but—crucified to the world in accordance with the Gospel—the burdens and heat of this age. To him it is rightly said: “If anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two.” It is as though he said: “Go with him two, so that you may be ready not merely in your feet but in your heart.”

But why did he say one thousand paces, and neither more nor fewer? I do not think this was done without a mystery, especially since he commands us to go the additional two with him, yet does not allow us to depart from the measure of one thousand paces. For if two additional miles are added to one thousand paces, the total is three thousand. Thus, just as the perfection of sufferings is proclaimed through these three examples, so the final limit of the word is concluded by a threefold number, and perfection is consecrated in it through the number one thousand.

For in the Law the Sabbath journey is one thousand paces, since on the Sabbath it was not permitted to go more than one thousand paces. This Sabbath journey therefore signifies spiritual perfection. On the Sabbath it is not permitted to perform servile works; rather, one must always pursue freely and generously the things that belong to perfection. We ought to do those things that pertain to the future Sabbath, concerning which Isaiah says: “There will be Sabbath after Sabbath” (Isaiah 66:23). For whoever here and now has kept a perverse Sabbath by his deeds will there rest from those deeds in heavenly recompense.

He rightly goes with the other two who is reduced to servitude only in body, provided that his spirit and soul remain whole and devoted with him in that service under compulsion. According to the Apostle, the whole perfected human being is counted in these three parts; and therefore the number one thousand is tripled.

Yet this must be understood so that, outside the perfection and freedom of the Sabbath, agreement to servitude does not exceed what is proper. Rather, let us freely endure without sin whatever compulsion is imposed upon us, in body, soul, and spirit. For by this compelled journey the servitude of labor is signified: we must patiently endure not only the deprivation of our possessions, but also, if we are reduced to servitude, freely and with equanimity carry it out.

Paul expresses this well when he enumerates the sum of these three sufferings: “You endure it if someone enslaves you, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone exalts himself, if someone strikes you in the face” (2 Corinthians 11:20). Behold, by “enslaves” he indicates that servitude belongs to compulsion; “devours” and “takes” refer to the robbery of those who violently seize and consume what is ours. But “if someone exalts himself” refers to those three situations: no one seizes another’s property, no one imposes compulsory service upon another, and no one strikes another in the face except through an arrogant persecution.

All these things, however, must be patiently endured by a Christian and carried out with a spirit of freedom. For in all these forms of injury the Teacher of truth teaches that the most merciful disposition of a religious person must be exercised, and that his mind must be fully prepared to endure still more for the accumulation of righteousness.

But because it is not enough to tolerate all these things unless one also provides whatever benefit one is able to provide, he adds accordingly:

“Give to everyone who asks you; and if anyone wishes to borrow from you, do not turn away.”

It is therefore clear that all these additions are parts of righteousness, so that complete righteousness is proclaimed through them all. From this it is also clear that when he says, “Give to everyone who asks you,” he means things that can be given honestly and justly. Otherwise, if something were demanded dishonestly and contrary to justice, how could justice be fulfilled by giving it? Especially since there are innumerable things which, if granted to those who ask, would utterly destroy justice.

Therefore the passage must be understood in this way: if anyone asks you justly and honestly, give willingly, if you are able. But if you lack the means, let justice itself at least be extended through affection, speech, or service. In this way it will sometimes happen that you give something better even to everyone who asks you.

As for what he says—“If anyone wishes to borrow from you, do not turn away”—it must be considered whether he speaks only of one who receives with the intention of repaying, or also of everyone, even one who does not intend to repay. For all who rightly show mercy to others expect to receive more from God, with interest. Thus everyone who receives is a borrower, since he presents himself as the patron of the lender; and the one who gives lends the same things that he sows in the other.

Nevertheless, by these words the Lord has embraced two kinds of giving. One is what we give freely for the love of Christ and the integrity of justice, without expecting to receive it back in the present; the other is what is requested and supplied as a loan. He therefore commands us not to be sluggish.

Divine Providence rightly urges us to this, because those in need are very often greatly relieved by such assistance. For this reason the pursuit of gain and interest are everywhere condemned. Lending, however, is highly commended as a component of justice when it is done according to the commandment. We must not think that the Lord is displeased even if the person repays, since you do this from obedience to the commandment: only do not turn away, and pursue no earthly profit, because before the one who commands, it will not be fruitless.

Earlier he taught what we ought to do against persecution and the violence inflicted upon our possessions; now he teaches what voluntary benefit we should offer to those who ask without any force.

Some, however, shrink from understanding these words as referring to the use of money. They argue that if we give alms to everyone who asks, even if someone is rich, his means will soon be exhausted; nor, if he gives continually, will there be anything he can keep giving forever. Unless, perhaps, the statement is defended in this sense: that to everyone who asks or wishes to borrow, one should give what is just and honorable, distributing it in equal measure according to our duty, first to those known to belong to our household of faith, and then impartially to all, so that we are found guilty of no injustice or dishonesty—which would be wholly unfitting.

If someone wishes to understand this of wisdom or spiritual gifts, the meaning is sufficiently clear: once these gifts have been divided, they increase, and when you give them you do not lose them. Such wealth will therefore always remain inexhaustible. Although this interpretation appears richer, as befits the apostolic office, it should nevertheless be accepted insofar as it teaches that no one should neglect acts of humanity; for all these things will benefit us more when, without loss of possessions here, they are multiplied a hundredfold before God in the future.

“You have heard that it was said: ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy,’” and so forth.

Since he had come to fulfill the Law, the text must be considered from the beginning, and we must examine the end with which he brought everything to completion. The goodness of God plainly advanced it, by fulfilling it, all the way to complete love.

The Law said, “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy,” not with the voice of one commanding, but of one permitting. It relaxes their inclination toward vengeance, yet commends a certain degree of equity by commanding, “You shall love your neighbor.” Those who are often restrained in their affection because of faults are held within this degree—for example, lustful children, or our relatives bound by any other vices. One may love them even while pursuing them harshly according to the Law, because this is done not from hatred but from love.

Love of one’s neighbor is therefore required, while permission is given to hate one’s enemy, so that the infancy of the unformed people might be moderated by both. But in the Gospel this is done so that the fullness of righteousness may be increased for those who are more perfect.

“But I say to you,” he says, “love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you.”

This is the breadth of love and the complete armor of righteousness, which extends even to the love of enemies. The fury of persecutors wages war against the Church of Christ in three ways: through hatred of the mind, curses of words, and the tortures of injuries and sufferings. Against these Christ taught that love should be offered in place of enmity, benefits returned in place of hatred and its injuries, and prayers poured out in place of their persecution and slanders.

Through these parts love wages war, so that it may conquer every evil with good. Each thing is opposed by its counterpart, so that every aspect of wickedness may be conquered by goodness. If the enemy is near, let love soften his heart; if he is far away, let our benefits seek him out by visiting him; and if his location is unknown, let poured-out prayer find him, even though hidden, before God.

Nevertheless, in all things the discernment of virtues must be carefully moderated, and we must diligently investigate why John forbids prayer for brothers who sin unto death, while the Lord commands prayer even for enemies (1 John 5:16). Nothing else seems to present itself except that there are some sins among brothers which appear more serious than the persecutions of enemies, and for these it is not permitted to pray. There are also such people, according to the Apostle, with whom one is not permitted even to eat (1 Corinthians 5:11). Yet vices must be hated, while human nature itself must be loved by us because they are human beings.

As for the words uttered by the holy Fathers and in the divine Scriptures that seem to sound like curses, they are rather prophecies concerning the future than outbursts of envy or hatred.

Nor should we think, as some do, that these commandments are impossible because they say, “It would have been enough not to hate one’s enemy.” They fail to notice that even in the Old Testament many fulfilled this command. How much more possible will it be for those aided by the grace of Christ, when the children of adoption ought to imitate the one who, coming into this world, found all people his enemies and made friends for himself from those very enemies?

But it is asked how he did not abolish the Law, since he said, “Love your enemies,” especially when the Law says, “You shall hate your enemy.” This question is resolved by the word we mentioned earlier: the statement is not one of command, but of permission, granted because of their hardness and imperfection. But when grace arrived, by which our weakness is strengthened, what had been cut short because of the weakness and sluggishness of the carnal people was restored to the Law in the perfection of righteousness.

For this reason, elsewhere, speaking of love, he says: “I give you a new commandment,” although “You shall love your neighbor” had already been stated (John 13:34). He calls it new because, among that carnal people, it had become old and only half-spoken: scarcely any of them loved anyone unless he was related to him by flesh.

But Christ, our new man, commanding those renewed in himself to love, orders us to love everyone either in God or for God. He therefore set forth a new commandment, because what has been renewed renews everything and makes children of adoption from children of wrath.

Hence it follows:

“So that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven.”

Behold, adoption as children is acquired by love alone; love is completed through the parts of righteousness previously mentioned and is confirmed through love of enemies. This is the power of which John said: “He gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

The Holy Spirit testifies to this within us: through him the love of God has been poured into our hearts, because we are children of God. Otherwise, unless we are reborn through faith and love, how can we be said to be born from God? Love is God; therefore whoever is reborn from it is born from God.

Notice that he does not say, “Do these things because you are children,” but: “Do what I command so that you may be children of your Father.” From this an extraordinary mode of speech arises. For what can a son be to his father except a son? And yet he is already called Father, although the ability to become children is still being offered to believers.

“So that you may be children of your Father,” he says, as though he were saying: “Do these works, so that you may not be degenerate, because you are not yet in reality what, by divine hope, you have already become.”

We often speak this way in ordinary language: “May you prove yourself such a son of your father”—not with regard to nature, which already exists, but with regard to imitation, which does not yet exist. How much more appropriately this expression can be used of us and God the Father, where one nature of God and of us is not being proclaimed, but we are urged to remain in the grace of adoption through which we are already called children and through which the same person is called our Father.

Furthermore, I think we should ask whether this statement depends only on the words, “Love your enemies,” or on everything stated earlier. It is sufficiently clear that all those things are fulfilled in this one love, through which we are also commanded to love our enemies, and that everything is recapitulated in it.

Therefore the statement, “So that you may be children of your Father,” must be referred not only to this command but also to all those things from which love is composed. It is as though he were saying plainly: “Mercifully love your enemies, and by this one love fulfill everything I have commanded, so that you may be children of your Father.”

Having received the power, therefore, act through works so that you may be children, because he is already Father. What is, cannot fail to be. Therefore, through rebirth in love, become what you have been called to be. Otherwise, although he is Father, you will not be children unless you are born from God; for God is love.

This is suggested by the prodigal son. Although he does not dare, and does not consider himself worthy, to be called a son, he nevertheless calls him father, knowing that he cannot change. It is as though he were crying out plainly: “If I have sinned against heaven and am not worthy to be called your son, you never cease to be a father, nor do you ever cease to possess a father’s compassion. Make me as one of your hired servants.”

The Lord of the New Testament, wishing to prevent the children of adoption from degenerating in this way, fulfills the righteousness of the Law, removes the quarrels of the carnal, extends the sum of the commandments even to love of enemies, sets forth paternal examples which good children ought carefully to imitate, and gives the reason for all the commandments: “So that you may be children,” he says, “of your Father who is in heaven.”

He is said to be in heaven, although God the Father is everywhere, so that his heirs and Christ’s coheirs may claim their dignity there, lest they later lament that they sinned in the place where the prodigal sinned.

“He makes his sun rise,” he says, “upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust.”

This example of divine kindness can indeed be understood spiritually of Christ, who is the sun of righteousness: he rose in the flesh for the redemption of the good and the evil and poured the rain of evangelical preaching upon the just and the unjust. Yet it is better to understand it as referring to this sun and this rain, which are necessary for daily use.

For although Christ came for everyone, his rising did not shine upon everyone. Hence, in the book entitled *The Book of Solomon*, it is said: “The sun of righteousness did not shine for us.” Otherwise, if he shone upon everyone and poured the rain of his preaching over all, the unjust would never remain dry and fruitless, without the fruit of repentance. Nor would the prophet have said: “He rained upon one city, and upon another he did not rain” (Amos 4:7).

The meaning is therefore clear: the statement concerns this sun and this rain. In them the Father’s considerable kindness is proclaimed, since he gives these temporal goods equally to everyone, while reserving eternal goods for the just alone.

This clearly provides an example appropriate to those who are adopted, so that they ought to imitate their Father’s works of compassion and, without any exception, embrace and illumine the good and the evil, the just and the unjust, with their benefits. They should also irrigate and drench them with the rain of love, in case those who seem barren may at some time be converted for the better and bear fruit.

“For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have?”

Here he shows that, although in our time scarcely anyone perfectly loves those who love him, there is little righteousness in loving only those who love us, as the Law’s commandments prescribe. Therefore he says: “What reward will you have?” As though he were answering: “None.”

This does not mean that such people receive no reward at all, since the love by which one is loved by another whom one loves is already the reward of love. But because the reward promised abundantly in heaven is not granted for such acts, it is spoken of as though it were nothing. For although it can be a reward, before God it is nothing; therefore it is rightly not called a reward. The reward of children is believed to be adoption alone.

Therefore, if anyone desires to attain it, let him hold fast the examples of adoption. Otherwise, what more does your love offer than the publicans? Do they not also love those who love them?

Publicans were the collectors of Roman taxes. The Jews called them by this name because they administered public affairs. They pursued profit, exacted taxes, and practiced commerce, frauds, thefts, and criminal perjuries. Compared with their mutual love, the love required by the Law appears to have no merit, since it comes not from the duty of owed love but from an exchange for profit.

“And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing? Do not even the Gentiles do this?”

These words are not spoken to imply that one ought not to love those who love one, or to greet one’s brothers humbly and with every courtesy. Rather, when these things, or things of this kind, are omitted from the perfection required, they appear small. Worse still, the inflated pride of some of our own people sometimes no longer permits even this: they refuse to anticipate one another in greeting, although pagans are known to do this out of regard for propriety.

I have said this so that the simpler hearers may know that the teaching of those who came before must in no respect be neglected. They so carefully established even the mutual greeting of blessing among other things because, if we do not deign to offer this in turn because of our insolence, we pursue a standard of courtesy lower than that of pagans.

“Therefore you shall be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.”

Behold the summit to which Christ raises his followers, and the perfection in love that he declares they must possess. If we wish to be children, let us pursue the perfection of love. By keeping the commandments we shall be children—not by nature, but by grace, through which it appears to have been placed within our own choice whether we remain children.

Someone may perhaps ask: How can any mortal human being be so perfect as God the Father is perfect, especially since no one ever remains in the same condition? Whoever asks this should know that to be made like God the Father means nothing other than to restore, through love poured into our hearts, the likeness in which the first human being was created, and to restore it to something better.

No believer denies this, since humanity was made in the image and likeness of the whole Trinity. Why then is it surprising if that image is renewed in such a way that the human being is said to be perfect, just as God is said to be perfect, when perfection of image and likeness was formerly attributed to humanity?

But because some, seeking this likeness of perfection with excessive subtlety, have fallen into some sort of darkness, at least lest they fail to return to what they were made for, let us explain a little more fully what philosophers have thought about this manner of speaking.

Everything that is similar—everything by which one person is made similar to another—is considered in two ways: either according to a certain relation of forms, or according to the nature of things. All likeness is contemplated under these two aspects.

Now consider which of these you would choose as the means by which you could possess the perfection of God the Father through likeness. If you choose to be perfect according to the relation of forms, know that there is no such relation in him except that he himself is. For he himself is the form from which all things are formed.

But if you say that you possess the likeness of perfection according to nature, it immediately follows that his nature—if nature is to be predicated of him—and the relation of forms are not different, because he himself is both form and nature.

Accordingly, our inner person must be raised up, so that what he possesses by essence we may begin to possess by the grace of adoption. Just as, in relation to us, he is called our Father through the adoption by which he adopted us as sons, so we too, through the same likeness by which we are children of adoption, must remain perfect in that adoption.

Otherwise, how can one be called perfect who was never made, and is believed to have neither beginning nor completion? God is called perfect not by a term proper to him, but, as in many places, for the sake of our weakness, so that by this language God may be proclaimed wholly good and supreme.

The human being, however, is found to be perfect not in reality but by grace. If he is compared with God, what in him will be perfect? “No one is good except God alone.” And if no one is good, who among us will be perfect in goodness?

It is therefore clear that this likeness is understood not with respect to the whole but with respect to a part. If a human being were wholly equal or similar to God, he would certainly be God. But since, according to the measure or quality of divinity, nothing can be equal or similar to him, it remains that a human being or an angel may be called perfect according to the capacity proper to him.

This perfection nevertheless comes only from the very image or likeness of God, in whose image he is read to have been made. For each person is more perfect the more similar he is. He is similar or perfect not through his own property, but through the grace of divine generosity and the integrity of the virtues.

Thus what God possesses by nature, the human being begins to possess by adoption, through participation in God’s goodness. Accordingly, each person is rightly called perfect as God the Father is perfect when, insofar as he can attain it by grace, he participates in the integrity of the virtues and in the gift of adoption.

Just as God is called perfect in himself according to the nature of his divinity, so we are called perfect through him, in part, according to the grace of holy adoption.

But since from the beginning—when the Lord God Sabaoth first gathered an army for battle against the aerial powers, intending to fight on their behalf—we have traversed immense seas of teachings, prayer now demands an end to the book, lest the reader’s mind, wearied by the long course of toil, grow sluggish.

Yet let us close the apprenticeship of this military service with a fitting conclusion, so that where we end the book, there the perfected virtue of the triumphant may attain completion in us.

Whether the abyss of knowledge has been sufficiently and correctly traversed, let the secure authority of the Fathers, upon whose support I relied in attempting this work, determine. If the fruit of my labor smiles upon us through the aid of divine grace, the glory of the completed work will be attributed to the one from whom its effect and the capacity for devout understanding have come.

Wherever I have understood less or otherwise than I ought, the fault belongs not to those whom I followed but to my own sluggishness. Accordingly, their streams will make up whatever the weakness of my imperfect work has subtracted.

It will nevertheless not be unwelcome to the reader if, with faithful desires, I have drawn something from the fountain of truth and offered, at the expense of my own labor, what I could for reading as a gift of service.

## PROLOGUE TO BOOK FOUR

[Column 0267]

[Col. 0267B] Whenever a ship casts off from harbor, with the sails of its wings spread, it is no longer under the rower’s control amid the immense waves of the waters, as to which parts of the route it should choose; rather, wherever the force and breath of the winds carry it, the skilled helmsman goes, together with the wind, even against his will. So, too, once the teacher’s tongue has parted from the harbor of silence, it does not remain sufficiently within his own control which paths of doctrine he should pursue as he advances in speech, nor with what words he should more suitably commit to writing the judgments he understands.

Hence it is clear that, if the breath of the Holy Spirit blows inwardly upon him, he will devotedly take the straight paths of understanding without turning aside. But if he is abandoned by it, it is dangerous to proceed farther, lest he should rashly plunge into crooked tracks and rough places from which he cannot extricate himself. For this reason the divine Spirit must always be entreated to grant a good life to one who has been brought to this task, and sound doctrine, so that a good life may wisely commend the teacher to his critics, while sound doctrine may crush those who resist and prudently show his hearers that the truth of Scripture, by whatever teacher it may be proclaimed, must never be rejected. Conversely, if it should happen to be false, then—even if the person through whom it is taught is outstanding in his life—it must never be accepted, and certainly never venerated.

But because I do not boast of possessing a suitable life, I nevertheless persist in the service of monastic religion, subject to be nourished by the disciplines of noble elders and advanced toward better pursuits of life. Moreover, in proportion to the smallness of my understanding, I rejoice not only that I have grasped sound doctrine, but also take pleasure in still being helped by the support of my instructors’ learning and the gravity of their character. [Col. 0268B] I desire that this task at least be granted me: that I may benefit those for whom I labor. As for those to whom our work has not been pleasing, I ask them to refrain from disparaging it before they have understood it, lest—God forbid!—because they disdain the progress of others and cannot bear to please them, they greatly harm themselves in what might perhaps have profited them.

Carried forward by this hope, I shall at last come to reconsider what the Lord commands concerning purity of heart. For just as what is commanded is not rightly carried out by flatterers and those who seek empty glory, so, unless the person who hastens to explain or teach others returns to himself, so that with the eye of his mind always thoroughly purified he refers himself and his words to the praise of his Creator, he never reaches the end without the danger of superficial praise. [Col. 0268D] Therefore I commit myself wholly to God. May I, carried by his inspiration to the harbor of salvation and eventually to the completion of this work, pass safely amid the various snares of the Scyllas. And I implore him—since this book deals above all with purity of heart—to make the one who commands purity also enable me, with the eye of my heart cleansed, to attain that same vision of contemplation concerning which it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0269]

## (CHAPTER VI)

Up to this point the righteousness of the Gospel has been restored in all its parts, including the full love of enemies, so that it might be greater than the righteousness of the Pharisees and scribes. Now Truth carefully intimates by what vision and purity of heart this same righteousness ought to be fulfilled in the works of believers.

“Beware,” he says, “of practicing your righteousness before men, in order to be seen by them.” It is not unreasonable to ask what our righteousness is meant to signify. Are we perhaps seeking to establish our own righteousness, like the Jews who were ignorant of God’s righteousness? Thus we read in Paul concerning them: “Being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and seeking to establish their own, they were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Romans 10:3).

Similarly, when he says, “Beware of practicing your righteousness before men,” we must ask whether he means: Beware lest you make the righteousness that belongs to God your own by displaying it before men for the sake of empty glory, so that you may be seen by them. By striving after such righteousness, you cannot be subject to the righteousness of God.

It is evident that, according to the sacred Scriptures, righteousness is called by various names. It is called the righteousness of God, and the righteousness of faith and of the Gospel, which are at once God’s and one. It is also called the righteousness of the law, of the Jews, and of the flesh. Yet now the righteousness of God is called ours as well. From this it is clear that, since under Christ we live in the faith of the Gospel, it is rightly called our righteousness; but it is God’s because “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” It is ours because it is fulfilled through grace in godly works.

Accordingly, he speaks of that righteousness which, as was shown above in the Gospel, is proclaimed as greater after being fulfilled in all its parts than the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, which is declared to be theirs, not God’s. Our righteousness, moreover, is that of which it is said: “The righteous shall live by faith” (Romans 1:17). Faith, however, belongs to God and is brought to completion through love of God and neighbor.

The meaning is therefore clear: this is the righteousness that has already been fulfilled above through commands concerning actions and commands concerning signs, and is now presented as more glorious. Let the prudent executor open the eyes of his mind, then, and examine himself in every undertaking, every duty of praise or action, every kindness of charity, and everything by which this righteousness of Christians is commended; and let him withdraw himself from worldly favor and from every regard for present praise. Whatever he does, let him transfer it through fixed hope to God, and let him not pursue the display of the crowd—not religious ostentation, not verbal superstition, not the empty pomp of eloquence—lest, while he seeks with the Pharisees to establish his own righteousness of praise, he not be subject to the righteousness of God.

For the righteousness of God is that everything commanded by him should be fulfilled, and that all things, once fulfilled, should likewise be referred to the praise of the Creator. Otherwise, unless they are done with this intention, they slip away, and even the few things we accomplish perish uselessly into the wind.

But we must ask how he said a little earlier: “Let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven”; whereas now, on the contrary: “Beware of practicing your righteousness before men.” Whoever carefully considers the boundaries of these statements will understand, without the labor of our explanation, what he forbids us to avoid and what he commands to be done before men.

There he says: “Let the true light so shine before men that they may glorify your Father”; here, however: “Beware of practicing your works so that you may be seen by them.” It is as though he said: Act so that those who see may glorify your Father, and do not act before men merely so that you may be seen by them.

Nothing is more foolish than to perform greater or lesser works of righteousness solely in order to be seen. If, in the greater matter, you wish to become a martyr, or, in the lesser, to give a cup of cold water, so that you may be seen and praised, then you who act have established yourself as the end of your action, and perhaps you possess what you sought. In this way, being seen has profited you nothing; rather, you have incurred empty glory.

But if you act publicly for the sake of making your works shine before those who see them, so that God may be praised and glorified, then even if what you sought does not occur, you have nevertheless, in your conscience, retained the end of righteousness. Hence it is not said, “Let your light shine, and if they see it, let them glorify God,” but simply, “so that they may see and glorify.” It is as though he said: Act for this purpose, that they may glorify your Father; what pleases him will rest in the divine judgment.

The preacher’s duty is indeed to persuade through words and works toward the praise of the faith. But it belongs to God if these gifts obtain firmness among those who hear them. The precise wording must therefore be noted everywhere. There it was said, “Let it shine”; here, “Beware of practicing your works before men merely for this purpose.” Thus he does not prohibit their shining, but only their being done in order to be seen by them.

For if they were works of virtue, they would shine. But now, because they are works of vice and darkness, let the dark see their own darkness. Since God is light, he can neither regard such works except to punish them, nor approve them.

Different wills and intentions of mind therefore produce different ends of merit. One end is that your works may be seen by men alone; another is that through them God may be praised. Tell me, I ask: what farmer, however rustic, ever cultivated and sowed his field merely to be seen by passersby? Or who, unless he is foolish, places the end of his labor in the sight of men, seeking nothing else from it?

For this reason the mind must always be attentive to what it does, how much it does, why it does it, and where, when, and in what manner it does it. For unless what is commanded is done as it is written; unless it is done in the proper measure, in an amount sufficient for righteousness; unless it is done for the purpose and in the place required—that is, for the love of Christ and in the Church; unless it is done at the appropriate time, while the seed is being sown; or unless it is done with the fitting haste of fear or love of God, as is proper and commanded—then, as Truth declares, there is no reward with the Father who is in heaven.

[Col. 0271A] Sons ought to pursue the glory of their Father, for the glory of children is the dignity of their parents. It is therefore right that we refer everything belonging to good works, and whatever in us rightly pleases, to the one from whom we are.

Otherwise, if we please men, we do not belong to Christ, no matter whom we please. Thus the Apostle said that he did not please men (Galatians 1:10), although elsewhere he commands us, like himself, to please everyone (1 Corinthians 10:33). For precisely insofar as he proves that he serves God, he does not hesitate rightly to please others on account of the form of virtue; and for that reason he invites others to please men.

It follows:

“When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you.”

This means: I do not want you to raise a proclamation of praise before you, so that you may be seen by men. Nor should you take pleasure in announcing yourself through your deeds, but rather God. He sounds a trumpet before himself who, seeking his own praise, continually makes known before others the greater things about himself, so that he may appear greater.

But whether, in the literal sense, the hypocrites among the Pharisees sounded a trumpet before themselves whenever they went to distribute alms—as though they were being summoned and proceeded ceremonially, for the favor of the crowd, as to a spectacle—is not sufficiently clear. Nevertheless, since they did many superstitious things, there is no doubt that they also had this custom. The Lord, taking the opportunity to speak of it, warns his own not to seek the proclamations of self-display as hypocrites do, but to carry out everything humbly and religiously in their conscience, for the praise of God.

The name “hypocrites” is therefore taken from the ancient theatrical disciplines, because they were impersonators. Indeed, the Greek word *hypocrite*—ὑποκριτής—is understood to mean “one who acts a part.” Like speakers in an assembly, they fictitiously performed the roles of persons in theaters, and their entire tragic or comic affairs were displayed as though they themselves were the persons whose roles they assumed.

They narrated not their own stories but those of others, and before the spectators, for the favor of the crowd, they represented in turn their conduct, movements, voices, and expressions. So also are those who display good works through a counterfeit service of praise, not for God’s glory but for their own. They play the parts of the righteous and assume their persona, though they are impersonators, for the favor of men. They do not possess the works of righteousness; they merely pretend to possess them.

If their works were truly righteous, they would refer everything good that they do not to themselves but to God. But now, like mimes, according to tragic piety in the theatrical games, they flatter themselves before men, with the devil approving, and desire to appear righteous. When the King of armies comes, he will find that they were not those whose parts they played outwardly, but imitators of actors whose appearance they held in their hearts.

Whoever therefore desires to appear outwardly as something he is not inwardly is certainly a hypocrite and a deceiver of men. When he has deceived them through his pretense, he destroys not them but himself.

Concerning such people it follows:

“Truly I tell you, they have received their reward.”

He says this of those whom human praises had already nourished in synagogues and streets, and with whom those who became their imitators are also included: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward.” Their own reward, that is, and not God’s. Their own, because the praise they sought they received, bringing with it the payment of error and the punishment they deserved, exacted by their sins.

Observe how carefully the Teacher of truth touches upon every part of righteousness. First, he teaches what one should do; then, that one must not be deceived by one’s own praise and be condemned along with hypocrites on account of that same righteousness; finally, he indicates how one should do whatever one can, so that one may afterward be crowned by it in the future.

Hence also it follows:

“But when you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing.”

This is not something that the nature of the body permits us to understand literally. Rather, through so obvious a bodily secret, it compels us to consider another meaning. Who could ever say that the soul, which is wholly present everywhere throughout every part of the body, could fail to perceive in the left hand what is being done in the right? For just as all the members suffer if one member suffers, so, through the life-giving soul, all the members suffer with it when one member suffers and perceive whatever is perceived in one.

The soul, which is in all the members, therefore knows no less what is being done in the left hand than what is being done throughout the whole body, because it is wholly present everywhere and consequently knows and feels everything.

We are therefore compelled to seek another meaning. We are taught that whenever Scripture speaks in this way about the members—as we have already seen above when it spoke of the hand or eye, or of those who castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdoms of heaven—we must not take it according to the letter, but through it consider the mystical workings of doctrine.

Unless perhaps the saying is expressed hyperbolically in this passage: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing”—that is, let it be done so secretly that the left hand is not even permitted to know it. But what if alms are offered with the left hand? Or what if the right hand has been cut off? Is it not permitted to give anything with that hand?

It is therefore clear that God made both hands. Accordingly, it is not rightly believed that God hates the good thing done through a hand, but rather the evil signified by it.

Our inner person has a right hand and a left hand. Would that our whole person were right-handed! The right hand signifies works of virtue; the left signifies vices. Thus it is said, “Let not your left hand know”—that is, let no operation of vice know—what your right hand is doing.

This is to say plainly: Let the vice of self-exaltation, pride, empty glory, or whatever belongs to that side not know what the right hand of virtue is doing. For just as darkness does not know light, so vices ought not to know virtues. Indeed, just as light drives them away, so vices should be driven away by the light of right action.

Let what I have said here suffice, lest anyone wish superstitiously to insist that what is commanded must be done so secretly that no one else, or even we ourselves, may be permitted to know it—especially since it was said: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may glorify your Father.”

Moreover, there are many who, although they seem to perform good deeds secretly, nevertheless know what their left hand is doing with their right, because they mix light with darkness. Thus they confuse the good things they do, so that all are obscured by darkness and deprived of light.

Nor should it be thought that “Let not your left hand know” refers only to glory. All the members of vice are left-handed and opposed to the virtues. Therefore whatever vice has been implanted in us as the law of sin must in every way fail to know the action of a good work; that is, it must in no way be admitted so as to obscure the things that belong to the light. Rather, everything should carefully be brought into the light and made bright.

“Let your alms,” he says, “be in secret.”

Almsgiving is rightly done in secret if it is mixed with no darkness, because darkness is always external to the light, while light is always inward. Whatever is done inwardly—that is, in the light—is therefore always secret. Whatever is done in darkness, that is, is mixed with vices, is always external and deprived of the light of truth.

In that light—in secret—whatever is done is approved, because God is light. For God's seeing is approving. Whatever is in the light is not rejected; whatever is external—that is, in darkness—is rejected.

Many people, inventing many things about this passage, have produced various opinions. Some of them decreed that the left hand should be understood as pagans; others, as enemies; and very many, as one’s wife. But the contradiction of these interpretations compels us to reject them and retain the understanding we are following, although above we said that by the right hand a wife or friend who scandalizes us may be understood, and that such a person ought to be cut off from us.

The idiom of speech is nevertheless preserved, so that whatever has been proposed generally in this discourse may be expounded particularly. This is why he began above by fulfilling the righteousness of Christians and distinguishing it from that of the Pharisees, which he strictly forbade us to display in order to be seen by men.

Now, just as that same righteousness was fulfilled in parts, he explains in parts how it should be practiced. Almsgiving is one part of righteousness, as are the many things that follow. Hence he says: “When you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing.”

The Pharisees therefore give alms in such a way that works of empty praise are mixed with them on the left side. Thus he teaches specifically what he had taught shortly before in general. There it was said to all in the plural: “Beware of practicing your righteousness before men.” Here it is said to one person in the singular: “When you give alms, let not your left hand know.”

From this it is understood that there one person is taken for all, and here all are taken together in one. Everyone must nevertheless take care to act faithfully in the secrecy of conscience, before God—not merely by avoiding temporal concerns and every advantage of praise or external recompense, but also by removing every cosmetic disguise of vice.

For if he commands the left hand not to know what the right hand does, then the left hand can much less perform anything pleasing or anything counted among the works of the right.

This, then, is the discipline of sons. Therefore the virtue of righteousness must always be displayed before the Father’s face in the secrecy of conscience. This does not mean that others must not see what we do, but that nothing should be mixed into holy works; rather, everything should advance toward the praise and glory of the Father. Nothing else should be sought from it as an advantage. Everything should be hidden where our life is hidden with Christ and where an abundance of sweetness is reserved for those who fear him.

There our conscience is rightly hidden, so that our heart may be there where our treasure is. There God the Father sees; there he looks upon and approves; there everything pleases him. Outside that secret, there is nothing he sees and approves, nothing that pleases, nothing that endures.

Therefore everything must be done for Christ and in Christ, because nothing outside Christ pleases the Father or is approved by him through his sight—Christ in whom he was well pleased.

Hence it follows:

“And when you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites,” and so forth.

This statement is joined to the preceding one, and from that conjunction a similar order of speech is repeated. First he had said: “Beware of practicing your righteousness before men”; then he adds: “And when you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites.”

Just as the Pharisees became impersonators—that is, hypocrites—so also in prayer they gloried, and only superstitiously. In order to be seen by men, they prayed in synagogues and at the corners of the streets. At the corners, as though hiding their prayers, yet in the streets so that they might be seen; and thus they gloried all the more through both circumstances.

Often, when weaker people looked upon them, they thought them to be something they were not. Anyone who prays at a corner, turning away from a right conscience, covers himself with darkness and pretends to be hidden. Yet although he pretends to pray in secret, he prays in the street, because in his pride he seeks the public and broad reputation of men.

There is no doubt that they also observed these practices superstitiously in the literal sense. We, too, frequently pray not only in public or at some corner, but everywhere, because we are commanded always and everywhere to pray no less than to give thanks. This must be understood in the same manner as we explained above concerning righteousness.

He does not forbid prayer everywhere, but speaks with precision:

“When you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites, who love to pray standing, so that they may be seen by men,” and so forth.

It is by no means unlawful to pray to God in any place and to be seen by men. What is wrong is to pray in order to be seen, and to establish the end of prayer in being praised. The following words demonstrate this well: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward.”

They have received the reward by which they were seen praying and praised as though they were religious. It is not that true praise is harmful; rather, to pray for the purpose of being seen and praised by men—which is the practice of hypocrites—not only brings no reward, because the fruit is emptied within by the evil intention, but also increases the vice of pretense and mockery against God.

God is not mocked. He knows, as the one who is broader than our heart, what is weighed in our conscience for him and what for empty glory.

“But you,” he says, “when you pray, enter into your room.”

Here what was said above concerning righteousness in the plural is taught in the singular. From this it is understood that unity is gathered here for the universal Church. Nor is it without reason that universal commands are often directed as though to one person, while plurality is contained in that one.

Thus it is said so often in Deuteronomy and in other passages: “And now, Israel, hear the commandments and judgments that I teach you, so that by doing them you may live, enter into, and possess the land” (Deuteronomy 4:1). Throughout that entire book he speaks as though to a single person, so that the unity of the whole people may be commended.

What, finally, can be more one than the body of the Church, which is composed of many parts? It is expressed more significantly as one because it is supported by one love of Christ, generated by one faith, and ruled and enlivened by one Holy Spirit. Through one person universality is expressed, and thus the divine word is addressed to all as though to one alone.

In this way one person in all, and all in one, are animated together, through which the greatest communion of the Church is displayed.

“But you,” he says, “when you pray.” It is as though he said: Because all the Churches have one body, therefore you, my beloved and my bride, who are my body, whenever you pray, enter into your room.

By “room” he means the more secret recess of the mind, where no one can see what is in it except the spirit of the human being that is within. Concerning this chamber David sings by way of admonition: “What you say in your hearts, and be pierced in your chambers” (Psalm 4:5). Something more secret seems to be signified by these words, since we are commanded first to be pierced inwardly by what we bring forth from the heart.

At the door of this chamber the Wisdom of the Father knocks, saying: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock” (Revelation 3:20). This door is opened to him through faith, concerning which the bride speaks in the Song of Songs: “I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved” (Song of Songs 5:6).

Christ therefore knocks at the door whenever he moves the mind through the inspiration of a good work. His voice, which he often repeats with the affection of one who caresses, says: “Open to me, my sister, my beloved, my dove, my undefiled one” (Song of Songs 5:2). If she does not open to the one who knocks, she returns inwardly empty into herself.

What good is it to pray in that chamber of the mind where neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit has yet been received as he comes, and where they have made no dwelling?

Whoever therefore wishes to pray to God in the chamber of his heart as he has been commanded must first open the door through faith to the one who knocks, kiss him through charity, and devoutly point him out within the chamber of his mother, where he may be taught by him.

Otherwise, what good is it to pray where one does not wish the one being prayed to be?

But if through faith you already hold the one whom you love with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength, then you rightly enter the chamber of the mind. There the Triune God is worshiped through faith, embraced through charity, and made more deeply firm through hope.

Such a temple is already holy, as the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

What good, then, is it to enter for the sake of prayer where there is no place for religion? Therefore, because Christ comes freely, knocking at the door, let him be received, and let the Triune God be embraced inwardly by a silent conscience through charity. Then, as commanded, let the door be shut, and let God the Father be prayed to.

He is not to be prayed to merely with the noise of words; rather, what we seek should be obtained inwardly through faith, hope, and charity. This, I say, is the true religion of Christianity: the mind should not scatter itself in searching for God beyond the heavens, beneath the abyss, or around the boundaries of the earth, but should hold inwardly through faith the one whom it loves and pray to him more attentively through the same virtues by which it worships him.

Thus it is fitting to adore the one who is confined by no place and bounded by no limit. Hence also he says to the Samaritan woman: “The hour is coming when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4:23).

It is as though he said: They will worship the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, because the Triune God is worshiped and honored nowhere except in himself.

Happy indeed is the chamber that is enlarged by such a capacity of faith that it embraces the immense and incomprehensible One. Whoever enters it and prays asks without hesitation for whatever he desires, because through faith he possesses within himself the one to whom he prays; from him the devout person will very easily obtain faithfully whatever he asks.

Hence the Psalmist says: “With me is my prayer to the God of my life” (Psalm 41:9). And a little earlier: “I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me” (ibid., 4).

“Within me,” he says, “I poured out my soul,” because the one whom he holds by faith, loves through charity, upon whom he relies with certain hope, and whom he humbly implores through religious worship is within him.

Thus we read concerning Hannah, when she multiplied her prayers before the Lord and Eli watched her mouth, that she was speaking in her heart, and only her lips moved, while her voice was not heard at all (1 Samuel 1:13). Do you think she was praying in order to be seen? Certainly not. With the door shut—that is, with a silent conscience—she asked God, so that she might be heard in the chamber, for all things are present to him.

She was therefore heard because, weeping abundantly with the one who is present everywhere, she was turned inwardly toward herself.

Whoever, with the door shut, prays to God repels by the power of the spirit and by guarding the door barred whatever things improperly intrude from outside, so that they may not steal in completely. Visible things and all the temporal concerns of this life press upon our inner beings and clamor at the door of the heart.

Therefore the door must be barred, and the whole inner person must be gathered inwardly, so that it may enter the chamber. Concerning this chamber the bride rejoices in the Song of Songs because the king has brought her into his chamber (Song of Songs 1:4).

From this chamber one reaches him.
