Therefore the faithful soul must first enter itself and receive God into the dwelling of its heart, so that afterward, carried through him toward himself, it may eventually arrive and may now enjoy in hope what it will then enjoy in reality, blessedly, in its homeland.

For although glory is granted to us for eternal grace, each person nevertheless carries within his conscience what he desires to obtain through his labor in prayer.

Hence it is written: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their chambers” (Psalm 147).

They shall therefore exult in glory because of the glory freely received through grace; they shall rejoice in their chambers—that is, in their consciences—because while they were placed in the struggle, Christ’s grace produced joy in them.

For this reason the Teacher of truth commands each person to enter the chamber of his heart and there begin to pray or act, so that afterward he may be able to rejoice. Each person will have glory in himself alone, and not in another.

The Teacher of life instituted all these things so as to educate the son, and therefore says: “With the door shut, pray to your Father.”

It is as though he said: Pray as a son, and pray according to the fact that you have been reborn. His fatherhood should teach you with what confidence and affection you ought to pray. You are praying to the Father; enter into his presence in your conscience and pray to him as a son.

“And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

Do not pray in order to be seen by men. Rather, pray inwardly with the door shut, so that your Father may see; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

He will repay not words for words, nor prayer for prayer, but the fruit of prayer and the reward of faith.

### “When you pray, do not speak at length,” like the Gentiles.

He plainly calls the Gentiles “pagans,” or philosophers, who prayed at greater length for two reasons. For they thought that, just as they were accustomed to speak persuasively in business dealings and legal proceedings, so they ought to speak in prayer, supposing that God could be persuaded by words. And just as by eloquence they won over judges to favor them, making them attentive and well disposed, so they tried to charm God, because they imagined that in each matter he could be moved by persuasive words. [p. 314; Col. 0277B]

Or perhaps they spoke at such length because they did everything not from conscience but from the surface of words, not knowing that God is present everywhere. Their faithless supplication sought that, if the one whom they were asking happened to be absent, he might eventually come, as demons do; and, on coming, might learn through verbal circumlocutions what he had previously not known. It is therefore no wonder that, when they served idols, they poured out many foolish words before the deaf—especially since the demons themselves could not know what those entreating them wanted before they had been instructed by their speech, while the demons remained ignorant. [Col. 0277C]

But the faithful worshiper of God does not need many words, nor does he need to tell him many things to whom everything is open, who everywhere searches out the secrets of hidden things, who scrutinizes hearts and distinguishes thoughts and inmost parts. Yet he certainly does not condemn many tears or many supplications offered with purity of heart; rather, he condemns wordiness that arises from faithlessness and impurity of mind. [Col. 0277D]

Otherwise, we also read that Hannah multiplied her prayers before the Lord, and that many of the saints prolonged their prayers for two or three days without any interruption. The Lord, too, spent the night in prayer and prayed at greater length in his agony, so that his sweat dripped onto the ground like drops of blood. From this it is understood that what is condemned is not the multiplication of prayers, nor the continual outpouring that proceeds from the affection of divine love, nor the intercession for pardon, but the attempt of those who, without devotion and in faithlessness, merely fill the empty air with words.

Indeed, just as it is blameworthy to pray with the hypocrites so that we may be seen by human beings, so it is faithlessness to suppose, with the Gentiles, that we are heard through wordiness, and not to understand—even if only by believing—that God, before whom things that are, things that were, and things that will be are present, knows beforehand what we need before we ask. [p. 315]

Concerning this the question is rightly raised: if God knows beforehand what we will ask, why is it necessary to ask before his knowledge, or why, although he commands us to pray, does he command us to use few words? Some philosophers have even called it superfluous to weary with prayers one who knows each thing even before it is requested. [Col. 0278A]

But this question is very easily resolved if the proper order and justice are considered. For it is one thing to report to someone who is ignorant what he does not know; it is another to pray in religious worship to one to whom you ought to be subject, and to ask the one who knows that you may receive freely what you did not previously possess in yourself. It is altogether different to implore devotedly the assistance of one who is greater than you and to report to a weak person what he does not know. In the one case there is an indication of ignorance; in the other, an act of obedience to justice. There we faithfully report to one who does not know; here we humbly entreat and ask from the giver.

God wishes to be asked so that his goodness may be distributed to many, while the devotion and condition of justice are preserved among those subject to him. He is not taught as though he were ignorant; rather, as a good Lord, he is reverently worshiped in supplication and is graciously pleased to grant what is requested. [Col. 0278B]

For this reason he composed a very brief prayer, so that perhaps, in his mercy, he might quickly grant salvation and no lengthiness of words might impede it. Indeed, the brevity of the words should inspire confidence that the merciful Judge, who wished to be asked in a brief utterance, would more quickly grant the petitioner’s request according to his desire.

Nevertheless, although he composed only a few words by which he teaches us to pray, I think we must still ask why even these few words are necessary for one who knows everything and, as has been said, knows what we need before we ask.

To this we must immediately admit that before God we ought to act through the matters we carry in our minds and through the intention of our hearts, with pure love and sincerity of feeling, rather than through words, so that we may obtain what we seek. Therefore we must understand that he taught us words in order, through those words, to teach us what ought to be prayed for, so that from them the mind might conceive and commit to memory a rule of prayer—not the words one should merely recite, but the reality and understanding of the meanings, and what one should seek from devotion. [Col. 0278C]

Otherwise, one should never pray in any words other than those in which he gave this instruction. But now the matter is understood quite differently. We do not act before him through words, but through the disposition of mind that we have received from those same words, devoutly imploring him with faith, hope, and the service of charity, so that our heart may be kindled by the words and become serene in prayer. Then, enlightened by that very intention of heart, we may more confidently obtain what he himself taught us to seek. [p. 316]

Thus, through his teaching, our heart is enlightened by a few words concerning what it ought to pray for. Once enlightened, it does not inform the one to whom all things are open; rather, by supplication to the one who can do all things, it pours itself out more fervently and asks with charity for what it is already presumed to have received through the hope of faith. [Col. 0278D]

“Hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” In that Spirit we already cry, “Abba, Father.”

From this it is perfectly clear that we ought to pray for nothing other than what the teacher of truth taught. Although we frequently pray in other words, we nevertheless have no doubt that we are not permitted to pray for anything else.

Therefore let the person reborn in Christ consider that, from the time the righteousness of Christians began to be wonderfully fulfilled, the adoption of sons also began to be restored. If he sees that he favors those same elements of righteousness, let him know that he is rightly called a son by adoption, and that through this same adoption he obtains the fatherly compassion that moves to mercy. [Col. 0279A]

But if he pays insufficient attention to what has been said above, he should fear lest his prayer become accursed. To live otherwise than he taught is to fall away from the grace by which God the Father adopted us as sons; to pray otherwise is to be weighed down not only by ignorance but also by the guilt of error.

Hence he himself says: “You have rejected the commandments of God in order to establish your own traditions” (Matthew 15:3).

Let us therefore pray as the Father’s only Son taught us—the one who made his own Father, namely his Father by nature, our Father by grace. He bestowed on human beings his own honor, so that what he alone possessed as the excellence of consubstantiality, he might grant to all by his goodness through grace. [Col. 0279B]

For this reason he first taught that we ought to be conformed to him; then he granted us to possess, through the grace of adoption, what he possessed by the nature of his deity.

What, then, can be called more orderly, more powerful, kinder, or more generous than what he bestowed on us? He taught us to share in his name and made us participants in his dignity.

This, then, is why, among his other saving admonitions and divine commands by which he counseled believers toward salvation, he also set forth a form of prayer, established its character, handed down its discipline, instructed us what should be requested, and granted the boldness of adoption, so that, while inwardly asking the Father within us, we might more easily be heard. [p. 317]

Finally, he fulfilled what he had promised: “True worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.” We are true worshipers because, according to the sanctification of the Spirit and the tradition of truth, we worship the Father without any obstacle of error. [Col. 0279C]

For we do not know how we ought to pray; but it is the Holy Spirit who teaches us about everything, pleads for us, and carries us over into all truth. Therefore there is no prayer more spiritual or more abundant than the one we received from the Son, who is the Truth, from his own mouth.

It is a friendly and familiar prayer to ask God for what is his own, at his own command, and for Christ’s commands to ascend to the Father’s ears. What, then, do you think? Will the Father recognize the words of his Son?

Therefore, when we make our prayer, we are commanded to enter into our inner room so that Christ, who dwells within the breast, may himself also be present in the voice. Otherwise, we can certainly pour out prayers before God without God and complete the matter in words; but we will by no means obtain the effect of the deed. [Col. 0279D]

### “Thus,” he says, “you shall pray.”

What does “Thus you shall pray” mean except this: “You shall pray not like the hypocrites, so that you may be seen; not like the Gentiles, with much speaking; but as I teach, what I teach, and in the manner in which I teach, you who are mine shall pray”?

Here, therefore, we must consider not only the effect of prayer, but also the posture of the body, the manner of the voice, the quietness of Christ’s discipline, and the modesty of humility.

For this reason he adds: “Thus you shall pray,” as though he were saying: “As I hand it down, as I instruct, as I command, as I prescribe.” [Col. 0280A]

God is a hearer not of the voice but of the heart. Concerning him the Prophet says: “Your ear has heard the preparation of their heart” (Psalm 9:20).

Therefore whoever prays should already hold in his heart, through faith, the one whom he is praying to, and love him through charity. If he prays only what is commanded, let him confidently rejoice that he will receive in reality what he anticipates in hope from the one who denies nothing that is required.

For this prayer is public to all who are reborn in Christ, and common to all, since it is poured out not for one person but for everyone, because we are all one in Christ.

God, therefore, the teacher of truth and of peace and concord, established the unity of those reborn. For this reason he wished one person to pray for all in the same way that he himself carried all together in one person.

To pray as one person for everyone is greater than to pray for someone in oneself alone. Therefore the power of prayer must not be considered small in that place where all pray together for one, because one is consecrated in all. [p. 318]

And when it is said by everyone:

### “Our Father, who are in heaven,”

if you are truly united in Christ’s body, they all take you with them into their prayers and together implore that his will may be done in you. [Col. 0280B]

This unity must therefore be considered no small matter, nor should such a firm fellowship in Christ be lightly valued—where everyone’s voice is one, where all together carry God in their minds with one faith, love him with one charity, and now share one hope; where all together ask for one thing, seek one thing, and knock together at the one door of mercy.

Nothing, therefore, is stronger, richer, or better than for all to be one and for all to keep watch for one, just as one person stands among all for everyone, so that all together may be found one in Christ.

With what faith, what hope, and finally what charity he taught this! No believer should separate himself from this unity. Therefore no one should distrust that he can obtain from the Father what the only Son taught. No one should lazily neglect the works of sons that he taught. [Col. 0280C]

This, I say, is that power which he gave to human beings: to become sons of God. For this reason he first set forth the works of power, so that the adoption of our freedom might remain from him.

Therefore he grants the boldness to pray with the prayer he gave and taught, so that whatever is lacking in us may be fulfilled by grace.

Hence, whenever one of us, even though separated from the others and living secretly in more secluded places, calls God “Father,” he should understand that the gift of so great a privilege has been given not separately to individuals but commonly to all.

Therefore no one should flatter himself by saying, “My Father, who are in heaven,” but rather, “Our Father,” because this belongs properly to Christ alone, whose Father God is by nature.

Hence elsewhere he expressly says: “I am going to my Father,” and then adds, “and your Father” (John 20:17). By this statement he carefully indicates that the special glory of being Son belongs to him by nature, while the general grace of adoption has been granted to all together by grace. [Col. 0280D]

Suppose, for example, that a householder has someone as a son by nature and nevertheless possesses many servants. Does it follow, merely because he is called the householder’s father, that the servants are held by him on equal terms with the son—especially since this same Son is proved to be Lord of all?

It is clear, therefore, that in the one case there is consubstantiality of nature, while in the other there is the goodness of the ruler; yet in both cases the common name of fatherhood is received. [p. 319]

Hence we are taught that all whom the water of baptism washes ought to be brothers in him and to be joined to one another by the bond of brotherhood. [Col. 0281A]

Accordingly, we are instructed at the same time to return to the Father the affection of adoption and to serve our brothers not with hatred but with the devotion of kinship.

If bodily birth from one mortal binds us with so great a bond of love, brotherhood born from God the Father must be considered worthy of much greater reverence—a brotherhood that no one can recognize except spiritually.

Otherwise, if a person is not spiritually reborn, how can he grasp or feel, according to the inner person, the affection of this love?

If this fatherhood were honored and loved with true faith and the surest hope, through the charity poured out by the Holy Spirit, bodily kinship would never again prevail among some people. They would prefer nobility from God and the grace of adoption to corruption, and would take care not to become degenerate and unworthy of so great a parent because of the oldness of the flesh. [Col. 0281B]

See how faithful and blessed the prayer should be considered, the prayer that the teacher of life and heavenly master taught us. See how blessed we can be if we preserve these things not merely in the duty of the lips but in the faithful conduct of our lives. See what certain hope of salvation has been given to believers; how great the Creator’s love is poured out upon us; how much mercy and compassion are bestowed; how great a grace and gift of confidence are granted, so that we, who were not worthy servants, dare to call God “Father.”

Therefore we must live and conduct ourselves as God’s sons, proving by spiritual action and conduct that we are what we are called, according to what John says: “Whoever has been born of God does not sin” (1 John 5:18), because God’s birth guards him, and the devil does not touch him. [Col. 0281C]

But whoever commits sin is not from God, but from the devil, because the devil sins from the beginning.

Therefore, preserving the sacrament of our birth, let us keep ourselves free from every stain of sin, so that we may truly be sons of God.

Isaiah prophesies this on our behalf when he says: “For you are our Father, because Abraham did not know us and Israel did not recognize us; but you, Lord, are our Father. From the beginning your name is upon us” (Isaiah 63:16).

Instructed sufficiently by this name, we rightly ask.

### “Hallowed be your name.”

But first the question arises: since God the Father is believed to be everywhere, why is he addressed only as “who are in heaven”? Likewise, what of the statement, “To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven” (Psalm 122:1), and the many other passages in which God the Father is said to be in the heavenly places? [p. 320; Col. 0281D]

To this we must reply that these heavens in which God dwells are to be understood not as bodily but as spiritual, since God is not extended through spaces or confined by a place.

We are instructed, however, not to desire anything earthly, but rather to hasten with the greatest longing toward that region in which we confess that our Father is remembered, so that even now we may dwell there in mind, where he is proved to be our Father and Creator.

Hence Paul says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). And elsewhere: “He makes us sit together in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2:6). Likewise: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, not the things that are on earth; for you have died, and your life is hidden with God in heaven” (Colossians 3:1). [Col. 0282A]

Come now, I ask you, investigator of heavenly things, and inquire what heavens these are in which you recognize both God the Father and your life as hidden. Are they perhaps the highest bodily regions of the world, which cannot exist except in a place? If that were so, the birds of heaven would be of greater merit, since their dwelling is closer to God. But that is altogether impossible.

Therefore we must acknowledge that God is nowhere to be sought or conceived as occupying the place of bodily things, nor is there any place in which he is not, since every place is present to him.

When it is said that he is everywhere, this does not mean that he is locally in every place—for he cannot be in a place at all—but that every place is present to him and open to his apprehension, while he himself is not received within a place. For this reason he is rightly said to be nowhere in a place. [Col. 0282B]

God the Spirit is everywhere, although not in a place, but in spiritual beings and in the saints. Hence David also says: “God, who dwell in the saints” (Psalm 21:3). This is plainly what it means to say that he is in heaven.

Therefore, whoever desires to dwell with God in heaven, transfer yourself from earthly things into what is holy, spiritual, and intellectual. For those who set their minds on earthly things cannot share with God in the inheritance.

This is also why the spirit of wisdom meditates in good sons, not intervening for the benefits of earthly things, but devoting the whole affection of piety to the glory of our Father, saying:

### “Hallowed be your name.”

The Father’s name, then, belongs to sons, since “Father” is spoken only in relation to a son, just as “son” is spoken only in relation to a father. This is a relation referred to the Son, since neither of them is named according to himself but according to the other. [p. 321; Col. 0282C]

Thus the Son is related to the Father in order to be Son, and the Father to the Son in order to be Father. These things exist in mutual relation, because one is named from the other.

From this it is perfectly clear that the Father’s name is in the Son, just as, conversely, the Son’s is shown to be in the Father. Otherwise, if one were not in the other, neither would be called Father nor the other Son.

Therefore, because the name of God the Father is in us, so that by adoption we may rightly be called sons, we pray: “Hallowed be your name.”

This does not mean that he can become more holy, since he sanctifies all things from himself. Hence he says: “Be holy, as I also am holy.” Rather, we ask that his name be sanctified in us so that he may cause the increase of his sanctification, namely by granting us his Holy Spirit, through whom the love of God has been poured into our hearts and we cry, “Abba, Father.” [Col. 0282D]

For the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God.

For this reason the Father’s name is then sanctified in us, when we are sanctified by him from whom all sanctification is granted. For just as the father’s dignity is referred to his sons, so the sons’ sanctification is attributed to his name.

What else is the sanctification of the name but the infusion of the Holy Spirit, through whom we prepare a devout, gentle, peaceful, and pure heart, furnished with every virtue, for his entrance, so that the adoption of freedom may be sanctified?

Thus the name of God the Father is sanctified in us, just as the Son himself elsewhere testifies that he has been glorified in his disciples, although he always shone with the clear light of divinity, without any addition or diminution.

Among other things he says: “I have been sanctified in them” (Ezekiel 39). And elsewhere: “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit” (John 5:18).

Where, therefore, he finds the place of his sanctification, there he says that he is sanctified. The supreme piety of the Father declares that whatever it mercifully bestows upon its servants is conferred upon itself. [Col. 0283A]

Thus he is sanctified in us, just as he is magnified by us.

Hence the virgin Mary sings with joyful heart: “My soul magnifies the Lord” (Luke 1:46). This does not mean that the great and exalted Lord, who has no limit or completion, can become greater or smaller; rather, as we grow in him, he is, so to speak, magnified in us.

It is as though we were saying: “Father, hallowed be your name, so that we may be such people as are able not only to understand your sanctification but also to receive it, so that you may appear holy through our spiritual way of life.” [p. 322; Col. 0283B]

This is rightly accomplished when, seeing our good works, people glorify the Father who is in heaven.

But how wretched are those through whose evil works the name of God the Father is blasphemed! Therefore, lest this occur, because we sin daily, we pray daily that the vivification and sanctification received from God’s grace may be preserved in us by his protection.

Accordingly, the name of God the Father, which is in us, is continually sanctified through the cleansing of the Holy Spirit, lest anything worse befall us.

Some therefore rightly ask: of what name is it said, “Hallowed be your name”? Is it because we are called Christians by Christ, or because we are named sons by God the Father through the grace of adoption? [Col. 0283C]

This is immediately indicated by the context of the reading, when we begin with: “Our Father, who are in heaven.” No name is exalted in us with greater honor than that we are named and are sons of God through the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

This name is sanctified by growing in two ways: either when it is spread more widely through the increasing number of believers, or when it is more abundantly diffused among believers through the increase of their merits.

In both ways it is sanctified daily, as those reborn are increased by his gift.

I do not say this, however, to suggest that the name of Christianity ought not to be sanctified in us, but because, in rebirth, adoption is consecrated as a higher degree of merit. Otherwise, neither Christianity is granted without adoption, nor adoption without Christianity. [Col. 0283D]

Hence in the Apocalypse of John it is said to the one who conquers: “I will give him a white stone, and upon the stone a new name, which no one knows except the one who receives it” (Revelation 2:17).

By the stone, the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is signified. In this stone, each person reborn in Christ, when through the grace of adoption he becomes one body in him, receives a new name, so that he may be called the Father’s son and become Christ’s coheir in the Father’s kingdom.

It is as though he plainly said: “To the one who conquers the world and the author of death, I will give Christ as coheir and companion, through whom the enemy is conquered; and in him I will give a new name, of which Isaiah previously foretold: ‘You will be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord will pronounce’” (Isaiah 61:2). [Col. 0284A]

No one knows this name except the one who receives it—as though it were said that no one defends the dignity of adoption by conduct and life except the one who has merited to know that name itself by divine predestination unto eternal life. For “to receive” refers to the grace of predestination. [p. 323]

Hence John the Baptist, speaking of this same mediator of ours, says among other things: “No one receives his testimony” (John 3:32); but whoever receives his testimony certifies that God is true.

Therefore a white stone is given to those who conquer, and on that stone—that is, in the same body of Christ—a new name is given: namely, holy adoption, through which we are named sons.

In this adoption the name of those predestined to love God and their neighbor is consecrated. [Col. 0284B]

For it is written: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13:34).

No love, therefore, can be greater than that which the Lord commends between father and sons, and among sons as brothers. This is the new name bestowed on the disciples in the stone, which no one knows except the one who receives it.

It is as though it were said: Whoever does not preserve love of his brother in the commandment with paternal affection is utterly ignorant of the power of this name.

Indeed, concerning this name it is promised in the same Apocalypse: “I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which descends from heaven from my God, and my new name” (Revelation 3:12).

This inscription, therefore, is nothing other than the sanctification of the name. Hence we pray: “Hallowed be your name.” [Col. 0284C]

Let us hear with what stylus or pen the name of God the Father is inscribed upon the victorious:

“My tongue,” he says, “is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Psalm 44:2). This, I say, is the Spirit of the Son and the Father, by whose grace the name of adoption or of Christianity is inscribed and sanctified.

For, as Paul says: “Because we are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’”

Hence comes the dignity of the name; hence the height of merits. Hence we are kings; hence priests; hence conquerors; hence a new creation; hence we are called Christians; hence we are sons of God.

Therefore, where the whole sum of salvation is concerned, let us pray with the innermost feeling of our hearts:

### “Hallowed be your name.”

Then follows:

### “Your kingdom come.”

What do we ask in this supplication? Do we perhaps doubt that he reigns without beginning and without end, continually? Certainly not, because he is the king of all ages, whose dominion is neither enclosed by an end nor terminated by a beginning.

Rather, we ask that the kingdom of adoption may come, in which we shall be heirs of God and coheirs of Christ. [Col. 0284D]

The order of the petitions is entirely appropriate: since in the first supplication the adoption of sons is consecrated, in the second we ask for the kingdom that is owed to sons. For we do not pray for what benefits him, but for what benefits us.

Just as, when his name is sanctified in us, we are sanctified, so, when we ask that his kingdom come, we also pray that our kingdom—sought through Christ’s blood and passion—may come as promised.

When Christ has abolished every principality, authority, and power, he will hand us over to God the Father as a kingdom, in the triumph of his power, so that God may be all in all. Then we shall contemplate what “eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and what has not entered the human heart,” what God has prepared for those who love him.

Concerning this kingdom he will say to his elect at the end: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

But lest the mind become sluggish through delay, let the devout inquirer know that, just as the Father’s name is sanctified daily in us so that we may be able to advance to better works of virtue, so the kingdom that we desire to come is also felt to arrive daily, as principalities and powers, and the spiritual forces of the air, are abolished in us, when vices are abolished and the desire of the world is extinguished. [p. 324; Col. 0285A]

Then, certainly, when these things have been driven away, the good things of the virtues have blossomed in us and the fragrances of merits have sprinkled the chamber of the mind, we have no doubt that the Father’s kingdom is already coming in us.

By a taste of this kingdom we are strengthened more firmly amid the pressures of the world, and we pray with the greatest urgency that it may come more completely to what we are entering.

Come, then, whoever rejoices that you have been adopted into the kingdom: enlarge the bosom of your faith, extend the perseverance of your hope, increase the greatness of your love, and pray with every virtue of mind and every earnestness of heart that this kingdom may daily increase not only in the number of believers but also in you and in all who are already counted by the Christian name, expanding through the measure of their merits and being glorified in virtues once evils have been abolished. [Col. 0285B]

Moreover, extend the eye of your mind toward that final day of promise, when, if you remain in adoption, you will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom.”

Therefore extend the eye of faith and charity, and grasp in prayer all that the teacher of truth has compressed into a few words.

Pray that the kingdom of God the Father may come among all. Pray that, once evils have been abolished in believers, virtues may increase and shine with the fitting honor of divinity, so that the age may come to an end and be gloriously concluded in the blessedness of eternity.

No criminal dares to say or desire these things, because he does not wish to see the judge’s tribunal: at his coming he does not hope to receive the palm of reward, but, with his conscience bearing witness, fears that he will immediately receive punishment for his offenses. [Col. 0285C]

Come, then, whoever you are: at least desire now, in this present age, to be stripped of the evils of vices and for the kingdom of virtue to come in you, because God is the God of virtues and not of vices.

Desire to be gathered among the members of Christ, and let whatever the whole body prays for as a whole reach even to the member, if you have perhaps been restored by hope, faith, or charity. Thus, by praying, acting, living, and conducting yourself, cooperate faithfully from now on with the head and the members.

Otherwise, even if you do not wish him to come, you will not escape this judgment; and, having lived badly, you will receive the punishment you fear.

Learn, I ask you, perseverance, and accustom yourself to labor without weariness. [Col. 0285D]

See how long it has been since the holy Church of God began to pray, “Your kingdom come”; yet, although it increases daily, it is still delayed.

I say this so that, if you ask and perhaps do not obtain it immediately, you will not grow weary but will sweat more earnestly in the struggle: the kingdom of God is sought through delay, already held by certain hope; toward it we advance through faith, overcome by the immense ardor of charity whatever stands in the way, and through that same charity we labor tirelessly until we arrive there.

### “Your will be done.”

The meaning is parallel to this understanding. No one can resist or contradict God so as to prevent his will from being done, especially since it is written: “Everything that the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 134:6).

But we pray that we may join the freedom of our will to his will through grace, so that the one who lives may no longer live for himself, but that God’s free will may be fulfilled in everything. [p. 326; Col. 0286A]

Concerning this will the holy Apostle bears witness, saying: “The will of God is your sanctification, that you abstain from carnal desires” (1 Thessalonians 4:3).

And elsewhere the Lord says: “This is the will of the Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life” (John 6:40).

Here, therefore, we devoutly pray not for what benefits him but for what benefits us.

When we say, “Your will be done,” we must consider with what faith and with what charity we say it, because no one who doubts the Father’s will ever prays rightly.

It requires great faith, great devotion, and great confidence to know, concerning the unchangeable goodness of the Lord, that he wills nothing evil; indeed, according to the Apostle: “He wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4). [Col. 0286B]

No one can say these words sincerely except one who firmly believes that God orders everything visible and invisible, prosperous and adverse, for our benefit.

For devout faith requires us to believe that he is continually provident and solicitous for our salvation, without interruption and according to his dispensation, more than we ourselves are for ourselves.

Therefore, if anyone deliberately or firmly holds this in mind, he always depends upon his will, presuming nothing about himself, and night and day continually implores that his will be done in us—a will that can never be deceived, never changed, and never corrupted by any emotions.

For his will is the salvation of all.

This the same only Son, the teacher of truth, knew when he said: “Father, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (Matthew 26:39). [Col. 0286C]

And elsewhere: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 6:38).

The humanity of the man assumed by the Son relied more on the Father than on itself, in order to show everyone how great and what kind of confidence ought to rest in his will.

No one doubts the truth of John’s statement: “Whoever does the will of God remains forever” (1 John 2:17).

Therefore let our spirits expand, let our devotion grow, and let us conceive in our minds what we pray for, because whatever the heavenly master taught by words or examples is the will of the Father, so that everything may be fulfilled.

For this purpose the things written or done have been handed down, so that we may faithfully carry them out in works for our salvation. [Col. 0286D]

Therefore let each person consider what he wants within himself and what he carries in his heart. If he sees that his will differs in anything from God’s will, let him correct his perversity, lest he contradict in his conduct what he prays for in words.

Hence it is written: “Turn away from your own desires” (Ecclesiasticus 18:30).

But because the soul is from heaven and is a part of heaven, while the body is from earth and is demonstrably a part of earth, therefore, as the Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17). [p. 327; Col. 0287A]

Thus, although willing for a time lies within our power, we do not find the ability to accomplish the good.

Therefore we pray:

### “Your will be done, on earth as in heaven.”

That is, in the spirit, so also on earth, so that flesh and soul may be that spiritual person of whom David sings: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Psalm 83:3); and again: “My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh also thirsted for you” (Psalm 62:2).

For who does not know that the will of God exists among angels and spiritual beings, since God is spirit? “Whoever clings to God is one spirit.”

Where unity reigns, therefore, there can be no disagreement.

But if someone is earthly, he will go into the earth. In this passage, too, “earth” signifies carnality, through which access is given to evil spirits within us.

Concerning this David says: “When evildoers draw near against me, to devour my flesh” (Psalm 26:2).

And to the serpent in paradise: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Genesis 3:14).

In this earth, because action is taken against the will of God and our carnal person opposes God, we pray. [Col. 0287B]

[Col. 0287C] “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” Not that the earth should remain, so that while it remains your will may be done in it, but that whatever is earthly or carnal in us may pass away, and become spiritual and incorruptible. Otherwise, in the earth—which is the fourth of the elements—what is ever done less than the will of God? All the elements of creation, and whatever is in them or from them, are subject to his power. Every nature serves his commands; at his sovereign order it even passes into contrary kinds or forms, and there is nothing that resists his words.

But because freedom of choice was granted on earth only to human beings, just as it was granted to the angels in heaven, we are finally taught to pray that, just as they already cleave by grace to his will, so that they neither wish nor are able to sin any further or do anything contrary to his will, so we too, who are still on earth, may be joined to him, so that through his will we may be one with him. For what could we possess more happily than to preserve God’s will perpetually within us? To will what he wills is the highest good, the consecration of all virtues, the destruction of vices, and the perpetuity of eternal blessedness.

By this will, earthly things are joined to heavenly things. Therefore, let the faithful soul consider how dead it ought to be to itself and to the world, if it truly wishes to pray for what the Teacher of truth teaches. Otherwise, whoever still cherishes his own willing and his own refusal, drawn away in his heart, is certainly not asking that the Father’s will be fulfilled in him. Having been warned of this, let him beware lest it ever be said to him: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me”; far, certainly, from salvation, because the will of God is believed to be our salvation.

Therefore, even if we wish otherwise, we must always pray that not our will but his will be done. And if, by his inspiration, we now wish the very things that God wills, this is not our gift but God’s. Therefore, placing our confidence more in him than in ourselves, and submitting to his most excellent will, we rightly pray: “Your will be done on earth,” that is, in us, in that part by which we are earthly, “as it is in heaven,” where you dwell.

In heaven, as we have said, not in these material heavens, but in the holy angels, in whom God the Trinity works perfectly; or also in the saints, whom, raising from earthly things to sublime realities by grace, he has already made heavenly. In these heavens, certainly, God’s full and perfect will is accomplished, since none of them can any longer disagree with it or turn aside from it.

Of this will David sings: “That I may see the will of the Lord, and visit his holy temple” (Psal. VI, 24). Likewise, the prophet Isaiah says in the person of the Father: “And in all things my will” (Isa. XLVI, 10). Therefore we pray that, just as it already is in heaven—that is, in his angels and saints—so also in us, because we are still partly earth, the will of the Father, about which no faithful person rightly doubts, may be completely fulfilled, so that spiritual and divine things may be done in all things and in each person, while earthly things fail.

But the soul must be searched, faith nourished, and understanding more abundantly enlarged, so as to recognize how rich, how holy, how just and perfectly righteous, how merciful, and how beneficial to all the Father’s will is. For the existence of all creatures came from the will of God alone, because his willing was his making. Therefore it is right that the will by which we were created and through which we exist should be done and remain in us, lest, deprived of it, we should immediately be condemned as guilty.

Nothing, then, is more just than that the will of God, by which we subsist, should be done in us, so that from it, through it, and toward it we may at last arrive more happily. For just as there is no other reason why we exist except the will of the Father alone, so there ought to be no other reason why we live except that his will be fulfilled in all of us, and that we may reach, with sufficient devotion, the state for which he willed us to exist.

But the fact that we are earth comes from the curse, because it is said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19). Therefore we ask that God’s will—which made heavens out of earth—be done in us, so that we too may be heavens.

And it should be noted that he does not say: “Let our will be done as yours,” or: “Let the will that is on earth be done as it is in those who are in heaven.” Rather, he says: “Let the will be done, as in heaven, also on earth” [the Latin wording is textually irregular]. Thus, just as they no longer live for themselves, but his will lives in them and through them accomplishes what he wills, so also in us and in all who are still earthly, God’s will may be done and may accomplish what belongs to salvation.

For we do not pray merely that we may will what is good, because to will and not to accomplish is weakness. Instead, we openly ask that his will, which is exceedingly rich and possesses no weakness and admits nothing evil, be done in us, so that he himself may accomplish everything in us. “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.”

But those who are still permitted to follow their own wills, like children of wrath, feed upon their own misery, unless at some time they are overcome by his goodness and brought to God’s will, and Christ’s exceedingly rich virtue deigns to come to their aid.

Moreover, those who, already divinely inspired, ardently will what God wills, but do not attain such a will in their works, seem to hold a degree of perfection, yet are not considered so blessed. Hence the excellent teacher, as I stated earlier: “To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find” (Rom. VII, 18).

Therefore we earnestly implore what is more perfect: “Your will be done as in heaven and on earth.” For although your will is done on earth by power, it is already done in heaven in a very different way, by grace. Therefore we pray not in just any manner, but: “Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” Just as in heaven your will alone reigns and works in all things, so may it work in all things on earth, and may your grace, rich in willing, take possession of everyone.

From this the devout soul may perceive with how broad a bosom of charity one must pray, with what faith the supplication must be strengthened, and with how great a hope devotion must be nourished. For the will of the Father is the same as that of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. The Father wills nothing other than the Son, nor the Son anything other than the Father and the Holy Spirit. But just as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one Godhead, one power, and one authority, so also they have one and unchangeable will.

Therefore, when we pray to the Father that his will be done in us, this must be understood so that the will of the Son and of the Holy Spirit may also be fulfilled in us. Accordingly, whatever the Son taught, or whatever the Holy Spirit divinely inspired, we must beseech God to bring about in us through works. For this is the will of the Father: that we live according to God and observe his commands in all things.

But because we are less capable of these things, setting aside our own wills, we earnestly pray that his will be done in us and that we be subject to him, so that the adoption already granted to us may at last be bestowed more fully.

And it should be noted that, just as three commandments in the Decalogue are shown to belong to God, so also in this form of prayer, according to the inner person, God the Trinity is consecrated in us. Indeed, by calling upon him within us, we ourselves are more fully consecrated through these three things, with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength.

The four petitions that follow pertain to the supports of the present life, while these three are directed toward the grace of future adoption. For our earthly human being subsists through the four elements, and therefore we are rightly strengthened daily by the fourfold number of petitions. But that future adoption, surrounded by the will of God, will be the kingdom of God the Father, when God is all in all; thereafter there will be the rest of the sabbath and the fullest sanctification of blessedness in all things.

Then, certainly, our whole human being will fulfill the commandment of charity: to love God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his strength. Meanwhile, however, we pray that what is destined to be may be done in us, so that we may be sons and imitators of Christ, who said: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matth. L, 12); and likewise of himself: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (Joan. VI, 38).

But in order that his will may be done in us, first, by the inspiration of divine grace, let a willing disposition according to God remain ready; and thus let us pray, “Your will be done,” so that what is less possible from us may be completed by his gift, and so that we may begin to live where we are destined to be.

Some wish the will of the Father to be referred to the person of the Holy Spirit, and the coming kingdom to the person of Christ, concerning whom the children who went before and who followed cried out, saying: “Blessed is the kingdom of our father David” (Marc. XI, 10). But who could doubt that the sanctification of his name belongs to the person of the Father?

We, however, confess in the catholic faith that, just as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one will, so they have one kingdom and one sanctification, belonging to the whole Trinity. Although the outpouring of charity—that is, a willing disposition ready and devoted to God—is referred to the grace of the Holy Spirit, just as the kingdom is referred to Christ’s triumph, by which he triumphed after conquering his enemies. Through his victory we have been reconciled to God the Father, and through adoption we glory in being divinely consecrated as his heirs and fellow heirs with Christ.

This offspring of adoption will receive these things more fully and perfectly in the future; therefore, let these few remarks about them suffice. But let us now turn the eye of the mind to the things necessary here, so that, having understood these matters, we may at last come to those more sublime things [Col. 0290C].

**Give us today our supersubstantial bread.**

In this petition, he seems to have taught that everything necessary for the present life, so that we may reach the future life, should be requested. For when he says “our bread” *ἐπιούσιον* (*epiousion*), that is, “supersubstantial,” he signifies the quality of its nobility and substance: that it is above all substances, and that the sublimity of its nature surpasses all creatures.

He expressed this more significantly when he used “supersubstantial,” because he is that living bread which came down from heaven. Those who eat of it still hunger, and therefore another Evangelist called it “daily” (Luc. XI, 3). Nevertheless, it is daily on the way, but eternal in the homeland. Hence, through John: “If anyone eats of this bread, he will not die.” He says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world” (Joan. VI, 51, 52).

A little later, while the ever-unbelieving Jews were arguing about these things: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you do not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink,” and the other things that follow (Ibid., 53, 54, 55, 56, etc.).

It is therefore clear how earnestly we ought to ask for this bread, without which we cannot live in Christ [Col. 0291A]. “Whoever eats me,” he says, “will himself live because of me.” He will live by another life, for whoever eats this bread will live forever.

But if this is to be understood of that bread, namely, of Christ’s body, the question is not unreasonable: why do we not eat it every day, without interruption of days, just as we pray that it be given to us daily? For in the Eastern Churches it is the practice of many not to communicate daily, especially since this bread is called daily. Otherwise, if the command were to communicate daily, this would never be done so indifferently in the Church. Let those who wish do it without scandal, and there is no priest who either forbids daily celebration or commands that communion never be omitted.

From this it is evident that the matter must be understood otherwise, since we cannot all be prepared to receive it daily; for whoever eats unworthily eats judgment upon himself. We therefore understand it as daily either because it may be offered daily and faithfully received by those who are prepared, or because it is daily in that the same bread continually refreshes us inwardly through faith and charity, by religious devotion and hope, and comforts us with the nourishment of its sweetness.

For without it we can never live spiritually. Therefore, when he says “today,” he shows that it must be received daily; it is not enough that we received it yesterday if we do not still receive it today and continually to the end. Finally, he teaches us to pour out this prayer daily before the Father, so that from this daily need of life we may be reminded that there is no day on which the heart of the inner person should not be strengthened inwardly by that bread [Col. 0291C]. Concerning it David says: “And bread may strengthen the heart of man” (Psal. CIII, 16).

What is said here, “today,” may also be understood quite suitably of the present life, while we remain in this age. It is as though he said: Grant us this bread for as long as we are on this journey through the world. For we know that unless someone receives it in this life, he will in no way share in it in the future. Often “today” is taken to mean the whole of the present time, as in: “Today, if you hear his voice” (Psal. XCIV, 8).

If it is understood this way here, then it should rightly be understood of the body and blood, so that the meaning is: “Give us our bread while we are in the present life, so that, never excommunicated from it, we may not be cut off from Christ’s body.” For if anyone does not keep his commands, he receives this bread unworthily.

We believe that this was sufficiently indicated through Adam when he had sinned while still in paradise: “See that he does not perhaps take from the tree of life and live forever.” No one who reads the sacred Scriptures can doubt that the tree of life is to be understood as Christ. We are forbidden to take from it whenever we sin more grievously, lest, being unworthy, we receive his body and blood.

From this we are rightly taught to pray: “Give us our daily bread today,” that is, make us such that we may rightly receive it from you.

But some, examining this meaning more deeply, have more plainly decreed that “daily bread” should be understood as the spiritual and divine commandments that we ought daily to meditate upon and perform, since we ought not to transgress this rule of prayer by adding anything, subtracting anything, or changing anything.

Therefore the capacity of understanding must be enlarged, and, if we do not dare to receive the Lord’s body daily, let us daily receive him in our mind, together with all his commandments, with ardent spirit. And so that we may grasp them more fully, let us pray each day: “Give us our daily bread today.” For the true food is the will of the Father. Thus the only-begotten Son, teaching us, says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (Joan. IV, 34). And elsewhere to the disciples: “Work for the food that does not perish, but remains unto eternal life” (Joan. VI, 27).

For meditation on the divine law and the performance of the commandments are food for souls. There is no doubt that, just as the present life consists in the food of bread, so eternal life consists in the work of the commandment.

Hence blessed is said to be the one who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night. Concerning this meditation David says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth” (Psal. CXVIII, 103). There he shows that the words of the commandments ought to be called food, since he says they are sweet to the palate, not to the ears.

Likewise the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal; I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III, 1), calling spiritual teaching food.

Therefore, who could doubt that Christ was sacrificed so that he might be saving food and the drink of life? Hence the Apostle cries out: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed; therefore let us feast” (I Cor. V, 7).

But that we may overflow more abundantly with these delights, let us pray more earnestly: “Give us our daily bread today.” In the conclusion of this petition, a threefold sense of interpretation is more plausibly disclosed, although all the divine Scriptures ought to be interpreted in this way.

First, according to the literal sense, we rightly ask him who created all things to grant us the daily sustenance of necessity. But perhaps someone will be troubled as to why we pray to obtain the things necessary for this life, especially since the Lord says: “Do not be anxious about what you shall eat or what you shall wear. Seek first,” he says, “the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matth. VI, 25, 33).

From these words and examples of this kind, some think it is to be taught that these things should not be requested from the Lord in supplication, but that we should always seek only those things that are spiritual and eternal. If this is to be understood in that way, then the general custom of the Churches would be mistaken, since in their prayers they very often earnestly ask for the things necessary to the present life, and many such petitions are recited in the prayers of the sacraments.

From this it is plainly evident that, just as we ought to labor with our hands without being anxious, so we ought especially to pray that we may receive these things from him who grants all things. Otherwise, should we be ungrateful? Or do we receive them without him? And if, even with the wicked, we share in these goods from him, then we, whose faith is adoption, ought humbly to ask to obtain mercifully what we wish to receive.

Nevertheless, when we say “our bread,” we are separated from those who possess neither faith nor adoption. For although this bread is common to everyone, we seem to ask more particularly for another bread, which is proved to be ours alone; for the food of Christ’s body or blood belongs only to Christians, and likewise the nourishment of the work of the commandments and of doctrines is counted as belonging only to sons.

But, they say, this common food cannot properly be called ours, since it also belongs to others. To this we acknowledge that, just as this world was made and is believed to subsist for those who are predestined to life, so also those others freely receive these things for their sake—things that are owed to those who love God. Hence it is rightly called ours, because it is extended to them for us, so that his goodness may be spread to all.

But it is not their daily food, because they have planted the permanence of love in the root of their hearts, although they themselves are not permanent here on earth. Those, however, whose adoption is assured, since they ought not to be anxious about tomorrow, ask only for their daily ration, always hoping for God’s generosity for the future.

This was well commanded to the people who were leaving Egypt as they journeyed through the desert: each person was to gather no more than one *gomer* for daily sustenance. If anyone gathered more, or stored some of it for the next day, worms immediately swarmed from it, so that the food was of no further use.

By this the present rule of Christians was signified: even the perfect ought not to be anxious about tomorrow. “Sufficient for the day is its own evil; for tomorrow will be anxious for itself” (Matth. VI, 34).

And if this is thought laborious and difficult, nevertheless this perfection ought to belong to sons: that they live each day as though they were about to die immediately, and always hang in hope upon the place to which they believe they will soon come.

Therefore, praying daily, let us receive this threefold food of life each day, as faithful children from the hand of the Father, lest perhaps, having received our substance, we wander away from him as the prodigal did.

But such a rule is observed by few people and very rarely, and such love of the Father and devotion of his children is scarcely maintained. Therefore, trusting in his mercy, let us reject the things of the world and live so that, here on the journey, we may also be nourished daily with this bodily food, without which we cannot live, while giving thanks.

Then, in a moral sense, let us occupy ourselves day and night with the law of the commandments, because “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matth. IV, 4).

It is therefore clear that just as our outward person is nourished by this bread, so the inner person is renewed day by day by that bread. Through both, meanwhile, we are sustained: by this one the body is nourished on the journey, while by the other soul and body together are nourished for eternal things.

We eat spiritual food daily, either when we receive his flesh or blood in the sacrament, or when, loving, believing, and hoping in him, we inwardly ruminate upon him in the mind alone. By this food we are incorporated into Christ for eternal life and become one body with him.

Therefore we must pray no less that we may be worthily nourished by him with that food, without which we cannot be saved. “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.”

Accordingly, we must live in such a way that we may be found worthy of him, and pray in such a way that each day we may receive all these things from him suitably and soberly: from one, whatever is presently necessary for us; from the other, that inwardly, through doctrine and mystery, we may daily share spiritually in the delights of the angels for as long as we live in time.

Let us have no doubt in any matter that God the Father has given us all things together with Christ, whether present or future. Therefore, because a child has been born to us and a son has been given to us, let us pray to him as our treasure; let us pray to him as our food. He is ours, and therefore all things become ours together with him.

For this reason let us ask for him as ours, so that, just as we already hold him in faith, we may enjoy him in reality and obtain all things from the Father through him. For he is ours because he is now rightly owed to us. Therefore we pray that what is ours by gift may be granted daily in its effect.

Let him only be our daily food, and all things will be ours together in him. This is what is meant by: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you.”

All the rest is foreign, because we are not of this world. Therefore let us first pray for what is ours, so that we may rejoice that we have obtained all things in it. The evangelical saying teaches that all the remaining things are foreign, where it says: “If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luc. XVI, 12.)

Therefore, let us seek what is ours before and above all things, so that he may be our bread, our food, and our life. For love of him, let us set aside all that belongs to the world as foreign. And therefore let us ask the Father for this nourishment, whether bodily or spiritual, only day by day, so that in him, from him, and by him we may always be nourished.

For no richer storehouse can be found, nor anything more excellent and fully prepared; it is indeed ready and continuous. Therefore let us seek nothing other than what is proper and paternal.

It follows:

**Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.**

Here let each person attend to himself and understand that by his own voice he has presented a binding undertaking before the judge. The Teacher of mercy taught this not only to bend us mutually toward mercy, but also to grant forgiveness himself to those guilty of sins against him.

In one petition he comes to our aid; in the other he releases the debts of brothers who have sinned. Yet in both he mercifully provided forgiveness for both parties, and willed that each person should come to the freedom of adoption through some act of charity.

Therefore, let each person recognize more carefully the petition contained in his undertaking: just as he proves ready to forgive his debtors, so he will have God propitious in his own affairs. We are taught to hope this from the Lord, and it has been placed in our power: what we are seen to have forgiven our fellow servant.

We are bound by our own promise. Therefore, just as we do not wish to be debtors, so we should not desire to have debtors, because in their persons we are either bound or released.

But if it is thought uncertain what debts or what debtors are meant here, every basis for excuse must be cast aside, and the meaning must be understood more plainly as referring to every debt, both of faults and of financial burden: whatever matter in which your brother is liable to you, release him from it.

For the frequent presumption of offenses and the dishonest handling of money and pursuit of profit show that we too are entangled in many bonds. Therefore, according to the measure of their strength available to all, each person ought to release his debtors from the burdens of the means by which they are held oppressed by debts.

For whoever is inhuman toward the needy denies to God what belongs to him. His infinite mercy so takes upon itself the distress of the poor that whatever you have generously bestowed upon a poor person through benevolent stewardship, he counts as given to himself.

We are held liable as debtors in three ways: when we commit what the Divinity has forbidden; when we do not fulfill what he has commanded; or when we are bound by our own vows. For even then we are debtors, since, having freely received Christ’s benefits, we owe all that we have promised until we faithfully render each thing.

Likewise, what we are commanded to forgive is incurred in us in three ways, so that we may be released from our own guilt: when we are unjustly wounded in mind; when we are afflicted by sufferings in body; or when, in outward matters that rightly belong to us, we are burdened by some injury.

Whether the debt is the price of sin or of possessions—which is sometimes held without wrongdoing—we must release it entirely to our brothers, so that our debts may be released to us by the merciful Judge.

Above all, if the burden of sin is shown to belong to us, let us forgive it willingly. For although we sometimes rightly demand a monetary debt, we never refuse, without our own condemnation, to forgive the debt of offenses to those who ask it.

Hence this command is given in this very Gospel: “When you stand for prayer, forgive whatever you have against anyone, and your Father who is in heaven will forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive,” he says, “neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive you your sins” (Matth. XVIII, 35).

No excuse is left to us, because each of us will be judged on the day of judgment according to this saying. But we must be careful not to forgive those who sin against God as though the offenses were ours, or to repay what is ours, as though out of zeal for God, for the sake of vengeance.

We commonly do what is more serious: toward offenses that erupt against the omnipotent God, we behave as though merciful; but toward those committed against us, even if very small, we are harsh and inexorable. For this we earn from the Lord not forgiveness for either kind of deed, but condemnation, because by our own petition we are condemned more severely.

What, then, does it mean to say, “Forgive as I have forgiven my debtors,” when you have not forgiven? Does this not provoke the merciful Judge, through your cruelty, more sharply to the severity of vengeance?

Therefore he has imposed upon us the model according to which we wish to be judged. To those who forgive, supreme confidence in obtaining mercy already responds before God; but for those who exact payment, punishment gnaws at the conscience because of the condemnation they incur.

Yet God prefers to find someone to whom he may show mercy rather than someone whom he may punish. Therefore he has placed in our power the means by which each person may call forth God’s judgment against himself, and may moderate the sentence of so great a peril.

Let no one, therefore, consider himself free from debts of sin, because no one can live without fault. Concerning this the Apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I Joan. I, 8).

Nor did the Teacher of truth teach his disciples to pray this superficially. Nor is the universal Church proved to say this falsely. We are all debtors, and therefore Christ’s forgiveness is necessary for all.

For this reason, let us devoutly forgive everyone from the heart, so that the merciful Judge may also forgive us more serious and more numerous debts.

He proposed a monetary image in prayer, likened to sins, since not only covetousness but also avarice is shown to be the root of all evils; without its vicious seed, scarcely any crimes are generated.

Therefore, in both kinds of debt, this must be observed: that we help our fellow servants in every way we can. Otherwise he who examines the hearts of all either approves prayers when charity burns in the soul, or rejects them when it has grown cold.

For he first examines the hearts and strength of each person, and then weighs the offering of the vow or the prayers of the suppliants according to that. Hence it is written that he first looked upon Abel and then upon his offerings; therefore he accepted them favorably, because he found the one whom he had first regarded as righteous before him.

Accordingly, let no one deceive himself; let no one circumvent himself. Whoever does not forgive from the heart those who sin against him offers prayers in vain before the Judge whose commandments these are.

**And do not lead us into temptation.**

This does not mean that the Lord and Teacher of truth, who is the way for believers, leads anyone into the snare of temptation. Rather, when he abandons those who neglect to obey his teachings and permits them to go wherever they are enticed and led, he is then said to lead them in.

This manner of speaking occurs very frequently in the divine Scriptures: through what he permits or enables to happen, he is said to do it himself.

You have an example of this in a good sense, when the Holy Spirit is said to plead for us with inexpressible groanings (Rom. VIII, 26), while he causes us to plead. You also have an example in an evil sense, when he says: “And I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. IV, 21), while he permitted Pharaoh to be hardened.

And the prophet says: “You have hardened our heart, Lord; you have hardened it so that we would not go after you” (Isa. LXIII, 17).

This does not mean that the merciful Lord leads anyone into the snare of temptation or hardens anyone so that he cannot receive the word of instruction. Rather, when, by his true and just judgment, he abandons us, he is figuratively represented in the sacred writings as leading us in; and when he permits us inwardly to grow cold through hardness of heart, he is said figuratively to harden us, because he does not melt those whom he knows to be growing cold away from him who has placed his seat toward the north.

Hence the bride says in the Song: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, that its spices may flow” (Cant. IV, 16) [Col. 0297A].

Otherwise, unless the soul is aided by divine assistance, it is quickly driven to ruin when the wind of temptation blows.

This is why we ask: “And do not lead us into temptation,” that is, do not permit us to be led into it by the one who tempts for evil. For God is not a tempter of evils. Hence it is written that God tempts no one—not because he did not test Abraham and Jacob, or very many of the elect for salvation, but because he tempts no one for evil. Therefore he is called the one who does not tempt to evil.

We are led into temptation when temptation has weakened us even a little. For we do not pray that we may not be tempted, but that we may not be led into temptation—that is, that temptation may not overcome us even briefly.

This is what is meant by saying, “Do not bring us into temptation,” which Paul states beforehand when he says that, with the temptation, God will also provide that we may be able to endure (I Cor. X, 13).

For no one is blessed because he is not tempted, but because, after temptation, he is crowned by God as a victor. Hence it is written: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life” (Jac. I, 12).

It is therefore clear that temptation is necessary for everyone and that all are tempted. But because our strength is insufficient to overcome these things, we pray from the depths of our hearts: “Do not lead us into temptation”—that is, do not permit us to go forth so that we may be conquered.

It is as though we were saying: “Bring temptation, so that we may be tested, and grant assistance so that we may not be conquered, so that after triumph we may be crowned as victors.”

Winds come, rivers surge, waves strike, immense whirlpools pile up. We ask, “Do not lead us in”—that is, do not deprive us of your help so that temptation may conquer [Col. 0297C].

For you cry from heaven to soldiers still fighting in the contest: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (Joan. XVI, 33).

It is as though you were saying: If you are afraid among innumerable enemies; if you are fearful because of the immense savagery of the world; if your strength is broken by distrust before their violent assaults; if snares are stretched out on every side; if the darkness of shadows is scattered so that, pressed by blindness, you may stumble; if you are hemmed in by countless calamities; and if, surrounded by a rampart, your faith is at last weakened—“Take courage; I have conquered the world.”

For in my victory your triumph will be accomplished.

Amid these evils, which our sins demand, we rightly pray that he not abandon us and not lead us into temptation. And then we add:

[Col. 0297D] But deliver us from evil. By these two petitions we are stripped of the devil’s kingdom: that is, insofar as we have been led out from it, so that we may not again be infected by it; and insofar as we are still in it because of the weakness of the flesh, so that we may be freed from it as quickly as possible. For when we say, “Deliver us from evil,” we ask to be delivered no less from invisible than from visible evil. Above all, however, we ask to be stripped of that evil by which we are held captive, namely, the devil and sin, which is propagated daily from the devil. Nevertheless, the prayer is also directed toward the end, because then we shall be wholly delivered from every evil. For as long as we are here, we cannot exist without that evil by which the flesh is worn down and the soul restrained; but when this corruptible has put on incorruption and this mortal has put on immortality, then indeed we shall be entirely free from every evil, with that freedom by which Christ will free us.

Meanwhile, however, we also ask to be delivered from the evil of this world, so that we may not be weighed down by the anguish and pressure of corruption. In this petition the eye is extended both to past time and to the present, and also to the future: so that by every means we may be delivered either from what we have committed, or from the evil by which we are still held, whether inwardly or outwardly, or from what threatens in the future. For every corruption is certainly evil, because it arose from evil—that is, from the devil. Therefore, when we pray, “Deliver us from evil,” we ask to share in the integrity of the future life, so that at last we may be able to reach it more happily.

What, then, is lacking that is not contained in these seven petitions, whether for the present life or, what is greater, for the future? From this it is plainly evident that in them Christ taught realities rather than words. Hence we rightly believe that nothing else ought to be prayed for, since whatever is done for salvation—which is to ask in the name of Jesus—we ask for altogether in this prayer. If we consider it rightly, a wondrous order of ascent is displayed here. For just as the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit begin from the highest and descend step by step toward the end, that is, as far as the beginning of wisdom, so the order of the petitions extends from the highest down to the end, so that we may be delivered from the evils of the world.

Thus, in both cases, if we begin from the end, a graded order of the seven virtues is made toward perfection; and if we begin from the highest, because we likewise receive these things from above, there is again an order of descent. But because through the operation of these gifts we rise from the lowest to the highest, the seven beatitudes, as we have stated above, which are sought through our labor by means of the same gifts so that they may teach us to rise to higher things, proceed step by step from the lowest to the highest.

We therefore have in the petitions the request that we may receive the gifts; in the gifts, the request that we may carry out the commands of the Holy Spirit; and then, in the activity, the beatitudes by which we may be crowned immediately follow. Accordingly, let us pray that we may receive them; once they have been received, let us carry out what has been commanded; and while acting, let us anticipate the time when, aided by God, we may eventually reach each of the beatitudes.

For just as we are delivered from evil through the spirit of fear, so, once delivered from it, we desire to be poor in spirit no less than in possessions. Then, when we say, “Do not lead us into temptation,” we ask for the spirit of piety, so that our inner person may become gentle and we may be meek, lest, without anyone warning us, we fall into the snares of temptations. Rather, let us be moved by the spirit of piety, so that we may not be embittered by any evils and, walking along the way of justice, may escape without any impiety of mind or body.

For when we ask that our debts be forgiven us, we ask only through the spirit of knowledge, because by that gift we are able to know or understand our sins. Hence David also says: “Who understands his offenses?” As though he plainly said: No one except the one who has received, as a gift, the spirit of the knowledge of God. He said “understand” instead of “know,” because divine and spiritual things are understood, whereas earthly things and those belonging to the flesh are properly known.

Hence some teachers have defined this distinction between wisdom and knowledge, saying that wisdom pertains to contemplation of the future life, while knowledge pertains to the use of temporal things, so that we may use them well. This virtue of knowledge is concerned with avoiding or understanding evils and seeking good things, because through it, once evils have been rejected, we first share in the recognition of truth. For this reason we are urged, with unwearied prayers, to mourn the contagions of our own lives and those of others, and to burn more abundantly with desire for the heavenly aspirations of our celestial homeland.

342 We make good use of these two ends—of vices and of reward—when, mourning the former, we wholly avoid them, and, desiring the latter, we long for them with the fullest ardor of charity. Great, therefore, is whoever is raised up by these three steps. For when he is delivered from evil, he already clings to the highest good; and when he asks for it, he confesses that it must be pursued. When he sees himself delivered, he asks the one from whom he is delivered not to lead him into temptation, lest he fall again into evil.
