Here the power of the one without whose permission the adversary can do nothing is openly proclaimed; and because permission is granted on account of sins, he appears, as it were, to lead us into temptation. Therefore let all our fear, hope, and devotion be directed toward him in religious worship, since it is established that in temptation the enemy is permitted nothing unless the power to harm is granted by the one whom we ask not to lead us into temptation.

Furthermore, because in this life it is not possible for those reborn to live without sin, we rightly make use of this petition, asking to be delivered from sins, so that through it we may be taught, in the duty of charity, what we ourselves ought to do for our brothers. But because we do not yet fully enjoy the vision of God and the fullness of the virtues, we need daily food on the journey, so that, refreshed by it, we may eventually return to our homeland.

Therefore we immediately ask for “our daily bread,” which no one reaches without the spirit of fortitude. Hence it is written: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. III, 19). Wherever sweat is required, labor is signified; and wherever there is labor, the spirit of fortitude is shown to be necessary. Wherever the spirit of fortitude is present, there the unwearied hunger for justice is anticipated, because the fullness of justice is eternal food.

It is called daily so that, hungering for it each day, we may fulfill the justice that Christ taught: so that in the petition there may be the bread that came down from heaven, in its practice justice, and in its refreshment the spirit of fortitude. By these four gifts of the virtues, the remaining three are finally brought to fuller completion, since the will of God on earth, just as in heaven, is governed by the spirit of counsel. For God wills nothing other than what belongs to counsel, and through it all things are directed. His willing and his counseling are, in truth, one. He is not divided in such a way that he has one thing in willing and another in counseling. We, however, very often do not will one thing and recognize another as advisable.

For this reason we sometimes walk perversely; and therefore the spirit of counsel is necessary, so that through it the will of God may be directed in us, in order that we may rightly be able to be merciful. The spirit of understanding plainly remains, through which the future kingdom is disclosed to those entering it, and purity of heart is granted. When this eye has been opened, we shall see God reigning there as he is, and there the spirit of wisdom will complete that seventh sanctification of his name. This sanctification was not fitting to be requested in the number six, which everyone declares to be perfect, nor in any other number preceding it, but in the number seven, in which the sanctification of the seventh day is signified: the day on which God is related to have sanctified his rest after resting from all his work.

This does not mean that he rested after labor, but that, because he made all things perfect, he permitted them to rest in himself. For everything that exists is from him and through him in such a way that everything owes him its existence. Therefore the coming of the kingdom is requested in the perfection of the number six, so that we may all attain “to a perfect man and to the measure of the fullness of Christ”; and then, as we rest in him, he may be sanctified in us while we are sanctified in him.

This sanctification he promised from the beginning to those who believe in him, when he is read to have sanctified the day that followed the perfection of all things. In it God, resting in himself, permitted it to rest nowhere other than in himself. We rightly ask that this rest be sanctified in us, so that, sanctified forever, we may rest in him.

This, then, is the finger of Christ the High Priest, with which his blood is sprinkled seven times, so that in it we may be sanctified from the leprosy of uncleanness. For through the finger the grace of the Holy Spirit is signified, by which our prayers and the blessedness of the gifts are completed and all the contagions of the present life are expiated.

In this seventh sanctification the peace of true blessedness is firmly established, adoption is granted, and wisdom is bestowed in its fullness. Hence Paul also says: “Pursue peace and holiness, without which no one will see God.” Every dedication of the virtues, however, is extended toward this final sanctification, because after the perfection of the number six, clothed with the gift of immortality, we are sanctified by his sprinkling, so that thereafter, resting in him, we may remain unchangeable and holy through him.

I therefore urge the reader to contemplate more carefully these seven steps of the gifts and petitions, because it is not without reason that perfection and true rest are proclaimed in very many places under this number. For Christ Jesus came for everyone. He came to teach the wise and the foolish in heart alike, and to give the precepts of salvation to every sex and age.

Therefore he delivered, in a sufficiently concise form, not only the discipline of the commandments but also that of the gifts and petitions, so that through fewer words he might entrust to memory many things of the greatest necessity. Thus the simplicity of faith might quickly learn the sufficiency of its salvation, while the prudence of the gifted might be struck with amazement at the greater depth of the mystery.

Hence Isaiah prophesies, saying: “The Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth.” He shortened this word in such a way that people could suddenly grasp it by heart; yet he filled it with realities in such a way that at present no one without the grace of the Holy Spirit—and very few even with it—can either understand or receive everything.

Therefore we must labor in prayer so that we may receive the gifts from grace; through the gifts we must act so that we may reach the merit of grace; and then, according to our merits, we must hope for the blessedness granted to those who seek it. Otherwise one reaches neither the house without the prayers of faith nor the degree of blessedness without merits. The following conclusion makes this sufficiently clear.

“If,” he says, “you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses. But if you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins.” From this it is clear that each person is condemned by his own faithlessness. Yet in both cases the Father remains unchangeable, because he cannot lose the heart of fatherhood. Rather, because you do not wish to be a son, you are rightly condemned by your own cruelty.

For this reason, after the prayer, he concluded everything with this one matter, in order to bring back to memory what you had promised in prayer, so that you might recognize that it lay within your power to obtain the pardon (*veniam*) for which you ask. The judge before whom you plead first demands nothing else than that you be toward your brother such as you ask him to be toward you as his son.

If you do not spare your brother, you also inflict an injury upon the Father whom you entreat, and therefore you are rightly condemned as doubly guilty: first, because you owe him for your sins; and then because, warned by the judge, you did not grant forgiveness to your brother when he asked for it out of love for the Father, so that you yourself might receive forgiveness. For this reason let no one deceive himself, because the one who composed the prayer penetrates the secrets of the heart, and he regards you in prayer as you have been in your heart.

[Col. 0301C] With these matters thus examined, let us now complete what follows.

“When you fast, do not become like the sad hypocrites,” and the rest. He next instructs all his children how they ought to fast. He explains that they should not appear sad, like hypocrites, when they fast before people. This does not mean that on a day of fasting one ought not to grieve for sins and the various circumstances of misery; rather, he wants the sadness that seeks empty praise to be far removed from us, so that God may be glorified in everything and everything may be referred to his praise.

Hence he does not simply say, “Do not be sad,” but adds: “Do not,” he says, “become like the sad hypocrites.” Otherwise, how shall we humble our souls before God, especially since we ought to grieve unto repentance? For “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart.” Thus he also condemns that sadness which pursues empty praise and teaches that it must be avoided. This is immediately explained in what follows.

For they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting. As above, he also criticizes the end toward which their intention is directed, and teaches that the fruit of fasting must lie outside the display of an emaciated body; they must not seek popular favor by exhibiting squalor. For it is fitting that all our fasting be placed in the beauty of holy action, so that we may please the one whose glory we ought always to pursue and whose praise we must seek without weariness.

It should be observed that just as arrogance is stolen upon the proud through the brightness of clothing and the beauty of appearance, so vanity deceives the unwary through excessive squalor and emaciation of the body. “They disfigure,” he says, “their faces”—which is plainly to say: They draw them outside the bounds of ordinary human custom, and, afflicting themselves with an unusual kind of ugliness, seek pallor so that they may appear unlike others and, on account of the very wretchedness of their flesh, be praised as more than human.

We nevertheless say that “they demolish their faces,” as it is found in certain books, is better than “they disfigure.” For “to disfigure” is, as it were, to lead outside the boundary; “to demolish” is, as it were, to scatter and, by covering the face with sadness and squalor, to reduce all its beauty to nothing. But whichever reading you accept, it belongs to hypocrites: wearing the masks of a stage performance, they carry one thing in their hearts and present another on the surface to those who see them. They do not strive for the virtues of Christ through the practice of true religion, but to arouse the favor of the crowd.

Hence what follows:

“Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward.” Their own reward, therefore, and not the adoption promised to the faithful, because, seeking their own glory, they are alien from Christ. Indeed, “God is not mocked.” Thus, in the present they have received the smoky praises of the crowd, and in the future the reward of their hypocrisy: condemnation.

“But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face,” and so forth. It is an idiom of the Holy Scriptures to speak in the singular to one as though to all, and to all as though to one. Therefore he said in the singular, “But you, when you fast,” so that each person might understand that this statement was addressed particularly to himself.

The passage should also be noted because not all the precepts of the New Testament are to be observed according to the letter. Otherwise, while fleeing in our fasts the awareness of people and the vanity of empty praise, we would appear to fast all the more when our heads were anointed, and we would become ridiculous, smeared with the richness of oil.

Nevertheless, he speaks according to the custom of the province of Palestine, where on feast days people habitually anoint their heads while celebrating solemn occasions. From this it is clear that those who fast ought to be festive, and that on days of abstinence they should grow rich in spiritual joy.

For our inner person exists, and just as all the bodily members are governed from the head, so the parts of the inner person share in what proceeds from the mind. For this reason “head” is often used for “mind.” It is the mind, finally, that ought on days of fasting to be anointed with sacred ointment—namely, that of which the bride speaks to the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “Your name is poured-out ointment; therefore the young women love you” (Song I, 3).

When our mind has been anointed with this ointment, it rightly loves him whose love has been poured into it inwardly, whose fragrance it exhales, and whose perfumes of virtue it scatters everywhere, adorned with good works.

But the head of hypocrites is anointed with the ointment of flattery, concerning which the Psalmist sings: “Let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Ps. CXL, 3). Christ, therefore, has become our ointment: poured out through the passion of death, he filled the whole house—namely, the holy Church—with his fragrance.

Therefore it is not fitting to fast for the sake of anyone else; rather, suffused with his spirit, we ought through abstinence to mortify the flesh, so that we may share in his sufferings. Otherwise, unless we are anointed with the spirit of his love, our fasts will be empty.

Jesus was anointed with that oil above his companions. Let us also be anointed with it, so that works of mercy may abound, imploring the spirit of charity by which we may be inwardly watered by God’s dew. Concerning this the Prophet says: “You have anointed my head with oil, and my intoxicating cup—how splendid it is!” (Ps. XXII, 5). For unless we are anointed with that oil of anointing, the cup of our fasting is not intoxicated with any feeling of devotion.

“Anoint your head,” he says, “and wash your face.” This is plainly to say: Pour over your mind the spirit of joy by laboring in good works, and wash your face—that is, your conscience—with tears, so that your mind and conscience may be clean in all your works before God. For “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 6).

Otherwise, on the days of our fasts, it is not enough for the head to be anointed with works of mercy without a pure conscience; nor is it enough for the conscience to be washed clean from sinful works if we do not earnestly do the good things we can. Therefore, so that the head may shine, suffused with the grace of the Holy Spirit, let the conscience be cleansed from every stain of sin and washed in a fountain of tears, so that the fast may become acceptable and may commend us, anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit, as purer and brighter.

“Do not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret. And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.” The one who fasts for people is caught by their favor and seeks empty glory; the one who fasts for God the Father mortifies himself for his love and gives to another what he takes away from himself.

Likewise, the person fasts for himself and not for God who, enticed by greed, reserves for the future for himself what he has abstained from. But the one who fasts for God offers his fast inwardly, in secret, with a pure conscience, precisely where God the Father sees.

For if he is believed to be inwardly present in secret through faith, one must fast in the place where he sees, since he who is absent nowhere can see only where he is known to be. Therefore the person who fasts must live in such a way as to please the one whom he carries in his breast.

“Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth,” and the rest. This statement is circumstantially connected with the words, “Do not appear to people to be fasting.” For whoever fasts, whether by reserving what he has not eaten or by seeking glory for himself because of what he has abstained from, certainly stores up treasure for himself on earth.

Everything we do for earthly advantages we store up on earth; everything we do for God we transfer to heaven. Here “heaven” is used for eternity, while “earth” is used for transitory things. Therefore whatever we do, and however much we do, we ought to do for eternal things and in spiritual matters, so that we may be able to live happily forever.

Nor should we think that we shall find these earthly things, distributed for the uses of the commandments, gathered together there according to the letter. Rather, through the works of our service we acquire in Christ those treasures of wisdom and knowledge. For no other treasures are possessed in the heavenly places, nor can other treasures be transferred there from here. But while we lose these things for Christ’s sake, we store up for ourselves the things that are in him.

Although we are specifically admonished concerning almsgiving, the passage must nevertheless be understood generally of every work of virtue. For whatever we spend temporally for Christ, we shall receive back eternally in him. Therefore we must always take care to perform the things we do with this purpose: that we may please Christ and, through this, diligently prepare for ourselves in him the hidden treasures laid up for us.

“Where neither rust nor moth consume, and where thieves do not break in and steal.” Having therefore abandoned concern for empty praise and the slander of the envious, by which alone the precious treasures of souls are corrupted, let us place all our hope in heavenly things and store up treasure there—where we already are through hope, where we still walk by faith, and where we embrace through charity.

Here, however, rust consumes all the splendor of metals, and moth or age destroys the brightness of garments. To speak more plainly, whatever is possessed in the world will pass away. Thus, in these three words, every desire of the world and the extravagance of greed are condemned.

Morally, too, if we carry out anything in the flesh, we bury treasures on earth, when we occupy the precious senses of the body with earthly desires. Thus, when gluttony or fornication is practiced, a talent is buried in the earth and consumed by rust, because lust subdues and corrodes minds that have become hard as iron. Then anger, pride, fear, arrogance, and the whole army of vices ravage the garments of character. If anything remains after these, thieves—namely, the multitude of demons—dig it up and steal it.

Hence blessed Job, touched by anguish of heart, laments, saying: “Those who consume me do not sleep”; “by their multitude,” he says, “my garment is consumed, as by a moth” (Job XXX, 17). By these words he shows that even those whom God tests are sometimes gnawed and worn down by the many teeth of ambushes, and are gradually consumed as by a moth, while their garments are corrupted by the deceitful schemes of those who seek to steal them. The Teacher of truth, instructing his people to beware of this, wisely comprehended everything in a few words.

“Store up,” he says, “treasures for yourselves in heaven.” As though he were saying: When you fast or perform some good work, store it where neither flattery nor empty glory can corrupt it. When, because of abstinence, you withdraw something earthly from yourselves—something that nature itself also demands—place this and whatever else you possess there, to be preserved where neither thieves nor corruption can ever approach.

Finally, whatever it is that must be done in action, do it spiritually. For “the one who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, and the one who sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit.” Therefore store up treasure in spiritual things, that is, in heaven, so that from spiritual things you may receive eternal life.

It should also be noted that he does not say, “Store up treasures for me,” but “for yourselves,” because whatever good work we do for love of him benefits not him but us. Hence David says: “Preserve me, Lord, for you have no need of my good things” (Ps. XV, 1). He therefore has need of nothing from another, and thus whatever we give to him is kept for us.

Moreover, when he says, “Where neither rust nor moth destroys,” he shows that the future riches of the saints will be incorruptible. When he says that there thieves neither break in nor steal, he makes clear that there no fraud of the devil will ever prevail against God’s elect. Thus their glory will be incorruptible without end, and, enjoying it forever without any transgression of sin, they will be blessed unchangeably by grace.

The text continues:

“Where your treasure is, there is your heart also.” Whoever stores treasure on earth has his heart below; whoever stores it in heaven—that is, in spiritual things—is already present in the heights through hope and has his heart fixed in Christ, in whom are all the treasures of riches.

“The lamp of your body is your eye,” and the rest. He continues concerning the purity of our heart and teaches metaphorically, from the exterior, the function of the inner person. For just as all the members of the body are directed in an orderly way toward action by these bodily eyes, so by the mind’s intention and the light of faith every kind of virtue is illuminated, so that they may perfect a luminous body.

Here only one and simple eye is sought, concerning which the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “You have wounded my heart, my sister; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes” (Song IV, 9), where he expressed the purest light of her heart. For although many kinds of virtue shine forth here and there, Christ is wounded by the one eye of faith that works through charity, through the love of affection. For a lamp contains light; so charity, the love of Christ, shines in faith. But when faith has ceased, charity alone will shine for us.

“But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark.” That is, if the intention of the mind is not from faith, it is evil. Therefore your whole body, even if virtues seem to be present in it—that is, the whole inner person—will be evil. For whatever is not from faith is sin; all sins are evil, and therefore the body that consists of them will be dark.

Nothing condemns more than faithlessness and the evil intention of hypocrites, which descends from faithlessness. Even if something good appears to be done there, it is counted among vices because it is born from the origin of vices.

“So if the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be?” That is: If the good things you have done become dark because of an evil intention, although they could have been light had they proceeded from faith, what do you think will be the case with those things that are evil in themselves and are not done from faith, indeed arise from an evil intention? Since they are darkness, how great will their darkness be?

For an evil intention is darkness. If something resembling light—a virtuous deed—arises from it, the very light of the virtue, because it is done badly, will be a vice. If, in turn, a vice is performed with an evil and faithless intention, darkness is generated from darkness. Who, then, could explain such great darkness?

Christ therefore wants good things to be done and to arise from a good purpose of mind. Otherwise, if our justification is from faith, who can be justified by that faith which is ambiguous in itself? Here it must be asked: If virtues performed with an evil intention are vices, should vices that in turn appear to be performed with a good purpose be interpreted as light, when we are deceived in God’s judgment? Otherwise, severity seems more inclined toward the punishment of guilt than the origin of good toward the increase of virtue.

But “the judgments of God are a great abyss.” For who knows by what judgment of God we are deceived even in the same good purpose? Or who understands whether our will is judged rightly in view of all our circumstances? Nevertheless, we must trust in the Lord’s goodness: if we stumble while acting with a right intention, we shall quickly be cleansed by the light of faith and confession. But if obstinacy persists, we must fear all the more that this has proceeded from the root of an evil intention.

For if something contrary happens to a good will, humble confession, which is born from good will, will quickly cleanse it, so that everything may shine in the light. Therefore let the soul always be subject to God, and let it follow the saying: “Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he himself will act.”

“You cannot serve two masters,” and the rest. He is speaking, therefore, of things opposed to and in conflict with one another. For we often see two things that agree well with each other being served with one purpose and with an even mind, without any disturbance of the mind. But he is not speaking of these, because he sets these matters before us on account of the conflicting interests of the things themselves.

Thus the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three Lords, since their divinity, will, and power are proclaimed to be one. But equal obedience in service fails wherever a different will is introduced. This statement is connected with the three matters that we explained above.

It is as though he were saying: You cannot merely do good things so that you may appear before people and thereby please God. Nor can you simultaneously store up treasure on earth and deposit it in heaven. Nor, certainly, can you serve vices and virtues at the same time, by which, on opposite sides, one serves either God rightly or the devil.

But because the kingdom of Christ and the kingdom of the devil are far divided from one another, we cannot serve as soldiers in both at once. For this reason, at the beginning of faith no one enters the baptismal font, through which one enters the kingdom of Christ, until he has renounced the devil, all his works, and all his pomps.

A foolish soldier, therefore, is one who has rejected a tyrannical domination and begun to serve under the most pious heavenly authority, if he should again despise the one whom he had devoutly received, casting away his immortal weapons and refusing to obey his laws and disciplines—the one through whom he had also been rescued from death and acquired perpetual salvation.

What is more foolish than to return to the dominion of the one by whom he had previously been held captive, assigned to death, and tormented under the cruel laws of the Furies? Therefore let each person consider within himself what he rejected in baptism. Each of us repudiated the devil, all his works, and all his pomps; and yet a remarkable deception occurs when we pursue either the works of the flesh or the pomps of the world.

For what are the works of the flesh if not the works of the devil? And again, what are the pomps of the world considered to be if not the devil’s? When we serve or succumb to them, before whom do we prostrate ourselves if not before the devil? Thus the proper meanings of the words are remarkably exchanged in turn.

“Either,” he says, “he will hate the one and love the other, or he will support the one and despise the other.” Certainly the devil must always be hated, while Christ must surely be loved. No one has ever openly hated God; even the pagans confess that they love him, although they are led astray by various errors while inventing false gods for themselves. But the name of the devil they all alike execrate.

Thus every vicious person, oppressed by his own desire, supports the devil as a tyrant, as though he were ruling over him by an unjust exaction; but God, his Lord and Creator, who still calls him back, he despises, overcome by his own desires and by the devil’s persuasions.

Nevertheless, he does not hate the one whom he knows with certainty loves him and wills his salvation; rather, he despises returning, while, perfected in evil by desire, he lies oppressed under the devil. There are therefore two outcomes of these two positions, because the whole human race is gathered into these two divisions.

All people either hate the devil and, by obeying, love the true God, or else, overcome by their own desire under the devil, they endure a tyrannical domination and, refusing to keep the commands of their Creator, blinded in mind and presuming upon his mercy, despise him.

[Col. 0307C] “You cannot serve God and Mammon.” Here he explains more openly what he had proposed above: that they cannot serve God and the world together, nor temporal and eternal things together, nor heavenly and earthly things together.

For in the Syriac interpretation, “Mammon” means riches; to serve them is to deny God. He does not say, “You cannot possess riches and carry out the service of the Lord,” but deliberately says, “You cannot serve God and riches at the same time.”

For it is one thing to possess the wealth of the world and another to serve it. Whoever possesses it and uses it lawfully, as its master, is rather its steward than its servant. But the person who neglects himself and wears himself out excessively in the profits of greed is rightly called a servant of Mammon.

Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons and martyr of Christ, says that this name belongs to a demon, as though it were the demon presiding over the riches of this world—not because the wealth of the world belongs to him or lies under his control, but because he uses it for deception, ensnaring the unwary in the traps of riches.

But whichever interpretation you accept, whoever is so entangled in the bonds of riches that he must rightly be called their servant serves the devil.

Therefore I say to you: Do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat, nor about your body, what you shall put on. The structure of this statement does not seem entirely to correspond to the propositions set forth above. Is a servant, then, of one master unable to be anxious about clothing and food? Or, because he cannot serve two masters equally, what reason is there that he should not think anxiously about food and clothing? Yet if we examine this connection carefully, it carries forward the meaning of the preceding statements. For throughout the whole preceding discourse he had commended contempt for the world and confidence in the future, as though addressing sons and heirs of eternal life: he commanded them to endure injuries patiently, to bear losses willingly, and in no case to take revenge; likewise to love their enemies, and then to flee human glory. Now he labors to strengthen us through faith in his promises, so that we may hope for eternal blessings. For there are many whom love of present things and despair of the future render sluggish, while unbelief envelops them in complete darkness.

This is why he says, “You cannot serve two masters,” and then, “Therefore I say to you: Do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat”—as though plainly indicating what it means to serve riches. “Do not be anxious,” he says, because to be anxious on their account is to serve them; and therefore, to prevent you from being servants of money, I forbid anxiety about food or clothing. For it was not said, “In anxiety you shall eat your bread,” but, “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread.” Therefore labor is to be undertaken, but anxiety is to be removed. Otherwise, even if superfluous things are not sought, the heart may become divided under the pretext of necessity.

Hence we ought to entrust all our hope to God, lest we serve things that perish. For worldly anxiety is occupied with its own concerns, lest possessions decay or the fruits of labor fail to arrive; from these anxieties and fears arise, which greatly disturb the wretched soul, although by such means we can acquire nothing more and retain nothing further except as much as he shall have determined—to whom we ought also to entrust ourselves.

But it must be asked: since the soul is spiritual and incorporeal, how can this bodily food be said to pertain to it? The reason is that “soul,” as elsewhere, is here understood of this life by which we live. For it seems to consist of two parts: its higher part is the mind, by which our inner person is called not only spiritual but also spirit, namely, the soul itself; its lower part, however, is called the animus, from which the animal person takes its name. This person does not yet perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God, but lives only this present life, which is nourished by food, and lives together with the beasts. Whoever loses this life for Christ’s sake will find it again as a spiritual life, made alive by the Holy Spirit for eternal life.

Thus, according to one part, the soul requires food in order that life may be nourished; according to the other part, it is believed to require something far greater than food. For this present life was not created for the sake of food, but food for the sake of this life. Similarly, the body is not made for clothing, but clothing for the body. Therefore the animus should not be anxious lest it fail to receive what was created for its sake. Rather, one ought to believe the words of God, because he is truth, and because the efficacy of all creatures lies in his word; therefore a person should not be uncertain. For in the promises of him who made these pledges there is nothing ineffective or ambiguous. Let a person be what he ought to be and what he was made to be, and immediately all things will be present for whose sake they were made.

“Look at the birds of the air, because they neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns.” Are we, by their examples, therefore forbidden to sow or to labor for the things necessary to human use? Far be it from us to understand it so. Rather, here as in all passages of Scripture, we must seek the meaning that accords with catholic truth and offers spiritual understanding. This example does not concern human labor, to which it was said, “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread,” but the removal of anxiety and the instilling of confidence in the supreme and most excellent Father among his children. Since the birds of the air live without any care or fear of earthly nourishment, how much more ought those for whom all these things were created to serve the Lord without any anxiety of mind, and to cast all their care and anxiety upon him, so that they may live for him whom, once they believed, they embraced.

“And your heavenly Father,” he says, “feeds them.” He therefore magnifies and strengthens the confidence of the children. Thus he testifies that the Father feeds even those things that are least significant and were created for the sake of his children. If the goodness of the giver extends even to them, how much more does it extend to those whom he has perhaps reckoned among his adopted children?

**355** “Are you not more valuable than they?” Here “more valuable” does not refer to number, but to the fact that rational children are more precious, having been joined to adoption by grace. Nevertheless, this comparison of the saints, as is customary when the greater is compared with the lesser, is not improperly made with the birds of heaven, because the saints penetrate the secrets of heaven farther than birds do. And just as they are preeminent by nature and merit, so by grace they occupy the heights of heaven, flying more sublimely.

The prophet marvels at them, saying: “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60:8.) Moreover, very many of them are so separated from the affairs of the world that they now do nothing earthly and undertake no other labor, but, occupied with the word and with divine contemplation alone, already dwell in heaven through hope.

“Which of you can add one cubit to his stature?” Thus far he has exhorted them concerning food; now he speaks about bodily clothing. By excessive diligence and ingenuity no one can add anything to his body, and therefore concern for the body should be relaxed, since it is believed to have been made by providence, whereas creating anything in it lies outside our power. By these words he not only instills confidence concerning clothing, but also demonstrates that the size and quality of the body are measured by his power, and that whatever is lacking in the future he can restore. Therefore the care of clothing should be entrusted to him who provided the body’s measure when it was formed.

This does not mean that a person ought not to labor and provide these things, just as with food. Rather, one must cast away all fear and anxiety concerning them, entrust one’s hope and confidence to God, and reserve no fear for oneself concerning food or clothing. Paul aptly teaches this elsewhere from the same passage, expressing it in a single statement: “He who plows ought to plow in hope” (1 Cor. 9:10). He did not forbid the act, but commanded that even in such matters hope be entrusted to God. Nor did he say that the one who plows ought to plow anxiously; rather, he specifically indicates that one ought to plow in hope.

Unless someone should perhaps interpret this as meaning that he has hope in the seed itself when it has been cast into the earth—something no one but a fool would ever say. Rather, whatever we prudently undertake for this life must be understood in such a way that we always place our hope in the Lord both concerning these things themselves and concerning the future.

“Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow.” He confirms the exhortation concerning clothing with an example sufficiently suited to the earlier one concerning food. It is not necessary, as some devout people wish, to allegorize these things, teaching that by the birds we should understand demons, by the lilies the higher angelic orders, and by the green grass **356** the nations. Rather, Christ simply reveals to them that all things exist by his power and wisdom, and that nothing is lacking in his might. Nor do bodies escape his providence—bodies that he created, formed according to their measures—since he bestowed such beauty even upon herbs and plants, and therefore they too must be clothed.

It is true, therefore, that not even Solomon, who is said to have flourished in the glory of the world above the kings of the earth, was clothed with such beauty as that of the lilies. For no art can color anything so vividly that it shines like a lily or glows red like a rose. Yet the lilies do not labor to adorn themselves with dyes, just as the birds do not sow in the earth; nor do they spin, so as to fashion coverings with which they may be clothed.

At this point some unlearned person, pretending to be clever in a kind of physical argument, criticizes the simplicity of the Gospel, saying: “Why should insensible things seek what nature has bestowed upon them? Or why should they labor to produce a beauty that the Creator granted not to them but to us? Or how are they covered, since it is written that not even Solomon was covered like one of these?” For lilies are born rather than covered. And as someone has said: “Covering or clothing belongs to the body, not to the body itself. Therefore, if the matter is referred,” he says, “to the understanding of human beings, the whiteness of the lily’s color could rival the brightness of a garment.”

These words do not reveal the truth of the matter, nor do they attend to the context of the reading; rather, they obscure its meaning. For he proposed an example in which the Creator’s manifold providence and effective power are proclaimed: he who granted so much to insensible things will also grant what is needed to us, for whom these things were created. This does not mean that he granted them more excellent things than he granted us, but that, while possessing an inward grace of beauty, we should not seek this outward beauty with less confidence.

Everything colored is rightly said to be “covered,” even if it grows—not because it has some other external covering, but because, according to the manner of speaking, the color itself is called a covering. Thus we often say, “Paleness covered him,” or “Blushing covered him”; “blindness covered him,” or “the wasting of the body covered him,” and other expressions of this kind, referring to conditions that arise within the body. No one, therefore, should doubt that just as there is a disposition of the mind, so there is a disposition in the body and a disposition outside the body.

Moreover, although any color of clothing may rival the whiteness of the lily, it can in no way equal it. Therefore, if he grants such things to any one of the plants, the Christian should have no doubt **357** that he will ever defraud him of his promises.

[Col. 0311A] “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith?” Thus, by the authority of examples, he divinely confirms the inviolable confidence of our faith, so that no one may be permitted to doubt, since doubt is removed by such evident proof and unbelief is refuted by Christ’s promise. If the grass, which exists today, is clothed with such beauty of greenness, how much more is he prepared to clothe those whom he has made participants in eternal fellowship?

“And tomorrow it is thrown into the oven.” Other manuscripts read, “into the fire.” There is no doubt that it is thrown into the fire when necessity requires, although it is regarded as unsuitable for this purpose and is rather kept for the use of animals. More figuratively, however, it is said to be thrown into the oven because, when what flourished today with the beauty of its appearance is gathered tomorrow into a heap, that is to throw it into the oven: since that heap resembles the shape of an oven, it is rightly called an oven.

“How much more you, O you of little faith?” The verb “will he clothe” is understood. Since he persuades us to place all our confidence in faith in his promises and in the power of his own majesty to fulfill them, he commands us, leaving aside anxiety about the things we need, to ask everything without hesitation from him, from whom we ourselves received the beginning of life. We should hesitate over nothing small, since we ought to hope for heavenly and eternal things without any uncertainty and to await them patiently.

For if concerning earthly and perishable things we do not believe his promises, so that we may cease to be anxious, and yet, although ungrateful, receive these things from him, how can we rightly hope for invisible and heavenly things? Or how can we believe without doubt in the promises of eternal things when we are not confident even concerning these? Therefore the trumpet of truth cries out in such a way as both to instill confidence in us concerning these matters and to condemn our unbelief.

Faith is exceedingly small—if it is to be called faith at all—when it does not provide an immovable assurance even concerning the least things. Worse still, very few possess even this measure of faith. Thus, although elsewhere the Lord condemns it, they suffocate the word of divine preaching beneath worldly cares and anxieties, and they do not produce the fruit of faith by entrusting all the hope of their life to their Creator and seeking first, as justice dictates, the things that are heavenly.

[Col. 0311C] “Therefore do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘With what shall we be clothed?’” He therefore repeats and reinforces more fully whatever he taught from the beginning of the discourse, so that all Christians may live without anxiety concerning the present life, because worldly anxiety suffocates the word, preventing the soldier of Christ from bearing fruit.

O unbelief of the heart! You press so heavily upon human hearts that scarcely anyone is permitted to breathe fully toward the things above. Nearly everyone is weighed down by this anxiety, including at times those who seem to be dead to the world. Hence they are so often scandalized over food and clothing. Wretched, therefore, is their perfection, when anxiety over these things makes them equal to the Gentiles.

“All these things,” he says, “the Gentiles seek.” What, then, does the person who is still troubled by unbelief and fatigued by the cares of this life have more than a Gentile? He who places his confidence in the Lord concerning these things alone possesses at least a little faith; but he who is still anxious about them is judged an unbeliever. Hence perfect faith is rare and belongs to few.

Therefore, when Peter still doubted after the Lord’s command, he was rightly told: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14:31.) Whoever, then, doubts in any matter concerning God’s commandments, or trusts in the almighty God less than he has promised, is of little faith. Hence James also says: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask for it in faith, doubting nothing; for he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind” (Jas. 1:5).

If it is unfitting for a Christian to doubt in divine matters, how can he, after God’s promises, doubt faithfully in human and perishable matters? What, then, are you fleeing, Christian? The more you have doubted God’s promises, the fewer things you will find for which you may labor anxiously. And if, by God’s goodness, even while doubtful, you receive what you sought anxiously, it was not your anxiety that made it effective, but God’s generosity, for he makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked.

[Col. 0312B] “For your Father knows that you need all these things.” He therefore recalls the Father to the minds of his children, so that through him they may become more secure concerning his goodness and providence, without worldly anxiety. Thus elsewhere, to make us more certain, he says: “If you, though evil, know how to give good things to your children, how much more will your Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” (Matt. 7:10.)

To this unbelief might perhaps reply: “I know that he knows we need these things, but I do not know whether he wishes to give them.” Fool, you hear that he is a Father, and you doubt his willingness? What good father has ever closed his heart against a faithful son? And if he did not spare his own Son for us, what has he that he ought to deny? Therefore, whenever you do not receive what you rightly ask, it is not his but your own perversity or unbelief that causes it. For he has given his children nothing more powerful than faith, nothing stronger than love, nothing richer than hope. Therefore whoever abounds in these three things can do all things in Christ and possesses everything through him.

“Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.” I do not think “first” should refer to order, as though we ought afterward to seek these other things, since he says, “All these things will be added to you.” It should rather be referred to quantity, so that nothing outside this need be sought, because, together with it, all things are granted to the faithful.

Therefore he says, “Seek first the kingdom of God,” as though it were the highest good, which ought to be sought not for the sake of anything else but for its own sake, and not referred to something else. For all necessities will be added to you—not indeed to be embraced for their own sake, but so that you may practice righteousness and eventually attain happily to the kingdom. In the meantime, while you are on the way, these things are to be used, not for their own sake but for the sake of that kingdom. Thus we should use these things on the way so that we may enjoy the kingdom in our homeland: all these things are necessary for us because of that kingdom, whereas the kingdom is necessary for its own sake.

Hence it is said: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things, which are necessary for you because of him, will be added.” They are added because that one thing alone, and that supremely, is necessary, in which the whole sufficiency of the children is fulfilled. This is diligently sought through faith, hope, and love, if in everything we do and everything we desire we always seek it in our mind.

Here the order is aptly inverted: “Seek first the kingdom of God”; then he adds, “and his righteousness.” Therefore the righteousness of the kingdom must first be sought, by which one reaches the kingdom, and afterward, through that same righteousness, one must proceed to the kingdom itself. For no one can find it except by carrying out works of righteousness.

He put “first” at the beginning in order to charm the hearing, and afterward introduced the righteousness that must be sought, which is fulfilled only with considerable labor. If what charms us is pleasing, then the righteousness he taught everywhere must be fulfilled laboriously, even if what is commanded causes grief.

[Col. 0313B] “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” The righteousness of the kingdom therefore consists in observing all that Christ taught, together with the three virtues mentioned above, and then seeking the kingdom; and in fulfilling that same righteousness in works for no other reason than that God may be glorified **360** and that we may please him in all things.

The Gentiles seek earthly things in unbelief, since no hope of the future is shown to them, adoption has not been given to them, and no kingdom in heaven is granted to them. But because the faithful have been chosen for grace, it is rightly said to them: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you.” For although goodness is proclaimed at present to all—namely, to believers and unbelievers alike—in the future, however, he is everywhere proclaimed as just.

Therefore he warns his children: “Seek first the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world and promised in the Gospel; then seek its righteousness, because no reprobate will enter it, but the King of virtues will repay each person according to what he has done.” For this reason, to strive after virtues belongs to the children; to seek the things of the world belongs to the nations, that is, to unbelievers.

Nevertheless, because everything belongs to the children, these things will also be added to those who do not seek them. When they are withdrawn from them, this happens for their testing; when they are supplied, it is for thanksgiving, because for those who are called according to his purpose all things work together for good.

“Do not be anxious about tomorrow.” And if you ask, “Why?”—because all these things will be added to you. Here, while forbidding anxiety about the future, he at least permits care for the present. For Paul labored with his hands day and night, and he gave instructions concerning the collections made for the saints. Moreover, according to Agabus’s prophecy, famine was relieved by the saints; and we also read that the Lord had a money box. Thus it is not labor or provision, but anxiety and care that suffocate the mind, which are condemned.

“Tomorrow” is used of the future. For it is not anxiety about eternal life that is forbidden, but worldly anxiety. Hence it is clear that to be anxious in acquiring these things, fearful in preserving them, sorrowful in losing them, and also joyful in enjoying them is to serve them; but to be free from these and similar passions is to reign. For we cannot serve two masters, since worldly anxiety is one thing, and anxiety for the righteousness and kingdom of God another.

[Col. 0314A] “Tomorrow will be anxious for itself.” This does not mean the anxiety of the virtues, but the anxiety that disturbs the mind only through fear, joy, sorrow, and the distress of cares. Hence: “Sufficient for the day is its own evil.” That is, the anxiety and affliction of the present life. The Greek word κακία (*kakia*) has both meanings at once, namely “evil” and “affliction.”

Nevertheless, it would have been better here to translate it as “evil”; but there is an evil of sin, and an evil of labor and torment. Thus “sufficient for the day is its evil” means that it has its own labor and distress; therefore it is superfluous to think about uncertain things. Yet we do not insist that both senses of evil must be understood here together; certainly, we incur this evil by sinning. The point is not that some day is evil in itself, but that both evils occur in it.

Finally, Job and Jeremiah, observing such a day, rightly curse it, because it is not the day that the Lord made, but the day the devil devised—a day of evil and darkness. Therefore its evil is sufficient for it, and it does not need another’s. For if we scarcely endure in the light at present, how much more difficult will it be if we join the evil of the future to that of the present? The mind is so overwhelmed by present cares that it can scarcely look upon the light; how much more if the evil of that very day is doubled? Therefore he gives commandments for life, lest in this exile we be weighed down by double burdens.

**(Chapter 7.)** “Do not judge, and you will not be judged.” He is speaking about hidden and doubtful matters, whose manner or intention cannot be openly interpreted. Otherwise, why do both the apostles and the universal Church judge and decide concerning manifest crimes? It is because, concerning manifest matters—the judgment of which belongs to their office—they ought indeed to decide.

But concerning things that are hidden, or whose intention we do not know, no one judges without danger. There are, however, certain crimes of vice that can never be committed with a good intention; concerning these no one doubts that judgment must be made. There are also deeds that can be good if performed with a good intention and evil if performed with an evil one. When people carry them out under the appearance of religion, judgment must not immediately be made concerning them, until the Lord comes, who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and make the counsels of hearts manifest.

Nevertheless, through the simulation of some people these things are sometimes revealed. Concerning such persons the Lord says: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:16). Where matters are manifest, judgment must indeed be made, so that they may be exposed by the light, because they were not done in truth.

“For with what judgment you judge, you will be judged. And with what measure you measure, it will be measured back to you.” From this some philosophers, I do not know who, have scattered a cloud of darkness, so that the simple truth might be covered. They say: “If God is going to repay sinners with punishment according to measure, and every measure is bounded by time, what do the threats of infinite punishment mean?”

To this it must be admitted that not every measure, as one of them supposed, is prescribed by time. Nevertheless, lest we appear to evade the question, it is proved to be plausible, or altogether true, that every measure is bounded—not only by time, as he imagines, but also because certain things are specifically bounded by the dimensions of places, or by the capacity of things, which are likewise referred to place.

Therefore we must ask whether there is anything that is called eternal and yet is in some way held within certain boundaries. Consider the human being himself, who is confirmed by divine authority as destined to be eternal and yet is bounded by place, although he is also limited by an end. Otherwise he would be without location. The sun itself, which the philosophers consider eternal, is nevertheless thought by them to be contained within geometrical figures.

Thus, in many other ways also, it can be shown that something can be eternal and yet have a definite measure according to its mode. By this statement they are compelled, whether they wish it or not, to accept something eternal together with measure. In this way the punishments that Christ threatened will be eternal, although they will have a measure corresponding to the manner of the fault.

Nevertheless, it was not said, “What you have measured, that will be measured back to you,” but, “With what measure you have measured.” There is no doubt that the thing in which something is measured differs from the thing that is measured within the measure. It can happen that, with the same measure by which someone measured something for another person, something may be measured back to him. For example, with a bushel-measure of wheat, barley or gold—or something else—may be measured for him, or one hundred thousand may be assigned in the same measure. Thus the nature and quantity of the things may differ without comparison, and yet it can be stated most correctly that with the same measure by which he measured, something was measured back to him.

The source of this statement becomes clear a little earlier: “Do not judge,” he says, “and you will not be judged; for with what judgment you judge,” and so forth. If they judge with an unjust judgment, will they therefore be judged unjustly by the most just judge? Or if they do not judge in matters concerning which they are forbidden to judge, will they not be judged concerning their other crimes? Far be it from us to think so. There is no iniquity with God, nor does he allow any sin to go unpunished.

Rather, this is what is meant: “With what judgment you judge, you will be judged,” as though it were said, “With what intention you do good, by that same intention you are set free; or with what intention you do evil, in that same intention you will be punished.” It is as though one were to say: if someone, using his eyes, gives himself over to shameful desire, and is therefore commanded to be made blind, then in the very eyes with which you sinned you will suffer. For by the judgment of the mind, in which it judges, the mind itself will either be condemned or purified.

Therefore it is not unjust that a person should suffer punishment by the judgment of his own mind in the very matter about which he judges, since he suffers the same evils that pursue the mind when it judges wrongly. This should not be understood of every other kind of sin, but of judicial sins in particular. In these matters we either offend by judging rashly, or are excused when we examine each matter mercifully with right judgment, or, when things are doubtful and possess the appearance of justice, interpret them favorably and leave their discernment to the Lord alone.

Other sins that we commit will not be punished according to this measure or judgment; rather, each sin will avenge itself in itself. That is, according to the quality or quantity of the sin, the unhappy soul will be punished, with its own conscience accusing it. For in the mind itself, where the will’s desire is formed, lies the measure of all human acts; in that measure punishment follows guilt.

Therefore, when he had said, “With what judgment you judge,” he added, “And with what measure you measure.” The good person measures, according to his own will, the good deeds of his works; the wicked person measures the evil deeds and the miseries of his guilt. For each person is good where he wills good and wicked where he wills evil.

Thus the statement is doubled, so that each person may know that he is punished in the very offense, or in the very conscience of his mind. There he is either miserable or blessed—namely, in the inclination of his own will, which is the measure of actions and merits. These are not measured by the periods of time in which they are slowly carried out, but by the will with which they are done.

The will itself is punished, whether by the suffering of the mind or of the body, so that the very thing that delights in sins may itself be punished in penalties. Therefore those whose will was to sin without end, although they sinned within a finite time, are justly condemned without end. And those whose judgment was without mercy will be judged without mercy.

This, I say, is the measure: one does not receive what one did not provide. Therefore the judgment by which a person is himself judged will be eternal, although what he himself judged could not be eternal. It is just, then, that whoever wished to possess eternal enjoyment of sin should find eternal severity of vengeance; and that those whose will had no end of sinning should have no end of torment, bearing without end the avenging punishment.

Some among our own people, preserving the continuous context of the reading in this chapter, understand it as forbidding judgment concerning his promises. For just as judgments are made among human beings concerning uncertain matters, so this judgment is sometimes directed against God on account of the ambiguity of one who feels or conjectures. This he wholly removes from us, so that steadfast faith and confidence in his promises may be retained. For, unlike other matters, it is not merely a sin, arising from a lack of confidence in God’s promises, to have judged something wrongly; it is the crime of unbelief.

“What do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not see the beam in your own eye?” A great moderation in judgment is proposed here, but few are free from this vice, since each person, while favoring his own faults, easily censures those of others. Each person also tolerates the faults of others less than his own, and therefore assumes authority to rebuke without offering any example of his own correction.

By the eye, as has been said, the intention of the mind is signified. When a person carries a beam in it—that is, the guilt of a greater offense—he cannot see himself, because, pressed down by the darkness of sin, he lies inwardly blind. But that outer eye, which was opened in paradise after the Fall, always sees openly what is harmful to itself, not what would benefit it.

It sees the boastfulness of empty praise: while blind concerning itself, it attempts to heal another’s mind, not so that the other may improve, but so that it may fall more conspicuously through empty glory. It is difficult for someone to give another what he himself lacks; therefore no blind person offers guidance to another.

He is speaking metaphorically. We should therefore draw the example from the body to the mind: by the eye we should understand the intention of the mind, by the speck the smallest offenses, and by the beam the more serious disgrace of crimes. When hatred still remains in the intention of the mind, a person rashly rebukes another for anger; therefore he is reproved by the judge of salvation, because he sees the lesser things in his brother while failing to consider the greater things in himself.

And what is more serious: how does someone wish to appear as a physician of souls when he does not care for his own soul? Hence the Lord immediately adds:

**365** “Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your eye.” A hypocrite is anyone who desires to appear to be what he is not. Therefore each person is brought back to the careful examination of himself, so that he may first heal himself and then, enlightened by virtues, seek the salvation of his brother insofar as he is able.

“Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before pigs.” By proposing these sayings proverbially, he warns the stewards of the churches to come to the correction of others only after cleansing the eye of the mind. Then he warns them not to throw what is holy before dogs—that is, the word of preaching. For just as it is dangerous to hide the Lord’s money, so it is certainly wasteful to give it to dogs.

And just as it is a vice to conceal the truth, so it is dangerous to place the word of life before those who cannot endure it. By dogs are understood those who attack the truth by barking against it; by pigs, those who despise what they have heard and trample it underfoot. Concerning them the apostle Peter says: “The dog has returned to its own vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (2 Pet. 2:21).

Thus by dogs heretics, or deniers of the truth, are signified—those who return to the vomit of unbelief. By pigs are signified those who persist in their own uncleanness and do not know how rightly to ruminate upon the knowledge of God. The truth of allegories should not be disclosed to them, because they are polluted by every uncleanness of vice; rather, the more obvious teachings should be opened to them, or, if one may call them so, the more ordinary ones.

The mystical teachings of the divine utterances, however, should be kept silent for a time, until individuals are able to bear them, and the measure of wheat is supplied to everyone, so that neither the former tear apart what they have received nor the latter trample upon what has been offered to them.

Nevertheless, in whatever way one considers it, it is more dangerous to offer holy things to the perverse than precious things to the impure. He aptly tempered this statement with one small adverb of uncertainty: “lest perhaps.”

Lest they trample them under their feet and tear you apart. For it may happen that they repent of their uncleanness and pass from the herd of swine into the company of sheep. Nevertheless, this is no reason rashly to give that thing to dogs, contrary to the Lord’s command, nor to throw these things before the feet of swine, lest they trample them as well and tear you apart. Contemners of the truth trample the exceedingly precious utterances of God when they despise and regard as worthless the beauty of his promises, and, like swine, return to uncleanness. But if those who strive to bark against the truth are given the things that are commanded to be concealed beneath a veil, overshadowing the holy of holies—things which they are permitted neither to touch nor even to see—then, he says, they will immediately tear you apart, not the sacred mysteries of God’s utterances—for they remain incorruptible—but the simplicity of your faith.

[Col. 0318A] Hence it is that the unity of the brotherhood suffers such great pressures, and that we are torn apart by so many divisions and mangled by so many refutations in words: because those to whom the mystical sacraments should be disclosed are not first tested; rather, everything is revealed indiscriminately to certain people. Such persons are rightly judged not stewards of money but squanderers and destroyers of treasures, since they take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.

For they do not know that what is concealed is sought more eagerly, that what is hidden is regarded more reverently, that what has long been sought is held more dearly, that what is received in measured portions is taken without distaste, and that what is suitably granted for a time to those who are hungry is received without harm to the stomach.

[Col. 0318B] Hence it is that Peter denies Simon the grace of the Holy Spirit, and yet, because he had been admitted for a time to knowledge of the faith, he hastens to tear the believers apart. Hence it is that many heretics divide the Church and attack its unity. Hence it is that Julian the apostate, through tyrannical domination, raises blasphemies and weapons together against Christ. Hence also it is that today the Church’s indulgence of repentance is so often trampled upon, and security is promised, so that it sometimes becomes more a deception than a remedy for those stained by sin; for when it is easily granted, it is held in less esteem, and once received it is guarded more carelessly. Moreover, guilt is sometimes repeated more boldly in deed because of the hope of pardon.

I have not said this in order to teach that a teacher should be cruel, but to lead the unwary back to caution. For just as it must not be denied to those who seek it with the faith of love, so it must not immediately be granted to deceivers and unbelievers, lest they not only trample underfoot the pearls of our hope, but also, by being wrongly enticed while repeatedly immersing themselves in filth, provide others with encouragement to sin. This is why the sacred canons do not readily admit those who repeatedly return to penance. We too ought not to transgress those boundaries indiscriminately, but weigh everything with discernment.

[Col. 0318C] Ask, and it will be given to you. Seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. By these steps, the way, the truth, and the life are duly granted to those who strive. First, walking in the way—which is Christ—they find the truth while seeking him with whom is the fountain of life. Then, knocking at the door, although through the narrow gate, they enter into eternal life. For Christ is the door, as he himself says: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X, 9).

[Col. 0318D] Therefore, one must ask for nothing other than what is to be sought, nor seek anything other than that at which one must continually knock in order to enter. For this is the living bread that came down from heaven, the food of the children. This is the kingdom, and the righteousness of the kingdom by which we are all justified. Therefore, we must first ask for it no less than we must seek it, and indeed find what we have sought; once it has been found, we must ceaselessly knock at that very door, until, by knocking, we enter through him into him.

[Col. 0319A] From the beginning of this sermon, therefore, he taught the children and heirs of the kingdom nothing other than righteousness. For this reason he withdrew their minds from every worldly anxiety, so that they might devote themselves to that righteousness and seek only the heavenly kingdom with devotion. Otherwise, we cannot reign in it unless we first seek to learn—and not merely to learn, but to fulfill—its laws and righteousness. Thus, to seek the kingdom first means to love God with the mind before and above all things, and then to accomplish the works of love.

But lest this seem impossible to anyone, he composed prayers, taught us what we should ask for, and now supplies confidence, so that we may ask for nothing hesitantly. For the Truth itself promises this, and therefore we must not hesitate in our prayers, provided that we ask for these things in the manner he commands. Nor should we seek them at any other time or place than where he commands.

[Col. 0319B] Hence the Prophet says: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice; seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Psalm CIV, 3). Here, if we examine the passage carefully, he taught that none other than the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is to be sought, and commanded that he always be sought with a joyful and steadfast heart. This is not because there is more than one God, but because he himself, one and the same, is immeasurable and eternal.

We ask in faith, advancing by it toward Christ; we seek in the safest hope, penetrating through it until we sometimes reach the interior of Christ’s veil; and finally, we possess it as a secure anchor already fixed in heaven. [Col. 0319C] We knock in love, as we sweat through our labors by steadfastly persevering at the door, which is Christ, so that at last, once the evils have been conquered, we may obtain the one thing we ask for and seek. And to provide greater constancy for perseverance, diligence in seeking, and confidence in obtaining, he added, saying:

For everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened. Therefore, to anyone who is not given what he asks for, there is no doubt that he does not ask rightly, nor seek rightly, nor knock rightly at the door of mercy. For everything that we ask or seek, and at which we knock, as I have said, must be directed to one thing and for the sake of one thing, because only one thing is necessary.

[Col. 0319D] Hence David also says: “One thing I have asked from the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Psalm XXVI, 4). Otherwise, how will he deny himself to those who ask, when he first freely offered himself to those who did not ask? Or how will those who seek him fail to find him, when he granted even those who did not seek him the means of finding him? Or how will he not open to himself for those who knock, when he cries out to us daily: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock” (Revelation III, 20)—speaking, of course, of the door of our heart—“If anyone opens to me, I will enter in to him and dine with him”?

It is therefore clear that whenever we do not receive something, we have not asked for it rightly; when we do not find something, we have not sought it well; and when it is not opened to those who knock, we have not knocked rightly. The text continues:

[Col. 0320A] “What man is there among you who, if his son asks him for bread, would give him a stone?” He begins to explain more clearly what should be asked for, and from the very human benevolence shown toward children he commends the Father’s superior and incomparable care for us. Here the excellence of our dignity must be considered and the confidence of the mind strengthened. For if fathers give good gifts to their children, how much more will our Father, who is incomparably good, give his good things to his children when they ask him?

He therefore compares bread with a stone, so that by bread Christ may be understood, the Life who came down from heaven. If we ask for him with right faith, will he give us that stone of stumbling and hardness of heart? Far be it from us to think this of the highest and unchangeable Good, when it is not permissible to think it even of a mortal and unchangeable person!

[Col. 0320B] “Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent?” The fish, certainly, is the one that Peter first caught by fishing, hidden among the waters of Scripture; in its mouth he found the stater that he was to give for himself. If one of the children asks for this fish, will a benevolent father give him the serpent that killed Eve with the poison of its deceit, so that he may die, deceived by his father’s trickery?

By these two statements we are confirmed in the knowledge that we never receive anything from God the Father except good things, however they may appear to us. For “all things work together for good for those who, according to his purpose, are called saints.”

[Col. 0320C] Therefore, if you, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him? He calls them evil either as apostles or, in general, by comparison with divinity. By “good things” he means worldly goods, either as they are judged by worldly people or because all things are rightly called good by nature, since they come from the good God. Yet we possess these goods only from him.

But there are other goods, incomparably greater, which we must ask for and seek, and at which we must knock perseveringly in order to receive them. These goods are granted only to children, and they are the things for which we must always keep watch, strive, and be concerned. For worldly goods will be added to us, whereas these, because they are eternal and spiritual, must be asked for without ceasing, sought with perseverance, and approached by tireless knocking. For they are received only by those who ask, found only by those who seek, and entered only by those who persevere.

[Col. 0320D] The first thing, however, is to ask in order to possess what you seek; then to hasten forward by seeking, so that you may find; and, once it has been found, to preserve it, so that you may enter into it and enjoy it without end. Thus the order is fitting, and according to Luke it is well compared to three things in turn (Luke II, 11): by the bread, in which the whole of life is signified, love is understood; by the fish, faith, which is nourished beneath the flowing waters of the Holy Spirit; and by the egg, from which a chick is still hoped for, a sure hope is held. From these virtues, all the gifts of grace follow.

[Col. 0321A] Hence the Evangelist mentioned above did not simply say “good things,” but: “How much more will your Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” For through that Spirit all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge that are in Christ are acquired; without him nothing precious is received. For “anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.” Hence that same Spirit is called, in the Catholic tradition, “the gift.”

Therefore, whatever we pray for, first and above all, must be none other than the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—which is the eternal kingdom of Christians—and its righteousness, so that we may fulfill all the works of love toward God and neighbor, as they have been commanded. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0321B] “Therefore, everything that you wish people to do for you, you also do for them. For this is the Law and the Prophets.” In certain manuscripts it is written: “Therefore, everything that you wish—good things—that people should do for you…” For he is certainly speaking of nothing other than good things. But because the word “good” is not found in the Hebrew truth, it is superfluous, although some have wished to add it so that the sentence might sound clearer.

Yet if we attend to the proper force of the words, “will” is rightly understood only with respect to the good, just as, conversely, “desire” is rightly understood with respect to evil. Although in many passages “will” is improperly used of evil and “desire” of good, in this passage it concerns only the good and is spoken with reference to the good. That is: the good things you wish to receive from them, do the same for them, so that love of neighbor may be fulfilled.

[Col. 0321C] This love, however, no one rightly fulfills without love of God; therefore he added: “This is the Law and the Prophets.” For this reason elsewhere he says that the whole Law and the Prophets depend not upon one of these two parts alone, but upon both—namely, love of God and love of neighbor.

Unless perhaps we take the statement simply to mean that the Law and the Prophets depend upon love of neighbor, while upon love of God together with love of neighbor the whole Law and all prophecy depend. But it is better to say that they depend upon both together, because the love of God cannot rightly be preserved without love of neighbor, nor love of neighbor without love of God.

Hence the Lord says: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John XIV, 15). And the Apostle says: “Let the one who loves God love his neighbor also.” Otherwise, “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his neighbor, he is shown to be a liar” (I John IV, 20).

[Col. 0321D] Therefore, let one’s neighbor be loved for God’s sake, and God for his own sake, so that his commandments may be kept. Thus the love of neighbor will exist in the love of God, just as the love of God exists in the love of neighbor. Hence, because they are always together, the whole Law and the Prophets are rightly said to depend upon either one of them.

Here he clearly indicates why he says that we should do for people what we wish them to do for us. For he is not speaking of just any desire, but of the desire that pertains to love of God and neighbor: whatever we wish to be done for us, we too should do for others for God’s sake.

Otherwise, if a drunkard wishes another person to make him drunk, should he rightly make others drunk himself? Or if he wishes the indulgence of lust to be granted him, should he immediately commit fornication with the woman who has agreed to him? Far be it from us to think so! Rather, whatever the love of Christ dictates, let us render to one another.

[Col. 0322A] “Enter through the narrow gate.” Although love is fulfilled only with an enlarged heart and is often shown in Scripture to be broad, nevertheless, once it has filled the mind, it hastens to lead it away through difficult and narrow places.
