No one swollen with the pride of exalted status can enter this gate; no one who is lowly and abject—not one whom true humility inclines, but one whom the devil casts down into the dust and tramples upon; no one honored by the goods of this world, since it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter through such narrowness.

[Col. 0322B] It is therefore sufficiently lofty when it is raised up to the love of God; yet it is sufficiently low and narrow when it commands us even to be willing to die for the love of neighbor and to love an enemy. Thus, although love is called broad, it is nevertheless narrow: few find it, and, if they find it, fewer still strive to enter through it.

Nevertheless, when a gate is mentioned, the city must also be considered—what and what kind of city it is that has so narrow an entrance, which few find, and, if they find it, fewer still strive to enter through it. No one enters there without the burden of sin, no one without labor, and no one without purity of spirit.

For it is sufficiently narrow to abandon everything else and love one thing alone, attend to one thing, seek one thing, and knock daily at one thing; to turn neither to the right nor to the left—that is, neither to pursue prosperity nor fear adversity; to seek what is unseen, but to reject what is seen; and thus to drive everything away from the mind on either side for the sake of the narrow path.

[Col. 0322C] “For broad is the gate and spacious the way that leads to destruction.” Although no one seeks this way, everyone finds it, because they are born in it; even if they withdraw from it, it offers itself spontaneously. Hence few reach out their hand toward the virtues, whereas pleasure invites everyone, like an importunate prostitute, with its allurements. Therefore many enter through it.

[Col. 0322D] But how narrow is the gate and constricted the way that leads to life! Hence the bridegroom and bride marvel in the Song of Songs: “Who is this that comes up through the wilderness like a column of smoke, from the perfumes of myrrh and frankincense?” (Song of Songs III, 6).

It is as though he were saying: Who is this who ascends by the way that few find—and, even if they find it, few pursue? How, then, is this way directed and made so slender that it is compared with a column of smoke—not just any smoke, but smoke from the perfumes of myrrh and frankincense? Christ taught above what these perfumes signify: that, bearing his mortification in our body, we should be a sacrifice of frankincense to God, so reduced and refined that we may rightly be compared to a column of fragrant substances.

[Col. 0323A] Few find this wilderness path, yet more walk upon it where there is a multitude of people. Few undertake the wilderness path, in which Christ’s followers do battle. They are called few only in comparison with those who walk along the broad way. Therefore the gate and the way are sufficiently narrow, since they admit only a few.

[Col. 0323B] “Beware of false prophets who come to you in sheep’s clothing.” He speaks of those who walk in humility and false religious observance, whom Scripture calls false prophets. Speaking hypocritically from their own hearts, they seek their own interests.

Therefore, because he had said that the difficult and narrow way is found by few, the Lord wished to teach his own in every respect. Lest they see many people passing along it more through pretense than through simplicity of heart and become entangled in their errors, he immediately added: “Beware”—that is, guard yourselves—from false prophets, lest you be polluted by their errors.

[Col. 0323C] They will come to you to deceive you in the clothing of sheep, because you are truly sheep. Thus they bear your appearance outwardly in their clothing and conduct, so as to mock your simplicity; inwardly, however, they will be ravenous wolves—namely, unclean spirits who have taken possession of them. Therefore beware of them, lest they tear you apart with the bites of their words, the allurements of food, and the elaborate construction of their pretense.

[Col. 0323D] “By their fruits,” he says, “you will know them.” Therefore let none of the false ones say: “How do you know me? Why, then, do you judge me?” Or: “Why do you not share with me? Or why do you despise me, when you ought not to judge me?”

[Col. 0324A] Certainly, because you display a garment outwardly and present in advance the appearance of religion, but inwardly I fear the wolf, since I do not find in you the fruit of Christ’s peace and love, or of the other virtues. I recognize the outward appearance, but I fear what lies within. Even if you teach hidden things, as though you were speaking in a mystery, I seek something else in you that I do not see.

Let them therefore understand by what name they should be judged—those who are covered neither by the appearance of humility nor by the fruit of piety. If we must beware of those who both offer prophetic preaching and wear the garb of holy religion, what indeed must we avoid in those who adorn themselves with more refined worldly clothing, pursue the glory of the world, and in every utterance, in the pomp of their conduct, in their food, and in their worldly dignities demonstrate themselves to be sons of this light, yet so often claim for themselves a teaching office among Christ’s sheep?

[Col. 0324B] For, whether they wish it or not, the clothing of sheep belongs properly to the sheep. Although wicked people may use it, a sheep of Christ ought not therefore to abandon what belongs properly to it. Rather, it must beware of those who disguise themselves in such clothing in order to deceive, and must not imitate those who boast that they carry Christ’s cross amid the pleasures of the world—especially since the cross possesses mortification of the flesh and proclaims contempt for the world.

[Col. 0324C] “Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” Although a thorn may shine with flowers at the beginning, it does not therefore produce grapes, because it does not remain in the vine, even if grapes appear to hang upon it. The vine, however, is Christ, and all his members are branches. Therefore only they can bear grapes—namely, the works of the Holy Spirit, which intoxicate the mind. When you see grapes among thorns, know that they do not come from the thorns; therefore gather the grape in such a way that you avoid the thorn.

[Col. 0324D] It belongs to thorns to tear and wound the one who touches them, because heretics mangle and pierce everyone with the barbs of their words. Moreover, thistles produce no sweetness of figs, because fornicators and lovers of crimes flourish for a time without fruit. By these two images all who belong to the mass of perdition are aptly represented: even if they come to us, they are destined outside us for the fire, without fruit.

[Col. 0325A] Hence it is said to the first man: “When you work the ground, it will produce thorns and thistles for you” (Genesis III, 18). These wretched people, nourishing thorns and thistles in flesh and soul—for they are earth—cannot bear clusters for the vine whose cultivator is the Father and from which all the branches are propagated. Nor are figs produced from thistles; the fig tree produces the larger figs from its own stock. Those who are of the flesh perceive what comes from Adam and pursue only those things.

[Col. 0325B] “Thus every good tree produces good fruit, but the evil tree produces evil fruit.” This is so because grapes cannot arise from thorns, nor figs from thistles, but the fruit of each remains from its root. Likewise, fruit cannot be exchanged between a good and an evil tree; each thing sprouts from its own root.

He did not say: “A good tree cannot become evil.” Otherwise Judas could not have changed from an Apostle into an apostate and betrayed the Savior, nor could Paul have become a vessel of election from a persecutor, if what was evil could not become good.

[Col. 0325C] We therefore do not preach from this passage, in accordance with the Manichaeans, two natures, one good and one evil. Nor do we say, with Jovinian, that the evil cannot be changed so as to become good, or that the good cannot again fall into wickedness if they are not saved by the grace of God.

Since no one is evil by nature, but is changed by vice—for the earth subject to curses produces thorns and thistles—from these no grapes or figs are ever gathered. For even if a wicked person or evil teacher sometimes appears to offer some benefit by preaching well while living badly, the fruit is not really theirs, but belongs to the vine that at times overflows above a hedge of thorns.

[Col. 0325D] Therefore, as I said, the cluster must be gathered and the thorn avoided, lest the thorn that grows wickedly in the hand of a drunken person pierce the unwary.

Thus Moses, hearing Jethro, his father-in-law, gathered a grape, yet was not stained by the fault of paganism. Nor can we say that he gathered grapes from a thorn, because what appeared in Jethro for a time did not come from him but from the one whom Moses served. Therefore, devoted to God and among the people over whom Christ already presided, he ordered everything as the Truth taught.

[Col. 0326A] Those who come in sheep’s clothing also seem to possess contempt for the world, fasts, the lavish distribution of alms, and public prayers in the forum and in the street corners; but these are absolutely not their fruit, since they are counted against them as a vice. This fruit is foreign to them, and therefore they are called hypocrites, because they fictitiously perform the parts of others. Their fruit should therefore rather be judged to belong to those whose own it is recognized to be.

The fruit of evil trees, moreover, is the works of the flesh: fornication, luxury, uncleanness, the service of idols, and other such works of darkness. The fruit of the good tree is joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, kindness, and the other marks of virtue, inwardly made fruitful by heavenly dew. Such fruits are never produced except by a good will, just as, conversely, an evil intention always nourishes evil fruits.

[Col. 0326B] A good will, therefore, never produces evil fruits, just as an evil will never produces good ones. For this reason the will of each person is rightly signified by a tree: just as a tree is rooted in the earth, so the will of each person is rooted in the soul. Even if a tree of evil nature is planted in good earth, good fruit does not therefore immediately arise from it. Similarly, even if the soul is shown to be good by nature, an evil will implanted in it can never produce good fruit; and conversely, neither can a good will produce evil fruit.

[Col. 0326C] Therefore it is more correctly understood figuratively that the good or evil will of each person is the tree, while the soul, with its nature remaining intact, is corrupted or changed for the better each day by the inclination of the will. Unless, perhaps, the slander of the heretics prevents this, as though things that are not substances could not, by metaphor, receive likenesses from substances. Especially since secular learning itself teaches that figures of speech can pass both from soul to body and outwardly from body to soul.

Thus countless examples of things are found everywhere, and likenesses are seen to be drawn from things that are not substances to things that are substances, and again from things that are substances to things that are not. [Col. 0326D] The present passage confirms this quite clearly. Even if the good or evil trees themselves are understood simply as human beings rather than as their wills, the fruit will nevertheless, whether they wish it or not, be the works of virtues or vices—works that no one but an ignorant person will regard as substances.

[Col. 0327A] Accordingly, the human will is rightly called a tree, because, just as a tree is rooted in the earth, so the will is rooted in thoughts within the mind. Hence the Lord says that the axe has already been laid to the roots of the trees, as he prepares, by the word of his divinity, to cut off the thoughts of individuals by which an evil will is rooted, and to judge everyone by them.

This will, if it is good and its intention is upright, does not produce evil fruit, just as an evil will cannot produce good fruit. For all works, although they may appear good or evil, draw the sap of their root and the vigor of their seed from that root. By this statement he condemns all hypocrites and all false prophets, and confirms, by this one example of unalterable nature, everything he taught above concerning purity of heart: no one obtains good fruit from an evil will, nor does anyone reap from a good intention anything other than what is good.

[Col. 0327B] A human being’s good will—that is, the good tree—cannot be good unless it possesses the planting and vigor of the will of God, so that it may bring forth fruit for those who taste its flavor. For whatever degenerates from it is corrupted by vice and is counted among the evil parts of discernment.

This, I say, is the narrow way, regulated by such an unalterable course and by the rule of justice. The broad way is that of the world, because it is scattered from the right hand of this one toward the left in an immense expanse, and is broadly spread here and there through all the grasses of vice. Hence it follows.

[Col. 0327C] “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father,” and so forth. What is required is that God’s will be done in us, not an outpouring of words. Therefore, beware of false prophets and recognize them by their fruits, because their perverse will cannot produce good things.

Even if they say, “Lord, Lord,” they are not immediately to be believed. For “with their lips they appear to honor me, so that they may be received by you, but their heart is far from me.” Therefore not everyone who says to me, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven.

[Col. 0327D] Although he appears to have brought the thief into paradise solely through the invocation of his name, it is clear that the thief had drawn near inwardly with a heart of faith and had offered the service of love. Christ did not prohibit himself from being invoked with the voice; rather, he showed that not everyone who repeats “Lord” with the voice believes in him with the heart or loves him through works.

Here we must ask how the Apostle Paul’s testimony can be true: that “no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (I Corinthians XII, 13). If we say to him, “Lord, Lord,” in the Holy Spirit, will he not hear us knocking at him, so that we may enter? He certainly will hear us. Therefore the meaning of Scripture must be sought, and the foolishness of heretics must not be heeded.

[Col. 0328A] No one can doubt that there is a great difference between the two statements. For what uneducated person cannot say with the voice alone, “The Lord Jesus”? But to say it in the Spirit is rare, and possible only for one who perseveres as a predestined person. Many indeed say with the voice, “Lord, Lord,” but at the final coming the foolish are rejected. Those whose lamps are adorned with the oil of the Holy Spirit are brought in through the door, though they are few.

Therefore, to say “the Lord Jesus” in the Holy Spirit is to adorn the lamps—that is, to confess Christ the Lord with heart and mouth together and with worthy works through the Holy Spirit. To say “the Lord Jesus” is to confess him. One says him who believes in his heart for righteousness and confesses him with his mouth for salvation, and then bears witness through works to the one in whom he has believed.

[Col. 0328B] Otherwise it is of no benefit if they deny him by their works. Therefore truly to say and confess the Lord Jesus is to proclaim him with heart, mouth, and good works. One without the other is denial. But the one who confesses and declares him fully is the person who carries inwardly in the heart, through faith and understanding, the intelligible word that can be spoken; whenever it is appropriate, he brings forth with his mouth and declares what he possesses inwardly as a word that can be spoken; then, through actions and works, he confesses in himself that what remained intelligible in his mind is true.

With reference to this integrity of speech, the Apostle cries out that no one can say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit, because without him no one can understand Christ. Peter makes this clear: when he feared death, he denied Life. Moreover, who will rightly receive the works of virtue—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit—without the Spirit himself? No one, therefore, can say “Lord Jesus” without him, because no one can belong to the members of Christ without the Holy Spirit.

Thus these false prophets, hypocrites, or false Christians, although they say “Lord, Lord” in words, since they neither love him in their hearts, nor preach him rightly with their mouths, nor confirm him through their works, do not do the will of the Father and are therefore driven out as exiles from the kingdom. Behold, all cry out with the voice, but not all are received. Those are received who invoke the Lord in the Holy Spirit and possess an anointing from him. For this reason he taught that all people are to be understood by their fruit.

For not only are those who name the Lord by name alone excluded; so too are those who prophesy without works, cast out demons, or perform many mighty deeds. Hence it also follows:

“Many will say to me on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’ Did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty deeds?” He wishes us to be watchful in every direction, lest we be led astray. Therefore, just as above he warned us to beware of false prophets, so he also indicates that we must be cautious concerning those who cast out demons and perform many mighty deeds.

For even wicked people can preach the hidden things of Scripture out of a desire to learn; and we see how often men of the most shameful character possess intellectual power and are learned in the divine writings. Moreover, who does not know that wicked people have often prophesied and will still become their accomplices? Balaam the diviner, Saul the rejected, and Caiaphas the wicked prophesied, as did many others whom Scripture does not name.

Furthermore, many cast out demons not by their own merits but through invocation of Christ’s name, just as we read in the Acts of the Apostles that the sons of a certain priest, Sceva, did this (Acts XIX, 14). In the same way, miracles are performed by the reprobate through the overflowing grace of God, for three reasons: first, so that those who refuse to believe the things already fulfilled and taught by the teacher of truth may be deceived by their wicked error; second, so that others may be healed through them, whom the Lord has determined to help, and so that both those persons and others may believe, stirred by the miracles; and third, so that the faithful of Christ may learn that they should not strive especially to perform miracles, even though these are done through them despite their being reprobate by divine power, but should imitate Christ in all things.

For Christ said: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matthew II, 29), and he taught them to pursue love. Let no one therefore doubt that the former performed many miracles in Christ’s name and cast out demons. If anyone wishes to deny this, let him read what the Lord himself says concerning the future: “Then,” he says, “if anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is the Christ,’ do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise, and they will give great signs, so that even the elect, if possible, may be led into error. Behold, I have told you beforehand” (Matthew XXIV, 23).

Therefore the eye of the mind must be cleansed, wisdom sought, faith strengthened, and the steadfastness of faith reinforced amid the evils of so many perverse people and the scandals of so many snares, so that we may escape and guard ourselves against such persons. Sound doctrine must therefore always be sought, and a perfect life imitated. For the performance of miracles is the work of the Holy Spirit, but living well is the imitation of Christ.

Therefore he will say to these people: “I do not know you”; but to those who act rightly: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV, 34). For this reason the Lord also forbade the disciples to rejoice because demons had been subjected to them: “Rejoice,” he said, “because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 20). Likewise Paul commends not the powers of tongues, nor knowledge of secret mysteries, nor prophecies, nor faith that might prodigiously move mountains, but love alone, which Christ taught (I Corinthians XIII, 1–2).

“And then I will confess to them: ‘I never knew you; depart from me, all you who work iniquity.’” I will confess what they did not wish to confess in order to return to me; I will confess what I patiently endured for a long time. I will indeed confess: “I do not know you.”

How, then, does the one who formed the hearts of human beings individually and understands all their works rightly say that he does not know those whom he created? Is not the face of the Lord always against those who do evil, so that he may destroy their memory from the earth? Accordingly, “not knowing” on God’s part is understood figuratively: he knows those whom he approves and saves, but he does not know those whom he destroys and condemns.

For we say: “The light does not know the darkness,” that is, it does not look upon it; for if it looked upon it, the darkness would no longer exist. Therefore not to look upon it was to reject it. Hence he must be prayed to continually, that he may illumine our blindness; for unless he looks upon us, we are nothing other than darkness.

For God’s knowing means approving and choosing by grace. Hence we also read: “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the path of the ungodly will perish” (Psalm VI). And: “The Lord knows those who are his.” And to Moses: “I know you by name” (Exodus XXXIII, 12). He therefore knows those who know him, and approves those who keep his commandments in simplicity of heart. Hence it follows:

Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a wise man who built his house upon rock.

The conclusion of the whole sermon is confirmed by a marvelous example of faith. It excludes all who are either deceived by hypocrisy or oppressed in some respect by the burden of unbelief, and compares only those with the highest degree of wisdom whom the practice of truth proves to be inwardly firm upon the rock of right faith. “Everyone,” he says, “who hears my words and does them.” He did not say, “who merely hears,” but “who first hears and then does them.” For no one truly hears unless he does them.

Hence how often it is said: “Whoever has ears for hearing, let him hear” (Matt. XI, 15; Luke VIII, 8). For one thing is to hear with the hearing of the body, and another with the hearing of the mind. Whoever hears, therefore, with the hearing of the mind understands, and strives to fulfill in deeds what he has understood and desired. But whoever perceives the word outwardly in its sound, unless he inwardly grasps the reality of the word that cries out within him, returns deaf. For when the voice has fallen silent, nothing remains for him that he can hear.

And therefore he says, “who hears my words,” not “the sound of the speaker.” For what takes place outwardly is the word of the reader or teacher; but what is inwardly perceived and understood is the word of Christ. Hence David says: “I will hear what God will speak within me” (Ps. LXXXIV, 9). He then speaks rightly within us when, while the organ of the voice sounds outwardly, we are inwardly awakened to the voice of Christ speaking with us divinely. Therefore the Apostle cries out: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God” (I Pet. IV, 10). And if this man speaks the words of God, what else should that man inwardly hear except those same words? For he did not say, “Everyone who teaches my words,” but “who hears.”

It is therefore safer to hear than to teach. Nevertheless, the one who teaches, if he teaches rightly, certainly first hears in his heart what he teaches. Accordingly, it is Christ who teaches everyone; and those whom he teaches are first hearers of the words of God and then doers. Yet although doing is more perfect than learning, one must first hear in order to practice the discipline of the one who commands, and then to make the teaching one has learned equal to it through one’s works.

And if perhaps you have heard only once, you ought to take delight in hearing continually the trumpet of salvation, because enemies against whom we must fight are never lacking. Nor is the food of a single day sufficient for the whole life of the present age. Therefore the words of the Scriptures must be meditated upon continually, so that through them we may possess life, and so that by the exercise of works we may be nourished by that from which we live. Otherwise the words are neither rightly heard without the fruit of works, nor can one rightly act without the food of such great sweetness.

The one who does both together—who, that is, rightly hears and then does the words he hears, namely, those words inwardly which he hears—“I will compare him,” he says, “to a wise man who built his house upon rock.”

It must therefore be asked who this architect is who built his house upon rock, to whom the one who hears and does the words of the Savior ought to be compared. I do not think this should be understood simply of some ordinary builder of houses, since houses often built upon rocks collapse precipitously when struck by winds, but perhaps of the one who says: “As a wise architect I laid the foundation” (I Cor. III, 10).

It is a great thing, then, to be compared with Paul. He himself says this; but if we look at it truthfully, what is promised is greater still. For unless the Lord builds the house, all who build it labor in vain. Therefore, although Peter builds, although Paul builds, although any one of the saints or teachers builds, Christ is the wise man who builds—not just any houses, but one heavenly house in the heavens, placed upon himself, who is rightly called the rock, as upon the foundation of faith.

Hence in this same Gospel it is said to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18); that is: “From which you, Peter, derive your name on account of the firmness of faith, upon that same rock I will build the Church, founded upon faith, which is the house of the living God constructed from precious heavenly stones.”

There no heretic builds, no hypocrite, no hoarder of earthly treasures, no follower of vices, but only those who hear what he taught and do as he taught. These, to be sure, build their houses upon the rock. For although the house that Christ builds in himself is one, individuals build together upon the foundation of faith the merits of their own houses.

Hence elsewhere: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John XIV, 2). Those who build them are fellow-builders with Christ, who builds those dwelling places together with them; and therefore they are rightly compared with him. For where he is, there they are also; and what he does, they too strive to raise through their works and to construct as a house. This, then, is to hear his words and do them: to build that house in the heavens.

Its foundation, certainly, is the faith of Christ; its summit is raised by certain hope; the framework of its joints is fitted together by charity; and its columns are erected by the gift of the Holy Spirit. Upon these seven columns of gifts the whole house rests, and the house is strengthened upon the foundation of Christ.

Thus he plainly teaches that the entire structure—that is, every work which has grown upward in the faith of Christ—cannot be shaken by any assaults.

Hence he also says:

“Rain fell, rivers came, winds blew, and they rushed upon that house, and it did not fall.”

By the rains, therefore, he signifies the alluring enticements of pleasures and the showers of desires that gradually seep in. Through them faith first becomes dampened by the cracks opened through negligence; the rigor of faith is dissolved, and the strength of charity is corrupted. Hence James says: “Each person is tempted when he is enticed and drawn away by his own desire” (Jas. I, 14).

For when the mind is intoxicated by the desire of the flesh, it is dissolved from the firmness of its state, as though by rains.

Concerning these rains, David threatens, speaking of those who are rejected: “He will rain snares upon sinners” (Ps. X, 6). Snares indeed, because each person, if left without God’s help, is entangled by his own desire.

And if he is not moved by such things, greater rivers of temptations are released, so that he may experience more grievous movements of the waves and, as though carried along by the force of rivers, be overwhelmed more violently by the floods of desires.

Nothing is weaker in human life than the one who is conquered by his own desire; nothing is stronger than the one who is not overcome even by the devil. But the one who is truly founded upon the rock is tempted in one way, and the one who builds upon sand in another: the latter in order that he may fall, the former in order that he may be crowned and conquer.

Yet upon both the rains of enticements descend, and the rivers of prolonged temptation come in flood. But the former collapse; the latter, in whom Christ builds from himself, remain steadfast, and their work is always made firm in the heavens.

Hence the prophet says: “The Lord is in the whirlwind and in the storm; his ways are in the tempest” (Nahum I, 3). For a fiercer and more violent storm rages against those who are built together in Christ. Although lesser enticements of vices beat against them, although rivers of exaltation and pride flow, and although the devil then moves all the winds of temptations more forcefully from every side, if we still stand unshaken, the Lord in the whirlwind of the winds and in the storm is greatly to be feared, lest perhaps he find us weaker.

Nevertheless, we must remain fixed, although these three kinds of attacks rage against us and he expend every kind of temptation through them. For none of them can prevail against us unless he finds that we have built upon sand.

The devil always fights, so to speak, with three kinds of weapons: either with the desires of the flesh, or with the outward pleasures and favors of the world, or through himself, when he has unleashed from every side all the winds of assaults, bringing about the ruin of those whom he finds to have built upon sand.

Yet he plainly shows why this particular man did not fall when he says: “For it had been founded upon rock.” Otherwise, if it had not been founded upon it, it would have fallen completely. Hence it is understood that all who collapse are not built in Christ; but all who remain do not owe this to themselves, but to the firmness of faith, and the power of faith is consolidated in them by Christ.

Thus, once the illustrative exhortation has been completed which warns that everyone who builds upon sand will, by contrast, be compared to a foolish architect whose structure rests upon no foundation of virtue, we see that vices are always fluid and collapse like sand.

For sand can never be solidified or joined together; it is always drinking in water, yet never softening for any length of time from its dryness. So, too, the desire and craving for vices is never satisfied by the flow of pleasure, and yet it is always hardened by the dryness of an evil ardor without satiety. It does not receive the joining of charity, so that it could possess firmness when the heat comes; but, like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth, it is carried here and there by assaults, plainly because such desires are propagated not in the spirit but in the flesh.

Hence the promise concerning Abraham’s offspring is stated twice: “Your seed will be like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore.” By the sand, the carnal offspring is signified, separated from Christ by the vice of unbelief and by the dryness of carnal desire. Whoever builds upon it, whatever the things he does may be, awaits not the height of an erected summit but the ruin of a fall.

There the Gentile, still in the flesh, builds without Christ, as does the Jew; the heretic, condemned in faith; the hypocrite, deceived by pretense; and the false Christian, entangled in the snares of vices. All these build not upon the rock but upon the sand, and therefore they are scattered by Christ. Their ruin is all the greater the higher they are found to have built upon sand.

For he speaks of those who hear these words and do not do them. They hear with the ear of the flesh and not with the ear of the mind. They hear, therefore, so that they may not have an excuse, and not so that they may accomplish the work of faith. Thus, as it is concluded at the end, the ruin of those who have despised such saving admonitions of Christ becomes great.

And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these words, that the crowds were astonished at his teaching.

What crowds are said to have been astonished, when above only the disciples are recorded as having approached him? Perhaps the crowd of disciples, from whom he had chosen the Twelve, is said to have been astonished—those whom, after spending the night in prayer, he had summoned when day had come. Or certainly, when he had descended, according to Luke, and stood in a level place where a multitude of the people is also said to have been present, then, when he had finished the same sermon which he had perhaps already delivered above, the crowds are said to have been astonished, and not the disciples.

For faith and love were more fitting for the disciples than astonishment. Astonishment, therefore, is a sign of unbelief, because the mind, not yet thinking rightly about the power of God, is stunned by things that it had not previously believed. Indeed, miracles are performed for this reason: so that the mind may be moved by them, begin to believe, and doubt in nothing concerning the one for whom nothing is impossible.

The completion of the sermon, then, should be understood as the fullness and integrity of its teachings, because Christ’s sermon contains no imperfection.

Hence also:

“The crowds were astonished because he was teaching as one having authority, and not as the scribes and Pharisees.”

His authority, therefore, was not in the domination of exaction but in teaching. He showed himself to be Lord of the Law, adding authoritatively to perfection what had been lacking in it and removing what had belonged to the shadow by revealing it through the light of truth. Then, by word and example, he confirmed those same precepts which had been given for the perfection of a life to be practiced.

In everything he displayed himself as Lord, teaching not superstitious doctrines as the Pharisees and scribes did, but setting forth what belonged to salvation. They demonstrated through their works that the things they taught in words were impossible; but he, teaching more perfect things, confirmed everything by power and works.

His teaching, bearing witness from the Law and the Prophets, was also commended by the power of signs. He had not learned from the scribes and interpreters of the Law the teaching of the Law that he proclaimed in the synagogues; rather, it served him as though eloquence of words and abundance of meanings were themselves his handmaid.

Thus it was plainly understood from every side that he himself was the giver of the laws, whose authority and power were evident in all things. For it is said that grace also shone most swiftly from his face, so that it affected the minds of his hearers on every side.

But they are said to have been astonished chiefly on account of his teaching. We, therefore, who constantly attend to that teaching, should not be astonished with the crowds but should act with the apostles, so that after the end of life we may be crowned with them.

But how unhappy are those who are still carnal today in the Church: they neither wonder with these people, because they do not care to understand what is said; nor believe with the faithful, so as to devote themselves to the practice of works; nor act with the apostles, so that they may be able to attain the kingdom promised to those who seek it rightly.

But because, with the grace of Christ as our oarsman, we have crossed the immense rivers of the Holy Spirit and traversed in our minds the heights of the Mount of Olives, where these words are believed to have been spoken, we must return to ourselves, so that, descending the mountain with the leper, we may disclose our wounds to the physician.

And because we have by no means yet fulfilled the things we have said, let us at least, worshiping below and falling before his face, obtain pardon in confession. For this reason, let us close together the end of the book and the completion of the sermon, so that at the beginning of another work we may be more fully cleansed from the leprosy with which we are defiled when the Lord touches us with his hand.

## PROLOGUE OF THE FIFTH BOOK

[Col. 0331]

[Col. 0331D] To the most holy brothers in Christ, whom divine wisdom abundantly and sufficiently illuminates with its virtues, and heavenly grace adorns with wondrous gifts, dwelling at Centulum under the holy commitment of monastic discipline: Paschasius Radbertus, the refuse of all monks and the least of the Levites.

[Col. 0333A] Beloved, I had once begun the exposition of Matthew, intending to fulfill according to my desire the duty of my service to the brothers in that office. But afterward, having undertaken a position of governance, I was hindered by many anxious cares and entangled in various affairs of secular business. I was carried so far away from it as I was removed from the study of letters. I not only left unfinished what I had begun, but, abandoning the benefit of quiet, I delivered myself almost to shipwreck, buffeted by the assaults of innumerable winds.

But because God, as that poet says, has made these periods of leisure for us, brothers who had come from you to us repeatedly urged me with diligent exhortation to complete the work I had begun and dedicate it to your name, lest I should be mocked, according to that saying from the Gospel, because I had begun as though to build a tower but had not been able to complete it.

Therefore, moved by their exhortation, and as though touched by a divine utterance, I resolved, when asked, to offer this service of devotion [Note: [Col. 0333D] Understand “myself,” or “my efforts,” or “my labors.”] both to your charity and to my brothers, who themselves also impelled me to do this by the gift of their affection.

Accordingly, I decided to rewrite the little works of four books on the same Matthew which I had long ago composed for them according to my desire, as though they were the beginning of this work, if perhaps upon them, as upon a foundation, I might be able to raise the summit of the entire structure, offering it to you as a gift and to them as the payment of my service.

Thus, since one inviolable and undefiled charity remains among those whose love is one, whose devotion is one, and whose commitment is one, this reading might become one solidity of love, one threefold cord of faith, hope, and charity that is never broken, and one structure of perfection that is never violated.

I therefore consider myself blessed if I should pay something of mine as a contribution, whatever might be pleasing, and offer you, as a gift—although small—a talent of no sluggish weight, enriched with whatever might give pleasure. For you have deigned to receive me in Christ with the most grateful affection in all things and toward all things in the present, to cherish me in the bosom of charity, and to entrust me to God through your prayers, especially at the time when, according to that ancient proverb, a friend and a physician are tested in need.

For this reason, beloved, I have so often resolved to come to you with such eagerness for the sake of visiting you, desiring to see you and to correct in myself what I had long neglected too carelessly. You consoled me in your prayers with the affection of love against every adversity, so that at the present I thought nothing was lacking for me, since your great benefits toward me burned with perfect charity.

For you have become debtors to everyone, while owing nothing else to anyone—because you have set the root of your heart in heaven—except charity. By always owing it, you have paid it, and by paying it you have become more and more indebted.

But because your generosity overflows greatly in giving, I believe that in receiving also your liberal and holy goodwill will rejoice more in the gift of a word than in the payment of any material offering.

For this reason I thought that whatever I might offer devotionally would be pleasing to those to whom I owe whatever I can and whatever I am.

Nevertheless, I am not so ignorant that I do not know that I cannot worthily penetrate with my limited understanding the chariot of the four Evangelists, nor understand even one of them completely—not merely I, so insignificant, but, I scarcely know whether anyone among those who make much of their virtues can do so.

For this chariot is the many-formed chariot of God, in which Christ, the heavenly charioteer, traverses the whole fourfold world: now flying through all things in time; now beyond time, above all things and beyond the heights of the heavens, always remaining with the Father as the same God in one eternity; now, God made man, surveying all things below time; now going forth from the summit of the heavens and running down even to the underworld; now returning from the underworld to the heights above.

And therefore these living creatures, which appear to draw this chariot throughout the world while flying everywhere, are also said to have winged backs. Their bodies are full of eyes in front and behind, then within and without. From them flash sparks like glowing bronze, and lightning bolts dart about.

Each of them therefore has straight feet, always stretching upward. Hence they are not unfittingly called Cherubim, because they possess within themselves an abundance of the knowledge of God.

How well, then, was it said through Ezekiel: “They did not turn back as they went, but each one proceeded straight before his face” (Ezek. I, 9), because they strive toward eternal things.

These living creatures, prefigured in many places and—what is astonishing—shown first in the heavens to this prophet in the Spirit of God before they were born upon earth, cannot therefore fail to be ineffable and incomprehensible in what they perceive.

And yet whatever we rightly know or understand comes from their sayings and words, because their words are the words of God. In those words, assuredly, not human wisdom but spirit and life shine forth. Therefore those words are rightly called words of life, because they do not exude the flower of secular eloquence but the fruit of life.

Consequently, although no one can speak fully about such things, no human being ought on that account to remain altogether silent, even in a polished manner of speaking, lest he fail to speak what he perceives by divine inspiration.

For the understanding of the Gospel does not consist in persuasive words of human wisdom but in the wisdom of Christ. Paul, although—as he himself says—unskilled in speech, is nevertheless not unskilled in knowledge and rejoices that he speaks among the mature (II Cor. II, 6).

Meanwhile, although an old man’s speech ought in itself to be composed and graceful in meaning, it ought nevertheless to be gentle, especially in matters of this kind. Even if its language is elegant—which I do not require, as someone says—it ought to be calm and restrained.

If eloquence in secular studies ought to be such as to contain the sap of moderation, how much more ought I, amid these blazing examples of virtue, not to seek, if I could, the polish of secular eloquence that carries with it the splendor of words, but rather the purity of meaning and the understanding of truth?

For this wisdom of Christ is hidden in mystery in him, in whom all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God are stored up. Therefore we must ask him that our speech may possess more the benefit of perfect understanding than the incitement of vanity.

But since these four living creatures are described in different ways, it must be asked altogether why John said that the first living creature was like a lion (Rev. IV, 7), when the prophet Ezekiel declared that the first living creature had the appearance not of a lion but of a man.

For he describes their order in this way: “The likeness of their faces was the face of a man, and the face of a lion on the right side of the four of them, and the face of an ox on the left side of the four of them, and the face of an eagle above the four of them” (Ezek. I, 10).

It is indeed very astonishing that John places first a living creature like a lion, while the prophet places first one like a man. From this statement a major question arises for us.

Although Ezekiel says of these living creatures that one had four faces and one had four wings, the faces of each individual are nevertheless made clear. Therefore, why the order written by the prophet Ezekiel is changed, so that John says “lion” in place of “man,” is not without a great mystery.

Accordingly, it must be understood that the mystical words of the Scriptures do not always preserve the historical order. If they did, they would no longer be mystical but merely historical.

Thus, if we return to the description of the Gospels, the prophet, in describing the living creatures he saw, preserved the order corresponding to Matthew, who is narrated as having had the human face, because he began to write first about the humanity of Christ.

To Mark is assigned the form of a lion, since he began with the cry, as of a lion roaring in the wilderness. Luke, third, bears the appearance of an ox or calf, because he began his Gospel from the priesthood. John, likewise, is represented in the likeness of an eagle, because, flying higher than all things, he ascended even to the divinity of the Word. There he fixed the sight of his eyes more clearly and from there disclosed to us more fully the mysteries of the hidden Word.

Our teachers also hold different opinions on this passage, just as different accounts are read: Matthew is said to have appeared in the lion, and Mark in the man.

But if we fix the eye of our mind upon the dispensation of our Redeemer—a dispensation which these same living creatures declare to have been accomplished—not even the prophet preserved the order, since he placed the lion second. For our same Redeemer, born as a man, was first offered as a calf before he was raised from the dead as a lion.

Therefore let us see why their order was reversed, since, as has been said, one had four faces and one had four wings. Here the concord and unity of the Evangelists and of the Gospel of God are plainly demonstrated: each one possesses both his own form and the forms of the other three, so that in one there are three, and in the three there is one.

If three living creatures are found in each one of them, each is first and none is later than another, because the one face of all four belongs to each individual, just as four belong simultaneously to the one.

For the Christ whom they all proclaim was a man; and he was a lion because of his extraordinary strength, since by dying he conquered death; and he was also a calf because he was offered in sacrifice to God the Father, as all four testify; and he was represented as an eagle because, as soon as he fell in death, his youth was renewed, he rose again, and by his flight he ascended higher than all the angels when he returned to where, in the beginning, he was God with God.

And therefore not unfittingly there are “the face of a man and the face of a lion on the right side of the four,” “the face of a calf on the left side of the four,” and “the face of an eagle above the four”: because all of them have one face, and yet each has its own, so that both the distinctiveness of their proclamation shines wondrously in each and unity is commended in all.

Although each has its own characteristic manner of narrating, you will not find in one a face that the other does not also possess. Thus, so to speak, four faces ineffably belong to one.

For if you ask what Matthew thinks about the incarnation, he certainly thinks what Mark, Luke, and John do. If you ask what John thinks, it is undoubtedly what the other three likewise think. If you ask what Mark thinks, it is what Matthew, Luke, and John think; and if you ask what Luke thinks, it is certainly what John, Matthew, and Mark think.

For their knowledge of faith is one, by which they are known by God. Accordingly, that same knowledge is the face or understanding of faith in one, and it is simultaneously in all four.

Since these things are so, beloved, if in this passage I follow another order, on account of which our teachers differ among themselves, let no one rashly reproach me. For I am recognized as attacking neither the order of John, as some have done, nor that of Ezekiel, just as they themselves are not shown to attack one another even in their differing narration of the order.

One of them—that is, the prophet Ezekiel—sets forth the order of the Evangelists, as I said, according to the order in which they were appointed by the Lord and each wrote his Gospel, each in accordance with his own prefiguration and the character of his beginning. The other—that is, John—rather pursues the mysteries prefigured and fulfilled in Christ, because Christ himself is the lion who slept securely in his passion.

Hence Jacob said of Judah in the person of Christ: “You have lain down like a lion, and who will rouse him?” (Gen. XLIX, 9). He himself is man and calf, and he is rightly prefigured also as an eagle.

But John preferred to place the lion first because, when writing the mystery of his resurrection for believers, he judged it more fitting first to declare the event through which the world chiefly believed than to present the person of a man or calf.

For all generations did not believe in him because he was born a man into the world, nor because he was sacrificed as a calf, but because after death he rose victorious like a lion, raising himself, just as Moses had written that Jacob had once prophesied.

Otherwise, if he had merely been born as a man, suffered, and been preached without being raised again, who would believe in him?

Accordingly, John very carefully placed the lion first in the mystery of Christ’s resurrection, because through the fact that he rose again after dying, he compelled the world to believe in him. For this reason he placed the lion first.

Although man or calf may be first in the order, the lion is nevertheless first in power, and Christ in strength.

Hence Paul said: “Even if we had known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer” (II Cor. V, 16), as though he were saying in other words: We no longer attend to the man who was destined to die among the living creatures, but to the lion who rose after death to live forever.

Thus, as far as I can see, both the order of the Evangelists is rightly preserved, as has been said, and the reversal of the narrative made by John in the Apocalypse is not without a great mystery.

But whether our preface preserves the proper sequence of reasoning, while respecting the authority of the earlier Fathers, I leave to the judgment both of your community and of my brothers, for whom I seem to labor.

For if, both in this argument and in the whole of this work, I am approved by the judgment of you both and defended by your decision, I fear no arrogance of rashness and will not dread undeserved criticism, since I know that I am supported and strengthened by the authority of such great men, whose teaching in all the knowledge of God is proclaimed far and wide and whose wisdom is powerful—not merely in word but also in every good work and discipline of virtue.

Whatever you have learned in teaching, you exhibit more richly in deeds, so that Christ is glorified everywhere in you.

For this reason I consider myself not without cause fortunate if, as an old man, I should produce in this work something worthy of you, at least something that may benefit the young, to the advantage of learning and the pursuit of piety.

For, as someone says, just as wise old men delight in young people endowed with a good nature, and the old age of those who are honored and loved by the young becomes lighter, so good young people rejoice in the instructions of the old, by which they are led toward the pursuit of virtues.

Therefore, beloved, my old age ought not to have been merely feeble with regard to you and my brothers, whom I ought to have exhorted when I presided over them. It ought not to have been idle, nor even inactive in its very leisure, but industrious and always doing and attempting something by which the life of those now living might be formed and an example provided for those to come.

This was so that the sacrament of salt which I once received as a little child in my mouth might not be emptied out in old age or decline.

Suppose, then, that I possess neither such holiness, nor have been endowed with such a measure of the salt of wisdom, nor have been instructed in such a discipline of letters that my old age might be rich in mercy, nor have been so illumined by the splendor of virtues that I might seem worthy to write about such people and such matters. Nevertheless, it is your merit and grace that, though unworthy, I presume to obey.

And if someone should wish to stifle me so completely that I would not dare to do this, let him behold me, ineloquent and as though sprinkled with the filth of all vices, as the leper who first appears in this work, in whom and with whom I trust that I shall be healed.

Let him look upon every kind of disease and, together with me, implore the will of the Lord alone as the cause of salvation.

Let him therefore hear the Lord commanding, if he thinks me mute, in the Gospel: “Ephphetha” (Mark VII, 34), which means “Be opened.”

And because long ago, as an infant, I tasted the saliva of his mouth, I do not blush, now an old man, to speak the truth when asked by you.

Indeed, because I feel his fingers inwardly in my ears, I must not be silent about what I hear to myself and to my own people.

And even if the most merciful Jesus himself commanded me not to speak, those whom he commanded to be silent would sufficiently invite me not to remain silent: the more he commanded them, the more they preached, and all the more they marveled, saying: “He has done all things well; he has made the deaf hear and the mute speak” (Mark VII, 37).

For this reason, I ask that no one trouble me and no one reproach me if I speak, lest he appear ungrateful for the works of Christ, who by his goodness grants the deaf to hear the mysteries of life and the mute to speak, so that they may proclaim the mighty works of God.

For the rest, I ask my reader not to judge the progress of this discourse, scarcely sufficient for the meanings of the Scriptures, to be tedious prolixity, since our speech is extended not by words but by meanings.

Although brevity that is barren sometimes pleases many readers more than the useful length of explanations, nevertheless a richer meaning rightly offers more to the diligent than a shortened exposition.

Here we have followed neither the allegorical interpretations of the Gospel in our explanation nor the mystical understandings of its statements; we have explained only the simple meaning of the words, briefly, as was appropriate.

Therefore let those who are fastidious take, in abridgment, the rules of truth which the authority and force of mind of the earlier Fathers first dictated in the Gospel, so that they may not be disgusted by greater length.

But those who are more diligent, I ask, may deign to read our work, since I wished to satisfy those asking for a fuller treatment.

If neither this nor that pleases those weighed down by any kind of laziness, let them read what they imagine for themselves in the silence of sleep and slumber; or, if they are otherwise entertained, let them, still children, gnaw the pods of secular literature like swine, or nibble its husks.

For us, however, whom the divine Spirit has instructed, it was not permissible to refrain from speaking to you, our beloved, of whatever had been composed by the holy teachers. I believed it would be useful and did not doubt that it would please the more diligent.

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0337]

[Col. 0337D] **CHAPTER VIII.** At that time, as Jesus was coming down from the mountain, behold, a leper came and worshiped him (Matthew 8:2).

Because, as the Lord was descending from the mountain, the leper was the first to meet him, we must hasten so that we too may arrive with him, since we were also present in that man, insofar as through him the human race and the care of our salvation are represented. Nevertheless, let the prudent reader understand from this, and in all the other passages [Col. 0338D] of the holy Gospel, that allegorical figures diminish nothing of the faith in the truth of the event itself. For everything was arranged in these matters by divine providence in such a way that faith might arise from the miracle, and that the teaching of faith, proceeding from that same work, might advance the formation of character through its mystery.

Therefore, everywhere the setting, time, order, and every circumstance [Col. 0339A] of the history must be considered, so that both the truth of what happened may become evident for the sake of faith and the spiritual understanding may shine forth for the sake of instruction. Hence it is that on the mountain he teaches spiritual disciples spiritual matters, as though they had been placed near heavenly things. But as he descended below, a leper was the first to meet him.

In that leper, unquestionably, the human race is represented allegorically, as I have said, because leprosy had sprinkled all people with the stain of a defiled life; and therefore no one had a way back to the camp of paradise. The allegories of the divine Scriptures are chiefly formed in two ways: by things and by words—though in one way through things and in another through words.

That which is made through words is called verbal or proverbial allegory, and it is recognized in four forms. It occurs either through the transference of words, as in: “Heaven was opened and the Holy Spirit descended” (Luke 3:21), and: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16:28). These expressions transfer to God, metaphorically, causes drawn from human activities.

Or it occurs according to the images of parables, as in: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers” (Luke 10:30), and in the parable of the vineyard and its tenants (Matthew 21:33). In such cases, what is demanded is not a historical event; rather, the transformation of persons and affairs refers to something else.

Or it occurs comparatively, through the comparison of similar things. This differs scarcely at all from the preceding form, except that no narrative is woven together, as in the examples above; instead, only the effects of causes are brought into relation.

Or it occurs simply in a proverbial manner, as in: “Do not cast your pearls before pigs” (Matthew 7:6).

The allegory of things, however, of which we have spoken, is always represented mystically in such a way that it is rightly believed to subtract nothing from the events themselves. For typological interpretations do not remove the truth of things that happened, as the present passage proves: the leper is said to have been immediately cured as the Lord descended from the mountain, signifying that the human race, when the Lord descended from the heavenly realms, was cleansed from the leprosy of sin.

Nor is it inappropriate that the multitude of believers should be signified by one person, since teachers comprehend the whole of the human race under the single designation “man.” For when “man” is mentioned, whatever has been generated from our humanity is also understood according to the customary usage of secular disciplines.

Thus, most clearly, through one man sprinkled with the spots of leprosy, the unity [Col. 0339D] of believers—defiled by the stains of sins and cast away amid the squalor of impurities—is shown. Therefore let no one glory in his own merits, because we were all children of wrath and excluded from heavenly fellowship. This race, when it had descended, is immediately shown to have met him in one person.

Otherwise, unless he had descended—having been found through the incarnation in the condition of a human being—this man, expelled from the joys of paradise, would not have ascended as a leper in the condition of a human being. Therefore, mystically, we all meet together with him; together with him let us all say from the heart: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.” Though all unclean, let us approach in faith and ask the will of him whose power we do not doubt. And let us draw nearer in proportion to the firmness of our faith.

[Col. 0340A] What undertaking, then, in all disciplines is as effective as the will of God? The will of God is the cause, origin, and existence of all things, because all things are created from nothing by the will of God and are brought forth from their formlessness into form.

Here, therefore, he most wisely disclosed the cause of origin and existence to those deformed by the contagion of sin, when Christ did everything that he willed, and to have willed alone was to have done. Since the unity of believers was represented beforehand in this man, it was entirely just that, according to his teaching—the cause of all things—the will of God should be entreated together with faith.

For it is not faith merely to believe that he created all things unless we also believe that by that very will through which we were created, we can again be restored from formlessness to the form of eternal happiness, and restored for the better. This subject of argument [Col. 0340B] none of the philosophers of old discovered; rather, he himself taught it who created it.

Therefore let every believer say: “Lord, if you will,” seeking the cause of his origin and having no hesitation about his restoration, since he wills all people to be saved: “You can cleanse me and restore me to the form of salvation.”

Nor is there any doubt that, according to the truth of the history, as the Lord descended this man, first covered with leprosy, met him. For blessed Matthew, undertaking both the care of sinners and the apostolate, instructed them and impressed upon them the form of teaching—those whom leprosy had made wanderers, exiles from the city of Zion, whose foundations are on the holy mountains.

[395] And appropriately, at the beginning of the healing, he records that no one other than a leper met him together with the crowds: a man commendable in faith, devoted in confession, and endowed with heavenly teaching, who indeed asks: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me,” wisely teaching the cause and efficacy of all things: the will of God.

The philosopher Plato had not attained this discipline, although he taught something else. The man therefore confesses Christ’s power and implores his will, because his power is as great as his will—indeed, his will itself is power. For this reason he devoutly begs that, from the one by whom he came from nothing, he may again be reformed from the formlessness of sin into the original form of his nature.

Then Jesus, stretching out his hand, touched him, saying: “I will.” He stretched out his hand because the man had gone far away. And unless he had first taken pity and stretched out his hand, the man could never have returned and been healed. Therefore the Prophet, groaning, said: “Why, Lord, have you withdrawn your hand and your right hand from the midst of your bosom forever?” (Psalm 73:12).

If that hand had not been extended, since we had been plunged into the deepest depths, it would never have taken care to touch us. Concerning its power, elsewhere the Prophet asks again: “Has your hand been shortened, or made small, so that you cannot save?” (Isaiah 50:2). If it were indeed short in mercy or small in power, it would never raise those sunk in the depths and weighed down by such a burden of sins.

But because Christ came already extended—that is, the Father’s right hand clothed in flesh, for the sake of mercy—he is rightly said to have extended his hand and touched him. Otherwise, according to the literal sense, what need was there for him to extend his hand and touch the leper, when by his word, indeed by his will, he created and restores all things? It was because in one man he most effectively accomplished what he had once promised, through the many utterances of the prophets, that he would do at the same time in the whole race.

Therefore he is rightly said to have extended his hand and touched him, because, if he incarnate had not cleansed our stains by touching them, we would still be under the leprosy of sin and not yet purified from the contagion of our offenses. For this reason he extended his hand, so that he might grasp us, however deeply submerged we were; and he touched the badly wounded through the mystery of the incarnation, so that he might heal us.

According to the literal sense, moreover, he is believed to have touched the man in order to show himself Lord both of leprosy and of the law. Since the law prohibited lepers from being touched by priests, he touched the man because that leprosy of the law could not defile him. It was a shadow, although it was a bodily affliction.

[Col. 0341B] Yet it was rightly the case that Jewish priests did not touch lepers, because they could be defiled and could not heal anyone. But there was one mediator, God and man, the promulgator of the law, for whom it was lawful both to touch through his humanity and to command through his divinity; his purity could not be defiled, just as his health could not be weakened.

And therefore, because he was Lord of the law, he removes leprosy by his authority and drives it away by his command, just as darkness is driven away by light. Hence I think that the hand did not touch the leprosy; rather, just as darkness disappears before the face of light, so leprosy immediately disappeared before the face of the hand.

For it is not right to believe that he touched the leprosy of sin, but that by his incarnation alone and by the power of his word he destroyed all things. For this reason what is touched by the hand is healed by the word.

After the touch, therefore, he also commands: “Be cleansed,” so that the divinity may be understood in the word of command and the humanity in the touch of the flesh. For neither did the divinity do anything in this mystery without the flesh, nor the humanity without the divinity.

“Immediately,” he says, “he was cleansed.” He is therefore immediately cleansed because the effect always follows the will and command of God.

If the reader wishes to examine this passage according to tropology, it will provide no small moral teaching. For the form of tropology in the sacred Scriptures is always twofold: either mystical, or bare and simple. It is mystical when the events themselves are drawn toward the improvement of conduct, so that through this leper the healing of each individual human soul is understood. It is bare when sacred Scripture simply instructs conduct, as in: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none, and let the one who has food do likewise” (Luke 3:11).

Therefore each person’s soul, though sinful, is healed daily by the Lord if, humbly and devoutly worshiping him everywhere, it confesses him in faith, saying: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.” For with the heart one believes unto righteousness. Thus it is necessary to ask with complete faith, doubting nothing of his power.

And if one prays through the faith that works through love, the divine will for salvation will undoubtedly be present—effective in command and powerful in accomplishment. Therefore the supplicant leper is immediately told: “I will.” For when the soul begins in this way to pray through believing, it already begins to be healed of its leprosy by the Savior’s hand.

He himself, descending daily, looks upon and touches our sins, when he inclines himself toward mercy in order to lift up our infirmities. For we who are sick are unable first to ascend through contemplation to the mountains, that is, to heavenly things. Only Moses and a few elders with him were chosen from among all; likewise, only the disciples were led to the heights.

Below, however, the weak crowd and the worshiping leper are healed because they do not wish to pursue contemplation, being hindered by many snares. To them, therefore, the Lord frequently inclines himself, touches them with the hand of his clemency, and commands by the word of his majesty.

From this it is clear that the Lord’s hand touched not the leprosy but the leper’s clean body. Likewise, whenever he determines to touch us with the gaze of his mercy, our crimes are immediately driven away and the soul is restored to purity.

For surely, wherever salvation deigns to act, no sickness can remain; where there is light, no obscurity of sin can prevail; where there is life, no invasion of death can occur; where there is power, no difficulty in healing exists.

Therefore this man is an outstanding teacher of supplication. He does not doubt the Lord’s will as though he disbelieved his compassion, but, conscious of the enormity of his sins, he does not presume. Rather, we praise in him the steadfastness of faith, because he declares that the Lord can cleanse him if he wills—thus acknowledging the Lord’s authority in power.

For sound and true faith ought rightly to be as great as a gift as the power of the Creator’s mercy is in its operation. Otherwise faith itself, when weakened, must first be healed, and only then can bodily or spiritual health be obtained through it more effectively.

Concerning this faith the Apostle says: “Purifying their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). And if the hearts of believers are purified by faith, the power of faith must be considered, because whoever doubts is, as the Apostle says, like a wave of the sea (James 1:6).

Sound faith is loving, steadfast in perseverance, patient in delay, humble in confession, strong in trust, devout in supplication, and prudent in the deliberation of petition. Such faith will everywhere hear the Lord saying: “I will.”

For this reason the sequence of the words is wonderfully joined together. The leper had first said: “Lord, if you will,” and the Savior answered: “I will.” He had said: “You can cleanse me,” and the Lord, by the word of his power, commanded: “Be cleansed.” Whatever the true confession of the sinner had embraced in faith, mercy and power immediately displayed in granting it.

And lest anyone despair because of the enormity of his sins, this very man who is healed is described by another Evangelist as being full of leprosy. “All have sinned and lack the glory of God.”

For just as God’s power is rightly believed to exist everywhere, so his will must necessarily be believed as well. He wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. The knowledge of the truth is that, just as the Father and the Son are one Godhead, so their will is one; and the will belonging to both is also their power. Therefore it is no less lawful to believe him powerful than willing.

Hence it is written: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 134:6).

Therefore this excellent man seeks the Lord’s will, doubting nothing concerning his power and presuming upon his compassion. Jesus said to him: “See that you tell no one.”

Why, then, is he commanded to tell no one what he wanted to be made known to everyone? It is because [Col. 0343A] he himself was made for us the way from God, so that he might teach that the works of our virtue are not immediately to be publicized, but sometimes are to be concealed in silence for the preservation of humility, so that we may abstain not only from the reward of the deed but also from praise and approval.

What he did for the salvation of all must by no means be concealed. Yet, in one and the same work, he wished to teach what we ought to do and to indicate how cautious we must be even in our own actions, lest from the very place where we are raised to the summit, we should fall more grievously into sin.

Hence Mark says that the leper immediately began to preach and spread the report, so that Jesus could no longer enter a city openly. Certainly, divine works are to be disclosed, whereas the works performed in us are sometimes to be concealed lest we slip.

We are indeed commanded, in the person of that man, to tell no one; he, however, is released from the command, so that without fault, in praise of the Savior, he might also show himself cleansed to the priest. “But go,” he says, “show yourself to the priest.”

Otherwise, how could he tell no one, when, for his cleansing, he publicly offers a gift to the priest in the temple? Unless perhaps our works are everywhere to be disclosed for the glory and praise of God, including the works God performs in us, but are not to be displayed for our own praise or the gaining of favor.

Or perhaps the mere display of virtues is sufficient to encourage the deed, so that it is superfluous to proclaim in words what everyone is permitted to see for imitation, and so that one should not seek praise for oneself but present oneself as an example to many.

“Go,” he says, “show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded as a testimony to them.”

Not because the Lord then cared greatly for that Mosaic command, which was soon to be abolished [Note: *Satis* means “much, very much,” as when one says in French, *il est assez habile, assez savant*—“he is quite able, quite learned”—etc.]; rather, he was giving all who come to the faith and are healed a model of offering daily to Christ, the supreme priest—of whom that priest bore the figure—the sacrifices of thanksgiving and the gifts of due praise.

These sacrifices of the law are to be offered spiritually for our cleansing, since they were commands signifying life and promising that Christ would suffer in the flesh for our cleansing. These are indeed the sacrifices of our redemption, without which we cannot please God. Therefore, continually sprinkled with the blood of Christ through baptism, we too must offer these sacrifices for ourselves in faith.

Nevertheless, he commanded the man to go to the priest so that the priest might understand that he had been healed not according to the order of the law but by the grace of the holy [Col. 0343D] Gospel, which is above the law.

Hence what follows: “And offer the gift that Moses commanded as a testimony to them.” The gift is offered as a testimony so that they may believe. And if the Jewish priests should refuse to believe, it would become evident that the one whom the severity of the law had been unable to cleanse from leprosy had been made healthy and whole by the grace of Christ.

Indeed, that very gift, because it was a shadow, typologically foreshadowed the one who would mercifully free the entire human race, sprinkled with his blood, from the leprosy of its uncleanness.

All the Savior’s miracles performed through the flesh were testimonies to his divinity, demonstrating that Christ Jesus was the same God and man. Therefore he said: “If you do not want to believe me, at least believe the works” (John 10:38).

The priests and scribes are convicted by the testimony of the law and the prophets, because he was testified to by the law and the prophets. They are also convicted by those same works, which are shown to be no less above the law than above human power.

For this reason the man is sent with due foresight to the priest, so that the priest might also depart from the leprosy of his own impiety. He has testimony from the law that the law had never been able to do such things; testimony from the law’s own typological ordinance; testimony from the work of healing itself and from the word of command—at least so that he might recognize the one who had once created all things by his word.

It does not appear that he approved, as some suppose, the Mosaic sacrifice, which thereafter the Church of Christ did not believe should be offered. Rather, he did so solely for the sake of testimony, especially since that holy of holies—namely, his body—had not yet begun to be offered as a sacrifice [Col. 0344B], because he had not yet offered himself in his passion as the holocaust of our redemption.

For this reason, the significant sacrifices of the law did not yet need to be removed, until what they signified had been revealed and confirmed through the fulfillment of the work. Then, with the figures of the passion already set aside, what had been concealed would be embraced more fully by the faith of believers: the sacrifice of Christ.

When Jesus had entered Capernaum, a centurion approached him, entreating him and saying (Matt. 8:5). Concerning this passage, Luke and the present Evangelist seem to differ greatly, 400 since Luke says that he first sent the elders of the Jews to him, asking him to come and save his servant. When they had come, they earnestly begged him, saying: “He is worthy that you should grant this for him, for he loves our nation, and he himself built our synagogue for us.” Jesus was going with them, and when he was already not far from the house, the centurion again sent friends to him, saying: “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof. For that reason I did not consider myself worthy even to come to you,” and so forth (Luke 7:1–7). Yet in this passage it is said that he himself approached him, although according to Luke he declares himself unworthy to come.

But there Luke, pursuing the historical truth, did so; Matthew, however, asserted this according to the most customary manner of speaking. Luke too, as though recalling the matter, published elsewhere and much later the account of the leper—what is inserted here immediately after the descent from the mountain, as having truly occurred [Col. 0344D]—but concerning the centurion he says: “When he had finished all his words in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum” (ibid.). The sense is that he did not enter before he had finished these things. Yet he does not indicate how much time passed before he entered there after completing his discourse. Thus, in this respect also, the two accounts do not disagree.
