One wished to state what should be understood according to the historical truth; the other, which is the greater matter, what we should understand according to faith.

Especially since we commonly say that the arrival at a person, for the sake of attaining whom someone approaches, has taken place, even though the person who heard of it may not see the one who arrives, when the arrival has occurred through a friend, whose favor is often necessary in such matters. Hence common usage has established that we call those “intercessors” through whom we reach the minds of powerful people—even when they are inaccessible—by the interposition of persons, as though through the art of solicitation. How much more rightly is this man said to have approached through friends, since he had approached more than all others through faith, according to what is written: “Approach him, and be enlightened” (Ps. 33:5).

Therefore, because the Evangelist wished to say that the centurion had approached Christ rather than those through whom he had sent his words, he praised the centurion’s faith—the faith by which each person truly approaches God—in such a way that he said: “I have not found such great faith in Israel” (Matt. 8:10). For Luke, understanding this, wove together the historical truth in order to lead you back to faith, just as another said that the woman had approached him who could not possibly have lied (Luke [Col. 0345B] 8:43). Thus that woman who suffered from an issue of blood is said to have touched the Lord, although she touched only his fringe, rather than the crowd’s having touched him.

For this reason it is not surprising if the man who is believed to have approached him is regarded as having done so all the more because he had approached him greatly through faith and later, when he had arrived at the house, met him as a suppliant with complete devotion and approached him with his whole mind. He approached him, therefore, in proportion as he believed more deeply. And whatever humility and devotion he most wisely expressed, although through another acting officially, he undoubtedly approached him wholly—not less in the intention of his entreaty than in the faith of his religious devotion—saying: “Lord, my boy lies paralyzed in the house and is suffering terribly.”

At that time many were asking for different illnesses: one for himself, another for a son or daughter, another for someone else. Yet no one is recorded as having asked for a servant except this man, who alone pleaded so earnestly. Let our people therefore listen—those who sometimes not only fail to pray for their own servants, that they may not suffer terribly, but themselves become cruel and utterly savage torturers, so that at times it seems worse to serve under their hand than under the hand of pagans.

This man had already learned the Apostle’s teaching: “Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear” (1 Pet. 2:18), and “obey, not by serving merely to attract the eye” (Eph. 6:6), knowing that “you have one Lord in heaven” (Col. 4:1). He therefore knew that Jesus Christ was this common Lord, and, full of faith and charity, devotedly pleaded for his fellow servant.

He did not bring him to Jesus because he believed that Jesus, perfectly present everywhere, was able to do everything. Nor did he ask him to go there, since he believed that Jesus was absent nowhere in his majesty, although he saw him living among human beings locally in the flesh. This is evidently the greatness of his faith, and it surpasses the faith of all who were then in Israel.

Yet his faith was not bare or dead; it was a faith that worked powerfully through love toward God and neighbor, increasing its reward through concern for a fellow servant. He plainly understood Christ’s power: it is not confined by place or bounded by limitation, but is effective everywhere. Therefore, just as he did not believe that Jesus needed to come to him, so he did not think that the servant had to be brought from the house to Jesus. “But speak with a word,” he said, “and my boy will be healed.”

And indeed the boy was immediately healed by that word, because “by the word of the Lord the heavens were established.” What remarkable teaching from the centurion! I openly confess that, from my earliest years, although I was able to read whatever philosophers I could, just as Christ found no such faith in Israel, neither was I able to find such wisdom in them. What they had been unable to understand from the whole structure of the world, this man perceived entirely in one small body, and he sensed the fullness of divinity dwelling in it. 402

The Word had certainly approached him, the Word through whom God the Father had created all things—not an emanated word, but one consubstantial and coeternal. Therefore he asks: “Speak with a word,” because the Son is plainly the Father’s co-worker; and just as the Father either says or does all things through him, so he himself works and commands together with the Father and through himself.

Understanding this correctly, he says: “Speak with a word”—that is, from your consubstantial nature, because you are the Word and Wisdom of God the Father. Wisdom, moreover, is the health of the world. “And immediately my boy will be healed.” For the efficacy of the word reaches everything. Therefore, do not trouble the body, which I confess to be truly human. I do not desire you to fatigue yourself with the sufferings and labor of the flesh, which I fully recognize that you have taken upon yourself for us; rather, work by your majesty, namely, by the power of the Word. For in one and the same person my faith proclaims for me both God and man. Nor does it teach, like certain heretics, two persons; rather, he says: “Speak with a word”—that is, by your majesty—“and my boy will be healed.”

The Lord says to him: “I will come and heal him.” What a marvel! Behold, something is offered to him that he himself does not request. But to a certain royal official who asked him to come down before his son died, the request is entirely denied. Is God therefore a respecter of persons, especially since the one is recorded as a royal official and the other as a centurion? Far from it! Otherwise, it would have been more honorable to go to the royal official’s house and grant his request than to offer to go to the centurion’s house when he was refusing.

But faith is the issue. The royal official was to be instructed because he believed that Jesus could not heal someone who was absent, even though Jesus was wholly present everywhere and could be present to the son. The centurion, however, was to be exercised toward greater things, and it was to be made known to us by how many virtues he surpassed others—he to whom the Lord was glad to go willingly.

“Lord,” he says, “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” Thus everyone humbles himself who is unable to bear Christ’s divinity when it is present. Hence Moses, speaking from his conversation with God, even though he speaks enigmatically, says: “I am not eloquent, Lord, nor worthy from yesterday and the day before, since you began to speak with your servant” (Exod. 4:10). Hence Abraham confesses before the Lord that he is dust and ashes (Gen. 18:27). Job too, after the vision, promises to carry out repentance in ashes and dust (Job 42:6). Peter himself, moved by the miracle, cries out at the catch of fish: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8).

Yet the centurion does not drive the Lord away from himself; he confesses that he is not worthy for the Lord to enter under his roof, and he fully acknowledges the majesty of the Word in him. He implores him who is absent to show himself present, whose unfailing presence is everywhere [Col. 0347A] and whose power fills all things.

Then, finally advancing to higher matters, although covertly, he teaches more clearly from his own example that human concerns are also cared for through the service of angels. “For I too am a man,” he says, “placed under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

What remarkable prudence in the centurion! In a single moment he pursued such profound secrets of majesty: he showed that visible and invisible things are subject to Christ, through whom all things subsist and by whose angelic service they are administered. Hence the same Lord is so often proclaimed in the sacred Scriptures as the King of hosts.

The centurion did not insert the words “I am a man placed under authority,” as some suppose, to suggest his humility, as though he were thereby to be understood as more sinful. Rather, like a perfect advocate or philosopher, he introduces an example by which, in accordance with his own official position, he might move the mind of the most merciful judge to action and finally offer believers an example of his devotion.

The very connection of the words proves this, since he says: “For I too,” joining or arranging the meaning. It is as though he plainly said: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but since you are the eternal King commanding under no one’s authority, only speak with a word, and my boy will be healed. For I too, although under another’s authority—perhaps that of a commander or king—and appointed to an office of honor, have soldiers under me. I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and yet he goes, and so forth. How much more can you, who have an army of angels under no one else, arrange all things with power through their service?”

First you can do all things by a word; then, through the service of mighty soldiers, you possess them with authority: in the one case having the command of majesty, in the other the obedience of rank. If I, under another’s authority, can accomplish such things effortlessly through subordinates, how much more can you, through your distinguished attendants, who can do everything at once by a word?

Our philosopher here makes an argument by comparison from the lesser to the greater. Therefore he begins: “If I, under another’s authority, can accomplish such things”—showing that Christ, according to his divinity, is under no one’s authority and yet presides over armies, even according to his humanity. Hence he is also called the King of Sabaoth, that is, of armies.

For, as they say, every argument is made in two ways: either by induction or by reasoning. But induction gradually proceeds by means of an example, as it does among certain wise men of the world, so that our advocate here might move the judge’s mind to action. In this way, certainly, he himself makes an argument for us from an undisputed matter—or rather, through him the divine Spirit, by whom he was enlightened, more plainly leads us to believe what had previously been uncertain.

In a similar way, shortly before, he heightens the opening of his plea to the Lord, both through himself and through messengers, in the manner of rhetoricians. First he recounts acts of kindness and benevolence: that the centurion had built a synagogue for the Jews and had loved that nation, which he knew the Lord had loved. Then, calling him Lord in humble supplication, he says: “My boy lies in the house,” and not merely that, but “he is paralyzed,” and afterward: “He is suffering terribly.”

That alone would have been sufficient to indicate suffering, if he were being tortured; nevertheless he added “terribly,” in contrast with those who are sometimes tortured so that they may be corrected or tested. This boy, however, is suffering terribly because of the misery of sin—not so that he may be corrected, but so that he may already be deservedly punished. Having said this, the heavenly advocate falls silent, as though plainly saying: “I have opened my wounds to you; you are the physician. You know better how to fulfill your office and grant the salvation for which you came, since you are believed to be the salvation of the world.”

It is nevertheless remarkable that he says: “I have soldiers under me, and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” I think he had examined all heavenly things, since he both perceived divinity in a human being and fully understood the functions of the heavenly army. He also distinguished, as I believe, the service of servants from that of the others.

For that inward arbiter sometimes says to one of the angels, “Go,” when he frequently sends them to us. The heavenly spirits have been appointed to this service for the sake of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation: to arrange the affairs of our life each day and report the deeds of individuals to the Creator. To another he says: “Come,” and he comes.

For he commands both those whom he sends and those whom he keeps tirelessly within for his praise to come to him. This does not mean that they ever depart from him—from the sweetness of that eternal vision—when they come to us. Rather, “to go” means for them to turn their attention to the cause of creatures and to our cause; “to come” means to gaze ever more intently upon the contemplation of that immeasurable majesty. Hence it is rightly said: “Into which things the angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1:12). For in proportion to their greater desire, they are believed to come more greatly to him, because he whom they behold is immeasurable and supreme blessedness.

But when he says: “And to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it,” he seems prudently to have distinguished the service of demons from that of the others. He calls them servants, and by his example he indicates that they neither return from him nor come from him. For they never cease to direct themselves and their wicked deceptions—not at divine command, but driven by their own enticement toward pride. Yet just as it belongs to them to go, and they never cease from such activity, so, through the power of the Lord, who makes good use of their evil, whether they wish it or not, they accomplish everything that has been commanded them.

Even in the ancient Roman people, those whom the freedom of their lineage ennobled did not themselves torture anyone whom a judicial sentence condemned; rather, their servile condition afflicted such people with punishments. How much more, among the ranks of the elect angels, is no one in some sense believed to be lawfully an exactor of punishments.

Those torturers, then, are understood to be the ones whom power constrains to obey what has been commanded, while their sinful condition corrupts them so that they become ministers of punishment in evil. However wickedly they may wish otherwise, they are never able to do anything except what divine justice has decreed. Hence in this same Gospel they are rightly called torturers.

Understanding this wisely, the centurion humbly suggests that the Lord can accomplish everything through the service of angels. Through their service, bodily illness—or hostile powers, by which the boy may perhaps have been tormented—would be driven far from the man, since those malign beings can do nothing more than what is commanded, especially when the Lord himself could heal by a word alone.

Though he was still a Gentile, this man was able to understand many things about the divine and to speak wisely about hidden realities. Therefore it follows: “When Jesus heard this, he marveled.” What, then, did he marvel at? Was it a faith that he himself had not previously given, or did he not foresee that the man would possess such great faith? Certainly not. Rather, he praises and approves the faith that he himself had given, and he marvels in order to make us marvel.

Likewise it is said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22:12), that is, “I will make it known.” This manner of speaking is exceedingly common in the sacred Scriptures. Yet just as perfect fear in Abraham is divinely approved in so great a work of faith, so in this centurion, as though in the first fruits of the Gentiles, perfect faith is displayed through the Lord’s marveling.

Therefore nothing in the world is marvelous in his sight, and he marvels only at the faith of one person. For this reason he says in what follows: “Amen, I say to you: I have not found such great faith in Israel.”

We do not think that this was said about all the earlier patriarchs and saints; he is speaking only about the people of that same period. The centurion’s faith is therefore preferred to theirs because, although the Law or the prophets had led them to faith through prolonged instruction, the Father alone fully instructed this man, without another teacher. Flesh and blood did not teach him these things; the Father of Christ revealed them from heaven.

Thus, rightly, the faith of the Gentiles is praised through him. For in the earlier leper the whole human race is signified, the race sprinkled with the leprosy of original sin; in this centurion, however, the Gentile world alone is gathered together. His faith is proclaimed in many places as surpassing that of the Jews because the Gentiles, once they had received the grace of preaching and signs, immediately believed fully.

“Israel,” he says, “has not known me, and that people has not understood me” (Isa. 1:3). This does not mean that there was no faith at all among the Israelites who were then saved; rather, abundant and exceptional faith is approved in this man, as though in all the Gentiles.

Finally, he shows in the centurion the elect from among the Gentiles by grace. For this reason his faith, together with the fruits of good works, is placed before Israel. The fruits of faith were charity, by which he loved God and neighbor; prudence and understanding, by which he perceived divinity in a human being; and deeply grounded humility, by which he confessed himself unworthy for Christ to receive him under his roof.

He is justified by faith, and he does not despise the original condition of the flesh, since he takes care of those in his household. Therefore he is not inappropriately called a centurion, surrounded by the army of virtues.

“Centurion” derives its name from “one hundred.” The number one hundred, transferred from the left to the right, always signifies the crown of heaven and blessedness, indicating those who will be placed on the right. Since these are perfect, they must intercede with God for the imperfect, because the latter are still oppressed by servile fear under the spirit of slavery, as children; so that perfect charity may gradually drive fear out from them.

Yet the same Gentile world is still said to be under the authority of another because it has not yet been reborn, having under itself no fewer soldiers than it has lords over itself—those who served it most zealously and wickedly in everything belonging to the flesh.

But according to the tropological sense, if someone reaches the perfection symbolized by one hundred, like Abraham begetting Isaac according to the promise, he will find within himself a wretched place of inward groaning. For one part of us is still in the womb, like a child in the house, lying paralyzed and terribly tormented by the sicknesses of vices.

One part in us is indeed “one hundred,” through which we are spiritual; the other is animal, so that we do not yet rightly understand the things of God, because “the animal person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God.” From the part by which we understand, we make supplication for our errors and cry out each day: “From your fear, Lord, we have conceived and given birth, and we have brought forth the spirit of salvation.”

The more perfect freedom of the man prays for the servant. Although the servant has not yet been reborn from God and, while still in fragile flesh, sins—for, as John says, “if he had been born from God, he would not sin at all” (1 John 3:9)—nevertheless, because he is “one hundred,” he entreats God, who is to be placed on the right, and is healed daily through faith, saying: “Lord, my boy lies paralyzed in the house.”

In the house, I say, of which we read that it was said to the soul: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44:11). In this house, namely, in this world, every soul lies paralyzed—that is, inwardly disordered—and, not without reason, is called a child, since it is still partly animal.

“And the child, though one hundred years old, shall die” [cf. Isa. 65:20]. Such a one, so long as he is a child, is always terribly tormented by demons. Therefore, so long as he remains such, he is not considered worthy for Jesus to enter under his roof. It is a great thing for Christ to deign to enter into someone and make his dwelling with him.

For this reason our weakness must first be presented through humble confession: the evils by which we are tormented inwardly in the mind. Then, after healing, lodging must be prepared through the virtues of good works.

Sometimes, although we are under the power of the prince of this world, all the desires of the flesh are believed to be subject to us, and we rule them by right. Hence, when he spoke about sin at the door to Cain, he said: “Your desire shall be under you.” If we rule these desires well, if we always pursue the things that belong to freedom, so that we may be transferred completely from slavery into freedom, then we present true faith to the Lord together with good works.

Indeed, there is a great difference between faith and faith, although the faith of all is one, as the Apostle says: “One faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4:5). Hence faith is rightly said to belong to individuals—not because one person has one faith and another another, since there is only one faith, but because within the one and same faith there is a great difference in degree according to the gift of grace and the virtue of the soul.

That is why it is called the faith proper to individuals, while nevertheless it is proclaimed universally as one faith belonging to all: unless this one and same faith is held, there is no other faith. For this reason the Lord did not say: “I have not found this faith in Israel,” since, if he had said that, everyone would be outside the faith. Rather, he said: “I have not found such great faith,” so that the unity of the substance of faith might be understood, while the varying measure of merits within that same faith might be recompensed by the Lord.

Hence also he says to the Canaanite woman: “O woman, great is your faith” (Matt. 15:28), but to Peter: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14:31). If there were no great difference, the faith of the latter would not be censured as little, nor that of the former praised as great. Nevertheless, in both—and in all who understand rightly—the one faith is either corrected, advanced, or proposed for imitation by others.

But although “false faith” is a phrase that may be used, it is not faith, because it is fabricated from the heart. If we falsely believe something false about the Trinity, our hope is empty and our charity uncertain. For when what is false is loved, what is true cannot be present.

For this reason the centurion is praised as having true and great faith for no other reason than that he may be imitated. If we wish to be counted among his imitators, Marcion must not be heeded, nor the others who said that Christ was a phantom without true flesh. Nor Arius, who considers him a creature, together with the Word that was in the beginning with God, through which he creates all things and restores everything by speech alone.

Nor should the new Felician heresy be followed, which wished to disturb the ashes of the ancients by introducing two persons in Christ: namely, the Word, the proper Son of God, and the adopted son of God, the human being. Yet this man understands the human being to be God when he says: “Speak with a word.” Otherwise, if the same person were not both God and man, one ought to pray inwardly to God rather than outwardly to the human being.

Although he saw him made lower than the angels, he nevertheless teaches most openly by this example that this same human being, because he was one with the Word, rules over the army of angels. Therefore we must believe that the human being, because he was made medicine for us by God the Father, speaks the Word and heals.

Yet he is not someone other than the Word, nor is the Word another person, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”: one and the same person. 409

“I say to you,” he continues, “that many will come from east and west,” and the rest that follows. We must therefore ask: How will they come? Will they come by the steps of their feet? Certainly not, but by the steps of faith, charity, and humility, by which this man approached him. Each person will reach him in proportion as he believes more deeply through faith that works by love.

But how can many truly be believed to come, when elsewhere it is said that “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22:14)? From the beginning to the end of the world, few are gathered from among all people in comparison with those who perish, although many are called. Yet when those coming from every direction are gathered together at the same time, they will undoubtedly be found to be many.

Concerning them the Prophet says: “I will number them, and they will be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. 138:17). When he says “from east and west,” this does not mean that they are believed to come only from these two regions; they will also come from the south and the north.

Rather, he says “from the east” because it is the first part of the world, as though from the beginning of the age, and “from the west,” as though from the end of life. All will come from every direction to the one mediator, God and man, through faith—to the one whom this man had approached. That is: those who rightly believed in him before his coming will rest, as will those who, after his coming, received him by faith, having been born not from bloods nor from the will of the flesh, but from God.

Or alternatively: “from east and west,” that is, from every nation under heaven, from the rising of the sun to its setting. For just as he must be preached among all nations, so people from all nations will come to the kingdom of heaven.

Within these regions the two intermediate directions are certainly also understood, so that the figure may be made solid by four equal sides. But the first and last are mentioned so that the day may always be fixed in memory when “lightning will come out from the east and appear as far as the west,” for then will be the coming of the Son of Man.

At that time only those will recline in the kingdom whom the beginning of right faith and the completion of good works have proved worthy. Hence these patriarchs are brought into the discussion, whose God is not ashamed to be called their God. He says: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:6)—the God, certainly, of those whom these men hold as examples before him who knows all things.

In Abraham, faith is signified: faith by which he pleased God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. In Isaac, hope is generated, as a sacrament of faith and grace. Through Jacob, charity is signified; through various struggles it labors and sweats sufficiently until Israel can see the God of gods in Zion.

From this charity the twelve tribes are propagated, that is, the entire order of the predestined. Hence in the last age the twelve apostles will sit over the twelve tribes, where no others will be numbered except those whose faith, hope, and charity believed in, hoped for, and worshiped the God of these patriarchs with complete love.

Born again through these virtues, they will recline with them—not lying carnally, but resting spiritually from their labors. And when they have been gathered together from different regions, they will be one flock and one shepherd.

“But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into the outer darkness.” Thus the Jews are understood as the children of the kingdom: God led them out of Egypt, established them in a kingdom, and adopted them as his sons. In them he long held his kingdom, until they rejected the Son of the King, Christ, when he came to them. Therefore, because they refused to believe along with the Gentiles, whose faith this centurion displayed, they shall be cast into darkness.

The children of the kingdom may also be understood as those of this world, over whom the rulers of darkness hold sway; thus the entire order of the condemned is comprehended, since no fewer Gentiles than Jews will go into the same darkness. For from the beginning of the world these two kingdoms, Jerusalem and Babylon, are gathered: that Jerusalem is built in heaven; Babylon, because it always wished to reign on earth by itself, without God, is hurled headlong into darkness and into the furnace of burning fire. They are called children of the kingdom just as there are children of darkness, children of Gehenna, or children of wrath—which we were, but through Christ’s grace have become children of adoption.

But one must ask how they are to be cast into outer darkness, when darkness is always inward. Unless he is not speaking of the darkness which we see obscured by bodies, in the midst of which we ourselves often rest, but of that which the gloom of vices and unbelief has prepared for itself together with the devil. It is called outer because they will be exiles from Christ’s kingdom. For whatever is within that heavenly kingdom will altogether be light, as also life, because all will be blessed in his light and life. But whatever is outside it will be nothing but darkness and death, because all will be wretched without end in the fire of torments prepared for the devil. They are wretched, therefore, because they loved darkness rather than light; and because they carried the inward darkness of their minds with them, they are justly driven, as strangers to the light which they never loved, into outer darkness.

“There,” he says, “will be weeping and gnashing of teeth,” from which the future true resurrection of the flesh is proclaimed, although the character of the punishments is indicated: so that the mind may weep without end through the eyes, without the fruit of repentance, for the things—or sins [Note: [Col. 0353D] Before *which*, supply *the things* or *sins*.]—to which it wickedly consented; and so that the teeth may gnash from the horror of torments, in order that through them we may understand how greatly the wretched flesh suffers for evils.

Then he says to the centurion: “Go, and as you have believed, let it be done to you” (John 11:25). Without doubt, the same is promised to each person according to the measure of faith. For this is the power by which he gave us freedom to become children of God: that we may daily be born anew from God in Christ through faith, and that, according to its measure, the remaining gifts of charisms may be bestowed on each person, according to the Apostle. Therefore he says to this man: “Go, and as you have believed, let it be done to you.” Let us too believe, then, because if anyone believes in him—as he himself testifies—even though he has died, he shall live. And the boy was healed from that hour: that is, from the hour when Jesus said, “As you have believed, let it be done to you.” Faith obtained the reward of healing because it receives power: whatever it asks in prayer it shall receive, if it believes rightly. But whenever we do not receive, either we do not believe rightly or we certainly ask for evil things.

And when Jesus had come into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying ill, and the rest. He had come in order to see the feverish woman, and therefore, as soon as he came, he saw and healed her. For the cause of his coming was the illness of one lying down, not a need for eating: in a house where a miserable fever was rending a person, the concern was not for a meal and rejoicing, but for an outpouring of tears. A wonderful dispensation of almighty God, who seeks even those who do not seek him and mercifully comes to those unable to come to him; for if he had not first come to us, we could never have returned to him.

But fittingly, after he came down, this woman is read to have been healed in third place, although the other Evangelists mention her in another place (Mark 1:30; Luke 4:38). It makes no difference to the truth of history where each places a matter, whether he inserts it in sequence, recalls it, or anticipates an event which happened later by relating it earlier, provided that they do not contradict one another—which you will never find. Yet it always greatly advances mystical understanding that, with the Holy Spirit teaching, individual matters are placed by each writer in such a position that both the truth of the deed may be evident and spiritual teaching may appear more abundantly from the circumstances of the reading.

For, as I said, that leper signifies the whole human race, defiled by the leprosy of original sin; the centurion’s boy signifies the Gentile world alone, dissolved by the disease of idolatry as by paralysis and almost dead in every vital joint. Once these had been healed, it was most fitting that the woman, who had been the author of diseases and death, should herself be healed after the man. For the Lord had come to heal both sexes. But he who was created first had first to be healed, and then she too was not to be passed over by the Creator. Hence Scripture says:

“He took her hand, and the fever left her.” What do you suppose? Was he unable to heal her by a word because he took her hand? Or why does he touch the leper and heal him by a word, whereas he takes this woman’s hand and the fever immediately departs? He touches the leper, then, though the Law had forbidden it, in order to show himself above the Law, as we have already sufficiently said. But he took this woman’s hand, which she had stretched out against the command toward the tree, so that she might take from it the deadly taste of its fruit. Therefore there was reason for his taking her hand, that she might recover life, because Adam had received death from the hand of a woman. Thus all the Savior’s works are harmonious. For it was just that the hand of the Creator should repair what the hand of the presumptuous woman had committed, and that she who had brought death upon all should receive pardon.

She rose and served them. This was contrary to the usual condition of those suffering from fever, since they ordinarily become weak when recovery begins and feel the discomfort of their illness; but the health bestowed at the Lord’s command returns all at once, although, for the sake of a higher meaning, she herself immediately began to serve. Otherwise there was no maidservant in Peter’s house, no attendant, no member of the household, no relative—certainly not even a wife—who might have anticipated the younger woman in serving her mother; but an old woman, long tormented by fevers, did for the Teacher what the disciple, whose house it is said to have been, ought to have done. I said “had been,” because although it is called his, since there is no doubt that it had formerly been so, it is nevertheless proved that it was no longer his, because he had left everything. There were also many other servants with him; therefore Christ did not need her service, but leads us onward to understand higher things. For Peter’s house too is mentioned, as I believe, not without mystical significance. So too her service—even if for no other reason, at least tropologically, to demonstrate what the Apostle says: that the members which served iniquity unto iniquity should bear fruit and serve righteousness unto sanctification. Indeed, he also wanted her to serve for this reason, so that she might be evidence that health had been restored. For where power heals, no trace of illness ought to remain. [Col. 0354C]

Jesus therefore came into Peter’s house so that Peter’s house might come to him. He came at that time when he assumed the condition of our flesh. For Peter’s house is itself the house of Judah, or Bethlehem, which is interpreted as “house of bread,” from which Christ came according to the flesh. When he had come to that house, he saw Peter’s mother-in-law lying there and suffering from fever: that is, he saw the Synagogue lying in its unbelief and reclining on the bed of its vices. He took her hand, because he worked salvation for the Jewish people not only by word but also with his hands. Hence the Prophet says: “He worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. LXXIII, 12). He strengthened her weary hands and made firm her trembling knees. When he had taken her hand, he gave the sacrament of life to her who had drawn death to herself [Note: Before “who,” supply “to her”; that is, the word omitted through the ellipsis already indicated by us.], and she rose serving Christ—the woman who had previously lain feverish on the bed of infirmity.

The Synagogue was therefore tormented by fevers while the lust of desires and greed inflamed their wretched minds, and the chill of unbelief froze their hearts. Fever, alternating continually between flame and cold, tears apart the wretched limbs of human beings. Hence she who had been lying is raised by the hand, and she serves Christ, while she now sanctifies her hands in good works, though previously she had defiled them with her sins. [Col. 0355A]

When evening came, they brought him many who had demons, and he drove out the spirits with a word. It is strange if the crowd was so large, or if those bringing them were so slow, that, disregarding the day, they brought many afflicted people only in the evening. But even if this was due to the Savior’s excessive occupation, it is nevertheless expressed so carefully that we should understand the event mystically. For it is evening when the day ends; so too it is the end of the age, when the world, having passed through the light of the ages, was entering its final period, in which Christ restored to us an everlasting day. In this evening many afflicted people were brought through the ministry of the apostles—including us Gentiles, who did not know the one true God—and from them he drove out unclean spirits by the word of his power. Hence it is written: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Psal. XCV, 5). For Christ came to us through the word, because “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God.” By this he plainly set captives free from impious condemnation and healed all of us who were sick. For this had been written: “He sent his Word and healed them, and delivered them from their destruction” (Psal. CVI, 20). [Col. 0355B]

Wishing to explain this, the evangelist says: “so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘He himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses’” (Isa. LIII, 4). Let those who say that although the Savior is said to have suffered, or to have been weary or hungry, he endured such experiences without any experience of pain or labor, listen. For if this is true, he neither took our infirmities nor bore our sufferings. Rather, he truly suffered because he felt pain, and, wearied by labors, he endured the weakness of the flesh. Otherwise that man of the Lord would have been insensible, and there would have been neither a true passion nor, consequently, a true redemption. Therefore, in accordance with Catholic faith, we confess that he assumed every weakness of the flesh without sin, so that by his weakness he might heal us, drive unclean spirits from us by his word, and, having become medicine for our sins through the true weakness of his flesh, heal them; while through the divinity of the Word, the one and same Christ, God and man, would drive demons from us and restore all things to a better condition. [Col. 0355D]

When Jesus saw the crowds around him, he ordered them to go across the lake. The Lord sometimes had refuge from the crowds at sea, sometimes in the mountains, sometimes in the desert. Hence he now orders them to go across the lake, so that both he and his own might rest for a while from the tumult and labors of the crowds. This also gives teachers an indication that sometimes they ought to be occupied with preaching and the affairs of the churches, but at other times live in greater seclusion and devote themselves to God alone in prayer and the practice of contemplating God. [Col. 0356A]

Alternatively, when the Lord saw the crowds around him, not yet fervent in faith but merely tumultuous in body, he saw that in the consciousness of their unbelief they were still being battered by a storm and suffering shipwreck as they were tossed about. He ordered them to cross the lake so that he might remove them from the waves and have them follow him across the lake of temptation, granting them from time to time an opportunity to turn from their foolishness. He alone orders them to cross the lake so that, when the temptations of the world have been completed, we may reach our homeland. [Col. 0356B]

When he had given this order, one scribe approached and said to him, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” He approached not with faith, like that centurion of whom we spoke, but merely saying with his lips, “Teacher, I will follow you.” Thus falls the one who promises, either rashly or deceitfully, that he can follow God in everything. For an unbelieving and foolish promise displeases God. The wretched man did not yet know who or how great the one was whom he promised to follow wherever he went. Otherwise, how could he promise what no mortal in this life can do—although after the end of life it is said of the saints, who were purchased from the earth as firstfruits for God and the Lamb, that “they follow him wherever he goes” (Apoc. XIV, 4)? The text immediately adds the reason: they are virgins and were purchased from the earth as firstfruits for God and the Lamb, and are without blemish. [Col. 0356C]

But this man neither measured his own capacity nor considered Christ’s exalted greatness, ignorant of what and how much there was between himself and Christ. It is therefore clear that he considered him nothing more than a human being; hence he calls him “Teacher.” He believed that Christ was one of the teachers of the law, and so addressed him. He wanted to follow him not in order to imitate him, but to gain profit from his miracles and powers, or to seek empty glory. Simon Magus likewise desired to follow him (Act. VIII, 13). Peter, however, the chief of the apostles, follows him across the sea but sinks (Matth. XIV, 30); he follows him also to the Passion, but denies him. If so great a man, together with the others, abandons him and is unable to follow him in everything, what do you suppose this rash promiser would have done had he been present then? [Col. 0356D]

Nevertheless, he speaks as though he could endure with Christ the disgrace of the cross, break down the gates of hell, destroy death by death, restore life by rising again, and accomplish all the other things that it is difficult to enumerate concerning Christ. Therefore each person must first consider what he can do, for whom or what he is making a vow, and with what spirit and intention. But that this man had deceitfully made these promises is soon revealed by the one who sees everything and searches the hearts of individuals. [Col. 0357A]

“Foxes,” he says, “have dens, and the birds of the air have nests,” and so forth. He does not repel the man because he offers himself devoutly; rather, by implying what sort of person he was, he exposes him. For this man represents heretics or hypocrites, who always pretend to confess and follow God for some other purpose. Their service is not approved, because they do not possess the dwelling of faith in their hearts.

Hence it is fittingly said: “Foxes have dens.” Otherwise, if such people did not have dens, with their deceits and frauds, they would not be foxes. Moreover, unless they had dens and earthly caves of ambush, the birds of the air—that is, demons flying in this atmosphere—would have no nests in them. And if those demons had not first nested in them, these people would not dig dens for themselves in earthly depravity. But now heretics always seek dens because demons have nests of vices in them. [Col. 0357B]

These, then, are the birds which Abraham drove away from his sacrifice at evening, always ready to devour (Gen. XV, 11). How well heretics are compared with foxes: the fox is a very deceitful animal, always intent on ambush, practicing the plunder of fraud everywhere—now outside, now within, now around houses, seeking deceit amid human dwellings. It constantly prepares dens in which it seeks either to hide or to take refuge. Finally, as a predator of domestic birds, it tirelessly strives to carry off the chicks of hens. Concerning these the Lord says to Jerusalem: “How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings!” (Matth. XXIII, 37). Heretics are always pursuing these chicks and attempting to snatch them from beneath the Lord’s wings. [Col. 0357C]

This animal never becomes so tame that it abandons its deceit. For this reason the Lord rejected the man, because he promised to follow him in the bitterness of gall—not indeed in order to bear fruit, but in order to destroy. Concerning such people he says in the Song: “Seize for us the foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Cant. II, 15). Samson therefore ties torches to their tails (Jud. XVIII, 4), because heretics always drag fire behind them to burn the crops. The Lord rightly repels this man, lest under the pretext of discipleship he consume the Lord’s harvest.

The passage can also edify the reader by showing that the Lord was so poor that he had not even a hut on earth. It is as though he said: “Why do you follow me for ambitions and profits, when I am shown to be so poor that I do not even have a place upon which to recline my head?” But a deeper meaning should be understood in this man and in all who perhaps have dens of depravity in which demons nest: the Son of Man does not have in them a place to lay his head. Christ’s head is God, and God reclines only in clean minds, cleansing their hearts first through faith. But in those who dig dens of depravity for themselves, in whom birds of demons nest through the practices of vices, God is not believed to recline. [Col. 0357D]

Therefore the Lord seeks from all people followers in whom, through faith, the things belonging to charity may be fulfilled. It is clear, then, as I said, that Christ exposed this scribe as one who did not wish to follow but was pretending, and recoiled from him because he was presumptuous. Otherwise, how would he have repelled one who wished to follow, when he prevented another who wished to go from departing? [Col. 0358A]

Nevertheless, in both cases the judgments of the Redeemer are astonishing and fearsome. He justly rejected this man, whom he had not first removed inwardly from the coldness of his unbelief through the anointing of the Spirit; and he mercifully restrained the other, who wished to go, whom he had divinely chosen beforehand for life. What else, then, can we say about these matters but the words of the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. XI, 33.) “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.” Although we perceive outwardly the things that belong to human beings, the Lord looks upon the heart and sees most penetratingly what is in each person. [Col. 0358B]

Then another disciple said to him, “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.” After those three miracles, the dispenser of all things brought these two forward together for this reason: so that you might learn that neither those who are saved are saved by their own merits, nor those who perish perish except by the just judgment of God, so that no one may boast in himself, but all may flee to the physician of salvation.

When he says, “Permit me first to go,” he is mistaken, although not in his devotion, since he hastens to perform an act of piety. This ought not to have been first for him, but second. For the first tablet of the law commands that God be loved, while the second commands that one’s father be honored. An earthly father was therefore to be placed after the heavenly Father; hence he immediately says, “Follow me.” [Col. 0358C]

This is what he commands all whom he calls to life, for he came in order to offer himself as an example to everyone. “Follow me” means: follow me to sufferings, to obedience, to humility, and to the fulfillment of all that belongs to the Father. The son of faith ought not to go to the house of unbelief. Indeed, he would not have commanded him, “Follow me,” if his father had not been dead, concerning whom it is said: “Forget your father’s house” (Psal. XLIV, 11). Once the father was dead, he took pity on the man and called him to discipleship, although he was imprudent; but he immediately instructed him, knowing that the man did not reject discipleship in his heart, and that, once he had completed the pious duty owed to his father, he would follow Christ more freely.

“Let the dead,” he said, “bury their own dead.” Does he forbid the religious duty of burial, which we have received from the authority of the sacred Scriptures, by prohibiting the burial of a father’s body? I would certainly not say so, because the perfection of Christ’s discipleship is one thing, and the beginning of religious observance another. Human things must always be placed after divine things, and what is highest must be preferred to human things, because, when attention is divided among many things, it becomes weaker for what is exceptional. [Note: The text apparently requires *intentione* (“by intention/attention”) rather than *intentio*.] For this reason the Lord does not permit preachers of the Gospel to greet anyone on the way (Luc. X, 4)—not because an act of goodwill toward God displeases him, but because irrevocable execution and the intention to evangelize please him more. [Col. 0358D]

For this reason the apostles choose ministers for the service of the poor, so that they themselves would not become occupied and cease for a time from the work of preaching. We must therefore ask how the dead bury their own dead, unless it is when the impious and the dead to God bury the corpses of the deceased. It is evident that just as the flesh dies when it is abandoned by the soul, so the soul dies when it is abandoned by God. [Col. 0359A]

Hence he says: “Allow the dead to bury their own dead”—that is, allow unbelievers to bury those who had died in the flesh. It is as though he were saying plainly: “You who live by faith and are proved dead to the world have nothing to do with the dead; leave that to your companions. But you, together with the elect, follow me into life; otherwise you will be counted among the dead.”

He says this not to deny burial to the dead, but to disclose the teaching everywhere to believers; not to recall the son from his duty toward his father, but to separate him from the company of the impious, and to arrange all things mystically according to the occasion, the teaching, and the duty. [Col. 0359B]

As he went up into the boat, his disciples followed him. This is what he had ordered above, that they should cross the lake; and it corresponds to the middle of the account concerning these two men. Hence one of them said, “Permit me first”—that is, before he went with Christ across the lake. For they were still inexperienced and lukewarm, moved by affection for their parents, by which they were hindered from following Christ to sufferings and to the duty of preaching.

But the Lord orders them to put everything else after this, and to cross with him in the boat, which is his Church, amid the various waves and storms of the world, lest without him they be overwhelmed in the midst of the depths. Hence it follows: “And behold, a great storm arose on the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves.” [Col. 0359C]

A marvelous dispensation of God! The sea that subjected its swelling waves to his feet, that brought the peaks of the waves down to level ground, that made a flowing path firm like dry land so that the Lord might walk upon it with dry feet—why does it now rage so fiercely when the Lord enters the boat? Or was he, although foreknowing future events, so ignorant of present ones that he failed to avert the approaching storm and time of danger? Rather, we believe that he entered the boat and stirred up the winds for the sake of bringing about another effect. Otherwise, in such great danger, how could he alone, as we read that Jonah once did (Jon. I, 5), be so weighed down by sleep that he fell asleep while his own were caught in such peril? [Col. 0359D]

But, he says, Christ’s power governs all things providentially, so that faith may be increased through the miracle and another matter may be taught inwardly through the mystery. For the skill of a helmsman is not proved by calm serenity, but by the violence of a storm.

Therefore Christ entered the boat at the time when he would teach by this event that from the beginning of the world he acts powerfully within his Church while it is in peril. What the apostles did after they saw that the skill of human weakness in steering had failed, observing that the sea raged more fiercely and that the whirlwinds of the winds battered the waves more and more against them—this Christ’s disciples do daily while the Church is in danger.

They immediately and rightly flee to the true helmsman, the conqueror of the world, the Lord of the elements, asking him to calm the waves of affliction, remove the danger of temptation, and restore salvation to those who labor. [Col. 0360A]

This is what we sing in the Psalm: “Awake; why do you sleep, O Lord? Awake, and do not reject us forever” (Psal. XLIII, 23). This does not mean that the one who guards and governs the Church amid the crashes of the world ever sleeps; but whenever he does not provide aid to those in danger, he is said, as it were, to have fallen asleep.

Therefore, from the point at which he falls asleep, the ship—that is, the Church—and those who are in it are governed, because from that point faith is more fully trained for victory against temptations. Christ boarded this ship when he came to us incarnate, intending to cross the sea of this world. But immediately the whirlwind and storm of persecution rushed in: King Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. From then until the end of the world, a fiercer storm of demons rages against him and his own; the fury of the whole world roars, the waves of kings foam in turn, and the depths of the peoples roll about in unbelief, always preparing shipwreck for believers. [Col. 0360B]

Therefore the dragon who is in this great and spacious sea, to mock it, never ceases anywhere or at any time. Yet whenever the disciples approach Christ, they awaken him as though he were sleeping in slumber. He immediately commands the winds, rebukes the storm, restores calm to the Church, subdues the powers of the world, and establishes peace for all. Hence he was often thought to have fallen asleep while they were trying to destroy his Church: Diocletian was trying to overthrow it, Decius to extinguish it, Maximian to overwhelm it with waves, and many others to strike it with the weapons of the devil.

Then, it says, rising up, he commanded the winds and the sea. [Col. 0360C] He rose as one powerful from the sleep of death and cast down the enemies; previously he had slept while the winds blew and the sea seethed with waves. Yet although in his humanity he sleeps bodily, in his divinity he watches over all things, and, rising, commands by his majesty.

At one time, while sleeping, he disturbs the seas; when he awakens, he makes everything calm. Then, and now, he did this to reveal his majesty to his own and to train the hearts of believers in faith. For Christ sometimes sleeps in order to awaken his sleeping disciples. They are awakened when they recognize their own weakness and, enclosed amid distress, understand his majesty.

Hence they say: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” He is awakened by their prayers because he commands by majesty as God. But he immediately rebukes their fear, saying: [Col. 0360D]

“People of little faith, why are you afraid?” For he had fallen asleep precisely so that their faith might be tested. When they became afraid, they were increasingly pressed by danger. So too Peter, seeing the strong wind, became afraid, and immediately began to sink. It is therefore clear that faith without confidence and courage is everywhere weakened.

No one ought to place confidence in himself but in God, just as this very faith is truly proved to come from God. Therefore, if it is to be great and effective, it must expand through prayer in proportion to the greatness of the one from whom it comes, and it must grow through confidence in Christ’s generosity. The more it fears, the less strength it has, because fear itself comes from our weakness; but the confidence of faith, arising from the power and goodness of divine assistance, everywhere and always makes believers firm and effective. [Col. 0361A]

“This,” says the Apostle, “is our victory that conquers the world, our faith” (I Joan. V, 4). Otherwise, what are we without faith? If their faith had been perfect, I admit, they themselves could have prevailed through it against that same temptation. For this reason Christ fell asleep, so that its weakness might be demonstrated; once demonstrated, it might be nourished by the miracle, and the Teacher might show in a small matter what he himself, governing his Church, does at all times amid all the dangers of the world.

I have read that a certain teacher said that the sea, leaping for joy at the Creator’s arrival, could scarcely contain itself, and that the event was therefore not a storm caused by winds but a movement of gladness. This is a pious interpretation, although it does not agree with the understanding of the reading. For the winds by which the sea is often disturbed are restrained by the Lord’s command, so that this may show that all things yield to him and feel him giving orders. [Col. 0361B]

But I believe rather that he commanded by a word that fury of the winds [Note: After “winds,” supply “fury,” so that the sense is: “he commanded that fury of the winds by a word.”], concerning which the Church says in the Song: “Rise up, north wind, and come, south wind” (Cant. IV, 16). For that same wind—he who established his seat in the north—always signifies the coldness of unbelief, which it stirs up against the Church of Christ. Hence even the disciples are endangered when their faith grows cold.

Then, as though sleeping, Christ briefly withdraws his aid, showing that it is we who have rather fallen asleep. When we are finally awakened from the sleep of doubt or fear, we must say with true faith: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.”

Then the men were amazed, saying: The disciples go up to the Lord in the boat and awaken him, humbly asking him to save them. The men, however, are said to have been amazed that the elements obeyed, not knowing that, as I said, every creature perceives the commands of its Creator. [Col. 0361C]

They were truly men and not disciples, since they thought that insensible things could not perceive at God’s command, just as the people of the world are amazed that, at Christ’s command and will, he suddenly converted the world in this way. Nevertheless, we believe that those who were amazed were sailors, or at least people from the crowd who had boarded the boat, not the apostles. Although the apostles may have been overcome by fear and returned to the amazement of uncertainty because of the miracle, they had already seen many other signs and wonders. Moreover, nowhere do we find the Lord’s disciples called anything other than by an honorable title; they are always called apostles, disciples, or something similar.

The men were therefore amazed and said: [Col. 0361D]

“What sort of man is this, that even the sea and the winds obey him?” These words are not spoken in the manner of a questioner, but as an assertion. “What sort of man is this?” means: How great, how strong, how powerful, how mighty must he be, when even insensible elements obey him—elements that possess neither hearing, speech, nor any kind of sensation? Yet in the very substance in which they exist, they are moved by his nod and serve the command of the one who orders them.

We do not, however, thereby deny that at times he moves the creature of the world through angels. Rather, we truthfully assert that all things yield not merely to his commands but to his will, and that the nature of things obeys him who commands. [Col. 0362A]

It is therefore clear from this miracle, as from all the others, that the one and same Christ is one person: he himself is the one who commands, and he himself is the one who sleeps. Insofar as he sleeps, he is man; insofar as he commands, he is God. From both aspects, the one and same person is everywhere proclaimed—not as a certain man has recently invented, but as the one person of the Son of God, who is also proclaimed in accordance with Catholic faith as the Son of Man.

When he had come across the lake into the region of the Gerasenes, two men possessed by demons came out to meet him from the tombs. They were exceedingly fierce, and so forth. Christ had come for the sake of human salvation. Therefore he walked—not to see places, but to find those who could neither seek nor find him. For this reason he wished to cross the lake, so that he might also draw to himself these men, whom he knew to be full of demons there. [Col. 0362B]

They immediately came out of the tombs to meet him, exceedingly fierce, so that no one could pass along that road. Before he crossed, he foresaw what evil existed in those places and determined not only to help the afflicted and wretched, but also to help those who were suffering from their madness. [Note: Before *qui* (“who”), understand *illis* (“to those people”).] For the devil always increases his malice. He persecutes not only those whom he possesses, but also unsuspecting and defenseless travelers who are passing through this world toward the homeland by the road that is Christ, so that he may deceive them.

Therefore, when we see such fierce people opposing us, let us not hate the people themselves, but attribute their fierceness to those who act through them, so that no one may pass unharmed along the road, but that they may all either be touched by his bites or torn apart by his hands. Hence also comes such great pressure upon the churches and persecution by those nearby. [Col. 0362C]

Where do such people come from? From tombs, certainly, because their mouth is an open grave, where they bury those whom they have killed with the bites of their words. Or else they themselves are whitewashed tombs, full of the bones of the dead; unless they came out from these, they would never meet the Redeemer. This does not mean that they had already been stripped of the demons’ power, but that they were to be stripped of it—like that prodigal son who admits that he is not yet worthy to be called a son.

Therefore, reader, consider the demons’ violence, their fury, and their rage against the human race: they cannot bear to see human beings die, yet they eagerly seek to bury the living and consign themselves to tombs so that they may reduce human beings to tombs. A fitting condition for both kinds: those who do not wish to preside over heaven are fed on corpses and fattened on decay; they delight in stench, since their entire pleasure lies in serving vices. [Col. 0362D]

But it is a very fearful example that they are said to be so fierce that no one could pass along that road. They had closed the road and denied passage to those coming to God. Therefore no one should think that it is possible to reach God without Christ. Hence Christ himself became the road for us, because, as the evangelist pointedly says, no one had previously been able to pass along that road.

It was that road, not this one which is Christ, because no demonic power can prevent those who come to the road by the road and to God through God. But one cannot reach God except through God. [Col. 0363A]

It is therefore clear that these men met Christ in accordance with their own wishes, but were brought before him like robbers before a judge—drawn there unwillingly together with the spoils of their fraud. The order of things was wonderfully reversed. Previously, while the devil was robbing, an innocent human being was tormented; now the human being runs to the one who is our refuge, while the devil incurs the penalty for his fraud.

Otherwise, if they had not been bound and dragged there unwillingly, they would not have come before the light, nor would these men have run to worship. Perhaps, then, before Christ crossed the lake, they had stirred up the winds against him by permission and agitated the waves so that the judge would not come to them. When, having crossed the boundary of the wavering world by the vessel of the cross, Christ reached what were, as it were, the shores of our salvation, he flooded the region of blindness with the radiance of his light. [Col. 0363B]

Thus two men, as though from two peoples, immediately rise through faith from the tombs in which they had long been tormented by various mockeries of robbers. But as soon as the enemies perceive Christ’s power, they cry out:

“What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” This confession is not an expression of their will, but an exaction of necessity, which sometimes compels the unwilling, through the torments of punishment, to confess what they do not wish to confess. It is like fugitive slaves who, after a long time, see their master and ask for nothing except relief from blows, while their conscience accuses them.

So the demons, seeing from their conjecture that the Lord was suddenly moving about on earth, believed that he had already come to judge them. For the Savior’s presence is torment for demons, just as the tribunal of a judge is torment for the guilty. Hence they cry out: “What have we to do with you, Son of God?” It is as though they were saying plainly: “What has the author of life to do with the dead, the inhabitant of heaven with tombs, the judge with the accused? We were expelled from the paradises of heaven; although we are worthy of such things, what have we to do with you, especially since you do not deserve such an injury?” [Col. 0363C]

Their confession is therefore false in every respect, denying that the Creator has anything to do with the creature, or the Savior with the lost [Note: Here *aliquid* (“something”) appears required in place of the printed negative *nihil* (“nothing”), because of the negative force of *denegans* (“denying”)], although there is much between us and him: we should remain devoted to the one from whom we come—he, so that he may rule and save those whom he created; we, so that, bound to him by the affection of charity, we may serve him faithfully and devotedly.

If they had deserved an answer, it might at least have been said to them: “Give back the human beings whom you have invaded, and restore to their Creator those whom you have taken captive. But if you have nothing to do with me, I know that I have much to do with you, because you too are mine and cannot escape my hand. But you have nothing to do with those whom I created in my image and whom you deceived by your frauds.” [Col. 0363D]

They suspect doubtfully that he is the Son of God. For inwardly they had sensed the power of his majesty, which wretched heretics refuse to acknowledge. These demons proclaim him Son of God, while Arius preaches him merely as the son of man. “You have come,” they say, “before the time to torment us,” and they prescribe the time as though they knew when the judgment would be. They presume to know more than they know, caring nothing for falsehood.

Thus they confess him as Son of God, cry out that the judge has come, and speak of the time as though they had foreknown it before the time—although that time is not only unknown to them, but also to any of the saints, since the Father has placed it in his own power. But to the wicked, even a long period of patience always seems short, just as vengeance seems slow to the good. Hence they speak in this way not because they know when it must occur, but because, although it seems to them exceedingly long, it appears short since a more intense torment is imminent; and when the time of their desires has passed, it becomes as though it had never existed. [Col. 0364A]

There was a herd of many pigs feeding not far from them. Mystically, the herd of pigs was not far from them because the unclean are always near them, and the demons, wherever they are driven out, return to them because of their uncleanness. These are the pigs before whose feet the Lord earlier forbade that pearls be thrown (Matth. VII, 6), and whose food the younger son desired to use to fill his belly, while no one gave him any. [Col. 0364B]

This herd signifies all the unclean, whom demons always possess, wherever they are driven out from. Hence, although doubtfully, they say: “If you drive us out, send us into the pigs,” because they certainly know how to change the stench and uncleanness without abandoning them. There is no doubt that they themselves had been the pigs from which they were being expelled; therefore they seek to enter pigs again.

To them the Lord says, “Go.” Hence we must trust that if they cannot harm pigs, they can harm human beings much less, unless human beings first submit themselves to their wicked persuasions. They are permitted to possess people only when, having become strangers to God through uncleanness, those people become worthy of such an inhabitant. [Col. 0364C]

It is certainly fitting that those who fall from heaven seek only mud and pursue pigs’ wallows. From this we should note how much better a human being is than an animal, since for the sake of only two human beings a herd of pigs was exposed to the demons and suffocated. Nor, as Manichaeus dreams, is the soul of all animals equal, since for the sake of these men, whose souls were immortal, so many animal souls were given over together with death to perish.

Otherwise, if their condition were equal, it would be absurd for him to destroy so many souls for their sake from his own kingdom—or rather, as they themselves say, from his own substance. Compared with a few elect people, therefore, the multiplied number of animals is insignificant; indeed, so is the multitude of human beings who perish. Hence many are handed over for the sake of the few, because all the chaff is handed over to the fire for burning once the wheat has been nourished. [Col. 0364D]

Let wicked Christians therefore beware of imitating this confession and malice of the evil devil. They prove themselves to be partly his own when they believe, confess verbally, and tremble—not so that they may be corrected and seek salvation, but, hardened, so that they may advance toward worse things. For this reason they always fear the judge’s arrival. But let the righteous rejoice, since they humbly implore the arrival of the kingdom and not only do not fear punishments, but also desire the kingdom.

“Behold,” he says, “the whole herd rushed headlong with a violent movement into the sea and died in the waters.” The devil seeks everyone for this purpose: to plunge them down headlong, extinguish them as they rush violently into the waters of wicked pollution, and suffocate them through the teaching of evil persuasion. [Col. 0365A]

It must not be overlooked that the Savior did not permit them to enter the pigs because of their requests, but for the sake of the salvation of those to whom they belonged, so that the herdsmen, having seen the miracle, might report all these things to them, as they did. Hence it follows:

And behold, the whole city came out to meet Jesus. They came out, moved by faith and devoted religious feeling, although they were still immature and fearful. When they saw this, they asked him to depart from their territory. It is astonishing if they did not already sense something in his appearance that they could not bear, since they had earlier come out to him with such devotion. Hence it must be understood that they were not speaking from unbelief, but from astonishment and reverence for his majesty. Thus Peter too, when he saw the miracle of the fish, immediately prayed: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8). So also these people, considering themselves and not yet imbued with faith, were afraid before such great divinity and could not endure the brilliance of so great a light. Nor is it surprising if eyes that had long been unaccustomed to light sometimes, dazzled by such splendor, become unable to see.

**(CHAP. IX.)** And when he had climbed into the boat, he crossed over and came to his own city. It is not surprising that Christ is found everywhere either climbing into a boat or sometimes making use of perishable aids, although he can do all things. For he came especially to take upon himself our weaknesses and to bestow his virtues upon us. Therefore, as we have already said above, it was fitting that he should endure our weaknesses. Otherwise, if he had remained in his own powers, he would have had nothing in common with human beings; and unless he had fulfilled the order of the flesh, his assumption of flesh in him would have been pointless. Thus, when he makes use of these things, he is to be believed true man; and when he walks upon the sea on foot without a vessel, he is to be understood as the one and the same God.

Why did he climb into a boat to cross the strait and come to his homeland? We have already said above that he climbed into the boat of his Church, which he himself guides amid the waves of the world, so that he may eventually bring all who sail in it with him as citizens to the heavenly homeland—those whom he has willed to be fellow citizens of his homeland or city. For it was not he who needed the boat, but the boat that needed Christ; without him it cannot reach the harbor without shipwreck amid the waves of this world. In earthly matters, moreover, from the place where he had a homeland, there too he needed a boat.

When he had arrived there, they brought him a paralytic lying on a bed. When Jesus saw the faith of those who were bringing him, he said to the paralytic—here the holy Gospel proclaims great teaching and the great power of faith, which powerfully comes to the aid not only of the one who possesses it but also of others, even if they lack faith themselves. I say “powerfully,” because complete and true faith enjoys this privilege through the great gift of God.

“Jesus,” it says, “seeing their faith.” It must be asked with what eyes faith in another can be seen, since no one can see it even in himself except with spiritual eyes. Yet because no one but God looks into the hearts of individuals, he demonstrates himself to be God by seeing and weighing their faith. From this passage the authority of the whole Church is undoubtedly confirmed: infants, still ignorant of the faith, are brought to be baptized on the faith of another and are dipped in another’s faith, so that they may be reborn from it, just as this man is saved through the faith of others. Therefore, the faith of those who bring them must first be examined, so that it may be proved; afterward the infant must be consecrated through the sacrament of faith. Otherwise, do you not think that Christ first examines the faith of the one who brings the child? And if that person is an unbeliever, how will he be able to help another? Therefore, those who bring children must be chosen from among the faithful, and only then is the order of salvation to be followed.

“Take courage, son,” he says; “your sins are forgiven you.” It is clear from this passage that many illnesses arise on account of sins; therefore, the fountain and origin of the illness is first healed by the true physician. And remember that he calls “son” one who is still burdened by unbelief. Yet he is rightly called son, since the confidence of faith is first restored in him, without which everyone is shown to be dead. Thus, by saying “Take courage,” he raises him again to life. By calling him “son,” he pours into him love and an affection of compassion. Without these two, every soul—not merely a paralytic one, but a dead one—lies prostrate. For by these sins are forgiven, because Christ cleanses the hearts of believers through faith, and love covers a multitude of sins.

Thus, what he approves in those who bring the man, he first bestows upon the sick man. Then, because faith belongs to souls, the soul of the one being brought is immediately healed through the faith of those who bring him. Let paralytics hear this—let those dissolved by their crimes hear it—that another’s faith is of great value on behalf of another. Therefore, if they still desire to rise, let them seek faithful intercessors. Where shall I find such people, so that, brought before Jesus through their faith, I may first deserve forgiveness of sins and then obtain the healing of salvation from the paralytic condition of perverse weakness?

The wretched and unhappy soul has its own paralysis: laid low by this disease of perversity, it lies helpless on the bed of vices. Of this bed David says: “Every night I will wash my bed; with my tears I will water my couch” (Psalm 6:6). On this bed the miserable man lay, and therefore he could neither rise nor come before Jesus. But blessed is the one who finds people to bring him!

So you too, burdened soul, bound by crimes, if you distrust the forgiveness of sins, bring in intercessors; bring in the Church; bring presbyters over you—elders, that is—so that Jesus, seeing their faith, may mercifully forgive you what he might perhaps refuse you. He must therefore have patrons, since he cannot yet come by himself. But no one comes to Christ except through faith. This faith, if strengthened by virtues, can immediately bring salvation.

Hence another Evangelist reports that he was carried by four (Mark 2:3). We know that there are four general virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. By these the soul is carried and brought before the Savior, provided that they remain grounded in faith. Whatever is not from faith is sin. Therefore, it is said that he saw not those who had brought him, but their faith (Col. 0367A), because the faith of the soul is always examined first, and afterward the works of faith are required.

And behold, some of the scribes said within themselves: “This man blasphemes.” This utterance was a thought of the heart, through which the envy of the Pharisees shows us that he is God who says, “Your sins are forgiven,” while they slander him—as Mark says—on the ground that no one but God can forgive sins (Mark 2:7). Indeed, their own testimony proves him to be God, although, while slandering him, they affirm the work of divinity and deny the person. They confess God in words, yet do not abandon their unbelief. Unbelief can confess in words; it cannot believe. But the physician of souls always brings remedies of salvation.

“Why,” he says, “do you think evil in your hearts?” (Col. 0367B). This is a word of the heart.
