Nevertheless, it must be asked how they thought evil, since it is true that no one can forgive sins except God alone. It is certain that this is what they thought. But they thought wrongly in directing that thought toward convicting him of blasphemy: because he was a man, they claimed that he had arrogated to himself the power belonging to God alone, refusing to believe that he was God. To this he immediately replied—not to their spoken words but to their thoughts, as God. It was as if he said: “Why do you not remember that it belongs to God alone to know the thoughts of human beings, as it is written: ‘You alone know the hearts of human beings’?” (2 Chronicles 6:30). For just as it belongs to God alone to forgive sins, so also it belongs to him alone to see the thoughts of each person.

Hence he also says: “Why do you think evil, imagining me to be merely a man? Behold, while I perceive your thoughts, you can prove that I am God, since I see them, and no one except God can do this. By what you cannot possibly deny, convict yourselves and overcome your unbelief.”

For which is easier to say: “Your sins are forgiven,” or to say: “Rise and walk”? Among human beings there is a great difference between doing and saying; with God, however, both proceed from power, so that a visible sign may be produced and the spiritual statement—“Your sins are forgiven”—may be understood to have been accomplished in truth. Otherwise, just as no one but God can cleanse the soul’s defect, namely sins, by command, so also no one but God can cleanse the defect of the flesh. From this it is clear that, contrary to Manichaeus’s delirium, the whole human being was created by one Maker. Therefore, “Your sins are forgiven” involves no less power than “Rise and walk.”

The Savior made this argument against their unbelief so that, if they evaded the issue of his thoughts, a visible miracle might occur, whose divine work they could not deny.

“Then,” he says, “so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralytic: “Rise and walk.” In saying “so that you may know,” he is speaking to the Jews; but while the sentence is still incomplete, the Evangelist inserts, “Then he said to the paralytic,” and afterward follows the Savior’s authoritative command: “Rise and walk.”

He commands three things together: “Rise, walk, and take up your bed.” It is as if he plainly said: “Rise from the deep ruin of vices, and go to the dwelling of eternal happiness from which you fell; meanwhile, take up the bed of your infirmity, until you are clothed with complete immortality.”

Wonderful was the unbelief of the Pharisees, but more wonderful still the perversity of the heretics, who do not keep silent even when overcome by the same truth [Note: [Col. 0367D] “The same” seems to be the reading that should be adopted.]. Behold, the Son of Man has the power of divinity, and therefore, as God, he forgives sins, knows thoughts, and commands those lying prostrate to rise again. He is not, as they wish, one man and another God, but one Christ, God and man.

Here, as in very many passages, he calls himself the Son of Man because the Pharisees were slandering him: since he was truly human, why did he make himself God? He proves by this work that he is God, because he possesses power in all matters belonging to divinity. Yet he does not deny that he is the true Son of Man, as Marcion and the others from the school of the heretics do.

By these deeds God forestalls the wicked designs of minds and demonstrates the power of his divinity by the testimony of his work: he strengthens the limbs of the loosened body and, at his command, restores its former health. Here resurrection is shown in its completeness, namely of soul and body. Through what became outwardly evident, what had also occurred in the soul is confirmed.

This is what Christ still does today in the Church: he alone forgives our sins, and at times he also heals what belongs to the flesh. Who does not see that the soul deprived of virtues lies upon the bed of vices? Therefore we must run continually for forgiveness. And because we are less capable, intercessors must be brought in until we rise inwardly.

As testimony to this he says to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.” His power will be the same at the resurrection, when the dead who are in the Lord will rise first.

But he says, “Take up your bed,” for two reasons: so that the true health and restored strength of virtue might be evident to all, and so that what this sign mystically represented might become clearer. The bed signifies the weakness of the flesh. It is also the bed of pain on which our soul lies afflicted and tormented by the anguish of conscience.

It is astonishing that, while sins are forgiven, the weakness of the flesh is not removed; therefore the bed on which the sick man was previously carried is carried by the man himself. There is no doubt that everyone is loosened and entangled in mortal bonds only through weakness of flesh or soul. But sins are forgiven in baptism—or certainly are always forgiven through indulgence—while the weakness that leads to sin or corruption remains.

Hence the Psalms also say: “He who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your infirmities” (Psalm 102:3). One work is shown in forgiving, another in healing. Therefore he is also commanded to take up his bed, so that everyone may understand that he must always carry his weakness with him. We do not lie in this weakness except when we succumb, because the Lord gives aid upon the bed of our pain, even though he has turned the whole human race’s bed into a condition of weakness.

Therefore, after the healing of salvation and after forgiveness of sins, one must not lie on that same bed of weakness, but must bear it courageously and guard against vices. Hence he plainly says: “Take up your bed and go to your house.”

Our house is paradise. Concerning that house, the Prophet sings joyfully: “I rejoiced in those things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Psalm 121:1). Returning to that house, we must carry the bed of our weakness, praying: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak” (Psalm 6:3). And the more fragile we are, with the Lord’s grace supporting us, the more earnestly we are commanded to lean upon Christ and go to the house. For the bed of pain produces refreshment through grace and the repose of blessedness.

Then he rose and went to his house. In a single moment the fulfillment of the command in deed is displayed before the slanderers, so that they might understand that he was the one of whom it had been said: “He himself spoke, and they were made” (Psalm 32:9). Hence it follows:

But when the crowds saw this, they were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings. What remarkable hardness of the Pharisees! When the crowds saw the man rise, some at least were afraid, although they had not yet believed so as to love; others glorified God. The Pharisees, however, were moved by even sharper envy, and therefore slandered him as a blasphemer.

It should be carefully noted that even those who were still imperfect are said to have glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings. But it must be asked whether they glorified Jesus as the God who, before their eyes, gave human beings the authority to heal by a word, or whether, in the manner of the Jews, they glorified God who gave the man Christ Jesus, together with those same apostles, such great authority to heal that they understood him to be merely human, although he possessed works of divinity.

Whichever of these you wish to assert, the meaning is clear: the power of divinity was in him. Nevertheless, because he had forgiven sins—which belongs to God alone—had detected hidden thoughts, and had given this man, as well as very many others, authority to be healed and to rise by a word before their eyes, we more rightly understand that they glorified and feared Christ as God, whom the wretched Pharisees refused to believe.

This, I say, is the power of divinity that they glorify: the power by which he has granted those who believe in him not only to be healed but also to become children of God and to arrive as quickly as possible at the house of the heavenly homeland.

[Col. 0369D] And as Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man sitting at the tax office, named Matthew, and said to him: “Follow me.” It is the custom of the saints in the divine Scriptures, whenever they speak about themselves, to speak as though about someone else. Not without reason, since although they themselves appear to speak, the Holy Spirit speaks in them; and he himself bears witness, without the false coloring of distortion, to the truths concerning them as though he were another, even though by this manner of speaking they conceal themselves out of humility.

Thus Moses often speaks, and Isaiah, and John as well, as though about another, so that the truth might be adorned by their virtues.

“He saw,” it says, “a man.” It says “a man,” not Matthew, because Matthew means “gifted” or “given.” Although he already existed in predestination, he had not yet been called to grace. Therefore he did not yet see Matthew, but only a man called Matthew by name, not yet by grace.

He saw, I say, a man of those about whom it is said: “But you shall die like human beings” (Psalm 81:7). For he had abandoned heavenly things and longed only for earthly profits. This, then, is what he saw and rescued. In Matthew he saved the man.

He therefore saw the man with the same gaze with which Nathanael is said to have been seen under the fig tree (John 1:48). He saw him, I say, with the affection of his compassion—this man at the tax office, the other beneath the fig tree, where the first Adam had covered himself with leaves—yet he saw this one farther away, in proportion as he longed for earthly things.

To emphasize the accumulation of his greed, he is therefore said to have seen him sitting. He sat like a master of robbery beside the furnace of avarice, burning with the heat of desires. He was neither standing in order to conquer nor departing in order to escape, but sitting like a prince of robbery in order to seize the prey of his servants.

For τέλος in Greek means “tribute” or “tax.” Hence one reads in Greek: τῷ τὸ τέλος, τὸ τέλος—that is, “to the one to whom tribute is due, tribute” (Romans 13:7). From this it is clear that he was seated in a tax office, where profits, tributes, or taxes were collected.

The question arises why Matthew is now said to have been called, when Luke sets forth much earlier that the twelve apostles were chosen together (Luke 6:13) and heard from the Lord the sermon on the mountain that we discussed above. It is therefore clear that this was done mystically. The others, by marking the historical sequence, indicate that they were called before this sermon on the mountain. But Matthew preferred to insert himself here, after the healing of the leper and the curing of the paralytics and the others, so that, where many weak people are healed, he too might display himself as weak and unclean, healed by the merciful Lord, as an act of humility.

At the same time, it should be noted that the Gospel does not state when or where the calling of all the apostles took place. Yet when Jesus saw this man sitting at the tax office, he said to him: “Follow me.”

What a wonderful dispensation of God! Nathanael, already coming to him, whom he praises, although he had seen him beneath the fig tree with the affection of compassion, he does not call to the office of apostle. But this man, from the deeply entrenched seat of such iniquity, he immediately and mercifully raises to the throne of apostleship. I think this was so that the Apostle’s statement might be fulfilled: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 1:20). He willed him to be not only an apostle but also an evangelist.

The craftsman knows how individual things, even when unformed, can be made useful through his work. Therefore, as he passed by, he saw the material for his own work and chose the material from which to fashion a vessel for honor, although it had previously lain in dishonor. He saw him when he approved him—not because he was already good, but because there was in him something from which the Craftsman could make him worthy of approval.

Thus all things that God made in the beginning are said to have been “seen” by him—that is, approved. Whatever he brings back to himself for the praise of his work, he first approves by his own mercy, so that he may see it; and whatever he sees, he approves for the praise of the completed work, so that he may restore it.

Hence he says: “Seeing I have seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt” (Exodus 3:9). Otherwise, if he had not first seen them, although they belonged to him, they would not have returned to him. Thus he also looked upon Peter after the cross, when Peter had wrongly withdrawn by denying him, so that, weeping, he might return.

So too he first sees with the eye of compassion all whom he calls to his grace, wherever they may have withdrawn; then, through the office of his favor, he calls them to strive to follow him.

He does not call this man so that he may remain rich, but so that, having left everything, he may love blessed poverty and follow the example of his Teacher—not only in the movement of his feet but also in the imitation of a perfect life. Therefore he sets no one else before him for imitation but himself.

It should also be noted that he saw and called him while passing by. This was so that he too, passing from this world, might hasten to eternal things. In the same way he called Peter and Andrew not while standing or sitting, but while walking beside the sea; and he called James and John while passing by, as the same Matthew testifies (Matthew 4:18, 21).

Therefore, reader, do not think that events of this kind happened by chance. Rather, all things were divinely prepared for our instruction, so that faith might shine forth from the command and teaching might shine more abundantly from every circumstance.

And rising, he followed him. He follows after rising because, while sitting, he had fallen badly. He could not stand, weighed down by the burden of perverse desire. He rose, no less in faith than in body. He rose entirely because he had fallen entirely; and he followed him in conduct, in the teaching of faith, and in the example of discipleship.

It was not, as the madness of certain people has dared to bark in accusation against us, that the apostles were foolish or stupid because, while still ignorant, they so suddenly followed someone whom they had not yet tested. Those wretched people do not know that they acted because of the authority and majesty of the one commanding, rather than from fickleness.

If such power is said to exist in amber or in a magnet stone that they draw to themselves even light objects placed opposite them, how much more did the power and virtue of divine majesty affect them inwardly and release them from the torpor of unbelief by the flame of his love? The chill of doubt could not persist before the heat of the face that burned within them. Their mind, melted by the feeling of love, immediately ran after the fountain whose sweetness had sprinkled it, unable to doubt the one by whose spirit it was already inwardly moved.

The mind ran, yet they were drawn. Of this the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song of Songs 1:4). It is as if she plainly said: “Draw me first, so that I may rise, while I still appear weak and feeble, while I am numb with sickness; draw me after you, so that I may recover. Then we shall run—not without assistance, but in the fragrance of your perfumes.”

Revived by these fragrances, they went after him without weariness. They had touched—there is no doubt—these perfumes of virtues with their nostrils, while the fragrance of life passed before them. Therefore, without any hesitation of mind, they quickly followed what inwardly exhaled fragrance, having left everything behind.

Indeed, divine power drew them—the hook of apples, so to speak, which the Prophet had seen—and therefore nothing could impede them. They were apples of the valleys; for this reason they could not resist the hook held by the divine hand.

Porphyry and Julian Augustus, ignorant of this, criticize the matter, as I have said, accusing either the ignorance of a lying historian or the stupidity of the apostles, on the ground that they followed irrationally just any man who called them, whereas such great virtues and signs had gone before—signs which they had undoubtedly seen before they believed.

As they say, he could draw those who saw him by his appearance, while the very radiance and hidden majesty of divinity shone upon his face. But those who falsely claim that he was merely a man cannot understand by what power the apostles immediately followed the fragrance of life.

[Col. 0372B] And it happened that, while he was reclining in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and reclined with Jesus. There is no doubt that, as Luke asserts (Luke 5:29), this took place in Matthew’s own house, and that Levi had prepared a banquet for him in his house, as Mark says (Mark 2:15). Thus he plainly fulfilled the Apostle’s statement: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, it is fitting that we reap your material things” (1 Corinthians 9:11).

The order was therefore proper: first he should receive faith, and then, intending to renounce everything, he should prepare a banquet of hospitality for the Lord—not by distributing extravagantly, but at his own expense.

Yet he had first offered that banquet in his heart, according to the saying: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens the door for me, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20). He prepared this banquet at the moment when, through faith, he received Christ into his heart for love.

Thus, thus, each person rightly prepares a banquet for the Lord when he first devotes himself, and then his possessions. He wished to repay Christ in kind, and therefore immediately prepared a banquet for him in his house, so that he might give his temporal goods to the one from whom he already hoped for eternal blessings.

The Lord, however, did not so frequently go to banquets for the sake of earthly food, but in order to have an opportunity to bestow grace. Hence, whenever he is said to have attended, either the things he taught are recorded or the things he did, so that through this he might invite everyone to come to the banquets of life.

Therefore he enters not only among sinners but also among those who considered themselves righteous, so that all may understand themselves to be sinners and run to the fountain of mercy. For these people who dine with the Lord in the house—those whom the Pharisees accuse as sinners—do not recline with him so as to remain sinners, but so that from then on they may adhere to his teaching together with Matthew.

Hence the following is brought against their slander:

“The healthy do not need a physician, but those who are sick,” and also: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice.” By these answers he shows why he entered the banquets of sinners: not to receive food, but to offer mercy and to aid the wretched and sick through forgiveness.

It should not be overlooked that Matthew was chosen from the tax office for this reason: so that no one might despair because of the enormity of his crimes, being drawn by the Lord’s goodness, when he sees this man raised from such base and disgraceful profits and suddenly numbered among the apostles.

Thus, immediately, in his house—which had been a workshop of cruelty, a storehouse of fraud, and a den of iniquity—a fountain of compassion sprang forth, so that many tax collectors and sinners, as though raised to life, might share a meal with the Lord. Otherwise, if they had decided to remain in their sins, they would never have dared to eat with the one who is without sin.

Indeed, the conversion of one sinner offered many an example of repentance. Matthew therefore changed his business and did not lose it: in the house to which he had previously brought many people with him for the sake of profits, he now invited them to forgiveness. He who had been a master of robbery became an example of forgiveness.

Hence he immediately brings to the school of life those whom he had previously brought to the gain of death. He received different talents, and therefore he brings back different gains. Just as the blessed fishermen now catch other fish in Christ’s net, so this man, in the business of forgiveness, invites many other sinners and tax collectors to accompany him; and all recline with Jesus in the house of mercy.

Concerning them the Evangelist Mark says: “Many sinners and tax collectors were reclining with Jesus and his disciples” (Mark 2:15). For there were many who followed him. They followed because it had been said to this man: “Follow me.”

It is therefore evident that those who had previously sought present profits through ignorance were suddenly swept toward divine things by the conversion of one person. What is judged worthless in comparison with what has been gained is easily despised. The mind is rightly called noble when it so quickly, through faith, abandons what it had considered great and is so easily captured by love of the better life.

But envy is always tormented by another’s good. Therefore the Pharisees approached the disciples, saying:

“Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” First they approach the still-weak disciples, because they do not dare openly to rebuke the Teacher. Then they display their ignorance, since they understand neither themselves nor the one whom they are trying to slander.

The wretched people do not know that no one is without sin; and if he did not associate with sinners, no one would be worthy of life. This superstition came to them from boastfulness, not from righteousness, since, as the Prophet sings: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142:2).

Therefore, when the Lord heard this, he said: “The healthy do not need a physician, but those who are sick.” He did not thereby exclude anyone healthy from the medicine of his salvation, but showed that all were guilty. If medicine is not applied to the sick, what benefit can it provide to the healthy?

For this reason he came to Matthew, because Matthew was sick: to heal the wounds of avarice and extinguish desires. Yet he does not say this as though those who were trying to rebuke him were healthy, but in order to show medicine to those who declared themselves sick.

As for those who relied upon a false righteousness of the Law, he addresses them more by reproach than by acknowledging them to be righteous. It is as if he plainly said: “I came for everyone, because I know that everyone is oppressed by disease; but to you, who boast from the height of an evil presumption, I appear unnecessary. Rather, I devote myself to the humble and to sinners.”

These words are spoken more gravely against those who falsely claimed to be righteous; salvation, however, is offered to the humble and to those who confess. Hence the blessed Apostle says: “For God has enclosed all under sin, so that he may have mercy on all” (Romans 11:32). And David says: “All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one” (Psalm 13:3).

Therefore it is better to share a meal with Christ and with tax collectors and sinners in the house of blessed Matthew than to be falsely justified without him among the Pharisees. They were fasting from the food of salvation, and therefore did not perceive themselves to be sick; filled with the boastfulness of false justification, they did not know how to hunger for mercy or seek the physician of perpetual health.

Otherwise, who was healthy in the human race, when human nature itself was sick with the sin of its first origin? Hence the kindly physician still admonishes them as though they were weak:

“Go,” he says, “and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’” By producing the testimony of the Prophet, he reproves those who considered themselves righteous for avoiding the company of sinners and tax collectors. Therefore he invites them to instruction, so that they may say what is meant by what is written: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6).

Divine compassion therefore desires mercy, so that it may have mercy on all and so that all may implore it; and so that, by showing mercy to one another in sympathy, no one may remain wretched through weakness. These people, however, disdainfully cared neither to show mercy to others nor to seek it for themselves, believing that they were justified by sacrifices, Sabbaths, and new moons.

By condemning these practices, he shows that their followers are sinners and urges them to hasten as quickly as possible to mercy. He wishes to be understood as the physician who knows the weaknesses of those who, through a superstitious presumption, were swollen with confidence in the righteousness of the Law. To those who are sick—those who, overcome by awareness of their own frailty, seek grace—he freely offers himself.

At the same time, as I have already indicated, he shows that those whom the Pharisees blamed did not remain in their former vices, but, practicing repentance, went before into the kingdom of God by coming to Christ. For this reason he was wounded for our iniquities, so that by his bruising we might be healed. He was crushed for our crimes, so that we might be justified by him freely. Hence he says:

“‘I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.’” But perhaps someone may be troubled by how he could have said, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners,” since it is evident to all that he also called many whom he found perfect according to the righteousness and ordinances of the Mosaic law to the summit of evangelical perfection. For if he called sinners alone, and not also the righteous according to the law, Nathanael would certainly not have adhered to his discipleship, since he considered him worthy of being praised so highly when he came to him. Nor would he ever have raised the others to higher things—men whom no one doubts to have been righteous according to the law—if he had not also chosen from among them, by grace, those whom he would call.

Luke perhaps explains this passage more clearly (Luke 5:32): “I have not come,” he says, “to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance”; as though he plainly indicated: The Lord indeed calls all the elect to the kingdoms of heaven, but he calls only those to repentance whom more serious offenses bind. He calls the former so that they may grasp the summit of a more perfect life; the latter so that, through repentance, they may condemn the sins of their former errors.

Yet it can also be interpreted in another way: “I have not come to call the righteous,” because he did not call those by predestination who, wishing to establish their own righteousness, were not subject to God’s righteousness. Rather, he called those who, conscious of their own weakness, were not ashamed to confess that all had sinned and lacked the grace of God, and that “we all offend in many things.” Certainly, he also called those who had previously been puffed up by a false righteousness, correcting them toward repentance. Nevertheless, it is clear that those who are saved—whether these or those—are justified for forgiveness by the grace of Christ, not by presuming upon their own righteousness or that of the law.

Therefore he is rightly said not to call the righteous: even if they possessed the righteousness of the law, they are found justified before God only by the grace of Christ. For this reason he intimates that he does not merely love sinners, but calls sinners absolutely to repentance, so that through that same repentance of baptism, about which we spoke at length above, he may receive them as already righteous into forgiveness.

By these words he proves that they were deceived by a twofold error: they considered themselves righteous, and they accused as unrighteous those who, by turning back from evil, were already drawing near to righteousness. Thus they knew neither themselves nor the others. Therefore, as Judge, he distinguishes them: he restrains these toward humility, and raises those toward the hope of forgiveness; yet to both he freely offers himself as physician.

But in the case of these, I think, it is the elder son who, standing outside, is envious and fasts wrongly; in the case of those, it is the younger son who, having returned, is glorified by the father’s gifts and is justified while dining. Blessed is such an evangelist, who by his own conversion deserved to draw a flock of publicans to Christ.

Therefore, as I had said at the beginning of this work, he shows concern for sinners throughout all his work. Perhaps his meal, at which he had brought them together with Christ, demonstrated this: by his own examples, his teaching, and the ministry of his preaching, he cared for those who were held guilty of unspeakable crimes, so that they might be nourished with Christ by the banquet of eternal life.

But the literal question arises: since, as Luke indicates (Luke 5:28), he followed Christ from the tollbooth after leaving everything, how did he later feed him at his own expense in his house, together with publicans and sinners? From this it is clear that what is vowed is abandoned more by intention than by the hand. He left everything when he recognized that he must imitate him; and therefore, in his own house, over which he presided at the tollbooth, he disdains and wisely administers perishable things—not as the master of the house, but as a faithful servant—for he was to be entrusted with eternal things.

In whose banquet, I earnestly ask, may I dine with Christ, even as the last, and may I be healed by his medicine of the evils by which I am hindered.

“Then,” he says, “the disciples of John came to him, saying: Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?” Great was the Jews’ envy and treacherous cunning by which they attacked, assailed, harassed, and sought to overthrow Christ—now flattering him with questions, now reproving him, now using deceit, now ambushes, now the open blasphemies and insults of hatred—though no one could deceive him and no one could oppose him.

This is why the Pharisees had first composed, among the disciples, an accusation against the Master concerning the banquet of publicans. Now these men, together with the same Pharisees, deceitfully accuse the disciples before the Master as though they were ignorant of fasting and devoted to gluttony. Thus they set traps of hatred before the disciples concerning their Master, and again sow among the Master the seeds of discord concerning the disciples. In both cases they acted so as to uproot his teaching and stir up plots against him.

Sometimes they send opposing parties: now Sadducees, now Herodians; now the Pharisees themselves rage against him with their bent bows and arrows. On this occasion they send John’s disciples, so that they themselves may come against the one whom their master had preached. Otherwise, what association could they have had with those same Pharisees, whose doctrine was different? Envy joined together those whom discipline kept apart: the Pharisees, so that they might set Moses before Christ; the others, so that they might place John before him. Both were equal in error, and both raged together through jealousy.

Because they had been formed by John’s discipline, the Lord therefore presents himself to them as the bridegroom, of whom their teacher had foretold: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom rejoices with joy because he stands and hears the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29). It was entirely fitting that, from the voice of their teacher, they should believe this, and not force the bridegroom’s joyful times to be mingled with the sadnesses of Pharisaic law through their plotting.

There is no doubt that those fasts were not among the commandments for the fulfillment of life, but belonged to the Pharisees’ tradition, by which the observance of the present Church was prefigured. Hence he plainly says: “The children of the bridegroom cannot fast.” This does not mean that he did not want them to fast, especially since their life consisted in nothing other than fasting. Rather, he showed us higher things: they could not fast those Pharisaic fasts that arose either from the rigor of the law or from the superstition of teachers. Nor had those fasts yet arrived which, later strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, they fulfilled more perfectly.

Meanwhile, because he seeks a bride, he sets fasting aside and leaves austerity behind. Whatever tender affection requires of the bride, he gives entirely to spiritual joys and indulges in banquets, so that toward the children whom he leads as nursing infants he may be wholly gentle, wholly lovable and sweet, wholly festive.

“For he came forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber, and rejoicing he ran from the highest summit of the heavens to its farthest summit, until he should confirm the bride with his gifts.” For this reason he sometimes presented himself at tables and took part in banquets, showing himself equally to all, until he joined the human to the divine and made a heavenly fellowship out of earthly things.

There is no doubt that in the calling of blessed Matthew, although he was a Hebrew, because he had transferred himself—against the ordinance of the law—to serve the Romans’ profits, the calling of the Gentiles is signified. Therefore many publicans and sinners immediately come with him, celebrating a banquet—not an ordinary one, but a great one, as Luke says (Luke 5:29). This is plainly shown mystically to be the banquet at which the bridegroom and the bride, redeemed with heavenly gifts, are joined in covenant.

And, to speak more profoundly, the same bridegroom is that fattened calf which is slaughtered according to the parable in another passage, from which this banquet is divinely prepared. Yet it is prepared by those who receive Christ by faith with the affection of love in their hearts. There are publicans and sinners; there is Rahab the prostitute; there are Tyre and the people of Ethiopia, whom the same evangelist called to Christ’s grace.

Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “From beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, there will come my suppliants” (Zephaniah 3:10). Therefore Levi is not without reason said to have prepared a great banquet, since this Gentile people offered all these things to Christ in its house—that is, in the Church.

For this reason it was said in the person of the Lord: “I will remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me” (Psalm 86:4). These people already knew Christ, and therefore the Lord remembered them. He had called them not only to faith, but also, admitting them to the banquet with himself, had clothed them in the wedding garment.

Therefore the children of the bridegroom and the bride cannot fast as long as the bridegroom is with them. They are called children because, reborn from the faith of Christ and the Church, they were still being nourished by their mother’s teachings. All are indeed children of the bridegroom and the bride, although the one bride is formed from all, so that the children, gathered together in the unity of faith—which is also the bride—may be joined by the bond of charity. Thus it is not without reason that the bride ate in the same house with the bridegroom.

They are called the bridegroom’s children, however, in order to indicate the tenderness of their faith and the beginning of their discipleship; for this reason nothing burdensome ought to be imposed upon them.

“But,” he says, “the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.” From this passage it is evident that all the days during which Christ was in the flesh were, as it were, days of the banquet and wedding of the bridegroom and the bride. Those who had already been created as apostles through the spiritual marriage could not mourn so long as they rejoiced that the bridegroom was with the bride in the bridal chamber.

“But,” he says, “the days will come when the wedding has passed, and the time of the passion, resurrection, or ascension has arrived; then they will fast”—that is, then, when the bridegroom will be taken away from them. From this passage they multiplied those fasts which were to be observed immediately after the forty days of the Passion, until the Holy Spirit came and consecrated those days of Pentecost as festive.

On this occasion, moreover, the old women Prisca and Maximilla taught that a forty-day fast should be undertaken after Pentecost, as though, once the bridegroom had been taken away, the bridegroom’s children ought immediately to fast. But the Church of Christ postponed this until the Passion and resurrection, so that souls might be better prepared for the Paschal mystery by fasting from spiritual nourishment.

Nevertheless, the apostles did not begin to weep only after Christ’s ascension, but already during his Passion. After the ascension had been completed, during the days in which they awaited the coming of the Holy Spirit, they were undoubtedly both weeping and abstaining, and continued to do so thereafter.

But how could the Lord prohibit the disciples from fasting, when he himself also fasted? Moreover, he tells them that that most wicked kind of demon could be overcome only by fasts and prayers. If he wishes them to conquer demons, how could they not have fasted while he was with them? Or how were they not fasting when the whole crowd that remained with him had nothing to eat, especially since among them no more than five loaves—or, elsewhere, seven—were found? Do you suppose that, while all those people were fasting, Christ and the apostles alone were dining? Far be it from us to be so foolish.

Rather, what is truer is that the bridegroom’s children cannot mystically mourn or fast while the bridegroom is with them, because inwardly they rejoice with spiritual joy and feast upon the banquets of eternal blessedness. John rejoiced with this joy because of the bridegroom’s voice—not because he was the bridegroom, but because he was his friend.

This is why he says that the bridegroom’s children cannot fast, although those who had not yet entered the wedding feast did fast. For all those who do not know the bread of life fast. Christ, however, is both bridegroom and bread, and he is the banquet of delights. Those who had not yet been renewed and could not take part in the wedding feast were fasting from him.

From this the following passage proceeds:

“No one,” he says, “puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, lest a greater tear be made; nor do they put new wine into old wineskins,” and so forth.

Thus he calls the furnishings of the ancient law old: a garment worn down by Jewish zeal, corrupted in its understanding, torn by sects, and made obsolete by its practices. He calls the patch of unshrunk cloth the garment of the Gospel. For just as the body is covered by a garment, so the soul is covered by teachings.

But one garment is old and another is new. The old suffers corruption, consumed by age; if an unshrunk patch is sewn onto it, the tear becomes worse, since both what had been promised for the sake of signification is corrupted, and what had been promised for the salvation of all is judged unable to suffice by itself.

The Ebionites, plainly failing to understand this, mixed the new with the old, thinking that the Gospel of Christ could not suffice without the law of Moses. The law, indeed, was of great benefit by itself up to the time of grace, although it had been worn away by the traditions of the Pharisees. But when grace began, the garment of the Gospel, woven from the fleece of the Lamb, ought not to have been sewn onto it.

Rather, when the figures had ceased and had been emptied by age, the things belonging to the conduct of life that were contained in that same law ought to have passed into newness. Hence John, speaking of love, says: “Little children, I give you a new commandment” (1 John 2:8), “the commandment that you heard from the beginning.” For all those things belonged not to oldness but to newness.

But Sabbaths, New Moons, the rites of fasting, and the other institutions intended to signify life had passed away like an old garment, already consumed, as shadows vanished when the light became clear. Therefore the patch of the new teaching was not to be sewn onto these things.

Nevertheless, both teachings are rightly called a patch or garment. Clothed in them, the soul will not fear the cold of unbelief, nor be disfigured by nakedness. For this is that richly woven garment, adorned with marvelous variety, which Wisdom perfected for us in Solomon.

Some also say, concerning philosophy under the appearance of a woman, that it possessed garments made with delicate craftsmanship and of indissoluble material, which she herself had woven with her own hands. Their appearance was almost like smoky images, covered by a certain darkness of neglected antiquity. At the lower ends there was the Greek letter Π, signifying the practical life; at the upper ends the letter Θ was read, intending to express the theoretical life.

By this she plainly indicates that the clothing of souls is the teaching of wisdom, although human traditions have defiled it. When these traditions are removed like shadows, the truth of the light becomes evident. It cannot, however, be admitted to an old garment, lest a worse blindness result if the light is obscured in darkness—or rather, lest their darkness be more rightly made bright in the light.

Nevertheless, when you hear of a patch of unshrunk cloth, do not understand it as a part of a tear, but as the beginning of a fabric. For then the royal garment’s cloth was first being woven from Christ’s fleece—the fleece given by the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world.

At that time the beginning of the Gospel was being woven; therefore it is rightly called a patch, that is, a joining. This does not mean that it ought to be joined to the old things, but that it ought to be extended and spread over the hearts of believers to the end, so that there may be one seamless, undivided garment for all, woven from above, embracing everyone and leaving no one naked except those who have deprived themselves of such ornaments.

He doubles the example, however, speaking of garments and of old and new wineskins. By the old wineskins we must understand the scribes and Pharisees, or anyone outside Christ’s grace who has not yet been washed by the water of baptism. Since they have not yet put off the old person, they cannot endure the heat of Christ’s teaching.

The new garment’s patch and the new wine signify the commandments of the Gospel, which the Jews cannot endure, lest a greater tear be made. The Galatians likewise wished to do something of this sort when they mixed the commandments of the law with the Gospel. But the Apostle says to them: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you so that you do not obey the truth?” (Galatians 3:1).

The evangelical word and the teaching of the Holy Spirit therefore had to be poured into the apostles rather than into the scribes and Pharisees, or into John’s disciples who were envious of Christ. Corrupted by the traditions of their ancestors, they could not preserve the purity of Christ’s commandments.

One thing is the virginal purity of a soul polluted by no contagion of former vice; another is the obscene lustfulness of one that has lain under the filth of many things. Some, however, have wished to transfer this interpretation to the imperfection of the disciples, on the grounds that they were still carnal and weak and could not bear more severe commandments.

But if this is so, they too were still in the old condition—which is absurd to understand, since they had already been separated from the yoke of the law and were called the bridegroom’s children.

It is better, therefore, to understand these words as spoken against those who were asking: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?” They seem to have wished Christ to release them from the yoke of fasts and the burden of the law.

For this reason they immediately hear that they cannot keep the commandments of the Gospel while they remain in the old condition, lest a worse tear be made in them. Their teaching, worn down by age, could not bear the newness of the commandments.

They themselves, as wineskins, could not contain the wine of the wedding feast—the wine about which the apostles spoke while intoxicated in various tongues. Concerning this wine the master of the feast is said to have told the bridegroom: “You have kept the good wine until now” (John 2:10).

The Pharisees, corrupted by age, were not yet able to bear this wine. The new wineskins—that is, the apostles and their imitators—were filled with it. For just as leather skins are first cleansed of every impurity and internally rubbed with fragrant spices, so, once prepared by the divine winepresses, they were judged suitable for virtues and restored by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

David, foreseeing that they would come, lamented about himself, saying: “My eyes have failed at your word, saying: When will you comfort me? For I have become like a wineskin in the frost” (Psalm 118:82). Without doubt, the frost of unbelief had frozen these men; therefore, consumed by age, they could neither hold the new wine of evangelical preaching nor keep the commandments.

The steward of salvation, foreseeing this well, fills the new wineskins with the intoxication of the Spirit from the press of the cross, but leaves the old ones empty, lest a worse tear be made.

And behold, one ruler approached and worshiped him, saying: “My daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.” Mark and Luke, however, do not say that she was dead, but that she was at the point of death, or about to die shortly, that is, near death (Mark 5:25; Luke 8:42).

This evangelist therefore declared that she was dead because the father had despaired of finding her alive. For this reason the two accounts say different things while agreeing in substance: he had asked both that he heal her if she were about to die and that he raise her if she were already dead.

Hence the father, desperate about his daughter’s life, asks for help with such mournful lamentation. He was not, as I think, an unbeliever, but had been instructed by the law. Although he knew that God had created all things by a word in the beginning, he had read that the human being had been formed by God’s hand. Therefore he believed that by that same hand his daughter, by which she had been created, could be recreated and brought back from death to life.

Thus he plainly asks: “But come, lay your hand upon her.” You who earlier placed your hand willingly in order to create, may you now, entreated, place it again in order to restore. This is what the Prophet confesses when he sings: “You formed me and placed your hand upon me” (Psalm 138:5). He who placed his hand when he formed her from nothing withdrew it in order to place it again and reform her from destruction.

According to the allegorical sense, what he says also has great force: “But come, lay your hand upon her.” Without doubt, each detail is filled with mysteries, and everything is prepared by the Lord with great foreknowledge.

Nor is it without mystery that, in the sixth place among the signs, he frees people possessed by demons. The one whom he had formed from the earth with his hands on the sixth day, by the same number of healings—according to this evangelist—he recalls to himself, frees from the dominion of the deceiver, and reforms according to the image of the first creation.

Thus, in the seventh place, he heals the paralytic through the faith of those who bring him, forgives his sins, and commands him to return home. Through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit he heals every wound of sins and grants the grace of returning to the homeland.

Therefore the divine word, with keen insight, now presents the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue in the eighth sign of healing. It does not wish to exclude her from the mystery of true circumcision. But a woman suffering from a flow of blood enters between them and is healed in the eighth place.

By this number the Synagogue is divinely removed, so that at least it may come to the new, according to what is sung in the Psalms: “Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to God” (Psalm 67:32); and: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25).

The ruler who approaches to plead for his daughter typologically designates, in a special way, the people of the patriarchs. Pleading tirelessly for the Synagogue, after the Church’s entrance and healing from the flow of unbelief and from the menstruation of idols, he scarcely obtained health for the daughter.

This is also why he pleads: “Come and lay your hand upon her.” He asks him to come who fills all things everywhere; that is, he asks that visible flesh appear. By the laying on of his hand the Synagogue is healed and raised to life.

Indeed, with the Church she also sings in the prophetic voice: “The right hand of the Lord has acted with power; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” (Psalm 117:16). As though she plainly said: The right hand of the Lord restored what it had created; therefore I shall not die, but live.

The people of the patriarchs had foreseen such things, and therefore this man is rightly called Jairus by another evangelist. Jairus is interpreted as “illuminating” or “illuminated.” He was illuminated by the law and the prophets through the grace of the Holy Spirit; and therefore he is rightly called “illuminating,” from the fact that he had already been illuminated.

So too the apostles were called the light of the world—not substantially, but through participation in the true light.

This ruler of the synagogue humbly descended from the stronghold of Pharisaic tradition, came devotedly, and worshiped in supplication. Some, however, think that he came still from unbelief, because he asked Christ to come to his daughter and lay his hand upon her, as though he had not yet understood, like that royal official in the Gospel, that Christ was present everywhere.

But he who knows all things immediately obeys him. By healing the daughter while absent, he nevertheless teaches that he is present everywhere. Yet if this ruler had held such a thought in his heart, the one who examines the hearts of all would have corrected it.

Perhaps, then, the woman suffering from the flow of blood is brought into the middle of the path so that the ruler might learn that Christ is not to be carried about from place to place, nor wearied by travel, nor sought only in bodily presence, but that he must be believed to be God, powerful everywhere, wholly everywhere, and always everywhere.

Meanwhile, perhaps because he knew what would happen, he hastens to go with the ruler so that he may first mercifully heal this woman on the way, and thereby remove the knot of uncertainty concerning that healing.

For the ruler says: “My daughter has just died,” which means: Her spirit is still on the way; she is still at the point of death; she is still at home. Tartarus has not yet seized her. Therefore, if you can retain her, hurry.

In this, the Jews’ doubt and dullness are signified. Hence the Gentiles, adopting their customary course—that is, having received faith—immediately come into the middle, so that they may be healed before the Synagogue.

Nevertheless, although Christ confesses that he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, because of their hardness of heart he mercifully heals the Church from the Gentiles first, from the menstruation of idols. Thus, while he is making his way toward one matter, another takes the opportunity to seize healing by faith.

For this reason we read: “They provoked me with that which was not God, and I will provoke them with that which is not a people; and I will anger them with a foolish nation” (Deuteronomy 32:21).

The ruler of the synagogue, instructed by the law and the prophets, did not yet know that Christ God was perhaps present everywhere, nor did he regard Christ as God; whereas the woman, rightly suffering from the menstrual flow, is healed. “If I touch,” she says, “only the fringe of his garment, I shall be saved.”

Both senses can therefore be applied to the Jewish people. Through those who believed Christ to be God, Jairus is called “illuminating” or “illuminated”; through those who doubted and thought him merely human, the Church is said to have entered into faith, as the Apostle commends. For he says: “Their unbelief is the salvation of the Gentiles. But when their fullness has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25).

And behold, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years approached from behind and touched the fringe of his garment.

According to Luke’s Gospel, the ruler’s daughter is also said to have died at the age of twelve (Luke 8:42). For, mystically speaking, this woman—the Church gathered from the Gentiles—began to be sick and to suffer a flow of impurities from the time when the Jewish people began to believe and was then divinely instructed through the institutions of the law.

Now vices are better displayed by comparison with virtues. But when the woman, having reached maturity, is converted from the idolatrous rites of her menstrual impurity—during which, according to the evangelist, she had spent all her patrimony—and is healed by coming to Christ, the other immediately dies from the sickness of her faithlessness.

For this reason both are rightly said to be twelve years old. Even the laws of the world commonly restrain people by their commands from the twelfth year of age, and they themselves are sometimes subject to the reward of the law for good deeds or to punishment for evil ones.

Thus, according to the allegorical senses of Scripture, the woman is rightly healed by the Lord because, having reached mature life, she received understanding, and her former actions are reckoned as ignorance.

The other, likewise, although by law she had reached maturity and ought to have received Christ, promised through the law, because she refused to believe, is immediately announced as dead by the prophets and patriarchs.

It should also be noted that the woman suffering from the flow does not approach God in a house or in a city—since according to the law she was excluded from human society—but on the road, while the Lord is walking. Thus, while he proceeds toward one matter, he shows another, namely the Church, healed on the way.

The divine word indicates this elsewhere, when certain people invited to the wedding refused to come. “Go out,” it says, “to the crossroads, and compel all whom you find, good and bad, to enter” (Matthew 22:9). For the Church is called from the roads of this world.

She is therefore prepared while he is going to another, so that she may meet him first on the way.

For she was saying within herself: “If I touch only the fringe of his garment, I shall be saved.” Wonderful dispensation! Behold, between God and the woman a secret salvation is taking place, yet it is a great exchange.

The ruler of the synagogue approaches devoutly, prostrates himself completely on the ground in worship, explains the matter, reveals his grief, moves compassion, obtains a promise that Christ will hurry, and asks him to come to the healing.

But the Lord, who was not sought by the woman, encounters her as he passes by and, at least, presents himself to her, so that through this general work of mercy he might give a clearer forewarning.

“She approached,” he says, “from behind.” She approached from behind because she believed after the Savior’s ascension.

According to the historical sense, although the magnitude of her grief compelled her to approach Christ, the foulness of her wound prohibited her. Yet, with trembling judgment born of faith, she preferred to be judged on the basis of confidence rather than to perish from so foul a wound.

Let the wicked and unclean hear this: let them break through their harmful shame, discover the counsel of faith, and find the medicine of salvation.

She knew that Christ was God and man. Otherwise, if she did not believe him to be God, how could she seek salvation outside the human being, in his fringe? If he were not God, how could he perceive outside himself what had happened in the fringe?

It is therefore established that she believed God to be in the human being, and that God existed beyond the human being. For this reason she devoutly touched his fringe, the one whom the faith of the Church confesses to be everywhere.

He is wholly everywhere, and wholly in the human being Christ Jesus, since he grants nothing outside himself. For he says:

“I perceive power has gone forth from me.”

Power went forth from him because in him was the fullness of divinity, and in the divinity omnipotent power prevailed. Divinity, however, was everywhere.

Yet it was one way in the human being Christ and another in the fringe of the garment. In the human being Christ, it was so that God might be man, because the Word became flesh; in the fringe, as also in the whole world, it was not that God should rightly be believed to be the world or the fringe, but because, outside and within, he powerfully holds and governs all things.

Thus the woman is prepared, in whose type the universal Church is portrayed under a figure; therefore such great things are divinely proclaimed through her.

“If I touch,” she says, “only the fringe of his garment, I shall be saved.” And what extraordinary confidence! For in the law, if anyone touched a menstruating woman, or one flowing with blood, or anything that she had touched, those things were unclean. But she says: “If I touch only the fringe of his garment, I shall be saved.”

It is therefore clear that she believed him to be God, who is contaminated by no impurity, but rather wipes away wounds, cleanses uncleanness, and empties out sicknesses.

Could he not have granted this to her without her touch, especially since she did not ask to be touched by him, but herself dared, in faith, secretly to touch the tassel of his garment? From this it is clear that divine mysteries and realities are proclaimed everywhere in the Gospel. For this reason she is said to have touched it, so that the faith by which Christ is touched by his own might be revealed with the greatest clarity.

As far as the historical sense is concerned, because she judged herself unworthy, she is said to have approached from behind—not because she was unaware that Christ saw everything, especially since she believed divinity to be present even in the fringe, but so that she might avoid the gaze of the crowd.

She wished to remain unknown to the people, not to Christ. Therefore she judged that she could hide what she was doing not from God, but from human beings. Otherwise, how could she have believed that she could hide from the gaze of divinity, in whom she judged nothing to be lowly and nothing weak, since she sought power and salvation even in the fringe?

Thus the mystical sense is evident, as I said: this woman, namely the Church, touches Christ by faith, while the crowd presses upon him.

She is indeed the woman who, wounded first by the sin of original transgression, flowed with blood and was stained with the menstruation of sins. With sound faith she secretly seized healing, while the faithless daughter of the ruler of the synagogue—that is, the Synagogue, instructed by its teachers—was announced as dead.

Thus, truly, Christ is touched when he is believed to be powerful everywhere and God is worshiped in the human being.

For this reason he says to someone who did not yet believe: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 19:21). But this woman had already ascended to the Father in her understanding, because she believed him to be equal to the Father; therefore she touched the fringe of his garment with perfect faith.

What, then, is signified by the fringe except the power of divinity? This is the fringe of the commandments that Moses commanded to be made at the edge of the priest’s cloak. Through it this woman entered inwardly, and through the fringe she touched the summit of the head.

She drew a drop of salvation from the tassel and dew of mercy from the head. Hence the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “My head is full of dew, and my locks with drops of the night” (Song of Songs 5:2).

She reached the fountain of dew and secretly drew a drop of salvation from the fringe, because she believed that the ointment descending from the head had reached the edge of his garment.

The seven locks of Samson, that Nazarite—that is, of Christ—were filled with this dew of the Holy Spirit. Such power was in them that he was unconquerable. But while he seeks the embraces of Delilah—that is, of the menstruating Church—he is weakened unto death, the death of the cross.

Understanding this, the woman approached from behind and touched the fringe of his garment.

The fringe of the garments can also rightly be understood as any one of the holy apostles. The whole Church is often designated as Christ’s garment, and therefore it is also sung that the ointment flowing down from the head descended to the edge of the garment (Psalm 123:2), so that we may not doubt that all whom divine power has clothed are full of the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Whenever one of them is touched by faith, the teaching of salvation is drawn from him. Concerning them the Father says through the prophet to the Son: “As I live, you will clothe yourself with all these as with a garment” (Isaiah 49:18).

These are, as I said, the tassels filled with drops of the night, while the bridegroom knocks at the door. The Church of Christ, touching them everywhere by faith, confesses: “If I touch only his garment, I shall be saved,” because through their teaching she is saved from the flow of unbelief.

She touches from behind, as I said, because she believed after his ascension; or because it is said: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12:26); and elsewhere: “You shall walk after the Lord your God.” Hence Moses, seeing the back of God, descended radiant from the mountain.

But Jesus turned, and seeing her, said: “Take courage, daughter; your faith saves you.” He did not say, therefore, “Your faith will save you,” but “has saved you,” as though he were saying plainly: “By the fact that you believed, you have already been saved.” It should be noted that faith acquires salvation, and not salvation faith, since faith is shown to be the beginning and root of all virtues. Although some first require virtues and then promise faith, faith must nevertheless come first, so that afterward anyone may arrive at salvation.

When Jesus is said to have turned toward the woman, this should be understood not merely as a movement of the body, but also as an act of divine vision preceding it: the woman was to turn toward Christ and then, through faith, receive the care of healing. Hence we must acknowledge that he saw with divine rather than human eyes. He saw in order to restore her to salvation, not in order to discover what he certainly knew before she herself knew that she needed to seek God.

What more need be said? By this woman’s example Christ taught how greatly faith advances salvation. This is the power we employ not only to be healed but also to become children of God. Hence he says: “Your faith has saved you.” Yet unless he had first turned and seen her, she would not have touched him in faith at all. He first restored what he was about to do and gave her the means by which she might touch him. Since she had thereby been reborn, she is rightly called a daughter, and, having received the power of faith, she is healed. Otherwise, if she had not first received it, she would not only have failed to bring back salvation from the physician but would not have touched him either.

In the tropological sense, this ruler properly signifies any human being who pleads for his daughter—that is, for the flesh—because our whole mortality is rightly believed to be destined for its final end. But the soul first seeks healing, having suffered badly from the flow of vices, and touches at least the smallest of God’s commandments, restored by faith, so that it may arrive at salvation. The proper order is first that the human being be healed in the soul, and then that he long for the resurrection and salvation of the flesh. Hence the Prophet says: “My soul thirsted for you; how manifoldly my flesh longs for you” (Ps. LXII, 2).

Nevertheless, every Christian should hear this and, each day partaking of Christ’s body from the altar, consider how great a medicine he can receive from it, since the woman seized such healing from Christ’s fringe alone. Perhaps through this woman he taught how great a thing it is to receive Christ’s body from the height of the altar before the eyes of the divine majesty, since from the fringe a fountain of healing immediately flowed at her touch.

But what must be lamented most bitterly is that she received medicine for her wound, whereas for us the medicine itself is sometimes turned back into a wound. Hence the Apostle says: “Whoever touches, or whoever eats, Christ’s body unworthily, receives judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. XI, 29). Rashness therefore takes hold of sickness where faith ought to have received healing. For this reason, he says, “many among you are weak and sick, and many are asleep” (ibid., 30). By “those who are asleep” he calls the dead, whom he sharply deplores and mourns as already buried alive in the body.

It should also be noted that neither does the touch of an unclean woman pollute Christ, nor does the sight of a blood-stained woman offend him, nor does the smell of foulness exasperate him, nor does the hearing of human contagion defile him. For if the sun touches dung and yet is not polluted, how much more is the Creator of the sun undefiled when he touches our wounds? The wounds of sins offend and displease him more than bodily sufferings, and the festering of vices more than the flux of the viscera. For although each person voluntarily falls into sins, he is held unwillingly in illnesses.

Therefore let everyone beware of touching the sacrament of life unworthily; rather, let him first cleanse himself from his menstrual impurities, and only then let the faithful person receive it. Let no one at all doubt that Christ’s divinity is present in the flesh of his body, if it reaches even to the fringe. Faith everywhere attains the power of the divinity, because it is everywhere and is absent nowhere; nevertheless, it is more fully present in the body and flesh of Christ, through which “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14).

And although the taking up of Christ’s body has been carried across to heaven, the majesty of the Word, free from unbelief, is everywhere and has not withdrawn from us. Therefore let every devout person touch him everywhere in faith, lest, when pressing upon him wrongly with the crowds, he crush and trample Christ.

Then follows:

“And when Jesus had come into the ruler’s house and had seen the flute players and the crowd making a tumult, he said: ‘Withdraw; the girl is not dead but sleeping.’”

Behold, he says that she is sleeping, although above the father had announced her as dead. And as another evangelist reports more explicitly, while these things were taking place on the road, servants declared that she was dead, saying: “Do not trouble the Teacher, for the girl is dead.”

Wonderful is God’s dispensation! Behold, one had declined toward death for twelve years, while the other, her equal in age, rose again to life. This number does not, of course, encompass the period of human life, but signifies the year divided into twelve months. Hence the Prophet proclaims “the acceptable year of the Lord” (Luke IV, 19), and the Apostle, commending the fullness of time, says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. IV, 4).

When he came, he restored life to believers but thrust unbelievers into death—namely, those whom the unbelief of the Jews had killed. The servants are rightly called servants because they do not want Christ to be troubled by coming to the dead synagogue. They regard him as the teacher of the Law, although they pronounce her dead, since they have lost hope of resurrection and do not wish to return to him.

It is therefore clear that the scribes and Pharisees despised God in the flesh. Yet Christ, with the prophets and patriarchs interceding for her, hastens to enter the house in order to raise the synagogue, which is dead. When he saw the flute players and the tumultuous crowd, he ordered them to withdraw. These are the supporters whose reading of the lamentations presses the synagogue down in the sleep of unbelief even to this day.

It is customary for a mournful song to sound on the flutes at vigils, together with the singing for the dead, so that they may rouse the hearts of the sluggish to lamentation. Thus the Jews, following the letter that kills, bring mourning through their own songs and lamentations, and to this day bewail the dead synagogue. When Christ, or his disciples, says to them, “The girl is not dead but sleeping,” they ridicule him, crushed beneath the weight of their unbelief.

But Christ, after expelling all of them together with the crowd, enters and takes the girl’s hand, because all things live to God. Hence he says: “The girl is not dead but sleeping,” as though he were saying openly: “She sleeps in the superstitions of the Law and in the traditions of a perverse persuasion.”

Thus Christ expels from the house of resurrection the tumultuous crowd of unbelieving Jews, and the flute players—namely, the wicked teachers—from the office of the letter, excluding them from the gift. In that house, finally, only seven persons remained, signifying that among the Jews those are raised to the light in whom the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit has been poured out and consecrated by that number.

But perhaps it is asked why he held her hand, just as we read above that he held the hand of the man whom he healed from fevers in Simon’s house. It is therefore evident in both cases that the female sex is restored to life. For this reason, according to the literal sense, the hands of both are held, so that she may be healed who, contrary to the prohibition, had offered the taste of death from the tree to the man.

In the moral sense, however, once the demons that had been falsely chanting over the wretched soul and the crowd of vices have been expelled, it is raised again to life. It is held by the Savior’s hand, from which no one who has been predestined can be taken.

The salvation restored to all through these healings is signified when one of them is raised from illness and the other from death. The prudent reader knows that everywhere the particular mystically returns to the universal, and that, while faith is confirmed by the miracles of the events, the universality of those to be saved is proclaimed through the virtues. Thus the particular is enclosed within the universal, and the limit of the meaning of particulars, both in moral matters and in allegories, does not exceed the universal.

Therefore, through the woman, the Church from the nations is signified, or any soul utterly deprived of the beauty of virtues and the strength of courage. Through the dead girl, however, the synagogue is signified, which had formerly lived by the Spirit of faith; or a soul killed by the illusions of demons. The former suffered the flow of vices; the latter had already fallen, and was continually falling, into death. The former was deprived of the beauty and strength of blood; the latter was killed by the worst incantations of demons.

For beauty and strength of body are supplied in the blood; when it flowed away, the virtues of a good life had fallen, and the wretched, tearful soul was stained with its own impurities and bloodied. But just as the former is not healed except through the touch of faith and virtues, so the latter, dead through the crimes of vices, is raised to life only by the Savior’s hand.

As Jesus was passing on from there, two blind men followed him, crying out: “Have mercy on us, Son of David” (Matt. IX, 27).

Matthew alone speaks of these two blind men and of the demon-possessed mute (Matt. XX, 30). Those two blind men about whom the other evangelists are also shown to have written are not these men; nevertheless, the event was similar. Thus, even if Matthew himself had not remembered them as well, what he now recounts could have been understood as something said by the others about two men.

We must carefully commit this to memory: there are certain similar events in the sacred Gospel, even when the same evangelist recalls both. Thus, whenever we find such individual accounts in different evangelists and encounter in them some contradiction that cannot be resolved, we should not conclude that the event in one passage is merely similar to that of another.

For when the Lord was passing from the ruler’s house and going toward his own house, as we read above—when he had gone up into a boat in order to cross over and go to his own city—the two men cried out, saying: “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” Yet they were not healed in passing, or on the road, as they supposed. Rather, afterward, when he came to his own house, they approached him and entered. There, after being questioned more carefully and instructed, they received sight.

Certainly no one can receive light outside Jesus’ house, that is, outside the Church. Their faith is therefore examined first, to determine whether they are able to believe that he can save them. Then, once they have received the light of faith, the sight of their eyes is immediately restored.

Nevertheless, as I said above, faith does not arise from the miracle; rather, through faith, light is restored to their eyes as they ask for it. Faith is therefore required first, because all things are possible to the one who believes.

This miracle explains the event concerning the ruler’s daughter and the woman with the flow of blood. Accordingly, just as death and weakness appeared there, so here the blindness of the two is displayed. Both peoples were blind in this world while the Lord was passing by, longing to return to their own house. Unless they confess Christ as the Son of David and cry out, “Have mercy on us,” they will be raised neither from the flow of sins nor from death.

Then they are also questioned:

“Do you believe that I can do this?” They answered: “Certainly, Lord.”

They believed, and their faith is strengthened by this question, just as in the case of the man who said: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark IX, 24). For this reason, I think, they are not healed beforehand.

Their cry, however, reveals the deep affection of their hearts: “Have mercy on us, Son of David,” as though they were saying openly: “You are our mouth and our flesh; have mercy on us”—if for no other reason, then because of our kinship in the flesh.

When they are questioned whether they believe, they say: “Certainly, Lord.” First, by crying out “Son of David,” and afterward by confessing him more fully and perfectly as “Lord,” they invoke Christ’s humanity and divinity, so that their faith may be accepted.

Otherwise, whoever proclaims Christ’s human flesh without divinity, or divinity without true humanity, does not yet believe but is blinded by errors. For this reason such a person cannot receive the light of the heart.

Let Marcion and Mani, and the others who deny that Christ came in the flesh from David’s line, or who deny true divinity in one and the same person, hear this and learn to call Christ the Son of David according to the flesh, and to confess that same one as Lord.

As for those who place themselves outside the Catholic Church, let them return to Jesus’ house, because they cannot receive light anywhere else, so that through true faith they may recover what they have lost. Let them know, therefore, that whatever they ask within Christ’s house must be obtained by faith, and that faith is not to be derived from commands imposed upon them, since salvation is not granted to such people before they believe.

Then he sternly warned them that no one should know; but they spread his fame throughout that entire region. These things are contradictory, yet just. The humble Lord teaches the avoidance of boasting; they, on the other hand, cannot keep silent about the benefit of salvation because of their remembrance of the grace they received.

The Savior does not yet wish great and divine things to be proclaimed about himself, lest glory precede the Passion. Such things are reserved for the apostles; therefore he rightly tells these men not to usurp what belonged to others. But they spread his fame throughout that entire region, in accordance with what was to come, since “the sound of the apostles went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5).

According to the moral sense, the outer and inner human being receives light fully from the Lord within the unity of Christ’s Church when he believes that Christ came in the flesh from David’s seed for righteousness and confesses him with his mouth as God and Lord for salvation.

As they were going out, behold, they brought him a mute man who had a demon. When the demon had been expelled, the mute man spoke.

The word used in Greek is κωφόν, which in ordinary speech is understood more as “deaf” than “mute.” But it is customary for Scripture to use κωφόν, “mute” or “deaf,” without distinction. It is therefore clear that three signs were exhibited simultaneously in one and the same man: when the demon had been expelled, the mute man spoke, and through the ambiguous word it is signified that the deaf man also received hearing.

It may seem strange that, if the demon had invaded the whole man, it occupied some parts of the body while leaving others free—sight, smell, and touch, for example. Yet it is clear that he had done this deliberately. He had blocked the man’s hearing so that he could not grasp the word of faith or Christ’s teaching; he had paralyzed his tongue so that he could not utter the voice of confession or supplication. Through the eyes and other senses, however, the demon could perceive nothing but bodily things.

Let the prudent reader therefore ask whether the enemy possessed the soul inwardly while thus tearing apart the limbs outwardly, using some of them so that they had no use at all, as though they were an instrument, so that the wretched man seemed meanwhile unable to do anything.
