Nor is it surprising if he dominates the flesh, where the law of sin dwells, concerning which the Apostle Paul says: “I know that good does not dwell in my flesh” (Rom. VII, 18). Accordingly, the enemy rightly approaches it as though it were his own law.

But it is one thing when he inflames his own laws within us toward desire, and another when he possesses the whole person, handed over to him for the destruction of the flesh. Whether, however, he rightly holds some people in flesh and soul together, and others in the flesh alone, so that the spirit may be saved, is a question worth asking.

The matter is easily understood from those whom the divine judge preserves as predestined for himself. They are not handed over to the enemy so that he may thereafter possess their souls more wickedly; rather, once punishment has been completed, God reclaims what was his own and vindicates what belongs to God, so that the enemy may justly lose it in the end, since God does not judge twice for the same matter. Others, alienated from God, he sometimes holds in such a way that, like an unrelenting exactor, he possesses the entire structure of the person.

He had nevertheless afflicted this man through such a stratagem because he had discovered that the Lord had come upon the earth. Thus neither the hearing of the word, nor the power of the divine name, nor confession could reach him. For this reason he made the man’s breast the hiding place of his cavern, blocked his ears, and bound his tongue, so that, with the doors closed, he could neither utter nor receive the word of life.

This does not mean that an unclean spirit is divided among human limbs or confined by the senses. It is a spirit, and in a single moment it flies around the whole world, changes into various forms, penetrates hearts, mocks souls, and breathes wicked and evil thoughts into them. But while the strong enemy holds the wretched limbs of a human being, that human being can do nothing of himself.

“And when he had expelled,” he says, “the demon, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marveled.”

It is therefore evident that the demon himself had closed the windows. For this reason the author of salvation first drove out the author of the affliction; once he had been expelled, the mute man immediately recovered the function of his tongue, and the crowds marveled.

They marvel, but they do not believe or confess God. Instead, they say that nothing like this had ever appeared in Israel. Although ignorant and unbelieving, they understand that what has happened surpasses the Law; they proclaim Jesus above all who had previously existed. For although Elijah, Elisha, and the others performed mighty deeds, none did so by such power or command. None of them ever performed things of this kind or magnitude.

But the Jews were saying that he cast out demons by the prince of demons. Wretched people! What they could not deny, they slandered as the work of divinity.

The admiring crowds say that nothing like this had appeared in Israel. These men, blinded by envy, say that the Savior’s works were accomplished by Beelzebul, the prince of demons.

According to the anagogical sense, this mute man signifies the people of the nations, who were brought to the Lord through the ministry of the apostles and enslaved to the worship of idols. He is shown to have been plainly mute because he had not yet learned to speak the truth. He was deaf because he had neither heard the Lord’s commandments nor received the word of faith. Finally, he was full of a demon because his limbs were filled with an unclean spirit.

Once the demon had been expelled, they hear the word of truth each day and proclaim the confession of salvation with their mouths. Hence unbelievers still marvel today, as they did at the beginning, when the Church spoke in various tongues, while the Jews slander us because they do not believe in Christ.

It is therefore clear that, just as the faith of the nations was displayed beforehand through the wonder and confession of the peoples, so the unbelief and blasphemy of the Jews are signified to this day through their slander.

It is evident that every soul, while still being tossed about in the world by crimes, is shown to be mute and deaf. Otherwise, if it were not deaf, it would hear and receive the word of salvation. Hence the Lord so often says: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XI, 15; XIII, 9, 43; Mark IV, 7; VII, 16; Luke VIII, 8; XIV, 35).

But because the wretched soul is weighed down by the torpor of deafness, it is clear that it is tormented by a demon. Therefore it can neither utter the word of confession nor draw in the salvation of life by hearing.

Hence the Prophet, striking fear into us, says: “But to the sinner God said: ‘Why do you recount my righteousnesses and take my covenant upon your mouth?’” (Ps. XLIX, 16). It is as though he were saying openly: “Because you are driven by an unclean spirit, it is unworthy of you to presume to tell anyone the word of salvation.”

Therefore teachers must take care, whenever an auditor is so senseless that he neither wishes nor is able to understand with the ear of the heart what is said, to offer him to the Savior through their prayers, since he is oppressed by an evil spirit. Once that spirit has been expelled, let the auditor confess the hidden things of the heart and thereafter devoutly remain alert, hearing with the ear what is divine. Otherwise everyone labors in vain unless God provides the inward growth that enables hearing.

And Jesus went around all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues.

He went through all the cities and villages so that no one would be excluded from the duty of salvation. Yet he first taught the apostles on the mountain, prefiguring that their way of life would be in heavenly places; the others he taught in the synagogues, since they were not yet able to comprehend higher things.

In a marvelous order, he first taught the Gospel of the kingdom, and then, after preaching and teaching, healed every disease and every infirmity. Thus, for those whom the word had not persuaded to faith, the works of his powers might provide persuasion. For he was, as two of the disciples say while walking, “powerful in deed and word” (Luke XXIV, 19). Accordingly, he first offered the instruction of the kingdom, and afterward powerfully commended the same teaching through signs and wonders, so that people might be moved to faith.

You will find nowhere that anyone other than the Lord is said to have healed every disease and every infirmity, although the disciples also healed many, as we read that even more people were cured by Peter’s shadow.

But it should be asked whether, from the place where he descended from the mountain, he healed every disease and every infirmity of those who were brought to him, since only ten are counted as having been healed afterward, or whether he healed others as well—which is evident. For he certainly went everywhere with such diligence in order to heal all people and so that they might receive the Gospel of the kingdom.

It is clear that just as he taught in their synagogues in the cities, villages, and all the hamlets—the Gospel discourse explains and promises these things individually—so he plainly performed countless miracles that were not written down. Indeed, there was no disease or infirmity among them that he did not heal.

The disciples, however, could not heal the demon-possessed man who was brought to him. Concerning him it is said that this kind of demon is cured only by prayer and fasting. But Christ, as Lord, drove out every disease and every infirmity, inwardly and outwardly, proving that nothing was impossible for him.

Just as that discourse delivered on the mountain is believed to be sufficient from among all his teachings, and was therefore handed down in writing by the Holy Spirit for the instruction of later generations, so only a very few of all his works are narrated. They commend the mysteries of faith through their events and number and suggest that all the Savior’s works were full of mystical gifts.

For we often read in this very Gospel, without an account of events and without distinction of persons, that all were healed and that every disease and infirmity was driven away, without any particular individual being identified.

But at times the blind unbelief of the pagans refuses to believe. They say that no signs appropriate to such majesty shone forth in Christ. They claim that the theatrical healing of the weak and the restoration of life to the dead are small matters for God, if others who performed wonders are also taken into account.

We too acknowledge that the prophets performed such things. For in these signs, what is more excellent than raising the dead to life? Elijah did this in the Old Testament, and Elisha did it as well; countless others did so after the Lord’s coming.

As for the miracles of the magicians, of which the pagans boast, let those who invent the claim that they performed them decide whether they raised the dead. They also vigorously defend Apuleius against the efforts of magical arts and attempt to convict him, not by accusing him but by praising him.

We read that the Egyptian magicians were highly skilled in such powers, yet they were decisively overcome by Moses, God’s servant. For they and all the wise men of the world, if they accomplished anything, did so only by diabolical art; our people, however, do so only through Christ’s power and in the Savior’s name.

By prophesying and preaching about him, they gave him great glory, presuming nothing about themselves. They announced him not as their equal, nor merely as one superior to them in the same power of miracles, but plainly as God and Lord of all, made human for the sake of human beings.

For this reason he himself also wished to perform such things, lest what they had done through him seem absurd unless he performed similar works himself. Nevertheless, he also had to do something proper to himself: to be born of a Virgin, to rise from the dead, to ascend into heaven, to sit at the Father’s right hand above all the choirs of angels, and to make demons subject to God.

If anyone considers this little, I do not know what more he could expect. For I think that, since in the beginning all things were made through him, once he had assumed humanity he ought to have made another world, so that we might believe that he was the one through whom the world was made. But no world greater than or equal to this one could be made in this world. If he had made a smaller one below this, that too would likewise have been considered little.

Therefore, since it was not fitting, he made new things within the world. Perhaps what he did in the last times is more powerful than what he did in the beginning.

How astonishing, then, is human blindness! The Son of God performed in the flesh works smaller than or equal to those performed by others, and they despise him; he performed greater works, and they do not believe. He performed what, in their judgment, was believable, and they consider it insignificant for God. He performed divine works, but they refuse to believe because such works belong to God.

The wretched do not understand that Christ did not come again to make the world, for what he had made remains; rather, he came to save what had perished—namely, the human race—for whose sake he had long ago created all these things.

For this reason he performed what is known to pertain to salvation, and he made visible signs of his powers in the outer human being, so that through them the mind, eager for knowledge, might learn sufficiently what it should seek inwardly.

For inwardly, in the soul—the part in which the human being is believed to be better—he had fallen entirely. Therefore the works of power that bring salvation are performed outwardly, so that through this benefit the human being may be summoned inwardly to salvation, love the author of life, believe, and devoutly seek from him the medicine of salvation.

If it is still asked what Christ did that no one else did, let us briefly review a few things among many. He fulfilled in himself the prophecies of all the prophets, which no one else did. He was born of a Virgin, at whose birth a new star shone forth and led devoted magi to him by the way.

An army of angels sang to shepherds listening beside his cradle: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke II, 10). And Gabriel declares: “Behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born for you.”

Nothing of such kind and magnitude is read of anyone else from the beginning of the world. He certainly performed miracles that his own prophets had also performed earlier, so that they might be proved true prophets of the true God. But the works he performed by his own power and without invoking anyone else are of such a kind and magnitude that they are never read to have been performed by anyone, as had been foretold.

Hence he so often says that he healed every disease and every infirmity. By his own power he also gave the witnesses of the Gospel authority to perform similar works, but through faith and invocation of his name—something no one else did.

Only those things from his deeds that are sufficient for faith and suggest to us the mystical lessons of his powers are written down. Therefore, prudent reader, I ask you not to become weary, since all things respond to divine gifts. For if everything that he did in the flesh had been committed to writing, as John testifies, the whole world would not be sufficient to contain it (John XXI, 25).

And I do not mean merely the signs of such great deeds; even the works he afterward performed in his own members would not fit within it. Hence he is rightly proclaimed so marvelous in his saints, to whom he gave power to perform not only similar works but even greater ones.

Accordingly, the things that are narrated in the course of this discourse for the confirmation of faith and as testimony to the teaching are spoken more for their usefulness through mystical mysteries than to display the quantity of the works performed. Their conclusion is greater without a defined number than the multitude of signs without understanding of the mystery.

From the beginning of the signs in this Gospel there are nearly ten miracles, or somewhat more, from the time Jesus began to perform signs: ten people are read to have been healed, while the sea and the winds were calmed by a word of command.

It is clear that long ago Egypt was struck with ten plagues because of the hardness of its heart, and finally all its cavalry was drowned in the sea. Through these plagues our present world likewise lay crushed.

Therefore, just as ten commandments were formerly given on the mountain for healing, so now the disciples are taught above, more than Moses and more perfectly, in the higher places. Below, ten healings are divinely displayed, so that those who had been tormented by the number of the plagues might be relieved by the same number as a medicine of salvation.

Perhaps this is why he is said to have healed every disease: in these events he provided an example of complete health, showing that he healed every kind of pain—leprosy, that is, impurity; paralysis, that is, dissolution; fever, that is, burning; demonic affliction; the flow of unbelief; the onset of death; the blindness of ignorance; deafness; and the impediment of the tongue in speaking.

If you examine these carefully, you will see why, after the eight beatitudes of the teaching, an equal number of kinds of healing follows: the meaning is that whoever has fulfilled these eight beatitudes in his soul has received complete health and emptied himself of every infirmity.

If two signs are joined into one—namely, deafness and the binding of the tongue—seven are counted, just as the petitions in the Lord’s Prayer are arranged under the same number.

Thus, if you take note of it, everything harmonizes with divine mysteries: the number ten corresponds to the persons, while the number eight corresponds to the kinds of diseases, since when the two paralytics are joined together, one infirmity is healed in them. Again, when two demoniacs are healed, one enemy is expelled.

When seven, eight, and ten are recognized step by step, the sacred number is given meaning here and there, and the power of the mysteries is disclosed more abundantly.

Moreover, when the sea, stirred up by a storm, is calmed by a word, this occurs so that all who have been restored to health with Christ may reach the harbor of salvation.

Therefore, as I said earlier, two disciples are prepared first. One is cast out because of the fault of his unbelief; the other, liberated by Christ’s grace, is transferred to life. Once he has been transferred, legions of demons, together with the swine that they held, are drowned in the sea.

Thus, while the true Israel is carried back to its homeland, Pharaoh’s cavalry is enveloped amid the waves.

And in a marvelous dispensation of God, the whole human being is healed. In the mute man, the lips and taste are cleansed; in the deaf man, the ears are purified and hearing is opened. In the blind man, the darkness of shadows is dispelled and sight is illuminated. In the leper, the stench is rejected from the nostrils and the beauty of the whole body is restored, so that confession may be present in speech and beauty in the restoration of appearance.

Then, in the feverish mother-in-law, touch is cleansed in the hands. The sea is calmed, so that, once the enemies have been drowned with Christ, he may be carried back to his homeland as quickly as possible.

A diligent investigator should consider these and similar matters more carefully, and will see that neither the conclusion is without a mystery, nor the miracles without a secret meaning, nor the teaching without an understanding of the narrative. Step by step, while faith is still being nourished in the tender hearts of the disciples, these things are described continuously.

But since the sequence of the mystery is concluded from the beginning of Christ’s preaching, I wish the book of explanation also to be brought to its conclusion, so that, at the beginning—as though at the opening of a new narrative—the restored mind may take greater delight in what follows and, delighting, grasp it more fully.

**PREFACE TO BOOK SIX**

[Col. 0393]

[Col. 0393D] My exposition, beloved, belongs to many highly learned teachers whom an earlier age produced and the authority of truth established. Yet its novelty, commended by my own style, makes it mine, so that the treatise gathered from all of them may truly appear to be one work and specifically my own. I have made the common understanding of many teachers my own through Catholic faith and understanding.

For I have not thought it right to explain the mysteries of divine understanding or the sayings of God the Savior solely by my own boldness—as many have done, who refused to understand what the divinely inspired sacred Scripture inwardly understands, but perversely applied it in many places to their own errors. Thus they strayed so far from the truth because they could taste the wisdom of the divine word inwardly with the palate of the heart so little; they gave greater assent to human efforts than to submitting themselves and their own understanding to divine utterances.

For this reason I preferred to follow the footsteps of the Catholic Fathers, whom the instruction of heavenly wisdom seasoned with salt, and, as I said, I made their teaching my own, so that I might bring you, most learned in divine law, nothing other than what had been proved. Even if I drew something of truth from elsewhere, it did not belong to those among whom truth itself was living as a stranger. Rather, it was ours to recognize it and restore it, so that it might flourish in its proper places.

But since we are preparing to forge the sixth book on Matthew, I believe it will greatly contribute to the perfection of our understanding if the human being—formed on the sixth day from the clay of the earth under the perfect number and created in the image of God—is led from the beginning of Christ’s birth to this point along the lines and way that is Christ, so that the faithful soul may understand the ascents in its heart, advancing daily from virtue to virtues. For all Christ’s works are described in such a way that through them he himself is shown to us as the way.

[Col. 0395C] For he himself came to us, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills, looking through the lattices, so that he might always call us to higher things. Therefore let the prudent reader first come to Ephrata, where the union of marriage had long been heard. Hence David, rejoicing, does not wish to give sleep to his eyes or rest to his temples until he finds a place for the Lord, who is everywhere without locality, and the tabernacle of the God of Jacob, which Christ himself set up in the sun.

“Behold,” he says, “we heard of it in Ephrata” (Psalm 131:4), that is, in Bethlehem, where Christ was born. At his cradle a multitude of angels sings: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). The shepherds proclaim the Word and behold the Word in flesh—the Word that in the beginning was with God—which the Lord showed them.

[Col. 0395D] Let the faithful soul first go out from Babylon, that is, from confusion, where for a long time we lay grievously wounded, and see where it ought to ascend and worship with the Magi and offer the gifts of its faith. For where else could one exiled from paradise lie, if not in his own confusion? And where ought it first to ascend, if not to the house of bread? For there that living bread descended from heaven. Whoever reaches that house suffers hunger for the word no longer, because whoever lives lives in him who is living and true bread and descended from heaven.

Then, because we had been sold into Egypt and weighed down by many burdens, he is brought there by his own will, as though to become our protector, so that he might indicate that he had shared our griefs and sorrows and endured many things for us. [Col. 0396A] With him the heavenly soul, afflicted by many tribulations and anxieties, ascends again into Judea by the grace of God—that is, to true confession—so that it may confess the Lord’s mercies in all things and faithfully recount the wonders of the Lord’s works.

Afterward it is nourished with him in Nazareth, that is, in the flower of good works, so that it too may be called with Christ “the flower of the valleys,” because it has blossomed in the palm, in order to bear the fruit of righteousness. Thus, having reached maturity, it can ascend, according to the other evangelist (Luke 2:42), to the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem, where Jesus always remains, because he must be occupied with the things that belong to the Father.

Nevertheless, although he himself is the wisdom of God the Father, he still questions the scribes and priests about the Law and the prophets—not in order to be taught, but to provide an example from himself of what children ought to do at that age. Thus all were astonished at his wisdom in questioning and at his answers.

[Col. 0396B] Nor is it without mystery that he is read to have been twelve years old, because at that age the entire human race begins to flourish in understanding and reason and to reach physical maturity, so that the soul may transfer itself wholly to heavenly things and learn to question what is divine. At the same time, it must repel in its mind the vices that oppose it and question them inwardly in its conscience, so that it may answer each matter wisely.

Otherwise, because at that time the eyes are opened—the eyes that are read to have been wrongly opened in paradise—youth might be confounded by errors. Therefore it ought to ascend to the temple and there ask how it may advance in age, grace, and wisdom before God and human beings.

[Col. 0396C] Otherwise Jesus advanced neither in grace nor in wisdom through the stages of life, since he was wholly, even in the Virgin’s womb, the grace and wisdom of God the Father. Hence John says: “And we saw him as the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Therefore it is for our sake that he is said to advance, although he came full of these things, so that we too may be urged to grow in virtues, and so that as age increases outwardly before human beings, the grace and wisdom of God may daily increase inwardly in our conduct.

But lest youth and the power of wisdom—which sometimes tends to inflate those who possess it—lift us up, we must come to the descent of the Jordan. For Jordan is interpreted as “descent,” and through this descent humility is signified. We must humble ourselves in all things, because we are washed and saved in baptism not by our merits but by grace.

[Col. 0396D] Then, already saved, we are led with Christ into the desert, so that each of us may learn to fight against invisible enemies and against the vices of the flesh through abstinence and vigilance over our mind, if somehow our soul may reach the triumph of victory once the enemy has been driven away.

All these advances of our soul are therefore ascents, so that with unfailing faith and good works we may follow Christ. Through these steps, the soul, thoroughly exercised, may find the grace of pious formation and reach the summit of virtue.

But because, after Adam was expelled from paradise, the human condition was confined within the strongholds of vice, the most kindly Jesus is said to have gone around everything and to have traversed all the twists and turns of the roads. [Col. 0397A] I think we must consider at what age Jesus began this, so that the prudent soul may learn to presume nothing about itself before being trained under Christ’s discipline, nor seize a place of authority before learning what it ought to teach once mature.

Hence I think it was established that no presbyter should be ordained as teacher and master before the age of thirty, around which age the most kindly Jesus began to go around the villages and preach the word of life.

He began first near the borders of Zebulun—that is, near nocturnal streams, namely, beside the more obscure riddles of the prophets. There, to those sitting in the region of the shadow of death, light arose. When the Sun of righteousness began to illumine them, he led them onward to higher things, where only disciples can ascend, [Col. 0397B] and taught the mysteries of heavenly life, which can be grasped by the mind only in heavenly places.

But because the weak multitude could not follow him there, he came down and healed the sicknesses of souls, and continued as far as Capernaum, which is interpreted as “most beautiful village,” so that they might pass from such squalor to the habitation of the countryside and the beauty of dwelling.

Proceeding from there, when he wished to reach the territory of the Gerasenes, he boarded a ship [Col. 0398A] and taught by his example not to fear the waves and storms of this life. For Christ has an intelligible ship which he governs, and in it he conveys pious freight toward the homeland. In its stern he rests in tranquil sleep like a good helmsman. When awakened by its movement, he rebukes the winds, so that he may restore tranquility to his own.

He also crossed over to the Gentiles and freed souls that had been tormented by many demons, and, as I said, concluded the sequence of salvation by healing and teaching everyone.

A truly wretched and exceedingly unhappy soul may be called one that receives no healing through so many advances. Yet it must not despair, because even afterward the gracious shepherd, as though at the beginning of another narrative, deigned to visit the flock of his sheep, so that he might bring everyone tirelessly to the medicine of salvation.

I have said these things from time to time so that from them the mind might grasp what is more excellent and learn that nothing else shines forth here and there in the Gospel except life. For Christ was made for us by God the way, and the truth, and the life. Therefore, in the things he did, the way must always be sought, the truth held fast, and life enjoyed.

BOOK SIX.

[Col. 0397]

[Col. 0379B] “When Jesus saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were harassed and lying like sheep without a shepherd.”

[Col. 0397C] In this chapter the statement of Ezekiel is fulfilled, where he speaks in the person of the Lord: “Behold, I myself will seek out my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is in the midst of his scattered sheep” (Ezekiel 34:11–12).

They were harassed by various illnesses of vice and lay prostrate beneath the feet of their enemies, because through faithlessness they had previously lost their gracious shepherd and, scattered, were tormented by many wounds inflicted by demons.

Therefore the Lord goes around all the cities, teaching and healing, so that he may find everyone and raise up those who were lying down and had been unable to stand. He saw the crowds not in one particular place, but while he was going around villages and settlements where the wind of faithlessness had scattered them; for this reason he is read to have gone around them.

The entire human race had strayed like a sheep that had been lost. Therefore, seeking it, he found them harassed and lying like sheep without a shepherd, because in their wandering they had lost the true Savior.

He found them harassed by demons and lying prostrate while they were oppressed by various illnesses of vice and had no one to care for them; all, torn by the bites of wolves, lay on the bed of great sickness. Otherwise, unless he had first sought them out and, moved with compassion, seen them, the whole flock would still be lying in its illnesses.

Now, once their sickness has been healed, the restored flock vigorously carries the bed of its sickness, and all, refreshed with green grasses, may eventually reach the fountain of satiety. Then he said:

“The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest” [Col. 0398B] (Matthew 9:37–38).

A sufficiently remarkable and ornate variety of figures! Those whom he first designates as sheep without a shepherd he calls the same people a harvest without laborers. He calls them sheep because they had departed from the pastures of paradise for many reasons; but he calls them a harvest because of the nature of seed, since we all grew from the earth, as though in yearly seasons, from one origin.

In this harvest the laborers were few—those who, by cultivating it, might bring it back by grace to the granary of paradise from which the seed had gone out because of sin. Others had indeed worked in this field, although the apostles entered into their labors; nevertheless, they were still few. Therefore they are commanded to ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest.

It must also be noted that although the harvest has been choked by thorns and thistles, it does not belong to another, because he himself made us, and not we ourselves—as certain natural philosophers wish, introducing nature as the maker of the human race.

[Col. 0398D] Thus he declares himself to be the Lord and Creator who ought to send preachers into his harvest. Otherwise, how will it be preached unless they are sent? Preachers therefore cannot be what they are unless they are directed by him so that they may prosper. Hence the Lord of the harvest, who cares for all things, must be asked to send cultivators to work the soil.

For certainly the sickness of the sheep, the barrenness of the crops, and their choking by thorns and thistles result from the lack of farmers and shepherds. Perhaps, therefore, he warned these twelve for this reason: so that they would not be moved by envy, but rather ask, like excellent farmers, for companions whose support might strengthen their small number.

For in choosing seventy-two disciples, the provident teacher first directs them to pray for such workers rather than to envy them. Thus, while he goes around [Col. 0399A] all the villages and settlements, he sees crowds lying not so much from bodily sickness as from depravity of conduct and unbelief of mind, because they were harassed by various demonic deceits. Therefore, moved with compassion, he said:

“The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few.”

For this reason he had already called these twelve above; for this reason he had instructed them more fully apart on the mountain; for this reason he had performed miracles before them. But because he had not yet sent them to preach, he wishes them to ask, so that they may learn from him to seek the one without whom they can accomplish nothing.

Their abundant fruit is a gift, for although it is received by everyone, it always overflows. Therefore he commands that it be requested, because he desires to bestow it freely. The grace of the Holy Spirit is granted to those who knock [Col. 0399B] and ask, so that they may be fellow workers with the grace of God. Otherwise reapers labor everywhere in vain without the abundance of the Holy Spirit, since they cannot rightly preach unless they are sent.

Hence the force of the words must be considered no less than that of the deeds, because the same meaning of the events is revealed equally in what is said and what is done. For through those of whom he is read to have compassion, he designates the entire human race, since all were harassed by various deceptions of wickedness.

Some had been enticed by philosophical arts and magic; others had been imbued with the perverse teachings of the scribes’ and Pharisees’ traditions; others were occupied by idolatries through the deception of demons; others were weighed down by the burdens of sin and intent upon worldly concerns, lacking the power to rise again.

The law of nature had perished, the patriarchs had died, there was no prophet, and the whole world, so to speak, lay uncultivated, including the Jews themselves, among whom their fathers had once sown the seeds of life. Compared with the magnitude of this multitude, the laborers, namely the apostles, were few, and they themselves had not yet been so illumined by the grace of the Spirit as to suffice.

As a clear figure of this matter, we read that, at the advice of his father-in-law, Moses established several levels to instruct the people of one nation (Exodus 18). How much more, then, must one ask in this multitude of the human race that Christ send more laborers, through whose teachings the harvest and the vineyard—whose farmer is the Father—might thereafter be cultivated more abundantly, flourish more richly, and bear more fruit?

(CHAPTER X.) “Then, having summoned his twelve disciples, he gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every sickness and every disease.”

In this passage it is not sufficiently clear from either of the evangelists whether the order of the narrative followed according to recollection or according to the actual sequence of history. Hence Mark and Luke each indicate that the following discourse was delivered in some other place, yet none of them anywhere departs from the path of truth, since it is clear both that they were sent by the Lord and that they had been called.

For Luke says that they were called and named together on the mountain, but elsewhere that they were sent. Then, in a third place, he narrates the commissioning of the seventy-two disciples to preach. Here, too, the passage comprehends that the same thing happened at some point.

It must also be noted that in the distribution of this grace Judas is not excluded, but is counted both in the order and in the gift. [Col. 0400A] Thus the teacher is gracious, who does not begrudge his own the granting of powers and gifts.

But it is one thing to possess something essentially, another to give it generously, and another to receive it mercifully. Knowing this, they always confessed their own weakness, saying: “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise,” or whatever else was appropriate by the command of healing.

Therefore, although the disciples heal every sickness and cure every disease, it is Christ who acts; his power worked in the disciples. The order is indeed remarkable: first he taught, so that they might know what to follow, and established instructions for salvation; then he confirmed their faith by miracles and made their teaching firm.

But when he sends them to preach, he also gives them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every sickness [Col. 0400B] and every disease. First the instruction of wisdom is granted to them through speech; in the middle comes faith through the works of divinity; finally, the power of faith is brought to completion by grace.

Thus neither teaching should exist without the power of signs, nor power without the teaching of wisdom, nor the power of signs or wisdom without faith. Rather, each end depends upon faith in Jesus Christ, so that the teaching may rightly understand it and the power may derive from faith alone.

Musicians admire and praise this kind of alternation: the middle of a symphony made of two parts answers equally to the endings of both its parts, and they themselves finally form the middle.

Faith is produced with testimony from the Law or the prophets and is brought to completion in the middle by the power of signs. Therefore he first taught so that they might be instructed by the Law, and added whatever the Law lacked; then, through the work of divinity, he established faith that he was God, and afterward, imparting to his own the power of signs, he confirmed it most forcefully.

First, therefore, he taught them to live by faith, as it is written: “But my righteous one will live by faith” (Hebrews 10:38). Then, once faith had been received, through the work of his divinity he also granted that if they had faith like a mustard seed, they could move mountains from their place by a word, so that they too, powerful in every deed and word, might establish for all the truth concerning Christ.

It must also be noted that authority over unclean spirits is granted first, so that we may know that various kinds of diseases are inflicted upon bodies by those same spirits. Once these spirits have been expelled, he grants the ability to heal whatever has been imposed by them. Otherwise, unless the author of the torments were first driven out, the poison of sickness and disease would remain.

Therefore authority over unclean spirits is rightly bestowed beforehand, and then the power to cure whatever they have inflicted. [Col. 0400D] The dispensation of the Almighty is remarkable. For although no authority exists except from God, one kind is that which he sometimes permits to have power, though it always opposes the good of piety, even if it is rightly believed to be just; another is that which always obeys his will and which the Lord has mercifully granted to his own.

Although the former exalts itself above everything called God and is so effective that no human power can resist it, human beings are nevertheless granted not only the ability to resist it but also to dominate it and exercise authority against [Col. 0401A] everything that is opposed to the Lord.

Let the Manichaeans therefore hear this. They assert that the Lord fought against the God of darkness and contend that bodies belong to the kingdom of darkness. How can they think it fitting that the one who granted to so few and insignificant people authority over everything that strives against the Lord should have waged war against them?

Or how can bodies rightly be believed to belong to the kingdom of darkness, when the Savior came to empty them of all the enemy’s deceit and to heal every stain of corruption?

It is therefore clear that no virtue or power exists except from God, and that God himself is the one who granted his own such great power that they could act. For he gave them authority to tread upon every power of the enemy. Bodies too were created by none other than him, so that what the enemy had wounded might rightly be healed by its maker. Therefore he gave his own, by his word, the power to heal every sickness and every disease, and bestowed grace upon them.

Nevertheless, it is asked what difference exists between “every sickness” and “every disease,” even by those who think that nothing in the divine writings is devoid of mystery or superfluous in the narrative. Thus it may be supposed that “sickness” pertains to the soul’s unbelief, whereas “disease” pertains to affliction of the flesh. These two kinds of illness clearly arise from demonic possession.

Therefore the demons first had to be driven out, then the soul had to be cleansed through faith, and afterward bodily health had to be obtained.

Hence faith is so often required in miracles and is more fully confirmed through benefits, so that the whole person may somehow be saved and no grace of salvation may be lacking to the apostles.

Some interpret “sickness” as prolonged affliction of the flesh, but “disease” as sudden corruption that comes upon it. Others judge that the enemy’s affliction belongs to diseases, while illnesses belong to bodily intemperance.

Whichever of these is more correct, the meaning is clear when he says “every sickness and every disease”: he excludes no human evil by which a person might be corrupted outwardly or inwardly, and there is no adversity to health against which he did not give the apostles grace, so that their power might appear weak in nothing.

For every corruption is from the evil one. Therefore perfect power is granted to them, so that they may have from the Lord the ability to bestow what exists in him. He himself is power, salvation, and goodness, and the source of all incorruption.

[Col. 0401D] Therefore by grace he granted to his own what he is by nature, solely so that their hearers might receive both the teaching he presented and the faith he commended by signs and powers.

The text continues:

“These are the names of the twelve apostles.”

From the title itself it is foreshadowed that false apostles would come, so that no other might be received; therefore they are immediately counted. In these men the consecrated order and the number twelve are established.

Accordingly, after the Savior’s teaching and the wonders of his signs, they are immediately named when authority is granted to them, so that no one bringing something outside their teaching—even if it might appear to some to involve certain arts—would be received either into the apostolate or into the teaching of salvation.

These twelve are the foundations of the city of God shown beforehand in the Apocalypse, and likewise its gates and corners, because they are made firm. It was therefore necessary that they be counted and defined by their own marked names.

Thus, although others are called apostles, in these men the complete variety of figures has been established: over them the bronze sea is set, and they, like twelve oxen consecrated by the number three and facing the separate regions of the world, bear in a marked way the baptism that is the bronze sea, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

That only twelve are chosen also has a mystical significance. For this number is formed either by three times four or by four times three, in alternating arrangement, so that neither three without four nor four without three answers to its respective parts. This is because the four Gospels of Christ have been entrusted in a special way to these four in the name of the Trinity, and they ought by their office rightly to carry them to the four regions of the world and proclaim the Trinity in those same regions.

For this reason, too, the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel, ascending from Egypt (Numbers 2), likewise encamp: three toward the east, three toward the south, three toward the north, and three toward the west, prefiguring the form of the apostles. Concerning them it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:4).

The true Jacob begot twelve sons, whom he blessed spiritually with the blessings of the everlasting hills. These twelve springs flow with the abundance of life at Elim, around which seventy-two palm trees are said to have grown (Exodus 15:27)—namely, the seventy-two disciples who are sent to preach, whom the fountain of the apostles nourished healthfully.

The twelve lions bearing Solomon’s throne (1 Kings 10:20), when three are joined together in a square number toward each of the regions of the world, likewise foreshadow the strength of these men. The true Solomon, Christ, is rightly believed to preside over them on the throne of his Church, because the faith of his majesty is founded upon them alone, and the city is made firm, concerning which it is said: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Psalm 86:1).

These foundations are immediately called gates, which the Lord loves above all the tabernacles of Jacob. Therefore, if anyone does not enter the Church of Christ through them—that is, through their faith and teaching—he will nowhere and never find the door, of which the Lord says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10:9).

There are therefore many examples of figures by which the number of the apostles is foreshadowed and their primacy, order, and exalted status are declared. Hence, through many indications in the divine Scriptures, the praise of offices and persons is very frequently woven under the same number, so that both their number and their merits may be commended mystically.

For the true Solomon has only these twelve leaders set over all Israel, to whom the Lord said: “You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28).

These are the twelve stones of the altar and the twelve loaves of the bread of the Presence before the Lord (Leviticus 24:5). These are taken from the middle of the bed of the Jordan and carried away (Joshua 4), and their names are soon written upon the front of the gates of the city according to the Apocalypse (Revelation 21:12). They too, as we said, are called gates, because through them alone entry is opened to everyone.

Thus, through many such and similar figures, their number is very frequently prescribed and assigned in the divine writings, so that, as I have acknowledged, their dignity might thereby shine forth, and so that it might be clear that precisely that number—and neither more nor fewer—was to be received.

For although there are still other apostles, such as Paul and Barnabas and the others to whom the rights of apostolic office were divinely entrusted, the mystical number of the mystery has been consecrated in these twelve, and the Church of Christ founded upon the same number, so that Paul and the others may also be gathered to them, and all may sit among their number, judging upon the twelve thrones.

Just as the number of the twelve tribes does not exceed the number that crossed out of Egypt, while the nations too are incorporated into that same number, so neither does the order or number of preachers exceed it; rather, all who are propagated from them are joined to their assembly through faith in Christ and united to the number.

It was necessary that the evident dignity of their mysteries be commended by many and frequent praises in the Scriptures. Therefore, prudent reader, pay attention: the more diligently you examine these matters, the deeper the wonders of God’s Law you will perceive.

“The first,” he says, “is Simon Peter, and Andrew his brother.”

The divine dispensation, which knows the merits of each, now begins their catalogue. But concerning Simon Peter it must be asked whether the word “first” refers to order and number or to merit. There is no doubt that it can refer to both, because just as he is placed first in this catalogue, so too in every other place; he is everywhere set before the others, both individually and generally with them.

He is individual when it is said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18); and: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32).

He is therefore rightly regarded as first in merits, through whom and in whom gifts are transmitted to the others. The others all receive in him the keys of the kingdom of heaven when they are entrusted to him by the Lord in a special way; and the Church of Christ is founded upon them. Hence they are called foundations by the prophet, while they too are made firm upon the rock that is Christ.

Yet what is granted to him as though to him alone is granted to all through him. Therefore in Peter power has precedence and authority excels.

Simon Peter is named to distinguish him from the other Simon, who was called the Cananaean, so that no error concerning them may entangle us; rather, the prescribed and prearranged order may be maintained, so that neither one may ever be received in place of another, nor another outside these, nor any of these be rejected as though he had not been enrolled.

Their order, they say, is distinguished in this way for three reasons: either by the grace of calling or by the perfection of merits. For this reason Peter is perhaps placed at the beginning and Judas Iscariot at the end; an inscription of condemnation is rightly always attached to him, so that both his guilt may thereby be revealed and he may be distinguished from the other apostle also named Judas.

In this matter it must be understood that the sole searcher of hearts, who knows the merits of each, distinguished and arranged them in this way, so that their account might breathe forth mysteries and divine things might be revered in their dispositions.

They acknowledge a third reason as well, as though based on kinship of the flesh, but I do not sufficiently approve this. Although Peter and Andrew, James and John, are joined together as brothers, they are placed in pairs rather for this reason: they were to be sent to preach in such a way that the twofold love they were to preach—love of God and of neighbor—might be displayed in them, and their brotherhood might be made firmer in the spirit.

Thus the brotherhood of Peter and Andrew is designated almost everywhere from the beginning. It is clear that love can exist no less between two people; therefore, I think, the two are joined together quite deliberately, so that they themselves might first be fastened together by the same clasp of love and might join the others, two by two, under the yoke of affection in this cultivation of the Lord.

In this way, the whole structure of the house might grow compact and joined together in the Lord. For God’s cultivation requires that under one yoke of faith two people be bound by the strap of love, lest brotherhood be broken apart and become unruly.

For certainly “no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9:62). Therefore how fittingly they are joined two by two, so that their pairing may rise to the number six.

It is agreed that all things were made in the same reckoning of days, and that humanity was created on the sixth day because six is a perfect number. But because the whole cultivation of the world had been overrun by the thorns of sins and the thickets of unbelief, it was just that an equal number of yokes of oxen should draw the plough of the holy Gospel, in the perfect number, to break up the clods of hearts and scatter the seeds of the word.

Thus, yoked together by the bond of love, they would display the perfection of six, and, counted individually upon the twelve thrones of the tribes, would strive more gloriously to judge them.

[Col. 0404C] Their first double name, Simon, is interpreted as “obedient,” while Peter is interpreted as “acknowledging.” For all perfection of Christian religion begins from obedience, just as the apostasy of the first Adam begins from disobedience; and it arises not from ignorance when one pleases, but from acknowledgment of the truth.

Therefore Peter is rightly said, as I have stated, to mean “acknowledging,” rendered into our language from the Greek. Yet this name is no less derived in Latin from petra, “rock,” which is Christ, and signifies the firmness of his faith.

Thus obedience, which struggles even unto death, possesses not only acknowledgment of the truth but also strength of faith. Hence scharioth, which is placed last in the catalogue, is rightly interpreted as “memorial of the Lord” or “remembrance of his death,” because the true obedience of the apostles must be extended through martyrdom into the remembrance of Christ’s death and become an imitator of his passion even unto death.

Simon is also interpreted as “put away sorrow,” quite fittingly because of the dispensation of his denial, concerning which he wept bitterly in great sorrow and grief. He laid aside that sorrow when, already filled with the Holy Spirit, he poured forth the new wine of joy. He also abandoned the sorrow he had drawn from Christ’s passion when he saw with bodily sight that Christ had risen.

Andrew his brother is joined to him in name according to the tropological interpretation, so that the virtue described above might be supported by courage. For Andrew is interpreted from the Greek as “manly,” so that the meaning may be that neither obedience without manly strength of mind nor manly strength without acknowledgment of the truth and obedience before the Lord is brought to completion.

His first exercises in faith demonstrate how manly and noble he was. The name seems to sound alike in Greek and Hebrew: when John immediately declared, “Behold, the Lamb of God,” he preferred not merely to see Christ but to follow him, and took care to bring his brother to him. Together, leaving everything behind at the sound of a single command, they followed the author of life (John 1:29, 40–41).

His end also clearly reveals his manliness: how vigorously he came to the cross, how courageously he endured, and how nobly he shone in all things. Thus the names of the apostles are proved to have been given by prophetic foreknowledge rather than by chance.

For this reason other names are also imposed upon them: Peter, whose name in both languages is derived from the rock that is Christ, and Boanerges, so that its bearers may be understood as “sons of true thunder.”

Therefore Simon is also interpreted as “hearing sorrow,” because he heard from the Lord: “When you grow old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21:18).

It must not be judged otherwise; rather, it must be understood that all these things are filled throughout with mysteries, so that divine wisdom may correspond to each detail.

The text continues:

James of Zebedee and John his brother. He is called “son of Zebedee” [Col. 0405C] to distinguish him from the other James, so that their names may not be confused in any catalogue. His name is interpreted as “supplanter,” because, when the Lord called him, he was pleased not only to supplant the vices of the flesh but also, when Herod struck the flesh, to despise that very flesh for Christ before all the other apostles. John, however, sprinkled with the grace of Christ, shone forth in the glory of his virginity, and alone at the supper reclined upon the breast of the Savior, so that, wholly possessed by the grace of God, he might clearly indicate that he had derived his name from a prophetic foreknowledge. Hence they also bear, together with the memory of their father, the ancient names of their merits, so that it may plainly be suggested what merit they previously possessed, or by whose grace they were ultimately saved.

Thus Zebedee is interpreted as “fugitive,” representing the one who from the beginning has always fled from the face of the Savior [Col. 0405D], although his power continually apprehends him everywhere. Concerning him the Prophet admonishes the father: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. XLVI, 11). After abandoning him, they are immediately called by the Lord “Boanerges,” that is, “sons of thunder”—at least because they had heard the voice of the Father thundering terribly from heaven concerning Christ: “This is my beloved Son; hear him” (Matt. XVII, 5); or because one of them, as though thundering from the heavenly heights, brought forth that theoretical voice which no one had previously attained: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1). If he had flown still higher, I think that not even the whole world could have contained him.

The other, immediately preaching Christ as though with a trumpet, and preceding the others as an imitator of his passion, gained the palm of martyrdom [Col. 0406A]. Both of them are often led apart by the Lord onto the mountain, and by I know not what privilege of grace are honored together with Peter above the rest.

Philip and Bartholomew. Philip is interpreted as “mouth of the lamp.” And rightly so: when John was preaching, he shone forth first into the recognition of the truth like a lamp that had been kindled, and illuminated another disciple with heavenly light. “The one whom Moses wrote about in the Law and the Prophets,” he said, “we have found: Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth” (John I, 45). See why “mouth of the lamp” is rightly interpreted here as a prophetic indication of things to come: like a torch in the darkness, he taught from the mouth of truth what was contained in the Law and the Prophets.

Bartholomew, although his name is Syriac and not Hebrew, is nevertheless interpreted as “son of the one who suspended the waters”—that is, the streams of teachings in the clouds, which rain upon one city but do not rain upon another, according to the distribution of the divine judgment [Col. 0406B]. Moreover, the saints are rightly called clouds: while they fly toward higher things, Christ suspends in them the waters of life, by which the visited earth is refreshed and enriched with heavenly teachings. Among them this man is rightly called “his son,” because he carries out these things in each person according to the abundance of grace, so that through him the Father’s generosity may also be transmitted to others. It follows:

Thomas and Matthew the tax collector. The other Evangelists place Matthew first in the catalogue of the apostles and Thomas afterward; and they do so without the addition “tax collector,” lest, by recalling his former life, they seem to reproach the apostle whom Christ deigned to illuminate with so great a grace of his compassion [Col. 0406C]. Matthew himself, however, places himself after Thomas and calls himself “tax collector,” plainly for the sake of humility, so that it may be evident to all that where sin had previously abounded, grace abounded still more.

Indeed, by this he also teaches that we ought always to set our former sins before our eyes, and not conceal our offenses after receiving pardon, so that others may be consoled by the hope of forgiveness after guilt, and so that humility may be preserved in the heart through the means of repentance.

Thomas is interpreted as “abyss.” Certainly, the abyss over which the Holy Spirit was once borne (Gen. I, 2), so that, from the weakness of his heart, he might eventually proceed toward the form of right faith when illuminated from above by that same Spirit. Otherwise, after so many proclamations, after the miracles, after the raising of the dead to life, when the others announced that they had seen the Lord [Col. 0406D], how could he have failed to believe, unless his mind was an unformed abyss over which the Holy Spirit was borne, so that he might warm and nourish it toward faith?

For this reason, after carefully touching the wounds, he immediately cried out, saying: “My God and my Lord!” (John XX, 28). Otherwise, unless the same Spirit revived him, he could never have been formed out of such great doubt into the light, so as to recognize divinity in one and the same person. He touches the flesh of the man, yet exclaims “God and Lord.” Therefore Thomas is rightly interpreted as “abyss”: from such great deformity he arrived at such great profundity of mystery.

In Greek he is called Didymus, which is interpreted as “similar” or “twin,” because, as they say, he resembled the Savior in appearance [Col. 0407A], just as two twins customarily reproduce one figure of form and face in alternating likeness. Matthew, moreover, is said to mean “given”—and how fittingly, since from the tax office the grace of the Holy Spirit gave him to us as an apostle and evangelist. Every gift, therefore, is believed to be a gift derived from the gift of the giver. For this reason the Holy Spirit is also very often called “gift” in the sacred writings, because he is the gift of the Father and the Son. This man, too, is rightly called “given” by him, because he was filled with that gift and, without any preceding merit of his own, was immediately changed from the tax office into something better.

James of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus. He called James “of Alphaeus” in the same way to distinguish him from the other James, perhaps because his father was, as the other’s father was, [Col. 0407B] the father of that James. This James is plainly written in the Gospels as the brother of the Lord, although both are surnamed from their fathers. For it is established that Mary, the wife of this Alphaeus, was the sister of Mary, the mother of the Lord; John is read to have called her “Mary of Clopas” in his Gospel, perhaps taking the name from her father or from some member of her family; or certainly because, after Alphaeus died, she married another man, Clopas; or because she bore the surname that had been given to her for some other reason.

Alphaeus, in the Hebrew language, is interpreted as “thousandth” or “learned,” so that he may be the son of a learned or perfect man, who was destined to be ordained the first bishop at Jerusalem by the apostles. It should be noted that, just as there are two Simons, so there are two Jameses and two Judases, counted together with their surnames. For just as perfect obedience consists in heart and deed, so the supplanting of vices must exist no less in the soul [Col. 0407C] than in the flesh, and faith in the heart must contribute no less to righteousness than confession by the mouth to salvation.

Hence the Prophet also sings: “He will confess to you, O God; he will confess” (Ps. LXXIV, 1), as though he plainly said: “He will confess to you with heart and mouth,” lest perhaps one without the other be condemned by you, who are the searcher of hearts. These six are doubled, so that the perfection of the number six may be made firm through twelve, and the twofold substance of the human being may be united in honoring the Trinity through these three virtues: beginning with obedience, then supplanting the assaults of vices on every side, and proceeding from confession of the heart to confession of the mouth, even—if it should occur—through the suffering of martyrdom unto salvation.

I have said this so that the prudent reader may not think that anything in these matters is devoid of mystery.

Thaddaeus himself [Col. 0407D] is the one whom Luke names in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles as “Judas of James”; elsewhere he bears the surname Lebbaeus, from “heart,” which we may render, as a diminutive, “little heart.” Perhaps he used these two names first for the sake of accommodation, as though expressing something playful, because the diminutive “little heart” seems to sound more agreeably—expressing a mother’s affection amid the infant’s playthings—than if he were called “heart,” a word that conveys the tenderness of love.

He is the one whom ecclesiastical history records as having been sent by the Savior to the city of Edessa, to King Abgar. For he was the brother of James, the brother of the Lord, as he himself writes in his Epistle. Hence he too is called the brother of the Savior, as his fellow citizens testify. Astonished at the miracles, they said [Col. 0408A]: “Is this not the carpenter’s son and Mary’s, the brother of James and Joseph and Judas and Simon?” (Matt. XVII, 55). They were not brothers of the Savior through his mother, as Helvidius foolishly claims, but through kinship of race, just as it is customary in the Scriptures for relatives to be called brothers.

Simon the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed the Lord. He placed these men with the addition of their surnames in order to distinguish Simon from Peter and Judas from James. This Simon was from the village of Cana in Galilee, where the Lord changed water into wine. Luke calls him “the Zealot” in his Gospel, because Cana is interpreted as “zeal”; hence, by a proper interpretation, Cananaean is called Zealot on account of his excessive fervor of charity. The zeal for the house of Christ had inflamed him, and therefore he was brought to completion in martyrdom [Col. 0408B].

Judas, however, took the name Iscariot either from the village in which he was born or from the tribe of Issachar, by a certain foreshadowing of the future, for his condemnation. Issachar is interpreted as “reward,” because he pursued the reward of betrayal, concerning which the Prophet says in the person of the Lord: “They weighed out my reward, thirty pieces of silver, the price at which they valued me” (Zech. XI, 12).

Moreover, Iscariot sounds like “memory of death,” so that he is inexcusable because he betrayed the Lord not by accident but after meditating upon death; he carried for a long time in his mind the memory of him, considering how or when he should betray him. He is also called “memory of death” because, whenever we remember him, we immediately remember the Lord’s passion, so that the obedience which began [Col. 0408C] in Simon might be brought to completion in the flesh through the other Simon, and so that, persevering in confession on both sides, we might always retain the memory of Christ’s death until, if it should occur, we too might be brought to completion in martyrdom for his sake.

It must not therefore be thought that he was chosen among the apostles without God’s foreknowledge: the interpretation of his name corresponded to him, and he was chosen last, as though he were already to be rejected from their number. Christ preferred to risk his judgment concerning him among the unskilled rather than its fulfillment. Especially since, in a similar manner, others are now chosen in the Church: some so that they may be tested and, once approved, may attain the crown; others so that they may test others, in whom the devil works as in “sons of distrust,” whom the Apostle also calls false brothers.

Some are chosen so that they may be saved [Col. 0408D], others so that through them the good may be exercised. Yet all are chosen, for different reasons, according to God’s foreknowledge and providence. This does not mean that they are predetermined so that they could not be other than evil; rather, they are foreknown as the sort of persons each will become, although they do not yet exist as such: the former by grace, the latter by God’s just judgment abandoned in the mass of perdition, since they were not predestined to life.

All, nevertheless, as I have said, are known and foreknown. God’s knowledge is mistaken in nothing; his judgment deviates in nothing from what is true and just. This is the depth of his riches, concerning which the Apostle exclaims: “How incomprehensible are his ways!” (Rom. XI, 33).

Therefore, whenever a faithful person is deserted by a companion, whenever he has been wronged or even betrayed, let him bear it patiently. For just as all these things had been foretold concerning this man, so [Col. 0409A] nearly every page testifies concerning wicked and false brothers that they too will arise. Hence the Lord wished to be betrayed by a disciple and wished also to be deserted, so that you would not be broken when you saw your judgment fail or your benefaction come to an end.

These twelve Jesus sent. Hence they are specifically called “sent,” since apostle in Greek is interpreted by the Latin word missi, “sent.” Although others have also been sent, these men are more particularly appointed under the mystical number twelve, so that the order of Christ’s wisdom might serve the realities and figures of all the Scriptures.

For this reason it is pointedly said: “These twelve Jesus sent,” as though they had been fixed and marked out in their number, the ones whom Moses once sent to explore the land (Deut. I, 23) [Col. 0409B]. Those men, because they were a figure, are sent without their individual names; these men, in whom the truth shines forth, and whom Rahab the prostitute alone received, are assigned with their names displayed and fixed in advance, so that no one might take offense at them.

They are joined together two by two with great appropriateness, so that they might carry on their shoulders the cluster with which the nations would be intoxicated—two and two, because charity cannot exist to the same degree except between two persons. These are the twelve months, which, with the sun of righteousness shining upon them, together complete the favorable year, the acceptable year. These are the twelve hours of the day; whoever walks in them certainly does not stumble.

Therefore Jesus sent these twelve, so that no one might seek another light except the one they display, and no one might receive any doctrine other than what they bring. For these are the true explorers who explored all truth concerning Christ [Col. 0409C] and the divine majesty, and who carried the mortification of Christ on the cross upon their joyful shoulders all the way to us, with glad steps.

And he commanded them: “Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles.” Here, then, the force and meaning of the commandments must be considered, because not all commandments are bounded by an equal weight or purpose. Some serve only to signify life; others to govern the conduct of life; still others are to be observed dispensationally for a time and fulfilled continually in a tropological sense. Such is the command: “Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles.” Otherwise, what he said to these same apostles would be contradictory: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

How, then, would they teach all nations if, for the sake of teaching, they were not to go not only to their cities and roads but even to their companionship and fellowship, and if they were not to leave Judaea? And from where did their sound go out into all the earth and reach to its very ends, if it did not flow to the Gentiles after being carried by them? [Col. 0409D]

Therefore one must not fail to recognize that commands of this kind were given dispensationally for a time and must be continually carried out according to the tropological sense. They were to be observed for a time, until, rejected by Judaea, they might proceed divinely to all peoples.

He gave this command so that the Jews, to whom Christ had been promised and to whom he had come as the lost sheep of the house of Israel, would not take offense if the apostles went first to the Gentiles, with whom it was not lawful according to the Law to associate. He remembered his own command: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble” (Matt. XVIII, 6). This was especially so because they did not yet believe in him [Col. 0410A] and therefore could be more greatly scandalized if the apostles abandoned those to whom the promise had been made and went to outsiders.

But as soon as the Jews judged themselves unworthy of eternal life, this command was dissolved—not because it had been a shadow, but because it had been given for a time. From this it is clear that all the commandments of the divine Law must be understood according to the sense in which they were given, and must not be entirely violated through human presumption.

Nevertheless, in the tropological sense this must continually be observed: pious preachers must never go onto the roads of the Gentiles, which are the actions of a wicked life. Nor may they ever enter the cities of the Samaritans, which are the fortifications of heretics. Thus those who were sent to the salvation of the Gentiles are rightly warned to abstain in conduct and life from the ignorance of paganism, and morally not to enter [Col. 0410B] the cities of the Samaritans—especially since he himself took care of the Samaritan woman.

It is therefore clear that they were forbidden to approach the doctrines and depraved practices of those whose speech spreads like cancer, but were to preach freely and everywhere to all the sincere and undefiled discipline of the true teacher.

As a literal matter, the Samaritans are those whom Sargon placed in charge of guarding the land of Israel after the ten tribes had been taken captive. Hence they are interpreted as “guards.” They were the first to begin corrupting the Law of the Old Testament, receiving only the five books of Moses, and those same books corrupted by the perversity of the scribes. For this reason they are rightly shown to bear the person of heretics, who know how to divide what is solid and violate what is whole.

He therefore first forbids entering among them before the Passion, because they too were from the Gentiles [Col. 0410C], so that, after the apostles’ preaching had been rejected by Judaea, the holy preachers might come afterward, in due order, to the calling of the Gentiles.

“Going forth,” he says, “preach, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’” This, then, the first herald of truth taught; this Christ made the beginning of his preaching: that the kingdom of heaven had drawn near. This he also first commanded the apostles to preach, because the whole power of the Lord’s might was transferred to them, so that those who had been earthly in Adam and had lost the image and likeness of God might now receive the perfect image and likeness of Christ, differing in nothing from the virtues of their Lord through the power they had received.

Therefore those who had previously been earthly rightly first become heavenly, and are commanded to preach that the kingdom of heaven has drawn near—that is, that the image and likeness are now [Col. 0410D] being taken into fellowship with the truth, so that all the saints who are called by the name “heaven” may reign with Christ, and so that Christ may henceforth possess an everlasting kingdom in them.

For the soul of the just is the seat of wisdom, and wisdom is Christ; Christ, however, dwells nowhere except among heavenly things. Concerning them we read: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII, 1). Therefore he immediately granted them the power of adoption, by which he gave them authority to become children of God, and then granted them the works of divinity.

“Cure the sick,” he says, “raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons.” Thus, by concentrating on visible things, they might not only recognize the deity in Christ, but also have no doubt that those same apostles would be gods [Col. 0411A].

Let us not be surprised that the first man was told, “You are earth, and into earth you will go” (Gen. III, 19), if those who are reborn in Christ hear: “You are heaven, and into heaven you will go.” Not, of course, into the heaven of the firmament, which is local, but into spiritual heaven, plainly because God is Spirit. In this heaven God is believed to dwell and, in a certain manner, to walk locally, although he is without limits and without locality; we believe that he is everywhere not by place but by power.

Hence he himself says elsewhere: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (II Cor. VI, 6). And elsewhere: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII, 21). This kingdom of heaven is rightly said to have drawn near—not through an inclination of the heaven [Col. 0411B] called the firmament, but through the illumination of faith by which human beings are made God’s own.

The kingdom of heaven is therefore called the present Church not only because it already reigns in heaven through hope, but because, having spiritually become heaven, Christ reigns in it, just as he reigns in the angels who are spiritually called “heaven.” For Christ is the kingdom of the saints; and the saints, as we have said, are called heaven.

Their kingdom is rightly said to have drawn near when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. By this gift human beings became heaven, and Christ himself became their kingdom, so that they might also attain the kingdoms of heaven. First, because he descended, drawing near, and we ourselves became the kingdom of heaven.

“Cure the sick,” he says, “raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons.” There is no doubt that all these things [Col. 0411C] had come about through the devil’s deception. Therefore it was fitting that, once a human being had been healed, he should again be given the power that what the devil had inflicted by deceit and malicious persuasion these men should heal by the power of faith, and that they should drive the very rulers of the world from the bodies they had possessed.

This was a great power and a great gift, a great restoration and a great confidence for those who had fallen. Otherwise, while the world flourished, while the human race had long been sliding into faithlessness, and while the world had grown insolent against God through ignorance of its blindness, with the propagation of the flesh flowing forth not merely for increase but for the wickedness of pleasure, who would ever have brought invisible realities visibly to light? Who would have believed in another life? Who would have recalled himself from so long a habit? Who would have restrained himself from the broad road on which everyone walked and confined himself to one so narrow and constricted?

No one, unless he had been moved to faith by great miracles, so that through what was visibly done he might grasp inwardly by faith the invisible things that were preached. These things were granted for this purpose—not as theatrical phantoms, as the unbelief of the pagans asserts [Col. 0411D], but as divine miracles of power, corresponding to his power alone: so that, invited by the benefit, people might believe through hearing in the greater things that are invisible; moved by visible events, they might understand from the report the power of the Godhead; and, through the outcome of health, they might rejoice to escape the devil’s deceit.

Hence the Apostle plainly says: “Signs were given not to believers but to unbelievers” (I Cor. XIV, 22), so that faith might be born in them through these things; and once faith had been received, the power of adoption might be granted. Through the power of faith evils would indeed be driven away and the devil conquered; and once he had been conquered, liberty and triumph would be owed to human beings.

“You have received without payment,” he says; “give without payment.” For he plainly wishes the true image and likeness of the Godhead, which human beings had lost, to be restored in them.
