He first granted them the power to correct whatever the devil had corrupted through his prompting; then, just as they receive benefits from God, to give benefits freely, so that the preaching of the holy Gospel might be free to all, and the restoration of the image and likeness complete—lest either the administration of so great a mystery be corrupted or the likeness restored in conduct be violated for the sake of avarice.

“Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts. No bag for the road [Col. 0412B], nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff.” These commands therefore belong not only to the apostles but to all those to whom the preaching of the holy Gospel has been entrusted, although many corrupt them.

Yet unless they are rightly understood, they not only drive any careless person into error, but also seem to create disagreement among the holy Evangelists. Thus, first [Col. 0412A], since he commands them to give freely, the prohibition of gold, silver, and money appears superfluous—especially since Judas, by the Lord’s commission, had a money box from which they bought what seemed necessary to them. Elsewhere, too, the disciples went into a city to buy food for themselves.

From this it is plainly evident that the Lord did not forbid necessities but cut away excess. Hence he pointedly says: “Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money” [Col. 0412C]. For it is one thing to have the necessities of food and clothing for the moment, and another to possess with anxiety or greed what has been acquired through long concern.

Nevertheless, as I judge, he teaches not that a grudging or costly store of gold, silver, and bronze should be kept only in one’s belts, but that preachers ought to have such confidence in the Lord that, even though they do not foresee them, they should not at all distrust that the expenses of the present life will fail them.

He therefore cuts away riches with sufficient foresight: he hastens almost to remove even the necessities of the present life, so that our heart may be where our treasure is understood to be. And lest the apostles seem to preach more for the sake of profit than for human salvation, he removes everything that could cause scandal and grants necessities from the Gospel, so that none of them might appear to think about tomorrow.

But it must be asked why Matthew and Luke report that the Lord prohibited them from carrying a staff on the road, whereas Mark [Col. 0412D] grants them nothing except that they may carry only a staff and walk wearing sandals—although Matthew pointedly forbids them entirely to possess footwear. For this reason some monks of the East who live in monasteries observe these commands literally even to the present day, and, following barefoot practices, insist that they ought to be observed.

Therefore, lest the Evangelists seem to hold contradictory views, one must seek the manner—here as elsewhere—in which Holy Scripture may be understood catholicly and the authority of so great a mystery not violated.

According to Matthew [Col. 0413A], the Lord is reported to have said that they should not even carry a staff (Matt. X, 10). According to Mark, however, that they should take nothing on the road except a staff (Mark VI, 8). They do indeed seem to speak contrary things, but the things are mystical and true, so that we may understand one staff to have been mentioned with one meaning—the one that is to be carried according to Mark—and another with another meaning—the one that is not to be carried according to Matthew and Luke.

It is like the statements: “The Lord your God is testing you” (Deut. XIII, 3), and “God tests no one” (Jas. I, 13). The latter concerns seduction: God tests no one in the sense that he deceives him. The former concerns proof: Abraham and Job, and the other saints, were tested so that, once proved, they might be made manifest, according to what is said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. XXII)—that is, “I have made it known.”

Likewise, what was said above, “To know whether you love him” (Deut. XIII, 3), means “to make it known whether you truly wish to love him.” So also in this passage, the staff that is to be carried on the road [Col. 0413B] is the power of the Savior, which they had received from him, and the governance of souls.

Concerning this power he immediately added, saying: “The worker is worthy of his wages.” The Apostle explains this wage when he says: “Those who serve the Gospel should live from the Gospel” (I Cor. IX, 14). And: “Do we not have this authority?” (Ibid., 4). Therefore, when the Lord had said, “Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money,” and the rest, he immediately added:

“The worker is worthy of his wages.” From this he sufficiently shows why he did not want them to possess these things: plainly because he was sending them in such a way that he showed they ought to receive these things from those to whom they were already preaching the Gospel as believers [Col. 0413C].

Thus he spoke to them so that, secure, they would neither possess nor carry the necessities of this life—not even great or small ones. For this reason, according to Matthew and Luke, they were to receive all the necessities of life from the faithful, by the authority and arrangement of the Lord, and were to demand no superfluous things from their hearers. For just as rightful authority comes from the Lord, so wrongful presumption comes from the devil.

Hence it is clear that the Lord said both things: that they should carry a staff on the road and that they should not carry one. For just as there is the staff of the righteous, concerning which it is said, “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. XXII, 4), so there is also “the staff of sinners,” which the Lord will not leave upon the lot of the righteous (Ps. CXXIV, 3).

The staff, therefore, concerning which the Lord warned [Col. 0413D] that his disciples should not carry it on the road—which is Christ—was the staff by which, under the pretext of the authority due to them, through which they were worthy of their wages, they might oppress their hearers with costly demands, as though by permission.

This does not mean that they were not permitted to seek necessary food with their own hands, as Paul and others worked with their hands so as not to use this authority. Rather, he grants the permission when he says:

“Worthy is the laborer of his wage.” And he is commanded to carry nothing on the road except a staff, from whose authority, certainly, the necessities of life would come; no teacher of the faithful should doubt this (Exod. 4:20). For this is the staff from the root of Jesse, which Moses once carried with him, and by whose authority he performed many signs [Col. 0414A] (Num. 20:11). When he doubted its power at the waters of Contradiction, he offended. So also preachers, unless they use it lawfully and by Christ’s authority, and unless, faithfully and without doubting, they depend entirely on him, are driven far away backward. Therefore preachers must not seek gold, silver, money, or anything else superfluous from the faithful, as though from the staff that belongs to sinners; rather, they must presume upon the Lord’s authority.

But one may ask how they are to give freely what they received freely, if “the laborer is worthy of his wage,” and if from this wage they may receive the necessities of life from their hearers. The matter is resolved as follows. It is one thing to expend the mysteries of the word for the sake of profit as a wage, and to seek from this the conveniences of the present life; 487 it is another to receive scarcely sufficient food, [Col. 0414B] not merely so that we may live, but so that we may preach freely. Although these things are already a wage for the work, they are nevertheless the gains of the Gospel. Therefore it is just to receive living expenses from those to whom we offer the rewards of heavenly life, since these things are sometimes necessary for the sake of evangelizing. Thus such provisions are granted to preachers out of necessity, not sought for the sake of profit; and the mysteries of life are imparted to the faithful freely, though not as payment. This wage indeed begins here, from the labors performed for the faithful, so that there it may be completed for believers by right, in the vision of truth.

That no sandals are to be carried on the feet should be understood more according to the sense; for, as I said, according to Mark he commands them to go about wearing sandals (Mark 6:9). Hence even today the Lord’s sandals are kept at Rome, and they are displayed with the feet both covered and uncovered—that is, neither bare below, toward the ground, nor covered above. He wished to show that they ought to be shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace, thereby indicating that the Gospel must neither be concealed nor entangled in earthly advantages.

But when here he did not permit them to carry sandals, he suggests the examples of foolish deeds: they are not even to look upon them, lest anyone think that the works of his own body are protected, as it were, by dead skins. For there are some who try to defend their wickedness by the wickedness of others: when they see others doing such things, they think themselves more freely permitted to do them. Thus, just as feet are covered with the skins of the dead, so they protect themselves, as it were, by a kind of stripping away. For just as these two Evangelists—Matthew and Mark—give contrary commands, so elsewhere the same Lord commands holy Moses: “Take off your sandals from your feet” (Exod. 3:5); and likewise Joshua (Josh. 5:15). But at the eating of the lamb something quite different is proclaimed. For he says:

“This is how you shall eat it: let your loins be girded, and you shall have sandals on your feet” (Exod. 12:11).

Moreover, the true Lamb of God is Christ, whom John points out: “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God; behold, he who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). Therefore, whether we are faithful in the ministry of the Lord’s body and blood or are all believers together in faith, we ought to eat him and commit him to the innermost places of our hearts in such a way that we have not only our loins girded with chastity, but are also shod in preparation for the Gospel [Col. 0415A] of peace, 488 since, just as sandals protect bodily feet, defend against the severity of cold, and resist the bites of serpents and the pricks of thorns, so the precepts of Scripture—with which we are commanded to fortify the steps of our minds—repel the deceits of the serpent, the devil, and the harsh cold of the north wind, as well as the thorns and thistles of the nations and heretics attacking from every side.

Therefore all who celebrate the Lord’s Passover ought to use such sandals. What good is it if you have your loins girded with chastity but are careless, as though stripped of the protection of the holy Scriptures, like sandals made of skins? For we know what was said to the devil: “And you shall lie in wait for his heel” (Gen. 3:15). His snares are many, and every day we are wounded by them. Therefore it was not without profound reason that one Evangelist said that we should have our feet shod with sandals, while another said that we should carry no sandals on the road.

So also in the Old Testament, while we eat the Passover, we are commanded to be shod. And we read that Moses and Joshua received a quite different command. But if the order and reason are considered, the great difference is immediately resolved without ambiguity, when the reason itself is added at once: “Take off your sandals from your feet,” he says, “for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. 3:5). It is therefore shown that the land of Egypt, where the earlier command concerning the Passover was given, is holy ground; and for this reason the people of God are commanded there to have sandals and to carry them on their feet, whereas in holy ground they are ordered to remove them.

These matters, however, must be considered carefully, because they foreshadow great mysteries. Therefore, as long as we remain in this Egypt, celebrating the Lord’s Passover, we must walk with shod feet and fortify our steps with the coverings of the holy Scriptures, because our walking is not secure unless our feet are furnished and covered with the Lord’s commandments—until we enter that land of holy promise which is owed to the righteous and prepared for God’s elect. Of it it is said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4). In it there are no thorns or thistles, no serpents or scorpions; there the devil does not approach with his ministers.

We also have the Lord Jesus, as I said shortly before, testified by John to have been shod: “Of whom,” he says, “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandals” (John 1:27). But the meaning is quite different in Christ. He was shod not for his own sake—that is, clothed in flesh—for the earth could not endure the bare footprints of his majesty. Yet when he speaks of his sandals, he indicates the steps of the holy Scriptures, by which his way of life and knowledge walk and range among all who dwell upon the earth. Therefore John judges himself unworthy to loosen the strap of his sandals, because his revered footsteps, as though still shod in this age, are those of the Word of God, which no one can fully unfasten. For now “we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face”; then nothing will remain covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known.

And for this reason, in this Gospel the apostles are forbidden to carry sandals, when it is said to them: “Do not possess gold,” and shortly afterward, “nor sandals, nor a staff.” Mark, however, says that the Lord commanded them to take nothing with them on the road except a staff, and, as I said, to have their feet shod with sandals. This is so that they may preach the word of God as though it were shod and covered in the mystery, because of the thorns and thistles of blasphemers and the poisons of heretics, lest holy things immediately be exposed to dogs and precious things be thrown before swine.

But those who listen with faithful and devoted minds, and desire to know divine things with sound intention, are treated as though they were already walking in holy ground. [Col. 0416B] Since they are considered perfect in faith, they are rightly commanded not to carry sandals; secure, they can bring forth the naked testimonies of Scripture, walk there with uncovered footsteps, and unlock divine secrets.

Therefore Peter, at the angel’s command (Acts 12:8), put on his sandals in prison, and thus went out to the hostile Jews and opposing powers, so that, with his feet shod in preparation for the Gospel, he might tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon all the power of the enemy. The bride also is praised in the Song of Songs as beautiful in sandals, since she too is said to flower like a lily among thorns (Song 7:1; 2:2). For this reason, walking through the wilderness of this age, she must be shod, lest she be harmed by the bites of serpents or the pricks of sin.

Moses also says in the blessings he pronounced upon Israel, speaking in the person of Christ: “Iron and bronze shall be your sandal” (Deut. 33:25). These two metals appear very strong. One of them cuts through and breaks whatever seems hard; the other does not at any time decay through the defect of rust. Thus, as though shod with these, Christ came to trample and crush all the heads of the dragon and to break all the power of the enemy. He would not be affected by any contagion of vices in the world, but would walk victorious in all things, until he had subdued all his enemies and cast them beneath his feet.

But we must return to the deeper reason why he expressly forbade carrying weights of gold, silver, and money in their belts, unless it was both to cut away avarice and to reveal something else through allegory. For in the belt he signifies the equipment for ministry and the effectiveness of the work; from this we are warned that nothing in the ministry of the Gospel should be for sale, and that the work of the apostolate should not be the profit of gold, silver, or money. Hence the Lord says: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35). They are commanded to gird themselves for this purpose, so that they may be more ready for the work of ministry.

Paul also urges us to have our feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace (Eph. 6:15), although, as I said, Moses is told: “Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. 3:5). From this it is clear that these things have a mystical meaning, although some are to be observed literally; and therefore we must be shod, lest the dust of sin cling to our steps. If, however, while unshod, the dust of the faithless should again cling to us in some respect, it must certainly be shaken from our feet, lest we be defiled by any of their deceits.

“Nor a bag,” he says, “on the road, nor two tunics.” Thus, having cut away the treasures of avarice, he immediately restrains gluttony and rebukes the philosophers called Bacchionites or Baccroperitae, who, considering all the things of the world worthless, carried their storerooms with them. One of them, carrying none of his possessions except a cup from which to drink water, saw someone drinking with hollowed hands and immediately threw it away: “If I had known,” he said, “that nature had given me this skill, I would not have carried even this.” How much more unworthy it would have been for the apostles to carry sacks of food, when they were permitted to receive necessities from the Gospel.

Nevertheless, we read [Col. 0417B] that Judas had a money box (John 13:29), in which he carried not burdens of food, but necessities for living and certain things for the use of the poor. It is clear that he forbade carrying two tunics—not because in regions of Scythia stiff with icy snow, or on many of the peaks of the Alps, one tunic could suffice for everyone, but because “tunic” is rightly understood here as necessary clothing. Otherwise, when he forbade two, he might not have prohibited other kinds of garments. Hence Paul orders that his cloak be brought to him from Troas (2 Tim. 4:31); but it is more correctly understood that “tunic” means the complete and necessary clothing of life, although Saint Basil judged that one simple tunic could suffice for his own people.

This, then, is what he says: “Nor two tunics,” lest any of them should think that, after the one he was wearing, he ought to carry another, anxious that he might be in need—especially since, from the authority mentioned earlier, he could receive what was necessary from anyone already instructed. Accordingly, Mark forbade them not merely to carry or possess two tunics, but more explicitly to wear them (Mark 6:9), indicating that they ought not to walk in the Gospel with duplicity, but simply, clothed in the wedding garment. That garment is the one uncut and seamless, woven from above throughout; whoever has it will not fear the cold of snow, but will walk confidently, protected against everything.

Nevertheless, because the apostles’ condition appeared harsh in all these matters, he concludes by saying:

“Worthy is the laborer of his wage.”

As though he were saying openly: “Receive only as much as is necessary for you in clothing and food.” Hence Paul says: “Having food and clothing, with these let us be content” (1 Tim. 6:8). In this second preaching, therefore, after granting them the power to heal the weak for the sake of love of neighbor, he turns his speech to his own friends, indicating the manner in which they should show that they preach the Gospel for the sake of salvation rather than profit. And just as the discourse on the mountain was immediately confirmed by works of power, so to these men, because the commands given are harsh, an abundant operation of virtues is granted.

“Into whatever city you enter, inquire who in it is worthy.”

The pious teacher sets before the disciples everything useful and honorable, lest the Gospel be disgraced by any infamy. But when entering an unfamiliar city, how could the apostles know who in it was worthy, except through the report of its citizens? Therefore they are commanded to inquire. This does not mean that they should seek someone possessing the dignity of faith in those cities, but someone worthy in character and of good reputation—like many among the Gentiles and Jews who pursued honesty and nobility of birth. What remarkable dignity belongs to the apostles, for whose hospitality a host is sought not merely as anyone might ordinarily be sought even by the great, but as someone worthy—not less so that he may impart something than that he may receive it. Otherwise the dignity of such great preaching would be disgraced by infamy if the host were unworthy and conspicuous among his fellow citizens. Great, therefore, is the dignity of those to whom God grants benefits; but greater still is the dignity of one who, if found worthy, receives grace from him. Yet whoever is found fit for these things is praiseworthy in both respects.

[Col. 0418B] “Remain there,” he says. Do not wander about, running here and there, so that, since a worthy host has been found, hearers may be able to gather in that same place. He therefore taught what they should do when entering a city, and then what they should request for the host’s house: “Say,” he says, “Peace to this house.”

He teaches in particular what he presented in general. For the heavenly army of angels, at Christ’s coming to us, presented this peace to the world: “Glory,” they say, “to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). And this is why a worthy person is sought: namely, that he should be a host of good will, since nothing richer or more prosperous can be found. Indeed, he does not command them to ask peace of walls, but of human beings, from whom houses in heaven are also built.

If the house is worthy—that is, of good will—“your peace,” he says, “will come upon it.” Paul also very often first asks peace for those to whom he writes, so that, having received peace with God, those who are children of wrath may become children of adoption. It should be noted that the peace of God is now called the peace of the apostles, because they too, having been reconciled to God, bestow the gift of peace on others from the gift of the giver.

But if the house is not worthy—that is, if it is not of good will, since peace cannot come to others—“your peace will return to you.” It will return because it had gone forth through speech, not so as to abandon those by whom it had been sent, but because the host refused to receive the peace offered to him on account of the wickedness of his heart. Thus both the reward of the peace offered and peace itself overflow entirely upon the preachers, refreshing them with its dew, insofar as they were not received and therefore suffered no scruple of mind.

But if there is a son of peace in the house through good will, the Lord’s peace will rest upon it, causing the mind reconciled to God to rest from every disturbance of the world. Otherwise, peace suffers no annoyance, since it repels all internal rebellions. But if not, “your peace will return to you,” because none of the preachers will be without fruit.

“And whoever does not receive you or hear your words, when you go out of the house or city, shake the dust from your feet.”

Both points must be observed, because there is neither reception of the apostles without acceptance of their preaching, nor acceptance of the preaching without the duty of charity. Therefore he joins them together: “When they do not receive you or hear you,” and, “when you go out of the house or city.” First from the house, if perhaps someone worthy may be found in the same city, because one person does not prejudice all the others; and likewise, if someone in the city receives them, that does not excuse the house that disliked the peace offered to it.

“When you go out,” he says, “shake the dust from your feet.” What if the city is muddy, so that mud rather than dust clings to the feet? I think this should be understood more according to the sense than literally. Those who did not receive peace remained in their impiety, of whom it is said through the Prophet: “Not so the impious, not so, but like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:4). And elsewhere concerning the devil: “Dust shall be his bread” (Isa. 65:25).

Therefore the dust is the anathema of the wretched city or house, so that it may not cling to the steps of the apostles who refused to receive the peace of their reconciliation. They are to remain cast away from the face of the living, possessing no solidity of faith, but being dust in the devil’s food, unwilling to receive the rain of teaching brought to them from heaven by which they might be watered.

Hence another Evangelist expressly says: “As a testimony against them” (Luke 9:5). For if they had received them or their teaching, they would not have remained dust. Therefore the dust is shaken off as a testimony, to indicate what they had remained through their guilt, and that, cast away from the apostles’ feet, they are driven here and there toward darkness by the force of the winds. Or the dust is shaken off as a testimony to the apostles, as a sign of their labor: they came to those people, and those people refused to receive peace. Thus they had shared none of earthly things with them, so that they would not even allow dust to cling to their feet, but left everything belonging to them under anathema.

They shake the dust from their feet when they leave, because holy teachers, while fleeing the wickedness of their hearers, must allow no sin to cling to them; and if anything does cling, they must shake it off quickly, so that they may be found fit for others.

“Amen I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom than for that city.”

What remarkable dignity, then, and what great consolation belong to the apostles, since such grace is bestowed through their reception, and God is so greatly offended by their rejection. But we must examine what he means by saying: “It will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom.” Will the very land, which was once consumed by fire, come again in the judgment? Certainly not. Rather, he placed the land for its inhabitants, who, although they were once condemned for their crimes, will nevertheless suffer more tolerable punishments in the future. For human beings are rightly called “earth,” since it was said to Adam: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19).

But the wretched Sodomites are both now consumed by fire and tormented in the future, though more tolerably. For a comparison is made from lighter things to heavier ones; and therefore, for those for whom it will be more tolerable and lighter, it will nevertheless be punitive. Let those who carelessly pass judgment on anyone hear that God does not judge twice for the same thing, unaware that some begin to be tormented here—not so that their torment may end at the end of life, but so that those who see them may be terrified, and so that they themselves may mourn without end for what they have done. Otherwise, even Pharaoh would retain hope of pardon, which is absurd.

Therefore we must believe that only conversion to God puts an end to evils, and not the torture of guilt without grace—a torture that begins here in order to rage forever. From this passage, however, it is gathered that just as the reward of the saints is deferred until their rest, so the punishment of torments is deferred until their penalties. But he who searches hearts and knows all things most justly discerns what he should restore to each according to his deeds.

Otherwise, who can contemplate why it should be more tolerable for Sodom and more severe for that city? We can nevertheless say that the peace of reconciliation was not preached to the Sodomites, nor was anyone sent to announce to them the life of salvation; rather, angels were immediately sent to destroy it. When they entered to Lot, they found at least one person with whom they could turn aside. Or perhaps Sodom suffered punishment here so that, for this reason, it may have something lighter in the future.

But wretched is the city that rejected the peace offered to it and refused the grace of hospitality. It despised both laws—the law of nature and that of Moses—and resisted the grace of Christ, whereas the Sodomites had trampled upon only the law of nature, which had almost entirely been abolished, though they had long been enticed by it.

“Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves.”

This utterance is full of all authority, as though it plainly thundered: “Although you are few and insignificant, lowly and unlearned, behold, I am the one who sends you as sheep in the midst of wolves.” If the savage and innumerable ferocity of the wolves terrifies you, take courage, because I am the one who sends you.

What a remarkable height of power! It would indeed be frightening if wolves were sent among sheep, even if they were few. But now a very few sheep are sent to overcome thousands of wolves, whose rapacity had occupied the whole world. Yet the Lion from the tribe of Judah had brought forth these sheep; therefore he himself sent them as unconquerable. These are the ones of whom it was said shortly before: “Jesus sent these twelve,” designating them as innocent by the name of sheep. He rightly compared the wolves to the scribes and Pharisees, as well as to heretics and philosophers, who are always lying in wait for the simplicity of the Lord’s flock.

“Be,” he says, “wise as serpents and simple as doves.”

He seems to command things that are opposed to one another, but they agree sufficiently through their resemblance. For Moses also healed the people from the bites of serpents by the sight of the bronze serpent that he had raised up (Num. 21:9); Christ, hanging on the cross, expressed its truth.

They are not commanded to possess the cunning of the ancient serpent, but, according to the natural philosophers, to imitate their natural prudence. Some of them say that serpents carry extremely precious gems in their heads. When people wish to charm them so that they may take these gems away, the serpents press one ear against a very hard stone and cover the other from above with their tail, so that they may not hear the charmer’s voice. By doing this, they both guard what is precious and do not lose their lives.

Thus the holy apostles are warned to guard with their prudence the pearl which they purchased after selling everything, and firmly to press their mind—which is the principal part of the human being—against the rock that is Christ. They must cover the ear of the flesh with the tail, that is, with the end of life, even if this should occur through suffering, so that they may not hear the voice of the charmer.

Great, therefore, is the prudence of carrying Christ within us and guarding our life, lest he be taken from us by any deceits of the wicked. For the scribes and Pharisees, as well as heretics and philosophers, strive by their enchantments and wicked persuasions to take Christ away from us.

Another prudence of the serpent is also mentioned: it presents its entire body in order to guard its head, in which its life resides. When it grows old, it enters a narrow opening in the rocks so that it may strip off its old skin. So also, while guarding within us our head, which is Christ, we should lay down the body and, entering by the narrow way, strip off the old garment, so that we may be renewed in all things.

This is the good prudence of the serpent which Paul explains when he says: “Be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil” (Rom. 16:19). Christ therefore placed prudence first, so that simplicity might be secure. Then follows the simplicity of the dove, lest our prudence before God be found foolish, concerning which it is said: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the prudence of the prudent” (1 Cor. 1:19; Isa. 29:14).

For this reason these qualities should support one another by alternating their outlooks, lest there be in us that simplicity of which it is said that the simple believe everything. Indeed, in the world the children of light are more prudent, and more simple in their own folly. Perhaps we should be found simple before the prudent in the affairs of the world, but prudent in what is good before the simple.

The natural philosophers also report that whenever serpents wish to drink water, they first cast off their poisons. So also, if we wish to draw the water of teaching from the fountain of the Savior, let us vomit forth, through humble confession, the poisons of our vices, so that afterward we may be able to drink the streams of teaching.

These four examples of the nature of the serpent that we have set forth seem well suited to the imitation of prudence. Two of them teach us to guard Christ, who is our head, within us above all things through faith; the other two teach us to imitate its way of life, so that, stripped of vices, we may walk in newness of life.

But some have said that this should not be referred to the nature of the serpent, but to another matter that we read in Genesis: before it deceived Adam in paradise, it was wiser than all the animals of the earth. Therefore the serpent first attacked the mind of the weaker sex; then it enticed her with hope, when it promised her a share in immortality with the gods. Through such great rewards it persuaded her to carry out the plan and desire it had proposed.

They therefore say that a teacher ought to act with a similar prudence: first examining the nature and will of each individual—what he intends, what he can do, and how much he is capable of understanding. Then he should employ prudence in speech; afterward he should disclose hopes of future blessings and promise the heavenly rewards of faith. Thus, in opposition to what the serpent falsely promised, teachers should preach truthfully, according to God’s promise, that we shall become like the angels.

By such prudence in words and promises, they would draw the minds of the enraged and the rage of wolves toward faith. But which of these interpretations more appropriately fits the Savior’s command, let the prudent reader judge, while fleeing the venom of poison and not losing the simplicity of the dove. For just as the absence of gall in the dove is greatly to be loved, so in the serpent we must greatly fear the spreading within us of poisons arising from wicked understanding.

There are four features in the nature of the dove by which simplicity is especially commended. First, it does not injure with its beak, tear with its claws, or strike with its wings in order to cause harm, as other birds do. Rather, because it has no gall, it preserves the simplicity of love within itself without bitterness.

Another feature is that, sitting above streams of water, it sees the shadows of those lying in wait for it, as is read concerning the Church in the Song of Songs (Song 5:12); 497 a third is that it feeds its own young with the greatest care and also feeds those of others. By these examples it teaches us to be beneficent toward everyone and indicates that we should harm no one.

The final feature, as I said earlier, shows that we should do and teach everything without the bitterness of gall, lest we be found bound by deceit with Simon (Acts 8:21). Rather, always dwelling beside the streams of teaching, let us avoid the snares of the malicious and, contemplating God in our hearts, put aside the things outwardly to be desired.

Hence the prophet says of holy preachers: “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60:8). The saints rightly look toward their own windows, so that they may guard the simplicity of innocence within, seeing nothing outwardly that might please them. Indeed, they make themselves available even to strangers, while striving by every means to nourish their own.

Doves are also said to conceive through their mutual kisses or through gazing at one another. From this we are morally instructed to sow virtues and bring forth children of adoption through charity, without any desire of the flesh, regenerating them inwardly through spiritual love.

It follows:

“But beware of people.”

Everything that preceded serves this purpose: “Be wise and simple,” so that we may beware lest we be deceived outwardly by wicked persuasions, or cast out improperly the simplicity that has been poured into believers through the Holy Spirit. This is what it means to beware of people—not that we will not be handed over, which the Truth declares will happen, but that we should not be deceived by any treacherous snares. This passage refers back to what he said: “Behold, I send you.” Therefore beware through prudence, lest you lose the simplicity of the dove.

“For they will hand you over to councils.”

The excellent teacher Christ foretells to the disciples what was going to happen—not to frighten them, but to instruct them, so that they may be more prepared to endure everything for his sake. Hence the apostle Paul, when he was in chains, says: “For this we are appointed” (1 Thess. 3:3)—that is, to suffer and endure the things inflicted upon us.

There were four things that could disturb the apostles, and these are mentioned here beforehand so that a silent thought might not suddenly seize them: simple and unlearned men would be led into a council. Therefore he says: “For they will hand you over.” Because they were weak and lacking in physical strength, lest they should perhaps become frightened in heart, he adds: “In their synagogues they will scourge you.”

Because they were lowly and rustic, they would stand before kings; hence he says: “You will be led before kings and governors.” Because they were ineloquent and, so to speak, uneducated, they would have to dispute about Christ and about the law and the prophets, in which everything concerning him had been foretold. Therefore he immediately says: “Do not consider how or what you are to speak.”

Hence the excellent teacher Paul says: “I came to you, brothers, not in loftiness of speech or in persuasive words of human wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of God, but in a demonstration of the Spirit, of signs, and of truth” (1 Cor. 2:4). Thus he indicates that we must attribute everything to God and believe that we have nothing from anywhere else except from him, in whose hand we and our words are.

“All these things,” he says, “will be for my sake, as a testimony to them.”

Here faith must be sought more than understanding, because whatever might happen to the holy preachers of the word could come from no one other than him, and could happen only in him by whom they had been sent. When he says, “as a testimony to them,” he distinguishes Jews and Gentiles, just as above, where it is said that they came to them as a testimony, so that they might be without excuse. As the Lord says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John 15:22).

Otherwise both Jews and Gentiles would in some way be excusable if the apostles and apostolic men had not come to them. This passage should be understood not only of the apostles, but also of all teachers down to the end of the age who will suffer before the rulers of the Gentiles or in the synagogues of the Jews.

“When they hand you over”—that is, as he said above, “Because they will hand you over”—“do not consider how,” that is, whether the speech should be eloquent and polished or simple and unadorned, “or what you should speak,” that is, what subject you should address. Let it be from a good conscience and an unfeigned faith, so that prudence may go before you and the simplicity of the dove may not escape you.

For in these two words, “prudence” and “simplicity,” the Lord and Teacher wonderfully prepared for his disciples a great brief lesson: they were to guard everything that he announced would have to be endured, however harsh and difficult, because the Holy Spirit was within them, teaching each one about everything.

“For it will be given to you,” he says, “in that hour”—that is, when you are questioned before kings or in synagogues, or wherever you may be questioned. For he wants the teacher’s heart to depend upon God and to act and speak in all things for God’s glory through God’s gifts.

“Brother will hand over brother to death, and father his son.”

For there is no faithful affection of the flesh where faith is different. Thus he intensifies the constrictions of persecution and oppression, when hope is left nowhere except in God alone, and when even sons are said to rise against their parents. This is the sword of the divine word which Jesus came to send upon the earth, to separate the religion of faith from every affection of the flesh, and love of neighbor from devotion to God.

“And you will be hated,” he says, “by all people because of my name.”

The name of God is great and ineffable. Yet his name is also the name over which many are scandalized and by which all who rightly invoke the Lord’s name are marked; hence we are called Christians. Because this name will be in you, those who hear it will persecute you. When he says “all,” he does not mean everyone who hears, but all who oppose you in hostility.

“Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”

Not whoever perseveres in hatred, or in any other undertaking—namely, in handing over a brother or son—but whoever perseveres in faith in the name of Christ, as Mark states more clearly (Mark 13:13–14). Whoever endures—that is, all the insults and persecutions inflicted upon him, which have been imposed upon the holy martyrs sufficiently and abundantly—if anyone endures these things to the end, he will be saved.

By “the end” we understand either the end of life, or the point at which he completes his testimony, which is the martyrdom of suffering; or until he reaches Christ, who is the end of every consummation, through whom each person may attain true and perpetual life.

For four elements of salvation are commended in this chapter. First, the rashness of presumption is driven from us when it says, “Whoever perseveres,” so that no one may presume upon his own strength. Then, when it says, “will be saved,” hope is granted, whatever death may bring him to completion.

Third, when it says, “to the end,” it shows two things at once: every tribulation has an end, but the reward of good labor has no end. Therefore, at the end of labor or struggle, it rightly adds, “will be saved,” so that you may understand this to mean eternity, in which there will be no end. Otherwise, eternity would be commended as something destined to end in the words “will be saved,” if salvation too were to end, just as the temporal struggle of the contest comes to an end.

[Col. 0424C] When they persecute you in one city, flee to another. Since he had said, “You will be hated by all people on account of my name,” he seems to answer their thoughts as to what should be done thereafter. When he said, “In this city,” he did not speak demonstratively, but referred to whatever city persecution might occur in: for example, if it happened in Jerusalem, flee to Rome, just as we read that the people also did from Damascus (II Cor. XI). He therefore commanded, or permitted, flight so that the weak might have a place to breathe while confessing Christ, if someone still considered himself insufficiently able; lest rashness be endangered; and lest someone should meet martyrdom for Christ prematurely, before he had faithfully spent his ministry of preaching for the salvation of those who were to believe.

It is foolish, therefore, in warfare for a soldier to offer himself to death before he has struck down any of his opponents with his weapons; rather, it is advantageous that he hasten to overthrow as many as possible before he falls. Thereafter, even if it happens that he is preserved for other duties, let him rejoice. So also in this warfare of Christ one must seek the palm of martyrdom in such a way that one does not shrink from enduring the loss of one’s own life for the salvation of others, and from bearing for a long time the struggles of one’s own labor.

Others, however, understanding this passage more explicitly, have said that when he says “in this city,” he wished to indicate Jerusalem, as the metropolis of the Jews, so that they would not go first to Samaria and the Gentiles before persecution had arisen there. We read that the primitive Church also observed this under Claudius. The order, then, would be: when they have persecuted you in Jerusalem, [Col. 0425A] then, driven from the city, flee first to Samaria, which is called another city and by which all Gentile peoples are signified.

Therefore, because he had said for a time, “Do not go along the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans,” he indicates how long what he had commanded was to be observed. It is as though he said: “When persecution has driven you from Judaea, flee to Samaria, and let the Gospel be preached everywhere among all peoples and be brought to completion among the Gentiles.” Hence elsewhere the Lord says: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts I, 8).

This does not mean that the apostles alone were to accomplish it; rather, what he says to them he says to all those through whom this was to be completed until the end of the age. Otherwise, what does he mean when he says, “You will not complete the cities of Israel until the Son of Man comes”? (Matt. X, 23.) Or what does “you will not complete” mean? Perhaps, then, the preceding phrase, “flee to another city,” means that you will not complete them by fleeing from city to city. But that interpretation is entirely untenable. Rather, you will not complete them by preaching and converting them until the Son of Man comes at the end of the age. Thus he seems to have said this to the apostles alone, just as he says: “I am with you all the days until the completion of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

Yet there is no doubt that he promised this to the universal Church, in which, while some die and others are born, it will be preserved until the completion of the age. So likewise the statement, “When you see all these things, know that he is near, at the doors” (Matt. XXIV, 33), applies only to those who will be elect in the flesh. This manner of speaking is very often found in the divine Scriptures.

Thus the statement seems to have been made to show that some would believe the apostles’ preaching, while the remainder of Israel would believe in the last times—those whom we see not yet brought to completion in faith, but whom we do not doubt will receive it at the end, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered. This does not mean that those who belong to the Antichrist will believe, but all who have been predestined to life. This will be the completion of the apostles’ preaching, followed by the coming of the Son of Man.

Unless, perhaps, it seems absurd that he said the cities of Israel would not be completed, since their cities are rightly called the people themselves, who dwell together so as to become fellow citizens. This too may be understood simply: [Col. 0425D] “You will not complete them until he comes”; that is, the labor of preaching will not be completed until the Son of Man comes to your aid after the resurrection from the dead. But this interpretation seems forced, since they had not yet begun to preach with such perfection, although they had been sent two by two.

I nevertheless think that he answered their thoughts, since they were anxious about converting them to the faith. He also gave them to understand that the statement concerned the Gentiles, because the whole matter must be referred to the time when the apostles were being sent to preach. They were not to fear the fury of their persecutors; rather, each was to act successively, so that the teaching of the Gospel might reach all the nations, as it is written concerning them: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 4).

Morally, however, the meaning is that if one of the heretics persecutes us in one place of the Scriptures, we should flee to other testimonies of the divine writings until we complete the perfect faith that is in Christ and obtain the palm of victory.

The text continues:

“There is no disciple above his teacher.” He therefore encourages them concerning what he had said, “They will persecute you.” It is as though he said: “If I, your Teacher, suffer and endure freely on your behalf, how much more ought you, disciples and servants, not to disdain suffering for love of me, but to endure and bear it with the greatest patience?” And if they called the master of the household Beelzebub, how much more his disciples, since “there is no disciple above his teacher”? [Col. 0426B] Therefore you ought to endure insults and mockery with equanimity.

Beelzebub, moreover, was the idol of Accaron, which in the Book of Kings is called the idol of the fly (IV Kings I). At times it is called Baal, because it was worshiped in the mountains; at times Beelphegor, from the city in which it was the idol of the children of Ammon. Bel was the father of Ninus, king of the Assyrians, whom some have said was Saturn. As for the addition “Zebub,” they relate that it received this name because of the servant Abimelech, who killed his seventy brothers with the sword. This servant is said to have been the first to worship this idol in the land of Israel.

“Zebub” is also interpreted as “fly” or “man of flies,” because of the great quantity of filth and the putrefaction of the sacrifices which the flies pursued and defiled before the idol of the Fly, destroying the fragrance of the oil. Since this idol appeared utterly filthy, they called the prince of demons by the name of this demon; they slanderously claimed that Christ was possessed by him and worked miracles in his name (Matt. XII, 24).

Just as this idol held precedence among many in wickedness over all the other idols, so they thought that this demon, through whom Christ—as they admitted—worked such marvelous and unheard-of deeds, bore the idol’s name above the rest. “How much more his household?” By Christ’s household he wishes to be understood both the apostles to whom he was speaking and all who wish to live devoutly in Christ until the end of the age, so that all may be prepared to endure for the Lord whatever is inflicted by their adversaries—things which he himself first showed that he had endured in his own person.

[Col. 0426D] Hence he had said above: “Beware of people, lest through fear, or through anyone’s seductive deception, they deceive you.” The Teacher of truth could set before his household no more glorious example than himself, the eternal light, who is the immortal King of glory. It is indeed glorious if we embrace through faith—which works through love—the one richer than anything else, and are made like him in every condition of suffering, as the apostles were.

For although we may appear to live in peace, it remains true that all who wish to live devoutly suffer persecution.

“Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, and hidden that will not be known.” He says this so that no one would fear the disgrace and accusations of blasphemers, [Col. 0427A] even if he should be called Beelzebub or something worse, if such a thing could be imagined, because everything will be made manifest at the last judgment.

He proposes two terms: “covered” and “hidden.” Nothing is done in the body or in the soul that will not be revealed on the day of the final examination, or remain unknown when God judges the hidden things of human beings. Whatever has been done and committed will be revealed; whatever has been thought will be known. Therefore those who belong to God should not fear the blasphemies and reproaches of people. For, as the Apostle says, “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I, 12).

This revelation, or this knowledge, will equally concern good and evil things—whatever has been done or contemplated. Therefore he teaches that threats, conspiracies, blasphemies, reproaches, and the powers of persecutors are not to be feared, because the day of judgment will declare all these things to have been nothing and empty.

“What I say to you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops.” What does he mean by “in darkness”? I do not think he meant the darkness that we see, since we do not read that the Savior discussed many things at night. Rather, he certainly speaks of the darkness of which John says: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John I, 5). If it had comprehended it, it would no longer have been darkness, but light in the Lord.

In this darkness, therefore, the Lord was speaking, because all his speech is darkness to the carnal, and his word is night to unbelievers. Whatever he said secretly, as though still within those darknesses, or in figures and riddles, he commands them to preach in the light—that is, openly before people. Whatever he taught in their ears, as though under cover of silence, he commands them to expend like a talent entrusted to them upon the housetops.

He speaks according to the custom of the province of Palestine, where there were terraces above the roofs, upon which they very often addressed the people. Thus the Lord commands that the proclamations of life be set forth on high, and that whatever the holy preachers have heard from the Lord—not only with the bodily ear but also with the ear of the mind within—be announced steadfastly.

It was said to these same disciples: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables” (Luke VIII, 10). Therefore what they truly understood inwardly with the ear of the heart, he asks them to communicate to all without fear, bringing the knowledge of the truth into the light; for through the revelation of the true light they themselves have become light, so that all may be illuminated by the light.

“Do not fear,” he says, “those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.” He strengthens them to remain fearless in preaching, because although the body can be tortured for a time, the soul—which is the life of the body—cannot be harmed or killed by torments, because it is immortal by nature (for its death is of another kind). Nor can anyone tear it away from the body unless God wills or permits it.

In this testimony we must also take note of the argument against those who say that the soul is corporeal according to the thickness of our body and can be measured by bodily outlines, since with dull senses they are unable to understand anything other than the forms and patterns of bodies. The Lord denies this here when he says that the body can be killed, but they cannot kill the soul. The soul is not a body that can be killed; if it were, it would be mortal, just as the body is. And just as all corporeal things pass away and have their own end, it would likewise pass away with them into destruction if it were such a body. But it cannot do so, even when it is in punishments.

Hence the merciful Teacher immediately adds:

“Rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.” Here the true resurrection of the body is proclaimed, because unless it rose to life, it could not be sent into Gehenna to experience punishment. But since the soul cannot be killed and the body is to rise from death, that death is to be feared by which both body and soul can be tortured without end.

The name “Gehenna,” moreover, is not found in the Old Testament, but is first introduced here by the Savior. It is said that the idol of Baal stood near Jerusalem, at the foot of Mount Moriah, where the stream of Siloam flows. This valley is said to have contained a small, level, irrigated, wooded plain, full of delights; that place had been consecrated to the idol Baal.

Alas! The ruined people had descended into such madness and folly that, abandoning the temple, they sacrificed and offered victims to the gods there. Nothing more insane can be found than this deed: for the sake of pleasures they abandoned the worship of God; moreover, they consecrated or initiated their children to demons through fire.

That place was called Gehennon—that is, the valley of the sons of Ennon—as we read in Kings and Jeremiah, and also in Chronicles. Hence Jeremiah, or rather the Lord through him, threatens (Jer. XIX, 16) that the place itself will be filled with the corpses of the dead, so that it will no longer be called Topheth [Col. 0428C] and Baal, but Polyandrium—that is, “a burial place of the dead.”

By the name of this place the future punishments and everlasting penalties of sinners, by which sinners will be tortured, are signified. Job plainly declares that Gehenna and punishment are of two kinds when he says: “They pass from extreme heat to cold” (Job XXIV, 19). These punishments, with God as witness, are truly more to be feared and dreaded than the momentary pain of the body and the separation of the soul from the body. For then, although the soul is invisible and incorporeal in relation to the substance of our body, it is punished together with the body and will experience everlasting punishments with the body with which it had previously sinned while it was in this world.

“Are not two sparrows sold for an as, and not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father?” The Teacher of truth therefore instructs his own sufficiently and abundantly through the clearest examples not to fear the present. For this reason he continues to magnify God’s providence, without which nothing happens on earth, since he himself is power and might.

It is as though he said: If small and worthless animals do not fall to the ground without God as their author, but in all things his power and providence are present, even in such small things that what is destined to perish does not perish without God’s will, then you, who are eternal, ought not to fear that you live without God’s providence.

This same meaning was already presented above, where he says: “Look at the birds of heaven, for they neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth more than they?” And so forth.

Nevertheless, since Paul says, “Does God care for oxen?” (I Cor. IX, 9), it is rightly asked how even the smallest things are governed by God’s providence if God has no care for them; or how they remain or fall according to his will if they are not governed by his decision.

Here, prudent reader, I ask you to heed what was long ago taught by our predecessors: beware of a superstitious interpretation. Do not say, “How does God himself personally arrange the outcomes of birds and beasts, and even of flies or of all things?” Rather, truly believe that he formed and created everything in such a way that each thing was prescribed and ordered within its own condition and bound by the laws of nature. Because he willed this once, all things remain and come to an end as he willed.

Only the human being in this world, created in the image of God and elevated by a greater grace so that he is called a son of God, is governed by continual providence and ordered by the care of divine mercy. Therefore, since God does not care for the other things with regard to eternity, they remain entirely in their first condition, in which he willed and arranged that they should remain and exist.

But for the human being alone, for whose sake he created all things, so that he might attain eternal grace, he provides assistance and benefits, and governs him by his providence. All other things, as I have said, happen and pass away as he willed and ordered.

Therefore nothing happens on earth without his will, not even among the smallest things; rather, all things are nourished by his benefits, subsist, and are clothed with coverings appropriate to their nature. Therefore, O human being endowed with reason, avoid superstition and understand these modes of expression simply. Do not attribute matters to yourself and to your nature, reducing the Scriptures to your own understanding and assigning everything to yourself so that you attribute nothing to God, from whom all things come.

I have dwelt at length on this so that the mind would not be deceived by its own sluggishness, when divine power is encouraged by such great teachings and grace, and illuminated by such great benefits.

As for what he says, “Two sparrows are sold for an as,” he says this because it was customary in the temple for sparrows and the other things offered in sacrifices to be available for sale, so that those arriving from the various cities would find everything prepared. But the Evangelist seems to have mentioned only two sparrows being bought for an as so that you might understand that even such insignificant creatures do not exist or perish without God; and that, all the more, your body and soul will not perish, since Christ, the Son of God, was sold and killed for your sake, while these creatures are sold for such coins.

To commend God’s providence further and drive away fear, he adds that even all the hairs of our head have been numbered by God. In this he multiplies and commends his ineffable and incomprehensible care for us.

But miserable and vain are those who continually turn God’s benefits and the immensity of his wisdom into accusations against his promises. They say that it is superfluous to promise the restoration of hairs that have been cut off unnecessarily or fall out daily, because they do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh. They do not wish to understand the force of Scripture, especially since it does not say, “All must be restored” or “All must be saved,” but “All have been numbered”—numbered, that is, according to the number in which they were created.

To put it this way, they have been numbered according to the same weight and measure by which they were measured, since wherever there is number, the knowledge of number is also demonstrated. Yet these foolish talkers may still wish to criticize the enumeration itself as superfluous. If it seems superfluous to them, let them consider whether they may perhaps rashly judge as superfluous the wisdom by which all things were created.

To this wisdom it is rightly said: “You made all things in wisdom, and then in measure and weight and number” (Wis. XI, 21). If all things were created in number, then so were the hairs. And because they were created in number, they have truly been numbered.

Since they are therefore within God’s foreknowledge, how much more are the soul and body, for whose adornment these hairs were created? In all these matters the divine Teacher strengthens the faith of his disciples. If those things that fall away and perish have been numbered by God and comprehended according to the number, weight, and measure in which they were created, how much more should no misfortune affecting our bodies be feared for God's sake, especially in view of his saying: “You are worth more than many sparrows.” For all those things will shortly no longer exist, whereas the human being, called to eternity, will always exist forever.

Having been sufficiently and abundantly instructed in faith by these teachings, let us hear what follows:

“Whoever confesses me before people, I will also confess him before my Father.” It is as though he said: “As you will be my witnesses before people, so that by your life, conduct, and confession you may proclaim me unweariedly on earth, so I will commend you by such a testimony before the Father, whose sons you also are, in heaven.”

Everything he had said earlier leads to this: remaining steadfast in this testimony of faith, they were to fight bravely until they attained the palm of martyrdom.

There are four kinds of confession in the divine writings, and they occur in two settings. There is the confession of praise, and there is thanksgiving, which is always made in heaven. The third is the confession of sins, which is never profitably made except on earth. The fourth is the confession discussed here: confession in martyrdom before people, in time, so that each person may receive it before the Father and the holy angels in eternity.

This denial or confession must be understood not only in words but also in all good works and purity of heart. Hence, conversely, Christ says to the elect: “Come, blessed of my Father”; and to the rejected: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity, for I do not know you” (Matt. XXV, 3).

“Do not suppose,” he says, “that I came to bring peace upon the earth.” It must be asked how the song sung by the angels at the Savior’s birth is to be understood: “Glory in the highest to God, and on earth peace to people” (Luke II, 14). This appears contrary to the present passage, unless we note that the angels added, “of good will.” When they said, “Peace to people of good will,” they separated them from those who are of evil will.

Likewise, when the Lord says, “I give you my peace” (John XIV, 27), he is shown to have spoken only to his own members, among whom peace is preserved for those who love God until the end.

“I did not come to bring peace, but a sword.” [Col. 0431A] This is certainly the sword of the word of God, concerning which the Apostle Paul says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI, 17). For God is Spirit.

This is the sword that proceeds from the mouth of God, sharp on both sides. It is rightly sharp on both sides, because it equally destroys sinners and the impious: they first die to sin and afterward live better for God. By this same sword of the word those who refuse to convert and do penance are also struck, so that, dead to God, they live wickedly, having been destroyed by eternal punishments.

This is the sword with which the incarnate Son is commanded by the Father to gird himself: “Gird yourself with your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one” (Ps. XLIV, 4). With this sword, while he takes a bride for himself, he comes to conquer and overthrow all his adversaries.

Hence it follows:

“For I came to separate a son against his father and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a person’s enemies will be those of his household.”

Unless this division were already familiar to us through custom and experience, such an expression would seem exceedingly obscure. How can the Lord, who commands that one love mother and father according to the law and everywhere gives such great and fundamental commands concerning love, say that he came not to bring peace but discord and a sword? The authority of the most merciful Savior thus became a seedbed of impiety.

From this came hatred everywhere at the beginning of the preaching; from this, wars and seditions, when the Lord’s sword—that is, the word of preaching—began to divide father from son and daughter from mother. The whole world became so divided against itself and raged so fiercely that it stirred up many persecutions.

For the Teacher, by the ineffable sword of his power reaching even to the division of soul, joints, and marrow, separated everything, so that from all peoples one Church might be chosen, in which peace would rest, and so that he might separate the chaff from the grain.

Therefore, reader, I ask you to consider, from the beginning of this instruction, how forceful the speech is, how sublime the commands, and how far the discourse rises above all philosophy. Here later things answer earlier things, and higher things answer lower ones; everything is fulfilled by everything, if only Christ is in some way completing the one body of his martyrdom.

In each individual statement there is one continuous sequence of causes and one connected order of discourse. The parts of this teaching also agree with one another and are joined together as a whole. Thus in this testimony he appears as a marvelous craftsman and examiner of nature, probing even the deepest things in the innermost recesses, while by the sword of the word he separates son from father and daughter from mother.

He also leaves behind old age, and in this passage consistently chooses the younger members of families. Clearly, later age, accustomed to or entangled in longer-standing errors, is scarcely or never freed, because a long habit of the worst life is almost like nature itself. Younger age, however, is more easily recalled to the faith and is shown to grasp rational teachings more effectively and to believe more quickly.

This was not said because many parents did not believe before their children, but because the Teacher, in his kindness, introduces what more commonly follows from human nature. He did not come, he says, to bring peace, but to separate a son from his father—that is, in place, faith, or conduct—when someone is converted from unbelief to true faith, from death to life, and from perversity to the straight and true way of life that is in Christ.

Thus a person’s household members become his enemies when children rise up against parents and parents against children, or daughters-in-law against mothers-in-law and mothers-in-law against daughters-in-law, so that no association is secure anywhere.

Alternatively, “a person’s enemies”—that is, the enemies of Christ, who is the Son of Man—become his household members when the Jews, who had previously been his friends, apostatize from the faith.

Some, wishing to distinguish the words more subtly, place “a person’s enemies” first and then add “his household,” with “will be” understood: those who were previously enemies will finally become God’s household through the preaching of the Word, as the whole Gentile world became.

Spiritually, everyone who comes to Christ is separated from the father, the devil; the daughter, that is, the Church, is separated from her former Gentile condition; and the daughter-in-law is separated from her mother-in-law when the Church of believers is divided from the Synagogue.

This passage may also be understood morally, but I leave that treatment to the reader’s discretion, since we have not undertaken to expound this Gospel in three ways.

“Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.” Since he had said, “I came to separate a son against his father,” he moderates the statement lest he seem to contradict himself in commanding love of one’s father. He shows that he does not forbid love of father or mother or other relatives, but forbids anyone to place devotion to parents or the flesh before Christian religion, since we are reborn and adopted so that we may be and be called sons of God.

He therefore teaches us to have ordered love: first, to love God with our whole heart; then, our neighbor as ourselves. If these two loves cannot be held together, devotion to God must take precedence and faith must be preserved. Hence the law commanded that a priest should not be defiled on account of his father or mother (Lev. XXI, 2).

In all these teachings, therefore, the Savior portrays, forms, and instructs the evangelical person. It is not necessary to magnify individually everything we discuss in an exceptionally elevated manner or draw it out at greater length, because these matters are themselves lofty and have great force for those who consider them. Thus even the envious and rivalrous are compelled to judge them divine and necessarily to extort a confession of the truth.

It should also be noted that the son whom he came to separate from his father he now warns not to love his father more than God. The same must be understood in the other relationships, lest anyone be loved more than God.

“And whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” Lest you think it sufficient merely to have left one’s father, he adds that one must also take up the cross; and lest you think it sufficient to take up the cross, he adds that one must also follow Christ.

Hence we find in another Gospel: “Whoever does not take it up daily” (Luke IX, 29). It is not enough once to have conceived the ardor of faith; the cross must always be borne after Christ, so that we may always be taught to love him.

There are certain hypocrites who appear to bear the cross but do not follow Christ, because they do not seem to love him with a perfect heart, seeking something other than Christ. The cross is therefore taken up in two ways: either the body is afflicted through abstinence, or the soul within is moved through compassion for one’s neighbor.

Since he was crucified for us, we too are crucified for him, no less in secret than openly. Otherwise one is not worthy of me—that is, not worthy to attain the victory of my passion.

Hence the Apostle also says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. V, 24). Anyone who has not taken up his cross—through which we suffer with Christ, dwell with him, are buried with him, and also rise with him—and who has not in some way followed by imitating Christ, which means walking in newness of life, is unworthy of grace.

Take heed, diligent reader, of the beautiful order of preaching taught in each statement. It clearly points out no dangers of the present life to be feared, subjects every affection of the flesh to religion, and completely removes dependence on gold and money.

Therefore, lest anyone think the condition of such evangelists burdensome and ask where they would obtain expenses and the necessities of life, he tempers the austerity of the commands with the hope of the promises and the blessedness of eternal reward.

Hence it follows:

“Whoever finds his soul will lose it, and whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it.” Nothing, therefore, is more necessary for a person to do than to spend his soul for Christ and for his neighbor—not merely to hand over the flesh to suffering for him, but also to rejoice in losing for the present the soul, which is more than the flesh.

This is the very cross that he commands us to bear to the end, so that we may be saved. The soul that every carnal person finds is the present life. He is rightly said to have found it because he has taken no care to know another life. He believes this one alone sufficient for him and rejoices to have received and found it; he prefers to abuse it according to the freedom of his will rather than be crucified for Christ.

It should be noted that “soul” is used in various senses; but nothing is lower in it than the life by which one lives merely with the beasts. Therefore whoever refuses to lose for Christ this part by which one lives with cattle will lose the life that he could have enjoyed with angels in Christ.

He says that one loses it in the future, when one will no longer enjoy it according to one’s own will but will be deservedly condemned to eternal torments. Whoever loses it and carries his cross, however, will find that angelic life and everlasting rewards.

Some have interpreted the passage differently, taking it to mean: whoever finds his soul and wants to save it should lose it—as though it should be read in the imperative, “Let him crucify it.” He finds it who has lost it in this world, acquiring the gain of immortality at the cost of his brief life.

He now moderates the whole austerity of the commandments and displays to the apostles the great rewards of their merits when he says:

“Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.” He says this concerning the reception of the apostles because they are Christ’s members, so that each believer may rejoice that he has received Christ.

But because there were false apostles, false prophets, and false Christians, he anticipates the thoughts of those who would receive them, should they be unable to distinguish which were false and which were worthy to come to them, provided only that they received them in the name of a true disciple.

Hence it follows:

“Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward.”

He is not speaking about the prophet or the righteous person themselves, but saying that whoever receives a righteous person or a prophet will receive the reward of the righteous person or the prophet.

This is in accordance with what the Apostle says: “He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will also supply and multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness” (II Cor. IX, 10).

But if the reader wishes to consider the matter more deeply, all these passages in which the hospitality of human kindness is commended display a great and evident mystery. Above, he had already set forth the danger of those who do not receive them, when he ordered that they be warned by the testimony of shaken-off dust. Now, however, he commends the merit of those who receive them beyond the grace of the service that was expected, [Col. 0434C] and teaches that the office of the mediator consists in this: when he has been received by us, and because he was born from God and came to us, God is believed to have been poured into us through him.

Thus whoever receives the apostles and holy ministers of God receives Christ; whoever receives Christ receives the Father of the Lord, who is in the Son. For in the apostles one receives nothing other than what is in Christ, nor in Christ anything other than what is in God. Through all these relationships, to receive the apostles or ministers of God is nothing other than to receive God, because Christ is believed to be in them and God in Christ.

Thus it comes about that Christ Jesus, the Mediator between God and human beings, contains all things in himself: God as the head, and the members of his body. For this reason he himself is rightly received in his members.

But if he himself is received in the Apostle, he indicated only the apostles, as though by pointing with his finger, when he said, “Whoever receives you”; all the others he excluded. For Christ himself is received in the apostle, a prophet’s reward is promised to the one who receives a prophet, and so the honor of these twelve apostles is commended, whom we rightly call Christ’s vicars.

A reward corresponding to the office of a prophet is promised to those who receive prophets, and likewise to those who receive the righteous, as to fellow workers with the prophets and the righteous. Yet it may happen that someone is a false prophet, or that one who appears righteous is found not to be righteous but false and wicked.

Nevertheless, if no one beyond the number of the twelve apostles were to be received, no one would have received the Apostle Paul; and if only a true prophet and a true righteous person could be received, there would be great difficulty. He tempered this matter with a single expression when he said, “In the name of a prophet” or “in the name of a righteous person,” indicating that it is not the persons but the names of their offices that are to be received, and that the recipient does not lose his reward, even if the one received proves unworthy, until the weeds are mingled with the wheat. This nevertheless provides great encouragement to those who receive them.
