Regarding the apostles, however, he does not say “in the name of an apostle” or “in the name of Christ,” because that would be superfluous. For *apostle* in Greek means “one who is sent” in Latin. No one is rightly called one sent by Christ unless he has been sent by Christ. Therefore whoever receives an apostle receives the one by whom he was sent; and because he believes that the apostle came in Christ’s name, he is rightly said to have received Christ himself, since in receiving him he received the one for whose sake he received him and in whom he believes.

Whoever, he says, gives one of these least ones a cup of cold water, only in the name of a disciple—amen I say to you, he will not lose his reward. This is indeed what he had said above: “Whoever gives only in the name of true religious devotion,” because he will not lose the reward of true religion. Hence, when he gives a command concerning the greatest precepts, he proceeds all the way down to the least, that is, to a drink and a cup of cold water. Just as in individual matters he anticipates the frauds of slanderers, so also in this he anticipates the defenses of those making excuses, lest someone should say: “Poverty prevents me; lack of means keeps me from being able to practice hospitality.” He dispels this excuse by a very slight command, when he indicates that a cup of cold water is to be offered with the readiest disposition. For this reason too he says “cold,” and not “hot,” because in the case of hot water some excuse of poverty might perhaps be possible; but now it is evident that the duty of benevolence and piety cannot be excused in any respect. For “God is not mocked, and whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (Gal. 6:7).

The teaching of almighty God is wondrous: it pursues everything in such a way that the reward of a good work is defrauded in no respect, and no excuse of impossibility has any place if honor has not been rendered to the name of a disciple of Christ, however insignificant. For the insults of the one who deceives himself do not harm the duties of the one who obeys piously, since the Lord recompenses the reward according to the faith of the giver, and not according to the falsehood of the recipient. It should also be noted that, by the cup of cold water, he shows that individual acts of piety are not empty, even when they are very slight; rather, just as the greatest things done for the Lord are recompensed in the greatest things, so also the least are recompensed in the least, so that the reward of a good work may in no respect be voided.

Although some wish these various degrees of service to be understood only as referring to the members of Christ, for whose reception, they say, a reward alone is promised, they maintain that, concerning wicked and false brothers, even when they have been received with the utmost courtesy, there is no recompense. Hence they affirm that the Lord will say in the judgment: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. 25:40). Here he makes this sufficiently clear when anyone is received in faith in the name of a prophet, or of a righteous person, or of a disciple, because he does not lose the reward of righteousness, in accordance with the Psalmist’s statement: “He scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever and ever” (Ps. 111:9). For each person becomes righteous through the honor paid to righteousness, when righteousness is brought to completion in the name of a righteous person through faith.

[Col. 0436A] **(CHAP. XI.)** “And when Jesus had finished instructing the twelve.” He indicates the perfection of apostolic teaching from the point at which he says: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matt. 9:37). Therefore what follows—“He passed on from there”—means: from the house in which the twelve had been healed much earlier, so that he might teach and preach in their cities. He thus came to those cities which he shortly afterward rebukes and reproaches, after the inserted account of John, as though in a narrative, because they had not believed in the signs and wonders that had taken place among them, nor in the preaching of the Savior himself. The text continues:

“But when John had heard in prison about the works of Christ.” Since, when Christ heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee, John, now sending his disciples to him from prison, said: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” This was not because he was ignorant of Christ, whom he had pointed out to everyone with his finger, saying: “Behold, the Lamb of God” (John 1:29, 36), and over whom he had seen the Spirit descending and remaining in the form of a dove. Nor was it because he was ignorant of the one concerning whom he had heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

Moreover, in the Greek we find something that our manuscripts do not contain: when he was being baptized in the waters of the Jordan, “a great light,” he says, “shone around from the water,” so that everyone—that is, those standing nearby—was afraid. From all this it is sufficiently clear that he was not ignorant of the one whose coming he had previously announced as herald, whom he recognized as a prophet when he came and stood among the crowds, and whom he revered as a confessor when he approached him, concerning whom he had said: “After me comes a man who has been made before me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen” (John 1:27).

How, then, did error creep into such abundant knowledge of his, so that he did not know the one whom, instructed inwardly by the Holy Spirit, he had recognized through so many indications and proclaimed through his declarations? Unless perhaps he had been touched only partially by the spirit of prophecy, so that he knew that he was the Son of God but did not know many things about him; while in another respect he had not yet been touched, and therefore faithfully asked him about certain things he did not know. For this reason he pointedly says: “Are you the one who is to come?” and does not say, “the one who has come.” He was not ignorant that he had baptized the Son of God, but perhaps he did not know whether he himself would redeem the world through death and descend to the underworld on behalf of his own. Therefore he says: “Or should we expect another?”—as though he were saying: “Just as I announced you on earth by preaching, shall I likewise announce to those in the underworld that you are to come, so that they may await you?”

Otherwise it cannot be believed that, placed in prison for righteousness and truth, he had been deprived of the grace of the Holy Spirit with which he had been filled, since the same Holy Spirit, the light of his power, was likewise ministered to the apostles when they were imprisoned for Christ.

Nevertheless, although it can rightly be understood in the manner we have explained, the response of the Lord and Savior compels us to understand something else, since he did not answer in the words corresponding to what had been asked. From this it is plainly established that John was asking not so much for himself as for the disciples whom he directed to Christ. In this he asks in the same way that the Savior asked where Lazarus had been laid, so that those who pointed out the place of the tomb might at least in this way be prepared for faith when they saw the dead man rising.

For the Forerunner and prophet of the Lord knew that his disciples were still acting proudly against the Lord and harbored some sharpness toward him, arising from jealousy and envy, as was shown above when the Evangelist reports: “Then the disciples of John came, saying: Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?” (Matt. 9:14). And elsewhere: “Teacher, the one to whom you bore witness across the Jordan—behold, his disciples are baptizing, and everyone is coming to him” (John 3:26). It was as though, provoked by envy, they had said: “We are being abandoned, and the crowd is running to him.”

The blessed Forerunner knew all this most fully, and, as I have said, fashioned the question not for himself but for them, sending it through those whom the blindness of envy had obscured, so that greater understanding and a more effective expression might be perceived in the same act: the prophet himself might prophesy in this form of his office, and, like a provident teacher, heal the dullness of his disciples.

For in John himself there was a figure of the Law. The Law indeed announced Christ, preached remission in him, and promised the kingdom of heaven. John also completed the whole work of the Law. Thus, with the Law now ceasing—the Law that had been held confined because of the sins of the peoples, and that was shut up, as though in bonds and prison, by the vices of the people, so that Christ could not be understood—the Law sends two of its disciples to behold the Gospels, namely, scribes and Pharisees, so that unbelief might contemplate faith no less in deeds than in words, and so that what had been bound within it by the deceit of sins might be washed away through the understanding of evangelical freedom.

Using such an example of John and the wondrous instruction of the Holy Spirit, as though with an artisan’s skill, he both wove prophecy into an action and attended to the ignorance of his disciples, so that they might know that he had preached no one other than God. For this reason he sent his disciples to observe Christ’s works, so that the works might lend authority to his words and proclamations, and so that no other Christ might henceforth be expected than the one whose works had provided testimony to his divinity.

Thus it is made fully intelligible that John was filled with the same Spirit who had rested wholly upon Christ. Therefore Christ entirely foreknows the purpose for which John had sent them, and John had no doubt about Christ, to whom all the secrets of the heart are open. For this reason also, as I said, [Col. 0437D] he did not answer the words of those asking, but displayed signs of divinity.

“Go,” he says, “and tell John what you hear and see.” He wanted them to be witnesses to their own consciousness of the purpose for which their teacher had sent them. The arbiter of all secrets answered them not according to their words but according to the intention of the one who sent them and the scandal of the messengers: “The blind see,” as though he were saying: “Go, tell John that I am the one of whom the prophet said: ‘God himself will come and save us’ (Isa. 35:4); and elsewhere: ‘He himself will bear our infirmities’ (Isa. 53:4); and also: ‘Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened; the lame walk’ (Isa. 35:5).” For it was said in the same prophet: “Then the lame man shall leap like a stag” (Isa. 35:6). And next: “The deaf hear,” from which it follows that the ears of the deaf will be opened.

As for what he says, “The poor are evangelized,” these are precisely the poor of whom it was said: “He sent me to evangelize the poor” (Luke 4:18), so that you might understand the needy—or, what should rather be understood, the poor in spirit—and so that there might appear to be no distinction in preaching between the noble and the lowly, between the rich and the needy.

“And blessed,” he says, “is the one who is not scandalized in me.” Thus, as I have said, he strikes their conscience, or that of all who doubt concerning Christ’s death, because although he died through the weakness of the flesh, as he himself willed, he nevertheless lives through the power of God. Therefore he wishes to heal both those who had been sent and all others from the scandal of unbelief; and if they are not scandalized, blessedness is promised to them.

Otherwise, in these words or deeds, the disciples of John could have admired more than they could have been scandalized; nor had anything yet been done in Christ on account of which John might have been scandalized and sent them such instructions. Indeed, he speaks to those very disciples to whom they had been sent in order that they might be healed—not only to them, but also to all to whom, from the beginning of the course of his discourse, Christ’s death and the passion of the cross had been preached. He says: “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it, and whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:38–39).

Since the whole of the passion was to converge upon the Lord, and since his future cross would become a scandal to many, blessedness is therefore promised to those who persevere in faith without scandal. Hence it appears that these same messengers had always been among Christ’s disciples from the beginning of the preceding discourse, in which the blind had first been illuminated, the lame healed, and the poor evangelized, and they had been fully instructed to endure all things even unto death.

But lest what had been asked and what had been answered cause anyone to suspect infamy or suspicion concerning John, as though he had been scandalized in some respect concerning Christ, the most kindly Jesus said to the crowds about him:

“What did you go out into the desert to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” He speaks this also as though in a narrative. By “the desert,” certainly either the place in which they were is designated, or perhaps the fact that they themselves were empty of the Holy Spirit, in whom there had not yet been any dwelling of God. Hence he speaks these words more in the spirit of rebuke than of confirmation.

It is as though he were saying: “Why did you go out to see a person empty of the thought of God, wandering here and there like a reed under the blowing of unclean spirits?” He is believed to have said this in order both to exalt John with wondrous praises and to restore those whose hearts he had inspected to a firm faith concerning John: John did not doubt about Christ through any softness of mind, since he had previously preached him. Or perhaps he answered their vain thoughts, lest he appear to be agitated against Christ by the goad of envy, as though he were pursuing empty glory from his own preaching.

Nevertheless, whatever the crowd may have thought about John, he surrounds him with wondrous praises, showing that he was neither like a reed amid the waves and the twisting currents of the winds, so as to be moved by any impulse from the faith, nor inwardly empty of the dew of the Holy Spirit, nor clothed in soft garments.

“For behold,” he says, “those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings.” It is as though he were saying: “He does not seek empty glory from his preaching, nor flatter worldly life in order to be clothed in soft garments. Rather, he seeks you, who, like reeds empty within, shine outwardly as flexible things bending here and there.”

For in the sacred Scriptures the reed or cane is spoken of in four ways. At times it signifies the word of sacred eloquence, which flows and pours forth, as in: “My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Ps. 44:2). At times it designates the skill of a teacher, as in: “In the dens where dragons formerly dwelt, verdure of the reed will arise” (Isa. 35:7). At times it signifies the splendor of the glory of the saints: “The righteous will shine, and like sparks they will run through the reed-bed” (Wis. 3:7). They themselves were that reed-bed to which the Lord was speaking: wavering in what they had previously heard from John, and in the other things he had proclaimed about him with many praises.

Now they were hearing him ask: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” Would Christ’s hearers, then, remain amid these waves? He strengthens them also by John’s example, showing that John had not been empty within, not dry outwardly, not a follower of softness, and not a flatterer of earthly kings. Moreover, he added what is greater:

“Or what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.” After recalling them from the error of their minds, he immediately explains how and what sort of person they ought to believe him to be. First he removed their error; then at last he brought forward the truth.

Why, then, is he said to have been more than a prophet? It is clear. John was permitted to prophesy Christ, and then, unlike any other prophet, to see him, point him out with his finger, and baptize him with his own hands. Thus he is rightly more than a prophet no less in deed than in name. The office of a prophet is to proclaim future things; but John extended his hand and showed as present the one whose coming he had foretold.

Indeed, how great he was is suggested by the divine voice when it says: “Behold, I send my angel before your face” (Mal. 3:1). Malachi, moreover, whose name is interpreted from Hebrew as “angel,” foretells in the person of the Holy Spirit that this one will be an angel—not because John was an angel in the fellowship of nature, but through participation in office. For the name “angel” also refers not to nature but to office.

Now the face of Christ is his knowledge, just as Christ is the face of the Father, through whom the Father is known. Long beforehand John is announced as coming before his face, so that Christ may be known.

“Amen I say to you, among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist.” Perhaps, therefore, as I said, because he was sent in the capacity of an angel before God, lest he be thought to be above human nature and more than human, he immediately qualified the statement and numbered him among those born of women. Yet he did so in such a way that he is understood to be included among those generated through the intercourse of man and woman, and is not equated with Christ, who was born from a virgin without the union of a man.

Thus the divine arbiter qualified his judgment between the two: he showed what John was, and prevented him from being thought more than human—something he was not, except insofar as, sent in the power of an angel, he prepared the way for the human being who is God.

Nevertheless, it is rightly still asked whether John was greater than Elijah, in whose spirit and power he is said to have come; or whether he should be regarded as greater than Elisha, in whom a double portion of Elijah’s spirit is said to have rested (2 Kings 2:9). It would be very presumptuous for us to determine this, unless perhaps John is rightly said to be greater than Elijah or Elisha because he precedes in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17) the one who will come at the end of the age. Perhaps “greater” is understood in this way.

Accordingly, he does not say “will follow,” although Elijah existed before, but “will precede”—the one who, when he comes, will perhaps possess a grace so much greater than before as the struggle he will have to endure will also be stronger.

Meanwhile, the Savior did not prefer John to the prophets and patriarchs, or to all human beings, but made the others equal to John. Hence what follows:

“He who is lesser,” he says, “in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.” Although he called him an angel, the one who is in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he: after the struggles and battles of pious combat, he is already with God and has ascended victorious to heaven, having escaped the various deceits of this life, whereas the other, still amid the uncertain battles of his own struggle, fights and sweats uncertainly over the outcome.

Some, because he had called John an angel, said that this should be understood as spoken of the angels. It would mean that any angel in the kingdom of heaven, although lesser than the others, is greater than John because he sees the face of the Father, even if, in his office, he is last among beings of that nature.

Hence it is rightly asked: since an angel surpasses human beings by nature, will he finally be made equal to holy human beings in glory through merits and grace? Yet no one here dares presume anything about himself, unless he also needs the aid of those whose assistance protects us everywhere. Hence David says in the Psalm: “He will send his angels around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Ps. 33:8).

The angel of great counsel himself sends his ministering spirits and makes them angels when they come to us, on behalf of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation. But it is not right to judge rashly about this: either about how much they differ among themselves, or about how much the highest of the saints ought to be made equal to them or exalted through their fellowship.

Nevertheless, the blessed and glorious Virgin Mary, already by ecclesiastical authority and the tradition of the holy Fathers, is everywhere sung and proclaimed to have been most gloriously exalted above the choirs of angels. Yet, to put it so, this is not by nature but by the gift and privilege of divine grace, because she was established by the same Word by which the heavens were established, and filled with the same Spirit by which her strength and power are proclaimed to be greater.

Some have said that Christ—who at that time, in age and reputation, still appeared lesser in the flesh—was greater than John in the kingdom of heaven, that is, in the present Church, which certainly already existed in the apostles, or which he himself ruled above in heaven.

“From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.” Since each saying of the most kindly Savior is pregnant with mysteries and full of sacramental teachings, I have resolved to treat each one individually. But because the subject surpasses my ability in speaking, and because I cannot produce a work worthy of all who ask, I shall at least briefly display an image of the truth. Even if I cannot provide what is called the principal and authoritative exposition of everything, I shall nevertheless strive to explain the Evangelist’s meaning, in however unlearned words, to those who desire to know it.

When I consider what has been said—“From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence”—I am greatly astonished at what he wishes to indicate. For although baptism and repentance, by which the kingdom of heaven is seized, were first preached by John, it is sufficiently obscure what is meant by “until now.” When he says, “from the days of John the Baptist until now,” he seems to have set two limits for its seizure. But if no one seized it either before or afterward through faith, then all the hope of the patriarchs and prophets was empty, and the promise of eternal life in Christ was empty as well.

It is true that before the preaching of repentance announced by John, and before the baptism that he administered, none of the saints received the kingdom of heaven, because, as the Savior says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5). Hence it is plainly established that the kingdom of heaven suffered violence from the moment Christ opened the gate of paradise to those who believed in him.

But what does “until now” mean? We know that “now” is an adverb of present time. If the kingdom of God suffered this violence from the days of John until the time when Christ was speaking these words, and not thereafter, then he excluded from the kingdom of God all who believed in Christ either before or afterward.

Unless perhaps a particular kind of violence is to be understood—one that prevailed at that time but not at another—although this violence was nothing other than faith in Christ, “which works through love” (Gal. 5:6). Therefore, when the Savior says “until now,” he certainly intends the time extending up to himself, because he is always the same: yesterday and today, that is, both now, while the present age runs its course, and always. Thus the same kingdom of heaven is opened to no one either before him, whom John preached and pointed out with his finger, or after him, who is always present everywhere in time.

Meanwhile, it is rightly asked what sort and degree of violence it is by which the violent seize the kingdom of heaven, because it is altogether great and wondrous. Truly wondrous is the power by which sinful human beings acquire through grace the kingdom of the citizens of heaven, which they did not possess by nature, and by which an earthly human being formed from the clay of earth attains eternal and angelic life.

What, then, could be more violent than to acquire heaven through strength, when we never possessed it by nature? For, as the nature of things requires, what is stronger always inflicts force, and that upon which force is inflicted is weaker. Hence, from the beginning of Christ’s discourse, a wall of faith is constructed and defenses are prepared, with which every violence of faith is armed, so that it may seize what is freely offered.

Moreover, the Jewish apostle John is not believed. The works do not earn Christ’s authority. The future cross was a scandal to almost everyone. John’s prophecy comes to an end. The Law is fulfilled in Christ, and then preaching is brought to completion. The spirit of Elijah is sent ahead in John’s voice. In him the old things are brought to an end and the new begin.

Therefore, let every believer consider what greater force there could be than what happened when Christ was preached to the Jews and was immediately received and acknowledged by the Gentiles. He is born among the Jews and loved by the Gentiles. His own reject him; strangers seize him. His own persecute him; enemies embrace him. The Gentile world, alienated from God, seeks the inheritance; the household rejected it. O wondrous power of God! “How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33.)

The children reject the testament of the promised inheritance, and servants obtain it through faith. Hence it is said: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12). As someone has said, the glory owed to Israel’s fathers, announced by the prophets and offered by Christ, is occupied and seized by the faith of the Gentiles.

“All,” he says, “the prophets and the Law prophesied until John, that no one greater than he had arisen among those born of women.” Therefore John is rightly the boundary of the Law and prophecy, and from this he also makes use, as it were, of a privilege proper to himself.

It should be noted that he says “all the prophets.” Does this expression also include those who lived after Christ’s coming? Properly, he is speaking of those who prophesied Christ’s coming, although those who came afterward also prophesied only up to Christ and about Christ.

“Law” is a single name, but it has a threefold meaning. The first part of the Law concerns God; the second consists in commandments for the conduct of life; the third concerns new moons and the Sabbath, various foods and circumcision, as well as various sacrifices. He says that this part prophesied as a whole until John, because whatever is contained in these commandments and riddles is nothing other than a prophecy of future things.

As for everything else in the Law, Christ came not to abolish it but to fulfill it. Those things that are only partly complete are fulfilled so that the Trinity may be understood from the Law. The commandments concerning the conduct of life are fulfilled so that they may be brought to greater completion, as in “You shall not be angry,” and similar teachings. The final part, which signifies the life to come, was fulfilled when Christ—who had been promised through its figures and riddles—was shown everywhere through it as having already come in the flesh.

It should also be noted that the Law is prophecy, since, as Paul says to the Hebrews: “In many portions and in many ways, long ago God spoke to the fathers in the prophets” (Heb. 1:1). He spoke in one way through things and in another through words. Yet prophecy of future things was made through things and words together, up to John.

“If you wish,” he says, “to know, he himself is Elijah.” This statement would certainly seem very obscure if it had not already been clarified by the many declarations of the holy Fathers, to such an extent that some, no less heretically than philosophically, wished to assert that souls return again to bodies and ought to accompany one another through different bodies. The Catholic faith certainly does not accept this.

Therefore John and Elijah are one not in person, as though the one who is Elijah were John, but in the Spirit and grace, and also in the proclamation of truth. The text continues:

“Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” Wherever the Holy Spirit presents this statement, he urges the hearer to seek a mystical understanding, both in the Gospel and in the Apocalypse of John. For he requires spiritual ears when he says: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Rev. 2:17).

Who is so inexperienced, so ignorant and uneducated, that he does not know that there is an inner and an outer human being, or that the mind has ears within, the ears of the heart? The external voice strikes the bodily ear: when it touches and beats the air, it becomes a voice, flows in, and touches the ears so that hearing may be moved. In the same way, when the Holy Spirit proclaims divine things, our mind inwardly hears and sees them at once.

Its seeing is understanding, and understanding rightly is perfected perception. Just as an external voice moves a person to hearing, so the divine voice teaches and instructs the soul inwardly, when the soul itself perceives the things of God with its own ears.

But because there are few who possess these inner ears, he vigilantly seeks them out among the countless: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” No one can possess them unless they have been given to him. But let such a person also take care not to appear to have received the grace of God in vain, as did those of whom it is next said:

“To what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplace who call to their companions and say: ‘We played music for you, and you did not dance; we lamented, and you did not mourn.’”

He seems to be speaking of those who had been sent to John as two disciples, to whom he spoke continuously while they were doubting concerning him. Indeed, in their likeness, the whole race of the Jews is blamed, whose hearts were oppressed by excessive unbelief.

Nevertheless, the outstanding Teacher presents a wondrous proverbial comparison from the game of children and the custom of mourners. In certain places, they say, it is customary to arrange two groups opposite each other, which alternately praise whatever they wish and sing dirges, calling out together to their companions. Hence the Lord introduced this appropriate sentence of rebuke for his hearers.

For this entire discourse is a reproach of unbelief, and descends from the feeling of a superior complaint. The rhythm of the singers is beautifully adapted to the voices of those dancing, and to the lamentations of those mourning, according to the plain sense. Applause accompanies songs of joy, and mourning accompanies laments of contrition.

In laments, good things are also recounted concerning those who are mourned, as well as the disasters of dreadful misfortune, as we read that Jeremiah did in his Lamentations. Another prophet orders the women who lament to be summoned for mourning, so that they may stir up greater weeping among the people. Moreover, that dancing should accompany song is taught by David, when choirs on every side sang psalms and he himself leapt before the ark, even dancing naked.

Therefore we are not given unlimited freedom of interpretation concerning these things. Whatever is said about the children and the generation, which he seems to rebuke because of the hardness of their hearts, must all be referred to the Jews, and to Christ, the prophets, and the apostles, who are called children because of their innocence.

For these children who sit in the marketplace are those of whom Isaiah speaks in the person of Christ: “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me” (Isa. 8:18; Heb. 2:13). And in the Psalms: “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Ps. 8:3). Also: “The testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones” (Ps. 18:8).

These, then, are the little ones or children sitting in the marketplace, who conduct Christ’s profitable commerce. They carry pearls and precious stones in the marketplace; they offer gold and silver—the words of God—for sale. Finally, they offer milk and wine freely to the young, even without silver and without any price.

Where Latin says “in the marketplace,” the Greek has ἐν ἀγορᾷ, which is more expressive: it is a place where many things are offered for sale.

And because the Jewish people, always heavy of hearing, did not wish to listen, the prophets and apostles not only spoke to them but also raised their voices as though with a trumpet and cried out, saying: “We played music for you, and you did not dance” (Matt. 11:17)—that is, “We invited you to our song, and you answered nothing through the work of your hands. We preached Christ’s coming in the flesh, and you did not believe.”

It should be noted that all the proclamations of virtues form one harmony and one melody of the sweetest song, and that the prophecy concerning Christ is a trumpet of salvation. “We lamented,” they said, “and invited you to repentance; you did not even wish to do this.” Thus you rejected both forms of preaching: the pious exhortation to virtue and the call to repentance after sins.

For what could be harder in either case, when the mind is neither urged toward better things by the attraction of good nor frightened by the threat of punishment so that it may turn back, lest it thereafter remain bound by sin, live wickedly, and suffer punishment? The Savior makes clearer the purpose for which he proposed this judgment:

“John came,” he says, “neither eating nor drinking.” This is what is meant by “We lamented for you,” because his manner of life and frugality of food were nothing other than a form of lamentation and repentance.

This does not mean that John did not eat and drink, since no one presently lives without these things, but that he never ate the ordinary foods of human beings in excess or those unnecessary for life. Moreover, he did not drink wine or strong drink, abstaining from every beverage by which one can become intoxicated.

Then the Son of Man came with the manner of joy, which is to say, “We played music for you.” He came eating with tax collectors and sinners, taking food from every kind of dish with you at banquets, and yet you were not pleased in such a way as to devote yourselves to pious joy in response to his songs of gladness.

It is as though he were saying plainly: “If the sorrow and abstinence of John’s way of life please you, why did John displease you? And if joy and the use of all foods please you, why did Christ not please you?”

“Wisdom,” he says, “is justified by her children.” It is as though he were saying: “Because you were unwilling to receive discipline, I, who am the wisdom of the Most High God, have been approved and accepted by my apostles and disciples”—namely, by those who, using force, seize the kingdom of heaven itself, justified through faith.

And because they have been reborn in wisdom, they are rightly called children of wisdom. It is therefore worthwhile in this place to consider the force of the statement. “Wisdom,” he says, “is justified by her children,” intending the statement to be understood of himself, for he is the Wisdom of God the Father.

He is not something accidental arising from the effects of things, but exists by nature. Every thing has power over its own nature, whereas an activity is the effect of power; for the work of power is not the same as power itself. The effective power by which what is effected comes to be is therefore distinguished from the work itself as much as the Creator is distinguished from the creature.

Thus, in this statement—that wisdom is justified by the children whom she has generated so that they may be wise—the nature of wisdom should be understood rather than the efficacy and work of power. For Christ is proclaimed by the Apostle as, by nature, truly the power of God and the true Wisdom of God the Father.

Here he has most openly called himself Wisdom and has shown that he is Wisdom essentially. This is the great gift and privilege of children: to understand him sincerely in this way, because the king’s children rejected her, so that Wisdom may rightly be proclaimed justified by her children, and they may thereafter pass into the adoption of children.

Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida; for if the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, etc. Among the other cities which, as was said above, he went through in order to preach the Gospel of the kingdom, there is no doubt that he also preached in these. Matthew has placed this here by way of recollection rather than according to the sequence of the text. For it is clear that these two cities were in Galilee; but which mighty works the Lord performed in them is not sufficiently evident, unless perhaps, at the time when he was going through the other cities, he performed very many works there as well, and this is now being recalled. Nevertheless, since they were performed, no one doubts it. From this passage, however, a very difficult question arises—one that even the holy Fathers have been unable to resolve: why were mighty works not performed in Tyre and Sidon? If they had been performed there, according to the Savior’s word, those cities would have repented at his preaching. But now, since he did not preach to them [Col. 0445D], nor did they receive the signs of miracles, they seem not to be at fault because they did not believe. Indeed, the fault of silence lies with the one who refused to preach to those who would have acted in repentance—something no believer dares to say.

Therefore, as I have said, all the holy teachers give the same true, straightforward, and entirely open answer: that they do not know God’s judgments, nor understand the mysteries of his individual dispensations. Hence the Apostle Paul exclaimed: “How incomprehensible are the judgments of God, and how unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. XI, 33.)

For the Lord’s intention had sometimes been not to go beyond the boundaries of Judea, lest he first give the Pharisees and priests, who were ready to accuse him, a legitimate occasion for persecution. Thus, before his Passion, he also instructed the apostles: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (Matt. X, 5). Therefore the Gospel was preached and signs were displayed in the Jewish cities which the Lord reproaches, so that they might be without excuse.

In these words the Lord Jesus reveals to us a deeper mystery of predestination: the word of God is preached both to those whose hearts were hardened and whose ears were burdened, and not preached to those among whom, had the mighty works been performed, they would long ago have repented in ashes and sackcloth, as the utterances of truth declare. Nevertheless, on the day of judgment these cities too will be punished more leniently, though with a lesser penalty; while those cities in which the Lord himself performed miracles and signs will be punished more severely, because of the obstinacy and disobedience which the Lord foreknew they would have, even before those works were performed in them [Col. 0446B].

The Lord therefore foreknew both: that these would deny him when the works were performed, and that those would repent and confess if the works were performed. It is evident that they did so later, through the preaching of the apostles. Therefore, do not ask when this happened, once you look to the salvation of believers; but why the former were treated more leniently, even though they did not believe, and the latter more severely, although the Gospel was preached to them, the Lord came to them, and divine signs and wonders were displayed before them—that is clear.

Those cities were without the true God, like all the Gentiles; lacking knowledge of the Law and the Prophets, they had transgressed only the law of nature. But Judea and the cities which he reproaches despised everything: the law of nature and the Prophets, the Law given through Moses, in which Christ’s coming was foretold [Col. 0446C]. In addition, they rejected the Lord himself, who was present and had been shown to them through signs and mighty works. Therefore, so that they might be without excuse, these signs of his divinity were displayed before them.

Nevertheless, from all this it is our duty to confess that, although the things being said are hidden, what God does is certainly true and just. Hence it is sung in the Psalm: “The judgments of God are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV, 7). And: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XIV, 11), because there is no iniquity with God, nor any injustice.

A certain Catholic disputant of no little distinction, wishing to escape the depth of the question, has nevertheless expounded this Gospel passage as follows: God had foreknown that the Tyrians and Sidonians would later depart from the faith, although they would have believed when miracles had been performed among them; and for this reason, out of mercy, he had not preached there or performed mighty works, since they would have become liable to a more severe punishment if they had rejected the faith which they had received [Col. 0446D].

Whether this solution is true, let the prudent reader judge. One may nevertheless object that, if this was the Savior’s compassion—that he preferred those people not to approach the faith rather than to depart from it with a much graver crime—why was it not rather done in the most merciful way, so that they would first believe, and then, through the grace of the faith they had received, be enabled not to abandon it? Or why did they not depart from this life before they abandoned it, lest wickedness, as it is written of certain people, change their hearts?

Thus God’s judgment in both cases remains hidden, but is just in everything [Col. 0447A], although many people pile up numerous questions on this subject and entangle the unwary in the chains of syllogisms. Therefore, I ask—since the matter is difficult—whether I possess such excellence and facility in teaching that I can satisfy eloquence in every art and discipline and unravel the impenetrable mysteries of the divine words, lest they mark our ignorance in matters which God wished to reserve as known only to himself.

I hope they will not unjustly criticize me for this, since they ought rather to be grateful and accept with appreciation whatever our labor and industry have managed to obtain worthy of faith, though not of eloquence. For we, weak in intellect and insignificant, attempt things great and almost incredible. Indeed, we dare and presume more from God than we deserve or are able to do. Nevertheless, whoever presumes in true faith upon God more than he deserves or can accomplish is not ineffective. Because the cities mentioned above refused to receive this faith, Capernaum too is denounced—the city in which he dwelt for a long time—and threatened.

“You, Capernaum,” he says, “will you perhaps be exalted to heaven? You will descend to the underworld.” But in Greek it reads: “And you, Capernaum, which have been exalted to heaven, will descend to the underworld.”

There appears to be a twofold interpretation. Either you will descend to the lower regions because you resisted my preaching with the utmost arrogance; or, because you were exalted to heaven through my hospitality and through my signs and mighty works, possessing such a privilege, you will be punished with greater penalties because you refused to believe these things.

For it is written that Capernaum was beside the Lake of Gennesaret in Galilee of the Gentiles [Col. 0447C], and in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali: a very beautiful village. Yet, as appears from the threat against it, Jerusalem is blamed as though it were guilty, just as elsewhere it is said to it: “Your sister Sodom has been justified in comparison with you.” This makes evident the disgrace of its pleasures, its excessive pride, and the foulness of its vices. Hence he says:

“For if the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day.”

Here one must first note that the crimes and shameful deeds of human beings sometimes shorten their present life. It is as though it were said of them: If they had not sinned and acted against God, they would certainly have remained until this day—that is, the day on which he was speaking. Nevertheless, when he says “perhaps,” an adverb suggesting doubt, this does not mean that the Lord doubted anything; rather, it leaves room and opportunity for free choice to remain, if they had been unwilling to sin after accepting faith through signs and wonders. For all salvation comes from faith.

Therefore, where so many miracles had been seen, the spectacle of those deeds should have summoned them not only to fear and drawn them to faith; even hearing of them, though from a distance, should have invited them to believe. But the wretched Jews, among whom such things were performed and to whom these exceptional events were foretold—the enormity of whose sins makes the sins of the Tyrians and Sidonians seem light, and even those of the Sodomites and Gomorrhans seem light, because perhaps they would have been inclined to believe had they witnessed such mighty works [Col. 0448A]—were more culpable. What is more, they had not sinned to such an extent, nor had they yet received the divine Law. Nevertheless, in all this the difference between future punishments is shown, just as the differing quality of merits is shown [529].

At that time Jesus answered and said: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones,” and so forth.

It is asked how he is said to have answered when he had not been questioned. For it has not been stated beforehand that anyone asked him anything, or what anyone asked him. We read this kind of expression also in the Apocalypse. But whether it belongs to mystical meanings, or whether this expression should simply be understood in its ordinary sense, I leave to the judgment of the reader.

Unless, that is, there are divine realities within which the saints see and hear while they are still in the flesh, and to which they often seem to respond and speak. How much more, then, did the Savior—who did everything inwardly and divinely with the Father and outwardly answered what he beheld within—do so? Hence Luke says: “In that hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit” (Luke X, 21), because he was always inwardly with God the Father in the Holy Spirit.

For what Matthew says here, “At that time,” and what Luke says, “In that hour,” are one and the same. But concerning what time or hour is meant, some say that it was after he reproached the cities; others, that it was after the seventy-two disciples returned, rejoicing over the mighty works and signs, and were consequently warned that they ought not to be exalted. Others have said that he spoke these words at the time and place where it was said: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. XIII, 5), to which declaration what he says now—“I confess to you, Lord Father”—seems to respond [Col. 0448C].

It is as though he said: “I give you thanks because you have hidden these things from the wise of the world and revealed them to little ones, so that they may understand me and know that you are in me and I am in you; and for this reason I confess and rejoice in the Holy Spirit.”

“Father, Lord,” he says. Appropriately he calls him Father who said: “This is my beloved Son.” This passage also stands against those who say that Christ was not born but created, since he calls him Father.

In every other respect, he is Lord of heaven and earth, although he also took the form of a servant. He calls him Lord of heaven because a voice had sounded from heaven, and on earth the Son of God was shown through the Father’s indications. Otherwise it would be inconsistent not to call him likewise Lord or Father of himself, of heaven, and of earth.

“You have hidden,” he says, “from the wise of the world those things concerning me which you revealed to little ones, by whom wisdom was justified as by her own children” (Matt. XI, 19), and not by the Jews, who were unwilling to mourn with John or to leap and rejoice at the song of the Son of Man. But you revealed to the humble and the little ones the profound mysteries which you hid from the wise and the scribes. Otherwise, if those things concerning Christ had not been hidden from them, they would never have gone so far astray.

The apostles, or all Christ’s disciples, are called little ones either because they are free from wickedness, or because they were humble and innocent. Moreover, they were inexperienced in wisdom, so that they possessed nothing from themselves, but everything that was in them came from God.

For this reason also, in a tone of affectionate flattery, he speaks to the Father because he had disclosed the ineffable mystery to the apostles, while leaving those who presumed upon themselves empty and deprived, so that all the benefits of divine compassion begun in the apostles might be brought to completion [Col. 0449A]. He continues:

“All things have been handed over to me by my Father.”

Reader, understand mystically both the Father who hands over and the Son who receives. Otherwise, if we wish to understand the statement according to our frailty, when the one who receives begins truly to possess, the one who gave begins not to possess. But lest you should think that there is anything less in Christ than in the Father because he had submitted himself in an attitude of affection, he says that all things have been handed over to him by the Father.

For just as he himself says to the Father: “All that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine” (Luke XV, 31), and thereby shows one nature of the Godhead and one divinity, so also, by saying that the Son alone knows the Father and the Father is known by the Son alone—or by anyone to whom the Son has wished to reveal him—he teaches that in this revelation the substance of both is the same, with their mutual knowledge unchanged.

Whoever has known the Son also knows the Father in the Son, because all things have been handed over to him by the Father, since he is begotten from him and is the consubstantial Son in whom the Father himself is. Thus, in this secret of mutual knowledge, it is understood that the Son is nothing other than what is in the Father, because the Father himself is in the Son, just as the Son is in the Father.

Everything that belongs to the Father has been handed over to him, since, by being born, the Son is made equal to the Father, so that he is equal to him in every respect—in nature, honor, and power.

Therefore, reader, I ask you not to understand the statement that the Son is in the Father, or the Father in the Son, according to bodily modes of existence. Do not imagine that God, remaining in one place, cannot exist elsewhere, as a human being does, or as something similar to a human being does: when it is in one place, it is entirely absent from another. For whatever exists is contained where it is. But God possesses immeasurable power; he is living everywhere, a power that is absent nowhere and never. The Son is wholly in the Father, and the Father in the Son; they are one true God.

Accordingly, when the Son says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father,” and when he says to the Father: “All that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine,” he shows himself and the Father. For “what is his” signifies nothing other than himself, begotten from the Father, so that wherever his possessions are, he himself is rightly understood to be.

This is not to be understood bodily, as though he were absent somewhere and not believed to be everywhere. Through his own things and through those things handed over to him by the Father, he does not cease to be in everything, since he is wholly in the Father. Thus, as has been said, he himself is nothing other than what he is, and his possessions are what he is, because all these things must be referred to an understanding of his nature [Col. 0449D].

Hence, when the Apostle spoke elsewhere about the Holy Spirit, he said (John XVI, 12, 15): “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that one, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will direct you—or, as others read, he will teach you—all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come. He will honor me,” or, as other books read, “he will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine.”

Then he added: “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said to you that he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.”

The Holy Spirit therefore receives from the Son, because everything that belongs to the Father belongs to the Son, and he is sent by the Son, who proceeds from the Father [Col. 0450A]. Hence one must ask whether “to receive from the Son” and “to proceed from the Father” are the same thing. They appear to be the same and a single thing: to proceed from the Father and from the Son, and to receive from the Son as from the Father. For he said: “He will receive from what is mine,” and: “Everything that the Father has is mine”; therefore, he says, “I told you that he will receive from what is mine.”

Thus, whatever he says “he will receive”—whether it is power, strength, teaching, or anything else which the Son was to announce to them—he says that it must be received from himself; and he indicated that this same thing must altogether be received from the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds.

For when he says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father,” he makes known that everything belonging to the Father belongs to him. Therefore, what must be received from the Father is also received from him, because everything belonging to the Father belongs to him, having been handed over to him by the Father, since he is begotten from him.

This unity, therefore, contains no diversity, nor does it matter from whom something has been received [Col. 0450B]. What is given by the Father is from the Father, and the gift is also attributed to the Son, because everything that the Father has, the Son has, since all things have been handed over to him.

From this it is evident that no one rightly divides the Father’s nature from the Son, and no one in a Catholic manner cuts apart this unity or introduces any dissimilarity into it, by which the Son would not share the unity of the nature whose Spirit is one communion, one natural love, and one consubstantial unity.

Therefore, everything that belongs to the Father belongs likewise to the Son, because all things have been handed over to him by the Father.

For this reason, as I have said, one must distinguish carefully, so that one says: “I confess to you, Father,” and then adds: “Lord of heaven and earth,” because he is Father by nature, but Lord and creator of heaven and earth.

These are the things that have been revealed to little ones and hidden from the wise of the world, because this was pleasing to God the Father.

I have said this so that the prudent mind may always be gradually led, together with the apostles, to attend to divine things. For no one rightly knows what must be known about the Father or the Son except the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal it. Nor can anyone know the Father who does not know the Son, nor the Son who does not know the Father. For no one can know one without the other.

Therefore he says to the Father: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3).

The Father had already spoken from heaven above, crying out: “This is my Son.” Here the Son too says: “I will confess to you, Father.” The Father who cries from heaven that he is his own Son is himself confessed by that Son to be his Father, and is identified as Father.

But lest this be understood as merely a simple confession of names—“This is my Son,” and “I confess to you, Father”—and lest we suppose that the Father is merely titular, or the Son merely adopted, and that “father” is a title of honor, as the heretics wish, he therefore added all these things concerning himself and said: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. XI, 27).

But when the Father reveals the Son to whomever he wishes, what more need be sought, since the Father himself says: “This is my Son,” and the Son himself says to Peter concerning the Father: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 17).

From these words the meaning is clear when he says: “No one knows the Son except the Father,” and no one knows him in any way as he is except the Son. For neither of them is known except through mutual testimony: the Son through the Father, and the Father through the Son.

The Son is as unknowable as the Father; and the Father too is unknowable, just as is the Son to whom all things have been handed over [Col. 0451A].

For this reason, dearest brothers, as I have said, these additions have been made so that nothing at all may be understood to be excluded in matters concerning those whose nature, power, authority, and divinity are one and equal in everything, and whose secret mutual knowledge is equal.

If their nature is equal, and their power and authority are equal in everything, it cannot naturally be the case that they are not what they are called: Father and Son.

Therefore Christ cannot be merely titular by name, or adoptive, as the recent heresy has asserted. He is one, and, contrary to the opinion of Arius and the other heretics, he is not less than the Father, nor other than what the Father is. In everything he is what the Father is. Therefore he alone knows the Father, just as he himself is known by the Father alone. Their natural right is equal in power, and there is no difficulty in their mutual knowledge.

Thus, through these statements, the only-begotten God, the wisdom of God the Father who was justified by her children, teaches that he is not merely the Son of God by the testimony of a name, but truly united to the Father in everything and naturally his Son, so that we may truly believe what was said by the Father: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. XVII, 5).

And because the Jews did not believe that he was such, the most gracious Savior said to them: “You know neither me nor where I am from. For I have not come from myself, but he who sent me is truthful, whom you do not know. But I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me” (John VIII, 19, 26).

Therefore it is true that no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him. This confession is repeated so frequently for the definite reason that the Father is known only to the Son, because the Son is naturally from him.

But if he is from him and is known by him alone, the Arians must be questioned. Since they call him a creature, is what is from the Father in him the work of creation, or does it show through this that he possesses the nature of generation?

If it is the work of creation—and everything that has been created is from God—how is it that not everything knows the Father, especially rational creatures? Christ certainly knows him precisely because he is altogether from him [Col. 0451D].

But if he appears to have been created rather than born, insofar as he is from God, and since all things are from God, how is it that he does not, together with the others, remain ignorant of the Father? In the same way, all things that are from him, apart from the Son, are ignorant of him.

But if the Son knows him precisely because he is from him, and this is proper to him, how will it not also be proper to him, because he is from him, that he is truly Son by nature of God the Father?

No one other than God knows this nature and generation in the clearest manner. He alone knows God because he alone is from God the Father.

Otherwise, if he were the work of creation, how could the Jews have failed to know who he was and from whom he came, since everything is proved to be from God, even though all things were made from nothing?

Therefore, whatever is not known as to where it is from is certainly unknown in respect of the divine nature from which it comes, since, if its origin is unknown, it is unknown what it is. For the origin of anything that subsists from nothing cannot be unknown.

But no one knows the Son except the Father alone, just as no one knows the Father except the Son alone.

You therefore have, reader, the distinctiveness of knowledge arising from the distinctiveness of generation: in the Son there is nothing other than what is in the Father, nor has anything unknowable to either arisen between them [Col. 0452A].

Hence the question arises: If the Father, as God, is known only to the Son, and the Son is known only to the Father, what does the Apostle mean when he says: “But God has revealed this to us through his Holy Spirit”?

If God the Father or God the Son has been revealed to them, how is the Father known only to the Son? Unless it is because he added: “And to whomever the Son wishes to reveal him.”

Nor is the Father or the Son known to anyone—not even to the angels—in the manner in which they know each other. In this mutual knowledge the Holy Spirit himself is often included, where it is said that “the Holy Spirit searches even the depths of God,” because he too possesses the nature of the Godhead.

Finally, in this passage the rashness of Eunomius is condemned. He says that a human being has as much knowledge of the Father and the Son as they have of each other. But it is one thing to know what one knows through equality of nature, and another to know, with certainty, as much as one knows through the condescension of the one who reveals.

Some ask why, when he says, “and to whomever the Son wishes to reveal him,” he did not say “the Father and the Son,” since neither of them can rightly be known without the other. They do not consider that he had already spoken above concerning the Father: “You have revealed these things to little ones.”

Thus, since they have one nature, they also have one operation of revelation through the Holy Spirit, in whom the profound mysteries of the Godhead are disclosed to us. For he is the Spirit of both, in whom all things exist [Col. 0452C].

Nevertheless, in this handing over by the Father, one must not understand heaven, earth, the elements of the world, and the rest, which he himself made and established. Rather, one must understand those who, through the Son, have access to the Father.

Hence it had long ago been said in the Psalms: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Ps. II, 8). When the Father gave or handed all these over, he did not lose them but acquired them, since previously they were enemies whom he adopted as sons.

It must therefore not be understood in the way some have wrongly wished, as though the Son could be known by no one except the Father alone, while the Father could be known not only by the Son but also by those to whom the Son wished to reveal him [Col. 0452D].

Rather, it must be understood in this way: we should believe that both the Father and the Son are revealed through the Son, because the Son appeared visibly so that he might be the inner light of our mind.

Yet the Son too was revealed and shown by the Father, as I have said, since no one knows one of them without the other. Thus, just as the Father declares himself through his Word, so the Word, the Son, declares not only what is declared through the Word but also himself.

Therefore, because all things have been handed over to him, he invites everyone to himself, since he is the mediator, so that he may bring them to the Father.

“Come to me,” he says, “all of you, and I will refresh you.”

This call is read in three ways when he says, “Come.” The first is the one spoken of here: “Come to me.” The second is the call by which we are taught, as he says: “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. XXXIII, 12). The third will be in the future, when he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matt. XXV, 34).

Furthermore, when he says:

“You who labor and are burdened,”

he appears to call Jews and Gentiles together. One of them was afflicted by the excessive labor of the Law without making any progress; the other was weighed down by the burdens of sins and, worshiping idols, was unable to look upward toward God.

The burdens of sin are indeed heavy. Hence Zechariah says that iniquity sits upon a talent of lead (Zech. V, 7), and David: “My iniquities have risen above my head, and like a heavy burden they have become too heavy for me” (Ps. XXXVII, 5).

The Law too was a heavy burden, as Peter teaches: “Neither we nor our fathers,” he says, “have been able to bear it” (Acts XV, 10).

And so the most gracious Savior calls to himself those exhausted by heavy labors or weighed down by burdens, intending to remove all these things, provided only that they accept his yoke, which is easy, and his burden, which is light, in accordance with what Isaiah says: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger” (Isa. I, 3).

The ox signifies the Jews, who drew the exceedingly heavy yoke of the Law; the donkey signifies the Gentiles, irrational and burdened with very many crimes.

They are first called to come to faith, and each is to receive what is especially his own: the Jews the labor peculiar to them, and the Gentiles, having laid down the burden of the camels, the lightness of Christ’s gentleness.

This is the yoke of which he said above that each person should take up the commandments of God together with the mystery of the Cross and follow Christ, because he is humble and gentle. He sets before believers these consolations, so that they may learn to refrain from evil and to do good.

For nothing is sweeter than to will what is good; nothing lighter than to live without guilt, to love everyone, to hate no one, to attain eternal things, not to be held by present things, and not to wish to inflict upon another what one does not wish to suffer oneself.

“And you will find,” he says, “rest for your souls.”

He said “for your souls,” not “for your bodies,” because at present bodies are afflicted so that souls may rest from vices and from the labors of this age. This does not mean that in the future the flesh will not also be restored to rest; rather, it means that the soul should already here rest in God, in whom true rest exists, and be refreshed daily with heavenly goods, lest, exhausted by the labors and pressures of the journey, it fail.

But Jews and Gentiles together are commanded to bear one yoke, joined and bound together, two by two, in the place of love, so that, laboring over the seeds of the word in the Gospel, they may grow more abundantly and the Lord’s harvest may increase with an increase of fruits.

This yoke of sweetness is, as I have said, the Cross of the Savior himself. And so that we may be able to bear it, he immediately adds the discipline of the Cross itself.

“Learn from me,” he says, “because I am gentle and humble in heart.”

Otherwise, no one but the humble can bear what he commands, and no one but the gentle can endure all that belongs to the Cross.

Therefore he commands us to learn from him—not to fashion the world, not to raise the dead, not to perform mighty signs, but to be humble and gentle, so that we may be able to endure everything.

One must also note that he says: “Because I am gentle and humble in heart.” This means not merely on the surface of the lips, but with the integrity of the heart; not through any mere outward arrangement or lowering of one’s appearance, although humility and gentleness must also be displayed bodily and verbally before human beings, but through complete devotion and abasement of mind.

For humility and gentleness must first be borne and possessed there, where God sees them; afterward they must be displayed outwardly from the fountain of the heart, so that they may be pleasing to God and acceptable to human beings.

Therefore, they must be learned from the gracious Lord and most merciful teacher precisely where they can remain and from where they can flow forth to everyone.

Meanwhile, it is rightly asked how the yoke of the Gospel can be called easy and the commandments of grace light, since adultery is condemned in the Law and desire in the Gospel; in the Gospel one is not permitted to become angry or to repay evil with evil, but is even commanded to render good for evil and to pray for enemies.

Moreover, the Law requires deeds which, as the Apostle says, the Jews were unable to bear. In the Gospel, however, even when the good intention has not achieved its effect, the will itself is required for what is good, while the will is condemned even when tested in what is evil.

But because the commandments of the Law were kept under fear, so that a person might live merely by observing them, they are called heavy and unbearable. The Gospel, however, now given to children through the grace that is in Christ Jesus, seems exceedingly light.

The fear of the Law brings punishment; the love of the Gospel brings sweetness, because whatever one desires is altogether more pleasing. For the earthly Law promises earthly and temporal things, whereas the Gospel promises heavenly and eternal things. There the guilty person is condemned without any mercy; here, by contrast, not only forgiveness but also grace and adoption are granted.

Therefore, since the whole Law and the Prophets are fulfilled in two commandments, grace perfects love—which is the foundation of everything—so that it may be preserved whole. Nothing is sweeter, lighter, or more pleasant than this love, because through love of God and neighbor we are not merely pressed down or burdened; through these two commandments we are even lifted up to heaven, so that we may become companions of the angels.

**Chapter XII**

At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath.

Mark and Luke relate the same event, but they do not assign it to this particular time. It therefore appears that Matthew has preserved the chronological order here. When Jesus answered, “I confess to you, Lord Father,” and what follows, he proceeded according to the order of narration; and for this reason he expressly says: “At that time Jesus went through the grainfields.”

But his disciples, being hungry, began to pluck ears of grain and eat them. Here the wondrous dispensation of God must be considered, and the sequence of events carefully observed, since from the point where he says, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matt. 9:37; Luke 10:2), up to this passage, an abundant variety of teaching overflows in the individual sayings. I have traversed these sayings, as best I could, more briefly than their importance required. But because they possess the splendor of divine utterance, because they are magnificent and divine, I have employed no verbal elegance or rhetorical ornament, nor sought a beautiful and praiseworthy style of discourse [Col. 0455A]; I have sought only to open the meaning to those of lesser capacity, and briefly to show the disciplines by which the perfect disciple of Christ is formed.

Now, after so great a vastness of divine wisdom and depth of understanding, let the attentive hearer consider to what work the pious Teacher invites those whom he has instructed and who are now at last becoming hungry. “At that time,” he says—as though he were saying, “when they had been instructed by these sayings”—“Jesus went through the grainfields,” so that they might remember what he had said: that the harvest was indeed plentiful and the laborers few. For this purpose, then, he had trained them: that they might be reapers of souls, and that they themselves might now harvest what others had previously cultivated. Hence they too began to hunger and to pluck the firstfruits of the ears of grain.

Did they not hunger before, since it is said so pointedly [Col. 0455B] that they then first began to hunger? They certainly did hunger before, but he orders everything in such a way that each event is filled with mysteries. For he speaks everywhere mystically—in words, in places and times, and in the things and deeds of his provident activity. Therefore, after such an abundance of the divine word and after such outstanding and wondrous discourses of teaching, the disciples are said, as though they were reapers, to have gone through the grainfields at that time when he had confessed thanks to God the Father for the salvation granted to the nations. Thus the same meaning might join what came before to what follows, so that the disciples might fulfill by their action what he had taught. And therefore, with what providential significance it is said that they began to hunger and to pluck the ears of grain!

Consider carefully: at that time the fervor of charity first began more abundantly to desire the salvation of souls—to tear human beings away from the world, to rub them with the teachings of the word so that they might grow warm, and to transfer them into his own body, so that together they might become members of Christ. For the harvest in the field is the human race in the world. But the fact that on the Sabbath those who are hungry as they journey pluck the ears of grain signifies leisure and rest from every work of the present age. [539] They are not sluggish through the indolence of the Jews, but journeying toward their homeland, hungering for the salvation of souls, and plucking them away from earthly actions—souls whose salvation the disciples hasten to satisfy.

Otherwise, food made from ears of grain is not sufficiently appropriate for a human being, nor is the eating of detached awns useful; but the outward form already enacts the faith of what was to come, and the force contained in the intervening words brings the mystery of hunger and satiety to completion. There is no doubt that if you wish to examine more diligently the meaning hidden in the deeds of the Savior, wherever it may lie, and to investigate what its singular understanding is, you will find that the reality is not as small as the sound of each individual word, but that the mysteries concealed within are immense, once the garment has been removed from the covering of the letter, so that the truth may be seen and grasped [Col. 0455D].

For so great is the ingenuity of the divine work and the wisdom of the Savior that he speaks through all things and deeds to those who desire to seek and receive salvation. Nevertheless, because they eat the ears of grain rubbed out with their hands, swollen and full, the austerity of life is signified; and this is an indication of the virtue of frugality, where not elaborate preparation of food but simple nourishment is sought.

That the apostles take ears of grain from another’s labor, and are not at all reproved, is a defense of the Law, which commands only that they not carry away a great quantity from it. But because they go on the Sabbaths, pluck, and rub the grain, they are condemned by those who zealously defend the letter of the Law. It should also be noted that he says “on the Sabbaths,” not “on the Sabbath,” because he indicates that they did this not only once or twice, but even more often, so that from this it might become evident, after the whole instruction of the new Law, that the letter of the Law was to be abolished and the observance of the Sabbath brought to an end. What common observance was there between a human being and sinners? For this reason it is first destroyed by the apostles, since Christ—the spiritual and true rest, and the true Lord of the Sabbath—was present.

To him they said:

“Why do your disciples do what they are not permitted to do on the Sabbaths?” That is, the things I mentioned above: going, plucking, and rubbing the grain, or doing anything of that kind. Since this was said in the plural, “on the Sabbaths,” it appears that the disciples did these things without observance of the Law on other Sabbaths as well. But the Lord answered on behalf of his disciples against the Jews who were slandering them:

“Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him; how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests?” [Col. 0456B]

The authority of an event in the past is brought forward, when David, fleeing from Saul, came to Nob (1 Sam. 21:1), where, received by Abimelech the priest, he asked for food. Since he had no ordinary bread, the priest gave him consecrated bread, which it was lawful for no one to eat except the priests and Levites. Thus we read in the Book of Kings [Col. 0456C] that he gave them the bread of the Presence, judging it better to rescue human beings from the danger of hunger than to preserve for himself and his own the loaves offered to God, because they had been sacrificed. He decided rather to fulfill that prophetic saying: “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Matt. 12:7).

Divine Wisdom uses this as an argument from events: what had once happened was already contained in prophecy, and from the logic of that prophecy he teaches most clearly that the earlier event was an example of this one. For David, being holy, is not believed to have done without guilt something that was unlawful. But because he did it, and the event is handed down to posterity as a memorial without the stain of guilt, there is no doubt that it was more truly a prophecy: that David, together with his companions, might be filled by the bread of the Presence.

This shows that Christ, together with his apostles, hungered for the salvation of the nations, about whom he had said above, “The harvest is indeed plentiful,” and that through them he transferred those nations into the body of the Church. From this it is perfectly clear that nothing was found among the deeds performed by the Savior that had not been foretold beforehand. He takes each matter concerning himself in such a way as though it were a testimony belonging to his own work, by which the salvation of human beings is the acceptable sacrifice.

Therefore, in this passage he proposes the matter and speaks to the Jews who were making accusations from the Law, as though offering an argument by which the truth of the event might be established.
