It is as if he were saying: “If David is holy, and Abimelech the high priest is rightly not reproved by you—indeed, if both are shown, by a reasonable defense, not to have violated the commandment of the Law—why do you not approve the same hunger in my disciples? Especially since there is a great difference between the two events.

“He ate Levitical loaves; these rub ears of grain with their hands. He was in the tabernacle; these are in a field. He acted on the day of the New Moon, when his place at the king’s table appeared empty; these act on the Sabbath, at the time appointed for rest. He was merely a human being; I am God and human being. He fought with his earthly soldiers using earthly weapons; these, sent by God the Father and by me as preachers, are sent to conquer the whole world—twelve men against it all.”

This figure, brought forward as an example, surpasses all the philosophical arguments by which plausible proofs of events are woven together. For here, as I have said, an external example is set forth with complete clarity, while within it the truth itself, long prophesied and hidden, is disclosed: the twelve loaves of the Presence prefigure the twelve apostles, and the harvest from which they pluck the grains is the totality of the nations.

Moreover, the scribes and Pharisees, like Saul pursuing David, pursue Christ the King; in Abimelech the high priest they desire to kill him, while Doeg the Edomite represents Judas in the deed.

“Have you not read in the Law,” he says, “that on the Sabbaths the priests in the Temple profane the Sabbath by violating it without guilt? But I tell you that something greater than the Temple is here.” He refutes them most openly by showing that on each Sabbath the priests do worse things in the Temple and violate the Sabbaths: sacrificing victims, slaughtering bulls, placing burnt offerings upon a pile of wood, and consuming them in the fire, without regard to the charge of necessity. It is as though he were saying: “While you wish to observe one part of the Law, you certainly violate and destroy the Sabbath.”

Moreover, as we read in another Gospel, they circumcised boys on the Sabbath so that circumcision might be preserved on the eighth day. Many such examples are found in the Law, and for this reason I do not think that the laws of God are contradictory to one another. Yet Christ, who is the Wisdom of God the Father, wisely directs this example against those same people who had brought an accusation against his disciples, and sets before them more serious violations of the Law, although these appear to be without guilt.

Everything is presented here so that he might prove his own disciples innocent and convict those who accused the apostles as guilty and full of envy. Now, when he says, “because something greater than the Temple is here,” the Greek wording shows that this is not a pronoun but an adverb of place: the place that contains the Lord of the Temple is greater than the Temple. The Lord himself was also holier and greater, although he was bodily present in that place, than the Temple at Jerusalem [Col. 0457D].

He further confirms from the divine Scriptures what he had brought against them. “If you knew,” he says, “what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice’” (Matt. 12:7), you would never have condemned those who not only defiled themselves but also violated the Sabbath and the Temple. The meaning is: “If you accept Abimelech’s action with mercy and approve it because, when David and his companions were endangered by hunger, he refreshed them with bread consecrated to the Lord, why do you condemn my disciples, who, because of hunger, take not loaves offered to God but merely grains?”

This example should be noted because it teaches that the work of our salvation lies not in sacrifice but in mercy. For once the Law has ceased, we are saved solely by the goodness of God. If they had understood this gift, they would never, out of envy, have condemned the innocent—that is, the apostles. Especially since, with the Law ceasing, the newness of mercy was to come to the aid of all through them. Hence the meaning is clearer than daylight: it is better mercifully to refresh the hungry with food than to observe the Sabbath rest.

“For the Son of Man,” he says, “is Lord even of the Sabbath.” That is, Christ, the Son of God and human being, is truly Lord of the Sabbath. He established and created the Sabbath not for the sake of the Sabbath against the human being, but the Sabbath for the sake of the human being. Indeed, every human being also appears rightly to be lord of the Sabbath, because the Sabbath was made for that person, and out of mercy one may lawfully set aside the regulations of the Sabbath.

But Christ, the Son of Man, rules and is Lord even of the Sabbath in a wholly different way, because all things were created through him and the universe subsists through him.

It follows:

“And when he had passed on from there, he came into their synagogue.” Luke, however, says that he came into the synagogue not on the same Sabbath but on another. This shows that some days intervened during which he discussed the matters stated above; afterward he passed on from the grainfield and, on another Sabbath, entered the synagogue from the field.

“And behold, there was a man who had a withered hand.” This, then, is the thirteenth person healed in their synagogue. It should be noted that he was healed not on the road or outside, but in the assembly of the Jews, where his hand had withered and had become sluggish through the dryness of good works.

Moreover, in the Gospel used by the Nazarenes, it is said that this man was a builder, and that he asked for help in these words: “I was a builder, earning my livelihood with my hands; I beg you, Jesus, to restore my health, so that I may not disgracefully beg for food.”

That hand remained withered in the synagogue of the Jews until the Savior’s coming. But after he came, it was restored in the believing apostles; the right hand was restored to good works and granted health.

“When he had come into their synagogue, they questioned him, saying whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbaths, so that they might accuse him.” Mark and Luke, however, report that Jesus asked them whether it was lawful on the Sabbaths to do good or evil, to save a life or destroy it. It appears from this that they first questioned the Lord, testing him so that they might be able to accuse him on account of the Sabbath. Understanding their wickedness, Jesus placed in the midst the man who was to be healed and himself asked the question, as these two evangelists explicitly testify.

When they remained silent, he again put forward a very striking comparison involving a sheep. The seemingly unavoidable question was thereby loosened like a spider’s web. For if he said that it was lawful, he would be held as a transgressor of the Law; but if he said that it was not lawful, he would be accused of being merciless or powerless in the face of the infirmity presented, since he would not help the one who asked.

“Who among you,” he says, “if he has one sheep and it falls into a pit on the Sabbaths, will not take hold of it and lift it out? How much more valuable is a human being than a sheep?” The sheep was made for the human being, and not only the sheep but also the Sabbath on which the sheep fell. Therefore, because you violate the Sabbath for the sake of a sheep and are not held guilty, much more ought I not to be held guilty, since I left the ninety-nine on the mountains and came to seek the one that had wandered and fallen into the pit of death.

This figure both refutes the Jews and reveals the Savior’s deed: he came to save what had perished. But the wretched Pharisees, blinded by malice, could not understand the wisdom of God, and therefore tried to resist. They are refuted by their own deeds and bound by their own chains.

Christ, who heals by his word and drives away infirmities by his power, indicates in a particular instance what he was going to do universally. The Jews themselves are healed in the man with the withered hand, because they did not possess the substance of salvation to be given, and the hand’s function had ceased. The ministry of the body, by which something is done or imparted, had also withered.

The Lord commanded him to stretch out his hand, and at once it was restored to health like the other. Its healing took place through a word, and the hand was made sound like the other; thus, in a wondrous and admirable example, the power of salvation was displayed—not by human agency or by chance, but by divine providence and, so to speak, by prophecy of God’s supreme work.

The ministry of the apostles in the work of giving salvation is brought into effect before they begin to pluck the ears of grain. The hand of the human being had withered more from the stupor of faith than from the dryness of the nerves, and more from the guilt of conscience than from bodily weakness.

This was the ancient hand, which at the very beginning of the world had contracted its sickness. It could be healed neither by human skill nor by human favor. It had been dried up by the just indignation of God, because it had touched what was forbidden and presumed upon what was not permitted when it reached out toward the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Therefore it needed an author of salvation—not one who would apply a poultice, but one who could loosen the sentence imposed and, by forgiving, release what he had justly bound in indignation.

For this reason, as I have said, the man with the withered hand is divinely prepared so that in him an argument for our salvation might be made, because perfect salvation is restored to us in Christ. The dryness of our pitiable hand is dissolved when it is drenched with the blood of the Lord’s Passion; when it is stretched out upon that life-giving wood of the cross; when it plucks from the suffering of the Passion the fruitful power of pain; when it embraces the tree of salvation; when the body is fastened by the nails of divine love, so that it may never again return to the tree of desire belonging to a withered will [Col. 0459C].

But wretched are the Jews, who do not receive Christ when he enters among them, do not recognize him when he is present, and do not understand that he is acting divinely! From this one must consider how little bodily presence accomplishes when the mind has been miserably separated from God; and, conversely, how bodily absence does not hinder when the hearts of the faithful have been joined to God through faith and possess the integrity of a good will.

Otherwise, good things always offend the wicked, holy things the impious, and sacred things the profane. For this reason the worst priests watched on the Sabbaths not to see whether he sinned, but whether he healed, so that they might accuse him. They plotted accusations against acts of virtue, as though the Sabbath had been established against salvation rather than for salvation.

He is therefore commanded to stretch out his hand, so that he might display the generosity of good works. But they immediately make an accusation from the man’s healing, because a human being is healed on the Sabbath—as though none of them stretched out a hand or moved a foot on that day, at least to carry food to his mouth or extend a cup.

On the Sabbath and in the Temple, as was said above, they performed even greater actions, especially since the Law permitted a journey of up to a thousand paces. Hence it is clear that they were troubled by the zeal of bitterness and envy, not by concern for the Sabbath, but because they were plotting against him out of hatred.

“But the Pharisees went out and took counsel against him, how they might destroy him.” As another evangelist says, they entered into this council with the Herodians (Mark 3:6), that is, with Herod’s soldiers, so that they themselves might appear innocent while the others killed him, as we later read that they did during the Passion.

Every evil is more serious when it is long premeditated and carried out, as though after deliberation and counsel. But there is no counsel against God. Therefore he says, “Jesus, knowing it, withdrew from there.” He knew secretly what they were doing—he who knows the hearts of all—and what sort of counsel they were undertaking. For this reason he withdrew, to take away from them the opportunity for impiety; either because the time of his Passion had not yet come, or in order to give his own an example of avoiding dangers for a time.

“And many followed him, and he healed them all, and he ordered them not to make him known.” He hastens, then, to lead aside and separate from unbelievers those whom he intends to heal. Those who desire salvation follow without weariness, and he heals all who follow him. No one who wishes to follow him in imitation is excluded from salvation.

He orders them not to make him known, not because of fear, but so that he might not provide an occasion for boasting about himself. Rather, he teaches the avoidance of ostentation by commanding that both himself and the works performed by him be concealed. The salvation restored to each person was itself a witness. Yet by commanding silence about himself, he provides greater knowledge of himself, because the observance of silence proceeds from the matter that is to be kept silent. The deed itself displays its reality openly, even while suggesting that one should remain silent about it.

Thus, just as had been foretold through Isaiah, he demonstrates with complete clarity that he is Christ, the Savior of the world, when he commands that they not make him known, because they were unworthy to have him announced publicly. To confirm this, the Evangelist introduces the testimony:

“As it was spoken,” he says, “through Isaiah the prophet, saying: ‘Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul has been well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will announce judgment to the nations. He will not contend or cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. He will not break a bruised reed, and he will not extinguish smoking flax, until he brings judgment forth to victory; and in his name the nations will hope.’”

I have set all this down together so that the discerning reader may consider that not all these testimonies pertain to this passage. For he confirms the foregoing statement with only one phrase, when he says, “Nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets.” The other parts appear to establish other places in his narrative. For example, “Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul has been well pleased,” corresponds to the passage where he says, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). The remaining phrases likewise correspond to their respective places.

Yet all these passages portray Christ and mark him with their own distinctive features. This figure is called *characterismos*, “description” in Latin. It describes his innocence in such a way that this long narrative of the chapter seems to fit no one else but Christ, who was never seen to be turbulent or anxious, according to Jerome’s interpretation, because he maintained an even expression at all times—a quality which philosophers falsely boast of in Pythagoras, as though he had never been sadder or happier than usual.

But so that the explanation of this testimony concerning Christ may become more evident, let us proceed through each phrase according to the variety of interpreters. At the beginning of this passage, the Septuagint has, “Jacob is my servant,” and “I will take hold of him,” “Israel is my chosen one,” “I have received him.” But Matthew, because he followed the Hebrew truth, included neither “Jacob” nor “Israel,” but only, “Behold, my servant.”

For whenever prophecy concerns the apostolic choir, they are always called “Jacob,” or “Israel,” or the seed of Abraham; and to them, as human beings and servants, it is accordingly said: “Do not fear, Jacob, you worm, and Israel, small in number” (Isa. 41:14). But wherever the prophecy concerns Christ, perfect as he is in the present reality, “Jacob” and “Israel” are always omitted.

It is therefore no surprise if Christ is called a servant, for the Evangelist says, “Behold, my servant,” since he was made from a woman and made under the Law: “Though he was in the form of God, he humbled himself, taking the form of a servant, and was found in human likeness” (Phil. 2:7). In him the soul of God the Father was well pleased. This does not mean that God the Father, from whose person the Prophet speaks, possesses a soul; rather, it is spoken figuratively, in human fashion, just as in very many passages where bodily members are also attributed to God.

He testifies that the Father was well pleased in him because all virtues were in him and no sin. Indeed, he himself is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

“I have given,” he says, “my Spirit upon him”—not partially, but wholly. The Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove and remained wholly in him. He is called a servant because, although lesser in the form of a servant, the one and same Christ is coequal with the Father in the kingdom and in the form of God.

Because he is equal in divinity, he has one will with the Father. The Father placed his entire pleasure in him who was born from Mary. Therefore those who desire to please God should please him in Christ, outside whom nothing can please God.

“And he will announce judgment to the nations” (Matt. 12:18), or he will bring forth what they previously did not know. Hence he says of himself: “For judgment I have come into this world” (John 9:39), since the Father has also given all judgment to the Son, because he is the Son of Man (ibid., 5:22).

“He will not contend or cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets.” For broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction (Jer. 7:13). On that way no one hears his voice, because he himself is the narrow and constricted way by which the few strive to enter, so that through him they may arrive at him.

Many do not hear him because they walk along the broad and spacious way, on which Christ is never heard, although Wisdom cries out publicly and raises her voice in the streets, at the head of all the roads. Unless someone passes from this street to the narrow way that leads to life, he cannot hear Christ inwardly.

Alternatively, he is said not to cry out because he was gentle and meek, without loud speech, not opening his mouth; and he will not show partiality in judgment. Or, “he will not raise”—that is, it may be understood, he will not raise his voice on high. According to Symmachus, “he will not be deceived,” because he will understand all the devil’s snares.

The Septuagint, however, says here, “He will not be left”; that is, he will not abandon the Jewish people unless he calls them to repentance. Nor will his voice be heard outside, that is, beyond Galilee, nor will he preach the Gospel outside Judea among the other nations.

Even if we read that he was in the region of Tyre and Sidon, or in the territory of Caesarea, which is now called Paneas, we must nevertheless understand that it is not written that he entered those cities or preached in them.

That he did not contend even when condemned is clear: he did not defend himself when assailed with many insults, reproaches, blows, and lashes; nor did he cry out when it was said to him, “Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?” (Matt. 27:13).

“A bruised reed,” he says, “whether broken or shattered, he will not crush” (Isa. 42:3), because he was conciliatory toward all and granted forgiveness to sinners, saying to the woman, “Take courage, daughter; your sins are forgiven” (Matt. 9:2).

“And smoking flax,” or, as others translated it, “what is dim and darkened,” “he will not extinguish” (Matt. 12:20). For all shouting, anger, indignation, and bitterness were far from him; therefore he harmed no one. Whoever does not extend a hand to the sinner and does not carry his brother’s burden crushes the bruised reed or cane. Whoever despises a small spark of faith, justice, or good work in a little one extinguishes the smoking flax.

Christ is proved not to have done this, because those who were near death and darkened by the shadows of sins were saved by his mercy. They were kindled by the flame of charity, for he came to enlighten those darkened by sin and to save what had perished.

Alternatively, the kingdom of the Jews was bruised and broken because it stumbled against the stone of offense. It was not Christ but their sin that crushed it, because they received him. The smoking flax that they possessed—that is, the priests themselves—was extinguished not by him but by their unbelief, because they brought forth stench and blindness rather than the flame of charity.

Yet he rejected neither the nations nor the Jews from faith. He bound up what was broken and sought what had perished. Moreover, he rekindled the small spark of the Jews, to whom alone he had been born, so that from the little light of the knowledge of God, and from the spark of punishment that was dying, immense fires might be kindled throughout the world, so that the whole earth might burn with the fire of the Lord Savior—the fire he came to cast upon the earth and which he desires to burn still more.

It follows: “And in truth he will bring forth judgment” (Isa. 42:3). Then, according to the Hebrew, “He will not be sad or turbulent until he establishes judgment on the earth.” The Septuagint, instead of “sad” and “turbulent,” has “he will shine” and “he will not be crushed”; the Evangelist included neither version here.

Indeed, this appears to have resulted from a copyist’s error, because above it says, “In truth he will bring forth judgment,” and below, “until he establishes judgment.” The intervening phrase, whether according to the Hebrew or according to the Septuagint, was omitted by the copyist.

But since I have already discussed one of these versions above, let us see what the Septuagint says: “He will shine and will not be crushed.” He will shine when he rises from the dead, ascending victorious from death and illuminating all. Or he will shine, as some say, when a certain radiance flashing from his face struck back against those opposing him, so that they could not endure the sight of his countenance—as happened (John 2:15) when he made a whip from cords and drove everyone from the Temple, and likewise in other passages.

This happened so that he would not be crushed by his enemies, but might pass unharmed through their midst whenever he wished.

As for the statement that “in truth he will bring forth judgment; he will shine and will not be crushed until he establishes judgment on the earth,” there is no doubt that the Savior judges every judgment according to truth. To him it was said: “Give the king your judgments, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71:1), who will repay each person according to his works.

Nevertheless, in the present time he showed no reverence toward the scribes and Pharisees; he publicly rebuked them with confidence and branded them with the name of hypocrites. He will shine in his Church and in his members, and he will not be crushed, although the Church may often appear to suffer persecution and to be obscured, until the end of the age, until he brings his judgment forth to victory, so that, already victorious, he may say to death: “Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your victory?” (1 Cor. 15:55).

His judgments are truly true in all things, justified in themselves. Hence David says elsewhere to him: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50:6).

Therefore, let every teacher of the Church act with confidence, because the teaching of Christ will shine and will not be crushed, even by one who exalts himself and rises up against God, until Christ brings his judgment forth to victory. Then, with the power of death removed, he will display the glory of his judgment to all and demonstrate that in everything he has conquered in truth.

These things establish, as it were, a fixed limit within a certain period of time, until his will is done, “as in heaven and on earth,” and his judgment passes into victory. Hence Aquila and Theodotion translated the passage in this way: “He will not obscure, and he will not run, until he establishes judgment on the earth.” The meaning is that no sadness of countenance will frighten anyone, nor will he hasten toward the punishment of the impious; rather, he will reserve everything for the judgment of the final time.

What follows, “And in his name the nations will hope,” has in Hebrew, “And the islands will hope in his law.” The Evangelist interpreted the sense rather than the words: instead of “law” and “islands,” he used “name” and “nations,” saying, “In his name the nations will hope.”

This was done not only here, but wherever the Evangelists and apostles brought forward testimonies from the Old Testament. According to Jerome, they did not merely follow the words, but the sense; and where the Septuagint differs from the Hebrew, they expressed the Hebrew sense in their own language.

That the nations hope in the name of Christ is already witnessed by the whole world. The islands—that is, the Churches—have received his law, namely, the Gospel. Although they may be shaken by various waves, their foundation remains immovable, because they have been founded upon the firm rock.

“Then a demon-possessed man was brought to him, blind and mute, and he healed him, so that the blind and mute man spoke and saw.” The phrase “then he was brought” indicates the time when many followed him and he healed them all. Luke tells of this event, though not in the same order, and he does not mention the blindness.

Here, clearly, three signs occurred together: the blind man sees, the mute man speaks, and the one possessed by a demon is liberated. If Luke is silent about one of these features, he should not therefore be thought to be speaking of another person, but of the same one. Through this man, as through a figure, the entire human race is represented.

This healing occurs most appropriately here: after all the crowds, charity is now held in common, while a blind and mute man having a demon is brought forward outwardly [the Latin syntax is uncertain]. Thus the order of interpretation appears to have been mystically preserved without any ambiguity.

The apostles were accused by the Pharisees for plucking ears of grain—that is, for snatching human beings away from the world. In response, mercy is proclaimed above sacrifice. Then the man with the withered hand is brought into the synagogue and healed. These miracles not only accomplish nothing toward converting Israel; the Pharisees even enter into a conspiracy to kill him.

Therefore, after these events, it was necessary that the salvation of all the nations be represented in the figure of one human being: the people who had been the dwelling place of the demon should become capable of God, see God in Christ, and praise Christ’s works in the confession of the whole Trinity.

When this was done, the crowds were astonished, but the envy of the Pharisees grew heavier. Since they saw that these great works of his surpassed human weakness, they avoided the shame of acknowledging the truth by committing a greater crime of unbelief.

Because they could not regard these works as the works of a human being, they refused to confess them as God’s works. They maintain that all this power of his is in Beelzebub, the prince of demons, and proclaim that it was accomplished by the power of a demon.

But all the crowds were astonished and said: “Can this be the Son of David?” The blindness of the Pharisees was exceedingly wretched. The crowds marvel and are struck with amazement at the signs, and they ask about and confess the Son of David, whom they knew from the prophecy of the prophets to have been promised. But the Pharisees slander him and maliciously turn the matter toward blasphemy.

But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste.” He answered their thoughts, so that they might at least in this way be compelled to believe that he is God, since he alone knows human thoughts and, by his own power, observes the hidden things of hearts. Then he employs against them a remarkable argument: every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste. Thus he provides an abundance of understanding concerning himself and of examples, whether it is understood simply [Col. 0465A] or examined more deeply.

His response is therefore exceedingly rich against those who slanderously claimed that his works had been performed in the name of Beelzebub, so that it may be understood in two ways. First, the condition of the response itself may be turned back against that same kingdom of theirs—namely, the kingdom of the Jews—which, being badly divided, cannot stand. The Law was given by God, and the promise or stability of the kingdom of Israel derives from the Law. Christ’s birth or coming, however, is the fullness of the Law. If the kingdom is divided against itself, as they caused it to be, it must necessarily be laid waste; and this is what happened. For every power is weakened by division, and the strength of a kingdom, separated and fighting against itself, is consumed.

Accordingly, Israel lost its kingdom according to the Law when the arrogance [Col. 0465B] and pride of the rulers and Pharisees, in their bitter jealousy, resisted Christ, even though he brought the Law to fulfillment. The consequence of this division was that the people, the city, and the kingdom were brought to destruction.

But they also prove, by their own words—although they did not understand what they were saying—that the kingdom of the devil cannot stand, since they spoke against themselves in precisely the same manner. By the very kind of statement they had made, he condemns them: he shows that, according to their slander, they had confessed that the kingdom of Beelzebub was divided against itself. Even if he had been compelled to bring about this division within his own kingdom, so that the most filthy demon disturbed the other demons, the division itself was nevertheless against him, and therefore his kingdom plainly could not stand.

Here too it must be acknowledged that the one who divided them had greater power than those who were divided and expelled. His kingdom, therefore, is already divided and compelled to oppose itself; under such division it has already been dissolved and destroyed. Moreover, when he says:

“Every city and house divided against itself will not stand,”

the reasoning or analogy is the same as that concerning the kingdom. Yet “city” here may be understood as Jerusalem, in which the worship of God was once honored in glory. But after the people, hostile to God, burned with fury against their Lord so that they might kill him, and drove out his apostles because they would not believe, division occurred: the kingdom fell, the city was destroyed, and the house was demolished down to its foundations, in accordance with the Savior’s threat.

Nevertheless, the most merciful Lord does not cease to set before the hardness of their hearts still clearer examples.

“But if Satan,” he says, “casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how, then, will his kingdom stand?” [Col. 0465D]

It is as though he were saying: if the demon is his own enemy and attacks himself—when he drives his soldiers from the bodies they have possessed—how can his kingdom stand once peace has been restored to those whom they had dominated? The hostile powers have no place in such a kingdom, since, while they quarrel, peace is restored, all the inner and outer members of the body are healed, and the whole human being is cured through faith.

And if demons always desire to harm human beings, while the one who is greater than they in wickedness heals them by invoking his own name, how can his kingdom stand? It is as though he said: judge among yourselves and convict yourselves by your own slanders, because their will—always evil and eager to inflict harm—cannot be compared with my most merciful works. For the kingdom of the devil is the malice by which he harms, and through which he reigns over those whom he harms. Kindness, however, and the bestowal of health no longer belong to his kingdom, but to the grace of the Holy Spirit and to the work of God, the mediator between God and human beings.

“But if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?” [Col. 0466A]

He still refutes them by the example of exorcists among that people, who are said, through invocation of God’s name, to have cast out demons and, by their invocations, to have healed those badly afflicted by unclean spirits.

Or, as I judge more probable, this should be understood of the apostles, to whom authority was given to judge the twelve tribes of Israel. “Therefore,” he says, “they will be your judges.” The Jewish exorcists also could not be judges possessing such great authority; yet, by comparison and by the faith with which the invocation was made, they are rightly said to be future judges. For what was done among these men, who were less than Christ, the Pharisees did not believe had been done through him, who was God in Christ.

Thus, by an exceedingly prudent question—as in all matters he presses them—he compels them to confess that the work which had been performed was accomplished by the power of the Holy Spirit. It is as though he openly cried out: if the casting out of demons by your sons is attributed not to the demons but to the Lord, why do you not approve the same work in me? Or why do you not assign the same cause to me? They will therefore be your judges because you believe that they act in the Spirit of God; and I will contend with you before their judgment, since they attribute the entire work of human salvation to God, whereas you assign it to Beelzebub—something that is directed against him and does not even suit him.

What, then, is more fitting than that they should be the judges of those who are not hesitant to believe that Christ gave them authority against demons, while denying that he himself possessed such authority? Therefore, if the disciples work in Christ, and Christ in the Spirit of God, then surely the kingdom of God has already been poured into the disciples through the office of the mediator.

For this reason he says (Matt. XII, 28): “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God—and you believe this—then the kingdom of God—and of the whole Trinity—has certainly come upon you.” In this deed the whole Trinity is declared: Christ, in the Spirit of God the Father, works power in the human race, through which the kingdom of God—namely, the forgiveness of sins—is rightly believed to have come upon believers.

But “the kingdom of God” must be understood in three ways. It may mean God himself, of whom it is said elsewhere: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII, 21). Or it may mean that sublime kingdom of which John and Christ himself preached: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. IV, 17). Or, in a third sense, Holy Scripture or the Law is called the kingdom of God, concerning which it was said: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI, 43). The Jews lost all these things together when they did not receive Christ.

It should also be noted that Matthew says “by the Spirit of God,” whereas Luke is found to say “by the finger of God.” What Luke set forth more obscurely, Matthew is shown to have established more clearly. This, then, is the finger of God of which Pharaoh’s magicians confess: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VIII, 19). The Law, too, is read to have been written by the finger of God on Mount Sinai. By this finger, certainly, the depth of the holy Scriptures was inspired in holy men, and the law of truth was opened.

Therefore, if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God or by the finger of God—whoever those may be from whom I cast them out—then the kingdom of God, and of the whole Trinity, has certainly come upon you. Otherwise, unless the Trinity is believed to be God and the one equality of the Godhead is commended to us, neither are demons driven away nor can it rightly be believed that the kingdom of God has come.

But the pious Teacher continues to touch upon and refute the hardness of their hearts more broadly, showing that the expulsion of demons and the healing of human souls are works of the Godhead. Hence he adds:

“How can anyone enter the house of a strong man and plunder his possessions, unless he first binds the strong man? Then he will plunder his house.”

Against the monstrous and senseless obstinacy of the Jews—if I may put it so—the most merciful Savior employs many new arguments. Thus, once again, he introduces the likeness of a very strong man, just as he had already spoken of a kingdom and a city: no one can enter or plunder such a house unless he has first conquered and bound the strong man.

The present Evangelist makes it sufficiently clear that the Lord himself did this immediately after his baptism, when he was led into the desert and confronted the devil—indeed, that very one whom those utterly insane men called the prince of demons. He confronted him and defeated and rejected him three times.

This is why the statement is now made here, as though he were expressing the matter in other words: how could I cast out demons unless I had first defeated and bound their prince, who consented to them in every wicked work?

That he himself is strong and unconquerable, the Lord describes and indicates most clearly to his servant Job, saying that there is no power on earth that can be compared with him. For this reason Luke appropriately adds: “But when one stronger than he comes upon him and defeats him, he takes away all his armor in which he trusted and distributes his spoils” (Luke XI, 23).

There he plainly shows that Christ, the stronger one, defeated and bound that strong man, fastening him with the very bonds of his own wickedness, so that he could do no more harm than was permitted to him. Having bound him in this way, the Savior stripped him of his spoils and took away his house—that is, us, whom he redeemed; whom, after defeating the Devil, he brought under his own dominion; and from whom he dedicated a new house for himself, sanctifying the Church.

Those whom, in his just judgment, he abandoned, he bound in their hearts, as in an abyss, like a condemned strong man together with his followers, and he removed from him all those whom he redeemed. Otherwise human beings could not free themselves by their own strength, since he was strong and held them captive, unless they were liberated by the grace of God and Christ, stronger than he, had bound the strong man. Christ took away his power, so that he could not obstruct the will of the faithful, preventing them from following Christ and obtaining the kingdom offered to them.

Therefore, when I say “offered,” the present passage indicates that even those who are not yet willing are compelled to receive it. For this reason he continues:

“Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.”

By this syllogism he decisively proves that the demon Beelzebub is far from him—as far as light is from darkness or good from evil—for nothing is found to be more opposed to him. Thus he argues not only that he borrowed nothing from Beelzebub or acted in his name and power, but that he cannot agree with him in any respect. Whoever is not with him is against him, and whoever does not gather with him scatters. From this it follows that the immense unity of Christ’s body is distinguished from the divided condition of Satan’s body: whoever is proven to scatter against Christ is not gathered into that which is God the Trinity, nor into him.

In all this he acts so that it may be understood that he, sent by God the Father, works in the Holy Spirit. In this way the unity of the Father and the Son is commended—the Spirit belongs to both, and the same love belongs to both, of which it is said: “God is love” (I John IV, 16).

Therefore no one is with Christ, even if he appears to bear his name and is called a Christian, unless he possesses the Holy Spirit, in whom unity is commended as a gift. For the Spirit is not only undivided against himself, but also makes indivisible all whom he gathers: by forgiving the sins that were divided against themselves, and by dwelling in those who have been cleansed, he makes them members of Christ and the body of Christ. In that body unity is commended and gathered.

Those, however, who are on the opposite side are neither with him nor do they gather with him; they scatter until they are divided from the unity of Christ’s body.

If this is so, what are we to make of the disciples’ report that they had seen someone casting out demons in Christ’s name and had forbidden him because he did not follow them? The Lord said to them: “Do not forbid him. Whoever is not against you is for you. For no one can do anything in my name and then speak evil of me.”

How, then, was he not against them—or rather, against the Lord—since he was not yet in the body of Christ and had not been reborn in the Holy Spirit so as to follow the Lord, through whom this unity is gathered? If he had been, the disciples would certainly not have forbidden him to cast out demons in Jesus’ name, nor even to perform any miracles, which they themselves were undoubtedly performing.

Since, then, he was outside this unity, how does the Savior say: “Whoever is not against you is for you”? If this is to be understood in an absolute sense, it appears that everyone who is outside the communion of the Church and separated from the fellowship of the Christian religion is with Christ and gathers in his name. In that case the statement found here would be false: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. XII, 30).

Anyone who works some good or performs miracles in Christ’s name outside the Church of Christ might therefore seem able to remain secure; but the catholic faith does not accept this at all. For this reason, whenever statements appear to disagree in the divine Scriptures—especially in the words of the Lord—great discrimination of meaning must be applied, lest he be found, God forbid, to contradict himself.

In this deed the man was not against them but for them, since he was performing healings in Christ’s name. Therefore, so that both statements may be true—as they unquestionably are—we must seek the manner in which both can rightly be understood according to the Lord’s meaning.

Thus, in this particular deed, he was not to be forbidden, in accordance with the Lord’s command. Rather, he was to be confirmed all the more in his reverence for so great a name. He was not against Christ, nor against the apostles, nor against the Church. Nevertheless, he was blameworthy in that he did not follow Christ or join himself to him, since he had not yet been reborn in the Holy Spirit and had not been united with him in the love of Christ, so as to be his member.

Since he was separated from the unity of Christ and the Church, although he himself was gathering, he was nevertheless scattering outside, because he was not yet with Christ. If he had come to Christ and to the Church, he would not have retained what he already possessed, but would have corrected in himself what was erroneous and received what he did not yet have.

For surely the prayers of Cornelius, a Gentile, were not unheard, nor were his almsgivings unaccepted (Acts X, 31). Indeed, he was deemed worthy to see an angel sent to him. But because these things could not benefit him except through the bond of Christian fellowship and peace, so that he might be incorporated into the Church, he was ordered to send for Peter, in order that through Peter he might learn Christ and, after being baptized through him, might be gathered into the fellowship of the Church’s sacred communion and unity.

Otherwise, if he had refused to receive the good that he lacked—the fellowship of Christ and the Church—he would have scattered in that which made him opposed to Christ and to his Church, proudly remaining outside on account of what he possessed.

Christ therefore appears in this saying to address both those who are inside and those who are outside: either those who are outside may wish to enter with Christ, be in the Church, and become one body; or those who are inside, as though already gathered in the house, may refuse to gather with Christ and to assemble their virtues, so that they may remain stable, founded and firmly established upon the rock.

Those who build their house upon sand and store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath do not gather with Christ, who is the rock, so as to possess a stable foundation; rather, they scatter. When the wind and the breeze blow upon them, they are carried here and there like dust before the face of the wind.

Therefore those who are outside—whether pagans or heretics—even if they possess God’s sacraments, through which they may perhaps perform miracles, are not with God, because they are not in the Church and are not gathered into the unity of peace through the Holy Spirit. For this reason they are against God.

Likewise, those who are inside through the sacrament of baptism, as though in the house, but do not build upon the rock, which is Christ, scatter themselves because they do not wish to gather in the unity of Christ, so as to be in the Church of God and themselves become one, incorporated and joined together in the Holy Spirit through the bond of peace.

From this it is also gathered, on both sides, that the body of the Devil is never with Christ and never gathers with him, either inside or outside, according to the inner person who is renewed day by day in the knowledge of truth and joined through love in the unity of Christ’s body.

Although they may possess certain benefits of God’s sacraments, through which they may appear to be with God, inside or outside, they are nevertheless rightly called Antichrist’s, since in many respects they are shown to be against him. Yet they are not against the Church but for the Church in that what they possess consists of his gifts, not of the gifts of those who misuse them—misusing them to their own destruction and condemnation, but to the Church’s testimony.

Thus both groups, although in certain respects they are with God, are shown, inside or outside, to be against God, because they are not according to God and they scatter.

It follows:

“Therefore I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings, but the blasphemy of the Spirit will not be forgiven human beings. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.”

The brilliance of the most distinguished teacher Augustine demonstrates that this passage is exceedingly obscure, for he delivered many discourses to the people concerning its questions. No one ought to criticize us if our pious labor and industry has produced anything beyond these discussions; and because we are weak and insignificant, no one should despise us for attempting great and incredible things, since the matters we treat are great and exceptional.

Therefore, if we venture and presume more than we can accomplish, I ask that no one preemptively bar the gift of grace—at least not the good thing we desire. For the matter under discussion is not only obscure but also extremely necessary to understand, and exceedingly frightening once understood: “Every sin and every blasphemy will be forgiven human beings, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.”

A matter is often better understood through comparison among interpreters; what lies hidden is often discerned by comparing the opinions of teachers, and what is evident is grasped more fully in the Holy Spirit. Thus comparison among the Evangelists often produces a fuller understanding. In the present case Mark states the cause of such great anger more clearly: “Because,” he says, “they were saying that he had an unclean spirit” (Mark III, 30). The present Evangelist likewise shows by his own indications that this threat arose from the same blasphemy, because they were saying that he cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.

For, as the catholic faith knows, all forgiveness of sins and all sanctification take place in the Holy Spirit. In this gift all gifts of power are bestowed. If someone therefore blasphemes against the one in whom all these sacraments of perfection exist, how can he obtain forgiveness of sins? How will he be sanctified from his uncleanness? Or how will he receive any gift when he has cursed the one in whom all gifts of power exist?

Although the Father grants every gift—including himself and the Son, which is greater than all gifts—the Father and the Son grant nothing except in the Holy Spirit, because the Spirit is the gift of them both. When the Spirit himself is given, then whatever has been contracted, so to speak, against the Father and the Son is truly forgiven in him, in whom all forgiveness is given. Or forgiveness of sin itself is denied, and blasphemy is held as a crime, when someone blasphemes the one in whom all the gifts of the Father and the Son exist.

When this gift is given, God—the whole Trinity—is possessed, believed in, and loved. When it is denied, no sin and no blasphemy is forgiven, since the Spirit himself is blasphemed and his works are said to belong to the prince of demons, whereas in him grace is given and all hardness of heart is dissolved.

Therefore the holy father Augustine, after various arguments concerning the matter, after all the propositions of Scripture, after the sharpest argumentative syllogisms, after the broadest introductions of definitions, declared that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is impenitence of heart.

For just as no one can call Jesus Lord except in the Holy Spirit, nor confess him through works of salvation except in the Spirit, so no one can repent of sins or cease from blasphemies without the Spirit. How much more, then, is this true of someone who clearly understands the works of God but, unable to deny their power, slanders Christ, the Word of God, driven by diabolical envy, and calls the works of the Holy Spirit Beelzebub?

This does not mean that such blasphemy will not be forgiven if the blasphemer ceases blaspheming, genuinely wishes to repent, and confesses the one without whom no one says that Jesus is Lord. For to confess Christ the Lord in him is rather to praise and venerate him than to blaspheme him.

This offense of blasphemy is not forgiven such people, neither in the present age nor in the age to come, so long as their hearts remain impenitent. Their boldness is not overcome by such great threats, nor their shamelessness subdued by such great teachings, nor their faith—in which nothing is holier—instructed by such divine utterances.

Christ therefore exercised against them, so to speak, the arguments of his discourse, divinely ordered in words in such a way that within they display the truth more clearly than light, while outwardly they bring offense to those who do not understand.

“For,” he says, “every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings, unless the blasphemy of the Spirit holds them guilty. Even whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven.”

It is as though he were saying: if someone has been scandalized by my flesh and has regarded me merely as a human being—thinking that I am the son of a craftsman, a man who eats and drinks wine, and that I have brothers—such an opinion and blasphemy, although not free from the fault of error, may nevertheless have forgiveness. This is not so if he persists in that blasphemy of faith, but if he accepts confession and repentance of heart, so that he may not appear to blaspheme against the Holy Spirit, from whom Christ was conceived.

Otherwise, how would certain people receive into their former rank heretics who had blasphemed the Holy Spirit—namely, bishops and presbyters—and likewise receive all blasphemers into repentance? It is therefore evident that forgiveness of sins never occurs without confession of the Holy Spirit, never without his advocacy. Without him no one can grieve as he ought, nor pray as is proper, since the Apostle says: “For we do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. VIII, 26).

For, as I said, “No one can say ‘Lord Jesus’ except in the Holy Spirit” (I Cor. XII, 3). To nullify this and to say that demons are cast out by Beelzebub, or that divine works are performed in him, is exceedingly destructive and deadly.

Therefore he will never obtain forgiveness who is abandoned by the intercessor and sanctifier—that is, by the Holy Spirit, who is the forgiveness of all sins. Hence it is said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John XX, 23).

In what, then, do you think sins are forgiven when pardon is received, if not in the Holy Spirit, who is given to believers because he belongs to the Father and the Son? He is the one perfect and supreme gift in whom the remaining gifts are bestowed. When he is denied, the pardon that is received in true confession of the Holy Spirit is also denied.

For all who truly believe in Jesus Christ possess the Holy Spirit, through whom the love of God the Father and the Son has been poured into the hearts of believers; and this love covers a multitude of sins. They also possess the grace of forgiving sins, yet only in that same Spirit, in whom there is every gift and all grace, as has often been said, and the forgiveness of all sins.

Because we are filled less fully by the weight of the water flowing through the narrow channel of a clepsydra, and because the mind, less thoroughly flooded with the grace of the Holy Spirit, slips inward toward these matters, we are now, in our failing old age, reminded by the clapper of the tongue of the winding lines of divine understanding that the Spirit of God, through the blessed Evangelists, has arranged and distinguished in measured form.

For this reason I refer my reader, wearied by these brief remarks but not rightly to be called impatient, to blessed Augustine and the other holy teachers, who have published separate works on this subject.

Meanwhile, it is appropriate to know that when he says that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come (Matt. XII, 32), this implies that certain sins are forgiven after this life, in the future age—either through purgatorial fire, as they say, or through offerings, prayers, and vows of the faithful.

The only condition is that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit must not burn them, so that they deny that the Lord Jesus works in the Holy Spirit with whom he is filled. For although forgiveness may release other deeds and words spoken against the Holy Spirit, whoever, through this hardness and impenitence of heart, has denied that God is in Christ lacks mercy.

What is farther from forgiveness than not only denying that Christ is God, but also blaspheming that he acts through an unclean spirit and removing the presence of the Father’s Spirit, in whom and through whom every blasphemy and every sin is forgiven? When he is denied, every sin is retained.

For in the Spirit of God Christ completes every work, so that he himself is the kingdom of heaven, and God in him reconciles the world to himself (II Cor. V, 19). Otherwise, whatever insult has arisen against Christ will all arise against God, because God is in Christ and Christ is in God.

Hence there follows an even clearer syllogism, which, as blessed Jerome says, we may call unavoidable. By its bonds it encloses them on every side if they are questioned.

“Either make the tree good,” he says, “and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad.”

Thus he presses them from both sides. It is as though he said: if the Devil is evil, he cannot perform good works. But if the things you see being done are good, it is clear that the one who does them is not the Devil—that is, the bad tree. For it cannot happen that good comes from evil or evil from good.

Therefore, attribute the good works that you see being done by me to the fact that the one from whom they come is good. You cannot deny that they are good, since they are godlike and divine. For this reason he elsewhere says to the same Pharisees: even if you do not wish to believe me, at least believe the works.

By this argument he decisively refutes both the Jews present and the adversaries of the future. He condemns those who understand that Christ’s works are not accomplished by human power but nevertheless refuse to confess that they are God’s works.

In the future, moreover, he thereby rebukes every perversity of faith—namely, that of those who take away from him the dignity and communion of the Father’s substance.

Thus he indicates that he is the tree which gives its own fruit, and not another’s, in its season, while he is placed in the body. Through the fecundity of his inner nature, abundance is sent into the Church, and every fruit of righteousness overflows.

Therefore he now says, in a remarkable way: “Either make the tree good with its fruits, or make the tree bad with its fruits,” because, as he says, the tree itself is known by its fruits.

Can a bad tree, according to the nature of trees, be made good, or can one that is good become bad, together with its branches and fruits, by being changed? Rather, by the nature of trees they are convicted of being unable rightly to judge Christ useless or evil, since his fruits are shown to be good and godlike. Indeed, according to the fruit of his work, God must be acknowledged, and the Son of God must be venerated in all things as God.

Otherwise, although you do not dare, out of admiration for such great works, to remove the name of God, you may nevertheless, through the malice of your mind and the nobility of your understanding, diminish in the fruit the particularity of the nature which he possesses with God the Father—even though you have been compelled to confess it in name—by denying his communion with the Father’s substance.

Hence: “Woe to those who call good evil and evil good” (Isa. V, 20). For this reason the Lord displays less of his goodness, and therefore they must distinguish either the bad tree with its bad fruits or the good tree with its good fruits, lest, if someone is good, they say that he can perform evil works, or lest those who themselves were evil suppose that good or true things can be spoken.

Hence it follows:

“Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”

He shows more openly that they are a bad tree and brings forth judgment in truth, showing that they bear such fruits of blasphemy as the seeds of the Devil that they had received within themselves.

For this reason they are rightly called a brood of vipers—not by nature, but because of the vice of the Devil by which they had already been corrupted, so that they could neither speak nor do good as long as they persisted in that same vice of blasphemy.

“For the good person brings good things out of a good treasure, and the evil person brings evil things out of an evil treasure.”

This does not mean that a human being is evil by nature, but that he makes himself evil by storing evil in his own heart. From that treasure of wrath against God he brings forth evil things. Having stored up such a treasure, he becomes evil, just as one becomes good from what is good and brings forth good things—even though the human being himself is good by nature.

If doubt should creep into the judgment of what is good or evil, forgiveness is reserved in the secret of God’s mercy when there is a good confession. Nevertheless, he taught that all human corruption proceeds from a fault of nature when he spoke of a good person and an evil person—not according to what a human being is, but according to the vice by which he has been corrupted.

Hence it follows:

“For every idle word that human beings speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment.”

This is connected with what precedes, and its meaning is: if an idle word, which does not at all edify those who hear it, is not without danger for the one who speaks it, how much more will you have to give an account of your slander, since you slander the works of the Holy Spirit?

An idle word is one spoken without benefit to the hearer or the speaker. For example, if, setting serious matters aside, we speak about frivolous things and tell ancient stories. But if someone repeats vulgar words, or words intended to provoke laughter, or anything shameful, he is not held guilty of an idle word but of a criminal one.

By such vices we often offend when we dissolve our mouths in laughter, since divine speech and the rules of the holy Fathers have condemned such things to eternal silence, lest the mouth of Christ’s disciple be stained by such utterances.

Hence it follows:

“By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”

For, as was said above, “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. XII, 14)—that is, out of the heart’s own treasure. Vanity, vulgarity, and the other things that abound within the mind frequently accustom the mouth to reveal what is worse within.

Where the grace of the Holy Spirit abounds and goodness remains stored up, the tongue brings forth what it possesses within its treasure. The pen of the tongue flows from what abounds inside. From an evil treasure it cannot habitually bring forth anything except what is evil.

Then certain scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying: “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.”

Whenever the Evangelist uses “then,” he indicates the time and order of events. Accordingly, up to this point all these arguments have been directed against them in response to the blasphemy concerning the earlier sign.

But the faithless Pharisees and scribes again ask him for a sign, as though the signs they had seen had not existed. Another Evangelist explains more clearly what is set forth here more obscurely, when he says: “We wish to see a sign from you from heaven” (Matt. XII, 38).

Thus they were asking either for fire to come from heaven after the manner of Elijah, or, in the likeness of Samuel, for thunder to crash, lightning to flash, and rain to fall in summertime. Yet even if these things had occurred, they could have slandered them by saying that they resulted from hidden and various disturbances of the air.

For those who slandered what they had plainly seen with their eyes, what they could touch with their hands, and whose usefulness they could experience in the healing of human beings—what would those senseless men have done with things that came from heaven by hidden means? Perhaps they would have replied that the magicians in Egypt had also performed many signs from heaven.

They will regard him as nothing but a human being. For this reason they call him “Teacher” more out of flattery and deceit than from faith or religious conviction.

I do not think that they were unaware of the star seen by the magi and proclaimed at his birth, since, when Herod inquired, they themselves announced from prophecy the place of Christ’s birth. Nor were they unaware that angels had announced Christ’s birth to the shepherds; they had heard or learned that the Father’s voice had come to him from heaven and proclaimed him his beloved Son, even though they themselves maliciously claimed that the thunder had come from heaven.

For these slanders and blasphemies he fittingly said:

“An evil and adulterous generation.”

Adulterous, because it had abandoned its husband, Christ, according to Ezekiel, and had mingled with many lovers. When he says “evil generation,” he does not condemn the nature of those born from the seed of Abraham, but the vice by which they had been corrupted by the Devil. Through imitation of him they are called sons, just as above they were called a brood of vipers.

For just as offspring kill the mothers from whom they are born, so the Jews killed Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God (I Cor. I, 24), who is the mother of all who possess true wisdom.

He seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to him except the sign of the prophet Jonah. Every sign, therefore, is a sign of something. Moreover, the sign that Christ promises to give is the reality of that sign of Jonah. Yet it is called a sign because whatever was prefigured in Jonah was wholly fulfilled in Christ. Accordingly, although it is called a sign, it was, as I have said, the reality of that sign. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster for three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth [Col. 0475C] for three days and three nights.

Although some affirm that everything Jonah did was a sign concerning Christ—for the prophet was sent to the Ninevites after Israel had been rejected, just as Christ was sent to the Gentiles after the faithless Jews had been rejected, as well as the other things that are read about him—nevertheless, the evident sign in this instance was that he not only prefigured the Lord’s death, but also distinctly expressed the very time of the Passion, three days and three nights.

Yet on this account some doubt and attribute to the Savior’s words a falsehood, because he did not lie in the tomb for three days and three nights. They do not understand how often they encounter this manner of expression in the sacred Scriptures, which is called the trope of synecdoche, in which a part is taken for the whole. It is not that the Lord was in hell for all three days and three nights, but that you should take the part of Friday on which he was buried, together with the preceding night and day, as one whole day. Then there was the Sabbath, consisting of an entire night and day; thereafter, the Lord’s night, together with the day that was beginning, with a part being taken for the whole. Thus you have three days and three nights, if you take a part of each day, or of each night, as the whole.

For example, if someone left his lodging at the ninth hour of the day and, traveling, arrived at another lodging at the third hour of the following day, and if we said that he had made a two-day journey, would we immediately be accused of lying? The one who traveled did not spend all the hours of both days on the journey, but only a certain part of them. Likewise, one Evangelist says that the Lord showed himself on the mountain after six days [Col. 0476A], while another says, after eight days. We count the latter part of the first day, on which what he had promised was fulfilled, as the whole and complete days, so that you may understand that the one who said “after six days” counted only the middle days, which were true, whole, and complete.

This trope, however, is capable of conveying meaning and full understanding, when Scripture states more or less than the precise total. For it either shows the whole by a part, as in, “The Word became flesh,” or conversely, as in the passage: “Therefore, because it was the preparation day of the Jews, since the tomb was nearby, where they had laid him” (John XIX, 42). Moreover, when it says “in the heart of the earth,” it likewise speaks tropically: not that the earth has a heart, as though it were an animal, but it signifies Jerusalem, of which it was said: “For he worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Psalm LXXIII, 12), where the Lord was crucified and buried. 565

**The men of Nineveh will rise.** He continues the wondrous and admirable prophecy that was made through Jonah’s prophecy, concerning which Christ prophesied and the prophet himself also prophesied. In order to fulfill his own prediction, Christ himself was also quicker in rising than the prophet had foretold and prefigured.

Moreover, he demonstrates that the faith of the Gentiles would be greater than that of the Jews, and therefore declares that, because of the faith of the Ninevites, the Jews will be condemned in the future because they did not believe. For the Ninevites, when Jonah preached, did penance and by their confession obtained from God forgiveness for their repentance; but these, when Christ the Son of God had been foretold and when he himself preached, did not receive him.

Thus it is said that they will rise, because they will be more praiseworthy in the likeness of two denarii, one of which shines more beautifully and brightly because of the craftsman’s workmanship, while the other, debased into the most worthless state by its weight and luster, is despised. Here the very great faith of the Gentiles is proclaimed. They will condemn them, not by the power of judgment, but because they themselves will be condemned by comparison with them.

It should also be noted that the Gentiles will rise to better things on that day and will receive loftier gifts according to their faith.

**And behold, something greater than Jonah is here.** Here, however, the word should not be understood as a name but as an adverb of place. Christ was present at that moment, speaking of himself as though he were speaking of another, as if he were saying: “Here among you is one who is greater than Jonah here.”

For, according to the Septuagint, Jonah preached repentance to the Ninevites for three days, but I have done so for a much longer time; he preached to the Assyrians, an unbelieving nation, while I preach to the Jews, the people of God; he preached to foreigners who were outside God’s law, while I, to my own fellow citizens, always display what was promised to the fathers through the Law and the Prophets; he spoke only with his voice, simply, performing no signs, whereas I—even though you slander me as performing them by Beelzebub—have freely bestowed innumerable benefits upon the sick.

Because these are works of divinity, they indicate that the one who is here at this moment, from whom such marvelous and unheard-of things are done, is greater than Jonah.

**The queen of the South will rise in the judgment with this generation, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon.** No mortal possesses so teachable a nature or so excellent an intellect that he can fully penetrate the treasures of the divine Scriptures by his own knowledge or learning. No one can reveal every individual riddle, demonstrate the allegorical meanings and explanations of the parables, express the comparisons suitably in their proper places, or disclose all hidden things.

Yet because he cannot do this, he must not therefore suppose that anything in those sacred writings has been placed there superfluously or without a sacramental meaning, even if that meaning is hidden. For this reason, labor must be applied, and God’s grace must be entreated with earnestness in the search for understanding, so that he who holds the key of knowledge may deign to unlock what is obscure for us.

For, as has been said, the truth itself lies deeply submerged in the depths. Which of the most eloquent philosophers would have discovered that this queen of Sheba prefigured these things, or that Jonah, having perhaps been submerged for three days in the belly of the sea monster, displayed such profound realities? Only Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, who opens and no one shuts, could reveal that this had been said concerning him.

For just as an unheard-of conveyance preserves its ruler and brings him back to the heights after three days, so Christ, descending through death to the lower regions, ineffably fulfilled the truth when he returned victoriously to life.

And this is the sign that he promises to give only to those who seek it: through it they would know that the glory they had rejected in Christ was to be bestowed entirely upon the Gentiles, just as Jonah gave himself back to the Gentiles, whom he had deprived of himself by fleeing from the Jews.

For this reason the queen of the South is also proclaimed as coming to judgment. Just as Jonah was foreseen as coming in the figure of Christ, so the queen of the South was foreseen as a figure of the Church, which comes to Christ.

Therefore, I say, we are blessed, because what preceded in type and was promised in figure, we possess wholly in its actual form. We venerate the very wisdom and embrace, love, and hold fast the very Solomon in the reality of faith. We venerate the very wisdom and embrace, love, and hold fast the very Solomon in the reality of faith.

For certainly Christ is here, greater than Solomon. His going forth from the highest summit of heaven sought out her who came from the ends of the earth to hear his wisdom and contemplate the ineffable mysteries of his sacraments.

The Jews therefore report that this woman was called Meroe, seeking only the name and understanding everything carnally. Yet they do not recognize the mystery that Christ taught concerning himself and the Church, which is truly queen.

This comparison therefore further increases the Jews’ guilt, because the faith of the Gentiles leaves them without excuse. While the Gentiles believe the prophets—that is, Jonah and Solomon—and embrace the teaching of wisdom, the Jews do not believe Christ to be greater than Jonah or Solomon.

And therefore the Gentiles will condemn them in the resurrection of judgment, because fear of God and faith were found among those to whom the Law had not been given and among whom the power of true wisdom had not been proclaimed. For this reason those who are unbelieving though they possess the Law are even more undeserving of pardon, while those who did not know the Law pursued a greater fellowship of faith, when grace and pardon are freely proclaimed to the former. 567

Another rebuke follows:

**When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it travels through dry places seeking rest, and does not find it,** and so forth.

The continuous order of the reading is shown to proceed from the beginning of the preceding discourse, while, because of the hardness of their hearts, a more terrible punishment is accumulated upon them and a greater vengeance threatened. Indeed, the whole comparison in the present passage is directed toward demonstrating that graver punishments threaten the Jews. He makes this clear at the end, when he says:

**So it will be,** he says, **also with this most wicked generation.**

The person from whom the unclean spirit goes out designates the nation of the Jews, from which the Law that had been given drove out the unclean spirit through its intervention. For previously, in Egypt, they had contracted many grave sins against God by worshiping idols and serving demons.

Moreover, after they had seen God’s signs and wonders in Egypt, after the crossing of the Red Sea, and after innumerable benefits and miracles, at times, while the Law was being fashioned by God, they sacrificed victims of metal and stone. Together with choruses and songs of dancers, they worshiped as gods the golden calves that they had cast for themselves, offering sacrifices to metal and stones.

But the Law, like a kind of guard—a wall of surrounding power—after rejecting the demons, enclosed God’s people against them and excluded the adversary. When he went out from there, traveling as though through dry and waterless places, wandering around for a long time, he roamed through the wastelands of the nations. In them no fountain of life had yet flowed, nor had heavenly rain drenched them; and therefore, scorched by excessive dryness, they lay barren.

After he had long traversed and rested in these wastelands and dry places, being badly at peace in them, eventually, when they had been watered by God’s grace, washed in the bath of the water of life, and a living spring had begun to flow in them, there was no place for him to dwell with them.

Since he no longer found rest in them, and reflected that he might rule in them, he finally judged it best—and believed it possible—to return to that house from which he had previously been expelled by the Law, as though he had gone out invited to greater things.

Returning to it, he found it vacant through idleness and Sabbath rest. The temple of the Jews was vacant because it was without Christ, without God, and without the guardianship of angels. For, as we read in Josephus, after the Lord’s Passion a cry was publicly heard, with many people listening, in that same fortress of the walls: “Let us depart from these places.”

And not without reason, because they did not wish to have the Lord of the angels as their inhabitant. Therefore, stripped of its defenses, their house was vacant, idly and most vainly at leisure, adorned with the proclamations of the prophets and the traditions of the ancestral Law, as well as with superstitious observances.

Because of those traditions, indeed, the very protection of the Law had also withdrawn far away. For the whole Law and prophecy had been given until John, so that they might announce Christ. Once he had been rejected, the Law itself, as I have said, remained empty, without an inhabitant—not only the nation itself, but also the Law, because there was no other person whom it could prefigure or whom it could reveal within itself.

Nevertheless, it is read by us as full of mysteries, for the testimony and confirmation of our faith, and for their reproach and condemnation.

When that house of the Jews was thus adorned, cleansed, and also vacant, so that it would not remain empty, it was filled again with demons. They are taken in the number seven because that number signifies complete perfection.

Since so many gifts of grace had been destined for them, if they had received Christ, in whom all these things were present, so great and numerous a possession of iniquity would thereafter, conversely, arise in them. For through the seven principal vices the whole enormity of vices is expressed, so that as great as the working of grace is among the good, so great is the fullness of iniquity among the wicked.

But they are called worse than the one who had previously possessed them because the vices committed after the Law or grace has been received are graver than those we practiced when we had received neither Law nor grace.

Therefore, because we see fulfilled among the Jews what was threatened, let us be afraid to commit what has been forbidden. For, according to the Apostle, it would have been better not to know the way of God than, after receiving grace, to turn backward or to live falsely and most viciously under hypocrisy (II Peter II, 20).

When anyone has fallen from the summit of God’s righteousness, thereafter he will possess simulation. For when the desire of the flesh has been expelled through repentance and excluded from its customary works, if it does not find pleasures in which it may rest, it returns more eagerly to the person’s former mind and occupies it again, if, after it was expelled, negligence follows and the mind falls away from the fervor of charity.
