Then it will possess not only those seven vices that are opposed to the seven spiritual virtues, but will also pretend through hypocrisy to possess virtues within itself. Therefore, with seven other spirits worse than itself—that is, with that sevenfold simulation—the desire returns and takes possession of the same house, so that the last state of that person is worse than the first (Matthew XII, 45).

Indeed, it is more serious for the Jews now to blaspheme Christ every day in their synagogues with stubborn intent than it was for them, before they knew the Law, to serve idols and sacrifice to demons in Egypt.

And, to show more plainly what the parable was about, he said: **So it will be with this most wicked generation.**

Although this may in some manner also be understood of heretics, since heretics must be judged to be in a much worse condition than pagans: among the latter, hope of faith still remains, whereas among the former the conflict of dissension persists.

Nevertheless, so that the truth of the understanding may not be weakened, all these things can plainly be seen fulfilled among the Jews. Unless it were graver for them to have rejected Christ and remained empty than it would have been to worship idols as before, they would certainly not have been expelled to the end of the age from their own land and from their very head, without any reconciliation.

For now they do not worship or venerate idols, and yet, without any mercy, they are scattered throughout the whole world and are found wandering without the true God. Because they did not wish to be God’s house, they have become the house of the worst demons.

When the demons returned to it with their prince, surrounded by their wickedness, they dwell in it, and everything belonging to them is worse than before.

[Col. 0480A] While the Savior was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and his brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him. Someone said to him: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you.”

Although the Lord was occupied with teaching the word, a deeper meaning must be sought in this passage. For it is the mark of a perfect and wise man to examine each statement keenly and discover the meanings hidden within it; to distinguish individually what is signified, said, or done in particular places, times, and circumstances; and to define briefly in words what is explained more fully, expanding what is said through meanings, without arrogance, ambition for praise, or boastful vanity.

For, as I said above, all the divine things that have been narrated were accomplished in mysteries, and nothing in them was said that is not full of meaning. Such is the statement: “While he was still speaking, behold, his mother and his brothers were standing outside,” and someone said to him: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you.”

This does not mean that they did not have the power to enter to him, as the others did. Rather, divine Providence arranged matters in such a way that the outcome of the event might show what the Jews themselves would later do: refusing to enter through the door—that is, through faith—to him.

Hence it was said: “I am the door” (John X, 9), and because “he came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John I, 11).

In the mother and the brothers, the Synagogue and the Jews who were born from it are understood. They despise his teaching and turn everything into reproach.

Thus someone, so that the race might be understood from one individual, speaks as though taunting him: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you.”

It is as if he were saying: “Why do you spread such things about yourself among the people? Why do you make yourself God and reproach and threaten us with such great things, as though it were in your power to inflict worse things upon us? Is this not your mother and your brothers? Since you are merely a human being, the son of a carpenter, and lower in standing than the others by birth, why do you display such extraordinary claims about yourself and heap so many accusations upon us?”

This is still the voice of the Jews today, who believe that he is merely a human being, the son of a carpenter, generated from a woman according to the condition of human flesh.

Although it appears that the one who reported this, and who also intended another accusation, did not report it by chance or merely as an insult, but rather was laying a trap: whether, in carrying out the ministry of the divine word, he would prefer the flesh or blood of his mother and brothers out of emotional attachment, contrary to the command he had previously given concerning his mother and brothers.

But the most benevolent Savior, who examines hearts, moderates his response so as not to deny his mother or his brothers—for whom he also showed concern while hanging on the cross—but, at the same time, to strike back at the one laying the trap and not conceal that he was the Son of God.

Therefore, stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said: “Behold, my mother and my brothers.”

It is as though he were saying: “These are my mother and my brothers. Through their service and teaching, the souls of believers are daily brought forth into the light, so that they may be in my body. These are the brothers who do the works and will of my Father; therefore they too are adopted as sons.”

For, as I said, he did not deny his mother, as the heretics claim, so that he might be thought to have been born from a phantom. Rather, he placed the apostles before his fleshly kin, so that we too may always prefer the Spirit to the flesh when comparing the objects of our love.

But lest he seem to be speaking only of the apostles, the provident Teacher added that he was also speaking of each individual who believes rightly.

**And whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, and sister, and mother.**

Meanwhile, lest he should again be slandered in reference to Joseph when he spoke of doing the Father’s will, he added, “who is in heaven,” so that it might be shown more clearly than light itself that he himself had come from heaven, although he appeared in the flesh as the Son of Man.

He also established himself as a model for everyone in acting and thinking, showing that the right and name of all relationships must henceforth be understood not according to the condition of the flesh, but according to the fellowship of Christ and the Church.

For the Church, which is gathered together in Christ, has become a mother by conceiving and giving birth to Christ within the heart. She is called sister because she is so often addressed by that name in the Song of Songs; and she is called this because Christ, the Son of God, became the son of man, according to which he is both bridegroom and brother.

Thus already at that time, among the apostles, Christ’s mother and brothers were within; outside stood the Synagogue, from which he had been born, and the Jewish brothers, blinded by envy. They did not wish to enter within to the banquet at which the younger son was mercifully received and feasted.

From this passage some have said that the Lord’s brothers were sons of Joseph, born from another wife. They supposed, following the fantasies of a Jewish apocryphal work, that a certain little woman named Estha existed, from whom he had sons who were called the Lord’s brothers.

We, however, understand the Lord’s brothers not as Joseph’s sons, but as the Savior’s cousins: the children of the Lord’s maternal aunt Mary, who is said to have been the mother of James the younger, Joseph, and Jude. In another passage of the Gospel we read that these men were called the Lord’s brothers. That brothers may therefore be called cousins is demonstrated by all Scripture.

When they came to him, the Lord was occupied with the entire multitude of the people: no less in the work of preaching to the crowds than in teaching the disciples inwardly, in the ministry of healing, and in responding to those who were laying traps for him.

Yet in all things he was working one salvation for all, “who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Timothy II, 4).

Therefore his mother and brothers delayed entering, so that reverence might be preserved in their approach and the mystery of divinity might be represented through the outcome.

Since we have proceeded in an unpolished style of speech from the place where the most benevolent Jesus went through all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues and preaching the Gospel of the kingdom (Matthew IX, 35), up to this point, where a new order of narration begins, reason demands that we restore the reader’s strength.

Let us therefore bring the book to an end, so that perhaps, with our strength renewed, we may return with greater steadiness, however imperfectly, to the new manner of narration.

For we possess neither such abundant skill in speaking nor such ability to persuade appropriately that I can complete everything that is best in expression. Nor am I endowed with such outstanding intelligence that I can easily untangle and explain these very difficult matters.

Therefore I have decided to keep within my own limits, which divine mercy has granted me, lest I exceed the measure of grace given to me. For I seek neither great human praise nor glory.

Thus, although I do not claim eloquence for myself, I desire to unfold orthodox meanings. For if no one had treated the divine Scriptures except diligent, prudent, and most distinguished orators and eminent men, discussion of the divine utterances would be rare, and human eloquence would be praised more than heavenly grace.

For it is foolish, in this school of Christ, to pursue worldly and empty philosophy, especially in the passage we have treated. Here fishermen and peasants are chosen as apostles and sent “as sheep in the midst of wolves” (Matthew X, 16) to endure every kind of torment. Here the apostles are trained as disciples for spiritual contests and are commanded to seek no eloquence.

Therefore, now that these matters have been traversed, let our discourse, together with the most excellent Teacher of the divine utterances, hasten to bring its manner of speaking to an end. And, together with the most benevolent Savior—for he too is hastening—may we be able to board the ship, so that what was said to those who were with him in the ship may also be said to us: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables” (Luke VIII, 10), lest perhaps we be found with the crowds on land.

# PREFACE TO BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0481]

[Col. 0481D] Let the mind briefly review what we have treated, since I have spoken timidly, because scarcely anywhere at this time are the things that are commanded found being fulfilled. For the divine discourse describes the Gospel man and portrays him—not with brush or pen, but through the reason and discipline of heavenly instruction—so that the whole and complete human being may be inwardly reformed.

From this point let us join together what was said in the house, matters attributed with the greatest clarity to the more perfect, with the parables that were more obscurely sketched for the crowds and common people, so that with the apostles we may know the mystery of the heavenly kingdom and understand the riddles established by the authority of divine testimony.

Therefore let the most discerning mind hasten, between the two parts of the books, to weave them into one texture of its character, so that it may behold the luminous teachings of the Gospel from a somewhat higher vantage: how splendid and how excellent they are, if only it can see how greatly his teaching excels and what a beautiful image of himself it produces from the vision of truth.

Thus, to the extent that the sublimity of the commandments, divinely commended to our ears within the house, has terrified us, let the sweetness of the parables soothe everything, lest the commandments be judged impossible, and let their variety adorn it.

In this way, with the light evenly poured into our hearts, no radiance between the two parts will deceive us. But if we seem to be led higher, let no dizziness of the head mislead us. Rather, let us be secure, because the one whom we follow is true and cannot be deceived.

Therefore let us follow him fearlessly; let us follow him securely. For he has places of refuge whenever he is wearied by the crowds: on the mountain, in the solitude of the wilderness, or at sea. Since the weak multitude cannot approach these places, the disciples alone follow him, withdrawn from the teaching in every respect.

Therefore they have already received on the mountain what the crowds cannot attain; and, having now entered the boat with him at sea, they ask more privately about the mysteries of heavenly life, which the crowds are still hearing in parables.

Their strength is not weakened in anything, their courage is not broken, their steadfastness is not wearied, and the excellence of divine love is not weighed down by the burden of weakness. Rather, they continue to follow him in all things without fatigue [Col. 0483B], even amid the waves of the sea, and entrust themselves to the little boat governed by Christ.

For it is built with the firmest joining of its planks, by divine craftsmanship; it is more solid in Christ than it is merely strong. It breaks the waves, yet is not broken; it is whirled about by storms, yet does not sink; it evades and breaks apart the waves of the winds, which it does not admit; and it calms disturbances through the measured use of the oars.

Since we have now boarded this ship, brothers, let us remain firm and steady in it, always following Christ’s teaching. And if there are matters we understand less well—for there are many—let us ask about them confidently and not be moved by any waves of wind.

For even if those waves rise as high as heaven, they cannot overwhelm us with their collisions, since Christ is sailing in the boat with us. Therefore he says: “I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII, 20); and: “Take courage, because I have conquered the world” (John XVI, 33).

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0483]

[Col. 0483B] **(CHAPTER XIII.)** On that day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea, and great crowds gathered to him.

It appears, then, that Matthew here followed the order of his narration and of the time when he says, “on that day,” as though it meant: when these words that have been spoken came to an end.

Unless perhaps we take “day” to mean “time,” so that he went out of the house in which he had been when he commanded those who had been healed not to make him known, or in which he had taught the things just mentioned.

And crowds gathered to him—those who could not enter the house, where the apostles were inside listening to the mysteries. Therefore he went out so that they might gather to him, because he is merciful.

Otherwise, if he had not come out from that hidden dwelling of his, in which he is always with God the Father, those who were scattered and afflicted by various illnesses would never have gathered to him.

He sits beside the sea of this world so that the crowds may gather to him and hear at the shore what they were not worthy to hear inside. But the most benevolent Teacher also indicates through his actions what he is doing.

He then went up into a little boat and sat amid the waves, where the ship is struck on every side by very mountainous storms. But the crowd stands outside, so that through the circumstances that follow the reason may be shown for his speaking in parables.

By this action he signifies that those who are outside, beyond the Church, cannot grasp any understanding of the divine word. For the ship presents the type of the Church, within which the word of life has been placed and is preached.

Those who are outside are compared to sand and are barren, without fruit and useless. Therefore they cannot understand what is put forward in parables.

Or perhaps they stand on the fixed shore so that they may hear more attentively what is said, because they were not yet able, with Jesus and the apostles, to endure the dangers and temptations by which Christ was already being pressed by his own plotters.

Hence it follows:

[Col. 0484B] **And he spoke many things to them in parables.**

Many things, certainly, but not everything. For if he had said “everything in parables,” the crowd would have departed without benefit. The crowd, however, is not of one understanding, but each person has a different will.

Therefore he speaks many things to them in parables, so that, according to their various wills, they might receive different forms of instruction. Here he mixes clear things with obscure ones, so that through what they understand more plainly they may be drawn toward knowledge of what is obscure, seeking it more eagerly and understanding it more clearly.

**Behold, the sower went out to sow.**

He was inside, dwelling in the house and speaking to the disciples the mysteries of life. Through these matters he teaches, as I have said, that he went out from heaven and came into the world, which is represented by his sitting beside the sea; or that he came from the Jews to the Gentiles and went up into the ship, that is, the Church.

The crowds standing on the shore signify the present life. For the one who sows the word of God went out from his house in order to sow among the Gentiles. Thus he speaks of himself as though of another, because he alone is the sower and the seed of all.

Therefore he introduces himself without any surname, because he is the one who is properly and uniquely called the sower.

At the same time, observe that this is the first of the parables that is presented together with its interpretation. We must be cautious: whenever the Lord explains one of them, and, when asked by the disciples, himself expounds his own words, we must not superstitiously wish to understand either something different or something more than what he has explained.

Some heretics, moreover, take this parable to support their own heresy, wishing to introduce three natures—namely, a spiritual, an animal, and an earthly one—although four sowings are counted here: one beside the road, another among rocky places, a third among thorns, and a fourth said to have produced fruit in good soil.

Let us seek the meaning of these from the Lord himself. For the moment, however, the matter must be postponed briefly, until we are able, together with the disciples, to hear the same explanation in private.

And his disciples approached him and said:

We must ask, then, how his disciples approached him when Jesus was sitting in the boat. The explanation must be that they had boarded the boat with him earlier and, standing there with him, asked about the interpretation of the parable.

It should also be noted that they approach and ask, while the crowds stand and listen. Jesus, secure in his majesty, sits in the boat like a teacher and judge. Therefore he teaches those who approach in faith amid the waves of temptations, while he distinguishes the others and permits them to hear only in parables, because they were not yet capable of enduring temptations, not yet having been tested.

And therefore he says:

**To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0485B], but to them it has not been given.**

Let the Pelagians listen, who boast that they possess something without the grace of God: nothing is received without God’s gift. Hence the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Corinthians IV, 7).

Therefore no one should presume upon himself, because he possesses nothing from himself except sins. Let him approach eagerly, devoted in faith and strengthened by grace in charity, so that he may hear with the apostles in the boat and understand what has been given to them, because what has been given to them has been promised to all.

Great, then, is what has been given to them to know, because this is eternal life: “that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3).

This knowledge is a great mystery. Hence it was said: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII, 21). And because the apostles truly believed this, they already possessed—not from themselves, but from God’s gift—that in which eternal life consists.

Therefore it follows:

Whoever has will be given more, and he will have abundance; but whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him. That is: whoever has the mystery of the kingdom of God and possesses an undivided faith—which comes from me—as you do, will be given an increase of grace, as the Apostle says, “according to the measure of faith.” For faith is the root of all virtues and their foundation; upon it the structure of all virtues is built. Whoever possesses it will also receive knowledge, according to the measure of faith. Charity in the Holy Spirit will likewise be given, so that the true Christian may grow, together with gifts corresponding to the greatness of his faith; and he will abound even unto the fullness of charity. Whoever does not have this—that is, true and upright faith—will have what he possesses taken away from him.

Yet, conversely, here he touches upon the Jews, who gloried in the Law, and upon the crowd that heard in parables, because they did not yet possess the faith that is in Christ. Therefore whatever they had possessed through the Law will be taken away from them. He also touches upon those who seem to possess, by the natural good [of their disposition], or through virtues feigned without faith, a certain good; for these things will be taken away from them, since “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI, 6). Nor can those understand anything wisely who do not possess within themselves the head of wisdom. But lest someone suppose that he has faith because he believes in Christ without works of righteousness, let him know that if his faith has no work, faith is dead. And if he has some work of goodness without faith, that very work is empty, because it is not in Christ. But whoever has Christ in faith, according to the work of faith, certainly also has the Father. Whoever has the Father and the Son truly has the Holy Spirit as well, who is their Spirit. Since whatever is without faith is sin, as the Apostle testifies, therefore whoever truly does not have this faith will have taken away from him what he appears to possess.

This, then, he says concerning those who stand on the shore and are separated from Jesus by the disturbances of the world, and do not hear clearly what is said. Therefore, according to the prophet Isaiah, everything they hear is in parables. He says: “You shall hear with hearing and shall not understand; and seeing, you shall see, and shall not see.” These things were prophesied concerning the crowds, who do not deserve to hear the word with the hearing of the heart, because concerning Christ they perceived nothing beyond what they saw with their bodily eyes. They saw flesh and body, but they did not understand his divinity performing divine works. The Father’s voice was indeed heard saying, “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. XIII, 55), but they did not hear it, because they said: “Is this not the son of the carpenter?”

Therefore let us also approach Jesus with the disciples and ask for the discernment of the parables, lest, like the crowds, we appear to possess ears and eyes in vain. Yet what we read in Isaiah according to the Hebrew truth is much more obscure, where everything is expressed in the imperative: “Hear by hearing, and do not understand; see by sight, and do not recognize.” And afterward: “Make the heart of this people blind, and make their ears heavy” (Isa. VI, 10), and “close their eyes,” or the rest. Here, however, it is not expressed in the imperative but in the indicative, just as Luke also rendered it in the Acts of the Apostles. Hence it continues:

“For the heart of this people has grown dull, and they have heard heavily with their ears.” I am therefore greatly surprised why Matthew, a true Hebrew writing in the Hebrew language, placed this testimony here, contrary to his usual practice, according to the Septuagint rather than according to the Hebrew text. Jerome, too, in his commentary, interpreted this passage according to the Septuagint. Nevertheless, he raised no question about this variation, either in this work or in his exposition of Isaiah—unless perhaps because the sense is one and the same in both translators. Yet the Septuagint is easier, since there is difficulty in the Hebrew: how God himself should command the people to hear with hearing and not understand, and to see with sight and not recognize; or how the Prophet should be introduced as acting toward the Lord through his prayers: “Make blind,” he says, “the heart of this people, and make heavy their ears, and close their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted and healed” (Isa. VI, 10).

If this was done by divine judgment and authority, and what was commanded was truly commanded, I do not see how those who do not see are at fault, but rather the one who blinded them and gave them eyes not to see. Therefore the Septuagint seem more to preserve free will when they say: “The heart of this people has grown dull, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes,” or the rest. Thus, by their own actions, they are judged unworthy, by God’s just judgment, of understanding divine things.

But apart from this testimony, which we are now attempting to explain, the same question remains in the churches. For whether it was spoken in the imperative or in the indicative, the point is one: God condemns no one without his just judgment. Nor does he prescribe anything in such a way that one could say that he is the author of evil; rather, he has mercy on whom he wills and softens them so that they may be converted, while he hardens whom he wills. This does not mean that God blinds anyone so that he cannot see with the eye of the heart, or hardens anyone so that he cannot be converted; rather, when someone is already blind and hardened, he leaves him in his just judgment, neither illuminating him so that he may see the light of life nor softening him so that he may be converted and healed.

Therefore, when this question has been resolved, the other questions in very many passages will also be resolved; or, together with the others, this one will remain unresolved here as well. For according to the Apostle: “God has shut up all things under sin, so that he may have mercy on all” (Rom. XI, 32–33). Marveling also at the Lord’s mysteries, he added: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways!”

Nevertheless, three things ought to be considered in this passage. First, that because of the greatness of their crime, even those who are blinded and have pressed their ears so as not to hear the words of life were judged unworthy of repentance. Second, that if anyone is converted, does penance, and hears the mysteries of the true faith, he will truly be healed by the Lord and will be saved, even if he is held fast in any crime whatsoever. Third, concerning all those who perish—who are said to hear heavily and to close their eyes lest they see and be healed—we must understand that this is not a defect of nature but the choice of an evil will. It continues:

“But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.” They are therefore blessed because it has been granted to them to know the mystery of the Kingdom. And the expression is remarkable: “Blessed,” he says, “are your eyes because they see, and your ears because they hear.” Did not everyone, whether good or evil, see and hear—and even the beasts? Luke the Evangelist makes the point clearer when he says: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke X, 23).

Accordingly, from this passage we must derive a rule by which we may understand more clearly the modes of expression used in the divine Scriptures. For it had been granted to them to know the mystery of the kingdom of God (Mark IV, 11). Hence it was that they saw and heard in the heart, whereas the crowds and those who were outside had been blinded. But because all possessed bodily eyes and ears, he therefore required the ears of the heart when he said above: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Apoc. VI, 13, 22). For blessed are those eyes that can recognize Christ’s mysteries, and which Jesus commands to be lifted on high so that they may behold the fields already white with grain.

Those ears, too, are blessed of which Isaiah speaks: “The Lord has opened my ear.” And Job says: “With the hearing of the ear I have heard you” (Job XLII, 5); for one can hear only with an ear. Yet he rightly says that he hears, because what he heard was within, the one who spoke was within, and that by which he heard was within. Hence David says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me, for he speaks peace to his people” (Ps. LXXXIV, 9).

Otherwise, there is no blessedness in hearing and seeing what everyone hears and sees—for example, good and evil alike saw Christ in the flesh, and all who come to the Church hear the Gospel, although they do not understand what is read. As for what follows:

“For many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.”

This seems contrary to what is said elsewhere: “Abraham desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced.” Yet he did not say, “All the prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see,” but “many.” Among the many, therefore, it could happen that some saw and others did not. But it is rash to define anything about them or to distinguish the merits of the saints.

For Abraham saw in a riddle; he saw in form, while the apostles saw in the very completion of truth. They are therefore blessed because what those men perceived in the spirit as something future, these already saw fulfilled in Christ; and they questioned him about everything according to their desire and ate with him in all the mysteries. And the more present they enjoyed his words and teachings, the more clearly they knew everything.

“Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it—the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart.” From this it is shown that whoever does not understand what he hears truly does not hear with the hearing of the ear, because he does not grasp what he hears with the sense of the flesh. Hence he exhorts us to hear more attentively what is said in the divine Scriptures: “The evil one comes,” he says, “and snatches away what was sown in his heart.”

The evil one therefore snatches the good seed from nowhere other than the heart in which it was sown. This is not because there is any difference in the letter—that is, in the souls of believers—but because it fell beside the road, and therefore the birds of heaven devoured it (Luke VIII, 5). The seed of the word falls beside the road, then, when the demons themselves make a road for themselves in the soul, as in the saying: “Bend down your soul so that we may pass through it” (Isa. LI, 23). For unless the soul were bent—that is, entangled in vices—the demons would have no passage through it. But because it offered them a passage within itself, whatever good is sown in it is immediately snatched away by the evil one. Nor can it be otherwise until the wretched soul has provided such spirits with a path through itself.

The expression is remarkable: when the word of the kingdom is said to have been sown in the heart, it immediately passes over to the one in whom it is sown, as follows:

“This,” he says, “is the one who was sown beside the road.” Thus the word is seed, and the one in whom it was sown is himself also seed. Yet both are beside the road—not beside that road which is Christ, but beside the road which the demons have claimed for themselves, when they found it deflected and bent away from the state of uprightness. Therefore Satan immediately snatches it from the heart, lest those who believe should be saved.

This mode of expression is found according to the idiom of the sacred Scriptures, so that the parable may not be understood carnally. Hence Mark the Evangelist says more significantly: “These are those beside the road, where the word is sown; and when they have heard it, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that was sown in their hearts” (Mark IV, 15). It is as if he said: They are beside the road and have provided a road within themselves for the demons; therefore what was sown in them is taken away. Matthew said this so that everything stated above might be understood spiritually concerning the seed. And so it continues:

“But the one sown on rocky ground is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy.” Yet it was stated above that some things fell—that is, seeds—on rocky ground. Now the one in whom the seed of the word was sown is himself said to have been sown on the rocky ground, because he has become entirely stony and hard in his heart through his own vice.

He nevertheless had a little earth, though not much—that is, some affection for the good, even if only for a time—and therefore he is said to have received it with joy. But because he had no depth of earth—that is, endurance and persevering patience—the hardness of his heart overcame the rain of the divine word, and the seed had no moisture of virtue by which to establish its root. Since he was temporal and did not strive toward eternal things, it is rightly said:

“But when tribulation and persecution arise because of the word, he immediately falls away.” What he had said above was, “they withered.” It should be noted from the Lord’s words that the rising or heat of the sun often signifies temptation or persecution in the divine Scriptures, as in the saying: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Ps. CXX, 6). Those whom temptation or persecution burns, because they do not have the moisture of perseverance in charity, quickly fall into denial when questioned about the word.

But there is a great difference between someone who is compelled by many tribulations and punishments to deny Christ and someone who immediately falls away and stumbles at the first persecution. Likewise, there is a difference between someone who is inclined to sin daily and someone who is eventually overcome by more serious temptations, if he is immediately renewed by divine mercy.

“But the one sown among thorns is the one who hears the word, and the anxiety of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes fruitless.” Similarly, it was said above that other seeds fell among thorns. Here, however, the one in whom they were sown is himself said to have been sown, because he had the seed of the word within him; thus, through the fact that the seed was sown, he who received it is understood to have been sown as well, growing amid the riches of the world and the deceptions of vanity.

Nor is this mode of expression surprising, since the thorns themselves are also called such, as in the Song of Songs: “As a lily among thorns, so is my soul among daughters” (Song I, 2). Although they blossom, they never produce fruit, just as the cares of the world do not, even if they appear to possess food that brings salvation. Hence, even to Adam, according to the literal sense, he speaks figuratively: “When you work the earth, it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you. By the sweat of your brow you shall eat your bread” (Gen. III, 19).

For whoever gives himself over to the pleasures of the world and the cares of this present life eats heavenly bread and true food only among thorns—and even then in sweat and immense labor: “For a rich man will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty” (Matt. XIX, 23). He aptly added, “and the deceitfulness of riches,” because riches are seductive. They do one thing and promise another; their possession is slippery. Through their attractions and deceptions the word of God is choked, while, on their unstable course, they quickly abandon those who possess them and restore those who do not.

These three kinds of seed correspond to the passage where he says: “The rain descended, the winds blew, and the rivers rushed upon it” (Matt. VII, 25–27). For these are three things by which not only agriculture is overturned, but also the structure of God’s building.

“But the one,” he says, “sown in good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it and bears fruit.” The order is appropriate: first one hears the word, then understands it; for merely hearing with the ear of the flesh and not understanding with the ear of the mind is little. Yet these stages themselves indicate what the aforementioned differences of fruit are in the bad soil, since in both parts three varieties of the one seed are found, although the qualities differ—not because there was any defect in the seed, but because the quality of the cultivation produced this result.

Thus, in one and the same good soil, three fruitful abundances of the one seed are said to be produced: the hundredfold, the sixtyfold, and the thirtyfold. Nevertheless, neither in that part nor in this is the substance of nature changed; rather, it is the will and cultivation of the faithful or the unfaithful. Because the evil one comes into their hearts and snatches away what was sown in the heart, he says a second and third time: “This is the one who hears the word.”

Likewise, in the exposition of the good soil, he says: “This is the one who hears, then understands, and thus brings forth the fruit of teachings, no less in action than in understanding.” For whatever he deserved to hear, he hastened to know and understand; and what he understood, he fulfilled in action.

From this threefold stage of progress arises the summit of complete perfection, so that the whole Church of Christ may be two-chambered or three-chambered. Through these stages, as though through the levels of the true temple of Solomon, one ascends to the citadel of complete perfection.

This number—the hundredfold, the sixtyfold, and the thirtyfold—is also depicted according to the ages of human nature. When a man is thirty years old, he is considered strongest for all things, embraces the rights of marriage more fully, and children are begotten on either side. Therefore, under this number, the fruit of married people is rightly explained by all ecclesiastical writers.

Then the sixtyfold is increased, because when someone reaches this age, he ceases from waging war and sometimes also from begetting children. Under this number is found the order of widows and of all who practice continence. Their fruit is therefore more abundant because they are more removed from the actions of the world and are known to devote themselves to God under the constraint of repentance and the tribulation of pious labor. Hence the Apostle commands that a widow who is truly a widow and desolate be chosen only if she is not less than sixty years old.

From this they are also called celibates, because thereafter they ought to lead a heavenly life, so that they may ascend to a doubled fruit, as widows can in their destitution; thereafter, when the passions of this life have been quieted, every condition may be allotted to the affairs of the better life.

We believe, moreover, that the hundredfold fruit is consecrated and reserved equally for virgins and martyrs. Although one of our writers contends that it should be referred only to martyrs, because of their contempt for death, and assigns the sixtyfold to virgins because, as he says, of their inner repose, since they do not fight against the custom of the flesh.

But this is a remarkable interpretation, in which grace is not considered, nor is preserved incorruption—which is the companion of angels and ought to be honored for its privileges. If this were so—which it is not—the order of celibates and widows, and of all who practice continence or repentance, would appear to be excluded. Yet after their military service or repose, like those already sixty years old, they rightly receive a doubled reward for their contempt of the world.

Because the compassionate Teacher did not express, separate, demonstrate, or define these divisions, we must not therefore wander freely from the rule of truth. Otherwise, throughout the entire text of this parable, how do you suppose the truth of so great an understanding could shine forth unless divine authority had disclosed it? Even the perfect can scarcely agree concerning that truth in what remains.

Therefore the most kind Savior, in the other parables, wished to show a rule for interpretation. Like a prudent orator, he explained this parable by itself in a few words, so as afterward to provoke his hearers to understand the remaining parables that he set forth.

He did this, as they say, after the likeness of someone carrying a vessel full of wondrous and varied objects. When he has brought them into a land where they had not previously been seen, he displays one of them as especially rich and adorned with many colors, so that by means of this one he may provoke the merchants of the kingdom of heaven to seek the others that are more obscurely wrapped within.

Therefore he proposes such varied things in order to remove all weariness, because the heavenly orator knows how, according to the custom of his homeland, to speak in parables with gravity, abundance, and ornament. He also knows most skillfully how to teach, to move the minds of his hearers greatly, and to persuade them effectively, so that he may delight the differing wills of his hearers with the sweetest allurements of the parables.

Therefore, from one and the same earth he promises the thirtyfold, the sixtyfold, and the hundredfold fruit, according to the quality of the cultivation. But no one can worthily marvel at how great the diversity of these stages is, how great the majesty of divine wisdom, how great the power of his eloquence, or how much weight he possesses in speaking; no one can explain it fully.

Let us therefore also see, in the reckoning of the Greeks, who are always seeking wisdom, how this number is formed. They refer the number thirty to marriage, because in the left hand the joining of the fingers, as though beneath a gentle kiss, depicts husband and wife together.

They assign sixty to widows or celibates, because they are placed under the yoke of tribulation and distress. Hence the index finger is pressed down from the thumb by the bond of widowhood, so that the greater the difficulty of the burden and its weight, the more the reward may increase.

The hundredfold, because it is referred to virgins or martyrs, passes from the left hand to the right, so that the fingers by which marriage is signified, and the widow’s finger forming a circle, express the crown of virginity. This is what is sung in the Psalms: “The queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. XLIV, 10), because true incorruption is the sister of the angels, whose fellowship in Christ is placed at the right hand.

He proposed another parable to them, saying:

“Another,” rightly, because there are many; and not “a different one,” lest they should understand that there were only two—the two that the author of life himself graciously explained, though with a few things inserted between them, so that the understanding of the others might be sought more eagerly from these.

Because their meaning is rich and their hearing sweet, they greatly invite the reader to seek what follows among the other things that are obscure. For the most kind Savior, like an exceedingly wealthy householder who invites people to the banquet of eternal satisfaction, meanwhile takes care to refresh them on the way with various foods of delight, so that each person may receive nourishment for salvation according to the nature of his stomach.

But because, as I said, he himself explained only these two, although with a few things inserted between them, I judged that they should be joined together. And just as heavenly wisdom illuminated them with the splendor of divine understanding, so I resolved to assign them together to readers, just as they were presented.

“The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like a man who sowed good seed in his field.”

This likeness, then, he proclaimed very obscurely before the crowds, together with the others. Then, after dismissing the crowds, he came into the house, and the disciples approached him as household members, as his closest intimates, and said to him: “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.”

If this parable had not appeared more obscure than the others, they would certainly not have asked about it alone as though ignorant of it—a parable that the people neither deserved nor were able to hear. To them the compassionate Teacher said:

“The one who sows is the Son of Man; the field is the world; the good seed is the children of the kingdom; the weeds are the children of the evil one. The enemy who oversows is the devil,” and the rest.

I have prefaced these matters so that greater freedom to speak might be granted, and so that from the few things disclosed by the Lord we might understand more perceptively the many questions involved. For what has been explained and left to our understanding must be sought out more precisely and briefly noted.

The divine judge covers the truth with closed figures, shades it with mysteries, and obscures it with secret meanings so that the faithful and devoted may be exercised by these things. He explains certain matters more secretly so that they may become more eager for what is concealed.

“The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like a man,” because Christ became man in order to help the human race that was perishing. “This man sowed good seed in his field.”

You hear how God himself, made man, the sower of the world, made the beginnings of all things good, and how no evil proceeded from the author of the first creation, but he made all things exceedingly good. Therefore the Manichaeans, or the other heretics who say that something evil was created by the God of darkness, must not be heeded, since evil was oversown by the enemy and was not created by God the author, who made all things exceedingly good.

But the enemy, man—that is, the devil—oversowed weeds “in the midst of the wheat” (Matt. XIII, 25): first in Adam while he was in paradise, then in Cain already in the world, and thus throughout the entire race that was disseminated from one man to the end of the age.

And, not to prolong the discussion, from the beginning he has always mixed evil with good, vices with virtues. It is therefore established that from one man God filled the whole earth, and that from one seed the compassionate sower multiplied the entire human race into such a great harvest.

But the enemy, man, who is called an enemy because he ceased to be what God willed him to be, has always turned our life-giving things toward ruin. He has turned the creature created for the knowledge and praise of God toward insult, so that God would not be known in the world, since he falsely claimed to be God.

Hence he made the wise men of the world foolish; he taught the observers of the world to see nothing; he made teachers of the sciences possess no knowledge; and, according to the Apostle, he left investigators of reality ignorant.

Thus, by oversowing and confusing the entire crop sown in the world with heavenly seed through heretical depravity and deceptive illusions, he made sheaves bound with the cord of faith and charity into bundles for Gehenna, to be burned in everlasting fire, lest the heavenly wheat reach the granary.

This was not because he changed the nature of the wheat, but because he infected it with vices, so that what had been created good in the world would not obey its author and reach the granary. He accomplished this through deceit, schemes, and fraud, so that the wheat might degenerate and become darnel—not by nature, but corrupted through vice.

Hence there are heresies in the world, sin among the saints, quarrels among the peaceful, deceit among the simple, and wickedness among the innocent. He does not therefore strive to acquire weeds, but to destroy the wheat. Nor does he seek to besiege the dead, but to attack the living. Nor does he seek to capture those whom he possesses as subjects, but to capture the righteous who have already been corrupted by his vice.

And he does all this not during the day, while someone is awake to keep the Lord’s commandments, but while people sleep in the sleep of sluggishness and negligence. The enemy comes in the midst of the wheat and departs; nowhere else does he go than into the midst of the wheat, because evil exists nowhere except in something good. From the good, because he is evil, he makes evil by his own vice.

Yet even this happens only while the one whom he deceives is asleep. Hence David says: “They all slumbered and slept their sleep, and none of all the men of riches found anything in their hands” (Ps. LXXV, 14).

Therefore the enemy oversowed weeds so that the entire Lord’s harvest might perish. He did this by his deception, while darkness concealed it, so that the guilt of the adulterated harvest might rebound upon the servants, and they might suffer punishment from the very thing from which they had hoped for a crown.

For this reason the servants, awakened by fear and concern because this had happened, were terrified, fearing that the growth of the weeds might rebound to the offense of those whose conscience contained nothing except the sowing of the good seed.

We must therefore consider how dangerous it is for those in authority to pursue something else or to grow sluggish through negligence. The enemy might oversow weeds in the harvest entrusted to them—that is, crimes or heresy—through which the good seed sown by the Lord might perish.

For although someone sows the word of preaching, it is Christ himself who sows, because he himself went out to sow, and that which is sown in the hearts of believers.

“But when the grass had grown and produced ears, then the weeds appeared.” What was hidden in the grass is revealed in the ear, and what was concealed in the shoot is disclosed in the fruit. Hence the Lord also says: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII, 16), since in the Church of Christ many blossoms promise a multitude of fruits. But when temptation arises, very few remain for the fruit of good works.

Hence good reapers are always vigilant and afraid, lest while they sleep the wheat be soiled and mixed with foreign seed. Hence also they anticipate access to their Lord, neither secure concerning their innocence nor free from fear of incurring guilt through silence.

[Col. 0494B] “The servants of the householder came and said to him.” They approach in mind, not in body; not by place but by faith. They do not speak with an audible cry, since it is a parable, but silently in the heart and with grief: “Did you not,” they say, “sow good seed?”

“You sowed,” they say, “and we did not sow.” For whatever good we do, we ought to attribute wholly to the author and not to ourselves.

“Where then does it have weeds?” This voice is full of wonder, astonishment, and fear. How could human nature, created good by the good God, have become so corrupted and degenerate that it became something other than what it was created to be—not by nature, but through vice?

They therefore show that they are entirely ignorant by what judgment of God it happened that human beings, made rational and good in the image of God, could so wander from God that they became so vain and barren, alienated from fruit, appearing to be nothing but darnel, prepared rather for Gehenna than worthy to be stored in the granary of paradise, for which they had been created.

Therefore let human presumption cease, and let the depravity of heretics cease—those who rashly presume to define or whisper something about God’s judgment and foreknowledge—since even the angels themselves, piously asking, confess that they do not know by what judgment it occurred.

But the divine judge removes both himself and the holy angels far from guilt. “The enemy, man,” he says, “did this,” because he infected and corrupted the good that had been created by the good and sown in the world.

If someone should wish to ask further why he from whom nothing is hidden permitted this, even before it occurred, the answer is surely that nothing can be lost to him, and that it was better to distinguish the mystical meaning than to prohibit the mystery. For it is greater to restore what has been lost than to preserve what is unharmed.

At the same time, observe what has already been answered: that weeds—that is, heresies—must exist so that those who are approved may become manifest.

Then the devoted servants say: “Do you want us to go and gather the weeds?” Tireless, they offer their labor and cannot endure seeing such foulness in the Lord’s harvest, even temporarily.

Yet the compassionate Lord, whom time does not weary and who, whenever he wishes, can remove the injuries done to him, says: “Let both grow until the harvest.” And he immediately adds why he commands this:

“Lest, while you are trying to uproot the weeds, you uproot the wheat along with them.”

Otherwise, if the most merciful Lord had not commanded this, he would seem to abolish repentance. But inexperienced cultivators, ignorant of God’s work and lacking the knowledge of discernment, sometimes, while wishing to uproot the darnel, uproot the wheat as well.

I do not say this to contradict the Apostle’s command, “Remove the evil one from among you” (I Cor. V, 13), which seems to sound contrary to this passage. For it is one thing to judge in the Church concerning manifest and open crimes, and another to judge concerning things that are still hidden, as though in the grass.

For the weeds, which we call darnel, before they come into the stalk, while they are still grass, resemble the wheat so greatly that they can scarcely, or never, be distinguished. Therefore the Lord says: “Let them grow until the harvest.”

For it can happen that what appears today to be a weed may tomorrow become wheat, and what at present appears to be wheat may in the future turn into darnel, when one thing is displayed in appearance and another is produced in the blossom.

Thus it can happen that someone who is a heretic today may tomorrow be not only faithful but even a defender of the faith. The same must rightly be understood concerning the other vices. For unless God’s patience had come to the aid of Matthew also—whose Gospel this is—we would not possess him, nor would we possess Paul as an apostle after he had been a persecutor.

From this it follows that, where something is ambiguous, the teacher of the Church should not quickly pronounce sentence. Rather, let us reserve the end of judgment for God, so that when the day of judgment arrives, he may cast the guilty person from the assembly of the saints not according to suspicion of a crime but according to manifest guilt. The saints, however, because they are called wheat, he will receive into the granaries—that is, into the dwelling places of eternal life.

Moreover, the harvest is called the consummation of the age because afterward there will be neither sowing of the field nor further increase of the fruit of human seed. Then will be the time of that harvest—that is, the day of judgment—when each person will be judged.

Furthermore, the reapers to whom it is said, “Gather the weeds first,” are, with God as witness, the angels themselves, who assist God’s Church. The Apostle Paul calls them ministering spirits, placed in service for the sake of the saints who are going to receive the inheritance of salvation.

When he says, “Gather the weeds first,” this does not mean that there is one resurrection of the righteous and another of sinners or the impious. Rather, the evil are first to be separated from the good, and then the saints are to be gathered together into the kingdom.

“And then they will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII), because through the death of the Son of God they have been adopted as sons.

He proposed another parable to them, saying:

The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed. A wondrous and ineffable comparison: behold, the whole greatness of heaven is compared with a mustard seed. Yet what it means that the majesty of the kingdom is enclosed within the likeness of such a small and insignificant seed must not be passed over without serious consideration. It is as though that heavenly Wisdom had found nothing richer than a mustard seed with which to compare the omnipotence of the power above. Therefore let no one read the Gospel in passing; let no one receive Christ’s parables as though they were something worthless. For that kingdom of heaven ought not to seem worthless: by its uniqueness it is powerful, blessed in eternity, radiant in divinity, spread throughout the whole heaven, and extended over the whole earth. Yet I am not sufficient to contemplate it, nor able to penetrate what that divine Wisdom means when it compresses so priceless and ineffable a mystery into a mustard seed and confines it within the narrow limits of so very small a seed.

Hence, I ask, let heretical perversity cease its barking because God deigned to become human, if the majesty of the heavenly kingdom itself descended to the likeness of a seed. What objection can be raised to the Lord of the whole world’s taking the form of a servant? Now, as I have already said above, the kingdom of heaven is understood in three ways: either as Christ himself, as here; or as the present Church, as in very many passages; or certainly as the Gospel, which here too is signified not incongruously. For it is clear that it has grown beyond all the doctrines of the philosophers and the mysteries of the holy Scriptures. Nevertheless, it is better understood as spoken of Christ, from whom and through whom the Gospel itself grew and spread abroad. For just as “what is weak in God is stronger than men, and what is foolish is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1:25), so this least thing of God is found more magnificent, in its whole greatness, than both human beings and angels.

This is so, however, if we sow this mustard seed within our own breasts in such a way that the greatness of understanding grows inwardly in us into a tree—not just any tree, but one such and so great that all the birds of heaven may rest among its branches (Matt. 13:32), and our perceptions may be lifted toward heaven, while the whole body of knowledge spreads through its branches. Then let it be crushed in the heart so that it may set our mouths, burning with lively taste, aflame with the savor of its fruit. Indeed, let tears run from our eyes because of its excessive ardor; let the fire of its seed burn so intensely in us that it purify the brain and touch the crown of the mind. Let it flame in the breast, so that by its tasting it may remove from us all distaste for ignorance and make us ardent.

The understanding of mustard, then, of this and such a nature, indicates that it was not without reason compared with the seed of this vegetable. A man—namely, God the Father—took it and cast it into his field; or, as other books have it, into his garden, that is, into his Church, or into the world. But when it says that it is the smallest of all vegetable seeds, this is not surprising, since he says of himself in the Psalm: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. 21:7).

When it grew—that is, when it rose again—it became a tree and ascended to the heavens. Its branches, namely the apostles, spread out and grew, because “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5). Thus the birds of heaven, who are understood as the saints, dwell in them—that is, in their teaching and authority—while they despise earthly things and seek heavenly ones.

If this mustard seed is referred to the Gospel in another sense, then the man sowing the Gospel word is understood to be Christ. It is called the smallest in comparison with human philosophy because it seems worthless to unbelievers. But when it has been sown in the heart of the faithful, it becomes an excellent tree as it rises and spreads beyond all worldly wisdom. In the meantime, however, the teaching of the Gospel seems small in comparison with all disciplines. For at the beginning of the teaching of the new institution it lacks credibility: it asserts that a man is God and that God died; and from this the whole scandal of the cross seems to arise.

Compare this teaching, then, with the doctrines of the philosophers and with their books, which exude an excessive brilliance of eloquence and shine through the arrangement of their speech. Thus you will see how much smaller the seed of the Gospel is than the seeds of the liberal arts. Yet while those seeds grow and increase everywhere, they bring nothing living and show nothing conducive to salvation, nor anything vigorous directed toward eternal continuance. Rather, everything weak and everything decayed puts forth leaves and blossoms into vegetables and herbs that quickly wither.

But the preaching of the Gospel, which seemed smallest—or little at the beginning of faith—once it has taken root in the soul of the believer or in the whole world, as we see it has done, grows entirely into a tree, so that the birds of heaven—that is, the souls of believers or the virtues devoted to God’s service—come and dwell in its branches. The branches of this tree are rightly understood to be the various doctrines of the holy preachers, in which the holy fellowship of the birds mentioned above rests.

Let us therefore take to ourselves the wings of a dove, so that we may be able to fly toward higher things; and let us also dwell in the branches of this tree and make nests of teachings. Yet many, when they read that this mustard seed is the smallest of all seeds—and likewise what is said elsewhere by the disciples, “Lord, increase our faith,” to whom the answer was given, “Amen, I say to you, if you have faith like a mustard seed and say to this mountain, ‘Move from this place,’ it will move” (Luke 17:5–7)—entirely suppose that the apostles had little faith, or that the Lord reproved them because their faith was small.

They do not understand that the apostle Paul judged this faith, compared with a mustard seed, to be great and excellent: “If I have,” he says, “all faith, so that I remove mountains, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2). That faith which removes mountains is itself the faith compared by the Lord with a mustard seed; it is the whole and complete faith in which all faith is present. For through it the Triune God is truly and confidently worshiped and loved; in it Christ is wholly present, through whom all things exist, and through him faith itself accomplishes all things.

Its branches then spread out when the expositions of the holy Fathers grow from this doctrine, and in them the birds of heaven—namely, lovers of true wisdom—rest securely. For what is sown comes from above; therefore it is received with confidence, rooted by faith, grows upward through hope, is spread abroad by love, and extends into branches; it is stretched forth by confession and grows green each day through virtues. To this pleasant abundance of foliage the birds of heaven continually invite us—that is, spiritual meanings. It receives those meanings into the same branches as into a quiet dwelling, where they make nests and nourish everlasting offspring for themselves in the mind.

If, again, you seek this seed sown in the garden, where it lay in the tomb, you will find it first sown in the Virgin’s womb and afterward in the Church. From this garden the Bridegroom speaks in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed is my sister, a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Song 4:12), “the two outpourings,” he says, “of paradise.” In that garden, plainly, because this seed grew, the whole sum of the kingdom remains in it.

This is the kingdom of Christ, who grew upon the tree of the cross and spread throughout the entire world. The more he was crushed by his passion, the more abundantly he poured out the savor of his fruit in the world, and the more ardently love, once spread abroad, burned. His power appeared all the stronger when he was reduced to dust and melted in the press of his passion. From this comes the whole origin of his reign; and therefore we faithfully sing: “The Lord has reigned from the wood.”

Let no one therefore doubt that this seed was already long ago rooted in the patriarchs, born in the prophets, grown in the apostles, and brought to completion as a great tree in the churches. It produced many branches through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which the Apostle rightly numbers. In these branches the spotless birds of heaven rest in the security of faith.

“And he spoke another parable to them.” Let us therefore ask Christ not to speak to us also with the crowds in parables. For although what is said in parables is sometimes heard more pleasantly, it is nevertheless very unfruitful unless the things adorned and concealed by figures in them are understood.

“The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened.” The good and excellent teacher explains, varies, and adorns the likenesses of his kingdom through fitting comparisons in such a way that he does not draw them from what is hidden or from heavenly things, but brings them forth from daily use and ordinary human life, so that what is beneficial to everyone may reach every kind of person, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “Hear this, all nations; perceive it with your ears, all you who inhabit the world, both earthborn and children of men, rich and poor together” (Ps. 48:2–3).

Otherwise, if he brought forward something from the hidden things of divinity, something from the secret places of heaven, or something from the impenetrable riches, the poor would not know it, ordinary people would not grasp it, and simplicity would not recognize it. But now he speaks in such a way that his skill in speaking suits everyone. For in God’s calling the human being is sought; in God’s preaching no person is singled out.

Therefore he first says that a man—that is, a male—took the seed of his kingdom, the mustard seed; but now he asserts that a woman took the leaven. He shows that the small seed grew into a great tree, while the woman hid a small amount of leaven for the benefit of the whole mass. For, as the Apostle says, “Neither is man without woman, nor woman without man, in the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:11). A varied likeness brings the two sexes to one kingdom. Christ’s calling therefore does not separate the man from the woman; rather, it joins them together. For what God made to arise from one another, and what nature unites, this parable renders similar through its wondrous likeness and composes into a pattern of growth.

These parables make the two into one in one body, so that there may be neither an isolated individuality left helpless nor a confused union. But why, I believe, did the Lord shape the likenesses of his kingdom through a man and a woman? Why did he compare and join so great a majesty of the kingdom with examples so lowly and so different? This was not done without reason, especially since the Apostle says: “This mystery is great; but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32). I therefore think that something precious lies hidden in this mystery.

Through these comparisons, then, the affair of the human race is being conducted, and through the man and the woman the cause of the world, long ago prefigured from the beginning of the ages, is brought to completion. The mustard seed grows into a tree by which both sexes are cleansed, so that whatever was sinned in that which is called the knowledge of good and evil may be undone in this which is called the tree of life.

And the leaven is hidden in three measures of flour so that everything visible and corrupted by the sin of the first transgression may be wholly leavened. The woman who had corrupted the whole mass of the human race in Adam restored the whole mass of our flesh in Christ, the leaven of righteousness, through the new regeneration and renewal of a new birth. The woman who had prepared the bread of sighing and sweat would again bake the bread of life by the fire of the Holy Spirit and salvation. She would be, through Christ, the mother of all the living who had first been the mother of all the dying.

Here the matter is drawn from ordinary life: a man plants a tree in the mustard field; at home a woman hides leaven in flour, bakes bread, and prepares food. For it is the man’s task to labor outside, while domestic care confines the woman within. Hence, brothers, Sarah, barren and aged, through this preparation of leaven and from the three measures offers three cakes baked under the ashes in the mystical service of the Lord’s hospitality. The world’s barrenness, now enclosed in complete old age, would place in the three measures—that is, in the equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the leaven of her faith or the teaching of perfect understanding.

That woman, plainly, was right to set three loaves from the Gospel before her Lord as a gift, in confession of the Trinity. From this kneading of right faith, the whole offspring of the Christian name became fruitful, and, leavened in Christ, became one kneading.

As you see, reader, this woman bears the figure of the Church. She received the leaven—that is, the faith of Christ or the teaching of the holy Gospel—and became one new kneading. Thus whatever was concealed in the prophets and patriarchs, and also throughout the whole Old Testament, where we see manifold and mystical meanings, is all one mass of perfect faith in the Word: it is not hidden from the faithful, but is hidden from unbelievers and the faithless.

When he says “until the whole was leavened,” if you refer it to the human race, the meaning is that the whole integrity of this leavening extends to the end of the age, and its expansion is to be commended. Leaven comes from flour, but a certain uniqueness is attributed to it because it possesses a special and proper power, and I know not what sharpness of potency, so that from a little of it much of its own kind is produced with the Holy Spirit. Thus the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel are thoroughly dissolved, as it were, and all these things are worked together under the three measures.

From one grain of leaven he makes one whole, because what the Law established, the prophets announced, and the Gospel itself fulfills. Everything is made through Christ of the same power and meaning, so that everything has one taste, and nothing is found to differ from another when leavened in equal measures.

Some, however, seem not unreasonably to refer these three measures of flour to the calling of the nations descended from Shem, Ham, and Japheth. The meaning of “until the whole was leavened” is then that “we know in part and prophesy in part,” until what is partial is abolished and the one whole which is perfect is found.

I do not say that the calling of all nations has been saved and united in this kneading, so that the whole human race has been leavened; rather, the unity of those descended from the three is commended, in whom no admixture of leaven is found from without, but the whole unity is commended in Christ. Thus neither is leaven found without the flour from which it comes, nor flour without the leaven in which it is and by which it has been leavened, so that through this all things may become one and have one taste in the Trinity, which is perfect.

Yet because this parable was not interpreted by the Lord, as were the two above of which we have already spoken, the weakness of human intelligence invents for itself various interpretations and differing doctrines. For some hold that these three measures refer to spirit, soul, and body, so that these three, brought into one through the preaching of the word, may not disagree among themselves, but the whole and complete human being may become a new kneading in Christ. For if two or three of these agree well with one another, as is read elsewhere, they will obtain from the Father whatever they ask.

This passage is also explained otherwise by some, because human opinion, as I have said, often proceeds unsteadily and variously, so that each person may seem the more learned insofar as he finds something novel in its meaning which at least appears plausible. Accordingly, in this place they take an example from Plato, the most learned of philosophers, which is commonly known, and say that there are three possessions in the human soul: the rational, the irascible, and the concupiscible. And, as that philosopher thinks, our rational faculty resides in the brain, the irascible in the gall, and the concupiscible in the liver.

With these matters thus recognized and determined, if we receive the evangelical leaven and the teaching of the holy Scriptures, of which we have already spoken above, and if these three passions of the human soul are brought into one and kneaded with the leaven of righteousness—so that wonderful prudence flourishes in reason, perfect hatred rises against vices, and in desire or concupiscence love of God and neighbor is substituted, so that there is always in the human being a fresh desire for virtues—then all this comes through evangelical teaching, which mother Church has rightly kneaded and hidden within us in our hearts. Hence David says: “I have hidden your sayings in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. 118:11).

I neither sufficiently approve nor reject this interpretation, because the clearer meaning of this parable, which has its fragrance within, is that which we have already touched upon above, though in few words. Yet even if it is understood as we have said, it sufficiently edifies the hearer, though it does not greatly instruct the reader. For meanwhile, while we are on the way, it is always necessary that the leaven of the divine word be kneaded within us for the increase of righteousness; for divine knowledge enlightens the senses, raises hearts, increases abilities, enlarges virtues, and intoxicates, so that the mind may always flourish at every hour, rekindled by the fire of God’s love. It spreads the increase of love, and thus the whole kneading is well leavened and continually renewed, until incorruption comes; then the whole will be leavened, so that thereafter no injustice may reign in us.

Those three measures of flour are also understood by some, as I have said, in the three distinct sons of Noah, from whom every nation of the human race was begotten. But because faith does not belong to all of them, it cannot rightly be said that everything which comes from them is leavened, unless the part is taken for the whole. Therefore some, avoiding this difficulty, have understood the three measures to be the three fruits of the Church, kneaded together; in these the whole Church is leavened through the teaching of Christ, until the Gospel is preached throughout this entire world and kneaded into the hearts of the faithful.

A *satum* is a kind of measure according to the custom of the province of Palestine, containing one and a half *modii*. This measure, tripled among the three persons mentioned, is also interpreted—not incongruously—by a certain distinguished teacher as leaven kneaded and hidden: namely, Noah, Job, and Daniel. For in these three persons the whole order of the elect is represented.

Thus it is said through the prophet: “If Noah, Job, and Daniel were in the midst of the city, they would save neither sons nor daughters, but they alone would be saved by their righteousness” (Ezek. 14:20). Through them, as I have said, the whole number of the elect is understood as kneaded together in God’s teaching and faith, until the whole Church of Christ is gathered into one at the end of the age—leavened under that number in the perfect faith of the Trinity, and kneaded in the unity of Christ’s body and the fullness of love.

No one can properly criticize my having explained these matters in various ways according to the understanding of some, since I did this to satisfy the curious reader. Let him himself prudently choose from the many interpretations whichever pleases him, or else decide in sound faith that all these interpretations correspond to this parable without impropriety.

“All these things,” he says, “Jesus spoke in parables to the crowds, and without parables he did not speak to them.” Christ speaks in parables not to the disciples but to the crowds. And what is more serious, even to this day the crowds and the people of the present age hear everything in parables and do not seek to understand; they hear only what reaches them in the sound of the voice.

But the disciples, he says, because they are true disciples, question the Savior more privately at home and ask to understand. We read that David prayed for this: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me; he will speak peace to his people, and to his saints, and to those who turn their hearts toward him” (Ps. 84:9).

“This was fulfilled,” he says, “which was spoken through the prophet: ‘I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world’” (Ps. 77:2). There is no doubt that Matthew understood this as spoken in Christ’s person; and because these parables are exceedingly obscure, he concluded at the end: “Let the one who has ears for hearing hear.” Thus he says:

“I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world.” Whatever seems to sound historically in Genesis, Exodus, or the other books of the Old Testament was altogether spoken in parables and hidden in riddles. Although some have translated the term as “propositions,” others as “hidden things,” in Hebrew it is nevertheless said to mean “riddles,” because a riddle is not merely what is said but what is signified inwardly.

Therefore the sense is one, whether you say “hidden things,” “propositions,” or merely “riddles”: Christ opens his mouth and speaks inwardly in the heart the propositions and riddles that had been hidden and greatly obscured from the beginning of the world. Hence the divine word says pointedly: “Incline your ear to the words of my mouth” (Ps. 77:1). It does not say “raise” your ear, but “incline” it humbly, so that what sounds within may be understood—not through the sound of the voice but through the hearing of the mind—as the mystery of the divine word, which was hidden from the beginning of the world and prefigured in the holy Scriptures.

Then, after dismissing the crowds, he returns home, so that there the disciples may hear what the people neither deserved to know nor could hear inwardly, since the crowd is always more involved in the tumult of this age than in the silence of the heart. But what the disciples then heard and asked about we have already anticipated, so that the two parables explained by Christ might be joined together.
