For, without doubt, he concludes the parable with his explanation in this way: when the wheat has been gathered into the barns—that is, into eternal dwellings—then the righteous will shine like the sun in their power. For now, like the light of the moon in the night of this age, the light of the saints is present; then it will be enlarged like the light of the sun. Hence Isaiah says: “The light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun”—that is, of Christ—“will be like the light of seven days” (Isa. 30:26), because in him there will be the whole fullness of eternal brightness, and from the seven spirits who stand before his throne the grace of all gifts will shine in him with everlasting splendor.

It follows:

“The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field,” and so forth. The meaning of this parable is itself obscure, since the treasure is proclaimed both hidden and found, and then hidden again by the one who found it, so that it may remain concealed and secret for the time being until it is purchased together with the field in which it lies.

What, then, shall I do, poor in understanding? How shall I find what is hidden with such care? Or how shall I dig out what is concealed so deeply, even if I find it? For, as has often been said, the truth of perfect understanding is wrapped in figures and obscured by riddles. It lies in the depths. Therefore, although the discourse is excellent and the eloquence lofty, divine mercy must be implored, so that these parables may be expounded by the same Spirit by which they appear to have been composed.

For, as I perceive, in this present parable all the resources and riches of our hope appear to be sufficiently wrapped and hidden. To this treasure, because it lies hidden in a field, the kingdom of heaven is divinely compared. Here he plainly shows that in Christ the man God was found—not discovered by our skill, but revealed by his own grace. In him, according to the Apostle, “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:3), but in the field of flesh.

If, following others, I take the field to mean the knowledge of faith and the treasure to mean faith itself, the interpretation seems insufficiently suited to an understanding of such sublimity. Others have interpreted the kingdom of heaven as the work of righteousness, which they say was hidden in that man as in a field. Others understood the treasure in the field as both Testaments, shadowed in the Church by figures. That treasure is not hidden out of envy, but so that it may be placed in the heart. The Jewish people sold this treasure, and the nation of the Gentiles bought it. There are other interpretations of this sort, which seem more to invent than to explain, especially because the matter is obscure; and therefore some have been allowed, so to speak, to rave freely.

But supported by the grace of the Holy Spirit, let us say, as we have already said above, that Christ’s flesh is the field, full of heavenly mysteries. The Lord blessed it long ago, and all the resources of the world must be sold as its price, so that we may purchase the eternal riches of the heavenly treasure.

Yet it must be carefully considered that neither is the treasure purchased without the field, nor is the field found without the treasure. Here every heretical perversity is condemned—those who have thought wrongly about the Lord’s incarnation and doubted his flesh. For neither is his flesh possessed without the treasure of divinity, nor is the treasure found without the birth of flesh from the Virgin’s womb; and once found, it is purchased through faith and good works.

Whoever discovers this treasure of wisdom and knowledge in Christ, the good man, will recognize that it is deeply concealed because of the weakness of the flesh. But the one who finds it goes away and hides it, lest it meanwhile be secretly taken away; lest, if it were taken away from the midst of the field, the whole necessity and opportunity of purchasing it should lose the fruit of the discovery.

But the reason both of the matter and of the saying had to be explained. The treasure is hidden again by the one who found it because the field also had to be purchased in which the treasure of all riches was concealed. The treasure in the field, as we have said, is Christ in the flesh, in whom “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily,” and who is hidden from unbelievers.

To find this field is undoubtedly free, because the whole preaching of the Gospel is offered openly and given freely. But the power to use and possess this treasure cannot be obtained without paying the price of the field, because heavenly riches are possessed only at the cost of the world. Therefore it is said:

“When a man has found it, he hides it, and in his joy over it goes and sells everything that he has and buys that field.” When it says that he hides it, he does not do this out of envy, but from holy fear, wishing to preserve it and not lose it. He therefore hides in his heart the treasure he has preferred to all the resources of the present life, to such an extent that in his joy over it he chooses to sell everything—to possess in its entirety the field, namely Christ’s flesh, because, as I have said, in him is the whole fullness of divinity (Col. 1:9) in one person.

Otherwise, what necessity or obstacle was there to prevent him from immediately taking the treasure he had found from the field? If he rejoiced because he had found it, does it not seem to you that this discoverer of the treasure acted rather unwisely? Surely, during that very period of leisure and secrecy in which he had found it, he could have carried it away; and with such an easy and economical acquisition, he would not have needed to purchase the field at the expense of his own resources, since he was glad to possess the treasure as his own.

But the very prudent man recognized that possession of this treasure without the field was ineffective and useless, indeed dangerous. For observe: just as he had found it hidden, so he himself hid it. He did not dare to strip and empty the field of its treasure, but hastened to sell all his possessions according to lawful right, so that he might obtain both the treasure and the field together.

For neither is Christ’s humanity possessed without his divinity, nor his divinity without his humanity, in one and the same person according to right doctrine. Therefore every confession concerning Christ is altogether useless, vain, and impious if it confesses the Lord Christ as God alone or as man alone, and does not confess him as both God and man.

That Christ’s field is figuratively called his flesh is indicated both by the present passage and by many other testimonies of Scripture. Isaac especially bears witness to this field in his blessings, saying: “Behold, the odor of my son is like the odor of a field that God has blessed” (Gen. 27:27). For Christ’s body gives off the fragrance of the great variety of virtues. Hence the Apostle says: “We are the good odor of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2:15). And the Church says in the Song of Songs: “We run after you in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:4).

He himself speaks of the beauty of this field in the Psalm: “And the beauty of the field is with me” (Ps. 49:11). In Solomon, a woman is introduced as having purchased this field, for it is said: “She saw a field and bought it” (Prov. 31:16). Precious is the possession of this field, which holds hidden within itself the divinity of Christ.

Therefore neither is the treasure of divinity, without the field, nor the field, without the treasure, lawfully purchased or possessed, as the heretics wished. Although the distinguished teacher Augustine said that this field is the two Testaments, it is better understood in such a way that the error of Photinus, who says that Christ is merely a man, is destroyed no less than the impiety of Eutyches and the falsehood of Nestorius are condemned by this passage, as also in other places.

It follows:

“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls,” and so forth. In different words and another manner of speaking, he seems most elegantly to repeat the same thing—not to alter the same wisdom, but to introduce his hearers to it through various riddling statements.

The only apparent difference is that he seems to designate more particularly a merchant who had long been engaged in the Law, although this parable can clearly encompass in general all who follow the faith of Christ. By calling him a merchant and saying that he seeks good pearls, he foretells at length the desire of those who, represented by one man, wish through long and sustained labor to attain knowledge of the pearls.

After he has carried on his commerce through continual meditation upon the Law and discovered the meanings contained in the Law, at last, among those he had found, he finds one singular pearl, Christ, whom he desired. In comparison with him, although the Law is good and prophecy is good, and although the foremost ornaments of teaching are found in them, the merchant—like the apostle Paul—despises all the mysteries and former observances of the Law and the prophets, in which he had previously lived blamelessly, as refuse and rubbish, so that he may gain Christ.

For the most precious pearl is knowledge of the Savior, the mystery of his passion, and the secret of his resurrection. The discovery of this most precious pearl does not mean that the former pearls are condemned, but that in comparison with Christ every gem—that is, every understanding of the Law and prophecy—is less valuable.

This exceedingly diligent merchant of gems can also signify the whole order of Christ’s Church, so that the genus may be shown in one example and the kingdom of heaven may itself be understood as the Church. The Church labored for a long time in the patriarchs and sought in the prophets, although secretly, because the glory of the saints had not yet been revealed. Yet many of them brought forth the appearance of gems and adorned them beforehand by prefiguring Christ and the future Church.

But no one among them was found who bore within himself the price of human redemption. Therefore no stone was found so precious that this prudent merchant would sell everything belonging to the present life in order to acquire that one gem, in which are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge and the price of human salvation.

For this reason this most precious stone is purchased at the same price at which the field and the treasure were purchased in the other parable. This does not mean that the other stones sought—and perhaps found—by the merchant were not good and precious, but in comparison with this one no one is good, because all derive from it whatever makes them good and precious.

This is the new stone from the Apocalypse of John, on which a new name is written, which no one knows except the one who receives it. Therefore every shadow must be removed from the meaning of the Law and the Prophets, and truth alone must be embraced. The present life and the things of the present must be sold, so that this alone may be possessed in which all things are good and eternal.

It should also be noted that the text does not say how much the present merchant paid to purchase it, but only that whoever finds it gives as much as he possesses. Hence it says:

“He goes and sells everything that he has, and buys it.” For the kingdom of God is worth as much as you possess.

Nevertheless, it is not purchased in such a way that you give your possessions to God while giving yourself to vices and the devil. Rather, you must first restore yourself to him, and then give him what is yours, so that you may be able to follow him freely.

Nor, once you have found him and purchased him through faith and good works, will you cease seeking and finding him while you remain in this life. But as the Prophet sings: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice; seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Ps. 104:3).

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind, and so forth.

Most rightly, then, did the Lord and Savior compare the preaching of the holy Gospel to a dragnet cast into the sea, so that in these words the prophecy of the prophet Jeremiah might be fulfilled, when he says: “For behold, I am sending many fishermen to you” (Jer. XVI, 16). These fishermen will certainly labor in this fishing for human salvation from the beginning of the Gospel to the end of the age. The first of them were those to whom it was said: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. IV, 19).

Thus these four—two and two—first wove for themselves, in accordance with the voice of their Teacher and Savior, the Gospel net of doctrine from both the Old and the New Testament. After them came the succession of all the holy preachers. This net is drawn by two interwoven cords through the midst of this sea, stretched from the highest point down to the depths: upward, indeed, it is raised and firmly established by hope above all the waves of the age; downward, it is submerged as far as the lowest depths by fear of divine judgment, but it is never dragged all the way down, so that it may not always be aloft, raised more highly by the love of Christ and lifted up to heaven.

For *sagena* is the Greek word for what is commonly called a *verruculum*, from its being drawn. The sea in which it is drawn is called “great and broad” in the Psalms (Ps. CIII, 25). In it are creeping creatures whose number is beyond counting, and in it the dragon has been placed to be mocked, so that he himself may be mocked by all—not merely by human strength, but by the grace of the divine gift and by the instruction of so great a fisherman.

In accordance with the pattern of this instruction, the net is woven, as custom requires, with large and small knots of two kinds, so that it may catch every kind of fish and no large or small fish may escape. In the same way, these two Testaments duplicate their greater and lesser commandments, so that no one may escape the nets of salvation. If someone cannot fulfill the greater commandments, let him at least fulfill the smallest.

Just as the Gospel is rightly drawn in such a way that it penetrates the whole sea, passing through the entire body of this deep element of the age and drawing out into the light above, and into the light of the true sun, all whom it has enclosed within the limits and embrace of its net, so that no one born and nourished in this darkness of the waters may remain submerged.

This likeness is composed for the purpose of showing why he chose as apostles those same men to whom he spoke—fishermen—and made them fishers of men: namely, so that the pattern of divine judgment might be displayed through the skill of a fisherman. The catch gathers fish, confused and undistinguished, of whatever kind; but in the vessels the discrimination of divine judgment separates the chosen. So the call of the Gospel summons and draws both the righteous and the unrighteous, the good and the evil, to faith.

The end of the age and the day of judgment will show what kind of creatures the nets have drawn. For amid the waves of this sea—whose swelling pomp foams through many collisions, whose rising summit the world lifts up, which makes itself turbulent through sects, divides itself through errors, becomes noisy through disputes, rages with the vapors of anger, grows savage in storms, suffers shipwreck through crimes, and is submerged in impiety—amid the waves of this sea, then, over which the ancient enemy ruled, Christ sent his fishermen, namely Peter and Andrew, James and John, proven in their craft when he said: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. IV, 19).

He sent these men carrying nets knotted with evangelical commandments and heavenly admonitions, surrounded and woven together with the gifts of virtues. This net, spread wide in the Gospel’s embrace, draws out a long catch of the human race until the end of the age.

“When it was full,” he says, “they drew it out, and sitting beside the shore they chose the good into vessels, but threw the bad outside.” The Savior himself explained this third parable, because the parables are obscure, so that “every word” of Catholic interpretation might stand “on the testimony of two or three witnesses.”

“So it will be,” he says, “at the consummation of the age. The angels will go out and separate the evil from the midst of the righteous.”

This does not mean that the angels require bodily seats, but that their judicial authority is being indicated. Hence he says expressly: “The angels will go out” from that inward judgment of divine majesty in which Christ will sit with his senators. They will go out to carry out the divine judgments that they learned within, but not before Christ’s net has been filled—that is, before the whole number of those predestined to life and foreordained before the foundation of the world has been completed.

At the end of the age they themselves will be gathered into vessels, that is, into eternal dwellings; but the evil will be sent outside that kingdom and away from the glory of eternal life. And this is the consummation of the age. It does not mean that the elements of the world will perish, since there will be a new heaven and a new earth; rather, “consummation of the age” is understood as the fullness of perfection, when the world will take its beginning from its end.

The end will not, as I have said, be the destruction of the elements, but their renewal, when the form of this world has passed away. For even if it comes to an end, it will not perish for its Creator, but for sin, since “death will be no more” (Rev. XXI, 4).

There is no doubt that the merciful Savior will then complete the work of his angels, through whom the Church of Christ is now governed and assisted. The impious will be removed from the midst of the righteous, lest they see the glory of God, and they will be sent outside into the outer darkness and into the furnace of fire, “where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

I am greatly astonished at the rashness and folly of certain people who say that there are no punishments or tortures of penalties except the consciences of sinners themselves—as though they too were not conscious of their guilt while they were still living in the flesh. This is especially astonishing since the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels is also said to exist, and those whom the eternal fire will burn are to be cast into it.

Since there will be a resurrection of the flesh, the gnashing of teeth and weeping of the eyes are therefore proclaimed—not as arising from consciousness of sin alone, but from the eternal punishment that has been prepared. Unless, perhaps, the advocates of this lie wish to assert that the Author of life also prepared those very consciences in such a way that they are believed to be tortured only by themselves, so that he himself is the author of the punishment; for the torments by which they will be tortured, as well as the fires and punishments, are said to have been prepared by him.

Hence he says: “Have you understood all these things?” He says this only to the Apostles, to whom it was given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God (Mark IV, 11), and to the crowds. Therefore they too, as teachers and as sharers in the kingdom, answer—not instructed by common gossip, nor by the school of philosophers, but instructed by the Holy Spirit as future teachers and educated by heavenly teaching.

Then he said to them: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure new things and old.”

He calls them scribes and indicates that they are learned and trained in heavenly disciplines. By explaining the parables to them as though they understood them, he gives them worthy testimony, since they alone, like the Savior’s scribes and those acquainted with his secrets, stored his words and commandments in the treasure of their hearts and inscribed them on the tablets of their purest breasts.

For this reason he compares them to a householder, because they had drawn in full from the treasure of Christ’s breast the teaching of the New and Old Testaments—that is, of the Law and the Prophets. Therefore he calls them scribes learned in the Law and the Gospel. And he makes them not merely learned, but like himself:

“Who brings out of his treasure new things and old.”

Thus what they all drew from was one treasure. Therefore, whatever the apostles taught in the Gospel, they confirmed by the words of the Law and the Prophets in every respect, so that they might be found like the one whose treasure they carried in their hearts.

For this reason also the bride sings in the Song of Songs (Song VII, 13): “My beloved has kept new things and old things.” No teacher, therefore, ought to exist in the Church—which is the kingdom of heaven—unless he can bring forth the treasure of the New and Old Testament to the peoples.

He must proclaim the ancient transgression of Adam in such a way that he is able fully to preach the benefits of Christ’s new grace and the new redemption of the human race. He must also be found rich in virtues, so that he can display from the treasure of his heart good works belonging to the new life, and skillfully cure, like a physician, vices and sins belonging to the old person. He must openly declare the punishments of hell and the torments of the underworld, so that he is able, from faith and with the full authority of the Scriptures, to exhort and teach what is heavenly and spiritual, and to invite his hearers most clearly to the things that are eternal.

Thus he must temper new things and old—not so that fear of Gehenna overwhelms the faithful, nor so that the hope of blessedness arrogantly exalts us, but so that humility always hides within itself the virtues it produces.

Behold, Matthew has now set forth eight kinds of parables. If you wish, reader, to compare them with the eight beatitudes, you will find that they correspond very closely to one another, not only in number but also in their example of teaching. Some, however, have wished there to be seven, saying that the final repetition belongs to the preceding one.

They said this so that the number seven might correspond to the seven days in which the world was made. Thus the first of the parables seems to refer to the beginning of the world, when everything that later grew into fruit was sown, or when everything that eventually appeared in the seed was corrupted. The final parable, which is compared to the net, tends toward the end of the age, in which it is said: “So it will be at the consummation of the age.”

They assigned the other six to the six ages of the world, because whatever is said in each parable seems to correspond to the respective periods of the age. Thus, in the first age of the world, beginning with Adam and then Cain, the devil, like an enemy and adversary, sowed weeds over the wheat and corrupted the nature of the human race throughout that whole age.

Then, in the second age, in the time of Noah, the mustard seed, small in number, grew into a great nation as the branches of the genealogies spread out, and it became a very leafy tree.

The leaven of the third parable designates the age in which the faith of our father Abraham fermented and thereafter leavened God’s world, in whose seed all the nations of the earth would be blessed. In this age of the world the Synagogue also first received the leaven of the Law, with which the whole mass of the New Testament was leavened, as testified by the Law and the Prophets.

Then, in David’s time, as though under the fourth age, a treasure was found to have been hidden in the field of prophecy. Hence one of the prophets, when he had found it, said: “You are a hidden God, and we did not know you” (Isa. XLV, 15).

Meanwhile, when the captivity that occurred among the Chaldeans had come, the pearls that had long been sought failed, until at the end of this period the one most precious pearl, Christ, was found, because Christ was born in it.

And so, in that final age, which is called the sixth, the whole order of preachers, in the likeness of Christ who brought forth new things and old from his treasure, placed the mysteries of the Law and the Prophets in their earthen vessels and continued to pour forth until the end of the age the most precious ornaments of the divine words, the new and old mysteries.

Since some teachers hand down this interpretation as we have described it, let it be enough for us to have touched upon it briefly rather than explained it. But the diligent reader should consider whether the eight parables, together with their eight beatitudes, correspond more fully when joined together, or whether they correspond as those teachers wish when compared with the ages of the world.

This much is certain: these parables, so many and of such a kind, are joined together not without a mystery. In them the number eight is conformed, and the mysteries of human salvation are hidden from the Jews and disclosed to the apostles.

Hence he says: “And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these parables, that he departed from there.”

The completion of the parables is the work of perfect preaching, which will never be completed except through the eight beatitudes. For this reason a certain psalm is sung “for the octave,” and it is sung about the Lord’s Passion, because in it the entire perfection of blessedness will be brought to completion.

And when he had come into his own country, that is, Nazareth, he taught them in their synagogues, so that they were astonished.

Here Matthew did not preserve the order of the narrative, because after these parables, when he had gone out from the house, he first turned to other events that Mark and Luke narrated, where they say that he slept in the boat and that demons were expelled in the region of the Gerasenes. Luke also placed this episode not long after the baptism, saying that his fellow citizens were amazed at his power.

Do not be surprised, reader, that he says, “He came into his own country.” He is not speaking according to his divinity, but according to his humanity. Otherwise, according to his divinity, from where does he go forth, since he is absent nowhere? Where does he enter, since no place contains or confines him? To what country, then, does he go, who made and possesses everything?

He therefore came to his country and to his fellow citizens according to the flesh, in order to teach them in their synagogues. “In their synagogues,” he says, and not in God’s, because those who did not know him could not have God. Therefore they were astonished and said:

“From where does this man have this wisdom and these powers?”

What astonishing folly and lack of understanding on the part of the Nazarenes! They wonder from where eternal Wisdom has wisdom, and from where eternal Power has powers. But their error is obvious, since they suppose him to be the son of a craftsman.

Oh, how great is human error, and how great the folly that conceives envy and gives birth to hatred over virtues and divine things! Night does not cover day, nor darkness the sun, as envy’s jaundiced stain blinds and darkens the mind of those whom it possesses.

They marvel at his wisdom and powers, but they do not wish to believe. Their astonishment does not arise from devotion but from envy. Yet whether they wish it or not, the teaching they hear is divine, and the powers they see are divine. They confess that he is more than a human being, and therefore they are moved by the miracles; but they do not wish to confess him as God, even though they see in him the works of divinity.

They marvel in such a way that they invent another source for what they cannot deny. Therefore, blinded by envy, they immediately turn their eyes back to the man:

“Is this not the son of the craftsman,” they say, “and is not his mother called Mary? From where, then, does this man have such wisdom and such great powers?”

So speak those who do not know God, from whom wisdom comes and from whom power comes. Thus the one who does not see and does not know that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God both denies and confesses against his will.

But I wonder why they name Mary while saying nothing about his father, unless they call him the craftsman’s son more mockingly, so that, on account of the usefulness of the work, they may despise him more deeply. Yet by God’s will, even unwillingly, they speak true and divine things about him, since he is truly the Son of God the Father, who is the Maker of the world.

Hence Mark calls him not the craftsman’s son but the craftsman himself. They believed him to be a craftsman for the same reason that they believed him to be the craftsman’s son: from the craft of his father he was truly himself a craftsman, because he is the Maker of the universe, through whom all things were made.

It is therefore not surprising that his relatives and fellow citizens should err with the Jews concerning Christ, since they err concerning his father and mother, and also concerning his brothers. They cunningly introduce brothers and display sisters, so that they may either invent that his father had had another wife, or cast disgrace upon the greater number of births of the holy Mother, so that her holy virginity may remain hidden, her integrity obscured, and everything human may be perceived in Christ, with nothing divine.

For if blessed Mary had had sons, as some chatter, why, at the very time of the cross, would the Virgin have been entrusted by Christ to the virgin disciple, and why, at the very moment of his death, would she have been commended to a stranger?

Rather, the brothers and sisters of Christ were the sons of Mary, the sister of Cleophas, who was Christ’s maternal aunt. They were therefore the Savior’s cousins, who are rightly called brothers.

He would never, contrary to the order of devotion, have entrusted the Lord’s Mother to an outsider—to John, that is, from the cross, as I have said—if she had borne other sons afterward. But because there were no others, he entrusted the Virgin to a virgin, so that among outsiders he alone might have responsibility for the mystery, and there might be only the fellowship of religion. The great disciple was not to serve worldly concern, but, since he was going to preach the birth that came from virginity, the Virgin was to be kept at home.

Otherwise, could not James, who is called the Lord’s brother, have cared for his mother if he had been the son of the same woman? He was the one who, both in the beginnings of the Church and amid the Jewish unbelief then prevailing, governed the Church of Jerusalem in a singular manner.

Thus it is clear that this error of the Jews arose not from truth but from envy. Therefore it is not surprising that they err concerning the brothers, since they also err concerning the father.

But Jesus said to them: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country.”

It is almost natural for fellow citizens always to envy their fellow citizens. Therefore they do not perceive the wisdom of divinity in him, nor the extraordinary works of divine majesty, because they remember his fragile infancy, count his parents among his relations, and assign him a genealogy.

Behold how carnally his fellow citizens understand; behold how worldly relatives think about the honor of kinship.

“And he did not perform many powers there,” he says, “because of their unbelief.”

This does not mean that he could not perform them even though they did not believe, but that, by performing many miracles, he would have condemned the unbelieving citizens more severely. Or he performed a few freely for this reason, so that they might be without excuse, although in his divine judgment he postponed performing many, because they did not deserve to understand the things that had been done so that they might believe.

### Chapter XIV

At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus and said to his attendants.

When it says, “At that time,” this is to be understood as the time when he came into his own country, that is, into Galilee, where Herod was.

This Herod the tetrarch was the son of the Herod under whom Christ was born. Augustus granted him a fourth part of the kingdom of the Jews, so that his rule would be humble, just as he did to his other three brothers. Hence each of them derived his title from the Greek, so that they were called tetrarchs, because each held a fourth part of a single principality.

Matthew says that, when he heard the report about Jesus, he said to his attendants: “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore powers are at work in him.” Mark reports it this way: “Some were saying that John the Baptist had risen from the dead” (Mark VI, 14). Luke says: “When Herod heard what was being done by him, he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had risen from the dead” (Luke IX, 7), followed by the rest of the passage.

It is therefore to be understood either that, after his perplexity, he confirmed inwardly that he should believe what was being said and then said to his attendants, “This is John,” or that, while still perplexed, he asked as a question, “Is this John?” The passage can therefore be understood in either way.

He did not say, “Surely this is not he?” as though he were confirming the matter, nor, while uncertain, did he say, “Perhaps this is he.” He simply said: “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore powers are at work in him.”

Some ecclesiastical interpreters seek the reasons why Herod suspected this, so that he thought John had risen from the dead and that powers were therefore working in him. But an explanation of another person’s error seems superfluous, unless perhaps the sect that the Greeks call *μετεμψύχωσις*—metempsychosis, which they say occurs through necromancy—is to be restrained and condemned. They say that the souls of individuals return to bodies after thirty years.

This cannot at all apply to John and Christ, because at the time when John was beheaded, the Lord was already thirty years old. Metempsychosis, as I have said, teaches that after thirty years, or even more, after many cycles of years, human souls enter different bodies and return to them. This is utterly contrary to Christian doctrines and is an utterly insane belief.

But Herod seized John.

The evangelist had earlier said, in Herod’s person: “This is John.” He introduced that passage above by way of recapitulation, because none of the evangelists narrates John in the chronological order in which this tragedy occurred, although Matthew and Mark agree with one another at this point. Luke, placing these events long before the Lord was baptized, narrates them earlier. John merely touches upon them, saying that Jesus came into Galilee, where he made wine from water, and then, he says, returned to Judea, where he baptized many before John was handed over.

He was handed over, bound, and placed in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother.

For John was saying: “It is not lawful for you to have her.”

An ancient history tells that Philip, the son of Herod the elder, under whom the Lord fled into Egypt, and the brother of this Herod under whom Christ suffered, married Herodias, the daughter of King Petiphere. Later, when certain quarrels had arisen between her father and her husband, her father took his daughter away and, to the grief of her first husband and as an insult to this Herod, his enemy, joined her in marriage to him, although Philip was the actual brother of Herod himself.

But John the Baptist, who had come “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke I, 17), rebuked Herod with the same authority with which Elijah had rebuked Ahab and Jezebel, because he had contracted an unlawful marriage. According to the Law, it was not permissible, while a brother was alive, to take his wife, although it was permitted after his death.

Therefore, since his brother was alive, Herod was rightly condemned as guilty and incestuous on account of this crime. The herald of truth preferred to endanger himself before the king rather than, through flattery, become forgetful of God’s commandments.

For this reason the Lord rightly repaid him with the blessedness of martyrdom, saying in this very Gospel: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 10).

Accordingly, certain people today must be rebuked who say that kings and the powers of this age ought not to be rebuked or sharply reproved, lest they be provoked to fiercer anger. I heard one of the bishops say this: “A king has been reduced under no one’s authority, nor is he under anyone’s government, because he belongs to everyone in common and does not dwell in a single parish.”

If this is so, John ought to be judged blameworthy and rash, since he came from the desert into the presence of the king to rebuke adultery. But because John was the friend of the Bridegroom, he could not tolerate incestuous people, whom this flatterer is more pleased to caress and soothe with praise than to rebuke. Many who appear to exercise the care of shepherds are endangered by this fault.

I do not know whether, if the time of martyrdom came, those who now dare not say anything for the sake of justice would remain faithful. But John, although Herodias was plotting against him, did not fear Herod, who was bound by such great evils, nor was he softened by his favors. As the evangelist says, Herod often heard him in many matters and willingly inclined himself toward the things that Christ’s herald admonished.

For he was wretched in every respect and exceedingly deceitful; hence the Lord calls him a fox.

And therefore the evangelist says:

“Desiring to kill him, he feared the people, because they regarded him as a prophet.”

But because he postponed killing him, in order to satisfy his wicked wife he placed him, though innocent, bound in prison, so that Herod’s whole deed might be a mystery of guilt. John is hidden while Christ is exalted. In John the Law and prophecy come to an end, because all the prophets prophesied until John.

Therefore, reader, as I have very often warned, every diligence must be applied to reading the Gospels, because within the events that are narrated there are hidden the secrets of inward understanding. The narrative of every deed has its own order, and from the effects of the events the form of the underlying causes is prefigured.

Thus Herodias signifies the Synagogue, which attempts, together with her daughter who danced at the banquet—as the nations also danced before idols—to cut off the head of John, that is, Christ. She took John’s head, that is, the body of Christ, to the altar, because it was given to the girl, that is, to the Church from the Gentiles.

Again, the girl carried it to her mother, because the faith she received concerning Christ she herself will offer at the end of the age for the conversion of the Jews, so that they may receive him as their head.

On Herod’s birthday, the daughter of Herodias danced in the midst of the company, and she pleased Herod.

They say that this daughter was Philip’s, so that through her it might be demonstrated publicly before all his associates that Herodias had been the wife of two brothers, and that through conjugal affection she had violated brotherly affection—simply so that she might be joined to Herod, and that those who were no longer unlike in crime, character, and life might be alike in name.

Those whom the shamefulness of their crimes had joined were united by a common title. But the daughter was more shameful, since by her games she dishonored her uncle and further defiled her mother. For she was the daughter of the first husband and publicly exposed all these things. As a result she became still worse, according to the saying in Revelation: “Let the one who does wrong continue to do wrong, and let the one who is filthy continue to be filthy” (Rev. XXII, 11).

Therefore, when he had sworn to her, he promised to give her whatever she requested.

Without doubt he swore deceitfully so that he might appear excusable and innocent, although, as the evangelist had testified above, he had long wished to kill John. He knew from his wife’s desire what the girl would ask.

Otherwise, if she had requested something else, she perhaps would not have obtained her mother’s death, nor half the kingdom which he had promised. He did not make the promise in order to give it, but so that it might appear more unanswerable when she requested what he himself was plotting.

We find no one in the divine Scriptures who celebrated his birthday except Herod and Pharaoh. Since their impiety in unbelief was alike, they had one shared solemnity of pride.

Amid these deceptions, Herodias feared that Herod might someday come to his senses, or become reconciled with his brother Philip, and dissolve the unlawful marriage by repudiation. She therefore advised that John’s head be demanded immediately at the banquet itself—a reward of blood worthy of the dance’s deed.

“And the king was grieved,” the evangelist says, “because of the oath.”

This grief revealed not repentance of heart, but an attempt to deceive his fellow diners through pretense. A craftsman of lies and a murderer displays sadness on his face while holding joy in his heart, so that he might fool the banqueters.

It is customary in Scripture for the historian to report the opinion of the multitude, describing how everyone believed matters to be at that time. So here, perhaps, the diners thought that Herod was genuinely grieving.

Hence he says: “Because of the oath and those who were reclining with him, he ordered it to be given.”

Therefore, at the Lord’s command, oaths are to be avoided, especially those that give rise to banquets prolonged through whole nights and hours. Wine purchased in moderation but drunk without moderation quickly produces shipwreck.

Thus Herod, although he kept faith with his oath, committed murder. It would have been better to repent of an unfortunate oath—as we read that David did when Abigail’s words appeased him concerning Nabal—than to shed the blood of the holy prophet and carry out the deceit that he harbored in his heart.

“Give me,” she said, “here on a platter.”

Why on a platter, unless so that the mystery of our redemption might be represented? For “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV, 15). Thus, on the platter and table on which Christ’s body is consecrated—the body that is the head of the martyrs—the martyrs themselves might share with their head in the offering of eternal salvation.

But the serpent’s offspring always demands the head of John and of the human being whose head it knew had once been condemned by the sentence of the supreme Judge, when the Lord said: “She will watch for your head, and you will watch for her heel” (Gen. III, 15).

But miserable and deadly was the royal hall, and unhappy the rage that received a martyr’s head as its food, drank the fluid of sacred blood as its drink, and, thirsting for the prophet’s death, looked upon it.

O cruel dish! O platter sprinkled with drops of blood, but exceedingly deadly to the banqueters! For in so great a banquet there was no one who would restrain the king’s audacity. Rather, as Scripture says, “because of those who were reclining with him, he ordered it to be given.”

By this act he made them all accomplices in his crime. In the luxurious and impure banquet, the bloody food was made still more defiled as the head was brought on the platter.

The head that had been brought was given to the girl, and she carried it to her mother.

It is recorded in Roman history that Flaminius, a Roman commander, agreed to the request of a little prostitute reclining beside him, who said that she had never seen a man beheaded, and had a certain criminal convicted of a capital offense beheaded during a banquet. Later he was expelled from the Senate by the senators because he had mixed food with blood and had displayed the death even of a guilty man for another’s pleasure, so that lust and murder might be mingled together.

How much more criminal were Herod and Herodias, and also the girl who danced and, as the price of her tragic performance, demanded not a goat but the prophet’s head, so that she might control the tongue that had boldly denounced the unlawful marriage.

The very shameful daughter therefore answered her even more shameful mother. Such a daughter deserved to be born from an adulteress, and, with crooked steps, disordered body, and every joint of her limbs dislocated, to be disfigured by entrails flowing this way and that through the art of sorcery, becoming in every respect far more deformed than her mother by her own deformity.

It should be noted that he says:

“Because Herod sent and beheaded John.”

From this it is understood that the one who orders something done is the one who kills, just as, in every guilt, the one who commands an act to be performed makes himself the author of the crime.

Let this suffice according to the literal sense. Many of our own people have eloquently declaimed in the churches about this tragedy of wretched Herod and his accomplices who were involved with him. Therefore, in this treatise, a few things out of many should suffice for the reader.

“And his disciples came,” he says, “and took his body and buried it, and they came and announced it to Jesus.”

Here we must understand that those who took him were no less Christ’s disciples than John’s, because those who had previously belonged to John had already become Christ’s.

Yet John’s honor is preserved. In him so many mysteries were fulfilled that, in his severed head, we see the Jews remaining without Christ even to this day, although he is the head of all the prophets.

When Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a deserted place by himself.

When the death of the Baptist was announced to him, he withdrew again to his customary refuge—not, as some have thought, out of fear of death, but for three reasons.

First, to spare his enemies, lest they add murder to murder; second, to postpone his own death until the day of Passover, on which, because of the mystery, the lamb was always sacrificed; finally, he withdrew in order to provide us with an example of avoiding rashness, because not everyone perseveres with the same steadfastness when placed amid torments with which they sometimes offer themselves to be tortured.

Hence it was also said above: “When they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. X, 23).

The evangelist also says elegantly not that he “fled” to a deserted place, but that he “withdrew,” to show that he avoided his persecutors for a time rather than feared them.

But after the head of the prophet had been cut off by the Jews and by the king of the Jews, and prophecy had lost its head, tongue, and voice among the Jews, Jesus passed over to the desert and to the place of the Church, which previously had had neither husband nor head.

When he says that after John’s beheading he withdrew in a boat and went into the desert, the narrative is continuous. It therefore appears that after these things the report about Jesus was heard, and the events narrated above took place.

He may also have withdrawn for this reason: to test the faith of believers. And therefore it follows that the crowds followed him on foot. They did not come on animals or in various vehicles; rather, the evangelist indicates the hardship of the journey through the labor of their own feet, in order to show the ardor of their minds.

Before he came into the solitudes of the Gentiles, he was worshiped by one people alone. But after the Lord came to the Gentiles as into a desert, many crowds followed him.

Therefore this testimony is placed before the following miracle, because, once the head had been cut off from the Law, he immediately withdrew from the Jews and climbed into a boat—that is, into that primitive Church—and went into a deserted place, as I have said, because they did not possess knowledge of the teaching.

They came on foot because they were humble and did not come with the pomp of the age. The Lord had compassion on them, healing their souls. They had come to him from the cities—that is, from various sects—and he cured them, because when faith is complete, it immediately receives the reward of salvation.

Hence it is said:

“And when Jesus had gone out, he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, and he healed their sick.”

You see that spiritual mysteries are always disclosed in the Gospel’s words. Therefore it says that Jesus “went out”: this signifies that the crowds had the desire to come to him, but did not have the strength to reach him. For this reason the Savior goes out from the place and comes to meet them, just as we read that he ran to meet the repentant prodigal son.

When he saw them, he had compassion on them and healed every sickness, so that complete faith might immediately receive the rewards of salvation.

When evening had come, the disciples approached him, saying, etc. No one is able to examine all the mysteries of the Gospel with complete thoroughness, because everything is full of mysteries; and concerning individual passages, as we have often said, one thing is spoken about places, another about times, another about the action and its causes, and also about sentences joined together. He therefore withdraws from Judea and comes into a deserted place, as we have already said, and Jesus goes out to meet them and has compassion on them; and he does this not in the morning, not as the day was advancing, not at midday, but in the evening, when the sun of righteousness had set.

[Col. 0517A] But Jesus said to them, “They do not need to go away; you give them something to eat.” Yet it remains to ask how the disciples approached Jesus, according to Matthew and the other two evangelists, or how they could have said this—that he should dismiss them so that they might go away—when John describes Jesus as having first said to Philip: “Where shall we buy bread, so that these people may eat?” (John 6:5). From this it is rightly understood that after the disciples’ statement the Lord spoke to Philip: “Where shall we buy bread?” When they say that the place is deserted, this is shown, literally, by the fact that they were far from the cities. “And the hour,” he says, “has already passed”—that is, the hour for eating. Or “hour” is used for the whole day, because the day had already passed.

Matthew, moreover, says that they should buy food for themselves, as though he were speaking about the crowds. Mark, however, relates [Col. 0517B] that the apostles said this on their own behalf: “Let us go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread” (Mark 6:37). Concerning this passage John says: “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for them” (John 6:7). We must understand here that everything said by the individual evangelists is true, and that none of them contradicts another’s account by his own words. John, for example, does not contradict the others when he says that the Lord questioned Philip, although the other disciples had already said to him what the other evangelists relate. Rather, it is shown that after the disciples’ words the Lord said to Philip: “Where shall we buy bread?” Likewise, Andrew is said to have said: “There is one boy here who has five loaves.” Others said: “We have nothing here except five loaves.” No one should doubt that both statements were made.

Thus, reader, [Col. 0517C] throughout the harmony of the evangelists you will find that they differ in no matter of substance: “They do not need to go away,” he says; “you give them something to eat.” It is as though he were saying: They do not need to seek and buy different food and unfamiliar loaves for themselves, since they have with them the heavenly bread. “You give them something to eat.” He urges the apostles to break the bread and to exercise care according to their own ability, so that, when they testify that they do not possess it, the power and greatness of the sign might become more evident to everyone.

Therefore, I ask that each person recall what I have often urged him to keep in mind, especially in this miracle: although the things performed by the Lord and Savior are wonderful, those prefigured in them appear far more wonderful, since they are expressed so clearly that no one can doubt that all these things were divinely prepared for this purpose. Accordingly, [Col. 0517D] consider what was done and how it was done, and in all these matters attend to the persons, the effects of the causes, and the individual causes, as well as the numbers and the modes, the places and the times, and the other details that would take too long to enumerate. For the things that occurred, as I have said, point far beyond the function of their immediate performance to the gift of our salvation. Therefore these things did not happen by chance or according to the event itself, but according to the divine dispensation.

When the disciples were questioned, they said: “We have nothing except five loaves.” Another said: “There is one boy here who has five loaves.” John testifies that Andrew said this. But none of these details is without mystery. For although Moses is to be understood through this boy, as our teachers relate, because the five books of the Old Testament are called his, nevertheless [Col. 0518A] the law was the same for all the apostles, because it was given to all of them, so that whoever does what it commands may live by it.

Especially because, before the Lord’s Passion and the flashing forth of the Gospel, the apostles had nothing but five loaves, and those loaves were barley, because the law of Moses, divided into five books, [Col. 0518A] was tightly bound by an excessive adherence to chaff. And the two fish—according to others, the two fish that moved about in salt pools, in waters, and in the waves of the sea—are understood as the two books that remain after the five, namely Joshua and Judges, since they too contain great mysteries according to their mystical meanings. [Col. 0518B] Others have said that the fish are the sayings of the prophets and the preaching of John.

But we, together with certain others, have interpreted the two as Moses and Aaron, through whom kingship and priesthood were represented. By their seasoning the people were fed as they went out of Egypt through the desert, and in the future the people are governed by these two persons. For just as the life of the Jews was contained in the five books mentioned above as loaves, so it was governed by the royal and priestly offices represented by the two fish.

Yet these two persons prefigured our Lord: he bore both offices, and fulfilled them alone not figuratively but in reality. For our King is the Lord Jesus Christ, who showed us an example of fighting and conquering. Thus, with him as our leader, we are freed from the burdens and labors of this pilgrimage, as from Egypt; [Col. 0518C] and the sins pursuing us are overwhelmed as we escape through the sacrament of baptism.

For he is our priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. He offered himself as a holocaust for our sins and entrusted to us the celebration of the likeness of his sacrifice in remembrance of his Passion, so that we may now be seen, throughout the world in the Church of Christ, to offer that which he offered to God in Melchizedek. The genealogy of Christ also appears to have been woven through these two persons. Matthew, descending from Abraham to Christ, traces it through the royal person; Luke, ascending from Christ to Adam and to God, inserted it through the priestly lineage. This prophecy concerning Christ lay hidden in these five books. Therefore these two fish alone are found and held together with the five loaves.

[Col. 0518D] And when he had ordered the crowd to recline on the grass, taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, blessed them, broke them, and gave them to his disciples. Listen to the order of the miracle—or rather, not only of the miracle but also of the parable—so that faith might be strengthened by the miracle and the soul nourished by the mystery, because the truth is not concealed in the event, while the parable of the event is proclaimed as greater and deeper in the sacrament.

He therefore commands them to recline on the grass, according to another evangelist, because there was much grass in the place. In accordance with the custom of those dining, he commands them to sit upon what they had trodden underfoot and upon all its flowers, because “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isaiah 40:6), and all its pleasures are like withered grass.

[Col. 0519A] But that Jewish crowd reclined on grass because it had received the Old Testament, in which a temporal kingdom and a temporal Jerusalem were promised to them. It is therefore clear that they had been placed in a carnal hope, whose glory blossomed like grass and whose splendor was like the flower of grass. Yet each of them was not merely lying on the ground, but was supported by the law and, as by the grass of the earth—that is, by the fruits of his works—was cushioned beneath.

Hence it is rightly said that the Lord fed them on the mountain. Although through the letter of the law they climbed for a time toward higher things, because they were still carnal, as I have said, they were fed with barley and not with wheat. [Col. 0519B] Thus barley signified the law of the Old Testament, just as wheat—of which the Gospel elsewhere shows that there were seven loaves—signified the law of the holy Gospel.

These are the two Testaments, that is, the two laws, from which the whole human race is nourished at present, while this age is passing, through the blessing of God our Savior Jesus Christ. Therefore he used this second miracle, neither more nor less, to show himself also in this deed as the one who had established two laws for the sake of our nourishment, from which every faithful soul is daily fed and refreshed.

But because that earlier people was still carnal, such a law was given to it as concealed the life-giving nourishment of souls beneath bodily sacraments. And just as the marrow of barley is covered by extremely tenacious chaff, so that same law, through its carnal institutions, was given to a carnal people not yet stripped of carnal desires; and that desire clung to their hearts like barley chaff.

[Col. 0519C] Therefore they are condemned by the prophet as uncircumcised in heart, because they could not be purified by any scourges of tribulation or pressures of threshing, so that, with their spiritual understanding opened, they might lay aside their carnal coverings. In the same way, barley is not stripped of its chaff-covering by the threshing of the threshing floor, even though the ears are broken.

For this reason the Lord then provided and prepared only these five loaves for himself among that entire people, so that from them he might teach what he would do with the five books in his own time. He took them, blessed them, broke them, and gave them to his disciples. [Col. 0519D] Otherwise, if he himself had not taken them in his hands, so that they might be fulfilled by his work, they would have been without the fruit of salvation and without life. And if he had not blessed them in himself, in whom all spiritual blessing exists, those who were under that law would have remained under a curse. And if he had not broken them, they would have nourished no one unto salvation.

“And he gave them,” it says, “to his disciples; and the disciples presented them to the crowd.” For through them the gifts of divine grace were to be distributed to the peoples.

Then the crowd of the people is fed, and five thousand men, apart from children and women, are abundantly filled from the five loaves and the two fish. The number five therefore corresponds on both sides to the carnal people, who scarcely used their five carnal senses properly, although many were devoted to them. Therefore [Col. 0520A] how pointedly the Lord seems to signify this when he says: “They do not need to go away to buy elsewhere or from someone else; you give them something to eat.” For they were kept under the law, in which there was food for perfect understanding, if it were broken up and explained by the Lord and handed over to the disciples.

The Wisdom of God the Father knew everything: what he had given to each person and what he was going to do. Therefore he does not ask, “How many loaves do you have?” out of ignorance, but because of the mystery. According to Mark, he also asks how many loaves they had, in order to expose the fact that they did not understand the mystery that was already evident in what had been given and entrusted to them, and that both they and the whole crowd bore under the yoke.

[Col. 0520B] When these loaves had been blessed and broken, they increased. The five are not multiplied numerically into a greater number; rather, fragments follow upon fragments, and in the breaking they continually elude those who break them through their multiplication. The substance of the bread therefore grows—I do not know whether in measure, or in place, or in the hands of those taking it, or in the mouths of those eating it.

One thing, however, I affirm: in Christ’s hands was the source of increase, just as it is the nature of a spring to flow, of grapes to be present on vines, and of wines to be poured out; and just as all the riches of the world flow in various directions in a certain yearly course. For the author of this universe is the source of such an increase of bread.

Everyone marvels at what is rare, but no one marvels at what has become cheap through habitual use, because it happens every day. In the visible work, the demonstration of invisible things is carried out: the power of the one acting surpasses all nature, the reasoning of the power exceeds the understanding of the deed, and only wonder at the power remains.

[Col. 0520C] But before these things happened, he looked up to heaven and gave an example, so that we should always direct the eyes of our minds toward the Father and, following his example, bless food and all things that come from God. For every blessing through him is either an increase of things or their sanctification, so that, if it is considered attentively, the blessing of things reaches as far as wonder, while wonder reaches as far as the measure of the underlying cause.

For the broken loaves, together with the fish, are sometimes afterward heaped up with increase, so that as many thousands of people as there are may be filled with bread, apart from the children and women—as is more generally believed—whose number, just as it has no limit, so also has no limit in the amount required to fill them.

[Col. 0520D] Moreover, the splendor of grace is increased, so that twelve baskets are filled according to the number of the apostles. Thus measure is made equal to number, and number obeys the measure of the mystery, so that reason, enclosed within its own limits, may encourage the restraints of divine power toward the condition of the effects that follow, since the work performed surpasses human understanding.

And although many things frequently occur that speech, once conceived by the senses, cannot explain, in these matters the subtlety of perception itself is overcome. The mind is struck with astonishment at the contemplation of the thing because of the magnificence of the difficulty and the miracle of the invisible work, to such an extent that it is not sufficient either to think what it perceives or to express in words what it understands.

[Col. 0521A] Yet no one among those whom heavenly grace fed was permitted to remain hungry. And twelve baskets of leftover fragments were taken up. Perhaps, apart from the aforesaid ineffable mystery, the fragments were collected so that, over the course of time, they might demonstrate to the faith of believers that the loaves had been real and not an apparition.

Although, because of the difficulty of the event, many immediately ask where the twelve baskets in which the fragments were gathered could have been found in the desert, as though they could not have been brought from the neighboring villages by the same power by which the loaves had first been prepared—especially since, according to Luke, they were in a deserted place near Bethsaida. The baskets brought there were filled with the fragments and with ineffable power, although the thing itself and the substance itself could never have filled them.

Five thousand were satisfied from five loaves, together with the mystery of eternal salvation and perpetual sweetness. “Apart from the women,” he says, “and the children.” [Col. 0521B] These seem to me to signify that within the people of the Old Testament there were some so weak in fulfilling the righteousness that is according to the law—righteousness in which the Apostle says that he lived without reproach—and others who could easily be led astray into the worship of idols.

These two classes, namely weakness and error, are represented under the names of women and children. The female sex is weak for actions, and childhood is easily inclined to play. What is more like childish play than the worship of idols? The Apostle also referred this kind of superstition to that comparison when he said: “Let us not serve idols, as some of them did, as it is written: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (1 Corinthians 10:7).

[Col. 0521C] Those like women were people who, in the labors of expectation, while waiting until they should come to God’s promises, did not persevere manfully but tested God. They were like the children who sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play. Such people also exist in the New Testament: they cannot attain mature manhood, either because of weakness of strength or because of fickleness of mind. They are rightly compared at times with women and children.

Therefore, neither in the Old Testament nor in the New are such people admitted to the number, whether in military matters or in any affairs of importance. Thus in the Book of Numbers, whenever the priest, the Levites, the army, or crowds of combatants are described, servants, women, children, and the ignoble common people are omitted from the count.

[Col. 0521D] Yet they were still among the people. Therefore, as David sings to the Lord in the psalm: “You open your hand, and you fill every living creature with blessing” (Psalm 144:16). He filled them with heavenly gifts, and they too are satisfied every day, each according to the capacity of his understanding and the measure of his faith.

The apostles, moreover, to whom he gave all these things into their hands, received the mysteries first revealed to them. For this reason they preached the Gospel of eternal life to everyone, and they took up twelve baskets of fragments, which the whole crowd could not contain. Each apostle had his own basket, because all the mysteries of heavenly life had been disclosed to them.

[Col. 0522A] But wretched Judas lost what he took up, because it had been reserved not for himself but for another. Hence blessed Peter sought a decision by lot from the Lord; although both men were good, he set them before the Lord so that the one who was to be chosen might be chosen not by a human being but by God, with whom these things had been laid up, and who could receive what had been prepared and preserved by divine privilege for the apostles alone.

Therefore no saint dared to claim such honor for himself, because both a mystical number and a sacred order are present in these things, as well as a distinction of honor granted by the Lord only to those whose hearts are so filled with virtues and divine wisdom that they stored within themselves and left to their successors all that the diners could not take from the divine feast, and preserved it for them.

Thus, immediately after the Lord’s Passion, five thousand were filled with faith and imbued with the Lord’s sacraments, corresponding to the number prefigured in this meal, even if the figure itself is believed to be the truth.

[Col. 0522B] Let these few remarks about this first sacramental feeding suffice, so that when we come to the second, in which a new order is formed, we may, with the Lord’s inspiration, discuss these matters more fully. In the meantime, we are forming the infancy of those who are learning, so that later, with the syllables distinguished, we may give forth a clear confession concerning these things. For now, as we are about to sail among saving waves, let us prepare our vessels.

Indeed, let us ask with the apostle Peter that he himself command us to come to him upon the waters, lest, while sailing with the Word, we sink in faith, and so that we may be able to find the shining pearl hidden in the depths. Otherwise we might seem, now that we have learned to do so, to be playing idly among tranquil fruits.

“And immediately,” he says, “he ordered the disciples to get into the boat and go ahead of him across the strait, until he dismissed the crowds.” And after dismissing the crowd, he went up the mountain alone to pray. In other copies, however, it is not “he ordered” but “he compelled”: he compelled his disciples to get into the boat and go ahead of him across the strait.

This word suggests that they withdrew from the Lord unwillingly, because, out of love for their most compassionate teacher, they could not bear to be separated from his presence even for a moment, nor did they wish to be parted from him.

But what he says now seems very contradictory: after dismissing the crowds, he went up the mountain alone to pray, whereas John, as I stated above, implies that the Lord fed the crowds on the mountain. If he fed them on the mountain, and now, after dismissing the crowds, went up the mountain, how does he say that he went up the mountain on which he had been when he satisfied them with bread?

From this it plainly appears that he descended from the mountain on which he had previously been to the lower places to feed the crowd, because they were unable to climb to the heights. [Col. 0522D] From that lower place, after dismissing the crowds, he again went up the mountain, so that the crowds would not seize him, since they wanted to make him king.

For this reason John did not say that he ascended, but that he “fled to the mountain alone to pray” (John 6:5). Here he shows that, for the sake of prayer, we must not only withdraw alone but also flee passing and earthly honors, so that we may devote ourselves to God alone in contemplation—that is, on the mountain. For the contemplative life is always more removed and richer in its fruits; concerning it the Lord says: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42).

[Col. 0523A] It should be noted that Matthew says the Lord dismissed the disciples first and then went up the mountain to pray. John, however, says that he first fled to the mountain and then dismissed the disciples. From this it appears that John, later recalling what had happened earlier, mentioned what he had omitted, just as all the evangelists often return to things they had forgotten and mention them not in their literal chronological place but for some other reason.

When he says that he went up alone, it is clear that Peter, James, and John were not with him. If they had been, since they perhaps saw the glory of his transfiguration, they would have gone up with him. They were therefore mentioned beforehand for the sake of the mystery: he prayed alone for all, just as he alone died for all in order to redeem all.

Thus it is said:

[Col. 0523B] “When evening had come, he was there alone.” This makes clear to everyone that his prayer is the salvation of all. It should also be noted that he is said to have been alone when evening had come. Evening signifies the end of the age, when he came alone for the salvation of all.

Above, too, it is said that the hour had already passed, because, as the Apostle says, “It is the last hour” (1 John 2:18), and it has already passed, because it flees like a shadow.

Do not be surprised that he went up alone to pray—alone and solitary. Yet although he was alone, you must not apply the fact that he prayed to the one who fed five thousand people from five loaves, apart from children and women, nor to the one who walked firmly on his feet over the waves of the sea, but to the one who, after hearing of John’s death, withdrew into a deserted place.

[Col. 0523C] I do not say this, brothers, in order to divide the person of the Lord into two, but so that the Savior’s twofold operation may be considered throughout the entire Gospel in the one and same person, the mediator between God and human beings. For just as God and human were in him, since “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), so too there was an operation of divinity and an operation of humanity.

There is indeed a twofold operation, but one and the same Christ performed all these things. He is the one who hungered and thirsted; he is the one who fed so many people from five loaves; he is the one who, wearied from the journey, sat down; he is the one who also walked on foot over the sea. One of these operations is plainly that of his humanity, while the other is that of his divinity.

Unless a prudent reader distinguishes and understands these operations in a catholic manner, he may stray from the catholic faith as far as he is blinded by the darkness of confusion.

[Col. 0523D] “But the boat was being battered by the waves in the middle of the sea.” Therefore the apostles had earlier withdrawn from the Lord unwillingly and reluctantly, lest, with him absent, they should suffer shipwreck. For they knew that without him they would be troubled, just as the Church, whenever she is presently abandoned by Christ, is battered by waves and driven by winds.

That entire peril of the boat was a figure of the present time. Meanwhile, while the Lord lingered on the summit of the mountain, a contrary wind immediately arose, the sea was disturbed, and the Church was endangered. The threatened shipwreck continues as long as Jesus remains away and does not come to help.

[Col. 0524A] Therefore he promised that he would be with his own until the present age comes to an end: “I am with you,” he says, “all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Otherwise, without him, the Church is endangered and sinks.

Thus, whenever she is struck by various waves and driven by gusts of wind, so that she seems about to sink, the Savior must be invoked. We must trust that he is nowhere and never absent in his majesty, even though he dwells on high in heaven. Hence it is said that, while they were laboring at the oars:

“In the fourth watch of the night he came, walking upon the sea.”

When he says “in the fourth watch of the night,” he shows that they had been endangered and battered by the waves throughout the entire night. For, according to military watches, there are four watches and twelve hours; each watch contains three hours.

[Col. 0524B] Therefore, when he says that Jesus came in the fourth watch, he indicates the end of night and the beginning of dawn, as the darkness grows thin. In a few words he depicts the whole period from the time when the Savior returned to the Father, alone as high priest interceding for us until the end of the age, when he will come again. Then, when all things have been trodden underfoot, the darkness will be driven away by his light, the streams and the force of the winds will cease, because God is now walking where no trace of human power can be found, where the ordinary manner of walking fails.

From this single event miracles are heaped together from every side. Custom does not account for the sign, just as its uniqueness admits no example; rather, divine power works the mystery and the miracle together: the miracle in the deed, and the mystery in the sacrament of its prefiguration.

[Col. 0524C] Nature does not possess this; human ingenuity and the philosophy of the world cannot grasp it. Therefore the power belongs to the author, not to human nature, so that divinity and humanity may be declared in one and the same human being.

Divinity is shown in the fact that he is perceived as exceeding humanity; humanity is shown because the man himself is seen upon the waves. This work is plainly that of the heavenly power, because flesh cannot experience it, nor can the human mind understand how something can occur that neither nature permits: that something heavy should walk upon the water and that liquid should support a weight, although neither nature allows it.

In the same way, no human reasoning proves that the loaves grew to the extent described, and no understanding detects how it happened—unless you choose to imagine either that he lightened the body so that it was an apparition, or that he made the waters thicker and congealed, so that human flesh could walk over them with dry footing.

[Col. 0524D] That too would be a marvel if reason admitted it. But now no one explains the cause of the deed, no human sense receives it, no human mind grasps it, and no human being can say how it could have happened so freely—except the one to whom all power is subject whenever he wills, so that his twofold operation may be demonstrated, as we have said.

For it is wholly an act of divinity that he walks contrary to human nature upon the waters, and an act of humanity that he appears visibly in the form of a servant and in true flesh.

Therefore, when they saw him walking upon the sea, they were troubled and said, “It is a phantom.” Thus they had already proved that he was truly the human Christ, and for that reason they were now disturbed, thinking that they were seeing something contrary to his nature. Otherwise, if, according to Marcion and Mani, our Lord was not born of the Virgin Mary but appeared as a phantom, how could the apostles now fear and be troubled lest they should see a phantom? They cried out through fear. For a confused voice and an uncertain cry are signs of great fear.

Yet their fear is the strength of our understanding, since concerning Christ they feel nothing without examination, nothing that they do not investigate, and they understand in him nothing of either humanity or divinity without due consideration. They establish everything so fully that thereafter no one should doubt, no one lose confidence, no one despair, and no one collapse through unbelief concerning Christ.

But divine mercy quickly comes to the aid of those who seek devoutly and do not doubt impiously. While they were crying out through fear and, because of the miracle, were uncertain how to receive in faith the God and man in whom they had believed, he immediately said to them, “Take courage, and be confident: I am he.” Thus the physician came to the place where the first difficulty lay. For, according to the apostle, the one who loses confidence and hesitates is like a wave of the sea (James 1:6).

“I am he,” he said, and he did not add what or who he was, because from a voice so familiar to them they could understand who was speaking to them through the darkness or twilight of night.
