They knew that this was his most familiar expression, and therefore he said, “I am he.” It was as though he were plainly saying, “I am the one who is; I do not change, as you think, into a phantom.” There is no doubt that they retained in their minds the very Being whom they knew had once spoken to Moses: “I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3:13).

When Peter heard this voice—“I am he”—he answered correspondingly, saying, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” For he perceived that in the words “I am he” was the one whose being is always essentially identical. Therefore he said, “If it is you,” as though he were saying: “If you are the one who is always one and the same with the Father, your command is the manifestation of power, since you are omnipotent.”

Do not be surprised, reader, that he asks with faith and yet doubts. He doubts not as an unbeliever but as a cautious and seasoned examiner, lest he should rashly fall into ruin. He invokes the one whose essence is truth, and he doubts nothing concerning his power or might.

Otherwise, to attribute any unbelief to the apostle Peter, as though he were the foundation of the Church, is exceedingly rash. To him, according to the merits of his faith, the power of binding and loosing was assigned. Who, then, is found so suitable for fear of God and love, if guilt is imputed to this man—especially when the Lord himself bore witness on his behalf?

It is therefore not surprising that many who are uninstructed, because they do not understand the reason for what happened, fall into snares of offense and believe that true faith was absent from the words spoken to him: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” Such people fail to consider the greatness of the faith expressed in the words, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” Certainly, the one who says, “Command me,” believes in the power to command.

Great, then, was this act of faith: with a daring leap and fearless descent from the boat, he entrusted himself to the deepest element and confidently entered upon a path unfamiliar to human feet. He did not fear that the weight of a human body would be extremely heavy or that the liquid wave of the sea would not support a solid step. He had conceived such confidence in the word of God that, when Christ said, “Come,” he believed the unstable surface would be made firm beneath his feet, as though solid earth lay beneath him.

For the fact that, out of all who remained in the boat, Peter alone dared to answer and asked to be commanded to come to the Lord upon the waters was a sign of the ardor of love, the strength of faith, and a foreknowledge of what was to come. Thus also, in the Passion, he displayed a greater expression of love than the others, always clinging to the footsteps of the most merciful Redeemer, although the timidity of his future denial foreshadowed the weakness of the coming temptation.

For this reason, although he had dared to walk, he was sinking because of the weakness of the flesh, just as eventually he was compelled by necessity to deny him, even to the fear of death. No mortal can be compared with the footsteps of the Lord. When the Lord journeyed upon the sea, the element wonderfully obeyed his feet: the sea neither withdrew from him nor failed to carry the revered soles of the Lord.

It is therefore not surprising that the nature of the waters served him, by whose ordering all things were perfected. Accordingly, it made itself passable beneath him, as was fitting for the Lord, while serving Peter according to the command of the one who gave the order, in the manner of a servant.

Yet reason required, in view of human frailty, that the wind should frighten Peter and the waves disturb him by their collisions, lest there appear to be no distinction between God and man. Otherwise, if they had seen Peter doing here what Christ had done by his own power, there would have been no small uncertainty among human beings. Nor would the honor due to God have been rendered, since what was accomplished by God would not have seemed wondrous if it had also been accomplished by a human being.

Moreover, by this power Christ indicates that he alone is the one who by his own strength treads down and restrains all the haughtiness of the present age and all its waves. Therefore it had to be shown in Peter, as one individual and unique example, what he does in all who seek his help while the present age is passing.

For in this age we are placed as though upon a sea, in which we daily endure the storms and most violent assaults of spiritual wickedness, continually striving with every care to avoid shipwreck. This is especially to be feared when we are lifted above ourselves by virtues and miracles. Therefore blessed Paul is given a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan (2 Corinthians 12:7), just as now the wind of temptation is given to Peter, so that strength may be perfected in weakness.

For it is better for us to be delivered by calling upon the Lord than, through concealment and failure to pray—or rather, through pride—to incur the danger of death. Human presumption would claim far too much license for itself if it began to share power with God.

For this reason it rightly seemed that Peter, in whom the unity of all the apostles is commended, was overwhelmed by excessive fear in a carefully ordered way, so that we might know that we ought to attribute nothing to our own actions, but ascribe everything we accomplish rightly to God and invoke God’s help in all things.

Nevertheless, when Peter was trembling, the Lord did not grant him the power to reach him freely, although he had first commanded him to come. Instead, he stretched out his hand, grasped him, and supported him. As I briefly indicated above, this was a typological order: the right hand of God was to be exalted from the waves, for it accomplishes strength in all things. The power to tread upon the movements and storms of the age and to rescue everyone from the pressure of temptations belongs to the Lord alone.

For he alone was to suffer for all; he himself took away the sins of all and admitted no associate or partner into this work. Whatever he granted to the whole human race came from him alone. Thus, although he himself was the one and unique redemption of all, he first redeemed Peter and trod everything beneath his feet. Finally, Peter himself, raised up by God’s help, would meet martyrdom—not unworthy to approach, since he preceded the others in faith, but instructed and glorified through the testing and multiplication of his strength, so that he might precede the others.

Therefore, however Peter may have fallen, whether because of the mystery or because of weakness, it nevertheless remains certain that his body was real. If he, being merely a true human being, was able to walk with upright step upon the waters, how much more was the one who was God and man—not a phantom but the truth—he who in both natures was none other than the true Jesus Christ.

Therefore let no one be weakened concerning Christ’s power in company with heretics; let no one fabricate for himself a falsehood about the reality of the flesh, claiming that it had no weight; and let no one doubt Christ’s divinity. “You of little faith,” he said, “why did you doubt?”

But if this is rightly said to Peter, whose faith, so to speak, shone forth as incomparable among the others, what do you think will be said about us, who are shown to possess not even a small portion of this faith? He was permitted to be tested for a short time so that his faith might be increased through weakness and the greater excellence of Christ’s power might be proclaimed through his assistance.

No one, therefore, can call Peter’s faith small, since he surpasses everyone everywhere in faith. Yet no one can deny that it was limited, since the Lord rebuked him by calling him “of little faith.” Still, the faith compared with a mustard seed is the faith of all the apostles; it appears small because it is compared with the size of a tiny seed.

What, then, shall we say? Is that Canaanite woman believed to have had greater faith than Peter, to whom it was said, “O woman, great is your faith” (Matthew 15:28)? I believe that no one would dare to assert this. We must therefore seek the proper manner of understanding how the faith of one who is proclaimed to be the most ardent in all things, both in faith and in love, can be called small.

When the disciples were asked who they said Jesus was, he confessed before them all: “You are the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16). Thus, in all other passages as well, you will always find him superior in faith.

Indeed, such faith—so great that it is rightly considered great in comparison with the magnitude of the things in which faith is placed—is, in my judgment, small in comparison with their greatness. For “faith is the proof of things hoped for, of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1), and every proof is less than the things of which it is the proof.

Therefore Peter’s faith is not improperly rebuked as small in comparison with the immense majesty of God, in whom faith is placed—especially since through such experiences Peter’s faith had to grow and be nourished until it reached completion. Thus, although Peter sometimes errs through the ardor of his great faith, he is nevertheless found more fervent in all things, because in him is the pattern of all, in whom the unity of the Church is commended.

And when he had entered the boat, the wind ceased. Then those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying, “Truly you are the Son of God.”

In this miracle, as I briefly showed above, the whole faith and order of the Church are represented. Throughout the period until the end of the age, when he returns, the Church is endangered by many waves. Jesus, walking upon the waves of the sea, is thought by very many to be a phantom.

For this reason he is rightly said also to have come in the fourth watch of the night. Above we showed that this portion of the night signifies its end. In this watch, when Christ comes because of the temptations of Antichrist, he will find the Church exceedingly unsteady and shipwrecked, with winds blowing from every direction.

It is called the fourth watch because the first was the watch of the Law, in which the Law was given; the second, that of the prophets; the third, that of the Lord’s own coming; and the fourth, that of his return, when he will come in glory, having trampled down every movement of the winds. Then he will find the Church exhausted and greatly wearied by the assaults of Antichrist.

During that temptation, Christ’s Church, harassed by anxious waves, will be exceedingly troubled by every new form of temptation, so that it will even be said to fear the Lord’s coming because of false images of things and deceptive fragments of lies intruding upon the eyes.

But the good Lord will immediately be present with his own and will enlighten them with a voice of consolation, so that they may have confidence and drive away fear. Without doubt he will inspire faith in their hearts and will say, “I am he,” lest they be led astray by the errors of Antichrist.

His entering the boat signifies this: at his coming he will immediately cause the wind to cease, and the sea will rest from the fury of temptation; there will be great peace and tranquility. Thereafter, when eternal brightness has shone forth and he himself has appeared openly, all will say in wonder, “He truly is the Son of God.”

For the confession of all will then be complete and public, when he will no longer be seen partially but wholly, face to face, according to the Apostle, when that which is perfect has come. Then the whole Church of the saints will see the Son of God—not in bodily humility but in the brightness and glory that he has with the Father—and will worship him forever and ever.

But now, while waves rise on every side and storms rage, although the truth already shines forth more clearly than light itself, many—even among ecclesiastical people, which is worse—still think that Jesus was a phantom. They believe either that he did not possess a true body or that, if he did possess one, he was not the true or proper Son of God.

But the catholic faith confesses both: that he is the proper and true Son of God, as the apostles confessed in this passage, along with those who were with them in the boat—“You are truly the Son of God”—and that he possessed a true body, as catholic teaching proclaims. As I have said, his body had the weight of bodily heaviness without sin, and a bodily burden; and with that weight and bodily burden he walked upon the waters without his feet being immersed.

The distinguished Dionysius, among the other ecclesiastical teachers, expressly argued this point in his works *On the Divine Names* and left it written for us; other teachers likewise confirmed it. For among other things he writes:

“We do not know how he was formed from virginal blood by another law, contrary to the natural one, nor how, with feet not immersed, possessing bodily weight and a material burden, he walked upon a pure and unstable substance.”

Here the aforementioned teacher shows that he walked in this manner, and the Gospel proves it: his body was nothing other than a true body, and the waters were nothing other than real, liquid waters flowing past. The whole deed was the work of divinity, while the reality of humanity appeared.

I have mentioned these matters, though briefly, because many people are still foolishly mistaken about them and attempt to explain what neither the truth permits nor they themselves understand. Therefore, I ask that no one consider this digression and return concerning such exceptional matters too lengthy, since in them the very same truth is proclaimed as wondrous and ineffable.

Moreover, the significance of these events is found to be more complex in its multiplicity and broader in its mysteries than the miracle of the event itself. Whatever he now accomplishes in time was prefigured in the miracle.

Therefore those who were in the boat and reached the shore confess and worship him as truly the Son of God, believing him to reign with the Father in the unity of divinity.

And when they had crossed over, he says, they came to the land of Gennesaret. Gennesaret is a region, from which the lake is also called the Lake of Gennesaret in some places. It is called Gennesaret because it generates winds for itself. From there, as though from the shipwreck of persecution, the most merciful Jesus brings the Church’s boat to shore, so that he may make it rest in a most tranquil harbor.

It should be noted that after the five thousand men who ate and were satisfied, and through the many intervening events that have been related up to this point, the meaning is the same throughout. For when the times of the Law had ended and five thousand men from Israel had been placed in the Church, while Jesus prayed alone on the mountain where he is with the Father and trod upon the waves, the disciples struggled at the oars.

Meanwhile, whenever the Savior looked upon them and entered the boat, he calmed the winds and restored tranquility. Thus, from those five thousand whom he first refreshed with loaves, he himself, now saved and satisfied through faith from the Law, came to meet the many peoples of believers. Thereafter, from among his own, he presents the weak and sick to God for healing, because they recognize him as Savior.

Therefore the Gospel says:

“And when the men of that place had recognized him, they sent word throughout the whole region.”

They recognized him more by report than by sight, although, because of the greatness of the signs he performed, his face was already known to many. But all this faith and knowledge arose from the power and efficacy of his miracles, or from the grace of his countenance, just as with us, who have never seen him in the flesh.

Therefore let your prudence consider how precisely he says: “When the men of that place had recognized him, they sent word throughout the whole region and brought to him all who were ill.” So also the Church does now. They ask him to let them touch the fringe of his garment. Here the remarkable faith of the people of Gennesaret and of the Church is proclaimed: the Church is not content merely with the healing of its own members but sends word to all, so that they may come and be healed.

Thus Gennesaret is appropriately interpreted as “the beginning of origin,” because through that primitive Church, which at the beginning saw him by faith and understanding, in which Christ arose and from which the apostles were born, he became known and believed throughout the world. That Church itself sent word throughout the whole world, so that Christ might be proclaimed everywhere and all might be healed of their sins and illnesses.

“And they begged him,” he says, “to let them touch even the fringe of his garment.” The fringe, as we all know, is part of a garment and hangs from it. In the same way, the power of the Holy Spirit proceeds from our Lord Jesus Christ. Given to the apostles, who themselves proceed from the same body of Christ, it supplies salvation to those who are able to touch them.

For this healing does not come from an apostle or from any saint, but from the fringe—that is, from the grace that is in the apostle or in the saint. The woman who suffered from the flow of blood had touched this fringe, because she had reached Christ’s grace; therefore she was healed of her discharge.

For this reason no priest enters the sanctuary worthily without fringes, because whoever approaches in order to minister without the grace of the Holy Spirit shows himself empty and intrusive rather than dutiful and worthy.

“And all who touched him,” he says, “were saved.” No one is excluded from eternal salvation who has touched the grace of God, because whoever possesses one of its gifts will possess them all. And, “Whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all” (James 2:10).

From this it is evident that those who are still unwell and sick in mind are so because they do not touch the fringe of his garment. Whoever touches even one, in order to possess them all, is immediately saved and is no longer sick.

**(Chapter 15.)** Then the scribes and Pharisees came to him from Jerusalem, saying: “Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders and not wash their hands when they eat bread?”

Wonderful was the foolishness of the Pharisees and scribes: they reproached the Son of God, who had given the divine Law, because he did not observe human traditions and precepts. For whatever was blamed in the disciples was maliciously turned into an accusation against the Master by the scribes and Pharisees who had come from Jerusalem.

But the evangelist rebukes them on two grounds: they were scribes and teachers of the Law who were plotting against him, and they had come from the holy place, the metropolis where they held the stronghold of divine authority and the teaching office of doctrine.

But the divine Teacher and herald of the Law, like lightning, often strikes them back with a terrifying clash and blunts them with the flash of his words. Thunderously he frightens them, corrects his own with saving instruction, and reforms them, as we marvel that he does here, when the Pharisees and scribes eagerly seek to disparage and rebuke his disciples.

I marvel that nothing was prophesied about him that he did not fulfill, and that he did nothing on earth that had not previously been announced. Because it had been foretold, “He shall judge in favor of the meek of the earth” (Isaiah 11:4), he fulfilled it here by rebuking and confuting the scribes and Pharisees on behalf of his apostles, who were exceedingly meek.

Yet when anyone hears this, let him not suppose that the Lord’s disciples, under the appearance of contempt for themselves, habitually ate with unkempt and unwashed hands, as though they were peasants—especially since they shared as guests at the Lord’s table. It is more reasonable to believe that they observed ordinary decency, since neither nature permits such behavior nor the affection of hospitality allows it.

Who would not immediately offer water for the hands of a visitor as an act of service? Or who would refuse this courtesy as an insult to the one who offered it? Especially since the Lord himself rebukes Simon, who had invited him to table: “You did not give me water for my hands” (Luke 7:44).

The Lord therefore wishes this to be done, as we are clearly taught that he required it. But the Pharisees were demanding from the Lord’s disciples not bodily cleanliness but the baptisms of their superstition, by which, as was the custom of some, they repeatedly washed at table. They did not know the one baptism by which the Lord was to wash and renew both body and soul, a baptism prepared not for the adornment of the skin but for the cleansing of the conscience.

For this reason the Prophet prayed, saying, “Wash me yet more from my iniquity” (Psalm 50:4).

The evangelist Mark makes these superstitions of the Jews clearer to us when he says: “The Pharisees and scribes do not eat unless they wash their hands repeatedly; and when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they have been baptized” (Mark 7:3–4). They also observed the baptism of cups, jugs, bronze vessels, beds, and many other things, according to the purification of the Jews.

They demanded this purification of the hands, which arose from superstition rather than from decency and daily custom, while they themselves were impure and unclean. Their tradition was such that the apostles rightly refused to imitate it superstitiously.

The Lord answered them:

“Why do you also transgress the commandment of God because of your tradition?”

See how freely the excellent Teacher responded, with all divine authority, wisdom, and the utmost propriety. He refutes and strikes down the false accusation with a true question, since it is wrong to neglect the commandment of God because of human traditions, even when those traditions are superfluous and empty.

It was as though the Savior were saying: “If you disregard God’s precepts or commandments because of human tradition, why do you rebuke my innocent disciples, who are fully conscious of their innocence, because they do not keep the institutions of your elders as though they were God’s commandments? Is it not a more serious crime to neglect God’s commandments than to omit superfluous human traditions?”

Thus the evil knot is dissolved by a very strong wedge. Thus the heavenly orator not only confirms his own deeds and those of his followers but also crushes and destroys the opposing deeds. He plainly shows that the relief of souls must always be pursued more than that of bodies.

For God said: “Honor your father and your mother. And whoever curses father or mother shall be put to death.”

“But you say: ‘Whoever says to his father or mother, “Whatever gift is from me will benefit you,” and does not honor his father or mother—’”

The brevity of expression frequently generates obscurity in the divine Scriptures and produces difficulty of understanding, as in this passage when it says, “Whatever gift is from me will benefit you.” For in sacred writings honor is preserved not so much through greetings and services rendered as through alms, gifts, presents, and offerings.

Thus Paul says, “Honor widows who are truly widows” (1 Timothy 5:3). Elsewhere he says that elders should receive double honor, “especially those who labor in the word of God” (ibid., 17). That honor is understood as a gift.

By this commandment we are also ordered not to muzzle the ox while it is threshing (1 Corinthians 9:9), since “the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Matthew 10:10).

Therefore, considering the weakness, age, or poverty of parents, the Lord had commanded that children honor their father and mother, even by providing the necessities of life, and minister to their parents.

The scribes and Pharisees, wishing to overturn this most provident law of God so that they might cloak impiety under the name of piety because of their own avarice and financial gain, taught wicked children that if anyone wished to dedicate to God, who is the true Father and Lord, whatever he owed and ought to have offered to his parents for their necessities, the Lord’s offering should be preferred to the gifts owed to the parents, and the offering should be irrevocable, so that the parents would no longer receive assistance in their distress.

Or else, if the parents saw things consecrated to God, they avoided touching them lest they incur the charge of sacrilege, and so they were consumed by poverty. Thus the offering of the children, under the pretext of the Temple and God, became a source of profit for the priests.

This wicked tradition of the Pharisees arose from another circumstance. Many people who had others bound to them by debts, and who did not wish to repay what had been entrusted to them, assigned the money to the priests so that the money, once collected, might serve the ministries of the Temple and the priests’ own needs.

They therefore taught people to say to their father or mother: “Whatever gift from me has been offered to God by vow benefits you, O father, because it is offered to God on your behalf.”

By these words they cunningly emptied the honor due to the father and caused people to transgress God’s commandments for the sake of their own greedy profits, refusing to consider what the Lord himself said: “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13).

The statement may also be understood in another way, so that this very brief expression can have the following sense: “The gift that comes from me will benefit you,” as though he were saying: “You compel children to say to their parents, ‘Whatever gift or offering I was going to dedicate to the Lord by vow, I am now using for your needs, and it benefits you, O father, or O mother.’”

Thus the parents, fearing to accept what they saw as dedicated to God at least by a vow of intention, were willing to lead a life of poverty rather than eat from what had been consecrated.

Father Augustine, that outstanding resolver of every kind of question and most acute investigator of difficulties, resolves this interpretation quite differently. He says: “Whatever gift you offer on my behalf”—as though a son were saying to his father: “The matter concerning me belongs to you.”

By these words the children indicated that they no longer needed their parents’ offerings on their behalf, since they had reached an age at which they could make offerings for themselves. Once they had reached this age, the children could freely say this to their parents. When they had said it, the Pharisees denied that the children were guilty if they did not render honor to their parents.

But I do not see how this interpretation fits the context of the reading, except that at the end those who did not honor their parents were blamed because they had been led astray by pride and did not obey the divine commandments.

“Hypocrites, Isaiah rightly prophesied concerning you.”

They were hypocrites because, out of avarice, they taught children to say, “Whatever gift is from me.” Here he indicates that honor is empty of reward if it is offered only with the lips and not in the heart.

For one honors God in three ways: in the heart, in action, and in speech. But because the Jews had become empty in these matters through their traditions, they were far from God and from God’s traditions. Since they were more troublesome to God than religious, they worshiped God without purpose: God was not present in the worship they practiced, since they taught vices by their way of life and abandoned the commandments of God’s Covenant.

To them he himself said, “Hear and understand.” He requires the ears of the whole human being. For no one properly hears inwardly if he despises what belongs to God when he hears it outwardly; nor does anyone hear outwardly as he ought if inwardly he does not understand what he hears outwardly.

“It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person.”

This was said because they were rebuking the disciples for not washing their hands. When they heard him say, “What enters the mouth does not defile a person,” they were offended. His disciples therefore said to him concerning this saying, “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?”

They were especially offended because he was abolishing the Law of Moses. By this one statement the whole superstition of Jewish observances had been struck down, since they believed that their entire religion consisted in eating certain foods and rejecting others.

For this reason, when he said, “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person,” they were offended, because by this one statement a very large part of the Law was being dissolved.

Or they are said to have been offended because he had spoken not to them but to the crowds.

Since the word “scandal” is frequently found in our writings, let the careful reader know that it is more Greek than Latin. For where the Psalm says, “They set a scandal before me,” the Greek has: **Σκάνδαλα ἔθεντό μοι**—“They placed scandals before me.” We can render the word as an offense, a ruin, or a stumbling of the foot. Therefore we must give no deed or word that can become an occasion of ruin to anyone.

It should also be noted that where our copies have, “What proceeds from the mouth, this defiles a person,” other books read, “This makes a person common.” I have mentioned this because blessed Jerome, in this passage also, explained the word itself by saying that “common foods” are those used by all people—for example, pork, oysters, hares, and animals of that kind which do not divide the hoof and do not chew the cud, nor do they have scales among the fish.

What is common, then, is what is open to other people and eaten in common, as by those who are not part of God’s people. Therefore such foods are called common and unclean by the Jews. Thus one interpreter said, “This defiles a person,” while another said, “This makes a person common.” The meaning is the same.

When the disciples approached and reported this saying to him, he answered them:

“Every planting that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted.”

Christ’s response was exceedingly remarkable and prudent in every respect: he both taught and instructed the disciples and, by divine authority, struck back at those who were plotting against him.

“For every planting,” he said, “that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted.” The whole Jewish tradition from which the discussion began was not from God the Father but was a human superstition. For its sake they even transgressed the precepts of the Law. Therefore he very prudently threatens that this teaching will be uprooted, as though he were saying:

“For this reason these people rightly deserve to be uprooted: they do not remain in the teaching in which they were planted by God.” Concerning that planting God himself says through the prophet Isaiah, “I planted you as a choice vine” (Isaiah 5:2). But because they had been deceived by their own perversity, they were now called by him the wicked seed.

Someone might ask: “If the planting of the apostle Paul is to be uprooted, concerning which he says, ‘I planted, Apollos watered’ (1 Corinthians 3:6, 9)—”

I certainly would not say this, because what follows is, “But God gave the growth.” He also says elsewhere, “You are God’s cultivation; you are God’s building.” And in another place: “We are God’s fellow workers.” If we are fellow workers, then while Paul plants and Apollos waters, God plants and waters together with his fellow workers, because they themselves plant and do nothing other than what belongs to God.

But the Pharisees did not teach what belonged to God; they taught what belonged to human beings. Therefore the true and just Teacher rightly says, “Every planting that my Father did not plant will be uprooted.”

Those who introduce different natures misuse this passage, saying: “If the planting that the Father did not plant will be uprooted, then the planting he planted cannot be uprooted. Therefore no one can be transplanted for the better or for the worse; each person will bear fruit according to his own nature.”

Let such people take care lest they hear the prophet speaking in the person of the Lord: “I planted you as a choice vine; how have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?”

God did indeed plant it, and no one can uproot his planting, which he himself planted, unless the person in whom the true seed—the seed of justice and goodness—has been planted or sown gives assent. For this planting lies within the will of free choice. No one else uproots it except each person himself, deceived by his own vice.

He calls the unbelief of the Jews itself a planting, one that the heavenly Father had not planted in them but the devil. Therefore elsewhere he says to them, “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44).

By these words Peter and the other disciples were also deeply disturbed, because he said that a person was not defiled by those foods which the Law calls unclean and which enter a person through the mouth. For they too were entirely Jews, and from childhood they had received from the Law of Moses established commandments instructing them to avoid the flesh of certain animals. Through these observances they firmly believed that they were justified.

And so, coming to him, they speak quite inquisitively:

Do you know that the Pharisees, when they heard the saying, were scandalized? Perhaps they too were nevertheless disturbed by this statement, since a long-established habit regarding foods had been implanted in them, as though it were a law of nature, which is scarcely or never removed—even if the habit itself appears to be bad. How much more, then, was that practice to be revered which had been handed down through legal commandments and commended with the greatest authority by the traditions of their fathers? [Col. 0535B]

And so, undoubtedly because he had called the Jews blind, and guides of the blind, they thought that he had spoken these things about foods entirely in parables. For, being still inexperienced, they could not yet understand anything else from the reference to foods, nor could they judge that the commandment concerned the meaning of life: that by the uncleanness of certain animals’ flesh the law designated human practices which the Church, being the body of Christ, cannot receive into the stable and everlasting bond of its unity, rejecting them as unclean foods and not turning them into its own entrails. For they were not yet capable of understanding that all those commandments imposed upon the carnal people to signify life prophetically foreshadowed the future discipline of the spiritual people. [Col. 0535C]

Therefore they too could not accept the Lord’s judgment as meaning that he was speaking about those foods which the law and ancestral tradition called unclean. Hence, long afterward, Peter, still ignorant of the mysteries of this commandment, gloried when the angel ordered him to kill and eat what had been brought to him from heaven in a vessel: “Lord,” he said, “nothing unclean or common has ever entered my mouth” (Acts 10:13).

For if the Apostle had understood fully at this point that the saying “Whatever enters the mouth does not defile a person” had been spoken about foods, I think that afterward, on hearing “Kill and eat,” he would never have been so greatly terrified. Therefore he understood neither point: neither that these commandments had been given prophetically to signify life, nor that here the Lord was speaking about foods. And so he said: [Col. 0535D]

“Lord, explain this parable to us.”

He believed that this was an inviolable commandment, which he and the other Jews, so to speak, observed inviolably. This judgment undoubtedly refutes and condemns the Manichaeans, who abominate and reject all flesh, even claiming that human flesh was made by the God of darkness. They sometimes permit their hearers, as though they were still unclean, to eat flesh, although they themselves—being nothing other than flesh—consider it sacrilegious to be defiled, and say that the Lord spoke the words “Whatever enters the mouth does not defile a person” not to the perfect but to the crowds. Thus they forbid this to their few saints while perversely allowing it to their hearers. [640]

Yet the Lord, not as they falsely claim but plainly and universally to everyone, says and testifies that whatever enters the mouth does not defile a person. Therefore he also rebukes the apostles quite sternly, although they were Jews. “Are you also,” he says, “still without understanding?” Therefore they were without understanding of the judgment, since they did not yet understand what the Lord was speaking plainly.

And so, at the Lord’s command, one must first listen carefully to the Scriptures and then understand them wisely, so that we may understand each thing as it was said. Thus Paul, because he had understood wisely, said: “Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a festival, or of a new moon, or of a sabbath, which are a shadow of things to come” (Col. 2:16–17). [Col. 0536A]

Because all these things were truly shadows, they were now being removed by the Lord, so that the servile obligation might be dissolved and the freedom of the children restored. Nor is the law of the Old Testament in such matters contrary to the Gospel, nor does the Gospel conflict with the law, as the Manichaeans babble. Rather, it fulfills and explains what was concealed in the law.

Therefore those things which were figuratively called unclean are shown by the Lord to be naturally clean in themselves, since they do not defile a person when they enter the mouth. Nevertheless, he commands the apostles not to cast their pearls before swine, wishing to indicate by the swine unclean and wicked people. For this reason, when such people have been exposed, the Church rightly abhors them and does not admit them, because they are unclean, into its own body. [Col. 0536B]

Accordingly, the Savior, who gave the law, says concerning foods and flesh: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person.” Those foods were not unclean in themselves, since everything that God created is very good and is to be used with thanksgiving. But the meaning represented by them in human beings was sometimes very unclean and had to be rejected, lest it be touched or mingled with the body of Christ.

When blessed Peter heard this, as though struck by a new astonishment, he could neither take the words literally as having been spoken about foods nor suppose that Jesus had said this without reason. Therefore, first, as though seeking an explanation on account of the Jews’ scandal, he asks what he meant by the saying. But when the Lord answered them rather sternly, the meaning seemed still more obscure to him, and he believed that the Lord had spoken in parables. [Col. 0536C]

For he had said, as though addressing those who understood correctly: “Leave them; they are blind and guides of the blind.” They were blind because they could not see the light of the knowledge of God; they were guides of the blind, not so as to show them the way of God, but so that, because of human traditions, they might plunge them into the pit of death.

Hence they taught children to say to their parents: “Whatever gift from me might benefit you.” But when he said, “Leave them,” this means that he commands the apostles, after one or two admonitions, to avoid a heretical person, knowing that such a person is perverse and self-condemned. In this sense the Savior commanded that the worst teachers be left to their own will, because such people are difficult to correct and change from their perverse understanding. [Col. 0536D]

But Peter, hearing what had been said, as I explained, suspected that the Lord had spoken in parables, and therefore replied: “Explain this parable to us.” The Lord said to him: “Are you also still without understanding?” From this we should recognize the defective hearer: one who wishes to interpret or understand obscure things plainly, or plain things obscurely—as we see Peter doing here, seeking a mystical interpretation in a matter that was so evident. Nevertheless, the most kindly Teacher further explains the judgment from which this suspicion had arisen and says:

“Do you not understand that everything which enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the latrine?”

Brothers, all the passages of the Gospels are full of stumbling-blocks among heretics and the perverse teachers of their unbelief, because they set traps for themselves and tie knots in order to overthrow the doctrine of salvation and deceive the unwary. Thus, in this saying, they slander the Lord, the creator of all natures, as though he were ignorant of natural philosophy: they claim that he thinks all foods go into the stomach and are expelled into the latrine, whereas immediately after food has been swallowed and consumed, it is distributed through the limbs, veins, marrow, and nerves, so that each member receives its portion, by which the whole body is nourished and sustained, and all the bodily fluids are generated. [Col. 0537A]

Thus these slanderers, craftily seeking to criticize the Savior’s judgment, display their own ignorance. The Lord speaks according to nature and ordinary human practice, not to teach natural philosophy, but to instruct human beings in heavenly discipline. For he knows all nature so much more fully because it is certain that he himself fashioned and created it.

Nevertheless, although this speech may appear simple, let us inquire how much truth of reason and sound understanding it contains. The natural process of nourishment operates in this way: what enters the mouth, as soon as it has passed through the throat, first goes into the stomach. Then the more fluid food and the richer juice of the food and drink are distributed through all the veins and limbs, so that the various fluids and the several functions of the members receive their portions. [Col. 0537B]

Finally, when these things have been cooked and digested, whether the adversary wishes it or not—for the Creator himself established this in nature—they descend through the hidden passages of the body, which the Greeks call πόροι (*poroi*), and which we may call “openings,” toward the lower parts. First, the cooked ash of the food, and afterward the flesh itself that is nourished from it, together with all the rheums, descend to the lowest parts as they diminish, except for a few fluids which, as I said, are expelled through their own pores. [Col. 0537C]

All these things have their own outlets in the human body, although their ash and material, having first been digested and descended to the lower regions, have already become rotten and foul. Thus nature itself shows how vain and unwarranted are those who criticize these things, and the truth of the saying refutes them.

But what he says—

“It is not what enters the mouth, but what proceeds from the heart, that defiles a person”—

raises no smaller question. For although the things that come out of the heart or mouth are truly capable of defiling a person—for example, when someone drinks or eats, and when food or drink is taken through the mouth—if the person happens to vomit while drunk and bloated, surely, because it has come out through the mouth, it does not defile the person? [Col. 0537D]

It is exceedingly absurd and foolish to think that a person is not made unclean when he eats to the point of surfeit and gets drunk, but that he is not made unclean when he vomits because the vomit comes out of his mouth.

For the Lord says: “It is not what enters the mouth, but what comes out, that defiles a person.” As for what can be said about food sacrificed to idols, the Apostle Paul resolves it: a person is defiled when he eats only because of conscience. Every creature is good in itself, but because it has been sacrificed to idols, it is evil.

Can this be explained here in such a way that when you eat you are not unclean, but when you spit you are unclean? Or, what is more serious, when you have reached the point of nausea because you have drunk, you are defiled, but because you have vomited, you are unclean? [Col. 0538A]

Nevertheless, the Apostle says: “Drunkards will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10). And the Savior says: “See to it that your hearts are not weighed down with drunkenness” (Luke 21:34). For it is not, he says, as though this were contrary to every Christian. Rather, when you spit because something has come out of your mouth, and when you have drunk because something entered your mouth by which you are defiled, it is such that you cannot possess the kingdom of God.

What, then, did the Lord mean by saying, “It is not what enters the mouth, but what comes out, that defiles a person,” except perhaps what the Evangelist Mark, following immediately in the same passage, said: “Do you not understand that everything external which enters a person cannot defile him, because it does not enter his heart but his stomach, and goes out into the latrine, cleansing all foods?” (Mark 7:18–19). [Col. 0538B]

Otherwise, if the body were not defective, so that it could become drunk or admit something of that kind, it would certainly not happen.

Therefore we should understand that the mouth from which the evils that defile a person come out is not merely the mouth of the body, but rather the mouth of the heart. Hence Matthew also says here: “But the things that proceed from the mouth come out of the heart, and these defile a person.” For the heart has its own mouth, just as the inner person has ears and eyes of its own, by which a person sees or hears the things of God.

Therefore, unless desire, will, or assent to an evil thing goes out from within, nothing that defiles can enter from outside, because “all things are clean to the clean” (Titus 1:15). [Col. 0538C]

For this reason the Apostle also forbids eating food sacrificed to idols if one knows that it has been sacrificed, lest one become defiled through conscience—which cannot happen through the creature itself, since the creature is good in itself. The same must be understood of every food and drink: they do not defile a person in themselves, but people are defiled by the vice through which they are wrongly consumed. And so it follows:

“For from the heart come evil thoughts, fornications, murders, thefts, blasphemies.”

“These,” he says, “are the things that defile a person.” Although they are carried out externally, the impulse that causes them proceeds from within. Therefore the will alone is first at fault, and afterward the guilt of the deed is subject to punishment. For the things that defile a person are those which come out through the mouth of the heart.

And lest anyone ask whether the heart has a mouth, hear David saying: “Then our heart was filled with joy, and our tongue with rejoicing” (Ps. 125:2). [Col. 0538D]

Otherwise, how could the bodily mouth be filled with joy? It is not ordinarily filled except with food, drink, or something of that kind; and even when we have it full, we cannot speak. But within us there is a mouth—that is, in the heart—from which whatever proceeds does not defile us indiscriminately: if it is evil, it defiles us; if it is good, it cleanses us.

Therefore, whatever enters the mouth of the body that is unlawful or inexpedient does not first defile a person; rather, it is the mind and conscience, which were already unclean, that defile him. This is the perverse will that flows from the mouth of the heart. For it is not only when we speak, or when we carry out our will in action, that we are stained.

No one should say: “When we speak, words come out of our mouth, because the sounds of words come out of our mouth; and when we speak evil, then we become unclean.” If someone does not speak but merely thinks evil, is he clean because nothing has proceeded from the mouth of his body? No: God has already heard it from the mouth of his heart, from which and in which the perverse will to speak or act has arisen. [Col. 0539A]

Therefore, in accordance with the Lord’s saying, whatever evils proceed from the mouth of the heart defile a person, because from there come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, and blasphemies. Mark lists more kinds of vice, which he testifies come out from the root of the heart.

Yet even he has not counted all the evils of the heart. For I do not know whether the breadth of the earth, the size of cities, or the extent of regions could bear so many enemies, or contain so many adversaries, or withstand so many nations, as the vices, offenses, and crimes that rage against and seize human senses, devastate human hearts, and plunder the goods of the virtues. [Col. 0539B]

A new order of warfare arises daily: human beings against human beings, within the human being himself. Therefore it is not what is external, but what is internal—what has already been corrupted within and comes outward in deed or word—that defiles a person.

Thus those who think that thoughts are sent by the devil and do not arise from their own will must be corrected. The devil may be the helper and instigator of evil thoughts, but he cannot be their author, because he is external. If, therefore, while lying outside in ambush, he first detects a slight spark of our thoughts and then inflames it, we should not suppose that he can search out the hidden things of the heart. Rather, he investigates or infers from the posture or movements of the body what we are turning over within. [Col. 0539C]

Therefore he is the instigator of all evils, not their author; the inciter, not the restrainer.

Moreover, when the most kindly Savior says, “For from the heart come evil thoughts,” the fashioner and creator of all natures indicates that the governing principle of our soul is not, according to Plato, in the brain, but, in accordance with the truth, in the heart, which is the center of the living being. Thus, from the center—as from the point of a circle—the rays of light shine forth, and illuminate and brighten everything above, as though the brain were the sky and the luminaries surrounding it shone from the fountain of the heart. [Col. 0539D]

The head is naturally brighter in proportion as it is healthier, and it shines more splendidly by grace in proportion as the heart has been divinely illumined by heavenly wisdom.

And Jesus, departing from there, withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon, cities near the sea. Indeed, Tyre is an island in the sea, near Circeium, a land of Judea. And behold, a Canaanite woman came out from those borders. [Col. 0540A]

We are instructed in new and great mysteries throughout the entire text of the holy Gospel, since whoever follows Jesus now penetrates the heavens, now descends to the depths, and now enters into mystical and novel sacraments. The various kinds of healings also embrace different effects of their causes. But the event and the saying derive their order from what came before.

After the unbelief of the Pharisees had been reproved and their blindness condemned—for they were blind and guides of the blind—Jesus then came to the regions of Tyre and Sidon, so that he might foreshadow new mysteries through the miracle, and so that the event might wonderfully prepare the way for faith, while the power of the sacrament might rise to the highest level in order to demonstrate still greater things. [Col. 0540B]

For this was, in appearance, a general presentation of events, and in this deed lay the salvation of the Gentiles, together with the promise already made.

Therefore the Savior departs from the Jews and comes to the borders of Tyre and Sidon. Then that Canaanite woman herself comes out from her own borders. O mystery! Behold, a partial blindness has come upon Israel so that the whole multitude of the Gentiles might be saved.

For this reason the Savior has now, in accordance with the cause, left the Jews, and that woman, who represents the Church from the Gentiles, has left idolatry. Coming out from her borders, she cries out and prays after the Lord, and confesses him as the Son of David, whom the scribes and Pharisees above denied. [Col. 0540C]

Therefore, not undeservedly, they lost the one whom she found, because they denied the one whom she confessed. Yet God’s dispensation is wondrous: he does not yet leave the borders of Judea, lest he give them any opportunity for slander, but nevertheless offers himself to them in order to heal the Tyrians and Sidonians. Thus the woman comes out from her former borders so that, by crying out, she might obtain healing for her daughter.

But the providence of almighty God is wondrous, so that each event, divinely ordered according to its own meaning, corresponds to its sacrament. Behold, a woman comes from the Gentiles, and her daughter is healed in the fifteenth place, so that she might receive, as part of her remission, seven and also eight, and thus pass over to the worship of the New Testament—but not before she had left her borders and come to Christ. [Col. 0540D]

Mark and Matthew both exalt and praise her faith. They commend the wisdom of her belief and magnify its ardor.

But Mark generates for us no small question from this event, for he says:

“Jesus departed from there and went into the region of Syria and Sidon. And entering a house, he did not want anyone to know, yet he could not remain hidden” (Mark 7:24).

No one can read this without amazement, because the text says, “He wanted to, and he could not.” For to want and not be able is not characteristic of divine majesty but rather of human weakness. It is written: “Everything that the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Ps. 134:6). [641]

And the Apostle says: “Who resists his will?” (Rom. 9:19). Necessity therefore overcomes him; the will is not free and absolute, and the ruler’s power is diminished, while his will endures the constraints of certain difficulties. [Col. 0541A]

The leper mentioned much earlier says: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me” (Matt. 8:2). And the Evangelist says: “He wanted to, and he could not.” I do not believe that this was said without a mystery. Therefore let us inquire more carefully what “he wanted to” and “he could not” mean.

Christ, formerly promised to the Jews, had come for salvation, mindful of his promise. Hence he also said: “I was sent only to the sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). But they, fiercer than beasts in their own savagery, hardened themselves to tear apart and kill their shepherd continually rather than receive him in faith.

Therefore Christ could not fulfill the purpose of remaining hidden among the Jews, as though in a house—not because of any inability in himself, but because of the wickedness of those who betrayed him. [Col. 0541B]

Thus what he had assigned to some he was compelled to bestow upon others, since he himself said: “The kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12).

Therefore this woman, in the sacrament of the Church, used force while he was still hidden in the house, according to the Evangelist Mark. As soon as she heard of him, she approached him, so that, through the faith of the Gentiles, she might, within the divine dispensation, seize the inheritance of the Father and herself pass over into the lot of the children, although she had been called a dog.

Because he had wanted to save the Jews to whom he had come, but could not, they themselves made themselves unworthy of eternal life. He could not remain hidden, lest the Gentiles seize this salvation, because in God’s dispensation it had been arranged that he should come first to them and afterward to the Gentiles, when they themselves had driven him away. [Col. 0541C]

Hence Mark expressly says: “For she was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth, and she was asking him to cast the demon out of her daughter” (Mark 7:26). He said:

“Let the children be filled first, for it is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

Matthew, however, says that he did not answer her a word. From this it is shown that, according to Mark, the woman first entered the house and cried out: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.” Then, on the road—indeed, along the entire road—she proclaimed this, now before him and now behind him.

But because he did not first answer her a word, this was not due to the Pharisees’ haughtiness or pride. Rather, he did not want to appear contrary to his own command, by which he had said, “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. 10:5), nor did he want to give an opportunity to those who would slander him. [Col. 0541D]

He wished to reserve the perfect salvation of the Gentiles for the time of his passion and resurrection.

Nevertheless, she did not cease crying out on the road: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.” Thus she confesses both natures in Christ, since she calls him Lord and proclaims him the Son of David.

Meanwhile, we should ask where this woman of the Canaanite race learned the faith which the Pharisees and scribes themselves denied. There is no doubt that this is the Catholic faith: that Jesus Christ is understood and worshiped as one and the same God and human being.

What, then, is the reason that this Gentile and Canaanite woman, uneducated in the law and perhaps not yet even counted among the proselytes, confesses him in this way? From where did she obtain the insight to recognize divinity in a human being and to understand that this same human being was the Son of God promised long ago? [Col. 0542A]

If we say that she learned it from the tradition of the Jews, among whom she perhaps lived as a tributary, the Gospel refutes us, since it says that she first came out from her borders upon hearing the report about Jesus. Unless she had come out, I do not think she would have uttered this confession.

Therefore I acknowledge that she came out for this reason: so that she might find the Savior, because he himself had first illumined her and sought her. He had sought her when he came into the region of Tyre and Sidon, so that in the particular event he might foreshadow the whole, whose figure and form she embodied. Thus the faith of the Church, already present in her, shone forth.

Then his disciples approached him, asking: “Send her away, because she is crying out after us.” [Col. 0542B]

The disciples appeal to the Lord on her behalf for various reasons. Perhaps they still understood the Savior’s mysteries only imperfectly. Therefore it seemed harsh to them that, in response to such pleading cries, he had for so long given no answer. Or perhaps, wearied by such a great outcry, they wished to help the unfortunate woman because they were moved by compassion. Perhaps also, out of love for their most merciful Teacher, they begged him lest he appear harsh toward anyone, or rather so that he might show mercy.

To them the merciful Lord said:

“I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

And what is this, most kindly Savior, that you say: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel”? Do you not elsewhere say: “I have other sheep which are not of this fold, and I must bring them also” (John 10:16)? What, I ask, is the meaning of your denial? Is she not one of those sheep whom you must bring? [Col. 0542C]

And behold, she has now come devoutly and faithfully, confessing you and worshiping you as Lord, asserting that you are also the Son of David, just as you were promised. Why, then, do you drive her away? Or why do you deny the salvation of the world by refusing to save her daughter?

What you are doing is certainly not without a mystery. From this it is understood that there is a hidden matter and a sacrament of the Father’s will: namely, that it may be clearly revealed that this Canaanite woman represents the Church, while she asks for what is being offered to others.

This does not mean that salvation was not also to be granted to the Gentiles. But the Lord, because he had come among his own, was pleased first to grant salvation to his own, so that he might receive the first fruits of faith from those among whom and from whom he had arisen. [649]

Then, through his apostles and holy preachers, salvation would pass to the Gentiles, and there would be one salvation for all.

But the woman mentioned above does not cease or give way. She had appealed to the company of the apostles, and although they had not obtained her request, she herself again persists by crying out. [Col. 0542D]

The Lord says to her:

“It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

For although giving bread to dogs is not an act of human kindness, it is nevertheless consistent with human reason. Since the bread of life was promised to those who did not wish to receive it, it would not be good to take it away from them; yet, when those who seek and ask for it with faith come, it is not right to deny it.

Therefore the merciful Lord delays for this purpose: to preserve the Father’s sacrament and not take away from those to whom salvation had been promised. But since it had been offered to them and they had refused to receive it, the order was finally that it should pass to the Gentiles and bring into the apostles’ fold those sheep that are not of this fold. [Col. 0543A]

The honor once promised to Israel is deferred, so that it might not appear frustrated unjustly or denied. Yet the affection of the most merciful God thereby brings upon the Jews envy and hatred rather than the effect of mercy.

Meanwhile, the Canaanite woman, already saved through faith and possessing an inner knowledge of the mystery, not only does not refuse to be called a dog, but humbly proposes that the little dogs often eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table. Thus she effectively turns the insult directed against her into an appeal for favor.

Nor does she refuse to understand the Jews as the masters to whom authority over the Canaanites had been assigned by the Lord, and to acknowledge that she and her people were rightly called dogs. But because the Jews had attempted to trample upon the bread offered to them rather than take it for life, she humbly begs with all her desire that she may at least be permitted to lick the crumbs like little dogs. [Col. 0543B]

For this would not be to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs—especially since the bread, brought to them many times, had been rejected, and, though offered with great care, had been trampled upon. Although it had been assigned to them, they never received it.

This is why, brothers, this woman, already imbued with faith in Christ, answers so effectively and so humbly. Thus she who confessed herself a dog is finally transformed into a human being, while those who barked against the Lord are turned into dogs. Of them the Prophet says: “Many dogs surrounded me; the assembly of the wicked besieged me” (Ps. 21:17). They rightly received this name, because they did not wish to be children of God. [Col. 0543C]

This is why I said above that the true justice of God explains why he could neither give his promises to the Jews nor deny them to the Gentiles. Therefore the Savior cries out: “O woman, great is your faith!” So that we might understand that the Lord’s long silence and refusal arose from the reason proper to the time, not from any difficulty of will.

Therefore, I ask the prudent reader to consider what I often emphasize: no one should judge that such things, or things of this kind, happened fortuitously in God’s works. Rather, they were prepared by the Lord’s dispensation in such a way that the miracles would provide incentives to faith, and that through them the greater operation of the Godhead might be proclaimed throughout the teaching.

For, as has often been said, this woman represents the Church. Already instructed in perfect faith, she comes to the Lord, whom she does not cease to confess as God and human being, and she pleads for her daughter to be freed from the malignant enemy. The Church likewise does not cease to do this for those born anew from her in Christ. [Col. 0543D]

Since it is said, “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19), the Gospel’s account and the Lord’s response demonstrate how patiently she endured all these things and how perseveringly she continued to plead.

Her humility was equally great, as was her admirable wisdom: she recognized God in a human being and, again, the human being assumed into God, so that God and human being are one Christ, one person, one Son of God to be worshiped, and one Son of Man—not by a confusion of substance, but by a unity of person.

The Lord praises this faith in the following words: “O woman, great is your faith!” It is not merely any faith, but great faith. In it every soul is reborn, so that it may become a daughter of the Church. [Col. 0544A]

Therefore the Lord says to her: “Let it be done for you as you wish,” so that the healing of your daughter may rest in your will and power. Likewise, “To all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

And from that hour her daughter was healed. Therefore those who say that children, not yet capable of believing, cannot be saved in baptism through another’s faith must not be heeded.

It should also be noted that Christ did not come in person to the centurion’s child or to this woman’s daughter, in whom great faith is proclaimed, in order to heal them. Rather, they were commanded to be healed from a distance, so that he might show that the Lord is able to save everyone not only by touch but also by word and will. [651]

In these cases, above all, he signifies the salvation of the Gentiles: to them he did not come in person, but all are healed and delivered through the word of faith, just as the woman’s daughter was delivered from all domination by unclean spirits through the washing of salvation.

Then faith immediately follows the deed, when at once on the mountain those afflicted by various kinds of diseases are brought by the crowds to the Lord—that is, unbelievers and sick persons are instructed by believers to worship and fall before him—but not before he ascends the mountain. For the Evangelist says:

“When Jesus had crossed over from there, he came beside the Sea of Galilee, and ascending the mountain, he sat there.”

Because he ascended from this world to the Father. Then great crowds came to him, bringing with them many mute persons, blind persons, lame persons, the infirm, and many others. They threw them at his feet, and he healed them all.

For where the Latin translator rendered “the infirm,” the Greek has κύλλους (*kyllous*), which is not a general term for weakness but the name of a particular infirmity; in ordinary speech we may call such a person “maimed” or “crippled.” [Col. 0544B]

But because the precise meaning of this word cannot be expressed in our language, the translator preferred to say “the infirm” rather than render it incorrectly with a non-equivalent word.

As for the fact that Jesus ascended the mountain, he thereby challenges his earthly young birds to fly, so that they may always seek higher things. For he himself, from the highest dwelling places, never ceases to heal all who are infirm and return to faith. But after they are healed, lest they fail on the way, the Lord has such compassion on them that they ascend to the mountains. Hence the Evangelist expressly says: [Col. 0544C]

Having summoned his disciples, he said to them: “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat; and I do not want to dismiss them fasting, lest they collapse on the way” [Col. 0544D].

He maintains the order of the course of action and teaches mystical meanings through these same deeds, as the work of virtues proceeds in sequence. For in the daughter of the Canaanite woman the faith of the Gentiles is prepared; then bodily weaknesses and diseases are cured by the Lord from the mountain through that same faith; and thus food is offered, lest after their illnesses they should fail, as sick people do, since in all these things there is a representation of the Church. Hence the interpretation of these events receives authority from what follows, so that they may not collapse from hunger along the road of the present life.

Thus the pious and kindly Lord summons his disciples, with whom he takes counsel concerning the restoration of the people, so that they might be ignorant of nothing that he was about to do. He does this also to provide an example for future teachers of the churches: whenever some important matter is to be undertaken, they should share their deliberations with their subordinates and disciples, just as the Lord does, so that through this conversation the rationale of the deed and the fellowship of agreement may be commended; and also so that, from the difficulty, they may understand the greatness of the sign and become ministers of so great a sacrament, companions in the administration of salvation.

“I have compassion,” he says, “on the crowd, because they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat.”

In this reading, as in every text of the holy Gospel, one must therefore consider, in our one and the same Redeemer, the twofold and distinct operation of divinity and humanity, so that in both works the truth of his humanity and divinity may be commended. Thus the error of Eutyches, which presumes to teach that there is only one operation in Christ, is condemned [Col. 0545B].

For who would not see that the most kind Jesus’ compassion for the crowd, his conversation with the disciples lest the crowd should fail either from hunger or from the labor of a longer journey, expresses the affection or compassion of human weakness? But that he satisfied four thousand people with seven loaves and a few small fish is clearly a work of divine power. And, what is greater, these things are so balanced throughout all the miracles, sayings, and deeds that the truth of the event is commended in the miracle as its outward form, while the sacrament is proclaimed through the divine operation in its general meaning.

For this reason, I ask the Catholic hearer to understand why Almighty God performed this miracle of the loaves no more than twice, feeding the crowds and leaving an abundance of leftovers. He was not powerless, as though he could not have done it more often if he wished; but reason required that he should perform neither more nor fewer such deeds in outward form, so as to stir faith at that time, than he performs at every time for the instruction, through grace, of the whole human race [Col. 0545C].

For he established only two laws by which every faithful soul is instructed and nourished unto life: namely, the Old and the New Testament, in and from which every soul lives. “For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV, 4).

This twofold nourishment proclaims God, who did not present himself more or less in the miracle than he manifested himself in the New or Old Testament. He established these two laws, giving one of them to the earlier people and the other to the people whom he redeemed with his blood. Thus, once and twice, he provided these two meals in the miracle: one of them, which we discussed above, represented the earlier law; but the one of which we are now speaking, as its distinctions will demonstrate, expresses the figure of the New Testament, in which the grace of Christ is commended [Col. 0545D].

And therefore this nourishment was rightly made from seven loaves, because through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit the fullness and grace of the whole Church are supplied. For this reason it is rightly understood to belong to the New Testament.

None of the Evangelists said that these loaves were barley loaves, as was said of the earlier ones; rather, they are believed to have been wheat loaves, so that Christ’s Church might be nourished by that grain of wheat which, falling into the earth, was dead and then produced much fruit.

For the sake of this people, the Lord himself, moved by compassion because they had already remained with him for three days and had nothing to eat [Col. 0546A]—without doubt, the Gentiles, because they did not possess the law, that is, the five books of Moses, nor the prophets, nor the preaching of any saint, but first came to Christ through faith alone. How rightly, therefore, they have now remained with him for three days, while they rightly believe in his birth, passion, and resurrection; and they remain in the faith of Christ with him for three days, when they believe in the Father, in his Son, and in the Holy Spirit, and persist in the confession of the Trinity, as the Savior says: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22).

And this is what is meant by “They have nothing to eat”: they do not have the law, nor the word of preaching, without which no one lives [Col. 0546B]. “And I do not want to dismiss them fasting, lest they fail on the way”: those who had believed in Christ through faith were henceforth to be nourished unto salvation by the word of faith.

The order, therefore, is the same in the Lord’s sermon as it remains in the attainment of grace. Hence, even today, those who are coming to baptism first confess that they believe in the Son of God, in his passion and resurrection, and faith is given in return for this sacramental profession. And so that the truth of these very events may correspond to this pledge of words, throughout the period of the Lord’s Passion they remain in fasts, joined to the Lord in a certain fellowship of compassion; and thus, whether through the pledge of the sacrament or through fasting, they pass with the Lord through the whole period of the Lord’s Passion.

The Lord, having compassion on them, says that they have already been with him for three days. He wishes to nourish them with his food, lest failure in the course of secular life—that is, in the work of the present age—should weaken them, and to strengthen them with the power of his bread for continuing the whole journey [Col. 0546C].

But it is very remarkable why the apostles are said earlier to have been concerned about the restoration of the people after a single day’s fast, and to have asked Jesus, because the place was deserted and the hour had passed, to dismiss the crowds so that they might go to the neighboring places and villages where they could buy food for themselves. Here, however, although the people have already continued for three days and labored with the Lord amid the crowds, they say nothing of the sort but remain silent; and the discussion concerns the bread, because there is no means by which these people can be satisfied.

Therefore, since the cause of the events is being sought, and not without reason, it seems to me that the earlier feeding demonstrated the salvation of the Israelite people and the measure of eternal satisfaction for those who were to be saved. For this reason the apostles’ concern was directed toward seeking the salvation of their own nation, just as we read that Jonah did.

For the Gentiles, on the other hand, there was no salvation from the law or from the prophets, but through the grace of Christ alone. Seven loaves are first prepared and broken for them, so that they may be nourished freely by the grace of the Holy Spirit and fed by heavenly gifts. Since the apostles had not yet been sent to preach to them, but rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, they therefore not only remain silent about these people but even complain and say: “From where can anyone satisfy these people with bread in the wilderness?” (Mark VIII, 4) [Col. 0546D].

Otherwise, if this had not been said mystically, the apostles’ unbelief would deserve severe blame. For even if from nowhere else, they could at least have remembered from the earlier miracle of the five loaves and known that nothing was impossible for God. But perhaps unbelief and forgetfulness held them for so long that they did not remember what he had done with the five loaves and two fish, until the mysteries of the events had been completed.

For in the earlier sign, since they were still using only the five senses by which people are nourished, and were close to bodily senses, the Lord himself did not remember those who were laboring for even one day; rather, the disciples did, because they were still under the tutor of the law. Therefore, when evening was near and the sun was already declining, since they could endure no more, they pleaded on behalf of the crowd that Jesus should dismiss them, as though they were pleading for the imperfect.

Here, however, the Lord himself remembers them and is said to have compassion, and he explains the reasons for his compassion: “Because they have remained with me for three days,” he says, “and I do not want to dismiss them fasting, lest they fail on the way” [Col. 0547B].

Unhappy Jews, who even today do not spend these three days with God, nor remain in the things that belong to God, because they do not wish to believe in the Trinity of the Godhead, nor confess the birth, passion, and resurrection of Christ.

Some, however, wish to interpret this three-day period differently. They say that it was the third day since they had clung to him while fasting. For in the whole age of the human race it was the third period, when the grace of Christian faith was given: the first before the law, the second under the law, and the third under grace. And because a fourth period still remains, when we shall come to the fullest peace of Jerusalem, toward which everyone who rightly believes in Christ is journeying, the Lord therefore says that he is restoring that crowd, lest they fail on the way [Col. 0547C].

For this dispensation, by which the Lord deigned to appear to us in the flesh, does nothing other than enable us to arrive without failing at the prize of the heavenly calling. For “we walk by faith, and not by sight.” Hence the apostle Paul says that he has not yet apprehended what is perfect, but, forgetting what lies behind and stretching toward what lies ahead, he pursues, as he says, “toward the prize of the heavenly calling” (Phil. III, 14).

Nevertheless, in whatever we have attained, let us walk, so that, because we are clinging to the Lord on the third day, we may not fail after being nourished by him.

And Jesus said to them:

“How many loaves do you have?”

They said: “Seven.”

This question of the Lord does not arise from ignorance, but from divine providence, so that the apostles would not remain uncertain about the gifts they had received. Since they were to become teachers of the churches, they were to know what they had received in Christ. For, according to the prophet Isaiah, these seven gifts were in Christ, and by them the whole Church was to be nourished, gathered—or to be gathered—in Christ under the square number.

“And the spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him,” he says, “the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI, 2–3) [Col. 0547D].
