According to this number, an equal number of loaves was provided and prepared, by God’s deliberate purpose rather than by chance, so that the apostles might learn that by grace they possessed what they had not possessed by nature, in whom there was the whole satisfaction of the people.

It should also be noted that above there were five loaves, whereas here seven are offered; there only two fish, whereas here an indefinite number is given, though with the implication of fewness; there five thousand men, in accordance with the Pentateuch, whereas here four thousand, in accordance with the Gospel; there twelve baskets, whereas here seven baskets, are filled; there the people reclined on grass, whereas these recline on solid ground; there they spend only one day with Christ, whereas these remain unmoved for three days [Col. 0548A].

I think enough has already been discussed above concerning some of these matters, and I have indicated that everything has been fittingly set forth according to the person of the people. Now, too, reason appropriately demands that what has been omitted should be completed briefly by explaining the causes of each matter, so that it may become clearer than daylight to which people each table corresponds.

The four thousand are therefore compared with the people of the New Testament because this order is shown to live under the four Gospels and is gathered into the unity of the Church from the four quarters of heaven. This number is always placed in praise, because a square stone does not waver and is not unstable. Through this number, plainly, the innumerable multitude gathered from the four parts is represented, and that multitude is strengthened by four virtues so that it may stand.

By this same number, the Gospel itself is made firm, so that it may endure: it is strengthened by the square number and, in the solidity of unity, is perfectly squared, lest it waver in any age.

The few fish—not two, as above—are those who, first caught from the false whirlpools of this age, clung to the Lord through faith, were joined in his name, and were sent to preach the Gospel. They were to act as ambassadors on behalf of that great Fish, that is, Christ, so that the souls of the faithful might be satisfied by their seasoning and the weak people might suffer no distaste [Col. 0548C].

Or the indefinite number of fish signifies the divisions and ministries of different gifts and charisms, by the diversity of which the faith of the Gentiles is satisfied.

And he commanded the crowd to recline on the ground.

The earlier crowd, fed with five loaves, reclined on green grass. Now, when they are restored with seven loaves, they are commanded to recline on the ground, because through the Scripture of the law we are commanded to trample down and restrain the desires of the flesh: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass.” But in the New Testament we are commanded to leave the earth itself and temporal possessions [Col. 0548D].

Yet both peoples are led toward the mountains. There, height is exalted for carnal people by carnal hope and desire as the earthly Jerusalem; here, with every carnal possession removed, he has taken care to lead the guests of the New Testament toward higher things in the hope that endures, and to establish them in the solidity of incorruption.

And therefore, as though placed upon the solidity of Christ’s own mountain, they were not softened by any intervening grass, but were restored by the sole eternity of incorruption [Col. 0549A]. Thus, after blindness, lameness, and countless weaknesses—because they had already remained with the Lord for three days for the sake of the cures and healings of various illnesses—they are restored from the Lord’s hand through the ministry of the apostles, so that they may eventually reach those things, because, according to the angel’s word, a great journey still lies before them.

“And taking,” he says, “the seven loaves, giving thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people. And they set them before the crowd.”

For all these divine sacraments were to be distributed to the churches through the hands of the apostles. But the most kindly Jesus first gave thanks to God the Father for the salvation of believers; then he blessed the loaves, so that they might increase through his blessing; and he broke them, because unless he first broke them, no one could open the divine mysteries and unlock the sacraments hidden from the ages.

For who would reveal the Son of the Father? Or who would know the Father unless the Son did? He himself says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. XI, 27).

For he is the bread of life that descended from heaven. And who could show us this bread by himself, or how could we have penetrated to perceive its interior mysteries, unless he himself had opened for us the seven seals of the sealed book? Without doubt, these seven loaves were sealed in that book. Therefore, long ago the prophet, weeping, said: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. IV, 4) [Col. 0549B].

In other words, the unlearned and uninstructed sought the food of the divine word by which they could grow strong for good works and be restored by the divine utterances, but there was no one to open for them the secrets of the Scriptures and instruct them in the way of truth.

Therefore, after taking the loaves, the Lord gave thanks to instruct us to offer thanksgiving to God the Father and to implore his assistance, and also to show how greatly he rejoices in the salvation of the human race. For this reason we too must be instructed and prepared both to implore grace and to give thanks for it, so that whatever benefits we receive from him, we may thank him with unwearied praises [Col. 0549C].

“They ate,” he says, “and were satisfied.”

This had long before been foretold through the prophet David: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied; and those who seek him shall praise the Lord, and their hearts shall live forever and ever” (Ps. XXI, 27).

Therefore, because these people sought, they found; and because they found, they remained for three days; and because they remained for three days, he had compassion on them, and they were satisfied; and because they were satisfied, “their hearts shall live forever and ever” [Col. 0549D].

But as blessed as these people are, who are restored by such food and satisfied with divine banquets, so unhappy are those who eat and are not satisfied: they hear and taste the bread of the word by which man lives, but do not complete through faith and works what they hear, and receive none of its inward sweetness by which their hearts may be strengthened so that they remain.

Indeed, I will not say that such people came from far away, but that they were far from salvation and alienated from grace. Some of those who are saved and satisfied with heavenly gifts came from far away; others, like Nathanael and many in whom there was no deceit, came from nearby. Yet all who have come through faith, unless they withdraw from sin, grow weak and, so to speak, are dead, because salvation is far from sinners.

And they gathered what remained from the fragments, seven baskets.

Certainly, because the crowd, placed on the road, could not reach the end of its eating, food was left over. But the company of the apostles and teachers did not allow the fragments of the leftovers to perish; rather, through a wonderful sacrament they filled seven baskets. These are the seven churches, in which universality is signified, and the seven shining lampstands illuminated before the Lord by divine light [Col. 0550A].

For once the little ones have been satisfied together with the great, there will not be lacking in Christ’s Church, together with the apostles, those who fulfill and store in their vessels these higher precepts—or rather exhortations and counsels—of perfection, which the general multitude of the faithful cannot grasp with its understanding or fulfill in its works.

Thus the seven baskets in which the fragments of the Lord’s food were stored are rightly mentioned, on account of the sevenfold Church, which itself, because of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, is generally consecrated by the number seven. It is rightly recognized as filled with the remnants of the Lord’s meal and said to be satisfied, because everything is completed at the summit that the breadth of the carnal multitude below cannot contain [Col. 0550B].

Nevertheless, all are said to have been fully satisfied, because although there are people in the Church who cannot leave all their possessions or fulfill what is said concerning virgins, each is satisfied according to his measure, as each hastens to fulfill what he understands and what his own order requires, so that he may attain eternal life.

“And when he had dismissed the crowd,” he says, “he went up into the boat.”

The crowd is not dismissed until it has been satisfied and filled. Yet he remains with us throughout all the days of our life [Col. 0550C]. Hence it is significant that he went up into the boat, which is the Church, and from which and in which he himself governs and guides the people of believers, lest, after being fed, they fail amid the waves; lest, after being instructed, they wander amid the winds of languages; lest, after being strengthened, they be broken by the long journey; lest, even after reaching harbor, they be driven back by the winds; and lest, when Charybdis rages, they be shipwrecked in the whirlwinds.

And he came into the district of Magedan. In Mark we read Dalmanutha. But because the order of the narrative is the same in both Evangelists, there is no doubt that it is the same place under both names. Some manuscripts likewise have Mageda according to Mark, although in Greek it is Magdalan.

## Chapter XVI

And the Pharisees and Sadducees came to him, testing him, and asked him to show them a sign from heaven.

O how hard-hearted they were! They ask for signs, as though the works of divinity that they had seen had not been signs. But the Evangelist shows what kind of sign they sought when he says: “And they asked him to show them a sign from heaven.”

They were therefore seeking a sign from heaven, either—as above—in the manner of Elijah, for fire to come down from on high, or, after the likeness of Samuel, for thunder to resound in summer, lightning to flash, and rains to pour down. Yet they could have slandered these things, too, and others like them, by claiming that they arose from hidden and varied disturbances of the air.

For this reason the meaning is clear: they did not seek a sign from heaven so that they might believe, but so that they might invalidate what had been done twice with the loaves. In the Gospel of John, moreover, it is shown that after this miracle of the loaves they asked for manna to be given them from heaven after the manner of Moses [Col. 0551A].

For John says that they spoke in this way: “What then do you do, so that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform? Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat’” (John VI, 30–31).

As though they were saying: “Since you have fed many thousands of people twice in the wilderness with a few loaves, do for us, in imitation of Moses, that manna may come from heaven, so that we may believe you.”

And they truly did not say this from purity of faith, just as their fathers did not when they said: “Can God provide bread, or prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Ps. LXXVII, 19). That utterance, like theirs, arose not from belief but from unbelief and hardness of heart, so that they might slander and nullify what had been done by the Lord, lest by believing they should be saved [Col. 0551B].

But he answered them.

In Mark it is written that he said, sighing in spirit: “An evil and adulterous generation”—omitting in the middle the matters that Matthew records. For just as above, when he was about to restore the believing crowd with heavenly benefits, he gave thanks, so now, because of the foolish faithlessness of the unbelieving Pharisees and their crafty, fraudulent request for a temptation, he sighs and is saddened.

He said to them:

“When evening comes, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red’; and in the morning, ‘Today there will be a storm, for the sky is red and threatening.’ You know how to judge the face of the sky, but you cannot recognize the signs of the times?”

This passage is not found in many manuscripts. But its meaning is clear, even among the Gentiles. Hence Virgil sings:

> The sun, too, when it rises and when it sinks into the waves,  
> will give signs; the sun will be followed by the surest signs.  
> And what it reports in the morning, and what with the rising stars.  
> Finally, what the late evening brings, from where the wind drives  
> the clear clouds, what the damp South Wind intends—  
> the sun will give you signs. Who would dare call the sun false?

It is therefore established as true that, from the order of the elements and the harmony of things, clear and rainy days can very often be predicted. And for this reason the Pharisees and scribes, who appeared to be teachers of the law, are rebuked because from the more certain prophetic prediction they could not understand the coming of the Savior, concerning whom it had been said: “He shall descend like rain upon fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth; in his days righteousness and abundance of peace shall arise” (Ps. LXXI, 6) [Col. 0551D].

These were open and manifest signs by which the time of his coming could be recognized. Therefore they are rebuked because they knew how to judge the seasons from the condition of the air and to detect what was useful to themselves, yet did not attend to or understand what was useful for their salvation: the signs from heaven of God’s coming in the flesh.

In these words, a marvelous response of God is commended in every respect. For they observed the humility of Christ’s flesh and body, and disdained to receive doctrine from what he bore under the appearance of a human being. Mocking their insolence and empty boastfulness, he replied that they were accustomed to infer much about the nature of the sky, predicting clear or stormy weather either from the rising of dawn or from evening [Col. 0552A].

Since they could predict and know such things, he teaches them that it was exceedingly foolish for them to be ignorant of the signs of his coming, when the whole law and the prophets announced that he was to come and foretold when and how he would come. The indications of the works he performed also already bore witness, with every sign of wonder, that he had come.

Thus, just as the redness of the morning or evening sky inspires belief in a coming storm, so the manifest knowledge of the times should have been supplied by the signs of his virtues and works, if they had not been blind.

And the comparison is remarkable. For when evening came, through the blood of Christ’s Passion at his first coming, forgiveness of sins was given; and today there is a strong storm at morning, “for the sky is red and threatening.”

His first coming is rightly compared to evening, because it occurred at the end of the age. Therefore, although the sky is red, made purple by Christ’s blood like a rose, it is nevertheless very serene. But at the second coming, when he arrives, it will be like morning; and although the sky may then be red or glowing, it will not be serene but stormy, certainly because that redness will come not from blood but from fire.

For, as the psalm sings: “Fire shall go before him” (Ps. XCVI, 3), “and around him there is a mighty storm” (Ps. XLIX, 4). In Greek, the word used here is more expressive: πυρράζει, which we might call “fiery,” because all that glowing then will come from fire [Col. 0552B].

“Therefore,” he says, “you know how to judge the face of the sky, but you cannot recognize the signs of the times?”

This is the voice of one rebuking or reproaching them, because they could not—or would not—recognize the signs and prophecies concerning his first coming, or concerning his Passion and resurrection, to which the rosy evening sky is said to be comparable.

Nor did they carefully consider the tribulation that would precede his coming, to which the rosy and threatening morning sky is comparable, from which and by which a storm is foretold.

Let the faithful soul weigh how worthy of every admiration the Lord’s response is: how true, how powerful in refutation, how prudent in instruction. Just as the redness of the morning or evening sky gives assurance of a coming storm, so the miracles of his virtues and works, or the indications of the Scriptures, ought to have supplied manifest knowledge of the times.

He so tempered his response, so to speak, ineffably, that he himself, having arisen from heaven, gave them not a heavenly sign but an earthly one, mercifully drawing them back within a confession of humility and teaching what the law had foretold concerning him.

“An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah” [Col. 0552D].

Therefore, if they had not been adulterous, they would have preserved the faith of Abraham, from whom they had been born. But because they had fallen away from the faith into apostasy, they were adulterous. Hence the prophet says: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. XVI, 3).

To these he promises that he will give a sign—not just any sign, but the great and marvelous sign long ago promised by God in a figure of himself. For just as Jonah was sent to the Ninevites to preach repentance, so Christ presented the whole reality of this in himself, fulfilling the sign [Col. 0553A].

For every sign is the sign of something: it marks a hidden and concealed thing, or something future. Therefore Christ’s Passion is rightly called the sign of Jonah—not because Christ’s Passion itself prefigures something else, but because it is the fulfillment of Jonah’s sign.

This is a well-known usage among grammarians: a thing may be called a sign even though it no longer signifies anything beyond itself, because it represents in itself the form of a sign formerly promised.

For Jonah was thrown into the sea when the winds were raging, and was swallowed by a sea creature or beast; after three days he was sent forth alive from the abyss and from the belly of the beast. He was not held by the sea creature, consumed in the abyss, or destroyed in its belly as food is destroyed; rather, contrary to the nature of the human body, through the power of the Lord’s prefiguration he emerged after three days whole and unharmed into the upper air [Col. 0553B].

Christ therefore demonstrates the sign of his power that had been established concerning him, and promises that he will fulfill it as it was prefigured.

Let the devout soul consider this, even if inadequately, and understand wisely the marvelous sacrament, full of omnipotence. It was promised then in prophecy, and now fulfilled more wonderfully in Christ.

For he is the one who, having left the Jews, came to preach repentance and bring salvation to the Ninevites—that is, to all the Gentiles. He is the one who by his death calms the winds and stills the storms. He is the one who was handed over to the judgment of the age and judged by human beings, so that Caiaphas, as though speaking by lot, might say: “It is expedient that one man should die, lest the whole nation perish” (John XI, 50).

Therefore, swallowed and devoured by death, he was cast down, descending as far as the underworld, as though into the depth of the abyss, and the whole abyss surrounded him [Col. 0553C].

I do not mean that the dragon who is in the sea and was formed for sport swallowed him in order to transfer him into its own body, but in order to destroy him—though he was unharmed—not knowing that he had not been given to it for food, but so that he might return alive and victorious to the regions above from the tomb.

A sign was thereby given that Jonah had come in his proclamation: immediately after three days he emerged alive from death and the abyss, contrary to the condition of the human being whom he had assumed, neither held nor corrupted.

Therefore, because his death and condition are full of miracles of power and sacramental signs, he wished it to be understood that what had been promised as an example would occur concerning him, so that it might be recognized all the more clearly through the sign of prophecy, since the sign itself was again reproduced in the example of a human being.

Then, leaving them, he went away.

This does not say, as in other passages, that he went away after dismissing the crowds, but that he left them, in order to establish some distinction in the matter. Since the error of unbelief had hardened the minds of the insolent, he is therefore said not to have dismissed them but to have left them.

And when he had crossed over the strait, his disciples forgot to take bread. He said to them: “Look and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” The fact that they had forgotten to take bread, and that he commanded them to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, is the occasion on which he teaches not only the apostles but also us what the five and the seven loaves signify, as well as the five thousand men and the four thousand who were fed in the wilderness. For although the greatness of the signs is clear and wondrous, nevertheless, through spiritual understanding, they demonstrate something far higher and more wondrous.

Accordingly, he teaches that the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees signifies not bodily bread, as the apostles supposed, but perverse traditions and heretical doctrines. Likewise, the food by which the children of Israel were nourished in the wilderness signifies true doctrine and the bread—Christ—who descended from heaven.

But it is rightly asked: “How could they have had no bread with them, when, immediately after filling the seven baskets, they went up into the boat and came to the region of Magedan, where they heard, as they sailed, that they should beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees?” Finally, the Evangelist explains why they did not have those loaves with them: “They forgot,” he says, “to take them.” But how they could have forgotten them seems to have been caused solely by divine providence. Therefore he sets before them the proverb about leaven, so that from it both they and we might arrive at an understanding of the twofold nourishment.

And through this saying about leaven, because the apostles were thinking something else—that they had not taken bread—every obscurity of this mystery was removed and the divinity was made clear, since only God knows human thoughts. But when he commands the apostles to abstain, lest they become mixed with the doctrine of the Jews, he teaches with complete authority that this must be understood carefully and broadly: all the works of the Law were directed toward the fulfillment of faith and established as a prefiguration of future realities, so that, whenever and in whatever ages the truth of the signs should become clear, nothing further would remain in the likeness of truth or in hope to be shadowed forth, nor would Jewish superstition, or *deuterosis*—that is, their second tradition—be judged to promise anything true.

Therefore this is a great lesson for the whole Catholic Church: it must beware of everything that is outside Christ and outside the spiritual Law, lest the truth of the Gospel Law be corrupted in any respect. But if human frailty or forgetfulness should happen to creep in, so that someone neglects to take the seven baskets with him, let him beware of becoming like them by forgetting God’s benefits. Rather, let him hear the most gracious Jesus rebuking and teaching, since every forgetfulness of God’s gifts must be wholly avoided.

And if it should happen, one must remember God’s teachings concerning the five and seven loaves, because the one who fed so many thousands of people from them is also powerful to restore life—not from loaves alone, but also from the doctrine of eternal refreshment—to those whom forgetfulness has overtaken for a time in the boat or on the road, provided that he offers those things which the Law commands as a remedy for the offense of forgetfulness.

But since we have now traveled a long road and traversed broader fields, we must not linger any longer over these matters, lest an overly extended speech or an overly elaborate reading displease those who are weary and eager to learn, and impede them; for an untimely narrative by the speaker often tires the patience of the listener.

Therefore I must warn my reader not to hear as one deaf the portion of the parables of the most gracious God, for it was said concerning them: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XI, 15). Let him not receive God’s healings ungratefully; let him not come to the banquets of the twofold refreshment with distaste; let him not approach as an undevout intercessor on behalf of the daughter.

Therefore let no one despise our very serious and simple discussion, since there is in our speech no ambition for praise, no display of empty eloquence: nothing that shines with festivity except understanding alone; nothing that sounds slippery or childish, nor anything heated with youthful ardor. And, as I believe and hope, nothing that may rightly be mocked as senile, since I no longer take pleasure in feather-light frivolity, nor delight in a milky abundance and childish charm.

For long ago I abandoned the study of human letters, and therefore I now draw nothing deceptive or ornamented from alien studies, because I do not desire an adulterated doctrine or the voice of a shouting populace that courts acclaim. Therefore, my brothers, as I proposed at the beginning, since our speech does not possess a painted beauty, I pray that it may have within it a natural vigor and the truth of its own image, so that it may not crown its head with any flowers of words, but be supported by understanding alone and in simplicity.

And we have followed Jesus through the ineffable lessons of his parables and the miracles of his virtues. Let us draw breath for a little while, so that we may return without weariness to the matters that remain to be treated, if only we may first grasp the faith of blessed Peter, inspired by God the Father.

# PREFACE TO BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 0555]

[Col. 0555B] It is known to everyone, even to those who read secular literature, that wisdom—especially divine wisdom—is to be pursued more than human eloquence. For, as Cicero says, the king and teacher of the eloquence of the whole age, “If someone, neglecting the most upright and honorable studies of reason and duty, spends all his effort in the practice of speaking, he is raised up as a citizen useless to himself and harmful to his country. But the one,” he says, “who so arms himself with eloquence that he can use it not to attack the common good but to defend it seems to me most useful both to his own interests and to those of the state.”

Therefore, although I do not possess such great eloquence of speech, since understanding has been granted to me in part concerning the divine Scriptures, let no one, I beg, criticize me because I wished to serve in this undertaking the brothers to whom I owe my whole self, [Col. 0555C] and to fasten the fleeting meanings of thoughts in writing, at least for those who understand less, in order to stimulate their minds.

Indeed, I have resolved to unravel divine things in simple speech, since this is altogether more fitting than artificial ingenuity, lest a marketable discourse be blamed more than it is approved as useful and profitable to its readers. This must especially be observed as the discourse proceeds, where neither flesh and blood accomplishes anything, nor human learning avails, but rather the outpouring of the Father, who by himself revealed his own Son to the most blessed Peter in the flesh and taught him the hidden mysteries of his sacrament—mysteries which no human tongue has ever been able to unlock, nor provide mortals with the form and method of understanding that were granted to the chief of the apostles—so that he might know most fully that in one and the same Christ the Son of God the Father had always existed, and that the Father’s right and name had always remained in him.

This, then, is the true and inviolable faith given by God the Father to Peter: that if the Son has not always existed, neither has the Father always existed. On this faith, assuredly, the whole Church is founded and firmly established, believing in God the Son of God, for whom there is with him, from the eternity of the Father, one eternity, one power, and one authority.

This faith, therefore, was taught neither by human eloquence, nor by secular philosophy, nor by verbal fluency, nor by the discipline of any art. And so it is foolish in this part of the discourse to bring forth persuasive words of argument, where divine inspiration accomplishes everything. Nevertheless, we must beware lest bitter and poisonous sweetness be mingled with good and most holy teachings, since the confession of blessed Peter concerning Christ is altogether clear and plain, so that no one may be permitted to stray from the faith or deviate from the truth.

Therefore, after declaring Christ’s majesty, divine Wisdom, wishing to introduce the apostles to the mysteries of human redemption, began to show them, now that he himself would suffer, now that they themselves and all the elect must follow Christ through the same sufferings and mortifications of the flesh. Until he returns again to the customary works of his ministry, divine power labors to make everyone understand that he is true God and man, both subject to suffering and immortal.

Using, so to speak, his own arguments, he introduces them to himself—not with persuasive words based on human wisdom, nor according to the introductions of the dialectical art, which the Greeks call *Isagogai* [Introductions], but in a marvelous and ineffable manner: sometimes through inspirations for understanding divine things, sometimes by demonstrating what belongs to his humanity, sometimes by promising that he would come in the glory of the Father. Then he showed himself glorified on the mountain, and thus, through a new manner, so to speak, of acting and speaking, he arranged matters so that they might understand truly who and what this one and unique person was, and why he had come.

So that they might see, believe, and know the mysteries of human redemption, the most gracious Teacher invites them to follow him and thus reach him.

# BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 0555D] Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi and was questioning his disciples, saying: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” Great and evident is the understanding concerning Christ that the Evangelists commend. Therefore he describes the place where this question was asked and where such a great, remarkable, and wondrous answer was given. Since many have discussed that place, I have judged it superfluous to say anything or to speak at length about it. For it is necessary only, as I said, to note that the Evangelist would never have described the place and time if the things said or done in those places had not been great and extraordinary, since he himself was about to narrate them.

Jesus questioned his disciples in that place, saying: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” Whatever anyone might have thought about him, he asks no other question than what they would say concerning the Son of Man. For he clearly wishes first to lead the disciples to faith, whatever others may have thought, so that they might truly think, believe, [Col. 0557B] and understand that this same Son of Man is the Son of God—not, as we have sorrowfully observed in the case of an old error that has recently sprouted again and stirred up ancient ashes, so as to divide the one and same Christ into two persons, saying that Christ’s humanity was by adoption in God, while confessing the Father’s Word, which became flesh, to be the true Son.

Thus he was teaching as dogma that there were two sons in Christ, according to the two natures, and fabricating two persons. But here he himself asks only about the Son of Man, and Peter answered the question concerning this very one:

“You are,” he said, “the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

Without inserting or distinguishing anything concerning the unity of the person, he confesses the whole reality that is in Christ to be the true Son of God. Nor is it surprising that the man of whom we spoke went astray, since he was human, just as those also went astray who, because of Herod’s deception, called him either John, or Elijah because he was still believed to be yet to come, or Jeremiah, because God had said to him: “Behold, I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms” (Jer. I, 10), “to uproot and tear down, to destroy, and again to rebuild and plant.” All these opinions certainly arose from error, because they were human. Therefore, leaving these things aside, let us pass on to others, since the faith revealed to Peter builds up more than the place in which this question was put forward. And leaving aside also the errors concerning Christ and the opinions of individuals, lest we seem to prolong an idle treatment, let us come to the question addressed by Christ to the apostles.

“You, then,” he said, “who do you say that I am?” It was as though the gracious Teacher were saying: “Since those people, merely human beings, think wrongly about the Son of Man—for ‘every man is a liar’ (Ps. CXV, 11)—you, who are more than human beings, who do you believe me to be?”

This is shown by what follows in the text of the Lord’s discourse: the apostles are rightly called not human beings but gods. For when he had said, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” he immediately added, “You, then,” as if he were saying: “Since you are gods, whom do you testify me to be?” Or, “Whom do you judge me to be?”

Attend, prudent reader, to the marvelous and astonishing question. Before their eyes he himself appeared to be nothing other than a man; he even said that he was the Son of Man, which he truly was, and yet he required something else from them. Therefore I would by no means say that he asked about himself what he himself had confessed—what was before their eyes and in that very place, what could be touched with the hand. Rather, he was asking about something hidden: in this hidden reality the foundations of the Church were to be laid, and the faith of all was to be commended.

Hence blessed Peter’s marvelous and unheard-of answer burst forth, so that he might perceive everything that was in the Lord and see what was in Christ, who was God. He did not deny that the man who was speaking with him was a man, the one whom he saw present; yet, going beyond this without delay, he confessed what none of them had confessed: “You are,” he said, “the Son of the living God.”

Perhaps he calls him the living God in comparison with those gods who were thought to be gods but were dead and were nothing except the phantoms of idols. Therefore blessed Peter was more than human, because his understanding went beyond humanity. When he saw the Son of God in a man, he saw and understood beyond human eyes.

For this reason he was praised by the Lord himself: he did not attend only to what was of flesh and blood, but, seeing the Son of God through the Father’s revelation, confessed him in one and the same person. For he did not say, “The true Son of God is in you,” as the Word was in the prophets, so that there would be one son of man and another Son of God. Rather, as soon as he heard, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” he confessed without any delay or insertion that the one speaking with him, the Son of Man, was this: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

Certainly, according to John, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14). Therefore he is the Son of God, God from God, and man from man, one in both, full of grace and truth. For by being born he received what he was not, and the Word, which had always been in the Father, was born. Thus the eternal Son was born, because in him nothing was born except what is eternal.

The fact that he assumed the body that was openly visible and became man is the complete and unambiguous confession of blessed Peter. For just as eternity received the body of our nature, so it must be understood that the nature of our body was able to receive the power of eternity.

Therefore, since the highest good consists in this faith, he very necessarily asks the disciples whom people would say him to be, and adds: “The Son of Man.” This is the firmest principle of confession and the faith to be preached: that just as we believe and adore the Son of God, so we should believe and adore the Son of Man in one and the same person. For either one without the other contributes nothing, in appearance, to salvation.

Moreover, Peter answered first before them all because of the precedence of his office and the excessive ardor of his faith, so that the unity of the Church might be commended and the faith of all the apostles maintained, as though in one head: “You are,” he said, “the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

In this example you have the whole Trinity and the true confession of Catholic truth: God the Father is proclaimed, as is the Son of the living God, anointed by the Holy Spirit; and one power, one nature, and one operation of the Trinity are understood.

Furthermore, the addition “of God” is more exalted than to admit comparison with those who are not gods. But what is greater, it also excludes comparison with those who seem to be something by grace, because God is called “the living God” according to the excellence by which he surpasses all who possess life in themselves. Life is not accidental to him, just as it is not accidental to his Son, who was born from him as Life.

And therefore, from the one by whom he has it that he is life, the apostle Peter revealed that he is the Son of the Father. “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John V, 26). Accordingly, the Son who is life is the Son of the living God the Father.

This confession undoubtedly has an eternal reward, just as it has the prize of blessedness. Hence Christ says to him:

“Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.”

Blessed is the one who has entered the treasuries of God; blessed also is the confession drawn from the treasuries of God, since it brings the reward of blessedness.

Therefore he is called blessed both by predestination and by the gift of grace, which he did not yet possess in fact when Satan was rebuked, when he denied, and in the many other circumstances through which salvation was being worked by the weakness of the flesh. Yet his blessedness remains secure in the one “who calls those things that are not as though they were” (Rom. IV, 17).

But why this blessedness is returned to him by Christ in reciprocal fashion is explained by his confession; the cause of his confession, however, is gift and grace. Thus God the Father, who reveals his Son, is the cause; the Son who is revealed is the cause of our salvation; and the Holy Spirit, the gift of both—the Father and the Son—is the one through whom the Son is revealed.

Therefore he also says to Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona.” Why? “Because flesh and blood has not revealed these things to you”—flesh and blood derived from father or mother—but “my Father who is in heaven.” What flesh and blood could not reveal was revealed by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Hence Peter also receives a name from his confession, because he had the revelation from the Holy Spirit, whose son he must also be called. For the Holy Spirit is called *Ruha* in the Hebrew language, feminine in gender, and not inappropriately so, since from him—or from her, if I may put it that way in Latin—the whole Church is born again.

Indeed, in our language *bar* means “son,” while *Jona* is interpreted as “dove,” so that the whole expression may be understood as “son of a dove.” Others, however, take it simply to mean that Simon Peter is understood according to the flesh as the son of John, in accordance with the question in another passage: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John XXI).

They wish this to be attributed to a scribal corruption, so that *Bar Joanna* has been corruptly read as *Bar-Jona*, with a syllable removed. *Joanna* is interpreted as “the grace of the Lord,” while *Jona*, as I have said, means “dove.”

But both names can be understood mystically, so that the dove signifies the Holy Spirit, and grace signifies the spiritual gift of God—the very thing about which he said: “Because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you.”

Compare the apostolic account, which says: “Immediately I did not consult flesh and blood” (Gal. I, 16), where “flesh and blood” signifies the Jews. Thus it is shown that Christ the Son of God was revealed to him not through the teaching of the Pharisees but through the grace of God.

And, to speak more truly, he received this grace neither from a human being nor through a human being, nor did he learn this doctrine through any human faculties, since, just as “no one knows the Son except the Father,” so “no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. XI, 27).

Accordingly, just as the Son alone reveals the Father through the Holy Spirit, so the Father reveals the Son through that same Holy Spirit.

“And I say to you: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

If you wish, reader, to set each word against and join it to the preceding words, you will find an eloquence of marvelous response. It is as though he were saying: “Because you have said to me, ‘You are the Christ,’ I also say to you that you are Peter.” Then: “‘The Son of the living God,’ and I say that you are Bar-Jona,” that is, “son of a dove,” so that Peter himself might also be understood as a son of God through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore what he says—“And I say to you”—must be considered and read with great gravity. It is as though he were openly saying: “I do not speak with an empty word that produces no work, but I, whose saying is doing, say to you, because my word is full of omnipotence: ‘You are Peter.’”

The name is derived from *petra*, “rock,” that is, from me, upon whom the whole Church is built. For Peter is not, as some wrongly think, the foundation of the whole Church: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. III, 11).

Although Peter may rightly be believed to have been placed first upon that same foundation, as though its head, nevertheless the whole heavenly Jerusalem is built and firmly established upon that rock from which he drew his name as a gift—upon Christ—so that it may remain firm forever.

Abraham is likewise read to have been first established and strengthened upon this firmness in the Old Testament, and then Peter in the New, so that every promise might remain firm in Christ through their faith.

Nor is it surprising that Peter was named from the rock, since he was destined to become firm through the Holy Spirit with the firmness of faith, just as they are called the light of the world from the Light, who is Christ.

Thus it is a common name, as they say, among the Syrian, Hebrew, and Latin languages. And it should be noted that this name was not first imposed upon him here, but much earlier, according to John, when Andrew brought him to Christ. “You are,” he said, “Simon, son of John; you will be called Cephas,” which is interpreted as “Peter” (John I, 42).

He did not say, “You will be called Peter,” by which name he had already been called, but he said pointedly: “You are Peter, and upon this rock”—from which rock you have been made—“I will build my Church.”

This was not because he was already so firm, as I have said, but because he was destined to become so through Christ, “who calls those things that are not as though they were” (Rom. IV, 17). And through the Holy Spirit he would be made so firm that “neither death nor life, nor things present nor things to come, nor any creature” could separate him “from the love that is in Christ” (Rom. VIII, 38–39).

Therefore he was not yet blessed in reality, but only in God’s predestination. He was loved by the Lord not as he then was, but as he was destined to be.

Nathaniel too, in whom there was no deceit, according to the Lord’s testimony, held almost the same earlier confession when he said: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel” (John I, 47–49). But he seems to ask rather than affirm, with the attitude of one still questioning and doubting, and this because he had been seen under the fig tree.

Peter, however, expressed such a great confession from his heart that his confession is the confession of all the apostles. And just as they are all questioned together, so in him there is one answer belonging to all, upon which the Church is founded and against which the gates of hell shall not prevail.

For whether you say that they do not prevail against this faith, or that they do not prevail against the Church founded upon Christ by this faith and strengthened in him, it is one and the same thing: neither is the foundation dissolved, nor is such a great faith weakened, nor is the Church overthrown amid countless storms or by the assaults of the winds.

[Col. 0561B] But such faith is born only from the revelation of God the Father and the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, so that every Peter who possesses this faith is called firm with the firmness of the rock—not because flesh and blood has revealed it, but because God illuminates him, so that, with the Apostle, “our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20).

But if we live according to flesh and blood and confess Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God—for example, accepting such a doctrine as something handed down to us by our parents—then perhaps the Father has not revealed it to us, but flesh and blood has (Rom. VIII, 13).

Therefore we are neither stable in his faith nor firm like Peter, and so we do not receive the blessedness or a similar grace of blessing. And it should be noted that each believer is a rock to the extent that he is an imitator of Christ, and is light to the extent that he has been illumined by the Light.

Accordingly, the Church of Christ is founded upon them to the extent that they themselves are made firm by Christ. Therefore God’s Church is built not upon Peter alone but upon all the apostles and their successors. Hence David says: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI, 1).

But those mountains are first built upon the mountain, Christ. Then Christ the mountain is raised above all mountains and hills.

As for the promise that “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it,” or, as some manuscripts have it, “shall not prevail against him,” it is rightly asked: against whom? Or, against what? Is it against the rock upon which the Church of God is built, or will they not prevail against the Church that Christ builds upon the rock?

Because he does not state this explicitly, it must nevertheless be believed without doubt that they prevail neither against the rock upon which the Church is built nor against the Church that is built upon such a rock.

Otherwise, if the gates of hell prevailed against someone, that person could be neither the rock upon which Christ builds the Church nor the Church built upon the rock. For if it were built upon the rock, even though the rivers flooded and the winds blew, as Christ testifies, no one would fall, because he had been founded upon the rock.

We know that the gates of hell are vices and sins. For every sin through which one descends to hell is a gate of hell. Therefore every soul that contracts sin against itself, within itself, is neither the rock upon which Christ builds the Church, nor the Church, nor a part of the Church that Christ builds upon the rock, because the gate of hell has prevailed against it.

Therefore, while we live here, we must labor lest any gate of hell prevail against us. For if it prevails, we are not in the Church, nor are we a part of the Church.

Hence the Apostle says: “Those who do such and such things,” which he enumerates, “shall not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal. V, 22). And the Lord says: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke XIII, 24).

For just as the gates of hell are vices and sins, so the gates of righteousness are virtues, through which the righteous enter into rest. Hence David sings to the Lord: “You lift me up from the gates of death, so that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. IX, 14).

Through these gates one happily reaches that one gate concerning which he himself asks: “Open for me the gates of righteousness; entering through them I will confess to the Lord” (Ps. CXVII, 19). Then he added that one gate which is Christ: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (ibid., 20).

Since, then, there are many and innumerable gates of hell, none of them prevails against him, because he is either the rock or the Church built upon the rock.

Therefore we must pray continually: “Lest at any time the enemy say, ‘I have prevailed against him’” (Ps. XII, 5). For he truly prevails if he conquers to the end, so that the gate of sin may swallow us up and we can no longer rise again to virtue or overcome sin.

And perhaps he said “they shall not prevail” concerning the future, not the present, because there are few in whom, after grace has been received, none of those gates of sin prevails. Indeed, to confess the truth, even Peter himself was not one against whom the gate did not prevail while he was denying, although he did not fall away from the faith.

Therefore, after he was finally and truly converted through the grace of the Holy Spirit, nothing further prevailed against him, and he shone forth victorious at the end.

“And I will give you,” he says, “the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

Accordingly, it was fitting that he first promised that the gates of hell would not prevail against him, and afterward said: “To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

For the one who has closed the gates of hell so that they do not prevail against him is worthy to receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven from that very Word. As a reward, so to speak, after the firmness of faith and the strength of victories, the keys of the kingdom of heaven are given in second place to the one who has been able by his virtues to close the gates of hell, so that he himself may open for himself the gates of the kingdom of heaven—gates closed to those who are conquered by vices and confined by the gates of hell.

For every kind of virtue, when it has been fulfilled from the heart, appears to be itself, as it were, a key of the kingdom, so that the same virtue is found to be at once the key of the gate and the gate through which one enters the kingdom.

Therefore it is not without reason that as many keys are said to exist as there are virtues possessed. Especially since each virtue, and often all the virtues together, are called the kingdom of heaven.

For this reason, whoever possesses them and lives according to them appears to be in the kingdom of heaven and in the city of virtues, against which the laws of hell, the gates of Tartarus, and all the barriers of death will be dissolved, and the doors of life will be opened.

It follows:

“Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.”

I ask each person present to attend carefully to the context of this reading, but especially bishops, to whom this power seems to have been more particularly attributed by the Lord together with Peter and all the apostles, although the same power has also been granted to the whole Church.

For whoever wishes to claim this grace for himself must hold fast to Peter’s weakness in the rock, and preach faith by his conduct and by his speech. Then he must possess the keys of the kingdom that I have mentioned, and guard those same keys not as coming from himself but from the Lord and through the Lord, as a heavenly doorkeeper.

Otherwise, unless his judgments remain firm in Christ, as though God were judging through him, he must fear that the gates of hell may prevail against him who binds or looses, if he judges unjustly and not according to the word of God.

But the one against whom the gates of hell have not prevailed judges justly, because he carries with him the keys of the kingdom already received from the Lord.

For this reason he opens to those who have been loosed on earth, so that they may be loosed and free in heaven. And he closes to those who have been bound on earth by his just judgment, so that they may be, as it were, bound in heaven and judged.

I said “as it were,” because they will not be in heaven; rather, expelled from it, they will carry the heavenly judgment with them into hell, if they have been justly bound.

Therefore a fearful necessity rests upon both: upon the one who judges and binds, lest he bind or loose unjustly; and upon the one who is judged and bound, lest, having been justly bound or judged, he depart from this life before he is loosed.

Nevertheless, for Christ’s sheep, however the shepherd may bind, the shepherd’s sentence must always be feared and revered, lest, through contempt, one incur a fault that one did not contract by one’s actions.

But although they retain the power of binding and loosing, unless they bind or loose justly—forgive me for speaking thus to those who bind or loose—it is ridiculous to think, and even more dangerous to do, that someone who is bound and painfully constrained by the chains of his sins should, merely because a bishop is said to possess such power, be loosed by him so as to be loosed in heaven, or, if bound on earth, be bound in heaven—that is, in the judgment of heaven.

Far be this, then, from that senate of heaven: that, according to the impulse of the mind of anyone who is proud or angry, they should themselves bind or loose unjustly before the eyes of the supreme Judge, who sees everything.

Rather, the judge of another’s life must fear that he may incur judgment, since the Truth said to everyone: “In whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged” (Matt. VII, 2).

Therefore, those who judge in divine matters must beware above all, because before the Lord not only the sentence of priests is sought, but also the life of those judged.

In Leviticus too, concerning lepers, where they are commanded to show themselves to the priests, and, if they have leprosy, the priest is then commanded to declare them unclean, the priest does not make lepers clean or unclean. Rather, he has knowledge of the leprous and the non-leprous and is able to discern who is clean and who is unclean.

Just as the priest there makes someone clean or unclean, so here a bishop or presbyter binds or looses—not those who are guilty or innocent according to his own judgment, but by his episcopal office. When he has heard the various conditions of sinners, he knows who are to be bound and who are to be loosed.

And if anyone presumes to act otherwise, it does not come from justice and truth but from the arrogance and presumption of the Pharisees. For they were not sent to destroy and kill, but to gather and save even those who have fallen.

Then he commanded his disciples to tell no one [Col. 0564B] that he was the Christ. For it was necessary that other spirits should bear witness to him than the apostles—namely, the Law and the prophets. But the testimony of his resurrection belongs properly to the apostles.

Therefore they are not confirmed before that time, so that they might become suitable witnesses in the Spirit of truth. In this command it is clearly shown that the blessedness of those who know Christ in the Spirit has been revealed. But the danger of denying his humility and passion is again declared.

Therefore:

From that point he began to show, he says, that he had to go to Jerusalem, and suffer many things from the elders of the people and the scribes, and be killed by the chief priests, and rise again on the third day. [677] But I do not know how dispensationally he introduces the apostles to this faith, or whether even a few understand it. For above Peter scarcely at last reached the point of confessing, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” and this only because the Father had revealed the Son; and immediately afterward he commanded him and all the disciples, “They should tell no one that he was the Christ.”

What do you think they preached earlier, when they were told: “Do not go into the roads of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,” and so forth (Matt. X, 5–6)—the words he spoke to them when he sent them to preach? If, then, they were already being sent to the ministry of apostleship, what else could they preach except Christ, who daily showed by marvelous and varied works that he was Lord? And if he now still sends them and wanted them to announce him, why did he now command those same disciples to tell no one [Col. 0564D] that he was the Christ?

But if he did not want himself to be preached, how are the things foretold to them fulfilled? What of this saying: “For they will hand you over to the council, and in their synagogues they will scourge you because of me, as a testimony to them” (Mark XIII, 9)? Or this: “When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you are to speak; for it will be given to you in that hour what you are to say” (Matt. X, 19). How were they to be scourged or handed over because of Christ, if they were not going to announce Christ?

Perhaps, then, someone may dare to say that he did not want to be preached at that time as Jesus himself being the Christ—when the first messengers were sent two by two—nor by the apostles until the time of the resurrection. Concerning all these matters Origen, in his treatise, proposes and develops many questions [Col. 0565A]. He considers it necessary to investigate in this passage, if perhaps these matters and others like them pertain in their proper places to a future time, and whether, when they were sent, they already knew that he was the Christ. “And if they already knew,” he says, “Peter undoubtedly knew as well.”

How, then, after so many such events, which are recorded earlier in various passages, does he ask them, “But who do you say that I am?” And when Peter answered and said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” he said to him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven”? By these words he demonstrates that Peter had then confessed him for the first time as Christ, the Son of the living God; and the other apostles also are believed to have confessed and learned this in the same confession. [678]

But if previously they did not know that he was Christ, the Son of God, how could they preach one whom they did not know—or confess him? And what earlier confession does he now require? For he says: “Everyone who confesses me before human beings, I also will confess before my Father” (Matt. X, 32).

From these words and statements, then, the meaning is plainly made clear: at that time the apostles and the other disciples knew something about Christ, but they did not know the greater and higher mysteries of our salvation. Therefore the aforementioned teacher asks whether believing Jesus to be the Christ is less than knowing him. He gives the example of John, where he says: “If you remain in my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John VIII, 32).

He says that we may put it this way: when they were sent to preach, they did believe that Jesus was the Christ, but they did not yet know him. Later, advancing through instruction and many miracles, they came to know him, when, having been questioned, they confessed: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” But I admit that Peter too, when he made this praiseworthy confession through the revelation of God the Father, still did not know everything about Christ—as was immediately shown when he rebuked the Lord because he had said that he would be killed, along with the other matters attested by the present passage.

Thus there is a great difference between knowing and knowing. At that time the apostles already possessed the beginnings of knowledge; afterward they advanced until they arrived at fullness, especially when they received the Holy Spirit for complete knowledge of the truth.

Why say more? The present saying of the Savior is relevant, in which he says that afterward he began to show them that he would suffer. This explains why he had commanded them to tell no one that he was the Christ. By “afterward” he means the time after Peter had confessed him as the Son of the living God. Even if Peter then learned, together with the other apostles, something about him that he had previously not known, he was immediately scandalized—the one who was to become a teacher, already appointed head of the Church. What, then, must we think the others could bear, to whom he was being preached, if everything about him had been announced as it was destined to occur in his passion?

Or if the apostles were then learning these things about Jesus, which they had not yet known, how much less, do you think, did those whom the apostles had previously instructed know about Christ? Therefore the Lord Jesus Christ did not initially wish to be preached [Col. 0566A], lest any disturbance should arise from it.

For this reason Luke says more openly that he rebuked them, so that they should tell no one that the Son of Man had to suffer many things, be rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes, be killed, and rise again on the third day. Perhaps he adds that he rebuked them because the Lord knew that even the disciples would find it difficult to believe in his passion and resurrection.

This is why he himself first chose to be the witness of his passion and resurrection, and afterward the apostles: so that faith would arise from what had happened, and not disagreement from what had merely been heard. Nor did he wish to boast before undergoing his passion; rather, he preferred at times to appear of lowly status.

For under the one and same name of Christ there are many things both difficult and mysterious that had to be preached [Col. 0566B]. He is the Christ who was born of the Virgin and conceived by the Holy Spirit; he is the one who performed countless miracles; he is the one who died for our sins; he is the one who rose from the dead. And the one who suffered and rose again is the one who in the beginning was the Word, God with God, without whom God the Father never was, through whom all things were made.

Such things, and many others that are taught about Christ in accordance with the catholic faith—he is the Christ. For if you remove any one of these, you have removed your salvation. Heretics too appear to possess Christ and preach Christ; none of them denies the name of Christ, but they deny Christ because they do not confess everything that belongs to Christ.

For many reasons, therefore, he commands the disciples to remain silent: perhaps so that he might deceive the prince of this world; so that he might appear to avoid boastfulness and teach humility concerning himself; and, more importantly, so that the disciples, still inexperienced and imperfect, would not be crushed beneath the burden of the highest preaching. If they had faltered in their preaching, as they did in the passion of Christ, they would have produced in their hearers the scandal of error rather than perseverance in perfect love.

If it is asked whether he gave this command for the first time here—that they should not announce him—or earlier, when they were sent not only to preach but also to heal and cure everyone, we rightly say that here too the command does not seem to mean that they were forbidden to preach Christ, the Son of God. Rather, it means, so to speak, that they should not announce that he was going to suffer something, be killed, or rise again from the dead. For no one is properly said to rise from the dead unless he has died and risen from death to life. [680]

But because this command is a mystery of sacred dispensation, it was given with such moderation that this principle is to be observed in all preaching and at every time: the teacher should not take upon himself more than has been entrusted and committed to him, nor more than the hearers themselves can bear or understand, so that each person may receive, at the proper time, his measure of wheat (Luke XII, 42), which he can effectively carry and fulfill in his works.

This, then, is why they are forbidden, as I said, to proclaim Christ—or to proclaim everything that Christ is—so that afterward they might preach him more fully and perfectly, even as crucified, and thus commend the cross itself together with Christ, in which Christians were to glory [Col. 0567A]. For this is the true glory of our faith: to understand truly the cross of Christ. Other crosses do us no good; only the cross of Christ is useful and altogether necessary for us—the cross through which the world has been crucified to us (Gal. VI, 14), and we to the world.

Wonderful is the dispensation of almighty God! How subtly and carefully he leads his people into faith, lest they either be overwhelmed by majesty or cast down by the weakness of the flesh; and lest they reserve for a later and more suitable time the fuller teaching about him that was to be preached, when they were already able to announce individually what they had seen. Thus, if the death of Christ disturbed anyone into unbelief, the resurrection and ascension to the Father would lift up and sustain the minds of believers in faith.

Otherwise, the apostles, who had always been with him, had seen all the miracles he performed, and had heard from him the words of life (John VI, 68), to which they had also borne witness—if they were scandalized on the night when he was betrayed, what do we think would have happened to those who knew nothing of such things? If they had heard that he was the Christ, this is why, sparing them, he commanded the apostles to tell no one that he was the Christ.

Nevertheless, I do not mean that when the apostles were sent, or when they spoke to the crowds, they announced nothing about him. Rather, they did so with such moderation that they drew people to faith in him, while not making public the secret mysteries of Christ before the proper time.

And because they had already been led to the Lord through faith by the revelation of the Father, so that they not only fully believed but also knew him to be the Son of the living God, it was now appropriate that they understand that this same Son of God and man would die for all and rise again. For it is absolutely necessary that Jesus Christ crucified be preached. Otherwise it is useless to preach Christ while remaining silent about the cross.

Therefore he commanded them for the time being to tell no one that he was the Christ, until he had prepared them for faith and for the mysteries of the mystery, so that afterward they might say more perfectly and appropriately that he truly was the Christ.

Accordingly, we must consider more carefully that he does not say, “From that point Jesus began to say or teach,” but says: “From that point he began to show his disciples.” Just as bodily things are said to be shown more clearly to bodily people, so Christ still showed these things to them as though they were mortal and little ones, so that they might recognize more openly [Col. 0567D] what they were discussing.

I do not think that what he suffered, or what they saw and what was done by Christ, was shown to them through the sight of their eyes in the same way that a rational and intelligible discourse about the mystery of his passion and resurrection was shown to the disciples. Therefore he said that at that time he began to show them these things: afterward, when they had become more capable through words and deeds, he would demonstrate the same things more fully, no longer speaking to them as beginners who were still unformed, but completing the revelation so that they might understand more fully that everything Jesus began to do or teach he also brought to completion.

And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you.” But he turned and said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to me, because you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of human beings.” [Col. 0568A]

From these words it is apparent what many have often said: that Peter possessed exceedingly ardent and extremely great love for the Lord and Savior. After his confession, divinely revealed to him by the Father, and after the reward bestowed by the most kindly Savior, when he had heard, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven,” he suddenly heard from the Lord—and I say, immediately—that he had to go to Jerusalem, suffer many things there, be killed, and so forth.

He cannot bear what he hears, nor does he want his confession to be weakened and destroyed, because he does not think it possible that what he truly knew and confessed without hesitation—that the Son of God should be killed—could happen. Thus, out of the ardor of love, the firmness of faith, and the reverence of devotion, he takes him aside, both to restrain the Master from such statements and so that he would not seem to rebuke him rashly in the presence of his fellow disciples. When they had withdrawn, he began to rebuke him with the deepest affection and with the desire to prevent it, saying: “Far be it from you, Lord.”

The Greek expresses this better: ἵλεώς σοι, Κύριε—“May it be gracious to you, Lord,” or “May God be gracious to you, Lord.” And, to add what was in blessed Peter’s mind: “This shall not happen to you; it cannot happen; my ears and my heart cannot accept that the Son of God should be killed.”

It had not been revealed to him that the Son of God had to suffer and be killed—such a great Christ, God the Son—for these things seemed unworthy even of God the Father. Hence he said: “Be gracious to yourself, Lord, because if you do not wish it, it will not happen to you.”

And this was true. Yet he did not know that God the Father had appointed him as a propitiation for our sins in his blood (I John IV, 10). Christ accepted Peter’s affection but reproved his ignorance, saying: “Get behind me, Satan, because you do not have in mind the things of God,” that is, the will and mystery of God.

But because through ignorance you have ceased to go behind me—because you do not have the right understanding—go behind me, behind my back, and hear the voice of one admonishing you, so that you may understand rightly.

When he calls him Satan, it is the voice of one rebuking him, because no one, even through ignorance, ought to be contrary to God. For “Satan” means “adversary” in our language. Satan had prevailed in Peter, though through ignorance, so that he ceased to go behind God and follow the one whom he desired to precede him for his own sake. Therefore he is rightly called an adversary, so that he might now learn not to be a stumbling-block to the Son of God. [Col. 0568D]

From the beginning of his calling Peter had walked behind the Lord, before he began to be a stumbling-block and oppose him. Therefore he is struck immediately at the beginning of his sin—if it is proper to call it sin—and is admonished to fulfill what had been commanded to them by the Lord at the beginning of their calling. For he had said: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of human beings” (Matt. IV, 19).

It should be noted that to this man he says, “Get behind me, Satan,” but to the devil only, “Go,” as though he were saying, “Into the eternal fire.” Peter was overcome by the affection of love and by ignorance.

Thus this apostolic error arose from steadfastness of faith more than from an instigation of the devil. Yet we cannot entirely deny that, after the preaching of the passion, the devil received an opportunity to tempt him; for until that time he had withdrawn from him. But, seizing this opportunity presented by human unbelief, and—if it is permissible to say so—through the affection of love, he insinuated himself outwardly into Peter in order to set this before Christ. Peter’s mind was not infected with the poison of unbelief; rather, it had been wrapped in ignorance.

Knowing both the devil’s deception and Peter’s ignorance, the Lord rebuked them. To Peter he said, “Get behind me,” as though he were saying, “Until the passion of the cross”; and rebuking the devil he said, “Satan, you are a stumbling-block to me.”

For just as it is God’s gift to know Christ as God in the spirit, so it is the devil’s work not to know Christ in the human being. It is equally perilous either to deny the body without God or to deny God without the body, because Christ, the Word, is in the body he assumed for the sake of human salvation.

Therefore Peter was rightly told to follow; but the one from whom such a suggestion of error came was rebuked with the words, “You are a stumbling-block to me.” [Col. 0569B]

Yet it is astonishing that after such a confession, such blessedness, and such an admirable grace—so that the Church of Christ was to be built upon him and through him—and after such power of binding and loosing had been granted to him, he should suddenly hear—however and to whomever the words may be spoken, they are nevertheless spoken to him—“Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to me.”

What is this so sudden a change, that after such great rewards had been divinely conferred upon him he should be called Satan? But if a prudent mind pays close attention, all these things concern not the present, as I said above, but the promise of future things. For if such grace had immediately been granted to him and his blessedness had already been made firm, the error of a wicked persuasion would never have found a place.

For this reason, I think, Mark and Luke wrote that Peter answered, “You are the Christ,” without adding what is found here in Matthew, “the Son of the living God.” Therefore they did not relate this blessedness to that confession, nor the grace of the blessing, nor the gift of such great power, nor the other things granted to him.

From this we state with certainty that these things were not granted freely to him in the present, but were bestowed and freely given in God’s predestination and in the future. For this reason the present error also crept in and found an opportunity for contradiction, and later, in the passion of Christ, for denial.

Whether error can ever exist without sin, or be well-intentioned, as some wish, I leave to those to discuss who know how to present the intricate knots of syllogisms and penetrate the inner thoughts of minds—whether perhaps someone can err, or be a stumbling-block to one of the lesser ones, or be contrary to God in a way that is not truly opposition. [684] Even if it is opposition, it is against him.

For although at some time error may have benefited someone, so that it is called a good error, this may happen on the way of the world, but not on the way of God.

Then it follows: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”

Let the army of the Christian religion hear, I ask; let all who are reckoned under the Christian name hear; let them hear Christ the King addressing the people of the heavenly army and speaking to his soldiers. “Whoever wishes,” he says, “to come after me”—for above he had told his own that he would suffer and be killed; he had said to Peter, “Get behind me,” because he had found in him something opposed.

Now he says to everyone that all should follow him into the campaign—not fighting for himself, but fighting for us. Let all follow, and let no one wish to go ahead, no one oppose, no one turn aside, no one go backward. Let all follow him, because he alone is the one who fights, he alone the one who conquers, he alone the one who crowns.

Nevertheless, he preserves free choice in all things. He establishes a rule for everyone, but grants freedom. Therefore Mark says: “Calling the crowd together with his disciples, he said to them” (Mark VIII, 34). And Luke says: “He was saying to all” (Luke IX, 23).

For this invitation to everyone is the salvation of believers, since following Christ and going after him is no ordinary virtue. Its first rule is this: whoever has the will to follow him must deny himself, because he cannot go after him in any other way unless he has denied himself.

He denies himself who renews and changes his carnal life and his evil conduct through a good way of life, and thereafter walks in newness of life—that is, abandons vices and pursues virtues—so that through these he may confess Christ, no less by faith than by good works. For in these each person either denies Christ and confesses himself, or again confesses Christ by denying evil works through faith, so that he may live entirely in confession and praise of God, fulfilling good works.

Thus every thought of ours, every understanding, and every word and deed demonstrates our self-denial and produces confession and testimony to Christ in each virtue.

“Let him take up,” he says, “his cross, and follow me.” For it is not enough to take up the cross unless you follow Christ. The philosophers of this world also abandoned everything of theirs, and sometimes even their vices, pursuing good conduct and enduring many things. But because they did not have faith and did not follow Christ, “while claiming to be wise, they became fools,” because they did not glorify God but became futile in their thoughts (Rom. I, 21), and wandered away from the truth.

Therefore everyone who wishes to follow Christ must take up his cross. Unless he has gloried in the cross of Christ, believed in it, made Christ’s cross his own, and carried it after Christ with Simon, under compulsion, he cannot follow him, because no one follows Christ empty-handed. [Col. 0570D]

Therefore whoever dies to sin should die in no other way than according to the flesh, so that he may say with the Apostle: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of the Lord, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14).

For whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it. And whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it in eternal life.

O blessed loss, happy ruin! He wishes to save us through the loss of soul and body, and urges us to become like him. For although he was in the form of God (Phil.
