II, 6), he became humble and obedient unto death, and for this reason endured the death of the cross, so that each person might glory in the Lord through the cross and through it die to the world and to himself.

Although someone may appear to abstain from sin and be dead, insofar as sin is concerned, nevertheless, unless he believes in the cross of Christ and in the faith of the one who was crucified, and unless for his sake he abstains from sin, he lives for himself and not for Christ. He has not been crucified and died with Christ, so that Christ might accomplish all these things in him.

Therefore he says pointedly: “Whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it.”

We can understand this saying—“whoever loves his soul” or “whoever hates his soul”—in this way: if someone loves the present life more than the eternal one, and thinks that this present life is the highest happiness, and spares his soul so as to fear death more, thinking that his soul will perish through this death of the flesh, then by wishing in this way to save his soul he will lose it, since he will have made it foreign to eternal life.

The superior part of the soul is also called the mind, by which the whole life of a human being is governed. There is also a lower part, by which the body is given life, and which is called animal life. Yet “soul” is used for the whole by reference to the part through which the body is animated.

If someone loves this soul—that is, this present life—more than living according to God or dying for God, he will lose the whole life in which he ought to have lived according to God. Thus neither part of the soul, by which the body lives and is governed, will thereafter live in that eternal life through God, because he did not wish to die to himself and to the world in order to live well according to God. [686]

Similarly, whoever despises the present life for the sake of the word, and trusting in eternal life struggles for the truth unto death, or lives in the present not for himself but according to God, will indeed lose his soul with respect to the present life—whether he hands it over to death for the sake of Christ’s devotion, a death that is improperly so called, or, being entirely dead to the world, can say with the Apostle: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II, 20).

Such a person, because he has lost his soul for Christ’s sake, makes it more truly safe in eternal life. For he renounces the devil and all his works, as well as the world with its deceptions and its pomp, so that he takes up his cross and follows Christ.

All these matters are set before free choice. Therefore, as though returning to what was said above, he says: “Whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it.” By saying “whoever wishes,” he shows that the preceding and following statements have one meaning.

Therefore, if what he said above—“Let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me”—refers only to death, we must likewise understand what he says, “Whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it,” as referring only to death. But if denying oneself and taking up the cross means not only dying for Christ but also rejecting carnal conduct, then without doubt losing one’s soul means not only dying for Christ but also laying aside carnal desires and dying to oneself and to the world.

He does not say, “Whoever has saved his soul will lose it,” but “Whoever wishes to save it will lose it”; and “Whoever first loses it for my sake will save it.” For the reasoning is consequently this: first we must lose what we already possessed wrongly, and afterward seek to attain what we could never have possessed from ourselves.

Thus we must live in such a way that we attain the salvation of our souls through a better way of life. Although the statements vary, their meaning is one; nevertheless, the understanding is disclosed more fully and perfectly when one statement is proclaimed from another, and a more elegant manner of expression is commended.

Whoever denies himself and takes up his cross is the one who loses his soul for Christ. By losing it, he saves it better, since it is wholly expended for the one who is life by essence. And whoever loses his soul with respect to carnal desires is the one who denies himself, takes up his cross, and follows Christ.

What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?

I think that the one who does not deny himself, does not take up his cross, and does not follow Christ according to what has been said, and who does not lose his soul in order to save it in spiritual love, gains the world—the one who has all carnal desires within himself.

For just as Peter indicates that the one who desires nothing carnal leaves everything, so he gains everything and keeps it for himself, even though he cannot attain it, because he longs for and busies himself with all its desires. Therefore the one for whom the world is not crucified suffers the loss of his soul.

Thus a twofold choice is set before us, so that each person’s recompense may remain according to his decision. If we wish to gain the world, we lose our souls; but if we wish to gain our souls, let us deny and lose this world, renouncing all its desires.

Let the faithful soul therefore see what ought rather to be chosen and what ought to be pursued. One of these will either destroy or save it, although it cannot retain the world and possess anything without itself.

Or what exchange will a human being give for his soul?

If you do not know from elsewhere, human being, read what the devil said to God when he sought permission to lay his hand upon Job: “Skin for skin,” he said, “and everything a human being has he will give for his soul” (Job II, 4).

He did not say this because he wished to preserve the soul, but in order to find an opportunity to harm it. Nevertheless, he knew that no other exchange for the soul lay within human power, although even this is insufficient unless the soul is redeemed by the precious blood of Christ.

For this reason every possible exchange must be rendered. David says also (Ps. CXV, 12–13): “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” As though he were saying: “I find nothing else that I can repay, except that I will take the cup of salvation”—that is, the cross of Christ’s passion—“and I will call upon the name of the Lord.”

For neither the cross nor the cup of the passion has any value without invocation of the Lord, nor does invocation of God have any value without the cross of which we spoke above, the cross that must be taken up for salvation.

The exchange for the soul is, first, the substance of the world: a person must leave himself and the things that belong to the world, insofar as he is of the world, and follow Christ, who is not of the world, so that through him he may acquire himself, having lost the world, and whatever lies beyond the world. [688]

Otherwise, if he gains this world while losing himself, to the detriment of his soul, what will he give in exchange for himself?

Behold the marvelous conclusion of God! Let those who glory in their own deeds hear, I ask, and who despise the simplicity of the holy Scriptures, while proposing, assuming syllogistically, and concluding, and thus joining together their plausible arguments for the capture of souls.

For this heavenly Teacher does not set forth a probable argument as his premise, but the truth itself, as an argument concerning free choice, when he says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” and so forth. Then he adds the assumption when he says: “Whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it,” and the rest.

But if someone refuses this and gains the world with the loss of his soul—because he lost the world by gaining it—what exchange will he give for his soul, when the world is his gain and his soul is his loss?

And thus, not by the law of dialectical art but by the divine law, through which he wisely orders all things, he concludes everything in such a way that all understand that the world will either be gain to a person and his soul loss to him—or, what is much more to be desired, the soul will be gain to God and to itself, while the world will be loss.

For no one can have Christ together with the world and follow him who is beyond and outside the world. Therefore there is no other exchange for the soul except that it leave the world and the things of the world, take up its cross, and follow him who calls us.

Perhaps someone will say that not everyone can leave the world and the things of the world. I reply that the divine word compels no one, but leaves them to their own choice. Nevertheless, the Apostle exhorts us that those who have should be as though they did not have, those who use this world as though they were not using it, and those who possess as though they did not possess (I Cor. VII, 31).

Although such people may appear to be in the world, they are no longer of the world. Therefore, since there is no other worthy exchange that can be given for us, let us leave the world and follow Christ, who was sold and handed over for us, lest we perhaps be entangled among the Egyptians and Ethiopians, who, according to the prophet, are given in exchange for Israel.

That exchange is ruinous for them. Therefore either there is no other exchange, or this is the true and only one: that all the gains of the world perish and the soul alone be saved. [689]

For the Son of Man

“will come in his majesty, and then he will repay each person according to his works.”

From the passage where the disciples are asked, “Who do they say the Son of Man is?” and Peter confesses, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” everything there and afterward concerns the Son of Man. The one who was declared by Peter, through the Father, to be the Son of the living God is to be understood as the Son of Man, because “the Word became flesh” (John I, 14). The Son of Man, the true Son of God, is shown in one and the same person as the one who must be killed and scourged. [Col. 0574A]

For his sake the cross must be taken up, and he must be followed unto death; for his sake the soul must be lost and the present life relinquished.

But if you fear, human being, enduring such great things for the sake of the Son of Man—or if you think that he is merely human because he shows himself destined to be crucified and to die for us—hear that he will come in the glory of his Father with his angels. There are not two persons, but one person and one Christ.

A great terror had gone before among the hearers, so much so that, when this was heard, Peter, the chief of the apostles, was scandalized, until he was rebuked by the sentence of God. Therefore joyful things follow sorrowful ones, and Peter’s confession is confirmed: although he had declared that he would die, he is the true Son of the living God who promises that he will come alive after death, in the glory of his Father with his angels.

For although he was made a little lower than the angels (Ps. VIII, 6) because of the death of the flesh, he is greater than the angels because they are his creatures, and he is their Lord. He is not greater by comparison, as the Arians wish—as though he were one of their number, although greater than they—but by divinity and majesty, which he possesses coequally with the Father. Therefore he is foretold as coming in the glory of the Father with his angels.

And it is not another person, but this same one, who will come in glory with his angels: the Son of Man. For in respect of his divinity he is rightly never said to come in glory, since he never departed from it.

I have said these things for this reason, reader: always be vigilant on account of heretical perversity, since heretics have thought wrongly about Christ in various ways.

“And then he will repay each person according to his works” (Ps. LXI, 13).

These promises are made to those who have denied themselves, taken up their cross, followed Christ, and lost their souls for Christ, so that the faithful Christian may be frightened by nothing and scandalized by nothing—not by death resulting from the sufferings of Christ, since he will come in the glory of the Father with his angels; nor by his own torments or the loss of possessions, since he will find a better substance laid up for him in heaven and enduring there, if he has lost here what is destined to perish; nor by the loss of life, since, as the Truth promises, whoever loses temporal life here will find eternal and everlasting life there, where Christ is in the glory of the Father, eternal life.

He also touches upon those who either do not wish to believe, or, if they believe, do not wish to possess the works of faith because they do not perform them.

But since the unspoken thought of the apostles or of those whom he had summoned to hear could have generated such a scandal within them, and they might say inwardly in their hearts: “You promise us your killing and death, and urge us to death and to endure everything; and because you promise that you will one day be present in the glory of the Father with your angels, and further assert that you will repay each person according to his works, you present this as something that will happen only after long days, if it happens at all, and defer it to a distant time”—the most kind Jesus, who knows all hidden things, foresaw such thoughts and temptations, which could arise in the minds of the weak and, once arisen, could be set before them.

Therefore, to drive away their present fear or thought, he repays believers with a present reward, so that those who desire to rejoice in a future vision might be consoled by a promise close at hand.

For he says as follows:

There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.

The discourse and promise of almighty God is therefore wholly filled with joy and consolation in hope of future things, since all could hope for what he had previously promised to everyone concerning the future, while here he confirms to a few that he would show himself coming in his kingdom before they had tasted death. This indeed was because he transformed himself in that glory on the mountain before the disciples whom he had taken with him [Col. 0575B], in which he had promised that he would come in the glory of the Father with his angels.

It should be noted that the kingdom of Christ in which he was to come, so that they might see him coming in his kingdom, is itself the glory of the Father. For just as the kingdom of Christ is the Father’s kingdom, so the glory of the Father is Christ’s glory, which was displayed on the mountain, though to only a few. Thus those who had seen it, and the others who had heard it from them recounting that they had finally seen it, would be strengthened in faith concerning the Son of Man, because he had been seen in glory: namely, that he was the true Son of God who is also the Son of Man.

But those are chosen and taken up who can still, while in the flesh, be suited to that vision which is perceived more deeply in the mind; concerning this some discuss more extensively. For what shone before their eyes corresponds to those [Col. 0575C] of whom Peter says: “Like newborn infants, desire rational milk without deceit” (I Peter 2:2). Paul also spoke of them, saying: “I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able, nor are you even now able” (I Corinthians 3:2).

That vision, however, which is heavenly, and the understanding of the Word, belongs only to the more perfect, who have weaned senses, so that together with these three who are taken up they may understand divine things.

These, then, were the ones standing of whom he speaks: those who have their steps firmly planted with Jesus and were standing with him where Jesus, the Word of God, stood. Yet they did not all stand equally. For among them there is with the Lord a great difference in the manner of one person’s standing compared with another’s. Therefore it is said not of all who were standing with Jesus, but of some of them—those who stood, as it were, more firmly [Col. 0575D]—that they would not taste death until they saw the Word of God who came to human beings and became flesh.

Nevertheless, he does not expressly name those of whom he speaks, lest perhaps the others should be moved by envy; rather, he says without qualification that there are some among those standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.

For this reason he teaches the faith of our hope by deeds and words, when he both showed himself transfigured to some of them on the mountain and shone forth. At that time he was speaking to the people, at least in the hearts of the apostles, so that they might see and hear inwardly what Paul declares that he saw and heard when he was caught up to the third heaven, where he truly heard and saw unspeakable things (II Corinthians 12:4).

We therefore [Col. 0576A] can neither deny nor ought to deny that the apostles, before they departed from this life, saw something of this kind, in which they perceived the kingdom of God inwardly and understood the Son of Man coming in his kingdom in the power of the Holy Spirit.

This vision, brighter at times than the sun, flashes forth and shines in the understanding of the saints. Hence it is that sometimes it is first found by faith and then by understanding, even while one remains in the flesh, among those who seek it, when it enters the thoughts of the faithful. Thus someone sees and comprehends the excellence of the Word of God, which dissolves and refutes every persuasion of falsehood and introduces confession of the truth, so that he sees the Son of Man—that is, the Word of God—coming with flesh in his kingdom, by faith and understanding.

Whoever sees the Word of God in this way—that is, Christ, God [Col. 0576B] and man—not only dissolving and refuting the persuasions of his adversaries, but also making clear the evidences within his own mind, sees not only the kingdom but also the glory of the Word of God.

If something of this kind sometimes occurs in God’s elect, what do you think the inspiration and illumination of divine understanding was like in the apostles at that time? They were undoubtedly instructed by words, and instructed also by realities. Thus both things can stand together: inwardly, some of those standing there saw him coming in his kingdom in the power of God before they tasted death; and outwardly, on the mountain, with their bodily eyes, they saw him transfigured in the glory of eternal brightness. In this way they were instructed inwardly and outwardly.

For he had imposed a heavy burden upon human weakness when, once human beings had begun to possess the sense of life [Col. 0576C] through the desire for living, they had to lose the fruit of life—which presently delighted their bodily senses—and deny themselves, that is, refuse to be what they had begun to be, although they had acquired the beginnings of this perception through the inclination of the will.

Otherwise, if the apostles had not been strengthened in every respect, they could not have abandoned the attractions and pleasures of the present life, held back by uncertainty and doubt concerning hope; nor could they have desired the things of the cross and death or denied themselves.

Therefore the apostles, and all who are perfect in life, saw these things in whatever manner, so that thereafter they would not hesitate to taste death for their sake.

For two deaths are said to exist—although a third, the death of the soul through sin, is also mentioned—the first and the second. The first, which is bodily death, is called the tasting of death; the second [Col. 0576D], however, is called true death, by which human beings are condemned eternally.

If the statement that those standing there did not taste death until they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom is to be understood of this death, it follows that afterward they certainly tasted death, because they died by this momentary death.

But if the promise concerns that eternal death—that those who have remained beside the life which is Christ cannot die, because they already possess eternal life when they see Christ coming in his kingdom, since they understand, believe, confess, venerate, and adore him—then it was said that such people would not taste death because they stand more perfectly beside him who is life.

Hence [Col. 0577A] “the gates of hell will not prevail against them,” since they will not taste death eternally—unless perhaps the word “until” means that they would taste it afterward, when they had seen the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.

But it would be utterly impious to believe this concerning the saints. For “until” does not define a period such that, once it has passed, something that had not previously happened will occur; rather, it explains the necessary reality.

Similarly, elsewhere he says to the disciples: “I am with you every day until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 24:14). This might seem to mean that he will no longer be with them after the age has been consummated, so that the disciples would have a better state in the time before the consummation of the age than in the future, when we say that they will reign with Christ.

It is therefore absolutely necessary to understand [Col. 0577B] that if he will not abandon us until the end of the age, so that he is with us every day of the age, he will much more be with us after the end of the age, when the saints, completely stripped of mortality, will reign with the Lord.

Thus in this passage “until” is not set as a finite limit, but as an indefinite one. Whoever has once seen the Son of Man coming in his kingdom and in his glory, and has seen him coming into his kingdom in power, will no longer taste death for eternity.

If someone wishes to ask what difference there is between tasting death and seeing death—for divine Scripture seems to vary in these expressions—it says that death comes upon some, that some are followed by death, and that death absorbs others.

Origen [Col. 0577C] asks about the differences among these expressions, lest perhaps tasting death should be more serious than seeing it, and following death worse than tasting it. But for death to come upon those whom it was following and to seize them seems likewise to be more serious; being absorbed by death, however, appears to him the most serious of all.

And so, as I said above, “not tasting death” in this passage seems rather to have been spoken of temporal death.

## Chapter XVII

After six days Jesus took Peter, James, and his brother John and led them up a high mountain privately, and he was transfigured before them.

Why Peter, James, and John are separated from the others in certain passages of the Gospels, and what privilege they possess, is clear if Peter’s dignity, his merits, and the firmness of his virtues are weighed. For they are the ones who appeared to be pillars [Col. 0577D], of whom he had said: “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom” (Matthew 16).

Meanwhile, reader, do not think it a small thing to stand with Jesus. For unless they had first been established so that they might stand firmly upon the rock, they could by no means have followed him as he went before them and ascended the high mountain of his ascent, and by contemplation looked inwardly upon the divine majesty.

Therefore, although the other apostles also possess the same firmness in Christ, these are chosen by him, who looks into the heart of each, for the sake of the divine dispensation.

These two, James and John, are called “sons of thunder,” because they were born from the majestic utterance of the thundering God, who cried out to them from heaven with magnificence [Col. 0578A]: “Come after me” (Mark 1:17). For this reason they follow him.

Although these same words seem to have been spoken also to Andrew, these alone are chosen to be led to the heights—not because Andrew should be judged inferior, since he is placed before those two in the catalogue of the apostles, but because of the mystery. We are to understand that only those who are established with Peter upon the rock which is Christ will not taste death, and that it is granted to them alone to remain steadfast.

These are also the sons of thunder, because they received their teaching from no other source than heaven, from the voice of the most high God who thunders. Jesus certainly cries out and thunders to them every day, saying: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew 11:15).

Only three are taken up onto the mountain because in them the order and number [Col. 0578B] of the heavenly kingdom are prefigured. The whole Church is to be gathered from the origin of Noah’s three sons, and from them will come the entire future election of those who will ascend into heaven with Christ.

Christ is the firmness and strength of these people. Their teaching sounded in the voice of thunder from heaven and terrified everyone with the flashing proclamation throughout the world, so that the various regions of the earth were shaken—those regions described under three names. Thus it should not be said that Asia alone believed; Africa also and Europe, redeemed by Christ’s blood, are led from the depths to the heights.

“And after six days,” or, as Luke testifies, “after eight.” For in this passage Matthew is read to have said “after six days,” while Luke says “after eight.”

Yet neither is believed to have departed from the truth according to the letter [Col. 0578C], nor does anyone disagree with the truth while they seem to consent to one another as though neither agreed with the other.

It should be understood that Matthew, having mentioned days, spoke of the whole by the whole, while Luke expressed a part by the whole. For on the day when it was said, “There are some standing here who will not taste death,” part of the day had already passed; and on the day when he took them up and ascended the mountain, part of the day still remained.

Therefore, the parts that Matthew omitted to mention—virtually the two outer portions—Luke counted together as the whole day, so that there would be eight days.

Here we recognize the customary figure of speech called in Greek *synecdoche*, which in Latin may be called either “the whole from a part” or “the part for the whole.” This figure is very often found in the sacred Scriptures.

Here both evangelists employed it, not without great mystery [Col. 0578D] concerning the realities signified. For when Jesus had said, “There are some standing here who will not taste death,” one of the evangelists spoke of six days afterward, while the other spoke of eight.

One evangelist counted the first and the last days so that there would be eight; the other, holding only the six in the middle, omitted the two outer days. Thus, when the six ages of the world had been completed, the glory of God—which will appear in the seventh, that is, at the end of life—was proclaimed.

Luke, however, who says that they were taken up after eight days, suggests that whoever follows Christ, carries his cross, and loses his soul for his sake, persisting in faith, will not taste death forever until he sees the glory of the resurrection of the eighth day and rejoices with the Lord, himself also taken up onto the mountain [Col. 0579A].

For whoever hears Christ’s words sounding from heaven in the voice of thunder and establishes his steps upon the rock which is Christ will see the glory of Christ, which came to be on the eighth day through the grace of the resurrection.

Hence many psalms are also written “for the eighth.” For the one who loses his soul for the sake of the Word of God will save it when Christ fulfills his promises on the eighth day of his resurrection.

The same applies to the six days in which the works of the world were created, so that through the days, the times, and the world we may understand its completion. When these have been fulfilled, the future resurrection will be shown.

Those who have been led out of the world with these three, so that they rise above the world and transcend the cycles of this age and the fleeting courses of life, as though placed in a high position, will see the brightness of the future resurrection and receive the fruit of eternal life.

Such is the evangelists’ varied weaving of sentences [Col. 0579B], their varied alteration of words, the insertion of certain actions, and, in some places, a kind of recollection.

For in the Gospel Christ’s garment is fashioned in many colors and painted with heavenly texture; it is also adorned with a manifold understanding of sentences, as though marked with the precious stones of the most valuable gems. Thus it appears woven throughout from above, one tunic of Christ’s fleece, adorned with the diverse and countless flowers of virtues and miracles.

In considering its appearance, diligent reader, you will scarcely find what you ought first to admire.

Therefore, as I have already said above, no syllable, no arrangement of words or sentences [Col. 0579C] in the Gospel, and no alteration in the statements, should be read casually in passing. Nothing in these things is empty of mystery; everything is full of sacred meanings.

This is especially true of the transformation that took place on the holy mountain, where only three chosen disciples saw it, because “on the testimony of two or three witnesses every word stands” (Matthew 18:16).

Two men from among all the patriarchs are chosen to be seen by those same three with the Lord as witnesses. Both their number and the choice of these persons are a great sacramental manifestation.

The three whom we have already mentioned are perhaps also taken up for this reason [Col. 0579D]: no one can see the glory of the resurrection unless he has preserved the entire mystery of the Trinity with the uncorrupted sincerity of faith, gathered into this fellowship of faith from all three parts of the world.

The first of them, and not without reason, is Peter, because he was the first to receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Next is John, to whom the Virgin Mother was entrusted because of the privilege of virginity. James, too, was the first from the company of the apostles to ascend victorious, his priestly throne marked with his own purple blood and whitened in Christ.

For such reasons, and others of this kind which I have briefly enumerated above, these three are led to the heights. They were already above the world, so that they might see Christ not in the form of a servant but in the form of the glory of God. For those who are below cannot see him in the form of God, but only in the form of a servant.

Therefore he shows himself to each person according to what he sees [Col. 0580A] to be beneficial. But after the six days have been completed, on the eighth day, already above the high mountain and the elevated throne, he will appear glorified to the elect only in the form of God.

It was not said without reason that he was “transfigured,” since he was transfigured before them—namely, before those who ascended with him privately and separately onto the high mountain, withdrawn from all the crowds of the world and from the tumult of earthly disturbance.

For although Jesus came in the valley of humility, he is rightly seen crucified only above a mountain as well. Isaac, too, as a figure of Christ, is read to have been offered only on a mountain.

Therefore, what he did in this passage, and the miracle that shone before those who saw it, signified far more by the event itself than they had seen, so that the place and the transfiguration itself [Col. 0580B] indicated the height of the Godhead. The transformation took place where the height of judgment was symbolized and the contemplation of truth appeared.

Nevertheless, the question is raised: what kind of transformation was this? Did he lose his former form and the reality of his body? Or was the body that appeared spiritual or aerial?

I believe neither of these alternatives: neither that he lost the former form or appearance of his body, nor that he changed it for that moment into an aerial or spiritual body.

But how he was transformed the Evangelist shows when he says: “His face shone like the sun, and his garments became white like snow.” These words proclaim nothing other than the brightness of his face and the whiteness of his garments.

Thus, where the brightness of his face is shown and the whiteness of his clothing is described [Col. 0580C], his substance is neither denied nor removed; rather, his glory and brightness are commended and increased. That brightness shone as though from the treasures of God, so that the reality of his body was not taken away, while the glory that was to be in Christ was not concealed.

It is therefore clear that the brightness which flowed outward through Christ’s garments proceeded from that inner light of his which no bodily eye of the human race can behold, as it is written: “No one has ever seen God” (I John 4:12).

Thus the divine majesty tempered the form of this vision so that the vision would be wondrous, proclaiming the divinity in Christ, and yet human sight, belonging to mortal beings, could endure it.

One form was therefore present in the garments and another appearance in the face, but both were wondrous. Thus he who was visible in the flesh suddenly appeared before his own people radiant with light.

It is not without reason, however, that the question is asked: since we know that it is written of the saints, “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in their power” (Matthew 13:43), why is Christ’s face here rightly compared with the brightness of the sun?

Will the saints therefore have such great brightness in the kingdom of the Father—which it is impious to believe—as the one who will justify them in himself? Who but a heretic could say this?

Therefore, because what is accomplished in the dispensation of human salvation is divine and wondrous, we must believe that it was shown in this way not without great instruction.

It seems to me that this happened for four reasons among others:

First, because he was still mortal, and the mortality of his flesh [Col. 0581A] did not allow the brightness of his divinity to be displayed as it truly was;

or because, before the eyes of those who saw him, he moderated it so that they could behold the magnitude of his radiance, lest the light of the sun should appear in him seven times brighter than it now is;

or also because the light of his glory was then modified in him so that he displayed only the form which he knew he would show to the elect and the reprobate on the day of judgment;

and, to speak more fully and appropriately, because he was already displaying the very form of his limbs, showing beforehand with what and how great a glory the saints themselves will shine in the future, in their own glory.

For he who “calls into existence the things that do not exist as though they did” (Romans 4:17) caused to appear in Christ things that did not yet exist, so that through them those things which had been seen in him and were still to come might be known with greater certainty.

Thus the Lord was transformed into that glory [Col. 0581B] in which he would afterward come in his kingdom, which is the Church.

For this reason these three did not taste death until they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. To have seen him transfigured in the form of glory was already to have seen him coming in the kingdom of his glory.

In this transformation, the glory of the majesty of the Godhead was added, but the face of his humanity was not removed. Therefore, when the brightness of his face and the whiteness of his garments are shown, as I said, neither the reality of his face nor that of his garment is denied; rather, it is made abundantly clear whose brightness and whiteness shone forth.

Hence some wish to assert that at the resurrection of eternal judgment we will not possess naked bodies, although they will be incorruptible, but bodies spiritually and incorruptibly woven about with the outlines of garments [Col. 0581C].

For this reason his garments are read to have become white like snow. And, as another Evangelist says: “Such as no fuller on earth can make” (Mark 9:3). What a fuller can make on earth is corporeal and subject to touch; it is not spiritual or aerial, deceiving the eyes and appearing only in a phantasm. Likewise, if the coverings of the body that will exist in the future exist at all, they will be spiritual and real, not otherwise.

Moreover, when Mark says, “His garments became shining, exceedingly white like snow, such as no fuller on earth can make white” (Mark 9:3), he indicates the spiritual or moral understanding of this passage.

I therefore believe that Christ’s garments, with which the most glorious Jesus is clothed [Col. 0581D], signify the teachings of the Gospels. When those who ascend with him onto the high mountain are with him, these garments become exceedingly white and shining.

Since there are many kinds of white garments, the teachings about Christ in the Gospel, with which he deigned to be clothed, become, for those contemplating divine things, not merely white but white and shining like light.

If the humanity of Christ is seen so illuminated by splendor in his divinity when the mind is raised to higher things, what do you think is the greatness of the brightness with which the divinity shines in the humanity of the flesh?

Therefore both Evangelists significantly say: “His face became like the sun, but his garments white like snow.” For he is the sun of righteousness who shone forth and illuminated believers unto righteousness.

But such and so great a one is seen nowhere except on the high mountain [Col. 0582A] by those who have deserved to ascend with him to the heights and to understand the divine and human things in Christ.

For both natures in him are white and glorious. One aspect is seen by those who understand only the things above as more splendid than the sun from heaven; the other, which is of the earth, is whiter than snow, when his glory is recognized and the one and same Christ, the Only-Begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth, is seen (John 1:14).

Everything in the Gospel that concerns his garments and proceeds from him has this brightness in the face and this whiteness throughout the weaving of its words and sentences. All these things concerning him are so white and so brilliant that they are “such as no fuller can make on earth.”

We may therefore understand these fullers, as Origen taught [Col. 0582B], to be the wise men of this age who cannot make such garments of doctrine—without prejudice to a higher interpretation. They devote themselves to philosophy and all the liberal arts, study them daily, and delight in them, so that by their eloquence they may persuade people to their teaching and bend the minds of individuals toward their deceptions.

They greatly boast that these teachings are splendid, and seem to adorn them with their words, so that by the skill of their art they may lead people into their shameful interpretations and perverse doctrines.

From this they attempt to whiten their discourses, as though by the art of a fuller, and to make them white through their eloquence.

But none of them on earth could forge or fashion anything of this kind, because they were of the earth [Col. 0582C] and therefore understood only earthly things, and those very few.

Our most merciful Savior and most skillful teacher Jesus, however, showed his shining garments to those ascending with him above the mountain—not to just anyone, but to those who were worthy and most pleasing.

Although the fastidious and unlearned despise them, he showed garments more splendid than the art of those fullers could make.

Therefore, as I have often warned—and must frequently continue to warn—let no one read the Gospel or the divine Scriptures carelessly. Let no one judge the higher utterances of the philosophers to be such that any of them, anywhere or at any time, has been able to make or say anything like what has been described.

And so that the things taking place on the mountain might be shown to be even more wondrous:

“Behold,” he says, “Moses and Elijah appeared to them [Col. 0582D], speaking with him.”

Whoever understands that the Law is spiritual, that the Law is signified through Moses, and that the prophecies of all the prophets are represented through Elijah—prophecies which no faithful person at all doubts were spoken beforehand concerning Christ—understands perfectly why these two alone appeared with him on the mountain and in glory.

Luke shows this sufficiently clearly when he says that these two were seen with him speaking in glory: “And they were speaking of his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem.”

Here he shows that the Law and prophecy are always with Jesus and speak with him, and that they proclaim with repeated voices everything that he did in the world and everything that he was to suffer in Jerusalem.

Therefore, so that the faith of the apostles [Col. 0583A] might be confirmed and their understanding increased, they are seen here with him in glory. One of them is mystically understood to have come from heaven, to which he had been caught up; the other to have risen from the underworld.

Concerning this sign it had been said to Ahaz through the prophet Isaiah: “Ask for yourself a sign from heaven or from the depths of hell” (Isaiah 7:11). We also read that the Jews asked for a sign from above.

But here reason more appropriately required that those two be shown, between whom Jesus was seen in glory: for the Law and prophecy never cease to proclaim him, and, like two witnesses, they always speak with the Word.

For there can be no Law without the Word, nor prophet or prophecy unless it prophesies concerning the Son of God.

Thus Peter and the sons of thunder behold Moses and Elijah speaking with Christ in bodily glory [Col. 0583B]. We too, although unworthy, hear them conversing with him every day, and contemplate them glorified in the Gospel, because the Law and prophecy have been fulfilled in him.

For this reason, when those two departed, Jesus alone remained, because “the Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16).

Then the glory of their faces was set aside, so that Jesus Christ alone—whom they had proclaimed, concerning whom they had foretold all that was to come—might be seen in the glory of God the Father and announced among all the nations by those who are able to see them continually speaking with him.

For these two alone teach concerning his departure and all the mysteries of everything he accomplished.

Although they seem to have departed, because they now proclaim nothing new, Moses still teaches us about him today, and Elijah—that is, prophecy—speaks about him.

Today we see Moses glorified with Christ on the mountain [Col. 0583C] in greater glory than the sons of Israel, and we now venerate him, not with his countenance unveiled, but with his face unveiled.

We do not find Moses or Elijah without Christ, nor is Christ proclaimed without these two witnesses.

Although these two alone are joined to the Lord in a fast of forty days, the Lord nevertheless is the only one who is read to have fasted without the support of another, even though both of them fasted in the wilderness.

By these indications it is clearly shown that the Law and prophecy announced in words and deeds only what Christ fulfilled.

Otherwise, wherever one of them is seen without Christ, he is certainly proved to be without glory [Col. 0583D]. For whoever sees Moses alone or Elijah alone cannot see together with them the Word of God who came to that prophet or the other.

And wherever the Word of God is not present, such prophecy or Law is truly empty of the truth, because Christ, the Word of the Father, is truly the truth.

But Peter answered Jesus: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make three tabernacles here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”

O the profound blindness of human ignorance, enveloped in such dense darkness that it can scarcely, or never, rise up to see the light of God’s glory! Behold, blessed Peter is instructed by so many lessons and raised up by so many praises; yet immediately afterward [Col. 0584A]—although he spoke out of the affection of his love for Christ—we must consider, so to speak, how foolishly he speaks and in how many errors he becomes entangled.

For when God came in the flesh, “the Tabernacle of God” was made “with human beings” (Rev. XXI, 3). Not three, certainly, but one; for although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons, their luminous and glorious tabernacle is nevertheless one. Likewise, although three appeared in glory—namely Christ, Moses, and Elijah—one cloud alone overshadowed them and, as one tabernacle, covered and overshadowed them all. That tabernacle, because it is Christ himself, is the luminous cloud which, without sin, protects from all heat both itself and those who are with it, and illuminates them. For this is the proper function of a tabernacle: to overshadow certain persons beneath it.

Hence the luminous cloud, in which the Holy Spirit was present, overshadowed those who were one with Christ in the Gospel; and it did not exclude these three, who were below, but made them one. Nevertheless, by its example of repose and rest, it showed all of them a more divine and splendid rest: the rest of eternal peace, which would protect and illuminate them all at once.

While these things were taking place, behold, Peter, in this assertion of three tabernacles, fell into four errors, and even more. The first was that he resolved to make three tabernacles from which they would soon depart; for God does not dwell in things made by human hands (Acts XVII, 24), nor beneath arrangements of leaves, since there is one tabernacle—the Gospel—in which the law and the prophecy are joined together and fulfilled.

Another error is that he equates servants with the Lord. A third, as far as can be understood, is that he did not think the day of judgment was already approaching without death intervening; and therefore he says: “Lord, it is good for us to be here.” This too, as I have said, is false; for if it were truly good, they would certainly have remained in that place, and then no one else would have received their assistance—not to mention the human race, but not even their fellow apostles, who had not ascended with him to that same place. For Peter does not seem to consider those in whom charity was especially commended.

A fourth error is further disclosed by his supposing that tabernacles would be made in the kingdom of God by human hands, where there will be neither heat nor cold, neither rain nor heat, and certainly no disturbance of any kind.

Thus, although blessed Peter was surrounded by so great a light of glory and so great a radiance, and enticed by the sweetness of an immense delight, no one can deny that he was mistaken, even though he spoke without knowing what he was saying. Therefore I ask you, blessed Peter—most humbly—if you were taken up with Christ onto the mountain so that, by fixing tabernacles, you might possess the Lord alone with a few others: if this pleases you, why do you equate servants with the Lord? What, then, do you think of yourself and of your fellow apostles? Perhaps you wish to associate two persons with each tabernacle? Perhaps this glory appears so great to you that you are pleased for them to be the Lord’s, while you prefer that you and the others should be servants of the lords in the individual tabernacles you intend to construct.

Nor do you consider that Moses and Elijah would never and nowhere wish to be without God the Lord. But now, since you are so intent on this, which of you will be the Lord’s servant, which Moses’ servant, and which Elijah’s? It would therefore be more tolerable if you had said that one tabernacle ought to be made for the Lord, with whom the five of you could all be together.

But now, if I may speak with pardon, you seem to me to be mistaken; and the evangelist too testifies that you did not know what you were saying. Therefore we must consider with the fullest attention, throughout all that was done and said before the apostles, how difficult it was for them to arrive at firmness of faith and solidity of doctrine, so that before the coming of the Holy Spirit they possessed little strength.

This, then, is why blessed Peter is moved by such powerful impulses. Although his love for Christ and the magnificence of his faith are evident, error is nevertheless responsible for his promising to make three tabernacles: one, as though privately, for Jesus; another [Col. 0585B] for Moses; and another for Elijah—as if one tabernacle could not contain them, or as if all could not remain together in one.

And, as Origen holds, this was maliciously brought about by the prompting of the devil, who was working through one who did not know the mysteries of God or what he was saying, wishing Jesus, Moses, and Elijah not to be together but to be separated from one another under the pretext of three tabernacles—a thing that could not happen.

For if Christ, the law, and the prophets are one, then Christ is truly proved to be the Son of God; and thus the law and the prophets are found to have prophesied truly. The law and the prophets bore witness to Christ, proclaiming beforehand what was to come in Christ; and Christ bore witness to the law and the prophets that they had prophesied truly, when he fulfilled their prophecy in the very events themselves.

Neither of them is proved to have spoken the truth without the other, if they are separated from one another—as cannot happen. Perhaps this was what the enemy, as that teacher perceived, desired to bring about by his evil suggestion, when Peter said: “Let us make three tabernacles here,” while, as the evangelist testifies, he did not know what he was saying.

Nevertheless, there is a remedy for the error: before beginning to do what belongs to error, the will of the most benevolent Master is devoutly sought. Yet it cannot be denied that Peter testifies that it was good: “Lord, it is good for us to be here,” he says. But if it had been good for them to be there, they would certainly have remained there and would not have failed to do what was good.

But because it was not according to the truth, it is not denied that it was false, just as with what he said: “Be merciful to yourself, Lord; this shall certainly not happen to you” (Matt. XVI, 22).

Nevertheless, since Peter had already been called blessed and holy by the Lord according to his purpose, and a son of God’s grace, what is the meaning of his error? We must therefore believe and confess that, according to the apostle Paul, everything works together for his good (Rom. VIII, 28), even if he was in some respect being goaded by the adversary; for what proceeds from devout love is close to forgiveness.

For he himself, as Luke says (Luke IX, 39), was suffering from sleep; and the others who were with him are said to have been weighed down—not by bodily sleep, but by sleep of the mind. Thus, just as we do not approve Peter’s ignorance in this saying, so we should venerate his outstanding love for the Lord and the fervor of his faith. He was so mighty an executor of his love that he could not keep hidden within him the signs of it that he so often displayed openly; rather, the fire he carried within burned outwardly.

That is why, when the disciples were asked above whom they said he was, he alone first answered for them all: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

That is why he did not want him to suffer, but rebuked him, saying: “Be merciful to yourself, Lord; this shall certainly not happen to you” (Matt. XVI, 22).

That is why, when the hour of his Passion was approaching and he himself said: “You will all be scandalized because of me on this night,” while the others were troubled, this man answered fearlessly: “Even if everyone is scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized” (Matt. XXVI, 31–33).

And again: “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death” (Luke XXII, 33).

And once more: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. XXVI, 35).

That is why he drew his sword and cut off the ear of the servant Malchus.

All these things, and many others, arose from the fervor of his faith and the ardor of his devoted love for Christ, although, in accordance with the divine dispensation, he was sufficiently exercised by temptations. As we believe, although he believed in these things, they immediately worked together for his good, since he was destined to become the shepherd of the Church, so that from his own weaknesses he might learn not only to be humbled but also to bear with others.

Yet it is pious to consider this: if, having seen the brightness of the Lord’s face, he wished thereafter to remain on the mountain and not descend even for a moment; if he rejected the glory of the world and everything that charms in the world, and was pleased only by the radiance that shone from Christ’s face—what may we suppose would have pleased him if at that time he could have looked upon Christ in his mortal body as he now beholds him, already stripped of mortality?

To speak plainly, no one could say how greatly he would have been pleased—beyond anything the mind could conceive.

Yet Peter should not be reproved so severely, as though he had departed from himself, having already been enticed by the grace of the future resurrection, when amid the mystical wonders of his astonishment he said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here.” For blessed Paul desired, with the same ardor of faith, to depart and be with Christ (Phil. I, 23).

Perhaps this man too, because he had been weighed down by sleep, thought that, released from the flesh, he was already seeing in ecstasy the likeness of the resurrection. And since he rightly believed that glory good, it was not enough for him to praise it: with a devotion superior to that of others, the energetic servant came forward and promised the ministry of a common service.

Although he did not know what he was saying, he nevertheless offered the service of servitude. His action did not display ill-considered insolence, but premature devotion, by which he sought to accumulate for himself the reward of labor.

For his not knowing what he was saying was a matter of human condition; but what he promised was an act of devoted service. Therefore Peter was not rebuked by the Lord: although it displeased God that he did not know what he was saying, such great devotion nevertheless pleased him.

And so, amid these words, a cloud appeared, most luminous, to cover and overshadow them, so that Peter might know that there was no need for three tabernacles to be made, since he saw them covered by a heavenly cloud and, as it were, sheltered beneath one tabernacle.

Hence the evangelist continues:

[Col. 0587A] “While he was still speaking, behold, a luminous cloud overshadowed them.”

There is no doubt that this is the cloud which received him from the eyes of all the apostles when he was lifted up into heaven (Acts I, 9). But in the Old Testament too we read that, before the children of Israel, a pillar of cloud went before them by day and a pillar of fire by night (Exod. XIII, 21); yet we do not find that either of these was luminous.

Indeed, before the coming of the Mediator, as it is written, “dark water was in the clouds of the air” (Ps. XVII, 12): that is, the knowledge contained in the law and the prophets was hidden and obscure, although many sought it. Some ask whether this cloud itself was corporeal or not; but what remains to be understood is that, whatever its nature was, it contained a great mystery.

For the teaching of the New Testament is no longer covered by a dark cloud, but through the luminous cloud the Father’s voice is clearly heard as it thunders. This cloud is proclaimed to have been neither fiery nor dark, but luminous. For Christ now comes not in the fire of terror, nor in the gloom of blindness, but illuminated by the light of truth—made radiant by the patriarchs and illumined by the prophets with the light of glory.

It should be noted that the luminous cloud holds and overshadows Moses and Elijah. How is it luminous if it overshadows? The power of the Most High also overshadows Mary (Luke I, 35). Therefore this cloud must be understood as something that illuminates and shines with respect to one thing, while overshadowing another.

It consequently takes Moses and Elijah away and conceals them. And although it holds and conceals them, Moses and Elijah no longer speak from the cloud in which they are hidden; the Father alone speaks through the cloud, and the luminous cloud alone expresses the Father’s voice.

Thus, clearly, the grace of the New Testament overshadows and preserves the law and the prophecy: it holds, conceals, and overshadows them in the letter; it preserves them in the spirit; it conceals them in riddles and figures; and it holds them in mysteries.

Thus it comes about that whatever the law and prophecy say, although it is retained for spiritual observance, is no longer heard through the Old Testament but through the New, just as God the Father alone seems to speak through the luminous cloud.

From then on Moses is silent, Elijah is quiet, and through the cloud alone the Father’s voice sounds and is heard:

“This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him.”

“This is”—as though he were saying: “This is the one who is my Son by nature, and this is the one who is beloved by me by nature.”

Therefore “this” is not an adverb of place but a pronoun indicating a person, because no one other than this one is nearer. And behold, the concern about fixing tabernacles has been removed, because Moses departed, and Elijah departed—men who were servants, not lords.

They departed, therefore, so that there might be no doubt about which of them the Father was speaking. But now, since he alone remained, it is certain that both the law and the prophecy had passed over to him, and that the Father’s voice was addressed to the disciples about no one other than him.

It was as though the divine voice were saying: “This one who alone remains is the Lord. This one alone whom you have followed is the beloved and only Son. In this one alone, and not in Moses or Elijah, I am well pleased. Therefore, above all and before all, listen to him.”

And when the disciples heard this, they fell upon their faces on the ground and were very much afraid.

That voice, then, which struck the disciples’ ears—whether the Lord caused it to sound through himself, through an angelic creature, or through an element that shone with light—nevertheless sounded through the cloud.

Because the voice proceeded from the cloud and cast the disciples down upon the ground, it was formed like thunder, just as on the occasion when, as his Passion approached, the same Son said to the Father: “Now my soul is troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name.”

Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”

The crowd that stood by and heard it said that thunder had occurred (John XII, 27–29).

But why did the crowd hear thunder there and not fall, whereas here, when the disciples heard the voice, they fell upon their faces? Unless it is because there pride swells, while here humility trembles.

Yet the mind does not tremble without reason when, through grace, it already possesses the reward of such trembling—the reward it has received.

Many explanations present themselves for why the disciples fell face down upon the ground.

First, they could not endure the glory of so great a voice from the cloud, nor the radiance of the cloud itself, which overshadowed Christ, Moses, and Elijah. These three were already one with Christ under one tabernacle, not three—the three tabernacles that Peter offered to build.

For the splendor of his face shone like the sun, and the brightness of his garments delighted Peter as he gazed in wonder. But amid all these things, unable to bear the power of the voice, they could not endure the voice that descended from the Father through the cloud. Therefore, as though moved by the attitude of one supplicating, struck by fear, they fell upon their faces.

They were exceedingly terrified by the novelty of the spectacle and by the testimony of the Father’s voice.

Regarding this testimony, since I recall that I have already said enough above, I have refrained from repeating the same matter. Except that some ask whether this voice came from the cloud for Moses and Elijah, who desired to see and hear the Son of God in the flesh, so that they might see and hear the things already fulfilled that they had believed about him and had once foretold would occur.

Or perhaps—and this is more fitting—the Father was teaching the disciples about the Son: that he was the Son proper to the Father, the one whom they had followed [Col. 0588D] and whom they now saw transfigured in glory, so that thereafter they would have no further doubt about him.

Hence the voice itself was such and so great that they could not endure it when they heard that he was the Son of God the Father, the one who had appeared to Moses and had said to him: “No human being shall see my face and live” (Exod. XXXIII, 20).

Perhaps, therefore, when they saw the face of the Son of God made radiant like the sun and heard the testimony of God the Father concerning him, they could not help being afraid. And so they were immediately humbled beneath the hand of God, just as we read that Moses and the patriarch Abraham were humbled.

Then the gracious Teacher approached, touched them, and said to them: “Rise, and do not be afraid.”

It was as though he were saying openly: “There would have been cause for fear if the voice had called out that Moses was to be heard, or that Elijah alone was to be imitated, since even they are certainly not pleasing without me.

“Moreover, the fact that he approaches after such great glory signifies mercy; the fact that he touches signifies the power of restoration—so that they might be revived for faith by the hand by which they had been created for life.

“He therefore commands them to rise from sleep, and by commanding drives away their fear. He touches them in order to restore their weak limbs to health; and those whom he heals with his hand, he also heals by his command.

“Do not be afraid,” he says, because those whom such violent fear possesses cannot receive sound teaching. Therefore he first drives away their fear, and then raises and lifts them up to himself [Col. 0589A], so that they might seek and attend to no other, but to the one whom the Father had sealed and shown to be unique and singular.”

And they, lifting their eyes, saw no one else except Jesus alone, because everything is in him. In him indeed are the Father and the Son; in him also is the Holy Spirit; in him are Moses and Elijah, even when they depart; and in him are the disciples as well.

Therefore it is not necessary for more than one tabernacle to be made, because when he alone is possessed, everything is possessed.

But Jesus is not shown alone on the mountain until the bright cloud covers him and, from the cloud in which the Holy Spirit was present, the Father’s voice sounds: “This is my Son,” and so forth.

Then, when the cloud shone above and the Father’s voice thundered through the cloud, Jesus was found to be alone. Although there had been three, as I said, one alone remained: Jesus Christ, who makes one all things that have been perfected.

For in that kingdom which is prefigured, Christ God will be one, “all in all,” when all together will fear him in the judgment that is to come.

Meanwhile, since it was good for us too to remain for a long time with Jesus on the mountain, only a few of the things we saw have been brought forward, and even those in the unpolished words we have offered. Therefore let no one regard these things as burdensome, since what we have omitted is of a higher order to speak about; indeed, we ourselves were unable to penetrate it.

As they were coming down from the mountain, the most gracious Savior therefore commanded them, saying: “Tell no one about the vision you have seen until the Son of Man rises from the dead.”

He wished to reserve this reward of faith for the future, so that honor might be rendered at the proper time to all the apostles, among whom the authority of the commandments would be shown to be no small matter.

For the form of the future kingdom and the glory of the triumphant one had been displayed on the holy mountain. It was in no way fitting that, before the victory had been completed, this should be proclaimed by the apostles; otherwise, because of the magnitude of the event, it might appear unbelievable, and after such great glory the cross that followed might produce scandal in inexperienced minds.

Accordingly, everything we explained above concerning his command that they tell no one that he was the Christ must be understood here in full: the cross of the Passion and the glory of the triumphant one were not to be proclaimed before their proper time.

Then the disciples questioned him about these matters, saying:

“Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”

The apostles, having now returned to themselves, compared what they had seen and asked about what they had heard. They had heard, according to the prophet Malachi, that the Pharisees taught that Elijah would come before the Savior’s advent, in order to turn the hearts of fathers toward their children and restore everything to its former condition (Mal. IV, 5).

But the disciples, thinking that the transformation of glory which they had seen on the mountain was the fulfillment of that coming, asked—as though they were saying: “If you have already come in glory, how is it that your forerunner Elijah, who has just appeared and departed, did not come first? Why then do the scribes say this?”

They asked this because the vision that had taken place on the mountain, in which Elijah too had appeared, seemed to them not to agree with the scribes’ tradition: Elijah appeared not to have come before Christ, but with Christ.

They therefore judged the scribes’ tradition to be false, because Christ had plainly come before Elijah appeared on this mountain.

Let us consider how prudently he answered them. He did not reject what had been handed down by the scribes about Elijah; rather, he indicated that another coming of Elijah before him had already taken place—a coming of which the scribes and Pharisees were ignorant.

And it should be noted that they say that, unless Elijah first comes according to the Scriptures, the Savior’s second coming cannot take place.

But he answered: “Elijah will indeed come at my second coming, in accordance with the reality of the body. Now, at the first coming, he has already come through John in spirit and power, because John was truly Elijah in spirit.

“But they did not recognize him, and they did to him whatever they wished.”

That is, they despised him, imprisoned him, and beheaded him.

“So,” he says, “the Son of Man will also suffer at their hands.”

By this statement he plainly indicates that, just as John went before in voice and word, announcing Christ the Word to the world, so, by announcing his Passion beforehand, he went before by the example of insult and harassment.

Hence he says: “They did to him whatever they wished,” because they were likewise going to do this to Christ.

Regarding this deed, it is not without reason that the question is asked: by whom was what he says—“they did to him whatever they wished”—done? For above there was mention of the scribes, not of Herod or Herodias, who killed him.

Likewise, even if we rightly understand Christ to have spoken about those who killed John, how are we to understand that these same people killed Christ? For he says this about John: “They did to him whatever they wished.” And then: “So also the Son of Man will suffer at their hands.”

Here [Col. 0590D] he does not distinguish the individuals who killed them, but gathers together as one the whole generation of persecutors of the saints.

Otherwise, Herod did not kill Christ, nor did the scribes and Pharisees kill John. Nevertheless, from both sides it is gathered that these did in Christ and those in John what they wished.

Accordingly, those who did something to John and those who acted against Christ were one body, one offspring, and members of one head.

Thus it is clear that the former and the latter were conscious of one another and accomplices in evil, so that Scripture speaks indifferently of either group or the other: that they did in John whatever they wished, and that the Son of Man would suffer at their hands—that is, at the hands of the same persecutors of righteousness by whom John also suffered.

Although we can truly say that the faction of the Pharisees consented to John’s death, and that Herod very plainly joined his own will to the Lord’s killing, when he sent him, mocked and despised, back to Pilate so that he might be crucified.

And when Jesus had descended from the mountain to the crowds, a man approached him, falling on his knees before him and saying: “Lord, have mercy on my son, for he is epileptic and suffers terribly.”

The works of the Lord are therefore great, since, even when we are silent, they themselves cry out. The prophet also testifies that they are great and mighty: “Sought out according to all his desires” (Ps. CX, 2), and prepared.

Therefore, as I often say, they do not arise from the outcome of events, but from God’s providence and from his dispensation for human salvation.

This is why, much earlier, when Jesus descended from the mountain after teaching his disciples the eight beatitudes, a leper first met him, so that, when they saw the miracle, the disciples’ hearts might be strengthened for faith.

Likewise here, because the crowds and some of the disciples could not ascend the mountain with Jesus, he descended to them for the sake of the dispensation of human salvation—as though from the lofty mountain of his divinity, where he had transfigured himself in glory before the more perfect.

And immediately: a man approached him, falling on his knees and asking on behalf of his son, who was grievously tormented by a demon.

He would not have approached him if Jesus himself had not first come with his disciples to the crowd below, which was suffering under the torments of many demons.

From this passage we must understand that all the cures and healings of diseases performed by Christ, and every kind of infirmity, when considered more deeply in their mystery, teach the profounder mysteries of souls and the different kinds of healing.

Therefore, those who are able to hear with greater attention or understand more subtly should have these matters examined before them, so that the powers of healing bodies and souls, compared and examined in relation to one another, may communicate many teachings about healing and demonstrate differences of character and the qualities of infirmities.

For that episode in which the leper appeared and pleaded for his own healing was quite different from this one, although it may seem close to it, in which a man, falling on his knees, pleads not for himself but for his epileptic son.

There are some who suffer, believe, and ask for themselves; and there are others who suffer while others plead for them: the centurion for his servant, the royal official for his son, the ruler of the synagogue and the Canaanite woman for their daughters.

Among all these came the woman who suffered from an issue of blood. No one pleaded for her; she pleaded for herself—not by asking with her voice or speaking, but merely by thinking: “She touched the fringe of his garment” (Matt. IX, 20), and she was healed.

The principle behind all these infirmities and healings is that all the ailments and weaknesses among the people which the most gracious Savior healed should be referred, according to the differences of their sufferings, to the infirmities of souls.

But since my subject now is not all the varieties of infirmity and healing, but the healing of the man brought before us, let us consider what ought to be understood from it.

For this epileptic is enveloped in many sufferings. First, he is often tormented most grievously by his infirmity; then, by the demon himself, because he is painfully afflicted and tortured, so that, driven mad, he throws himself into fire and water—or, what is worse, so that he could not even be healed by the apostles.

As I suppose, this was not without reason, since the apostles had remained below with the crowds and with the epileptic himself. During these delays, while the Lord remained on the mountain and performed exceedingly astonishing and wondrous signs of power, the disciples, separated from him, grew weak in faith; and consequently their faith did not accomplish the healing, in accordance with the promises of their devout Master.

Therefore he rebuked them most severely, together with those with whom they had sometimes associated:

“O unbelieving and perverse generation,” he said, “how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?”

Here he shows that, in his absence, the habit of their ancient unbelief had stolen upon them. By this saying he indicates that discipleship of Christ can contribute no power if, at the time of its exercise, it withdraws from faith as though the Lord were absent.

If anyone wishes to maintain that the apostles had already become perfect in faith, and that there was no unbelief in them by which the man could not be healed, he will entangle himself in many questions; and, overcome by Christ’s authority, he will cease to assert what he cannot confirm.

Therefore, when the father had brought him, wishing to move the most gracious Jesus to compassion:

He said, “I presented him to your disciples, and they could not cure him.” [Col. 0592C] They had no power other than the faith that is in Christ. Yet I presented him, and they could not cure him—perhaps so that Christ’s omnipotence alone might be proclaimed, while the apostles’ weakness was commended. Held back by this weakness, as was said above, they had not yet deserved to ascend with the Lord to higher things; indeed, remaining below with the crowds, they grew weak in faith.

Nevertheless, they were not weakened to such a degree as were the children of Israel while Moses lingered on the mountain, because they are immediately restored by what they hear, when the others recount what they had seen, and they are also restored by the miracle. Moreover, the father of the boy and the crowds are rebuked along with them as unbelieving, because they did not yet possess such faith that the demon could be expelled. Thus they wonder that those to whom power had formerly been granted—to cure the sick, cleanse lepers, drive out demons, and even raise the dead—had been entirely unable to cure this boy. The Lord plainly tells them the reason: “Because of your unbelief.”

Therefore faith must always be earnestly implored, because it is exceedingly rare. If the apostles are told, “O unbelieving generation,” what will he say about us? Like that lunatic, we now appear sound in faith and now weak; we believe for a time, but in the hour of temptation we wither, inclined to sin. Thus we are either hurled into the fire of our desires—“for all of them commit adultery; they are like a burning oven” [cf. Hos. VII, 4]—or we are submerged by the waves of the sea, where the dragon, king of all those who are in the waters, lies; he casts us down from the freedom of the soul into the depths of the sea, that is, into the evil and most wretched practice of this life, so that we are covered by the waves of our vices.

Of such people Wisdom says, while apparently commending the steadfastness of the righteous: “The wise person remains like the sun, but the fool changes like the moon” (Eccli. XXVII, 12). In such people one can indeed observe certain surges, as though they possessed the works of the righteous, so that they may steal praise from people who do not know the hidden conscience of their hearts. But if you examine them a little later, you will see such people diminish and fail like the moon from the light of righteousness, and be darkened by the shadows of their vices. Yet when you see such a person, what else will you call him but a lunatic? This does not mean that something descending from the defect of the moon causes a person to fall into the madness of sin, but that, just as the moon is darkened, so he is rolled about in the monthly cycles of his sins.

It should also be noted that the Evangelist calls him a lunatic in accordance with the father’s words and the common judgment of the people. This does not mean that he suffered any affliction from the moon, since he was tormented by an unclean spirit, but that the cunning enemy worked through his mockeries in the man according to the course of the moon, so that the people would think that he suffered from it. In this way God’s creature—which was created good and is extremely useful and necessary to human beings—was brought into disrepute, and its dishonor was turned against the Creator.

The devil does this by his artifice, so that faith may be preserved in nothing. Hence physicians speak about such cases however they wish. They do not think that these people have an unclean spirit, but some bodily disorder caused by the corruption of the brain’s humor during the moon’s course, since the moon also has a moist nature. We, however, because we believe the Gospel, say that an unclean spirit produces this affliction in human beings. Therefore such physicians must be addressed in a way that does not neglect God, from whom and through whom all healing comes; otherwise, when someone considers God’s creature blameworthy, he may seem to think something against God and thereby offend him even more.

Behold: in this miracle three persons are blamed together—the father, because he presented his son and secretly accuses the apostles; the apostles themselves, whose unbelief is marked; and finally the lunatic son himself, who was tormented by a demon. Nevertheless, although their faith is different, all are marked by one rebuke from Christ: “O unbelieving and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?”

Yet they are not all rebuked in the same way. Although the apostles were still unbelieving, as the Teacher of truth declares to them, we must not consider them perverse, since he had once sanctified them for himself. In one and the same body the members are diverse; therefore Christ speaks in such a way that everyone may see what applies to each one. Although the apostles had not yet been cleansed of unbelief so as to be wholly illumined by divine light, they were nevertheless far removed from the darkness in which that lunatic was tormented. Although they had not yet been fully illumined by the light of the sun, those who followed the Sun of righteousness were no longer entirely in darkness. But because they had remained below, the fervor and heat of the light were perhaps less intense.
