Therefore he still rebukes them together with those with whom they had been and from whom they had not yet been set free, so that they might be purified.

As for those who are counted with the father and those who are numbered with the lunatic, they are rightly rebuked together as one generation—not merely unbelieving but also perverse. To them, with the emotion of one who mourns, he says: “How long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?” This does not mean that the most gentle Lord and most meek Lamb, who “did not open his mouth before the one shearing him” (Acts VIII, 32), had been overcome by weariness or burst into words of anger. Rather, he speaks in the likeness of a physician who, seeing a sick person act contrary to his instructions, might say: “How long shall I come to your house? How long shall I waste my skill, while I command one thing and you continually do another and remain sick?”

For a long time already he had been enduring those with whom he was always present in affection and compassion. Thus he was not angry with the human being but with the vice. Through this one man, therefore, not only the apostles and the father are blamed, since they were still burdened by the vice of unbelief, but all the Jews and unbelievers are also touched, with whom the Word of God is laboring at the present time. Yet they do not hasten to receive healing.

Accordingly, in this one lunatic a great and evident mystery of Christ was displayed, just as in that leper when he came down from the mountain—except that the leper came of his own accord, whereas this man neither came nor cared to come, because he was being grievously oppressed by the demon. Nor are those who had received power to heal, or the father who pleaded on his behalf, free from blame, although the inability to heal does not always refer to the weakness of the healers but to the faith of those who are to be healed, as the Lord says: “Let it be done for you according to your faith” (Matt. XIX, 19).

Nevertheless, as I said, this entire rebuke must not be referred to the apostles, because although they were still unbelieving, they were not perverse. The lunatic, however, and the Jews whom he represents were both unbelieving and perverse, because malice had been introduced into them through perversity, so that they suffered evil from demons contrary to nature. Here the perversity of the whole human race is also rebuked. As though weighed down by their malice and conduct, he says to them: “How long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?”

The race is blamed in one representative person, since one generation is said, on account of its faithlessness, to comprise the whole human race—unless it is continually reborn into faith. For after receiving knowledge of the faith, many, as was stated above, grow lukewarm in the faith that works through love. Therefore they are not unjustly called lunatics until they become firm and steadfast.

But if the Lord had not come down from the mountain and first sought us on earth, no one would have come to him, no one would have healed us, and no one would have become sound. Thus the difference between the leper, when the Lord came down from the mountain and set forth the lessons of life, and this lunatic is shown in the kinds of sins; yet it is shown that there is one healing, from God alone.

For this reason he came, and for this reason he wished to suffer—but for how long? His suffering was not postponed for a long time from that moment, although Christ’s Passion began long ago and is still completed today in his members. That suffering he was already enduring in himself through patience, so that there might be a passion before the Passion; just as, after the Passion, it is fulfilled in his members until it reaches its completion.

After saying these things, the most merciful Savior said: “Bring him here to me.” The excessive torment of the sick man is shown by the command that he be brought, since he could not come. He commands those whose faith, however small, and whose ability to carry him were present—the apostles and the crowds, with the father also among them. Nor is it surprising if we say that the faith of the patriarchs was present, which could offer this demoniac, since he could not be saved without faith.

And Jesus rebuked him, and the demon came out of him, and the boy was cured from that hour by Christ’s power. The reason why he rebuked the one who was tormented by the unclean spirit, rather than the one who tormented him, although he ought rather to have rebuked the spirit, is clear. Since the boy was suffering and had been oppressed because of his sins, he ought rather to rebuke the one who needed correction than the one who can never again be corrected. Yet the sick man is struck by that word when he is recalled from madness and made sound.

Then the disciples came to Jesus privately and said to him: “Why could we not cast it out?” He said to them: “Because of your unbelief.” This is what he says elsewhere: “Whatever you ask in my name, believing, you will receive” (Matt. XXI, 22). Therefore whenever we ask and do not receive, the fault is not the inability of our Savior but the fault of those who pray, either because they ask wrongly or because they do not ask with complete faith.

After the lunatic had been cured, they came to him privately, as was their custom, to question him and be instructed more secretly, like members of his household. When he answered that it had happened because of their unbelief, he taught and trained them concerning how great their faith ought to be and what must be done in this work through faith.

“If you have faith,” he said, “like a grain of mustard seed, and say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ it will move.” By saying, “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed,” he showed—as one who looked into their hearts—that they did not yet possess such faith. Their faith was still being born, now through teachings and now through miracles, and was being instructed so that they might have perfect faith in him.

Nevertheless, no one should consider faith small if it is as great as a mustard seed. We have already said enough above about this seed, in the parable in which the kingdom of heaven is said to be like a mustard seed. In that passage we must understand that the thing to which the kingdom of heaven is compared is great. Therefore we must attend not to the smallness of the seed but to the one who is said to be like it. For this seed is entirely the seed of faith, which, when sown or planted in the garden of the Church, bore fruit. That is, it is the humanity of the incarnate Word, which grew into a great tree, and its branches spread over the whole world, so that the birds of heaven—that is, the saints—might dwell in it and rest from the heat beneath its shade.

It should also be noted that he says: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed,” so that our faith may be such and so great as Christ is. For if it is such and so great as the one from whom it comes, then it is complete and perfect faith. But not everyone’s faith is of this kind or of this magnitude. Therefore, when the apostles’ faith was made equal to a mustard seed, so that their faith concerning Christ and in Christ might be as great as he is, do not think that it was small—unless you foolishly think that Christ was little or nothing.

For although he was made lower than the angels and compared to a worm, as he himself says through the Prophet, “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. XXI, 7), he is nevertheless greater than the angels, because he is coequal and consubstantial with God the Father. Therefore this faith, which is as great as a mustard seed, is complete and incorrupt faith.

It is also the faith of which the Apostle says: “If I have all faith, so that I move mountains” (I Cor. XIII, 2), because through its command it can move mountains, as the Lord promises. This is the whole of faith, and therefore it is great faith. Because the heretics refused to possess it, their faith was not true faith; because sinners and false Christians violated it, their faith was not incorrupt or undefiled. For this reason they did not free themselves either from the torment of the full moon or from their own monthly afflictions.

Although every creature in some way hears the Creator, so that faith might command even mountains, Christ does not here speak of the mountains that we see with bodily eyes, but of the one that had been moved by the Lord and cast out by the lunatic. Pointing to it as though with his finger, he says: “If you say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ it will move.” Otherwise we do not read that Christ himself did this in bodily appearance; such an act would display ostentation rather than progress.

Therefore those who argue that the apostles had no faith at all must be refuted, because none of them moved mountains. That is not what the Lord intended, although it could have been done through faith. His entire intention and will concern the salvation of the human race, so that the apostles may receive power through faith where every opposition to faith and every corruption of what is good are found.

“And nothing,” he says, “will be impossible for you.” It is as though he said: Whatever good you ask for, since all things are possible to the one who believes. Some people, however, when they try to read this statement with excessive subtlety, weaken its simple meaning through their syllogisms, as though only what is nothing ought to be impossible for them, while everything else that exists ought to be possible. They even want “nothing” to be something, or perhaps they say that they could not make something from nothing, as God did.

But this interpretation belongs to idle people, as does the one in which they say that “without him nothing was made,” while arguing as though nothing were some entity that had not been made by God. In imagining this for themselves, they are themselves, not unjustly, found to be without God. Such argument is plainly far from the truth. I mention it so that those who are accustomed to raise this issue may restrain themselves from such language; for although it may provide an exercise, I do not know whether it can provide any fruit of understanding.

“This kind,” he says, “is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.” Thus, while teaching by what means the most wicked demon can be expelled, he instructs everyone in the way of life. [Col. 0597A] Hence the canonical authority says concerning monks who renounce the world: “In the places where they have renounced it, let them serve the Lord with fasts and prayers.” For through these two things soul and body are entrusted to the Lord, and the devil is excluded from the whole integrity of the human person, so that the devil’s cunning cannot operate in the soul, where prayers are vigorous, nor in the flesh, which fasts chastise.

Since he says, “This kind,” understand that he means either the lunatic alone, or every kind of demon, as capable of being overcome by these practices. For just as prayer prevails against the vices of the soul and reaches even to the flesh, so fasting hastens to suppress the vices of the flesh and reaches even to the purity of the soul.

While they were staying in Galilee, Jesus said: “The Son of Man is to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again.” And they were exceedingly grieved.

The excellent Teacher, in order gradually to lead the minds of the disciples to faith, always mixes sad things with favorable and gentle things, and joins opposites to miracles, so that he may raise their minds to divine matters and prepare them for every adversity. Thus, after Peter’s confession of faith, he announces what is contrary; and now, after the transfiguration on the mountain and after the miracle displayed before everyone, he again announces that the Son of Man is to be delivered, and so forth.

He is laboring to make them understand equally that he is the Son of God and the Son of Man, while remaining one and the same Christ. He appears to repeat here the same things about his death that he had said above, but this is not entirely so. It is one thing to show the disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things, and be killed; it is another to say, while he is in Galilee—a point we had not learned above—“The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men,” although he says all the remaining things similarly.

Since all scandal concerning his death was to arise, he repeats the same things many times and gradually introduces what he had not yet said, in order to lead them into faith. Above, it was said that he would be delivered; here, however, it is said not merely that he would be delivered, but that he would be delivered into the hands of men. There we learned from whom he would suffer and in what place he would suffer; here we learn that he would suffer many things from those already mentioned, though they themselves did not provide the cause that he should suffer many things. Rather, he—or those who delivered him into the hands of men—provided the cause of his Passion.

But perhaps someone may say that Judas delivered him into the hands of men, although Judas himself was also a man, and into whose hands he was delivered by someone else I do not know. The Apostle, therefore, recounts that the Son was delivered by God the Father, saying: “He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him for us all” (Rom. VIII, 32). To whom, do you think, did he deliver him? Was it first to the prince of this world, who put it into Judas’s heart to betray him and into the Jews’ hearts to kill him? Or did God the Father deliver him to those same Jews? Or did the Son himself deliver himself as an offering to God the Father for a pleasing fragrance?

Job too, and everything he possessed, was first delivered by God into the devil’s power; then, by the adversary himself, all his substance and possessions were delivered into the hands of plunderers who would seize them, after the devil had first received power from God. So perhaps we may say that, through some operation, the prince of the power of the air, who works in the sons of disobedience, receiving from God the Father the one delivered to him, delivered him into the hands of men, among whom Judas also was found—Judas, into whom Satan entered after the holy bread.

Consider, however, that God the Father delivered him in one way—or that the Son himself, because of his most merciful kindness, delivered himself—in order to save the human race. The hostile powers delivered the Lord into the hands of men in another way, after receiving authority: not for anyone’s salvation, but, so far as they were concerned, because they did not know the wisdom of God hidden in the mystery.

They delivered him not so that, by dying, he might destroy death, but so that hostile death might subject him to itself, like all the human beings who died in Adam, through whom death entered the world. Likewise, all those who killed Christ, to whom he was delivered by the devil because they were members of the devil, did this not according to the will of God, which had already been foreordained by God, but according to the will of the powers that wanted the Son of God to become subject to death.

It is therefore true that he was not delivered by men into the hands of men, but by the powers to whom the Father delivered him for us all, so that, in being delivered and becoming subject to the one to whom he was delivered, he might destroy the one who held the power of death. I do not mean the power of that death by which we all die bodily in common, but of that death which is contrary and hostile to the one who said: “I am life.”

“And they were exceedingly grieved,” he says (John XIV, 6). This grief did not come from unbelief, although they were still ignorant and did not know the mysteries of God; it came from love for their merciful Teacher. Otherwise, they knew that Peter had been corrected because he did not understand the things of God but the things of men (Matt. XVI, 23). Therefore Peter gave no further answer, nor did the others say anything; they were simply exceedingly grieved out of affection for his love.

They did not sufficiently understand or reflect upon what he had said: “And on the third day he will rise again.” Their grief over his death ought not to have been as great as their joy ought to have been over his resurrection. They were not considering how great was the power of the one for whom three days were sufficient to destroy death.

When they had come to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachma approached Peter and said to him: “Does your teacher not pay the didrachma?” Whether this statement is read as a question or spoken as an assertion, the meaning is the same: it was done deceitfully, so that they might entrap him while the Jews were plotting against him.

It is known to everyone that after Augustus Caesar, Judea became tributary, and all were bound by a head-tax. Hence Joseph departed with Mary, his kinswoman and wife, for Bethlehem. Since Jesus had been raised in Nazareth, which is a town of Galilee subject to the city of Capernaum, they demand tribute from him. Yet, because of the greatness of the signs, those who collected the didrachma do not dare to demand it directly from him; they approach the disciple, or maliciously ask whether he pays the tribute or contradicts Caesar’s will by refusing to pay the tax.

In accordance with this, elsewhere they ask: “Is it lawful to pay the tax or not?” (Matt. XXII, 17). From this it is clear that the payment here should not be understood, as some wish, as the tax of God’s temple and altar, but as Caesar’s tax, which had been imposed on them per head. Hence the Lord says: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Mark XII, 17).

In the Law, however, a sanctuary shekel was given, containing twenty obols. Here the didrachma is demanded, on which Caesar’s image was engraved. This tax is called a coin. The didrachma is so called because it contains two drachmas; these amount to six scruples, or thirty-six carats. It is believed that the Lord was in death for this many hours on our behalf, so that he might redeem us from the tax of the world and make us tributaries to himself.

When Peter entered the house, Jesus anticipated him and said: “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth collect tribute or tax—from their own sons or from strangers?” Peter said to him: “From strangers.” Jesus said to him: “Therefore the sons are free.”

Jesus anticipated Peter before Peter could tell him what had happened, and asked about what had been said or done in his absence, so that the apostles would not be scandalized by the demand for tribute. When they saw that he knew what had been said privately, they would believe that he was God and be consoled.

It was as though he said: “According to the flesh I am the son of King David, and according to divinity I am the Son of the living God; I am free from every tax according to human laws, and therefore I ought not to pay tribute.” For in every kingdom of individual nations, the sons must be understood to be free, so that they are not subject to taxation.

If this is so in the condition of human flesh, then much more should the sons of that kingdom be free in every earthly kingdom—the sons of the kingdom under which all earthly kingdoms exist. Christ and the apostles were outside the world, insofar as this Lord was of the heavenly kingdom and they were its sons.

But how wretched we are, who are counted by the Christian name, when he endured the cross for us and paid tribute, while we, for love of him, neither fulfill our vows nor pay tribute. We are free from taxes as though we were the king’s sons, except insofar as we take up again Caesar’s image in order to desire earthly things.

Otherwise, if we were outside the earth, we would indeed be free. If Egypt did not oppress us in slavery—for whose liberation the Son of God assumed the form of a servant—we would be free, although he did no work of clay or servile labor. Yet simply because he possessed the form of a servant, he paid tribute and tax, no different from what he paid for his disciples.

One stater was sufficient: one coin given for Jesus and for his disciple. Jesus did not owe it, but he paid it so as not to scandalize them, lest perhaps they kill him before the appointed time and give us an example that, insofar as it depends on us, we should scandalize no one.

Then he said to Peter: “Go to the sea and cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up,” and so forth. [Col. 0600A] In this miracle God’s foreknowledge and the greatness of his power are wonderfully revealed.

First, he was able, as God, to know beforehand that such a fish of such a size was in the sea and that it would have a stater in its mouth; or he may have foreordained that this fish should be the first to appear. Therefore there is no doubt that the stater in the fish’s mouth was created through him, and that by speaking he brought about what was to happen.

He did not wish to pay the tribute from Judas’s purse, lest he appear to turn the substance of the poor to his own uses, but from Peter’s trade. Therefore he sends Peter back to his own occupation, both to display humility concerning himself and to reveal higher mysteries through the miracle. The fish was in the sea, and the stater was in the mouth of a sea-fish.

I see this fish, divinely prepared, rising to Peter’s hook—Peter who had already become a fisher of human beings. I cannot determine which should first be admired: the foreknowledge of his divinity or the power of his majesty, by which he immediately brought it about through speech that a stater should be created in the fish’s mouth.

According to some, the stater is the sanctuary shekel, containing twenty obols. Others say that it is a half-ounce; we interpret it as a double didrachma, so that it could suffice for two. It should be noted, however, that the Savior did not say, “Pay it for us,” but distinctly, “Pay it for me and for you,” so that it might be understood that there is a great distinction between the Lord and the servant, between him who was without sin and him who was liable to many sins.

Nor should anyone wonder that he received Caesar’s image from such an appropriate place as the sea, so that he could give it for himself and for his disciple. In this way he demonstrated that he was not a debtor to the earthly kingdom, and yet he paid the debt—although he had not assumed it as something he owed, nor acquired it as something he wished to possess. He never wished Caesar’s image to dwell in us alongside the image of the invisible God.

According to mystical interpretations, this fish appears to be the first one that was caught. It dwelt in the depths of the sea, in the salty and bitter whirlpools of the world; it was the one who rose first from the dead. The stater found in its mouth is the solidity of faith contained in confession, to be paid for Peter and for the Lord—that is, for Christ and the Church—for Peter signifies the Church.

For them two didrachmas are paid: namely, the four Gospels that flowed from Christ’s mouth, which are four drachmas. Therefore the stater is not kept in the fish’s belly but in its mouth, in which grace has been poured out; for although one believes with the heart for righteousness, confession is made with the mouth for salvation (Rom. X, 10).

Otherwise, unless an interior meaning were present in these visible things, it would not be the nature of a fish that it should happen to be found on the shore of the sea, that it should hold a stater in its mouth rather than immediately hide within its entrails and swallow what it had absorbed with its mouth.

From all this it is clearly gathered that nothing in these events occurred by chance. They were known and prepared by God, so that the reality of the event might strengthen faith through the miracle and so that each detail might teach a lesson of virtue.

Thus neither the first fish caught by Peter, which others follow, is without a mystery, nor is the stater found in its mouth without a great miracle of instruction. For Peter, who had already become a fisher of human beings, is sent by the Lord to catch the first one, whom many others will eventually follow. Yet none of them is worthy to be drawn by Peter from the waves at Christ’s command unless he carries this coin of the tax in his mouth.

Hence the blessed Hilary, an outstanding teacher, says that this fish, the first caught by Peter for Christ, is the first martyr, Stephen, who was the first to be offered in martyrdom for Christ. In his mouth the stater of true confession was found, with the image of Christ impressed on its surface and engraved within and without.

As the first to be crowned with martyrdom, he rose to Peter’s rational hook; having been caught and saved, he was the first to pay, so that he would no longer have in his mouth the stater bearing the image of an earthly king, but instead would have the sanctuary didrachma, that is, the image of God. For “the words of the Lord are pure words” (Ps. XI, 7), and they were in him.

Thus, in a marvelous manner, one stater—that is, two drachmas—is found in the fish’s mouth, because he was already included in the census of human salvation. First Caesar’s tax was paid, and then the coin of God’s sanctuary, which was holy.

Concerning this it is said according to the Septuagint: “You shall take five shekels according to the holy didrachma,” which was also given for all the children of Israel according to the head of each one. But since it is not permitted for the sons of the heavenly kingdom to possess together the sanctuary didrachmas and the didrachmas of this world—defiled in metal, weight, and inscription—they must first pay, according to the Lord’s command, to Caesar, who is the prince of this world, and renounce the age; then they must pay to God the holy didrachma prescribed in the Law, so that from this didrachma the Law and the Gospel may be fulfilled.

Therefore, when they said, “Your teacher does not pay the didrachma,” the Savior commanded that the stater found in the fish’s mouth be given, in which there were two didrachmas. One didrachma was to be paid for us, since we had renounced the world; the other was to be paid to the heavenly God, with his image restored in us.

Otherwise no one is free from tribute, because “whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John XXI, 23). But those who remain in Jesus’ words are free with the freedom with which Christ set them free.

And you who are free—may your charity, acting freely in all things, defend our freedom as our advocate and desire that we be exempt from every tax under this example, so that we owe nothing else except to love one another. For this love is the tax owed to God and neighbor.

Therefore Christ, so as not to give scandal about himself to the impious and to instruct us, both provides and pays the tribute. He acts carefully, since he is free and belongs to himself, so as not to scandalize those who demand the didrachma, whether the kings of the earth or their sons.

For this reason he asks Peter to seek by his own craft how the price of the tribute may be paid, so that the preaching of the Gospel may remain free. He thus gives an example to everyone, as I said. Even if those who demand taxes are wicked and greedy, we should not scandalize such people over private matters, lest, having been scandalized, they sin still more—or lest, if some favorable circumstance should occur, they might be moved by God’s inspiration to convert to Christ’s teaching and be healed.

For such payment of the tax is freedom in Christ. Therefore the heavenly orator shows that he acts on behalf of his own, since all are free, provided only that they do not turn Christ’s freedom into an occasion of scandal.

### (Chapter XVIII)

“At that hour” his disciples came to Jesus, saying, “Who, do you think, is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” It was not without reason that “at that hour”—or “on that day,” according to the true readings of the manuscripts—was added. And therefore I think it should be asked why Matthew, with such care, added this phrase when he says: “At that hour the disciples came to Jesus, saying, ‘Who, do you think, is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?’” I certainly would not say that he did this without reason. Rather, as I have often pointed out, the wording of each event and its circumstances are full of meaning. Thus Mark says that when they came to Capernaum and were in the house, he asked them, “What were you discussing on the way?” But they kept silent, because on the way they had argued with one another about which of them was the greatest (Mark 9:33–34). Luke, however, relates that a thought arose among them about which of them was the greatest. From these statements we learn that the Evangelists do not disagree with one another in any respect, but explain one and the same meaning, so that we may understand that the apostles were still being stirred by envy among themselves. Since the Lord wished to heal them of the envy arising from jealousy, according to Mark and Luke he presents himself everywhere as God, to whom no secrets of the heart are hidden. For this reason he asks them on the way what they had been discussing. But Matthew, wishing to show from where this dispute had arisen, [Col. 0602B] says: “At that hour the disciples came to Jesus”—that is, when they saw the same tribute paid on behalf of Peter and the Lord. For they thought that by this the Lord had conferred the greatest honor upon Peter, so that, both on this occasion and because of the many privileges he had often received above his companions, they might judge among themselves that he would be superior to the other disciples in the kingdom of heaven. Accordingly, they suspected that if they questioned the Lord—as indeed they did, although they had already been convicted of discussing this among themselves on the way—they might cautiously discover from his answers whether Peter ought to surpass the others in rank and honor, or whether John, who was more greatly loved by the Lord, could be considered his equal, or whether James too should be counted with them, since he likewise had been taken up with them onto the mountain. Wishing to make clear that the disciples had previously been plotting this among themselves, Matthew therefore says that, after Jesus had spoken to Peter about the coin of the stater, “Take this and pay it for me and for you,” “at that hour,” or “on that day,” the disciples came to Jesus, saying, “Who, do you think, is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?”

Perhaps their opinion was recalled once more for this reason: Jesus had already said to Peter, in a way he had not said to the other disciples, “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, because you do not understand the things of God but those of men” (Matthew 16:23). Perhaps, then, for such a reason or something similar, Peter would not be the greatest, but one of the two brothers who, together with him, enjoyed privilege of honor in many respects. Nor were they unaware that the Lord had already said of John, “Among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:11). And therefore, since in that kingdom many would be great, they asked who ought to be greatest among the great. Since this question had perhaps boiled within them on the way, like the flame of zeal, they were convicted, once they had been received into the house, of having stirred one another to envy by such conversations. Then, according to Matthew, they did what they ought to have done first. They had already come into the house and, having been convicted, like disciples before their Teacher, they put forward the aforesaid question: which of them was the greatest.

We too must be their imitators in every respect whenever something arises among us as though doubtful, from which some scruple might arise between us. But the compassionate and most merciful observer, Jesus, seeing their thoughts and understanding the causes of so great an error, wished in his kindness to remove the desire for glory from their hearts and to heal their disputes with the antidote of humility, so that he might wisely treat all their wounds.

He called a little child and set him in their midst.

Many indeed ask about this child: whether we should simply understand that he set any one of the little children there, or whether perhaps he presented himself to them as an example, or certainly John, who appeared younger than they in age. To some, the comparison seems inappropriate if it concerns any ordinary child, since at such an age a child still possesses no prudence by which virtue can operate; nor are children so free from vices that the law of sin is not implanted in them, by which they become angry and are moved even to tears. Such people do not attend to the simplicity of divine speech and the purity of the word, especially since every comparison must be referred to the point toward which the comparer directs its meaning, and not to everything that happens to the person or thing being compared. Consider, for example, what was previously said about serpents and doves: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matthew 10:15), although there are many things in them that must be avoided. Yet in the serpent there is such wisdom that it can suffice as an example, and in the dove such simplicity that its imitation likewise suffices for salvation.

So here too the innocence of a child is elegantly proposed as an example, to recall the apostles from empty glory and envy to humility and contempt for the world. The Gospel saying itself also seems to convey this more clearly than if it introduced any other person: “Jesus,” it says, “called a little child and set him in their midst.” It does not say that he called himself, or John, or the Holy Spirit, as some wish, but one of the little children, whose natural and unaffected innocence and humility could be a teacher of salvation. Hence it follows:

> Truly I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

And it should be noted that, although he set one in their midst, he did not say, “like this child,” but “like little children,” so that the humility and innocence of all of them might be affirmed, and so that the child he had set there would not appear to possess something beyond the nature of his age. By setting him in their midst, he indicates that this virtue is no nearer to one person than to another—not to Peter, not to John, any more than to the rest—but is common to all who choose to follow it. They are not to possess a child’s age, but the humility and innocence which children possess by reason of their years, while adults are to possess purity through discipline and virtue.

The imitation of such children is therefore by no means a small virtue. For if a man, having reached adulthood, mortifies his masculine desires in spirit and his bodily acts to such an extent that he always carries the death of Jesus in his body, so that he becomes like the child who has not yet attempted feminine things or experienced masculine impulses, then such a man, having turned, has become like a child whose eyes have not yet been opened—eyes which, having been wrongly opened in Adam, we still greatly lament today because of the punishment of sin.

For this reason, I believe, he set such a little child in their midst: in the child’s innocence and simplicity of heart he represented the holy Adam who had existed before sin, perhaps already reborn in himself. They were not to follow all the ignorance that belongs to an age below maturity, but all the innocence and purity that exist in a child’s nature without vice. Thus, the more each of them approached true innocence by progress, withdrawing from the passions that later arise and grow in us, the more he would be regarded as greater in the kingdom of heaven than others who remain continent but cannot rise to perfection.

Let each person apply this rule to himself and observe, even in children of that same age, how sound children are in all the passions and ailments of the soul—ailments that we later contract in ourselves. A child does not first fall into these things before beginning to speak a complete sentence. Before that, no desire of the flesh touches him: neither anger, nor sadness, nor hatred, nor envy, nor the irritation of any other passion. Indeed, even at the death of his father or mother or some friend, he plays and delights in his rattles more simply than anyone at a feast. He does not know how to exalt himself; he does not know how to seek lofty things; he does not reject what is lowly; he seeks none of the precious things or those associated with pride; he rejoices in everyone’s sight and loves everyone as parents. What more can be said? He does not even fear death itself.

If I wished to enumerate all the virtues of his innocence, it would be lengthy. Nature, though corrupted, preserved and retained these virtues in the succession of generations. Thus, after receiving grace, the apostles are sent back well to that integrity, so that thereafter they may not be seized by any snares or entangled in the errors of desire. And although the form of Jesus Christ and imitation of his example are more perfect, this is nevertheless a sufficiently complete proposal for a perfect life, provided that each person observes the grace he has received, so that he harms neither himself nor another, while doing whatever virtue later bestowed through Christ directs him to do. For although a child cannot possess any great wisdom, no boastfulness concerning lineage, wealth, or other things regarded as good delights his mind. And therefore it follows:

> Whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. And whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.

Since all these things must be referred to Christ, he concluded at the end: “Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.” It is as though he said: “He receives me because I am in such people—those who cast themselves down in this way and, for my sake, wish to return to such innocence, so that they may receive within themselves by reason and faith the condition that children possess by age.” These matters concerning children must be considered with the greatest depth if someone, having turned, wishes to return to them. Unless their character is examined with the utmost care, scarcely any capacity for explanation will suffice.

The figure passes from lower things to higher when he says: “Whoever receives such a one in my name receives me.” This does not mean that such children, who do not yet know how to seek anything, are to be received as guests, although nothing is lost from the good deeds done for Christ in them. Rather, whoever receives in Christ’s name, or in a disciple’s name, one such as the compassionate Teacher wishes him to become—one whom he invites to attain such innocence that, for God’s sake, he timidly avoids nothing and seeks neither honor, nor sensual delights, nor anything voluptuous—receives him. For this is the form of virtue: a child claims nothing for himself and seeks nothing.

“And whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble,” he says, “it would be better for him if a millstone turned by a donkey were hung around his neck and he were sunk into the depths of the sea.”

There are many things in these verses on which many people construct doctrines. We, however, as elsewhere, seek only the plain and simple understanding of the passage and, for the sake of brevity, omit much that could usefully be said. Nevertheless, we must ask how the apostles, or the other disciples of Christ who could attain this perfection to which they are so carefully invited by the Lord—as though to a spectacle of virtues—are called “little ones.”

We know, therefore, that he is not speaking of those children who do not yet know how to be scandalized, but of those who have been able to imitate their innocence. Even if he places himself before them as a little child, as some wish, a greater perfection is commended in these little ones—and if those who imitate Christ are to be called little ones. But if such people are great, as he wishes them to become; if he hastens to form them according to the example of children; and if they are called great in the kingdom of heaven, how can such people be scandalized? Especially since it is written: “Great peace belongs to those who love your law, and there is no stumbling block for them” (Psalm 118:165).

Although this saying may appear general, directed against all who cause any of those who believe in Christ to stumble, nevertheless, according to the context of the passage, it can also be understood as spoken especially against the apostles, who, by asking which of them was the greatest in the kingdom of heaven, seemed to be contending among themselves over rank. If they had remained in this vice, they could undoubtedly have destroyed by their scandal those whom they were calling to the faith, since these people, still weak in faith, would have seen them fighting among themselves for honor.

For this reason the compassionate Teacher recalls them to the humility and simplicity of a child who does not know how to quarrel over honors. Unless someone turns according to this example, it is certainly impossible for him to enter the kingdom of heaven. Here too the meaning is clear: many turn in order to become like a child and assume the character of Christ’s discipleship, but not all who turn have already reached the point of becoming like such children. Each one possesses less of the likeness of children to the extent that he is farther from a childlike disposition concerning carnal passions, fears, and the enticements of vices.

[Col. 0605C] Within the entire multitude of believers, then, there are some who have only recently turned, in order to become like children, but who have not yet become so, although they appear to have turned. They are regarded as little ones and children in Christ, receivers of scandal, because they can be scandalized—and for this reason they are children. Otherwise, if they were not little ones and children, they would not receive scandal. We must in no way provide these people with an occasion for scandal, since they too are already in Christ.

Of these it is said in the Psalm: “He has blessed all who fear the Lord, the little with the great” (Psalm 113:21). Concerning these little ones, who have already been blessed by the Lord and reborn in Christ, he says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a millstone turned by a donkey were hung around his neck,” and so forth.

Jerome testifies here that Christ is speaking according to the custom of the province, although other teachers teach this differently: among the ancient Jews, he says, it was customary, for the gravest crimes, that the condemned culprit should be punished in this way—namely, that a stone was tied around his neck and he was sunk into the depth of whatever abyss was at hand. According to Matthew and Mark, the Lord calls this stone a millstone turned by a donkey, although Luke merely calls it “a stone.” There is no doubt that such millstones existed among the Jews, as among many nations. Therefore, although the person who was plunged into the water might have been punished with any stone, since that stone was so large, they say, as the millstone turned by a donkey, the Lord rightly commends the same punishment for such people in these words. Thus he both announces to the guilty what is more useful for healing their evil and, from the ordinary use of the millstone, gives all readers a clearer understanding of his teaching.

At times, however, it should be understood literally in this sense: it is better and much more useful for someone who has caused one of them to stumble to receive immediately a brief, although severe, punishment than to be preserved for eternal torments, because God does not judge twice for the same matter. But many of our people customarily diminish the force of these statements, saying that such a thing ought by no means to happen, since death itself, however severe, is sufficient as punishment; and I do not know how that can be called useful which is the last of all evils as punishment.

Therefore, what should be understood from this must be investigated, especially since the Lord does not command it when he speaks of it, but indicates what is more useful for each person. Nevertheless, these many and weighty details are not believed to have been spoken by the Lord without purpose: a millstone is to be hung around the person’s neck, not just any millstone but one turned by a donkey, and he is to be sunk not anywhere but into the depths of the sea. If this were not a great offense, he would certainly not be condemned so atrociously.

Moreover, when the customary practice of causing scandal for small and trivial matters is considered, it seems impossible—or even necessary—to preserve and observe, not only literally, the things that are enjoined, but even to attend to the scandals of those who are scandalized. Therefore, just as there is a difference among those who are scandalized, so there is a difference in the thing over which they are scandalized and in the degree to which they are scandalized.

We should not simply say that every disturbance of the soul is a scandal, although disturbances are the thorns of scandals. For even if the soul is stirred to anger or sadness, it is not thereby separated from the bond of charity or from the unity of the body. Therefore, concerning such scandals and similar ones as can occur even among brothers who are most closely related, although they must be avoided and lamented if they occur, I would never say that such a severe punishment should be imposed upon the guilty person for whose fault they occurred, although there should be mutual groaning over them.

For even though the one who caused the disturbance is guilty, the one who is scandalized by so small a matter is not entirely free from blame. But if a brother, because he is perfect and has greatly loved the law of God, could not be scandalized by a small or great matter, is the other person therefore free from guilt? Otherwise, if that were so, Alexander the coppersmith, who inflicted many evils upon Paul, would be free from guilt. But because this is not so, Paul says, “The Lord will repay him.” To him, if I am not mistaken, it would have been better if this millstone had been hung around his neck and he had been sunk into the depths of the sea for his crime than if he had persisted in such conduct.

Guarding against this, the Apostle says, lest he provide scandal through himself to anyone: “It is good for me neither to eat meat nor to drink wine forever, rather than cause my brother to stumble” (Romans 14:21), because it is evil for a person to eat or drink through an offense. The same applies to other actions in which scandals are generated or nourished.

We must therefore take care not to provide an occasion for anyone, since there are many kinds of scandals. Yet none, in my judgment, are more serious than resistance to teachers—or when teachers themselves corrupt their hearers by their example.

There is, however, another meaning of the millstone turned by a donkey, which must not be passed over. They say that the work of the mill is labor performed in blindness; that nothing is so blind as folly, and nothing so heavy as greed. Thus the desire or greed for temporal things is appropriately represented: it is bound to the heart of a foolish and blind person, so that it leads the same fool, together with his burden, to destruction.

They say that millstones are driven around with the eyes of the animals closed. Under the name of the donkey, gentile society is frequently signified. Not without reason, since the nations do not know what they are doing, and, detained in the work of their life, they are held in the blindness of ignorance.

To the Jews, however, the knowledge of the law had been entrusted and the way of life had been granted. If they scandalized Christ’s apostles, who were called the little flock, it would be more tolerable for them to be bound with a millstone around their necks and sunk into the depths of the sea—that is, to be weighed down by the turning motion of the nations and dragged into the deepest ignorance of the world—because it would have been lighter for them not to have known Christ than not to have received him who had been proclaimed by the prophets.

For the healing of sin, it is indeed more useful for a person who is dragged down by the heaviest burden of sins to be sunk into the depths of the sea, where the dragon is said to dwell, whom God formed to mock him, and for the body that so greatly weighs down the soul to be punished. Afterwards the person who has endured, as it were, a long repentance in the depths of the sea for the destruction of the flesh, dragged downward by the millstone turned by a donkey, will be outside the pains.

The different kinds of millstones are also rightly sought from this passage, because there are human millstones, millstones turned by donkeys, and millstones belonging to beasts of burden. The human millstone is that of which it is said: “There will be two grinding at one millstone; one will be taken and one will be left” (Matthew 24:41). The millstone turned by a donkey is the one imposed upon the person who causes one of the little ones who believe in Christ to stumble, so that he may be sunk into the depths of the sea. For just as there is a great difference among sins, so there is a difference among punishments.

Therefore, as I said, it may reasonably be said that the very heavy body of an evil person is the millstone turned by a donkey which he has bound to himself as though with the leather strap of sin, by which he is always pressed downward. For this reason such a person must be cast out of the Church and reduced to repentance. But no one drags this millstone along with him except a blind person. Hence that very strong Samson is not sent to the mill to grind until his eyes have been torn out. Whoever is struck by this blindness walks around like an impious person, sunk down to the lowest depths of hell by the cares of the world and the burdens of his crimes.

[733] “Woe to the world,” he says, “because of scandals. It is necessary that scandals come. Nevertheless, woe to that person through whom the scandal comes.”

Our Lord and Savior discusses many things concerning scandals, since there are many kinds of scandals and many occasions through which scandals arise and come about. Nevertheless, only those who are in the world and of the world are ever scandalized. Therefore he says, “Woe to the world because of scandals,” because everything that causes scandal brings woe to those who are of the world. But those who are outside the world, I think, can no longer be scandalized.

Accordingly, when he says, “Woe to the world because of scandals,” I do not believe that he is speaking of the elements of heaven and earth, but, according to the custom of the Scriptures, designating all earthly and carnal people who have fixed the root of their hearts in the love of the world. Concerning this world it is said elsewhere: “The world is set in the evil one” (John 5:19). In this world, “there was the true light which enlightens everyone coming into this world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1:9–10).

And because it did not know him, it was left in the evil one, although, before he came, the true light had been placed in this world. Woe therefore threatens that world because of scandals, since in it and from it scandals arise and are nourished throughout the whole earth.

The disciples of Christ, I acknowledge, were no longer of that world, just as their Teacher was not of that world. Therefore none of them was subject to woe because of scandals, insofar as each of them was already outside the world in mind. For this reason the compassionate Teacher says to the Father: “Father, I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me from the world” (John 17:6); and shortly afterward: “I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me” (John 17:9).

Here he plainly shows that, according to God’s predestination, these people were no longer of the world. Therefore they had great peace rather than woe, because they already loved the law of God from the heart. Indeed, although scandals rage and multiply everywhere in the world against Christ’s disciple, no woe threatens him, provided that he is not of this world in which woe abounds, because scandals flare up everywhere in it.

But if some little one who already appears to be a disciple of Christ receives the scandals of the world into himself—either because of the instability of his faith, because he has not believed with his whole heart, or because he has not consented to obey God completely—then scandals will entirely seize him in proportion to the number of things by which he is bound to the world.

It should also be noted that he says, “It is necessary that scandals come.” If they come, we must ask from where they come, through whom they come, and to whom they come. For although it is necessary that they come, they never come except from evil and through evil people to the imperfect. Their instigator and producer, who approaches through evil people as though through his own vessels, is understood to be none other than the devil, who rules over the children of disobedience and, through them, exercises his arts so that he may secretly inflict further harm.

Therefore the person who causes scandal is much worse than the person who is scandalized. And since scandals must come, it is more tolerable for them to come through those who are estranged from the worship of God than through those who appear to be faithful. The woe is also greater for those through whom they occur than for the little ones and the world to which they occur. For it would have been more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon than for those cities which the Lord was unable to correct and convert by his miracles.

Nevertheless, even though there is woe for those who, being of the world and in the world, sow and nourish scandals, those who are subjected to guilt and blame are not free from guilt, and woe is also spoken against them, because they mingled with the world, whose entire woe they willingly accepted by choosing to be scandalized with the world.

Yet a more serious woe remains for those through whom scandal comes, because they have offered themselves to unclean spirits in order to scandalize weak and worldly people and have made themselves servants of Satan.

Even if they were great in the Church and unable to scandalize those who could not be scandalized—as we have already said above concerning Paul, against whom Alexander the coppersmith inflicted many evils so that his Gospel might be scandalized—they are not for that reason free from guilt, although they may have been less able to accomplish what they wished.

The same will apply to all who serve scandals and are not afraid to scandalize God’s servants in any office of Christ’s service. Even if punishment is not immediately inflicted upon them, no lesser vengeance will follow than that which the Lord threatens.

Those who preside over others must also beware of this sentence, lest they scandalize their subjects by their actions. For all these things are demanded more severely from those who are in authority: not merely scandals, if they cause them, but also the failure to bring back profits from the talents entrusted to them will bring punishments for those committed to their care.

Now, when he says, “It is necessary that scandals come,” he may seem to free from guilt those who cause scandals for others, since they do what must happen, according to the compassionate Teacher’s statement. But it must not be understood in this way, even though Luke states it still more explicitly: “It is impossible that scandals should not come” (Luke 17:1). If it is impossible that they should not come, then it is necessary that they come. We must ask how this should be understood, because the Savior’s sentence cannot be weakened.

Nor do his words contradict one another when he says, “Whoever causes one of these to stumble, it would be better for him if a millstone turned by a donkey were hung around his neck,” and so forth. Therefore we must ask what kind of necessity he means when he says, “It is necessary that scandals come.”

I do not believe that he means that it is necessary in such a way that it is beneficial either to the person who causes scandals or to the person who is scandalized, but rather in the sense expressed more carefully by Luke: “It is impossible that scandals should not come.” Many things are called necessary in this way. Just as a human being, being mortal, must die; and just as someone who is walking must move, because things cannot be otherwise.

This necessity must therefore be referred to the world, which is subject to woe because of scandals, and not to that world which has been redeemed from evil. Although scandals are stirred up against the redeemed world by the one to whom woe belongs because of scandals, there is no necessity in that world that scandals should come; rather, through God’s grace it possesses great freedom to repel and overcome them.

But in and from that world, since there can be nothing but woe, scandals must come, because from those who have fixed their hearts in it nothing else can come, even if they promise peace, insofar as the enemy rules within them, and nothing but scandals can come from him.

If this necessity is to be understood in a straightforward manner—when it is said that scandals must come—it should rather be understood as referring to the passion of Christ. The humility and passion of Christ are certainly a scandal to the world from which scandals come, especially because human ignorance is held fast and oppressed and does not believe or accept that the Lord of eternal glory could humble himself under the appearance of the cross and choose to be hung upon a tree.

Nothing is more dangerous to the world set in the evil one than its refusal to receive Christ crucified. Nevertheless, under the single designation of “the world,” the Jewish people are plainly signified, through whom all the scandal came upon this world, so that everyone might deny Christ in his passion, although the law and the prophets had always proclaimed that he would suffer.

Therefore, as he says, it was necessary that scandals come, so that in Christ’s passion the law and prophecy might be restored according to their figures and all the mysteries of our redemption might be fulfilled in that humility. Thus, although many are scandalized by Christ’s death, it was nevertheless necessary—indeed, absolutely necessary—not so that scandals should arise, but so that Christ’s passion might be fulfilled through the cross, through which these scandals would come.

I ask that no one condemn the devout, though diverse, meanings handed down by the holy Fathers, nor reproach any of them. Rather, let everyone always attend to the circumstances of the reading and thus determine, in each case, what best suits the understanding of the passage under discussion. For although the very extensive doctrines of their teachings are venerable and delight the soul, the author’s own meaning must first be investigated, lest someone, preferring to gather flowers, lose the fruit.

But if your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. For it is better for you to enter eternal life lame or maimed than, having two hands or two feet, to be cast into the eternal fire.

Earlier, when he had said, “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28–29), he immediately added these words: “If your right eye or your hand causes you to stumble,” showing that he was speaking of those scandal-causing members which are within us and in our body. Therefore, in that passage we explained that the passions of the soul or the will are the members that cause scandal.

Here, however, after saying, “Woe to the world because of scandals; it is necessary that scandals come, but woe to the person through whom the scandal comes,” he immediately adds: “If your hand or your foot or your eye causes you to stumble.” Here he shows that he is not speaking of the scandal-causing members that are within us, but of people who are outside us and yet belong to us, so that they may rightly be called hands, feet, or eyes, because they are joined and bound to us by so great a grace of charity and affection.

Therefore, because scandals can come to us from such people, he commands that if one of those who appears to be such a member causes us to stumble and draws us back from the way of Christ, we must cut him off and cast him away from us. It is better to remain attached to Christ, the head, than to perish with these rotten members.

For this reason the Church customarily cuts off such members from itself by divine authority, with the sword of the word, and casts them outside, lest “a little leaven corrupt the whole lump” (1 Corinthians 5:6; Galatians 5:9).

See how carefully the compassionate Teacher and most kindly physician of souls instructs his people, so that they may not be scandalized in any respect. As I said above, because each person is tempted by his own desires according to the Apostle, he commands that all harmful affections be cut off. Here, however, because scandals must come from those who are outside, he warns us beforehand that it cannot be otherwise than that they will come, so that we may avoid them before they come, since woe belongs to the one through whom they come.

But lest someone wonder what should be done about brothers who often cause scandals within the Church, he immediately speaks of them: “If your hand, or your foot, or your eye causes you to stumble, throw it away from you.”

If someone in the Church is a hand by doing good, or a foot that first walks well on the way of God, or an eye that teaches the light of life, remaining attached to its head, Christ—but if any one of them turns backward, no longer clinging to its head or keeping the commandments of life, and causes the healthy members of Christ to stumble—the head must say to such an eye, foot, or hand, “I have no need of you,” and, cutting it off, cast it away from itself. For it is better for the remaining body to enter eternal life without the scandal-causing member than for the whole body of the Church, with the disease of scandal raging through all its members, to be cast into Gehenna.

We must also use this testimony against those close to us who, as members, are joined and compacted with us by affection—whether parents or very intimate friends. We must not spare those who harm our souls. We must cut them off from us, even if the person is our father or mother, before we withdraw, because of scandal, from Christ the head. For this is why Jesus came to cast a sword upon the earth: so that with it we might cut away from ourselves all harmful passions and all the members that produce scandals for us.

“See to it,” he says, “that you do not despise one of these little ones who believe in me; for I tell you that their angels always behold the face of my Father who is in heaven.” He imposes the strongest bond of mutual love especially upon those who truly believe in the Lord, whom one ought not to despise. But we must consider who the “little ones” are whom he forbids us to despise, and whose angels always behold the face of the Father (Matt. 18:10). Does he mean those children or little ones of whom there was one whom he placed in their midst, and to whose innocence he commands the apostles to return? Does he command those same apostles not to presume to despise such people, when among those little children there is nothing they ought to command, nor do the apostles have anything to despise? Unless perhaps he means that they should not despise their innocence. But I judge this to be a general command: that all should obey the apostles and apostolic men, whom he had summoned to the innocence of children. He passed from the particular form, as divine Scripture very often does, to the general category, from one form to another—from those little ones who, because of their age, still retain innocence, to those who have been made innocent and little ones by grace and now labor for others. These laborers ought not to be despised, lest Christ also be despised in them.

Nor ought we to wonder that apostles or apostolic men are called little ones, since they too have been made such through the power of Christ and have been reduced to the innocence to which they are summoned. Hence they are also called by the Lord himself “the little flock” (Luke 12:32). On the other hand, although many maintain that the little ones and other children within the Church are those who are still fed with milk, since they are heirs of the heavenly kingdom, nevertheless these are especially called little ones; and the saying is more properly understood of those whom he appointed teachers and masters, so that no one may despise them, because none can be more humble, nor ought any to be more truly innocent, than they themselves.

“Their angels,” he says, “always behold the face of my Father.” Great is the dignity of those who have been able to attain this innocence, or who are such that their teaching must not be despised. For even if they themselves still understand or accomplish little, their angels understand and accomplish much: they always see God, and in him they accomplish much. I believe that no one can doubt—and this is confirmed by the authority of the divine Scriptures—that angels have been appointed to minister to those who are to receive the inheritance of eternal life, so that individual angels preside over individual provinces or kingdoms. Indeed, individuals have their own angels, especially those who have been predestined by God and whose inheritance is the promise of eternal life.

Hence, as I said, the authority is unequivocal: the angels of these little ones offer their prayers to God, once these little ones begin to offer something worthy of God. For, as is fitting, they have been appointed ministers of the churches of God; and Paul the apostle calls them “ministering spirits” (Heb. 1:14). They offer to God the vows and prayers of all, but through Christ; through their ministry, the prayers of believers are brought daily before the supreme God, and what has been obtained is brought back to us.

Therefore, although it is terrifying to despise the little ones who are still small in faith and in their office, it is more terrifying to trample upon those who seem to offer the vows of all. Many say that princes have been placed above their offices, above their mouths, as it were, and that these princes unquestionably perform the duties of those who are proved to be ministers of the altar. Thus those whose desires and petitions the angels offer daily are despised with the greatest peril.

For no mortal, while still in the flesh of sin, is worthy in himself. Therefore the most merciful God has provided that the vows and prayers of human beings be carried by the hands of angels to that eternal and invisible God with due reverence, so that whatever is lacking in us by nature may become an acceptable sacrifice through angelic service.

In these words, sentences, and statements there are certainly many matters that many people propose and investigate concerning this subject. But, steering a middle course between the two approaches, we have selected a few points from many, in which true doctrine may be commended.

Those who wish to establish that this saying concerns the children in the Church say that Christ had no need to command that great and more perfect believers should not be despised, but simply spoke of those who are little in faith. Hence, they say, he did not say, “Do not despise one of all these,” but “one of these little ones,” whom he himself knew to be little.

Likewise, those who are perfect, such as the apostle Paul, who calls himself “the least of the apostles” (1 Cor. 15:9), cannot receive scandals, because “there is great peace for those who love your law, and there is no scandal for them” (Ps. 118:165). Yet, according to Ezekiel, a person who has acted in accordance with everything that a righteous person ordinarily does may still depart from God’s commandments and do what the wicked ordinarily do; then his earlier righteousnesses are handed over to oblivion. If he could not be scandalized and pass from good and holy works to iniquity, just as, conversely, one may pass from evil to good, the prophet would never have made such declarations against the watchman from whom the soul is required.

They transmit another interpretation as well when he says, “Do not despise one of these little ones.” They say that he said this because, under the figure of the hand and foot—but not the eye—he commands us to cast away from the Church any dear and distinguished persons who are placed within it if they scandalize us, lest perhaps we should wish to be more severe toward them than is expedient. He moderates his judgment lest we despise them as though we were driven by zeal for God but not according to knowledge or the charity of Christ. It is as though he said:

“I command you to maintain severity toward the members of the body in such a way that you teach at the same time the compassion of charity and the mercy of brotherly love, so that through your own salvation you may also seek their healing.”

“For their angels always behold the face of my Father.” Through their ministry and prayers they may be reconciled and healed in the body of Christ.

Therefore it must not be denied that each person reborn in Christ has his own guardian angel. But how they always see the face of the Father, “into whom they desire to look,” as the apostle testifies, while the Triune God is also said to be invisible, is no small question—unless he is invisible in the sense that none of the angels sees him wholly, exactly as he is. Nevertheless, each of them sees him insofar as it has been granted to them, according to the excellence of their nature and grace. Thus neither their love nor their desire produces the anxiety of a denied vision, but rather satisfaction; they see as much as they desire. Nor does the satisfaction of vision bring them disgust, since the vision itself fills them with brightness. They see him as much as their nature can see, and therefore they desire this: to love him continually without disgust. They love the one whom they see, so that, always seeing him, they love and desire him without any anxiety.

If it is asked what they do when they come to us—whether they see him then—we must believe that they are never anywhere except in him, since they run and come through him who is everywhere; and therefore they never withdraw from his vision.

He calls the face of the Father by a figure of human speech. This does not mean that there is anything corporeal in the Father or in that indivisible Trinity, or any bodily features. Rather, Christ calls himself the face of the Father: the angels always see him, and through him they see the Father. For just as no one comes to the Father except through the Son, so no one sees the Father except through that same Son, because no one knows him except the Son and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him (John 14; Luke 10).

For the Son of Man came to save what had perished.

Because he had said, “See to it that you do not despise one of these little ones,” he adds that “the Son of Man came to save what had perished,” as though he were saying: He came to seek and save what is little; therefore, now that it has been saved through faith, do not destroy it. The text continues:

“What do you think? If someone has a hundred sheep, and one of them goes astray, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go in search of the one that went astray? And if it happens that he finds it, and so forth.”

He repeats and presses home the same points he had made above, so that no one may despise those whom the Son of Man came to seek and save, and whom he would carry back to the flock on his shoulders, as a shepherd. By this he shows how dangerous it is to despise those whom Christ, the shepherd of the sheep, sought on earth with such great diligence that he carried them on his own shoulders back to heaven and into the fellowship of the heavenly citizens, whose angels always behold the face of the Father.

He left the ninety-nine on the mountains, or in the desert, and came to seek the one that had gone astray. By this he greatly magnifies the dignity of our redemption, so that those who believe in Christ, whose shepherd he is, may not be despised. For their sake he left the angelic dignity in the heavenly places, since the angels are their companions; and he appointed them by God to serve them, carrying out prayers and vows in their ministry.

Hence Daniel says in his vision: “A thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10). For although some are those who stand before him, others are those who have been appointed to minister; and these always behold the face of the Father.

According to Luke, this man whom Matthew presents without distinction is Christ himself, who came to seek what had perished through the fact that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). He came to seek one sheep—not one in species, but one in kind—for through this one sheep he designates the entire race of those who, sought and found, are daily carried back by the Lord to the flock.

This is what he had said: “The Son of Man came to save what had perished” (Luke 19:10). Concerning this sheep David, lamenting and grieving, had said long before: “I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost; seek your servant, Lord” (Ps. 118:176).

But what he prayed for, the Evangelist proves and declares: having become human, Christ had already fulfilled what the Prophet, groaning, prayed: “Seek your servant, Lord, because I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost.” The patriarch David perceived that he had gone astray and perished through Adam; therefore he said, “I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost.” He knew that he had perished and gone astray in that very Adam; since “in Adam all die” (1 Cor. 15:22), he asks that all may be made alive through Christ.

Thus some Greek manuscripts have ζῆσον instead of what we have, “seek”—that is, “make alive.” The sense would then be: “Make your servant alive, because he lies dead in Adam.” But other manuscripts have ζήτησον, which means “seek,” and this is better, although the sense is one. “Seek your servant, Lord” is more appropriate to this passage, since the sheep that had gone astray had to be sought by the shepherd so that it would not perish.

The Prophet confesses his fall in that condition which he shares with all others. No one has not died in Adam, except the one who alone was found to be “free among the dead” (Ps. 87:6). But because this man had perished like a sheep, having gone astray from the way in that first Adam, he asks the good shepherd to seek him.

No one perishes who perfectly recognizes his error. What, then, does “seek your servant” mean except “seek your fallen and straying sheep”? Come, Lord Jesus, shepherd; seek like Joseph’s sheep, because your sheep has gone astray while you remain on the mountains. Leave your ninety-nine sheep securely, because there is no wolf where you leave them, no evil laborer, no hired hand. Come yourself; seek the sheep that went astray; carry back the broken and weakened one that had perished.

And so it happened as he prayed: he came, sought, found, and, as the present parable testifies, carried it back on his own shoulders.

For that sheep which was lost in Adam is found and lifted up by Christ, placed, as I said, upon his own shoulders. Since it was weak and weary, afflicted by many diseases, it could not return by itself, nor through free will, as some wrongly think.

Therefore it is lifted onto his shoulders, upon which even the glorious principality was established. These shoulders are certainly the arms of the cross. There he took up and bore our sins. Upon that noble neck of the compassionate shepherd, made noble, we rest and are carried. Although one sheep is spoken of, we were all that one sheep, because we are all one body, though many members.

Rich, therefore, is our shepherd, of whom we all are scarcely the hundredth part. For he has ninety-nine sheep on the heavenly mountains, where the pastures are always pleasant and always green.

It should also be noted that the angels themselves are called sheep, of whom Christ is shepherd, and they themselves are sheep and lambs. Yet the angels are not sheep by nature, any more than human beings are; they are called sheep figuratively because their innocence, indefatigable, follows Christ the Lamb among the pastures of life, and he himself leads them to springs of water.

If you ask, reader, why the ninety-nine sheep are said to have been left on the mountains, when there are innumerable flocks in that desert which he left, know that we have selected a few points from many that ought to be discussed, because this parable has been very famously explained in the writings of the earlier Fathers, both Greek and Latin.

But since all have said that this finite number is used for an infinite one, we must ask why only ninety-nine are said to have been left. I therefore do not doubt that the statement is not without mystery. Divine Scripture testifies that there are nine orders of angels. We therefore believe that this number was chosen because the ninety-nine signify as much for the sacrament of prefiguration as the nine alone, which is the third square number. Since nine orders of angels are said to exist under this number, it is as though ninety-nine were mentioned so that only nine might be understood.

But since no definite number has been prefigured in the individual orders, and no mortal can know how great their number is, a finite number is not inappropriately used for an infinite one. Thus the third square number is rightly understood, so that neither the Trinity may be absent from the number nor the squareness of the number absent from the firm and stable Trinity, perfectly squared so that it may never be moved or confused throughout the ages.

He left all these on the mountains of righteousness, concerning which the Prophet says to God: “Your righteousnesses are like the mountains of God” (Ps. 35:7). And because he left them established on these mountains, he came securely to us, since “the heavens were established by the word of the Lord, and all their host by the breath of his mouth” (Ps. 32:6).
