Hence there is greater joy in heaven over one converted sinner than over the ninety-nine righteous who do not need repentance, because the joy of righteousness has been preserved for them in the heavenly places.

If, however, one distinguished teacher understands the number of the sheep left behind as referring to those sheep whom he left in the desert—not to angels, but to various human beings who are proud—he means that they are proud as though they were carrying a desert within their minds, since they wish to be seen as solitary and lack unity, which leads to perfection.

“For,” he says, “whenever someone is torn away from true unity, desiring to belong to himself, he is certainly torn away through pride.” He does not follow the One who is God; therefore, as he himself says, the signification of such people is placed in the ninety-nine sheep. They presume upon themselves and place themselves before sinners who are returning to salvation.

One is therefore lacking: one is lacking from nine in order that there may be ten, and from ninety-nine in order that there may be one hundred. If you consider the matter through other numbers of this kind, you will find the same thing. Numbers may vary in their smallness or greatness, but one is lacking from them in order that they may be made perfect; the one itself remains without variation in itself.

When that one is added to the ninety-nine dwelling in the solitude of their sins, the perfect hundred is restored. For unless all sinners receive this unity within themselves through repentance and are reconciled to God, they will remain outside that number which, raised on the right, expresses the crown.

This is certainly a devout interpretation of a most holy teacher, but the other interpretation is commended as more truthful, in which all the other teachers, both Greek and Latin, seem to agree. The whole parable indicates that the compassionate shepherd came to us from the place where he left the sheep—not imperfect or defective, but reduced in number because of those who had fallen.

That number is restored from unity, so that the perfect hundred may be found on the right. Therefore he did not say fifty or two hundred, but one hundred. Of these he lost one, to show that the grief in heaven arose not only from the loss but also from the number. The loss of one had disrupted the whole hundred, because it had also reduced the right hand to the left: by the loss of one, the left was closed in upon itself, while the right had nothing.

The ninety-ninth number lies hidden on the left, shut in, bound, and held enclosed. But when it receives and feels the increase of one, it immediately passes to the palm of the right hand and immediately reaches the crown of the hundred. This is not because there was any imperfection in those angels who remained and whom he left, but because the diminution of the number was a definite imperfection.

For the one who causes what does not exist to exist seeks the lost in such a way that he holds on to what he left behind; and he finds what was lost in such a way that he does not lose what has been preserved in the heavenly places.

Therefore we believe that this was said more particularly of the angels, in whom and for whom joy is henceforth neither diminished, increased, nor changed, just as it is concerning the human beings whom the author of salvation sought, found when sought, and, once found, carried back on his own shoulders to the joys of eternal life.

Hence he calls those same angels, his friends and neighbors, and says: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep which I had lost.” He had lost it because, although it had first been created on the right, it had fallen to the left. Perfection therefore could not exist while the number of one hundred had been diminished.

But as soon as the number is transferred from the left to the right, the hundred is restored. Once it has been restored, the crown is immediately displayed in it. Hence Christ the Judge will in the future place the sheep—which is the whole Church—on his right, but leave the goats on his left.

But how did he leave the angelic hosts on the heavenly mountains, when he never left the heavens any more than he left the Father? This, I think, must be investigated, so that we may understand what it means that he left them. For one is not rightly said to have left those with whom he is proved always to have been.

Thus we must admit that, just as he says in this Gospel that he left the Father and came into the world, so he left the angels in heaven and came to earth. He left them when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7). In that form, because he assumed our nature, he came into the world where he had previously been, without in a certain sense leaving those sheep with whom he had also been before.

This was what it meant for him to leave himself: to empty himself, just as this sheep wandered away from the flocks. For the first human being, placed in paradise, lost the pastures of life through sin.

The text continues:

“Amen, I say to you, he will rejoice over it more than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray.”

Luke, for his part, marks the celebration of this joy when he says that the shepherd of this sheep calls together his friends and neighbors and says to them: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that had perished” (Luke 15:6).

Although this rejoicing belongs jointly to the friends and the shepherd, the shepherd’s joy nevertheless appears greater, since his friends and neighbors rejoice with him because the sheep has been recovered. These neighbors and friends are rational beings; therefore they rightly rejoice over the redemption of rational human beings. Filled with charity, they are advanced through their service and ministry into the fellowship of those human beings, and they rightly rejoice over so great a triumph of their king.

Therefore the Lord, wishing to display this immense joy over the salvation of the little ones whom he forbade us to despise, proposed this comparison as an example, so that they might know that those who cause such people to stumble first injure God, and then all the fellowship of the angels, whose protection guards these little ones and whose joy honors them.

Nor should it contribute little to us, small and insignificant as we are, as an incentive to goodness, if each of us believes that his conduct is pleasing to God and to the assemblies of the angels. We ought either to implore their protection through prayers and labors offered with devotion, or to fear giving them offense.

When the heavenly speaker had thus led them by divine guidance to the preceding judgment, he concludes by explaining why he set all these things forth:

“So,” he says, “it is not the will before our Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.”

And therefore he shows that everything said in parables must be referred to what came before, when he says: “See to it that you do not despise one of these little ones.” He makes this clear through many indications, including the statement: “It is not the will before your Father who is in heaven that one of these should perish.”

He says this so that, moved by reverent affection, we may take care to obey the Father and not despise our brother, however contemptible or insignificant he may appear.

Therefore we must know with certainty that whenever someone perishes, he does not perish by God’s predestination, as some wrongly think, nor by the will of the Father, but by his own sin and by God’s just judgment.

The Lord Jesus, looking upon his disciples, said to Simon Peter:

“But if your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone.”

We must therefore ask whether this statement still depends upon what came before: that we should not despise or scandalize one of these little ones who believe in God. Does he therefore say that if one of them sins against us, this is what we ought to do?

If someone sins against us or injures us in any matter, we have—or rather, are under the necessity of exercising—the power of forgiveness. We are commanded to forgive the debts of our debtors, just as we wish our debts to be forgiven us by the Lord (Matt. 6:12).

But if someone has sinned against God, it is not within our discretion to forgive. Hence divine Scripture says: “If a human being sins against another human being, the priest will pray for him. But if he sins against God, who will pray for him?”

A brother must first be rebuked privately, lest, if he once loses his shame or embarrassment, he thereafter become shameless and remain in sin. Yet he seems to be speaking here of sins that concern us, and not absolutely, as some manuscripts have it, “if your brother sins.”

Hence Origen, because this may be how it is read in the Greek manuscripts, proposes several questions from this passage. But since our more carefully corrected manuscripts have only “if he sins against you,” the sense is easier, although much discrimination is still necessary concerning these sins, so that we may know with certainty which are committed only against God and which only against us.

For there are certainly offenses that occur within us and against us, yet are referred to the injury of God. We must therefore examine and distinguish everything with the greatest diligence and prudence, so that we may readily forgive our neighbors and brothers—who share with us the one name of Christianity—those things that concern us and were done only to our injury.

Although God is offended by all evils committed against one’s neighbor, since his commands are violated, the compassionate Lord has nevertheless provided a remedy for both kinds of offense, so that through the salvation of the other, salvation and grace may also be acquired for us in the same matter.

But, perversely, we are lenient where God is injured, while, insofar as we can, we exercise vengeance and hatred over injuries done to ourselves.

If it happens, my brothers, that we now wish to correct the person who injured us, we must take care that we do not wish to do this merely because he injured us. If we act more out of love for ourselves than for our neighbor, then what we are doing is nothing. But if we do it out of love for him, then without doubt we are performing a great work, as is shown in the same words of God.

“If he listens to you,” he says, “you have gained your brother.”

Therefore act for his sake, so that you may gain the one who would have perished if you had not gained him.

But since many distinguished teachers maintain that this applies to every sin, because there is nothing in which our neighbor can sin that ought not to injure us, an excessive difficulty arises in interpreting how, under this exalted mercy of Christ, a greater opportunity for sinning is not given to sinners. For they say that the statement applies generally to every sin, if forgiveness is granted to criminals and guilty persons after such a slight rebuke.

On the other hand, if we rebuke the sinner for minor and human sins, including those committed against us, and say that after the rebuke the matter must proceed to witnesses or to the Church, so that he may be treated as a gentile and a publican, we must be especially careful not to introduce a kind of cruelty for sins that are not unto death.

For I do not think that one can easily be found in the Church among those subject to vigilant discipline—someone who has not already been rebuked three times or more for the same fault: for example, slandering a neighbor, being inflated with pride, feasting, drunkenness, drinking, speaking a lie or committing perjury, saying to his brother “Raca” or “Fool,” or committing the other lesser daily offenses of injury from which long-standing or evil habit can scarcely remain free.

Therefore, as I said, we must consider with the greatest prudence which offenses committed against us we ought to forgive privately while they remain secret. I do not mean seven times, but, according to the Lord’s word, “seventy times seven” times. We must also consider which offenses are committed against God and must be reserved for God’s judgment.

Above all, however, we must watch over our neighbor with vigilant charity. If no one else knows that a brother has sinned, but you alone have witnessed the sin against God that leads to death, rebuke him and, insofar as you are able, restore him privately between yourself and him alone, because he sinned against you, since he sinned with you as witness, and you know that he sinned.

Therefore, since it was secret when he sinned against you and against God, seek privately and with every care how you may correct the offense.

But we must ask what the Apostle means when he says: “Rebuke those who sin in the presence of all, so that the others may have fear” (1 Tim. 5:20). Does the Apostle give a contrary command, when Christ himself was speaking through him?

What could be more contrary than the Lord’s command, “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone,” while the Apostle says, “Rebuke those who sin in the presence of all”?

If we examine the matter correctly, both statements are true, and the command is rightly given that we do one at one time and the other at another, lest the discipline of Christ be confused—lest what ought to be corrected privately become public, and what is public become private.

Your brother has sinned against you when you alone know of it. Therefore the matter must be dealt with between yourself and him, since there are no other witnesses, so that he may be rebuked privately.

But if, in the presence of others who heard or saw, he inflicted an injury upon you, he sinned against those whom he made witnesses of his iniquity. Perhaps he would not have done it in their presence unless he thought that it would please them. Therefore such matters must be rebuked before all: the sins committed before all must be rebuked before all.

Those committed more secretly must also be rebuked more secretly. But the sins intended in this passage are those of which he says that they must be rebuked—sins by which a brother might perish unless you rebuke him between yourself and him alone, and by which, if he listens to you, you gain him.

What does “you have gained him” mean, then, except that he would have perished if you had not gained him?

Therefore, although we ought to contend with one another concerning every offense, according to this interpretation we must judge a sin to be of such a kind that, unless it is corrected, the brother might perish. And if he appears incorrigible before the Church of Christ, he may rightly be treated as a gentile and a publican.

Perhaps you too, the one who suffered the injury by which he sinned, may become worse by despising and neglecting to correct him as far as you are able, becoming worse through your silence than he was through his injury or insult.

For although it is glorious to forget our own injuries, we ought truly to forget our own injury, not the wound of our brother.

If he refuses to listen to you, to those whom you later bring with you, and even to the Church in which he lives, and if he defends his sin as though it were righteousness, then he must no longer be counted among the brothers or continue to live within the Church.

Nevertheless, even for the lesser offenses listed above and for injuries of this kind, if the person who has been rebuked refuses to humble himself, make peace, or offer satisfaction to the one whom he injured, the holy Fathers have decreed that, if he appears stubborn or proud, he must be separated from the fellowship of the congregation.

Nor should we overlook the interpretation of those who assert that this passage concerns the smallest sins. They say that a sinner who has been convicted twice or three times, has become puffed up in pride, and has not amended his ways should be treated as a gentile and a publican—not merely because he sinned at first, but because he remained proudly obstinate.

Meanwhile, we must consider more carefully with what wondrous arrangement divine mercy judged this matter, so that what God first fulfilled in the people whom he chose, each person might fulfill toward the neighbor joined to him, and so that, “on the testimony of two witnesses,” the trustworthiness and truth of the word might remain uncorrupted.

The law of rebuke was first sent to the insolence of the sinful people, and the lawgiver alone contended with them by rebuking them. Then prophecy and John were sent to them with that same law, and the same people were summoned by these witnesses to cease from sinning.

Third, at the very coming of the Lord, they were admonished as though he were observing them in the presence of the whole Church. When these rebukes had been rendered fruitless, they were thereafter rightly regarded by the apostles as publicans or gentiles, because “every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matt. 18:16).

This does not mean that a lie cannot be found in the mouth of two or three human beings, but that in these three witnesses—that is, in the law, the prophets, and the Gospel—every word of doctrine and every truth stands. All truth stands in them, which is the whole word, because it never falls.

Therefore the witnesses by whose testimony one’s neighbor is to be summoned must, in accordance with these three witnesses, correct and condemn the person who refuses to listen to them. Then they must make the matter known to the Church, just as Christ did with the Jews whom he endured for a long time, until the Church was instructed.

Because they did not listen to the Church, they became like gentiles and publicans: although they had already been convicted and rebuked by the testimony of many, they persisted in their unbelief and refused to believe.

I tell you truly, whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose will be loosed also in heaven. For the one who has been rebuked and convicted so many times and before so many witnesses, and before the Church, by everyone, is justly bound if he refuses to amend and to harm anyone further. Therefore, such a person, bound and condemned while still in the flesh, is rightly bound before all who are in heaven—provided, nevertheless, that at some point he amend, so as to make satisfaction to the Church which he injured, according to the rebuke of the three [Col. 0622B] witnesses; then he will no longer be bound by the cords of his sins, but will be justly loosed, even by those who are in heaven.

For this power of loosing and binding depends upon what has been said above. You have begun, then, to regard your brother as a gentile and a publican: you have bound him on earth. But, if you are to bind him justly, see to it that justice breaks apart unjust bonds. When, however, you have corrected him and been reconciled with your brother, you have loosed him on earth. Once you have loosed him on earth, he will also be loosed in heaven. You have therefore done something very great—not for yourself, but for him—for he did great harm, not to you, but to himself.

This power of loosing and binding appears to be the same as that which was given above to Peter; but it is not entirely so, since Peter had to possess some privilege over those who are commanded to rebuke three times. For that reason it was said there: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in the heavens” (Matt. XVI, 19). Here a considerable difference is perceived: the keys given to Peter are not the keys of one heaven, but the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that whatever he binds on earth will be bound not only in one heaven, but in all the heavens; likewise, what is loosed on earth will be loosed in all the heavens.

How perfect is Peter’s apostleship, how common our way of life, and how exalted the authority of the apostles! Therefore, whoever reaches that perfection which belongs to the apostles’ loosing will be wholly absolved, because just as “star differs from star in glory” (I Cor. V, 11), so too the saints differ from one another. Thus, although the authority of the apostles is rightly proclaimed as greater, the agreement and power of the Church are not for that reason to be despised—since neither the apostles nor the Church received them from anywhere other than Christ.

And therefore, because our contemptuous opponent might have had this hidden reply or silent thought—“If you despise me, I too will despise you; and if you condemn me, you too, conversely, will be condemned by that sentence”—he granted the power so that they might know that, when such people are condemned, God the judge is in their midst: lest these men bind unjustly, or that contumacious person be wrongly condemned. “For this reason I tell you,” he says, “whatever has been bound on earth will likewise be bound in heaven.” It is as though he were saying: “I am in the midst of those who bind.” Hence it follows:

[Col. 0623A] “Again I tell you: if two of you on earth agree about any matter whatever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. And where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them.”

He is so concerned for concord that, in the merit of unity, he confirms that everything which ought to be asked of God will be obtained. And wherever two or three have been gathered in the Lord with equal spirit and equal will, there he promises that he will be in their midst. For he himself is peace and love, which makes the hearts of many one and joins together countless souls of the saints with one another, so that they are one soul, and places his seat and dwelling in their midst.

This entire discourse depends upon what was said above, where he had summoned everyone to concord; and now he explains what fruit they will receive from it, so that whatever they ask they will obtain, and will always have God in their midst. But perhaps even a few people do not agree with one another in everything with such unanimity and power; therefore he perhaps moderated the statement: “if two or three of you agree,” as with Peter, James, and John. As though they agreed with him in everything, he showed them the glory of his brightness on the mountain, changing from the appearance in which he had “no form or beauty” into such great glory that his garments became shining before them, as certain manuscripts read, “like light.”

In the Old Testament also, the three sons of Korah agreed in this unity, and therefore escaped, so that they represent the form of all those who are to be saved from that eternal fire [Col. 0623C]. Since they agree with the law and the prophets, they are called two. Then, because they are gathered together in the Gospel, three harmonious persons are found in the unity of Christ. Especially since the law and the prophecies are not divided, but agree in the Gospel as though from one Spirit, one soul, and one voice.

When their agreement operates in God’s elect, if two or three are gathered together in the same unity, they will rightly obtain whatever they ask, because, gathered only in unity, they ask for one thing. Concerning this petition David says: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek” (Ps. XXVI, 4). And to show that many such people are one, as though one person were speaking for many, he says: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. XLI, 2).

The Apostle commends this unity: “that you may be perfect in the same understanding and in the same knowledge” (Philip. II, 7). For just as disagreement separates from the concord of love, so agreement gathers together and joins the structure of love into one, so that God can be in their midst through this unity.

Otherwise, if we are one body, although we are many members, we maintain unity, because God placed the individual members in the body for this purpose: that they should all have the same mind, say the same thing, agree in the same way, and be concerned for one another, “so that if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (I Cor. XII, 26), and when one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it.

Thus it ought to be among all people; so also within one person, so that, if we wish to rejoice together in our cooperation, we may preserve one musical song, and body, soul, and spirit may remain whole in one structure of God’s love and in one bond of peace. You know from music that, unless there is harmony of voices—unless singing produces one harmony from differing voices—the listener takes no delight, even if one of those voices should first fall out of the concert. So too in the churches, and certainly within one person: unless there is agreement among the chorus of virtues and harmony of love, God takes no delight and does not hear their voices.

For as the Apostle says: “Whoever stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. II, 10). Therefore, while we live together, let us be gathered in body, soul, and spirit in the name of Jesus, so that Jesus may be in our midst—that is, the Word of God, his wisdom and his power—in order that we may not be separated either by place or by time from the love of unity. For neither places nor times divide or separate those whom one love joins together.

Therefore, if two or three who agree well with one another in Christ can more confidently obtain from the Father, in his name, whatever they ask according to Jesus, how much more when individual churches pray, or the whole Church! But whenever we are not heard, the reason is that two or three of us do not agree in every respect, in understanding or knowledge, nor do we preserve Christ’s unity in the bond of peace.

And therefore, in these statements, the prudent mind should weigh how terrible it is to despise the agreement, testimony, or correction of two or three, and how great is the confidence they possess in obtaining what they ask. For that statement answers these matters: “If two of you, or three, agree” (Matt. XVIII, 16). He says, “Take one or two with you,” so that so small a number might not appear contemptible; because whatever these two or three agree upon or ask for on earth will also be agreed upon and obtained in heaven.

Great, therefore, is the consolation of the faithful, whose small number is strengthened by the Lord’s such great power, so that the one who “rules with the rod of his power in the midst of his enemies” (Ps. CIX, 2) also testifies that he is in the midst of these people. It must therefore not be doubted that they are heard in heaven, although they are still on earth, because they have the Lord in their midst.

It should be noted that he did not say, “I shall be in their midst,” but “I am in their midst,” because he will not merely become their mediator, nor will he delay being their mediator; rather, as soon as they sincerely agree, Christ is found in their midst. For Christ himself is their agreement, while they too agree in the same unity with those whose fellowship is “in the same unity” (Ps. CXXI, 3).

Then Peter approached him and said: “Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him—up to seven times?” Jesus said to him: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.”

For Luke joins together this statement about the forgiveness of a brother and the other statement in which correction is commanded—statements which the Lord explained while teaching. He introduced these statements with one injunction: “Pay attention to yourselves.” This both makes the meaning of the two commands clearer and makes his hearers more attentive.

For although he might seem to be speaking to one person, he did not say, “Pay attention to yourself,” but “Pay attention to yourselves.” Whatever a person pays attention to in these two commandments, he pays attention to for himself also; and whatever he sees in another, the other will see in him as well.

Therefore, this unusual form of speech, as it seems to me, was most helpfully placed beforehand, and this admonition was given beyond ordinary usage, because there are many things we rebuke in brothers who appear to sin against us, and many things we ought to forgive. For this reason it was said with sufficient foresight: “Pay attention to yourselves”—lest a wandering, indiscriminate eye and an immoderate gaze should look more curiously upon the ruins and faults of others than upon its own; lest, while blind to its own crimes, a person rashly undertake to rebuke those of another, and while failing to consider the injuries he inflicts daily upon others, bear more heavily those inflicted upon him by someone else.

For this reason the most kindly Teacher and most merciful Lord prudently fortified the minds of his hearers with a few words, saying: “Pay attention to yourselves.” Whatever there is in these two commandments that we do, we must first attend to it so that it benefits us, and then attend to our neighbor no less than to ourselves. If he sins against us and we correct him, so that through us the brother is gained, we receive a double reward: one because we willingly forgive him, and another because we have gained him.

Otherwise, unless you do what is commanded at God’s order, you pay attention neither to yourself nor to your neighbor. And because you cannot care for yourself without your neighbor, nor help your neighbor before helping yourself, it was rightly said: “Pay attention to yourselves, being diligent to preserve among yourselves the unity of peace in the bond of love” (Eph. IV, 5), because you give and receive as you render mutual services to one another. Even if he sins today, you too will sin tomorrow.

Perhaps tomorrow the one who was guilty today will be your judge. And even if you could disregard the fact that you had sinned against him, you will not escape God, who commands you to act—the one from whom more has been forgiven you, and to whom you owe countless things.

Therefore, know that in this number the merciful judge does not narrow forgiveness, nor does he confine it by this law and enclose it within a limit; rather, under the sacramental meaning of a sacred sign, he set this finite number in place of the infinite. Nevertheless, many ask why Peter thought that sins should be forgiven up to this number, and no further.

Perhaps it was because he knew from the law that this number signified forgiveness or rest. Hence the Lord is said to have rested after completing everything on the seventh day (Gen. II, 2); and it is also written: “The righteous falls seven times in a day and rises again” (Luke XVII, 4). Thus Luke expressly says that the Lord answered in this way: “If he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turns back to you, saying, ‘I repent,’ forgive him.”

The seventh year was also a year of rest according to the law; and after seven times seven had passed, the jubilee year of great remission was celebrated. Many other things in the law are likewise prefigured through such groups of seven. From this, some constructed for themselves an argument for their interpretation; likewise, because there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, in which there is forgiveness of all sins; or because there are seven principal vices, and when these are forgiven, everything is forgiven.

Others say that, because vengeance was exacted sevenfold upon Cain, the Lord therefore added, in accordance with what sacred History judged should be exacted from Lamech, that forgiveness should be granted as many times: so that, in proportion as vengeance had grown greater, indulgence and forgiveness might become greater.

Therefore, since the Lord set a limit for forgiving, perhaps no one would dare to spare a wrongdoer beyond it. No one, then, would dare to cross beyond this boundary. But the following parable releases the limit of forgiveness when the man who owed ten thousand talents was found and everything was forgiven him.

Therefore, let no one say that he ought not to forgive his brothers beyond this point because the Lord does not command greater forgiveness. For if he had wished this to be fixed as a limit, he certainly would not have added what he himself did. By the ten thousand talents he clearly expressed all the sins which he found in us and forgave.

Therefore, do not withhold mercy; rather, let us consider together the solution of this number. For Lamech did not first introduce this number as a measure of his vengeance without reason, nor did the Lord again establish it as a measure of the forgiveness of all sins without reason.

But I think we should first inquire into the number itself, because some multiply it by calculation in one way, while others constrain this same number toward a mystery rather than merely toward arithmetic. Why does he say “seventy times seven”? Let it be understood as seventy and seven—not, as I said, chiefly according to arithmetical multiplication, but according to the mystery of the sacrament.

For seventy times seven makes four hundred ninety, so that we should forgive a brother who sins that many times in a day, after which he can no longer sin. But if your brother sins against you again, whether in a day or at another time, will you not forgive him again? For, as will immediately be discussed in the following parable, ten thousand talents are more than seventy times seven, and one hundred denarii are more than seventy-seven.

Perhaps one hundred denarii amount to one thousand asses; and therefore, through the ten thousand talents or the one hundred denarii, he indicates all the offenses committed against us, because we ought to forgive just as we pray to be forgiven. For we do not prostrate ourselves each day and ask forgiveness according to a number; rather, we pray: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” [Col. 0626D] (Matt. VI, 12).

What debts do we ask to be forgiven— all of them, or only some part of them? No one doubts that we ask forgiveness for all those innumerable offenses which we commit daily, although all our sins have already been forgiven in baptism.

What, then, does “seventy times seven” mean? I think that the number is not to be brought to an end here according to the rule of calculation, but is to be treated according to the great mystery and wondrous sacrament.

For Luke the Evangelist, whose praise, according to Paul, “is in the Gospel” (II Cor. VIII, 18), began to count Christ’s genealogy upward from the place where the Lord was baptized—and rightly so, because that is the beginning of ascent to God. Although Matthew, counting downward from Abraham to Christ, also fulfilled a mystical sacrament, Luke, as I said, began by counting upward, and by counting completed seventy-seven generations.

He therefore began to count from Christ, in whom all sins were erased, and by counting through all the generations reached Adam himself, who was the first human being to sin and who generated all of us under the obligation of sin, because we are all, as it were, condemned in one mass.

Therefore, by a great sacramental mystery, seventy-seven generations are gathered from Christ to Adam through the entire line of those born, and likewise seventy-seven from Adam to Christ. If no generation has been omitted, no fault is passed over that ought not to be forgiven.

And the acts of vengeance for sins which raged through the entire succession down to Christ, and which Lamech enumerates, are seventy. But, so that this sacrament might be concealed more obscurely, he did not say that these same acts of vengeance would be seventy-seven, but seventy times seven; and no one should doubt that this is to be understood as the same number.

The Lord commended this number for the forgiveness of all sins when he began counting from baptism, where all sins are loosed. He then carried the line of Christ’s genealogy all the way to Adam, to show that just as vengeance was exacted sevenfold upon Cain, when he fulfilled seven acts of vengeance, as many report, so also seventy times seven were exacted upon Lamech, as he himself had foretold and prophesied. Thus seventy-seven are completed up to Christ, in whom every transgression and the vengeance for sins receive their end.

For, as some report, Christ knew that certain people would extend their sins beyond this forgiveness. Therefore Christ added seventy to seven, to say that forgiveness of sins ought to take place in this number only for those still living in this world and sinning according to the affairs of this world. For the number six, in which the world was made, appears to signify work and labor, while seven signifies rest and forgiveness.

Therefore, if someone loves the world and practices the things that are in the world, and directs his attention only to secular matters, he may aptly be said to sin six times and to receive the end of sins in the number seven, so that within it he may reach forgiveness. Perhaps Peter, perceiving this, therefore asks whether he ought to forgive up to seven times.

But the Lord, knowing that in the things enclosed by the number six we sin daily by acting against the ten commandments of God, fixed the boundary and end of sinning so that, in the number which signifies forgiveness, each person might willingly forgive his brother and neighbor.

If someone goes beyond these sins, which ordinarily occur in worldly and secular matters, and deliberately wishes to sin still further—if it were possible for him to live longer—because he has not brought an end to his sins and has not worthily sought forgiveness for his deeds, he will rightly have no forgiveness beyond the forgiveness of his sins. For whatever is accumulated in the world against the Lord’s commandments is granted forgiveness, whether he converts quickly or slowly, provided that he seeks forgiveness by making satisfaction, as Luke testifies, to the one whom he injured—since, even if no other person is offended, God is offended in every sin.

Perhaps, then, the condition of this number is that all sins which, mystically, lie beyond seventy-seven are extremely evil, whereas forgiveness is granted within that number. Therefore the most merciful Jesus exhorts and commands his Peter to forgive his brothers’ sins up to this number. The following parable will treat this matter at greater length, so that, while life in this world continues, forgiveness may be denied to no one who asks for it.

“Therefore,” he says, “I tell you: The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants.”

This parable is the conclusion of the preceding statements, which speak of concord and of the forgiveness to be shown to brothers. For just as it is exceedingly dangerous to cause one’s neighbors to stumble, so it is dangerous to deny forgiveness to those who sin against us. And just as he concluded concerning those who cause others to stumble by showing what would be better for them, so he foretold what danger threatens those who refuse forgiveness.

But let us examine who this man is who is a king, to whom the kingdom of heaven may be likened, and what is meant here by “the kingdom of heaven.” For in this Gospel the kingdom of heaven is sometimes called the present Church, sometimes the virtues and preaching of the Gospel, and sometimes Christ himself, since he himself is the kingdom of heaven, just as he himself is the wisdom of the Father, justice, truth, and power.

In this way he himself is the kingdom—not the kingdom of any of those who are below, nor of certain beings who are said to rule above in this air, but of all those who are above, who are called heavens and who strive toward heavenly things.

Accordingly, they are called heavens because Christ belongs to them, inasmuch as he himself is the kingdom that reigns daily in their hearts, just as justice reigns, and wisdom and truth and the other virtues reign in the one who became heaven for us by bearing the image of the heavenly one himself.

This kingdom of heaven, then, became like a king when the Word became flesh (I John I), and when he came “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. VIII, 3) and condemned sin through sin. Then indeed it became like a king, joining the man to himself and making him one with himself in every respect without mixture of natures, so that God and man are one Christ, the king of kings.

Accordingly, God-man Christ, because he was appointed king by God the Father over his holy mountain Zion (Ps. II, 6), wished to settle accounts with his servants. For he was appointed king for this purpose: to rule those whom he created, and then those whom he redeemed.

But lest this statement—“he wished to settle accounts with his servants”—seem obscure to you, know with certainty that he speaks parabolically by anticipation, narrating what he wished eventually to fulfill as though he had already done it. This is entirely correct, because he wished it in the sense that he prepared himself and his own things in this way, arranged all the sacraments in this way, and distributed to each person his gifts of talents until he returns.

Then he began to settle accounts with those to whom he had given his talents, at the time when he wished and when he himself determined each matter. This accounting will end when all the affairs of the present life have been completed, so that he may then begin to examine each person concerning the profit he has brought, when the time for trading will no longer exist.

“And when he had begun to settle accounts,” he says, “one who owed him ten thousand talents was brought to him.”

You have heard, brothers, how often in this same Gospel, whenever the Savior in parables entrusted his money and talents to his servants for trading, he gave them according to the measure of each and then departed. One received more, another less—each according to his own ability. For the one who distributes alone knows the strength of each person and how much he ought to give to each.

To one he gave five talents, perhaps because he was able to manage that much; to another two, as one who was able to manage less; to another one, according to the capacity of his particular quality. So also in the other passages where he divided many things among his servants, for all of which he will settle accounts with them when he returns.

But who this one person is who, when he began to settle accounts, was brought before him is not unreasonably asked. For even if we understand this as referring to that final examination, when each person will give God an account of his individual works, so that this debtor of ten thousand talents is to be brought before him when he begins to settle accounts, it will be impossible for such a person thereafter to afflict his fellow servants or, I will not say, choke one of them, but even demand money from him.

Therefore, we must ask when this accounting began, so that, after his talents had been forgiven, this man might again dispute with his fellow servant over debts. And afterward, when the Lord heard what had been reported by the fellow servants, when could he recall him to judgment for these matters?

Otherwise, unless there were some period after the forgiveness granted to him in which he could commit such offenses—offenses which, after the judgment that is to come has been completed, will certainly no longer be possible—he would perhaps never have reached so great and unhappy a danger.

Therefore, because it could not be otherwise, perhaps the Evangelist, or rather the Lord himself, who presented this parable to us, expressly says:

“But when that servant had gone out, he found one of his fellow servants.”

The wretched man would never have committed such things so cruelly if he had not gone out from the Lord’s forgiveness and from the observance of his commandments. [Col. 0629D]

But since this parable appears extremely obscure and very difficult in many respects, its meaning must be sought by whatever method may allow it to be understood soundly. For there have been some who, because of its difficulty, departed from the truth in certain places; and the interpreters themselves who translated their statements from Greek for Latin ears did not sufficiently purge their errors, lest the simple reader stumble over them, nor did they close the mouth of the pit.

For such and so great is the difficulty in these matters that are proposed that Origen confesses in his little works that no one can fully understand the text of this parable. To use his own words, he says:

“Truly I confess that no one can explain this except Christ alone, who secretly explains everything to his disciples, entering into their understanding and opening to them the obscure, hidden, and invisible treasures of the parable, confirming them with undeniable demonstrations. Then, lest he exclude other teachers from this reading, he added: ‘or perhaps the one whom he wishes to illuminate with the light of his knowledge, so that he may understand everything in this parable.’”

And after he had set forth the individual persons—who this king is, who the servant brought before him is, who those are who brought him forward, who the wife and the children are, and what all his possessions are, as well as the other matters too lengthy to enumerate—he says:

“For it is the work of God’s wisdom, so to speak, to discuss all these things.”

Therefore, let the faithful mind consider how great a difficulty there may be here, where the teacher of the Church of that time held such divine and remarkable opinions. Although he wished to exalt and allegorize these matters more deeply than the Catholic faith permits—for, as Scripture testifies, “whoever presses the breasts more forcefully will not draw milk but blood” (Prov. XXX, 33).

And therefore let us return to ourselves, and then to the end of the parable and to the Savior’s conclusion. For this parable is not to be referred to heavenly and angelic falls, but to us, to whom it is said: “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive your brother from your hearts.”

Therefore, the very force of the words must be considered, so that perhaps the meaning may shine upon us from the Lord’s own statements. For he says:

“When he had begun to settle accounts, one who owed ten thousand talents was brought to him.”

What, then, do you think the Lord meant when he said, “When he had begun to settle accounts”? He did not say, “One was brought to him while he was already settling accounts in the judgment itself,” but “when he had begun to settle accounts,” so that judgment is implied.

For the time of the future judgment is one thing, and the time when the account of that judgment was established is another. Our king Jesus Christ began to establish the account of judgment, because he became human, when in his first coming he wished to be judged and to suffer for us; or when he gave the law, when from heaven he “looked down upon the sons of men, to see whether there was anyone who understood or sought God,” because all had turned aside, and “there was no one who did good, not even one” (Ps. XIII, 2–3).

That one whole human race—because all had become one in the mass of sin—was brought before him in its entirety on account of the transgression of the first human being, bound with chains and wrapped in crimes. He owed ten thousand talents, because this iniquity was spread throughout the whole human race. According to the prophet Zechariah, this iniquity sits upon a talent of lead.

The ten thousand talents are said to be owed because the law is commended in ten commandments. If you investigate more carefully the secrets of this number and search out its hidden places, the justice established by God’s law will be shown to you. Whoever has despised it is held guilty as a violator of God’s commandments, since he has kept neither the natural law implanted in the first human being nor the law given through Moses.

Therefore he owed ten thousand talents because he had corrupted that memorable Decalogue, written by the finger of God and handed down to God’s people. He owed ten thousand talents on account of the number of the law, because, as a criminal, he had contracted all the sins condemned in the law.

His fellow servant also owed one hundred denarii, no less according to the same number; for ten times one hundred makes one thousand, just as ten times one thousand makes ten thousand, and ten times ten makes one hundred. Thus, in neither the debtor of ten thousand talents nor the one who owed ten times ten denarii has the legitimate number been abandoned—and rightly so. In both you will find both kinds of sin.

Both, therefore, are debtors, and both implore forgiveness; both likewise obtain it from the Lord. But that servant, the wicked, unjust, and ungrateful servant, was unwilling to repay his fellow servant what he himself had received from the Lord; he was unwilling to grant what had been granted to him, though he was unworthy of it.

For the ten thousand talents were forgiven him. And do not think that one hundred is perhaps a small amount, since as many sins made him liable as are also contained in those ten thousand, in which all sins must likewise be understood.

I do not wish to say that one talent encompasses all sins in this passage, but ten thousand talents, because no one doubts that the man who was brought before him owed everything.

That servant who owed one hundred denarii also owed more than seventy-seven. But there is no doubt that all those ten thousand talents were forgiven in baptism, when the most merciful Savior restored to us freedom from the guilt under which we were held as sinners.

Under that sin we had already been sold—both we and our wife, namely, sinful flesh, and our children, and all the things that are works of the flesh: the things which the carnal inclination itself, or the pleasure of the flesh, had borne for us as children. This inclination, having wickedly become adulterous to our spirit, is the wife from whom we received those same numerous and most wicked children.

The king orders them to be sold together with their mother—not because he had destroyed or sold us by his authority as his own possession, but because he shows parabolically that we and everything that seemed to belong to us had already been sold under the same sins. Thus “to have sold” means that he showed us to have been sold.

For not everything in parables can be made figuratively equal to the realities in such a way that the account appears to be history; rather, it is expressed so that the things proposed may fully indicate the point for which they are shown.

The Lord clearly demonstrates the reason for this presentation when he says:

So also my Father will do to you, if you do not forgive people their sins from your hearts. [Col. 0631D] Here he makes clear that from his first coming he forgave us many talents of sins, and therefore we too must forgive many things committed against us. For first he presented the guilty man and freely absolved him; he released the talents; he also released his wife, so that she would not remain in servitude when she came into it; he absolved his sons, so that they would not remain sold forever; and all that belonged to him, which had been assigned to servitude under the devil by God’s just judgment because sins demanded it, the pious and merciful king granted.

All these things were ordered to be sold as punishment for this wicked servant because he had first sold himself of his own accord and handed himself over under the devil. And this is what it means to order him to be sold, as I stated with certainty: to show that he had already been sold. This figure is very well known in the divine Scriptures and is expressed in various ways, as here also, by the fact that what he orders to be done he demonstrates, by his just judgment, to have already been done. Yet he does not order him to be put into prison, which belongs to that final judgment still to come.

As for the wife and sons, whatever that aforementioned teacher may have thought, one ought to understand nothing other than what can pertain to this same servant himself—that is, the flesh or carnal affection. For very often in Scripture, figuratively, the mind or spirit, called in Greek *νοῦς* (*nous*), is taken for the husband, while the flesh is taken for the wife, so that “the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24), as Christ and the Church; thus the mind rules the body, and the flesh is subject as a wife is to her husband. For the right order is preserved when the mind is subject to God [Col. 0632B] and the flesh duly obeys the soul or spirit. The children generated from them—that is, the actions of good works—will be perfect and worthy of God.

But because this wicked servant had not yet been redeemed, as I have said, nor granted freedom, he could only remain sold under the one to whom he had handed himself over in the first parent. Therefore he had nothing with which to repay, because he himself, his wife, and his sons—that is, everything that could belong to him—had all been sold under the hand of the devil. Nor could he generate anything free from himself [763] until, having received freedom, the king began to settle accounts with his servants, distributing to each the measure of talents with which they were again to trade for the profit of their lord. Thus this wicked servant was required to observe all those commandments that pertain to God and those that pertain to his neighbor.

For those ten thousand talents must certainly be referred to God, while the hundred denarii refer to the debt owed to one’s neighbor. But this servant, so forgetful of God’s benefits, observed neither those things that pertain to God nor those that pertain to his neighbor. Rather, he cruelly exacted what he himself ought first to have granted to his fellow servant. For he was obliged to do for the other what he wanted his fellow servant to do for him. Nor ought he to have inflicted upon his fellow servant the penalties that he absolutely would not have wanted another to inflict upon him. Ensnared again in these debts through his own wrongdoing, he is accused. Accused and convicted of such cruelty, he is rightly condemned: he had wished to spare neither himself nor anyone else, and moreover had not considered the talents once again entrusted to him after forgiveness had been granted.

For the money that he had first lost in Adam he ought, after being incorporated into Christ, to have spent for profit. We have already said more above about these probable “moneys.” Therefore the text does not say that, when the king had already begun to settle accounts, one was brought to him, but rather “when he began to settle accounts”—that is, when he had set forth in himself and in his death all the seeds of the rational life to come, through which all the debts of our servitude were forgiven and perfect freedom was restored to us in Christ.

Thus, if the husband and wife—that is, the spirit and the flesh, since “the two are one flesh”—or the children, namely the works of faith in Christ, remain in the adoption of the sons of God, servitude passes away. For in the past we bore the losses of many thousands of talents and had brought God no profit at all. But every day [Col. 0633A] we heap up greater losses for ourselves and commit more serious sins, because we follow the woman sitting upon the talent of lead, whose name is Iniquity.

Jesus, our king, began to settle this account, as has been said, when he came into the world incarnate; and even today this same account is being handled in this age. For this one servant is offered each day when we approach Christ through faith, having previously been sold under sin and convicted as debtors of talents. But because we had nothing with which to repay—and no mortal is believed to have had anything—we turn, therefore, to this same king and adore him, asking him mercifully to forgive us our debts.

But when, having been brought before him through the ministry of whatever ministers—namely, angels, priests, or other ministers—we descend into the font, where we are washed and consecrated in the blood of Christ, all the documents of the talents are cancelled. Freedom is restored to all mortals through Christ’s grace, and this one who was brought forward—which is the entire body of the Church—passes from servitude into the adoption of the sons of God.

Therefore he says very aptly that “he forgave him.” He sent him away free of charge, and moreover forgave him all the debts of the talents. Once this man had become free, no further mention was made of his wife and children, because with his freedom the freedom of the entire body was granted, so that the whole man—soul and spirit and flesh, whole and pure—might be free, absolved from every debt.

But this one servant, after leaving the font, found one of his fellow servants. Alas! One left the font, and behold, now there were two. Had they not again been divided, he would have found only one, because just as formerly all were one body of the devil, although many members, so also all who are reborn in Christ are received into the unity of Christ’s body. He has become their head, while each individual is a member of another, and thus in all of them there is one body.

Nevertheless, even if this one who had become one again divides himself into two, he does not divide the one who has remained one in Christ: a man whose head is one and whose members are many is still one body. This wretched one, who had left the body, left the unity of brotherhood, left the grace of God, and left charity, found one of his fellow servants. Both were servants, and therefore the other was his fellow servant. Yet one was a servant in one way and the other in another. Still, they had one Lord.

But unhappy and most wretched Cain, because he went out from the face of the Lord; blessed Abel, however, because, with his offering accepted by God, he remained within with God. Thus all human beings, although they are servants of one Lord, were made servants in different ways: Esau became a servant in one way, afflicting his brother Jacob, and Jacob himself in another, suffering his brother’s persecution, for which he fled and became an exile.

Therefore, although this account which he began to settle with his servants pertains more particularly to the time of baptism, when all debts are forgiven in it—both those we contracted from Adam and those we ourselves afterward committed—nevertheless the law of nature had to be observed among the earlier people as well, just as the law of Moses did. Moreover, in both cases fraternal charity had to be maintained, without which no one is absolved, even if he hands over his body to be burned, so that he might appear to some to be a martyr of God.

Yet the main point of the whole parable is better interpreted with reference to baptism, when our sins are forgiven more fully and perfectly, and when the charity of brotherhood, adoption, and freedom are all more abundantly released to us. Therefore the time when forgiveness is received is, as it were, the time when an account is to be rendered, so that all debts that are found may be forgiven.

The servant is not, however, said afterward to have lent his fellow servant money, which the latter could not repay, so that he might show him mercy. Rather, the wording suggests that this fellow servant already owed him when he himself, in rendering an account to his lord, was compelled to pay such a great debt. For it does not say that he forgave his fellow servant what the latter owed him and only afterward approached so that the lord might forgive him. In truth, in this act of exaction both were debtors, because both were one body from the mass of sin, and both had been forgiven by the merciful Lord.

It would therefore have been more right, and more fitting, for one who was about to render an account as such a great debtor and who was awaiting the mercy of his lord first to forgive his fellow servant whatever he owed him. Then he could approach the rendering of the account—where he was to implore his lord’s mercy—with greater reason and greater confidence in obtaining pardon.

But the fact that he did not forgive him is indicated by the fellow servant’s words, who simply says: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.” Otherwise he would have said: “You had already forgiven this; why do you demand again what you granted?” And therefore the wording may perhaps mean that at baptism we ought to forgive whatever is owed to us and no longer demand anything concerning the past.

The Lord’s own words make this clearer. For he says: “That servant went out and found one of his fellow servants, who owed him a hundred denarii,” and he does not say that the man had already been forgiven his debt. If he had forgiven him, he would certainly not owe him; but since it says that he owed him, it appears clear that he had not forgiven him. Therefore perhaps we are compelled to understand none of this as referring to what people afterward contract against one another.

But the conclusion of this parable has a very different force, when it says: “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive your brothers their sins from your hearts.” Here he shows that both the sins committed before baptism and those subsequently contracted against one another are to be most kindly forgiven. For the new birth and the transformation of the heart bring about this result: that afterward we owe nothing else except that we love one another.

Nevertheless, in this a great mystery of divine mercy is revealed: the fact that what he had not yet forgiven his fellow servant—and the hard heart which he had hitherto carried even at the font—could not prevent the Lord from forgiving him, at the beginning of the accounting, everything that he owed, if he was willing to receive what was being given.

But what did it profit the wretched man that he had been forgiven, when, because of his hardness of heart and his persistence in hatred, everything was immediately brought back upon his head and all his former and present debts were demanded from him again? Hence the question properly arises: if they were forgiven, how do they return? Could the grace of baptism perhaps be prevented from forgiving all sins, especially if fraternal hatred persists in the mind of the one who is forgiven?

It is therefore established, and the Catholic Church confesses, that yesterday is cancelled, together with whatever was contracted on that day or earlier; the hour itself and the moment immediately preceding baptism are also cancelled, and so is what occurs in baptism. But thereafter he immediately begins to be guilty, when, falling from freedom, the servant begins to be a servant of sin.

Consequently, not only the sins of subsequent days, hours, and moments, but also those of earlier days, hours, and moments, return; once everything that was forgiven has returned, he is held guilty and it is exacted from him, as though the entire debt had come back to life. Thus in some people sins appear not to have been forgiven, as in Simon Magus and in the many who have approached or approach the font hypocritically, because “the holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit.”

Therefore, because such a person approaches hypocritically, perhaps his debts are not forgiven. But this is entirely false. Hence the Apostle says: “All who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III, 27). Whoever, therefore, puts on Christ is consecrated in the body of Christ. It cannot be that, through the holy power of so great a sacrament, his sins are not forgiven, at least at the very point in time when it is received.

But through hypocrisy and hardness of heart, because an unrepentant heart remains in him, they are immediately shown to have returned, on account of his persistence in lust or hypocrisy. For, as I have said, “the holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit,” because the baptized person did not wish to receive or preserve his gift. When that Spirit has fled, even though the debts were forgiven, they return, because his eyes are directed toward darkness forever.

Nevertheless, as blessed Augustine says: “The light can only flood him while passing through, as he passes through the light,” even if he passes into the darkness appointed for him, with the sins immediately returning—sins that the holiness of baptism had forgiven in that moment—as darkness returns, darkness which the light, in passing through him, had shaken off or driven away.

The present passage also demonstrates this, when the Lord declares that the forgiven sins return because of fraternal hatred or the exaction of a debt, ordering all the debts of his former and subsequent life to be demanded from him. For “everyone who does not love remains in death; and whoever hates his brother is a murderer and walks in darkness, because he does not know where he is going” (I John III, 14–15).

I have said these things so that everyone may understand that there is no one whose debts are not forgiven wherever he has been baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. But this grace of freedom is not preserved except in the unity of the Church and in the bond of love of God and neighbor, whether a person appears to be within or outside.

Thus this servant, who seized his fellow servant and throttled him, is himself said to have gone out, because he went out from the unity of love, from the bond of concord and peace. Therefore, although he is within in number and bodily presence, he is nevertheless outside; he is not in the unity of the Spirit or in the bond of peace, because the Spirit of discipline has departed from the hypocrite, or from one who has openly become or remained wicked.

For this reason, throughout the whole time of our life, we ought to work out our salvation with fear and trembling, lest in any respect we grieve the Holy Spirit in whom we have been sealed. For neither can the one who approaches this grace of forgiveness hypocritically, nor the one who afterward, having matured in faith, withdraws from the unity of love and from the bond of fraternal affection, be saved.

The sacrament of God’s gifts and consecration is not therefore repeated, whether within or outside; rather, one waits for the person to return to the unity of love and to the bond of concord and peace, so that he may learn and begin to forgive and grant to others rather than exacting those things that belong to mercy, love, and grace.

But one must ask whether it is only hatred of one’s neighbor that causes all the debts already forgiven to be recalled, or whether it is also the other crimes enumerated by the Apostle—crimes whose perpetrators, as he himself testifies, will not inherit the kingdom of God. No one at all can deny that this is so. But here only hatred, the throttling of a brother, or cruel exaction is made the issue, because every iniquity is hatred either of oneself or of one’s neighbor, and is hatred of justice and equity.

Hence David says: “Everyone who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X, 5). Therefore no one rightly loves another who hates himself. Scripture also recalls each of us to ourselves: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Eccli. XXX, 24). For whoever has mercy on himself as he ought will be cruelly exacting toward no one else.

And whoever loves iniquity in himself cannot perfectly love equity in anything, because it is most equitable that each person first love himself according to God, and then his neighbor as himself. Otherwise let everyone know for certain that forgiven sins return wherever there is neither fraternal charity nor love of oneself according to God.

For if “everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III, 15), much more is the one a murderer who hates himself so greatly that he has mercy neither on himself nor on another in a way that could please God.

Therefore, dearest brothers, the text of this parable and the accusation of the eternal Judge must be considered. For in the Church of Christ there are only two peoples and two nations, although they appear to be twins, just as two struggled in Rebecca’s womb before they were born. Of them it was prophesied that “the elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. XXV, 23).

This does not mean the condition in which Christ’s faithful serve in the Church of Christ under the fear of God, not serving merely to be seen, but the servitude in which Esau served his brother Jacob, afflicting and tormenting him and compelling him by his hatred to live as an exile, so that his cruelty might benefit his most gentle brother for the testing and advancement of his salvation, while the other’s hostility might add to the accumulation of his own condemnation.

Yet both are servants of one Lord. But the elect serve in a very different way, while they are tormented by fraternal hatred and hostility; differently serve those who persecute them, whether within or outside. Thus the good serve to God’s praise and their own justification; the wicked also serve, but to the detriment of their own salvation and the punishment of their condemnation. The just are refined by their torments, through which their merits are increased, while the wicked and criminal do not escape the eternal punishments prepared for them.

For all whom Christ foreknew and predestined to life serve, and those who have gone out, although they appear to be within, also serve—those who afflict their neighbors. It would take too long to discuss the ways in which those whom they falsely call brothers, these cruel exactors, afflict and hold within the Church of God the members of Christ, or the many ways in which the good are throttled and shut up in prisons. I think no one could state or enumerate them all.

Perhaps the fellow servant owed a hundred denarii. Because he owed them, the wicked servant refused to repay his fellow servant with the benefits he himself had received from his most generous lord. For the wicked, ungrateful, harsh, and unjust servant refused to grant his fellow servant what had been granted to him.

If such a man is held guilty because he did not forgive his debtor when the debtor asked him, what do you think of those who repay good with evil even to people who owe them nothing, and who often attempt to torture them without cause?

This is the source of all the affliction in the Church of God, of every calamity, and of the exceedingly harsh oppression: that wicked and cruel servant does not cease to crush his fellow servant—now through losses of property and external possessions, now, with respect to the inner person, through many vexations, while such men do not blush to strike at the consciences of individuals.

But because this parable refers to what he had said earlier to Peter, who asked whether he ought to forgive a brother who sinned against him up to seven times, and he replied, “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy-seven times,” we must conclude by asking how the number corresponds to these matters.

For this reason, observe both numbers, and observe also the sin of the one talent. The number eleven signifies transgression of the law: the law is established in the number ten, while sin is expressed through eleven. Why is sin represented by eleven? Because it is transgression of ten, bringing one to eleven. In the law there is a fixed measure of commandments, while transgression of the limit of these commandments is sin.

Therefore a great mystery is figured in the number eleven, when eleven curtains of goats’ hair were ordered to be made in the tabernacle. For he said that we must forgive all sins when he said “seventy-seven times,” just as he would have said the same if he had said “seven times,” because sevenfold is customarily reckoned as the whole: all time revolves through seven days, and when the sevenfold cycle is completed, it returns again to the beginning.

He said “all sins” when he said “seven times,” because eleven multiplied by seven makes seventy-seven. He therefore wished all sins to be forgiven when he prefigured them by the number seventy-seven. Therefore let no one retain anything against himself by refusing to forgive, lest what had been forgiven be held against him.

For if he refuses to forgive his neighbor a hundred denarii, the ten thousand talents that had been forgiven are brought back before his face. For he says: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt because you begged me.” Here he declares what the ten thousand talents signify.

And if these things that the good and merciful king forgave are brought forward as a reproach, how much more those which the ungrateful and wicked servant afterward committed—the one for whom there was no other reason to forgive him than that the Lord was good and that he begged him while adoring him?

But this wicked and ungrateful servant, having obtained forgiveness, went out from the king and throttled his fellow servant, saying: “Pay what you owe.” He throttled him, and he still throttles him today, because he had gone out from the king and from his commandments in order to afflict and test his brother. Otherwise he would not have throttled his fellow servant if he had not gone out from the king.

Therefore, attentive reader, I ask you to consider carefully the subtlety of the words. The servant who was in debt for many talents fell down and adored the king, because he is the King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. XIX, 16). The text demonstrates that he is a king, and therefore introduces him as being adored—the one who had received the kingdom from the Father and had come to settle accounts.

This accounting, as I have said, takes place throughout this entire period, when the Lord’s money is dispensed and the servant seeks profit by trading with the talent he has received. If anyone claims that he did not receive a talent, he cannot deny that he received at least this: that which was forgiven him. And even if he received nothing more, he nevertheless received this: the grace which he himself ought to have remitted to his debtor, rather than exacting the debt from him.

No one can deny that he has a debtor, since someone owes him a hundred denarii. Even if this debtor does not fall down and adore him—for no one else is to be adored except the king, God, whose servants all are, both good and otherwise—he nevertheless asks his fellow servant to have patience with him until he can repay everything.

If he had nothing with which to repay, the wicked servant ought to have considered how much had been freely forgiven him by their common Lord. Since the one who owed him was his fellow servant, and since everything had been forgiven to the wicked servant himself, he ought in turn to have released everything to his debtor, at least in hope of eternal recompense.

But the wretched man, holding him fast, throttles him. Would that we did not know such things to occur in this age, to such an extent that the wretched are not permitted to breathe toward forgiveness! [771] They are often thrust into prison, so cruelly that the whole world becomes one prison for them.

And if the debt relates to offenses, the exactors become still more savage, laboring in their hearts lest their victims be able to find in them forgiveness for the offenses they themselves have committed. This is to send them into prison: they do not wish to show them mercy, but to retaliate against them, even beyond what they can requite or avenge.

When the text says, “He sent him into prison until he should repay the whole debt,” it does not speak as though it forgot that good servants will not remain in prison after the present age has ended—especially since the retribution of the most wicked exactor intervenes. Rather, it says this because “he sent him into prison until he should repay the whole debt,” since the cruelty of certain people against their enemies burns so fiercely that they never wish to bring their punishments to an end.

Therefore he himself, as though by a reciprocal sentence, is immediately justly condemned by the Lord, so that what he inflicted upon another as punishment through his rage he himself may deservedly receive according to the sentence of his own cruelty.

It should also be noted that he does not say, “He forgave him the whole debt because you adored me,” lest he appear to have forgiven him on account of some service owed by his servitude, but rather, “because you begged me.” Through this expression Christ wished us to understand that he forgave us the whole debt freely, without any merits of our actions intervening.

What a just recompense! The servant did not wish to remember God’s benefits; he did not wish to have mercy on his fellow servant, as his lord had had mercy on him; he did not wish to grant him time for repentance; he did not wish to remit vengeance and release the debt.

“Seeing what had happened, his fellow servants were greatly grieved. And they came and reported these things to their lord.”

The lord is therefore rich, since he has such and so many servants. For he has many who daily distribute among their fellow servants the various talents of gifts for the profit of their lord, and entrust them to moneychangers and merchants for trading. He also has others whom this servant most wickedly scourges.

He has this wicked servant as well, in whom are all those who disturb and tear apart the entire Church of God and do not fear to rend it. He has also those who cannot endure the injuries inflicted upon it and who are greatly grieved by the things done by such people in the Church.

This does not mean that any punitive sadness falls upon the angels, but that they do not approve of the evils that are done. Therefore they are said to be greatly grieved, and not without reason, since the Lord too is said to become angry and to rejoice, and to possess the other emotions of the human mind.

Moreover, that our deeds—whether good or evil—are daily reported by the angels to our Maker and Judge is declared in many places of the holy Scriptures and is also proclaimed by many teachers. As I have already said above, it is through their ministry that the present Church is governed and assisted.

For if on earth there is no king who is not supported by his attendants, who is not served with due honor, and for whom ministers do not administer affairs, how much more should we believe that the angels obey and minister to the Lord of all, appointed for the assistance of the Church and the defense of the saints?

Those who do not fear these angels, and who constrain and oppress God’s servants through their own taxes and exactions, will, willingly or unwillingly, experience them as accusers and exactors. For they are said in this very Gospel to come in order to gather all scandals out of Christ’s kingdom—scandals which these most wicked servants and evil men have cruelly introduced.

It should also be noted that, because they wished to help the one who had been sent into prison, the text does not say that they disparaged or inflicted anything, but that they reported what had been done, as something accomplished and not fabricated or false.

“Then his lord called him and said to him.”

He did not speak as before, concerning the loss, but more harshly because of the fellow servant who had been sent into prison. At first he spoke like a pious and merciful king, and did not reproach him by calling him wicked or evil. But because he had nothing with which to repay, he ordered him to be sold for the debt, as I said—that is, he declared that he had been sold.
