Then, when he had been entreated by the servant’s pleas, he released him as a free man and forgave him everything. But now he reproaches and rebukes him; finally, in anger, he hands him over to the torturers [Col. 0640A] until he should repay the whole debt.

From this sentence those who wish to maintain that, after the exaction of punishments, one must return again to forgiveness derive abundant material for constructing their doctrine. They imagine that people are handed over to torturers until the entire debt has been paid through sufferings, and that only then freedom ought to return to a person in full. The Catholic faith entirely rejects this.

I recall that I have already said enough above in this same Gospel about this type of expression, where it says: “Agree with your adversary quickly, while you are on the way with him, lest perhaps the adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be cast into prison. Truly I say to you, you will not come out from there until you have paid the last farthing.” [773] For what he says here is of the same kind:

“He handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the whole debt.”

It is like this: “The judge will hand you over to the officer, and you will be cast into prison, and you will not come out from there until you have paid the last farthing.” For “until” and “as long as” are shown to have one meaning in the divine Scriptures. In Greek, too, the same word, *ἕως* (*heōs*), is used indifferently for “until” and “as long as.”

These terms are very often used for what is infinite, as in this passage, because the punishments of the reprobate are believed to be infinite. But where the other passage says “the last farthing,” this one says “the whole debt,” because there he will pay all the debts of his offenses. Thus, just as he did not wish to bring his cruelty to an end here, so there the punishments owed will not come to an end.

Here, however, he is more clearly handed over to torturers than above, where it says, “The judge will hand you over to the officer,” because good angels may be understood through the officer. By their ministry that judgment will be administered when the good are separated from the evil, and the wicked exactors of punishments will receive all the reprobate, when the Judge will say to those on his left: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

He preserved his metaphor from the beginning, from the moment when he said that the kingdom of heaven is like a king who began to settle accounts with his servants, all the way to the end. Then the same Judge, who above was called the king, will complete the accounting of the judgment which he began at his first coming, or from the beginning of the age, and will bring everything to completion: restoring to the good what they have done—the good whom this wicked servant afflicted—and reckoning to this most wicked servant the things he stored up for himself and the evils he inflicted upon his fellow servants through his cruel conduct.

It must therefore be understood that throughout the whole period this one servant, because of the unity of the body whose head is the devil, signifies the entire race of wicked people. This is preferable to transferring this general sentence to another interpretation, as some wish to do when they interpret the torturers as the Roman army that came against the Jews, to whom they were handed over.

Let them see how the whole parable can fit that interpretation, when neither its beginning, nor its end, nor indeed its middle, agrees with those claims. Hence what follows:

So will my heavenly Father do to you, unless each of you forgives his fellow human beings from your hearts. Here the merciful Lord makes most clear the meaning in which he presented this parable: it is to be understood as entirely concerned with the pardon and forgiveness that we ourselves have freely received from God, so that we, in turn, must most devotedly extend the same grace to our brothers and fellow servants.

From this statement we must note two things: first, what he says, “So will my heavenly Father do to you”; and second, “Unless you forgive your fellow human beings from your hearts.” For by these two statements he reveals something terrifying: in one and the same servant, as though in a single figure, he describes the punishments of the whole race and of all the wicked. It is not that this servant whom he presents is one person and those said to be condemned in his likeness are others; rather, this servant will be anyone who does not forgive his brother from his heart.

Yet freedom of choice is preserved among the countless servants: one may wish to imitate his master’s forgiveness toward himself, while another may wish to exercise cruelty toward those little ones whom Christ called, healed, and undertook to carry back to the flock on his own shoulders. “So also,” he says, “will my Father do to you, if each of you does not forgive your fellow human beings from your hearts.”

I beg anyone hearing these words not to assume and impose upon himself the right to judge the one who forgives, or to persuade the offender against him through empty presumption of when or to whom he ought to grant pardon. For the merciful physician has arranged matters in such a way that the healing of the person whom you spare may redound to your glory, and that person’s pardon may become your reward, just as your correction or indulgence becomes that person’s pardon.

Therefore a fearful sentence has been pronounced by him who examines the hearts of individuals: “If you do not forgive your fellow human beings from your hearts.” We are thus to believe that God’s judgment is bent and changed according to our disposition. We must therefore be certain that if we do not forgive people their small offenses—not merely with our words and in pretense, but unless we forgive with our whole heart and complete purity of mind—we remain guilty, because charity has been violated.

Let no one therefore say hypocritically, “I have nothing against him,” as people commonly say: “He knows; he has God as his judge. I am not concerned with what he chooses to do; I have forgiven him.” Such a person contradicts his own statement and is convicted by his conscience. For where true charity does not reign, false peace puts on a show of color.

Therefore he overturns every pretense of counterfeit peace when he says: “So will my heavenly Father do to you, if each of you does not forgive your fellow human beings from your hearts.” He does not say how many times, as Peter asks—“up to seven times?”—nor, as he himself replies, “up to seventy-seven times,” but, “If you do not forgive your fellow human beings.” From this it is clear that the prescribed number does not restrict forgiveness but enlarges it: obedience is bounded by the command, while freedom of choice is left without limit. Thus, if you forgive as much as God commands, the reward is the reward of obedience; but if you forgive more, as the mystical number indicates, it is the reward of grace.

For God does not command forgiveness so many times in such a way that grace can have no further place—although obeying all God’s commands is itself also a gift of grace. Hence the very number seven that Peter proposed, although it seems small numerically, is found to be exceedingly great in its sacramental meaning, as is also that number when multiplied seventy-seven times.

If you consider this number throughout the entire sequence of the Old Testament, you will find it to be the mystical number of the weeks: whether it proceeds through days and produces the Sabbath; or through weeks and fulfills Pentecost for us; or hastens through months and consecrates the feasts of the seventh month; and likewise, when it proceeds through the yearly week, it makes the year that grants rest to the earth.

Then the seventh number of years releases every bond of fraternal obligation, when, after seven weeks, it produces the fiftieth year, which, as I have already said, is called the Jubilee. That year brings the complete fullness of forgiveness and the remission of all things: all servitude is removed and complete freedom returns; when every debt has been laid to rest and the bonds have been broken, the debtor rises free.

By this number, indeed, all quarrels are buried, and all greed perishes, together with every transaction arising from greed. Therefore, whenever seven is multiplied, it brings nothing other than pardon and forgiveness, if the Christian reader rightly reckons and understands it.

For when that number has been completed, then truly the contract of credit and debt will cease. Then the entire condition of servitude will truly be abolished. Then glorious freedom without end will come. Then the eternal field, ever green and flowering, will return.

Let your Charity know, dearest ones, that just as gold lies hidden in the earth, so divine meaning is concealed beneath human words. 776 Therefore, whenever the Lord’s words are discussed, let the mind awaken and the spirit attend, lest the understanding depart empty. Rather, let it labor with every desire of the heart so that it may enter into the secret of heavenly knowledge.

Whatever we have been less able to penetrate in this parable, or in the other statements that we have treated as exceedingly difficult in this book, let the faithful person approach, instructed by the Holy Spirit himself, so as to hold the perfect faith that not flesh and blood, but the heavenly Father, revealed to Peter.

Then let him hasten, with earnest vows, to fulfill the commandments that he has commanded, so that he may climb to the mountain of vision, where he may always hear Moses and Elijah speaking radiantly together with Jesus. Thus the sheep that has already been carried back to the flock on God’s shoulders may never stray from the faith or deviate from the truth.

Finally, I ask that the religious devotion of the faithful consider the passage in which the most merciful Savior placed one of the little ones in the midst of the apostles, so that all might take from him an example of perfect life; and consider that what follows was discussed concerning unanimity and the harmony of peace, what was proposed concerning individuals, and what was concluded at the end in this parable.

For its entire proposition, all its assumptions and confirmations of its statements, and finally such a great and comprehensive conclusion, have this purpose above all: that we may be of one mind and be one, that we may wish to harm no one, and deny no one what we desire to be granted to us, so that we may piously obtain from him whatever we ask.

For that true forgiveness, that perpetual release, will certainly come when, by the Lord’s own favor, the very necessity of sinning is abolished. When impurity has perished, that redeemed world will truly now be called pure; when life returns, death will no longer exist; and then there will be nothing [the text is uncertain here], when Christ reigns, the good alone will rejoice and all the wicked, together with the devil, will be outside these boundaries.

Therefore pray, brothers, because the length of the book demands an end, that the Lord may increase faith in us and in you, reveal the splendid mysteries of heavenly life, and carry us back to the flock on his own shoulders, until we are able to see the good things that he promises in the land of the living and hold them without end—he toward whom we are striving.

## 779 PREFACE TO BOOK NINE

[Col. 0643]

Philosophy can never be praised worthily enough, dearest brothers. Whoever obeys her can pass, in a certain sense, through every period of his life without distress, because those whom she has nurtured from childhood she does not abandon even in old age.

For this reason, although I had abandoned her, she did not allow me at this age to wander any farther from her. As soon as I returned to her, after having long been sorely troubled by the cares of worldly affairs, I recognized that the path of my former life was not the true one; and she began to nurse me like a child and restore me with her own breasts.

It is fitting, therefore, since the condition of children and old men is almost the same, and their death seems to me equal, that the minds of both alike should always be nourished by the milk of the divine Scriptures: the child so that he may grow, the old man so that he may not fail, indeed both so that they may progress toward what is better and live, nourished by divine breasts.

For just as they have one entrance into life, so also they have one exit after decline. Therefore both must labor so that each may know everything that is understood to belong to the divine page.

If someone wishes to reproach an old man for not having labored in his proper time, let him learn that it is more fitting for him first to listen, so that he may teach. Let him also hear that it is better to labor in the word at some time than never. Therefore no time of old age ought to be idle or unprofitable.

Especially since we remember that the study of the Scriptures progresses in others, I scatter at least among the young the divine seeds of the word. Perhaps their affection will be encouraged by this, because devoted labor conquers all things.

Therefore, in response to the pledge of my first promise, although the thinness of my exhausted intellect is already drying up, I return willingly, because I am speaking to dearest brothers. For among men so capable, illustrious, and wise, I would not dare to speak of anything, even the least thing, unless their charity had compelled me.

Often the merits of children grant the teacher an abundance of speech; and therefore there ought to be no lack of confidence in exposition when complete love overflows in affection—especially in my case, since together with you I am preparing for my sons the expenses of understanding that are their due.

For, as you have read in secular writings, “Age bears all things.” In this matter too, this proverb has come upon me and my dearest son, in an immeasurable way, so to speak, while the alternating proportion of our lives, by the dispensation of divine judgment, at a sufficiently opportune time and in a manner suitable to both, has brought each of us the wages of our actions.

For me, after countless worldly activities and the wearisome labors of life; after the anxieties of so great an administration and the long losses of the present life, it finally granted a prudent man a sufficiently desirable leisure.

So much so that those who were plotting something else accomplished nothing, while it placed upon my son, then especially dear to me and scarcely finished with his apprenticeship, a very burdensome yoke of business, because he was vigorous in mind and body—and, as I also hope, deserving in holiness.

Since divine power increased the burden of grace upon him, it enlarged the danger of his administration, weighed him down with the cares of affairs, occupied him with duties, and raised him to honors.

Yet the Almighty allowed those who were devising otherwise to accomplish nothing; he always puts our evils to good use for their outcome, and bestowed on us, in our son, the great gift of his grace: the office of leadership.

To him, dearest ones, although I write to you as a service of affection, I also pay my brothers the tribute of servitude. Not without reason am I preparing the expenses of the word, by which he himself may discharge to all, no less through my office than through his own, the debt of service and the duty of preaching—in the word, in teaching, and in every grace of religion.

Thus he too, when the time comes, may perhaps be able to complete another work. Let him nevertheless not neglect this paternal gift, however small—for it is not a gift of negligible weight—and let him regard it as offered to him together with everyone else.

Indeed, even if it is of little value, let him embrace it more dearly, because a son’s nobility derives from the honor and reverence shown to his father. For every inheritance prepared and received from a father is usually more precious than all the riches that he might have acquired for himself elsewhere.

Therefore I ask that he embrace this small possession of paternal right in the word in such a way that the divine things I turn over may bring the fruit of life inwardly to their minds, and may also raise them toward the things that are divine and toward the secret mysteries of God.

I ask also that these things please you, for they will then be acceptable to the God who dwells in you, when what I offer is pleasing to you, dearest ones, in accordance with your desire.

For although the brothers have become debtors, so that they must listen and handle the money of the word, expended for their profit rather than their loss, nevertheless you too ought, in charity, to consider the talent that I am paying out.

For although, according to the Apostle, parents ought to store up for their children, and not children for their parents, it is nevertheless fitting for children to guard more carefully what has been stored up and cultivate it diligently, lest the capital of labor perish in vain. It is demanded, with interest of merit and with the profit of good work, by the Lord himself, to whom the money belongs.

For in this solid square number of the Evangelists are the great treasures of wisdom and knowledge that I am excavating. Therefore, since the whole world consists of four elements and the entire globe is joined together in its four regions, the supreme Craftsman, God, has most appropriately arranged that, just as the four seasons continually run their course, so the world might be watered by these four divine fountains.

For one fountain divides into four heads, and they flow from the paradise of the living God. By their showers of the word of Christ the Church is watered, so that it may be spread universally under the sacramental meaning of this material number.

Therefore four disciples are chosen: two, namely, who followed the Lord, and two who believed when the apostles preached. Thus there is to be no difference in preaching between those who saw the Lord and those who did not see him, provided that they believe rightly.

Nevertheless, their order must be sought: why Mark and Luke, who did not learn from the Lord himself and are not counted among the apostles, are placed in the middle, as though enclosed by two posts; while Matthew and John, at either end, followed the Lord, saw his miracles, were instructed by his teaching, trained by his disciplines, shown examples by him, and confirmed by the glory of his resurrection.

The other two learned later and completed what many had attempted. The Holy Spirit placed them in the middle between two distinguished men, like sons to be embraced, so that no imperfection might appear in the body of the Gospel.

But let Christ the man be the beginning of our salvation, and the same Christ, God and man, its end. Thus what is the beginning is the end, and what is the end is the beginning: that is, α and ω, Alpha and Omega.

Meanwhile, although some may have wished to arrange them differently, they have more correctly been placed in this order: those whose grace is that of the apostolate are placed at the ends, while those of a lesser order, who learned from a man what was approved and confirmed by the apostles, are placed in the middle.

Therefore, to speak truly, they are rightly placed in the middle like sons, so that they may be enclosed on either side, just as the two at the ends are more firmly established—if it is permissible to say so.

For what the two at the ends are in office, in the unity of the word, and in all the preaching of the holy Gospel, the two in the middle are also. Thus throughout the square world the four-horse chariot of the word, more enduring than heaven, may run its course, and the unity of all those who believed in the Gospel and followed the Lord in preaching the word, whether before or after the Passion, may be commended.

## BOOK NINE

[Col. 0645]

## (CHAPTER XIX)

When Jesus had finished these sayings, he departed from Galilee and came into the regions of Judaea beyond the Jordan, and great crowds followed him, and he healed them.

The most merciful Lord left Galilee, namely, his own homeland, and came into the regions of Judaea [Col. 0645C], as the just Lord of all, who loves his own so greatly that he does not abandon the others; for just as all of them ought to preserve faith and offer glory as to the Lord, so he ought to assist all and show mercy as to servants, lest one place should always hold him according to his humanity.

But he did not leave the Galileans before he had finished these sayings—that is, until he had brought everything he had set before them to a perfect conclusion of peace and concord. And so he came into the regions of Judaea beyond the Jordan, where baptism was administered to people. Perhaps the words “and he healed them there” are said of the crowds that followed him, because he was urging them toward healing. For no one is perfectly healed unless he has been reborn through the baptism of Christ, which is prefigured in the Jordan [Col. 0645D]. The Jordan is formed from two springs, according to the mystery of Christ, to demonstrate that the same Christ our Lord is joined from two substances, as it were from two springs—namely, divinity and humanity. Thus Christ became one, and the crowds followed him, and he healed them all.

Yet the Apostles followed him in one way, and the crowds in another. So even today some follow him because of him himself and because of eternal life, while others follow him temporarily for some other reason, even as far as the regions of Judaea beyond the Jordan, in order to be reborn in the fountain of baptism.

And the Pharisees came to him, testing him and saying, “Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any cause whatsoever?” [Col. 0646B] The miserable blindness and hardness of heart of the Pharisees! The crowds follow him as though to bear witness to his saving teaching, like sheep accompanying the shepherd whom they were leading along, like little children accompanying a loving father who is setting out on a journey or traveling far away [Col. 0646C]. But these men, as soon as he approached them, cunningly put him to the test, and attack him from either side with a kind of horned syllogism, so that whatever he answered, he might be trapped.

But the excellent Teacher orders everything in such a way that they are left without excuse and he is trapped in nothing. First, therefore, after healing the crowds, he immediately dismissed them, because they were ready to follow him into the regions of Judaea. Otherwise the blind detractors, the Pharisees, might perhaps have said that, in order to spread the reputation of his teaching and to provide testimony to his miracles, he had brought this crowd along with him for the sake of boasting—the people whom he had healed. And so he immediately dismissed them once they had been healed.

Then he so carefully framed his answer that they could neither deny what he said nor seize and entangle him in the snare they had prepared. For if he had said that it was lawful to dismiss one’s wife for any cause whatsoever, the Lord, the preacher of chastity, would seem to be teaching the opposite. But if he had answered that she ought not to be dismissed for every cause, he would have been treated as guilty of sacrilege because he was speaking against Moses; and they might perhaps have accused him of saying that Moses had spoken against God.

They do not even consider how shamelessly they are asking the question when they assign no specific cause, lest they confine themselves within the limits of definite causes. Instead they say “for every cause”: whether, for any one of these causes, a wife ought to be dismissed, since desire knows no restraint. By their question they first bind themselves and prove themselves adulterers. For where the law concerning dissolving a marriage is invoked, divorce is already being sought out of hatred for the former spouse, and desire for the next spouse gives birth to adultery.

Therefore, when a man or a woman entertains such thoughts and seeks, for any cause whatsoever, to dissolve what God has joined, if it is a man, he is lustful and already an adulterer in his heart. But if it is a woman, she is plainly shown to be a prostitute.

How well, therefore, the Lord brings forward Holy Scripture as testimony—and not any other Scripture than that written by Moses himself—so that he may pass unharmed through their trap, bind them with their own cords, and prove by divine authority that it was not so from the beginning. “Have you not read,” he says, “that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female? And he said, ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’?” [Col. 0646D]

This passage is presented differently in Genesis. There the whole matter is related as Adam’s words; here, however, the Lord indicates that all these things were spoken by the one who fashioned the man and made the woman from the man’s rib. I have therefore taken care to admonish the reader to consult himself on this question and to inquire carefully wherever anything of this kind is found in the divine Scriptures [Col. 0647B].

Nevertheless, whatever Adam is shown to have said concerning this matter, we accept as truly spoken in prophecy. Therefore, whatever was said through him, we have no doubt was spoken by the Lord, who formed a wife from his side. For he himself built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman for him; and it was a sacrament of the future, since at that time the Lord was speaking mystically through Adam.

The Apostle understood this, saying, “This is a great sacrament in Christ and in the Church” (Ephesians 5:32), because Christ is the head of the body, and the whole Church is the body and members of the head; and thus “the two have become one flesh” [Col. 0647C].

Therefore, as I have said, let the most diligent reader weigh the force of the words, and the words with which the Lord answered, and those words which the disciples used. Let him also consider the disposition of the Apostle Paul concerning this matter, whether he is silent about it or treats it occasionally in other passages: how he unfolds the hidden sacrament of God.

How did Christ leave his Father when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and also leave his mother, namely the Synagogue, and cling to his wife, that is, the Church, which was formed from Christ’s side and is daily built into a woman, just as every succession of those who are born is propagated from wife and husband? “Thus they are no longer two, but one flesh.”

Therefore, “what God has joined, let no human being separate.” Behold, the most merciful Jesus calls conscience to testify to divine authority, so that he may convict those who do not ask in order to learn and restrain themselves, but in order to slander him and excuse themselves for doing what they were inexcusable in doing [Col. 0647D].

He says “male and female,” not “one male and many females,” as though one man might be permitted to take many wives; nor “many males and one female,” as though one woman might be permitted to take many husbands. For the Lord did not take two or three ribs, or more, from the man’s side.

Therefore the mind must be recalled to continence, so that you may say to your wife what we read that Adam said: “This is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh” (Genesis 2:23). Otherwise, even if that woman whom you have taken beyond the first is a rib, from whose rib she may be, she is nevertheless not yours. And if you say that she is yours, take care that you are not lying, since from the one Adam only one rib was taken, so that it might be joined in the companionship of one spouse [Col. 0648A].

This union, being a natural law, approves God’s first judgment. Second marriages, however, were permitted not according to God’s will, but according to the necessity of sinners. Therefore the Lord shows by these words that second marriages ought to be avoided, when he says concerning the bill of divorce, “Because from the beginning it was not so.” But he who made them from the beginning made them male and female. “For this reason,” he says, “a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.”

When he says “for this reason,” he expresses the cause of the matter. The wife is from the husband, and both are from one flesh. Although, according to the Apostle, this is a great sacrament “in Christ and in the Church” [Col. 0648B], nevertheless according to the nature of flesh it is as creation teaches.

Others may wish to say that greater love ought to exist between brothers and sisters because they come from the same parents, whereas a husband and wife are now understood to come from different parents, and not as they came from that one Adam. Here, I ask you, reader, to attend a little more carefully, because according to this bond of marriage also, the bond of wedlock is exceedingly great, and it is a sacrament of piety in Christ.

For even if they now say of brothers and sisters that they are born from one flesh already made, nevertheless the unity made one at the beginning, which remains, is itself stronger. God’s ordinance from the beginning must be believed stronger than the subsequent power of human nature. For God’s commandments are not subject to nature; rather, nature must necessarily obey God’s commandments [Col. 0648C].

And so in individual cases it is as it is in the case of three. Although they are born from one marriage, afterward they too seek different paths. Marriage, however, always returns to the beginning, so that the two may be one flesh. Although husband and wife are born from different parents, nevertheless by God’s commandment they are born so that they may come together as one.

Attend, I beg you, to the divine law, examined according to all the wills of God. Brothers and sisters, although they are from one source, were created by nature so that they should not come together as one. But male and female, although they are not from one source, were created so that they should return to the beginning, from which they came as one, because they were created for the purpose of being one.

Thus every nature follows God’s ordering, though it does not follow itself. And although this bond of marriage is a grace of God when it is joined and preserved lawfully according to God, nevertheless, because husband and wife sometimes love each other carnally, it is rightly said: “And the two shall be one flesh” [Col. 0648D].

But the Pharisees, because they do not receive sound teaching and cannot refute it, return to the hardness of their hearts and ask, “Why, then, did Moses command that a bill of divorce be given?” See how greatly the teaching of righteousness displeases sinners and the lustful, since the preaching of chastity is burdensome to fornicators. Yet because they cannot answer reason, they are unwilling to believe the truth.

They put forward Moses as their patron, whose person was revered by everyone as though he were God, and whom everyone feared to oppose in anything. Therefore they tried to destroy Christ’s teaching, which they could not overcome by reason, through the authority of a supposedly greater person, so that while Moses was considered irreproachable and feared to be criticized, the interpretation of the truth might be silenced [Col. 0649A].

Hence they also say to him, “Why, then, did Moses command that a bill of divorce be given and the wife dismissed?” He says to them, “Because Moses permitted you to dismiss your wives on account of the hardness of your hearts; but from the beginning it was not so.”

Their question proceeds from great disdain and much arrogance. They bring forward Moses while inwardly despising Christ as well, as though they were saying: “Why do you contradict what so great and so eminent a man, Moses, commanded in the Law? He was like the visible tongue of the invisible God. He saw the incorruptible glory of God and bore the testimony of divinity in his face before the people. But you, a most insignificant man, a craftsman’s son—why, then, are you destroying what he established?” [Col. 0649B]

But the gentle Lord does not cease to teach and refute them. “Moses,” he says, “because of the hardness of your hearts, permitted you to dismiss your wives.”

It is as though he were saying: “Moses often permitted you many such things because of the hardness of your hearts and the perversity of your minds—things that God did not command. Thus, in the wilderness, he ordered sacrifices to be offered to God, sacrifices that he had commanded you to offer, although through the prophets he reproaches them and says that he does not want them and had not commanded anything of the kind.

“But Moses saw that your minds had not yet departed from Egypt, nor had you abandoned the sacrifices that you were accustomed to offer to demons. Rather, you were still carnally inclined toward the practice of sacrifices. If he had commanded you to withdraw from sacrifices and offerings, you would certainly not have obeyed him. For such a long-standing passion, or such a cruel disease, is difficult to cure. He therefore ordered you to sacrifice—but to God, and no longer to demons.”

By a similar reasoning, the Author of human salvation thoroughly teaches that this matter too came about: the bill of divorce which those most wicked people put forward. Because of the hardness of their hearts, Moses judged it less harmful to allow them to give a bill of divorce and dissolve marriages than to have hatred perpetually in their hearts and murders take place [Col. 0649D].

This does not mean that such dissolution was good. Rather, like a compassionate physician, he permitted them to do something evil so that they would not fall into worse crimes and the worst diseases would not continually arise among them.

“From the beginning,” he says, “it was not so.” See how powerfully he refutes them and how forcefully he strikes back, proving by divine authority that it had not been so from the beginning.

It is as though he were saying: “Since it was not so from the beginning, can God be contradictory to himself, so that he commanded one thing at the beginning and afterward, with a new command, should break his own most just judgment?” We must not think this of God, who does not repeat the very thing he has once spoken, because he speaks unchangeably.

But Moses, as we have said, used his own judgment in many matters concerning which he had not received a command from the Lord, just as Paul also testifies that he did. Moses, however, according to the hardness of their hearts and according to the desire for second marriages that was passionately sought among that people—so that they might have wives who were either more beautiful or younger—permitted such things by his own judgment, and not by divine command [Col. 0650A].

The Lord therefore did not say, “According to the hardness of your hearts, God permitted you,” but “Moses.”

“But I say to you: whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery; and whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery.”

Behold how brief and unqualified the Lord’s judgment is concerning the broad opportunity which the Jews were abusing in dismissing their wives: he says that fornication alone can overcome a wife’s marital bond, since it is itself what first divides one flesh into two.

Some, considering this judgment insufficiently, think wrongly about it, saying: “If a wife commits adultery, it is in her husband’s power either to retain her as an adulteress and sleep with her as she is, or to dismiss her.” Yet the Lord showed that one of these actions is lawful: to dismiss her if she has fornicated. He did not say that retaining her is lawful, just as it does not appear that he openly prohibited it in this passage, unless this is considered from other passages and from the context of his words [Col. 0650B].

He says, “What God has joined, let no human being separate.” Therefore one must first inquire into the law of marriage, whether God is its cause and whether the union has been established lawfully according to God. Only then should the question of divorce be discussed, because not every marriage is from God or through God. Otherwise, how could the Apostle say, “If the unbelieving partner separates, let him separate” (1 Corinthians 7:15)? In this he clearly shows that not every marriage is from God, since there is one that is to be dissolved.

Therefore, even if a wife or husband commits adultery, the union is not God’s union when those involved do not have God’s law and the law of nature is not preserved. Whoever, whether male or female, acts against God’s commandment is an adulterer and has already been separated from his or her own body and from that grace which exists in lawful marriage.

This is especially true because such a person has taken himself, a member of Christ, and made himself a member of a prostitute with whom he has committed fornication. Therefore I do not consider it a small matter if a prostitute is retained and abuses herself wickedly in both respects, since, because she is an adulteress, she no longer appears to be a lawful wife to anyone.

Thus, just as the man who dismisses a chaste wife for any cause whatsoever is cruel and unjust, so the man who retains a prostitute or a disgraceful woman is foolish and unjust. For he appears to be her defender of disgrace, concealing the crime and consenting to his wife, just as, conversely, chastity possesses the reward of marriage when it makes one flesh from two.

When chastity is joined to the spirit, one spirit and one flesh are formed in them. This can in no way happen if one of them adulterates the flesh [Col. 0650D]. Therefore, when a woman has divided the one flesh into another and separated herself from her husband through fornication, she ought not to be retained, because she has committed adultery, lest perhaps she cause the husband who has preserved his chastity to come under a curse. Scripture says: “He who retains an adulteress is foolish and impious.”

Wherever, therefore, fornication exists, the wife may freely be dismissed. But since it could happen that someone, driven by some jealousy, might bring a false accusation against an innocent woman and, because he desired a second marriage, charge his lawful wife with adultery, the most equitable Judge commands the first wife to be dismissed in such a way that he may not take a second wife while the first is alive. The Lord neither commands him to kill her, as Moses commands in the Law, nor to retain her [Col. 0651A].

It must also be noted that he says, “What God has joined, let no human being separate.” He did not forbid separation where the cause is against God and the union is not God’s union. Nor did he forbid separation by mutual consent for the sake of God, since the time is short, so that afterward, being free, they may devote themselves to the Lord in holy continence. For where God is the cause, there is also lawful freedom.

Nevertheless, since it is not permitted to take another wife while the first, who is an adulteress, is alive—just as a woman may not marry another man if her first husband was an adulterer and was dismissed by her—there is no other path of salvation left to them than either to reconcile themselves to one another after worthy satisfaction before God or the Church, or for both to submit themselves to perpetual continence, lest perhaps what one of them did wrong should have been contracted through the fault of the other. This often happens where the rights of chaste love are not preserved and no care is taken for the discipline of lawful observance [Col. 0651B].

But the disciples of Christ, considering all these dangers that can occur and often do occur to those who live in the world with wives, were astonished by the novelty of his words and the consequences of the matter, and said: “If such is the situation of a man with his wife, it is not advantageous to marry.”

They did not say, “If such is the situation,” because of uncertainty about the Teacher’s teaching, but because of the magnitude of the dangers that ordinarily befall married people. A wife is a heavy burden when men are not permitted to dismiss their wives, nor women their husbands, whatever their mutual condition, for any cause except fornication—and even that only with very careful judgment, lest, as I have said, what one of them did wrong should be the fault of the other [Col. 0651C].

Therefore both must recognize their own danger. And as the excellent teacher Augustine defines in his book *On Adulterous Marriages*, neither of them should shrink from forgiving the other after repentance, just as Christ forgave the adulterous woman who was brought to him and caught in adultery. Thus both should consider their danger, perhaps suffering from a similar disease, and flee to the mercy of the same Savior, so that thereafter each of them may live continently.

Or, if after repentance and worthy satisfaction before God they choose to be reconciled to one another, let them praise God’s patience in each other and practice repentance together throughout the days of their lives, so that in the future they may receive perfect forgiveness. This is not so that one of them may consent to the other’s wantonness, as some now wickedly and openly do. Rather, let them consider their shared condition and shared danger, even if the wound is not shared, so that they may have a shared salvation, faithfully and humbly sought [Col. 0651D].

For the evangelist Matthew, because he expressed one case and omitted the other, perhaps makes this difficult to understand. He appears to give men an opportunity to choose something other than the truth, because they wrongly suppose that what is not permitted to women is permitted to themselves—as though, because he remained silent, he seemed to have granted them permission. [790]

Therefore the other evangelists have expressed the matter generally, so that what they say may truly be understood of both.

Thus Mark says: “Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery against her; and if a wife dismisses her husband and marries another, she commits adultery” (Mark 10:11) [Col. 0652A].

Behold, one judgment is given concerning both.

Luke also says: “Everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a woman dismissed by her husband commits adultery” (Luke 16:18).

Since her husband is alive, therefore, she commits adultery, although she has been dismissed, because she is his wife as long as her husband lives. Consequently she cannot lawfully belong to another man, since she is another man’s wife. But the man to whom she belongs does not join himself to another man’s wife, but to his own; therefore he does not commit adultery. Nevertheless he is guilty if he consents to her adultery and conceals his wife’s adultery.

Here, therefore, a common remedy of salvation must be sought. For if he dismisses her on account of fornication, she nevertheless has not ceased to be the wife of the man who dismissed her. Since she has not ceased to be what she was, she belongs to the man whose wife she was, and not to the man whom she married. Scripture does not call the latter her husband, but an adulterer [Col. 0652B].

Therefore reconciliation of the marriage is neither disgraceful nor difficult even after one of them has committed and purged adultery, where forgiveness of sins is believed to take place through the keys of the kingdom of heaven. This is not so that the adulteress may be recalled after the husband’s divorce, but so that, after fellowship with Christ and reconciliation, she may no longer be called an adulteress.

Nor is it surprising that the Apostle either urges them to be reconciled to one another or to practice continence together. For as long as her husband lives, the wife is bound by the law of her husband, so that she may not join herself to anyone else; nor may the husband take another wife, because, while the other lives, each of them remains bound by the law of marriage, since they continue together in the body [Col. 0652C].

But if one of them departs from the body, the other is released from the law of marriage, so that she may marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord, and may be with another man.

A great sacrament is therefore prefigured here: a woman cannot become the wife of any later husband by any arrangement unless the first husband has died and thereby she has ceased to belong to him. For if she commits fornication, she does not thereby cease to be the wife of her first husband unless he first dies.

Although a wife may lawfully be dismissed on account of fornication, or a wife may leave a husband who has committed adultery, the bond of the first marriage nevertheless remains. Therefore the man who marries a dismissed woman is guilty of adultery even if she was dismissed because of fornication; likewise a dismissed husband is guilty if he takes another wife [Col. 0652D].

Just as an excommunicated person guilty of any crime, while the sacrament of regeneration remains in him, does not lose that divine sacrament even if he is never reconciled to God, so, while the marriage covenant remains, when a wife is dismissed because of fornication or a husband is released, they will never be without that bond between them, even if they are never reconciled to one another. They will be without it only if one of them dies.

But an excommunicated person guilty for any reason will never lose the sacrament of regeneration, even if unreconciled, because God never dies, to whom the virgin soul had been joined by the marriage portion of betrothal and by the right of spiritual marriage. This is the great sacrament made evident in Christ and in the Church.

Therefore the Apostle exhorts: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the Church” [Col. 0653A].

If a wife is to be loved for the end for which, and in the manner in which, Christ loves the Church, then the covenants of lawful marriage and the chastity of purity must certainly be preserved.

But if some corruption of divorce should occur, the salvation of the other must be sought rather than death: either they should preserve themselves chastely by abstaining together, or, after worthy satisfaction before God, they should be reconciled to one another in peace, just as Christ is reconciled to souls that love him worthily after the fall into sin. Thus he says that he rejoices more over those who have been converted and repent worthily than over the righteous who stand firm and perhaps have no need of repentance for any crime.

For this reason I have departed at greater length from the duty of an expositor, though not more broadly than was fitting, because many questions arise concerning these matters [Col. 0653B]. Augustine, the most abundant resolver of all questions, so to speak, treated them at greater length in the book mentioned above, which he composed on this subject. Anyone who wishes to read it will find that I have said little about these matters, and scarcely anything necessary.

As for the other vices by which human nature can be defiled—whether someone has been contaminated or disfigured inwardly or outwardly: for example, if one has been drunken, or angry, or both spouses have been raised in the worst habits; if the woman has been lustful, or a poisoner, or a murderer of her children, or promiscuous, or polluted by any bodily disgrace, or weighed down by illness, or affected by the other evils that would take too long to enumerate—if one or both of them are entangled or corrupted, nevertheless their union must be maintained and preserved, whether they wish it or not, and such a great bond must be endured [Col. 0653C].

For when we were free, we voluntarily subjected ourselves to servitude—unless perhaps someone wishes to act against God’s judgment or interpret this passage differently, as some have attempted. They hold that if one of the spouses has committed crimes perhaps worse than adultery, the wife need not be retained, since this appears unreasonable. Yet to decide against God and act against his teaching appears impious.

Some say that Christ did not command or order anyone to dismiss his wife by precept on account of fornication, but, as though explaining the matter, said that whoever dismisses her except on account of fornication makes her commit adultery—that is, he dismisses a woman who is not committing adultery. If she became an adulteress while her husband was alive, and is with another man, then without doubt the man who dismisses her gives her the opportunity for a second marriage and thereby makes her commit adultery. But if she was already an adulteress and he dismissed her, he does not make her commit adultery, because she is already an adulteress and separated from the body of chastity [Col. 0653D].

Therefore the husband now appears rightly guilty if he dismisses an adulteress, just as he is guilty when, for any cause whatsoever, he dismisses a wife chaste in body and makes her commit adultery.

Considering this, the Apostles, with closer attention, put forward so grave a yoke, expressing the movement of their minds under the weight of the burden, and say: “If such is the situation of a man with his wife, it is not advantageous to marry.”

For if a woman does not marry, both parties, man and woman, will be free. But if she marries, and one of them sins against God and corrupts the marriage bed, both will suffer destruction from one another [Col. 0654A].

Their punishment is inescapable; it is a necessary evil, a natural temptation, a calamity that is desired, a domestic danger, a pleasing loss: the power of evil painted in the color of good. To dismiss her is sin, while to retain her is torment, so that by dismissing her we commit adultery, or by retaining her we endure daily quarrels and bitter disputes.

The Apostles, horrified by all these things that can be said, imagined, or happen, said: “If such is the situation, it is not advantageous to marry.”

The Lord did not answer them that it is advantageous. Rather, by saying something else, he agreed that it is not advantageous. Nevertheless, seeing the weakness of the flesh, he said: “Not everyone accepts this saying, but only those to whom it has been given.”

He did not say, “Not everyone can,” but “Not everyone accepts.” It is as though he were saying: “Everyone can accept it, but not everyone wishes to.” For even if the victor’s crown is set before them, not everyone competes for victory; even if they desire glory, not everyone sweats through the labor. It is given to those who are willing to understand, strive, and labor [Col. 0654B].

Here it must be noted that the virtue of true chastity or perpetual virginity is never possessed except by the grace of God. Nor are the covenants of marriage lawfully preserved in Christ except by his gift. Let no foolish thought therefore seize us, as though we could excuse ourselves by saying that because we did not receive this gift, we cannot prevail, but that it belongs only to those to whom it has been given.

For although this grace is a gift, nevertheless, in order to receive it, labor must be expended with faith and charity. For it has been said: “Ask and it will be given to you”; and, “Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matthew 7:7–8) [Col. 0654C].

This makes clear that grace is not denied to those who ask and desire it perfectly. And to show what chastity that comes from God ought to be like, he said:

“For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb; there are eunuchs who were made so by human beings; and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdoms of heaven. Let the one who can accept this accept it.”

The Apostles, therefore, seeing the dangers of married people, said that it is not advantageous to marry if such is the situation of marriage. But the Lord immediately indicates that not everyone possesses the reward of continence. The virtue of continence is perfect when it is preserved wholly by vow and free will, for love of eternal life, rather than from necessity.

Therefore the Lord presents three kinds of eunuchs, distinguishing between those who practice continence more from necessity than from free will and the desire for chastity, and those who castrated themselves of their own accord for the sake of the kingdoms of heaven. Those who belong to the latter group neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God, remaining in chastity [Col. 0654D].

Following their example, the eunuchs whom Isaiah describes have consecrated and castrated themselves for the Lord. Not with iron, as some wrongly teach, but by the word—by that word which, according to the Apostle Paul, is the living and effective word of God, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, cleansing everything within, discerning the joints and marrow, and purifying all things [Col. 0655A].

For it is a great matter, on account of the kingdom of heaven, for a man to castrate himself. It must be done through love of Christ, so that no sexual impurity (*venereus*) may infect his mind or body, and not like that eunuch of whom it is said that, embracing a virgin, he sighs. Rather, he must be wholly cut through by the sword of the Holy Spirit, which is the word of God, and circumcised inwardly and outwardly, so that no itching of desire may prevail in him. Indeed, only chastity and purity should reign.

Not everyone accepts the word by which these people are thus castrated, because they neither ask nor seek, nor knock as they ought in order to receive it; rather, it is accepted by those to whom it has been given, because none of us possesses anything that he has not received.

As for the other two kinds of eunuchs, because some are born from their mother’s womb so that they are incapable of this, while others afterward become eunuchs through iron or by some other means, such people are not God’s eunuchs. Through the prophet Isaiah he himself speaks to them [Col. 0655B]. Their will has not been cut off, but necessity has been imposed upon them; their conscience has not yet been circumcised, nor has a new will been begotten according to the Holy Spirit. They are either the playthings of married women or effeminate figures fashioned for some purpose. Since they have no vows of chastity before God, no reward is owed them, because they were not castrated for the sake of the kingdoms of heaven.

Nevertheless, we do not say that God is so lacking in mercy that he does not reward those who were born this way or later became so by whatever means, if it is granted to them to possess by vow and desire what they previously possessed by necessity, so that they remain chaste in mind and body. For although such people have less bodily power, they can still be corrupted in mind at every moment.

Therefore, although they have a lighter struggle against the desires of the flesh, they do not overcome all the affections of the mind without conflict. Whatever happens to them, for whatever reason, they turn into a vow and do not cease giving thanks to God, who granted them the grace of chastity, even if they received it unwillingly [Col. 0655C].

Nor should we listen to those who teach that this third kind of becoming a eunuch—the strongest and holiest kind—ought to be accomplished by iron or by some other artifice. They would have us believe, according to a literal argument, that all the desires of the flesh can be cut off not by striving and much sweat in battle, but by a single stroke, something that cannot be done, as we have discovered that very many, including monks, have done.

For even if the will was good at the moment when someone castrated himself for the sake of eternal life, it was not according to knowledge if he thereby corrupted the struggle of the Christian religion and afterward lay useless and idle [Col. 0655D].

Therefore the Author of our salvation set forth three kinds: one who is born according to the flesh, as though by nature; another who is made so by some necessity and is rendered chaste, as it were, only outwardly; and a third who becomes chaste for God by vow and free will.

In one of them nature is defective, namely in the one who is born so. In another, a necessity has been imposed, on account of which he is mutilated. But in the third, the hope of the heavenly kingdom, begotten through faith, is propagated in charity, through which he is believed to beget many children more by spirit than by flesh [Col. 0656A].

He urged us to become like this one, if we are able. For the Lord says this to his eunuchs:

“Let none of them say, according to Isaiah, ‘I am a dry tree’” (Isaiah 56:3). “For if they keep my commandments and choose what I will, I will give them in my house and within my walls a chosen and renowned place, better than sons and daughters.”

After hearing these rewards, the Lord nevertheless so moderates his judgment that he places no snare of ruin before anyone. For he says: “Let the one who can accept this accept it.” This is the voice of God exhorting.

It is as though he were saying: “Let each person consider his own strength and the grace he has received, whether he can fulfill the commands of virginity; for it is better to travel along level ground than to climb to higher places from which one may fall more grievously.”

Thus, in the manner of a king exhorting his soldiers, he says: “Let the one who can accept this accept it”—that is, let the one who can fight, fight, and engage the enemy, so that he may overcome and triumph [Col. 0656B].

Then little children were brought to him, so that he might lay his hands on them and pray; but the disciples rebuked them.

“Then,” that is, when he was speaking about chastity and declaring those eunuchs blessed who had castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. On hearing this, certain people brought him infants and children, most pure by the virtue that was being preached. Perhaps they thought that the Lord praised only those who were bodily pure, not knowing that he did not bless those eunuchs whom the necessity of infancy makes chaste, but those whom the virtue of continence does so. Especially since he did not say, “The kingdom of heaven belongs to these,” but “to such as these,” thereby showing that they reign not according to age but according to the conduct of perfect discipline and according to a similar innocence [Col. 0656C] and simplicity. He promises them the kingdom of heaven not on account of bodily childhood but on account of purity of heart.

The Apostle also, agreeing with this same meaning, says: “Brothers, do not become children in your understanding, but be infants in malice, and mature in understanding” (I Cor. XIV, 20). A great figure was indeed set forth beforehand in these children: namely, those children who are daily offered to God by angelic spirits or by the ministers of the altar. Of them the Savior says: “Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me” (Hebr. II, 13). These children he himself received from God the Father, as it were as a trust, so that he might save them.

But because one of the Evangelists called them “little children,” another “infants,” and a third said, “Let the children come to me,” I think that this variation was not without some sacramental significance. [Col. 0656D] For there is much difference among those who are offered daily, whose form these children represent. There are children, there are little ones, and there are also sucklings, whom we say are smaller than infants. Since he says that children have been given to him, he perfects his praise for himself from the mouths of both groups, so that, recognizing his benefits in children, we may say: “Out of the mouth of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise” (Psal. VIII, 3), so that no age is excluded from Christ.

Yet it seems strange that the disciples forbade infants to come to Christ, or rebuked those who brought them so that he might lay his hands on them and pray for them. I do not think this should be understood literally, as though they were unwilling for them to be touched by the Savior’s hand or blessed by his voice. Rather, because they did not yet possess the fullest faith or understanding [Col. 0657A] concerning Christ, they thought that he, like other human beings, might grow weary through the persistence of those who brought them.

Nor did they sufficiently remember that shortly before, the most gracious Savior had taken a little child, placed him in their midst, and said: “Unless you become like this little child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” And behold, immediately forgetting the innocence of childhood, they forbade children to approach Christ, as though they were unworthy or troublesome—although they themselves had been summoned to that innocence so that they might become its imitators.

Nor did they consider the faith of those who brought them so that he might touch them, as though they had already learned his power from what had preceded. For through the laying on of hands and through prayer—not only of Christ but also of his ministers—the deceptions [Col. 0657B] of the adversaries are driven away, and the grace of sanctification is bestowed.

But if the apostles already believed by faith that these children were to be sanctified and that in them was the form of things to come, the Evangelist so balances the effect of the present event and of future things that he reveals a middle and fitting explanation of both: through what was being accomplished in the children, the prophecy of the future was displayed.

For infants were truly brought forward and truly restrained, because they prefigured the Gentiles, for whom salvation was prepared through the touch of faith and the hearing of the word. But, in the manner of the prophet Jonah, the disciples hindered them from approaching because of their attachment to their own race: they had decided that the Israelites were to be saved first. Otherwise, the intention of preventing children from coming to Christ would not have accorded with apostolic generosity.

[Col. 0657C] Yet an impulse arose, in the typological fulfillment of the infants who were to be prevented, on account of which the Lord said that they ought not to be prevented, because the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these. For, with the work of the Law coming to an end, the gift and grace of the Holy Spirit was to be granted to the Gentiles through the laying on of hands and through prayer.

Therefore let us also become such as these, so that even those who are children in understanding may be saved through us. Let us not merely refrain from preventing children from coming to Christ; let us ourselves also become like children with children, and in humility fulfill the Lord’s will. For the apostles became such, at the Lord’s exhortation and instruction. Concerned for the benefit of children, they became like children to those same children, so that they might win the children.

[Col. 0657D] It should also be noted that, although Matthew says that these same children were brought for two reasons, he did not introduce at the end the same two reasons that follow. “And when he had laid his hands on them,” he says, “he departed from there,” and he did not add that he had prayed. For he could have said, “And after laying his hands on them and praying, he departed.” Perhaps some sacramental meaning lies hidden here, as though the laying on of hands alone were sufficient for these little ones, while Christ’s prayer is reserved for those who are older—those who are able to receive not only the laying of his hands upon them but also his prayer to the Father, by which he prayed for himself.

Moreover, as I said, the laying on of hands may perhaps be sufficient for the younger children, whom he deigns to touch, saying that the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these. In this he urges that no one in the Church of God should be so wise as to glory against Christ’s little ones. For he does not say that the kingdom of heaven belongs to those who are without understanding, but to such as have become like children through humility and true innocence [Col. 0658A], while remaining mature in understanding and intellect.

Luke the Evangelist commends this meaning more openly when he says: “Truly I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will not enter it.” For those who are called children are nevertheless more perfect, because they do not receive the kingdom of God in the manner they ought.

And behold, one who approached said to him: “Good Teacher, what good thing must I do in order to have eternal life?”

I have often said above, and shall say again, brothers, that all the sayings of the Gospels and all their deeds are full of sacramental meanings, so that future things are foreshadowed through those things that are now taking place. For Christ often acts in this way [Col. 0658B]: when he is about to speak of the mystery of some matter, he first introduces a bodily action or saying signifying that same thing, whether it belongs to a past event or to one that is still to come. Then, finding in it an occasion for the bodily narrative, he brings it into conformity with the mystery he has proposed.

For example, when Luke was about to speak of restraining the Pharisees’ boastfulness, he first introduced a man suffering from dropsy and healed him, so that the boastfulness and inflation of the Pharisees might be portrayed in the bodily swelling of the disease of dropsy.

So here also, as in very many places, when he wished to expound the mystery of the rejection of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles, he introduces this young man—something we have already foreshadowed earlier in the little children. Hence, at the end of this passage, when he had concluded his speech to Peter, [Col. 0658C] he said: “Many who are last will be first, and the first last.” Then from this he constructs the entire parable that follows.

Therefore here too he first sets before us this rich and frivolous young man, boasting and loving his carnal goods more than Christ’s heavenly promises, so that in the person of this young man the entire condition and suffering of the Jewish people might be expressed—the reason why they were unwilling to believe Christ: namely, their attachment to what pleased them, their boastfulness, and the profits they obtained from the Law.

Accordingly, whatever is said about that young man should be understood as having been said about the Jewish people. The Jewish people, then, was a young man not in age but in frivolity: immature in conduct, though not in years. It also committed all the carnal or youthful vices [Col. 0658D] of which the Apostle says: “Flee youthful desires” (II Tim. II, 22).

[Cols. 0658D, 0659A–D, 0660A; pp. 799–800] The most arrogant youthful vice, however, is empty boasting, by which one wishes to seem more than to be—as we know was true of the Jewish people. Of them the Lord says: “They do all their works in order to be seen by people, and they love the chief seats in the synagogues,” and so forth (Matth. XXI, 25). For this reason they are compared to a fig tree having leaves without fruit.

And observe the character of this people at the very beginning of the narrative. He says: “Good Teacher, what good thing must I do, so that I may possess eternal life?” For they were always boasting in the Law and, through transgressing the Law, dishonoring God.

Consider also that he asks nothing about knowledge of God, nothing about faith, nothing about how he might truly know God. He asks only how, through works performed in accordance with the Law, he might possess eternal life. For among the Jews all hope of salvation was placed in works, not in faith. Israel, pursuing the righteousness of the Law, did not attain the law of righteousness, because it was not from faith but from works.

But when they asked Christ elsewhere, “What shall we do, so that we may perform the work of God?” he answered: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent” (Joan. VI, 29). They, however, neglecting the work of knowing God, were always boasting in works; and, as though by a privilege inherited from their fathers, they claimed the righteousness of God on the basis of the works of the Law.

For this reason they lost the knowledge of God and never fulfilled works of righteousness, because the power by which righteousness is performed is the knowledge of God.

Jesus says to him: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God.”

This is an incisive answer—not because he himself was not good, since he was the Son of God and himself God. Rather, through this man he recalls the Jews, so that they may understand that he too is God: since he himself is God, he is the Son of the good God and nothing other than the good God.

For the Father is the good God, the Son is the good God, and the Holy Spirit is also the good God. They are not three gods, but one good God. Accordingly, he did not say, “No one is good except the Father alone,” but “No one is good except God alone,” because these three persons are one God.

Nevertheless, the Jewish people, possessing knowledge of one God, never wished to understand either the Son of God or the triune God in persons. For this reason Christ rejected the praise offered to him by that man: he had not reverenced him as the good God but, as a human being, called him good.

Thus, insofar as the Jews are concerned—those who worshiped one God of heaven and did not recognize Christ as the Son of God—no one was good except one God. Among the faithful, however, just as the one God the Father is good, so too the Only-Begotten God is good, and the Holy Spirit is one good God. They are not three good gods, but one good, holy, and righteous God, together with all those things that are said essentially of God.

Therefore he did not exclude himself from the nature of deity; rather, he praised the good nature of God itself. Goodness, then, belongs to nature, not to the vice of falsehood, since “every human being is a liar” (Psal. CXV, 11).

The nature of God is the Son himself, because he was born from God the Father, and he is what the Father is. Therefore Christ added what the young man did not believe, so that he might believe him to be the Son of God—not merely a good teacher in part, but wholly the good Lord.

What wonder, then, if this young man is so foolish as to regard him as a true and pure human being, when a certain heretic named Felix, who was recently condemned, said that Christ was merely titular and not true, and that he was an adoptive rather than a proper Son, insofar as he was human—as though there were two sons in Christ?

“For this reason,” he says, “he did not allow himself to be called good, because no one except the one and true God is good.” Thus he attempts to tear Christ away from the fellowship of the one God, because he deigned to become human, and from all goodness of nature—so much so that even insofar as he is human, he is not essentially good, but only titularly, like any ordinary human being who is not one person with God the Word.

He does not consider that “the Word became flesh” (Joan. I, 14). As though Christ were not also naturally a good human being. As though he had been born human from corrupted human nature and from the mass of perdition.

The wretched man does not consider that Christ was born from the holy Virgin and brought forth by the Holy Spirit, without any concupiscence of the flesh. Therefore, even according to the flesh, insofar as he is human, he is truly and essentially good.

For this reason he did not say, “Because I am not good,” as though he were saying that this would be false; rather, he said, “No one is good except God alone,” wishing to make known that he truly was God. For in Christ, from the moment he was conceived in the Virgin’s womb, there was nothing other than God, because he was God and human being. Just as there was one Christ, so there was one God and one mediator between God and human beings; and therefore he was wholly good in both natures, because he was wholly God.

[Cols. 0660B–D, 0661A; pp. 801–802] Behold, brothers, in this very saying—the one from which heretics rejoice and attempt to establish their wickedness—how they are overthrown: Photinus no less than Arius and the others who say that Christ was merely human or an adoptive Son of God.

For Christ did not deny himself to be good in this saying, when he said, “No one is good except God alone.” Rather, while preserving the distinct properties of the three persons, he showed himself with the Father and the Holy Spirit to be one God, perfect and good in the Trinity.

Therefore he did not say, “Because I am not good,” nor did he say, “The Father alone is good,” which would be a relative designation. He said instead, “No one is good except God alone,” because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God.

Elsewhere, however, he says of himself: “I am the good shepherd” (Joan. XI, 14). And in another place: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matth. XX, 5.)

Therefore he did not deny that he was a teacher, since the teacher of all is one Christ, as he himself says. Nor, as Felix—or rather, as the unhappy man—lies, did he altogether deny that he was good. Rather, he taught what he was, so that the whole Christ, God and human being, might be understood as one good God, and the perfect God might be loved in the Trinity.

Christ was not divided within himself, as this man foolishly imagined, so that one might be God and another human being, one the proper Son of God and another an adoptive son. Rather, he is one and the same, wholly God, wholly good, and wholly the proper Son, because he is one and the same Son of God.

And the Lord and Savior did not answer according to the sound of the voice, as a human being, but properly according to his deity, because it belongs to God alone to see the hearts of individuals and to discern everyone’s thoughts.

Therefore he did not answer in response to that hypocrite’s cry or favor, but in response to the unbelief of one who did not believe. He exposed the cunning of his deceit, because he himself was reading inwardly the tablet of his heart, written with fraud. And in that young man he was already condemning the heretic who makes Christ a human being outside God and who therefore says that he denied himself to be good.

Especially since Christ did not reject the simple title “Teacher,” nor the honor attached to so great a name. But because the man was still blind in heart and did not believe Christ to be both God and human being, he called him merely a human being under the title “Teacher,” when he ought to have believed and confessed him truly to be Lord.

Thus this man confessed him not to be essentially good, but only such a teacher as the young man understood him to be: a mere human being. He also held him not to be good because, as he wishes it, Christ did not dare call himself good, since “no one is good except God alone.”

This blind disputant does not know that the words “Why do you call me good?” are the words of one reproving or rejecting a claim. It is as though he were saying: “Why do you imagine in your heart that I am something other than good, when I am the good God and human being? I say that no one is essentially good in the way you suppose me to be merely human, whom you falsely call good.”

Therefore, if he wished to have life, Christ commands him to return to the commandments of the Law, so that by reading them he might learn how to recognize him as the true God in the mystery of the Trinity [Col. 0661B]. This is what all those heretics refuse to confess: they deny that Christ is true God and the true Son of God and of humanity; they neither believe nor say that he is the proper Son, but an adoptive one.

I have explained these matters at such length, brothers, so that hearers devoted to God may understand how great is the madness of the heretics concerning Christ. For from the very point where they impiously think they are constructing their falsehoods, they are more fully exposed and more easily refuted by those same sayings, if these are examined faithfully and thoroughly and brought forward wisely, when and as circumstances require.

[Col. 0661C] They do not wish to know or understand what wisdom itself teaches, but only what they themselves foolishly think, because they are wholly senseless. Anyone can observe and prove this in the present saying. For nowhere is Christ more clearly commended as good than when he is proclaimed God; and the one true Son of God is approved. For this reason he himself invites the one praising him to understand, and recalls this heretic so that he may believe him essentially to be God, personally united in both natures, and the good Son of God.

For “a good tree produces good fruits”: so too Christ is essentially good in both natures. And the one Son of God makes us, through the grace of adoption, exceedingly good in himself, coheirs and brothers with him, and true children of the living God.

Consider, then, how wisely the Wisdom of God answered the one asking how he could enter eternal life. “If you wish,” he says, “to enter life, keep the commandments.”

He did not say, “Learn the commandments,” because God had taught him, as the maker of a rational nature. Even if he had forgotten what Moses had commanded, he knew whatever the law of nature had taught. Therefore he did not say, “Learn the commandments that you know,” [Col. 0661D] but “Keep them,” because he plainly was not keeping them, and for this reason he commands him to keep them.

For the truly good person is one who keeps the commandments and does what is good, not one who asks in order to put someone to the test. And he says to him: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery,” and so forth.

[Cols. 0662A–D; pp. 803–804] He speaks appropriately to this man—whoever he may be—in words that fit the person of the Jews. For, as God, he knew that this people would act either against him or against his disciples. Therefore, anticipating this in the young man, he warns and says: “You shall not kill”—which they did, not only to Christ but also to the prophets and apostles.

“You shall not commit adultery.” Those who departed from God committed adultery when they sacrificed to idols.

“You shall not steal.” They stole the faith in Christ’s divinity, as well as the truth of his resurrection, when they gave a large sum of money to the soldiers so that they would say: “While we were sleeping, his disciples stole him.”

Likewise, they spoke many false testimonies against him. Thus, if you investigate carefully, you will find that everything said to this man applies to the Jews. And therefore, like this young man, they did not enter into life.

It should be noted that he says: “If you wish to enter into life”—not because this young man was outside this present life, but because, in comparison with that life which is eternal or blessed life, this life ought rather to be called death than life.
