Yet even in this life he is, in a certain sense, outside life, because he is outside the one who said: “I am life.” Otherwise, whoever is still in the flesh, even if he appears righteous, is in the shadow of life, because he is not yet in that blessed life. He is in the body of this death and sits in the region of the shadow of death, since he has not yet come into the land of the living.

Therefore, insofar as each person keeps the commandments—which are works of life—in that measure he enters into life. For people enter into life according to their observance of God’s commandments.

And so that we may at least learn their beginnings, the Lord, in response to the man’s question, enumerates those commandments that concern one’s neighbor: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery,” and so forth. For whoever transgresses even one of the commandments will not enter even the beginning of life.

It should also be noted that both the things he forbids and the things he commands to be fulfilled are called commandments. Just as the person who does what he forbids is driven away from life, so too is the person who fails to do what he commands to be done, namely: “Honor your father and your mother.”

Then the gracious Lord leads him toward the greater and more useful commandment, which he orders him to fulfill: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

For the Apostle too, after enumerating “you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not commit adultery,” says: “And if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’”

This recapitulation of the commandments is rightly interpreted as their summation because it is the perfection of God’s commandments: whoever fulfills this appears to be perfect.

But if the person who fulfills this is already perfect, we must ask how the Lord answers the young man as though he were not yet perfect: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you possess, give it to the poor, and come, follow me”—when the man himself says: “I have kept all these things from my youth.”

For this reason some have suspected that this was not written by the Lord in this passage but was added by someone who did not sufficiently understand the subtlety of these sayings. When Mark and Luke touch upon this passage, neither of them adds the words, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

Therefore we think that these words were added unnecessarily by editors who were not sufficiently skilled, especially since Origen testifies that he did not find them in many manuscripts.

Nevertheless, we must also consider what he says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you possess, give it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.” For not everyone who sells or abandons his possessions is immediately found to be perfect.

[Cols. 0663A–B] They are not found to be perfect to the extent that they do not follow Christ. Therefore whoever wishes to be perfect should hasten to fulfill both requirements: namely, to distribute all his possessions completely and then, as is said elsewhere, to take up his cross and follow Christ. No one follows Christ perfectly without the mark of the cross.

The Jews too, whose person this young man represents, did not enter into life because they did not fulfill these things, although they boastfully say that they fulfilled everything. This is also prefigured in another parable, where the elder son, moved by envy against the younger, says to his father: “Behold, I have always been with you, and I have never transgressed your commandment” (Luc. XIII, 20). This is altogether proved to be a lie.

So too this young man proves by his actions that he lied. For if he had fulfilled everything that was said earlier, he would neither have possessed such great wealth nor have been saddened on its account, if the love of his neighbor—which he was commanded to practice—had been in him. Unless, as I said, the Lord had not actually said this to him, and he had kept only the other commandments previously enumerated. Having kept these, he could also have been rich.

Nevertheless, the Jewish people had killed the prophets, had continually committed adultery through idolatry, and had continually stolen when it corrupted the truth of the Scriptures, as the Lord says of them: “You have nullified the commandment of God because of your tradition” (Matth. XV, 6). It also brought forward false testimonies against the Lord.

Finally, because it was rich and boasted in the Law, it was unwilling to sell and abandon the things in which it gloried—its sacrifices and offerings, and the other matters that would take too long to enumerate [Col. 0663C].

Therefore, as the blessed Virgin Mary sang: “He has filled the hungry with good things, and he has sent the rich away empty” (Luc. I, 53).

[Col. 0663D; p. 805] Then follows:

> But when the young man heard these words, he went away sorrowful, for he had many possessions.

Wretched is the soul that is torn away only with such difficulty from the goods of the world or from the desire for empty glory. We want more to obtain the things we wrongly desire than to be freed from evil desires.

But observe that an older person is not introduced here, nor a man who had emptied himself of the things that belonged to a child, but a young man who, after hearing the word, went away sorrowful.

He was a young man according to the soul, and for this reason, after abandoning the Savior, he went away sorrowful. From this it is clear, as we said, that neither this man nor the Jewish people had done the things stated above; and therefore they lie when they say that they had kept everything from their youth.

For even if he is truly called a young man, he does not know how to consider his own age. Adolescence is below youth, and a later stage of life cannot be contained within the limits of an earlier life.

But this is presented in this way so that it may be clearer that this young man represents the Jews, who boastfully glory in the Law from their youth, as though they had served it for a long time. Therefore he calls himself a young man in order to display the lengthy period of the Law, under which he boasts that he struggled and persevered with much exertion and kept the commandments contained in it.

Thus the principle of the typological construction has been preserved, so that you may see that this young man has been introduced for no other reason than to reveal how much abundance the Jewish nation possessed in the Law [Col. 0664A], how much glory in riches, and how much pride.

And because it always sought carnal and earthly things more than heavenly ones, it departed from Christ sorrowful and deeply offended. Although he had said to it, “You will have treasure in heaven,” it was unwilling, for the sake of hope in eternal happiness, to love anything other than visible things.

For, in accordance with what was said earlier, seed had been sown in it among thorns. Therefore the pleasure of the flesh and the anxiety of the world choked the word by which he had commanded it to sell its riches and tear them from its heart, so that it might store those same riches for itself in the treasuries of heaven in the future.

But because it was wholly fixed upon earthly things, from the place where it ought to have drawn life it drew death, and therefore departed sorrowful. This was not the sorrow by which the heart is pierced toward repentance [Col. 0664B], but the sorrow of the world that produces death, because, as I said, the thorns choked it.

Alas! Behold how, after so many labors and after such observance of God’s commandments, while he was still asking what he lacked, he suddenly cast himself down into death. From the very source by which he was outwardly enlarged through many possessions, he was inwardly constricted, and, miserably suffocated by them, he perished.

Therefore, as he departed, Jesus said: “Truly I say to you, a rich man will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty.”

He did not say that it is impossible for the rich to enter the kingdom of heaven, but that it is difficult. Wherever “difficult” is stated, impossibility is not being asserted; rather, rarity is being indicated.

Otherwise, how did Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob enter it? And likewise Matthew and Zacchaeus in the Gospel, who are commended on the Lord’s testimony after abandoning their riches?

[Cols. 0664C–D; pp. 806–807] Riches by no means exclude people from the kingdom of God if they use them well—so that those who have them may be as though they did not have them, and those who use them as though they did not use them.

Here riches are not condemned; rather, the difficulty of entering is emphatically proclaimed. For a rich person can, although with difficulty, overcome the passions of his flesh and mind, resist vices and crimes, and distribute lawfully the possessions he owns.

This difficulty clearly also affected the Jews, so that they would abandon the things in which they gloried. And therefore so few Jews were converted to him, because they were held bound by many crimes and by many carnal profits that the customary practice of the Law provided for them.

For this reason they disdained to look toward the spiritual things that Christ promised for the future because of the things immediately present.

If we cannot now persuade Christians that the riches of the world ought to be despised—for they say, “If God had not wished human beings to use riches, he would never have created them in the world”—how much more difficult was it to persuade the very wealthy Jewish people, rich in all the riches of the Law, to abandon the wealth of the Law, the worship divinely handed down by God, the traditions of their fathers, and all the institutions of the Jewish religion that they had received from God?

They would say: “If God had ever wished this Law to be despised, together with the Temple, which at that time shone in majesty throughout the whole world, and all the things performed in it, he would never have handed it down in ancient times with such reason and care, nor commended it through so many signs and wonders.”

[Col. 0665A] Therefore the Savior added again, saying: “Again I say to you, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.” By this statement, not the difficulty but the impossibility of entering is demonstrated. For if, just as a camel cannot enter through the eye of a needle, so a rich man cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, then none of the rich will be saved—much less one who says that the former is more possible than the latter.

Hence some seem to doubt this statement, because they hear that, contrary to it, rich people also come to the kingdoms of heaven. Since this is not read as having happened, what is proclaimed as easier appears to remain impossible. Such people clearly do not pay attention to those figures of speech which even secular men—especially those called philosophers—so often use in their discourses. This figure is called hyperbole. Its expression frequently exceeds credibility, as they themselves perceive.

But we rightly understand this both of the rich of this world and of the Jews, whom this young man represents: it is impossible for them to enter blessed life so long as they proudly hold such opinions against Christ and place their hope in the uncertainty of riches. If, then, we first turn our attention to the Jews, it immediately becomes clear that it is easier for the Gentiles—who are understood under the figure of the camel, and who had been crooked and weighed down by many burdens of sins—to enter the kingdom of heaven through the narrow opening than for the Jews, who appeared rich in the Law, in the prophets and patriarchs, in the divine Scriptures, in the temple, in the priests, [Col. 0665C] in the Levites, in sacrifices and tithes, and in the other ordinances of the Law.

Moreover, Isaiah describes how the rich from the Gentiles or from the Jews come or enter that heavenly Jerusalem, saying: “The flood of camels shall cover you; the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah; all those from Sheba shall come, bringing gold and frankincense” (Isa. 60:6). Thus those who were previously bent and oppressed by a hump, distorted by the crookedness of their vices, enter through the gates of Jerusalem. All the orthodox rightly understand these people as the rich, as the Gospel declares this young man to have been.

Therefore the Lord says: “It is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle”—if it has laid down the burdens [808] under which it was previously weighed down—than for a proud man who places his hope in his riches to enter the kingdom [Col. 0665D] of heaven.

Because of the difficulty of this matter, some have said that the eye of a needle was a small gate in Jerusalem called by that name, through which loaded camels could not enter Jerusalem. Others have said simply that he was speaking of the needle with which clothing is sewn. Certain others, taking refuge in a spiritual interpretation, have said that the eye of the needle is the confession of faith that is in Christ, or repentance. Still others wish Christ’s Passion to be understood, in which he himself was pierced by a lance; and therefore the Passion itself is rightly called the eye of a needle. All these interpretations fit this passage sufficiently, when either a rich man or any Jew lays down the heavy burden of his sins, the exceedingly heavy burdens of the Law, Jewish superstitions, every impiety toward idols, greed for possessions, and all the distortions of mind and body, so that they may enter through the narrow and constricted way that leads to life.

If we understand correctly, that way is itself the eye of the needle; it is the true confession of faith and the true repentance by which one enters the kingdom of heavenly Jerusalem. A needle has two forms: its front part is exceedingly sharp, piercing and penetrating everything, while its back part is pierced and draws the thread behind it. Thus Christ himself is not improperly understood through the needle, pierced in his Passion; through that opening he draws everything to himself and behind himself. His divinity penetrates and reaches everything. His humanity, because it suffered, draws everything behind it.

Through the wound of his Passion the Gentiles entered eternal life. He alone is able, through that wound, to sew together all our wounds, while his divinity, like the front part of the needle, penetrates and searches all our inward places. By him the garment of immortality, once torn apart through Adam, has been sewn together. He is the needle by which flesh and spirit are sewn into one, so that they can no longer be separated. By this needle the Jewish people and the Gentiles have likewise been joined together and made one flock, because “he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14).

What more need be said? Everything torn apart and broken is restored to unity through him.

When the disciples heard this, they were astonished, saying: “Who then can be saved?” Jesus looked at them and said: “With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” [Col. 0666C] He shows that, just as of itself it is impossible for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle, but possible with regard to God, so likewise, with regard to himself, it is impossible for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven, but possible with regard to God, who by his ineffable power can make the camel’s bulk thin and straighten its crookedness.

He can also lessen the folly of the brutish human being and enlighten the mind, so that either he makes the narrow entrance capable of receiving that person, or makes the person himself worthy of God and of such great glory. Christ employed this example of the eye of the needle and the camel because of the difficulty of entering, not because of impossibility.

The apostles, greatly astonished, also said: “Who can be saved?” The Lord said to them: “With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” With God it is possible for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle, though not with men. How these things are possible with God, he himself knows, and the one to whom it has been revealed. We know one thing: every nature is subject to divine commands.

But one who is wise and instructed in divine discourse may perhaps dare to expound more fully on the needle and its eye. Yet the entire text of this passage tends toward this: among human beings you are to find one camel constituted as entering through the eye of the needle, and another—a rich man—entering the kingdom of heaven, impossible with regard to human beings but possible with regard to God. Therefore, whatever is called the camel and whatever is understood as the eye of the needle, even if Christ is said to enter through his Passion, through that entrance the multitude of the Gentiles will enter the kingdom of heaven.

The Savior introduced this comparison in order to show that their entrance would be easier than that of the Jews who gloried in their riches. For in the things in which the Gentiles were called poor, the Jews gloried in being rich. Whether our discussion has fulfilled any limits in this interpretation—according to the mysteries of the most benevolent God, by what ways it is possible for God alone to fulfill what he promises, even if it appears impossible to human beings—let the prudent reader investigate. Let him understand only this: the young man was provided here by the Lord as a great sacramental figure, not by chance but foreordained in the wisdom of God, so that through him he might show what was going to happen. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0667B]

**Then Peter answered and said to him: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what, then, will there be for us?”**

Peter heard what he had commanded this young man and what he had proposed. Taking the opportunity, he confidently responded and asked about these matters. He declared that he and his fellow disciples had fulfilled what was commanded and asked what good they would receive in return.

He is suddenly stirred to ask, as though he had become a witness to the power of God, and confirms God’s promise concerning himself and his companions. For Peter himself and all his fellow apostles, as well as very many who believed from among the Jews, believed in Christ by God’s grace, contrary to human possibility, as he himself testifies to Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:17).

Peter’s great confidence and virtue are revealed when he says: “Behold, we have left everything.” When he had heard that those who had left their possessions would have treasures in heaven, and had considered the young man’s sadness and the difficulty for the rich of entering the kingdom of heaven, he spoke forcefully, as one who had accomplished no easy task: “Behold, we who have left everything.”

He does not consider only how little he and the others left, but what they left and how much it was. For many things are left by one who abandons himself and everything that can be desired in the world completely for the love of Christ.

There is no doubt that the apostles and their followers, although they had little, left more than everyone else, because they trampled more perfectly upon everything that can be desired. They despised not only every vice but themselves also, together with the world.

Recognizing that this had been accomplished through Christ’s power, he confidently asks: “What, then, will there be for us?” This is so that Christ’s greater power might be commended, and that they themselves and all believers might be made more certain of the promise and strengthened in faith.

In this new question itself there are many things that do not allow us to receive the Gospel statements with a simple understanding. For when the apostles say that they have left everything and followed Christ, how are they said above to have been sad or astonished? Or how do they fear, saying that no one can be saved, especially when others could similarly do what they themselves had already done?

This sense appears contradictory. We are therefore warned that we ought to seek more deeply the reason belonging to heavenly understanding: from where this fear or sadness— as some manuscripts have it—or astonishment arose, when they glory in having done everything that is proclaimed to be most difficult.

The Lord’s answer, moreover, is that these things, impossible with human beings, will be possible with God. Or were the things they themselves glory and rejoice in having done impossible with human beings? The Lord immediately confirms that they did these very things; and afterward there were many who happily left themselves and all they possessed, even unto the blessedness of martyrdom.

Therefore this whole discourse must be understood spiritually. As I have shown briefly above, the Lord introduced the discourse about the exceedingly rich young man with deliberate providence, so that he might foreshadow the rejection of the Jews on account of their sins.

If the apostles, understanding that no one could be saved from the Law, realized that they themselves were still within the Law—for the powerful love or favor of the Law still held them—then they were especially in fear because they had not yet fully discovered the mysteries of the Gospel or entirely understood the truth of this sacrament. Therefore they fear and marvel, and they also become sad at the rejection of their own people, just as Paul was saddened, for whom on this account there was continual sorrow of heart.

How much more were the apostles still inexperienced, for whom the heavenly mysteries had not yet been fully opened? They still placed all their salvation in the Law and their hope of life in observance of the commandments. Perhaps they therefore feared that they too could not be saved without the Law.

Seeing this, the merciful Teacher says: “What is impossible with men is possible with God.” For what seems so ineffectual to a Jew as expecting salvation from a human being rather than from the Law? What seems so detestable to him as the scandal of the cross—that for the sake of the cross the legislation, the covenant, adoption, and inheritance of the Law should be abandoned?

By contrast, what is so possible for God’s power as that a person should be saved through faith, regenerated through water, conquer through the cross, be adopted as a son through the Gospel and the grace of Christ, and be made alive through the resurrection of Jesus Christ?

Perhaps after hearing these things, setting aside their sorrow over the unbelieving Jews, they quickly ask out of concern for themselves and confess that through his obedience they have already left everything. To them the Lord says:

[Col. 0668D]

“Amen I say to you, you who have left everything and followed me: in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

[812] Behold, every difficulty of coming to the kingdom has been resolved, and every reward for labor has been promised by the Lord. Here he also confirms that they have done what they professed and displayed perfection. For it would not be sufficient to have left everything—which philosophers did, and many others as well—unless they had followed the Lord: not merely with their feet, as many then did for various reasons, but in conduct and imitation.

Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought to walk as Christ walked, obedient to God the Father even unto death, and himself likewise walk so that he may remain obedient to the end. The apostles had not yet completed this to the end, although what was to happen was already present in God’s predestination. Therefore he promises them rewards in the present as though they had already earned them, although they were to come according to their merits.

The phrase “in the regeneration” appears to be an amphibology—that is, an ambiguity of expression—since it can be applied in either direction. Some report that it should be punctuated this way: “You who have left everything and followed me in the regeneration.” For at that time the apostles had already been reborn in Christ through the font of baptism.

It is as though he said: “You who have followed me in the regeneration of new birth, in the washing of faith, in the sanctification of eternal consecration, in the adoption of perpetual inheritance, and in the resurrection from the dead.” Hence the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Col. 3:1).

This is the regeneration in which the apostles followed Christ, which the Law could not give, nor could anyone be glorified in this way from the Law.

Although this distinction may be understood in that manner, it is better applied to what follows: “in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty.” Then the dead will awaken and rise from corruption and the dust of the earth, incorruptible and immortal.

That regeneration is a certain new birth and recreation established by God, when a new heaven and a new earth are created for those who have renewed themselves through that second regeneration from the dead. To them the New Testament is given, together with the cup of that New Testament. Its reward is that regeneration, just as the mystery of that newness is this renewal.

One must consider what we were born as from Adam, what we were reborn as in Christ, and what we shall be in that third birth of eternal regeneration. For in the first, which is in Adam, we are all children of wrath; in the second, through which we passed to Christ, although we were reborn cleansed from defilements, we still remain in weakness.

Therefore David speaks to his soul, saying: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your infirmities” (Ps. 102:3). [Col. 0669D] For this reason, as someone says, it seems to me that this birth—by which we are truly cleansed from defilements and reborn in Christ—is as though it occurs “through a mirror, in an enigma.”

But whoever reaches that regeneration in which Christ is the firstborn from the dead will thereafter be utterly clean from defilements and healed, incorruptible, and free from every weakness or corruption. In that regeneration they will be conformed to the holy and glorious body of Christ, who sits on the throne of his glory.

The Son of Man will then sit fully upon the throne of his glory, when no one contemptible or inglorious remains in his kingdom. Then his prayer to the Father will also be shown to have been fulfilled: “Father, glorify me with yourself with the glory”—or “the splendor”—which I had before the world existed (John 17:5).

For the Greek word δόξα (*doxa*) signifies both, that is, both “glory” and “splendor.” Accordingly, since some manuscripts have *clarifica* (“glorify with splendor”) and others *glorifica* (“glorify”), understand that they are one and the same. Some manuscripts also have: “Glorify me with yourself”; others, at the end, have: “With the glory which I had with you before the world existed.”

The sense is nevertheless one: when he existed in the form of God the Father, he possessed the same glory and splendor as the Father. When the Father restored and gave him the name that is above every name, he was glorified with the same splendor that he had with the Father before the world existed.

This is what is now said here: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty.” God the Word, who became flesh, will sit upon the throne of his majesty and in glory. He is not one God and another man, but one and the same Christ, God and man. He is not God’s adopted Son, nor a supposed son of man, as many heretics wrongly thought, but the true and one Son of God and the true and one son of man.

Thus, because the man is commended as taken up into God and God is made man, it is fittingly said: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty.” No one should doubt that Christ as man is himself God, established by God the Father in the form of God upon the throne of his majesty.

And because the apostles had been made conformed to Christ, he says: “You also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel,” thereby depicting the entire dignity of a senate. Since he is said to sit as King and Lord upon the throne, the thrones of the apostles—namely, twelve seats—are introduced, because in Greek θρόνοι (*thronoi*) means “seats” in Latin.

He joined the twelve thrones for judging the twelve tribes to the glory of the twelve patriarchs, so that the twenty-four elders may be said to sit around the throne, worshiping the one who lives for ever and ever. But only the twelve receive this judicial power: they condemn the twelve tribes of Israel, who refused to believe when the apostles believed and refused to receive the words of life when the apostles preached them.

Moreover, they hated and expelled the apostles as evildoers on account of the Son of Man, and persecuted them. Therefore they will rightly be their judges: they followed the Lord, which was the apostles’ distinctive role. The Jews, however, unjustly put both Christ and the apostles to death.

[Col. 0670D] Another person introduces from this a subtler interpretation, though I do not know whether it is more secure. He says that Christ is not speaking here of the time of the future judgment, but of the calling of all the Gentiles. For, he says, he did not say, “When the Son of Man comes, sitting upon the throne of his majesty,” but, “when he has sat upon the throne of his majesty.”

He says that Christ began to sit upon the throne of his majesty from the time when the Gentiles began to believe in him. From the time Christ sits upon the holy throne of his majesty, the apostles also sat upon twelve thrones—that is, in all Christians according to the differences of their souls.

He explains that, just as the Jewish people were divided into twelve tribes, so the entire Christian people is divided and, together with those who believed from the Jews, gathered into twelve tribes according to certain properties of souls and differences of hearts. Only God, who knows and distinguishes all the hidden things of the heart, can recognize these. Thus some souls belong to the tribe of Reuben, some to the tribe of Simeon, or Levi, or Judah, or the others.

He says that, just as all the saints are called five wise virgins, although they are innumerable, on account of the five spiritual senses, so all sinners are understood as the five foolish virgins, although they too are innumerable, on account of the five senses of the flesh.

[815] Then he added: “And just as all the churches of Christ are called seven churches, although there are many, because of the sevenfold grace of gifts—for example, all those in whom the Spirit of wisdom abounds are counted as one church—so also in the other virtues of the Holy Spirit one universal Church is gathered because of the unity of that same Holy Spirit. It is divided into seven because of the distribution of gifts, so that only seven are found.

“Likewise, because of the twelve gifts or graces which the angel expounds in the person of the twelve virgins in the Shepherd, if anyone wishes to accept Scripture in this way, all Christians are found to be twelve tribes, each distinguished according to its particular grace, which that angel designates in the same virgins.

“Thus all souls in which the virtue of truth excels above the other virtues constitute one tribe, just as one virtue excels in those virgins. The same applies to the rest, since not all graces are found equally in everyone: one person excels in this virtue, another in that. All Christians, however, in whom Christ dwells are seats of Christ.

“This is why he says: ‘In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones.’ Through this he promises them the future age of Christianity after his ascension, when all have received the apostles’ word within themselves as the word of Christ.

“That is the time of regeneration, when people, regenerated through baptism, became thereafter sons of God from sons of men. From that time Christ began to sit upon the throne of his majesty, as the Prophet testifies concerning the unity and faith of the Gentiles: ‘God shall reign over the nations; God sits upon his holy throne’ (Ps. 46:9).

“Therefore whoever perfectly receives Christ into himself by believing is a throne of his majesty. The apostles’ thrones are also those who received their teaching. The Prophet rightly commends this, saying: ‘There the thrones sat in judgment’—speaking of Jerusalem, which is the Church of the living God—‘thrones over the house of David’ (Ps. 121:5).

“To that Jerusalem, which is built as a city, the tribes ascended: the tribes of the Lord, gathered from the Gentiles as a testimony against Israel, because they refused to believe and confess the name of the Lord, and for the condemnation of the unbelieving.

“Therefore the thrones will sit in judgment, because the apostles themselves, upon whom Christ first sits, will also sit upon their thrones—that is, upon those same twelve tribes and thrones which ascended [Col. 0672A] and are built together in that city Jerusalem, which is the throne and temple of God.

“If all the elect are the apostles’ thrones, or those associated with them, even though they are arranged according to their number in twelve seats, why are all of them again said together with the apostles, in the person of Christ, to be one seat or throne? For he did not say, ‘When the Son of Man sits upon his thrones,’ but, ‘when he sits upon the throne of his majesty.’

“They are not read as being many, but one, because no equality between Christ and the apostles is being proclaimed. Although all the apostles possessed the same kinds of virtues, not every one of them possessed all of them perfectly. Rather, each was more perfect than another in some particular good. Therefore they could by no means possess among them all the gifts of the Holy Spirit which Christ alone possesses upon his throne.

“They are all read as having sat around the throne, whereas Christ, raised to the Father’s right hand above the whole Church and above every seat, is worshiped by all.

“Christ, however, possessed all the virtues equally. Those virtues perhaps shone forth in the apostles in separate parts and in a distinctive manner, but Christ was equally perfect in every virtue and grace, because in him the whole fullness of divinity is believed to have dwelt bodily, together with every grace.

“Therefore he has one seat with the Father, with whom he is worshiped and glorified as God.”

It follows:

[Col. 0672B]

**“And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for the sake of my name, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.”**

This passage agrees with the statement in which the Savior says: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34). “For I have come to separate a man from his father, and a daughter from her mother, and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household.” I have already discussed this above.

But here, when Peter asks in the person of all the apostles, lest those who later read these promises of Christ should think that they had been promised only to the apostles, he appropriately adds: “And everyone who has left”—that is, whether Jew or Gentile, or anyone of any other condition.

Although no one leaves in as perfect a manner as the apostles, whoever leaves anything, however much, for no other reason than the name of Christ, will receive a hundredfold even in the present age and will possess eternal life in the future.

Many carnal people doubt this statement because they do not perceive in the present what spiritual people receive a hundredfold. For example, one who has left a mortal father, whatever his condition, has he not chosen someone better for himself by acquiring God as his father? Is not fatherhood multiplied a hundredfold in him, so that he may serve the one whose inheritance he will receive and never lose?

Once he has handed over his property to his own people, he will never die and thereby leave his children orphans afterward. What shall I say about brothers and sisters, when no kinship is happier or truer than that which is found in Christ?

The same applies to everything else, if he truly has the Church of Christ as his mother. With her and in her he will presently possess all that belongs to Christ, with his blessings multiplied.

The apostle Peter likewise commands his people to glory as possessing nothing and possessing everything.

From this passage some who think carnally introduce the fable of a thousand years, saying that after the resurrection we shall receive a hundredfold of every possession we abandoned, together with eternal life, understanding nothing except material things.

Even if the promise is worthy in other respects, it appears shameful and disgraceful with regard to wives: that one who left a single wife for the Lord should receive a hundred in the future. Yet the Lord says in this same Gospel that in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels in heaven (Matt. 22:30).

Therefore the meaning is that whoever has left material things for the Lord will receive spiritual things a hundredfold in this Church of Christ, while retaining his treasure in the heavens, where he has stored everything.

These blessings, in comparison and according to their worth, will be so abundant that it is as though a small number were compared with the number one hundred, which is crowned as perfect on the right hand.

But if we leave everything that can be left in this world without first leaving vices, sins, and carnal desires, what we do is of little value. Therefore much is contained in what Peter gloried in saying: “We who have left everything and followed you—what, then, will there be for us?”

It follows:

[Col. 0673B]

**“For many who are first will be last, and the last first.”**

The Savior now introduces, from much earlier, figures concerning the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews, to instruct his disciples about such great mysteries. He now concludes them more openly, presenting this statement in a marvelous way so that he both confirms more clearly what was previously prefigured and declares in this one verse what he is about to say in the following parable.

The Jews, who were first and gloried in the Law, became last because of the hardness of their hearts and their betrayal of Christ. But the people of the Gentiles, who came last in the final hour and believed in Christ, became first.

Consider how carefully the Savior speaks. He did not say, “All who were last will be first,” but “many,” because there are certainly some from the Jews who were first and nevertheless remained first because they believed in Christ, as the apostles did, and as did many Jews descended physically from Abraham. Even now they are counted and regarded as first among the first in faith.

Likewise, many from the Gentiles are last and nevertheless remain last, because they either do not wish to believe or conduct themselves badly, even though they appear to be in the Church when they are not.

The Apostle speaks of both groups: remnants from the Jews have been saved, while many from the Gentiles, although they appear to have been grafted into the good olive root, perish. For when the Jews were branches of their own olive tree, they were broken off because of their unbelief, while the Gentiles were wild olive branches. “If God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he perhaps spare those who have been grafted contrary to nature into the olive tree.”

Here we must not listen to those who wish this statement to be understood of apostate angels and human beings, as though the angels, created earlier and more glorious than human beings and therefore first, became last because of their deserved punishments, while human beings, who had been last, became first.

Although there may seem to be some reasoning in this, that interpretation does not sufficiently accord with the circumstances of the reading, especially since what was said earlier and what follows in the parable appear to fit the Jews and the Gentiles much better.

Nor, therefore, are apostate angels rightly called last in this parable, since they are not within the order of bodily beings and are not saved in the way we say the Jews will be saved. “When the fullness of the Gentiles has come, then all Israel will be saved.”

Nor should we accept those who say that the first are to be understood as those who are saved by receiving the faith of Christ because of their observance of God’s commandments, while the last are those who are not worthy to be saved in such an order or with such grace, but are saved only after punishments and penalties, from Gehenna, once what they deserved through their own sins has been completed and paid.

This interpretation must be condemned both in this passage and in any other passage; therefore it must be especially avoided in the parable that follows.

(CAP. XX.)

[Col. 0674B] **“The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard.”**

The obscurity of the parables spoken by Christ Jesus is exceedingly great when they are not explained. In him “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Col. 2:3). Yet this parable is especially obscure, concerning which a certain prophet testifies that he spoke more particularly: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter propositions from the beginning” (Ps. 77:2). And: “I will bring forth hidden things from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 13:35).

Therefore the Savior’s grace must be implored, so that the parable may be understood in the same Spirit in which it was spoken, from the treasure of God’s wisdom and knowledge.

The whole comparison is complete in itself, although the persons must be distinguished and the times differentiated. Accordingly, the householder is rightly understood as none other than our Lord Jesus Christ, because he is both man and the guardian of the entire human race, and at every time he never ceases to hire all people for the cultivation of the divine Law.

This figure is understood from what was said previously, namely: “Many who are first will be last, and the last first.” Here the Lord does not proclaim a difference of times but distinguishes the merits of faith.

For this reason the whole parable seems to have been introduced so that we may learn how our Savior possesses all those subject to him in this world and, as Lord in his house, arranges the elect. That Lord and householder has a vineyard—namely, the whole Church—which is gathered from righteous Abel to the last elect who will come at the end of the world.

He himself is Christ the householder, who says of himself in the Gospel: “I am the true vine, and you are the branches” (John 15:5). Accordingly, all who have been saved from the beginning of the world have remained in this true vine like branches, because without faith in Christ they could produce no fruit.

Therefore Abel, first as a figure of Christ and as an exceedingly righteous prophet, is read as having offered and sacrificed a lamb to God the Father. He showed by his faith and works that the Lamb was to come, the one who was to be offered to God the Father as a sacrifice of pleasing fragrance for the salvation of the whole world.

Thus Abel himself, because he remained in the faith of Christ like a branch in the vine, was killed as a figure of Christ, and became a shoot from the vine and a faithful witness.

From that point onward the Church of Christ is propagated and cultivated, as though it were a vineyard whose cultivators are the laborers whom the householder himself hired to cultivate it in return for the reward of eternal life.

Accordingly, from the beginning of the world he sent as many saints as there are branches, so to speak.

This householder therefore hires laborers to work in his vineyard early in the morning and at the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours. From the beginning of this world to its end, he has not ceased to gather and summon preachers to instruct the people of the faithful.

This does not mean that the laborers and hired servants who are hired are one thing and the vineyard another. Rather, all who are called to the vineyard together constitute one Church and one vineyard propagated from the vine, which is Christ.

In it and toward it, whoever enters or is hired must not be idle, but all must be laborers. For there is no one who, even if he does not exercise and cultivate others, ought not to exercise and cultivate himself, so that he may bear fruit for Christ and remain in the vine.

Whoever truly remains in Christ knows how great and arduous the labor of this vineyard is, and what its cultivation requires: lest the branch grow luxuriantly and lest vices creep in; and how great a guarding of God’s commandments is needed for the vine to remain fruitful.

But what does he mean when he says, “He went out early in the morning”? Would it not have been sufficient to say, “He went out in the morning”? But by adding “early in the morning,” he wished to suggest something. Perhaps he wanted us to understand that he was speaking of the beginning of the world, when God first went out and created man and placed him in paradise to cultivate and guard it; when, concerning each of his works, he said, “And it was morning.” Although that morning is rightly understood as the first, perhaps it is called “first” in comparison with the other days. For at each succession of hours, during which the master of the household shone forth like the sun and went out to hire workers, there was a morning: when a new daylight arose for them, until the sun of righteousness, having been darkened in the hearts of individuals, as the day declined toward sunset because of the darkness of sins, turned into night. And thus there was, as it were, a morning at each hour, so that he is rightly said to have gone out early in the morning when he hired Adam, Abel, and the other Fathers to work in and cultivate the vineyard—that is, righteousness.

But none of them except those who were called last answered, “Because no one hired us.” For all those Fathers of the Old Testament had been hired; they had knowledge of God and knew his promises. The Gentiles, however, neither knew God nor his promises, and therefore they could justifiably answer, “Because no one hired us.” [Col. 0675D]

Moreover, he appears to have joined the sixth and ninth hours together because at that time, from Abraham to David, God had a greater and more frequent association with the holy Fathers, with whom he decreed that he would establish covenants for the salvation of the human race, as you, reader, can enumerate more carefully. For after Noah we read that God spoke to no one except first to Abraham, then very frequently to Isaac and Jacob; and not long afterward to Moses and Aaron, to whom he gave the Law. Thus he went out very frequently to hire workers as far as Joshua; then he proceeded to Samuel and David, when the choir of prophets shone forth in the world like a new light, and with them he again established new covenants. During these periods, as though in two hours joined together, he established his covenant more urgently with each successive generation and most openly promised that he would come in the flesh. Therefore, if you consider the matter carefully, reader, you will find that as many covenants were established for the human race as the number of times he is said to have gone out to the marketplace.

Yet he agreed on a denarius with none of these except the first whom he sent; with the others, he merely promised that he would give them whatever was just. But to the last, after reproving their idleness, he says only, “Go you also into my vineyard,” because it is a free gift of God that he deigned to hire them from the marketplace, even at the eleventh hour. But because in this parable he wished the whole present age—from the beginning of the world to its end—to be understood as one day, he says that he went out early in the morning, so that you may refer the word “first” not merely to sequence, [Col. 0676A] but also to the beginning of the world, when, as I have said, he first created and established man so that he might preserve and guard what had first been entrusted to him.

Here I admonish my hearers concerning this day, by which we understand the entire span of the present life, lest they consider it something great or impossible. For in relation to us it may be a great day, but in relation to the eternity of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the day of the whole age is short and very small. For in that eternity there is only one day, of which it is said: “Because one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. LXXXIII [84], 11). And if that eternity is one day, do not be surprised that he set this whole present age as one day, in which the master of the household is said to have gone out five times to hire workers for his vineyard. [Col. 0676D]

I do not think that this was said without a sacramental meaning. A curious reader may perhaps ask why certain workers were hired in the morning; and afterward he went out not around the second hour but around the third, and others were hired; and after hiring them, why he went out not around the fourth or fifth hour but around the sixth and sent others into the vineyard; likewise, not around the seventh or eighth but around the ninth. Finally, why he went out not around the tenth but at the eleventh, when he found people standing idle all day, since it was already the last hour?

I therefore certainly believe that it was not without reason that between that morning and the third hour there was a short interval, as though one hour had been inserted, and not the same periods as those set between the third and sixth hours, where twice as much time intervened, or between the sixth and ninth. Finally, between the ninth and eleventh there is again one hour, just as earlier between morning and the third hour.

In these five orders something musical seems to resound: the two outer intervals have a simple number and one, while the two middle intervals have the double; thus each of the double middle intervals corresponds to its simple counterpart and produces what is called in Greek the *diapason*—the octave. For this reason certain learned teachers, moved by these considerations, referred these five calls of Christ to the five senses of human beings, by which we know that we presently perceive.

They said that in the first calling he instituted touch, because the woman told the serpent what God had said: “You shall not eat from it, nor shall you touch it.” Smell, however, is consecrated by the Lord in the second calling, because Noah offered to the Lord a sacrifice of good odor; hence it is said: “And the Lord smelled the fragrance of sweetness” (Gen. VIII, 21). Taste was especially pleasing to God in Abraham, because he fed the angels—or rather, God in the angel: he set before them hidden or ash-baked loaves of fine flour and a tender calf that was killed for the feast, because the prodigal son, who had been lost and dead, had come to life and been found. Of this taste it is rightly said: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII [34], 9).

Hearing, according to some, is consecrated to the Lord in Moses, when the voice of God was heard by him from heaven, having been produced by the Lord. Others understand this sense to have been consecrated to God through David and in David. For through him, no less than through Moses, Christ, who had been promised, came forth to us from the fruit of his womb. He himself heard of all these things in Ephrata and found his bride in the fields of the forest, whom Moses had previously taken as his wife, the Ethiopian woman, as a figure of Christ. [824]

Sight, moreover, which is more honorable than all the other senses, is wholly illuminated at the coming of Christ. Concerning these eyes, because they saw Christ, he himself said to the apostles: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see.”

I have said these things so that the prudent hearer may understand that the works and words of God are full of mysteries. For just as the soul, while it is in the body, goes outward through these five bodily senses and perceives bodily things, [Col. 0677D] so Christ went forth through these five ages, as though through an equal number of hours, although he is wholly present everywhere, when he made himself more manifestly known and, instructing them in his laws, came to hire workers for his vineyard. Through these five senses, we are wrongly dispersed toward outward things; he would recall us most graciously inward to himself, lest souls that had slipped outward in an evil manner perish completely.

This was his going forth when, through some effective intervention with the holy Fathers, he established new laws and promised covenants of peace, so that at that time he appeared to those same holy men in visible form. He went out early in the morning when he established his laws and gave commandments to Adam the first-formed man, whom he placed in paradise to work and guard it; with him he made an agreement for only a daily denarius. [Col. 0678A]

For God knew beforehand that Adam would transgress, although, possessing the covenant of life, he could have avoided death, and that afterward all would perish in the flood. Therefore he made a definite covenant with him, as if for a denarius of eternal life, so that the workers of that hour might never say that they had neglected God’s commandments because they did not know what rewards had been promised to the good or what punishment to the wicked.

Afterward, with the remaining workers there is no mention of a denarius. He made no definite covenant with them and promised no fixed reward, but said, “Whatever is just, I will give you.” For the most kind master of the household knew his own generosity and mercy: he was prepared to give them as much as the hired workers never expected to receive. Thus the workers of that hour were hired until the flood. Those who labored during that period received the same denarius with righteous Abel when Christ descended to the underworld, and they will yet receive it in full when all immortality has been restored to them as their reward.

The third hour was when he went out to Noah, after the world had been renewed because of the waters of the flood. With him he again made a new covenant, established agreements, and gave commandments—to him and to his offspring as far as Abraham. He sent them as workers from the marketplace into the vineyard, where he found them idle, as though they were merchants pursuing profits and the gains of the present age. He found them idle because he found them doing nothing that could benefit them, and he said to them, “Go you also into my vineyard.”

They were in the marketplace, and therefore outside the vineyard; that is, they were pursuing worldly profits, situated amid the commerce of the age. For this reason it is rightly said that he found them in the marketplace. There, according to another parable, a wife is taken, a farm is purchased, and five yokes of oxen are tested. Therefore, while such people are in the marketplace, pursuing only temporal things, they can neither come to the bridegroom’s wedding nor enter Christ’s vineyard and work in it.

The master of the household went out, as it were, at the sixth hour to Abraham, when he also received him as a guest. Then he gave him new commandments, instructed him in many teachings, and trained him in disciplines. He made a covenant with him, and he confirmed even with an oath that the blessing of all nations would be in his offspring.

Thus he sent him, and all the Fathers and patriarchs who lived in his time up to Moses—or, better, up to David—into his vineyard, not so that they would grow sluggish in idleness after being placed there, but so that they would labor and cultivate it. Then, from Moses or from David, whose offspring and the fruit of whose womb was promised to be Christ, he himself hired them and all the cultivators of faith as workers into his vineyard.

That vineyard, according to the testimony of the Prophet, was the house of Israel, carried out of Egypt and transplanted; it was called *Sorech*, that is, “chosen.” In that vineyard the entire ancient Hebrew people of God labored. The master of the household himself—namely Christ—chose and instructed them in faith from the very beginning of the world. And as along a straight line, through all the Fathers and patriarchs up to Christ himself, he did not cease to teach and establish their genealogy in faith, nor did he cease, through those same men, to labor and cultivate that vineyard. [Col. 0679A]

At the eleventh hour, according to the promises of Holy Scripture, he went out incarnate to the Gentiles and came into the world to hire workers for that same chosen vineyard, which he acquired for himself by the strength of his arm and arranged to lead out of Egypt, so that there might be one vineyard, with its cultivators joined together in faith and sharing alike in the reward and in the labor.

When God, having become man, came to them, he found the Gentiles standing outside the vineyard. He said to them: “Why are you standing here idle all day?” We must by no means follow the ravings of the heretics who say that they are described as having been ready to stand idle for work all day because souls, removed in the heavenly places, had not been hired for the labor of work but were waiting to come into bodies. Hence, they say, the Gospel speaks as though there were many who were to be hired, but no one who would hire them.

They allegorize many things from this parable according to their own interpretations, mixing their errors with divine mysteries. But we say that they stood idle all day because they were not engaged in the labor of the Law, nor in any worship of God; rather, they stood idly, wickedly contending for their own rights, set upright against God so that they would not believe. They stood like upright stones, which they worshiped as gods, having become like them. They did not advance but remained immobile all day, as though from the beginning of the world to the final time of Christ’s coming.

Hence John also says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (I John II, 18). In that hour, when they are steadily questioned or reproved, they say, “Because no one hired us.” For no patriarch had come to them, no prophet, no teacher of life, and no preacher of salvation. What, then, does “No one hired us” mean except that no one preached to us the ways of life?

It should be noted that there is one master of the household, who went out five times throughout the whole age and, on the final occasion, fully manifested himself as the promised God made man, in order to teach the unconfused workers the word of truth and send them into his vineyard. He himself is the true vine; for the reward of a denarius he hires laborers so that, through the works of the vineyard, they might pass into adoption as children of God and become, through him who is the true and proper Son, children of the eternal Father.

Therefore it is not without reason that on each day, at these hours, the Church of Christ, as a memorial, celebrates praises to God, so that it may recall itself to the things within and that the whole mind may return to God. Thus, early in the morning, it gathers itself entirely in praises, when it is accustomed to recite the morning hymns, and joining the First Hour to them, consecrates itself wholly to God. Then, performing the Third, Sixth, and Ninth Hours and retracing the footsteps of Christ’s Passion, it completes in evening praises, as though at the final hour of the day, the fivefold pattern of our calling in praise, so that through this each person may direct himself toward the praise and glory of his Creator. [824]

When evening had come, the lord of the vineyard said to his steward: “Call the workers and give them their wages, beginning with the last and going on to the first.”

Consider that “evening” is mentioned because it is the end of the very day on which the workers were sent into the vineyard, and not another morning. Therefore, at that same end of time, before that blessed day dawns, judgment will take place. The righteous must be separated from sinners, so that the wicked may be removed and not see the glory of God.

At that judgment, each will receive what he has done: the workers of the vineyard, or each individual branch the fruit of its labor, those who have remained in the vine. The denarius will be given to them—that is, eternal life—for this is the reward of the blessed, which will be one and everlasting for all and for each. Yet within it there will be different degrees of merits, because it is said that he will repay each according to his works.

It is rightly asked who the steward is to whom the master of the household says, “Call the workers,” and so forth. The Arians especially labor from this passage to establish their error, saying that the steward is another—the Holy Spirit—because, they claim, the two cannot be of one substance, nor one person, nor have one dignity. If, they say, one is the master of the household and the other the steward, they are not equal with the Father, since they are not of one substance. Therefore the Son is less than the Father, and the Holy Spirit is also less than the Son.

Alas, how ready heretical perversity always is to distort what is right and mix poisons of falsehood with the truth! It is therefore necessary to inquire more carefully who this steward is, whom the Lord of the vineyard calls as though he were subordinate, lest some hierarchy—as the Arians wish—or any distinction be imagined within the Trinity, which is God, between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, since there is one Godhead, one substance, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and one equality. [Col. 0680C]

Therefore, although the Holy Spirit may rightly be called a steward, just as he may be called the Comforter, more properly that angelic order which cares for the Churches of God is called the steward. For, as the Apostle says, as long as the heir is a child, until the appointed time he is under guardians and stewards; so the Church of Christ is preserved under those spiritual stewards who have been appointed by Christ for the ministry of the saints. We rightly call them *oikonomoi*—stewards—on account of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation.

Nor should you be surprised that one of them is introduced in place of many, since even in secular literature one is very often said tropologically to stand for many. To him it is said, “Call the workers,” because at the trumpet of God and at the voice of the archangel those who are dead in Christ will rise first; this is the calling of the last to their reward. Through the ministry of these angels also, even now, when the souls of the saints are carried to rest, they are rewarded with the denarius of eternal life.

But through these same angels, at the Lord’s command, the reward begins with the last, because those who came to the vineyard last under grace have been made first, rather than those who came earlier under the Law and bore the burdens of the Law and sweated through their own labors. For the gifts of Christ are greater than the reward of the Law. Therefore the Apostle calls them the immeasurable riches of Christ, gifts of his mercy and goodness. A reward arising from a gift is not a reward, since it is owed on account of work; but God gave all people free grace through faith and justification, not merely through the reward of the Law.

Therefore, because Abraham believed God, it was reckoned to him as righteousness. Observe, I ask, how natural reasoning is placed first when the reward begins with those who live under grace. We always give more readily to those to whom we give something solely for our honor and goodness than to those to whom we return something under compulsion of a payment. For all who lived before Christ’s coming are justified, even in the faith of Christ, as though by works of the Law. But the Gentiles received the gifts of salvation solely through the mercy of God. Hence the Apostle says: “But the Gentiles glorify God for his mercy” (Rom. XV, 9).

It therefore belongs to the goodness of God that the last should receive free grace, while nothing is defrauded or diminished for the first. Thus, to display his immeasurable mercy and the riches of his goodness, God did not observe the order presumed by human arrogance.

When the first came and saw those who had come around the eleventh hour receiving one denarius each, they thought that they would receive more. They did not consider the agreement made with them for a denarius, though they had seen the goodness of the one who had hired each person whenever he wished. Nor did they consider by what goodness of God, or by what disposition and power, each had been hired, since it was not in their power to be born first, just as it was not in the power of the others to be born last.

Therefore they do not rightly murmur, since they too received one denarius each. Otherwise, if it were in a person’s power when he would be born, or in what order a worker would come to Christ’s vineyard, perhaps the one who came first to the work of the vineyard ought to demand that he receive the first reward.

Nevertheless, although one denarius is given to all—in which the image of Christ is shown to everyone and eternal life is granted—there are certainly different dwelling places within that same eternal life, according to the merits of each. Therefore one must attend to what the lord of the vineyard said to his steward: that he should begin with the last and proceed upward until he reached the first. Thus those hired around the eleventh hour receive first, like the thief on the cross; second, those hired around the ninth; third, those around the sixth; fourth, those around the third; and last, those hired in the morning.

This is what he had indicated when he said, “Give them their wages, beginning with the last and going on to the first”: those who are closer to the grace of our redemption should receive earlier, according to these same lines of human calling. Through these lines and intervals of hours, as I have already said, a new light arose for us after the darkness of human blindness, so that it might hire workers for the vineyard planted by his right hand.

But not all bore the burden and heat of the day, and therefore not all murmur against the master of the household. Not those who were hired around the third and sixth hours, nor those around the ninth, since they did not bear the burden of the entire day. But each bore a portion of the day, its heat, and its burden, according as he was called, in proportion to the hours and the spans of time.

Therefore those who came first, with whom an agreement had been made for a denarius, are said to have murmured, although no one who murmurs or is envious can receive the kingdom of heaven. This murmuring, then, also arises not from justice but certainly from envy, because the last are made equal in reward to those who were hired at the first hour, although the latter received the denarius for which the agreement had been made.

In these matters and words there is great obscurity unless the parable is examined more carefully. For there is no partiality, but complete justice, when he gives one what he owes and grants another what he wishes; and this is to act justly: “I do what I wish.” Yet he called both groups freely and placed them in the labor, so that they might deserve to receive.

Here the whole Jewish nation, which was called through these five stages to cultivate the vineyard, is depicted together, as one body. There is no doubt that among them there were murmurers and envious people. Like the elder brother in another parable, placed in the field and at work, it complains that it has always been with the father and has never transgressed his commandment. But when the younger brother, while the elder was outside, is mercifully received inside by the father and a banquet is prepared for him, the elder, indignant, refuses to enter and murmurs, moved by envy.

It is not that the father did not wish to receive him into the feast and joy, but because the younger brother—that is, the last Gentile nation—was made equal, he refused to enter. For this reason the same people are perhaps introduced in this passage as murmuring figuratively, after the custom of those who always gloried carnally in the Law and considered themselves better than all the Gentiles, not because of God’s grace but because of their own works.

Therefore even those among them who are saved—not only by works of the Law but also justified by faith—together with the faithful patriarch Abraham, are sometimes said to have murmured, or are marked as having done so after the manner of their race. This should not, however, be understood to mean that anyone who murmurs or is envious, as I have said above, ought to enter the kingdom of God. Their murmuring consisted in having endured, with very great desire, the delay of the kingdom until Christ’s coming.

For this reason it must be asked why the master of the household did not answer all those who came first and thought they would receive more, since they are also said to have murmured. He said to one of them: “Friend, I do you no wrong, because you agreed with me for a denarius.”

Here, as it seems to me, although one is taken for all, the earlier order is designated, even though all the Jews bore the burdens of the Law and all the heat and weight of their desires. Those alone suffer no wrong and receive the promised denarius for their righteous labors who remained in the unity of Christ’s faith with the Fathers and patriarchs. No injustice was inflicted upon them when, in reciprocal order, the grace of Christ was also bestowed upon them, because, according to the Apostle’s testimony, no one will be justified by works of the Law.

They are not said to have borne the burden and heat of the day as though some one of them had endured the yoke of the Law and its desires throughout this entire period, by which alternately “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V, 17). Rather, because that entire nation, until the grace of Christ cooled the heat of their passions and lightened the weight of their sins, was exhausted by immense heats of desire and weighed down by burdens of sin.

Hence the Savior says to them: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28). Since they had borne heavily the burdens of the whole day, which neither they nor their fathers could bear, they ought therefore to have been grateful rather than ungrateful, because grace was given to them also, just as to the Gentiles, so that all might rely not upon their own merits but upon the goodness of God.

Hence he says, as though to an envious person: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” For the envious person always grieves, as though whatever has been added to another had been entirely taken away from him. He thinks that everything belonging to him is diminished when he sees someone made richer than himself—or even when he sees someone made equal to him. All this arises for him from empty glory.

Accordingly, he speaks more according to the custom and habit of those who gloried carnally in the Law than according to the disposition of those who are rewarded, even though they receive their reward after a long delay.

He says: “So the last will be first, and the first last.” He repeats the same statement he made earlier concerning Jews and Gentiles. Although the Jews were called first, before the Gentiles, the Gentiles nevertheless received the one who had been promised to them and became first in grace. And when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then the Jews, who were formerly first, will finally be saved as the last.

This is the whole point of the parable; this is its complete resolution. For this reason the last received the denarius, although they were first. Perhaps this does not mean that the last are to be considered holier or more worthy than the Fathers, but that they are made equal in the one hope of calling, because it is not the circumstance of time but the grace of merits that makes a difference.

Hence all the saints are like a crown in the hand of God. For in a crown, which turns around in a circle, you will find nothing that can be called first, or that has a beginning or an end. So among the saints, insofar as time is concerned in that age and in that life signified by the denarius, no one is called last and no one first.

Therefore how fitting it is that those who were born and called earlier should be rewarded last, and that those who were reborn last in Christ should be rewarded first with the denarius of life! The former, possessing the first grace, are made equal to the latter through this grace; and the latter, though last, are incorporated through that same grace of Christ so that they may become first in Christ.

But because both the earlier and the last workers were all hired into the master’s vineyard to cultivate it, we must not listen to the heretics—Jovinianus and the others—who wish there to be no difference among them because all were sent into the vineyard and hired for its cultivation. Hence, they say, all receive one denarius at evening, without exception, and none of those who were called is excluded from the reward.

This interpretation is strongly contradicted by the statement: “For many are called, but few are chosen.” Therefore it must be acknowledged that not all who were called were called according to the grace of election; nor were all called, but many were called, and from among them few were chosen.

For all the Jews were called to cultivate the vineyard, yet because they did not remain in the faith of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, nor in the promise made to them, they too were rejected—along with all who did not persevere in cultivating the vineyard so as to remain in the faith of Christ, which works through love.

Therefore this is not to be understood only of the Gentiles, as the heretics wish, but of the whole calling of the five hours, among which there are found both the rejected and the faithful and chosen. For no one hires a laborer for work merely so that he may eat, drink, and grow sluggish in idleness, but so that he may labor and cultivate what has been assigned to him.

In the marketplace—that is, in the affairs of this age, from which they were called—many are either dead or languish in idleness. But in the cultivation of Christ’s vineyard no one ought to be idle if he wishes to remain in the vine. Otherwise he too will be cut off, although he may appear to be a branch, and will be thrown into the fire because he neglects to bear the fruit of good work.

Therefore the first praise of a Christian is to be separated from the marketplace, from the affairs and frauds of this age, and to have no cause of litigation with anyone, because no one contends in the marketplace except for profit. From that marketplace we have all been called to work. [Col. 0684B]

But because this whole parable has been corrupted by the frauds of the heretics, their interpretation must be avoided. They say that none of those who were called among the workers of the vineyard will be counted among those receiving the reward if they have fallen away, departed from the vineyard, and returned again to the marketplace to pursue the profits of their pleasure; nor can they return as penitents to work in the vineyard from the beginning.

For, they say, they can no longer tell the master of the household, “No one hired us.” They had already been hired at the first time, when they were called to the faith. Nor, they say, will it be said to them, “Why are you standing here idle all day?” Especially since they have fallen into death, they refuse to consider that if they wish to return and rise from the place where they fell, we read in the Apocalypse: “Remember from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the former works” (Apoc. II, 5). The most merciful Savior invites sinners to forgiveness in many other passages as well.

If anyone dislikes this lengthy exposition, let him understand the workers as the individual ages of human life. The workers of the first hour may be understood as Samuel, Jeremiah, or John the Baptist, or others of the same kind who can say: “From my mother’s womb you are my God” (Ps. LXX [71], 6/7). The workers of the third hour will be those who began to serve God from puberty. Those of the sixth hour are people who, having reached full maturity—that is, youth—took up the yoke of Christ. The workers of the ninth hour are rightly understood as those who, when they already seem to be declining toward old age, come to the faith. The workers of the eleventh hour are those who are very old, whom the Greeks call not *presbyteroi* but *gerontes*, that is, extremely aged men. Yet all receive the reward of eternal life, although the labor of these hours differs.

In that life, although eternity will always be one, the splendor of merits will nevertheless be different. Therefore those who have been rewarded ought to be grateful in every respect, just as the master of the household is shown to be merciful in everything and unjust in nothing. For if the master of the household were unjust in any one matter, he would be unjust not in one but in all. Hence it is rightly demonstrated that eternal life is granted to all not from the merit of their work, but from the grace of Christ.

As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside privately and said to them: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and crucified; and on the third day he will rise again.”

This is already the third time that he repeats this to the disciples, as we remember having explained above, except that there he is said only to be killed, whereas here even the manner of his killing is more clearly declared, when he says that he will be crucified, so that no doubt about his death might remain for the apostles.

And because, after many intervening discussions, what they had heard might afterward have slipped from their memory, as he was going to Jerusalem and taking the apostles with him, he prepares them for temptation and introduces them to the mystery of the cross, so that when persecution and the disgrace of the cross came, they would not be scandalized by being suddenly struck with fear.
