Hence he says pointedly: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem.” For “behold” here is the speech of one bearing witness, so that they might store the memory of this foreknowledge in their hearts, as though he were saying: “Behold, now for the third time, or even more, I foretell to you the mystery of my Passion; I testify to you so that you may know it.”

What do you think, brothers? If at that hour of Christ’s Passion the faith of the apostles failed and bodily fear swallowed up the preparation of their souls, so that they all abandoned him and fled, how great do you think their despair would have been unless God’s foreknowledge and his will concerning his Passion had been at work?

Therefore he foretells so often what is to happen to him so that, from the foreknowledge of his divinity, it may be fully understood, and so that reflection on his divinity may strengthen and confirm their faith all the more at the time of his Passion. Thus they may attribute everything he suffered to the dispensation of his will, not to the necessity of nature.

Because this was a great mystery, while a very large crowd followed him, he took only these twelve aside privately and expressed the mystery of his Passion more fully to them alone. For the more precious and sacred a treasure is, the more faithfully it must be entrusted to the faithful and stored in more precious vessels.

But wretched Judas, who was still numbered among the Twelve and was drawing such treasures from the foreknowledge of God without knowing what would happen through him, paid no attention. Until then he had not been marked out by the Lord in any way; in everything he had been counted and sent to preach together with the other apostles. The devil had not yet put it into his heart to betray him.

And therefore, because we do not know what the coming day will bring forth from us, that apostolic saying must always be kept in mind: “Work out your salvation continually with fear and trembling.”

It should also be noted that on this occasion none of the apostles replied—neither Peter, who had earlier rebuked him, nor any of those who had heard the Lord rebuke Peter. For it was fitting that they remember and observe what the Lord had said to Peter, lest they perhaps hear even harsher words of rebuke from their pious and most merciful Teacher.

Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee approached Jesus with her sons, worshiping him and asking something of him. This occurred, as he says, on the way, when Jesus said to his twelve disciples: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem.” But Mark explains not that the mother approached and made the request reported by Matthew and worshiped him, but that her sons themselves approached, as though on their own. Hence it is clear that she asked the very thing which they had persuaded her to ask, and therefore they are said to have approached as though on their own, since their suggestion was that their mother intercede for them. We can also understand this from the Lord’s words: he did not answer as though to a woman making the request, but as though to the sons who had themselves prompted it.

“You do not know,” he said, “what you are asking.” For I think that when they had often heard the Lord prophesying about his passion and resurrection, and understood that he would suffer of his own accord, they began to think among themselves—since they were already devoted in faith: “Behold, the heavenly King is ascending, so that he may destroy the kingdoms of death, and the king and kingdom of the underworld. What else remains, once he has ascended victorious from the battle, except that the glory of the kingdom should follow?” Especially because they had heard him earlier promising: “At the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

Thus, being greatly stirred by the prospect of glory, they put forward their mother to plead for them, with sufficient subtlety and ingenuity. Perhaps this was so that no suspicion would arise that they themselves had asked for it, and no envy would arise among their fellow disciples because they desired this for themselves; and if there should be any reproach, a woman’s error would be borne more lightly. For her sex itself, being prone to such a mistake, excuses her error. And if importunity should go somewhat further, it is endured more gently. Great, indeed, is the force of love in mothers. Thus she perhaps believed that the Lord, who had filled maternal hearts with love for their children, would more readily heed her affection, because they had not only left their father for Christ, but she herself had left her husband and followed Christ together with her sons. [Col. 0686B] For this reason she may have been more ready, since she had left her husband alive for his sake, as the Evangelist shows when he says that they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed Jesus. Unless someone should say that he had meanwhile died, and that she therefore followed Christ only afterward. Nevertheless, she followed him, and marital affection did not overcome her.

Although someone might say that in this passage carnal love overcame spiritual reverence for Christ, since she still did not know the spiritual things she was seeking. Jesus said to her: “What do you want?” He certainly did not ask as though he did not know, in order to hear what she wanted; rather, when she made the request, he exposed the unreasonable petition of those who were asking, as though they were devout lovers of heavenly glory, yet without possessing true knowledge. Therefore, when she asked, “Say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand in your kingdom and the other at your left,” although she had requested heavenly things for them, the heavenly Judge answered not the woman’s words but the purpose and suggestion of her sons: “You do not know,” he said, “what you are asking.”

It was as though he said: “Have you not heard that those who will be on the left will be accursed and rejected? For this reason I called you from the left to the right, so that you might always remain on the right. Why, then, do you wish by your own design to return again to the left? Perhaps the devil, through the woman, is returning to his customary weapons, seeking an opportunity for error through feminine affections.”

Moreover, since it belongs properly to Christ, the only Son of God, to sit at the right hand of God the Father, how could one of them sit at the left hand of the Son unless he sat between the Father and the Son—and that is impious to say—or nearer to him? Therefore the Savior immediately said: “You do not know what you are asking.” Although the desire may appear good, the request was ill-considered. It is thought to have arisen from love of the Lord, and therefore he did not perhaps condemn their will or intention, but their ignorance concerning what they were asking. Thus the woman is neither put to shame nor angered; rather, her error is recalled and her ignorance reproved.

“Can you,” he said, “drink the cup that I am about to drink?” He asks this in order to draw from their confession what was going to happen—as if he were saying: “Unless you are prepared to receive it and to be brought to completion through martyrdom, you cannot sit at my right hand.” It has been granted to all generally that they should be on the right, although you may wish to claim this specially for yourselves, so that you alone may sit on the throne where angels are said to stand around.

“You will indeed drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand or my left is not mine to grant to you, but belongs to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.”

What a remarkable answer! Does he not have authority to grant it to whomever he wishes? What does he mean by saying, “It is not mine”? Does the Father not love the Son, as he says elsewhere: “He has given everything into his hand”? And the Son himself says of the Father: “Everything belonging to the Father is mine.” If everything is his, how is it not his to grant that someone should sit on his throne at his right or left, whomsoever he wishes? For even if it has been prepared by the Father that those who are to sit there should sit, surely the seat itself is also prepared by the Son. He says elsewhere: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places; and if it were not so, I would have told you, because I am going to prepare a place for you” (John XIV, 2).

Therefore the place, seat, or dwelling of each person was prepared for each one from the beginning in God’s foreknowledge, and is prepared daily through the faith of those who believe, so that they may attain it. Thus he rightly says that it is not his to give, but that it belongs to those who will receive it to earn through faith what has already been prepared for them by the Father and is prepared daily also by the Son himself. Hence he is read as saying at the end: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV, 34).

Christ does not, then, deny his own authority to give, although the Felician heresy joyfully rises up here against the Catholic faith, as though, because he was the nominal or adoptive Son of God according to his humanity, he therefore said: “It is not mine to give you.” But he himself says something entirely different by the words “It is not mine.” It is as though he said: “My form in which I am man, as you believe, does not possess the power to grant what you ask.”

Thus, although this must be understood in that way, blind presumption did not consider the reason why the Savior said this, although the Father had given everything into his hands (John XIII, 3). It was not “not mine to give” because he lacked the power, but because they were asking wrongly. Immediately afterward he made the reason clearer: “You do not know what you are asking.” This, then, was the reason for the impossibility, not the one which that wretched man turned against Christ concerning the adoption of the Son of God—a doctrine which he read nowhere and never.

Therefore, when he had said, “It is not mine to give you,” he did not immediately add, as would have followed: “But it will belong to those to whom my Father gives it.” Nor would he have spoken in such a way as to show himself, through adoption, to be the Son of God the Father. How much more is this evident now when he says: “But [to those] for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” By this he indicates that nothing was impossible for him, nor was granting it difficult; rather, the quality of the request produced the difficulty for those who made it.

Accordingly, one must first ask in every matter whether one is requesting rightly or wrongly what pertains to salvation. Otherwise, no one asks in the name of the Savior except the person who asks for what pertains to salvation, what ought to be asked, and in the manner in which it ought to be asked. Otherwise, it is not his to give to one who asks wrongly.

Thus the Lord did not speak generally about everyone, who very often ask rightly and as they ought, so as to say, “It is not mine to give to any human being,” but specifically to them. It was as though he plainly said: “To you, certainly, who do not know what you ought to ask or how you ought to ask; who do not yet know me as you ought, the one whom you are approaching in prayer.”

Nor did he conclude his statement in such a way as to deny himself this authority, but he added: “To those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” It was as though he said: “It is mine to give to those for whom it has been prepared by the Father, so that they may believe and understand me to be equal to God the Father; to those to whom my Father reveals it, as he did to Peter, so that they may confess me as Christ, the Son of the living God. For then it will be mine to give to them also, just as I gave Peter eternal blessedness and the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

To those, therefore, whose minds the Father prepares so that they may believe perfectly and ask rightly, it belongs to the Son to give the kingdom of heaven. For no one rightly believes in the Father without the Son, nor in the Son without the Father. Hence he himself says, speaking to the Father: “This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3).

Because that man did not believe this, he foolishly went astray and was condemned. Christ had not ascended to the Father for him, any more than for Mary; and therefore he called him the nominal or adoptive Son of God. For that wretched man had not touched him through faith, since he did not believe him to be truly God or omnipotent, but divided the one Son of God into two: one whom he called the proper Son and another whom he called adoptive. Thus God would no longer be a Trinity but a quaternity. Whoever holds this doctrine is wholly foolish.

I have said these things at greater length so that the prudent reader may avoid the poisons of heretics, both in this passage and in very many others, and may understand chastely and seek devoutly what ought to be requested, how it ought to be requested, and from whom it ought to be requested. For in the request of the two brothers is contained, in summary, the error of almost all who ask wrongly, and the presumption of those who make improper requests is exposed.

The height of his divinity is also shown when he wishes to confess himself equal to the Father, while he rejects those who, as though they understood him to be merely a man, had such thoughts. In accordance with the intention of their hearts, the Wisdom of God the Father so tempered his answer that through it they might understand him more fully as God.

It was as though he said: “Because you still believe me to be a man and do not yet believe perfectly, ‘it is not mine’—that is, it is not the power of a man or of human nature alone—to give that. But because I am at once God and man in one person, it is mine to give, but to those for whom it has been prepared by the Father, so that they may believe in this way and ask rightly.”

But because heretics spread their poisons through almost every passage of Scripture, especially wherever it speaks about the Son, the Catholic faith must always be carefully observed, according to the divine Scripture itself, just as Paul said of himself and his associates: “To one we are the fragrance of life leading to life, and to another the fragrance of death leading to death” (II Corinthians II, 16). For rightly understanding people it grants eternal life, but upon its corrupters and those who understand it wrongly it brings perpetual death.

In all the statements of his teaching, however, the most benevolent Master provides from God a good fragrance to those who are good and right in heart. It is not as the Arians chatter that the Son is proclaimed inferior to the Father in this passage. Rather, the most gracious Master so tempered his statement that he both blunted their stupidity and did not deny them what they had asked, if they would devote themselves to faith.

And in this answer the excellent Master gathered together and instructed not only the other fellow disciples but all who are saved through faith, so that no one might be scandalized by the two brothers, and so that none of them might seek that thing through vain presumption. For if their rivalry was not accepted by the Lord, although they were asking good things for themselves, the other apostles were indignant that they had dared to ask for even this. How much more would they have been disturbed if their request had been accepted by the Lord?

For if their rashness or presumption had been heard—since they were asking such things without the help or grace of the Holy Spirit—the others, who still thought carnally, could have been even more scandalized if what was owed to all, and what all ought to hope for, had been granted to two alone. The ability and glory of that kingdom, however, are to be given commonly to all, not stolen away by two.

Therefore it is pleasing to consider how wisely Wisdom answered them. He tempered his statement in such a way that he could offend no one. He did not say, “You will never sit there,” lest he put the two to shame; nor did he grant their request by saying, “You will sit there,” lest he provoke the others to scandal.

What, then, does he say? “It is not mine to give you.” Thus the most gracious Master arranges everything prudently, so that both they and the others may be instructed, and so that unanimity and brotherly love may not be destroyed among the brothers.

For this reason also he had asked them earlier: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” This was so that, when they answered, “We can,” the others too might hear and acquiesce. They would understand that if they themselves were prepared to die for Christ, they too could sit beside Christ, and that they were not excluded for the sake of the two.

As it was promised through the Prophet in the person of the Lord: “My eyes are upon the faithful of the earth, that they may sit with me” (Psalm C, 6).

Here it must be asked why Mark, after saying, “Can you drink the cup that I drink?” added: “And be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” (Mark X, 39), whereas Matthew omitted this entirely. We must see whether perhaps both meanings are expressed in this one statement, which Mark is shown to have explained more openly in two statements.

The cup is rightly understood as the pain or passion that occurs before death; baptism, however, is death itself, through which the soul is reborn to salvation. In Greek it is called βάπτισμα (*baptisma*), but in Latin *tinctio*, “dipping,” by analogy with dyed wool: for example, wool that has its natural color, when dipped, is changed into purple or takes on the dignity of some other color. So too, when a person enters death with Christ, even if he has been stained by some color of sin or corruption, he passes wholly to Christ cleansed, renewed, and already made spiritual, as the Apostle says: “It is sown in weakness, it rises in power; it is sown in dishonor, it rises in glory; it is sown an animal body, it rises a spiritual body” (I Corinthians XV, 43–44).

Every death certainly contains suffering, but not every suffering contains death. For many have suffered without being killed, as did the many confessors of Christ. They all drank the Lord’s cup, but they were not baptized with his baptism—that is, with death—except in the baptism by which they had first been reborn.

Thus John, although he was not brought to completion in martyrdom through bodily death, nevertheless drank the Lord’s cup, since he suffered in many ways. Death itself is also not improperly called a cup. When the Lord had come to the hour of his passion, he said of it: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew XXVI, 39), to show his own people that, although passion involves pain, the prospect of death nevertheless brings great fear.

Perhaps these men were still inexperienced in that fear. Therefore, when asked so freely whether they could drink it, they answered, “We can.” Their error, if I may call it that, was a blessed one, since it removes so great an error from believers. For unless they had erred, we could not have learned that not everything which appears good should be sought rashly.

For one thing is a good work, and another is the primacy of honor, to desire which is vanity. Hence the Apostle says: “Whoever desires the office of bishop desires a good work” (I Timothy III, 1), because he wishes a person to seek not the honor but the work associated with the honor. To accomplish this good work belongs to our will, granted by God, and to our own work and labor; but to attain primacy must belong to God’s judgment, not to our desire.

Therefore it follows:

“And Jesus, calling the twelve disciples, said to them: You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you. But whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your minister; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant.”

He recalls them to the satisfaction of humility, setting heavenly primacy as the fruit of humility, just as in earthly primacy he showed confusion to be the fruit. Thus whoever desires heavenly dignity should follow humility; and whoever seeks the honors of the world on earth and wishes to rule will find confusion in heaven.

Therefore he calls all twelve together, lest, by reproving only those two for the desire and greed by which they had exceeded their measure—seeking alone what was being prepared for all—he should put them to shame; or lest he should appear to rebuke the remaining ten more harshly for their indignation and envy.

Accordingly, the most gracious Master set forth an example by which he teaches that the greater is the one who, out of humility, wishes to be the least, and who, out of devotion to Christ, is not lord but servant of all.

It was as though he said: “It shall not be so among you as it is among the rulers of the nations, because they delight only in ruling and exercising authority. Therefore these men seek high or excessive things in vain, and you are indignant at them without cause because of the pride of the two who ask for greater things. The summit of virtue and the height of true honor are reached not through power and domination, but through humility and gentleness.”

And lest anyone should think that such a command to humility was impossible among those who appear to be rulers, princes, and teachers of the Churches, he sets himself forth as an example:

“Just as the Son of Man,” he says, “did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life for many.”

Accordingly, whoever wishes to be a teacher in the school of virtue should first desire to become a minister of the work and a servant in that virtue which operates through love, so that afterward he may teach from himself the things which the Savior taught through his own instruction. For he says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew XI, 29).

Everyone who already holds a position of governance in the Church of Christ ought to display this pattern in himself; and before he approaches that grace, he must nourish it more fully when God calls him. Otherwise, to seek or desire the primacy of honor in the Church is neither reasonable nor justified, if it is sought in any other way, because it can be neither just nor useful.

Perhaps for the rulers of the world, even if it is not reasonable merely to rule, at least their only motive is their own will, although what they consider just or useful may not be so. Yet no wise person can rightly subject himself voluntarily to dangers for another’s life when he does not know how to govern his own; bind himself to servitude without the reward of its fruit; involve himself in labors and pains; and, what is greater, endure the daily loss of his life as though on behalf of the whole Church, while he himself is held guilty because he does not rule rightly according to the pattern of the true teacher, and is therefore condemned at the head by the true Judge.

Who, then, would wish in a worldly manner to seek what the Lord and Judge, the avenger of all, forbids, except one who does not believe that judgment will come for these things?

Therefore let no one presume carelessly upon himself, even if he appears holy. For although we cannot deny that there is a distinction between the saints and the common people, no one is permitted to know for himself whether he is better or worse in God’s sight.

Therefore we must listen to the gracious Lord and Teacher, who did not come in the form of a servant to be served—although angels ministered to him—but to minister and serve his own, and also to give his life for many in death. No other just person did this for the unjust.

For he does not say “for all,” but “for many.” Although he suffered for all, in order to give forgiveness to all, not all received it perfectly, just as Judas did not, who, when Jesus was speaking these things, was one of the twelve. He was in the number, but not in merit. So too those who are in the grades of the Church, because they pursue profits and honors more than the salvation of souls, are called by the merciful Judge hirelings, and wolves, rather than shepherds.

As they were going out from Jericho, a great crowd followed him. And behold, two blind men sitting beside the road heard that Jesus was passing by, and cried out, saying: “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.”

Let the attentive hearer consider how providently divine Wisdom orders all things. For above he had said: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes,” and so forth—things which, already for the third time, could greatly disturb the minds of the disciples.

And behold, immediately, before fulfilling what he had announced, he performs the work of human salvation in a divine and godlike manner. He introduces his future death in such a way that he always declares himself God, introduces the minds of the disciples to the mysteries of human redemption, and raises those very disciples toward God.

Thus, although he first promises things about himself that are frightening, he immediately displays divine things and joins the marvelous to them. He places what follows after what came before so that in the hearts of the apostles Christ, God and man, one and the same, may be formed, and faith may be strengthened through alternating sequences, so that his whole humanity may be believed, in his divinity, to perform what is divine, just as his divinity, in his humanity, suffers what is human.

Nevertheless, he did not suffer mixture, nor was he separated by division; rather, he is one Christ in the unity of his person. Therefore the entire sequence of the Gospels, the alternation of events, and the connection of statements are arranged in alternating order, so that all his divinity may be believed, without confusion, to exist in the one and the same Christ, just as all his humanity is proclaimed, in Catholic fashion, to be personally united in his divinity.

Thus it came about that he is the Mediator of God and human beings (I Timothy II, 5), joining in himself what is divine to what is human and what is human to what is divine.

Accordingly, how providently, as he was leaving Jericho, these two blind men encountered him on the road! In their appearance was shown what was to occur in the whole human race, so that faith might be strengthened by the miracle, and so that Christ might be proclaimed in the figure of the human race as illumination when he went out from the world.

For this reason he descended into Jericho, so that he might draw a great crowd along with him. There were many robbers in it who were accustomed to attack, kill, and wound those descending from Jerusalem. Therefore the Lord came into it with his disciples, so that he might free the wounded and draw a great crowd with him.

Unless he had gone there, neither would the crowds have followed him nor would the blind have received sight. There came there also that Rahab who had committed fornication with many lovers. Nor is it surprising that, after abandoning their former ways, the crowd followed the Lord, since a great fragrance of divinity breathed from him.

For he himself is that rose planted in the fields of Jericho, of which Wisdom speaks through Solomon: “Like a palm tree I was exalted in Gades, and like a rose plantation in Jericho” (Ecclesiasticus XXIV, 18). For he is “fairer in form than the sons of men” (Psalm XLIV, 3), “white and red” (Song V, 10): white, adorned with holiness, justice, and virtues; red, however, through his own blood.

His divinity in him was perceived like fragrance in a rose before he was seen, and it breathed forth the perfume of his virtues before he was found. Therefore the crowd followed him, and the blind, while he was still far away and before they saw him, perceived the fragrance of his divinity.

Thus it was not by chance or accident, but by the preparation of God who orders all things, that behold, two blind men sitting beside the road heard and perceived that Jesus was passing by. For when he says “Behold,” he declares the providential appropriateness of the event: they were offered most opportunely by God’s providence before Christ, as an instruction concerning future things, so that with their eyes opened, like witnesses of his power, they might ascend with him to Jerusalem against the conspiracies of all who opposed him.

And, what is greater, they were to represent all believers who wish to ascend to the homeland of paradise.

Therefore it must be asked—for many teachers report the matter differently—which persons these two blind men represent. Some say that they represent the two peoples who believed, from the Jews and from the nations, and confessed him as Lord and Son of David. They are said to have sat not on the road but beside the road. They were blind because the Jews, sitting according to the letter of the Law, had not yet been illuminated by the spirit of truth; while the nations, lying inert beside the law of nature, were struck by blindness and worshiped idols.

Others, however, say that the Pharisees and Sadducees are better represented by these same two men. Some also say that they represent two peoples from the Jews, namely Judah and Israel, who all sat blind in Jericho, because they could not yet say to God the Father: “In your light we shall see light” (Psalm XXXV, 10). For they did not yet know the Son of the living God, and therefore they call him Lord and Son of God with a common designation.

Some, avoiding this interpretation, have understood both to be signified from the nations, so that one was from Ham and the other from Japheth. They sat blind because the only-begotten light born from God the Father had not yet appeared to them.

But when they heard that Jesus was passing by, they were positioned beside the road—that is, near the truth. This can also rightly be understood of all those mentioned above, because all sat blind without Christ, in a state of decline—that is, in Jericho.

Jericho is interpreted as “moon,” and the moon is taken as a figure of the decline of the flesh. No one doubts that both peoples sat blind in this decline until Jesus descended and came to Jericho with his own.

As he returned from there to Jerusalem, from which he had descended, they heard that he was passing by and, according to his humanity, the two began together to cry out: “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us.”

They sit beside the road because they already perceived him who is the road passing by. If they had not perceived him and understood themselves to be blind, they would not have cried out; and unless they were already beside the road, which is Christ—because he had come to them—they could not have followed him, since they were in darkness.

But when the day of light arrived, they began to cry out; and after receiving light, they were able to follow him—those who had been sitting in darkness and the shadow of death—because formerly all had lost the way: the Jews, because they wished to establish their own righteousness and were not subject to the righteousness of God; the nations, because they had abandoned God, gone farther away, and worshiped idols.

Both peoples, hearing that Jesus was passing by—the Word made flesh—cried out together, saying: “Have mercy on us, Son of David.”

O how wondrous and admirable is the twofold operation of God: that God should pass as man in his humanity, and that man should stand as God in his divinity! For passing belongs to his humanity, while standing belongs to his divinity, since he is always everywhere and unchangeable.

When the Gentiles heard the noise of those running at his passing, and when the others were hastening from every side—for these two blind men alone were sitting ahead of everyone, darkened and bound by an unbreakable gloom, with nothing loosened throughout their bodies except their voice—they could not follow him. They had only the voice of confession and a heart already believing, saying, “Have mercy on us, Lord, Son of David.” But those who went before rebuked them, telling them to be silent.

Thus, those who went before the Gentiles are the Jews, who, always moved by envy, still forbid people today to invoke Christ as Lord and confess him as the Son of David. They rebuked them, so that nothing might be said about Christ. But every day, too, crowds of our thoughts go before us in our hearts, especially when Jesus is passing and does not remain in us. When we begin to cry out to him, they rebuke us and do not allow us to cry freely, because our foolish heart has been darkened, and, blinded, we cannot see the light that is Christ.

But if we steadfastly cling to faith and persist in crying out inwardly with the cry of the heart, Jesus, who had been passing by, immediately stands still for us, so that thereafter we may no longer suffer such phantoms. For it is not honoring Christ when we are ordered to cease from the prayers and cries of the heart. That honor and that wisdom are foolish if we think Christ is wronged when he is exercised inwardly by prayers.

Therefore, brothers, whenever we are restrained by such phantoms of thought, we must cry out more and more, saying: “Have mercy on us, Lord, Son of David.” [Col. 0694C]

Such, then, is the nature of faith. We therefore know that the Church of Christ has grown more amid persecutions, because the more it was afflicted, the more intensely it was always kindled within. Thus it was conquered in nothing; rather, amid the very dangers, it was strengthened by the warmth of faith. It expands and is not overcome by terrors.

Jesus, standing still, commanded them to come to him; and when he commanded this, no one could prevent them. Hence he is rightly said to have stood still, so that the crowd might not prevent them. For, as I have said, his standing belongs to his divinity, against which no force of the enemy can prevail.

And he asked what they wanted. I would certainly not say that this question arose from ignorance, since their blindness was evident, but from the dispensation of the mystery, so that their greater faith might be proclaimed. Here they no longer call him the Son of David, but only Lord. “Lord,” they say, “that our eyes may be opened.” [Col. 0694D]

For opening the eyes of the blind belongs solely to divinity. It is not, as some chatter, a kind of phantom-like cure, but the full, mystical, twofold operation of Christ Jesus as God and man, full of the sacraments of God and man. Therefore he touches their eyes as man and heals them by his power as God. For neither does Christ the man do anything without God, nor does Christ God do anything without man.

Accordingly, God and man are one Christ; one and the same is the Son of David and the Son of God. Accordingly, the Lord and the Son of David are not two, but one Christ, whom the blind beseech to have mercy on them.

In this faith all those who were sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death were enlightened. They were enlightened so that they could leave Jericho, where there are many pits and many snares, and follow Christ to that heavenly Jerusalem—not to the Jerusalem that he soon laments as destined to fall, but to the Jerusalem above, which is the mother of all the elect.

Mark and Luke, however, presented this episode quite differently, so that, according to some, they seem to be explaining this same story, while, according to others, they are composing another. Thus the difference in the bodily events is to be understood as arising from Christ’s healing these two blind men on a different occasion.

On one occasion, they say that he healed the one whom Mark records, alone on the road as the Lord was leaving Jericho; Mark also gives his name and indicates his father. On a third occasion, Luke records the man he describes in these words: “And it came to pass,” he says, “when he drew near Jericho, that a certain blind man was sitting beside the road, begging.” Although he appears to have been healed at a different time, the place was nevertheless the same—that is, beside the road—and in all three accounts the event seems to have occurred there.

Matthew and Mark say that this happened as Jesus was leaving Jericho, whereas Luke says that it happened as he was entering. Thus it may be that, when Luke says that a blind man was healed as Jesus approached Jericho, and Mark similarly says that another was healed as he was leaving, Matthew gathered these two blind men into a single account for the sake of brevity, since both are said to have sat blind beside the road and to have cried out.

Perhaps, since one Evangelist says “Lord” and another “Rabbi,” they may be said together: “Have mercy, Lord Rabboni, Son of David”; as they often do, one first gives what the other sets forth.

Nor does it conflict with the truth, according to ordinary usage, if Matthew says that this happened as Jesus was leaving, since the event occurred on the road at that time, as it is narrated. If this seems less fitting to anyone, there is no difficulty in saying that there were so many, provided only that we acknowledge that they were enlightened; for in their figure and likeness we believe that the whole human race was healed by the Lord.

It may nevertheless rightly be judged that, although the man mentioned by Luke was another and was healed at another time, the one whom Mark records—who was the son of Timaeus and was named Bartimaeus—was one of the two whom Matthew narrates. Mark may therefore have recorded this one alone because he was better known and most famous, as his name itself indicates: he is called the son of Timaeus because *bar* means “son” in the Hebrew or Syriac language. Thus it was quite appropriately arranged that this man should be called *Bar-timaeus*, “son of Timaeus.” [Col. 0695A]

Nevertheless, even in the mystery there is no departure from the truth if this one man is taken as a figure of the whole human race. For just as the Savior granted him what nature had not given, or weakness had caused him to lose, so he granted all people, through grace, greater gifts of salvation: he remitted guilt and bestowed gifts.

Only, if we wish to follow him as he leaves Jericho, together with those who accompany him daily to that heavenly Jerusalem, we shall be able to reach it happily with praises.

For when he ascended from Jericho—that is, from the world—through the resurrection and ascension into heaven, many crowds followed him, because peoples and nations immediately believed in him. Therefore Matthew, whatever their number may have been, rightly narrates two blind men sitting beside the road. He signifies that, from both peoples, some were already joined by faith to the temporal dispensation, according to which Christ is the way for us.

That is why, desiring to be enlightened—that is, to understand something of his eternity and the incarnation of the Word—they cried out. Since Jesus was passing according to his humanity, they rejoiced to obtain what they sought through the merit of faith: faith in which it is believed that the Son of God became man, was born from the seed of David, and suffered for us. He ascended to Jerusalem—that is, to heaven—and through this dispensation Jesus passes, because such an action was temporal.

Therefore it was necessary, and is always absolutely necessary, for each of us to cry out until we overcome the noise of the crowd resisting us: that is, to devote ourselves with such perseverance—in prayer, seeking, and knocking at his door—that we may attempt to see the light of eternal truth, and by the strongest concentration overcome that crowd, whether of carnal people, thoughts, or desires, which obstructs our attention and our cries.

Thus our most merciful Jesus, who says, “Ask and you will receive; seek and you will find; knock and it will be opened to you,” immediately stands still for those who come to him with the ardor of desire and attain what they rightly desire inwardly; he touches the eyes of our heart and enlightens us. For, as I have said, just as that temporal dispensation passes, so does not the eternity of the Word, which, remaining in itself, renews all things. [Col. 0695B]

Therefore, because the temporal faith of Christ’s incarnation prepares us to understand eternal things, when Jesus passes we are admonished to be enlightened. Accordingly, since all temporal things pass away while eternal things stand, let us follow Jesus to Jerusalem, where he hastens to ascend, so that we may be enlightened by him who stands on the road and, ascending there with him, may arrive as quickly as possible.

## Chapter XXI

“And when he had drawn near Jerusalem, and had come to Bethphage at the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two of his disciples and said to them: ‘Go into the village that is opposite you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her.’”

After the Savior’s many miracles and glorious works, it is not without a great mystery that the Evangelists wished to describe so carefully the donkey and the colt, and the things that were done or said at Jerusalem when he drew near.

Although he had often entered the city, we never read that he needed or sought any vehicle, even though we read that, tired from his journey, he sat beside a well. He always went around all the villages on foot, as we read that he did when, leaving Jerusalem and passing through Samaria, he went into Galilee.

Why, then, does Jesus now command that a donkey and a colt be presented to him with such care? Why does he also order that the animal be untied? Were the disciples so dull that, when they saw it tied, they would not first untie it, since otherwise they could not bring it? Moreover, he commands that when someone asks them why they are untying them, they should say, “Because the Lord has need of them.”

It is perfectly clear that an event of such importance is filled with divine mysteries, especially since Zechariah had long before foretold concerning it: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout aloud, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your King will come to you, righteous and Savior, himself poor, and riding upon a donkey and upon a colt, the foal of a donkey.”

The Septuagint rendered this as “a beast under the yoke, and its young colt.” But Matthew did not set down this passage either according to the Hebrew or according to the Septuagint. For “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout aloud”—or “proclaim”—“daughter of Jerusalem” is not the same as “Say to the daughters of Zion,” or “Do not fear, daughter of Zion,” or the other expressions that John also presented quite differently, merely mentioning this prophecy. Matthew likewise gathered only the sense, and therefore did not even name the prophet Zechariah, but simply said, “what was spoken through the prophet.” [Col. 0695C]

We must therefore ask why the prophet commands the daughter of Zion to rejoice greatly and the daughter of Jerusalem to shout aloud because of him who sat upon the donkey and the young colt, when shortly afterward the Lord, seeing Jerusalem, wept and said to it: “If you had known—even you,” that is, you would weep; and elsewhere, with the affection of one lamenting, he said: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets,” and so forth (Matt. 23:37).

In these words, surely, not joy or rejoicing but the lamentation and mourning of the wretched city are proclaimed. Knowing this, the Evangelist preferred to say, “Say to the daughters of Zion,” rather than “Rejoice.” He knew without doubt that, when the message was announced to it and he himself came, Jerusalem would kill the Lord.

Therefore the prophet perhaps does not address his speech to the Jerusalem that crucified the Lord, but to that heavenly Jerusalem which, rejoicing reverently, received the crucified Lord. Of it the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Heb. 12:22). For, according to the same Apostle, “the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. 4:26). All these mysteries of the Savior properly belong to her.

And so, before Christ’s passion, such a great triumph is rightly celebrated for two reasons. One is that Jerusalem below is the slave-woman and serves with her children. Since the time of his passion was approaching, it heard such glory and such praises at his entrance that it thereby aroused still more intensely the rage of their envy against him, because the time of his passion was already at hand, so that they might complete what they had long plotted by many acts of treachery.

On other occasions Jesus had often come to Jerusalem, as I have said, but he never employed the services of beasts, nor did he arrange green branches as ornaments around himself, nor did he stir up the minds of those who gathered with the terrifying praise of his divinity. As we have said, this is reasonably believed to have happened in order that he might release those who were already hostile to his death, so that they could do what they had often wished to do before.

Now that the appointed time had been fulfilled, when it had long been decreed by him that this should happen, they were given the opportunity to act. Their will was not changed, nor were they driven to the crime, except insofar as they themselves were inflamed by their own envy and perverse hatred.

The other reason is that, as he ascended from Jericho to Jerusalem, he went up with such a great triumph—as though with palms of victory and praises—to declare that ascension when, having conquered the world, he would ascend victoriously to that Jerusalem which is above.

Therefore, because Christ’s passion was the triumph of his victory, he ascended to his passion in such a way that, in that very ascent, he foreshadowed by signs everything that would occur after the resurrection, when, already victorious and most glorious, he would ascend to heaven.

Earthly kings, after conquering their enemies, erect triumphs for their victories and rejoice to have their praises celebrated. But Christ, whose victory lies in his own power, who calls things that are not as though they were (Rom. 4:17), before fearlessly undertaking the single combat on behalf of all, wished to fulfill in reality what the prophet Zechariah had foretold long ago, as I have said. He wished his own to recognize that, just as had been foretold, Christ himself—the prophet—would, through the fulfillment of events, commend to all future readers a prophecy of his greater glory and of his more glorious triumph.

Although the prophetic word extends also to that triumph of Christ’s ascension, nevertheless, as the Evangelist understood it, it must also be applied to the things now taking place, so that they may be seen already fulfilled literally, while the things that are to come through Christ may be understood as more deeply prefigured in those same events.

Accordingly, in a marvelous and ineffable way, the event that is taking place embraces both dimensions: it retains the truth of the prophecy already given, and that very truth ultimately possesses the prophecy and figure of future things. Therefore, let us run through the details, if in some way we can understand how divine and mysterious are the things being done. [Col. 0695D]

“When he had drawn near Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage at the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two of his disciples, saying: ‘Go into the village that is opposite you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me.’”

As Jesus was leaving Jericho—that is, as I have said, this world—having led out from it very many crowds and having already restored health to the blind, when he had drawn near Jerusalem, enriched with the great treasures of the salvation of believers, he wished to return and desired to enter the city of peace, the place of the vision of God, the citadel of contemplation.

But first, when he had come to Bethphage, “the house of the jaws,” which was a priestly village and bore the figure of confession, situated on the Mount of Olives—where there is the light of knowledge and the rest of labors and sorrows—he sent two of his disciples from there and commanded that the donkey and the colt, already untied, be brought to him.

For there was that spring which is recorded in the Book of Judges as having flowed most abundantly from the jawbone of a donkey. Hence that place was called “the spring of the jawbone,” from which the very strong Samson drank sufficiently and abundantly. A house was also dedicated there, rightly called “the house of the jawbone,” so that from it a spring of water might flow for everyone, leaping up into eternal life (John 4:14).

Mark likewise records, with even greater significance, that they were sent from Bethany, so that by obeying they might lead to the house of obedience those who would believe and be released from the bonds of sins. This is what Bethany means.

Thus those who have been released from the bonds of their sins and refreshed by the spring of salvation—which now, by God’s favor, flows from the jawbone—are led to the house of obedience. They arrive at the priestly house, which is the house of the jaws, or of endurance, so that Jesus may ascend upon those whom his disciples, according to the command of the Lord and Savior God, have released and brought to him.

The mountain on which these places are situated is the Church of Christ. In it, the faithful who bear fruit can say with the prophet: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Ps. 51:10).

Those who were first brought to Christ through the ministry of the Apostles, possessing the beginnings of faith, were like young olive shoots around Christ’s table, and they became his children. Although all the Apostles were sent to release and bring them, two are introduced in this figure either because of the twofold love that they all preached, or because of the *theoretikē* and *praktikē*—that is, knowledge and works.

He sends them into the village that is opposite them. There is no doubt that this signifies the world, which was unwilling either to accept the yoke of instruction or to submit to the virtues of good works.

But perhaps we may more suitably understand those two disciples first sent by the Lord—although the other interpretation is also plausible—as Peter and Paul, who gave each other the right hand of fellowship, so that Peter would go to the circumcision, to the synagogue, which was called “under the yoke” because it had been subdued under the yoke of the law, while Paul would go to the Gentiles, whom the Septuagint calls “the young colt,” because they had newly come to Christ as untamed creatures. [Col. 0696A]

Both peoples—the people from the Jews and the people from the Gentiles—were still rural and wild with respect to faith. Therefore they were tied in the village by the bonds of sins, and not in the city of Zion or Jerusalem, which is the Church of the living God.

The Apostles, sent to them, release both and bring them to Christ, so that he may ascend upon them in the house of obedience after they have been released from the bonds of sins and received remission of them. For Jesus does not sit upon those who are still tied and shackled by the bonds of their sins.

Do not be surprised, reader, that I also said that the wanton colt was tied by bonds. According to Luke and Mark, it too is introduced as tied, and no human being had ever sat upon it. It is rightly said to have been tied for this reason: those whose figure it bears were bound by demonic ropes, and no human being had sat upon them.

For no prophet, nor any other human being sent to them, had done so. Therefore there was still nothing rational in them, nor any instruction according to the discipline of God’s teaching. Yet they obtained everything freely from God, without their own merits, so that the Word of God might sit upon them—that is, in their hearts—and so that, with him guiding them, as though presiding in his chariot, they might ascend happily, bearing God in their body, to that heavenly Jerusalem.

Nor should you be surprised if the Gentiles are said to come from the Jews, as though the colt came from its mother. For, according to God, Judea is the mother of the Gentiles through faith.

Thus the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah concerning the synagogue of the Jews: “I will appoint your rulers as at the first, and your counselors as at the beginning. And afterward you shall be called the city of righteousness and the mother of cities” (Isa. 1:26)—that is, faithful Zion, the mother of the Churches.

Because of certain similarities, therefore, the Jews and the Gentiles are compared to animals of this kind. Both Jews and Gentiles lived too deeply in the world before Christ’s coming, weighed down by many burdens and bound by chains.

This animal, compared with nearly all other beasts of burden, is irrational, exceedingly brutish and foolish, quite lowly, greatly burden-bearing, and weak. In the same way, almost all human beings were before knowing Christ, even the Jews themselves.

That is why they so often sacrificed in the high places and worshiped idols, forgetting the works of the law and frequently being ignorant of God. It is therefore no wonder if human beings are called beasts of burden, especially since the prophet says to the Lord: “I became like a beast before you” (Ps. 72:23).

For, in relation to God, we are beasts of burden—not only we, but also those who were much more prudent than we are, and especially those who behaved so irrationally in the flesh, living according to the flesh.

This is why, according to Luke, the same colt, impatient of the bridle, had many masters; it was not subject to one error or doctrine alone. Yet, although many masters had long exercised unlawful power over it, when they saw the true Lord and his servants had come—those who had been sent to release it—they did not dare resist, just as the one to whom it belonged did not resist.

Hence the Savior says: “And if anyone says anything to you, say, ‘The Lord has need of them.’” This statement refers more to the mystery than to an invitation.

He says it figuratively, as though they had no other lord, even though certain people were ruling them unlawfully while they were bound by the chains of sins, so that he might show himself to be the one true Lord. Therefore, “immediately he will release them,” because no one could resist his power, although some manuscripts read: “And immediately he will send them back.”

The sense would then be that, after they had come to Christ—because the Lord had need of them—and had been improved through faith and fully imbued with his discipline, and had once again received Christ as their rider upon themselves, they should be sent back to the Jewish people or to the Gentiles who did not yet believe. Returning as believers, they would proclaim the Lord Jesus Christ to them; hence the Lord is said to have had need of them.

But not everyone received the grace of evangelizing. It is therefore better to understand that the Lord had need of them so that they might do the Father’s will by believing and acting, just as he himself says: “My work is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven.”

As for the testimony of the prophet that Matthew added—“This happened so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled”—we have already discussed it. Let us now see how it applies to both ascensions of Christ.

The Lord, intending to ascend to death in Jerusalem, wished long ago to proclaim in advance a great prophecy about this ascent, leaving it to the whole world, as though in a testament of peace and concord. They would see that what had been foretold had already been fulfilled, and that what had been fulfilled and foretold would again, in his ascension, be completed in a more universal way, so that he might judge Jews and Gentiles together worthy of his service.

But because the Jews were going to oppose Christ as he ascended into the temple, the prophecy was proclaimed beforehand. It was then fulfilled in actual events, and it remains for us even today a testimony. What was then fulfilled in the wisdom of God according to his humanity is still being fulfilled today in the mystery of salvation.

Thus the prophet says: “Say to the daughters of Zion: Behold, your King comes to you.” For “behold” is a word of pointing, as if he were saying: “See—not with bodily sight but with spiritual understanding—the works of his virtues, and not the form of a servant.”

What is now being fulfilled was spoken before the ages. The prophet already saw spiritually what had been spoken concerning Christ, although he had not yet been born in the flesh. Therefore he said “behold,” to show that the one of whom he spoke before his birth already existed.

If the wretched Jews had understood this, they would never have asked, “By what authority are you doing these things?” For although the things being done seemed great, the things prefigured in them are greater still.

Therefore, my brothers, we must consider how clear was the vision of the prophets and how far-seeing their judgment: in one and the same event they foresaw so much that they saw both the things that were to be accomplished in detail and the future things that were to be signified through them.

Accordingly, extending his gaze to that ascension into heaven, he added: “And he will destroy the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem; and the war bow will be destroyed, and he will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth.”

Then the prophet turned his speech to the king himself, humble, gentle, and saving: “And you,” he says, “by the blood of the covenant have released the prisoners from the pit in which there is no water.”

I have said this so that the prudent reader may understand that the prophetic word applies to both ascensions. But the whole of that triumph is now celebrated for him in heaven, as though for one already victorious. [Col. 0696B]

It should certainly be asked how, according to the literal sense, the following statement can stand: “The disciples went and did as Jesus commanded them, and they brought the donkey and the colt, and placed their garments upon them, and made him sit upon them.”

Although they placed their garments upon both animals, he certainly could not sit upon both during so short a stretch of the journey, nor does human nature permit this. Either he sat upon the donkey while the colt remained without a rider, or, if he sat upon the colt—which was more untamed and unruly for riding—the donkey was led along free.

Since the historical account therefore contains an impossibility—and even an indecency, if it happened in this way—we must know that the Evangelist directs us toward higher meanings, just as we believe he did above concerning the blind men.

The donkey, which was under the yoke and had been tamed, and which had borne the yoke of the law, is therefore to be understood as the synagogue. The donkey’s colt, wanton and free, is the people of the Gentiles. Upon both the Lord happily sat.

The Apostles found both of them naked and filthy, because they had no covering of salvation and were frozen by the cold of unbelief. Although the Jews seemed to be covered with fig leaves—that is, with the commandments of the harsh law—they were nevertheless naked of grace and disfigured by that nakedness in which Adam saw himself stripped in paradise. For this reason he could not immediately bear himself, but covered himself with fig leaves. Thus the Jews too were still, as it were, naturally in sins.

For this reason Paul says: “We too were by nature children of wrath” (Eph. 2:3), like the others. When people are stripped of grace, the Lord shows that they are naked when he speaks through the prophet Hosea concerning the synagogue: “I will take away my garments and my linens, and I will expose her shame before the nations.”

From this it is plainly evident that the Apostles prophetically placed their garments upon them—that is, the commandments and the grace that they themselves had already received from Christ. They placed them upon Jews and Gentiles when they handed on to them the baptism of salvation, so that they might put on Christ and keep his commandments.

Thus they made the Lord Christ sit upon them—that is, they made him dwell through faith in their hearts. For Christ could not otherwise rest or sit in them unless, after the old nature had been expelled, they were covered with faith and had received his commandments and grace.

Long ago Habakkuk sang of his riding: “You mounted upon your horses, and your riding is salvation.” Jacob too, when he blessed his son Judah, prophesied in a figure of Christ concerning these two animals, saying: “Binding his colt to the vine, and his donkey, O my son, to the vine” (Gen. XXIX, 11).

What Jacob called “the vine,” Christ himself testifies in the Gospel to be himself, when he says: “I am the true vine” (John 15:1). To this vine he bound the vineyard that was brought out of Egypt and transplanted in the East.

Again, to this vineyard he bound his young colt—that is, the Church from the Gentiles—and did what Noah said: “Let Japheth dwell in the tents of Shem.”

All these things were accomplished not by the power of the Apostles but by the word of Christ. Their ministry was to go and say, “The Lord has need of them,” and then to untie them, and afterward to clothe them with garments. The power and authority belonged to Christ.

For they could not have taken beasts belonging to another master, from a lord who did not know who they were, unless the Lord Christ and his Spirit had gone before them in the prophecy of future things and prepared the hearts of their masters to release them.

Accordingly, whatever the Apostles, so few and insignificant, were able to accomplish in the world was entirely the power of Christ and the grace of the Savior God.

## [Column 0703C]

Most of the crowd spread their garments on the road; others were cutting branches from the trees and spreading them on the road. A great multitude, therefore, was going up with Christ to Jerusalem; but far greater was the multitude prefigured through them in the spirit of prophecy. Here, quite appropriately, three orders are introduced. One consists of those who were cutting branches from the trees and preparing a certain beauty for the road along which he was proceeding with the peoples toward Jerusalem. Although they were perfect in faith, holy in virtue, and learned, those of another order were nevertheless more learned, holier, and more perfect: clothed in Christ’s garment, they spread the ornaments of their teaching and the garments of their virtue on the road along which the she-ass and the colt—that is, the congregation of the faithful—were to pass toward that heavenly homeland. They labored so that the animals might walk most cleanly and not encounter rough places.

Yet they do these things so that they do not even touch the earth, or anything dusty belonging to earthly affairs, but so that all the roads of their journey may be level for them and the crooked ways made straight.

## [Column 0703D]

Although those who are moved by that spirit are more perfect and more learned, no one can reach the summit of those who, first at God’s command, both loose them and bring them to Christ, spread the ornaments of their virtues over them, and make him sit upon them.

And because every comparison, even according to secular learning, is made in three degrees, the entire order of the apostles and of those who imitate them is rightly called the most perfect and holiest. In these three orders, by God’s favor, no one is compared with God except one who is good and devoted in faith, so that Christ’s Church may be directed by the straight road toward that heavenly Jerusalem, with Christ himself presiding. Let what we have said about these matters according to our capacity suffice, although others have explained this passage in a very different way.

## [Column 0704A]

They wish the garments and branches from the trees that were thrown onto the road to be understood as the commandments of the Law, together with the figures, diverse forms, and ceremonies of the Jewish religion. All these things, they say, were to be trampled underfoot by Christians on the road—that is, in Christ. For this reason, they spread them beneath the feet of the animals, so that we might understand that Christians are laid beneath the commandments and teachings of the apostles and are urged onward; but the commandments of the Law and its ceremonies are all to be trampled underfoot.

Therefore, not only the commandments and ceremonies, but also all the glory that those who came from the circumcision had derived from the Law, they cast away in order to gain Christ. I leave this interpretation to the reader’s judgment, asking only that he understand the events that took place as a figure of the whole Church and as a prophecy of great things.

## [Column 0704B]

Hence also those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” The crowds who had gone out with him from Jericho and had seen the wonders he displayed to them—the blind receiving sight and Lazarus rising again—were deeply stirred by the miracles and healings he had performed for them. In their exultation they perhaps poured themselves into praises, so that the words might be fulfilled literally which, as we have already recalled, were spoken above through the prophet: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem.” For the people, both those who went before and those who followed, perhaps cried out such things not without great rejoicing of heart.

In these two groups the two peoples are understood: those who believed in Christ before the Gospel and those who believed afterward. They are the ones who both go before and follow. Yet they all say one thing; those who go before do not say one thing and those who follow another, but all cry out together with a harmonious voice.

## [Column 0704C]

While praising Christ’s human dispensation, they also proclaimed his divinity in saying, “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” For he could not have come in the name of the Lord in any other way unless he were God. But because God became man, they wondrously proclaim his restoration in that holy, heavenly Jerusalem, in the words “Hosanna in the highest.”

The crowd takes this verse from Psalm 117, which openly prophesies about Christ and was read very frequently in the synagogues of the Jews; consequently it was more familiar to that people. ## [Column 0704D]

They therefore take up the same verses to show that the one who had been promised there and elsewhere as coming from the family of David has now come to save Israel. David says in the same psalm:

> “The stone which the builders rejected  
> has become the cornerstone.  
> This was done by the Lord,  
> and it is wonderful in our eyes,”  
> and so forth.  
> *(Psalm 117 [118]:22–23.)*

For this reason the writing of the Evangelists also records that the Pharisees and scribes immediately became indignant when they saw that the people understood the prophecy of the psalm to have been fulfilled in Christ, and that the children were crying, “Hosanna to the Son of David.” They said to him, “Do you hear what these people are saying?” Jesus answered them, “Have you never read, ‘From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?”

## [Column 0705A]

As you can see, reader, the assertion that could easily be expressed—“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”—is stated consistently by all the Evangelists. But concerning the word *Hosanna*, since it could not be translated into Greek, just as neither *Alleluia* nor *Amen* can be translated otherwise, they placed the Hebrew word itself, saying *Hosanna*. Luke, who was the most learned among them in the Greek language and wrote his Gospel in Greek, saw that he could not transfer the word’s exact character and therefore, as Jerome testifies, judged it better to remain silent than to introduce something that would cause difficulty for the reader.

For *Hosanna*, as the same author says, is corruptly read as *Osanna* through ignorance, and it means “save,” or “save, I pray,” as is established by the interpretations of all. For *anna* is an interjection among the Hebrews used by one who begs, just as among us *heu* expresses grief, *papae* expresses amazement, and other such words do likewise. Thus among them one says *Anna Adonai*, which our people render “O Lord, save.”

## [Column 0705B]

Accordingly, it is interpreted as “save,” or “save, I pray.” Moreover, as I have said, *anna* is the interjection of one who begs. If you wish to make a compound word from these two elements, you will say *osianna*, or, as common usage now has it, *osanna*, with the middle vowel omitted, as is customary among poets in meter. The Greeks do this very frequently, even in prose.

Therefore, since *anna* belongs to one who begs, we may read this Hebrew verse in the following sense: “I beg you, Lord, save me”; “I beg you, Lord, grant prosperity.” For among them the interjection is repeated: *Anna Adonai, anna Adonai*, just as we say “O Lord” among ourselves.

## [Column 0705C]

When it says “save,” the meaning is that we should understand “your people Israel,” or, more generally, the world. But since our manuscripts have *Hosanna to the Son of David*, some have thought that, according to this interpretation, it would be more Latin to say *Hosanna, Son of David*, with *Son* in the vocative case. The sense would then be: “I beg you, Lord, Son of David, save me.” Several have already dared to correct their manuscripts in this way.

Yet this does not without reason appear rash, since both the Greek manuscripts and the Latin ones—at least all those that I have been able to inspect—have the dative case. Matthew too, who wrote this Gospel in the Hebrew language, placed this word at the end as *Hosanna rania*, which means, “Say again: salvation in the highest.” The reason is that, when the Savior was born, salvation reached as far as heaven, even to the heights,

## [Column 0705D]

peace having been made not only on earth but also in heaven, so that the saying might at last cease: “My sword has become drunk in heaven.”

Thus, when the crowds first say, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” they repeat the same words with rejoicing voices: “Hosanna in the highest.” If the matter is examined correctly, *Hosanna to the Son of David* seems to sound better than *Hosanna, Son of David* in the vocative case.

Nor should we think, as some have supposed, that the word *Hosanna* is composed from two words, one Greek and one Hebrew. Rather, it is entirely Hebrew and exceedingly obscure. Anyone who reads the letter of blessed Jerome sent to Pope Damasus will be able to notice this, together with many other matters that we omit for the sake of brevity.

## [Column 0706A]

When he had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred, saying, “Who is this?” As Jesus entered with the crowds and their praises, it was not without reason that the city of Jerusalem was stirred by such unusual cries, astonished at so great a multitude of people and at the unheard-of restraint of his procession. Not knowing the truth of the matter or the mysteries of salvation, they say, “Who is he?”

As we have already said briefly above, because all these events take place through parabolic mysteries, they marvel and the whole city is stirred, just as we read that the heavenly Jerusalem also did when Christ ascended, while the angels said: “Who is this King of glory?” *(Psalm 23 [24]:8.)*

The powers of heaven and the angels—who are the true city of Jerusalem—marvel and ask this because of the new clothing of his body.

## [Column 0706B]

When it was said to them, “Lift up your gates, princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” *(ibid., 10)*, they rightly say, as though struck with amazement: “Who is this King of glory?”

So also in Isaiah: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments stained from Bosor? This one is beautiful in his robe, walking” *(Isaiah 63:1–2).* I repeat these things for this reason: to show that the mysteries of future events are contained in what is being done and said.

Thus, as he ascends into Jerusalem, it is said, “Who is this?” because the whole city is stirred. Through the effects of these deeds, the form of future things is fashioned and divinity is proclaimed. All the beauty that the Jewish people possessed, so to speak, was adorned by the teachings of the patriarchs and prophets.

## [Column 0706C]

And lest they stumble against the stone of stumbling, the road was laid and leveled by the commandments of the precepts. Then the Gentile people, through the apostles’ labors, were made subject to God and imbued with divine instruction. Through their service, the branches cut from the trees are spread in order along the entrance to the heavenly road, to such an extent that they also most devotedly lay down the coverings of their bodies in death, so that Christ’s Church may proceed securely and without stumbling, carrying God within herself.

Otherwise, if these things were not mystical, what benefit would there be in such reverence? It could impede rather than help. For this reason, as I said, the whole account is shaped by prophecy of the future.

Therefore even when questioned, the lowly common people answer with a confession, beginning with lesser things so as to reach greater ones, and say:

## [Column 0706D]

> “This is Jesus the prophet from Nazareth of Galilee.”

In saying, “This is Jesus the prophet,” they imply that he is something greater than a prophet. For this reason, among the Greeks the phrase is written with the article, just as we place *this*—not an adverb of place but a demonstrative pronoun—so that he may be understood to be the one whom Moses said would come, like himself.

“From Nazareth of Galilee” is said because he had been brought up there, so that he might be nourished like a flower of the field in the flowering of virtues.

I therefore do not think that those who followed him with such praises and unfolded such divine matters in their words did not know what they were saying, as some maintain, or whom they were praising. They so clearly demonstrate him as the prophet promised in the Law. Although the others were stirred with indignation, these people do not remain silent.

## [Column 0707A]

For this reason the others were increasingly disturbed when they heard the astonishing thing: that a man was being praised by the crowds and that God was being proclaimed in a man. It might have happened that the Holy Spirit suddenly breathed upon them, without their understanding in their minds the words of truth that they uttered. But it should not be believed that the Holy Spirit so breathed within all those who went before and followed that they failed to understand what they were saying or know what they were doing. Some of the Greeks have wished to say the same both about these people and about the prophets.

Certainly, these people were speaking in their own language, and, on the authority of the psalm—as I said, a psalm in which many things are said about Christ—they were singing that passage. Above all, they chose the verse in which his coming to them is proclaimed and his divinity and humanity are shown together in one person.

## [Column 0707B]

And, so that the meaning might be clearer, inspired by God and as though adding something of their own, they added, according to Mark: “Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that comes,” and they repeated, “Hosanna in the highest.”

When questioned, they faithfully continued and proclaimed that he was the Savior and the prophet from Nazareth. How, then, could it be that they did not know what future things their actions were prefiguring?

This should not be believed, especially since all the apostles and many other disciples who had already believed were accompanying him. Nor should we suppose that the women who had come with him from Galilee failed to understand. The crowd, which had witnessed so many miracles, was doing all these things for no other reason than to praise and glorify the one whom they celebrated with such wondrous praises in a harmonious voice.

I do not say that they did these things without the Holy Spirit. Rather, what they did, they did under divine inspiration, devoutly and with proper reverence, in return for all that they had seen or heard him accomplish so gloriously.

## [Column 0707C]

For this reason Christ’s Church fittingly celebrates these same events each year before the feast of Easter, both in memory of what happened and as an example. Each person carries green branches of trees, with palms and flowers, in his hands, as though they were the victorious standards of Christ, rejoicing worthily to glorify the triumph of his Passion and to proclaim his most wondrous entry, with victorious palms, into that heavenly Jerusalem.

The text continues:

## [Column 0707D]

And Jesus entered the temple of God and was casting out all those who were selling and buying in the temple. He overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves.

First, we should marvel at the event itself, since it surpasses human nature. According to what he appeared to be—the poor son of a carpenter and of Mary, a poor woman—he nevertheless used such confidence and such power in casting everyone who was selling and buying out of the temple, which shone forth as the most august and most revered place in the whole world.

For perhaps not even the ruler of any nation, using whatever power he possessed, could easily have accomplished what Jesus did. And, as I remember having said above, unless something divine had shone forth in his face when these things were being done, something that would strike his adversaries, I could never say that he was able to do this by human strength, when I do not know how many thousands of priests, Levites, and other people had gathered there for the feast.

## [Column 0708A]

Therefore I openly confess that, given the smallness of my understanding, I cannot—not merely explain in words, but even adequately marvel at—the things woven together in this discourse and the deeds that are narrated, while wondrous events follow wondrous actions.

For I cannot express how, in one and the same Christ, divine miracles shine forth and cooperate with human actions in the one person of Christ; and how the things belonging to his humanity lift themselves up and are joined to divine things, so that the divine things do not occur without Christ’s humanity, nor does his humanity accomplish anything without his divinity.

This twofold operation is joined together in one Christ in such a way that the whole matter may be understood: what we ought to attribute to God and what to man. ## [Column 0708B]
