From the beginning of the Gospel, sentences are joined to sentences and miracles to miracles in such a way that, according to Ezekiel, they are full of eyes within and without, and do not allow the reader to breathe until the things of God and the things of man are joined together in the one and same Christ.

Therefore, although what is now being done in the temple appears to have been done according to his humanity, because it is wondrous it is nevertheless proved to be divine. The very things that God, then appearing as man, accomplished, he now performs divinely in a general sense every day.

Let us first examine literally what he overturned, whom he cast out, and from where he cast them out: from the temple itself. For the whole religion of the temple had been gravely violated through the greed of the priests. Oxen, sheep, and the other things offered in divine sacrifices were being brought into the temple for sale, as John indicates more fully, ## [Column 0708C]

so that nothing seemed to be there except a marketplace and a forum for merchants.

When he had entered there first and seen everything, as Mark relates—“having looked around at everything” *(Mark 11:11)*—he did not act rashly. When evening had already come, he went out to Bethany. Returning in the morning and entering the temple, he began to cast out, with a whip made of cords, all those who were selling and buying.

At that time the people had flowed together there from nearly every region of the Jews, and innumerable victims were being sacrificed, especially on feast days: bulls, rams, goats, and the other animals that were called clean in the Law.

The greed of the priests had therefore arranged that all these things should be available for sale in the temple, so that no one would lack anything to offer and so that none of the poor would be without a sacrifice on that day. ## [Column 0708D]

Young pigeons, turtledoves, sparrows, and the other birds offered in sacrifice were also sold.

For it often happened that those who came from far away did not have victims. Therefore they devised a way to make a profit from the people, and everything necessary for the sacrifices was sold, so that they could receive the price of the goods and then take back for themselves what they had purchased.

Their cunning was often frustrated by the poverty of certain people, who not only had no victims but did not even have the means to buy birds or inexpensive offerings. For this reason they also placed money-changers there, who would lend money under security to those who had none.

And, as Jerome testifies—

## [Column 0709A]

having lived among them, he had learned their practices thoroughly—because the Law commanded that no one among them should take interest, the money lent at interest could bring them little profit, since it yielded no advantage and sometimes even involved the loss of the principal. They therefore devised, as he says, another scheme: they made *collybistae* serve in place of money-changers, a word whose precise meaning, he says, cannot be expressed in Latin.

But what they call *collyba*, he says, we call *tragemata*, or inexpensive gifts: for example, fried chickpeas, raisins, and various kinds of fruit. Since the *collybistae* who had lent money could not receive interest, they accepted various commodities as interest, so that what they were not permitted to exact in money they might demand in goods purchased with money—as though Ezekiel had not proclaimed precisely this when he said: “You shall not take interest

## [Column 0709B]

or increase” *(Ezekiel 18:17).*

Would that we also did not know such things to be happening in this Church of Christ.

Seeing such commerce in his Father’s house, the Lord could not tolerate it. The house was also his own, as the present Evangelist testifies that the Lord said, according to what is written: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” *(Mark 11:17).* John says that he said: “Do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce” *(John 2:16).* No one should doubt, therefore, that the Lord said both things, since everything belonging to his Father is his, and therefore his Father’s house is his own.

“But you,” he says, “have made it a den of thieves.” A thief is one who turns the temple of God into a den by plundering it, one who pursues profit through religion, ## [Column 0709C]

so that his worship is not so much the worship of God as an opportunity for commerce.

This is enough to say according to the historical sense. But all these things were done mystically, because what he then did visibly he always does in the Church, which is truly the house of God. For he casts out from it every day those who sell and buy, especially those who consider gain to be godliness and regard everything done in ecclesiastical affairs as merchandise, although it has been commanded: “You received without payment; give without payment” *(Matthew 10:8).*

Otherwise, it is a matter of grave danger that, because of the greed of priests, the altars of God should be called the tables of money-changers and the temple of God should become a den of thieves. For those who sell the gifts that belong to Christ sell the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Clergy and ministers of the altar were not appointed for this purpose: to serve, as though on behalf of religion, the commerce

## [Column 0709D]

and profits of the world, and to conduct buying and selling as though it were God’s cause. Such things do not suit those for whom they are inappropriate, nor should they take place in a setting where they do not belong—especially where they ought to devote themselves only to prayer.

We have spoken of this temple built for God from material things, in which no one ought to sell, buy, or do anything unbecoming. How much more, then, should we reflect upon the temple of God constructed from living stones, of which the Apostle says: “You are the temple of the living God” *(2 Corinthians 6:16),* because the Holy Spirit dwells in you.

Therefore, whoever is the temple of the Holy Spirit should take care not to return to the marketplace from which he was called and placed in the vineyard. The soul of a Christian ought not to be a den of thieves or

## [Column 0710A]

engage in commerce for the sake of profit, since such activity is scarcely ever, or perhaps never, undertaken without sin.

Much more, then, must God’s servants and clergy devoted to divine offices beware of doing this in the house of God, acquiring riches and many possessions for themselves, lest the Church in which they live become, under their rule, a den of thieves, with themselves already transformed into merchants.

As for the sale of doves, the holy Fathers have discussed it sufficiently and abundantly in many places, especially against the simoniacal heresy, which has often been opposed in Gaul but never conquered. For thieves have become both those who buy what properly belongs to the Church and those who sell it.

Although this heresy could be condemned, it has not yet been conquered for this reason: just as a thief is called a *latro* from *latere*, “to hide,” so these people very often act secretly—or act so boldly, though shamelessly, that no one dares oppose them.

## [Column 0710B] What has happened today, to speak frankly, is felt and lamented throughout Gaul.

And rightly so, because Jesus did not weep over that wretched Jerusalem without cause or without reason. How much more reasonable it seems, then, that Christ should grieve in his Church over such people, making those who grieve and groan on their behalf.

For this reason, according to their own will, they entrust the Churches of Christ to some people whose concern is not the things of Jesus Christ but their own interests—people who seek shameful profits and luxury. I do not say that those who at this time occupy the seats of the Churches sell doves. Rather, Churches are entrusted to people to whom they ought not to be entrusted, not for the profit of souls but for luxury and personal desires.

## [Column 0710C]

Here, I think, we must take the greatest care lest it be counted as selling doves when they hand over Churches consecrated to the Lord Christ to disgraceful and greedy men—tyrannically, to those who ought not to receive them, to the undisciplined and irreligious.

For this reason the Evangelist says only that Jesus overturned the seats and the tables of the money-changers. Would that those who glory in such things would hear this—those who sell Churches, which we rightly call doves, and entrust them not to shepherds but to hirelings and plunderers. For their sake it is now more fitting to weep than to explain evils that are already exposed.

Although Jesus is now believed to be silent, a time will come when he will inspect his Church and examine everyone, as he is also read to have done then; and he will cast out or overturn those whom he finds not worthily seated in the place of governance.

## [Column 0710D]

And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.

Behold: miracles follow mystical matters and deeds, so that in the one and same temple he might show what he himself does in his Church throughout all time. First he did things new and previously unheard of, and then wonders familiar to him, so that by the one the reprobate might be terrified, while by the other the sick might be restored. For although he is just in chastisement, he is kind and merciful in assistance.

There are indeed blind and lame people in the Church. Therefore he acts with his customary compassion to make himself known as God: without his grace no one sees the light, and without his guidance no one walks on the road except as a lame person.

There are three things that he condemns and two that he presently restores:

## [Column 0711A] the blind, so that they may see the light, and the lame, so that they may walk happily with straight steps toward their homeland along the road that he himself is.

But those who not only return to the marketplace but also, as though they were still in the marketplace, sell and buy within Christ’s Church, pursuing markets and shameful profits—these he casts outside, scourged with the cords of their sins.

For this reason he appears to have made a whip specifically from cords or ropes: each person is rightly scourged and cast out by the cords of his own sins, by which he is bound.

Then he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves, because where the bread of the Presence had previously been offered to God, tables were set up for nothing other than the pursuit of shameful profits. The seats of teachers, from which the Law and teaching ought to have flowed freely,

## [Column 0711B]

are utterly overturned because they pursued commercial gain, although they ought to give Christ’s free gifts freely.

But because the blind profaned everything and had taken away the key of knowledge, so that neither they themselves might enter the holy places nor others be able to enter, how mercifully such people are overthrown, so that others who are blind in the temple may be able to receive light from their corruption.

Otherwise, if Jesus had not overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves, the blind and the lame would not have deserved to receive their former light and active steps.

The Evangelist mentioned doves alone in this passage, when speaking of the overturning of the priests’ seats, for this reason: so that no one might receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit in vain; lest, God forbid, if he attempted to sell or buy them, he should receive, together with Simon, the sentence of condemnation—condemned as a heretic rather than recognized as a teacher.

## [Column 0711C]

When the chief priests and scribes saw the wonders he had performed, and the children crying in the temple, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” they became indignant and said to him, “Do you hear what these people are saying?”

What astonishing blindness in the Pharisees, and what excessive hardness of heart! The crowds proclaim him Lord with their words, while Christ demonstrates himself by his deeds. He himself becomes their witness when he heals the blind so that they may see and the lame so that they may walk, so that those who were themselves blind and lame—the leaders—might direct their steps toward the Lord and be enlightened by the miracles. Yet they become indignant at the very means by which they ought to have been healed and grow worse.

They had not seen only these things, but also greater and countless others. They had recently seen Lazarus, who had been dead for four days, rise again; and perhaps he was then present as a witness. For this reason, as the Evangelist testifies, they already wished

## [Column 0711D]

to kill him. They had also seen the man blind from his mother’s womb receive sight.

If we go back to still greater things, they had heard the Father’s voice thunder from heaven over him in the Jordan: “This is my beloved Son” *(Matthew 17:5).* These things are great, as are the countless others that he performed.

Yet, as I said a little above, among all the signs he performed, this seems to me the more wondrous: that one man—at that time lowly among them, contemptible and despised, so lowly that he seemed worthy of the cross and was afterward crucified—could, while the scribes and Pharisees raged against him, especially because they saw their profits being destroyed, drive out so great a multitude with the blows of a single whip, overturn their tables

## [Column 0712A]

in the temple, throw down and shatter their seats, and do things that an immeasurable army could not have done.

Therefore, as I said above, something fiery and star-like must have radiated from his eyes, and the majesty of divinity shone forth in his face, as our predecessors have said.

Because they did not dare lay hands on him—the time had not yet come—they nevertheless attacked his deeds and challenged the testimony of the people, whose cries rang out loudly and without interruption from the descent of the Mount of Olives all the way to the temple and within the temple.

They turn these praises into an accusation because they understand that “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” cannot properly be said to anyone except the Son of God. Therefore they say to him, “Do you hear what these people are saying?” ## [Column 0712B]

As though they were saying: “Since you are a man, the son of a carpenter, why do you permit them to acclaim you with divine praises? Why do you not rebuke them and make them keep silent?”

Jesus answers them, “Certainly.” He means: “Certainly I hear and confirm through my miracles what they proclaim with their voices.”

And he added: “Have you never read, ‘From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?”

His answer is wondrous, as it is in everything, and prudent. He did not say what the scribes wished to hear: “The children are doing well by bearing witness to me.” Nor did he say: “They are mistaken because they are children and foolish, and therefore you ought to forgive them.” Instead, he brings forward an example from Psalm 8 with such moderation that his statement can suit both sides without exposing the speaker to accusation.

## [Column 0712C]

Thus, by divine authority, he silences those lying in wait for him, and, through the testimony of the Scriptures, while he himself remains silent, he confirms the words of the children or of the people, because what they were saying had long before been foretold in the Holy Spirit.

They too, inspired at that time by the same Spirit, could not remain silent lest they fail to cry out. God himself perfects his praise in such things. Giving thanks to the Father for them, the Son said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to infants” *(Matthew 11:25).*

He does not mean that those who were crying out were infants and nursing children in age, since it was said shortly before that “the crowds who went before and those who followed were crying out.” We understand, therefore, that they were called infants not because of their age but because of the simplicity of their hearts.

Otherwise, infants can neither understand anyone nor praise anyone. But they are rightly called infants and nursing children because, as though stirred in their minds by the sweetness

## [Column 0712D]

of milk, they cried out, kindled inwardly by delight in God’s miracles.

The work of Christ’s miracles is therefore rightly called milk, because unbelievers and those still little in faith need it in order to believe and be strengthened. Teaching, however, like solid food, belongs to the mature; and these people are shown not yet to have reached that state.

See how the accusation of those who blamed Jesus for not silencing the cries is suppressed by the authority of Scripture—as though he were saying: “Even if it is my fault that these people are crying out, is it my fault that the prophet foretold this would happen so many thousands of years ago?”

Perhaps there were people in that crowd who would later cry out, “Crucify him, crucify him!” *(John 19:6.)* ## [Column 0713A]

But once stirred by the miracles, as I said, they could not remain silent about what was being done in the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, according to the Evangelist, the Savior added another saying: “If these people were silent, the stones would cry out” *(Luke 19:40).*

It is therefore no wonder that these people, moved by the miracles, sing the Lord’s praises, even though they themselves may be harder than rocks, when stones themselves, contrary to their nature, answer—stones that are also said to have been split during his Passion.

For every creature, even if it is without sensation, perceives its Creator and is subject to his commands, when the divine order exercises its dominion.

The text continues:

And leaving them, he went out to Bethany, a place outside the city, and stayed there. When morning came, as he was returning to the city, he was hungry. Seeing one fig tree beside the road, he went to it and found nothing on it except leaves [Col. 0713B]. He said to it: “May no fruit ever come from you again.”

Events follow upon events, and miracles upon miracles. The evangelists do not all relate everything in the same place, lest they seem merely to be weaving together the Savior’s history. Rather, they arrange everything in turn, so that each adorns his own account, and each one externally embellishes and reshapes in his narrative what he inwardly perceives to fit together wonderfully in the mystery. Thus, even if he appears to be a learned and discerning teacher, no one knows what he ought first to admire: what one of them places in sequence, or what another changes, while divine providence nevertheless weaves their accounts together in such a way that each tells the truth, differing in nothing from the others. In their meanings, figures, and events, each places more beautiful things—as though setting precious stones into a structure—and constructs the mysteries of what happened with greater ornament [Col. 0713C].

Accordingly, in this passage Mark says that what happened concerning the fig tree occurred in the morning of the second day, according to the order of his narrative, and then repeats on the third day that it had withered; he also adds that it was not yet the season for figs. Matthew, however, relates everything together on the third day, when the disciples marveled that it had suddenly withered. For, as the Gospel makes clear, on each night he left them, went out with his companions from Jerusalem, and stayed in Bethany—that is, in the house of obedience—with Lazarus and his sisters, since their village was Bethany.

Even then he was prefiguring the calling of the Gentiles, because he could not remain in Jerusalem, as has already been shown by many indications. For this fig tree signifies nothing other than the barrenness of the Jews. Otherwise, what does Christ’s immense power and wisdom mean by his coming hungry to the fig tree and seeking fruit on it, when the evangelist says that it was not the season for figs? Could he who knew everything, even hidden things before they occurred, have been ignorant of what was plain to everyone? Or how can he rightly be believed to have been hungry when it is said to have been morning? It is therefore clear—as I recall having said very often—that everything he did, although marvelous so that faith might be strengthened, is full of mysteries, and full of things meant for the inward and outward eye.

Accordingly, when the darkness of night had been dispelled, the morning light was already shining, and midday was drawing near—the hour in which the Lord was to illuminate the world through his passion or resurrection—when he was returning to the city, he was hungry. He was either displaying the reality of human flesh, or, as must rather be acknowledged, he was hungry for the salvation of believers and burning with zeal against the unbelief of Israel, in which he could not remain.

Their unbelief was indeed astonishing: in that great city, during those days, he found no host and no lodging. When he saw one tree, by which the Synagogue of the Jews could be understood, as though by a divine utterance, and all their assemblies beside the road—for they were not on the way, which is Christ, but beside the way of the Law, beside which they seemed green yet fruitless—he came hungry for salvation to the Synagogue and found it barren, without fruit, clothed only in leaves: that is, boasting in empty words and devoid of fruit, sterile in good works [Col. 0714B]. And because the time for repentance had passed for it, the sentence of the heavenly Judge remains forever, as we ourselves see, with it withered as a testimony.

I do not know whether anything can be found that more clearly commends the person of the Synagogue through the image of trees than if it may reasonably be compared with this one. For this tree is said to flourish very differently from other trees, both by nature and by its condition. Its first flower is itself a fruit; but not all the fruits that first emerge reach maturity. These are called *grossi*—the common term in use—and are also attested by prophetic authority. Later, as we see, when the power of its inner fertility overflows, fruits again burst forth in the same appearance and form. As these emerge, the earlier ones are pushed out; when the tails by which they were held are loosened, they fall, while the others continue onward until they reach maturity [Col. 0714C].

It also often happens that some of those earlier fruits remain permanently and do not fall like the other *grossi*. They simply cling to the tree, being fruits that come to maturity before the rest. That tree also produces from itself these very beautiful fruits, which, emerging together with the other *grossi*, are brought forth from the middle of the two little branches.

Therefore, from the condition of this tree, the Lord proposed a likeness to the Synagogue that is both appropriate and exceedingly fitting. The Synagogue lost the first fruits of the people that it had produced from its beginning, as in the case of the *grossi*. For the faithful people arising from the Gentiles, steadfast in the greenness of faith and remaining in the faith of the patriarchs until the consummation of the ages, displaced its useless populace.

Then the first believers from Israel—the apostles—clinging between the Law and the Gospels in the manner of the *grossi*, would precede the others in the glory and time of the resurrection. Indeed, at the beginning of Genesis, as a figure of this matter, Adam and Eve covered their shame with the leaves of this tree when they hid themselves from the advent of the Lord who was calling them.

For the unbelieving Synagogue, transgressing the commandments of the Law, was to cover the filth of its shamelessness and the confusion of its disgrace with the fruitless coverings of words, like fig leaves. But the merciful Lord, returning to it in the morning, was hungry—not as a human being, but as God—for their salvation; not as though he needed our righteousness or faith, but as the merciful one desiring from us the fruit of good works [Col. 0715A]. If he had been hungry as a human being, he would never have hungered for human food. But he was hungry in the morning because he has always hungered for our righteousness and for the salvation of the Jews.

For at the first morning he hungered for their righteousness and the work of goodness, when, so many thousands of years ago, he went out to hire laborers for his vineyard. And because one who bore the fruit of faith was rare, after the night of unbelief he again went out in the morning to Noah, then also to Abraham, and to the others about whom we have already spoken above. Each of these ages of the world had its own evening and its own morning; in each period he came to them, hungering for their righteousness.

But because they accumulated their iniquities more and more, Christ withdrew far from them like light from night. Yet because the Sun of righteousness returned again and again through the successive ages, he brought them a new morning, until he himself, having become human, came to them as if at the eleventh hour. When morning came, he found no fruit in them [Col. 0715B].

And therefore, because they had been fruitless throughout so many ages while occupying the land, he said prophetically to the tree what was to occur among the Jewish people: “May no fruit ever come from you again.” He did not curse the tree and thereby cause the Synagogue not to bear fruit; rather, because it did not bear fruit, he cursed it so that it would not even produce leaves.

The Jews did not lose the righteousness of faith because God abandoned them; rather, God abandoned them because they were not bringing forth righteousness, so that not even the outward appearance of piety or its speech remained in them. For truly, just as it is better that a tree should not exist than that it should stand in a garden of delights and bear no fruit, so it is better that a person should not be a man of God than that he should be one who never bears fruit or undergoes conversion according to God [Col. 0715C].

And the fig tree immediately withered. When the disciples saw it, they marveled at how quickly it had withered. They marveled because his word descended to its roots more quickly than flame, since the word of Jesus is sharper than any two-edged sword (Hebrews 4:12) and stronger than the axe laid at the roots of the trees.

This happened figuratively with reference to the Synagogue, because he found nothing in it except leaves: namely, the Pharisaic traditions, the promises of the Law, the noise of boastfulness, and the adornments of words. He said to it: “May no fruit ever come from you again.” These are therefore not frivolous words issuing from an outburst of bile, but the severity of judgment and a sentence long suspended, full of equity.

Moreover, when he says “forever,” it is as though he said “for the age”; both expressions are signified in Greek by **εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα**. He speaks concerning the reprobate—those who refused to receive the faith of Christ—from whom no fruit will arise in this age until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and then Israel will be saved. Or, because Christ is eternal, those who are found outside him as reprobate and barren will bring forth no fruit in Christ.

Therefore, whoever remains in that Synagogue which degenerated from the vine and produced thorns will never have from it the fruit of righteousness. Its branches and leaves withered in such a way that the trunk itself remained, as the Apostle says: because its branches were broken and withered, you are grafted into the root of greenness [Col. 0716A]. From that root, even if they themselves should refuse to believe, shoots of faith will at least sprout in the final age, and Scripture will be fulfilled which says: “There is hope for a tree: it must sprout again at the scent of water.”

In the literal sense, however, the Lord, who was soon to suffer and to bear the scandal of the cross, ought to strengthen and instruct the minds of the disciples by many indications and to make them firm through anticipatory signs. Hence they themselves marvel, saying: “How did it wither immediately?” Through this miracle they may perhaps have understood that the Synagogue had been rejected by the Lord. From this they could also have reflected that by the same power he might have withered and destroyed his enemies, had he not awaited their salvation through patience, giving them time for repentance [Col. 0716B].

Behold, in Lazarus he showed them that he possesses the power to give life; behold, in the fig tree, that he also possesses the power to kill. But how mercifully the destruction is postponed is shown by this very example: a tree, not a human being, is condemned, so that a rational human being may be instructed by the event itself. For this reason the tree’s withering is hastened, while the penalty of death is delayed for the Jews.

Jesus answered and said to them: “Amen I say to you, if you have faith and do not hesitate, you will do not only what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Take yourself up and throw yourself into the sea,’ it will happen.”

Although, then, such things are not recorded as having been literally done by the apostles, as certain pagans have slanderously claimed and chatter against us—asserting in their own writings that the apostles did not have faith because they did not move mountains or dry up fig trees by a word—our predecessors have already answered that, according to the Gospel of John, the Lord performed many signs which, if they had all been written down, the world could not contain. This does not mean that the world could not contain the volumes, since even a single small bookcase could contain them, however numerous they might be; rather, it means that the world could not bear the greatness of the signs, in view of the miracles and the unbelief of the impious.

We therefore believe that the apostles literally did these things, or even greater ones. But they were not written down so that unbelievers would not be given a greater opportunity to contradict them. Otherwise, they should be asked whether they believe the signs that are recorded or not. When we see them to be unbelievers, we shall consequently prove that they would not have believed greater things either, since they do not believe lesser ones [Col. 0716C].

As for the fig tree toward which this sign is directed—that is, the Synagogue—the faithful disciples of Christ themselves indicate how it withered, without hesitation, when they say to it: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). Leaving it dry, they transferred from it the greenness of grace and the life-giving power.

This is what the apostles had understood in that fig tree, and this they accomplished in faith, without hesitation: that they would wither, as we see, while the Gentiles would receive the grace of the Holy Spirit, as we rejoice.

But concerning what they did to the fig tree, he promises them something else as well: “If you have faith,” he says, “without hesitating at all, and say to this mountain”—because it was visible from Christ himself and manifest, and therefore was pointed out as though with a finger—“Take yourself up.”

When it is removed from the hearts of believers and cast outward into the sea, a greater and more beneficial power for human beings is demonstrated than if they had made mountains fly. Accordingly, this mountain of which he speaks may rightly be understood as the opposing power, which exalts itself even against God.

The apostles said to it by their word: “Take yourself away from here, from the hearts of believers.” And Satan—that is, that height of total wickedness—was sent into the sea, that is, into the abyss, the place of Gehenna.

Concerning this sea it is said in the Psalm: “This sea is great and spacious; there ships will pass through; there are the small animals with the great, and the dragon which was formed to play in it” (Psalm 103:25–27). And elsewhere: “You crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters, and gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Psalm 73:14).

This is the one whom the prophet calls a corrupted mountain, because he is always proud and raises himself against his Maker. When he is commanded by the apostles, or by holy believers, to leave the hearts of believers and go into the sea, where the storm always rages, this is indeed accomplished: he is transferred to places most salty and turbulent, always bitter, which possess none of the sweetness of God.

Concerning these mountains, in the person of the apostles or of other believers, it is read in the Psalm: “We will not fear when the earth is troubled and the mountains are transferred into the heart of the sea” (Psalm 43:3).

Some wish to understand this as spoken of Christ, raised on the summit of all mountains, upon whom a city built cannot remain hidden. This mountain, when the fig tree had withered, the apostles transferred from the Jews and sent and established in the heart of the sea—that is, they planted and transferred Christ by faith into the hearts of the Gentiles, when through their word he came from the Jews to the Gentiles [Col. 0717C].

“And everything whatever you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive.”

A great grace of faith is revealed here: a great gift and a great mystery. Yet great things are shown in what is small, and only the great can receive them—those whom faith, which works through love, makes great. For not everything is immediately perfect, complete, or strong as soon as it begins. Otherwise, if nature produced nothing unworthy and all virtues were immediately given in perfection, piety would certainly be abolished and the pursuits of religion would cease [Col. 0717D].

Therefore faith must be sought and cultivated, and charity must be nourished. There is a small faith, and there is also a great faith that hesitates at nothing, especially since Truth himself declared that nothing would be denied to those who ask and desire piously, saying: “If two or three of you agree on earth concerning any matter whatever that you ask of my Father, it will be done for you” (Matthew 18:19).

Every Christian must therefore reflect so that his faith may be complete—not just any faith, but that by which God wholly dwells inwardly in the mind, and through which all things are possible for the one who rightly asks.

There is no Christian who does not profess to have faith, but few possess faith of such a kind and such magnitude—so instructed and so full of hope and charity—that they first ask well, then already attain by certain hope what they ask for, and already possess through charity what they continue to seek, since they have the whole of God within themselves, the God whom they ask—not outside themselves, but within, where the devout person approaches him confidently according to God, so that by persevering he may at length receive what he asks from God in a manner worthy of God.

When he had entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people approached him as he was teaching and said: “By what authority are you doing these things? And who gave you this authority?”

These things were said on the third day, when, according to Mark, the disciples also marveled at the withering of the fig tree. They approached then, not in the disposition of believing, but bodily in order to test him.

It is unclear what authority they are asking about, since there is no authority except from God. Do they mean the authority of Caesar, of the governor, or of the priests? Or perhaps they were asking whether he wished to say that he acted by the authority of some prophecy, although elsewhere they accused him of performing these things not by the authority of another but by Beelzebub, the prince of demons [Col. 0718B].

There were many things he had done, and they were great and divine: he had raised Lazarus, illuminated the blind, entered the temple amid such great praises, overturned the tables and the seats of the teachers, healed the blind and the lame again in the temple, and withered the fig tree by a word. Yet, despite such deeds and such greatness, they ask: “Who gave you this authority?”

From this it is most plainly evident that they deny him to be the Son of God, since they think that he performs these things not by his own power but by another’s.

Although I have said that it is uncertain what authority they are asking about, their question seems to sound as though they understood only two authorities: one, God’s, who can do such things; the other, the devil’s, to whom they attributed these deeds. But it is wholly unfitting that he should perform such signs.

Blinded by their own depravity, they ask for no other reason than to deny that these things are from God and to bring an accusation against him in his reply. But the Lord did not answer what they had asked. Instead, answering their two questions with one, he said to them:

“I too will ask you one question. If you answer me, I also will tell you by what authority I do these things. The baptism of John—where was it from: from heaven or from human beings?”

The Savior therefore did what is commonly said: a bad nail or a hard wedge must be driven into a bad knot. He set two questions against two, so that whatever they said, they would be caught by their own answer. They could not ensnare Christ if he said that he acted only by God’s authority, since no believer doubts that this is true.

On the other hand, they could not say that he acted by the devil’s authority. Even the man of sin himself, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped, would not answer what was true, since he will perform all the signs and wonders by which he may deceive God’s elect.

If even he would not say this, how much less would the Lord and Savior give any other answer, if he wished to answer, than that he acted by God’s authority?

Therefore, in the face of so obvious an argument, their question seems sufficiently clear—unless someone wishes to say that the chief priests and elders of the people were asking this not merely from the disposition of questioners, but by the cunning of threatening or intimidating, as we often speak to our own people when we disapprove of what someone is doing.

We say to such a person: “Who ordered you to do this?” We do not want to hear an answer, but wish to frighten him, so that, knowing that no one ordered him, he will desist from the action.

Perhaps these people likewise questioned the Lord, not to learn, but to frighten him as a human being, so that he would no longer teach so publicly in the temple or anywhere else, nor perform such things again.

But if this question is to be understood in the way some wish, it seems to me that he would never have answered them in this manner if they had wished to tell the truth and receive an answer from him. Rather, we must hold to what I said above: that, according to the traditions of their own people, they recognized two general authorities—one belonging to God and the other belonging to the devil [Col. 0719B].

Within and from these two sides they distinguished many particular and diverse authorities. The Apostle speaks of them when he says that all things were created by God, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or authorities (Colossians 1:16). In these orders he did not mention one authority, but many authorities and dominions, and so forth.

Likewise, on the devil’s side, many principalities and authorities are named, as the same Apostle testifies: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and authorities” (Ephesians 6:12).

Knowing such things, and many others, about authorities and the ranks of heavenly mysteries—whether aroused by the tradition of their ancestors or by certain secrets, rationally or irrationally—because they saw Jesus performing many signs and wonders, the chief priests and elders perhaps thought that these things were not being done without some authority subject to him. They therefore wished to hear from Christ the kind and particular nature of that authority.

If, however, they were asking only about the teaching by which he taught the people in the temple—asking who had given him authority to teach—the preceding interpretation may fit.

The Lord refuted their cunning by questioning them, so that they were condemned either by their silence or by the conclusion of their answer. If they had answered that John’s baptism was from heaven, they would have spoken the truth, though in their malicious cunning they had considered the consequences. The appropriate reply would have been: “Why, then, did you not believe him, and why were you not baptized with his baptism?”

If they wished to say that it had been devised by John through human deception and possessed nothing divine, they feared the rebellion of the people. For the entire assembled multitude had received John’s baptism and regarded him as a prophet.

But the most impious faction answered, using words that seemed humble: “We do not know.” To them he said: “Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things.”

Thus Christ acted wisely through his question: he both drove them away from himself and did not disclose divine mysteries to them, as though giving what is holy to dogs.

In saying that they did not know, they lied. According to their answer, it would have followed that the Lord should say: “Neither do I know what you have asked.” But Truth cannot lie. By this he showed that he knew that there is no authority except from God, and that he possessed this authority properly as God; nevertheless, he did not wish to answer them.

He therefore refused to tell them because they had deliberately concealed what they knew with malicious intent. For this reason he did not ask about John by chance, nor merely to drive them away from himself. He also wished to expose their false view of John—that his baptism was from human beings.

Accordingly, answering their thoughts as God, who knows all things, he introduces a parable that is both remarkable and entirely fitting.

“What do you think?” he said. “A certain man had two sons. Approaching the first, he said: ‘Son, go and work today in my vineyard.’ But he answered: ‘I will not.’ Later, moved by repentance, he went. Approaching the other, he said the same. But he answered: ‘I am going, Lord,’ and did not go. Which of the two did the father’s will?”

They said: “The first.”

Jesus said to them: “Amen I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God. For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him. But tax collectors and prostitutes believed him; and you, though you saw, did not afterward repent so as to believe him.”

I have presented this entire parable together and in full so that the hearers may understand how great the Savior’s wisdom was both in answering and in proposing his argument. Although, as the Jews themselves slanderously claim, he had not studied letters, he surpasses all the eloquence of philosophers and the fluency of all those whom they call rhetoricians. In presenting what belongs to his own case, refuting what has been brought against him, and overturning what belongs to his opponents, he brings the very persons whom he sets up as defendants against himself to act as judges.

He therefore seems to act more remarkably against the legal advocates and the expertise of the priests than any juridical art could teach, compelling those who oppose him to judge from the very objections they themselves have raised. Truth itself defends itself with its own hand; and, in order to conquer its opponents gloriously, it binds them with their own chains and attacks them with their own weapons. Thus the deliberation of the judgment is just: those who condemn themselves by their own judgment deserve acquittal from no one.

From this it is evident how great is the confidence of righteousness when the case is entrusted to the adversary himself. Yet, because the matter is frightening, and lest naked truth should initially deter the opponents from pronouncing a judgment of equity, the good Teacher uses the argument of actual events and represents their persons in parables, so that they themselves, as though judging another, may pronounce sentence concerning their own guilt [Col. 0720D].

We likewise read that David once acted in this way after he had fallen into sin, when Nathan ensnared him in the nets of parables, so that he pronounced a sentence of death against himself. But the situation was different in his case from that of these people: David was summoned to repentance, whereas they were stirred up more deeply toward wickedness.

This is the characteristic difference between good and evil people: when a good person is caught in sin, he groans because he has sinned; but an evil person rages and wastes away, not because he has sinned, but because he has been caught in sin.

“The man who had two sons” is God, who created all human beings with a father’s affection. Although he is by nature Lord, he nevertheless wishes to be loved as a father rather than feared as Lord. For this reason the Law does not say, “You shall fear the Lord your God with all your heart,” but “You shall love him.” To demand love from human beings belongs not to a lord but to a father.

He had two sons: one, the people of the Gentiles; the other, the Jews. The earlier son was the people of the Gentiles, which began from the time of Noah. The younger was the Jewish people, which from the time of Abraham was separated from the Gentiles by circumcision, so that there might be two sons of God: one in uncircumcision, the other in circumcision [Col. 0721A].

At first, when he established the natural law in the mind, he said: “Son, go work in my vineyard today”—that is, throughout the entire time of this age, as has already been shown in the other parable of the vineyard. He did not speak to them face-to-face as a human being, but in their hearts as God—not outwardly in their ears, but inwardly in the understanding of the mind.

The first said: “I will not.” How did he say “I will not,” except in thought and will? Human beings know by nature what is good and evil. When a person abandons the good and follows evil in his mind, thoughts, and pursuits, he seems to answer against God, who established the natural law: “I will not.”

Thus it is said in the Psalm: “The unrighteous person said within himself that he should sin” (Psalm 35:2). Therefore, from the beginning, the Gentiles abandoned God and all works of virtue; they refused to cultivate the faith of Christ or those things that belong to the cultivation of virtue and the salvation of souls.

Then the master of the household, seeing that the law of nature had been abolished in their hearts, spoke similarly to the younger son when he gave him circumcision and the Law through Moses. When Moses and Joshua son of Nun questioned them, they said: “Everything that the Lord has commanded us, we will do” (Psalm 17:46).

But afterward they turned away and lied, as the prophet says in the person of the Lord: “Foreign sons have lied to me; foreign sons have grown old and have limped from their paths.”

He asked them which of the two had done the father’s will. They answered: “The first.”

Behold how, as we said above, they were introduced and drawn into the parable, so that, agreeing with the truth against themselves, they pronounced sentence by saying that the first son had done the father’s will, and not the one who, in the other parable, says to his father: “I have never transgressed your commandment.”

Because they had bound themselves by their own judgment, he confirms that judgment abundantly, saying: “Amen I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God” [Col. 0721D].

It was as though he said: “Not only are the people of the Gentiles better than you Jews, as you have judged, but even the tax collectors and prostitutes among you, whose exceedingly wicked life you know well.”

In these two persons he includes every category of sinners: in the tax collectors, all men who are shown to sin through greed and various profits; in the prostitutes, all sinful women. For just as greed and the pursuit of financial gain chiefly abound among men, so fornication abounds among women.

He immediately explains the reason why tax collectors and prostitutes will go before them. “John came to you,” he says, “in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him; but tax collectors and prostitutes believed him. You, however, though you saw, did not repent so as to believe him.”

Consider how greatly he magnifies John’s office and person when he says that John came to them “in the way of righteousness.” If he had preached only a baptism of repentance, you, as prudent priests and judges not of persons but of matters, ought to have believed him—not necessarily as a righteous man, but as one teaching what was righteous and true. How much more now, since he came to you in the way of righteousness!

His conduct was so evident, and his life so venerable and angelic, that it shook even the hearts of tax collectors and prostitutes and, once shaken by fear, bent them toward repentance. But your hearts could not even be touched by what he said. Therefore tax collectors and prostitutes rightly go before you into the kingdom of God.

Consider, I beg you, how the holy conduct of a preacher gives such power to his preaching that it sometimes subdues even hearts that cannot be tamed.

It should be noted that, when the Lord concluded his parable, it would have followed that he should say: “Amen I say to you, the Gentiles will go before you into the kingdom of God.” Instead, he says: “Tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you.”

Perhaps here he is showing the condition of the ordinary people, or rather the state of sinners rather than that of the Gentiles [Col. 0722B]. They should see that even the common people and the lay population at that time were better than they were—unless, indeed, those who came from the Gentiles are rightly understood as tax collectors and prostitutes. If this interpretation seems less adequate, what we said above is sufficient: he introduced tax collectors and prostitutes for the sake of emphasis, to show that they would precede them into the kingdom of God.

To the other son, who said, “I am going, Lord,” but did not go, he applies this statement: “John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him.” He then returns to the first son: “Tax collectors and prostitutes believed him,” and therefore repented.

The distinguished teacher Hilary interpreted this parable quite differently, perhaps because of a corruption introduced through false manuscripts. For in some copies, when he asked which of the two sons had done the father’s will, they are found to have answered not “the first” but “the last.”

It must nevertheless be known that the more numerous and more accurate copies do not read “the last” but “the first.” Likewise, the Greek does not have **ἔσχατος**, which means “last,” but **πρῶτος**, which means “first.”

Thus, according to the sequence of the parable and the context of the reading, I think it better to understand that, since they were previously shown to be dry in the fig tree, it was fitting that they should condemn themselves by their own judgment, as they do quite openly in the following parable.

Even if someone wishes to read “the last,” the interpretation will be clear: we may understand that the Jews did not wish to speak the truth but to evade the issue, and did not wish to answer concerning themselves what they felt, just as, although they believed John’s baptism to be from heaven, they refused to say so.

It follows:

Hear another parable: “There was a householder who planted a vineyard,” and so forth. The length of the book was indeed demanding an end by now; but reason does not permit these two parables to be separated, since they were delivered together as a response to the chief priests and the scribes. Through these two parables in the Temple, he strikes the hardness of their hearts with extraordinary force, as though the mind were being beaten with two hammers. Accordingly, they could not soften the hardness of their hearts so as to make progress; nevertheless, in both parables they are introduced as hard-hearted in such a way that they condemn themselves by their own judgment. Thus, although the figures are different, the intention of the one who introduces them is the same. Therefore, even if the parable is called another, it is the same hand that strikes, so that they may be without excuse.

For the most merciful Lord wishes them at last to feel the pain of their wounds; and therefore, like a compassionate physician, he applies to the wound another injury of harsh incision. The Savior expends in them, as it were, the whole skill of his art, so that the fault may not be thought to lie with him, but so that it may be shown that the disease in them was incurable. For a physician is praiseworthy even when he sometimes does not cure, provided that he has exhausted all the skill of his art and applied every diligence in treating the patient.

“There was,” he says, “a householder.” By the name “man,” as commonly occurs in parables, God the Father is understood—not according to nature. Even if, in some likeness adapted to our smallness, God the Father is called a man, this must not be understood literally, as though anything could worthily be compared with him or he himself could be said to resemble anyone. He is called a human householder, although he is invisible and incorporeal, because heaven and earth and all created things are, as it were, one house. In this house, since he is by nature the Lord of angels and human beings, he rules and governs them with all the benevolence and affection of a father.

For this reason he preferred to be called “Father”: so that all, considering his goodness, might serve him willingly—not as evil servants, but in free will, like good sons serving a most loving parent.

“He planted a vineyard.” Since different parables, both in the Gospel and in the prophets, speak of a vineyard, we must ask whether “vineyard” is to be understood as referring to different realities, or to one and the same reality—especially since at the end of this parable he says to the chief priests and scribes: “Amen, I say to you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

What do you think is meant by the kingdom of God, which is taken away from wicked teachers, unless it is the vineyard itself, which is leased to other husbandmen, after the wicked have been destroyed? Perhaps, then, the vineyard is the very thing that was cultivated, namely the kingdom of God, which is taken away from the earlier tenants and given to another nation; or ought we to judge that the kingdom of God is one thing and the vineyard another?

The prophet Isaiah shows us more clearly what we should understand the vineyard to be. “I will sing,” he says (Isaiah 5:1–2), “for my beloved a song concerning my beloved’s vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a fertile hill. He fenced it around, dug it, and planted it with the choice vine.” And, to indicate that this is the same vineyard spoken of in the Gospel, he adds: “He built a tower in its midst and dug a winepress in it.” A little later he says: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is his tender plant.”

In that parable, or song, some things are similar to those in the present passage, while others are dissimilar. Let us therefore examine the dissimilarities, so that from unlike things we may learn the differences between unlike realities.

The similarity lies in the statement that he planted a vineyard, fenced it around—or enclosed it with a wall—dug a winepress in it, and built a tower. The difference is that in Isaiah the planter of the vineyard accuses the vineyard itself, saying: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns.” In the Gospel, however, the vineyard is not accused, as though it had failed to produce fruit in its season; rather, the tenants are accused, because they took possession of it, treated the householder’s servants with various insults, and finally killed the householder’s son.

Again, in Isaiah he threatens the vineyard itself, saying: “I will remove its fence, and it shall be for plunder; I will destroy its wall, and it shall be for trampling” (Isaiah 5:5), and so forth. He also promises that he will command the clouds not to rain upon that vineyard, which, according to the same prophecy, was the house of Israel because it had produced no fruit.

In the present parable of the vineyard, however, we find the vineyard suffering nothing; rather, it has received God’s providence so that it may produce more abundant fruit. Therefore it is taken away from the wicked tenants and given to a better nation. The evil and wicked tenants, meanwhile, receive the whole of the anger, and pronounce sentence against themselves by their own condemnation when, questioned, they say: “He will put those wicked men to a miserable death,” and so forth.

Concerning the same vineyard Jeremiah says to the people: “I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly genuine seed; how have you turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jeremiah 2:21). You see that in the prophets the Jewish people are called a vineyard, and that in those same prophets the householder’s threat is directed against the vineyard. In the Gospel, however, the vineyard is not blamed at all, but the tenants are.

For this reason certain outstanding teachers have understood the vineyard in this passage not as the people, but as the teaching of the Law, or the righteousness that comes from the Law, because the worship and providence of God are implanted in those sacred Scriptures. Hence the Lord says: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruit.”

By this mystery the Lord clearly wished the vineyard to be understood as the kingdom of God—that is, the Law and the Prophets, and all the divine Scriptures—which the Lord entrusted to the vineyard. First he entrusted them to the tenants, to that earlier people, because the oracles of God were first committed to them; then, after rejecting them, he entrusted them to the Gentiles, who produce the fruit of the Scriptures.

From this vineyard, it is believed, neither the fence is now removed nor the wall destroyed, nor is it any longer exposed to plunder and trampling. Thus, thereafter, both the winepresses are handed over from those same Scriptures, and the tower—representing contemplation and the repulsion of enemies—is fittingly raised by them.

But because, in another parable of the vineyard, we have said that the very cultivators of the vineyard, the laborers who were sent to work in it at different hours, represent the vineyard itself—for they were branches of the true vine—and because Christ gathered into himself as many saints as he brought into it from the beginning of the world to the end, propagating them in himself like so many branches from which the whole vineyard bears fruit and grows, we must therefore understand that the vineyard leased to the husbandmen is none other than that same vineyard in which he earlier hired laborers at the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours.

“And he went away to a distant place.” This does not refer to a change of location, but to the freedom of the will: he says this so that the vinedressers might be given the opportunity to work for a time. Otherwise, from where could God be absent, since he fills and surrounds all things, as he himself says through Jeremiah: “I am God who is near, and not far away”?

This parable of the vineyard therefore appears different from the earlier one, or from those about which the prophets speak, because, as we have shown above, the figure of the vineyard is introduced here in a very different way. In this parable no rewards are promised to the cultivators of the vineyard; rather, they themselves, as though speaking with prophetic inspiration, condemn themselves by their own judgment.

Indeed, this parable is introduced against those who arrogantly confronted the Lord while he was teaching in the Temple, so that it might convict them of having been destroyers of the vineyard rather than cultivators. Thus the present parable of the vineyard is very deliberately varied: just as it is customary in many passages of Scripture for one and the same reality to be represented in different ways in parables, with each figure receiving its own proper attribution according to place, persons, and circumstances.

Accordingly, the earlier parable of the vineyard encompasses the whole period from the beginning of the world to its end. It brings laborers into the vineyard, yet deprives none of the agreed denarius; rather, everyone whom it hired is rewarded at the end with the payment for his labor. Therefore, in that parable we rightly understand that only the elect are called—those whom God foreknew and predestined. All of them, both the last and the first, labored together in the unity of the vineyard and are glorified together in the one blessed eternity of immortality.

In the present parable, the very same vineyard is commended, and greater care and diligence are expressed; indeed, whatever was omitted there is described here, as well as in the prophets, in full detail. Moreover, the wicked laborers or tenants who had been called to cultivate it—whom the other parables had passed over—are openly condemned here in the persons of the Pharisees and scribes.

For this reason the parable is composed in this way: good and evil had long been mixed together, from the beginning of the Law and as they are now; and the part of the vineyard that, although small in number, was destined to receive the faith of Christ is entrusted for cultivation to other tenants without defilement. But the other part not only refused to bear fruit; it also, like the vineyard’s laborers who had been sent to it, killed the servants sent to it.

Therefore this parable appears to extend no farther than from the time when the Jews were brought out of Egypt to Christ. Of this vineyard David sings:

“You brought a vine out of Egypt;
you drove out the nations and planted it” (Psalm 79:9).

That vineyard was not only already present in Egypt; it was also propagated from the beginning of the world among the holy fathers and patriarchs. But from there, as though at the sixth hour of the day, it was transferred: the nations were driven out because they were unfruitful, and the right hand of God planted it in the land formerly promised to the fathers. Its shadow covered the mountains, its branches were like the cedars of God, and it extended its shoots to the sea and its offshoots to the river (ibid., vv. 11–12).

In this vineyard there were different vines: some were changed into bitterness, “foreign vines,” according to Jeremiah; others produced fruit pleasing to God. Concerning both groups the prophet David testifies that one part was destined to be destroyed miserably, while the other was to be perfected for the better and set over the Son of Man and over the mountain.

Thus, prophesying and lamenting over one part of it, he says:

“Why have you broken down its wall,
or its fence,
so that all who pass along the road pluck its grapes?” (ibid., v. 13).

Because that vineyard refused to repent, the boar from the forest destroyed it, and the wild beast devoured it (ibid., v. 14)—that is, the Roman army under Titus and Vespasian, which was sent to destroy the wicked and most evil tenants of the vineyard. They not only refused to cultivate the vineyard entrusted to them so that it would bear fruit for God; they also cut themselves off from the stock of the true vine, and continually desired to kill those who, remaining in the vine through faith, took care to bear fruit.

Concerning that vineyard which remained in the vine, the aforesaid Prophet prays:

“God of hosts, turn again;
look down from heaven and see;
visit this vineyard
and perfect it,
which your right hand planted,
and the Son of Man whom you strengthened for yourself” (ibid., v. 15).

Because they had been planted in him and strengthened in faith, they remained in the root of their richness. The other branches, however, or shoots of the vineyard, because they were broken off, withered.

These were brought in by the right hand of God, as Mary, the sister of Aaron, sings in the Song: upon the mountain of God’s inheritance, they were planted in the firmest dwelling-place of God, which God—not man—had made, and in the sanctuary that his hands established.

This vineyard, after the wicked tenants had been destroyed and expelled, was leased and entrusted to the apostles, or to apostolic men. Every nation of the Gentiles was grafted into it by God’s authority and propagated in it from the vine that is Christ, in whom the Father is the cultivator; and it is daily expanded throughout the whole world.

For the present Church is often called the kingdom of heaven. Christ too, who is its head, is frequently called the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, when those most wicked tenants judged themselves unworthy of eternal life and refused to receive Christ, Christ was taken away from them, the Church was taken away, and all the sacraments of salvation were taken away. They were given to those who believe in Christ, both Jews and Gentiles, so that each might render the fruit of faith in its proper season.

Consequently, it is not necessary to understand the kingdom of God as the divine Scriptures alone, as some wish, thereby allowing themselves to speculate at greater length about the vineyard and to introduce certain elements of their own error.

The vineyard which the prophets lament as having degenerated, because it did not remain in the true vine, is therefore represented in this passage as Christ’s wicked tenants. He transforms his parable with reference to them, so that they may be called not the vineyard but the husbandmen. In this way the chief priests and scribes may clearly understand that the words are spoken about themselves, condemn themselves by their own judgment, and recognize that they are strangers to this vineyard.

Thus the elders of the people who asked the Lord, “By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?”—and who wanted to catch his wisdom in his words—were defeated by his words and bound themselves with their own chains, so that they no longer dared to speak to him.

Alternatively, since wicked teachers say that the sacred Scriptures themselves are the way, or the kingdom of God that is taken away from the Jews, how is that taken away from them which they possess? It is taken away when Christ, who is proclaimed in those Scriptures, is taken away from them—or rather, when he is rejected so that he may not be believed. Every understanding of the Scriptures is emptied and removed from them.

When, therefore, it is transferred through the apostles to the Gentiles, to whom the Church has been entrusted, it is rooted in their hearts, and Christ, the true vine, is planted in them, so that all may be propagated from him and the one vineyard may grow throughout the whole world. Christ entrusted this vineyard to good and better husbandmen, who will render him abundant fruit in its proper seasons.

These points have been said against those who claim that no one can perish from the vineyard. They maintain not only that no vine is blamed in this parable, but also that the vineyard, preserved, is entrusted to better tenants.

Let us finally return to the order of the parable itself, since everything said to have been built in it is now seen in a more exalted form in the Church.

“He fenced it around,” he says—that is, with the wall of Jerusalem, or, better, with the protection of angels. No one can doubt that angels were appointed over them for their protection, since this is shown in many passages of Scripture. Hence, as Josephus himself relates, when the wretched city was already about to be destroyed and the people were under siege, voices were heard crying within it: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

“And he dug a winepress in it”—that is, the altar on which all their vows were refined. Or he may also be speaking of the winepresses mentioned in the titles of three psalms, because in them the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion and the sacraments of the Church are foreshadowed.

For the Jewish people were not without the pressure of temptations, nor was their whole Synagogue without the fervor of the Holy Spirit. When these winepresses were transferred into the Church, they filled the hearts of believers with the new wine of the Holy Spirit. After drinking from its fervor, they were called drunk and full of new wine.

Hence the prophets and all the saints, burning with the Holy Spirit, were affected by the ardor of charity. Concerning their sufferings and pressures it is rightly said: “Your winepresses will overflow with wine” (Proverbs 3:10).

Otherwise, if all the saints had not been intoxicated with this new wine, they would never willingly have endured such great and extraordinary things as they suffered—those whom the Holy Spirit cleansed.

It is rightly said that “he dug a winepress in it,” because the inner abundance of the fruit of grace would not have had anything to flow forth unless hearts had been dug out more broadly in charity. The winepress was dug for this purpose: so that from the pressure of tribulation the intoxication of love and the new wine of eternal sweetness might flow more abundantly and widely.

“And he built a tower.” There is no doubt that this means the Temple, concerning which Micah says:

“And you, tower of the flock,
misty daughter of Zion,
to you shall come the former dominion” (Micah 4:8).

But perhaps it is better to say that the summit of the Law, and the understanding concerning Christ, is meant, since all contemplation of the Law and all strength against enemies are found in it. Thus we rightly pray to him:

“Be for us, Lord, a tower of strength
against the face of the enemy” (Psalm 60:4),

because from him and in him is all our contemplation, so that we may not be captured by enemies; and he himself is all our strength, refuge, and protection.

Because the Jews rejected him, they were captured by enemies, their winepresses were overturned, and their fence was taken away from them.

Some have said that the fence placed around the vineyard on the outside represents the Scriptures according to the letter, because, like a wall or fence, they enclose externally what is within, so that the fruits of the vineyard, which are hidden, may not be seen. The severity of the Law and its heavy yoke are understood as the winepress imposed upon them. Concerning this yoke or pressure the Apostle says that neither we nor our fathers were able to bear it.

The tower, as I have said, is built in it and represents the ascent of the Scriptures, the eminence and height of understanding, rising above the vineyard itself, the fence, and the winepresses. It is the word concerning God himself, concerning Christ’s dispensation, and the temple of divine understanding constructed in him. Whoever remains established in Christ’s protection is never easily wounded and is never carelessly deceived by the enemy.

But the wretched priests and scribes neither drew the new wine of the clarified vintage from the prophets’ winepresses, in which the grace of the Holy Spirit flowed, nor ascended to the height of the Law and the Prophets. From that height, like watchmen, they might have foreseen Christ’s coming and observed the things foretold in them.

“When the time of the fruits had drawn near, he sent his servants to the husbandmen, so that they might receive its fruits. But the husbandmen seized his servants, struck one, killed another, and stoned another.”

He had given them commandments for their work and established the cultivation of the vineyard, so that they might manifest in themselves the fruit they had received. But they presented no fruit of the vineyard; instead, they killed the servants of their Lord. Therefore he rightly said “the time of the fruits,” and not “the produce.” For no fruit of righteousness existed in them, and there was no advance in faith toward Christ, who is the true vine.

Of this vineyard he himself says: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns.” Thus their winepresses did not overflow with the wine of joy or with spiritual new wine; rather, they poured out the blood of the prophets.

It should be noted that only the householder truly knows when the time of fruits must approach for each person, or when the time is still farther off. This ought to be carefully considered with respect to each age—not only the ages of time, but also the stages of a human being’s life.

Therefore one must consider from what point each person was called, and the time of our faith must be examined, so that each of us may see how much and what kind of fruit he bears according to the period of his life and the growth of his faith. Otherwise, when someone ought to be a teacher according to the time of maturity, he may again need to be taught the elementary principles of the oracles of God.

And when it would already be fitting for him, like an early-ripening grape, to mature, produce new wine, and display the joy of the Holy Spirit, he may only then be swelling into a bud.

This is why some, although according to the time of God’s dispensation and according to their calling they ought already to be producing abundant fruits, have no fruit at all; or, although they ought to possess mature fruit, they have only clusters blossoming out of season and not at their proper time.

But the householder knows with certainty when the time of the vintage should be and when the fruit of each person must be demanded. Therefore he says of them: “When the time of the fruits had drawn near.” For a long time had passed since they received the Law through Moses; and, instructed by many benefits from God, it was already time for them to return the fruit of faith in Christ and in God the Father, at least in the time of the prophets, who themselves proclaimed it more abundantly and perfectly.

But they, weighed down by the yoke of unbelief, struck one, as they did Micah, when Zedekiah son of Chenaana struck him on the cheek and ordered him not to prophesy. They killed another, as they did Zechariah, between the Temple and the altar. They stoned another, as they did Naboth, of whom, although we have received no prophetic word, we have nevertheless received a prophetic deed: by his own blood he prophesied that many future martyrs would suffer for this vineyard.

They also tormented Jeremiah with many tortures and finally cast him into a pit. They likewise sawed Isaiah in half more readily—from the crown of his head down to his feet—than they could break his faith and steadfastness.

Thus, because the time of fruits was approaching, it happened that he sent many other servants to receive the fruits, so that they might receive the fruit of each vine. No one, therefore, doubts that the servants are the prophets, who were sent to them so often.

But someone might perhaps say that the prophets were not sent to receive fruits, but rather to work themselves and cultivate the vineyard, and should therefore be called laborers.

Let us see, then, whether we can say that the Jews, having been instructed in the Law, ought already to have offered spiritual fruits and divine offerings to God the Father and the Son in faith—especially the Levites and priests, and the rulers of the people, who had cultivated the vineyard and ruled over them. The prophets were sent to them so that they might receive a perfect understanding of the Father and the Son, and also of the Holy Spirit, as well as all the works of right faith that had been handed down in the Law, both to signify and to practice life; and so that, like priests, they might offer these things to God.

And because the time of the vintage was already fully ripe, so that they might receive from them the abundance of spiritual fruits and full knowledge of the Godhead, they were sent in such a way that they themselves would also be the most perfect laborers of the vineyard, bearing abundant fruit like branches of the true vine.

Then, after the fewer servants had been killed, the householder sent more than the first to the same tenants of the vineyard, and they treated them in the same way. The whole sequence of the Scriptures of the Old Testament is filled with the account of their killing innumerable prophets. Paul too describes their struggles, saying that through faith they conquered kingdoms, and so forth, as is read in that passage.

Therefore, the fact that more are sent to them again is evidence of extraordinary goodness and tireless patience. After so many benefits, and without the need for God’s exaction or the admonition of the prophets, they ought to have paid the Lord the tribute due from their righteousness and their faith in Christ, together with the debt of good works; instead, they returned evil for good.

Yet even when they did not believe, although he ought rather to have become angry over the insults they had inflicted upon his servants, he sent still more—namely, the minor prophets together with the major ones, whom he gathered almost all at one time together with the priests and Levites.

After these too had been killed, so that Jerusalem was filled with blood, because of his goodness and extraordinary patience he sent them his Son—not as one bringing a sentence of punishment to the guilty, but the mercy of pardon after so many crimes, after every loss of fruit, and after their insolent wickedness, while still preserving for them a place of repentance—so that by clemency he might overcome them even then.

And he says: “Perhaps they will reverence my Son.”

He therefore wishes them to be brought to shame and reverence rather than punished. Otherwise, after such great injuries, vengeance for their crimes ought already to have been inflicted. But for the most benevolent God, the sole punishment of shame is sufficient for forgiveness, and sincere conversion alone is sufficient for pardon. For every injury inflicted upon servants is directed against the Lord as an insult.

Nevertheless, he sends his Son—not an adopted son, not one begotten from some source other than himself, but his own Son, who by nature possesses the things that belong to the Father—saying: “Perhaps they will reverence my Son.”

This proverbial expression of hesitation does not arise from ignorance, nor from any uncertainty in God’s foreknowledge. For what could the householder not know, especially when God the Father is understood in this passage? Rather, he is said to hesitate in order that their free will might be preserved and grace offered.
