Therefore the heretics who say that the Son is ignorant because he said that no one knows the last day except the Father must be refuted. He says that no one knows that day except the Father alone, and the one to whom he himself wishes to reveal it; yet the Son is nowhere proclaimed inferior to the Father—neither in power, nor in knowledge, nor in anything else.

Accordingly, just as the Son there says that he does not know something in a certain respect, so here the Father is believed to hesitate in a certain respect. For this reason he moderates the statement—not because he is ignorant of what was going to happen, but so that he may introduce a mode of speaking, thereby catching in their own judgment those to whom he speaks and granting them, as it were in human language, an opportunity for conversion.

But whatever the heretics may answer here in defense of their position, let them understand that their entire answer applies also to the Son, who says that he does not know the day of consummation.

Unless perhaps this question is resolved in another way: perhaps some among the Jews reverenced the Son of God, while other tenants were those who said, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him.” Yet he speaks as though all the Jews would kill him, although not all the Jews killed Christ, but only those Jews who were servants according to the flesh.

So here too the expression “They will reverence my Son” may perhaps be stated universally with reference to the Father, as though all would reverence him, although not all received him—only the few who were enlightened by the Holy Spirit and believed in him. Thus he speaks generally as though of all, although there were only a few who offered him the reverence of faith.

We have therefore proposed both interpretations, so that no one might think that God the Father was ignorant. For according to the present text of the Gospel, the Jews plainly do not appear to have reverenced him. But to say that something happened other than what had been foreknown, or that the Father could not have foreknown it, is an impious thought.

The statement “This is the heir; come, let us kill him” was fulfilled in those who saw Christ and recognized him as the Son of God, yet nevertheless killed him. It was not spoken by those who reverenced him and believed in him, but by those wicked and obstinate men.

They did not fail to know that he was the Son of God the householder, as some carelessly assert. Rather, blinded by envy, arrogance, and the desire for possessions, they hardened their faces against him, just as Joseph’s brothers did, refusing to acknowledge him as their brother.

They did recognize him, but called him a dreamer; hence their jealousy arose. In the same way these men called Christ a blasphemer and claimed that he performed all his miracles by Beelzebub—although no sane person denies that they were divine works.

Thus, even though they raged in the blindness of fury, they said to one another: “Is this not the Christ?” Others, eager to resist the truth, replied: “When the Christ comes, no one will know where he is from. But we know where this man is from.”

By this denial they asserted their falsehood more strongly than they expressed ignorance of the prophets, who had demonstrated with the utmost clarity everything about him that was to happen—where he would be born, from where he would come, and in what manner.

But when they saw the signs and wonders, they understood that he was the Christ, whom they refused to confess. Rather, they sought to kill him because they were unwilling to believe in him.

So did the most wicked Herod: when he learned from the Magi that the king of the Jews had been born, he was inflamed all the more and sought to destroy the one whom he had learned from the divine oracles had been promised.

It is therefore established that the chief priests and the elders of the people knew that Christ was the Son of God. Even if they did not know that he was holy, they nevertheless dared to kill him, just as Herod killed the children.

For if he had not believed that Christ was destined to be king of the Jews, he would certainly not have killed all the infants according to the time he had learned from the Magi.

In the same way, the hard-hearted Jews knew—from both prophecy and miracles—but, as though they did not know, they hardened themselves. They refused to proclaim among the people that he was the Son of God, or to allow their words or assent to reach the populace.

Nor is it surprising, since even today those who are scattered and expelled are harder still, so that they cannot receive the truth about Christ according to the Scriptures—harder than stones.

Thus, hardened by their excessive hatred, they cast him outside the vineyard and killed him. Hence the Apostle says that the Lord was crucified outside the gate—that is, outside Jerusalem, on Mount Calvary.

For, as far as they themselves were concerned, the most wicked tenants judged him to be a stranger to the vineyard, that is, to the people of God, when they passed sentence of death against him.

But he was rightly cast outside that vineyard which produced thorns, and there he was killed, so that when the Gentiles received him, the vineyard might be leased to other husbandmen.

When, therefore, he says, the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants? The Lord asks them this, not because he does not know what they will answer, but so that they may condemn themselves by their own response. Indeed, among other things, they themselves testify why they killed him: “This is the heir,” they say; “come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance.” This they said, if not with their voice, nevertheless in their hearts—especially when he entered the Temple and drove out all those selling animals of various kinds, which were sold for sacrifice. The avaricious priests were inflamed by the profits from these animals.

[Col. 0732B] It was then, as it seems, that they especially resolved to kill him, perhaps saying within themselves: “If the people or we have this man as God, it will be necessary for the entire custom of sacrifices to be abolished, which he is already trying to destroy for the present; this religion, which pertains to our profit, will cease; and our glory will be humbled by him. Moreover, the worship of the Temple, which is preserved for the glory of God, will perish; and this people, who now offer these things, will no longer be subject to us. The Temple and the sacrifices will not be our possession, but this man’s; the whole inheritance will be his. Therefore let us kill him, and everything that he says belongs to himself and to the Father will be our inheritance, so that, just as today, so also always, everything may belong to our profit and our glory.” For this is what it means to say, “The inheritance will be ours.”

[Col. 0732C] But they, wisely trapped by the wisdom of God, answered very differently when questioned, already condemned beforehand by their own conscience. For they say to him: “He will put those wicked men to a miserable death and lease the vineyard to other tenants.” Moreover, the expression they used, they say, is not a plural nominative, so that it should refer to them, but a singular dative, as is made more evident from the Greek [αὐτῷ, “to him”]. Thus what they answered truthfully was not theirs at all; rather, by God’s will it happened that Truth itself forced them, lest they be able to conceal it.

So also Caiaphas the priest did not speak the truth from himself; but, because he was high priest that year, he prophesied (John 11:51). Likewise these men did not prophesy against themselves of their own accord, but by God’s will, as I have said: all the words of God that concerned Christ were to be taken away from them, and Christ, together with all religion and the worshipful service of God, was to be transferred to the Gentiles after they had been rejected, so that each nation and each individual might produce the fruit of a good work in its proper time.

Meanwhile, because Luke gives a very different account, an obvious question arises: the priests did not say, “He will put those wicked men to a miserable death,” but the Lord said this; and when he had said it, they replied, “May it not be so.” For according to Luke they understood that he was speaking against them, and therefore immediately contradicted Christ’s judgment, saying, “May it not be so.”

This question is resolved in two ways, so that each evangelist tells the truth and the respective meanings of their accounts resolve one aspect of the priests’ dispute. One interpretation is very easy if we consider the people who said, “He is good,” and those who said, “No, but he deceives the crowds” (John 7:12). For among the same crowds there were two parties: one favored Christ, for whatever reasons, while the other opposed him. Thus on this occasion there were some who answered the question put to them, “He will put those wicked men to a miserable death”; perhaps these were the same people who had cried out, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Again, there were others who, contradicting the Lord’s words, gave the answer reported by Luke: “May it not be so.”

Another explanation is that, by God’s will, although they were unwilling, they uttered in prophecy, “He will put those wicked men to a miserable death,” while in their hearts they said the contrary, “May it not be so.” Thus one of the evangelists reported what they carried in their hearts. As it is said in the Psalms: “With their mouth they blessed, but in their heart they cursed” (Psalm 61:5).

[Col. 0733A] Every human being possesses knowledge of good and evil; therefore, whatever these men said of the two alternatives, they said something else against it as well. Hence the question was directed at their thoughts according to their wickedness. For although they said in words, “May it not be so,” they confessed in their conscience, “He will put those wicked men to a miserable death.”

Scripture frequently explains the thoughts of the heart as though they were spoken words. Thus Job says: “The wicked man says to God, ‘Depart from me; I do not desire to know your ways.’” And elsewhere the Prophet says: “They said, ‘The Lord will not see, and the God of Jacob will not understand’” (Psalm 93:7). The same is true in very many other passages.

Otherwise, the matter seems contradictory: they had understood that the parables were spoken against them, so much so that they wanted immediately to seize him, and thus agreed in heart and mouth with what was being said. Therefore, when they did not accept this, Scripture introduces another testimony, saying, “Have you never read?”—as though it were saying: “If you do not understand my parable, or do not wish to accept it, then at least turn over this Scripture that was given to you in prophecy, which you cannot contradict: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.’”

For if they had accepted what was said above and declared themselves worthy of punishment, it would not seem necessary to bring forward this further statement. But now he calls those whom he had called tenants “builders of a house”—and rightly so, because the vineyard itself, according to the Prophet, was the house of Israel. It is as though he were saying to them: “Since you are builders of the house, why do you not consider at which corner of the building that stone must be placed of which the Prophet says: ‘You, the builders of the house, have been found to be rejecters of this stone’? Is it to be placed in your structure, seeing that you reject it? Certainly not, but in another building, at the corner of two peoples, so that there may be one house, just as the one vineyard and the one Church have also been transferred from you. And if another building is to come into being, your building is contemptible.”

[Col. 0733B] This construction of the verse, according to the literal wording, appears to be a solecism, like the expression, “The city that I establish is yours,” instead of what should have been said, “The city is yours.” But this is a manner of expression found in the divine Scriptures. What should have been said is: “The stone that they rejected—he himself has become the cornerstone,” so that he might join two walls in himself. For if they had been approved builders, they would never have rejected such a stone.

Isaiah had spoken of this stone when he said: “Behold, I lay in Zion a stone as a foundation, an elect stone, precious, corner-stone; and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Isaiah 28:16). For he is the stone of help, the stone that Jacob set up as a sign and poured with oil, because he was anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit beyond his companions.

Peter also speaks confidently to the Jews about this stone: “This stone, which was rejected by you builders, has become the cornerstone.” For this stone is both the cornerstone and the foundation of the Church. “From the Lord,” he says, “this has been done, and it is marvelous in our eyes” (Psalm 117:22).

[Col. 0734A] This is the confession of the saints: it was not made by a human being or by human power, but by the power of God and the might of the Father. Therefore it is marvelous, not in the sight of unbelievers, but in the eyes of all who have been enlightened through faith by believing.

What is more marvelous than all other miracles is that God should become man, and that this stone, growing according to the Prophet, should fill the whole earth; that it should join heavenly and earthly things together and gather two laws into itself as one.

Therefore it is exceedingly marvelous in the eyes of the saints, whose voice this is, because it is the head of the heavenly building and the foundation of the house granted by God the Father.

“Therefore,” he says, “the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.” We have already discussed this sufficiently above, except that what he says—“It will be given to other tenants who will return its fruit at its proper times”—must be examined more carefully.

For the kingdom of God, that is, the mysteries of the word of God, is given to no one except those who produce fruit in it and from it. If this is so, it is given to no one who sins.

[Col. 0734B] At this point someone might say: “If the kingdom of God is given to no one except one who produces its fruit, how was it given to that people from whom it has been taken away because it did not produce its fruit?”

But we must consider that above it was not said of that people, “He gave it to the tenants,” but, “He leased it,” or, as it is better expressed in Greek, “He handed it over to the tenants.” Here, however, he says, “It is taken away and will be given to other tenants.”

If he had said above “he gave it” in the same sense as “he leased” or “he handed it over,” the question would be insoluble. But now he says, “It will be given,” because what is given is understood to be given freely, whereas what is leased or handed over is not given entirely free of charge. Nor did he hand it over or lease it as though they were chosen or faithful, in the manner in which he freely gave it to those whom he gave it through the judgment of election and not on the basis of the merit of their virtue, so that they might be subject to the justice of God and not justified by their own works according to the law. For such justice has merit, but not from God.

[Col. 0734C] It follows:

“And whoever falls upon this stone will be shattered; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.”

He speaks of himself, because he wishes to be understood as having been placed as the foundation of the whole Church. It is one thing to offend Christ through evil works, and another to deny Christ and drive him away from oneself.

Therefore the sinner who nevertheless believes in him does indeed fall, but falls upon the stone; and thus he is shattered for repentance, but is not completely crushed into destruction, because, though bruised by the contrition of his heart, he is preserved for the forgiveness of salvation.

But upon whomever it falls—that is, whoever is crushed by the stone itself, rejected and driven away from the heart, namely, whoever has denied Christ—it will crush him so completely that not even a potsherd will remain with which to draw a little water or carry a small ember from a fire.

Some, however, wish those who fall upon the stone to be understood as those who, for Christ’s sake, handed their bodies over to death—that is, those who have died upon him and whose flesh and bones are shattered.

But upon those over whom Christ has fallen—that is, those who, as I have said, have utterly denied him—he will come from above in judgment, with the punishment of destruction. Therefore he said, “It will crush them,” so that they may be like the wicked, like dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth.

Others, following the text and the context of the reading, say that these are the nations that have been dashed against Christ. They fell well from their pride upon him and were broken into humility so that they might be saved. For when the righteous man falls in this way, he is not crushed, because the Lord supports him with his hand.

[Col. 0735A] But upon whomever it falls—that is, upon the Jews who drove him away from themselves—it will fall crushingly. Therefore, when he comes to judgment, they will be so crushed and pulverized that nothing else will come upon them except sudden destruction.

Great, therefore, is this stone, and strong. Consequently, whoever falls upon it and strikes it dashes and breaks himself; but no one injures Christ the stone. The sinner indeed corrupts himself, because he falls upon the stone. The stone does not merely shatter him because it is benign; rather, he himself dashes against the stone.

For no one is broken according to the stone’s own nature as a strong stone, but according to how forcefully he himself has fallen. A fall is forceful either because of the weight of one’s own burden or because of the height from which one has fallen—that is, the higher someone has been exalted.

[Col. 0735B] Therefore not every fall breaks the one who is falling to the same degree, just as, according to the Apostle, not everyone builds equally upon the foundation, which is Christ.

Let each person therefore weigh how far he falls, from what height he falls, and what it is that falls. For one person falls through humility so that he may rise again, while another falls so that he may be shattered and lie there miserably broken.

Nevertheless, while someone falls upon the foundation—that is, upon the rock that is Christ—he is not shattered in such a way that the potter is unable to fashion from those same fragments a vessel again for honor, unless someone has perhaps become hardened, so that he will not receive the bitumen of charity and cannot again be softened for the cleansing of sin.

[Col. 0735C] But when the stone falls upon someone, it is not asked how heavy or how light the thing crushed beneath it was, whether it came from a height or from a low place, because it is crushed completely.

Therefore perhaps the Christian who sins does not perish as much as Christ can destroy him, or as much as Christ possesses power, but as much as he himself has destroyed himself according to his works.

For this reason the Christian should consider, while there is still time and while he is upon the rock, by what weight of sins he is being pressed, or from what height—that is, from what rank—he has fallen: for example, whether he is a cleric or one who practices continence; whether he is a priest, a Levite, or a monk; whether she is a widow or a virgin.

Likewise, the magnitude or enormity of the sin must be considered. For, as I have said, each person is shattered to the extent that he has sinned more greatly and more gravely.

[Col. 0736A] But one who has fallen neither from a high rank of honor nor under the weight of a grave sin against Christ, and who has not been burdened by the sand of transgressions, is sometimes not injured, or at least is not greatly injured, because he is cleansed daily through prayer.

But because the length of the book demands an end, God must be prayed to continually: may he who has granted us understanding of our danger also grant us the ability to avoid it, so that we may neither fall again from a height nor sin more grievously thereafter, nor become weighed down each day by an increasing number of lesser transgressions.

Rather, let us continually wipe away through weeping the things we have committed, so that through Christ himself, who is the living stone, we may be renewed and made more firm for the better, and through him and in him may be numbered among his members.

[Col. 0736B] So that in Christ, from whom and in whom the book has its end, the end of sin and the beginning of every good may henceforth be in him and through him.

# PROLOGUE OF THE TENTH BOOK

[Col. 0735]

[Col. 0735C] Let no one, when reading the evangelists, suppose that they fabricated anything false about Christ, as many Jews slanderously claim; or that they attributed more to him than the truth contains, as certain pagans falsely assert; or that, although they may appear to differ from one another in their wording, they presented anything contrary to one another in meaning, as very many enemies of the truth have judged.

For there was one Spirit in them, one perfect knowledge of Christ, and one faith. So that you may recognize this more fully, prudent reader—how harmoniously and concordantly they spoke, although they varied their words in many ways because of the dispensation of God’s mysteries, omitting some things, saying others in their own manner, postponing certain matters, sometimes anticipating them, and often recapitulating them—I ask you to read the four books of blessed Augustine that he published on the Harmony of the Evangelists.

[Col. 0736C] In a short time you will perhaps be able to discern their meaning completely: how great their unity is, how great the agreement of their statements, how great the harmony of their virtues, and how brilliant their variety; how great the adornment of their expressions, the multiplicity of their meanings, and the clarity of their words.

Thus, from the fact that they vary, one may understand that a more divine meaning is present in them and that the abundance of the Holy Spirit is richer. For although there are four Gospels, there is one fountain rising from the earth from which truth arose, irrigating the whole earth and Paradise from the beginning of God’s first creation.

This fountain divides itself into the heads of four rivers and drenches the entire fourfold world, pouring itself over everything. Therefore they cannot be different from one another, as wicked men try to claim, because they flow from the force of one fountain and are proved to flow from nowhere other than the Paradise of God, whence this heavenly justice looked forth from heaven and came even to us, because we are all justified.

[Col. 0737A] It is therefore established that what is one cannot be different. For even before they were born in the flesh, they were seen in Paradise—that is, in heaven—through whom, as though through living beings, Christ flows here and there.

Hence afterward, through John, when he himself was one of them, they were seen in heaven as four living creatures. When they gave glory, honor, and blessing to the one seated upon the throne, the twenty-four elders came forward, casting down their crowns and worshiping the one who lives for ever and ever.

If, then, my brothers were seen in heaven, and at their voices the senate of that eternal court—that is, the entire order of preachers—is said to rise and worship the one who lives for ever and ever, how much more ought we to listen and attend to their voices? For they are neither different nor discordant, since there is one Spirit and one fountain in them.

Therefore they all say one thing together and have one understanding, because they are nothing other than the instrument of the Holy Spirit.

But because a stream flows from nowhere other than its fountain, those who maintain that Christ ought rather to have written his deeds himself than through men who do not even agree among themselves must not be heeded, since they wrote nothing other than what he showed and said.

[Col. 0737B] Nor, I think, should it be said that Christ himself did not wish to write about himself and did not do so, since his members—that is, the hands and fingers of his body—wrote what they heard inwardly, with Christ the Head dictating.

For it is certain that whatever he wished us to read concerning his deeds and words, the divine Spirit commanded his own hands to write.

Therefore whoever rightly understands this fellowship of unity and the harmonious ministry of the members in their diverse offices under one head, Christ, will not understand it otherwise when these men, who were foreordained for this Gospel in its fourfold form before the foundation of the world, narrate one thing than if he had seen the Lord’s own hand, which he bore in his proper body, writing.

[Col. 0738A] Therefore, just as the twenty-four elders come forward at their voice before God’s throne and worship, so we too ought with a harmonious voice to give honor, praise, and glory to God, and worship the one who lives for ever and ever, who rose from the dead and is to come for judgment.

Because many and ineffable mysteries concerning God have been disclosed to us in their voices, let no one doubt what the Holy Spirit dictated through them to the churches. Yet even if what they say appears clear, let no one presume that he understands everything that was proclaimed by them.

[Col. 0738B] Their speech is not contemptible, as some think, but divine; in it not eloquence shines forth, but the power of wisdom.

Meanwhile, although I too may appear unworthy of so great a work and may not understand it, I would rather be pleasing in my thoughts and effective in understanding than eloquent in words. For, as divine Scripture says: “He who is pleasing in speech will grasp greater things.”

In Greek, “pleasing” is called Χρίστος (*Christos*; perhaps χρηστός, *chrēstos*, is intended), a term said to signify “good,” “pleasing,” “gentle,” and “anointed.” All these qualities suit a good man, especially one who has been softened by the Holy Spirit, so that he may speak more wisely than eloquently.

[Col. 0738C] Therefore, although I believe that I am sufficient for none of these things, nevertheless, because I am indebted to both groups—to you, my beloved, to whom I write, and to the brothers to whom I repay the vows of service—I trust in prayers and rely upon merits, confident that he himself will grant effectiveness in speaking who granted me the resolve to fulfill the duty of charity.

# THE TENTH BOOK

[Col. 0737]

[Col. 0737C] When the chief priests and Pharisees had heard his parables, they recognized that he was speaking about them, and, while seeking to seize him, they feared the crowds, because they regarded him as a prophet.

Behold: because of the hardness of heart, unbelief, and wickedness that they possessed toward the Son of God, they hear with their ears what they refused to believe in their hearts. They hear from Christ explicit statements that they could not deny, and they understand that all the Lord’s judgments were directed against them—judgments by which they ought to have been moved toward faith.

But from the very point at which they ought to have turned toward forgiveness, they instead turn toward wickedness, so that, seeing, they do not see, and understanding, they do not understand.

In wishing to seize him in order to kill him, they feared not God but the crowds, because they regarded him as a prophet. Their desire to seize and kill him, as I have already said above, did not arise merely from ignorance that he was the Christ, but from unbelief and contempt. For, according to Solomon, “when the wicked man has come into the depths of evil, he despises.”

Therefore they do not spare themselves either, because, buried beneath many evils, they are no longer able to look toward the light.

[Col. 0738C] Whoever, then, wishes to seize Jesus falsely, deceitfully, or treacherously—or to grasp the word of truth—can never seize or grasp him.

There is, indeed, a great difference between those who seek to hold him through love and those who seek to hold him through hatred. These men seek to seize him in one way, while the bride in the Song seeks him in another. Rising, she went through the streets, going around the city and its marketplaces; and after passing through them all, scarcely finding him, she held him and said: “I will hold him and will not let him go.”

In the same way those women held his feet after the resurrection, when they worshiped him. Yet the woman who supposed him to be the gardener was not allowed to do so, to whom it was said—because she did not yet believe him to be the Word of the Father—“Do not touch me” (John 20:17).

Therefore, as I have said, no one can hold Christ, and no one can touch him, except one who does so in faith and to whom he himself permits it.

The crowds whom the rulers of the people and the priests feared were themselves being dragged here and there by waves, because they were imperfect. Perhaps they were the same people who had earlier sung “Hosanna” and said, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

[Col. 0738D] But because the wretched priests had taken away from them the key of knowledge, they could not stand firm in faith. Therefore the one whom they now venerate as a prophet, later—even if not all of them, at least some—cry out against him to please the elders: “Crucify, crucify!”

The crowds understood many true things about him, but nevertheless did not understand his greatness, just as our own common people do not.

Jesus was indeed also a prophet, as Moses says: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him according to everything that he speaks” (Deuteronomy 18:15). “Whoever does not listen to that prophet shall perish, or be exterminated, from his people.”

Nevertheless, the eminence of his majesty is not expressed by the fact that he is called a prophet, but by the fact that he is the firstborn Son of God of all creation, through whom all things in heaven and on earth were created.

[Col. 0739A] Therefore his eminence is expressed in the words: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), and so forth.

But the crowds did not yet understand this, although they were prepared to fight for him. The chief priests and scribes feared them, and therefore did not dare to seize him.

And if the crowds understood nothing great about Christ because they regarded him only as a prophet, still less did the priests and scribes, blinded by envy and hatred, who were unwilling even to accept the knowledge possessed by the common people.

For although they knew him in part to be God, they would not allow anything worthy of him to be declared to anyone.

Such, therefore, are all heretics: they themselves do not wish to believe rightly concerning Christ, nor do they permit others to confess the true faith in a catholic manner.

## (Chapter 22)

And Jesus answered and said to them again in parables:

“The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son,” and so forth.

Matthew alone appears to have narrated this parable. Nevertheless, Luke too is shown to have narrated, in his own place, something similar in large part. Hence some maintain that it is one and the same parable in both accounts, although one of them said something more—for example, concerning the man who was not clothed in a wedding garment, which the other omitted.

But this is not so, because Luke makes no mention of a wedding. Moreover, Matthew calls it a midday meal, while Luke calls it a dinner; and even if he had wished to introduce there the man who was not clothed in a wedding garment and was rejected, he could not properly have done so.

[Col. 0739B] For by that dinner the final banquet that the saints will have in the kingdom of God is certainly signified. But by the midday meal and by this wedding, to which good and evil people are summoned and enter together, the present Church is entirely understood.

For after the midday meal comes dinner, and after dinner no banquet remains, unless perhaps that same dinner is placed in the role of the midday meal, as was the custom among the ancients to dine only in the evening. In this way, to some extent, the present Church and the banquet of the Scriptures and their mysteries may be understood through the dinner itself—mysteries of which good and evil people alike feast daily until they reach that final banquet.

A response does not always refer only to what has been asked, but also to the merits of the matter and to those things that are rightly touched upon by the response, as happens here.

For he had said that the kingdom of God was to be taken away from the Jews, along with the other things he mentioned, and they were neither terrified nor moved to repentance. Instead, they were further inflamed to anger, wishing to lay hands on him.

[Col. 0740A] Understanding this, the Lord nevertheless responds through another parable and touches upon the hardness of their hearts. Because they refused to receive the antidote of salvation, after the remedies of exhortation and the ointments, he would apply the cauterizing iron and announce that a harsher vengeance was to come upon them.

Otherwise, the most merciful Savior might appear to have been afraid because they had become more exasperated, and therefore to have kept silent.

For if wickedness made them bold, immense power made Christ secure, and charity urged him to invite them tirelessly to forgiveness.

The King is more terrifying in his vengeance when he sends out his armies to destroy those murderers than the householder, who appears to take away nothing except what belongs to him.

But we must ask why he added, “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who was a man,” when he could have said it without adding “man.”

[Col. 0740B] Hence it is not without reason that the question is asked why it was necessary to add “man.”

We also have many other examples in the Gospels in which God the Father is compared to a man and represented allegorically in the person of a man. In the same parables God the Father is called “a man.”

These examples are very necessary against certain heretics who criticize the God of the Old Testament when he is introduced with human features and said to be subject to passions. From this they pretend that the God of the law and of the prophets is evil, cruel, and bloodthirsty.

Therefore let them hear from the Gospel that, in accordance with the parables and not according to nature, God the Father is called a man; and according to the sequence of the parables, one must accept an angry God, just as in the Old Testament, together with his fury and patience, the turning away of his face, and God’s sitting, standing, walking, and sleeping.

All these things are written about God in the law and the prophets and are displayed from the beginning.

If God has nothing figuratively in himself that appears or is called human, since he is immense, incomparable, and incorporeal, then let the heretics say whether this God who, according to the Gospel parables, is called a man and presented as angry according to human nature is the Father of Christ or someone other than him.

[Col. 0740C] They are necessarily compelled either to say that someone else besides this God is the Father of Christ—although the parables also show this man to be the Father of Christ and present him as similar to human nature—or, if they say that this same God is the Father of Christ, they are compelled to confess that many things are said of him according to the passible nature of human beings.

This does not mean that the Father is passible, but that, because of our weakness, these things are said about God according to the passible nature of man, so that our infancy may be able to grasp something concerning him, at least in accordance with human customs.

For as long as we are human beings, we cannot grasp God according to himself, nor comprehend the multitude of his greatness with our understanding. Therefore it was necessary to add, “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who was a man,” so that he might speak to human beings among human beings as a man.

[Col. 0740D] For if he were to speak according to himself, inasmuch as he is God, no mortal could endure it.

God accommodates himself to human beings who are unable to be sufficiently accommodated by God, because he is wholly God even in the way he accommodates himself to human beings. Hence it was necessary to add “man.”

For God the Father did not speak to us human beings according to himself, but according to our customs; and he still speaks in a human manner, until it is said to us: “I have said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’” (Psalm 81:6).

Then, I believe, these comparisons will cease, when God is seen as he is and when the Son himself openly announces to us the Father who made the wedding feast for his son.

Since the persons of the Father and the Son are now manifest—the one for whom the wedding was made and the one who made it—this parable must be distinguished according to the times in which the wedding took place, because to make a wedding belongs both to an author and to a time.

[Col. 0741A] We read in another parable that the time of the wedding will be in the future, when five of the ten virgins who are prepared will enter with Christ the bridegroom into the wedding for which these are believed to have been made.

Therefore, if the present passage concerns that wedding, it is a new problem that he should have invited them to the same wedding while also saying that it had already taken place.

But because this wedding is the entrance into heavenly life, and the mystery of eternal glory is to be received through the resurrection, it is not without reason that the wedding is said already to have been made by the Father.

For the fellowship of this eternity and the dispensation of the new body had already been perfectly accomplished in Christ. This new and unheard-of union took place when, in the Virgin’s womb, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

For just as the resurrection of all the elect is in Christ’s resurrection, so this wedding was celebrated in him; and the Church was joined to the bridegroom by the right of betrothal when the God-man received the gifts of the Holy Spirit in their fullness and the entire divinity dwelt bodily in him.

[Col. 0741B] From these gifts, as I have said, the bride has already received, by the right of betrothal, the gifts of the same Holy Spirit as her dowry and pledge—the Spirit who remained wholly in Christ from the time he became man and came forth like a bridegroom from the Virgin’s womb, because her womb was his bridal chamber.

But the Church, reborn in the same Spirit through water, becomes one body in Christ, “so that the two may be one flesh,” which is a great mystery in Christ and in the Church (Ephesians 5:32).

The time of the wedding extends from the beginning of Christ’s incarnation until Christ himself returns, so that all the mysteries of the wedding may be completed.

Then those who have lawfully preserved the rights of so great a betrothal and are prepared will enter with him, in the proper manner, into that eternal wedding.

Meanwhile the wife and bride is being given to Christ the man, and is betrothed daily in faith and mercy until he himself returns.

[Col. 0741C] Hence Paul said: “For I have betrothed you to one man, to present a pure virgin to Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:2), so that when he comes, the Church gathered together from both Jews and Gentiles may be embraced as one bride, spouse, and wife.

For all the saints of the Old Testament who existed from the beginning of the world belong to this wedding. Through faith, though they saw it from afar, they believed that Christ would come in the flesh for the salvation of the human race.

Hence it is said that Abel offered a lamb as a figure of Christ. “And the Lord looked upon him and upon his gifts” (Genesis 4:4). He looked upon him, as we read elsewhere, because he kindled him.

[Col. 0741D] Therefore we rightly say that every nation of the human race was invited to this wedding through the law of nature.

For some copies have here not “his servants,” in the plural, but “his servant,” in the singular; and by this servant Moses may perhaps rightly be understood.

But if we read “servants,” as it is also found in the Greek, we must understand most clearly the prophets proclaiming Christ’s incarnation.

But they were unwilling to come at first, because they refused to believe.

Again he sent other servants, saying: “Tell those who have been invited: Behold, I have prepared my meal; my bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding.”

He sent twice because prophets were sent first, and then apostles, so that what the prophets had previously announced as future might afterward be presented and administered through the apostles, and confirmed by deeds. Although some say that he sent twice because he sent prophets of a second rank, it is better to refer this second invitation—since more servants were sent above—to the apostles, through whom it is now expressly said: “Behold, I have prepared my meal,” and so forth.

For by the bulls the Fathers of the Old Testament are rightly understood, since, by the strength of the body, they were permitted, as it were, to strike with the horn and to take vengeance on their enemies, as it is said **[Col. 0742C]**: “And you shall hate your enemy.” Moreover, by the fattened animals the Fathers of the New Testament are signified, because they were more abundantly and perfectly fattened by the grace of the Holy Spirit. For in Greek it does not have *altilia* (“fattened animals”), but “fattened things”; hence *altilia* is also said to derive from *alere* (“to nourish”). And therefore we rightly call the apostles and apostolic men *altilia*, because, while they are fattened by the grace of inward richness, they are lifted on wings toward the higher gifts of contemplation.

All these things are rightly said to have been slaughtered and prepared, and he says: “Come to the wedding.” It is as though he were saying: “Look upon the mountains of the preceding Fathers, on account of their faith; and, instructed by their examples in faith, consider the remedies for your life and seek the food of the eternal banquet.”

How fitting, then, that in the first invitation nothing is said about bulls, whereas in the second **[Col. 0742D]** both bulls and fattened animals are mentioned as slaughtered, and everything as prepared. For almighty God, when we are willing to hear words, very often joins examples to them, in order to convict human perversity, so that no one may plead impossibility.

Nevertheless, the bulls and fattened animals said to have been slaughtered would never have been slaughtered for Christ’s wedding as food for the banqueters, unless they themselves had first **[908]** already been fed and nourished by the banquet of the word of God. For whoever is hungry with respect to this banquet of the Word does not truly live, because “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV, 4).

Truly, the words of God are the meal of eternal life; and whoever has been fattened by them grows rich at the spiritual banquet, is filled with the Holy Spirit, and expands in understanding; he is nourished **[Col. 0743A]** by faith and grows in charity. But whoever fasts from these things is emptied of spirit, weakened in understanding, and dried up in faith. At times, moreover, through deprivation of nourishment, he falls into death.

And because all were invited from the beginning of faith to this wedding meal, we ought to go out with faithful Abraham from the land of our flesh and from the kinship of vices. To him it was said: “Come into the land that I shall show you” (Gen. II, 1). This land, unquestionably, is the land of the living, for which David sighs, saying: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI, 13).

And if you ask, reader, when this invitation of the Jews began, hear the Lord inviting our father Abraham, who was called the father of many nations. To him it was said: “All the land upon which your foot shall tread I shall give to you and to your seed after you forever”—the land, certainly, flowing with milk and honey, by which every soul that takes part in God’s banquet is nourished and fed.

**[Col. 0743B]** God the Father established this banquet in Christ and prepared the wedding meal. For it is not from this earth, since eternal fellowship is celebrated in it; nor is it from the earth of this age, since milk and honey have never flowed from it. Rather, it is that rational land which Christ assumed, from which our infancy is nourished, from which every sweetness flows, and in which the wedding feast is prepared.

When Christ was saying these things, the wedding was already in him, because of the joining and assumption of the new human being, which is the great sacrament in Christ and in the Church.

Perhaps, then, someone asks whether those who lived before Abraham were invited. We have already shown this in Abel. Let him himself look through all the Fathers and understand in whose figure Noah built the ark, lest anyone perish; and he will be able to see that from the beginning all were invited to this wedding and to this banquet, although they were unwilling to come in faith.

**[Col. 0743C]** So even today there are many who do not wish to enter this ark—that is, the Church of Christ—nor to accept with us the covenant of marriage or the banquet. This meal, like the wedding itself, is tasted beforehand here, but in that eternal **[909]** satisfaction it will be enjoyed in full.

Meanwhile, as though it were a royal banquet, it is adorned with many kinds of delicacies and decorated with various Scriptures as with dishes and courses, so that there you will find whatever sweetness exists and whatever eternal pleasantness.

**[Col. 0743D]** But although everything had thus already been prepared in Christ, “they went away, one to his own farm and another to his business; but the rest seized his servants, treated them outrageously, and killed them.”

These things are shown to refer both to the first calling of the Jews and to the second. For they treated not only the prophets but also the apostles outrageously, and killed many of them. Yet not all the Jews did this, but the scribes, Pharisees, and elders of the people.

Therefore those who, occupied with other matters, were unwilling to come are guilty of a lesser crime than those who not only despised the command of the one calling them, but also turned his benefits, kindness, and gracious favor into injury and extreme cruelty. For the insult offered to those who are sent is proved to be contempt for the one who sent them. Their insolence even reaches injury against the bridegroom and insult against the wedding.

**[Col. 0744A]** It should also be noted in this parable that he was silent about his own sacrifice, although in another parable above he had already spoken of himself, on account of whose hatred these things also occurred.

The distinction between the two groups—those who go to the farm and those who go to the business—depicts all the activities that people carry on in this world as necessary to life. Their activity is of two kinds: it either cultivates a farm or conducts business.

To go to the farm, therefore, is to work the land or to perform some earthly task with one’s hands—for example, to work a field or vineyard, or to carry out work in wood or iron, or some other craft. While they work all these things with their hands, to inhabit the farm means to engage in earthly labor.

**[Col. 0744B]** But when they obtain profits not through the labor of their hands but from elsewhere—for example, when they seek honors, remain in military service, trade for the sake of some merchandise, or toil in some other pursuit—all these things are properly called business.

With these two words he has enclosed every human activity. But in this passage he condemned only what is done dishonestly and immoderately. What can be done honestly and moderately he does not reproach, as Solomon says: “Do not hate farming, for it was created by the Most High” (Eccli. VII, 16). The Apostle also labors with his own hands by day and night, and commands others to labor. “I urge you, brothers,” he says, “to make it your aim to live quietly, **[910]** working with your own hands, so that you may lack nothing from those who are outside.”

For every activity or business undertaken for the sake of shameful profit is rightly judged dishonorable.

**[Col. 0744C]** Someone might perhaps say in response: What sin is it to go to the farm? If business, military service, or the pursuit of honor is scarcely ever, or never, without sin, cultivating a farm is not sinful.

Nor do we say that it is—unless any of these things recalls you from faith or from the religion of Christ, and becomes an impediment preventing you from following Christ. That is sin.

Therefore cultivating farms is not sin; rather, by preferring it to God, you make it sin for yourself, because whoever wishes to be a friend of this age will be established as an enemy of God.

And therefore some works are works of righteousness, which we ought to perform attentively; others are for our sustenance, and these we should carry out only in passing and without anxiety, because no one serving God entangles himself in worldly affairs.

**[Col. 0744D]** This twofold distinction produces one kind of negligence, but it signifies two classes among the Jews. Through occupation with the farm he indicates the common people, or the popular multitude, whom love of the world separated from Christ. Through business, however, he signifies the priests, rulers of the people, and the other ministers of the temple, whom the pursuit of profit, the favor of honor, or avarice and ambition for possessions drew away from faith in Christ.

They themselves, suffocated by anxieties and riches, bore no fruit.

Among all these, then, there are some who were unwilling to come at first; some who neglected the invitation, entangled in the loves of the world; and others who stubbornly laid hands on the king’s servants and killed them.

But in the wedding also, if you consider the customary order of weddings carefully, there is one bride who marries, there are various invitees of different ranks who issue the invitations, and there are those who are invited to the wedding. Although different degrees of merit are represented, there is nevertheless one bride in all these things for whom the wedding is prepared; and within her are both those who invite and those who are invited.

God knows all these orders of individuals, as well as the virtues and causes of their souls, and how each one is received into the union of the bride.

**[Col. 0745A]** Nevertheless, all ought to be one Church, so that no one in it fails to call both himself and others to the wedding banquet; and no one fails to understand that he has been invited and remains in the body of the bridegroom and the bride. Likewise, we have said that the workers of the vineyard are one vineyard, renewed through faith in the vine that is Christ.

Accordingly, whoever has been invited, according to the Apocalypse of John, and hears, should also say: “Come,” so that the activity **[911]** of all and the hope of each person’s calling may be one.

**[Col. 0745B]** But when the king heard this, he was angry.

He preserves the particular character of the parable, but not without a great lesson in understanding. For above he had said: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who was a king.” Here, however, he is not called a man, but only a king. I would say that this was not done without reason: where God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is called both king and man, he prepares the wedding for his son in a sufficiently figurative comparison; here, however, he is called only king, when he is also introduced as angry, because he has heard that his servants were treated outrageously and killed by those to whom he was freely preparing to grant his benefits.

And because vengeance had justly to be exacted upon them, he is rightly represented as angry. For, if above he had not been represented as a man in the parable, we would have been less able to understand the wedding of the son.

So that our understanding might be able to receive these attributes in relation to God, he is first introduced as king and man when he invites to the wedding and performs works of mercy. At that point the name “man” is openly supplied. Now, when the discourse hastens toward vengeance, “man” is properly left unmentioned; he is called only king and is introduced as angry, because the king’s anger is a messenger of death—not because anger falls upon God, but because the parable preserves its figurative logic.

He sent out his armies, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city with fire. For he has countless armies of his own, and therefore he is rightly called *Dominus sabaoth*, that is, “the Lord,” or “the king, of armies.”

**[Col. 0745D]** The armies he sent may be understood as avenging angels, or as the sending of punishments—of which it is said in the Psalms, “a sending through evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII, 49)—or we may understand the Roman army under the command of Vespasian and Titus. After killing and dispersing the peoples of Judaea in God’s vengeance, they burned the treacherous city and laid everything waste.

Before these things were fulfilled, however, they stoned Stephen and even rejoiced at the death of James; they also stoned James the son of Alphaeus. Because of all these things, wretched Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans.

It should be noted that the Roman army is called God’s army and his avengers, because it would never have come against it unless the Lord had summoned it, as we often read in the prophets.

Then he said to his servants: “The wedding is indeed ready, but those who had been invited were not worthy.”

**[Col. 0746A]** It is as though he said: “Neither those who were unwilling to come at first, nor those who eventually **[912]** neglected the invitation, nor those who killed my servants: Go therefore to the exits of the roads, and invite to the wedding all whom you find, both good and bad.”

For the apostles did not first go to the exits of the roads until the Jews themselves had judged themselves unworthy of eternal life and cast them out from themselves as something evil. Then, compelled by God’s command, they went out to the Gentiles, whom they found not on the roads of God but at the exits of various roads.

**[Col. 0746B]** For just as the ways of the Lord are straight, so the ways of the world are diverse and innumerable, according to the errors and inventions of individuals. For example, there is the profession of philosophy, which tends toward various doctrines; or the practice of worshiping many gods; and also the will of individuals, in accordance with what the poet sings: “Each person is led by his own will.”

All these roads outside the road of God are the exits of the roads of the world. There also, outside, at the head of all the roads, Wisdom cries out and raises her voice in the streets, saying: “If anyone loves wisdom, let him turn aside to me and come to me; he will find her, and when he has found her, he will be blessed if he holds fast to her.”

And the servants went out, according to the command of their master, from Judaea—or, if they are angels of peace, from the inner boundaries of Jerusalem—and gathered all whom they found, good and bad; and the wedding hall was filled with those reclining at table.

They are not called bad so that they should remain bad; nor does he say that they called the good so that their goodness would be sufficient for them unto life.

Hence the question is not without reason: How are those called good who had not yet received the gift of grace, without which no one is good?

**[Col. 0746C]** This question is easily resolved if the Apostle’s words are brought into consideration, where he says that even among the Gentiles, in some sense, people are found good by comparison with the Jews. For he says thus (Rom. II, 14): “The Gentiles, who by nature do the things of the law, show the work of the law written in their hearts; and although they do not have the law, they are a law to themselves.”

Yet they are not thereby so good that they do not need the grace of God. Therefore they are, in some sense, called good together with the bad, so that all may become good together through the gift and grace of God, by which all the crimes of their former life are forgiven and gifts are bestowed.

**[Col. 0746D]** For this reason those who were sent to the exits of the roads are commanded to go out: because, at the end of time, all past faults are forgiven when the failure of human activity has come to an end.

He therefore rightly commands the good and the bad to be called together, since God’s calling is holy and supremely good, making all good together—unless someone remains, through an incurable vice of pleasure, in a state of **[913]** peril.

Thus it follows: “But the king entered to see those reclining at table.”

Wonderful and ineffable is the meaning of saying that the king enters, although he is everywhere and is absent nowhere and never, and although there is no place where he is not, since he fills all things.

His entering, however, means that he examines and looks upon the minds of individuals, into which no other person can enter or look. For, according to the usage of Scripture, when he looks upon someone—whether by approval or by rejection—he is said to be present; but where he wills neither of these, he appears absent, while each person is left to his own judgment.

**[Col. 0747A]** When the day of inspection, or judgment, comes in the resurrection, then he will enter to inspect the consciences of all and will penetrate the assembly of that resurrection, to see the deeds of each person and to approve the condition of all.

“When he looked around,” he says, “he saw there a man not clothed in a wedding garment.” This does not mean that on the day of that examination this one individual alone will be found without a wedding garment; rather, according to the usage of Scripture, one is placed for all whose lot and interrogation will be one.

The question will not concern bodily clothing, but the clothing of the mind and the garment of virtues.

Hence he says: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” This is the question of which it is said: “There will be an interrogation in the thoughts of the ungodly” (Wis. I, 9).

Had the king specified the clothing of those to be invited when he commanded that everyone, good and bad, should be invited? Or could everyone in that assembly have possessed the same clothing or disposition of soul? Especially since, if there ought to have been some customary external clothing among those attending a wedding, the invitees and attendants might perhaps have prevented such a person from entering.

**[Col. 0747B]** But it is not given to everyone to discern the wickedness of the bad within their consciences, since human simplicity can scarcely detect the fraudulence of a feigned mind. Therefore this wicked assembly of sinners, whose sins will neither be forgiven nor covered, will be discovered by God alone—the terrible and great King, who sees the consciences of individuals.

**[Col. 0747C]** And because all come to this wedding badly clothed, the Apostle cries out to us every day: “Put off the old man with his deeds, which is corrupted according to the desires of error; and put on the new man, who was created according to God in the **[914]** righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. IV, 23–24).

What he says, “in righteousness,” pertains to our entire manner of life, so that, as Solomon says, “our garments may be white at all times” (Eccl. IX, 8). But “in the holiness of truth” pertains to the pure conscience of faith.

For just as the works of sinners are filthy and corruptible, so the works of the righteous are white and beautiful, incorruptible and holy; and in them charity reigns above all.

**[Col. 0747D]** When he calls him “friend,” this is more a reproach than an expression of affection. It is as though he were saying: “Friend by faith, by the pretense of faith, and by hypocrisy, but not friend through conduct—how did you come in here without a wedding garment?”

This does not mean that anyone brought the garment to this wedding from himself, but that all who are baptized put on Christ, the new man, so that thereafter they might walk in newness of life, in righteousness and in the holiness of truth.

If this man had not lost that righteousness and holiness, he would never have been questioned so severely, nor, once questioned, would he have become so completely silent. For where there is no excuse, the response is rightly unwilling in those whom an evil conscience accuses inwardly and against whom it cries out.

**[Col. 0748A]** Then the king said to the attendants—that is, to the attendants of punishment: “Bind his feet and hands, and cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Therefore, just as there is a difference in glory and a differing brightness among the saints, as the Apostle testifies, so there are also differing punishments of torments.

There are inner darknesses, that is, of the heart; and there are outer darknesses, concerning which we have already said that it is not without reason that the one who has been blinded inwardly in his soul by the darkness of sins until the end of life is justly cast into the outer darkness.

**[Col. 0748B]** Because he does not say that the king entered to reward his friends, nor that he gathered everyone together at once, some suspect that this is not said of the future judgment. Especially since he does not say, “Cast him into the lower darkness,” so that we might understand by “lower darkness” the lower regions of hell, as in the passage: “You have delivered my soul from the lower hell” (Ps. LXXXV, 13).

For just as there are inner darknesses, so there are outer ones; and just as there are lower ones, so there are also final ones, which are in the furthest places.

Therefore, even now, as they themselves wish to understand it, when some approach the banquet of Scripture, or the body and blood of Christ, stained by vices and crimes and not clothed in a wedding garment, they are sometimes blinded for the worse by the spirit of error through God’s just judgment. Thus those who were hidden within become manifest outwardly, and, while he walks over precipices, what John says in his **[915]** Apocalypse comes to pass: “Let the one who does harm still do more harm, and let the one who is in filth become still filthier” (Apoc. XXII, 11).

Thus, with their feet and hands already bound, they may be driven by an unclean spirit, so that they can never free themselves.

**[Col. 0748C]** But we judge that all these things are better understood of the future judgment, lest despair arise in anyone, when the whole multitude of the wicked, gathered together, is driven from that inner banquet of eternal satisfaction and sweetness and is cast outside, with hands and feet bound, into the outer darkness, so that they can no longer do either good or evil, nor pass from evil to good.

For the works of a person are rightly understood as the hands, just as his movements are understood as the feet. These hands and feet are then rightly bound by the strictness of the sentence, because here, while it was permitted through amendment of life, they were unwilling to be bound from evil works; so then punishment will bind those whom guilt now bound from good works.

Moreover, where hands and feet are bound, and where weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth are mentioned, the truth of the resurrection is altogether proclaimed.

**[Col. 0748D]** And when they are cast into the outer darkness, they will not be scattered everywhere indiscriminately, as some have recently begun to chatter; nor will the rejected be locally mixed indiscriminately with the good.

For whether they wish it or not, if they have bodies, they will truly be in a place and will not be everywhere. They will indeed be separated from one another: heaven and the new earth will retain the righteous, who will have been renewed, as the divine voice cries out: “Behold, I make all things new” (Apoc. XXI, 5); the places of punishment will retain the others, outside this new heaven and new earth.

Therefore, in the outer darkness they will be alienated from the light, where there is a fire prepared for the devil and his angels, with whom these too will be.

For this reason, as they wish to understand it, they will not be without the punishments of flames, in which there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

**[Col. 0749A]** He said “there will be,” and not “there is,” because before the day of the resurrection there will be no human bodies in hell.

Although the aforementioned *philocumphi*—more *philocumphi* than philosophers—whisper that in this air, in which demons sometimes move about according to the Apostle, souls also dwell there in punishment, and that they are tormented there more by their own conscience than by other forms of punishment.

They do not consider that the things prepared by the Lord for the devil and his angels were not prepared in this way by them for themselves, or by these men for themselves; rather, they say that, through God’s foreknowledge, those things were prepared by which they would be punished for their wickedness, and that these men likewise, together with the bodies in which they sinned, would be tortured against their will for their crimes, by God’s just judgment, in the place where “there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Luke XIII, 38).

By this metaphor of bodily members, the magnitude of the torments is shown. **[916]**

“Many are called, but few are chosen.”

**[Col. 0749B]** The small number of those invited is not being described, but the small number of the chosen. For in the invitation, without any exception, there is the greatness of immense goodness; but among those invited there is the discrimination of judgment and the choosing of virtue.

This sentence embraces and concludes all these parables: the one concerning the work of the vineyard, the one concerning the building of the house, and this one as well. In all of them, it is not the beginnings of works that are sought, but their end.

Then the Pharisees went away and took counsel in order to trap him in his speech.

**[Col. 0749C]** That is, this happened when the chief priests had heard these parables and recognized that he was speaking about them. For although Mark and Luke omitted this parable of the wedding, which was inserted in the middle, the Savior nevertheless, at the point where they recognized that he was speaking about them and wished to seize him, brought this parable of the wedding against them.

And because they did not dare to seize him on account of the crowds, they went away and took counsel quite treacherously, in order to trap him in his speech.

From this it is clear that they sinned not through ignorance, but because they were blinded by deliberate evil. Therefore, after everything that had been brought against them, they were not moved to repentance, but went away with deceit.

And where did they go? To the Herodians, certainly, and they took counsel with them: the wicked with the worst.

Truly, the chief priests and the officials of the temple did not deliberate with them about counsel, but about fraud and deceit, because there is no counsel and no knowledge against God.

**[Col. 0749D]** And since the counselors were of such a kind, they received counsel of the same kind. Therefore, through an evil plan, they now send their disciples with the Herodians, as though the disciples were less well known and less suspect, so that either they might more easily seize him secretly, or, if they could not trap him, might themselves suffer less shame.

Although they had often been caught in evil counsel, they were proportionately less ashamed as their minds, blocked by treachery, became worse.

The disciples whom they sent, although lower in rank, were nevertheless their equals in wickedness, like children of vipers and serpents: although younger in age, they are equal in venom.

**[Col. 0750A]** They say to him: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth.”

They call him “Teacher,” but craftily; and they flatter him as truthful, so that, captured by their honor or praise, he might disclose the mystery of his heart to them in simplicity.

For this reason they had sent these men with the Herodians: through the former he might be deceived by soothing words, and through the latter, by contradicting Caesar and saying that tribute ought not to be paid, he might be held as guilty before Caesar.

For the Herodians were servants of King Herod, whom Caesar Augustus had recently appointed king over Judaea. Judaea had not long been subject **[917]** to the Romans when the census was proclaimed throughout the whole world and the country was made tributary to them.

**[Col. 0750B]** Hence there was still a great sedition among the Jewish people. Some said that, since the Romans served on behalf of everyone for security and peace, the Jews ought to pay tribute, as had been decreed by the Senate.

But the Pharisees, who applauded themselves for their own righteousness, resisted in the opposite direction and said that the people of God, who paid tithes and gave firstfruits and observed the other things commanded in the law, ought not to be subject to human laws.

Accordingly, as history relates, there arose a certain Judas the Galilean, whom Luke also mentions in the Acts of the Apostles. Gathering a large multitude of Jews with him, he taught that tribute ought not to be given to Caesar, and that neither a lord nor Caesar ought to be acknowledged. He also attempted to defend this with arms, but the king’s soldiers suddenly crushed such efforts.

**[Col. 0750C]** Therefore they send these men with the Herodians—that is, with Herod’s soldiers—or with those Jews who paid tribute to the Romans, whom the Pharisees mockingly called Herodians as being more devoted to Herod than to divine worship.

Sent together for this reason, they say: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth. You are not concerned with anyone, nor do you regard the person of human beings. Tell us, therefore: What do you think? Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar or not?”

With flattery, but craftily and deceitfully, they provoke him to answer, so that he might show that he feared and venerated God more than Caesar and say that tribute ought not to be paid. Then the Herodians, hearing it immediately, could hold him as guilty—as the author of sedition and an opponent of Caesar—although they themselves had not dared to kill him; or otherwise he could be accused as guilty before God.

**[Col. 0750D]** But Jesus, knowing their wickedness, said: “Why are you testing me, hypocrites?”

For it is a power of divinity to know and look into their thoughts and consciences. Therefore he did not answer the flattering words, but addressed what they had maliciously and venomously gathered in their hearts. To their hard hearts he returned a hard answer, calling them not disciples but tempters and hypocrites.

It is characteristic of hypocrites to conceal one thing in the heart and to pretend something else in their actions or to display something else in their words.

Therefore the Savior strikes what they had within them with the hammer of his word when he calls them hypocrites, so that they may find within their hearts what they hear externally with their ears, and may recognize Christ as the knower of human hearts, lest they dare to carry out what they had very treacherously planned to do.

“Show me,” he says, “the coin of the tribute.”

And they offered him a denarius.

Wisdom always **[918]** acts wisely in all things, and so distributes its answers that it refutes its tempters by their own words.

**[Col. 0751A]** “Show me the coin of the tribute”—that is, the denarius, which was counted as ten coins and bore the image of Caesar.

And the most gracious Jesus said to them: “Whose image and inscription is this?”

This question clearly does not arise from ignorance, since no one was unaware of what everyone observed and saw publicly; rather, it was asked so that he might respond appropriately to their words.

For in them he was seeking nothing more than his own image.

How fittingly, therefore, he says: “Give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

It is as though he were saying: “The image of God is not painted in gold, but sculpted and formed inwardly in the heart. I see that image violated because of your wickedness. Therefore, since Caesar’s coin is gold, give it back to Caesar; and since God’s coin is the whole human being, created in the image of God, give yourselves back to God.”

**[Col. 0751B]** You cannot do this at all unless you first strip yourselves of Caesar’s tribute, so that thereafter you may be free.

Therefore first give back what is alien, so that you may be able to possess what is yours. Just as Caesar’s image is paid back on the coin, so let the true image of God be restored in your hearts, where the heavenly treasure is kept in the conscience; and the divine hand has marked that image with the strokes of the Ten Commandments.

**[Col. 0751C]** Thus, although God must be honored before and above all things, a proper order must nevertheless be observed in this matter: not first to give to God what belongs to God, but to give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar.

Then, once freed from these matters, give to God whatever belongs to God, so that you may not again have to entangle yourselves in such affairs.

Otherwise, to offer yourselves first to God while retaining another’s interest is a perverse order, if you are again reduced under the rule of your former life.

O how provident in all things is God’s wisdom, and how effective is the response! So that no one could bring an accusation against it by deceit, he commanded with perfect order what all must fulfill who wish to leave the world and come to Christ: let him give to Caesar and to the world what belongs to Caesar—the gold—and let him give to God what belongs to God.

It can also be understood simply: just as he commands money and tribute to be paid to Caesar, so he also commands that what belongs to God be given to God—that is, tithes, firstfruits, offerings, sacrifices, and everything contained in the law.

For he himself paid tribute for himself and Peter; and he gave to God what belongs to God, fulfilling the will of the Father **[919]** in all things.

He also tempered this response, full of divine mysteries and a perfect exposition of the heavenly saying, with such wondrous balance between contempt for the world and avoiding insult to Caesar, that he freed minds devoted to God from every human concern and duty when he decreed that what belonged to Caesar should be given back to Caesar.

**[Col. 0751D]** But wretched is the custom of Gaul, which is held so tightly bound by debts in the affairs of the churches and by the burdens of unlawful exaction.

If the world did not know how to hold us by its laws, we would never be compelled, under an imposed condition of servitude, to give back to it what belongs to it.

Therefore blessed is the one who first made himself free from these things. More blessed is the one who gives himself wholly to God—body, soul, and will, increased daily toward what is better—so that he may serve willingly and entirely the one from whom he remembers that he has received his origin and growth.

**[Col. 0752A]** It follows: “And when they heard this, they marveled; and they left him and went away.”

Behold, those who ought to have believed at such teaching marveled. From this both the hardness of their hearts is shown and the divine nature of the teaching is proclaimed.

For although they had come maliciously, they were moved to admiration because their cunning attempt at entrapment had found no opening, and they no longer dared to question him.

Therefore, having left him, they went away, carrying their unbelief with them along with their amazement.

On that day the Sadducees, who say that there is no resurrection, approached him. On what day? Surely on the day when the Pharisees had withdrawn. For although they were divided from one another, in this one matter they were united, as though wicked men, in hating Jesus and capturing him by their schemes. For this purpose they take turns approaching one another, again and again, to weary him with their plots, competing to see who, by the ingenuity of his entire art, might catch him first. Thus, if they could not overcome him by reasoning, at least through the repeated exercise of their cunning they might confuse his understanding, so that he would be unable to anticipate what they would answer. For each wished to show himself wiser than the others if he could ensnare him in his traps.

There were indeed two sects among the Jews: one of the Pharisees and the other of the Sadducees. The Pharisees possessed traditions and observances, which they call in Greek *deuterōseis* (“second laws” or “additional traditions”), by which they set themselves above others as more righteous; hence they were also called “separated” from the people. The Sadducees, however, whose name is interpreted as “righteous,” likewise applauded themselves for their own righteousness, saying that there was neither resurrection of the body nor of souls; nor, according to the Acts of the Apostles, did they say that angels or spirit existed. 920

These are the two houses of which Isaiah speaks plainly. Hence I wonder why they were called “righteous” among the people, since the whole virtue of conduct by which anyone is righteous consists in hope for the future. For who would devote himself against himself to daily struggles unless because of the hope of resurrection? Otherwise the whole practice of piety is dissolved.

But since these men did not believe in resurrection, how could they believe in marriages after death? I would certainly not say that they believed this could happen when they denied resurrection itself. They did not believe that souls existed after death or that bodies would be raised; rather, like the Pharisees, they sought to butt with both horns and to shut him inescapably into defending their error and magnifying their own praise.

They thought they could entrap him in this way: just as it was impossible for a woman who had been the wife of seven husbands afterward to belong exclusively to one or to be held in common by all, so it was impossible for there to be a resurrection of the dead.
