And so, cunningly, when they had seen that the Pharisees had already been defeated and silenced, they asked him:

“Teacher, Moses said that if someone dies without having a son, his brother should marry his wife and raise up offspring for his brother. Now there were among us seven brothers, and the first, after marrying a wife, died, and so forth.”

They therefore invent this extremely sordid marriage story—whether it actually happened among them or not—in order to make the claims of those who assert the resurrection of the dead appear delirious. Hence they say: “In the resurrection, then, whose wife of the seven will she be? For they all had her.” They bring forward the indecency of the story in order to deny the truth of the resurrection, as though he would not dare to say that any one of them ought to claim her for himself by the legitimate right of marriage. If he could not answer them honorably, then, whether he wished it or not, he would have to concede the palm of victory to their side.

It seemed difficult to them to prove that one man would have her. But if he said that all would have her equally, he would be accused of teaching an utterly shameful matter in that blessed life, since at present two are said to be one flesh, not eight.

In reply Jesus said to them: “You are mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.” But the question arises what the kindly Savior meant when he said, “You are mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.” Is it stated somewhere in the Scriptures of the Old Testament that there will be no marriages in the resurrection, or that human beings will have to become like angels, since it is not openly apparent where such things are written? Yet he speaks as though this had been stated in some Scriptures.

But, as I have said, this is plainly not read in the Old Testament, unless, as some wish, it is found in allegorical figures which, as if in a mystery, indicate an understanding of this kind. When the marriages of Abraham are explained and mention is made of his concubines, they do not wish the statement to be understood principally of those marriages alone, but of marriages such as we have interpreted as referring to Christ and the Church, and such as will exist in that age, in which equality with the angels will be compared. Let them see what they say, provided that they speak as Catholics. We, however, say that the wisdom of God wisely rebukes their negligence when it says: “You are mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.”

Because they did not read, they were ignorant of God; and they were ignorant because they did not understand Christ as God in those same Scriptures. Otherwise, just as knowledge of God arises from diligent reading, so ignorance is the daughter of negligence. Yet not everyone who reads comes to know God, because some read wrongly while others do not wish to live worthily before God. And so, in reading, they do not seek God; rather, they seek knowledge of God for empty glory. For this reason they rightly never find him, like the philosophers and the other wise men of the world.

When the Lord had said, “You do not know the power of God,” he referred this to the fact that in the resurrection “they neither marry nor are given in marriage,” as other codices have it, “they do not take wives.” But when he says, “You are mistaken because you do not know the Scriptures,” he explained this with reference to indicating the resurrection of the dead: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” If they had perished by dying, as these men wrongly believed, he would never be called the God of those who did not exist.

Thus the most kindly Teacher gave two answers because they were both slandering and questioning him. Against their slanders he set the authority of sacred Scripture; against their question, an argument. He first presented the argument, because through ignorance they thought they knew something, gently teaching them that in the resurrection “they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but will be like the angels in heaven.” Then, to crush their slander, he brought forward the authority of Scripture, saying:

“Regarding the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was spoken when God said to you: ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’?”

So also, when people question us with whatever intention of mind, we ought first to set out the argument and afterward confirm the same matter by authority, so that, if it is a slander, it may be refuted, but if it is a simple question, it may be instructed. And it should be noted that the Jews’ confrontation with Jesus is always weaker. Their first question above was made with terror and threatening authority: “By what authority do you do these things?” The second was made with deceit: they did not threaten him but surrounded and sought to deceive him with praise. Against the former came the sharpest wisdom, just as against their terrors came unconquerable strength.

Here, in the third place, they approach neither with terror nor with much deceit, but out of great presumption and the blindness of ignorance, supposing that they could defeat Christ while he proclaimed the resurrection. As for the reading found in our codices, “neither will they marry,” Latin usage does not correspond to the Greek idiom. *Nubere* properly refers to women, while for men it means “to take wives,” as another translator rendered it. Let us nevertheless understand the statement simply: *nubere* is said of men, and *nubi* of wives.

To prove the truth of the resurrection, he could also have used many clearer testimonies, among them this one: “The dead will be raised, and those who are in the tombs will rise.” And elsewhere: “Many of those sleeping in the dust of the earth will rise, some to life, others to disgrace and everlasting confusion.” It is therefore rightly asked why the Lord did not wish to bring forward this testimony. Perhaps it seemed ambiguous, or not sufficiently suitable for proving the resurrection.

And so, after producing the present testimony, as though he had proved what he wished, he immediately confirms and concludes by saying: “He is not the God of the dead but of the living.” For this reason the crowds, hearing the mystery and recognizing it, marveled at his teaching and answer. He fully instructed them concerning what they did not know and in which they were mistaken, by the authority of God and the testimony of Scripture; and he showed the power of God when he proclaimed the resurrection and declared fellowship with the angels.

He does not mean that bodies, or the members of the body, or either sex will not rise, as some heretics have thought. Rather, human beings will be immortal, and the members of the body will be spiritual. In this age, because we die, we are born; and because we are born, we take wives. Remove the necessity of dying, and the usefulness of being born will disappear. Remove again the usefulness of being born, and the reason for marrying is dissolved.

Therefore human beings will remain human in their own nature, not transferred into the nature of angels, but made spiritual in their own nature, 923 just as the angels in heaven are immortal and incorruptible, joined to them in glory as equals, without marriage.

Nevertheless, as I had proposed, the Lord used this testimony concerning the resurrection because the Sadducees, who did not believe that an angel or any spirit existed and did not confess the resurrection of the flesh, also preached the destruction of souls. They accepted only the five books of Moses and rejected the prophecies of the prophets. It would therefore have been foolish to produce testimonies from a source whose authority they did not accept and whose teaching they did not follow.

For this reason, with great foresight, to prove the eternity of souls he takes an example from Moses: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” and immediately adds: “He is not the God of the dead but of the living,” in order to prove that souls remain after death. For the God of truth would not say that he was their God if they did not in any way subsist. Thus, having won the palm of victory concerning souls from their own books, he could more freely introduce the resurrection of bodies, which performed good or evil deeds together with the souls.

For Abraham and the other patriarchs could not have God if they did not exist, since it belongs to the nature of reality that one thing must exist if another belongs to it. Accordingly, God is the God of the living, not of those who are not. God is also eternity; he is not the God of things that are either dead or altogether nonexistent.

How, then, can he be denied to be the God of those whose God eternity itself declares him to be? For the God who exists says of himself: “I am who I am” (Exod. III, 14), “and this is my name forever.” Therefore it is impossible to say that he is the God of those who do not exist. And because this is impossible, he is the God of those who exist, who live, who experience his benefits, and who understand that they possess God, whose they themselves also are.

But it must be asked why he said separately, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” when he could have said, “I am the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” Elsewhere he declared himself to belong collectively to all when he said to Moses: “Go and say to Pharaoh, ‘The God of the Hebrews has sent me.’” We should not think that he said this without reason.

For although he is one God of all, he is most perfectly the God of those who are devoted to God and are found to be more perfect than other human beings in God’s presence; therefore they possess the whole of God more fully within themselves. For this reason God is rightly said not collectively but wholly and individually to belong to each of these men.

For example, if it is said, “That field belongs to them,” we show that each of them possesses some portion of that field, whatever its extent, and that none possesses the whole of it. But if we say, “That field belongs to him,” we demonstrate that he possesses the whole field. So when he said, “I am the God of Abraham,” he showed that Abraham, as a perfect patriarch, possesses him wholly; Isaac possesses him wholly; and Jacob possesses him wholly. Therefore he is not called collectively their God, but “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” because each of them possessed God in his entirety.

Likewise, elsewhere it is said, “the God of Elijah” (IV Kings II, 14). But Christ’s God and Father is something altogether different. As for the expression “the God of the Hebrews,” it demonstrates their imperfection, since each of them possessed something, however little, of God.

Christ bestowed this benefit upon the apostles as a great gift when he said: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John XX, 17).

When the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together, and one of them, a lawyer, questioned him in order to test him. What we read about Herod and Pilate in the Lord’s Passion—that they returned to harmony—we now also see in the case of the Pharisees and Sadducees. Previously they had been enemies of one another, but in testing God they agree with one mind.

For whoever contends against the truth is never appeased, even when his malice is defeated, because he does not seek to defend the truth but to overthrow it. Thus, although these men had been silenced and made mute, they were not appeased so as to consent, having been defeated by the truth in every respect through faith. They gather together because they could not repeatedly be refuted by reasoning, so that by their combined multitude they might be able to contend. And because they had seen the Sadducee faction collapse so suddenly, they ought to have been warned by its example not to devise further plots.

But malevolence and envy always nourish greater and greater shamelessness. Hence they armed themselves sufficiently with their multitude, although one man speaks on behalf of them all. For all of them contend and speak through one, so that if he wins, they may all appear to have won; but if he is defeated, he alone may appear disgraced.

“Teacher,” he said, “which is the great commandment in the law?”

He calls him “Teacher,” although perhaps he does not wish to be his disciple. For he asks about a great commandment, not the greatest, so that whatever Jesus should answer, since everything God commanded is great, he might have an opportunity to accuse him by asserting that one among several was great. Whoever asks falsely and deceitfully is a brother and companion of this Pharisee. For every disciple is the disciple of a teacher, just as every teacher is the teacher of his disciple. Therefore no one calls someone “teacher” properly except a disciple.

And so, because he was testing him, he is rightly shown to have spoken falsely—unless perhaps we understand, as Matthew says, that he did not wish to test Jesus of his own accord, but that, having been persuaded by the Pharisees, he approached, as far as his own intention was concerned, not to test him but to ask as though he were less learned.

Hence, although Mark appears to differ in many respects when he recounts the matter, he nevertheless does not introduce this man as testing Jesus, as Matthew does. At the end of the conversation Mark says that the Lord told him: “You are not far from the kingdom of God” (Matt. XII, 34).

This could also have happened if he approached while testing him, or even unwillingly, and, insofar as he himself was concerned, asked devoutly, so that by the Lord’s answer he might truly be corrected toward faith. Or certainly, the “testing” that Matthew describes may not have been proposed with evil intent—as though he wished to deceive Jesus as an enemy—but rather out of curiosity, because this matter had long been debated, so that he might discover whether the Lord knew and learn whether he was ignorant of what everyone still asked about as something uncertain.

Luke appears to say something similar in a nearby passage, but he inserts it far elsewhere. It therefore seems more correct that the man about whom Luke tells this story is another person—not only because of the difference in order, but also because when he asks the Lord, “What must I do to possess eternal life?” Luke reports that the Lord answered quite differently and proposed many things that do not seem to fit this passage.

The man whom Matthew and Mark introduce, however, is rightly commended by the Lord for having received the answer and remained silent, when he says to him: “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And because he perhaps asked faithfully which commandment in the law was great, the Lord answered not only which was great but also which was first.

Hence I think that the distinction among the commandments must be investigated. For where there is a great and a first commandment, there are also subsequent ones; and perhaps one must proceed in order until reaching that least commandment, concerning which whoever breaks it and teaches others to do so “will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.” It is therefore clear that if there is a great commandment, there is also a least one, as well as a middle one, and many others in between, arranged in order.

Meanwhile, in answering him, the Lord teaches us that it is not only a great commandment to love God, but also the first. “First” does not refer to the order of Scripture but to the dignity of virtue, and this is what should be considered as appropriate to the passage. It is as though, after many commandments had been established, he now called this commandment great and first.

The second is like the first, and is great because of its likeness: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Perhaps from this we may understand that there is another commandment which in greatness and order is third, and another which is fourth, and so on, counting the commandments of the law in order.

But only God can arrange and reckon them as far as the least. Unless Christ, who is the power and wisdom of God, fulfills this, no other saint would dare to do so. Perhaps, then, from the time of Moses until Christ people had been asking which commandment in the law was great, yet no one had defined it with complete clarity. Otherwise the Pharisee would not have asked this question unless it had long and extensively been sought among them but not discovered or determined. Then Christ came and taught not only which commandment was great, but also which was first, and afterward which was second and like the first. It would likewise be his task, if he wished, to complete or discover the third and fourth and the remaining commandments in their order.

There is, however, another commandment elsewhere that is called first, but not “like” the first, so that it is called both great and first. Concerning it the Apostle says: “Honor your father and mother” (Eph. VI, 2). It is the first commandment with a promise, or in the law, since it was read as the first commandment placed on the second tablet of the law. Thus, although it can be called first, it is not immediately also great; just as perhaps another may be great without immediately being first.

Nevertheless, we must consider what the Savior says: “On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets.” Then consider what the Apostle says to the Romans (Rom. XIII, 9): “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal,” and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up—or, as other codices have it, recapitulated—in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

Whatever, therefore, hangs upon these two commandments is wholly summed up or recapitulated in this one. Hence it must be asked whether “the law and the prophets hanging upon these two commandments” is one thing, and “everything being recapitulated in this commandment” another. Since this has already appeared so to earlier Fathers, it is necessary to understand that all the commandments—or the law and the prophets—hang upon and are summed up or restored in the twofold commandment, because neither God without one’s neighbor nor one’s neighbor without God is rightly loved.

Accordingly, love of God and love of neighbor are one commandment, one complete charity, and one true love. To put it frankly, when the Apostle says, “If there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying,” even this commandment—“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind”—is entirely recapitulated or restored in the second, so that what the Apostle says may be true.

And if the first commandment is recapitulated in the second, then the second must be restored in the first to an even greater degree. Therefore, if every commandment is recapitulated in the second, this great and first commandment is also recapitulated there; and in these two the whole law and the prophets rightly hang.

It is not without reason, then, that the Lord defined the great and first commandment in the law as follows: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.” If you subtract anything from its greatness and primacy, you subtract it from the whole. Whoever subtracts anything from that entire commandment—that is, from “with all your heart,” or “with all your soul,” or “with all your mind”—corrupts what is great and first if it is not observed in its entirety.

Therefore whoever wishes to love the Lord his God wholly must carry out the complete parts of love and fulfill them entirely, so that he may love not only the whole Lord God with his whole self, but also offer the three things by which God is loved wholly.

He must love him with all his heart, so that he stores the whole God within his heart as though in a treasury, in every action and thought. He must love him with all his soul, so that he is ready to place his soul in death for him who created all things, lest any part of the soul be torn away from him who gave it. And he must love him with all his mind, so that nothing else occupies our understanding except understanding and thinking about God.

By these three parts, therefore, the whole and complete human being is said to consist—not because, as some wish, the human being is composed of three substances, but of two, namely soul and body. Although the Apostle says, “May your spirit be whole” (II Thess. III, 3–23), the soul and body, the soul is both soul and spirit. Nevertheless, the part by which the body is given life is called “soul,” while its higher part, by which we understand and reason, is called “mind.”

The heart, moreover, is understood as a part of the flesh, so that we may strive with all our being for the flesh too to thirst for God and to love God. 928 For this David promised God: “My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh [thirsted] for you” (Ps. LXII, 2).

When the whole and complete human being is transferred wholly to the love of God through these parts, he is rightly believed to fulfill God’s greatest commandment.

Although loving one’s neighbor is a great thing, it is not called first but “like” the first. For one’s neighbor is loved in God, and God is loved in the human being, whose image he is. It is therefore not without reason that the commandment is called “like,” especially because of the mystery of Christ, who is our neighbor: he assumed our flesh and became, as he himself shows in another parable, our neighbor.

Therefore the first and greatest commandment is to love the Lord God. The second, like it in every respect, is to love, know, and venerate the Son of God—namely Christ—who became the Mediator between God and human beings, likewise with one’s whole self and without measure. Then we must love our other neighbors in Christ Jesus, with measure, as we love ourselves, so that one commandment may be fulfilled in all things through Christ.

Otherwise, as John says: “Whoever says that he loves God and does not love his brother is a liar” (I John IV, 20). And: “Everyone who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X, 5).

We must therefore labor with the grace of God, because the commandment concerning love of neighbor is called “like” the first, so that one’s neighbor may be loved in the same way: with all the heart, just as one is commanded to love. For who would not wish to be loved with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his mind, when the commandment says, “as yourself”?

Yet a certain distinction is placed between God and one’s neighbor, lest anyone wish to worship the neighbor whom he is commanded to love as himself as though he were God—although God must be loved more than oneself and more than every human being.

Therefore, when he says, “The second is like this,” this likeness should be referred to the love of Christ, so that just as God the Father is loved, so also God Christ, the Father’s Son, who is our neighbor, should be loved. And because we ought to love the rest of our neighbors, a measure is established in that same love: “as yourself.”

Therefore the second commandment is like the first: Christ is to be loved without any measure, with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all the mind. And so that this love or charity may be properly ordered, it says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

Since, as has been said, the whole law and the prophets hang upon these two commandments, this second, like commandment is better referred to Christ, who is truly our neighbor. For the law and all the prophets foreshadowed Christ’s coming, and all the riddles and figures of the law depended upon him. His coming supplied the understanding by which God is known, through their fulfillment.

But if the commandment is to be understood equally of the love of Christ and of one’s neighbor, how are we forbidden in this same Gospel to place father, mother, and the other affections of the flesh before the charity of God? How is love of neighbor a commandment like love of God, so that there is something that can be made equal to the love of God?

Rather, the likeness of the commandment requires an equal charity in loving the Father and the Son, and a corresponding understanding drawn from the law and the prophets, upon which commandment everything depends. Thus, so that the law itself and prophecy may be challenged by their words, and a clearer understanding concerning one’s neighbor may be opened,
Having gathered the Pharisees together, he asks them, saying what they thought: whose son would Christ be? They say to him, “David’s.” And he says to them: “How, then, does David in the Spirit call him ‘Lord,’ saying:

> The Lord said to my Lord,  
> ‘Sit at my right hand,  
> until I place your enemies  
> as a footstool for your feet’?

This question, then, miserable Jews, because they saw that it was directed against them, although perhaps they knew from the prophets both how he would be Lord and how he would also be David’s son, nevertheless refused to answer him and kept silent. They could not deny what David had once prophesied about him in the Psalms, nor evade it in any other way than by silence. Therefore, trusting wrongly in themselves, and as though they were defendants, they remain silent.

But the Lord Jesus neither explained the question to them nor resolved its method; rather, through Paul—in whom he himself was speaking—he fully disclosed it to us Christians. For he says, speaking to Timothy:

> Remember that Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, is from the seed of David according to the flesh, according to my Gospel (I Tim. II, 6).

Behold how Christ is David’s son: namely, according to the flesh, because he was born from the seed of his flesh. But how is he David’s Lord? Let us ask the Apostle himself—or rather, Christ, who was speaking through him. For he says this about him:

> Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider being equal with God something to be seized (Phil. II, 6).

Since he was not equal to God the Father by robbery in the form of God, but by the nature of eternal birth, in which he remained God, begotten from the Father: according to this form, I ask, because in being born he came forth as God from the Father, recognize him as that same Lord of David. And if you recognize him truly as David’s Lord, you will certainly recognize him as God and Lord of all creatures, including the angels, because as God in the form of God he is equal to God the Father. Behold from what source he is David’s son, and from what source he is David’s Lord.

Therefore he is David’s son because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross. For this reason God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of the Lord every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. II, 7–8).

He therefore emptied himself, as was said. But if you ask how he truly took flesh from David’s seed, so that the Word became flesh, and thereby became what he was not: the Lord who was David’s Lord became David’s son. And therefore, in the Holy Spirit, he was rightly called the Lord of the one whose son he also became—not one Son and another Lord, but one and the same Christ, simultaneously Lord and Son.

But if the blind Jews, perhaps ignorant of these things, nevertheless knew that he would certainly come from David’s seed, they ought to have questioned the one whom they falsely called teacher, especially since he had brought forward David’s testimony, foretold in the Holy Spirit. But the miserable men did not wish to discover this because of their dullness, nor to inquire into what they could not deny, although they eagerly desired to contradict it.

If they had wished without doubt to believe the prophets, where they had read that Christ would be David’s son, they could have found that he was the one who was speaking and that he himself was David’s Lord. For where they read that they themselves would also kill him—what marvelous blindness and excessive inward obstinacy of mind! They hoped that he would come, and when questioned about him they foresaw him everywhere; yet they did not see their own most cruel crime, which they had long been plotting to carry out, although they had already been softened by his benefits.

Otherwise Christ would never have openly questioned them as though they knew him, if they had never before heard his name pronounced in the sacred Scriptures or among the people. But because this was very well known among the people and was read everywhere in the divine writings, they could not conceal that they knew he would come or that they expected him. They still expect him even today, and therefore they are in error. For we too expect him to come, but not to be judged, since he has already been judged; rather, we await him as judge, because the prophets foretold both advents. And therefore, blind because they went astray regarding the time of his coming, at the end they will encounter as judge the one whom, at his first coming, they condemned unjustly.

This passage, prudent reader, therefore serves not only against the hard-hearted Jews but also against heretics who deny that God came in the flesh and do not confess God as a true human being and the true Son of God. For Photinus, who denies Christ’s humanity, is condemned by this passage. Arius and the Manichaeans, as well as very many other heretics, are here overthrown because they do not confess Christ as God equal to God the Father, so that the whole Christian redemption may be emptied of meaning and their Catholic faith corrupted.

Therefore, so that we may strongly refute them all from every side, let us carefully examine both the present passage and other passages wherever necessary concerning Christ, so that we may understand them and question all of them together with the Lord: if he is merely a human being, as they say, and not God, how does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying:

> The Lord said to my Lord,  
> “Sit at my right hand,  
> until I place your enemies  
> as a footstool for your feet”?

The Pharisees themselves provided the opportunity for their refutation, for they had gathered in order to trap the Lord in some way. And because they had already proposed many questions deceitfully, it was fitting that at least once he should question them and make them understand that the one being tested was not merely a human being but also God, whom no one can deceive.

Meanwhile, because he could not openly speak the truth about himself while the Pharisees were lying in wait, nor remain silent, since he had come for this purpose—to announce the truth and show himself to be God, the Son of God the Father—he therefore puts this question to them, so that, while he is silent, the divine Scripture might declare what the Holy Spirit had uttered long beforehand about Christ.

First, therefore, he asks: “What do you think about Christ? Whose son is he?” This was known to everyone, because the promise had been made concerning David’s lineage. Then, when they immediately give the true answer, “David’s,” the Wisdom of God the Father again asks very wisely how David calls him Lord in the Spirit, if he is rightly believed to be his father.

He does not ask this in order to prove that they have spoken falsely, but to show himself to be the Lord and Son of God the Father. For he could not be the Lord of one who was to be born from him unless he were the Son of the Most High.

This question still has great force against the Jews today and, as I said, refutes nearly every heretical depravity concerning Christ: that one and the same Christ is truly David’s son according to the flesh and David’s Lord according to divinity—not a simple and ordinary human being, as the Jews then thought and as they still foolishly suppose today, asserting that a holy man from David’s race will come.

But he is proclaimed by David himself, whose son he is, in the Holy Spirit, as David’s Lord. This does not mean that there were two sons, as the recent heresy suspects, but one and the same Christ is both Lord and Son—not one God and another human being, but one God and human being in both respects.

This faith does not arise from uncertain error, nor is it fashioned from private will; it is shown to have been declared in the Holy Spirit by the Lord himself. For David does not deny that he is his son, which the Pharisees confess; rather, he also reveals himself as the Lord of the prophets.

Therefore he takes testimony from the hundred and ninth Psalm, so that all the Jews who invent for themselves many foolish and empty arguments to evade the truth of the question may be convicted from it. They say that the man in question was Abraham’s household slave, whose son was Damascus Eliezer, and that this Psalm was written in his person—that it was his voice, and that after the slaughter of the five kings the Lord God said to Abraham, “Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet.”

It is necessary to ask them how God said to Abraham the words that follow:

> With you is the beginning on the day of your strength,  
> in the splendors of the holy ones;  
> from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you,

and the other things that are read in that Psalm.

All these things, just as on that day they closed the mouths of the Pharisees, so that from that hour no one dared question him any longer, enable us also to convict every Jew and every heretic from this passage: Christ is true God and human being, begotten before the morning star, from the womb—that is, from the substance of God the Father—in the splendors of the holy ones by the Father himself; and at the end of time he was established as priest according to the order of Melchizedek, just as God the Father had once sworn.

It therefore appears frivolous either to say that that servant was the prophet of so great a mystery, or that David composed such a statement about him—something that, as they suppose, fits neither him nor Abraham—but rather that the similarity of the name and the equality by which the Lord was saying to the Lord that he was equal to the Father placed him at the right hand when he ascended into heaven, where he had always been.

This is wholly as unsuitable to Abraham as it is to say that he was equal to God the Father; nor could he sit at God’s right hand. For there is nothing on the left in God, and therefore the Son is rightly commanded to sit, in the plural expression, at the right hand of God the Father:

> And the Lord at your right hand  
> shattered kings on the day of his anger.

For this reason there is no need to introduce a bodily sitting into matters that must be understood spiritually. For just as the Son is at the right hand of the Father, so the Father is at the right hand of the Son.

How, then, the Father places the enemies as a footstool beneath the feet of the Savior is not asked without reason, since God’s kindness is proclaimed here more than any indignation of wrath. For it is pious and very desirable to be subject to God. Therefore I do not think that God places Christ’s enemies as a footstool beneath his feet in the same manner as earthly kings place their enemies beneath their feet when they destroy them.

Those kings afflict their own enemies without mercy, but the Lord places Christ’s enemies as a footstool beneath his feet not for their destruction but for their salvation, so that they may be subject to their most merciful Savior and liberator.

For we read in the Lamentations of Jeremiah how the Lord in his anger darkened the daughter of Zion and cast down from heaven to earth the glory of Israel; he did not remember his footstool. Concerning this, in the same work that we published on those Lamentations, we have already said what could then be brought forward, and we say it still: to be God’s footstool is immense glory. For when the daughter of Zion was God’s footstool, she was gloriously in heaven.

But after she was cast down, so that she was no longer his footstool, she ceased to be in heaven. Therefore pay close attention to what he says:

> He cast down from heaven the glory of Israel,

and she became his footstool when he rejected them and cast them down to earth, so that they would be written not in heaven but on earth.

Yet earth is sometimes also mentioned in praise, as in the words:

> Heaven is my throne,  
> but the earth is the footstool of my feet (Isa. LXVI, 1),

where he wishes to show not the earth’s disgrace but its glory, since it understands some portion—however small—of God.

For this reason that woman who was doing penance wept at the feet of the most merciful Jesus, because she was a sinner. It was desirable for her to sit and weep beside the Lord’s feet, because she was not yet fit to reach his head and pour perfume over it.

When they had thus been questioned about the Psalm:

> No one was able to answer him a word,  
> nor did anyone dare from that day to question him any longer.

What do you think would happen if they were compelled to explain the whole text of the Psalm, which most manifestly seems to resound entirely concerning Christ? I believe that the mouths of all the Jews are closed by this one Psalm, if there is a diligent investigator who can plainly confine their evasions by means of it.

## Chapter XXIII

Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples.

That is, after the questioning had ended, when no one dared to question him any longer, he spoke freely to the crowds and to his disciples. Matthew also makes this distinction, preserving the privilege of the apostles and of those who adhered more faithfully to Christ, since the disciples of the Savior were better than the other crowds, for they were already following him more fully through faith.

Therefore, although they are often instructed by him alone, whenever they hear him together with the crowds they are distinguished from them, so that their dignity may be commended. For above, when Matthew had said, “As Jesus was speaking to the crowds,” and someone had said, “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to see you,” he immediately stretched out his hands not toward the crowds but toward his disciples, saying, “Behold my mother and my brothers,” and so forth.

You will find the same thing, reader, in the remaining passages: the honor of the disciples is always preserved.

Luke does not seem to disagree in this passage when he says that the Lord spoke these things in the house of a certain Pharisee. For Matthew does not specify the particular place where these words were spoken; rather, from the time he came from Galilee to Jerusalem, even the earlier events, up to these speeches, may rightly be understood to have occurred there, wherever they are taken to have occurred.

But he is no longer speaking these words to the Pharisees; he is speaking to the crowds and to the disciples, because the Pharisees were unworthy. Nevertheless, he does not wish sound teaching to be utterly despised on their account, and therefore he says:

> The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat.  
> Whatever they tell you, observe and do;  
> but do not do according to their works.

By “Moses’ seat” we are to understand the Law itself and its teaching, upon which those men sat who either boasted that they interpreted it correctly or professed that they ascended above it according to their traditions.

And because it was soon to be removed, so that it would not be followed according to the letter, he seems to have said, “They have sat,” as though he were saying, “up to the present,” rather than “they will sit” or “they are sitting.”

He commands that the things belonging to the Law be observed and done, because the Law is spiritual. Therefore he placed before them the glory of the Law that testified about him, which had expressed within itself the image of future truth and had foreshown in its decrees both kinds of commandments: those concerning the conduct of life and those signifying future realities. In all things, however, it obeyed Christ and meditated upon his coming.

Whatever is contained in it is of great value for the advancement of the manifest knowledge of Christ. Therefore he commands obedience to the precepts of those who sit on Moses’ seat, so that they may teach the things belonging to the Law. He does not ask that they be obeyed if they teach something vicious from their own invention; rather, because they sit on Moses’ seat, he mystically commands obedience in all things to the commandments of the Law and abstention from their deeds and works, so that only the perversity and faithlessness of the men may be avoided while the teaching of the Law is preserved.

Some say that the scribes are those who do not depart from the letter of the Law, while the Pharisees are those who profess to know something greater in the Law. Therefore they separate themselves from the rest as though they were better and more learned; hence they are called Pharisees, which is interpreted as “divided” or “separated.”

The others, who understand and explain Moses’ Law according to its spiritual power, do indeed sit on Moses’ seat, yet they are not scribes and Pharisees but better than them—such as the apostles and the other disciples of Christ.

This sitting is rightly said to have existed up to the Lord’s Passion. Thereafter, Catholic teachers sit more gloriously upon the seat of the Church, which is the seat and throne of Christ, and teach the words of life.

Whoever sits or teaches well and does not abolish these things receives honor and grace through that seat. But whoever teaches well and lives badly acquires guilt from his priesthood rather than dignity, because he sits unworthily—although more unworthy still is the one who neither teaches well nor lives well.

The dignity of teachers is indeed diverse, but their nature is one. If a priest lives well, he has his own gain; if he teaches well, he is an instrument for the people. Therefore the people ought to receive the teaching that belongs to it and not scrutinize what belongs to another, because Moses’ teaching is according to God.

For one seat is the seat of pestilence, and another is the seat of Moses, which is also called the Lord’s Law, in which the will of the blessed man is meditated upon day and night. For the Lord overturned the seats of those who sold doves, seats that were seats of pestilence.

Although the teaching of all these people is to be heard insofar as it comes from the Law of God, their way of life is nevertheless not to be imitated.

For they bind heavy and unbearable burdens on people’s shoulders, but they themselves do not wish to move them with their finger. They bind them and place them on people’s shoulders—not because these words are to be understood literally, but according to a figurative interpretation. The heavy burdens signify the commandments of the Law; and the “unbearable” burdens are those which they themselves were unwilling not only to work at with their hands and fulfill, but even to touch in the slightest.

Concerning these burdens of the commandments the Apostle says that neither we nor our fathers were able to bear them. Although they were heavy and unbearable, the severity of the Pharisees made them even heavier.

Nevertheless, on account of the dignity of the priestly office and of the name—which certainly has a sacramental significance—the most merciful Savior urges the people to be subject to them.

Therefore:

> Whatever they tell you, observe and do,  
> although they do not do what they say,

because truth is to be followed, from whatever person’s mouth it has been spoken.

These commandments ultimately apply to all priests of the Churches, even though they themselves do not fulfill the smallest commandments while commanding greater ones. This is what is signified by the finger. The seat, as I said, and the burdens, shoulders, finger, and bonds by which the burdens are tied must all be understood spiritually.

Everything must be treated mercifully by good and discerning men, lest they be reproved by the Lord together with such teachers. First, therefore, let them themselves fulfill the greater commandments and not neglect the lesser. Then, according to the measure of each hearer’s strength, let them distribute, bind, and impose them one by one.

For the measure of grain is not to be determined according to the size of God’s commandments but according to the ability and capacity of each person. Otherwise, if teachers compel people without moderation and place words heavier than the hearer can bear upon their shoulders, they may force the hearer to fall beneath the burden, contrary to the will of Christ, who says:

> My yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Matt. XI, 30).

It follows:

> They do all their works in order to be seen by people.

It is therefore evident that all such men generally love the first places at banquets, greetings in the marketplace, and being called “Rabbi” by people, or something similar to this.

After he had been harassed above by the plots of the priests and Pharisees and had not been heard in his answers, he rightly turned to the people and to the disciples and taught that such teachers in the Law were to be heard but not imitated.

Then, in these words, he wishes to show the reason why they could not believe: namely, because they did everything for empty glory, so that they might be seen by people and praised by them. For it is impossible that someone who seeks empty glory from people and desires earthly praises more should believe Christ when he proclaims heavenly things, just as he himself says elsewhere:

> How can you believe, when you seek glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God? (John V, 44.)

For that which destroys the thing itself arises from the thing itself. For example, a worm arises from wood and eats away the wood; a moth arises from clothing and consumes the clothing; similarly, worms arise from vegetables and spoil all the vegetables.

So too, vices arise from the disposition of each person in the present life, and by them the soul is consumed so that it may not live for God. Therefore remove this vice from the clergy—the desire to be seen by people—and the other vices will immediately be cut away as well.

When they disdain one another, how often do they refuse to have someone better than themselves placed over them, just as the Jews refused Christ!

They enlarge their phylacteries and magnify their fringes. From this passage the blessed Jerome, lamenting the evils of the clergy, says:

> Woe to us miserable men, upon whom the vices of the Pharisees have passed.

He would certainly lament our present crimes even more if he were in the flesh today and knew how many things, and of what kind, are now done among us without shame.

This superstition of the Pharisees had arisen because, when the Lord had given the commandments of the Law through Moses, he added and concluded by saying:

> You shall bind them on your hand, and they shall be immovable before your eyes always (Deut. VI, 8).

He commanded that they be carried on the hand so that they might always be fulfilled in deed, and that they be kept before the eyes so that we might meditate on them day and night.

Meanwhile, the Pharisees, interpreting these words badly, wrote Moses’ Decalogue—that is, the ten words of the Law—on strips of parchment, folding and binding them on the forehead and making them like a crown for the head, so that the written Law and the memory of the commandments might always revolve before their eyes—not in true faith, so that they might fulfill them in their works, but so that they might be seen by people.

They wrote them on two pieces of cut parchment. One they carried on their heads in their houses, placing it there like a crown, and carrying the writing on their forehead as though it were before their eyes; the other they placed on the upper part of their arm. These parts they called phylacteries.

They still do this today, as we read, among the Indians and Babylonians. Those who wear them are judged religious by the people.

Similarly, they magnified the fringes on their cloaks, which they had taken from the commandment in Deuteronomy, so that by them they might show themselves to be greater observers of the Law.

They therefore tied large fringes at the tops of the four corners of their cloaks, so that their holiness might appear greater, because the Lord had commanded this to be done so that by means of the hyacinth-colored fringes the people of Israel might be distinguished from the other nations: just as they had a difference in the flesh through circumcision, so they should have a difference in their clothing.

But those superstitious teachers, pursuing popular favor, as Jerome reports, and seeking profits from women, made the fringes large and fastened them with very sharp thorns, evidently so that as they walked or sat they would sometimes be pricked and, as though under this reminder, be drawn back to the duties of God and the ministries of his service.

Therefore the Lord says:

> They do all their works in order to be seen by people.

Would that our own people today, who seem to be more learned among the people, did not do the same!

The miserable men did not understand that these things ought to be carried more in the heart than on the body. Nevertheless, that fringe of the Lord was of this kind, though small and short, a precept from the Law. The woman who was suffering from a flow of blood touched it on the Lord’s cloak, yet she was not pierced by the Pharisees’ superstitious thorns; rather, she was healed by touching it.

Therefore the Lord does not condemn them merely because they had fringes at the tops of their cloaks, but because they were excessively large and spread out, seeking glory from people. In the same way, he condemns them in all the other statements that he distinguishes in detail: why they seek the first places at dinners, the first seats in the synagogues, the pursuit of gluttony, and greetings in the marketplace.

He does not blame them because they reclined in the first place or because they pursued greetings in the marketplace, but because, as he says more explicitly, they loved the first places at banquets for the sake of empty glory, and greetings in the marketplace and the first seats in the synagogues for the sake of their own praise.

Because their mind was corrupted in its desires and pursuits, seeking avarice and empty glory in everything, their conduct is condemned and the reproach is directed toward their vices, not toward actions when those actions are done honorably.

For it is most dutiful to preserve one’s order at table, to offer greetings to one another, and to anticipate one another in honor; it is honorable. Moreover, when these things are observed religiously, they build up the minds of individuals in charity.

But if we proceed carnally, and someone desires and loves his own boasting more than moral propriety and the excellence of humility, he is an imitator of the Pharisees.

It can happen that someone reclines in the last place who not only does not lose the boasting of his heart but nourishes it inwardly all the more from that very action, seeking empty glory as though he were more humble than everyone else and wishing to appear just and humble so that he may be honored more by all.

How many, do you think, are found either in the first places or in the last, while inwardly they are condemned by the Lord, who sees the hearts of all, for pride?

God is Spirit, and therefore he examines everyone spiritually, not carnally. He does not merely consider where someone sits or in what voice another person greets him, whether reverently, with head or body bowed—although all these things ought to be done honorably and suitably for each person—but rather with what mind and conscience each person does whatever he does.

Therefore, as I said, he directed the blame toward the love of the Pharisees and not toward duties that can be performed honorably.

“But you,” he says, “do not be called Rabbi,” and he immediately gives the reason: “For one is your teacher; you are all brothers.”

“Rabbi” is Hebrew, and in Latin it means “teacher.”

“And do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven. Nor be called teachers, because one is your teacher, Christ.”

Behold why we are called brothers: because we have no other father than God, who formed and created us. For although one human being begets another, there is one Father of all, who formed and created everyone.

Therefore we are sons and brothers of our earthly fathers because, so to speak, we were not born from them in an absolute sense but through them. We do not have the beginning of life from them, but through them we received, as it were, a passage into life.

For even if a tree seems to produce branches from itself, the life of the branches and of the tree, so to speak, is the root. Much more, then, is God the Father, author and creator of all human beings.

Similarly, although many teach, Christ is the one teacher of all, who teaches all human beings inwardly—not artificially but naturally. For if one human being completely taught and instructed another, all human beings would learn equally from one teacher.

But now, because it is not a human being who teaches but God, who gives sense and understanding, Paul cries out that neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God, who gives the growth (I Cor. III, 7).

For a human being does not provide understanding through teaching; it is provided by God, who gives understanding to the little ones (Ps. CXVIII, 130), and who says:

> I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you will walk (Ps. LXXIII, 130).

Hence David also says:

> Blessed is the person whom you instruct, Lord,  
> and whom you teach from your Law (Ps. XXXI, 8).

But perhaps someone will say in response that a person becomes learned through his own efficacy and the intelligibility of his mind, although no one possesses even these gifts except by God’s gift, enabling him to be instructed.

Therefore whoever professes to be Christ’s disciple ought to call him “teacher,” since he generates in us not a carnal but a spiritual discipline; and he ought to call him “father,” since through Christ’s teaching and fellowship he mercifully granted us this name and grace.

We are sons of God through adoption rather than of an earthly parent. For we profess ourselves to be heavenly from the moment when, reborn with faith, we began to say in heart and mouth:

> Our Father, who are in heaven (Matt. VI, 9).

It is therefore unworthy for us to call anyone on earth “father,” since we have been made heavenly and do not doubt that we have a Father in heaven.

It is asked, however, why Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, calls himself a teacher in opposition to these commandments; or how, in ordinary speech, in monasteries, according to the common practice of all monks and the rule’s command, monks call one another “father,” in which paternal reverence is preserved.

This is rightly resolved when we say that one thing is a father or teacher by nature and another by indulgence. Thus, if we call someone “father,” we show honor to his age or reverence for his merits; we do not say that the one whom we call father is the author of our life. In the same way, we rightly call someone teacher not for any other reason than through customary usage and fellowship with the true teacher.

And, not to prolong the discussion indefinitely: just as the fact that by nature there is one God and one Son does not prevent the saints from being called gods by name and sons by the grace of adoption, so the fact that there is one Father and one Teacher does not prevent others from being called fathers and teachers in an improper or secondary sense.

For it is one thing to be a teacher by skill and another to be one by authority and nature.

Therefore, in all these matters, remove empty and personal presumption, so that favor born of empty glory may not be loved, but the honor of God and the devotion of moral propriety may be preserved. You will find that he does not prohibit anyone from ever being called such by others; rather, he seems to introduce this teaching so that Christ’s disciples will not desire, for the sake of empty glory, to be called these things by people or to be honored in some superstitious way beyond what is appropriate.

> The one who is greater among you will be your servant.  
> Whoever exalts himself will be humbled,  
> and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

Because he had said, “Do not be called teachers,” and had forbidden them to love the first places at table and the rest, he sets himself forward as the form and example of humility. He is called teacher by nature rather than by indulgence, because all things exist through him, and through the dispensation of his flesh we are all instructed unto life and reconciled to God—through the fact that he is greater than us.

It is as though he were saying: “Do not love the primacy of honor, nor be called teachers, just as I do not seek my own glory, but there is one who seeks it” (John VIII, 50).

So you too must look to me, because:

> The Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve,  
> and to give his life for many (Matt. XX, 28).

In this passage he instructs not only his disciples but also the teachers of the Churches, so that no one may seek honors through ambition. Rather, whoever wishes to be greater should first become, as he himself became, the servant of all.

And if anyone desires something from these things, let him desire the work and not the height of honor; let him serve and minister to everyone rather than have everyone serve and minister to him.

One of these attitudes comes from the arrogance of the Pharisees, while the other comes from the teaching and instruction of Christ. Those who pursue and seek honors for themselves are the ones who exalt themselves; those who rejoice in ministering and serving are the ones who humble themselves, so that they may be exalted by the Lord.

And it should be noted that he does not say, “The one whom the Lord exalts will be humbled,” but, “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled”—clearly by the Lord. Nor does he say, “The one whom the Lord humbles,” but, “Whoever humbles himself of his own accord will be exalted,” in turn, by the Lord.

This teaching is appropriate to all good Christians. Conversely, this threat applies to the devil, to the Jews and Gentiles, and to all apostates who refuse to humble themselves under Christ’s yoke; and therefore all these will be humbled by God’s just judgment.

To avoid this, the apostles and all good men preferred to anticipate one another in honor and to be all brothers—that is, children of one parent—rejoicing through the regeneration of the new birth that they had passed beyond the beginnings of earthly origin and had one heavenly teacher presiding over them all.

Therefore, because Christ specially retained this teaching authority in himself, he immediately provided the form of the teaching: whoever wishes to be greater should be the servant of all.

Then he immediately added a twofold reason for such great humility: one, namely, for attaining the glory of eternal life in Christ; the other, for demonstrating to the proud the confusion of eternal humiliation.

And because he claimed the name of teacher essentially, though in other words, and proposed the same form, he says:

> Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart (Matt. XI, 29).

Therefore whoever wishes to be his disciple must diligently learn the teaching that he professes to teach. For each person will then be perfect if he is like his teacher.

Otherwise, I will not say that he is a teacher, but he will not even be a disciple, if he is unwilling to learn the teaching that the teacher teaches.

“Woe to you,” he says, “scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before people; for you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter.”

Let those who perhaps still remain accomplices of the Manichaeans hear this—those who say that the God of the Old Testament is not good because of the curses he placed in the law against sinners and transgressors. If they call him cruel and bloodthirsty, what will they say in this passage about Christ, whom they call kind? Yet with one accord he shows himself to be the true Son of God, the Son of him who gave the law. Indeed, he also intimates that he himself is the lawgiver, for, following the pattern of the blessings he placed in the law, he too set forth in the Gospel the beatitudes of those who are saved. Likewise, he presents here [Col. 0770D] the counterparts of the curses that he had set forth in the law, as he does elsewhere against sinners and transgressors, so that they may repent of their evils, saying: “Woe to us, and to you.” He immediately gives the reasons why he says this, just as in the law.

Thus, both here and in the law, these things were spoken by the one God—that is, by Jesus Christ, most benevolent—in a sufficiently benevolent manner, whether they are the curses in the law or this “woe,” which is rightly understood as spoken with the affection of the one pronouncing it. It is not that sins come upon each person from the pronouncement of the one who pronounces it, but that each person, because he sins, receives it through the judgment of a just condemnation. And I do not mean merely because he sins, but also because, after such warnings have been issued, he sins according to the impenitence [Col. 0771A] of his heart and presents himself as deserving what God uttered for the sake of discipline against them, so that they might turn to goodness and correct themselves.

For at present, just as true blessedness is granted to no one except in hope, so neither is that curse, or this woe, yet brought to its final end. But just as great happiness in heaven is called blessedness, and true blessedness itself is completed in the kingdom of God, so the lamentation and weeping of these curses is brought to completion in hell. There, infinite misery and the torment of the second woe are found, according to the Apocalypse of John, since it is said that the first has passed away. This is the woe that is announced at present not only to scribes and Pharisees but also to all the reprobate, so that in the future they may be without excuse and be punished by the just judgment of God.

It is therefore not without reason that the question is raised why there are eight beatitudes, whereas the Savior pronounced “woe” seven times in this passage. I do not believe that this was done without purpose. Since we read concerning the eighth day, “This is the day which the Lord has made” (Ps. CXVII, 24), perhaps the seven beatitudes are in some way granted by the grace of God to human beings, as though to his own people in hope, through righteous works. But that eighth day is the one which the Lord alone made and freely granted to those who love him. Because they ran in hope through the seven courses, the courses of the days, filled with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, they performed these seven beatitudes.

In contrast, because of the seven principal vices, this woe, repeated seven times, is set against them in number. It did not proceed farther, because that evil completion, situated below it, enfolded its own. But the elect, nourished at present by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, have reached that eighth beatitude which the Lord made. These others, grievously afflicted by seven crimes and running badly toward punishments through the seven courses of the days, carried away with them this one woe, repeated seven times, which they themselves fashioned.

Therefore, when the Lord was speaking to the Jews far above, he said: “When an unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it wanders through dry and waterless places, seeking rest and not finding it. Then it says: ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds the house swept and adorned. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; and entering, they dwell there, and the last state of that person is worse than the first” (Matt. XII, 43–45).

Because this had happened to the scribes and Pharisees, of whom he had already spoken above, he did not exceed either the number of the vices or the number of the punishments. Rather, he declared that woe threatened them as many times as they were oppressed by demons and entangled in vices. For the number seven is commonly counted as representing totality, as in this passage, since they had drawn into themselves a mass of crimes and all the filth of vices had flowed down upon them. Therefore, the totality of demons rightly reigned over them.

“For you shut,” he says, “the kingdom of heaven before people.” And Luke says: “You have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and those entering you prevented from entering” (Luke XI, 52).

Let whoever wishes ask what could be worse among human beings and among the demons themselves: that they neither wish to cease from evil nor to return to God, nor allow others to follow their creator or pass from death to life. What, then, remains for such people except that, since their impiety is one, the punishment of their torments should also be one?

He assigns to each vice its own clause concerning the vices. Because they enlarged their phylacteries, pretending to be holy, and magnified their fringes, it was just that they should be called hypocrites. But they shut the kingdom of heaven before themselves and before others whom they did not allow to enter, because they bound heavy and unbearable burdens upon people’s shoulders, burdens which they themselves were unwilling even to move with a finger, while seeking plunder and desiring glory from the people.

They certainly knew from the law and the prophets that he himself was the Christ. Therefore they were called hypocrites, and not without reason, because they pretended not to know the true Christ whom they knew perfectly well. Yet, for the sake of their greed and their honor, they were unwilling to confess him. Thus, through a perverse interpretation, they shut before the people’s sight the door of the law and the prophets, which had spoken most clearly about Christ’s coming, so that they might deter everyone from faith in Christ, no less by threats and seditions than by their traditions.

They feared that, if the people believed in him, all the sacrificial gifts, glory, honor, worship, and offerings of vows would pass to Christ—things from which not God but they themselves grew rich and gloried in honors.

Therefore the kingdom of heaven is called those very Scriptures in which Christ the Son of God was proclaimed. They had shut them before themselves and before others, since they did not allow Christ to be believed in them and from them. And because Christ himself is the key of David, who opened and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens, when they did not allow him to be believed in or understood, they had taken away not only the key of knowledge but also the very entrance or door. They had blocked it so completely that they themselves did not enter, in order to understand those same Scriptures concerning him, and did not allow others to enter.

These two things therefore appear, as it were, naturally inseparable from each other. Whoever sins in one of them cannot restrain himself from the other; conversely, whoever abstains from one of them seems unable not also to abstain from the other. Suppose, for example, that someone enters happily into God and into the holy Scriptures, or penetrates the kingdom of heaven. You will immediately find that he not only does not prevent others but also exhorts and draws in as many as he can.

For whoever prevents others from entering the kingdom of heaven has, for his own expulsion, a sufficient cause in this very act: that he does not permit others to enter. Whoever causes one of the little ones of the Church to stumble, preventing him from entering by living badly, will suffer what the Lord threatens.

And let no one say, “I do not prevent anyone, because although I am evil, I nevertheless want everyone to be good and to enter the kingdoms of heaven.” If this is humility, and if what he says is true, I agree. But if he is openly evil, I do not know to whom he can be good, since he is proved wicked to himself; nor how he can desire what is good while loving iniquity and serving as an example to others of sinning.

If someone is filled with charity so that, with God acting, he causes others to enter through his labor, I do not see how he himself could fail to enter first. For even though charity does not seek its own interests (1 Cor. XIII, 5), nevertheless the person who has charity not only causes others to enter but also seems already to reign with God, insofar as he is aided by charity. Charity is from God, and it is a heavenly gift. Iniquity, on the other hand, is also from the devil, and sometimes even the punishment of sin—the punishment by which the scribes and Pharisees, weighed down, neither entered themselves nor, insofar as it depended on them, allowed others to enter.

They did this by their words, when they interpreted all Christ’s works, which were divine, as having been performed by Beelzebub. They did it by threats and by every kind of deceit and fraud, so that they cruelly killed the Lord, the Son of God, innocent though incapable of suffering, lest anyone should thereafter believe him to be the Lord. Thus they shut the kingdom against themselves so that they would not enter, and they utterly prevented others, insofar as they could, from entering.

It should be noted that he did not say, “Woe to you because you do not open the kingdom of heaven,” but “because you shut it,” lying and acting falsely in one matter for another, so that the Scriptures might not be rightly understood concerning Christ. This is still done today by those who remain like brands from a fire, prepared for destruction. The double woe that John mentions in his Apocalypse threatens them: he says that he saw an eagle crying out and saying, “Woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth” (Rev. VIII, 13).

For, expelled from their land and from the city of Jerusalem, they long for and seek nothing but earth. Far from them is that first beatitude of which it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V, 3). Their manner of life is in heaven, and therefore that second woe will not touch them, because they are not of the earth.

The present passage also concerns those who appear to be rulers of the churches, if they live badly, or indeed if both things are true: if they live badly and teach badly, or if they teach nothing good and do not abandon the position of hirelings. The prophet Hosea also rebukes and reproves them: “The priests,” he says, “have hidden the way of the Lord and killed the sick person” [the reading *sicennam* is uncertain]. [Col. 0771B]

Otherwise, if wicked priests had not in some fashion corrupted the Lord’s teaching, the truth itself concerning Christ in the divine Scriptures, although obscure, would not have been hidden. It is obscure not so that those who seek it may not find it, but so that those who do not wish to seek it may not see it. Its obscurity contributes to the glory of those who desired and sought it and found it, and conversely to the confusion and condemnation of those who neither desire nor seek nor find it.

Ignorance of the truth cannot be an excuse for a just condemnation when the opportunity to find it existed, if only the will to seek it had existed. If Christ is the truth, salvation, and life of those who know him perfectly, how great, do you think, is the woe that threatens those who shut those same Scriptures by lying about one thing in place of another?

For what could have been said more openly about Christ than what Isaiah says? “The Lord himself,” he says, “will come and save us; then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear, and the tongue of the mute shall speak clearly” (Isa. XXXV, 5), along with the rest.

These signs had indeed been signs of Christ’s coming, and those people saw all of them, and even greater ones, take place. Yet, as I said, they claimed that all had been done by Beelzebub, the prince of demons, in order to turn the people away from faith in Christ. Not only this, but they also issued a decree that if anyone said he was the Son of God, he should be expelled from the synagogue. [Col. 0771C]

The passage continues:

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who travel around sea and dry land to make one proselyte; and when he has become one, you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as yourselves.”

The Jews traveled around sea and dry land for the sake of trade and traversed every part of the world, going by sea and land, even to islands and regions, just as they still do today and in many places. Amid these business pursuits, they did not seek the glory of God, so that God might be worshiped more devoutly by his worshipers; nor did they act out of mercy and love of God and neighbor, wishing to save the person whom they taught to Judaize. Rather, they acted either out of greed, so that the offerings of sacrifices might be increased for them, or out of empty glory, so that they might appear to convert Gentiles to the worship of God.

Those who were converted from Gentile error to the worship of the one God, abandoning idols, were called proselytes. Once circumcised, they were received into the people of God under the law and mingled with them. But when a person had become a proselyte—that is, had been circumcised and consecrated to the Lord—and was then again ruined by their evil examples, he became a son of Gehenna, being compelled to imitate them and follow their disposition.

These were the people who at that time said concerning Christ, “Crucify him, crucify him” (John XIX, 6). They said not only that he should be accused but also that he should be blasphemed daily in their synagogues, so that no one would receive the faith of Christ, just as they still do today.

But we must ask what he means by saying: “And you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as yourselves.” Could a disciple who had become a proselyte become twice as miserable as the scribes and Pharisees, so that he was not equally their son of Gehenna but twice as much? Is not every perfect disciple in both matters one who is like his teacher—if someone can perhaps be called perfect in evil?

The meaning becomes sufficiently clear if the proselyte’s earlier Gentile condemnation is considered. I believe that every person who, from a Gentile way of life, became a proselyte under the law was previously a son of Gehenna; baptism in Christ absolved that sin. But the circumcision of the Jews, since Christ has already come, is of no benefit. Therefore it no longer frees a Gentile from guilt; rather, through transgression of the law, it adds to him a greater measure of condemnation, so that, even according to Judaism, he becomes a son of Gehenna.

Because the earlier condemnation remains unabsolved, when he becomes a proselyte he becomes twice a son of Gehenna through the teaching of an evil teacher: he begins both to blaspheme Christ and to gain nothing from the law. Thus he who taught him becomes the cause of his second error, and the proselyte becomes twice a son of Gehenna beyond the one who taught him evil.

For everyone is very commonly called the son of the one whose works he does; thus people are called sons of perdition and sons of this age.

A person also becomes a proselyte guilty in a twofold way. Previously he was a transgressor under the law of nature; after becoming a proselyte, while still an ethnic outsider, he saw the vices of his teachers and, by transgressing the law, was justly punished with a greater penalty, that is, a double one—just as you are, who possess neither faith nor works.

Others wish *quam*, taken adverbially in the sense of “as,” to be understood, so that the meaning is: “You make him a son of Gehenna twice over, as you yourselves are,” because you reject the faith of Christ, foretold in the law and the prophets, and possess no works of virtue, but are full of vices. Through these vices you have become savage and have lost all gentleness of heart; therefore you can no longer be blessed, since “blessed are the meek and gentle, for they shall possess the earth.”

That is the land of the living, for which David sighs, saying: “I believe that I shall see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI, 13). Because you pursue earthly things, you have unhappily lost it.

It should also be noted that, when Gehenna is promised as a punishment twice as severe for those who transgress more grievously, a difference in torments is indicated. One who is simply a son of Gehenna is tortured in one way, and one who is doubly so is tortured in another. In the same way, we should consider whether someone might be tortured still more abundantly—threefold or multiplied according to the multitude of his sins.

Yet we must not listen to those who say that there are no places of punishment, or that those whom Gehenna has overtaken are tormented by no punishments except the consciousness of their own sins. Many passages of Scripture show both that places of punishment exist and that punishments and torments have already been prepared; the authority of the holy Fathers also confirms that this is so, even though each person is said to become a son of Gehenna according to the particular kind of crime.

For example, the fornicator becomes a son of Gehenna; the adulterer, however, is tortured doubly, and the same applies to the other vices. It does not seem unjust if, according to the measure of each person’s guilt, the punishment of torments is applied within one and the same punishment.

We have already spoken sufficiently above about the name “Gehenna.” Nevertheless, I warn the reader always to beware of the snares of heretics on every side, lest he become entangled in the snares of false teachers, who are not teachers but deceivers of souls.

For just as those empty talkers whom we have now mentioned, so also there are others who wish, by allegorizing, to introduce the idea that Gehenna—which in the Scriptures is called the valley of the sons of Hinnom—and Jerusalem are not far from one another. Although Jerusalem is situated on a mountain and Gehenna is called a valley, they claim that the lot of those places is one, and that they are counted within one tribe, like the other most distinguished cities.

Therefore they assert that those who sin, even if they are cast into Gehenna and are called valleys because they have sinned, will at some time return to one lot and be counted within the same tribe in which that heavenly Jerusalem receives its lot. How absurd this opinion is, all the authority of the Scriptures and the Catholic faith proclaim, even without our speaking.
