Nevertheless, because these evils came to us transferred from the turmoil of the Greeks, I ought not to omit them. Those who hold or have held such opinions, already possessed by evil, are hastening headlong toward that final woe which remains, unless they are corrected. Concerning it the text continues: [Col. 0775D]

“Woe to you, blind guides, who say: Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound. Fools and blind! For which is greater, the gold, or the temple which sanctifies the gold? And whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is upon it is bound. Blind! For which is greater, the gift, or the altar which sanctifies the gift? Therefore whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by all the things that are upon it. And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by the one who dwells in it. And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by the one who sits upon it.”

The scribes and Pharisees are reproved for doing everything for profit and not out of fear of God. As above, in their enlarged phylacteries and fringes, they sought nothing but empty glory; through the occasion of glory they also pursued monetary gain. Therefore they are rightly called hypocrites and blind guides, although they sat upon Moses’ chair.

Under the appearance of holiness they sought neither the worship of God, nor glory, nor honor, nor observance of God’s commandments. As we already said above concerning the gift, when they said to father or mother, “Whatever gift is from me will benefit you” (Matt. XV, 5), so that everything might come to their own profit, these men likewise treated the temple and altar as insignificant and commanded that the gold and all the gifts of the law offered in them should be revered, so that everything might advance their own advantage and profit.

Because they delighted in these things—the gold and the gifts that they used for their own purposes—they said that these were holier than the temple and the altar themselves, so that those making offerings might become more ready to offer voluntarily a multitude of material gifts than to pour out prayers before the holy altar in the temple.

Accordingly, so that their gifts and vows might be made more firmly acceptable to God, they devised a very clever trick. If someone entered into a dispute or some controversy in which, because of the ambiguity of the quarrel, he ought to swear, he was not held guilty in the temple if he had sworn falsely. But if he had sworn by the gold, and was later convicted of having sworn falsely, he was held guilty of the crime. Immediately he was compelled to pay the gold by which he had sworn, so that everything might fall to their own uses.

Likewise, if someone had sworn by the altar, he was not at all judged guilty of perjury, even if he was convicted of having sworn. But if he had sworn falsely by the gifts and offerings presented to God at the altar—by sacrifices and victims or by any gifts—they diligently demanded these things from him, exacting from him that by which he had sworn falsely. [Col. 0776D]

The Lord therefore rightly rebukes them for venerating the gold of the temple and the gifts of the altar as objects of religious oath, when the honor of the altar and temple ought to have been more important. For, as figures of things to come, gold is dedicated to the temple and the gift to the altar.

When Christ came, all these things of the law were already useless for those offering them, because Christ was not sanctified by the law; rather, the law was sanctified in Christ. In the law, as in a seat and throne of God, he had previously been placed—the one who was proclaimed from it as destined to come [the transmitted reading *mike* is uncertain].

For this reason they are rightly called blind guides and hypocrites, because they pretended to revere the law and were accustomed to swear by the throne of God or by heaven, observing these things more religiously than the one who was judged to sit in them. They neglected the one who sanctifies and venerated the sanctified things, passing over Christ. Therefore a kind of likeness of heaven is introduced, so that the one who sits in it—or in the law—may be recognized.

For because of their traditions the Jews had corrupted all the commandments of the law and emptied out every understanding concerning Christ. He therefore wishes to lead them back both to the commandments of the life that must be practiced and to those that signify life, so that from the one they may understand that Christ has already come, and from the other, by keeping what has been commanded, may advance in Christ.

But because those people, possessed by demons, were unwilling to accept these things, let us, because we all offend in many ways (Jas. III, 2), follow Christ with groaning. “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V, 5).

First let us cleanse our consciences, so that we may understand how holy the holy Scriptures are and how full of God they are—Scriptures in which God dwells and from which he speaks to us. Then let us believe that no gold is holy except what has been dedicated within the temple of God; that is, let us accept nothing outside the divine Scriptures, however brightly it may shine.

For every meaning that seems to shine outwardly, even if it is admirable, is not thereby immediately proved holy. The Holy Spirit alone is the consecrator of the holy Scriptures. Through him the gold of eloquence is sanctified within and by those same Scriptures, so that what we bring forth may be found to be holy.

But if we offer any gifts upon the altar, let us first make pure the heart upon and within which we offer them. Let us first act through vows and prayers so that what is primary in us may be sanctified; then the gifts and offerings that we offer daily upon it will be holy.

Therefore we must persist in tears and prayers, so that this beatitude may be nourished in us by God and so that we may cleanse the heart from which and in which a vow is offered to God. For it is the human heart that makes every human vow acceptable to God—not by its own gift but by the gift of God.

Therefore the human heart, toward which God first looks and from which the vow is offered, is more honorable than the gift of the heart, which God considers only after the heart from which the vow is offered. [Col. 0777D]

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have left the weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy, and faith. These you ought to have done, without leaving the others undone.”

Woe to them, because they strained out all their works so that they might appear before people; therefore they are rightly called hypocrites.

But the question arises how the scribes and Pharisees tithed, since he was speaking to and about people who were especially priests and Levites, who were more accustomed to receive tithes from the people than to give them—unless some of them were priests and Levites, while others were ordinary members of the people.

Therefore it is not inappropriate to say that this passage has a twofold distinction: one part concerns the ordinary people, who gave tithes, although hypocritically; the other concerns the priests, who received tithes. The wording itself seems to leave the matter uncertain when it says, “Woe to you who tithe,” for both the one who receives tithes and the one who gives them can properly be said to tithe.

Perhaps the scribes and Pharisees gave tithes from their smallest vegetables, although they were priests, so that they might thereby be considered more righteous among the people. Those who saw them would say: “Consider how these men do not neglect to offer God tithes of all their possessions, since they do not even fail to give tithes of insignificant vegetables. Consider how their life is preserved according to all God’s commandments, so that they do not appear negligent even in small matters.”

Perhaps, therefore, they offered such things under the appearance of religious devotion so that they might avoid expense while gaining more favorable glory among the people.

The Lord therefore selected three vegetables from all those they gave, in order through them to show what they were seeking. They are extremely fragrant, and through their fragrances he indicated the reputation of empty praise that they drew toward themselves through their nostrils and the pleasures in which they delighted.

“And you have left,” he says, “judgment, mercy, and faith.” To the three things badly offered he opposed three things neglected even worse. Once these are omitted, all justice toward God and neighbor is frustrated.

The justice of God, by which each person is just and lives, is preserved through faith, because the ungodly person is justified. And unless you are found upright in judgment, you can never be just, nor justified in that justice by which a person departs from iniquity.

Therefore it was justly commanded that what is just should be carried out. This is rightly done when, in judgment, what belongs to God is justly rendered to God and what belongs to each neighbor is justly rendered to each neighbor. Thus the virtue of judging, divine no less than human, is included so that you may be found just.

How well, therefore, it has been said: “In all your judgments always consider God.” There are secular judgments, and there are ecclesiastical judgments. Yet secular officials may not presume upon what belongs to divine matters, nor may priests, who hold divine things in their hands, pass over into matters belonging to the world. Each of them must carry out what is just justly, without partiality.

Moreover, to live among brothers without mercy is already to incur divine judgment, because judgment will be without mercy for the one who has not shown mercy at the present time. But the primacy of mercy is that a person should begin with himself, as it is written: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX, 24). Then mercy proceeds through all one’s neighbors, because, according to the Gospel, only the person who shows mercy is rightly considered a neighbor.

These are the commandments of the law that the Lord calls weightier, along with many others. Yet all justice and charity are preserved in these three. It is therefore not without reason that the scribes and Pharisees are corrected by the Lord because they had neglected them.

But it is not unfitting to ask why they are called weighty, since every burden of Christ is light. If these are weighty, the others cannot be light; and if they are light, how, as the Savior says, are these called weighty?

Consider, please: even if the magnitude of the commandments is called light, it is nevertheless called a burden. But if it is a burden, how is it light? Unless there are one kind of burdens—the burdens of vices, which weigh a person down to the depths of hell—and another kind, the burdens of God’s commandments, which, when kept, lift a person to the heights of heaven.

These two kinds of weight seek opposite directions: the more blessed is the weight that draws upward, the more wretched is the weight that plunges downward.

The Lord did not criticize giving tithes of vegetables, but because they did not attend to the principal matters, whether the people observed them or not—matters which they themselves were unwilling to move even with a finger. Therefore he says: “These you ought to have done, without leaving the others undone.”

O divine wisdom, how carefully you speak in all things! Above, he had said that not one stroke or iota would pass away from the law. Therefore now also he does not release even the tithe of the smallest things, but requires that everything be fulfilled completely.

He had commanded them to preserve true judgment and justice, to show mercy, and to have faith. For the glory of his name he had also commanded that tithes be offered. Although the tithes themselves belonged to the honor of God, they were nevertheless given for the benefit of the priests, so that they might serve their needs.

Perhaps, therefore, those who did not care about greater things—whether they themselves or the people neglected them—demanded even the smallest vegetables as tithes. Nor did they correct anyone when he committed more serious offenses against God. [Col. 0779B]

Thus he concludes his judgment very well at the end: “Blind guides, who strain out”—or, as other copies read, “who strain out the gnat and swallow the camel.” Here one must understand the “woe” that he had said above.

By offering the smallest things they made them conspicuous. For “straining out” or “filtering” signifies more expressively that they prepared mint, dill, cumin, or whatever small things are denoted by the gnat, so pompously and brightly for offering that all diligence was commended in these little vegetables.

Because, through the fault of those offering them, these things themselves also became unclean, they are rightly compared to a gnat, which is both a small and an unclean animal, just as the camel is large.

The wicked priests swallowed the camel when, because of their greed for the belly, they absorbed the greatest commandments of God and did not care what either they themselves or the people committed as sin against God. They did not hunger or thirst for justice. Therefore, possessed by a demon, they swallowed the great works of virtue as though they were unclean and twisted, weighed down by the hump of greed, so that the commanded works would not be fulfilled.

All people are either judges or rulers—spiritual or worldly—or else they are subject to judges and rulers. Both those who rule and those who obey need true faith and good works, so that they may receive those beatitudes that are joined in opposition to this passage: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice” (Matt. V, 6).

Here two beatitudes come against this one woe. They are never rightly separated from each other, because neither should judgment, in which justice is preserved, exist without mercy, nor is mercy crowned without justice. Joined together in this way, they contend on every side against the vices: just as those vices make their followers wretched, so these virtues make them blessed.

Because the scribes and Pharisees strained out and offered the smallest things while swallowing judgment, from which justice arises, and mercy, which they plunged down as though into the gluttony of the stomach, they had not unjustly lost these two beatitudes and incurred one sole and eternal woe. For in this one matter they trampled upon the faith that is directed toward God and swallowed up the virtues most necessary among neighbors, so that they would share them with no one.

Therefore, doubled in all things by the just judgment of God, they received the losses of their lives in accordance with their iniquity.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who cleanse the outside of the cup and dish, but inside you are full of plunder and uncleanness. For under the appearance of vessels he designates human beings; and by what he adds—“inside you are full of plunder and iniquity”—he makes this clearer.

Indeed, whenever the Jews were about to enter the temple to offer sacrifices, or to celebrate feast days, or when they were returning from a journey, they washed themselves externally, their garments, and all their utensils; but inwardly they did not wash their heart and conscience, nor did they take care to cleanse them of the filth of wickedness. Hence, in Matthew, the cleansing of the outside of the cup and dish is introduced figuratively; whereas in Luke the washing of the cup and bowl is mentioned. [955] Both writers certainly speak of a cup, since it is always used as a vessel for drinking. Thus they did not both use the word *dish*: one used “bowl,” the other “dish.” Both, however, refer to a vessel prepared for eating. Therefore, through these two vessels, the whole human being—body and soul—is not improperly understood, so that by the vessels through which we are nourished with food or drink the entire person may be represented and admonished to be washed and nourished inwardly by the word. For “man shall not live by bread alone” (Matt. 4:4), but by spiritual food and drink, through which the inner person is refreshed.

And so that you may understand that these vessels have not been chosen for their own sake, hear what follows: “Blind Pharisee, first cleanse what is inside the cup and dish, so that what is outside may also become clean.” It does not seem consistent that the Jews should wash their vessels externally while they remained unclean inside, since they devoted such great care to their baptisms and purifications. Nor should one think that the Lord reproves them concerning the washing or not washing of their vessels in order to make them concerned about those vessels; rather, he draws an example from the cleansing of vessels so that through it they might return to themselves and cleanse themselves from every defilement, inwardly as well as outwardly, so that they might be holy and clean in mind and body.

If they had been willing to hear this, they would certainly have been blessed, because “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). This beatitude is plainly opposed to the woe assigned to them, because they were filled inwardly with every evil. For they themselves were the cup and the bowl: outwardly they displayed themselves as polished—in dress, speech, clothing, phylacteries, and all their pretended works—but their mind and conscience were polluted with every kind of filth and the dirt of vices.

For whatever a person does without a good conscience and not according to God appears clean outwardly, but inwardly is full of deceit and hypocrisy. Such are all who seek the glory of the world more than God’s, and who are more eager to please human beings than God. Whatever good they do benefits them nothing when they do it without a good motive; indeed, it harms them, because in the very thing through which they shine outwardly in action, they become more soiled inwardly in mind.

And if such people appear to do good, it is sin; how much more so when they themselves commit crimes! Thus the comparison with vessels is entirely appropriate: their outside is washed, although their use is internal. For if a vessel has become dirty within, what does it accomplish if it is washed only on the outside? Therefore the splendor of virtues and purity of mind must always be sought inwardly. For “blessed are the pure in heart; they shall see God.”

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful outwardly to human beings, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and of every kind of uncleanness. Although he seems to repeat the same thing in different words and sentences, he is always repeating the same single woe against them and condemning their one hypocrisy. Hence what follows: “So you also appear righteous outwardly to human beings, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.”

But as sins are piled upon sins, and the good things done falsely pass over into crimes, that one woe is multiplied as it increases, until that final single woe is completed in its seven parts. For the hypocrisy and iniquity with which the scribes and Pharisees were filled are themselves the bones of the dead and every kind of impurity. Hypocrisy, although it is some semblance of good—as though it were a bone—is a dead virtue. Hence virtues are also called “bones” in the sacred Scriptures.

Yet those bones with which tombs are filled possess nothing living, since what appears good is done hypocritically. They are bones, so to speak: virtues that are pretended; dead justice, dead chastity or virginity, and every other thing done falsely. The most merciful Savior wishes to show that every pretended virtue is a dead virtue—or rather, is not a virtue at all, because it is without faith. Therefore such virtue and such justice are dead when they have not been done for God; hence they are not justice or virtue, but pretense.

Accordingly, it is not without reason that the bodies of sinners are called “tombs of the dead,” and whitewashed, since outwardly they glitter with every kind of adornment while the soul within is dead and filled with the stench of many vices. Nor should that be considered alive which does nothing clean or spiritual within the body of sin.

And just as a tomb, while it is closed, appears beautiful from outside but is horrifying if it is opened, so pretenders to goodness, as long as they are not known, are considered praiseworthy; but once they are known, they are found detestable. For such people to be peacemakers is wholly contrary both to God and to themselves. Therefore, first, while they destroy themselves, they can neither be blessed nor be called children of God, because they are full of the bones of the dead. There are as many bones of uncleanness in them as there are works of darkness. [957] For this reason, by way of exaggeration, they are said to be tombs full of bones and whitewashed tombs of hypocrites. When people are filled with hypocrisy and iniquity, they are filled with every evil.

These vices leave no rank of the ecclesiastical order untouched, since even pretenders to martyrdom are found, and some are shown to have been false apostles. Likewise, in every order one finds persons pursuing the outward display of virtues without possessing them. Therefore such people prove to be enemies of the very virtues which they pretend to have.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous, and say, “If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partners with them in the blood of the prophets,” and so forth.

As far as the surface of the words is concerned, he does not seem to threaten very justly or reasonably those who were building the tombs of the dead and adorning the monuments of the righteous, just as we now do for any saints who are known to rest among us. Indeed, they were doing something praiseworthy when they built and adorned their tombs; nor did they consent to the deeds of their fathers, who had dared to lay hands on them, saying, “If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partners with them in the blood of the prophets.”

How, then, if they were such people, was it fitting that he should foretell that a woe threatened them? They were not culpable merely because they were their children, since it does not depend on anyone’s choice whose child one is, whether of a good or an evil man. And if there was no offense in any of these things, it remains that they were not guilty because they were good, but because they were imitators of the parents whom they condemned.

It is therefore clear that they performed the good works of virtue which they seemed to perform not for God, but hypocritically, so that they might be praised by human beings. Hence he says, “And you, fill up the measure of your fathers.” He does not command them to do what ought not to be done, but foretells what they themselves were going to do and were already plotting in their minds. They themselves bore witness to their crimes and showed themselves to be children of those who had killed the prophets, although they honored the tombs, since they trampled underfoot everything in the prophets’ words concerning Christ.

And, completing what was still lacking in the killing of the prophets and righteous, they brought it to fulfillment through the killing of Christ. Therefore, although the impious descendants professed to detest the deeds of their parents, they revered the books of the prophets, adorned the memorials of the righteous, and restored their tombs, in order by such reverence to show themselves free from guilt for their fathers’ crime. [958] Do you suppose that those who killed the Lord of the prophets, who foretold everything that happened concerning him, are free from guilt and from the stain of so great a crime?

Therefore the Lord says, “Fill up the measure of your fathers,” as though he were saying: “You who detest what was perpetrated by your fathers, complete the measure by multiplying the interest of your crime. For the persecution of the members and the killing of the whole body are brought fully to completion when the head is cut off and all the limbs are shattered on every side.”

The fathers of the scribes and Pharisees, unable to endure the rebukes of the prophets, persecuted and killed them. Likewise, their children, unable to endure Christ’s rebukes on account of their sins, although they knew him to be the Christ and God, the Son of God, because they were incapable of turning back from their guilt, did not fear to lay hands on him.

Thus, reader, throughout the entire succession of the Jewish people you will find that the children consistently honored as saints those whom their fathers had killed as though they were evil, and that they revered the prophets of those whom their fathers had rejected. They did not do this so that each might preserve his own innocence, but so that they might condemn one another by a domestic judgment.

This vice must also be avoided among Christians, because each person is always quicker to criticize another’s sins than his own. Therefore, if we pay attention, the vices of the Pharisees, repeated seven times, now touch our consciences most plainly. So too does this matter: many now honor dead saints while persecuting living people whom God commands them to love.

Let each person therefore take care, because these things were not spoken only to them, but also to all of us who would be born afterward. If they had been spoken only to those people, they would have remained spoken to them and would not have been written down; but now they were both spoken and written. They were spoken on account of them, but written on account of us.

For in these seven, so to speak, curses, although what he counts may seem small to some, the whole body of vices is portrayed, composed of seven principal crimes and doubled through hypocrisy. Thus, when seven woes are pronounced against them, as though the future were being announced prophetically, the entirety of Gehenna is described. Although there is one woe in it, there are many differing punishments; just as in paradise, although there is one blessedness and eight beatitudes are enumerated, there are very many dwellings and a diversity of degrees according to merits.

There is a certain likeness in this Evangelist: on either side, as though from Mount Gerizim, he sets forth seven beatitudes, and from Mount Ebal, as if opposite them, he prophetically displays an equal number of curses against the impious and criminal Jews, more in a prophetic manner than in the spirit of one who merely wishes evil, so that each generation may be distinguished according to its merits.

And just as we now see that what was then proclaimed has been fulfilled in the Jews, so now the Evangelist, writing according to the ancestral manner, makes it clear that these things also, which were spoken from the Lord’s mouth, will certainly be fulfilled in the saints and in sinners.

Thus, just as the final beatitude is, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:10), so this is the final woe: because they were full of the bones of the dead and were to fill up the measure of their fathers by killing prophets and wise men, and even the Lord himself.

On account of all these things, the voice of the saints beneath God’s altar cries out: “Avenge, Lord, our blood which has been shed” (Rev. 16:10). And through the prophet: “Repay our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom” (Ps. 78:12). This multiplication of the number is rendered here, just as it was foreshadowed in Cain from the beginning, so that the multitude of the wicked may presently understand the fullness of their punishments. It follows:

“Serpents, offspring of vipers, how will you escape the judgment of Gehenna?”

It is true that serpents are more cunning than all other animals, but their cunning is not directed toward good, rather toward evil; for they are always watching so that they may harm and conceal themselves. Thus every hypocrite and deceitful person wishes to be more cunning than other human beings and considers how he may deceive another by his cleverness; and when he has deceived him, he behaves as though he had harmed no one.

“Offspring of vipers”: although I have already spoken above about this passage, they are called this here because, through successive generations, they condemned one another’s deeds, and the fathers were always reproached by their children, just as the children in turn were cut off by their own descendants. Such, indeed, is the nature of vipers.

“How,” he says, “will you escape the judgment of Gehenna?” As though he were saying: “Is it because you build the tombs of the prophets? Does God not judge the secrets of the heart?” Therefore it is no holiness or justice to honor and venerate the saints while despising holiness. The first step of piety is to love justice and holiness, and only then to love the saints, because those are saints whom holiness has consecrated to the Lord.

“Therefore, behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes; some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues,” and so forth.

Here we must consider what reason he gives when he says, “Therefore, behold, I send to you prophets.” For above he had said, “Fill up the measure of your fathers.” He certainly did not say this in order to command them, nor so that they should do what he appears to order.

Nor does he send them prophets and wise men here so that they may kill, scourge, and crucify them, as the enumeration might suggest. Rather, he does so because they had said, “If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partners in the blood of the prophets,” wishing to justify themselves before human beings and not before God, who sees the heart of each person and distinguishes the consciences of hypocrites.

He therefore says, “Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men,” as though he were saying: “For this reason I send them to you, so that the murderous deeds you are going to commit may become evident, and so that you may be convicted as children of murderous fathers; and so that everyone may understand that I am God, who sees and tests the hearts of individuals.”

And therefore I foretell to you that you will kill them, and that you will scourge them in your synagogues; then you will fill up the measure of your fathers. For although those who long ago foretold the coming of the Son of God killed them, you will destroy those who testify that he has already come.

And this is the measure which your fathers did not properly complete. But because they killed prophets and saints, you will complete that same measure; and you will do still worse, since you will also kill the Lord of the prophets.

Yet, as far as Christ’s words are concerned, he does not seem here to be speaking about his own death, since his death, which he willingly accepted, was the salvation of all—even of them, if after committing the crime they wished to return to him. Hence on the cross he prays for them.

Rather, he seems now to be imputing to them the deaths of the apostles and of the other saints, who were killed against their will. Perhaps, therefore, he says, “Fill up the measure of your fathers,” and not, “Exceed the measure.” If he had spoken more openly about himself, he would have shown them what was going to happen.

For it is characteristic of a kind and just judge to disregard injuries done to himself more readily and to avenge those done to others. Therefore, because the Lord is just and upright, seeing their hearts full of deceit and fraud, and the sins of their parents and of themselves heaped together, the measure of their fathers was already complete in the sight of God, insofar as their will and the purpose of their hearts were concerned. God examines hearts; they were already, as it were, murderers, since their wickedness existed in their intention and will.

Hence the prophet also says: “But those who turn aside to their obligations, the Lord will lead away with the workers of iniquity.”

By “prophets and wise men and scribes” he means the apostles, or those whom he sent with them to preach. For, as the Apostle writes to the Corinthians, there were various gifts in the Church of Christ, which the Holy Spirit appointed: some prophets, who foretold future things; some wise men, who possessed the fullest knowledge in Christ and knew when they ought to speak; and some scribes, highly learned in the law, who knew how to bring forth new things from their hearts, and so forth.

“And some of them you will kill,” as Paul was beheaded, along with many others; “and you will crucify,” as Peter was crucified and Andrew was hung upon the same kind of cross; and likewise Stephen was stoned, the first martyr to come before the Lord, chosen for this purpose long beforehand.

Hence it is not without reason that he is believed to have received his name: *Stephen* in Greek means “crown” in Latin. Thus, suitably designated beforehand by his name as by a prophecy—for the Greek name *Stephen* means “crown” in Latin—he was the first to wear a crown upon his head and came before the Lord as a glorious, crowned servant.

The disciples who were scourged are also read of in the Acts of the Apostles. No one can enumerate all the subsequent sufferings—what and how great they were, or where they endured them. But just as by this threefold number he gathered together all who suffered at their hands, so he also included every kind of torture they endured.

Hence it follows: “And you will persecute them from city to city.” How often they did this, history itself reveals: they expelled them from Judaea so that, unwillingly, they might cross into the wildernesses of the Gentiles.

[Col. 0785D] “So that,” he says, “there may come upon you all the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar.”

And this is the full measure of sin. For this reason it was impossible for those who were confined and held fast by such deeds to escape the judgment of Gehenna.

Finally, I do not think that what he says—“upon you”—should be understood as though he meant only those who were present at that time, with whom and about whom he had been speaking for a long time. By saying “upon you,” he includes together the fathers of whom he had spoken above, the children, and all their accomplices, as though they were one body; and shortly he shows that they are all one evil generation.

For in Abel’s time the Jews did not yet exist, but Cain’s accomplices were already evil and murderous. Therefore, although according to human usage there are many generations, in accordance with the custom of Scripture no more than two are gathered together at the end. From the beginning two cities are constructed: miserable Babylon and blessed Jerusalem.

And just as all good things are promised to one of them throughout all the pages of Scripture, so all evils are prophetically invoked and announced against the other, as though against a single person.

“From the blood of righteous Abel,” he says, “to the blood of Zechariah.” There is no ambiguity concerning Abel: he is the one whom his brother Cain killed. He is shown to be righteous not only now by God’s judgment but also by the testimony of Genesis, where his offerings are said to have been accepted by God.

But concerning Zechariah, who is said to be the son of Barachiah, there is much uncertainty, because we read of many Zechariahs. And so that we would not be given free opportunity for error, it is added: “whom you killed between the temple and the altar.”

Blessed Jerome testifies that he read much about this in his commentary. Origen, however, attempts to argue a position which, he admits, he could easily refute. He tries to establish that this Zechariah was the father of John, especially because Christ attributes his killing to the very Jews to whom he was speaking, and not to their fathers.

“Whom you killed,” he says, “between the temple and the altar.” He directs the word to them as though they themselves could not deny that this was so. Yet how he was the son of Barachiah, he confesses, cannot be proved from the holy Scriptures, unless perhaps—because *Barachiah* is interpreted from Hebrew as “blessed of God,” as Jerome himself attests—Zechariah may rightly be called the blessed son of God, since he was the son of a high priest from a priestly family; and if he were not blessed by God, he could in no way have been a priest.

As for his killing, Origen says that he received the following tradition. There was a place in the temple where only virgins were permitted to stand, and she was not permitted to stand there. But blessed Mary, after giving birth to the Savior, entered the temple to pray and stood in that place assigned to virgins, conscious of her own modesty.

When the scribes and Pharisees, who knew that she had borne a son, prohibited her, Zechariah, already fully aware of the divine mystery, is said to have resisted them and to have said to those who opposed him: “Do not forbid her, because she is worthy to stand in the place of virgins, since she too is a virgin.”

For this reason the chief priests were provoked. Because Zechariah was preaching Christ, and because he was allowing a woman—of whom it was not denied that Christ had been born—to stand in the place of virgins, as though he were acting most openly against the law, the men of that generation, or perhaps those with whom he was speaking, killed him between the temple and the altar.

After saying these things, Origen continues and adds that, if they do not believe this kind of tradition, we should demand of them an explanation: how, as though they were the children of those who killed the prophets, Jesus reproaches them with killing Zechariah, and does not refer the deed back to their fathers, but speaks as though the children themselves had killed him between the temple and the altar. For he addresses the Pharisees and scribes who were present: “whom you killed.”

If they had not done this, they could certainly have denied that they had, and accused him of falsely charging them. Hence Christ wishes to introduce something like this: “You who excuse yourselves from the blood of the prophets and say, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partners with them in the blood of the prophets,’ and who build their tombs—in daring to kill this man you give testimony against yourselves that you are children of the murderous fathers, and therefore in everything you complete their measure.”

If someone objects, “Why did he not say, ‘to the blood of John’?” the answer is that they did not kill John, but “to the blood of Zechariah,” in whom there was the end of all the prophets and of the king, just as there was in John.

Otherwise, what reason was there for him to choose these two, from the one to the other of whom the blood of all the saints that had been shed was to be demanded? Unless it was because persecution began with Abel, and this man was the last among the ancient saints who were killed before Christ’s Passion, as the aforesaid writer relates.

Nevertheless, blessed Jerome, as his commentary records, asserts that this Zechariah was the son of Jehoiada the priest, killed by King Joash, although Origen speaks very differently about the name.

“We read,” he says, “of Azariah being stoned, the son of Jehoiada the priest, because he rebuked the people.” But Jerome proves from both the name and the place where he was killed that he was Zechariah, and also from the fact that Joash repaid his father with evil for good.

Therefore they say that these two were mentioned so that the magnitude of the offense might be demonstrated and the enormity of the crime might be brought into comparison.

[964] Cain killed his brother without any cause; and Joash killed Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada the priest, who had raised him, rescued him from death, and concealed him in the temple for seven years, while all the royal offspring were being killed. Afterwards he established him in the kingdom and instructed him throughout his life.

But that man, forgetting all these benefits, killed his son—what is more criminal—his foster-brother, between the temple and the altar; that is, as some wish it understood, between the temple wall and the altar of incense, so that the criminal nature of the deed might be made still more evident.

We, however, can understand “between the temple and the altar” according to a manner of speaking: between the priests and the people, in whom the whole matter is comprised—referring the temple to the people and the altar to the priests, among whom the remaining blood of the prophets was also shed.

Others understand it as between the ruins of the temple and the outer altar, which was the altar of sacrifices. They say this happened because, since he was a prophet of God, he never ceased rebuking the king and the people for abandoning the law and sacrificing to gods.

From all these accounts it is gathered that a great crime was committed by both those whom the Savior set before us. Nevertheless, let the prudent reader judge which of these accounts is more accurate.

For my part, I would certainly not say that the Savior chose these two without reason, since the blood of the saints that was shed upon the earth was to be demanded from one point to the other. And he did not say “which is to be shed upon the earth,” in order to frighten them away from their purpose, but “which has been shed.”

It follows:

“Amen I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation.”

We have already said above that there are two generations in the divine Scriptures: the generation of the wicked and the generation of the good. Of the latter it is said: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob” (Ps. 24:6). And in another psalm concerning all the saints: “The generation of the upright shall be blessed” (Ps. 112:2), and in very many other passages.

Of the wicked, however, and in the present passage, there is the “generation of vipers.” And all these things will be demanded from this generation.

In Ezekiel (14:14, 20), after he had described the sins of the earth, he says: “If Noah, Job, and Daniel were found there, the sins of that land would not be forgiven.” By these three he wishes all the righteous to be understood, those who would be like them in virtues.

Thus these people, who acted against the apostles or against any of the saints in a manner similar to Cain, Joash, or any of the persecutors, are all counted as one generation. When the whole of this generation has been gathered together at the end, all these things that they did will certainly come upon it.

Conversely, the good things which, throughout the successive generations from the creation of the world, all the saints have done, will finally be received by those who have received Christ.

Thus all the evils which, throughout the successive generations from the creation of the world, all the wicked and killers of the saints accumulated for themselves came upon the final Jews, who not only rejected Christ and the saints but also killed them.

For just as such great and abundant grace of God was never given to holy people as was given in Christ, so there was never an extermination so great and terrible as that which came upon the wretched Jews, who killed Christ and persecuted the saints without any repentance of heart.

And I say this apart from all the other things which they suffered at the hands of the Romans and continue daily to suffer as captives. I do not mean that the sins of all the preceding wicked people would come upon those who were present at that time and did the deeds that are recounted; rather, we say that just as the righteous deeds of all the saints did not merit blessings from God as great as those granted through Christ, so also the evil that increased upon the Jews who crucified Christ and persecuted his disciples was such as no others had previously endured.

Nevertheless, all the blood and all the deeds they committed will come upon this generation, so that all together may endure and receive in common their individual portions of what they accumulated. Since their wickedness was united from beginning to end, it is just that their punishment also be one, as though they were a single body.

Otherwise, let the prudent reader read Josephus and see how many things came upon the Jews even in the present life, so that they suffered bodily afflictions such as those they endured from the Romans. They were so rejected by God that even today they are a mockery to all nations. Then he will be able to consider how many and what kinds of things remain for the impious and the wicked, when God comes to judge all things and to repay each person his due.

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you.”

This is the voice of one mourning and grieving, just as it is said elsewhere: “When Jesus saw the city, he wept over it” (Luke 19:21). The compassionate and merciful Lord did not lament only the death of his saints, nor the blood of all the prophets that had been shed by them, as much as we read that he wept and grieved over this wretched city, knowing that glory was being prepared for his elect through these things.

[966] But he was grieving over their destruction, as a kind and just Lord over those whom he had loved greatly. His excessive mercy bent him toward lamentation, while justice recalled him, lest he allow so great an evil to go unpunished for too long.

Therefore he shed tears for the impious, wishing to show them mercy, but their impiety and the power of justice prevented this. For mercy is true only if justice is not violated.

Accordingly, this voice in which he says “Jerusalem, Jerusalem” is no less a voice of warning than of lamentation, in case they might, struck by fear, cease from their guilt, and, moved by his lamentations, be formed for the mourning of repentance.

Thus the meaning is clear: the impious and sinners provoke wrath upon themselves, so that they do not deserve any mercy.

“You who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you.”

Again Origen seems to reopen questions he had discussed above. He asks how the Savior, speaking before Jews—including scribes and Pharisees who gloried in their knowledge of the law and the prophets—could have said that Jerusalem killed the prophets and stoned those sent to it. The divine history does not establish this very clearly, since the history read daily in their synagogues mentions only Azariah, son of Jehoiada, whom we read was stoned.

Therefore, he says, we must consider whether this word of Christ may need to be demonstrated from more secret books, which are read among them—not only the word of Christ, but also that of his disciples, namely Stephen, the protomartyr, and the apostle Paul.

For Stephen says: “Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of this one, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become” (Acts 7:52).

Paul likewise says to the Thessalonians: “You became imitators, brothers, of the churches of God that are in Judaea in Christ Jesus, because you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews, who killed both the Lord and the prophets and persecuted you” (1 Thess. 2:14).

And to the Hebrews: “They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they died by the sword” (Heb. 11:37), along with the other things he enumerates. It would be lengthy to pursue all these matters, which the aforementioned teacher repeats.

We need know only this: there are certain things among them which we cannot affirm from the divine books unless we follow the authority of Paul and blessed Stephen the protomartyr. For they said nothing else before those same Jews except what was well known to everyone.

Thus, if the matter concerning Zechariah cannot be established from authoritative books, Origen nevertheless confesses that he received it from tradition in the same way. He also teaches that only Isaiah was sawn in two, that Azariah alone, the son of Jehoiada, was stoned, and that Zechariah alone, the son of Barachiah, died by the sword.

Perhaps this discrepancy in the name was caused by a difference among interpreters or by the variation of manuscripts.

But how Jerusalem killed the prophets is rightly asked. It is not believed that the buildings of the walls themselves killed them, just as the Lord is not shown to have lamented stones and walls. Rather, it is said in the manner of ordinary speech, as when one says, “The whole city cried out,” or, “The whole city went out to meet him,” meaning those who were in the city.

Thus those who killed them are themselves rightly called fellow citizens, and Jerusalem is said to have killed the prophets on account of them.

It should also be noted that he did not say, “which you killed and stoned,” but, “which you kill and which you stone.” As though he were saying: “This is your distinctive and almost now natural habit: to stone and kill the saints.”

For even after Christ had been killed, Jerusalem did not cease from then on to kill those sent to it. It did to the apostles the same things it had previously done to the prophets sent to it.

As though he were saying: “How will you be healed, since you allow no physician to come to you? Indeed, you trample underfoot every medicine. Therefore how shall I spare you, since you do not spare those of mine who are sent to you?”

How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings—and you were unwilling! And it must be asked whom he calls “children,” and why he says “how often I wanted,” as though he had frequently wished to gather them, when it is evident that he taught them bodily only once. And if he wanted to, what is meant by the fact that he did not do it? For the Lord did everything whatever he wished, as the Prophet sings: “The Lord has done whatever he wished in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 134:6).

Although I have already dealt sufficiently with this question above, I shall now say further that, if he had not wished to gather them to himself—prophets and apostles—he would never have sent so many of them to them. He spared his own so that he might spare her, the sinful woman; he disregarded their lives so that he might not see her death; indeed, he handed himself over to death. But what does it mean that he did not do what he wished, unless it is because he is just and has always loved justice? For this reason he could not act otherwise, because he ought not to have done so: her affliction was incurable. In a manner of speaking, she defeated divine skill, and all the spiritual physicians sent to her failed in everything they did on her behalf; therefore she was not healed. If he had wished to destroy her, he would never have come to her himself. But what could he do with her, when she was proved in every way unwilling to live?

When he says “how often,” this refers not only to the time when he was in the world in the flesh, but also to the rest of time. For Christ was substantially present with them in Moses and the prophets, in the fathers and patriarchs, and even in the angels who ministered aid for human salvation through each successive generation. Thus what he says, “How often I wanted,” was fulfilled. For in each succession children were born to him, and he wished to gather them all into the unity of faith, so as to accomplish the Father’s will; but their perversity always prevailed.

Over them he spread his wings in the manner of a hen. Hence Moses, in the Song, says that he spread his wings like an eagle, stirring up his chicks to fly, and took them up and carried them upon his shoulders (Deuteronomy 32:11).

This work properly belongs to Christ: to gather. For this purpose the Son of Man came, “to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10). It should also be noted that throughout the earlier time it was always the same one who wished to gather them, not one person who wished to do so then and another who wishes to do so now. Hence God is neither recent nor alien, since the one who wished to do so then was himself the one who came. He came not to some place other than where he was, nor as another than the one who always was. Although he assumed humanity into God, he did not change his person, for he is immutable; nor did he assume a person other than the one he had always possessed, as someone recently and wrongly thought: that in Christ there was a merely nominal or adoptive God, while the true God was the Word of God. He was so foolish as to introduce two gods and two sons of God, one proper and the other adoptive.

But Christ, who was then speaking to the Jews in the flesh, showed himself to be the one and the same person who had often wished, in the Old Testament, to gather them under his wings and carry them upon his shoulders for the sake of redemption. These wings of Christ may appropriately be proclaimed as the twofold charity, because of Christ’s twofold substance in one and the same person; under him we are gathered and protected. Although some have wished to interpret the two wings as Moses and Aaron, it is better for us to understand them as the powers of the divine majesty, concerning which the Prophet sings: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Psalm 16:8)—namely, hope and grace. Although these people did not possess such wings, divine help was never lacking for them while they pleased God.

A remarkable comparison is proposed in the hen. For no animal becomes weak in the way a hen does when brooding over and nourishing its chicks. She becomes wholly weakened, entirely ruffled and hoarse. She continually hurries about, as though trying by certain cries to gather her chicks, and does not cease calling them to herself with constant clamor, lest, wandering here and there in different directions, they be seized in the talons of kites.

But Christ bestowed this affection in vain and without fruit. Like a hen, he assumed the weakness of flesh so that he might warm them beneath the wings of his teachings with the heat of charity and restore them to life. For this reason he became, in a certain sense, an earthly and domestic bird, so that, like the protection of wings, he might pour the warmth of his body’s great covering over his chicks, grant them immortal life, and raise them to flight as though through a new birth.

Chicks have one mode of being born and another of being nourished. At first they are enclosed within the shells of eggs, as though in a bodily enclosure. Then, after the eggs have been warmed by the parent’s attentiveness, they are born; afterward they are brooded over until they emerge for flight. In the manner of this bird, therefore, Christ wished to gather them within himself and nourish them, so that those who had already been brought forth by the condition of their first birth might, through the origin and warmth of another regeneration, be brooded over by the nourishing God, be born again from water and the Spirit, and fly up into the heavenly kingdom as though with winged bodies.

Hence, very appropriately, in the passage where we read, “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Genesis 1:2), the Hebrew has *merephet*, which is said to be interpreted as “was brooding” or “was warming.” This showed that from the waters, through its warmth and sanctification, a new kind was to be created. Because these people were unwilling to receive either Christ or the Holy Spirit, he said: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.” It is as though he said: “Because you were unwilling to be gathered under my wings.”

It should be noted that he says “your,” although that house had previously belonged to God. Now it is no longer mine or my Father’s, but yours, and it has become a den of thieves—although once it shone with greater splendor throughout the whole world. Now the Synagogue also will be left desolate by God, when all religious observance passes over to the Church; or because, as a punishment for Christ’s cross, that temple too was destined to be destroyed by the Romans.

Nor will you see me from now on until you say, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” According to Luke, the meaning is more straightforward, because he had not yet come to Jerusalem, nor had this acclamation been made by the children; he foretells that it will occur. Nevertheless, according to both Evangelists, it should be understood as though he had said to them: “Unless you repent and confess me as the Son of God, you will never see my face—that is, the true knowledge of me—in your heart. For I will no longer come to teach you, since from now on there will be no time for gathering, as I wished before.”

The Jews therefore have time granted to them, if they wish, for the veil to be removed from their hearts and for them to be able to see Christ’s face, if they say and confess concerning him: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord God the Father.” For the Father’s name belongs to the Son, just as the Son’s belongs to the Father. The Father is never named without the Son, nor the Son without the Father. Accordingly, he himself is in the Father, just as the Father is in the Son. Therefore whoever wishes to see his face should say and confess: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” because he himself is both God and Lord.

We may also understand figuratively, through the example of the hen, the Church, which is Christ’s body. Every day she gathers her chicks—that is, her children, whom she generates through water and the Holy Spirit—into the unity of faith, under the guidance of the virtues. And just as a hen also broods over and warms eggs that are not her own, so our mother the Church, gathered from all nations, raises and nourishes foreign children through the grace of the Holy Spirit and makes them her own. She continually warms them, broods over them, and protects them beneath her wings.

These wings are the teachers and governors of the churches. With their wings extended toward every doctrine of the virtues, they rightly do not allow the chicks to be exposed to any deceitful ambushes, but nourish them by their teachings toward lofty things, until they are able by themselves to fly into the heavenly realms.

I have said this so that the prudent mind may learn to consider many other things as well—things that we omit for the sake of brevity—in many passages. For the divine discourse is found almost everywhere to be like the ark of God, with two or three chambers.

## Chapter 24

“And Jesus went out from the temple and was going away, and his disciples approached to show him the buildings of the temple.”

Here Mark and Luke relate that, before he left the temple—as though he were about to go to the nations—a poor widow, in the figure of the Church, brought two small coins, representing the Law and the Gospel, in order to receive Christ in faith. Therefore she cast in more than all the others.

They showed him the buildings of the temple because they had heard him say: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.” They were as though amazed and grieving that such a great and magnificent structure of the temple should be reduced to nothing, and wished to move him by the grandeur of such a work. For this reason they said to him, as the Evangelist expresses it more clearly elsewhere: “Teacher, do you see what kind of stones and what kind of buildings these are?” Evidently they wished to bend the most merciful Jesus toward pity for that place, so that he might not permit what he had foretold to happen.

Or they showed them to him in amazement at the hardness of their hearts, as though they were saying: “Alas! How great is the adversity—or the blindness—of this people, who do not believe so that they may be converted, lest so great a structure of the temple and city should perish!” Jesus answered them and said: “Do you see all these things? Truly I say to you, not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed.”

Nevertheless, these words were sometimes spoken while he was leaving the temple and going away. But as soon as he had completed his statement of what was to happen, he departed from the precincts of the temple—the temple that he had preserved from destruction until he was within it, though afterward it was destroyed by the Romans. For Jesus was already preparing another eternal temple for his own in heaven. As long as the word of God was among the Jews, the kingdom of God was not taken away from them. But now that it has been taken away, they and their city have been left empty and vain: “Like a shelter in a cucumber field, and like a city that is laid waste” (Isaiah 1:8); and they have been scattered among all the nations.

When the Lord departed from the temple, all the structures of the Law were destroyed, and the stones of the sanctuary were scattered into every wind, as though they were ashes, so that no saving religion might any longer be found in them.

This passage also touches morally upon the hearers and teachers of the churches. For although that structure was admirable, far more admirable is the structure of human nature, which was not built according to the pattern of just anyone, but was made in the image and likeness of God, so that it might be his temple, formed according to his image.

Perhaps the apostles are doing this very thing: they display the wonderful works of God toward the human creature, placing it before God’s sight and interceding so as to move the most merciful Savior not to abandon the human race because of its sins. Rather, they urge him toward pardon and toward the very wonderful works of God, rather than toward anger on account of their iniquities, lest the temple of the living God should be destroyed and reduced to nothing.

Therefore we must carefully consider why that temple, once utterly cast down to the ground, is destroyed a second time or even more often. For there was always room for repentance; hence, as an image of penitents, after it had been burned, it was restored. But now, according to the hardness of their hearts—because they were unwilling to receive the word of God—they have fallen into something worse.

Thus every soul, so long as it receives Christ within itself, is a temple of the Holy Spirit. But when, after sin, it has completely fallen away from the word of God and does not care for itself sufficiently to repent, it continually slips away from the faith and runs downward. Although it gradually withdraws from life while abandoning God and is diminished day by day, eventually it collapses completely into sin.

When these things have taken place, what follows is exceedingly dreadful: “Not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed.” For even if it seemed to possess something of good work, those were not stones of the sanctuary, but straw and hay long prepared to be consumed in the fire.

Therefore, while there is opportunity, we must carefully examine ourselves, so that every structure of piety built together within us may remain intact. And if it should happen—which God forbid—that someone should fall, the author of our building must be implored and the Holy Spirit invoked, so that what has been corrupted and defiled may be recovered and cleansed within us; what has been distorted and destroyed may likewise be renewed, so that, through the power of the word—for the sacraments of our redemption remain—he may restore within us what has perished while repentance is still possible. He restores all things by his word alone.

Otherwise, “not one stone will be left upon another” when evil thoughts and deeds are destroyed. For when a perverse mind adds an even more perverse thought to a perverse thought, it does nothing other than place stone upon stone. But in the destruction of the wretched city, no stone is left upon stone, because when the unhappy soul is led to the vengeance of divine judgment, every structure of evil thoughts is scattered from it. Then the entire city of the mind will be laid waste, as though in an enemy’s devastation, when the wretched soul, deprived of its works, is led to death by the enemies whom it wickedly served as a captive during life.

Because the Lord is hastening to the Mount of Olives, and the discourse he is about to have there with his disciples is more extended, it must not be cut short; rather, everything he spoke on that most holy mountain must be treated together. For this reason the book must finally be brought to an end, lest either this work be extended and burden the reader’s mind, or that discourse—which would not be fitting—be divided.

# Prologue to the Eleventh Book

## [Col. 0793]

Amid the deep silences of the heart and the very busy leisure of monastic discipline, we who are bound by divine vows ought to consider highly desirable, lest we be found idle without the fruit of eternal contemplation, that example of Cato—especially for me, an old man—if I should ever truly be able to say what he himself, already an old man, wrote concerning the man first called Africanus. He said that Africanus was accustomed to declare that he was never less at leisure than when he was at leisure, and never less alone than when he was alone.

This is a magnificent saying, my brothers, worthy of a great and wise man; but it is suited and necessary to no one more than to us monks. It shows that such a great man, even in leisure, reflected upon the concerns of the good life, and in solitude was accustomed to speak with himself about useful things; he never ceased to think about good and necessary matters.

How much more ought we, dearest brothers, never to cease, in leisure, from thinking about divine things, since we are devoted to heavenly disciplines; and never to be alone in solitude, since always and everywhere we live before God: “In whom we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28). We are also before the whole assembly of the citizens above, lest our enemies perhaps mock our sabbaths if at some hour we are not only useless to ourselves but also—as must sadly often have happened—are found harmful to others.

Therefore, as I have often said, at the final boundaries of life, at your urging, I have resolved, amid the retreats and sometimes the solitudes of our silence, to undertake again the work I had left unfinished and, in devotion, to dedicate it to you.

Accordingly, let each person carefully consider, as I have already advised above, how each of the Evangelists regulates his own order, so that all say one thing while each possesses something proper to himself. Although one may speak more excellently on some point and another more modestly, all nevertheless speak both their own material and what they share with the others. It is a pious task to consider and investigate how they communicate these things with one another—how one speaks together with another, or with two, or with three—and to examine the particular features of each. The labor yields no small fruit.

For in these writings you will find nothing empty of mystery, nothing superfluous, and nothing omitted from Christ’s teaching that the Holy Spirit judged necessary for us to know. Everything is so interwoven and so adorned with the figures of events and sayings that it appears both as one seamless garment woven from above throughout (John 19:23) and as a marvelous beauty of works, with a many-colored variety of meanings displayed in individual blossoms.

In these writings it is not merely history that is woven, in the manner of those who are known simply to narrate events; rather, the divine mysteries of things are arranged in their proper places, as though gems had been inserted wherever the Holy Spirit determined to adorn the same garment of Christ.

These matters must therefore be searched out fully, so that the meaning of each may be understood in its proper place and the unity of the whole understanding, dispersed here and there by the Holy Spirit as though from one fountain, may not be corrupted.

# Book Eleven

## [Col. 0795]

First, the sitting of Christ on the Mount of Olives must be treated; thereafter, the same discourse, which he delivered there at greater length in response to the disciples’ questions, must be explained section by section.

Matthew, Mark, and Luke follow this discourse in nearly the same sequence, because great divine mysteries are disclosed in it. Therefore—as I have very often said—nothing in it is empty of mystery: not the time, not the order, not the place, not the posture, not the setting, nor anything whatever that is said on that mountain.

For just as the things he previously taught on another mountain are extraordinary and ineffable, so are these things—indeed, to speak frankly, some of them are obscure and incomprehensible as well.

The mountain itself contains an ineffable mystery, not only because it is a mountain, but also because it is called the Mount of Olives, that is, the mountain of light, and because it lies to the east of that city. For when Jesus departed from the temple and from that earthly Jerusalem, leaving the Jews and the Synagogue, he ascended this same mountain, on which fruitful olive trees had been planted and are planted daily. In these our wild olive tree has been grafted, because the branches were broken off.

On this mountain, and from it, the Lord came to his passion and prayed to the Father. From there again, after completing all the mysteries of our redemption, he ascended into heaven. For this reason he foretells more things there concerning the future, and not without reason, since—as many teachers maintain—the Lord will descend there to carry out the future judgment, just as it was foretold and proclaimed to the apostles by the angels: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

Although others understand this differently, we judge that, just as he ascended from earth to heaven, so, according to the angels’ statement, he will come from heaven to earth and carry out judgment on earth.

Therefore it is not without reason that the judgment is thought to be destined to occur at the place where the author of life was sentenced to death, so that at that place the impious and sinners may receive the sentence of condemnation—those who always preferred to remain in death.

Perhaps, therefore, the prophet literally says: “The Lord will go forth and fight against the nations, and his feet will stand upon the Mount of Olives, which is toward the east” (Zechariah 14:3–4). For from that mountain, whose name is interpreted as “light,” he came to his passion; shortly afterward he ascended from it to the place of light and glory, which is the true light of the world and the mountain raised to the summit of all mountains.

Accordingly, it is not inappropriate to say that he came to the Mount of Olives and sat there with his disciples, because they are read as sitting with him in judgment. From there all the elect will ascend to the place of rest and repose, through Christ, who is the mountain and the true rest of souls.

Below there is also a valley, which perhaps, as a foretelling of future things, is called and interpreted as the Valley of Jehoshaphat, the valley of judgment. The mountain signifies the Church, which will ascend above with Christ; the valley of judgment signifies the company of the lost, who, condemned in judgment, will descend to the depths with their head, the devil—that is, to hell.

Therefore the Church is not without reason represented by this mountain. It is God’s throne, in which the Lord will sit as judge of the world. There will be some who do not believe and have already been judged; others with whom he will judge others in judgment; and others who are to be judged, among whom the elect will be mixed with the reprobate.

But the elect will be gathered to their head and, transplanted like fruitful olive trees, will take root upon the mountain, which is the Church. They will be established by the root of charity so that they can no longer be moved. Each of them will be able to say: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Psalm 51:10).

There is no doubt that on this Mount of Olives, which is Christ, the Synagogue was first planted and took root. From it the branches were broken off, and wild olive branches were grafted in their place—those branches that were broken off because of unbelief.

At the summit of the mountain, as though the Lord were seated there as a farmer, “the disciples approached him privately, saying…”

Here we must consider the disciples’ approach to Jesus. They are said to sit with him, as though in judgment. Then some approach more privately, thereby showing that they have greater confidence with him, as members of his household. We can see that they did this above as well, when they questioned him about the parables.

Others, however, do not question him privately but openly and in the presence of the crowd. Therefore, reader, observe everywhere the difference among those who approach Christ.

Those who approach like the Pharisees, testing him, approach and question him in one way—not from faith, nor do they ask or pray from faith. Others sometimes seek and ask because they desire to learn; yet they never do so privately, but within the crowd.

These chief apostles approach in another way: Peter, namely, James, and John, and now Andrew is added to them. Because those who approach are great, the things they ask are also great. They do not speak with a feigned heart, but because they have been struck with fear by the Lord’s words and are taking one thing for another, they say to him: “Tell us when these things will be.”

What are these “things” about which they ask as though pointing to something? They are the things he had said above in the presence of all: “Not a stone will stand here upon another stone that will not be destroyed.” From this they took the occasion for their question, and they ask three things at once: when Jerusalem and everything in it will be destroyed; at what time Christ himself will come again; and when the consummation of the age will occur.

They do not merely wish to learn when it will be destroyed; they also seek the sign of his coming and the sign of the consummation of the age. For, like human beings, they thought that the temple would not be destroyed before he himself returned and the end of the age came. They therefore asked whether the destruction of the temple might be the sign of his coming and of the consummation of the age.

Many people believed these things, but absolutely no one knew when they would occur, and even today they do not know. Jesus answered them and said: “See that no one deceives you.” For they were seeking the sign of his coming, and many false Christs were destined to come into the world in his name, performing signs, like Simon Magus and others. Therefore he warns them beforehand and says: “See that none of them deceive you through the signs and wonders that you seek.”

## [Col. 0798A]

“For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ,’ and they will deceive many.”

Who these many are who are said to come in Christ’s name is not sufficiently clear. For, as the history of the readings shows, there were not many people in the time of the apostles who said that they were Christs—unless perhaps Dositheus the Samaritan and Simon Magus, of whom it is said in the Acts of the Apostles that he declared himself to be the great power of God.

Nevertheless, there were many heretics who perhaps came in Christ’s name because they claimed to possess Christ’s teaching. In his name they asserted many things; they even displayed and proclaimed that they performed exceedingly wondrous works, and urged many to believe what was being said, to such an extent that they deceived very many and plunged them into various errors.

Concerning these, John says in his Epistle, as you have heard: “Antichrist will come, but now many antichrists have arisen” (1 John 2:18). And the Antichrist who is said to be coming—what else will he say that he is but Christ God? Scripture declares that he will exalt himself above every name that is said or named.

Therefore, if there are already many antichrists, what else can they be called, together with their head, except false Christs? They are opposed to Christ. Indeed, any word that is foreign and alien to the truth and to the faith, yet asserts that it is the word of God—what else do we call it than antichrist?

And because this one Word is true, if there is some other word that is spoken against Christ, whoever carries it in his heart is rightly himself called an antichrist. Therefore many false Christs have already come and will come in Christ’s name; they have led many away from the faith and will lead them away.

For this reason he warns them and says: “See that no one deceives you.” Lest some deceiver suggest falsehood to the ignorant, and lest the right faith be weakened by a destructive lie, the warning of the loving Teacher went before them.

He says this not only to the apostles, but through them to all his own people who will be members of Christ until the end of the age. Nevertheless, these signs and the others that follow began almost from the time when they are said to be destined to occur.

Because the apostles asked three things—when Jerusalem would be destroyed, which was the occasion of their question; when he himself would come; and when the end of the age would occur—it must therefore be asked whether the three signs he enumerates pertain to these three matters, and whether each should be assigned to its corresponding part.

For the destruction of that wretched city is one thing, and his coming in his body, which is the Church, is another. From the beginning of faith to the end, he does not cease to come into the Church; and he is recognized as coming in his members, as its members are born and gathered every day.

Concerning this coming he himself says: “From now on you will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds” (Matthew 26:64). Concerning these clouds the prophet says: “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isaiah 5:6).

His coming at the very end, when he will come to judge the living and the dead, is also rightly understood to be asked about here. Thus the coming may be distinguished as twofold: one is his coming in his body, and the other is his coming in the head of the Church, who is himself.

But which of these signs should be referred to which of the three matters—whether each corresponds to one, or all correspond to each—must be considered with careful examination.

Otherwise we may perhaps think that what belongs to the overthrow of Jerusalem should be referred to the end of the age; or conversely, affirm that what belongs to the end of the age pertains to the destruction of that wretched city; or say that what belongs to his coming in his body, which is the Church, pertains to his final coming, when he himself, who is the head of the Church, will come personally.
