Conversely, what belongs to his final coming in person we might again assert to pertain to the coming that takes place through the whole Church. Among all these matters, some are clear, while others are obscure, so that it is laborious—or even rash—to judge them. And so long as they are not understood, it is exceedingly presumptuous to define anything concerning them.

Because Luke and Mark also relate in this Gospel nearly the same signs that are said to be future—for they do not differ in the events, even if one says something that another omits, or expresses it in another manner—they are more useful to one another by comparison, so that the reader’s understanding may itself be assisted.

Who does not see that the following refers to that city, Jerusalem: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation is near”?

Again, who does not see that the following refers to the Lord’s final coming: “When you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near”?

But what is said—“Woe to those who are pregnant and those who nurse infants in those days, and pray that your flight may not occur in winter or on the Sabbath, and then there will be great tribulation,” and the rest (Mark 13:17–18)—is placed in this Gospel and according to Mark in such a way that it can be referred to both the end of the age and the destruction of that city.

We shall explain all these matters in their proper order.

I have spoken of these signs for this reason: so that the prudent hearer may know that from the beginning of the Church some of them occurred then, some occur now, and yet some of them have always occurred. Therefore he says to the apostles, and through them to all: “See that no one deceives you,” because there have always been deceivers and corrupters of sound doctrine, as well as certain other things that follow.

He likewise says to everyone when he tells the apostles: “Watch, because you do not know the day or the hour” (Matthew 24:42). Although he says this to everyone, he speaks as though it concerned only those who were present at that time, just as with many other things read in Scripture.

In this way, what was said then applies to everyone, because for each person the final day and the end of the age will come when he departs from this life. Therefore everyone must take care to depart in such a condition as he will be judged on that day. Accordingly, every person must take care not to be deceived and must remain watchful, lest the day of the Lord’s coming find him unprepared.

That day will find him unprepared whom the final day of his life has found unprepared. I certainly do not believe that it was uncertain to the apostles that the Lord would not come for judgment in their own days. Yet who could doubt that they both guarded against being deceived, kept watch, and observed everything that had been said to everyone, so that they might be found ready?

Therefore Christ’s coming must always be watched for in two ways. One is when he will come and we will have to give an account of everything we have done; the other is his daily coming, when he continually visits our consciences and comes to us so that, when he comes, he may find us ready.

What good does it do me to know the day of judgment, burdened as I am with so many sins, if the Lord comes—or when he comes—unless he first comes into my mind and returns into my thought; unless Christ lives in me and speaks in me? He comes well to me only if Christ first lives in me and I in him.

Then his second coming has, as it were, already come to me when the world’s decline has taken place in me, so that I can say, insofar as I am able: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

Consider also the very words he says: “For many will come in my name.” Although the Antichrist alone falsely assumes this name, and his body does so without Christ’s work, without the word of truth, and without his wisdom, you will nowhere find the Lord using this very expression to say, “I am the Christ.”

It was sufficient for him to show his own people through his teachings and miracles that he was the Christ, because the Father’s work was in him, as was the word of the teaching he gave and the power that cried out, “I am the Christ”—more powerfully than if a thousand voices had proclaimed it.

Therefore, I do not know whether you will find that he said this in words; but he displayed himself through the Father’s works and through the teaching of piety. The false Christs, lacking these things, promised in words that they were what they were not.

Thus Manichaeus is reported to have said that he was the Holy Spirit—something the Holy Spirit never did concerning himself, neither in words nor by indicating in any prophecy that he would come in the flesh.

So too Simon, whom I mentioned above, who said not only this but many other things as well. Jerome says that he found in Simon’s books that Simon had said: “I am the Word of God; I am the Beautiful One; I am the Paraclete; I am the Almighty; I am all the things of God.”

What would he not say, who said this and so many other things? Thus the other members of the Antichrist confessed nothing other than that they were Christs or, at least, members of Christ.

It is therefore no wonder if they deceive some through signs and wonders, when the Lord says that they will deceive many.

For you will hear of wars and reports of wars; see that you are not disturbed. For these things must happen, but the end is not yet. This sign, therefore, is not a sign of the age to come, nor a sign of Christ’s coming. For both before Christ’s coming and afterward, innumerable kinds of wars soon arose and were heard of and seen, just as many false Christs also came at that time and thereafter. For this reason it is rightly asked what sign this should be of the things to come, since wars have never ceased at various intervals of time and in different places—wars by which the earth has now been battered and drenched with human blood.

Even if wars ceased at the time of Christ’s coming [Col. 0801A], by God’s providential arrangement, under Augustus Octavian and for a little while afterward, so that the Gospel might be preached more freely throughout the world, nevertheless, not long afterward barbarian nations overran the Roman provinces more frequently everywhere, just as the Romans themselves had previously conquered the whole world by waging war. For this reason I do not see at all how these things can be signs of the future, when the end of the age comes—unless they were foretold in such a way that they are to be understood rather in relation to the Church.

For there are two peoples and two kingdoms: one, that of Christ, and the other, that of the devil. Of these it may perhaps have been said: “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom” (Luke XXI, 10). This has not ceased to happen since it was said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew III, 2). [Col. 0801B] And from the time when this was said, how many years have passed? Yet although it was said most truly of the final hour, when the Lord was born from a virgin in these last days, throughout this entire final hour all those things are happening which the Lord foretold would occur as his kingdom drew near. Thus, while terrifying events and signs of the future take place, each person may always be found prepared, since our punishment compels us to confess that the end is already at hand, while what was proclaimed is continually being fulfilled.

By these words, surely, no one can be a greater witness than we, whom—as I might put it—the end of the world has overtaken. We see daily such great civil wars, and wars worse than civil, among brothers and relatives; we continually endure such slaughter of human beings and desolation [Col. 0801C] of cities at the hands of barbarian and pagan enemies; and every day we await nothing else but our own end, with groaning. Yet, as the divine word says, the end is not yet.

Although barbarians rise against us and there is no one to bring help—for civil ambushes and massacres rage more fiercely against one another—so that both within and without nothing but death strikes our ears, all these things have been preceded by famine, plague, and every kind of calamity. And because we are at the setting of the age, so many illnesses of the world precede it, such as—I do not know whether they have been heard of since the beginning of the age. All these evils have been produced for us by greed, pride, and luxury, so that there is no place that is not afflicted by enemies and even troubled by its own citizens.

But if these evils that we see and suffer are certain indications that the Lord is already about to come, what of the apostle’s saying: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them”? And, conversely, the Gospel says: “People will faint from fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world” (Luke XXI, 26). Then it continues: “The powers of heaven,” he says, “will be shaken, and then they will see the Son of Man coming with great power and majesty.”

Therefore it must be asked whether such things are the heralds of Christ’s coming, so that people faint from fear and from expectation of the evils said to be coming. What, then, is meant by the statement: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thessalonians V, 3)? Perhaps the words seem to introduce two periods, which I altogether do not believe. Rather, there will be one and the same period. [Col. 0802A] Just as there are two peoples, and as we have said that there are two kingdoms, those of Christ and of the devil, so then also there will be the Church of Christ throughout the whole world.

At that time such a great tribulation will come upon the Church during the days of Antichrist as has never been from the beginning—a tribulation that will then exist throughout the whole world, that is, throughout the entire Church. But there will be others by whom the Church will then be troubled, and they will say, “Peace and security”; sudden destruction will come upon them when the Lord’s coming, like a thief in the night, finds them secure. There will be others who are troubled; then they will all rejoice and be glad, because they will not be in darkness, so that that day may overtake them like a thief in the night, since they will all be children of day and of light.

But if we believe that nothing in the Gospel is superfluous, I think it must be asked what is meant by the words: “You will hear of wars and reports of wars.” For it is one thing to hear of wars and another to hear reports of wars. It may be that the children of peace keep themselves from seeing wars because they do not wish to see evil things, yet they hear of wars and reports of wars.

Perhaps one matter is distant and another near, as indicated by the difference in the words. For it is not the same thing to be far away and to hear reports of wars—which may or may not be true—as to be near the battle and even hear the voices of the combatants themselves. Each statement therefore has its own meaning: the one who is far from the wars hears reports about them, but not the wars themselves; the one who is near hears the wars themselves and the voices of the combatants.

In both cases, therefore, there appears to be an understanding of a certain distinction. For not all members of Christ’s Church are equally perfect, nor are they equally peaceful and removed from all the tumult and fear of wars. Otherwise there would not be so many seditions and scandals within Christ’s Church. From all these things the disciples of Christ and that entire primitive Church were free; they had one heart and one soul. For they had been confirmed in the same understanding and the same judgment.

“All these things,” he says, “are the beginning of sorrows.” What things? Wars, certainly, and reports of wars; nation rising against nation and kingdom against kingdom; plagues and famines; and earthquakes in various places.

For just as, when death approaches, the bodies of the sick languish, so that through the weakness of their limbs and entrails the soul may be separated from its body, so this world’s creation, such and so great, is corrupted. The corrupted air brings plagues, and the weakened earth brings famine, providing, as it were, a beginning of sorrows before death.

And because heaven and earth will pass away (Mark XIII, 31), they must first languish in corruption: the earth must be shaken by its own movements, and the air, filled with disease, must be drawn in so that plagues may arise; and the earth, exhausted of its strength, must fail and wither in producing what grows from it, so that it too may be without fruit. We know all these things better because we already see them all.

But the end is not yet. For neither are these things coming to an end, nor do we, badly nourished amid them, wish them to end. And therefore, just as Christ’s coming brought peace among very many nations, according to what the Prophet says of him: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace” (Psalm LXXI, 7), until the moon—that is, the Church—is exalted and peace [Col. 0803A] increases in the world because of the growth of the churches, so that this peace might become an occasion of salvation for many, since they were no longer compelled, as before, to go out to war and fight for their ancestral lands—so, by consequence, because of the abundance of iniquity, since the love of many has grown cold, God’s wars and seditions will again arise because of the increasing wickedness of human beings, which is the cause of all the evils that occur.

And because these things are increasing daily, this worse final evil is near: the evil that the present passage announces will come. “And then,” he says, “they will hand you over to tribulation and kill you, and you will be hated by all nations because of my name.”

The word “then” seems more explicitly to indicate a time and to refer to that moment when nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom, or the other events. Yet as soon as the Apostles became witnesses of the truth, they were handed over and killed—some even before Jerusalem was devastated by the Romans in punishment for Christ.

Therefore, as I have said, it is better to understand the rising of nation against nation and kingdom against kingdom as referring to the kingdom of Christ and the kingdom of the devil, and to the nation whose treachery raged against Christ’s Church as soon as faith began. Before this, the world, badly pacified, had been oppressed by the rule of one power; but as soon as Christ’s faith came, nation rose against nation, because Jesus came not to bring peace on earth but a sword (Matthew X, 34), and kingdom rose against kingdom.

These two kingdoms and two peoples can never have peace with one another. Therefore the merciful Teacher deliberately says: “These things must happen, but the end is not yet.”

It is necessary, however, for each of the enemies to fight with his own weapons: they with carnal and diabolical weapons, but the elect with virtues and heavenly weapons. Thus they will fight among themselves and against the saints; but the saints will hear of wars and reports of wars, yet will not see them with their eyes, because blessed are the eyes that see the things which they themselves rejoice to see.

“And you will be hated by all nations because of my name.” Christ always wishes himself to be regarded as the cause when the elect fight against the reprobate, the saints against vices, and the good against the wicked; likewise, whatever they suffer from the unjust, he wishes them always to do and endure for Christ.

For this purpose he instructs and strengthens them to endure sufferings, and announces that the public hatred of all nations [Col. 0803D] will rage against them because of his name. “Afflicted by these vexations, many will be scandalized.” This rule of Scripture must certainly be considered, because he is not speaking only about the Apostles, but about all his elect, so that this general hatred of all nations against Christ’s members is to be understood as coming generally.

Otherwise the Apostles themselves did not first come to the knowledge of all nations, although it is said: “Their sound went out into all the earth” (Romans X, 8). It did go out, but through their successors. Therefore when he says, “You will be hated by all nations,” he either speaks by way of exaggeration, meaning “many nations” by “all,” or, as I have said, the entire order of preachers is gathered into the unity of the Apostles. [Col. 0804A]

For just as the order of preachers has succeeded and continues to succeed throughout all parts of the earth, so also their hatred, because of Christ’s name, extends throughout all nations. The martyrdoms of the saints prove this: today they flourish in nearly all nations and kingdoms.

But this persecution and hatred of the saints, begun from the start of the faith, will be brought to completion at the end. Then the tribulation will be such as has never been from the beginning. Therefore all the things that have occurred up to now are “the beginning of sorrows.”

Thus he says: “For then many will be scandalized, and they will hand one another over, and they will hate one another,” and so forth. For although from the beginning of the faith some were scandalized or handed others over, there were not so many betrayers of their brothers, nor so many false prophets who are recorded as deceiving and leading many astray.

But then they will betray one another especially, because the love of many will grow cold, and they will lead very many astray as never before. For as yet we are not hated by all the nations to which Christ’s name has not yet reached. In the north there are certain regions and peoples to whom Christ’s Gospel has not yet been preached.

Nevertheless, I do not know whether there is any nation to which no preacher has reached, even though their savagery has not allowed them wholly to receive Christ’s faith. As for the remaining islands toward the west, as far as the British Ocean, all now believe throughout the entire world.

And let no one object to me concerning the Saracens, who by God’s will have occupied many kingdoms of the earth with their arms and rule almost everywhere over Christians, as though Christ’s Gospel had not yet reached them. [Col. 0804C] It did reach them, and they received knowledge of God; but, badly led astray by certain false apostles, so to speak disciples of Nicolas, they established for themselves a law drawn from both the Old and the New Testament. As though under the worship of one God, yet unwilling to hold anything in common either with us or with the Jews, they have perverted everything.

While they desire to subject all things to their own dominion, they do not ask which God each person worships, but only that service be rendered to them. Perhaps because they received the spirit of error by God’s just judgment—as many think—the Antichrist is to be received by them. With their assent and under their dominion he will be able to accomplish such things and so great things as are plainly read in the Apocalypse of John.

I have said this so that the prudent reader may know that the mystery of iniquity is already at work, but the end is not yet: “But the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.” That is, amid so many scandals, amid everything opposed to sound faith, amid torments and deception, amid demonic signs and wonders, whoever perseveres faithfully in Christ to death will be saved.

“And this Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world, as a testimony to all nations, and then the consummation will come.”

For to say that the end of the age will come before this Gospel is preached throughout the whole world is a claim of great rashness and of a person who does not understand. For as the Savior says: “Then the consummation will come.” And what does “then the consummation will come” mean, except that it will not come before that? When it will come afterward is certainly uncertain to us; yet we must not in any way doubt that it will not come beforehand.

For this was surely promised by God, even with an oath, to our father Abraham: all nations would be blessed in his seed. From that promise it has already come about that many nations have received the Gospel, and from them all one Church of Christ has been formed. It still bears fruit today and grows throughout the whole world.

Yet, as I have said above, it still has room to grow, until what was promised to Christ comes to pass. “And he will rule,” says the Prophet, “from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Psalm LXXI, 8). From the river in which he was baptized, that is, because from there the Gospel began to be preached; from sea to sea, however, means the whole world with all its nations, since the entire world is encircled by the greater Ocean.

Otherwise, how will that prophecy be fulfilled: “All the nations that you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord”? (Psalm LXXXV, 9.) They will not come to him by migrating from their places to one in whom they have not believed; rather, each nation will come in faith, believing in its own place.

Hence the Prophet says: “And they will worship him, each one from his own place, all the islands of the nations” (Zephaniah II, 11). He said “all the islands,” as though he meant all the churches. Here he shows that no regions of the earth will be left where the Church will not be present.

Very many of the islands situated in the Ocean have already certainly received the Gospel. Whatever have not received it will indeed receive it, so that it may reach all nations, however gradually, by growing and bearing fruit.

“And then,” he says, “the consummation will come.” Even so, when he says “then it will come,” we cannot determine how long afterward the end of the age will come, since the Lord says to the Apostles: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons that the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts I, 7).

Therefore, even if it were already absolutely certain to us that the Gospel had reached all nations, we still could not say how much time would remain, although we could truly say that his coming was already very near.

Nor do we say this in such a way that everyone who is in every nation must believe, but rather that throughout the whole world, among those nations where the Church does not yet exist, it ought to exist. Thus recently we learned that churches had been established and built among certain peoples of the Danes, and that some of them had been baptized in those same churches.

For although all nations have been promised as coming to the faith, this does not mean all people of all nations, since faith does not belong to everyone. Accordingly, in all nations there will be unbelievers who hate, and believers whom the wicked and evil hate.

Otherwise, as I have already said above, how will this be fulfilled: “You will be hated by all nations because of my name”? Nor should it be said that all these things were completed among all nations through the Apostles, although the Truth says to them: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts I, 8).

For he does not speak to them as though they alone were to accomplish this ministry of salvation, but he speaks in them and with them to all preachers of the word. Thus he speaks as though saying: “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII, 20). This does not mean that the Apostles would remain in the flesh for so long, but that Christ himself would always protect them and be present everywhere with his elect.

“When therefore you see the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place—let the one who reads understand.”

In this brief statement, then, great obscurity is generated. By asking the reader to understand, he wishes to exercise us and call us toward the mysteries of spiritual understanding.

Since, as I showed above, all three Evangelists spoke about these matters either in similar words, or nearly similar words, or in expressions proper to each one, they must therefore be compared with one another, so that from all of them we may understand what is very obscure.

For Matthew, after prefacing the statement cited above from Daniel, said: “Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; and the one who is on the roof must not come down to take anything from his house; and the one who is in the field must not return to take his cloak. Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days.”

Mark, however, says this: “When you see the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not to be—let the one who reads understand—then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; and the one who is on the roof must not come down into the house, nor enter to take anything from his house; and the one who is in the field must not turn back to take his garment. Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days” (Mark XIII, 14–17).

Luke, more clearly showing that this abomination and desolation foretold by Daniel occurred when Jerusalem was conquered and occupied by the Romans, recalls the Lord’s words at the same place: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army,” he said, “know that its desolation has drawn near” (Luke XXI, 20).

It is evident that the abomination of desolation of which Matthew and Mark spoke was then placed or seen there. Therefore Luke, to show that what he had said referred to the same place, continues with what they also say: “Then,” he says, “let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.”

Accordingly, as all three make clear, this prophecy of Daniel is not to be referred to the time of Antichrist, when there will be one general and savage persecution of all Christians throughout the world, as some maintain, but to the first coming of the Savior. At that time the number of the weeks was completed, the continual sacrifice and the offering were taken away, and the Holy of Holies, Christ, had already been anointed and had come. He himself had foretold what would be fulfilled concerning Jerusalem and Judea alone, not concerning the whole world.

Otherwise, if someone wishes to interpret Daniel’s prophecy—which the Lord here says, “Let the one who reads understand”—as referring to the future time of Antichrist, he seems to depart far from the truth. I do not know whether he could in any way make it fit that time, even by falsifying the number of the weeks. In that case an outstanding and exceedingly firm prophecy concerning Christ’s coming would be mutilated, which could never be done, even if he wished to overturn the number of years by calculating it differently from our predecessors.

For if, from the time of the Lord’s first coming up to this passage, those things were not fulfilled and are to be fulfilled at the end of the age, it is certain either that the Apostles were ignorant of this or that they knew it but were forbidden to teach it—which I do not believe. If they knew it, their question is superfluous.

But if all the remaining things he foretold have been fulfilled because the Holy of Holies was anointed, then both the number of the weeks and the desolation of the temple itself have been fulfilled in Christ. For just as Christ foretold, so it plainly came to pass when Jerusalem was surrounded by the Roman army and the whole city was destroyed to its foundations.

Then, indeed, the abomination of desolation was brought upon the temple by the army. The Prophet says that it will remain until the time of consummation, because it will never be restored until the consummation of the world. Thus the same prophet says: “Consummation will be given upon the desolation of Jerusalem” (2 Thessalonians II, 4, 8).

But if the temple is to be rebuilt in that place, it will be built for the one “who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped, so that he takes his seat in the temple, displaying himself as though he were God.” [Col. 0807B] “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming.”

Even now, in the same place in the city, there is a sanctuary of the Saracens in the form of a temple, into which no Jew dares to enter. Moreover, in the very place where the Holy of Holies formerly stood, a mounted statue of the emperor Hadrian is said to remain erected to the present day.

In the ancient Scriptures, however, “abomination” is the name given to an idol. For this reason “of desolation” is added, because in the desolated, abandoned, and deserted temple an idol was undoubtedly placed there by the Romans.

For this was not fulfilled, as some think, before the Lord’s Passion by Pilate or anyone else, when he set up Caesar’s image in the temple, although that too would have been an abomination. Otherwise, what does the Lord mean when he warns and says, “When you see the abomination of desolation standing,” and so forth, except that Luke testifies that this happened when Jerusalem was overthrown?

Therefore it should not be believed that it happened before the Passion, nor should we think that it is still to occur at or near the end of the age, since it has already been fulfilled. Although the abomination of desolation itself, because of the obscurity of the statement, may be understood in some other way, nevertheless it must be believed to have occurred when the Lord foretold it and that the same prophecy was fulfilled when he foresaw and announced that it would be fulfilled.

“Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and the one who is on the roof must not come down to take anything from his house.”

In these words, as in the other two Evangelists, the command concerns more the haste of the Jews’ flight than the time of Antichrist, when there will be no place—as we read in the Apocalypse—where a cruel persecution will not rage.

Therefore this should not be understood as referring to flight at that time, when I do not know whether anyone could physically escape the evil that will then exist everywhere on earth. For this reason we refer these words more plainly to the siege of that wretched city, when the abomination of desolation is said to stand in the holy place.

This abomination, although I have interpreted it differently, may itself be understood as Vespasian, who surrounded Jerusalem with an army, devastated it, and violated the temple. Through him such terrible things occurred that those who were in Judea would scarcely flee—not to the temple, not to the Holy of Holies, nor to the city of God, but, as it is said, [Col. 0808A] to the mountains and the hiding places among the rocks. For so great and terrible would the persecution be at that time that the one who was on the roof would not have time to come down and take anything from his house before beginning his flight, if he could; and the one who was in the field would be unable to return to the city and take his garment, because there would be no time for mercy, but only for vengeance. Thus they would spare neither pregnant women nor nursing mothers, and therefore he says that woe would befall both.

It is as though the Lord were speaking to those same Jews who boasted of the Sabbath: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath,” when it is not permitted to act or travel farther than the Sabbath journey, and in winter, when it is extremely difficult to seek safety by flight.

There is, however, a certain flight of human beings according to the command of God’s Word, which must always be pursued. Therefore blessed Ambrose composed two excellent books on flight from the world. Whoever undertakes this flight is better than the one who does not flee, because anyone who does not flee commits greater sins by that very fact.

And because one must always flee, Christ the Lord established six cities to which a guilty person who has sinned ought to flee—but not on the Sabbath, when he ought already to rest in rest, nor in winter, when it is not permitted, because the cold of unbelief already holds all those whom the Sun of righteousness does not now illuminate.

In place of what Matthew and Mark said—“The one who is in the field must not turn back to take his garment”—Luke says more clearly: “And those who are in the regions must not enter them, because these are days of vengeance, so that all the things that are written may be fulfilled” (Luke XXI, 12).

I have said this so that the prudent reader may understand that all three are speaking together about one and the same matter. The words can also be understood quite appropriately in a spiritual sense: in all tribulations one must beware lest anyone, overcome by desire or by any kind of exaltation, descend from the height of a good life to a carnal life; or lest one who has made progress, stretching toward what lies ahead, fall away from a good purpose and return to what is behind.

If these things must be guarded against in every tribulation, how much more must they have been commanded in that tribulation which is announced as destined to come upon that city—such as has not been from the beginning and will not be again? And if this applies to that particular tribulation, how much more to the general tribulation that will finally come upon God’s holy Church spread throughout the whole world?

For Luke appears to narrate these two sayings, about the roof and the field, at a place where they can more readily be referred to that final time of Antichrist, when the Pharisees asked the Lord when the kingdom of God would come.

This is not surprising, especially since it is a rule of Scripture that it sometimes speaks indifferently of Christ’s coming: at one time, in a single and the same statement, it speaks of Christ’s first coming in such a way that certain things must be referred to his final coming; and of his final coming in such a way that certain things must be understood of the first.

Therefore one must beware in every case, lest we refer what is said of the first coming to the second, and what is said of the second to the first, as learned men have also done in this passage.

Nevertheless, as I have said, because the command that those who are in Judea should flee to the mountains, and so forth, can refer both to the desolation of the temple, to the future time of Antichrist, to every tribulation that takes place in the Church, and against all the perverse doctrines of heretics—when we see these standing in the holy place, that is, in the Church, and displaying themselves as though they were God—we must flee from Judea to the mountains from which help may come to us.

That means abandoning the dead letter and Jewish perversity and drawing near to the eternal mountains, from which the Lord may wonderfully enlighten us. We must remain on the roof, in the height of heavenly understanding, where the fiery darts of the devil cannot reach. We must not descend and take anything from the house of our former way of life, nor seek the things that are behind, but rather sow in the field that the Lord has blessed, so that we may receive from it the fruit of life.

“Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days.”

For the heaviness of the womb and the burden of very young children are not suitable for those who are fleeing. Nor indeed are these things suited either to that flight which then took place in Judea or to those who wish to escape the dangers of tribulation.

For woe to those creatures that have not brought forth the shoots of virtue to maturity, but possess only the beginnings of faith and therefore need the milk of teachers. It may also be said that in the persecution of Antichrist, just as in the Roman captivity, pregnant women and nursing mothers, weighed down by the burden of the womb and of children, could not make an unencumbered flight. Therefore it follows:

“Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath.”

For in winter the severity and harshness of the cold do not permit them to flee quickly into deserted places or hide in the mountains and wilderness. On the Sabbath, either there will be transgression of the law if they wish to go out to flee, or imminent death if they remain.

This command applies both to the destruction of Jerusalem and to the time of Antichrist, and also to every Christian’s flight from the world, so that one may not begin to wish to flee when it is no longer permitted, or when, oppressed by excessive sickness and unbelief, one is no longer able.

It is therefore clear that these commands were spoken more proverbially, because some of them, taken literally, admit neither a human rationale for the action and statement nor a divine understanding. What reason is there not to come down from the roof, when, if one remains on the roof or in the house, one can neither depart nor escape, especially if the flight occurs on the Sabbath or in winter?

It is not the letter that must be observed, but the moral meaning of things must always be observed in every case. So also, when he says, “Woe to those who are pregnant,” we must consider what the condition of sex and the order of generation have deserved.

Unless, perhaps, the sex and age of women happened to fall into a time in which their curse properly applies—not because of fault, God forbid, but because of the outcome. Therefore, when the Lord says, “Woe to those who are pregnant,” he is not speaking of the burden of pregnancy or of the weight of children, in which blessing is confirmed, but of the burden of sins and the weight of the womb when souls are weighed down by crimes and wicked deeds.

Woe threatens those who did not wish to pass into the form of a man and be strengthened by virtues, but always pursued womanish things. Accordingly, the statement must be understood equally of both sexes, when the birth of sin is badly nourished and the whole person, inwardly and outwardly, is confused and burdened by the worst affliction of sins.

As for the tribulation that was then to come upon Judea and that is still to come upon the whole world, enough has already been said. “And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened.”

We have already said above that Luke makes clear in this passage what was uncertain: whether the statement about the abomination of desolation and the shortening of the days referred to the end of the age or to the conquest of Jerusalem. For although he did not say these things himself, he stated other matters more clearly concerning the same subject, which he showed above to belong to this passage.

Therefore, although according to the rule mentioned earlier some things may refer to the time of Antichrist, some to the overthrow of Jerusalem, and some to both, we must not doubt that, when Jerusalem was overthrown, there were among that people elect ones of God who had believed or were going to believe from the circumcision—elect according to God’s foreknowledge before the foundation of the world. For their sake those days would be shortened, so that the evils might become bearable.

The same must be understood of the time of Antichrist; no one can doubt it, and John also declares this in his Apocalypse.

But it must be asked how those days are said to be shortened: whether they have been or will be shortened in number, as some think, or whether the days themselves will be shortened in their duration, just as, when Joshua prayed, the day was made longer.

I certainly do not think that the moments of time ought to be changed, since we read: “By your ordinance the day persists.” Therefore we should understand, more appropriately according to the quality of the times, that the days are shortened not in the measure of their hours but in their number—not because anything has been taken from the course of time, but because they have been diminished in quality.

The fifteen years granted to Hezekiah are likewise said to have been increased, not with respect to the course of time, but because years that were to be his were granted to him for life. So also it is said in the blessings: “I will satisfy him with length of days” (Psalm XC, 16), because when someone is filled with a good life he is said to be full of days.

Therefore, when the evils of those days are shortened, the days themselves are rightly said to be shortened. The divine Scriptures also speak of evil days, not because the days themselves are evil, but because the evils that occur in them are evil.

Thus, when it is promised that those evils will be shortened, so that by God’s gift they may at least be felt less severely through endurance, they are not improperly said to be shortened, since their quality is changed: what would have been evil, unless God shortened it, becomes good and tranquil.

As I have said, Luke did not say these things, but Matthew and Mark. Whoever follows only them can refer these matters to the end of the age and the time of Antichrist. But Luke stated the matters from which he taught that what they said more obscurely referred to the overthrow of Jerusalem.

For anyone who wishes to know about the tribulation of those days should read Josephus, who says that such things then happened to that people that they scarcely seem credible. [Col. 0811A]

Therefore the merciful Lord did not undeservedly foretell to that same people that there would then be a great tribulation, such as had not been from the beginning of the world until then—as you should understand, when he was speaking these words—and such as would never be again.

But even if there will perhaps be a tribulation as great or greater throughout the whole world in the time of Antichrist, it must be understood that this was said only of that people: no greater tribulation of this kind would ever again come upon it in this age.

For, as is reported, they will be the first, and above all others, to receive Antichrist with complete joy of heart. Consequently, that same Jewish people will then cause tribulation in Christ’s Church rather than suffer it.

Then if anyone says to you, “Behold, here is the Christ,” or, “There,” do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise, and they will give great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect. Behold, I have foretold it to you.

He therefore foretold those evils that were to come so that they might be avoided. For this reason, this passage must be expounded in three ways, since these dangers are shown to be guarded against in three periods: namely, at the time of the Roman siege, when Jerusalem was besieged and the whole region of Judaea devastated; also at the consummation of the age, when the Antichrist, [Col. 0811C] together with his head, the devil, and also with all his members, will fight against the Church of Christ; and then throughout the entire intervening period, when the cunning of heretics never ceases to rage against catholic doctrine and the apostolic institutions.

In all these cases there will be one deceit of the antichrists, so to speak: under the appearance of knowledge of Christ, even though it is false, they will never cease to fight fiercely. For during the very siege and captivity, among the Jewish people, many heresiarchs arose who claimed to be Christs. So much so that, while the Romans were besieging them from outside, there were three factions within. Yet at the consummation of the age, greater and more numerous things are believed to be destined to occur.

Nevertheless, I do not know whether greater signs will be produced by diabolical arts than those already displayed [Col. 0811D] in all the lies of human beings and in the utterly false teachings from whose instruction the power of wonders will perhaps sprout anew, with more numerous heads cut off. For just as one abomination is said to stand in the holy place, so one Antichrist is proclaimed as destined to come at the end of the age. But because the abomination of desolation has been established in the holy place by the just judgment of God, many false Christs are born from it, and false prophets arise. Although all these belong to one genus, their species are many; although they are one body, their members are diverse.

It is as if we were to say generally that there is one falsehood, but according to the differences of false doctrines and the perverse teachings of heretics, there are many falsehoods. And just as one falsehood differs greatly from another, so the doctrines of false prophets are often attacked by perverse doctrines, and many arise even with their heads cut off. Whoever has arisen after them—even if they perform signs and wonders as though they were acts of power—are members of one head. For just as there is one true Christ, the Lord Jesus, with innumerable members belonging to one head, so there are many false Christs and very many antichrists.

Therefore do not be surprised: just as the members of the one true Christ were made up of all the holy prophets who existed from the beginning of the age, announcing Christ’s coming and sufferings, and afterward his future glory, so, I ask, understand many false Christs and false prophets in relation to the one Antichrist. They are not teachers of one falsehood only, [Col. 0812B] but of all falsehoods. These false prophets are indeed prophets of that Antichrist whose false words they proclaim and teach as though they were true.

Thus the pious teacher says on their account: “If they say to you, ‘Behold, here is the Christ,’ or, ‘There,’ do not believe it.” He says this to his own people so that they may guard themselves against being deceived by the errors of false teachers, or certainly by diabolical fantasies.

Therefore it must be considered very carefully in the divine Scriptures lest a false Christ be painted and fashioned here or there and pointed out with a finger, something that we read many have already done, sufficiently and abundantly. For this reason the faith of Christians must be so firm and so learned that it can never deviate from the truth, nor from the doctrine of Christ, which the universal Church, the holy Mother, learned from Christ and preserves.

If anyone teaches or holds anything beyond this faith, one must say to him the words of the apostle Paul (Gal. 1:8): “If anyone should evangelize or teach anything else—even an angel from heaven, or anyone exceedingly learned, or powerful in the Scriptures, even if he performs signs and wonders—beyond what has been evangelized by Christ the Lord and by his apostles, let him be anathema.”

For just as true and steadfast faith receives no doctrine other than that which Christ taught, so it does not seek signs, because, as Paul bears witness, signs and wonders were not truly given for the faithful but for unbelievers.

This is why, once the faith of Christ has been received, such things are now performed only at the relics of the saints who stood as witnesses to the truth. How many have already been deceived by false teachers, and also enticed toward death by signs and wonders through excessive curiosity, I think no one can say.

Therefore, lest this happen, the most gracious Savior said to his chosen ones: “Behold, I have foretold it to you,” because such things have already occurred, and greater things are perhaps believed to be destined to occur, so that, if it were possible, even the elect might be led into error.

This does not mean that the elect—those perfected and predestined by God—could actually be led astray into error, but that they can be tested in such matters, even though they cannot be overcome. Although the freedom of the will is preserved here, grace must nevertheless be proclaimed all the more, since they cannot go astray.

Thus the Lord so moderates his statement that both the help of grace is sought in temptation and greater confidence in that help arises. Therefore, when he says, “Behold, I have foretold it to you,” this refers to both matters: that many will be scandalized, and that the temptation of the saints will be so great and so severe that, unless God’s election saved them, they too would fall into error.

If therefore they say to you, “Behold, he is in the wilderness,” do not go out; “Behold, he is in the inner chambers,” do not believe it.

The matter of the locations is clear, because in the Scriptures he did not promise that he would come in this way, but rather as it is said: “Our God will come manifestly” (Ps. 49:3). For he seems to introduce four distinctions when he says “here” or “there,” and when he says “in the wilderness” or “in the inner chambers.”

There are two distinctions in “here” or “there,” because there are two Testaments, beyond which he does not seem to me to extend his finger outward; rather, within these he says “here” or “there,” that is, in the New Testament or in the Old Testament.

This does not mean that Christ must be sought somewhere else or from some other source, since he was long ago proclaimed and displayed in these same books. Rather, false Christs and false prophets, interpreting the divine Scriptures differently, seek to defend their own false doctrines from those Scriptures against the truth. They say: “Behold, this is the Christ whom I proclaim in this passage of the holy Gospel,” or, “There, in that passage of the Old Testament.”

Thus, traversing every place in the Scriptures, each one chooses whatever seems to defend the error of his falsehood, and from these passages fashions and paints his Antichrist as he pleases, from the Law and the Prophets as well as from the Gospel and the apostles. We know that many have already done this: each of them, according to his own pleasure, has offered falsehood in place of truth, and the Antichrist in place of Christ God.

Therefore the teacher of truth warned us: whoever among them evangelizes anything beyond what has already been evangelized, and displays through fabricated verbal deceptions, “Behold, here is the Christ,” or, “There,” is told: “Do not believe it.”

If they say, “Behold, he is in the solitude,” that is, in the teaching of philosophers, do not go out to them, because they are outside the faith and outside the Church.

If they again produce the claim, “Behold, he is in the inner chambers of houses,” that is, within certain secret or apocryphal Scriptures, do not believe it, because they present things that are uncertain or false—not things that are authoritative, publicly known, or issued by the holy Fathers, but stories suited to their own fables and lies.

Or, if they formulate some doctrine from the divine Scripture itself, as though it were in the house, but it is false, do not believe it, lest you be deceived in any way, whether within or without. Even if they promise something new concerning heavenly matters, which is the house of God, do not depart from the rule of the catholic faith; do not believe what is not catholic, because it is not wholly true.

For truth, although it is hidden from the wicked, is nevertheless bright to the good, as though it were lightning. Hence it follows: “For just as lightning comes out from the east and appears even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.”

Therefore do not go out and do not believe that the Son of Man is either in the wilderness of the nations or in the inner chambers, or in any secret places of their words, since the lightning of faith concerning Christ shines from east to west through all his catholic Churches.

But according to the literal sense, the Savior’s second coming must be manifested not in humility, as before, when he came gently, “Like rain upon fleece” (Ps. 71:6), and “Like dew upon grass” (Prov. 19:12), but in immense splendor and the glory of his majesty.

Therefore, from the point where the apostles asked for the sign of his coming and the sign of the consummation of the age, no single sign was given. Rather, those things were stated that had to be guarded against throughout the entire age, because such great things were destined to occur before the end of the world that they could terrify people away from the faith and, if it were possible, lead even the elect astray.

For this reason he openly foretold the future destruction of Jerusalem and, finally, declared what kind and what magnitude his coming would have, without any other sign. For he himself will be such that it will be evident to all, even more than lightning, to which he is compared.

This comparison was made from the lesser to the greater, because nothing can be found among created things equal to the day of the Lord’s coming. And although lightning penetrates and terrifies everything beneath the heavens, that day will be more penetrating and more terrifying: it will move all the hidden things of the heavens, penetrate all the realms of the underworld, and disturb all the elements of the world.

The presbyter Juvencus gave his book a remarkable beginning:

> Nothing immortal is held by the structure of the world,
>
> neither the globe, nor the kingdoms of men, nor golden Rome,
>
> neither the earth, nor the fiery stars of heaven, and so forth.

Hence the prophets cannot adequately describe that day even with its many names. And so, when the disciples asked the most gracious Jesus for the sign of such a great day, he judged it necessary to show them nothing else except those things that each person ought to avoid and foresee, continually placing these matters before them so that they might be prepared.

For it is exceedingly foolish to seek in a small or hidden place the one who fills all things, and who will then shake the universe and examine every individual thing. Therefore no one should be curious or doubtful about these matters in the faith. Since many divine miracles preceded his first coming to confirm the faith, one should not now seek signs any longer, as though one were an unbeliever.

For the whole Church has been full of these things from the beginning, full of the radiance of faith from east to west, and full of true light. It has itself become the immovable pillar and foundation of truth. In it the entire coming of the Son of Man is wholly present; he is wholly everywhere, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

Hence it follows:

> Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.

A remarkable comparison has been made from the most common behavior of eagles. For this reason the Greek word πτῶμα, which means “corpse,” is used more significantly according to the pattern of Christ’s passion. He fell into death and became a corpse in order to raise up those who had fallen.

And because what had fallen rose again, it is fitting, for the sake of those for whom he had fallen, that where the body that rose again is, there also the saints should be gathered. This is what he says plainly: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.”

Not just any birds, but eagles: namely, the disciples, concerning whom the prophet had once foretold: “They will take wings like eagles; they will fly and not grow weary” (Isa. 40:3). One of these, Paul, speaking of the resurrection and wishing to introduce faith, said: “We who are alive, who remain, will not precede those who have fallen asleep, but together with them we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:16).

Therefore he did not say, “Wherever the body is, there vultures and ravens will be gathered.” Rather, he wished to point out his elect, whose youth had been renewed like that of eagles, and to show them as magnificent beyond all birds, exceptional—as he wishes all to be who, having died and been buried with him, rose again to life.

To these he properly and rightly says: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.” He says “they will be gathered” because perhaps they will be led by the service of angels to the place of Christ’s passion, where he will descend to earth, since he departed from there and, as I have already said above, will judge there; many also believe this.

Saint Hilary likewise says:

> His coming in glory will be awaited there where, through the passion of bodily humility, he brought about for us the glory of eternity.

Luke also seems to show more clearly that this is so when he says that the disciples asked, “Where, Lord?” and the Lord answered them: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Luke 17:37).

For it is certain that the apostles are asking about the place. If they say, in connection with what Luke has related above, “Where, Lord?” after he has said, “There will be two in the field; one will be taken and the other left,” the meaning is the same. They are asking where that one who is taken will be taken, and the Lord answers: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.” The unity of these eagles is the totality of the saints, who, carried along by the rowing of their wings, are joined to the body of Christ.

Therefore he takes an example from irrational birds, which sometimes smell out and see corpses even across the seas, and do not hesitate to fly to them, so that the multitude of believers may much more confidently hasten to him whose lightning comes from the east and flashes throughout the whole Church, in which his body and blood are offered and received, even to the west.

I know, however, that some doubt this interpretation and raise several objections, which are easily refuted. In their desire to empty catholic meanings of their force, they display their ignorance. They understand it as though it said: wherever the sacrifices and blood of the Jewish victims are, there the Romans, swifter than the eagles of heaven, will gather for the slaughter and devastation of the wretched city.

But we give a better interpretation concerning the man Christ: wherever he is—or where he suffered, rose again, and from where he ascended into heaven—there, at the resurrection of the flesh, the eagles, that is, the saints, must be gathered from the four winds of heaven and thereafter be with the Lord.

I do not say this as though I were unaware of the various opinions that arise from this interpretation. Therefore let no one prescribe to me a definite location, so as to deny me the right to entertain a possible conjecture that I hesitate to affirm, except insofar as reasoned reflection in such matters gives us an occasion for forming an opinion. At the appropriate places I shall also touch upon what anyone may think concerning this.

For although the blessed apostle Paul affirms, moved by love for Christ, that he and his companions will be caught up in the air to meet Christ, he does not deny that Christ will come to earth for judgment, where he was judged and from where he departed.

I therefore do not know whether anyone could or would maintain that, if Paul and the other supreme saints are to be caught up above to meet him, all must likewise be raised from the earth before the judgment has been completed and must go wherever they are to be judged, as some wish.

But, as Isaiah says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. 3:14).

Others, for their part, say that wherever the bodies are—in tombs or in the earth—there the souls will come and receive their own bodies. Although it is true that this will happen, it does not follow that this passage is speaking of that matter.

Immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken; and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.

Here he shows that after the tribulations of the Antichrist a short time will elapse, when he says “immediately,” until the day of judgment comes. Some, however, wish to understand this as a very brief interval after the apostles’ tribulations, until the desolation of the temple and the dispersion of the Jews came as vengeance for Christ’s cross.

That interpretation does not follow from what comes next: “The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light,” and so forth. I do not think these words refer to a diminution of light, especially since Isaiah says: “The light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be like the light of seven days” (Isa. 30:26).

Although these words may receive another interpretation, it is by no means rightly believed that the stars will fall from heaven. Rather, in comparison with the true light, all the luminaries of heaven are prophesied by the Lord to become as though they were dark. They will be very obscure—not in their own nature, but when compared with the radiance of eternal light.

If this sun, which now glows and shines throughout the whole world, and the moon, which is the second luminary, and the stars, which were given for the consolation of the night, as well as all the powers of heaven—which we understand as the multitudes of angels—are all, at Christ’s coming and in comparison with his radiance, reckoned as darkness, as though because of excessive brightness, what do those think who, with raised eyebrows, consider themselves saints and, as though secure in their own righteousness, do not fear the presence of so great a judge?

For in that fearful judgment no one will be secure. When the glory of his splendor shines forth, no one will think himself to be anything, because then no one will be able to think of or look upon anything other than him, who alone will then appear glorious.

At his coming, therefore, the darkening of the sun, the eclipse of the moon, the falling of the stars, the shaking of the powers of heaven, the manifestation of the saving sign, and the lamentation and mourning of all the nations are proclaimed. At that time he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice to gather his elect.

Although I have put it this way, there is such great obscurity in these words that no one should rashly define anything concerning them. Some say that just as at Christ’s passion, during the dispensation of the cross, darkness came over the whole earth when the sun failed to give its light, so at Christ’s coming, when the same sign of the Son of Man appears in heaven, the light of the sun will again fail, and afterward that of the moon and stars, because of the great brightness and power of that sign.

If the sun is darkened or suffers an eclipse, it is not surprising that the moon and stars, which do not possess their own light, will be unable to display any brightness. Yet even so, the stars are not rightly said to fall from heaven; rather, according to their eclipse, they will grow dark and cease to appear.

The curious reader should examine fully whether this can be established from Isaiah, Joel, and the other prophets, and whether it ought to be understood literally in this way, or as we said above. For it is not to be believed that the stars will fall, since the wise men of this age are said to consider their magnitude to be as great as that of the earth. If so many of them fell, to omit other considerations, there would be no place for them to fall.

Others say that, from the conflagration by which the world will be burned, smoke will be condensed and raised upward from the multitude of fires, as commonly happens with fire, until it reaches the highest heavens, so that the darkness will be so great that neither the sun, nor the moon, nor the stars will be able to shine.

This seems entirely inconsistent, because it is not sufficiently clear how long this fire will precede the Lord’s coming. Even concerning this very fire, some hold different opinions.

If Matthew and Mark had not added these signs after the tribulation of those days, we would better understand them spiritually, as some wish, concerning the Church: namely, that this took place during the persecution itself, so that the sun of righteousness was darkened in the hearts of many, although it had previously begun to shine in them.

For at that time many will fall away from religion, and the clear faith in them will be darkened, covered by the cloud of unbelief. It is therefore no wonder if, after the tribulation of those days, they are said to be darkened. These things do not happen only after that entire persecution has passed; rather, the falling away of some will precede the restoration of serenity.

Because this will happen throughout all those days, it will occur afterward within those same days, when there will be nothing but darkness. Therefore the moon, which is the Church, will not have its light in them, and the stars will fall from heaven, when many who were thought to be saints, overcome by temptations, will be inscribed not in heaven but on earth.

Because the love of this present life excluded them from the light that is Christ during the persecution, they are said, as it were, to fall from heaven like stars. For it was said to Abraham: “Your seed will be like the stars of heaven” (Gen. 22:17; 26:24).

But because the harshness of persecution and love of the world tore carnal people away from the faith, they fall violently from heaven to earth, just as the one who fell from the heavenly seats fell like lightning.

Hence the Lord says: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke 10:18); and: “The powers of heaven will be shaken” (Luke 21:26).

They will indeed be shaken by the glory of Christ’s majesty, although they always attend him and see his splendor. For when he rises to strike the world and destroy sinners from it, I do not know whether any of the angels will glory in his own conscience, trusting in his own strength.

Or the powers of heaven will be moved to avenge the enemies when they see the judge of all coming prepared to take vengeance on his enemies.

“And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.” This sign is certainly the sign of the cross—not because it will signify something yet to come, but so that it may show that the one who was crucified on the cross in humility is glorious. Thus the elect may rejoice with every act of thanksgiving, while the impious and sinners may see the one whom they despised in humility and suffer all the more.

Hence it follows: “And then all the tribes of the earth will mourn.” These are the tribes that loved earth more than heaven and therefore remained miserably on earth. There will be various tribes according to the diversity of merits, because neither in hell will there be one uniform quality of punishment for all. There they will rightly mourn because here they destroyed themselves through evil.

[Col. 0818B] “And then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty.”

“Then” is an adverb referring to a predetermined time, and it can refer only to that predetermined time. Therefore it must be sought out with the greatest care what all these things refer to.

The same word was similarly placed above: “And then all the tribes of the earth will mourn.” Nearly everyone has referred this to the end of the age, and I have followed them. But if the whole context of the reading is considered and a comparison is made among the evangelists, a very great difficulty arises: whether all these things should be referred to that time of destruction or to the Savior’s coming.

For if they are referred to that event, the divine speech exceeds it in many respects and raises matters greater than seem to belong to that time. A little farther below it says: “When you see all these things taking place.” He speaks as though he wishes all the things mentioned above to be understood by these words.

After saying these things, he then says: “Know that he is near, at the gates.” This does not mean that the end of the age is already present, as the preceding words seem to suggest; rather, he is near and at the gates, as though at the entrance.

Therefore perhaps we shall know that he is near when we see not some of those things, but all these things that have been stated above. Among them are these: then the powers of heaven will be shaken, and then they will see the sign of the Son of Man.

“And then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty. And then he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest heavens to their boundaries,” and so forth.

All these things he brings about in this final hour, coming in his members as in a great cloud, while the Church bears fruit and grows until the Gospel is completed and preached throughout the whole world among all the nations.

This Gospel began when he wished to preach and say: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4:17).

Therefore, from the beginning of this discourse, certain things were spoken by these three evangelists in such a way that, if they are carefully compared with one another, some may perhaps be found to have been spoken about his coming, and some to pertain to the overthrow of Jerusalem.

The remaining things, however, are shown either to pertain to this: that he comes daily in his body, which is the Church, concerning which coming he said: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God and coming in the clouds of heaven”; or to that final day of future judgment, as I have said, when he will come in himself and judge the living and the dead.

Therefore it will be the task of a prudent man to understand which of all the things mentioned above are intended. Perhaps they should be understood in such a way that some of the statements are excepted—those that are shown to pertain only to his coming, when he himself will come in person, as is beyond doubt in that final parable:

“When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then all the nations will be gathered before him,” and what follows.

Perhaps the same applies here to the statements: “The powers of heaven will be shaken. And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn. They will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty. And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice,” and so forth.

Although these things can also be interpreted concerning the Church, they seem better to refer to his final coming in person.

We can nevertheless say that the powers of heaven are to be removed from Judaea, lest they bring aid to the wretched city; that then the cross is to be preached in the Church and raised up as a triumph of Christ’s power; and that then, during that siege, all the tribes of the Jews will mourn.

Thereafter they will see the Son of Man in the clouds of heaven—that is, coming through the holy preachers in the Church with great glory and power of the word.

I have said these things so that I may not be mocked by those who refer nearly all of them to one time: either to the coming in which Christ comes daily in his Church, as though in his members, or to the coming when he himself will come in person at the end of the age.

I do not think either of these interpretations sufficiently fits or accords with the passage. Therefore I shall continue, although these things can also be interpreted concerning the Church, preferably so that they are understood of his coming in his own body, in which he sits at the right hand of the Father.

In that body he also died, rose again, and ascended into heaven, according to what is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “And a cloud received him from their eyes” (Acts 1:9). There the angels also said: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.”

Therefore he is rightly believed to come not only in the same body, but also, as it is said here, in the clouds, because he will come as he departed, and a cloud received him as he went away.

This interpretation is certainly more straightforward and clearer, so that whenever anyone hears or reads, “Then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and majesty,” he should understand this precisely as his coming—not through the Church, but in person, when he will come to the living and the dead.

For this reason the sacred Scriptures must be searched, and nothing should be defined rashly, in case someone else may be able to discern in these matters something higher than we can. No teacher—not even I, who am insignificant—has ever been able to disclose everything.

“And then,” he says, “they will see the Son of Man,” that is, at the end of the age, coming with great power and majesty.

But the elect will see him in one way, and the reprobate in another: the elect so that they may rejoice, and the reprobate so that they may grieve.

For this reason it is said: “Let the impious be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.” Although the good and the wicked will see him, the impious and sinners will see him so that they may be put to shame, while the righteous will be glorified through him.

Nevertheless, because it is said, “They will see him coming in the clouds of heaven,” it must be asked whether they will see him with bodily eyes or in some other manner.

But because it is said that they will see the Son of Man, I do not believe it can be understood otherwise than that they will see him in the human form in which he ascended, coming in the heavenly clouds, so that all who crucified and rejected him will see him.

It should also be noted that when he was taken from the eyes of the apostles, a cloud received him. Now he is said to come in the clouds with great power and majesty, and yet he will come entirely as the angels promised.

For he will truly come in the same bodily form and in the same flesh, but in the clouds with great power, great glory, and great majesty.

Therefore, since we have already read that he was transformed in great glory and splendor, it must be asked whether he will come in that same splendor or in a greater one.

At that time, before his chosen disciples, “his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white as snow”; other manuscripts read, “like light.” “And behold,” he says, “a bright cloud overshadowed them, and behold, a voice from the cloud said: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him’” (Matt. 17:5).

Therefore it is not unreasonable to ask—since great power and majesty are proclaimed as destined to accompany his coming—whether he will be transformed into that glorious form, just as he was then transformed before the three disciples, or whether, as is more consistent with what follows, he will already be wholly transformed into a greater and abiding glory, beyond what he was on the mountain.

For it is clear that he was then transformed before only three disciples. In the future, however, at the consummation of the whole world, he will undoubtedly appear in great glory, so that all the elect may see him.

Perhaps for this reason, just as a bright cloud overshadowed them then and also at his ascension, many clouds will carry the Son of Man when he comes at the end to judgment, coming with an array so great and so magnificent that it is wholly worthy of his glory.

This is not because he needs such things, nor because “God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2:9). We must not understand this according to the divinity of the Word, but according to the fact that “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14) and “emptied himself” (Phil. 2:7), so that in every respect everything that is in Christ—body and soul—might be wholly God and wholly exalted.

For it was fitting that the body he assumed from the Virgin, through the power of the Most High God, should be honored by the Father in such a way that he would come upon clouds of this kind—not upon darkened atmospheric clouds, but upon rational and angelic ones. Otherwise it would seem unfitting that irrational creation should serve as the vehicle of the glorified Son of Man.

We ought not to understand the clouds in any other way than those of which it is said: “And your truth reaches to the clouds” (Ps. 35:6).

Nor do I think that the bright cloud at the Transfiguration was merely an atmospheric cloud, especially since it follows: “And behold, a voice from the cloud said: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’” (Matt. 17:5).

That cloud was not the Father of the beloved Son, nor did the Father speak through an irrational creature. Rather, so to speak, the Word of God came to that cloud just as it came to the prophets—for example, to Isaiah, when he says: “I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have rejected me” (Isa. 1:2).

In this voice we do not hear Isaiah speaking, but God the Father speaking through Isaiah. Likewise, in this cloud, when he says, “This is my Son,” we understand an angelic office and the person of the Father bearing witness in it to the glory of his Son.

If such a cloud proclaimed and overshadowed him before the dispensation of the passion, what ought we to think here of the clouds of heaven upon which they will see the Son of Man coming with great power, majesty, and glory—those who are then to see him not without immense brightness?

Therefore, although the sentence is joined to the mourning of the tribes of the earth, I do not think that they will see him inwardly in his glory. Rather, he will be so covered by clouds that it will be sufficiently clear why they are put to shame and grieve: because they did not heed such a great Lord.

If, when the Lord came to Jerusalem, the apostles loved him so much that they spread their garments on the road so that the ground would not be trampled bare by the donkey on which he sat, why should it be surprising if the Father and God of all spreads heavenly clouds beneath the body of his Son as he descends to accomplish the consummation?

When Jesus first came, he came full of every power, and therefore powers went out from him. But in comparison with the power with which he will come again, glorified at the end, those powers that were performed then appear small.

For the glory with which he will come is the glory of restoration—the glory that he possessed before the world was made, from which he never departed, even when he hung upon the cross.

From the beginning of his preaching until the end, he also comes daily in the clouds, as has already been said, so that the Church, which is the body of Christ, may be glorified and grow, and so that she herself, glorified again through him, may ascend to him.

Hence it follows:

And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest parts of the heavens to their farthest boundaries. Some, as I said, understand this—as they do the other passages mentioned above—as referring to the Church. But we think that, without prejudice to the other interpretation, it should rather be referred to the future, and to the present chapter. For in nearly all these statements, some expressions seem capable of fitting the present Church, while others so far surpass the words and meaning that they may rightly be said to concern that second coming of Christ in himself.
