And therefore perhaps he concludes the passage in this way: “This generation will not pass away until all these things take place.” They have been stated in such a way that some may be shown to have been fulfilled in the Church, while those that have been fulfilled in this last hour are to be manifested more gloriously. The apostles asked about these things in connection with the end of the age and with his second coming.

The Apostle also agrees with this passage, saying that, “at the voice of the archangel and at the last trumpet,” the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Likewise, in the Apocalypse of John, the angels prepared themselves to sound the trumpet. And it is said to Ezekiel: “Prophesy, son of man; prophesy and say to the Spirit: Thus says the Lord God: Come from the four winds of heaven, O Spirit, and breathe upon these slain, and let them live again” (Ezek. XXXVII, 9). Although the prophet, according to the historical sense, speaks of the Jews by the prophetic Spirit, he nevertheless directs his gaze toward that day of resurrection. So also in this passage the Evangelist speaks, even though holy preachers do not cease daily to fulfill this in the Church. [Col. 0821D]

Here we must ask whom he foretells will be gathered as the elect: whether only those whom that day will find alive in the flesh; or those who will be holy from the coming of Christ; or perhaps all who have existed from the foundation of the world, who, like Abraham, saw the Lord’s day and believed that Christ would come in the flesh. Since the discussion concerns the last day, it is fitting to consider all Christ’s elect, those foreknown and predestined. But what should I say meanwhile about whether they will be gathered in one place—although I have already stated above what many think concerning the place of his coming? To inquire further exceeds my limited powers and would perhaps be superfluous.

For “to gather” may also be understood as collecting them into the unity of predestination; and they may be said to be raised at the trumpet of God and at the voice of the archangel into life, so that all may share together in that first resurrection. Their unity and restoration to life is rightly called a gathering. Thus it is not that the impious and sinners will not rise; rather, because they will be unworthy of the company of these people, they are not mentioned. Nevertheless, they too will be somewhere in the sight of God, and they will be on the left because they will be reprobate.

What, then, is surprising if all the elect and the reprobate are said to stand there in different ways, since we also read in Job that, on a certain day, when the sons of God came before the Lord, Satan stood among them (Job I, 6)? So all these too will come before the Lord, although the multitude may seem incomprehensible. But those who are said to be gathered will be gathered only after the chaff has been rejected—not merely from the four winds of heaven, but, as the Evangelist says, “from the highest parts of the heavens and to their farthest boundaries”—so that they may always be with the Lord, and so that henceforth, wherever the body of Christ is, there also will the eagles be.

And, as I said, it should be noted that some things in these statements so surpass the present situation that they cannot be taking place now. I do not think that what he says—“They will gather them from the highest parts of the heavens to their farthest boundaries”—can apply to anyone on earth. It could happen from the four winds of heaven, that is, from the four regions, so that the holy preachers of Christ gather the Church. But I do not know whether they can gather them from the highest parts of the heavens, unless perhaps such people are found among human beings who, while still living among men, also dwell with the angels in the heavenly places.

Therefore, since it is not fitting that such hearers should be found, it remains that, through the offices of angels, those who have already become heavenly by the grace of Christ will be gathered at the resurrection from the highest heavenly powers to its boundaries, so that no exile from heaven may be found outside its boundaries. [Col. 0822A] For they will shine in that perpetual eternity like stars, or rather like the sun. And therefore they are not without reason gathered from the highest parts of the heavens, so that they may be established in the firmament of heaven, and to its boundaries, from among those who were foreknown and predestined, so that no outsider may be found.

We read in the Book of Numbers that, when the twelve tribes of the children of Israel went out from the land of Egypt, they encamped around God’s sanctuary on the four sides of heaven. Therefore, because its figure is fulfilled here, they are said to be gathered from the four winds of heaven, not without a great mystery. So also in Ezekiel the Spirit is commanded to breathe upon the slain from the four winds. And perhaps this is why the command is given, and why the angels will act in this way: just as at that time they encamped on the four sides and were brought by Jesus into Judaea and into the Lord’s inheritance, so also the angels will gather God’s elect from the four winds. [Col. 0823B]

These winds are not earthly but heavenly, those of the holy Gospel—that is, from the highest parts of the heavens to their boundaries—so that, gathered by Jesus Christ our Lord, they may receive the divine and true inheritance in heaven.

“Learn a parable from the fig tree: when its branch has already become tender and its leaves have grown, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see all these things taking place, know that he is near, at the doors.”

Luke says: “Look at the fig tree and all the trees: when they produce fruit from themselves, you know that summer is near” (Luke XXI, 29). No one doubts that both statements were spoken by the Savior. And therefore, since this is a parable concerning the future, we must investigate what one of them intends by the fig tree alone, and what the other intends by the fig tree and all the trees.

For the fig tree and all the trees in the winter season appear as though dead, although they possess within themselves a living power that is very deeply hidden. Afterwards, when the sun has grown warm and illuminated them with its appearance, and the cold has withdrawn, their living power immediately returns. Thus, warmed by the sun, after they have been drenched by the rains, they begin within to give birth and germinate; then they break forth into a sprout and swell into a bud. When spring has passed and the west wind is blowing, the buds begin to emerge on the branches through the strength of the sun itself, and they produce leaves, so that the tenderness of the branches is extended and fruit is produced. Thus, little by little, from the actual effect of the trees and fig trees, it becomes clear that summer is near.

For above he had said: “This Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world.” [Col. 0823D] But the wretched synagogue of the Jews, because it is winter, lies dead, without fruit and without any greenness of faith. So also many nations, although more and more of them have believed by God’s favor, are still oppressed by the cold of excessive unbelief. The Savior’s parable undoubtedly refers to them.

First, when that fig tree of the Jews has received the warmth of God’s word, and the sun of righteousness—that is, Christ—has illuminated it with his light and watered it with heavenly waters, as though winter had passed and it had received the living Spirit, then, when the Gospel has been completed throughout the whole world, all the trees—that is, all the nations—having received the greenness of faith, will bring forth fruits of righteousness.

Nevertheless, Matthew, writing this Gospel for Hebrews who had believed, placed only the fig tree, namely the synagogue, on account of its particular significance, so that he would not pass it over. For when all the trees have produced fruit—that is, when the fullness of the nations has entered—then all Israel will be saved.

Before these things take place, let no one say that Christ is here or there; let no one terrify us as though the Lord’s day were imminent. For unless these things first occur, he will certainly not come. But when they have taken place, he says, “know that the kingdom of God is near.” Indeed, it is near in this last hour, but no one can truly say how near, because it is altogether beyond anyone’s knowledge to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own authority (Acts I, 7). The text continues:

“So also, when you see all these things taking place, know that he is near, at the doors.” This is what I was saying above: the prudent reader must understand what “all these things” means. For it is proved that all these things which have been set forth from the beginning of the question do not pertain to the apostles’ times, nor even to our own. In the present age there are nothing but uprisings and wars, disasters and plagues, and indeed unheard-of calamities. More atrocious than all these evils is this evil: that love has grown cold and true faith has been abolished. From these things tribulation and every desolation of the citizens arise daily.

Therefore, as has often been said, each matter must be considered in its own time and distinguished according to its setting, lest someone try to reduce to a single moment everything that must be completed throughout the intervals of this one final hour. For when he says, “He is near, at the doors,” this is not stated simply, but with great subtlety, so that you may understand that all these things which have been taking place from the beginning of the preaching of Jesus Christ are “at the doors”—that is, at the entrance through which the whole Church enters, going forward and carrying its seeds, never ceasing to go, never ceasing to enter.

And therefore all the evils that take place are proclamations and messengers of one evil, while the things that are good and pleasing to God are seeds and fruits of one good. Yet when these things are happening, the Lord’s day is near, at the doors, so that it may receive no thief and reject no righteous person. And therefore, as long as these things are happening, it is near, at the doors, so that the entrance to life may not seem long to anyone:

“Amen, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.”

Behold how far all the things foretold must be fulfilled. Here, I ask, let the devout hearer fix his attention and understand that “this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.” Let us first see what “this generation” is; then what “will not pass away” means—or, as other manuscripts have it, “will not pass over.” For “to pass away” or “to pass over” may mean either moving from one place to another or being changed from one state into another.

If this is said of the generation of the Jews, any simple person might suppose that the meanings of the statements set forth above concern the destruction of Jerusalem and only those Jews who saw Christ’s passion at that time, as though that generation ought not to pass away before the destruction of that wretched city came. But I do not know whether all these statements can be expounded word for word concerning that generation, from the place where he says, “You see all these things,” to the place where he says, “He is near, at the doors.” Perhaps they can be so understood in some passages, but in others they certainly cannot. And if someone attempts it, being sufficiently constrained, I do not know whether he will be able to say what is fitting.

Therefore we understand either one generation of all human beings, from Adam to that last human being; or, from two generations—the Jews and the nations—we understand one Church, concerning which Solomon says: “One generation goes, and another generation comes” (Eccl. I, 4). For the Jewish people, which existed in its own time, has now gone away; and the nation of the Gentiles, along with a very large part of the Jews, has come to the faith of Christ. Together they say with one voice: “Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation” (Ps. LXXXIX, 1).

The one God justifies this one generation together: circumcision from faith, and uncircumcision through faith in Jesus Christ. This generation of the New Testament, which was then present in the face and sight of the Savior, will not pass away to those blessed promises of eternal life until all these things have taken place which the Lord spoke—namely, before Christ comes in the clouds; before his sign appears in heaven; before the angels are sent with the trumpet of God; and before the dead rise.

Neither will those who are then in the flesh precede those who are to rise, nor will those who rise to that blessed life pass away beforehand, until all these things have taken place. This is the true conclusion of God’s statements, toward which everything converges. And perhaps this is what it means to be “at the doors” when all these things have taken place: for then, as though placed in the middle—that is, at the doors—they can neither return to this present state nor arrive at the other without divine judgment. [Col. 0825C]

If anyone tries to constrain us by saying that this was spoken only of the Jews, let him know that that nation itself, wherever it may be, though dispersed, will still remain. Some attempt to establish that, at the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, one hundred forty-four thousand from all the tribes, marked with the sign of the cross and gathered from all the nations in Judaea, must believe. Thus neither that nation itself, nor its successors, nor those who are found in the flesh, will pass into that age before all these things have taken place.

Then, when these things have been completed in the manner foretold, each person will pass over according to the deeds of his merits, to the places long ago prepared for him by the Lord. The text continues:

“Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

This is very appropriately said: after the inhabitants have been transferred, the house itself will finally also be transferred. But perhaps judgment will first take place within some interval of time or in a moment; and then heaven and earth will pass away—not so that they cease to exist, but so that they may exist in a better form: a new heaven and a new earth. Thus those who are to be transferred will be changed and made incorruptible.

Hence the Lord also says in the Apocalypse of John: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. XXI, 5). Therefore how well he says that this generation will not pass away before all these things have taken place. And when they have been completed, then they themselves, as though placed at the doors, will pass over to other things.

And if all these things will pass away because they will be changed, the Lord’s words will not pass away. For the words that belong to the Savior will not pass away, since they are his own; they are active now and always in him, in whom, so to speak, they are ineffable and eternal. Human words, on the other hand, so long as they are imperfect, are not truly words; but when they have been perfected, then they truly exist. God’s words, however, cannot fail to exist.

Human words, because of the condition of their creation, have their beginning in nothing within themselves; therefore they return to the end imposed by their nature, so that they cease to be. But Christ’s words, born from eternity, always contain within themselves the power to remain.

He appears to introduce this statement in answer to the disciples’ question. They had asked about the structure of the stones, and he sets before them what is more firmly established: heaven will pass away. Therefore he warns them not to be astonished at the destruction of the temple, since even greater elements will pass away. But he confirms that his words—by which he had promised them the things that were to come—will never pass away in such a way as to fail to be fulfilled.

The divine things in Christ are always the same, and the things spoken and completed in him cannot fail to occur. Therefore whoever wishes to come to the things that remain must pass through the things that are slipping away and pass beyond them; for no one can pass over to those things until all these things have happened to him.

“But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven, but the Father alone.”

Many manuscripts have “neither the Son,” and this is how it appears in Mark. Yet nowhere has “neither the Son of man” been added. The Felician heresy added “of man” to its doctrine for this reason: to teach that, insofar as he was man, he did not know that day and hour. By this fraud it wanted to introduce the idea that, because he did not know what God the Father knew, he was an adoptive—or rather titular—Son of God rather than the true Son.

Thus, blind to what he was saying, the heretic wanted to show two sons in one and the same Christ. But nowhere in the entire sequence of Scripture will you find grounds for inventing a Christ who is sometimes the true God and sometimes not true; sometimes the true and proper Son of God, and sometimes not true or not proper. He is always the true God and the proper Son of God, both before and after the Virgin’s childbirth.

Therefore the Virgin Mary did not give birth from herself to two sons, but to one incarnate Son of God. Yet Arius rises up against this statement, and Eunomius rejoices, as though, because the Son does not know what the Father knows, he could not be equal to the Father.

To them we must briefly respond that everything was truly made through him, as the Gospel testifies, and that life was in him before the things were made. Therefore times too were made through him, because they are not eternal. And if they were made through him, and if what was life in him existed before they were made, he cannot be ignorant of what he himself made and of what was always in him before it was made.

Among all the times that were made is the day of judgment, which he undoubtedly established and made. He cannot be ignorant of what the Father knows, since he is wholly in the Father and the Father is in him. Nor can he fail to know what the Father possesses and what belongs to him, since everything the Father has, the Son also has, because everything has been handed over to him by the Father.

If the Son had been ignorant of the last day, he would necessarily have been ignorant of the penultimate day, or of all the preceding days as well. For it cannot happen that one who is ignorant of the first should know the second.

Nevertheless, the reason must be sought why the Son of man is also said to be ignorant, since the one who is both God and man is one Christ. His ignorance has a reason, especially since the Apostle declares that in Christ “all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God are hidden” (Col. II, 2). Therefore, in the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom are present, there is no ignorance.

But why are they hidden? When the apostles asked him about this day, he answered them most clearly: “It is not yours,” he said, “to know the times and moments which the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts I, 7). By saying, “It is not yours to know,” he showed that he himself knows, but that it is not expedient for the apostles to know, nor for that day to be announced to mortals, so that, always uncertain, each person may live as though he were to die tomorrow and come to judgment.

Whatever is in the Father is wholly comprehended by the divine statement that the Son knows when it says that the Father alone knows. For just as the Father is called by the name “Son,” so the Son is also called by the name “Father.” Therefore whatever is in one of them is wholly in the other.

Thus we must not listen to those who say that, before Christ fulfilled his own dispensation of passion and resurrection, he was ignorant of what he later learned, and that this is why Luke says that the child Jesus advanced in age, wisdom, and grace before God and human beings (Luke II, 52). From the beginning of the incarnation, God and man were wholly in him, together with all grace and all the wisdom and knowledge of God. Therefore nothing came to him that was not already in him, because he was complete God and complete man.

But toward what he advanced Luke himself faithfully explains: he advanced “before God and human beings,” so that he might attribute this appropriately and dispensationally to the man and to his age.

The manner of speech by which he says that he does not know that day and hour must itself be considered. Scripture often speaks in such a way that it says it does not know something because it left the apostles themselves ignorant of it. Thus it says to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. XXII, 12), as though it were saying, “I have caused you to be known.” Secular literature also speaks of bitter lupines because they make those who eat them bitter. This manner of speaking is exceedingly common among all.

Jesus may also rightly be said, in another sense, not to have known that day and hour which comes at the end: he did not know its shortening. Just as we say that a physician does not know jaundice even when he sees and understands it in another person, although he has never experienced it in himself, so it is said of him who “knew no sin” that he himself was made sin for us. Just as he never knew sin by experiencing it, so he did not know the end of that day and hour.

I have said this because many go astray in this chapter, so that it may be clear how many possible interpretations it contains. Even if no other explanation occurred to us for why he said that he was ignorant, we could say that Christ and the Church are one body. Since the Church, because it is expedient, is ignorant of that day and hour, and since it is his body, it is entirely fitting that he who is its head should confess ignorance in his members, until the day is fully understood to be known when all its members also know it.

There were also those who said concerning this passage that he stated that neither angels nor any mortals know the day and hour because no one can calculate the measures of times or the intervals of hours. Someone might perhaps know after how many months or years it will occur—whether after a thousand years, or after a hundred, or after more or fewer. Therefore he said “the day and the hour,” because such a small point within so many ages cannot be comprehended.

I confess that in this last hour, in which we are and in which Christ has come, as John says, “My little children, know that it is the last hour” (1 John II, 18), just as it cannot be detected how long it will extend, so neither can it be determined through how many years. Therefore he did not say that he did not know the day or hour because he could not gather the smallest divisions of the hours, since one hour might be so long; rather, he wished the day, time, and hour of the end to remain so uncertain that no human being could know when he would come.

It should also be noted that he says, “neither the angels of heaven.” From this it is clear that the angels do not comprehend God in his entirety. Although they possess an exalted nature, they do not understand everything that is in God, since they too are God’s creatures.

He added “of heaven” to distinguish them from those angels who, in this Church of Christ, strive daily to announce divine things. For “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature. And so, when even those who are more excellent in nature and nearer to God do not know, human frailty ought to be content, so that it may not seek with excessive curiosity to know what can unquestionably be most beneficial to leave unknown.

Meanwhile, however, with God providing something better for us, the angels of heaven themselves do not know that day and hour, so that all things may be completed in us. For the Son of God prepares knowledge of that day and hour for the coheirs of eternal life, so that all may know together, and so that all things in heaven and on earth may be restored in Christ. [Col. 0828C]

“As it was in the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of man. For just as they were eating and drinking in the days before the flood, and so forth, so will the coming of the Son of man also be.”

It must therefore be asked how it was said above, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom,” and how plagues, famines, and earthquakes were foretold at Christ’s coming, while now he recalls matters that are rather signs of peace.

We should therefore understand, in accordance with the Apostle, that after the battles and dissensions of those who lie in wait, and after the other things by which the human race is continually ravaged, a brief peace will follow for a short time. This peace will permit everything to become quiet, so that the faith of believers may be tested: whether, after the evils have passed, they expect God the Judge to come.

This is what we read in Paul: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thess. V, 3). It is rightly asked whether this sudden destruction will occur all at once, or gradually, just as we read that the flood grew over several days.

For all the signs of future things about which we have spoken up to now were, as it were, illnesses of the world, revealing the corruption that was to come upon the age. This is shown especially by the statement that the coming of the Son of man will be like the days of Noah, because then everything perished suddenly.

Some, however, wish to say that it happened gradually, since it follows that those who lived in the lower places first perished, then those in somewhat higher places, and finally those who dwelt on the highest mountains. In the same way, some say that at the consummation of the age, when fire descends, it will begin in the higher places and gradually descend to the lower.

Luke gives us an occasion, from the fire of Sodom, to understand that this world will be consumed by fire, but suddenly. “Likewise,” he says, “it happened in the days of Lot: they were eating and drinking.” And shortly afterward: “On the day when Lot went out from Sodom, it rained fire and sulphur from heaven, and destroyed them all. So will it be on the day when the Son of man is revealed” (Luke XVII, 29–30).

Blessed Peter confirms this in his Epistle: “The heavens,” he says, “will pass away with great force, and the elements will be dissolved by heat” (2 Pet. III, 10). Which heavens will pass away, the same Apostle teaches shortly before, saying: “The heavens that existed formerly, and the earth subsisting out of water and through water by the word of God; through these the world that then existed perished. But the heavens and earth that now exist have been preserved by the same word, reserved for fire on the day of judgment.”

Here we must not understand as “the heavens” those in which the stars are placed and which are called the firmament, nor the ethereal heaven, but this atmospheric heaven, near to the earth, from which the birds are called “the birds of heaven.” The waters of the flood once destroyed and overwhelmed it, and the fire of the final judgment, growing through the same extent, will occupy and destroy it.

All these things most clearly teach that the corruption of the world will come suddenly. This is also shown by what the angel says to Lot: “Hurry, then, and save yourself there, for I cannot do anything until you enter Zoar” (Gen. XIX, 22).

Hence some suspect that, just as Lot was saved, so that fire will not then take possession of the world before the righteous who have been saved shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, when the angels gather from Christ’s kingdom all the scandals of the tares and throw them into the furnace of fire (Matt. XIII, 42).

Therefore, although I said above concerning Christ’s descent to earth—according to where he ascended and from where he ascended—that he must return there in order to judge the world, there is great obscurity as to whether that final and universal judgment will take place there or elsewhere, and where, and in what manner, and for how long. No delay is indicated, since the Apostle says that “in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead will rise” (1 Cor. XV, 52).

And when the resurrection of the saints has taken place, the saints will immediately be caught up, as the Apostle testifies, to meet Christ in the air. But whether at that time the reprobate also will be raised higher from the earth to meet the coming Judge; or whether, after the judgment has been completed, fire will precede in the manner I mentioned above; or whether, when the saints ascend to meet him in the heights, the reprobate will be so weighed down by the burdens of their sins—although they possess immortal bodies—that they will be unable to rise higher; and therefore, while the Lord presides at the judgment, the saints will be raised on his right into the heights and rejoice more gloriously, while the impious and sinners, standing below and pressed downward, will be on his left—what of these possibilities is to be judged more correct must be left undecided, lest we rashly define what will then appear more clearly.

If that fire will burn everything on the surface of the earth, even the highest places, and if the unjust will not be raised to the heights, it is clear that, being placed on the earth, they will await—or perhaps will already have received—the Judge’s sentence.

But whether they will be burned by that fire, although they are destined to be condemned to eternal fire, I think no one can determine. No one should dare prejudge the matter except those who say that the reprobate will suffer no punishments other than those proper to the conscience of each individual.

Augustine, however, says in his book *The City of God* that by that fire the lesser sins of certain of God’s elect are purified. Pope Gregory says the same in his homilies, referring to the words: “Fire will burn before him, and will inflame his enemies” (Ps. XCVI, 3), and “a mighty tempest surrounds him” (Ps. XLIX, 3). “The tempest of such strict justice,” he says, “is accompanied by fire, because the tempest examines what the fire consumes. And if this fire will then be able to do something to those who will at that time be in it, let each person consider what that eternal fire will do—the fire that is prepared for the devil and his angels.”

By those who are eating and drinking he means those who, during the tribulation of those days, will remain in their desires, thinking of nothing except the present life, committing fornication and serving their lusts. “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thess. V, 3). But for the saints and righteous there will be eternal blessedness, because blessed are those who are prepared to meet him.

Then two will be in the field: one will be taken and one will be left. Two women will be grinding at the mill: one will be taken and one will be left. Two will be in bed: one will be taken and one will be left.

Similarly, above he had already proposed three groups: those in Judaea, those on the housetop, and those in the field. For, as some wish, there will be no more than three orders among these: married people in bed; widows at the mill of tribulation and poverty; and virginity in the field, entirely flourishing and white as a lily. But in the taking and leaving, another distinction must be sought, in which the future separation is shown.

Therefore, in the field, two are rightly said to be present—that is, among those dwelling in this world, the order of believers and unbelievers, who labor in this age as in the work of this life. When the day of the Lord comes upon them like a thief in the night, it will find the latter drinking and committing fornication; but it will find the former using the things of the world as though they were not using them, and possessing them as though they did not possess them. One of these will be taken: the one who seeks the things that belong to God; the other will be left in the fire: the one who seeks only the things of the world.

The same reasoning applies to those who are grinding, so that the mill may be understood as the work of the Law. It is as though there were a wheel within a wheel: while the Law itself revolves in its turning, the wheel of the New Testament is formed within it. But because part of the Jews believed through the apostles, and is still to believe through Elijah, and is to be justified by faith in Jesus Christ, one part of them, saved by that same faith of good works, will be taken into glory and into the body of the Church; but the other, pursuing the unfruitful works of the Law, will be left grinding and turning stone rocks in vain.[Col. 0831A] And because, by turning it, they draw the mill around without the grain that is Christ, they produce no flour of heavenly food.

Moreover, the two in bed proclaim the same rest of the Lord’s Passion. Concerning this faith, there is one confession among heretics and Catholics; but because heretics do not believe in the unity of the Father and the Son, nor in their communion, the Holy Spirit, they are rightly left behind: for they believe wrongly and live worse. The Catholic, therefore, will be taken in faith and works; but the other, namely the heretic, while he seems to rest in this rest of Christ—as though in a bed—will be left behind, as I have said, because he lives badly and teaches worse, wrapped in his errors.

This is proved, then, by the matter of agriculture in Genesis, where Cain and Noah are introduced as farmers. But one of them, namely Noah, a worker of the earth, placed in the field of this world, is taken by the Lord together with his fellow-workers, who will be like him; while Cain, the worker of the earth, is left behind together with his followers. Although he offered badly, he divided worse; he sinned, and did not rest so as to cease sinning.

The same must be understood of the human souls who grind: they are weighed down by a heavy burden and walk around in circles, blinded by the works of the body. One of them, if she turns this mill well so that she may eat heavenly bread, will be taken; but the other, if she remains blind at the mill, will be left turning in her blindness. Otherwise that very strong man Samson would never have come to this mill unless he had first received the grace of the Holy Spirit and then lost his eyes.[Col. 0831C]

Therefore, two are also said to be in bed. In this sickness of weakness we all lie. Concerning this bed David, groaning, said: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears” (Psalm VI, 7). And elsewhere, concerning the one whom he wished, he said: “May the Lord have mercy on him and help him upon his bed of pain. You have turned his whole bed in his sickness” (Psalm XL, 41). From this sickness no one is saved except through the grace of Christ. Since the whole human race lies in this bed, one will be taken so that he may recover from the sickness of his weakness, through the work of the most merciful Savior; but the other will be left, by the just judgment of God, in the corruption of death.

Accordingly, whatever is in the field should cultivate and labor over its field. I mean the field in which the treasure is found and purchased—he whom the Lord blessed. Isaac, as though perceiving him from afar by his fragrance, said: “Behold, the odor of my son is like the odor of a full field” (Genesis XVII, 27). For in him are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, whom the Lord blessed. Let each person also work his own field, lest, luxuriating in the abundance of the flesh, he produce thorns or thistles. For earth that produces thorns or thistles is rejected, and is close to being accursed.

Moreover, the soul that has been placed at the mill ought to gather for herself the grain of the word, so that she may always grind and make flour, or the bread of salvation, by which the inner person may live and be satisfied each day. The mill, as though made of two stones, should be turned by fear and hope: hope always drawing upward, fear pressing downward, bearing everything with equanimity and holding all things in common. From fear the soul conceives, so that she may give birth to the spirit of salvation.

When this mill is firmly secured both below and above and turns correctly—provided only that the soul ruminates and grinds Christ within herself—she never remains without the fruit of flour. Therefore such a soul will be taken, not just anywhere, but after her labors, into rest. The other, because the ungodly walk in circles, although she appears to grind while pursuing the things of the world, will be left empty and without fruit.

And because we all lie in bed, weighed down by excessive sickness, while there is leisure and time, the saving physician must be invoked, lest we lie dead for a long time. He must be invoked so that he may say to us: “Rise, take up your pallet, and go into your house” (Mark II, 9, 11). For at present no one goes without sickness, no one without a pallet.[Col. 0832B] But one is taken when the physician Jesus has mercy; the other is left by God’s just judgment, because we are all pressed down in one bed and under one sickness.

“Watch therefore, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come.”

Let Faustus the Manichaean hear this, since he slanders Moses, as though Moses either did not speak about himself when he spoke as though about another, or else some unknown person, speaking in Moses’ role, falsely published the words, “The Lord said to Moses,” when Moses was plainly speaking about himself as though about another. And because he accepts the Gospel, let him hear the Lord here speaking about himself as though about another. For, as is clear, he was present before the disciples when he spoke: “Because you do not know when your Lord will come.” He did not say, “Because you do not know when I shall come,” although he was speaking about himself.

This manner of speaking is, in fact, extremely common in the sacred Scriptures. Although someone may wish to understand this passage more profoundly, he may say that he spoke in this way because, insofar as he was God the Word, he was still absent from the hearts of the disciples. Therefore he significantly spoke of the future coming of the Word into the understanding of the disciples, because he was not yet in their perception as he was to be. For, as he intimates through this passage, every day he brings about the day of his coming in those who keep watch: he comes into the souls illuminated by the light of truth and illuminates them with the light of his glory.

Whatever he had said above about his coming, whatever he had taught, and why he had concealed the day and hour of his coming, he concludes here when he says: “Watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.” It is as though he said: “For this reason I wanted you not to know, so that you may always keep watch and always be ready for the time when your Lord will come, lest the darkness of night or the sluggishness of sleep overtake you.”

What he says to the apostles he certainly says to everyone. He does not say, “Because we do not know,” thereby confirming that he does not know—as the heretics chatter when they seize upon this as an occasion—but “you do not know,” separating himself from them and making them understand that he does know.

“But know this: if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly have watched and would not have allowed his house to be broken into.”

He therefore introduces the parable of the house and the thief, in order to warn the master of the house to keep watch and guard the things that are in the house. This parable touches everyone who has received the mysteries of the faith, but especially the superiors and rulers of the Churches, who must keep watch and be concerned not only for themselves but also for everyone. For whatever the just Judge finds lacking in the sheep entrusted to them concerns them.

Yet because he speaks to everyone, each person ought to watch in spirit and always attend more carefully with the mind, lest, while he has grown sluggish, the thief come and undermine the house in the darkness of blindness. Each person is the master of his own house. Our house, moreover, is soul and body, in which, according to the Apostle, we carry our hidden treasure in these earthen vessels.

The thief breaks into this house at night when either the body is corrupted externally by vices, or the soul inwardly—although she ought to watch and guard the house—overwhelms herself; then the devil strips her and breaks in.[Col. 0833B] If he knew when the thief would come—namely, the final day of his death—he would certainly watch and would not allow his house to be broken into.

What, then, does “he would not allow his house to be broken into” mean? Can anyone recall the day of death, which is said to come like a thief, so that it will not come? Certainly not. But it is one thing to open the door to someone who is knocking, and another to admit the thief—not through the door of good vigilance, but through sluggishness and the oppression of sins.

This is why, dearest ones, when death is already knocking at the door like a thief, we sometimes receive it so unwillingly: the adversary had first stripped us of heavenly goods. But good servants, who have long awaited the coming of their Lord, open happily when he knocks at the door and receive him. They receive him because they were ready.

Thus it is one thing to meet the final day as it comes and to open the door to it—or rather to Christ the Judge—and another thing, willingly or unwillingly, to admit it as an enemy or thief. For Christ does not come to the soul unless he knocks at the door; but the thief and robber, the devil, climbing up by another way, breaks into and strips her.

The final day itself is also a thief and robber to the weakened soul. Therefore, through the door of good faith, but secretly to one blinded by evils, it breaks into and overturns her, drives her out of the body, and tears her away. For in another parable it is said: “He who does not enter through the door is a thief and a robber” (John X, 1).

But the shepherd is the one for whom the doorkeeper opens. For the Lord of the house enters confidently through the door, himself both doorkeeper and door, in order to reward the one who keeps watch—one who so joyfully and vigilantly receives him when he comes. The thief, however, does not enter through the natural entrance of a good life. Rather, as one who had already first broken into it, destroying and overturning the natural foundations—that is, the foundations of the structure of faith—he enters through the openings made by that undermining when the final day comes, like a thief.[Col. 0833D]

Therefore, as long as human life lasts, this night-watch ought also to last. But because few keep continual watch throughout the whole time, one must nevertheless guard in every way against allowing the final time to find us sleeping like a thief—those whom he may previously, and often, have deceived as though enveloped in darkness.

Thus he says: “Be ready, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come.” For the one who is unprepared cannot prevent the day of his death from afflicting him like a thief. The Lord does not say this to the apostles as though the day of his coming in the flesh would find them, so that they might then be found ready; rather, he says what he says to everyone, and he says it so that no one may make himself secure.

For just as no one knows when the day of judgment will come, so each person does not know when the coming of his own death will be. Therefore he says: “Be ready.” This means: keep watch against the snares of the devil by abstaining from evil and meditating on good, lest the thief seize and overthrow you like the night. Indeed, watch attentively, so that whenever the Lord comes and knocks through whatever circumstance of death, each person may immediately open to him, rejoicing in his own day and hour.[Col. 0834A]

“Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent servant whom his lord has appointed over his household, to give them food at the proper time?”

Above he appears to have spoken generally to everyone; now, however, he addresses the apostles specifically—or the rulers of the Churches and apostolic men. This parable is directed especially to them so that, the more they rejoice that they have received more than others, the more concerned they may always be when rendering an account for themselves and for others.

Peter, recognizing that he had spoken this to himself and his companions, asks in Luke: “Do you speak this parable to us, or also to others?” (Luke XII, 4).

The steward is required to possess two qualities: that he be faithful and prudent. Yet although these two may seem insignificant to rash people, among the many stewards it is difficult to find a prudent and faithful man. Therefore he said, as though in doubt: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent servant?”[Col. 0834C] For such a person is found very rarely.

For this reason the Apostle said: “Let a man regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Here, moreover, what is sought among stewards is that one be found faithful” (I Corinthians IV, 1–2).

Many things come together in these two virtues, and it would take too long to enumerate them. Therefore such men are so rare that scarcely one is found among many. Rare are those who would rather serve their fellow servants than rule them, and would rather benefit than preside over them; those who seek nothing except the divine profits, advantages, and interests of the people entrusted to them, so that they may deprive no one of food at the proper time—for it belongs to everyone.

Whatever a bishop possesses, he ought to possess not so much for himself as for everyone, because he himself belongs to everyone in order to serve all. Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, he finds doing this: distributing his lord’s provisions prudently and faithfully to his fellow servants.

And he must not act as though he were exercising unrestricted authority. Luke adds: “To give them their measure of wheat” (Luke XII, 42). He must not give either to one to whom it ought not be given, or more than ought to be given; nor must he withhold from one what ought to be supplied, or more than ought to be supplied. Rather, he should distribute to everyone—as is proper to a prudent man—and to each his appropriate measure, recognizing the different qualities of all in character, capacity of understanding, and merit.

“Amen, I say to you: he will set him over all his goods.”

Let rash and exceedingly proud rulers take heed. It was recently said that one of them had declared—and had even left this written in his books—that it is of no benefit to pray to God at the relics of blessed Peter and the other saints, nor to go there for the sake of prayer and the service of devotion. He claimed that the one who now exercises the office of Peter and the other saints, or sits in their seat, can help more than the one who, in his own time, distributed the gifts of Christ—which the present officeholder appears to do.

This is a rash and blind presumption. Can Peter, Paul, and all the other saints not now help more, after conquering their enemies and trampling down their vices, because they reign with God, than those who are still laboring in the contest? Certainly, those who presume wrongly about themselves lie defeated.

For it is said: “Let not the one who girds himself boast as the one who ungirds himself” (III Kings XX, 11). The soldier who is still positioned in battle scarcely suffices for himself against his enemies; but the one who now boasts as a victor rests securely, even ungirded.[Col. 0835B]

At present, too, any priest or teacher, because he has been placed over others and many things have been entrusted to him for the use of his fellow servants—but not everything, nor has he been set over everything—does not possess all the goods of God. Therefore it is extremely rash to assert that anyone, by virtue of his office, can do what Peter cannot by virtue of his merit.

The one who sits in Peter’s seat flourishes by Peter’s authority, excels by his power, and is strengthened by Peter’s faith—the faith that Peter himself learned from God the Father and taught, and everything he taught concerning Christ he confirmed by martyrdom.

Therefore the merciful Lord has already done what he promised, just as he has done with the other saints whom he has set over all his goods—that is, whom he has placed in the glory of God, beyond which there is nothing better to possess.

[Col. 0835C] “But if that evil servant says in his heart, ‘My lord delays his coming,’ and begins to beat his fellow servants, while he eats and drinks with drunkards, the lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know,” and so forth.

See why no bishop, no priest, and no cleric ought to boast that he has been placed in a position of authority. For not only are faithful and prudent servants appointed over the Lord’s house, but also evil servants who say in their hearts: “My lord delays his coming.”

One of these servants, because he was faithful and wise, will be taken into glory; but the other, because he was unfaithful and foolish, will be left to disgrace and the shame of his dishonor,[Col. 0835D] so that he may receive everlasting reproach.

Let the rulers or stewards of the Churches take heed: they have been entrusted with a precious jewel. Therefore, according to both kinds of stewardship, they must be very faithful and prudent—something you will find extremely rare.

To give food at the proper time—both material sustenance and the nourishment of the divine word—a person needs great prudence, so that he neither removes, defrauds, nor withholds food from those in need at the proper time: namely, the word and bread. Great faith is therefore necessary.

For all the revenues of the Churches are entrusted in stewardship to the poor, so that they may not be diverted to any uses other than ecclesiastical ones. Prudence is likewise very necessary, so that we may minister to each person according to each one’s quality and merit: neither more lavishly nor more restrictively than is proper; to no one less, and to no one more, than is expedient. Nor should anything be given to one to whom it ought not to be given, or in any way other than is fitting and appropriate.

Because this requires great diligence, great glory is also promised: “Amen, I say to you,” he says, “he will set him over all his goods.”

Let someone give me a king who has beneath him an entire lofty kingdom, with many peoples, many cities, and many kingdoms or diverse regions. Suppose that he divides the greatness of his kingdom among his soldiers or commanders who have accomplished something outstanding, so that he appoints all of them over his entire kingdom, its provinces, and its cities—not each one over everything, but each over some part of his kingdom. For example, one over ten cities, another over ten cities, and another over five, as another Evangelist shows.

Thus all will be set over all his goods, especially in that kingdom where no one possesses anything from which another does not rejoice. The King himself, God, alone holds everything over all and alone governs everything.

I have said this so that no one may fail to understand this manner of speaking. If he does not understand it, we may wonder how it can be said of each person that he will be set over all his goods.

“But he will divide that evil servant and appoint his portion with the hypocrites; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

And why will he divide him? Because he was unfaithful and imprudent; he did not know how to provide for the future, especially since he preferred pleasure to future goods. Therefore, as though secure, he said in his heart, despising rather than loving his lord: “My lord delays his coming.”[Col. 0836C]

The evil servant says this more according to his wish—wanting it to be so, so that his lord might not come quickly, or might never come—than from any foreknowledge arising from faith. For this reason he holds out the prospect of long delays, wanting always to eat and drink with drunkards. Thus, as though dreaming, he says: “My lord will come after a long time.” And the poetic saying comes true: “Those who love, fashion dreams for themselves.”

Accordingly, while the lord delays, such a servant beats his fellow servants, eats, and drinks luxuriously, taking advantage of his ecclesiastical office. He does not bring the needy, the poor, and strangers into his house to feed the hungry; instead, he feasts splendidly every day with drunkards and *ambrones* [revelers]. Although one such person is mentioned, their number is great—would that we did not know them—those to whom ecclesiastical responsibility has been entrusted.

Their lord will come on a day they do not know and at an hour they do not expect, and he will divide them from his elect, whom he will set over all his goods. Without doubt this will happen because they hated the coming of their lord.

Removing such people, let us always set before our eyes good and watchful servants, carefully and soberly managing his household. One of them, out of desire and love born of charity, groans and sighs that his coming is delayed; another, because of the great ardor of his love, thinks and hopes that he will come sooner; a third, anxious about this matter, daily nurtures his ignorance with tears and sighs and confesses, groaning, that he does not know when he will come.

All of them love the manifestation of their lord and await it eagerly and vigilantly. Whatever each of them may say, the one speaks and groans best who says to his companions: “Let us watch and pray, because this life is brief and uncertain, and we do not know the day of death or when the Lord will come.”

Because the evil servant did not wish to foresee this, his portion ends with the hypocrites. Origen interprets this division differently, as though the Lord divides his spirit from him, and the spirit returns to God who gave it, while the soul goes with its body into Gehenna. Let the prudent reader beware of this interpretation.

For spirit, soul, and flesh constitute one human being; spirit and soul are one substance. The soul is the part by which a person is given life; the spirit, or mind, is the part that holds superiority in the human being, through which the whole person is governed.

Therefore this evil servant, because he allowed the flesh to rule, is wholly divided from the good and placed with the hypocrites: because he falsely held the place of governance; because he despaired of the Judge’s coming; because he did not obey the commandments; because he devoted himself more to present things than to future ones; because he lived the life of unbelievers; and because he afflicted the household entrusted to him with hunger, thirst, and slaughter, so that he is proved to have been faithful neither in divine nor in human matters. Therefore he is rightly joined to the hypocrites.

“There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” There, in the place where his portion will be with the hypocrites—for they too will be in a definite place, not scattered and indiscriminately, as certain rash disputants wrongly think—but in the fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

Although that fire may be of whatever kind it is, bodies too will be tormented in it, since bodies can exist only in a place. Thus the teeth that here rejoiced wrongly in eating will gnash, and the eyes that here continually fed insatiably on desirable things and seized upon the things of the present life with their sight will weep.

## Chapter XXV

“Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who, taking their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride.”

This, then, is that famous likeness among the parables. Many have discussed it, but few have restored it whole in its several parts, so that the individual meanings of the parable might correspond to its unity. Therefore I do not rashly presume to judge anything concerning it, lest, when someone approaches with a more effective understanding, a richer grace should bind us by its interpretations and enclose us within its expressions.

Nevertheless, I will explain briefly and carefully, as far as I can, what sometimes seems to me to be meant by these things. He had said: “Watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.” After other matters, to confirm and adorn what he had said, he adds this parable, which seems to signify nothing other than what was said concerning the two in the field, the two at the mill, and the two in bed, as well as what he proposed concerning the good and evil servant.

For among all these, one is admitted to the kingdom and one is rejected. So also in this parable, although it is treated more broadly and eloquently, since it is composed with sufficient splendor and appropriateness to instruct minds, lift up their spirits, and enrich the heavenly discipline, it is nevertheless shown to signify the same thing: that the good are to be chosen and the evil rejected.

But let us see why he proposed it at the beginning. “Then,” he says, “it will be like.” He shows that he is speaking of his future coming, and not—as some have wished—of the time when he comes daily in his Church, and she herself enters by faith to him, adorned with good works. Although there are certain elements that may have this meaning, they do not all have it, because the meaning and purpose of the parable are concluded with the end.

Why the kingdom of heaven is called the holy Church of God has already been explained sufficiently.[Col. 0838A] But why it is compared with ten virgins must, I think, be examined carefully.

As the two peoples mentioned above perhaps signify Christians and Jews, or the elect and the reprobate, who appear to be established in this Church of God and themselves to practice Christ’s agriculture—to plow and grind—yet do everything in hypocrisy, so now the ten virgins encompass all human beings within the Church. They appear to believe in God and applaud themselves in the divine Scriptures, whether they are churchmen, Jews, or heretics.

They are all rightly called virgins because they boast that they have been betrothed in the knowledge of the one God, just as the Lord himself says through the prophet: “I will betroth you to me in faith and mercy” (Hosea II, 20). Since they are brides through faith, they are rightly called virgins.

Yet we must not carelessly say, as some have done, that all human beings descended from Adam are virgins. We should say this only of those who appear to have received the faith of God and who, through that same faith, have in some manner gone out to meet the bridegroom Christ God, or the bride. Those who have no faith neither know nor begin to go out to meet him; rather, they lie defiled by idols or corrupted by demons.

Because five of them are wise and five foolish, the ten virgins are counted figuratively. The five wise and five foolish are introduced on account of the five bodily senses. For just as there are five senses externally in the body, from which the outer person is constituted and lives, so there are five inward senses by which the soul lives within, is renewed, and enjoys God.

Some, desiring earthly things, do not possess the nourishment of the true light with which to illuminate their hearts; others continually desire heavenly and higher things within and seek what is divine.

Concerning these senses the Evangelist and Apostle said: “What we have seen, what we have heard, and what our hands have touched concerning the Word of life.” Concerning taste David says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm XXXIII, 9). Concerning scent, the bride says in the Song of Songs: “We run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song I, 4); and the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (I Corinthians II, 15).

These virgins, because through these five senses they have inwardly perceived Christ, are rightly called five and wise. They are wise because they have passed from fleshly things to spiritual things, and from temporal things to eternal things. They are five because, through this number five, they are joined to God and consecrated in the unity of Christ’s body.

We likewise, not unreasonably, call the remaining five virgins foolish, because through these five senses they have learned divine things in some manner and have received the word of God somehow, whether by circumstance or in truth.[Col. 0839A]

For, so to speak, they have been made virgins through the word of God, which they perhaps believed, although no works followed, or which they claimed to believe. The word of God is such, and so powerful, that by its purity and virtue it accommodates itself to all who receive it, turn away from the worship of idols or of the elements, and approach, as though by faith, the living God—even if works of piety have not followed—so that they may be called virgins on account of their knowledge of the one God or their profession of faith in God.

Their senses are not defiled by idols, nor are they polluted by the worship of false gods, although, deprived of the word of wisdom, they are inwardly made foolish.

It should be noted that whoever has one of the five senses defiled by idols, so that he is not called a virgin, must also be polluted in the other senses, so that he is not a virgin. Similarly, whoever has one of these senses wise, so that he diligently practices the things that belong to wisdom, will have all the remaining senses wise as well.

For just as Christ cannot be separated from himself, so all the senses, according to the inner person—or rather, in relation to one another—follow one another. Therefore, if you have one of the senses inwardly wise, so that the person may be established by God as a virgin, Christ must pour wisdom into the other senses as well.

For this reason, one does not find among the five senses in a person one foolish and another wise; rather, all five will be wise virgins, or truly foolish. For in one person these dispositions of the senses are not separated from one another.

Therefore those who have reached the knowledge of the one God, or received faith after abandoning idols, are rightly called virgins, because they do not commit fornication with gods nor pollute themselves with idols.

But because, as I have said, these senses are twofold in a human being, the ten are rightly said to be virgins once faith has been received.

Having taken their lamps, they went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. In this parable they are said to go out to meet the bridegroom not only once but also a second time. We must therefore understand that the first going out by faith to meet Christ and the Church is one thing, and that rising again at the consummation of the age and hastening to meet the eternal Judge, so that each may receive according to what he has done, is another.

For the first going out to meet him takes place in this last hour, throughout the entire period from the beginning of the incarnation of Christ, when the bridegroom and the bride are “two in one flesh,” when our Lord, becoming God, became man in the body. Thus, just as the spirit is the bridegroom for the flesh, so the flesh is the bride for the spirit. Ten virgins come to meet him, taking up their natural instruments—that is, all souls when they first received, through faith, the saving trumpet sounding forth the proclamation of the word of God.

They do indeed go out from the world and from the errors of many gods, and so come to meet the bridegroom and the bride through the grace of new regeneration, so that all may enter first into the hope of blessed immortality. For as soon as any soul has encountered him through faith, the bridegroom is ready to come to meet the virgin and receive her into his body, which is the Church, in sweet embraces.

(This whole parable is therefore better understood of those virgins who come to meet Christ so that they may be received within the Church. For no one meets the bridegroom worthily without the bride, nor does anyone enter the bride—namely, the blessed Church—without Christ. Thus it is rightly said that they went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride, taking their lamps [Matt. 25].)

This going out is celebrated in this last hour, until all meet in the unity of faith. While this delay continues, after faith has been received, the light of the faithful must shine before human beings, so that, seeing their good works, they may glorify God the Father, who is in heaven. This is what it means to take oil in one’s vessels, as nourishment for eternal light: while soul and body live here, they must continually be filled with good deeds, so that they may always have with them the oil of gladness and the joy of the Holy Spirit.

Because the other virgins did not wish to take this oil with them and nourish it after receiving grace, they are called foolish. Hence it is said that five of them were foolish and five wise, though all were virgins because they had received the grace of faith. By this one name the whole Church is called a virgin; concerning it the Apostle says: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2). He also added: “But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted” (ibid., 3) from the chastity that is in Christ.

This parable therefore does not portray only those virgins whom we call religious women, but the whole Church. For few possess virginity in the body, but all ought to possess it in the heart. Accordingly, abstinence through all five bodily senses is good, so that the human mind may abstain from everything unlawful. From this abstinence virginity received its name, and through this incorruption the whole Church of Christ is called both virgin and bride.

Nor is she just any kind of virgin, but a wise one—provided that her abstinence from vices shines forth to the praise of God. Otherwise, if she acts well for some other reason, whoever seems to be doing good will be counted among the foolish, because she does not possess the salt of wisdom. For this reason she is found to be foolish: many appear to have faith without works, while some also abstain from unlawful things and perform good works, but not sincerely for God’s sake, although those works are judged praiseworthy.

Thus five are admitted because they were wise, and five are rejected because they were foolish. The foolish are foolish because, having received lamps, they did not take oil with them; the wise, however, took oil in their vessels along with their lamps. Oil is the fruit of the Spirit. The vessels, although made of clay, are our bodies, within whose inward parts this same fruit of good works must be stored.

The lamps are the shining light of souls, which, clothed with the sacrament of baptism, have shone. Behold: the foolish are called virgins, are said to have received lamps, and went out with the wise to meet the bridegroom and the bride. What more, then, do you think must be sought except that they did not take oil with them, lest the light of their burning lamps fail?

For this reason alone they are called foolish. We must therefore understand that this oil signifies something great—indeed, something exceedingly great. We are anointed with oil in baptism, so that we may be called Christians. The Savior Christ our Lord was also anointed with oil. Concerning this anointing we sing in the Psalm: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”

This oil is the oil of exultation and gladness, for which David, because he had sinned, prays, saying: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit” (Ps. 50:14). Perhaps, then, this oil of exultation and gladness is the Holy Spirit. Whoever does not have him is not of Christ here, nor does he possess the charity of Christ. For “God’s charity has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). Without this charity, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 13:3), whatever a person may possess profits him nothing.

This charity is rightly signified by oil. For just as oil rises above all liquids, so charity surpasses all virtues. Hence the same Apostle Paul says of it: “I show you a still more excellent way.” This way is prepared and laid out here and now through charity, so that the wise virgin may carry oil with her, and a light that will shine forever.

Therefore, through the oil by which charity is nourished and diffused, the Holy Spirit is rightly signified: by him the hearts of believers are gladdened, and all works of virtue are enriched. Charity, which is the richness of the Holy Spirit, never fails. Whoever loses it after receiving grace, although he may appear to have gone out through faith to meet the bridegroom and the bride, will nevertheless be counted among the foolish.

All ten virgins are joined together in faith. Through the pledge of faith they all strive to go out to meet the bridegroom and, as it were, await his coming in their hearts. But because they neglect to preserve the grace they have received, to nourish it, and to take it inwardly with them in their souls for the glory of God the Father, they become foolish.

The wise, however, not only preserved the grace they had received in their bodies, but also continually took in oil and accumulated for themselves, through the gift of charity, the fruit of the Spirit. Therefore “the yoke of sin has rotted away before the oil.” For in the Holy Spirit they not only preserved the remission they had received, but also stored within their vessels outstanding works of virtue, so that they might shine like burning lamps.

These vessels may also be understood as the five bodily senses, in which they stored the abundance of oil that they had drawn from the firm rock, so that the senses themselves, saturated with oil, might pass over to spiritual things. They did not cast their inward things outward, but hid within themselves, in their conscience, the gifts of eternal life.

Concerning these gifts, for which they grieved here, it is said: “They shall exult in glory and rejoice upon their couches” (Ps. 149:5)—that is, each of them in his own conscience. It must also be noted that it is said that the wise virgins took oil in their vessels, together with their lamps.

They received it as a gift of grace and stored it in their vessels until the time of their visitation. They are therefore called wise because they foresaw what would come afterward: that, by the gift of grace, they would have to render an account.

But it was not so with the foolish. For, according to Solomon (Eccl. 10:1), “Dead flies destroy the sweetness of the oil”—that is, the anointing with which they were anointed by the Holy Spirit. The Greek word χρηστότητα means “sweetness” and “anointing,” as well as “goodness” and “gentleness”; all these are bestowed through the Holy Spirit.

Because they did not wish to receive him or preserve what they had received, but cast away their inward things after the empty praises of human beings and the favor of the crowd, they remained empty of every brightness of light and of all the verdure of charity.

[Col. 0842B] While the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and slept. What does “all” mean? The wise, of course, and the foolish. And what does it mean to say, “They became drowsy and slept”? Does “they became drowsy” mean, as someone says, that they languished before death? Or what sort of sleep is this?

Perhaps, because the bridegroom was delayed—and because iniquity abounds—the charity of all of them grew cold. Are we to understand this sleep in that way? Is it that they first weakened or became drowsy, and then went into death, which is what “they slept” means?

Far be it from us to understand it that way, since the wise are present among them. For when the Lord said, “Because iniquity has abounded, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24:12)—which is to say, the oil of many has failed—he immediately added: “But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.” Therefore these virgins were wise: they took oil in their vessels, preserved it, and remained faithful to the end. For this reason they are admitted inside without hesitation, because they were ready.

The chill of sluggishness therefore did not creep over them, nor did their charity grow cold; rather, it burned fervently to the end. Therefore the doors of the bridegroom stood freely open for them to enter, and it was said to them, as to that excellent servant: “Enter into the joy of your Lord.”

What, then, does this delay mean, during which the bridegroom delays coming and they all become drowsy and sleep? We rightly understand the delay as extending from the beginning of the Church’s calling to the end of the age, until the last hour is completed, in which all are lulled by the sleep of death, which no one escapes: neither the learned nor the unlearned, neither the wise nor the foolish. All, in the meantime, until the bridegroom comes, are enclosed by one end, death.

Why are they called sleeping? Because on their last day all will be raised as though from daily sleep, and all will be found alive. Whether a virgin is wise or foolish, all will nevertheless undergo the sleep of death. But the oil of the wise, which was received and preserved in their vessels, will not perish in death.

When it says, “They all became drowsy and slept,” it speaks according to our customary usage. Just as no one sleeps unless weighed down by sleep, so no one dies unless overcome by weakness; and to become drowsy means to be brought low by weakness.

Yet it seems better to me that, since it had said, “They all became drowsy,” it then found the expression “they slept” so that we might understand that it was speaking of the sleep of death. It is as though it had said: They slept because, as soon as the cry was made, they all rose from sleep.

This is why it said “they became drowsy”: after the sleep of death, all rose at the voice of the living God and at the trumpet of the archangel. Here it clearly indicates that no one lives who does not see death. Therefore it says: “They all became drowsy and slept.” The wise and the foolish alike—all slept.

Behold, at midnight a cry was made. What is “midnight”? It is unexpectedly, when it is not hoped for, when it is not believed at all. He therefore used “night” for ignorance, because it will happen suddenly, as in the deepest night, when all who are secure are overcome by the heaviest sleep, as was said above.

Then, through the cry of the angels and the trumpets of the preceding powers, the coming of Christ resounded. At this point blessed Jerome says that there is a Jewish tradition that Christ will come at midnight, in imitation of the time in Egypt, when the Passover was celebrated, the destroyer struck all the firstborn of the Egyptians, and the Lord passed over the dwellings that had been consecrated by the blood of the lamb.

Hence that outstanding teacher believes that, from apostolic tradition, the practice descended and continued of keeping vigil on the day of the Passover vigils, so that the people might not be dismissed before midnight while awaiting the coming of Christ. Once that time had passed, everyone could celebrate the festal day with greater security. Hence the Psalmist also said: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (Ps. 118:62).

[Col. 0843C] Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps. Lamps are so called from the Greek word λάμψαι, that is, “to shine,” from brightness or radiance. Hence the Apostle says (2 Cor. 4): Ὁ εἰπὼν ἐκ σκότους φῶς λάμψαι, that is, “the one who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness.’”

All indeed arose, but only those who had taken oil with them in their vessels before they slept trimmed their lamps with their radiance. From this brightness of grace each adorned her senses, in which she had stored the oil of the knowledge of God and the works of charity, so that she might have works of virtue in her hands with which to shine before the eternal Judge.

Indeed, they received from him the splendor of glory to whom they had entrusted their good deeds. Therefore the true Judge will then restore the deposits of each person, with whom the oil of those who had entrusted to him the adornments of their virtues has not been emptied.

When they rise, having received these things from the Lord, they will adorn themselves inwardly in their consciences and raise the senses of their souls to those eternal joys, because they will see the works of their deeds that they had once entrusted to the Lord before they went into death.

But the foolish said to the wise: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.” By complaining that their lamps are going out, they show that they had possessed lamps that were lit and illuminated, and that had shone to some degree. But because they did not possess lasting works—that is, works of eternal charity—or unfailing light, they go out, because they acted only temporarily and shone in the world through unfruitful works.

Then that prophetic saying will be fulfilled: “All the foolish in heart were troubled” (Ps. 75:6). And if you should ask why, it is because “all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands” (ibid.), since they had no lamps of these works in their hands.

Hence the Lord says: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35). Therefore, if anyone has a virginal soul and is a lover of eternal life, let him not be content with insignificant things that quickly fade through their works, lest what appears good wither from the heat.

When the Judge begins to examine the consciences of individuals, the lamps that seemed to shine may suddenly go out. For after the day of the resurrection there will no longer be any opportunity to earn merit; rather, whatever a person has sown in this life, he will then reap.

Therefore the wise answered and said: “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you; go instead to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.” These virgins must not be judged moderately wise, for they are the ones who preserved for themselves the opportune time for working, when, at the first coming of the Lord, they accumulated much oil of charity in their bodies. They prepared with themselves what is eternal and heavenly, and loved heavenly things.

They did not live carelessly and negligently like the foolish, who were concerned only with the present and its affairs, forgetful of God’s promises, and did not extend themselves toward any hope of resurrection.

Yet they were not so imprudent, although they were foolish, that they did not understand that they ought to go to meet the bridegroom with the light of good works and have all their lamps illuminated. They saw that they had less oil of good works because they had not cared for these things while there was time.
