Therefore, as the darkness was already approaching, the lamps that had previously seemed to shine—illuminated for a time by their own pleasures—grew dark, because the oil of delight and gladness was failing. The sinner’s oil did not delight them, nor were their minds driven by the praises of others.

But the wise, because they were wise, also gave a wise answer: “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you.” For at that dreadful examination no one will boast that he has a chaste heart, nor will anyone’s merits be sufficient for himself, much less for giving to others, since perhaps there will not be enough to satisfy everyone.

For they understand that at that examination no one will be helped by the works and merits of another; each person must have oil for his own lamp. They urge them to go and buy, if perhaps, even late, they might obtain through the merits of the greater saints—who were accustomed to distribute the Lord’s money for the profit of souls—what they need, thereafter obeying God’s commands so that, with the light of their lamps, they might be made worthy to meet the bridegroom.

The lamps of those other virgins, however, did not go out before they slept, because the praises of human beings were not lacking. But when they rise, no one will praise them, for then every person will attend only to his own case. No one, therefore, will exist who does not think about himself; no one will sell oil through flattery.

And so their lamps began to fail, so that they would not shine. Then the foolish turned to the five wise virgins: “Give us some of your oil.” They seek what they had been accustomed to make shine with another’s oil, rather than by their own conscience, and they seek the praises of others.

“Go instead,” they say, “to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.” This is perhaps not the voice of advisers but of mockers. For wisdom was in those virgins, and therefore wisdom itself was speaking through them—the wisdom that elsewhere confesses concerning fools: “I also will laugh at your destruction” (Prov. 1:26).

What wonder, then, if the wise mock the foolish, when Wisdom itself admits that it laughs them to scorn? What else does “Go to those who sell” mean except: “This is what you have been accustomed to do, and therefore we do not give to you, lest there not be enough for us and for you”?

Nevertheless, even if these words can partly be understood of those who always preferred to possess human praises in a flattering rather than a truthful manner, there are many other advantages, cares, and concerns of the present life through which the rewards of eternal life are neglected, and into which sluggishness and idleness sometimes intrude.

Therefore, I believe that he is speaking not only of flatterers but also of all who have pursued something else. To them it is said: “Go instead to the customary affairs of human life in which you have been accustomed to live. That is why you did not take with you the oil of the Holy Spirit.”

For this reason we do not give it, lest there not be enough for us and for you—now, when there is no time for anyone either to give or to buy. And therefore, while they go to buy, the bridegroom comes; that is, while they seek too late to buy what they had neglected to prepare earlier, while they seek those who might praise or console them and do not find them, the bridegroom comes.

Those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast, because the door was opened to them. It should be noted that it says, “The bridegroom came.” Above, the ten virgins went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride; here, however, only the bridegroom comes.

What, then, is this? Or where did the bride go, who earlier came with the bridegroom among these ten virgins? It is certainly not without mystery that she came with him then, while the divine discourse is silent about her now. It is not truly silent, but speaks openly about her, saying: “Those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast.” For she is the bride who enters with him, because she was ready, ever watchful through the immense love of charity, and spending the night in prayers, anxious for the bridegroom’s coming and yearning with all her desire to come to him.

Earlier she came with the bridegroom in order to bear children: receiving those who had been begotten within her womb, she gave birth to them and nourished them. But now, rising from the dead, when the door of life has been opened to her, she hastens joyfully to meet the bridegroom and enter with him into the wedding feast to which she had long been invited.

But the one who had loved less, who had loved something else more, who had not possessed the oil of charity, who had been concerned about many things but had neglected the one necessary thing, remained cold within herself while seeking too late. Therefore it is not said that they bought or received the oil of perfect charity, because their very seeking was certainly not prompted by the affection of chaste love.

It is therefore difficult, and known by few, to understand how Christ is called the bridegroom and the Church the wife and bride. For although we may be called Christ’s brothers and God’s children, and may also be brothers to one another through God the Father, nevertheless no one other than Jesus Christ is the bridegroom of the Church.

Thus John, although he is the friend of the bridegroom, is not the bridegroom, nor is any of the saints. It is therefore a very hidden and difficult matter to understand how the human soul is joined to the Word of God so as to be a bride, or how it is united with him.

Yet no one enters this wedding except the bride. For what is more wondrous, since whatever Christ is, he is God, while she is a creature; and accordingly he is the bridegroom and she the bride—Christ and the Church as husband and wife?

Hence the Apostle says: “And the two shall be one flesh” (1 Cor. 6:16); and he says: “This is a great mystery, but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32). The Apostle calls this a great mystery, and therefore not everyone immediately understands how great the matter is of which he speaks.

We know by what kinship all the saints are Christ’s brothers: not by earthly blood relationship, but through divine grace, because we have one Father in heaven, God. Although he is the proper Son of God, nevertheless, through the grace of adoption, all the saints are brothers because they are sons. Through the same grace they are also brothers to one another.

But no one from that society is the bridegroom of the others, nor can any of them be called so. Therefore it is a matter of the highest importance for the Church to recognize and confess Christ as the most excellent bridegroom of righteousness and wisdom.

Hence Jeremiah said: “And he is a man, and who will know him?” He is therefore a man, and from this it is shown that he is a brother and can be known. But what does “and who will know him?” mean? He is truly known as man, as brother, and as God; but it is exceedingly hidden how he is the bridegroom, because it is a great mystery. And yet he is the bridegroom, and she is the wife.

Thus John says in his Apocalypse: “The wedding of the Lamb has come” (Rev. 19:7). Of this the present passage says: “Those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast.” For in all these things there was one chosen Church, one beautiful dove, one lovely bride, whitened in the blood of her bridegroom.

While the foolish go too late to buy oil so that their lamps may shine, she enters the wedding feast with all her members. For above, when she came with the bridegroom whom these ten virgins went out to meet, she was already, in a wondrous way, bride and virgin; she had already received the dowry of her betrothal and the pledge, the Holy Spirit.

Then, having been betrothed with divine gifts, she now, having received the gift of immortality, enters joyfully into the immortal wedding feast—something she had not previously been able to do.

And the door was closed. If only we could taste with the palate of the heart what kind and how great the joy will be—how pleasant and blessed it will be for those who enter, and how bitter it will be for those left outside, since it says: “And the door was closed.” From then on no wretched person will enter it to become blessed; nor will anyone leave it afterward to be found outside.

For he strengthened the bars of the gates of that city (Ps. 147:13), blessed all within it, and set [an unspecified thing] throughout all its boundaries. There no one will hunger any longer, satisfied with the richness of grain, and every blessedness of eternal life will surround them.

At last the remaining virgins come, saying, “Lord, Lord, open to us.” 1039 Behold, as I had said, the foolish virgins who had been sent to purchase oil are not said to have bought or received any. Rather, this is passed over in silence, since there was no longer any time for buying; it is simply said that they come afterward, whereas he could have said, “Afterward they came, having received or purchased oil.” But because they had not found any, he appropriately kept silent about it, lest, when they had oil or were at the last adorning their lamps, he should say, “I do not know you, who you are.” For it is not written that they came with their lamps adorned; indeed, I do not know whether it could ever have happened that he would say, “I do not know you,” since God is charity and would never have rejected virgins full of charity, nor said that he did not know them. For the Lord knows only those who are his; those whom he rejects he certainly does not know, because they themselves were unwilling to know God as they ought. And therefore it is said, “If anyone does not know, he shall not be known.” For the Lord does not know workers of iniquity, nor does he approve the reprobate.

Therefore, although they are virgins, even according to the flesh, so that they boast of bodily purity as well as of the confession of faith, nevertheless, because they do not have the oil of the knowledge of God and of charity, it is punishment enough for them that they are not known by the bridegroom. And therefore, in this parable, the conclusion of the saying is this: “Keep watch, therefore, because you do not know the day or the hour.” This is what he had already said above: that each person should always be ready. For he wished us not to know the day of our departure for this purpose: that we might watch in spirit and be ready before the door is closed.

Behold how, concerning the end of the age, different parables are introduced. Above, angels are sent to gather the weeds from the field of the present Church and hand them over to be burned in the fire, while they gather the wheat into the Lord’s granary. Here, however, under another figure, ten virgins are set forth, five foolish and five wise. Under yet another form, five who cry, “Lord, Lord,” are rejected, while five with adorned lamps are admitted. Likewise in the other three parables previously mentioned, although more briefly, the meaning of future events is nevertheless varied in no unequal way.

Then, in this parable, which we shall explain shortly, a very different figure is formed and sketched, although it may seem clearer. In all these passages, different judgments are not introduced; rather, one day of terror and the cause of so great a separation are scarcely expressed in all of them. And therefore another comparison is now proposed, as it were, concerning those set over others, to whom the utterances of God have been entrusted, so that all of us together—rulers and people alike—since the day of judgment is unknown, may diligently prepare for ourselves the light and profit of good works, lest the Judge come while we are still unaware. Hence it follows:

“For just as a man going abroad called his servants and handed over to them his possessions.”

This is a new and unusual expression. For the logic of the speech does not seem to have been supplied, as though he had said in the customary manner, “Just as a man going away called his servants”; so also the Son of Man—or certainly, “so also I,” since he himself is the householder—who, after the resurrection, ascended victoriously to the Father, called his servants, that is, the apostles, and handed over to them the evangelical teaching and the money of the divine word.

Other copies, however, read: “For just as a man intending to go abroad called his servants.” He is said to go abroad because by his power he led our captivity away, as though, by going abroad, he had taken captivity captive. But it must be asked how he went away as though he were a stranger, when he himself promises his disciples concerning himself: “I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 18:20). And again: “Where two or three have been gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” And also in John: “There stands among you one whom you do not know” (John 1:26).

If, then, he is always present with all his own, how do the parables introduce him as going away or traveling abroad? Unless it is because, insofar as he is the only-begotten Son of God, the Word and Wisdom by nature of the Father, he is not enclosed within bodily limits, but is wholly present everywhere; in that nature he is never a stranger. He travels abroad, however, according to the dispensation of the body, and goes away when God, having become man, is placed in heaven at the right hand of the Father.

Nor do we thereby introduce two persons, as the Felician heresy wishes, or two Christs, or two sons. Rather, there is one Jesus Christ, one Son of God and man: according to his divinity, present everywhere; according to his humanity, ascending to the Father. Thus we do not separate the man from God, nor the Word from the flesh. For “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), since it is written in John: “Every spirit that separates Jesus is not from God” (1 John 4:3). Therefore God and man are one Christ.

Unity does not admit division or separation, and for this reason there is a great mystery in Christ. For the unity of his person is to be revered in him, while the property of each substance must be preserved. If every human being who is joined to the Lord is one spirit, how much more must that man whom Christ assumed according to the dispensation of the flesh not be separated from him who assumed him, nor be called another? For “the Word became flesh,” uniting it to himself by his power; and therefore there is one Christ, one Son of God, and one Son of man.

He, then, insofar as he is the Son of man, “going abroad,” gave five talents to one, two to another, and one to another, to each according to his own ability, and immediately went away. This is the proven money of the Word, concerning which it is said in the Psalms: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, proved upon the earth, purified sevenfold” (Psalm 11:7). For whatever is in it from the Holy Spirit has been thoroughly refined, and therefore everything in it is precious and excellent.

To each person, then, who observes the abilities of individuals, he distributed the money of the talents according to his own measure, and not according to merits, so that no one could excuse himself from gain on the grounds that he had no material with which to work. For the one who bestowed understanding also entrusted the talents according to their abilities—not giving more to one and less to another out of generosity or parsimony, but entrusting them freely to all according to the capacity of those who received them.

We read that the Apostle did the same when he gave milk to certain people who were not yet able to receive solid food. It should also be noted that in Greek, for the money he gave to each person, the word ἀργύριον (*argyrion*) is used, so that the utterances of God may be understood more pointedly as silver. For silver is called ἀργύριον in Greek.

Thus, concerning those who received from Christ the administration of the utterances of God, you will see that some received more and more divinely, while others received less, and, so to speak, did not understand even half of the business of these matters; while others possessed still less capacity. If you consider their differences, those who received the master’s money in order to administer it, you will see that the ability and effectiveness of mind of those to whom five talents were given was one thing, that of those to whom two were given another, and that of those who received only one another—because one person did not possess the measure of another.

The one who received one talent did not receive a contemptible gift. For it is a great thing even to have received one talent from so great a master; and therefore care must be taken lest it be received in vain. But when we consider the countless servants of the one who went away as a householder, and as a father, what is the reason that he sets forth only three classes among those to whom he distributed his possessions?

Perhaps he does this as an example of the good soil, concerning which he had already said above in the parables that, when it was sown, it produced fruit—one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, and another thirtyfold. Yet above, the one who produced thirtyfold is saved; here, however, the one who received one talent and hid it in the earth is condemned. Thus, although the figure in number is one, the deed is nevertheless different. The earth in which the seed is sown is one, but the cultivation is different, as is the unequal labor of those who put their hand to the plough.

Therefore, while he depicts the various forms of the parables with appropriate diversity, and brings out the brightness of their causes, specifying more fully the business of each person, here, because the subject is the talents entrusted to them, he proceeds down to one. For no one exists who has not received either five, or two, or one. Just as no one exists who does not possess either the five bodily senses, or understanding and activity, or at least reason, by which he is distinguished from animals and knows himself to be rational.

Nevertheless, no one is found without some talent for which he must render an account to the Lord, since he was created rational. And just as those who double for profit what they have received are blessed, so those are wretched and unhappy who plunge themselves into earthly activities and hide in the earth the talent they have received.

The wretched man is not wretched because he received one, but because, weighed down by earthly burdens, he choked in the earth what he had received and buried it in the carnal activities of the present life, so that it might bring no profit for heavenly life.

Hence many ask which of them received more: the one who received five talents, or the one who received two. For three kinds of talents are also said to exist. And therefore, not without reason, those are understood to be more perfect who received from God a more divine and loftier understanding and practice of the Scriptures, so that they may instruct themselves and others in divine matters.

For this reason, the account of the talents must not be referred only to number, but also to weight and quality, since it is more to receive two talents of gold than five of silver. The one who distributes his possessions to his servants knows the abilities of each person; and therefore each person must consider what and how much he has received.

Above all, this must first be understood: that a human being has nothing, in the whole range of things, inwardly or outwardly, that he has not received. And whatever there is in the five, or two, or one that he received, nothing more is required if he returns it doubled.

For, insofar as we can judge, it is a great thing if we are able to explain all the sensible things of the world that lie beneath the five senses, or transform them toward eternal and divine things, so that the senses themselves may burn more divinely within us, trained upon those things that are always the same, in order that from transitory and temporal things we may gain what is everlasting.

This is what it means to gain another five talents from the five talents: to work through them in temporal matters, so that, exercising ourselves through those same faculties and instructing others, we may raise ourselves to the heights of greater virtues, and thus return everything doubled, both in ourselves and in our neighbors, acquiring eternal things from temporal ones, and things that always remain from fragile and transitory things.

It should also be noted that he says: “He worked with them and gained another five.” Certainly, no one easily receives another person’s profit in virtue except from the gift of the grace whose seeds he has received—for example, the faithful person in faith, the wise person in wisdom, the rich person in the administration of his possessions, and so forth in everything else that he has received.

Therefore, as I said, let each person observe what and how much he has received—in skill, understanding, or any kind of natural ability.

Likewise, the one who had received two talents worked with them and gained another two. Thus he went away in the same way as the one who had received five.

But where did he go? Surely into a distant region, like the younger son? Certainly not. Where, then, did he go? He went to himself, having received grace, to the place where that younger son is also said to have returned. For the younger son had gone away, having wickedly poured himself out beyond himself, and had lost all the patrimony he had received from the Father.

This man, however, went into himself and exercised the gifts entrusted to him, lest he retain the grace bestowed upon him in vain. Hence Paul also gloried, saying: “And his grace toward me was not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:16).

This is the grace of faith and activity that he freely bestowed upon the whole human race, and the power of evangelical preaching granted to holy teachers. Each person received this grace, as it were, in the form of two talents, according to the measure of his faith—that is, according to his own ability.

For this is the incorruptible and eternal substance from the Father, the patrimony of Christ reserved for eternal heirs. Therefore, because he called two peoples to this grace, it is not inappropriate that he is said to have given five talents to one—namely, first to the one who believed from the Law.

Going forth from the Law, as I said, he went into himself and toward the grace of evangelical preaching that he had received. In this grace, rightly and in accordance with what I said above, he doubled everything that lies beneath the five senses: he referred to the glory of God the Father even those things that are presently perceived, and from these gained another five inwardly, so that the whole inward person, converted to God through these five senses, might enjoy eternal things.

Because five had been entrusted to him, when the Lord returned he presented ten from the five. For he doubled the things of the Law, when he learned to speak in the Church the five words of the New Testament—spiritual words, according to the Apostle Paul, in the inward person and beyond these five senses—more spiritually than ten thousand words. He also fulfilled the utterances of the five books of Moses by obeying through evangelical justification.

Likewise, the people of the Gentiles are signified by the one who received two. What they believed in the heart for justification, they confessed with the mouth for salvation. This people confesses Jesus Christ as God and man, the one mediator to whom two talents were entrusted in the confession of faith, so that it might have in God what it should understand and in man what it should imitate and do.

Accordingly, whatever it actively does through love, it transfers into contemplation. And whatever it contemplates through faith, it should refer intellectually in its entirety to him who is within it and whom it ought to love with its whole being.

Thus the two talents appropriately signify understanding and activity. These two come to profit, and one’s neighbor is loved perfectly, as commanded. Accordingly, by teaching another the very virtues that someone possesses in himself, he acquires and doubles them in the other, causing that person, together with the grace of God, to possess the virtue that he himself has possessed.

Therefore, according to either interpretation, the one who had five or the one who had two is said to have acquired no more than double. For no one can provide or teach anything more than what he knows and himself possesses.

For this reason every teacher ought to keep in mind the talents he has received, especially since he has put his hand to the plough—that is, to teaching the doctrine of Christ—lest he turn back or be found sluggish in teaching, when he ought to plough the souls with the word of doctrine insistently, in season and out of season. Then, after receiving the seed of the word, they too may bear fruit, doubling for themselves the knowledge of heavenly things from earthly perceptions, understanding the Creator from created things, acquiring incorporeal things from bodily ones, grasping invisible things from visible ones, and eternal things from temporal ones.

But the one who had received one went away, dug in the earth, and hid his master’s money. Some wish this servant to be the Jewish people, remaining in the Law, carnally foolish and understanding nothing spiritual. They say that he was unwilling to receive the power of evangelical preaching, but through envy hid the talent of the knowledge of Scripture in the earth, so that Christ would not be recognized in it; neither using it himself nor distributing it for others to use.

Although this meaning may seem evident, it is better understood of all who were created rational and do not wish to use reason, nor distribute it for gain, so that either they themselves or others may understand what they were created for.

Hence it is said: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand” (Psalm 48:13), because he did not use the talent of reason with sufficient diligence to know that he had been created in the image of God. Instead, he hid everything he had received in earthly activities and the pleasure of the flesh, preserving himself carnally while neglecting to fulfill God’s commandments.

For this reason another Evangelist says that he had tied up his master’s money in a napkin, because by living softly and delicately he had weakened the householder’s teaching through excessive fear. He tied up everything he had learned, as it were, in a napkin, when he entangled all his reason and prudence in carnal activities; concerning this it is said: “The prudence of the flesh is death” (Romans 8:6).

After a long time, the master of those servants came and settled accounts with them. The time from Christ’s ascension until his coming, when he will come for judgment, is therefore a long time. For the manner of the sacred Scriptures uses the past tense for the future, when the examination of judgment is displayed in the settling of accounts; for the business of the heavenly word will be demanded, and the return of the profit from the talent entrusted will be required.

Then the one who had received five talents came to the returning master and offered another five. What is yet to happen is spoken of as already accomplished. For with the Lord whatever is foretold is unchangeable, and therefore is rightly believed as though it had already happened.

“And the one who had received five talents came,” he says, “and offered another five, saying: ‘Lord, you handed over to me five talents; behold, I have gained another five.’”

The first therefore approached with great confidence, and as though of his own accord, because he had worked faithfully and gained profit. Indeed, the confidence produced by the profit, like assurance of good hope, made him dare to approach his master joyfully and devotedly and speak about the talent entrusted to him.

At once the master uttered to him a voice greatly desired by all good stewards: “Well done,” he said, “good and faithful servant. Because you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.”

Perhaps, then, this voice or meaning is like that which is also said concerning Abraham: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Galatians 3:6). Thus the faith of these servants was reckoned to them as righteousness, because they were faithful in a small matter.

Everything belonging to this life is small in comparison with future things, whether it is the teaching of the word, knowledge of the Scriptures, material resources, or anything else that can be turned to profit. For eternity surpasses all present goods, and the mystery of resurrection unto immortality surpasses everything that can come to an end.

If only we could know how great and how excellent are the things he means when he says, “Enter into the joy of your master,” we would certainly know how small are all the things we presently seem to possess or own. Since these things have been entrusted to us and commended to us for profit, whoever is faithful will receive what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Corinthians 2:9), things prepared for the faithful and for those who love God.

But it must be asked why there is one promise both to those who offer ten from five and to those who offer four from two. Both the one who received two and the one who received five return the money doubled. Both approach with confidence and devotion when they pass from this world to God. To both the master speaks one voice, gives one praise, and returns one reward.

To both, therefore, he says: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.” The same voice is the voice of exultation when he says, “Well done”; the same praise is given, since both are called good and faithful.

Therefore, because the same words are spoken to both, it is rightly asked whether perhaps the one who possessed lesser ability and exercised all of it as he ought will have nothing less with God than the one who received more and, possessing greater ability, acquired more.

I would not say this at all. For although the joy they receive is one, and their life and eternity are one, nevertheless, in that same joy and in that same life, each will receive his own rewards according to his own labor.

It is not as some wish, that there should be one brightness and one glory for everyone, in accordance with the saying that the one who had little did not lack and the one who had much did not have an excess. They wish to establish and demonstrate, from the commandment, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind,” that the reward of such love is the same for the person who has a lesser capacity of soul as for the one who has greater strength of heart and a more eminent soul.

Hence they say that this alone must be sought: that whatever a person has or has received from God, he should use wholly for the glory and praise of God. This is indeed a good exhortation and an abundant virtue of spirit. But whoever has labored more than all, according to Paul’s words, must confess in faith that each person will receive his reward according to his labor.

It should also be noted that the faithful servant is called good as well. If every faithful servant is called good through the gift of grace and participation in the good, how much more is Christ, God, good, since he is good essentially.

It is not as the Felician heresy slanders him, claiming that he did not allow himself to be called good because “no one is good except God alone”; and therefore, according to his humanity, that he is not true but adoptive or titular God. Rather, he wishes to show himself God precisely from this, because he was called “Good Teacher” and says: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God” (Mark 10:18).

He does not wish to be understood as good in the way these servants are called good, through an accidental good; rather, he is goodness essentially, because he is God. Therefore he was not afraid to be called good, as that man chatters; instead, by this he indicates that he is what God is, since in comparison with him no one is good.

But the one who had received the one talent came and said: “Lord, I know that you are a hard man, reaping where you did not sow and gathering where you did not scatter; and being afraid, I went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.”

He approaches through the resurrection, just as earlier he went away through freedom of choice—not so that he might labor with the grace he had received, but so that he might rest in his own sloth and torpor, abusing what was his. And now he approaches not devotedly and humbly asking pardon, but as an ungrateful accuser, reproaching the one whom he ought to have confessed to be kind. Thus, although he was in the filth of sin, he became still filthier, in accordance with the prophetic saying, “to make excuses for sins” (Psalm 140:4).

He ought to have confessed his sloth and inactivity and prayed to the householder; instead, by accusing him, he calls the master harsh. He claims that he acted with prudent judgment, lest, while seeking monetary profits, he should perhaps also be endangered by the talent entrusted to him.

For the nature of present things does not possess what he imputes to the master when he says, “You reap where you did not sow.” You will never find a harvest without seed, nor can anything be gathered that has not been scattered. But because the whole speech is parabolic, we must receive it figuratively.

We have said that some understand this servant to be the people who, from the Law, were not ignorant of the Lord’s coming, envied the salvation of the Gentiles, and remained in unbelief. They knew that the fruits of righteousness would be reaped where the Law had not been sown, and gathered from Gentiles who were not descended from Abraham’s stock.

For this reason he calls him harsh, since he demands from the Law something other than the carnal meaning that they preserve according to the letter, as though buried in the earth, while he is going to gather among the Gentiles without scattering and reap without sowing.

Thus, even while he tries to excuse himself, he is shown to be guilty without pardon, because he concealed the preaching entrusted to him or buried the talent beneath the coverings of the letter, obscured by the figures of things.

Although this meaning may seem clearer, as I said, the saying is better understood as applying to all who received human reason, so that, placed in the dignity of rationality, they might understand and transfer themselves through reason into fellowship with the angels. Otherwise, by badly preserving the talent of reason, they would be compared with foolish beasts and become like them.

Nevertheless, even if this is to be understood of all who received human reason, special care must be taken concerning those who possess the money of the word and hold a place of governance, because, according to the Apostle, woe hangs over them unless they preach and distribute to their fellow servants the money of their master entrusted to them for distribution.

Thus this servant is not improperly numbered among believers. For no believer is found who has not received from the Lord the talent entrusted to him, although not all act faithfully in the faith. For they either wish to remain hidden in their own pleasures, or at least to lie concealed so that it may not be known what they have received.

Therefore, although they may seem to preserve the talent they possess, they add no work, do not trade for the profit of their master, and do not act confidently with what they received. In this way they benefit neither themselves nor others so as to acquire eternal life.

Those who are like this, then, although for their own ruin they may seem to possess fear of the Lord and to understand that he is severe and implacable toward sinners, nevertheless, because they are oppressed by great sluggishness, they grow torpid in their laziness. They preserve the talent, as it were, not for profit but for themselves, so that everything they live may benefit them only in the present.

1049 But his master answered and said to him: “Wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I did not sow and gather where I did not scatter,” and so forth.

The good master repeats some of the things that the wicked servant had alleged, but keeps silent about others. He does not admit that he is harsh, as the servant supposed when he accused him. For it is not from his nature that he should be called severe or harsh; rather, the servant abused God’s mercy for negligence and not for his own conversion, as the Apostle says: “See, therefore, the kindness and severity of God” (Romans 11:22)—severity toward those who fell, but kindness toward you.

Therefore let no one be secure and say that God does not care—not only about the sins of those who transgress, but even about the grace entrusted to them, if they have not worked with it.

As for the remaining words, he seems to have agreed that he reaps where he did not sow and gathers where he did not scatter. But it must be asked how this is to be understood according to the present meaning.

For just as no one has anything that he has not received, so no one works except with what he has received. With that, perhaps, he works the fruit of righteousness in the present, a fruit that the righteous person will reap for eternal life. For he has sown in the Spirit, from whom he will receive greater profits.

When these profits are reaped by the righteous, the one whose possession the righteous person himself is reaps them. The righteous person has distributed and given, and has perhaps sown his substance—or the money of the word—among the poor and needy. But the Lord gathers everything in his members, as though into himself, when he counts as given to himself whatever has been faithfully distributed to his poor.

Hence in another parable he will say: “As long as you did it for one of these least of mine, you did it for me” (Matthew 25:40).

The reason he calls him wicked, however, is plainly evident: he makes an accusation against the master out of his own fault. He calls him lazy because he was unwilling to double the talent entrusted to him, so that he might be condemned in one respect for pride and in another for negligence.

Accordingly, he receives an answer suited to him, as though the master were saying: “Since you knew me to be cruel and harsh, and to pursue other things that I had not given, reaping where I had not sown, why did such a thought not inspire fear in you? For you knew that I would diligently demand not only those things, but also my money—or silver—given to the money-changers.”

For, as I said, the Greek word ἀργύριον (*argyrion*) signifies both. Therefore the whole of this parable is understood of the money of the divine word and the teaching of preaching, which is the administration of the Gospel and the speech of the utterances of God.

This money ought to have been given to money-changers and bankers—that is, to holy teachers in the individual churches, just as the apostles appointed presbyters and bishops throughout the individual provinces—or to all believers who, handing on the divine mysteries, could double their Lord’s money, skillfully engraving the image of the supreme King in the hearts of each person, as though in coins, and returning everything with interest.

Thus whatever they had learned in word they would fulfill in deed, and from earthly and perishable things would gain heavenly and eternal things for themselves and others.

“Take the talent from him,” he says, “and give it to the one who made ten talents.”

According to the earlier interpretation, the meaning is easy. All the mysteries of the divine word were taken away from the Jews, who did not receive Christ, and were entrusted to the apostles and apostolic men who believed from the Jews, and to those who labored most in the word.

We should understand that, although the Lord’s joy is equal in the labor of both for the faithful and good, and is given to all who return ten talents from five or four from two, nevertheless a greater reward is owed to the one who has labored more with the Lord’s money, as divine Scripture teaches.

It is not as some wish, claiming that the one who received more should have nothing more, nor the one who labored little anything less, provided only that each loves with his whole being and doubles what he received.

Although he reaps among the Gentiles, where he did not sow the words of the Law, and gathers them to the faith where he did not scatter them, the reward is nevertheless not granted without the merit of faith. For just as each person labors from no other source than the gift of God and the talent entrusted to him, so he is rewarded only according to his labor and the abundance of grace.

For to everyone who has, more will be given, and he will have abundance; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away. For whoever does not possess a correct and complete faith will also lose the other virtues which he seemed to have. Elegantly, therefore, he says “what he seemed [Col. 0856C] to have,” because whatever is without faith is not virtue but sin. What he seemed to have is therefore taken away from him when it is made clear in the examination of God’s judgment that what he had did not proceed from faith, by which the ungodly person is justified and in which the righteous person lives. And this is what “it will be taken away from him” means: his work is not reckoned to him as righteousness, nor is the reward of righteousness assigned to him in recompense.

For even when many naturally possess considerable mental ability and a sharp, prudent intellect, if through negligence they corrupt the good of nature by indolence, such people lose the reward of nature that had been promised to them; and they sometimes see it pass to others who, through great labor and diligence, make up for what nature had given them in lesser measure. Although this saying does not seem sufficiently clear—how, in whatever manner, the talent that the evil servant had received is taken away from him, or how it is given to another who had possessed ten talents, more or fewer, so that he may have this also in addition to what he had acquired—it is nevertheless possible to understand it in terms of the office of the one who rewards: the person who presently has may abound, since it is easy for a faithful and good servant to grow rich through increase, either through an increase of generosity or through the abundance produced by labor. But I do not see how, from the one who does not have, though he seemed to have, what he did not have can be taken away; nor how something that does not exist can be given to anyone, since in the one who had possessed it, it has been emptied out.

Unless perhaps it is to be understood in this way: that for those who possess the grace of the Gospel, the honor of the Law is also added on account of the faith of Christ, together with the gain of the Gospel; whereas from the useless servant, who does not possess faith in Christ nor the mysteries of the Law, but seemed to have them, these are taken away; the letter that kills, in which he boasted that he possessed, is also taken away; the honor of the Law and all its superstitious observance are also taken away. But how this saying applies more generally to those who are sluggish and negligent in the faith of Christ must be examined with more diligent inquiry, since all such people are represented in this servant.

Sometimes, however, I admit that God, whose divinity is powerful and effective, sharper than any sword (Hebr. IV, 12), is able to cut away from him and take away the sufficiency he possesses—the sufficiency by which he pretends to be something while living idly and indulging in the pleasures of the flesh—and to give grace and the rewards of merit to one who, like Paul and many of the saints, has contributed more than he had received, through labor and diligence, beyond the talents assigned to him by God’s commandments; for he received freely even this very ability to do so.

“Take the talent away from him,” he says, “and give it to the one who has ten talents”: that is, take away from the one who possessed faith what he seemed to have, although it was not faith, because without works it was dead in itself (Jac. II, 26). This faith, and the grace of faith, is given to the one who has it, and he will abound in that same grace of faith by working daily; he will be found firmer and more abundant in what he possesses. Likewise, one who has received from nature, as I said, mental ability and intellect, when he exercises it in the faith of Christ, receives that same gift twofold; through God’s grace he becomes more abundant [Col. 0857B] and stronger in the very thing he possessed. And if someone is perfect in understanding, according to Solomon, among the children of men, but the grace and wisdom of God are absent from him, he will be regarded as nothing. The same must be understood of every talent, skill, and virtue.

Therefore, if we wish what we possess from God to remain ours, let us act so that a more perfect virtue may be given to us, and so that what is perfected by God’s grace may abound in us; otherwise it may be taken away from us and given to another, and another may receive our place, as we read in the Apocalypse, if our lampstand is moved from its place. For this reason, let us act with every diligence and constant earnestness, so that we may both retain what we receive and acquire from it something else in which we may abound.

“But throw the useless servant into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” We have already spoken above about this saying; nevertheless, because it is exceedingly fearful, we must consider what is blamed in the person who is not said to have done anything evil, although he is called evil, but because he was lazy and useless. Likewise, the five foolish virgins above are rejected for no other reason than that they did not take oil with them. This servant too is called useless because he did not offer his master any profit from the talent, but placed it entirely in a cloth—that is, in the flesh. And for this reason he was sent by the torturers into the outer darkness, because he too did not have God, the light, within himself. God is eternal light; and because he is not illumined by God, he is outside God—not locally, certainly, but under punishment. For in God there are no darknesses at all, since he is wholly light. Therefore this evil servant, when he is rejected by him, is sent into the [Col. 0858A] outer darkness. For if these darknesses were not outside God, they would nowhere and never be darknesses.

“When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty, and all the nations will be gathered before him,” and so forth.

This parable, unless it is more carefully examined and worked through, appears very clear, a simple and open narrative, as though exhorting people to perform acts of human kindness, to give alms, and to bestow grace; condemning all inhumanity in a few words and reproving every withholding of pious action. Therefore, since to many it seems to be a simple narrative, and to many it is the more obscure the more terrifying it is, we must ask what difficulty of mysteries it contains. This is especially necessary because there are those who think that nothing else is to be sought in this discourse than an exhortation to humanity and generosity, just as in the parable we have recently discussed they see nothing else than the dispensation of the word and the talent of preaching.

No one doubts that this passage speaks of the final coming: the Son of Man, who is also the Son of God, who was taken up into the glory of the Father—a glory in which he was previously and always present—will return here just as he departed, for judgment, in his own appearance and beauty, so that his body will be present and will appear in the glory of eternal incorruption. He will not merely be transformed before three disciples, as he was shown on the mountain, but glorified in the glory of God the Father [Col. 0858C] before all the nations gathered before him through the resurrection of the flesh, when it will appear that he was judged in the world so that he himself might judge the world.

He will sit as judge upon the throne of his majesty, and then he will separate the sheep from the goats—that is, the good from the evil. Consider for yourself, reader, all the preceding parables, and understand how mystically they were spoken. The angels have already gathered all the weeds and separated them from the wheat. The good fish have already been gathered into vessels, and the bad have been thrown out. The foolish virgins have already been rejected. The useless and evil servant has already been sent into the outer darkness, along with the other matters that would take too long to enumerate.

What, then, is the meaning of the fact that now, at the end, he himself is introduced and seated as judge upon the throne of his majesty, and that all the nations are placed before him, whom he himself judges and separates, as a shepherd, dividing the sheep from the goats? He himself is the good shepherd who says: “Know mine, and mine know me” (Joan. X, 14). Those whom he himself recognizes as his own he will set at his right hand; all the rest he will reject in judgment and assign among the goats at his left. Therefore, in this final examination and in this last of all the parables, he introduces no person other than himself, to show how powerful and discerning he is: he who was to be judged for all would himself come again to judge.

For this reason he put forward this last parable so that it would be continuous with his Passion, and so that everyone might attend simultaneously to these two judgments. How justly and appropriately the powerful Son of Man will come to judgment, he who was judged so humbly and contemptibly, and unjustly, on behalf of all. Since he endured an undeserved death for all, he powerfully makes clear that he did so because he willed it. He shows that he is king and judge of all ages before all the nations are gathered to be judged concerning all those things for which he himself endured so much.

But we must ask whether “all the nations” means all the nations that existed throughout all the generations of the age, or only those that will still be in the flesh at the consummation of the age, or only those who believed the Gospel of Christ, from whom the sheep will be separated from the goats. For, as it is sung in the Psalm: “The ungodly shall not rise in judgment” (Psal. I, 5). Or does it also concern those who received the faith of Christ?

As far as the simple text of the narrative is concerned, it seems ambiguous whether he speaks of all or not all, especially since among those who will be at the right hand no other cause is praised, nor are they introduced into the kingdom prepared long ago for any other reason, than the sole grace of human kindness and generosity in almsgiving. Nor is any other cause condemned in those who will be at the left, or are they assigned to the fire, except their inhumanity and the fact that they did not refresh the members of Christ with their good works.

What, then, if some people were humane and generous with the goods they possessed? If they were negligent in the other virtues, or perhaps committed crimes, will they immediately receive these promised things? Or if others were not devoted to such services, but fulfilled other and greater virtues, will they immediately be cursed [Col. 0859C] and altogether condemned to eternal fire with the devil?

Therefore, insofar as it pertains to sound understanding and the teaching of truth, this passage must be examined with prudent consideration, so that it may agree with catholic instruction. For it cannot be understood in any other way than Christ the Truth foretold, nor could he preach or teach anything that did not entirely accord with the ordinances of the holy Scriptures. Accordingly, their humanity is not praised merely because it was generous, but because it was for Christ; as he himself says, it was such and so great through faith and love of Christ that it seems to have been offered to no one other than Christ himself, because it was done for his love.

Otherwise, according to the Apostle (I Cor. XIII, 3), if all one’s possessions are distributed as food for the poor, and one hands over one’s body so as to be burned, but does not have love, it profits nothing. Therefore, this humanity and kindness, which is rewarded with so great a recompense, was the fulfillment of love; and love is the infusion of the Holy Spirit. Thus, even if these people did not leave all their possessions in the world for love, they nevertheless devotedly offered themselves and what they had to the Lord. Hence it is not the amount of what is given that is rewarded so much as its fruit. According to the Apostle, the fruit of what is given is love, and love covers a multitude of sins (Jac. V, 20). Therefore, where the love of God, poured out through the Holy Spirit, works generously, the integrity of the virtues is preserved.

As for the throne of Christ’s glory, when he sits upon the throne of his majesty: although the Son of Man is said to sit, there will not be some bodily seat there, since thrones are also said to have been set in that judgment, and Daniel sees books opened. In these books, all the deeds of mortals are held written down, and the names of all who gave themselves in baptism to the service of Christ are recited, together with how they contended in the struggle, as though everything were preserved in the annals of the supreme King.

Hence we read in the Apocalypse that one seated was seen sitting on a throne, and around the throne twenty-four seats were placed (Apoc. IV, 4), where the king, coming to judgment with his senators, will sit. Therefore, whoever wishes to understand all these things carefully must be filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, since they are spiritual; no one comprehends spiritual things except in the Spirit.

For we read that thrones and dominions are ranks of angels. We also read that the Church of Christ is called the seat of his majesty. Accordingly, either the angels themselves are called seats in this passage, and no believer doubts that the Son of Man presides over them; or certainly the more perfect saints are meant, concerning whom it is sung in the Psalm: “For there the seats sat in judgment, seats over the house of David” (Psal. CXXI, 5). Therefore the King of the ages, God the Word who became flesh (Joan. I, 14), the Son of Man, will sit upon such a throne of glory with all his saints, to whom he promised, saying: “You who have left everything and followed me will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luc. XXII, 30).

“And then all the nations will be gathered before him.”

I have already spoken above about Christ’s coming to earth, saying that he will descend for judgment to the place where he was judged according to the flesh. I am not so ignorant as to think that there is any single place capable of containing within one human view—not to mention all the ranks of angels who will come with him to judgment—even all the nations that are to be gathered before the throne of his majesty.

And yet it is truly said that all the nations will be gathered before him when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty. There is no doubt that this same Son of Man will be in one place. But if he will be in one place, how will those whom one place cannot contain be gathered before him? The nations themselves, whatever nations are gathered, will truly be local and will be gathered before the face of the Son of Man, as the Gospel says.

They will be gathered through the resurrection of the flesh from the four winds of heaven, all released from every worldly duty and from every activity of the flesh. They are therefore truly said to be gathered, because they will no longer be dispersed in different directions, nor wandering as though possessing free will, but all will be present before one judge.

I say this, brothers, because of those who are troubled by such matters. Perhaps, if I were entirely silent, the difficulty of speaking would generate still more difficult questions concerning such a great and terrible examination. Therefore, first of all, let us think of the Son of Man as coming to judgment in such a way that he is understood and believed to be God—not made threefold or doubled into two, but understood by all of us as one Christ, God and man.

Accordingly, wherever God-man is present—for he is everywhere—let Christ be understood to be wholly present everywhere. In this way all the nations can be gathered before the Son of Man, who descended from heaven, because while the Son of Man was saying these things, according to his own word he was already in heaven. Since the person of Christ is thus undivided, it is not absurd to believe that all the nations will be gathered before him. For he is nowhere absent, nor is there any place where Christ is not; therefore all will be before him.

He must not, then, be divided. For “whoever divides Jesus is the antichrist.” At his coming there will be such a manifestation according to his humanity that not only will none of the righteous, but not even any sinner, be unaware that Christ has come to judgment, when he will go forth like lightning from the East and appear as far as the West.

Then all the sinners of the earth will recognize their own offenses, and the righteous will clearly see the seeds of their virtues and to what end those virtues brought them. Perhaps this is what he means when he says: “All the nations will be gathered before him.”

For if, even now, when not everyone recognizes Christ as he is, and even the elect do not openly recognize him except insofar as they recognize him in faith, people nevertheless enter to him and come before his sight when they possess knowledge of him and are at least illumined through faith—as we sing in the Psalm: “Enter into his presence with rejoicing” (Psal. XCIX, 2)—how much more rightly can all the nations be said to be gathered and set before him when he will be manifest to all, good and evil, faithful and unbelieving alike.

He will be present before the eyes of their minds, no longer discovered through the inquiry of faith or of any human diligence, but manifested through the appearance of his flesh so openly that no one will be unaware that he is the Christ, and no one will doubt that he is God.

Accordingly, perhaps in this sense, when the Son of God and Son of Man comes in his glory, he will not appear in one place and fail to appear in another, but, as he has deigned to show through the radiance of his manifestation, he will be visible. Therefore, manifest everywhere to all, he himself will be before everyone’s sight, all will be everywhere before him, and each person will be manifest in his presence.

Nevertheless, his bodily appearance will in some manner be known and manifest—either according to the way he shone on the mountain, or according to the way he was visible after the resurrection. “They will see him whom they pierced, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him.”

Then, by contrast, the righteous will rejoice at the great splendor of the most loving judge and at the great glory of his majesty. Yet that vision will not be the vision of him in the form of God, nor will it yet be the reception of the kingdom. But because, in the examination of so great a judge, no one will boast that he has a pure heart, in the glory of his manifestation he will illumine the hearts of those who served him, so that each may understand his own works, and so that even the wicked may possess in their consciences what they have done. This is what it means to separate the good from the evil, and for the books to be opened: the consciences of each will be naked and manifest.

For this reason he himself also says through the Prophet: “Behold, I am coming upon their thoughts, to gather them.” And the Apostle Paul says that the thoughts of those who accuse or excuse will be present for each person on the day when God judges the hidden things of human beings.

For surely it belongs to the good Shepherd to know his own sheep, so that he may rescue them from among the evil, according to what Ezekiel says: “Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I myself will seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock, on the day when he is among his scattered sheep. Thus I will visit my sheep and deliver them from all the places in which they had been scattered, on the day of cloud and darkness” (Ezech. XXXIV, 12). This means the present time, when there is scarcely any distinction between the good and the evil, until the shepherd himself comes, when he is to sit upon the throne of his majesty. Then what is now said through the prophet will be fulfilled: he will separate them from the peoples and nations [Col. 0862B], gather them, and place them at his right hand.

Therefore the holy Evangelist set this last of all the parables not in the person of another—as above, where he says, “The angels will go out and separate the evil from among the righteous”—but solely in the person of him who says: “I am the good shepherd; I know mine, and mine know me” (Joan. X, 14). The angels will indeed gather the evil from among the righteous; but Christ himself, because he is the good shepherd, will personally seek out and visit his sheep, since no one else has the task of examining the consciences of individuals.

“And he will set the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left.” Appropriately, therefore, foreseeing that after two days he was to celebrate the Passover and then be handed over to the cross, mocked by human beings, and given vinegar and gall to drink, he first sets forth the glory of the triumphant one and the judgment of eternal recompense, so that he might compensate for the scandals that were to follow with the promise of a reward and lift the spirits of the disciples from the sorrow of so great a temptation.

As for the statement that he will set the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left, understand it according to this passage: “The heart of the wise is at his right hand, and the heart of the fool at his left” (Eccle. X, 2). No one has his heart anywhere other than in the part of the body where it is naturally placed in everyone. But because Christ’s sheep were wise, they chose to place their hearts at the right hand, because the Lord knows the ways that are at the right hand. The foolish, or senseless, held to the left, and placed their hearts there. Therefore each flock is rightly assigned to the side it chose to occupy through its works.

Hence the Lord says in this same Gospel: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing.” It should also be noted that he will set the sheep at his right hand, but the goats only at his left—not at his own left, because the ways and works of the left do not belong to him who has nothing left in himself. He therefore speaks in the plural of the right hands and left hands, because the actions of both sides are many.

Accordingly, we must not direct our attention to a place, as though to a physical location, but to the merits and distinctions of the individual sides. Otherwise, according to the human meaning of right and left, there is no space capable of containing the respective groups of sheep and goats. All these matters must therefore be considered at a higher level, according to the insight of the mind.

The sheep, therefore, are called the elect because of their innocence. From this it is understood that he does not reward the righteous, as some suppose, solely because of their humanity, but also because of their blameless life, so that they are rightly called sheep. For this is the perfection of human life, as the prophet teaches: to turn away from evil and do good.

Their works are rightly praised because they did good works—not for just anyone, but because they served Christ. And because they lived innocently, they are not undeservedly called sheep.

The reprobate, however, are not sheep, nor are they goats that are offered in sacrifices and nourish their young, goats that, after being shorn, ascend from the washing, among which none is found barren. Rather, they are called goats, an animal that is exceedingly lustful and wanton, always rushing toward intercourse. Therefore the reprobate, because they have always pursued luxury and the pleasure of the flesh, are rightly called goats; their sterility in good works is condemned.

And because they pursued the pleasures of the world in luxury and did not wish to redeem themselves through their own good and just works, they are condemned on both counts by God’s just judgment. Hence what follows.

“Then the King will say to those who are at his right hand: Come, you blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

In a marvelous way, therefore, the form of the reigning king is introduced, so that none of the disciples may be ashamed of the disgrace of the cross. He calls them blessed of his Father because of the eminence of the divine blessing by which immense glory is bestowed upon them. They are called blessed by the Lord who made heaven and earth (Psal. CXIII, 15), and there is no greater blessing than that by which they are blessed by the Father through the Son.

Following this rule of faith, the Apostle Paul said: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ Jesus in the heavenly places” (Ephes. I, 3). Therefore, because the Father blesses his elect not with just any blessing, but with every spiritual blessing in Christ, he rightly calls those whom he himself has chosen and invites to receive the kingdom “the blessed of his Father.”

He calls those who have followed him through faith and love, so that they may pass over to the vision of eternal reality; because they lived with God in the world, they may become closer to him and co-heirs in the kingdom through contemplation of the whole Trinity.

Beware, I ask you, reader, always of the snares of heretics, who say that he called them here “the blessed of God the Father” in order to distinguish them from those who are indeed blessed, but blessed through Christ at a much lower level—as though anyone who is called blessed could remain outside this blessing. The catholic faith does not accept this at all, just as no one is outside that curse which the reprobate will hear.

Accordingly, there will be only two groups and two cities, gathered from the beginning of the age. One will receive only the children of blessing; the other will receive those of the curse.

“Receive,” he says, “the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” Moreover, where the Latin has a constitutione mundi, “from the foundation of the world,” the Greek has ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, that is, “from the laying down” or “casting down of the world.” For this word does not simply mean “constitution”; more significantly, it indicates what is cast down into foundations and sent into a lower place from above, or the moment when something begins.

Thus those who lay the first foundations of houses are said to have καταβεβληκέναι, that is, “to have cast down the beginnings,” because, as one of the Greeks says, the expression is broader and the language more fortunate. Therefore the word καταβολή rightly seems to signify the beginning of a foundation. You will not find this word used of the creation of angels, archangels, or the other spiritual beings, but only of the beginning of the world or the establishment of bodily things.

The kingdom of the saints is therefore proclaimed as having been prepared from the foundation, or origin, of the world. Nor is this strange, since the saints themselves are said to have been foreknown by the Lord and predestined by the Apostle before the foundation of the world; in that kingdom many dwellings are already prepared.

The kingdom prepared from the origin of the world already contains within itself the dwellings that the Lord Jesus went to prepare when he ascended into heaven [Col. 0864B]—and they were not prepared in any other way than they already were. For one comes to them only through faith. Thus they must be prepared in the faith of the predestined, just as they already exist in that heavenly kingdom.

“For I was hungry, and you gave me food.”

A great unity of Christ and the Church, and a great mystery, is commended in this passage. Concerning it the Apostle says: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24), that is, Christ and the Church, so that he is the head and all the elect are members of one body under one head.

Accordingly, wherever so great a mystery is commended, the mind must awaken, so that it may live in the one body of Christ in such a way that it recognizes itself to be a member of Christ. And just as the body has built up each of its individual members, so each person must be built up honorably in his own place, in a manner fitting his head, and so that, in order to live in the body [Col. 0864C] of Christ, he may be governed by the Spirit of God.

For whoever is led by the Spirit of God is a child of God, a brother of Christ, and lives in the body of Christ. In these people such unity is commended here by the Lord that whatever one does for one of them, he declares, in a marvelous way, to have been done wholly for himself. He magnifies the gift of the work done for him, so that the deed may be commended more gloriously.

Hence he says: “For I was hungry, and you gave me food. I was thirsty, and you gave me drink,” and so forth—all of which appear to be acts of human kindness. But, as I said, we must not understand this as though, with all the other virtues set aside and crimes admitted, only one kind of righteousness were rewarded in them, as some think.

For it is absurd to understand that those who are so rewarded possessed no other virtue deserving reward than the sharing of human kindness. But because, as I said, the persons represented are those who, while possessing worldly goods, did not leave everything that belongs to the world, it was right that they should be praised more especially for having served the Lord with great devotion in those matters by which they were still, as it were, bound to the world.

The Apostle also commends this in his Epistle to the Corinthians, speaking to those who used their own possessions: “Let your abundance supply their need” (II Cor. VIII, 14–15). That is, let the abundance of those who have left their possessions for Christ be a supplement to your need, so that equality may be achieved, as it is written: “He who gathered much did not have too much, and he who gathered little did not have too little.”

He says this only to the faithful and devoted, whom he praises as rich in many virtues. Therefore, in all things we must strive both that those who possess these things should practice them and that they should not omit the other foundations of virtue, without which these accomplish little or nothing.

It should therefore be understood that just as these things alone do not suffice to obtain the eternal inheritance, so it is not possible to fulfill all the others in such a way that we never do anything against God’s commandment, because “we all offend in many things” (Jac. III, 2). Accordingly, these deeds that are enumerated must be performed in such a way that other bodily benefits also are not neglected toward anyone; that is, in addition, we must by every possible means and to the fullest extent of our ability not omit spiritual benefits.

For whether a person does good in this way or that, so that either the body is refreshed with bodily food or the soul with spiritual food, he certainly feeds and refreshes God in his members. For just as Christ’s food is to do the will of the Father, so his food and drink is that, for love of him, his members should mutually support and nourish one another in the will of God.

Therefore, in these matters the members of Christ must necessarily serve one another, so that the abundance of those who possess the things of the world may supply the need of the saints, and so that the riches of those who possess the spiritual substance of the Word may also be a supplement to the merits of these others.

Hence everyone must certainly believe that whatever a person sows, that he will also reap (Galat. VI, 7). When these matters have been enumerated, ...

Then the righteous will answer: “Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you; thirsty, and give you drink? [Col. 0865C] When did we see you as a stranger and take you in?”—and so forth. Now, if some rational explanation were intended to be understood in their words at that judgment, the righteous certainly could not have forgotten, perhaps at that moment, what they had read, or what they had done for his sake toward God’s elect. Just as today no one is unaware that whatever he gives to Christ’s poor he renders to God.

But this effect of their words is either caused by profound humility or is the stupor of great astonishment: how could they have seen him whom they behold in such glory and majesty, if they had ever been able to see him hungry or thirsty? Or, if I may put it this way, it is the result of the excessive stupor and astonishment of disbelief that they should ever have seen him sick, or that they could have ministered worthily to one so great, when he was placed in prison or sick, [Col. 0865D] or have come to him. Hence, as I said, if they proclaim themselves unworthy out of humility, they do so more by the feeling of the mind than by the cry of the voice.

But he himself, as though pious and merciful, raises them up, gently caressing and encouraging them, and wishes to show them the compassion of his kinship. He says: “Amen, I say to you, insofar as you did it to one of these least of my brothers, you did it to me.” He plainly declares that they had been among his own, indeed that they had ministered everything to himself more than to them; and, so to speak, that they had been so completely united with him that in one and the same deed he says that they had done everything both for himself and for them. Thus he also plainly says: “Insofar as you did it to one of these least, you did it to me.” He testifies that they had fed him, given him drink, done it for him, and come to him.

Nevertheless, this is in the form in which he is properly the Son of Man, while in that one and the same person he is equally the Son of God and the son of man. Since he is singularly the Truth, he cannot lie. Therefore we must believe that he receives all these things in his members as though in himself; this is shown most clearly in many passages of Scripture, as in the saying: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever receives you receives me indeed” (Luke 10:16). Likewise, from heaven he said to Saul: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9). And there are many other such passages. In all of these, when he says “to me” or “me,” he undoubtedly wishes it to be understood that what is done for him and that those who come to him are understood with reference to his members.

Nevertheless, we must consider that he is speaking with those who will be on the right or on the left. The people of whom he speaks are the least: those to whom the people on the right did good, or to whom those on the left did not do good, and therefore did not do it to Christ the Son of Man. Who they are who are called “the least,” and yet, because they are brothers, will be great and may be received as Christ, is a question by no means irrelevant.

In fact, since at that judgment there will be no others than those who are on the right or on the left, and since these people did the deeds that are praised, or failed to do the deeds that are condemned, he nevertheless says demonstratively: “Insofar as you did it,” or “did not do it,” “to one of these least of my brothers.” Hence the meaning is clear: those of whom he speaks will be present, and he seems to point toward them with his finger. For this reason they too will be at the same judgment with the Lord—not, as I think, in order to be judged, but in order to judge: those who left everything of theirs, even themselves, for Christ. These were judged in the world for Christ, and therefore they themselves, as was promised in this very Gospel, will judge others. They themselves were in hunger and thirst, as Paul enumerates (2 Cor. 11:17). They were in cold and nakedness; these people fed them from their just labors and covered their nakedness. They came to those who had been placed in prison for Christ’s name and ministered to them; they also supported them in sickness.

Therefore it does not seem to me that this was said generally of all the poor, but of those whom the Apostle calls Christ’s poor, who are also called blessed because they are poor. To them, extending his hand above, he said: “These are my brothers and my mother, those who do the will of my Father” (Mark 3:33–34). Therefore the will of the Father is Christ’s food and drink.

Otherwise, our understanding would be free to suppose that Christ is fed in every poor person when hungry, given drink when thirsty, received under a roof when a stranger, clothed when naked, visited when sick, and comforted in prison by those who console him—unless their identification were so evident that he does not allow us to look elsewhere than toward those whom he points out as though with a finger, whom he calls his brothers, although they are the least. They are called least not in comparison with those whom he rewards on their account, but in comparison with himself.

Or they are called least because they will be exceedingly gentle and humble. Since they will be exceptional, perhaps even he himself will be least in comparison with all. Hence elsewhere he says: “I confess to you, Lord Father, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10:21).

Yet we do not repeat these matters in order to deny that whatever good anyone has done, or to whomever anyone has done it in the name of righteousness, he ought not to lose the reward of the righteous. Rather, we say this so that those who belong more closely to the household of faith may always be chosen, and those who labor in the word of God and embody Christ’s discipline in themselves may be honored more greatly with every human service. For a greater reward is acquired through such people, and the religion of Christ is honored.

Then he will say also to those who will be on the left: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels,” and so forth.
