You will therefore nowhere find that he said that the goats stood “at his left” or “at his own left,” but only “on the left.” First, in relation to God, as I said, there is nothing sinister. Second, what is on the left does not belong to God, but to those who placed themselves on the left through their own wickedness, unwilling to follow the footsteps of those on the right.

That he first rewards those who are on the right is the goodness of God the Savior, because he always prefers to grant benefits freely rather than repay sinners with punishment, even when punishment is deserved. He is therefore an imitator of the Father; for the Father prefers to bless those whom he placed on the right rather than curse those whom their own iniquity caused to stand on the left.

For this reason he does not say: “Depart from me, accursed ones of my Father,” since the Father is rather the giver of blessing, while each person is the author of his own curse when he does deeds deserving of curses.

And we must note that he says: “Depart from me.” He orders them to depart from himself, with whom, because he is “the mediator of God and human beings” (1 Tim. 2:5), they seemed to have been joined through the mysteries of the new birth. But because they had first withdrawn from him so as not to cling to him in faith and works, he decrees by his just judgment that they should go into the eternal fire. For they had previously fallen into that fire themselves when, living in the world without repentance, they loved the world more than God.

Nor is it believed that only their inhumanity is condemned, any more than only the generosity of those who will be on the right is rewarded. Rather, because they misused the things of the world in pride, handed themselves over to their desires, served their own luxuries and pleasures, and were unwilling to render to God what would redeem them, it is entirely reasonable that, as though the whole of iniquity were condemned at its root, inhumanity alone is censured and their refusal of kindness to their brothers is condemned.

As for the eternal fire of which he speaks, no one doubts that it is a fire of another kind than the one we now use. No fire of the present age is eternal. I do not know whether the sun, since it is said to be fire, ought to be called eternal or not, because it is changeable, even if it will be changed for the better.

But that fire of which he speaks here is certainly affirmed to be eternal, because the one who promises that it has been prepared for the devil is the Truth. Therefore we must believe no differently from what the Truth itself says. Although certain recent advocates of falsehood, wishing to deceive the unwary, try to assert that there are no other kinds of punishments and no places of torment, the consciences of human beings themselves contradict them, since God, who is the Truth, already declares that this fire has been prepared and is eternal.

Of this fire Isaiah plainly says that “their worm will not die, and their fire will not be quenched” (Isa. 66:24). Perhaps that fire is of such a kind and such a substance that it can burn even incorporeal and invisible things. Hence many hold that it too has been constituted invisible, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “The things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4:18).

But perhaps he is speaking about the things that exist at present. Otherwise, if only the things that are not seen are eternal, while the things that are seen are temporary, that fire is invisible, lest it be thought temporal when it is called eternal.

If the devil himself is also eternal, then the fire prepared for him must rightly be believed eternal, since it is said to be prepared for no one other than the devil. Perhaps, when this fire was prepared for the devil by the just Judge, the human being did not yet exist. Therefore it was prepared for him who had fallen before the human being existed.

And although the one for whom it was prepared is spiritual, he is nevertheless not denied a body. If the devil, although believed to have a spiritual body, possesses a body, what wonder is it if the fire prepared for him is also believed to be spiritual and corporeal? Hence it is not unreasonable to believe that, at the resurrection, the human bodies—because they will be spiritual—can be burned by that fire, both body and soul, in Gehenna.

Gehenna is said to be a twofold punishment, perhaps because body and soul are burned by that conflagration: since the human being sinned in two ways, he is punished in two ways.

Therefore do not be surprised if that fire is said to be visible or invisible, because its visibility will not be according to the mode of our present vision, just as corporeal spiritual bodies will not be such as they now are. Nor is it surprising if that fire, foreseen and prepared by God the wise Judge, is of such a kind that it can torment that angelic spiritual nature and burn the human nature once it has been raised as spiritual.

The kingdom, however, is said to have been prepared from the foundation of the world for no others than the righteous and the holy. Therefore it is given to those for whom it was prepared, so that they may be with their King, Christ.

The eternal fire is not prepared for those to whom it is said, “Depart from me, accursed ones,” as the kingdom is prepared for the righteous; it is prepared for the devil and his angels. For, insofar as God is concerned, he did not create human beings for destruction, but for life and joy, so that the number that had been wickedly diminished in the devil and his angels might be restored.

But they themselves, by sinning, joined themselves to the angel of darkness through disobedience. Therefore it was just that, just as those who are saved are made equal to the holy angels in the resurrection and become children of God, so those who perished should be made equal to the devil’s angels and become their companions.

To these it is said: “I was hungry and you did not give me food; I was thirsty and you did not give me drink.”

A wondrous unity of the Lord Jesus Christ with his body is proclaimed, so that you may understand the head to suffer with, or rejoice with, its members, just as the soul in a human body suffers with the body, although it does not hunger according to its own nature. Yet it hungers for the body’s food because it is joined to its body, and it is fed.

So Christ too hungers and suffers in his body, which is the Church; he is also fed and refreshed, although he himself is impassible and lacks no nourishment. In each of the saints he is nourished with food and refreshed with drink; when naked, he is clothed; when a stranger, he is received; in prison, he is comforted; when sick, he is visited. No one understands these things unless he is truly faithful and illuminated by the Holy Spirit.

If Paul is truly made weak with the weak and suffers with all the brothers, how much more does Christ, the head of the whole Church, who says to every sufferer, “I am with him in tribulation,” do so?

I ask you, prudent reader, to consider how carefully he lingers, while enumerating the righteous’ good deeds, over each word, praising them individually and exalting their acts of kindness. But observe how concisely he cuts short each matter concerning those who will be on the left, and gathers together briefly the deeds neglected by them, according to certain manuscripts, although he had reviewed the good deeds above at greater length.

For it belongs to the most merciful Judge to proclaim such deeds more fully and enlarge them with praise, but to remember their evil deeds only in passing and briefly, as though grieving over them.

The righteous also, answering in the interest of their Judge, linger over each word and enumerate their deeds in the same order as the Judge, but, as I said, with an excessive display of astonishment and humility. For it is characteristic of the righteous to receive humbly the good deeds reported to their face, and sometimes even to deny them, out of humility.

Therefore, when they repeat each deed, it is as though they were saying: “We do not recognize that we worthily did either this or the other good deeds you praise.” But the unrighteous, as though overcome by excessive shame or grief and covered with such great reproach, say hurriedly and briefly: “Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?”

Perhaps, struck with terror, they say all these things while denying them, as is customary with wrongdoers. They seem to wish to excuse themselves by saying that they never saw him hungry or thirsty, or in the other conditions mentioned. They refer the single expression “we did not minister to you” to everything.

They do this as though minimizing their crimes, lest they appear more serious when each is enumerated individually and carefully. It is always characteristic of the wicked, for the sake of excusing themselves, to present their faults as nonexistent, trivial, or few.

Christ’s response to both groups also seems to signify this. To the righteous he says: “What you did to one of these least of my brothers, you did to me.” But to the unrighteous: “When you did not do it to one of the least, you did not do it to me.”

He did not add “of my brothers,” as he did when speaking to the righteous, because he wished to show the righteous’ good deeds as great and outstanding, while not exaggerating the faults of the guilty in any respect.

For a good deed done toward Christ’s holier and more distinguished disciples, who can say with the Apostle Paul, “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11:1), seems more worthy of favor than one done toward those who are less holy. For those who more fully do the Father’s will are especially called Christ’s brothers.

Nevertheless, even if I speak in this way, those who did no good either to Christ’s brothers and principal members in the Church, or to any of the least to whom such deeds were enumerated, will in no respect be excusable.

He calls any of them “the least” either because they are considered least in the world, or because they judged themselves least in their own eyes, since they lacked humility in their own sight, so that they might be found great before God if they followed him who said: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29).

And these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.

Let those who wish to diminish the torments of hell and claim that all will eventually return to forgiveness listen. The Lord himself confirms the eternal fire, and these people are sent into eternal punishment. If the eternal life of the saints is perpetual, and the saints will suffer no further downfall thereafter, then it must likewise be confessed that the punishments of lost human beings [Col. 0870B] and angels are to be believed eternal.

These three accounts, or parables, which the Savior seems to have joined together, when compared with one another, are shown to have one meaning, and each is brought to a conclusion with the same ending. Their parts are twofold, namely, concerning the good and the wicked.

For the five who are called wise virgins are the sheep who are placed on the right; they are also the two good servants who doubled for profit the talents they had received—one receiving two, the other five.

The foolish women, however, are the goats who are separated onto the left; they are also that wicked servant who did not wish to seek profit from the talent.

Meanwhile, the profits from the talents are the oil that is prepared and stored daily in vessels of mercy. They are also the wages of good works, by which those who are hungry are fed, those who are thirsty are given drink, and the naked are clothed.

The time when all these things are carried out is the time of the present life. The time when all these things are shown completed is the time of the final resurrection, when the five wise virgins will come to meet Christ, and these two servants will carry their profits with them. Then all the good things they did will be reckoned to those same people, who will now be on the right.

It is clear who will reckon them: the king himself, who is both the bridegroom of the Church and, since servants are under discussion, is also called the master of the household.

Therefore, as I said, this entire discourse, wonderfully composed concerning the future, must be compared with the two preceding ones, so that the understanding of each may be increased by the others, and a more ornate discourse may be introduced, if something concerning such great majesty can in any way be understood worthily.

For he himself is the Son of Man who comes in the seat of his majesty. He himself is the Lord of those servants who comes to settle accounts, at the time when the cry of the angels is said to occur in the middle of the night.

Then, before the seat of his majesty, all the nations will be gathered in the manner of a judge. Those who brought oil with them in their vessels and those who made their talents double will be the sheep on the right.

To all of them it had been said above: “Watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.”

There is one thing expressed by “they will be gathered,” and by the fact that the one who had made five talents double approached; likewise by the statement, “Then they all arose.” Similarly, there is one thing expressed by the separation of the sheep from the goats here and by the foolish women going to buy oil there, as well as by the judgment of the useless servant.

For until the matter comes to judgment, all are mixed together. But when he says to those who will be on the right, “Come,” then those who are ready will enter with him into the wedding feast, since they are the ones to whom he gives the command.

What else does it mean when he says to the good servant, “Well done; enter into the joy of your Lord”? As for those who will be on the left, what does it mean when he says to them, “Insofar as you did not do it to one of these, you did not do it to me; go into the eternal fire,” except to reproach the useless servant and say, “Take the talent from him and throw him into the outer darkness,” and to answer the foolish virgins when they knock, “The door is closed; I do not know you”?

For the Lord knows the ways that are on the right, but those on the left will be perverse.

I have introduced these few matters so that the prudent reader may learn from a small number of examples how profound are the mysteries of God’s utterances and the sacramental meanings shadowed in his sayings; how varied and flourishing are the enigmas of the sentences, so that the figures adorning their subject matter may exercise the reader’s mind and remove weariness.

The Truth itself, concealed within them, arouses the reader’s eagerness, and, when it has been disclosed, the understanding of those who hear, so that in obscure matters the truth may always be sought with greater eagerness.

## Chapter XXVI

And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these words, that he said to his disciples.

Five times in this Gospel you will find this completion of discourse, and it always indicates the perfection of events. For there is nothing that Jesus began without also bringing it to the completion of perfection.

But someone may think there is a contradiction in the fact that Matthew and Mark, after saying that Passover would take place after two days, mentioned that Jesus was in Bethany, where the account of the precious ointment is told; whereas John, six days before Passover, says that Jesus came to Bethany in order to relate the same event concerning the ointment.

Thus the question arises: how, according to these two evangelists, was Passover to occur after two days, when after saying this they are found with John in Bethany, narrating what he himself records about the ointment, at the time when John foretells that Passover will occur after six days?

Those who are troubled by such matters do not understand how deliberately the evangelists act in relation to one another: they neither conceal the truth of the event nor fail, often in the manner of gems, to adorn things placed in other passages so that their words may shine more beautifully, according to what the consequent order of the argument requires.

We see Matthew and Mark doing this here. They placed by way of recapitulation the anointing that had already taken place in Bethany. Therefore it occurred not after those two days, but before them, when six days still remained until Passover.

For this reason neither of them, after saying that Passover would be after two days, immediately added, “After this, when he was in Bethany.” Instead, both deliberately said only, “When he was in Bethany.” This is understood to have taken place before the statement about Passover was made, or before the other matters said to have been spoken.

For according to John, Jesus had come there six days before Passover, and it was then that the meal took place, at which the remarkable account of the ointment was given.

I have said this so that each person may understand from this example the agreement of the evangelists in detail, and may diligently gather and discern what they themselves do not say in the many places where, for the sake of brevity, I have omitted much. No one could encompass all these things in writing.

For among these omissions, variations, and transpositions, nothing that has been said is anywhere without a mystery. Hence, wishing to show above that God established all things in measure, weight, and number, the evangelist first introduced the completion of perfection and began to show how near was the hour of which he had said elsewhere to his mother: “My hour has not yet come” (John 2:4).

Therefore he said to his disciples, showing what he meant: “You know that after two days Passover will take place.” This is the foreknown and foreordained hour, established before the foundation of the world.

Of this hour he says to his Father: “Father, save me from this hour” (John 12:27), and it becomes still clearer how evidently it was foreknown by him. “For this reason,” he says, “I came to this hour.”

And when he prays to the Father, he cries out: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:11).

Therefore, if the Son so clearly foreknew the hour of his passion from far off, we cannot doubt, as the heretics wish, that he was ignorant of the day of his coming and of when the end of the world would be, since he established and reckoned the hour and day of his passion.

For this reason, whenever he suffered ambushes from the Jews, whenever he was sought, he could not suffer before the hour and time came. And although he taught them every day in the temple, he could not be seized until he had completed all these words that he had proposed to disclose to his disciples.

After he had completed all these words, he then said to his disciples, already in Bethany: “You know that after two days Passover will take place.”

It should be noted that he did not say merely “all the words,” but added “these all,” that is, the words he had spoken before them on the Mount of Olives—not the words he was still going to speak at supper with the disciples, or in the house of Simon the leper concerning the woman who approached him, or the many other matters that a careful reader can consider and observe here, since nothing is empty of meaning but everything is full of mysteries.

“You know,” he says, “that after two days Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.”

He had frequently foretold these things much earlier, but now, as I said, he declares both the hour and the day. Therefore he had previously set forth the words concerning the glory and splendor of his coming, and concluded them in this one statement, in which he most fully declares that he will come in the kingdom with his angels and sit on the seat of his majesty.

Immediately afterward, with great deliberateness, he declares that he will suffer shortly, so that the disciples may understand with complete faith that the mystery of the cross has been joined to the glory of eternity, and may in no respect fear the event, since they hear of the glory and majesty of the one who reigns.

He announces that Passover will take place after two days so that they might know that the foreordained hour had already arrived, according to what we have shown: that he could not die before he had completed all the mysteries of his teaching.

It was therefore necessary first to dissolve that typical Passover and then to hand over to the disciples the New Testament, when the appointed other day was at hand, so that Christ our Passover might be sacrificed.

The former took place in the evening; then, after these things had been completed, Christ was immediately handed over on that same night. This was the hour of the passion, which had not previously come before all these types had been fulfilled.

The year and day had come of which the prophet spoke: “He has sent me to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of reconciliation.” This is the day of our salvation, on which the victim was offered for the salvation of the whole world.

It is also the first month of Passover among the months of the year from the beginning of the world.

He foretells these things to his disciples, warning them before they begin to occur, so that they may fix them in their hearts and understand what was soon to come. Thus, when these events began and they saw him who had said and displayed such things as to be believed God handed over to the cross, they would not be astonished or, through excessive fear, be driven away from returning to the faith.

Therefore he says: “You know that after two days Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.”

He is not speaking only, as some think, about that typical sacrament which was known to everyone. For if he had meant that, he ought rather to have said: “You know that after two days Passover will come,” or “Passover will be,” or “Passover will be celebrated according to custom.”

But he says something far different: “Passover will be made,” because what was happening was new—something that had never happened before—so that through this new Passover the old one might grow old.

For this reason the former is rightly called the Old Testament, because after two days the New succeeded it. This was that very two-day period: after two days, as though after the two most brilliant lights, the Old and New Testaments, the true Passover for the world was to be celebrated—not in the blood of an animal, but in the blood of the truest Lamb.

For this reason he added: “And the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.”

After two days Passover took place, as he had foretold, when he was handed over on the night of the fourteenth day of the moon.

From this it is clear, as the excellent teacher Augustine says, that this was Wednesday when it was foretold; or certainly, as others hold, he foretold these things earlier, and, since the Jews reckon their days by the moon, it was the eleventh lunar day when he had completed the parables mentioned above.

Thus it is fitting that “after two days” should be said according to the manner of Scripture, with two complete days passing in between, and with Passover already celebrated on the evening of the fourteenth moon, Christ being sacrificed around the sixth hour of the day, as though on that very day.

For the most learned among the Jews reckon the lunar day from the moon’s illumination, when, as they say, it is illuminated by the sun, until its next illumination. Accordingly, the mystery of Passover is more fully commended at the end of the fifth day, as it were toward evening.

Nevertheless, whichever of these interpretations is more accurate is not of great consequence, since the meaning is one.

But when he says that the Son of Man will be handed over, it is rightly asked by whom he was handed over, since that is not said here.

Yet it is said of the Father that he did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all. We also read of him that he handed himself over for us.

Judas too handed him over, and for this reason he is called “the betrayer” to this day. The devil also handed him over, having put it into Judas’s heart to betray him. Likewise the chief priests and elders of the people handed him over to the condemnation of death.

Perhaps, therefore, the impersonal form is used here—“he will be handed over”—without saying by whom or through whom, so that the word may refer to all the persons involved, although they did not all hand him over with one intention or the same will. To whom he was handed over he had already foretold above.

“For he will be handed over,” he says, “to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and crucified”—that is, to the Roman soldiers, who received him from the hands of all those who had handed him over to death.

Let those who attempt to assert that the Savior feared death and, terrified by the passion, said, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”—of which we shall speak in its proper place—understand and blush. For, knowing that after two days Passover would come, he knew that he would be handed over to be crucified.

He had always known this from the beginning, since he came for this very reason; yet he did not avoid the ambushes or retreat in fear. Indeed, while the others were afraid and unwilling to go, he himself proceeded voluntarily and fearlessly.

Hence, in the Psalms, speaking in his own person, he says: “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily” (Ps. 53:8); and: “I desired to do your will, my God” (Ps. 39:9).

If he had been altogether unwilling, he would not have suffered. Therefore, because he came willingly in order to bring the shadow of the carnal festival to an end, he said: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15).

But he could not suffer earlier, because his hour had not yet come.

Then the chief priests and the scribes and the elders of the people gathered in the courtyard of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas.

This happened when Jesus had completed all these words and brought to an end what we have discussed at length. Then they gathered and took counsel to seize and kill Jesus by deceit.

In a truly wondrous and ineffable way, these men carry out God’s counsel against their own counsel, so that they may kill the innocent one who was life. Therefore not everything that can be called counsel is always counsel; nor, wherever the chief priests and the wise men of the world or the rulers of the people gather, are matters of counsel always being discussed.

For this reason four things are rightly condemned in this counsel: first, that they gather in deceit; second, that they are not just any people from the crowd, but chief priests; third, that they are scribes, that is, teachers of the law; and fourth, that they deliberate to kill Christ the Son of God.

They do this at the very time when, with Passover near, they ought already to have been preparing victims and sacrifices, smoothing the walls of the temple, sweeping the floors, cleansing the vessels, and purifying everything according to the rite of the law, so that they might become worthy to eat the lamb and so that their religious worship might be more acceptable to God.

Instead, they gather not just anywhere and not with just anyone, but in the courtyard of the high priest, in order to deliberate with him how they might kill the Lord. They do not fear God, do not respect the festival day, and do not care about a popular uprising if one should occur on that day, as the plain sense of the passage shows.

They urge one another to take every precaution only against the possibility that he might be snatched from their hands by the assistance of the people.

For they imitate Cain, whose prophecy they wish to fulfill, so that they may freely kill his brother Abel by deceit. Hence Cain says: “Let us go out into the field” (Gen. 4:8), so that he might kill him and prevent his escape.

But Judas—or rather, the devil through him—anticipated their plan before the festival when he sought an agreement concerning what they were willing to give him. From that point he sought an opportunity to hand him over to them.

Therefore, rejoicing at such an event, they no longer cared on what day it might happen. On the night when they ought to have eaten Passover, they all busied themselves and deliberated together with the betrayer, so that as soon as they found a suitable place they might seize him.

But because the day had already come, and the hour known to the Lord from the beginning of the world, it could neither be delayed nor brought forward.

After the plan had been made, as they say, on Wednesday before the day of Passover, on the following day toward evening the legal lamb was immediately killed; at once our Lamb was slaughtered for the salvation of the whole world, as though at the full moon.

Thus it came about that he was not killed on their festival day, but that the event was deferred to another day, so that, after all the things that were shadows had been completed, Christ our Passover might be sacrificed in the clear light.

Then, abandoning the Jews’ unleavened bread, let all hasten, as a new dough, to celebrate the new Passover with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, and not remain with the Jews in the oldness of the letter.

But because the gracious Savior came to Bethany six days before Passover, and on the following day, with triumph and palm branches, celebrated his return to Jerusalem as though already victorious, ascending again to Jerusalem the glory of his single combat, which he was soon to complete, the chief priests were themselves stirred and gathered in the courtyard of the high priest.

Thus was fulfilled what was said in the Psalm: “Why did the peoples rage, and the rulers gather together against the Lord and against his Christ?” (Ps. 2:1–2).

Since they labor to form a deceitful plan against the Lord, let us leave them and hasten to bring the book to a fitting conclusion, so that we may once again meet our Savior in Bethany.

For Bethany is interpreted as “house of obedience,” so that there, with the disciples, we may see with the eye of the mind and understand the things done by the Lord, because they are exceedingly mystical and wondrous.

Let us pray that, with Lazarus, our sins having been loosed, although last at the banquet at which we dine with the Lord, we may be found worthy to take part.

**1075 — PROLOGUE OF THE TWELFTH BOOK**

[Col. 0875]

[Col. 0875C] Once, when I was still a boy and wished to swim across a vast sea, shortly before reaching the shore I caught sight of something. And behold, from a distance an excessive height seemed to rise, and the inaccessible harbor of the river appeared to grow. Struck with fear, and already wearied by great exertion, I began to discern that I could neither turn back nor find an exit to a safe harbor in so immense a stretch of sea.

So now, too, dearest brothers, after the eleven books of explanations on Matthew have at last been completed, it occurs to me, in this final work of my labor, that so great is the depth of God’s mysteries and so great the obscurity of the divine utterances that it seems I can neither omit what I began here and there at your earlier urging, nor confidently complete the little that remains. For a sorrowful prayer, long [Col. 0875D] fasting, and worn out by the cares of worldly matters, greatly fears even to speak what it perceives, when it sees that it cannot suffice either in understanding or in talent.

But because an unfailing abundance of the word is always promised to those who rightly seek divine things, the all-abundant Lord says to his petitioner: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX, 11). Therefore I will demand this from myself, trusting that, through your merits intervening, it will come from the gift of the giver. I shall proceed as I began, if somehow I may worthily explain a few things concerning the fullness of the mystery of Christ’s Passion, at least for young people who seek it. I believe that facility in speaking will not be lacking in the treatment, when the will to complete it has proved ready and devoted.

For it can scarcely happen that the capacity for virtues abandons a mind of good will. Conversely, it is exceedingly difficult for an abundance of understanding to follow a person who wishes to share with no one else the wealth of the word. Therefore, although the discourse may seem lowly, its excessive length may be criticized, and some may condemn its uninstructed boldness, my defense will be that very good will; your intercession, together with the truth I have put on, will be my breastplate of righteousness. For if no one who holds the office of teaching can be secure about the talent entrusted to him, no one can rightly reproach me if, at your request, [Col. 0876C] I wish to supply, in whatever words I can, while no longer idle, what I long neglected while occupied with the labors of others.

For just as I was your debtor in completing whatever I was then less able to repay, so now you—and those for whom I labor—are themselves my debtors, that they may hear what I now faithfully offer to both. For they will be liable to blame if they do not gratefully receive, as an act of service, what I devotedly—or at least belatedly—return to you and to them together.

## BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 0875]

[Col. 0875D] When Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came to him carrying an alabaster vessel of precious ointment [Col. 0876D] and poured it over his head as he reclined.

Many scholars doubt concerning this passage whether the four evangelists each spoke, in their respective places, about one and the same woman—for they said almost the same things about her, or things closely related—or whether there were in fact several women about whom a single account was composed, not so that she would be thought to be one, but so that, from all of them as one, Christ’s woman might be commended through diverse figures and incorporated members.

For that reason, what each evangelist says in common, and in what they differ, must be considered very carefully, so that from these matters we may understand whether they all relate the story of one woman, or of three or more, lest we presume anything rashly. For it is impossible that these four men, speaking about one and the same woman, should have held contrary views, since they were perfect in the same understanding, consummated in the same Spirit and the same judgment, and were appointed to minister the salvation of the word to the churches.

There is much similarity and close correspondence concerning the place, the person, the house, and the host with whom these things occurred; there is also considerable agreement in the account of the woman, since Matthew, Mark, and John say that these things happened in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper. Although John does say that it was in Bethany, he states: “They made him a supper, and Martha served, while Lazarus was one of those reclining with him. Mary therefore took a pound of precious ointment of pure nard and anointed Jesus’ feet” (John XII, 3).

From this it appears that they themselves made him a supper in some house, whether Simon’s or their own. Luke, however, although he does not call this Simon a leper, nevertheless identifies him by name from the Lord’s words, and declares that he was a Pharisee who invited him to eat with him in his house; yet he does not name Bethany, but a certain town.

All of them, moreover, speak of an alabaster vessel of ointment, except that John says “a pound of precious pure nard,” while Luke, like Matthew and Mark, relates that it was precious. They all relate that the ointment was poured over Jesus’ head, but only Mark indicates that the alabaster vessel was broken. Luke, on the other hand, records something quite different: that she anointed the Lord’s feet, stood humbly behind him out of shame, bathed them with tears, wiped them with her hair, and emphasizes that she was a sinner. John, however, names her Mary, the sister of Lazarus and Martha, and recalls that she anointed the Lord’s feet and wiped them with her hair, but does not say that she wept over them; rather, he says that the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.

[Col. 0877D] Therefore some say that there was not one woman but three, or, as I have said, four. For the woman who poured the ointment over Jesus’ head, according to Matthew and Mark, does not appear to be the same as the one who anointed his feet, as Luke and John explain.

They say that it is neither possible nor fitting that the woman who was scarcely judged worthy to approach the feet should have approached the Lord’s head; and for that reason she stood behind him and wept, because she was a sinner. Nor do they consider it believable that Mary, whom Jesus loved—the sister of Martha and Lazarus, who had chosen the better part—should be called a sinner in the city, as prostitutes customarily are. Jesus is often shown to have lodged among such women.

Origen therefore agrees more readily that there were three women: one, namely, of whom Matthew and Mark wrote in harmonious agreement, making no difference in their accounts; another, of whom Luke wrote; and a third, of whom John wrote, since his account differs greatly from the others—not only in what is said about the ointment, but also because Jesus loved the woman whom he even places before her sister Martha, since she chose the best part, which will not be taken away from her.

Although this woman too is said to have been in Bethany, as was the other woman about whom Matthew and Mark speak, there is nevertheless a considerable difference. They say that she came into the house of Simon and anointed his head there, when the Passover was to take place after two days. John, however, as I have said, relates that Jesus came to Bethany six days before the Passover, where Lazarus, whom he had raised, was; and that Mary and Martha made him a great supper.

But if we say that one and the same Mary did all this as many as three times—once and again in Simon’s house, and a third time in her own house—the account of one event seems remarkable, with great variety in the statements, so that such diversity and repetition of the event appears to signify hidden mysteries.

Nevertheless, whether one woman is introduced so many times, or whether there were two or three, the evangelists’ faith does not waver, their authority is not weakened, and there is no disagreement in the understanding of their statements or in the particular identity of the persons. Rather, the narrative of a great mystery is supplied in an ordered way: in one of their houses Lazarus, who had been raised, is introduced as dining with him, and she is not called a sinner; nor is she called one in Simon’s house, since Simon is mentioned as having been a leper.

[Col. 0878C] In the house of a certain ruler, however, though he was not a leper, the woman who first approached is called a sinner; then she is said to have wept and bathed the Lord’s feet with her tears. Yet the things she did are not said to have occurred in Bethany.

Thus in these three women the great virtue of repentance is displayed, and God’s clemency toward sinners is proclaimed. For just as in Lazarus the resurrection of those who are falling into the death of sin is declared, so in Simon the leper the cleansing of all crimes is commended. And in the woman who is called a sinner, the washing away of all offenses is shown. Throughout all of this the marvelous kindness of almighty God is proclaimed: he does not shun the leper, avoid the sinner, or abhor the unclean, so that he may wash away the stains of the human mind and body.

[Col. 0878D] This leper’s house was in Bethany. Bethany is interpreted as “house of obedience,” by which the whole present world is understood. It is rightly called the house of obedience because we have been placed in it for this purpose: as though in an arena, to be obedient to God, so that through this obedience we may be able to ascend to that heavenly Jerusalem which is near to it.

If every place of the present age is understood as Bethany, then rightly a portion of the whole place is Simon the leper’s house, because through his house the Catholic Church, which is in the world, is signified. Jesus is believed to be in that house, and he dines with us whenever we render him the service that is his due.

The house is called Simon the leper’s for two reasons: either because he was once a leper, as we all were, and, though now healed of his ancient fault, is still called so by the Lord; or because we all still remain under sin. For “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I, 8).

[Col. 0879A] Into this house, then, because Jesus entered and dines there, the woman came—that is, the Church. She came, but not empty-handed, because she brought an alabaster vessel of precious ointment; and, as John says, “ointment of pure nard,” because she came faithfully. For *pistis* in Greek means “faith” or “faithful”; this woman therefore brought complete faith. Otherwise she could not approach Jesus or enter the house of obedience unless she brought precious and fragrant ointment of faith.

Of this ointment the bride of Christ, which is the Church, says in the Song of Songs: “My nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song I, 12). John therefore speaks with great precision when he says “ointment of pure nard,” for the name of the Bridegroom is also an ointment poured out.

There are indeed many kinds of ointments, and therefore there is much variation here. One is that with which the Lord’s feet are anointed, yet which is not poured out and is not called especially fragrant, because the sinful woman is accused; another is that which is here said to have been poured over Jesus’ head; and another is that with which the Lord’s feet are anointed in John, which is said to be pure nard, whose fragrance fills the whole house.

All these fragrances derive from the name of the Savior, which has been poured out over the minds of believers; therefore the young women love him. One of them anoints the Lord’s feet with weeping and tears; another, who chose the best part, always knows to sit at his feet in order to hear the word of salvation. She indeed anoints those same feet with ointment, but with such a wondrous and mystical ointment that its fragrance fills the whole house.

[Col. 0879C] The third woman, of whom the present account speaks, brought another ointment and poured it over his head; it is proclaimed to have been precious—precious, certainly, because it was divine. Otherwise, if it were not divine, it could not be poured over Christ’s head, because upon the head of Christ, who is God, nothing falls except what is divine.

Accordingly, whatever it is with which Christ’s humanity, which is below, is anointed must be pure and completely faithful, and its fragrance must fill the whole house, just as Ezekiel relates that he saw the Lord seated upon a high and exalted throne, and that the things beneath him filled the temple—not less with fragrance than with the brightness of virtue.

Therefore, through these distinctions among the things described, whether there is one woman who does this repeatedly—which I do not believe—or whether there are two or three, the distinction among the faithful is entirely demonstrated. The diversity of the evangelists is therefore very helpful, since it shows that in Simon’s house some pour precious ointment over Jesus’ head, some merely anoint his feet with tears, and some pour it out so lavishly that the whole house of the Church is filled with the fragrance of Christ’s divinity.

Observe also that the owner of the house himself is called Simon. For Simon is likewise interpreted as “obedient,” because in the house of obedience no one except the obedient dwells worthily. In this house the most gracious Savior descends from those heavenly mountains, because he came from heaven into the world.

He was not previously visible in this world; rather, sent by the Father through the devotion of obedience, he came into this world, as he himself says: “As you sent me, I came into the world.” When this woman heard that Christ had come and was in Simon’s house, she too approached, for she could not be healed unless Christ had come to earth.

But, as has been said, the agreement of the evangelists and the particular meaning of their statements must be sought. For although Luke says something similar and the name of the man with whom the Lord dined is the same—so that he too is called Simon—he does not call him a leper. It is therefore not contrary to custom or reason to believe that there were two men, or more, with the same name. For if one man can have two names, much more can two or more men have one name.

It is therefore more credible that the Simon who was not a leper was another man, into whose house the woman called a sinner entered, whether that house was in Bethany or not. For Luke neither names Bethany nor any city or town, and his account does not seem to concern the same event in the same place.

[Col. 0880B] Accordingly, it may be, as the eminent fathers Ambrose and Augustine think, that the same woman was the one who is said to have been a sinner in the city, to whom, because she loved God greatly in accordance with the example, many sins were forgiven. Yet it is clear that this same Mary did this twice, because she loved greatly.

Thus she first approached with great humanity and profound modesty, and by the abundance of her tears and her greatest love she merited the forgiveness of sins. And because whatever she had first devoutly offered had been pleasing to God and praised by the Lord, she did not hesitate to repeat the act and to offer something more precious, so that the whole house might be filled with the fragrance of the ointment.

It is therefore not surprising if, through grace divinely inspired within her, she not only dared to repeat the act, but also deserved to understand more fully the things that are divine in Christ. Nor is it surprising that the woman whom the Lord loved greatly should be called both a prostitute and the sister of Lazarus and Martha. For it was not she who first chose and loved the Lord, but the Lord who first chose and loved her, so that thereafter she would love the Lord greatly.

For this reason, out of her excessive love, she ardently held to the best part that she had chosen as one who had been chosen; and therefore she never wearied of remaining at the Lord’s feet. John too indicates that she is this woman.

“For there was,” he says, “a certain man who was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, from the town of Mary and Martha, her sisters. Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill” (John XI, 1–2).

In saying this, John confirms that what Luke narrated happened in the house of a certain Simon. Mary had already done this. What she is said to have done again in Bethany is another event and does not belong to Luke’s narrative.

But what is reported by three evangelists alike as having happened in Bethany—namely, by John, Matthew, and Mark—as the blessed Jerome and the aforementioned Origen believe, was not done once by one and the same woman, but by two. Therefore it must be considered how the accounts agree in another way.

In John, the event is not narrated as having occurred in Simon’s house, but only as follows: “Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus had been dead, whom Jesus raised. They made him a supper there,” he says; and he does not say where, except that you are to understand Bethany; nor does he say who made him the supper, except that Martha served and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him (John XII, 1–2), and so forth.

Matthew and Mark, however, state that the events they relate took place both in Bethany and in the house of Simon the leper. Thus either there were two women, as the distinguished interpreters mentioned above maintain, or, if we wish to say that there was one woman and that the event occurred once, as Father Augustine judged more likely, we can understand nothing other than that Simon the leper, the two sisters, and Lazarus were fellow citizens and neighbors, their houses adjoining, and that they lived together in the closest familiarity, as though in one house.

Hence it is said that “they made him a supper there,” rather than that this or that individual made it. You are to understand that, both because of their constant association or their proximity, their house was one, and because of the Savior’s frequent presence: he had healed Simon of his leprosy, raised Lazarus from the dead in that house, and forgiven Mary the sinner her many sins because she loved greatly (Luke VII, 47).

From these considerations we ought to conclude that there was one Mary, who had already anointed the Lord’s feet, washed them with tears, and wiped them with her hair, [Col. 0881C] and who is now said both to have anointed his feet according to John and to have poured ointment over his head according to Matthew and Mark.

Although their accounts may seem different, the evangelists are not opposed to one another when they narrate different things concerning one and the same woman. This is also demonstrated by the rule according to which one writer often gives a part for the whole, while another explains and states the entire event or statement; at times, too, one of them recalls one part of an event and another a different part, so that together they both speak one true account.

For example, when they related the account of the five loaves mentioned earlier, one said that groups of fifty and one hundred reclined, while another mentioned only groups of fifty; yet neither statement can be considered contradictory, any more than what is said here.

Accordingly, it was not only the Lord’s feet that this one and the same Mary anointed again in this passage, but now also his head—or perhaps his head first and then his feet—unless it is because Mark relates that his head was poured over after the alabaster vessel had been broken.

Perhaps some hostile slanderer will be so troublesome as to deny that anything remained in the broken vessel, arguing against the truth of the Gospel. But another, more wisely and religiously, argues the contrary in defense of the Gospel’s truth: that it was not broken in such a way that everything was poured out, but that enough remained in the intact vessel for the head to be poured over.

If that person should still persist, so blind or so violent an opponent of the truth that he wishes to sever the harmony of the evangelists because of this alabaster vessel, let him first accept the orderly explanation that the feet were poured over or anointed before the vessel was broken, so that, while it remained intact, enough was left to pour over the head. Then the breaking of which Mark speaks so carefully caused the remainder to be poured out completely, so that the whole house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment (John XII, 3).

The evangelist therefore does not mention this event without reason. Through this woman the whole Church of Christ is signified; she carries with her many ointments of good fragrance, received from the Lord, in which she delights greatly and frequently. Thus the ointment that descends from the head and is poured over the members—perhaps even as far as the feet—may, in proper order, flow back from the feet to the head. For from him and through him all anointing comes to us, who are the feet.

Jesus has many and most precious ointments. Therefore the bride sings to her bridegroom, the Lord, in the Song of Songs: “We run after the fragrance of your ointments; therefore the young women have loved you exceedingly” (Song I, 4).

But since many of the saints, because of the pouring out of this most precious ointment upon their bodies, surrendered their lives for the Lord, one evangelist rightly mentions the broken alabaster, while the others are silent about it. For although they all refer the anointing of grace, the pouring out of the ointment, and the act of good fragrance to Christ, this applies especially to the martyrs, whose bodies were broken and crushed in death for Christ. Once they had been slain, the whole Church was filled with the fragrance of Christ’s name; this is the ointment that, as I have said, is rightly named in the Song of Songs.

[Col. 0882D] Therefore it is called precious in this passage. Because of it the disciples were indignant and grieved, especially Judas: “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?”

Perhaps the disciples were indignant because they did not yet understand God’s mysteries, while Judas was indignant because he was a thief and a robber. Otherwise, what beauty or propriety would there have been in pouring the ointment that flowed from Christ’s head over the rest of his body and over the head of so great a teacher, unless the event itself revealed a great mystery?

Therefore, although it could have been sold for a great price and given to the poor, this ought not to have been done, because it was more fitting that it be poured over Christ’s head in a holy and marvelous outpouring. That ointment was not intended for the poor, nor was it appropriate that it be divided among many; rather, it was to be poured out whole and most precious, even after the alabaster had been broken (Mark XIV, 3), solely over Jesus’ head.

For this reason Jesus gratefully accepted the woman’s wise action, and, when the disciples were indignant, said: “Let her alone, and do not trouble her, for she has done a good work for me.”

So effective is this kind of action, and so great is the praise of such a good work, that all are exhorted by so great an example. This woman is proclaimed throughout the world, wherever the Gospel is preached, and what she did is proclaimed in memory of Christ.

Those who wish to understand this woman’s action according to the literal sense should say what benefit this ointment, poured so laudably over Jesus’ head, had, or what advantage and beauty it possesses according to the wording of the account—unless it is because she did a good work in the mystery, and in the sacrament of this event her devotion prefigured many things.

Thus he also said: “You will always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me.” It is as though he said: You will always have the poor, toward whom you may perform works of mercy, but you cannot always have me bodily; therefore this must be done once for me, so that the whole house may be filled with the fragrance of the good odor, and all the members of the head may be anointed.

For unless this ointment flows down from the head, it can benefit nothing in the body. But if everything we do contributes to the praise of God, and every work is referred to the glory of Christ, then we anoint Christ’s head with precious ointment; from there it runs through his entire body, that is, through the whole Church. This is the very precious ointment whose fragrance fills the whole house, namely, the Church of God.

From this passage some raise objections: why one evangelist alone says that Judas was grieved because he had the money box and had been a thief from the beginning, while Matthew now writes that all the apostles were indignant, since they do not know the figure called *synlepsis*, in which one is spoken of for many, or many for one.

It can also be said that the apostles, because they truly did not yet understand God’s mysteries, were indignant on account of the poor, whereas Judas was indignant solely on account of profit. Therefore the evangelist records his murmuring together with the charge against him: he did not care for the poor, but because he was a thief and a robber.

For this reason John took the occasion to reveal his habit of stealing and to express how greedy he was for money.

It is asked, however, why he said: “You will not always have me,” when after the resurrection he says to them: “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20). As I have said, he is speaking of the presence of his body; after the resurrection he would not be with them in the same way as he was then, in all their companionship and familiarity.

Mindful of this, the Apostle also says: “If we have known Christ according to the flesh, now we know him no longer.” But true faith knows that God the Word is everywhere and will always be with his own.

“In pouring this ointment on my body, she has done it for my burial.”

Let the heretics who say that Christ had no body hear this; and let those who divide him hear it too, wishing to introduce in Christ two persons, an adoptive Son of God and a proper one, just as it is certain that he truly had two natures.

Let them hear that, from both natures, Christ is one and the same; therefore the one who speaks is one, and the one whose body is anointed is the same. He does not say, “She did this for the burial of my body,” but “She did this for my burial.”

Thus in the Creed we rightly confess that Christ the Son of God suffered and was crucified, died, and was buried, although only the flesh suffered, only the flesh was crucified, died, and was buried.

[Col. 0883D] Hence here too he says, “for my burial.” Who is it, then, who says this? Truly Christ, the Word of God made flesh. And because “the Word was made flesh” (John I, 14), he rightly says, in the unity of the person, “She did this for my burial,” while the flesh of the Word is prepared for burial.

He therefore descended to the lower regions who lay in the tomb: one and the same, undivided Christ. The flesh did not lie in the tomb without God the Word, who became flesh; nor did the soul descend to the lower regions without him, because in all things Christ is one and the same, God and man, true Son of God and of man.

God therefore neither died nor was buried, and yet it was he who said: “By pouring this ointment on my body, she did this for my burial.” What was poured upon his body was done for his burial; yet he himself and what belongs to him are not identical. Nor is it the same thing for his burial to be prepared and for his body to be anointed; for it is not fitting to say that the body is his and that he himself is buried in the same manner.

The point of this divine mystery—that is, the understanding of piety—is not to fail to acknowledge as God the one whom you know as man, nor to fail to acknowledge as man the one whom you do not doubt is God. This is what it means not to divide Jesus Christ, because the Word was made flesh.

Therefore the right faith is neither to think that the one whom you understand to have been raised was not buried, nor to doubt that the one whom you do not dare deny was buried has been raised.

Jesus Christ was buried because he also died. Therefore it is not right to divide him into three persons, or to divide Christ by saying that the Word, the soul, and the body are separated in one place or another. But because he is one, he was also buried, just as he confesses that he was anointed for his burial.

“Amen, I say to you, wherever this Gospel is preached throughout the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”

This ambiguity of expression, as some wish to understand it, creates no difficulty or doubt. For whether you punctuate it so as to say, “Wherever this Gospel is preached throughout the whole world”—which belongs to what follows—or whether you punctuate it so that “throughout the whole world” is taken with “it will be told,” nevertheless, wherever this Gospel is preached, it will also be told that she did this in memory of him.

The Gospel will not be preached without the memory of this woman, who is the Church; nor is her memory to be proclaimed without the Gospel. For the memory of this woman signifies the present Church: she received the Lord, buried the Savior in her faith, and anointed his head with the most precious ointment and his feet, believing him truly God and man in her heart and confessing him with her mouth, together with good works.

Consider, I ask you, his knowledge of future events. He foretold that after two days he would suffer and on the third day rise again, since he was to die. Then he says that the Gospel will be preached throughout the whole world, together with the memory of the woman, because she did this for the burial of Jesus Christ.

And then one of the Twelve, named Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said to them:

This was then, certainly, when he was in Bethany and had said, “You know that after two days the Passover will take place.” Or it was when the leaders of the people and the scribes had gathered in the courtyard of the high priest. For when the true Passover came, darkness fled, and Judas passed over into darkness during the night; when the presence withdrew, he came even to the Jews in order to hand over the Lord.

“One of the Twelve”: one in number, but not in merit; in outward appearance, not in virtue; joined for a time to the body, but not bound by love.

It is therefore not without mystery that two of the apostles were called by this name: one Judas is called the son of James, the other Iscariot, because Judas is interpreted as “confession.” The two were therefore among the disciples so that one might represent those who truly confess, whose portion remains faithfully with the Lord, while the other expresses the portion of those “who profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus I, 16).

For this reason all who follow this one pass over into greed, deceit, and fraud, and mingle with false brothers.

I have read that, according to a Hebrew interpretation, Iscariot is said by someone to mean “the strangled one.” If this is so, the name corresponds remarkably—as though prophetically—with the outcome of his death, since he hanged himself with a noose and died strangled.

As for the region or village from which he came, and from which he derived his surname, and what the name means, we have already spoken above.

This man therefore went to the chief priests against the one who was truly established forever as priest according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. CIX, 4), and who had become the high priest.

“What will you give me,” he said, “and I will hand him over to you?”

They fixed for him thirty pieces of silver.

Our writers report that wretched Judas wished to compensate with the price of his Teacher for the loss he believed he had suffered through the pouring out of the ointment. In his misery, he did not even ask for a definite sum, so that his betrayal might at least appear profitable; rather, as though handing over a worthless slave, he placed the price in the buyers’ power, leaving it to them to give him as much as they wished.

He could not have done what he promised—“I will hand him over to you”—unless Christ himself permitted it; but Judas’s shamelessness is shown in the fact that he did not care whether he lied. For the member of the devil was now speaking, although earlier he himself had spoken with the Lord: “All these things I will give you” (Matt. IV, 9), when he attacked the head so that afterward he might more easily scatter the members.

They therefore set the price of a slave for him, because Christ had taken the form of a slave. In his figure, Joseph, though free from his brothers, was once “sold into slavery” (Ps. CIV, 17), so that in the time of famine he might distribute grain to his brothers.

He was sold not, according to the Septuagint, for twenty gold pieces, but, as the Hebrew truth has it, he was bought for as many pieces of silver as the years he sojourned in this world, up to his baptism. For Joseph, as a figure of Christ, is also read to have been that many years old when he stood before Pharaoh as Christ was when he was baptized and began to preach the Gospel.

“From then on,” he says, “he sought an opportunity to hand him over”—that is, from the time when he spoke with the chief priests and they agreed to give him thirty pieces of silver.

Thus enticed by such an evil bargain, he sought an opportunity to find him alone with the disciples, so that he might hand him over as though freely and without the crowds. Luke makes this clearer. Therefore, like a careful conspirator, after the supper, in the silence of night, when he was in greater seclusion with his own in the garden of Gethsemane, they came upon him with swords and clubs, so that they might secretly seize him as though he were a thief.

On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples approached Jesus, saying: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?”

The first day of Unleavened Bread is the day on which the lamb was sacrificed among the Jews, on the evening of the fourteenth lunar day, once the leaven had been removed, as is shown in Exodus: “For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; on the first day there shall be no leaven in your houses” (Exod. XII, 15).

The days of Unleavened Bread were seven, but there was only one Passover, concerning which Anatolius says: “Count from the end of the thirteenth lunar day, which is the beginning of the fourteenth, and thus continue to the end of the twentieth lunar day; for seven days Unleavened Bread is celebrated. During these days, whichever day the fourteenth moon occurs—since those seven days were symbolic—the truest Passover is celebrated.”

The apostles’ question, “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” [Col. 0886B] shows great concern and devoted obedience, so that everything might be done according to his will, just as wretched Judas, according to the devil’s will, handed over the price of this blood.

The Passover they mention was the lamb called the Passover among the Jews, which was sacrificed in the evening. It had to be eaten because Christ, having been made from a woman, was made under the Law.

This was not, as the Ebionites wrongly think, because the Lord celebrated this Passover with the Jews so that it should thereafter be observed according to Jewish custom. Rather, he did so in order to transfer his own from the oldness of the letter to spiritual mysteries and to redeem those who were under the Law.

If he came to drive those who were under the Law out from under the yoke of the Law, much less is it fitting that he should bring under the Law those who had previously been found outside the Law.

To them the Lord says:

Go into the city to a certain man and say to him: “The Teacher says, ‘My time is near; I am celebrating the Passover with my disciples at your house.’” Mark and Luke explain this more clearly, when they indicate by certain clues that he was the master of the house or the owner of it. He was going to show them a large upper room, furnished and clean, where they might prepare the Passover.

But Matthew, when he says that the Lord said, “Go into the city to a certain man,” seems, for the sake of brevity, to have added the words “to a certain man” in his own voice, wishing somehow to indicate him. For no one who wishes to speak fully would say to his servants, “Go to a certain man.” It would be more acceptable to say, “Go to anyone,” or “Go to whomever you please”; yet even then the person to whom they were being sent would not be identified with certainty. Mark and Luke, however, show that the Lord indicated a definite person, although they suppress his name. For the Lord knew to whom he was sending them, and those whom he sent knew how they could find him by whatever signs were given them. Since they knew this, it could not properly be said, “Go to anyone.” The completeness of ordinary speech may permit such an expression, but not in this passage; still less could it have been said so absolutely, “Go to a certain man.”

It is evident that he sent them to someone definite. The Evangelist could therefore have said in his own voice: “He sent them to a certain man, to say to him, ‘I am celebrating the Passover at your house.’” Or certainly: “He sent them to a certain man, saying, ‘Go and say to him, “I am celebrating the Passover at your house.”’” Accordingly, as the most learned Father Augustine wishes, when the Evangelist had set down the Lord’s words, “Go into the city,” he himself inserted, from his own wording, “to a certain man.” This was not because the Lord had said it, but so that he might indicate, without naming him, that there was a certain man in the city to whom the Lord was sending his servants to prepare the Passover for him.

But whether these are the Lord’s words or the Evangelist added them from his own wording, the expression is less familiar to us nowadays. Therefore the outstanding teacher Jerome says that in this passage the New Scripture preserves the usage of the ancients. “We frequently read,” he says, “that one person said to another, in this place or that, which in Hebrew is called Phelmoni and Helmoni; yet the persons and places are not disclosed.” It is therefore certain that for some reason the Lord did not identify the person by name—perhaps so that, with every path left open, an opportunity for the celebration might be provided to all.

Nevertheless, what the others said about the man carrying a pitcher of water and about the large upper room, whether furnished or spread with coverings, belongs to the words of the Lord and Savior. These statements contain great mysteries in themselves, which must be explained in their proper places.

Moreover, when he says, “The Teacher says, ‘My time is near; I am celebrating the Passover with my disciples at your house,’” he does indeed seem to be speaking of the time of the Passover solemnity. That time was not his alone but belonged to all the Jews. Yet he more subtly indicates to us the time that he recognizes as his own, now close at hand, when he had come for the purpose of suffering. This was his time and the hour that had arrived: “to pass from this world to the Father,” which is to celebrate the true Passover.

He was about to celebrate this with the man to whom he was sending his servants, since that man represented all those who would ascend to the heavenly Jerusalem. Entering it, he does so neither without the water of refreshment nor without the water of baptism, because he had already drawn salvation for himself from the fountain of life. He hastens to enter the city where he had prepared a large upper room, furnished for Christ, in which the Teacher of truth might recline.

Thus he calls him “Teacher,” perhaps in accordance with the custom of the one to whom he was sending his servants. In that man’s house he was also going to celebrate the Passover of the New Testament with his disciples. Perhaps he was saying that his time had already arrived sacramentally, since on that same day he was to complete it when he passed over to the typological Passover.

For this reason that house was not below but in an upper room. It was large, so that it might contain Jesus, the Word of God the Father, together with wisdom and truth; none but a large house can contain all these things. And for it to be worthy of so great an inhabitant, it must necessarily be cleansed, containing within itself no filth of wickedness.

This house is shown to be in the city of Jerusalem—that is, in the Church. Therefore the man, namely the master of the house, is presented without a name, so that this mystery may be common to all who wish to prepare a lodging for Christ, where the Passover may worthily be celebrated by the Lord.

This is why he says, “Go to a certain man,” so that they may say to the one who desires to prepare the Passover for Christ:

When evening had come, he reclined at table with his twelve disciples. That is, on the very first day of Unleavened Bread, when he had sent them to prepare the Passover for the evening. Judas was among them both when he sent them and when he reclined at the supper. He was like a wolf lurking among lambs, because the devil had already put into his heart that he should betray him.

While they were eating, he said: “Amen I say to you, one of you will betray me.” As usual, the Truth, because it cannot be deceived, speaks with an oath. For he knew what was in a person; therefore there was no need for anyone to testify to him about a person (John 2:25).

He could therefore have pointed out his betrayer immediately and specifically. Yet he did not do so; instead, he placed the crime within the number, both to test the disposition of each one and to give the wretched betrayer an opportunity for repentance. Since he had foretold his own Passion, it was fitting that he should also foretell his betrayer. By both predictions he showed that he had come voluntarily to that same Passion.

Yet he did not openly accuse the man whose hidden intentions he secretly detected. Perhaps, once exposed in his conscience, he might have believed that the Lord knew this as God, although he had thought that it was hidden from him as from a human being. But the wretched man, after he saw that his conscience could not remain concealed, was blinded by excessive unbelief. Thus he dared to proceed, or, seized by excessive shamelessness, did not blush when secretly detected.

And they became very sorrowful and began, each one, to say: “Surely it is not I, Lord?” This is indeed the virtue of the apostles: they believed the words of their Lord more than their own consciences. Each of them already knew from the Lord’s teaching, although they had good consciences and were free from every betrayal of the Teacher, that human mortality never remains in the same condition. Therefore, each fearing for himself, each considered whether he might perhaps be the one who had been foreknown as the betrayer.

If they, who were conscious of their innocence, nevertheless feared and trembled as weak human beings, what ought we to do, who have never received a conscience of perfect purity or perfect love toward God? If the Apostle subjects his own body to servitude, lest he himself should be found rejected while preaching the word of salvation to others, how much more ought we to fear and commit ourselves to God in all things?

Those whom he foreknows, he also calls; those whom he calls, he also sanctifies; and those whom he sanctifies, he also justifies.

“He who dips his hand with me into the dish,” he says, “will betray me. The Son of Man indeed goes, as it is written concerning him.” He says this on the testimony of the prophetic word, as though he were saying: “He who eats bread with me has magnified his treachery against me” (Psalm 40:10).

This meaning therefore does not differ from what he says: “He who dips his hand with me into the dish will betray me.” By these words he releases the disciples as though they were free, while identifying only the betrayer. Yet the man could not withdraw his hand from the dish, although the others had done so, after he had already been warned privately once and then again.

Here the Lord displays his benefits toward him, while Judas does not conceal his own shamelessness. The Lord had embraced him with such great honors that he was one of the Twelve and the treasurer of what was distributed to the poor. Yet, remembering neither the salt, nor the same table, nor the bread, nor the flesh of the lamb that he had eaten, he shamelessly hastens to betray the giver of good works, although no one could count all the wondrous and divine deeds he had seen or heard from him.

“The Son of Man goes, as it is written concerning him.” He goes to his Passion because he is the Son of Man, destined to suffer through the cross, as the prophets had foretold. Yet he remains with his disciples in the world, according to the word, preserving them in faith. Otherwise they would not have remained in his faith, especially after seeing him hanging on the cross and afterward dead.

It should also be noted that he did not say, “Woe to that man by whom he will be betrayed,” but rather, “through whom he will be betrayed.” He wished to identify another from whom the betrayal came, namely the devil, while Judas was the devil’s servant, through whom the betrayal leading to the Passion was carried out.

For the third time he now touches him, so that punishments, announced at last, might correct the man whom neither conscience nor shame had moved. It would have been good for that man if he had not been born.

Many sharpen the points of their syllogisms on this statement and argue as though it could in no way be good for him who would not exist at all if he had not been born. They therefore assert that he existed before he was born, so that he might be such as he was. For they say that what exists can possess something in addition to what it itself is. Thus he could possess some good even if he had not been born, since it is one thing simply to be something and another to be something in that which exists.

Just as everything that participates in being, so that it may exist, participates in something else so that it may be something, so perhaps Judas, because he participated in being, existed before he was born, in order that it might be good for him to exist and that his condition might be better.

But since these are the arguments of philosophers, who can raise their reasoning from probabilities and introduce certain falsehoods, let us return to the simplicity of divine speech. It says that it would have been good for him if he had not been born, because even when he existed he was not worthy of this good, and he was born beforehand when he did not exist.

Since he came by his own choice to complete this work of betrayal, and the Lord used him for it, he was born to his own harm, so that he might fall into the evil that had been according to his purpose, having been most justly appointed for this by God’s foreknowledge.

Thus it is not said that it would have been good for him not to exist, but that it would have been good for him not to have been born. For although evil befell him, it arose from an accidental fault; his having existed is not thereby denied, although, because of his guilt, it would have been better for him not to exist, according to the just judgment of God, since he had been foreknown for punishment.

This is not because souls existed beforehand, as some maintain, in heavenly places, so that it might be good for them; nor could any good have existed for him, since there was no one for whom any good could exist. Rather, according to the simple understanding of the holy Scriptures, it would have been good for the one who already existed not to continue in existence rather than to continue in such an evil condition that existence itself became evil for him. This would not have happened at all if he had not been born.

Then Judas, who betrayed him, answered and said: “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?” He said to him: “You have said so.”

Here too it is not explicitly stated whether he was the one. Perhaps the answer was so restrained that the others would not perceive it, and so that he might still be given an opportunity to repent of the crime that was in his conscience. His words therefore seem to sound more like defiance than like a genuine inquiry about something uncertain.
