The speech also shows that he was not sorrowful as the others were, nor religious and devoted in faith, so as to address the Lord gently with the others. Instead, hardened in spirit and without any modesty of heart, he speaks as though he were excusing himself: “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?”

He said this so that, by remaining silent, he would not seem to reveal the crime in his heart. He joined to his words the manner of one who flatters, although deceit was not absent from his heart. He therefore calls him “Rabbi,” which is a sign of unbelief, because, after so many signs and miracles, he did not believe that he was God and Lord. Or perhaps—I do not know—he regarded him merely as one of the teachers, and, without any repentance in his heart, was therefore so cruelly and shamelessly hastening to betray him by deceit.

To him the Lord said: “You have said so.” Thus the betrayer is refuted by the same answer as Pilate, so that he might condemn himself from his own mouth. He did not ask because he doubted his own conscience, but pretended to doubt, feigning fear. The shameless man did not care whether he could still be excused; he wished only, for a time, to conceal the plan of his betrayal.

As they were eating, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body.”

Let those who wish to diminish the meaning of the word “body” hear that the flesh of Christ celebrated now in the sacrament of the Church of Christ is real flesh, and that his blood is real blood. I do not know what they wish to applaud or invent, as though the sacrament possessed merely some power of flesh and blood, so that the Lord should be lying and his flesh and blood should not be real—although in them the true death of Christ is proclaimed—when the Truth itself says: “This is my body.”

Likewise concerning the cup he says: “Drink from this, all of you, for this is my blood of the New Testament,” not just any blood, but that which “will be poured out for you for the forgiveness of sins.”

When he broke the bread and gave it to them, he did not say, “This is,” or “In this mystery there is,” the power or figure of my body. Rather, without pretense, he said: “This is my body.” Luke added: “which will be given for you,” or, as other copies read, “which is given.”

John too records the Lord saying in his Gospel: “The bread that I will give is my flesh,” none other than that which is “for the life of the world” (John 6:52). And afterward: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (ibid., 6:57).

Therefore I am astonished at what certain people now wish to say: that the truth of Christ’s flesh or blood is not present in the reality, but that there is only the power of flesh and not flesh, the power of blood and not blood; a figure and not truth, a shadow and not a body. This is said even though here the form receives truth and figure: the body of the former sacrifices.

Thus the Truth says, when he extended the bread to the disciples: “This is my body,” and nothing other than that which “will be given for you.” And when he gave the cup: “This is the cup of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.”

It had not yet been poured out, and yet the blood that was going to be poured out was already offered in the cup. It was already in the cup, although it was still to be poured out as the price. Therefore the same blood was already in the cup as was in the body, just as the body, or flesh, was in the bread.

Christ was whole, and Christ’s body was placed before the eyes of all; likewise, his blood was in his body, and that blood remains wholly intact even today. It was truly given to them for eating and drinking, for the forgiveness of sins.

Let anyone say, if he wishes, whether there is forgiveness of sins in anything other than Christ. It is certain that there is not. Since forgiveness of sins is in this body and blood, it is truly Christ’s flesh and blood.

Therefore those who worthily eat and drink truly eat and drink eternal life, and life remains whole. Then Christ’s body and blood will be life for each person, if what is received in the sacrament is eaten spiritually in the very truth—as I remember having said on an earlier occasion—and is drunk spiritually. For, as the Apostle says, “the flesh profits nothing”; how much less does bread profit without the Spirit, which is seen, “but it is the Spirit who gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

I have said these things at greater length and with greater explicitness because I have heard that some people criticize me, as though in the book I published on the sacraments of Christ I wished to attribute more to these statements than the Truth itself promises. Perhaps they feared that I wished to create divisions and divide Christ’s members one by one, cutting them apart or distributing them, just as those are said to have thought who were scandalized and went away backward.

To them the Savior said: “Does this scandalize you? What, then, if you were to see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?” (John 6:62–63). It is as though he were saying: “If you could understand this, you would certainly know that the one and same Christ, who can ascend whole to where he was before, cannot be consumed piece by piece or divided by teeth.”

This is very difficult to perceive, because it belongs to the Spirit. Who can explain by this understanding how the one Christ, the Son of Man, ascended to where he was before? And what reason can grasp that “the Son of Man who is in heaven came down from heaven” (John 3:13)? Likewise, what words can express that “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), so that what is unchangeable is said to have become something?

Or how can he who was a human being, the Son of Man, placed before their eyes on earth, be said to be in heaven? How, then, did he come from heaven, from which he was never absent? He ascended while descending, because Christ is dissolved in no respect. He is what he was, and what he is was not previously present.

In all these passages, and in very many others, divine power surpasses human minds. Heavenly and divine reason does not submit to human senses, because an inferior nature neither grasps nor understands the cause and reason of a superior and immeasurable nature.

Therefore, concerning such matters as divine power accomplishes, doubt must be removed and hesitation banished. Their knowledge consists in faith; their reason in power; their effect is in things, proceeding from authority; their cause is in the will.

Thus a human being has nothing with which to complain about the individual things God has spoken and willed: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 148:5), as he willed.

The sacraments performed for the salvation of the human race in such matters are very similar to these divine acts. Every day they are celebrated mystically in this mystery, just as they were delivered to the apostles.

For this reason the Passover is celebrated in the upper room: only those who have ascended can comprehend these things, so that they may drink and eat what was poured out for the forgiveness of sins, and yet remains whole.

The Truth itself says here also: “Drink, for this is my blood, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of all sins.” But if it has already been poured out, how is it poured out again now? And if the flesh has been consumed, how does it still remain whole and continue to be eaten?

Behold: what is drunk is poured out every day; and what was sacrificed once is sacrificed even today. Therefore only what is living is sacrificed. It is drunk for the forgiveness of sins, and it is poured out.

But if you ask how it is poured out so that what has been poured out remains, understand how “the love of God has been poured out in our hearts” (Romans 5:5), and remains there. In this way, perhaps, you will be able to recognize that whatever the Holy Spirit accomplishes is ineffable.

And if the love of God has been poured out while remaining in itself, then truly the blood of the New Testament of God is poured out into our hearts for the forgiveness of sins. When it has been poured out, our sins are forgiven in it.

For Christ himself is the high priest who offers us this bread, his body, and pours out this cup; he does not withdraw from his priestly office. And if he remains in us, he too drinks it new with us; and this is so in his whole body and in all of us, because without him we cannot receive it, nor eat of that bread, nor drink from the cup.

Do not be surprised, brother, if perhaps you do not believe these things, because what we are saying is not ours. The Word of God is almighty and effective for everything he wills, according to the multitude of his powers, while he himself is one, the power of all powers.

His words are not the words of anyone other than the one Word who is himself. Therefore they are full of truth, because they are “spirit and life” (John 6:63). They contain nothing other than what the Truth itself openly professes: “Take; this is my body.”

And concerning the cup: “For this is my blood.”

At that time the apostles could have replied, if they did not believe the words of life and truth, or could have asked how that bread and cup of wine could be Christ’s body and blood, since Christ himself, whole in his body, was before their eyes.

But because they believed what he had said, they confess it in silence and receive from him what they afterward delivered to us. They delivered not another supper, but the very same supper that they themselves had then eaten and drunk.

Therefore let the faithful mind consider the difference between that typological Passover, in which the lamb was sacrificed and eaten at the same supper, and this Passover, which is continually celebrated in bread and wine according to the order of Melchizedek.

Concerning this he said at that very hour to all his own: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15).

But if this mystery contains nothing more than a figure of Christ’s body and blood, and is not what he himself said, why was it necessary for him to repeat it in deed, since the whole matter had already been prefigured in the lamb?

Luke therefore also records that two cups were given to the disciples at the same supper: one earlier, after they had eaten the lamb and before he received the bread; the other afterward, once he had blessed the bread, broken it, and given it to his disciples.

Likewise, he says, after he had supped, he said: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which will be poured out for you.”

Here it is made clear that the legal lamb, together with its cup, went before as a figure of Christ’s Passion. Then the body and blood in the cup were made for the completion of the truth, so that everything that had gone before in Melchizedek might be fulfilled in Christ.

No one who reads this Gospel doubts that the cup signifies Christ’s Passion. Therefore it is asked whether Luke intended to indicate that Jesus received two cups, or one and the same cup, because he had anticipated mentioning it and then recalled it again, mentioning it twice.

Some indeed think that there were not two cups but one, which is mentioned as having been given to the disciples both before it was divided and afterward to be drunk. But others, as I stated earlier, more appropriately affirm that two cups were offered to the disciples: in the one, that is, the first, he wished to express his own Passion; in the other, he prefigured the passion of his faithful.

Still others maintain that in both cups he wished to show what was commanded in the Old Testament: that whoever did not celebrate the Passover in the first month by eating the lamb should celebrate it in the second month by eating it. For this reason, they say, the Lord gave two cups to the disciples.

They further assert that in both cups what must be understood is the two Testaments: one of them therefore refers to the lamb, while the other refers to the mystery of the body.

But whether someone holds this view or that, none of them is found to be outside the true faith, provided that he understands this fact: the most merciful Jesus, taking bread and a cup from the figure and shadow of the truth, passes over to the true sacrament of the Passover, so that not even the smallest letter or jot might be cut away from the law.

Indeed, because he is the cornerstone who holds and fulfills both laws, like the true Melchizedek he offers bread and wine, which had been prefigured as the sacrament of his body and blood.

It should also be noted that he says: “He blessed and broke.” Through this blessing and breaking, a new creation is brought about, so that the bread, offered to God in faith in remembrance of Christ’s death, is truly called his flesh.

Likewise, through the same thanksgiving, when he gave thanks to the Father, the blood is created so that it may be believed to be true blood: “which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.”

“For many,” indeed, but not for all, because not all obey the Gospel or believe in him.

Nevertheless, many who do not follow a simple understanding ask from whom Jesus received this bread or this cup, since he is said to have received it. They do not think that “received” should be understood in a bodily sense; rather, they attempt to explain it in a higher way, as though he received it from God the Father, from whom he has all things.

What he first receives, giving thanks, he gives to those who are worthy to receive this bread and cup from God. Hence John says that the Lord declared in his Gospel: “It was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven” (John 6:32).

The Savior receives this bread from the Father and gives it to those who worthily share the supper with him, so that, according to the Apostle Paul, it may be for us “to eat the Lord’s supper” and not another’s (1 Corinthians 11:20, 26).

Therefore, because he received that bread from the Father, he gave thanks to God the Father, blesses it as high priest, and breaks it. As Jeremiah laments, no one else was found who would first break bread for the little ones who asked, except Jesus alone. Receiving it from the Father, he gives it to his disciples and members according to what each one can grasp and receive by faith.

Therefore the Apostle commands: “Whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you will proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26).

“Until he comes,” he says—not the death that is proclaimed in this sacrifice, but Christ himself, so that he may come for judgment. Then these mystical sacraments will no longer remain in faith, but the very truth, which is now rightly enacted in mystery, will be opened with a light clearer than day. What we now receive in mystery will then be openly present to all in fruition.

For this reason he himself also says to his own: “And I will openly proclaim the Father to you” (John 16:25).

This mystery of Christ’s death has, in remembrance, what the flesh and blood of Christ had once in the Passion, so that it is one flesh and blood in the sacrament. By it the human being, a member of Christ, is nourished, and blood is poured out for the washing away of sin at the present time, without which no human being lives as righteous.

“For this is the blood of the New Testament.” Because, in figure of this blood that was to be poured out, Moses once said to the people: “This is the blood of the covenant.” He did not say “of the New Testament,” but rather, “which the Lord has commanded for you.”

This, however, is the blood of the New Testament, because it is not the blood of that lamb, nor of a calf, nor of bulls or goats, but Christ’s own blood. With it he entered the holy places once for all, offering himself to God for us; and he is offered daily in this sacrament, because we sin daily, so that we may be without sin.

Otherwise, how is it called a sacrifice unless Christ is sacrificed in it? For according to the proper meaning of the name or word, an offering cannot rightly be called a sacrifice unless the slaughter of the victim also follows.

Nevertheless, in this bread and wine the priest is rightly said to sacrifice, because in it Christ is, so to speak, slain for God the Father in this offering, either as a victim for our sins or as the food of our salvation.

Amen, I say to you, he said, I shall not drink from this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I shall drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father. But Luke says similarly concerning the bread: “I shall not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.” Behold, as I said, he passes from carnal things to spiritual ones. Therefore all these things that are handed down in the sacrament must be understood spiritually. For if the flesh profits nothing unless it is given life by the Spirit, much less can this bread and wine, which is believed to be blood and flesh, profit unless it is understood that it is all brought about in the Spirit. Otherwise, what benefit could there be in what is digested within us or sensed upon the palate of the mouth? Only that they are sacraments until Christ himself comes, openly presents himself, and shows us the Father.

Meanwhile, with a mind devoted to God and with faith intact, a person truly receives intelligibly in these things what has been newly created—namely, the body and blood—even if the body digests what is outward, because this is how it has been handed down to us by the Lord in the sacrament. In the meantime, whether we read “this fruit of the vine” or “this creation of the vine,” as other codices have it, the question is rightly raised whether the gracious Teacher extended his finger as though pointing toward the bread and cup, before they became flesh and blood, or toward the things he had previously performed according to the Law, certainly so that he might indicate the Synagogue itself, which was the Lord Sabaoth’s vineyard and which he himself transplanted from Egypt; for both interpretations seem to fit.

But if we look to the bread and the cup, then certainly after that he ate no more of them, nor drank, until after the resurrection, when he ate and drank with those same disciples, already incorruptible and immortal. If, however, he is speaking of the things performed according to the Law, he speaks truly, because thereafter he tasted none of the sacrifices and victims of the Jews, until all the sacraments had been transferred into the Church and renewed. But if the subject is the Synagogue itself, from which he willingly received the cup of passion when it was brought to him, he brought none of them through faith into his own body, which is the Church, until after the resurrection, when through the grace of the Holy Spirit he received very many who had been renewed.

That the vineyard transplanted from Egypt is the Jewish Synagogue, Jeremiah shows when, speaking in the person of the Lord, he says, as though the Lord were lamenting: “I planted you as my chosen vineyard; how have you been turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. II, 21). Isaiah says the same in the Song, as does the rest of Scripture in very many places.

Concerning this vineyard the Lord plainly says that he will by no means drink the cup of sweetness until the kingdom of his Father. That kingdom is rightly understood as the Church of God, or the faith of believers, concerning which the Apostle says to believers: “The kingdom of God is within you.” Therefore, whatever you understand by “this fruit of the vine,” of which he says that he will not drink until he drinks it new in the kingdom of his Father, consider how great a unity of the body with its head is commended when he says, “Until I drink it with you.” For when he promises that he will drink in the kingdom, he nevertheless shows that he will drink it new in the kingdom of his Father not without them, but with them.

Only those who have been renewed can drink new wine; the old cannot contain the new. Nor can these renewed ones drink it except with Christ, just as Christ cannot drink it without them. Therefore, since he did not separate his own from participation in the kingdom, nor from participation in his drinking and sweetness, it must in no way be believed that he separated them from the presence of his dignity and glory.

And it should be noted that he says, “in the kingdom of my Father.” He did not say, “in the kingdom of God,” but “in the kingdom of my Father,” because every father is the name of a son. No one comes to the Father except through the Son, just as no one comes to the Son unless the Father has drawn him. And when the Father has brought his own to the Son, then the Lord Christ will drink with them in the kingdom of his Father from the wine of their joy and gladness; and all will be drunk with the wine of God’s charity, just as Joseph was, as it were, drunk at midday with his brothers.

Attend, I beg you, my brothers, to how you ought now to drink or eat at the table of God and in the kingdom of Christ’s Father; for he does not drink that new wine with you anywhere else, nor at any other time than in the kingdom of his Father. Attend to what the Apostle says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink” (Rom. XIV, 17), nor is it what is bodily consumed as flesh; rather, this food and drink that we take from the altar is the food of angels.

Therefore Scripture says: “Blessed is the man who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God” (Luke XIV, 15), because the bread of true life is never eaten anywhere else. For here we are already in the kingdom of God the Father, but still in the sacrament; there, when this kingdom has been fulfilled in us, what exists in part will be brought to an end, and then we shall enjoy him face to face, when he himself and that which is perfect come.

Come, brothers—if I may speak with pardon—for this reason I have labored at greater length on this supper of Christ than the brevity of a treatise requires: in these mystical matters many think otherwise, and many are blind, since this bread and cup seem to them to be nothing other than what is seen by the eyes and sensed by the mouth.

Therefore, so that they may understand more clearly how great is the unity of the body, let them understand the ways in which Christ’s body is spoken of. There is the Lord’s body in which God suffered, but not according to what he is as God. And there is this body in the mystery, which is created in the Spirit and by the power of the word so that it may be Christ’s body, and none other than that which suffered—his own body.

Christ’s body is also the whole holy Church of God, formed from his flesh and bones into one flesh and joined together in the unity of his body. Therefore there is truth in both, and unity of the body; and for this reason this body, which is the intermediary by which we are nourished on the way, is not separated from the unity of Christ’s body.

Nor, because Christ is the head of the Church, is he rightly cut off from his own members, just as the members are not separated from the head, so that members and head may be one body—a mystery which, according to the Apostle, is great in Christ and the Church.

Therefore whoever wishes to live in the unity of the body should mystically understand these three to be one body: for God’s eternal covenant has been established through them in the blood of Christ. For this reason he does not rightly say, “This is the bread,” or “the body of the New Testament,” but: “This is the cup of the New Testament in my blood, which will be poured out for you.”

Nor is it without reason that he rightly calls this mystery a testament, since it is confirmed by the death of the testator. For according to the Apostle, where a testament is confirmed, there must necessarily also be the death of the testator, since, according to him, every testament is confirmed by the dead. The Apostle, following his customary practice, himself a Hebrew with the Hebrews in Christ, also establishes that a testament is of no value to its heirs if the death of the testator does not intervene. Otherwise it is not yet valid while the one who made the testament is alive.

Hence, brothers, the testament that he ordained from Abraham, and that covenant which he made with Israel on Mount Sinai, since it did not come through the death of the one who made it, was therefore weak until it was confirmed by the one and unique death of our Lord Jesus Christ, who made the testament. That death truly became the death of death.

And therefore how beautiful and how necessary it is that this sacrament is offered in memory of Christ’s death, so that it may be the body of our redemption and the nourishment of life within us, and also the blood of the New Testament in the death of the testator himself.

The Old Testament, on the other hand, although all the laws proper to testaments were solemnly observed in it, was nevertheless weakened through the flesh because it had not been strengthened by the death of the Mediator, as the Apostle teaches. But this New Testament, since it was completed when the death of the testator was already imminent, as provision for the journey and as an inheritance of salvation, is firm and ratified forever and will remain throughout the ages.

For only the space of a single night intervened between the proclamation of this series of the testament and the death of the most holy testator, Christ. Therefore, on that same night, he specifically inscribed in the text of this testament those whom he made heirs, just as he instructed them individually concerning what they were to observe. So also, concerning this sacrament of the cup—that is, of his passion—he established that they should perform these things in memory of his death; and thereby, having become participants in his flesh and blood, they should remain one body.

And because our mortality slips daily into the death of sin, it is necessary that the human person be renewed daily into the life of righteousness. When all these things had been duly completed at the same supper, the evangelist immediately says:

“And when they had sung a hymn,” he says, “they went out to the Mount of Olives.”

This is what we read in the Psalm: “All the fat ones of the earth have eaten and worshiped”; for no one who has been satisfied with the fatness of this grain, or made drunk with the sweetness of Christ’s blood, ceases, once filled, from praising God.

But what kind of hymn this was, and in what words it was sung, is not sufficiently shown by any of the evangelists. For this reason many religious men inquire whether a hymn of such great sweetness and delight may perhaps be found written somewhere, even obscurely, in the Gospel, or handed down by one of the apostles. Indeed, they earnestly and carefully desire to know whether a hymn of such great sweetness and delight was omitted by all the evangelists, unwilling to accept that all of them would have left this out.

Hence some wish this to have been that hymn: the wondrous prayer that John records, when, lifting his face toward heaven, he prays to the Father, beginning in this way after the many things he had spoken to the disciples at supper: “And having lifted his eyes to heaven, he said: Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John XVII, 1), continuing until he says: “When he had said these things, he went out across the brook Cedron” (John XVIII, 1).

“If it is not written there,” they say, “then it is not written anywhere at all in the Gospel.”

But that ineffable prayer—or thanksgiving, if I may call it so—does not seem to belong to the same occasion, nor is it rightly believed to be that hymn which the most gracious Teacher was accustomed to sing after the meal. For whatever the Savior deigned to perform through the dispensation of the flesh was either a mystery or an example. In the fact that he prayed there are great mysteries; in this hymn there is an example, just as he himself says: “I have given you an example, so that you also may do likewise” (John XIII, 15).

It is therefore a great example of piety that even today the Church, established by God, does not fail to do this no less before food than after food. But what those words were with which the gracious Lord then sang a hymn to God the Father does not sufficiently appear. Nor is it clear what he said when he cried out again from the cross, “with a loud voice, and gave up his spirit” (Matt. XXVII, 18). What he said there is not manifest.

Likewise, when he took bread and gave thanks, it is not clearly evident whether he did so only in his heart, without words, or aloud; nor is this clear concerning the cup. In such matters, scarcely any composed words are found written. Yet although they are not recorded, because the sequence of the thanksgivings that were to be offered has not been explained, no one doubts that a hymn of praise to God was then spoken in words, at least for the sake of the example, just as thanksgiving was offered, even though the evangelists have not carefully set down such words anywhere.

Nevertheless, we know that our Lord Jesus Christ had also dined before this mystical and unique supper in the house of Matthew; likewise, he had graciously reclined in the house of Simon the leper; and he had also supped with the same disciples in the house of Mary and Martha. In these banquets, who does not know that the author of life and Teacher of our salvation, before taking food, gave thanks to God the Father insofar as he was human, and then, after the meal, according to custom, sang a hymn?

That hymn was already known and manifest to everyone through custom. Therefore the evangelists, hastening to other matters, considered it superfluous to reproduce it in writing. A hymn is properly the praise of God; for it is not a hymn unless God is praised and it is sung aloud in praise of God.

Therefore this was the hymn that was sung to God at all the banquets at which he was accustomed daily to give thanks to God the Father and sing a hymn. Perhaps for this reason the evangelist, as I said, postponed writing about something that occurred so frequently, since it was always in the mouths of them all.

“When he had said this, they went out to the Mount of Olives.”

For they ascend from a high place to higher places, because the most gracious Lord always leads them from virtue to virtues. But long before—not merely before the hymn, but even before the prayer or thanksgiving mentioned above had been offered to the Father—the wretched Judas, possessed by a demon, went out, alienated from the company of all the apostles, before he had shared in Christ’s blood.

Thus the thanksgiving and praise were spoken for and in those who were to remain with the Lord, already blessed in life—as though only those were believed blessed who would ascend with him to the Mount of Olives, where there is refreshment from labors, rest from sorrow, and knowledge of the true light.

Then Jesus says to them: “You will all be scandalized because of me on this night.”

He foresaw everything as God and foretold what they were soon to suffer as a provident Teacher, so that, once they had suffered these things, they would not despair of salvation but would return through repentance and be freed from the scandal of unbelief. Therefore he immediately added the testimony of prophecy—not because what was foretold could fail to occur, but so that all things might happen and be fulfilled as they had been foretold.

To console them, at least after the flight, the scandal of such great fear, and the dispersion caused by excessive trembling, he immediately added: “But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee.”

If anyone asks how, after such great and extraordinary signs of power and miraculous wonders, after so many proofs and the countless mysteries of Christ’s preaching, and after the works and examples of his divinity, the disciples could so suddenly be scandalized, without any firmness of mind or strength of courage, let him know that just as no one can say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit, so no one can endure such things without the grace of the Holy Spirit.

For the Holy Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. And therefore Christ, the provident steward, arranges everything so that he alone may appear to have suffered for all, and that no one may presume upon himself; for only those who are led by the Spirit of God are truly sons of God and remain in the faith.

And notice that the Savior added, “on this night,” so that you might know—as I have often said in these matters—that nothing is without a mystery: neither time, nor place, nor order, nor any narrative of the holy Gospel. For just as, according to Scripture, those who become drunk do so at night, so those who suffer scandals are scandalized at night—those who are in darkness and in the ignorance of night.

But those who belong to the day and to the light do not stumble, because night has passed from them and day has drawn near. Hence the Savior says: “Whoever walks in the day does not stumble.”

But what is written, “I will strike the shepherd” (John XI, 9), without saying where, seems to have taken its meaning from the prophet Zechariah, rather than the exact wording of the passage. For there it is said to God in the person of the prophet, “Strike the shepherd”; here, however, the person of God the Father himself is introduced as saying, “I will strike the shepherd.” Concerning him the Psalm says: “For they persecuted the one whom you struck” (Ps. LXVIII, 27).

It is therefore not surprising if God the Father says that he will strike the shepherd—that is, his Son—to death, since he handed him over to passion for us all. Nor is it surprising if the sheep of the flock are scattered, having suffered the scandal of fear because of their extreme weakness, so that at last they may be gathered into one when Christ rises and follow him into Galilee of the nations, where, because they all fled in darkness according to the Prophet, they may see a great light.

And because in the land of the shadow of death they suffered the scandal of fear, let light arise for them from Christ’s death in their migration.

But Peter answered and said to him: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized.”

He says this altogether from the ardor of faith rather than from rashness or falsehood, insofar as his conscience was concerned. An ardent affection toward God produces this response; it is not the frivolity of his mind.

And Jesus said to him: “Amen, I say to you, on this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.”

The Lord speaks as God, who knows all things before they happen; Peter speaks as a human being, because “every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV, 1). And therefore he says: “If I must die with you, I will not deny you.” Likewise all the disciples said.

Yet Peter does not deny for this reason—that the Lord foretells it—but rather Truth says that it will happen because he is Truth and cannot be deceived. Nor is every human being a liar because the Prophet says this and commands every human being to be a liar; rather, he declares what is true and says universally, “Every human being is a liar.”

Here he shows that Christ is more than human, so that he alone, because he is God, may be truthful. But Peter, inflamed by excessive fervor of faith and love, does not sufficiently consider that the one who said, “I am the truth” (John XIV, 6), cannot lie.

For this reason, as I judge, whereas the other disciples did not presume so far as to go against the truth and were merely scandalized because of Jesus, Peter considered it a small matter if Christ were lying. Perhaps he thought that Christ could more readily be lying than that what he carried in his heart should happen otherwise.

Therefore, because he rashly presumes upon himself, places himself before the others in faith, and does not sufficiently attend to the fact that the one who says these things to him is Truth, he was not only scandalized like the others, but was also abandoned because of the boldness of his rashness, so that he denied the Lord three times.

And if you carefully examine the judgments of all four evangelists concerning this matter, you may perhaps find that Peter was moved a third time by the Lord’s words to make this declaration of his presumption that he would die with the Lord or for the Lord. Matthew and Mark speak of this in the same continuous manner; Luke and John, however, by narrating it in different places, make it more necessary to understand that he uttered this presumption three times, and that the Lord answered him three times that he would deny him before the cock crowed.

It should not seem incredible that, with intervals of time between them, Peter was moved by the Lord’s words to presume, just as he was moved to deny him by various sayings. Nor does it seem absurd that the Lord answered him three times in this way, since after the resurrection we also read that, even consecutively, with no other matters or words intervening, he asked him three times whether he loved him, and Peter answered three times; and afterward he was commanded three times to feed the sheep.

For this reason even our father Augustine considers it more credible that this happened in this way: that Peter presumed rashly three times and therefore heard from the Lord three times about his threefold denial. From the actual words of the evangelists, reader, and from what they recall having been said by the Lord, you will be able to learn this fully for yourself.

To show it briefly, in John, after the Savior had said: “Little children, I am still with you for a little while. You will seek me, and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come’” (John XIII, 35–37), Peter, certainly moved by these words, said to him: “Lord, where are you going?” The Lord answered him: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now, but afterward you will follow.”

Then Peter said: “Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.” To this presumption the Lord immediately responded by foretelling his future denial.

Luke, after saying: “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII, 31–34), has Peter say to him: “Lord, I am ready to go with you both into prison and into death.” And the Lord said to him: “I tell you, Peter, the cock will not crow today until you have denied that you know me three times.”

Who does not see in these three passages of the evangelists by which words of the Lord Peter was moved to presume? I think no one can fail to say that one thing is being spoken of there and another elsewhere, and that in all these passages the origin of such presumption was the same.

Mark, moreover, says these things in the same place as Matthew, almost in the same words. But the other two, because they narrate them quite differently, compel us to understand that the Lord gave a threefold prophecy concerning this matter, because Peter’s threefold presumption preceded it, and because his impulse to presume arose from three different sayings in different places.

And therefore, so that the teacher and master of the whole Church might be corrected, God’s just judgment wisely permitted the one who had refused to yield three times to the Lord’s most firm statements himself to deny the Lord three times.

Otherwise, I do not know why someone so great and such a person would have been permitted by the Lord to enter into temptation more abundantly than the other apostles, unless it was because he considered neither the majesty of the Lord nor his own fragile and slippery life.

Therefore, so that the boldness of his incautious promise might be reproved, he is permitted to enter the temptation of denial according to the number of his pledge. Since he had promised that thing three times without due consideration, he also denied the Lord three times, fearfully and with an oath.

From this we are instructed never to promise anything foolishly, without considering our strength, beyond the measure of our ability. After Peter heard from the Lord that he would deny him, he ought rather to have begged the gracious Lord not to permit this than to presume so upon himself.

For he was not fit to die with the Lord or for the Lord before the Savior tasted death for all. Therefore, because he incautiously presumed upon himself more than all the others, he denied him three times, with extreme weakness, more than all the others.

Some, however, wish to defend Peter by saying that he denied him only with his voice and not in his heart, and that he did so more by pretense than truly. But their assertion is one and the same, and the tears that came from his heart expose them: when he returned to himself, he wept most bitterly, seeing that he had sinned grievously.

They are pious defenders of Peter, who try to defend him in such a way that they prove the Lord to have lied. But their blind defense does not understand how, as part of the divine dispensation, not only Peter but also the other apostles were permitted to enter into temptation.

Among other reasons, this happened so that those who were to become teachers of the churches of God might learn from their own experience never again to presume upon themselves; so that they might know how they ought to bear with others in their guilt; and so that, recognizing their own falls, if someone should stumble—as mortal weakness very often does—none would ever learn to despair of pardon when he saw the teachers of the churches suddenly fall.

Matthew says that the Lord said, “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times”; Luke and John say the same. Mark alone seems to differ from them, saying that Jesus said: “Today, on this night, before the cock gives its voice twice, you will deny me three times” (Mark XIV, 72).

Otherwise, if Mark were not indicating something more precisely, he would never have added “twice,” which the others stated without qualification. For those who speak by one Spirit cannot disagree in any matter.

What must be understood is that Peter’s threefold denial was conceived before the first cockcrow. This is what the three evangelists intend—not that he would complete the whole denial with his words at that moment, as Mark indicates more clearly, but that what was to occur at intervals of time had already been conceived and determined all at once in his mind, because of his excessive fear and dread of death.

Thus all speak truly and with one meaning: that threefold denial was wholly conceived in his heart before the cockcrow and, because of his extreme terror, resolved upon in advance; then, before the second cockcrow, it was carried out with his voice, just as it had already been conceived.

For the whole force of his mind and the disposition of his heart had already been thrown into confusion by the magnitude of his grief and sadness, by fear of such a great danger, and nothing of his strength remained, since anguish and terror had entirely overwhelmed him.

Then Jesus came with them to a farm called Gethsemane and said to his disciples: “Sit here until I go over there and pray.”

Gethsemane is interpreted as “the very rich valley,” or “the valley of rich things.” On the summit of this valley the Lord’s temple was situated. Concerning this valley Isaiah says: “Woe to the crown of pride of the drunkards of Ephraim, who were on the summit of the very rich valley” (Isa. XXVIII, 1), signifying the priests and scribes, drunk with the wine of error, who arrested and killed the Lord there.

Luke calls it a farm without explicitly naming the estate, when he says: “Jesus went out and proceeded, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives” (Luke XXII, 39). “And his disciples followed him. And when he had arrived,” he says, “he said to them: ‘Pray that you may not enter into temptation.’”

This, then, is the place whose name those two evangelists said was Gethsemane. Here we understand that there was the garden beyond the brook Cedron that John mentions. Judas knew the place, because Jesus often entered it with his disciples.

Wonderful is the ordering of almighty God, who so dispenses all things and so foresees them that everything is full of mysteries. For it was not fitting that Jesus should be handed over in the place where he had eaten the Passover with his disciples. Rather, a place was chosen through which this world might be signified, in which the Lord was handed over.

Hence the prophet mentioned above says: “Woe to the falling flower of the glory of exultation” (Isa. XXVIII, 1). When he was identifying the place of the passion, he called it flowering.

And it is said that there was a garden there because the Church of God is in the world, planted with the flowering fragrances of virtues. Jesus often enters it to see whether the pomegranates are in bloom and whether the garden plots planted by skilled perfumers are being watered by divine springs. Concerning these garden plots David says, according to the Hebrew: “As the garden plots long for a fountain of water, so my soul longs for the living God.”

But this garden of delights could not flower toward fruit or sprout before Jesus had crossed the brook Cedron, from which brook he himself also drank on the way (Ps. CIX, 7).

Before he was handed over, therefore, it was fitting that he should pray, and nowhere other than on the Mount of Olives, where the garden was also situated in the valley. It was necessary for him to pray for its sake and in it, because Christ’s Church is truly called a house of prayer.

The Lord therefore does not choose without reason a place of prayer that is most pure and secluded. He wishes that, by virtue of it, the prayer of the one who prays may be purer and more acceptable, in accordance with what is written: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. XXI, 13).

Concerning this place we also read elsewhere: “The land on which you stand is holy ground.” Hence I think it should be asked whether perhaps a place must be chosen in which one may pray more reverently—and whether those with whom one prays must be chosen, as we see the Lord doing.

When the Lord was about to pray above for Jairus’s daughter, he expelled everyone, choosing only three to remain with him; he had also previously decided to lead these three with him onto the mountain, so that they might be witnesses of his transfiguration.

Perhaps, therefore, this is also why the custom of Christ’s Church, divinely handed down by the apostles, is that those discovered in manifest crimes should be expelled from the common prayer. For prayer does not seem to differ because of the place, although opportunity and reverence must always be sought. But this must be understood: it is better for us to pray alone than to pray with the wicked by agreeing with them so that they may remain wicked.

We do not say this so that anyone should rashly judge another or place himself above others. Nor is it fitting to suspect anything sinister concerning the apostles. Rather, one should consider that he alone knew why he said to them, perhaps as a model of secret prayer: “Sit here until I go over there and pray.”

The ineffable dispensation of God commands the apostles, while he is about to pray for all, to remain seated, and takes only three with him. Yet he did not begin to be sorrowful before he took these three and left the others. Therefore all his grief began from that point.

Hence this sadness does not seem to have arisen from himself, but from those whom he allowed to sit there, or for the sake of those whom he took with him. From this, perhaps, all his sorrow is believed to have arisen, since those whom he leads with him are the very ones to whom, placed upon the mountain, he showed what he would be like when he came in his kingdom.

And, taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and deeply troubled. He takes these same men whom he had previously taken both onto the mountain and to Jairus’s daughter. But why he took only these, he alone knows who is the knower of all secrets. Although someone may say that God chose them for a special honor, as above, [Col. 0904A] so that there might be three witnesses, in whom, it is said, every word stands. And just as above they are chosen to be witnesses of his glory, so here they are taken as witnesses to establish the truth of his humanity: namely, that he assumed in himself, without sin, the whole infirmity of our nature. Hence he says: “Then he began to be sorrowful and deeply troubled.” I have already spoken above about passion and propassion: propassion is the infirmity of passion, which falls upon the soul of one who is weakened before the passion itself. For this reason the Evangelist says deliberately, “He began to be sorrowful and deeply troubled,” to show that the propassion of infirmity was present in him and had begun. This was not so that passion might dominate his soul, but so that through propassion the true man, who also suffered, might be revealed.

For it is one thing to be sorrowful and deeply troubled, and another to begin to be sorrowful. If someone should wish to maintain that he was wholly troubled because of his own death, or for some other reason, let him hear the Apostle, who says that he was tempted in every respect according to likeness, except that he committed no sin in himself, and that he sympathized with our infirmities; for he possessed in every respect the likeness of sinful flesh. Therefore, according to the nature of his humanity, he became sorrowful and deeply troubled—not according to that which in him was the treasure of wisdom and of saving knowledge. Thus he says that he began to be sorrowful, for many reasons, and deeply troubled.

Let every Catholic, I beg, attend to Christ’s soul and to what exists in Christ’s soul, so that he may understand the Mediator, God and man. For according to his humanity he assumed the nature that belongs to man; but according to his divinity, the nature that is God exists in Christ himself. When we speak of Christ’s soul, we are speaking of that rational spirit to which God not only came by grace, but which the divinity itself assumed in the unity of person. That soul, together with the Word, is one Christ; that soul, together with the Word, is the one-begotten God. And because the one-begotten God is equal to the Father, he cannot fail to possess and know and will everything that belongs to the Father. And because he is the Son of man, it is clear that he assumed by nature everything that belongs to man. And because the Holy Spirit wholly remained in him—God did not give the Spirit by measure—all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge were in him. Therefore he could not be weakened, although the nature of infirmity was in him, except insofar as, and in those matters in which, he himself willed it according to nature.

Because, then, he was deeply troubled and sorrowful, we must understand that he suffered greatly not for himself but for us, for many reasons. First, after Adam’s fall, we had to depart from this world by such a passage that it was necessary for us to die. God had not made death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living. And therefore he rightly found it distasteful to assume upon himself what he himself had not made. For he saw the company of the Apostles, whom he had nourished with such great care, about to be suddenly scattered; and among them there was also cause for grief on account of the most wretched Judas.

Accordingly, although this is a cause of sorrow, it is not without reason that the question is asked why, at that time, when he had reached the place where he was to pray to the Father—a place where he had so often been accustomed to meet—he is said now to be so sorrowful and deeply troubled. Perhaps it was to express the cause of our prayer: that, at such a time, we ought to become sorrowful especially for two reasons—either because we are involved in evils, or because we are still deprived of blessings.

But since he himself was to be offered in sacrifice for the salvation of the whole world, he saw kings standing by and rulers gathering together against the Lord and against his Christ (Ps. 2:2). Perhaps at that moment, according to his humanity, he saw all those evils which are always before him according to his divinity: the evils threatening the human race and which the world admits piecemeal. Perhaps, then, at the moment of his death, he saw, as I have said, those aerial powers gathered together against him and against the human race. For all these things he groaned and prayed—not for himself, but for us—not casually, but at greater length in his agony, so that a drop of blood fell from him onto the earth through the sweat of his labor, in order that by his prayer he might drive away all things opposed to us and brought against us.

He was also sorrowful for the Jews, whom he had specially chosen for himself as a people and had nourished so tenderly, because he saw them all rushing toward his death. It is therefore no wonder if he is sorrowful for these people, for whom we have read above that he wept. This, brothers, is a great mystery: that he wept, that he was sorrowful and deeply troubled, and that he grieved. Therefore we must not merely defend, as some have done, the claim that he did none of these things for us; rather, we must confess and say that he grieved and became sorrowful for us—he who had nothing for which he should grieve on his own behalf, nor any affection by which he might become sorrowful for himself, and who nevertheless willed to die for all.

Why, then, should I not confidently proclaim his sorrow, his anguish, and his grief, when I read of his tears and his death? Although the function of tears belongs to the body, it is nevertheless the soul that pours them forth through the body’s service; for a kind of grief of the soul, as it were, sweats them out externally. Therefore, wherever tears are proclaimed, the presence of pain and sorrow must not merely be defended but also proclaimed.

Thus, whoever proclaims the cross and death acts foolishly if he denies pain and grief. Christ did not assume merely the appearance of incarnation or of an image, but its reality—not in order to suffer for himself, since he assumed no cause of pain in himself, but in order to suffer for me and to grieve for me, not for himself. Likewise he died for me, in order to restore me from death to life.

And therefore God assumed the whole human being, so that in him he might endure all those things which he could not suffer in himself, because in his entirety he was immortal and impassible. Thus it is not I who am sorrowful, but my soul is sorrowful. Accordingly, faithful hearer, distinguish each point and understand wisely, lest in any respect you confuse the divine mysteries. For although Christ is one, there are in him many divine mysteries.

Behold, the one who reigns dies, and the one who has died reigns. Behold, the one who is unjustly condemned before the judge’s tribunal is believed to sit in heaven as King and glorious. And the one who suffers in the mystery—the Son of man—is himself the Son of God, who suffers in him and not in himself, because God and man are one Christ. [Col. 0906A] Therefore do not be afraid to confess what belongs to the mystery of our salvation, and do not confuse what belongs properly to each nature. For Christ Jesus, God made man, came for this purpose: that, according to the prophet, he might know, placed in affliction, how to bear our infirmities and sustain our pains. Therefore those who proclaim rather the insensibility of his wounds than his pain, and rather a simulation of the soul than its sorrow, must not be heeded.

Then he said to them: “My soul is sorrowful unto death; remain here and keep watch with me.” He says this to those whom he had taken with him from among all the others. It is as though he were saying: “I do not want you to go farther. Let it be enough for you to have seen and heard me sorrowful on your behalf, since I allowed you to come this far so that you might be witnesses of what you hear from me and behold in myself.” For since he had begun to be sorrowful and deeply troubled—these are Matthew’s words—the three had seen with their eyes what he himself had experienced, and they had heard with their ears what he further declared about himself: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.”

He had therefore not brought them this far without reason, as though they were stronger in the struggle of the agony, but so that, although from a distance, they might labor with him in vigils and prayers. To the others, according to Matthew, he had ordered only that they sit; to these he orders that they keep watch and pray with him, as though they were participants in so great a peril. Yet he also commands them to remain within their own rank, so that each person may learn to stand in the place and condition of his calling and not seek what is above him.

For however great may be their grace, and that of all others, Christ is always greater than all; and his uniqueness, because he is God, surpasses everyone. Hence it follows: “And going forward a little, he fell on his face, praying and saying.” Behold why he led them out: so that they might learn not to presume rashly upon themselves, but first to obtain through vigils and prayers that they may see and understand where human ability lies and how far it extends, and in what manner they ought to seek to obtain what they ask.

Let them see him falling and worshiping on his face, and let them hear him say: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” O heavenly instruction, and medicine of salvation! Behold what antidote is set against the disease of such great presumption: they must learn not to think great thoughts of themselves, but to estimate themselves as human beings; not to be quick to make promises, but earnest in seeking to obtain them. Perhaps for this reason he wished to show these things to those who were more prudent or stronger in faith, so that no mortal might thereafter presume upon himself.

“My soul,” he says, “is sorrowful unto death.” What was displayed in his face when he began to be sorrowful is confirmed by his voice when he says, “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” And if his soul received sorrow, then surely his flesh also felt pain, because he truly received wounds and blows.

First let the Apollinarists hear this, since they say that Jesus did not have a soul; then let the other heretics hear it, who suspect that he assumed an irrational soul: how could he have become sorrowful? For although brute animals also appear to experience sadness, they do not know the time of their sadness or the cause of their pain. But he testifies how far he ought to become sorrowful, and he makes the cause of his sorrow clear through many indications. [Col. 0907A] For he does not say, “My soul is sorrowful because of death,” but “unto death.”

Therefore, as one distinguished teacher says: “If this sorrow arose from death, then he who had come for the purpose of suffering death, and for no other reason, ought certainly to have referred the cause to that same death through which he was to suffer, rather than saying that he was sorrowful unto it. For it is one thing to be sorrowful unto something, and another to be sorrowful because of it. Where sorrow is because of death, death itself is the cause of sorrow; but where sorrow is unto death, death is no longer the cause but the end. For what is at the end does not make the cause of death.”

Therefore we should not labor to prove that he did not suffer, or that he was not sorrowful or deeply troubled, or anything of this kind; rather, we should understand that he was not sorrowful because of death. For he had come for this purpose and was prepared of his own will to undergo it, the very death which he urged his followers to meet, and toward which he himself went fearlessly. As I have already said, there were many other causes for which he was truly sorrowful and deeply troubled.

Yet it is not contrary to truth that, since he was human and had assumed all the infirmities of our body, he may also have admitted into himself fear of death—not so that fear might conquer him, but so that by the strength of his virtue he might destroy the fear of death, since the sting of death was not in him. Therefore he alone was “free among the dead” (Ps. 87:6), and he was sorrowful unto death, because his death was the destruction of death and the restoration of life.

As for those who say that all sorrow over death arises only from fear, let them say what they wish. We, however, say that although he possessed in himself all the affections of our infirmity, none of them was present so that he might suffer except insofar as he willed, in whatever measure he willed, and admitted it into himself.

“And going forward a little, he fell”—not backward, but on his face, as is fitting for the saints—“praying and saying: My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” Luke indicates how far he went, saying, “About a stone’s throw” (Luke 22:41). The most gracious Savior did not wish to go far from them, but to pray in their sight, so that they might learn.

It is therefore no wonder if he fell on his face, praying humbly, who became obedient to God the Father unto death (Phil. 2:6), and who commands us to learn that he is gentle and humble of heart (Matt. 11:29).

What he says in prayer is clear: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” With the affection of one entreating and pleading, he asks that, if it is possible, not merely a cup but “this cup” pass from him. He asks this not according to the divine and impassible substance, but according to the weak and passible nature of humanity.

He does not ask out of fear of suffering, nor does he ask not to suffer—he who had come for that very purpose and had often foretold to his disciples what would happen to him. For he undoubtedly knew that it could not happen otherwise. Rather, he asks out of mercy for the former people, so that he might not drink the cup of suffering from them—a cup foreknown and predestined for him before the foundation of the world.

Hence he says pointedly, “This cup.” It is not that he shrinks from the cup of death, but from this cup which was being aimed at him by the Jews, lest it be brought about by those who would have no excuse. For he does not say, “Let this cup pass me by,” but “from me.” The meaning seems different if the cup passes him by, so that he himself may be spared the troubles of the cup that is passing by, and different if it passes from him so that it may not remain with him.

He does not ask that he himself be passed over, so that he might not drink the cup into which he had come—for he was also in that cup—but that it pass from him so that it might not fall upon the Jews. Or, alternatively, he may mean: “Let it pass from me to them”—that is, just as it is drunk by me, so also by them, with every hope of forgiveness and every confidence of salvation.

Otherwise it was impossible for Christ not to suffer. Did he, then, not wish to suffer, when shortly before he had consecrated the blood of his body to be poured out for the remission of sins? If someone should wish to be still more contentious and say that he prayed not to taste death, although he himself had foreknown and foretold it, let him know that we do not entirely deny this either. For it is not surprising if, as man, he refuses death, while, as God, he preserves his own judgment and one will together with the Father.

It is always characteristic of man not to wish to suffer pain. Thus he perhaps says, “My soul is sorrowful unto death,” because “death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9). Although I said above that “unto” means as far as the limit, before death began, it can also be understood as referring to the limit of completed death, at which the end of his sorrow and pain occurred. To say “unto death,” then, would mean “unto the end of completed death.”

This is the customary manner of speaking in many passages, when we say “unto the end of a place,” or when we say “unto the third hour” or “unto the sixth,” intending “unto the completion of that hour.” It is by this manner of speaking that the statement of the Apostle is also explained: “Death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who had not sinned” (Rom. 5:14). This does not mean that the reign of death, which is sin, was dissolved by Moses or by the law, but that Moses, or the law, continued until Christ.

To say “until Moses,” then, means “until Moses is read and completed.” So also, in the case of Christ’s death, since every groaning and sorrow of all people is abolished and every corruption healed, he appropriately testifies that he is sorrowful for all “unto death,” that is, until through his death every death and sorrow is dissolved.

Therefore, just as we must always discern two operations in Christ, through which the one and same Christ performs what is divine in his humanity and what is human in his divinity, each form acting, through communion with the other, according to what is proper to itself, so we must not deny that there are two wills in him. Just as both are everywhere together in Christ, so we understand both here.

He wills and prays according to what belongs to humanity when he says: “My Father, remove this cup from me, if it is possible.” Then, because it is not possible, he returns to the will which he has with the Father, whose will is always one and undivided, and says what belongs to divinity: “Your will be done.”

This does not mean that his will was ever one thing and the Father’s another, but that because he was human he prayed with the affection of humanity, and because he was God his will returns to that in which it had always been. This is a great mystery in Christ, given to shape the minds of the disciples: whenever someone wishes something as a human being, he must pray not that his own will be done, but God’s.

After returning to the disciples, he found them sleeping and said to Peter: “So, you were not able to keep watch with me for one hour?” This is the voice of one rebuking and convicting. It is therefore said to Peter alone because, more than the others, he had boasted and promised that he would not be scandalized, contrary to the Lord’s warning, and would not deny him.

He had not commanded them to keep watch over bodily sleep, whose time had not yet come while the danger of the Passion was impending, but over the sleep of unbelief and the drowsiness of the mind. Perhaps unbelief was already at work in Peter’s soul, and for this reason, because of the magnitude of his sorrow, he could not overcome the sleep of unbelief. We do not therefore defend him so absolutely that we deny that he was weighed down by bodily sleep, since he was already being drawn away from faith through the sorrow of his mind.

To them he says: “Keep watch and pray, so that you may not enter into temptation.” Consider, I beg, the mysteries of Christ. As long as Jesus was with them, the disciples were burdened by no sleep. But when he went forward a little away from them, they could not keep watch for even one hour in his absence. Therefore we must always pray that he may remain with us, as he himself promised.

He commands two things: to keep watch and to pray, because prayer is powerless without watchfulness of mind, and the mind cannot keep proper watch without perseverance in prayer. He keeps watch who continually performs good works attentively and meditates earnestly, lest he ever be overwhelmed by the darkness of sin. For the prayer of one who keeps watch in this way will be heard.

Therefore, if you wish to be heard, you must first keep watch; then, so that you may keep watch well, you must always pray. Neither of these is effective without the other. And the author of salvation himself teaches what you ought to pray. Since human life on earth is a time of temptation, he commands us to pray that we may not enter into temptation.

For he does not say, “Pray that you may not be tempted,” but “that you may not enter into temptation”—that is, that temptation may not conquer you, but that you may be able to overcome it as victors. They themselves were to be tested courageously, and therefore he forewarns them to strive to be victorious.

Hence the Apostle says: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations” (Jas. 1:12), because temptation contains the gain of joy.

“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Many wish to establish that the Savior said this about himself, but that does not seem to follow; rather, this entire speech is addressed to those to whom he was speaking. Otherwise, how could the Spirit of Christ or his soul be said now to be willing, when shortly before it was proclaimed to be sorrowful unto death?

Perhaps, however, Peter is still being addressed here, as though he were being told: “O Peter, how is it that your spirit was so willing to promise that you would die for me, while now your flesh is shown to be so weak that you could not keep watch for even one hour?”

But if the Savior is speaking of everyone’s spirit or flesh, we must consider whether this fits, or whether he is speaking only of the spirit of the saints. Although everyone’s flesh is weak, I do not know whether everyone’s spirit can be called willing, since the spirit of unbelievers is always sluggish toward what is good, as is also that of those shown to be lukewarm.

Therefore perhaps this should be understood of the spirit of the Apostles, or of all the saints. Although their spirit is always fervent and willing, because it desires and struggles against the vices of the flesh, the flesh is nevertheless always weak, even when it appears entirely subdued or possessed by the spirit.

Yet, so that the Savior’s saying may be true, the strength of the saints is perfected in weakness. Hence one of them says: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12:9–10). And because the strength of the saints is perfected in this way, he says: “Keep watch and pray. Even if your spirit is willing to suffer and endure many things for me, your flesh is nevertheless weak. Therefore devote yourselves to prayers and works, so that you may not enter into temptation”—that is, so that the weakness of the flesh may not conquer you, because “the earthly dwelling weighs down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15).

Again, for the second time he went away and prayed, saying: “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done.” He calls the Father his own not by adoption, but by the proper relation of the nature in which he was born from the Father.

He repeats the same words, knowing that the cup could not pass. Yet this possibility of the Father and the Son does not arise from weakness, for all power is subject to them, and they possess one power just as they possess one will.

Rather, because the Father, almighty God, is merciful and just, this impossibility arises from God’s justice and goodness. He is almighty in such a way that he is also just, good, and merciful. Therefore, insofar as both natures are concerned, it was impossible that he should not save by his goodness, justice, and mercy those whom he had created.

He asks pointedly that this cup pass from him. [Col. 0910C] And if it cannot pass as he himself wills, he asks that the Father’s will be done, so that when he has drunk it—that is, when he has tasted death—it may pass from him and from all for whom he drank it.

For if he did not drink it, it would indeed have passed from him, since it would not touch him; but it would not pass from humanity. Rather, death would remain reigning in human beings from Adam until Moses—that is, until the end of the law—which Christ did not come to abolish but to fulfill, until he had drawn all people along with himself and brought them to completion in death.

He therefore wished this cup of passion and death to pass from himself and from his own people, perhaps so that he might not taste a drink of such bitterness, if it were possible—which it absolutely was not, because it was not just. Therefore, so that all justice might be fulfilled in him, the Father’s will must be done. For only those things that are just are possible with him, since he alone is good, just, and powerful.

And he came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. The burden by which they were oppressed had not yet been removed from their eyes: the blindness of their hearts. The Holy Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. And therefore, already weighed down by their imminent denial, they could not keep watch, oppressed by excessive sorrow of heart.

He did not rebuke them as before, but went away again for the third time. The first time he returned and reproved them; the second time, when they seemed more deserving of rebuke, he remained silent and did not rouse them from sleep; the third time he ordered them to rest.

I do not think that he did this without reason, since he testifies that he is the way, and all his works are either mysteries of things prefigured or examples of virtues. If this is true of everything he did, it is especially true here, where the triumph of glory is commended to God the Father through prayers.

No one should doubt that at that time he displayed in himself all the infirmities of our body; no one should be unaware that he fastened to the cross all our sins, for which he was weakened and grieved; and, in addition, he showed us how and in what things we must struggle.

As he was about to engage in the battle of the Passion against the aerial powers and their legions, he first conquered them through prayer, so that all things opposed to us might die in that one man. Therefore he went away alone and prayed, because he alone was to suffer for all.

He therefore prays once, a second time, and a third time, not without a mystery. First, so that we may learn never to cease from prayer, especially on the day of battle and in the time of tribulation. Perhaps this was also because Peter was going to deny not merely the man, as some say, but God and the whole Christ, three times. Rather, the Lord asks three times in prayer because he was to be three days in the heart of the earth for the salvation of the whole world, so that he might be heard before descending to the underworld.

For this reason, perhaps, Paul also asked the Lord three times, until the answer was given that strength is perfected in weakness (2 Cor. 12:9). It is therefore clear that the Lord prayed under this number for a great mystical reason. He could either have continued his prayers or obtained what he sought with one prayer, but he prays three times in order to teach us.

We pray for three things: that he may rescue us from past evils, from present evils, and also from future evils. And we rightly pray only to the holy Trinity, who is one God. We return to ourselves, as it were, threefold, because we live and exist in body, soul, and spirit. Whenever we are burdened in these, we must always return to God, so that at last through God and in God we may rest.

The Lord also, in this threefold mystery of his visitation, prefigures a threefold pattern of future events. Why would he wish to revisit them a third time unless he were prefiguring something great in this? As I have said, the first time he returned to them, he reproved and rebuked them; the second time he was silent; the third time he said, “Sleep and rest.”

The condition of future events is therefore prefigured in them, showing what they themselves would later be. Immediately after the Resurrection, he rebukes and reproves them as scattered, having fled, and also distrustful and frightened. Secondly, after the Holy Spirit has been sent, he finds them still weighed down by the sleep of the law, whose darkness burdened their eyes so that they could not see the freedom of grace and the brightness of the Gospel.

Yet he does not harshly rebuke them during his visitation, until they themselves awaken, lest, held too long by love of the law and oppressed as though by the sleep of faith, they should suffer lethargy. Thirdly, when everything has already been obtained from the Father, he commands them to rest securely in the light of his glory and urges them to sleep in the sleep of peace, so that they may no longer suffer any danger of unbelief.

For it had been obtained through the Savior’s prayers that none of them could fall away from the faith. Hence he says:

“Sleep now and rest. Behold, the hour has drawn near, and the Son of man will be delivered into the hands of sinners.”

But a difficult question arises from this, because after saying, “Sleep now and rest,” he immediately adds: “Rise, let us go. Behold, the one who betrays me has drawn near.” [Col. 0912A] Matthew therefore appears to contradict himself—or rather, the Savior appears to command contradictory things, as though he had first spoken impulsively, not knowing that Judas was approaching with the crowds, and for that reason had said, “Sleep now and rest.” But when he suddenly discovered that they were already nearby, as though suddenly disturbed, he changed his statement and immediately said, “Rise, let us go.”

Far be it from the hearts of the faithful to wish to think this about Christ, as though he had been ignorant of what was happening, when he is always wholly present everywhere. Catholic faith absolutely does not accept this. Therefore some, disturbed as though by a contradiction between the statements, have tried to pronounce the earlier words, “Sleep now and rest,” as though they were the voice of one reproaching and rebuking rather than of one beseeching. Then they take the words “Rise, let us go” plainly, without any contradiction.

If this were necessary, it would nevertheless be better to understand the passage in this way than to bring any criticism either against the Evangelist or against the Savior. But since the Evangelist Mark, after saying, “Sleep now and rest,” adds “It is enough,” and then continues, “The hour has come,” followed by the other words, it may be understood that after saying, “Sleep now and rest,” the Lord remained silent for a little while, allowing what he had announced to occur, and then, after a short interval, said, “Behold, the hour has drawn near.”

Therefore, when Mark adds “It is enough” after the earlier words, we should understand that he spoke as though he were saying: “It is enough that you have slept or rested until now.” If this phrase had been included in Matthew, there would seem to be no ambiguity, which arose from the brevity of the words: “Behold, the hour has come; rise, let us go.”

After he had therefore prayed three times, so that, just as every word stands on the testimony of two or three witnesses (Matt. 18:16), so also all our prayer might be commended through these three supplications—for in these prayers everything that he asked was granted to him on our behalf—he now goes forth secure concerning his Passion and advances fearlessly to meet his persecutors.

He goes voluntarily to be sacrificed, not unwillingly.
