Therefore he says, “Rise, let us go.” This is the hour of which I have already spoken above, known to God from eternity and often foretold in the Holy Spirit. This is the hour that had not yet come when he said to his mother, “My hour has not yet come” (John 2:4). And now, so that you may recognize it, he says: “Behold, the hour has come; rise, let us go,” lest they find us unprepared.

This voice is certainly not one of fear. He addresses the disciples so voluntarily and commands them to rise as though they were the bravest soldiers. For in the spirit he saw Judas—[at what place? the reading is uncertain]—meditating the madness of his betrayal; he saw him approaching, not in faith or in the love of charity, since by his sins he had withdrawn from salvation.

He approached in order to hand over the one whom he had already sold. Judas therefore did what all transgressors do: first they betray Jesus, and afterward they hand him over, because “when sin is complete, it gives birth to death” (Jas. 1:15).

While he was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the Twelve, came, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, and so forth. Perhaps someone asks why they sent so large a crowd with swords and clubs, and the entire cohort of soldiers, to seize Jesus, a most simple and unarmed man, who relied upon no human defenses. It cannot be that they brought so great a multitude without cause. Perhaps they feared the multitude of the people who had already believed in him, lest a great crowd of believers snatch him from their hands.

But I think there was another reason why the multitude came against Jesus. Perhaps some of them thought that he cast out demons by Beelzebub (Luke XI, 15), as though by certain magical arts he might be able to escape, so that they might hold him by force. Others had heard that once, when he was about to be thrown down from the brow of the mountain, he had escaped the hands of those who were holding him; they thought that he had not escaped by an ordinary flight, but had been able to do something beyond human nature. There was indeed much speculation about him among the people.

Hence Mark also says that Judas declared: “Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him” (Mark XIV, 44), “and lead him away carefully.” He seems to have said this maliciously and treacherously, with much slander, as though he were saying: “Unless you carefully seize and hold him, lead him away, and guard him, he will escape from you whenever he wishes, by whatever arts and by whatever power.” Thus, according to Judas’s persuasion, as though Jesus were not acting in his own divinity and in fellowship with the Father’s name, or performing the many other things he had done,

they arm themselves with a multitude of soldiers; they arm themselves with swords and clubs; they arm themselves with deceit and fraud in a kiss, lest he should be able by any means to escape through his power. Hence it follows: “Now the one who betrayed him had given them a sign, saying: ‘Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him.’” O fraud, O ambushes, O cunning deceit! He had preached for a long time throughout the individual cities, villages, and synagogues, so that his fame had gone out into every region; he had performed many miracles among the people; and in the temple he had often taught openly before everyone. Thus, for nearly all who lived in Judea, he was manifest. Why, then, does he give them such a careful sign? And not just any sign, but a sign of peace, a sign of harmony and charity, although he was known to those who had come, who perhaps could have seized him even without a sign.

For since he was manifest to them, he himself shows this when he says: “As against a robber you come out with swords and clubs to seize me, although I sat with you every day in the temple, teaching, and you did not arrest me.” Similarly John reports him as saying: “I have spoken openly to the world; I have always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where the Jews gathered” (John XVIII, 20). And therefore, because he was so manifest to everyone, I do not think it happened without reason that he was handed over by means of a sign involving the eyes.

Hence that tradition seems true which I mentioned above: that there was sometimes on Jesus’ face a certain sprinkling of his divinity, so that two forms appeared in him by turns—one according to which everyone saw him, and another according to which he is read to have been transfigured on the mountain. He modulated this form in alternation in such a way that he appeared to each person according to what that person was worthy of, and according to what he himself judged expedient.

Otherwise, what was the meaning of John’s statement (chapter XVIII, 4), when, after he had said, “Whom do you seek?” and they had replied, “Jesus the Nazarene”—what do you think was the nature and greatness of the power that shone forth from him?—when he said, “I am he,” they all went away and fell backward. What, then? Was this terror in his voice, or in his face, or in both? Whatever it was, and wherever it was—in his voice or in his face, or however it happened—it is evident that divine power was in him, just as it was in the temple when he drove everyone out.

Yet it was fitting that he be handed over with a kiss, since he commands his own to love their enemies, and therefore did not refuse a kiss of peace to his betrayer at the very moment of his betrayal. By this example we are taught even more clearly to love our enemies and not to refuse the kisses of peace, nor to love such people hypocritically. For, so far as it depended upon him, he neither hypocritically calls Judas his friend nor extends a kiss to him deceitfully or dissimulatively. Hence, according to Luke, he says: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke XXII, 48). He intensifies the question with much questioning and with the affection of pious love, reproving and rebuking him. He expresses much grief and love toward him; therefore, although it is to be read interrogatively and with complete solemnity, it should be understood as spoken with the feeling of one who mourns—especially because he calls himself the Son of Man, as though he were saying: “Although I was the Son of God, for your sake I became the Son of Man.”

O pious one, O most wretched man! Why do you so contemptuously betray your Savior, your Redeemer, your Teacher and Lord? You betray that which I assumed for your sake; and not in just any manner, but you betray me with a kiss, which is a sign of love and an indication of true affection. You offer a pledge of true peace, but inflict a wound and the serpent’s poison.

All these things, as I have said, and many others, are to be spoken in the form of a question, as though with the feeling of one who loves and grieves. For the words seem to have been spoken in such a way that both reproof resounds in the voice and the affection of love and sorrow is understood in the mind. Moreover, he is expressly said above to have been one of the Twelve, so that the betrayer’s guilt might be impressed more forcefully and the prophecy concerning him might be more carefully shown to have been fulfilled—the prophecy that says in the person of the Lord: “The man of my peace, who ate my bread, has magnified his treachery against me” (Psalm XL, 10).

“Immediately he approached Jesus and said: ‘Hail, Rabbi,’ and kissed him.” Alas! The wolf still wishes to hide himself, and therefore first greets him, as though constrained by modesty. Yet he does not call him Lord, just as he did not at the supper—for he had not sincerely followed him; he did not believe him to be God, nor did he regard him as anything other than one of the scribes and Pharisees. What is worse, he thought that Jesus acted by magical arts, and therefore treated him so hypocritically and cunningly in everything, as though he were a most worthless slave.

To him the Lord says: “Friend, why have you come?” He calls him “friend,” perhaps by antiphrasis—that is, calling him a friend by name, though not a friend in his actions. Yet, so far as Christ himself was concerned, he was Judas’s friend, for Christ loved him even as an enemy. How, then, is he not rightly called “friend,” at least according to the former name and fellowship, since the Psalm says: “But you, a man of one mind with me, my leader and my acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food; we walked with one accord in the house of God” (Psalm LIV, 14–15)?

Thus there was one accord and one fellowship; it is not inappropriate, therefore, that he is called “friend” according to the former designation—not hypocritically, but according to the truth of the former name. For the Lord does not teach us to pretend, but reveals to us his own simplicity, lest he should seem to shrink from his betrayer, since he commands us also to love our enemies.

Therefore, if you consider Peter’s wounds, for which the Lord rebukes him, and Judas’s kiss, you will acknowledge that the wounds of one who loves are better than the kisses of one who hates. Judas’s kiss was not the same as the kiss of the woman who says in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I, 1). Yet the most kind Lord does not drive his betrayer away from him. He does not refuse him the service of love, and with a rebuking voice says: “Friend, why have you come?” As though he were saying:

“For what you have come, why do you show yourself to be doing something else? You offer a kiss, but it is the sign of betrayal. You do one thing when you kiss me and another when you hand innocent blood over to my persecutors. Do what you have come to do, and complete what you have begun; do not linger over kisses, since your kiss is not a sign of peace or the power of friendship. Therefore do what you have come to do, because you do not have peace with me, since you have not loved it.”

We often read this name used in Scripture to rebuke the wicked, as in: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matthew XXII, 12), and: “Friend, I am not doing you an injustice” (Matthew XX, 13). All such expressions are more characteristic of one who rebukes than of one who approves.

Then they approached and laid hands on Jesus, because they feared that he might somehow slip from their hands. Although, according to John, they had been struck down by his word and had fallen backward to the ground, nevertheless, since they had come for this purpose, with his permission they seized him and led him away bound to the house of the high priest. Meanwhile:

“Behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand, drew his sword, and striking the servant of the high priest, cut off his ear.”

I often admonish—and it is necessary to admonish—the reader of the holy Gospel to learn the differences among the evangelists’ statements by comparing them. For no one can understand one of them fully and accurately unless he follows all of them with the same spirit in which they either differ among themselves, or one says something more and another something less, or one of them inserts elsewhere, in whatever manner was appropriate, things that were said or done.

Although this work involves great labor, its fruit is certainly profitable, and its understanding rich. For example, in this passage, who is the one of those who were with Jesus who stretched out his hand and drew his sword? According to John, it is reported to have been Peter; and the one whom he struck is called Malchus. The ear that he cut off is remembered, according to Luke and John, to have been the right one.

All these details both increase the meaning and, when they are all compared together, commend even higher mysteries in the event itself. Finally, Luke says: “When those who were around him saw what was about to happen, they said to him: ‘Lord, shall we strike with the sword?’” (Luke XXII, 49, 51). This raises a considerable question, especially because they had heard the Lord answer: “Let it be until this point.”

The present Gospel relates that the Lord said to Peter: “Put your sword back into its place,” and so forth. Thus Luke speaks of the disciples’ question and the Lord’s response—“Let it be until this point”—as though this had been said after the striking, and as though the Lord had permitted this act alone, up to that point, but nothing further.

Yet, according to the passage we are treating, the Lord’s words are understood rather to mean that everything Peter did with his sword was displeasing to him. And marvelous is the ordering of God! If he did not want them to strike with the sword, why had he commanded each of them to sell his tunic and buy a sword, along with the other things said here and there concerning the sword? All these matters raise questions for us and, without doubt, generate greater mysteries for those who understand.

With regard to Luke’s question—“Lord, shall we strike with the sword?”—it must first of all be understood as having been asked before Peter drew the sword. It is therefore clear that the Lord answered: “Let it be until this point.” As though he were saying: “Do not be troubled by what is about to happen, but permit them to approach me, so that they may seize me, so that the things written about me may be fulfilled,” and so forth.

But amid the pauses in the questioners’ words, while they were speaking with the Lord, and before the words of his sweetest response, Peter, as was his custom, driven by the fervor of the faith and love that he always had for the Lord, by his eagerness to defend his pious Master, and by his greater agitation on the Lord’s behalf—as a human being who did not yet fully understand the mysteries of God—was moved to vengeance. He paid little attention to what the others were saying or doing, or even to what the Lord was answering.

During these pauses in their words, he struck the servant of the high priest. The evangelists, however, could not state simultaneously all the things that happened or were said at the same time. Luke demonstrates that this is so: the Savior’s response is shown to have been directed not to Peter’s action but to the disciples’ question.

Peter, therefore, did not yet retain the evangelical patience that the Lord had given him, nor the peace that he had bestowed upon them. He was still thinking of avenging himself upon his enemies according to the institution of the Law, and he had certainly not yet learned why the Lord had instructed them to buy swords. For he had not commanded them to strike, but perhaps so that they would not be found unprepared, or because he was speaking of something else.

Thus, when they had said: “Lord, here are two swords,” he said: “It is enough.” For the disciples of Christ need neither more than two swords nor, appropriately, fewer: one in the word, by which a person is struck so that he may be brought to life; the other by which every crime and disobedience is avenged, and, if the person involved does not amend, he is cut off and severed from the body.

Therefore, not only the things that the most kind Savior did or said are full of mysteries, but also the things that Peter did in his disturbance are veiled with mysteries.

Hence Peter did not inflict just any wound, nor upon just anyone: he cut off the right ear of the servant of the high priest. For the high priests themselves were already servants of sin, and all their hearing was not on the right but on the left side of the Law. Therefore whatever belonged to the right was rightly cut off from them, lest they should continue to glory in the things that they themselves had wickedly lost.

Hence the servant is also rightly called Malchus. Malchus is interpreted as “king,” because although the Jewish people had been chosen by the Lord for kingship, they made themselves everlasting servants, compelled by their guilt. Therefore their right hearing is cut off when the understanding of the divine word is taken away.

For this reason the prophet says: “Blind the heart of this people and make their ears heavy, lest seeing they see and hearing they understand, and be converted and I heal them” (Isaiah VI, 10).

Nor was it without reason that Peter cut off his ear, because he had received the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Therefore he rightly condemns who also absolves, since he received both powers from the Lord. Yet the Lord alone is he who heals what has been cut off; he alone restores hearing to very many of the Jews.

Otherwise, unless the good Lord restored hearing to some of them, they would certainly have remained deaf even to this day. None of them would have heard the word of wisdom, because all were servants, sold under sin. For “whoever sins is a slave of sin” (John VIII, 34). And unless they had been servants who ought to have reigned, their ear would never have been cut off by Peter.

The Lord said to him: “Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword.”

Many dispute this passage, as though all who use this sword in warfare and in public affairs must perish. Concerning this sword the Apostle says: “For the judge does not bear the sword without cause; for he is God’s minister” (Romans XIII, 4), for good, for the punishment of evildoers; “but if you do evil, be afraid.”

For if this statement had to be observed literally by everyone, I do not know whether such a custom ought to exist among the laypeople in the Church, so that all of them would serve with the sword insofar as its use is concerned. Yet the Savior made no exception: “All,” he says, “who take the sword will perish by the sword.”

He does not say that they ought to perish by the sword, or for what purpose they took that sword—whether perhaps for homicide or for the punishment of evildoers—but he says indiscriminately: “Everyone who takes the sword.” Nor does he sufficiently explain by what sword they will perish, or in what manner.

This, however, we know with certainty: all who use the just sword do not always perish by it, especially when they use it precisely so that they may not perish. Nor can it be that those who now carry this sword or strike with the sword are all struck, without any reconsideration, by that divine sword in punishment for sin.

Indeed, the sword that turns before Paradise is itself said to be turning and flashing, and the sword proceeding from the mouth of God in the Apocalypse of John is sharp on both sides (Revelation I, 16).

Therefore, when the apostles had said, as I mentioned above, “Here are two swords,” the Savior said: “It is enough.” Accordingly, it is certain by which sword all who use the sword will perish: either by that sword by which they rise from guilt and return to life, or by that sword by which, because they refused to be corrected, they fall under divine judgment and are cut off from the body of Christ.

If this is so, those who use the sword in whatever manner have already been judged, because by using the sword they will perish through it. But, as I have said, death by the sword is not customary for all who use the sword. Many are destroyed by some other accidental event, although they use the sword either for the sake of judgment or in the service of military duty.

Nevertheless, he commands Peter to put his sword back into its sheath because all those who had come against the Lord armed with swords and clubs were to be slain not by a human sword but by the sword of his mouth. For Peter’s sword was rightly drawn for their destruction, so that he might slay with the sword of the word those who used their own sword for crime.

Yet Peter himself is not read to have been slain by the sword that he used, unless perhaps he received a greater punishment. This kind of expression must therefore be understood in the same way as the Apostle’s warning that we should not present our members as weapons of sin.

Whatever member it may be by which we have sinned, or whatever carnal desire it may be, is rightly called a sword or a weapon of sin. Whoever uses that sword, because he has struck himself or another with the sword of sin unto death, will perish by the sword of sin—that is, he will justly be condemned in his own sin, whatever he may have committed.

For just as there is no sword more penetrating unto death than sin, so there is no sword more penetrating unto life than the power of the word of God. Each sword, therefore, slays a person, either unto death or unto life.

And therefore, without qualification, whoever takes up or uses the sword—whether the sword of sin unto death or the sword of righteousness unto life—will perish by the sword: either by the word of God, so that he may rise wholly to God for the better, or by the sword of sin, so that he may perish for the worse and fall into death.

“Or do you think,” he said, “that I cannot ask my Father, and he would provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” Immediately he introduces the question of prophecy and indicates that the alternative cannot happen except as it had been foretold, saying: “How then would the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen in this way?”

As though he were saying to Peter: “Why are you hastening to provide me assistance, and why do you think that you can conquer by your human sword? Do you think that, for the sake of the twelve apostles, I cannot obtain from my Father even more than twelve legions of angels?

“I do not need your help, then, or a human sword; therefore put your sword back into its place. Even if the twelve tribes of Israel wished to bring me assistance, I could have had more legions of an angelic army to provide help, if I wished, with their unconquerable sword.”

From these words it is clear that, after the manner of a human army, that angelic host is much more numerous, and that its legions, assigned to provide human assistance, are more numerous. Hence Luke says that, at the Savior’s birth, a multitude of the heavenly army sang and praised God. The Apostle Paul also testifies that they have been placed in defense of the saints, for the sake of those who are to receive the inheritance.

Jacob too encountered a multitude of the divine army, which would relieve him of his fraternal fear and guard him. Hence he called the place where they had been stationed Manaim, that is, “the camps of God.”

I have said these things so that the faithful soul may learn to trust in divine assistance and the protection of angels more than in human strength. For wherever there are people who truly fear God, there the camps of angels are rightly believed to be around them. Concerning these David says in the Psalms: “He will send the angels of the Lord around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Psalm XXXIII, 8).

For he himself is the angel of great counsel, who sends legions and armies to those who fear him and to himself; he himself is the one who now professes that he can obtain from the Father more than twelve legions.

Therefore let those who say that he was afraid at the moment of his Passion listen. Behold, already among the hands of those persecuting him, among swords and clubs, and amid the entire cohort, he testifies that he has God the Father and that, if he wished, he could obtain angelic legions.

Yet he does not say these things as though he himself were inferior to the angels and needed their assistance, although according to Luke he is read to have been strengthened by an angel while in agony. For if, according to Elisha—as the Book of Kings relates—a very great army stood by him for his assistance, it is much more credible that such an army was not absent then, even though the angelic legions were not displayed.

But the Lord arranged everything in this way so that the Scriptures might be fulfilled, and so that it might be shown that “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Corinthians V, 19), while he himself, as man, suffered because it had to happen in this way. Through this event a higher understanding would always be shown, as, for example, through the twelve legions.

For, according to the ancients, one legion is said to consist of six thousand men. If you multiply that number, there are seventy-two thousand angels—not without a great mystery. For seventy-two human languages are believed to exist in the world.

Therefore, by the wisdom of God, this number has been included here with great wisdom, so that you might understand that, even if the whole world had come against him, nothing could prevail against him unless he wished it. Against each nation of the human race he could have sent more than one legion of heavenly citizens.

But he chose that the Scriptures should be fulfilled, because it was necessary for him to suffer in this way, to rise again, and to enter into his glory.

At that hour Jesus said to the crowds: “As against a robber you come out with swords and clubs to seize me, although I sat with you every day in the temple, teaching you, and you did not arrest me.”

As though he were saying: “It is foolish to seek with swords and clubs the one who freely handed himself over to your hands; and it is utter blindness and great madness of heart to seek with torches and lanterns in the night the one who is always with you—as though he were a robber hiding in the darkness, or as though he were avoiding your sight—when I sat with you and taught everyone openly every day.

“What need was there, then, to seek me through this betrayer and investigate as though I were fleeing, when I sat with you and taught all of you openly every day? What are you doing, except demonstrating that you are in darkness? For your power is the power of darkness. Therefore you have come to seize me in darkness because you have lost the true light.”

But all this happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Much is contained in this one event; therefore he says: “So that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.” For in this passage the Scripture of not merely one prophet is fulfilled, but of nearly all the prophets, who spoke of these matters in many forms and in many ways, by words and by deeds.

I do not know whether anyone could select or collect how many and how great are the prophetic utterances fulfilled in this passage. To mention only a few among countless examples: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter” (Isaiah LIII, 7), along with the other things foretold there. Elsewhere: “He was led to death by the wicked of the people,” or “by the ungodly.” And also: “Many dogs have surrounded me; the assembly of the wicked has besieged me” (Psalm XXI, 17), along with all the other things read in that Psalm.

Accordingly, since it would be lengthy now to repeat each individual testimony of Scripture, let the prudent reader understand that everything done in this passage—from the place where it says, “While he was still speaking, behold, Judas,” and so forth, through the end of his Passion—was done so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.

Then all of them, leaving him, fled. These were the disciples who had previously boasted that they would die for him and promised that they would never deny him. Their dispersal represents the scattering of the flock and the fulfillment of the truth, as he himself says through the prophet:

“I have become a reproach to all my enemies, and exceedingly so to my neighbors, and a terror to those who knew me. Those who saw me outside fled from me. I have been forgotten as one dead from the heart.”

But they, holding Jesus, led him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and elders had assembled. He did not therefore first come to the house of Caiaphas; according to John, he was led first to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who himself was also high priest. In Annas’s house he endured many insults until morning, during which Peter also denied him three times.

But since it would be lengthy and more difficult to distinguish what happened in Annas’s house from what happened in Caiaphas’s house—because the evangelists seem to disagree among themselves, although they speak with one spirit—one of them intends first to explain Peter’s denial and only afterward to record these insults against the Lord, while another inserts these events in between. Another first relates the Lord’s insults and then Peter’s temptation.

Nevertheless, each of them, according to his own manner, gives the individual events in their proper places, so that the whole truth may be seen woven into Christ’s garment, and so that the variation itself may be shown to adorn it in a marvelous way. Whatever one of them omitted is fully supplied by another.

Thus we must consider how carefully Matthew speaks. He does not, like John, specify where Jesus was first led; rather, he says simply: “They seized Jesus and led him to Caiaphas the high priest.” He does not say “first,” nor when this happened, but only that he was led to him.

John, emphasizing this more carefully, says: “Then the cohort, the tribune, and the attendants of the Jews seized Jesus, bound him, and led him to Annas first” (John XVIII, 12). In Annas’s house, therefore, many kinds of insults were inflicted upon him until morning, after Peter’s denial had already taken place.

Then, as John testifies more fully, Annas sends him bound to Caiaphas the high priest. This is what Matthew now says, omitting Annas, to whom he had first been brought and by whom he had been insulted. The present evangelist also recounts some of these events by way of recapitulation, as he does with Peter, so that, unless one considers the matter carefully, they may appear to have taken place in one and the same house.

Nor does it matter greatly if their house is called one house and their authority one authority—that of Caiaphas—because Caiaphas held the higher place in the priesthood, and whatever Annas had done belonged to Caiaphas. They had one purpose, one will, one iniquity, and one agreement in wickedness.

It is therefore no wonder if wicked high priests devise wicked counsels, judge unjustly, and wickedly encourage the wicked toward iniquity. They had not obtained the priesthood by succession, as the Law promulgated by the Lord commands; rather, as Josephus relates, he had wrongly purchased from Herod a high-priesthood lasting only one year.

Such priests, therefore, are always to be feared—those who pursue the honors of the Churches for a price and not by the grace of the Holy Spirit. With them a false council is always assembled, false witnesses are sought, and with them not truth or religion but unjust authority is always preferred in matters of judgment.

Now Peter was following him from a distance, as far as the courtyard of the high priest. Having entered, he sat with the attendants to see the outcome of the affair.

All these events concerning Peter, and the many insults and punishments inflicted upon Jesus at Annas’s house before he came to Caiaphas, are rightly understood to have taken place in this sequence, as I have said. Yet Peter, above all the others, still follows out of the fervor of his faith, although from a distance. Because he had already been overcome by fear in the first confusion, he did not dare to follow closely, as it is said: “Those who were near me stood far away” (Psalm XXVII, 13).

He followed either out of a disciple’s love, or out of human curiosity, wishing to know what would happen to him, or what judgment the high priest would give concerning him—whether he would hand him over to death or release him after scourging. He did not sufficiently remember how often he had heard from the Lord that he would be scourged and crucified.

Nevertheless, Peter’s constancy still appears greater than that of the other apostles: while they flee, he, although far away, at least follows the Savior from a distance. He does not withdraw from him completely, but neither does he follow him closely.

He reached the courtyard of the high priest—not Caiaphas’s, but Annas’s—where he was going to deny the Lord. For what the Lord had foretold could not fail to happen. Having entered, he sat with the attendants—not to serve, but to see the outcome of the affair, which he could not see in the courtyard, nor where the elders of that people had assembled.

I do not know whether someone might perhaps be able at present to see the outcome of Jesus, which some manuscripts have: the consummation’s end. For whoever can see this will see the Word of God and Wisdom, which is Christ, who says: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Revelation I, 8).

The chief priests, and the whole council, and the elders of the people, were seeking false testimony against Jesus in order to hand him over to death, and they did not find any, although many false witnesses had come forward. What, then, did they not find? Did they not find false testimony against the Lord, which they were seeking? But if they did not find false testimony, far be it from any mortal to believe that they found true testimony against him, so that they could justly hand him over to death. Otherwise, how would they have been false witnesses if they were speaking the truth? And since those who came forward were false witnesses, how did they not find the false testimony they were seeking? They certainly found the falsehood they were seeking, and not the truth; for Jesus was innocent, and those wretched and blind men were not seeking the truth, but were all deliberately considering how they might hand him over to death.

Hence, as some manuscripts have it, as I said, they “did not find the outcome”—that is, they could not determine either how to frame the false testimony itself or how to present it fictitiously in such a way that it might appear even remotely credible. This is what the evangelist means when he says, “They did not find it”: not that they found no falsehood, but that they could not shape it in such a way that its falsity would not also be apparent to Pilate. Therefore Pilate clearly knew that they had handed him over out of envy. [Col. 0922B]

Another reading in the manuscripts says: “Although many false witnesses had come forward, they found nothing in him.” From this it is evident that, according to the prophet Isaiah, among that people, from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, there was no soundness, but only one iniquity in all of them and one common intention. [Col. 0922C] Yet their cunning was not so subtle that even their falsehood could seem to possess some likeness to truth. Among wicked judges, false testimonies ordinarily have force when they are deceitfully presented with some semblance of truth. But Christ’s utterly pure conduct and blameless life prevented this, because no deceit was found in him. Thus he gave them no opportunity against him by which they could support their lies.

Wretched is the people whose rulers are wicked and whose elders are perverse, because false witnesses are never lacking in their councils. A ruler who willingly listens to lies will have all his ministers impious—how much more so if he actively seeks them, as we see these men doing! Hence it is said: “The synagogue of sinners is a heap of stubble” (Eccli. XXI, 10). Yet among such people the praise of a righteous man is condemned though innocent. [Col. 0922D]

Meanwhile, even in this passage, the arrival of many false witnesses, the favor shown to Caiaphas, the agitation of the chief priests, the convocation of the priests and scribes, and likewise the conspiracy of the elders and the entire council—all this serves to magnify the praise of Christ, and to proclaim the blamelessness of his life and teaching. He did and taught everything so irreproachably that many lying, cunning, and crafty rulers could find in him nothing resembling evil.

Then follows: “At last two false witnesses came forward and said: ‘This man said: I can destroy [lacuna] of God, and after three days rebuild it.’” Yet these two themselves disagreed with each other, as Mark shows when he says: “And some others arose and bore false witness against him, saying: ‘We heard him say, I will destroy this temple made with hands, and after three days I will raise up another, not made with hands.’ And their testimony was not consistent” (Mark XIV, 58–59). [Col. 0923A]

Thus their testimony was inconsistent because one man perhaps reported his words in one way, as Mark recounts, and the other in another way, as Matthew does. Yet both were liars with one spirit, and both were therefore false witnesses. Whether they said these things twice, as the two evangelists report, or whether one said this and the other that, if you consider what John says the Lord said about this temple, you will prove that both were false witnesses. Each evangelist makes this clear when he declares that they were false. [Col. 0923B]

For John says that Jesus said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” John himself then adds: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John II, 19). Consider, therefore, the craftiness of the two false witnesses, who, using their false persuasion, construct false testimony for themselves from a saying of Christ. The Savior did not say, “I will destroy this temple made with hands,” nor that he would rebuild another after three days, as Mark reports. Nor, according to Matthew, did he say, “I can destroy the temple of God.” He was not speaking of that stone temple, but, as John says, of the temple of his body. They altered his words in order to magnify the charge and make it appear impossible, twisting them into an accusation against him so that they could make him seem a liar by means of their own lie. [Col. 0923C]

Jesus had not said, “I can destroy the temple of God,” but, “Destroy it”—touching, as it were, the temple of his body with his finger. Nor did he command them to do so; rather, he permitted the destruction of his body in accordance with the purpose and impiety of their hearts, allowing them to do what they wished. They were suited to such a deed, so that the crime they were already plotting in their minds might become the salvation of all believers.

Why, then, would the evangelists single out these two, since many false witnesses had come forward? The reason is obvious: these two alone had something that appeared plausible, which they were seeking so earnestly, as I said. But even their testimonies did not agree with one another, nor were they true, although by their lie they could deceive the unwary. [Col. 0923D]

And the high priest rose and said to him: “Do you have no answer to what these men are testifying against you?” But Jesus remained silent.

The high priest therefore rises in anger, driven by the madness of his fury. He rises because there was in him no modesty, no dignity of character, and no integrity of discipline. He rises especially in anger, inflamed because he found no place in Christ for the slander of falsehood, and so wished to display the madness of his own mind.

But Jesus remained silent, judging him unworthy of an answer, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “When the sinner stood against me, I was silent and was greatly humbled, and I was silent concerning good things” (Psal. XXXVIII, 3). None of those to whom he might speak was worthy. [Col. 0924A]

Thus savage anger and fickleness of mind drive the deranged high priest from the seat of judgment. The more benign Jesus remained fearlessly silent, the more that man, overcome by madness, provoked him to answer on any pretext, if he might perhaps find an opportunity to accuse him. But the most gentle Savior nevertheless remains silent, because, as God, he knew that whatever he answered would be twisted entirely into an accusation.

More deeply provoked by this silence, the high priest said to him: “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.” He adjures him as though in accordance with the Law, just as a woman who is held liable to the ordeal of jealousy is adjured. But he does not do so with the intention of believing, for when he heard Jesus confess, he could not endure it; rather, he acted so that he might condemn him. He questions him with the same disposition as the devil. [Col. 0924B]

Thus he does not ask without doubt, just as we read that the devil himself once did. Nor is this without reason: since he was from the devil as his father, he asks in this way, “If you are the Christ, the Son of God,” just as the devil did—except that he adds something more to his deception by administering an adjuration when he says, “By the living God,” in order to force a confession of the truth. Whatever had been said in the Law about Christ and the prophets was not accepted by them; and if Jesus said what he was, he would be punished.

Peter’s confession is one thing, when he says, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI, 16), and the confession of this high priest is another. Although he knew that Christ was the Son of the living God, he did not understand the mystery that was to come, and he disdained him as God. He does not confess him; rather, by asking, “If you are,” he denies everything he had heard in the Law and the prophets, everything he had learned about his divinity through miracles and deeds. Therefore, as blessed Peter was above all, so this Caiaphas was more wretched than all. [Col. 0924C]

Because he was unworthy of Christ’s teaching, Christ neither taught nor instructed him. Instead, he took the words from his mouth and turned them back against him, saying: “You have said so.” Thus he neither appeared to deny that he was the Son of God—for that would have been a lie—nor did he wish to confess in plain speech that he was, lest he be seized.

He therefore gives him a reply like the one given to Pilate, because it was fitting that, since they were alike in deed, they should be made alike in the punishment of condemnation—except that this man was more criminal in condemning than Pilate was in acquitting.

“Nevertheless, I say to you: From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.”

The “nevertheless” connects what he says with what came before, as if he were saying: “Although I have answered, ‘You have said so,’ from now on you will see what has hitherto been foretold fulfilled in deeds. And because you are ignorant of the Law in which you glory, and know neither its mysteries nor the prophecies of the prophets, and do not seek by faith to know that I myself am the Christ—as though the Law and the prophets had spoken obscurely about me—although I have said, ‘You have said so,’ from now on you yourselves will see openly all that has been written about the Son of Man fulfilled and revealed more clearly than daylight.” [Col. 0924D]

Matthew and Mark say “at the right hand of Power,” without adding “of God,” whereas Luke is read to have added it. I do not think, as some wish, that this introduces a new problem. Rather, we should ask what is meant by the words: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power.” [Col. 0925A]

All three evangelists write in the same way: “You will see him sitting.” We must ask who will see this, whether they will see him sitting from the time when these words were spoken, or to whom he is speaking. In the word “sitting,” the form of a reigning figure is introduced—as if he were saying that he is established above Power or firmly enthroned. Thus it was said: “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear”; and elsewhere: “I saw God sitting upon a high and lofty throne,” along with the many other passages in which this is read concerning him.

A diligent investigator will be able to compare each of these passages with the present one and investigate what he means by “from now on”: namely, that Christ, who at that time was held in such low estimation, stood accused before the entire council, while now the Son of Man is proclaimed as seated in such glory—not the Son of God, but the Son of Man—unless perhaps his enemies were there, those who were persecuting him, concerning whom the prophet had foretold: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Psal. CIX, 1). [Col. 0925B]

Perhaps those men were among the enemies to whom he was saying: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power.” Those who are said by God the Father to become his footstool are surely the very ones over whom, when he rises as victor, he promises that he will sit.

For from the time when the Son of Man rose from the dead, as he himself says, “All power has been given to him in heaven and on earth” (Matt. XXVIII, 18). From then onward all the elect saw him, through faith, presiding at the right hand of the Power of God—that is, of his Church, which by the power of God has been placed at the right hand.

This Church, whether it is called the throne or the seat of Christ, has been gathered and assembled from the time of his resurrection and will continue to the end. In it the Son of Man is seen both sitting as victor and coming on the clouds of heaven, because those clouds of heaven are the very ones of whom it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psal. XVIII, 2). Through these clouds he himself comes to individuals, and in them he scatters the rains of his utterance, sifting waters from the clouds. [Col. 0925C]

That there were in that council people with whom and about whom Jesus was speaking in this way is proved by the Acts of the Apostles, where we read that among the Jews three thousand believed in Christ on one day, and on another day five thousand. They saw him through faith sitting at the right hand of the Power of God and coming on the clouds.

They themselves were those clouds, because from that primitive Church of Christ, in which the author of life presided, the whole world was watered. In these clouds of heaven, we ourselves who are speaking even now see that same Son of Man, who was speaking before the rulers of the people, coming—if we think and understand rightly.

This prophecy has already filled the whole world and will be fulfilled to the end. Mark also concludes his Gospel in this way: “And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God” (Mark XVI, 19). Indeed, Christ sits in heaven in his Church, because the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom. [Col. 0925D]

Then the high priest tore his garments, saying: “He has blasphemed. Why do we still need witnesses?” The same rage or fury that had earlier driven him from the priestly seat of judgment compelled him to tear his garments. This tearing of his clothing was, so to speak, a prophecy or sign: it showed him confessing himself guilty with his garments torn, and it demonstrated that the Jews had entirely lost the glory of the priesthood and that their high priests would thereafter possess an empty seat. [Col. 0926A]

It is therefore not surprising that, though he prophesied unknowingly, he now displayed in his madness something against himself and against his own people. It was the custom of the Jews, whenever they heard something blasphemous against themselves or against God, to tear their garments; we read that Paul and Barnabas did this as well. It is also the custom of some peoples, when they grieve over having been found guilty, to tear their clothing and bare their breasts as though these were guilty, and thus lament while covered with many accusations. [Col. 0926B]

But because he had said, “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting,” and so forth, the high priest said that Jesus had blasphemed. Therefore, as though in accordance with the Law, the frenzied crowd, seeking to please the elders, cries out—as the mob is accustomed to do: “He is guilty of death!”

Then they spat in his face and struck him with blows. Others slapped him in the face, saying: “Prophesy to us, Christ. Who is it that struck you?”

As I have already said, the Lord is understood to have suffered these things in the house of the high priest, where he had been brought. These events continued until morning, when Peter too was being tested in the same house.

Because Christ had made great claims about himself, saying that he would sit at the right hand of the Power of God, they thought they were bringing shame upon him. But he willingly allowed these things to happen so that everything spoken about him might be fulfilled. [Col. 0926C]

For it was written: “I gave my body to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who pulled out the hair; I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isa. L, 6), along with many other things that were fulfilled in him just as they had been written by the prophets.

Perhaps they had earlier heard him prophesying about the Temple and Jerusalem, saying that it would be destroyed. Therefore, to mock him, they ordered him to prophesy which of them had struck him. But it was foolish to answer those who were beating him, for he had come for this purpose like a lamb, not opening his mouth, so that Scripture might be fulfilled.

Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. He was sitting outside so that he might see the outcome of the affair, and he did not approach Jesus, lest the servants form any suspicion about him, since he was already possessed by fear. [Col. 0926D]

Here too Peter’s perseverance with the Lord is remarkable. Although he was afraid, he did not abandon him. Fear came from nature, but care came from the affection of piety. What he fears is alien to him; what he does not flee is his own. What follows is the devotion of piety; his denial, however, is the sudden intrusion of fear. The falling away from faith is common, but the repentant grief and the bitter tears are his own gift.

And one servant girl approached him, saying: “You too were with Jesus the Galilean.” But he denied it before everyone, saying: “I do not know what you are saying.”

What, then, does it mean that a woman is the first to expose him? Men could certainly have recognized him more readily. I would say that this did not happen without reason. It happened not by chance that this sex went before in the devil’s work and in the Lord’s death, so that the deception of the first woman might be remembered and that this sex might be redeemed through the Lord’s passion. Thus it also received the first testimony of the resurrection, in order to erase the ancient error of transgression and cleanse the crime of this betrayal. [Col. 0927A]

Some, out of pious affection, say that Peter did not deny God but the man, as though he were saying in his heart: “I do not know the man,” or, “I do not know what you are saying in your womanly manner, because I know the Lord.” But I prefer to understand Peter as having denied him rather than to suppose that he deceived God in any respect.

What, then, did Peter deny? In every way, what God had foretold, because there was nothing in Christ other than what God is. And just as Christ, God and man, is one, so the whole Christ, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one God.

Nevertheless, we must consider where Peter denies him: not on the mountain where he had been with the Lord, not in the Temple, and not in his own house, but in the Jews’ praetorium and at night, in the house of the high priest. There he denies him where truth is absent, where Christ is bound, where Christ is mocked, where the female doorkeeper had let him in and questioned him with her deceit, and where innocence is difficult to preserve.

For this reason his fault is more pardonable than Adam’s was in paradise. Concerning Peter’s threefold denial, there is great variation among all the evangelists in the wording, but one completion of meaning. Therefore a prudent reader should compare their accounts, so that together they may complete one meaning.

Then follows:

As he was going out through the gate, another servant girl saw him and said to those who were there: “This man too was with Jesus the Nazarene.” And again he denied it with an oath: “I do not know the man.” [Col. 0927C]

He did not deny him again outside in the courtyard, where he had been before, nor before the gate, where he is said to have gone out, but when he had returned to the fire. Matthew does not say when he returned. But Mark says that he went outside before the courtyard, and the rooster crowed. Then, again: “When the servant girl saw him, she began to say to those standing around: ‘This man is one of them’” (Mark XIV, 68–69). He says this, then, when Peter had returned inside to the fire.

This was not the same servant girl as before, though she too was a servant girl. It should be noted that it was cold and night. If we consider the time and the places where Peter denied him, we can perceive the evils that pressed upon him: the night of unbelief had blinded him, and the cold of fear had frozen him, since he was illumined by no sun of righteousness. [Col. 0927D]

He was not in the courts of the Lord, of which it is sung in the Psalms: “Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem” (Psal. CXXI, 2), nor in “the courts of the house of our God” (Psal. CXXXIII, 1), but in the courts of Caiaphas and in his house, where Jesus was held bound. Therefore Christ was not recognized there, because there was no one in that place who saw the light.

There was indeed a burning fire there, but it consumed evilly. It neither drove the cold from the mind nor banished the darkness of night; rather, with the heat of impiety, it inflamed them toward crime.

When it says, “Your speech makes you known,” this does not mean that Peter belonged to another nation. All were Hebrews, both those accusing Peter and the one being accused. But each province and region has its own peculiarities and its native manner of speech. [Col. 0928A]

Then, it says, he began to curse and swear: “I do not know the man.” And immediately the rooster crowed.

In his first denial, before everyone, he says only: “I do not know what you are saying.” In the second, he denies with an oath: “I do not know the man.” In this third denial, it is said that he began to curse and swear that he did not know the man.

He denies more gravely each time. The deeper he goes into denial, the more seriously he sins by adding an oath. Therefore those who say, as I mentioned, that he did not deny God but the man must not be heeded. To deny Jesus as a man is itself a lie, and to affirm that lie with an oath—what else is it but perjury? Especially since Jesus, as man, is truly called God, and thus he is rightly said to have denied God. [Col. 0928B]

Peter could not yet recognize the Lord Jesus in the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit had not yet been given to human beings, since Jesus had not yet been glorified. Therefore he denies at night before the rooster crows, because he did not yet possess the Spirit of the Father, by whom he might confess Jesus Christ and who might speak in him.

Then follows: “And he went outside and wept bitterly.”

See, brothers, what I often say: all places and times are filled with mysteries. While sitting in the high priest’s courtyard, Peter could not—not merely stand firm in faith, but not even do penance after his fall. He goes outside from the council of the impious, because the Lord had looked upon him in order to wash away the filth of his fearful denial and cleanse the stains of his mind with bitter tears. [Col. 0928C]

Do not suppose, reader, that when it is said that the Lord looked upon Peter, this means that he saw him with bodily eyes, since Peter was outside in the courtyard while the Lord was being mocked inside. Rather, the Lord looked upon him where he lay—in his mind he looked upon him by his divinity.

And where the most gracious Lord looked upon him, there Peter immediately wept most bitterly. These things have been written, brothers, so that each of us may learn to presume much more on God than on ourselves. If you should perhaps fall in some matter, know that God is always present as a witness to your hidden deeds. [Col. 0928D]

He looks upon you so that you may remember and confess your errors and falls in humble confession. Imitate Peter, so that you may mourn your evils and thereafter love as Peter loved. When you are questioned a third time about what you denied three times, confess it fully with love and with a threefold affection of love—with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind. For no one loves perfectly except one who loves with his whole being.

## Chapter XXVII

When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus in order to hand him over to death. They bound him, led him away, and handed him over to Pontius Pilate, the governor.

Consider, I ask, the zeal of the priests during the night of Passover, when they ought to have been “in the unleavened bread of sincerity” (I Cor. V, 8), throughout the entire night in which the lamb was eaten. What watches they keep, what vigils they maintain, so that they might commit murder and hand Jesus over to death!

When this counsel had been completed and their decision made, in the morning, after he had been sent to Caiaphas, they immediately sent him bound to Pilate. It should be noted that the apostles deny and flee at night, whereas these men, when morning had come and they were in the light, enter into counsel and conspire together “to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him.” [Col. 0929A]

They therefore bind him with chains because Satan had bound them. They do not remember that he himself was the one who had earlier set free the daughter of Abraham whom the devil had bound for eighteen years, so that she could not look upward at all.

Nor, then, was that most powerful Samson stronger than Christ, who could not be held bound because of his hair. Samson went before as a figure of Christ, and no one can doubt that what Samson did whenever he was bound, Christ also did. Christ has freed us all by his bonds.

For this purpose, after the signs and countless mighty works he had performed, he allowed himself to be bound and consented to be tied—not by the cords of sin, but by sacramental bonds, whose mysteries were represented by those bonds of Samson. Christ broke them as soon as they surrounded him, when he rose victorious from death, in order to break ours. [Col. 0929B]

Concerning these bonds the prophet said: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Psal. CXV, 17).

It was the custom of the Jews to hand over to the judge anyone whom they had condemned to death while he was bound. Therefore they bring him bound to Caiaphas, as John testifies. Shortly afterward, he again relates that they bring him into the praetorium. “It was morning,” he says.

Matthew likewise says: “When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders took counsel to hand him over to death. And they led him away bound and handed him over to Pontius Pilate, the governor.” [Col. 0929C]

Here we understand that he was handed over to Pilate in the morning as well—perhaps when Caiaphas entered the praetorium, after Jesus had just been judged, and Jesus was brought to him to be handed over. This may have compelled Caiaphas to enter the praetorium.

Or perhaps, while Caiaphas was elsewhere, Jesus had been condemned to death by the entire council; nevertheless, from the beginning he was led from the house of Annas to Caiaphas, to whom he was brought at the end. But because Caiaphas had already determined that Jesus should die, and because those who brought him bound immediately resolved without delay that he should be handed over to Pilate the judge to be killed, both events took place in the morning: both his condemnation by Caiaphas together with the entire council, and his suffering of certain things before them, and his being handed over to Pilate. [Col. 0929D]

Then Judas, who had handed him over, seeing that he had been condemned, was moved to repentance and returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: “I have sinned by handing over innocent blood.”

O deed, and wretched condition of humanity! When a person is drawn into sin, he is enticed in such a way that he sees what he is doing but cannot foresee, with the clear vision of his mind, the destination toward which he is being dragged.

See how weak the betrayer’s mind had been. Now he sees and understands that the man he handed over was righteous, although before he could not foresee it. He now carries confusion in his mind because of his guilt, though previously he could not feel shame even when he was rushing to kiss the most gracious Savior. [Col. 0930A]

Up to this point, while Jesus was being scourged and subjected to many insults and injuries, the wretched man perhaps thought that he would escape. But when he saw that Jesus had been condemned to death and handed over to Pilate, the unhappy man understood with certainty that he had been condemned and could not endure his shame. Confused in mind, he was unable to find sound counsel.

This is how confusion and disturbance usually operate: a person sometimes becomes unable even to find himself. Thus, for the first time, under the weight of his impiety, Judas overcame the magnitude of his greed. Moved to repentance, he returned the thirty pieces of silver to those worst of merchants.

Yet, overwhelmed by grief and the enormity of his shame, he could not maintain a proper measure of repentance; he soon hanged himself. The devil, who had earlier seized him by his craft, caused him to repent—not perhaps for forgiveness, but in order to drive him further into ruin. [Col. 0930B]

The devil brought before the eyes of his mind the enormity of the crime he had committed, not so that he might follow sound counsel and flee to the most merciful Lord, the physician of souls, but so that, through the disturbance of his dreadful mind, he might fall into something worse.

Origen, in his customary manner, raises several opinions concerning this matter. Judas, he says, may have thought—although foolishly and not according to knowledge—that he could anticipate the Lord who was about to die, meet him in the soul he had separated from the body, and perhaps ask him by his prayers for forgiveness and mercy.

If such a thought did come into his mind, as I have said, it too arose from confusion and not from the teaching of the compassionate Master.

Origen offers another opinion: after the devil, as a most cunning investigator, had done in Judas and through Judas whatever he wished, so that Jesus would be handed over to death, he immediately withdrew from Judas. Once the devil had departed, Judas at once understood the evil he had done, because he had handed over innocent blood, and he saw that he himself had been condemned by God. [Col. 0930C]

Or perhaps, after the devil had withdrawn from him, Judas was able to consider repentance and return to them the price they had given him. Because he had perhaps been freed from his adversary, he could say, with rational awareness: “I have sinned by handing over innocent blood.”

But although the devil withdrew from him for a time, he later resumed possession of Judas—and of all whom he temporarily abandons—according to his own cunning, so that they might sometimes be swallowed up by even greater sorrow. We do not doubt that this man was likewise swallowed up and overcome in an evil way.

Therefore those who repent must always seek healthy counsel, and the medicine of salvation must be applied with the greatest care. Once the adversary has recognized each person according to his sin, he watches him and craftily lies in wait, so that he may deceive him to the very end. [Col. 0930D]

Let those who attempt to introduce different natures answer this. They say that Judas the betrayer possessed an evil nature and could not preserve the election to apostleship, because the fault was not in him but in his nature, which could not turn toward the good.

Let them answer, I ask, how an evil nature could have perceived that Christ was righteous. Or how could Judas have practiced repentance in any manner at all, so that he was not overcome by the desire for the thirty pieces of silver?

Although he did not turn perfectly, nor as he ought to have turned, he nevertheless condemned the state of his most evil greed, which he had wickedly accepted, and he certainly recognized his sin. Otherwise, if there had been in him no nature of a good planting, he could not have perceived the virtue of repentance and justice at all, nor recognized the madness of his impiety. [Col. 0931A]

It was sufficient that he said: “I have sinned by handing over innocent blood.” It would also have been sufficient that he rejected the money, if afterward he had preserved his heart for repentance and, while wisely grieving, had taken care, in accordance with the Apostle, not to be swallowed up by excessive sorrow into the ruin of his condemnation.

But they said: “What is that to us? You see to it” (II Cor. II, 7).

O blindness of the Jews and perversity of mind! They act as though they were innocent, although they had purchased the murder with the price they paid. O hardness of heart! Even one possessed by a demon is moved to repent of his guilt, but they refuse to acknowledge that they have acted wickedly.

They say: “What is that to us?” as though they themselves had done nothing evil and cared nothing about the guilt of their neighbor. It is no wonder that they think of nothing concerning themselves, but say: “You see what you have done,” since they consider themselves entirely free from guilt in everything. [Col. 0931B]

Therefore let those beware who sin so easily against their brothers. For when someone sins against another in such a way that he cannot make amends, there is very great reason to fear that he has sinned grievously.

It was no longer in Judas’s power to absolve the one whom he had handed over. Therefore he assumes the voice of repentance in vain, because the works of impiety remain. This is what is sung in the Psalm about that most wretched Judas: “Let his prayer become sin” (Psal. CVIII, 7). He not only failed to correct the crime he had committed, but also added the crime of his own death to his sin.

If you examine carefully the Psalm that is sung about him, you will find in it, in place of the thirty pieces of silver that he received, thirty curses formerly pronounced against him by divine utterance and preserved, as though by hereditary right, in the price—not because he sinned only once, but because, though repeatedly corrected by the Lord so that he might cleanse himself, “he refused to understand, that he might do good” (Psal. XXXV, 4). Thus he received the reward of his price, to the corruption of all future things, so that everyone might know that all things lie within the foreknowledge of God and might fear, because “the judgments of God are a great abyss, and his ways are unsearchable” (Psal. XXXV, 7; Rom. XI, 33).

The chief priests, having received the 1,145 pieces of silver, said: “It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood.” O false religion and blind justice! If this is not lawful because it is the price of blood, [Col. 0931D] why, then, is that innocent blood so impiously poured out? This is precisely what is said much earlier: “Straining out gnats and swallowing camels.” Therefore, after taking counsel, they bought with it the potter’s field as a burial place for strangers.

All these things, as you see, do not happen by chance or through some accidental turn of events, as they suppose, but entirely by the disposition of the living God, so that what had been foretold might be fulfilled, although they themselves intended something else insofar as it lay within their power. For perhaps they saw that this blood-money was more appropriately used for the dead and for the burial places of the deceased than put into the treasury or used for any respectable need of theirs. “Corbona,” moreover, is interpreted from Hebrew into Latin as “gift”; it was the place, or chest of money, [Col. 0932A] into which gifts and offerings were deposited, or any funds set aside for the uses of the Temple, or for whatever other purposes or needs.

But, impelled by God’s directing will, they decided to buy with the very price—not just any field, but the potter’s field—and to use it for burial—not for just anyone, but for strangers. For there are many distinctions among the places of burial and much diversity among merits. Some are buried according to the wishes of the noble; others according to the estimation of the common people. Yet no one is buried in the potter’s field, bought with the price of Christ’s blood, except one who is buried with Christ through baptism into death. This field is truly the field of strangers, and of those who are strangers in the world, who can say to God: “Be not silent, for I am a sojourner with you, a stranger, as all my fathers were” (Ps. XXXVIII, 13). [Col. 0932B]

Therefore this field that is bought is a field of blood and a potter’s field, because our potter is Christ, whose strength “dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. XXI, 16). That field itself is called Acheldemach—that is, “Field of Blood”—even to the present day. And rightly is this world, or the Church of Christ, or the paradise of God, called the Field of Blood, because it was bought for us with Christ’s blood, so that the saints who are strangers on earth might rest there. Their cry is: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar; my soul has been a long-time sojourner” (Ps. CXIX, 5). [Col. 0932C]

Such people, then, are buried with Christ. Therefore, from the price of his blood, a field is bought for their burial, as a place in which they may remain and rest forever. With faithful Abraham, they sojourn in this age according to God’s command. But because this testimony is not found in Jeremiah, they say that it was rather taken from Zechariah, where it is found, in some fashion, with very different words and in an entirely different order.

First, according to the Septuagint, it reads as follows: “I will say to them, ‘If it is good in your sight, give me my wage; or refuse.’ And they weighed out my wage, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: ‘Put them into the smelting furnace, and see whether it is tested, as I have been tested by them.’ And I took the thirty pieces of silver and put them into the house of the Lord, into the smelting furnace” (Zech. XI, 12–13). How far this translation differs from the Evangelist’s testimony is clear to all who read it. [Col. 0932D]

But in the Hebrew, according to Jerome, although the sense is the same, the wording is very disordered and almost entirely different. It reads: “And I said to them: ‘If it is good in your eyes, bring my wage; and if not, refrain.’ And they weighed out my wage, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: ‘Cast it to the statuary—the splendid price at which I was valued by them.’ And I took the thirty pieces of silver and cast them to the statuary in the house of the Lord.”

I have set this out so that everyone may weigh the difficulty of this passage, since many have tried on this account to accuse the Evangelist and prove him an advocate of falsehood, because he appears to agree neither with the Hebrew nor with the translators of the Septuagint. And, what is more, they say that he is also mistaken in the name, having falsely written Jeremiah instead of Zechariah. Yet our Catholic interpreters have never wished to alter or correct this, as certain rash and presumptuous people have attempted to do, just as we know they have done in very many other passages. [Col. 0933A]

But far be it from the faithful to think that Christ’s Evangelist said anything other than what he read and proclaimed in the Spirit of God to the children of Christ’s Church. The Church is concerned not with arranging words or syllables in sentences, nor with preserving the rights of translators, but with setting forth the very sentences of truth in the teaching of the Holy Spirit, as they were formerly proclaimed.

Although blessed Jerome says that he read, in a certain Hebrew volume offered to him by a member of the sect of the Nazarenes, an apocryphal book of Jeremiah, and found in it, written word for word, this passage attributed to Jeremiah, it nevertheless seemed to him more likely that the Evangelist’s testimony had been taken from Zechariah. He held that it had been set down in this form according to the custom of the apostles, who, frequently omitting the order of the words, nevertheless brought forward the meanings of the Old Testament as examples. [Col. 0933B]

Therefore, in this passage we must seek an interpretation by which the Evangelist’s authority remains firm and no rash impulse to correct intrudes upon us. Rather, together with the holy Fathers, we should speak about it by conjecturing than by asserting what we do not know to be certain.

The first point that presents itself is that not all copies of the Gospels say that this was spoken “through Jeremiah,” but only “through the prophet.” Yet this does not mean that we should immediately assert that greater credence ought to be given to those copies, so as to call the manuscripts that contain Jeremiah false. Where the text says “through the prophet,” Zechariah is more appropriately understood. For the holy Fathers long ago explained that this was more likely the bold ignorance of someone who, troubled by the question of not finding this testimony in Jeremiah, rashly chose to correct it rather than appear ignorant. [Col. 0933C]

Perhaps, however, this was done through a higher mystery and by God’s providence, by which the minds of the Evangelists were inwardly moved. For those living creatures were “full of eyes all around,” and therefore it cannot be that Matthew wrote something through forgetfulness and put Jeremiah in place of Zechariah. He would certainly have corrected it when others admonished him—at least those who could have read it while he was still alive—unless the Holy Spirit had willed that this testimony be written through him in precisely this way. [Col. 0933D]

But why did he will it so? The first and most useful reason occurs to our father Augustine: all the holy prophets spoke by one Spirit, in wondrous agreement with one another, so that they might say far more than if every statement of all the prophets had been spoken by the mouth of one man. Therefore, whatever the Holy Spirit said through them must undoubtedly be accepted as belonging to all of them individually, and everything spoken through them as belonging to each one. [Col. 0934A]

Accordingly, what was spoken through Jeremiah belongs as much to Zechariah as to Jeremiah; and what was spoken through Zechariah belongs as much to Jeremiah as to Zechariah. For this reason Matthew did not need to correct what the Holy Spirit had spoken through him, when by divine revelation he found the name Jeremiah written by him in his Gospel. Through this, he wished to show us that such harmony exists among the prophets and among the Evangelists themselves that whatever is said to belong to one of them may, without absurdity, appear to belong to another as well. Thus, what we clearly see was spoken through Zechariah is not improperly proved, with the consent of the Holy Spirit, to belong to Jeremiah.

It is customary to speak in the same way of very close friends whose agreement and will are one. If one of them says something that is attributed to the other, people say: “Do not worry which of them said it, for it was spoken so harmoniously that it is the same whether this one said it or that one did, since they share one spirit, one fellowship, and one purpose of mind.” [Col. 0934B]

Consequently, the prophets and Evangelists possess among themselves a greater constancy of mind and unanimity of truth than would exist if all these things were spoken by a single, however learned, man. Therefore no unbeliever or ignorant person rightly reproves such statements as these, as though they displayed disagreement among the Evangelists. Rather, learned and faithful people should derive from them an argument and authority for demonstrating the unity and harmony of the Evangelists and the holy prophets.

There is also an evident reason in Jeremiah that may demand that this testimony should have remained under Jeremiah’s name. It seems to have been confirmed by the authority of the Spirit because of that field which we read that Jeremiah bought while he was in prison. For although thirty pieces of silver are read in Zechariah as having been given for the Lord and rejected in the Temple, that same prophet also records that the field was bought by his brother’s son, and that the price of the silver was given to him. [Col. 0934C]

It was not, indeed, under this name, nor with the same number given in Zechariah. Yet that account of the field bought also pertains to the prophecy concerning the thirty pieces of silver. That what was fulfilled concerning the Lord was the price assigned to him is clear; and it is true that the Field of Blood was bought with those same pieces of silver. Thus, mystically, one testimony appears to exist between the two prophets: what one expressed more explicitly concerning the silver, the other expressed concerning the field.

Accordingly, if the name Zechariah had been given, it would have referred to the price. But because the name Jeremiah is given—the prophet who spoke of the field bought—it does not appear to have been done incongruously. Therefore, the wise mind should strive to bring both together rather than rashly reproach the Evangelist or hastily erase or alter what he wrote. It should instead examine the meaning more carefully, asking how both passages pertain to the fulfillment of the testimony, rather than neglecting one and preferring the other. [Col. 0934D]

For even the deed of purchase in Jeremiah, which was written concerning the field together with its attestation, was commanded to be placed in an earthen vessel. And the potter’s field was bought with the Lord’s price, [Col. 0935A] for the burial of strangers. Likewise, that deed of purchase was sealed in a potter’s vessel as a memorial for the future, so that it might signify the permanence or rest of the people for a long time in the land of captivity or sojourning, until, by God’s gift, that captivity itself should be released into the freedom of the children of God.

As for what Matthew added to this testimony when he said, “Whom the children of Israel valued, and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed me,” this is found neither in Zechariah nor in Jeremiah. It is therefore uncertain whether it was elegantly and mystically supplied from the person of blessed Matthew himself. For he too, through the Lord’s revelation, understood that this kind of prophecy pertained to the matter accomplished concerning Christ’s price.

We must therefore ask who received those same pieces of silver, since here too there is a variation among the manuscripts: some read “the children of Israel,” while others read “from the children.” If we refer it to Judas, who received the price of Christ, valued by the children of Israel, the plural number will stand for the singular. But if “the children” is to be read, they received it—that is, the priests of the Temple, when Judas threw it back into the Temple—the price of Christ, whom the children of Israel had valued; or the price of Christ which Judas had valued from the children of Israel. “And they gave them for the potter’s field.” [Col. 0935B]
