I leave it to the reader’s judgment which of these is preferable, since the sense is almost the same. For this variation was caused either by the rashness of correctors or by the diversity of translators.

Jesus, however, stood before the governor, and the governor questioned him, saying: “Are you the king of the Jews?”

Behold, Christ’s prophecy has been fulfilled, in which he had said above that he would be handed over to the Gentiles to be mocked. He stands in humility before the tribunal of a proud judge. The judge sees someone standing before him as though he were a criminal and asks whether he is the king of the Jews, because this had been the Jews’ chief accusation against him: they wished to stir up the judge’s envy and anger and to strike him with fear, in case he wanted to defend him as Caesar’s representative. [Col. 0935C]

But the treacherous leaders are condemned even by this charge of their impiety, since they could not find anything—even anything false—to bring against the Savior. They pretend such intense hatred that they were unwilling even to accept the testimony of the prophets concerning him, that he was the king whose coming had been foretold.

Although they had brought forward other false and implausible charges, Pilate nevertheless asks about the title of king, which he feared most. The Lord answered him: “You say so.” [Col. 0935D]

Pilate’s question and that of the chief priest are different, and Christ’s responses are different. The chief priest says: “If you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Although he knows the Law, he asks doubtfully, and therefore adds the conditional “if.” Pilate, however, though ignorant of the Law, asks more in the manner of a declaration: “Are you the king of the Jews?” even though he appears to be asking a question.

He confirms this also in the inscription when he ordered that it be written above the cross: “JESUS OF NAZARETH, KING OF THE JEWS.” For he thought that he was the king of the Jews. And therefore, when the Jews wanted it erased, he said: “What I have written, I have written.”

Because Pilate asked in such a way that he wished to know, the Lord answered him: “You say so.” Through the faith of this confession, the salvation of the Gentiles and their belief are already proclaimed. Thus Pilate, who is ignorant of the Law, speaks of himself in this way what those deny who had always previously spoken of it in the Law.

Therefore the chief priest also received the answer: “You have said so.” This is because the whole Law daily proclaimed that Christ would come, as though he were saying to him concerning the past: “You have said so,” because in the Law and from the Law you have often proclaimed him, although unwillingly. [Col. 0936A]

I say this because I do not believe that anything superfluous exists in the divine Scriptures, nor that anything in the Lord’s words is empty of saving instruction. Therefore, because Pilate uses an interrogative that is really a declaration, the Lord gives him a confirming answer. But when he says to the other, “You have said so,” he wisely exposes his doubt by an oblique rebuke.

In all this, however, he so measured his answer that he both spoke the truth and left his speech free from accusation. When he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing. He deigned to answer Pilate something because Pilate was unwillingly pronouncing judgment against him; he judged the priests and leaders of the people unworthy of an answer.

Then Pilate says to him: “Do you not hear how many testimonies they bring against you?” [Col. 0936B]

The governor urges him to clear himself of the charge, knowing that the accusations brought against him were empty and false. But Jesus does not wish to answer or to excuse himself with any words, lest the triumph of his Passion be delayed by the governor, who was glad to free and acquit him because he saw that he was subject to no crime. Yet he was not worthy of answering him, because Pilate proceeded in doubt and did not remain firm in faith; therefore he could give no settled judgment concerning Christ.

But the wretched Jews, to whom the Word of God remains silent even to this day and speaks nothing while they accuse Christ—neither through himself, nor through the prophets, nor through any oracles of his divinity, because they killed the Lord of the prophets—received no word from him. The governor therefore marveled exceedingly.

He marveled at his steadfastness; he also marveled at how he could remain so silent, since he was able to remove the false accusations brought against him and clear himself of the charge. Who could fail to marvel amid such rage from his accusers, the shouts of the crowd, and the fury of the elders, when he saw him standing so tranquil, so gentle and quiet, undaunted with complete dignity? He was being demanded for death, yet no address moved him. [Col. 0936C]

For the power within him was stronger than human nature ordinarily is. Therefore Pilate could not merely marvel, but marvel exceedingly, since it seemed worthy of great wonder that a man brought before a criminal tribunal and sentenced to death should remain undisturbed and fearless; that he should stand before death, which is terrifying to all, without any fear of death, and should remain silent without defending himself, although he could have defended himself in court if he had wished. [Col. 0936D]

On the solemn day, the governor was accustomed to release to the people one prisoner whom they wished. Do not be surprised, listener, if Roman authority was still in its beginnings among them. It had been the custom of the Jews, especially at their Passover solemnity, when they had been liberated from Egypt, to ask their rulers for any one guilty person they wished, no matter what crimes he was involved in.

And because the Jews had only recently taken upon themselves the yoke of the Romans, their law and custom were preserved for them, so that, attracted by such benefits, they might serve the Romans more willingly, until their yoke over them was firmly established.

This is why, when the people asked for Jonathan, Saul immediately released him from death, although he had been held guilty for tasting honey, even though God had exposed the matter. Saul had determined, indeed, even with an oath, to kill him, although he was his son. Yet when the people of Israel asked for the man whom he was preparing to kill, he released him to life. [Col. 0937A]

For such and similar reasons, the custom grew in the Church of Christ of petitioning secular judges for the life of the accused and criminal, and indeed of entreating God, the Judge of all, on behalf of sinners, that they may be freed from their faults and restored to pardon. For no one rightly entreats him without hope of forgiveness.

At that time they had a notable prisoner called Barabbas. When they had gathered, Pilate said to them: “Whom do you want me to release to you—Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?”

“Barabbas” is interpreted as “son of their master.” He had been condemned because of sedition and murders, and therefore is called notable not for virtues but for vices and crimes. Perhaps Pilate deliberately selected such a man from among the other guilty prisoners so that the enormity of his crimes would compel the Jews to ask for Jesus and hand Barabbas over to death. [Col. 0937B]

For this purpose he offers them the choice of releasing whomever they wished: such a criminal thief or Jesus. He did not doubt that they would choose Jesus rather than one held guilty of such great crimes. For he knew that Jesus had been handed over solely because of envy, and that no other cause of Christ’s cross existed than hatred and envy.

But the wretched Jews, who provide us with a kind of sacramental lesson from their own guilt, choose the man who was guilty of seditions, wars, and murders, and reject Jesus the Son of God, who has been appointed for us as peace from God the Father, the Word of God and the Wisdom of the Father.

These two, then, are bound in human affairs and bodies, because God became man: the first Adam and the last. But that faithless people continually asks that Barabbas be released, on whose account they never cease to make seditions, robberies, and murders, because they do not think rightly about Jesus and do not believe in him. [Col. 0937C]

For in a soul where Jesus is absent, there are seditions, quarrels, and scandals. But where Jesus is present, although the body is dead because of sin, the spirit is life because of righteousness. There all good things and innumerable riches of goodness are present together, because Christ is our peace, who made both one (Eph. II, 14). [Col. 0937D]

All who do evil are released from that body, whereas Christ and his own are held bound in the bond of peace (Eph. IV, 3). From that bond, Barabbas—that is, “the son of their master”—and those held liable by their own crimes are loosed and released to a life of the worst sedition; from them all evils are generated in this world.

While he was seated on the tribunal, his wife sent to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him.”

The Evangelist does not explain what she saw in the dream or from whom she suffered. Therefore our interpreters have been given the opportunity to interpret this vision in different ways. [Col. 0938A]

Some say that the vision was sent by the devil, and that she was scourged by him, since he already perhaps sensed that he was being overcome by Christ’s Passion and that the world was being saved. For this reason he acted by his own craft so that Christ might be freed through the woman—not because he cared about Christ’s death, but so that through Christ’s death he might not lose the guilty people whom he held captive unto death.

Others say that it happened through God’s goodness, just as dreams are often said to have been revealed by God to Gentiles, so that Pilate’s wife might signify the Gentiles. By confessing the righteous Lord, she gives testimony for faith to those who do not believe.

Therefore the Evangelist did not wish to pass over an event belonging to divine providence and containing praise of Christ, who deigned through a dream to bring Pilate’s wife to confession. Perhaps she suffered what she suffered in the dream so that she would not suffer more greatly. [Col. 0938B]

For this reason, as I said, the Evangelist did not explain the vision, so that we might be permitted to think more broadly about Christ’s compassion. They call Pilate’s wife blessed because she suffered many things in a dream on account of Jesus and received in the dream what she was destined to suffer during her life.

From this some wish to argue that it is better to receive evils in a dream than to receive them in life. For who would not choose this, unless perhaps there are many for whom it is more beneficial to receive harsher things in their life than lighter ones in a dream?

Thus Lazarus is comforted and rests in Abraham’s bosom because he receives evils in his life, and not the evils that she received in her dream and through her senses. Whether, however, this woman began to turn toward God because she suffered many things in a dream on account of Jesus, God knows.

One thing, however, we know: the Church of Christ from the Gentiles, which was once Pilate’s wife—Pilate signifying the devil—is no longer his wife but Christ’s. Joined to Christ through faith in his Passion, she does not cease to confess God by faith and to summon to him everyone she can. [Col. 0938C]

But the chief priests and the elders persuaded the people to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus. The governor replied and said to them: “Which of the two do you want me to release?” They said: “Barabbas.”

What shall I say about this except that almost all the wickedness and transgression of peoples comes from the elders of the people? By their evils they are stirred up to every sin, and everyone observes and obeys what they want and what they do not want.

The crowds believe their leaders and priests, and pay little attention to what the governor wishes, since he was still using new laws among them. He attempts nothing except persuasion, but they themselves choose Barabbas, whose footsteps they follow more closely, and therefore they want him released to them. [Col. 0938D]

Pilate says to them: “What, then, shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” They all say: “Let him be crucified,” and so forth.

He wishes to bring upon them shame for such great iniquity. But they not only do not blush, although Pilate was confessing him to be Jesus Christ; they actually increase the fury of their impiety and cry out more savagely, without any assent to reconsideration: “Let him be crucified.” [Col. 0939A]

If they had merely asked that Barabbas be released to them, that would have been enough to increase their impiety. But now, on the contrary, they also demand Christ’s death. If the most wretched people had left Jesus to Pilate’s authority, allowing him to do with Jesus whatever he wished, provided only that he release Barabbas to them, this would have been a grave crime of impiety, since they had asked that a criminal be given to them and were unwilling, when they could, to release the righteous man to life.

But now they do what is more criminal: they proclaim him for death—not just any death, but the most disgraceful death—and demand with loud voices that he be crucified.

This is what Isaiah says: “I expected them to do justice” (Isa. V, 7); but they did iniquity and not justice, only a cry. And David says of them: “Many dogs surrounded me; the assembly of the wicked besieged me” (Ps. XXI, 17). And Jeremiah: “My inheritance has become for me like a lion in the forest; they raised their voice against me” (Jer. XI, 8). [Col. 0939B]

Yet Pilate does not cease to act against their impiety, so that they might be confounded and turn back from their crime. Again he says to them: “Why, what evil has he done?”

Since they had no answer to this, they cried out even more, as though their eyes had been closed so that they would not remember God’s judgments. They did not lay aside their malice but increased their blasphemy, saying: “Let him be crucified.”

Thus Pilate, insofar as it depended on him, acquitted him in every respect, especially by declaring that he had done nothing evil. His question is itself an acquittal, or a rebuke, because they wished to kill an innocent man. He acquitted by judgment the one whom he later crucified in the mystery. [Col. 0939C]

Therefore, when Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing but that the tumult was increasing, he took water and washed his hands before the people, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; you will see to it.”

He did this according to Jewish custom, wishing to demonstrate Christ’s innocence to them not only in words but also in deeds, if perhaps he might pacify them; or else to prove himself innocent and show them to be guilty. He did not wash his hands according to any Roman custom, but in accordance with the prophetic saying: “I will wash my hands among the innocent” (Ps. XXV, 6). [Col. 0939D]

In this washing, unknowingly signifying that the works of the Gentiles were to be cleansed, he prefigured that we should be shown to be separate from the impiety of the Jews. Pilate professes himself innocent and Jesus righteous, as his wife had also confessed.

But the wretched man does not wash away his own deeds, since he submits to the designs of another’s cruelty. He washed his hands, but he did not wash away his guilt, because a judge ought not to have believed envy, fear, or any pressure from his adversaries so as to condemn innocent blood—the blood of one whom he declared righteous.

This, then, is what he says: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man,” as though he were saying: “I wanted to free an innocent man, but because a sedition is arising and the charge of rebellion against Caesar is being brought against me, I will demonstrate my innocence in every direction.” [Col. 0940A]

Nevertheless, the guilt of a judge who is compelled to pronounce sentence against the Lord is more tolerable than that of the Jews, who in their faithlessness demand the death of an innocent man. Pilate does not condemn the one brought before him, but repeatedly rebukes those who bring him forward. He declares righteous the one whom, compelled, he condemns to death, as though he were saying: “I am the minister of the law, but your voice and the cry of your fury pour out innocent blood. You will see to it.”

The whole people answered him: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” [Col. 0940B]

This imprecation of the Jews continues to the present day. The Lord’s blood, which cries from the earth against them together with the blood of Abel poured out upon the earth, does not cease even now to cry out, nor is it removed from them. Therefore he speaks through Isaiah: “When you stretch out your hands to me, I will not hear you; for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. I, 15).

O most wretched Jews, who left such an inheritance to their children! For this reason they became guilty not only of the blood of the prophets whom they shed, but also of the blood of Christ, in which they completed the measure of their fathers.

Therefore their city was devastated with hostile devastation, and they themselves, faithless as they are, were scattered over the whole earth even to the present day.

Then he released Barabbas to them, but after scourging Jesus he handed him over to them to be crucified.

Thus, in Barabbas they did what they will also do in the Antichrist. The secret of future faithlessness had already gone before in this robber. They therefore choose one reserved for condemnation rather than the author of their salvation, so that the prophecies of the prophets might be fulfilled in every respect and so that, by their deeds, they might still reveal what the children of the master will do in the Antichrist, whose master is the devil. [Col. 0940C]

And therefore, as I said, Barabbas is interpreted as “son of the master,” so that they may follow the error of the one whose children they are.

Pilate, overcome by fear of Caesar, forgets his own words by which he had begun to defend Christ’s innocence. He bends his judgment toward the crime of impiety, and not only hands Jesus over to be crucified, but first has him beaten with whips, as was customary with criminals. For Mark says that he did this in order to satisfy the people and put an end to their desire to kill him, when they saw that he had been scourged.

Then the soldiers of the governor, taking Jesus into the praetorium, observing no order of discipline and no gravity in judgment, and holding him in the Roman manner, make Jesus their sport: “And they gathered the whole cohort around him; and stripping him, they wrapped him in a scarlet cloak.” Taking him into the courtyard of the praetorium, as Mark says, they summoned the whole cohort, clothed him in purple, mocked him, and fashioned him in the appearance of a king, just as is usually done in the theaters when one person is introduced in place of another [Col. 0940D]. Yet their error was not without a mystery, since he himself was the King of kings; and for this reason he accepted all these things as mockery, so that by the pattern of humility he might make all his own people kings.

Moreover, what Matthew says—“they wrapped him in a scarlet cloak”—Mark expresses as, “they clothe him in purple” (Mark XV, 17). For that cloak was given by the mockers as royal clothing; in John also it is called a purple garment, because it was a kind of red purple, very like scarlet. It is also possible that the same cloak was both purple and scarlet, even though it was scarlet. Matthew seems here to relate all these events more by recollection than in their chronological order, because, as is shown in John, these things took place earlier in the praetorium before Pilate, [Col. 0941A] before he had handed him over to the soldiers to be crucified. After they had mocked him and performed all these acts of derision against him, they removed the cloak, dressed him in his own garments, and led him away to crucify him.

Earlier, however, before Pilate, all these events that the Evangelists narrate in different ways had taken place. I think, therefore, that in that same spectacle there were not lacking the princes and soldiers of darkness who had assembled—as though that cohort were against the Lord and against his Christ—and that these men, deceived by them, were contriving such things contrary to custom. And so this mockery was rather the work of demons than of human beings, so that in these things also Jesus might triumph. For they could not foresee the wisdom of God in this dispensation of the mystery; “but if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 8).

That cohort, therefore, was a multitude of soldiers, since in one cohort there are said to be three hundred soldiers, or many more. Their number signified that invisible host against which Christ had come to fight. Thus, even though they were unaware of it, they did these things with a great mystery. They had heard that he had been called king of the Jews, and therefore they mocked the name, not understanding what they were doing when they placed upon him the appearance of a king.

For that cloak, as I have said, whether scarlet or purple, was a mystery of the scarlet sign that Rahab the harlot had once tied in the window for the salvation of her household. Tamar likewise tied scarlet to the hand of the infant being born, as a sign of Christ’s passion. Therefore, because it was a mystery foretold long ago, Jesus took it upon himself, so that you might recognize him who had come to save the world by his own blood [Col. 0941C]. They themselves, unaware of this, mocked him in order to depict him as a king, and said: “Hail, King of the Jews.”

This was the charge that the scribes and priests had brought against him. They strip him of his former garments and clothe him in a purple robe; in place of the rose-colored border used by ancient kings, and in place of a diadem, they set a crown of thorns upon him; in place of a royal scepter, they give him a reed, and they worship him in mockery, as though he were a king.

We, however, understanding all these things mystically in prophecy—like Caiaphas, who said, “It is necessary for one man to die for all,” without knowing what he was saying—understand that these men, whatever they did, although they did it with a perverse spirit, nevertheless worked for us the mysteries of salvation. For in the scarlet cloak are signified the bloody works of the nations, which are changed by the love of Christ into twice-dyed scarlet; for in the scarlet, the love with which Christ is clothed, is wholly expressed.

In the thorny crown that ancient curse is dissolved, so that thereafter our earth, which had produced thorns and thistles of sin, might compose garlands for Christ’s head, and the Church might become the bride adorned for her husband, wearing the diadem of salvation.

He therefore bears the reed in his hand, with which he may kill the poisonous kinds of serpents. Or he carries the reed for this reason: to enroll his soldiers for eternity, and not to omit enrolling the sacrilege of the Jews. “And spitting on him, they took the reed and were striking his head,” so that what was written might be fulfilled: “I did not turn my face away from those who rebuked and spat upon me” (Ps. L, 6).

O patience of the most gracious God! How calmly he bears everything! He neither turns himself away from the disgrace of the spittle, nor is he moved when he is struck with the reed, in accordance with the prophet Isaiah. He will not break the bruised reed, but bears in himself all our sins, which were red as scarlet, so that through him they might be whitened like snow and our garments might become white—“such as a fuller cannot make upon the earth” (Mark IX, 3).

But it is remarkable what the Evangelist intended when he says that they again removed the scarlet cloak from him. Concerning the thorny crown, that they removed it from his head after placing it upon him, he was silent; nor is it written that they pulled it off. I think this too was not without a great mystery. Although in the scarlet cloak [Col. 0942B] and in the thorny crown he wished to show that he had taken our sins upon himself, the matter is nevertheless quite different: he removed the garment, but did not change the thorny crown; rather, so to speak, he consumed it in himself, so that thereafter there would be no thorns in him or anywhere else.

Thus, by the scarlet cloak, the flesh assumed in the likeness of sinful flesh is signified. Hence also in Zechariah the soiled garments of Jesus the priest are mentioned—not because they were stained by sin, but because they were corruptible, in the likeness of sinful flesh, and were completely purpled by his own blood. Since he lost this corruption, he changed it, as though it were a scarlet garment, through the passion of the cross, when he received back the immortality that he had always possessed.

But the thorns that he wore upon his head he did not change or transfer elsewhere; he consumed them, so that upon the head of Jesus there might shine not thorns but precious stones. For this reason it is also said that stones of the sanctuary would shine upon the diadem of Aaron’s head. The head of Christ is God; thorns cannot exist in him. Therefore stones are rightly said to shine upon him, because those who are in him cannot possess sin.

For this reason the Evangelist does not say that that crown was removed or taken off: the sins consumed by Jesus from his head are rightly believed no longer to exist as thorns. He took them up upon his venerable head, removed them from us so that they would no longer exist, and consumed them.

In his right hand the reed is placed, to put it another way, so that the frailty of Egypt—whose king is called a reed-like staff—might be represented in him, as they themselves imagined. But it is a mystery of the reigning God, whose tongue is also called “the pen of a swift-writing scribe,” and whose “rod of uprightness” is “the rod of his kingdom” (Ps. XLIV, 2, 7).

He accepted from our hands the scepter of a fragile kingdom, upon which we had wrongly relied and long leaned, so that he might triumph over it and crush it upon the wood of the cross. In place of that reed, he gave us the scepter of the heavenly kingdom and the rod of righteousness, concerning which we sing in the Psalm: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. XXI, 4).

Thus the entire appearance of a king is depicted in him by these men, so that the person of the king might be introduced and the mystery of our redemption declared, whether they wished it or not. Concerning this rod the apostle Paul boasted: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness?” [Col. 0943A] (I Cor. IV, 21).

We too must properly celebrate Passover with the staff in our hands. For whatever was light in us, whatever was empty and vain, we have entirely lost, so that we may be supported by Christ’s staff and corrected by the rod of God’s rectitude.

But miserable is the power of the world, and vain the presumption of human beings, which relies so greatly upon the pomp of the world and the reed of empty presumption that even today it strikes the venerable head of Jesus with a reed. And while the most impious raise themselves up against God the Father, they strike the head of our Savior with a reed—their power being vain— and attempt to destroy his kingdom.

Behold, Jesus has been clothed in a scarlet cloak and likewise in a purple garment; behold, upon his head is a thorny crown, and in his right hand a reed. Yet, with knees bent, he is worshiped in mockery [Col. 0943B]. Having therefore taken upon himself all the infirmities of our body, he triumphs and shows what he has done in his members.

Behold the whole order of the holy martyrs, whose kingdom consisted in him and which is most gloriously drenched in the color of blood, like scarlet. Behold the number of the prophets and patriarchs clothed in purple honor and crowned with thorns—that is, with the barbs of all our sins—so that, emptied of evils, we may be a crown upon his head. From all these things Christ’s victory and diadem are woven.

So also, in the reed, the weakness of all the nations and their emptiness, grasped by the Savior’s hand, is healed, and fragile nature is strengthened. Thus, held in Christ’s hand, it shines as something precious upon his head, like a crown of honor.

In all these things, as I have said, Christ is worshiped while he is mocked; and, having been worshiped, he is honored as God.

When they went out, they found a Cyrenian man named Simon. They compelled him to carry his cross. This man is said to have been from Cyrene, which is the Pentapolis near Libya. And because a great mystery is formed in him, the Evangelists discuss with such care who he was and where he came from.

He was from the nations. He did not happen to come upon them by chance, but, as I have often said, by the providence of God, so that it might already be shown in him that the nations would have to bear Christ’s cross and become sharers in his passion.

No Jew was worthy to carry Christ’s cross, because it had been granted to the faith of the nations to receive it and carry it after Jesus. Although John said that “they took Jesus and led him out,” and that “carrying his own cross he went out to the place called the Place of the Skull,” it is nevertheless true what the other three say: when he went out from Pilate’s praetorium, he first carried the cross himself, as was fitting, so that he might come carrying it to Golgotha, where he was to be crucified.

Both accounts are therefore true: first what John says, and then what the others say. For afterward, when that Simon came upon him, he was compelled to carry Jesus’ cross to the place [Col. 0944A].

This is entirely appropriate, since Jesus first carried it for us; only then, on the way, is it necessary for us to carry it for him. In this same act the royal honor is proclaimed, lest the King proceed to victory without a servant to carry his triumph.

Nor is it without reason that Simon himself is called by that name, which means “obedient,” since no one carries Christ’s cross except by obeying. It makes no difference whether we say Simeon or Simon, because both names, according to the character of the Hebrew language, signify obedience.

Therefore one of them, after Jesus, hastens to carry the cross under compulsion; the other, receiving him into his arms at the temple in Jerusalem, rejoices to carry him exultantly between his arms, although he is already an old man. Both, however, by obeying, earned the privilege of being worthy of so great a gift. Although this forced service is called an angaria, it is never borne worthily except through obedience. Thus, from his name it is rightly called obedience, and by the command of our salvation it is nevertheless proved to be a forced service.

But Jesus graciously carries it first and is finally crucified upon it himself, also whenever any member of Christ is crucified to the world and the world is held fast, crucified to him.

Nor is it without a mystery that, according to John, Christ is said to have carried his cross alone, whereas according to the others someone else is introduced carrying it, not Christ himself. The same is true when he was tempted: because the only-begotten God had accepted that same temptation according to his humanity, these three explain it; John, since he had undertaken to expound his divine nature, made no mention of that temptation.

So here, when they who had taken him placed his cross upon him, he himself carried the cross that belongs to all and, according to his divinity, went out free from all labor to the place called Calvary. Nevertheless, Simon himself, made obedient to God the Father, carries it together with his members, who are counted and found under this name along the way.

According to John, he himself, as victor, raises up his own trophy, when the cross is placed upon his shoulders; and, according to the prophet, “the government shall be upon his shoulder” (Isa. IX, 6). For whether Simon or Christ himself carried the trophy of the cross, in the mystery it is almost one and the same, since Christ carried it in a human being, and a human being carried it in Christ.

The statements of the Evangelists therefore do not conflict when the mystery is harmonious, and the good order in which our perfection is proclaimed is preserved: first he raises up in himself the trophy of his cross; afterward he hands it over to the martyrs and to all believers to raise up.

The one who carries Christ’s cross does not go before him, but follows, as he himself says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me” (Luke IX, 23) [Col. 0944D].

He does not carry his own cross, but ours; and therefore we are commanded to carry our own cross. For even if it is his, in which the God-man suffers, it is nevertheless ours, by which we are redeemed and saved.

Therefore, just as God cannot be tempted, so neither can he suffer. Hence Christ, about to ascend the cross, beautifully removed his royal garments, so that you might know that he suffered as a human being, and not as the divine King. For although Christ is both, it is as a human being, not as God, that he is crucified.

And wonderful is God’s dispensation: the soldiers, unknowingly, wisely know in prophecy at what time, and what kind, of garments are fitting for Christ.

The Place of the Skull was the place of those who had been beheaded and of those who were afflicted with various tortures unto death. The Lord is therefore crucified there where previously there had been a field of the condemned, so that there the banners of the martyrs might thereafter be raised.

And just as for our sake he became a curse upon the cross, so, for the salvation of all, he is hung as though guilty among the guilty, scourged in the midst of them.

For this reason that account which some transmit concerning Adam does not seem plausible: that he was supposedly buried there, so that Christ’s blood might drip upon his tomb. They therefore say that the place was called Calvary, that is, “of the head,” because of the head of the human race, so that the first-formed man himself might find resurrection with the whole people through Christ’s resurrection.

For, they say, it would be inappropriate that, while many who were born from him received forgiveness of sins and the grace of resurrection in Christ, the father of all should not himself obtain such grace through Christ, as though he could not otherwise be saved unless divine Scripture were shown to be false, since it says that he was buried in Hebron.

But if this were so, why were others also condemned in that place? From this it is evident that Golgotha was not the tomb of the first man, but the place of those who had been beheaded, so that it might be shown that where sin abounds, grace abounds still more.

“And they gave him wine to drink mixed with gall. And when he had tasted it, he would not drink.” This is the myrrh-flavored wine that Mark mentions, since Matthew used “gall” for bitterness. For myrrh-flavored wine is extremely bitter. It is also possible that they mixed gall, wine, and myrrh together to make it more bitter, so that this drink might express all the bitterness of their flesh and soul—or spirit—and thereby signify the fullness of the bitterness of the passion.

But Christ, when he had tasted it, as the present Evangelist says, would not drink. This is what Mark means when he says, “he did not accept it”—that is, in order to drink it—even though he tasted it.

And wonderful is God’s dispensation, which orders all things in such a way that the fulfillment of prophecy is completed in the deed, and the event itself reveals the divine mysteries. For tasting is one thing, and drinking is another. He tasted death, but did not wish to drink it completely, because he rose on the third day.

It is enough for us that he tasted death for us. Therefore, when he had tasted it and would not drink it, he said: “It is finished.”

For this reason God speaks through the prophet concerning Jerusalem: “I planted you as a choice vine” (Jer. II, 21); “how have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” A bitter vine produced bitter wine, which it offered to the Lord Jesus, so that what was written might be fulfilled: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII, 22).

The Evangelist speaks of the present passage by anticipation, because this was fulfilled after the Lord had ascended the cross; and this fulfillment was, in fact, the tasting of death. Thereafter no bitterness of corruption is mingled with Christ’s eternal glory and incorruption. For the wine mixed with gall that he tasted is one thing, and that other wine is another—the new wine that he promised to drink with his disciples in the kingdom of God.

After they had crucified him, they divided his garments among themselves, casting lots [Col. 0946A]. This is what he had foretold about himself through the prophet in the Psalm: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my garment they cast a lot” (Ps. XXI, 19).

John explains this prophecy more fully when he says that, after the soldiers had crucified Christ, they took his garments and made four parts, a part for each soldier (John XIX, 23–24). But the tunic, because it was seamless and woven from above throughout, they said to one another: “Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, to determine whose it shall be.”

Not all of them received it, but the one who obtained it by lot received it as the lot of Christ’s inheritance. Woe to those who try to tear this tunic, which was woven from above throughout! Even the soldiers, without understanding its significance, produced a wondrous work.

Nor did they all receive him, but the one who obtained it received it by a good lot. We do not believe, therefore, that any of his garments was torn in the other division, but that each of them remained intact for the individual to whom it fell.

Nevertheless, we do not know what those garments were like; we desire to know how great are the mysteries contained in them. Each of the Evangelists received a share of these garments by lot, but one seamless garment, woven from above throughout, remains with one—and with all as one [Col. 0946B].

Of these garments, whoever has no share under the entire vault of heaven is wretched, because he walks naked; and whoever wishes to tear what all possess in unity is still more wretched. Therefore Christ’s garments must be divided among all by lot in such a way that unity is not corrupted; and unity must be preserved in such a way that each person guards his own portion.

“And sitting down, they kept watch over him.” The diligence of the soldiers and priests benefits us even to the present day, so that the truth may appear greater and the power of the risen one more evident. For they were already guarding the body of the crucified man, having been ordered to do so by the chief priests, as though it might be stolen by the disciples if it were not guarded. Thus, if they wished to proclaim the truth, he made them witnesses of the resurrection.

“And they placed above his head the written charge against him: THIS IS JESUS, KING OF THE JEWS.” It was their custom to write the charges against the condemned, and therefore Christ’s title and charge are wondrously written above his head.

It was not written simply as in the case of others, but was inscribed in three languages, in which the whole world, divided into three parts, is especially governed by the study of letters. Nor was it placed in an insignificant location: it was raised above his head, as though it were the trophy of a reigning king, so that it might be evident to all who read it.

I cannot sufficiently admire, in view of the greatness of the matter, God’s providence, which everywhere prepares his mysteries from the errors of his adversaries. Behold: the false witnesses have already been bought; behold: sedition has been stirred up by the chief priests and elders through many acts of persuasion; behold: the wretched people have been hired to cry out and demand Christ’s death.

Yet they find no charge by which he might rightly be put to death, except that he was the King of the Jews. Although they did this to mock him, the truth of it is nevertheless confirmed by prophecy, which says: “Do not corrupt the inscription of the title.”

Pilate, as though obeying divine Scripture, although ignorant of it, gives and confirms this testimony: “What I have written, I have written,” so that the title might not in any respect be corrupted against the divine prophecy. It is as though he were saying: “What I have written, I have certainly written truthfully—not only because, as you say, he himself claimed it, but because he truly is the King of the Jews.”

He speaks of himself in the Psalms: “But I have been established as king by him”—that is, by God the Father—“upon Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. II, 6).

Behold, brothers, as you see, whether by opportunity, or in truth, or for whatever other reason, Christ is proclaimed King and God; every letter of the Scriptures bears witness that his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, whether of the Hebrews, the Greeks, or the Latins. Pilate therefore did not do this by chance, but was driven by a divine impulse.

The charge against Jesus is written above his head and placed there as a priestly crown, like the one that the priest under the Law wore upon his head, bearing the form of Christ’s high priesthood. For this reason he wore a written golden plate upon his forehead, to foreshadow Jesus as the true high priest. Now his title—who he is and what he is—is placed upon the cross, without corruption, as though upon his forehead, so that it may be clear to all who read it that he himself is Jesus, the true high priest and King of the Jews.

Then two robbers were crucified with him, one on his right and one on his left. This too was done through the great providence of God, so that the King and ruler of all the saints might not be raised upon the cross alone; for Christ’s cross is raised like the tribunal of a judge.

Therefore two were crucified with him, so that the entire case of judgment might be represented together upon the cross: two guilty men are placed on either side, one on the right and one on the left, while the innocent Christ is condemned in the middle [Col. 0947C].

The punishment is equal, but the cause is different. The sentence of the judge does not make the merit of all one and the same, nor does equal punishment lead everyone to one outcome. Thus Christ the innocent King is afflicted in the middle, as though he were about to judge those who would be on the right or on the left.

Otherwise, if the judge were not innocent and almighty, he could neither mercifully grant forgiveness to those on the right nor determine by his righteous judgment the punishment of those who would be on the left.

Therefore innocence, although unjustly condemned, is more gloriously vindicated and acquitted, while the punishment of the guilty is decreed. For although all are guilty because of the punishment of sin and are justly punished, only those are saved to whom the righteous Judge, God, grants indulgence and the confession of piety.

But to those who will be on the left, blasphemy and unbelief are justly left according to the hardness of their hearts, in which they will be punished.

And therefore, as I have said, the entire case of judgment, and the condition of the cases, is prepared in advance, as though before the tribunal of the eternal Judge. Thus what was done upon the cross is the fulfillment of the judgment of the whole world and the manifestation of the prophecy concerning which it is said: “He was counted among the wicked” (Mark XV, 28).

He was placed not merely in any position, but in the middle, as King and Judge between Jews and nations, so that he might place the sheep on his right and determine the goats on his left, because “his right hand is full of righteousness” (Ps. XLVII, 11).

Thus it happened that he was recognized in the midst of two animals. If you consider this carefully, you will find that in this triumph of the cross all the mysteries of salvation are determined, all judgments are brought to completion, [Col. 0948A] and the rewards of eternal life are bestowed.

Those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying: “Ah! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days, save yourself.” They said this as though he had said: “I can destroy it and rebuild it.”

Some manuscripts also read: “You who destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself.” But the meaning is one, because at times they spoke these words mockingly to the crowd and to him.

What is said as “those passing by” is expressed better in Greek as “those going past,” so that we may understand the passage distinctly from the Psalm: “Why have you broken down its wall,” that is, the wall of the vineyard that he had brought out of Egypt, “and all who pass along the way pluck it,” it says (Ps. XCVII, 13).

Those going past were the ones who, after the wall of the vineyard had also been broken down, were stripping those who had remained in the faith, praising God [Col. 0948B]. For as long as anyone does not turn away from the way of God, he can say to God: “You have set my feet upon a rock.”

Therefore he does not blaspheme Jesus, who is the head of the Church, because he stands fixed in faith in him and cannot shake his head like one who goes past, crosses over, or turns away from the way of God.

But if he does this, then he blasphemes and insults him, saying: “Ah!”—in accordance with the words: “They saw and shook their heads” (Ps. CXIII, 7). “Ah!” is an interjection of one who insults or mocks.

For all who do not have a firm head, but move it up and down, are not wise. They do not have their eyes in their head, nor do they hold their head—their mind—firm in faith, lest it be moved; rather, their mind and conscience whirl about like a sling at every circumstance [Col. 0948C].

They did not wish to walk along the straight road of the Scriptures, nor to know the ways of life, so that they might stand in the way of God. Therefore they went past, shaking their heads, because they had moved their feet away from standing upon the rock, which is Christ.

And they said: “Save yourself, if you are the Son of God; come down from the cross.” In their folly they foolishly mocked him, saying: “Ah! You who destroy the temple.”

They were saying what the false witnesses had earlier falsely fabricated for themselves. He had not said that he himself would destroy the temple of God, but: “Destroy it, and I will rebuild it after three days.” What others destroy, he rebuilds—whether the temple of his body, or the temple of his martyrs, or that of all who possess the testimony of God within themselves.

Hence he himself says: “For the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and will come forth” (John V, 28).

1166 Likewise the chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and elders, said: “He saved others; he cannot save himself.” How wretched were the priests and scribes, who had read everything that had been foretold about Christ by the prophets, who had seen what they themselves confess—for they had certainly seen that he had saved others—and yet they mocked him. Thus, Pharisees, your own sentence condemns you, since you refused to believe. For they were stirred up by the outcry of the crowd. The crowd, then, says—although in mockery—“Save yourself!” and, “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross.” These men, by contrast, deny and cry out that he could not save himself, while nevertheless confessing that he saved others. Hence they are worse than the crowd: they do not believe or inquire into what they had read, namely, that he is the Son of God; they despise what they had seen; and what he plainly could do for others, they deny that he could do for himself. They deny and confess at the same time.

Yet if he had wished, he truly could have saved himself—the one who was able to raise himself from the dead on the third day, as he had foretold. “If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe him.” A thoroughly deceitful and false promise! What was greater: to come down alive from the cross, or to rise dead from the tomb? He did rise, nevertheless, and they absolutely refused to believe when he rose; indeed, they gave the soldiers a large sum of money so that they would not testify to his resurrection but would lie that he had been removed. Jesus knew and foresaw everything; therefore he did what was necessary all the more firmly than he would have done had he come down because of their mockery. For this was what he had come to do.

Perhaps the elders of the people also said this at the instigation of his adversaries, rather than on their own judgment, as it seems to me. For as soon as the Lord was crucified, they immediately felt the power of the cross and understood that their strength had already been broken. Hence, through those whom they had seized, they craftily attempted to make him come down from the cross before he triumphed over them and destroyed the dominion of death. But the Lord, knowing their plots, remains upon the gibbet, so that he might conquer all the legions of Tartarus and return victorious from the underworld.

Here, as was his custom, the devil—just as in the first temptation—employs the arguments of an evil exhortation: “He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he wants him,” for he said, “I am the Son of God.” Above also the crafty tempter had asked whether he was the Son of God—not as a devotee, but as a plotter. And so he provokes him to confidence, just as above he provoked him to seek the help of angels: not in order to rescue him, but in order to test him, and, having tested him, to deceive him by fraud. For it would have been no small deception had he come down from the height of the cross, contrary to reason, in response to their insult, against his own purpose, against the authority of all the prophets, against the whole order of our salvation, and against the Father’s will—before, by dying, he had conquered death and ascended victorious from the underworld.

Therefore the plots of the worst of plotters must always be guarded against, lest we be recalled from a good purpose by his deceits before the palm of victory is placed in the hands of those who conquer.

1167 The robbers who had been crucified with him also reproached him. Luke, however, relates the matter quite differently when he says: “One of the robbers who were hanging there blasphemed him, saying, ‘If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.’ But the other, answering, rebuked him, saying, ‘Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong.’ And he said to Jesus, ‘Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.’ And Jesus said to him, ‘Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise’” (Luke 23:39–44).

I have said all this so that you may see how differently the evangelists often speak with one another, or how variously they speak—yet with one Spirit and not with a different understanding. Even if one says more than another, or if they appear to speak differently—as here, where Matthew and Mark introduce two men blaspheming: “And the robbers who had been crucified with him reviled him” (Mark 15:32), or “blasphemed him.” Luke, as I have said, does not say that two blasphemed, but only one; the other, he says, not only believed, but also restrained his companion and pleaded on his own behalf. This very diversity calls for a prudent hearer, not a quarrelsome person contradicting the truth.

Hence we must seek to understand the manner in which they speak, since two are said to have blasphemed or reviled the Lord on behalf of one robber. This often occurs in Scripture, both divine and human: a plural number is used for a singular, as Matthew and Mark did here for the sake of brevity, using the plural for the singular. Thus also Paul says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “They shut the mouths of lions” (Hebrews 10:33, 37), although Daniel alone is understood to have done this. Likewise, “They were sawn apart” is plural, although Isaiah alone is traditionally handed down as having been sawn from the crown of his head through the middle all the way down.

1168 But since pagans are accustomed to slander the Gospel of Christ, let them also observe how the authors of their own literature spoke, using “Phaedras,” “Medeas,” and “Clytemnestras” in the plural, although each was a single woman. For this figure of speech, which they call synecdoche, is very commonly used: one is put for many, or many for one, or a part for the whole. For example, I may say, “The peasants insult me foolishly,” even if only one is insulting me. Likewise it is said in the Psalm: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together” (Psalm 2:2); the plural has been used for the singular. This is explained in the Acts of the Apostles, where Peter understood the kings as Herod and the rulers as Pilate when he applied the testimony of that same Psalm.

It could have happened that at first both men reproached him, and then one of them, seeing the wonders that were taking place, turned and confessed the Lord, moved by his clemency to repentance. This fits both peoples: both insulted him, but afterward one remained a blasphemer, while the other became a confessor of Christ and did not cease to implore forgiveness. To him the most merciful Savior, as though seated upon his tribunal, said: “Today you will be with me in paradise,” because those will be with the Lord to whom forgiveness is granted.

This interpretation does not seem contrary to the harmony of the evangelists, although the fuller meaning above appears preferable. In particular, they did not say that both robbers reviled the Lord; for then one could not be understood under a plural number. But now, since it is said merely “the robbers,” or “those who had been crucified with him,” and “both” is not added, one person could, as I have said, be signified by the plural according to this manner of speech. In these two men, the order of the elect and of the reprobate is displayed.

For just as those who will be on the right are never saved without the gift of forgiveness, so those on the left are rightly believed to be condemned never without the spirit of blasphemy, which is impenitence of heart. Thus the man who was saved bears the mystery of the Jews and of those who, after many iniquities and sins, believe in Christ. They can say, being conformed with the Apostle to Christ’s death: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

1169 The other, persisting in his blasphemies, represents those who believe neither in Christ nor in the resurrection of his body after the temple of God was rebuilt on the third day, since this is exceedingly great and difficult for them to believe. Therefore they reproach Christ’s condition and passion, in which, while he was placed there, he performed greater works of power in communion with the whole of nature. For by dying he destroyed death; he conquered the aerial powers; he shattered the rights of hell and freed his own from there. The earth trembled; the rocks were split wherever they were; the tombs were opened; the bodies of the dead were restored to life; and the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom.

1170 “From the sixth hour,” he says, “darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour.”

There were those who said that the Lord was crucified at the third hour and that darkness began at the sixth hour and lasted until the ninth, so that the three hours from his crucifixion until the onset of darkness are understood to have elapsed; for Mark says: “It was the third hour, and they crucified him.” This could indeed be understood quite correctly in that way, were it not that John says that at about the sixth hour Pilate sat upon the tribunal at the place called Lithostrotos, and in Hebrew Gabbatha. For he continues: “It was the preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour, and he says to the Jews, ‘Behold your king,’” and so forth (John 19:13–14).

But if it was the sixth hour when Pilate sat upon the tribunal and Jesus was handed over to the Jews, how was he crucified at the third hour, as some have wished to understand the words of blessed Mark? Mark had already said earlier: “And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments.” If, therefore, he wished to mention the time when that event occurred, it would have been enough for him to say only, “It was the third hour.” Why then did he add what he had already said earlier, “and they crucified him”? Unless he wished, by recapitulating, to signify something that learned men, with the Holy Spirit revealing it, would seek and discover.

For this Scripture was already being read in the time of blessed Mark, when it was universally known to the Church at what hour the Lord had been hung upon the wood of the cross. Thus his error could have been corrected, or his falsehood refuted by many. But this happened by divine counsel, because the evangelist knew that the Lord was crucified by Pilate’s soldiers, and not by the Jews, as they themselves say: “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.” In this way the fraud of the Jews might be exposed more fully.

He wished to show by this statement that those who cried out for the Lord to be crucified crucified him more truly than those who obeyed their governor and the laws of men. For the soldiers, fulfilling the service of their military office, did this according to the duty of Roman discipline. It is therefore shown that the third hour was when the Jews cried out, “Let him be crucified!” Hence the evangelist most truthfully demonstrates that they crucified him more at the time when they cried out. Pilate, unable to withstand their tumult, handed him over to them, after deliberating for a long time within himself about his crucifixion.

But because they did not wish to appear to have done this—as their words make clear, especially in John—the evangelist therefore revealed that they did it at the third hour. He most truthfully proves that their tongue killed the Lord more than the soldiers’ hands, because their tongue raged like a sharp sword: “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Psalm 56:5); and “The venom of asps was boiling under their lips” (Psalm 13:3).

Whoever says that it was not the third hour when the Jews first cried this out should read blessed Augustine’s work On the Harmony of the Evangelists, and will find that he is laboring in vain. Even if he should find another way to resolve the question, this explanation must not be omitted, since each detail is full of mysteries. The interpretation of each statement proves more fruitful the richer it is in meanings.

If someone should perhaps discover something else that does not agree with these statements, he still has no grounds for proving that it was not the third hour when the Lord was crucified by the Jews’ tongues, and the sixth hour when darkness came over the whole earth and the Lord was hung upon the wood. Thus neither evangelist departs from the truth: neither Mark, who says that the Lord was crucified at the third hour, nor John, who says that it was about the sixth hour when Pilate sat upon the tribunal—for it was not yet fully the sixth hour, although some part of the sixth had already begun.

Thus, throughout that entire hour, the events narrated in the Lord’s crucifixion took place, until, when the sixth hour had been completed and he was already hanging there, darkness came—darkness to which the three evangelists, Matthew, Mark, and Luke, bear witness as having occurred over the whole earth.

If this explanation does not seem sufficient to someone, lest the evangelists appear to disagree, let him hear what Jerome says: it could have happened through the fault of copyists that a discrepancy of hours arose among the evangelists, because of two Greek letters—gamma, namely, and episemon. The letter Γ signifies three in their numerical system, whereas episemon signifies six. Since they have a certain similarity in their written forms, it could have happened in Greek that one of the scribes found episemon written for six, as is customary among the Greeks, mistook it for gamma, which expresses three numerically, and therefore wrote the third hour instead of the sixth in Mark. Thus, through the fault of a single manuscript, the others may subsequently have been corrupted. 1171

Or, as others wish, the evangelists are describing one and the same hour in different ways, calling it third or sixth. For during the night in which the Lord was captured, three hours remained until the beginning of day, and then three more until the third hour of the day. Mark rightly calls this the third hour, while the other evangelists call it the sixth, because it is the sixth from the time when the Lord was captured.

But since we have said that this may perhaps have occurred through the fault of Greek copyists, an error could likewise have arisen among Latins through two numerals, again because of a scribal mistake. For whenever we wish to signify six, we often write V and I. If the letter V is divided into two I’s, there are three. Thus it would be the third hour in Mark, which is read as the sixth in the other three. I do not approve this explanation at all, although I have reported the opinion of some.

For even if something of this sort could have occurred among Latins and Greeks, Matthew could not have been corrupted in the Hebrew version with respect to this matter. He says that from the sixth hour, when the Lord stretched out his hands upon the cross, darkness came over the whole earth; and Luke added: “Because the sun was darkened” (Luke 23:45). Therefore the darkness was caused not by something else, as some maintain, but by the failure of the sun, although at that time it was not an eclipse of the sun—the sort that occurs only when the sun and moon come together, when the moon, passing beneath, obstructs the sun’s rays so that it cannot shine upon us, and by its encounter dulls the sun’s light.

But since no one doubts that at the Lord’s passion it was the fourteenth day of the moon, when there was no conjunction of the moon with the sun, nor any encounter by which the sun could be deprived of its light, some people, disturbed and unable to answer fully the arguments of those who slander the faith, preferred to choose a plain and very easy path. They argued that if so dark an obscuration and so evident a miracle had occurred over the whole earth—as the wise men of this age and the critics of our faith maintain—it could not have remained hidden, nor could it have happened without being recorded in the chronicles or histories of the Greeks or Latins. Such an extraordinary novelty, they say, would have moved every person whom they call wise.

This is the principal objection raised by those who believe neither in divine miracles nor in the testimony of the evangelists unless they first accept it with judgment and critical examination. 1172 Hence, as I have said, certain learned men, so that no contradiction might be brought against them by anyone who is always eager to criticize, refute what is true, and assert what is false, said that, just as the other signs that occurred during the Lord’s passion took place only in Jerusalem, so these darknesses too, as they are called, occurred only over the whole land of Judea, until the ninth hour.

For the veil of the temple was torn in that place; there the earth trembled, and the rocks were split; there the tombs were opened; and there many of the dead rose and appeared to many. It is therefore not surprising if these things also happened in the land of Judea, and yet did not occur elsewhere, so that they came to the knowledge of everyone—for example, in India, Ethiopia, or Scythia. If this had happened, they say, it would certainly be found in their histories or annals.

But since we read that the earth trembled, this should be referred to the land of Jerusalem, or, if more broadly, to the land of Judea. Likewise, these darknesses occurred either only over Jerusalem or, at most, over all Judea. Otherwise, while trying to demonstrate the greatness of the miracle, our assertion might fall into ridicule and produce unbelief rather than faith in those who do not believe—especially since Matthew and Mark did not say that the sun was darkened, but only that darkness came over the whole earth.

It follows, they say, that very dark clouds should be understood—perhaps not one, but many and very large clouds—having gathered over the whole land of Judea or over Jerusalem, just as palpable darkness may have occurred in Egypt for three days. It would not have resulted from the sun’s failure, which occurs through the moon’s conjunction with it, but because exceedingly dark clouds gathered together from opposite directions into one mass. Yet there was light for all the children of Israel, wherever they dwelt, as Holy Scripture testifies.

It was impossible, they say, for such darkness to have lasted three continuous days through the encounter of the sun and moon. This, they maintain, was another cause of the darkness, although the Book of Exodus gives no other cause than that Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and darkness and gloom came over the whole land of Egypt for three days; no one saw his brother, nor did anyone rise from his place.

Suppose, then, that the darkness during Christ’s passion is described by exaggeration in this way, and that it extended over all Judea when he stretched out his hands upon the cross. With reference to this event, Moses may rightly be said at that time to have stretched out his hands toward heaven, so that God’s servants might be freed from the yoke of slavery.

Yet no one can rightly believe that Moses was more effective in Egypt than Christ was upon the cross. 1173 Therefore, since Egypt signifies the whole world here, it is better to believe that darkness began at the sixth hour—when the first man was formed from the clay of the earth—and lasted until the ninth hour, not merely over Judea, as these people think, but over the whole earth that the sun is seen daily to illuminate.

I am astonished at what such wise men intended to devise in statements of this kind. It is as though unbelievers and the wise men of this age ought more easily to believe the other things in the Gospel if these statements had been falsified. For Matthew and Mark say that from the sixth hour darkness came over the whole earth—not merely over Judea, nor over Jerusalem, but over the whole earth.

Suppose, then, that we say, as they wish, that it occurred over the whole land of Judea. What, then, shall we do with Luke’s statement that the sun was darkened? Wherever the sun was darkened, nothing remained except darkness. And because the sun did not shine at that time, since it was darkened over the whole earth, there was absolutely nothing in the entire world but darkness until the ninth hour.

This also happened, among other things, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “The sun shall go down at noon, and the day shall be darkened over the earth” (Amos 8:9). And elsewhere: “The sun went down while it was still day” (Jeremiah 15:9). Therefore darkness is reasonably said to have come at the sixth hour, when it is noon, so that no one might think it was the darkness of the preceding or following night.

The Lord is also said to have been crucified in the middle of the earth, because it was fitting that he should suffer at noon—in fullness, that is, and not in deficiency or increase of charity, but in the full fervor of love. Concerning this love, when the bride asks in the Song of Songs, “Where do you pasture? Where do you lie at noon?” (Song of Songs 1:7), he replies, “At noon.” At noon, because in that love with which he suffered for the world, delights and glory flourished.

The darkness therefore lasted three hours, because the whole world had lost the light of the Trinity, which is God. Those who were in the whole world were deprived of light for three hours: of the light of God the Father, of the radiance of his Son Jesus Christ, and of the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore it was not merely that clouds were thickened, as these people say; rather, as Luke testifies, the sun itself was darkened—the greater light—so that it might neither see the Lord hanging there nor allow the wicked blasphemers to enjoy its light.

It is not surprising, then, that the sun withdrew the rays of its light so as not to see the disgrace of Christ, whose figure had gone before in the sons of Noah, who covered their eyes and turned their faces away so as not to see their father’s nakedness.

1174 If they do not believe that such things happened to the sun throughout the whole world by the marvelous power of God—since they could not have occurred through the customary course of nature from the beginning of the world—I do not know whether unbelievers can believe that the earth trembled in the manner reported by the Gospels, that the rocks were split, or, greater still, that the dead rose from their tombs.

As for their claim that these events are found in no histories, let them hear what our Paul Orosius writes: on the day when the Lord was fastened to the gibbet, after a tremendous earthquake had occurred throughout the whole world, rocks in the mountains were split, and many parts of the greatest cities collapsed in an upheaval greater than usual. On that same day, he says, at the sixth hour of the day, the sun was darkened throughout the whole world, and night suddenly covered the earth; and, as it is said:

> And the impious ages feared everlasting night.

Then he added that the miracle shone forth so brilliantly that it was clear that neither the moon had obstructed the sun’s light nor clouds had stood in its way. Rather, on the fourteenth day of the moon—as is known to all—the moon, having crossed the entire expanse of the sky, was far removed from the sun’s sight. The stars too, he says, shone throughout the whole sky during those daylight hours—or rather, during that dreadful night.

This, he says, is attested not only by the faith of the holy Gospels, but also by certain Greek books. Therefore the truth of the Gospel shines forth manifestly, not as these people wish, without witnesses. For a certain pagan named Phlegon, according to Origen’s testimony, recounts this event in his chronicles during the reign of Tiberius Caesar, except that he indicated that it occurred at the full moon.

Dionysius the Areopagite also, writing to his fellow philosopher Apollophanes, says among other things about this miracle:

“When the supreme light of the Father’s glory resolved, according to its own purpose, to make its radiance shine upon the darkness of your mind, it immediately poured into the innermost chambers of my heart, so that I might remember most devoutly for you, my brother, how we were living together in the city of Heliopolis, almost of the same age. I was then completing about twenty-five years of life, when one Friday, at approximately that hour, the sun was horribly darkened, as though the moon had come between it and us. For since it is not God but God’s creature, the sun cannot shine when its light has set. I complained to you, asking what your most prudent judgment was concerning this.

1175 “Your answer remained so firmly fixed in my mind’s heart that it could not be erased by any oblivion or destroyed by any image of death. For, when the world had been uniformly obscured and was wasting away beneath a fog of darkness, and the sun’s disk returned purified, we took up the [uncertain: *philipplari*] of God. When we discovered what was already widely known—that the sun ought not to suffer the troubles of an eclipse through such an extended course—we learned that the moon, from the east, usually seeks refuge at the western hour while covering the sun’s splendor with Ethiopian veils.

“But at that time, when the darknesses that had arisen seemed to us to be extending and hiding the sun’s light as far as the boundaries of the Nile, especially since the moon was lacking and the time of conjunction was not approaching, I said to you, still ignorant of the mystery of so great a thing, ‘O sanctuary of profound knowledge, what do you ascribe to these secrets, mirror of Apollophanes’ teaching?’

“To this you replied to me, speaking, as though by divine rather than human understanding: ‘These things, good Dionysius, are the requitals of divine deeds.’”

Behold what human philosophy thought about these darknesses. Behold what Greece possesses in its authoritative books. Behold what this Apollophanes gave in answer. Perhaps he then understood from the philosopher’s [uncertain reading] what our people are unwilling to believe from the Gospels. He recognized that these darknesses had not occurred in Judea alone, but perceived that the whole world had been uniformly covered with a fog of darkness. And, more wonderfully still, he answered as though from a divine oracle: they were the requitals of divine deeds.

Then blessed Dionysius, as though awakened and roused from sleep by so great a miracle, said: “When I discovered that the day and year had been recorded and agreed with the Annunciation which our Paul proclaimed with attentive ears, with signs crying out in agreement, I yielded to the truth and was released from the bonds of falsehood.”

Alas, how grievously even today the darkness of ignorance obscures the world, especially among those who refuse to submit to the truth, refuse to believe the Gospels, and refuse to understand what the holy evangelists express with such ineffable power and proclaim concerning events so wondrously that no one who possesses understanding or life can deny that what they say is divine.

Therefore, since such people cannot be thoroughly instructed by human words, we must pray to the one who enlightens every person, that he may enlighten them also and lead us into all truth.

And about the ninth hour, he says, Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani.” 1176 That is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” [Col. 0956D] Behold, at the ninth hour he cries out with a loud voice who in the afternoon walked in paradise and cried out, saying, “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9). But here he cries out with a loud voice, which is, so to speak, contrary to the nature of the dying. Therefore we must ask in what respect Christ’s voice was loud: whether merely in the sound of the cry, or whether it was “loud” in a mystery because of mystical realities. If it was externally loud to the sensory hearing as an example, I nevertheless believe that sacramentally it is loud as a remedy for the inner man; for every voice of Christ is clearly loud, and so loud that at the last all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God (John 5:28), by which we are now redeemed twofold. And wherever the cry of Jesus, or the cry of God, or the cry of Wisdom is read in the sacred Scriptures, one must always understand some great and ineffable mystery.

Moreover, Eli is interpreted as “my God,” since *El* is one of the ten names of God. Aquila, wishing to express its etymology, translated it as ἰχυρόν (*ischyrón*), which means “strong”; and he used this at the beginning of the twenty-first Psalm, so that it reads in Hebrew: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” because the words that we sing in the middle—“Look upon me”—are superfluous. I ask you, reader, not to be troubled because other manuscripts have *Heloi, Heloi, lamazaptani*, since *Heloi* is the same as *Eli*, because οι is a diphthong among the Greeks and is to be read as a single *i*. Further, in Hebrew *lamazaptani*, as they say, is the voice of one who is angry, full of complaints. *Lemasabachthani* is Syriac, the complaint of one who laments with devout affection; nevertheless, both expressions mean, “Why have you forsaken me?”

And, as I recently heard from a certain Hebrew, *lamazapthani* seems to mean, “Why have you examined me so thoroughly?” Its sense is: “Why have you examined me so thoroughly, so that you might complete everything in me, down to the last jot of what was foretold about me in the Law and the Prophets?” For this reason it is read in both Greek and Latin, according to the proper character of the Hebrew language, in this form. Although an interpretation of the same utterance immediately follows in both languages, this is done so that the honor and reverence due to Christ’s most sweet voice, which he poured forth at the moment of death to the Father, may be preserved. The same practice is followed with *Alleluia*, *Hosanna*, and *Amen*, so that, with voice and mind in harmony, we may all sing praises to God with one accord, sharing unity of expression with one another.

Indeed, [Col. 0957C] since there is a great mystery in this utterance, the evangelists themselves quite properly, as I have said, provided 1177 that, out of honor and reverence for so great a cry, the exact form of the same words should be preserved in every language. For I do not know whether what is supplicated with such intense emotion in the sacrament of our salvation can be translated with sufficient dignity. Nevertheless, in the version believed to have been corrected by Jerome, the form *lemazabacthani* is consistently found. In the version that, as I think, was formerly read in the churches, the form is *lamazaptani*. But Christ, hanging on the cross, uttered one of these forms, and the evangelists perhaps followed it more closely. It could have happened that someone found a different form written in the Hebrew Psalter, from which this variation in a single word arose; for I have also found *lebasambacthani* in Greek manuscripts.

[Col. 0957D] Therefore, I ask that in words so obscure and unknown among us no Latin speaker be quick to alter them, as though correcting something whose force we cannot understand. Let us therefore follow our Latin translators, who all with one voice said, “Why have you forsaken me.” Nor should we be surprised at the lowliness of the words and the complaints of one who has been forsaken, when we recognize in him the form of a servant and see the scandal of the cross. Yet we must understand that Christ’s death is nothing other than the abolition of death and the humiliation of the powers; it is the confidence of victory and the triumph of one who fights. Although it comes from the weakness of the flesh, it was not necessity but will.

Therefore this utterance must be understood sacramentally rather than as the expression of one who is grieving.
