We must not alter the meaning of so great a mystery into an insult against the weakness of our nature, since it is will, and a sacrament that signifies power, confidence, and triumph. It is plainly a triumph to complain at the cross and, as one offering himself voluntarily, to proclaim the complaints of his innocence; to stand under sentence, yet from there to depart to the right hand of God’s power; to be fastened with nails, yet pray for his persecutors; to drink vinegar and say sacramentally, “It is finished”; to be counted among the wicked, yet grant paradise to one of them; to be lifted up on the wood, yet make the earth tremble; to hang on the cross, yet drive away the sun and daylight; to release his soul from the body, yet recall souls to their bodies and restore the dead themselves to life; to be buried dead as a human being, yet rise again as God; [Col. 0958B] as man, to suffer all the weaknesses on our behalf, yet as God, to triumph in all these things.

Therefore, no one can insult us because of these words, since he says, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”—as though, amid so many causes of blessedness, he had feared to die, and therefore complained that he had been abandoned by God as though compelled to die. If that were so, my brothers, I think this would not be the loud voice of Christ, the Son of the living God. Since it is loud, I believe that in these words he shows us some great sacrament and that a most profound mystery is hidden in himself when he cries out to God, “Why have you forsaken me?”

For it is not permissible to say that he lies when he says, “Why have you forsaken me?” Nor should anything lowly be supposed in it, because what he says in a plaintive voice is true, although spoken through the humility of the human condition. Christ was not divided in this utterance, nor divided into three, as though God the Word had departed from himself while the man was exposed to sufferings. Rather, this voice is loud because, while he existed in the form of God and was equal to God the Father, he took upon himself the form of a servant. Descending, therefore, from that greatness, he emptied himself (Phil. 2:7) by taking the form of a servant. Thus there is one will: that of the Father who sent him and of the Son who voluntarily accepted it.

Therefore, with regard to that nature in which he had been the image of the invisible God in the form of God, the same Christ was forsaken by the Father when the flesh was handed over to death, although he is believed to have remained impassible. He was forsaken not on his own account—for he was always one with the Father—but for the sake of us all, so that God and man, Christ, might endure such and so great things that he would come even to death, and to the death of the cross, which among human beings appeared most shameful. He was not forsaken so that he would cease to be God with God and in God; rather, he was forsaken in order to come even to the cross, to the scourges and spitting, to the crown of thorns, and to various insults.

In this, then, you can understand what he means when he says, “Why have you forsaken me?” He is comparing the glory that he had with the Father with the disgrace that, despising it for our sake, he endured. I do not know, my brothers, whether any mortal can understand in the mystery of this plaintive voice how great and of what kind are the sacraments that he offers. For in these words hangs the salvation of all who have been predestined to life and the judgment of all the condemned, so that he may present to God the Father in himself everything belonging to all the ages. These, then, are his complaints, so that all may understand that, in the fact that he was forsaken even unto death, the cause of everyone’s salvation is at stake.

There are indeed many great things in this voice of Christ, which he briefly recalls before God the Father, but he wishes 1179 each person to consider them with broader understanding. For it is the same voice by which it is said, “You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled.” And also that utterance, as though crying out to the Father: “What profit is there in my blood, while I descend into corruption?” (Ps. 29:8, 10.) He represents to God the Father the obedience of his labor and humility and offers it as the price of our salvation. He asks for the cause—or rather, the fruit of the cause—so that he may commend to God the Father the whole reason why he came even to this death.

I have said these things at greater length so that no one may turn the great sacrament of piety toward the impiety of unbelief. For it is the same voice and speech of one who complains that he has been forsaken and who declares that he reigns. Therefore let no one divide our faith by a principle of unbelief, but let us confess with our whole heart that it is the same one, at the same time, who died and who reigns immortally.

It follows: “But certain people standing there, when they heard this, were saying, ‘He is calling Elijah.’” Therefore, when he says “certain people,” he does not intend everyone to be understood. But, as I think, some of them were Roman soldiers who did not understand the character of the Hebrew speech; when he said, “Eli, Eli,” they thought that he was calling Elijah. Hence others also said, “Let us see whether Elijah will come to save him.”

If we understand Jews to have said these things, it is not surprising that they acted according to their customary manner, slandering the Lord on account of his weakness, as though he had called upon Elijah for help. They did this also to persuade the Romans, who did not know the character of the words, that he was weak because he had been unable to help himself.

But we too, because Christ has become our way, should learn at least at the end of our lives to cry out to the Lord with a loud voice for all our tribulations—not with the sound of the voice, but with the cry of the heart, just as we read that Jonah cried out from the belly of the whale. We cannot deny that his cry was great, since it was heard from the belly of the whale in heaven and from the depth of hell. But Christ’s cry on the cross was altogether greater, because of the greatness of the things completed in Christ and because of the great devotion of his voluntary passion.

[Col. 0959D] Immediately one of them ran, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, placed it on a reed, and gave him something to drink. He did this because, according to John, Jesus had said, “I thirst.” He said this in order that everything that had been foretold about him might be fulfilled, including: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” 1180

To this day the Jews and all who disbelieve in the Lord’s resurrection give him vinegar to drink, and they give him gall: gall, that is, the bitterness of vices, and vinegar, unbelief. For just as new wine signifies honor and the virtue of immortality, so vinegar signifies the corruption of vices. Wine often turns to vinegar in vessels through vice and neglect; so too human nature, when it first fermented in Adam, became sour and corrupt. Taking this nature upon himself, he drank it as though from the reed of our frailty.

But we give him myrrhed wine to drink, and vinegar mixed with gall, whenever we suppose that we can make him sleep so that he will not see our evils. Yet, as far as we are concerned, because we inflict injuries upon him, when he had tasted our mortality he refused to drink the kind of beverage we offered. Not because it was wine, but because it was mixed with gall, and because the wine of joy that was in us had been wholly corrupted by the bitterness of sin.

But to show that the bitterness of vices ought not to have been mixed with the sincerity of a good nature, when he had tasted that corruption itself he refused to drink what had been mixed into it. Instead, taking up the sincerity of nature, in which he would bear what belongs to us and fasten it to the cross, [Col. 0960B] he subsequently demonstrated in himself that, without the bitterness of sin and corruption, the immortality of those who rise again would come to be. Since this immortality had fermented in the vessels of the human race, it is restored in Christ.

Consider carefully, I ask, the things that are narrated and that were done in Christ, and do not suppose that anything lowly happened by chance. O human being, everything was prepared and ordered by providence in such a way that the prophecies might be fulfilled through the events, Christ might be shown in the flesh through the prophecy itself, and through that manifestation the causes of the events and the works accomplished might be revealed.

Otherwise, at the cross, why vinegar? Why a sponge? Or, in such a spectacle, why myrrhed wine? Why so many reeds? Unless all things had been ordered by God so that the objects from which what had been foretold would be done might be present, and might be used at the proper time—and so that in these objects, from which things were done and by which they were done, the prophecies might be proclaimed.

For what else did that sponge signify than the Jews themselves? Whoever considers the nature of a sponge—how porous, swollen and inflated, soft and fragile, and slack it is—can recognize what it signifies. Although it draws in liquids when it swells, it quickly disappears and, when squeezed, expels everything from itself. So too the Jews, or anyone who is swollen with pride, carry within themselves nothing other than the vinegar of sin and corruption. They draw into themselves every filth of wickedness; pride raises them up on the reed of their frailty, and if they are pressed down in any way, they immediately vomit forth what is within them and remain empty and weightless.

Thus they are the very ones who offer themselves as a drink of death, [Col. 0960D] from whom and in whom the Lord’s death is administered. He drinks it in order that it may be abolished in the reed and absorbed from the human body. For unless Christ had absorbed our vices on the cross, we would have remained like an empty reed and a sponge full of the cup of death.

Therefore, since we are so fragile, let us pour out all the inner depths of our hearts to Christ—first through baptism, which we received once, and then daily through repentance—so that our sins may be erased on his cross and death may be swallowed up through him in victory.

Hear a great and marvelous sacrament. Behold, when he drank the vinegar that had been offered to him in the sponge on the reed, according to another evangelist he said, “It is finished.” Everything was indeed finished in him, because, having assumed our mortality, the mystery was fulfilled: he himself on the cross bore in his own person all the wounds of our corruption. Therefore it is one person who runs up, unknowingly, and completes the great mystery in which all things are fulfilled.

For this one person is the unity of all those whose bitterness and corruption the Lord absorbed and emptied out. When all vices had been drained away by grace, only the joy of immortality remained. The vinegar that had become sour returned to its nature, was poured into Christ’s body, and became new wine, the wine of joy, because it flowed from the shoot that is the true vine. This wine he now drinks with his own in the kingdom of his Father; he will no longer drink from what had become sour, from which he received this cup of death.

Jesus, crying out again with a loud voice, gave up his spirit. Here an error could have stolen upon us regarding what Jesus cried out according to Matthew, when he says that Jesus cried out again, unless Luke had expressly stated what he cried out, namely: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” Otherwise our ignorance would more easily say that he cried out again the same voice that he had cried out above, saying, “My God, my God,” and so forth.

Now, however, we must understand that the voice he cried out again as he gave up his spirit was the voice that Luke says he cried out: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” But when he says “again,” this is not to be referred to the fact that he cried out the same thing, but to the fact that he cried out again—and not with just any voice, but again with a loud voice, because what he cried out is great and ineffable.

He commends a great deposit to God the Father, in whose hands are all things. And rightly the Son’s spirit is commended to his most beloved Father, because in the Father’s nature nothing is dearer than the Son, just as in the Son nothing is greater than the Father. For the nature of the Father and the Son is one, their equality is one, and the love of the Holy Spirit is one.

Therefore whatever is commended to the Father by the Son is not lost but preserved. It is thus a good deposit, a good pledge: the Son’s spirit, which is commended. Hence he once confidently said: “You will not abandon my soul to hell, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10).

No one other than the Father can contain Christ, the Son of God; therefore he commends the great spirit, in which are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, to the great God the Father. And he gave up his spirit. He gave it up, certainly, and did not lose it. For to give up or hand over the spirit is one thing, as John says, that he bowed his head and handed over his spirit; to lose it is another. For what we lose, we are sometimes proved to have destroyed.

But whether Christ gave up his spirit, handed it over, or, according to Luke, breathed his last, it was within his power: when, in what manner, and to whom he would commend or hand over his spirit. Otherwise it is not within human nature by itself to breathe out its spirit. Therefore the unity of Christ must be considered carefully.

Here, I ask, let those who say that Jesus did not have a soul hear this: his spirit is his soul, concerning which he himself said, “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18). Both, therefore, were within his power: to take it up again when he wished, because the power of the Father and the Son is one.

Thus he gave it up without departing from his own power when he commended it into the hands—that is, into the power—of the Father, because the one who commends it is the one and the same Christ the Lord. He commends his soul to the Father so that the flesh may be handed over to death. Death is, as the wise men of this world say, the separation of the soul from the body, and this is simply to die.

But it is something altogether different for Christ to cry out with a loud voice and give up his spirit, as Matthew explains; to breathe his last, as Luke testifies; or to hand it over, as John says—and nowhere to anyone other than into the hands of the Father. For it belongs to all human beings to die, even the wicked, since the souls of both the guilty and the holy are separated from the body. But they cannot say this so freely from the bond of sin, nor so absolutely, by their own power in the freedom of grace, as Christ said when he departed from his body—in the mystery, not divided from himself, nor divided into three.

For “whoever dissolves Jesus does not belong to him.” And because he was not dissolved or divided from himself—that is, because he remained in unity with the Father in the soul that he gave up from the body, and in the body in which he was buried in the tomb, that is, in the form in which he is everywhere wholly with the Father and in the Father—therefore, because he is such and so great, it is a great mystery that he cried out with a loud voice and thus gave up his spirit, or handed his spirit—his soul—into the hand of God.

He did not dissolve himself, nor did he dissolve the body whose passage into death he permitted. Because his body died, Christ the Son of God is rightly said to have died and, in the sacrament of our salvation, to have died and been buried.

What, then, is it other than the fulfillment of the words, “I have power to lay down my soul,” when he bowed his head and handed over the spirit commended to God the Father? And what else is it than the fulfillment of what is said in the Psalm: “In peace, in the same place, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. 4:9)?

Therefore Christ rested more securely in this sleep of death than we do in daily sleep, sleeping and resting in peace. Yet he did this in order to invite us to the same peace, to the same hope of sleep and rest, and to the same glory of resurrection.

Therefore, dearest brothers, if we have understood what it means to give up or hand over the spirit into the hands of the Father, let us hasten also to preserve our life, so that at our departure we too may be able to cry out with a very loud voice and thus give up our spirit in peace, or bow our head and hand over our spirit, so that thereafter we may rest in the bosom of the Father.

I have said these things, beloved, so that in matters belonging to his humanity no one may be weakened in faith, nor divide Christ God by separating the Word, the soul, and the body, nor say that the whole Christ, God the Word, was contracted into a mere man of the human race. Rather, the whole Christ, in his twofold operation, worked both the divine and the human things together. This is the great sacrament of piety, manifested in the flesh and revealed in the spirit.

Jesus Christ both handed over his spirit and commended it into the hands of the Father; on that same day he was in paradise; and he himself who was in paradise on that same day is also the one who complained that he had been forsaken. For, as I said, the complaint of the forsaken dying man is weakness, whereas the promise of paradise belongs to the kingdom of the living God. The voice of the one commending his spirit is the confidence of that same person who commends it; the handing over or giving up of the spirit is the passage through death.

Therefore I ask you again, brothers, as though I had said nothing: who died? Surely the one who handed over his spirit. Next, the one who handed over his spirit is also the one who commended his spirit to the Father. And if the one who commended it and the one who handed over the spirit are the same person who died, I ask whether the body commends the soul, or whether God commends the soul of the body.

For there is no doubt that “spirit” frequently signifies and is called “soul,” as is evident at least from this: Jesus, about to die, handed over his spirit. If, therefore, someone thinks that the soul should be understood to have been commended by the body—by that which was about to be dissolved from life—the living by that which was about to decay, the eternal by that which was to be raised—and doubts that the same person commended his spirit to the Father who was also in paradise with the thief on that same day, I ask: did he remain in paradise after being received into the tomb? Or, while remaining in paradise, did he complain that he had been forsaken by God?

It is certain that the one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, the Word who became flesh (John 1:14), signifies himself through all these things. When he cries out that he has been forsaken unto death, he is man; in paradise, Christ God reigns. Moreover, while reigning in paradise, the Son of God commends his spirit to God the Father; and the spirit thus commended is handed over by the Son of Man to death in the sacrament of piety, so that Christ may be dissolved in nothing, the distinct properties of the natures may be confused in nothing, and the unity of the person may be divided in nothing.

When he gave up his spirit, signs occurred above him of his divinity, and miracles testified to the truth, as well as powers bringing salvation.

“And behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. And the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split,” and so forth. Truly the veil of the temple was torn, and all the sacraments of the Law that had previously been hidden beneath the veil were opened. For the one who alone, having been appointed priest forever with an oath according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. 109:4), had now come.

He alone, through the dispensation of his death, was able to enter once for all, through his own blood, into the holy and eternal redemption. By his entrance, immediately after his death, he deigned to tear the veil of the temple in two, from top to bottom, so that the hidden things that had been concealed and veiled within the Law, in the temple, and in all the ceremonies might be seen.

They had to be veiled until the one who alone could reveal them made them manifest to the apostles and to all who awaited him for salvation. Everything had previously been veiled and overshadowed, including the very face of Moses. But it is not now the time to explain what all those things were, since the highest sacraments of God were revealed in them, and especially at the moment when the most kind Jesus, crying out with a loud voice, gave up his Spirit [Col. 0964A] and did not lose it—for to lose it, as I have said, belongs to necessity.

He gave it up by his own will, he who holds the key of David and disclosed everything that had been obscure from the beginning of the world and wrapped in figures. Now, when the veil had been torn, all the mysteries concerning Christ that had been hidden were made manifest to everyone.

Therefore, brothers, this power and the tearing of the veil must be considered and admired. It is much greater than any mortal could admire: that the veil was torn at the very moment when Christ, through death, entered into that blessed rest of the eternal inheritance. For from there came all these forms and mystical sacraments of the realities represented, which had been hidden in the veil, concerning which God had said to Moses: “Make everything according to the pattern and form that was shown to you on the mountain” (Exod. 25:40).

And because everything was shown to Moses on the mountain—that is, in Christ—it is rightly in Christ and through Christ that everything has been opened to us.

The veil, therefore, is torn, and the Synagogue is profaned; the letter of the Law is destroyed; the heavenly sacraments hidden in it are opened in the Spirit—for the Law is spiritual—and the Church is brought in with the gaze of the mind unveiled, so that it may see the eternal and mystical mysteries once promised to it.

For this reason the rocks also were split through Christ’s passion: so that old things might be cut away and new things arise. Thus, through the broken cliffs of the rocks, new things to come are shown. For human hearts harder than rocks had to be split open by heavenly words, so that the water that had flowed from the rock might itself flow from them and within them, divinely poured over them.

Moreover, in the Gospel that properly belongs to the Hebrews, blessed Jerome says that he read that the temple lintel, of immense size, had then been broken and split apart; we believe this happened to signify the abolition of the Law and the destruction of the temple.

Josephus also relates in his books that the angelic powers, once guardians of the temple, cried out together at that time: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

As for the earth being shaken, this was the fulfillment of prophecy. Although the earthquake itself contains greater sacraments within it, it is said that in that earthquake many cities, wherever they were, and many buildings collapsed. Nor is it surprising that, when the Lord was dying, the earth trembled, since at his resurrection all human flesh was moved and shaken, so that by words and events people were awakened as though from death to life, from flesh to spirit, and from the oldness of the letter to the New Testament; and in the new song all things, even the trees of the forests, would sing and become new.

When did these things happen? Certainly, as the Prophet says, when “the Lord reigned from the wood” (Ps. 95:12). Then the earth saw and was shaken. All who saw these things were also disturbed, and every human being was afraid (Ps. 63:9–10).

This is that great shaking which perhaps at that time occurred only in Judea, in Jerusalem, but whose significance reached beneath the entire expanse of heaven, even to the ends of the earth. These signs may seem small and insignificant to unbelievers, as they wish, but to believers they are immense and, so to speak, ineffable.

Although, as they themselves claim, these events did not extend beyond the borders of Judea or Jerusalem, the fulfillment of their significance had already overtaken the whole world. Likewise, the resurrection of the dead, when the tombs were opened, is more reasonably believed to have occurred only in Judea or around Jerusalem, since only the bodies of the saints rose—not immediately when the tombs were opened, but soon after the Lord’s resurrection. For Christ is the firstborn from the dead.

No one doubts that all these things are great in themselves: that, when the Lord was crucified, none of the elements could endure not to show him to be dead; that the sun was darkened and all the holy of holies was opened; that the earth trembled and the rocks were split; that the tombs were opened and the dead whom the underworld held were restored to life.

Nevertheless, as I have said, what these things signify is greater than the signs themselves, although the signs themselves are astonishing. The same is true of this resurrection of the dead, when many who had fallen asleep rose, came out of the tombs after Christ’s resurrection, entered the holy Jerusalem, and appeared to many.

Although this resurrection was exceedingly astonishing and marvelous, that future general resurrection is still greater, and this one testified to it, since many rose as a testimony to the true resurrection of Christ. They came into the holy city and appeared to many, so that those who had truly seen them rise might themselves be witnesses to the people of the true resurrection.

For many who rise rightly make many witnesses. This is difficult to believe, even though it is desirable. Therefore Christ, although one person died and he alone died for all, did not wish to rise alone, but with many, so that he might first have witnesses of the resurrection. Then he himself, together with many, became a witness of perpetual resurrection, so that he might pour hope into the despairing.

It was fitting that, because he had illuminated the darkness of our minds through his teachings, he should also illuminate the obscurities of the underworld; that he should make his saints visible through the resurrection of the flesh, so that they might instruct the minds of the faithful; and that, ascending alive from the underworld as a victor, he should display the spoils of death before those who saw them.

Otherwise unbelievers might say that a pure man could not rise by the power of God. But what Christ could do by his own power, he did as God and man.

For what else does the opening of the tombs signify than that, once the barriers of death had been shattered, it signified the resurrection of all the dead? In their appearance there was the faith of those who saw them; in their coming forth, a type of future things. By coming forth into the holy city, they declared the form of present things; and in that same form they displayed the pattern of future things.

Hence many ask whether that resurrection was perpetual, or whether, just as Lazarus rose again only to die again, so these people also rose again only to die once more. The Gospel does not make this clear. Nevertheless, several people seek to affirm that their resurrection with Christ was perpetual, although others think differently.

For if they were true witnesses of Christ’s true resurrection, it is pious not only to suppose but also to believe and confess that they rose perpetually, never to die again. Otherwise, how could they have been true witnesses of the true and perpetual resurrection if they had soon returned to the dust of the earth?

But since we can persuade those who do not contradict us less readily from the Gospel on this matter, let it be enough for us, if they refuse to believe, that they cannot contradict it either. Together with certain holy teachers, we devoutly suspect this to be the case.

For even if the things we assert seem great, what they signify is greater still, as I have already said above: these things are signified in human souls and happen daily until everything is fulfilled that has been promised generally through Christ.

But meanwhile these people came into the holy city, namely that Jerusalem, and appeared to many. It is called holy either because of the temple that was in it, or because of the Holy of Holies; or because it had formerly been holy and still retained that ancient legal name, just as Matthew was not ashamed to call himself a tax collector—not because he still was one, just as Paul was not still a persecutor, but because he had been one.

It is also possible that the evangelist is speaking of that heavenly Jerusalem, saying that they reached it and appeared to many, so that Jesus would not return alone to the heights, just as he did not rise alone from the dead. They certainly ascended there with him, although they were first seen in this earthly city, having risen immortally so that they would no longer be subject to death.

But the centurion and those who were with him keeping watch over Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, were greatly afraid, saying, “Truly this was the Son of God.” O how hard-hearted the Jews were! Behold, meanwhile the insensible elements perceived the Lord’s death; the dead heard the sound of his cry; the underworld restored them alive. The centurion believed when he saw these things, as did those who were with him, and they confessed him to be the Son of God. Only the wretched Jews neither perceived what was happening, nor believed, nor revered, nor reconsidered what they had done.

The centurion believed, although imperfectly. Imperfectly, indeed, because when he said, “He was,” he supposed that he had been so in the human manner, not knowing the mystery of his divinity, nor that he had ceased to live through the death—which itself he saw to be wondrous. Hence Mark says: “When the centurion who stood facing him saw that he had breathed his last with such a cry, he said, ‘Truly this man was the Son of God’” (Mark 15:39). For he does not say, as Matthew does, that he saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, but only that “he had breathed his last with such a cry.” Thus the centurion understood something great in that cry and in the manner in which he gave up his spirit. If it had not contained something especially astonishing, Mark would never, leaving aside the other miracles that had moved the centurion and those who were with him to wonder, have related this one thing alone.

Accordingly, in such a miracle Christ’s divinity is truly declared. But we must examine this one point thoroughly, since we have already discussed the others above: what is so wondrous about his giving up his spirit? For unless that same centurion had understood in it the magnitude of its meaning according to his own capacity, I think that, however greatly he was astonished at this one event, he would not have said, “Truly this man was the Son of God.” But when he gave up his spirit, what else did he do except die? If that alone had occurred, and nothing further wondrous had appeared in it, the Apostle would never have said that “there are three that testify on earth” (1 John 5:7)—namely, the spirit, the blood, and the water, testifying to Christ because he is God. The spirit, certainly, which he gave up, and the blood and water which, after his death, flowed from his side contrary to human nature, as a sacrament of our redemption.

But since the spirit is now under discussion, we must ask how and what testimony it gave. We believe that it gave no other testimony than that Christ is the true God. But how it gave this testimony is not obvious, unless perhaps it was because such liveliness and such radiance were in his face that all could understand that he was dying of his own will; and because his voice had been so powerful when he said, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit,” that each might recognize that it was not merely a matter of humanity, but that the mystery of divinity was also present. Therefore, when he had prayed, he immediately bowed his head and surrendered his spirit, as though lulled into the sleep of peace.

Nevertheless, although it was clearly shown in him by his appearance, his voice, and the understanding of his words that he was the Son of God, our predecessors transmit another explanation. It was the custom of the Romans, and of all those who scourged people destined for crucifixion, first to strike those who were held guilty for their crimes and to wear them down with many punishments, so that they would not endure a greater torment. For after crucifixion they suffered longer and exceedingly severe agony, with much pain, if they had not first been tortured by blows beneath the arms and upon the sinews.

But these things had not first been done to Jesus. Pilate, wishing to satisfy the whole populace who had cried, “Crucify him, crucify him,” and fearing their tumult, had not ordered them to be done to Jesus, so that he might die quickly on the cross. Those whose death was not hastened on the cross ordinarily lived until the third day, and even until the fourth. Since Jesus had not previously been beaten in this way, it was expected that he would live for a long time hanging on the cross and suffer still greater torments.

But because his hour had come, so that he might rise on the first day after the Sabbath, he prayed to the Father and was heard; and when he cried out, he was received peacefully, as one possessing authority to lay down his life. Therefore, with his head bowed (Song 1:7), he laid it down when he wished and in the manner he wished. Seeing this prodigy, contrary to the custom of all those who were tortured on the cross, the centurion said, “Truly this man was the Son of God.”

It was a great miracle that, after three hours, the one who might perhaps have lived two or three days on the cross was received, if he had lived according to the custom of those who were hanged. For this reason it seemed to the centurion a great benefit of God that he expired so quickly, and more the result of the merit of his prayer than of the violence of the cross.

Otherwise, if what happened to Jesus’ body had occurred according to the custom applied to those whom they wished to take down quickly from the cross, why was it necessary for the centurion and the soldiers to keep watch over him on the cross? Or why was it necessary, as John writes, for them to ask Pilate and offer petitions that their legs be broken, so that death might come more quickly and they might be taken down from the wood on account of the Sabbath—as the Evangelist testifies, lest they remain hanging on the cross on that day?

But when they broke the legs of those who had been crucified with him and came to Jesus, they did not break his legs, because he had already given up his spirit. For this reason the miracle was new and unheard-of, not only to the centurion and those who were with him, but also to Pilate. When Pilate heard from Joseph that he was already dead, he was greatly astonished, as Mark testifies; he summoned the centurion and asked whether he was truly dead.

Therefore, among the other miracles that occurred during Christ’s passion, this was by no means the least. Astonished by it, the centurion and those who were with him also reported it to Pilate, overcome by the amazement and novelty of what had happened.

Yet it is not contradictory that Matthew here says that the centurion and those who were with him were astonished when they saw the earthquake and the things that had happened. Among the many wondrous events that occurred at that time, the Savior’s death itself was also wondrous, full of God’s power and awe. Since there were many great events, the Evangelists were free to relate whichever miracles each wished to recall, or to say which of all these things had caused those who saw them to wonder.

For the Evangelists do not appear to disagree in any respect when one says that something else was wondered at. All of them rightly wondered at everything, and all at each individual event. Who could fail to wonder, when he ascended the cross, that suddenly so dreadful a darkness came over the earth at midday? Or who would not rather be struck with amazement at the hour when he gave up his spirit, that such serene light returned? For it is clear that the same darkness continued until the ninth hour, when he gave up his spirit.

Then the veil of the temple was also torn, the earth trembled with an unusual movement, the rocks were split, and the tombs of the dead were opened. Therefore, when the centurion and those who were with him saw the earthquake and the terrifying things that were happening, they not only wondered but were also greatly afraid, saying, “Truly this was the Son of God.”

If he truly was the Son of God, he certainly could not have ceased to be; for what truly is remains altogether the same forever. Meanwhile, this centurion and those who were with him, by confessing the Son of God, foreshadow the faith of the nations and the true faith. For, as Mark says, he confesses him as both God and man, saying, “Truly this man was the Son of God.” Luke says that he declared, “Truly this man was righteous.” Or perhaps they said both things about him, since he was both a human being and righteous, and truly the Son of God.

The two statements converge upon one judgment and one faith. Nor is it in any way contradictory that one Evangelist omitted “this man” while another included it. Whatever the manner in which that man believed, Christ remained always the same—not as he is perhaps said to have supposed, so that he did not truly believe him to be the Son of God but merely righteous and holy, just as many righteous people are called sons of God.

Whatever, however, he may have perceived, we rightly believe and confess him to be truly God and man, the Son of God, and in his righteousness truly most righteous.

Finally, among the other miracles, nothing less clearly appeared after the Lord’s resurrection: many who had fallen asleep rose and appeared to many. Yet they did not appear to everyone, but only to those who were worthy to see such things, so that they might be witnesses foreordained by God.

From this we must understand that, just as not everything has been written about those to whom they appeared, or for how long, except that they came into the holy city and appeared to many, so likewise not everything concerning Christ’s resurrection has been committed to writing. The Apostle Paul proves this when he says that, after he had risen, he was seen at one time by more than five hundred brothers (1 Cor. 15:6).

I have said this so that an intelligent mind may understand that not all the Savior’s miracles have been written down, nor all the things he did narrated, but only a few out of many, solely so that we may believe.

There were also many women there, watching from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee and ministered to him. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.

Concerning these women, a considerable ambiguity often arises, as it does here. Matthew says that the mother of the sons of Zebedee was with the other two, whereas Mark recalls that she was Salome. It is therefore not surprising that both Evangelists, although they name three, imply that there were more women who had followed him from Galilee and were looking on from a distance. Among them were these three whom Matthew names, and whom Mark likewise names, except that, in place of the mother of the sons of Zebedee, he seems to put another woman, Salome.

It could indeed be that she was the woman whom Mark places third among these many women. For it makes no difference to the truth which women the two Evangelists together, or each individually from among the whole group, chose to name.

Origen, however, suspects that this same Salome was the mother of the sons of Zebedee, who is rightly called by that name. “Many,” he says, “were waiting by the cross of Jesus, but the principal women among them were named, as though watching him more attentively, ministering to him more generously, and following him more faithfully and perfectly.”

For it was the custom of the Jews, and was not considered blameworthy according to the ancient practice of that people, for women to provide their teachers with food and clothing from their own resources. Because this could cause scandal among the nations, the Apostle Paul recalls that he had renounced the practice: “Do we not have the right to take along believing women, as do the other apostles?” (1 Cor. 9:5).

These women certainly ministered to the Lord from their own means and followed him on account of his holy teaching. It was not that the Lord needed these things, but that he might display a type and pattern for teachers who followed him, since they ought to be content with food and clothing supplied through the service of their disciples.

But let us see what sort of companions the Savior had. Mary Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, took an appropriate surname from the village or place of Magdala, where she had been born. Now Magdala is interpreted as “magnification.” This Mary had been magnified by the magnification of God, because she had followed the most gracious Jesus, to whom many sins had been forgiven because she had loved much; and she ministered to him especially among all the women. As the Gospel declares, she awaited the mystery of Christ’s passion and resurrection more than all the others.

Among these principal women there was also Mary, the mother of James the younger and of Joseph. She was the sister of Mary, the mother of the Lord, and Christ’s maternal aunt—great in offspring, but greater in holiness. She followed the Lord more through the affection of her mind and desire for virtue than through carnal love, and she ministered to the Lord until the moment of his death.

But Jerome, writing to Hedibia concerning these Marys, says that Mary the Lord’s maternal aunt was the wife of Clopas. If this is so, let him consider how James and Joseph are called the Lord’s brothers—unless they were his relatives according to the flesh, being, as we believe, the sons of the sister of the Lord’s mother. Many agree with this, although the aforementioned teacher appears to contradict it in that passage.

Among the others there was also a third principal woman, the mother of the sons of Zebedee. Having left her husband—or after his death—she followed Jesus. This too has a meaning, since her sons were called “sons of thunder.” Perhaps she herself was called Thunder because of her faith and holy life—not because her sons were so named, but because she had been awakened by the same thunder of Christ to follow him and minister to him, awaiting the events that took place around the Lord. Her sons were James and John.

John, the son of thunder, himself heard the seven words of thunder which, because they were more exalted and the world could not comprehend them, he was commanded not to write down.

Thus it is permissible, as we have said, to suppose and to say that the mother of the sons of Zebedee was indeed Salome, since both Evangelists unquestionably designated the principal women among the others by name. Perhaps she is called Salome because Salome is interpreted as “peaceful.”

Since the other two women were of great merit, I not unreasonably suspect that this third woman too was the mother of the sons of Zebedee, who is herself called Salome by Mark. These women had followed the most gracious Jesus from Galilee and gone up with him to Jerusalem, so that they might celebrate the Passover with him.

This is the end appointed for all who leave behind the Galilee of the nations and follow the Lord: that they may ascend not only into Jerusalem, but also, ascending into it with Christ, celebrate the true Passover, so that they may joyfully see the risen Lord again in the transmigration.

When evening had come, a certain rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, arrived; he too was a disciple of Jesus. He went to Pilate and asked for Jesus’ body. Then Pilate ordered that the body be given to him.

He is called rich not through the writer’s ostentation, as though he wished to present the Savior’s disciple as rich or noble, since the Lord himself says, “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). Rather, Joseph is called rich to show why he was able to obtain Jesus’ body from Pilate and how he had access to him.

First, according to Mark, he was a decurion—that is, he belonged to the order of the curia and administered its office, on account of which he was also called a curial, that is, a senator of the curia. This is expressed more clearly in Greek as εὐχήμων βουλευτής, that is, “an honorable councillor,” because he managed civil and public affairs. Second, he was rich and noble according to his birth.

Otherwise, a poor and unknown man would not have had the means to approach Pilate, the governor of Roman power, and obtain the body of a crucified man concerning whom so great a sentence had been pronounced before everyone, or upon whom so many things had been declared.

He was, as we are told, from Arimathea. This is the city of Ramathaim, associated with Elkanah and Samuel, in the region of Thamnitica, near Diospolis.

You should recognize that the Lord chose and foreordained such a man for this purpose in both respects, so that he might be worthy to perform for the Lord, before so great a ruler, the great office of burial. Hence Mark says: “Joseph of Arimathea, an honorable decurion, who was himself awaiting the kingdom of God, came and boldly went in to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus” (Mark 15:43).

If he had not been a man of great dignity, this would not have been said of him in such terms. And unless he had possessed greater standing before God, he would never have been praised as being of such great merit. For, he says, he was “a good and righteous man,” because he too was a disciple of the Savior, although secretly, out of fear of the Jews.

It is therefore not without reason that someone may wonder why the man who had been a hidden disciple because of fear of the Jews, or how he dared to ask for Jesus’ body, when none of those who followed him openly had dared to do so.

We must understand that he did this with the confidence afforded by his dignity. Because he possessed that standing, he could enter familiarly to Pilate, since he was honored by everyone, and obtain his request with greater ease.

For this purpose he had long ago been chosen by God’s providence as a disciple, to such an extent that some say that the first psalm was sung concerning him: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly,” and what follows (Ps. 1:1).

Since he was, so to speak, a senator of the Jews and a decurion of the commonwealth, he could more easily obtain what he requested. Pilate summoned the centurion who had guarded Jesus on the cross, as Mark relates, and, being greatly astonished, asked him about Jesus; then he ordered that the body be given over.

Although this man had previously been a secret disciple of Christ and, when listening to the word of God, had been accustomed to avoid the hostility of those others, at the final moment he openly performed, with every care, what he had previously kept hidden. He generously carried out the duty of burial, caring nothing for Jewish offense, because he was righteous—and because he was righteous, he was therefore good.

Because he was good and righteous, he understood that he had been chosen for this purpose: to fulfill with devotion the duty of so great an office at such a time.

Having received the body, he wrapped it in a clean linen cloth and placed it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock; he then rolled a great stone against the entrance of the tomb and departed.

John, however, says that this burial was arranged not by Joseph alone but also by Nicodemus. He begins by relating that Nicodemus, who had first come to Jesus by night, brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds’ weight (John 19:39). He then adds Joseph and says that they took Jesus’ body and bound him in linen cloths with spices, as is the Jews’ custom of burying.

“There was,” he says, “in the place where he was crucified a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid.”

I have said this so that everyone may more fully consider what sort of disciples these two were under a hidden appearance, and with how much honor and reverence they carried out the burial of Christ. Otherwise, someone who does not understand correctly might think that John contradicts the others because he relates something more than they do.

Although the others are silent about Nicodemus, they do not affirm that Christ was buried by Joseph alone, even though they mention Joseph alone. Nor do they appear to disagree in saying that Joseph wrapped him in a single linen cloth, while John relates that he was wrapped in linen cloths. Nicodemus could have added other linen cloths out of reverence and a concern for propriety.

Even on account of the face cloth and the bindings with which the head and the whole body were tied, it can rightly be said that he was bound in linen, since these too were made of linen, even if he had been wrapped in a single linen cloth.

Nevertheless, none of them commends anything other than that the body of the Lord was wrapped in linen cloths, or in a single linen cloth, although those who buried him were very rich. It is specifically said to have been clean because it was fitting that the Lord’s most pure body should be wrapped in clean linen.

The simple burial of the Lord condemns the ambition of the rich, who do not wish to be without riches even in their tombs, where purity from sin ought to be sought more than wealth.

The body of Jesus, however, provided greater purity than did the material in which it was wrapped, because whatever the Author of life touched became new and clean. How appropriately, therefore, that tomb is said to have been new, in which, according to John, no one had yet been placed, and which had been hewn out in rock.

The Evangelist seems to commend this so carefully lest any of his opponents be able to invent the claim that some other person rose from that tomb, since it is established that no one else had ever been placed there.

Thus it does not seem to have happened by chance or accident that he wrapped him in a clean linen cloth and placed him in a new tomb. Jesus is buried only in a new heart and in the purest faith, by which the hearts of believers are cleansed.

This tomb is never hewn out except in the rock, which is Christ, most firm. In our hearts, too, this burial of Christ is cut out as though in the hardest crag, and Christ’s body is placed there. From this we must believe that it is not he who is sanctified by us, but we who are sanctified by the body, so that we may be purer if we receive it with right faith and a good conscience. Otherwise, without Christ’s body, we are empty and unclean.

But because we are buried with Christ, perhaps John therefore expressly says, “in which no one had yet been placed.” He says “in which no one had yet been placed,” as though someone might afterward have been placed there. I do not believe this at all, since even today it is carefully and gloriously guarded and preserved.

Concerning this Isaiah says, “And his tomb shall be glorious” (Isa. 11:10). Therefore, when John or Luke says that no one had yet been placed in it, this should rather be referred to the mystery.

For we are buried with Christ through baptism into his death, so that he may be believed to have been buried there first on our behalf, in a tomb in which no one had yet been placed for him. Then we are buried with him through baptism into his death, as though in a new tomb, so that thereafter we may walk with him in newness of life (Rom. 6:4).

Everyone also wraps Jesus well in a clean linen cloth when he embraces and loves him within himself with a pure mind. Hence how suitably the practice has arisen in the Church that the altar-sacrifice, which is the Lord’s body, should not be wrapped and celebrated in a garment woven of gold, nor in silk, nor in any dyed cloth, but in purest and clean linen.

This was therefore rightly ordained by the holy Fathers, because the Lord’s body was wrapped in a clean linen cloth, so that this body too might be received in the same linen and might be consecrated in it with the greatest purity. Our people, with due foresight and on account of the mystery, appropriately call it a corporal.

I therefore wonder at those who say that this truly is not Christ’s body which we receive daily from the Lord’s table: why have they chosen to call this cloth by that name, if this is not Christ’s body, which is consecrated in it and upon it? It is demonstrably from this that it derived its name; and the name is falsely applied if it is not what it is called.

“And he rolled,” it says, “a great stone against the entrance of the tomb and departed.” From this it is understood that Christ’s tomb was not cut in the manner in which tombs are formed in this earth, since it is said to have had an entrance.

We therefore believe that what many have handed down who saw it is true: inside the entrance of the tomb there was a round chamber cut deep within an enormous rock, of such height that a man standing inside could scarcely touch its roof with an outstretched hand. Its entrance faced east, and that very large stone had been rolled against it and placed there.

There were not many stones, but one, and it was large—so large that the strength of those lying in wait could not quickly roll it away, nor could anyone, even with a light movement, remove it from the entrance of the tomb after so many centuries.

Yet it was not so much larger than the strength of the angel descending from heaven that he could not quickly roll it away from the entrance of the tomb and sit upon it—not wearied, but terrifying by reason of the mystery.

Since we have begun to describe the shape of this tomb and the manner of its arrangement in order to explain the visions, we must set it out fully. As I said, its entrance faced east. Then, for those entering, on the right was the place on the north side specially prepared to receive the Lord’s body.

It was seven feet long and three palms higher than the rest of the floor. This place was not made open above, as is customary with ordinary tombs, but from the southern side, along its entire length, so that the body could be placed there.

From this it can be understood more clearly what Mark says: that when the women entered the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right (Mark 16:5). The place of the Lord’s body, where the angel was sitting, was indeed on the right for those entering. Yet the places there were not separated; all these features were continuous and not divided from one another, since they had been cut out in one and the same rock.

Now, as those who come to us from that place report, there is a church there of remarkable workmanship, circular in form and divided by a triple wall. In its center is the tomb, and to the east of it is a church that is still called Golgotha today.

There is much construction in these places. Indeed, one can see there that Isaiah’s prophecy has been fulfilled, where he says: “On that day the root of Jesse, which stands as a sign for the peoples, will be sought by the nations, and his tomb shall be glorious” (Isa. 11:10).

For the place where he overthrew the kingdom of death preserves the memorable victory of judgment, just as the supplication of the nations, extending to the ends of the earth as a sign of our salvation, flourishes everywhere.

Mary Magdalene and the other Mary—whom we have learned from Mark was the mother of James and Joseph—were there, sitting opposite the tomb.

An intense fervor of love for Jesus’ body had bound these two to the new tomb. These two, together with the mother of the sons of Zebedee, who above is perhaps called Salome, are also said to have been among those who watched from a distance the wonders of Christ’s passion.

But since the three did not remain together, neither the mother of the sons of Zebedee nor Salome is mentioned here. Perhaps, therefore, these two, as greater in charity, remained steadfast in the struggle all the way to the tomb, and for that reason deserved to be the first to see the risen Lord. When the others, even the men, had departed, they remained faithful and strong in the duty of devout love, awaiting what the most gracious Jesus had promised.

“For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”

On the next day, which is after the Preparation, the chief priests and Pharisees gathered before Pilate, saying, “Lord, we remember that while that deceiver was still alive he said, ‘After three days I will rise again,’” and so forth.

After the Preparation comes the Sabbath, that is, the seventh day. For *parasceve* in Greek means “preparation.” The Jews were already using this word at that time, since Greeks were then living among them.

It is called the Preparation of the Passover not only of the Jews but of everyone, because the Lord was crucified on the sixth day, when “Christ our Passover was truly sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7). That day is rightly called the Preparation because on it all the sacraments of our salvation were prepared.

It was not enough for the chief priests and scribes to crucify the Lord and Savior unless they also guarded his tomb, received a cohort from Pilate, and sealed the stone, which could scarcely be moved by many people. And, as far as they were concerned, all this diligence concerning the tomb was insufficient unless they also opposed the risen one, so that such conspicuous care might contribute to the strengthening of our faith. For the more carefully the tomb was guarded, the more fully the power of the resurrection was displayed.

Therefore, by divine providence, he was placed in a new tomb that had been hewn in rock, so that no fraud could find an opportunity to fabricate anything about him. If it had been built from many stones, people would undoubtedly have said that, after the foundations of the tomb had been undermined, he had been secretly removed.

But now even the testimony of prophecy is fulfilled in it, which says, “He will dwell in a lofty cavern of a very strong rock.” Immediately afterward, two verses later in the same passage, it continues, “You will see the king in glory”—which is truly the glory of the one who rises again.

But because the Jews’ cunning always attempts to act craftily in every matter, we must consider how their impiety and fraud attack themselves through their own words.

They say that the Lord said, “Destroy this temple, and after three days I will rebuild it” (John 2:19). Accordingly, they accuse him as though they were false witnesses. Yet now, conversely, they interpret that statement as referring to the destruction and resurrection of his body.

For this reason, it is worth asking through these words how craftily they act. If they then understood the statement as referring to his resurrection, how could they give testimony against him that he had said this about that temple which had been built? Or if they truly understood him to have said this, how did they testify against him? How do they now know that he said, “After three days I will rise from the dead”?

In both matters they are found guilty of deceit, and in both they are enemies of the truth. Through these words they themselves condemn their own testimony: truly understanding that he had spoken of the resurrection of his body, they knowingly turned the statement into a charge and said that he had spoken of the destruction and rebuilding of that temple.

We must consider another fraud as well. If he openly told the people that he would rise from the dead after three days, how could it appear plausible that he had secretly commanded his disciples to steal him by night and say, “He has risen from the dead after three days”?

The very circumstances prove this incredible: that, after so much teaching which he had given before the whole people, and after so many and such great deeds which he had displayed before human beings throughout all Judea, he would have deceived his disciples by his words.

With what face, then, could any mortal make such a claim? Or what advantage would his death have displayed? There can be no doubt that the disciples, terrified in this way, would not have done what he commanded, especially because of the danger threatening them if they were caught doing it.

Therefore it is true, by divine providence, that the chief priests spoke these things to their own condemnation and to strengthen our faith, so that they themselves might be inexcusable in every respect and no doubt whatever might remain for us.

They provide guards; the stone is sealed with the impression of their seal; and all these things become for us testimony to our faith, while for them they become condemnation of their faithlessness.

Nevertheless, although they fabricate and arrange everything in this way, they are always conscious within themselves of their own fraud and are its witnesses.

Thus some of the guards came into the city and reported—not to others, but to the chief priests themselves—all that had happened, so that their impiety might be found in every respect without excuse.

Yet, although they were trapped on every side, they still refused to receive Christ as the Son of God or to turn back from their impiety. Instead, after all these things, according to the hardness of their hearts, they continued to store up for themselves wrath on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment.

## (Chapter XXVIII)

“On the evening of the Sabbath, when the first day of the Sabbath was dawning, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb.”

As I understand it, a remarkable and unheard-of manner of speaking arises here. For the day of this world does not know such an evening, nor does ordinary human usage: evening ends the day and does not begin it; it grows dark and does not grow light. Hence Genesis preserves the order of nature: “And there was evening and morning, one day” (Gen. 1:5), and likewise concerning the remaining days—except that the Sabbath, that is, the seventh day, which is said to be rest, has a morning without any evening. [Col. 0976B]

For plainly the evening of the Sabbath is itself, in mystery, that which dawns into the first day of the Sabbath—not so as to give birth to night, or be the mother of night, but so as to change the order, recognizing its author, and to become wholly bright as day. And not just any day, but that day which the Lord made outside the whole order of days, so that it might serve not time but its maker and the creator of all ages. Therefore this entire expression shines with mystery, answers to novelty, and breathes forth joyfully to present the dawn of light, so that the whole evening may grow bright—the evening which, occurring at sunset, dawns into the first day of the Sabbath, which is the day of light; the day, I say, of light that knows no setting.

Thus the first day of the Sabbath is now called the Lord’s Day. It was the first created in the beginning, and the first to merit seeing the risen Lord. It gave the world its beginning before all other days, and through Christ it was first deemed worthy to be restored. But the fact that the Evangelists describe the women as coming at different times is not a lie, as the impious slander, but reflects their diligent service of visitation. What they report is therefore not different in substance, but one and the same event; the time is to be understood as somewhat later than midnight, namely, at cockcrow, though they called it by different names.

Matthew writes, “On the evening of the Sabbath,” meaning “late”—that is, not at the beginning of the night, but when it was already deep and a large part of it had passed—that Mary Magdalene, or the women, came to see the tomb. For although it was late, they came during the evening of the preceding Sabbath, which dawns into the first day of the Sabbath, so that thereafter in the New Testament the night does not follow the day but precedes it. For, according to the Apostle, “the night has gone before, and the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13:12), and it certainly drew near when the Lord rose.

Indeed, “evening” may reasonably be taken tropologically for the whole night. At the end of that night—that is, at the evening of the Sabbath—the women mentioned above came to the tomb, when that same night was already dawning into the first day of the Sabbath, or, as it is found in Greek, “on one [day] of the Sabbath” (*in una Sabbati*). The Evangelist himself therefore interpreted “the evening of the Sabbath” when he added, “which dawns into the first day of the Sabbath,” that is, when the light of the following day was already approaching.

Nevertheless, we must consider how much the Evangelists appear to differ on this matter. For although Matthew speaks in this way, Mark seems to narrate the very same event quite differently: “And very early, on the first of the Sabbaths, they come to the tomb, when the sun had risen or was already rising” (Mark 16:2). Luke and John are shown not to differ greatly from him: Luke says, “very early in the morning” (Luke 24:1), and John, “Early, while it was still dark” (John 20:1).

Mark too is understood to mean this when he says, “very early, when the sun had risen”—that is, from the east, when the sky was already beginning to grow pale, although darkness still lay over the earth. This happens only because the rising sun is already near: when the dawn, as the sun’s forerunner, begins to appear, the dense darkness nevertheless still remains. It is gradually weakened as the light preceding the sun rises higher.

Therefore, when Mark says “very early,” this should not be understood as though the sun itself had already been poured out over the earth, but rather in the sense in which we commonly say “morning,” or “very early morning,” when the crowing of the roosters has sounded like a herald and we say, “Let us rise, for it is already morning.” This does not mean that the sun has already risen, but that it is known or believed to be close at hand, and that day will soon arrive.

But when we see some part of the eastern sky reddening, or something beginning to grow white, we immediately proclaim that dawn is present; and this we rightly call “very early morning.” Thus the Evangelists say one thing and mean one thing. The “very early” of Mark is the same as the “very early dawn” of Luke, and also the “morning while it was still dark” of John. “When the sun had risen” means when, rising upward at its appearance, it begins to illuminate the earth.

But how does Matthew accord with these three, when he says—as we are now discussing—not “very early,” not “at dawn,” nor “morning while it was still dark,” but “on the evening of the Sabbath, which dawns into the first day of the Sabbath”? Although I have already said many things about this, it must still be investigated.

As I said, the first part of the night is called evening, and by this part Matthew wished to signify the whole night. At the end of that night—at dawn, or in the morning while it was still dark—the holy women came with spices to the tomb. But among the other mysteries of the events, Matthew says that they came in the evening because, once the Sabbath day had passed, they were now permitted to bring the spices, which they had prepared insufficiently on the Sabbath. Perhaps he called it evening for this reason also, in order to express that permission.

When he says, however, “which dawns into the first day of the Sabbath,” it is as though he were saying: “In the morning or at dawn, when the night of the preceding day was dawning into the first day of the Sabbath, while it was still dark, when the night was already beginning to be brought to an end, so that the whole night of the preceding Sabbath might pass into the first day of the Sabbath.”

Since, therefore, by “evening” he signified the night, and in this expression of the divine word disclosed the hidden mysteries of God, we must marvel at the wisdom of the divine word and at the power of its meaning, even though others have expressed this time more simply and without obscurity. Each of them wished to indicate only one particular time: perhaps a period somewhat later than midnight, or the time of cockcrow. Although three of them wished to indicate the end of the night, Matthew wished to indicate its beginning.

Hence Jerome thinks that Matthew, composing the Gospel in Hebrew, said not so much “evening” as “late,” and that the translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, translated it not as “late” but as “evening.” For according to customary speech, *serum* can signify not “evening” but “late.” We say, “You came late,” meaning “you came tardily,” and, “Do at least late what you ought to have done earlier”—that is, do it tardily.

In all these matters, although the outcome of the exposition is extremely rich, the manner of speaking is nevertheless, as I said, both remarkable and admirable. In it the truth of the history is preserved, while an ineffable mystery, so to speak, is constructed. Indeed, the Latin language itself seems to have been corrupted when it says, “in the evening which dawns,” an expression that is likewise written in Greek with the same feminine gender, although among Latins *vesper* may be of any gender. For the proper manner of speaking is not corrupted wherever divine mysteries are commended in an ineffable way according to divine rules.

Even if there were no other manner of speaking by which this expression could be understood, we might say that “the evening of the Sabbath” means not the day becoming evening, but the night itself, so to speak, becoming evening—that is, the night already coming to an end.

“Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came.” Some say “another,” but it is the same one: “another” in person and significance, but “the same” in name and the novelty of her will. Some think that this other woman was the mother of the Lord. But I do not think so. She was afflicted by such powerful emotions and tormented by such great sorrows that she would not have wandered about in this way, since from that hour the disciple had received her into his own home at the Lord’s command.

It should also be noted that the Evangelist does not say “they came” but “she came.” Two women come under one name—not by accident but in mystery—because two churches were destined to come to Christ. They are two because they come from two peoples; yet there is one Church, one dove of God, the chosen mother of her offspring. Therefore we rightly say that she is “the same” in name, but “another” in offspring; another according to lineage, but the same in the mystery and name of betrothal.

There is no obscurity concerning Mary Magdalene regarding the hours at which she is said to have come to the tomb. She first saw the risen Lord and afterward is reported to have wept at the tomb. For she first came alone, then with the other woman, or even with others, mindful of God’s benefits, which the Lord had bestowed upon her. She frequently ran to his tomb and, so to speak, never ceased from her service. She now worships the one whom she encounters as she runs; then, overcome by excessive love, she weeps for the one whom she seeks as absent and mourns.

When it says that they came “to see the tomb,” the greatness of their love is shown. Since they could not see him, they burned with loving devotion: if only they could see his tomb, where he had been laid. Nevertheless, their coming to the tomb was not without purpose, as another Evangelist reports more fully when he says that they came with spices. They do not come empty-handed, but filled with the service of love and with the fragrant offerings of virtue.

“And behold, a great earthquake occurred. For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and coming near, rolled back the stone from the entrance of the tomb, and sat upon it.” [Col. 0979A]

The earth trembled, therefore, not because an angel descended from heaven, but because the Lord and ruler rose again from the realms below. Hence a great earthquake occurred; nor, I think, was it lesser than the earthquake that took place when he gave up his spirit, since both movements of the earth were truly extraordinary, at a time when many great cities of Asia are said to have collapsed.

And rightly so: the depths of the earth split open, chaos was shaken, and the foundations of the world were struck. What wonder, then, if the earth trembled beyond the borders of Judea, in a region unaccustomed to earthquakes, and heavier masses were moved, when the Lord of the whole world descended into the realms below and rose again from them?

When all the rights of death are believed to have been broken, and the gates of hell are opened after their strength has been dissolved—if all this had not taken place in the depths, I do not think that the earth, which is below and rests above the abyss, would have trembled in this way.

It did so not once but twice: first, when almighty Jesus gave up his spirit and descended to the underworld; then when he rose again from that same underworld and, as victor, led out with him the captives whom the prison of hell held. Therefore we must not listen to those who say that hell is located anywhere other than in the depths of the earth. For if those places were situated elsewhere, they would certainly have sensed the Lord coming to them, just as the earth sensed and trembled when Christ died and when he rose victorious from death.

Nor is it surprising that Tartarus is shaken and the regions below are torn apart when Christ runs all the way to them. Death, which held the guilty, is condemned when it rushes upon the Judge. And because, raging against human beings, it burned fiercely and leapt upon God, the rights of Tartarus were rightly removed. Its power is taken away when the dead are raised from the underworld.

“For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven”—indeed, angels. They did not raise the Lord, but announced that he had risen from the dead, and showed us that heavenly communion had now been restored to earthly beings.

“And coming near, he rolled back the stone.” It does not say that he “turned” the stone but that he “rolled it back.” When rolled into place, the stone proved Christ’s death; when rolled back, it became the defender of his true resurrection, since it displayed the empty tomb. He could not have been taken away, for so great a stone enclosed him, a seal secured it, and soldiers guarded it.

The stone was rolled back before the eyes of the women so that it might open the hearts of unbelievers through faith, just as it opened the tomb, and show that the Lord had risen from it without any deception.

The angels guard the remains of his body and ask the women not to seek the living among the dead. “And he sat,” it says, “upon it.” What was the reason for the angel’s sitting? Was he suffering from some weariness? Had he perhaps been tired from travel or some labor, and therefore sat down to rest?

Certainly not. No weariness can exist in him, since his nature is incorruptible. Rather, he sat as the defender of faith and the teacher of Christ’s resurrection. He sat as the teacher of the heavenly school upon the rock, so that the firmness of the one sitting might give believers firmness of faith. By his sitting he was already preaching Christ, upon whom he himself, rising victorious, would sit upon the rock—that is, upon the solidity of faith and the foundation of his Church, whose name is derived from the rock, which is Christ.

“You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18).

“His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow” (Matt. 16:18). In the lightning, the terror of judgment is signified; in the snow, the soothing gentleness of whiteness, which calms the devout and strikes the impious with fear. In another respect, however, lightning is not sufficient to express the angel’s glory, nor are garments suitable to a heavenly nature. Yet beneath such a great splendor he displayed before human eyes the form of our resurrection, and the appearance and condition into which those who will be raised through Christ are to be transformed in glory.

Hence the Lord says: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in its power” (Matt. 13:43).

But we must ask what Mark means when he says: “And entering into the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe, and they were astonished” (Mark 16:5). If this angel was sitting outside upon the stone, what does Mark mean when he says that they entered inside and saw a young man sitting there?

Perhaps two angels were seen at that time: one of whom Matthew speaks and Mark leaves unmentioned, and another of whom Mark speaks and Matthew leaves unmentioned. Thus they saw two angels and heard separately from each of them what they said.

First they heard the angel who sat outside upon the stone, whom they saw. His words initially encouraged them, for he had said to them: “Come and see the place where the Lord was laid.” When they came and entered, they saw the young man on the right whom Mark reports and Matthew does not mention. From him they heard almost the same words: “Do not be afraid; you seek Jesus of Nazareth,” and the rest that follows.

They could not previously see the angel who sat on the right inside the enclosure of the tomb, until the first angel, with great kindness, encouraged them to enter. After the stone had been rolled away from the eastern side, they entered that rounded chamber through the entrance of the tomb. There they immediately saw the angel—the young man—sitting toward the southern side of the place where Jesus’ body had been laid.

This was the right-hand side because Jesus’ body, which had lain on its back, had its head toward the west. Consequently, its right side necessarily faced south, and the angel is rightly understood to have been sitting on that right side according to the position of the place.

It is therefore extremely necessary to understand the structure of the Lord’s tomb, so that we may understand the angelic visions more fully, bring the apparent disagreement of the Evangelists into a single harmony, and comprehend the meaning of the visions. We must also understand how, according to Luke, they entered the tomb and found two angels standing or sitting there. Unless the position of the tomb separates and distinguishes these things, what the Evangelists vary for the sake of mystery appears contradictory.

“But the guards were terrified because of him, and became like dead men.” Ministers of unbelief and executors of another’s death could not endure the sight of heavenly things, nor take confidence from above.
