How wretched they were: fear of death struck them at the very moment when security of life had been restored to believers.

Since, then, the ministers of death were guarding death so that Life might not live, the angel’s arrival rightly struck and overthrew them, and they became like dead men. If they had not been, so to speak, more than dead, Christ’s resurrection ought to have awakened them to life, and the sight of the angel ought to have illuminated their eyes so that they might believe in the one who had risen.

The empty tomb and the rolled-back stone ought also to have shown that the one who had returned to life had not been found in the tomb after the stone was sealed. The miracle of the deed ought to have become hope of resurrection; Christ’s return to life, certainty of faith; and the angel’s appearance, honor and triumph for the risen one.

Since such madness had seized them that they could accept no faith in Christ at all, they were rightly made as dead as they were.

“But the angel answered and said to the women: ‘Do not be afraid, you; for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified.’”

The angel is said to answer as though he had been questioned, although the women ask nothing aloud. But because the angel speaks to what was taking place within their minds, he is rightly said to answer as though responding to a question. He consoles them, teaches them, and urges them not to fear—not those who lay dead in heart through unbelief, or rather struck down by terror, but the women whom devotion drew onward and the love of pious affection moved.

Thus he pointedly says: “Do not be afraid, you.” It is as though he were saying: “Let those who do not love and do not believe be afraid. Why are you frightened, you who see your fellow citizens? Among them let dread and terror of judgment remain, since unbelief and faithlessness of mind remain in them.”

“But you, because you seek Jesus who was crucified, do not be afraid. Rather, rejoice and share in the joy, because he has risen on the third day and has fulfilled for you what he promised.”

“He is not here”—that is, in the tomb where you seek him—“but come and see the place where the Lord was laid.” If you do not believe my words, at least believe the tomb, which is now empty.

See how pious a teacher he is, how modest and how kind an inviter. Although he shines like lightning, he moderates his speech so as to soothe the minds of women rather than terrify those whom he teaches. In the angel’s face, the brightness of the heavenly nature is displayed; in his garment, the power of common grace is represented.

Let proud and arrogant teachers listen—those who always desire to appear impressive in speech and clothing and in every display of glory, rather than to be useful and to teach simply. Behold, the angel, splendid by nature, moderates his appearance in speaking so that he may soothe his hearers rather than frighten them. The brightness of his clothing is restrained so that he may appear gentler, although in his face he displays the brilliance and terror of the one whom he announces to be living, as well as the likeness of his author.

It should also be noted that he says: “I know that you seek Jesus.” He does not say that they seek his body, which had been laid in the tomb, but that they seek Jesus. The angel does not separate Jesus or divide him into three, as though his body were in the tomb where it had been laid, his soul in the underworld where it descended, and the Word in heaven with the Father, where he always remains.

The angel does not understand him in the manner of wretched heretics, who frequently strive to divide Christ. What, then, does he say? “Come,” he says, “and see the place where the Lord was laid.” Not merely the dead body, but the place where the Lord was laid—the one who cannot die, because he is Lord of lords and lives immortally.

Therefore we also confess in the Creed that we believe “in the Lord Jesus Christ,” who, among the other things he did, also died and was buried. How well, then, the angel who sat as an eminent teacher upon the seat of eternal solidity does not say, “Come and see where the body was laid,” but, in its fullness—because Christ is one and indivisible—“Come and see where the Lord was laid.”

Let those who wish to cut him apart and introduce two persons into Christ listen: one according to the flesh of adoption, the other according to the proper nature of God, so that one is called the nuncupative Son of God and the other the proper Son. [Col. 0982B]

The angel teaches and shows that he is the same in both and that there is one Lord: one in the burial of the body, one in the Word, one also in the soul; one, therefore, in both natures, indivisible and inseparable, remaining in one person as God and Lord. The Word is not divided from the flesh, nor the flesh from the Word, nor the soul from the Word and flesh. In all these there is one God and man, one mediator between God and human beings (1 Tim. 2:5), the Lord Jesus Christ.

Thus, as I said above, Christ is rightly proclaimed the proper Son of God, crucified and suffering, dead and buried in the unity of his person, although only the flesh suffered. Therefore the angel says splendidly: “Come and see where the Lord was laid.”

Behold, the angel proclaims the Lord, whose passion he speaks of, whose death he acknowledges, but whose resurrection he immediately confesses. If the angel, after so many insults, after such terrible sufferings inflicted upon the flesh, and after the tomb, recognizes Jesus as his Lord and confesses him, what is it that the heretics babble when they say that he is the Son of God only by adoption?

Behold, the angel speaks of his own servitude; he offers devoted service to the one whom he serves, and he perceives that the whole injury of the passion has passed into the glory of the resurrection. He does not judge the Lord to have been diminished in the flesh, nor think that his lordship was exhausted in the passion, nor that the power of the ruler had failed. He calls him Lord and offers him service.

He is not ashamed to call him Lord whom he says was crucified, and he devoutly shows the place where the Lord was laid—the Lord whom no place can contain or confine. He therefore shows the place in which he had lain, lest it be believed that someone else, and not this same one, had risen from the dead.

The angel then commands the women:

“Go quickly,” he says, “and tell his disciples that he has risen, and behold, he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him. Behold, I have told you.”

It is not without mystery that the women become Evangelists, so that through a woman the faith of the resurrection might first be announced in the world, just as through a woman unbelief first entered the world. It was an order of justice that judgment concerning resurrection to life should be given to human beings through the woman through whom the counsel of temptation and ruin had first been brought to humanity.

Nor, therefore, are these two women appointed for this purpose without reason: under one name they are to evangelize Christ’s resurrection to the disciples. In the mystery they are prepared for the tomb so that they may represent the form of the two churches through which the Gospel is proclaimed far and wide.

Two women are sent under one name to signify the one Church that is daily gathered from Jews and Gentiles. They are commanded to go quickly because nothing in the office of preaching ought to be done slowly or lukewarmly; everything must be completed as quickly as possible with the speed of perfect intention.

Nor is it without a great mystery of faith that the disciples are commanded to go into Galilee, although they were destined to see him first in various places. Since “Galilee” is interpreted as “transmigration,” whoever desires to see the Lord must first migrate from vices to virtues, from corruption to incorruption, and from death to immortality, so that, once this transmigration has taken place—that is, once he has reached Galilee—he may be able to see the Lord.

“And they went out quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, running to announce it to his disciples.”

When it says that they went out from the tomb, it indicates that they examined all the mysteries of the burial, concerning which the other Evangelists are shown to narrate more fully. A twofold emotion moved them, so that they went quickly and ran: fear and joy. Fear had seized them because of the greatness of the miracles; joy arose from their desire for the risen God.

Possessed inwardly by these emotions and overcome by excessive love, they hastened toward the apostles so that through them the seeds of faith might be scattered among the people.

“And behold, Jesus met them, saying, ‘Greetings.’ They came near, took hold of his feet, and worshiped him.”

Do not be surprised that those who had sought him in this way, who had visited the same place throughout the night, and who were now running so eagerly, were found worthy to meet the risen Lord, so that they might more certainly proclaim as living the one whom they had previously sought as dead.

In those two women there was already a figure of the whole Church, as I said, for the whole was present in the particular. Accordingly, Jesus himself, hastening to meet his bride as a bridegroom, greets her first out of loving affection, saying, “Greetings.” He does not terrify them by his power, but anticipates them in love. He does not disturb them by the authority of his majesty, but greets them according to the law of the bridegroom, and wholly gives himself to the greeting.

Thus the angel had greeted Mary so that Eve’s curse might be dissolved in her; Christ also greets her so that the Church’s blessing might be bestowed and the rights of betrothal confirmed.

This, then, was the first gift of greeting that the Exalted One brought after he rose: through it the curse of the first woman might be dissolved.

He himself had said to the disciples: “Greet no one on the way.” What, then, does it mean that, having risen, he so quickly meets them on the way and greets them? He does not first wait to be recognized, nor does he ask anything of them, nor permit himself to be questioned. Rather, wholly impelled by the ardor of pious love, and as though rejoicing, he goes, as I have said, to greet them, and himself fulfills his own command.

For even though there are those who betroth the one Church, a pure virgin, as a bride to God, he alone is the bridegroom; and by his greeting he rightly fulfills his own command. The power of love conquers and surpasses everything, since he has made her whom he greets in himself his body, and he is shown to be her head.

“But they came near and took hold of his feet,” in accordance with what the bride sings in the Song of Songs: “I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him” (Song 3:1), and, “I will not let him go.”

They do not wish to let go of the one whom they hold with their hands, whom they worship and believe. If they had not believed, they would not have held him.

But we must ask how, according to Matthew, Mary Magdalene, on the evening of the Sabbath, lies prostrate with her companion at Jesus’ feet, holds them, and worships him, while according to John, on the morning of the Sabbath, she hears the Lord say, when she wishes again to hold his feet: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17).

If, as Matthew testifies, she first saw him risen with the other Mary and fell at his feet, which they are said to have held together, why, after returning—since she could neither remain at home for even a short time nor stay still—does he reject her in this apparently indignant manner?

When she came to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed from its entrance, the stone that had closed the tomb (John 20:1–2), she ran to Simon and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved greatly and said to them: “They have taken my Lord from the tomb, and I do not know where they have laid him,” and the rest that follows.

When those two arrived and entered, “Mary stood outside at the tomb, weeping.” Bending down, she saw two angels in white sitting in the place of the tomb, one at the head and one at the feet, and the rest. Turning around, she saw Jesus standing and said to him, among other things: “Rabboni,” which means “Teacher.” Jesus said to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.”

If she first believed in him, held his feet, and worshiped him, why was she then judged so unworthy by the Lord that she was forbidden to touch him again? If astonishment had seized her, and terror at the vision, I am surprised that her faith and recognition of the earlier vision should so quickly have failed, so that, terrified by the miracles and blinded as though by a mist, she did not know what she had done before.

This difficulty makes clear that unless a careful mind understands, as we have said, the position of the tomb and balances the narrow intervals of time, as well as the continual presence of the women and the appearances of the angels according to the arrangement of the place, there is a great opening for the arguments of slanderers, and we become entangled in many knots of insoluble questions.

I shall therefore say what seems more probable to me.

Behold, at dawn on the first day of the Sabbath, as all agree, they came to the tomb. That earthquake occurred which Matthew narrates, the stone was rolled away, and the guards were terrified, so that some of them lay there like dead men.

Mary came first, precisely as John says—Mary, certainly Magdalene, without doubt more fervent in her love of Christ than the other women who followed the Lord. Hence John does not improperly mention her alone, leaving unmentioned those who had been with her.

She came, and when she saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb—or perhaps saw it being rolled away by the angel—before she examined anything more carefully, she did not doubt that Jesus’ body had been taken away. She ran and announced this to Peter and John.

Those two ran and carried out what John himself narrates. Meanwhile Mary, while those two runners were completing everything, stood outside at the tomb weeping—or perhaps had already returned from the house.

She stood before the rocky place of the tomb, but nevertheless within the courtyard into which she herself and the other Mary had already entered, along with the other women whom the Evangelists omit except for these two, because of the mystery involved.

At that time they saw the angel sitting on the right upon the rolled-back stone, the angel of whom Matthew and Mark speak, who said to them the words that have been read.

During these words, as it seems, Mary, while weeping, bent down and looked into the tomb. She saw the two angels whom John mentions, initially sitting there.

Then, when they spoke to her, the angels are believed—according to Luke’s testimony that she saw them standing—to have risen and to have said what Luke narrates.

Between these various visions of angels and signs of miracles, she was perhaps so terrified that, struck with astonishment, she did not know even the angels she saw. Turning her face this way and that, she desired nothing except to see the Lord.

“Turning around, she saw Jesus standing, and she did not know that it was Jesus” (John 20).

This was not because the Lord had changed his form, as Mani and other heretics claim, so that he might appear different and varied according to his will. Rather, because Mary was astonished by the miracles and the place was a garden, she thought that he was the gardener.

The Lord spoke to her in almost the same words as the angel. Amid the many confused words she had spoken, the most kind Jesus called her by name and said, “Mary,” so that the one whom she did not recognize by his face might understand him by his voice.

She, overcome with grief, called him “Rabboni,” that is, “Teacher.” When, still disturbed in mind, she wished to touch him, he said to her: “Do not touch me,” and the rest that follows.

Then she went out from that small courtyard of the tomb, or from the place where there was an open space in the garden, together with the other women who, according to Mark, had been seized by trembling and fear and, as they went, said nothing to anyone.

Behold, on the way, as Matthew says, Jesus met them and said: “Greetings.”

They, now better instructed or restored in faith, came near, took hold of his feet, and worshiped him. They would not have worshiped him unless they had recognized him. Nor would Jesus have permitted himself to be touched by them unless they had believed—something Mary had not done earlier, when she thought he was the gardener.

Thus, brothers, by examining the place, the succession of the women, and the appearances of the angels, we can understand that the Evangelists do not disagree with one another in any respect.

We understand, therefore, that they spoke with the angels twice: first with the one who sat above the stone, and then with those who were inside the tomb.

So too they spoke with the Lord twice: first there, when Mary thought he was the gardener, and now again, when he met them on the way. By this repetition of his appearance and conversation, he strengthened them and restored them from fear and trembling and from all the uncertainties that had arisen in their minds.

First he said to them: “Do not be afraid.” Then: “Go and announce to my brothers that they should go into Galilee; there they will see me.”

See how much they profit from the vision of God: immediately they are sent to the apostles and become Evangelists.

Hence it follows: “Mary Magdalene came announcing to the disciples, ‘I have seen the Lord,’ and that he had said these things to her.”

This does not mean that she alone announced these things. Rather, a distinction is made between the vision that she alone saw and announced, and the vision that she saw with the others, whom Luke mentions as having announced all these things to the Eleven and to all the rest.

And behold, some of the guards came into the city and reported to the chief priests everything that had happened, etc.—what follows through: “This report has been spread among the Jews to this day.” These things were said by the evangelist Matthew and done by the guards so that from them it might become increasingly evident to everyone that the priests were without excuse.

For although the guards had been struck down and become as dead from terror, they nevertheless saw and heard many things, since they were able to behold the angels themselves, the stone rolled away from the entrance of the tomb, and the other events that had now taken place. Hence he says that they reported everything that had happened—certainly the truth—to the chief priests. But those who ought to have turned to repentance and carefully investigated all that had been said and done, so that they might find true life and prove that the one whom they undoubtedly knew to have died had risen, persisted in their unbelief, just as they still do today.

They turned the very money that had been given for the needs of the Temple and the sacrifices of God toward the purchase of a lie, just as earlier they had given thirty pieces of silver to the betrayer. Let the stewards of the churches hear what blessed Jerome thinks here about such people: Everyone who misuses the offerings of the Temple or altar, and what is contributed for the uses of the Church of God, for any other purposes by which they may satisfy their own will or obtain profits, is like the scribes and priests who purchase a lie and the blood of the Savior.

But the blind leaders, blinded by such great evils, give a large sum of money to the soldiers so that they may lie. Yet they find nothing plausible to say, except that they persuade them to say: “While we were sleeping, his disciples came and stole him.” But if those utterly deranged scribes and Pharisees—guards of so great an event—were asleep, how could they know who had taken him or where they had gone?

The soldiers say what they themselves perceived, and what they saw and heard; but you, on the contrary, buy a lie so that they may say that they slept and did not see what happened. Tell me, I ask: What judge would hear such witnesses? Who would fail to recognize so great a lie? And if others are unable to detect your plots, the soldiers themselves understand how faithless and deceitful you are.

Therefore, although you gave them a large sum of money to conceal the truth and affirm a lie, behold, it has been spread among the Jews—men of your own nation—what you did and how wickedly; and not only among the Jews, but also among all nations, wherever this Gospel has been proclaimed throughout the world.

Men of blood and deceit, you poured out money—the price of falsehood—and destroyed the Law, your homeland, and the Temple. By your counsel you discovered an instrument of faithlessness, a commerce in cruelty, a fraud against your own faith, and a robbery of the truth. You bought with a price the assertion that what was the mystery of the resurrection was theft. And behold, what you did has been publicized, just as the whole world still protests against you.

The eleven disciples, however, went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them. When they saw him, they worshiped him, but some doubted.

Here a major question arises: Why does the angel first command them to go to Galilee, as though they were to see the Lord only there—a command that the Lord likewise repeats to the same women—when he had already appeared to them earlier, in the places reported by the Gospel? Nor do they hasten to go there. Of this one appearance, in particular, they are instructed by command.

I therefore do not think that it happened without some mystery that they were ordered to go to Galilee, as though they were to see the Lord only there. Perhaps this appearance is, so to speak, no less prophetic than sacramental. For Galilee, as has often been said, is interpreted as “migration” or “revelation made.” Thus it was prophesied that the apostles themselves would migrate from the Jews to the Gentiles and that, among those same Gentiles—that is, in the Church—they would see the Lord more fully and perfectly after the grace of the Holy Spirit, as though they were to see the Head in his members, since Christ and the Church are one body.

In these words, moreover, a sacrament still future is revealed: when the apostles and the whole Church of God shall have reached that perfect migration in which the very vision of God’s glory will be revealed in the future, then they will see him—not only the apostles, but all God’s elect—just as he is. To this vision, without doubt, all are invited to migrate and go to Galilee. For there, on the mountain upon which that city described by Ezekiel was founded, the city that turns toward the south, the Lord will be revealed; and there the members will see the Head, where he himself has gone before as the beginning.

Hence it is said: “Behold, he will go before you into Galilee.” Because the mysteries of this vision are so profound, perhaps the apostles therefore sometimes delayed going there, so that the mystery might be shown in the event and the literal appearance might also be fulfilled in its proper place.

Matthew passes over many things that happened or were said after the resurrection, leaving each evangelist his own particular material. Nevertheless, he relates the perfect conclusion of the divine work, where the eleven disciples were permitted to see the Lord. I do not believe that only the eleven reached that spectacle: the angel had earlier instructed them to come, and the Lord had given this command and prediction to the women. How could it be that the love of the women or of the other disciples cooled so quickly that they did not desire to come to such a spectacle and enjoy so great a joy?

The eleven alone are designated because they had been appointed as witnesses to the people; all the others, however, were included under their teaching. As for the women, whom no fear of the Jews could restrain from the cross or the tomb, I do not think that anyone could have deprived them of so great a joy or kept them from sharing in such a desired fellowship.

The mountain on which this appearance was shown is not explicitly stated, unless perhaps it was Mount Tabor, or some other mountain where the Lord was accustomed to speak with those same disciples. Therefore, when they were told to go to Galilee, the place in Galilee to which they were to go was known to them according to their custom. For this reason it is said: “As the Lord had appointed for them.”

When they saw him, they worshiped him. Previously they had seen him, but I do not know whether as clearly, as familiarly, or after conversing with him for so long as they did then. Therefore it is said that they worshiped him, because they recognized in him all the signs of deity and truth: that he was the very same one who, before his passion, had shown himself to be God and man; the very same one who, after the resurrection, showed himself to be living immortally, instructing them and teaching them about the kingdom of God. Thus, now secure and instructed in all things, they worshiped him as God.

When he says that some of them doubted, he says this in recollection of Thomas, who is recorded earlier to have doubted at another appearance, or of the occasion when, all being terrified together, they thought they were seeing a spirit. Perhaps it is in that appearance that they are said to have doubted. For although they had previously doubted in all these matters, they had been confirmed and instructed concerning him so that they would no longer doubt—until they were clothed with power from on high by the Holy Spirit.

He therefore appears to them on the mountain, so that the mountain itself might show us the perfection of the vision. Behold, on the mountain he manifests himself more fully and perfectly. Perhaps it was on this same mountain that he had already taught the eight beatitudes; and on it, long before his passion, he had displayed himself transfigured in glory, although to fewer witnesses.

It is therefore not surprising that he displays or teaches such things on a mountain, thereby signifying that we should understand higher realities. In the Apocalypse of John, too, he is seen revealed on a mountain. Thus John says: “I saw the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand” (Rev. 14:1). From this it is entirely clear that neither here nor there should the fact that he was revealed on a mountain, or that he taught on it, be understood without a great mystery, as I have often said.

And he approached and said to them. He approached them bodily, because they had come to themselves and drawn near with complete faith, and he said to them:

“Full authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

He is not speaking here of the coeternal divinity of the Father, in which he is equal and consubstantial with God the Father, but of the humanity he assumed. By assuming it, although he existed in the form of God, he was made a little lower than the angels; and in that humanity, rising from the dead, he was crowned with glory and honor as the victor.

This is what he now says: “Authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Ps. 8:6), because he had already been established, in the unity of his deity, above all the works of the Father’s hands. For everything had been subjected beneath his feet. Among all these things was death itself, which for a time had prevailed against him; it was subjected to him, destroyed by his dying and trampled underfoot by his rising again.

Although Matthew passes over many details that the others narrated, in this one statement he sufficiently displayed all the mysteries of our redemption, perfectly completed and consummated in Christ. He showed the Lord himself speaking and declaring the glory of his majesty when he said: “Full authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.” The one who shortly before had been crucified, had died, and had lain buried in a tomb is shown to have risen, and all authority in heaven and on earth is now proclaimed to have been conferred upon him.

When it is said that all authority was given to him, he is rightly proclaimed omnipotent in the unity of deity and in hope. Otherwise, if he himself is not Omnipotent, then all authority was not given to him by the Omnipotent—perhaps because he did not wish to give it, or because he was unable to do so. But because he is truth and cannot lie, he is rightly believed and proclaimed Omnipotent.

This is not by adoption, as some chatter, introducing two sons, but through the unity of person, in which the one and same proper Son of God is proclaimed according to the Catholic faith. For he is the one and the same who says: “All things that belong to the Father are mine”; and to the Father: “All your things are mine, just as my things are yours.”

Hence the question is rightly raised: If all that belongs to the Father belongs to the Son through equality of nature and through the omnipotence of his deity, why does he now say that everything was given to him, as though he had not possessed everything before it was given to him?

Here a great mystery of piety is certainly revealed, and the perversity of all heretics is condemned in one and the same person. The one who receives grace has by nature all that belongs to the Father; and there is no other person than the one who possesses it. Therefore the very same one says to the Father: “All your things are mine,” and also says here: “Full authority has been given to me.”

For Christ is one in two natures, namely in humanity and deity, and there is one person in the Trinity of the deity. Since Christ is one person according to his humanity, he says: “It has been given to me”; but according to his divinity, in which he is equal to the Father, he says: “All your things are mine, just as my things are yours.” Accordingly, Christ in both natures is one God, one Omnipotent.

For this reason Paul says that the Father gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2:10). This is the full authority that was given to Christ.

Although Matthew is silent here concerning the authority of the underworld, when he says “all,” he includes everything universally, because the underworld is included under the designation “earth.” Therefore those who say that the underworld is everywhere and not in a place must not be heeded; for unless it exists in a place, it exists nowhere. To say this against the whole authority of the Scriptures is utter madness.

It is also an error to say that the angelic powers were not subject to him before the Author of life rose from the dead. For the heavenly powers knew that they themselves were rightly subject to the human being whom they saw specially assumed by his Creator into God. Therefore, from the beginning of his conception, they revered, proclaimed, and worshiped the twofold nature in him, and served the one whom the angel who first came to Mary commanded to be called Emmanuel, that is, “God with us.”

Hence the angel speaks to Joseph, and the same angel proclaims joy to the shepherds. Then, at the infant’s cradle, the angelic choir is heard singing: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). When he was tempted in the wilderness, after his solitary combat and singular struggle, the angels immediately served and ministered to him.

Now also, at the tomb, an angel in white clothing proclaims the glory of the triumphant one, and others are seen attending upon his resurrection. All of them, nevertheless, proclaim and confess his resurrection. Nor were angels absent at his ascension—not angels who carried or lifted him up, but angels who proclaimed that he would come again.

In all these events, Christ, one person in two natures, is proclaimed by the angels as God and man, the true Son of God. This is the twofold operation that must be considered throughout the whole text of the holy Gospel, so that in one and the same Christ a twofold nature and a twofold operation may be understood in one and the same person of the deity.

For the person of the Son of God, which he always possessed, he did not assume; rather, he assumed the nature of humanity. Accordingly, in everything, if you understand correctly, you will see the human being throughout his entire earthly life sometimes displaying the glory and power of his greatness through signs and miraculous works, and at other times presenting the form of his humility and humanity in the unity of one person.

For this reason, while still on earth, that most merciful Mediator himself, God and human being, considered it necessary to declare to humanity, after he had conquered death, that “full authority had been given to him in heaven and on earth,” so that through this one statement he might confirm all the other mysteries of the holy Gospel.

John sees this Gospel-bearing angel in his Apocalypse passing through the midst of heaven, and says that he carried an eternal Gospel. Therefore it fittingly and providently ought to be preached and taught on earth that which is now openly proclaimed and declared in heaven.

“Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.”

The most correct order of preaching is therefore handed down and proclaimed for the most diligent observance of the present-day preachers of the churches of God: first, they should teach their hearers; then they should hand on to them the sacraments of faith and of the new birth; finally, they should urge them to observe completely everything that had been commanded them.

For neither does baptism profit without faith, nor does faith profit without the works of God’s commandments. Faith must therefore be taught first—the faith by which God is rightly believed and through which all things are granted to believers as possible—as well as the power of adoption, so that we may be called and may be the children of God (1 John 3:1).

Then, once they have been instructed in these matters, the sacraments of faith must be handed on, and the person must be immersed in baptism so that he may be wholly reborn in that sacrament. Only then should the preacher and teacher apply himself so that, in this new birth, works of faith may follow and the commandments in which love is fulfilled may be observed.

Let all heretics and schismatics hear in what faith the whole Church of Christ is reborn, and in what words a person is immersed in the font: “In the name,” he says, “of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” For he does not say “in the names,” but “in the name,” because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have only one name.

These three are spoken of relationally with respect to one another, so that they may be called three: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Although they are three, God is one, the Omnipotent is one; and whatever is said of God in relation to himself is one, because in him there is only one nature, one deity, one power, one greatness, and one authority.

Therefore it is believed that there is one name in the three. For this reason we are commanded to be baptized in that one name, in the Trinity of unity, just as in the unity of the Trinity. For neither is the Trinity rightly believed as God without unity, nor is unity truly proclaimed for salvation without the Trinity.

Here a quaternity is not asserted on account of the two substances in the Son; rather, the Trinity is affirmed, because the whole Christ is rightly believed to be only one person in the Trinity. To make this still clearer, let us hear what follows:

“Behold, I am with you every day, until the consummation of the age.”

It is the same Christ who, returning to the Father, ascended into heaven according to the flesh, while never departing from the Father; and it is the same Christ who promises that he will always be present on earth with his elect. He is never divided from himself or separated from himself anywhere after the Word became flesh (John 1:14), so that one Christ might be God and man.

Therefore I urge devout hearers of the word of God always to be attentive from the beginning of the Gospel to the fact—as I have often urged previously—that Christ’s teaching must not be corrupted in any respect. For it is universal and nowhere contradicts itself; rather, one complete understanding of Christ remains throughout.

The conclusion of the Gospel clearly confirms that he is one and the same: he is, he remains, and he goes. When he says, “Behold, I,” “behold” is the adverb of one pointing something out. When he says, “I am with you,” this is a great and wondrous declaration of his deity. Thus, in one and the same sentence, the humanity of the flesh is displayed to the eyes, while the ineffable nature of the Word is proclaimed intelligibly in one and the same person.

For he does not say, “I was with you, and I will be,” as though speaking of the past and the future, but “I am with you,” which is proper to divine majesty. The deity of the Word has neither past nor future, but is always the same being.

Therefore it was once said to Moses, when God wished to display his unchangeable deity: “I am who I am”; and, “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14). God could not say anything more proper about himself than “I am who I am.”

Here too, wishing to show the disciples that he was the one who had earlier spoken to Moses, he said almost the same thing: “Behold, I am with you,” as though he were saying: “Because I am always the same and present everywhere.”

Yet he is everywhere in one way, through his majesty by which he fills all things, and with us in another way, according to grace. In this statement he gives great confidence to all who believe in him. For he promises this not only to his disciples but also to all Christians.

The apostles were not going to live in the flesh until the end of the age, so that he might be said to be with them always. Rather, he faithfully makes this promise to his Church: that he, the Head, will always be present with his members, with whom and in whom he must complete and fulfill whatever is lacking in his body and in his members.

This confidence, however, so that it may be constant and enduring, is born only from true faith and from the faith that works through love. Whoever possesses this faith perfectly feels and understands that God is always present, wherever he may be.

Although the divine majesty is present everywhere, it is present in a very different way with the reprobate, so as to erase their memory from the earth, and with the elect, through the grace of his protection. Nevertheless, he himself knows everything everywhere, the latest and the earliest; he understands the thoughts of all human beings and penetrates all things. He also foresees and distinguishes the ways of each individual.

Therefore it belongs to the perfect to live always as though in his presence, while it belongs to the condemned to live negligently as though he did not see them.

When he says that he will be with his own until the end of the age, he does not mean that he will abandon them at that time, when he is to give them the rewards of eternal life, as he himself says: “Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Rev. 2:10).

Rather, this is what he says: “I am with you until the consummation of the age,” through the help of loving protection and defense, through the grace of divine inspiration, and in all good works; in struggles, so that you may conquer, and afterward, as conquerors, be crowned. For afterward there will be no more struggles, no contests in which you will need my help. Meanwhile, because I will be with you through the gift of my grace until the end of life, nothing will be lacking for you.

After these afflictions of life, I will grant eternal life, so that you may see my glory more fully and perfectly, in which thereafter you will lack nothing.

Reader, observe that “until” and “as far as” in the divine Scriptures do not always signify a limit, because it is an idiom of the Scriptures that they are sometimes used indefinitely. For example, when he says, “Until you grow old, I am he,” he does not mean that as soon as they have grown old he will cease to be God. To think this would be utter madness. Rather, “They will all grow old like a garment” (Ps. 101:27), and all things will be changed, while he himself remains always the same and endures forever.

Understand this statement as particularized in such a way that, in the part where he says “I am,” you should believe the meaning to be indefinite, while in the part where he says “until you grow old,” the sentence is understood as having a limit.

In this passage too, insofar as it concerns the end of the age, the sentence has a limit, just as labor itself must have an end. Until the labor of the saints’ tribulation is ended, God is promised to be present with his own in everything, both as the help of their defense and as the aid of their good works. Finally, as the reward of eternal recompense, God’s presence with his saints will be without end, because all labor certainly has an end, but the reward of labor has no end.

I have already spoken at length above, as far as I could, about this kind of expression. Since the meaning here extends so far and wide, it is unnecessary to gather more examples, many of which have already been treated in earlier places where the discourse has labored.

But since the whole narrative of the holy Gospel ends in this faith and is brought to its conclusion in hope, let us believe what we read and remain in the faith in which we were reborn, so that all who have believed perfectly in Christ may live confidently under God’s protection. For Christ is the power and wisdom of God the Father, and he is with those who belong to him.

God himself made the promise, and he does not lie: “I am with you until the consummation of the age.” Therefore, for those who possess such great confidence of faith, the power and light of the Father are entirely present.

Concerning this light David, in the magnificence of his heart, said with complete confidence: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. 26:1). He said this when the Lord Emmanuel had not yet come to us, because he had not yet been incarnate, although he was always with the Father and everywhere with his own.

How much more ought we now to have confidence, when, just as he promised through the mouth of all the prophets, he has been given openly and has become God with us. Since he has become God with us, he cannot fail to be with us.

We must therefore believe confidently what he says—he who is always the same, who is everywhere, without past or future, so that he may be understood always to be present—for through this faith the saints conquered kingdoms and pleased God. In this confidence, therefore, they remained secure amid torments, and in this hope they entrusted their souls peacefully to God, for whose love they did not fear to die.

Behold, dearest brethren, urged by your love and desire, I have attempted this, wishing to obey your commands and to complete in words what I do not know whether I have accomplished for anyone in deed. Behold into what sea of divine matters I have plunged, trusting in your merits and urged on by your prayers. Behold, I have now traversed difficult paths. Behold how I, poor in understanding, have pierced treasures that cannot be searched out.

Nevertheless, possessing the firmness of my rebirth, I believe that I escaped not through my own strength but through God’s grace, by which I learned what I did not know and hold what I had been ignorant of. For I have always trusted in the one who declares that he is with us, and in whom I live.

Therefore, even though I am a sinner, reborn already through the Holy Spirit, I confidently embrace in love what he himself says and recall it with devotion. For “the Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John 3:8). Thus is everyone who is born from him.

Therefore, dearest ones, although I do not grasp perfectly by my understanding the things that he himself speaks—for at times I have become dull and ignorant of divine matters—I nevertheless firmly retain the rules of faith and the teaching of Catholic discipline in those things I have heard inwardly, insofar as I learned them from him who is in us. For this reason I offer them devotedly to my readers.

The Holy Spirit’s manner of speaking has no fixed manner: he speaks when he wills, to whom he wills, and as he wills. Hence, in this work, which I have labored beyond my strength, I was driven to it by love, because love compelled me. The cause of his coming or departing, as the Savior says, lies in the will of the one who inspires, although his coming or departure is unknown while he fills all things.

Therefore no one rightly prevents him from speaking through whomever he wills, since he possesses the power to teach and inspire all things that he wills. Without him I do not think rightly; nor can the angels, who are powers, ever think or understand rightly without him.

For, as the Prophet sings: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32:6). And if this is true of them, it is certainly true also of the saints.

---

## The Exposition of Saint Paschasius Radbertus, Abbot of Corbie, on Psalm 44: “My Heart Has Uttered a Good Word”

For the holy virgins dwelling at Soissons, in the monastery of Saint Mary.

*(From the edition of Sirmond.)*

## Book One

### 1225–1226

When, by God’s disposing judgment, I had at last been freed from the responsibilities of pastoral office, the cares of governance, and the business of active duties, I returned to those studies which, though retained in my mind and postponed for a time amid the various winding paths of worldly affairs, I had cast aside. Thus, after a long interval, I recalled what had been interrupted.

Amid the deep silences of the heart and the pleasant retreats of the Holy Scriptures, I reviewed in my mind what I had once vowed to write for so holy a mother and for some of you. But since she now reads in the book of life ineffable things that human speech cannot contain, I ought to return to you, her daughters, what I had resolved to give.

For just as it is characteristic of a shameless debtor to deny what he has promised, so it is characteristic of an honorable and generous person to offer freely, without delay. Especially since the Mother, heir of the blessed inheritance, was appointed by God—she who was the dearest daughter of the mother to whom I wholly devoted myself, promising to be present with all that I am and to pay in Christ the debt of love that I owed.

For the interest of love is rightly owed when it is repaid, and by being repaid it is always lawfully owed.

In this very matter the prophecy of the present psalm has been fulfilled, where it says: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes” (Ps. 44:17). Therefore she was established by God, dearest daughters; and she who was the daughter of the blessed Mother has become an excellent nurse, to whom we owe everything that we know.

Thus, pressed by your abundant kindnesses, I began to consider those to whom I owed the most: since, being occupied, I had not benefited you, I might at least benefit you somewhat in my leisure.

Perhaps I might apply to myself what Cato said about Scipio, who was first called Africanus: that he used to say he was never less at leisure than when at leisure, nor less alone than when alone.

This is a magnificent saying, dearest daughters, worthy of a great and wise man. It shows that, in leisure, he was accustomed to think about the business of life and, in solitude, to converse with himself; that he never ceased thinking and did not need the conversation of another. These two things, which bring weakness to others, sharpened him: leisure and solitude.

I would wish that I might truthfully say the same of myself. But because, by imitation, I am unable to attain such excellence of intellect, I certainly approach it in intention, which is especially fitting for us, who live under monastic discipline and have the contemplative life as our vocation.

Therefore the Lord says: “Be at leisure, and know that I am God” (Ps. 45:11). By this example, the Lord commends a most dutiful occasion for devoting ourselves to leisure under religious observance.

This is appropriate only if idleness, sluggishness, negligence, or laziness do not overwhelm us, because idleness is the enemy of the soul. Otherwise, at the present time, to devote oneself more fully to the contemplative life is as most blessed as it is most demanding.

For this reason the Lord says in the Gospel: “Mary has chosen the best part, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42).

Therefore, because you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, it is especially fitting for you always to pursue these things and to seek the contemplation—theoria—of the one whose daughters you are. For a share in this same discipline is fruitful and fertile in every respect. Its fruit always remains; no part of it lies uncultivated or desolate and barren.

Since you have chosen it and have been dedicated to God for this purpose, you ought all the more earnestly to cultivate it, because at present no activity is more blessed or more genuine than to participate in angelic service, to mingle with divine conversations, and to be presented before divine manifestations.

Thus a more blessed leisure is commended to us than any lofty earthly occupation. For this reason, leaving everything behind, you vowed yourselves to God. Therefore, although we may sometimes appear solitary and at leisure, since we ought always to be most busily engaged with God and in his presence, we are never alone or idle.

If, then, we wish to compare our solitude or leisure with the intellect of that Africanus, it is far more excellent than all their studies—not established so that we may grow sluggish through the vice of boasting, but so that we may meditate on God’s commandments, on divine praise and contemplation, on the Holy Scriptures, on the Law and the Prophets, on the Gospel and the teaching of the apostles, and on the traditions of the holy Fathers, so that somehow we may present to Christ the things we know.

Among these, then, most excellent pastures of doctrine and the richest honeycombs of delights, there was held a discussion of Psalm 44. When I had recited it, I found it to be a marriage song and your epithalamium, since it treats entirely of the marriage of the bridegroom and the virgins, whose one body becomes one Church and the spouse of so great a man—he who is described and praised in it as more beautiful than all the sons of men.

But when, as I desired, I was treating these matters, so that I might briefly repay what I had promised, I immediately found at the entrance of the psalm, that is, in its title: “For the end, for those who will be changed; for the sons of Korah, an understanding; a song for the Beloved.” Then, considering the Hebrew truth according to blessed Jerome, in which it is written: “For the Victor, concerning the lilies of the sons of Korah, a song of instruction, of the most beloved,” I found that Symmachus, in his customary manner, translated it more plainly as “a triumph concerning flowers.” When I read these and other different expressions of this kind in the title, I believed, most beloved women, that what is sung in general to all virgins—indeed, to the whole Church of Christ—could not belong to only a few.

But because virginity, which is always compared with flowers, surpasses the other members of the Church as its more glorious portion, and because it is shown to be a special virtue among them, it occurred to me most opportunely to write to you about all these things, since you truly are Christ’s flowers and the lilies of the Churches. First, so that I might discharge what I owed to the mother mentioned previously; then, to you, whose song concerns marriage, as though I were generally delivering a discourse under the heading of a dowry, although I would not refuse to speak in a humble style.

For lilies also grow well among thorns; and when the Holy Spirit speaks of meanings—or, certainly, when the bridegroom of the Church himself, the mediator between God and human beings, speaks—he teaches and instructs Moses. Perhaps, therefore, through the intervention of your merits, he will not disdain to bring forth something through the service of my thorny heart that may benefit those who desire to hear, since the subject of my discourse arises from the dowry of your betrothal.

Accordingly, how fittingly the entire psalm is continually expended at the vigils of virgins and sung in their praise, [Col. 0996D] since they truly are the flowers of the Churches and the lilies of paradise. Yet although it is solemnly sung concerning those virgins who, having already been happily released from death with Christ, have entered into the marriage feast, it nevertheless celebrates hymnodically your marriages in Christ at the present time and describes the most joyful bonds of marriage. It paints the bridegroom as beautiful and wealthy above all others; and it testifies that the bride stands glorious at his right hand, exalted with royal honor.

For the sake of those who are still laboring on earth, it gives this admonition: “Hear, daughter, and see,” and the rest that is spoken. Therefore, most beloved women, since I recognized it as your epithalamium, although unlearned and unable to sing, I ought not to remain silent before the bridal chamber of so great a king and of so many virgins. For we read that it was commanded: “Before the bedchamber of this virgin, sing for us the sweet songs of the drama.” If, then, at the bridal chamber of a single virgin, such funeral rites are fittingly celebrated with alternating choirs and according to one’s desire, how much more festive ought the discourse to be—if only I possessed eloquence—at the banquet of so many virgins, where psalms are sung in praise and readings are recited as delicacies for the feast?

On every side the choirs rejoice, in the manner of those who sing at weddings with the fullest jubilation of praise. I do not know, most beloved women, what invites us more to joy: the divine readings or the songs of so great a solemnity. The readings instruct; the singing lightens arduous labors and consoles distress. They demonstrate that song has been naturally given to us for the consolation of work: hence sailors overcome the dangers of the sea by singing; hence they bring relief to an immense burden through songs. Hence a sonorous voice enables travelers to cross steep hills, and the sweet modulation of song makes them pass through the wilderness without fear.

To say nothing more, whatever work is difficult and whatever labor is harsh, sweet singing triumphs over it through the musical song and makes it light. So may the harmony of this song, most holy women, relieve your continual burdens and awaken your minds. May David’s flute delight you; may the marriage-gifts entertain your spirit. For David himself, who is believed to have first sung this epithalamium, is undoubtedly thought to have devised this kind of song for weddings as a favor of singing. By singing he learned to overcome the hardships of war; by singing he deserved to stir the people toward salvation; by singing he invites the nations to Christ, recalls the Jews, drives away demons, summons the children of God to the service of the heavenly Father, and instructs and prepares you, O virgins, for the bridal chamber of Christ, the eternal King—provided that your conduct accords with the bridegroom and your deeds answer to your songs.

Therefore, most beloved women, as I said, since I am unable either to sing harmoniously before the bridal chamber of the supreme King, to exhort the guests with brilliance, or to address my fellow-banquet guests with wit, I have decided, in this heading of the dowry, merely to scatter flowers, in case our discourse should find some pennyroyal of ours pleasing to someone—a fragrant gift that I have sent. Since I cannot offer anything more precious, at least I scatter what I can, so that the chamber of the heart may glow within before the bridal bed.

For wherever I turned my eyes, I found none to whom our offerings would be more pleasing, none for whom my skill would labor more earnestly, none to whom I owed more, and none for whom this would be more fitting than you—who, according to the nobility of your lineage, are flowers of the Church, and, according to the brightness of your virtues, lilies of paradise.

You are the women who, through the green freshness of chastity and the radiance of pure love, arrange garlands for the bridegroom and daily transform the crown of thorns into the glory of the triumphant one. Across the fields of Scripture, like bees, you continually gather flowers; through the green meadows of the mind and body, by labor, you collect the nourishment of virtues. When these are stored away, the honeys of Christ are prepared, as though in the hive of the heart. Therefore it is rightly sung to the bridegroom:

> “How sweet are your words to my palate,  
> more than honey and the honeycomb!” (Psalm 118:103)

Ezekiel, having tasted this beforehand, says well:

> “It became like sweet honey in my mouth” (Ezekiel 3:3).

For this purpose you pluck various flowers from the divine books, so that spiritual honeys may become sweet to you in your spirit, inwardly adorned with various ornaments of virtue. Thus you strive to reach him who says of himself in the Song of Songs:

> “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2:1).

Since, therefore, the Psalm also concerns lilies and flowers, and Christ the bridegroom confesses himself to be a flower and a lily, I too ought to pluck a portion for you while absent in body, although you yourselves always flourish among flowers, so that I might have something to offer you—your foster child, present though absent, devoted and not idle in these matters.

For, in the poetic phrase, “God has made these periods of leisure for us.” Therefore, lest I be found wholly inactive, I quietly spend my time among the pleasant volumes of books, which is the better occupation. [Col. 0998B] For Christ, who feeds among lilies, rewards the flowers of virtue that send themselves to him, and grants those who seek that they may find.

But because I cannot be a flower, I at least send you, who are shining lilies, whatever thoughts I can, so that both “the one who sows,” according to the Apostle (John 4:36), “and the one who reaps may rejoice together.” Yet because sowing belongs to the great, would that I could bring irrigation as well; for then someone sows rightly if he understands what, when, and where he is sowing.

But in you the word of life has already been sown, since “you are God’s agriculture, God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3:9). Therefore the seeds of virtues sprout in you, and a multiplied harvest grows in the Lord. For no one other than Christ sows virginity, since he himself is both the sower, the seed, and the fruit.

The hearts of the faithful are a garden of delights, plowed by the plowshare of the holy Gospel. Although it is presented generally as a garden, nevertheless in you—because you are its particular form and beauty—it is sung in the Canticles as enclosed and sealed: cleansed of every evil weed by the faith of Christ, sown with the seed of the word, adorned with the lily of chastity, lovely with the verdure of virtues, and fragrant with everlasting flowers.

But because thorns and lilies arise together in one and the same earth, the field of the heart must be cultivated constantly, lest the lilies of chastity be injured by thorns. Therefore the soil of the mind must continually be drenched with the dew of Scripture. For the divine word is a virginal dew. As dew, God’s words descend and refresh the hearts of virgins from the burning of harmful heat.

Otherwise the pleasure of the flesh has its own flowers, by which the mind is wrongly delighted. Hence the Prophet says:

> “All flesh is grass,  
> and all its glory is like the flower of grass;  
> the grass withered, and the flower fell,  
> but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Psalm 39:6).

Therefore, most beloved women, establish within yourselves, with firm root, the word that remains and exists forever, and implore that it remain in your hearts. Of this the present Psalm speaks:

> “My heart has poured forth a good word.”

Make the foundation square: in your hearts, establish the four-sided structure of virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—in which Christ, as a charioteer upon his own chariot, may preside over and direct the movements of the heart, and may say of you:

> “I have compared you to my cavalry in the chariot,  
> O daughter of Pharaoh” (Song of Songs 1:9).

For without these four, the integrity of the other virtues can never be rightly governed, nor can a foundation be laid on which one may remain rooted and grounded in that cornerstone “in whom the whole structure grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:21).

In this corner of the structure, therefore, ground your hearts by faith, so that no voice of the Epicureans—that is, of carnal people—may deceive you. They say what is written:

> “Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither;  
> let no pleasure pass us by,  
> but everywhere let us leave signs of our joy” (Wisdom 2:8).

I say this because Symmachus interpreted this psalm as concerning flowers, lest any blandishments of the lilies or flowers of the present age deceive you. You trampled and rejected them at the very beginning of life, and you spurned all the enticements of pleasure as dung. You also renounced empty joy and empty glory, so that through this shortcut of life you might more swiftly grasp true life and true joys.

You endure these things courageously, most beloved women, because you have fixed the root of your hearts above, where Christ the bridegroom is seen. For there are roses that grow rich and red within through Christ’s blood, so that they may flower forever; and there are others that take root in the earth, flowering quickly and then withering. All luxury in the present life is vapor, and the foam of empty joy.

Therefore, matrons of Christ, always pursue virtues, so that they may flourish and the lilies of chastity may increase. Let the rose, sprinkled with the blood of Christ, redden upon your cheeks. For every adornment of the soul and every moral excellence shines upon the face of the virgin.

Therefore, I ask you, raise your aim—that is, the intention of your heart—continually before your eyes, and do not neglect the *telos*, that is, the end. For *telos* (τέλος) is the end of all things. Hence it is written in this title: “For the end, for those who will be changed.”

But “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” Christ is not therefore the end of the law in the sense that it should cease to exist; rather, its end is that it may possess completed righteousness through faith in Jesus Christ. For without Christ the law is imperfect; but it is perfected through Christ when Christ, promised in the law, is believed, received, and, once received, held by complete faith.

Christ is not called the end so that whatever God has established to exist may come to an end in him and cease to be. Rather, in him and toward him all things arrive so that they may exist rightly. Otherwise no virtue is perfected without him; nor does virtue have a beginning if it does not begin from him, since he is the Alpha and the Omega. From him the righteousness of faith is conceived, and in him it is brought to completion—not so that it may cease to exist, but so that it may be perfect in that righteousness which has looked forth from heaven.

Hence David, instructed by the Holy Spirit, says:

> “I have seen the end of all perfection” (Psalm 118:96).

Nothing is perfect or complete unless it is perfected in Christ so that it may remain forever. Whatever ran toward Christ did so lest it be found without Christ. Hence also the Apostle exhorts us:

> “So run that you may obtain” (1 Corinthians 9:24).

Therefore, brides of Christ, whatever you do, let Christ always be the reason for it, so that you may please him to whom you have vowed yourselves. For the virtue of virginity is then well supported by the virtues when whatever the virgin does is adorned inwardly by love for her bridegroom.

Just as there is no bridegroom without a bride, so there is no bride without the relationship and covenant of betrothal, so that after the faith of betrothal “the two may become one flesh.” Thus God came into humanity so that humanity might be in God, and so that God and humanity might be one Christ. Therefore, most beloved women, it is necessary that the Church somehow become one with the bridegroom—not that it become God, which Christ is, but that it become one flesh in him, one body, so that there may be one union of flesh and God.

Because God passed into flesh, may the whole human being pass into God, and may Christ and the Church become one body and one flesh. If this is believed concerning the entire body, what does the virgin of God, the matron of Christ, think—she who is still wholly in the flesh in such a way that she is already in God without the corruption of the flesh? She preserves the rights of betrothal to the bridegroom in their entirety, since she loves nothing other than him and nothing except for his sake.

Already the whole reality shines forth in its particular form that is promised as future in general. Therefore the Virgin must answer to the title of the dowry, answer the bridegroom in her conduct, and assert by mind and action, by nature, the heavenly life that she has obtained by grace; and she must follow the Lamb wherever he goes.

Virginity follows the Lamb wherever he goes (Revelation 14:4), provided that it maintains harmony among the virtues. For Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, is the beginning of all ways, and he himself is the virtue of all virtues. Therefore whoever hastens after him and wishes to follow him wherever he goes must first preserve incorruption of mind and body, then enter upon the paths of the remaining virtues, while love guards all the members.

Otherwise virginity of the flesh, without the other virtues, does not follow the Lamb wherever he goes. For Christ, the Lamb of God, is the form of all God’s ways; he himself is the way and the beginning.

Therefore, for the virgin of Christ to be a bride and to follow in all things him to whom she has vowed herself, she must, according to the Apostle, be holy and undefiled in body and mind, lest the devil corrupt inwardly the mind that the outward purity of the flesh flatters.

Christ seeks a virgin who is wholly his, to whom he has offered himself as the way, so that she may follow wherever he, the only-begotten Son of God, goes—the only-begotten one also born of a Virgin. He is the one bridegroom of all holy virgins, the fruit, beauty, and gift of holy virginity: bodily, holy virginity gave birth to him; spiritually, holy virginity marries him. By him holy virginity is made fruitful so that it may remain untouched; by him it is adorned so that it may remain beautiful; by him it is crowned so that it may reign eternally in glory.

He himself makes a holy virgin his own through his freely given gift, because he does everything whatever he wills. For this reason holy virginity is given by him without any preceding merits, so that pure thanksgiving may always be returned to him with humility of heart.

If the sublimity of so great a name is pleasing, the virgin must follow the work of virtues, so that the work may be consecrated by the name and the name completed by the work. For God willed the good of virginity to be so great that it would derive its name from no other source than the word for virtue.

If anyone wishes to consider the name “virginity” more carefully, it is derived from the name of virtue. For *virgo*—“virgin”—is said as though it were *virago*, a manlike woman; and Holy Scripture indicates that *virago* was so called for no other reason than that she was taken from man. It is clear that the name *virgo* descends from *vir*—“man”—and there is no doubt that *vir* was named from *virtus*, “virtue.”

This is well confirmed by the testimony of Genesis (chapter 2:23), and the Apostle makes a pointed allusion to it concerning the Church when he says:

> “For I betrothed you to one man, to present a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2).

Christ is altogether called “the man whose name is the Rising” (*vir Oriens*), from whose side and power the Church is formed in faith and mercy, betrothed, according to the prophet, to Christ through love.

Hence, in general, the whole Church is rightly called a virgin and a bride, because she was taken from the man Christ Jesus. Therefore she is neither deceived by seduction nor overcome by violence, strengthened in Christ; nor is she defeated by any kind of persecution, because she is supported by the virtue of inward virginity.

Isaiah says of her in the person of Christ:

> “The young man will dwell with the virgin,  
> and your children will dwell in you” (Isaiah 62:5–6).

And to show that the young man is the bridegroom and the virgin the bride, he continued by saying:

> “The bridegroom will rejoice over the bride,  
> and your God will rejoice over you.”

This, then, is the virgin who is a mother, to whom it is said: “Your children will dwell in you.” And this is the virgin mother of whom it is said: “The young man will dwell with the virgin.” This virgin is the bride of whom it is said: “He will rejoice over his bride.”

This, therefore, is the one and perfect dove of God, the true catholic mother, bride, and virgin. She is a mother because she gives birth; a virgin because she perseveres in incorrupt faith. Virginity is not corrupted by fruitfulness, nor is fruitfulness hindered by virginity.

Such is the marriage of this virgin that virginity is made fruitful by this man precisely because no corruption can ever exist in this marriage. And such great virginity and integrity remain in this mother that, unless she were always a virgin, she could not be a mother.

Therefore she always flourishes spiritually, because she always produces fruit; and when she has ceased giving birth, she herself will always remain both flower and fruit.

For this reason a triumph is sung to Christ the Victor “concerning flowers,” or “concerning those who will be changed.” Those who will be changed will flourish like the cedar of Lebanon in the courts of the Lord, as it is said:

> “The righteous will flourish like the palm tree;  
> he will multiply like the cedar of Lebanon” (Psalm 91:13).

For the virtue of all the elect is the triumph of the Savior, who triumphed in all things and proved victorious. Hence he himself says:

> “Take courage, because I have conquered the world” (John 16:33).

Christ is believed to be victorious especially in the Church’s outstanding members, for he is no less victorious in virgins than in martyrs. Therefore, when he distributes gifts among his various members according to the grace given to believers, he nevertheless gives the greater grace of the gift to those members of the Church in whom she is called spiritually a virgin and also possesses the integrity of bodily virginity.

According to the different orders of the members and the variety of virtues, and according to the rule of the catholic faith, the Church is rightly praised as adorned with many forms. She preserves virginal purity in all, guards widowed chastity, and keeps the marriage bed undefiled.

Hence it is sung in this same psalm:

> “The queen stood at your right hand,  
> clothed in gilded garments  
> and surrounded by variety” (Psalm 44:10).

Each of the elect has a particular gift from God: one in this way, another in that. Yet all alike will be changed at the end—that is, in Christ—in whom he triumphs and conquers.

Therefore this entire psalm is sung as an epithalamium in praise of the bridegroom and the bride. It introduces the bridegroom into the world and describes the bride as exceedingly glorious and adorned with countless varieties of virtues; it also testifies that she stands at his right hand. Thus, on every side, it frequently brings forward sweet songs of the drama for its participants, adorning now the bridegroom and now the bride with marvelous brief praises. It joins them by the covenant of marriage and binds them together in chaste embraces.

First, it commends the grace of Christ in the title, so that whatever virtue is praised in the body may be attributed entirely to the bridegroom and head. For it is his praise that his own power freely bestowed on the bride. Everything glorious that is said of her is his gift.

Therefore let us all say, and let each one say:

> “Not to us, Lord, not to us,  
> but to your name give glory” (Psalm 113:1).

Certainly his holy generosity is always free, since no demand based on human merit ever precedes it. Even if there is some merit that is good in any human being, it is from him—from whom comes “every good gift and every perfect gift” (James 1:17). A person cannot possess it unless it has been given, nor possess it perseveringly unless it has been guarded by him.

Therefore I too, aided by your merits, ask him to grant me the ability to return this debt worthily to you, from whom I received the will to return it. I would not wish to repay it because of any merits you had previously shown toward me unless he himself, in his mercy, granted me the desire to do so.

If, therefore, I say something in this work that pleases you and is sufficient for you—or rather, that pleases and benefits your holy desire—the virtue will not belong to my foolishness but will be the fruit of divine sufficiency. Conversely, if I perhaps say something that can neither suffice nor benefit your holy desire, this will not be the emptying of divine sufficiency but the condemnation of my foolishness.

Therefore let your charity temper both possibilities equally—in yourselves no less than in me—so that your prudence may humbly recognize God’s benefits in everything, and your charity may patiently forgive whatever is lacking in my speech.

For the things we discuss are obscure, and the matters we propose are exceedingly lofty. [1236] Hence what follows in the title: “An understanding of the sons of Korah.” Otherwise, if the matters were not obscure, the psalm would not have been commended so diligently by all interpreters under the heading “the understanding of the sons of Korah,” so that “whoever has ears to hear may hear.”

Whenever understanding is required in the sacred Scriptures, something carnal or earthly is not being commended, but everything spiritual and hidden, divinely revealed. Hence in another psalm he says:

> “Who is wise and will keep these things,  
> and will understand the mercies of the Lord?” (Psalm 106:43).

This understanding is said here to belong not to just anyone but to the sons of Korah. From this it is plainly evident that what is described in their understanding is deeply hidden and marvelous.

For, as the divine word says, a marvelous sacrament took place in the rebellion of Korah: when the father perished, the sons remained unharmed by that death. Therefore what is divinely proclaimed under their understanding must not be interpreted without significance.

Now, in our language, Korah is interpreted as “bald” or “baldness,” and they are said to be his sons. But who this bald man is may rightly be asked. Perhaps, then, it is Elisha ascending from Bethel, whom the boys mocked, saying:

> “Go up, baldhead! Go up, baldhead!” (2 Kings 2:23).

But we find no indication of what sons he had, for whose understanding this psalm is sung. Nevertheless, by events and deeds he wove a prophecy concerning Christ, to show that Christ would come in the flesh, whom Elisha himself prefigured in his actions.

The boys mocked Elisha because Christ was to be mocked by the Jews. Two bears from the forest—namely Titus and Vespasian—killed them as vengeance from God.

Yet Christ is indicated as bald, or as having his head shaven, for no other reason than that he was lifted up and mocked on the cross at the place of Calvary. All those who received him are his sons; to them he gave “the power to become children of God” (John 1:12), and they have been redeemed by his blood.

Their understanding consists in believing that he came to us in the flesh, begotten from the heart of the Father, and in believing all that the present psalm suggests about him and that is proclaimed in the Church of Christ according to the catholic faith.

This is the understanding of the sons of Korah: that they understand him as substantially, without beginning, begotten coeternal and coequal with the Father according to his nature, and that this very same one became human for us at the end of the ages. The Church marries this bridegroom, and in his praise all these things are wholly celebrated.

This, then, is Korah, which, as I said, is interpreted as “bald” or “baldness.” His sons attained such great grace that through their understanding the mysteries of divinity were opened.

He is Korah, the bridegroom of the Church, whose sons cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them. Therefore they are sons of God because they are sons of the bridegroom, and they were not entangled in the rebellion of their father, who descended alive into the underworld.

Concerning him, the bride is told in this same psalm, as though she were his daughter:

> “Forget your people and your father’s house.”

For we were all “children of wrath,” that is, children of the devil. We are commanded to forget him together with his house, lest we perish as his accomplices in the rebellion that he continually stirs up against God and against God’s members.

Therefore we are sometimes moved by the pious Father to whom we have been reborn, lest we become entangled in the arrogance of the one to whom, because of the transgression of our first parent, we were born as children. For he too is rightly called Korah, since he has been stripped and divested of every grace of God and of the virtues.

Let us therefore cling to him to whom we have been reborn: he is the creator who made us when we did not exist; and although he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7), in order to acquire for himself a pure and glorious virgin bride, “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27).

At the place of Calvary he was made bald; on the cross he was lifted up and put to death. Therefore, because of truth, gentleness, and justice, he was marvelously exalted.
