Even in the hearts of his enemies he rules and exercises dominion, because he has been established upon the throne of God the Father as King forever.

This is the true understanding of the sons of Korah. This is the praise, glory, honor, virtue, triumph, and strength that are sung in the choir of the sons of Korah to Christ the Victor, “concerning those who will be changed.” For, according to the Apostle, “although we shall all rise, we shall not all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51–52).

Although different readings concerning this change are found in various books, especially Greek ones, there will nevertheless be one resurrection of all. Some books read:

> “We shall indeed all rise, but we shall not all be changed”;

others:

> “We shall all sleep, but we shall not all be changed.”

Paul explains this more clearly when he says:

> “The trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality.”

The teachers of the Church say that this will happen so that each person may remain forever in one of two conditions, either in punishments or in the kingdom of heaven.

Otherwise, why was it necessary to say, “The dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed”? Both statements are understood to mean that all will rise changed for the better and incorruptible.

Was it not enough to say one of these things: “We shall all rise incorruptible,” or “We shall all be changed”? Unless he wished it to be understood that incorruption is common to all who rise, whereas change properly belongs to the righteous, since they attain not only incorruption and immortality but also eternal glory.

Sinners and the rejected, however, will be raised incorruptible so that they may receive forever, for enduring punishments, the incorruptible bodies which they previously had and in which they sinned.

Therefore the Apostle pointedly says, “we also shall be changed,” wishing to distinguish himself and those who will be found righteous with him—those who will be transferred from virtue to virtue and from glory to glory.

The same Apostle, speaking of the incorruption of the dead, added:

> “This corruptible body must put on incorruption.”

But to what he had said, “we shall be changed,” he added:

> “And this mortal body must put on immortality.”

Immortality is one thing, and incorruption another, just as a mortal thing is one thing and an incorruptible thing another. For whatever is mortal is corruptible, but not everything that is corruptible is immediately mortal. There are bodies without a soul, since they have never possessed life, which properly belongs to living beings.

How well, therefore, the Apostle joined incorruption to corruption and immortality to mortality as the future resurrection, occurring in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye. Hence the very incorruption of the dead will be a change.

But one kind of change will be that by which all become incorruptible, whether for punishment or for glory; another will be that by which Paul and all the saints will be glorified. There will be one splendor of the sun, another splendor of the moon, and another splendor of the stars, with eternal permanence, “for star differs from star in splendor” (1 Corinthians 15:41).

Hence it is also said here: “For those who will be changed,” or “for the flowers,” because all will flower in the courts of the house of God. And just as star differs from star, so flower differs from flower.

Thus virginity, which is common to the whole Church, is specially compared with lilies in virgins; martyrdom is compared with flourishing roses, so that individuals may correspond in splendor to their respective kinds. Each of them, sprinkled with his own blood and with Christ’s blood, may redden beautifully like a rose in Jericho and may come forth gloriously from battle with Christ into the kingdom.

Virginity, clothed in the whiteness of the lily because of its incorruption, will also emerge made equal to the angels.

Therefore I think that blessed Hilary understood the Savior’s words in the Gospel—“Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow” (Matthew 6:28), and what follows—as having been spoken about angels for this reason: virginity, which is compared with angels, is very often prefigured in the sacred Scriptures by lilies.

And therefore the Lord said that “not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these” (Matthew 6:29). In these flowers, the incorruption of the true flower shines inwardly, together with the beauty that comes through the perfect love of chastity.

For this reason I want you to consider how excellent virginity is, since it is raised up by such and so many praises. As I have acknowledged, the Church in general is compared with these two flowers: she is red because she has been sprinkled with Christ’s blood, sprinkled outwardly and inwardly, since in both places the color is scarlet; and she is white as a lily. Of her it is said:

> “As a lily among thorns,  
> so is my beloved among daughters” (Song of Songs 2:2).

Although she presently lives among the wicked, she is wholly flower-like and exceedingly beautiful, adorned with many gifts.

But because I have decided to write to virgins and true widows who are living the heavenly life, it seemed most appropriate—since they are also flowers of paradise—to explain to them many flowers in which the bridegroom delights.

Hence the Church says in the Song of Songs:

> “Support me with flowers,  
> surround me with apples,  
> because I am sick with love” (Song of Songs 2:5).

But because there is great diversity among flowers, the Holy Spirit must be entreated to breathe upon the field of the mind, so that its aromas may flow forth from it; for this field of the Church is made fruitful from no other source than the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

This is the field from which Isaac said concerning his son:

> “Behold, the scent of my son  
> is like the scent of a full field  
> which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27:27).

This field is full of flowers, full of the fragrances of eternal life. In it that hidden treasure mentioned in the Gospel is found, for which the faithful sell all they possess; seized by love for it, they even leave themselves behind so that they may reach the one flower who says of himself in the Song of Songs:

> “I am the flower of the field  
> and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2:1).

The fruitfulness of this field is said always to be with God. Elsewhere in a psalm, after describing all that belongs to heaven and earth as his, he says:

> “The beauty of the field is always with me” (Psalm 49:11).

From this it is clear that although he possesses all things through the dominion of his majesty, he himself inwardly possesses, according to the grace of election, the flowers and fruit of this field from which such fragrances of virtue flow.

In this field he himself is the true vine, from which the whole Church is propagated together with the fruits of her produce. Therefore the bride rightly invites the bridegroom in the Song of Songs:

> “Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field;  
> let us stay in the villages;  
> let us rise early and go to the vineyards;  
> let us see whether the vine has flowered,  
> whether the flowers have brought forth fruit,  
> whether the pomegranates have blossomed”  
> (Song of Songs 4:13; 7:11).

The bride knows, therefore, and the true virgin knows, that the bridegroom, the flower of the field, wholly proceeds toward fruit and delights in flowers. Therefore she asks and urges him to go out into the field and visit the flowers of the vineyard, because without him they cannot bear fruit. She also promises that the mandrakes have already given their fragrance at the gates. Hence one of those who are called “gates” said: “We are the good odor of God in every place” (II Cor. 2:15).

Yet no one is adequate for these things. But let no one be discouraged when he hears that such excellent flowers bloom and exhale such immense fragrances of virtue in the Lord’s field. For in that same field of the Gospel there are lilies, roses, nard, and saffron, and humble violets, which by their color surpass the purple of the king’s murex dye. There are also heliotrope flowers, which rejoice at the rising of the sun; inwardly and outwardly they are colored by its radiance and follow its tracks as far as is permitted, so that they know nothing except to gaze upon the sun. Therefore, dearest ones, it is as though you have shut yourselves in for the night, so that at the rising of the eternal sun you may, as though newly reborn—for you have known no darkness—receive the light.

[Col. 1006C] There are also many other heavenly flowers of the sacred Scriptures, in which the cultivation of souls is everywhere formed and the Church of Christ adorned. In these virginity works crowns for itself and, with heavenly dew, gathers sweet honey for the bridegroom. For who does not know that virginal purity and widowed chastity know how to work at nothing else except in those things in which the bridegroom delights? Hence, like bees of the sacred Scriptures, you gather flowers, because he who feeds among the lilies (Cant. 6:2) wholly proceeds among flowers and delights in flowers—not in just any flowers, but in those that have blossomed in the valley of humility.

For virginity blossoms in the valley of tears, while it always attends to what belongs to humility and chastity, because it bears in its breast the flower that is “the lily of the valleys” (Cant. 2:1), and grows in the gardens of delights watered by the Holy Spirit. The bridegroom himself shows in the Canticles what the gardens of delights are: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Cant. 4:12). For in gardens of this kind the image of God, impressed with his seals, is preserved enclosed and drenched with the water of the purest fountain. Concerning this it was said to the Father: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35:12).

That fountain, truly sealed in the virgin’s heart, rises and flows continually, so that it may irrigate all the flowers of delight and the fruits of paradise—that is, the heliotrope flowers of which I spoke, which know how to gaze upon no one except the sun, Christ; they know how to rejoice in nothing except the brightness and warmth of the Word. [Col. 1007A] Thus at midday you may see the circles of that flower extended and widened, so much so that its circumference appears wider in the circle than it is, through joy. With their little blossoms spread open, you might think that they perceive and rejoice in the brilliance of the light.

Perhaps, then, nature perceives, although it does not possess the faculty of perception, and asks that question from the Canticles: “Where do you feed your flock? Where do you lie down?” It is answered: “At midday.” And because at midday the bridegroom feeds among the lilies and casts his shade in the gardens of delights, rightly the flowers of virtues most dutifully open and expand themselves, so that they may receive the radiance of the true sun and be warmed within by the heat of the Word.

Therefore, wherever the sun goes as it circles, they incline themselves and always gaze upon him. Exulting, as it were, with joy and serving in humility, they seem always to adore him with their wings stretched out like oars, so that in the evening, when the sun has withdrawn and the heat has ceased, the flowers too gradually gather and draw themselves together, enclosing their inner parts in one place as though in their own chamber. In this way they show that they cannot endure the sun’s absence: with their doors closed, they mourn in the night from sorrow as much as they had shown themselves joyful in the daytime.

Hence the bride says in the Canticles: “On my bed, in the nights, I sought him whom my soul loves” (Cant. 3:1). For the bride’s true love does not permit her to endure the bridegroom’s absence; rather, beneath the chambers of her heart, she continually meditates in faith and desire upon holding in her mind him whom she cannot behold with her eyes.

But because I have entered into the parts of this flower, lest I seem improperly to impose upon virgins things that are not read in the divine writings, nature itself teaches what we are suggesting, since, according to the Apostle (Rom. 1:20), “through the things that have been made, the things that are understood are seen.” I am not laboring over our own words so that they may possess as much brilliance of expression as elegance of meaning and adornment of understanding. Therefore I do not employ the eloquence that adorns faces, so that our speech may be beautiful and praiseworthy; I seek only what can entice younger brides into love of the bridegroom and increase the affection of their espousal.

For an old man’s speech ought to be restrained and serious, not adorned with verbal harmony or the elegance of urbanity. Rather, it should be mature, flourishing with wisdom, commended also by the judgment of integrity, full of truth, pure of cosmetic coloring, worthy of old age, and honorable. For it is one thing when, after the budding of puberty, youth begins to flower—green and bright with colors; it is another when aged old age, long wearied by labor, seeks the gain of salvation. If the latter wishes to adorn itself with the trappings of another age, it will seem more laughable than eloquent; it will be mocked rather than honored.

Therefore, I ask you not to think me offensive if I obey the young by speaking about flowers, because in this song everything is sung concerning lilies and flowers, so that the true flowers of Christ may learn to dwell with Christ. Hence, like bees roaming through the fields of the sacred Scriptures, you make honey not only for the bridegroom but also for yourselves and for everyone.

For you have flown together from every side as though to Christ’s beehive, and you have chosen one to preside over you, so that, after the manner of bees—because “honey comes forth from the mouth of the wise”—you may return honeycombs to God and the fruit of life. Truly this place is rightly called the beehive of monastic discipline, since you have shut yourselves within an eternal enclosure, lest the camp consecrated to the Lord be violated by any deceitful ambush.

It is therefore, if I may say so, more than a beehive, because you nowhere and never wander elsewhere to gather flowers. Within, you ceaselessly gather every honey-sweet thing from the sacred Scriptures, where the Holy Spirit intoxicates your hearts with nectarean dew and drenches and illumines them with the splendor of divine light. There you gaze upon nothing except heaven, because for this purpose you have shut the flesh—which “desires against the spirit” (Gal. 5:17)—as though in a prison, so that your free mind may fly to where the bridegroom has gone according to his humanity and sits at the right hand of God.

There, although nine orders of angels are said to exist, thousands upon thousands stand before him—without number—and, as Daniel testifies (chap. 7:11), “ten thousand times ten thousand” minister on behalf of those who are to receive an inheritance. There the apostolic chorus, the judges, rejoices in their fellowship, and the white-robed army of martyrs sings with crowns. There the trumpet of the patriarchs sounds beforehand, and the discerning company of the prophets answers, because everything promised through them is now read as completed before the eyes of all.

There, amid eternal joys, the senate of the holy confessors, clothed in their robes, intercedes for its peoples. There the hymn-singing choirs of the holy virgins, with their victorious palms, follow the Lamb wherever he goes and sing upon instruments things that no one can utter except those who follow with them in white garments.

There the flocks of celibates and widows are joined together; there the holy fellowship of married men and married women is adorned; there the little ones with the great, and the crowd that no one can number, sing with immense rejoicing the joys of Alleluia through all its streets.

When the faithful mind is at times carried away among them by desire, faith—which is “the substance of things hoped for”—does not see these things as outside itself. Rather, among the unseen chambers of the heart, because they are in God, it believes and understands them according to purity of heart, and loves all things. When someone is with them in mind, I think that person is nowhere alone; when he does what they do, he is never idle.

And if you ask what they do, David says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5). If someone wishes to address any one of them, or any of the saints, he is immediately present in him who is everywhere; and with him we too are always all together, because “in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28).

But we are with him and with the saints in one way if we love what they love and devoutly do for his glory and praise what they do; in another way we are with him when, always before his eyes, we are subject to him and in him wherever we may be. If we will or do anything otherwise than he wills, then without doubt we are far from him, to the extent that we are unlike him. Hence we rightly say each day in prayer: “Your will be done as in heaven, so also on earth” (Matt. 6:10).

[Col. 1009A] All these things, which faith certainly opens as credible, hope approaches and anticipates through the things believed by faith. But love perseveringly knocks until it offers prayers and vows within, before the supreme God and before the saints. It does not return until it carries back, with those whom it addresses, the result obtained through sincere faith.

But because I know that you are such, dearest ones, whenever I enter in my mind the oratory of the blessed Virgin Mary, I see that ladder of Jacob erected, by which I do not doubt that angels ascend and descend to you. I do not doubt that this place is the house of God and the gate of heaven.

Therefore, even if I have said something about these flowers of the heavenly powers, because you are their fellow citizens, I believe that you know these things better through the practice of contemplation than speech could express. For you, who are already bound in the heavens by every devotion and by the ardor of faith and charity to those whom you ceaselessly invoke, and with whom you offer inward conversations and prayers to God, cannot possibly be ignorant of them.

I am certain that they are with you in charity. Although you are still on earth, as I have said, your minds are already above; you say one Alleluia with them and worthily offer one glory to God the Trinity. From this place thanksgiving, praise, and honor are offered.

Therefore, dearest ones, I ask you not to think this place narrow, where you have shut yourselves in, because the house of God into which you have entered is vast and great—great, I say, because it has no completion. No mortal can penetrate it utterly as it is, where God is splendor and infinite possession.

John, contemplating that house, could scarcely recount even what he saw. Paul, who was carried up to it, although he was a leader of the Word, confessed that what he heard “it is not permitted to man to speak” (II Cor. 12:4).

Therefore, brides of Christ, enlarge your hearts; enlarge them, and do not be confined with unbelievers! For the house is great, and the possession immense, which is owed to you as a dowry; it is bounded neither by the spaces of places nor closed by the limits of time.

Let the dwelling that has received you from the world, as though you were doves flying toward heaven, suffice for the needs of nature. For in the world, according to the Apostle, there is nothing except “the desire of the eyes and the pride of life” (I John 2:16). Let it suffice simply that you are free for God alone, where sufficiency does not exceed necessity and necessity does not deprive sufficiency of its measure.

A small income is enough when the only eternal possession is God [Col. 1009D] (Luke 10:42). For Mary chose the better portion when she held only the Lord’s feet, which she watered with her tears.

The Mother of God also, through whose intercession you have vowed yourselves to God’s service, did not seek spacious palaces, when in the lodging place she had no room except the manger of the animals, in which she laid the infant God.

The apostles, praising God together in prison, are heard; how much more ought you, Christ’s flock, to take confidence before the holy altars, where the blessed and venerable Virgin is venerated and worshiped, exalted above the angelic choirs! Interceding for you before the supreme God, she commends your prayers and offers the vows of your tears, which you pour forth continually in abundance together with her prayers.

There also the relics of many saints and many virgins are venerated. By their vigils they illumine your watches for the praise of God and guard the camp.

For what else, dearest ones, is this house in which you dwell except God’s camp, the school of divine service, the workshop of virtues, the tower of eternal contemplation, and the guardhouse of perpetual chastity? Therefore it is rightly a camp, because it is a camp. Nor is this without reason, because your way of life is the discipline of a heavenly army; and it is the most valiant kind of monastic community, where virginity excels and a multitude of angels moves about for the watches of the supreme King.

There, plainly, the choir keeps vigil with divine praises and watches to see at what hour the bridegroom may come, so that with lamps prepared you may enter worthily with him into the wedding feast, to which you have already been invited.

Hence this hall continually resounds with harmonious praises; hence your groaning strikes the divine ears; hence tears rise from your cheeks and, according to Jeremiah, pierce the heavens; hence fasts mortify the flesh and affliction weakens the body.

This, then, is the understanding of the sons of Korah; this is the song of instruction, according to the Hebrew. For among them *Melchil* signifies “instruction” or “most learned.” *Idida* is an ancient name of Solomon, signifying both “peaceful” and “beloved.”

Therefore at the end of the title it concludes: “A song of instruction of the most beloved,” which the Septuagint rendered by “beloved,” because Greek has no ablative case. But when it says “the song of the most beloved,” it is one and the same as if it said “the song of instruction of the most beloved.”

Moreover, instruction and understanding differ in no respect in meaning, according to the saying: “Now therefore, kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth” (Ps. 2:10). For true understanding brings complete instruction, just as true instruction brings the understanding of a prudent man.

Accordingly, as I said a little above, the mystery of this song requires a spiritual and attentive reader. Otherwise, where the meaning is simple and open, why would the hearer need to be warned by the word “understanding,” and be told: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 11:15)?

The song of instruction is sung for the most beloved and the beloved; it is sung for the victor and for triumph; it is sung for flowers and lilies; it is also sung for those who will be changed. Hence, as I stated earlier, it is rightly called by the holy Fathers an epithalamium.

For we read that the first epithalamium was composed by Solomon in praise of Christ and the Church. From him secular men later drew their own dramatic compositions, so that at weddings, in honor of the bridegroom and bride, they might sing songs of praise back and forth before the bridal chamber.

David also, who is said to have been wholly musical, set forth in this psalm the form of this drama. Therefore he introduces not himself alone, nor one of the prophets, but the entire choir of the sons of Korah singing together; and he introduces the bridegroom, begotten from eternity from the Father’s heart, coming to the wedding.

He calls him “beloved,” and without any addition “most beloved,” because, in comparison with him, no one is rightly considered beloved. This figure is called by grammarians antonomasia, as though a kind of renaming from things, drawing the force of a proper name, when some person excels in a title to such an extent that no one other than the person spoken of is understood.

This occurs in many ways, often even in the divine Scriptures. Thus in the ninth Psalm, in the phrase “concerning the hidden things of the Son,” he wishes to indicate Christ as the Son alone. Likewise concerning John: “This is the disciple whom Jesus loved” (John 21:7)—not because he did not love the others, but because he loved him especially and above all.

So also in this passage the song is called “of the beloved” or “of the most beloved,” because although others are loved through the grace of adoption, this one is loved through the propriety of nature. Not because he received from outside himself something by which he might be lovable, but because by nature he possesses within himself the reason for being beloved.

For the holy natural unity, equality, and charity of the unity derives from itself, not from elsewhere, the fact that it is loved, just as adoption gives this to those whom it adopts. In that substance of the Trinity, there is unity in origin, equality in the offspring, and in the love of the Father and the Son a communion of unity and equality.

Therefore there is no division of unity, but a natural love of the whole majesty. He is beloved by God the Father as his own, concerning whom the Father himself says in the Gospel: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5).

Isaiah says in a song: “I will sing,” he says, “to my beloved, a song concerning my kinsman and his vineyard.” And then: “The vineyard of the beloved was made on a hill, in a fertile place” (Isa. 5:1). That vineyard is plainly the Church of Christ, which was made the bride of the only and beloved Son.

Yet the Church too is beloved, but because of him who reconciled her to himself and rescued her from the wrath of condemnation, so that she might be beloved. He, however, is beloved in himself, because he is Son by nature, so that no one else is rightly called beloved in comparison with him.

Rightly, therefore, he alone is to be loved by every rational creature as God and Lord, and to be venerated together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Meanwhile, because he alone, God, became man for human beings, he alone among human beings is rightly called beloved and most beloved above all. And because the title of the Psalm is one in which the song concerns him and the bride, it is rightly inscribed without ambiguity “of the beloved” or “of the most beloved,” so that the bride may seek no one to be loved apart from him. Rather, whomever the bride of Christ loves must either be he himself, or be loved in him, or for his sake, so that all may be one in charity.

Hence the Apostle says: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the charity of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (II Cor. 13:13). That communion makes all those to whom it is communicated one in him.

Moreover, in the Trinity there is no discord in love, because the equal love is dear and one, while the unity is equal and dear. Furthermore, love that is naturally equal and one persists incomparably.

And because God the Father was sending his own Son into the world, so that God himself, having become man, might by his power take a bride among human beings, it was fitting that in the mystery of this Psalm’s title— which precedes a song about the wedding—there should be “a song of the beloved,” or “a song of the most beloved.” Through this, the Son’s complete belovedness is commended: he is called beloved without addition, so that he alone is understood as beloved; in him those who are beloved are loved, and in him God the Father is well pleased, so that in him all the rest, whom he adopted as sons, may also please him.

With these matters concerning the title set forth beforehand, so that the mind may proceed to the song and to the mystical matters, the first book must be brought to an end, and the Holy Spirit must be entreated, so that they may be written upon our hearts with the same stylus with which they were disclosed to all God’s holy prophets.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1011]

[Col. 1011C] Although much and for a long time has been discussed, virgin of Christ, concerning hidden and obscure things, ignorance has not been so far driven away from us that we are no longer always entangled in those same obscurities, except insofar as we are illumined by grace.

Therefore certain philosophers, when they were without God, said that everything was doubtful. Others, removing this far from themselves, presumed that they knew what they did not know. Hence it is rightly said to be part of knowledge to know that you do not know.

Yet this lack of knowledge is called knowledge for this reason: although ignorance is a part of knowledge—namely, to know that you do not know—it is still much more ignorance if you do not know what you are seeking.

Hence some have said that there are three kinds of obscurity. The first is when a thing is evident to the senses but what it is remains obscure to the mind. The second is where the thing would be evident to the mind if it were not closed off from the senses. The third, however, is proved to be the most obscure: when something is grasped neither by the senses nor understood by the mind, nor comprehended by reason, even if it exists.

By this kind we are obscured and entangled in many things, except insofar as divine mercy deigns in some manner to disclose them to us, so that we may be able to grasp them. Hence, giving thanks to God and rejoicing in him, he said: “You have manifested to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Ps. 50:8).

These two things excessively obscure our mind when they confront us: not only what is hidden but also what is uncertain. For example, if someone wishing to make a journey arrives amid the darkness of night at a certain crossroads, knowing already what a road is but not knowing that there is any road or path there, he is enveloped in obscurity. When morning comes, what was hidden has been revealed; but it remains uncertain which road among all of them he ought to take, or where each one leads.

The prophet, freed from these two errors, now gives thanks to God, who had divinely inspired him concerning what was uncertain and hidden from the ages and generations, as is declared in this epithalamium of virgins.

Therefore we too, dearest ones, ought to give thanks to God our Savior, who has rescued us from such great darkness and led us to the true light. He not only showed himself to our senses as light visible in bodily form, but also illumined the eyes of our hearts within, so that the mysteries of the deity, which had been hidden and obscure, might become fully manifest to us.

Hence Isaiah too, rejoicing and himself illumined, said: “You are a hidden God, the God of Israel, and we did not know you” (Isa. 45:15).

But even when the prophets, inspired by God, said these things, they were very obscure and hidden, because what had been predestined had not yet been completed and manifested in realities. God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit certainly existed; but because the way of the saints had not yet been revealed (Heb. 9:8), God the Trinity was entirely unknown except to a few.

Hence, as the Apostle says: “Although they knew God through the things that had been made, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts” (Rom. 1:21). They did not find the way that is Christ—the way, namely, of the city of God, toward which we are journeying.

Therefore, so that divine mercy might wholly cleanse the folly of our hearts, long afterward it fulfilled what had been said, so that all obscurity might be driven away, and so that in one and the same Christ there might be what the eyes could see, what the hand could touch, and what the mind could understand—so that you might touch a man and understand God.

Hence John also said: “Our hands have handled the Word of life” (I John 1:1).

Do you hear, then, that the hands of the apostles touched the Word of life? Wherever the hands handle and touch, understand flesh. Wherever you hear “the Word,” recognize him who “was in the beginning with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

Nevertheless, understand the same one, truly God and man, as one God, whom the Prophet in the Psalm describes as bridegroom, as though in the title of the dowry, and joins to the holy Church.

Consider, I ask you, bride of Christ, how hidden or obscure it was when it was not known among human beings whether God even existed, except only in Judea. Hence it is sung in the Psalm: “God is known in Judah” (Ps. 75:2). In that land too, it had previously been unknown whether God the Son of God existed.

But when, through the prophet’s paternal voice, it is said: “My heart has poured forth a good word” (Ps. 44:1), it was uncertain of which word this was said, except to those whose eyes were illumined, so that they might know with certainty what was uncertain and believe in their hearts what was yet to come.

But for us, because everything has been disclosed and completed, nothing obscure and nothing uncertain remains. Therefore, because the faithful soul receives in this epithalamium the Word begotten from the Father’s heart, let the bride receive the little book of the dowry, and let incorrupt virginity receive the bridegroom sent to her from the innermost heart of God.

Concerning him the Father expressly says: “My heart has poured forth a good word.” A good word indeed, which “was in the beginning with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

And do not wonder, prudent virgin, that I have called this Psalm a little book of the dowry, in which such covenants of marriage are first disclosed from the beginning of the world. For you have in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding for his son” (Matt. 22:2).

If you pay attention, you will find that in this passage that wedding is first established by a covenant—not merely betrothed, but as though written in the tablets of marriage—where God the Father says that he poured forth from his heart the Word “who was in the beginning,” so that “the Word might become flesh.”

To this Word, namely to his Son the King, the divine majesty declares its works and indicates everything that is to be done through him. When you hear this, virgin of Christ, that the Father, through prophetic speech, indicates to his Son the King the works of his power, you ought to consider that he is the swift scribe. For the one who brings forth from his treasure “new things and old” (Matt. 13:52) discloses the secrets of heaven, hidden not from him but from the ages.

But because a scribe, however swift, cannot write what he hears without a pen or stylus, it immediately follows, as though from the Father’s voice: “My tongue is the pen, or stylus, of a swift-writing scribe,” according to the Hebrew.

By these words the bride has nothing else to consider than the covenant of marriage, which is never lawfully confirmed without a dowry. Therefore, most sacred sister, when you hear the Father dictating and the tongue declared to be the pen of a swift-writing scribe, know that the three persons have one nature, one power, and one operation, so that this little book of the dowry may be written for virgins.

In it the bridegroom’s origin is first shown: the Word from the Father’s heart, the Word that was in the beginning, plainly with God, and God was the Word. Receive, then, this good Word that has poured forth from the Father’s heart. For this is what he himself is, and from him he is; through him all these good things that are seen were made.

Concerning this good Word of his the Father said: “My heart has poured forth a good word.” Through him alone all good exists, and therefore he is to be loved because he is good, and whatever good we may possess comes from him.

For if you, a human being, have in your heart and counsel whatever good you intend to do—what that good will be and when it will be done—how much more did God, in this one coeternal Word of his, possess all that was to be done? Hence, according to John’s statement, “what was made, in him was life” (John 1:3–4).

Therefore he added, as though repeating what he had said: “I speak of my works to the king.” It is as though he were saying plainly: I speak of my works to him because I begot him as the Word, in whom are all my works that are to be done by me through him.

Otherwise visible and invisible things would not exist in reality unless they had first existed in the Word, just as in you there would be no construction of things or work unless it had first existed in your plan.

All the works of God were in the Father’s Word. They were not yet works, but the Word existed; and because the Father begot him coeternal, he disclosed to him all that was his, whatever this may be.

Therefore he is incomparably good, because this very Word is God. Hence what shone forth from the heart must be received by the bride there, and she must embrace the dowry of eternal salvation from the place from which it poured forth to us.

For what proceeds from the heart is held or grasped only by the heart. Therefore the most beloved Son and the good Word from the Father’s heart is announced as sent to the bride for the wedding, so that he may be loved in the soul with still greater charity.

The Father must not be believed to be corporeal, as though he possessed a heart, womb, and other bodily members. Rather, through the names of bodily activities, the mysteries of his divinity are to be apprehended. God does not consist of bodily members.

For elsewhere, when he wished to mention the generation of the Son, he said: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3). In this way he commended, through the truth of his divinity and for the faith of understanding, the ineffable birth of the Only-Begotten Son from himself: he whom he generated from the womb as Son before the morning star, that is, as eternal; whom he poured forth from the heart as Word.

In all these expressions he spoke of his divine realities according to human nature, in order to educate the understanding of human nature toward knowledge of the faith: so that he should not appear to subsist from nothing or from elsewhere, as though created, but so that the natural birth of his Only-Begotten might be taught as proceeding from himself.

Thus in this passage the Son’s true essence is commended as deriving from the Father’s nature. But because he had called him beloved or most beloved, so that he might be loved and complete love commended to believers, he indicates that he had poured forth his Word—always existing in himself—from the innermost and life-giving viscera of his heart.

Not that the Word departed from the place in which he remained, but because “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), he came to us without departing from there.

Therefore, to show this mystery to believers, the Father indicates the Word of whom he had spoken. He indicates that this Word is the one who is “beautiful in form above the sons of men” (Phil. 2:7), and this in the form of a servant.

In the form of God, however, no one can be compared with him so as to call him more beautiful or more handsome. For according to his divinity he is comparable to no one, since no form of any created thing exists without matter except the divine form.

That form is plainly nothing other than one; and therefore this one is always what it is. There is no accident in it, although from it all being derives. But it derives from no other. Therefore it lacks matter and motion and exists always immutably in itself.

All other things formed and created by him are not what they are in themselves, because each of them has its being only from those things of which and from which it consists—that is, from its parts.

Therefore God, in the form of God, is comparable to no one, since he is from no other than himself. But the wretched heretics were unwilling or unable to perceive or understand that in this form of divinity there can be nothing but a Trinity that is unity, one equality, and one essence of divinity, for which there is never and nowhere any being other than the same eternal being.

Therefore he said to his servant Moses: “I am who I am” (Gen. 3:14), because for him there is nothing except always to be the same and to be capable of all things.

While the Son of God existed in this form, he was not equal to God through robbery but through the nature of his true birth, because he was begotten by God the Father. He “emptied himself,” not so that he might be someone other than himself, but so that, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7), he might be the same God and man for our redemption.

In this form, therefore, he is said to be beautiful above the sons of men. This emptying was not a change of his divinity but a merciful act of compassion in the assumption of humanity.

For if Paul, when he removes from himself the things that belonged to a child when he became a man, is not changed—lest he himself no longer be the same person and possess the same things as before—how much more is God the Son of God himself unchangeably the same when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant?

For he is whole in both: God and man. But because the form of divinity was hidden in visible man, the Apostle rightly proclaims that he, presenting himself as one and the same in the form of a servant, emptied himself.

In this form, therefore, as blessed Basil is said by all to have declared, a certain new, manly operation of God was being displayed, as the text of the holy Gospel also makes clear to the end. For just as the aforementioned [Col. 1016B] doctor most eloquently alluded to it in that statement, showing that God had become man, so that in one and the same person there was a twofold substance, there was likewise a twofold operation: one, namely, by which he was shown to be true God; the other, by which he was shown to be true man. This mystery remains no less secret in speech than it is unknown to the understanding; whoever cannot discern it clearly must believe. Otherwise he will stray from the truth as far as he has been buried in ignorance of the truth and deceived by his own presumption. For in the one and the same undivided person of Christ, divine and human works are displayed throughout all the pages of the Old and New Testaments. And this is a certain new and ineffable twofold manly operation of God, in the form of man in which Jesus Christ, most kind, is proclaimed beautiful beyond the sons of men and blessed forever.

Why, however, is he called beautiful beyond the sons of men, rather than beyond all the angels, since he is so much higher than the angels as he has inherited a name more excellent than theirs, the name “Son” (Hebr. I, 4)? The question is not unreasonable, unless the meaning is clear: in the form of man, the only-begotten Son of God the Father is commended as destined to be, so that man should not be denied in comparison with the angels. He is proclaimed beautiful beyond the sons of men so that you would neither believe him to be outside humanity, [1253] nor regard him as merely one of the common multitude, since he was man among men and, even among the sons of men, beautiful in form.

Nevertheless, in the Hebrew text, with regard to the beloved king himself and victorious Word of the Father, about whom everything previously stated has been said, as though the preface were now concluded, he begins the narrative here and makes an apostrophe to that most loving victor, to whom he attributes all his works, and all the things spoken concerning him have come to pass. “Concerning the sons of Korah,” he says, “more beautiful than the sons of men.”

But the question is asked again: how is he more beautiful than all the sons of men, when we read in Isaiah: “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty, but was despised by men; his appearance was dishonored and deficient in comparison with the sons of men, a man set in suffering and knowing how to bear weakness” (Isa. LIII, 2–3), together with the other things that various interpreters interpret concerning him in that passage? If you consider the matter carefully, no disagreement among the Scriptures arises. There the lowliness of his body was not on its own account, but because of the scourges, spittings, and blows; because of the nails as well, the mockeries and insults of the cross, and the many other disgraces that our most kind Savior endured for us, so that he was not even counted among men. Here, however, the beauty of virtues and the nobility of life, the integrity of his conduct and his form, are praised in him no less than his justice and complete goodness. It is not that Christ’s divinity is said to be more beautiful by comparison with human beings—for, as I stated shortly before, it is comparable to no one—but that, in the form of a servant and the appearance of a man, without the insults, injuries, and sufferings of the cross, he shone more beautiful than all human beings. In him divinity also shone forth in his works, brighter than the sun, while his humanity, even in those same sufferings and injuries, is shown to possess the virtue of mercy. And therefore he is rightly proclaimed and revered by all as beautiful on the cross, beautiful in the scourges, beautiful in everything, in all his works.

For although it is wondrous that one who was a virgin was born of a Virgin, it is no less wondrous that the same one was born not by the will of man but from God (John I, 13): born at the end of time, yet begotten without beginning before all time.

This, then, is why, in the form of a servant, every kind of insult and the acceptance of weakness is a virtue of piety. That form is more beautiful than all the sons of men because in it the divine glory of majesty shone forth, while whatever human weakness existed in him was either a form of virtue, an example of perfect imitation, a triumph of our salvation, or certainly the price of our redemption—yet in everything he was more beautiful than all. For this reason the holy fathers also say that he possessed something star-like in his face and eyes, by which he divinely caressed the pious and terrified the reprobate.

Otherwise the apostles would never have followed him immediately at a single command; nor would those who had come to seize him have immediately fallen prostrate at his mere voice. Likewise, when he is said to have made a whip from cords, he could never have driven all the dissenters and proud men from the temple with such authority, unless something heavenly had terrified them, so that, struck with fear, they yielded to his threat.

Finally, in the testimony cited above, where he says, “A man set in suffering and knowing how to bear weakness,” he gives the reason why he endured these things. “Because,” he says, “he turned his face away”—that is, with the assistance of his divinity withdrawn for a little while, he abandoned his body to insult and torments; otherwise, unless he had willed it, he would not have suffered, since he had come for this purpose. Hence there is no doubt that, in this form of a servant, in which he was more beautiful than the sons of men, he possessed grace diffused through him, so that he could do whatever he wished as God and suffer whatever he had determined to suffer as man—not as one unwilling, but as one possessing authority, no less in every word than in every deed.

Hence also follows: “Grace has been poured forth upon your lips.” According to the form of his humanity, in which he came to make the covenant of marriage, he is believed to have been full of grace—not according to the form in which he is equal to the Father. For in that form he could not receive the Holy Spirit, since according to the divine nature the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. In that nature the Father alone is as great as he is with the Son and the Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit alone is as great as he is together with the Father and the Son. Among the three persons, none possesses anything less than the other two. For in each person the deity is so complete that it is one in the three persons and wholly present in each.

The Son’s divinity, therefore, could not receive the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father, and is given by the Son just as he is given by the Father. That nature, therefore, from which the Holy Spirit has his origin could neither await nor receive generosity. Indeed, the Holy Spirit is wholly the Father’s and wholly the Son’s, because he is naturally one with the Father and the Son. Thus no one doubts that he proceeds wholly from the Father and the Son and remains wholly in the Father and the Son, because he remains in such a way that he proceeds, and proceeds in such a way that he remains. Hence by nature he possesses with the Father and the Son the fullness of unity and the unity of fullness, so that he is wholly possessed by the Father and wholly possessed by the Son. The Son’s divinity, therefore, could not receive the Holy Spirit, since it is of one nature with him.

It remains, then, that Christ the God-man received the Holy Spirit, through this outpouring, in the form of a servant that he assumed. Yet we read that he did not receive him according to measure, because he received him wholly. Therefore, when grace was poured forth upon Christ’s lips, it possessed the fullness of perfection; for where there is no measure, there is the perfection of fullness. The saints indeed received the gift of grace according to the measure of Christ’s gift, but Christ, just as he is beautiful in form beyond the sons of men, is also full of the grace of the Holy Spirit beyond all his partakers.

Hence John, speaking of the Son himself, says: “God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John III, 34). For with all God’s saints there is the generosity of the giver’s abundant gift, whereas in Christ the fullness of the Spirit remains forever. Therefore the blessed Apostle says that the Spirit is given “according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. IV, 13), indicating that other human beings receive him by measure. John, wishing to show that the whole fullness of grace was in Christ, says: “God does not give the Spirit by measure.”

Isaiah also clearly indicates this when he speaks of him: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit filled him with the fear of the Lord” (Isa. XI, 2–3). It is therefore clear that Christ received the grace of the Holy Spirit, but not according to measure. And if God gave the Spirit to the man Christ not according to measure, then Christ must likewise possess wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety. Consequently, that prerogative of perfection belongs not only to his divinity but also to his humanity—the prerogative that the blessed Apostle assigns to Christ himself when he says: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II, 3). Since he did not receive the Spirit according to measure, he possessed all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. For if any portion of his fullness were lacking in him, it would follow that he should be proclaimed to have received the Spirit according to measure.

If the Apostle speaks truly—and indeed he does, since he says that God gave him the Spirit not according to measure—it is established that he possessed in himself the entire fullness of divinity. And where the fullness of deity was present, it is manifest that the power of that same divinity was present as well. Therefore he attributed to him all power according to his every will, death already conquered. Here there is no adoption, no division of substances, no confusion or commingling, no deprivation of anything, but only the unity of Christ’s person and the distinct property of his nature are proclaimed. To him belongs in its entirety the ability to know the things of God, because in him nothing is found except God.

All the remaining members receive the gift of grace according to measure and receive it from Christ’s [Col. 1019B] fullness. Hence the evangelist John says: “We have all received from his fullness, grace upon grace” (John I, 16). This means that, in that grace of form which is given in place of the grace of faith, the fullness is not itself the grace diffused upon Christ’s lips, but that fullness which all receive and with which the whole Church is filled, insofar as each person is shown to be capable of possessing it through his grace.

Hence also the Prophet says: “You will fill me with joy in your presence” (Ps. XV, 11); and again: “We shall be filled with the good things of your house” (Ps. LXIV, 5). But in order that we may be filled, we have received from his fullness, by which the house that is the Church of the living God is filled.

Moreover, the Apostle Paul says of him: “In him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II, 9). I ask you not to regard as trivial what is great, or to treat without reverence what is divine. For although it is joyful for virgins that God, as a bridegroom, is described to them as a man beautiful in form, it is nevertheless ineffable that the frailty of the flesh is called to the glory of so great a union, so that it has God as Father, the only Son of God as brother and bridegroom. The angels marvel at him; the powers of heaven are afraid. Heaven does not contain him whom a womb contains; the sun does not see him; earth does not sustain him; the whole of creation does not comprehend him.

What can a mortal breast do in the face of these things, dearest women? What can the weak human mind do? How can it contain the Word that has burst forth from the Father’s heart, the Word that is eternal in the Father? What can the narrowness of human understanding do before this? What can human nature, or the human voice, [Col. 1019D] say before it, when it is the ineffable and unheard Word through whom all things exist? [1257] The Word remaining in the Father, “which ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the human heart” (1 Cor. II, 9).

When Isaiah had heard of this Word with spiritual hearing, inspired by God, he wondered how it could reach human hearing, saying: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isa. LIII, 1.) Concerning this, Jeremiah, having conceived it with divine affection and scarcely able to endure it, cried out: “My belly, my belly, I am in pain, and the senses of my heart are troubled” (Jer. IV, 19). Habakkuk says of it: “Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works, and I was terrified.” And then he says: “Trembling entered my bones, and beneath me my strength was shaken” (Hab. III, 2). Behold, such a great prophet, raised up by the power of God, felt that his own strength had fallen beneath him.

So also all the saints throughout the ages, whenever they experienced such things, confessed that they were nothing. But because it would be lengthy to pursue the fears of the saints concerning this mystery, let Christ’s virgin consider much from a little and prepare her heart so that she may be able to contain such a great Word; for nothing is closer than heart and word. A heart without a speakable word seems dead; the word, however, remains nowhere but within the heart, proceeds nowhere but from the heart, and is received nowhere but in the heart. This Word, although clothed with a voice, comes forth only from the heart, yet does not depart from the heart when it comes forth; it comes to the heart so that it may remain where it has come.

By these indications the divine nature is surely revealed to us: that the Father and the Son have one substance. And when the bride, to whom this wedding song is sung, receives him, she possesses him only in her heart, so that she may love the Father’s beloved, whom she holds by faith.

Symmachus, however, translated the passage very differently: “My heart has been stirred by a good word.” He seems to mean that the prophet’s heart, or the heart of some other speaker, was stirred by another’s speech, while the Holy Spirit disclosed beforehand the mysteries of Christ, causing the prophet himself to burst forth into eloquence, so that he too, like the other prophets, might speak of Christ’s coming. Even so, he also proclaims the good Word of God, but he is silent about the fact that the Word came forth to us from the Father’s heart. Therefore it is better to understand the statement as spoken in the person of the Father: that he himself begot the Word, who is God, from himself, and that he is said to have uttered him forth.

Indeed, the words of the title harmonize with this no less than the text of the Psalm itself completes the same meaning in the manner of a song. For the sense in which the Word is said to have been uttered forth fits both interpretations well.

[1258] Properly speaking, a belch is the digestion of food and the exhalation into the air of digested nourishment. From this exhalation, according to the quality of the food or the state of the stomach, a breath of good or bad odor bursts forth; this is called a belch. But divine providence does not disdain to assume lowly words in order to shape our understanding of it, since he deigned to assume the weakness of our flesh. He did all these things so that he might instruct us through our own words, uses, and examples, and commend his humility to us in everything.

Finally, from the beginning all the saints—that is, patriarchs and prophets—perceived this breath of fragrance inwardly in their hearts through the Holy Spirit, who is often called breath in the Scriptures and by whom the one who was to be sent was revealed even before he came. Hence one of the saints says: “The ruler shall not depart from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. XLIX, 10).

All the sacrifices of the Old Testament, which prefigured Christ’s coming in the flesh to be offered to God the Father for us as a holocaust, will exhale the fragrances of this Word’s belch. Concerning these sacrifices it is often said: “The Lord smelled the fragrance of sweetness” (Gen. VIII, 21). The patriarch Jacob had sensed this fragrance when, as I said not long above, he declared: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. XXVII, 27).

Who this one is whom the Lord has blessed, the present Psalm declares when it says: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured forth upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever.” The Church had already sensed the fragrance of this aroma through her nostrils in the Song of Songs, when she said: “Your name is an ointment poured out; therefore the maidens have loved you exceedingly” (Song I, 3–4).

There is no doubt, dearest women, that you are the maidens of whom it is said: “You are those who sing among the same virgins, whose number is without end”; you say to the bridegroom in that same Song: “Draw me after you; we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments.” Otherwise, unless his fragrance had sprinkled you, you would never have desired, after despising the things that belong to the world, to come to such mortification of flesh and spirit and to carry the cross under compulsion after Christ. Thus, having trampled everything beneath your feet, you look toward and follow Christ the Sun no differently than the heliotropes of which I spoke, because you have loved only the author of life and have set your minds on things above.

And rightly so, beloved women, because the alabaster jar of the most precious ointment was broken, broken certainly for you, and the house was filled with the fragrance of that pure nard. Hence, together with the Apostle, you are a good fragrance to all people in this world, so that the fragrances of virtues flow from you. Hence charity is enlarged; peace and patience adorn your conduct; goodness and kindness are fragrant. Hence deep humility strikes heaven; modesty and gentleness beautify your appearance; contempt for the world, long-suffering, and frugality in food flourish in you. Hence virginity blooms, chastity and purity are fresh. Hence, from the good treasure of the heart, the teaching of virtues and the gifts of the Holy Spirit flow, so that each of you may say—not from yourselves, but in him through whom you received the word of salvation and the gift of grace: “My heart has uttered a good word,” because in him to whom you have vowed yourselves, whom you carry in your heart, are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

Hence follows: “I speak of my works to the king.” The voice of the Father continues, proclaiming of the Son that he shows him his works, in accordance with the statement: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. CXLVIII, 5); and in Genesis: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Gen. I, 3).

It is not that God the Father uttered a spoken voice, saying “Let there be,” since God the Trinity is incorporeal and has neither members by which words might be formed nor ears with which he might hear. Rather, the Son is himself the Father’s Word, consubstantial and coeternal. When the Father begot him, he showed and spoke all things to him, not by utterance but by eternal begetting, because he begot the one through whom he made all things.

For him to speak his works to the king means that he begot the king—not only the one through whom he would create all things, but also the one through whom he would redeem and govern the universe. Therefore, in this passage he ought rather to have named as king the one to whom he shows his works, in accordance with the text of the Psalm, because he was coming to acquire the kingdom by his own power and to take the bride.

Finally, in the Gospel he himself says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding for his son” (Matt. XXII, 2). Since in this song a wedding was being prepared for Christ the king, the son of the king, the Father shows the Son his works for the praise of his name and the glory of the distinctiveness of his nature, because “no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. XI, 27). Therefore the Father shows him his works because he is the Father’s Word, and he alone knows all that belongs to the Father and to whom he wishes to reveal it.

For this reason the Father cries from heaven not once but twice: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” It is as though he plainly said: [Col. 1022B] “He is the one to whom I have disclosed everything, whom I have begotten according to his own nature, who is wholly in me and I in him; therefore I have established my good pleasure in him. Listen to him.”

Hence it is said that everything the Father does, the Son also does in the same way, and that the Son can do nothing except what he sees the Father doing.

According to Symmachus, however, the prophetic chorus, about to speak of the mysteries of Christ’s Church, speaks so that it may not seem unworthy of the song. Together with them, you also, holy women consecrated to Christ, leading your choruses in turn, proclaim your works to God the king, your bridegroom, lest because of consciousness of sin it be said: “Why do you recount my statutes and take up my covenant in your mouth?” (Ps. XLIX, 16.) Confess your works to God the king, so that, if they are good, he may accept them, or, if they are evil, may have mercy and cleanse them, in accordance with the saying: “Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified, because the righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. XVIII, 17).

Therefore, with that same prophetic chorus of the sons of Korah, consecrate to God whatever you do: the mortification of the flesh, vigils, prayers, the singing of psalms, and praises, in your hearts. Give yourselves solely to him, and to him alone disclose the secrets of your hearts. Pay him the service owed to him, so that you may please him alone, to whom you consecrated yourselves from the beginning of your religious life. A virgin is never alone when God is with her.

“My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe.” Jerome translated this as “My tongue is the stylus of a swift scribe,” wishing to express the speed with which notaries write. But the Father’s tongue is swifter: it signifies the Holy Spirit, whose coming is the teaching of the whole world. Through him the law, as though written by the finger of God, was written on tablets of stone; through him all the holy men of God, inspired, spoke of future things and published what is divine.

The most kind Savior therefore says in the Gospel: “The Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything” (John XIV, 26). Hence it is not without mystery that the same Holy Spirit is said to have come upon the apostles in tongues of fire. For he is the one through whom the Father distributes his gifts to believers, and writes him into the hearts of individuals; and whoever he fills, he makes at once ardent and speaking.

For he possesses knowledge of speech in that which contains all things (Wis. I, 7). Therefore he is rightly called the Father’s tongue and the pen of a swift-writing scribe, [1261] because he is the Spirit of both, namely, of the Father and the Son. For Jesus Christ, the Father’s Word, is himself the learned and swift scribe in the kingdom of heaven, who brings forth from his treasure things new and old (Matt. XIII, 52). Isaiah declares that he would come: “Write quickly; strip off the spoils; plunder swiftly” (Isa. VIII, 1).

The Holy Spirit is therefore rightly called the pen of a swift-writing scribe, because to will something is, for him, not merely to write it but also to accomplish and teach it. For where there is one will, one divinity, and one power, there is no inequality because of differences in words, but one divinity, one nature, and one cooperation.

God the Father, the king from whom all things are, was willing to make a wedding for his Son, the king through whom all things are. Therefore, in this same wedding song, he declared the Holy Spirit, who contains all things. Otherwise, such a great inheritance as is displayed in this song would not be attributed to the bride except through this mystery of faith: that God is believed to be the Trinity of unity and the unity of the Trinity, possessing one majesty, one kingdom, and one will.

For this reason, in this wedding song three witnesses are inscribed, as though in a marriage contract: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Thus the Apostle John says that there are three on earth who bear witness to these mystical gifts: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and, as is found in the more corrected manuscripts: “And there are three who bear witness in heaven, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one” (1 John V, 7).

Otherwise, in the conscience of the virgin, as though in a covenant document, unless these three witnesses are inscribed, she will obtain no inheritance from God; in Greek this is called κληρονομία (*klēronomia*), “inheritance.” To speak plainly, this inheritance, as though in a marriage contract, sets forth under seal the splendid faith of the Trinity and assigns to the bride the Son’s form and the rights of marriage.

The Son, like a swift scribe, because he is the Father’s heir and the Church’s bridegroom, hands on to his bride the inheritance received from the Father, as though in a marriage contract, when he is placed at the right hand. Yet it is not written with a corruptible pen and ink, but by the grace of the Holy Spirit, through whom the love of God has been poured into the hearts of all who are to enter these nuptials.

Otherwise, whoever does not bring this marriage formula of the faith will fear that, when the king has entered, he may hear from the Gospel: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matt. XXII, 12.)

Therefore let Christ Jesus, the most kind bridegroom, teach and write the marriage covenant for the virgin. Let her listen attentively, I say, and observe it; let her also persist with complete purity of heart and watchfulness, lest she be rejected among the foolish virgins. Indeed, let her say of herself, let her say to God the Father, and let her say to the bridegroom:

“My heart has uttered a good word, and I have consecrated all the little works of my actions to you, Lord. Meanwhile, let my tongue, like the pen of a swift-writing scribe, not only teach my companions what the Spirit has infused and sounded forth as though through his own instrument, but also continually offer the sacrifice of praise to the Lord, and perseveringly pay to the end the vows that my lips have pronounced” (Ps. LXV, 13). “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. I, 21). In him I have placed the end of all my perfection: that I may remain in him without end.

And, to speak more plainly . . . [lacuna] Therefore it is rightly believed that no fullness of divinity is lacking in him, whose person is one with the Word, whom the wisdom and power of the Father assumed in such a way that he himself is that same wisdom and power. For God the Son assumed human nature, which he had not previously possessed, not a person, which he had always possessed eternally in the Trinity.

This humanity passed into God in such a way that there is one person. In this unity it was made mistress of all things to such an extent that, together with his divinity, it is one person and one power in the Trinity. Hence John says: “We saw him as the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I, 14).

From this it is plainly established that the fullness of truth in him contains the fullness of grace, which is the whole of humanity in his divinity, and that the fullness of grace contains within itself the fullness of truth, which is the whole of divinity in his humanity. This grace was diffused and poured throughout Christ’s entire humanity, so that the fullness of truth in the unity of person contains within itself the fullness of humanity, and humanity contains the fullness of truth.

By assuming a complete human nature—namely, soul and flesh—into the eternal person of his divinity, he is naturally wholly true man and wholly true God. For just as in his divinity he possesses the entire nature of his begetting, so in his humanity he possesses the whole substance of his divinity, the whole majesty, the whole power, the whole wisdom, immutability, and omnipotence.

This, then, is your bridegroom, dearest women: the one who is God and bridegroom for you is man, and the same man is God, the true and proper Son of God. This is your beloved from the Song of Songs, “white and ruddy” (Song V, 10): white because he was born a virgin from a Virgin; ruddy because he was sprinkled with his own blood. He is white in you and ruddy in the martyrs. From his mouth this grace flowed; in his mouth this reconciliation was accomplished.

Hence the bride says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I, 1). For she knew that this omnipotent grace had been poured upon Christ’s lips, and therefore from afar she implores such sweet kisses. It is not that the fullness of grace was poured only upon his lips and not throughout his whole being; rather, it is in his lips as a part representing the whole, because the grace of the divine Word flowed from the fountain of Christ’s mouth and filled the entire world.

Thus in the Gospel: “Opening his mouth, he taught them” (Matt. V, 2)—opening it like the fountains of life, like things hidden from the ages, like the secret things of God’s mysteries. The two Testaments as well, the Old and the New, are called Christ’s lips, in which these mysteries are disclosed and the divine sacraments are revealed.

The mouths of the patriarchs and prophets were also suffused with the grace of the Holy Spirit, as were those of the apostles; but Christ’s lips were so in a wholly different way. Therefore, just as in the first clause the Father’s voice concerning the Son says, “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men,” so in the next two clauses we should understand the words to mean: “Grace has been poured forth upon your lips beyond the sons of men, and God has blessed you forever beyond the sons of men,” because in everything he was beyond man.

Let the faithful soul understand this; let holy virginity understand it; and let Christ’s bride attend to the praises spoken of him, because this is the understanding of the sons of Korah—that is, of the sons of God. Why he said, “Therefore God has blessed you forever,” is clear from the reasons already given: because he is beautiful in form, because grace has been poured forth upon his lips beyond the sons of men.

Otherwise such a great blessing would not belong to him unless he were beautiful in everything beyond the sons of men and possessed within himself grace diffused beyond all others. For this is the blessing in which all who are blessed on earth will be blessed.

Hence the Apostle says: “Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (Eph. I, 3). This is not an earthly or Jewish blessing, nor merely a temporal one whose eternity extends only to a jubilee—for example, the Hebrew slave who did not wish to leave in the seventh year and, with his ear pierced, became a servant forever—and similar cases in many passages where a determined number of years signifies eternity.

Rather, the eternity in which Christ is blessed is an immeasurability of ages, just as the grace with which he is suffused is an immeasurability of gifts. True eternity, as some define it, is the complete and perfect possession of interminable life all at once, because it is enclosed by no end and deprived of no blessedness.

In that eternity Christ, already blessed, is proclaimed in the prophetic voice through the gift of grace, with the past tense placed in the future’s stead. He is therefore not proclaimed blessed with just any blessing, but, as the Apostle explained, is said to be blessed with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.

It must also be noted that this is not according to the nature in which he was begotten by the Father, but according to that in which he was born and in which he received grace—though an immeasurable grace. He is the one who gives and the one who receives. Since he is powerful enough for others to receive according to measure, while remaining in the form of God he gives the Spirit, and in assuming the form of a servant he receives the Spirit. He receives wholly the very one whom he gives according to measure. He gives to many sons according to measure, but the only Son does not receive according to measure, because he is true man in such a way that he is true God.

By these and similar words the law of the New Testament, witnessed by the law and the prophets, testifies that he is the Christ to whom the name was given that is above every name (Phil. II, 9). For “the Lord magnified his holy name above every name” because of mercy and truth, and in that name he placed the whole blessing of divinity.

And so that you may not think, virgin of Christ, that blessing always consists in invocations and prayers by which the gifts of charisms or whatever else is employed in the sacred writings are obtained, know that blessings are more properly called gifts and offerings. Hence the Greek also calls any gifts or little presents *eulogia*, just as by common usage we call the bread received from the priest’s hand “eulogies.”

But in Christ that blessing in the heavenly places is truly called a gift—one that is above every gift—because in him everything has been given to us. Therefore let no one applaud herself, and let no one presume upon her merits. If Christ, that whole man in flesh and soul, received from the gift of the giver that he should be blessed forever, full of grace and truth, much more does no mortal, and not even an angel, possess anything good except from the bounty and gift of the giver.

Therefore, dearest women, I beg you: guard the gift of chastity; guard the offering and honor of virginity, because the rewards of the one who rewards are certainly great. If these gifts are worthily preserved, they are already themselves the rewards of the recompense, because you do not possess from yourselves what you know, but from the gift of the giver; still less can you preserve the outstanding gifts you have received unless he himself grants that you remain in what you have vowed.

For “unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain; and unless the Lord guards the city of our heart or flesh, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. CXXVI, 1). Therefore, beloved women, labor in this way, and build yourselves together in one another; watch more diligently in everything, so that you may attribute to God all that you possess, because the things you have received are great.

Commit to him everything you have received, because the gifts are his, so that, kept safely with him, they may be preserved for you until the day of eternal recompense. Follow that beauty by which your bridegroom is proclaimed beautiful and handsome; preserve that grace which is praised as having been given to you in him, so that he himself may say to you what is written in the Song of Songs: “You are beautiful, my beloved; my dove, my immaculate one, beautiful; your cheeks are like those of a turtledove, your eyes like those of doves” (Song II, 10).

The marriage covenant is therefore well preserved if love of chaste affection and the modesty of perpetual chastity are offered from both sides; if beauty of form and dignity answer one another; if integrity of conduct and the diligence of chaste observance remain watchful, so that the right of love is not injured in anything. For the more tenderly the inward love burns, the more sharply the bridegroom is wounded when offended by the bride.

[Col. 1026D] Therefore, lest the virgin of Christ perhaps flatter herself because of the bridegroom’s gentleness, let her hear that he carries a sword and threatens to be jealous. Hence it follows: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one.” If you do this well, if you keep the covenant of your betrothal, the powerful and mighty Son of the King whom you have taken as bridegroom is able to complete the marriage contract of your dowry. But if you live wickedly, be afraid, because from his mouth has gone forth a flashing sword, sharp and honed on both sides.
