Hence, too, after the outstanding beauty of his appearance, after the grace poured upon his lips, after the blessing received from the eternal inheritance, the Father commands him to gird himself with the sword of his strength: for the vengeance of enemies, the rebuke of those who oppose him, and the preservation of the rights of all things, so that everything he possesses may be in peace (Luke XI, 21). Let no one, therefore, think about the vengeance of servants when he sees the Lord fighting, girded with the sword of retribution. And therefore rejoice, virgin, even though fragile; rejoice, bride, although walking here and there amid enemies and full of fear; because you have taken as bridegroom one who is most powerful and armed.

Indeed, arm yourself also with the sword of the divine word, of which the Apostle says: “And take the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians VI, 17), so that you too, armed, may answer your champion and defender. I do not doubt that you understand this passage better, you who, girded manfully with the sword of Christ from your earliest years, have learned to fight bravely, as though in battle, with the comfort of many others. But so that you may know that virginity must always be armed, as though in battle, I think it should be recalled what paganism, deceived by various errors, imagined for itself, since they displayed their virgins armed and always girded with the sword in many fictions.

The Lord also commands us to have our loins girded and to carry lamps in our hands. Solomon likewise describes in the Song of Songs sixty mighty men, from the strongest of Israel, around the litter, all holding swords, most skilled in war, men girded with swords upon their thighs (Song of Songs III, 8).

That “thigh” signifies the works of marriage is taught by Abraham (Genesis XXIV, 2), who commands his servant to swear by his thigh, by the God of heaven who was to be born from him; and likewise in the passage where a ruler is promised from the thighs of Judah. Jacob also, when dying, adjures Joseph by his thigh (Genesis XLVII, 29) not to bury him in Egypt. All these things, [Col. 1027C] and in whatever other passages they occur, are mysteries of the birth of Christ.

It is also customary, especially among those who wish to be strong and vigorous in war, always to carry a sword girded upon the thigh. Here the bridegroom is commanded by the Father to gird himself, not with just any sword, but, as it is written in Hebrew: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O strongest one, your glory and your beauty.” Here, for some reason, it is wrongly divided in all copies, both Greek and Latin, so that “your appearance and your beauty” is read as joined not to the preceding verse but to the beginning of the following one.

However this sword is understood, Jesus came to cast it upon the earth, as he himself says: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth but a sword. I have come,” he says, “to separate a son against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law” (Matthew X, 34); and, he says, “there will be two against three, and three against two. And a man’s enemies will be those of his own household.” Without doubt Christ’s sword has brought this division to us; and, as we still see it happening daily on earth, it acts lest the mind wrongly possess the things granted to it by nature. [1267]

For this reason, dearest women, you stripped yourselves of all things; for this reason, having left parents, relatives, loved ones, and friends, you shut yourselves here beneath the yoke of Christ in perpetual enclosure. Having left father or mother, relatives, acquaintances of every kind, and children, you clung to the Lord alone. Why should I enumerate more, since it is evident that whatever you could have held dear, you too have left behind, enduring the harsh losses of the present life for the love of Christ, and pursuing eternal things through tireless labor?

No one was able to draw you back: neither the love of a husband, nor the dear bonds of children, nor the harshness of any way of life, nor the frailty of the flesh, nor the pleasures of luxury. You have indeed trampled upon and bravely conquered everything, most holy women. I urge you only to apply endurance to it until the end, until you seize the prize. For, according to the Apostle, “tribulation produces endurance, endurance approval, and approval hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans V, 3–5). For love of him you endure everything and have left whatever you could have possessed as precious; moreover, united inwardly by the love of Christ, you have crucified yourselves together with your vices and desires.

Therefore the place where bones are laid after the end of life was once dedicated by our forebears in honor of the holy cross, so that the limbs that bore Christ’s cross for a long time and at length, under compulsion, might rest there buried, like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies, where the triumph of that same holy cross and its honor are exalted. Beneath the aid and protection of him who hung upon it, they will more happily germinate in the future with everlasting freshness, like the lily of paradise. Though now humbled in the dust of the earth, they will eventually rejoice and flower with Christ forever.

Always place this hope confidently in your breast, and continually moisten it with faith and tears like a heap of testimony. For these are the instruments in which the seeds of eternal verdure have blossomed. Thus, dearest women, your camp has been irreproachably dedicated, so that it may teach you to bear Christ’s military service and carry the cross after him under compulsion.

Among you the effective word of God, sharper than every two-edged sword, is active (Hebrews IV, 12); it divides the thoughts of individual hearts, like a discerner of thorns and lilies, and, stretching over them, examines how each of you loves him, how she strives to run after him, and with what forms of virtue each adorns herself according to his will.

If carnal love sometimes demands such pledges of its love from married couples—that one should desire nothing other than what the bridegroom desires—what do you think, sister, does Christ consider in his virgins, happily dedicated to him? How carefully does he consider with what virtues they may be made beautiful, with what ornaments they prepare themselves according to his will, and with what they adorn themselves inwardly? For he is altogether jealous, and “to the division of soul, joints, and marrow,” he discerns thoughts, examining everything.

For God dwells much more deeply within the soul of each one of us, sister, than the soul inhabits its own body; and therefore he does not fail to know what it thinks, since that Spirit is the Creator, while this is created. Therefore we must always pray that God’s visitation may guard our spirit, enlighten and cleanse it with the sword of the word, cut away the corruptions of our thoughts, wipe away every tickling of flesh and mind, and always gird and illuminate us with his power, so that afterward we may be able to attend to what he commands.

[Col. 1029A] Hence there follows also the Father’s voice to the Son: “Direct your course,” he says, “prosperously, advance, and reign.” In Hebrew it again has “in your beauty,” so that the sense is: “In your beauty, ascend prosperously, and gird your sword—your glory and your beauty.” With “in your beauty” read a second time, it means: “Advance prosperously.” I have said this so that no one may think there is a scribal error in the Hebrew. Rather, it is a figurative repetition of the name, in the manner of a panegyric, the kind in which rhetors and secular men speak when they exalt with praises the subject they have determined to commend.

Thus God the Father, wishing to establish his Son as leader of the human race, urges him, armed for battle with his army, to advance to war, lest he abandon the single combat once undertaken. Rather, advancing as victor over the slaughter of his enemies, let him proceed so as to prepare a kingdom for himself from those whom, rescuing from the power of the devil, he has joined to his rule, and let him say: “Yet I have been established as king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Psalm II, 6). At the time when the Prophet sang these things, Christ had not yet come, nor had he advanced to the kingdom; but now it has already happened.

Attend, therefore, to the world, and you will see that, according to the Father’s voice, he has advanced prosperously, gone forth, and now reigns, placed upon his father’s throne. What was then seen in the spirit is now seen as accomplished in reality. [1269] At that time the Prophet was proclaiming what had always been in the Father’s eternal plan; now what had been hidden has been displayed, and what was announced beforehand has come to pass. And, to speak according to the custom of singing, in accordance with the Septuagint, “he has advanced in his appearance and his beauty,” which are truth and justice, by which he is always beautiful and fair.

He advanced prosperously by himself; he advanced through holy preachers; and his kingdom has been extended and is still extended today, as all nations are subjected to him. The Gospel was therefore preached, because “truth has sprung from the earth, and justice has looked down from heaven” (Psalm LXXXIV, 12). In this truth and justice the saints of God, themselves made beautiful and fair, advancing and proceeding prosperously, planted Christ’s churches.

One of them, namely Paul, reached as far as Illyricum, and many others afterward, scattered here and there, advanced prosperously, because, secure, they subjected the world to his rule. In all these people he himself has always advanced, and his kingdom is extended everywhere, [Col. 1029D] not by anything other than himself, since he is always beautiful and fair, because he is truth and justice, himself sprung upon the earth and come from heaven.

He alone is commanded to attend in his appearance and beauty, and also to advance prosperously by himself, because he alone was found “free among the dead” (Psalm LXXXVII, 6). All the others are not beautiful and fair from themselves, because they were servants of sin, but from him by whom every Church is justified and made beautiful. Otherwise no one was found free or just.

Hence he says in the Gospel: “Then you will truly be free, if the Son makes you free” (John VIII, 36). Therefore, dearest women, let none of you attend to herself in order to please herself; let no one attend to the beauty of the flesh, no one to freedom or nobility of lineage, lest she be found ignoble [Col. 1030A] in Christ; let no one attend to knowledge, which puffs up, nor to any matter of present glory. “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians I, 31).

Hence Paul says: “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth (Galatians VI, 14). If you wish to boast, virgin, boast only in him who is the radiance of the glory of God the Father, the bridegroom of the Church, the form of beauty. Boast in him in whom there is every renewal of life, and the will of the race—that is, the newness by which we are reborn—so that, as though in the appearance and beauty of Christ, you may attend to him and ensure that the honor of heaven and the dignity of beauty are in no way defiled.

Indeed, you are a virgin: attend. You are a nun: attend. You are a widow or a holy woman: attend. Then advance prosperously from virtue to virtue, so that you may reign with him who alone advanced by his own power and gave to all the ability to advance. [Col. 1030B] He said to the bound: “Come out,” and to the blind: “Be revealed” (Isaiah XLIX, 9). [1270]

Hence follows: “Because of truth, gentleness, and justice, your right hand will lead you wondrously.” All these things are proclaimed in the head so that afterward they may be required in the body. Yet they are very different in him, because he is himself and in himself the Father’s truth—not accidental but natural—and justice. Hence he says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). And the Apostle says: “Who was made for us by God justice, and redemption, and sanctification” (1 Corinthians I, 30).

No one doubts that Christ is also shown to be gentleness, since his victory is displayed in the triumph of his servants and the disciples’ progress in the teacher’s instruction. Nevertheless, Christ is eternally truth. Therefore it is said above to him: “Attend in your appearance and your beauty,” because truth is never deceived in itself.

Finally, to be led wondrously because of gentleness is the same as to advance prosperously. For Christ’s passion and humility are the advancement and progress of all nations toward faith and the kingdom. Christ suffered, and the martyrs also suffered as members of the head. They did not fail or resist; they spoke the truth, concealed nothing, and were ready for everything, refusing nothing. Great gentleness indeed went before in the head; therefore Christ also advanced greatly toward the kingdom in them, and he still advances today.

The most gentle body of Christ does this because it learned such things from its head. For he himself was led first, like a sheep, to slaughter, so gentle that, hanging upon the cross, he said: “Father, forgive them; they do not know what they are doing” (Isaiah LIII, 7).

Therefore he brought forth, advanced, conquered, and reigns, having conquered death; and because of justice he will come to judgment and will repay each one according to his works. He himself is truth in himself, and therefore he is commanded to attend to himself.

But you, virgin of Christ, although holy, although incorrupt and undefiled, although endowed with every good thing, do not attend to yourself and do not presume upon yourself, because all these things that you have are not from yourself for yourself, but from him from whom you received the ability to have them. “If you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians IV, 7.)

It is not your right hand that leads you in these gifts, but his right hand, mercifully; and it leads him wondrously by his own right hand. The bride in the Song of Songs knew this, and therefore she says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song of Songs II, 6). For unless the bridegroom’s right hand embraces the bride, she cannot remain chaste. True chastity does not know another’s embrace or foreign kisses. [1271]

Therefore she says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs I, 1). Everything, then, that inviolate virginity knows is Christ. Therefore such and so great a bridegroom is described, in whose embraces his bride may rest secure and by whose right hand she may be led, because “the heart of the wise is in his right hand, and the heart of the fool is in his left” (Ecclesiastes X, 2).

For this reason the elect always pass to the right, while the rejected remain on the left. Hence, significantly, according to the Hebrew interpretation, instead of “your right hand will lead you wondrously,” it has “your right hand will teach you terribly.” For the teaching of heavenly life is exceedingly terrible and wondrous. Hence elsewhere in the psalm, in the person of the Lord: “Terrible in counsels above the sons of men” (Psalm LXV, 5).

By these disciplines, because the works of the Lord are terrible, every soul of a righteous man is taught and instructed by the right hand of most merciful correction.

“Your arrows are sharp; peoples will fall beneath you into the hearts of the King’s enemies.” I think that in Hebrew and also in Greek it has: “Your arrows are most powerful.” For certainly, unless the Lord’s arrows were most powerful, they would not suddenly have struck down the whole world raging against Christ, nor would they have powerfully darkened the hearts of all.

The bride declares in the Song of Songs that she has been wounded by their dart: “I am wounded by love,” she says. With this wound, dearest women, your hearts have been pierced; and therefore, having left worldly things, you have devoted yourselves so earnestly to Christ’s service for his love.

What power, dearest women, do you think it was, and what reason, that drew you, after casting aside parents and friends, brothers and relatives, and every nobility of lineage, to the heights of so laborious a life, so that for the Lord it should please you more to be afflicted by hardships than to be exalted in the world by honors and various pleasures?

It is therefore no wonder that your bridegroom has wounded you inwardly with his arrows, with “desolating coals” (Psalm CXIX, 4). These arrows are rightly called most powerful. By these arrows, surely, those were pierced and wounded who said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV, 32.)

He himself speaks of himself through Isaiah, saying: “He made me like a chosen arrow; in his quiver he hid me” (Isaiah XLIX, 2). There is no doubt that the Father protected him beneath the covering of flesh, and therefore as though beneath the shadow of his hand.

Whatever soul is wounded by this arrow is inflamed with the love of chaste devotion, and all the hardness of unbelief is dissolved. The itching of vices is boiled away; the flame of desires is driven out by the ardor of charity. Fire is conquered by fire, so that the furnace of Babylon, kindled sevenfold by unclean spirits, is extinguished.

These arrows in the hand of the Mighty One have powerfully wounded the whole world, and now the entire world lies prostrate before God. [Col. 1032A] Now the victor rules and dominates in the hearts of his enemies, because from enemies and children of wrath he has made friends for himself, whom he rules by his power and governs with most holy authority.

Happy is the heart that is daily affected by such arrows, wounded by such darts, and consumed by the fire of divine love! Such a soul is the throne of God, because, as Scripture testifies, the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.

Hence follows: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom.” In Greek, “throne” is read in place of “seat,” and in Hebrew “scepter” is found in place of “rod.”

In this passage the speech is addressed to the King who is God. Above, the Father of the bride whom he was going to take as wife commended him in his proclamations and exalted him with praises so that he might be loved all the more. He taught three things pertaining to rule by which the throne would be strengthened. Then he equipped him to defeat enemies and instructed him to overcome adversaries.

When these had been struck down and subjected to him, the throne of sovereignty and the scepter of the ruler are offered to him, according to what was written to David: “From the fruit of your womb I will place one upon my throne” (Psalm CXXXI, 11). The angel also announced this to Mary: “The Lord God will give him,” he says, “the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke I, 32).

Because the scepter had departed from Judah, it is said: “And the scepter of equity, the scepter of your kingdom.” The scepter is the insignia of the one who reigns and the visible sign of the one who rules. Hence the power of the judge is also declared through the throne.

He always possessed this throne with the Father, but it is offered to him from the time when he began to exist in the world. Therefore the form of the ruler was mentioned first, since no one is rightly considered a king except through truth, gentleness, and justice. Without these virtues, each person is proved to be a tyrant rather than a king.

Hence follows: “You have loved justice and hated iniquity.” Nothing is so proper to kings as truth and justice, and nothing so honorable as gentleness. For justice cannot be preserved when received without truth, nor can truth in judgment be fulfilled without justice.

Between these two virtues, therefore, gentleness is placed in the middle, so that truth may be chosen more diligently and calmly in affairs, and justice may be fulfilled in its own parts by preserving what belongs to each person with greater moderation. [1273] Therefore the Lord says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew XI, 29). For, as I have stated, this virtue greatly commends us to God.

When he says, “You have loved justice and hated iniquity,” this means that because of these things his right hand is wondrously raised toward the kingdom, and because of them he is now anointed above his companions when the throne of sovereignty is conveyed to him—clearly because he loved justice and hated iniquity. Likewise he is said to be anointed with the oil of justice for the kingdom. For it is not enough for anyone to love justice unless he also hates iniquity with perfect hatred. For this reason he was commanded a little earlier to gird himself with a sword, so that as avenger he might be able to restore rewards to the just and the punishment owed to sinners.

What follows—“Therefore God, your God, has anointed you”—must be understood with the first occurrence of “God” in the vocative case and the second in the nominative. For the God who is anointed is one, and the one by whom he is anointed is another.

When he says “your,” it refers to the author through whom he is anointed as king, to whom he had said: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever,” and: “The scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom.” Therefore the scepter of equity, or the rod of uprightness, is the love of justice and hatred of iniquity. By this rod all things are terribly directed in divine judgment.

Hence he says: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you.” God, then, has been anointed for the kingdom by his God because of the merit of loved justice and hated iniquity—that is, the Son by the Father.

No interval confuses our understanding here, where a distinction only between the persons is marked by the two names previously mentioned, namely “you” and “your.” It is not that the nature of the Godhead is distinguished when it says, “God has anointed you,” and then adds, “your God.” For when it says “God” and “God,” it shows one nature and one Godhead, because the God who is anointed is from the God who anoints.

And if God is from God, he is nothing other than God, as the Prophet narrates in this order: “God has anointed; your God.” This does not mean that the earlier or later God is from God, since Father and Son are one and eternal God; rather, the prophetic voice declares the mystery of the incarnation.

Otherwise, through the Prophet he says of himself: “Be witnesses for me, and I am a witness, says the Lord God, and my servant whom I chose, so that you may know and believe and understand that I am, and before me there is no other God, and after me there will not be.” Here the Father and the Son are declared, because he himself is the witness of his own word, yet in his testimony he has joined testimony about his servant whom he chose.

Their testimony is one: that there is no God before him, because all things are from him, nor will there be a God after him. He certainly does not deny that God was from him. For the servant already existed in the Father’s testimony—the servant, clearly, chosen from the tribe from which he was to be born. Hence also in the Gospel: “Behold my beloved servant, whom I chose, in whom my soul was well pleased” (Matthew XII, 18).

There is therefore no God before him and none after him, because the Son is always with him and in him, from whom he is—the eternal and unchangeable power—having weakness in this respect: that he shows no God besides himself before or afterward.

He placed his servant both in the testimony and in the name. The Father who anointed him is therefore his God, because he was born from God into God, although by this expression his assumed humanity may also be understood as taken into God.

By this statement he establishes both Father and Son in the naming of the same nature and dignity, so that both may be believed to be one God. Nevertheless, when he is said to have been anointed with the oil of exultation above his companions (Hebrews I, 9), he speaks not according to some other mystery but according to the dispensation of the assumed body.

Those who were called his brothers could not have been his companions according to the nature by which he was begotten from the Father before Lucifer; they were his companions according to the assumption by which “the Word became flesh” (John I, 14), in which he is testified to have been anointed by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Otherwise this anointing would have contributed nothing to the blessed and incorrupt birth remaining in the nature of God the Father; rather, it is shown to have benefited the sacrament of the body, so that Christ Jesus might be wholly in God.

Moreover, according to the fact that “in the beginning the Word was God, with God” (ibid., 1), there is no reason to speak of an anointing of that nature, because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and also from him, since he is the Spirit of both.

Before the dispensation of the flesh, there had been many anointed ones under the Law. But Christ, who is now anointed above his companions, is later in time; he is placed above his anointed companions because he is God and man.

Thus the Spirit of prophecy tempered the Word, so that, while God is anointed by his God, he may be both what his God is in the dispensation of anointing and what God is in nature. [1275]

Therefore know, virgin of Christ, that the Church of God recognizes in Christ a dispensation but does not recognize a division of person. It does not allow Jesus Christ to be divided into two persons, so that Jesus would not himself be Christ; nor does it distinguish the Son of Man from the Son of God, lest the Son of God perhaps not also be understood to be the Son of Man.

It does not take the Son of God into the Son of Man, nor the Son of Man into the Son of God, but says that the same Son exists in both natures. In the same person, the Word is wholly God, and Christ is wholly man. In the sacrament of its confession it retains the one reality: it believes no Christ other than Jesus, preaches no other Jesus, and proclaims nothing other than Christ.

Accordingly, in both natures there is one Christ, God, Son of God and of man, whom God anointed with the oil of exultation above his companions. There is no doubt that the oil of exultation is the Holy Spirit, as blessed Peter says: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts X, 38).

He therefore anointed him above his companions when he did not give him the Spirit by measure, in whom “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians II, 9), and in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Admiring the depth of this wisdom and knowledge, the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans XI, 33.)

The catholic faith confesses and proclaims Christ to be most high not only according to his divinity but also according to his humanity, according to the passage: “Mother Zion will say, ‘A man,’ and he himself was born in her, and he himself founded her, the Most High” (Psalm LXXXVI, 5).

Therefore, who would dare deny that he is Most High and Son of the Most High, whom God not only begot from himself as Most High, but also exalted most highly when born from the Virgin, and granted him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians II, 10)?

From this anointing of the Holy Spirit all who share in Christ are called Christians. But Christ himself, because he was anointed above all his companions, is truly called and worshiped as God, not adoptively, in both natures united in one.

Hence David says elsewhere: “His going forth is from the highest heaven.” Therefore here also: “My heart has poured forth a good word,” and: “His course reaches to its highest point” (Psalm XVIII, 7). For in the same form he wholly returned from which he had emptied himself in order to receive the form of a servant.

Thus blessed Ambrose says in a certain hymn:

> His going forth is from the Father,  
> his return is to the Father,  
> his journey is even to the underworld,  
> his return to the seat of God.

And this is the seat, dearest women, which he possessed before the foundation of the world and which is offered at the end of time, because in both there is one Christ, one God, one bridegroom of the Church—or, so to speak, one husband of virgins, God the Son of God—to whom, as a demonstration of his betrothal, the following is added.

[Col. 1035B] “Myrrh and drop and cassia are from your garments, from ivory houses, from which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor.”

In place of “drop,” some have translated “myrrh,” others “stacte.” Cassia is the same substance that is elsewhere called “cane” or “cinnamon-stick.” I have no doubt that you, holy women of Christ, know these substances and virtues more fully, since they are the aromatics of virtues that you offer daily as a sacrifice to the Lord King, having put to death your members upon the earth; hence you are a good odor to God and to all people.

You know that in the title I found it written “for flowers” or “for lilies”; therefore I have chosen to write this from the psalm for you. It follows that you offer yourselves first to God as myrrh, for an odor of sweetness, so that I may explain at greater length something about these substances in which you continually devote yourselves to works, in order to please the bridegroom in every respect.

Those who have written about the properties of aromatics report that stacte is a flower of myrrh, although others have called it an ammoniacal drop. No one doubts that it is a flower of excellent quality, although there appears to be a great difference between one myrrh and another. One kind flows from the tree like dew; another is extracted through incisions and various tortures, or is prepared elsewhere for the odor of incense.

Therefore Scripture most fittingly calls you, virgins of Christ, “first” or “chosen myrrh,” because you carry the Lord’s mortification in your body. Cassia, or cane, by its heat boils away all the phlegms and rheums of pleasures in you until they are completely purified, and wipes away every itch of vice.

For what is written in certain copies as “drop” or “stacte” has “aloes” in Hebrew. Hence Nicodemus prepared a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes for the Lord’s burial. Therefore the bridegroom speaks to the bride in the Song of Songs about these things: “Myrrh and aloe, with all the finest perfumes.” And she replies: “My hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of most proven myrrh” (Song of Songs IV, 14).

Here the Holy Spirit shows that these aromatics are examples of the virtues of virgins. For the forms of earthly things seem to demonstrate to us judgments concerning heavenly virtues. What else could we know about that majesty unless the divine word made something of it known to us through such likenesses?

Therefore, dearest women, cast away the works of death. Buried with Christ in baptism and consecrated to the Lord beneath the veil of betrothal as a dowry, you are dead to this world; think of nothing other than heavenly things. Speak to your bridegroom, each one of you; speak, all of you: “My hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of most proven myrrh” (Psalm CXV, 15), because “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”

It is not only death, therefore, but also the mortification of the flesh. You have mortified your members in the world for the love of Christ; rejoice and exult, because your reward remains glorious in heaven with the saints.

This mortification first flowed from the Lord’s garments; therefore you have followed him so vigorously after the fragrance of his perfumes. The Lord’s garment was his mortal body, because just as the limbs of mortals are covered by clothing, so the majesty of the Word was concealed from unbelieving eyes by the veil of flesh.

From this garment—the mystery of the incarnation—these three substances are appropriately said to have come: myrrh, drop, and cassia. The Church greatly rejoices that you have learned to work with these gifts, for you anoint the Lord’s body daily; and because he was stripped and hung upon the cross, you clothe his nakedness with your faith.

You reject the scandals of the Jews and the foolishness of the nations through a confession full of words, knowing that “the Lord has reigned from the wood.” Therefore, with the Lord’s favor, you now put on the grace of the cross with him, in which you have learned, in deepest faith, to glory with the Apostle Paul.

[Col. 1036C] If you truly consider the matter, you too are now the Lord’s garment, to whose edge that perfume has reached which descended from the head into Aaron’s beard (Psalm CXXXII, 2). Christ was indeed anointed with the oil of exultation and the perfume of the Holy Spirit above all his companions (Hebrews I, 9), because in him the entire fountain of anointing flowed from his divinity into his humanity, in one and the same Christ.

Then, as though from the beard, which is the mark of masculine maturity, it flowed through all the members of the churches, which are his body and garment, even to the furthest parts. In that body, dearest women, you are above all the adornment of the garments, in whom this perfume of blessing has flowed forth, because you are Christ’s most precious members in the body.

I shall tell you, matrons of Christ, something new, confirmed by the authority of the Scriptures. You are Christ’s garment because by your confession and works you have adorned him, and again you have put him on yourselves. Hence the Apostle exhorts: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans XIII, 14).

Put on Christ, I beg you, dearest women, more fully and perfectly, because Christ first deigned to clothe you in his own body. It is therefore clear that just as there are different kinds of Christ’s garments, so there are different fragrant perfumes.

For this reason the Holy Spirit has signified these three for you in particular—myrrh, drop, and cassia—so that in all the perfumes of the garments the Trinity, God, may be sensed in complete faith and smelled in perfect understanding here and now.

If you attend carefully, virgin, from the beginning of this psalm the Trinity of things is declared in each verse. Therefore here too he chose only three kinds of perfume from among them all. In these aromatics he proclaimed the virtue of good works and the grace of faith.

Cassia, moreover, if it is boiled in oil while it is in flower, is said to produce from itself a very fragrant perfume, so that through it the power of Christ’s holy incarnation and the sweetness of perpetual blessing may rightly be understood as perfuming all things.

Therefore the bride says in the Song of Songs: “We shall run after you into the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song of Songs I, 4). You too, then, holy virgins, run—how well you run after various perfumes, after the fragrance of the bridegroom, yourselves anointed with the most precious perfumes.

Therefore, dearest women, as I said, you are now a good odor in every place and in every affair of life. This fragrance of aromatics, by God’s gracious ordering, is believed to come to you from the ivory houses, just as it comes from the garments. [1279]

From these [houses], he says—so that “from these spices” may be understood—“the daughters of kings have loved you in your honor.” But “from the houses” is found neither in the Hebrew nor in the Greek, as blessed Jerome testifies, although he himself translated it thus. Indeed, the Greek has ἀπὸ βαρέων, as does the Hebrew. In Greek, a house is rather called οἶκος, whereas βαρύς means “heavy.” Hence we read that some translated ἀπὸ βαρέων as “from the heavy things,” deceived by the ambiguity of the word.

According to the particular usage of the province of Palestine, however, βαρύς denotes a kind of house enclosed on every side, built in the form of a tower and resembling public fortifications, which were sometimes clad in ivory. Therefore it has rightly been translated by all as “ivory,” because buildings of this kind were houses adorned with ivory. Let us accordingly apply these houses not only to the riches of the homeland but also to the virtues of souls. For the elephant, whose bones these are, is said to possess exceptional chastity and to be endowed with greater intelligence than all quadrupeds. It also uses marriage temperately, as they say, and does not take a second female. This is rightly applied not only to the most chaste men but also to women.

Thus those are known to have dwelt in ivory houses who, through purity of mind and body, preserved Christ’s commandments and loved only monogamy. From such houses, therefore, and in such houses, not only is monogamy guarded with the utmost chastity, but true widowhood is also practiced; moreover, incorrupt virginity is clothed in the whiteness of ivory. These ancient spices of the virtues are proclaimed to diffuse their fragrance everywhere for Christ God and for all as an odor of sweetness. Finally, when that fragrance is scattered in turn from the garments and from the ivory houses, the whole house—which is the Church of the living God—is filled with the odor of sweetness.

And although there is one house and one spouse, she nevertheless has many dwellings and houses built together, in which Christ will be fully known when he receives them into unity. Among these houses, surely, you are the matrons of Christ: you are that βαρύς—that is, that kind of house—built in the form of a tower, together with its fortifications and armor of virtues, made from ancient ivory and adorned with perpetual chastity.

You are the daughters of kings who make the bridegroom glad in your beauty, in his honor. For your bridegroom himself is the Lord of lords; therefore he has many kings under him, whose daughters you are. Drawn by their fragrances and teachings, you have indeed been steeped in their ointments and adorned with their flowers. For under so great a king there are many lesser kings and princes, whose daughters you are—and they are themselves your fathers, since through Christ’s Gospel they gave you birth. You have been filled with their teachings and nourished by their instructions, so that you are both the house of God and brides and daughters.

For this reason, dearest ones, you have made the bridegroom glad in all your garments, because your garments are the virtues of your souls, in all the fragrances of good works, so that you may please him to whom you have vowed yourselves. For he is more beautiful than the sons of men, nobler than all, chosen from among thousands, more gracious than everyone, more powerful than all, higher than the heavens, deeper than the depths, broader than the world, and longer than the ages. There is nothing in him, virgin, for which you should be ashamed; let no disgust with goodness estrange you from the good.

Therefore, bride of Christ, rejoice in the Lord—not in yourself or in another, but in the honor of your bridegroom. For thus the Father says to the Son: “The daughters of kings have loved you in your honor” (Ps. XXXVI, 4). Otherwise, unless the bridegroom is loved in his glory, praise, and honor, he rejects any love by which something other than himself is loved.

Therefore, if there is a woman who loves to commit adultery, it must be feared that she may be called not a daughter of kings, not the bride of the king, but an adulteress—one who loves something other than God, or loves something in God or for God’s sake. Hence David says: “You have destroyed everyone who fornicates away from you” (Ps. LXXII, 27).

Then the true chastity of the bride is such that she knows neither adulterous fragrances nor kisses nor embraces. Rather, the daughter of kings continually prepares herself for Christ’s marriage and delights in his embraces. Therefore she runs after the fragrance of his ointments, whose scent diffuses and scatters itself throughout the whole world. Accordingly, he is sometimes loved through the garments with which he is clothed; and from the ivory houses, through an everlasting covenant, he is loved whose throne is forever and ever.

Strive, then, in turn, with God’s help, to make such fragrances of the virtues shine forth everywhere in the world. Such is the effect of the fragrance of the ointments, so that, inwardly purified by such ointments, you may be able to enter happily into the wedding prepared for you with lamps adorned—for those who are ready, as Christ testifies, will enter with him into the wedding.

Since prayer now demands the conclusion of the book, I ask those who read this little work of love, which I have dedicated to sacred virgins out of love for Christ, not to despise it before testing it; for what belongs to charity can be read well only from the fountain of charity. Therefore I ask that they not judge me in eloquence, nor compare any drop, however small, with great rivers. I must be judged not by the talents of great men but by my own strength, since the authority of those whom I have followed always lives on in greatness.

And therefore the mind must sometimes be restored with greater security, so that at last we may be able to raise ourselves more clearly, with lamps kindled, to contemplate the queen at the right hand of the virtue of God.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1039]

It is known to all that holy Moses received the two tablets of the covenant of the Testament, both written by the finger of God. On them the earlier Synagogue was joined in covenant to the Lord as wife from Mount Sinai. So also, in this nuptial song, as though two pages of tablets were alternately subscribed with the marriage covenant, they have been written out by the stylus of a rapidly writing secretary. One of them has its origin from the Father and the nature of the Word; it praises the bridegroom’s noble birth and appearance, depicts the beauty of his form, magnifies his virtues, and multiplies the gifts of blessing forever.

Thus, by a wondrous account of the marriage-bed between the two pages, it describes both the man and the bride. This figure is called in Greek characterismos, and in Latin informatio or descriptio—“formation” or “description.” For it brings before the eyes of the understanding things that are not seen by bodily sight, as though they were visible.

In this passage, through the armor of warfare, it commends him greatly, exalting him in virtue and power, until he unquestionably lays the kingdom low by his strength and subjects his enemies to his rule. Then it adorns his judicial character with praise. His throne and the scepter of equity are recounted, and his power is glorified. Finally, as though on the first tablet, it shows from where the bride’s wondrous beauty and immeasurable fragrance come.

This is done because the discourse concerns a wedding and the joy of a wedding, lest the fragrances be lacking among the mysterious gifts of sweetest things, by which the delight of souls is greatly pleased. Everything has been narrated in such a way that no possibility of further praise remains, since above all the sons of men, and beyond all others in every respect, the bridegroom is praised.

Thus he passes, as it were, to the second tablet of the wedding, in which he begins by saying to this same bridegroom: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold, surrounded by variety.” Here he adorns the wife’s form with almost the same features, dedicating her as queen to his Son, because she loved the kingly God, as has been shown, and the heavenly man.

Therefore, having first praised the throne of the most gracious Savior, he says that this queen and wife stands at his right hand, because the right hand is, so to speak, the more honorable part of the bridegroom, who is acknowledged to be the head of the Church. The Prophet—or rather, the pen of the scribe and the Father’s tongue—runs through all the lines of praise with which the bridegroom is praised. Accordingly, she too is placed at the divine right hand, adorned with mystical riddles and precious virtues, just as Christ has been exalted to the Father’s right hand.

Nevertheless, he is to be worshiped with the Father as God and King; she, however, is honored and loved on his account, because the merciful Savior graciously took her as his wife. She is loved because she was chosen first.

Therefore, most beloved women, as I reflect on your excellence, as I consider the rights of your betrothal and the divine praises everywhere, I fear to speak, lest I offend precisely where I desire to please, if I do not show the reverence due to you throughout my writings. I understand you to be honored in heaven, where you have given your names, so that you are not only brides but also flowers of the Church and the bridegroom’s adornment.

When I behold you adorned with manifold variety at the right hand of our most gracious God and Savior Christ, I groan deeply, because the crown that I received as a little boy before the holy altar of the Mother of God, together with your prayers and the ministry of praise by which your hearts and heads are consecrated to God, the immortal King and bridegroom, I lost after a long exile in the world, stained by many worldly deeds.

Therefore, wounded, I ask that, while you lift your hearts upward, you remember me in prayer before the divine grace already granted to you, so that through your merits as intercessors the most merciful Judge may remove from me the punishments I deserve and, in his goodness, restore the lost crown. For it is not unfitting for Christ’s brides to ask their gracious bridegroom for such things; nor is it at all unfitting or impossible for him mercifully to forgive sinners for whom he suffered.

But lest a virgin perhaps hesitate to pray for such things, let her know that she herself was taken from the shameful prostitution of infidelity, so that she might attain such great grace as to be called not only a faithful wife but also a queen.

Hence blessed Jerome, according to the Hebrew truth, says: “The wife stood at your right hand.” The Septuagint, however, said, “The queen stood”; but Symmachus and the fifth edition have: “The concubine stood.” These interpreters show that in one and the same bride, just as there is one bridegroom, so there is one Church but different orders of merit.

Then, where the Septuagint said, “In a garment of gold,” Jerome says: “The wife stood at your right hand, in a golden diadem.”

She is therefore rightly said to stand with a diadem, because she is proclaimed the king’s wife. But perhaps this does not seem to apply to all the members, since it is attributed to the head of the body. Therefore, dearest ones, I would call you happy, since not only is a crown of virginity promised to each of you individually, but you are also inserted into the very crown of Christ and the Church as most precious gems, and are its beauty and adornment.

For in Aaron’s diadem upon his head, we read that precious stones shone. In his priesthood, therefore, Christ’s crown and the Church’s crown are already prefigured. For this reason I would rightly call you happy, matrons of Christ, because you are already in God’s presence, as though predestined and chosen for the workmanship of Christ’s and the Church’s beauty.

Hence blessed Paul says: “He chose us before the foundation of the world” (Eph. I, 4). And because you have been chosen for the chastity of purity, there is no doubt that you will remain either in virginity or in widowhood. Remain, I ask, worthily in that calling to which you have been called. For you did not choose him; your bridegroom Christ chose you from the world and gathered you in this place, so that you might please him and be for the praise and glory of his name, just as he himself is the praise, glory, virtue, and honor of God the Father.

For you have been called for this purpose: to possess worthily the things that belong to Christ. This is the victory of the lilies and the triumph of the flowers, so that you may be the beauty and adornment of the body of the Church.

Symmachus, however, says “in pure gold”; Aquila and the fifth edition, as we have found them, say: “In the coloring, or gold, of Ophir.” From all these versions, as I have said, it is clear that there is one Catholic Church, one perfect and intimate dove, although she stands at the right hand of God’s virtue and has nothing on the left. Just as the members of one body are diverse, so she possesses different kinds of forms and adornments.

Thus, regarding the words “in a garment of gold”: because the saints are always raised toward higher and heavenly things, they are surrounded, as it were, by a gilded garment when they understand divine things from the human meanings of Scripture and seek heavenly realities. In these gilded garments, clothed in the splendor of divine speech, they go forth gloriously, as though in pure gold.

As for the words “in the coloring, or gold, of Ophir,” which some have interpreted in this way, they indicate the Church’s marvelous variety and the appearance of adornments of different colors. The Septuagint, understanding this well, alone added “surrounded by variety,” which is not found in the Hebrew. Yet it shows that neither the Church nor any soul possesses this beauty and loveliness by nature, but by the gift of grace.

Therefore she is praised no less for being clothed in a gilded garment than for being surrounded by the variety of colors. For he did not say “in a golden garment” but “in a gilded garment.” We call something gilded when a layer of gold is bonded onto some kind of metal; and by this charity is rightly understood. For the remaining virtues, with which Christ’s garment or the Church is woven, possess little or no brightness or splendor in themselves without charity. The Apostle makes this sufficiently clear when he says: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIII, 1), and so forth in what he says there.

From this the meaning is clear: all kinds of virtues, if they are to possess splendor and the beauty of glory, must be gilded and overlaid with love of God and neighbor. For the splendor of charity surpasses all virtues and shines forth above them all with its own radiance.

If some distinction of charity is also shown in the pure gold of Ophir, we must understand that charity is ordered. Hence the bride says in the Song: “Order charity in me” (Cant. II, 4). For there is a charity that scarcely gives even its means of subsistence as food to the poor; and there is one that gives even its life for the brethren. Concerning this the Savior says: “No one has greater charity than that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John XV, 13). Therefore, unless there were a lesser charity, this would not be called greater; and unless there were a second or last kind, this would not be called first.

Of this the angel of the Church says in the Apocalypse: “I have this against you, that you have abandoned your first charity” (Rev. II, 4). Therefore, even within these same virtues there is great diversity, and, as though through a variety of colors, there is a manifold and varied adornment of merits.

Yet the one Church is called one wife and queen; there is one fabric of virtues and one garment, in which everything is simple and one. But variety and beauty are praised within that very unity of faith, because of the difference of virtues and merits, the diversity of languages, the particularity of each, the ascent of degrees, the multiplicity and distinction of churches and orders, and also the differing sounds of those who sing psalms and of the offices, although the praise is one. In all these things the one and manifold Church is rightly proclaimed with varied praise.

She is adorned as though with the first gold of the apostles; she shines with the silver of the prophets, as though in the pallor of gold, glorious within and without (Ps. LXVII, 14). She is illumined with the gems of virgins among the remaining splendors, as though with stars. Then, reddened by martyrs, like scarlet dyed twice, she is adorned with embroidered and pictorial workmanship. The purple of penitents, as though changed from sackcloth, is transformed into the adornment and beauty of the wife.

This wife, or queen, is said to stand before God because the bridegroom still stands in battle, although he possesses the throne of empire, until all his enemies are subjected and hostile death is destroyed according to the Apostle, and he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, who subjected all things to him, so that thereafter God may be all in all.

Up to this point, then, this garment is woven; this wife and queen is gathered together. Meanwhile, having already been placed at the right hand because of grace, in the place that is with God, she too must fight courageously, girded with weapons.

Therefore the same bridegroom says to Moses, his servant: “But you, stand here with me.” He commands him to stand with him for this purpose, lest he fall. Hence the Apostle also says: “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X, 12).

But no one stationed in battle can stand idle lest he fall, because either he strikes—not as one beating the air—or he is struck more severely by the enemy and thrown down.

But how happy you are, dearest ones, who have deserved both to enter into marriage with Christ and to become an adornment of beauty in the Church’s garments. Hence, as I said above, this entire Psalm concerns the flowers and the lilies, and is wholly sung in praise of virgins.

Happy, I say, are you who have separated yourselves from the works of the world, rejected everything that belongs to the age, and vowed yourselves to God alone. Therefore, since you have already been established at God’s right hand, near him, for battle, I ask you to accustom yourselves to fight with the weapons with which your bridegroom and teacher of all taught you by word and displayed to you by example.

Let no one here, even though the barriers seem fortified and shut, rest securely or be overcome by pride. For the devil found in heaven itself a place in which to sin, from which he first fell; then in paradise he deceived the human being.

Therefore, in the person of the Father, he speaks to one woman in such a way that all are addressed: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house.” It is a remarkable thing: he calls her “daughter” while commanding her to forget another father.

From this it is plainly evident that although she had been born in the flesh to another, she had already been reborn in the Spirit to the one who urges and commands her to forget her people and father. And because she was reborn, she was therefore joined in marriage; because she was joined in marriage, she was therefore queen; and because she was queen, she was therefore exalted at the right hand.

Nevertheless, she is the queen who is also the daughter. And just as she is one queen among all, so she is also one daughter. She is a daughter because she was reborn and adopted; she is wife and queen because she had taken as bridegroom the King, the Son of the King. Through him she now gives birth in faith to many sons for God.

She is established at the right hand, where the place of the blessed is, and is warned by the Father that, as I have said, the time for battle still remains. Some say that from the beginning of the Psalm up to this verse the voice is that of the Prophet. But this seems hardly to fit; rather, for this reason it is believed to be the voice of the Father, or of the Holy Spirit through the Prophet.

From this point, they say, the voice of the Father is first introduced as speaking. Yet what we have explained as spoken in the person of the Father—I do not say is discordant, but seems to fit everything better. Some teachers also affirm this, and we have followed them. Nevertheless, neither view departs from the truth, whatever either of them may have said; rather, a broader meaning is opened through all of them.

Meanwhile, the Father’s voice, just as above concerning the bridegroom, now teaches and instructs the bride more gently. He openly calls her daughter because, by a personal and eternal covenant, she has married his Son.

“Hear, daughter,” he says, as though he were plainly saying: Hear carefully what the prophets taught from this marriage, and now see all things fulfilled in works, whatever has been foretold concerning them.

It should be noted that, just as above in the praise of the bridegroom he often joined three things together, so here he has now joined three. First he said: “Hear.” For this is the discipline of all who desire to be instructed: that they listen carefully. Then he said: “See.” For whatever one hears, it remains to understand; otherwise, if you have not understood, what benefit is there in hearing?

Just as each person sees bodily things with the eyes of the body, so one sees divine things entirely through understanding. For just as the body sees through the eyes and bodies are seen, so the soul sees itself through itself, and through understanding it also sees spiritual things.

When he says, “Hear, daughter,” there is a great mystery of piety: she who had been the daughter of the devil because of idolatry and blindness of heart is called the daughter of God the Father. Therefore, when he adds “see,” it should be read with complete rejoicing of heart, as though he were saying: See, for the bridegroom who was promised to you for so long has arrived; in him are true love, glory, virtue, power, and every joy.

Then follows: “Incline your ear.” Here he teaches the humility of hearing and makes known that the words of divine speech, or the teachings of teachers, must be heard reverently—not with an exalted heart, nor with disgust or sluggishness of spirit, but with a devoted mind and the ears of the heart.

Hence the Lord says: “Let him who has ears for hearing hear” (Matt. XI, 15). Therefore, so that the mind may always be ready to hear the word of God, he commands it to be prepared and always brought down into humility. And lest its former vices or its badly accustomed secular pursuits, through the worst of habits, should make the mind perversely deaf so that it could not hear freely, he says: “Forget your people and your father’s house.”

Hence someone says: “We ought to pass by the song of the Sirens with deaf ears.” But long ago it was said to Abraham: “Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Gen. XII, 1).

You too, dearest ones, because you are his daughters, have done this in imitation of so great a father. Under Christ’s leadership, you have gone out from the land of your birth, from houses and fields, and also from whatever possessions of the Lord you could have had in the world.

You have gone out from all kinship according to the flesh, and for love of eternal life you have submitted yourselves to Christ’s yoke, which is exceedingly gentle for those who love him. You have taken up the burden that is light for those who desire it, and you have chosen the Lord himself, the most gracious Savior, as your bridegroom.

Indeed, he himself chose you and appointed you to preserve the gift of grace that you received. May you flourish in mind and in virtues, and bear fruit in works, so that your fruit may remain in tribulation.

For this purpose you chose this place, dedicated to you by the Lord, even though it is narrow, because “narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life” (Matt. VII, 14). You did not choose, so to speak, a place, but Christ the bridegroom, of the whole Church and of yourselves.

His possession is therefore not merely the whole world that you have trampled underfoot, but the entire immense inheritance of Christians, that heavenly Jerusalem, concerning which and for which this Psalm is sung to you here, as though in the title of a dowry.

In that inheritance, the bride and wife now stands not only at the right hand of God, but is also said to reign as queen with the diadem upon her head.

And lest an unbelieving mind say, “This crown is not for me; one crown is promised collectively to all,” know, sister, that what will be given to all who deserve it will not be denied to one person—provided that you are with all and incorporated with all into Christ, a garden of delights, a fountain sealed with the seal of faith, and enclosed by the protection of charity (Cant. IV, 12).

That is, within the holy Church of God you are dedicated to the Lord more by your vow than, during the time of your life, you are badly confined and constricted by necessity within this Vesona.

Therefore, sister, I ask you to beware lest this Suession in which you dwell become a persuasion to you, and lest you begin—God forbid—with an apostate mind, since you are no longer permitted to flee from here bodily.

Rather, hear your Lord, the Father of your bridegroom, who adopted you as a daughter and sent you his own virgin Son, born from a Virgin, as your bridegroom through the Virgin’s womb, so that you might remain his bride and virgin, queen and wife.

Hear what he says: “Forget your people and your father’s house.” Hence in the Gospel the Lord also says: “Allow the dead to bury their dead; but you, follow me” (Luke IX, 60).

It should be noted that he said “forget,” and did not merely command her to abandon them bodily, because what is forgotten is retained by no affection of the heart. In this forgetting, the devil and the whole offspring of vices that belong to the devil are erased from the hearts of the faithful.

That the devil is the father of unbelievers, the Lord testifies to the Jews: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII, 44).

Therefore, faithful virgin, if you have forgotten your ancient father and have shown yourself in such a way, laying aside the filth of vices, that you may ascend, whitened, above your bridegroom and brother, such as God the Son can love: Then God the Father says: “The king will desire your beauty.”

Do not think that he is one among the crowd or among the number of the other kings by whom you are to be loved. Know that he is your King and your Lord God. For the other kings, although they are lords or kings because they exercise power, are nevertheless of the same condition or nature as those over whom they rule and reign.

But because this one is God, I command you: worship him. For the Hebrew truth has it thus: “Worship him.”

The Septuagint, however, did not say “worship him” but “they will worship him,” so that the sense may be: This one who will love you, who will love your beauty and your loveliness, is God and Lord and is to be worshiped by all. Therefore you too, daughter, worship him, although by his condescension he is said to be your bridegroom or brother.

From this the Catholic faith is evident: the whole Christ, namely God and man, is to be worshiped and honored as God. He is not divided in persons or confused in substances, but the whole and one Christ is to be worshiped as the true God.

He is not the adoptive Son of God or the titular son of man, as someone recently presumed wickedly, ignorant of the mystery of God. Rather, in both natures he is wholly and truly Christ, true God and true man.

In his divinity and humanity alike, he is the only-begotten and true Son of God, one true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit. And, as I have said, he is not titular in his human nature and true in his divine nature, nor proper Son of God in his divine nature and adoptive in his human nature, so that the one person of the Son might be divided with Nestorius into two persons—that is, the true Son of God and an adoptive son.

Rather, the whole Christ is one true God and true man; he is truly and wholly the Son of God, and truly and wholly the son of man. Hence blessed Mary is proclaimed Catholicly the Mother of God and true bearer of God.

Christ’s person is not divided when he is called the Son of God, nor when he is called the son of man, but he is one and the same Son of God and man.

Therefore, the Son of God was not a titular God born from the blessed Virgin, nor was Christ the man an adoptive Son of God. Rather, he is believed to be the true and proper Son of God the Father, because Christ is one, not divided into two sons. He is not called putative, adoptive, or titular, but wholly true, wholly perfect, God and man, Son of God and son of man.

Therefore he did nothing exclusively in the human nature, nor anything exclusively in the divine nature. Hence the Lord is truly said to have suffered and died in the mystery. For although he is immortal and incapable of suffering, to unfold one point among many, he is also said to have been buried.

Speaking of the woman, he says: “By pouring this ointment on my body, she has done it for my burial” (Matt. XXVI, 12). You hear, then, that what was poured upon his body was done for his burial.

Although, therefore, “to be himself” is not the same as “to be his body,” and “to be made for burying himself” is not the same as “to anoint his body,” nevertheless, it is by no means fitting to say that his body is one thing and that he himself is buried. Rather, this belongs to an understanding of the mystery of divinity: not to be ignorant of the God whom you know to be man, nor to fail to know the man whom you do not fail to recognize as God.

Therefore, from all the passages of Scripture we must gather that the most gracious Jesus Christ is one undivided person, God and man, whether he is called God, man, dead, or buried. For “the Word became flesh” (John I, 14).

Nor, when it is said here, “For he is the Lord your God; worship him,” is a newly introduced God meant. Hence it is said: “Israel, if you will hear me, there shall be no new God among you.” Therefore we worship no other and no one other than the proper Son of God.

I have said this because it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Matt. IV, 10). Just as we are commanded to serve him alone, so also we are to worship him alone.

Let there not be those who doubt that Christ’s humanity is to be worshiped as God, especially since here the prophecy, speaking with the Father’s voice, commands the whole Church whom Christ took as his bride, according to the Hebrew truth: “Since he is the Lord your God, worship him.” Or, according to the Septuagint, since all the sons of the Church are addressed, it is said: “They will worship him.”

Some, however, wished to apply the words “They will worship him” to the following verse concerning the daughters of Tyre; the Hebrew truth does not permit this.

When he says, “The King will desire your beauty,” or “your appearance,” it is as though he were saying: If you remain in the condition of the covenant and not in the lot of the devil in which you had been placed, then, because you are beautiful, because you are lovely, because you are immaculate, the King will desire your appearance.

It is as though he were saying: The King, my beloved Son, to whom this Psalm is sung, to whom I speak all my works, who is beautiful beyond the sons of men, and all the other things that are praised concerning him—this such and so great a King desires your appearance, which he himself made beautiful.

He does not desire it because he found it beautiful, since you were foul when the invading devil held you; rather, behold, you have been made beautiful.

The praise then proceeds through almost the same lines of praise that he had set forth above concerning the bridegroom, although in a gentler manner. For he is said to be beautiful in his own appearance; she, however, is beautiful and lovely because the Lord joined her to himself in marriage.

Thus, just as the bridegroom was beautiful in his own appearance from the beginning, so she too is praised as beautiful because she ascended, whitened.

Concerning her, even the angelic powers marvel in the Song: “Who is this who ascends through the desert, rising like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arranged for battle?” (Cant. VI, 9).

Therefore, dearest ones, your virginity is exceedingly happy and blessed; happy also is your holy widowhood, which ascends daily in such a way that it stands at the right hand of God, and stands girded with heavenly weapons so that it may ascend.

Thus, under monastic discipline, which is the warfare of men, any one of you is sufficient to fight alone, with one hand or one arm, as though in single combat, armed with the weapons of the virtues.

Your holy society is the first battle line in the King’s procession, ascending like the dawn of a new day. Beautiful in face and lovely, because you have trampled the filth of the flesh and the deceits of the world, you ascend after Christ, like an army arranged for battle, and take up the yoke of youth.

Who would not marvel, most beloved ones, at the beauty of your religious life? Who would not marvel that the fragile sex advances with such a single force toward the heights, so that while still within the world it already appears, through its virtues, to be outside the flesh and outside the world?

It is therefore no wonder that the King, the Son of God the Father, desired your appearance, since he himself restored in you his image and likeness.

Hence follows: “The daughters of Tyre will entreat your face with gifts; all the rich of the people.”

In the Hebrew it reads: “O daughter of the mighty one, with gifts the rich of the people will entreat your face.” For the Hebrew word Sor can be interpreted as both “Tyre,” “tribulation,” and “the mighty one” or “the mighty woman.” Hence disagreement has arisen among translators in the present passage.

Jerome, however, following Symmachus, translated it “Daughter of the mighty one,” so that she to whom he had said above, “Hear, daughter, and see,” may be understood as the daughter of the mighty Father; or else she herself may be understood as mighty, according to Solomon: “Who will find a strong woman?” (Prov. XXXI, 10).

She is called strong because she placed all her strength in Christ when she says: “I will guard my strength for you” (Ps. LVIII, 10). Concerning her the bridegroom says in the Song: “Your love has become strong as death” (Cant. VIII, 6).

Meanwhile, according to the Septuagint, “The daughters of Tyre will entreat the face of the Church with gifts,” because the Church began first from the Jews, so that she is the one whose beauty the King desires.

Here there is a second mode of praise: just as he had said to the bridegroom, “Direct your attention, prosper, proceed, reign,” so here the dignity and glory of the Church are commended when the devout people, coming to her, entreat her face in the confession of faith. Her face is the knowledge, practice, and beauty of true religion.

That glory and honor are said to come from the bride’s worship of Christ is therefore made clear. Thus Tyre is a city formerly situated in the midst of the sea, not far from Jerusalem, about which Isaiah speaks much as a figure of the whole Church.

Among other things he says: “Her profits will be consecrated to the Lord” (Isa. XXIII, 18). Therefore, by the daughters of this city, which is wholly tossed upon the waves of this age, he means the souls of the faithful, or particular churches founded in Christ throughout different places. For it was not Tyre alone that sent faithful daughters to the Church; rather, the united diversity of the whole world has rushed toward her.

Among these is Vesona as well, the city in which you dwell. Formerly she played the harlot after idols of fornication, but she comes with gifts and has become faithful—she who had been the daughter of the most powerful devil. And, as you can see, just as Isaiah said, her revenues are now sanctified to the Lord: for she shines, filled throughout with churches, and has become the possession of the most devoted Savior—she who had been the daughter of perdition and the spoil of the destroyer.

For to her east she now has the camp of monks, together with her holy confessors and martyrs; but to the west, as though behind you, the trumpet of the holy Gospel resounds in the voice of one admonishing. Thus it comes about that no place is deprived of heavenly gifts in which you are established. You, however, established as though in the midst, chose only one corner of narrow Soissons, because you loved that cornerstone which was made for you by God the Father as the foundation at the head of the corner (Ps. CXVII, 22).

If you look carefully, there rises there that tower from the Gospel of which it is said: “And you, tower of the misty flock of the daughter of Zion, to you shall come the former dominion, the kingdom of the daughter of Jerusalem” (Mic. IV, 8). For although your bridegroom Christ was born in that little city called Bethlehem, near which, at his birth, the angels sang, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14), nevertheless that former dominion which was once promised to it has reached you also, dearest ones.

There can be no doubt that it has reached you, because Christ himself chose and raised you up as a mirror and protection for the whole city, so that this place may rightly be called “the tower of the illustrious, misty flock.” In this flock the Savior himself has become the shepherd. Here, we believe, the descending and ascending angels sing “Glory to God in the highest,” and peace of good will continually flourishes and rests more abundantly among you.

Here the guard of vigils and the observance of virtues are unceasingly carried out; here praise and rejoicing, insofar as mortality permits, never cease; here prayers, groans, and tears daily strike heaven and flow with every force of love toward God; here vows and gifts of thanksgiving are offered to God.

Therefore, although that [vineyard] which the wicked cultivate was called misty or desolate, because they killed the householder and cultivated it, you, because you have set up the tower in the midst and raised Christ—the winepress, that is, the altar—in your hearts, will not lack the help of angels, according to what David says: “The Angel of the Lord will encamp” (Ps. XXXIII, 8)—that is, the angel of the great counsel—“around those who fear him, and he will deliver them.”

For unless the Lord guards you, narrow Soissons, being very small and ruined within the circuit of its walls, will save you from no enemy. Therefore place your confidence in this all the more, because the former dominion has reached you. This dominion is the kingdom of the daughter of Jerusalem, for “the kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII, 21); and his rule and principality have reached you—he who said: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last” (Rev. I, 8).

You also have, to the south and in view of the east, the holy martyrs of God, your patrons, Crispinus and Crispinianus, reddened by their own blood and whitened by the blood of Christ. They founded this city in the faith and rescued it from the precipice of death. Now it flourishes so greatly in Christ that it appears full of lilies and roses, for which this Psalm is sung.

Indeed, your holy martyrs are sweetly fragrant roses, dearest ones; and you are lilies, from which the whole city shines on every side and the angels rejoice. These, then, are the gifts that are shown to be exceedingly pleasing to the divinity: Vesona, once dedicated to demons, now consecrated to God and joined to the angels, sends them to Christ.

All look toward her face and, as the Psalm sings, entreat her; likewise, with gifts, all the wealthy of the peoples of Gaul do so, because they rejoice that they have gathered lilies from roses. The wealthy who venerate and entreat the Church of Christ in all good works are religious men, or the wealthy who are called wise men of the world, trained in the disciplines of the philosophers. Assisted by their eloquence, the Church flourished greatly at the beginning, together with signs and wonders.

There were also wealthy men to whom the utterances of God were first entrusted, possessing knowledge of God’s Testament, and understanding of the prophets and of the heavenly mysteries. Among them, Paul and Apollo were first compelled, along with very many others, to bring numerous gifts. Through these the Church from the nations was enriched, although they entreated that they might be received into the faith within the Church of Christ, so that they might find in the faith of the nations the salvation they had lost in the synagogue of the Jews. For, as the Lord testifies, he did not find such faith in Israel (Matt. VIII, 10) as he found among the nations.

It follows: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, clothed around with golden borders in varied workmanship.” In Hebrew it reads: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; in golden bands she is clothed with latticework.”

For instead of what is written according to the Septuagint in Greek, ἔσωθεν (“within”), Jerome translated “from within,” or “inwardly,” and says that in certain manuscripts he read *Esebon* in place of this word, which signifies “thoughts.” From this he shows that all the glory of the Church—to which it was said above, “Hear, daughter, and see,” and “O daughter of Tyre,” or “of the mighty one,” and which he now calls the daughter of the King—is within, in thoughts, namely in the inner person and in the circumcision not made by hands.

She wishes to have confidence before God in spirit and conscience, and to possess all her beauty inwardly in the mind, more in the silent thought of the heart than in the flower or eloquence of words. But the Septuagint said, “All the glory of the daughter of kings is from within,” wishing likewise to show that all the glory of the Church—to which he had said above, “Hear, daughter, and the king will desire your beauty,” and so forth—belongs to the daughters of princes, or of the righteous, when they turn to the Lord and continually offer themselves to the Lord in the secret devotion of the heart. This is what “from within” signifies.

Here no empty glory is sought, no display of works is exhibited, no clatter of boastful lips is cultivated, and no swelling of mind is present. Rather, the whole inner person, with silent intention, reflects on what pleases God—indeed, reflects only on what pleases God—and delights in and practices only what it knows to belong to the divine mysteries. This applies above all to God’s ministers who serve at the sacred altars, and to holy virgins, because the closer they appear to be to God, the purer they must also be inwardly, since God dwells among them.

Otherwise, how could Christ’s bride say what is written in the Song of Songs: “The King introduced me into his chamber” (Song I, 14)?
