The chamber of so great a King does not receive adulterous friends who are foul in conscience. For his eyes always see what is in human hearts, and he considers everything.

Therefore all the glory of the King’s bride, whom he himself calls “daughter” above, comes from unfictitious faith and a good conscience. Hence Paul said: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I, 1). Such glory comes only from newness of life and the clothing of virtues, by which every soul in which God dwells through faith is beautified and adorned, and in which he rejoices in the abundance of love.

Although this beauty shines outwardly in good works, the force and adornment of love are nevertheless within. Hence it is said to the bride in the Song of Songs: “How beautiful you are, my beloved, how beautiful you are! Your eyes are like those of doves, apart from what is hidden within” (Song I, 15).

Although the whole Church may shine outwardly with glory and beauty, she is more beautiful inwardly, where Christ dwells and all the ornaments of virtue shine. From this it is clear to everyone that all the glory of the Church, or the beauty of the soul, is within, where the character of the virtues is illumined by heavenly wisdom and the integrity of love gleams.

For, as the philosophers say, virtue is a disposition of the soul in the manner of nature, always consonant with reason. Therefore, from within—where God is, as he is the origin of the virtues and the fountain of goodness—all glory and brightness are produced and grow outwardly.

Hence it is said: “Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from what is hidden within” (Song VI, 7). For what is outwardly red in the cheeks comes from within, so that it may be red, from what lives and flourishes inwardly. Therefore, while this outward beauty withers, it is the inward part that lives, so that life may remain in the fruit and what falls away outwardly may, through what is within, live most beautifully and be restored.

Therefore, dearest ones, consider your calling carefully and examine your consciences, because there is no true glory except that which comes from one’s own conscience. There are wise virgins, and there are foolish ones, whose praise is sometimes false rather than true—especially those whom the tongue of flatterers adorns and empty glory delights.

For this reason, let the devoted virgin test herself, according to the Apostle, and then she will have glory in herself and not in another, since each person will be judged according to his or her own conscience. Hence David sings: “The saints will exult in glory; they will rejoice upon their couches” (Ps. CXLIX, 5).

They will therefore exult in the glory that they always held inwardly in their hearts, under the hope of eternal recompense. They will rejoice upon their couches, in which they lived fruitfully and innocently before God through a good conscience.

It should also be noted that he says, “The daughters of kings from within,” because this expression is never found in secular writings but is counted among the distinctive utterances of divine Scripture.

It follows: “Clothed around with golden borders in varied workmanship.” Yet in Hebrew it reads: “In golden bands she is clothed with latticework.” Although the words differ, the meaning is one, though broader and more remarkable.

For the borders of any garments always hang from the warp, into which the weft is woven. The entire strength of the garment lies in the warp, from which the beauty of the borders descends. But when they are called golden, a more divine meaning is introduced.

For when above the queen is said to stand in a gilded garment, here the borders of that same garment are read to be golden. From this it is understood that the end of life must always be more perfect and precious than its beginning.

This garment is continually woven while human life is spent upon earth. Hence Hezekiah wept most bitterly, saying: “My life has been cut off like that of a weaver, while I was still beginning to weave” (Isa. XXXVIII, 12). He signified that, according to the prophet’s threat, he would depart from here earlier than was appropriate to the age of a human being; or, in accordance with God’s eternal plan, that he would depart before the order of Christ’s generation had been woven from him.

Therefore, by the borders the final portion of human life is signified. It is shown that this portion must not merely be gilded, as the garment above was shown to be, but must be entirely golden, because at the end of life the whole perfection of the love of God is sought.

Yet she is clothed around with varied workmanship on account of the various virtues of the faithful, which, as is clear, have already been explained above. Since the daughter of the King, the Queen—that is, the soul clothed with the faith of Christ—is dressed in these diverse colors, she necessarily wears a multicolored garment, just as the Catholic Church is clothed.

This is that garment signified by the one worn by Aaron, which is said to have been woven with gold, purple, fine linen, scarlet, and hyacinth-blue. Women adorned this garment with mystical mysteries, women to whom God gave wisdom for weaving. In it many divine mysteries were prefigured.

It is also the long robe with which Joseph was clothed, which Mother Church wove for him. From its borders the woman in the Gospel who suffered from a flow of blood touched one.

As for the Hebrew reading, “In golden bands she is clothed with latticework,” although the words differ, it seems to signify the same thing as “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.” For the breast-bands entirely cover the swelling of the womb and regulate the looseness of the breasts; then the inner organs are tightened, so that the belly may not swell more broadly.

But some bands are those with which virgins adorn themselves; others are those by which married women, as we have said, are bound. Hence the prophet Jeremiah says: “Does a virgin forget her adornment, or a bride, or a woman, her breast-band?” (Jer. II, 32).

From this Christ is clearly shown to be the bridegroom of the Virgin Church, while the Synagogue is called a bride more as an expression of reproach than as an honor of virginity. And because she had already been defiled by idols, what she had possessed is recalled.

Nevertheless, through the clemency of the most kindly Savior, she is invited to repentance, so that she may at least receive the band she had as an ornament of beauty as a covering and bond for her deformity.

But Christ’s Church is called virgin and bride because she has neither spot nor wrinkle (Eph. V, 27). Therefore she is girded with golden bands and adorned with latticework as well. But that woman who has withdrawn from the Lord and followed foreign loves has lost her adornment.

Even so, she is not abandoned by the Lord. Rather, he urges her to return to her husband, receive her former love, and perform her first works of love, lest she be found naked in her blood, though she had been whitened by the bridegroom’s blood.

This also indicates how great is the honor and glory of the virgin who is said to have an ornament upon her breast, where the rational—containing teaching and truth—was carried by the high priest.

The virgin of Christ therefore carries nothing less: she bears her bridegroom and Savior in her breast. Thus she is covered with golden bands of understanding, and within them the divine mysteries are wrapped and hidden in the mind. There the virgin’s faith is a sanctuary, and love is a treasure.

For if, as Wisdom herself confesses through Solomon, it is her delight to be with human beings, much more is it believed to be the delight of the bridegroom, who is himself the wisdom of God the Father, to be with them, so that they may fulfill their vows to God and may reach the temple of the King with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves (Ps. CXXV, 6).

Let them be brought to the temple in such a way that they are priests; but to the chamber of the King as brides and wives. Indeed, of them all, let the virgin be one bride and wife.

This is the temple that John saw in his Apocalypse. And the Prophet says: “One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. XXVI, 4). And again: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Ps. XXIII, 8).

To contemplate that glory, dearest ones, one must come with joy and exultation. But because we are daily invited and instructed by evangelical duties to those heavenly joys, it is rightly said, “They shall be brought.”

This applies above all to virgins and widows, because they are invited by great rewards and will rejoice with great joys, since in fragile bodies they have conquered the gravest passions of the flesh. Therefore, “to the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree of life” (Rev. II, 7).

Thus, in John’s Apocalypse, rewards are promised to none but those who conquer. Therefore let the widow fulfill the vows of widowhood, and let the virgin fulfill the vows of her parents. Indeed, those who belonged to their parents, since they are now mature, should make those vows their own, because they have been offered to no one other than the one to whom they owe their whole selves.

For since a daughter is the fruit of the womb, parents have the right either to bring their children to God or to give them in marriage. Hence the Apostle says: “He who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not give her in marriage does better” (I Cor. VII, 38).

Therefore, sister, do not be displeased with your parents’ vows, since they chose for you what is better. Rather, consider more carefully what you owe your parents and what you owe God. For you are held by both laws if you violate the vows of the sacrifice, since they vowed that you should fulfill it; they offered you so that you might remain.

You hear, dearest one, how Isaac carried out his father’s offering even to the sword and to the fires. For insofar as the vow is concerned, he does not shrink even unto death; he does not resist or object.

Perhaps you will say that he was a man. Let the daughter of Jephthah come to your mind, who, so that her father’s vow should not be frustrated, offered herself to death. Her father had opened his mouth, and she not only did not shrink back but urged her father to fulfill the gift promised to God.

So you also, dearest ones, fulfill in yourselves the happy vows of your parents; fulfill what you have vowed to God. Persevere with Samuel in the temple, who lived as the Lord’s Nazirite to the end. For you were born for no one but God—not for your parents, nor for any mortal—but bound by eternal laws to the bridegroom Christ. Before you came forth from your mother’s womb, you began to belong to him through an eternal bridal covenant.

Therefore, although we all belong to him, you belong to him in a special way, because you are the vows of your parents and have received the title of a dowry, so that you might remain happily consecrated in virginity to the virgin Bridegroom.

For everything in this bridal epithalamium of the dowry that was set forth beforehand has been prepared for you. Your bridegroom is everywhere present, beautiful beyond the sons of men, ready to meet you and introduce you into his temple, where are those things that “no eye has seen and no ear has heard” (I Cor. II, 9).

For it cannot happen that he is absent from you who seek him in the Scriptures, love him in your inmost hearts, knock in prayer, persevere in faith, and hope in mercy—he who revealed himself to those who were not seeking him and was found by those who did not ask about him.

It follows: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth.”

The bride is therefore praised in the same order in which the bridegroom was praised above by the Father. First she is praised for her ivory houses and the fragrances of her garments. She is also praised because she is established at the right hand as queen and instructed as the Father’s daughter.

Third, she is proclaimed glorious in her members. And observe how powerfully he preserves the order of praise. “Virgins,” he says, “will be brought to the King after her; her companions are brought near.” This means the Church, because it was fitting that her unity should first be commended, and that afterward the distinction of her parts should follow.

To show the abundant gifts of God’s Church that are to be bestowed, he says that she is to be brought in joy and exultation, through angelic ministries. And that they are to be brought he immediately adds, saying: “They will be brought to the temple of the King.”

He says “to the temple” as though to the bridal chamber or sanctuary, where there is joy and glorious exultation. Finally, he indicates how far the Queen, who has been established at God’s right hand among the virtues, has advanced through the increase of teaching, when it is added: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you.”

For until the end of the world there will be no lack of teachers from her who will be honored in place of their parents and will fulfill the vows of their sons, so that they may be fathers and sons at the same time, lest they appear to have been born from anywhere other than her and the faith be endangered.

Thus, in place of the patriarchs came the prophets, in place of the prophets the apostles, and so thereafter the apostolic order continued, so that there might be one understanding among all their sons, like that of the sons of Korah, in the Church from beginning to end, because the Church is propagated in this way through them all.

But if he is speaking only to the one to whom he had said, “Forget your people,” we ought to understand as fathers those from the nations whose sons were born to them, all of them worshipers of idols. Jeremiah spoke of them: “Our fathers falsely possessed idols, and there is none among them who brings rain” (Jer. XIV, 22).

Or perhaps philosophers are meant—Plato, Aristotle, and the rest, whom it would take too long to enumerate, teachers of various doctrines or errors. In place of all these, sons were born to the Church from the nations: namely, teachers and rulers, whom she appointed as princes or teachers.

It is as though it were said to the Church herself: “Your sons, whom you have begotten for yourself, will be turned into fathers when you have made them teachers from disciples.” We see this happening daily in the Church, and we have no doubt that it will happen until the end of the world, so that bishops, the successors of the apostles, may continue by succeeding one another.

But if we understand Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as the fathers, and wish to understand as the sons of the Church those who were born to her in their place—the apostles who were sent by the Lord to preach to the ends of the earth—we must immediately ask how the Church from the nations had the patriarchs as fathers, when it was said to her above: “Forget your people and your father’s house.”

Unless it is because, as we read in the Gospel, “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. III, 9)—that is, from the nations—which we believe has indeed happened. For if they were Abraham’s sons, they would do the works of Abraham.

Therefore, after those others were disowned, all the nations are blessed in the seed of Abraham (Gen. XXII, 18). For just as he was justified in faith while uncircumcised, so we too are justified in his faith, so that we may be his sons, since this faith was reckoned to him as righteousness (Rom. IV, 3).

It follows: “I will remember your name throughout every generation and generation.”

Previously the divine voice was speaking to the Church herself. Now, by contrast, as often happens—especially among the prophets—the speaker changes person. Having understood herself to have been exalted and enriched with rewards for all these benefits, she turns her voice toward the bridegroom himself and promises that she will remember his name throughout every generation and generation—that is, throughout all the generations of the world.

This is still being fulfilled today, and we see it fulfilled to such an extent that the Church herself has taken the name of Christ. Hence all Christians are called from Christ, in remembrance and confession of Christ’s name, which is the new name in which all the families of the nations are blessed.

In this name you too, dearest ones, have been gathered here, as his brides and members, persevering in confession of his name. It is a wondrous glory and the highest praise of the churches never to cease praising him through so many successive generations of human beings.

But it is more glorious and happier in you, who never cease from praise at any hour or place. Insofar as the weakness of the flesh permits, may you desire by your vow to be made equal to the angels.

Thus even in the world thanksgiving is rightly offered, because what is fragile and unclean is conquered and the future life, where incorruption reigns, is already displayed on earth.

Therefore, he says, “the peoples will confess to you forever and throughout the age of the age.”

This confession is eternal because it is true and devout. Thus the thanksgiving, praise, or confession that exists at present will become life throughout the age of the age, because it already begins to be what will remain forever, when love alone reigns after death has been conquered.

Therefore, dearest ones, while you are still in the contest, since you have overcome the things belonging to the present life, nothing remains except to persevere to the end and receive that portion of eternal life which you have chosen. For Mary, as the Lord testifies, “chose the better portion” (Luke X, 42).

I know, therefore, that you greatly love the blessed Virgin Mary, to whose service you have devoted yourselves. Let her described virginity be for you as an image; let her humility be an example; and let all her virtues be a model of beauty.

You truly love her when you strive to imitate her, when she shines for you in the mirror of chastity and when she is the form of virtue. Take from her examples for living, a pattern of purity in which models of goodness are expressed: what you ought to correct, what to shun, and what to retain.

The first incentives to learning are the nobility or reputation of the teacher. The reputation of the blessed Virgin is that she is blessed by all because her humility has been regarded. Her nobility is that nothing is nobler than the Mother of God; nothing is more splendid than she, whom the splendor of the Father’s glory chose and illumined; nothing is more chaste than she, who generated God as man without bodily defilement.

You truly love her when you follow her completely in conduct and life, since she loved nothing other than God.

You have, dearest ones, the trifles of my leisure; you have what I once vowed to the mother—not because I was capable of worthily fulfilling the divine mysteries under the title of a dowry, but so that I might prove my devotion in service.

Therefore I traversed the glorious epithalamium that the Prophet had sung with exultation, so that I might show you the bridegroom whom the Psalm depicts, as though in the title of a dowry: exceedingly illustrious and beautiful beyond all, glorious in everything and more gracious than all.

It also adorns the bride with wondrous variety. I have shown that the marriages of spiritual union, especially among virgins, are acceptable to God—marriages in which love of chastity endures and the modesty of integrity is obscured by nothing; in which eternal chastity exhales its fragrance and the bond of perfect love is dissolved by no end.

Their bridal chamber is one house, and their joy is one and unceasing. All these things are recorded in this Psalm, as though in the title of a dowry.

In it the drums of the prophets, full of foresight, sing beforehand with exultation of heart what we now rejoice has happened. In it the principality of the apostles is established; their trumpet has subdued all nations, and with their instruments they invite the whole world to your wedding, dearest ones, and sing together with their melodies and with the words of the prophets.

In it the harps of the martyrs celebrate perpetual praises—not with strings but with virtues—and sprinkle roses upon the bride’s bridal chambers. Through Christ they have happily begotten you for him.

In it the chorus of the holy confessors, born from the apostles, brings forth a most pleasing sound on spiritual lyres, so that through them whatever is apostolic has reached the whole earth. The virgin himself walks about, rooted in his virgins and founded in their hearts, loved all the better and more perfectly the more joyfully and perfectly they rest upon the breast of Christ in love.

Hence John, because he was a virgin, is said to have reclined more familiarly upon the Lord’s breast. The priest also, among the other portions of the separation, received the breast-piece from the sacrifices of the victims. The virgin appropriately covers and wraps it entirely with golden bands, because she hides within, with love, the one whom she loves—love which nothing in the world can overcome or violate by any deceit.

When the virgin is said to be clothed in latticework, that very variety, as has often been said, signifies the virtues. There is a lattice-work garment which elsewhere is called *stragulata*. Concerning this Solomon, speaking of the valiant woman who is the Church, says: “She made herself a woven garment; fine linen and purple are her clothing.”

A lattice-work garment is well woven from these two materials. It is called lattice-work because of the white circular shapes of wheels, or of another beauty, which it has among the purple, or because of the beauty of any wondrous color.

Only virgins possess this robe, garment, or band; they bind their breasts so that they may not be found nursing and nourishing children. These bands cover and constrain thoughts, because virgins cherish, conceal, and nourish in their breast all the gifts granted to them and the mysteries of the King, until the time comes to fly away from here and be reborn in heaven.

Hence it follows: “Virgins will be brought to the King after her; her companions will be brought near her. They will be offered in joy and exultation; they will be brought into the temple of the King.”

According to the Septuagint, the first verse still concerns the adornment of the daughter, while the following verse is directed to the King himself. According to the Hebrew, however, the whole passage is addressed to the bride, up to the place where it is written: “You will appoint them princes over all the earth.”

The division of verses often creates ambiguity in Scripture, especially in the Psalms and the prophets, and alters the meanings. The change of persons does likewise, as this Psalm clearly demonstrates.

Therefore, here too the phrase we discussed, “in latticework,” is applied to this verse and made its beginning: “In latticework the virgins will be led to the King, and her companions will follow her. They will be led there; they will be led in joys and exultation into the temple of the King.”

This shows not so much the difference of meaning as the distinction among the souls who believe in Christ, when it says, “Virgins will be brought to the King,” and then, “Her companions will follow her.”

For the statement “They will be brought” declares the grace of the Lord, which makes us come to him, just as he himself testifies in the Gospel, saying: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him” (John VI, 44). And the Church says in the Song of Songs: “Draw me after you; we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song I, 4).

The faithful soul knows well that unless the Lord’s grace draws, no one is capable by himself of arriving. But what virgins are brought so specially to the King and to the King’s bridal chamber?

I think, dearest ones, that this was said of virgins such as I believe you to be: those who follow the Church together with you and follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and who are placed in the first rank because, like you, they have remained faithful in virginity of body and mind.

Otherwise, what good would it do to preserve the chastity of the flesh intact if they did not preserve the integrity of faith? Therefore, amid every form of teaching and combination of virtues, virginity of mind and body in Christ must be guarded.

For she who is perfect and holy in body and spirit is called in the Song of Songs an immaculate and intimate dove, of whom it is said: “The daughters saw her and blessed her; queens and concubines praised her” (Song VI, 8).

From this the meaning is clear: although there is one Church, one wife, and one queen, there are different orders and a great diversity of merits. Sixty queens, eighty concubines, and maidens without number are also counted there.

Therefore, in the first rank virgins are brought to the King, whom the bridegroom himself, beautiful beyond the sons of men, chose and joined to himself in a worthy marriage, so that he himself, a virgin at the head, might remain with his virgins.

Among these I consider you, dearest ones, consecrated to the Lord. You have vowed your complete virginity to God; moreover, following the example of the apostles, you have left everything. And not this alone: you have also placed yourselves under monastic discipline.

But because the female sex seemed more fragile, while love was more fervent in you, by a long-standing custom you also shut yourselves into perpetual enclosure, persevering with one accord in the temple of the Lord. Your heart and soul became one (Acts IV, 32), burned up by the fire of divine love, so that many might become one, following the example of that primitive Church which the Holy Spirit fused into unity, so that it might also be one mass of love in many virtues.

At your beginning the same Holy Spirit joined you together—the Spirit who works all things in all—and made one body in Christ, and one heart and one soul.

But because this virtue belongs to few, it rightly follows: “After her, her companions will be brought near to you,” that is, after this one in whom divine grace has established you as flourishing flowers, companions or intimates will be brought to that same Church, so that they too may be faithful members in the unity of the body.

These companions or intimates are widows living chastely, joined to the virgins in a lower rank. Since virginity bears a hundredfold fruit and widowhood a sixtyfold, widows are honored as being near them.

Thus how fittingly, dearest ones, your compact and united body has been formed from these two orders. Virgins are said to be led because they are stronger in bodily integrity; widows, however, are said to be brought, because they are often broken by many and various troubles and exhausted by great bodily weakness.

They are offered by gratuitous grace, since they have handed themselves over to the cost of life amid diverse cares.

At this point perhaps youthful cleverness might say that I ought to have said that virgins should be brought and widows led. This is especially so since widows come to you of their own accord and by their own devotion, whereas virgins are offered to God the King almost from their beds and, so to speak, while still tender amid the toys of childhood, more through the vow of their parents than through a choice of their own minds.

Hence it might seem more correct to understand that virgins should be brought and widows should come of their own will and present themselves through their own vows.

Yet such a person does not consider the matter sufficiently, because virgins always come through a vow and are offered through the will of their parents, rather than through compulsion. Widows, on the other hand, are often compelled by necessity, especially when, as the Apostle testifies, they are released from the bond of servitude.

Even if they remain in freedom, rewards are promised to them. Hence the Apostle says: “She will be happier if she remains so, according to my counsel” (I Cor. VII, 40).

But the necessities by which they are pressed in marriage, and how they are freed from marriage, would take too long to enumerate. They themselves, however, know better what they have escaped when Christ is their vow.

Virginity alone in the world is free—with the freedom of Christ—subject to no vices, bound by no chains, contaminated by no corruptions. It alone on earth is compared with the angels; it alone is free. It follows Christ the bridegroom wherever he goes, as though accompanying him into a remote place.

And therefore, dearest women, I should call you happy, because you have not known a marriage-bed in sin; you will bear fruit in the visitation of holy souls. Happy are you who drank, together with the milk of the flesh, the milk of eternal life, and were immediately dedicated to God at birth. For you are nothing other than a sacrifice to God, the vows of your parents, the possession of the Holy Spirit, by whose infusion you were sacrificed and nourished. Indeed, nourished from earliest childhood with the milk of the Word, amid the throngs of angels, beneath Christ’s flock, among the pastures of life, as though in God’s paradise, amid perpetual alleluiatic joys, amid God’s sacrifices and burnt offerings: you learned nothing but Christ, and knew how to love no one but him.

Although the vows of your parents led you here, dearest women, happy are you who remained steadfast in the contest of the struggle: for the faith that consecrated you to God in baptism itself, in accordance with your vow, also offered and dedicated you here, with the Church as witness. Therefore you have the first grace in baptism, and a second grace, pleasing to God, after the manner of Samuel, because you were offered to God as a burnt offering. Finally, you have the last grace, because you abandoned everything. You have indeed abandoned everything if you disdain to possess anything; for this is the true mortification of the world: that in the world you neither possess anything nor wish to possess anything.

These vows, brides of Christ, are held in common among you here, which you have vowed: so that together, both the unmarried woman and the virgin, according to the Apostle (I Cor. VII, 34), may think upon the things of the Lord, so as to be holy both in body and in spirit. That unity, coming from different quarters, was joined together by that stone, Christ, who is the cornerstone and made both one (Eph. II, 20). You have placed this cornerstone in the foundation of your hearts, and therefore you have hastened to this corner of Vesona. Not because you loved the corner of a small city, but because you have loved—and must love—the arduous and narrow way that leads to life, since broad and spacious is the way that leads to death.

Therefore, dearest women, because Christ the living stone has made you one flock and one fold in this corner, raise up for yourselves that tower from the Gospel, the tower of the corner, so that you may be for one another an aid to virtue and a school of chastity. Thus let virginity learn from the example of chaste marriage to offer chastity to Christ, so that, just as marriage has preserved an undefiled marriage-bed, virginity may preserve for God, even more than it vowed, the integrity of mind and body. For it is scarcely an inferior virtue to abstain from marriage and to know nothing of its delights.

Widowhood, too, must learn much from the example of virgins: much that it should mourn, much that it should imitate, and much also in which it should rejoice, so that what the widow lost in marriage she may possess wholly, rejoicing with charity in the flower of virginity. And so, strong in both forms of virtue, dearest women, raise up from the Gospel that tower—one and strong, fortified with its armor and defenses—for in both virtues together the rewards of eternal recompense have been promised to you.

When a tower is built, it is raised in the form of fire: for although fire always burns more broadly at the bottom, it narrows toward the top and always strives toward what is above. Hence this tower, as they say, is called *pyrgos* among the Greeks, because it narrows and rises in the form of a flame. You build this tower truly well if you continually kindle within yourselves that charity by which the hearts and souls of many become one, because the charity of God and neighbor strives to fly upward like fire.

Indeed, no ranks of the Church are more suited to one another than the virginity and widowhood of consecrated women. Their vow of obedience is one; their manner of life is one; their stability of place is one; their way of living is one; their promise of the kingdom is one. And lest one of them become puffed up against the other, one is called a virgin and the other a neighbor or friend. To them both it is said in the Song of Songs: “One is my dove, my friend, my neighbor” (Song II, 10), because the bridegroom always seeks one thing in all, and always wishes all to be one.

Accordingly, all who are offered and all who are brought together should be brought in joy and exultation (II Cor. IX, 7), so that no one may act out of sadness or necessity, but each one—[lacuna]—had sounded with sweetest harmony upon her instruments. In this place the bridal chamber of all virgins is dedicated, and the bridegroom is brought in, anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit, as though in the arena, before his companions, while all kinds of music resound in this song and the whole world, together with the citizens above, holds one harmony.

In this bridal song, therefore, the virgins of Christ set such musical instruments sounding before your vigils that, through their honey-sweet tones, all human joy may for the present be surpassed, and the joys of what is to come may already, even now, be celebrated. In that joy, dearest women, I wished to sprinkle your most sacred marriage-beds of the heart with flowers. But because I was not equal to the task, I sent humble pennyroyal, very sweet-smelling, so that at least the feet of those going before the doors might be sprinkled with it. For although it may seem worthless in Gaul, among the Indians it is dear and more precious than pepper because of its fragrance.

From this it is clear that not everyone possesses everything, nor does one flavor taste equally sweet to everyone upon the palate of the heart; just as one and the same medicine is not equally effective for all. For this reason I believe that among you this little work of ours may find some to whom it will be useful and pleasing. Not, I say, because it is ours, but because it is God’s; for in what comes from us, only rusticity is unsightly. Otherwise, within the good King are delights with which we, hungering, have been nourished from your wedding feast, and which, as far as permitted, we have [uncertain: “set down”] here in the title of your dowry.

[Col. 1059B]

**The Five Books of Saint Paschasius Radbertus, Abbot of Corbie, on the Lamentations, or Laments, of Jeremiah.**

*(In Sirmond’s edition, Works of Saint Paschasius Radbertus.)*

[Col. 1059]

**Prologue to Odilmannus Severus**

[Col. 1059C] 1307–1308

**Paschasius Radbertus**, the refuse of all monks, sends the most abundant and everlasting greeting to the old man Odilmannus Severus.

I am compelled, worn out by the long weariness of life, to take up the mournful melodies of tears. For already, as a matter of fact, groaning, old age has come upon me unexpectedly and unbidden, weighed down by my misfortunes. When I look upon it, disfigured in appearance, I shudder at what is foreign, because, although my mind has not suddenly changed, I do not find in myself the person I was. Yet I cannot escape that which deceives me—the very thing I have lost.

Thus, frozen and made harder by prolonged habit, I can no longer be softened by any tears, although I am pressed within and without by many sorrows of my wretchedness. Driven at least daily to sighs by these sorrows, I have resolved to explain the Lamentations of the prophet Jeremiah amid the final dangers of life, so that I may be softened by his laments and thus learn, at least in this way, to mourn the disasters of fragile life, in the manner in which that holy man mourns the misfortunes of others.

And because this age calls for other customs, although late, at the urging of Scripture, since I have once entered the house of mourning, I have resolved not to pass over without investigation a work of such magnitude—even though I have read no Latin author who has explained the Lamentations, which the prophet wished to commend to readers by joining them to metrical melody.

If in this work I should unravel anything worthy of being committed to writing for those who come after us, I send it to be judged by you, brother, because, among all to whom I have turned my eyes, I have thought no one more suited to our purpose than you: you are my equal in old age and surpass me in the daily tears of prayer.

## Preface

[Col. 1061]

[Col. 1061A]

Just as various songs are read in the divine Scriptures, so also, when the Holy Spirit unlocks them, there are various laments. And just as Solomon’s book is properly called the Song of Songs, so Jeremiah’s Lamentations may also be called the Lamentations of Lamentations. For just as those songs altogether surpass the others, in which bridegroom and bride enjoy sweet embraces, so these lamentations surpass all the laments of Scripture, in which the bridegroom’s departure from the bride is mourned with great tears and extraordinary grief. From this separation the solitary city is lamented, and the mistress of nations is bitterly mourned as though she were a widow.

In those songs, different persons are introduced for the joys of the wedding; in these, different persons are mourned. The former are fitting in the homeland; the latter in this pilgrimage of ours. Of the former songs it is said that they are fitting in that heavenly Zion, as David the Psalmist sings: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, and to you the vow shall be fulfilled in Jerusalem” (Ps. LXIV, 2). Of the latter the same Prophet says: “Blessed is the one whose help is from you” (Ps. LXIV). “He has arranged,” he says, “ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place that he has established” (Ps. LXXXIII).

The valley of tears rightly signifies the conduct of the present life. The place is the Church of Christ, in which each person, placed there and mourning out of desire for the heavenly homeland, has arranged ascents in his heart, so that one day he may devotedly reach those joys of blessedness. For one ascends only in the heart, where each believer, while meditating upon the various stages of his calling, is inwardly moved by various groans of the heart.

Hence it is clear that there are many kinds of weeping and many different kinds of tears. One person mourns his own losses, another the losses of others. One mourns out of love for the heavenly homeland, another because of the enormity of crimes and the terror of Gehenna. Another mourns because of anguish of heart and love of pious and holy remembrance. Divine Scripture explains these kinds of tears more broadly when, in different passages of Scripture, it displays the various emotions of individuals and repeats their laments.

Among them David says: “My tears have been my bread day and night, while it is said to me every day: Where is your God?” (Ps. XLI). And elsewhere: “I have labored in my groaning; every night I will make my bed swim, and I will water my couch with my tears” (Ps. VI). “My eye has grown dim with bitterness, because I have been consumed by all my enemies.” From these words it is evident that the saints are moved by many emotions, since they too have transferred inwardly into the understanding of their minds the whole scroll that was shown to Ezekiel (ch. II), in which were written “lamentations, a song, and woe.”

Lamentations, clearly, because repentance for sins and the weeping of all the saints are written in those same letters, as the Psalmist sings: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. CXXV). Confident in this true hope, the earlier saints “went and wept, casting their seeds” (ibid.). Therefore a song follows in the same book, from which the joys of the righteous are announced; yet woe is not silenced, since in many places the condemnation of the reprobate is plainly expressed.

But we are afflicted by laments in this valley of tears so that in the future we may be able to reach the joys of eternal life and songs of gladness (Joel II). Of these laments it is written in the same sayings: “Tear your hearts and not your garments” (James IV). “Be miserable and mourn,” because “blessed are those who mourn now.” “Let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow.” And so that you may rejoice at the promise of the joy that follows, you have in the collection of the same volume: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII).

And, as the heavenly Jerusalem is more splendidly proclaimed by a certain wise man: “All its streets shall be paved with precious and pure stone, and alleluia shall be sung through all its lanes” (Tob. XIII). The citizens of the heavenly homeland came to announce this song to us when they cried out together: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II).

Such songs, then, are the joys of the heavenly homeland. But the lamentations of the Holy Spirit are an infusion into the heart, whether from sorrow or from desire for eternal life. We nevertheless read the lamentation over Saul and Jonathan, and also over Absalom; these laments are certainly full of pain and grief. Hezekiah also wept with great weeping, and Peter wept most bitterly.

But these, as we have said, are rightly called the Lamentations of Lamentations, because they are universal. Thus the genus is extended to the species, and again the species is referred back to the genus. They mourn the destruction of that earthly Jerusalem and its people in such a way that they do not fail to mourn the losses of the present Church. They mourn the generality of the new and old people—their members who have fallen from the faith and are taken captive—in such a way that they do not cease to lament the loss of a single soul that was a temple of the Holy Spirit.

They direct their gaze toward the present captivity, under which he composed this same prophecy, in such a way that they do not wholly omit the final captivity, which took place under Titus and Vespasian. What more is there to say? Seeing all the causes and ruins of the present life, the prophet is moved with groaning to each particular thing, so that each person may learn to mourn his own things in the way he himself mourns common things and the sins of others.

Therefore, as I judge, he composed the Lamentations of the whole lament in a fourfold alphabet, because both we and this world were created from four elements—namely, fire, water, air, and earth—so that we who consist of four kinds of existence might rightly be mourned under four alphabets of letters.

That the prophet mourns not only the present but also the past and the future is indicated by the book of Chronicles (II Chron. XXXV), where we read that King Josiah died and was buried in the mausoleum of his fathers, and that all Judah and Jerusalem mourned him; “Jeremiah,” it says, “especially.” These words plainly show that this lamentation extends not only to the present and future but also to the past, so that beneath the fourfold vault of heaven he might mourn the sins of the present age with a fourfold alphabet and invite all to lament.

For this reason we too have decided to expound these same lamentations in three ways—over the ruin of that city no less than over the losses of the Church and the dangers of souls—and to direct the meaning, as appropriate, toward those three times.

Nor did we think it should be left unsaid that the holy prophet, as Jerome, the interpreter of the divine law, testifies, composed the Lamentations according to the rule of meter. Hence among the Latins, at the beginning of each sentence, individual Hebrew letters are prefixed, from which, as is reported, each verse begins in its own language. Nor should it be believed that so many letters are devoid of mystery, since not even one jot or tittle is to be omitted from the law (Matt. V). Therefore, because the individual letters are interpreted, an interpretation must be assigned to each sentence.

For *Aleph* is interpreted as “teaching.” That teaching is true by which God is known and the particular state or failing of each person is not ignored. For no one properly devotes himself to teaching who does not thoroughly know himself. Concerning this the prophet Isaiah says: “Glorify God in teaching” (Isa. XXIV). Therefore, the one who glorifies God worthily in teaching is the one who does not cease to praise him for his own deeds, and who does not fail to mourn what he himself has committed or what his neighbors have committed.

How well the prophet had grasped this teaching is shown when, filled with a sorrowful spirit, he said:

## Book One

[Col. 1063]

### ALEPH

[Col. 1063C]

“How the city sits solitary, full of people! She has become like a widow, the mistress of nations. The princess of provinces has become subject to tribute.”

Here he does not mourn the walls of the city of Jerusalem, but, figuratively speaking, bitterly laments the people led away into captivity through it. This accords with the prophet Isaiah’s statement (ch. I), that the daughter of Zion, deprived of all good things, has been left alone by her enemies, like a hut in a cucumber field and like a city that is laid waste.

Immediately the prophet’s vehement cry follows, full of tears, full of grief, full of the whole wonder and astonishment of one who mourns. In it he plainly indicates the overthrow of the wretched city and the ruin of the sinful people: not only that these happened under the Chaldeans, but also that all would be fulfilled more fully under Titus and Vespasian.

Up to this point she is rightly said to sit alone only as an exaggeration of grief, since innumerable cultivators of the land, the poor, were left behind, and Gedaliah was ordered to rule over them. Yet the city was not destroyed; rather, its complete devastation was postponed until Christ the leader had been killed, when, according to the Lord’s sentence, neither stone would remain upon stone, nor would any people be left in it (Matt. XXIV).

Meanwhile, even after the return from such captivity, the rod of God’s anger gradually grew again, because the faithless Jewish people did not turn back to God after the warnings and corrections of the prophets. Instead, always ungrateful for God’s benefits, they brought upon themselves harsher punishments. Concerning this people Moses says: “I know your contentiousness and your most stubborn neck; you have always acted contentiously against God” (Deut. XXXI). And Stephen likewise says: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart, you always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did” (Acts VII).

Therefore, although often worn down by scourges, oppressed by enemies, and afflicted by almost every evil, they still did not believe with their whole heart, but “provoked the Most High and did not keep his testimonies” (Ps. LXXVII). And so, after the ten tribes had already been taken captive among the Assyrians, the two that remained, following the house of David and outwardly worshiping God, were taken captive more harshly in Chaldaea as their wickedness gradually increased.

Hence the city is mourned as though sitting alone, and as a widow subjected to tribute, although previously she had been mistress of nations—namely, of those nations that she had overthrown. She is astonishingly said to sit as a widow not only because, after the kings had been taken captive and the priesthood destroyed, she was desolate, but also because, after the temple had been profaned and the glory of all its vessels utterly scattered, she was immediately deprived of God’s help, emptied, and left alone among her enemies, full of disgrace.

Spiritually, however, the matter is more tearful whenever the Church, because her sins demand it, is widowed of her bridegroom Christ and is mourned by the prophet or by holy men: “How does the city sit alone?” She is rightly said to sit alone when, desolated of the help of God and the holy angels, she is ravaged within and without by enemies.

Otherwise, if she were not alone, she ought not to be mourned, because the children of the bridegroom cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them; rather, the friends rejoice with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. But when they perceived that the mother, namely the Church of Christ, had been widowed of her bridegroom, it was rightly fitting for all to weep—not only the children but also the friends.

Jeremiah the prophet belonged to this company; he mourned more bitterly than all and on behalf of all. He mourned not stones and buildings but the ruin of human beings. The city is rightly said to sit well, because sitting is the posture of one who mourns. Hence Job is also said to have sat upon the dung heap, in order to express the feeling of one who grieves (Job II), for his name itself is interpreted as “the grieving one.”

David likewise speaks of this same captivity: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Ps. CXXXVI). It is as though he plainly says: Because we did not wish to stand upon the throne of the kingdom, indeed upon the summit of heaven, we rightly grieve beyond measure, weeping and mourning beside the rivers of temptations, in accordance with the prophet Isaiah: “Descend, sit in the dust, daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground, there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans” (Isa. XLVII).

So too, whenever our Jerusalem comes into the confusion of sins, it has no seat, no throne, and no dignity of exaltation; rather, it is rightly said to sit in the dust of the earth. Therefore the prophet mourns not only because it sits, soiled by dusty and earthly works, but because it sits alone.

It sits alone because it is like a widow; and it is a widow because, on account of the foulness of its disgrace, it has been abandoned by its bridegroom. But it should be noted that it is called “like a widow,” not “truly a widow,” because even if it is despised by its bridegroom, the rights of its betrothal nevertheless remain, so that if it returns and fulfills its former works of love, it may recover its bridegroom at least through repentance and immortality.

Once reclothed in that garment, it lies under no tribute of debt, as the Apostle Paul indicates, saying: “You should owe nothing else except to love one another” (Rom. XII).

Tropologically, however, the soul is rightly mourned as sitting alone, like a widow stripped of the goods of virtue, because it has subjected itself to the dominion of the Chaldeans and despised the bridegroom of its youth. For the Chaldeans are interpreted as “those who take captive.”

Thus the soul is called captive when, subdued by vices and removed from the throne of the heavenly homeland, it is brought under the power of demons. The prophet then says to it: “Enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans” (Isa. XLVII), as though he plainly said: Because you did not wish to stand in the light of virtues, though made a daughter of God by the gift of adoption, enter, under a changed name, into the darkness of perpetual blindness.

Seeing this soul, deprived by its faults of the help of its bridegroom, the prophet groans and cries out: “How does the city sit alone?”—that is, the soul that once was full of virtues and the assistance of the saints, like a populous city, but now lies desolate. Formerly it flourished in divine works amid the company of its companions; now, amid the enemies of its adversaries, it is filthy and squalid. It has no fellowship with the saints, no sharing in the sacraments of God, no participation with the bridegroom to whom it had bound itself by the love of devotion. Reduced instead under the tribute of vices, it becomes daily more tightly bound by paying every debt.

(Cass.) Hence one of the elect mourned and said: “My father left me liable to many creditors, and I labor daily to pay them, but to one of them I have not yet been able to make satisfaction, as I lament the impulses of gluttony.”

It is therefore clear that there are many tributes of sins to which the soul becomes liable, unless it is freed again by God’s help and is able to recover its former liberty.

For this reason the merciful God, although provoked to anger by our evils, urges the fornicator soul, saying: “Mourn like a virgin girded with sackcloth over the husband of her youth” (Joel I). The soul is mourned as a virgin over the husband of its youth when, filled with the love of perfect charity, it considers the obligations of its marriage and is brought to shame.

Therefore it is commanded to gird itself with a sackcloth garment, to mourn its deeds, so that by repenting it may not be judged by the Lord, but may first be corrected among the sinful goats; then it is urged to complete works of love over the husband of its youth. Hence the voice of the mourner follows.

### BETH

[Col. 1066B]

“Weeping, she wept in the night, and her tears were upon her cheeks.”

Who she is who weeps is indicated by the letter Beth at the beginning of the verse; it is shown to be interpreted as “house.” Beth means “house”—namely, that house which entered Egypt with Jacob (Gen. XLVI) and afterward, with the Lord’s merciful help and amid flashing miracles, is proclaimed to have come out from a barbarous people (Ps. CXIII). Now, however, because its sins demand it, it is led back into captivity in Babylon, and therefore is said to weep most bitterly.

It weeps in the night because during the day no rest was granted them, not even enough to console themselves with their tears and wash their eyes late in the day—eyes that they had previously raised wickedly toward idols. And, what is more grievous, of all the friends who deceitfully flattered it, no one consoled it, as the Prophet testifies; rather, its friends are mourned as having become enemies.

Its tears, he says, were upon its cheeks, so that it might be clothed in greater disgrace among its enemies and be filled with their reproaches. The meaning is therefore clear: because of idolatry the people were led into captivity and, in Babylon, were treated harshly enough by their enemies, burdened with the full disgrace of their crimes.

But a harsher captivity was that which, according to Josephus, took place under Titus and Vespasian, so that it may rightly be believed that nothing more grievous could occur in the present time. From this it is plainly evident that God’s patience long endured them for repentance, and that the anger which they stored up for themselves greatly increased the fury of God.

Allegorically, however, this refers to the Church of Christ, namely that heavenly Jerusalem which is read to have descended from heaven from God, adorned with her jewels. “Weeping, she wept in the night,” amid the adversities of this life. For although she is foreknown and predestined for the glory of heavenly contemplation, she still moves amid the darkness of ignorance and the dangers of our blindness.

Hence the text significantly says, “Weeping, she wept,” because she not only groans and grieves over the evils she endures outwardly, but also weeps and groans over the hardships of her weaknesses and the stains by which she is afflicted inwardly. She weeps no less over what she feels within than over what she suffers without.

First she is pierced in the secret chambers of hearts; then she is outwardly—and inwardly—washed anew by tears. For from the fountain within arises the groaning and the tear that is brought forth outwardly.

Therefore, according to the idiom of the holy Scriptures, the Church of Christ is rightly said to weep with weeping, just as it is said to rejoice with joy and to live with life. For just as “to live with life” and “to rejoice with joy” are greater and more significant than simply “to live” and “to rejoice,” so it is greater to say, “Weeping, she wept,” in order to indicate the abundance of perfect inward compunction and to demonstrate the profusion of outward tears. Thus no less the outward than the inward person may be washed, restored in full.

Hence what follows: “Her tears were upon her cheeks.” By the cheeks, the rulers of the churches are signified, those who know how to care for and mourn their own sins and the sins of others, but not to expose them. Of them it is rightly praised in the Song of Songs: “Your cheeks are like a slice of a pomegranate, apart from what lies hidden within” (Song IV).

Thus in the cheeks not only the beauty of the Church is displayed, but also their office as preachers is signified, because through them we convey everything into the body, and through them the Church herself is daily reborn and gathered in faith in Christ. Therefore, since they labor more than others in the body of Christ, they groan and weep more than others.

They rejoice more when they nourish and bring the elect to faith; they grieve and mourn more over those whom they know to be wandering in the night of sins or in the blindness of error. For this reason she is said to weep in the night.

She weeps in the night because, placed in sorrow, she does not fail to recognize the darkness of her sins, and she carries tears upon her cheeks so that her beauty may be renewed daily.

They themselves are the cheeks of the Church, and also the rind of the pomegranate, because they not only bring us into the body of Christ, but also cover us, adorned with the red beauty of Christ’s blood, and conceal everything within his inward parts that lies hidden.

The cheeks of the Church are also said to be like a turtledove, to signify those who love a solitary and chaste life. They are also said to be like beds of spices planted by perfumers (Song V), to indicate those who pursue the contemplative life and devote themselves to prayer day and night. In them are truly the beauty of the churches and the fragrance of virtues; the rush of the river makes them glad within, and the abundance of tears intoxicates them.

Their tears, in fact, are the laments of all, including those who lead the active life, while these people above all groan and mourn for everyone. They are like beds of virtues planted by perfumers—namely, by the apostles and apostolic men.

Whatever Mary mourns beside the Lord’s feet benefits Martha in her labor. Therefore the tears of Christ’s churches are rightly shown to flow upon the cheeks, so that the vows of charity of all may become one burnt offering.

The bride therefore weeps, far removed from the embraces of her bridegroom, in this valley of tears as though in the night of ignorance, yet betrothed with the dowry of love and intoxicated with the wine of compunction.

First she weeps in her pastors and rulers, not only because of desire for that heavenly homeland, but also because of the corrupt life of some of her members. She also weeps in those who have mortified themselves to this world. She weeps in virgins, she weeps in widows, and she weeps in all who recognize themselves at present as pilgrims and needy, because “blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V).

Above all, however, it is fitting for the bride to mourn when, as the Prophet groans, “There is no one among all her beloved who consoles her.” For when the bridegroom is provoked by sins, she is not only deprived of the help of angels and all the saints, but is also frequently left desolate of the consolation of the Holy Spirit. Thus the friends who rejoice at the bridegroom’s voice (John III) and listen to him, when he is shown, bring mourning and sometimes laments rather than any comfort or solace.

Hence it follows: “All her friends have despised her, and have become her enemies.” For when God is offended, there is no saint who disagrees with his justice, until, through repentance and with Christ’s favor, the sinner is reconciled again to forgiveness.

Tropologically, however, the soul rightly “weeping, weeps in the night” when it understands that it is everywhere darkened by the blindness of its sins. The same prophet deplores and curses this night of sin far above. Concerning it, that grieving man Job says: “Let that night be solitary and unworthy of praise” (Job III).

When the soul is enveloped in this night, it is rightly said to weep with weeping—not by its own choice, but by the grace of the Lord. Therefore, in God’s person, the prophet first cries out with the voice of one who mourns: “How does the city sit alone?” and what follows.

Otherwise, if the Lord had not first seen her sitting alone and, moved by mercy, mourned her, she would not have mourned herself at all. Thus, when the Lord looked upon Peter, he himself, remembering Jesus’ word, immediately wept most bitterly (Matt. XXVI).

If you consider this carefully, you will find throughout all the holy Scriptures that those who returned perfectly to the lamentation of repentance after sin were first anticipated and looked upon by God’s mercy.

“Her tears,” he says, “were upon her cheeks.” The cheek of the soul is its innermost conscience. For just as the face is formed in the cheeks, so each person’s character is displayed in the conscience. Therefore tears are rightly said to be upon the cheeks, so that the sinful conscience may never be found dry from the fountain of tears, but, according to David (Ps. L), may always set its sins before itself and not fail to punish what it has committed with weeping.

“Nor does anyone console her among all her beloved.” She has lost her consoler, namely the Holy Spirit, who has been driven away, especially since all her most beloved friends—that is, the affections of her perverse love—have become her enemies. On the day of the final reckoning, according to the Apostle, they will rise up (Rom. II), accusing the wretched conscience, while their thoughts defend them.

Then not only will those most beloved private affections, which now seem like friends, despise the unhappy soul while accusing it, but the demons themselves, those worst persuaders who now flatter the unwary by deceiving them, will then press against them as harsher enemies, together with all that we have done.

Therefore, when the soul loses the divine Spirit who consoles it, let it earnestly implore him, so that, according to the abundance of its sorrow, the same consoler, who is also the Paraclete, may once again gladden the desolate soul when, after its enemies have been conquered, it reaches reconciliation and the kisses of its bridegroom.

What follows.

### GIMEL
The letter that is interpreted as “fullness.” For the fullness of sins caused wretched Judah to migrate into captivity, because, by heaping up for itself ever more grievous offenses, it provoked God’s anger. Otherwise, if its wickedness had not reached completion, that people—formerly beloved by God—would not have reached such disgraceful dishonor. For when the just Judge, the Lord, promised his friend Abraham (Gen. XV) the land of the Canaanites as an inheritance, he denied that he could yet give it, saying: “The sins of the Amorites have not yet been completed.” How much more would he hand over to enemies a glorious people, greatly beloved by him, only on account of the fullness and enormity of its crimes?

Therefore, in this sentence concerning Judah’s transmigration, the letter Gimel, that is, “fullness,” is appropriately set forth, so that the meaning is this: because of the fullness of its sins, it was taken captive among its enemies (IV Kings XXV; Jer. XXXIX). And it is mourned not only for having been carried far away among the Chaldeans to Babylon, but also—by way of intensifying its most cruel captivity—for having migrated from there still farther, because of its affliction and severe servitude, among foreign peoples scattered everywhere, without finding rest. This is what unfaithful servants do when they are oppressed by excessive servitude: they flee indiscriminately in every direction.

Nor is this undeserved. Those who had lost their freedom—despising the gentle yoke of the love of God and the promises concerning Christ—if they are crushed by excessive affliction and pressed by servitude, are like Cain, who did not tremble to kill Abel (Gen. IV), that is, Christ, his brother. They dwell as wanderers and fugitives here and there among the nations, finding no rest, but always carrying with them the disgrace of their confusion as they roam.

Hence it follows: “All her persecutors overtook her amid her distresses.” Those from whose captivity they had escaped, cruelly oppressed, by flight now pursued them again and overtook them—afflicted in many ways, without any rest—so that they were scattered among the nations under threat.

Our Jerusalem is also frequently understood in this way according to the anagogical sense: she is mourned most bitterly because, abandoning the freedom of Christ, she migrated into the servitude of the nations and into the excessive affliction of vices. Among these, indeed, she found no rest, but amid the distresses of unjust affliction she is overtaken and tormented by her persecutors.

If you wish to interpret such things literally also of this Jerusalem of ours, which is rightly called “confession,” you have abundant grounds for lamenting tearfully before God, whom we offend daily, on behalf of churches that, because their sins demand it, are pressed beneath the yoke of pagans and devastated by excessive affliction, oppressed under their most cruel servitude. If our people, moved by divine fear, feared this in the present, they would certainly not continue to tear apart and lacerate Christ’s Church in this way, nor, so to speak, draw God’s offense upon themselves with their own hands. Yet when enemies have advanced from every side, they will be found—only amid civil wars and the flames of discord, amid the devastation of the homeland and the plundering of God’s churches, amid seditions and frauds, scandals and robberies, the oppression of the poor and murders—persecuting one another, without regard for God, and caught shamefully amid ambushes and crimes.

Therefore, with the prophet, we too can cry out with groans: we have no rest anywhere, even among the ministers of the altar, either within or without. Rather, we migrate from evil to worse, long oppressed by the weight of our sins, and everywhere we are overtaken amid distresses by hateful persecutors.

The soul likewise, morally understood, afflicted by the servitude of our vices—in which alone the confession of Christ sounds forth—migrates disastrously, being taken captive daily from one vice to another. Concerning these things the Apostle cries out with a groan: “I see in my members another law opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin” (Rom. VII). This migration comes already from the law of sin, so that no other way of escape remains except the one he himself indicates: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” Then he immediately adds confidently: “The grace of God, through Jesus Christ.”

But wretched is the woman who, exhausted in the extremity of her condition like a woman in labor, is found amid the distresses of her enemies and persecutors. Hence the Lord says: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing on that day” (Matt. II, 4).

It follows:

## DALETH

“The roads of Zion mourn, because there are none who come to the solemn assembly. All her gates are destroyed, her priests groaning, her virgins squalid, and she herself oppressed by bitterness.”

Having already set forth the general category, he now passes to the particular classes of persons, so that, as the general is divided into its species and the species are gathered back into the general, the mourning may be enlarged and the grief increased.

Because the prophet chose to compose his laments according to metrical rules, he occasionally adorns his discourse with figures from secular eloquence, so that he immediately renders the literal meaning through metaphor according to the rules of rhetoric. Hence he says: “The roads of Zion mourn.” He does not mean that roads, which possess no sensation, can literally mourn, but that they could arouse mourning in passersby and appear mournful because there are none who come to her solemn assembly.

Nor should it seem strange that the roads of Zion are said to mourn, since Moses too, when giving the Law, calls heaven and earth as witnesses: “Attend, O heaven, and hear, O earth, the words of my mouth” (Deut. XXXI, 32). Then Isaiah (chap. XIII), after the transgression of that same Law, again brings them forward as witnesses, so that all the elements may recognize that God has been justly stirred to anger in avenging his commands.

Thus the roads of Zion are rightly said to mourn, so that it may be understood that God’s offense has justly occurred among that same people. According to the anagogical sense, the squared form of the tablets is introduced, which the letter Daleth is said to signify, for Daleth is interpreted as “tablets.” By their function, the house of the Church, joined together, rises with a square summit.

Whenever our Zion, within or without, is filled with the bitterness of God’s anger because of its own sins, the roads rightly mourn, the gates lie destroyed, the priests groan, and the virgins are lamented as squalid, so that the entire house, marked by the fourfold number of its tablets, appears to have been shaken.

Concerning these roads the same prophet says much earlier: “Stand on the roads, and see, and ask about the roads of the Lord” (Jer. VI). Other copies read: “Ask about the roads of the Lord; inquire which is the good road, and walk in it.” Lest we wander from the road, he commands us not only to stand but also to see and then to ask about the everlasting roads—that is, the patriarchs and prophets—which is the good road, and thus to walk in it.

Therefore I have not improperly said that those through whom one reaches the one true road are rightly called “roads.” Just as the holy preachers are called lights and exalted by other names taken from Christ, so they are interpreted as the roads and gates of the heavenly Zion. Hence one of the poets, Prudentius, calls Abraham “the first road of faith.”

Whenever these roads fail, and there are none who come to the solemn assemblies of the heavenly homeland, they mourn and groan, especially because the gates appear destroyed: neither do those who are said to preside by virtue of their office enter themselves, nor do they permit others to enter. The prophet therefore howls that the roads of Zion mourn, and the gates also howl because they lie destroyed. Their single function had been to lead people to the joys of life; therefore there is one lament and one mourning directed toward severe repentance.

Then, after the priests are said to groan, her virgins are called defiled, so that squalor corresponds to the destruction of the gates and groaning to the mourning of the roads. Virginity is rightly joined to the priesthood, since all are rules for the priesthood; and the priesthood is no less suited to chastity than to the adornment of virginity.

When these steps have been violated, it is rightly not merely their life that is lamented, but also the wickedness of those who follow, deplored in their children. Hence she complains, filled with bitterness in every respect, according to what has been said: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (I Cor. XII).

Moreover, even if some come with bodily steps to the thresholds of the Church, very few attend frequently as far as the horn of God’s altar to celebrate her festive joys, while the gates are destroyed and the roads, filled with the filth of thorns, lie unused. The priests groan because of their sins; virginity is squalid from the foulness of vices.

The soul, filled with the same evils in the moral sense, mourns; the virtues once possessed groan because there are none who come to her solemn assembly, since her bridegroom has been taken away. The soul’s bridegroom is immediately offended when the soul, after its fall, casts itself down from the citadel of heavenly intention into external actions.

Therefore, wishing to recover the effect of its former life, so that they might come to celebrate its inward joys, it will perceive that there are none who come to the joys of its desired solemn assembly. Its solemn assembly is therefore the inward enjoyment of heavenly life, into which, having first entered through contemplation, the soul was worthy to be called not only Zion but also paradise.

Its roads mourn, that is, its effects, because, when evils press in, there are none who come to the solemn assemblies of divine contemplation. The gates—namely, the five senses—also lie destroyed. For just as there are gates of death, so there are gates of righteousness. Concerning these gates the Psalm says: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; entering through them, I will confess to the Lord. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Ps. CXVII). Isaiah likewise says: “Open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter” (Isa. XVII).

When the angels open these gates, it is not that rejected people of the Jews who enter, but the nation of the faithful and the companies of the virtues. No one enters them unless he has been raised up from the gates of death—that is, from vices—so that he may proclaim all the praises of Christ in the gates of divine contemplation.

But because death entered us through our windows (Jer. IX), the virginity of the soul is squalid and our royal priesthood groans, while we are filled with the bitterness of sins instead of virtues. Therefore let us first go out from the gates of death, which cannot prevail against the Apostle. Then let us rebuild the gates through which death entered—namely, our senses—again asking which is the good road among the roads of the Lord. For there are roads that seem good to people, but their end plunges them into the depths of hell.

Therefore, although there are many roads and many gates, let the one at the head of all things always be held fast: through it alone the righteous enter into life and proceed along it.

## HE

“Her enemies have become her leaders; her foes have grown rich, because the Lord has spoken against her on account of the multitude of her iniquities. Her little ones have been led into captivity before the face of the one who afflicts her.”

We must ask when or where the Lord spoke against her, and what he said, lest someone say that such things happened to them merely because “the Lord spoke,” as one often finds this stated simply in many passages of Scripture—as though God’s sentence seemed to predetermine what follows.

But it must not be understood in this way, lest God appear unjust. For concerning this sentence we read in Deuteronomy that Moses commanded Reuben and the other tribes to stand on Mount Ebal to pronounce a curse if they were unwilling to hear and keep God’s commandments, while on the opposite mountain they were to pronounce a blessing if they obeyed and did not turn aside from his commands.

Among those curses are these:

“If you are unwilling to hear the voice of the Lord your God, to keep and do all his commandments, the Lord will cause you to fall before your enemies. You will be scattered through all the kingdoms of the earth, oppressed by violence, and you will have no one to free you. Your sons and daughters will be handed over to another people; your eyes will see this, but your sight will fail as you look upon them all day long, and there will be no strength in your hand. The fruit of your land and your labors will be eaten by a people whom you do not know; you will always suffer accusation and be oppressed throughout all your days. You will beget sons and daughters, but you will not enjoy them, because they will be led into captivity. The foreigner who dwells with you in your land will rise above you and become higher; you will descend and become lower. He will be the head, and you will be the tail” (Deut. XXVIII).

Why have I said all this? So that from it you may understand what, and of what kind, the Lord spoke against the iniquity of Jerusalem—not to predetermine her guilt, but to recall her by warning. Because she was unwilling to obey, all these things happened by God’s just judgment, which the prophet tearfully deplores; and nothing was lacking from any of the prophetic words that Moses had threatened.

For this reason, I think, He is placed before this chapter. He is interpreted as “this.” It is a relative or demonstrative term, so that the meaning is: these are the judgments fulfilled, which Moses formerly threatened would come upon them if they sinned against the Lord.

Whenever similar judgments for sins befall our Jerusalem—that is, the present Church—we must groan deeply. Her enemies become her leaders, namely heretics or pagans, as we now see in many churches; or certainly wicked and utterly depraved Christians, who are rightly called enemies no less than the others. The enemies grow rich in argumentative eloquence, while there is often great poverty of understanding among men, even among ecclesiastics, so that what the prophet threatens is rightly understood to have been said of them: “I will send among them not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos VIII).

When that word is removed—for it is the sword of the Holy Spirit (Eph. VI)—the enemies, namely heretics and those who seize God’s churches, rightly become the leaders and grow rich in doctrines from the sacred Scriptures, because of the multitude of our iniquities.

Then there are “mute dogs,” because we have not been able to bark—that is, to defend the orthodox faith or to provide the people with the instruction in doctrine owed to them (Isa. LVI).

The little ones are said to be captives before the face of the one who afflicts them. Since they are little ones in doctrine, lacking rulers and defenders of the churches who would exercise pastoral concern and care for them, they are led—either captive by invisible enemies or certainly by visible ones—not less into error than into the shameful deeds of vices, before the face of the one who afflicts them.

Thus, enticed, they have those by whom they are led; bound by the chains of their sins, they already go before the face of the one who afflicts them, even unwillingly, unable to return or shake off the yoke of vices.

According to the moral understanding, the captivity of our soul is unhappy and greatly to be lamented, when its enemies have become its leaders after it has lost the freedom of Christ, and hostile spirits—having grown rich from our own powers—have become stronger. Hence we are piously warned: “If the spirit of one who possesses power rises against you, do not leave your place” (Eccl. X).
