Otherwise, if it had not first listened to its enemies when they were persuading it, they would never have become its leaders. Then, gradually, as the practice of vices increases, our adversaries grow richer and stronger from our evil acts, so that we cannot escape except by God’s help.

But how can we escape, when the merciful Lord, provoked by our evils—now on account of the punishment of sin and the vengeance for our iniquities—has spoken these things? He speaks once, according to Job, and does not repeat the same thing (Job XXXIII).

Nevertheless, we must not despair so completely or cease from the struggle, because only the little ones or the weak—or certainly the negligent—are captured in this way. Their captivity is utterly dreadful when you are dragged, entangled in many snares, unable to turn away from or cease the things you have badly begun, before the face of the one who afflicts you.

At times you see where you are being led and perceive from whom you are threatened, yet you cannot prevail in resisting or withstand them until, through God’s mercy, the bonds are broken and the captivity is again released.

Anyone who has been weakened and entangled in such bonds understands what I am saying: he wishes to free himself but cannot, while the punishment of sin now rages against him and enemies who have grown richer and stronger from his own powers attack him so forcefully that at times they even defile his good intention.

They possess it more completely insofar as they hold dominion over it from the beginning. Moreover, prolonged habit and the pleasures of the flesh often hinder and entice the resisting soul, according to what Solomon says in Proverbs: “Whoever indulges his servant from childhood will afterward find him rebellious” (Prov. XXIX).

He wishes to display the flesh and carnal desires, from which we are scarcely or never freed except by God’s grace. And the more difficult and harsh this is, the more those desires dominate the perverse mind as though they were superior and stronger at its head.

## VAU

“All her beauty has departed from the daughter of Zion. Her princes have become like rams without pasture.”

Vau is placed before this passage; it is interpreted as “and,” so that the meaning is that the things stated above and those now being said proceed from the reciprocal relation of punishments. Thus, through this letter, two sentences of God’s judgments are joined under a single copulative conjunction.

Besieged Jerusalem had externally lost all the beauty of her loveliness and delight; inwardly, her possessions had been stripped away, her temple and priesthood destroyed, and she herself was suffering from hunger and pestilence, sustained by no one. Her princes and rulers, their strength dissolved, as Moses had foretold in his curses, had hearts filled with fear and were considering not the defense of their citizens but flight. Before this final captivity, they had no pastures of Christ, whom they had killed; in sluggish torpor they were contemplating only their escape.

Mystically, however, all beauty departs from our Zion, that is, from the Church of Christ, which is truly called not only a daughter but also a bride. Concerning her it is said in the Song of Songs: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are like those of doves” (Song I); and shortly afterward: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song IV).

All beauty departs from her when, corrupted by the fury of heretics, the faith within is defiled. Concerning this faith the Psalm rightly sings: “You have put on confession and beauty, clothing yourself with light” (Ps. CIII).

But then her beauty is rightly mourned as having wholly departed when her rams—that is, her shepherds and rulers—do not find the pastures of life in the sacred volumes. They go without the strength of divine food wherever error drives them before the face of the one who afflicts them. Those who fail to lead the flock entrusted to them before themselves to the pastures of holy life, and who do not find those pastures themselves, having now become utterly insignificant, are driven into errors and go without the strength of virtues, held captive before the face of their enemies. Their end is destruction, because they set their minds on earthly things (Phil. III).

All beauty is found in the entire ecclesiastical order, but especially in Christ’s priests, the ministers of the sacred altar, and the virgins, who were previously mentioned as defiled. The loss of all beauty from these is rightly lamented when not only the rulers and ministers of the sheep but also the virginity of the faith that works through love (Gal. V) are stripped inwardly and outwardly. They show no concern for the cultivation of piety and no care for the holy virtues through meditation on the divine Law. Rather, at the prompting of the compelling enemy, they are led away by the luxury of their pleasures and by the various desires of their crimes.

The danger of this evil especially concerns those who, established in a position of rule, follow worldly desires rather than the footsteps of the commandments. By their examples and negligence they have destroyed not only themselves but also others.

Through the judgment that follows, the glory of their garments perishes and is darkened by wicked deeds. Thus the soul, enticed by evil morals, abandons its beauty when, through neglect of its thoughts, it loses the ornament of the virtues. Nor do its princes—namely, the rational movements of its mind or the interpretations of the teachings of the holy Scriptures, in which it ought to have resisted its pursuing and threatening enemies—come to its aid. Rather, with the strength of its virtues weakened and bound by the chains of its sins, it is driven into the pit of eternal confusion.

## ZAIN

“And Jerusalem remembered the days of her affliction and transgression, all her desirable things that she had possessed from ancient days, when her people fell into the hand of the enemy.”

Jerusalem is said to remember not for consolation but rather for increased pain and mourning, when her people fell into the hand of the enemy together with all her desirable things that she had possessed. For this is perfect vengeance: that you should suffer no less for the good things you once possessed and that enemies have plundered than for the evils they have inflicted upon you without any consolation.

This is Zain, which is noted at the beginning. The letter Zain is therefore said to sound forth this meaning: this is the divine and perfect vengeance for sins, long promised by the Lawgiver of the divine Law to the Jews, when they would fall into the hands of their enemies and no helper would be found for them. Indeed: “Her enemies saw her,” he says, “and mocked her Sabbaths.”

We too do this to the present day: when we see the Jews’ idle and superfluous Sabbaths, we mock them, because by killing and losing the one in whom they ought to have rested with true rest, they lost him.

This is, as we have said, the perfect recompense for sins: first to fall into the hands of enemies; then to remember continually not only the days of affliction but also the transgression, and to yearn for the use of all desirable good things. Thus from affliction a new pain is born each day, from transgression the sorrow of confusion, and from the good things once possessed the fire of incurable desires is continually rekindled. There is also the disgrace and derision of their religious observance among those who afflict them, as the passage proceeds to indicate concerning their dreadful cruelty.

What do you think that people could remember amid so many distresses? The days when it departed from Egypt with signs and wonders (Exod. XIV); when God was its leader and companion on the journey; when the pillar of fire went before it at night and the pillar of cloud by day; when manna flowed down for it from heaven (Exod. XVI); when the armies of angels encamped around it; or the many similar deeds done for that people which are recorded?

What do you think—that when they remembered all their desirable things, they could be weighed down by how many sorrows? According to the spiritual understanding, when our Jerusalem often sees that her people fall into the hand of hostile enemies and remembers the days of our transgression and the afflictions with which we are attacked by our enemies, what do you think is the magnitude of the mourning and groaning that threatens?

When one falls into crimes through pride, another through avarice, another through lust, and others through the pleasures of the world and the desires of the flesh; when she sees many falling daily into the hand of hostile enemies, what do you imagine the bride of Christ does amid so many crimes and losses of our wretchedness? How great are her lamentations and how many her tears on our behalf?

Then, when she remembers, filled with love, all the desirable things given to us in the heavens—the fellowship of all the saints—from which we fall away while she herself remains in exile, I ask you not to shrink from considering how much sorrow affects her. This is especially so since the solemn assembly and Sabbaths of our festivals are violated by us no less than they are mocked by our enemies, and since people frequently ask where or who our God is.

Hence one of the saints says: “My tears have been my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. XLI).

According to the moral understanding, the soul, even if late, then remembers all its desirable things when it sees itself hemmed in on every side by unclean spirits and all the affections of its heart falling into the hostile hand. Whatever in it seemed to stand more securely, it sees coming entirely to ruin for itself because of the devastation wrought by demons and the vengeance of divine judgment.

Then all the deeds of its transgression come before it. Then the memory of its worst affliction, through which it had wandered amid many crimes, comes forward—not to provide consolation but to increase its punishment, according to what the impious are said to declare in hell, as Scripture testifies:

“Therefore we wandered from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine upon us; the sun did not rise for us. We grew weary in the way of iniquity and destruction; we traveled difficult roads and did not know the way of the Lord. What did pride profit us, or what did the wealth of riches contribute to us? All those things passed away like a shadow of death; we were consumed in our wickedness” (Wis. V).

There is no doubt that the great spirits themselves mock the idleness which the negligent spend uselessly throughout the intervals of the present life. Hence it follows: “The enemies saw and mocked her.”

The enemies then mock the soul’s Sabbaths when the evil spirits themselves drag the leisure of our rest into unlawful thoughts. This must be carefully guarded against by monks and by those who appear to be free from worldly actions, lest they become occupied with vain pursuits and their Sabbaths be not only condemned by the judgment within but also mocked by their enemies.

Every soul that is believed to serve God while withdrawn from external actions serves their tyranny all the more by thinking unlawful thoughts. If our Sabbaths are mocked because of vain thoughts, we must greatly fear what should be done concerning those who, throughout the very course of life, also commit various crimes.

Therefore, if we wish to be free, let us be free for God alone, according to the saying: “Be still and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Ps. XXXIII).

## HETH

“Jerusalem sinned with sin; therefore she became unstable. All who glorified her despised her.”

At the beginning of this sentence he expressed the cause of the vengeance: because of the magnitude of her crimes, that Jerusalem which bore children into the servitude of exile merited destruction.

But we must ask what sin she committed, so unspeakably wicked that this one sin should be reckoned to her as an accumulation of condemnation covering all the others.

I think that this is also what the Lord says about the Jews in the Gospel: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John XV). What does he mean by saying, “They would not have sin”? Were they without sin before Christ came to them? Who, even among the most foolish, would say this?

Rather, there is a particular great sin: the sin that Jerusalem committed, and that the Jews had because Christ came and spoke to them. The statement must not be understood as referring to every sin. There is a certain sin that holds all sins together; if a person does not possess it, all sins are forgiven him.

This is plainly the sin of unbelief, by which that people was always held captive while worshiping idols. They refused to believe in Christ, who came for the very purpose that people might believe in him. This sin they would not have had if he had not come (John XV). His coming became as salutary to believers as it became destructive to unbelievers.

Hence, when the Lord saw that city, he wept over it, saying: “If you had known—even you,” with “you would have wept” understood. Then he announces the cause of his weeping: “They will not leave in you a stone upon a stone, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation” (Luke XIX).

Because Jerusalem did not recognize it, and because she had always remained idolatrous and unbelieving, she became unstable, and not one stone was left upon another in her. “And all who glorified her despised her,” because they saw her disgrace, according to Isaiah: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy—or disturb—the way of your steps” (Isa. III).

He wishes to indicate the scribes and Pharisees, whom the same prophet called exactors, not teachers, and also called mockers above. Because of the gifts that blind even the wise, they not only failed to correct the sinners among the people but, for the sake of riches and their own advantages, extolled them with great praises. Conversely, the sinful people called them blessed and pillars of God’s house, and used the other expressions that flatterers customarily utter.

“She,” he says, “groaning, turned backward.” He describes the condition of captives: while they go before the face of those following them, they frequently look back in grief toward the soil of their homeland, thinking about and groaning over the sweetness of the things left behind.

According to the anagogical sense, whenever our Jerusalem is corrupted by some heresy in its members, because it has sinned with sin, it wanders unstable and is fixed nowhere with any solidity of faith. Although it seemed to be founded upon the solidity of the rock, which is Christ, it was unwilling to remain in him.

Those who glorified them with popular affection, when they see their disgrace exposed and trampled underfoot by orthodox and truly catholic people, despise and detest them, abhorring the fact that they have turned backward.

But since Heth is placed before this sapphic stanza and is interpreted as “life,” we must ask how “life” can rightly be set at the beginning of a passage in which nothing but the destruction and punishment of sin is announced. The answer is that it signifies what the end of this lament indicates: from the beginning of this work, it is the prophet who groans and speaks.

Now, according to the tropological sense, the soul’s life after the fall into sin, after bonds and captivity, is not to direct itself always toward Babylon—that is, toward the confusion of vices—and to go into foreign darkness, but to look backward toward the light and toward the homeland from which it has been led away captive, sighing continually in grief.

The unhappy or unstable condition results from the sin of faithlessness, through which the soul is dragged in different directions. Otherwise, if it always kept its steps fixed upon the rock of the virtues, neither the force of winds nor the rivers of storms would drive it from the station of its faith.

Sometimes, however, it happens that the soul, full of filth and despised because of the disgrace of its confusion, looks back at what it had lost and, even late, groans. This is life: to look from darkness toward the light, from the confusion of sins—that is, from Babylon—toward that heavenly Jerusalem; to groan while looking backward, and to turn one’s steps from vices toward virtues.

For it is not always evil to return backward and to hear the voice of the one who warns from behind, according to what Isaiah confesses: “Your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the word of one warning from behind you” (Isa. XXX).

Because we have turned our backs on him, the merciful and compassionate Lord does not disdain to recall us from behind, though angered by our evils, so that we may turn our face toward him as though backward and return to the place from which we fell.

Hence the angel says in the Apocalypse of John: “Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do your former works” (Rev. II). This is the soul’s groaning backward: to return to him through daily lamentation and to fulfill works filled with love.

When Mary doubted the Lord’s resurrection and, looking into the tomb, fixed her attention upon the angels seated in white, she did not find Jesus whom she was seeking until she looked backward. Hence the Evangelist says: “She turned backward and saw Jesus standing” (John XX).

He was standing behind her, at least so that he might warn her from behind, while she had turned away. When she turned backward in grief, she immediately saw the one she was seeking—the one whom she had previously believed dead with the Jews.

Thus that Jerusalem which is mourned for having sinned with the sin of impiety, because many from among it recognize Christ and believe, groaning as they turn backward toward him, soon found in the Law the one whom it had thought dead.

But those who freely resolved to go to the right hand remain unstable to this day, wandering here and there. Thus, like Cain, they carry the sign of their disgrace (Gen. IV), and as perpetual captives they are dragged to Babylon, that is, into confusion.

Therefore, soul, I would have you awaken at last. Do not, I beg you, though you are submerged in the depths of evils, disdain to remember from where you fell, sighing backward toward the works of virtue that you had abandoned.

If you ask, “From where?”—from heaven, certainly, where our citizenship is said to be. Hence Paul says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III).

Remember the name you gave when you entered into the grace of baptism and sent it to be carefully inscribed in the book of life. If you recognize that you have fallen and suppose that your name has been erased because of the evils pressing upon you; if you have directed your attention to nothing but darkness and death, look backward, turn around, and listen in grief to the voice of the one warning you from behind (Isa. XXX). I assure you that you will soon find life—namely, Jesus standing by you.

If you do not cease to follow him in faith as he ascends to the Father, you will find that same life placed there from which you had fallen.

## TETH
Its uncleanness is on its feet, and she did not remember her end. She has been utterly deposed, having no comforter.

She continues the lament she has begun, because Jerusalem has become exceedingly unstable. Therefore, like travelers always on the move, [Col. 1079D] she laments that she has uncleanness on her feet—not that so great a prophet mourns her merely because she literally had dirty feet, which would seem quite frivolous, but because, according to the inner person, she has polluted steps. Hence he says, “Her uncleanness is on her feet.”

The Synagogue, moreover, had feet of its own: namely, those who ought to have carried her along the way—which is Christ—toward every incentive to virtue. Since these feet certainly bore her uncleanness, that is, crimes and sins, she did not remember her end. For this reason she was utterly deposed, from the throne of her kingdom to the disgrace of so great a captivity.

He laments her in two ways, or even three: either because that great nation committed such offenses against God, or because, on account of them, it endured such wicked disasters in the present without the fruit of repentance. Then, what is more serious, [Col. 1080A] after the scourges, because she was unwilling to return to God, she drew upon herself more atrocious punishments. Hence also he says, “She did not remember her end.” Now, “the end of the law is Christ for righteousness” (Rom. X). Everything that she suffered came from this: she was unwilling to remember or receive him who is the end of that same law—of its very name unto grace—and also the end of the whole consummation of the age unto perfection.

For this reason, after suffering such evils, she finally cries out with her own voice, “See, Lord, my affliction, for my enemy has become exalted.” From the beginning of this lament up to this passage, the prophet’s words have been lamentations. From here onward, however, she herself begins to mourn her sins, or the punishments of her retribution. Therefore, I think that the letter Teth is rightly placed here: for Teth is interpreted as “good.” “It is good,” says the prophet, “that you have humbled me” (Ps. CXVIII).

[Col. 1080B] Thus Jerusalem, having been utterly humbled in every respect, no longer has the prophet weeping for her, but herself cries out with immense mourning, saying, “See, Lord, my affliction.” Then, in judicial fashion, she wishes to arouse God the judge to zeal and hatred against her enemies: “For my enemy,” she says, “has become exalted.” It is as though she were saying: “He has become proud against you, because he does not judge what has been done to me as the result of your judgment, but attributes it to his own strength and praises his own gods. Therefore, first see my cruel affliction, and not the crimes for which I suffer these things; then see that my enemy has risen up against me.”

[Col. 1080C] Mystically, however, our Jerusalem bears uncleanness on her feet, because in the solitude of this life no one walks without the squalor of vices, at least upon the feet with which we press the earth. Hence, when the Lord was giving his disciples the pattern of humility, he washed their feet and commanded them to wash one another’s feet (John XIII), so that we might understand the discipline of humility in this dusty life, in which no one walks without uncleanness.

For this reason, elsewhere also (Matt. X; Isa. LII; Rom. X), he commands the apostles to shake the dust from their feet, although, according to the Apostle, the feet of those who evangelize good things and proclaim peace are called beautiful. He wished the apostles, or apostolic men, to be understood—men whose feet, as I have said, the Lord washed so that they might be beautiful and clean for preaching, and so that they might run throughout the whole world, clean and beautiful, and quickly fill the world with the teaching of Christ.

[Col. 1080D] Of these preachers Christ plainly says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “How beautiful are your steps in your sandals, daughter of a prince” (Song VII). They are praised as beautiful because they run along the way of God’s commandments and provide guidance to the other members of the Church—not through the nakedness of their own will, but through the fortification and protection of divine restoration. Hence their steps are praised as beautiful in sandals, and their feet are commanded to be shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace (Eph. VI).

Otherwise, the grieving elect rightly lament the reprobate life of the priests at the present time, and say that the uncleanness of Christ’s bride is on her feet, and that she has not remembered her end. For if their fault were wholly their own, the ruin of the entire Church would not have occurred. They too have their own beauty, but not that beauty which comes from the Lord and is praised.

[Col. 1081A] Therefore, whenever the bridegroom comes, knocking at the door of the Church, he finds her either afflicted by many tribulations, or secure and overflowing with excessive delights and occupied with works of the flesh. Through these things the enemy has entered her, shut the door of her heart, and left no place for the bridegroom to enter, when he says: “Open to me, my sister, my beloved, my dove, my undefiled, for my head is full of dew” (Song V), along with the rest that follows.

How often, indeed, evil priests, lulled by such flatteries, fail to understand that she is Christ’s sister and beloved; they do not strive to rouse her so that, with steadfast heart, she may mourn the coming of her bridegroom and remain simple as a dove and undefiled. [Col. 1081B] Rather, if she herself speaks—not in words about such men and on behalf of such men, but in action—she says: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on again? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” (Ibid.) For an utterly evil habit is scarcely, or never, removed.

Thus teachers stripped of the tunic of charity, which alone covers the uncleanness of sins, grow sluggish, as though some delicate girl, having bathed and removed her garments, were unwilling to rise from her bed of rest and abandon the pleasures of her wicked habit. In the same way, having been stripped of the tunic of love of God and neighbor, such men do not wish to put it on again; they do not wish to direct once more toward preparation for the Gospel, with great contrition of heart, the feet that they had once withdrawn from the narrow way through the evil habit of pleasures and sloth, as though those feet had been washed with water. [Col. 1081C] They find every lowliness and contempt of the world hateful, together with all the examples and rigor of the saints and the discipline of Christ’s poverty (Eph. VI).

Although they may rest softly, carefully tending their bodies, they nevertheless bear the uncleanness of vices on their feet. Hence the choir of the saints, lamenting, says: “Her uncleanness is on her feet, and she did not remember her end.” For if such people remembered their end—namely, the judgments—they would never stray so far from the way, even though it is called narrow.

“Therefore,” he says, “she has been utterly deposed, having no comforter.” For even if they seem to stand adorned with the insignia of their pleasures, they have already been deposed in the sight of the divine majesty, having not the Holy Spirit as comforter—though they ought to have comforted others and delivered them from every distress.

[Col. 1081D] In the tropological sense, the soul has uncleanness on its feet when, polluted by the uncleanness of vices, it has lost the throne of heavenly life and the brightness of its former way of life. Of it Isaiah rightly says: “Rise up, Jerusalem; shake yourself free from the dust; rise up and sit” (Isa. LII). For it cannot happen that a soul which has exposed its ways outside to passersby and associated itself with earthly actions should not have uncleanness on its feet.

Hence one of the saints says: “Our soul has been humbled in the dust; our belly has clung to the earth” (Ps. XLIII). From these uncleannesses, then, our feet must be washed daily, lest we perhaps forget our end and be deposed to the disgrace of our faults, without any comforter within.

[Col. 1082A] Let the soul speak, and let the Church also, soiled or deposed by dusty actions, say: “See, Lord, my affliction, with which my enemy afflicts me without cease; consider not my sin in order to punish me, but the affliction by which I am afflicted, so that I may be delivered. For my enemy has become exalted: he does not attribute his success to your judgments, but mocks you as though you were unable to deliver me.”

Hence the prophet David says: “Many say to my soul, ‘There is no salvation for him in his God’” (Ps. III). Therefore the soul now implores with a great groan: “See, Lord,” and the rest that follows.

## JOD

“The enemy stretched out his hand toward all her desirable things, for she saw the nations entering her sanctuary, concerning whom you had commanded that they should not enter your Church.”

[Col. 1082B] As far as I understand, Jod is rightly placed here, so that we may know that this was the beginning of the ruin of Jerusalem and of those souls: the Lord saw the nations entering his sanctuary—namely, unclean spirits and carnal passions—concerning whom he had previously commanded that they should not enter his Church.

Therefore, because nations of unclean thoughts first entered their souls, the enemy boldly and powerfully stretched out his hand toward all her desirable things, that is, toward the Holy of Holies, which no one except the priests was permitted to enter once a year with blood (Exod. XXX). He stretched out his hand, took away all the vessels of beauty, and profaned God’s sanctuary; he prostituted, cast down, and polluted the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies (Ezek. XXIII).

[Col. 1082C] For previously, because of the enormity of their crimes, the Lord rejected the things in which he had dwelt among men, delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hands of the enemy. “He shut up his people to the sword and rejected his inheritance” (Ps. LXXVII).

According to the anagogical sense, even though we have briefly mingled these matters together, Christ’s bride Jerusalem, who is our mother, also has her desirable things, from which those who are opposed to her are not permitted to eat. The enemy sometimes stretches out his hand toward them, because nations first enter God’s sanctuary, embracing the foreskin of the flesh and lacking the circumcision of Christ—namely, wicked ministers of the altar or heretics, who provoke the eyes of the divine majesty still more to offense.

[Col. 1082D] Because of their sins and errors, the enemy stretches out his hand toward all her desirable things: he contaminates faith in the undivided Trinity, cuts apart baptism, handles the body and blood of Christ unworthily, corrupts his teaching, and, like a wolf ravaging the sheep of Christ, destroys all the precious vessels—that is, the sheep of Christ. This is the beginning of so great a crime: the unworthy enter the Church of God.

This evil, however, falls upon those leaders who, although they could prevent such things from happening, neglect to do so. Tropologically, the prophet and holy men also lament the soul, which is contaminated by perverse thoughts and wicked pleasures when they enter it, although they had no right to touch it. Those thoughts and pleasures destroy the sign of our circumcision, which is the sign of faith, and the sanctuary of so great a profession is polluted by the foreskin of an uncircumcised mind.

[Col. 1083A] Then, once the temple of the heart has been profaned by vices, the enemy finally stretches out his hand boldly toward all its desirable things and removes all its ornaments of virtue. Sometimes he first weakens faith, then takes away judgment, empties the treasures of the whole majesty of God, stirs up incentives to vice, and sharpens the poison.

Then, while the mind deliberates whether it should open to those who knock, he sometimes changes hope and, in place of hope for all invisible things—which are not seen but are believed—promises hope of future repentance, while carnal pleasure has already been enticed. Thus, as though made more secure, the soul is stripped of love of God and neighbor; then all the armor of faith is removed, its strength is overthrown, and thereafter the enemy does not fear stretching out his hand toward everything.

[Col. 1083B] Then modesty is corrupted, chastity violated, and that chief cook, the prince of cooks, intensifies the concupiscence of gluttony in order to destroy and inflame all the walls of the soul. He gouges out the eyes of prudence, tears the garment of justice, removes peace and concord, strikes down gentleness, crushes moderation, inflames kindness, and finally takes away the sword of the Holy Spirit. Thus, as though she had been stripped of all good things, he leaves the wretched soul without a comforter and naked in her own blood.

## CAPH

[Col. 1083C] “All her people groan, seeking bread. They gave their most precious things for food to revive the soul.”

See what benefit came from the prophet’s having mourned Jerusalem as one who was not himself mourning: above, the grieving prophet complains that he had mourned certain parts of her as though they were her nobler members. Now, however, after receiving the life-giving Spirit, all the people are said to groan.

For this reason a hen warms her eggs, and by her heat they are, as it were, brought to life together, so that everything within may be formed for life. In the same way spiritual men are accustomed to give life to, cherish, or lament those who do not know why they are being lamented.

The divine books make clear how many evils the Jewish people endured through famine, pestilence, and slaughter, and Josephus’s history does not keep silent about it. The whole people, oppressed by evils, groaned, and no one could enumerate the precious things they gave to revive the soul—not because the soul is nourished by such foods, but because he uses “soul” for the present life, as in other passages where this usage is found.

[Col. 1083D] Spiritually, however, the interpretation is sound. All the people are said to mourn when they suffer hunger for the word of God and seek from teachers the bread that descended from heaven, but it is not found (John VI). Those who see this evil grieve and groan, because they gave their most precious things for food: they lost heavenly things for earthly, eternal things for transitory ones. “To revive,” he says, “the soul,” not to satisfy it, because all such things can for the present revive the wretched soul, inflamed with countless desires, but can never satisfy it.

[Col. 1084A] Hence all the people are said to groan and seek bread, because the perverse multitude of human beings is afflicted and, as though tortured, suffers when it is not filled according to its desire with the delights and pleasures of the present life.

Tropologically, every soul gives precious things for food when it inclines the virtues of the mind toward the appetite for transitory pleasure and strives to revive itself by attempting to satisfy its perverse desires. Hence every people is lamented as groaning and seeking bread, because although they have given all their precious virtues for food, none of the passions of their desires is satisfied by sight, taste, or the other senses.

Therefore, if any virtues have returned inward to the soul, or if the soul itself has been restored by the Spirit of God together with the whole multitude of the elect, it is rightly said to cry out in lament: “See, Lord, and consider, for I have become vile” (Job XIX). It is as though one said: “I have therefore become vile, because the hand of the Lord has touched me.” This, they say, is what Caph signifies among the Hebrews.

[Col. 1084B] When, therefore, the hand of the Lord touches either to punish or to relieve punishments, or indeed to instruct the wretched soul and the negligent Church, the returning voice rightly says in its own words: “See, Lord” (as we said above), not the crimes of my sins, but the evils and punishments that I suffer; and consider the work belonging to you, for I have become vile.

[Col. 1084C] The people of God become vile when, as the number of the wicked increases, they pursue within the Church not the highest and heavenly things, but whatever is lowly and earthly. The soul, previously corrupted by many pleasures and wrongly exulting, lifted up by the arrogance of vices, recognizes itself as having become vile when the hand of the Lord touches it—although it was formerly created in the image of its Creator.

Otherwise, unless the hand of the Lord touched it, it would never return to such humility and groaning before its Creator. Therefore Caph, which is interpreted as “hand,” is not inappropriately placed here, although the meaning is indicated only implicitly. And so that you may understand what I have said, listen to the cry of lamentation that follows.

## LAMED

“O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow. For he has harvested me, and he has spoken in the day of his anger.”

[Col. 1084D] The letter Lamed is placed first because Lamed signifies discipline or the heart. We must see whether such a great sorrow over sins or crimes, and such a conversion of the heart, is not prophetic discipline.

For first, after the laments, she is read as having turned backward above; then, little by little, as though she had returned to her senses once and then again, she begins to cry out in her own voice: “See, Lord,” she says, “my affliction,” and the rest that follows. In one of these passages, however, playing poetically with the meter, she concludes at the end: “For my enemy has become exalted”; in the other she ends with: “For I have become vile.”

Now, as though her strength had been restored, some Sion has been raised from the citadel of the mind to the height of a summit, and from there looks down. “O all you,” she says, “who pass by the way.”

[Col. 1085A] Literally, this is recognized as proper to mourners, who judge their own suffering greater than that of others to the degree that they have taken less care to understand the suffering of others. The more deeply they feel their own pain, the less they agree that the pain of others should be compared with theirs.

Nevertheless, if any remnants had been saved before the Lord, they rightly cried out together with the people when all sanctification was abandoned and destroyed; the altars of incense and burnt offerings were demolished; the temple was razed to the ground; their psaltery was brought low; the hymn fell silent; all rejoicing was dissolved; the light of the lampstand was extinguished; the ark of the covenant was plundered; all holy things were contaminated; the most precious vessels were carried away to foreigners; and, most grievously, the name of God that had been invoked over them was profaned. The books, moreover, were burned to the disgrace of the sacred law; the priests and Levites were taken captive; virgins were wickedly violated; women suffered adultery.

[Col. 1085B] Then the just, together with the impious and wicked, were carried away to destruction; infants were dashed to pieces; young men were crowned with servitude; and the strong were made weak. The greatest of all these signs was that Sion herself, expelled from her glory, was delivered into the hands of the impious, who had always hated both her and God.

Let those whose minds are capable of seeing consider whether, in circumstances such as these, that choir and holy city could refrain from wailing, when the people were losing heavenly things no less than earthly ones, along with prosperity and the pleasures of luxury. For the Lord had harvested her in his just judgment, stripping her of all good things in the day of his wrath, as he had spoken in the curses of his law and in the utterances of the prophets.

[Col. 1085C] But let us consider our Sion, whose citizenship, according to the Apostle, is in heaven (Phil. III). Let us see how, placed upon the earth, she looks down from the lofty summit of heaven upon her members and sees all the things we have mentioned concerning that earthly Sion fulfilled—or daily being fulfilled—in us.

Therefore she cries out to those who pass by the way, weeping and wailing: “O all you,” she says, “who pass by the way.” And who are those who pass by the way, or what is the way by which they pass, unless they are certainly the saints, of whom David sings: “Going they went and wept, casting their seeds” (Ps. CXXV)?

As the elect go forward, although they may seem to be occupied with many affairs, they are always traveling the road they must travel, since whatever they do, they do with faith for the love of heaven. Then, along the way—which is Christ (John XIV)—following his footsteps and turning neither to the right nor to the left, they hasten onward.

[Col. 1085D] For having been called to the paschal feast and celebrating paschal vows, they hasten to eat the lamb, as was commanded in the law (Exod. XII). When the Church sees them walking along the royal way toward their homeland, she herself, pregnant because she nourishes and gives birth to children, impeded by many cares for her little ones, cries out in grief and groaning:

“O all you”—not in order to delay them on the way, but to invite them to the gifts of charity—“attend,” she says in your minds, “and see with the gaze of love whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow.”

[Col. 1086A] For according to the saying of our Redeemer in the Gospel, “When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow” (John XVI). This bride of Christ, a virgin because she gives birth and brings forth, nourishes and suckles, the mother of us all, is saddened in sorrow and mourns in humility, because she sees that almost all are going toward destruction and the ruin of life.

Some are endangered even unto death; others she pursues as she gives birth; some tender ones she suckles; others, made harsh, she scarcely recalls to the ways of life; she waits for others who are unwilling and sluggish to go; others, rushing headlong, she chastises so that they may go with her, lest the enemy perhaps find them outside the camp. For all these who pass by the way are fighting in the camp together with Christ’s bride.

Of her the Song of Songs says: “Who is this that rises through the desert like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army in battle array?” (Song VI.)

[Col. 1086B] To these, then, who pass by or ascend, a voice comes from the higher members: “O all you, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow.” For there are some things for which I groan on behalf of all these; others which I endure on behalf of those who are within or outside; and still others which I suffer because I am delayed by longing.

For these and other such losses I appeal to you: you who have a heart, attend—even though tireless devotion is carrying you toward the prize of the heavenly calling (Phil. III). See, I beg you, my sorrow. According to the pattern shown to me, I wished to bring forth and join together the children whom I had begotten, but they wander, despise, or languish, and few make the journey successfully.

For them I am drawn in different directions (II Cor. XI): “I am weak with the weak, and I burn with those who are scandalized. I became as a Jew to the Jews, and I became all things to all people.” Yet I cannot lead everyone forward to better things; therefore I lament without ceasing even those who have sinned and have not repented.

[Col. 1086C] I am stretched by great concern for all the Churches of God; I rejoice with those who rejoice, and I also weep with those who weep (Rom. XII). Therefore I beg you: attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow, especially on behalf of such people, because I am delayed on their account.

Raise your eyes to the time of the final judgment, and see that on the day of his wrath the Lord reaped or harvested me, as he had spoken, when he would repay each person according to his works. Therefore he delivered the multitude of chaff and straw, together with all the weeds or whatever had degenerated from the true seed, to unquenchable fire (Matt. XIII; III).

Let it not seem absurd to you, reader, that we have interpreted the past tense as referring to the future, following the custom of the prophets. For things that are future are already present with God in the manner in which they are future; therefore, in the divine Scriptures, past events are very often understood in place of future ones.

[Col. 1086D] Morally, however, the soul sees itself weighed down by vices, yet not so blinded or deposed that it cannot see others hastening with immense longing toward the heavenly homeland by steps of virtue—or rather, not merely hastening or passing by, but even flying with the greatest speed. They have wings like those of a silvered dove, and the backs of their wings are golden pale (Ps. LXVII).

When any soul, as we have said, oppressed by the evils of sins, sees such people walking—or rather flying—well along the way of virtue, what do you think the languishing soul says? If it has eyes with which to see and a heart with which to understand, does it not immediately cry out with a great grief, even though corrupted by evil habits:

[Col. 1087A] “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see with what wounds I lie wounded, with what evils I am tortured, with what bonds I am bound, with what burdens of crimes I am weighed down, and by what things I have been weakened and enticed. I fall daily into sufferings, because the Lord, in his just judgment, when my sins pressed upon me, harvested me as he had spoken.

For the punishment of sin, I have not merely lost all the good things of virtue with which the bridegroom adorned me; I have also turned backward and, from the highest summit of heaven, sought the depths of hell. He delivered me, provoked by my evils, on the day of his wrath into a reprobate mind, so that I might do things that are not fitting (Rom. I).

[Col. 1087B] Therefore, entangled in so many crimes, I beg you—all you who despise the present life, who do not set your steps firmly upon it and do not regard it as a way, you who have chosen for yourselves the way that is Christ (John XIV)—all you who pass by, consider whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow. Enticed by evils, I have lost heavenly and eternal things, and have stored up such dreadful punishments for myself on the day of wrath.”

But if I still seem to have something of virtue in the womb of my mind, as though pregnant, and wish to nourish these affections, I immediately hear the bridegroom crying out: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse” (Matt. XXIV). For, burdened by the stench of my own sins, I cannot fly with you—or rather, I cannot even walk.

Hence what follows:

## MEM

“From on high he sent fire into my bones, and he instructed me. He spread a net for my feet; he turned me backward. He made me desolate, exhausted with grief all day long.”

[Col. 1087C] That he sent fire from heaven into the bones of Jerusalem indicates heavenly vengeance. Perhaps this is the fire of which we read in Job (chap. I): the fire of God that descended from heaven, struck the sheep, and consumed the young men, indicating heavenly powers who have been given power to torment them even to this day.

The fire is rightly said to have been sent into the bones, so that all the things of the Jews that seemed strong, possessed inwardly and outwardly, might be instructed through scourges. They had previously been unwilling to hear God’s loving admonitions, and so they might learn to whom they must henceforth be entirely subject. Hence he says, “And he instructed me.”

[Col. 1087D] “He spread a net for my feet,” because he did not permit them, after their pleasures and the desires of their hearts, to proceed prosperously all the way to the end. Rather, he turned them backward, so that they might experience the pains and harshest troubles of tribulation on account of their wicked inventions.

As for the statement that she was made desolate and exhausted with grief all day long, the very appearance of the matter proves that the Jews will remain desolate all day long—that is, until the end of the age—worn out by the grief of their distress.

According to the allegorical sense, however, those among them who believed, or our Jerusalem, which has been formed as one from the nations, rightly says: “From on high he sent fire into my bones,” so that all the strong things of virtue might be strengthened inwardly in the Church; so that she might be divinely instructed and no longer serve idols or take pleasure in the various blandishments of the world.

[Col. 1088A] This is what the letter Mem signifies: Mem is interpreted as “from them.” From the gifts of the Holy Spirit, therefore, which have been sent through fire, Christ’s Church, rejoicing in her bones, groans that he instructed her in the teaching of chaste love; and from those same gifts she is confounded and ashamed of the errors and vices that she had previously served wickedly.

“He spread a net for my feet,” he says, “and turned me backward.” Certainly he spread the net of holy preaching before the feet of God’s elect, so that they would not follow after the vanities of error and the desires of life (II Pet. II); thus he turned them so that they would go backward after him.

He entrusted this net to the apostles to spread (Luke V), or to apostolic men—not only so that they might draw the one who laments back to the way of truth, but also so that they might entangle and capture people and turn them backward.

Hence one of the elect says: “I have kept my feet from every evil way” (Ps. CXVIII).

[Col. 1088B] But how did he make her desolate, when she had been enriched with such great gifts? The answer is that the Church now appears desolate because she does not seek present goods but eternal ones. She has been made desolate of all those things that she previously pursued, and all day long she is exhausted by the grief of sorrow and love. Hence, above, she also sends out immense cries of tears to those who pass by: “O all you,” and the rest that follows.

Moreover, when the soul is subject to sins and is sometimes corrected by the Lord on account of its iniquities, it returns inwardly to itself and is pierced by salutary grief. It is then as though fire has come from on high into its bones—that is, into the thoughts of its marrow. Touched by God, it is chastened and instructed in divine disciplines.

[Col. 1088C] And because it perceives the nets of God’s teachings spread before its feet, it turns backward by abstaining from what is unlawful. It changes its former luxury of pleasures and its desires into tears, and, binding itself more firmly, laments, exhausted by the grief of mourning. It is unwilling to receive the harmful consolation of the present life, all the more intensely because it recognizes that it has wandered for so long through various desires and with such wickedness.

## NUN
The yoke of my iniquities kept watch in his hand: they were rolled together and laid upon my neck.

She laments, therefore, that the yoke of her iniquities kept watch in the Lord’s hand, because the time of delayed vengeance had finally come upon her. [Col. 1088D] Thus, as it were, the yoke of their iniquity was asleep when they rested securely and without punishment in the torpor of wickedness. But it kept watch in the Lord’s hand, according to what this same prophet answered when the Lord asked him, saying: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” And he said: “I see a watchful rod.” The Lord said to him: “You have seen well, because I too shall watch over my word, to carry it out” (Jer. I). For although sins lie hidden while we are torpid, they always keep watch in the Lord’s hand, accusing us so that we may receive the vengeance of just retribution.

Hence the Lord said to Cain, when he denied it: “What have you done? Behold,” he said, “the voice of your brother Abel’s blood cries out to me from the earth” (Gen. IV). “And they were rolled together,” he says—that is, iniquities of such weight that I am crushed beneath them—“and laid upon my neck.” How rightly, I say, instead of a golden necklace (Isa. III), Jerusalem is surrounded by a cord of iniquity around her neck and pressed down as by a yoke, so that the vigor of virtue fails: for she groans that the mass of sins, which she accumulated over a long period through various transgressions, crushes and constricts her almost to suffocation. Hence it is written: “Each person is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. V).

And therefore the strength of the Jews was weakened, and the Lord gave them into a hand from which, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, they will not be able to rise (Rom. XI). This is also declared by the letter Nun, which is interpreted as “everlasting.” For everlasting is their yoke, and the weakness of transgression and the captivity of perpetual condemnation—those who, if they could sin without end, resolved to do so. [Col. 1089B]

According to the mystical meanings of allegory, the Church groans whenever she is subjected to innumerable temptations, because the yoke of her iniquities has kept watch in the Lord’s hand. For this reason she is subjected within and without to affliction by both visible and invisible enemies. Having lost the jewels that she had received from her bridegroom as ornaments (Cant. I), she groans over her iniquities. Hence she says: “They were rolled together and laid upon my neck.”

Isaiah had long before spoken what the Lord had said: “Because the daughters of Zion were exalted, and walked with outstretched necks, and went about with the glances of their eyes, clapping and walking, and advancing with measured step on their feet” (Isa. III), all their ornaments would be taken away. Among these, prophetic speech describes necklaces and jewels, all of which must be referred to virtues. The necklaces, hanging down as far as the breast, signify understanding and the ruling faculty of the mind in the heart; the jewels signify, in a single expression, all the ornaments of the virtues.

When these have been lost, ecclesiastical men are stripped of such ornaments: for they walk with womanly affectation, with outstretched necks and speaking through the gestures of their eyes; they clap with their hands and their feet, and advance with measured step, pursuing the glory of the world and the many other things mentioned above. There is no doubt that the yoke of their iniquities keeps watch in the Lord’s hand, by which they are rightly pressed down and dragged along, since they have stripped themselves of such great ornaments of virtue.

Hence the iniquities rolled together in an unbreakable cord are lamented by the Church, because they have been laid upon her neck—that is, upon her members—perhaps for suffocation, just as we read that Judas hanged himself with a noose (Acts I), or for being dragged away to punishment. Hence, lamenting, she says: “My strength is weakened; the Lord has given me into a hand from which I shall not be able to rise.” For the final vengeance awaiting all the impious and sinners will occur at the end of their calamity, and the torments will never cease, since in the outer darkness “their worm does not die, and the fire is not extinguished” (Isa. LXVI). Once a person enters there, he is no longer permitted to depart, as the Lord indicates: “You shall not go out from there,” he says, “until you have paid the last penny” (Matt. V)—that is, until each soul has paid its debts for its sins.

For just as the preceding statement, beginning with Mem—that is, “from these things which the Lord sent from heaven”—turned her backward toward repentance, so, because of the yoke of iniquities that kept watch in the Lord’s hand, although judgments had been removed from her sight, she stored up wrath for herself on the day of wrath (Rom. II). Nun, which signifies “everlasting,” struck her, so that the meaning is this: by the just judgment of God, the person who gathers wrath for himself through an unrepentant heart incurs everlasting punishment, from whose hand he will not be able to rise. This does not mean that the Church, foreknown and predestined, is to be handed over to such punishments, but that whatever happens in her members she attributes to herself. Therefore she laments and mourns that such dreadful things have happened to her.

The tropological meaning is evident: the yoke of iniquity keeps watch in the hand of the Lord over the soul that has submitted itself to vices and crimes, unless it sets them daily before its eyes in repentance. Hence David also says: “My sin is always before me” (Ps. L). He himself wished to keep watch in opposition, so that he might wash it away with tears; therefore he had continually set it before himself. And so that the yoke of his iniquities, which he himself had placed upon his neck, might not keep watch in the Lord’s hand, he said, weeping and groaning: “Turn your face away from my sins and blot out all my iniquities” (ibid.).

It is as though he said: “I do not want them to keep watch in your hand; consign them to oblivion, and let them always stand before me, so that they may be punished with tears and make me keep vigil.” But because the wretched soul sometimes lies in a falsely secure state, it consigned to oblivion, through its impenitence of heart, the yoke of iniquities that it had woven for itself. It keeps watch, however, in the Lord’s hand, because no sin will go unpunished.

Thus the just Judge will soon restore the iniquities rolled together around its neck to the person who has consigned them to oblivion, so that he may bear what he stored up for himself. Finally, he is handed over to the hand from which no one who has once entered can rise, because, while he was able to foresee the everlasting punishments which the present element announces, he did not wish to do so. [Col. 1090B]

## SAMECH

The Lord has removed all my mighty ones from my midst. He summoned a time against me to crush my chosen ones.

There is no doubt that these things happened more fully to the Jews in that final captivity, when no prophet is believed to have remained among them; no priest to offer sacrifices, no scribe learned in the Law whose teaching could instruct them. Thus Daniel laments, saying: “Lord, there is not,” he says, “at this time a prince, or prophet, or leader, or burnt offering, or sacrifice, or incense, or place of firstfruits before you, so that we may find mercy” (Dan. III).

But these things, as I have said, are better referred to that final captivity, because in the captivity that occurred under the Chaldeans, it is beyond doubt that Daniel was among them, and Ezekiel also began to prophesy there, together with the other prophets. Therefore, in the final period under Titus and Vespasian, all the mighty ones—something Samech indicates—were taken away from Judah.

Samech signifies “help.” At that time, therefore, all help departed from them, when not only were all their mighty ones led away captive, according to Isaiah—“I will take away,” he says, “from Jerusalem the strong and mighty, every strength of bread and every strength of water, the prince and the captain of fifty, and the counselor,” speaking mystically (Isa. III)—and all those whom we considered it too lengthy to enumerate above, but after Christ’s Passion all graces and gifts were also taken away from them. At that time, too, we read that the angels themselves cried out at the gates of Jerusalem: “Let us depart from these dwellings” (Josephus).

Moreover, mystically, whenever our Jerusalem is oppressed by tribulations and troubles, whenever she is harassed by persecutions or attacked by the enemies of heretics, there is no doubt that she laments, saying: “The Lord has removed all my mighty ones from my midst.” So great is this deprivation that we read that often, throughout the whole world, only a few bishops or mighty priests remained who could rightly defend the Catholic faith with sound teaching.

As for her groaning because the time was summoned against her to crush her chosen ones, among whom there was no defense of faith or teaching, this does not mean that time was contracted for another purpose. Rather, because her sins demanded it, the cause was the vengeance of God. Whenever this occurs, she mourns, laments, and groans. [Col. 1091B]

According to the tropological sense, the soul mourns that all its mighty ones have been taken away when it perceives that the sound faculties of virtue within it have been taken captive. Against it the Lord then summoned the time of vengeance, when he removes his divine help. This, as we have said, is what Samech signifies. Once that help has been removed, the enemy immediately leads the soul captive to vices and from the state of right faith and good conduct into the confusion of error. By removing from the sight of its heart, through forgetfulness, the teaching and examples of holy preachers, he crushes the chosen endeavors of its mind, so that, stripped of virtues, he may more easily possess it in a foreign land and prevent it from returning to the state of its former conduct through remembrance of sound doctrine and improvement of life.

## AIN

The Lord has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah. Therefore I weep, and my eye pours out water.

According to the custom of Holy Scripture, the winepress is sometimes used for the vengeance and punishments of sinners, and sometimes for the gathering of new fruits; here it signifies punishments and torments, as in the present passage, where Jeremiah, lamenting the overthrow of Jerusalem, says: “The Lord has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah; therefore I weep.”

Isaiah is also said to have answered when the Lord, as though ascending into heaven, was questioned by the angels: “Why is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” He replied: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and no man from the nations was with me” (Isa. LXIII).

The Lord alone trod this winepress, in which punishments are trodden out for the wicked and rewards for the good, because he had no helper. For neither an angel, nor an archangel, nor thrones or dominions, nor any of the heavenly powers assumed a human body, suffered for us, trampled down the opposing forces, and crushed them—no one except him who speaks in the psalm: “Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed” (Ps. XI).

The Lord therefore trod this winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah [Col. 1092A] on the day of his Passion, so that rewards might remain for believers, but for unbelievers, persecutors, and those who crucified him, vengeance involving perpetual captivity and the punishments of eternal condemnation. He trod this winepress because he reduced every opposing force under his own power.

But the prophet, seeing the hardness of the Jews’ hearts, laments and groans that the Savior trod for the virgin daughter of Judah the winepress of her hostile oppression in order to free her. She, on the contrary, brought upon herself, from this remedy, the torments both of the extreme captivity and of perpetual condemnation.

Therefore, he says in the person of the Synagogue: “I weep, and my eye pours out tears,” because “the consoler who turns my soul has been made far from me.” How far the consoler who turns their soul has been made from the Jews, we ourselves prove when we repeatedly confront the hardness of their hearts. For just as “the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. CXLIV), so he will be far from those who seek him falsely and do not wish to receive the truth—especially because Christ is the truth (John XIV).

All of this the prophet laments while preserving the metaphor: the vineyard that the Lord planted out of Egypt (Ps. LXXIX), which is said to have remained barren and fruitless for a long time: he expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes instead (Isa. V). Hence the Lord trod the winepress that he had prepared, and, as though with the worst grapes, he prepared the captivity of the worst invasion.

Allegorically, the Lord trod the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah when, through his Passion, he subjected all the aerial powers to the Church. She is the virgin daughter of Judah from whom the Church arose, because “the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II). The Lord alone trod the winepress for her—the yoke of the worst oppression—so that she might be free.

But because, while Christ is treading it, many beneath him return to the dregs (amurca), the prophet laments: “My eye,” he says, “pours out water.” For this reason the Hebrew word Ain is placed first, because it is interpreted as “fountain” or “eye.”

That fountain flowed from Christ’s side when the pressure of the cross bore down upon him; from it, as the Evangelist testifies, blood and water immediately came forth (John XIX). From this fountain the bride of Christ is not only reborn but also enriched. For he is our fountain of life, opened in Christ’s death, from which flow all the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge.

And because Ain is also said to be interpreted as “eye,” it is not without reason that the one who has been refreshed from the fountain is lamented as pouring out a stream of tears: “The consoler who turns my soul,” he says, “has been made far from me.”

Whenever the Church is afflicted by tribulations, whenever she is deprived of divine help, she returns to tears as to her customary weapons. It should also be noted that, whenever she is not converted outwardly despite the teacher’s admonition, the Paraclete Spirit is far from her—the Spirit who should instruct and teach her inwardly. For this reason her children so often become lost.

Therefore, whoever wishes to fulfill the office of teacher, whenever he sees that the Church entrusted to him is insufficiently converted, should draw from the fountain of love the source from which he may produce tears, until he summons the Paraclete Spirit, who consoles and converts. Otherwise, as long as the enemy is provoked and rises up against God, the children who have not yet been weaned and are not yet able to advance to mature manhood will be lost and dashed to pieces, until they are restored and consoled by the Spirit of God. [Col. 1093A]

Tropologically, the Lord treads the winepress for the souls that are barren of virtues, empty of good works, and produce no fruit of faith, whenever he compels them to pay the punishments of deserved vengeance for their barrenness and idleness.

Hence, in accordance with the unending lamentation described above, the eye pours out water with such severity because the soul, having lost its consoler, has consented in an impenitent heart to rush continually toward the place where the weeping of the eyes and the gnashing of teeth are proclaimed. From this a great weeping of the grieving soul is described, so that it may know that, after the empty joy of this world, every consolation of the present life will be taken away from it; the fruit of its womb—that is, its evil works—will be scattered, and the enemy alone will rule over it amid various torments.

## PHE

Zion has stretched out her hands, and there is no one to console her. The Lord commanded against Jacob; his enemies surround him. Jerusalem has become like a woman polluted by menstruation among them.

The fact that Zion is lamented as having stretched out her hands signifies the pains of a woman in labor. Hence elsewhere: “As a swimmer stretches out his hands to swim, so also does Zion amid distress” (Isa. XXV). And Isaiah says: “Distress has seized me like the distress of a woman in labor” (Isa. XXI).

This distress is of the heart, and the cry is expressed through the hands. Therefore Phe is written at the beginning of the verse, for Phe is interpreted as “mouth.” When Zion stretches out her hands amid distress, it is a sign of the mouth, unable through speech to express her groans because she is oppressed by great anguish without a consoler.

Therefore another prophet says: “Depart from me; I shall weep bitterly. Do not press upon me in order to console me over the devastation or destruction of the daughter of my people” (Isa. XXI).

When he says that the Lord commanded against Jacob, he shows that the Lord himself brought upon her not only the Romans afterward but also the Chaldeans previously. From this the meaning is clear: no nation ever rises against her—or, indeed, one nation against another—unless God commands it according to his just and true judgment.

“And Jerusalem has become like a woman polluted by menstruation among them.” Just as a woman is detestable during the time when she suffers menstruation, so those Jews were detestable, and remain so to this day, both to us and to their enemies.

Moreover, whenever our Jerusalem is surrounded by the army of heretics, let us understand that the Lord commanded against Jacob—that is, against the Church, which ought to trample down vices and perverse doctrine—that she should be surrounded by a siege of heretics. For she has lost the Holy Spirit, her consoler, and the teacher without whom no one is instructed in the true faith, no one is raised up from vices, and no one can be consoled among enemies.

Therefore she often stretches out her hands as if in prayer amid pains and pressures, and has no worthy voice of the mouth with which she can defeat her enemies and defend her doctrines. Hence she often becomes like a woman polluted because of the filthiness of carnal works, stained among her enemies by bloody and alluring desires of life, by whom she is attacked within and without.

Therefore the Lord says concerning such people: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse infants in that day” (Mark XIII).

Morally, the soul of the believer, which was once the mirror of God and the trampler of vices, when it is spiritually handed over to wickedness because of its evil deeds, seeks an inner consoler in vain. Thus the Lord rightly commanded against Jacob, who once trampled vices, but now only bears that name in relation to the soul adorned with the same title. Because it refused to submit to God and obey his commands, its enemies surround it on every side, so that it cannot escape.

Thus, seeing itself so often surrounded, it stretches out its hands amid the distress of its thoughts. There is no voice of the mouth and no excuse in speech, except that it has become like a woman polluted by menstruation among enemies—that is, stained by bloody deeds.

How can the soul be free from such menstruation, especially since the prophet says that all our righteousnesses before God are like the cloth of a menstruating woman (Isa. LXIV)? The text continues:

## SADE

The Lord is just, because I provoked his mouth to anger. Hear, I beg you, all peoples, and see my pain: my virgins and my young men have gone into captivity.

At the beginning of the verse the letter Sade is explained; it is interpreted as “justice.” Therefore, because the Lord’s justice is believed to be upright, it is rightly proclaimed that the Lord is just: “because,” he says, “I provoked his mouth to anger.”

I rightly endured the judgment of the mouth in the preceding verse through the letter Phe. Therefore I did not delay confessing Sade—that is, his justice—because the Lord is just, since I provoked his mouth to anger from outside, having lost spiritual consolation.

Above, she mourned the filthy virgins and the little ones who had been led away captive; now she laments that the stronger young men and virgins have been taken captive. Therefore, as the evil increases, so the groans of grief multiply. Hence she does not address merely any people walking along the royal road, but invites everyone to lamentation: “Hear,” she says, “I beg you, all peoples, and see my pain,” because it cannot be discerned without great attention and consideration.

Mystically, the Church rightly endured above the judgment of the mouth, because she provoked the mouth of the Lord to anger in the Holy Scriptures. Corrected by that judgment, she learned to confess to the Lord: “The Lord is just,” she says, “because we provoked his mouth to anger.”

The complaint of so great a disaster is brought to recognition of the sentence of the just Judge, so that all may learn that nothing occurs on earth without cause: the bride of Christ, redeemed by precious blood, is not struck by such waves of temptations and attacked by enemies without the providence of God (Job V).

She confesses that she provoked the mouth of the Lord to anger—not because she teaches that God has human limbs, but because, just as human emotions are tropically attributed to him, so are limbs. For that unbounded light and immeasurable majesty of God do not possess bodily features; rather, she confesses that she provoked to anger the Word proceeding from the mouth of the Father.

It is as though one were to say: “By my wicked deeds I provoked the just Judge and compelled him, naturally merciful, to pass a harsh sentence against me.”

Therefore: “Hear, I beg you, all peoples, and see my pain.” She invites everyone to see her pain because she weighs her manifold and immeasurable calamity, so that, through the compassion of others, she may in some way lighten her anxiety.

It is enough to say that this meaning was already explained above, except that here she more fully laments that her young men and virgins have gone into captivity.

Finally, the young men whom the Church brought forth from the fountain of baptism, and the virgins whom she consecrated in faith to Christ, her immortal bridegroom, are, whenever they are corrupted by the perversity of heretics and defiled for the uses of vices, taken captive—not bodily, but in mind—into Babylon, that is, into the confusion of sin. For “the one who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body” (1 Cor. VI).

Hence such great mourning and pain are applied that scarcely do all people even see or understand it. [Col. 1095C]

The soul, however, which is already being chastised by punishments according to the judgment of the mouth, rightly confesses that the Lord is just in what it suffers. For previously enticed by wicked desires, it provoked the mouth of the Lord to anger, so that he might pronounce against it a sentence worthy of punishment for its sin. For he cannot act otherwise, because he is just in all his ways and in all his works (Ps. CXLIV).

By that sentence of its confusion, therefore, the soul, covered with disgrace, does not dare to raise its eyes before the just Judge whom it provoked to anger. Instead, it does not cease to cry out to all its companions, so that they may hear its pain and see its mourning.

Finally, because this is the nature of our human feeling, whether of pain or of joy, we so often seek others to share in our experience, so that, supported by their consolation, we may bear the burden of sadness or the splendor of joy more lightly and pleasantly.

Hence the man in the Gospel who sought the lost sheep, and the woman who found the drachma, call together their friends and neighbors because they wish to have sharers in their joy and companions in their gladness (Luke XV).

How much more ought the soul to summon everyone when, oppressed by shame over its confusion, it does not dare raise its eyes to God, whom it had brought to anger by its evil deeds, so that they might become intercessors with the merciful Judge through compassion for its pain and love?

That her young men and virgins are taken captive shows that she grieves especially over this, when she sees the stronger affections of her heart, or her virginal thoughts, going into the confusion of miserable captivity, and the hope of her womb being violated by enemies. For whenever anyone sees his offspring perish, he is certainly aware that he has lost the hope of future generation.

## COPH

I called my friends, but they deceived me. My priests and my elders perished in the city, because they sought food for themselves in order to revive their souls.

First, we must ask what Coph signifies. Coph is called “calling.” Hence, immediately playing upon the letter, she says: “I called my friends, but they deceived me.” She wishes to signify the Egyptians, whose friendship the Jews always used.

But during the time of the first captivity, or the final captivity under the Romans, they deceived them when, although called upon—those in whom, as Isaiah testifies, they had placed their greatest confidence—they offered no help. We also read that Rabshakeh proclaimed this in the same prophetic book, that they had placed great confidence in them (Isa. XXXVI).

But how they deceived those who called them, Isaiah reveals: “The land of Judah,” he says, “will be a terror and a fear to Egypt on the day of their destruction. Everyone who remembers it will tremble at the presence of the counsel of the Lord of hosts, which he has planned against it” (Isa. XII).

They are rightly said to have been deceived, therefore, because, having been abandoned by God’s help, they placed greater hope in the Egyptians. I do not say that the Egyptians provided them help; rather, because of them, fear and terror increased, on account of their remembrance, while God was offended even more.

As for the lament that the priests and elders perished in the city, there is no doubt that this occurred under the Babylonians and under the Romans.

According to the anagogical sense, the Church often calls friends—namely, those whom she thinks she has as companions in the faith. Yet they deceive her, corrupted inwardly in faith because they remain hidden, or outwardly when they have gone out from us, precisely because they fight against us (1 John II).

Likewise, any wicked Christians placed in positions of higher authority, whose friendship the Church often uses, sometimes deceive her through various devices of their depravity or through examples of an alluring life. They are not truly friends, but, according to antiphrasis, they are called so because they are, as it were, table companions, wicked in faith and deceivers of the Church through their works.

What is worse, such people then rage more cruelly against them when the priests and elders—whom the Greeks call γέροντας, “elders”—are consumed among us by hunger for the word of God. For, pursuing the profits of carnal life, they seek food with which to revive their miserable life, as we have already explained above, rather than those heavenly banquets from Solomon’s table (Cant. III), and from the meal proclaimed as prepared in the Gospel (Matt. XXII), and from the banquet of wisdom, to which the calling of all is signified by the letter Coph, which, as we have said, is interpreted as “calling.”

Morally, the soul also calls its friends—that is, the sweet and pleasant affections of its flesh. Yet, while it enjoys their friendship, they immediately deceive it. Although it ought to be a royal priesthood (1 Pet. II), enticed by pleasures and desires, it labors, as though for food, to revive the lusts of its flesh.

Consumed by these things, it loses the dignity of the priesthood and the maturity of counsel through lack of wisdom and poverty of virtues. Egypt will indeed help in vain (Ezek. XXIX), because the world is passing away, together with all its desire. It is a staff of reed, broken and fragile; therefore it tears those who lean upon it and pierces their hands, and it can never grant perfect prosperity to its lovers.

## RES

See, Lord, for I am in distress; my belly is troubled, my heart is overturned within me.

Now Jerusalem is confounded by shame and does not dare raise her eyes to God; now she is lifted up by hope of pardon and presumes upon mercy. Therefore she says: “See, Lord, for I am in distress,” so that suffering may bend the merciful Judge toward clemency, and shame toward pardon.
