When she says that her belly is in pain, she expresses the condition of a woman in danger within the womb: “I have been filled,” she says, “with bitterness.” She thus indicates that she has not been touched only in part, but filled with every bitterness of pain and sorrow; she laments that her heart has been overturned under the weight of tribulation, because outside the persecutor’s sword rages, while within there is a similar death because of the bitterness of affliction.

Let us now proceed to the anagogical meaning and see what the letter Res signifies. Res is interpreted as “head.” The disturbance of the belly or overturning of the heart is a groaning of the mind. The mind is the head of every soul; consequently, the perturbation of the head and its overturning are rightly said to occur when it is filled with bitterness and wounded by many of its misfortunes.

There is no doubt that the Church daily sets forth and reveals her pain and tribulation to the most merciful Judge. Yet the Church has a belly, of which she herself proclaims in the praises of the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “His belly is ivory, studded with sapphires” (Cant. V).

No one is unaware that the belly is the receptacle of all foods, where the nourishment and substance of the whole body are gathered and digested. Through it those people are rightly understood who, although they do not strive to teach others by their speech, nevertheless do not fail to store and ruminate inwardly the food of souls—the bread that came down from heaven (John VI)—together with the Holy Spirit, after the manner of clean animals (Lev. XI).

They first receive this food through faith; then they digest it by the fire of charity through good conduct of life and meditation. Their voice cries out through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “Because of your fear, Lord, we conceived and gave birth to the spirit of salvation” (Isa. XXVI).

The Church groans with this belly disturbed whenever she is struck by various temptations, to such an extent that those within and without are weighed down by torments.

Then she says: “My heart is overturned,” because the command of the bridegroom in the Song of Songs is not fulfilled: “Set me,” he says, “as a seal upon your heart” (Cant. VIII). If she had set him there, the enemy would not have approached to overturn her.

Therefore, because she did not wish to retain the sweetness of such great love, so that her love might be strong as death, she is often filled with every bitterness of tribulation, inwardly and outwardly: outwardly, she is struck by the sword of persecutors; inwardly, by the more bitter gall of heretical teaching, or else, because of the wickedness of her conduct, by death itself, with a similar seasoning of vices.

Morally, the soul afflicted by various pains laments that its belly—that is, its mind—is greatly disturbed, because in sacred speech the mind is often designated by the word “belly” or “womb.” Hence Solomon says: “The lamp of the Lord is the breath of a human being, searching all the hidden places of the belly” (Prov. XX).

The light of God is therefore said to search all the hidden places of the belly because it penetrates the secrets of the mind, bringing before the eyes of the soul deeds that had been hidden from it. And because, as I have said, the mind signifies the head of the soul, this groaning is rightly said to belong to the head, as is shown through the letter Res.

Thus she reveals that everything within her is disturbed and overturned, saying: “See, Lord.” Hence Jeremiah himself said much earlier: “My belly, my belly, I suffer pain” (Jer. IV). And to show what he meant, he added: “The senses of my heart are disturbed.”

The mind is rightly understood by the name “belly,” because, just as offspring are generated in the womb, so thoughts are generated in the mind; and just as food is contained in the belly, so thoughts are contained in the mind.

The faithful soul, wearied by various temptations, rightly laments that it has been battered inwardly and outwardly by a similar death, because it knows that it is torn outwardly by persecutions and inwardly by distress. Often we are battered outwardly by scourges, while inwardly we are wearied by carnal suggestions.

Hence it says: “Outside, the sword kills, and at home there is a similar death.” Outside, the sword kills when vengeance strikes us outwardly and consumes us; but at home there is a similar death because, although the soul endures scourges, its conscience is not clean within from the filth of temptations.

How rightly, therefore, this is the voice of the head—that is, of the mind grieving and lamenting: “See, Lord, my affliction,” and so forth. Hence the text continues:

## SIN

They heard that I was groaning, and there was no one to console me. All my enemies heard of my evil; they rejoiced, because you did it.

There is no doubt that all the enemies of the Jews rejoiced at their desolation, as Isaiah testifies, especially because they saw them deprived of God’s help and consolation, in which they had previously gloried so greatly.

Jerusalem was indeed situated among her enemies like a ship amid the waves of the sea. They often drove her back, yet they could never harm her except when she offended God. Recognizing this herself, instructed by divine teachings, she does not attribute it to her enemies or assign it to their strength, but to God’s judgment, which she declares: “Therefore they rejoiced,” she says, “because you did it.” It is as though she said: Although they rejoice as though because of the outcome, you nevertheless decreed in your just judgment what I suffer for my guilt.

The text continues: “You have brought the day of consolation, and they will become like me.” Jerusalem therefore saw that the day of her consolation would come; indeed, the prophet promises it as though it had already passed, and he did not doubt that it would come under Cyrus. Meanwhile, he announces what is more strongly demanded by the prophetic spirit, in order to terrify them: after all the other kingdoms had been destroyed and led into captivity, finally Babylon itself and its kingdom would also be destroyed.

Hence the text continues: “They will become like me.” He speaks in the manner of those who are always striving to win the favor of judges and to inflict punishment upon their enemies.

## SIN

Spiritually, the Church, weeping over the evils presently inflicted upon herself and her members, groans as represented by the letter **SIN**, which is interpreted as “teeth.” The weeping, therefore, belongs to the teeth of those of whom we read in the Song of Songs:

“Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing” (Song 4).

“All of them bear twins, and none among them is barren.”

I think that these teeth are those who do not need the milk of instruction (Heb. 5), but have already passed beyond infancy. They are able not only to chew solid food for themselves, but also to divide and ruminate the strong bones of virtues for the members of the Church. Hence, when the Lord sent down from heaven the sheet containing every kind of creature, he said to one of them: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10).

Such people, exceptionally discerning through the sharpness of their learning, know how to kill vices and, by chewing, transfer the souls of believers into the body of Christ. But since we have mentioned teeth, let us recognize that their functions in chewing are various: some divide, others crush and ruminate, and others form sounds and distinguish them together with the tongue.

Thus some saints are like “flocks of shorn sheep”: stripped of their old nature, they provide their young with the milk of instruction and the garments of virtues. Others are like the teeth prophetically described in relation to Judah, which were “whiter than milk” (Gen. 49); through their office they offer the beauty of adornment in the utmost refinement of speech.

1356 Concerning these teeth the Apostle likewise says to the Hebrews that solid food belongs to the mature (Heb. 5), who, according to the capacity of those who receive it, have trained faculties for discerning good and evil.

These teeth, since they exercise more than all others care and concern, “heard,” he says, “that I groan, and there is none to comfort me.” The enemies heard this—those whom he immediately indicates as having rejoiced. They heard, I say, that the bride was mourning, deprived of the bridegroom, although he promised that he would always be present with her until the consummation of the age (Matt. 28).

For although he is always present, never absent anywhere or at any time in his majesty, he nevertheless often, for many reasons, allows the bride to be tested without the apparent consolation of his help. Hence she says: “They saw that I groan.” It is as though she were saying: “They saw what they had never suspected, what they had always desired to see: not only that I groan, but also the immense evils that I endure. Therefore they rejoiced, because they heard of my evil—what I suffer, what I mourn, and how, even without a consoler, I commit worse things in my members.”

Who the enemies of the Church are is clear: all spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places, the airy spirits, and the powers of this darkness that oppose her (Eph. 6), as well as heretics and false Christians, by whom she is attacked both within and without.

Yet Christ’s bride knows that, however fiercely they rage, they have power only by God’s permission. Hence she says: “For you have done it,” just as he says elsewhere through the prophet: “I am the Lord, creating evil and making peace” (Isa. 45). He therefore makes peace and creates evil when, by his just judgment, he permits evil to be done.

“You have brought,” she says, “the day of consolation, and they shall become like me.” These words apply more appropriately to the Church, since no consolation remains for the final captivity of the Jews. Hence the Apostle Paul says:

“It is just with God to repay tribulation to those who trouble you, and to you who are troubled, rest with us at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power, in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Thess. 1).

This is the day of consolation that all God’s elect possess in hope. For its sake they patiently endure everything in the present, because the one who will render to each according to his works (Matt. 16) will assign punishments to oppressors and rewards to the saints.

According to the tropological sense, however, the soul laments because the enemies have heard that she groans after offending God and that she magnifies the evils she endures. This is especially so because, for a soul troubled and afflicted by pain, it often seems to increase her sorrow that the one in whom she had placed her hope delays offering the help of consolation and assistance.

Hence the enemies’ mockery causes her the greatest grief—namely, the invisible enemies who previously flattered her inwardly with evil designs. Nor are they alone: her own conscience also insults her by accusing her more gravely, and the vices that once seemed sweet reveal themselves as more atrocious and bitter.

If our crimes ever become known even to those who share in such evil, it becomes clear whether they are enemies or friends, according as they mock when they ought to have pitied and mourned. David says of them: “Those who guarded my soul took counsel together, saying: ‘God has abandoned him; pursue and seize him, for there is no one to deliver him’” (Ps. 70).

Yet although the adversaries rage in this way, the soul has her own teeth, fashioned inwardly from the flesh and bones of Christ. Their voice cries out to God in groaning and mourning: thoughts strong in hope, which know how to distinguish between prosperity and adversity, which know how to seek the consoling Spirit and never to despair of God’s mercy.

Hence she says: “You have brought the day of consolation,” because the strong soul knows that penitents merit pardon after their afflictions, while punishments of retribution are inflicted upon those who insult them by the just Judge.

From this follows:

## THAU

“Let all their evil come before you, and gather them as you gathered me, because of all my iniquities.”

These verses bear **THAU**, together with those signs that are signified in many places throughout the divine writings; they occur here no less than elsewhere. For **Thau** means “signs,” in the plural, because this sign is set forth for the reason that through it all the secrets of God, which have been sealed, are opened.

Concerning this sign the angel—or rather the Lord himself—said to the prophet Ezekiel: “Pass through the midst of Jerusalem, and mark with Thau the foreheads of the men who groan and mourn” (Ezek. 9).

There is no doubt that this sign designates the Lord’s cross and his passion, as can also be recognized from the character itself. It lacks little of the form of a cross, except that the upper part projects above the shaft. Thus, by its mystery, it is said to be marked upon the foreheads of men who groan and mourn.

And lest this seem insignificant to you, know that it is the final letter of the Hebrews, just as **omega** is the final letter of the Greeks. Concerning this the Lord says: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1; 22). If Christ himself is called Alpha and Omega—that is, the beginning and the end—what less, do you suppose, can be signified by Thau than the cross, by which the foreheads of all who groan and mourn are commanded to be marked and consecrated, so that they may not be harmed by those who carry vessels of slaughter through the midst of Jerusalem to destroy souls?

All letters are signs of words; words and expressions, in turn, are signs of things and deeds. Through them and in them all things are prefigured—not only present things, but also future ones.

But since we have said that Thau is interpreted as “signs,” let us examine what these signs are, or whose signs they are. Every sign is the sign of something, for the thing that signifies is altogether different from the thing signified. It is therefore not unreasonable to ask what signs are designated by the character of this letter, or whose signs they are.

We have already said above that Thau is a sign—or, according to its interpretation, signs—of the cross; indeed, to speak more accurately, it is almost the cross itself. Hence it was commanded that the mourners and those who groan should be marked with it, as was stated earlier. At that time it was the sign of the future cross; now it is the cross itself, or rather the reality of our redemption contained in it.

Since Thau is the end of the Hebrew letters, and since the Hebrew letters are as numerous as the books of the Old Testament, of which they themselves are signs, I reasonably believe that, just as Thau is the end of all the letters, so the cross—the passion of Jesus Christ—is the end of all the books of the Old Testament. He is the end of the whole law unto righteousness.

Therefore all those signs contained in the books of divine authority are sacraments of the Lord’s incarnation and of our redemption. Thau is accordingly and rightly interpreted as “signs,” so that through these signs one thing might be announced: the reality from which, as I have said, all signs are opened and all things disclosed.

It is also a fitting end to our lamentation, which from the beginning has contained many signs of God’s judgments. Thus the reward of their labors may be repaid by the Lord to those who now groan and mourn, upon whose foreheads the cross shines marked; and those who have afflicted them and refused to recognize the signs of so great a work may receive the vengeance of a fitting retribution.

Hence the words are spoken not in the disposition of one making a wish, but in the spirit of prophecy:

“Let all their evil come before you, and gather them as you gathered me, because of all my iniquities.”

As regards the literal sense, this happened also among the other kingdoms hostile to the Jews. Read the prophets, and you will find everything fulfilled.

But these words apply more fully to our Jerusalem, which unceasingly prays, even from beneath the altar of God, as we read: “Why, Lord, do you not defend and avenge our blood?” (Rev. 6), together with the other words that follow.

So here also the chorus of the faithful recalls before God the cruelty of their persecutors, so that the vengeance of divine retribution may even now seize, humble, and destroy those who, in their pride and cruelty, did not fear to harass, afflict, or punish Christ’s Church.

Hence they say: “Let all their evil come before you.” For when their malice grew so fierce and so great, it was as though God were thought not to know or see it, although nothing is hidden from him (Heb. 4).

“Let all their evil come before you,” so that, measured according to these deeds, those who refused to put an end to their wicked works may be punished without end.

“Gather those who gathered me.” To gather each person as in a harvest is to collect the fruit of his works. The metaphor is taken either from the vineyard that he brought out of Egypt (Ps. 79), or from the vineyard that he himself planted in the Gospel (Matt. 21).

The Lord therefore gathers his enemies as they gathered his saints in this world—those whom he himself permitted them to oppress for their testing—when, in the future judgment, each person will receive everlasting retribution according to what he has done.

But the saints have been gathered in one way in this world, and the wicked in another way in the future. The saints lost and despised temporal goods; the wicked, who loved the world, will lose eternal goods. This is an equitable compensation: just as the saints were stripped of all the joys of this life, so that they might confess, from a true humility, that this occurred because of their iniquities, so the wicked will be deprived of future goods because of their impiety and evil.

Moreover, just as the saints endured their afflictions by God’s just judgment, so the wicked will suffer everlasting punishments for their errors.

To prevent such things from happening, the Church, weeping and groaning, says: “Many are my groanings, and my heart is sorrowful.” For since there are many transgressions, there are also many groanings; and since the pain is great, so also is the sorrow of the heart.

Perhaps at last, through the Lord’s mercy, she may say: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93). Here the multitude of sorrows is sometimes inwardly consoled by hope in the Spirit, but elsewhere the recompense of consolation will be given.

Therefore, until the things that are to come arrive, the Church—or the holy soul—more fully instructed concerning all things says: “Many are my groanings, and my heart is sorrowful.”

This soul, considered also in the moral sense, prays before the Lord, saying: “Let all their evil come before you.” Let the evil that they frequently impose upon me, and that they frequently display and inflict inwardly and outwardly, come before you, so that you may refute and weaken it, since I cannot escape by my own strength.

For wherever I turn, I see nothing but their evils; and what is more grievous, I find that even within myself they have been fashioned upon my back (Ps. 128).

Therefore, since you recognize the thing formed, let their evil come before you, so that I may be stripped of it and so that, when you are judged, you may prevail against the charge that you do not care for such things (Ps. 50). Gather them from all their deceptions, lest they obtain fruit from me, just as you gathered me when, moved to anger, you withdrew your gifts from me and removed from me, for all my iniquities, the present joy of the perfect life.

Then joys may again grow for me out of sorrow, and punishments for them out of their unchangeable cruelty.

These are the signs for which all the miracles of signs have been performed. Hence David says in the Psalm: “You have given signs to those who fear you, that they may flee from the face of the bow” (Ps. 59). Those who refuse to guard against these signs will come upon the things that Holy Scripture consistently foretells.

Hence Wisdom, looking toward the end, says: “Renew the signs and change the wonders. Glorify your hand and your right arm. Stir up fury and pour out anger. Raise up the adversary and afflict the enemy. Hasten the time and remember the end” (Ecclus. 36).

She therefore asks that the signs that occur daily be renewed, so that justice may be turned into judgment, so that the saints may not always be afflicted, but that each person may receive according to what he has done. It is as though she were saying: “Because these things have hitherto been done so that people might escape, now change the wonders according to what they signify, so that they may reach their appointed end.”

Thus, at the conclusion of this lament, he announced beforehand through the letter Thau the signs that were to come, and in these tearful verses he completed by prophecy everything that would happen.

Therefore let us also, having completed the first alphabet as best we could, bring the book to its end. And I humbly beg, in the prayers of all and the lamentations of everyone, that he wash me in the heart of Jesus Christ; for I am not sufficient for myself, so that I who have sinned monstrously with all and above all may, in all things and together with all, merit to be heard mercifully and obtain pardon.

# PROLOGUE TO THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 1103]

1361 Among us, as has been said, dearest of men, in the giving and receiving of gifts, those services are especially to be valued if it is clearly established that I have brought you nothing more suitable than this, according to my ability, once it has been completed; and that I have never received from you anything that benevolence would embrace as dearer.

For as we grow old together, it is evident that this has always been our longstanding practice: to devote ourselves to prayers, to persist in lamentations, and to mourn either our own crimes or those of others.

Hence, having completed the first alphabet in the Lamentations, we extend our hand to the second, so that you may have more to lament—pierced with charity, if there is nothing in me over which you can rejoice, and embittered by evils.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1103]

I have therefore rendered in the preceding book, in the individual closures of the Sapphic meter, the individual letters, in groups of three verses, together with their interpretations—perhaps not in the manner in which the same prophet more perfectly understood why he inserted them. But according to the understanding of my little intellect, at least the reader might recognize from this that nothing in those letters is devoid of mystery.

If only those with greater capacity were willing to search the divine utterances with such diligence, they would undoubtedly discover higher and deeper meanings. The same applies to the style of the work, which possesses a kind of eloquence surpassing that of any secular discipline—not because holy men sought to imitate such eloquence, but because eloquence itself seems, like a little maidservant, to serve wisdom.

Therefore, since there are twenty-two letters by which everything spoken in Hebrew is written and through whose signs the human voice is expressed, it pleased the prophets to make the same number of verse-beginnings arise from those same letters, so that poetic discipline might serve the verses and divine mysteries might be opened to us through them.

But because it would be lengthy to insert, throughout the individual sections of this second book, the individual interpretations of these letters and to explain their meanings from them, we have decided, following the practice of teachers, to note their connections at the beginning, leaving it to the reader’s judgment how he himself may render each interpretation according to his own understanding.

The sequence is as follows.

The first connection consists of four letters: **ALEPH, BETH, GIMEL, DALETH**. Their meaning is: doctrine, house, fullness, tablets.

If the two outer letters are joined, the result is “the doctrine of the tablets,” on which the law was written by the finger of God. If “fullness” and “house” are joined, the meaning is that the fullness of the house of God is filled from the doctrine of books or tablets. But if you join “fullness” with “tablets,” the meaning will be that the house is filled with doctrine from the fullness of the Scriptures.

Since the whole house of Solomon is described as paneled within (1 Kings 6), if you wish to interpret “tablets” as referring to those whose joints and breadth of charity cover and join the entire house with their excellence, it must be understood that their doctrine is the fullness of the whole house.

The understanding of these doctrines arises from the fountain of the fear of God, so that one may reach the summit of wisdom, as the prophet says: “From fear of you, Lord, we conceived and gave birth to the spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26).

The second connection is **HE, VAV, ZAIN, HETH**, which is interpreted as “this, and, these, life.”

If you join their outer letters and connect the two middle ones, the meaning will be an understanding of why the things that we have set forth, and these things here, are necessary for life; and that knowledge of the Scriptures is the life through which Christ is recognized and eternal life is prepared for believers.

In the books of these tablets, nothing other than a song, lamentations, and woe are shown to Ezekiel. Therefore, as I think, such things are prefigured as ought to be pursued, lest anyone incur that final woe; and this is presently the life of those who are weaned from infancy into a mature man.

The third connection is **TETH, IOD**, which sounds as “good beginning.”

This is rightly believed to be the truly good beginning in which, together with doctrine, we conceive from the fear of God the discipline of lamentation, until we arrive fully at the spirit of salvation. For, as has been shown above, lamentations are appropriate in this valley of tears; and this is the good beginning: to pursue dirges and lamentations, because, as the Gospel bears witness, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5), and afterward arrive at the songs of heavenly life.

Otherwise, unless this good beginning is accepted here, one does not reach those things. For “we know in part, and we prophesy in part. Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13), when God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the elect and mourning will cease (Rev. 21).

Furthermore:

The fourth connection, which is also the middle one of the seven, is **CAPH, LAMECH**, meaning “the hand of the heart” or “of discipline.”

The hand refers to the fact that hands are extended toward the works of perfect charity; the heart refers to mourning or meditation; and discipline refers to understanding directed toward making all things clean for us before the Lord.

What more is needed?

The fifth sequence of letters explains to us **MEM, NUN, SAMECH**, which means “from them, everlasting, help.”

I think these three require no explanation, especially since the upper elements are supplied by the two middle ones, while the lower three are rewarded from them. Hence:

The sixth connection is **AIN, PHE, SADE**—namely, “fountain” or “eye,” and “the righteousness of the mouth.” For from the groaning of the heart a fountain of piety flows, and the inward eye is illuminated by God, so that we may be able to see God at the end.

Indeed, through the hand and the eloquence of the mouth, treasures are stored up in zeal for righteousness. Thus someone, composing an epitaph for a certain man, rightly wrote:

“Here lies a man who despised the world and triumphed over earthly things; he stored his riches in heaven, by mouth and hand.”

These riches are rightly understood as the righteousness of perfect life, with the Holy Spirit bearing witness, who says: “He distributed; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever and ever” (Ps. 111).

The final connection, which is the seventh, contains **COPH, RES, SIN, TAU**. These are interpreted as “the calling of the head, of the teeth, signs,” so that an articulated voice may be understood as overcoming.

For these names of the letters, which have been set forth above, are signs of all the voices of the sacred Scriptures and of the work of lamentation; they are also the calling of our supreme Head, Jesus Christ, through whom one comes to the Father and to the everlasting kingdom (John 14).

There is no doubt that the holy Fathers—or rather the Holy Spirit—placed mystical meanings in this number seven. Thus the middle group corresponds to the two groups of three letters on either side. If you attend to the meanings of the joined letters, you will also find that they correspond to the meanings of their respective connections.

Let us now see what the actual text of the lamentation conveys.

## ALEPH

“How the Lord in his fury has covered the daughter of Zion with darkness; he has cast down from heaven to earth the glory of Israel.”

In these three alphabets of Sapphic meter there is one beginning of the expression and one exclamation, full of pain and full of every kind of wonder and astonishment.

Therefore, reader, I ask you not to pass over such words casually, but to consider the emotion of so great a lament with more careful attention. Understand with what charity and love the saints were affected, and with what flame of devotion they were inwardly moved toward everything, so that they made the causes of all people their own and attended to each matter with immense concern.

For this reason Jeremiah, since it is not enough for him to contemplate what happened to Jerusalem, repeats the same exclamatory word at the beginnings of the Lamentations not once or twice but three times: “How she sits,” or “How the Lord has covered her,” or “How the finest gold has been darkened”—as unexpectedly and unforeseeably as the people whom God had chosen for himself from all the nations, so that he might be their God and they might be his people (Deut. 26).

“How,” he says, “has the Lord in his fury covered the daughter of Zion with darkness?”

There would be a question concerning this darkness if he had not added “in his fury.” For the darkness into which Moses entered on the mountain, where God was (Exod. 19), is one thing; the darkness seen beneath his feet (2 Sam. 22), and proclaimed beneath his feet in the Psalm (Ps. 17), is another; and the darkness with which Jerusalem is covered in God’s fury is another.

This darkness is possessed by a gloomy storm, which is also often rightly interpreted as God’s fury. In the first darkness God is said to be present; and he is likewise proclaimed to preside over the darkness beneath his feet.

Considering, therefore, everything God had done for this people—how great, innumerable, terrifying, and inscrutable those deeds were—and seeing what had happened, Jeremiah cannot refrain from crying out with a great groan that a people raised to such adoption that it was called God’s daughter, raised from such immense glory, from the highest summit of heaven and from great happiness, had fallen into such vast misery on the day of the Lord’s fury and vengeance.

It was the day of fury, not simply the day of the Lord. For although it was indeed the Lord’s fury, this was a day of vengeance, a day of fury.

The daughter of Zion did indeed have the day of the Lord, which Abraham her father saw and rejoiced in (John 8); but because, on the day of her salvation, she refused to observe the day of the Lord, she stumbled upon the day of God’s fury.

According to the anagogical sense, we should likewise mourn whenever Zion, our mother, is covered with the darkness of sins, error, or ignorance, although she is believed to have been enriched with such great gifts and praised with such great acclaim.

What is worse is that she then had people who, although God was offended, lamented her with tireless groaning. I do not know whether our Zion has even a few who understand or reflect upon the evils by which we suffer and are afflicted.

We see the glory of Israel cast down from heaven when we see her pursuing earthly and carnal things. In particular, although, according to the Apostle, “our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3), we, by contrast, now devote ourselves to nothing but transitory and worldly affairs and meditate upon shameful things.

What more should you suppose, except that the Lord, because of the evils intervening among us, has rejected us and cast us down to earth? “Nor did he remember his footstool on the day of his fury” (Joel 3).

Although that Zion is described as God’s most beautiful dwelling, supported by angelic ministry, guidance, and divine protection, and although she was educated in the wilderness for a very long time through Moses and Aaron and the other holy fathers by many miracles and divine consolations, so that she rightly possessed the designation “the footstool of the Lord’s feet” because of the order of divine worship, nevertheless our Zion is proclaimed as more glorious by both Testaments.

Moses foresaw and perceived her when he ascended the mountain, together with Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and the seventy elders. “They saw the God of Israel,” he says, “and beneath his feet there was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear” (Exod. 24).

These words plainly reveal the meaning: he foresaw in the Spirit that the Church would be present beneath the feet of God. Therefore he says, “like the sky when it is clear,” because “the heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18).

Desiring to retain her, the Lord showed her beneath his feet, in the sacrament of baptism and under the appearance of a sapphire stone, as in a mystery.

Therefore, I think that the prophet, foreseeing in the Spirit not only the ruin of that people but also the dangers of our Zion, mourned together with us. She has so often been cast down on the day of God’s fury that God no longer remembered his footstool.

This often happened because of the sins of the people, and it is rightly lamented as having happened now: Christ ought to preside over her and walk in her, but at present the worst enemy rules over her.

He did not remember his throne or his footstool on the day of his fury, when God’s rights are attacked in us and evils dominate.

Moreover, in the moral sense, the sinful soul, which once possessed the light of knowledge and the mirror of divine contemplation, and whose name was written in heaven, is believed to deserve no less mourning when she is prostituted and profaned on earth, when she is polluted and defiled by vices, and when the feet of the Lord—that is, the traces of his commandments—are erased from the heart by departing footsteps.

When God was a temple dwelling in her and walking in her, she has now, because of blindness of heart and the wickedness of evil action, fallen from the summit of virtues, as from the highest peak of heaven, into the foulness of vices. On the day of the Lord’s fury she is trampled, plundered, and torn apart by enemies.

The Lord has not remembered her because she refused to stand in the light of virtues. Therefore he handed her over on the day of his fury.

Concerning this day the present prophet says: “Cursed is the day on which I was born, the day on which my mother bore me; let it not be blessed” (Jer. 20).

This day, as I have already said above, is rightly called the day of the Lord’s fury. When a soul falls into it, removing herself from the members of Christ through sin and making herself a member of a prostitute—that is, of the devil, with whom she commits fornication—she is not remembered on the day of wrath, because she did not stand in the day that the Lord made.

Therefore, despised and abandoned by God and trampled by enemies, she is rightly mourned by the prophet and by all the members of Christ, because she has rolled herself down from such a height of honor into such great mockery and madness, and has cast herself into such ruin.

Hence it follows:

## BETH

“The Lord has hurled down and has not spared all the beauty of Jacob; in his fury he has destroyed the fortifications of the daughter of Judah; he has cast them down to the ground and polluted the kingdom and its princes.”

It is clear that all these things happened to the Jews. But because the Lord is lamented as having done them, this must not be understood as though he compelled Jerusalem to sin. Rather, by a just and true judgment, he permitted her first to sin here and elsewhere through countless transgressions, and then, as punishment for sin, to be hurled down, together with the other events that follow.

Because of the Jews’ sins, committed in imitation of the other nations around them, the Lord was provoked and handed his people over into the hands of the nations; those who hated them ruled over them.

He did not spare all the beauty of Jacob—that which they possessed in the adornments of their famous temple and in the observance of ceremonies by which they believed themselves more glorious than the other nations.

The Lord hurled these things down and destroyed them in his fury, so that you might understand that the Lord did not seek those things for himself, but sought from them worship, glory, and praise of his name. They, on the contrary, preferred the things in which they gloried and surrendered themselves to impurities and crimes.

These matters are fulfilled more fully in the final destruction that occurred under the Romans, as though all the things read in the Law had been carried in shadow within earthen vessels: in the kingdom, the people, the leaders and ministers, the temple and all its vessels, the Sabbaths and solemnities, the garments and sacrifices, the practice of religion, and all the things that are proclaimed as prefigured in them.

Indeed, all these things were nothing other than a great prophet or prophecy.

When Christ came, and the individual things concerning him that were concealed in those same vessels had been fulfilled, all those things were hurled down and shattered, destroyed and cast away, polluted and profaned, so that all peoples throughout the world might see, clearer than daylight, the mystical and ineffable mysteries that had been concealed and now lay open.

Therefore, he says, “he polluted the kingdom and its princes,” when he rejected all their beauty and, after Christ had been put to death, spared none of it, judging that without him—for all this prophecy concerned him—everything had been prostituted and defiled.

So completely was this done that of all those things not even a potsherd remained in which to carry fire from the burning.

Such is the prophet’s lamentation—so monstrous and unbearable.

Mystically, these things are rightly referred to the Church when the people sin; for, according to the Apostle, if God did not spare the natural branches, how much less will he spare us, who, though we were wild olive trees, were grafted into a good olive tree (Rom. XI)? And if he despised their offices, how much more are ours polluted when both mind and conscience have been polluted?

How beautiful and fair the Church is, it is often praised throughout the Song of Songs, and also in the Psalms: “The queen,” he says, “stood in a garment of gold, clothed in manifold colors” (Ps. XLIV). Hence it is clear that she is exceedingly beautiful and sweet, “beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun” (Song VI). Yet how often, as her sins increase, either in part or wholly, the Lord casts down her splendors to insult and disgrace into the hands of enemies. She is splendid indeed, because she shines like a lily among thorns (Song II), when the thorns that have arisen together choke her beauty (Luke VIII).

To cast her down is God’s act of permitting each person, in his just judgment [p. 1368], to follow his desires, and of withholding the help of his grace and mercy. If we had tears for these things, we would continually see why we ought to weep; but what is more grievous is that now scarcely anyone reflects upon such matters.

Her fortifications, therefore, are destroyed when the vigilant men and guardians of the churches—those who ought with every care and concern to fortify and surround her with their assistance and teaching—are corrupted by the amusements and pleasures of this life. Because they do not understand that they have been destroyed and scattered by their evil deeds, the chorus of the saints sighs and weeps for them: for in them beauty perishes and the strength of the flock is weakened.

The Church of Christ is indeed like Jerusalem, which “is built as a city” (Ps. CXXI), and like the tower of David with its battlements. “A thousand shields hang upon it, the whole armor of the strong” (Song IV). But when her walls—namely, the shepherds and guardians of souls—are destroyed by their own deeds, the enemy easily casts down and plunders everything splendid within the city, and it becomes like a city that is laid waste.

Hence it follows: “He cast her down to the ground.” The Church, therefore, is cast down to the ground when she is occupied with earthly deeds and vices, and there is no one to sustain her with the virtues of teaching or with examples of good works.

Therefore, whenever such things occur in any church, divine vengeance justly follows at once: “He polluted,” he says, “the kingdom and its princes.” He polluted them when his justice exposed as polluted those who ought to have kept themselves and others before God pure and undefiled. “And having become a royal race, a holy priesthood” (1 Pet. II). They are rightly pronounced polluted when, cast down from the throne of so great a dignity, they are found to be slaves of vices.

Hence I think that one ought to mourn with the prophet rather than explain anything in these words, because, as we read elsewhere: “The guilt of the priests is the ruin of the people,” as it was also among the Jews.

Tropologically, the Lord casts down the splendors of every soul [Col. 1110A] and does not spare it when the mind has been occupied by wicked desires, having abandoned within itself the chaste love of God, to which it had been said: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear” (Ps. XLIV), and so forth, “until the king desires your beauty”; and he destroys all its fortifications round about in the anger of his fury (Eccl. IX). This happens when faith is weakened and the soul is unable to withstand the temptations of its enemies, which are brought against it, because it first lost within itself the appearance and beauty of chaste love.

Otherwise, unless the soul had first been corrupted within and defiled by vices, it would by no means be deprived of God’s help, so that the walls of its virtues would be destroyed outwardly—the virtues by which it had previously been protected from enemies lest they break in.

“And he cast her,” he says, “to the ground,” because she then falls altogether from the throne of the kingdom to the ground, when within herself she has violated the marriage of chaste love and mingled herself with the filth of vices. Hence everyone should greatly mourn with the prophet, because we are cast from heaven’s summit to the ground whenever we pursue earthly things and become entangled in vices, lest it should at some time be said to us: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III).

For unless the soul, beautiful with virtues, had first lost its beauty, the Lord would never permit its fortifications to be destroyed outwardly; and unless they had first been destroyed all around, it would never have fallen from heaven to earth, so as to savor everything earthly. But because it lost its beauty within, it ceased to be God’s throne. Thus it is both cast down upon the earth and the Lord pollutes it.

“He polluted,” he says, “the kingdom and its princes.” To pollute the kingdom, therefore, is to judge polluted the soul in which God had established a temple for himself, but which, prostituted and profaned by the devil through vices, is polluted [Col. 1110C] together with the very faculties by which it is wrongly ruled in a carnal manner. The Lord immediately strips it of the honor of the kingdom and of the rule that it possessed through receiving baptism and the anointing of sacred chrism.

Hence it also follows:

### GIMEL

“He broke in his furious anger every horn of Israel, turned his right hand backward from before the enemy, and kindled in Jacob, like a devouring flame of fire, all around.”

For the Lord not only destroyed the kingdom of the Jews—which is to break every horn—and turned away from them the defense of his right hand, delivering their land into the hands of enemies to be devastated; he also polluted our Jerusalem, which is rightly called the bride of the Lord, when she has departed from him and served, through various crimes, those who are not gods. He broke all her horn, which he had raised for her in the house of David his servant (Luke II), so that she would have no strength to resist her enemies.

Indeed, he also turned his hand backward from before the enemy, the hand that he had held out for vengeance against those who pursued her, unless she herself had first turned backward from God. But because she first went backward, God justly at some time withdrew from her the help of his right hand.

By the right hand, indeed, is understood the power of the Father, that is, the Son, who immediately withdraws the help of his grace from the Church when she has exposed herself to adulterous lovers. Nor is it unjust that, when she has despised her bridegroom and gone after her lovers (Jer. III), the bridegroom should withdraw from her the right hand of his protection.

Hence, when she is thus left without help, the prophet mourns that the Lord has broken all her horn. The Church has her horns, and heretics and false prophets also have theirs. But then her entire horn is rightly broken when she, neglecting the love of her bridegroom, who raised up for her the horn of salvation, does not fear to go after the allurements of her desires.

Thus, deprived of God’s hand, she is stripped of good things and corrupted by the luxury of lust. Therefore the grieving prophet adds: “He kindled in Jacob, like a devouring flame of fire, all around.” For when she is deprived of God’s grace and weakened in her own strength, various lusts of desire plunge themselves into her. Set aflame by these fires all around, so that she cannot escape, she is devoured, as if by fire, within and without.

Typically, this is also well referred to moral conduct, since the soul too is said to have horns. Concerning these horns it is written: “I will break all the horns of sinners, and the horns of the righteous shall be exalted” (Ps. XCXVII). The horns of souls are every kind of strong virtue, by which the faithful soul knows how to strike back at everything opposed to it and, as though it were hay or dust, toss or scatter it into the air.

Let no one, therefore, be unaware that horns are not born at the same time as young animals, although the cause of their coming into being is present in them. The soul, however, is not armed with virtues by instinct of nature, but by God’s gift. Nevertheless, it first received from the good of nature the grace to conceive and the effectiveness to nourish what it had conceived.

But because it has lost both itself and nature’s freedom, some things that are born from the origin of sin are broken, while others are exalted and grow from the strength of divine grace. Because these oppose one another, the Lord will break every horn of carnal Israel, so that vices may no longer exalt themselves.

Hence the prophet groans, not because they are broken, but because in God’s fury they are crushed together with the soul. Trembling at this fury, David said: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger” (Ps. VI).

The Lord also draws back and turns his hand from before the enemy—the enemy pursuing the soul—because the soul itself first exposed itself to its enemies and received an adulterer within. Therefore, because the soul went forth from God’s bosom to look, together with Dinah, upon the daughters of this world (Gen. XXXIV), it was wounded by the devil, and he was joined to its members. Now in his fury the Lord turns his hand away from before the enemy, so that he does not offer help against the one to whom the soul had previously subjected itself through evil.

For this reason he also permitted carnal Israel, namely the Jews, to go into destruction, because they too were previously leprous—not with an ordinary leprosy but with an enduring one. This was signified by Moses’ hand: when he extended it, it became leprous; but when he brought it back, it was clean (Exod. IV).

Hence David also says to God: “Why do you turn your hand away, and your right hand from the midst of your bosom, forever?” (Ps. LXXIII). Moses’ extended hand signified that the Jews had gone forth from God and stretched themselves out toward evil works; therefore Moses’ hand became leprous. But when they were mercifully brought back, as the hand of Moses was brought back into his bosom, they became clean.

This is why David, seeing their captivity to be irrevocable, speaks as though to an offended God: “Why do you turn your hand away, and your right hand from the midst of your bosom, forever?”—as though he were plainly saying: “As long as you turn your hand away and do not return it to your bosom, they will remain stretched out among the nations, unclean and leprous.”

I have said these things for this reason: the soul that casts itself from God’s bosom toward worldly desires will be contaminated. For the Lord cherishes and defends no others except those whom he carries and nourishes beneath his wings or in his bosom.

But concerning those who cast themselves away from there, hear what follows: “And he kindled in Jacob, like a devouring flame of fire, all around.” For surely, once the wretched soul has gone forth from God’s bosom through its increasing sins, the Lord in his fury freely permits unclean spirits to possess it—unless perhaps he again has mercy on it, so that it may return to his bosom. They set it aflame with the fire of desires, like a devouring flame.

And one must consider whether it is not kindled and burned sevenfold, like that furnace of Babylon (Dan. III), consuming whomever it finds among the Chaldeans.

### DALETH

“He bent his bow like an enemy, strengthened his right hand like a foe, and slew everything beautiful to behold. In the tent of the daughter of Zion he poured out his indignation like fire.”

It is clear that the Lord did all these things when he permitted the enemies fighting against Jerusalem—namely, the Chaldeans or the Romans—to fulfill his judgments, and did not repel them. They had been prepared and stretched out from afar, like a bow in God’s hand, for vengeance. But because Zion did not wish to return to him or receive him, in whose hand they were stretched out and kept until the fullness of time [Col. 1112C], it was so that, from the fullness and completed measure of sins, the fullness of vengeance might proceed.

And because they did not wish to be friends, he rightly became their enemy, for according to the voice of the Psalm: “With the holy man you will be holy, and with the innocent man, innocent” (Ps. XVII), “and with the perverse you will be perverted.” Thus, when enemies are concerned, he is rightly mourned as an enemy.

He strengthened his hand like a foe because they themselves had also become adversaries of the divine law, so that they might at least learn that they had not possessed the land by their own sword, and that their arm had not saved them (Ps. XLIII), but God’s right hand, his arm, and the light of his countenance (Exod. XV).

Because they refused to take this into account, he slew everything beautiful to behold in the tent of the daughter of Zion when he permitted everything to be exterminated and demolished. He did not merely let it drip, but poured out his indignation like fire.

This is better understood of the captivity that occurred under the Romans, when God’s indignation is seen to have been poured out in its entirety.

Allegorically, however, it concerns the Church, against which the Lord has often bent his bow like an enemy when she makes herself her own enemy and refuses to obey her bridegroom’s admonitions, so as to return to him through humble satisfaction. Therefore, because he stretches out his bow like an enemy, she is rightly mourned.

By the bow is understood judgment, by which each person is either struck at present so as to be corrected, or, because judgment has long been stretched out to the end, is released for harsher punishment once sins have been completed. In the one same bow, various arrows of God’s judgments are prepared for shooting.

Some are flashing arrows, sent as chosen arrows from the Lord’s quiver to slay the old man and strike vices. Others are sent to afflict various people, either for a crown, for correction, or for punishment.

But the Church groans and mourns over those arrows that the Lord, like an enemy, stretches out either through heretics, or through the devil himself, or through his members, to wound various people within the Church. Concerning these it is written in the Psalm: “Behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at those who are upright in heart” (Ps. X).

Such arrows come from God’s bow, that is, from his divine judgment. One of the elect says concerning them: “The arrows of the Lord are in me” (Job VI). And David says: “For your arrows are fixed in me” (Ps. XXXVII).

Because of these arrows, then, the bow is stretched by the Lord so that sinners may be struck more severely, and this is bitterly mourned—not because we are struck so that we may be corrected, but because the bow is stretched in fury, so that each sinner may become more hardened in heart and at last be struck more grievously because of the enormity of his crimes.

Hence also in the Psalms: “You have given a sign to those who fear you, so that they may flee from before the bow” (Ps. LIX). For the longer the time of judgment is extended by God’s patience, the more harshly the vengeance of retribution accumulates.

He therefore strengthens his right hand like an enemy against the Church when she sins, as he continually casts her down through punishments and torments her with severe penalties, until either, corrected by the blows, she returns to him, or, hardened in those things that perish, she is handed over to punishment after her sins.

Moreover, at times, while he angrily keeps his hand fixed like an enemy, he kills in her tent everything beautiful to behold, because he permits all her precious members to be plundered and slaughtered. Would that we might not see such things happen!

Hence it is more fitting for us to weep with the prophet, because the Lord’s indignation has been poured out like fire to devour, because we have sinned. And because we have brought these things upon ourselves through sins, they are now more atrocious and irremediable on account of the cause of sin that we daily commit; yet we neither perceive it nor try to return to the God who strikes us.

Indeed, contention poured out upon the princes has made us all wander in a trackless place and not on the way. Do you not think that the prophets beheld these things in the Spirit, seeing in him all that they spoke—he in whom are even those things that are not yet, so that the things we lament as having happened in our own times were future? [Col. 1113D]

I would by no means say that they were called “seers” for some other reason, unless it was because they foresaw in the spirit many things far in the future.

Hence, immediately, as though he were speaking about us, he says: “And he poured out his indignation like fire” (1 Kings IX). He poured out his indignation like fire in such a way that you see everything consumed by the fires of dissension and burned by the flames of desire. There is by no means any need to mourn in this manner over things that happened long ago, when we ourselves now commit more wicked deeds in the churches and sin more grievously.

Morally, the Lord stretches out his bow against the sinner like an enemy when he sees him sinning but does not soften him toward repentance. With his hand still extended, he permits him to proceed into more numerous crimes; and he does not turn it away, to such an extent that whatever was naturally beautiful to behold within him in his conduct, as though in a tent, the Lord is said to destroy when he permits the foulness of vices to defile him and all the decency of his conduct within to be violated.

Then at last, as though already in punishment for his sin, angered by his evils, according to the Apostle (Rom. I), he eventually hands him over to dishonorable passions and pours out the flame of lust, so that, already captive after the fires of his desire, he does things that are improper—even things that are against nature.

Hence it follows:

### HE

[Col. 1114B]

“The Lord became like an enemy; he hurled Israel down, he hurled down all his walls, he scattered all his fortifications, and he filled the daughter of Judah with the humbled man and the humbled woman.”

The literal reference of all these things to the Jews is evident, so that the words may stir up a fountain of tears and incline the understanding to lamentation: the Lord, who had once been their guide and guardian, who walked with them and spoke with them about each matter like a friend with a friend, merciful and compassionate (Gen. XXVIII; Exod. XIV, XV, XXXIII), now, on the contrary, when he repays them with vengeance, becomes like an enemy to them through the action of his judgment.

As far as the literal sense is concerned, he had already lamented these same matters above, where he said: “He did not spare all that was beautiful in Jacob; in his fury he destroyed the fortification of the daughter of Judah,” except that here he added “in his fury.” But the meaning is the same when he says that he became her enemy; and, because of the splendid things of the city, he has alluded metrically to its walls—not as though he were mourning different things, but so that, by unfolding the matter again, he might provoke himself more fully to tears.

For this reason, whoever has entered this work and come upon the things that are mourned should, with ever greater devotion and charity, seek tears and, together with the prophet, unfold what must be mourned in each instance, rather than look for something to disdain. Otherwise—for the Lord God of hosts calls us through Isaiah, on the day of distress, to weeping, mourning, baldness, and the wearing of sackcloth (Isa. XXII)—we may instead raise ourselves toward empty joy and gladness, eating and drinking as though we were to die tomorrow [Col. 1114D], so that afterward we experience nothing good or evil, but are like down to be carried away at this very moment (Wis. V).

Hence Solomon also says: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. VII).

Therefore, since we have entered the ordinances of this work of the Church as mourners, let us see spiritually what has happened (Song II). Whenever the bride and friend who is called beautiful and undefiled turns away from the embraces of chaste love, she brings hostility upon herself by acting against his commands, and her bridegroom becomes like an enemy to her.

With remarkable providence, however, he moderates the sentence of severity when he is said to be “like,” and not wholly, an enemy. For although he may seem to abandon her to the hands of enemies and afflict her at times, so that she is believed to have been utterly forsaken, this does not perhaps arise from the cruelty of enmity if she should finally turn back, but from the providence of mercy—even through the evils she has suffered—so that, chastened, she may return to him.

But it must be noted that he first hurls Israel down when he removes purity of heart, lest it be able to see divine things; then, he says, he hurled down all its walls. Our Jerusalem, therefore, has its walls, which pertain to the beauty and adornment of our religion. It also has fortifications by which the city is fortified lest it be breached by enemies.

It has honorable things, and it has dishonorable things. But, the Apostle says, “those members of the body which are dishonorable we surround with greater honor” (1 Cor. XII). For there are in the Church men who are simple and holy in their way of life, and there are also men covered with rustic lowliness. Both, however, are greatly necessary. Although all may seem to be built into the walls of the Church through a more honorable life, they are not able to fortify her by faith or teaching.

Therefore, as evils increase, the Lord frequently permits some who had seemed to be an adornment of the Church to be hurled down into heresy or some disgrace of life. He also often scatters her fortifications when he permits those who ought to be her defenders to go astray and be scattered by their own evil deeds.

Then he fills her with the humbled man and the humbled woman of both sexes—that is, he multiplies them—when he permits many in the Church to be defiled through the works of sin by the deceit of demons.

Morally, the soul has its walls of virtues. Just as in cities there are certain structures called walls for the adornment of beauty, and fortifications for defense by which the city is protected, so there are gifts that fortify us and others that adorn the soul and the Church together—for example, the gifts of prophecy, kinds of tongues, interpretation of speech, and kinds of healing.

These are, as it were, walls of the mind. Even if someone does not possess them, he can stand through faith and justice, although without the height of the gifts and virtues—without which he can nevertheless be saved—he may not appear adorned.

Faith, hope, and charity, however, are not our walls but our fortifications. If we neglect to possess them, we expose ourselves to the ambushes of enemies.

Regarding Judea, because the Lord removed prophecy, teaching, and the signs of miracles, he hurled down her walls. Because of her hardness, he permitted faith, hope, and charity to be taken away from her [p. 1376]. He undertook to scatter her fortifications.

A proper order is preserved here: when the sinful soul is abandoned, the gifts of virtues that were given for the manifestation of the Spirit are first removed from it; afterward, the foundations of faith, hope, and charity are destroyed.

All these things the Lord took from the unbelieving Jews and gave to the nations; and from what he took away from unbelievers, he adorned the mountains of the faithful.

When the soul is stripped of these things again, the Lord becomes an enemy to it, together with those same Jews. The one who had previously said, “I will be an enemy to your enemies, and I will afflict those who afflict you” (Exod. XXIII), at last makes himself an enemy to that soul and permits it to be afflicted.

Hence it is filled with the humbled man and the humbled woman—namely, with unclean thoughts and wicked perceptions—so that within and without it may be increased in insults, until perhaps, clothed in shame, it feels reverence and is converted to repentance.

It follows:

### VAU

“And he scattered his tent like a garden; he demolished his tabernacle. The Lord gave over to forgetfulness in Zion the festival and the Sabbath, and, in the indignation of his fury, the king and the priest to disgrace.”

First, one must note the structure of the words, how brightly it shines in Hebrew. When translated into our language, it possesses, through the beginnings of the verses, such an extended elegance of expression. For after he lamented, “How has the Lord covered the daughter of Zion with darkness,” he then mourned, one after another, with words that corresponded in gradual sequence, so that the word “how”—which is no less a particle of questioning than of grief and astonishment—can be fitted to all of them: “How he cast down, how he hurled down, destroyed, threw down, polluted,” and so forth.

Thus he laments and grieves over everything at once, so that astonishment, amazement, or lamentation never seems to change while he extends himself over each detail. Hence it is as though one were to say: “How did he scatter his tent like a garden?” or, “How did he demolish his tabernacle?” or the other things of this kind that are mourned.

All these things happened because of the sins of the Israelites: the Lord scattered his tent like a garden and demolished his tabernacle because he permitted enemies to demolish it.

Although “tent” and “tabernacle” may seem to convey one meaning—for tabernacles appear to have been so called because curtains, stretched by ropes and hung between supporting boards, sustained the tents—nevertheless, by “tent” we can understand the tabernacle that Moses erected in the desert, and by “tabernacle” the temple that Solomon later built.

Because of the crimes of the Jews, the Lord delivered both of these into the hands of enemies to be scattered and demolished. First he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle, where he dwelt among human beings (Ps. LXXVII). Then, as he himself says through the prophet: “I will do to this house”—namely, the temple of Solomon, in which my name was invoked and in which you trust—“as I did to Shiloh; and I will cast you out as I cast out all your brothers, the seed of Ephraim” (Jer. VII).

In the anagogical sense, however, it is greatly to be mourned that we see many people in the Church scattered and demolished like a garden. But let us see what garden is meant, after whose likeness the Lord is said to scatter or demolish his tent—namely, the rejected synagogue of the Jews or the Church that has strayed from Christ, which is rightly understood by the tabernacle.

There is also the garden of which it is said in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed is my sister, a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Song IV). In this garden a well of living waters flows forth, and there is a fountain of gardens where the south wind breathes, the north wind is removed, and its spices flow. Among these the bridegroom eats the fruit of apples and the honeycomb with honey.

Should we say that the members of the synagogue or of the rejected Church are scattered after the likeness of this garden, whose outpourings are nothing other than paradise? I would by no means say so. Rather, there is another garden of delights, like the paradise of God, of which Moses speaks in Genesis: Lot lifted up his eyes and saw the entire region around the Jordan, which was everywhere watered before the Lord overthrew Sodom, “like the paradise of the Lord and like Egypt” (Gen. XIII), so that it was a garden of delights and pleasure.

Longing for such delights, the Jews sighed over their pots of meat, desiring the garlic, onions, melons, and cucumbers of the Egyptians (Exod. XVI; Num. XI). All these things are found in the mind of those who savor earthly things.

After the likeness of this garden, therefore, the Lord scatters not only those in the Church who give themselves to wantonness and turn perversely toward the desires of Sodom and Egypt, but also those who stray from the synagogue.

The Lord demolishes his tabernacle when he permits those dwelling in the Church to be destroyed through crimes and wicked deeds, and everything within to be consumed by vices. Otherwise, as the Holy Spirit bears witness, “the one who enters without blemish and practices justice” can dwell in God’s tabernacle (Ps. XIV), nor can anyone be built into it apart from the things that follow.

When these commandments are neglected, the Lord also gives our festivals and Sabbaths of rest over to forgetfulness. This is not because the solemnities of our religion do not please him, but because God’s tabernacle, or the temple of the Holy Spirit, is first violated in us, and there is no place in which the remaining offerings can be presented so as to please God.

Hence he is considered to give them over to forgetfulness, because, without good and righteous works, they are reckoned to us as righteousness. Indeed, the king and the priest are given over to disgrace. They ought, according to Isaiah, to nourish the holy Church of God, for he says: “Kings shall be your foster fathers” (Isa. XLIX). But because they violate the temple of the Holy Spirit through evil deeds, these men are more a disgrace in the Church than an adornment.

Concerning them David says: “And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear” (Ps. II), and the rest that follows.

Thus he indicates that we are “a royal race and a holy priesthood” (1 Pet. II), if we wish to offer God pious and saving sacrifices. We must therefore guard more carefully the tabernacle of the Holy Spirit, in which they may worthily be offered, lest it be demolished by vices.

Morally, the soul has a tent and a tabernacle in which the Holy Spirit often speaks with it. This is immediately scattered like a garden if the soul dissolves itself into luxury and into the varied amusements of wicked pleasure.

The tent and tabernacle are scattered like a garden—not the garden of God’s delights, but like the garden over which Sargon, the leader of the Assyrians, is read to have presided (Isa. XX). For Sargon is interpreted as “prince of gardens,” devoted to pleasures and luxury.

Finally, King Ahab of Israel wished to turn Naboth’s vineyard into a garden (2 Kings XXI). Understanding this according to the laws of tropology, Naboth preferred to die rather than consent that his ancestral inheritance and such a great possession of virtues should be turned by an impious king into pleasures.

But because the unhappy and wretched soul consents outwardly to have its tent—namely, the flesh joined together by bones and sinews—scattered by delights and luxury, and inwardly to have its tabernacle—namely, itself—demolished by pleasures, what else is permitted to happen than that the vineyard and inheritance of the supreme Father be transformed into a garden of desires by the most wicked king?

Therefore the Lord at last gives all its festivals and Sabbaths over to forgetfulness, because the temple in which vows ought to be offered and solemnities celebrated has been demolished by these enticements of delights, and the tent of the flesh has been destroyed by the amusements of pleasure.

Its king and priest are given over to disgrace because, having abandoned these duties, the unhappy soul has subjected itself to the most impious kings: to one of them who devastates the Azotians (Isa. XX), serving generation and lust—for Azotus is interpreted as “generation of lust”; and to the other who wishes to have the flourishing vineyards of Christ changed for him into a garden of desires.

Hence it follows:

### ZAIN
The Lord rejected his altar and cursed his sanctuary; he delivered the walls of its towers into the hand of the enemy. He is said to have rejected his altar and cursed his sanctuary because he spurned all the sacrifices of the Law and the altar, together with all the implements on which the victims were offered, and handed them over, along with the city and the people, to be plundered by the hands of the enemies together with its fortifications.

Here also they entered the temple, the holiest place in all the earth, and raised their voice in the house [Col. 1118C] of the Lord, where once, on solemn days, praises were sung with various instruments according to an inviolable rite, and the glory of the Lord shone forth in greater majesty. Isaiah also laments this, saying: “Look,” he says, “behold, all of us are your people, and the city of your holy one has become deserted, Zion has become deserted, Jerusalem has become desolate; the house of our sanctuary and of our glory has become desolate. Where our fathers praised you, it has become a burning of fire, and all our desirable things have been turned into ruins” (Isa. LXIV).

The allegorical sense, however, does not seem sufficiently to fit the notion that the Lord rejected his altar from the Church, in which Christ is believed to be altar, victim and sacrifice, pontiff and priest. For no other altar can rightly be said to belong to the Church than this one, on which the vows and sacrifices of all the faithful are offered, although many altars are also mentioned, as in the Psalms: “Your altars, Lord of hosts, my king and my God” (Ps. LXXXIII). But the saints are altars in the same way as they are light, or as the other things that are proclaimed concerning them; therefore this one altar beneath which the souls of the saints rest is rightly called “altars” on their account. For it is by no means permissible to say that the Lord rejected him, unless perhaps this occurred in the Passion, when he prayed for the Jews, saying (Luke XXII): “Father, remove this cup from me”; and afterward: “If it cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done.” And this would be to reject him: not to hear him for those on whose behalf he prayed, but rather to undergo, through those for whom he prayed, the death of the Passion.

Thus, as though rejected by the Jews, he was transferred by the Father’s judgment [Col. 1119A] to the Gentiles. Concerning him David says: “But you have rejected and despised, you have delayed your Christ” (Ps. LXXXVIII). You delayed him so that, once the sacrifice had been taken away from the Jews, he would no longer be an altar on which they might offer their victims. For just as all those things connected with sacrifices bore the figure of Christ (I Cor. X), so too the altar built of unhewn stones that iron had not touched (Deut. XXVII) prefigured the Lord’s body, contaminated by no human work.

But because Christ was transferred to the Church, the faithful offer their devout vows in her. For them the Church, suffering together with the apostles, also mourns—not because she grieves that he was driven away and transferred from her, but because she grieves with the apostles over his death, so that together with them she may rejoice in his resurrection.

Hence it is believed that a custom arose among those same apostles: it is handed down that on the day on which he suffered, no sacrificial victim of Christ’s body and blood is offered mystically anywhere in the world. I think there are three reasons for this: either because he himself is sacrificed in truth, while these are his mystical sacraments on the other days; or because Christ himself, the pontiff who rightly offers these things, was slain on that day and descended by himself to the underworld; or because, when the temple was dissolved and the altar driven to its death, there is no mystery by which victims of the body and blood might be offered on another altar.

It follows: “And he cursed,” he says, “his sanctuary,” especially because, although he had no sin, according to the Apostle he was made sin for us (II Cor. V). Concerning him Moses says in the Law: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. XXI). To have cursed his sanctuary, therefore, means that he—in whom all our sanctification abides—was crucified on the tree for us.

And so what is lamented happened: “He delivered the walls of its towers into the hand of the enemy,” when he delivered the apostles—who are rightly believed to be the walls of his towers, that is, of the other saints—into the enemy’s temptation. The enemy had desired them like wheat to be sifted (Luke XXII), and, unless the good shepherd had prayed for them, they would have grown weary in faith and remained defeated in his hand.

As for what follows—“For they raised their voice in the house of the Lord as on a solemn day”—none of those who read the Gospel is unaware how great the confusion then was in the house of the Lord, how great in the courts and the streets, and how great throughout that entire city, especially since it was a solemn day. Yet those who raised voices everywhere, exceedingly loud and full of confused shouting, were not meditating on that solemnity. Hence Isaiah also says concerning the Synagogue: “I expected him to execute judgment, and behold, a cry” (Isa. V). This cry, it is believed, had already then resounded in the ears of the prophets.

In the tropological sense, the Lord rejected his altar in the soul when the altar of the heart is inwardly profaned and prostituted, so that its mind and conscience become polluted. For nowhere else is a sacrifice acceptable to God offered. David says concerning this: “The sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. L). But when the altar of the heart is inwardly contaminated by unclean spirits, it is not inappropriate that, together with the sacrifice that is rejected, its sanctuary also should be cursed, since it is shown to lie under curses.

Because it did not wish the name of God to be sanctified in it, it is punished with curses, and the walls of its towers are delivered into the hand of the enemy. The towers of the soul are faith, hope, and the other virtues, by which the soul, raised up, reaches even to heaven. But because these towers have their own walls by which they are fortified—that is, the works of the other virtues—the walls of its towers are struck down into the enemy’s hand when the soul is scattered inwardly or outwardly by its deeds.

And the enemies raise their voice in the house of the Lord as on a solemn day when all the monstrous forms of vice roar within, because, once the temple of the Holy Spirit has been violated, none but unclean spirits dwell in it, although it desires no other organs of virtue than those of the Holy Spirit to resound harmony [Col. 1120B]. Hence what follows:

**HETH**

“The Lord purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion; he stretched out his measuring line, and did not turn his hand away from destruction.”

The thoughts of God, therefore, are exceedingly deep and consequently inscrutable. How deep, then, was the thought by which the Lord purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion? And, lest the freedom to think about it in a human manner be granted, he “stretched out his measuring line,” so that punishment might proceed in proportion to the measure of the offenses. This does not mean that the Lord has the emotions involved in deliberation, but he speaks according to our manner of expression, because all things are present to him and nothing escapes his knowledge.

Therefore, in proportion to the fullness of their wickedness, the line of destruction was stretched out. Concerning that destruction it is said that he did not turn his hand away until he had repaid everything to them according to its measure, so that, by the line of distribution, the enemy divided their land among himself by lot. Elsewhere in the prophets that same hand is also said to be extended, because they still do not turn back.
