This is what is lamented: that he did not turn his hand away from their destruction, so as to draw them back into the bosom of his protection, lest they should appear throughout the whole day among the nations, leprous and unclean, as though Moses’ hand were extended.

“He mourned the outer wall, and the wall was likewise destroyed.” Tropologically, the outer wall is said to have mourned because, when they saw themselves abandoned by the angels whose aid had protected them, they were made mournful. But this is better referred to our Zion: whenever the Lord stretches over her the measuring line of the measure of our sins and the rule of the strictness of judgment, so that the Church is afflicted according to the merits of her offenses.

Hence her walls—namely, her defenders and rulers—are frequently destroyed, either when they are taken away prematurely by death or when, while still alive, they are overthrown by the assaults of enemies. But because this occurs by God’s just judgment, it is lamented that he does not turn his hand away from the destruction of those who fall, since the city of our strength, when God is offended, is devastated no less inwardly by invisible forces than outwardly by visible ones.

This, I say, is the city of our strength in which, according to Isaiah, the Savior is proclaimed to be established as wall and outer wall (Isa. XXVI). Yet it is not without reason that it is said to have mourned during this pilgrimage of ours, since it shows us to be mournful and grieving, because in us Moab—that is, what comes from the father—has not yet been humbled and crushed to the dust and trampled beneath our feet.

Otherwise, unless Moab is crushed beneath the feet of the Church, this song cannot rightly be sung in her. Hence the saints say: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” (Ps. XIII, 6). For that is a land in which Moab, born from the father who is the devil, still reigns undefeated.

Therefore it is rightly lamented that her outer wall has mourned, because everything found to be lamentable in the members is referred to the head. The wall is likewise lamented as destroyed whenever she herself is desolated by divine assistance—not because the wall can actually be destroyed, but because her protection is removed from her in accordance with her corresponding sins.

When the Lord was mourning Jerusalem’s coming destruction, saying, “If you had known, even you” (Luke XIX), what else was he becoming than her outer wall? But because they were making themselves unworthy of so great a defense, the Savior, as an outer wall, was transferred to the Gentiles: he knows how to suffer with and share the grief of our infirmities, and he became a wall for us.

Morally, the Lord purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion, that is, of the soul that is called a daughter, as the Psalm sings: “Hear, daughter, and see” (Ps. XLIV). But because the Lord sees her descending from the citadel of her contemplation toward the depths and growing cold, he purposed to destroy her wall. Yet he does not do so freely—although all things are naked and open to him—until he stretches out his measuring line and sees by what measure or weight each person’s sins must be punished.

First he deliberates, so that the soul may have the opportunity to return to repentance; and he considers whether, before her walls of assistance are destroyed, she may reflect upon herself. The line is stretched over her, showing how great or what kind her offenses are, if only she may understand them.

But if she recognizes that the Lord does not turn his hand of vengeance away from destruction, then what follows applies: “He mourned the outer wall, and her wall was destroyed.” This, then, the Lord had purposed—not yet freely, but searching, examining, and deliberating—so that the opportunity for conversion might also be granted.

But because she did not wish to convert, he too did not turn his hand away from destruction. At the end, as her evils increased, her wall was destroyed on every side, and she was plundered by the enemies.

Let those who rashly do not fear to pass judgment on individuals, and who do not wish to weigh the causes, take note: the Lord himself is said to bring judgment neither without measure nor without deliberation. Human frailty cannot grasp his examination; in his judgment lie both the magnitude and the measure of punishments.

As for the outer wall’s being said to mourn, once the soul’s wall has been destroyed, this is faith—not the faith that works through love, but the faith by which demons believe and tremble (Jas. II). Through this faith, before her wall was destroyed—that is, before the construction of the other virtues—Christ was the wall and outer wall of the soul, placed within her through that same faith.

But because the unhappy soul did not wish to have Christ as guardian and defender, the works of the virtues are destroyed, and the outer wall mourns: namely, the faith by which it believes in God’s future judgment and trembles. Yet it cannot free or defend itself sufficiently, since it has already been exposed to the enemies. This is not because a place of repentance is not open to it while it lives, but because “when the wicked comes into the depths of evils, he trembles” (Prov. XVIII).

Seeing this, the prophet laments most bitterly, because he sees a soul deprived of virtues, which, before it sinned, the river’s torrent made glad like the city of God (Ps. XLV). Concerning this the prophet had sung that the Savior would be placed in it as wall and outer wall, dwelling through faith in our hearts (Eph. III).

But now, besieged by enemies, instead of a song of joy it has only the outer wall mourning within it, because it has been destined for the underworld, where there is unappeasable mourning and the gnashing of teeth to be endured without end [Col. 1122B] (Matt. VIII; Luke XIII).

It follows:

**TETH**

“Her gates have sunk into the earth; he has destroyed and crushed her bars, her king and her princes among the nations. There is no law, and her prophets have found no vision from the Lord.”

According to the historical sense, by the gates sunk into the earth and the bars destroyed and crushed, he wishes to indicate the teachers of the Synagogue or its defenders, who fixed their minds on earthly matters and were scattered and crushed.

“Her king and her princes among the nations” seems to repeat the same point, so that by the gates kings may be understood and by the bars princes. All of them together were broken and destroyed among the nations, and, as though sunk into the earth, were unable to return to him whom they had refused to receive, although he had been promised by the Law.

When he says, “There is no law,” he may say this either because it was burned by the Chaldeans, or because for them it no longer exists, since, with Christ omitted in everything, it has been violated and destroyed to such an extent that among the Jews there is now no observance of it.

The prophets likewise found no further vision from the Lord because they had scorned to receive, present among them, the true lawgiver and Lord of the prophets, concerning whom the Law and the Prophets sang up to John (Matt. XI).

Spiritually, however, the prophet laments over the Church—or rather, the Church herself is shown to lament in her members—that her gates have sunk into the earth: that is, her teachers and masters, in whom the key of knowledge is turned upon the earth while they are occupied with carnal and earthly works.

He had already lamented above that they had been destroyed; now he grieves over something worse, because they have sunk into the earth. For what has been driven into the ground is not easily moved.

Hence David prays in the Psalms: “Rescue me from the mire, so that I may not sink in” (Ps. LXVIII). For what has been driven in, as I said, is not easily loosened. Indeed, I do not know whether it can be removed except by the one to whom all things yield before the abyss is submerged and presses its mouth over him (Apoc. IX).

Moreover, the bars are destroyed and crushed when those who ought to open the doors of divine Law to believers, or close them against unbelievers, and who ought to admit people into the circles in which divine mysteries are carried, are either crushed by the power of heretics or corrupted by their own depraved conduct.

When these have sunk into and been crushed in the mud of earthly desire, the kings themselves, about whom I spoke above, and the princes are taken captive in the nations—that is, in the vices of carnal life.

When he says, “There is no law,” he does not mean that the Law is not spiritual, but that, as evils increase, among the wicked it is not regarded as anything, since they think they can sin without the Law’s vengeance.

Such teachers of the churches, and such prophets of the Jews, do not deserve a vision of divine inspiration by which they might rightly teach concerning the future, because they presently entangle themselves in empty and wicked errors.

According to the tropological sense, the soul is rightly lamented whose senses have sunk into the earth, that is, into the mud of sin, and in which there is no substance of virtue by which to escape. Because it did not wish to enter through the narrow gate, it fixed its gates—its senses—into earthly pleasures, and destroyed and crushed the bars [Col. 1123B] and bolts of the virtues, so that no entrance of unclean spirits might be barred to it.

Once these have been broken, all the authority of God’s commandments by which it was governed is thereafter taken captive by vices, to such an extent that it has neither law nor vision found from God: it does not hear with the heart what God speaks within, but goes unrestrained after the vanities of its mind and pursues the desires of its heart.

Hence what follows is lamented in the ensuing words.

**JOD**

“They sat on the ground and were silent, the daughters of Zion scattered ashes upon their heads; the virgins of Jerusalem girded themselves with sackcloth. The virgins of Judah cast their heads upon the ground.”

The meaning is clear: in the manner of their fathers, the Jews, oppressed by such great tribulations, mourned in this kind of ascetic attire. Yet these persons especially are not without reason either mourners or mourned, in whom there would be great virtue of moral excellence and authority of religion if they preserved the vows proper to them.

In the mystical sense, the elders of God’s churches rightly keep silent when they sit upon the ground. Hence I do not know whether they ought to be called elders either because they sit upon the earth or because they are silent, unless perhaps those are meant who are like that chorus of senators who will come to judgment with the Lord. They know how to assume in themselves the form of those for whom they mourn, yet they do not descend from the throne of the Judge, although they seem, together with sinners, placed upon the earth, to lament the stains of our life.

Would that such elders existed among us! In that case I would certainly not say that they ought to be mourned. Rather, they mourn those whom the Greeks call *presbyteroi* (πρεσβύτεροι, “elders”), who are adorned by no work of old age but, like fools sunk in stupor, sit upon the earth while they are occupied with earthly and carnal works.

Such men, then, are lamented as those whom we read in Daniel to have raged against Susanna. Concerning them he says: “Grown old in days of evil, now the sins you practiced have come upon you” (Dan. XIII).

As for the daughters of Zion who scattered ashes upon their heads, and the virgins of Jerusalem, and likewise the virgins of Judah, they appear to have one meaning, although different names are introduced. For the souls of those who have been reborn are daughters of that heavenly Jerusalem, but they have their distinctions, whether from the contemplation of divine revelation or otherwise.

The languishing soul, overcome by love for the bridegroom, rightly adjures them in the Song of Songs—although struck by enemies and wounded by the guardians of this age, and although stripped of the garment of righteousness—saying fervently: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I am sick with love” (Song V).

I do not think that she believes these women whom she implores to be scattered with ashes or clothed in sackcloth, since she does not doubt that they can converse with the bridegroom. Otherwise, if she did not understand them to be the higher daughters of Jerusalem—the heavenly virtues and the souls of the exalted saints—she would never adjure them so tearfully on her behalf, asking them to make known to the bridegroom’s ears, together with their intercessions, the lament of her sickness and her love.

Thus he might recall the wandering soul among the flocks of its companions, console the sorrowful one, raise up the wounded from the blow, heal the injured by his own wound, and clothe the one who had been stripped with the garment of salvation.

Such a soul therefore knows how powerful the intercession of holy souls is with the beloved bridegroom. For this reason it adjures them with burning spirit. There is no doubt that, although she still speaks hesitantly on her own behalf, she says this through him than whom she thinks nothing is dearer to them.

But are those believed to be the daughters whom the prophet mourns? Do those who hasten to come, or rejoice that they have reached, the embraces and kisses of their bridegroom scatter ashes upon their heads and clothe themselves in sackcloth? No one could rightly say this.

Rather, these are daughters of Zion in name only and in the sacrament of regeneration. They have fallen from the throne of the kingdom either into heresy or into dusty actions of life, by which their mouth has been obstructed. They do not dare to raise their eyes upward to God, but scatter dust—earthly works—upon their heads, that is, upon their minds, and clothe themselves in a sack woven from the bristles of sins and goat hair.

And because once they have thrown their heads upon the ground—that is, rolled their minds in earthly pleasures—they do not wish to raise themselves up or shake themselves free of the dust, so that they might once again be clothed by the bridegroom in their garments of adornment.

Perhaps that woman who adjures them in this way belongs to their company and number. Although badly wounded, she had escaped already naked, seeking her beloved and languishing with love; yet she does not presume to approach him by herself, as though she were unchaste. Therefore, humbly, she sends and earnestly desires intercessors and messengers who have been adjured on her behalf.

But sometimes wretched souls, although called daughters of Zion, Jerusalem, and Judah, surround themselves so long with the cast-off garments of sins and wrap their minds in earthly clothing that they seem never to wish to rise up.

For them, surely, it is not Jeremiah alone—the lover of his brothers—but the entire chorus of the saints that rightly weeps and laments our most monstrous ruin. For if, after losing the bridegroom, after many persecutions and wounds, after nakedness and stains, they truly wished to do so, perhaps they would find—not immediately their beloved, but at least the daughters of Jerusalem, namely the souls of the saints. These would lead them back to the sweet kisses of the bridegroom through their prayers and merits, and finally through their admonitions and examples, if they would shake themselves free of the dust and raise their minds above earthly things.

Hence they are still called daughters of Judah and Jerusalem, so that, when they hear the name, they may receive the confession of the true faith and at some time turn toward the vision of peace through good will, until they are once again graciously received through adoption into the contemplation of the divine vision.

Morally, when the soul has lost the spirit of counsel, it becomes foolish, as though deprived of the gravity of old age and the dignity of mature life, while sitting among earthly things. For it is seasoned by no salt of wisdom when it longs for earthly things and pursues the allurements of the flesh.

This is what it means for the elders to sit upon the earth: all the thoughts of counsel and acts of prudence are occupied with the pleasures of this life and the profits of the world. When the soul is occupied with such cares, all the efforts of the mind fall silent before God.

Hence David, groaning, says: “Because I was silent, my bones grew old while I cried out all day” (Ps. XXXI). Therefore, the things that grow old within, while they pursue the profits of the old human being, are what other than decayed elders who have fallen from the watchtower of heavenly life onto the earth and keep silent concerning good things—even if they seem throughout the day, that is, in the present, to cry out for and seek the business of this life?

Hence the daughters of Zion—that is, souls—what do they do to the mind which they do not fear to pollute with such acts, other than scatter dust upon its head? Then, clothed all around with the bristles of vices and goat hair, the glory that it could have in heavenly places is rolled down by the mind lying upon the earth, until the flesh returns to the dust from which it was taken and its end becomes everlasting destruction (Gen. III; Phil. III).

**CAPH**

“My eyes failed because of tears; my inward parts were troubled; my liver was poured out upon the earth.”

There is no doubt that, seeing the people’s destruction and that the enemies spared neither sex nor age in the slaughter, the prophet, shaken by immense grief, laments with the greatest weeping, so that his eyes failed because of tears and every pleasant delight was changed into anxiety of heart.

For what could be more grievous than that an ancient nation, the offspring of patriarchs and friends of God, instructed in the divine laws and frequently comforted by the oracles of the prophets, should have come into such great apostasy that, having forgotten its God, it was delivered into the hands of enemies because of the enormity of its crimes?

Spiritually, however, “How the prophet’s eyes failed because of tears” should by no means, I think, be understood simply, but as David sings: “My eyes failed in expectation of your word, saying, ‘When will you console me?’” (Ps. CXVIII).

It is a praiseworthy and blessed failure, not arising from weakness of the flesh but from the strength of desire. For whenever the mind of the saints applies itself more ardently and intensely to the things that are unseen and eternal, it fails to gaze upon externally those things that belong to the present life and are empty.

There are, in fact, some eyes that are bodily; others were opened when Adam tasted the fruit of the forbidden tree (Gen. III); and others are praised in the bride, concerning which it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your eyes are like those of doves” (Song I).

But when these eyes, praised as the eyes of doves, are divinely illumined and contemplate the heavenly mysteries more purely and ardently, all the others fail, because the more ardently these penetrate and understand divine things inwardly, the less the others attend outwardly to objects of desire.

Hence the prophets were called “seers” (I Reg. IX), because they perceived more keenly the things that abide in the Spirit.

He therefore did not groan idly that their eyes failed because of tears, just as David added, “in expectation of your word.” It is a blessed failure, which suffers no loss but gains increase, since the eye grows toward the things upon which it gazes.

Thus, when the prophet’s eyes fail because of tears, they see no less the things they love than the things over which they grieve and mourn. Indeed, they direct themselves toward the things that abide all the more ardently because they see more clearly how bitter and harsh are the things over which they grieve.

Otherwise, tears are always sweet to the saints and suited to every present circumstance. For this reason David says: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. XLI)—in prosperity, that is, and in adversity. For just as bread seems suitable for everything used in life, so tears are suitable in sorrows and anxieties, in pressures and tribulations, in desire and the fervor of love, and even in joy and the compunction of divine remembrance.

I confess that no bodily fluid is seasoned with so much salt, nor does the soul, when moved by any affliction, find greater consolation in anything.

Hence the Church, together with Jeremiah, returns to tears as to the familiar remedies of her grief and pours herself wholly into tears on behalf of her members who have suffered evil, so that she may truly say with the prophet: “My eyes failed because of tears, and all my inward parts were troubled.”

He had already lamented these inward parts above, when he grieved that his belly was troubled, since the inward parts are the same as the belly, because they are within it like receptacles of filth.

Through them, as has already been said, the multitude of the faithful is understood: those who are daily filled within the womb of the Church with divine nourishment. But when they are shaken by the pressure of temptation, either because of the crudity of doctrine or because of the perversity of morals, they are immediately troubled and boil like the sea. For them the higher souls ceaselessly take care and show concern.

Hence the Church, as though in labor, says: “My inward parts were troubled, and my liver was poured out upon the earth.”

By the liver, I think, those are rightly understood who, being wealthy in the Church, devote themselves to cares and pleasures. Physicians likewise argue that pleasure and desire have their seat in the liver. Therefore the Apostle urges such people to be recalled, so that they may not hope in the uncertainty of riches, but, as he says, “let those who have be as though they had not; and those who use this world as though they did not use it; and those who possess as though they did not possess” (I Cor. VI).

Otherwise, when these people pour themselves out through the various desires of the world and loosen the reins of their appetites, what else is happening than that the liver of the Church is poured out upon the earth?

For those who, as the Apostle teaches, have—so to speak—the desires and pleasures of this life, that is, the things in which desire is nourished, can scarcely embrace them upon the earth without relaxing themselves; how much more so when all the reins of desire are loosened?

Hence the Church groans and says on behalf of such people: “My liver has been poured out upon the earth.”

It should also be noted that the liver is not found without bile; so too, I do not know whether wealth is ever possessed without bitterness. It is said that the liver draws the juice of food to itself by its heat and turns it into blood, which it supplies to the individual members for the purpose of nourishment and feeding.

Perhaps this is what the Apostle teaches: “Let those who have be as though they had not,” so that they may turn these things into the blood of their redemption and, from the abundance of blood, provide nourishment and food to each of the Church’s members.

Hence what follows:

“Over the destruction of the daughter of my people, when the little one and the suckling fainted in the streets of the city.”

It is as though he said: “My liver has been poured out upon the earth over the destruction of the daughter of my people,” because the Church of Christ, which is rightly called the daughter of the saints, is then crushed and afflicted by temptations when her liver—that is, the rich and powerful—pour themselves out in earthly desires and hunger only for the things of the present life.

Then the little one and the suckling faint in the streets of the city, when such people seem to abound in every worldly happiness. Otherwise, unless the little ones and sucklings were little in faith and doctrine, they would never faint in the streets on account of such people.

Hence David also says: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps were nearly poured out” (Ps. LXXII), because “I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners.”

The feet of the little ones are moved when those who are still weak in faith and not yet competent in doctrine become jealous of the happiness of those who devote themselves to earthly profits. They abandon the narrow way that leads to life (Matt. VII), go out into the streets, and pour themselves out so that they may perish.

Tropologically, the grieving soul rightly says: “My eyes failed because of tears” when, languishing with love, it sees its inward parts troubled, and cannot direct the conceptions of its mind toward the things upon which the eye is fixed.

For its inward parts are the conceptions of its thoughts. The eye of right intention sees these conceptions troubled within, and it fails because of tears; pressed by the pain of bitterness, it cannot freely contemplate the things it desires.

“For my liver,” it says, “has been poured out upon the earth”: that is, all its will and the luxuriance of its desires, by whose filth even the divine fire within it is extinguished.

And because, as the philosophers say, the fire of the human body is believed to have its seat in the liver, from there it rises up to the brain, then to the eyes and the other senses, and so is diffused through the limbs. Therefore, when the mind is inclined downward and its desire is toward evil, and that fire rises from the liver poured out upon the earth as far as the eyes, what else is it believed to bring about than the failure of right intention?

Hence it laments: “My eyes failed because of tears,” because from the grief that gives birth to tears the failure of divine contemplation is generated.

It should also be noted that the pouring out of the liver upon the earth occurs only because of the destruction of the soul that ought to have been the daughter of the saints, since it has been trampled by enemies. Thus both the outward sense, a little one in the vigor of grace [the wording is uncertain], and the inward mind, a suckling deprived of virtues, have strayed disastrously through the streets of this age. They have nowhere to turn except to tears, by which, although the eyes are weighed down, they are at least consoled through weeping.

Hence what follows:

**LAMED**

“They said to their mothers, ‘Where are grain and wine?’ when they fainted like the wounded in the streets of the city, when they breathed out their souls in the bosom of their mothers.”

No one doubts that even more atrocious things happened to the Jews. Our bitter Jerusalem, however, weeps because the greater part of her has been wounded and breathes out its life in the streets, after abandoning the narrow way and taking the broader paths (Matt. VII).

Among these, surely, that woman falls who, remembering her covenant, seeks her bridegroom mournfully in the Song of Songs: “I sought him,” she says, “and I did not find him; I called, and he did not answer me.” And afterward: “The watchmen who go about the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took away my cloak” (Song V).

She would certainly not have been wounded outside if she were enjoying the bridegroom’s embraces within. But because the little one and the suckling—so that both sexes may be included—desire the broader ways of life and seek more widely the streets of this age, by wandering together with the prodigal son of the Gospel they are stripped of every good and perish from hunger (Luke XV).

Hence the chorus of the saints mourns. “They said to their mothers,” they say, “‘Where are grain and wine?’ when they fainted like the wounded in the streets.”

But wretched are the mothers who have led their children far from the father into such great poverty.

From this it should be noted that “the little one and the suckling” are themselves the more grown-up son, the offspring of noble lineage, but impoverished through their wandering and squandering of possessions, and therefore they remember what foods they used in their father’s house. For they do not say, “Where is barley,” or “the pods” which the hungry gladly accept, but, “Where is wheat and wine?” Thus, although degenerate through their own fault, they know what kind of children their father originally begot them. Therefore that prodigal son too had desired to be filled with the pods that the pigs were eating. “How many,” he says, “of my father’s hired servants have an abundance of bread in my father’s house?” (ibid.)

Isaac likewise says of his son Jacob: “With wheat and wine I have established him.” For liberty is nourished by these two things: the human heart is strengthened by bread, and by wine—that is, by the joy of the Holy Spirit—it is made glad within (Gen. XXVII). Our liberty uses no other bread except that which is made from the grain of wheat that fell into the earth and died (John XII), and which is believed to have come from heaven (John VI); nor any other wine except that which is harvested from the vine of Sorek, and from the vine that is Christ (Isa. V; John XV).

This wine and this bread the little one and the suckling seek from their mothers. But because they are not found in the streets, and because the wounded do not receive them worthily, they breathe out their souls in the bosom of their mothers, who had badly nourished them and had most wickedly enticed them in the bosom of pleasure. For that other son, who looked up to his father in his need, was more instructed than these, who seek such things from the pleasures of the flesh as though from their mothers (Luke XV), since these things belong to the father. Otherwise, if they were with the Father, or returned home to the Father, they would not breathe out their souls from hunger. But because the flesh deceives them, they go astray; and even if not in the fact that they seek bread and wine, at least because, sluggish in the flesh, they ask these things from it. The wretched do not know that those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Rom. VIII). Therefore they perish in the bosom of the flesh, since they are sons of the Father who are born not from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God (John I).

In the moral sense, however, the meaning is almost the same: when the soul, abandoning the way of strictness, begins to expand outwardly, it seizes, as if through the streets of pleasure, the broad and spacious way that leads to death. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “Be consenting to your adversary while you are with him on the way” (Matt. VII)—that is, to the word of the Gospel, which appears opposed to your depraved desires—“lest perhaps he deliver you to the judge,” and so forth (Matt. V).

Otherwise, if your little ones—that is, your thoughts—and the suckling knowledge of your souls cast themselves toward the external things of the flesh and the streets of pleasure, they have nothing to demand from their mothers, namely, from the allurements that falsely flatter them. For they have neither the bread that strengthens the human heart—that is, spiritual teaching—nor the wine that makes glad, namely, the grace of the Holy Spirit within, by which the minds of the faithful are made drunk. And therefore, while they seek these things from those in whom and with whom such things are never found, they breathe out their souls—being such as are, as it were, in the bosom of Gehenna unto death, which bore them [the wording is difficult]—while the flesh that they believed to be a mother returns to the earth.

Hence how well it is said by a certain wise man: “In the day of good things, do not be forgetful of evils” (Ecclus. XI); and: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful, for he who is hard of heart will fall into evil” (Prov. XXVIII). Because that nation did not wish to be softened suitably toward repentance, the grieving prophet, with the affection of one lamenting, turned his complaints toward Jerusalem herself, saying:

## MEM

“To whom shall I compare you, or to whom shall I liken you, daughter Jerusalem? To whom shall I equate you, and console you, virgin daughter of Sion?”

It is certain that, just as formerly under heaven there was no nation so glorious as that Jerusalem, renowned above all kingdoms, so there was none happier than ours, which is the mother of us all and the daughter of the heavenly homeland. She has been called the bride and spouse of Christ, and also the soul consecrated in his body; she is believed to be most glorious, and there is no doubt that her citizenship and inheritance are in heaven. Her justification is believed to come from God alone, since one Church from all peoples is proclaimed to be destined for the heavenly places, so that she may be one body with her head (Gen. II), joined by faith and charity from his flesh and bones.

And just as in the heavens there is one glorious city gathered from all peoples, concerning which David says, “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI), so there is also that one Babylon which degenerates from Christ and commits fornication. Therefore, for the sake of the brevity of readers, over the ruins of these three, contrary to the order begun in the explanation—for their fall is almost one and the same, and one lament must be applied, so that what is said of all may also be said of each individually—let it be said:

“To whom shall I compare you, or to whom shall I liken you, daughter Jerusalem? To whom shall I equate you, virgin daughter of Sion?”

For just as no glory is higher for any mortal than that of those who have reached the prize of the heavenly calling (Phil. III), so no disgrace is comparable to such monstrous confusion. Indeed, the threefold repetition of the words, with one meaning, seems by its lamentation to gather these three into one incomparable blindness of madness: from such glory of their calling and the summit of their dignity—not to speak of the fellowship of angels, but of their being co-heirs with God in the heavenly places—they have cast themselves into so great a ruin and deformity of disgrace that I do not know to whom their fall can be compared except the devil.

Hence in the Psalms: “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High; but you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes” (Ps. LXXXI). Otherwise, those who had been gods and adopted sons of God (Rom. VIII), unless they had returned to the deeds of carnal men and become imitators of the devil rather than of God (Gal. IV; Eph. I), would never have died like men and fallen like one of the princes.

But now, because that nation—or Jerusalem, called the daughter of God—or any soul has fallen from such glory into so wicked a ruin, the grieving prophet, or the chorus of God’s elect, says of the one who has fallen:

“To whom shall I compare you, or to whom shall I liken you?”

As if he were saying: To no one except the one whom you imitate; only to him may you be equated, for you are worthy of it. There is no comparison or likeness where no form or beauty is found, but everything is possessed by deformity, horror, desolation, and destruction, and tends toward non-being. And I do not know whether what tends toward non-being can be recalled to being.

Therefore it is not easily found to whom the fallen soul, or the Church that has strayed from her bridegroom, or the nation cast down from the throne of glory, may be compared. For this reason there is no other fall or ruin from which any of them may take consolation.

“Great,” he says, “like the sea, is your destruction.”

That the destruction of that nation, or of the corrupted Church, or of the fallen soul, is mourned as great like the sea, is because, once one of them has been laid beneath or subjected to its enemies, it never ceases from the heat of trampling, just as the sea is continually struck by the waves of its waters and never rests. So these, after they have come into the hands of their enemies, are broken by ruins and temptations and worn down; they do not cease from the heat of sin until Gehenna receives them.

From this follows: “Who will heal you?”

As if he were saying: No one, until you return to him from whom you have turned away. Here “who” is used either because of impossibility, since one of them is shown to be irrevocable after falling, or because of extreme rarity, since there is no one who can heal the corrupted except the one who sinned—and it is uncertain whether even he is willing to do so.

He immediately discloses the causes of their ruin and the difficulty of their healing when he adds:

## NUN

“Your prophets saw false things and foolish things for you; they did not uncover your iniquity, so as to provoke you to repentance.”

Jerusalem certainly had her false prophets, as is shown in many passages. The Church too has her own—heretics, schismatics, or wicked teachers—who, according to Ezekiel, plaster the wall without tempering the plaster. Each of them overturns the hearts of the simple, through deceptive arguments or false opinions, away from the truth of right faith and the condition of good works. The apostle Peter bears witness:

“There were false prophets among the people, just as there will also be false teachers among you, who will introduce destructive sects, denying the Lord who bought them, and bringing swift destruction upon themselves. And many will follow their debaucheries; through them the way of truth will be blasphemed. And in greed they will trade in you with fabricated words. Their judgment long ago has not ceased, and their destruction does not sleep” (II Peter II).

There is no doubt that the fault of priests and of those who are occupied with the law is the ruin of the people: they either teach falsehoods without restraint, as though they were seeing, or, although they see their iniquity and crimes, they do not earnestly proclaim them to the people in order to summon them to repentance. Moreover, many, although they teach correctly, destroy by their wicked examples—not merely the least things, but even the greater things—that which they have taught well. They do everything either for profit, or out of error, or for boasting, or from laziness. They do not care for souls, but do everything for their own sake, speaking under hypocrisy, merely so that they may obtain what they pursue.

Thus all who do not teach the way of God in truth are proved to be false prophets (Isa. III, VII, XXIII). Hence it follows:

“They saw for you false assumptions and false castings down.”

In Isaiah, where our translator rendered *onus*—“burden”—of Babylon, Tyre, or Damascus, the Seventy translators used the word “vision,” while Symmachus and Theodotion interpreted it as “assumption.” This is what the false prophets do: when they see the burden of the people, by which word the sad things that follow and the punishments impending because of sins are signified, they strive by their own judgment to lighten those burdens, as though through examples from Scripture and their consolations, and to cast from the backs of sinners the burdens that have been fashioned.

But they see both falsely: both the assumptions and the castings down. For often, according to their own will, they pronounce and impose upon the people heavier burdens—or “assumptions”—from lighter offenses; and from heavier and innumerable offenses they make false castings down, or alleviations, as though by divine authority, for sinners. The wretched do not know that woe is impending for them, because they “call good evil and evil good” (Isa. V). And as Aquila translated it more plainly: “Woe to those who say to the good, ‘You are evil,’ and to the evil, ‘You are good.’”

Thus, by these two letters, the prophet laments both wicked teachers and wicked hearers according to the interpretation of the same letters. The sense is that from Mem—that is, from those who teach badly—and Nun, which is “everlasting,” punishment impends upon both groups: either because these teachers wickedly teach the wicked according to their merits, or because those who curse do not avoid the wicked.

The soul too has its false prophets externally, whenever it has subjected itself to them—namely, the senses of the flesh, which always display present things to it and neglect the future. It also has them within: wicked thoughts born from the wisdom of the flesh, which present false and foolish things to our sight. How often they judge as harmless whatever the mind relaxes into at present from pleasures; they do not declare to be iniquity whatever is acquired or repaid to enemies; they deem it permissible for the flesh; they promise us longer periods of time; they weaken the severe judgments of God; and they prophesy that many things which are said to be future will not happen, or will happen otherwise than they are said to happen. They suggest that one thing will be less serious and another more serious; they always consider their own actions lighter and favor what has been committed.

Hence the Apostle says: “The wisdom of the flesh is death,” because its thoughts continually see either false assumptions or false castings down (Rom. VIII). It is rare for them to forgive themselves so as to agree with another, or to forgive one person as they forgive all. They always either exaggerate, or assume, or cast down and diminish; and from these things, by obeying them, they acquire everlasting punishment for themselves.

And from this follows:

## SAMECH

“All who passed along the way clapped their hands over you; they hissed and wagged their heads over the daughter of Jerusalem.”

Some interpret this lament over the Synagogue, the Church, or the soul by saying that those who clap their hands over them are enemies, insulting them as though out of mockery and delight. But we say, on the contrary, that they are holy Fathers and friends, affected by zeal and charity and by immense grief. Whenever they learn that one of them has been cast down by God, they clap their hands not with the arrogance of mockery, but with the feeling of one grieving and lamenting that the Synagogue, Church, or fallen soul has suddenly and unexpectedly come from so great a summit and glory to so great a ruin.

Therefore they are called those who pass along the way. As for the enemies of the Church, or of souls, or of the Synagogue, I would by no means say that they pass along the way, since they have not known the way of peace (Ps. XIII); rather, wandering from the way and rushing tumultuously here and there, they fall to the depths.

When he says, “They hissed and wagged their heads over the daughter of Jerusalem,” he indicates the sudden and unexpected feeling both of one grieving and of one marveling: those who always strive toward divine things lament and are astonished at what has happened—that from such ineffable glory they have unexpectedly come to such madness of apostasy. These movements of the hands or head, and hissing, commonly display different emotions of the soul. Therefore we say that they signify grief and pain no less than insult, delight, or mockery.

From this follows:

“Is this the city, they say, of perfect beauty and the joy of the whole earth?”

The enemies of the Church or of souls certainly do not think it to be of perfect beauty or the joy of the whole earth when it flourishes in works. Only the saints and friends believe it to be of perfect beauty, as the prophets and authors of the divine Scriptures celebrate in many passages, and unhesitatingly affirm it to be the joy of the whole earth.

But the more gloriously and beautifully they rejoiced that it stood, the more they marvel and grieve when they see it defiled and cast down into the hands of its enemies. For “Is this?” is not said with the spirit of one questioning or rejoicing, but of one confessing, as though saying, “This is indeed,” and also of one lamenting. They say it so that, to the degree that everyone rejoices over it because it remains, they may grieve because it is defiled by filth and rushes to the depths.

Thus the prophet himself, grieving, displayed the groaning of the saints over it. Now, lamenting the joy and insult of the enemies, he says:

## AIN

“All your enemies,” he says, “opened their mouths over you; they hissed and gnashed their teeth, and said: ‘We shall devour.’”

The prophet is therefore moved by both sides: either because friends grieve over the three from which one city is gathered, or because enemies mock and insult it on account of the one among them who has fallen.

“All your enemies,” he says, “opened their mouths over you.” The mouth of the enemy is opened against us when many evil things are said about us. Otherwise, before the Judge who is deceived in nothing, it would have remained closed, unless there were innumerable crimes and sins in us that the enemy could bring forward.

They therefore opened their mouths against fallen Jerusalem; they open them also against the sinning Church and against the soul trampled down in the blood of its sins. Hence David says: “O God, do not be silent about my praise, because the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of deceit have been opened against me” (Ps. CVIII). Blessed is the one who, even if there are faults to be brought against him, also has praises to be spoken on his behalf.

“They hissed,” he says, “and gnashed their teeth,” like lions, I say, eager to devour. For just as those pierced by charity and moved by astonishment are said to have hissed above, grieving, so these clap and mock when they see one of them fall, deprived of God’s help and grace.

Hence follows:

“Behold, this is the day that we awaited; we have found it, we have seen it.”

Our enemies always await that day to come on which they may devour not only the soul of each individual, but also the whole Church together, as though with the sword of divine vengeance or destruction. But since this cannot happen unless, because of the multitude of our impieties, the Lord permits it to happen by his just judgment, just as Jerusalem is shown to have done, the grieving prophet immediately adds:

## PHE

[Col. 1133D]

“The Lord has done what he intended; he has fulfilled his word, which he commanded from ancient days; he has destroyed and has not spared; he has made the enemy rejoice over you; he has exalted the horn of your enemies.”

The Synagogue of the Jews had often provoked the Lord by its evil deeds and had long since deserved just punishment, had not the goodness of its Creator, enduring and patiently bearing with it for a long time, sustained it toward repentance. But because it did not wish to turn back after its sins or cease from wickedness, it received punishment worthy of it, according to its merits, because by its crimes it overcame God’s patience.

Thus, formerly, when the people had turned to idolatry and Moses was pleading for them, the Lord answered him, saying: “I will pardon according to your word; nevertheless, on the day of vengeance I will also visit this sin of theirs” (Exod. XXXII). This does not mean that the Lord would judge the same sin twice on the day of vengeance, for he does not judge the same thing twice; rather, it means that they had never completely ceased from or repented of this sin of idolatry. Therefore, on the day of vengeance, the Lord is said to visit this sin upon those who have persisted in it no less than in the future age.

This is why he now says: “The Lord has done what he intended and has fulfilled his word, which he had commanded from ancient days; he has destroyed and has not spared”—when, at last provoked to anger, he brought upon them the blows that he had often threatened and foretold in the Law and the Prophets.

If bodily enemies once did these things against that Jerusalem, what will the spiritual forces of wickedness and the servants of the ancient enemy do against the Church when, because of her sins, she has been handed over to them by the Lord, and they surround her with punishments and pains? I am not speaking of that Church against which the gates of hell will not prevail (Matt. XVI), but of those who have fallen, whether within or outside. Of them John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (I John II).

“He has exalted,” he says, “the horn of his enemies,” because when the Church of Christ is weakened, then the horn of her enemies—that is, their kingdom or power—is raised up and prevails against her.

Very terrible are the things that are mourned when the soul is handed over to the power of its enemies. In the day of prosperity it did not wish to foresee the future evils that threatened it. Therefore it struck upon the day that its enemies had always awaited, when the Lord did and fulfilled his word, according to what had been foretold in the sacred Scriptures.

Hence the Lord, seeing a soul of this kind surrounded by such evils, wept in the figure of perishing Jerusalem, saying: “If you too had known, even on this your day, the things that are for your peace—but now they are hidden from your eyes. For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart, and they will surround you and hem you in on every side” (Luke XIX).

The perverse soul therefore has its own day, which rejoices in transitory goods. The things it possesses are for its peace: while it rejoices in temporal matters, while it is lifted up by honors, while it is dissolved in the pleasure of the flesh, while it is terrified by no fear of future punishment, it has peace in its own day. But it will have the grave stumbling-block of condemnation in another’s day, when, because of its sins, it is handed over to its adversaries, who will surround it with their punishments and tortures.

Then whatever earthly happiness it possessed in the past will no longer help it; there it will be afflicted, where the righteous will rejoice. Everything that is now for its peace will then be turned into the bitterness of torments. Then it will begin to quarrel with itself, asking why it did not fear the condemnation it suffers, and why it closed the eyes of its mind against looking ahead to the evils that followed.

Therefore it is said to it: “But now they are hidden from your eyes.” The mind, relaxed by pleasures, hides the evils that follow from itself, while it refuses to see the future things that disturb its present joy. And when it neglects to foresee them, the Lord suddenly does what he had long deliberated while waiting, and fulfills the words he commanded, when he orders the things he foretold to come.

“He destroyed, and not partially,” so that the opportunity for sinning might not always remain; and what refused to spare itself, he hands over to the enemies to be deceived. This is what it means to exalt their horn: to give them power to rule over the one that refused to free itself from the yoke of its enemies.

Hence follows:

## SADE

“Their heart cried out to the Lord over the walls of the daughter of Sion.”

This cry signifies rather the intention of the heart than an exultation of the voice. Wicked people, or invisible enemies, cry out over the walls of the daughter of Sion—that is, over the soul or the Church—when they attribute to their own power the authority by which they dominate them, rather than to the judgment of divine permission.

Because their blasphemy cries out against God, they will not escape fitting torments. For just as a wall protects and defends, so divine power protects those whom it has fortified. But when he withdraws his help, the enemies are said to cry out over the walls of those whom they plunder, against the Lord, when they attribute everything to themselves and assign to their own power whatever they are able to do against them—although these people had previously been fortified by God’s help, as though he had been unable to deliver them, especially since what happens does not arise from weakness of power, but from vengeance and the equity of judgment.

Therefore, among the other lamentations of his grief, the prophet does not omit mourning this also. It should be noted that this clause of the verse, according to the law of meter, looks back more to what precedes than to what follows. Whenever they cannot complete the sense in one verse or two, they transpose it by poetic necessity and explain the intended meaning in the middle or at the beginning of another. This is why the discourse immediately turns to Jerusalem herself:

“Pour out tears like a torrent by day and by night; do not give yourself rest, and let not the pupil of your eye be silent.”

After completing many lamentations over her miseries and enumerating the evils that had occurred, the prophet turns toward her and urges her to pour out tears like a torrent in order to appease God for her errors.

The course of torrents does not always flow with one and the same force, but according as an inundation of rains has come from heaven; so tears are generated only from divine inspiration and compunction of heart. This does not mean that they can be as great as a torrent, although he seems to speak in exaggeration, but that the mind and eyes should always be ready for the outpouring of tears according to the grace of divine inspiration.

This is one exhortation for everyone: to weep without ceasing in prosperity and adversity, and not to grant any rest to one’s tears. This does not mean that any mortal can display this continually without interruption, but that, while living, no one should spare himself in such a way that he becomes sluggish, as though he had already received security. Rather, without rest and without any limit, let him at least carry repentance in his mind until, when mourning has finally ended, he may safely arrive at that true rest.

Hence how well it is said in the Apocalypse: “God will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Rev. XXI). As if he were saying: While they were going, going and scattering their seeds (Ps. CXXV), they wept without any rest, unwilling to set an end to their mourning until the Judge should come who would wipe it away. God will wipe away every tear of those who refused to spare themselves.

Their eyes were always toward the Lord, as the psalm sings, like the eyes of a servant-girl toward the hands of her mistress (Ps. CXXII), until he himself, taking pity, wiped the tears from their eyes. Therefore mourning must not cease until the Lord wipes away every tear of those who groan to him in their hearts.

He himself will wipe them away in order to show mercy. Do not justify yourself, nor become sluggish and rest. These are the true acts of justice of the soul, which are signified by the letter SADE.

“Let not the pupil of your eye be silent.” This does not mean that the pupil of the eye ought to speak, but that, when it is pierced with compunction through divine inspiration, it has greater efficacy in obtaining a result than the words of one who speaks.

Hence David also says in the Psalms: “My eyes have failed at your word, saying, ‘When will you console me?’” (Ps. CXVIII). As if he were saying: They say, “When will you console me?” so that you may wipe the tears from my eyes and restore perfect freedom, because at present there is no relief from misery, since the days of mourning have not yet been completed, until you put an end to evils, so that future consolation may remain for those who persevere.

It should also be noted whether there is another inner pupil in that eye of which the Lord speaks in the Song of Songs: “You have wounded my heart, my sister; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes” (Cant. IV). For although the bride of Christ is full of eyes before and behind, she nevertheless has one in which her gaze is always more brilliant and vigorous.

Its pupil is never silent in silence, but continually drips toward the Lord, as is read elsewhere. When it is pierced within, it then rightly produces tears outwardly, because “the force of the river makes glad the city of God, and the Most High sanctifies his tabernacle” (Ps. XLV). Otherwise, although the external eye seems to produce tears under compulsion, it is silent and generates them sterile and almost mute.

Therefore that eye must always be cleansed, and that pupil of it must be sought—one which, like torrents flowing from mountains and higher places, being drenched by rains from above, does not know how to be silent, does not know how to rest or look downward, but continually cries out indefatigably to God.

But because, as I have said, no one can always flow with one and the same force, the distinguished teacher of tears has moderated this, so that the eye fixed upon him may drip with burning desire at present, although it cannot remain fixed with an unbroken gaze.

Hence follows:

## COPH

“Arise; praise in the night, at the beginning of the watches. Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord.”

He rises in the night who, lifted up by hope from the tribulation or distress of the present life, shakes off from himself the torpor of negligence and, indefatigable against all things opposing him, fights like a soldier girded for battle. Then, whatever hard and harsh things have occurred, he always praises God.

Therefore he urges: “Arise and praise at the beginning of your watches.” For whenever the crafty enemy inflicts scourges, he immediately persuades us to blaspheme God. Job understood this well. When his wife urged him, “Bless God and die” (Job II), he answered her as one of the foolish women, and did not keep silent about the words of ancient counsel: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I).

This is to praise God at the beginning of the watches: to refer everything we do or suffer to the glory and praise of his name, lest, becoming sluggish at the beginning of our work, we be overwhelmed by the sleep of deception.

Concerning this the Apostle says: “Do all things for the glory of God” (I Cor. X). And so that we may fulfill what the distinguished teacher commands—since there are many watches in which God must be praised—we must take special care at the beginning of the watches, lest the work be condemned from the outset of its intention. When the work is begun well for the praise of the Creator, the remaining watches are left, so that it may be completed well to his glory.

“Pour out,” he says, “your heart like water.” He therefore pours out his heart like water before the presence of the Lord who, from the innermost affection of his heart, brings forth tears of compunction, because “a sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. L).

But when so great a rain of tears is not present, one must not immediately despair. Hence David, speaking in the person of the penitent, says: “Because the enemy has pursued my soul, he has humbled my life to the earth” (Ps. CXLI), and the other words that follow. Shortly afterward he says: “I stretched out my hands to you; my soul is like earth without water before you.”

Thus he spreads out his thirsty soul completely before the Lord, like earth without water, so that he may water it with his rains—the one who commanded waters to flow from a dry rock (Exod. XVII). But the heart flooded with a higher grace is poured out like water when, melted by love of God and neighbor, it is dissolved like ice by heat.

This is why he adds:

“Lift up your hands to him for the souls of your little ones, who have fainted from hunger and thirst at the head of all the crossroads” (Cant. V).

He therefore lifts his hands to God for these people who, out of sincere love of neighbor, apply works of mercy to the humble and little members of Christ, who are everywhere laboring in earthly things from hunger and thirst.

This is perfect charity: that the heart should be poured out to God like water through the love of true devotion, and that the hands should be raised for one’s neighbor; together with Moses, the slight thoughts of the little one of the Church—or of the soul—are overcome by enemies.

Of this woman from whom the bridegroom had turned away and passed on, the Song of Songs says: “My soul melted when he spoke. I sought him and did not find him; I called him, and he did not answer me.” For a melted heart or soul is not rightly dissolved like water from the cold of unbelief except through the heat of divine inspiration.

Therefore one must always pray that the north wind may rise, that the south wind may come, and that its spices may flow; for then the spices of prayers flow within, when the mind is breathed upon by the divine Spirit.

But lest the love of God alone seem sufficient without love of neighbor (Luke XVIII), the hands must be raised, as I have said, and care must be given for the little ones and for those who are in danger from hunger for the word at the head of all the crossroads (Amos VIII). Otherwise, if they had not gone out onto the roads and to the head of the crossroads, they would not have suffered from hunger or thirst.

They must therefore be called back from the crossroads and the exits of the streets, from the head of all the crossroads, to the banquet and the Lord’s meal (Matt. XXII), lest they perish from hunger to the end in their famine. The hands must be raised so that Amalek may be conquered and the little ones may not be crushed.

Therefore the prophet, lest perhaps, while preaching to others, he himself should be found reprobate (I Cor. IV), after he had summoned the wretched city Jerusalem—or rather, the Church, or each individual soul—to the tears of repentance and prayer, immediately turned his words of supplication toward the Lord himself, in order, if possible, to recall him from vengeance for sins, saying:

## RES

[Col. 1138B]

“See, Lord, and consider whom you have thus harvested.” I do not know whether anyone at the present time can comprehend the prophet’s mind, which, because of the abundance of its love, is drawn in different directions: now it repeats with sorrow the evils of its people; now it mourns their sins; now it redoubles its remembrance of the blessings they once possessed, and weeping recalls all their lost desirable things; now it grieves that God has been offended, yet does not cease to pour out prayers to him on their behalf. Therefore he now says also: “See, Lord, and consider.” He asks him to see who sees all things and from whom nothing is hidden (Heb. 4)—not because he does not know, since he sees, but so that by imploring him he may bend him toward mercy. He knows him, therefore, to be merciful by nature, and so he asks him to consider the evils of his people which he endures: “whom you have thus harvested,” as though he were saying: “Just as there is no nation to which you have granted such great benefits, so there is none to which, for just causes, such great punishments have been inflicted; for it produced wild grapes instead of grapes, and thorns instead of fruit” (Isa. 5). For the Lord has not harvested anyone in this way except those who imitate his examples. From them he took away all the ornaments of the Law and ceremonies that are read, and the oracles of his own responses. Why should I pursue the matter further, when they killed him who had provided them with everything? They lost all things, inwardly and outwardly, the present and future goods of heavenly life and earthly affairs—those who purchased offense instead of such great love of God, and disgraceful shame instead of such great glory. And therefore he asks God to consider, not that he may torture them more severely, but so that, because he is angry, he may recall mercy.

“Therefore, lest women eat their own fruit,” as though he were saying: “How can these women do what we read that they did in the Book of Kings, and what Josephus testifies happened under Titus?”—their children “to the measure,” or, as other manuscripts express it more clearly, “to the measure of a palm.” What, then, is incredible about their having eaten them to the measure of a palm, when among them there was such a scarcity of food that necessity and distress—or, to put it more strongly, madness—drove them to this? “If a priest and prophet is killed in the sanctuary of the Lord.” Here it is shown that they had first polluted that place with the blood of prophets, when they even killed them between the Temple and the altar, and stoned those who had been sent to them (Matt. 2). Therefore, by the just judgment of God, they reaped there the punishment for their guilt, worthy of such requital. From these evils the Church of Christ, no less than the soul, must certainly be afraid: for whatever happened to them literally, whenever we, devoted to divine offices, commit such things, the same offense will be measured back into our bosom, and all our religious observance will be profaned. The women too—that is, the souls of sinners—will eat the children of their womb to the measure of a palm, because whatever vices they have brought forth from themselves, they receive according to the measure of their deeds, and they will be filled with the fruits of their own miseries. Therefore, I think one should mourn for such people rather than rejoice, lest, because I have exalted them as far as the heavens, we should be lifted up on account of our religious observance and be condemned more harshly by the most equitable Judge for countless and even graver sins. It follows:

## SIN

[Col. 1139B]

“They lay on the ground outside, child and old man; my virgins and my young men fell by the sword.”

The prophet laments all their evils as his own, because, filled with love, he knows how to tear away whatever evil has occurred in the members. Thus every faithful person, in order to be clothed with love of God and neighbor, ought to extend himself to everything and mourn our common evils as though they were his own. He fixes his attention to see whether any among us, who seem to be members of the Church, lie on the ground, and how many and what sort of people they are—outside, that is, occupied with earthly business: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2). Those lie outside who go out from us and do not remain in works of faith; but there are more who seem to be inside and who, even when they are corrupted, are counted as lost before the divine tribunal.

Therefore the child lies on the ground because he is not strengthened by the virtue of the old; and the old man, a child of a hundred years, is punished with curses (Isa. 65). Virgins and young men in the flower of their age are struck in the soul by the sword of their adversaries. And what is more grievous: “You killed,” he says, “on the day of your fury.” For it is one thing to kill our old man so that he may fall and the new man rise; it is another to strike and kill on the day of his fury those who seemed to stand, so that they may perish without mercy. Hence arises an irreparable lamentation: those who are unknown are mourned; they are mourned because they have already been slain by the sword of God’s fury—not because, predestined by his judgment, they have arrived at eternal death, but because they have drawn it upon themselves by their own hands and desires. Therefore, because he did not recall them, they are mourned as having been killed.

## THAU

[Col. 1140A]

“You called,” he says, “as though to a solemn day those who would terrify me all around; and on the day of the Lord’s fury there was no one who escaped and was left behind.”

He describes, in the figure of the final captivity, and laments—not only the prophet but also the chorus of all the elect—the final destruction of all the reprobate. In this lament the letter THAU is placed as a heading, so that it may be found marked upon the foreheads of those who groan and mourn (Ezek. 9); otherwise, those upon whom it is not found will not escape, but will be set in the midst, with enemies gathered on every side as though for a solemn day. Concerning this the enemies had earlier said: “This is the day we were waiting for; we have found it, we have seen it.” It is therefore called their solemn day, not because that day pleases God, but because then their joy—the destruction, namely, of all the reprobate, which they had always desired—will be fulfilled. On the day of that solemnity, that is, of judgment, Satan too will be released from prison.

And this is what is said in the lament of the elect: “You called as though to a solemn day those who would terrify me all around.” For even the elect will see them gathered from every side and, terrified by the horrifying sight, will be purified on the day of the Lord’s fury; there will be no one who escapes, nor anyone who is left unexamined. Hence also the mournful voice of all the saints laments on behalf of the members taken away from them: “Those whom I raised through the discipline of a beginner and nourished with the milk of instruction” (1 Cor. 3; Heb. 5). For they did not reach the perfect man, so as to fight against the most savage enemies, who are said to have been called as though to a solemn day and to have defended themselves with heavenly arms. “My enemy consumed them.”

And because he first consumed them with the pleasures of men, none of them escapes except the one who has borne upon his forehead the signs of the letter Thau, marked beforehand. Hence the Lord also says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross”—and we have plainly said above that this cross is signified by Thau—and follow me (Luke 9). All the rest, in whom this banner is not found, will not escape the sword of God’s fury, even those whom the Church bore, raised, and nourished, but whom the enemy consumed through their sins. This is what the whole order of the saints laments and groans over: that the enemy consumed them.

But because we have entered the house of mourning and examined various kinds of lamentation and various persons, having completed the second alphabet of the second book, we appropriately impose an end to our vows that must be washed away by tears.

## 1407 PROLOGUE TO THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 1139]

[Col. 1139D] It is not the work of our undertaking, brother and fellow elder, to turn over again the false tales of the poets, or the Milesian stories, since our instruction demands other morals; nor is it our task to investigate the books of the philosophers, because in the one there is play and amusement, while in the other there is difficulty and labor mixed with sweat. Rather, it is more fitting for us to persist unceasingly in dirges and laments, if perhaps—as is read in Judges—when the angel warns us and recounts the evils we have committed, we may ascend with him to the place of those who weep, from Gilgal (Judg. 2), that is, from the place of rolling or wallowing. When he spoke there to all Israel, they raised their voice and wept. Hence that place was called by the name of those who weep, or of tears.

Because these things are sorrowful, it is difficult—indeed impossible—to please everyone. But because I know to whom belongs all that we live, I have therefore devoted myself wholly to this study, as though from a certain watchtower of the mind to behold amid these things we mourn the storms of this world and, with groaning and sorrow, the shipwrecks of our age. Therefore, as though approaching certain burning springs of the prophet for the third alphabet, I have decided to thrust my hand more deeply into those higher matters composed in another kind of meter, which are adapted to the trimeter. In this work, three verses begin with one and the same letter; this is not so in the three Sapphic alphabets.

But because some things here concern the Church, and because many matters are disclosed here more profoundly concerning the passion of Christ, a deeper meaning must be sought, although I believe it cannot be found without tears. Therefore, sitting as though above an ass—the untamed flesh—I ask this of you, fellow elder: since the Lord has given me a parched field of heart, obtain and ask through your prayers and pleadings that the merciful Physician may grant me, if not the upper irrigation, at least the lower, so that I, who have touched the veins of our lamenting people, may at last, even if late, be washed by the devoted spring of tears beneath the house of mourning.

## 1408 BOOK THREE

[Col. 1141]

[Col. 1141B] As far as I can discern, deeper mysteries concerning Christ and his body are opened in this mourning, as though for the whole body at a funeral. Thus the mournful prayer turns in different directions: now toward the Synagogue, now specifically toward the Church, now toward the passion of Christ, now jointly toward Christ and his body, as the first verse of this lament indicates. At times it also mingles moral instruction with these matters, though everything remains mournful, so that somehow the sorrow of the heart may increase—on behalf of those who fall away from the body of Christ, or who have fallen into Judaism, or for what happens in the head, or because of the evils suffered by the members, or even on behalf of those goods of which we are deprived until now.

But so that what belongs to the head and what belongs to the body may be more clearly distinguished, that rule should be recalled which Tichonius wished to be one of the seven rules (Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*), by which even the most learned are greatly helped in understanding the Scriptures. The first of these is the rule concerning Christ himself and his body: it applies when one passes from the head to the body without changing the person, or from the body to the head, or when the very same statement seems to fit the head no less than the body, while nevertheless one does not depart from one and the same person. This is rightly demonstrated in very many places of Scripture, and it is sometimes found in this lamentation also, as follows.

## ALEPH

“I am the man who sees my poverty under the rod of his indignation”; and also: “He has made my skin and my flesh old; he has crushed my bones.”

Although one of these statements suits the whole body, it suits the head better, while the other pertains to the members: by skin and flesh and bones are understood those who, within the Church, are made old by the antiquity of corruption and are crushed by the pressures of tribulation. But when he says, “I am the man who sees my poverty,” although it may seem to fit the lamenting prophet, it is more clearly understood as the voice of Christ, who was made like others in the hands of the prophets, and gathers everyone into himself and unites them, so that each of us may meet in the perfect man and in the fullness of his body.

Therefore, although what he says—“I am the man who sees my poverty”—seems to belong to everyone, it is pronounced more excellently of Christ, because just as all things that concern him excel, so too does this vision of poverty. Otherwise, what is surprising if someone sees his own poverty, by which nearly the whole multitude is afflicted? But just as Christ’s poverty is more glorious than all the riches of the world and more wondrous—he “did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2)—so this vision of poverty is also deeper.

Therefore what he says—“I am the man who sees my poverty”—must not be received casually, but read with great attentiveness of mind and considered with great concentration of heart. How well David, foreseeing poverty in spirit, said: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and poor” (Ps. 40). For this poverty is grasped only by understanding; otherwise, if this poverty were common, it could be felt and discerned by the senses, and understanding would not be required. But now blessedness is promised on this account.

It is therefore no wonder if Christ’s poverty is believed to be glorious and wondrous, since the Apostle also proclaims the poverty of the saints as exceedingly great and rich in wealth. This poverty is certainly not easily understood by everyone—how much less that poverty which even the angels marvel at and from which all our blessedness arises. For although the poor are blessed, they are believed and proclaimed blessed by that Spirit by which this poverty is understood, since it is comprehended only when the Holy Spirit reveals it.

Therefore, as they say, the beginnings of these three verses among the Hebrews begin with ALEPH. As I said above, Aleph is interpreted as “instruction.” I judge that this meaning requires much instruction: the supreme author boasts of it, and, as though he were unique in seeing and understanding, he says: “I am the man who sees my poverty.” It is as though he were saying: “I see my poverty, in which are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, which I willingly took upon myself for others, but which those wretched people not only do not wish to understand, but do not even wish to notice or recognize as their own, though it has been torn apart by every kind of misery.”

Meanwhile, this may also be the voice of all the saints, insofar as they are united in the body of Christ, insofar as they have imitated the same poverty, and insofar as they have been gathered by faith and works into the perfect man. Hence it follows: “Under the rod of his indignation.”

I think that the rod of God’s fury is one thing, the rod of guidance another, and the rod of his kingdom another; while the rod of indignation is something else again. One is the iron, flexible rod by which the impious are crushed like clay vessels in the anger of God’s fury; another is the rod by which the saints are guided in equity until they reach the prize of the heavenly calling (Phil. 3); and another is that of which the Lord says concerning Jerusalem: “In my indignation I struck you, and in my reconciliation I had mercy on you” (Isa. 60). Under this rod God strikes in order to have mercy; he wounds in order to heal.

Christ too was wounded by this rod—not because there was any indignation in him, but because of “the crime of my people I struck him, a man of sorrows and acquainted with sickness” (Isa. 53). This is what he says: “I am the man who sees my poverty under the rod of his indignation.” Because of indignation against our crimes, he endured the poverty of his passion, so that by his bruising we might all be healed.

I do not know whether any of the saints sees fully the mystery of this poverty: how great the goodness of God, how great the love poured out upon the children of wrath, and how great the mercy poured out upon the children of reconciliation. Therefore it is, as it were, his voice alone when he says: “I am the man who sees my poverty.” For he sees in himself his own wondrous and ineffable poverty; he sees the poverty of his members, which they too embrace while rejoicing in hope, having become imitators of him and knowing that “the patience of the poor will not perish forever” (Ps. 9).

Therefore there is rightly one voice of the head and the body: “I am the man who sees my poverty under the rod of his indignation.” For God chastises every son whom he receives and scourges those whom he disciplines for life (Heb. 12). This is a prolepsis in this passage, that is, an anticipation of future events, because at the beginning of this lament he speaks as though it had already been stated whose place he ought to bear: for he does not doubt that it is known to all the members that the Father struck the Son with the rod of passion.
