Therefore it is no wonder if his members too are struck by the same rod of indignation, for the correction that leads to perpetual health, so that the voice of all may be one groaning and lamentation in this valley of tears. Hence it also follows:

## ALEPH

“He threatened me and led me into darkness, and not into light.”

This was when he wished to crush him through sickness, according to the prophet Isaiah: for he was regarded as a leper and struck by God and humbled (Isa. 53). Then, certainly, he was led as though into darkness and not into light, and the darkness did not comprehend him.

But when he says that he threatened him, this refers not only to him (John 1), whom the Father handed over to the terrors and sufferings of the world, but also to the whole Church, which he subjected to himself through threats and terrors and led not into the light of the prosperity of this life, but into the darkness of afflictions, distress, and pressures.

Whose voice, then, is “He threatened me”? It is the voice of the Church, because God educates and advances her through many disciplines. Yet for the present he has led her “into darkness and not into light,” because he has called her more to mourning and sadness than to joy and gladness. Hence it follows:

## ALEPH

“He turned and turned his hand against me all day long.”

This voice equally refers to the head and to the members, because all who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution. Therefore it is the voice of the whole body: “He turned and turned his hand against me,” because those whom the discipline of faith did not convert he permitted to depart freely, each to enter his own ways. But the Church, whom he called from the Jews or from the nations, he afflicts with many painful disciplines and instructs.

Hence he says: “He turned and turned his hand against me.” He turned his hand to chastise (2 Tim. 3), because he scourges and corrects every son whom he receives (Heb. 12), and he turns it mercifully in order to have mercy on her, whom in paternal affection he constricts with many pressures of tribulation. To turn is understood in both senses: when he extends his hand to strike, or when he mercifully offers it for defense or reward.

God turns his hand all day long upon the members gathered into the perfect man and into the measure of the fullness of Christ (Eph. 4), in order to torture, amend, and correct them for the present, while this life is being lived; and he turns it by sparing and helping them in the future, so that he may have mercy.

But those whom God does not touch with any blow are those who have no regard for their own death (Ps. 72). They do not share in the labor of human beings, and they will not be scourged with humanity. Therefore pride possessed them; they are covered with their iniquity and impiety, and with the other things that follow.

This is well said concerning Solomon’s Temple when it was being built (1 Kings 6): “No hammer or axe was heard in it,” because all the stones had been so prepared externally and fitted together through their blows that each, having been hewn, was well joined in the places of the joints. This is what it means: he turned his hand, smoothing, cutting, and striking everything, in order to bring it forth so that it could fit into the structure; and he turned it away from these things by ceasing, when he restores the justified to their proper places and fits them into the dwellings prepared from the beginning (Matt. 5).

The structure of these saints is therefore one, the joining of the members is one, the voice is one, and the lamentation is one. Thus the body of the Church of Christ is so fitted together that there is one complete Christ.

In the moral sense, however, the spirit alone that is in a person knows what belongs to that person. Therefore whenever it is touched by the divine Spirit and understands its poverty, it is immediately moved by tears and groans, saying: “I am the man who sees my poverty under the rod of his indignation.” For when it is struck by God’s scourge so that it is afflicted with mourning, it suddenly recognizes that no strength remains in it, since there is no operation of virtue of which it can boast.

Let none of the saints therefore boast rightly that he possesses a pure heart. Rather, he confesses humbly with tears: “I am the man who sees my poverty,” because he presumes upon nothing in himself, especially when the rod of God’s indignation chastises him inwardly for correction.

Hence he says: “He threatened me and led me into darkness, and not into light.” Certainly, whenever a soul recalls God’s threats, examines the terrors of his judgments, and places its deeds before its eyes as though at the hour of departure, it sees itself turning nowhere except in darkness, stained with sorrow.

This is what it means: whenever inwardly it examines the poverty of its merits under the rod of God’s indignation, “He threatened me and led me into darkness,” because it senses nothing in itself except weakness; and when it considers and turns itself over, it mourns that it has been led to behold itself as though in darkness and not in light.

Such a soul, when it inwardly contemplates and attends to the rod of God’s examination and all the words of his threats, continually repeating its evil deeds before itself, as David did (Ps. 50), what else can it rightly believe except that it has been led into darkness and not into light? Indeed, it knows that it has been led into darkness so that it may weigh itself, lest, while the mind proudly presumes upon itself when lifted up by good things, it lose humility, the guardian of all virtues, and through pride fall into the judgment of the devil.

Thus the poor in spirit are rightly proclaimed blessed. The humble spirit, which knows what is in a person, always sees its own poverty and trembles, since it does not doubt that it still remains under the rod of God’s indignation. Through these blows of correction, the soul rightly understands that it has been threatened and led back to itself. This is the instruction that works inwardly in the soul through Aleph: that it should always turn back into itself, unraveling itself and mourning over itself, until the one who rises from on high enlightens it, the one who came to illuminate those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death (Luke 1).

It follows: “He turned and turned his hand against me all day long.”

With a mother’s affection God sometimes exposes the soul to temptations and casts it down; at other times, when it weeps and grieves, he draws it inward to himself and pulls it back into his bosom, suggests the milk of instruction in its heart, breathes into it words of his consolation, and promises eternal things.

This is what it means: “He turned and turned his hand against me all day long.” He does so while, throughout the whole time of the present life, he afflicts it now with threats and terrors, now with temptations and pressures, even with the thorns of sins; but now, inviting it to himself through divine inspiration and remedies, he encourages it with countless benefits. Thus it may become arrogant in nothing and be broken by no danger, but, subject in all things, may refer whatever happens to the praise and glory of God’s name.

## BETH

“He has made my skin and my flesh old,” he says; “he has crushed my bones.”

Although this is the voice of one lamenting and may seem to belong to the head, it can also suit the Church—not because Christ has been affected by the oldness of sin, as I have already said, but because within his body there are those whose life has grown old and corrupt through their deeds. On their behalf our head rightly groans, and all his elect members groan as well, because they see many within the Church consumed by the oldness of their sins.

Hence David, lamenting as though he were one of the sacred skins, says: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. 6). This man, then, who sees his poverty has an old skin and flesh; he also has rams’ skins dyed red to cover his tabernacle, and hyacinth-colored skins for the beauty and praise of his name (Exod. 25–26). In the former he is poor, because they are affected by oldness; in the latter he is rich, because they are dyed red with blood for the beauty of his name or compared with the colors of heaven.

The rams’ skins dyed red are the bodies of the saints dedicated to martyrdom, concerning whom it is sung: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. 28). The hyacinth-colored skins are those whom virginity has raised to the likeness of heaven, because such people neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven, as the Gospel testifies (Luke 20). Therefore in the tabernacle they are made nearer to heaven.

Hence the Church, speaking of herself in the Song of Songs, says: “I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skin of Solomon” (Song 1). This must rightly be understood not of that Solomon, but of Christ, whose skins are all the saints who have put their flesh to death by crucifying it with Christ, in the likeness of dead skins, beneath which the vital members of the whole body are covered, so that they may bear within themselves the likeness of Christ’s passion.

Solomon is introduced in his person, and his name is interpreted as “peaceful.” Whoever is worthy to be his skin will undoubtedly contain in the recesses of his soul the divine mysteries of the supreme King, as in the Holy of Holies.

The Church is like the tents of Kedar—Kedar is interpreted as “dark sorrow”—when she receives beneath her wings, through the teaching of her consolation, those who are converted from the darkness of error and who mourn as penitents. She is also like the skin of Solomon when she contains within herself orthodox men and all the things figured in the tabernacle.

But because skins have different effects—on some beauty is praised, under others the depth of God’s mysteries is hidden, while in others the Church of Christ is shown as defended and outwardly fortified—Satan says to the Lord: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his soul” (Job 1). For it is evident that God gave all his saints over to the sufferings and pressures of life so that their souls and the souls of all who would believe through their teaching and examples might be saved.

It is as though he were saying, when he was attacking the holy man: “Why do you hold back from giving this man over to passion and temptation, when you will at some time give all your saints over to passion, as skin for skin, and all that they have for their souls?”

Therefore, since such great glory is proclaimed concerning the skins, the man who sees his poverty—namely Christ and the Church—groans, because some of his members are affected by the oldness of sin; indeed, at present all are generally stained by the filth of sin. Hence the Apostle says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).

What else does the one who confesses himself infected by sin do except groan that he has been wounded by oldness? It is therefore clear to all sinners that all are infected by oldness, because vices belong to oldness, while virtues belong to new life. Hence Paul also says: “Strip off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new” (Col. 3). And again: “Our old man was crucified together with him” (Rom. 6).

Since the Church of Christ has been worn out by oldness and cannot yet in the present be without stain or wrinkle (Eph. 5), Christ rightly laments in his members and says: “He has made my skin and my flesh old.”

By flesh the multitude of the common people, or even the whole multitude within the body of Christ, is designated because of the tenderness of the people. Hence David groans: “When the wicked draw near against me, to eat my flesh” (Ps. 26). Otherwise, if they had not been flesh consumed by the oldness of sin, they would not have been food for enemies.

The prophet laments them in his own laments—indeed, Christ the head and his whole Church—as those consumed by the oldness of sins. And he adds: “He has crushed all my bones.” By bones the stronger members are understood, because in the passion of Christ even the apostles themselves were crushed and driven to flight by fear of death.

But when he says that God did all these things, he indicates that God permitted them by his just judgment in order to bring the passions to completion, and that what is lamented truly occurred in Christ’s body. From the beginning of this alphabet the person does not change; but some of these statements, as I said, pertain to the head, while others pertain to the body, as does the present verse. For neither inwardly nor outwardly did any oldness of sin touch Christ, nor is it proved that his bone was crushed. Rather, these things are rightly lamented as having occurred in his members, because inwardly and outwardly even the strong members seem to have been crushed in his body and consumed by the oldness of sins.

Moreover, Jeremiah appears to enumerate these things while plainly lamenting that they arose from the crimes of the wicked no less in that first captivity than also in the second.

In the moral sense, however, the sinful soul rightly laments the oldness of its crimes, saying: “He has made my skin and my flesh old.” For it does not lament skins in the plural, but groans over one skin in the singular, infected by oldness—the skin with which the first human beings, expelled from paradise, were clothed (Gen. 3).

It is rightly one skin, darkened by the oldness of many, because mortality, unquestionably contracted through the bruise of sin, clothed us all alike in the transgression of the first human being, with one sprinkling of sins and death. By this, not only the flesh of sin outwardly, but also all those things covered within the conscience, are rightly lamented as polluted.

Hence the Psalmist, speaking as though with the voice of the human race, caught among malignant spirits, says: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. 6). For away from the fervor of the mind, among spiritual enemies or among our various carnal neighbors, we grow old in some measure through the habit of living and darken the appearance of the newness we have assumed.

Therefore the soul, groaning, says: “[He has made my skin and my flesh old],” while its conscience grows old outwardly like skin, and all its inward beauty, like flesh corrupted by putrefaction, is consumed.

Hence David also says: “When the wicked draw near against me, to eat my flesh” (Ps. 26). By this flesh he designates the carnal affections in the soul, to which the devil approaches as though to his own laws, so that he may transfer into his own body those in whom these affections exist, as though eating their flesh.

When these fleshy parts have been brought to an end, what else will we be but spirit, so that the enemy may find nothing in us to eat? But because our mind and conscience are inwardly filled each day with such affections, what else is corrupted by oldness than the skin of our mortality and the flesh of our carnal desires?

“He has crushed,” he says, “all my bones.” By bones the virtues of the soul are shown, because just as bones are the supports of the body, so virtues are the strength of the soul. When these are broken, whether by the pleasures of the world, the terrors of threats, or any deceitful snares, the grieving soul rightly laments, because its bones have been crushed and its whole body, inwardly and outwardly, has been consumed by oldness and reduced to nothing.

It follows:

## BETH
He built siegeworks around me, and surrounded me with gall and toil.

By these verses, according to the historical sense, it is shown that Jeremiah laments no less the downfall and ruin of his people than the straits of his own tribulation. For God turned and directed his hand against them all day long, to test whether they wished to follow him. On their account Jeremiah’s skin and flesh were also afflicted by hunger, as though exhausted by the decay of old age; and all the vigor of the people was crushed beneath the hammer of the smiter, so that no strength for warfare remained in them.

But even now he laments the enemies’ siege when he says: “He built siegeworks around me.” The Lord had earlier bewailed this in the Gospel, saying: “If only you had known” (Luke 19)—as though he were saying: If you had known the evils that are impending, you too would weep, because your enemies will surround you with a rampart, press you hard, cast you down to the ground, and will not leave in you one stone upon another; that is, they will cast down and destroy every defense, both within and without. Hence also the prophet now mourns: “He built siegeworks around me, and surrounded me with gall and toil.” This is to say: He surrounded me—that is, the people of my nation—with the tribulation of misery and the toil of distress, no less in the second siege of the wicked city than in the first, during which Jeremiah himself was tormented by the people with great bitterness of heart and afflicted, on behalf of the people, by the toil of tribulation.

Meanwhile, mystically, Christ’s Church rightly groans—or rather, Christ in his members—because he too was seized in his Passion: “I have been handed over,” he says, “and did not go out” (Psalm 87). For the Father had built siegeworks around him when they seized him with weapons and clubs after he had been betrayed by Judas; and, lest he escape, they led him bound before the governor (Matthew 26). Surrounded by this rampart, the humanity of Christ is afflicted as though by the gall of bitterness and the toil of tribulation. This is to say: “He built siegeworks around me.” For from that very encirclement by the armed men who seized him, he was handed over to his Passion, where he was given gall to eat and was afflicted by the toil of tribulation. Hence also the Psalmist says: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm 68).

By “gall” every inward bitterness of the Passion is signified; by “toil,” outward tribulation in the flesh is expressed, so that Christ’s complete Passion may be understood in body and soul: for he suffered inwardly for us, and truly suffered outwardly in the flesh. By these passions he still suffers daily in his flesh and in his members, that is, in the Church, because she herself is formed from his flesh and bones, so that she may complete in herself what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ.

From these passions and afflictions she laments, saying: “He built siegeworks around me, and surrounded me with gall and toil,” since at the present time, besieged by every evil, she walks in the midst of snares, where Satan’s seat is. Hence she is so often surrounded by the army of heretics; within, she is afflicted by false brothers and filled with toils, as though with the gall of bitterness. With this gall Simon Magus was drenched; stirred by every kind of impiety and by the zeal of envy, he endeavored to overthrow Christ’s disciples and corrupt the Church of God’s elect.

Hence also she is oppressed by the punishments of outsiders and persecutors; hence she is soothed by the pleasures of this age and by the allurements of worldly things, so that, delighted by them, she may be deprived of eternal goods. Hence she is daily assailed by the deceits and frauds of invisible enemies, until she seems to be filled with the gall of sorrow and with the toils of tribulation.

Therefore, seeing herself hindered by so many snares, Christ’s bride says with a groan: “He built siegeworks around me, and surrounded me with gall and toils.” Enclosed within and without by evils on every side, she says elsewhere: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s? Then I would fly away and rest” (Psalm 54).

Besieged, therefore, by these deceptions and by the snares of her enemies, she is embittered inwardly in spirit, while outwardly she is wearied by toils in order to conquer. Any grieving soul likewise laments that siegeworks are built around it and that it is enclosed by the gall of wickedness, while it is wearied by many toils—especially when it sees itself hemmed in on every side and filled inwardly with its own iniquities.

For the evil spirits ceaselessly strive, if somehow, with God’s permission, they may entangle the wretched soul in perverse pleasures and fill it with the worst desires, whose end becomes for it more bitter than gall and harder than every toil, both within and without. Besieged by these snares, it rightly grieves in mourning because it is surrounded by evil forces and filled inwardly with the gall of bitterness.

It follows:

## BETH

He placed me in darkness, like those who have been dead forever.

This verse plainly suits Jeremiah, because shut away in the bottom of the prison, he was tortured with extreme harshness, almost to the point of losing his life, like one of those who, because of their crimes, are counted among the dead.

Yet because prophecy concerning Christ is woven through the deeds of the prophets, as Paul says, “In many and various ways God spoke formerly in the prophets” (Hebrews 1), he who was prefigured through the ministry of all the prophets fulfilled in his Passion the prophecy of this event. Hence he—or rather, the Lord through him—says: “He placed me in dark places.”

This lament seems to concern the Head more than the members, because he died for us, but not as the dead of this age die. The dead of this age receive the reward of their iniquity and draw death from the propagation of sin; Christ, however, came “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8). Therefore, placed in darkness in likeness, he drew sin out of death.

For this reason he says pointedly: “He placed me in dark places, like those who have been dead forever.” He was indeed truly dead, although he rose on the third day, and the Lord did not abandon him forever. He was placed in darkness—as in hell, as in the tomb, as in the Passion—like those eternally dead; yet he became “like a man without help, free among the dead” (Psalm 87). He was free because he was without sin; therefore, from darkness he soon returned as light to life.

These three verses fulfill the letter Beth, which according to another interpretation means “confusion” (*confusio*), so that the sense is this: Everyone who falls into old age, his strength broken, is surrounded by the siegeworks of the ancient enemy and filled inwardly with the gall of bitterness. Surrounded by these toils, where else does he dwell than in confusion—that is, in darkness?

Therefore, because he laments the confusion of the human race, he rightly laments under this letter the ruin of the whole house and the stains of old age. For Beth also means “house.” This house, groaning over its confusion, says: “He made my skin old,” and the rest that follows.

This old age may also be referred to the Head, because of the mortality assumed by the flesh; all the remaining statements under this letter, however, are more properly understood as spoken of the Head, that is, of Christ.

Morally, the soul placed under confusion laments that it has been progressively brought into ruin by these verses. First, it lies corrupted by the oldness of sin, its strength broken. Then, surrounded by the enemy’s deceit, sold under sin, it cannot escape to freedom; and within, caught among the adversary’s snares, it is filled with its iniquities, surrounded by the greater bitterness of gall, wearied by the toils of desire, and overwhelmed by the burdens of its crimes. Moreover, having lost the light and been placed in darkness, it is already, as though dead forever, unable to see itself—how wretched, how unhappy, oppressed by what evils, and stripped of what goods.

For the judgments of God are taken away from such a soul, lest it should be able to look upon itself any longer and, in the straight path of God’s judgments, see the great abyss (Psalm 35). Instead, deprived always of light, enclosed beneath its own confusion, it perceives only the things belonging to blindness. The enemy always rejoices in this, lest the wretched soul be able to unfold itself from darkness into light.

Hence, after capturing Samson, the Philistines tear out his eyes and then send him blind to the mill, so that, turning continually in a circle, he may never find the way of life with his light taken from him (Judges 16). Hence also, after capturing Zedekiah, Nebuchadnezzar first puts out his eyes and then leads him bound in a cage to Babylon (Jeremiah 39), so that, shut forever within confusion, he may never again see the light.

Nevertheless, whenever a soul enticed by such evils weeps while still bound in the flesh, it mourns itself not truly dead but “as though dead,” while an opportunity for repentance is still granted, before it is swallowed up by the deep and the pit of the abyss closes its mouth over it (Psalm 68). For when this has truly been fulfilled, there will be no return to repentance.

Meanwhile, when it lies in deeper sins, it grieves as though enclosed among the dead forever; yet often, through Christ’s grace and God’s mercy, it returns from the depth of iniquity to life.

The letter Gimel follows. It is interpreted as “retribution” or “fullness,” so that from its interpretation the reader may recognize the fullness of retribution. The following three verses indicate what sort or kind of retribution follows from the fullness of sins, when it says:

## GIMEL

He built siegeworks against me, so that I cannot go out; he made my fetters heavy. And when I cried out and pleaded, he shut out my prayer. He blocked my ways with squared stones; he overturned my paths.

The prophet seems to lament this sufficiently on his own behalf—or rather, on behalf of the people as well. Bound in prison and weighed down by fetters, he bitterly bewailed the siege built against the city and the people, because, as their sins demanded, he foresaw in the spirit that they could not be freed from it.

“And when I cried out,” he says, “and pleaded, he shut out my prayer.” Hence the Lord says: “Do not take up praise and prayer for them” (Jeremiah 7). For the cry of their deeds had risen up against them, so that the prophet would not be heard when he pleaded for them. This is why he says: “He shut out my prayer,” when, groaning and grieving over their sins, he did not deserve to be heard.

All their ways were also closed. Even if I spoke with him by means of a mound, they were blocked with squared stones, and the paths were overturned, lest they perhaps escape either the first or the second siege. It should be noted that the prophet laments his ways as closed and his paths overturned when he sees all the exits of the wretched city blocked in its overthrow by the enemies and the people ensnared for their persuasion.

The sense of these verses can equally be referred to the Head and to the members when he says: “He built siegeworks against me, so that I cannot go out,” as though he were plainly saying: He stirred up the hearts of the Jews against me and built legions and cohorts against me, raging so that I would not go out of their hands until I should go forth as it is written of me and the prophecies of the prophets should be fulfilled.

Therefore he shut out his prayer when he cried: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26), so that all things might be fulfilled.

The Church of Christ, too, often enclosed by the doctrines of heretics or surrounded by the punishments of persecutors, uses this voice in weeping and mourning. She attributes entirely to God whatever she has suffered from her enemies, as though grieving in her own voice she said: “He built siegeworks against me, so that I cannot go out; he made my fetters heavy,” whether because of the enormity of torments, the multitude of snares, or the density of a perverse doctrine—which is known to have happened frequently—so that the universal Church, like a single ship struck by waves in mid-sea, often grieves as though overturned and weighed down.

Amid these dangers she has very often groaned that her prayer was shut out by the Lord, for her testing, while possessing with the Apostle her anchor (Hebrews 6), namely, hope fixed in heaven, lest—God forbid—those who are foreknown and predestined should be submerged by the waves.

“He blocked her ways with squared stones,” when he closed all the paths of the holy Scriptures with what were, as it were, the squared expressions of philosophers, so that by them she might not hasten by the straight path, with the steps of faith, toward the homeland. He also permitted all their paths—that is, the most subtle understandings of divine matters—to be overturned by secular disciplines or by the snares of perverse doctrine.

As for the soul, whose retribution now threatens because of the enormity of its crimes and which lies submerged beneath the fullness of its sins: since we have said that the letter Gimel can be interpreted in both ways, it rightly laments what has returned upon itself.

“He built siegeworks against me, so that I cannot go out,” just as does the one to whom it is said: “The pains of death surrounded me; the dangers of hell found me” (Psalm 114). Weighed down by these fetters, it fears that it may not be able to escape punishment. For if its falling was its own doing, it belongs to the merciful God to free it from such snares.

What could be more pitiable for a sinful soul than to be held thus enclosed in the prison of the worst captivity, unable to go out any longer into the freedom of good action, and, moreover, bound by the fetters of sins and weighed down more grievously by crimes, so that it cannot even move itself toward the remedy of repentance?

Its fetters are all the desirable things of the world and the pleasures of the flesh, as well as all the deceits of its enemies, by which the feet of faith are bound. For “we walk by faith and not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5), and therefore they cannot freely direct themselves toward the things that are unseen and eternal. They are made heavier whenever we add iniquity to iniquity, because iniquity is rightly said to sit upon a talent of lead (Zechariah 5).

Thus he still enumerates the enormity of its miseries when he says that it is weighed down by such evils.

“And when I cried out and pleaded, he shut out my prayer.” For amid punishments, only tears and prayers console the guilty before the Judge, so that, moved by these, mercy may at last grant pardon for their sins. But a person can be greatly distressed in the end when the guilty mind perceives that it has so offended the Judge that, because its sins demand it, its prayer cannot pass through or reach the fountain of mercy.

The Lord shuts out the prayers of suppliants when he permits us to sin in such a way that our very crimes rise up against us and, with the Judge offended, close every path of mercy, so that prayer cannot reach him who is present everywhere and hears everything. For, as it is written: “Whoever closes his ears so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be an abomination” (Proverbs 28).

“He blocked my ways,” he says, “with squared stones.” Crimes and sins have their own squareness, as a certain poet says:

> These fear, desire, rejoice, and grieve.

By these squared stones, all the vices of our crimes are squared off.

May the exceedingly unhappy soul, infected by old age, its strength broken, surrounded by enemies in a circle and enclosed by the gall of iniquity and misery, wearied by empty toils, placed in the darkness of ignorance and beneath the gloom of blindness, against which countless enemies and vices rage so that it cannot escape—may it at last return to itself.

Let it return, bound by fetters and weighed down, and ask the merciful Judge unceasingly, with every insistence of its cries. For even if the truth does not promise that he will grant what is asked because the petitioner is his friend, it does promise, when indignation has been removed, that he will give as many loaves of life as the petitioner, knocking at the door, requests (Luke 10). For “the Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth” (Psalm 144).

Otherwise, even if the soul had been stripped of all these evils, how could it cross ways blocked by squared stones and paths overturned on the way to the homeland? For what else is there in the world but the desire of the eyes and the pride of life?

If it turns to the holy Scriptures as to the pastures of life, in which eternal life is rightly found (1 John 2), immediately the squared stones of the heretics appear. By these, faith, surrounded as though by walls, is entangled so that the straight paths may not be found; and the overturning of their paths is prepared there as a snare in place of a fountain.

Therefore the faithful soul says with the Prophet: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s? Then I would fly away and rest” (Psalm 54). And with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Romans 7). The answer is: “The grace of God,” so that we may know that we are freed from all these things only by grace.

Therefore, stirred by these straits, let the soul turn continually toward the Lord and, under the letter Daleth, weeping and groaning over more terrible things, see what follows.

Daleth, according to one interpretation, seems to signify “fear,” although above I said that it meant “tablets.” Hence it remains that the mind should conceive salvation from the fear of God, as it is written: “Because of your fear, Lord, we have conceived and given birth to the spirit of salvation” (Isaiah 62). And elsewhere: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling” (Philippians 2).

## DALETH

For what more terrible thing can be said, after such dreadful punishments of sin, than that under this letter it should be said of God:

> He became for me a bear lying in wait, a lion in hiding.  
> He turned aside my paths and broke me;  
> he left me desolate.  
> He bent his bow and set me like a target for the arrow.

What could have been said more terribly than that the author of our salvation should be described as having become for us like a bear lying in wait and like a lion in hiding?

A bear is a wild beast full of deceit, possessing great strength in its arms and in its loins. Yet the Lord is by no means compared here to the beast in himself; rather, through both animals Nebuchadnezzar, or Titus or Vespasian, is signified. Elsewhere they are called a boar and a solitary wild beast. In them, certainly, God’s power exercised vengeance and punishment upon the wicked. Thus God is lamented as having become a bear or a lion because, although he is a merciful and gracious Lord of forgiveness (Psalm 79), by his just judgment he brought against Jerusalem one who would besiege it with every kind of ambush and lay it waste by the power of his strength.

The Lord calls him his servant and his dove (Jeremiah 25), because he served in the vengeance taken against rebellious Jerusalem and overthrew the other cities as well. He left her desolate under hostile devastation, as the historical account reports, and like a shelter in a cucumber field, empty and without a guardian (Isaiah 1).

Therefore the Lord placed her like a target for the arrow, without doubt because she was set in the midst of her enemies so that she was surrounded on every side. Frequently wounded by them as though by arrows, she was at least compelled by necessity to return to the physician.

The Lord is often said to have sent these nations against her, as though from a drawn bow, while moderating them by his judgment, so that she might at least learn to fear God and defend herself, lest she be wounded by the ambushes of her enemies as by the darts of arrows.

But, abandoned by God, she rightly laments herself as set like a target for the arrow, because, under the just judgment of God, she was often wounded by her enemies as though by a drawn bow. The same adversary also overturned and broke her paths, which she says above that she mourns.

Meanwhile, this is the voice equally of the Head and of the body: that the unchangeable and eternal God became for him a bear lying in wait. This is not because he himself, as I said, is changed from his nature of goodness and mercy, but because of the effects of things: he permitted the adversary to rise up against his only Son, our Head, Christ, who, like a bear lying in wait, attempted by his deceit and strength to kill and deceive him. Nor did he do this only when he would tempt Christ’s whole body—that is, those who believe in him—from the beginning of the world to the end.

“And like a lion,” he says, “in hiding.” In these two beasts every ferocity of the devil is displayed. Hence the adversary of the human race is pointedly described by the lion; by the bear, however, all his members—that is, heretics and false brothers—are indicated. For although a bear is strong outwardly, it has a weak head; so do all these have the devil, who always, openly and secretly, seeks among the unity of Christ’s body those whom he may devour or deceive.

In hiding, because he always rages through deceit and fraud; openly, because he greatly trusts in his strength and is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth (Job 40). Hence the Apostle says: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5).

Otherwise, if he did not rely upon his own strength, he would never go about roaring in anger and gnashing his teeth; and if he did not deceive the unwary through the fraud of ambushes, the Psalmist would never say that he lies in wait in secret like a lion in his den (Psalm 9). But because he cannot overthrow all things by strength, he employs the deceits of ambushes.

By these two weapons of his strength he fights no less against the Head than against all his members. The grieving prophet—or rather, Christ and the Church—says:

> A bear lying in wait became for me like a lion in hiding,

so that through these two evils and, as I have said, these two beasts, the devil’s entire body and its head, even to the Antichrist, may rightly be judged to rage against God’s elect, and all may lament this.

These are the beasts that used to come against David, the shepherd of the sheep, and rise up to carry off the flock (1 Samuel 17). Against them David often sprang forth, rescuing a sheep even from the lion’s mouth, tearing apart its jaws, and overcoming its arms.

This is our David, who leads his sheep to the pastures of life, rescues them from the lion’s mouth, and binds the arms of the bears. For we are his people and the sheep of his pasture (Psalms 8 and 114).

Against them, therefore, this lion and bear—our enemies, the adversaries and hostile powers—often come, and they even take away a ram from the midst of the flock. Did not David himself take that very one and seize [or carry off] it like a ram? Had the Lord not rescued him from its jaws, he could not have escaped (1 Samuel 17).

Hence it was said in the person of Christ, because he pursued them: “I struck them,” he says, “and rescued them from their mouth” (Mark 14)—that is, Christ rescued his sheep who had been carried away: David, Peter, and all those who fled in his Passion, and afterward all whom he has rescued when they were almost consumed.

But they, as Scripture relates, “rose up against David” (Psalm 2), because they rise no less against the Head, namely Christ, than against his members. David says: “I seized them by the jaw and strangled them, and I killed them” (1 Samuel 17).

Thanks be to almighty God, because whatever the prophet lamented that they had been able to accomplish against Christ’s flock has all been overcome by God’s power—provided only that the sheep do not thrust themselves into their jaws. For it is clear that by his death the Lion from the tribe of Judah has killed them.

Hence also David says: “I was killing the lion and the bear, I, your servant” (ibid.).

It follows:

“He overturned and broke my paths.” He repeats here in grief the very thing he had already lamented above, and “he left me desolate”—that is, Jerusalem, which the Prophet earlier mourned as sitting desolate.

But now, perhaps having returned to herself—or rather, Christ’s bride, adorned with his blood—she grieves that she has been left desolate by Christ. For when she receives an adulterer in any of her members, she cannot have the Bridegroom with her.

“He bent his bow and set me like a target for the arrow.” Christ is therefore said to have been set by the Father like a target for the arrow, because he himself no less than his entire Church is seen to have been raised up as a standard against all the powers of the air and their deceit.

Hence one of his soldiers says: “We have become a spectacle to the world and to angels” (1 Corinthians 4). Christ alone undertook to raise this standard in himself, as though he were to complete a single combat against all the beasts of the forest, against their savagery, against the pleasures of the world, and against everything hostile to his name (Psalm 103).

Thus he laments that he has been set like a target for the arrow, because he received in himself, no less than in his members, all the darts of the enemy in order to repel them.

As for the soul, under the letter Daleth, struck with fear, it laments, saying: “A bear lying in wait became for me, and a lion in hiding.” For it receives wounds no less daily from the open violence of his arrows than from the secret ambushes of his deceit; and, deceived by such tricks, it rightly laments that it has been left desolate.

“He bent,” he says, “his bow.” By the drawn bow the force of divine judgment is expressed. Its coming is long delayed because Christ prefers to find those whom he may reward rather than those whom he may strike.

Hence David says: “You have given a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from the face of the bow” (Psalm 59).

Perhaps, therefore, by “bow” we may understand the holy Scriptures, from which, as from the strength of the New Testament and a certain sinew, the perplexity of the Old Testament is believed to have been subdued and brought under control. From them arrows are sent, as it were, to strike the hardness of the heart.

For another arrow has wounded the soul that says: “Bring me into the house of wine; surround me with perfumes, surround me with honeycombs, for I am wounded by the arrows of love; I languish with love.” From this bow of God’s judgments Christ has arrows with which to destroy vices and sins, and other arrows with which to wound souls with the love of charity.

Amid all these things the soul has been set like a target for the arrow, so that from one side it may receive the wounds of charity and from the other repel all the darts of the enemy, until it triumphs over its enemies and, victorious and crowned, receives paradise.

The letter He follows. It is interpreted as “I live” or “he is” (*vivo vel est*). From the beginning of this alphabet Christ’s self-emptying is shown, as the Apostle says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and being found in human appearance; therefore he endured every trial and suffering even unto death” (Philippians 2).

It was therefore necessary that under this letter it should become clear, amid the struggles and contests of the Passion, that he who so greatly emptied himself is always the same, exists unchangeably, and, since he is, certainly lives. Thus there is one voice among believers even amid the torments of punishment, when it is said concerning our soul: “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Psalm 3).

He is, because he is altogether always the same and everywhere present, never absent from his own and never far away. The faith of the Church holds this alone unchangeably: that he is.

He who is rightly believed to have died for us responds always and everywhere to those who trust in him: “I live.” Hence he also cries out to sinners, saying: “As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 18).

Let him turn to life, because life never desires death, but desires that all should live by life and turn from death to life.

This is the harmonious voice of the Bridegroom and the bride: let her confess with heart and mouth that “he is,” and let the Bridegroom immediately answer her, “I live,” so that she may be unable to doubt him in anything.

Hence, after death—or rather, before death, and always and everywhere without death—he says: “I have risen, and I am still with you. I was never absent, but I have always been with you and in you, just as you have been in me and I in you.”

This is to say: “I live in you, because you also live in me.” Let all hear that I live, and let them answer those who ask, “Where is your God?” (Psalm 41), saying: “He is.”

He is everywhere: in heaven, on earth, within all things, and beyond all things. He is also in my heart through faith and in my mouth through confession. Thus he is in me, so that I may be in him, just as he said to the Father: “Father, I desire that they too may be one in us” (John 17).

Now let us see what this lament itself indicates.

## HE
He shot the daughters of his quiver into my kidneys. I became a laughingstock to all my people, their song all day long. He filled me with bitterness; he intoxicated me with wormwood.

That this happened to Jerusalem is sufficiently clear, when the Lord, in his just judgment, like someone using a long-drawn bow—for she had refused to take precautions against being struck—sent his flashing arrows, the daughters of his quiver, into her kidneys, so that there they might first receive the vengeance of God’s judgments, in the place where she had sinned most. For, as the same prophet testifies: “Each one went in to his neighbor’s wife” (Jer. 5). By the quiver, moreover, the abyss and depth of God’s judgments are signified. From that abyss, Nebuchadnezzar and all the others against transgressing Jerusalem were sent as though they were arrows directed from a bow, to wound her, since the Lord had exposed her like a target for the arrow. When the prophet rebuked them, at least so that now, while besieged, they might repent, they turned all his words into ridicule. Hence he says with a groan: “I became a laughingstock to all my people, their song all day long.” He evidently indicates that this had formerly happened to him personally.

“He filled me,” he says, “with bitterness.” He laments that what the Lord, the God of hosts, had previously threatened was fulfilled: “Behold, I will feed this people with wormwood, and give them water of gall to drink” (Jer. 9). Jerusalem had now been filled and intoxicated with these things, for she had been filled with countless distresses and tribulations, no less in the second captivity under Titus than in the first under the Chaldaeans, when they were taken captive and scattered among nations that neither they nor their fathers had known. They were scattered throughout the whole world, as is seen today, where they were given wormwood to drink—that is, innumerable necessities and afflictions from their enemies—and received water of gall as their drink. This signifies the multitude of their evils, the everlasting yoke of their captivity, or certainly their ignorance of God’s law, because they have been filled with the bitterness of gall and will receive Antichrist in place of Christ.

Christ, however, who is and who lives, mourns as our head, no less for us than for them. Therefore he says: “He shot the daughters of his quiver into my kidneys.” The Father’s quiver is rightly understood as holy Scripture, from which the body of Christ daily receives, as from a bow, the arrows of God’s judgments and blows; these he himself first bore in the flesh, suffering them without the wound of sin. Various arrows are sent forth from Scripture’s quiver. Sometimes he makes them burn, so that cold hearts may grow warm with the heat of charity and be wounded by love. From that same quiver, heretics draw the poisoned arrows of their wickedness, with the venom of unbelief, and strike the hearts of the innocent. From Scripture too are taken the arrows of God’s judgments, by which the outward person is afflicted. Hence the Psalmist says: “Fix my flesh with fear of you, O Lord” (Ps. 113).

When he says, “He shot the daughters of his quiver into my kidneys,” he signifies the affections of divine love or fear, sent forth from those arrows of Scripture as from a propagated offspring. The propagation of the faithful is rightly understood as the kidneys, because just as the propagation of seed is said to be in the kidneys, so in faith, and through faith in believers, all the seeds of the virtues are propagated. Thus Christ’s posterity seems to arise from his kidneys. For Christ possesses all the members of his body in their integrity, including kidneys, from whose seed of faith others are propagated, born from the womb of the chaste mother, the Church.

“He shot,” he says, “the daughters of his quiver into my kidneys”—that is, arrows by which souls may be wounded either toward love or toward fear, so that through them vices may be destroyed and virtues burned with the heat of love. Hence David says: “Burn my kidneys and my heart” (Ps. 25). Therefore no soul exists that is not wounded by these arrows of God, shot as if from a drawn bow, either toward vices or toward virtues. Of these arrows David likewise says: “For his arrows are fixed in me” (Ps. 37).

All holy preachers too have been sent forth like arrows from the Lord’s quiver. Hence he says in the person of the Lord: “In his quiver he hid me” (Isa. 49). It is as though he plainly said: “The Father’s Word hid me for a long time, like a chosen arrow in his quiver, so that after a long period of concealment in the darkness of the Scriptures he might bring me forth from his bow, since I have been appointed judge of all to test kidneys and hearts.”

The remaining words of these verses plainly concern Christ: he himself became a laughingstock to the Jewish people and their song all day long while he lived in the flesh. Hence elsewhere he says: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. 22). “All who saw me mocked me; they spoke with their lips and shook their heads,” namely, in derision and insult, as the Lord’s passion most clearly shows.

“He filled me with bitterness and intoxicated me with wormwood.” Hence, in his passion, they gave him wine mixed with myrrh to drink (Mark 15), because the Lord’s vineyard—which he himself had planted, the vineyard of Sorek—had been turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine (Isa. 5). When he says that he was intoxicated with wormwood, he shows that he was affected inwardly by every sorrow of the heart no less than he was wounded outwardly by the bitterness of the passion.

With these sorrows and punishments the whole body of Christ is tormented inwardly and outwardly until the end, until all things are completed. It suffers derision from persecutors, heretics, false brothers, invisible enemies, and every pressure of the world (2 Cor. 11). Every soul likewise feels itself daily intoxicated with such and similar bitterness, so that for the present it senses nothing good, while it is continually afflicted by such evils.

This follows:

## VAU

He broke my teeth by number; he fed me with ashes. My soul was rejected, and I forgot good things. And I said: “My end has perished, and my hope from the Lord.”

No one doubts that Jeremiah was badly treated by the people, and that the people too were badly treated by their enemies. Hence he says: “He fed me with ashes,” because the Prophet was nearly killed by hunger, while the people endured every kind of punishment. Because of these anguishes of misery, he is mourned as having been fed with ashes, so that his soul is believed to have been rejected from the body.

Thus, amid punishments, the memory of good things quickly slips away; conversely, amid the joys of eternal possession, one does not remember evils. The prophet therefore mourns that the end of his people and the hope of their turning back to the Lord had perished, because, like the wicked person who has entered the depths of evils (Prov. 18), they had despised the Lord.

Meanwhile, this is the voice of the head: that in the passion he broke his teeth by number—that is, the apostles and disciples, who are rightly understood as teeth. For just as we chew and grind with our teeth everything that we take into the body, so through the apostles Christ admitted believers into his body and transferred them into it. Finally, when they had abandoned him and been struck with fear, they all fled (Matt. 26).

He is also said, through David, to have been fed with ashes: “For I ate ashes like bread, and mixed my drink with weeping” (Ps. 102). “My soul was rejected,” he says—that is, after all the evils previously enumerated, so that he was weary of living, since those whom he had loved most and for whom he had come were all pursuing him with hatred.

Under the letter Vau, therefore, these matters of pain and grief are intensified, and through it the harsher statements are moderated. Vau seems to sound either “thus not he,” although another translator rendered it “and,” or certainly “and not he.” For although he says, “My end has perished, and my hope from the Lord,” he did not judge thus, nor was he so forgetful of good things that he did not possess with the Father what is eternal, or that, according to his humanity, he did not believe he received those things in the unity of his person.

Of these good things David says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 27). Therefore, as I have said, he did not judge that his end had perished, nor that his hope from the Lord had perished, nor was he forgetful of good things, although his soul was rejected in him because of the hardness of the hearts of the Jews.

He does, however, indicate immense anguish of mind and grief: he was so intoxicated with the bitterness of the passion that he could not remember good things, and in his irritation at the evils he said: “My end has perished, and my hope from the Lord.” Although this was not so before the internal Judge, it seemed to the people who were present at that time to have perished to such an extent that they said in mockery: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (cf. Matt. 27).

So too the Church, often rejected because of the evils of heretics and persecutors, forgetful of former good things and oppressed by innumerable sorrows, may seem to have lost her end and her hope—not only to unbelievers, but sometimes even to believers. Hence the Prophet says: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had nearly slipped, because I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the prosperity of sinners” (Ps. 73), and the rest that follows.

Morally speaking, the soul, wounded inwardly by distaste for the holy Scriptures, rightly mourns: “He broke my teeth by number,” with which I ought to have chewed the word of God. For whoever inwardly receives the mysteries of the holy Scriptures by hearing them, but does not afterward chew them thoroughly through meditation or thought, is undoubtedly unclean. Hence in the Law every animal that does not chew the cud and divide the hoof is considered unclean (Lev. 11; Deut. 14).

The sinful soul therefore rightly mourns because the enemy has broken its teeth by number, so that nothing remains in it with which it might chew. Recognizing itself to be unclean, it laments that its teeth have been broken, with which it ought to have ground the nourishment of life: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. 8; Luke 4).

To unfold and chew the word of God with the faculties of the mind is the health of life. Hence Moses is praised because his teeth were not moved until the end of his life: he continually chewed the word of life in his mouth and heart and ate the bread of angels without ceasing.

But the one whose teeth have been broken by number rightly mourns that he has been fed with ashes, so that by ashes the grief of the heart and repentance may be signified. Hence, when Job had heard God with the hearing of his ear and seen him with his eyes, he said: “I reproach myself, and I do penance in dust and ashes” (Job 42). To do penance in dust and ashes means nothing other than to recognize oneself, in the contemplation of God, as dust and ashes.

Hence in the Gospel the Lord says to the rejected city: “If the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Sidon and Tyre, they would long ago have done penance in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. 11; Luke 10). To do penance in ashes means to recognize oneself as the ash of the dead. Ashes are therefore customarily applied to penitents, so that from dust and ashes we may discern what we have become through God’s judgment and the ruin caused by sin.

Hence the mourner says: “He fed me with ashes,” as though he plainly said: “Because my sins demanded it, and by his just judgment I delayed chewing the word of life, I groan, filled with the ashes of mortality.”

“My soul was rejected; I forgot good things.” He grieves that he has been rejected by God and exposed to temptations, so that he can no longer freely strive toward the good things he perceives. Rather, wounded within and struck back by every evil of the vices, he lies unable to remember good things, oppressed by more terrible pains.

Hence it follows: “My end has perished, and my hope from the Lord.” This is well indicated by the letter Vau, which, as I have said, is interpreted as “and not.” For one who perishes is not in the Lord, who is truly proclaimed to be the end of all consummation.

Or alternatively, “thus not he,” as one interpreter renders it: “Thus it is not that end of which he laments, in which all things are brought to an end, but the end that perishes and is not.” In this end, it is not the existence of things that is mourned, but their inward condition.

He likewise grieves that his hope has perished from the Lord, because, hindered by such snares, he cannot raise himself toward the things he perceives. Hence the letter Zain is significantly placed next.

According to some, Zain seems to sound “lead yourself there” or “hither.” This openly indicates what it means, as though it plainly said in the person of God or of the teacher: “Lead yourself far away from here, rolled backward into many evils.” And so that he might not wander indifferently, not knowing where to go, the double interpretation demonstrates the meaning, as though it said: “Lead yourself away from the things you oppose.” Then she asks where she should go, and he replies: “Hither,” and “Follow,” indicating the way of supplication.

What she ought to ask is immediately stated:

## ZAIN

Remember my poverty and my transgression, the wormwood and the gall. I shall surely remember, and my soul wastes away within me. Recalling this in my heart, therefore I shall hope.

From the beginning of this alphabet, he describes the miseries of the wretched city, the sufferings of Christ, and the tribulations of the Church. For all these things, as has been shown, he mourns that his end and his hope from the Lord had perished, as though through despair caused by the weight of his miseries.

But through the same letter, as though divinely admonished by what he heard—“Lead yourself”—the Prophet, immediately touched by a new kind of hope and restored in spirit, turns to God, offers prayers, and with wonderful freshness promises that henceforth he will hope for better things, as though he had forgotten his former offenses.

Let the prudent reader therefore observe that these letters are not marked in the divine writings without great mystery, nor without sacraments of understanding did the prophet wish this work of lamentation to begin with these verses, as though with a meter. It is not fitting to suppose that I have fabricated interpretations of this kind for each individual verse, especially since one finds the greatest teachers of the Church of Christ interpreting them in this way, or elsewhere—even if in another work—rendering these meanings in their own verses. The word of God is many-eyed; here and there it is shaded with mysteries.

When these mysteries are unlocked, it becomes clear how excellently the Holy Spirit, through those who produced the Scriptures, took care to foresee such things and things of this kind: namely, to remove the weariness of readers and to refresh their minds, even amid tears, through the exercise of pious work.

There is no doubt that these things ought to be interpreted concerning Christ and his body, since in this wretched voice of lamentation he joins the end to the beginning. The one who says, “I am the man who sees my poverty,” also says at the end, “Remember my poverty and my transgression.”

He therefore considers this poverty to be something great and, speaking as though on his own behalf, asks that it be remembered. Hence the Church rejoices to share in so great a poverty, because she believes by faith what the Lord said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

Therefore she too says with her head: “Remember my poverty and my transgression.” But it must be asked why he requests that his transgression be remembered, since Christ committed no transgression of sin, and no one rightly offers his transgression to the Judge for punishment. Rather, he asks with David: “Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities” (Ps. 51).

Yet there is a reason why Christ prays that his transgression be remembered. Although he committed no transgression of the Law or of God’s commandments, he became transgression for us. Hence the Apostle says: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2). “For our sake he was made sin and a curse” (2 Cor. 5), because “cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21).

Therefore, as I have said, because he was made transgression for us in order to erase our transgressions, it is a great thing to ask God the Father to remember his poverty and transgression. For although he was rich, he became poor for us, so that by his poverty he might enrich us (2 Cor. 8). He joins the body to the head, so that the body may be cleansed through the head’s supplication.

Because the body cannot pass through this present life without transgression, it is now filled with many bitternesses and with the misery of wormwood and gall. He did not simply say, “Remember my poverty and my transgression,” but added, “of wormwood and gall,” because the poverty and transgression of the churches are experienced in wormwood and gall. The Bride is constricted by many labors and wearied by sorrows, so that, if possible, refined in the furnace of poverty by the things she patiently endures for her transgression, she may be cleansed inwardly and, afflicted by sufferings, become thereafter more acceptable to her Bridegroom.

Hence he says: “Remember my poverty and my transgression, the wormwood and the gall.” He does not wish the Lord to remember her transgression as such, but the labors and struggles she endures on account of it—that is, the wormwood and the gall.

“I shall surely remember,” he says, “and my soul wastes away within me.” This is truly a devout voice of remembrance and of eternal life, because when there is remembrance—that is, when the matter is rightly remembered—the soul immediately wastes away within itself as it sighs for that life.

Hence David said: “My soul has fainted for your salvation, and it has hoped exceedingly in your word” (Ps. 119). Thus the prophet, wasting away within himself, says: “Recalling this in my heart, therefore I shall hope.”

For when the whole body of Christ directs itself toward the contemplation of his life, it certainly wastes away within itself and groans. Remembering this, he says, “therefore I shall hope.”

The expression “I shall surely remember” is an idiom of Scripture, as are “to live life,” “to rejoice with joy,” “to die death,” and other expressions found in the holy Scriptures. These are not superfluous forms of speech but are full of necessary significance. For to live simply is one thing, and to live life is another; to rejoice simply is one thing, and to rejoice with joy is another.

Thus “to remember with remembrance” conveys something far more significant than simply “to remember.” To remember with that remembrance means, through the memory of eternal life—which has been breathed into the affection of our mind—to give inward life by remembering, so that the members of Christ may learn to remember, think of, and love nothing except that memory by which everything in us is transformed from oldness into newness.

Here, I ask, let the prudent reader see how greatly Christ’s faithful Bride has advanced so suddenly under this letter, after she divinely heard, “Lead yourself.” Previously, amid lamentations, she had reached the point of despair; now, in the voice she heard, she desired heavenly things, wasting away within herself as she meditated on the word of God. Then, recalling what she had previously endured and having been led far away from those things by the word she heard, she says: “Therefore I shall hope.”

So too those men in the Gospel, who had labored all night and caught nothing, acted on the word. Hence Peter says: “But at your word I will let down the net,” and they enclosed a multitude of fish (Luke 5).

In the same way Christ’s Bride, previously afflicted by many voices of complaint and by tears, immediately upon hearing the word “Lead yourself” grew strong against hope and returned to hope. Refreshed by the memory of that eternal life, she says: “Therefore I shall hope.”

The soul too, after terrible crimes of wrongdoing and the punishments of its guilt, speaks from poverty. But immediately, upon hearing the word “Lead yourself,” it is reborn and brought to life, as the man in the Gospel heard: “Rise.”

Therefore, under this letter, she immediately sends forth a supplicating voice to God and says: “Remember my poverty and my transgression.” For in Adam, as in her first flowering, she transgressed and was exhausted by the poverty of nakedness. Yet, although secretly, when under this letter she is commanded to lead herself away, she immediately is said to remember with remembrance. Like Abraham’s daughter, through the promise she returns from against hope to hope and comes to the letter Heth, which, as we have said, is interpreted as “life” or, according to others, “fear.”

Thus, after the bitter tears of her complaints, she first conceives fear—that is, the fear of God—as it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 111; Sir. 1). Then at last she tastes the goodness of God as well.

She proceeds with the voice of confession:

## HETH

Because of the Lord’s mercies we are not consumed, for his compassions have not failed—and the rest that follows under this letter.

From this point onward, therefore, after arranging the complaints of lamentation, he begins morally to explain the way of returning to God and to presume nothing from oneself, because it depends neither on the one who runs nor on the one who wills, but on God who shows mercy (Rom. 9).

Hence he says: “Because of the Lord’s mercies we are not consumed,” since by God’s grace a remnant from Israel has been saved (Rom. 11), “for his compassions have not failed.”

Every soul likewise, afflicted by such great evils, rightly attributes entirely to the Lord’s mercy the fact that it has not been consumed amid the terrible crimes of its guilt, amid the weaknesses of its flesh, amid the enticements of this age, amid the snares and deceits of its enemies, amid false brothers and the traps of the devil. Though so many deceits and frauds of the enemy rage and evils multiply, the soul is not consumed. As I have said, it rightly attributes all this to God and to his mercies.

“For his compassions have not failed,” he says. David understood this well after his guilt and prayed: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy; and according to the multitude of your compassions, blot out my iniquity” (Ps. 51).

He implores great mercy against a great offense, however monstrous; and the multitude of compassions against innumerable sins, believing and confessing that no offense can be so great, nor sins so numerous, that the greatness and multitude of God’s mercies do not exceed them for forgiveness—provided only that the soul turns back so that it may live.

Hence he says: “For his compassions have not failed.” They fail in nothing, so that they do not flow from the fountain of mercy, provided that anyone’s way of life has not failed.

This is the beginning of our conversion: the Lord’s fear, or dread, and from him the beginning of life, as a gift granted by the Lord. For, as David says: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord” (Ps. 112). Those who fear God are therefore wise and blessed. “Blessed is the one whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach from your law” (Ps. 94).

The fear of the saints is likewise customary, as when fear fell upon Abraham while he was offering sacrifice (Gen. 15), and David says: “I said in my fear: Every man is a liar” (Ps. 116). It is therefore clear that those who fear God are blessed.

The fear of the Lord is holy, because it is truly the dread of the saints. From this it is evident that whoever possesses this fear passes into life.

The following verse indicates how acceptable confession or conversion under the fear of God is: “I have known at dawn; great is your faithfulness.”

What does “I have known” mean except this? After tears of complaint, after terrible punishments, after confession of crimes, after tribulations and distresses, after prayers and confession of God’s mercies, the voice of the merciful God is immediately present and comes upon her:

“I know your tribulation and your endurance; I know your distresses and poverty; I know that you groan because your prayer has been shut out. Since all these things are before me, I know your true confession and steadfast faith, because you confessed that my compassions had not failed.”

As though he said: “And I have known at dawn; great is your faithfulness.”

What does “I have known” mean except that amid all these dangers I approve what you have humbly enumerated in your groaning, and I make you know that after the night of blindness and the darkness of your distresses, at dawn there is great faith from the Lord?

She is praised even though previously, because of weakness, she seemed to have perished, as she said: “My end has perished, and my hope from the Lord.”

It is customary for the prophets quickly to change persons, and likewise in the Song of Songs (Song 2). Now the Bridegroom speaks to the Bride, then the Bride to the Bridegroom; now to companions and friends; now the same absent Bridegroom appears leaping over the mountains and skipping over the hills. He often seems absent so that the Bride’s love may be inflamed more intensely, but then suddenly, like a loving comforter, he is seen to be present.

So here, after under Heth she had reached the confusion of her distresses, she mourned as though abandoned by God. But then, hearing “Lead yourself,” she grew strong, as though passing from darkness to light and from confusion to joy, so that under the fear and dread of God she might preserve the purity of faith.

The Bridegroom immediately comes to her as a gentle comforter: “I have known at dawn; great is your faithfulness.” That is: “I approve you, and I show myself present, though you mourned me as absent and cruel: for at dawn your faithfulness is great.”

And she, as in the Song of Songs, after her lamentations, says: “The Lord is my portion, my soul has said; therefore I shall wait for him.”

How rare on earth is the person who can say: “The Lord is my portion”! How far removed from vices, how separated from every stain of sin, is the one who has nothing in common with the world!

David likewise placed a similar statement in the eighth position under this same letter: “I said, O Lord, my portion is to keep your law” (Ps. 119). This can belong only to the one who passes from the seventh to the eighth—that is, from the present life to the future and new life.

Only such a person can rightly say: “The Lord is my portion”—the one who exists under the eighth, who claims nothing of this world for himself, who possesses no carnal desires, whom lust does not inflame, greed does not goad, wantonness does not make effeminate, ambition does not overthrow, envy does not consume, and no other concern of worldly affairs troubles; the one who lives for God, not for himself.

Such a person can rightly say: “The Lord is my portion; therefore I shall wait for him.”

From here we proceed to the letter Teth, whose interpretation sounds like “exclusion” or “good.” A remarkable discord seems to arise between these two interpretations. If someone is excluded as a person is expelled from a house or lodging, deprived of God’s kingdom and his goods—as the virgins were excluded who did not bring oil with them (Matt. 25)—how can the excluded person receive goodness, being excluded from the kingdom of God?

I do not think the meaning should be taken in that way. Rather, the one whose portion is the Lord clings wholly to the good, possesses the whole of that eternal good, and is wholly excluded from the works of the world and the delights of the present life, because perfect love casts out fear.

Hence it follows:

## TETH
The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him. It is good to await the salvation of God in silence. Or, as another rendering has it: It is good to endure and hope for the salvation of God. For who endures the Lord except one who, through the pursuit of charity, has been shut out from every stain of vice? Who is it that hopes except one who both hopes for, desires, and loves what he hopes for? For what we hope for, we await with patience.

Therefore, whoever hopes endures; whoever endures with patience excludes all the passions of the flesh and all the tumult of troubles. For in goodness one is excluded from every evil. Thus both senses of the interpretations agree under this letter: the Lord is good to all who hope in him, since, according to David, those who hope in him do not transgress (Ps. XXXIII). Elsewhere also in the Psalms, under this same letter: “You have dealt kindly, O Lord, according to your word” (Ps. CXVIII). And what does “You have dealt kindly” mean except “You have been kind to me”? “How good, then, is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart!” (Ps. LXXII.)

To the others, however, Scripture makes this known in very many passages: although by nature he is good—indeed, goodness itself—for he becomes perverse with the perverse and opposes those who oppose him. Therefore he is rightly called good to those who hope in him. And so that hope might not be idle, he added: “to the soul that seeks him.” For whoever hopes does not yet possess in reality what he already holds and enjoys in hope. Therefore it remains for him to seek it through desire—not just any good, but the supreme good—as the bride says in the Song of Songs: “In my bed, by night, I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song III).

Here she beautifully suggests to everyone who seeks four things of the greatest necessity: first, that one should determine what one is seeking; then where, or when, one should seek it; and finally how long one should seek it. For when she says that she sought him in her bed, in the night, whom her soul loves—and there is no doubt that the bride is speaking of Christ—she appears to have sought him in the night and in the darkness of present circumstances, as well as amid the disturbances of worldly affairs.

It is easy to understand from the Gospel how the hearts of his disciples are troubled and the eyes of their hearts are darkened whenever the mind does not understand the things of God but the things of human beings. Whenever, therefore, our human nature does not see the things of God, it is rightly said to be asleep and to be in the night. Sleep closes the eyes of ignorance and blindness as though with slumber.

For this reason the Apostle denies that the children of God are in the night: “For you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day may seize you like a thief; for you are all sons of light and sons of day; you are not of night or of darkness” (I Thess. V). Therefore, let us not sleep as the others do, but let us keep watch and be sober.

For although the Lord is good to those who hope in him, he significantly added: “to the soul that seeks him.” Those who sleep sleep at night; and at night they seek him whom, while sleeping in the night, they cannot find. Nor can those relaxed in the bed of repose be found keeping watch in the first watch, or in the second, or in the third watch. Therefore the Lord is also reported to have frequently withdrawn to pray, remaining wakeful and devoting the night to prayers (Luke XII).

Nevertheless, whoever seeks must know how to seek him whom his soul loves. For one often seeks and does not find; one calls him, and he does not answer. As long as one delights in the place where one dozes and sleeps, one cannot find there the one whom one seeks. Let such a person hear Solomon say: “As a door turns on its hinge, so does the lazy person on his bed” (Prov. XXVI). So the lazy person turns—he seeks in his bed the one whom he seeks and desires, and he does not find him. Therefore the sleep of slumber must be abandoned; sleep must be shaken from our eyes. And although it is still night, watches must nevertheless be kept, so that the one who is sought may be found.

Although another rendering reads, “the fragrance of incense in my bed,” he is not rightly found by those who sleep. Hence the bride, when she had not found him in her bed, says: “I will rise and go around the city; in the marketplaces and in the streets I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him” (Song III). For although she had applied diligence and care, she did not seek him as she ought, and therefore she was entirely unable to find him.

Thus, for the soul that seeks God, the manner of seeking must first be determined, so that it may be able to find him: not with the idle in bed, nor in the marketplaces, nor in the streets, nor in any such place, where either blindness turns one about, or the hateful business of the world is contemplated, or wantonness roams.

For this reason Jesus took up a whip and drove all the buyers and sellers out of the temple, lest the house of his Father should be a house of commerce (Mark XI; Luke XIX). For what use is it to seek him in the streets, where, as the prophet says, his voice is not heard? Therefore the guardians of this city, going about the city, rightly find and seize the soul that seeks in this way while it is wandering, and they reveal its error: that he is not rightly sought in the streets, in the marketplaces, in bed, [Col. 1167B] or in the night of blindness.

The guardians of our city are the teachers, or the words of the prophets. If they are rightly questioned, he is found there more clearly and quickly.
