Thus the bride, when apprehended, did not pass them by without questioning them, but said: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” And, she says, “When I had passed a little beyond them, I found him whom my soul loves” (Song III).

From this it is plainly evident that the words and utterances of the prophets, and the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, are covered with a veil, and that Christ lies hidden within them. “When I had passed beyond them,” she says, “I found him whom my soul loves”—that is, in the patriarchs and prophets, and in the shadowy utterances of their sayings, in which God the man is both foretold and revealed.

He is sought in three ways, namely as the beloved: by faith and confession, and by conversion together with the integrity of doctrine. Hence David says: “Seek the Lord; seek his face continually” (Ps. CIV). See how long he must be sought: until you find him whom the soul loves, shining forth in the perfect light of the Father.

Moses indicates where he is to be sought—not as though above or below, or in the other things contained in Deuteronomy (Deut. IV), but, he says, “in your heart and in your mouth” alone, so that you may retain the peace granted by God; for “his place has been made in peace, and his dwelling place in Zion.” He speaks peace to his people and to those who turn back to the heart.

If we seek rightly, he must be sought there where he is found near. For, as the same lawgiver testifies, the word is “in your mouth and in your heart.” He is found, as we have said, in his holy ones; he also lives within and in the Scriptures.

Therefore, since he must be sought, he must certainly be sought where he can be found, and at the time when he is near, as the Prophet advises: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. LV). For the Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth.

Since, then, he is boundless, he must be sought in faith without weariness; and since he is one and the same, he must always be loved more and more, without any change.

Hence there follows: “It is good to await the salvation of God in silence.”

Let the prudent mind observe, after such great sorrow—once it has begun morally to recover its strength—how much the mind instructed in heavenly disciplines has advanced: excluded from all that belongs to the world and raised, even beyond angelic dignity, to the hidden things, so that it may find him whom it loves.

Thus, having found the supreme good of delights, it confesses that it endures and hopes in the salvation of God, and that it may always cling to this good. It confesses that it is good for a man when he has borne the heavy yoke of his youth. “He will sit alone and be silent.” This, then, is the good exclusion: that he should sit alone with himself and with God.

Whoever feels that he bears a heavy yoke in his youth “will sit alone and be silent,” because he has borne the heavy yoke. But since this instruction is learned only in a moral sense, we must ask what yoke is meant. There is a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam from the day of their birth; there is also the yoke of unbelief; and there is the Lord’s yoke, which is easy, whose burden of virtues is lightened by the hope of reward.

Perhaps this heavy yoke—that is, the yoke of correction—is rightly understood in accordance with the saying: “Come to me, all you who are burdened, and take my yoke upon you” (Matt. XI). If someone bears the yoke before being burdened with the heavy load of sins, he will sit alone; he is not to be compared with the many, but with the one who has been placed alone with God in hope (Ps. IV).

Nevertheless, we must ask how the yoke can be heavy when the Lord says that his yoke is gentle; and the Greek has only “yoke,” without adding “heavy.” Even so, he called the yoke gentle and the burden light, yet he did not wish to call the yoke light.

Therefore the yoke of the word can be heavy but gentle: heavy for young people, whose age is in fuller flower and who do not wish to offer their minds’ necks to be subjected to the yoke of the word. The heavy yoke of the word can also appear to belong to Christ’s Church, because of the burdens of discipline, the austerity of correction, the weight of abstinence, and the restraint of wantonness.

Christ accomplishes all these things in his body, so that the burden may be gentle through the fruit of grace, the hope of eternal reward, and the sweetness of a purer conscience. For he called the yoke of the word gentle and the burden of obedience light, since whoever receives the yoke of the word upon a patient neck will not be able to bear the heavy burden of discipline.

Therefore whoever bears the heavy yoke in youth because of the heat of youth, and sits alone with God and is silent, rejoicing in the eternal mysteries of divine reward revealed to him, will await the salvation of God beneath the yoke.

Certainly he will also be silent when, having need of an excuse for sin, he arrives at mature confession and lays the sin down through prompt correction. Such a person will not be told: “What you did not gather in youth, how will you find in old age?”

More simply, it can also be understood in this way: whoever has borne the yoke of the word from his earliest years—that is, whoever from youth has not mixed with young men—will sit apart until he has trained himself in the full perfection of virtue and has acquired great patience of spirit. Then, when struck, he will be able to offer his cheek, so that, when the time of blows comes, he may endure injury while obeying the heavenly commands.

It is a great thing for young people to abstain from vices and abandon them at the very threshold of youth. For the ways of youth are slippery and tangled. Hence Solomon understands three things as impossible for himself, and a fourth that he does not know: the tracks of an eagle, the way of a serpent, the paths of the sea, and the way of a man with a young woman (Prov. XXX). And David says: “The sins of my youth” (Ps. XXIV).

For a young man falls not only through the slippery weakness of his age, but often sins through ignorance of the heavenly commandments. And who is it that lifts the heavy yoke upon himself from youth except one who renounces all the delights of the world, flees luxury, and bears with equanimity the tumult of every trouble?

He is said to lift the heavy yoke upon himself because, unless aided by the grace of God, he cannot bear it according to his own strength. Therefore he is rightly said to have borne it upon himself, since whatever is commanded concerning ecclesiastical matters or the renewal of life exceeds the strength of corrupt nature.

The letter YOD follows. It is interpreted perhaps as “beginning” or “desolation.” Under it the man mentioned above is lamented: he will place his mouth in the dust, if perhaps there is hope. Or, according to another interpretation: “He will give his mouth to the burial-place, or to the pit; yet there is hope of patience.”

In these interpretations there appears to be great disagreement or dissonance. How can “beginning” be what he will place his mouth in the dust because of hope? Or what sort of desolation can there be, unless it is because, now acting morally after the punishments of his miseries and the dreadful anguish of his torments, faith having been restored to him, he begins our profession by placing his mouth in the dust and thinking at every moment that we are ashes and dust? From this, hope is again made to germinate in us and charity is enlarged.

Sometimes, however, it is a good beginning first to know ourselves and to endure everything for the Lord. Although all these things can be understood as having been said above concerning the Lord—for “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him”—it is said: “He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him; he will be filled with reproaches.”

And the Lord, teaching the virtue of patience in the Gospel, says: “If anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also” (Luke VI). He wants us to be patient even under injuries, not to strike back readily, but not yet even to strike. For patience is an indication of humility.

Therefore, because that Jerusalem was desolate and abandoned, it is said: “He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him.” But it is better understood of Christ and the Church—that is, of his whole body—to whom the Lord is good when he hopes, and to whom it is good to await in silence the salvation of God, and to whom it is also good to give his cheek to the one who strikes him, so that he may not withdraw from injury or avoid the pain of blows, but offer his cheek to be struck.

Indeed, after he had heard the words “Go far back, get behind me,” the Gospel describes him morally, and therefore says: “He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him.” You are to understand that, if someone wishes to strike—or even if someone has already struck—the voluntary body of Christ must offer itself for all the things that the grace of Christ has bestowed upon us. Thus it is an indication that Christ’s Church can be saved in no other way than through the discipline of the Gospel, and that a good beginning begins for it when it begins to observe the Gospel commandments and fulfill the Lord’s commands in its works.

It is as though one said with the Prophet: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXV). Otherwise, how can he lay down the heavy yoke of captivity from his neck unless he has submitted himself to Christ’s light yoke?

“And he will be filled with reproaches.” He did not say, “He will undergo reproaches,” but “He will be filled,” because it is easy to endure one or two insults. Hence he added, “he will be filled with reproaches,” since the abundance of reproaches would more readily move the Lord’s mercy, and would make him pitiable through the deformity of many insults. Here the eagerness of desire and the freedom of grace are shown, when it is said: “He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him and will be filled with reproaches,” since every fullness arises from eagerness to receive.

Therefore great grace is commended when it is said, “he will be filled with reproaches,” just as David, fleeing from Absalom, was filled with the reproaches of Shimei, who convicted and cursed him, calling him a bloodthirsty man. But David, wishing to appear more humble before God and to mitigate the Lord’s offense, said when Abishai wished to avenge him: “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse, because the Lord has commanded him to curse me; perhaps the Lord will see my humility and repay me with good for the curse” (II Kings XVI).

He therefore wished to be filled with reproach because, when humility has been completed, sin is dissolved, as Isaiah indicates when he says: “Speak to the heart of Jerusalem and comfort her, because her wickedness is complete” (Isa. XL). And as other copies have it: “When she has been humbled, her sin has been released; her iniquity has been forgiven, because she has received double from the hand of the Lord for all her sins.”

Thus a blessed desolation is displayed under this letter, because where there is desolation, humility follows; and in the proper order, patience follows humility, and hope follows testing. You also have this in the Apostle: “Hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit,” who is indeed the comforter of our affections (Rom. V).

Therefore it is good for a man, when he has borne the yoke, to sit alone, or at least to be placed alone in hope, because God, as they say, always delights in an odd number. Hence that needy and poor man, groaning and lamenting in the Psalms, says: “I kept watch, and became like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Ps. CI).

As I said above, according to another interpretation, “he will give his mouth to the burial-place,” or “to the pit,” indicates a certain manner of patient silence: as though buried, he does not speak; rather, he blocks his voice with a kind of mound of virtues, so that he does not admit complaint of pain. He asserts such a weight of patience, fostered by hope, that he buries and encloses his very voice in a kind of tomb or burial mound, so that no injury can wrest it out or rouse it.

The Lord gave a fitting example of this in his Passion. As the prophet says: “Like a sheep led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII).

Let the prudent reader observe how much this man, seeing his poverty after scourges, after contrition, after anguish, and after the cries of complaint, has advanced morally; and thus, instructed, let him proceed from here to the letter Caph.

For Caph is interpreted as “hand,” or also, according to another interpretation, “bent down,” because all who think rightly bend beneath the hand of the Lord. His hand is over all, either to punish or certainly to correct. Therefore, humbled by such great pressures and corrected by disciplines, he rejoices in bending his neck beneath the Lord’s hand, while he is humbled toward repentance; and, according to the inner person, he bends the neck of his heart and mind toward the Lord, hoping that the Lord will not reject him forever.

## CAPH

“Because, if he has rejected, he will also have mercy according to the multitude of his mercies. For he has not humbled from his heart,” he says, “nor rejected the children of men.”

The very sound of these verses indicates what it means to bend beneath the powerful hand of God: namely, to endure everything patiently, because the Lord does not reject forever. Whenever a man bearing the yoke inclines himself toward scourges, repentance, insults, and reproaches, he appears to bend himself toward humility.

Hence the prophet David says under this letter: “They almost consumed me on earth” (Ps. CXVIII), sensing that he had been cast down and exposed to struggles. Therefore he bends the neck of his mind toward the Lord. Concerning this neck it is said: “Do not bend your neck like a circle.” For whoever does not bend his heart toward humility and mercy bends his external neck in supplication in vain.

For this reason, now filled with reproaches and borne up alone in hope, he confidently says: “Because, if he has rejected, he will also have mercy according to the multitude of his mercies.”

The Lord afflicts and corrects for this purpose: that he may have mercy. Understanding this well, the man who sees his poverty, acting confidently toward God, says: “He has not humbled from his heart”—as though God were being satiated with our punishments—“nor has he rejected the children of men.” He prefers that we be humbled and bend before him, so that he may also have mercy.

Therefore, the same prophet, showing under this letter the groans and humility of the people, says above: “All her people groan, seeking bread; they gave their precious things for food, to revive the soul. See, O Lord, and look, for I have become vile” (Lam. I), or “without honor.”

Therefore whoever seeks refreshment for his soul is rightly bent by humility, so that he may more quickly reach the Lord’s mercy and experience it in his goodness: “Because, if he has rejected, he will also have mercy.” And so, as one bent down, let him bend himself wholly—much more in soul and mind than in body—toward the multitude of God’s mercies, knowing that he has not rejected or humbled the children of men from his heart in order to destroy them by punishment, but to correct and restore them to salvation.

The following letter, Lamech, pursues the consequence of this meaning.

## LAMECH

“To crush beneath his feet all the prisoners of the earth; to turn aside the judgment of a man before the face of the Most High; to pervert a man in his judgment—the Lord has not approved.”

As far as concerns the eloquence of our lamentation, the composition of the verses is remarkable, following the manner of meter: three verses begin from one part and end with one verbal clause, as though with the word “Lord.” Thus: “To crush beneath his feet all the prisoners of the earth, the Lord has not approved”; “to turn aside the judgment of a man, the Lord has not approved”; and “to strike a man in his judgment, the Lord has not approved.”

For God prefers to save those who have been corrected rather than condemn the obstinate. This is the great discipline of the verses, or the confession of the heart, under the letter Lamech. As I have already said above, Lamech is interpreted as “discipline,” or “of the heart,” or even “servant.”

Through these meanings, the great obscurity is considerably clarified, so that we may understand that, under the complete integrity and discipline of Christ, the things that are said must be carefully preserved with complete purity of heart. For whoever has the discipline of Christ professes that he preserves the commandments of salvation and purity of heart.

He did not reject all the prisoners of the earth in such a way as to crush them. The prisoners of the earth are all those bound by earthly crimes. The Lord did not reject them in order to crush them beneath his feet; rather, he placed them all under his authority, since he says of the Son: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. VIII).

Since he has been appointed judge of all, he faithfully confesses that “the Lord has not approved turning aside the judgment of a man”; rather, he will repay each according to his works. And although the statement “to pervert a man in his judgment” may for the present be understood without distinction, even when a man is judged, “the Lord has not approved” it, since the evils inflicted by the Lord are either just punishments corresponding to merits or tests of future rewards.

Therefore adversity that comes from the Lord is full of justice, full of equity, and full of mercy. In accordance with the discipline of Christ, he consequently professes innocence of heart. And the man who sees God, professing himself a servant of the divine words of command, says: even if there are heretics who falsely accuse God of cruelly afflicting souls bound in clay houses, and who claim that in the Old Testament he punished people as though in advance by prejudice, this man, trained by the scourge under the discipline of Christ, confesses the purity of his heart according to the prophet’s saying: “You will be chastised with a rod, daughter of Zion.” He confesses that everything is carried out under God’s just governance, so that he may grant salvation to all who call upon him in truth (Ps. CXLIV).

According to the interpretation of the letter, he freely cries out concerning himself: “I preserve the discipline of correction; I preserve the piety of confession; I preserve integrity of heart; I preserve the unblemished virtue of faith amid all the deceits of heretics; I preserve love, borne up alone in hope, carrying my soul under God’s protection with the possibility of turning back—for the Lord does not reject forever.”

A great advancement of the soul is thus shown: amid so many and such great dangers of life, it cannot be separated from the love of Christ. With the prophet David it says even amid scourges: “Behold, as the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so are our eyes toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy upon us” (Ps. CXXII).

After the steadfastness of this faith, he comes to the letter Mem, rising like a defender of justice against all Epicureans, and also against those who say that God does not care about mortal affairs. Against them Psalm LXXII is also raised, in which those who think perversely say: “How does God know? Or is there knowledge in the Most High?” The present verses also seem to rebuke them.

## MEM

“Who is this,” he says, “who has spoken so that it should happen, when the Lord has not commanded it? From the mouth of the Most High do not evils and goods proceed? Why should a living man murmur, a man because of his sins?”

As I have said, these matters are lamented under the letter Mem. Mem is interpreted as “from the innermost parts” or “from the very things”; and, as others say, “fire from the extremities.” Neither interpretation conflicts with the text of this lament, because it is the greatness of the ardor of love that now seems to contend in faith not so much for himself against the wicked as for God.

He thinks that he is rendering service to God if, against those who speak against him, he says mockingly, as though from a lofty summit: “Who is this who has said that it should happen when God has not commanded it?” It is as though he were plainly saying: “Who is this—though he is ashes and dust, inflated by his own spirit—who dares to dispute with words about the immeasurable and unbounded God according to his own condition, and to mock us who are being scourged, as though we, the children of adoption, had not yet been condemned by this world?”

These words plainly show that nothing happens in us without the command of the just and true judgment of God. Therefore whatever he previously brought forth against God in tears came more from the fountain of piety than from a prejudicial complaint.

Hence the present letter appears to sound “from the innermost parts,” since whatever he brought forward in his confession flowed from his innermost being; and the fire of God’s charity flowed from the furthest depths of his heart, so that, through a kind of bond of divine heat, it might burn inwardly into his bones.

Thus, far above in the same Lamentations, the text of the same letter seems to contain this: “From on high he sent fire into my bones” (Lam. I).

Good, therefore, is the God who sends this fire upon us, so that those who love him may find grace and the glory of their merits in his sight. Let him himself teach us what fire he sends into us. For he says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it should burn?” (Luke XII).

Good, therefore, is the fire that the Savior of all wishes to kindle more and more—especially since he himself is a consuming fire, which will consume our sins and pour into our innermost hearts the desire for divine knowledge, so that our heart may return to us, enabling it to grasp the sequence of the divine Scriptures and drink from the spring of water welling up to eternal life (John IV).

Cleopas said that his heart burned with this fire when Christ opened the Scriptures to them on the way (Luke XXIV).

We therefore see profound mysteries in the words of God. For this reason fire must be kindled from the innermost parts—or, as another interpreter says, “from the very things”—as though, from the deepest organs and bones, it might burn up within us hay, straw, or the lead of iniquity, or whatever belongs to secular life. Thus the iron hardness of sin may be melted by divine fire and softened in heavenly flame, to such a degree that, even against the insolence of the reprobate, we ourselves seem to contend for the faith and say: “Who is this who has said that from the mouth of the Most High neither evils nor goods proceed?”

This is especially so since evils proceed from him only according to his just judgment, while goods are granted only by his mercy—not merely to the good and holy, but also very often to the reprobate and condemned.

Therefore, in the voice of confession, he speaks concerning both: “Why should a living man murmur, a man because of his sins?” Paul says the same: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Can the vessel say to the potter—that is, a potsherd from the clay of the earth—‘Why have you made me so?’” (Rom. IX.)

Otherwise, in all things, why should a living man murmur, or what will a man say because of his sins, when God has confined everything under sin, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become subject to God (Gal. III)?

But let the slothful or senseless fashion for themselves from their hearts the claim, as I said, that God does not care about mortal affairs. Evils and goods come from him, as the soul instructed by the disciplines of Christ confesses. Therefore every iniquity has been stopped up, and man, formed by God, has nothing to answer—even if he becomes a vessel for dishonor—while the golden vessels are daily improved by God’s scourges, and the silver vessels are prepared for honor.

This is what Mem has “from the innermost parts”; this also is the fire “from the extremities”; this is “from the very things”: that every understanding of the wise, every speech of the prudent, every trial of burning passions, and every effort of action, reheated in the warmth of the love of God, may begin to become more precious.

Good, therefore, is the fire of God’s charity; good is the affection of love from the innermost heart; good is the persevering fear “from the very things.” Through it the whole body of the Church grows into mutual grace.

Good indeed is the fire of love, by which every saint is kindled to reverence for his creator. But whoever loves God, kindled by the fire of charity, does not love him superficially: he loves his law from the innermost parts, and from the very depths he keeps his commandments and justifies his heart—not by hearing words, but through the zeal of fulfillment and imitation of deeds.

Nevertheless, amid all these things, a living man has nothing to murmur because of his sins. “My righteous one,” says the divine Spirit, “lives by faith” (Hab. II). If a living man is not justified by faith, and one justified by faith and by righteous works of faith has nothing to say, how much less does the ungodly and sinner?

Hence he significantly says: “a man because of his sins.” “Man” is the name of the male sex, whereas “human being” is common to all. One of these exists by nature; the other is something that occurs through grace. Thus neither the one who is scourged because of the propagation of the first nature, nor the man who is already distinguished by grace, has anything to say.

Both, however, although living by faith, while they are afflicted because of their sins, have no argument to make against the potter, no question to ask: “Why did you make me so?” or “Why are you doing this?” Job understood this well. Although tormented by many punishments, he is rightly praised in everything because he did not sin with his lips or speak anything foolish against God (Job II).

Therefore, when someone lives by faith so that his merits may increase, or when a man already distinguished by grace from the weakness of his sex is corrected by the Lord so that he may be cleansed from his sins, he still has nothing to object to God. How much less does one who is rightly counted among the mass of perdition and condemned?

All these things—both evils and goods—are rightly believed to arise only from God’s just judgment.

Now the moral sense comes gladly to the letter Nun, whose meaning sounds as “eternal.” As I said, according to the Hebrew truth, its interpretation sounds as “eternal.” If another interpreter has said “one” or has wished it to signify “their pasture,” neither meaning is far from the text. For the Church has no pasture other than Christ, in whose pastures the Prophet rejoices to have been placed, saying: “He has placed me there in a place of pasture” (Ps. XXII).

For he himself refreshes and feeds us with the good things of his pasture, namely, with the divine sacraments, from the abundance of the field that the Lord has blessed, whose fragrance goes forth as an odor of sweetness, as though from the new flower of holy resurrection.

From the fullness of this abundance, in the person of the Father, he says: “The fullness of the field is with me.” From it the lily of the valleys is born, because of the brightness of eternity, and also the rose, because of the blood of the Lord’s Passion. These pastures are truly the mystical sacraments of the Scriptures, in which we are strongly admonished to examine our ways, to seek, and to return to the Lord.

For he proposed three things: that we examine our ways as precisely as possible, in the manner of the philosophers; that we seek what we have become, or what we were, or what we ought to have been; and that, when it has been discovered that we have inclined toward non-being, we be compelled by necessity to return to the Lord.

Here the beginning of the letter invites us, since, as I said earlier, it is also interpreted as “beginning.” Hence the only-begotten Son of the Father says: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII).

From this the meaning of the interpretation of the letters is clear: the elements of the Hebrews, with which childhood is accustomed to become familiar, do not shape the little ones from infancy all the way to the maturity of virtue so as to direct them secretly toward divine and mystical understandings.

Thus the same letter Nun is also said to be interpreted as “only one”—the one believed to be the true beginning—and as “their pasture,” namely, of those who return to him.

Good indeed are the pastures, and good are the studies of the heavenly Scriptures. In them we are fed by daily reading, renewed by grace, refreshed by disciplines, as we taste what has been written or repeatedly ruminate what we have received.

Good, therefore, are the pastures of Christ, by which the Lord’s flock is fattened. Good also are the pastures in which the only-begotten beginning of the Father’s life is fed among the lilies, in the splendor of the saints.

Hence he gives the excellent admonition: “Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God in heaven.” There are true joys, good pastures, lilies of the valleys, and roses in bloom.

But hearts are not rightly lifted to them without hands, nor hands without purity of heart, so that the integrity of our faith may commend us to God, and the working of faith, which works through love (Gal. IX), may carry us and what belongs to us no less into heaven.

And so, remembering our poverty, let us say to God: “We have acted wickedly,” so that the complete integrity of our confession may also be declared: “We have provoked you to anger.” For it is one thing that we have acted wickedly, and something altogether different that, by continuing to do evil, we have provoked the merciful Judge to anger.

## NUN
Therefore, he says, you are inexorable. For the understanding of these three verses renders the whole teaching of the Scriptures: that we should scrutinize our ways—that is, our actions—seek, and return to the Lord through lamentation, from whom we departed wickedly through our crimes. It is a great thing, then, for each person to know himself; for this reason we are commanded to scrutinize our ways, that is, our actions, the actions of our faith, so that we may be able to know ourselves. Hence Moses says in the Law: “Pay attention to yourself, lest there be a hidden word in your heart.” “Pay attention to yourself,” he says—not, certainly, to your money, your possessions, or your strength, but to your spirit and your mind, from which all counsels, deeds, and thoughts flow. Pay attention to yourself there where you know yourself to be most excellent.

What the pagans attribute to the Pythian Apollo, as though he himself were the author of the saying “Know yourself,” was, as we believe, taken from our tradition and transferred to theirs, since Moses was much earlier than those philosophers who invented such things. Thus Solomon too, following the divine oracle, says in the Song of Songs: “Unless you know yourself, beautiful among women” (Song I). This means: unless you recognize yourself as mortal, made rational in the image of God; unless you confess your former sins; unless you acknowledge your iniquities before yourself, so that you may be justified; unless you turn back and accuse yourself beforehand, before the door is closed, before the day of death comes like a thief (I Tim. V).

This, then, is what it means: “Let us scrutinize our ways, and seek, and return to the Lord,” so that by confession you may know how to acknowledge what you have lost, and seek again in the solidity of faith what you have forfeited. “Unless you know yourself,” he says, “O beautiful and lovely among women,” and say, “I am dark because I have sinned, but beautiful because I am loved,” a chosen race reborn from the faith of Abraham, a holy priesthood (I Pet. II); otherwise, “Go away after the tracks of the flocks, and feed your young goats beside the tents of Kedar.”

The man who sees his poverty and has been instructed by scourges made great progress; and he grew much stronger after he came to the letter Zain, hearing, “Lead yourself”; and still more after he placed the heavy yoke upon himself and sat alone. Amid those lofty silences he fully understood that this is our salvation: that we should scrutinize our ways and seek, because the ways of young men in their adolescence are slippery and crooked. But if someone takes the yoke upon himself late and sits alone at least in old age, how greatly must he be lamented with the dirges by which sinners are mourned—those who refuse to grasp the ways of life and the ways of righteousness!

It is therefore fitting to anticipate the years of youth with suitable correction, so that each of us may say: “God has fed me from my youth” (Ps. LXX). And elsewhere: “I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a pasture” (Ps. XXII).

These are the pastures under this letter. But there are also the pastures of eternal life, where the Only-Begotten of the Father feeds among the lilies; for “until the day breathes and the shadows incline” (Song II), this alone is our support in life: that we lift our hearts to him, together with our hands, into heaven, and say: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Ps. XXIV). For the wounds of old age are more serious than those of youth. One has the remedy of weakness; the other, the strength of salvation. Medicine is sought for a wound, but grace for health.

Therefore he says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke in his youth,” because, although for the old it is a remedy to cease from sinning, their sins goad them on, the habit of sinning harasses their conscience, and the long practice of error often makes them unstable. Thus the old man is in danger, but the young man is in a state of goodness. And I do not know, when you sit alone, whether a solitary person easily finds an equal companion together with the Only-Begotten Son of the Father, placed in a pasture—especially since he himself will be endowed with singular rewards and enriched with gifts.

For this reason, quiet and released from every interruption of worldly anxiety, free for divine oracles, he says: “Let us lift our hearts, together with our hands, to the Lord in heaven,” so that we may bring before him, individually, those things that are customarily given more happily to those who live with God. Meanwhile, because of past deeds, let us take care to implore God more earnestly with tears and prayers, and confess that we are the ones who have acted wickedly, we who provoke him to anger.

Therefore, because past sins abound and present ones do not cease, let us say with the prophet: “For you are inexorable.” And the reason he does not hear us is not his unsurpassable goodness, but our wickedness. Hence the letter Samech rightly follows; it seems to signify either “hear” or “firmament,” and, as our interpreter says, it means “help,” as the very text of the verses suggests.

## SAMECH

“For you have covered us,” he says, “in fury and struck us; you have killed and shown no mercy. You have placed a cloud before yourself, so that prayer may not pass through. You have made me eradication and indignation in the midst of the peoples.”

From these words the meaning of the letter is clear: help is justly taken away from those who neither lament the many sins accumulated from the past nor cease adding new ones to the old. By sinning daily they provoke the merciful Judge to anger and make him inexorable. Thus the same prophet earlier, under the same letter Samech, laments: “The Lord has taken away from my midst all my strong men” (Lam. I); or, as our codices read, “He summoned a time against me, to crush in me my chosen ones.”

For the Lord did not then take away all the strong men of Judea, when the Jewish people were led captive into the Babylonian region, but when Christ came, and the captive synagogue did not see the freedom of its soul. Bent beneath grievous sins, it did not know how to raise the neck of its mind upright or lift certain necks of faith toward the light of understanding. Therefore Christ was placed as eradication and indignation in the midst of the peoples.

Hence he himself says: “I came so that those who see may not see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX). And Simeon, receiving him, says: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed” (Luke II).

Therefore, since the Lord took away all the strong and mighty, the removal of help is rightly lamented among them, because with hardened hearts they abandoned God their helper. For the same prophet had already announced the voice of God far above, saying: “Behold, I have appointed you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and destroy, to ruin and demolish, and to plant” (Jer. VIII). Against these four sorrowful actions he set two joyful ones, because good things could not be built unless evil things had been destroyed, nor the best things planted unless the worst had been uprooted.

Here, however, he laments that he has been placed as eradication and indignation in the midst of the peoples, because all who strayed from Christ in his Passion were uprooted from the land of the living through perpetual indignation. Therefore the prophet introduces four statements on their behalf: “You have covered us in fury and struck us; you have killed and shown no mercy.”

In his fury he covered the face of the Jews with a veil of blindness, so that Christ would not be recognized. Hence a veil was also placed over the face of Moses (Exod. XXXIV), as is read to this day. He struck them with the wound of dispersion among the nations, yet we do not see that they perceived it. He killed them when he took away the spirit of the grace of life—for “the law is spiritual” (Rom. VII)—so that they might not receive the spirit of life in that same law. He showed no mercy when he expelled grace from the temple, from the Law, from the soil of their homeland, and from all the sacraments of faith.

Thus the cloud of sins placed against us, so that their prayer might not pass through, is rightly lamented. This passage is understood no less as referring to the person of Christ than it is interpreted concerning Jeremiah, because Jeremiah is said to mean “the exalted one of the Lord.” The Lord destroyed the kingdoms of the devil, which the devil had shown him on the height of the mountain, and he destroyed the hostile powers, erasing their bond on the cross (Col. II). From those powers, those who are members of this body have had all help taken away, and a great chasm has been established between those who are foreknown and predestined to life and those who, by the just and true judgment of God, are preordained to punishment.

Hence Abraham says to the rich man in the Gospel: “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can anyone cross from there to us” (Luke XVI).

For this reason some interpreters rightly explain this letter as “firmament,” or “hear.” It is not without purpose that it says “hear,” something common to all and available to everyone by the law of nature. It is not insignificant, I say, that “hear” is used, since even unwillingly or while occupied with something else, we are accustomed to hear a sound or a voice. But hearing is not merely what is available through the natural function of the body; it is something greater, so that you may hear not only through bodily use but through the understanding of the mind. Therefore consider more carefully the interpretation of this letter and the sequence of the verses, after their moral meaning, and what follows for those whose rage for sinning persists forever.

## SAMECH

Therefore: “You have placed a cloud before yourself, so that prayer may not pass through.” One cloud is read to be light, upon which Christ ascended; another is bright and shining; another, however, is dark. But the cloud that is lamented as having been placed before God signifies the density of sins.

The pillar of cloud that went before the Hebrews as they departed from Egypt, placing itself between the Egyptians and the Hebrews, was both light to the departing children of Israel and blindness to the Egyptians (Exod. XIII). So too the cloud of Christ’s body is light to believers, but to unbelievers it is blindness, a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense.

Therefore he says: “You have covered us in fury.” What did he cover, unless it was that he concealed the Lord himself in a human being? “And you struck us,” as though he were saying, “with the wound of unbelief.” “You killed them” in the contrition of their heart. “And you showed no mercy,” he says, because of the severity of judgment.

This cloud, I say, is placed before the eyes of the divine majesty, and the prayer of unbelief cannot pass through it as long as blindness remains in part in Israel. Therefore Christ is rightly lamented as having been placed as eradication and indignation, just as he threatens concerning unbelievers. Hence the prophet says, with what precedes and what follows: “God will destroy you forever; he will uproot you and remove you from your dwelling, and your root from the land of the living” (Ps. LI).

This is the text of the letter, as it says, “hear,” because the judgments of God are incomprehensible. Through this letter, which says “hear,” he therefore urges all to return to understanding and to grasp the intelligible meanings of the heart from what is said.

Hence earlier, under this letter, he says: “The Lord has trodden the winepress of the virgin daughter of Judah”—not, as I said, when the people were led captive, when the Lord removed the doors, but when Christ came. Then the Passion of the Savior became a pit for the Jews, while it displayed the gate of salvation to the nations. For the Lord’s cross is a precipice to unbelievers, but a harbor of salvation to believers.

Therefore the prophet first said “hear,” so that you might know what was to come: the winepress—or “pit,” according to another interpretation—which the Lord trod for the virgin daughter of Judah. He trod it so that from that winepress of the Passion the faith of believers might shine forth, or so that the dregs of unbelief might pass into refuse.

Morally, the soul rightly laments itself when it has been covered by the darkness of iniquity, so that it may feel itself struck and killed by the just judgment of God, with the wound of its own depravity at work. The cloud placed before it is lamented as the cloud of sins, which seems to cry out against us rather than plead for us.

Hence the Lord says to Cain: “Behold, the voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth” (Gen. IV). What does “it cries out to me from the earth” mean, unless earthly thought, the suffocation of goodness, and the enormity of sins prevent our prayer from passing through to God and prevent him from sparing those who pray, while the cry that rises daily against us from the earth grows stronger?

From this point to the end of the alphabet, the Passion of the Lord is disclosed with the greatest clarity. Having thus set these matters forth, let us explain what the letter Ain signifies. According to the Hebrew truth, Ain means “eye” or “fountain.” Therefore the prophet, under this meaning—for it is interpreted as “eye”—made a very apt allusion.

## AIN

“My eye is afflicted,” he says, “and has not been silent, because there was no rest”; and in the third verse under this letter: “My eye has plundered my soul” (Lam. III).

For it is the function of the eyes to announce what they have seen. Christ has been placed as a fall for some and as a resurrection for others. Through the letter Ain the functions of the eyes are declared, so that they may rightly mourn over offenses or groan from a desire for grace; for their function is always to delight in pleasant things and to be offended by adverse ones.

Hence Ennon is often interpreted as “eye of punishments,” “eye of temptation,” “eye of the kid,” “eye of the heifer,” “eye of generation,” or “fountain of generation,” in which John baptized, so that through the affliction of these eyes, by the fountain of generation, they might be reborn into the adoption of the children of God.

This is what it means: “My eye is afflicted,” with eyes and with sorrows, “and has not been silent.” Since no cry is believed to ascend to God more than the cry of tears—for even if voices are dull, tears before God are always shown, by the testimony of the Holy Spirit, to rise into heaven from the cheek with every cry of the heart—what else does it indicate that Ennon is interpreted as “eye of punishments,” in which John baptizes, except that the one who has been reborn desires his own sins to be forgiven, while he dreads their punishments with a watchful heart?

Thus, although it is called the eye of punishments, it belongs to one who foresees punishments, not to one who endures them. The eye of temptation is so called because through it we are often tempted. Hence the Savior says: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V). He did not simply say, “Whoever looks upon a woman,” but “in order to desire her.” He released the eye but bound the mind. Hence he did not say that he committed adultery with her through the eye, but in the heart.

The eye of the kid is the one on the left, because a sinner cannot see the things that are on the right. Therefore the holy man says: “I kept the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand, so that I may not be moved” (Ps. XXV).

There is also the eye of the heifer, because, as though drawn by a perpetual yoke, they drag along their iniquities, neither breaking nor cutting them off at their source, but dragging them far away on the rope of sins.

It is also called the eye of generation, or the fountain of generation, because from the sight of the eyes either good things or adverse things are generated. Therefore Ain is rightly called “eye” or “fountain”: for just as the drawing of rivers is seen to flow from a fountain, so from the sight of the eyes, as from a fountain, good or evil is generated in a long stream.

Whenever opportunities for accomplishing good are opened to us, the fountain of righteousness and the origin of grace seem to arise for us. But whenever opportunities for evil are opened, those eyes that were opened to Adam because of the punishment of sin are opened to us.

Hence the same prophet, much earlier in the same Lamentations, under the same letter Ain, says: “I weep, and my eye pours out water, because the comforter who turns my soul has been taken far from me” (Lam. I).

The prophet was not therefore grieving that he had been carried away from his lands, but that he saw the people abandoned by Christ and the consolation of future life lost. This, I say, is the captivity to be mourned: a captivity deprived of eternal freedom.

Therefore, at the present time, the eye is lamented as afflicted and not silent, because there was no rest. There is no rest, then, where the Holy Spirit, who consoles, has departed. For the Spirit Paraclete is called the Comforter, and therefore those who have departed from his sanctification will find no rest of the Sabbath day, on which God is read to have rested (Gen. II).

The prophetic eye, foreseeing them from afar, rightly mourns that it has found no rest, because of the anguish of their perpetual captivity, which the condemned people must pay as the price of their unbelief. Yet, although the eye is afflicted and has not been silent, he goes on to say that the Lord looked upon it and saw it from heaven, because “whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X).

For there are the eyes of the Lord, whose figure the prophet bears, as it is said to the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, at the gates of the daughter of the multitude” (Song VII). For what are the pools in Heshbon except rationality and the abundance of teachings in the thoughts that belong to the Church at the gates? To her, appropriately, a multitude of teaching is attributed.

The “daughter of the multitude” is the posterity of many judgments, because the prophet says: “Many days will pass, and knowledge will be multiplied” (Dan. XII). Her eye is not silent when it is filled with many tears, until the Lord looks upon and sees from heaven.

Meanwhile he says: “My eye has plundered my soul among all the daughters of my city.” Through this the prophet clearly announces the future judgment of Christ, since he foresees what is to come upon the cities of Judah and mourns it with a complete outpouring of tears, because he foresaw the evil unbelief of his impious people, by which they stubbornly denied their own creator.

But the eye is said to plunder the soul when it has poured out all the affections of pain and sorrow; when it has displayed through tears every sickness and ardor of the soul; when everything within it, as though a river from a fountain, has flowed forth, as the prophet David says: “My soul has fainted for your salvation, and my eyes for your word, saying: When will you comfort me?” (Ps. CXVIII).

The soul is plundered by the eye for this purpose: that, stripped of its own powers, it may cling to its Creator and pour itself entirely back into the fountain of devoted abundance. “It has fainted,” because it longs for him by whose Passion it has been saved. It has fainted so that it may pass into one spirit and become one spirit with God.

Therefore he says pointedly: “My eye has plundered my soul,” not “my eyes,” so that one mind with God may be understood, just as Christ says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “You have wounded my heart”—“you have wounded it,” he says, “with one of your eyes” (Song IV).

And rightly so, because Christ is seen and loved with one eye—not a bodily eye, but a spiritual one. Some eyes belong to the flesh; others, as we have said, are those that were opened in Adam (Gen. III); others belong to the mind, which pass into oneness so that the mind may be one with God; and still others are the eyes of the Church, because the bride bears two eyes, the moral and the mystical. The mystical sees God more fully and more sharply, although the moral may appear sweeter.

Therefore the eye filled with the love of Christ is said to plunder the soul, so that it may strip itself entirely of itself and pour itself into God beyond itself. “Among all the daughters of my city,” he says, because through each affection for sins and each thought of eternal life, it pours itself forth, as though plundered from itself, into God, so that it may be found as one with God.

This, then, is the letter interpreted as “fountain” or “eye,” so that neither an eye may be found without a fountain nor a fountain be believed to flow from us and within us without the eye of love. Thus, for its transgressions, the soul may be baptized anew in a fountain of tears, and this fountain may be nourished by the eye of holy contemplation, so that the soul bound to God may say: “I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind; I will sing praise with the spirit, and I will sing praise with the mind” (I Cor. X, 14).

The letter Phe follows, explained in its three verses. As I indicated above, Phe means “mouth”; according to other interpreters, it seems to signify “I have erred” or “I have opened my mouth.” Therefore the lamenting prophet speaks as though from the text of the letter itself:

## PHE

“All our enemies,” he says, “have opened their mouths against us.”

In many letters of the Lamentations you will find an allusion of this kind, so that the meaning of the letters may disclose the meaning of the words, and the words, sounding in harmony, may fulfill the meaning of the letters.

Thus the prophet also confesses that he has erred, according to the meaning of the letter, as the text of the following verse suggests, when he says: “Prophecy and crushing have become for us fear and a snare.” From this it is perfectly clear that the meaning concerns error, since the prophecy of the prophets and the crushing of their hearts urged correction and the satisfaction of repentance upon the people rather than error.

Conversely, because from the prophet’s prophecy an incurable fear had come upon sinners, and the crushing of the lamenting prophet had become a snare, he therefore signifies under this letter, pointedly, “I have erred”—not because the prophet had deviated in the steps of his faith and so gone astray, but because the people had strayed so far that their crushing and prophecy became for them a snare of ruin and a fear of correction.

Therefore, speaking in the person of the erring people, so that he might explain the element of their disgrace, he inserted into his words what had happened to them: because of their unbelief, the prophecy of the prophets and the crushing of their hearts were a snare and ruin to them, so that they might kill them, lest they speak to them in the name of God.

Seeing this, the prophet says: “My eye poured out streams of water because of the crushing of the daughter of my people.” Yet there was one crushing among the prophets arising from devotion to divine inspiration, and another among those who, afflicted by their sins with every form of contrition, were tormented by the spirit of error.

Otherwise, God would not despise the contrite and humbled person, unless they themselves had first rejected the prophecy and contrition of those who labored on behalf of the nations, and had exchanged fear—which was no fear except in rejecting God. Therefore prophecy became a snare for them.

There is no doubt that this occurred in the Passion of the Lord, concerning whom this may be spoken as though it were the person of all his members: “All our enemies have opened their mouths against us.” For them all the prophecy of the prophets became fear—not so that they might be corrected by it because of the hardness of their hearts, but so that what was being read might not happen concerning him.

Therefore the Passion and the contrition of Christ’s humility became a snare leading to ruin for all who did not believe. Hence the prophet speaks as though in the sound of the letter itself: “For I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. CXVIII).

“My eye poured out streams of water,” as though he were saying what is found in the Gospel: “If I had not spoken to them and preached, they would not have sin; but now they are without excuse” (John XV). Now, having become inexcusable, prophecy became a snare for them, because they did not believe in the things concerning which I opened my mouth (John I), so that they might be without excuse.

Therefore, under this letter too, a lamentable passage is shown much earlier: “Zion stretched out her hands, and there is no one to comfort her,” as though she were plainly saying: She receives the fitting reward of her error, because she neglected to listen to him stretching out his hands on the cross and refused to take refuge beneath his wings. It is therefore fitting that afterward she herself should stretch out her hands and be unable to find anyone to comfort her.

Hence the prophet says pointedly: “Because of the crushing of the daughter of my people.” For although he may seem to lament the captivity inflicted upon the Jews by the Chaldeans before the Lord’s coming, nevertheless, through the prophetic spirit, he more truly foresaw that captivity by which the intelligible Chaldean subjected them to the bonds of perpetual error, expelling them from the status of their ancestral devotion and depriving them of their native strength, and afflicted them with the exile of a distant domination.

He deplores this with pitiable grief. For in all this pilgrimage there is no truer homeland than faith. It made those who were far away to be near, and rightly joined strangers and foreigners to the citizenship of the heavenly homeland, as it is written: “Therefore,” says the Apostle, “you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. II).

But because they had been scattered from all these things—from the soil of their homeland, from God, from faith, from the Law, and from the holy covenant—he rightly says: “My eye poured out streams of water.”

For, as I think, he desired, together with the Apostle Paul, to be accursed for the sake of his brothers (Rom. IX). From this it is evident how great is the possession of charity, and what an exceptional garden of delights it is, in which every kind of virtue is nourished. From it, as from a paradise of pleasure, a fountain rises that waters every kind of virtue.

First it rises toward the four heads of the virtues, and then, as it were, through all the divisions of waters, so that it may intoxicate all the shoots of faith and conduct. For he expressed, in a grand manner, the feeling of one performing repentance; or, certainly, he indicated the love of devotion, according to what is written in the Song of Songs: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, rushing down from Lebanon” (Song IV).

These divisions of waters therefore wash away sins no less when they flow through all the plots of delight, so that they may water every kind of spice. The Church of Christ draws these divisions of waters with a rushing force from Lebanon, washing away sins; from the force of that pure fountain the bride flows from Lebanon, so that from the beginning of faith she may pass through the world and finally pass into the kingdom.

This grace of the Holy Spirit is a fountain to some, a well to others, and to others a garden, an enclosed garden, a sealed fountain; to others it is a stream of gardens, which is reckoned as a division in the Church. To others it is the rushing force descending from Lebanon, a great force indeed that never fails.

When he indicates, groaning and weeping, that his eye poured out these divisions, this may be because the channels of overflowing streams were like the courses of abundant tears, so that he poured out through each part of his heart the shoots of love; or because he poured them over the crimes of the heart that needed washing, to such an extent that the eye itself poured out those divisions through every danger of fear and every wound of love.

Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by love.” The force of the highest grief or love has this character: with tears, the eye of the mind itself seems somehow to pour itself out and draw forth those tears, so that from them, as from divisions of waters, the more powerful force of grief or love may be revealed.

Blessed, then, is such a flowing, and blessed are the divisions that come from the unity of the eye and the purity of the fountain of the Holy Spirit. Good is the rushing force that knows not how to harm but knows how to fill, since the holy apostles, filled with the Spirit (Acts II), were accused as though they had been intoxicated and filled with new wine by an exceedingly powerful grace.

That woman from the Gospel also drew forth these divisions of waters: she irrigated the Lord’s feet and purchased, at the price of her faith, the health of her soul and body.

David too led forth these divisions according to the greatness and multitude of his sins; from them he received grace instead of sin, and for his guilt he accumulated every gift of virtue from these divisions of waters.

From them the apostle also received the grace of his apostleship after his threefold denial (Luke VII). What, then, shall I say about these divisions, when the force of eloquence is diminished more than the abundance of tears or grace is opened to us in a hardened heart?

Therefore let David and many others be brought forward, so that from them we may understand what those themselves obtained for these same things, who increased their lamentations with tears according to the measure of their crimes.

He says: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears” (Ps. VI). And again: “My tears have been my bread” (Ps. CI); and also: “I mixed my drink with weeping” (Ps. CXVIII).

And so that you might see Jeremiah imitating him: “My eyes,” he says, “poured out streams of water.” He did not say, “Because I am afflicted, because I am scourged, because I am cursed, and cast down from my own soil or persecuted,” but rather, “Because I have not kept your law, O Lord.” As though he were saying: “With my eyes flowing, I mourn the things I committed while they looked on.”

He certainly had many other things to mourn—the incest of his daughter and the death of his sons (II Sam. XIII)—but here he says that he did not weep for these things, but because he had not kept the Lord’s law. For among holy men guilt is mourned more than misfortune.

Thus, when his son lay dying (II Sam. XII), he neither took food nor ascended the royal throne or his bed; but, lying on the ground, he fasted and wept. There he wept not so much desiring to remove the death of his son as to remove the punishment of his sin.

So too Jeremiah says: “My eye poured out streams of water because of the crushing of the daughter of my people.” He was lamenting not merely the crushing of the present life that she suffered from her enemies, but also the punishment of eternal suffering, because he knew that, on account of their impenitence and hardness of heart, the Lord would crush them with a double crushing, according to what is written, “from beneath the heavens.”

Thus the prophet wept over the hardships and distress of his people; he wept over the destruction of his homeland. But he is believed to have wept more because they themselves had opened their mouths against the Lord, as we read in the Passion, blaspheming and cursing Christ. For this reason they themselves received vengeance from the devil, as though in return.

Christ also wept in his Passion (Luke XXII), when, placed in agony, he prayed at length, and when a drop of blood fell from him to the ground as he grieved for us. He also wept over wretched Jerusalem itself (Luke XIX), and he wept over Lazarus, so that from this you might recognize by how many evils we are crushed and what lamentations we require (John X).

The saints also weep as they go forth and sow their seeds, drawing out divisions of waters in every part, so that the fruit of the eternal seed may rise more abundantly into the harvest. We can obtain these divisions of tears more effectively through prayers, by sowing seeds of piety, than learn them through instruction.

Therefore, let us pass on devoutly to consolation. The letter Sade follows, which is interpreted as “consolation” or “righteousness.” After the divisions of tears, after the heavy torrents of weeping, after the bitterness of such great grief, after fear of immense danger, after the snares of crushing, after the opening and assault of the enemies’ mouths, the letter Sade—consolation—intervenes most appropriately, so that those who have paid the penalty for their crimes through heavier sufferings may hope for the indulgence of righteousness and the consolation of forgiveness; and so that those who have washed away their sins with weeping and tears may deserve to obtain rest.

But no rest is proved to exist except through the Passion of Christ. Therefore, in the voice of the Redeemer, it is rightly lamented on our behalf.

## SADE
My enemies hunted me like a bird, without cause [Col. 1185D]. My life fell into a pit, and they placed a stone over me. The waters overwhelmed my head; I said, “I am lost.”

By these verses, the consolation of the faithful is shown through the Lord’s Passion, and the justifications by which we are justified are proclaimed with the clearest light—even though the impiety of the faithless increased. Like hunters pursuing a bird with swords and clubs, they seized Christ—namely, without cause (Matt. XXVI).

As for the prophet Jeremiah, it is clear that he was seized without cause, placed in a pit, and that the waters overwhelmed him, as though the waves of water, pursuing him, had risen over his head [p. 1463]; no one can doubt this. But the passage is understood still more clearly of Christ, who is lamented as having been captured like a bird in a hunt because of our sins. For he is that bird of which it is written in Job: “Man does not know the path of the bird” (Job XXVIII). Otherwise, if they had known him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. II).

Man did not know his paths; indeed, as the Apostle testifies (Col. I), they were hidden from ages and generations. And “who will declare his generation?” (Isa. LIII.) Blessed, therefore, is the bird begotten for us in the hope of the promise through the warmth and shadowing of the Holy Spirit, without intercourse. Although it was captured on earth in the hunt of its enemies, it always possessed the things of heaven.

Perhaps, then, he is the eagle which, when it stirs up its young—namely, the Jews—to fly, spreads its wings over them, takes them up, and carries them on its shoulders (Deut. XXXII). He was captured in their snare and ambush (Matt. XXIII). When he wished to gather them under his wings like a hen, he was seized in the weakness of the flesh.

Thus he significantly says: “My life fell into a pit” [Col. 1186A]. He alone truly trod upon that pit (Matt. XV), when by dying he destroyed death and by rising again restored life. “They placed,” he says, “a stone over me.” What could be clearer concerning Christ’s Passion, what more evident, since a stone is long proclaimed as having been placed over him at the tomb (Matt. XXVII–XXVIII), later sealed together with guards during the Passion, and afterward proclaimed to have been rolled away by an angel in greater glory?

Christ, therefore, was reckoned with those who descend into the pit (Ps. LXXXVII), “like a man without help, free among the dead.” For “his going forth is from the summit of heaven” (Ps. XVIII). And although he reached the deepest places of the pit, his coming forth reaches even to its summit [Col. 1186C].

It follows: “The waters overwhelmed my head.” By the waters, a multitude is lamented as having risen against Christ, who is believed to be the head of the whole Church. Although this may also pertain to his own words, on account of the enormity of the anguish of the Passion, it seems more fully to be the voice of the Church—that is, of the whole body—lamenting that the enemies, like a mass of waves, overwhelmed Christ in the greatness of their violence, without cause, in order to kill him.

Hence the bride, who already seemed to have been gathered for a while in the members of Christ, soon, as though deceived in her hope, is lamented as having said in a voice of doubt: “I am lost.” The whole assembly of Christ’s disciples was indeed lost when, having abandoned him, they each fled; it was lost when they denied him; it was lost when they all doubted.

Therefore the letter Sade, interpreted as “consolation,” was rightly placed before these verses [Col. 1186D, p. 1464], because unless the consolation of the Holy Spirit and of the Lord, the devout shepherd, had been present, their faith would immediately have vanished and all of them would have perished.

From this it is evident that all that trial of the Passion did not occur without the consolation of the Holy Spirit, who would raise them from unbelief to faith, from despair to hope, from sorrow to joy, and from the fall of sin to pardon. Hence also the Lord says to Peter: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII).

Nevertheless, insofar as it depended upon him, he undoubtedly denied him; but insofar as it depended upon God, he remained steadfast in foreknowledge. So also the voice of all of them, insofar as it depended upon themselves, rightly sounded: “I am lost”; but insofar as it depended upon the promise and foreknowledge of the devout Master, their faith, having received consolation, remained unconquered.

We are sometimes consoled in many ways through the Scriptures; we are consoled by God’s mercy; and we are also consoled in another way, when we pay the heavy penalties for our sins, as you have in Isaiah: “Be comforted, my people, be comforted, says your God. Speak to the heart of Jerusalem and call to her, because her wickedness has been completed and her iniquity has been pardoned” (Isa. IV). “She has received from the hand of the Lord double for all her sins” [Col. 1187A].

Even if Jerusalem lacked faith, punishment would satisfy for her. Those who are absolved through the consolation of merits are revealed through the consolation of punishments.

We are also very often consoled by various trials and by the words of the aforesaid disciples of Christ, because “trial produces patience, and patience hope.” We are consoled by tears when crimes are washed away, as in the Psalms: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping” (Ps. VI) [Col. 1187B].

We are also very often consoled by scourges, because God does not forget to show mercy, nor will he cast away forever those whom he has judged worthy of correction. Thus, when the punishments that we have endured because of our sins have run their course, we frequently perceive in hope that we belong to pardon. Punishment corrects and reforms the one who errs. If someone is such that he cannot be reformed, punishment sometimes either removes him from the midst of others or prevents him from committing more serious offenses.

From these and very many other kinds of trials and afflictions, the meaning is clear: the consolation of the Holy Spirit is never absent from scourges or trials, provided that hardness and impenitence of heart do not persist [Col. 1187C].

These are the Lord’s justifications, by which we are justified. For Sade, as we have said, also means “justice,” so that the meaning is this: through the Lord’s Passion, in many forms of mercy, while the Holy Spirit consoles us, we too are justified before the Lord through scourges, passions, and trials, when we are corrected.

This is well said in the Gospel to the rich man concerning Lazarus: “Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, while you are in torment” (Luke XVI). From this it is clear that no tribulation is without the consolation of its reward, unless impiety or impenitence of heart prevents the mind from being corrected [Col. 1187D].

Now, after the Passion, after the trials, and after the consolation of hope, let us see what follows.

There follows Coph, which is called “calling,” or, according to another interpreter, seems to signify “conclusion” or “look.” Accordingly, he immediately alluded harmoniously to the sound of the letter, by which it is called “calling.”

## COPH

“I called upon your name, O Lord.” We say that he also did this above, where, when he prefixed the same letter, he said—as though immediately from its sound—“I called my friends” [Col. 1188A].

This is the voice of Christ, according to the human form assumed in the Passion, addressed to the Father, because above he had grieved: “My life fell into a pit.” Now, however, even from the deepest places of the pit, he confesses that he called upon God the Father. In this figure, Jonah is read as having cried out to God from the belly of the sea-monster (Jon. II).

The reason is that what he previously prefaced, as though from the person of the Lord—not despairing, but speaking in the form of those who fled and abandoned the Lord—was a voice of doubt or unbelief: they had not yet been established in faith, nor strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Job, on the other hand, already tested by sufferings and certain of God’s help, says: “Even if I am plunged into the depths of hell, you will deliver me from there.” How much more certain of himself was the author of life, who confidently speaks thus to the Father: “On the day when I called upon you, O Lord, you said, ‘Do not be afraid.’”

Therefore he also says here: “You heard my voice. Do not turn your ear away from my sighing, and you drew near to my cries” [Col. 1188B]. He whose Father was present could not perish; he whose voice the Father had heard could not doubt.

But because Coph is also interpreted as “conclusion,” the one who has perished rightly prays, groaning: “Do not turn your ear away from my sighing and my cries.” Having become incarnate, he had descended, according to another prophet, to the farthest depths of the mountains. Enclosed by the bars of the earth, he confidently dealt with the Father, trusting that he would raise his life from corruption, under which he was suppressed and, together with us and for us, sorrowfully mourned.

Hence he says: “I called upon your name, O Lord, from the deepest places of the pit” (Jon. II). We read that Jonah did this from the belly of the beast in the prophecy of this mystery.

Coph is therefore rightly called “conclusion,” because God enclosed all things under sin so that the door of life might be opened to us, who had been enclosed under sin (Gal. III), through him who was detained in the corruption of the flesh and came down to the deepest places of the pit [Col. 1188C].

He was heard when he called, as a son—not one God and another man, but one and the same Christ, mediator of God and human beings (1 Tim. II). We, however, enclosed by a twofold confinement—namely, sin and corruption—are heard through him, and we believe that what preceded in him for us in hope will benefit us.

Therefore he says: “You drew near to me on the day when I called upon you; you said, ‘Do not be afraid.’” Thus, what our head confidently presumed concerning himself, as a son, we too may hope for in him and through him as members.

He impresses upon us the pattern of calling, praying, sighing, crying out, confidently presuming and hoping with complete contrition of heart [Col. 1188D].

Since, according to the literal sense, we are enclosed by a twofold barrier, we ought to examine ourselves and look upon ourselves, as the present letter indicates. For it is said to be interpreted as “look,” as though it were openly crying: “Look upon what mortality, corruption, and the harsh condition of our lot have brought you—to the deepest places of the pit. Look upon the snare of sin by which you have been irrevocably enclosed, and do not conceal the cause of your danger,” especially since it is a fatal peril for anyone not to look upon the dangers of his condition.

Everyone is enclosed within the swelling womb of the Church; everyone is enclosed by the snares of enemies and by innumerable dangers, as a woman, when she gives birth, according to the Gospel, “has sorrow” (John XVI). When the περιδρομή (*peridromē*) of the womb—the surrounding pressure by which the central region of the chest is constricted—oppresses her, she suffers immense and innumerable afflictions [Col. 1189A]. Thus the mind is enclosed by no lesser anguish than the body. The fevers and heats of souls are greater than those of bodies.

One enclosed by the swellings of the inward parts seeks a physician, so that he may drive away dangers and loosen what has been constricted. When the physician comes to him, he tests everything and examines the interior. Hence we too are admonished to look upon ourselves with the eye of the mind, to see by what evils we are enclosed, to consider our miseries, to know ourselves, and to seek the medicine of prayer.

Therefore Coph is rightly called “calling,” so that we may continually call upon the physician who came from heaven to heal our infirmities. Hence he himself also says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. IX) [Col. 1189B].

You have wounds; do not delay the medicine. Look with your eyes to see how you are enclosed—with the eyes, namely, by which David sought and obtained help. “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains,” he says, “from where help will come to me. My help is from the Lord” (Ps. CXX).

Look, therefore, and always look, because the eyes of the just are always turned toward the Lord. The same man urges this under the preceding occurrence of this letter, saying: “Rise up; awaken in the night, at the beginning of the watches; pour out your heart like water before the sight of the Lord; lift your hands toward him” (Lam. II).

From this he indicates the birth that results from our enclosure, displays our anguish, and urges us with complete devotion of heart to seek a saving remedy.

Therefore, under this letter he set before us the pattern of our Redeemer: how, even from the deepest places of the pit, he calls upon the Father; how he prays confidently; how he sighs and cries out—not with the voice, but with contrition of heart and a great cry of the mind; how he perceives God present everywhere; how, even amid affliction, he understands that God draws near on the day of invocation; how, with the hearing of the heart, he hears God saying, “Do not be afraid”—indeed, saying to all: “I have overcome the world” (John XVI) [Col. 1189C].

“And this is the victory that overcomes the world: our faith” (1 John V). Hence David said: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; from whom shall I tremble?” (Ps. XXVI.) As though he were plainly saying: No one who feels God present ought to fear. Even though “in him we live and move and are” (Acts XVII), we cannot rightly tremble at all.

Such a voice of the heart and such faith is a great cry to God—not because of the loudness of the voice, but because of the greatness of the heart [Col. 1189D]. It is the voice of the heart and the cry of tears, for there is also a voice of blood that reaches God.

Our heart cries out, therefore, not by the sound of the voice but by the sublimity of its thoughts and the harmony of its virtues. It is the great cry of faith by which, in the spirit of adoption, we cry, “Abba, Father.” And the Spirit himself cries out in us—or groans for us—with inexpressible groanings (Rom. VIII).

Great is the voice of justice, and great is charity, through which the dead speak. They not only speak, but, like Abel, they cry out (Gen. IV). Great was the voice of the apostles, which went out into all the earth, and great the cry that reached to the ends of the world (Ps. XVIII) [Col. 1190A].

With this voice our head cries out; his members also cry out; Rachel cries out, weeping for her children. “Do not turn your ear away,” he says, “from my sighing and my cries.”

Moses also cries out, to whom it is said, “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. XIV), when he was praying for the people. But some cry out in the heart, while others speak. Hannah was speaking (2 Kings XI), because she was praying for private matters—that is, for children. Moses cried out with the great ardor of charity; the saints under the altar of God cry out with an immense cry of devout affection.
