Hence, under this letter, the conclusion of our sinking is expressly set forth, and the need for invocation is shown, so that we may cry out more earnestly. To each person it is said: “Look upon the fact that you are held enclosed, and consider the afflictions by which you are pressed. Cry out in strength to him who is present: ‘Do not turn your ear away from my sighing and my cries,’ because God enclosed all things under sin so that he might have mercy upon all” [Col. 1190B].

Hence the Apostle says: “Be miserable and mourn; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow. Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (Gal. III). As though he were plainly saying: “Look upon your enclosure and mourn the miseries in which you have been enclosed. Call upon God from the deepest places of the pit; cry out wisely, because Wisdom cries aloud outside and raises her voice in the streets” (Prov. I).

The more greatly it is heard on high, the more fervently it pours itself out in the heart toward God with faith and desire. He is always perceived as present everywhere to true faith, because “the Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth.”

Let us therefore come with greater confidence to the letter Res [Col. 1190C]. Res is interpreted as “head,” or even “of the head,” or “primacy.” It is the head, or the form of the head, so that we may consider the author of life—our head, from whom all the members are nourished, who governs and fills all things with sense.

“For the sense of the wise is in his head.” From there the spirit is conducted through all the passages of the veins and distributes strength throughout every part of the body; the blood traverses everything and adorns everything. Once the head has been removed, the body is nameless: it is neither recognized, nor does any reason for living remain.

Let us therefore hear what the voice of the head thinks concerning itself, or what it presumes concerning itself.

## RES

[Col. 1190D]

“You have judged, O Lord, the cause of my soul, O redeemer of my life. You have seen, O Lord, the iniquity directed against me; judge my judgment. You have seen all their fury against me, all their thoughts.”

This voice belongs no less to the head than to the body, so that neither the body without the head nor the head without the body is found. Therefore judgment and redemption are commended together to the Father in prayer, as though in one person.

Judgment in the cause of the soul, so that it may be found just, is wholly attributed to the head for the sake of the entire body. Redemption, however, is granted to the body so that its members may advance from death to life. For the one who was never sold under sin is not rightly called redeemed, nor does the other, trusting in his own strength, call upon God for judgment—unless the righteousness of the head commends him to the Father in one body [Col. 1191A].

Christ, therefore, was the cause of our entire redemption. Hence, after the cause comes judgment, and after judgment the redemption of eternal life follows, because apart from the cause of Christ no judgment remains for us except that of punishment.

Here, in the manner of orators, he calls upon the merciful judge to show pity. First he confesses that the judge is just; then he explains the cause of his soul—why he came; he unfolds the redemption for which he came; he offers himself as the price; and, because of the spirit of charity, he declares our life to be his own, so that just as we live in him, he too may live in us.

Finally, he recalls the fury of his adversaries against him, so that, as the most equitable supplicant, he may bend the most equitable judge toward an equitable judgment through devout prayers:

“You have seen, O Lord, their fury against me; you have seen their iniquity,” although the following transmitted words are syntactically uncertain: “by rejecting the cause of my soul, choosing a judge” [Col. 1191B].

From these words it is clear how all judgments depend upon him: he punishes iniquity by condemning it; he directs judgment divinely; he examines all the fury directed against the Church of Christ and the thoughts of individuals. First, as I have said, in the manner of rhetoricians, he reconciles the kindly judge to himself; then he presents the cause of the adversaries, and thereby diffuses through all the members a spirit of action, confidence, and faith.

This is the voice of the elect within the body of Christ, who have obtained the primacy of blessing. Res seems to signify “primacy,” because there is one people that sold its birthright through Esau, and another—the one that bought it. Jacob quietly acquired the primacy of blessing; Esau, devoted to love of money, lost it.

This is the primacy that the letter Res seems to signify. Therefore the individual members of the body ought to share in the grace of the head and carefully preserve the primacy of grace, so that strength may reach each of the members from the head. Otherwise the body lies dead, deprived of its beauty.

In the head is the yoke of life; in the head is the primacy of our inheritance; in the head is the grace of antiquity. It is said that when the serpent is pressed by dangers, it always hides its head and gathers itself into a circle, presenting the remaining part of its body. Likewise the members of Christ guard the head, which is Christ, and observe its primacy, because “all things hold together in him, and he is the head of the body, the Church” [Col. 1191C].

For this, because of the misery of living, will have neither use nor fruit. [The transmitted Latin is corrupt and materially uncertain.]

In these three verses, therefore, all the rewards of the elect are commended to the Father through the head, which is Christ, and are offered as redeemed and justified by his judgment. Then all the iniquity and fury of the adversaries, together with the thoughts of the reprobate, are condemned, and the marvelous unity of the whole body of Christ is declared, when, under the yoke of all, it is borne before God the Father as though in the person of the head [Col. 1191D].

“Redeemer,” he says, “of my life,” where another interpretation has “defender.” From this it is clearly shown, as I said, that redemption belongs to the members, while defense belongs equally to the members and the head, so that the redemption and defense of the whole substance of our salvation may be offered through Christ to God the Father, and so that through his single death the redemption of our double death may be presented.

Therefore it remains that primacy be preserved for the head of the Church, and that complete salvation be guarded through the primacy of the head. Otherwise no one can lose the primacy if Christ has not been taken away from him [Col. 1192A].

For this reason, preserving the head becomes the chief concern and work of all our efforts, the chief object of our task, our hope, and our virtues. The whole aim of our effort is that we may be in the unity of the body of Christ and joined together in the unity of the head, from whom the whole body, supplied through its articulation and binding, grows and is joined together in holy growth in the Lord.

Isaiah also says: “He removes from Judah the head and the tail” (Isa. IX)—that is, the beginning and the end. Judah lost this head when it did not receive Jesus the Lord, in whom the primacy and beginning of the Church are chosen, who is “the firstborn from the dead,” in whom the affairs of life are offered to God the Father [Col. 1192B].

He is our primacy and our end, because he is first and last; he is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. Through him all iniquity raised up against us is cast down, our judgment is raised up, the fury of our adversaries is condemned, and, through their thoughts, their works are examined and rejected as though from the root, so that our primacy too may be glorified with the head and their love of money condemned.

Next, let us examine what the letter Sin brings against us, with a corresponding lament.

## SIN

1471

“You have heard, O Lord,” he says, “their reproaches and all their thoughts against me: the lips of those who rise up against me, and their meditations against me all day long. Look upon their sitting and their rising; I am their song” [Col. 1192C].

For, as was stated above, Sin means “teeth,” and, according to others, “upon a wound.” The reproaches of teeth against Christ are lamented. The Psalmist says: “Their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI). Their lips, rising up against the truth, spoke as deceitful lips, with heart and heart—that is, with a double heart.

Therefore David also says under this letter: “Princes persecuted me without cause” (Ps. CXVIII), to display the weeping of this letter, which is said to mean “upon a wound.” Elsewhere, prophesying and describing his Passion as though in the Gospel, he says among other things, as if addressing the Father: “For they persecuted the one whom you struck, and they added to the pain of my wounds” (Ps. LXVIII) [Col. 1192D].

To add to the pain of a wound is to receive death instead of medicine. Hence the iniquity of the Jews was added to their iniquity because of the hardness of their hearts, so that they would not enter into the righteousness of God, along with the other things that are said.

This too follows from the sound of the letter, which is interpreted as “upon a wound,” the text of the lament: wounds are healed by harsh medicine. But these people added more, returning evil for good, reaping unbelief from the faith of the prophets, and adding the murder of the Lord to their unbelief.

These evils, having been brought to completion, are offered by the just arbiter to God the Father for punishment, as though judgment too had been completed. Their unbelief was the wound; upon the wound came their faithlessness and the killing of the Lord [Col. 1193A].

But what is rightly placed upon a wound except medicine, by which the sharpness of the wound may be softened? Oil is poured upon a wound so that all its harshness may be made gentle. A soothing poultice, a bandage, and a binding are placed upon a wound, by which every wound may be cared for.

But these people, in their perverse response, rejected the medicine and added faithlessness and death to the wound of unbelief, as do all the reprobate, who abuse God’s patience (Rom. II). The goodness and patience of Christ invite everyone to repentance; they, however, according to the hardness of their hearts, store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment.

In these verses, he indicates that God is present everywhere (Isa. I), to whom their thoughts and meditations have been directed. “You have heard,” he says, “their reproaches and all their thoughts.” For to him hearing is the same as seeing, and seeing the same as knowing; nothing can remain hidden from him, and nothing can escape him [Col. 1193B, p. 1472].

The reprobate, however, through God’s patience, as though upon the wound of sin, store up for themselves, in repentance [perhaps an OCR corruption for “punishment”], for the day of wrath.

Hence it follows: “Look upon their sitting and their rising; I am their song.” By insulting and mocking, the reprobate rage no less against the head than against the body, like wicked judges and teachers sitting in the chair of pestilence.

None of them is now cared for by medicine, where no hope of restored salvation can be offered, because where every head is sick and every heart sorrowful, from the crown of the head to the sole of the foot, there is no soundness in it [Col. 1193C]. There, not a portion but the whole is in danger, and the entire body is consumed by a kind of corruption and decay.

There is no longer any place there for applying a soothing poultice, oil, or a bandage. Since the wound is consumed by impenitence, a mortal blow is inflicted upon it.

It is therefore better to have a wound that can be cared for, bound, and treated with medicine than to have death spread inwardly through the whole body without any wound.

There is not only a wound of the body but also of the mind. The latter is healed by the oil of the Holy Spirit, and by gentler words and the sweetness of peaceful speech. There are applications made from words, and medicines composed of heavenly commands, by which every poison of wickedness is driven away and stains are erased.

There are also bonds of the law by which those who are more tightly bound are loosed; through them certain bruised members of Christ are strengthened. This is what the present letter seems to signify [Col. 1193D].

But in these three verses the irrevocable madness of the reprobate against Christ and his members is lamented (Luke XVIII), because, rejecting the physician, they rejected the medicine for all their wounds.

The medicine placed upon the wound is the Lord Jesus himself, for, in order to heal our wounds, he poured wine and oil over the man who had been abandoned, half-dead, lying on the road; then, binding his wounds, he entrusted him to the innkeeper to care for him.

Therefore let each person beware of descending from Jerusalem through sin; rather, let him ascend to it through his merits. If he should happen to sin, we have a guardian of our mouth, a guardian of law and grace, who applies medicine to our wounds and places upon them the bandage of heavenly words, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. IV) [Col. 1194A, p. 1473].

Good, therefore, is the bandage that heals the wounded and joins together what has been broken. And so the prophet tirelessly laments under these verses those who, by every art and every device, continually rage against Christ and against his Church—reproaching, plotting, teaching, and rising up—so that nothing remains for them except to deride and mock those who wish to live devoutly in Christ.

Next let us examine the letter Tau, so that from it we may learn what, as has been urged in these words, is repaid to those who persevere according to God’s just judgment.

## TAU

[Col. 1194B]

He says: “You will repay them, Lord, according to the works of their hands. You will give them a shield of heart—your toil. You will pursue them in your anger, and crush them beneath the heavens, Lord.”

For *Tau*, as I have stated, is interpreted as “signs.” Another interpreter rendered it “he willed,” “he erred,” or “he completed.” From these meanings the interpretation is plainly evident: all these laments in the *Lamentations* are signs and manifestations of things to come. Hence the Psalmist says: “You have shown your people hard things, and have given those who fear you a sign, so that they may flee from the face of the bow” (Ps. 59).

But because the wicked refused to take heed, he says: “You will repay them, Lord, according to the works of their hands.” Therefore he first repaid the Jews, because they hardened their hearts beyond resistance, so that they would be driven farther from faith and truth and could neither enter the righteousness of God nor attain salvation. He grieves that God justly repaid them according to the works of their hands, because after they destroyed life, they find nothing but death.

This is why the letter *Tau* is also interpreted as “he erred.” The Jewish people erred from the way, and every assembly of the reprobate also errs because of the hardness and impenitence of their hearts. For this reason the Lord also “completed” his justice; this, too, we said is what the letter *Tau* signifies.

Hence what follows: “You will give them a shield of heart—your toil.” Because they disdained to venerate and believe in the labor of Christ’s passion, they held that very labor as a shield, so that the arrows of preaching would not pierce their hearts. In the same way the reprobate, while God’s patience invites them to repentance, set God’s very patience before themselves as a shield—as though, because he endures for a long time, he does not see—and, as the Apostle testifies, they store up wrath for themselves “on the day of wrath” (Rom. 2).

The bow of judgment is stretched when his patience is prolonged. But these people hold forth their hardness and various excuses, so that they will not receive the words of life. They do not allow the words of that preaching to reach them because they see him laboring and enduring even to death. The prophet laments that this happened to the Jews, since they set up the shield of hardness against themselves: they refused to believe, according to the flesh, in the mortal Son of God whom they themselves had killed.

In that flesh, of course, he endured the labor of the passion. Hence the prophet says: “I have labored, enduring” (Isa. 1). When the faithless saw the labor of his passion, they scorned to venerate him as God. Since they saw him mortal in the flesh, they disdained to believe that his divinity was immortal.

Therefore, as I said, after the signs and the meanings of the signs—because they scorned to flee from the face of the bow of judgment—there follows fittingly, more as a prophecy than as an exhortation, the sentence of condemnation: “You will pursue them in anger, and crush them beneath the heavens, Lord.” This is so because they persisted in their wicked thoughts, sitting in the seat of pestilence and rising up against the Lord, like dust that the wind casts away from the face of the earth.

They are therefore crushed beneath heaven because they were unwilling either to be heaven themselves or to cling to heavenly disciplines. Since they themselves persecuted Christ, his members, and all the goods of life, they too are justly pursued in anger and most equitably crushed by the good and just God, so that they may hear: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

These, then, are the signs that ran their course and the indications that were displayed, so that the elect might flee from the face of the bow and be delivered. But because the reprobate despised them, it was stated long before under this letter, in the voice of the whole Church: “Let all their evil come before you, and glean them because of all their iniquities” (Matt. 1).

Likewise, in another alphabet under this same letter, it says: “There was no one on the day of the Lord’s wrath who escaped and was left,” so that you may understand it of all the reprobate: “for my enemy has consumed them.” Therefore *Tau*, as I said, is rightly interpreted as “completion,” so that under it all impiety and injustice may receive an end and completion when God turns them into judgment—namely, righteousness receives its end, which is Christ, and the completion of perfection; but impiety receives the completion of its condemnation and an end beyond which it cannot proceed. Thus, in both cases, the signs that preceded may display the truth of their meaning.

For this reason the Lord first showed his people hard things under the sign of the cross, so that the elect might be delivered. But for those who wished to be marked with the sign of the cross, there will follow the truth of the signs and the crushing of eternal punishment, because they held the shield of faithlessness against the teachings of virtue and against the miracles of the saints. Therefore the crushing of God’s anger pursues them, so that they may no longer have strength to resist.

The elect have the shield of good will, by which they are crowned through divine protection, because those whom he protects by helping, he crowns by rewarding. The reprobate also have the shield of their faithlessness, concerning which Job rightly says in the person of the devil: “His body is like cast shields” (Job 41).

For what is meant by his body except all the reprobate, who are said to be like cast shields—fragile? Their shields are therefore cast: they are strong in receiving the blows of arrows, but fragile when they fall. They are not pierced at all by the blows of those who strike them, but by their own fall they are dissolved into fragments.

Hence the body of the malicious enemy—that is, all the wicked—is compared to cast shields: by their obstinacy they are rightly hard, but through their manner of life they are fragile. When they hear the words of preaching, they do not allow any dart of correction to pierce them, because in every sin they commit they set up for themselves the shield of proud defense or perverse denial.

When someone of this kind is accused of the guilt of his wickedness, he does not immediately consider how he might correct his fault, but what he can put forward in defense of himself. No arrow of truth therefore penetrates him, because he receives the words of holy correction upon the shield of perverse defense.

It is rightly lamented of such people here: “You will give them the shield, Lord, your labor,” because, on account of the punishment of sin, they acquire hardness of heart for themselves as a protection of perverse defense. Indeed, by abusing God’s patience for the sake of pride, while thinking that God does not care about such things and does not pay sufficient attention to what is right, they store up wrath for themselves “on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God.”

The first man also held this shield (Gen. 3). When he was asked why he had touched the forbidden tree, he did not attribute the fault to himself, but to the woman whom the Lord had given him; he slyly turned his guilt back upon the author of the gift, who had given him the woman.

The woman also held this shield when she was questioned. She did not turn the blame upon herself either, but threw it back upon the serpent’s persuasion, herself wishing to direct her guilt against the Creator, who had permitted the serpent to enter there and persuade such things.

Cain likewise had this shield when the Lord asked—or rather rebuked—him: “Where is Abel your brother?” He replied proudly and insultingly: “I do not know, Lord. Am I my brother’s keeper?” Behold: when he says, “I do not know, Lord,” he displays fraudulent humility and false denial; but when he says, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” he raises a defiant reproach against God.

Such an excuse is already the punishment of sin. When anyone abuses God’s patience for pride, his destruction and crushing suddenly come from beneath the heavens. Since the guilt of these people has been drawn out in the practice of sinners up to the present, it is just that the vengeance of condemnation should follow. For from the point at which each person ought to have brought guilt to an end, from that same point, through hardness of heart, he draws punishment upon himself.

And because he refused to fear the signs of judgment and did not bear the sign of this letter on his forehead, it is just that he should receive the vengeance of his condemnation. For he not only erred, but also completed and filled up the measure of his crimes, so that he may be condemned without end together with the reprobate.

Hence the Lord says to his patriarch: “The sins of the Amorites are not yet complete” (Gen. 15). When these were completed, both the promise and the vengeance immediately came.

Jeremiah sufficiently intimates this through this letter, which is interpreted as “he completed”; but when sin has been completed, it gives birth to death. Completion, therefore, is generated by hardness of heart and impenitence.

For this reason we must pray and groan that the Lord may soften the hardness of our hearts, so that we may be able to fear his signs, having drunk the wine of compunction, and lament the evils we have committed.

With these matters thus set forth, because the letter *Tau* is the end and completion of this alphabet, let the third book of the exposition of these same *Lamentations* also be ended, to be reread amid tears.

## PROLOGUE OF THE FOURTH BOOK

After the three alphabetical sequences of letters in the *Lamentations* have run their course, it remains for us to review the fourth, according to the mystical significance of the number four, because it is material, so that from it we may construct all the ornaments of the virtues.

It is material because humanity and the world are composed and held together from four elements; material because nothing temporal consists of anything other than four [elements], as, for example, all temporal things consist of four elements and four regions. Likewise, the age of the world consists of four seasons.

This number is therefore material, and it also squares and makes everything stand firm, because it is solid and square—not only material things, but heavenly things as well. Hence, although there is one Gospel, four evangelists are read. Four general virtues are also counted, from which all the others arise, as though from the four rivers of paradise, so that all the seeds of the virtues may be watered more abundantly.

And because under these four elements by which we subsist we sin inwardly and outwardly, it was just that under the same number we should lament together with the prophet and, as though from a material number, restore our inner person to newness of life through tears—the person whom we corrupted through the empty joys of our desires.

There are, then, my brother and fellow old man, four afflictions of character by which the four aforesaid virtues of our soul are corrupted. And therefore it was rightly provided that under these four alphabets the whole human being should lament inwardly and outwardly (Ps. 136), and restore all that belongs to us to the integrity of true expansion through tears or groans. Thus, as individual things belonging to character or body are corrupted, individual laments of the letters may be set against them. And so, carried away beside the rivers of Babylon, may our captivity be loosed and the true freedom of our Zion be restored in Christ.

## BOOK FOUR

## ALEPH

“How the gold has become dim, the finest color has changed. The stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street.”

By the dimmed gold the prophet laments the faithlessness of the Jews, because in them that ancient vigor of faith and splendor of innocence darkened itself with the night of wickedness as faithlessness advanced. They themselves were scattered, not only through every business of vanity, but were even led into captivity among foreign nations. And rightly so, because they had previously been scattered through the public affairs of the world, at the head of every street—that is, seeking the broad and spacious life of the world.

It was just that, because they had expelled the things of God’s sanctuary into the profane acts of the world, they should be driven from faith into faithlessness, and from there, as we have said, into captivity among foreign and rejected nations.

This utterance is no less the voice of one grieving than of one rebuking, just as is that other saying: “How the city sits solitary.” Under this voice, certainly, the hardness of the Jews is lamented. From among them the fathers, patriarchs, and prophets were rejected, like gold and most precious stones in God’s sanctuary, distinguished by faith and works. But when the reprobate and degenerate were made hard of heart, at Christ’s coming they turned to faithlessness.

Therefore, seeing them degenerate through filth and manner of life, the prophet rebukes and laments them: “How the gold has become dim; the finest color has changed.” They were gold because of their knowledge of God and the character inherited from the patriarchs, but they were darkened by the filth of sins and the contamination of faithlessness.

In a mystical sense, however, Christ’s Church, weeping and mourning for her own, says: “How the gold has become dim.” By the dimmed gold she laments the life of the elect, or of priests and ministers of God in their various orders—once bright through the glory of the virtues, but now darkened through base actions and worldly occupations.

Then it is said that “the finest color has been changed,” because that appearance of our holiness has been brought, through the earthly and contemptible works of the present life, to the disgrace of degradation.

Happy, therefore, are those whom the Lord has tested like gold in the furnace of tribulation and distress and received like a burnt offering. But wretched are we, whom the prosperity of the world and the pleasures of empty things have led to such darkness of sins and to such worthlessness of conduct, that rightly, by the prophet and by all God’s elect, our color and appearance of holiness are lamented as having been radically changed for the worse through the practice of sin.

So far has this gone that even the perverse, while trampling upon Christ’s sacraments, often—although reprobate—take an honored place among the elect and themselves rage against the holy Church as though with authority. They contemptuously disregard, as though knowingly, all the words of God’s commandments, and by their wicked conduct destroy the ordinances of ecclesiastical teaching.

Hence, too, the stones of the sanctuary are lamented as scattered at the head of every street. Previously they were always kept within, and were not even taken up for the use and honor of the high priest except when, entering the Holy of Holies, he appeared in the secrecy of his Creator.

What, then, do you think are the stones of the sanctuary scattered at the head of every street except the priests of Christ and the ministers of the sacred altar, as well as the holy society of monks consecrated to God, and the multitude of virgins and religious women? They should always appear before God’s gaze in secrecy; they should never need to be seen outside, nor ever be occupied with the activities of strangers and the world.

But what is more serious is that they are lamented as scattered—like the stones of the sanctuary at the head of every street—because, although they ought always to have been inwardly present in contemplation of God through their life and prayer, through a reprobate life they are busy everywhere outside.

Behold, now scarcely any activity of secular life is not administered by Christ’s priests; there are scarcely any worldly businesses in which the ministers of the altar do not occupy themselves; scarcely any wicked undertaking in which the monastic order does not entangle itself; scarcely any allurements of life with which the chastity of religious women does not defile itself.

Therefore, while those established in a holy habit and religious observance display outward things and pursue the empty pleasures of life, they lie like the stones of the sanctuary scattered outside at the head of every street.

In Greek, the word for “street,” πλατεῖα (*plateia*), derives from breadth. For broad and spacious is the way that leads to death (Matt. 7). The stones of the sanctuary are therefore scattered in the streets when religious people pursue the broad roads of the world. They are scattered not merely in the streets but at the head of the streets when, through desire, they carry out the works of this world, while nevertheless seeking the summit of honor or praise from their religious habit.

They are scattered at the head of the streets because they lie there through the ministry of their work while wishing to be honored for the appearance of holiness.

When the Lord, through the prophet, showed his Church the promises he had made concerning the order of these stones, he promised, saying: “Behold, I will lay your stones in order, and establish you on sapphires; I will place jasper stones as your defenses, and your gates in carved stones, and all your boundaries in desirable stones; all your children taught by the Lord” (Isa. 54).

Christ laid stones in the Church in an ordered arrangement because in it he distinguished the holy souls of the elect by the diversity of their merits. He established it on sapphires, stones that bear within themselves the likeness of an airy color, because the strength of the Church is made firm in souls that desire heavenly things.

And because jasper is green in color, he placed jasper as its defenses, because those who are set against adversaries for the defense of the holy Church are like jasper; during that drought of time, the reprobate wither away.

But because in our time many lovers of the world are counted among the various orders of the Church, it is rightly lamented that the stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street: we turn the mystery of the religion we have undertaken toward the increase of ambition; we bend the place of holiness toward earthly business; we become entangled in earthly activities. What is worse, wolves become shepherds; ministers of the altar become businessmen of the world; the society of monks becomes a fellowship of the vicious; the assembly of religious women becomes a dwelling place of vices.

Therefore Christ’s body—that is, his Church—rightly laments with the prophet: “How the gold has become dim with the soot of sins; how the color of beauty and holiness has been changed into the foulness of vices. How the stones laid in order in the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of the streets,” when they slip down into external occupations and fall.

They seek one thing from the honor of the religious life they have undertaken, but display something else through the duties they perform, and daily perish through many wickednesses. Intent upon worldly cares and vices, they become all the more insensitive as they are found more eager for external things and for the desires of the flesh.

Through habitual use of worldly things, the mind grows hard and becomes far removed from heavenly desire. And when it is made hard by that very habit, it cannot be softened by the demands of the world toward those things that belong to the love of God.

While only the faith of confession and the adoption of baptism remain in the heart, the person is rightly called gold and a stone of the sanctuary. Yet we are lamented as darkened because of the foulness of vices and scattered at the head of the streets.

That those reborn to God in baptism, or enrolled through circumcision, are rightly understood as gold is testified by Job when he speaks typologically about Judea: “The place of its sapphire is stones, and its clods are gold” (Job 28).

The glory that preceded increases the guilt of the fault that follows. For each person’s fall is a greater crime in proportion to the greater virtue he could have possessed before he fell.

Hence let it be said of Judea, reborn through circumcision; let it also be said of the Church, reborn through the sacrament of baptism, what it was and to what glory it was exalted, so that the greatness of grace and the number of virtues may increase in proportion to the accumulation of subsequent sins.

Hence it is said to Job, as was mentioned above: “Its place is sapphire, its stones, and its clods are gold.” For what do we understand by stones in this passage except the minds of holy and strong people, who, because of the grace and steadfastness of their minds, are rightly called stones of the sanctuary?

Hence the Apostle says: “You yourselves, as living stones, are being built up into spiritual houses.” These stones of the sanctuary are rightly lamented as scattered at the head of the streets because they extend themselves downward toward carnal things.

Even in Judea there were always holy souls who suitably led a heavenly life. Hence it is rightly said of it no less than of Christ’s Church: “Its place is sapphire, its stones.”

And because the elect in it shine with great clarity of life and wisdom through faith, it is added: “And its clods are gold.” What is meant by clods except the collections of individuals in the various orders and the unity of the multitude? Clods are bound together from moisture and dust.

All, therefore, who, infused with the dew of grace, confess with true knowledge that they are dust subject to death, shine like golden clods in the Church when they become radiant through the virtues of life.

The Synagogue also had its clods in the prophets, in its teachers, and likewise in the ancient fathers, who, through a great infusion of grace, held together in unanimity of profession and work. Of these it is rightly said: “And its clods are gold,” because the multitude of spiritual people shone in it with the greater virtue in proportion as they were bound together with greater unanimity toward God and neighbor.

But this gold of faithlessness was afterward darkened by shadows. Seeing its blackness, the prophet here laments, saying: “How the gold has become dim; the finest color has changed.”

Christ’s Church also, considering the members of the election blackened by the soot of earthly things, laments that the gold has become dim and that the finest color of the reborn has been changed. It once shone even in its later members with the pallor of gold, but now, on the contrary, it has been darkened by the shadows of sins.

The soul, too, rightly laments itself: formerly it had been made whiter than snow through the font of baptism and colored more beautifully than gold through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, but now it has either been infected with heresy or darkened inwardly by crimes.

The speech of holy souls shines more brightly than gold, and the splendor of their brightness radiates more beautifully than every color. But when the soul, delighted by evil desires, falls away from that radiance, what else is darkened in it except gold? And when it is blackened inwardly by carnal things, what else is changed for the worse except the finest color of brightness and beauty?

The soul has within it the word of divine eloquence, shining more precious than gold, colored incomparably within by charity. But when it is affected by desires for worldly things, what else happens except that the gold is darkened and the finest color is changed?

It is therefore a most evil change when love of eternal things and desire for the heavenly homeland are turned into love of temporal things and desire for vanities. For this the lament is rightly made: “How the gold has become dim; the finest color has changed.”

Since the desire for eternal life has been turned into love and desire for the flesh, the stones of God’s sanctuary—that is, the remaining virtues of the soul—are rightly scattered at the head of every street. For when charity has been lost, no virtue is made firm in the soul. Rather, it transfers all its affections to the broad roads and spacious endeavors of desire, at the head of the streets.

That stones represent the appearance of precious virtues in the souls of the saints is made clearer than light in many places by the words of the teachers. But when the mind extends its desires toward external things and the pleasures of the present life, it scatters all the ornaments of its virtues at the head of the streets, as it were.

The stones that it ought to have borne, fastened upon the breast over the breastplate of judgment, to the glory and praise of God and of its own beauty, it finally strips of their good things after the color of its love has been changed for the worse. It mourns them scattered at the head of the streets and lying there.

Nevertheless, the substance of the word of God within us remains incorrupt, even if it is darkened by the shadows of our sins. Therefore it is significant that it is not the substance of nature that is said to have been violated, but that it has rightly been lamented as darkened in us by our faults.

Heretics, too, although they seem to corrupt the integrity of the word of God, nevertheless leave the power and nature of the word itself intact, so far as depends upon it. It is darkened because of those who do not believe or who do not understand correctly, but the truth remains inviolate. For although it can be darkened for a time, it cannot be corrupted at all.

But the color of the word—namely, the charity with which we are suffused and clothed—is changed for the worse when we pass from love of God and neighbor into desires for earthly things. And when the mind exposes itself to each of them, it sends its actions and desires, as it were, to the head of the entire breadth of life.

When the wretched soul returns to itself, what else does it do but grieve and groan over these things scattered among the broad and spacious roads of death? It is as though it openly said:

“How has that fiery and splendid word of God become dim within me, so that, blinded by my sloth, I have been unable to see the luminous commandment of God that converts souls? How could that which shines for everyone become dim within me, and that which converts even fugitives? What escaped me and what I could not see shone for itself. Therefore the finest color has also been changed in me, and the stones of the sanctuary have been scattered.

“My soul was indeed a sanctuary faithful to God while the gold—that is, the divine word—shone within it like fire. But soon it began to grow dim through faithlessness and the darkness of sins. The finest color is also changed: what was beautiful becomes foul, and everything within is scattered, so that no ornaments of life remain, while all good things are driven outward and the interior is filled with evils.”

Great, therefore, is the force of this lament, and great the strength of the prophet’s grief, which extends to everything. He laments the blindness of the Jews; he also laments the dispersion and losses of God’s Churches; he laments the nakedness of souls and the foulness of all things; he recalls their beginnings, mourns what has been lost, and with groaning extends himself to everything.

Hence what follows.

## BETH

“The sons of Zion, renowned and clothed in the finest gold—how they have been reckoned as earthen vessels, the work of the potter!”

By this he indicates the dignity both of the Jews and of the privilege of the holy fathers: they were not only sons of that earthly Zion, but also renowned sons of the heavenly Jerusalem. Adopted through the teaching of the law and the privilege of grace, they were renowned in lineage, worship, and teaching, so that above all nations they were called sons of God and were named his friends. To them were given the promise and the lawgiving; theirs were the fathers, and from them came Christ.

They are therefore rightly called very renowned, since God, the wondrous teacher, is praised as having been in their midst and as having been their protector.

“Clothed,” he says, “in the finest gold.” By gold, the shining wisdom of God is signified. Hence the divine word says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 21).

In former times the Jews, clothed in gold, shone above all others like lights in the world. And they are marked not merely by any gold, but by the finest and purest gold, through which heavenly wisdom is understood.

Hence Solomon says: “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom and who abounds in prudence” (Prov. 3). “Its acquisition is better than the commerce of silver and its fruits better than the finest and purest gold.”

The Jews, imbued with this wisdom, are praised as clothed above all nations in the finest gold. For if, according to Scripture, “the root of wisdom is to fear God,” what are the fruits of wisdom except to see? (Eccli. 1.) These are the first and purest fruits born from the first gold of wisdom.

In this first gold of beauty, not only the Synagogue but also Christ’s Church glories as more gloriously clothed. But what is more tearful is that both the one and the other have been changed in their members, so that the reprobate Jews have been reckoned as earthen vessels and the members of the Church have been made baser.

For all these things the prophet—or rather, the voice of all the elect—rightly mourns: often the renowned sons of Zion, that is, of the heavenly Jerusalem, clothed in the finest gold and imbued with the wisdom of love of God and neighbor, fall toward the fragile works of this world. Thus they themselves become earthen vessels, although they had been prepared to become heavenly beings incorruptible.

The beautiful Church of Christ is therefore proclaimed “clothed in the finest gold, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army set in battle array” (Song 6). Hence her sons are called renowned, clothed in the finest gold. In the grace of their newness nothing defiled enters; reformed for the contemplation of God, they are clothed in the first grace, so that they may return to the dignity in which they were created.

For this reason, when the younger son returns repentant to his father, he is remembered as having received the first robe (Luke 15)—that is, the grace of immortality. Hence the renowned sons of Zion are rightly praised as clothed in the finest gold.

There is Arabian gold, which is also brought to the Lord from Sheba. There is also exceedingly precious gold, which is said to have been brought from Ophir to King Solomon (3 Kings 9).

*Ophir* is interpreted as “laughter” or “herb-covered.” It signifies coming from that laughter in which all the joys of life are found, where the souls of the saints rest in green pastures.

Therefore it is not without reason that the gold is called “first,” because wisdom and immortality, when we are reborn to life, are more precious than all riches (Prov. 3), and nothing that is desired can be compared with them.

When the sons of Zion, clothed in this gold, sin, they are rightly lamented as having been reckoned among earthen vessels. Job rightly said in mourning: “I have been compared to clay, and likened to dust and ashes” (Job 30). And the Lord says in the Psalms: “Like the mud of the streets I will wipe them away” (Ps. 17).

Earthen vessels are formed from clay. Yet among them some are prepared for honor, such as golden and silver vessels, while other vessels are earthenware and remain for dishonor.

The Apostle Paul says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (1 Cor. 4). The renowned sons of Zion glory as clothed in this treasure, but when they have been stripped of it, they are lamented as earthen and clay vessels prepared for dishonor.

Nevertheless, so long as one lives here, God is able to restore one of these to honor and another to dishonor. Those whom the furnace of tribulation and distress has tested are changed into gold, so that they may be vessels of honor. Of these it is said: “The furnace tests vessels of gold, and distress tests a just man” (Eccli. 27).

Hence David says in the person of the Lord: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21).

When the clay of the flesh has been fired, and the soul is inwardly filled with the desirable treasure through a good conscience, while outwardly the person shines, clothed in the gold of understanding, what else does he become except a vessel of honor?

They are therefore called the work of the potter’s hands, because just as the potter has power from the same lump to form one vessel for dishonor and another for honor, so Christ, our true maker, has power to raise us from clay to a beautiful appearance. Those whom he has decided to abandon to the confusion of condemnation are stripped of the heavenly treasure within and of the finest gold without, so that they become degenerate—but only according to his just and true judgment.

Otherwise, none of those heavenly sons of Zion, made renowned through the adoption of holy regeneration, would ever be reckoned inwardly as earthen vessels unless they had first been stripped, inwardly and outwardly, of divine things.

But although they have now fallen as their sins demand, because they are the work of the potter’s hands, we must recall the passage in which the Lord sends Jeremiah to the house of the potter. When he arrived there, the clay vessel is immediately said to have fallen from the potter’s hand and been broken (Jer. 18). It is significantly remembered that he formed another vessel again from the same clay.

The Lord immediately indicates to the prophet that he too is able to restore vessels of honor from us, who are indeed made of clay, and to make us worthy of his sacred mystery.

Therefore the prophet laments those who become degenerate and are stripped of heavenly things, so that they are compared with earthen and clay vessels. He does so in order that, pierced with compunction, they may return through repentance and the pouring out of tears to the grace of immortality.

Hence it is also written to the angel of the church of Ephesus: “Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do the first works.” This means plainly: “Know and understand what dignity you possessed through the grace and adoption of God—how renowned and noble you were, clothed in the finest and purest gold, indeed dressed in the robe of immortality—and afterward how base and clay-like you have become because of corruption and the punishment of sin, compared with earthen vessels.”

So that you may not fall into despair, imitate the prophet who mourns and laments that you have become such a person, and do the first works—that is, works of charity and love of God—so that through that same love of God and neighbor you may return to the adoption of sons, from which you fell because of the pleasures of perverse persuasion.

Hence what follows.

## GIMEL
But the lamias exposed their breasts; they suckled their young. The daughter of my people is cruel, like an ostrich in the wilderness.

By the lamia he reproaches the harshness of the scribes and Pharisees and their wicked teaching among the people: they were not even so demented as to offer milk or the breast of their teaching to the children of the Synagogue, like the most savage of all beasts, the lamia. For it is said of her that she is more cruel to her offspring than all other beasts. Hence, it is expressly said that she received her name: *lamia*, as though from *lania* (“a butcher”), is said by many to sound so because she tears her young to pieces and mangles them—which is also read quite plainly in the fables.

Thus the Pharisees, more savage than beasts, did not expose the breast to the little ones and infants, so that they might suck the nourishment of life. Rather, they became cruel like the ostrich, which, as soon as it has laid its eggs, abandons them, neither remembering them nor coming near to cover or warm them, because it gives no thought to its own offspring. So too the perversity of the Jews was at work among God’s people, doing nothing except tear them apart, plunder them, and lay everything waste, so that, as Scripture says, they themselves would neither enter into the promises of life nor permit others to enter.

The prophet, mourning and lamenting, says that the lamias suckled their young; he grieves that they did not do this for the little ones among the people. The lamia is called *Lilith* in Hebrew; some Hebrews suppose her to be an **ἐριννύς**, that is, one of the Furies, who are called *Parcae* (“the Fates”) because they spare no one—just like the scribes and Pharisees, who spared neither their neighbors among the people nor even the prophets.

What, then, shall I say about the prophets, when they did not withdraw their hands even from the one promised by God himself to the fathers? Therefore their cruel daughter, the Synagogue, laments, having become more cruel than lamias; and, like an ostrich, they left no hope for themselves or for their neighbors in the future.

But the Church of Christ also laments, in the figure of the lamias, the crafty perversity of hypocrites and heretics, who bear a human face but, through their impiety, carry bestial hearts. They expose the breast when they openly proclaim their error; they suckle their young when they perversely teach the immature souls of their followers and, by nourishing them wrongly, conform them to impiety.

Hence elsewhere the prophet, wailing as he deplores the deeds of heretics and hypocrites, says: “There the lamia has lain down and found rest” (Isaiah 34); “there the hedgehog has had its burrow”—namely, among the people of Christ, among a grave people full of sins. By the lamia, as I have said, hypocrites or heretics are signified; by the hedgehog, however, all the malicious are represented, those who cover themselves with various defenses.

For the lamia, as I have said, is said to have a human face but a bestial body. So too, in all hypocrites and heretics, what they display in their first appearance seems to arise from the reason of holiness, but the body that follows is bestial, because the things they contrive under the appearance of good are exceedingly wicked.

By the name “hedgehog,” as I have said, the defense of malicious minds is signified. For when a hedgehog is seized, its head is visible, its feet are seen, and its entire body can be observed; but as soon as it has been seized, it gathers itself into a sphere, hiding its feet inward together with its head. Within the hand of the one holding it, what had seemed to be seen in its entirety is suddenly lost.

So indeed—so are malicious minds when they are caught in their transgressions: by suddenly producing excuses, the malicious mind draws its head and feet inward, so that it hides all the traces of its iniquity. It withdraws its head because, by remarkable defenses, it makes it appear that it did not even begin anything wrong; and, like a sphere, it remains in the hand of the one holding it, because the person who rebukes it, suddenly losing all that he had already known, holds only something wrapped up within the conscience of sins. The one who had already seen the whole matter by detecting the wicked conduct, deceived by its excuses, is altogether ignorant of it.

Driven to such misery, let us now return to the order of the lament:

“The daughter of my people is cruel, like an ostrich in the wilderness.”

For who is the daughter of the people if not the Church that is lamented? Indeed, she is also proclaimed the daughter of the saints, because she has been reborn in Christ. But when entangled in such and similar bestial habits of sinning, she becomes cruel like an ostrich in the wilderness: thinking only of the present, doing nothing in hope, and even leaving neglected the acts and works she commits, lying without the warmth of charity; having no concern for future life and no care for her children, but attending only to the present, as we have said, and forgetting even the works she has performed, like an ostrich forgetting the eggs it has laid.

Leaving these evils of the Churches aside, let us now see what the soul ought morally to mourn in itself: how often the bestial ferocity of souls, which has been accustomed to caress them, is received into the piety of faith in Christ, so that they expose the breast of their teaching and suckle their own habits, as it were, with the milk of piety. Thus whatever previously appeared criminal within is wholly compensated by the abundance of piety and by love of God and neighbor.

For bestial souls, which previously seemed to assume a human form by reason but, through cruelty, ferocity, and their habits, produced the ways of beasts, are often quickly converted to what is better. They strip the breasts of their teaching of its coverings and then nourish the most discerning deeds of life with the milk of God’s utterances; they incline the mind toward piety and love of God and neighbor.

Hence the Lord says: “Would that you were cold or hot. But because you are lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Revelation 3). It is as though he said: “Would that I saw you grown old through the coldness of impiety and in your bestial and monstrous ways; certainly you would become hot through love of God and neighbor, by the flame of charity. But now, because you are lukewarm between the two, I shall begin to vomit you out and cast you from the body of unity.”

Therefore the integrity of conduct must always be pursued, ferocity must be tamed, and lukewarmness must be avoided. Hence the faithful soul should at last say with a groan concerning its deeds—and say also concerning its habits—that “the lamias exposed their breasts.”

For by the lamia, carnal prudence is rightly signified. Now carnal prudence, like the most savage of beasts, suckles and nourishes its young—that is, the deeds it has produced—with nothing other than death. But how often, when changed for the better, it passes from carnal prudence, which the Apostle calls death, into prudence of the spirit; then it uncovers what is cruel and exposes what is shameful, and, with the milk of teaching as though from the breast of piety, suckles and nourishes its young—that is, its habits and deeds—so that they pass from ferocity to gentleness, from savagery to piety, from death to life, and from infancy to maturity.

But carnal prudence, which had long and stubbornly hardened itself, is rightly lamented as “the cruel daughter of my people” and “like an ostrich in the wilderness.” For, as has often been said, when the ostrich has laid its eggs in the wilderness, it abandons them without the warmth of love, without the fostering care of piety, and without hope for future offspring, leaving them without care or concern. So too carnal prudence, directing all the acts of affection that it has produced solely toward the present, abandons them in death without hope or care. Hence, as I have admitted, it is rightly called death.

Therefore the prophet laments it as the daughter of the virtues, although cruel: when it ought to have foreseen for itself the fruitfulness of its seed in the future, it gave its deeds solely to the flesh and, without the fostering care of hope or the love of charity, abandoned them in death like an ostrich abandoning its eggs.

It follows.

## DALETH

“The tongue of the suckling has clung to his palate in thirst. The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them.”

This is an evident account of lamentation over the Jews: their mothers having been extinguished, the tongue of the suckling clung from excessive thirst to the palate, and when the older children, lacking strength, asked for bread, there was no one to break it for them—especially since they themselves were food for their mothers. Thus the youngest were consumed by thirst, while the older ones, without food, perished, killed by hunger.

According to the allegorical meanings, however, the tongue of the suckling clings to the palate in thirst without the milk of teaching when the cruel care of teachers, like that of an ostrich without concern for its flocks, has grown numb through loving something else, and the shepherd has not, with the Apostle, nourished the little ones by the milk of God’s teaching (1 Corinthians 3).

Hence the Apostle also says to his little ones: “I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able—but neither can you yet” (1 Corinthians 3). In the Church of Christ there are little sucklings, drawing the breasts of God’s commandments; there are also older ones, who are already able to receive solid food—that is, to understand the deeper mysteries of God—if only there were someone to break bread for them, namely, to expound the more secret sacraments of the holy Scriptures.

But the care and solicitude of shepherds are lacking. There is no one to expose the breast of teaching to the younger ones, nor anyone to break bread for the older ones. Seeing this well, the prophet rightly mourns their reprobate life and laments the cruel death of these people, because many teachers, enticed by their own impiety, are rightly judged more cruel than lamias and more negligent than ostriches.

For although lamias seem more cruel to their offspring, they nevertheless expose the breast and in some manner suckle their young. In comparison with them, these teachers are rightly lamented as more savage because they pursue earthly things and seek them. Through their negligence, the tongue of sucklings is often consumed by corruption, clings to the palate in thirst, and withers.

The ostrich too, although it appears to lay its eggs without care or any feeling of piety, is nevertheless said by natural philosophers to expose them in sand where the excessive heat of the sun grows hot each day; there, by the heat of the sun and the warmth of the sand, the eggs are moderately fostered until the chicks are formed. In comparison with this, those who meditate on something else without pastoral care and concern are rightly lamented as more negligent, since, when the little ones ask for bread, they avoid even breaking it for them.

For holy Scripture is sometimes food and sometimes the drink of milk. It is food in its more obscure passages, when it is broken by the teacher through exposition and swallowed by the hearers through chewing. It is the drink of milk in its more open passages, because it is written or sucked from the breasts of Scripture when they are presented and uncovered, just as it is found.

Therefore the prophet rightly teaches in the Spirit when he sees the sucklings and little ones of the Church wasting away from hunger and thirst. When these little ones have already learned to ask for bread, and there is no one to break it for them, let us nevertheless give thanks to God, who by himself has already broken five and seven loaves—the mysteries of the Old and New Testaments—and thus gave them to the disciples, and the disciples to the crowds. From what remained after those who had eaten, twelve baskets of fragments were gathered and stored (Mark 6).

Among these mystical mysteries of God’s utterances, teachers are necessary, so that, when weak people ask for the stronger meanings of holy Scripture to be expounded and broken into pieces, they may be able to explain them and supply what is necessary in each passage. But the prophet laments when the one who ought to expound cannot be found.

Holy Scripture is also the drink of milk, of which the prophet says: “All you who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no silver, hurry, buy and eat, without any exchange, wine and milk” (Isaiah 55). From this it is plainly evident that when he says, “Come to the waters,” holy Scripture is the true drink; when he says, “Eat,” it is the true food. When he says, “Wine and milk,” the nourishment of infancy and the drunkenness of the Holy Spirit are signified, so that by milk our tenderness may be nourished and by wine our hearts may be intoxicated.

And if God’s commandments were not altogether made clear in the holy Scriptures, Truth itself would not cry out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7). For he himself is our drink; he himself is our food; he himself is wine and milk.

The same prophet saw that these things were lacking to Judaea in this very work when he said:

“The nobles of it perished from hunger, and its multitude dried up from thirst.”

It belongs to few to know strong and hidden things; it belongs to many to perceive the open matters of history. Therefore he asserts that the nobles of Judaea perished not from thirst but from hunger, because those who seem to preside, while devoting themselves entirely to outward cares and the disciplines of empty understanding, do not find what they should commit to discussion concerning inward things.

When these fall away from inward understanding, the understanding of the little ones also dries up in outward matters. Hence it is rightly added there: “Its multitude dried up from thirst.” It is as though he were plainly saying: “While the common people abandon the pursuits of their life, they no longer seek even the streams of history, because, according to Job, ‘the earth from which bread arose in its place has been overturned by fire’” (Job 28).

For when the hearts of shepherds and teachers, from which the bread of life was accustomed to arise and the words of the divine utterances to flow, begin to be filled with earthly cares and vices, it is rightly lamented that the earth from which the bread that descended from heaven arose—or ought to have been drawn up in its proper place—has been overturned by fire.

It is overturned by fire in its own place when the mind of unbelievers, trampling upon the mysteries, is burned by the torches of vices. Therefore it burned, because it gave itself over to the flames of vices.

Hence we must act with lamentation and tears, lest our tongue cling to our palate from thirst; lest, when the little ones ask for bread, we perish, rejected by God’s judgment, consumed by poverty and hunger for the word; lest the earth from which bread arose perish, overwhelmed by fire. Rather, let us knock at the Father’s door with prayers and tears, asking for the three loaves from the Gospel, so that he himself may grant them to us—the one who urges us to knock, seek, and ask (Luke 11).

For this reason let us ask him to grant and break them for us as well—that true Teacher and Author who broke them in the wilderness. Refreshed by them, may none of us grow weary on the way. For because of the exceedingly wicked life of priests and the cruelty of their conduct, the dryness of the sucklings from thirst is lamented; and because there is no one to break bread for the little ones, their destruction is mourned.

We must therefore knock and ask for what is denied to no one who seeks in truth, lest, because our sins demand it, it be withdrawn from us, just as the Lord threatens elsewhere: “I shall send among them neither a hunger for bread nor a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of God” (Amos 8). For when the preaching and understanding of the word are withdrawn, hearing also ceases, and hunger and deprivation spread together through the death of these people.

Now let us see what is mourned morally. Our little thoughts and the inward affections of the mind quickly wither from thirst without the milk of gentle persuasion and the dew of the Holy Spirit. Their tongue, clinging to the palate of the flesh in utterance, causes the infancy of the tender mind to become mute and strangles with the sword of unbelief the conceptions of life within our heart, so that they cannot reach the light.

Hence it is rightly said: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10). Otherwise, whatever good is conceived in the mind, unless it is nourished by the milk of teaching and the grace of the Holy Spirit, quickly withers; and the tongue clings to the palate, unable to utter the confession of salvation.

The grace of the Holy Spirit divides itself into seven gifts, through which it has as many children. These are aptly signified when it is said that Job had seven sons and three daughters: “And his sons,” says Scripture, “went and made a feast in their houses, each on his own day” (Job 1).

The sons make a feast in their houses when the individual virtues, through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, nourish the mind with divinity according to the proper measure in which they exist. Hence it is also rightly said, “each on his own day.” For the day of each son is the illumination of each virtue.

Each gift has its own day, because it is not the same thing to have wisdom and to understand: many indeed have a taste for eternal things, but are by no means able to understand them. Wisdom, therefore, makes a feast on its own day, because it refreshes the mind with the hope and certainty of eternal things.

*(Gregory.)* But lest we seem to prolong our discussion, let us set down in full the words of the holy teacher Gregory, which have been cited above.

“Understanding,” he says, “prepares a feast on its own day; but they do not know how to do these things except those who, before their thoughts come forth into action, carefully observe and restrain their inward movements, and inwardly suckle them with the persuasion of teaching and with faith in Christ.”

They do not know how to do these things except those who know how to fortify the mind with every safeguard and understand how to nourish pious affections and promptings in Christ with the milk of teaching.

What else, then, is the tongue of such people but clinging to the palate of the flesh, when the inward inspirations of the virtues are suffocated by empty cares and, before it is uttered, the confession of faith is bound by the chains of evil?

Hence it rightly follows: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them.” Little thoughts, when they are conceived concerning Christ and eternal life, immediately seek that bread which descended from heaven. But the mind, weighed down by its own torpor and sloth and devoted to empty cares, does not know how to break bread for those who ask—by understanding it, by chewing it through meditation, or by distributing it through reception.

Therefore it is rightly lamented: “There was no one to break it for them.” For although a virtue inspired by God may for a time inwardly animate the hunger for life, outwardly it is emptied by desires and, weakened in its powers, is drained away.

Hence it follows:

## HE

“Those who ate delicacies perished in the ways; those who were nourished in saffron-colored garments embraced dung.”

Through these words the unbelief of the Jews is laid bare as clearly as daylight: they were darkened, and their finest color was changed—the color they had possessed in their fathers, patriarchs, and prophets. They were scattered, as we still see today, at the head of all the streets. Although clothed and arrayed in fine gold, according to the prerogative of their fathers, they were nevertheless reckoned among earthen vessels and the work of the potter’s hands, more savage than lamias and more cruel than ostriches.

Because of their unbelief, the sucklings and little ones perished, so that those who had eaten delicacies perished from hunger in the ways of God when Christ came. For all the mystical sacraments of Scripture and the institutions signifying realities—in which the fathers and patriarchs had feasted luxuriously—perished in the ways of God themselves, because they did not receive God and the Lord but denied that he was the true Son of God. He himself is the beginning of all ways; therefore, without him, they perished in the ways of the world.

Hence it follows:

“Those who were nourished in scarlet embraced dung.”

For the color scarlet is shown to be fiery. By this fire hearts are made aflame when they are filled with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. The holy fathers were nourished in saffron-colored garments, in the mysteries of grace; but the unbelieving Jews, denying the Lord, embraced dung.

Paul had rejected this dung when he said concerning Christ: “For whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and count them as dung”—namely, all the elements of the Law according to the letter, which were previously regarded as dung even by all Catholics, so that they might gain Christ and be found in him, not possessing the righteousness that comes from the Law but that which comes through faith in Jesus Christ (Philippians 3).

The unbelieving Jews, embracing this righteousness and the letter of the Law as dung, refuse to receive the righteousness that is in Christ. They were also often confined by siege and took dung for food, as we likewise read in the Book of Kings (2 Kings 6), where dove’s dung was sold for a price; yet even then they did not choose to turn wholly to God with their heart.

The Church of Christ also, according to the mystical meanings, laments its own people who abandon charity and the other virtues in which, because of the brightness of grace, they were nourished luxuriously in saffron-colored garments, but afterward fall and embrace the dung of their beloved things.

The prophet aptly lamented such people elsewhere, saying: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1). For beasts rotting in their own dung means that carnal people, in the stench of their lust, serve their sins according to the desires of their hearts.

The vinedresser promises to place this dung around the unfruitful fig tree when it is already due to be cut down: “Lord,” he says, “let it remain this year also, until I dig around it and put a basket of dung around it” (Luke 13).

What, then, is the basket of dung if not the remembrance of sins? Hence David said: “And my sin is always before me” (Psalm 50). The sins of the flesh are rightly called dung. When we bring them back to the memory of those who have committed them, we place, as it were, a basket of dung around an unfruitful tree, so that the person may recall the evils he has done and, through the grace of compunction and sorrow, may grow rich, as it were, from the stench.

A basket of dung is therefore placed at the root of the tree that was to be cut down when the mind is affected by awareness of its wickedness and the memory of its thoughts is touched; when the mind rouses itself through repentance to lamentation and reforms itself for the grace of good action, it returns at last to fruitfulness through contact with the dung.

For it comes back from stench to fruit when the soul raises itself from consideration of sin to good works.

But because there are many who do not wish to return to repentance, the Church laments them, though they do not know why they are lamented, because in their desire to sin they embrace the dung of vices. Whatever we embrace, we seem to hold with desire. Therefore those who, out of love of sinning, appear irredeemably to embrace dung—that is, crimes and shameful acts—are rightly lamented.

According to the tropological meaning, the virtues of the soul seem to be clothed in saffron-colored garments when they are made radiant by the rays of love of God and neighbor. For the saffron color often signifies in the holy Scriptures the brightness of holy love. Therefore, when charity is lost, the remaining virtues embrace dung; from the good odor of love of God and neighbor they immediately pass into the stench of wickedness.

Hence the angel says to the Church of Ephesus: “I have this against you, that you have abandoned your first charity. Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent. And do your former works”—namely, works of chaste love, without which no virtue of good fragrance is found (Revelation 2).

Paul aptly enumerates this, so that whatever virtue may appear highest is of no benefit without charity. Therefore the very virtues of works that are performed without love are rightly lamented as having embraced dung: without charity they lose the fragrance of good odor and come into the stench of a wicked intention.

It follows.

## VAU

“And the iniquity of the daughter of my people became greater than the sin of Sodom, which was overthrown in a moment; and hands did not begin in her.”

By an amplification of sin he describes Jerusalem and mourns the fall and crimes of the Synagogue, which was the daughter of the holy patriarchs and prophets, so that Isaiah says that from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there was no soundness in her.

Therefore, for many reasons, her iniquity became greater than the sin of Sodom. Ezekiel expresses what their sin was when he says: “This was indeed their sin: pride and abundance, fullness of bread and leisure; and also that they did not extend a hand to the needy and poor.” This is what the present verse means, because “hands did not begin in her.”

What does it mean to say, “hands did not begin in her,” unless one should understand “to do something good”? We read that the Synagogue did this. Nevertheless, although it received countless benefits and fulfilled the sacraments of God through very many works, because it committed more wicked crimes, its greater iniquity is rightly lamented.

Hence Ezekiel also says to her: “Sodom your sister was justified by you” (ibid.). She was the first to begin extending her hands to all the commandments of God, because the utterances of God had been entrusted to her. But afterward, when she began to apostatize from God, her wickedness surpassed all measure, so that Sodom did not commit even half of her crimes. Sodom lived in leisure and did not extend a hand to the needy and poor; nor, as the present verse indicates, did her hands begin to do anything good in her before she was overthrown.

Jerusalem, however, possessed knowledge of God and had received the commandments of life; she extended her hands to everything, although at last she killed the Author of life and, already defiled by many menstrual impurities, raised those hands to idols.

For all these evils, because she trampled upon such great benefits of almighty God and repaid good with evil, the punishment of her vengeance must be considered. If Sodom was suddenly overthrown in a moment for the faults listed above, how much more grievous a punishment did the Jews deserve, who not only despised benefits but killed the Author of life and committed greater and more numerous offenses?

Furthermore, the Church of Christ rightly deplores the sins of the people, because its iniquity has become greater than the sin of Sodom—especially now, at a time when faith and truth have departed; when humility, kindness, and nearly every goodness have perished; when the fires of discord and desire set the whole world ablaze; when the devouring flame of envy and treachery consumes everyone; when the Church of Christ laments that the poor are stripped by robberies and frauds, and nearly our whole world lies uncultivated; when the rights of all laws are violated and human and divine things are alike profaned; when right and wrong are confused together; when peace is preserved nowhere, in any place or region; when the bonds of name, kinship, and faith are renounced; when frivolity attempts everything and no consciousness of goodness remains; when everyone complains about what we do and scarcely anyone lives rightly.

The homeland is ravaged by civil war; from every side we are struck externally by the enemy’s sword; yet there is no end to the effort devoted to possessing and acquiring through every kind of deceit. Like a Vulcanian cauldron kindled by its own fires, the hearts of men and women are alike inflamed, and scarcely any age or class is spared.

For these and similar evils the Church—or rather the prophetic word—rightly laments, since the evils for which Sodom is condemned are increasing, and every day, after countless benefits from God, we commit many other offenses against God.

Therefore our iniquity is rightly lamented as greater than that of those who did not begin to do anything good in the faith of Christ. Hence let us fear punishments more terrible than theirs, for they were overthrown in a moment.

Everything in which we live is momentary; and therefore, by sinning each day, we are overthrown into punishment, as it were, in a moment. Perhaps Sodom bore lighter punishments in hell for its sins; we, on the contrary, who have extended our hand to the faith and made many vows, deserve worse things by sinning every day, according to what the Apostle says: “Do you not know, O man, that the patience of God leads you to repentance? For you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment” (Romans 2).

Morally also, the crimes of those who fall into hypocrisy are lamented, because their iniquity becomes greater than the sin of Sodom—especially when everything they do, even what is good, is full of guilt and dedicated sevenfold to demons. Therefore the iniquity of their works and habits is greater than the sin of Sodom.
