Thus every soul filled with vices under hypocrisy rightly laments and says: “The iniquity of my people has become greater than the sin of Sodom.” For just as one people rises against another, so the habits and deeds of hypocrites conflict, so that the virtues they appear to practice outwardly are shown inwardly to be worse than the vices of Sodom.

For when the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it travels through dry and waterless places, seeking rest and not finding it. Then, it says, “I shall return to my house from which I came.” And when it comes and finds it empty, swept with brooms, and decorated, it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; and they enter and dwell there (Matthew 12).

The unclean spirit goes out from a person when that person is reborn in Christ. But it returns to its house when it again finds the soul empty of the affection for good works, as though swept clean of filth by the brooms of hypocrisy and adorned with wicked actions as well.

Thus the soul is held in the embrace of a doubled number of unclean spirits, and the final state of that person becomes worse than the first. When the soul is filled with peoples of unclean spirits and hosts of vices, it not improperly laments that its iniquity is greater than the sin of Sodom: they descended into hell in a moment through open evil, whereas this soul, filled no less with simulated virtues than with hidden inward vices, is daily plunged into the depths of torment as though cleansed and adorned.

Therefore the iniquity of its people—that is, of its deeds and works—is proclaimed greater than the sin of Sodom: Sodom did not extend its hands toward the fruit of good works, whereas the society of hypocrites appears adorned with many works but is ensnared by vices more wicked than those who are openly held by the crimes of sinners.

Therefore it follows:

## ZAIN

“Her Nazirites were whiter than snow, brighter than milk, ruddier than ancient ivory, more beautiful than sapphire.”

According to the literal sense, the beauty of the Nazirites is rightly described: the whiteness of their abstinence and the beauty of their faces once shone more brightly than milk among the people, and the pleasing redness of their complexion gleamed in their faces.

But in the lamentation they are praised more greatly, so that their ugliness may appear greater because of the scarcity of hunger. Their faces are mourned as blackened above coals, so that, because of the affliction of hunger, they cannot be recognized in the streets.

Furthermore, the holy Church of God has its Nazirites, whiter than snow and brighter than milk. Through them the life of those who abstain and practice continence is signified, and it is rightly proclaimed in Christ’s chosen ones as whiter than snow and brighter than milk.

Snow is frozen from water that is seen to come from above; milk, however, is milked from flesh that is nourished below. What, then, is demonstrated by snow if not the whiteness of heavenly life? What by milk if not the administration of temporal dispensation?

Thus the Church of Christ has its Nazirites, who lead a heavenly life through contemplation and, through the administration of active life, shine more brightly than milk to the praise of their Creator. Often, indeed, continent men perform such remarkable works of virtue that many who have maintained a heavenly life appear to be surpassed by those who have administered earthly things well.

Therefore both groups are rightly called “whiter than snow and brighter than milk.” Because, through the fervor of the spirit, they sometimes appear to surpass the life of the ancient and strong fathers, it is rightly added: “Ruddier than ancient ivory.”

When the beauty of redness is praised, the flame of holy desire is expressed. Ivory, as is known, is the bone of elephants. But because they are expressly praised as “ruddier than ancient ivory,” the meaning is clear: some saints often prove more fervent in zeal before human eyes than certain fathers who preceded them.

To unfold the whole matter at once, it is added: “More beautiful than sapphire.” Sapphire is of an ethereal color. And because the Nazirites of Christ appear to surpass many who strive toward heavenly things not only through active life but also through the contemplative conduct of heavenly life, they are said to be more beautiful than sapphire, in recognition of the merits of the Churches.

Would that what is proclaimed for the beauty of Christ and the praise of his bride were not darkened by the favor of empty praise and the deception of wicked pretense! For often, when an abundance of virtues prospers beyond what is fitting, the mind is led into a certain self-confidence; and, badly deceived by presumption concerning a definite or empty praise, it is suddenly darkened when sin steals upon it. What for a long time seemed to shine more brightly through virtues is corrupted by the frauds of the devil.

Hence it is rightly added under the letter Heth:

## HETH
Their faces have become blacker than coals, and they were not recognized in the streets. Their skin has clung to their bones; it has dried up and become like wood.

Thus they become black after their whiteness: for when divine justice has been sent forth, as they seek the favor of their own praise, or when they presume wrongly upon themselves, they fall into sins even in matters they neither understand nor are able to foresee. And because after the bitter fire they come to bodily cold—or even, after the whiteness of life, to the sluggishness of empty praise—their faces are rightly compared to extinguished coals, blacker than they. Therefore one must walk along the royal road; and Scripture says: “Do not be excessively righteous.” For plainly, when some, presuming on their own confidence, sometimes abandon the fear of God, they become colder still in their frigid minds.

Of such it is rightly added: “And they were not recognized in the streets.” A “street,” a word derived from the Greek language, signifies the breadth of the present life. What, indeed, is narrower for the human mind than to deny one’s own wishes, break the desires of the flesh, and turn aside from what is just and right for the sake of no praise or deception? Concerning entry into this life, Truth says: “Enter through the narrow gate” (Ecclesiasticus XIX). But what is broader than to submit to no laws, serve one’s own desires, and resist no impulses? Otherwise, unless such people were seeking their own interests, they would never, adorned with such great virtues, have come into the streets. The breadth of the streets belongs to those who seek their own interests and defend themselves against everything.

For this reason they were not recognized in those same streets, because they are not what they seemed to be when, under God’s just scrutiny, they are found reprobate. Those who, through confidence in their holiness and having set aside the judgment of their betters, follow their own desires proceed, as it were, through the streets; but they are not recognized in the streets. For concerning their life they displayed one thing when, by breaking their own desires, they kept themselves on the narrow path, but another when, presuming on themselves, they proceed with greater confidence according to the intention of their hearts.

Hence it follows: “Their skin has clung to their bones.” What is signified by “bones” except the hardness of strength? What is expressed by “skin” except the softness of our weakness? Skin is therefore said to cling to bones because, among those who think perversely, the weakness of vices is regarded as the hardness of virtue. Or again, because skin covers all the inner parts, it is rightly said to cling to bones when everything done outwardly is joined inwardly to the bones by the favors of empty praise. For skin clings to bones when praise for outwardly well-performed deeds is inwardly joined to the virtues.

When these are thus joined together, the reward is emptied, since what they do is weak, while, deceived by confidence in their exaltation, they flatter themselves with stronger opinions about themselves. And because they think great things of themselves, they therefore disdain to correct themselves from their own wickedness.

Hence it is also added: “It has dried up and become like wood.” Their guilt is rendered so much more insensitive because among them it is praised as though it were even true virtue. He rightly declares it immediately to be dry, because no grace of true virtue grows green within; rather, it is lamented as having become like wood. Hence it happens that some, when corrected by their neighbors, remain as insensible as wood and, alienated from every greenness of grace, dry up inwardly.

This has also often happened to those who seek higher things while inwardly, as though they possessed good works, secretly serve vices. Outwardly they shine whiter than snow and brighter than milk; but their conscience has been blackened by vices, because they have inwardly lost all the warmth and ardor of God.

They were rightly not recognized by the more discerning in the streets, because, while they walk inwardly along the broad and pleasure-filled way of life, they are not recognized as being what they pretend to be. They are found to be dry, without the grace of the Holy Spirit; and when they are rebuked or reproved by their own people, they are found to be as insensible as wood, the more so the drier they are inwardly, and are proved to sin the more secretly.

They therefore disdain to appear other than what they pretend to be. Hence they boast that they are “redder than ancient ivory,” that is, better than the holy elect who preceded them, and more beautiful than those among them who already lead a heavenly life. Having long been hardened in the arrogance of shamelessness, they become inwardly insensible, dried up like wood.

Consequently, they are sometimes corrected neither by blows, nor by reproofs, nor by threats of any kind, nor by any words of persuasion or flattery; instead, they continually become worse.

The two verses also fit well the conduct of those who, under hypocrisy, boast that they possess more honorable virtues and outstanding works of merit. While outwardly they display works of their own that are “more beautiful than sapphire,” inwardly all the ornaments of their character lie there both blacker than coals and dead. Their virtue has dried up, and, like wood, everything belonging to them lies rotten and fruitless. The soul deceived by false colors cannot perceive how insensibly it lies inwardly cut off from God.

Hence it follows:

### TETH

“It was better for those slain by the sword than for those killed by famine, because they wasted away, exhausted by the barrenness of the earth.”

This verse plainly applies in the fullest sense to the Jews during that final siege. Those slain by the sword are shown to have suffered the lighter fate, since they endured the loss of life in a moment, beneath the blow of the sword, whereas those killed by famine endured death through prolonged and harsher torments. Afflicted by various punishments, they wasted away from thirst and were consumed by every kind of suffering.

The Church of Christ, however, judges those slain by the sword of God’s word happier than those killed by famine, because the former are killed in order to live, while the latter are consumed through the demands of their sins so that they may perish. Hence the Apostle asks us to take up the armor of God and says: “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians VI). By this sword the saints and elect of God are rightly slain, so that they may die to the world and live to God.

But because God’s sword is foreshadowed in many places with different meanings, that sword must be chosen by which death is killed, so that life may follow—not the one that cuts off life eternally, so that the soul may die. Hence the Lord says in the Canticle: “My sword has become drunk in heaven” (Genesis III). The whirling and flaming sword placed before Paradise to guard the way to the tree of life is also mentioned. Likewise, through the prophet, the Lord’s blade is said to be well polished and sharpened, on account of the violence of its slaughter: “How long,” he says, “will you not return to your sheath?”

It is also believed that a sword pierced Mary’s soul, when the Lord said: “And your own soul a sword will pierce” (Luke II). For plainly the sword of the Passion signifies Christ’s sorrow, and no believer doubts that Mary’s soul was wounded by it during the Passion.

The word of God, therefore, is a sweet and greatly desirable sword, by which a person is more rightly killed in order to live than if he lived a life by which he would perish. For this reason the Church of Christ rejoices more over those killed in this way than if they had perished from famine, being deprived of hearing the word of God.

It also mourns those whom it knows to have been consumed by famine or thirst because of the earth’s barrenness, since no death can be worse than that by which the soul is killed. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “I will send among them not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos VIII).

Whoever is killed by this famine will die an eternal death, because, as Truth itself says: “Man does not live by bread alone.” The complete human being consists of two substances, namely soul and flesh. Just as the flesh cannot live without food and drink, so the soul cannot live without the bread of God’s word and spiritual drink.

Therefore we also ask daily in the Lord’s Prayer: “Give us today our daily bread.” By “bread,” not only this daily nourishment is understood, but also that bread which descended from heaven, as well as that which the hungry and thirsty continually receive from the sacred Scriptures. “Blessed,” says the Evangelist, “are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew V).

Those who are killed by such starvation are rightly mourned as dead and consumed because of the barrenness of the earth. The barrenness of the earth is the unfruitfulness of the Church, when teachers fail and the Church itself is not drenched by the rains of God’s words. Hence it is clear that the fault of priests and negligence in teaching become the death and destruction of the people.

Morally, it is better to be slain by the sword of the word, so that the outward senses may not defend themselves and the soul may already live inwardly as though dead, than to perish, having gathered virtues but lacking the nourishment of divine love, as though from famine and thirst. The barrenness of virtues is the deprivation of charity; when the soul is barren of it, all the remaining virtues waste away from famine and thirst.

For this reason Job’s seven sons invited their three sisters to each of their banquets, so that they might be refreshed in their houses: for faith, hope, and charity are nourished by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Thus each of the gifts of the Holy Spirit rightly prepares a banquet in its own house, so that from them all there may be one house.

That house Christ, who is Wisdom, builds; it is supported by seven columns so that it may not fall, and nourished by seven gifts so that it may not perish. Otherwise, however many gifts of virtue there may be in the soul, unless they are nourished by those seven gifts of the Holy Spirit through which charity is poured into our hearts, they surely fail from famine and thirst because of the barrenness of the earth.

Therefore we should pray with the prophet: “That our soul may be filled as with fat and richness” (Psalm LXII).

### JOD

“The hands of women cooked their own children as though out of compassion; they became their food in the destruction of the daughter of my people.”

The letter JOD follows, and it is interpreted as “beginning” or “desolation.” The beginning of desolation was then threatening the Jews, when their women, seeing their children consumed by famine and thirst, cooked them as food, as though out of compassion.

No one who has read the histories can doubt that they did this, especially during that siege which, according to Josephus, is recorded as having occurred under Titus and Vespasian.

In the Church of Christ, those who, as though out of compassion, cook their children are likewise people elevated to the height of authority who burn the souls of their offspring with the flame of zeal and envy. They wish to appear righteous through threats, and by tyrannical power they torture those whom, as though out of compassion, they cook in the fire of zeal.

They too, according to the Apostle, have zeal for God—but only in this respect, “not according to knowledge” (Romans X). Their food is truly a cooking, when they burn them not only through cruel domination, as though on behalf of justice, but also when they gnaw at their weak and carnal life with their teeth.

All these things are done in the destruction of the Church, which is the daughter of God’s people—that is, of the apostles and saints—by those who burn souls with tyrannical harassment, whether through ecclesiastical authority or through secular office. Inflamed by their own desires, they consume their children or subjects, whom they ought to have nourished with the milk of instruction, through the scorching of wicked affliction.

Thus, tropologically, the virtues of hypocrites produce their conceptions in the soul when, pretending to act out of compassion, they kill virtues while still in their tender conception, through love of praise or the desire for favor; and they cook them as their food when they seek not future but present-life profits, and when they feed on the praises of their virtues, eating, as it were, their own children, born and cooked by the scorching of favor.

They are rightly said to have been women and to have acted in this way, because if they did not pursue womanly things in the mind of feigned virtue, they would not bring conceptions of the soul, well formed for life, into the death of empty praise.

Hence it follows:

### CAPH

“The Lord has completed his fury; he has poured out the anger of his wrath, and he has kindled a fire in Zion and devoured its foundations.”

The Lord then completed his fury against Jerusalem when its wickedness was complete, just as the sins of the Amorites were complete when they were destroyed. He poured out the anger of his wrath when Jerusalem itself spread into every crime of vice; and he devoured its foundations when it refused to receive the foundation, which is Christ.

It rejected that precious, cornerstone stone, founded as the foundation of our entire structure. When Christ saw that same wretched Jerusalem, he wept over it, saying that in it no stone would be left upon stone (Matthew XXIV), along with the other things that are read there.

As for us, which is greatly to be lamented, we see almost everything fulfilled over our Jerusalem that the prophet wept over irreparably for his own people with abundant tears. Otherwise, if the Lord’s fury had not been completed, contention poured out upon our rulers would not exist—contention which, as we see, makes them wander in a trackless place and not on the road, because of the anger of God’s wrath.

Wickedness, when completed, completed God’s fury, because punishment follows according to the measure of sins. For all these things that we see are already the punishment of sin. Otherwise, if our crimes had not been completed, the Lord would not have completed his fury.

If this seems not yet complete to anyone, let him observe those who are in filth, becoming still more filthy. Thus he will be able to see and mourn that such things arise from the completion of divine fury.

For “a fire has been kindled in Zion”—not that fire which descended from heaven upon the apostles, but the fire that consumed Job’s sheep and servants. God has a different fire, which he sends forth from his treasuries according to the manner of his dispensation; its fire is in Zion, and its furnace in Jerusalem. With this fire he inflames some in order to instruct them, and burns others in order to consume them.

When he has kindled them, he also tears away their entire foundation. If anyone builds upon that foundation wood, straw, hay, tin, and lead, he will suffer loss, because fire will test each person’s work. Their foundations are then overthrown when sound and true faith is destroyed in the heart by wicked and perverse works.

Since we already see such things in ourselves, there is no need to turn our eyes aside with the prophet toward the miseries of the Jews. Rather, it is more fitting now to mourn our own calamities, when the fire of our desires has been kindled; when, as I have said, the devouring flame of intrigues and seditions ravages nearly everyone; when, in divine matters and in the resources entrusted to God, Babylon’s pot, kindled from the face of the north, and the furnace of the Chaldeans, heated sevenfold, seize everything and burn all whom they find among the Chaldeans.

Just as our predecessors were kindled by the fire of divine love—those who gave these things to God and enriched the holy Church of Christ with their resources—so those who now devour and plunder them are proved to have been kindled by a foreign fire. They plunder the patrimony of the poor and are therefore punished as guilty in the manner of murderers, since, according to Scripture, one who takes away their substance is like one who slaughters a son in the presence of his father.

It is therefore greatly to be feared that this fury will not cease until God’s anger and wrath are completed and it devours even the foundations of the kingdom.

Tropologically, there is no doubt that all the foundations of hypocrites or heretics are devoured by the fire of God’s fury, because the fire of indignation already burns in their minds and the Lord’s fury has been completed against them. Hence Job says: “I saw a fool taking root, but immediately I cursed his beauty” (Job V).

What, then, is proved more wicked than the folly of hypocrites? Though they seem to stand with their own works, as though with a firm root, they are nevertheless accursed and rejected before God from the beginning of the beauty or splendor of their virtues. Their hearts are inflamed by empty praises and burned up by the favors of flatterers.

For all these things, how fittingly the following comes next:

### LAMEI

“The kings of the earth and all the inhabitants of the world did not believe that an enemy and foe would enter the gates of Jerusalem.”

According to the literal sense, as long as this city was surrounded by God’s help and fortified by the protection of angels—when judgment and justice were in it, and it was filled with the goods of virtues—no king or inhabitant of the world could believe that an enemy or foe would enter it. For the Lord had strengthened the bars of its gates and made its boundary peace.

But when they themselves turned away from him, by whose favor they had been protected, all God’s protection withdrew from them, and they became prey among their enemies. So also our Church is now, according to the mystical senses, plundered here and there by enemies, so to speak.

Who could ever have believed, or who could ever have imagined, in our regions that, after time had passed, we would see, grieve over, mourn, and greatly fear all the things that have occurred? Even today we fear no less that pirates gathered from widely diverse households might reach the borders of Paris and burn the churches of Christ here and there along the coast.

Who, I ask, could ever have believed that bandits of mixed nations would dare such things? Or who could have imagined that so glorious a kingdom, so fortified, so extensive, so populous, and so strong should be humbled or disgraced by the filth of such men?

I do not even speak of their carrying away great revenues, plundering spoils, or leading captives away. Rather, who could believe that such contemptible men would dare approach our borders? I confess that, not long ago—or so I think—none of the kings of the earth would have considered this, nor could any inhabitant of our world have heard that our Paris would be entered by an enemy.

Therefore, even if there is nothing here for me to explain, there is nevertheless something to mourn and lament, since, as the following verse indicates, all these things happened because of the sins of the people. And because of the iniquities of priests and rulers, such evils increase on every side: for they have long since perverted, in our midst, so to speak, the judgments of the just, and blood has touched blood. Thus, all polluted, they have now filled everything with their deceits and frauds.

These verses should therefore be interpreted more through lamentation and tears than unfolded through any verbal exposition of propositions. Nor should a threefold sense be sought, when the fall and ruin of us all is one. The sorrow of the heart must accordingly be sought in such howls and groans, so that, with the prophet, we may mourn the evils we have committed, since God’s sword is flashing and hangs over our necks.

Already the axe has been placed at the roots of the trees, because our mind is fruitless. Thus the sword of the Barbarians has raged, drawn from the sheath of the Lord, while we miserable people live numbly amid such monstrous evils of the Barbarians, amid such wars of cruel citizens, amid the spoils of plunderers, amid seditions and frauds—and yet each day we blaze up toward greater evils of crime.

For this reason, as though spoken concerning us, the voice of the mourning prophet follows.

### NUN

“The blind wandered in the streets, polluted with blood. And since they could not enter,” he says, “they held onto their torn garments.”

The meaning is clear: the scribes and Pharisees, blind, wandered in their streets; and when they were stained with the blood of human slaughter, perhaps restrained by shame, they refrained from entering the temple. Because they had poured out the blood of the righteous in the midst of Jerusalem, they walked polluted through the street and kept away from the temple—not mourning their own sins, but flattering themselves as they wantonly wandered through the streets.

They wandered like blind men, thinking that merely delaying the passage of time purified them if they refrained from the temple. They boasted of themselves as though they possessed strong works of every kind, and humility might be displayed; and when they could not enter, they held onto their torn garments.

“Torn garments” are pieces of old clothing, or curls of ripped cloth. Wearing these, they held onto one another like blind people following one another, so that one might be joined to another; under this false humility, the priests who had poured out the blood of the righteous and of the prophet might appease the people.

### MEM

“Because of the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests, who poured out the blood of the righteous in her midst.”

For this reason our Jerusalem mourns more abundantly with the prophet for her priests and teachers, who pour out the blood of the righteous in the midst of the Churches of God—people who could indeed have been righteous if they had not perished through their negligence.

Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel: “If you do not announce to the wicked all his iniquities, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel XVIII). Why, then, is the blood of the wicked required from the priest’s hand, unless because through his fault the wicked person’s blood—that is, his sin—is poured out even unto death?

Sometimes even those who seemed righteous descend all the way to the earth through their example and teaching of perversity, and, polluted by the more abundant blood of sin poured out, they perish.

Those priests and prophets, blind, wandered in the streets when, seizing the broad and spacious way of the present age, they refused to enter the narrow way of the Gospel that leads to the temple of the heavenly homeland. Polluted by the defilements of their sins, they neither entered themselves nor permitted others to enter.

This is what he means by saying that they “poured out the blood of the righteous in her midst”—that is, in the midst of the Church, which is the true Jerusalem and the mother of us all. In her midst the blind, wandering, pour out the blood of the righteous when, through the wicked examples of their lives, they invite them more readily to sin, and thus pour it out more criminally.

When they can no longer enter that temple of the true God, polluted by their own contagions, they hold onto their torn garments—that is, their rent and mangled old life, wandering about like blind people.

The priests of Christ hold onto one another’s torn garments, namely their old and defiled life, so that the Gospel saying may be proved true: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matthew XV).

This is what the prophet laments—or rather, the chorus of all the elect—especially in the present time, when all, thus blinded, walk along the broad and spacious way and hold onto one another’s torn garments, polluted with blood. They cannot grasp the ways of life, nor free themselves from the winding paths of their own ways.

They therefore hold onto one another’s torn garments like blind people following one another, because they do not wish to follow Christ as leader. Thus, clothed in the oldness of their sins, they follow a rent and disrupted life.

He also laments the blindness of heretics, who, abandoning the straight path of the Scriptures and the rule of the catholic faith, chose the breadth of error, polluted by the blood of those whose souls they kill through their errors. Since they cannot—or rather, will not—enter the catholic Church, they hold onto one another’s torn garments, namely the divisions of Scripture or the manglings that they themselves have torn apart through their deceit.

Thus, morally, the chorus of virtues, having lost prudence, walks inwardly blinded by its multitude. They walk like blind people through the streets along the way of empty desire, because they lack the light that is Christ. Unable to hold to the way and to Christ himself, they are always diffused outside themselves for the sake of empty favor; they hold onto one another’s torn garments of old age and cannot complete the ways of virtue, because they are clothed in the oldness of vices. Their polluted mind and conscience continually pursue the broadest streets of empty praise.

Concerning such people it is rightly added:

### SAMECH

“Depart, polluted ones,” they cried to them; “depart, go away, do not touch.” They quarreled and, being agitated, said among the nations: “He will no longer continue to dwell among them.”

Perhaps, by way of amplification, the prophet laments the monstrous crimes of the Jews: they had been so disfigured by vices and sins that their enemies and adversaries unexpectedly entered the gates of Jerusalem, overwhelmed them, and cried out in reproach: “Depart, polluted by your crimes; depart from God’s sanctuary, defiled by the many and immense contagions of your sins.”

Then the prophet, mourning, relates what the wicked Jews and their enemies did: “They quarreled,” he says, “and were agitated.” The former were agitated toward quarrels, the latter toward tears and contrition of heart; the former so that they might heap on still greater reproaches and blasphemies, the latter toward mourning and the shame of dreadful calamity.

“And they said among the nations: ‘He will no longer continue to dwell among them, their God.’” The phrase “among the nations” can therefore be referred to both sides. The sense may be that they said this among the nations during the captivity, or certainly: “He will no longer continue among the nations to dwell in them,” among whom they also abandoned the true and living God and worshiped idols.

But they themselves also, as the following verse suggests, may have quarreled among themselves because the face of the Lord divided them. Polluted with the blood of their sins, they may have cried to others polluted in the same way: “Depart!” Such is the custom of those who wish to appear righteous and despise the rest.

Accordingly, quarrels often occur among them. The Church of Christ, seeing such things among her members, mourns them as though they were profane: the former because, blind and polluted, they cannot enter the Church of the living God or participate in the sacred mysteries, perhaps having been brought under penance; the latter because, though polluted themselves, they despise others as though out of zeal for God.

When such people desire to appear righteous, though they cannot yet be openly exposed, and when they openly offend against others who have already fallen and been corrected, or who are still falling, they look down on them with an uplifted brow and rebuke them. What else do they seem to be doing than crying out to them: “Depart from us and from the sacraments of God, which we rightly enjoy. Depart from us and go away to those whose companions you are. Do not touch the holy things of God, you who are unworthy”?

We ourselves often experience such quarrels among us, when some, wickedly puffed up, conceal themselves in their own frauds; when, always seeking to appear holier, they not only despise some who have been publicly exposed or have confessed, but also disparage those who are holier, as though they were plagues of the Church, and gnaw at them.

What else do such people do daily than declare that everyone is unclean and polluted, merely to commend themselves as righteous and reproach the others? The Apostle may perhaps refer to such a cry when he says: “Let all anger and indignation, clamor, and blasphemy be taken away from you, with all malice” (Ephesians IV).

Such a cry arises only from anger or indignation of heart, from the arrogance of pride, or certainly from some form of malice. Therefore how beautifully he says: “Let it be taken away from you with all malice.” Otherwise, when we correct, rebuke, or reproach our neighbors outwardly, unless malice is first removed from us inwardly, we produce a cry.

Hence quarrels and disputes so often arise among neighbors because some of their rebukes and corrections come from the malice of wicked attack, and not from the love of pure affection exercised with discernment.

Therefore he pointedly says: “They quarreled and were agitated”—agitated because they had quarreled, and quarreling because they had been agitated. Otherwise they would not be agitated unless they had first been inwardly stirred toward quarrels, nor would they quarrel with one another unless they had first been agitated.

They were agitated because they did not stand in the one who is always the same and who is quarrelled with. They first lost peace inwardly and the love of charity. Hence it is rightly said of such among the nations: “He will no longer continue to dwell in them, their God,” because where peace and concord are not present, God cannot be. “His place was made in peace,” and his dwelling is in the watchtower of sacred contemplation.

“Among the nations” means, on our account, as the Apostle says, that the name of God is blasphemed. Such is the inflation of the wicked, such the quarrels of the proud, and such the mutual contempt and rejection of the reprobate, as well as of heretics against the catholic faith—especially the Donatists and those who call themselves Cathari.

These people say to you: “Depart from us, for we alone are clean, while you are polluted. Depart and go away; do not touch us, lest we perhaps be defiled by you.”

The heretics themselves also quarrel among one another as they attack one another with different heresies. They are agitated because they refused to stand in the right faith. They moved their feet from the east until they came into the plain of their confusion, that is, Babel, where, building a tower of pride, they deserved to receive the division of languages.

For this reason the following appropriately comes next:

### AIN
The face of the Lord divided them; he will not add that he should look upon them. And therefore this is entirely fitting, because they too, as follows, did not blush before the faces of the priests; indeed, in their priests they despised God. And because they did not reverence the face of the Lord in them, the very face of the Lord divided them, so that they might receive the retribution of their condemnation in return. For, as it is sung in the Psalm, because the faithless Jews did not fear the Lord, he stretched out his hand in requital.

Nor, when they had previously been corrected by many scourges of affliction, were they converted so as to receive Christ, who had been promised in the Law. Rather, they defiled his covenant when they rejected the one who had been proclaimed in the covenant of the Law for salvation. And therefore, because they rejected him, and did not blush before the faces of the priests and prophets, they were deservedly divided from the anger of his countenance; and this is what it means to say, “The face of the Lord divided them.” He divided them from the anger of his countenance by the final overthrow of their city, when he left part of them in unbelief, placing them with the faithless, and scattered them throughout all the kingdoms of the earth. But another part, as Scripture testifies (Luke XII), Christ received into the holy faith.

The face of God is, of course, the same as his countenance. But the anger that is often shown in the countenance or face divided them, because they provoked the most gentle God to anger when they refused to receive repentance for their evil deeds. Moreover, Christ’s Church mourns those irreparably who, rejecting the fear of God, do not blush before the faces of the priests within that same Church. For now, as their offenses have increased, the face of the Lord and the anger of his countenance have divided them from those who were foreknown and predestined for life: “He will not add that he should look upon them.”

And one must note how terrible it is to despise the priests of Christ, not to reverence them in their presence, and not to cease from evil deeds when they admonish us. This is what it means not to blush before their faces. Hence the Lord himself says of them: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X). Certainly, not to hear is not to obey; not to obey is to despise; and to despise is not to blush. Therefore, what follows is exceedingly dreadful: “He will not add that he should look upon them.” For those upon whom he does not look are not converted, and those who are not converted are certainly condemned, since the face of the Lord has divided them from his saints.

For this reason also, lest Peter should be divided from the anger of his countenance, the Lord looked upon him; and because he looked upon him, Peter, having been converted, wept bitterly. Thus, restored to the body of the Church, he deserved to hear: “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (Matthew XXVI).

Therefore, I wish our people to understand how terrible it is not to blush before the faces of priests, or of those whom they have received in Christ’s place, lest perhaps the offended Lord should not add that they be converted and that he look upon them.

Now what else does such a division signify except what will occur in the judgment of that final examination, when the faithless and wicked will be divided from the saints, the faithful, and the just? Then the straw destined to burn will, by the anger of God’s countenance, be separated from the grains of wheat, so that the wheat may be gathered into God’s granary, while the straw is given to unquenchable fire.

But when it is said that the face of God divided them, what else does this mean except that the anger of God separated them from God’s good, just, and chosen ones? Anger, or face, is used in place of retribution, since the same Lord judges all things with tranquility. His face judges and orders everything immutably and determines each matter calmly. But because they despised the faces of the priests and did not show mercy to the old, the face of the Lord rightly divided them.

It should also be noted that above he mourned those same priests as though they were murderers, saying: “Because of the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests, the enemy and adversary entered Jerusalem.” From this it is clear that, even if they are evil, they must not be despised. Rather, the one whose priests they are, and in whose name and person they come, must be revered and worshiped in them.

They themselves indeed wander blind through the streets, polluted with blood; but for that reason they are not to be trampled upon by the people, nor immediately despised in their office without prejudice. For from this arise quarrels and contempt for the Christian religion; from this, indignation and shouting on every side; from this, blasphemies and contempt. The preceding verse lamented this with deep grief when they cried out: “Depart, you polluted; depart! Go away, and do not touch us.”

It is therefore evident that wherever our religion is thus brought into confusion, there the anger of God rages, and no order is preserved. On one side and the other, these men applaud themselves under the appearance of hypocrites; those either defile themselves with public crimes or hide themselves badly beneath the sloth of torpor. All of them frequently quarrel with one another, because the face of the Lord has divided them from the saints and the faithful, even if they appear bodily to move about within them.

Meanwhile, the diversity of heretics is also indicated. They attack one another with the falsehoods of their own errors because, already condemned on account of the punishment of sin, they refuse to receive the sound teaching of Christ. They are divided from one another because of the distinctive character of their perverse invention, and therefore they can agree neither with themselves nor with any Catholic. Thus they do not blush before the faces of those who confess sound doctrine, nor do they show mercy to the old.

Since God’s vengeance divided such people because of their sins, not only from all the orthodox but also from one another, he no longer adds that he should have mercy or look upon them, just as he is said not to have looked upon Cain the fratricide or upon his offerings (Genesis IV).

All these quarrels therefore moved them from the position of right faith and drove them to every kind of vanity, so that they might think proudly. On their account the voice of the lamenting prophet appropriately continues:

## PHE

While we still remained, our eyes failed, looking in vain for our help, when we looked toward a nation that could not save us.

Here, according to the historical sense, the prophet laments the error of the wretched nation: they sought the help of Egypt and Pharaoh more eagerly than the help of God. Although they appeared still to be standing, they had already been almost consumed, and their eyes, as they looked toward them, had wasted away while looking toward a nation that could save neither itself nor them.

Jeremiah himself explains this at much greater length above, although here the prophet laments it more sharply and more grievously. Thus, within the Church, this is also the voice of those who lament, who for a long time soothe themselves with vain hopes and occupy themselves with worldly affairs. When they are touched by the weakness of death or by some temptation, they discover that they are not only naked but also blind, and they groan:

“While we still remained, our eyes failed, looking in vain for our help.”

In a certain sense, therefore, whoever remains in the flesh still stands, if he holds the faith, even though without works. But when he pursues the vanities of the world, touched by some affliction, he discovers that his eyes have failed—those eyes which he had fixed upon the perishable and fleeting things of the world—and that he had sought vain help. For the more intensely he had directed his heart toward obtaining those things, the more he had withered inwardly, away from the inner light and grace.

Thus, returning wisely to himself and groaning, he proves that what he had fixed his eyes upon in order to seek it was vain. And because, often through desire for acquired possessions, people entrust all their hope to the rich and powerful of the world, so that through them they may obtain more eagerly what they covet, it appropriately follows:

“When we looked attentively toward a nation that could not save us.”

Concerning this nation—that is, the rich—the prophet says: “Howl, you wretched ones, and weep over the miseries that will come upon you.” When attention is directed toward them and hope is placed in them for the help of salvation, what can follow but the lamentation of miseries, since they can save neither themselves nor others?

The prophet says: “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in man and makes flesh his arm, so that his heart departs from the Lord.”

This is also fittingly understood of heretics and of those who seek their vain help, because their eyes, examining vanities and the false utterances of Scripture, waste away and fail more and more. And when their hearers attend more carefully to a nation that cannot save, they raise their eyes in vain.

Therefore, from the person of those who grieve and of their nations, the following appropriately continues:

## SADE

Our footsteps slipped on the way through our streets; our end drew near; our days were completed, because our end came.

No one doubts that these lamentations suit the Jews, when each of them, at the point of death, turned over in his mind the deeds he had done. The prophet also takes upon himself the weeping and lamentations of them all, because the bitter and unexpected evils of captivity suddenly overtook them, demanded by the crimes of their nation.

This is no less rightly lamented concerning the Church of Christ, whenever we see those who take hold of the broad and spacious way of the world. The Church laments the wantonness of those who pursue the slippery path of vices and have not yet fixed their steps firmly upon the rock, which is Christ. For them she mourns and groans:

“Our footsteps slipped on the way through our streets.”

Otherwise, if they had not sought the ways of the streets, their feet would not have slipped from the straight path. Hence the Lord says: “Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city; compel the poor and the weak to enter, so that my house may be filled” (Luke XIV).

From this the meaning is clear: those who still hold to the broad and spacious way are, before the eyes of the inner Judge, outside, even if they appear to enter bodily. Outside the house that is the Church of Christ, they slip through wantonness. For the ways of the streets are slippery and downhill.

Therefore David sings in gladness: “He set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps” (Psalm XXXIX). And elsewhere: “He made my feet like those of deer and set me upon high places” (Psalm XVII).

But the broad way of the streets is foul, full of mud and filth. Whoever walks upon it proceeds not without the fall of his own ruin. Those whose feet are made firm upon the rock walk along the straight road, like the feet of deer. They fear none of the serpents’ poisons while they always hasten toward steep and lofty places.

They do not wish to avoid slippery footsteps or to place any hope in the uncertainty of riches or in the passing world. Rather, with the prophet they consider themselves blessed because they do not attend to vanities and do not pursue the false insanities of fools.

When such people refuse to foresee how quickly the things they love will slip away, they suddenly mourn that the end of life has drawn near, when they realize unexpectedly that the things they held were false. Hence they lament with greater fear:

“Our end drew near; our days were completed, because our end came.”

Completion is not always used in a good sense, as you find where it is said that the sins of the Amorites had not yet been completed (Genesis XV). Their completion was the end of those who had filled up their measure, and their extermination. So also with these, concerning whom the prophet, speaking in their person, mourns more bitterly that such things happened.

For the days are lamented as completed, since they had filled up the crimes and the measure of their fathers. When those days of sinning have been completed, the end comes. First it draws near while the axe, placed at the root, still hangs suspended in the hand. But when the crimes of offenses have been completed, the days are completed, because the end of eternal retribution has arrived.

Meanwhile, this is also the voice of heretics when they belatedly understand how slippery their footsteps have been in the sacred Scriptures, and how broad a way they have taken. They refuse to hold to the rules of the Catholic Fathers or to walk with straight steps along the way that is Christ. Instead, each of them bends the same Scriptures of God away from the straight path and spreads them more broadly along the roads of his own perversity.

And because they do not wish to walk within the boundaries prescribed by the Fathers or along the well-trodden path of the Scriptures, their footsteps slipped on the way through the streets. They pursued a broad and sprawling doctrine of disputation and corrupted not only the utterances of the holy Scriptures but even those of the philosophers.

Therefore, holding to slippery paths, they fell into death, and the end came with all the confusion and destruction of their condemnation. Hence it follows:

## COPH

Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven; they pursued us over the mountains; in the wilderness they lay in ambush for us.

These words are spoken hyperbolically of the Jews, just as Jonathan and Saul are praised in David’s lament as having been swifter than eagles.

But because the prophet, as we have said, takes upon himself the lamentations, persons, and voices of all, he mourns the persecutions of the Church. Her persecutors are rightly lamented as swifter than the eagles of heaven, because unclean spirits become swifter than holy preachers in tearing apart and devouring, through the wickedness of their deceit and the agility of their nature.

The Church has her own eagles chosen for her service, concerning whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Where the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Luke XVII). For wherever Christ’s passion is celebrated and his body is sacrificed for our salvation, there the eagles of heaven gather and come as though to food, so that from the death of his flesh they may receive life and the nourishment of perpetual satisfaction.

Accordingly, the prophet mourns, and the Church of Christ also mourns, because our enemies—the powers of the air and the unclean spirits—are swifter than we are, since there is no power upon earth that can be compared with them. Their power and violent speed in persecuting are therefore lamented: they move around and rage with greater speed, not only through their agents but even by themselves, seeking violently to snatch from the Church those whom they may devour.

“They pursued us over the mountains,” because, when we are raised to the higher summits of the ecclesiastical order, we provoke them more fiercely to persecute us. Although we appear to be placed upon the watchtowers of apostolic eminence, as though upon a mountain, we must not therefore consider ourselves secure. They persecute more forcefully those whom they see raised above the mountains for the purpose of observing the others more diligently and leading them to the heights of virtue.

“In the wilderness,” he says, “they lay in ambush for us.”

By the wilderness is signified the life of those who either live under monastic discipline or, tested for a long time, lead an eremitical life. These are the two orders in the Church that, contending more intently against invisible enemies in the struggle, wage war against them more swiftly and more strongly through persecution: the former openly, as though fighting upon the mountains; the latter, who lead a more withdrawn life, by lying in ambush.

Both are called eagles of heaven because they pursue heavenly and lofty things. But what must be lamented more grievously is that the enemies are often found to be swifter in deceiving them than they are in taking precautions or resisting.

Thus, with the prophet, Christ’s Church sometimes mourns that her enemies and adversaries are swifter than her chosen ones, who, having trampled upon all earthly things, dwell among heavenly realities. As a result, they sometimes deceive many—not only from the common people as a whole, but even from those who are pastors or who have chosen a life of perfect repose.

Hence, far above, the same prophet laments greatly, saying:

“My people became a lost flock; their shepherds led them astray and caused them to wander in the mountains; they passed from mountain to hill and forgot their resting place.”

Here he laments not only the seduction of heretics but also that of those who, by their evil examples, deceive the souls of their subjects within the Church. They cause them to pass from mountain to hill when, through the arrogance of pride, they strive to obtain offices and the power of worldly glory.

Heretics likewise pass from mountain to hill when they leap from one doctrine of their perversity to another, always wandering and never stable. Therefore the Lord’s flock has become lost, because those same heretics are often swifter in disputation than the eagles of heaven—that is, than the teachers of the Church and the leaders of the people whom they persecute—against the teaching of the apostles and of all the holy elect.

They lie in ambush for those who pursue the leisure of a more withdrawn life, using deceits, and they deceive them with the utterances of their cunning. The Church of Christ rightly laments all of them in one lament, because she is weakened in all these respects and, under such delusions, is hampered as though by the wing-beats of birds.

Hence we are pressed by such evils no less in secret than in public. In secret, indeed, they are active in the day; in public, persecution rages against the athletes of Christ over the mountains, so that it may destroy them and then, once they have been cast down, lay the people low more cruelly.

Hence also the Lord says through the prophet: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zechariah XIII). When he was struck, all the apostles fled. And from this comes what follows:

## RES

Christ the Lord, the breath of our mouth, has been seized in our sins; to him we said among the nations: “Under your shadow we shall live.”

The Jews understand this to have been said of Josiah: that the most just king was seized for death not because of his own sins but because of the sins of the people, in whom they had placed all their hope, even though they had come among the nations.

But this interpretation does not seem to stand concerning him, since he was not the breath of their mouth, nor could they finally have lived among the nations after being transferred under his shadow. Rather, whether they wish it or not, the passage must be understood of Christ: “Christ the Lord, the breath of our mouth, has been seized in our sins.”

From this it is plainly indicated that not only his divinity but also his humanity was seized under one and the same person. “The breath,” he says, “of our mouth is the Lord Christ.” When he says, “the breath of our mouth,” his divinity is declared; but when he says, “Christ the Lord,” humanity is plainly expressed. For “Spirit” is rightly understood as God, the whole Trinity, although in this passage it is understood specifically as the Word of the Father.

Hence Moses says in Deuteronomy: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.” This is to say: “The Spirit of our mouth and of our heart, God, is near,” because he fills and contains all things. In him, according to the Apostle, “we live and move and have our being.”

Therefore holy David, when he wished to distinguish the Trinity in its persons, prayed: “Renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm L), by which the Son is indicated; and then: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me,” when the person of the Holy Spirit is disclosed. But when he desires finally to be confirmed by the principal Spirit, the distinct property of the Father is manifested. Nevertheless, the whole Trinity is rightly proclaimed as Spirit and God.

In this passage, then, “the breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord,” is said, in a Catholic sense, to have been seized, because in one and the same person the divinity of the Word and the humanity are held together. Hence the incomprehensible is rightly believed to have been comprehended, and the uncontainable to have been seized, along with many other things that are spoken simultaneously of God and man under the one person of Christ.

But how fittingly is Christ the Lord called “the breath of our mouth”? The one whom inwardly we taste in our heart through faith, we confess with our mouth, so that he may be righteousness for us inwardly and our confession may be for salvation outwardly.

The mouth breathes in and breathes out, so that, through the infusion of grace, what is drawn inward may be breathed outward in a confession that leads to progress. Yet this is the voice of those who say: “Christ the Lord is the breath of our mouth.” They have nothing else in their mouth except the word of truth, which is Christ, and nothing else in their heart, since “the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart.” Thus this is the groaning and wailing of the saints:

“Christ the Lord, the breath of our mouth, has been seized in our sins.”

For he was seized and died for all, so that he might erase the sins of all—not for his own sins, since he bore no trace of wrongdoing, but for ours and in our sins he was held, so that he might erase them and remove the record of sins that stood against us.

Nor should one believe that so great a prophet is speaking of that aerial spirit or breath which we draw from the air below us when we inhale it, or which we give back when we exhale it. He is speaking of the Spirit who is God the Word, whom we believe in our heart for righteousness but confess with our mouth for salvation.

Otherwise, the breath of our mouth, or that aerial spirit, is neither Lord nor Christ; it is neither seized nor held when it is rejected. I do not say “for sins,” but not even for any use can it be understood as anything other than the one who is Christ in two substances. Thus the breath of our mouth—that is, the Word of the Father and the man Christ the Lord, one and the same God—was seized for the sins of all. To him we rightly said: “Under your shadow we shall live among the nations.”

Therefore we too, together with the prophet, await the grace of the promised adoption and groan within ourselves, saying: “Christ the Lord, the breath of our mouth, has been seized in our sins.”

And we say this worthily when we carry nothing else in our heart or mouth, but everything that we convey within the inner person is either him or from him, and everything we bring forth with our mouth is from him and directed toward him. In this way the inner person is made alive and nourished, and thus, being animated, is continually renewed.

He is made alive daily in the one who is in him, and the one who is in him is nourished. Through faith Christ is embraced and brought forth inwardly and outwardly. Just as this aerial breath has from that by which it is seized the fact that it breathes again toward it, and thus the outer person is restored to life in order to breathe, so our inner person must possess by faith the Spirit who is God, received inwardly in the heart, so that from him, through him, and in him it may live. By living, it must breathe toward him with all its desires and pour out all its inmost thoughts toward him and before him.

Such a person can rightly say: “Christ the Lord, the breath of our mouth, has been seized in our sins.”

He was therefore seized in our sins so that he might drive sins out from us and enter within us, so that God the Spirit might make us alive among those whom he possesses, and, having made us alive, possess us always, allowing us to breathe from him, in him, and toward him.

Finally, restored inwardly by this Spirit, let us say with the prophet: “Under your shadow we shall live among the nations.” For he is the expectation of the nations and their Savior; he is the seed of Abraham, in whom all the nations of the earth will be blessed.

To him the prophet had rightly spoken in his heart and confessed with his mouth: “Under your shadow we shall live among the nations.” For Christ the Lord was to come in the flesh, and the nations, receiving him as king and God, would thereafter be saved and rest with the saints under his shadow. This is what it means to say: “Under your shadow we shall live among the nations.”

This is not spoken of the present or the past, but of the future. It is as though he were saying: “We shall then live better with those nations when the promised Spirit, Christ the Lord, the breath of our mouth, comes—he who was seized in our sins, in which we were dead—and makes our mortal bodies alive through his Spirit dwelling in us, and removes the record of sin that stood against us.”

Elsewhere David says: “Under the shadow of your wings protect me from the face of the wicked who have afflicted me” (Psalm XVI). He had felt the heat of desire, tormented by the burning of lust, and therefore he longs to be protected beneath the shadow of God’s wings, so that he may rest unharmed from the flame of such grievous burning.

This is also what is promised to blessed Mary: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I), so that she might not be heated by any movements of desire or feel the burning of the fire, since she was to conceive from the Holy Spirit.

When Christ the Lord is said to have been seized, his flesh was nothing other than a shadow, because beneath the shadow of his passion he protected us, and beneath the shadow of his body he saved us.

What, then, do you think the unveiled brightness of his power and the sun of righteousness will be able to confer upon us when it shines forth, if the humility of the flesh and the emptying of divine majesty have conferred so much?

Through a shadow, then, the leper was healed; and through the fringe of the Lord’s garment the woman’s flow of blood ceased. Through a shadow also we saw him when he had neither form nor beauty. His flesh, as we have said, was a shadow: it cooled the heats of our desires, extinguished the fires of lust, and tempered the flames of greed and of the various passions.

And what shall I say about the shadow of the Lord, under which we live among the nations and in which we read that the nations hoped, when even the shadow of the apostles healed the sick and restored the languishing to life? When Peter came, the sick were brought out, and the shadow of the passing apostle restored them to health (Acts V).

What, then, was the Lord’s flesh other than a shadow? Concerning this flesh the prophet says: “Behold, the Lord sits upon a light cloud and comes into Egypt” (Isaiah XIV). The light and luminous cloud also overshadowed the apostles, lest the sun of iniquity scorch them.

Under this shadow, what the prophet announced as future is now fulfilled: we live among the nations and rest under the shadow of his protection. The same prophet saw him in shadow, although in the Spirit, when this first faith concerning him was still being announced to the nations. But now he illuminates the whole world, although we still see him through the shadow of his body, which is the Church of the living God.

For we do not yet see him face to face, since the eyes of no body can receive the brilliance of his divinity. Therefore, as though under a shadow, he daily protects the whole globe of the earth and allows us, regenerated among the nations in living hope, to live as though under a shadow.

There was no remedy except in the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, who could bring medicine to those who had despaired. Hence above, under the letter Coph, he lay as though enclosed. For this is said to be the sound signified by the letter Coph:

“Our time has drawn near; our days have been completed, because our end has come.”

This enclosure would bring despair unless the Lord’s coming raised us up. Therefore the same one is restored in the Spirit:

“The Spirit of our mouth, Christ the Lord, has been seized before our face in our sins.”

And it should be noted that the whole intention of the lament runs toward this end, in which the end of all grief and sorrow is imposed. Thereafter, in the following verses, a kind of crossroads is shown: heavenly and redeemed Jerusalem holds the right-hand path, while the same Jerusalem, defiled by the blood of sinners, seeks the left-hand path.

Therefore woe threatens the latter; but from Jerusalem Christ the Lord will wipe away every tear. For the Lord’s cross is shown to have been the tribunal of judgment, since one of those who hung on either side was received through faith, while the other, condemned for blasphemy, was left in the destruction of eternal death because he refused to receive life from the one hanging before his eyes through faith.

When he says “has been seized,” he uses the past tense for what was still future, following the custom of all those who, in divine promises, place future events in the past tense. This, then, is also within the lament: an exceedingly profound distinction in the lament that follows, by which the mourning of all the saints comes to an end and joy begins after grief and sorrow.

In those two verses of lament, the final woe begins from joy—a woe that ends with no remedy of pain or torment. Hence it follows:

## SIN

“Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Edom, who dwell in the land. To you also the cup will come; you will become drunk and be stripped naked.”

No one who has read the histories or the prophets doubts that Edom—and indeed all the surrounding nations—were always enemies of the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And because, in opposition to the Lord and to his help, they exulted and rejoiced over the evils that had occurred, they deservedly received, as a reciprocal punishment, the vengeance of the Lord’s fury.

Edom becomes drunk from the wine from which all the nations above drank, and from that golden cup of Babylon. Therefore it is said: “To you the cup will reach; you will become drunk and be stripped naked.”

For the Lord says: “Behold, those for whom it was not judgment to drink the cup will certainly drink; and finally, its cities,” he says, “will become everlasting desolations, and the whole earth was shaken by the sound of its ruin.”

Although all these things were fulfilled in that devastation by the sword of Babylon, and Babylon herself was again destroyed in the anger of God’s fury, it is better to understand everything of that final day of judgment, when everlasting desolation will follow vengeance.

Therefore this lament is also taken up against Babylon, because, according to the mystical interpretations, one and the same thing is signified by Edom and Babylon. From the beginning of the world, only two cities have been gathered and built: one Jerusalem, the other Edom or Babylon. One is the city that mourns, grieves, and labors with the prophet; the other does not know why some of its people are mourned, since Christ builds the one and the devil builds the other—the one whom the prophets often call Nebuchadnezzar.

That Babylon is the city of the lost, which makes the whole earth drunk with the wine of its iniquity. Concerning it the same prophet says: “Babylon is a golden cup in the hand of the Lord, making the whole earth drunk” (Jeremiah LI). “All the nations drank from the wine of its fury.”

Edom too is mourned as having drunk from the wine of that cup. Therefore against her the voice is uttered not as an admonition but ironically, as an insult or contradiction: she ought never to rejoice or be glad, since the fury of the Lord will finally reach her.

Edom is interpreted as “bloody” or “red.” He is therefore the bloody and shaggy people who pursue the things of the flesh and, for the allurements of the present life, have lost the birthright of eternal redemption.

Hence it is said: “Who dwell in the land.” For unless she had set her mind upon earthly actions, she would not have become drunk from that golden cup of Babylon, nor have been stripped of the garments of her virtues.

But Jerusalem that is above is the mother of God’s elect. She dwells not on earth but in heaven, where she has transferred herself completely, as Paul said: “Our citizenship is in heaven”; and: “Seek the things that are above, not the things that are on earth” (Philippians III).

For he feared what John says in his Apocalypse: “Woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, because the devil has come down to you in the anger of the Lord’s fury” (Apocalypse VIII). Therefore he admonished his hearers: “Seek the things that are above.”

But Edom, which chose to dwell on earth—that is, to defile its whole life with earthly and bloody works of sin—although for the present she appears to rejoice and be glad, shortly, once she has been made drunk with Babylon’s golden cup, will be stripped naked by the anger of God’s fury.

And not without reason: she resolved not merely to live on earth, but, as certain manuscripts have it, “in the land of Uz.” Uz is also interpreted as “counselor”—not the one who is called the angel of counsel, but the one accustomed to give counsel against God to those who move about on the perverse earth.

Edom is likewise interpreted as “earthly.” Therefore, by Edom, those are rightly signified who always pursue not heavenly but earthly things, deceived by cunning and by the devil’s counsel.

The golden cup reaches these people—the cup by which all the nations are made drunk—and they are stripped of the grace of God. Hence follows:

## TAU
Your iniquity is finished, daughter of Zion; he will not continue to carry you away. He will visit your iniquity, daughter [Col. 1234C] of Edom; he will uncover your sins.

These things seem, according to the literal sense, to have happened to both; but they are better understood generally of all who, at the final examination of the great judgment, are to be judged so that each may receive according to what he has done. Zion, indeed, is to pass from sorrow into everlasting joy and gladness; but Edom, reddened with the blood of its offenses, is to be visited so that it may receive the punishments of perpetual vengeance. These, as we have said, are the two constructed from the beginning: one is called Zion in this passage, the other Edom.

But through the prophet Isaiah it is also said of Zion that its wickedness has been completed, because its iniquity has been forgiven, in accordance with what David says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” (Psalm 31). Hence also in this passage he says: “Your iniquity is finished, daughter of Zion.” [Col. 1234D] Finished, indeed, because it has been forgiven. Thus, in the forgiveness of crimes, wickedness is proclaimed to be completed—that is, ended—because she has now received double from the hand of the Lord.

A very joyful promise immediately follows: “He will not continue to carry you away.” For when the judgment has ended, iniquity has ceased, and rest has been reached, there will thereafter be no change and no migration: neither from virtue to vice, from blessedness and joy to sorrow, nor from glory to punishment.

Conversely, over Edom the Lord will visit its iniquities, not in order to forgive but to punish; nor to release, since they remained in the same state, but to condemn. To them he will say: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which [Col. 1235A] 1525 has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25). Hence it follows: “He will uncover your sins.”

Whose sins, therefore, have not been covered and whose iniquities have not been forgiven through mercy—the Lord will then visit in order to punish, and they will be brought into the open. For all the crimes of transgressors will certainly be revealed in the future, while the offenses of those who were foreknown and predestined to life will have been forgiven and erased.

It is therefore rightly in that place that the crimes of those will be uncovered who here were unwilling to expose and confess them for repentance. But in those who confess their sins through lamentation and groaning, there will be nothing at all that can appear, because the things they acquired through guilt by sinning will have been erased and forgiven.

These are signs of the future judgment, toward which all the proclamations of divine speech [Col. 1235B] have run their course; and this is well signified by the letter Tau. For *tau* is interpreted as “signs.” Therefore these lamentations are also brought to their conclusion under that same letter. To those who fear him Christ gave signs and tokens so that they might flee from the face of the bow. But because they do not wish to foresee what is coming, it is just that they should be struck all the more severely, since they neglected to flee from the face of the drawn bow.

At the conclusion of so great a lament, let the mind rise higher, so that it may see at once to what exalted summit of heaven Jeremiah ascended. From there, contemplating with an expanded heart, he saw the many dangers of those struggling as in an arena in this age. Thus at one moment he extends the eye of his mind generally to all; at another he weeps over the individual falls and ruins of the Jews; at another he mourns the losses of the Church.

He also [Col. 1235C] deplores the wickedness of the character of each soul and, with tears, portrays the losses of its dreadful captivity. At one moment he beholds the glory and throne of Jerusalem, and likewise those of all God’s elect; at another, the wretched servitude of those tormented under the yoke of their adversaries; at another, he recalls them with every sorrow of heart.

Indeed, he introduces the Church herself as mourning, now herself, now her members. His lament therefore turns sometimes to the city walls and the adornments of virtues, but sometimes to the priests and leaders of the people, since through their faults they themselves no less than the flock have been captured and bound by the cord of iniquity, amid all the foulness of sin. His speech is also directed toward the little ones and infants who are groaning, because they have wasted away from hunger and thirst, while no outstanding teacher is found among the people.

Her virgins and those practicing continence are likewise [Col. 1235D] mourned as squalid, because, through the lack of the word of God, they have no freshness, [Col. 1236A] 1526 no beauty of face, and no loveliness of appearance: for all her beauty has departed from the daughter of Zion.

What more need be said? There is no distress, no disaster of the soul, and no affliction of crimes or adversaries, within or without, that he does not mourn and enumerate; no deprivation of good that he does not sorrowfully lay bare, no less in general than in particular. And just as there are no ornaments of virtue that these people have not lost in their several parts, so there are no forms of sorrow or grief by which the voice of lamentation and the streams of tears are not stirred.

As he brings in various persons, both from the common people and from the nobility, he is moved by various weepings; and through the individual persons the afflictions and increases of their tears are renewed. And just as there is no guilt of the present life in which she has not sinned, so there are no tears with which he has not lamented her. [Col. 1236B] Finally, on behalf of these same sins of ours, he presents God and the Lord as having been seized and having suffered in the flesh; yet, grieving most bitterly, he laments that all have returned from death.

Therefore, at the end, he rejoices over those who have heard and been converted, announcing that their wickedness and iniquities have been completed: the Lord will no longer add to their affliction, nor carry them away from the weakness of their virtue. Rather, they will be like the angels in heaven and will reign without end with Christ.

But those who have ended their lives in vices and crimes, and who have always acted advantageously in envy and deceit against God’s saints and elect—he will visit their iniquities, not to relieve and forgive but to punish and condemn, and he will uncover and expose all their sins.

Therefore, prudent [Col. 1236C] reader, carefully consider what I stated at the beginning of this lament: in the sacred Scriptures nothing is found except lamentations, a song, and a woe. Of these three, lamentations are appropriate for the present time; but in the homeland of eternal life there will be songs in the hymn-singing voices of the angels and in the rejoicing exultation of all the saints.

For this reason, I ask that lamentations and tears be practiced in this our pilgrimage, so that there we may be able to praise God in songs with the saints. But for those whom the joy and gladness of the present life have lifted up toward empty things, there will be an everlasting woe. Their iniquities will be visited in the wrath of God’s fury—not so that they may end and mourning cease, allowing them to rest, but so that vengeance may be renewed more fiercely and their offenses be punished without end: offenses which, if it had been permitted, they had resolved to commit without end. [Col. 1236D]

## PROLOGUE TO THE FIFTH BOOK

[Col. 1235]

[Col. 1235D] 1527 The fifth book, therefore, was not published according to the same method as the preceding four; rather, their conclusion is recapitulated in this single book, following the practice of rhetoricians, who at the end, in an epilogue, conclude, define, and briefly enumerate each of the matters they had treated.

They do this for the sake of recollection, setting before the eyes, as it were, in one place, the matters that had been scattered and spread out, while complaining in order to move either the indignation or the clemency of the merciful judge: clemency toward themselves or their own people, but indignation against their enemies, so that the judge may be stirred to more serious hatred and may incur offense because of the circumstances attributed to the persons or matters in question. [Col. 1236D]

For this purpose, a complaint is especially effective: it implores mercy from judgments and makes the listener’s spirit gentle and compassionate.

The first element of a complaint, therefore, is the condition in which they had once been, and the condition in which they now are, [Col. 1237A] as it says: “Remember what has happened to us,” or, “what has befallen us.” “Our inheritance,” he says, “has been turned over to strangers.”

He therefore laments before the most merciful judge all their misfortunes: that disgraceful and humiliating things have happened to them.
