He places everything individually before the judge’s eyes, as it were, so that the things he grieves to have happened to them contrary to expectation may be seen; and, in the manner of orators, as I have said, he recalls that he and his people have been brought down into the greatest misery.

If this is carefully considered, you will find that these same arts of speech have proceeded more from us than that our people borrowed such things from their disciplines. You will see this more clearly by examining each word, if you consider the prophet’s intention and feeling. Raised in spirit to a lofty height, he does not merely mourn his own sufferings and those of his people; through prophetic grace [Col. 1237B] he laments, as though under the appearance of his own people, the individual ruins of each person and the ruins belonging to all mortals.

For this seems to be the difference between the penitent and the lamenting: [Col. 1238A] sad tears are common to both. The penitent, however, prays for his own sins or for the transgressions of others, asking that the Lord forgive the offenses of sinners and not punish the errors of the wicked when he judges.

The lamenting, on the other hand, are those who, out of regard for compassion, grieve with lofty mind over the [uncertain: source reads *deflent*] ruins of cities, the destruction of their homeland, its depopulation and devastation, as well as the death of their fellow citizens, 1528. Among these things they count what they have already suffered—or are certainly going to suffer—through various tortures and countless insults (Romans 12).

Hence the Apostle admonishes, urging love of one’s neighbor: “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep.” And because, as the angel testifies, he is a lover of the brethren, one who prays greatly for the people and for God’s holy city Jerusalem, he rightly surpasses the lamentations of all in his own lamentations; and through his tears [Col. 1238B] he urges everyone to weep together over the ruins and sins of the whole age.

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1237]

[Col. 1237B] “Remember what has happened to us,” or, as other manuscripts read, “Remember, Lord, what has been done to us.” This lament is quite properly called, in a remarkable way, the song of Jeremiah, sung according to his prophecy—especially since he mourns the captivity of his people and the many miseries inflicted upon them by the Babylonian tyrant. [Col. 1237C] Hence it is clear that laments may also rightly be called songs; for just as joys full of misery are in the present age nowhere found without an end, so songs are scarcely, or not at all, found without laments. Therefore he rightly joined this song to the concluding lamentations, imploring the Lord’s mercy to put an end to their evils.

Monastic practice, however, has rightly determined that it should be sung in the manner of the psalms, although it should not be indicated by any headings merely because it bears the name “song.” For only songs are fitting in that heavenly Zion, whereas lamentations belong to this pilgrimage of ours. In the middle, as it were, before that final “woe” is reached, laments are rightly mingled with songs and songs with tears: there evils are mourned, while joys are celebrated in hope and faith.

For when he says, “Remember, Lord, and see what has happened to us; look upon and consider our disgrace,” he mourns the barbarous captivity recorded in history and places before the Creator’s sight the miseries endured by that people. Yet, more than any rhetorical discipline, the prophet regulates his statement in every respect—not to intensify the Judge’s hatred against the adversaries, but to implore mercy on behalf of his people’s deeds and crimes. Therefore he did not say, “Remember our enemies, so that they may pay what their deeds deserve,” but, “Remember what has happened to us.” It is as though he were saying plainly: “By remembering, remove the evils we suffer; but forgive those who caused them.”

When he says “what has happened” or “what has been done to us,” he distinguishes the evils we endure from nature, since they are not natural but accidental, arising from many causes of sin. To “look upon” or “consider” is likewise to see. The repetition by the one praying, however, reveals the affliction or earnestness of his heart. Therefore these verses must be reread with the emotion of one who is grieving.

Their disgrace was that a people so holy and so renowned, formerly celebrated for miracles and illumined by the presence of God, had fallen into such peril and destruction by God’s just judgment because of the enormity of its crimes. Alternatively, these words are shown to be the voice of the martyrs, who, afflicted by punishments and subjected to torments, say to God: “Remember, Lord, what has been done to us.” Since, at the present time, he does not avenge them but patiently allows the persecutors of the saints to rage, he in a sense forgets them; therefore they entreat him to remember, like the one who cried out in tears: “How long, Lord, will you forget me forever?” (Psalm 12); and again: “Will you forget our poverty and our tribulation?” (Psalm 43). When he remembers, he will also free us from the oppression of our persecutors, because his forgiveness alone will be our deliverance. Our deliverance will certainly be followed by vengeance upon our persecutors.

“Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses to foreigners.” He enumerates, piece by piece, the evils that had befallen them when the people were carried into captivity and foreigners possessed their land; what had been the people’s inheritance became the possession of the plunderer and devastator.

He also touches upon the prerogative of the Fathers and the authority of divine generosity: by whose favor the chosen nations became his inheritance, and that same people became God’s portion and possession. Their authority was of the greatest weight, and the defense of their inheritance was always under God’s care and protection. Then, what is most grievous of all, the inheritance of so great a privilege came—not to superiors, not to equals, nor to people of any standing, but to those alien and foreign to God. Their sins demanded this, although it was most unworthy and unjust: it came, that is, to the lowest and most arrogant of men. [Col. 1239A] Meanwhile, this conclusion also applies against heretics, who have handed the inheritance of Christ’s Church over either to demons or to corrupt institutions.

Accordingly, another translation says expressly: “Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, and our houses to foreigners.” For whatever is turned over once existed, but afterward is changed into another’s possession. This can rightly be understood also of the Holy Scriptures, which are the inheritance of the faithful, as I have said. This translation does not say, “has been turned over to strangers,” but “has been turned into strangers’ possession”—that is, into the possession of those who have been made alien to God, since Holy Scripture is “a fragrance of life unto life” to some, but “a fragrance of death unto death” to others (2 Corinthians 2). Thus it is turned over to such strangers unto unbelief, while it remains for the salvation of the faithful who understand it in the Catholic manner.

[Col. 1239B] “And our houses to foreigners or sojourners.” The meaning is therefore clear: everything that the same people possessed, outwardly or inwardly, was wholly possessed or transformed by foreigners.

In the tropological sense, however, the houses of Scripture are understood as divine understandings, in which we often establish the dwelling-place of our mind. We cannot dwell in them otherwise than by keeping hold of the breadth of their meanings, with our senses opened like doors. When heretics pervert these meanings according to the invention of their own depravity, our houses are transferred to foreign inhabitants.

The “foreigners” may also suitably be understood as spiritual forces of wickedness, who insert false depravity into the words of the divine Scriptures through perverse thoughts. Our houses—that is, human minds—are also turned over to foreign and unclean spirits when, through transgression and sin, they incline souls toward vices. Their inheritance is turned over to foreigners when unclean spirits take possession of our hearts, which have become accessible to them. Otherwise they could not enter us, since they derive the origin of their possession not from nature but from guilt.

The prophet, laying bare this misery before the supreme Judge, invites him no less against the enemies than toward mercy for us. Hence it follows: “We have become orphans, without a father; our mothers are like widows.”

Another translator says: “We have become orphans, as though we had no father.” From this it is evident that the prophet directs his gaze toward God the Father, who had adopted the Jewish people as sons. Hence he says: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exodus 4). Yet they became as though they had no father. Although they possessed him through the invocation of adoption, their sins had offended him, so that they no longer had him favorably disposed toward them in the affection of his compassion. Therefore he says pointedly, “as though having no father,” so that by lamentation and entreaty he might bend the paternal heart toward the mercy of a gracious remembrance.

“And our mothers,” he says, “are like widows.” The mothers are understood as the seven synagogues, which are known to have been established principally on the Mount of Olives. From them came the milk of instruction, or through them the law was proclaimed. But at the time of the siege or the Chaldean devastation, after their children had been taken away, they were abandoned and consumed by fire. He rightly mourns them as mothers and laments them as widows, since they used to raise children in the law and nourish peoples.

According to the anagogical sense, this statement often suits the voice of Christ’s Church: “We have become as though we had no father.” Whenever, amid anxieties and tribulations, we feel less than is fitting of the compassionate consolation of his fatherly heart, those who have lost God as Father through their own sins can plainly say this. They rightly lament that they have become orphans because they have lost their own parent.

For this reason, one of the interpreters said “not having a father,” while another said “as though not having one,” since at times the whole of him is lost because of sins. Often, even if he abandons us for a short time on earth, so that amid the pressure of persecutors we seem to have no father, we nevertheless do not doubt that we have him in heaven. Therefore we are sometimes “as though not having one.” He did not say absolutely, “and not having a father,” but “as though not having one,” whenever we are afflicted by various tribulations: we possess him through the affection of gracious remembrance, even though we may seem not to possess him through the aid of his defense.

The Churches of Christ, which are rightly called mothers, also often become like widows during persecution, when they are abandoned by their husbands, the priests who flee. They are likewise like widows when, in time of peace, through laziness and dullness they give birth to no offspring for God by the ministry of their preaching. For when they pursue worldly profits, become entangled in their own crimes, or feed upon the ignorance produced by their sluggishness, the Churches of Christ—which truly are mothers of Christians—become like widows. They are not widows, because their husbands appear to live, but they are like widows, because they bear no fruit from them for God.

The voice of such women is rightly mourned in the Church, because they still sigh toward God through the purpose of their hearts and the love they bear. The barrenness of heretics is also mourned. They are rightly called churches like widows because, although they are joined in some measure to the very strong husband, the Lord Jesus Christ—inasmuch as they in a certain way confess him, follow baptism, read the sacred writings, and pursue ecclesiastical functions—they are nevertheless rightly lamented as widows, because they produce no fruit for God through their teachers.

This is well represented by those concubines of David whom our true David entered at the beginning, but did not join to himself in a complete and marital union. Absalom, born more cruelly, entered them under the appearance of Satan and defiled them by the adultery of his depravity. Therefore David shut them away beneath their darkness in eternal condemnation. They are rightly mourned as widows, for they ought to have been mothers of God’s elect had they preserved the true covenants of faith with Christ and the chaste sacraments of marriage.

In the moral sense, however, we rightly understand “our mothers”—that is, the mothers of all virtues—to mean faith, hope, and charity. From these we are not only reborn for God, but all the other virtues of the soul are also generated. But when these begin to be corrupted in us by the vanities of the age, and Christ’s charity, through which the true marriage is preserved, together with the substance that is God, is changed by us into something else, these three virtues are mourned as widows rather than as true widows.

Although outwardly, in words and by the habit of Christian religion, they may appear to embrace Christ as husband, inwardly they have already lost the power of producing good works and the fruitfulness of chaste generation in Christ. For whatever is not from faith is sin, and works performed without charity cannot be beneficial.

It follows: “We drank our water for money; we bought our wood at a price.” The prophet describes the immense cruelty and affliction of his people. He describes their poverty and deprivation of what is good, to such a degree that they had to purchase even water, which is freely provided to all, at their own expense. Therefore he hastens, with tears, to move the mercy of the compassionate Judge at every point, lamenting before the most merciful Father things that are scarcely ever recorded as having happened to any nation.

This meaning also applies against greedy priests of God’s temples, who make God’s house a house of commerce. Because of baptism and the teaching of your preaching, or because of the spiritual gifts of God, they pursue profits and seek payment for their own gain. Against such men the people of Christ rightly lament and mourn.

“Our waters”—that is, the teaching of the Scriptures and the gifts of the Holy Spirit—we receive in exchange for monetary rewards. Of these the prophet Isaiah formerly promised us, and invited us freely to the waters: “All you who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no silver, hurry, buy, and drink wine and milk without any exchange” (Isaiah 55). When greedy priests sell these for a price, the people rightly grieve, because the wood—that is, the elements of the Scriptures and of Christ’s gifts, by which the fire of the Holy Spirit is daily nourished on the Lord’s altar—is bought for money. Everything given to us freely in common is cruelly put up for sale as private property, supposedly for our salvation.

In the moral sense, however, “they drink their own waters for money,” because they are filled by groaning with the fluid of their own tears: they possess the “money” of the Scriptures when they weigh in them the rewards of eternal life and the punishments. By meditating on these they nourish charity and fear within themselves. The mind becomes all the more ready to grieve the more it has been inflamed by the greater love of charity or pierced by fear because of the enormity of its crimes. Thus it comes about that, with the money of the Scriptures, we drink the waters of our tears.

Hence David also says: “You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us tears to drink in measure” (Psalm 79). We also buy wood as fuel for the Lord’s fire at a price whenever we exchange earthly and perishable things for spiritual ones. This too is to drink our waters for money: to give worldly wisdom and knowledge in exchange for spiritual things. Or, conversely, it means to lose the virtues of the soul within us as though in exchange, when vices increase.

Neither of these exchanges occurs without the price of labor or grief. No unjust profit is obtained without a just loss, nor is holy gain acquired without the expenditure of things that are passing away.

“We were threatened at our necks; no rest was given to the weary.” He indicates the contempt and oppression of the captives before the most righteous Judge, who scatters the proud and exalts the humble. He describes how those struck upon their necks by the hands of the proud were driven forward, so that, weary and exhausted by the cruelty of the enemy, they were forced to run unwillingly and to prefer the labor of work to rest.

Spiritually also, Christ’s Church groans in its martyrs when they are struck with blows, harassed by the hands of persecutors at their necks, afflicted by many insults and torments, and compelled to flee without rest from one city to another. Hence it is said: “No rest was given to us.”

By the blows upon the neck every affliction is signified, together with the contempt of humility, although, according to the Gospel (Matthew 5), those struck on one cheek might voluntarily offer the other as well.

Morally, our neck signifies pride, as Job says: “They set their neck like a shield”—that is, their pride as a means of protection. Through this pride we are driven as though by blows upon our necks into labor and are driven away from rest whenever the consciousness of our guilt strikes us inwardly. The exalted God looks upon the humble and knows the high from afar. He knows, recognizes, and approves them—but in order to strike and condemn.

This is the meaning of: “We were threatened at our necks, and no rest was given to the weary”: after the end of labor, no rest remains for those weighed down by sins and vices. For just as the spiritual life is tranquil, so the carnal life is restless and laborious. Hence it is said that “there was no rest for the weary.”

“We gave our hand to Egypt and to the Assyrians, so that we might be filled with bread.” Another translation differs greatly: “Egypt,” it says, “gave its hands to the Assyrians, for their satiety.”

Historically, he mourns that a people of such noble lineage, possessing the privilege of its fathers through a line of prophets and patriarchs, gave itself over to Egypt in order to be filled with bread, just as it is written elsewhere (1 Kings 2): “Those who were formerly filled hired themselves out for bread.” It gave itself not only to Egypt but also to the Assyrians because of its hunger for bread. God had formerly rained manna upon them from heaven and, through flashing miracles, had exalted them as a kingdom before all the nations.

But when he says, “Egypt gave its hands to the Assyrians, for their satiety,” he signifies that Egyptian and Assyrian soldiers came together with one accord to take the Israelite people captive, so that they might sell their spoils and satisfy their desires with wealth.

According to the allegory, Egypt conspires together with the Assyrians against Christ’s Church, not through charity but in order to attack the Church’s firmness. Concerning them one of the saints says: “I will not fear the thousands of the people who surround me” (Psalm 3).

Egypt is interpreted as “darkness,” and Assyrians as “those who direct.” By these are understood the aerial powers, who join themselves to human Assyrians—that is, to more powerful men—in order through them to inflict persecutions upon God’s elect. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “The hour will come when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John 16). They do this in order to satisfy the savagery of their own cruelty through the impiety of punishments.

Thus, in the tropological sense, Egypt gives its hands to the Assyrians for their satiety whenever heretics join themselves to heretics: the Maximianists to the Donatists, or the Marcionists and Manichaeans to the Valentinians, for the satisfaction of acquiring a people already led astray.

According to the Hebrew truth, however, the Church mourns its own members when the members of Christ and ministers of the altar give their hands, even for earthly things, to more powerful men and to secular persons who are darkened by the shadows of wealth or sins. The Assyrians, whose name is interpreted as “those who direct,” are joined to them so that they may be filled with bread: they direct themselves toward everything that belongs to the world, so that they may overflow with riches and exalt themselves with honors.

When Christ’s ministers give their hands to such men for perishable and worthless things, in order to serve their commands, what else do they become but lights of the world turned into darkness themselves?

By these words we are warned rather to lift our hands toward holy things and, with Moses, always to extend them toward heaven, lest they become heavy. Concerning them the prophet David says: “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God, lift up your hands in the holy places during the nights, and bless the Lord” (Psalm 134).

“During the nights,” he says, so that, if our hands are slackened in the darkness of this age and given over to Egypt, they may not become more tightly bound and subject to slavery. Therefore he says, “Lift up your hands during the nights,” so that, always meditating on holy things according to the Apostle, we may live continually to the praise of God.

It follows: “Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities.” Another translator says: “And we have paid the penalty for their iniquities.” This statement is forceful and obscure, wrapped in many shadows, although it appears sufficiently clear and straightforward with respect to the Jews. Following the antiquity of the letter, they drew all the curses of the law upon themselves, bearing its exceedingly heavy yoke—one which neither they nor their fathers were able to bear—because they refused to receive Christ, who would have freed them from the curse of the law.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “That upon you may come all the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah; all these things,” he says, “will be required from this generation” (Matthew 23). And elsewhere: “Fill up the measure of your fathers” (ibid.).

These words clearly show that imitators of the Fathers also draw upon themselves the earlier sins of the Fathers if they become followers of their evil. This is particularly grievous for us, since we are not sufficient to bear our own sins, even without being weighed down by the burdens of our preceding fathers.

Ezekiel appears to resolve this statement when he says: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son; but each one shall die in his own sin in which he has sinned” (Ezekiel 18). This statement would appear to settle the matter, were it not that the Lord speaks through Moses in Exodus: “I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, who repay the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and show mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments” (Exodus 34).

These words are said to occur here no less than elsewhere in parables and proverbs, so that one thing appears on the surface of the words while another seems to resound in their meanings. This does not mean that God’s injustice permits one person to sin with impunity while another suffers punishment for another’s crimes. Rather, the phrase that follows—“of those who hate me”—resolves the difficulty of the threatening judgment or command.

The fathers who existed and are no more ought rather to have been punished as sinners. But because their descendants became their imitators, hated God through an inherited evil and a hereditary right to impiety, and allowed guilt to grow like branches from a root, punishment rightly reached them.

This is the meaning of the words: “We have borne their iniquities,” spoken before the most righteous Judge, while also imploring a sentence of pardon so that he may put an end to their evils. The sons are not punished merely because their fathers sinned, but because they have taken up the yoke of iniquity. In this way the heap and measure of their own iniquity grows and accumulates.

This very disease is rightly lamented as having often flourished in Christ’s Church: when priests and rulers of the earth sin, the people are often scourged as though for their crimes. Their voice is: “Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities.” It is as though they were saying plainly: “They are not what they ought to have been, and because of their faults we bear, together with them, the vengeance for their iniquities.”

Therefore, we ask, let both groups hear how terribly the prophet mourns: he strikes the fathers for their own guilt, while warning his hearers not to deceive themselves with empty flatteries. Teachers are chosen according to the merits of the people, and the people suffer loss because of the teacher’s negligence. Punishment does not decrease when guilt succeeds guilt; rather, it increases. Thus Cain receives punishment sevenfold, but Lamech seventy-sevenfold. For although there is a distinction among murderers, a follower after the commandment and example does not thereby contract a smaller punishment than the originator and author of evil.

This statement can also be referred to original sins, since, when one sins, wrath rages against all unless they are freed by grace. In this respect, however, neither does the father bear the iniquity of the son, nor the son the iniquity of the father. Each is either freed by his own righteousness or dies in his own sin.

The statement “Our fathers sinned and are no more” also contains a meaning concerning how they are “no more,” since they are believed to exist even after death. Every sinner, insofar as he commits an offense and sins, is reduced to nothing and is no more. He is no more because he falls away from the One who is always the same, so that he does not exist, and slips away.

He did not say, “Our fathers sinned, and their sin is no more,” but “they themselves are no more.” For when the sinner has died, the cause of the sin remains entirely, and the sons often pay its penalty in two ways: either they are weighed down in the present by various afflictions because of their fathers’ iniquities, so that they pay the penalty for their fathers’ sins; or, by failing to put an end to their evils, they are assigned to eternal punishments.

But if the sons have been formed by better teachings or freed by grace, they are pressed by no yoke of iniquity. With the bonds of their sins broken through baptism, each is either punished for his own evils or acquitted.

“Servants,” he says, “have ruled over us; there was no one to redeem us from their hand.” He unfolds a summary of their miseries and introduces, one by one, new torments of his grief, so that in many ways he may incline the compassionate Judge’s benevolence toward mercy.

“Servants have ruled over us.” It is as though he were plainly saying: “You redeemed and liberated us by the arm of your power; you exalted and raised us to royal dignity; you glorified us through virtues and signs. Now, however, not just any people but servants have ruled over us, and there was no one to redeem us from their hand.”

He repeats this in order to call upon the accustomed mercy of the most merciful God by means of tears, inviting it with the whole affection of his mind and presenting his former benefits to the one who considers their errors.

Typically, however, the chorus of the saints—the holy nation, the people of God’s possession, the royal priesthood—mourns whenever spiritual forces of wickedness, who have lost their heavenly freedom, rule over us and afflict us with the slavery of sin. It also mourns whenever carnal or criminal men rule in the Church, and whenever the Redeemer, the Lord, appears for a time to abandon those who are under their power.

This grief therefore rightly belongs to penitents. Desiring to escape Satan’s snares, to whose dominion they had been subjected and handed over, they venture to breathe again toward God and direct their prayers to him.

Recognize also that heretics are servants of sin, who rule over those whom they have trained in their most evil habits and who have become servants of vices. Since they do not know how to moderate the yoke of their doctrine, there is at times no one to release those whom they themselves entangle in their disciplines.

“With our hands we brought our bread to ourselves, in the face of the sword in the wilderness.” Another translator says: “In our souls we acquired our bread.” From this the weariness of immense labor is described, when not only the body but also the mind is exhausted. There was outward labor in acquiring daily food; inwardly, however, there was immense fear before the face of the sword. This is the meaning: “In our souls,” because bread was sought at the risk of life.

The desirable typological sense, however, is that the conscience and the blessed mind—which always acquires for itself by its own hands the bread of life, or the food of the Holy Scriptures and various virtues—carry this food to themselves without weariness. We read in the Gospel that such loaves, both wheat and barley, were broken, so that the mind might gather for itself an abundant harvest from the New and Old Testaments and acquire bread for its understanding through labor, in the face of the sword of solitude.

The sword of solitude is rightly understood as the devil’s ambushes. Against its face the shield of faith is always carefully set, so that the mind may be safely preserved from the attack and the face of its assailant. Concerning this it is said: “Before his face is paradise, and behind him the solitude of the wilderness.” Before he invades the faithful soul flourishing with virtues, it is rightly understood as paradise; once invaded, he turns it into solitude. The soul is desolated and abandoned by God when it is overthrown by the enemy and brought down by vices.

Morally, the soul acquires the bread of virtues through its labors when the body is exercised in good works, inwardly and outwardly—for example, when it is directed toward benevolence, charity, peace, and piety. When it is brought to life by these virtues, it acquires heavenly and eternal bread “in the face of the sword in the wilderness,” because, after overcoming the ambushes and various temptations of the enemy, we are always engaged in labor and turn toward God as though in the solitude of a wilderness.

“Our skin has become like an oven, scorched by the face of the storms of hunger.” Or alternatively: “By the face of the wounds of hunger.” The scorching of the skin expresses the magnitude and immensity of the famine; or, as another translator understands it, it is expressed by livid flesh. Anyone who wishes to know this hunger should read Josephus, who says that parents devoured their children, and that brigands choked the throats of those devouring them, so that they tore out food already swallowed almost from their very entrails; thus the plunderers consumed the same flesh without horror.

Allegorically, however, this is the voice of the saints being mourned: “Our skin has become like an oven, livid or scorched.” It is called “skin” because our first parents were clothed in it and were miserably driven from the boundaries of paradise. Therefore he does not say “our skins,” but “our skin,” because from them we all contracted one skin of mortality.

Our mortality, stained by the lividness of sin, is burned like an oven—that is, like the devil, who is the furnace of vices—while the author of sin himself inflames it daily with new burnings of desire. Following this author, we incur the hell of condemnation. Through him we are afflicted by the famine of the storm, so that we may not be filled by any feasts of eternal life because of the wounds of hunger.

Another translation does not without cause say “by the face of the wounds,” or “of our storms,” in the plural, although bodily there is only one wound or storm of hunger. He therefore grieved rather because of the inward hunger, which is increased by many storms and afflicted by various wounds. When the soul has lost the food of life, it suffers the various wounds of affliction through all the senses of the body and through all the emotions of the mind: its inward light is darkened, and it can no longer hear the word of salvation inwardly with its ears.

Hence the Lord says: “I will send among them not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8). When the mind is afflicted by this hunger, it is tortured by various blows of wounds and tossed by the storms of tempests.

Hence it follows: “Women were humbled in Zion, and virgins in the cities of Judah.” That this happened literally to the Jews is beyond doubt. Many Churches of Christ have also often been corrupted and humbled in faith by the depravity of heretics through hunger for food and thirst to hear the word of God. To them the Apostle Paul said: “For I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds should be corrupted from the charity that is in Christ Jesus”; and below: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.”

These virgins, who had been betrothed to Christ in faith, are rightly mourned by the prophetic voice when they are humbled. Unless they were women and followed feminine wounds, they would not have been deceived by the frauds of heretics or humbled by an adulterous marriage.

In the tropological sense, whenever we are weighed down by the foulness of sins and, falling miserably from a height—that is, from Zion—into low places, are cast down, women—that is, our souls—are humbled in Zion, where they had been placed at the summit of the Church.

To be “in Zion” is one thing, and to be humbled outside it is another. Even if we are sinners, within the Church of Christ we open up the distress of our crimes in the house of the Lord, confessing and groaning, without despairing that the forgiveness of the good Shepherd may be granted. Thus we are humbled in Zion while mourning.

To such women the same prophet elsewhere cries out: “Hear the word of the Lord, women, and let your ears receive the word of his mouth. Teach,” he says, “your daughters lamentation, and each her neighbor mourning” (Jeremiah 9). From this it is also clear that we are all warned to wash the affections of our souls with tears, and, like daughters who must grieve and repent, to accustom them to mourning. We must cleanse the works of our body by lamentations as though they were our neighbors, so that those of us who have been humbled by our own sins may be purified through him who loves penitents and chastity.

The minds of the faithful are like virgins dedicated to the Lord. By God’s grace they have put on incorruption of faith and laid aside integrity.

The cities of Judah in which they were humbled are the various professions within the Church of God. There is one profession of priests, another of Levites, another of monks, another of the various degrees, another of virgins, another of widows and celibates, and another of married people. In each of these ranks certain virgins—that is, intelligible souls—are glorified by virtues as they make progress, advancing inwardly through the intention of their good will.

Others are humbled by vices because they do not follow Christ according to their purpose. More grievously still, some are inwardly defiled and cast down. Jeremiah also mourns these virgins much earlier in the same Lamentations, saying: “Hear, I beg you, all peoples, and see my sorrow. My virgins and my young men have gone into captivity” (Lamentations 2). The virgins are those who have received incorruption of mind; the young men are those who have put on newness of life but are subsequently corrupted by the enemies’ ambushes and the disgrace of crimes.

The prophetic affection rightly mourns them when they are carried away into foul and lowly defilements.

“Princes were hung up by the hand; the faces of elders did not blush.” That the Jews themselves were hung by the hands of their enemies upon the torture-horse or subjected to other punishments of torment is evident from accounts of still more atrocious penalties. Certainly they were hung by the hands of their enemies; certainly they were bound to the torture-horse by their own hands. In these punishments, as though to spare them, the faces of the elders did not blush.

Mystically, however, princes or rulers of peoples are hung by the hands of enemies in other circumstances: when, abandoning the purpose of good works or a right intention, they fulfill what they have conceived according to the enemy’s will, as though they were wholly suspended for punishment. Having conquered the works of their hands, they miserably endure, as upon a torture-horse, what they suffer.

Hence it follows: “The faces of elders did not glorify.” In these laments he shows that the storm of temptations passes through everyone. That most crafty dragon does not know how to spare children or young men in their sinning. Nor, when he has entangled adolescents in his allurements, does he grant rest to the old. Rather, he gathers every age and every dignity of ecclesiastical rank into one storm, and by his deceit overthrows sex, condition, and the grace of one’s profession. For an impious will does not know how to be satisfied with the fall of the wretched; it hastens all the more to deceive each person when it sees that he is more easily and unhappily obeying its suggestions.

The Church of Christ has also often endured such things from persecutors, when they hung the princes and elders of the people, harassed them with death, insults, and torments, and cast them away.
to disgrace: would that we might deserve to attain this, so that for the Lord’s sake we might be worthy to suffer such things, and that by this means our body might be cleansed by the price of his blood, and the soul sanctified when sprinkled with the stream of his own blood—our soul, which is ensnared and stained by so many of its own crimes.

It follows: “They abused the youths shamefully, and the boys fell upon the wood.” Another interpretation, however, has it quite differently: “The powerful were grinding at the mill, and the young men were fastened to the wood” [Col. 1248C]. Here, according to the historical sense, he laments Zedekiah, a powerful king whose eyes the king of Babylon put out at Riblah and whom he made to grind at the mill; but he also laments the other princes or young men whom he crucified upon the wood.

Moreover, what our edition reads—“They abused the young men with impunity”—touches upon the crime of the Romans, who indulged in intercourse with males in the manner of women for the sake of lust [1542]. Concerning them the Apostle Paul says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts; professing themselves to be wise, they became fools.” A little later he says: “For this reason,” he says, “God gave them over to a debased mind, to do what is not fitting. Their women exchanged natural use for that use [Col. 1248D] which is against nature; and likewise the males committing shameful acts with males” (Rom. I).

That these same people also perpetrated such deeds against the Jewish youths whom they had captured, the prophet reveals when he says: “They abused the young men shamefully.” That they crucified them upon the wood is likewise clear, on account of the enormity of their cruelty. But, according to our interpretation, how did “the boys fall upon the wood”? No other meaning is apparent than that they refused to believe in Christ hanging upon the wood. Hence a certain Apostle says: “The cross,” he says, “is foolishness to the Gentiles and a stumbling block to the Jews” (II Cor. I). Therefore they fell upon the wood because they refused to accept him who hung upon it, the Life who was to destroy death.

Those powerful men, then, [Col. 1249A] because they were scandalized by the wood, he left empty like boys. Hence “they were grinding at the mill,” since, using the law according to its letter and following their own tracks in it, they inflicted perpetual blindness upon themselves. When that very strong Samson came to this blindness, the Philistines made him grind, so that by this means he could advance nowhere; yet by turning the mill he retraced himself in his own footsteps, returning, like the Jews, to their errors.

Mystically, moreover, within the Church there are two kinds of powerful people. One consists of those who are powerful in bodily wealth and possess the power of temporal vanities; the other consists of those who excel in spiritual honors. In the former, the wickedness and obstinacy of desires and cravings revolve. Those who become powerful in spiritual things, however, turn the mill of the law, since they read, grind, repeat, and frequently revisit it. Thus there is a certain spiritual mill with which they grind the fine flour of wheat and prepare the meal of understanding, from which a sacrifice may be offered to God [Col. 1249B].

Those who are “young men fastened to the wood” also become martyrs. Concerning this wood the Apostle Paul says: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. II). For the boys, transferred into the Lord, died to the world and were fastened to the wood [1543] of the Lord’s cross.

It follows: “The elders have failed from the harbor; the young men from the choir of those singing psalms.” The veterans, worn out by long old age, were so consumed by hunger that, when they wished to go out through the gates to seek grass or any other food, they were found at those very gates half-dead, as though dead; and this is what “they have failed from the gates” means. Or certainly, when they were stretched and killed by the enemies here and there, they are rightly said to have failed from the gates, as counselors of the city and teachers of the law. Likewise, the young men are lamented as having failed from the streets, terrified away from their accustomed duties.

Typically, the elders are those who attain the gray hair of understanding through the grace of forgiveness and complete their work in the gentleness of quietness. If they offend God, they fail at the gates that are called the gates of righteousness, concerning which David says: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; entering them, I will confess to the Lord” (Ps. CXVII). At these gates, then, the elders fail when they are wearied by growing scandals. They are deprived of the straight course of the journey, so that, the path of repentance and mourning being cut off, they are overwhelmed by a certain negligence [Col. 1249C].

Their young men fail from the choir of those singing psalms when spiritual chanting comes to rest. Morally, however, an incontinent mind, although it knows God, cannot say, when it drives him from itself: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind.” Therefore the devout mind must cry out continually within its conscience, lest it ever cease to sing to God; indeed, it must always stand among the choir of the saints, praising God.

“Our heart’s joy has failed,” he says; “our choir has been turned into mourning.” The meaning is clear concerning the Jews: because they provoked God to anger, all the joy of their heart fell away, and all the inner parts of their gladness were dissolved into grief and sorrow and into various afflictions of misery, just as the prophet’s lament enumerates from the beginning [Col. 1250A]. Their choirs, moreover, which they used to lead during their various solemnities, had rightly been turned into mourning when they were tortured among their enemies by every kind of torment.

In another sense, within the Church this is the voice of penitents, who offer the contrition of their heart to God as a sacrifice, as David says: “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise.” Those, therefore, whose consciences are wounded by the injuries of crimes and sins rightly say: “The joy of our heart has been dissolved.” David again asks that this joy be given back to him: “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing,” he says; “you will restore to me the joy of your salvation.”

When the spirit rests in spiritual contrition and a constricted heart, this occurs whenever the soul, pierced by the misery of its afflictions, is wounded by torments. Isaiah [Col. 1250B] promises the healing of this contrition in his prophecy, saying: “On the day when the Lord binds up the wound of his people and heals the blow of its wound, because there is in it wound, bruise, and swollen sore” (Isa. XXX). Morally, whenever the soul is wounded by the bruise of sin, it is then also struck by the darts of its own crimes. Its joy is immediately dissolved when the mind is brought back to conscience and the choir of virtues is changed into mourning.

This is said to have happened well to Asahel, who was an exceedingly swift runner, like one of the deer that dwell in the forests, not knowing how to restrain the swift movements of his spirit with patience and gravity. Thus, while he pursued the enemy too swiftly, he perished when struck by a wound—where the violence of fornication dominates in the groin and the disease of lust rages.

But Ahab fell dead after being struck by an arrow in the heart (III [Col. 1250C] Kings XXII), between the lungs and the shoulders, signifying those in whom the virgin of wisdom is wounded by the arrows of falsehood. And rightly between the lungs, where the vital breaths are vigorous and the health of life is regulated, and the shoulders, where Christ’s easy burdens are carried. His heart’s joy was therefore dissolved and destroyed, because he himself failed, as did the joy of the present life.

That “our choir has been turned into mourning” signifies the mourning of perfect repentance: the choir of virtues preserves the harmony of mourning for what we have lost and maintains the concert of repentance, so that the same choir may, after sorrows and tears, reach lasting joys.

“The crown of our head has fallen,” he says. “Woe to us, because we have sinned.” This signifies the humiliation and casting down of the Jews from the kingdom, when the king’s honor [Col. 1250D] and glory perished. Hence the same prophet, far above, says: “Say to the king and to the queen: Humble yourselves and sit down, for the crown of your glory has fallen from your head.” Another translator has: “Descend.” But there is a great difference between a crown falling from the head and someone descending, because descent is lighter than ruin.

Thus, when one lives negligently little by little, to lose glory through neglect is to descend: for when someone does not run toward higher things, he descends toward lower ones. In the same way, the kingdom of the Jews, through successive retreats as far as Jehoiakim, descended from the heights to the depths; thereafter, through Zedekiah and those who remained of the people, it fell completely from its elevated state [1545] to utter ruin.

Hence follows the voice of all the captive mourners: “Woe to us, because we have sinned” [Col. 1251A]. From this it is evident that woe threatens those who fall; to those who sin through negligence, lamentation remains.

This aptly applies to the Church when priests and virgins in it fall—those who seem to be its ornaments and, as it were, its crown of beauty. Sometimes, too, when it loses the grace of faith, its glory falls from its head, because it changes the Lord of its beauty into the faithlessness of falsehood.

That the Lord is the crown of the Church Isaiah testifies, saying: “On that day the Lord of hosts will be a crown of glory and a diadem of exultation for the remnant of his people.” The Church then loses this crown of its head when those who are holier within it fall into faithlessness.

This crown sometimes falls, but it can be restored through lamentations and clothed again with the integrity of faith [Col. 1251B]. Otherwise the Church of Christ cannot be beautiful unless, crowned by Christ, she comes from Lebanon, as it is sung in the Song of Songs: “Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come—you will be crowned: from the head of Amana, from the summit of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards” (Song IV).

The crown of Christ himself is also understood in the passage that beautifully says in the Song of Songs: “Go forth and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal and on the day of the joy of his heart” (Song III).

The Church, truly Christ’s bride, loses this crown when she loses the beauty of faith and the integrity of his works in those who seem to be greatest among Christ’s members. Or certainly, “the crown of our head” falls when those who seemed to be honored for beauty and glory [Col. 1251C] fall, instead of receiving a diadem in Christ, who is the head of the whole Church, into faithlessness, crimes, or disgraceful deeds.

The crown of our head falls when those who seemed to be the ornament of beauty in Christ fall away. But then woe threatens when those who seem greatest also fall in various ways, and afterward the wanton populace comes into sins and disgraceful acts. Hence the prophet mourns together with the people, indeed on their behalf: “Woe to us, because we have sinned.”

Sinners therefore awaken and attribute woe to themselves, because by sinning they have offended God. Hence pain arises in the heart, either fixed there by wrongdoing or stirred by repentance.

Morally, however, the crown of our head perishes when good will is lost. Concerning it the prophet rightly sings in jubilation: “With the shield of your good will, Lord, you have crowned us” (Ps. V). Our mind is therefore adorned with the crown of virtues when it is not only adorned everywhere with the shield of good will, but also defended under God’s protection [Col. 1251D].

But when good will [1546] falls from the mind, what else is lost than the crown of virtues and the beauty of our salvation? Hence it is rightly lamented: “Woe to us, because we have sinned,” because everything we do is sin unless it is crowned with the shield of good will. Woe then threatens us because we have sinned after losing good will—not through excess, but through desires, when we sin with the intention of an evil will.

“Therefore,” he says, “our heart has become sorrowful” [Col. 1252A]; “therefore our eyes have been darkened.” How sorrowful the heart of the Jews was in both captivities, when they were afflicted by various torments, perhaps no one can comprehend; and how darkened their eyes were from tears and sufferings, no one can grasp. Yet there is the lamentation of all sinners who accuse themselves of having sinned against God.

Two kinds of sorrow and pain are considered. Concerning this Jeremiah says: “My pain is upon pain; within me my heart mourns” (Jer. VIII). By this statement he signifies that the pain of sinners is joined to the pain of compunction, so that there is “pain upon pain.”

There is therefore a bad pain, as in the saying: “In pain you shall bear children”; and there is a good one, as in: “My pain has been renewed,” namely, through repentance. Whoever therefore mourns healthfully after sin humbles his heart in sorrow, so that by medicinal pain the pain of infirmity may depart.

For this reason David says: “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. L). Therefore let humility and shame over the crime committed be present in the minds of all sinners, and let pain arise from repentance over the wound driven into them.

“Therefore,” he says, “our eyes have been darkened because of Mount Zion, which has perished.” Since wickedness in sinning had infected their eyes, they are rightly mourned as darkened, because their own wickedness blinded them. Thus they cannot see Christ, who is the stone cut from the mountain without hands and who grew into a great mountain, because Mount Zion perished—that is, because, although he was equal to God the Father, he emptied himself [Col. 1252C].

Those who previously saw now no longer see; those who contemplated the law become blind, so that they cannot discern either Christ or his Church, the spiritual mountain growing throughout the whole world. The eyes of all the faithless have been darkened because of the name of Zion, which has perished.

“Foxes have walked upon it,” he says—that is, persecutors or heretics. Because they held an evil opinion concerning Christ’s incarnation, they [1547] tore apart the whole Church of Christ and corrupted all catholic understanding of it by fraud and deceit. For this reason they themselves also belong to the company of foxes.

Herod was a persecutor of Christ and the killer of John, of whom the Lord says: “Tell that fox.” All heretics are also foxes lying in wait. Concerning them the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Catch for us the foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song II).

Heretics therefore destroy the vineyard of the Lord of hosts, the vineyard of Sorek that he himself planted. For this reason all Catholics must mourn because of their snares and frauds. Even those who seemed to be the eyes of the Church and who were appointed to provide the other members of the body with the light of knowledge have been darkened (Luke XIII) [Col. 1252D].

Therefore let each of us say, let us all say: “Illuminate, Lord, the sight of our hearts, and enlighten us with the worthy radiance of faith” (Song II), so that we may see what is worthy and avoid what is unworthy.

It follows: “But you, Lord, remain forever, and your throne from generation to generation.” Another translator says: “You dwell forever,” because one who rightly dwells is said to remain forever. His dwelling is eternal; “to be” itself is what remains—the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father—so that there may be in them one eternity and one substantial everlastingness, not a local habitation or a temporal dwelling, but one undivided essence of remaining in itself.

Although the Son emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, he is nevertheless rightly believed to remain forever one and the same, unchangeably, even though it is not improperly proclaimed that a throne has been prepared for him, according to his humility, forever and ever; this throne is understood to have been assumed on account of the mortality he took upon himself [Col. 1253A]. For this reason he is said to remain forever in both natures.

“And your throne,” he says, “from generation to generation”: when you contemplate the throne of the reigning one, you may fear the judge of supreme power; and although human mortality, worn down by many corruptions, grows old like a garment [Col. 1253B], may his essence and majesty be believed unfailing and unchangeable.

The prophet then turns his whole self toward God, despising all passing things, while God remains forever the same, so that from this he may receive consolation amid the various dangers of life. Hence he implores help with plaintive prayers: “Why,” he says, “will you forget us forever? Why do you abandon us for the length of our days?”

This does not mean that God has lost the treasures of memory or knowledge, but that by some hidden judgment he delays giving help immediately, while he seems [1548] to disregard those who plead and does not console hearts weighed down by distress. Indeed, he abandons them for a little while, so that through patience he may test them and through victory reward those whom he has tested. Because of human weakness, the mind oppressed by various troubles imagines that God has forgotten [Col. 1253C].

Forgetfulness covers over the fountain of charity, quickly removes the capacity for mercy, dulls the edge of the grace to be bestowed, and does not allow help to be given at once to those placed in misery. The prophet, knowing this well, laments: “Why,” he says, “will you forget us forever?” If, as though forgetting us for a little while, you delay granting grace, we who are weighed down by many falls will be subjected to numerous vices.

Therefore we must always entreat him not to abandon us for the length of our days. It is necessary that we always remember him, so that he may also remember us and have mercy. For he will not remember those who forget him except for this purpose: to make them understand through grace that he must be sought—the one whom the mind, previously ignorant, did not know how to seek.

Thus, while the things he has implanted in our memory slip away, unless he again inspires them through hidden grace, they are erased from the mind by the affliction of forgetfulness. God presides over the treasures of our memory, which are a great abyss; by a hidden dispensation of his, he in some manner governs, heals, and orders what has been stored there [Col. 1253D].

Hence it is said: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. XXI). They will first remember, so that they do not forget God’s commandments; then they will again turn to the Lord, so that what has been inspired into their memory may, through the grace of hidden inspiration, be fulfilled in all of you.

For what does one remember except that which was entrusted to memory? Or what does one forget except what was undoubtedly implanted in the mind? Hence the Lord says: “My people have forgotten me for innumerable days.”

Therefore the prophet asks in every way that the Lord not forget us—not merely for a little while, lest we be tested, but forever, lest we be swallowed up. Then, when we remember, may he guide us, not abandoning us to remain subject to sufferings, but strengthening us so that we may turn to him, whom we are commanded to love with our whole heart.

Hence follows: “Convert us, Lord, to yourself, and we shall be converted; renew our days as from the beginning” [Col. 1254A]. The prophet knows, therefore, that our turnings-away are many, and so he asks after many shipwrecks and storms, when his strength has been broken: “Convert us, Lord, and we shall be converted.”

In these words of perfect piety he first implores grace; then, through [1549] grace, he promises free choice, so that the result of salvation may be attained [Col. 1254B]. Otherwise, unless it is through grace, no one who has turned away is converted, because our falling is ours, whereas our rising again is God’s; or, as the Apostle says: “It is not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX).

It should be noted that when he says “to yourself,” we are to understand that whatever else we direct ourselves toward is turning away. For it is not enough for God to convert us unless we also, by grace, are converted to him through our own will.

There is, in a certain sense, a veil of our weakness placed before our senses. Unless it is removed by the illumination of Christ, we are in no way able to turn to God. Thus freedom is restored through grace, and the grace of freedom cooperates with the choice of good will.

Therefore God must be entreated to deign, after the apostasy of our turning away [Col. 1254C], to convert us to himself. For who, surrounded by darkness, can look upon the brightness of the sun? Or where can the one whom we know to exist be sought, whom we cannot find on earth?

It remains, then, that although we are surrounded by darkness, the Sun of righteousness may rise within us through grace’s shining rays. He is not obtained through any pleasures by the exercise of free choice; rather, charity shines forth through the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

Hence the prophet says concerning the converted: “And now,” he says, “we follow with our whole heart, we fear you, and we seek your face, Lord; do not put us to shame.” Whoever follows with his whole heart, once converted, does not delay in going after his God.

Therefore it follows: “Renew our days as from the beginning,” so that, once converted, he may at last reach the prize of the heavenly calling; for conversion is the beginning of the restoration of the former life [Col. 1254D]. The renewal of days, moreover, is the receiving of eternity.

Concerning these days of eternity the prophet sings in the person of Christ: “And his going forth,” he says, “is from the beginning of the days of eternity.” We are recalled to that beginning of renewal when we are converted; when we have arrived there, we shall be renewed.

What has grown old and is corrupted is renewed, because our days in paradise—the days possessed by the first human being—were immortal, had he remained in God’s commandments before we turned away from him. Since, through turning away [1550], we fell into old age and lost the days of eternity, the prophet knows that they can be restored through conversion. Therefore elsewhere also he prays: “Convert me, Lord, and I shall be converted to you,” and the other words that follow [Col. 1255A].

“But,” he says, “casting us away, you have rejected us; you have been exceedingly angry with us.” He laments the anger of the merciful Judge on account of the enormity of their crimes, when, in the time of fury, the punishment of sinners rages. He is also mourned as having driven them from himself in anger, although he is believed to be wholly present everywhere.

We understand two kinds of rejection. The first is when, as sinners, we are handed over to the tempter; the second is when we yield to temptations. When we are exposed to temptation, we are indeed rejected without God’s anger. But when we are overcome, and do not repent of our rejection, we are rejected.

Yet by this rejection, as David says, God never rejects the people whom he has foreknown and predestined; sometimes he rejects them only until they repent. When we are rejected in such a way that we are overcome, God is shown to be exceedingly angry with us [Col. 1255B].

Hence David says: “Who knows the power of your anger?” (Ps. LXXXIX), and who can count your anger because of fear of you? [Col. 1256A] For sometimes he is angry as a father, sometimes as a lord, and sometimes he is indignant as a judge.

As a father he is angry when, by words or corrections, he rebukes the sinner, yet does not withhold medicine from the repentant. Thus the same prophet said far above: “At least from now on call me ‘my father’; you are the guide of my virginity. Will you be angry forever, or will you persevere to the end?” From this it is clear that the father is rightly angry, but not forever—only until the time of conversion.

Therefore, when we are struck somewhat more harshly, the Lord is angry and immediately exacts punishment for sin. Moses perceived this well when he said: “Lord, let not your anger rage against your people.”

He is shown to be angry as a judge when he says to the wicked and sinners: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). After his presence, there is no longer any place for pardon [Col. 1256B].

But here he is sometimes shown to be angry with us when neither an end is put to evils nor the scourges cease as faults increase through the lack of repentance.

[Col. 1255]

## The Book of Saint Paschasius Radbertus, Abbot of Corbie, on the Body and Blood of the Lord

Revised and enlarged in a second edition by its author, and now finally corrected against manuscript copies and ancient editions.

(Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. IX.)

[Col. 1255C]

## Preliminary Observation

The two little works of Paschasius Radbertus, abbot of Corbie, which follow, were both written at the request of Warinus, abbot of New Corbie and formerly his pupil; both were composed for younger brothers who had not yet been touched by the waters of liberal learning; both have already seen the light, and yet both nevertheless now reappear as new works.

The book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, Paschasius’s first offspring, was composed long before he was raised to the dignity of abbot, especially at the time when Abbot Arsenius—whom his age regarded as a second Jeremiah—was living in exile. Hence those who understood “Arsenius” to mean Saint Adalard, exiled on the island of Herio from 814 to 821, commonly maintained that the book was written about the year 818; and this opinion has until now prevailed among almost all scholars. But since Warinus, to whom Paschasius dedicated his work, did not assume the administration of New Corbie until 826, after Adalard’s death, their reasoning cannot stand. Moreover, since Saint Adalard—who was at different times called Antonius and Augustinus—was nowhere surnamed Arsenius or Jeremiah, their view collapses entirely. It is therefore preferable, with Mabillon and Cointius, to assert that Paschasius’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* was written during the exile of Wala, his abbot, at a time when the world was almost collapsing amid the labyrinths of discord, while an imperial dispute raged among the great. Paschasius’s own *Dialogue on the Deeds of Wala*, or, as the book’s title has it, the *Epitaph of Arsenius*, shows that this occurred between 830 and 832. In that work Wala is continually called Arsenius and Jeremiah.

After Paschasius had been made abbot of Old Corbie in 844, realizing that his book was being read by almost everyone and not without profit, he revised it again, enlarged it with various additions, and presented it to King Charles the Bald. From this one may infer how highly that golden book was then valued, and how worthy it was considered of being offered to the greatest of kings by so eminent a man. Certainly, the doctrine handed down by the Apostles and the holy Fathers concerning the sacrament of the altar—especially concerning what is called Christ’s real presence in the Eucharist, the conversion of bread and wine into his body and blood, commonly called transubstantiation, and other mysteries—he explained so clearly and distinctly that he opened the way for the many others who later wrote on the subject. For, as Possevinus says, “he has been regarded as a prophetic writer because he extinguished Berengar’s heresy almost two hundred years before it was born.” Hence Mabillon rightly asserted that, in the controversy over the Eucharist, there is such a close connection between Radbertus and the Catholic faith that “it is almost the same thing to attack or defend the one or the other,” since “the Roman Church recognizes Radbertus as an outstanding interpreter and defender of the apostolic tradition in this matter.”

Indeed, Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, after citing several passages from Paschasius’s book in Book II, chapters 30 and 31, of his *Collations*, adds:

> “He wrote these and many other things from the sayings of the Fathers in order to commend the reverence due to the mystery itself and to demonstrate its majesty. If anyone—even a mere smatterer—reads them, I believe he will learn so much that he will think he has previously known very little about this mystery.”

Everyone can therefore see how important it is to present learned and devout men with a text that is pure and cleansed of every defect, especially one revised and enlarged by the author himself. Our Petrus Sabbatier had long ago undertaken this task. Since he intended to publish, after correcting them against manuscripts, the works of the holy Fathers who treated the Eucharist expressly, he had already compared Radbertus’s book with twenty manuscripts. But when he turned all his studies toward restoring the ancient Italian version of the sacred Scriptures, he freely entrusted the entire work to me.

The manuscripts he compared are these:

- The very ancient manuscript of the church of Aniciensis, written in Radbertus’s own age.
- The Puteanus, about nine hundred years old, now preserved in the library of the Most Christian King, no. 4356.
- Three other manuscripts in the same library: no. 4070, about five hundred years old, which contains additions made by Paschasius over the course of time; and nos. 4074 and 4357, about six hundred years old.
- Two Colbert manuscripts, nos. 939 and 3682, about eight hundred years old.
- Two manuscripts of Queen Christina of Sweden, nos. 1547 and 1544, whose variant readings, while he was in Rome, our Mabillon had arranged to have recorded. One of these contains the additions mentioned above.
- The Vatican manuscript, no. 3472, formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint Euphemia at Brescia.
- The manuscript of the church of Saint Mary at Laon.
- The Tours manuscript of Marmoutier, at least seven hundred years old, and another Tours manuscript of Saint Martin, six hundred years old.
- The Reims manuscript of Saint Remigius.
- The Rouen manuscript of Saint Ouen, five hundred years old.
- Three manuscripts of Saint-Germain-des-Prés: no. 462, six hundred years old; no. 647, two hundred years old; and another not much older.
- Two manuscripts of the monastery of Corbie: no. 297, five hundred years old and of excellent quality; and no. 361, six hundred years old.

I added the Florentine manuscript of the monastery of the Friars Minor of Santa Croce. From its library the late Cardinal Bona had the treatise *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* of Geso, abbot of Derton, copied and sent to our Acherius. With a few exceptions, that work contains Paschasius’s entire little book. And so that nothing might be lacking from our diligence, we also consulted the ancient editions, about which it is worthwhile to say something.

Paschasius Radbertus’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* was first published—or rather corrupted—at Hagenau by Johann Secen in 1528 by Hiob Gastius, a Lutheran. Philipp Labbeus rightly calls his edition, in Book II, p. 157, of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, “the disgrace and dishonor of the innovators and evil-believers” after Cardinal Perronius. Mabillon says the following about it in the preface to the sixth century of the Benedictine history, vol. II:

> “Among the Lutherans, Hiob Gastus of Hagenau published Paschasius’s book in 1528, and finally dared completely to pervert it, in a deed plainly shameful and detestable. For when he observed everywhere that Paschasius was no less a champion of transubstantiation and sacrifice than of the real presence, the audacity of that most shameless man proceeded so far that he not only deleted entire chapters of the book, but also inserted and substituted other words and sentences, in order to persuade people that Paschasius supported his error.”

Twelve years later, namely in 1540, Guillaume Ratus, doctor of theology, canon and penitentiary of the church of Rouen, received from François Quadratus, a monk of Bec, Lanfranc’s *Dialogue against Berengar the Heresiarch*. Lanfranc had formerly been a monk of Bec and archbishop of Canterbury. Ratus decided to publish the dialogue and, so that he might produce a suitably substantial volume, appended to it Paschasius Radbertus’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. He gave it the following title:

> *A little book, drawn with great skill from the divine Scriptures by Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Hesychius, and Paschasius, the most ancient orthodox Fathers, concerning the genuine understanding and use of the Eucharistic matter, against all those made giddy by a frenzied sacramentarian spirit, who obstinately rely upon the opinions of the Fathers themselves; a truly Achillean weapon recently drawn, under favorable auspices, from an ancient copy for the destruction of all fanatics.*

When I compared this edition with the manuscripts and examined its corruptions, I found it identical with Gastius’s edition, which Ratus had reprinted in good faith without any further examination.

I think the same must be said of the edition said to have been produced at Louvain in 1541, for I have not seen it.

The first to detect the heretic’s fraud and poison was Nicolaus Mameranus of Luxembourg. When he compared the corruptor’s book with the manuscripts, he could scarcely contain his astonishment at the shamelessness of so perverse a man:

> “I cannot know what came into that man’s mind, or what tormenting spirit he then harbored, when he so wickedly mangled this author that scarcely anything sound, complete, or uncorrupted remained in almost the whole book. He repeatedly inverted the very sequence of the words, omitted many words, changed some, newly inserted very many, removed and altered entire clauses, and in some places threw out half-pages, in others whole pages and entire chapters, stuffing something of his own into the place of what he had discarded. I believe no other treatise has ever been so miserably and unjustly handled by anyone.”

A little later he adds:

> “He hated the rites of the Roman Church so much that wherever he found in Paschasius the word ‘priest,’ ‘altar,’ ‘offering,’ ‘consecration,’ or ‘penance,’ he either omitted it or, after striking it out, substituted something else. In place of ‘priest’ he everywhere put ‘minister of the Church’ or ‘minister of the word of Christ,’ which is not Paschasian; in place of ‘altar,’ ‘the Lord’s table’; in place of ‘offering,’ ‘intercession’; in place of ‘consecration,’ ‘blessing’; and in place of ‘penance,’ ‘recognition of sin and of the disobedience committed.’ Likewise, for ‘be celebrated’ he sometimes put, without any rational sense, ‘be eaten,’ and many other things of this kind. If he had not sinned more extensively throughout the book, this alone would sufficiently mark the audacity and crime of the man in another’s work. But these things are nothing compared with the many others he corrupted,” and so forth.

When this Catholic and honest man had detected the wickedness of the forger, he omitted nothing to ensure that Paschasius should emerge into the light complete and uncorrupted. As he himself says, he was unwilling to spare either the greatest labors or any expense in order to advance the public good. Setting aside every other, however serious, concern as soon as possible, he wished to restore this excellent author to his integrity and publish him, lest he should once again appear monstrous throughout the world through Hagenau adulteration and be distributed to the great detriment of his own reputation and of the Church. Accordingly, when he came upon two very ancient manuscripts of Paschasius at Cologne—one in the famous monastery of Saint Pantaleon of the Order of Saint Benedict, the other in the Dominican friars’ convent in the same city—he did not delay in publishing Paschasius according to their testimony, sincere and cleansed of all the heretic’s filth; he published the work at Cologne in 1550.

About the same time, John Ulimmerus, prior of the canons regular at Saint Martin in Louvain, undertook a similar scholarly project. Having received several manuscript copies of Paschasius Radbertus from England, he had prepared a new edition of the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. But, forestalled by Mameranus, he waited out the entire decade. When Mameranus’s privilege expired and his complete edition had been distributed, Ulimmerus sent Paschasius to the press again at Louvain in 1561.

Finally, in 1618, the most learned priest of the Society of Jesus, James Sirmond, of revered memory, committed all of Paschasius’s works—and therefore the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*—to the press at Nivelles, from a manuscript in the library of Corbie. From there it eventually passed into various libraries of the Fathers.

In almost all these editions and manuscripts Paschasius’s work is divided into twenty-two chapters. Mameranus divided it into forty-nine; a recently examined manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés has sixty-two sections; the Laubian manuscript has ninety-nine. We have retained the division found in almost all the manuscripts, contenting ourselves with recording in the lower margin the chapter titles displayed by the Laubian manuscript because of its antiquity.

[Col. 1259A]

## Verses Written by Paschasius Radbertus, Abbot, to King Charles

When he sent him his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*.

[Note: This did not occur before the year 844, when, after Isaac, abbot of Old Corbie, had died, Paschasius Radbertus was appointed in his place.]

[Col. 1259B]

A note in the Colbert manuscript begins as follows: “Now, now, from the icy…” On its authority we have removed *gelidae* (“of the icy [rock]”), which is found in the Aniciensis manuscript; Mabillon was the first to publish these verses from that manuscript.

Now, now, from the icy rock of the Camenae  
We ask that they come; but you, virgin Sophia,  
Who preserve the snowy summit of shining Olympus,  
Golden light illuminating the world, whose summit rises,  
And whose most gracious face sends forth Phoebe’s rays,  
While purple with fiery jewels arranges your shoulders—  
I beseech you to deign to yield to our prayers,  
And hasten to the king’s throne, venerable in its majesty,  
With measured step and modest countenance,  
So that, when you stand before him, you may speak with radiant face:

“O king powerful in virtue, whom the splendor of wisdom adorns,  
Charles, whose name descends through the ancestral line,  
Behold, your servant Abbot Radbertus offers  
A gift with devoted heart. May your tranquil majesty  
Receive it, and with eyes and heart behold  
What it contains, or what it pleads through the writing pen.  
It promises nothing earthly, but the mysteries of heaven.  
For it reveals Christ’s body, or the rosy stream of his blood,  
Showing what mysteries there are, so that whoever reads it  
With a devoted and faithful mind may stand in awe  
Before the heavenly secrets in visible form.”

[Note: The Aniciensis manuscript reads *arcana pavescit*, “stands in awe of the secrets.”]

[Col. 1259C]

## Letter of the Same Paschasius to King Charles

[Col. 1259C]

To the most excellent lord, King Charles, his humble and insignificant Paschasius Radbertus, your servant, though an unworthy abbot and a levite of Christ, the least scrap of all monks, offers abundant greetings, illustrious king.

[Note: His proper name was Radbertus, the name with which he subscribed the Council of Paris and under which Lupus wrote to him. “Paschasius” was an additional name which he himself habitually placed before his proper name, says Mabillon in his historical biography, chapter 1.]

[Note: Since Radbertus was so modest that, even after becoming abbot, he did not wish to be promoted to the priesthood.]

[Note: The word *plurimum* (“very much”), omitted in the printed editions, is supplied by the Aniciensis and Colbert manuscripts.]

From every direction, as is fitting, gifts of gold and silver, vessels of various kinds, ornaments of clothing and other furnishings, decorated horses, and the choicest animals will be sent for the festivals of the approaching Lord’s Day.

[Note: That is, for Christmas, as Mabillon conjectures in the preface to the tenth Benedictine century, part II, p. 9.]
