Among these gifts, although last of all, because you have commanded it and because, as I hope, mine too will please you, I, devoted in faith, have decided to offer your majesty a gift not slight in weight: namely, a little book small in bodily size but great concerning the sacraments of holy communion.

[Note: From this passage the opinion of Louis Cellotius is refuted—namely, that Paschasius Radbertus wrote two distinct books on the Eucharist: one shorter, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, published up to the present; and another longer one, *On the Sacraments*, which he says has been lost. This passage shows that *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* is the same book as *On the Sacraments*, by which name Paschasius calls it in Book XII of his *Commentary on Matthew*.]

I had long ago dedicated this book to my devoted and faithful Warinus, my Placidius.

[Note: From this one may infer that “Placidius” was an additional name of Warinus, abbot of New Corbie, under which he long remained unknown.]

I therefore wished to temper my rustic style in this way, so that those who had not yet been touched by the waters of liberal learning might grasp more plainly, for healing, the nourishment of life and the draught of salvation: namely, what it is necessary to know concerning the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood.

Now I have not feared to send it to you.

[Note: The Colbert manuscript reads *curavi*, “I took care,” instead of *dirigere*, “to send.”]

By this means, through you, a richer fruit of reward for my labor might overflow, since, commended by you, it would reach very many, and the grace of the gift offered might answer to us. For the currency of the word—as you know more fully, my lord king—fills as many hearers with its resources as richly as it is itself enlarged by an abundance of merits.

[Note: Nearly the same words occur in the letter to Placidius.]

For this reason, may your greatness and discernment not read these things with a light spirit, drawn by love of more precious words toward other matters. Rather, may your wisdom attend to this little table of poverty as though it were Solomon’s banquet, surrounded by sixty chosen mighty men from among the strongest of the citizens above.

[Note: The Colbert manuscript reads *mea que*, “and my,” rather than *in ea quae*, “in those things which,” as found in the printed editions. The latter is plainly a copyist’s error: he made two letters from one *m*, and wrote *quae* instead of *que*.]

If anyone proud, envious, or unworthy should approach there, I speak confidently under the protection of those of whom the passage speaks: these things must not be despised without danger. For each man’s sword is brandished on either side.

[Note: The manuscripts read *custodiant*, “that they may guard,” rather than *custodiat*, “that he may guard.”]

[Note: The reference is to 2 Kings 11:7.]

It is brandished both to blunt the audacity of such men and to guard the king’s watch against his enemies. Although this work may be less distinguished in eloquence, it is far more excellent in substance, through which incorruptible and eternal life is bestowed upon those who believe worthily.

Therefore, most beloved of the Augusti,

[Note: Perhaps *clarissime*, “most illustrious,” is intended.]

do not think that I am weaving you a tale about Maro’s seasoning. Rather, beware that no one stumble over these things, for nothing is happier than to reach them worthily with an understanding taste. Here, if I understand rightly, whenever anyone reclines amid the matters under discussion, he dwells amid the throng of angels and the feasts of all the saints. For it is the banquet of the eternal King which he enters, where the bridegroom and bride enjoy the sweet gifts of delights, and the King of all creation enters daily to see whether those reclining have the wedding garment in which they were reborn (Matthew 22:11–12).

Therefore we must not esteem such great grace lightly, but must consider how we may confidently attain the pastures of eternal life. Hence, most excellent king, may it please you to attend carefully to this discourse of a brief reading, and to the great power contained in these same mystical sacraments: to receive eternal life even now, and daily to be nourished by Christ’s angelic food in his body.

For although everything is full of God, and we are always before the eyes of the divine majesty, and there is nowhere a safe place for the faithless, nevertheless we must attend and reverence the great company of angels contemplating God’s face before the holy altars, observing the divine rites; and we must search out such matters with greater earnestness of mind and soul.

And so that your keen understanding may read these things more carefully, although they may appear humble, I beg you with prostrate prayers that, once this book has been approved by your judgment, it may henceforth be held more securely, even though it has already reached many. For I have not published these things from myself; rather, I have entrusted to my style the teaching of the Catholic Fathers, written with the pen of truth.

If your dignity should graciously receive what I offer in devotion, and if these little things of mine should please you, I shall sing Maro’s words at the end:

> “Ten golden apples I have sent; tomorrow I shall send another.”  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues* 3.)

## Verses of Paschasius Radbertus on the Body and Blood of the Lord

[Note: The following poem may be viewed as a graphic, so that the acrostic ornaments in the text, which cannot be keyed here, may be seen.]

[Note: Mameranus and Ulimmerus mistakenly read *Legis* (“of the Law”) for *Regis* (“of the King”); with *Legis*, the acrostic fails at its first letter.]

Whoever wishes to approach the sacred solemnities of the King’s table,  
To touch Christ’s life-giving body with his prayers,  
To feed upon delights and drink the rosy blood,

[Note: The printed editions read *Deliciis vesci*; against the authority of ten manuscripts, which consistently read *Delicias vesci* (“to feed upon delights”). Although *vescor* is more often construed with the ablative, excellent authors also use it with the accusative. This passage further shows that Radbertus’s name must be read with *d*, *Radbertus*, not *Ratpertus*.]

I would have you preserve the Bacchic things that we once sent  
To the boy, and store snowy flowers in a chaste heart.

[Note: “The boy” means Warinus, or Abbot Placidius, whom he calls a boy because he had instructed him from his earliest years.]

The rustic things may perhaps seem worthless to the mind, but honey will flow.

[Note: Mameranus reads this, together with the manuscripts, as *mella manabunt*, “honey will flow.” Ulimmerus and Sirmond, however, read *mella meabunt*, “the honeys will pass.”]

Only what the pen supplies from Christ’s fountain

[Note: The Aniciensis manuscript and the two Colbert manuscripts read *Iste tamen calamus* (“Yet this pen”).]

May at least quench the boy’s thirst (*possint restinguere*; alternatively, *restringesi*)—

[Note: We have restored this verse from the manuscripts of excellent quality. The earlier printed editions read: “From which you may quench thirst and the flames of death.”]

—if he wishes worthily to follow the commands of the Thunderer.

For the freedom of faith never denies anyone  
The outstanding fruits of life from the turf of the flesh:

Life, salvation, peace, light, and finally wisdom  
Flow from him beneath the fourfold vault of heaven.

[Note: Mameranus reads this with twelve manuscripts. Four manuscripts read, “From there, I testify, it flows”; two have, “From there it always flows.” The Aniciensis reads, “From there it flows through the age.”]

If you have lived worthily of these gifts,  
You too, blessed in virtue, will receive the palm of the kingdom.

[Note: Here ends the poem prefixed by Marten to the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. The following verses were taken from Muratori’s *Anecdota*, vol. III. Editorial note.]

God arranges a cause suited to our needs,  
So that the bread may be his body and the wine his blood.  
But so that the same odor, color, and taste may remain,  
It becomes the reward of faith, whose power is greatest.

It is the law of nature that it be changed into whatever the author commands.  
The command follows him; immediately it passes into that  
Which the Almighty orders, transforming the thing into a miracle.  
At once, therefore, nature changes its accustomed form.  
Soon flesh becomes bread, and finally wine becomes blood.  
He gives priests, incorporating them all into himself,  
So that they may perform these mysteries through him, and he through them.

Could a man have changed any nature by himself?  
Could a man have made the wheat substance divine?  
But the Word accomplishes this work—the Word that created everything entirely.

For once he commanded the earth to produce grass,  
What it does thereafter, throughout all the ages,  
He commanded also to be done; thus the substance is changed.  
This work is performed everywhere by him in the Supper.

He has always accomplished many things through visible power:  
When he cleaves the sea, a serpent in turn becomes a rod;  
The rock pours forth water, and the cloud also provides food;  
The pillar bears fire, and afterward vapor as a covering.

These things are evident before us; the manifest power is seen.  
He made those things openly, but this he performs secretly.  
This hidden work is revealed by visible signs,  
For God made the manifest things so that this might be believed.

While the eye sees the former, let the sight of faith also perceive the latter,  
Faith which doubts neither the truthful one nor the almighty one.

Wheat and wine, which generate virginity,  
Generate beautiful companies from virginity.  
The greatest offspring of the Virgin chose these forms,  
So that he might sanctify, by offspring, those whom he adopts in number.

This fills the granaries with wheat and the storerooms with wine;  
This makes the human heart glad, and that likewise makes it firm.  
Thus these two generate virgin dances.

[Col. 1264A]

Those who share the cup must remain clean.  
He washed their feet when the time of the Supper had come,  
Urging his disciples to lead a clean life,  
As participants in the divine sacrament by which they might be cleansed,  
So that, unlike Judas, they might not receive greater losses in salvation,  
Since the unclean dare to take the clean offering.

For he teaches that some, in the cup, will become a birth for themselves [the reading is uncertain],  
Yet through the sacred mysteries they take judgment upon themselves.

Hence he permits Judas to sit among the friends who feast,  
That infamous dog, to taste the heavenly banquet.

What harms the sick ultimately benefits the healthy:  
He who rains upon the unjust and supplies the sun to the wicked,  
Who wishes all to be saved and to recognize the truth,  
Grants this common good to all for their use.

Yet let each person see what sort of thing he takes and in what condition,  
To whom it is the reward of life and to whom the increase of Gehenna.

When the law had established other matters which this subject requires,  
It placed this first and commanded those eating the lamb  
To make it their concern to gird their loins.  
By placing what is more expedient first, it makes this clear.

It teaches the guests of the heavenly feast to be chaste:  
Let him who sacrifices according to the ancient rite partake of the veiled offerings;  
Let him who has been washed abstain from lawful intercourse with his spouse  
For a lawful time, since one tribe supplies ministers.

Yet these things are the shadow of the ancient rite and the type of the burnt offering.  
How much more ought he to be clean who clings to such things?  
Death kills the one who rejects the worship of the shadow; from this  
Gather what awaits the person who perhaps profanes the reality itself,  
Since great sin burdens everyone and pollution is worse.

Nothing is more hostile to the virgin offspring than such defilement,  
And the majesty of the matter becomes an obstacle if it is not discerned.  
“He receives judgment who does not judge rightly,” he says.

[Col. 1263C]

[Note: The ancient Colbert manuscript gives this title. Two royal manuscripts read: “Here begins the prologue of Paschasius the deacon in the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*.” One Corbie manuscript reads: “In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. Here begins the book of Ratbertus Paschasius the levite *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. Here begins the prologue of the work that follows.” The manuscripts of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and Tours-Saint-Martin agree with this, with a few changes. The Vatican manuscript reads: “Prologue of the book to Placidius,” as do two manuscripts of Queen Christina of Sweden and Sirmond’s edition. In many manuscripts and printed editions this title is absent.]

## Here Begins the Prologue of Paschasius Radbertus to His Disciple Placidius Concerning the Work That Follows

[Col. 1263D]

Paschasius Radbertus the levite, the least scrap of all monks, to his dearest son, presiding as Christ’s representative, master of monastic discipline, and fellow disciple of truth through alternating successions.

[Note: Several manuscripts give the inscription of the preface as follows: “Paschasius Radbertus sends greetings to his Placidius, his most beloved son, presiding in Christ’s place.” But our reading, found in the Corbie and Saint-Germain manuscripts, is more genuine and more suited to the author’s style.]

I know, therefore, and I have no doubt that your practical skill in disciplines has taught you that our Arsenius—whom our own age has now produced for us as a second Jeremiah after that earlier one—entrusted you to me in the matter of faith.

[Note: Until now most people understood “Arsenius” to mean Adalard, abbot of Corbie, whom Paschasius observes was at times called Antonius and Augustinus, but never Arsenius. Mabillon demonstrated in the life of Wala, which he was the first to publish under the title *Epitaph of Arsenius*, that Wala, Adalard’s brother, who was also called Jeremiah, was designated by this name.]

For this reason, from your earliest years I tirelessly took care to snatch you away from amid the waves. But I confess to you that the father’s cloak over your head proved more beneficial; and, rejoicing that you were carried across by it, I also rejoice that I had not run in vain.

[Note: Seven manuscripts read, “I rejoice that, carried across, you were then [safe].” The Laon manuscript reads, “I rejoice that you were carried across then.”]

(But your father, as is customary among those who favor justice, endures exile for the sake of the faith—if I may use the comic poet’s phrase, because he knew the truth and would not remain silent, being full of cracks.)

[Note: These words in parentheses are absent from Sirmond’s edition and from the Saint-Germain manuscript, but occur in almost all manuscripts and in Mameranus.]

[Note: Wala underwent several exiles: first in 830 to Lake Geneva, then in the following year to the island of Herio, where his brother Saint Adalard had spent seven years in exile; and finally to a certain monastery in Germany.]

Hence we still wonder what God’s providence intends to do with him further, since we already see him being divinely driven here and there by the promises of merits.

[Note: Three manuscripts of excellent quality—the Puteanus, Colbertinus, and Reims manuscript of Saint Remigius—read *actitari*, “to be driven,” while Mameranus, with the Vatican and Rouen manuscripts of Saint Ouen, has *accitari*, also “to be summoned or driven.”]

You, however, have not followed youthful desires, as those usually do who are unwillingly weighed down by the fetters of prolonged disciplines. Rather, rooted in the faith of Christ, you have freely advanced day by day in conduct and life toward better things, with the Lord’s help.

Nor, as I often reproached you, have I written upon ice before the sun; instead, in the solidity of faith and the charity of Christ, while the spirit inwardly strengthened the seed, I sowed the seeds of life.

[Note: Sirmond’s edition omits *spiritu*, “in the spirit,” which all the manuscripts preserve.]

Therefore, child of my vows, through the judgment of faith and the grace of love—even amid the world’s storms, especially while our world almost collapses through the labyrinths of its own discord, amid the imperial dispute poured out upon the great, and after their quarrel had long and greatly shaken it according to divine judgment—the hidden things which had grown up piecemeal on every side from the beginning now lie exposed, as the reins of desire are everywhere let loose and their lightning now strikes the highest mountains. Nothing reaches our ears except confusion, reverberating everywhere through each passing hour.

[Note: Most manuscripts read *nostrarum*, “of our [discords],” rather than the printed editions’ *noster*, “our.”]

Nevertheless, I have not refrained from taking care, through my prayers, to wash you clean for divine purposes alone—even though you are confined in custody—and to invite you, though driven from milk by yearly anxieties, to grow more happily toward the immortality of eternal things, even in unpolished speech.

[Note: It is not easy to determine why Paschasius was confined in custody. Perhaps he refers here to Wala’s exile at Lake Geneva, where Paschasius, sent there by order of the Emperor, may have remained for some time.]

For this reason I have chosen to temper this in a common rustic style, and, under the guise of love for you, to touch upon the things you require concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s blood and body, so that others who had not yet been touched by the waters of liberal learning might grasp more plainly with you, for healing, the nourishment of life and the draught of salvation; that a richer fruit of the work might overflow for us, and that there might be a reward for our labor. For the currency of the word—as you know more fully—fills as many people with its resources as it is itself more richly enlarged by an abundance of merits.

[Note: Mameranus reads *fructus mercedis*, “the fruit of reward.”]

Therefore, I ask you not to read these things with a childish mind, drawn by love of more precious words toward other matters, but to sit at this little table of poverty as though at Solomon’s banquet. Around it stand sixty mighty men, chosen from the strongest of those above.

If anyone proud, envious,

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads *immundus*, “unclean,” rather than *invidus*, “envious.”]

or unworthy should ever approach, I speak confidently under their protection: he despises these things at his peril.

[Note: Mameranus reads, “He despises this protection at his peril.”]

For each man’s sword is brandished above his thigh,

[Note: The printed editions read *vibrat*, “is brandished,” rather than *vibratur*, “is brandished [passively].”]

both to blunt the audacity of such men and to guard the king’s watch against his enemies. For although this work may be less distinguished in eloquence, it is far more excellent in substance, through which incorruptible and eternal life is bestowed upon those who believe worthily.

Hence do not suppose that I am weaving for you, my son, a tale about Maro’s seasoned delicacies; rather, believe that, after the milk of infancy, nothing must be guarded against more carefully lest you stumble over these things, and that nothing is happier than reaching them with a worthy, intelligent taste. There, if [Note: The manuscripts of the best quality—Puteanus, Colbertinus, Vaticanus, Rhemensis of Saint-Remigius, Laubiensis, Rothomagensis of Saint-Ouen, Turonensis, Majoris-monasterii, and one royal manuscript—read: “If you understand rightly.” Mameranus reads: “which, if you understand rightly.” The manuscript of Majoris-monasterii adds: “Whenever it pleases you to celebrate or partake of that most holy mystery, whenever you recline, etc.”] I understand rightly, whenever you recline, you are mingled among the multitude of angels and the banquets of all the saints, because it is the banquet of the eternal King [Note: One royal manuscript reads: “which [belongs] to the banquet.”]. There the bridegroom and bride enjoy the sweet gifts of delights, and the King of all creation enters daily [Col. 1266C] to see those reclining, to determine whether they possess the wedding garment in which they were reborn.

Therefore, since, dearest one [Note: The Sirmondus edition reads “in common,” contrary to the testimony of all the manuscripts, which read “dearest one.”], it is more dangerous to presume upon such things, to defile the riches of Christ’s delights with the crimes of one’s life, and shamelessly to touch what is holy, I wish you to take care not to enter these things together with those who practice wickedness. Rather, wash your hands among the innocent [Col. 1267A], since you have already been devoted to sacred offices, so that you may approach what has been entrusted to you without danger and touch with confidence the pastures of life. Refreshed by them and worthily nourished by them to the end of life, may you be able to reach the place of the admirable tabernacle, even to the house of God, amid the voice of rejoicing and confession, where there is the sound of one feasting.

Do not therefore despise so great a grace, but understand from this small reading how great is the power of receiving eternal life in the present and of being daily nourished with angelic foods. For although everything is filled by God [Note: Thus Mameranus, together with eight manuscripts. Sirmondus, however, reads: “Although everything is full of God.”], we too are always present before the eyes of the divine majesty, and for the faithless there is nowhere a safe place; nevertheless, especially before the holy altars, where one contemplates the throng of angels and the face of God, one must observe and reverence the divine services [Col. 1267B] [Note: The manuscript of Saint-Ouen reads: “venerate.”].

But so that your infancy may read these things more securely [Col. 1268A], it pleased me, dearest one, to list at the beginning the Catholic teachers of the Church, from whom I have filtered out a little of much material, as it were milk of tenderness [Note: Three manuscripts read: “I have filtered out.”]: Cyprian, Ambrose, Hilary, Augustine, John, Jerome, Gregory, Isidore, Isicius, and Bede [Note: Mameranus omitted Isidore and Bede.]. Having been imbued with the teaching and faith of these men, you may be better able to advance to higher things. In my own style I now commend their meaning, now use their very words [Note: Two royal manuscripts read: “using their words and examples.”], adapting what was suited to my purpose. At times I have confirmed by sound reasoning what plainly seemed evident [Note: The manuscript of Saint-Ouen reads: “what did not yet seem evident.” Vaticanus: “what seemed not doubtful.”], and I have also taken care to place in the margin of this same book, opposite the relevant passages, the letters of the teachers whom I listed above, using the initial of each name. Therefore read confidently, and devotedly carry out what I have instructed.

[Col. 1268B] The Prologue ends.

[Col. 1267]

[Note: The manuscripts vary concerning this title. The manuscript of Rhemensis of Saint-Remigius reads: “Here begins the text of the book on the body of Christ.” Two royal manuscripts: “Here begins the book of Paschasius the deacon on the mystery of the Body and Blood of the Lord Jesus Christ.” The manuscript of Saint-Germain: “Here begins the book of Paschasius Radbertus the Levite on the Sacrament of the Body and Blood.” Corbeiensis: “Here begins the book on the Sacraments.”]

# HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF SAINT PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD

[Col. 1267]

## CHAPTER ONE. It must not be doubted that the communion of Christ is truly his body and blood

### 1

Everyone among the Catholics who rightly believes in his heart, for righteousness, that God created all things from nothing, and confesses this with his mouth, for salvation, will never be able to doubt that something can again be made from something—as though this were contrary to nature, but rather in accordance with the law of nature—namely, that which did not yet exist. (Augustine.) For the nature of all creatures does not exist from itself, nor does it itself again create all things that are natural births of things [Note: Thus the manuscripts of the best quality: Laubiensis, Vaticanus, Turonensis of Saint-Martin, Rothomagensis of Saint-Ouen, Rhemensis of Saint-Remigius, and two manuscripts of Saint-Germain, together with six Corbeiensis manuscripts. The printed editions read: “which feed on the natural births of things,” a reading supported by the manuscript of Majoris-monasterii.]. Rather, the nature of all things was established by the will of God. Therefore everyone who thinks rightly [Note: The printed editions, together with the Florentine manuscript, read: “if he thinks rightly.”] does not call nature the cause of things, but confesses that the will of God is the cause of all natures and of the things that arise from their own nature [Note: Mameranus and Sirmondus read *denascentia*, “arising again.” Laubiensis, Vaticanus, Rothomagensis of Saint-Ouen, and one royal manuscript read *denascentium*, “of those arising again.”].

Moreover, the will of God is so effective and omnipotent that its mere willing is its doing; and therefore, for him to have willed something is to have made it. Hence the will of God alone is rightly believed to be the cause of all things and natures. Therefore, whenever something seems to happen in the world contrary to nature, it is in a certain sense not contrary to nature, because the most important characteristic of the nature of created things [Note: The printed editions read *creaturarum*, “of creatures”; the manuscripts, more correctly, read the same form in this context.] is that it always obeys the commands of the one from whom it comes. Thus, just as God’s willing is certainly its being, so too, whatever God’s power has again decided that it should be, is rightly increased either by growth or by birth [Note: The manuscript of Saint-Ouen reads: “or by decrease.”], although it may be diminished on account of our offenses, or, by being changed into something else that was not, may be transformed while the order of nature is set aside. This he most rightly confesses.

Hence one of our poets—namely Sedulius—beautifully said:

> All nature is subjected  
> To your commands, and, its customary order released,  
> At the ruling command passes into contrary forms.

[Col. 1268D] Since nothing is outside God’s power, he can do all things [Note: In the Laubiensis manuscript, the first chapter begins here with this title: “That the will of God is the cause of all creatures, and that therefore no one ought to be disturbed by the fact that Christ’s flesh is true flesh, and true blood the blood which we take from the altar.”].

For God, the maker of all things, did not establish the natures of things in such a way as to remove his willing from them. The subsistence of all creatures [Note: One royal Anician manuscript and Rothomagensis of Saint-Ouen read *subtantia*, “substance.”] subsists in that same will and power of God. From it each thing receives its cause—not only so that whatever exists may subsist, but also so that it may be as the will of God itself has decided, since that will is the cause of all creatures. Otherwise no existence of any creature would subsist except in his will, from whom all its being flows. Therefore, whenever the nature of a creature is changed, increased, or diminished, it does not turn away from the one in whom it exists, because it is and becomes as he decides in whom it exists [Note: In Sirmondus’s edition these words are omitted: “in whom it exists, because it is and becomes as he decides in whom it exists.” They are nevertheless found in Mameranus and Ulimmerius, as well as in two manuscripts of Saint-Germain, two royal manuscripts, two manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden, Vaticanus, Laubiensis, Puteanus, Colbertinus, Laudunensis, and Turonensis of Saint-Martin.].

### 2

It is therefore clear that nothing can exist outside or against God’s willing [Note: Four manuscripts read: “against God’s will.”], but that everything yields entirely to it. Therefore let no one be disturbed about this body and blood of Christ: that, in the mystery, it is true flesh and true blood [Col. 1269B], since he who created it willed it so. For “he has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 113:2). And because he willed it, although it remains under the figure of bread and wine [Note: Puteanus, Anicianus, Remigianus, Vaticanus, and Florentinus read: “although the figure of bread and wine,” omitting *in*. Three other manuscripts add *maneat*, “remains,” while Ulimmerius reads: “although the figure of bread and wine is here.”], we must believe that this is entirely so, and that after consecration it is nothing other than the flesh and blood of Christ. Hence Truth itself says to the disciples: “This is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52) [Note: Anicianus reads: “This,” he says.][Note: In the Laubiensis manuscript, chapter 2 begins here, with the title: “That what we receive in the Eucharist is nothing other than the flesh born from the undefiled Virgin, and the blood that flowed from Christ’s side.”]. And, to speak more wondrously, it is plainly no other flesh than that which was born from Mary, suffered on the cross, and rose from the tomb. (Ambrose.)

This, I say, is that very flesh. Therefore it is Christ’s flesh, which is still offered today for the life of the world; and when it is worthily received, eternal life is restored in us [Note: The word *hodie*, “today,” is absent from the Vatican manuscript, as are the words that follow shortly afterward: “And when it is worthily received, life is indeed restored in us.”].

If what we say seems less credible to anyone, let him consider all the miracles of the Old and New [Note: The word “New” is absent from Mameranus and three manuscripts, although it fits very well, since below he relates miracles of the New Testament just as he does those of the Old.] Testament that God performed contrary to the order of nature [Col. 1269C] to strengthen faith. He will see with complete clarity that nothing is impossible for God, since the will of God is the being of all things, and whatever God wills, each thing is [Note: Mameranus and Laubiensis read: “these individual things come to be.” Rothomagensis of Saint-Ouen reads: “this happens in a singular way.”].

### 3

But if someone does not believe these things, if he had seen Christ on the cross in the appearance of a servant, how would he have understood that he was God unless he had first believed through faith? So also in this body, where another appearance is shown, how can he see Christ’s flesh unless he first truly believes through faith [Note: The printed editions, together with certain manuscripts, omit “first”; eight manuscripts read *veracius*, “more truly,” instead of *veraciter*, “truly.”]?

Let him consider whether the Red Sea once possessed by nature the power to divide itself [Note: Vaticanus reads: “possessed the nature of dividing itself.”], so that the people might cross through the middle on dry ground; or whether all that water of the Egyptians possessed from itself—even though it happened through Moses—the power to change itself into blood, and so forth. Was it not in God’s will to entice the impious toward faith and to show, in the appearance of its color, that all the sprinkling of their doctrine and conduct had been turned into blood? (Augustine.)

Then, in the Gospel, water drawn from a spring: from where did it obtain the power to change itself into the taste of wine? And, to mention only a few examples out of countless ones, from where did that Babylonian fire, into which the three young men were cast, obtain by nature the power not to grow hot [or: “not to burn”]? Was it not in God’s will that it should become like a spirit breathing dew [perhaps: “breathing”], so that it might provide the saints with refreshment rather than combustion?

Let each person consider whether those five or seven loaves in the wilderness possessed substantially from themselves the power to satisfy so many people and then fill so many baskets, or whether what happened was in the grace [Note: The printed editions, together with certain manuscripts, add “of God,” but this is superfluous, since “of the Creator” follows immediately; Laubiensis instead reads “of the one creating all things.”] of the Creator: for by being diminished they multiplied.

Likewise, did the Virgin Mary possess the power to bear God as a virgin without intercourse, or was it in the power of God? And, to put it more plainly, is not our flesh, or that of animals, from the earth [Note: Five manuscripts read: “is it not from the earth?”]? Indeed, it is earth, because it was said: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Genesis 3). Although earth is therefore true flesh, even though corruptible, if it keeps the laws and commandments of God, it will again be clothed with immortality. Through the things we are explaining, although it was flesh, it was nevertheless incorruptible [Note: Mameranus and Sirmondus omit *sit*, “is.” Laubiensis reads: “Although earth is true flesh, it is corruptible.” Florentinus: “Although earth is true flesh, it is nevertheless corruptible.”].

### 4

I ask you, O man, to attend carefully to these things and, with respect to everything that naturally appears to exist, or that is read as having been made contrary to nature from the beginning of creation, to consider more closely whether individual things come to be from themselves in their own nature [Note: Vaticanus reads: “whether the individual things that are increased, diminished, or changed come to be.”], or whether those things that are changed into something that they were not become so according to the order of their own law, so that they may be miraculous. Or rather—and this you will acknowledge more readily—whether both those things that are almost natural and just, and those that seem to come contrary to nature, are altogether in the will of God, and whether each is created in his wisdom for the reasonable benefit of rational beings.

Therefore we rightly confess that the will of God is the cause of all things that exist, and not without reason, since his willing was his making. Hence, whenever something is made from something, it is made by the power of the will [Note: The manuscript of Majoris-monasterii reads: “from some power”; two manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden read: “it is made by power and will.”], and in his wisdom provision is made for how it should be made. (Hilary.)

Therefore neither will without power nor power without wisdom accomplishes anything, because the will of God is power and wisdom. Therefore whatever he wills comes to be as he wills, and he is deceived in nothing, because he wills all things in his wisdom; indeed, his wisdom itself is his will. For this reason he wills nothing evil [Note: “Nothing evil” is absent from Sirmondus’s edition, but is found in all the manuscripts and in the other printed editions], and nothing that he cannot accomplish.

Therefore, since he willed this mystery to be his flesh and blood, do not doubt in any way if you believe in God. Hold in your mind with true faith [Note: Laubiensis and Laudunensis, together with Mameranus, read: “but hold true faith.”] that this is that flesh which was offered for the life of the world, and that whoever worthily eats it will not see death forever [Note: In the Laubiensis manuscript, chapter 3 begins here, with the title: “That Christ bestowed nothing greater on the Church than the sacrament of baptism, etc.”]. (Ambrose.)

For Christ left nothing greater in the mystery to his Church than this sacrament and that of baptism, and also the Holy Scriptures. In all these things the Holy Spirit, who is the pledge of the whole Church, inwardly works the mystical means of our salvation unto immortality.

Yet in these things nothing marvelous is offered to unbelievers, while to believers nothing better, nothing more marvelous, and nothing richer is offered in this world—not so that they may appear marvelous to the eyes of sight, but so that they may breathe forth divine mysteries in faith and understanding, and so that in these same mysteries eternity [Note: Florentinus and Praedicatus read: “the participation of eternity for mortals.”] and participation in Christ may be granted to mortals in the unity of the body.

### 5

For this reason this mystery is far removed from all the miracles that have been performed in the world [Note: Two royal manuscripts read: “it is more marvelous than those.” Laubiensis reads: “it is removed from marvelous things.”], because all those miracles were performed so that this one thing might be believed: that Christ is truth. Truth, however, is God; and if God is truth, then whatever Christ promised in this mystery is certainly true. Therefore Christ’s flesh and blood are true [Note: Ulimmerius and Sirmondus read: “Christ’s flesh is true.” In Mameranus and most manuscripts, *est*, “is,” is absent.], and whoever worthily eats and drinks it [Note: The printed editions omit “and drinks.”] has eternal life remaining in him.

Yet, for the sake of bodily sight and taste, they are not changed, so that faith may be exercised unto righteousness and, on account of the merit of faith, the reward of righteousness may be obtained in it. For Christ’s other miracles confirm this one sacrament of his passion [Note: The printed editions, together with Florentinus, read: “confirms.”]. Therefore these things are not outwardly changed in appearance on account of a miracle, but inwardly, so that faith may be proved in the spirit; and we confess this most truly.

Thus, because “the righteous person lives by faith,” let him possess the righteousness of faith in the mystery and receive life through faith, life remaining in him. Thus, being still mortal yet more securely nourished by immortality, let him hasten all the more quickly toward immortality [Col. 1272A], where one arrives not by feet but by faith together with good works.

### 6

It is therefore established in every respect that, just as there was in paradise a tree [Note: The printed editions, together with three manuscripts, read: “there was the tree of life.”] from which the human condition and immortality would have remained perpetual if humanity had kept the commandments, so in the Church this mystery of salvation has been provided—not because that tree possessed this power by nature, but because an invisible power worked inwardly through a visible thing [Note: The manuscript of Majoris-monasterii reads: “through the visible reality.”].

So also in this visible sacrament of communion, divine power, by its invisible might, sustains us both by the taste and by the power of wisdom unto immortality, as though from the fruit of the tree of paradise. Through this, as long as we worthily receive it, we are immortal in soul; and afterward, transferred to a better state, we are borne toward immortality. (Hilary.)

For this reason “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14): so that, through God the Word made flesh, flesh might advance toward God the Word. That flesh of the Word becomes food and nourishment for the faithful in this mystery, since it is truly believed to be the flesh offered for the life of the world, and nothing other than the flesh of Christ’s body. From it Christ remains in us, so that through it we too may be transformed into him, who became nothing other than God made flesh through his condescension, so that he might dwell in us.

If, therefore, he dwells in us so that we, as members of his body, may remain in him, it is right that, since we are in him, we should live from him [Note: Laubiensis reads: “that we should receive from him.”]. Therefore we feed on the flesh of the Word and drink his blood.

This, I say, is the firmness of our faith; this is the unity and sharing of life. Here, if the order of nature is demanded, reason yields; yet the truth of what has been done remains beyond human reason [Col. 1272C], so that, in the logic of faith, the force of the Godhead and its effective power are believed in every respect. For doubt of mind—even if the person who receives is of good life—excludes him [Note: The Anician manuscript reads: “excludes him,” making the object explicit.] from attaining an understanding of this sacrament.

## CHAPTER TWO [Note: The Laubiensis manuscript calls this chapter 5: “That none of the faithful ought to be ignorant of this mystery, because, even if the recipient is of good life, doubt of mind excludes him from attaining an understanding of that sacrament.”] That none of the faithful ought to be ignorant of this mystery of Christ

### 1

No member of the faithful ought to be ignorant of the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, which is celebrated daily in the Church; no one ought to be unaware of what in it belongs to faith and what belongs to knowledge. For neither is faith in the mystery rightly defended without knowledge, nor is knowledge rightly defended without faith; faith, which does not yet comprehend, is nourished so that it may in due course understand.

Therefore the power of so great a sacrament must be investigated, and the faith of Christ must be instructed in discipline [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “and the discipline of Christ by faith must be taught.” Another manuscript reads: “and faith must be instructed through the discipline of Christ.” The Anician manuscript and one Colbertinus manuscript do not read “must be instructed,” but “must be nourished.”], lest we perhaps be judged unworthy because we do not sufficiently distinguish or understand it: namely, how much dignity and how great a preeminence of power the mystical body and blood of Christ possess, and how it is distinguished from bodily taste, so that it is more excellent than every sacrifice of the Old Testament.

### 2

If someone is ignorant of this, he does not distinguish it. Therefore we must fear lest, through ignorance, what was provided for us as a remedy become a ruin to those who receive it. Hence the Lord says in Leviticus (22:14): “Whoever eats of the sanctified things,” he says, “through ignorance, shall add a fifth part to what he has eaten, and shall give it to the priest in the sanctuary. And you shall not profane the sanctified things [Col. 1273B] of the children of Israel which they offer to the Lord, lest they bear the iniquity of their offense when they have eaten the sanctified things.” And he added: “I am the Lord who sanctifies them.” Then: “They are holy of holies.” (Isidore.)

Here, plainly, the mystery of Christ’s body and blood is signified. From it the power to eat is withheld not only from every foreigner, resident alien, and hired servant, but even from one who is blinded through ignorance of so great a mystery. The person who receives it through ignorance is one who is entirely ignorant of its power, dignity, and circumstances: one who does not know that it is truly the body and blood of the Lord according to the truth, although it is received in the sacrament through faith. He receives the mystery, indeed, but does not know the power of the mystery.

Therefore Solomon—or rather the divine Spirit speaking through him—commands: “When you sit at the table of a powerful person [Note: One Colbertinus manuscript reads: “at the table of a rich person.”], in order to eat with a ruler, carefully attend to what is set before you.” That is, you must prepare such things for yourself: daily proclaiming the mortification of Christ while carrying it about in your body.

Therefore carefully to understand and worthily to receive spiritual sacraments with the palate of the mind and the taste of faith—as though legally adding a fifth part to what one had previously eaten through ignorance—is to have the inner person receive divine things intelligibly through the grace of Christ and, through them, be incorporated into Christ by the power of faith [Note: Rothomagensis of Saint-Ouen and one royal manuscript read: “by that power of faith.”].

Otherwise, how would the law command someone to add a fifth part to what he had eaten through ignorance, when those things would no longer remain to which anything further could be added? For nothing is added to a thing that no longer exists, but only to one that still exists. Hence the Septuagint rightly commands that a fifth part be added to the thing itself.

The fifth part of that thing is therefore rightly added by us to what was previously received through ignorance if the five bodily senses are inwardly converted spiritually toward intelligible things. For if we think and receive rightly, the divine Spirit who is in us is also enlarged through that same grace [Note: Other manuscripts read: “is amplified”; others: “is fulfilled.”], and he instructs and orders these same senses of ours to perceive those things.

Thus he leads not only the inner taste toward the mysteries, but also sight, hearing, smell, and touch, illuminating them in a certain way [Note: Ulimmerius reads: “he illuminates them in a certain way”; one manuscript reads: “so that we hold them illuminated in a certain way.”] to such an extent that nothing but divine things is perceived in them, nothing but heavenly things—and, what is sufficiently fearsome, what is communicated.

Hence how rightly it is said: “Let him add its fifth part upon it,” or, as other manuscripts have it, “with it,” “and he shall give it to the priest.” For the whole sanctification of the mystical sacrifice and its efficacy—how a sensible thing is transferred intelligibly, through the power of God and through the Word of Christ, into his flesh and blood, and how those who communicate through these things are nourished spiritually—must be attributed entirely and wholly to Christ, who is the true and supreme priest, and assigned to his power [Note: Rothomagensis of Saint-Ouen adds: “to attribute entirely.” In Florentinus, “and wholly to his power” is absent.] and to his own might [Note: Vaticanus and Florentinus read: “to assign”; the printed editions: “to designate.”].

For he frees us from all ignorance and removes us from the enticements of the flesh of this life [Note: In some manuscripts, “enticements” is absent]. He does not allow us to suspect anything earthly or base in that place, but teaches us to understand mystical and spiritual things in them, so that the senses of our body may be transferred more eagerly toward being sanctified inwardly for these things [Note: Mameranus and Vaticanus read: “transferred toward sanctifying them inwardly.”]. Thus the more eminent part of the human being may be able to say: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Psalm 83:3).

### 3

Therefore the whole person rightly rejoices in the living God. For although Christ’s flesh and blood are eaten daily by everyone [Note: One royal manuscript adds: “and drunk.”], the living and whole Lamb himself nevertheless remains. “He does not die now; death shall no longer rule over him” (Romans 6:9). Yet in the mystery he is truly sacrificed daily [Note: The printed editions read: “he is sacrificed.”] and eaten for the cleansing of sins. (Isidore.)

Hence the same sentence of the law immediately continues: “I am the Lord who sanctifies them” (Leviticus 20:16). He sanctifies those who, through these things, appropriately advance toward God who sanctifies, and who receive them with devotion in the manner in which they ought to be received. For he offered these things to those reborn in Christ as the cause of sanctification, not of defilement.

Otherwise, as the law says, “he shall bear the iniquity of his offense” (ibid.), namely, the one who has defiled the sanctified things by eating them through ignorance, or who seeks them unworthily out of contempt.

Therefore those who receive the sacraments of life must be instructed, lest, if someone negligently remains ignorant of the saving rudiments of the faith, he too should be entirely unknown to the Lord.

## CHAPTER THREE [Note: In the Laubiensis manuscript, chapter 6.] What the sacraments are, and why they are called such

### 1

A sacrament, then, is whatever, in some divine celebration, is handed down to us as a pledge of salvation, when a visible action [Note: The manuscript of Majoris-monasterii reads: “a visible gesture.”] inwardly effects something far different and invisible [Note: Florentinus reads: “effects something invisibly within.”], which must be received in holiness.

Hence they are called sacraments either from secrecy, because, through a bodily appearance, divinity inwardly effects something more secret than our capacity can grasp [Note: Vaticanus reads: “the divine power effects something more secretly, beyond our capacity.”]; or from the consecration of sanctification, because the Holy Spirit, remaining in Christ’s body, secretly works all these mystical things of the sacraments beneath the covering of visible realities for the salvation of the faithful [Note: Three manuscripts read: “the mystical mysteries.”].

Divine power therefore instructs the minds of believers through this toward invisible things more than if it visibly displayed what it inwardly provides for the effect of salvation: “For we walk by faith and not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7).

### 2

The sacraments of Christ in the Church are baptism and chrism, as well as the Lord’s body and blood. They are called sacraments for this reason: under their visible appearance, which is seen [Note: The printed editions read: “under the visible appearance which is seen,” using a plural verb in the alternative reading], the flesh is more secretly consecrated through divine power [Col. 1275C], so that inwardly they are in truth what outwardly they are believed to be through the power of faith.

(Isicius.) There is also the sacrament of a legal oath, in which, after the sides have been chosen, each person swears to what he has determined by his agreement [Note: One manuscript reads: “what he has determined for his side.”]. It too is called a sacrament because, through the consecration of an invocation of God or of something sacred, invisible faith is held more secretly, from the fact that outwardly the voice of the person swearing is perceived by sight or hearing.

The birth of Christ also, and the whole dispensation of his humanity, is a great sacrament, because, in visible humanity, the divine majesty inwardly and invisibly worked by its own power, for our consecration, those things that were being done [Note: Mameranus and three manuscripts read: “inwardly worked an entreaty.”].

Hence it is rightly called a mystery or sacrament that God became man. But it is called a Greek mystery [Note: Nearly all the manuscripts of better quality have this reading. Sirmondus, together with one manuscript, omits “is Greek.” The Laubiensis manuscript reads: “It is Greek, and therefore it is called so, because it contains within itself a secret and hidden dispensation.”] because it contains within itself a secret and hidden arrangement.

There is also a sacrament in the divine Scriptures wherever the Holy Spirit, by speaking inwardly and effectively in them, accomplishes something. Through the sacrament of the Scriptures, once instructed [Note: The printed editions, together with a few manuscripts, read “instructing,” and below “feeding.”], we are nourished inwardly by God, and, having been nourished, we are instructed in the practice of Christ’s discipline.

Through the sacrament of his birth and humanity [Note: Florentinus reads: “and his humility.”] we are redeemed for pardon; the Scriptures are opened to understanding; the way is shown to us through him; and power is granted so that we may pass from servitude into the adoption of sons.

Through the sacrament of baptism, the door of entry into that same adoption is opened to believers, so that thereafter, liberated from evil through the same rebirth among the members of Christ, we may become one body. In this baptism, and thereafter, the Holy Spirit is poured into the soul of the one being reborn, so that the whole Church of Christ, having received one Spirit, may be enlivened and become one body.

For just as all the members of our body are enlivened and governed by one soul, so that from the joining of the members one body may be formed, so the members of the whole Church are governed and enlivened by one Holy Spirit, so that they may constitute one body of Christ. “For if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9).

### 3

No one therefore doubts that each of us, while still enclosed in his mother’s womb, receives a soul, though secretly, so that he may be a human being possessing a living soul—sometimes in such a way that the mother does not know when life enters the child through that soul before the child emerges.

In precisely the same way, no one ought to doubt that, in the basin of baptism, before the infant rises from the font, the Holy Spirit comes upon the one who is being reborn, even though he is not seen [Col. 1276C]. For divine power is no less provident and effective for the regeneration of sacred adoption than it was previously at the birth of the flesh, when it gave life to the formed members of a human being, even though they had been conceived in sin.

From this there arises for us a convincing argument [Note: Thus the manuscripts of better quality. Sirmondus, together with a few manuscripts, reads: “so that it is not doubtful.”] that God, the examiner of all things and the effective giver, always dispenses fruitful grace [Note: Mameranus, Ulimmerius, and Sirmondus read: “dispenses fruitful grace”] so that what he has ordained may not be changed.

If, amid the occasional violations of the father and the crimes of the mother, members of a human being conceived from lust are brought to life, how much more does the Holy Spirit, everywhere present because he fills the world, offer himself readily, so that he may enter all who are reborn through faith, in order that through him the members of Christ may be of one mind, and that from them all one body may be formed.

[Col. 1276D] 4. Moreover, by the sacrament of the body and blood we are nourished and given drink in equal measure on the journey, so that, nourished by it, we may become one in Christ; and, invigorated by its taste, we may be prepared for immortal and eternal things [Note: [Col. 1277D] The printed editions, together with Flor., read *praeparemur*, “we may be prepared.”], so that, already spiritually fattened by angelic grace, we may be made alive in him. The divine Spirit works for us in all these sacraments. For in the Holy Scriptures he enlightens our hearts, since “neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7). Hence Ezekiel says: “For the spirit of life was in the wheels” (Ezek. 1:21). And John says: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Rev. 2:7).

Moreover, the same Spirit cooperates in Christ, because he is believed to have been conceived by him and of Mary the ever-Virgin [Note: [Col. 1277D] In most manuscripts *semper*, “ever,” is omitted. In the Tours manuscript of St. Martin, the following words, apparently omitted, are written in the margin: “And Mary ever-Virgin—not as though the Holy Spirit, God forbid, became seed for offspring in her most holy womb, but rather he employed the Creator’s virtue and power.”]. In a similar way, through water in baptism we are all regenerated from him; thereafter, by his power, we are daily nourished by the body of Christ and given drink of his blood. Hence [Note: [Col. 1277D] Ulim., with Flor., reads: “Hence it is not surprising if the Holy Spirit, who created the man in the Virgin’s womb without seed, himself also makes the substance of bread and wine the flesh and blood of Christ,” etc.] it is not surprising that the Spirit who created the man Christ in the Virgin’s womb without seed also, by invisible power, works daily through the sanctification of his sacrament to make the substance of bread and wine the flesh and blood of Christ, although this cannot be grasped outwardly either by sight or by the taste of its flavor. But because these things are spiritual, they are received with certainty, fully, by faith and understanding, just as the Truth foretold.

## CHAPTER IV [Note: [Col. 1277D] Laub., chapter VII.] Whether this mystical sacrament of the chalice is made under a figure or in truth

1. No one who believes the divine words doubts that, through the consecration of the mystery, the body and blood truly come to be. Hence the Truth says: “For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:56). And so that it might become clear to the disciples, who did not understand correctly, of what flesh and of what blood he was speaking, he makes the matter explicit: “Whoever eats my flesh,” he says, “and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (ibid., 57). Therefore, if it is truly food, it is also true flesh; and if it is truly drink, it is certainly true blood. Otherwise, how would what he says be true: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (ibid., 52), unless it were true flesh? And likewise, is the bread that came down from heaven (ibid., 51) not true bread [Note: [Col. 1277D] The royal manuscript reads: “It is true bread.”]?

But because it is not permissible for Christ to be chewed by teeth, he willed that this bread and wine should truly be made his flesh and blood in the mystery, through the consecration of the Holy Spirit and by his power; and, once made so, that it should be mystically sacrificed daily for the life of the world. Thus, just as true flesh is created from the Virgin through the Spirit, without intercourse, so through that same Spirit the same body and blood of Christ are mystically consecrated from the substance of bread and wine. Concerning this flesh and blood he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have eternal life in yourselves” (ibid., 54).

Here, plainly, he speaks of no other than true flesh and true blood, although mystically. Therefore, since it is a mystical sacrament, we cannot deny that it is also a figure. But if it is a figure, we must ask how it can be truth. For every figure is a figure of something, and it always refers to that thing, so that the thing of which it is a figure may be true [Note: [Col. 1277D] Seven manuscripts read “refers to him”; the Vatican manuscript, “refers to it.”]. No one who has read the sacred writings doubts that the figures of the Old Testament were shadows. This mystery, however, is either truth or figure—and, if figure, it is a shadow.

Or rather, the whole question must be examined: can it be called truth without the shadow of falsity, although such a thing ought to be called a mystery? It appears to be a figure when it is broken, when something other than what is perceived by bodily sight and taste is understood under its visible appearance, and when blood is mixed in the chalice together with water.

Nevertheless, that sacrament of faith is rightly called truth: truth, therefore, when the body and blood of Christ are made, by the power of the Spirit in his word, from the substance of bread and wine; but figure when, while the priest outwardly performs something else, the Lamb is sacrificed at the altar daily in remembrance of the sacred Passion, which took place once for all [Note: [Col. 1278D] Mamer., Sirm., and most manuscripts read: “while the priest … performing … sacrifices the Lamb.” Ulim., Flor., and certain other manuscripts read: “while the priest … comes to the altar, and what was performed once is sacrificed daily.”].

2. If we examine the matter truthfully, it is rightly called both truth and figure: the figure, or character, of truth is what is perceived outwardly; but truth is whatever is rightly understood or believed inwardly concerning this mystery. Not every figure is a shadow or falsehood [Note: [Col. 1278D] In the Laub manuscript, chapter VIII begins here, with the title: “That every figure is a shadow or falsehood.”]. Thus Paul, speaking of the only-begotten Son of God to the Hebrews, says: “Who, being the splendor of glory and the figure of his substance, and sustaining all things by the word of his power, having made purification for sins…” [Note: [Col. 1278D] The royal manuscript adds: “sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high.”].

By these words he plainly declares two substances in Christ, and both of them true. When he says that he is the splendor of the glory of divinity, he proclaims him consubstantial [Note: [Col. 1278D] The printed editions and manuscripts vary here. Laub., Putean., and two St.-Germain manuscripts read: “he proclaims him consubstantial.” Vatic. and Flor. read: “he proclaims him consubstantial with the divinity”; another manuscript: “he proclaims the divinity consubstantial”; the printed editions: “he proclaims him consubstantial with the divinity.”]. When, however, he calls him the figure or character of his substance, he designates the nature of his humanity, in which the fullness of the Divinity dwells bodily; and yet, in both, one true Christ God is proclaimed according to Catholic faith.

Thus he takes one thing to demonstrate two substances and calls it the figure or character of the substance. For just as, through the characters or figures of letters, our infancy first advances gradually to reading, and then to the spiritual meanings and understanding of the Scriptures, so from Christ’s humanity one arrives at the Divinity of the Father; and therefore it is rightly called the figure or character of that substance.

For what else are the figures of letters than their characters, through which their force and power, and the utterance of the spirit, are displayed to the eyes [Note: [Col. 1279D] Ulim. and Sirm. read *prolatione*, “by the utterance”; the manuscripts read *prolatio*, “the utterance.”]? Thus the Word is formed as flesh, so that through the flesh our infancy may be nourished toward understanding the divinity.

Nevertheless, neither are the characters of letters falsehood, nor are they anything other than letters; nor can Christ as man be called falsehood, nor anything other than God, although he is rightly called the figure—that is, the character—of the substance of the Divinity, because through himself he advances our infancy toward inward understanding of spiritual things and shows himself visible to our senses, so that we may grasp the things that are in him.

But because he had to penetrate the heavens according to the flesh, so that, reborn in him through faith, we might pursue them with greater confidence [Note: [Col. 1279D] The printed editions read: “might desire to follow them.”], he left us this visible sacrament [Note: [Col. 1279D] Vatic., Major Monastery, St. Audoen, St. Remigius, one royal manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, Putean., Mamer., and Ulim. read “a visible figure”; Sirm. reads “visible figure.”] as a figure and character of his flesh and blood, so that through these our mind and flesh might be nourished more abundantly by faith toward the apprehension of invisible and spiritual things.

The outwardly perceived thing is a figure or character [Note: [Col. 1279D] Another manuscript reads: “a figurative character.”], but everything that is perceived inwardly is truth and no shadow at all [Note: [Col. 1279D] Two manuscripts read “no obscurity.”]. Thus nothing other than truth and the sacrament of that flesh is disclosed on either side.

3. It is truly Christ’s flesh, the flesh that was crucified and buried; and it is truly the sacrament of that flesh [Note: [Col. 1279D] Sirm. reads: “the true sacrament of that flesh.”], divinely consecrated by the priest on the altar through the word of Christ and through the Holy Spirit. Hence the Lord himself cries: “This is my body” (Luke 22:19).

And do not marvel, O man [Note: [Col. 1279D] Anic. reads: “And do not delay, O man.”], nor seek the order of nature. If you truly believe that that flesh was created from the Virgin Mary in the womb without seed, by the power of the Holy Spirit, so that the Word might become flesh, then truly believe also that what is made through the word of Christ and through the Holy Spirit is his body from the Virgin.

If you seek an explanation, who could express or comprehend it in words? Rather, know, I beg you, that the explanation lies in Christ’s power, knowledge in faith, the cause in his authority, and the effect in his will; for the power of the Divinity works effectively against nature, beyond the capacity of our reason.

Therefore let knowledge be held in the teaching of salvation and faith be maintained in the mystery of truth, since in all these things we walk by faith and not by sight [Note: [Col. 1279D] At the end of this chapter Sirmond appends the following observation: “Paschasius sometimes speaks in such a way that by ‘the body and blood of the Lord being created’ he means that they begin to exist in the sacrament, and likewise that bread and wine are transubstantiated. Otherwise, theology teaches us that transubstantiation and creation differ, although they agree in some respect. See St. Thomas, *Summa theologiae* III, q. 75, a. 8.”].

## CHAPTER V [Note: [Col. 1279D] This chapter, which is chapter IX in the Laub manuscript, has the following title there: “What difference there is between the figures of the legal sacrifices and the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, and that the Lamb, manna, and all such things bore the figure of this same sacrament.” In the Vatican manuscript: “What difference there is between the offering of the old and the new Lamb.”] [Col. 1280A] What difference there is between the sacrifices and figures of former times and the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood

1. No faithful person rightly fails to know that the sacrifice of that lamb was a figure of Christ’s Passion and of our communion. But what difference there is between that sacrifice and this sacrament—or between the food that came down from heaven, and the water that flowed from the rock, and this spiritual and divine exchange—I think must be investigated, especially since the blessed Apostle cries out: “All our fathers ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink” (1 Cor. 10:3).

If they received the same food and the same drink, what need was there for what was itself to be changed, or for something seemingly different to be given, if there is nothing more? From this it must be acknowledged that it was the same food and the same drink as that which we now receive, just as it was the same rock from which the waters flowed; and, according to the Apostle’s testimony, Christ was proclaimed there.

It was the same food, for manna, when received spiritually, was a type of the food of Christ’s body; and that water which had flowed from the rock was a drink and figure of his blood. For in the prefiguration they were the same, and were the shadow of the body and its representations, but they were not the same in the fulfillment of truth: what was then shadowed forth in the designation of future things was an image of the truth; but now there is the mystery of fulfilled truth, and the Eucharist has become the flesh of Christ through the resurrection, which had previously been figured for believers by the lamb or by that same Church, as something that would come [Note: [Col. 1280D] The printed editions and Flor. read: “by that same food from heaven.”].

Of this bread David had sung in parables: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25). Otherwise, although that food came from heaven, and the drink likewise, because they were corporeal they were not suitable for angels; rather, it was that bread and drink which were foreshadowed by these things [Note: [Col. 1280D] The printed edition reads *praesagiebatur*, “was foreshadowed,” contrary to the reading of all the manuscripts.].

Christ, therefore, is the food of angels; and this sacrament is truly his flesh and blood [Note: [Col. 1280D] The printed editions, together with certain manuscripts, read: “truly flesh.”], which a human being eats and drinks spiritually [Note: [Col. 1280D] The passage that follows, up to “It is therefore evident,” is absent from the Putean and Rheims manuscripts of St. Remigius.]. Thus, by what sustains angels, the human being also lives, because everything in what the human being receives is spiritual and divine.

2. It is therefore evident that the legal lamb, the manna, and all such things that bore the figure of Christ’s flesh and blood—Christ who suffered once at Passover and is sacrificed daily on the altar, morning and evening—possessed nothing but the figure of this mystery [Note: [Col. 1281D] Three manuscripts read: “possessed.”]. And if some consecrating power lay hidden in them, it all shone forth from this grace of faith which we enjoy. Through these things, they participated in that grace by faith, sighing for it as something promised [Note: [Col. 1281D] The Putean manuscript reads: “as though sighing for the promised thing, they participated in it.”], and they understood the sacrament of truth from the figures.

We, however, have already received this grace, long ago promised to the fathers; and having received it, we venerate it. In venerating it, we are nourished and given drink from it—not shadowed by the figures of legal riddles [Note: [Col. 1281D] Mamer., together with Putean., one Colbert manuscript, the Remigius manuscript, and the Tours manuscript of Major Monastery, reads: “legal enigmas.”], but with these things disclosed [Note: [Col. 1281D] Sirm. reads “with these things defective,” contrary to the reading of all the manuscripts.] and emptied of their former obscurity, we enjoy truth alone, and in the mystery receive the true flesh and blood of Christ.

Hence the Savior says: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink; whoever eats this flesh and drinks this blood has eternal life” (John 6:49).

Moreover, the Lord said to the Jews: “Your fathers ate manna in the desert and died.” Shall we also, who eat these things, not die temporally as they did? We shall die, but not as they did in soul, because they died eternally by eating in a carnal manner [Note: [Col. 1281D] The printed editions read: “by eating carnal things.”]—although Mamer., Ulim., and certain manuscripts read: “in soul.” We, however, while perceiving nothing carnal in it, but understanding the whole spiritually [Note: [Col. 1281D] The printed editions read: “being spiritual.”], remain in Christ.

Therefore he himself cries out concerning those who receive rightly: “Whoever eats this bread will live forever.” For Christ’s flesh and blood are not received spiritually for the sake of this life, so that we may not die temporally, but for the sake of eternal life. Those who formerly received this in figure with due reverence did not enter into that life until the grace promised equally to us and to them should come.

3. Hence it is evident that there is a great difference, although the Apostle proclaims the same food and the same drink: they were the same not yet in reality, but in appearance [Note: [Col. 1282D] The printed editions read “in hope.”] and figure, where the promise of truth was present. Through this they were granted spiritual understanding and the sacraments of faith, although these things were still future, so that they did not lack in spirit what they already drank in hope [Note: [Col. 1282D] Three manuscripts read: “what they often drank in hope.”], nor do we lack what, by recalling them, may contribute more abundantly to the firmness of faith and the reception of life.

Both they and we [Note: An alternative reading has “however” for “and.”] are made alive by spiritual reception, because they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, signifying that Christ would come after them. We also spiritually drink and eat the spiritual flesh of Christ [Note: [Col. 1281D] Another manuscript reads: “we spiritually drink and eat.”], in which eternal life is believed to exist. Otherwise, to think according to the flesh is death, whereas to receive the true flesh of Christ spiritually is eternal life.

## CHAPTER VI [Note: [Col. 1282D] Laub., chapter X.] What it means to receive the body and blood of Christ worthily for life

1. Christ himself explains this: “Whoever eats my flesh,” he says, “and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57; Augustine, *Tractate 26 on John*, near the end).

To eat his flesh and drink his blood, then, means this: that the one who receives worthily remains in Christ, and Christ can remain in him. The person who remains in Christ is one who, reborn from water and the Spirit, is not held guilty of any mortal sin. Christ, in turn, is in the one who has opened for him the door of faith through the Holy Spirit consecrating [Note: [Col. 1282D] Five manuscripts read “through the consecrated Holy Spirit”; some read “the consecrated one.”], so that he may be a member in Christ’s body and a temple of the Holy Spirit; for “if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.”

Whoever does not belong to him cannot truly be either in him or in his body. Whoever does not remain in him does not live by the life of the Spirit in the body; in such a person Christ is not, nor can that person be in Christ, because Christ is altogether life. But one guilty of mortal sin is separated far from life.

Hence also he says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me and I in him” (John 6:57). Otherwise, unless he first remains in me and I in him, he cannot eat my flesh or drink my blood.

2. But what is it that human beings eat? Behold, all indiscriminately and repeatedly receive the sacraments of the altar [Note: [Col. 1282D] In the Laub manuscript, chapter XI begins here with the title: “What it is that the unworthy or the worthy receive in the Eucharist.”]. They certainly receive them, but one spiritually eats the flesh of Christ and drinks his blood, while another does not, although he appears to receive a morsel from the priest’s hand.

And what does he receive, if the consecration is one and he does not receive the body and blood of Christ? He truly receives condemnation, because he receives unworthily, as the Apostle Paul says: “He eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not first examining himself nor discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:29).

Behold what the sinner eats and what he drinks [Note: [Col. 1282D] Flor. adds: “not first examining himself.”]—not, certainly, flesh and blood beneficially for himself, but judgment—although he appears to receive the sacrament of the altar with the others. And why? Because he does not examine himself, nor discern the Lord’s body.

The unbeliever thinks that what is worthy and holy can be received by the unworthy, attending to nothing except what he sees and understanding nothing except what is perceived by the mouth [Note: [Col. 1282D] The manuscript of St. Audoen reads: “except what you perceive by the mouth.”]. He therefore neither believes nor understands what kind or how great a judgment he receives. He sees everyone eating from one thing outwardly, and by faith he does not sufficiently perceive whether there is any further power in it.

For this reason the power of the sacrament is taken away from him, and because of his presumption the guilt of judgment is doubled in the same person [Note: [Col. 1283D] Three manuscripts read: “the guilt of judgment.”]. Hence the Apostle says: “Let a person examine himself first, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the chalice” (ibid., 27).

When these two things have been observed, let him see whether he can receive worthily: namely, let him discern the Lord’s body—what the sacrament is, how great it is, and what kind of power belongs to the sacrament, since it is divine and spiritual. Then let him examine himself, to determine whether he is in the body of Christ, or whether Christ remains in him. Otherwise, unless he also spiritually judges that matter [Note: [Col. 1283D] Another manuscript reads: “discerns that matter.”] and proves himself fit to receive it, he eats judgment upon himself, because he uses a good thing badly. Thus he receives it not for life, but judgment for punishment [Note: [Col. 1283D] The passage that follows was recovered from the excellent manuscript 1554 of Queen Christina of Sweden and manuscript 4070 of the library of the Most Christian King.].

3. To confirm what we have said by more certain examples, we shall relate what happened to a certain unbeliever who, without discerning the Lord’s body and without examining himself according to the Apostle, presumptuously received these mysteries unworthily.

When the blessed Syrus, first bishop of the people of Ticinum, was celebrating the solemn Mass in the church of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, which he himself had dedicated, and a great number of his spiritual children—whom, according to the Apostle, he had begotten for God by the seed of the word—were devoutly attending the sacred mysteries, a certain Jew entered boldly. Instigated by an evil spirit, he attempted to receive the Lord’s body and throw it into a dung heap.

Having made his way, amid the crowds of faithful receiving the holy Eucharist from the bishop’s hand, to the man of God, he sacrilegiously received the Lord’s body with his unclean mouth and covered his mouth with it in order to cast it out. Struck by a fitting punishment, he began to cry out, though without intelligible words, so that all could hear and see.

He wanted to close his lips, but could not; he wished to utter words, but his rigid tongue did not provide the service of speech. As though carrying a flaming dart in his mouth, he was tormented by immense pains. The whole church resounded with the cries of his inarticulate voice, while the assembly of Christ’s faithful rejoiced at the power of so remarkable a miracle.

Thus was fulfilled: “He himself mocks the mockers” (Ps. 58); and what the Apostle writes to the Galatians: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked; for whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (Ps. 6:7); and also what the Truth himself promises in the Gospel, saying: “With the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Mark 4:24).

This unbelieving Jew had neither heard nor read these proclamations of Scripture. He had thought that he could deceive Christ and the Holy Spirit. The man of God ordered him to be brought before him, and when he arrived he said to him:

“Unbelieving mind, full of faithlessness, why have you fulfilled the counsel of so wicked an enemy, thinking that the body of Christ was worthless? Behold, the divine power has shown to all his faithful who that secret persuader was who induced you, miserable man, to do this.”

The Jew, overcome by excessive pain, did not cease emitting sounds without speech.
