He had the torture of his wickedness in his throat, because, according to the prophecy of the most holy Simeon, just as the Word of God is destruction and ruin for unbelievers, so it is life and exaltation for his faithful.

To those who looked closely, the Lord’s body appeared, in a pitiable suspension, to hang in the Jew’s mouth, so that it rested neither upon the structure beneath the tongue nor adhered above to the unclean palate.

When all the faithful pleaded for his misery, the man of the Lord, Syrus, stretched out his own hand and drew the mystery of the Holy Eucharist from the sacrilegious mouth, saying:

“Behold, unbeliever, now you have been freed. Henceforth beware of doing anything like this, and do not repeat it, lest something similar, or worse, happen to you.”

The Jew then fell at his feet and confessed that he would believe in Christ the Lord if Syrus would wash him in the water of sacred baptism and join him to his pious assembly. He also confessed with what intention he had rashly presumed to receive the Lord’s body. He declared that he would abandon his former guilt of unbelief and henceforth possess the firmness of true faith.

The blessed bishop Syrus said: “I give thanks to you, almighty God the Father, who do not disdain even to correct Jewish faithlessness, but in your great mercy turn it toward faith in your only-begotten Son.”

After he had been baptized, many Jews also, believing in Christ with him, were reborn in the sacred baptism and joined to the faithful of Christ and to the spiritual assembly.

We have inserted this punishment, divinely displayed before all, into our little work so that no unbeliever may rashly and negligently presume to eat of this bread and drink from the chalice before discerning what the Lord’s body is, or while guilty of mortal sin, before examining himself through repentance and being reconciled in peace to Christ.

What has been said in defense of sacred communion is sufficient. Let us now return to our subject.

## CHAPTER VII [Note: [Col. 1283D] In the Laub manuscript: chapter XII.] The ways in which the body of Christ is spoken of

1. In the sacred Scriptures the body of Christ is spoken of in three ways. The universal Church of Christ is his body: Christ is called its head, and all the elect are called its members. From them one body is daily gathered into a perfect man, into the measure of the fullness of Christ.

The body of Christ—namely, the bride, the Church of God—is rightly so called, according to what the Apostle says: “And the two shall be one flesh” (1 Cor. 6:16). “This,” he says, “is a great mystery” [Note: [Col. 1284D] The royal manuscript adds: “I say this to you.”] “in Christ and in the Church.”

If Christ and the Church are one flesh [Note: [Col. 1284D] The Major Monastery manuscript reads: “If Christ and the Church are one,” omitting “in the flesh.”], then they are certainly one body [Note: [Col. 1284D] In that same manuscript and in another Cologne manuscript of the Friars Preachers: “one bridegroom,” omitting “where the bridegroom is the head.”], where the bridegroom is the head and each of the elect is a member of the other.

Therefore whoever removes a member of Christ and makes it a member of a prostitute—or, through any grave offense, makes it a member of the devil—is plainly no longer in the body of Christ, because he has become a member of another.

For this reason he is rightly not permitted to eat of this mystical body of Christ. That body, so that it may be true flesh of Christ, is consecrated daily through the Holy Spirit for the life of the world; those who are opposed to him have no power to eat of it. [Note: Here chapter XIII begins in the Laub manuscript: “That only those who eat it worthily are in his body.”]

Those who are in his body eat it worthily [Note: [Col. 1285D] The Putean, Flor., Laub., and one Colbert manuscript read: “eat her”; Sirm. reads: “eat it.”], so that, while on the journey, the body of Christ alone may be refreshed by his flesh [Note: [Col. 1285D] One royal manuscript adds: “which is the Church.”], and may learn to hunger for nothing but Christ, to desire nothing but Christ, to taste nothing but Christ [Note: [Col. 1285D] Laub. reads: “to perceive nothing but Christ.” Three manuscripts omit the following words, “than Christ.”], to live from no other source [Note: [Col. 1285D] Three manuscripts add: “except from Christ,”] and to be nothing other than the body of Christ [Note: [Col. 1285D] In the Laub manuscript, chapter XIV begins here: “That body which was born of the undefiled Virgin Mary is truly the body.”].

2. Moreover, that body which was born from the Virgin Mary—the body into which this is transferred—which hung upon the cross, was buried in the tomb, rose from the dead, penetrated the heavens, and now, having become high priest forever, daily intercedes for us [Note: [Col. 1285D] Another manuscript reads: “interceding.”]—to him, if we communicate rightly, we direct our mind, so that from him and through him, while he remains whole, we may receive his body, his flesh.

This flesh, indeed, is himself and the fruit of his flesh [Note: [Col. 1285D] The printed editions, together with several manuscripts, read: “the flesh itself is.”], so that he always remains the same and feeds all who are in the body [Note: [Col. 1285D] Three manuscripts read: “in his body”; the St. Audoen manuscript reads: “in the body of Christ.”].

If a jar of flour, or a flask of oil, or loaves of bread increase when they are consumed [Note: [Col. 1286D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “increase through eating.”] and are not diminished while satisfying others, what do you suppose Christ’s flesh does?

Christ is now the tree of life in the Church, whose image in paradise was that tree. Therefore we should understand that here the truth is fulfilled which the figure had previously announced.

For if human beings had been permitted to eat from that tree forever, while observing God’s commandments, they would never have been mortal [Note: [Col. 1286D] Four manuscripts read: “could not die.” The printed editions read: “could never have been able to die,” or, as Flor. has it, “could die.”]. In the same way, all who spiritually eat from this tree of the body, if they observe the commandments, will never be mortal in spirit. Otherwise they must be cut off, so that they may be grafted in again more effectively. Hence it is rightly called the tree of life [Note: [Col. 1286D] In the Laub manuscript, “whence” and “it is rightly called the tree of life” are absent.], because just as the former tree, when consumed, would have granted bodily immortality, so this one—or rather, more securely—grants eternal life with the observance of God’s commandments.

Concerning this, Wisdom says: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her.” And John says in the Apocalypse: “To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.” For plainly he grants it, even in the mystery, to none but those who conquer.

3. Since we have spoken of the three names of Christ’s body, it remains also to understand that the holy Scriptures and the teaching of Christ are often to be interpreted typologically as Christ’s body, so that one body may be perfected from all. These things are nuptial and mystical, so that Christ and the Church may be more firmly confirmed as one body.

Otherwise, how would the Apostle dare to say that Christ’s Church consists of his flesh and bones? Whether Christ’s enemies wish it or not, this is certainly the great mystery in Christ and in the Church: “the two shall be one flesh.” And if Christ and the Church are one flesh, then the unity of the nature of both is more fully proclaimed.

Therefore, with the Lamb whole [Note: [Col. 1286D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “so that he may take away the Lamb’s whole flesh,” and so forth.], let us receive the flesh of the Lamb of the world, so that he may take away our sins; so that Christ may remain in us, and we, reborn in him, may become one.

## CHAPTER VIII [Note: [Col. 1286D] Laub.: chapter XV, “That nothing in the present age is more damnable than to receive the Lord’s body unworthily.”] Whether judgment or reward is received in this communion

1. At the present time nothing is more dangerous than to sin mortally and fall from the body of Christ before the eyes of the internal Judge.

Next, nothing is more damnable than, before being corrected, through human faithlessness not to withdraw one’s foot from the mystery of holy communion together with Judas. Hence, from the beginning of this celebration, he threatens judgment against those who receive badly, since immediately after Judas received the morsel from the Lord’s hand, the devil entered him.

Here it is immediately shown that judgment will occur in the Church, because these things are holy of holies. If anyone, having fallen from the body of Christ and become a member of a prostitute or of the devil, presumes to receive them, there is no doubt that he will encounter judgment on this account and, together with Judas, become liable to association in guilt—both because he fell and because, although condemned in his conscience, he dared to profane the sacred mysteries without repentance and the pardon of correction.

He did not fear the presence of the divine Majesty, since he thought of nothing beyond what was seen; and in his misery he did not understand that the flesh of Christ is never rightly received except from his hand and from the exalted altar where Christ, the high priest of future blessings, stands on behalf of all [Note: [Col. 1286D] The royal manuscript reads: “on behalf of human beings.”].

Therefore, when the priest begins to sacrifice these things, among the other prayers he says: “Command that these things be borne by the hand of your holy angel to your exalted altar, in the presence of your divine Majesty.”

And do you think, O man, that you receive it from anywhere other than the altar, where it is consecrated after being transferred to a higher place?

## 2.

But perhaps blind thought says to this: “And how is it suddenly raised to heaven before the sight of the divine majesty, when here, although it is called either bread or flesh, it is continually visibly held in the priest’s hand?” [Note: [Col. 1286D] The Laubach codex, chapter 16: “What blind thought says inwardly to itself.”] [Note: Thus read by seven manuscripts of excellent quality and by the printed editions: *offertur* (“is offered”). The Florentine manuscript has *transfertur* (“is transferred”); the Vatican manuscript has *transferatur* (“let it be transferred”).] [Note: The codices of the Monastery of Saint Martin and Saint-Ouen, and one royal manuscript, read: “although it may appear.” The Vatican manuscript reads: “Although it may be called bread or appear to be flesh in the priest’s hand, and be visibly held upon the altar.”]

This, unhappy man, is precisely what is called a sacrament or mystery. [Note: The printed editions, with several manuscripts, read “happy man”; the Florentine manuscript has “man,” omitting “happy.”] For if everything in it became visible, there would be no mystery or secret in it, no faith, no spiritual power—nothing other than what lay open to the eyes and the sense of taste. But now divine power works inwardly in a far different way, because “we walk by faith, and not by sight.” Faith has the reward of merit: whatever tastes sweet to you through faith, it supplies wholly within you. Hence we read: “You gave them, Lord, bread from heaven, possessing every delight and every flavor” (Wisdom 16:20).

Otherwise, unless through faith and understanding, what does anything besides bread and wine taste like to those who receive them? And therefore that carnal people grew weary of the manna, because there they sought nothing but carnal things. But for those to whom it provided every flavor and every delight, that same food from heaven which we now receive was tasted in the mouth by that spiritual and figurative reception. Hence the Apostle testifies that our fathers ate the same spiritual food, “but with most of them God was not well pleased” (Augustine)—plainly because, disdaining spiritual things, they tasted them carnally. They were not, in fact, our fathers who anticipated spiritual things, but plainly the unbelieving fathers of the Pharisees, of whom the Lord said that they “died in the wilderness.” Those indeed died in whom God was not well pleased; but these could not die spiritually while eating, because that heavenly food provided them with the flavor and delight of immortality.

In a similar way, this food is now life for some in the Church, but for others the punishment and penalty of sin. It is life for those for whom Christ is life; but death for those who, through flesh and ignorance, are members of the devil. Therefore, man, learn to taste something other than what is perceived by the mouth of flesh; learn to see something other than what is displayed to these fleshly eyes. [Note: The codex of the Monastery of Saint Martin: “see something else.” The Mamer manuscript: “learn to see something else.”]

Learn that God, being spirit, is everywhere without limitation of place. Understand that these spiritual things, just as they are not carried locally before the sight of the divine majesty, so likewise are not carried there carnally. Consider, then, whether anything bodily can be more sublime, when the substance of bread and wine is efficaciously changed inwardly into the flesh and blood of Christ, so that thereafter, after consecration, the true flesh and blood of Christ is truly believed to be present, and by believers the bread from heaven is judged to be nothing other than Christ.

Do you suppose that there is another altar where Christ the high priest stands besides his body, through which and in which he offers to God the Father the vows of the faithful and the faith of believers? [Note: More manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read: “and the faith of believers is offered.”] If that heavenly altar is truly believed to be the body of Christ, you will no longer think that you receive flesh and blood from anywhere other than from Christ’s own body.

## 3.

[Note: [Col. 1287D] In the Laubach codex chapter 18 begins here: “That we must not doubt the presence of angels.”]

Moreover, you must not doubt at all concerning the presence of angels, because, according to the Apostle Paul, “ministering spirits” have been appointed for service on behalf of those who are receiving the inheritance of salvation. [Note: The printed editions have *propter eos* (“for their sake”), but the manuscripts of better quality read *pro his* (“on behalf of these”).]

Therefore, amid the multitude of angels, each person ought to consider how terrifying it is to approach communion unworthily—indeed, how terrifying is the sacrament itself of the body and blood, in which the power of Christ is received in its fullness and which is extended by no one other than Christ himself, the high priest, although the visible priest may appear to stand before it and distribute it to each person. For what the latter, through ignorance, distributes indiscriminately to everyone, Christ, by the power of his majesty, divinely distinguishes inwardly, determining for whom it is given as a remedy and for whom as judgment. [Note: The Putean manuscript has “the divinity decides”; several manuscripts have “divinely distinguishes.”]

For who lawfully receives his flesh and blood except from him whose flesh it is? And therefore one person receives the mystery for the judgment of condemnation, while another receives the power of the mystery for salvation.

[Note: [Col. 1288D] In the Laubach codex chapter 19 begins here: “Concerning Judas, and that what is consecrated to the Lord is not food for others, except those who are in the Lord, since they alone shall see the Lord.”]

For the one who, because of his contempt and the fault of his crime, is held guilty together with Judas is certainly condemned together with Judas. [Note: The Mamer manuscript has “is held in contempt.”] But the one who faithfully and devoutly participates together with Peter and the others is consecrated in the body together with Peter and the other apostles. [Note: The Florentine manuscript has *participat* (“participates”). In the Mamer manuscript these words are missing: “faithfully and devoutly participates, together with Peter also.”]

(Isidore.) This judgment is therefore immediately encountered at the inception of the chalice, so that what awaits the contemptuous may be taught, if, though condemned by conscience, they do not withdraw their foot from the Lord’s table. [Note: The Vatican and Florentine manuscripts: “At the Lord’s Supper, at the beginning of the chalice.”]

Hence the Lord says in Leviticus to Moses: “Speak to Aaron and to his sons, that they beware of the things consecrated by the children of Israel, and that they not profane the name of the things sanctified to me. I am the Lord. Say to them and to their descendants: Any man of your offspring who approaches the things consecrated which the children of Israel offer to the Lord, while uncleanness is in him, shall perish before the Lord. I am the Lord” (Leviticus 22:2).

Here he addresses not only priests and ministers of the altar, but also everyone from the stock of true faith, even if he is regarded as the least in the Church, so that together they may observe this ordinance of the Law. One is called Israel in name only, the carnal Israel; another is truly a seer of God. [Note: Thus read by six manuscripts and the printed editions: “another is a man who sees God.” Two manuscripts have: “another, truly one who sees God,” omitting “truly.”] No unclean person from his stock ought to approach the things consecrated by the children of Israel, [Note: “Israel” is absent from three manuscripts.] because no one except one cleansed from mortal sin can worthily receive them.

But if anyone approaches unworthily—that is, if there is the uncleanness of sin in his soul—he shall perish before the Lord. [Note: The royal manuscript adds “approaches”; the printed editions have “receives.”] [Note: The Laud manuscript adds: “approaches this altar.”]

Thus, as the translators of the Septuagint rendered it, God turns away from such a person and rejects him from every communion of the Spirit. Therefore, if afterward, through the Lord’s mercy raising him up, such a person should perhaps be restored to the body of Christ and brought to life through repentance, he ought to lament from the depths of his heart no less over his contempt than over the guilt of his former sin, because he received the mysteries that give life for judgment; and, because he has escaped, he ought to burn with a more abundant grace of love.

## 4.

These things, therefore, which are consecrated to the Lord, are food for no one except those who are in the Lord, because they alone will see the Lord. Hence they are rightly called “the consecrated things of those”—that is, of the children of Israel. [Note: The Vatican manuscript has: “consecrated for their right.”]

Do not suppose that God the lawgiver established this ordinance only concerning the things that were consecrated under the Law, especially since those things were nothing other than a shadow of things to come. Therefore it is more terrifying for one who is unclean to approach those things where the priest is he who has power to destroy body and soul in Gehenna.

At the end it concludes: “I am the Lord”—as though he were plainly saying: “I am God, who searches hearts and kidneys” (Psalm 7:10). [Note: In six manuscripts “God” is absent.] I am the one who sanctifies those who receive worthily; I alone have power to destroy the soul of those who receive wrongly. And whoever you are who approach, look to him and fear the high priest: for it is not the one whom you think you can deceive, but him to whom all things are open, whom you must fear. [Note: The printed editions, together with several manuscripts, have “not him.”] [Note: The Laud manuscript has: “to whom such things are manifest.”] Fear, then, lest you receive not the power of the Holy Spirit, but the judgment of the sacrament.

## 5.

[Note: [Col. 1289D] In the Laubach manuscript this is the beginning of chapter 20: “That the sacrament is judgment.”]

The judgment of the sacrament is this: the guilty person bears the offense of his former fault and then, on account of his contempt, the sin of pride or sacrilege against God, because he dared to touch holy things, which are permitted only to the pure.

Hence it is clear that, for any such person, what he receives is a more grievous crime than what he had previously committed. [Note: The manuscripts vary greatly here. The printed editions, together with certain manuscripts, read: “That what such a person receives is a graver crime.” The codex of the Monastery of Saint Martin, together with one Colbertine manuscript: “It is graver that such a person receives a crime.” The Vatican manuscript: “It is graver that such a person displays a crime.” Other manuscripts: “It is graver that such a person receives a crime.” Finally, the Laubach manuscript: “That what such a person receives is a graver crime.”]

For Judas, until he received the morsel (John 13), although wounded in mind, was nevertheless gently and frequently admonished by the Lord’s goodness—sometimes with the others, sometimes alone. But after he presumed to receive the mystical thing unworthily, the devil entered him; and he who had previously been wavering, as soon as he received it immediately went out. [Note: The Laud manuscript, together with one royal manuscript and the Mamer manuscript, has “was being changed.” The manuscript of Tours, the Monastery of Saint Martin, and Saint-Ouen have “was wavering.”]

Likewise, in the Book of Samuel, when Eli was admonishing his sons concerning the sin of sacrifice, we read: “It is not a good report, my sons, which I hear about you. If a man of virtues sins against a man, God can be appeased for him; but if a man sins against God, who will pray for him?” (1 Samuel 2:24). [Note: The Sirmond manuscript reads “a man of virtues.”] That is: whom will he find to intercede for him with God, when, scorning the Lord of all creation, he unworthily approaches the things consecrated—or rather, now, his very body and blood—in insult against him?

[Note: [Col. 1290D] In the Laubach manuscript this is the beginning of chapter 21: “That he who thrusts himself into communion neither fears God’s presence nor dreads the multitude of angels.”]

Such a person plainly neither fears the presence of God nor dreads the multitude of angels, but thrusts himself forward as though there were no one who saw his conscience. [Note: The royal manuscript reads: “he fears [God’s] power, nor [does he fear] the presence of angels.” The manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden, after “he fears [God’s] power,” omits “nor dreads the multitude of angels,” but continues, after these omissions: “he thrusts himself forward as though there were no one who saw his conscience”; and then proceeds with the words “for which reason the Lord…”]

(Jerome.) For this reason, when the Lord showed Jerusalem’s sins and the abominations committed in the temple through a vision, among other things it is said that six men came from the road of the upper gate: “And behold, each of them had in his hand a vessel of slaughter” (Ezekiel 9:2). [Note: Two manuscripts add “of the prophet Ezekiel.”] The Septuagint said that they had brought an axe, concerning which the Lord says: “Behold, the axe is laid at the roots of the trees” (Luke 3:9)—namely, it is laid against the thoughts of each person.

In their midst was one man clothed in linen, with a writer’s inkwell at his waist. These men entered and stood beside the bronze altar that was in the court of the temple. [Note: [Col. 1290D] In the Laubach manuscript this is the beginning of chapter 22: “What this bronze altar signifies for us, where we receive the heavenly bread, and how anyone who approaches it unworthily, unless he hastens to be corrected, will be slain forever by the angels, the guardians of the altar.”]

Through this, clearly, the present altar is signified—the altar from which we receive the food of life and the allowance of our service—because we read that another altar, golden, was inside, beneath the Holy of Holies.

[Col. 1290C] 6. From this it is demonstrated that there is an intelligible altar where all the prayers and vows of individuals are offered by Christ the Lord, the high priest. Therefore we ought to reach that altar with a pure heart, but approach this one with mind and body alike, without any uncleanness. [Note: The manuscripts of Queen Christina of Sweden add “to approach.”] For the vows of the sacraments are offered for us upon that altar. [Note: The Vatican manuscript: “because the consecrated things are the Holy of Holies upon that altar.”] There Christ sees the concord of all and considers the faith of each; and there we pray that these things may be carried more gloriously to God the Father by the hand of the angel. [Note: The printed editions have *precantur* (“they pray”); one Colbertine manuscript has *hic precatur* (“here he prays”).]

And from that altar, before us, upon this visible one, [Note: Jerome.] because we cannot yet enter that altar by bodily passage, the truest flesh and blood of Christ are ministered daily.

For this reason they are expressly said to have stood beside the bronze altar that was in the court, because whoever has once entered that inner altar will never again suffer death. [Note: [Col. 1291D] In the Laubach manuscript this is the beginning of chapter 23: “That if anyone approaches this altar unworthily, he receives the judgment of condemnation.”] But whoever approaches this altar, which is in the court—that is, in the present age—unworthily receives the judgment of condemnation. For this reason each of those men is written to have carried in his hand a vessel of slaughter. [Note: Jerome.]

Hence the glory of the Lord, which had been taken up from the cherub, also stood at the threshold of the house, so that it might more fully recognize those entering. “And he called to the man clothed in linen, who had the writer’s inkwell at his loins.” This man, of course, we understand as Christ, clothed in the vesture of the high priest, of whom it is written: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4). He has the writer’s inkwell at his loins so that he may record the sins of all and separate the number of the saints from that of sinners, especially when they come to the altar. Therefore he is rightly said to stand beside it, so that he may divinely distinguish the soldiers who approach to receive the allowance of life.

When he stood in the midst of the golden lampstands, it was said to him: “Pass through the midst of Jerusalem and mark a *tau* upon the foreheads of those who groan and grieve over all the abominations that are committed in its midst” (Ezekiel 9:4).

Elsewhere also he says of them: “I will walk among them, and I will be their Lord” (Leviticus 22:12; 2 Corinthians 6:16). Whose people? Surely those upon whom the sign of the cross has been marked. [Note: The printed editions have “the sign of the *tau* has been marked,” that is, “the sign of the cross.” The manuscripts omit these words: “the sign of the *tau*, that is.”] They carry in their body the putting to death of Jesus; they mourn daily not only their own offenses but also those of others, and they can say with the Prophet: “The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us” (Psalm 4:7). [Note: The printed editions have “so that he may be able to say.”]

But immediately a voice is directed to those in whose hands were the vessels of slaughter, with the prophet listening: “Pass after him through the city and strike. Let not your eye spare, and do not have pity on old man, young man, and virgin; kill the little child and the women to utter destruction.” [Note: The Sirmond manuscript has *semen* (“seed”), contrary to the testimony of all the manuscripts, which read *senem* (“old man”).] [Note: Other manuscripts read “strike the women.”] “But kill no one upon whom you see the *tau*; and begin from my sanctuary” (Ezekiel 9:5), or, according to the Septuagint, [Note: [Col. 1291D] In the Laud manuscript this is the beginning of chapter 24: “That those who are the cause of sin among the people first receive punishment in retribution.”] “from my holy ones”—that is, from the priests and ministers of the altar—not because they are holy, but because they are called holy in the people on account of their ministry. [Note: The manuscript of the Monastery of Saint Martin reads “are sanctified.”] Thus those who are the cause of sin among the people receive punishment first, because it is time for judgment to begin from the house of God.

But lest you suppose that they stood beside the altar without cause, a divine voice is addressed to them—may it not be fulfilled in us: “Defile the house and fill the courts with the slain,” for there is no religious observance [the printed text has *regio*; read *religio*] in which the offense of sin does not defile those who make offerings. Therefore judgment rightly begins from the place where sin begins, because the person dead through sin first defiles the courts of the temple and profanes the holy things [Note: The Mamer, Ulm, and Sirmond manuscripts have “profane holy things,” contrary to the testimony of all the manuscripts.] while the unclean person touches them.

There is no error in this judgment, where the judge and recorder of his soldiers is the Word of God the Father, Christ, more penetrating than any two-edged sword and also the discerner of thoughts and marrow, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit (Hebrews 4:12).

[Note: [Col. 1292D] In the Laubach manuscript this is the beginning of chapter 25: “Who the many weak are, and who, according to the Apostle, sleep because they have received the sacrifice unworthily.”]

Hence the Apostle says concerning those who receive unworthily, not discerning the body of the Lord: “For this reason many are weak and sleep” (1 Corinthians 11). Many therefore sleep—not the sleep of peace, but the sleep of death—because they are slain by the ministry of those angels who have been appointed for this purpose. [Note: The Vatican manuscript has “many sleep in the day.”]

They became weak because some were afflicted with various illnesses so that they might be corrected, while others were already beginning to be tormented, so that the rest might be healed by fear of them. Otherwise, wounds and illnesses would never have multiplied so greatly among the people of Christ, especially since we read that among those who came out of Egypt as a figure of the holy Church of God, “there was not one who was infirm” (Psalm 104:37).

## 7.

For this reason also it is called the tree of life: it received from God the power that, if anyone ate from it, he would be strengthened in bodily health unto immortality. How much more does this provide—not that someone should not die in the flesh, but that no one should be harmed by the devil, while the power of the blood protects him! [Note: The manuscripts of Queen Christina of Sweden and one royal manuscript: “while the power of the flesh and blood of the Lord protects him.”]

[Note: [Col. 1292D] In the Laubach manuscript this is the beginning of chapter 26: “Why those who communicate unworthily do not openly become bodily weak and sleep.”]

But perhaps someone will ask concerning this: If many become weak and sleep for this reason, why does it not happen openly? [Note: Some manuscripts add “he says.”] Especially since those are punished more severely who are judged unworthy by God’s correction. Surely this is because the faith of the reborn must be exercised and tested, and because man must be instructed in the teaching of the commandments.

Nevertheless, there is no doubt that the faithful receive life, while the contemptuous receive death. Otherwise, if open vengeance were always inflicted upon sinners, terror would restrain people; faith or religious devotion would not educate them toward good conduct.

Therefore, according to the Apostle (James 5), when someone is ill, confession of sin must first be brought forward, then the prayer of many, and afterward the sanctification of anointing. [Note: The Laubach manuscript has “the anointing of sanctification”; the manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden has “the sacrificial anointing.”] For it is impossible for someone whom divine vengeance presses to be healed by the medicine of any human art. And even if medicine is to be pursued, this must nevertheless first be done by a Christian: for if perversity was found even among the angels, and the stars are not clean before him, how much more is an unclean human being proved to be if he is not cleansed daily by confession and good works!

## 8.

[Note: [Col. 1293D] In the Laubach manuscript this is the beginning of chapter 28: “That the person who approaches contemptuously stores up wrath for himself and accumulates sins all the more.”]

Nevertheless, because divine patience often spares sinners for a time, even when they presume to approach unworthily, and waits for them to repent, security must not steal over anyone. For by despising, he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and accumulates sins all the more against God. Let him be certain that the avenging angels would not spare even one person who communicated unworthily, unless the goodness of Christ—upon whose judgment everything depends, and to whom it has been entrusted to place a sign upon the foreheads of his own—were to suspend the sword and sometimes remove an instantaneous death. [Note: The manuscript of the Monastery of Saint Martin has “his servants”; the Vatican manuscript has “his own servants.”]

Therefore afterward, when one comes to one’s senses, mourning in repentance ought to be twofold: [Note: The Vatican and Florentine manuscripts read the singular “when one comes to one’s senses”; most manuscripts have the plural, “when they come to their senses,” although what follows appears to require the singular.] both because one acted badly and because at last one presumptuously approached judgment in a bad manner. This offense will be forgiven by no one other than Christ intervening.

Hence, in the Law, because he sinned against the consecrated things, a ram—by which Christ is understood—is commanded to be offered, so that God the man, the eternal high priest, may be believed through faith to intercede with God the Father, and so that the person himself may daily offer him through faith, clothed again in his conduct and life, as an offering for himself. [Note: The manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden has “as a burnt offering” instead of “clothed again.”]

Otherwise, since the one who has sinned against God—who will pray for him except God, who assumed our weaknesses for this very reason, that he might have compassion on us and through himself grant forgiveness even for offenses committed against God?

Nor do we say this so that someone suitable should not intervene for us in these matters, [Note: The Ulm, Sirmond, and Florentine manuscripts read “among the unjust” instead of “in these matters.”] but we must ascribe everything to Christ, who willingly forgives even the injuries done to him and, for those who offend against him, as he had earlier done upon the cross, intervenes as a suitable advocate by offering himself also to the Father.

# CHAPTER IX

[Note: [Col. 1294D] In the Laubach manuscript chapter 29 has this title: “Why this offering is repeated daily.”]

Why it was necessary for Christ to be sacrificed daily, although the event took place only once. [Note: In two manuscripts: “And what benefit these examples provide.”] Or: What good these mysteries provide to those who receive them worthily.

## 1.

This offering is repeated daily, although Christ, having suffered once in the flesh, saved the world once for all through one and the same passion of death; and, rising from that death to life, he no longer permits death to rule over him. [Note: The manuscripts of Queen Christina of Sweden and one royal manuscript: “He does not permit death to rule over him any longer.”]

For the wisdom of God the Father clearly provided this as necessary for many reasons. First, because we sin daily—at least with those sins without which mortal weakness cannot live—for although all sins have been forgiven in baptism, the weakness of sin still remains in the flesh. [Note: Another reading is “have been forgiven to us.”] [Note: One manuscript reads “the weakness of sinning.”] Hence the Psalmist says: “Bless the Lord, my soul, who is propitious toward all your iniquities, who heals all your weaknesses” (Psalm 102:1, 3). [Note: The Laubach manuscript has “all my iniquities, Israel.”] And therefore, because we stumble daily, Christ is mystically sacrificed for us daily, and Christ’s passion is handed down in the mystery, so that he who once conquered death by dying may daily, through these sacraments of his body and blood, forgive the recurring sins of those who fall again. [Note: The manuscripts of Queen Christina of Sweden add: “And by his death had taken away the sins of the world.”]

## 2.

[Note: The words in parentheses are added in two manuscripts, one belonging to the Most Christian King and the other to the library of Queen Christina of Sweden.]

Foreseeing that Christ would accomplish all this in us, that great lamp, burning and shining—namely John the Baptist, than whom no one born of woman has arisen greater—no sooner saw him coming toward him than, pointing him out with his finger and touched by the divine Spirit, he exclaimed: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins [another reading: “sin”] of the world” (John 1:29).

Therefore, believing in him with our heart and confessing with our mouth that he is the one who takes away the sins of the world, let us, together with that greater-than-a-prophet, the forerunner of Christ, joyfully proclaim his praises: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

Behold the innocent one, free from every sin: although he has bone from Adam’s bones and flesh from Adam’s flesh, he drew no stain of guilt from sinful flesh. Behold the just one among sinners, the gentle one among the ungodly—appearing, as it were, as a lamb among wolves—who also has the power to justify sinners and the ungodly.

But how he takes away the sins of the world, and by what order he justifies the ungodly, the Apostle Peter shows when he says: “You were not redeemed from your vain manner of life handed down by your fathers with perishable silver or gold, but with the precious blood, as of an unblemished and spotless lamb, Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:18).

And the Apostle John says in the Apocalypse: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Revelation 1:5). He not only washed us from our sins in his blood when he gave his blood for us upon the cross, or when each of us was washed in the mystery of his most holy passion and in the baptism of water; he also takes away the sins of the world daily and washes us daily from our sins in his blood, when the memory of that same blessed passion is renewed at the altar, when the creature of bread and wine is transferred into the sacrament of his flesh and blood through the ineffable sanctification of the Spirit.

Thus also his body and blood are not poured out and slain into the hands of unbelievers for their destruction, if they are received by the mouth of the faithful for salvation. The paschal lamb in the Law rightly displayed a figure of this: once freeing the people from Egyptian slavery, it was able, through its yearly sacrifice in memory of that liberation, to sanctify that same people until he should come—the one to whom such a victim bore witness—and, offered to the Father for us as a victim and an odor of sweetness, as priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, might transfer the mystery of his passion, with the Lamb offered, into the creature of bread and wine, approaching God through himself to intercede for us. [Note: Another reading has *transferret* (“might transfer”) instead of *transferetur* (“may be transferred”).]

Therefore, because our Redeemer continues to carry out, even to this day, through the daily commemoration of that same blessed passion, the whole work which he once accomplished at the time of his passion, I think this is above all the principal reason why we continually renew the remembrance of his most holy death, sacrificing his most sacred body and blood daily upon the altar. [Note: The words of this parenthesis occur in two manuscripts.]

Hence we pray: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:1), because if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

## 3.

Secondly, this is done so that, just as there was a tree of life in paradise, so the holy Church of God—which is called the paradise of delights in the Song of Songs—may contain within itself the mystery of life that was represented by that tree. Those who eat from it while keeping the commandments of life can in no way die forever.

But if, like Adam, they are disobedient and are again killed by the devil through the sin of death, they are removed from paradise, from the holy altars, and from the tree of life—that is, from the body and blood of Christ, who is the true tree of paradise, whose leaf does not fall and “all things whatsoever he does shall prosper” (Psalm 1:3).

They are removed so that they may not take from the tree of life and live badly, and so die—or rather, so that they may repent of their evils, be reconciled through repentance, and through this food be grafted again into the inner parts of Christ’s body. [Note: Thus read by manuscripts of better quality. The Sirmond manuscript, together with certain manuscripts, has “having been reconciled to Christ.”] [Note: Two royal manuscripts and one manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden have “be grafted into the inner parts of paradise, that is, the Church, and live happily.” Another manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden has “be grafted into its inner parts and live faithfully.”] Thereafter they may live happily forever.

This is what Christ’s priests do in the Church, and they show what will happen in that final judgment, when the just will be separated from the unjust. But here, just as hope of returning to life remained for Adam after his expulsion through repentance, so for those cut off from the tree of life the opportunity of returning to forgiveness remains, if they wish. When repentance has intervened, a sure hope is received, because once admitted again to life, a person cannot die if he remains reconciled in Christ.

[Col. 1295D] 4. Thirdly, Christ’s passion is also reckoned, so that all who, having been reborn, worthily receive this life may become one: just as they are already clothed with Christ through baptism, so Christ may remain bodily in them through this sacrament. [Note: Thus read nearly all the manuscripts. The printed editions have “they put on Christ.”] [Note: The Vatican manuscript has “may remain spiritually.”] Thus believers may be one in Christ and Christ may remain in them, so that what he himself prays to the Father may be fulfilled: “I pray not for these only, but for those who will believe in me through their word, that they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be in us” (John 17:20). [Note: The printed editions have “that they also may be one in us,” as does the text of John. But in all the manuscripts the word “one” is absent.]

This unity is not proclaimed between the Father and the Son, as the heretics wish, by will alone, as they endeavor to establish from the statement, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). They attempt to apply to it the agreement of unanimity, so that the unity in them is one of will, not of nature, just as it is said that the multitude of believers in Jerusalem had “one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

But following the footsteps of the Fathers, we ought to believe [Note: Three manuscripts have “we ought to believe without hesitation”] that God, begotten substantially from God, is naturally what the Father is (Hilary, Book 8, *On the Trinity*). Accordingly, the Father and the Son are proved to be one by unity of nature. [Note: The Vatican, Florentine, and first Colbertine manuscripts have “by this unity of nature.”] Likewise Christ is rightly said to remain today in us not only through harmony of will, but also by nature, just as we are in him.

For if the Word became flesh, and we truly receive the Word made flesh in the Lord’s food, how can Christ rightly not be considered to remain naturally in us? He, God born as man, assumed the nature of our flesh inseparably to himself, and under this sacrament he joined the nature of his flesh, which was to be communicated to us, to the nature of his eternity. [Note: Three manuscripts have “to the nature of his eternity.”]

And therefore through this we are all one in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, because the Father is proved to be in Christ and Christ in us. [Note: Two royal manuscripts and two manuscripts of Queen Christina of Sweden have: “Because the Father exists as one in Christ the Son and in the Holy Spirit, and Christ, remaining one in the Father and in the Holy Spirit, is also proved to be one in us through the nature of the flesh he assumed. Hence, therefore…”]

Hence we too are made naturally one body in Christ. And if anyone confesses that the Father is naturally in Christ, let him confess that he is naturally one in him—because the Word is flesh—so that natural unity may appear through the sacrament of truth. [Note: The printed editions have “because the Word became flesh.”]

Hence he says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57).

Truly, therefore, just as God the Father is in the Son through the nature of the deity, so the Son, God and man, is rightly said to be in us through the humanity [another reading: “unity”] of the flesh. Accordingly, he is proclaimed as the mediator between God and human beings, because through him we have communion in unity with God, while he himself remains in the Father and is also said to remain in us.

For this reason the Father earlier asks the Son that we be one in them according to his humanity.

5. See what these two sacraments accomplish: through baptism, therefore, we are reborn in Christ, and through the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, Christ is shown to remain in us—not only by faith, but also through unity of flesh and blood. Thus we are already members of Christ and feed on his flesh, so that we are found to be nothing other than his body, from which we live, and his blood. Hence no one ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven (John 3:13), because through these mysteries we are one with him.

This mystery is repeated also in remembrance of Christ’s passion, just as he himself says: “Whenever you do this, do it in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). Therefore, whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26). This should not be understood as meaning “until Christ’s death comes”—for he will die no more—but “until the Lord himself comes for judgment.” Meanwhile, Christ’s death must continually be proclaimed to those who come after us for the life of the world, so that they may learn with what love he loved his own, since he deigned to die for them. We all owe him a return of love, because he first loved us, when we were children of Gehenna, so that, now freed from death, we might love him.

[Note: The printed editions have interim (“meanwhile”), but all the manuscripts read interdum (“at times,” here meaning “meanwhile”), a word familiar in Radbertus for expressing “meanwhile.”]

6. Some also say that it is celebrated daily so that those who had come to believe from among the Jews might, through this grace, become accustomed to having sacrifices offered to the Lord each day, by which they could solemnly present the vows of their religion, and, once all the figures of the ancient sacrifices and holocausts had been set aside, might prefer the truth of this mystery.

[Note: This is the reading of the printed editions and several manuscripts. Some read immolare (“to offer”) instead of immolari (“to have offered”).]

[Note: The printed editions read suae religionis vota (“the vows of their religion”).]

[Note: The manuscripts vary greatly here. The Vatican manuscript reads: holocaustomatum sacris hujus mysterii (“of the holocausts, by the sacred things of this mystery”). The royal manuscripts and those of the queen of Sweden read: holocaustorum figuris hujus mysterii (“the figures of the holocausts of this mystery”). The manuscript of Marmoutier, together with five others, reads: holocaustomatum hujus mysterii (“of the holocausts of this mystery”). Ulm and Sirm read: holocaustomatum legitimis hujus mysterii (“of the lawful holocausts of this mystery”).]

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads virtutem (“power”) instead of veritatem (“truth”).]

But although this may seem to be so, the fuller and more perfect interpretation is the one we set forth earlier. For this mystery is celebrated in the Church no less for us than for them. This figure had already preceded it in Melchizedek, just as faith had preceded it in Abraham; but because the Law inserted itself like a dividing wall, the truth of this mystery was rather foreshadowed in all the sacrifices of the Law. Once these had been removed, what had been foretold was fulfilled: according to the order of Melchizedek, Christ, the true high priest, succeeded them, possessing an eternal priesthood.

Abraham had seen this by faith in Melchizedek, and therefore he is said to have offered him tithes and to have received a blessing from him. Hence that Melchizedek is called king—king of Salem, that is, of righteousness or peace—and priest, so that through him Christ, whose type he bore, might clearly be shown to be both king and priest.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads this passage as follows: “Hence that Melchizedek, king of Salem—that is, of righteousness and peace—and priest …”]

Otherwise, which mortal could rightly be called king of righteousness, when no one is found just except through the righteousness of faith?

[Note: Five manuscripts read “except through the righteousness of faith.”]

Let us therefore hold fast to this high priest and priest, Christ, and remain in him, because, since he is in us and we are in him, we too are all called and truly are priests. For he made us a kingdom and priests for God; therefore we are proclaimed by the Apostle to be a holy nation, a royal priesthood, and a people for possession.

This, then, is clear: because we are incorporated into him by this grace, and he into us, he transforms us into the body of his glory, so that with him and in him we may have a kingdom of peace. For this is what Salem signifies: peace and an eternal priesthood.

The Prophet also sings:

“Praise the Lord, Jerusalem;
praise your God, Zion,
who has established peace within your borders
and satisfies you with the fat of wheat” (Psalm 147:1, 3).

(Hilary.) It is with this wheat, surely, that the heavenly Jerusalem is nourished. It should be noted that this wheat—namely, Christ’s body—possesses fatness, and not fatness alone, but every delight; so too does the drink consist of blood. Hence what flowed figuratively from the rock is called at one time honey, at another oil, at another water, and at another a drink, because whatever you are able spiritually to taste beforehand, you will find there in its entirety.

For this reason the Jews relate that, when they ate manna in a bodily manner, it tasted in each person’s mouth according to that person’s desire: for example, if someone desired a pear, an apple, a grape, bread, meat, or anything else, the manna provided all these things in the mouth of the one who desired them.

[Note: The words “if an apple” are absent from three manuscripts.]

[Note: The printed editions, together with the manuscript of Marmoutier, read sapiebat (“it tasted”); all the other manuscripts read praestabat (“it provided”).]

They, always seeking bodily things, tell of bodily matters; but we confess by faith that spiritual and eternal things were provided in the hearts of believers—not only these but also those. Hence we ought confidently to believe through these things that, if anyone receives this sacrament worthily, he receives immortal life and enjoys delights with every pleasure, set in hope upon eternal things.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript, the manuscript of Marmoutier, and that of Saint-Ouen add: “May it be given by God to those who hope in him [or: in it]. So be it. Amen.” The royal manuscript reads: “of heavenly things, and therefore may it be given to those who hope in him. So, so may it be. Marmoutier reads: “May it be given by God to those who hope in him. So, so may it be, amen.”]

7. But since, with Christ’s help, we have taken care to show what good these mysteries bestow upon those who receive them worthily, I think it will be very useful for many in the future if we establish by certain examples the things we have expressed in words. Therefore, please read with pleasure what follows. Some of these examples we have excerpted from the writings of the blessed and most eminent man Gregory, bishop of the Roman See, and, just as that outstanding teacher left them in his writings, we have incorporated them into this little work, so that, with so great an authority brought forward, our words may be confirmed more firmly.

[Note: The following material was supplied by one manuscript of the queen of Sweden, numbered 1554, and by a manuscript of the Royal Library, numbered 4070.]

8. The son of a certain Jewish glassworker was being taught literary studies among Christian boys. One day, while the festival Masses were being celebrated in the basilica of the blessed Mary, ever-virgin and Mother of God, and the people, as usual, were coming forward to receive the Eucharist from the priest’s hand, the aforementioned Jewish child approached with the other children of his own age to receive a share in the glorious body and blood of the Lord.

As he drew near, divine providence—as I believe—revealing the matter to him, he saw upon the altar a woman of exceedingly dignified appearance seated on a chair, holding a little child on her knees. With her own hand she was presenting the sacred Communion to the priest, so that he might distribute it faithfully to the people who were approaching.

The Jewish boy received it as well, and returned home rejoicing. He reported the matter with joy to his father, who was occupied with his work, amid the embraces and kisses he received. But the father, hostile to Christ the Lord and to his laws, stirred by the gall of bitterness, said to him:

“If you have shared in the religion of the Christian children, then, to avenge the insult done to the Mosaic Law, I shall forget the affection due from a father and become a harsh parricide against you.”

He seized the boy and threw him into the mouth of a blazing furnace, then added wood and persisted in feeding the fire so that he might be burned more violently. But that mercy was not absent which had once sprinkled the three Hebrew boys, thrown into the Chaldean furnace, with a refreshing cloud of dew. The same mercy did not allow this child, lying amid the fire and piles of burning coals, to be consumed.

When the mother heard that the cruel father had resolved to burn their son, she ran to rescue him. But when she saw the flames spreading here and there from the open mouth of the furnace, with the fire raging, she threw her head-dress to the ground, tore her hair, and, crying out that she was wretched, filled the city with her cries.

When the Christian citizens learned what had happened, they all rushed together to witness so wicked a spectacle. Having drawn back the fires from the mouth of the furnace, they found the boy lying as though upon the softest feathers. After he had been taken out, they all marveled that he was unharmed, and the place was filled with their shouts. Thus the whole people blessed the mighty deeds of the Lord.

They also shouted that the perpetrator of this crime should be thrown into the same flames. Once he had been thrown in, the fire swallowed him completely, so that scarcely any small trace of his bones remained.

The Christians asked the child what shelter had protected him. He replied:

“That woman who was seated in the basilica, where I received the bread from the table, and who held a little child in her lap—she covered me with her cloak so that the fire would not devour me. The food I had received from the priest’s hand also helped me so greatly that I thought I did not feel even the breath of the fire. Therefore there is no doubt that blessed Mary appeared to him.”

Once the child had recognized the Catholic faith, he believed in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Washed in the saving waters, he was reborn together with his mother. Many Jews in that city were also converted to the faith through this example.

9. If, then, these mysteries benefited one who was without faith and had not yet been reborn through holy baptism, but who had been counted among Christ’s members, and benefited him as such a great protection of his salvation, how much more surely must we believe that, when the faithful receive them worthily—those who have already been made members of Christ’s body, which is the Church, of which he himself is the head—these sacraments contribute to the salvation of their body and soul?

10. Let us also bring forward, as we promised, the examples of the blessed Gregory, the supreme bishop. He reports (Homily 37 on the Gospels and Book 4 of the Dialogues, chapter 57) that a certain man was captured by enemies and taken far away. After he had been kept in captivity for a long time, and his wife did not recover him from that captivity, she thought he had died. For him, therefore, as though he were already dead, she arranged for sacred offerings to be presented to almighty God every week, so that the bonds of his soul might be loosed.

His bonds in captivity were loosed as many times as offerings had been made by his wife for the release of his soul. For after a long time he returned and, greatly astonished, told his wife that on certain days and every week his bonds had been loosed. When she examined those days and hours, she recognized that he had been released at the very times when she remembered that the sacrifice had been offered for him.

From this, my most beloved son, gather with certain reflection how powerful the sacred offering presented by us is for loosening the bond of the heart, if an offering presented by one person was able to loosen bodily chains in another.

But since I know that you are devoted to the sacred altars for offering these sacrifices, may you be more devoted and prepared—or more ready—to offer this victim continually. Listen, I beg you, to another example of that venerable man Gregory, which I append to this present page so that you may be inflamed more ardently to sacrifice yourself upon the altar of your heart.

11. The aforesaid teacher relates that there was a certain man named Cassius, then a bishop, whose custom was to offer daily sacrifices to God, so that scarcely any day of his life passed on which he did not offer victims to almighty God. His life was in complete harmony with his sacrifice. For he gave away everything he possessed in alms, and, when the hour for offering the sacrifice arrived, he would melt entirely into tears and first sacrifice himself with great contrition of heart.

One night the Lord appeared in a vision to his presbyter and said:

“Go and tell the bishop: ‘Do what you are doing; carry out what you are carrying out. Let neither your foot nor your hand cease. You will come to me on the feast of the apostles, and I will repay you your reward.’”

The presbyter arose. But because the feast of the apostles was already close at hand, he was afraid to announce to his bishop the date of his imminent death.

On another night the Lord returned, severely rebuked him for his disobedience, and repeated the same words of command. Then the presbyter arose to go, but again weakness of heart became an obstacle to revealing the vision. Hardened by the repeated command, he neglected to go and to disclose what he had seen.

But because contempt of a great kindness is usually followed by a greater punishment of anger, the Lord appeared in a third vision and added blows to his words. He was beaten with such severe punishment that the wounds on his body softened the hardness of his heart.

Thus instructed by the blows, he arose and went to the bishop. He found him already prepared according to custom, standing beside the tomb of the blessed martyr Juvenal to offer the sacrifice. He asked to speak with him privately and threw himself at his feet. The bishop could scarcely raise him, as he was weeping abundantly, and sought to learn the cause of his tears.

The presbyter, however, before relating the sequence of the vision, let his garment fall from his shoulders and revealed the wounds on his body. He displayed—as I may put it—the witnesses of the truth and of his guilt, showing with what strict severity of punishment his limbs had sweated beneath the blows, covered with bruises.

As soon as the bishop saw this, he was horrified and asked, with words of great astonishment, who had dared to do such things to him. The presbyter replied that he had suffered them for the bishop’s sake.

The bishop’s astonishment increased with trembling. But the presbyter no longer delayed answering his questions. He disclosed the secret of the revelation and related to him, in the words he had heard, the Lord’s vision:

“Do what you are doing; carry out what you are carrying out. Let your hand not cease, let your foot not cease. You will come to me on the feast of the apostles, and I will repay you your reward.”

When the bishop heard this, he prostrated himself in prayer with great contrition of heart. He had come to offer the sacrifice at the third hour, but because of the length of his prayer he prolonged it until the ninth hour. From that day onward, the profits of his devotion increased more and more, and he became as strong in his work as he was certain of his reward. For, by the promise, he had already begun to regard as his debtor the one to whom he himself had been a debtor.

It had been his custom each year to travel to Rome on the feast of the apostles. Therefore, troubled by this revelation, he did not wish to go according to custom. At the same time he remained anxious, suspended in expectation of his death, and likewise in the second and third years; and similarly in the fourth, fifth, and sixth years. He could already have despaired of the truth of the revelation, had not the blows given credibility to the words.

Then, behold, in the seventh year he reached the sacred vigils of the awaited feast in good health. But during the vigils he was seized by a slight fever, and on the very day of the feast, while his sons were awaiting him, he refused to complete the solemnities of the Mass himself.

Those who were likewise suspicious about his departure all came to him together and unanimously bound themselves by a promise that on that day they would by no means consent to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass unless the same bishop intervened before God on their behalf.

Then, compelled, he celebrated Mass in the bishop’s oratory and with his own hand gave everyone the Lord’s body and the kiss of peace. After completing the entire ministry of the offered sacrifice, he returned to bed. While lying there, and seeing his priests and ministers standing around him, he bade them a final farewell, admonished them to preserve the bond of charity, and preached how great a harmony they ought to maintain among themselves.

Suddenly, in the midst of these holy words of exhortation, he cried out in a terrible voice:

“It is the hour!”

Immediately he gave his attendants with his own hands a cloth, which, according to the custom for the dying, was stretched before his face. Once it had been stretched out, he gave up his spirit. Thus that holy soul, reaching eternal joys, was released from the corruption of the flesh.

Whom, then, my dearest son, whom was this man invited to meet in his death, except the one whom he had contemplated in his life? For when he said, “It is the hour,” he departed from the body, because Jesus also, after accomplishing everything, said, “It is finished,” bowed his head, and gave up his spirit. What the Lord did by authority, therefore, the servant did by calling.

Behold how great a harmony that sacrifice, offered daily with alms and tears, had with our Redeemer. Therefore, man of God, strive to offer it as far as you are able, with the fervor of charity and contrition of heart. For almighty God wishes to be appeased by our prayers, and he knows that we cannot bear him when he is angry. In a singular way, the victim of the sacred altar, offered with tears and kindliness of mind, comes to our aid for our release, because the one who, having risen from the dead, now dies no more, through this mystery nevertheless suffers again for us.

For whenever we offer him the victim of his passion, we renew his passion for our release. Through this victim souls are purified, sins are loosed, vices are driven away, demons are put to flight, virtues are acquired, the salvation of souls and bodies is possessed, and the whole world is saved.

But since we have shown at somewhat greater length, from the words of the blessed Gregory, how much benefit this offers to the living body, it is necessary to demonstrate how much it benefits the souls of the dead.

12. The often-mentioned teacher Gregory relates that there was a certain presbyter who, because of a bodily ailment, was advised by physicians to make a habit of bathing at the baths of Angulani, where the waters produce excessive steam. One day, when he had entered those baths according to custom, he found an unknown man prepared to serve him. The man removed the shoes from his feet, received his clothing, offered him a towel when he came out of the heat, and performed every service with great devotion.

After this had happened several times, one day, as the presbyter was going to the baths, he thought to himself:

“I ought not to appear ungrateful to the man who habitually serves me so devotedly when I bathe. I must bring him something as a gift.”

He therefore brought with him two little crowns of offerings. As soon as he arrived at the place, he found the man and, as usual, made use of his service in every respect. He bathed, and, when he wished to leave after dressing, he offered what he had brought to the man who had served him, as a blessing, asking him kindly to accept what he offered him as an expression of charity.

The man replied sadly and sorrowfully:

“Why do you give these things to me, Father? This bread is holy; I cannot eat it. I whom you see was once the master of this place, but because of my sins I have been assigned here after death. If you wish to grant me something, offer this bread for me to almighty God, so that you may intercede for my sins. Then know that you have been heard when you come here to bathe and do not find me at all.”

With these words he disappeared, and the one who had seemed to be a human being vanished, making it known that he was a spirit.

The presbyter then afflicted himself with tears for him for an entire week, offered the saving victim daily, and, returning afterward to the baths, no longer found him there. From this it is readily shown how much the immolation of the sacred offering benefits the souls of the faithful even after death, since the spirits of the dead themselves ask the living for it and give signs by which they later appear to have been released.

Indeed, if their sins have not been unpardonable, the victim of the sacred offering can benefit countless dead people for their release. But we must understand that the sacred victim benefits those dead who, while living, obtained that even after death the good works performed here on their behalf by others might assist them.

Meanwhile, we must consider that the safer course is for each person to do while alive the good that he hopes will be done for him by others after his death. It is more blessed to depart free than to seek freedom after being bound.

Therefore, while we live, we ought to sacrifice ourselves to God in heartfelt contrition, because, when we celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s passion, we ought to imitate what we perform. The sacrifice we offer will then truly be a sacrifice for us to God, when we have made ourselves a sacrifice.

While, therefore, we have the span of time granted by mercy, while the Judge bears with us, while he who examines sins awaits our conversion, let us melt the hardness of our mind in tears and form the grace of kindness toward our neighbors. I say confidently that we shall not need a saving victim after death if, while we live in this valley of tears, we ourselves have been a sacrifice to God.

Let these words suffice in defense of the sacred offering. Let us now return to the subject.

## CHAPTER X. Why this mystery is celebrated in bread and wine

[Note: In the most recent manuscript of Saint-Germain, the title is expressed as follows: “That this mystery is called both flesh and bread, and concerning the wine, which is poured from many grapes.”]

1. This offering is celebrated in bread because Christ is the bread that descended from heaven. But just as “bread” is understood to mean something far different from this bread, so “flesh” is distinguished by a great difference from our mortal flesh.

[Note: The manuscript of the queen of Sweden and two royal manuscripts add: “This offering.”]

[Note: The printed editions add ille (“that”), which the manuscripts omit. The manuscript of Marmoutier reads: “but just as that,” omitting panis (“bread”).]

[Note: Four manuscripts add terreno (“earthly”).]

Thus flesh, through the passion, and true flesh, completes the redemption of its condition; but bread provides nourishment for immortality to those reborn into eternity.

It is therefore not surprising that Christ’s flesh is called bread, since, when the flesh is presented under the visible appearance of bread, nothing other than flesh is presented.

[Note: The printed editions read: “while the flesh is presented.” But all the manuscripts unanimously read: “since the flesh also, under a visible appearance, is presented as nothing other than flesh.”]

It is called flesh because he is believed to have truly suffered in that same flesh; but it is called bread because the grain of wheat, falling into the earth, gave birth to us through faith, and we are nothing other than grain from it.

Hence he gave life from himself to his members born from him, and, by giving himself to us, was nothing other than the eternal bread. Nothing is clearer for the figure, nothing more evident for the mystery: Christ, the grain of wheat, fell into the earth, but produced many grains from himself. These grains are nothing other than the wheat gathered into the granary.

[Note: Seven manuscripts read this way. The printed editions read: “are nothing else.”]

[Note: The Florentine manuscript reads: “into the granary of the Church.”]

Hence the marvelous unity of our nature is proclaimed in him. For we all know that one loaf is naturally made from many grains. Through this our unity in Christ is commended, and the figure of the truth is confirmed in the mystery.

For this reason that one grain died in the earth: so that from its richness and fatness we might be made fruitful, as he himself says: “Unless it dies, it remains alone” (John 12:24).

[Note: The printed editions read maneret (“would remain”).]

But now, because it has died and risen, it bears much fruit in those who believe.

[Note: The printed editions add: “in those who believe in him,” but the manuscripts omit se (“in him”).]

From this fruit the one bread is made, because Christ and the Church are shown to be one body. Hence it is said: “And the two shall be one flesh” (1 Corinthians 6:16).

This mystery is rightly celebrated in bread, so that through it what takes place in him may be represented more profoundly.

[Note: Marmoutier, Ulm, and five manuscripts read generatur (“is generated”) instead of geratur (“takes place”).]

Likewise, it is celebrated in wine, which is poured from many grapes and flows together from many into one. These grains of virtue grew from that vine which had said: “I am the true vine, and you are the branches” (John 15:5). A branch cannot bear fruit from itself unless it remains in the vine.

Therefore the wine we drink is the blood of that same vine, which flowed from his side. The vine and the branch are one body, and therefore they appear to bear one fruit, because the grape borne by the branch has flowed from the root of the vine.

Hence Christ is also called a grape, which the true scouts—the chorus, that is, of the apostles and prophets—brought to us, carrying it vigorously upon their shoulders.

[Note: Most manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read viri exploratores (“the true scouts”).]

Thus Paul, the distinguished preacher, says: “You were bought at a price; carry the Lord Christ in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:20).

[Note: Nearly all manuscripts read: “carry Christ the Lord.” The printed editions read: “carry God.”]

Finally, when this grape was pressed in the winepress of the passion, the blood of salvation flowed from it.

Hence Moses sings in his song that the Lord established his people upon a high land, so that they might eat the fruits of the fields, suck honey from the rock, oil from the hardest stone, and drink the purest blood of the grape (Deuteronomy 32:13).

The whole Church of Christ is inebriated with this blood. Therefore it rightly retains the appearance of wine in its perception, while spiritually the blood is drunk in the mystery. Through this we are gladdened with spiritual gladness unto joy; through that we are redeemed from death to life and inwardly nourished by the price of our salvation.

David had sung of these two things figuratively: bread strengthens the human heart, and wine makes it glad—namely, with spiritual gladness.

Therefore this mystery of salvation is rightly celebrated in the same substances, because Christ is the bread that descended from heaven, and the wine by which the hearts of believers are gladdened.

It is in relation to this that Joseph is mystically read to have become drunk with his brothers at midday, the hour at which Christ suffered.

Hence we too, if we still do not taste anything more than water, are inwardly made drunk and rejoice in the Lord’s blessings, over grain, wine, and oil, with which we have been drenched in eternal gladness and exultant joy in the Lord.

For we are not only the Lord’s vineyard but also his vintage. Concerning this vineyard Christ says in the Song of Songs:

“I have gathered my myrrh with my spices;
I have eaten my bread with my honey,
and drunk my wine with my milk” (Song of Songs 5:1).

But we do not eat bread first, before the myrrh of mortification has swollen within us and the ointment of good fragrance has been sprinkled upon our nostrils.

[Note: Mamer. and Ulm, together with the manuscript of the Greater Monastery, read: “but first the bread is eaten.”]

Then we eat bread with honey, which flowed from the rock that is Christ, when we believe in him as possessing two natures, divine and human.

[Note: The words in parentheses are absent from the printed editions.]

Then indeed we drink the wine of sweetness with milk, when through sacred teaching we understand that the wine is his blood.

Because these mystical realities were hidden in these two substances, it was right that the divine sacrament should be made in them, so that the mind might strive to understand everything spiritually, where it is not permitted to perceive anything bodily.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “therefore Christ the bread.”]

Thus the same bread, Christ, who descended from heaven, is received in this mystery, just as the flesh that hung upon the cross is received, while thereafter Christ remains whole. Although he is eaten daily by all, he is bread for the life and strength of the soul, but flesh for the unity of our nature and the price of redemption.

Hence he himself says: “My flesh is for the life of the world, and my blood is truly poured out for you for the remission of sins” (John 6:62).

This is why the Wisdom of God the Father preferred that this mystery remain under the appearance of bread and wine rather than be changed into the color and taste of flesh and blood. For what is seen is not now what it is, nor would it be any more flesh and blood than it is perceived to be.

We eat in it the bread that descended from heaven. Therefore it is said: “I have eaten bread [or: honeycomb] with my honey” (Song of Songs 5:1), because in him the sweetness of divinity and humanity is proclaimed.

[Note: Eight manuscripts read “and of humanity” instead of “and humanity.”]

Therefore, just as in this case we do not consider the taste or color of bread,

[Note: In the manuscript of Marmoutier, “in this case” is absent.]

[Note: In two manuscripts the word non (“not”) is omitted.]

so also, if it were changed into flesh, Christ’s flesh would be nothing more than it is. Everything we eat is spiritual; indeed, it would be harsher, contrary to human custom, to receive the flesh of the man Christ—though it is the flesh of salvation—altered into his own appearance and color, and to receive wine converted into blood.

Hence those disciples, still inexperienced and thinking in bodily terms, said: “This is a hard saying” (John 6:61), when he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life abiding in you” (John 6:54). They could not endure it, plainly because they understood these words in a bodily way.

Thus the person who thinks bodily is also the one who does not believe Christ’s flesh and blood to be present because their outward appearance and color have not changed.

[Note: The manuscript of Marmoutier, with “orandum” crossed out, reads: “Hence Christ himself comes in person.”]

Therefore we should pray that Christ himself may come and eat bread with his honey in us and drink wine with milk. For unless Christ is truly understood as God and man, and unless wine—the blood of Christ—is mingled with the milk of teaching, the weak mind cannot grasp the light and mystery of truth, nor recognize what is divine.

Here the marvelous unity of Christ and the Church is declared, as in all the other passages, since what we do in him is shown to be done by him in us.

[Note: The printed editions read monstrat (“he shows”), but all the manuscripts read monstratur (“is shown”).]

For when we rightly eat bread with honey and drink the wine of the cup with milk, then he himself testifies that he takes these things in us, because through this he transfers us into his body, and we are made one in him.

2.
