Therefore, my dearest son, in matters such as these and of this kind, observe carefully that in bread and wine, without any alteration of their substance, this mystery is inwardly accomplished by divine power and efficacy. Thus the power of faith may shine forth in understanding, teaching may flow from one side to the other in the working of the sacrament,

[Note: Laud reads: “in the working of the mystery.”]

and the truth may shine in the prefiguration of the mystery.

For Melchizedek had previously offered bread and wine as a figure of this. It was therefore necessary that our true king of peace and high priest, according to his order, should offer the same things, so that through this the truth might become clear through the figures,

[Note: Marmoutier and four manuscripts read: “through this figure.”]

and so that those who hunger and thirst for righteousness might at times be satisfied by these two things on the way.

Hunger would be restrained by bread, which is very often used in Scripture for every kind of food and seems to correspond with all foods; while thirst would be moistened, as it were, by drinking the blood, like heavenly dew.

[Note: Two manuscripts read ante hilaresceret (“would earlier be made joyful”).]

Through this, the human being, further refreshed for righteousness, would labor more steadfastly in the strength of heavenly food.

[Note: Another reading is “made more upright.”]

[Note: Three manuscripts read “would labor more greatly.”]

It is said that Elijah, nourished by this drink and food from the angel’s hand, reached the mountain of God in strength for forty days, by which the present age is signified.

From this it is plainly suggested that this food is brought by angelic hands and returned through them,

[Note: The Vatican and Florentine manuscripts read: “It is brought to God and returned to us.”]

by which our weakness is divinely relieved. It is offered only to friends and brothers.

Hence the Bridegroom exhorts us in the Song of Songs: “Eat, friends, and drink; become drunk, beloved” (Song of Songs 5:2). For such food and drink are never worthily tasted without drunkenness in the Holy Spirit.

Hence David, drunk with joy in our person, sings:

“You have prepared a table before me against those who trouble me.
You have anointed my head with oil,
and how glorious is my inebriating cup!” (Psalm 22:5).

It is glorious indeed, because it shines more brightly with the radiance of all truth

[Note: The printed editions, together with the Florentine manuscript, read veritate et fulgore (“with truth and radiance”); several manuscripts of excellent authority, omitting et (“and”), read veritate fulgore (“with the radiance of truth”). Four manuscripts read veritate fulgoris (“with the radiance of truth”).]

and is illumined by the light of the Holy Spirit. Through this it makes the minds of the faithful drunk.

By this draught those people were drunk at the third hour, upon whom the same Spirit had poured himself more fully.

Therefore the hearts of us who receive must also be prepared,

[Note: The Vatican and Florentine manuscripts read: “that is, of those who receive.” The manuscript of the queen of Sweden reads: “to be received”; another reading is “for receiving.”]

so that, refreshed by such a feast, we may pass onward in strength to higher things. No one therefore receives worthily unless he passes over; hence Passover is called a passage.

Our Passover is Christ, who was sacrificed. Whoever wishes to come to it and see this vision must pass over with Moses, just as Christ passed over from this world, so that the wholly spiritual person may receive these spiritual things, how worthily indeed.

[Note: The printed editions read condigne (“worthily”), but ten manuscripts read quam digne (“how worthily”).]

## CHAPTER XI. Why water is mixed in the chalice

**[Note: In a recent manuscript of Saint-Germain this title is given as: “Why water is mixed with wine, although this is not recorded as having been done at the Supper.”]**

### 1

**[Col. 1307D]** The principal reason why water is mixed with the blood, although we do not read that this was done by Christ at the institution of the chalice **[Note: Ulm and Sirm add: “by Christ.”]**, is plainly that from Christ’s side, when his Passion was being completed, blood and water flowed together. **[Col. 1307C]** The apostles rightly understood this mystery fully and made it customary that it should be done in this chalice, so that nothing might be lacking for us in this sacrament as a memorial of the Passion—namely, of what was then present on the cross for the completion of our redemption. **[Note: Anicianus reads: “For the commemoration of our redemption,” omitting “of the Passion,” and continuing: “which then existed on the cross for the consummation of our redemption.” In the manuscript of Major Monastery these words are omitted: “which then existed on the cross for the consummation of our redemption.”]**

For after he had given up his spirit, one of the soldiers came, took a lance, and opened his side; from it, as from a living **[Note: The printed editions read “from one source.”]** fountain, blood and water flowed. And this is the true chalice, because he truly suffered for our salvation—pouring out no less the blood of the price than the water **[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “than the water of baptism.”]** of baptism. What then flowed from his flesh is now drunk by believers in the chalice.

The flesh is given as food; the blood and water truly as drink, so that our whole person, renewed by these two things, may drink all that flowed together from his side. Thus, if after the font anyone has contracted any stain of sin, he may have in this water **[Note: The Vatican reads “water of forgiveness.”]** the forgiveness by which all his iniquities may be washed away **[Note: In the printed editions and in the Florentine manuscript these words are lacking: “all his iniquities, and, all his infirmities being healed.”]**, with all his infirmities healed, and may have the price of his redemption, by which each redeemed person is renewed again from day to day.

### 2

Many others have also said that water ought to be mixed in so that baptism and the price of salvation may flow together in Christ’s blood, so that it may no longer be as though there were two things, but one—namely, blood. **[Note: Ulm and Sirm read: “Not now two, but one, namely the substance of blood,” contrary to the manuscripts, which read: “Not now as though two things, but one, namely blood.” Or, as the Vatican royal manuscript and the manuscript of Saint-Ouen have it: “Namely, blood or water”; or, with the manuscript of Major Monastery: “Blood and water.”]** For blood also grows in the body by being nourished by these two things. **[Note: The manuscript of Major Monastery reads: “By all these things it is nourished.”]**

From this it is clear that divine Wisdom, with sufficient foresight for the dispensation of our salvation, brought forth these two things together from his side, so that from the place where the woman who had deceived the first Adam was created, the Church might once again be formed—the Church whose sins Christ bore upon the cross.

It is thus established that he raised all people up in himself **[Note: Sirm reads “washed all.”]**, since he bore the causes of all upon the cross. For this reason the Church, which was together in him, is rightly said to have flowed from his side. It is well signified by water, as the most holy Cyprian says. Hence, in the Apocalypse, the angel interprets the waters as peoples. It was therefore rightly ordained that water flowed together with blood **[Note: The Vatican reads: “because water flowed together with the blood.”]**, so that in this mystery it might be mingled with the true blood, so that we too might be in him and, through this sacrament of salvation, might be mystically offered as united with him before the divine gaze. **[Note: The manuscripts of Mamer, Ulm, and Florence read “immediately united.”]**

For if wine is offered without water, Christ’s blood begins to be without us; but if water alone is offered, the people appear to be without Christ. When, however, both are mixed and joined together, then the mystery of the Church is rightly accomplished spiritually. **[Col. 1308C]**

No liquids unite themselves so closely **[Note: The Florentine, Remigian, Saint-Ouen, and one royal manuscript read “come together so closely.” Anicianus and one Colbertine manuscript read “mix themselves so closely”; the manuscript of Major Monastery, “unite themselves to each other so closely.”]** as wine and water. This is surely because the one is produced from water through the vine, just as Christ is born from flesh through Mary—although wine is far superior to water. **[Note: Here the Laubach manuscript begins chapter XXX: “Why the Lord changed water into wine.”]**

Finally, we read that the Lord changed those waters for this reason: so that, when our wisdom had been emptied, the wine of gladness might overflow within us. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “The king brought me into the wine cellar and ordered love in me” (Song 2:4). And thereafter: “We shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts” (Song 1:3). **[Note: Sirm adds “over wine,” a reading absent from all the manuscripts.]**

The faithful therefore rejoice when they understand that by grace they have been joined to so great a unity with Christ and have been advanced to so great a fervor of love. For this reason how fittingly our figure is admitted into this mystery through water, so that each person may understand that he has been received into Christ’s blood and transformed for the better.

**[Note: In the Laubach manuscript chapter XXXI begins here: “Although wine and water are first mixed, afterward only blood is drunk.”]** Hence, although wine and water are first mystically mixed, after the consecration only blood is drunk. For, having first been received through the water of baptism **[Note: The Vatican adds “we may be renewed.”]**, we drink him again every day by hungering and thirsting for him. There is no doubt that under this mystery we drink that water of which the Lord says: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water leaping up into eternal life” (John 4:14).

Therefore water is also consecrated there for this appropriate reason—not that the water remains water, but that it is changed into blood, to signify what faith receives. **[Col. 1309B]** For there are three things that bear witness that Christ is the Truth: spirit, blood, and water. This is because, after he had sent forth the Spirit from the fountain of his breast, contrary to nature there flowed the blessed water of baptism and the blood of redemption. Through these, only one work of salvation is mystically consecrated, so that the whole body **[Note: Mamer, Ulm, Sirm, and Florence read “our body.”]**, soul, and spirit may be preserved for life in Christ.

Here no one doubts that our flesh also is restored to life, because the whole person is redeemed. The flesh is spiritually nourished by flesh, because the Word became flesh; the soul is restored by Christ’s blood. For, as Scripture testifies, every soul is in the blood, so that where it has its seat in the body, and through which it is said to give life to the body, from that same source it may also receive from Christ eternal life remaining within it.

**[Col. 1309C] [Note: In the Laubach manuscript chapter XXXIII begins here: “That our spirit and soul are one substance.”]**

But since our spirit and soul are one substance—although “spirit” or “mind” is the name given to that part which predominates in a human being, from which he is sometimes called spiritual when it has subjected the whole person to its laws and is made alive by God, while the soul is its lower part, by which the body is animated, and a human being is called animal; yet the animal human being does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God—for this reason, perhaps, water is admitted into this sacrament, so that these three things may mystically be consecrated to those three realities.

### 3

It is therefore established that, although three things are first set forth, afterward only flesh and blood are rightly believed to be present, giving an indication that the whole animal human being ought to pass over into spirit and become spiritual. For every soul is in the blood. We understand this as spoken figuratively, because all its life, in order that it may live blessedly, is restored in Christ’s blood. **[Col. 1309D] [Note: The manuscript of Major Monastery reads “in Christ’s blood,” with “in” deleted.]**

How fittingly, then, is it in the blood! Since through it the soul has kinship with flesh, it was just that through it also it should have a return to life. Therefore on the way we are nourished and given drink by these two things alone, so that our whole person, which consists of two substances, may be completely restored.

Hence David also says: “My soul has thirsted for you; how manifoldly my flesh has thirsted for you” (Psalm 14:3). The whole person therefore thirsted, in order that from flesh and soul he might pass over into spirit, so that he might be wholly spiritual in God. For this reason, although I have said that blood pertains to the soul, in a certain manner both flesh and soul rightly thirst for and drink blood together, just as they are nourished together by Christ’s flesh, because these things are not received carnally but spiritually.

The soul thirsts to be refreshed by such things, and the body thirsts as well. The soul eats **[Note: In the Sirmian edition “the soul eats” is absent]**, and the body also eats, because such food pertains no less to the soul than to the body. Nourished by it until the end, the immortal soul passes into life, whereas the flesh, because of the sentence imposed upon the first human being, returns to the earth. Yet because it has been incorporated into Christ through the washing and nourished by the food of immortality, it receives the seeds of life and will never be held in death after the end of the world. Rather, what went before in the Head will be bestowed upon the members.

## CHAPTER XII. Whether this mystery has something more when it is effected by a good minister, or something less when it is effected by an evil one

**[Note: The printed editions, together with the Florentine and Anician manuscripts and the manuscript of Major Monastery, give this title as: “Whether this mystery has something more when it is effected by a good man, or something less than the Truth promises when it is effected by an evil minister.” In Laubach it reads, chapter XXXIII: “It must truly be believed that in the catholic Church nothing greater is received from a good priest and nothing less from an evil priest.” In a recent manuscript of Saint-Germain: “That this mystery is not consecrated according to the priest’s merit, and that no one receives more or less from the priest who ministers.”]**

### 1

We must truly believe and know without doubt that within the catholic Church, wherever this mystery is celebrated according to the catholic faith, nothing greater is received from a good priest and nothing less from an evil one. Nothing other than the flesh and blood of Christ is received when it is consecrated according to the catholic rite **[Note: Ulm and Sirm read “when it is celebrated according to the catholic rite and consecrated.” But “celebrated” is absent from all the manuscripts.]**, because it is made so not by the merit of the one who consecrates **[Note: The Vatican reads “of the consecrating priest.”]**, but by the word of the Creator and the power of the Holy Spirit. Thus the flesh and blood of Christ—which is none other than that created by the Holy Spirit—is believed with true faith and tasted with spiritual understanding.

For if it depended on the priest’s merit, it would not belong to Christ. But now, just as Christ himself is the one who baptizes, so he himself is the one who, through the Holy Spirit, makes this his flesh and changes the wine **[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads this way; the other manuscripts omit “the wine.”]** into blood.

Who else could create in the womb so that the Word might become flesh? Therefore in this mystery we must believe that by the same power of the Holy Spirit, through the Word of Christ, his flesh and blood are made by an invisible operation.

**[Note: In the Laubach manuscript chapter XXXIV begins here: “That he is asked to carry it to the sublime altar.”]**

Hence the priest says: “Command these things to be carried by the hands of your angel to your sublime altar, in the sight of your divine majesty.” Why does he ask that they be carried there **[Note: The printed editions, together with some manuscripts, read “that they ought to be carried”; the manuscript of Major Monastery: “Why ought they to be carried to the sublime altar?”]**, unless it is understood that these things take place through Christ’s priesthood?

For he himself was made a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, as the Apostle testifies, to intercede for us, offering himself to God the Father. For this purpose he entered the holy places once for all—not with another’s blood, but with his own blood. Therefore what is his own is rightly received not from another but from the supreme High Priest himself; nor is his flesh and blood created by anyone other than the one by whom it was created in the Virgin’s womb, so that the Word might become flesh.

**[Note: In the Laubach manuscript chapter XXXV begins here: “When it is not ineffective for him who made all things from nothing to do what he wills.”]**

For the Father’s Word was told: “Increase and multiply” (Genesis 1:21); and behold, even today all living creatures are created from it—not as new things **[Note: Mamer reads “not new.”]**, but from the same seed.

So also Christ’s flesh becomes flesh by the same Word, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Therefore, if such a multitude flows from that blessing, what do you think comes from Christ’s flesh? Is he ineffective in accomplishing things from himself **[Note: Three manuscripts read “is he ineffective in carrying it out?”]**, who made so many things from nothing? And just as he increased the loaves by a quantity of substance that nature had not supplied **[Note: The printed editions of Sirm read “which he had not given to nature”; all the manuscripts read “which nature had not given,” which seems better to us]**, is he powerless to make from something what he had created in the womb without seed **[Note: The Vatican adds “of the Virgin”]**?

That abundance of Christ’s flesh therefore brings forth shoots, while Christ remains whole, because, with nature remaining intact, all things also abound in created things for his use.

### 2

For this reason, although he said once: “Let the earth bring forth green grass” (Genesis 1:11), even today everything that is born year by year is created from that command. Thus also in what he once willed, and thereafter commanded to be flesh and blood in this commemoration, what is commanded comes to be. **[Note: Here the Laubach manuscript begins chapter XXXVI: “That whoever does not believe this is worse than an impious person.”]**

If anyone does not believe this, he is worse than an impious person: the latter cannot approve what he has not learned, whereas this person does not believe in Christ’s flesh what he has seen happen many times contrary to nature.

Therefore, human being, if you attend to the priest, attend to Christ, the Word of the Father who is flesh, and do not doubt that what happened once happens daily in the mystery **[Note: The printed editions omit “in the mystery”]**, while through this mystery flesh and blood become our eternal food **[Note: The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions omit “eternal”]**. For this purpose we too are to be his body.

The priest does not say of himself that he can be the creator of the body and blood, because if he could do this—which is absurd—he would become the creator of the Creator. Rather, he entreats the Father through the Son, through whom we have access to him.

“We ask for this offering to be blessed, through which we may be blessed; inscribed, through which we all may be enrolled in heaven; ratified **[Note: Anicianus adds: “That is, judged and made firm”]**, through which we may be reckoned among Christ’s inward parts; reasonable, through which we may be stripped of bestial understanding; and that he may deign to make it acceptable.” **[Note: Two manuscripts read “may you deign.”]**

Thus, because we have displeased ourselves, we may be acceptable in his only Son, “so that,” he says, “it may become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

### 3

Behold what faith establishes; behold what Christ has granted: that his body and blood may be ours, so that through this we may daily be transferred into Christ’s body.

Before Christ’s body becomes so through consecration, it is the priest’s offering, as he himself confesses, or that of the whole family of those who offer it. But through the word and power of the Holy Spirit it becomes a new creature in the body of the Creator, for the salvation of our restoration **[Note: The manuscript of Major Monastery reads “for our redemption.”]**

Accordingly, Scripture testifies that he always stands beside the sublime altar, so that from his immolation we may receive his body and blood. The priest, however, because he appears visibly to act in Christ’s place between God and the people, carries the people’s vows to God by the hands of the angel and brings them back.

He offers vows and gifts; he brings back what has been obtained through the body and blood, and distributes it to each person—not in the measure presented by outward appearance **[Col. 1312C]**, but in the measure received by faith.

**[Note: In the Laubach manuscript chapter LIII begins here: “Although the priest is proved evil in conscience, what he offers is not his own; rather, throughout the whole text of the canon he commends the prayers and vows.”]**

Although the priest may be proved evil in conscience, what he offers is not his own; throughout the whole text of the canon he commends the prayers and vows of all. The conclusion of the prayer is also confirmed by the voices of everyone, when all say “Amen” with one accord. **[Note: That is, the conclusion of the canon, which in Paschasius Radbertus’s time was formed by the prayer “Deliver us,” which followed the Lord’s Prayer. The celebrating priest pronounces or chants its conclusion in a loud voice, so that all may answer “Amen” with one voice. The preceding words were said in a low voice.]**

Therefore what is offered for many and confirmed by the prayers of many does not belong to one person alone. The Lord also says: “Which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28). If it were only for himself **[Note: The manuscript of Saint-Ouen and one royal manuscript read: “If it were only for one person.”]**, God might perhaps consider his merits **[Col. 1313A]** **[Note: Eight manuscripts read “would consider”; Sirm reads “would not consider.”]**.

But now, even if the one who offers is a leper, what is received is clean, because it is the flesh and blood of the Savior, and no uncleanness can defile it **[Note: Six manuscripts read “is defiled”; the printed editions read “are defiled.”]**. These things are therefore provided by virtue of the priest’s office, not by his merit.

Thus, even if he is guilty **[Note: One royal manuscript reads: “Although the priest is guilty”]**, the office of ministry **[Note: The Vatican reads “the office of the mystery”]** is sacred, and the rank of priesthood is compensated by Christ, the supreme High Priest, so that this mystery contains no less flesh and blood when it is presented by an unworthy person, provided nevertheless that consecration of apostolic succession be conferred **[Note: Florence reads “when it is presented by any unworthy person,” omitting the words “Nevertheless, the consecration of apostolic succession.” Mamer reads: “by any unworthy person consecrated through apostolic succession.” The Vatican gives this clause as: “Provided that the consecration is presented according to the institution of apostolic succession.”]**.

**[Note: In Mamer, Ulm, and the manuscripts of Puteanus, Major Monastery, Laubach, Saint-Remigius, one Colbertine, and one Saint-Germain manuscript, the following words are absent: “For he who is ordained possesses the sacrament of consecration.”]**

For the one who is ordained possesses the sacrament of consecration, because it is not from him but from his office, and from the supreme High Priest, that the grace promised by Truth itself is fulfilled, so that neither his priesthood nor the office of his high priesthood is diminished in any way by anyone’s merit.

**[Note: Here the Laubach manuscript begins chapter LV: “That the power of consecrating lies in what the ordained person possesses, namely, in the priesthood. Therefore heretics—even priests—as well as criminals and those who have been deposed are not ordained again. For just as there is only one baptism, so there is only one priesthood. They have not indeed lost it, but have been forbidden to minister and have assumed the office of doing penance.”]**

For the power of consecrating lies in what the one who is ordained possesses. **[Col. 1313B]** Therefore those who return to catholic unity, having previously been baptized, are not rebaptized; likewise those who were previously ordained are not ordained again.

They either minister, if the usefulness of the Church requires this, or, if not, they nevertheless retain the sacrament of their ordination. For this reason hands are not laid upon them among the laity **[Note: Sirm reads: “Therefore hands are laid upon them among the laity,” contrary to all the manuscripts, which read with the negative: “Therefore hands are not laid upon them among the laity.”]**.

The power of the sacrament therefore remains in them, useless to themselves—even when they are guilty and consecrate **[Note: Florence and Laubach read “even when they are consecrated”]**—yet their authority and ordination to consecrate remain sufficiently useful to those who, in faith, hope, and charity, communicate in the grace of the blessing and ministry they have received. **[Note: In the Laubach manuscript chapter LVI begins here: “That these sacraments do more harm than good to the perverse.”]**

These sacraments of life, flowing from the heavenly fountain, do not profit the perverse for salvation, because there is no sharing of righteousness with iniquity, just as there is none of light with darkness.

**[Note: In the Laubach manuscript chapter LVII begins here: “Although priests are adulterers and murderers, if they have not been legally deposed one must not consider what they are, but what they give.”]**

Yet, although such men may hate such things **[Note: In two Swedish royal manuscripts and two royal manuscripts, with “although they hate such things” omitted, the reading is: “Although today they are adulterers.”]**, they may be adulterers and murderers, and may have committed many things on the devil’s side, while they sacrifice before being cut off by the evangelical sickle, one must not consider who and what they are, but what they give—or what the person who communicates in faith receives **[Note: Laubach reads: “Or what they receive from those who communicate in faith.” The manuscript of Major Monastery reads: “but what he receives,” omitting “what they give or.”]**.

Nor should one ask who possesses the power of consecrating, but what he possesses **[Note: Four manuscripts read: “but from whom he possesses it.”]**. For just as, as Christ himself testifies, demons are driven out in Christ’s name even by members of the devil, and many miracles are performed through them, so by Christ’s power in the sacrament the body and blood are effected by evil men.

Although it is said that God does not hear sinners, all these things are nevertheless celebrated and accomplished in the sacrament through angels: over the water of baptism, over the oil, over the Eucharist, and over the heads of those upon whom hands are laid in the sacrament. **[Note: The printed editions omit “through angels.”]**

They are therefore effective even through murderers, because, although they do not possess the Holy Spirit, it is God who, through their ministry, gives that same Holy Spirit **[Note: Laubach reads: “Behold, nevertheless, through the office they perform, divine mercy presents the gift of its generosity.” The Vatican and another manuscript read: “Nevertheless, the one who gives the same Spirit through their ministry is not absent.”]**, and who consecrates the gift of his generosity through their office.

Otherwise the grace of Christ would be narrower than the fraud and cunning of the devil. If that garden of delights could contain the thorns of the adversary, then much more does the fountain of Christ’s grace flow outside it and upon those who are not members of Christ.

### 4

What prevails everywhere is not therefore emptied of its power, nor can what properly belongs to God belong to another. Even if there are people who claim that these things belong to their own merit and fornicate away from God, the sacraments belonging to divine law must by no means be dishonored, as though they were thought to belong to such people.

Thus the Lord says under the figure of the harlot-synagogue: “You took from my gold and my silver and made for yourself male images, and you fornicated with them” (Ezekiel 16:17). Then he says: “You took my variegated garments **[Note: Another reading: “of diverse color.” Laubach with three other manuscripts: “multicolored.” Florence: “of varied color.”]** and covered your idols with them. You also placed my oil and my incense before the faces of your idols **[Note: The printed editions add “your.”]**. And my loaves, which I gave you, and the fine flour **[Note: Another reading adds “you offered.”]**, after which I fed you with honey and oil.”

Certainly, although a carnal soul turns all the sacraments and words of sacred Scripture toward the image of its own fantasies, these things are nevertheless not its own, nor those of its lovers, but God’s, even though it possesses its own fornication, whether deceived or deceiving.

The Lord therefore declares that these things are his own. We must not attribute to such people what belongs to God, nor reject them as harmful **[Note: Laubach with three other manuscripts and the printed editions read “as though unknown.” Puteanus, Vatican, Laudian, Major Monastery, Saint-Ouen, one royal, one Colbertine, and the Dominican manuscript read “as things not to be done.”]**. Rather, even in a harlot woman we should recognize the gifts of her lawful husband and, if we can, correct her fornication by the word of truth—the fornication that belongs to the shameless woman—without condemning those gifts that properly belong to the merciful Lord.

For although God gives the sacrament of grace even through evil people, he gives grace itself only through himself. In it there is forgiveness **[Note: Another reading adds “of all sins.”]** of sins, which he sometimes grants also through his saints.

Therefore there is nothing greater or less from any minister **[Note: The printed editions read “from any minister in the ministry”; eight manuscripts read “from any minister in the mystery.”]**, even if he is still in darkness, since the sacrament is provided through office, while grace is provided through participation in and unity with the dove, in which the fountain of life flows and forgiveness of sins pours forth. Its priest and eternal high priest is Christ, who makes atonement and offers himself for us daily before the sight of the divine majesty.

## CHAPTER XIII. Why these things do not at all change color or taste in the sacrament

**[Note: The Laubach manuscript calls this chapter LVIII.]**

**[Note: Two Swedish royal manuscripts and two royal manuscripts give the title as: “Why these sacraments do not at all change their color or taste”; in Mamer: “On the color and taste of flesh and on the blood of a murdered man”; in Ulm: “Although nothing of this kind appears to carnal eyes, these things are nevertheless truly received by the power of faith.”]**

### 1

Although it does not present the color or taste of flesh **[Note: The Vatican and Florence read: “Although it does not present the color…”]**, the power of faith and understanding—which doubts nothing concerning Christ—nevertheless tastes and savors the whole of it spiritually.

For, as I said, the one who created all things by the word cooperates in this by the word together with the Holy Spirit. Therefore nothing is to be doubted where God the Trinity is rightly believed to be the maker.

Nothing is lacking in it where the effective power of the same reality is perceived, where the full likeness is present outwardly **[Note: In the Putean manuscript and four other manuscripts the following words are absent: “and the true power of the Lamb, and his spotless flesh, is devoured inwardly.”]**, while inwardly the true power of the Lamb and his spotless flesh are devoured.

For nothing is more reasonable than that, because we have already received the likeness of his death in baptism, we should also receive the likeness of his flesh **[Col. 1315C]** and drink the likeness of his precious blood **[Note: Mamer and Ulm, together with Puteanus, Major Monastery, two Colbertine, and two royal manuscripts, read: “And drink by the likeness of his precious blood.”]**, so that the truth may not be absent from the sacrament and the pagans may not ridicule us for drinking the blood of a murdered human being.

What is hidden is sought more eagerly, and what is sought with faith is more precious. For this reason, too, this mystery had to be arranged in such a way that the secrets of the mysteries might be hidden from the faithless **[Note: Anicianus reads “might be hidden in the faithless”]**, that merit might increase through the power of faith, and that nothing inward might be lacking to those who truly believe the promised truth **[Note: Two manuscripts read “the power of the promised truth.”]**.

### 2

Moreover—and this is greater—through what is more secretly provided here, they might strive toward that form of satiety in which Christ will no longer be sacrificed daily for our sins, but all will enjoy him without end, without any corruption, in the satiety of his manifestation.

Otherwise how would those still unbelieving endure these things, if the disciples of old, hearing such words from his mouth, could not endure them? For when the Savior said: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me” (John 6:57), and so forth, they said: “This is a hard saying; who can bear it?” (ibid., 61).

How much more harshly would the ignorant and faithless bear these things, and how would they condemn Christians as utterly unclean because they ate human flesh and drank blood? Thus what by faith we ought to believe desirable would become execrable, even though by understanding we ought to taste it—not carnally but spiritually.

“For we walk by faith, and not by sight.” If the appearance of flesh were visibly present in these things, it would no longer be faith or mystery **[Note: Major Monastery reads: “but the mystery would become a miracle.”]**, but a miracle would occur—either faith would be given to us, or a more troublesome execration from the faithless would assail communicants **[Note: Seven manuscripts read “or a curse for the faithless,” deleting “from.” The Vatican reads: “or a curse for faithless people who despise it.”]**.

These things, therefore, have been given also to believing faithful people **[Note: The printed editions read “and already.”]**, whereas signs and miracles are given to those who do not believe, so that they may receive faith. It was therefore fitting that these things should not be changed, and that believers should not doubt them even for a little while.

## CHAPTER XIV. That these things have often appeared in visible form

**[Note: In the Laubach manuscript this is chapter LIX.]**

**[Note: Four manuscripts add: “And concerning examples of those who saw them.”]**

### 1

No one who has read the lives and examples of the saints can be unaware that these mystical sacraments of the body and blood have often been displayed in visible form—either for the sake of doubters or certainly for those who love Christ more ardently—in the form of a lamb or in the color of flesh and blood.

This occurred so that Christ might still mercifully establish faith concerning himself among those who did not believe. Thus, when the offered host was broken or offered, a lamb appeared to be in the hands and blood to be flowing in the chalice, as though from an immolation, so that what lay hidden in the mystery might be disclosed to those still doubting through a miracle.

Divine mercy did this for certain people who already believed but still doubted, so that they themselves might receive confidence in the truth and others might be strengthened in faith by the miracle; and so that we might participate more abundantly in Christ’s grace through that same faith. **[Note: Nine manuscripts read: “And that through the same faith they might participate in the grace of Christ.”]**

For the things that the Truth promised must be believed without being seen. Yet because we are hard-hearted **[Note: The printed editions read “hard of heart.”]**, divine gentleness wished to satisfy everyone in certain cases, so that no one might thereafter doubt these things. **[Note: The printed editions read “so that another might not”; this is erroneous and contrary to all the manuscripts, which read “so that no one might thereafter.”]**

But if neither what has been displayed is believed nor the things that the Truth testifies to are received in faith, let anyone seek, for the sake of satisfying himself, what he is awaiting, since nothing exists outside the truth. Whatever the truth contains, a visible display represents whenever it pleases.

Therefore one ought to believe that these things were displayed most opportunely, and to doubt nothing of what the Truth promises, because whoever seeks anything outside the truth will find only falsehood. And if he does not accept the things spoken by Christ **[Note: The Colbertine manuscript reads “concerning Christ.”]**, he shuts himself outside the truth.

When I said that these things had often appeared in visible form to certain people **[Note: Sirm’s edition reads: “They often appeared in visible form to certain people who loved Christ more ardently.” Many manuscripts read: “They often appeared in visible form to certain people.” Laubach, Vatican, Laudian, Remigian, Tours, Major Monastery, Rouen, Saint-Ouen, and one royal manuscript read: “These things were displayed beforehand to those who loved them.” Florence, with Mamer and Ulm, reads: “They were often displayed beforehand to certain people who loved Christ.”]**, I shall disclose a few examples from among the many **[Note: Six manuscripts—namely, those that omit what follows concerning Saints Basil and Gregory—read: “One from among many.”]**.

## 2

When blessed Basil was publicly celebrating the divine mysteries, a certain Hebrew mingled with the congregation as though he were a Christian, wishing to investigate the ministry of the office and the gift [Note: [Col. 1318D] In one manuscript of Saint-Germain: “wishing to investigate the grace of the divine gift.”]. He saw an infant being divided in Basil’s hands; and when everyone had received communion, he too approached, and what was given to him was truly flesh. Then he approached the chalice, filled—as it truly is—with blood, became a participant in it as well, and, preserving remnants of both, returned to his house. He showed them to his wife as confirmation of what he had said and recounted what he had seen with his own [Col. 1317C] eyes. Believing, therefore, he said [Note: [Col. 1318D] The printed editions read: “believing therefore that truly”; the manuscripts read more correctly: “believing therefore, he said: Truly,” etc.]: “Truly, the mystery of the Christians is dreadful [Note: [Col. 1318D] One Colbert manuscript: “terrible.”] and wondrous.” The next day he came to Basil and asked to receive without delay the seal that is in Christ. Saint Basil did not delay, but, wishing to save all, offered the customary Eucharist and baptized him, together with his whole household, who believed in the Lord [Note: [Col. 1318D] Thus all the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “Wishing to save all.”].

## 3

But something should also be added from the life of blessed Gregory. A certain noble matron had been accustomed, every Sunday, to make offerings [Note: [Col. 1318D] The printed editions read *oblationem*, “an offering”; all the manuscripts read *oblationes*, “offerings.”] and present them according to ecclesiastical custom. One day, when she had come among the others to receive Holy Communion and to receive the body of Christ, the blessed pontiff handed her a portion [Note: [Col. 1318D] The Anician manuscript: “a particle and a portion.”] of the Lord’s body, saying: “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ benefit you for the remission of all [Col. 1318A] sins.” At once she smiled. When the man of God saw this, he withdrew the sacred communion from her and placed it upon the altar. After the sacred ministry had been completed, he asked her why she had laughed.

She replied: “I recognized that it was a small portion of my offering, which I heard you call the Lord’s body, and for that reason I laughed.”

Then Saint Gregory, addressing the people, urged them to entreat God in prayer to strengthen the woman’s faith, so that the Lord might show himself to her in visible form [Note: [Col. 1318D] Thus the Anician manuscript; the other manuscripts delete “himself.”], since she had been unable to believe this with the eyes of her mind. When this prayer had been offered, he rose together with the people and immediately, in full view of everyone—and with the woman also looking on—uncovered the altar. He found that the portion he had placed there, about the size of a little finger, was covered with blood [Note: [Col. 1318D] Another manuscript: “with blood poured over it.”].

Then the priest said to the woman: “Learn that what the Truth says is true: the bread that we offer is truly the body of Christ, according to his own word, and the blood is truly drink. Believe at last that it cannot be anything other than what the divine majesty has willed.”

Then the priest of Christ immediately prayed that the same flesh and blood might recover its former appearance. And so it happened: everyone glorified God, the woman’s unbelief was driven away, and she was healed after receiving the sacred and holy mystery [Note: [Col. 1318D] The printed editions read: “the sacred and holy mystery.”].

## 4

Abbot Arsenius is said to have been filled with such great holiness and compunction that, because of the excessive outpouring of his tears, he always carried a cloth in his bosom for wiping his face. He also very often related the story of a certain old man living in Scythia, who was great in active life but simple in faith. He was in error because he was uneducated, and said that this bread which we receive was not naturally [another reading: “by nature”] the body of Christ, but was its figure.

Two old men heard him saying this. Knowing that his life and conduct were exemplary, they thought that he spoke in this way innocently and simply. They came to him and said: “Abba, we have heard the statement of a certain unbeliever who says that the bread we receive is not naturally the body of Christ, but is its figure.”

The old man said: “I am the one who said this.”

They pleaded with him: “Do not hold this opinion, Abba, but believe as the Catholic Church has handed it down. We believe that the bread itself is the body of Christ, and that the chalice itself is the blood of Christ according to the truth, and not according to a figure. Just as in the beginning he took dust from the earth and fashioned a human being in his own image—and no one can say that this is not the image of the incomprehensible God—so also, regarding the bread of which he says, ‘This is my body,’ we believe that it is truly the body of Christ.”

The old man said to them: “Unless I come to know the matter itself, your request will not satisfy me.”

They said to him: “Let us beseech the Lord during this week concerning this mystery, and we believe that the Lord will reveal it to us.”

The old man gladly accepted this proposal and prayed to God, saying: “Lord, you know that I am not unbelieving in this matter through malice, but lest I go astray through ignorance. Therefore reveal to me, Lord Jesus Christ, what is true.” The other old men also went away to their cells and prayed to God in their cells, saying: “Lord Jesus Christ, reveal this mystery to the old man, so that he may believe and not lose the labor of his life.”

The Lord heard them. When the week had been completed, they came to the church on the Lord’s Day and the three of them alone sat upon a seat made of rushes, tied together in the form of a bundle. The old man sat between the other two. The eyes of their understanding were opened. When the loaves had been placed upon the altar, only the three of them saw what appeared to be a little child lying upon the altar. When the priest extended his hand to break the bread, an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, holding a knife in his hand, and sacrificed that little child. He caught the child’s blood in the chalice. When the priest broke the bread into small pieces, the angel likewise cut the child’s limbs into small portions.

When the old man approached to receive Holy Communion, flesh stained with blood was given to him alone. When he saw this, he was terrified and cried out: “I believe, Lord, that the bread placed upon the altar is your body, and that your chalice is your blood.”

Immediately that flesh in his hand became bread according to the mystery, and he took it into his mouth, giving thanks to God.

The old men said to him: “God knows human nature: it cannot eat raw flesh. For this reason he transformed his body into bread and his blood into wine for those who receive it in faith.”

They gave thanks to God concerning that old man, because God had not allowed the labor of his life to perish, and they all returned joyfully to their cells.

## 5

[Note: [Col. 1319D] In the Laub manuscript, chapter LXI begins here: “Announcement of a miracle concerning the same most holy mystery.”]

Sometimes, too, it is recorded that these things were shown to those who desired Christ according to their prayer. Such is the account in the deeds of the English: a certain priest, very devout, named Plecgils, frequently celebrated the solemnities of Mass at the shrine of Saint Ninia [Note: [Col. 1319D] The printed editions read “Nini”; the Major Monastery manuscript reads “Nili.”], bishop and confessor. Since, by God’s favor, he was leading a holy life with worthy discipline, he began to assail almighty God with devout prayers, asking him to show him the nature of Christ’s body and blood [Note: [Col. 1319D] The word “devout” is absent from the Major Monastery manuscript.].

He asked this not, as is customary, out of unbelief, but out of religious devotion. From childhood he had been instructed in the divine laws, and, out of love for the heavenly King, he had long ago left the borders of his homeland and its pleasant fields, so that, in exile, he might diligently learn the mysteries of Christ. Therefore, inflamed still more by love for him, he offered precious gifts every day and asked that the form hidden beneath the appearance of bread and wine be shown to him—not because he doubted Christ’s body, but because he wished to see Christ in this way also, whom no mortal, once he had been raised above the stars, can now behold anywhere upon earth [Note: [Col. 1319D] The Anician and Major Monastery manuscripts, together with the Ulm manuscript, read: “who suffered upon earth.” The Mamer manuscript, together with the Putean, Remigian, and one Saint-Germain manuscript, omits *passim* (“anywhere”) or *passum* (“suffered”).].

When the day came on which he was celebrating, he piously prostrated himself on his knees according to the customary rite of the solemn Mass and said:

“I beseech you, Almighty One: disclose to me, insignificant as I am, in this mystery the nature of Christ’s body, so that I may be permitted to behold him present with bodily sight and to touch with my hands the form of the child whom the womb of his mother once carried crying [Note: [Col. 1319D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “the womb of the Virgin mother.”].”

While he was praying such things, an angel came from heaven and addressed him:

“Rise quickly, if you desire to see Christ. He is present, clothed in the bodily garment that the holy mother bore.”

Then the venerable priest, trembling, raised his face from the ground [Note: [Col. 1320D] Another reading: “from the earth.”], and saw upon the altar of the Father the Son as a child, whom the righteous Simeon had been privileged to carry as an infant in his arms [Note: [Col. 1320D] The Vatican manuscript reads this passage as follows: “Upon the altar of the Most High Father, the only-begotten incarnate Jesus, whom the righteous old man Simeon …”].

The angel said to him: “Since you have desired to see Christ, whom previously you used to consecrate beneath the appearance of bread by mystical words, now look upon him with your eyes and touch him with your hands.”

Then, relying upon the heavenly gift—and wondrous beyond words—he took the child in his trembling arms and joined his own breast to Christ’s breast. Then, pouring himself into an embrace, he kissed God and pressed Christ’s holy lips with his own lips.

When this had been completed, he restored the glorious limbs of the Son of God to the top of the altar and filled Christ’s table with heavenly food. Then, prostrate once again upon the ground, he prayed that God himself would deign to turn again into its former appearance.

When the prayer had been completed, he rose from the ground and found that Christ’s body had returned to its former appearance, as he had prayed.

What a wondrous dispensation of almighty God: because of one person’s desire, he deigned to make himself visible in this way—not in the form of a lamb, as he does for others under this mystery, but in the form of a child—so that the truth might be revealed in what had been shown, the priest’s desire might be fulfilled through the miracle, and our faith might be strengthened through the account.

Nevertheless, it is not recorded that he received the child’s body and blood before it returned to the appearance of its former form, lest what he had presumed to do seem absurd; rather, faith is to be sought more abundantly inwardly in the same reality that he had seen outwardly.

For the present, let this suffice concerning the showing of Christ’s flesh in support of the truth. [Col. 1321A]

## 6

But if anyone does not believe, on the basis of this, what is proclaimed in the Gospel, he appears to be worse, I say, than those earlier people who, under the taste of a single kind, perceived every flavor and every delight through faith. Yet what was shown then was not something else, even though manna, under one and the same color, supplied inwardly whatever there is of flavor and delight.

The power of things is more important than their appearance and painted color [Note: [Col. 1321C] Seven manuscripts read “darkened color.”]. Therefore the power must be considered more than the outward color or taste [Note: [Col. 1321D] The printed editions read: “the power should be considered more.”]. For he who gave all things the power of their nature [Note: [Col. 1321D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “who gave all things their power”; the Florentine manuscript: “who gave every nature its power”] divinely granted this sacrament the power to be his flesh and blood, so that the whole sacrament of this mystery might accomplish what the flesh and blood of Christ bestowed upon the Church, and might mercifully lead his spotless people to immortality; and might cause carnal and corruptible people to advance toward spiritual and incorruptible things [Note: [Col. 1321D] The printed editions read “perfects”; the Florentine and Saint-Ouen manuscripts read “may perfect”; eight manuscripts read “may cause to advance.”].

For this reason it had to be celebrated spiritually, so that through it we might be carried from visible things to invisible things, and might seek with more insistent faith what still lies hidden [Note: [Col. 1321D] In the Major Monastery manuscript, “through it” has been deleted.]. There must be no doubt concerning the appearance, while the power of Christ inwardly supplies through the mystery everything that the Gospel promises by the divine oracle.

# CHAPTER XV

[Note: [Col. 1321D] In the Laub manuscript, chapter LXII begins here with the title: “There must be no doubt concerning the appearance, while the power of Christ inwardly supplies everything.” In the Mamer, Ulm, and more recent Saint-Germain manuscripts: “That this mystery is consecrated by no one’s merits except by the one whose will governs and sustains all things.”]

## By what words this mystery is accomplished

### 1

No one doubts that, just as when we are immersed three times in the font in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, we are then baptized—not by the virtue and power of the one who says these words, but by the power of Christ, who commanded this, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Mark XVI)—so also this sacrament is undoubtedly effected and consecrated not by human merits or words, but by divine commands.

For there is created there from something a new creation of salvation—not just any creation—namely, the flesh and blood of Christ, just as in baptism human beings become a new creation and the body of Christ [Note: [Col. 1321D] Six manuscripts read: “human beings are made new and become the body of Christ.”].

Therefore it must not be thought that these things are accomplished by another’s words, by the merits of anyone else, or by anyone’s power [Note: [Col. 1321D] The Laub manuscript has this reading; the other manuscripts commonly omit “by another’s.”], but by the word of the Creator, through which all visible and invisible things were created. Since they were first created by his power, they are certainly recreated for something better by his word, because Catholic teaching proclaims that no one is the creator or re-creator of anything except the one God [Note: [Col. 1321D] Five manuscripts read: “the creator of so great a thing.”].

For this reason we must come to the words of Christ and believe that these things are accomplished in those same words. All the other things that the priest says or the clergy sings are nothing other than praises and thanksgivings, or certainly the entreaties, petitions, and requests of the faithful [Note: [Col. 1321D] The Laub manuscript reads: “nothing other than praises, thanksgivings, and the entreaties of the faithful.” [Col. 1322C]].

But the words of Christ, being divine, are also effective [Note: [Col. 1322D] The Major Monastery manuscript reads: “effective in producing results.”], so that nothing happens except what they command, because they are eternal. “Heaven and earth,” he says, “will pass away” [Note: [Col. 1322D] All manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions read: “will pass away” with the future form], “but my words will not pass away” (Matthew XXIV, 35). Rather, they will accomplish everything for which they have been spoken, because the Word of the Father is one, substantive, consubstantial, and eternal.

Accordingly, the priest first takes up, among other things, even the words of the evangelists and says:

“On the day before he suffered, he took bread into his holy and venerable hands, and, raising his eyes to heaven, to you, God his almighty Father, giving you thanks, he blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples.”

Up to this point, these are the words of the evangelists. From this point onward, however, they are the words of God, full of power and complete efficacy:

“Take and eat from this, all of you; for this is my body.”

But lest you think that he commanded this only concerning that one loaf and at that one hour, he adds, saying:

“Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke XXII, 20 and following).

[Note: [Col. 1322D] In the Laub manuscript, chapter LXIII begins here: “It must be acknowledged that what the apostles received when Christ said to them, ‘This is my body,’ is the same thing that we receive, and not something else, if we receive it worthily.”]

Therefore it must be acknowledged that whatever that thing was which the apostles then received from him, it is entirely this same thing, because it is identical. And if you wish to hear what it is, he says: “This is my body, which will be given for you” [Note: [Col. 1322D] The printed Florentine edition and the Saint-Germain manuscript add: “In this word, therefore, that body is created, because it is the divine Word, full of omnipotence, present everywhere and filling all things. And when he says, ‘This is my body, which will be given for you,’ believe …”].

Believe, my son, that it is so, because he himself said it; and you cannot doubt that it was accomplished. He himself commanded, and it was created.

He therefore issued the command: “Do this in remembrance of me” [Note: [Col. 1322D] The printed editions add “saying”]. And therefore, whenever it is performed in Catholic fashion, what was said is truly performed: “This is my body.”

### 2

Likewise, after supper, the priest repeats the words of the evangelist:

“Taking this glorious chalice.”

And note that he received this chalice which we offer, and not another, into his holy and venerable hands [Note: [Col. 1322D] The words enclosed in parentheses are absent from the printed Florentine edition and the Saint-Germain manuscript.] [showing by what it contains what is contained, he says that he received it]; likewise, giving you thanks, he blessed it and gave it to his disciples, saying [Note: [Col. 1323D] The Vatican manuscript and another manuscript add: “Take and drink from it, all of you, for this is my blood.”]:

Do you hear everywhere that he himself gave thanks and that he blessed? Therefore, although we give thanks to God, he is the one who gives thanks for us through himself, while we do so through him. And because it is through him, his thanksgiving is rightly called ours.

Thus, although the priest blesses, he is the one who blesses and breaks; otherwise, if the blessing were not his, there would be no holiness in it [Note: [Col. 1323D] The Major Monastery manuscript reads: “no secure holiness.”]. Hence in Leviticus he says to Aaron and his sons: “You shall invoke my name over the children of Israel, and I will bless them” (Numbers VI, 27).

The priest therefore invokes, but he himself blesses and breaks; for unless he broke this bread, all the little ones would remain hungry. For this reason the prophet, sighing because Christ had not yet come, said in his Lamentations: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lamentations IV, 4).

Therefore he alone is the one who breaks this bread and distributes it through the hands of ministers to those who believe [Note: [Col. 1323D] Three manuscripts add: “and also distributes the chalice to believers”], saying: “Take and drink from this, all of you,” both the ministers and the other believers:

“This is the chalice of my blood, of the new and eternal covenant.”

In this word the blood is made what previously had been wine and water. It is therefore made blood—but that blood which he handed over to the disciples: plainly, the blood of the New and eternal Covenant. This covenant will never be changed, because it is eternal; it will never grow old and will never be annulled. And this is the covenant of our inheritance, through which divine and heavenly things are handed over to us.

### 3

This, then, is the mystery of faith. Through a figure of this blood the people of the Old Testament were sanctified. But in that blood there was a shadow; here, however, there is the truth:

“For you,” he says, “it will be poured out, and for many, for the remission of sins.”

For where Luke said “for you,” Matthew wrote “for many” (Matthew XVI, 28). We must therefore believe that Christ said both, because this blood was poured out both for the apostles and for the many who were to believe through their word.

It is this blood, and no other, neither anyone else’s [Note: [Col. 1323D] “Of another” is absent from most manuscripts], but the blood of Jesus Christ, that is made in this word. This word remains vigorous and endures:

“This is the chalice of my blood, which will be poured out for you and for many.”

Therefore, O human being, whenever you drink this chalice or eat this bread, do not suppose that you are drinking any blood other than that which was poured out for you and for all for the remission of sins. Nor suppose that you are receiving any flesh other than that which was given up for you and for all and hung upon the cross, because the Truth testifies:

“This is my body, which will be given for you.”

And concerning the chalice:

“For this is my blood, which will be poured out for you for the remission of sins.”

Therefore, just as it was then poured out and given for the remission of sins [Note: [Col. 1323D] Here we restore “then” from the Vatican manuscript; it is absent from the other manuscripts], so even today it is eaten and drunk for the remission of offenses [Note: [Col. 1324D] The printed editions read “for this purpose,” contrary to the testimony of all the manuscripts]. Since, as I said earlier, we cannot live on earth without daily and lesser offenses, may we, refreshed by such food and drink, be found without stain or wrinkle; and not only this, but may we also be filled with every heavenly blessing that is in them. Through this one thing may we remain one body with him and in him, where Christ is regarded as the head and we are all regarded as members.

# CHAPTER XVI

[Note: [Col. 1324D] Chapter LXV in the Laub manuscript.]

## Whether this body may rightly be called bread after the consecration

### 1

That this mystery may be called bread, even though it is true flesh, the Apostle proves when he says: “Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the chalice” (1 Corinthians XI, 28).

For Christ’s flesh is true flesh, and yet the living bread that descended from heaven is rightly and catholically proclaimed to be bread: flesh according to grace, but bread according to its efficacy. Just as this earthly bread supplies temporal life, so that heavenly bread grants eternal and heavenly life, because it is everlasting life.

Finally, this blood may likewise, according to its efficacy, be called wine in a figurative sense. Just as wine, when drunk in moderation, gladdens the hearts of human beings, so this wine of blood, far more abundantly, gladdens the heart of the inward human being and intoxicates the mind with spiritual love. Hence it is said: “How splendid is my intoxicating chalice” [Note: [Col. 1324D] Two manuscripts read: “How splendid is your chalice.”] (Psalm XXII, 5); and: “Wine gladdens the heart of man” (Psalm CIII, 15).

The bride rejoices over this wine in the Song of Songs, saying that Christ has ordered his love within her.

Nevertheless, according to the truth of the teaching set forth above, it is rightly believed to be nothing other than the flesh and blood of Christ. They are tasted not with the taste of flesh but with spiritual sweetness, and are understood by the reasoning of faith.

# CHAPTER XVII

[Note: [Col. 1324D] Chapter LXVI in the Laub manuscript. The title of this chapter in the Ulm and more recent Saint-Germain manuscripts reads: “The power and nature of this sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood are completely hidden from the perception of reason.”]

## Whether the devout person receives more who receives more or who receives less

### 1

If the figure of this sacrament preceded it in that heavenly manna, the meaning of this matter is truly and plainly demonstrated by what is said:

“He who had gathered more did not have more, nor did he who had prepared less find less” (Exodus XVI, 18; 2 Corinthians VIII, 15) [Note: [Col. 1324D] Two manuscripts omit “did not have.”].

In this mystery, visible quantity must not be considered at all, but the power of the spiritual sacrament. Just as the physical size of Christ’s human body is not to be measured, but the power and divinity in him are to be considered, so that woman in the Gospel received more who touched the fringe of his garment than the crowd that pressed against his whole body [Col. 1325A], because she conceived more of him in her mind when she believed with faith [Note: [Col. 1325C] We restore this passage with the help of the Major Monastery manuscript; the other manuscripts, having deleted *cum*, read: “And she believed by faith.”].

Therefore we must consider not how much is pressed by the tooth, but how much is grasped by faith and love [Note: [Col. 1325C] The Mamer manuscript and three others read: “by love and expansion of the mind” [Col. 1325D]].

For Christ’s flesh is not rightly received without divinity, nor is divinity granted without flesh. Hence the Gospel says:

“The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. When a man finds it, he goes away, sells everything, and buys that field” (Matthew XIII, 44).

For neither is the field—that is, Christ’s body—rightly acquired without the treasure [Note: [Col. 1325D] The printed editions add “of divinity,” but this is absent from all the manuscripts], nor is the treasure of divinity acquired without the field of flesh [Note: [Col. 1325D] The Florentine manuscript reads: “without the field, that is, the body of Christ.”].

And how well the treasure is said to be hidden in the field! For divinity, dwelling bodily in Christ’s flesh, is also withdrawn from the sight of the eyes in this mystery, so that it may be sought with more eager faith, found more truly when sought, held more dearly when found, and enjoyed more desirably when possessed [Note: [Col. 1325D] The printed editions and the Florentine manuscript read: “so that it may be enjoyed.”]. For in Christ all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

Therefore it is necessary that whoever has eaten his body should receive it by faith from the fullness of divinity. Hence the holy evangelist says:

“And we have all received from his fullness” (John I, 16).

Otherwise, if you do not first receive from the fullness [Note: [Col. 1325D] The printed editions read “from his fullness,” but the manuscripts omit “his”], you will not be able to reach even a small portion of the flesh, because the treasure is not bought for the sake of the field, but the field for the sake of the treasure.

For the treasure of the fullness of divinity is sold to those who believe with him and in him [Note: [Col. 1325D] The Mamer and Ulm manuscripts, together with five others, read: “is bought by believers”; two manuscripts: “is amended”; the Laub manuscript: “is cleansed.”].

Therefore, my son, whenever you receive this mystery, enlarge the bosom of your mind, cleanse your conscience, and receive not as much as the morsel displays, but as much as faith comprehends. For the fullness of divinity remains in Christ, while in you there is granted from the fullness not as much as it is, but as much as you are capable of receiving.

# CHAPTER XVIII

[Note: [Col. 1325D] Chapter LXVII in the Laub manuscript.]

## Why this mystery was handed over to the disciples before the Passion

This sacrament was celebrated before the Lord’s Passion so that, immediately after the legal Passover—for the shadow had to be removed—the light of truth might shine [Note: [Col. 1326C] The printed editions read: “so that the truth might shine clearly”; the manuscripts: “so that the light of truth might shine clearly.”]. A shadow can never cease unless light shines upon it [Note: [Col. 1326C] The printed editions read: “never, therefore”; the Florentine manuscript: “never, for.”].

Christ also knew something else: both the good, worthily, and the evil, unworthily, though presumptuously, would receive this mystery. He wished to give all communicants an example of what good or evil they receive. Therefore Judas is admitted to receive as a figure of all evil people [Note: [Col. 1326D] The Major Monastery manuscripts omit “to receive.”]. For if this had taken place after the resurrection, Judas could no longer have communicated with the holy apostles, since he had already been condemned by eternal judgment.

Through this mystery the Lord’s Passion and death had to be proclaimed. Therefore it was more fitting to hand it over at the very moment of the Passion than after the resurrection, because the Lamb was sacrificed for this purpose: that we might eat his flesh. Hence Paul says: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast” (1 Corinthians V, 7).

Moreover, because he himself was already passing [Note: [Col. 1326D] The Ulm and Sirmond manuscripts read “about to pass”; the Mamer manuscript, together with four others, “passing”; nearly all the other manuscripts “was passing.”] from this world to the Father—that is, from this mortality to immortality—he, while still mortal, did what we were to do after him and in him as mortals. Thus, refreshed by such food and inebriated by such a cup, we might confidently do for him, assured of immortality, what he first did for us as a mortal [Note: [Col. 1326D] Another reading: “for mortals.”].

For this reason he provided the nourishment of immortality, so that we might not fear death. But, finally, if he had given this after the resurrection, the heretics would have said that, once Christ was incorruptible and situated in heaven [Note: [Col. 1326D] This is the reading of nearly all the manuscripts and the printed editions: “that Christ, already incorruptible and situated in heaven …”], his flesh could not be devoured on earth by the faithful.

Now, however, because he remains whole and incorrupt [Note: [Col. 1326D] The printed editions read “remains incorruptible”; the manuscripts “remains incorrupt.”], we say against them that we receive these things in his death so that, until the end of the world, we may all be nourished by them, while what has been sown remains incorrupt when it rises again [Note: [Col. 1326D] Three manuscripts read: “will rise incorrupt,” omitting “remains.”].

For this reason the grain of wheat fell into the earth, so that it might bear much fruit. If he granted this to seeds, how much more did he grant it to himself, so that the same thing might remain incorrupt and thereafter provide abundant nourishment of immortality to believers from its fruitfulness [Note: [Col. 1326D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “and from his mortality.”].

Therefore, just as he rose, so also are these seeds of immortality, which make those who worthily receive them immortal. And whenever we eat these things, we proclaim the Lord’s death, because from this death we have obtained immortality, until he himself, living and immortal, comes [Note: [Col. 1326D] The printed editions read: “until he comes, living and mortal,” contrary to all the manuscripts, which read “living and immortal”]. Then, also refreshed with these things for a long time by such immortal food, we too may reign immortal with him through him.

# CHAPTER XIX

[Note: [Col. 1327D] Chapter LXIX in the Laub manuscript.]  
[Title:] Why a fragment of the body is mixed into Christ’s blood

[Note: [Col. 1327D] The Laub manuscript adds: “And that not only the soul but also the body is nourished by this mystery.” A recent Saint-Germain manuscript gives this title: “That receiving the Lord’s body and blood is necessary for our salvation.”]

### 1

The meaning is clear: the flesh is now broken because the blood is in the chalice that flowed from his side. Therefore how rightly the flesh is joined to the blood, since neither is flesh rightly communicated without blood, nor blood without flesh.

For the whole human being, who consists of two substances, is redeemed; and therefore he is nourished by Christ’s flesh and blood together. In the end, it is not, as some wish, the soul alone that is nourished by this mystery, because the soul alone is not redeemed and saved by Christ’s death. Rather, our flesh also is restored through this to immortality and incorruption.

Christ’s flesh, spiritually united with our flesh, transforms it [Note: [Col. 1327D] The Laub manuscript reads “is specially incorporated”; the Major Monastery manuscript: “is spiritually consecrated.”]—[Note: [Col. 1327D] The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the printed editions.] as Hilary testifies: “so that we may be one in him through this mystery naturally, and so that Christ’s substance may also be found in our flesh”—just as it is established that he assumed our humanity into his divinity.

Therefore, praying to God with the prophet, we say:

“Remember what my substance is: have you indeed created all the sons of men in vain?” (Psalm LXXXVIII, 48) [Note: [Col. 1327D] The printed editions, together with one manuscript, read: “Remember my substance.”].

What greater security is there for a human being than to pray concerning his own substance, to venerate that substance in God, and confidently, through the unity of person, to say:

“O God, my substance, who established and created me, did you create me in vain?”

Certainly not—even though the living human being is subject to vanity [Note: [Col. 1328D] The printed editions read: “every living human being.”], because God is the Creator, and the Word of the Father became human [Note: [Col. 1328D] The printed editions read: “the Word of the Father became human.”].

Thus it is evident from this that we are in him and he is in us, while he spiritually pours himself into the flesh [Note: [Col. 1328D] The printed editions read: “while he pours himself into the flesh”], so that through this we may be transformed into incorruption.

### 2

As I said, his blood is drunk so that the soul, which is in the blood of sin, may be renewed. For Christ’s soul, not in the blood of sin but in the blood of flesh, also vivified the human flesh that Christ had assumed, in accordance with human nature.

Therefore flesh is not rightly received without blood. Rather, flesh must have a relation to the soul, which is in Christ’s blood, and the soul, which gives life, must through the blood have a relation to God, so that the whole human being may be healed.

For this reason also, when the Lord had said: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life,” he immediately added: “And I will raise him up on the last day” [Col. 1327D] (John VI, 55).

He said “has” for this reason: as soon as the soul is released from the flesh, it enters the storehouses of life, where the souls of the saints rest. Then, concerning the body, he added: “And I will raise him up on the last day,” so that, just as the human being was created whole, so also he might be proclaimed redeemed whole; and thereafter, on the last day, believed to be restored in his entirety.

### 3.

[Note: [Col. 1328D] The following words, up to “nevertheless just,” are missing from eleven manuscripts.]

Moreover, in the chalice—as can be understood from the holy Fathers—body and blood are joined together in this portion because the chalice of Christ’s passion prefigures the mystery, as it is sung in the Psalms: “I will receive the chalice of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 115:13). For by the chalice of salvation the passion is signified. In that passion, certainly, Christ’s flesh was together with its blood; therefore, once Christ has been sacrificed through the sacrament of the divine tradition, the body is broken as food for the peoples and distributed to the faithful. The blood, however, as though poured out in the passion, is shown to us, spiritually consecrated, for drinking; it is offered to God the Father by the supreme priest, so that by the price through which we have been redeemed from death to life and incorporated into Christ’s body, we may be stripped of daily faults and lesser sins. Thereafter, let us be nourished and given drink by that same food and drink unto life, so that, refreshed from it and through it, we may be incorporated into Christ [Note: [Col. 1328D] The printed editions read “that we may dine together” (*convesceremur*).], in order that we too may be found to be one with him; otherwise, we cannot have life within us. Hence the Savior himself says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

### 4.

For this reason some also ask whether, if people are baptized and are then swiftly overtaken by death, so that they are not permitted to eat the Lord’s flesh or drink his blood, this harms them, and to what extent; or whether it does them no harm—especially since, having immediately been reborn in Christ and made one body with him, they are truly believed to have entered into adoption as children of God.

It is therefore clear that those reborn to life, immediately transferred through the death of the flesh to that same life which is Christ, are found incorporated into him without any stain of sin.

[Note: [Col. 1328D] The printed editions read “not incorporated”; this is less satisfactory.]

And for this reason we believe it does not harm them that they did not receive the viaticum of this sacrament for life along the way, because after receiving life they did not in any respect turn aside from the road.

[Note: [Col. 1328D] The royal manuscript reads: “they did not turn aside, but remained on the road.”]

Rather, they remained in the life which is Christ, and therefore they did not fail on the road until they reached the truth, in which life is eternal and true.

Nevertheless, for those who remain here for a while, that heavenly food and drink is exceedingly necessary for life, so that [Note: [Col. 1328D] The royal manuscript reads: “so that those reborn may thus be spiritually nourished through these things unto perpetual life.”], just as they are nourished for a time by earthly foods in order to live, so those reborn may through these things be spiritually nourished unto perpetual life, lest they fail on the road until they pass through the death of the flesh to perpetual life, where there is no failing, and to everlasting life.

### 5. *(Augustine on John, chapter 6.)*

Meanwhile, however, it is right and exceedingly necessary that the redeemed person be nourished unto incorruption and given drink unto life. Therefore the Savior immediately added: “For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:56). It is as though he said: Human beings generally desire food and drink above all so that they may not hunger or thirst and may not die.
