This ordinary food and drink does not provide that; my flesh and blood do, because they make people immortal and incorruptible.

[Note: [Col. 1329C] The printed editions read “which makes them immortal.”]

And therefore it is truly called food and drink.

[Note: [Col. 1329D] Some read “they are called.”]

It is therefore established and clear to everyone that in this mortal life one cannot live without food and drink. In the same way, one does not reach that eternal life unless one is spiritually nourished unto immortality by these two things. Thus they are rightly given together in the chalice.

[Note: [Col. 1329D] Four manuscripts read “they are believed.”]

For these two things flowed forth for us unto life from the one chalice of Christ’s passion.

But unhappy is the soul that does not sufficiently believe this, while nevertheless not doubting that human life is sustained by food and drink.

[Note: [Col. 1329D] Here chapter 70 begins in the Laubach manuscript, with an example of mortal food for mortal life.]

For if there is such power in this mortal food that it daily renews declining life and restores strength, what should we think of this immortal food and drink, in which eternal life is bestowed and immortality reigns?

[Note: [Col. 1329D] All manuscripts have this reading. Mamer. and Sirm. delete “reigns.”]

For God is truth, and Christ is truth, because he is certainly God. Therefore, O human being, if he is truth, believe that Christ’s flesh and blood are life. And therefore Truth declares: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life remaining in him” (John 6:55).

[Col. 1329C] Remaining, certainly, and not declining,

[Note: [Col. 1329D] Three manuscripts read “failing.”]

because in this life no one lives without, by living, declining toward death. In that life, however, one lives without failing, always remaining in the same condition.

Therefore, if anyone follows the way [Note: [Col. 1329D] The printed editions read “if anyone follows life.”], he holds to the truth; and whoever holds to the truth already has life remaining in him, because Christ is the way, the life, and the truth. Hence this mystery is sometimes also called the viaticum: if someone enjoys it on the road, he reaches the life which he already possesses within himself, and is deceived by no falsehood, because he is enlightened and strengthened unto life by the truth of the Lord’s body and blood.

[Note: [Col. 1329D] The Vatican manuscript reads “is enlightened and invigorated.” Mamer., Ulim., and two manuscripts read “is enlightened and strengthened.”]

## CHAPTER XX

[Note: [Col. 1329D] Chapter 71 in the Laubach manuscript.]

### Why the mystery of holy communion is now celebrated by those who are fasting, although the Lord entrusted it to the apostles after the supper

[Note: [Col. 1329D] The printed editions, with two manuscripts, add “generally.” In the Major Monastery manuscripts this title is expressed thus: “The mystery of holy communion is now generally celebrated by one fasting” [perhaps “by those fasting”]. The words that follow are omitted, as they are also omitted in the Rouen manuscript of Saint-Ouen.]

### 1.

It was therefore a sacrament that the Lord entrusted this to the apostles after the supper. For it was fitting that it be fulfilled toward the end of the day, in the evening, so that the very hour [Note: [Col. 1329D] The Vatican manuscript reads “the very hour of his sacrifice.”] of the sacrifice might show that the end of the age had already arrived. Hence John says: “My little children, it is the final hour.”

[Note: [Col. 1330C] The printed editions read “the final hour is already here.”]

Moreover, the apostles were no longer fasting for this reason: it was necessary that the typical Passover first be completed, and then that they pass over to the true sacrament of Passover. This was then done in mystery so that the shadow might come to an end once the reality had been revealed, and so that they themselves might thereafter immediately pass over to the true newness.

[Col. 1330B] For this reason it happened that, while not fasting, they did not initially receive the body and blood at all.

Nevertheless, throughout the Church it has universally become customary for everyone to receive communion while fasting with the greatest reverence.

[Note: [Col. 1330D] Florence reads “throughout the whole Church.”]

For the Holy Spirit, through the apostles, willed this to be established,

[Note: [Col. 1330D] The printed editions add “to ordain,” a phrase absent from all the manuscripts.]

so that, in honor of so great a mystery, Christ’s body and blood might first be received soberly, before any other food. And therefore this custom has quite properly and prudently taken root throughout Christ’s Church.

[Note: [Col. 1330D] Here chapter 72 begins in the Laubach manuscript, with this title: “That it is not to be observed, as some say, that the divine food should be mixed with this mortal food until it is digested.”]

Nor should one observe the rule laid down by apocryphal writings, namely, that one should wait until these things have been digested in the body lest ordinary food be consumed. Rather, one must take sufficient care to prepare oneself beforehand, and after receiving grace no one should make himself unworthy. These things must be received spiritually, not carnally.

### 2.

Although [Note: [Col. 1330D] Ulim., with Anic., Laon, and one Saint-Germain manuscript, reads: “Although bread [is changed] into flesh.”] flesh is changed into flesh and wine into blood, as nature itself appears to demonstrate,

[Note: [Col. 1330D] Mamer. and one manuscript read “as though it were proved by nature.”]

these things must nevertheless be considered at a higher level. Here not only are Christ’s flesh or blood changed into our flesh or blood [Note: [Col. 1330D] Florence reads “are not changed.”]; rather, they raise us above carnal things and make us spiritual.

[Note: [Col. 1330D] In Laubach, chapter 73 begins here: “That the divine food nourishes only what, being from God, is digested.”]

This food truly nourishes in us what has been born from God, not what is from flesh and blood. Christ therefore gave us power to become children of God, yet not from the will

[Note: [Col. 1330D] Three manuscripts read “not from the pleasure.”]

of the flesh, nor from the will of a man, but “we are born from God” (John 1).

That birth of ours which is from God is therefore spiritual [Note: [Col. 1330D] The Major Monastery manuscript repeats “spiritual.”], because God is spirit. And thus these mysteries are rightly understood as spiritual, not carnal, although they consist of flesh and blood.

[Note: [Col. 1330D] Some read “are believed to be spiritual.”]

Hence, far below, our temporal life is nourished by this ordinary bodily food and drink; but far higher and more preeminently, that life which is hidden with God, by which we are made like him and conformed to him, is nourished by that food and drink which we receive in the Scriptures and from the altar. It carries us over into spiritual things, so that from then on we may live there,

[Note: [Col. 1331C] Mamer. reads “so that we may live thereafter by faith.”]

where our eternal life is preserved.

[Note: [Col. 1331C] Some read “where our eternity is preserved.” In the printed editions and in the Major Monastery manuscript, the words “and therefore whoever receives it in this way receives it worthily” are absent.]

And therefore whoever receives it in this way receives it worthily; and whoever has received it worthily already has eternal life remaining in him.

### 3.

[Note: [Col. 1331D] Here chapter 74 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “It is foolish to ask whether it goes into excrement.”]

It is therefore foolish, as is read in that same apocryphal book, to think in this mystery about excrement, lest it be mixed together in the digestion of other food.

[Note: [Col. 1331D] Jacobus de Saincte-Beuve argues, in a special dissertation in manuscript possession of the editor, that Heribald of Auxerre and Rabanus, bishop of Mainz, fell into the foul heresy of the Stercoranists. Mabillon, in the preface to the fourth century of the Benedictine history, part II, pp. 32 ff., clears both of them of it.]

For when spiritual food and drink are received, and the Holy Spirit works through them in a person so that whatever is still carnal in us may be transferred into the spirit and the human being become spiritual, what mixture could there be?

Therefore, as far as that eternal life surpasses this mortal life, so greatly does this food surpass the ordinary food by which animals as well as we live. And it is called ordinary because it belongs to everyone—to the good and the wicked, and also to animals.

[Note: [Col. 1331D] Here chapter 75 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “That this food belongs only to the children of God.”]

But this food belongs only to the children of God, so that [Note: [Col. 1331D] The Vatican and Laubach manuscripts read “so that they may live from the source from which they are nourished.”] they may be nourished from the source from which they live. For we live through Christ, whose members we are. It has been sufficiently and providentially arranged that we should sometimes be nourished by him, so that through this we may be found to be one body with him and in him.

[Note: [Col. 1331D] Here chapter 76 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “Why we receive communion while fasting.”]

Nevertheless, the fact that we receive communion while fasting is done with sufficient foresight, so that, while sobriety burns within the body, while every carnal fervor is at rest, and [Note: [Col. 1331D] The printed editions read “and every sense of the soul.”] all the senses of the soul are more vigorously active in understanding and discernment,

[Note: [Col. 1331D] Mamer. and Ulim., together with four manuscripts, read “in understanding and the faculty of discernment.”]

our inner person may first be intoxicated by that food, so that thereafter what is preeminent in us, invigorated by heavenly sweetness, may govern and direct what is lower and may not relax into harmful and superfluous things.

[Note: [Col. 1331D] Three manuscripts read “may preserve and govern it.”]

It was therefore fitting that what is higher should receive greater honor, and then that what is lower, though necessary, should receive the indulgence of this life [Note: [Col. 1331D] Ulim., with six manuscripts, reads “indulgence”; two manuscripts read *indulgentit* [uncertain form].], while both are first more happily invited to heavenly and eternal things.

[Note: [Col. 1332C] The manuscripts vary here. Six read “more happily invited by both”; seven, with Mamer., read “more happily invited,” with “by both” deleted; two read “more happily invited” in the neuter.]

For this is the true and new mixture of sincerity and truth: that we should be unleavened, without the leaven of malice and wickedness.

[Col. 1332A]

[Note: [Col. 1332C] Here chapter 77 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “That in the chalice we receive nothing other than blood.”]

For in the chalice we drink nothing other than Christ’s blood, where we too are united through the water.

[Note: [Col. 1332D] The Vatican manuscript reads “we are commonly mixed in through it”; two royal manuscripts, “we are united to the mystery”; three manuscripts, “mixed in and strengthened”; Florence, “we are united through the mixing of water.”]

In the bread, however, there is nothing besides the body, where through Christ’s mixture we are already his members.

[Note: [Col. 1332D] Ulim. and Sirm. read “we are already his members”; “his” is absent from the manuscripts.]

This mixture is effected through the water of the Holy Spirit, concerning which Christ says in the Gospel (John 7:38): “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” And immediately the Evangelist adds: “He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive.”

This mixture, therefore, made one body from many grains—a body, I say, of sincerity and truth—provided that we are unleavened, that is, without the leaven of malice and wickedness,

[Note: [Col. 1332D] Two manuscripts read “so that we may worthily.”]

so that we may be able worthily to receive this bread mixed with this water.

O wondrous providence of almighty God, by which we are instructed in so many disciplines and strengthened by examples,

[Col. 1332B]

[Note: [Col. 1332D] Ulim. and Sirm. read “by how many disciplines we are instructed”; the Vatican manuscript, “through which we are instructed by so many disciplines”; Mamer. and seven manuscripts, “by which we are instructed in so many disciplines.”]

if only the mind is not ungrateful for such great benefits and doubtful concerning such immense promises.

Therefore, O human being, preserve the mixture of grace. For although you are wheat, unless by the teaching and power of the Holy Spirit you are thoroughly ground into flour for this unity and mixture, then mixed by grace and baked by the fire of charity, you will not be able to be strengthened into the solidity of faith.

Therefore,

[Note: [Col. 1332D] The printed editions, together with the Major Monastery manuscript, read: “Therefore may the lower millstone of fear and the upper millstone of perfect charity always be yours.” Mem. and Ulim. read “of perfect charity.” All the other manuscripts preserve our reading.]

may the upper millstone of the hope of promise and the lower millstone of the fear of perfect charity always be yours. Ground finely by these two, you may be united through the grace of the Holy Spirit into Christ’s body.

It is therefore clear that these things are mystical. And so, my son, you must think of them as heavenly; touch them as divine; receive them as saving, since eternal life is promised in them; believe them as they are spoken; and then live in such a way that, always mixed into Christ in truth and sincerity, you may be found to be his member.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Note: [Col. 1332D] Chapter 78 in the Laubach manuscript.]

### What the Lord means when he says: “I will not drink from this fruit of the vine from now on, until I drink it new in the kingdom of my Father”

### 1. *(Jerome.)*

From this passage, then, some construct a fable of a thousand years, claiming that Christ will reign bodily, at a time when he is to eat or drink these new things bodily; they say that he declared he would not do so until the consummation of the age.

[Note: [Col. 1332D] Anic. and two Colbert manuscripts add “saying.” In three manuscripts the words “he will be reigning, when these new things are also to be bodily” are absent, apparently through scribal omission.]

But we, seeking the Lord’s meaning in a catholic manner, should not follow the nonsense of heretics, but him who says: “Take and eat, all of you. For this is my body”; and let us say that the chalice is the one of which he likewise says: “This is my chalice of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.”

Of this chalice the prophet says: “I will receive the chalice of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 115:13). Through this chalice, certainly, the Lord’s passion is signified.

[Note: [Col. 1333D] Here chapter 79 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “What it means: Take this chalice away from me.”]

Hence he says to the Father: “Father, take this chalice away from me” (Luke 22:42)—that is, the passion of death, lest it take place at the hands of the Jews. And then: “Father, if this chalice cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done” (Matthew 26:42).

For this reason the custom has rightly become established that Christ’s blood is never consecrated in a dish, never in a bowl, nor in any vessel other than a chalice. Nor is it called by any other name, as happens with other vessels, but always, according to the proper usage of the languages, it is called a chalice, so that by this means the chalice of Christ’s passion may be brought back to everyone’s memory.

From this chalice—that is, from the same death—blood is drawn, and through the blood eternal life. When we drink it, what else do we proclaim than the Lord’s death?

Therefore it is necessary that each person first die to this age. For just as no one rightly proclaims death unless buried,

[Note: [Col. 1333D] Eight manuscripts read “buried.” Some omit “rightly.”]

so no one thereafter receives life unless, rising, he walks in newness of life and already remains in Christ.

Hence, if we wish to receive this life with Christ, let us ascend above into the upper room of life, specifically into a large and furnished upper room, because unless it is large, it cannot contain everyone.

[Note: [Col. 1333D] Here chapter 80 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “How serious it is for one receiving communion to lie below.”]

Let us ascend upward, for those who lie below do not drink this with Christ but, unhappily, drink the gall of dragons with Judas.

[Note: [Col. 1333D] The printed editions read “do not drink new wine with Christ.”]

Thus they are in the gall of bitterness. Hence Paul also says: “Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth” (Colossians 3:2).

For this chalice of the New Testament is received nowhere except above; and because it belongs to the New Testament, it is shared only by those who have been renewed and are without the oldness of sin.

He calls it the New Testament in distinction from the Old. For Moses, when he sprinkled the people with the blood of holocausts, poured half of it into bowls and half upon the altar, and said: “This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has commanded” (Exodus 24:8).

Only “the blood of the covenant,”

[Note: [Col. 1333D] The printed editions omit “only.”]

because it was a figure and shadow of this mystery, through which the Lord testified that he would give himself to us. With this blood the Christian people have been sprinkled, and half of it is poured out everywhere through bowls, because what we receive in it from the Scriptures is mystical and moral.

[Note: [Col. 1333D] In the Anic manuscript the words “half of it is poured out everywhere through bowls, because it is mystical” are absent.]

Then half of it is poured upon the altar for the removal of the sins of many. Hence we now receive the drink of salvation, since from it we also possess the wisdom of teaching, and from it we offer the price of redemption for us.

### 2.

Therefore, what that man is read to have done once for us, we do daily at his command. We also read in Solomon that Wisdom had poured

[Note: [Col. 1333D] Anic. reads “had mixed her wine in the bowls.”]

her wine into bowls. That wine is truly the moral understanding by which faithful souls are made drunk.

And that which is poured back upon the altar, when it is said, “Command that these things be carried by the hand of your angel to your high altar, in the sight of your divine majesty,” is done so that Christ’s blood may once more be taken from there as the price of redemption for removing our daily offenses, and so that through this our inner person may be more fully renewed and united to Christ—not only in conduct and life, but also in unity of nature through the body, here and there, so that we may be found in his form.

[Note: [Col. 1333D] The printed editions read “and be joined.”]

[Note: [Col. 1333D] Here chapter 81 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “What it means: When I drink it new in the kingdom of God.”]

For this blood is not received in its fullness unless it also morally intoxicates the mind and spiritually pours us forth from the altar of Christ’s body for our renewal.

[Note: [Col. 1333D] Put. and two Colbert manuscripts read “unless it also immortally intoxicates the mind.” A recent Saint-Germain manuscript reads: “unless it is also poured immortally from the altar of Christ’s body for our renewal.” Mamer. reads “unless it also mortally ...”]

There, certainly, Christ willed to be both our banquet and our guest.

Therefore, because [Note: [Col. 1334D] The Major Monastery manuscript reads “we are always his body.”] we are his body, of his flesh and bones, he drinks this new drink with us in the kingdom of the Father, because it is the blood of the New Testament.

But because we are his body and he reigns in us as the head, we are rightly called the kingdom of the Father. In this kingdom Christ now drinks that new drink whenever the faithful within the Church worthily receive it.

*(Jerome.)* Just as he suffers in his own people, hungers, thirsts, is clothed, and is received, so also he drinks that new drink in the kingdom of the Father—that is, in the Church—whenever we, his own people, worthily eat or drink him.

For from that vine which produced sour grapes he is given the gall of bitterness to drink, which is the chalice of passion. But in the kingdom of adoption he drinks from the fruit of the new vine, and from the vine of Sorech, which is interpreted as “chosen.” For red must is strained in the winepress of the cross, and when we daily receive Christ’s blood from the altar, whenever we drink new wine from it, Christ confesses that he drinks it in the kingdom of the Father.

[Note: [Col. 1334D] The printed editions read “in the kingdom of God.” Laubach deletes “of God,” or “of the Father.”]

For we are his members, including we who drink.

[Note: [Col. 1334D] One manuscript lacks the words “for we are his members, including we who drink.” In the Vatican manuscript, after the words “we are his members,” everything that follows up to “from which he...” is absent.]

Hence it is called our banquet, because Christ was sacrificed as our Passover; and he is the guest because we feast with him,

[Note: [Col. 1334D] The manuscript of Saint-Ouen reads “because we feast with him.”]

having been transformed into newness, because we are his body. From this he testifies that he drinks that new drink in the kingdom of the Father.

Otherwise, we do not believe that in that future kingdom he will rightly drink this drink with bodily taste or receive this food.

[Note: [Col. 1335D] Ulim. and Sirm. correctly omit “rightly.”]

Rather, we believe as the priest and author of salvation himself instituted: from the time when the holy apostles, renewed by the coming of the Holy Spirit from heaven, were made drunk with the wine of charity, this chalice has been consecrated in the Church. For the Spirit of truth, in whom they were renewed from their oldness, had led them into all truth and established them in the fullness of teaching.

[Note: [Col. 1335D] The printed editions and Florence read “because that Spirit.”]

Certainly, from then onward it is consecrated in the newness of the spirit, just as it was by Christ.

“But my food,” he says (John 4:34), “is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work.”

[Note: [Col. 1335D] The printed editions add “who is in heaven”; these words are absent from all the manuscripts.]

*(Jerome.)* Therefore, while we do the will of the Father and the work of charity is fulfilled,

[Note: [Col. 1335D] The Vatican manuscript reads “and it is fulfilled by us.” Three manuscripts read “and we complete the work of charity.”]

Christ certainly drinks his blood with us in the kingdom of his Church, because he is the head and we are the members.

This is the food that the patriarch Jacob desired when he said: “If the Lord is with me and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear” (Genesis 28:20).

### 3.

Therefore, all who are baptized in Christ put on Christ and eat the bread of angels.

[Note: [Col. 1335D] Three manuscripts read: “We are baptized, put on Christ, and eat the bread of angels.”]

[Note: [Col. 1335D] Here chapter 82 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “Why Isaac gave Jacob a blessing of grain and wine.”]

In this mystery Isaac blessed that same son of his, Jacob, as though there were no other blessing than grain and wine: namely, in the bread of Christ’s flesh and in the drink of his blood. These, from the field of the body, ripen for us daily through the ministry of the priest, and we drink

[Note: [Col. 1335D] The printed editions omit “we drink.”]

[Col. 1335C] and eat them.

Hence he likewise says: “May God give you from the dew of heaven and from the richness

[Note: [Col. 1335D] Four manuscripts omit “of the earth.”]

of the earth an abundance of grain and wine” (Genesis 27:28).

From the dew of heaven, certainly, because these mysteries are accomplished through the work of divinity. From the richness of the earth, because Christ’s flesh is believed to have arisen from the Virgin. There, without doubt,

[Note: [Col. 1335D] The printed editions lack “to the people.”]

the fullest abundance of bread and wine is provided for the Christian people,

[Note: [Col. 1335D] In three manuscripts “not” is absent.]

in which, without doubt, they enjoy the life of angels.

### 4.

Therefore, dearest son, do not think lightly of this life, in which such great mysteries are fragrant.

[Note: [Col. 1335D] The printed editions read: “Therefore, dearest son, do not think lightly of this, in which the sacraments of life are so fragrant”; seven manuscripts preserve our reading.]

You see from how far away so great a patriarch perceived the fragrance of this mystery in his son. For he says: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field full of blessings, which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27:27).

For undoubtedly, in this field of Christ’s body, a hidden treasure flourishes with unfading flowers and breathes the sweetness

[Note: [Col. 1336D] The printed editions read “breathes with sweetness.”]

of fragrance. Whoever finds it goes and sells everything he has and buys that field (Matthew 13:44), where all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are contemplated.

[Note: [Col. 1336D] Some read: “There he contemplates all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.”]

From that field, the bread of life—which is Christ’s flesh

[Note: [Col. 1336D] The printed editions read “that is, the flesh.”]

—and the drink of blood overflow daily for believers, and are harvested by the faithful.

[Note: [Col. 1336D] Here chapter 83 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “That without this sacrament no other blessing is beneficial.”]

In this field the true Jacob is blessed and established as lord of his brothers, because without this no other blessing of anything is beneficial. Hence the blessed man, when Esau—the fierce hunter—arrived too late to receive the blessing, since this blessing had already been granted to his brother, said: “Your brother came deceitfully”; and then: “I have established him by grain and wine” (Genesis 27:35, 37).

[Col. 1336B] This plainly means: “I have strengthened him by the bread of Christ’s body and the wine of his blood, in which that eternal abundance remains.”

“But for you, my son, what can I do beyond this?” (ibid.)

[Note: [Col. 1336D] Here chapter 84 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “That if anyone ungratefully rejects the divine mysteries of Christ’s body and blood, there is nothing better that God can grant him in this life.”]

What then? If so great and exemplary a worshiper of God found nothing more to provide for his son, except to pray that the same things might be fulfilled for him according to his desires, do you think—God forbid—that if you are unworthy of so great a grace, you possess any virtues by which you might obtain more, when nothing greater is offered in this life? Or perhaps you think lightly of it because it does not taste in your mouth as that which he had perceived from afar in the spirit and desired to enjoy?

But although Abraham too had once been refreshed by this in hope, for that reason he was called blessed by God Most High. Finally, because God had afterward saturated Isaac with the blessing, Isaac too enriched his son Jacob with the same blessings

[Note: [Col. 1336D] The printed editions read “enriched him with the same gifts.”]

and, in prophetic speech, prayed for what had been promised to all.

### 5.

A great good, therefore, and a secret of supreme blessing is mystically prepared in this Church of Christ,

[Note: [Col. 1336D] Mamer. reads “in this mystical Church it is prepared.” The Major Monastery manuscript, together with another Saint-Germain manuscript, reads “in this mystery of the Church it is prepared.”]

where Christ is both the guest of delights and the banquet.

Concerning this good, once promised, Zechariah says in wonder: “And what is his good, and what is his beauty, except the grain of the chosen and the wine that makes virgins spring forth?” (Zechariah 9:17.)

[Note: [Col. 1336D] Here chapter 85 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “That it is the food only of the chosen.”]

Here it should be noted that this food belongs only to the chosen, from which the good of the Church’s salvation and the beauty of its adornment are bestowed.

For although the Church becomes soiled daily, it is restored through this, so that the bride of Christ may be found sprinkled with such gifts, without spot or wrinkle. Otherwise, since we sin daily, even in the smallest matters, how can we be without spot?

That, then, is not immaculate which is disfigured by the foulness of blemishes. But because it is continually cleansed through these things, its body is beautiful: having already become fair through the washing, it grows more beautiful, adorned in this mystery with the whiteness of the lily and the redness of blood.

It is good because we advance toward eternal life; it is beautiful when we are clothed with the glory of immortality, so that inwardly we may enjoy the sweetness of life and outwardly shine more brightly through the grace of so great a benefit.

“And the wine,” he says, “that makes virgins spring forth.” Happy is the fruitfulness from which virginity springs.

[Note: [Col. 1337C] Here chapter 86 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “That in the wine of our fruitfulness chastity is corrupted, but from this wine virgins are produced.”]

For in the wine of our fruitfulness chastity is corrupted, but from this wine virgins are produced. And therefore the whole Church of Christ is rightly called a virgin, because, filled with this wine, it knows how to love no one besides Christ,

[Col. 1337B]

[Note: [Col. 1337D] The Major Monastery manuscript, omitting “to hunger for anyone,” adds “nor does it thirst for anyone.”]

to hunger for no other and thirst for no other, since its supreme good and supreme beauty is that garment woven above from the fleece of the Lamb, which elsewhere is called the wedding garment.

Moreover, every soul that is made drunk with the wine of charity and given to drink of Christ’s blood is rightly called a virgin.

### 6.

You have, dearest one, the good of the life of the saints, which has no equal.

[Note: [Col. 1337D] The Major Monastery manuscript reads “which has nothing else equal to it.” Others read “which has nothing else similar or better.”]

You have the beauty of loveliness with which to wash away the foulness of your childhood. Practice chastity, because this blood loves nothing more than virgins in Christ—virgins, I say, who are prudent and chaste. For there are also foolish virgins inwardly, in their souls, who do not have the oil of the Holy Spirit with them.

[Note: [Col. 1337D] Some read “with them from the Holy Spirit.”]

Whoever does not have this is not Christ’s. For neither does the grain of the flesh suffice without the wine of the blood, nor do flesh or blood without the oil of the Holy Spirit benefit us; rather, they do us greater harm.

[Note: [Col. 1337D] Here chapter 87 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “How one who is to receive communion ought to live.”]

Therefore, whoever wishes to receive communion rightly must necessarily live in such a way that he can always be a temple of the Spirit. For if anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him (1 Corinthians 3:17).

Hence Paul also says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you have been sealed” (Ephesians 4:30), clearly because without him no grace of Christ is possessed.

Therefore, when Joel promised forgiveness to the repentant, the Lord replied and said to his people: “Behold, I am sending you grain, wine, and oil, and you will be filled with it” (Joel 2:19).

[Col. 1338A] You will indeed be filled with it, although he promised three things, because flesh and blood are consecrated by that same Holy Spirit. Otherwise, for me there is neither flesh nor blood, but judgment, which I receive,

[Note: [Col. 1337D] Mamer. and Ulim., with Anic., the Major Monastery manuscript, and Saint-Ouen, read: “Otherwise, for me there is neither flesh nor blood, but judgment, which is received or receives.”]

because, without the one who gives, no gift from God is bestowed upon those who presume wrongly.

For the Spirit himself is also called a gift, whether the seven gifts belonging to him are mentioned, by which Christ and the Church are filled.

[Note: [Col. 1337D] Two manuscripts read “by which Christ fills the Church.”]

He possesses all these gifts in full; the Church, however, possesses them in portions, indivisibly, as it pleases the one who divides himself among individuals and apportions himself to all.

Nevertheless, in him we are divinely filled, because without him each person’s soul is found empty. Therefore let us always pray for him, let us continually desire him, so that our desire may be filled with his good things and our youth may always be renewed by him, like that of the eagle (Psalm 102).

### 7.

It is therefore clear that without him nothing exists that is possessed, and nothing that is received [Note: Four manuscripts: “that without him there is undoubtedly nothing that is possessed.”], because all the gifts of the virtues are enclosed in this one [Note: The Major Monastery manuscript: “are enclosed in this one gift.” Anicetus: “are praised by this one.”]. Therefore, if we wish to be enriched with heavenly gifts, let us earnestly ask for the gift of the Father and the Son, that is, the Holy Spirit [Note: Sirmond’s edition omits “that is, the Holy Spirit.”], who proceeds from them, consubstantial and coeternal, so that through him [Note: One Colbert manuscript: “through him the gift of charity”] charity may be poured into our hearts, and, being reborn in him, we may daily be sanctified for life. For we believe that whoever he has sanctified by the sprinkling of his dew is certainly inhabited by the Father and the Son.

Hence the Son himself says: “I and the Father will come to him and will make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23) [Note: Three manuscripts: “I and the Father are one, and we will come to him.”]—not as though the Holy Spirit had been passed over, but clearly indicating that the Father and he come only to those whom that same Spirit has sanctified by the advance of his inspiration [Note: Four manuscripts: “coming,” perhaps “they will come.”], although the whole Trinity is always cooperatively active in all things.

[Note: In the Laubach manuscript chapter 88 begins here: “That nothing is happier than the good, and nothing more unhappy than the evil.” Its text, however, reads: “For this reason, just as nothing…”]

For this reason, just as nothing in this life is happier than the Christian who is good, so nothing is more dangerous than he if, abandoned by such great grace, he becomes a member of a prostitute [Note: Here chapter 89 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “That it is more serious when those soiled by sins approach communion shamelessly.”].

And therefore, dearest one, keep yourself chaste, because this gift by which virgins are generated detests not only the lust of the flesh but also the laziness of the mind [Note: The printed editions read “detests”; nearly all manuscripts have “it detests.”], and everything by which our inner man [Note: Four manuscripts: “by which our outward man”] could be stained.

Since, by God’s ordering, you now serve at the sacred altars, wash your hands among the innocent, not with Pilate [Col. 1339A], because no excuse is effective where conscience is the witnessing judge [Note: Mamer­tus and six manuscripts: “conscience the judge.”]. And if you have first proved yourself pure [Note: The printed editions read: “and when you have proved yourself pure.” All manuscripts retain our reading.], then eat of that bread and drink from the chalice without fear. But if not, give honor to God [Note: The manuscript of the Queen of Sweden and two royal manuscripts: “give honor to such great mysteries.”], and correct as quickly as possible, through repentance [Note: The printed editions read “fullness”; all manuscripts read “repentance.”] of heart, the stain of your error, so that at last you may somehow be able to encircle Christ’s altars with pious embraces and enter the Holy of Holies with a pure and more devoted mind [Note: Another manuscript: “with a richer mind.”]. Otherwise, it is more serious to become still dirtier while remaining soiled, and, with God despised, to approach the unlawful mysteries of God shamelessly.

### 8.

[Note: In the Laubach manuscript chapter 90 begins here: “A lamentation over those living impurely and presuming to communicate.”]

I have said these things, therefore, for your caution, dearest son, because I know that many, like unclean swine [Note: Nearly all manuscripts: “like unclean sows.”], under the pretext of repentance return all the more readily to the mire of vices, the more easily they approach these things without prejudice to their guilt, trampling them underfoot [Col. 1339B]. Indeed, because God’s patience once endured them while they presumptuously approached the mysteries of life [Note: Five manuscripts: “unworthily.”; Vatican and Florentine manuscripts: “were rash.”], they prefer thereafter to believe that what we say is true [Note: The Vatican manuscript: “do not wish to believe these truths.”].

For they are more afraid to bear their shame before human eyes than to incur an offense before the divine majesty and the presence of all the heavenly citizens [Note: Mamertus and Sirmond: “the presence of the heavenly beings.” Ulim: “the presence of the spirit of the heavenly beings.” The Major Monastery manuscripts: “the presence of the holy heavenly beings.”]. Their hardness of heart, since they neither correct themselves nor are visited by the scourge of God’s mercy, is already the punishment of sin and the contempt of pride. But because the Lord does not immediately punish them, as we have said above, does he therefore not care, or does he in any way forget that his injuries have thus far gone unavenged? I would certainly not say this, especially since he sees them and is thereby further provoked to anger, because his sons and daughters provoke him to anger [Col. 1339C]—those whom he had graciously joined to the table of the angels.

Hence also follows this: “I will hide my face from them, and I will consider their end” (Deuteronomy 31:17).

### 9.

[Note: The words enclosed in parentheses were supplied by the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden, 1554, and by the manuscript of the Most Christian King, 4070.]

Regarding their manifest condemnation, the Apostle also delivers a terrifying judgment, saying:

“If anyone who rejects the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses, how much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by one who has trampled upon the Son of God, regarded the blood of the covenant as polluted, and insulted the Spirit of grace by whom he was sanctified?” (Hebrews 10:28).

He is rightly said to trample upon the Son of God who carelessly destroys charity, the root of all virtues, through which the only-begotten Son of God himself deigned to become man [Col. 1339D]. Thus, filled with hatred toward his brother, he presumes to offer these most sacred sacrifices before being reconciled to him in peace.

But his offering is not accepted by almighty God unless the discord with his neighbor has first been driven from his heart, as the Truth says:

“If you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, go first to be reconciled with your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23).

In this matter we must consider, since every fault is forgiven through the gift of this sacrifice, how serious is the fault of discord by which even the gift is not accepted.

Therefore, before we offer this sacrifice, we must go in spirit to our neighbor, however far away and however distinct from us he may be; we must submit our mind to him and appease him by humility and goodwill. Then, when our Creator sees such reconciliation of our mind, he releases us from sin.

We learn from the voice of Truth, moreover (Matthew 18:24), that when the servant who owed ten thousand talents repented, he received from his lord the remission of his debt. But because he did not forgive his fellow servant the debt of one hundred denarii that he owed him, the amount that had already been forgiven him was ordered to be exacted from him, and he was thrown into prison.

From these words it is evident that if we do not forgive from the heart what is committed against us, that debt which we rejoiced had already been forgiven us through repentance will be exacted from us again.

He therefore asks pardon for his own offense properly who first forgives what has been committed against him. Whoever refuses to do this, if he rashly presumes to handle the divine sacrifice, is said to trample upon the Lord’s body—not because it can be trampled upon by any mortal, but because for one who handles it badly it is turned into an occasion of trampling.

Whoever, despising the chastity shared with the angels, defiles himself with the filth of impure lust is not improperly said to pollute the blood of the covenant, namely, the new and eternal covenant. Such a person rashly presumes to approach participation in this table before being washed clean by humble confession, worthy fruits of repentance, and abundant streams of tears.

He also appears to commit the greatest insult against the Holy Spirit of grace, whoever doubts that the earthly substance of bread and wine, while it is sanctified by the power and consecration of that same Spirit, can be changed into that very flesh and blood which the blessed Virgin conceived and bore through the power and operation of the same Spirit.

From where, then, will he obtain forgiveness of sins who kindles anger against himself in the Holy Spirit, who is the remission of all sins, while doubting that he can accomplish something? It is therefore clearer than daylight with what severe punishment such people—who handle the Lord’s body and blood badly—must be chastised, since the Apostle judges that they deserve more grievous penalties of death [Col. 1340D].

For this reason such people often propose, after serious deliberation of mind, to reform themselves for a time, but again fall more badly under the force of temptation. Therefore, if you wish to be saved and to enjoy these things unto life, I ask you to conduct yourself in such a way that you always understand God to be present everywhere, and so live before him that you offend the eyes of his majesty in nothing.

For if anyone thinks he can hide from him anywhere, let him know that he will not escape him at all. He who is powerful everywhere will certainly not escape unoffended; with him all that he has done is stored away, and he will find it sealed in his treasuries.

## CHAPTER XXII

[Note: In Laubach, chapter 111. In the Vatican manuscript the title here reads: “That the immolation of the Paschal lamb refers to the body of Christ.” The text of this chapter, however, begins: “It is evident, therefore, from the divine law that, although Christ is sacrificed, the lamb is sacrificed in the Church.”]

### Whether there is any distinction in this mystery between the righteous person and the repentant person who has been reconciled

#### 1.

It is therefore evident from the divine law that, although Christ is sacrificed, the lamb is sacrificed in the Church, and that rewards are assigned according to the distinction of merits [Note: The manuscripts read “according to the provision for merits”; three manuscripts read “according to the foreknowledge of merits.”]. Hence, when the Lord was speaking of Passover in Exodus, he said:

“On the tenth day of this month each person shall take a lamb for his family and his household. The lamb shall be without blemish, male, and one year old; according to this rite you shall take also a kid” (Exodus 12:3).

The Septuagint has: “It shall be for you an unblemished lamb. From the lambs and the kids, they say, you shall take it.”

From this it is entirely clear that these commands are given because of the distinction of merits. If someone cannot attain a lamb because of the poverty of his life—that is, cannot offer an unblemished life—let him at least have a kid, which is always slaughtered in the sacrifices for penitents.

Regarding this, the blessed Jerome, interpreter of the divine law, says that Christ is sacrificed in the house of the Church in two ways:

“If we are righteous,” he says, “we eat the flesh of the lamb; if we are sinners and are doing penance, the kid is slaughtered for us. Not that Christ is a kid, the one whom he taught to stand on the left, but, according to the diversity of merits, let him be either a lamb or a kid for each person [Note: So reads the manuscript of Saint Audomarus. The printed editions, with other manuscripts: “whom he taught to stand on the left.”]. Otherwise, why would the law command that the kid be taken together with the lamb, except because of the distinction of merits?”

Then immediately:

“You shall keep it,” he says, “until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole assembly of the children of Israel shall slaughter it in the evening.”

Yet he does not explicitly indicate that, if this is to be understood only of the lamb, he likewise commands it concerning the kid [Note: Another reading: “that he commands it concerning the kid.”]. But by this, as is customary in the divine Scriptures, he secretly shows that one thing is commanded to the perfect and another is provided for those who have fallen and are sluggish [Note: The printed editions, with a few manuscripts: “that he secretly showed something intended for the more perfect in the divine Scriptures.” Mamertus: “that he secretly showed in the divine Scriptures something he commanded to the more perfect.”].

Therefore, he openly established what was to be done concerning the lamb alone, but, as though unwilling to speak about the kid, he kept silent more closely [Note: Another reading: “he touched on it more closely.”], because one thing is what he everywhere wills to be more perfect [Note: The printed editions: “what is perfect.”], while another is what he sometimes permits by indulgence.

Hence elsewhere it is commanded concerning Passover:

“If anyone could not celebrate Passover in the first month, let him celebrate it in the second”—that is, if, with the perfect in the first month, as in the first grace, he could not eat the lamb without the guilt of death, let him at least in the second month, that is, in the repentance of his guilt, receive the kid of indulgence.

For he says:

“If anyone is unclean because of a person, or is far away on a journey among you, let him celebrate the Passover to the Lord in the second month” (Numbers 9:10).

But if someone is neither unclean in soul nor, through sluggishness [Note: Mamertus: “through the sluggishness of the journey.” Ulim and Sirmond, with the Florentine and Major Monastery manuscripts: “through the sluggishness of life.” All the other manuscripts: “through the sluggishness of idleness.”], withdrawn from the temple of the Holy Spirit, and yet does not celebrate the Passover to the Lord, “that soul shall be utterly cut off from its people” (ibid., 13), because unless he eats the flesh of the Son of Man, he cannot have eternal life, since he has not offered sacrifice to the Lord at the proper time.

And lest you think that he might be speaking of those who are outside Christ, he added, “among you,” because all Christians are regarded as belonging to one generation.

It is certainly humbler to eat the kid with penitents than to eat Christ the lamb with the perfect and the holy. The elder son understood this well. Returning from the field, but wrongly moved by envy against his most gracious father, he complains, saying:

“For so many years I have served you, never transgressing your commandment, and you never gave me even a kid, so that I might feast with my friends” (Luke 15:29).

And how justly! For, blinded by sin [Note: The Major Monastery and Mamertus manuscripts read “for sins”; other manuscripts: “indeed.”], he did not wish to enter inwardly in his mind, nor to repent in his heart [Note: Two Colbert manuscripts: “lest he repent in his heart.”].

Therefore, he did not deserve to obtain even the kid of indulgence from all his father’s goods, while the tenderest father was sacrificing the fatted calf for his repentant younger son. And, what is more serious, with a stubborn mind he directs against his father insults which, because of his own carnality, he had conceived in an unrepentant heart [Note: The manuscripts read: “which, because of his own carnality or misfortune, he had conceived for himself with an unrepentant heart.” This reading appears interpolated.].

#### 2.

[Note: According to the Laubach manuscript, the following belongs here from chapter 95: “That it is better to do penance with a fervent spirit and thus mystically receive even the kid at the Lord’s banquet than to abstain from it longer.” The scribe who transferred the following chapters moved this passage to the place of the next chapter.]

Therefore, after the shipwreck, because repentance is a second plank [Note: The printed editions read: “Therefore after the shipwreck, which is the second plank…”], let us do penance with a fervent spirit. It is certainly better, since we are guilty and blameworthy, to feast at least mystically with our brothers on the kid within Christ’s banquet, where Christ the lamb is sacrificed, than to grow insolent in quarrels against the pious Father and, out of envy, disdain coming when we are at least invited to the Father’s ineffable joy.

There is no doubt that those who have been reconciled by God, ascending as quickly as possible by this path of humility to the pious embraces of their Father, will find in this heavenly banquet that not only Christ the kid of indulgence will be mystically sacrificed for them, but also, through his goodness, the lamb or calf, fattened by the divinity of the Word, will be mystically slaughtered for the joy of our salvation.

Otherwise, how among the lambs whom he will place on his right would the sinner, having received pardon, be restored as the hundredth sheep, unless, united to the grace of Christ [Note: Ulim and Sirmond: “unless united to the grace of Christ”], he is found already to be one body in him?

[Note: The following is absent from the Vatican manuscript up to “is made for the righteous and sinners.”]

Nevertheless, it is not surprising if in this mystery Christ is received as a kid for sinners, since in the law he is often sacrificed under the figure of a goat [Note: Another reading: “is sacrificed.”]. Therefore, because it consists of two substances, the law commands two goats to be offered together in one place [Note: The printed editions read “together in one place”; these words are absent from the manuscripts of Saint Audomarus and Saint Remigius].

One of them is slaughtered by lot for the Lord as a sin offering; the other is taken alive. The law calls it the scapegoat, and over its head they confessed all the iniquities of the children of Israel, invoking all their transgressions and sins upon it. Thus it was sent into the wilderness [Note: Thirteen manuscripts, together with Ulim and Sirmond: “They sent him away carrying all the sins.” One Colbert manuscript: “And thus it was sent into the wilderness by a man, carrying all the sins.”], carrying all the sins of the children of Israel into a solitary land.

From this it is entirely clear that Christ died for us in the likeness of sinful flesh, bore upon himself all the curses of the law and our sins, and hastened away to the wilderness where he had left the ninety-nine sheep in the desert.

He is not rightly believed to be a goat there or a kid here, but because for our sake he assumed the likeness of sinful flesh and condemned sin in the flesh, so that those who rightly ought to be placed among the kids on the left might mercifully be restored as sheep on the right.

Thus also, after the washing, the same one who is a lamb for the righteous becomes a kid for sinners [Note: All manuscripts read this. The printed editions: “the same Lamb is for the righteous.” The Laubach manuscript: “the same becomes a Lamb for the righteous.”], so that through this they too may be made righteous, and no one may be counted a stranger to the flesh and blood of Christ except one who, compelled by his sins, has cut himself off.

#### 3.

Behold the order: whoever does not eat the flesh of Christ and drink his blood certainly does not have life abiding in him; and whoever eats unworthily receives not the power of the flesh but the judgment of God [Note: Mamertus and Ulim: “he takes judgment upon himself.” Sirmond: “he eats judgment upon himself.”].

[Note: According to the Laubach manuscript, the following belongs here, having been placed in reversed order through a scribe’s error, as chapter 96: “That for one who is innocent in himself, the Lamb is received among the righteous; for penitents, not without the mystery of the figure, he is mercifully a kid, lest he reject them from his communion, at least as a kid.”]

But if someone is a sinner and has now ceased to sin, although Christ is a kid for him, the flesh of Christ nevertheless becomes a sacrament for him, so that through it he may return to true innocence and be counted among the lambs on the right.

Those who thereafter, after the washing, have remained in the body [Note: The printed editions and the Florentine manuscript: “have remained in the body of Christ.” Five manuscripts: “have remained incorrupt.”] under God’s protection, wrapped in no crimes [Note: Three manuscripts: “crimes of death”], rightly receive the flesh of the lamb and drink the blood.

Nevertheless, when we speak in this way, it must not be thought that one person receives something different from another: both receive the flesh and blood of Christ. For just as he is called a kid only dispensationally, because of the mystical meaning, so he is called a lamb only so that the true lamb who had often been prefigured in the law may be understood to have come, and that true innocence of mind may be revealed to all through him.

Moreover, although he is called a kid for me according to the quality of my merit and the obscuring of my offense [Note: Three manuscripts: “because of the obscuration”], he is nevertheless entirely as precious for the life of the world as the flesh of Christ, because for me he is nothing other than the flesh of Christ.

But for this reason he again becomes a kid for the penitent, in accordance with the mystery, so that he may expiate the curses of crimes and sins, just as the lamb expiates lesser matters.

Hence the “Lamb of God” is sung before it is eaten [Note: Here chapter 94 begins in the Laubach manuscript: “Why the Lamb of God is sung before it is eaten.”], so that faith may grow warm through this, because it is his flesh that was sacrificed for us [Note: The Major Monastery manuscripts: “the flesh of the one sacrificed”], in order once again to take away the sins of the world.

This sacrament accomplishes expiation for our sins, which we have finally contracted, if we cease from them and eat in the manner commanded—in one house, namely, the holy Church of the living God, outside which no one is permitted to eat the flesh of the lamb.

Nor are we to eat anything from it raw or boiled in water, but only roasted [Note: Anicetus: “but roasted.” The Putean and one royal manuscript: “but cooked.” The manuscripts of Saint Remigius and the Major Monastery: “but only roasted by the fire of Christ’s passion”] by the fire of Christ’s passion, with wild lettuce, without leaven—that is, we are to eat it in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, without the leaven of corruption.

Then let each person examine himself and conduct himself as commanded. “You shall gird your loins,” he says (Exodus 12:11), because these are the seeds of life by which virgins are generated.

Hence it is clear that no one touches these things more dangerously than the lustful and the incestuous. Therefore, in this passage the law of chastity is first fastened upon the loins, which God himself searches.

For if those who render the debt owed to their wives under the law cannot approach God, the showbread, or any consecrated thing of the law unless they have first been sanctified for at least three days or more, how much more, if we wish worthily to eat that bread which descended from heaven and the flesh of the Lamb of God, must we be free from every work of sin and direct the purification of our mind toward God?

“And you shall have sandals on your feet,” he says, lest, while we are on the road of this world, we be bitten by the serpent; “and a staff in your hands,” concerning which it is written in the Psalm: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Psalm 22:4).

After these things have been set forth, he says:

“You shall eat it hastily” [Note: The printed editions: “hastening.”].

For it is Passover, that is, the passage of the Lord.

[Note: According to the Laubach manuscript, chapter 98 belongs here: “That the sluggish and those lingering in worldly activities do not worthily eat Passover.”]

Otherwise, those who are sluggish through laziness [Note: Two manuscripts: “sluggish through desire”] and linger here in worldly activities do not worthily eat Passover, namely, the flesh of the Lamb. Therefore, such people must greatly fear lest, while the Egyptians are slain at night [Note: The Putean manuscript: “are overwhelmed”], they themselves be crushed by the sleep of sin.

Those whose minds have not been sprinkled with the blood of the Lamb are destroyed by the angel, both outwardly in the flesh and inwardly in conscience. But those are saved who are girded at the loins, shod on the feet, supported by Christ’s staff, and hastening from here toward their homeland with the greatest ardor or longing of mind.

For it is Passover, that is, the passage of the Lord.

#### 4.

Do you suppose, then, dearest one, that any person’s conscience is hidden from God? I do not mean if it is wrapped in crimes, but even if it grows sluggish through laziness [Note: In the Laubach manuscript chapter 99 begins here: “That unless they hasten toward heavenly things, they do not rightly eat of the Lamb’s flesh.”].

It is therefore evident that unless someone passes swiftly, with the fullest faith, certain hope, and sincere charity, toward the heavenly homeland above, where Christ is at the right hand of the Father [Note: One Colbert manuscript: “toward the heavenly right hand of peace, where Christ is”], he does not rightly eat of the Lamb’s flesh, because in this he violates the law of the one who commands.

Therefore, whenever we receive it [Note: Mamertus and Ulim: “whenever we receive it.” Sirmond: “whenever we receive him.”], let us raise our minds in longing and hasten through the ardor of faith toward so great a fullness of vision [Note: The Major Monastery manuscripts: “toward so great a vision of fullness”], because here there is tasting, but there fullness.

“I shall be satisfied,” says the Prophet [Note: The printed editions: “I shall be satisfied”; the Colbert manuscript: “He shall be satisfied.”], “when your glory is revealed” (Psalm 16:15).

Christ therefore passes in us from this world to the Father; let us also pass in him, because together with him we are all one person and one body, if we are counted among his members [Note: The Laubach manuscript, deleting “if,” reads only: “his members.” The manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden and two royal manuscripts: “if we are counted among his members.” Another reading: “if we are counted among his members.”].

But those who still sit idly beside the meat-pots [Note: Another reading: “and through negligence”] do not pass from here with him and do not hasten toward their homeland. Therefore they never rightly celebrate Passover, because Passover is named from passing over.

Therefore, child of vows [Note: Anicetus: “Therefore, by the vow of the holy faithful, let us pass from here.”], let us pass from here, hastening with minds girded and feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace [Col. 1345D], so that we may quickly attain those joys of the resurrection [Note: The Major Monastery manuscripts: “so that we may be able to reach them, through him who lives and reigns forever and ever.”].

#### 5.

[Note: The following passages, added by Paschasius, are found in the manuscript of the Most Christian King, 4070, and in the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden, 1554.]

Tell me, I ask: in this mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, what is more lovable when it is read, what more joyful when it is understood, what sweeter when it is worthily received, what more beautiful when it is someday seen in its own beauty as it truly is?

Let what has been said thus far in this brief work suffice for you, dearest son, to display the dignity of so great a mystery. You must believe this with certainty: we have not been able to explain it worthily or as fully as it is.

Nor is this surprising, since even the angelic powers themselves, contemplating these things in the subtlety of their nature, marvel and tremble, and can scarcely penetrate them. Since, then, the nature of the blessed spirits, free from the burden of flesh, scarcely suffices to investigate these matters, when will a human being be able to speak of God sufficiently or worthily—a mortal of the immortal, the visible of the invisible, the mutable of the immutable, the work of the craftsman, the creature of the Creator, the product of the maker, the small of the immense, the temporal of the eternal, the humble of the Most High, the one formed from clay of him who created all things from nothing?

His omnipotence is ineffable. By that omnipotence, together with the greatest mercy, he saved us. He freely brought into being the work of creative omnipotence and omnipotently completed the work of saving grace.

There, the only-begotten Jesus Christ, God’s Son and our Lord, has power to create and govern his creature; here, he has power to lay down and take up his soul for us. He lives, is glorified, and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit in perfect Trinity and unity, God and man, forever and ever. Amen.

## In the Laubach manuscript, after the end of the chapter that is chapter XXII in the printed editions, the following is found

[Col. 1346C]

What is the law for you, dearest one, in relation to what you have read and read through? What, I ask, have you now resolved? Speak openly. Have you become deaf or mute? Show it; I see both. As I consider you, I see you stunned by so much, and I am somewhat afraid of what is read in the prophet in such words.

Nevertheless, I advise you: if you find nothing else to do, with all confidence in every other avenue lost, give yourself wholly to the mercy of God. Do not first surrender entirely to sluggish idleness, but continue laboring, at least after renouncing in your mind those things which, on the authority of the Apostle, you do not doubt are mortal sins.

And because this is not enough, “turn aside,” he says, “from evil and do good.” If you are unable—I know that you are unable to do penance in proportion to the measure of your sins—for time, age, bodily health, vigor of mind, and the ability to complete it are lacking [Col. 1346D–1347A], do at least a little, and do it continually.

Permitted things present themselves from time to time; remember that you have more often seized what was forbidden. Beg resources from elsewhere, or force out the strength of wild lettuce; prepare the unleavened bread and cast away the leaven of malice; gird your loins; place the staff of discipline in the hand of reason; hasten through desire where you cannot aspire by merit.

Reconcile yourself to some through satisfaction, to all through affection. Thereafter offer sacrifice with all the greater fear, the more recklessly you had extorted it from your mind, when it would have been wiser not to do so.

Because you are unable, put cessation first, if possible with tears; if not, with inward sobbing. Let something of your own be given, as necessity demands, inserting the embassy of the most merciful Redeemer into your prayer for the hearing.

For who knows whether he may turn and forgive, and turn away from the anger of his wrath, so that you do not perish eternally? You have indeed perished criminally.

## The following prayers are appended in the same manuscript

Behold me, Lord, behold me, who was not worthy—wretched and unhappy—to enter the courts of your Church or to cross the holy thresholds into your house. Yet I approach to minister at your holy altars, and I stand guilty and a sinner before the sight of your divine majesty, without any adornment of good work, without any worthy fruit of repentance, and without even a single pure thought.

For I am exceedingly unworthy and most wicked. Yet, trusting in your ineffable goodness and mercy and in the merits of your saints, although trembling and fearful I presume to approach in order to offer sacrifices to your holy name [Col. 1347C].

And therefore, most merciful Lord, creator and most compassionate redeemer, who desire to correct every soul that confesses and repents rather than destroy it; who willed to become incarnate not for the righteous but for sinners; who not only spared the thief hanging on the cross and confessing your majesty, but also promised him that he would enter paradise with you—do not reject me, wretched and confessing my sins, and, though sluggishly, repenting of my sins, from your goodness and mercy.

Do not receive in vain the faith, hope, and trust that I place in your inestimable clemency. Just as you spared all criminals and sinners who believed in you and trusted in your mercy, so may you deign to spare and forgive me, wretched as I am, fleeing to you, renouncing the devil after my many sins and crimes [Col. 1347D], and returning to you.

May you deign, in your fatherly goodness, to make me worthy and receive me for celebrating the office entrusted to me, although I intrude myself more insistently than would be fitting. For I cannot fail to know the prohibition established by the judgment of both the Old and the New Law.

I know from your sacred oracles, without disbelief, that the angels who destroy the impious and guard your sacred altars are certainly present, carrying vessels of slaughter in their hands. Yet, having long ago conceived a certain confidence in your true mercy, I presume upon it: namely, that although I have reached this old age through a long course of evil days, always provoking you, those avengers of your injuries, Lord, have not killed me, as would have been deserved.

Perhaps they knew that your goodness was patiently awaiting me, who was storing up repentance, although I deserve wrath on the day of wrath and the revelation of your just judgment, while many of my brothers also have evils against me.

For, Lord, I stand here truly suspect and trembling, lest I suddenly be struck by you—as is just—while you are present in your body and blood, since by your divinity you are absent nowhere.

Yet spare me still, I beg you in my presumption, most merciful one; spare me. Delay the blow, suspend vengeance. Do not look upon the iniquities, crimes, and sins of my youth—and, as I confess more shamefully, also of my old age—but upon your many mercies and compassions, by which you have always been accustomed to pity the human race.

Receive the prayers and sacrifices which I presume to offer to your majesty for my sins and for the sins of your faithful, both living and dead [Col. 1348B].

Remember that we are flesh, formed from fragile matter. Even the heavens are not clean in your sight, and your angels were found blameworthy before you; how much more earthly human beings, unworthy and unclean?

For we cannot be clean unless, through your goodness and mercy, we daily deserve to be cleansed in heart and body.

Therefore you, Lord—you who willed to arouse my sluggish, wretched, and polluted intention and devotion toward the most sacred mystery of your altar, and permitted me, unworthy and sinful though I am, to approach and minister to you—mercifully restrain for now the anger I deserve.

Show gratuitous clemency [Col. 1348C], and graciously grant that the celebration of this sacred mystery, to which I approach lukewarm and fearful, may come to me not for judgment and condemnation but for the remission of sins and eternal salvation.

Again.

Thus, O Lord, guilty of immense crime, with conscience as our witness, we are so confounded that we can approach your service neither confidently nor freely. For who, weighing his sin, would not wish to hide from your face, if it were permitted to avert his eyes from such great majesty—if he might escape by hiding, or evade punishment by remaining concealed? Or who would not desire rather to see you, if he did not fear you all the more because you behold him in his sin? Therefore, since you find us everywhere, we flee to you, whom we can never escape. Nothing remains for the wretched but tears, since no hiding places intervene. May indulgence sustain those whom offense terrifies. Power threatens, but may mercy console. From you comes the will; through you comes pardon. Spare us, almighty Father, and deign to count those whom you see humbled by guilt among the upright in reward; and do not make those whom you recognize as wretched through confession confused at the judgment.

Again, another prayer.

Forgive, O God, whatever through the intemperance of our biting tongue, through the reproach of our careless mouth, has wounded our subjects; forgive whatever we have said that fell short of the perfection of goodness. Spare whatever we have uttered improperly or with insufficient restraint; you, forgive us. Let presumption not punish the unwary; rather, may your merciful kindness absolve me as I acknowledge my iniquities. And since I have no confidence elsewhere except in your mercy, sanctify both my mouth and my proclamation of the truth through arms and works, with fuller abundance, so that you may save me as one worthy and, in your goodness, justify the flock entrusted to me.

Whatever you see corrupted in them, heal; whatever you perceive defective in me, tend. If they have contracted or are contracting any stain through the defect of my lukewarmness or through negligence, overlook it. If, whether with my knowledge or without it, they have fallen into any crime, and if they have come into guilt through the offense caused by my example, forgive them; and for such faults do not repay wretched me with vengeance. Yet for those whom I seemed to subject to the force of reproof and judgment, may the reproof itself benefit them unto salvation, and may this prayer, interceding for the offense committed, recall them from error, so that they may not endure Tartarean torments, they for whom, as mortal men, we have prescribed laws of penance. Thus, sparing the hardships of both parties, grant forgiveness to their iniquities and wash away from me the offense incurred in undertaking the burden of governing them.

Give ear, O God, to our sacrifices. Inscribe me and those entrusted to me in your pages, so that, together with the flock committed to me, I may be cleansed from every crime and may deserve to reach you in peace. Make the dwelling-place of our hearts peaceful, by expelling carnal vices; and since I now strive to exercise the highest virtues among my subjects, may I, when the disorders of minds and bodies have been pacified, deserve, as a man of peace, to be crowned with the angels when you judge.

Do therefore, O God, that, as we behold you and burn in your sight, the zeal for your house may consume us through the gift of your grace. Let us govern our subjects with such restraint through the vigor of the Holy Spirit that they may gain profit from the disciplines of our rule, their hardness may be broken, and their life may bear fruit. Receive, Lord, the offerings of our vows, so that through them whatever correction we bestow upon our subjects, whether by word or by merit, may—rather than producing discord between us—be joyfully recognized as having profited both them and us unto everlasting sweetness. Absolve us from both the sin of others and our own, so that, desiring in both cases the effectiveness of spiritual grace, we may supplicate your name with greater confidence. Through the Lord.

Again.

The duty of ministering impels me to offer the saving sacrifice of the people for their offense. The conscience of an unworthy priesthood terrifies me because of my guilt: if I, the refuse of all priests, offer sacrifice, the crime of my polluted conscience is increased; but if it is not offered to such great Majesty, the Judge of all flesh, I am charged with the guilt of negligence.

[Col. 1350A] Amid these things I implore the balance of your mercy, Almighty God, whose day of vengeance I dread while my conscience accuses me. I ask that, in your mercy, you do not judge unworthy the one whom you do not exclude from the time of repentance. Suspend the axe until the cultivator of the vineyard brings a basket of manure to the root of the fruitless tree.

Spare me, most merciful Lord, a penitent, you who mercifully recalled David to forgiveness after his fall; you who, in your mercy, regarded Peter’s tears as he wept bitterly; you who illumined the thief, guilty of so great a crime upon the gallows of the cross, with divine grace. His confession soon obtained for him the clear sight of the Son of God: faith obtained a reward, punishment forgiveness, lamentation everlasting joys, while the confessor on the cross became the possessor of paradise after the cross.

But because my words need the forgiveness of your mercy, and the works of an unworthy priesthood do not commend me, at least receive the vows of those standing here, so that their prayers may obtain forgiveness for me before you, and that through their merits the sacrifices may beneficially bring us healing for our wounds. Since the Almighty became a sacrifice for all, for sins, be present to us as the sacrifice within the sacrifice for offenses, O Christ, Savior of the world, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit live and reign as God forever and ever. Amen.

In an old codex of the Major Monastery, at the end of Paschasius’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, the following prayer is appended; in some printed editions it is placed before the work.

Lord Jesus Christ, who by the will of the Father, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, took the form of a servant, and who, dying according to the flesh through your cross and passion, after conquering death and rising again, brought back to the pastures of life the hundredth sheep that had been lost: cleanse me by your mercy from every stain of vice, me whom you have made a minister of this great mystery not by the merit of election but by the gift of your grace. Grant that, cleansed for the salvation of my soul, I may receive your most holy body and blood, so that, vivified by them, I may obtain a share in the blessed resurrection on the day of judgment and, with the saints, sing glory to you in eternal joy without end. Amen. Blessed be God.

In the Corbie codex the following prayer of Paschasius Radbertus is found before the reception of the Eucharist:

May this sacrament of yours, Lord Jesus Christ, be for us forgiveness of sins. May this Eucharist become for us life, the inward parts of mercy, the grace of salvation, and the health of our souls. Amen.

[Col. 1351]

## Letter of Saint Paschasius Radbertus, Abbot of Corbie, on the Body and Blood of the Lord, to Frudegard

*(According to the edition of Jacques Sirmond, p. 1619.)*

[Col. 1351A] To his most beloved brother and fellow soldier, Frudegard, Paschasius, your old man and the refuse of all monks, sends the greatest and everlasting salvation.

After reading your letter, while I was occupied with the affairs of certain guests, I was quite unable to fulfill what you had instructed. Yet at times, filled with love for you and with the sweetness of your letter, I did not fail to reflect upon your request, because we have no part of the books with us in which I might find what you ask, so that I could answer one to whom I cannot refuse what you demand, even though you impose what I cannot fulfill.

You ask about a matter concerning which many people doubt. Even if they perhaps do not fully understand it, they ought certainly to believe the words of the Savior, the truthful God who does not lie, when he says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life remaining in you. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6). And to the disciples, when he offered them the bread, he said: “Take; this is my body, which will be handed over for you.” Likewise concerning the cup: “Drink from it, all of you, for this is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins.”

Therefore, when he says, “This is my body,” or “my flesh,” or “This is my blood,” I think he indicated no other flesh than his own, which was born of the Virgin Mary and hung upon the cross, and no other blood than that which was poured out upon the cross and was then in his own body. No one, therefore, who thinks soundly believes that Jesus had any other flesh or blood than that which was born of the Virgin Mary and suffered upon the cross.

[Col. 1351C] This same flesh must, I believe, be understood in whatever manner when he says: “This is my body, which will be handed over for many,” or, “This is my blood.” And lest you think that he was speaking in the sacrament of something other than his own, within that same mystery he said demonstratively: “This is my body.” For when he says “my” and “this is,” he does not wish some arbitrary body to be understood, but that body which was to be handed over, as he immediately added; nor does he mean any other blood than that which was to be poured out in his own body for the forgiveness of sins.

Otherwise, however it may be understood, if there were another blood and another flesh in this mystery, forgiveness of sins would not be in it. And if life were not in it, it would by no means bestow life. Otherwise, no ordinary food, unless it came from the living and eternal Lord, would provide eternal life to those who receive it for salvation. For, as he himself says: “Whoever does not eat this flesh and drink this blood does not have eternal life remaining in him.”

Therefore the sacrament that grants life contains within itself what it grants to those who worthily receive it; and in it is the flesh of the one who truly lives, and the blood in which eternal life truly exists.
