You say that you formerly believed this and that you read it in my little book which I published on the sacraments. But you confess that afterward, in the third book of blessed Augustine’s *On Christian Doctrine*, you read that it is a figurative expression for Christ’s body and blood to be so called. If it is figurative speech, you say, and a figure rather than reality, “I do not know how I ought to receive it.” Then you add: “And even if I believe it to be what he assumed from Mary his virgin mother, this outstanding doctor himself, conversely, declares it a great crime.”

This statement, if it is received with horror, seems to strike excessive fear into those who do not believe that the sacrament contains what the Truth openly testifies to be there. And if they believe it to be as some understand it, they nevertheless incur that crime because they believe falsely, since it was said in such a way that it would be permissible to tear him apart with the teeth.

Thus it would be a crime if someone believed it as those people believed to whom he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man.” They could not endure this because they understood it badly. Therefore, if someone says that this flesh and this blood are themselves present without mystery or sacrament, and that they are not to be received in a figure, as those carnal people, thinking carnally, understood them at that time, he destroys the whole matter.

For this reason, perhaps blessed Augustine says that it is a great crime to understand it in this way. Otherwise, how could that same outstanding doctor contradict himself, as I recall, in his sermons to the newly baptized? “Receive,” he says, “in the bread what hung upon the wood”; and concerning the cup: “Receive in the cup what flowed from Christ’s side.” I do not believe that anything other than flesh hung upon the cross, or that anything other than blood and water flowed from Christ’s side.

If this is so, believers receive this—that is, flesh and blood mingled with water—in the sacraments in which they were reborn, and for this reason these two are mixed in the cup: water, in which they were reborn, and blood, by which the faithful were redeemed. As Saint Cyprian testifies, neither should there be water in the cup without blood, nor blood without water, because by the water the people washed in the wave of baptism are signified, and by the blood Christ is signified, through which he redeemed us. Thus Christ and the Church are understood and formed as one body.

Therefore neither Christ without the Church, as eternal high priest, nor the Church without Christ is offered to God the Father. These things are mystical, in which there is the truth of flesh and blood—not of another, but of Christ—yet in mystery and figure.

Nor is it surprising if this mystery is a figure and the words of the mystery are called figurative speech, since Christ himself is called by the Apostle Paul a mark or figure, although he himself is the Truth. For he says: “In these last days God the Father has spoken to us in his Son, who, being the radiance of his glory and the figure—or character, as other codices have it—of his substance.” Behold: as you hear, Christ himself, the highest Truth, is called a character and a figure. Yet there was nothing fictitious in him, nothing empty of truth, just as we do not say that the characters or figures of letters are empty of their force and power when we call those same figures, figuratively, “letters.”

On this very interpretation I published a particular chapter in the same little book of mine which you say you read, so that this mystery and its truth might be understood, while it nevertheless would not be denied to be a figure.

For just as at present we know only in part whatever we know about God, and, as the Apostle testifies, prophesy in part concerning the future and the heavenly kingdom (1 Corinthians 13), so we partly taste beforehand—not with the palate of the mouth but with the palate of the heart—and through faith believe Christ’s body and blood to be present, so that we may live from him and, having been transformed and renewed into a new creation, live from this new creation in the one from whom, in whom, and through whom we have been redeemed and reborn.

Blessed Augustine says the following concerning this matter in his letter to Bishop Boniface, in the letter which you said had moved you:

“Just as we customarily say concerning the day of Christ’s passion during each of the solemnities of Easter, ‘Today is Christ’s resurrection,’ although it took place once, many years ago, and although it is said to have passed again through so many cycles of years, so that it may be believed to be the same event and understood to have occurred only once: therefore the one who says, ‘Today is Christ’s resurrection,’ does not truly lie, because, in a certain way, it is the same event on account of the recurrence of time.”

[Col. 1353D] Then that aforementioned doctor added the following, so that we might understand the manner of speaking—not so that he might be thought to contradict himself, or that he wished to apply his preceding statement to the newly baptized, but so that we could understand what he had shown elsewhere to have been said figuratively:

“Nor does the one who, when asked, answers that Christ is being sacrificed today lie, because from the similarity of the things whose sacraments they are, they receive their names. Otherwise, unless they had some similarity to the very thing whose sacraments they are, they would not be sacraments.”

Therefore, while the one who no longer dies and over whom death will never again rule (Romans 6) is sacrificed, this takes place in the sacrament. Hence the same doctor says:

“In a certain manner, just as the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body, so the sacrament of Christ’s blood is Christ’s blood.”

Behold, he is not contradictory here, as some think, nor is he contradictory to blessed Ambrose. His statement, I say, is entirely full and true in the book in which he says that it is the very flesh of Christ in the sacrament which hung upon the cross and was taken from the Virgin Mary, and the blood which flowed from his side.

Blessed Cyprian likewise confirms this in the work addressed to the people where he speaks about the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood. Following them, the aforementioned Father Augustine, that most subtle disputant, says, as I have stated:

“Receive in the bread what hung upon the wood, and receive in the cup what flowed from Christ’s side.”

And elsewhere, concerning the Jews:

“Afterward they drank in the cup, believing what they had poured out while raging at the cross.”

From this point Eusebius of Emesa likewise says:

“Let every ambiguity of unbelief therefore depart, since the one who is the author of the gift is himself also the witness of its truth. For the invisible priest, by his word and by a hidden power, changes visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood, saying: ‘Take and eat, for this is my body’; and, repeating the sanctification: ‘Take and drink, this is my blood.’ Therefore, just as at the command of the Lord who orders them, the heights of the heavens, the depths of the waters, and the vast expanses of the earth suddenly came into being out of nothing, so by equal power in the spiritual sacraments, where he commands, the effect serves the power of the reality.”

And shortly afterward:

“Look upon the sacred body and blood of your Lord with faith; touch it with the mind; honor it; marvel at it; receive it with the hand of the heart; and especially take it within by interior drinking.”

Then:

“Let no one doubt that the primary creatures can, at the command of power and in the presence of majesty, pass into the nature of the Lord’s body, when he sees that the man himself has been made Christ’s body through the work of heavenly mercy.”

This is the faith of the saints, beloved, although many doubt how he remains whole while this can be Christ’s body and blood.

They would not have believed it if they had seen the twelve baskets of fragments, the seven baskets, and the five or seven loaves (Matthew 14; Luke 9; John 6). For there was nothing in the fragments other than the loaves themselves, nor anything else in the eating of those who ate. Such abundance flowed from Christ’s blessing; and what was eaten and what was gathered up was nothing other than the five or seven loaves themselves.

How much more, then, does the flesh of the Word, who became flesh (John 1), multiply, and how does the abundance of Christ’s flesh and blood flow forth in the sacrament? It is not another flesh than Christ’s flesh, and yet Christ remains whole.

Therefore, as I think, blessed Augustine differs in none of these matters from the other holy Fathers, who in very many passages understood this to be as the Savior says, and believed what the holy Church of God believes.

“For thus it is,” says that same outstanding Father to the aforementioned Boniface:

“Christ’s body and blood, just as the sacrament of faith is faith. For believing, he says, is nothing other than having faith on account of the sacrament of faith, since the very answer by which, when questioned, we confess Christ to be sacrificed daily in the mystery also belongs to the celebration of the sacrament—something accomplished once, when he was sacrificed for the salvation of the world in himself.

“Thus, because we believe that this takes place spiritually, this is not without the sacrament that was then accomplished; nor is that event repeated in actuality so that Christ might die. Rather, he is sacrificed for us daily in the mystery, so that in the bread we may receive what hung upon the cross, and in the cup drink what flowed from Christ’s side.

“For we walk by faith and not by sight. Therefore we must believe these things spiritually in the Spirit, and not carnally, lest we incur a crime.”

Since, as that doctor himself says, the sacrament of faith is faith, so Christ’s body and blood in this sacrament are true flesh and blood.

“For believing,” he says, “is nothing other than having faith on account of the sacrament of faith, since the very answer belongs to the celebration of the sacrament.”

From this it is clear that not everyone who reads blessed Augustine understands him.

Blessed Gregory confirms the sacraments of this matter in the fourth book of the *Dialogues* (chapter 58), saying:

“We ought therefore to despise the present age with our whole mind, either because we see that it has passed away, and to offer daily to God the sacrifice of tears and the daily sacrifices of his flesh and blood.”

For this unique victim saves the soul from eternal destruction; through the mystery it restores to us the death of the Only-Begotten. Although, rising from the dead, he no longer dies and death will never again rule over him (Romans 6), nevertheless, living in himself immortally and incorruptibly, he is again sacrificed for us in this mystery of sacred offering.

There his body is received; his flesh is divided for the salvation of the people; his blood is poured out—not now into the hands of unbelievers, but into the mouths of the faithful. From this, therefore, let us consider what kind of sacrifice is offered for us: one that always imitates, for our absolution, the passion of the Only-Begotten Son.

For what believer could doubt that, at the very hour of the sacrifice, at the priest’s voice, the heavens are opened, and that in this mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present? That things above are joined to things below, earthly things to heavenly things, and one reality is made from visible and invisible things?

But concerning this sacrament also, Saint Cyril, together with the one hundred and fifty who assembled at Ephesus, said among the other statements of faith:

“We necessarily add this also: For while announcing, according to the flesh, the death of the Only-Begotten Son of God, that is, Christ Jesus, and likewise confessing his resurrection and ascension into the heavens, we celebrate in the churches the service of the bloodless sacrifice.

“In this way we also approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, becoming participants in the holy body and precious blood of Christ, the Redeemer of us all. We do not receive it as ordinary flesh—far be it from us—nor as the flesh of a sanctified man joined to the Word according to a unity of dignity, nor as though it possessed a divine indwelling. Rather, we receive it as truly life-giving and made the proper flesh of the Word himself.

“For since he exists naturally as Life, being God, and is united to his own flesh, he has confessed that it is life-giving. Therefore, although he says to us, ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood,’ we must not regard it as the flesh of one ordinary man from among us.

“For how could human flesh be life-giving according to its nature? Rather, it is the flesh truly made his own, since for our sake he both became and was called the Son of Man.”

Therefore, beloved, all who think carnally about this mystery do not think rightly. The sacraments in it are spiritual, and every merely natural person fasts from them because he does not grasp them with spiritual understanding and does not wish to believe what he does not understand.

For the present, dearest, you have what I have been able to bring to mind. Since you are a part of my soul, I ought not to conceal what I was unable to express as I should have.

But I ask that you reread our little book on this work, which you say you read long ago. If you find anything in it blameworthy or doubtful, do not hesitate to read it again. For even if I wrote nothing worthy for its readers, since I dedicated it to any child whatsoever, nevertheless, as I hear, I moved many toward an understanding of this mystery, so that they might know and understand how to think worthily about Christ.

While his body is not corrupted because it is spiritual, everything celebrated in this sacrament is wholly spiritual, because it is the Spirit who gives life and works within it for believers and those who receive it worthily; but for unbelievers and those who eat it unworthily, it is truly judgment and condemnation.

For this body and blood do what we read that Christ himself did upon the cross: to one of those who were with him on the gallows, when he confessed, he granted the kingdom of paradise; to the other, namely the blasphemer, he assigned the judgment of death.

I have also added to this response of ours the exposition concerning the supper which I had expounded from this mystery in my commentary on Matthew, so that from it you may consider what should be believed more intelligibly and what in me should be criticized charitably.

Nevertheless, whatever you judge of these matters, I ask that you append this letter and this exposition to the same little book, so that through them the reader’s understanding may be further increased and the authority of the Fathers confirmed.

## Exposition of Paschasius Radbertus, Abbot of Corbie, on the Passage in Matthew

“While they were dining, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, gave it to his disciples, and said: ‘Take and eat: this is my body,’ etc.” (Matthew 26).

[Col. 1356D]

While they were eating, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, gave it to his disciples, and said: “Take and eat: this is my body,” etc.

Let those who wish to diminish this word “body”—claiming that it is not the true flesh of Christ, which is now celebrated in the sacrament in the Church of Christ, nor his true blood—listen. I do not know what they wish to applaud or invent, as though there were some sort of power of flesh and blood in that sacrament, so that the Lord would be lying and it would not be his true flesh or true blood, in which Christ’s true death is proclaimed, when Truth itself says: “This is my body.” Likewise concerning the chalice: “Drink from it, all of you; for this is my blood of the New Testament,” not just any blood, but that which “will be poured out for you for the remission of sins.” [Col. 1357A]

Therefore, when he broke the bread and gave it to them, he did not say: “This is,” or “In this mystery there is some power or figure of my body”; rather, he said plainly: “This is my body.” And so this is what he said, not what anyone invents.

Luke added: “Which will be handed over for you” (Luke 22), or, as other codices have it, “is given.” John too, speaking in the person of the Lord, says: “The bread that I will give is my flesh,” none other than the flesh that “I will give for the life of the world”; and afterward: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6). [Col. 1357B]

Therefore I am astonished at what certain people now wish to say: that the truth of Christ’s flesh or blood is not present in the reality, but that there is some power of flesh in the sacrament, and not flesh; a power of blood, and not blood; a figure, and not the truth; a shadow, and not the body—when here the outward form receives the truth, and the figure of the ancient sacrifices receives the body.

Therefore Truth said, when he extended the bread to the disciples: “This is my body” (Matthew 26), and nothing other than that which “will be handed over for you”; and concerning the chalice: “This is the chalice of the New Testament, which will be poured out for you for the remission of sins” (Mark 14).

The blood had not yet been poured out, and yet the blood that was to be poured out was already being offered in the chalice. It was already in the chalice, although it was still to be poured out as the price. Thus the very same blood was already in the chalice as was in the body, just as the flesh, or body, was in the bread. [Col. 1357C]

Christ was whole, and his body was set before the eyes of everyone; his blood was also in his body. So even today he remains perfectly whole, yet was truly given to them to eat and drink for the remission of sins. (Augustine, *Sermon 2, On the Words of the Lord*.)

Let someone likewise say whether the remission of sins exists in anything other than Christ. It is therefore certain that it does not, and that the remission of sins is in this body and blood: truly, therefore, it is Christ’s flesh and blood.

Accordingly, those who worthily eat and drink truly eat and drink eternal life, and life remains whole. The body and blood of Christ will then be life for each person if what is received in the sacrament is eaten spiritually in the very truth, and drunk spiritually, as I remember having said on some occasion. For, as he says to the apostles (John 6), “the flesh profits nothing”; how much less does the bread without the Spirit, which is seen? “It is the Spirit who gives life.” [Col. 1357D]

I have said these things at greater length and more explicitly because I have heard certain people criticize me, as though in the book I published concerning the sacraments of Christ I had wished to attribute something more to these statements, or something other than what Truth herself promises. Perhaps they fear that I wished to make divisions, and to divide him limb by limb, cutting him up or dispersing him, just as those who are said to have been scandalized and to have gone back understood matters then.

To them the Savior said: “Does this scandalize you? What then if you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?” [Col. 1358A] As though he were saying: If you could understand this, you would certainly know that he who, whole and entire, can ascend where he was before—the one and the same Christ—cannot be consumed by teeth or divided into parts.

To see this is indeed a great matter, because it is in the Spirit. Who could explain by human understanding how the one Christ, the Son of Man, ascended where he was before? And what reason can comprehend that the Son of Man who descended from heaven is in heaven? Likewise, what words can express that “the Word became flesh,” and that what is unchangeable is said to have become something? Or how can he who was a human being, the Son of Man, placed before their eyes on earth, be said to be in heaven?

How, then, did he come from heaven, from which he was never absent? [Col. 1358B] He ascended while descending, because Christ is dissolved in nothing. He is what he was, and what he is was not.

In all these matters, and in very many others, divine power surpasses human minds; heavenly and divine reason does not submit to human senses. For an inferior nature neither grasps nor understands the cause and reason of a higher and immeasurable nature.

Therefore, concerning such things as divine power accomplishes, doubt must be removed and hesitation put aside. Their knowledge lies in faith, their reason in power, their effect in things proceeds from power, and their cause lies in the will. Thus a human being has nothing for which to complain about the individual things God has spoken and willed, since “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalms 32, 148), as he willed. [Col. 1358C]

The sacraments in such matters are sublime and divine: they are enacted for the salvation of the human race and, in this mystery entrusted to the apostles, are celebrated mystically every day.

Therefore this Passover is celebrated in the upper room, because only those who have ascended can understand these things: they eat and drink what has been poured out for the remission of sins, and yet it remains whole.

Hence Truth herself says: “Drink, for this is my blood, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins.” But if it has been poured out, how is it poured out again now? And if the flesh has been consumed, how does it still remain whole and continue to be eaten?

Behold: what is drunk every day is poured out, and what was sacrificed once is still sacrificed every day. Yet nothing is sacrificed except what is one. It is drunk and poured out for the remission of sins. [Col. 1358D]

If you ask how it is poured out so that what has been poured out remains, understand how “the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts” and charity remains whole (Romans 5)—namely, the Holy Spirit. In this way, perhaps, you will be able to recognize that whatever the Holy Spirit accomplishes is ineffable.

And if the charity of God has been poured out within us while remaining in itself, truly the blood of the New Testament of God is poured out into hearts for the remission of sins. Once it has been poured out, all our sins are forgiven in it, because Christ himself is the high priest who offers us this bread—namely, his body—and pours it into the chalice.

He does not depart from his office. And if he remains in us, he himself also drinks it anew with us, since he is in his whole body and in all of us; without him we cannot receive it, nor eat of that bread, nor drink from the chalice. [Col. 1359A]

Do not be astonished, brother, if perhaps you do not believe these things, because what we say is not ours. The Word of God is almighty and effective for everything he wills, according to the multitude of his powers, since he himself is the one power of all powers.

His words are the words of no other than the one Word who is himself; therefore they are full of truth, because they are Spirit and life, and contain nothing other than what Truth herself declares through them.

“Take,” he says; “this is my body.” And concerning the chalice: “This is my blood.”

At that time the apostles, if they had not believed the words of life and truth, could have replied or asked how that bread or chalice of wine could be the body and blood of Christ, since Christ himself, whole and entire in his body, was before their eyes. But because they believed what he had said, they confess it in silence and receive what they later handed down to us. [Col. 1359B]

They handed down no other supper than that very same supper which they themselves then ate and drank.

Let the faithful mind therefore consider the difference between that figurative Passover in which the lamb was sacrificed and eaten at the same supper, and this Passover, which according to the order of Melchizedek is continually celebrated in bread and wine.

Concerning that Passover, he said at the same hour to all his followers: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22).

But if this mystery contains nothing more than a figure of Christ’s body and blood, and is not what he himself said, why was it necessary to repeat it in reality, since the whole matter had already been prefigured in the lamb?

Hence Luke (in the same passage) recalls that two chalices were given to the disciples at the same supper: one first, after the eating of the lamb and before he took the bread; the other after he had blessed and broken the bread and given it to his disciples. [Col. 1359C]

Likewise, he says, after he had supped: “This chalice is the New Testament in my blood, which will be poured out for you.”

This gives us to understand that the legal lamb, together with its chalice, preceded as a figure of Christ’s Passion. Then the body and blood in the chalice were made for the fulfillment of the truth, so that what had preceded in Melchizedek might be completed entirely in Christ.

No one who reads this Gospel doubts that the chalice signifies Christ’s Passion.

For this reason some are uncertain whether Luke intended to indicate that Jesus received two chalices, or one and the same chalice, because he had mentioned it beforehand and then, in a recapitulation, mentioned it twice.

Some therefore think that there were not two chalices, but one, which is recalled as having been given to the disciples both before it was divided and afterward to be drunk. Others, more persuasively, as I have already said, affirm that two chalices were offered to the disciples: in one of them, the first, he wished to express his own Passion; in the other, to prefigure the passion of his faithful. [Col. 1359D]

Still others argue that in both chalices he wished to show what was commanded in the Old Testament: that whoever did not celebrate the Passover by eating the lamb in the first month was to complete it in the second month by eating a kid; and that for this reason the Lord gave two chalices to the disciples (Exodus 12). [Col. 1360A]

They maintain that both chalices truly signify that both Testaments should be understood, and that consequently one of them pertains to the lamb, while the other pertains to the mystery of the body.

But whether someone holds this view or that one, none of them is found to be outside the true faith, provided that he understands this fact: in receiving bread and the chalice, the most gracious Jesus passes from the figure and shadow of truth to the true sacrament of Passover, so that not one jot or tittle might be cut away from the Law—indeed, because he is the cornerstone, holding and fulfilling both laws.

Thus, as the true Melchizedek, he offers bread and wine, which were the prefigured sacrament of his body and blood.

It should be noted that he says: “He blessed and broke.” Through this blessing and breaking, a new creation is effected, so that the bread, offered to God in faith in commemoration of Christ’s death, is rightly believed to be his flesh. [Col. 1360B]

Likewise, the blood is created in the same thanksgiving that he offered to God the Father, so that it may truly be believed to be the blood that was poured out for many for the remission of sins.

## SAYINGS OF THE CATHOLIC FATHERS

Ambrose says in *On the Trinity*:

> “In the same way the Arians are accustomed to object to the Son’s obedience, because it is written (Philippians 12): ‘And being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death.’ He put ‘man’ first and said ‘unto death,’ so that we might understand that the obedience unto death belonged not to divinity but to humanity, in which he assumed our offices and names. We therefore say that the Trinity has one power, which he taught us in the Passion itself and after it. The Son suffers through the sacrament of the body; the Holy Spirit is poured into the apostles; the Spirit is commended into the hands of the Father; and God the Father is signified by a loud voice.” [Col. 1360C]

I have included these words of blessed Ambrose so that you may know, dearest son, that not only is the Lord’s Passion a mystery and sacrament of salvation, but so too are Christ’s birth and incarnation, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

All these things, I say, which God as man accomplished, are sacraments of the divine gift and mysteries of faith. Yet they are nothing other than the truth, because they are called sacraments.

Therefore the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, although it is called a sacrament, is nothing other than the truth and what Truth herself promised. [Col. 1360D]

Hence blessed Augustine says: “The sacrament of faith is faith”; and afterward: “So too the body and blood of Christ in this sacrament are true flesh and blood.”

“Believing,” he says, “is nothing other than having faith for the sake of the sacrament of faith.” Therefore whoever doubts this denies that he possesses faith, because in the faith of Christ there can be nothing other than truth.

And as Leo the apostolic teacher testifies:

> “What is believed by faith is truly received by the mouth. Therefore,” he says, “you ought to communicate in such a way that you have absolutely no doubt concerning the truth of Christ’s body and blood.”

That Christ’s flesh and blood are truly his own is testified by all Catholics; Cyril also testifies to it, together with his one hundred and fifty fellow bishops assembled at Ephesus. [Col. 1361A]

Among other things, he testifies that it is life-giving flesh, made the proper flesh of the Word himself, who exists naturally as life because he has been united to his own flesh.

Therefore, wherever there is this natural unity, there is no division. And if it is Christ’s own and one flesh, then surely it is the flesh that was born of Mary, because “the Word became flesh,” and it is the flesh that hung upon the cross.

To believe this in the sacrament is therefore faith, and the sacrament of faith is true flesh and blood.

Thus, as the Apostle testifies, just as no one says “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 21), so no one believes that this is so except through the Holy Spirit, through whom this faith has been given and through whom this sacrament is effected, so that it is true flesh—this very flesh, and none other. [Col. 1361B]

Without the Holy Spirit, however, just as the flesh of Christ profits nothing, so this sacrament of the flesh cannot profit anything.

For in all these things the Holy Spirit is the one worker, and Christ is one—he who was conceived of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary—and the same Spirit is the creator and sanctifier of the body and blood.

Without him no one says “Lord Jesus” in the sacrament; no one rightly believes these same sacraments; no one confesses that it is the very flesh that suffered, made his own and one.

Since faith comes from the sacrament of faith, if faith is true, the flesh and blood are also true. Thus the faith proclaimed by the Apostle may exist:

> “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11);

and yet it is a true substance, although it is called evidence. [Col. 1361C]

Therefore this flesh is not seen, nor is the eternal life that is hoped for, because it is the proper flesh of the Word. In faith there is the substance that already believes and receives, yet is still hoped for today.

It is therefore the evidence of things not seen, that is, because it is the substance of things hoped for. Through these things it is already wholly present in faith; indeed, it is faith itself.

Accordingly, whoever worthily eats this flesh and drinks this blood truly already eats and drinks eternal life. Christ remains in him through the true flesh of the Word and through his blood, just as we remain in him through the true human being whom he assumed.

If he is truly God and man, as we believe, then Christ’s flesh is true in this sacrament of faith; true unity is also granted in us through it, and there is true adoption into the body of Christ. [Col. 1361D]

Thus, although each person eats and drinks this life, Christ nevertheless remains whole and lives, because he is the way, the truth, and the life.

But certain people, extremely talkative rather than learned, refuse to believe these things. They raise every objection they can to avoid believing what Truth promises, saying that there is no body that is not tangible and visible.

“These things,” they say, “because they are mysteries, cannot be seen or touched; therefore they are not bodies. And if they are not bodies, they are spoken of as a figure of flesh and blood, not as the actual nature of Christ’s flesh and blood—the flesh that suffered on the cross and was born of the Virgin Mary.” [Col. 1362A]

See how well they argue against faith without faith, refusing to believe because, as the Apostle testifies, faith is not concerned with the things that are seen but with those that are not seen.

Since the mysteries are not seen, they are therefore mysteries and sacraments. Thus, in faith, they are what they are called to be, as Truth testifies.

Because they are things hoped for, they are rightly believed to be nothing other than the flesh and blood of Christ.

Otherwise, that holy Synod of Ephesus—which no one is permitted to contradict any more than the Gospel—would never have dared, except on the authority of the Gospel, to reject what it rejects and to affirm that Christ’s flesh in this sacrament is truly life-giving and has been made the proper flesh of the Word himself.

He exists naturally as life, as God, because he has been united to his own flesh.

I do not know whether these matters could be stated more openly or more clearly, when everything that Christ is is proclaimed—not in figure, but in reality, in proper identity, and in nature: he exists naturally as life, as God. Therefore it is rightly believed to be not merely a power but the proper nature itself. [Col. 1362B]

Consequently, those who deny that this mystery is visible and tangible do so for no other reason than that they do not wish to believe, and do not wish the words of Truth to be true: “This is my body, and this is my blood.”

Let them therefore ascend to where Christ is at the right hand of God the Father; there they will find the visible and tangible Christ himself, the very Christ whom they seek.

But because we walk by faith and not by sight, we believe and sometimes receive what is hidden, what is true in the mystery; for if it were not hidden, it would not be faith or mystery.

Thus what we receive becomes visible and tangible in Christ, visible in the mystery, and in faith the flesh of the Word is made proper in the Holy Spirit: one and the same flesh that suffered, and no other.

Likewise, the blood is present for salvation, and we enjoy it in life, because Christ is the mediator between God and human beings, so that through him and in him we may be found to be one. [Col. 1362C]

Behold, dearest one: in the cup of this little book you have the sayings of the Catholic Fathers, recorded in a brief compendium. From them you can learn that, long ago, when I was still a boy, I did not see such things under the impulse of presumption, but proposed them to those who asked on the authority of God and the holy Fathers.

Now, since it has become clear that faith does not belong to everyone, let those who still cannot understand that nothing is impossible for God learn, I ask, to believe with such people. Let them also learn to accept the divine words in everything and to doubt none of these matters.

For to the present day no one is recorded as having gone astray except those who also went astray concerning Christ, although very many have doubted or failed to understand the sacraments of so great a mystery.

Rather, let us marvel at the deepest counsel of God, which the Angel of Great Counsel established, desiring all human beings to be saved. [Col. 1362D]

Let us marvel, praise, and understand in these matters what blessed Hilary understood (*On the Trinity*, book 3): by what method, so to speak, Christ gathered us into himself, and by what mystery he willed us to be naturally one in him—not merely through agreement of will, but through the nature of his flesh and blood.

For he says:

> “How can Christ not be believed to remain naturally in us, when, having become man, he assumed the nature of our flesh, inseparable from himself, and mingled the nature of his flesh with the nature of eternity under the sacrament of the flesh to be communicated to us? Thus,” he says, “we are all one, because the Father is in Christ and Christ is in us,” etc. [Col. 1363A]

Augustine and the others likewise testify that Christ is in us in this way, and that we are in him through the human being he assumed. If anyone wishes to destroy this, he must destroy everything, to his own ruin: that God was pleased to become man in the sacrament for salvation.

Therefore what the most holy Ambrose says is true: the very same flesh and blood that we receive and share—the flesh that was born of the Virgin Mary and hung upon the cross for us.

Blessed Cyprian the martyr also testifies to this.

Therefore, if anyone denies that this is so because it is called a sacrament, then, as Saint Augustine testifies, it will be death rather than life for him if he considers Life a liar. [Col. 1363B]

Hence Leo the apostolic teacher says:

> “What is believed by faith is received by the mouth. And their ‘Amen’ is answered in vain by those who argue against what they receive.”

If you ask, dearest one, concerning what all people universally answer “Amen” throughout the whole Church of Christ, observe, during the celebration of the sacraments instituted by blessed Peter—as we believe—what the priest prays in the Canon, except for what is said after Communion:

> “May it become the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

When this prayer has been completed, we all say “Amen” with one harmonious voice. Thus the whole Church, in every nation and language, prays and confesses that this is what it prays for. [Col. 1363C]

Let anyone who wishes to oppose this rather than believe consider what he is doing against the Lord himself and against the whole Church of Christ.

It is therefore a wicked crime to pray with everyone and not believe what Truth herself testifies, and what everyone everywhere universally confesses to be true.

Since he himself says that it is his body and his blood, we ought not to doubt in any respect merely because we do not see with bodily eyes what we believe.

We have also heard what Pope Gregory thinks about this. We have heard what Saint Cyril thinks, together with all his fellow bishops assembled at Ephesus; what Greece thinks with them; what Egypt thinks; and what Saint Jerome the priest thinks, who also rendered the lives of the holy Fathers into Latin.

Therefore, although some people err through ignorance on this matter, there is still no one openly contradicting the truth of what the whole world believes and confesses. [Col. 1363D]

For, as I have said, by the great counsel of God this was ordained by God at the supper, so that the Savior, because it is an extraordinary thing, might say to the disciples:

> “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22). [Col. 1364A]

Otherwise, if there were no evident sacrament in it, he would never have said: “With desire I have desired.” For to say “with desire I have desired” is greater than simply saying “I have desired,” although even the latter would have been a great statement.

In the divine Scriptures this kind of expression is never used with such an addition except in reference to a profound meaning, as in: “Living, he will live, and he will not die” (John 6); and concerning the friend of the bridegroom: “He who stands and hears the bridegroom’s voice rejoices with joy”; and other expressions of this kind.

Therefore I do not think that it should be said without some great discernment, although no one rightly claims to desire except from desire. Nevertheless, since no jot or tittle in the sacred Scriptures is believed to be superfluous, such an intensification rightly suggests something more than if he had simply said “I have desired.”

We must not believe that this was spoken only about that legal lamb, since he had already eaten it with them according to Jewish custom, but about the truth of so great a mystery.

For in that shadow of future things, and in that prophecy, there was the body and blood of Christ truly—indeed, in Christ himself there was the truth.

He was the lamb whom Abel first offered, whom Moses long ago commanded to be offered to God as a sacrifice morning and evening.

At the same supper there was both that figurative lamb and the truth (Genesis 4; Exodus 29; Numbers 28); it was necessary to pass from the shadow to the truth. [Col. 1364B]

Therefore he rejoices with joy, giving thanks to God the Father, because what he had long desired with longing was now being fulfilled.

He had assumed the human being into God when the Word became flesh, so that through him we might be in him. But he had not yet mingled himself with us through his flesh and blood, so that each of us might be members in him and we might be one body.

For although the flesh by itself profits nothing, it is the Holy Spirit who gives life to the body, so that Christ may be one in all of us.

In one and the same Spirit we are given life, and we remain in him through the human being he assumed, just as he himself remains in us through this mystery of his body and blood.

Therefore, since the fullness of our salvation consists in this sacrament, he fulfilled his longing with the desire of his desire, so that with his own, before he suffered, he might eat this true Passover: in this way, before giving himself as the price, we might be one body in him and he in us. [Col. 1364C]

Therefore on the cross we were crucified together with him, in baptism we were buried together, and in the resurrection we were raised together.

Hence the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Colossians 3).

Therefore, dearest one, have no doubt about this mystery, which Christ the Truth has generously bestowed on us. For although he sits at the right hand of the Father in heaven, he does not disdain to be sacrificed daily under the sacrament, by the hands of the priest, as a true victim—not in unbelief but in faith. [Col. 1364D]

Although he does not die, and death will no longer rule over him (Romans 6), he is nevertheless truly communicated in the sacrament, so that he may remain naturally in us, just as we remain in him.

Hence he says: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me” (John 6).

He lives because of the Father, since he was born as the only-begotten Son from the Father; and we live because of him, since we eat him.

Therefore, dearest one, every Christian must take the greatest care that no one departs from this life without viaticum—that is, without the body and blood of Christ—so that he may have Christ in himself both in faith and in the food of flesh and blood, because “blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Revelation 14).

We die in the Lord if, through this mystery, we remain in him and he in us.

Meanwhile, we must take care lest, through negligence and sluggishness of mind, these things—which, God forbid, were handed down for our restoration with such longing for eternal salvation—become for us a cause of ruin and an increase of condemnation. [Col. 1365A]

Finally, I ask you not to follow the absurdities concerning the tripartite body of Christ. Do not mix salt or honey into it, as some have wished; add nothing and subtract nothing. Believe and understand it to be wholly as Christ instituted it, so that through this he may remain incorporated in us, just as we remain in him through the man-God whom he assumed, to whom God the Father swore:

> “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 107; Hebrews 6, 7), [Col. 1366A]

and not according to the ravings of certain people.

For this reason the tradition of the apostles must be followed (2 Corinthians 11), lest each of us presume to prepare his own supper for eating.

Their faith and their institutions must therefore be preserved. For one faith is required of all who truly communicate; zeal and care are considered, and deeds are sought, so that, always hastening from here through charity and through the desire for eternal life, we may pass into eternal and everlasting life.

Farewell, dearest one, and love the one who loves you.

[Col. 1365]

# A SHORT WORK OF PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS, ABBOT OF CORBIE, ON THE BIRTH OF THE VIRGIN

*(In Acherius, volume I of the* Spicilegium*.)*

## NOTICE

I had long been uncertain whether the short work *On the Birth of the Virgin* belonged to Hildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, or to Paschasius Radbertus, abbot of Corbie, when I first published the first volume of the *Spicilegium*. But since our Jean Mabillon has demonstrated with the most certain arguments that it belongs to Paschasius Radbertus [Note: Col. 1365D; *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, saec. II, observations on the Life of Saint Hildefonsus.], it seemed appropriate to set down those very arguments here, by which the work in question—which I now publish in full—is asserted to be Radbertus’s. [Col. 1365B]

> “Francis Feuardent, a Parisian theologian, published several short works of Hildefonsus in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Among them was a book *On the Virginity of Saint Mary against Three Unbelievers*, whose prologue begins: ‘God, true light, who enlightens every human being,’ etc., and whose opening is: ‘O my lady and my mistress,’ etc. To this book he appended another work likewise attributed to Hildefonsus, *On the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary and on Her Giving Birth*, beginning as follows: ‘Although the virginity of the blessed and glorious mother of God Mary is the adornment of all the Churches,’ etc. [Col. 1365C]

> “We have discovered by the most certain arguments that the first book is Hildefonsus’s, while the later one belongs to Radbertus, abbot of Corbie. Hildefonsus published a book on virginity full of testimonies from the Old and New Testaments, says Zixilanes; this manner of writing is clearly evident in the first book, but not in the second.

> “Furthermore, according to Julian, Hildefonsus wrote a book *On Virginity* against three unbelievers, namely against Jovinian, Helvidius, and the Jews, as is clear from the letter of Quiricius prefixed to Hildefonsus’s works in a manuscript codex. Hildefonsus explicitly addresses and attacks these very same unbelievers by name in this first book.

> “In the later book, however, the subject is entirely different: testimonies of the Fathers are repeatedly introduced in confirmation, among whom are praised and cited Gregory the Great’s *Moralia*, Augustine, Jerome, Cyril of Alexandria, Peter of Ravenna, and others, whom Hildefonsus does not even greet in his work.

> “Finally, there is a great difference in style between the two works. Hildefonsus presses his opponents with accumulated synonyms; Radbertus proceeds in the later book with greater gravity of expression, a manner appropriate to an old man. He dedicates his work to the abbess and nuns of Saint Mary at Soissons, where he had been educated, as will become clear from the inscription of the work given below. He often calls them his most beloved mothers and matrons. [Col. 1365D]

> “It should therefore be judged that the author of the later book was not Hildefonsus but Radbertus. In his time a certain controversy arose among Catholics concerning the manner in which blessed Mary gave birth to Christ. Some maintained that he was born by the natural and common way and law of other human beings; others, among whom was Radbertus, objected.

> “This question arose in Germany, as Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie who opposed Radbertus’s position, teaches in a short work he composed on this subject and dedicated to someone unknown to him—not, therefore, to Radbertus, the abbot of his monastery.

> “Radbertus appears to be replying to Ratramnus, addressing his opponents as ‘brothers,’ in these words: ‘But because the shameless boldness of certain brothers is again troubling itself with inquiries, I have decided to write to you, matrons of Christ, about matters which they endeavor to investigate more curiously than reverently against her modesty.’ [Col. 1366B]

> “And so that you may understand the state of the controversy: ‘I do not say,’ he says, ‘that they claim she lost her virginity—she who, without knowing a man, conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin—but because, while confessing this, they deny the very thing they confess when they say that she gave birth to her son by the common law of nature.’

> “From this a great difference between the works of Hildefonsus and Radbertus becomes evident. Hildefonsus acts against three unbelievers; Radbertus against brothers.

> “Hildefonsus argues against Helvidius and the Jews, who deny the Virgin Mother’s virginity. Radbertus argues against Catholic theologians who admit the same virginity of the Mother of God but do not explain it correctly—those who say that Mary gave birth to Christ by opening the barriers of her virginity. Jovinian had certainly already held this position, and Hildefonsus attacks him.

> “Radbertus divided his work into two books, dedicated to the nuns of Soissons, with this inscription, as it is found in Corbie copies: ‘To the venerable matron of Christ, together with the sacred virgins Vesona [read: Suessona] living a monastic life, P. R.—that is, Paschasius Radbertus—the vilest of all monks,’ etc. [Col. 1366C]

> “If Feuardent had seen this inscription, he would undoubtedly have attributed this genuine and proper offspring to Radbertus.

> “After this the book begins: ‘Since the virginity of all the Churches,’ etc., and this is what appears in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* up to the middle of the little work. For from the place where this note is found—‘Here something is missing’—the handwritten codices differ entirely from the printed editions. They substitute a portion of a sermon attributed to Hildefonsus, which among the printed works is entitled *On the Purification of Saint Mary*; but Radbertus’s second book is the very homily that in the printed editions follows that sermon, beginning: ‘Among the statements of the Holy Scriptures,’ etc.” [Col. 1366D; Col. 1367A–1368A]

This is what Mabillon says. When Acherius copied him, however, he forgot that it was his duty to note here that Radbertus’s work had been transcribed from an old Corbie codex and collated with another from the same monastery.

We shall immediately subject to examination the opinion held by both men that these two books were sent to the virgins living at Soissons.

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 1367]

## PREFACE

[Col. 1367B]

To the venerable matron of Christ, together with the sacred virgins Vesona [Note: “To the virgins Vesona.” Acherius comments on this passage as follows: “That is, at Soissons”; and this was also the opinion of the most learned Mabillon, who wished to read *Suessona*. We think the matter should be left open: since Vesona, or Vesonna, or Vesuna, was a city in Gaul, specifically in the province of Périgord, as all the children of geographers know, and since nothing seems to prevent Paschasius from having written to certain virgins living in that city, we think its name may be retained [Col. 1368D].] living a monastic life, PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS, the vilest of all monks.

I have resolved to answer for you, dearest ones, the question recently brought to me concerning the birth of the blessed Virgin Mary, since I do not doubt that you love it greatly. So that from this you may know how greatly [the sentence is syntactically incomplete in the supplied text], your foster child from boyhood long ago, now worn out by much old age.

Although the virginity of the blessed and glorious Mother of God, Mary, is the adornment, honor, and model of virtue of all the Churches, it is especially so for consecrated virgins, whose chastity is more particularly illumined by her virtues, shaped by her example, strengthened, and [Col. 1367C] confirmed by her merits. Therefore, to venerate and recount with the utmost devotion in mind and heart her most sacred childbirth is a grace of divine favor. But to fight against and overcome heretical perversity requires the work of the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High, who overshadowed her, so that without intercourse with a man and without any corruption she might bear the Lord, both God and man, and remain forever a virgin.

For this reason we read that blessed Jerome once wrote against the heretic Helvidius and his associates; he so thoroughly defeated and overcame them that from then until the present no recurrent error [Note: [Col. 1368D] “No recurrent error.” In another manuscript: “nothing remaining,” which is not at all unsuitable. Below we have chosen to enclose certain expressions as though in parentheses; we have done the same in two other places, because, since they disturbed the sense, they seemed to have been added by the copyist and to belong to that class of marks whose use few now understand. So that these parentheses might not mislead anyone, we have also added asterisks.] has arisen against her.

1. But because the shameless presumption of certain brothers is again troubling itself with idle questioning, I have decided to write to you, ladies consecrated to Christ, about matters which they themselves are trying to investigate with excessive curiosity rather than religious reverence concerning her chastity. In investigating her virginal childbirth and the womb of her purity, they introduce—as though they were highly skilled physiologists—the contamination of vices through a sufficiently crafty argument, in which very many perilous errors converge.

2. For they say that the blessed Virgin Mary could not, and ought not, have given birth in any other way than according to the common law of nature, and as all women customarily do, so that Christ’s birth may be called a true birth. Otherwise, they say, if he was not born as other infants are born, his birth is not a true one. Therefore, lest he be thought a phantom, or lest he be believed to have passed through the Virgin’s womb as water passes through a channel, being born without the normal process of birth, it is pious to believe that he was born according to nature’s law in the same way as other infants are born, and that she gave birth in the same way as other women do.

O blind piety, which thinks so impiously about the Virgin Mary, and blind presumption, which speaks so impiously about Christ! I do not mean that they say she lost her virginity—she who, without knowing a man, conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin—but that they deny the very thing they confess when they say that she brought forth her son in childbirth according to the common law of nature.

If what they assert and affirm were so—which God forbid—Mary would no longer be a virgin; Christ would have been born under the curse, a son of wrath from sinful flesh; and she who is proclaimed blessed by the angel, still remaining under the curse, would have given birth under the curse. Otherwise, why do they demand the law of nature in Mary, when the Holy Spirit possessed everything that was in her—she whom the power of the Most High overshadowed?

If the power of the Most High sheltered her from every heat of sin, then in conception and childbirth, just as she was free from every heat of lust, so also she was free from every pressure of the curse—not from herself, but by the power of the Most High, exempt and separated from it. Therefore, let them consider the laws of divine matters: divine laws do not depend upon the nature of things; rather, the laws of the natures of things are shown to flow from divine laws.

It is therefore rash to assert of Christ that he was born according to the common law of nature, since he was conceived in the Virgin’s flesh not according to the ordinary course of nature. Indeed, the very law of nature under which women now conceive and give birth is, so to speak, not truly the law of nature at all, but of the curse and of guilt. For unless Adam and Eve had first sinned in paradise, no one thereafter would be born under the guilt of sin. Therefore this common law of birth belongs not to nature but to corruption and defect.

But Mary, because she was blessed and did not possess the guilt of corruption, did not give birth to Christ in pain or under corruption. If Christ was born from corruption or with pain, then he was born under the curse. Concerning this curse, Genesis testifies that the Lord said to Eve: “I will multiply your pains and your conceptions” (Gen. III, 16). Symmachus rendered this, “your afflictions.” Origen, Theodotion, and the Septuagint rendered it “your sorrows” [Col. 1369B] and “groanings.” Theodotion and Symmachus likewise used “hardships” for “groanings.” In all these expressions, not the law of nature is indicated, as these physiologists quite incompetently wish, but the law of retribution is multiplied and the cause of sin increased: labors in childbirth, afflictions, sorrows, hardships, and groanings. In Hebrew it reads: [the Hebrew text is absent from the supplied source].

Therefore, all women who give birth do so not according to the nature of their first origin, but through the defect of guilt and through the curse of God’s just retribution. But the blessed and most glorious Virgin Mary—not merely did she give birth without the common law of nature, but she did not produce her son according to the nature of the first origin, nor from a man’s seed; rather, divinely produced by the Holy Spirit from her own flesh, she brought forth God and man without any contamination of vices.

[Col. 1369C] Her childbirth must therefore not be treated as the births of other people are, since, as the outstanding teacher Athanasius says among other things in his little work On His Faith (book IX), which he composed almost in the form of a dialogue: “The Incarnate and Only-Begotten One, in his own secret mystery, which he himself knows.” He continues: “It is ours to believe, and his to know.”

Let them therefore hear that it belongs to him alone to know how he was conceived, how he dwelt in the womb, and how the Word, God and man, was born from a virgin as one Christ. For, as he himself says, “God the Word, receiving all that belongs to man, is man; and man, receiving all that belongs to God, is certainly God.”

If this is so, as he confessed—or rather, because it is so—where, I ask, is the common law in his birth? Where is the contamination of vices? For Christ is God, who never failed to be God. From the moment he became man and was assumed in the unity of the person, he has always remained and remains true God and man—not two, as though one were God and the other man, but one and the same God and man.

Although he is one thing insofar as he is God and another insofar as he is man, in both he is one God and man, because there was never a time when a mere man was conceived or born without God. But because he was conceived by the Holy Spirit from virginal flesh and truly born as man, immediately from that ineffable conception the true God proceeded and was born as man.

How, then, can what is ineffable be called common? Or how is Christ not always wholly true God, since he was neither conceived nor born without the true God? Therefore, just as he is rightly believed to have been conceived with the womb closed, so also he was entirely born with the womb closed.

Nor did human incapacity prevent him from being born of a virgin, just as nothing ever prevented him from being God and one Christ. He willed to be born in the unity of true God and man so that everything about his birth might be wholly true, that his mode of birth might be ineffable, and that everything might be worthy of belief: that he was born from a virgin without the contamination of sin, just as he was conceived without any contagion of the first origin.

Let the rash investigators of so great a mystery therefore listen and understand that these are not human laws governing birth—not the law, I do not say, of condemned nature, but not even the law of the first origin before sin—according to which the one Christ, God and man, was born from a virgin.

For, as blessed Cyril says in his Letter to Nestorius, he was not born as an ordinary man from the holy Virgin. Rather, in the very womb of the Virgin, as he himself confesses, the Word united himself with flesh in the virginal womb and endured a carnal generation, because he made the birth of his flesh his own birth. He who, in the form of God, made man became man in the form of a servant: both God by the power of the one who receives, and both man by the humility of the one received.

Accordingly, such a birth does not follow the common law of nature. Just as he was wondrously conceived, so he was wondrously born as God and man. Adoption did not make him, as it made other adopted sons of God, into a son; rather, the nature of divinity exalted him as God’s own Son and gave him the name that is above every name (Phil. II), so that the whole Son of God might be man and Word. For he was never not the Son of God, remaining eternally the Only-Begotten of the one Father.

He was therefore never conceived as a mere man, nor born as other infants are born, so that by the grace of adoption or by the reward of virtues he might receive the prerogative of sonship. Rather, because the Word of God became flesh, he assumed man into himself without a human person, so that the whole Christ might be proper to himself—not reborn by a gift of grace as others are, but with the distinctiveness of both natures preserved.

He did not assume the person of a man, but only man, because he himself was always the third person with the Father and the Spirit, one God in the Trinity. Therefore, rightly possessing a person in eternity, he did not assume a person, but in time assumed the man whom he had not previously possessed, so that the one who assumed and that which was assumed might, as blessed Augustine says in his book On Predestination, be one person in the Trinity.

As he says elsewhere: “Born from the Father, God the Word; born from his mother, the Word made flesh; one and the same God, the Son of God, born before the ages and born in the age. Both births belong to the one Son of God.” Accordingly, the Virgin Mary is rightly called Mother of God, because she bore God and man.

The Word became flesh—not as other infants are born, nor as human beings become sons by a gift of grace—but, as blessed Gregory says in the Moralia, “with the distinctiveness of both natures preserved, he essentially assumed man into his own person.” Through this wondrous mystery, the eternal Son from the Father and the temporal Son from his mother would be one and the same true Son of God and man. For, as he says in the same work, “It is one thing for human beings, once born, to receive the grace of adoption through him; it is another for one uniquely to proceed as God himself, through the power of divinity, from the very conception.”

Therefore, I ask, let these men stop saying that he was born as other infants are born. The Virgin Mother of God did not bear him from the origin of the first transgression so that he might be reborn; she bore him from the Holy Spirit so that he might be believed to be God: without pain or groaning, without distress or hardship, without sorrow or affliction. All these things are the just retributions and punishments of condemned flesh in its first origin.

The blessed Mary, although she herself was born and begotten from sinful flesh, and although she was sinful flesh, was no longer so when, through the prevenient grace of the Holy Spirit, she was called by the angel blessed above all women. “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I, 35).

[Note: [Col. 1371D] “Unless because.” Of the two readings, we have preferred the one which Acherius relegated to the margin, although he chose to print “not because.” Here the reader must be warned that Mary the Virgin is written of differently when Christ’s conception is discussed and when the condition of her own birth is described. For after Paschasius had written that Mary was born from sinful flesh and was herself sinful flesh until the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit cleansed her, it is immediately added that, when she was born, she not only lay under no sins [Col. 1372D], but did not even contract original sin in her mother’s womb; and then that the Holy Spirit, when he came upon her, purified her from defilements and refined her. No writer, I think, ever contradicted himself more. Yet I ask the reader to judge from the rest of the work whether such shameful inconsistency can be ascribed to Radbert.] Otherwise, if she was not sanctified and cleansed by that same Holy Spirit, how was her flesh not sinful flesh? And if her flesh came from the mass of the first transgression, how was Christ, the Word made flesh, without sin, when he assumed flesh from sinful flesh, unless the Word made flesh first overshadowed her, upon whom the Holy Spirit came and whom the power of the Most High wholly possessed?

Therefore, her flesh truly was no longer sinful flesh. In her God poured himself out wholly, and the Word made flesh came to us without sin. Thus he rightly not only did not observe the law of corrupted nature in his birth, but did not observe even the law of the first origin that women would have possessed had Eve, the mother of all, kept the commandment in paradise.

Otherwise, how was she not without original sin when the Holy Spirit filled her? Her birth is gloriously proclaimed throughout the catholic Church by all as blessed and happy. Indeed, if it were not blessed and glorious, her feast would certainly not be celebrated everywhere by everyone.

But because she is so solemnly honored, the authority of the Church establishes that when she was born she was subject to no sins, nor did she contract original sin in the womb, having been sanctified there. Thus, although a curse is pronounced upon the days of Jeremiah and Job—that is, upon the days of their birth—the day on which Mary’s blessed birth began is pronounced blessed and is devoutly celebrated.

If she had been in sin, she would rightly have been called accursed, and, when it was announced to her father that she had been born into the world, she would have been mournful rather than blessed. But now, because the blessed Virgin Mary illumines the whole Church with her blessing, is she not rightly honored as one sanctified in the Holy Spirit?

No one’s birth is celebrated in the world except Christ’s, that of his mother, and that of blessed John. Thus, unless the blessed Virgin Mary had been sanctified in her mother’s womb, her birth ought not to be celebrated at all. But now, because she is venerated on the authority of the whole Church, it is clear that she was free from all original sin. Through her not only was the curse of Eve, the mother, dissolved, but blessing was also granted to all.

If, therefore, the splendid and most sacred birth of the Virgin is rightly celebrated and venerated everywhere as so holy and glorious, how much more should she be honored when she was most dutifully greeted by the angel as already full of grace?

When he said to her, “Hail” (Luke I, 28), he offered a heavenly service of veneration. When he said, “Full of grace,” he showed that wrath had been wholly expelled and declared that grace had been restored. When he said, “Blessed are you,” he displayed the fruit of blessing, because when the Holy Spirit came upon her, he cleansed the Virgin wholly from defilement and refined her, so that she might be holier than the stars of heaven.

Moreover, when the power of the Most High wholly overshadowed her, immediately the Word, who was eternal in the beginning with the Father, came into her womb so that he might become flesh in time and dwell among us. [Note: [Col. 1372D] “Immediately her.” We have emended it thus where it was corruptly read “her act,” and then supplied the necessary little word “that.”]

Let the new disputers and investigators of this new and unheard-of birth listen, then, and understand first that they are men: how can they competently dispute about the nature and sex of women? Let them next reflect that, when they seek nature and the common law of birth, everything here is divine and ineffable, and divine power is at work: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53, 8.)

Here “who” means “no one,” because there is no saint who can fully explain—not to mention the divine generation, but even the human generation of Christ—although all ought to believe both. From this it follows that their hesitation is superstitious and their argument unnecessary, since they say that he opened the entrances of the womb and vulva, and drew after him, as all others do, the contamination of blood and the filth of women in childbirth. In all these things groaning and pain are multiplied, and sorrow and hardship increased, so that no one gives birth to a son without them.

But far be it from the hearts of the faithful to suspect anything of this kind concerning the Virgin Mary, who brought blessing to the world in place of the curse of the first origin. Thus she herself, as I have said, is proclaimed blessed among women by the angel and is most dutifully greeted as the glorious mother of the Lord above all others. She is also declared blessed by Elizabeth in the spirit of prophecy, and the fruit of her womb is believed and venerated as blessed.

Therefore, in her and through her such great blessing blossomed and grace flowed forth; it cannot be believed that her childbirth was subject to pains and groanings according to the custom of women. Because the blessed Mother of God was not subject to sorrow or hardship, she was free from every stain of the curse. The Holy Spirit filled her and dedicated her wholly to the Lord; the power of the Most High overshadowed her; and from the sanctified flesh of the Virgin the Word assumed flesh and united it to himself in the unity of the person.

This is what is meant by “the Word became flesh”: not a mixture of natures, but a unity of person. Therefore, concerning this birth also, as I have said, we rightly believe it was said: “Who shall declare his generation?” For this wondrous birth of flesh is likewise ineffable—not, as these blind men imagine, common and governed by the law of nature, but a mystery of grace.

That God the man is born from a Virgin is not custom but mystery; it is not nature but power and condescension; it is not the ordinary order of birth but authority. Human wisdom therefore has nothing to investigate in this birth except that the Word became flesh and was born as he wished, or when and how he wished.

Otherwise, who could grasp what is unheard-of and ineffable? What right has fleshly understanding to investigate where everything that is related is both divine and incomprehensible? For the Evangelist says: “The generation of Christ was thus” (Matt. I, 18). This carnal generation was “thus”; he did not say, “Thus it was made,” but “Thus it was,” because Christ’s generation was ineffable with the Father when, through the aforesaid and ineffable generation, he was born from his mother.

Therefore, what “was” was always so. And what was always so from eternity could come to be in time; whatever came to be in him is not astonishing.

Hence those who say that he was born according to the common law of nature are exceedingly foolish, since it is clear that he was not conceived according to that law. The law of birth that is now called the law of nature arose from the defect of the first condemnation. Therefore the Apostle says: “We were all once children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. II, 3).

But far be it from the hearts of the faithful to believe that Christ was born as a son of wrath, as others are born in the defect of corruption, from which pain and groaning are multiplied. In the flesh, neither groaning nor pain exists without corruption of the entrails, nor corruption without pain and groaning. In women’s childbirth, groaning and corruption come only from sin and the curse of the first origin.

Let us therefore question these followers of the heretic Helvidius. Although they do not deny that she remained a virgin, they nevertheless stain her chastity and the grace of which she is proclaimed full when they say that she gave birth according to the common law of corrupted nature.

If she gave birth in that way, then—even as though—she still remained subject to the curse in the mass of the first condemnation, contrary to the angel’s proclamation, and the Word of the Father assumed man from sinful flesh so that it might become flesh—which God forbid.

But because it is contrary to the catholic faith to think in this way, the blessed Virgin, full of grace, neither felt pain nor suffered corruption of the entrails. Insofar as she was free from guilt through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit in her and through the power of the Most High by which she was overshadowed, she was likewise free from the curse of the first condemnation and from the groaning and pains that afflict all the daughters of Eve when they give birth.

Therefore the Prophet, speaking in the person of Christ to the Father, says: “You are he who drew me from the womb; my hope from my mother’s breasts” (Ps. XXI, 10). When he says, “You are he who drew me,” he declares the uniqueness of his birth: he came forth gently from the womb.

Every person who comes from the womb of his mother into the light of the world comes forth only by the will and activity of God. But Christ, begotten from the Virgin in a special and ineffable manner, entered the world without distress to his mother.

It is therefore pious to believe that God and man was born into the world not as others are, but in a new and wondrous manner. Hence Jeremiah testifies: “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI, 22).

If it was truly new and wondrous that a virgin conceived without seed and without a man’s corruption, then there could be no antiquated condition in his birth. We must therefore likewise believe that he was born into the world in a similar new and wondrous manner, without pain, without groaning, and without any corruption of the flesh.

Hence, as though in thanksgiving, he says in a special way in the psalm that is wholly about him, to the Father: “You are he who drew me from the womb.” It is as though he plainly said: “You drew me out, because I did not leave the womb in the manner in which others are born, with immense distress to their mothers, but by a new departure, without violation of modesty. You indeed drew me from my mother’s womb, and I did not corrupt the entrails of her integrity.”

And lest we think he was a phantom, as many heretics have said, he added: “My hope from my mother’s breasts.” Thus, where mother and breasts are mentioned, the reality of flesh, not a phantom, is proclaimed. Although he was born from a closed womb, which he himself made passable while preserving the seal of modesty, just as he was conceived, he was nevertheless produced from the Virgin’s flesh and is therefore rightly said to have been suckled at her breasts.

Everything was thus accomplished so that a new thing might come to be upon the earth when the Word became flesh and was called Emmanuel, which means “God with us” (Matt. I, 23).

This, then, is that enclosed garden in the Song of Songs, the sealed fountain (Cant. IV): an enclosed garden, because when God entered, he found her incorrupt; but a sealed fountain, because when God and man was born from her, she nevertheless did not violate the fountain of modesty or the integrity of her blood.

For the blood and fountain of modesty that was not corrupted in the conception of the child through intercourse with a man—I do not believe—ought to have been corrupted at his birth, with the torture of the mother and contamination of her honor. Hence the Church, on the authority of the holy Fathers, sings concerning his birth: “And she has the mother’s joy,” it says, “together with the virginity of modesty.” Others, outstanding men, emended this to “together with the virginity of honor.”

The honor of virginity is supremely great if a virgin gives birth to God and man, and yet, through the man born from her, suffers none of the *kakia* [κακίαι] that would violate the seal of modesty. *Kakia* is the Greek term for afflictions, by which body and soul are grievously tormented.

But blessed Mary suffered none of these things. She had joy in the fruit and honor in the childbirth. Hence it is also said that the Virgin conceived, gave birth, and remained a virgin. She is therefore said to have conceived and given birth under equal conditions, and to have remained so under equal conditions.

For women in childbirth do not ordinarily have intercourse with men at the time of delivery, so that one might deny that a virgin lost her virginity when there is neither desire nor possibility of intercourse. Rather, the integrity, honor, and incorruption of the virgin’s flesh are being commended.

Otherwise, since we men do not know the nature of that sex, let us ask virgins, and likewise ask married women. Let us ask virgins so that we may know what integrity of flesh [Col. 1375B] and blood is; but let us ask married women whether there is any corruption or pain in childbirth unless the contamination of blood and the reception of seed have occurred.

We do not willingly arouse shame in you, dearest ones, since we speak of these matters only with great modesty. But it is a mark of the highest piety and an ornament of virtue for you to proclaim the chastity of the most blessed Virgin pure and undefiled, and to confess that she was free from every contagion of the first origin.

If we question virgins about her, they know the grace of incorruption but do not know the fecundity of offspring. If we inquire of women dedicated to marriage, they know the pressures and groanings of Eve’s curse, and amid hardships and sorrows they know the fecundity of seed; but they do not know the integrity of virginity, either in conception or in childbirth.

The blessed Mother of the Lord, however, remained a virgin in both respects: a mother in conception and a virgin in childbirth. In none of these matters was she defiled according to the example of other women. She neither admitted Adam to herself, nor received a son from Eve’s contamination, nor, under the curse, gave birth to the Lord amid pain and distress.

It is therefore clear that, just as she conceived with her womb closed, so she also gave birth with her womb closed—not according to the common law of corrupted nature condemned by curses, but through the grace of the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High by which she is said to have been overshadowed.
