But these men, with all the effort they can muster, try to support the claim that the Virgin gave birth in a state of defect and to heap insults upon her chastity. They therefore cite the Gospel: “When the days of her purification were fulfilled,” they brought Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Luke II, 22–23).

“There,” they say, “when the Evangelist says that the days of her purification were completed, he shows that she was subject to the law of nature and was defiled with uncleanness, and likewise that Jesus opened his mother’s womb.”

These rash advocates, who think in this way, are utterly foolish and destroy everything that belongs to sound doctrine, everything that the rudiments of faith concerning Christ commended to the Churches, and everything that the grace of the Holy Spirit proclaimed in the mystery.

The days of her purification are not said to have been completed as though the blessed Virgin had needed purification from any sin, since she bore the Lord Jesus Christ, begotten by the Holy Spirit. Rather, because she herself was under the king, and the Lord Jesus Christ, having been made under the law and made from a woman, was under the law, the precepts and institutions of the ancient law were rightly observed in him for a time, until, when the law ceased, grace succeeded it.

This is the completion of the days according to the custom of the law, not according to any need for purification. For her blessed and undefiled virginity remained immaculate and incorrupt, stained by no defilements and afflicted by none of Eve’s torments.

It cannot be, in accordance with the angel’s proclamation, who brings joy to all, that Christ himself brought his mother torment at his birth. Amid the watchfulness and praises of the angels, I do not believe that he imposed upon his mother Eve’s groanings, pains, and sorrows.

That purification of women was therefore one thing: in it, the sins of souls no less than the defects of bodies were cleansed. The purification of Mary was another: in it the custom of the law was observed for no other reason than the sake of the mystery, because she had no need of any purification, since she gave birth from herself to God, incarnate, the purifier of all.

The completion of the days of her purification had no other cause than the fulfillment and custom of the law. The purification and separation of other women, however, occur for many reasons; in them both the defects of souls and the defects of bodies are cleansed.

Thus seven days are assigned as unclean, during which a woman is commanded to sit in her unclean blood, extremely unclean according to the days of her separation, and thirty-three days during which she is to sit in pure blood. Yet throughout all these days the woman was unclean and filthy in many respects, until the condition of her entire body was restored, her body was healed, and the blood ceased its corrupted heat. Once the defilements had been cleansed, the woman was purified by divine sacrifices and offerings.

But the blessed Mary did not need such sacrifices, since she gave birth from herself to the holy victim through whom the world was purified. When the Evangelist says, “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord,” he does not say this to compel us to believe that Christ opened his mother’s womb, as others do. Rather, he teaches that for this reason they presented him to the Lord, to perform what the law customarily required on his behalf: “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord,” in the mystery of the law and the sacrament of sacred transgression.

The Evangelist did not introduce this testimony from the law to show that Christ opened the Virgin’s womb as other firstborn children do, but to demonstrate that he was made under the law and proceeded from the Virgin’s womb—not merely one who would be called holy, but one who was essentially holy, for whom every closed thing is rightly open.

Blessed Ambrose, explaining this testimony in his Gospel commentary, says (book II, chapter 2 on Luke): [Note: [Col. 1375D] “For it was not.” What follows exists word for word in Hildefonsus, sermon 1, On the Purification.]

> “For it was not intercourse with a man that opened the secret places of the Virgin’s womb, but the Holy Spirit infused immaculate seed into an inviolate womb.”

The aforesaid teacher does not say that this seed was infused in such a way that it came from somewhere other than the Virgin’s flesh and blood, nor that the Holy Spirit should be thought to be the seed-producing substance of the flesh, as Irenaeus maintains. Rather, through the word “seed” the activity of the Holy Spirit is indicated.

He then added:

> “For he alone among those born of woman is holy in every respect, the Lord Jesus, who did not experience the contagions of earthly corruption because of the newness of his immaculate birth, and who cast them away by his heavenly majesty.”

A little later he says:

> “He alone, therefore, opened the womb for himself; and this is not surprising. For he who had said to the prophet, ‘Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and in your mother’s womb I sanctified you’ (Jer. I, 5)—he who sanctified another’s womb so that a prophet might be born is the one who opened his mother’s womb so that he might come forth immaculate.”

In these words, he does not seem to me to contradict himself or the other holy teachers when he says that he alone opened the womb for himself. He wondrously opened it for himself by his own power, so that it became a passable way, while the virginal womb remained closed, just as the doors were closed and yet he entered through them to the disciples; and just as the tomb was sealed and closed, yet when he rose he came out through it.

For this reason he also says elsewhere:

> “Christ’s gate becomes passable,  
> filled, full of grace;  
> the King passes through, yet it remains  
> closed . . . . .”

This he does not say so that you should understand him to contradict himself, but rather so that you may fully recognize that he was born from the womb and through the womb of the Virgin, which he himself made passable; and thus he himself opened the womb for himself. For himself, indeed: although the Virgin’s womb, while remaining closed, was open and penetrable to him, nevertheless, when he came forth and entered the world, he left it closed and sealed with the seal of modesty. For certainly nothing is difficult for God, since, as someone has said, all nature is subject to his commands in its accustomed order. Therefore it is clear beyond doubt that he was born in such a way that the mother’s secret genital place remained closed, yet by his own power he himself made it open to him.

Moreover, he alone opened the womb of the holy Church, which he dedicated to himself as a bride for the generation of peoples. Of this womb, surely, the prophet David sings, saying: “Sinners are estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the womb; they have spoken falsehood” (Psalm 57:4). He is declaring the person of the heretics, who are estranged from the womb of the Church’s integrity. The Apostle, for his part, strives to preserve that womb immaculate and to guard it as a virgin when he says: “For I have betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). He opened its secret genital place when he granted the grace of rebirth through water and the Holy Spirit.

To her the prophet says: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isaiah 54:1). Hence Hannah also says in her Song: “The barren woman has borne many, and she who had many children has grown weak” (1 Samuel 2:5). He, therefore, is the only one holy in essence—not one through whom the mother would be corrupted, but one through whom the womb of the Church would be opened—the firstborn among many brothers.

The divine ordinances prescribed through the utterances of the Law signified him in their firstborn, as a figure of the mystery to come. [Col. 1377D]  
[Note: “Through the utterances of the Law.” Perhaps *priora* (“the earlier things”), or *pia* (“pious things”), as is read in Ratramnus, chapter 6, not much after the particle of negation, where we have added “when they were not holy.”]

Not that they were truly holy, but because, by the mystery of the Law, they were called holy. Otherwise, if we follow the letter, how was every male who opened the womb holy, when it is well known that many were utterly wicked? Was Ahab holy, or Joram, or the others? Were the false prophets whom the avenging heavenly fire consumed at Elijah’s prayer holy? Certainly not. Rather, in the sacramental prefiguration of what was to come, they were called holy although they were not, until Christ came, holy in essence. He both opened the womb of his bride and poured into it the fruitfulness of bearing children.

For he was judged worthy of the Lord’s regard; no one can doubt that, according to the sequence of the Law, all the others were types of what was to come. And therefore they present him to the Lord, because he is the purification, through the resurrection of the eighth day, in Jerusalem, so that in him every adoption of the children of God might be pardoned and offered. For when the Law says, “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord,” it was promising the truly holy birth of the Virgin: the immaculate one who would open the womb of the Church, so that in him all the rest might be sanctified and become firstborn.

Hence the angel expressly said to Mary: “And what will be born from you will be called holy, the Son of God” (Luke 2:53). Not because, in being born, he corrupted his mother, whom he left an intact and inviolate virgin, but because God born from her as man opened the womb of the Church and made for himself a passable way in his flesh, while preserving the Virgin’s chamber closed, so that he might show that he had taken a virgin from the Virgin Mother as his bride. By such a great covenant of birth he showed that she would remain a virgin and immaculate.

It is therefore clear that he was offered according to the Law, just as he was circumcised. Otherwise, he had no need of circumcision, since he contracted no original sin from which Christ himself would have needed to be cleansed from his people by circumcision. Yet he was circumcised because he willingly placed himself under the Law, in order to redeem those who were under the Law; and he was likewise offered so that, in himself, he might offer to God the Father the sacrifice of us who were guilty.

Moreover, if—God forbid—he himself had been unclean so as to defile his mother, how would he have cleansed us in his offering and made us a sacrifice to God as a fragrance of sweetness? Therefore, although he took upon himself and bore our pains and carried our infirmities, far be it from us to believe that he afflicted his mother’s modesty with any injuries or vexations. Far be it from us to believe this of the woman through whom every curse of Eve was loosed, as though she herself had been subjected in childbirth to the curses of the first condemnation.

Far be it from us to believe it where virtue was born, that such a flood of vices existed; where the joy of all was proclaimed, that such sadness and groaning intervened; amid the movements of angels, that she sat for seven days in uncleanness amid unclean blood. If this had been so, the shepherds would not, so to speak, have been permitted to enter in the morning according to the Law. But now, because the angel devotedly invites them for the sake of proclaiming the Gospel, they come and see; they find and understand from the Word what had been foretold to them.

Therefore it must in no way be believed that they found Mary alone, overwhelmed by such filth, by many miseries, as women in childbirth commonly are, distraught and wrapped up. At her childbirth the multitude of angels sings: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). Therefore, where and through whom such great peace is proclaimed, I do not believe that those disgraces or the pains of the flesh befell the immaculate mother.

The Magi likewise then reverently enter the house and find what the shepherds found: Mary, Joseph, and the child. They find her not tormented by pains, but attending to the child. Then they fall down and adore him, offering gifts, the one whom they find with his mother. They adore, I say, her firstborn.

“Firstborn,” however, not one whom brothers would follow, but one whom no one precedes. Although some have preferred that he should be called “only-begotten” rather than “firstborn,” nevertheless, because it is the idiom of Scripture to call whatever first opens the womb “firstborn,” and to regard it as sanctified to the Lord, the Evangelist preferred to call him “firstborn,” according to the same custom, rather than “only-begotten.” This was not because he opened the womb according to the law of nature, as is customary with other women, as these people say, but because, born from her, he was both firstborn and only-begotten, made under the divine Law and under the Law, so that through him the whole Law might be fulfilled in spirit and in letter.

For he is also called the firstborn from the resurrection, from among many brothers. Since a genus is gathered in a species, although he could be called “only-begotten” by nature, he ought rather to be called “firstborn,” so that it might be an indication that already in him and through him many other brothers were being gathered as children of the Church by grace—of the Church whose womb he opened.

In the Old Testament, firstborn sons were very often given to those who had been chosen beforehand by God’s grace; their dignity was not preferred on the basis of nature, but their merit on the basis of grace. Therefore we too say that he is more significantly called “firstborn” than “only-begotten,” so that through him all who are gathered by grace, united with him alone, may be regarded in the heavenly places.

All those firstborn consecrated to the Lord under the Law bore this figure. And therefore it was right that, from among all those firstborn who opened the womb to the Lord, the Lord should be offered according to the Law, since all of them foreshadowed him, so that he might be the firstborn in all things, holding the primacy. Not one who would afflict his mother’s womb, but one who would open the womb of the Church.

I have said this so that the prudent reader may understand that it is not brothers following him who make someone firstborn. Christ is called firstborn because all who are only-begotten, just as he himself was the only-begotten of his mother, can be called firstborn; yet not all firstborn can rightly be called only-begotten. From this it follows that he ought to be called firstborn because no one precedes him and no one follows him—not merely because brothers follow him.

Christ is therefore rightly called firstborn from the Virgin, not because he afflicted the Virgin’s womb and opened the chamber of her modesty, but because he who was from the beginning the firstborn of the whole creation was born from her, both only-begotten and firstborn, in the manner he willed, without the mother’s groaning and without pain.

He is also rightly called firstborn in baptism, and he is said to have risen as the firstborn in the resurrection. In both natures and in both births, although he is called firstborn, he is rightly believed to be only-begotten, because he is both the Son of man and the Son of God—not one and another, but one, and one in both.

By these rules of Catholic truth, the meaning is clear on every side: no one but a heretic says that Christ was born only according to the common law of nature, and no otherwise than infants are otherwise born. Although the aforesaid doctor Jerome, in the work he composed against Helvidius on this subject, may appear to have yielded to him—particularly where he speaks of the womb’s lodging for nine months and of the lowliness of birth, which that heretic had mockingly proposed, as though it were unworthy of the divine majesty to humble itself to such condescension as to dwell among the organs in the Virgin’s womb or to be born, so filthy, between female thighs—the heretic thus opposed everything in a contrary sense, as a heretic, in order to destroy the truth of the Catholic faith.

That distinguished defender of truth did not yield, as these people maintain. Rather, by commending more fully the dignity of God’s most glorious humility, he said that the more lowly and dishonorable the divine majesty accepted or endured for our sake, the more dearly it redeemed us and the more earnestly it ought to be honored.

In this sense, although not, as I recall, in the same words, he appears to have answered the heretic in such a way that he brought upon the blessed Virgin no disgrace of any pollution or punishment of sin, but reverently commended the divine condescension and immeasurable self-emptying in the form of a servant. He did not do this to show the Virgin afflicted and dishonored by the Lord, but to demonstrate the mercy of the loving Creator even to heretics of this kind.

Therefore he did not yield to those who, with Helvidius, were in error; rather, he rebuked them, so that they might learn not to defame the Virgin and not to diminish God’s humility in the form of a servant. He does not teach that her chastity was injured in any respect; on the contrary, he triumphs so greatly in her praise. Nor did he yield even for an hour to her adversaries, since he fought so long and so earnestly on her behalf with the sword of the word. God granted him such grace for resisting her enemies and such power for defeating them that no one dares rise up against him.

I pray, most sacred virgins of Christ, through the intervention of your merits, that he who granted that man such skill in speaking and such strength for defeating adversaries may also deign to grant me the grace of speech, and may open in the Spirit of truth what is worthy of this mystery. Thus, through you and for your sake, O matrons of Christ, may I be found worthy—although I rely on none of my own merits—to defend fittingly the chastity of the mother of my Lord and to disclose the truth to those who do not believe rightly, so that they may come to their senses and cease henceforth to speak falsehood.

They say that Christ cannot be said to have been born otherwise than by the equal lot of nature, like everyone else—as though birth were always spoken of in the divine Scriptures as occurring under equal conditions. Yet this birth of all those who are born under the lot of the curse is very different from the birth that would have occurred if Eve had not sinned. The former is under a curse and in misery; the latter would have borne fruit wholly in the flower of blessing, without groaning and pain.

Therefore, I ask, let them at least grant Christ from the Virgin Mary that birth by which all would have been born according to the common law if Eve had not sinned—a birth now known only to God and perhaps unknown to human beings—and let them not attribute to him that he brought curses, groans, and miseries to his mother instead of joy.

The Virgin was all the more free from the corruption of suffering, from the pain of the flesh, and from the filth of disgrace, the more she was full of grace and incorrupt, the more she was consecrated by the Holy Spirit and overshadowed by divine power. For the Holy Spirit has within himself his own hidden places, according to which birth is spoken of in the sacred Scriptures and concealed by everlasting laws.

One birth is that of flesh from flesh; another is that of God from God; and another is that of countless other things. Yet the manner of birth is not the same for all of them, nor is their order of existence the same, although birth is equally spoken of in each case where it is rightly attributed to them that they are born from another. Thus Christ is rightly believed to have been born from the Virgin Mary in whatever manner, because he assumed flesh from her.

But how that birth itself came forth to us—whether under the condition in which Eve would have given birth had she not sinned, or gloriously, because she gave birth to God and man while remaining a virgin, something that Eve would not have been, nor the other women while giving birth—it is pointless to investigate. In this matter none of the saints wished to doubt. Rather, all proclaim as certain by Catholic faith that she conceived without sin, gave birth without sin, pain, or corruption, and that Christ drew no sin from her.

If he drew no sin from her, neither did he commit it, because he did not afflict his mother’s modesty with any torments in being born, nor in any respect stain her virginity.

We do not therefore say, as they claim, that he was born monstrously, but that, as was prefigured long ago in the prophets and handed down to us by the holy Fathers, she is the gate shown to Ezekiel, concerning which he says: “I saw a gate in the house of the Lord, and it was closed; and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of hosts entered through it” (Ezekiel 44:2).

Of this gate blessed Ambrose, in the same hymn of which I spoke, composed in honor of the most sacred Virgin, says:

“Christ’s gate becomes passable,  
filled, wholly filled with grace;  
the King passes through and remains,  
closed, as it was, throughout the ages.”

Therefore, when he says, “it becomes passable,” he explains himself and shows the passage of Christ’s birth; when he says, “it remains closed,” he shows the fulfillment of what had been foretold by the prophets.

It would not be called closed if her integrity had been injured in any respect. But because virginal modesty was violated in no respect, and the fountain was in no way unsealed, the meaning is plainly evident: he came to us with the womb closed, just as he entered to the disciples through closed doors.

The disciples’ own sight then proved both things: that the doors were closed and that the Lord, entering through them, stood present before them. So our faith holds both things concerning Christ as most certain: that her integrity was passable when the Lord was born from her, and yet that the womb was not opened.

Otherwise, how can that which was violated be said to have remained closed? Or how could a woman in childbirth give birth without pain and groaning if, in the manner of other women, she delivered a son with her organs afflicted? And if it was open in the way they claim, how did it remain closed as it had been before she gave birth? For those doors were no more penetrable while closed than the Virgin’s incorrupt womb.

Therefore it is not without reason believed that the Lord came forth to us in such a way that the birth of Christ from the Virgin’s flesh was proved, while the Virgin herself suffered no torments.

Perhaps they will say that a body already incorruptible and immortal would have been more subtle for penetrating wherever it wished than it had been before the resurrection. But no one who thinks soundly says this, because from the moment he was conceived as man, he remained the same one who had previously been God. Thus, when before the Passion he walked upon the waves of the sea, he was no less man than God.

If you consider the nature of things, either he carried a body without weight, or by his power he strengthened the waves so that they could sustain the body’s weight more solidly. [Note: “So that they might sustain [it]” (*quo sustinerent*). We have emended this; the corrupt reading was *quo sustinere*.] And therefore, as blessed Gregory says in his homilies (Homily 26), the works of our Redeemer, which cannot possibly be understood from themselves, must be assessed from another of his works, so that more wondrous deeds may give faith to miraculous things.

He says: “That body of the Lord entered to the disciples through closed doors—the very body that, through his birth, came forth to human eyes from the Virgin’s closed womb.” Then he adds: “What wonder, therefore, if after his resurrection, when he was to live forever, he entered through closed doors, since, coming to die, he came forth without the Virgin’s womb being opened?”

Behold what this great and eminent doctor, the supreme pontiff, thought about this matter, after reading all the distinguished Latin and Greek commentators who came before him. Behold how, from this one point—which he believed no one should doubt—he approved what might perhaps have been doubtful.

Therefore no one who thinks soundly should attempt to assert something uncertain about a matter that is greatly doubtful. Since the faith of those who looked upon the body that could be seen was wavering while they observed the doors closed, the teacher of truth removes all their doubt when he commands them to touch and see his hands and side.

So this distinguished author, from what he regarded as universally certain, constructed and established a matter exceedingly difficult to believe: that the Lord’s body entered through closed doors after the resurrection, and that it was at once incorruptible and tangible.

Nevertheless, by whatever manner he entered, the Gospel proves that he came to the disciples through closed doors, just as he was born from the Virgin’s closed womb. If, as these people wish, he cannot rightly be said to have been born through the womb in that manner, then neither could he have entered through the doors. Yet it is proved that he entered to them when he is said to have stood in their midst.

The same is shown when he came forth from the tomb while the monument remained sealed, when the angel rolled away the stone and displayed the tomb as empty.

Thus it is plainly established that, just as that stone doorway was passable and penetrable to him, and could not restrain the living one whom it had previously enclosed as dead beneath its seal, so too the enclosure of the womb and the Virgin’s genital place, although closed and sealed with the seal of modesty, could not obstruct the birth when the days of delivery had been fulfilled. Yet it did not need to be opened, because it was not fitting that it should be a torment to him who was the mother’s honor and joy.

For everything that was closed in her was passable to God; and the honor consisted in this, that all that was born was wholly divine [lacuna]. [Note: “With the tomb sealed” (*signato monumento*). Acherius had published *signatus* (“sealed”); he had also printed *Deificum quo natum*, where we restore *quod natum* (“that which was born”).]

I plainly confess that no subject for debate can be found as weighty as the question why he came forth from the sealed tomb or why he entered to the disciples through closed doors, compared with the question why he came forth from the Virgin Mary’s closed womb.

In those cases divine majesty is declared; in this case divine condescension is displayed, and, in keeping with humility, the honor due to the mother and reverence for modesty. Hence blessed Ambrose also bears witness in hymnic praises—in the hymn for the Nativity of the Lord—that the enclosure of modesty remained intact and that the banners of virtues shone in her, in whom the whole majesty of the Godhead dwelt, until the fullness of time for giving birth arrived.

Therefore, in her in whom the enclosure of modesty remained intact, there was no rupture, no affliction of the flesh, and no foulness of that dreadful condition. And in her in whom the banners of virtues glittered, no sin of original origin prevailed to torment her.

The banners of virtues shone in that sacred childbirth when the Virgin conceived without seed, the Virgin gave birth without pain or groaning, and remained a virgin with fruitful offspring. This is what it means for the enclosure of modesty to remain: the secret genital place opened to him was violated in no respect—not in conception, not in childbirth, and not in any confusion of labor.

For the whole Church of Christ, both Roman and Greek, confidently sings with the authority of its own divine tradition that the Virgin gave birth without pain and remained inviolate, because the Holy Spirit preserved her unharmed in every respect: she had a son as a virgin, and the honor appropriate to so great a gift was preserved for her, just as her womb had been consecrated to God with such sanctification.

The first volume on the Birth of the Virgin Mary, dedicated together with the holy virgins, ends here.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1383]

[Col. 1383C] Among the words of sacred Scripture, vain and superstitious interpretation must always be avoided, because, as it is written in Proverbs, “the perverse are difficult to correct, and the number of fools is infinite” (Ecclesiasticus 1:15).

Therefore, since the rashness of certain brothers once began to stain the mysteries of the divine gift by insolent disputation and to examine the mystery of the sacred birth through excessive inquiry, they prefer to err with heretics rather than correct with Catholics what they think wrongly.

Since they find openings for vain disputation, they introduce into the churches a foul and excessively fetid sewer of perverse pollution, to the drowning of souls, when they falsely say that the Virgin Mary bore the Lord according to the natural law, as other women give birth, and that she was incorrupt in childbirth for no other reason than that she did not conceive through intercourse with a man.

I believe that I have already said enough above, in the first volume, about her incorruption. But since these people do not accept what we have said, they obstinately insist that virginity can be corrupted only by intercourse with a man, and that Mary ought not to be called corrupted even if she gave birth according to the law of all women, because, they say, although her organs or secret genital place became open in the manner of other women so that Christ might be born, virginity nevertheless could not be corrupted. For this reason, they claim, the Mother of God alone remained a virgin and incorrupt after childbirth.

As they spread these and similar empty utterances and babblings, they put forward the authority of the holy Fathers and stain the Catholic faith. Therefore, since they disdain to hear us, let them hear blessed Augustine, whom it is not lawful to contradict, disputing among other things on this matter in the book of the *Enchiridion* (chapter 34). He says:

“It is not lawful to say that anything belonging to human nature was lacking in that assumption. It was not such as is born from both sexes through the concupiscence of the flesh with the burden of sin, whose guilt is washed away by regeneration, but such as ought to be born from a virgin, whom the faith of the mother had conceived, not lust. For if her integrity had been corrupted even through the one being born, he would no longer have been born from a virgin; and the whole Church, imitating his mother, which daily gives birth to his members and is itself a virgin, would falsely confess him—God forbid—as born from the Virgin Mary.”

Concerning this work, he writes quite elegantly in the work addressed to Volusianus, to which book he also refers us to read on this subject. But because these people are unwilling to read either that book or this passage, they err, deceived by their own rashness.

Otherwise, as this distinguished doctor admits, if virginal integrity had been corrupted even through the one being born, it would not be lawful to call her a virgin, since her virginity had been corrupted by the one born. And if it had been corrupted even through the birth, how would the virgin have been intact and unharmed?

Let these empty talkers therefore hear so great a doctor and come to their senses, lest through their false assertion they introduce Christ as conceived in sins and born in iniquities. For if he was not born from a virgin, then what the Church confesses is false, as he says here; and false too is what every Scripture of the New and Old Testaments testifies concerning her.

But because she remained wholly a virgin, she was pressed by no pains [Note: “She was pressed by none” (*nullis pressa est*). Archerius himself conjectured that this was the correct reading, having found *passa est* (“she suffered”) in his manuscripts.] and was corrupted in no respect. Therefore she did not undergo the uncleanness of the afterbirth, did not shed a flow of blood, and did not endure the corruptions of the organs within or without. If a woman in childbirth suffered torments of this kind, she would certainly not be a virgin, because virginal integrity would have been violated.

Hence Sedulius, rhetorician of the Roman Church, says in his *Paschal Work* (chapter 3, beginning):

“For the infant, small yet great—small in his limbs, exalted in his divinity—flowing through the pure chastity of the hospitable temple, did not injure the body as he departed, which he had not injured when he entered.”

If this is so—or rather, because it is so—he was not born as others are born, with the body corrupted, but God and man was born with his organs unharmed.

Hence the same witness to the secret of divine generation further shows the Virgin’s childbirth: he entered as the guardian of his mother’s modesty, conceived and created within closed organs.

Nothing clearer can be said; nowhere do these holy doctors speak more plainly about the Virgin’s childbirth: that the intact Virgin remained closed, just as she had been before giving birth. This would certainly not have been so if, in childbirth, she had been subjected to corruption in the manner of other women.

No virgin, therefore, is subject to sufferings of this kind; and for this reason she is rightly called truly a virgin, because she is intact and incorrupt. So also the blessed Mother of God, in order to be called truly a virgin while giving birth, is rightly believed to have remained wholly closed, in the manner of virgins, and incorrupt.

If she had not remained undefiled in this way, like other virgins, she would not truly have been a virgin. To demonstrate this, the prophet David, prophesying about her, says with a fitting example:

“He descended like rain upon a fleece, and like drops that fall upon the earth” (Psalm 71:6).

The senator Cassiodorus, explaining this verse in his *Exposition of the Psalms*, understands the fleece as the most sacred Virgin Mary, shorn from the sheep of Israel. He compares the rain with the divinity of the Word, because just as rain comes upon a fleece in complete silence, so it drenched and filled the virginal body and took possession of the virginal mind.

Thus, by a wondrous method and a wondrous example of comparison, he firmly established through prophecy the coming of Christ’s descent into the Virgin’s womb: just as rain drenches a fleece while leaving it whole and inviolate, so the divinity of the Word preserved the Virgin undefiled and unharmed.

It found her intact and incorrupt when it descended like rain upon a fleece; and it entered the Virgin’s organs. It also descended like drops falling upon the earth.

Therefore the same prophet explains the perfection of Christ’s incarnation in these two statements of prophecy. Through falling drops we see the earth bring forth growth; from it, through the infusion and moisture of rain, every plant of the field sprouts, and all the greenness of the earth arises.

So too the divinity of the Word, descending upon Mary like drops upon the earth, caused her to germinate the shoot of life—not from anywhere other than from itself, the same thing arising from the Virgin’s flesh through the infusion of divine majesty.

Therefore what was born from her was equally divine and human, so that from Mary neither the divinity of the Word is believed to have been born without man, nor man without the Word: for the Word became flesh, and thus God and man are one Christ.

Moreover, through the rain that descends upon the fleece, he expressed not the nature of germination from the fleece, but the manner of birth from the Virgin. For when rain, in clear weather, drenches a fleece, it preserves its integrity equally in entering and equally in departing when it flows back out, because the integrity of the fleece is in no respect violated by the rain.

Thus that heavenly orator mentioned above understands and confesses the matter concerning the Virgin Mary: that she was neither corrupted at the entry of the Son of God nor violated at his departure, but was preserved in every respect full of grace, intact, and unharmed. Neither when he entered were the womb or organs corrupted, nor when he emerged were they opened.

The secret genital place remains, but closed and immaculate; the womb is emptied like a fleece by the rain, but the organs are not shaken.

By these two statements, as the aforesaid doctor indicates, the Holy Spirit wished to declare what Isaiah later testifies concerning Christ, saying:

“As the rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again, but water the earth and soak it, and make it bring forth and sprout; so shall be the word that goes forth from my mouth. It shall not return to me empty, but shall accomplish whatever I have willed, and shall prosper in the things for which I sent it.”

Behold what David wished to signify by the rain, and what by the falling drops: surely, the infusion of the Holy Spirit and the divinity of the Word.

[Col. 1387]

# THREE BOOKS OF S. PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS, ABBOT OF CORBIE, ON FAITH, HOPE, AND CHARITY

*(In Martène, the Most Extensive Collection, volume IX, page 470.)*

[Col. 1387]

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION

[Col. 1387A] The second short work of Paschasius Radbertus, which we now present here to learned and devout readers as a new offering, comprises three books on Faith, Hope, and Charity. Learn briefly at what time they were written.

Since they were published at the command of Warinus, abbot of New Corbie, for the benefit of the younger brothers whom he was advancing from their novitiate toward greater perfection, it is clear that they were written before the year 856, when Warinus passed to heaven. It is also clear that Paschasius obeyed Warinus’s orders after the books on Matthew had been published, for he cites them in Book I, chapter 9. It is very likely that this occurred before he undertook the administration of Old Corbie, which he assumed in the year 844; otherwise one would have to say that he began this work not at Warinus’s command, but at his request.

The *Annals of Corbie*, inserted by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in volume II of the *Brunswick Affairs*, specify the year precisely. Under the year 843 I read: “The lector Preradbertus wrote an outstanding book on Faith, Hope, and Charity.” Concerning the year 839, the same annalist says: “Preradbertus, our fellow monk, distinguished himself in piety and learning and was greatly loved by Bishop Bathurad at Paderborn.”

The name “Preradbertus” is an error on the annalist’s part, caused by the inscription of a more recent Corbie manuscript, which, through the copyist’s own error, reads as follows: “Preradbertus to Warinus, abbot of Corbie and his archimandrite, greetings.” Had it been possible to consult the older books, he would have read not “Preradbertus” but “P. Radbertus,” as the preceding acrostic verses clearly indicate, whose initial letters form “Radbertus Levita.”

Our Bernard Pez first brought the treatise on Faith, Hope, and Charity into public circulation. He had received it from the distinguished George Eckart, who gave him a copy made from a Corbie manuscript, not sufficiently faithfully transcribed, for publication. It was so defiled with errors that it omitted or at least altered not only complete words but often entire lines.

We do not think this should be attributed to Bernard Pez, a most diligent man, but to Eckart or to the person who, in his name, copied the treatise with far too hasty a pen. Our Corbie brethren, indignant at this, gave me another copy, accurately transcribed and more carefully collated, so that it might have a place in this extensive collation.

This was especially desired by the most reverend and illustrious Lord Ansgar de Grass, prior of that place, intimate counsellor of the most exalted prince-abbot, and vicar general and archdeacon, who had prepared the work for publication.

## INVOCATION

[Note: The following poem may be viewed as a graphic, so that the acrostic ornaments in the text, which cannot be keyed, may be seen.]

[Col. 1387B]

Break, Muse, your delays; sing the covenant of virtues,

that I may climb perpetually to the chambers of heaven.

Tell where the snowy flowers bloom, in the dug-up turf;

leave behind the pastoral honeycombs and seize the heights.

I shall undertake to open the warm springs of life;

[Col. 1387C]

though hoarse for boys, I shall disclose heavenly gifts.

There are three sisters who come from one fountain,

with virgin steps, washed in the blood of Christ.  
[Note: The edition reads *totae* (“whole”) instead of *lotae* (“washed”).]

[Col. 1388B]

But Charity is the one among these who is higher than all,

while Faith, worthy of praise, governs the summit of the virtues.

She first seeks the weapons by which the holy conquer all things,

and blessed Hope, a virgin, directs her steps toward the heights,

reclining on a throne, secure beneath Christ’s protection.

[Col. 1388C]

These three weave the covenant of the virtues,

and compel the soul to ascend to heaven’s chambers.

[Col. 1387C]

## P. RADBERTUS TO WARINUS, ABBOT OF CORBIE AND HIS ARCHIMANDRITE, GREETINGS

[Col. 1387]

[Col. 1387D] There is no doubt that it is a most exalted task to discuss those things which no one knows except the one who receives them; yet they cannot be received [Col. 1388D] through art or eloquence, especially since the apostle James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (Jas. I, 17). Hence, after deliberating long [Note: [Col. 1389B] The printed editions omit *mecum* (“with myself”).] and earnestly with myself, my Father, I undertake what you demand: to say something about faith, hope, and charity—what they are and how they are possessed.

Indeed, since, as I have already indicated, no one can acquire an understanding of these virtues except through the gift of the Holy Spirit—and without them no one is called a Christian in reality, even if he appears to have acquired all the other virtues—for the salvation of the whole human race and the efficacy of the virtues depend upon them and in them; through them also all the depths and obscurities of the divine Scriptures are disclosed, not merely any clearer passages, and this not with the embellishments of poets [Note: [Col. 1389C] The printed editions read *falsimenta*, “false inventions.”].

Now I invent three sisters of the Muses, or, lured on, strike a Pierian [lyre; the object is implicit] [Note: [Col. 1389C] The printed editions read *Pieridum*, “of the Pierides.”]; but I am embarking upon the paths of life that flow from paradise. Therefore, moved by a new love and bound by a vow of devoted favor, I have believed that I should be aided by your prayers, lest I dare to speak of these things without them, since they are not committed to ink and paper but by the pen of the Holy Spirit, concerning which the Prophet sings: “My tongue,” he says, “is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Ps. XLIV, 2).

Nevertheless, I do not think that reading should be abandoned—or rather, that the discipline and instruction concerning these matters should not be pursued—so that the Christian may have something to understand and that all may have something to desire in these prayers. Otherwise, whatever we do or whatever teaching we pursue, we acquire nothing, because in these things lies whatever we believe has been given to us by God, hope for, and love through charity.

[Col. 1390A] There is therefore no page of the divine Scriptures that does not proclaim and imply these three virtues as the foundation and summit of all Christianity; through them the other gifts are bestowed and eternal life is attained. For they are nourished by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, as we read prefigured in Job: his three daughters feasted each day, throughout the cycle of days, in the houses of each of their brothers. That is, faith, hope, and charity are richly fattened by the dew of the Holy Spirit, so that they despise visible things [Note: [Col. 1390B] The printed editions read *contemnentur*, “will be despised.”] and hasten continually toward those things that are not seen [Note: [Col. 1390B] The printed editions read *festinetur*, “may be hastened.”].

For they are led by the Spirit of God, and therefore they keep ardent watch on behalf of the things already bestowed which they love [Note: [Col. 1390C] The printed editions read: “the gifts are ardently watched over because they are loved.”]. Hence, to speak of these matters as is fitting, as I have said, is a most exalted task; but to remain silent and not labor on behalf of these teachings [Col. 1390B] and prayers is utter foolishness.

Your Blessedness, moreover, did not ask, after the manner of the holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 1390C] The printed editions read *sanctorum primum*, “of the holy first [Fathers].”], that I dispute about faith; rather, you ordered me—whom you are bringing from apprenticeship to more perfect things—to disclose briefly and by headings what faith, hope, and charity are, what sort of activity they undertake, and what they contribute, whether individually or jointly, to believers in the bond of kinship [Note: [Col. 1390C] The printed editions read: “what they are and what sort of activity is being carried on.”]. Thus beginners may have something to taste in small measure, while the more perfect may read through all the volumes of the holy Scriptures [Note: [Col. 1390C] The printed editions read *omnia*, “all things”]; for in them, if they understand rightly, there will be no lack of material by which they may grow further and more perfectly as the Lord opens the way, and, growing, may happily arrive at those things that are eternal. Amen.

[Col. 1389C]

## [OF FAITH]

[Col. 1389C]

# THE BOOK OF FAITH BEGINS

[Col. 1389]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### What is faith?

1. We must first inquire what faith is, since it is the initiator of all the other virtues. For, as the Apostle says, although we may appear to strive after the various works of the Christian religion, “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. VI, 33).

Therefore faith must be sought with the utmost diligence—I do not merely say sought, but implored—for without it no one adheres to God. Through it the saints conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, and obtained the promises; through it even today they are proclaimed wondrous. Otherwise, who is justified except by faith? “But my righteous one,” he says [Note: [Col. 1389D] The printed editions read “the Apostle says,” omitting *meus* (“my”), which is present in the Apostle’s Epistle to the Hebrews], “shall live by faith” (Heb. X, 38).

We must therefore seek such a great and powerful faith, to which all things yield, without which no one lives, through which the remaining goods of the virtues are granted to us, and according to the measure of our faith, as the Apostle says (Rom. II, 3), all things are freely distributed.

It is therefore evident that, according to the definition of things and in accordance with the philosophers’ opinion, each thing is illuminated so that it may be better understood by everyone. For this reason we must seek a definition of faith—not, I mean, a physical or human one, but a divine one—so that through it what is being sought may also be grasped more clearly.

“Faith,” says the Apostle, in whom Christ was speaking, “is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. XI, 1); another translation has, “the conviction of things not seen.” Faith is rightly called the conviction of things not seen because it convinces and binds in our hearts things invisible and eternal, which therefore have not yet appeared. Hence it is also called religion. Religion is understood to be so called because it binds our minds back to God; or because through faith it binds invisible and eternal things in the heart with the bond of love, as though they were a treasure, lest they slip away from us [Note: [Col. 1390D] The printed editions read *prolabantur*, “lest they slip away,” plural].

This treasure, as it is written, rests “in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. X, 13). It is in the mouth because it flows from the heart. We know this treasure to be in Christ, “in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. XII, 3) [Note: [Col. 1391D] The printed editions read *in quo scilicet*, “in whom, namely.”].

Christ, moreover, is held in our hearts through faith, as the Apostle testifies (Eph. III, 17), joined and fastened by the cord [Note: [Col. 1391D] The printed editions read *thoro*, “bed,” rather than *loro*, “cord.”] of charity; and with him the Father and the Holy Spirit deign to make their dwelling in us [Note: [Col. 1391D] The printed editions read *dignatur*, singular, “deigns,” rather than *dignentur*, plural] (John XIV, 23), so that God—[Note: [Col. 1391D] The printed editions read “the Holy Trinity,” omitting *Deus* (“God”), though the latter fits the passage very well.]—the Trinity, the substance of things not yet seen, may already be in our hearts.

Behold what faith is: “the substance,” he says, “of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.”

Moreover, the substance of things hoped for is the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: the whole God, the complete God, the one God, as the Prophet sings: “The Lord is my hope” (Ps. LV, 5). For whatever God is, believers rightly hope for him in his entirety; because from him and in him full immortality is expected, full blessedness, full and unending eternity, and unfading life.

They therefore hope for him because he once promised the fathers under oath that he would give himself to us. We rejoice in believing that he has done so [Note: [Col. 1391D] The printed editions read *sperantes*, “hoping,” rather than *gaudentes*, “rejoicing”]; and by believing we hope. While hoping, we patiently endure until, after a little while—for he will come again and will not delay—the fullness of adoption is received, which has already been granted to us in hope through faith.

“The evangelist says: “He gave them power to become the children of God, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God” (John I, 12). Those who are renewed unto immortality through full faith, from water and the Holy Spirit, are therefore born again from God.

This, I say, is faith: full of God, the full substance of divinity, by which we are reborn—to believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God, true, abiding, unchangeable, and eternal. This, I say, is the substance of things hoped for, and this is the way of believing, filled with all truth. Through this faith, certainly, God in his entirety is, for the time being, believed, possessed, loved, and worshiped; in it there is nothing empty, nothing doubtful, nothing shadowy, but everything solid, complete, and true.

2. Faith, then, as some define it, is the origin of righteousness, the head of holiness, the beginning of devotion, and indeed the foundation of religion. Without it no one has pleased God, and no one has undertaken the way of holiness.

For it is an innocent and pure act of believing by which one goes to God, through which we adhere to his commandments [Note: [Col. 1391D] In the printed editions these words are absent: “through which we adhere to his commandments [Col. 1392D] and venerate God purely with devotion”], and rightly venerate God with devotion. It excludes doubt and establishes [Note: [Col. 1392D] The printed editions read “produces in the mind”] in the mind the absolute certainty of God’s promises. Hence it also displays signs, exercises virtues, and fulfills the charisms of the sacraments.

Faith therefore possesses God, and is possessed by God. Through faith we receive one thing from God, while from faith we owe another; for faith is a pact, or covenant, between God and human beings. Thus no one ought to abandon the agreement of the covenant whose pledge he sees himself retaining.

For if covenants are always preserved among capable and honorable men, and the one who either dissolves an agreement, breaks a pact, or changes a social relationship through treacherous cunning becomes guilty of violated faith, how much more must that which is contracted with God and entered into with Christ be kept inviolate, lest one be judged liable to eternal laws!

Whatever is joined with God in hope of heavenly promises must therefore be observed irrevocably. For although human beings sometimes deceive one another or are deceived by one another [Note: [Col. 1392D] The printed editions repeat *invicem*, “one another”], God can in no way be deceived by a human being.

Therefore he demands [Note: [Col. 1392D] The printed editions read *exigitur*, “it is demanded,” but *exigit* (“he demands”) is better; the subject is evidently God] what you have promised, since he is the rewarder of what you fulfill.

Hence the angel says in the Apocalypse: “Be faithful [Col. 1392B] unto death. To the one who conquers,” he says, “I will give to eat from the tree of life” (Rev. II, 10), because “this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith” (1 John V, 4).

It is faith, of course, that works through love (Gal. V, 6), not the faith that lies dead in itself without works (Jas. II, 20), by which even the demons believe and tremble.

3. Since unbelief expelled us from the tree of life, faithfulness must necessarily call us back. It was therefore said to the human being in paradise: “Why did God tell you not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil?” “God knows,” he said, “that on whatever day you eat from it, you will be like gods” (Gen. III, 1, 5).

This faith—or rather unbelief—came from the world and from the devil. It is therefore necessary that faith be from God and directed toward God, through which one goes to God, so that it may not arise from itself, from the world, or from the devil’s lie, but depend entirely upon God and remain in God.

Otherwise, how can faith conquer the world if it takes pleasure in and favors the things that are in the world? Therefore, so that it may be wholly unconquerable, as I have said, let it be directed toward God and come from God, consenting to nothing that favors the desires of the eyes or the deceptions of enemies, through which the pride of life is supplied. Rather, let it obey God’s commandments, cling to his promises, believe his words, and presume nothing from the flesh or from the world.

Whoever is born in this faith is rightly said to be born from God as his parent [Note: [Col. 1392D] The printed editions read “is said to be born from God the Father,” omitting *ipsius jure*, “rightly, by his right]. For such great faith is divinely proclaimed, as the Apostle testifies, to be the substance of things hoped for.

In this faith nothing is lacking except the contemplation of divinity, for “we shall see him as he is” (1 John III, 2). For the time being, however, we believe only that he is, although we do not yet grasp what he is, until “that which is in part” is done away. When it has been done away [Note: [Col. 1392D] The printed editions read *fuit*, “was done away,” which is less suitable], everything that is in faith will be found.

Therefore our faith is rightly called the very substance of divinity, which is the capacity for the things hoped for, provided that it holds within itself nothing concerning him except what he himself is.

Otherwise false faith presents a false hope; and therefore it is rightly called not faith but error, just as it is not hope but deception. We must therefore invent, think, or presume nothing concerning this substance except that he is, and whatever he has taught about himself—he who knows himself abundantly.

But if he were subject to our senses, he would be inferior to us [Note: [Col. 1393D] The printed editions do not have *nostri*; the sense is uncertain]; but because he surpasses [Note: [Col. 1393D] The printed editions read *prominet*, “stands forth,” rather than *praeeminet*, “surpasses”] and exceeds every sense, we must believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, a great and immeasurable God, who, as it is written, has no consummation.

He is wholly present everywhere—not by approach or withdrawal, since he is not confined to a place, yet touching every place. The Son is wholly in the Father, the Father wholly in the Word, and the Holy Spirit wholly in the Father and the Son: one God, one substance; three persons, but one equality.

The Father alone is not less than the Son and the Holy Spirit together; nor are the Father and the Son greater than the Holy Spirit alone. Certainly, they are one. Unity admits neither more nor less, but one quantity [Note: [Col. 1393D] The printed editions read *qualitas*, “quality,” rather than *quantitas*, “quantity”] is always proclaimed.

Therefore God is rightly believed by faith to be always one immensity and one capacity for the things hoped for; he is held in hope, venerated and loved in charity, and through these three together the one, immeasurable, and eternal God is worshiped.

It would be lengthy to traverse even briefly the volumes of Catholic teachers concerning this immense Trinity, especially since the assertion of our work has not proposed this, but only obedience to your commands: to show, by exhortation to simpler people, what faith, hope, and charity are, through which the Trinity who is God is worshiped [Col. 1393C] and proclaimed.

For it is one thing for wise and most learned doctors of the Churches to dispute more subtly about the faith of the Trinity in order to refute its adversaries [Note: [Col. 1393D] The printed editions read *disputari*, “to be disputed,” which is less correct], among whom very few are proved capable; it is another thing to explain briefly what faith, hope, and charity themselves are, without which no one is saved and no one is rightly believed to be a Christian.

4. Here too we must seek with the utmost intellectual care what the Apostle means when he says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.”

Is this evidence perhaps like the arguments philosophers use sometimes to deceive the unwary [Note: [Col. 1393D] The printed editions read *innocentes*, “the innocent,” but *incautos*, “the unwary,” is much better]? Certainly not.

This word, coming from an ambiguous Greek expression, is translated by many into Latin with various, though not entirely proper, terms, scarcely expressing the force of the Apostle’s word. Thus some translated it *argumentum* (“evidence”), others *capitulum* (“heading” or “foundation”), others *convinctio* (“conviction”), or *visio* (“vision”).

Yet *capitulum* seems to accord well with the sense: here faith is held as the beginning of things not seen, while there is the completeness of vision. And just as the wise men of this age are accustomed to persuade through whatever arguments are true, so Christ’s faithful investigate by faith those things that are most certain and true.

“For we walk by faith, and not by sight” (2 Cor. V, 7). Faith is therefore held as the evidence by which one investigates; but the sight sought through it is truth. Enlightened faith now seeks that truth—not something else, but the very one whom it already holds through faith.

For this reason the Prophet says: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice; seek the Lord [Note: [Col. 1394D] The printed editions omit *quaerite Dominum*, “seek the Lord”], and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Ps. CIV, 4).

It is as though he plainly said: Seek the Lord, and no other, but the very one whom it is clear you have already found through faith; that is, be confirmed more and more in the same thing until you arrive at sight, because “we shall see him as he is.” And do not seek anything else: “Seek,” he says, “his face always.”

Always, because he is immeasurable and admits no consummation. Faith is therefore commanded to expand and advance toward immeasurable things, lest it ever cease believing.

An immeasurable God requires an immeasurable faith by which he may be grasped. It is therefore fitting that faith should receive no consummation [Note: [Col. 1394D] The printed editions read *ne et illa ipsa*, “lest even that itself,” a difficult reading] concerning him until it is permitted to see the God of gods in Zion as he is.

Concerning him the bride says in the Song of Songs: “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song III, 1); and shortly afterward: “When I had passed by them,” she says, “I found him whom my soul loves; I will hold him and will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house” (ibid., IV, 4).

What do you think—where did she go, or where did she find him, or by what footprints did she seek him? By the steps of faith, certainly, in the heart [Note: [Col. 1394D] The printed editions read “by steps and in the heart”], where previously she had lain on the bed of weakness and had been unable to find him, because she was still oppressed by the knot of unbelief.

Hence she is significantly said to have sought him at night [Col. 1394C]. As soon as she passed through the darkness of blindness [Note: [Col. 1394D] The printed editions read “when she passed through”], she found him by faith. Therefore she firmly denies that she will ever let him go until she enters the house of heavenly Zion, where she may clearly behold his face and appearance.

She swears that she will always seek this face and never interrupt her effort to seek, because faith is indeed the evidence of things not seen and not yet the sight of perfect vision.

Therefore, while true faith is held, the one whom whoever has grasped must necessarily hold the faith of confession is present in the heart. Otherwise, if faith is not preserved, he cannot be in us who is apprehended only by faith and, once apprehended, is preserved and held in our hearts by faith.

5. We must note that the things which are seen are temporal, while the things which are not seen are eternal. Faith is always concerned with things not seen, because they are the pasture of things hoped for. Otherwise, who hopes for what he sees? (Rom. VIII, 24).

Faith is therefore the substance of things hoped for because it carries within itself all those things that are not seen. It despises temporal things and rises above everything visible, possessing nothing perishable, nothing empty, and nothing weak. Rather, it is full of God, full of truth, because God is truth; [Col. 1395A] full of eternity and full of immutability.

It likewise leads to the same assurance to which visible things lead. Therefore belief or unbelief cannot properly be spoken of concerning things that are seen, any more than faith can—unless it affords greater assurance concerning things not seen than concerning things seen.

For the things that are in hope seem somehow to exist without substance when they are considered without faith; therefore every faith bestows substance. To speak more clearly and truthfully, faith itself is their essence or substance.

For example, the general resurrection has not yet occurred and therefore, as it were, does not yet exist in substance. But because we believe that Christ, the head of the whole Church, has risen, we also believe that all the members of his body will rise in him—or rather, have risen in him [Col. 1395B], as the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Col. III, 1).

Here is something to note concerning a visible reality: it exists in Christ, though it does not yet appear as it will be. Faith grants it substance to us, and true hope makes that same resurrection already subsist in our soul.

This is what the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for.” Other manuscripts have: “The vision of things not yet seen.”

It is therefore a true vision, because right faith is more truthful than sight. Although we are often deceived by sight, as we can prove in many places, we are never deceived by faith, because faith never receives anything except truth. For this reason it can rightly be called more than vision, even though it concerns things not yet seen.

From where, then, do all the things that are seen arise in sight, by which we are often deceived [Col. 1395C], and temporal things that slip away at every moment and hasten toward nonbeing? But those things that are not seen remain at the end, because they are eternal.

Concerning them the prophet Isaiah says: “You have hoped in the Lord; you have hoped,” he says, “for the ages” (Isa. XXVI, 4).

Those things are therefore more certain which always remain as they are and are believed than those which are seen so as not to exist [Note: [Col. 1395D] The printed editions read “so that they exist,” *ut sint*, rather than “so as not to exist,” *ut non sint*], and which pass away.

“For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. VII, 31)—the form that is seen—whereas those things held by faith remain forever unchangeable, without end, and therefore eternal.

We come to them through faith, because for the time being “we walk by faith, and not by sight” [Note: [Col. 1395D] The printed editions read “because we walk by faith,” omitting *interdum*, “sometimes”].

Therefore, whoever hastens to come to them, do not fabricate some appearance for yourself, lest you cease to walk by faith. For the righteous lives by faith for the time being [Note: [Col. 1395D] The printed editions also omit *interdum*, “for the time being”], and not by the sight of things.

Otherwise you must beware lest, by rashly beginning to fabricate false things for yourself without faith, you cease to be righteous and be counted among the dead, because the righteous person lives altogether by faith.

## CHAPTER TWO  
### If faith concerns things that are not seen, will it be done away when they appear through sight?

One must not think that, when someone sees his faith—by which he believes what he does not yet see—he sees something eternal. For this condition will not always remain what in fact will not remain. Once this pilgrimage is finished, during which we are pilgrims away from the Lord, that sight will succeed by which we shall see face to face what we now believe without seeing, so long as it remains necessary to walk by faith.

Nevertheless, because we believe, we shall deserve to see, and we shall rejoice forever that faith has already brought us to sight. For there will no longer be faith by which unseen things are believed [Note: [Col. 1395D] The printed editions read “nor is there now faith,” a difficult variant], but sight by which the things formerly believed during this pilgrimage are seen.

Faith will then be reckoned among past and completed things [Note: [Col. 1396D] The printed editions read *computabitur*, “will be counted,” rather than *reputabitur*, “will be reckoned”], not among present things that always remain, which contemplation will make present. It will therefore exist rather in memory, just as infancy or childhood belongs to youth; when these have been done away, old age succeeds, yet the same person remains and his substance is not changed [Note: [Col. 1396D] The printed editions read *permutatur*, “is changed,” rather than *permutatus*, “changed”].

Thus, when faith has been done away, unchangeable truth will remain to be enjoyed in vision. It will not be another truth, but the very one toward which we advanced through faith and which we believed through faith, from which we had previously been pilgrims.

It is not another, but the same eternal and unchangeable substance. Therefore the Apostle defined faith in two ways when he said: “The substance of things hoped for” and “the evidence of things not seen.” For although faith is done away, the substance of faith nevertheless remains.

Faith is one thing, and the substance of faith another. The evidence is therefore done away when the truth has been revealed; but the substance of things hoped for remains, having been in faith and restored in vision.

Faith is consequently firm, because it carries nothing other than the substance of truth, which is never done away, but will be enjoyed without end in eternal vision.

Charity burns to reach this vision, and for this reason it is proclaimed by the Apostle to be greater than faith and hope. For although these three now remain, charity is rightly called greater because, when charity is more perfectly increased by blessed vision so that it may remain eternal, faith and hope concerning things not yet seen will be done away by vision.

Whatever one already sees is neither believed nor hoped for, but enjoyed in perfect contemplation. Yet a trace of remembrance of these things will remain fixed in memory, so that the joy of eternal blessedness may be increased, as we rejoice forever in having arrived at those things that we believed and hoped for [Note: [Col. 1396D] The printed editions read: “so that we may enjoy perpetual delight in having arrived at those things which we believed and hoped for”].

Otherwise, if no passing trace were left in us, nothing of it would remain in our memory by which we might return with joy to recall it as past [Note: [Col. 1396D] The printed editions read *recreamur*, “are refreshed,” rather than *recurramus*, “return”], especially since we shall love, as we recall them by sight, all the things that it suggested to us.

That substance itself will be what we now believe, also hope for, and enjoy through love. Concerning this substance the Lord says through Jeremiah: “If you had stood [Note: [Col. 1396D] The printed editions read *si stetissent*, “if they had stood,” and shortly afterward *fecissent*, “they had done”],” he says, “in my substance [Col. 1397A] and had made my words known to my people, I would certainly have turned them away from their evil way” (Jer. XXIII, 22).

To stand in God’s substance means, through faith, to believe God in the heart unto righteousness; and to make his words known to the people means to confess him unto salvation.

Thus, as long as the righteous lives by faith, he is directed through that same faith toward eternity, although the faith itself is temporal, having been established in eternal things. The things that are seen are temporal and therefore are not believed; the things that are not seen are eternal and therefore, for the time being, are present in the heart through faith until they are seen as they are.

This faith is nourished only by knowledge, through which we contemplate very deeply the things that are eternal.

## CHAPTER THREE  
### Is faith visible, since it is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not yet seen?

It is clear that we are commanded to believe what we cannot see. Yet we shall certainly see faith itself, since it is present in us. Faith is present to absent things, just as faith within us concerns things that are outside; and faith in things that are not seen is itself seen.

Yet faith occurs temporally in human hearts. If believers become unbelievers [Note: [Col. 1397D] The printed editions read *fiunt*, “become,” rather than *fiant*, “should become”], it perishes from them [Note: [Col. 1397D] The printed editions read *quia*, “because,” rather than *si*, “if”].

It is not rightly said to perish from their hearts when the truth that has been found— the truth that was present in faith—drives it out. Rather, the faith of true things passes most desirably into those same things, so that it is no longer the evidence of things not seen but the substance that was previously hidden in faith, now made present and displayed [Col. 1397C] so that it may be seen.

Therefore it must not be said to perish when the things believed by faith are now seen through sight, the evidence having been removed and the truth of the substance itself revealed.

Or should faith itself be called the vision of truth, since the Apostle defined it as the conviction or evidence of things not apparent? Certainly not. It is the truth laid open—the truth that was not merely in faith, but was faith itself—which, once the evidence has been done away, will be enjoyed forever by the sight of the faithful.

Sometimes, moreover, faith is applied in the present to false things, as when we say: “I was given faith, and it deceived me”—if such a condition should indeed be called faith.

The faith of the Christian religion is common to all, though not in the way that some bodily form is common to all eyes for seeing, being present to them all and giving shape to the sight of everyone who looks. Rather, it is common in the way that one may say the human face is common to all human beings. It is called common in this way, while each individual nevertheless has his own face [Note: [Col. 1397D] The printed editions read “and yet individuals”].

Accordingly, we rightly say that from one teaching faith is impressed upon the hearts of individual believers who believe the same thing. Yet the things believed are one thing, and faith itself, by which they are believed, another.

The things believed exist in realities that are said either to exist, to have existed, or to be future; but faith itself is entirely in the mind of the believer. It is visible only to the one whose faith it is, although faith also exists in others—not the same faith, but a similar one.

Faith is not numerically one, as the Apostle says, “one faith” (Eph. IV, 5), but one in kind. Yet because of its similarity and a certain diversity, we say that there is one faith rather than many.

It is therefore easier to say that there were many souls, each belonging to an individual, of whom we read in the Acts of the Apostles that they had “one soul” (Acts IV, 32), than, when the Apostle says “one faith,” for someone to dare to say that there are as many individual faiths as there are faithful people [Note: [Col. 1397D] The printed editions omit *dicitur*, “it is said,” before *multas animas*].

Nevertheless, when Christ says to one woman, “Great is your faith!” (Matt. XV, 28), and to another, “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. XIV, 31), he indicates that each person has his own faith, even though the faith of all is one.

This does not mean that there is another faith or several faiths, but that the one and same faith is distinguished in individuals by God’s distribution and becomes proper to each through the measure of believing and the quality of understanding.

Faith is not seen in the heart in the same way as images are seen—images which we form in memory from bodies we have seen with bodily eyes and contemplate in our hearts when we think about absent things. Nor is it seen like things we have not seen but which, from things we have seen, we somehow form in our minds through thought, so that, by remembering, we may return to them whenever we wish [Note: [Col. 1398D] The printed editions read *rememoramus*, “we recall,” rather than *rememoramur*, “we are recalled”].

Nor is it seen like a human soul, which we have not seen but infer from our own soul, while we observe that the person lives through the movements of his body.

Faith is not seen in the heart, therefore, in which it exists, by the one whose faith it is, in any of these ways. Although it is conceived in us through hearing, it does not belong to that bodily sense, because it is not itself sound; nor does it belong at all to sight, because it is neither color nor bodily form.

Nor does it belong to the sense called touch, because it possesses no corporeal substance; nor to any bodily sense whatsoever, because it is entirely a matter of the heart and not of the body.

It is not outside us, but in the inmost part of the mind. No human being sees it in another; each person sees and recognizes his own faith in himself, and sees it with a clarity proportionate to the greater strength of his knowledge and understanding [Note: [Col. 1398D] The printed editions read *tanta*, “so great,” but *tanto* (“the more”) is better, corresponding to *quanto plus*, “the more”].

No bodily imagination produces or nourishes it. Rather, devotion toward God holds it with the most certain knowledge, based upon what Christ taught or did in the flesh. A pure conscience proclaims it and, from what it sees to be understood, devoutly and ardently hastens in faith toward what it does not yet understand.

In another person, however, each individual believes that faith exists but does not see it. He believes it more firmly in someone the more he knows its fruits, which faith ordinarily works through love. If someone withdraws himself from faith [Note: [Col. 1398D] The printed editions omit *fide*, “from faith”], he will already begin to be counted among the ungodly as one who is dead [Note: [Col. 1398D] The printed editions read *incipit*, “he begins,” rather than *incipiet*, “he will begin], because, as it says, “the righteous lives by faith” [Note: [Col. 1398D] The printed editions omit *inquit*, “he says”].

## CHAPTER FOUR  
### Why faith is so called, and why faith is rightly complete only between two parties
Faith, then, is so called because it is made effective by words: whatever promise of things not seen is contained in the words spoken, one of the two fulfills what has been said, while the other holds in his heart by faith what has been said, sometimes until it is revealed. [Note: [Col. 1399D] The editor reads “in the meantime” (*interim*) for “sometimes” (*interdum*).] This faith, certainly, must be irrevocable between God and man, because it is fitting that human beings believe without any doubt what God, the Truth, has spoken; and each must preserve inwardly, so far as depends on him, by works and by grace, until death, what he has promised in faith to the Creator. [Note: [Col. 1399D] The editor reads, “must preserve by works until death,” omitting “inwardly.”]

Therefore, concerning him and concerning those things about which he wished to instruct us in the books of Sacred Scripture, even though we do not yet behold them, we must believe and firmly retain in our minds, without ambiguity, what has already been seen and substantially manifested through those same words, in greater measure and more perfectly. For, as has been said, the manifestation of past events is the certainty of future ones. Nothing is truer than Truth itself; and therefore the Apostle declares that God does not lie (Tit. I, 1). God, moreover, is truth—not accidentally, but essentially—and therefore he is unchangeable. Since he is unchangeable, whatever he has said unchangeably must certainly come to pass. [Note: [Col. 1399D] The editor reads “to be done” (*faciendum*) for “to come to pass” (*fiendum*).] Hence he says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Luke XXI, 23). [Note: [Col. 1399D] The editor reads *transibunt* (“will pass away,” plural) for *transient* (“will pass away,” singular).] Since, therefore, those words cannot pass away unless they are fulfilled, they must be believed.
