The faith in those words, because it is formed from truth, must itself be true and not feigned; it must not be darkened by any distrust of what has been said, but must shine ever more brightly, illumined by the Truth, who is Christ, until perfect vision. For Christ, the true light, came for this purpose: “to enlighten every human being coming into this world” (John XXI, 33), whom no darkness could comprehend. Hence it is said: “And the darkness did not comprehend him” (John IV). But because faith is illumined by God, it must not be darkened in any respect; it must continually set before the believer’s memory the substance of the things hoped for. For when each believer seeks the truth, he persistently seeks not another truth, but that very same truth which he bears in faith, so that through faith he may devoutly attain forever to the vision of that same fulfillment which he now believes temporarily in his heart to be eternal—not that it is itself temporary in the soul, but because the argumentation of faith is temporary until the mind strips itself of temporal things and puts on eternal things.

This, indeed, is the faith by which we truly believe and confess what God has taught or promised concerning himself, even if we do not yet understand it. Moreover, if that faith which works through love is to remain whole in us, we must do what we have promised to God in faith, so that the faith expressed in words may be proved by works. [Col. 1400A] Otherwise, he remains faithful, even if we are distrustful of him or fail entirely to fulfill in action what we have promised.

This, I say, is whole faith: if you believe in God with your whole heart and withdraw from none of his commandments; and if you keep watch lest you corrupt the faith by which you renounced the devil, his pomp, and his works. [Note: [Col. 1399D] The editor reads *observes* (“keep watch,” plural) for *observa* (“keep watch,” singular).] For this is the whole faith which the Apostle Paul boasts that he preserved: “I have kept the faith; I have finished the course” (II Tim. IV, 7); and elsewhere: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to preserve my deposit for that day” (II Tim. I, 12).

Paul therefore preserves the faith, and Christ also preserves it. Paul says of himself: “I have kept the faith”; but of God: “I am certain that he is able to preserve my deposit” (II Tim. I, 14). Yet, so that we might know that we too have a deposit from God within us, which must be guarded with whole faith, he says to Titus: “Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who dwells in you.” [Note: [Col. 1400D] The published editions omit “to Titus.”] Behold the deposit that we have entrusted to God, concerning which we ought to be certain that he will return it to us preserved—provided, of course, that we keep his deposit in our keeping inviolate in our hearts. And therefore, as I have said, whole faith is proved no less between the Creator and his work.

But if there is something concerning him that we do not believe, he is truthful and will not deny himself; we, if perhaps unbelieving, will be condemned. Since he too has entrusted himself to us, after we have renounced the devil, his pomp, and his works, it remains that we be found not guilty by preserving our promise in action, the promise in which we were reborn. [Note: [Col. 1400D] The editor reads “that we preserve it by action” (*opere ut conservemus*).] Concerning this the Holy Spirit admonishes us in the Apocalypse: “Be faithful unto death” (Apoc. II, 10). Clearly, after the end of this life there will be not faith but faith’s reward, the contemplation of the Godhead itself.

Meanwhile, while we are away from the Lord, the rights of faith must be preserved whole; [Note: [Col. 1400D] The editor reads “in the meantime” (*interim*) for “meanwhile” (*interdum*), though Paschasius usually employs *interdum*.] for it does no good to know God by faith while we deny him by our deeds and conduct. We did not first make our confession of the Godhead in baptism until after we had renounced all these things. Hence it does no good to say with the mouth of confession, “Lord, Lord,” unless you do what he commands and omit what he forbids, because “there is no partnership between light and darkness” (II Cor. VI, 14). For we who were formerly darkness have now become light in the Lord; therefore we must walk as children of light (Eph. V, 8). [Note: [Col. 1400D] The editor reads “therefore it is necessary” (*ideo necesse est*).]

Accordingly, what we once entrusted to God, so that our life might be kept hidden with Christ in heaven, we must not reclaim until Christ appears again, so that, when Christ our life appears, we too may appear with him in glory (Col. III, 4). Let us also preserve his deposit within us—the good treasure, namely, found in the field of Christ’s body, in which are “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II, 3)—carrying him in whole faith in these earthen vessels (II Cor. IV, 7), so that we may be found faithful on every side and, God forbid, be stripped by robbers on the road.

## CHAPTER V. That faith is twofold, though one and the same, just as charity is proclaimed to be one

Let this have been said about the faith that is directed toward God. Let us now see whether faith must also be preserved toward one’s neighbor, especially since we read in Solomon: “Possess faith with your neighbor” (Ecclus. XXII, 18). This is so because faith is a common possession; it is not rightly possessed by one person without a neighbor. Even if the person to whom you intend to preserve your faith lacks faith, you must nevertheless possess yours in him. [Note: [Col. 1401D] The editions read “if you intend to preserve yours,” omitting “to whom.”] Otherwise, how can anyone rightly possess alone what he immediately loses without the other?

Therefore each person must possess in another the faith that he carries in his own heart, and must not doubt it so as to lose it, even when his neighbor has lost his own. Faith without hypocrisy is therefore a great treasure, in which truth is preserved. For this reason it should shine back and forth among neighbors through reciprocal affections, so that the common possession of the mind may unite many: while it works love toward one’s neighbor, each person guards for the other the truth that he loves to have preserved in himself.

Hence, as I said, faith is rightly proclaimed to be twofold. For just as there is charity by which God is loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength, so there must also be faith by which that same God is believed with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength of faith; once believed, he is loved; once loved, he is held with certain hope. Therefore let us preserve wholly the faith that we have promised him concerning ourselves. [Col. 1401C] [Note: [Col. 1401D] The edition reads, “that he be loved,” omitting “with the whole strength.” The published text lacks “with the whole strength: just as he must be loved, so there must also be faith by which that same God is believed with the whole heart and the whole soul.”]

For faith without works is declared by the Apostle to be dead (James II, 26); “the righteous person lives by faith,” but faith is brought to life by its own and its righteous works. [Note: [Col. 1401D] The edition reads, “pious,” but “its own” is preferable. A little later it adds: “Let his faith live by its own and righteous works.”] If it has died, it cannot give life to its possessor.

Therefore let no one deceive himself. If he wishes the righteous person to live by faith, let his faith live through its own and righteous works. He himself must be brought to life through the faith that lives, lest he himself die through the faith that is dead.

Faith must be preserved toward one’s neighbor in such a degree and of such a kind as one wishes faith to be preserved toward oneself by that neighbor. Otherwise no one gives another the faith that he takes away from his own heart. [Note: [Col. 1402D] The editions read “another’s” (*alterius*), but “to another” (*alteri*) is preferable.] Therefore what we lose is ours, when we deny faith to our neighbor; and consequently, to the extent that we preserve it for ourselves, to that extent we bestow it upon another.

But this proposition does not correspond equally to its two sides. For we are not commanded to believe everyone concerning his own faith, as we know about our own faith. Many people say many things, and therefore faith is rare. But, as I stated above, we judge something more credible in another to the extent that, in the person whose faith it is, it has worked more fruitfully through love toward God and neighbor. [Note: [Col. 1402D] The published editions omit “is.”] Nevertheless, we read the Apostle’s statement: “Charity believes all things” (I Cor. XIII, 7).

Does this persuade us for that reason to believe the falsehoods of our neighbors? If it believes all things, we must ask: which things? Otherwise we might perhaps become entangled in errors. It believes, therefore, all credible things without exception concerning God, in whom there is no falsehood; and therefore it believes all things divinely spoken concerning him.

Toward one’s neighbor, however, it receives faith according to measure. If he is wise, he does not even believe himself with his whole heart, because “every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV, 2). Therefore only those things are credible in us that are supported by divine truth. But those things that are not yet grasped in our brothers by the light of truth, nor exposed by the falsehood of deception, must be endured in faith for the sake of charity until the Lord comes, who “will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the counsels of hearts” (I Cor. IV, 5).

The Apostle likewise says: “Receive the one who is weak in faith, not for disputes” [Col. 1402B] (Rom. IV, 1), lest, when he is not believed, he suffer the scandal of discouragement.

Therefore faith must be preserved toward all—from ourselves, from friends, and from enemies: [Note: [Col. 1402D] The editions omit “from friends, namely, in God; from enemies.”] toward friends, indeed, in God; toward enemies, for God’s sake. For just as God is charity, so truth is also proclaimed to be divine. Nor should it be thought that we owe our neighbors, or any human being, any other faith than that which works through love.

But the faith that fosters unlawful human desires is not to be called faith. Just as the intention by which iniquity is loved is not charity but hatred of the soul, so neither is it faith but unbelief when one supports a neighbor while knowing that he wishes what is harmful and what it is unlawful to approve. For the only faith of Christians is that which works through love. Hence each person is proved faithless when he is shown to be without the faith of Christians toward God and neighbor.

Moreover, to the extent that it harms us when our neighbor’s charity toward us is broken, so too does it harm us when faith is violated—provided, of course, that our own faith or charity toward God and neighbor is preserved whole within us.

No one unwillingly loses this possession; no one bestows it upon another without fruit; no one loses it after giving it; it is not diminished when given to many; and it is preserved for no one without being expended.

## CHAPTER VI. That this form of expression is never rightly understood of another, but only of God, when we say, “I believe in God”

1. The proper force of this expression must therefore be considered when, on the authority of the Creed that we confessed in baptism, we say: “I believe in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ, his Son,” with “I believe” understood. Then: “I believe also in the Holy Spirit.” In all three persons there is one confession handed down by the Apostles, one proper meaning of the word, to be confessed by all in intelligible speech.

No one rightly says, “I believe in my neighbor,” or “in an angel,” or “in any creature.” Accordingly, throughout all the divine Scriptures you will find the proper force of this confession preserved for God alone. From this it is clear to whom the one confession is owed: there is one Godhead. Whatever we believe concerning the Father, preserving the relation of the persons, we believe wholly concerning the Son and wholly concerning the Holy Spirit—namely, one consubstantial God, one omnipotence, one greatness, one life, and one truth. Whatever, as I have said, we believe the Father to be substantially, we confess the Son and the Holy Spirit to be wholly the same, without distinction of persons.

Yet we say, “I believe any human being,” just as we say, “I believe God.” Hence the Lord says: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also” (John V, 46). We therefore believe the patriarchs and prophets; we believe the Apostles and holy preachers; we believe the holy angels; we believe our neighbors, whom we do not doubt to be people of good faith. Yet we never read that anyone rightly believed in any one of them. [Note: [Col. 1403D] The editions read “in any one of them” in the feminine form, less well.]

We believe them because they participate in the truth and goodness of God; yet we do not believe in them, because they are not themselves believed or proclaimed substantively as truth, goodness, light, or life. Therefore, throughout all the passages of Scripture, the privilege of this expression is rightly reserved for God.

Thus, wishing to show himself consubstantial with the Father, the Lord says in the Gospel: “You believe in God; believe also in me” (John XIV, 1). Unless he were also God, it would not be right to believe in him. He therefore commands belief in himself so that he may present himself to his own as God.

2. But wretched heretics always find loopholes for their perversity through which they may escape. They say that the Creed must also be confessed as follows—not because they received this from apostolic authority, but because they added it from their own falsehood: “I believe also in the holy catholic Church.” It should not be understood in that way. The syllable added from the falsehood of the Macedonians must be removed, since they taught that the Holy Spirit was a creature; instead, one must say: “I believe the holy Church to exist,” just as one says, “the life eternal” and “the resurrection of the flesh.” Otherwise, if we believe in the holy Church, we seem to believe in a human being, which is not permitted.

For the holy Church began from human beings, not human beings from the Church. Therefore whoever says that he believes in the Church confesses that he believes in human beings. For this reason such an expression must be removed in every instance and offered to God alone, in whom one must believe with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength—namely, in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one God, the highest good, the highest blessedness, and the highest salvation of believers—and in no other, but only in his majesty.

Nevertheless, it is one thing to believe that God exists and another to believe in God. The demons believe that God exists and tremble (James II, 19), but, blinded by their own wickedness, they cannot believe in God. For believing in God is certainly not approved in anyone who has not hoped piously.

To believe in God means to seek him faithfully and to pass over wholly into him through love. Therefore “I believe in God” means: I worship him in hope and love; I adore him; and I transfer and pour my whole self into the service of his devotion.

3. This is the faith, as the Apostle Paul says, “that works through love” (Gal. VI). It works through love when it loves God for God’s sake and one’s neighbor as oneself, directing that love toward God. This love of God is preserved whole when faith is not denied to one’s neighbor.

This deposit must therefore be preserved for our neighbor among us according to the law. Paul admonishes his disciple concerning it, saying: “Guard the good deposit” (II Tim. I, 14). It is good, indeed, because without the deposit of faith we neither owe nor fulfill anything rightly; through it we preserve everything whole for our neighbors. Otherwise, “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV, 23). Therefore, through the faith of Christ, faith must be preserved for one’s neighbor; without it love is removed and the charity that is directed toward God is violated.

We therefore believe also in the words of God, because they are eternal and unchangeable. [Note: [Col. 1403D] The editor reads “since” (*quoniam*) for “because” (*quomodo*).] Hence it is said: “They believed his words, and they praised his praise” (Ps. CV, 12). We must believe in the divine Scriptures because they are from God, so that we doubt nothing in them at all. Otherwise, how do we believe in God with our whole heart if any wavering of faith has perhaps shaken the mind’s confidence in them?

This must therefore be believed first: that God has spoken in all the divine Scriptures, just as we confess according to the faith of the Council of Nicaea, that the Holy Spirit spoke through the prophets. And the Lord says of himself: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John VI, 63). “For I do not speak from myself,” he says (John XIV, 10), because he truly comes from the Father.

Therefore we must believe in the words of God as we believe in God, since they are from God; for they are eternal and unchangeable. [Note: [Col. 1404D] The editor reads *quia* (“because”) for *quoniam* (“since”).] We believe and hope in those words. [Note: [Col. 1404D] The editor omits “because” (*quia*).] For it is not permissible to believe in something if it is not permissible to hope in it; and it is absurd to hope except in God and in the words that are from God. Hence the Psalmist says: “I have hoped exceedingly in your word” (Ps. CXVIII, 147).

Therefore, whenever we do not believe the words of God’s saints because they are from God, we commit an offense. Hence Zechariah is rightly condemned by the angel: “Because you did not believe my words” (Luke I, 20). No one doubts that the angel’s words were words of God, and everything that is from truth is certainly from God.

Therefore, if someone does not submit to truth but believes in iniquity, he sins—even though we are not obliged to believe everyone. It is clear, then, that we ought to believe and hope in God, and in the words that are from God, with our whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength; but toward our neighbors we must merely believe them and, so far as depends on us, preserve whole faith for them.

## CHAPTER VII. How many kinds of credible things are there?

1. There are three kinds of credible things. Some are believed quite easily, yet, although believed, are never understood. Such are the histories of temporal events and accounts of things. Although they are believed, because they are not intelligible they never demand understanding. Rather, from the senses—through which we have perceived some things by seeing, hearing, tasting, touching, or smelling—we judge the things spoken to be credible by reimagining them in memory. But because the intellect is shown not to be subject to imaginables, such things are never understood, although they are believed.

They are believed from a kind of energy reimagined in memory, because neither past nor absent things are now subject to the senses, although they are not understood; for they are temporal. [Note: [Col. 1405D] The published editions omit “now.”] [Note: [Col. 1405D] The published editions omit “now.”]

Others are believed and immediately understood, such as all human rational principles by which rational matters are grasped. These are not merely believed once apprehended; they are immediately understood. For example, when we discuss numbers or any of the disciplines of the liberal arts: if we believe that one and two make three, who does not immediately understand that this is so?

We call understanding seeing with the eye of the mind. We therefore believe that everything numerable consists of one, because all numbers arise from one, proceed through one, and tend toward one; and we not only believe this but also understand it. For unity is never emptied by any multiplicity of number. Take two, for example: what is it except two unities? Unity and duality together are shown to be three. You will find this nowhere else among other numbers in the same way, since their extremes cannot exist without a middle.

One, two, and three placed together make six, which is the first perfect number of all numbers. Therefore the Triune God perfected all temporal things in the number six and rested on the Sabbath, which is the one and final everlasting rest.

We therefore believe, and as soon as we believe it we are rightly permitted to understand, that all things are gathered from one, through one, and into one. For example, six begins from one, is multiplied through one, and arrives at the number six in one; and so likewise ten, one hundred, and one thousand.

A human being and the world also proceed from one, through one, and into one, so that a human being is one and the world is one, although their members are many and are joined together individually into one.

Let these few remarks suffice concerning such matters. Yet, as I stated above, as soon as they are believed they are understood with certainty according to reason. If you examine everything, you will find that nothing intelligible exists without the unity of the Trinity and the Trinity of unity, because all things have been established in number, weight, and measure.

In individual things there is a multiplicity of unity, just as in the whole there is a unity of multiplicity. In God, however, there is the perfect Trinity of unity and the simple unity of Trinity.

2. Those things that are divinely spoken concerning God are both credible and intelligible; but unless they are first believed, they are never understood. Therefore they must be believed with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength, so that, with Christ illuminating us, they may be understood partly in this life and wholly in the future. We shall understand them here or there more fully and perfectly in proportion as we are purer in heart and more observant of God’s commands and precepts.

Hence the Prophet sings: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Ps. CXVIII, 104), because understanding arises from observance of the commandments and wisdom is granted. “The law of the Lord,” he says, “is immaculate, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, granting wisdom to the simple; the commandment of the Lord is also lucid, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. XVIII, 8–9).

The illumination of perfect understanding is therefore the reward of faith, because observance of God’s commandments descends from the perfect strength of faith. [Note: [Col. 1405D] The editions read “from the unity” instead of “from the strength.”] Otherwise, unless you first believe perfectly, human being, and unless faith lives through works, you will not be able to understand; for “the fear of the Lord is holy, a good understanding for all who do it” (ibid., v. 10).

Someone may stretch himself to the utmost, endowed with talent and vigorous in reasoning; he may desire to understand God as he is, invent examples for himself in his mind, form images, and set forth arguments. Yet he does not grasp what he hears or reads, and perhaps says, “Either it is so, or it is not so at all.” O unhappy and blind wandering of the mind, which carries an image of God within itself! It thinks that, though blind, it can comprehend what is immense and incomprehensible. It does not wish to believe, but immediately seeks to understand by its own skill, without the works through which understanding is acquired—or, worse, it fashions God in its heart from the visible imagination of material things.

Let such a person return to the proper order and say with the Prophet: “Give me understanding” (Ps. CXVIII, 34); and, if not so that I may understand you in the present, at least so that I may deserve to search out and keep your law with my whole heart.

It is enough to know or believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, one majesty, and whatever he himself has taught concerning himself, even if we do not understand how it is—provided only that we obey the commandments by faith. “If you wish,” he says to someone, “to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. XIX, 17). He does not say, “Understand how, what sort, or how great I am”; rather, he commands the fulfillment of the commandments. For, as we have already stated, understanding is increased daily from Christ’s commandments, so that the God of gods may be contemplated most clearly—not here to any great extent, but in Zion, as he is. [Note: [Col. 1406D] The edition omits “daily.”] [Note: [Col. 1406D] The edition adds “by him.”]

We do not say these things because no one ought sometimes to possess and investigate understanding of God, but because this belongs to few. We recall the Christian to caution: although we do not yet all understand, we must believe in our hearts the credible things that come from God, for righteousness, and confess them with our mouths, for salvation. Otherwise, as Isaiah says (Isa. VII, 9), unless we believe, I do not merely say that we will not understand; we will not even remain in Christ, through whom we might understand.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the true and undoubted discipline of faith

1. It is clear that everything known is known not from its own nature but from the nature of those who comprehend it. So too everything believed is rightly believed not from itself but through the efficacy of faith, illumined by the spirit of piety. Yet things that are believed from eternal realities must neither be believed within the limits of understanding nor understood outside faith. Rather, the faith by which the things that must be believed concerning Christ’s incarnation are believed in the catholic manner is supported by the knowledge that comes through the Holy Spirit, just as the understanding that concerns the divinity of the whole Trinity and its unity is illumined by the spirit of understanding.

Hence the Apostle says: “To one is given the word of wisdom through the Holy Spirit; to another the word of knowledge; to another faith in the same Spirit” (I Cor. XII, 8). This faith, so that it may be firm and undoubted, is instructed and strengthened on every side by the spirit of wisdom and knowledge.

Thus the things concerning Christ are entrusted to the mind of the believer by the spirit of knowledge. Although not everything concerning him is known, nevertheless, with whole faith, whatever the Teacher of truth has taught is believed—no less concerning his humanity than concerning the divinity of the Godhead, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—even if it is understood less fully.

A mind imbued with this teaching nourishes faith in a kind of inner retreat, the faith that Truth has disclosed to believers. It understands that nothing is left to it by its own nature in which it could render a greater service or gift to its Creator than to understand him only to the extent that he cannot be understood or known, although he can be believed.

Faith therefore takes precedence over our knowledge or understanding. Even though God is not yet known or understood as he is, because he exists, he is believed in faith as he is, together with everything that divine speech proclaims concerning him, so that through faith he may be understood more perfectly.

For this reason understanding has taken up faith as necessary religion, because the eternity and majesty of the Godhead surpass it. Yet because God is not comprehended from his own nature but is believed through the efficacy of faith, sometimes more and sometimes less, people occasionally go astray when they presume wrongly in faith—not because of the one who taught what he knew: that he himself is wholly and most fully the one God, immeasurable and incomprehensible. [Note: [Col. 1407D] The edition reads “incomparable,” but “incomprehensible” is preferable.]

Therefore true and undoubted faith is that which believes most fully everything that Truth has taught concerning itself and divinely inspired those whom it chose to disclose the canonical Scriptures to believers. If people believed those writers, they would certainly have believed God, since the writers uttered nothing other than what had been divinely inspired.

When those things are not believed or are interpreted otherwise than they were spoken, a human being is deceived by his own impiety or feigned faith. [Note: [Col. 1407D] The editor reads “are” (*sunt*) for “were spoken” (*dicta sint*).] [Note: [Col. 1407D] The edition reads “in piety,” which is not suitable; the editor correctly noted in the margin that “through impiety” should be read.] It would be better to believe without understanding than, by understanding wrongly, to be subject to errors. [Note: [Col. 1408D] The edition reads “the one understanding,” rather than “by understanding wrongly.”]

Hence it is also said: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not search out what is too deep for you” (Ecclus. III, 22). This does not mean that things unseen should not be sought, since they are eternal, even though they are higher than temporal things; it means that they should be investigated by faith rather than by human reason.

We forbid the use of reason to search out what is higher than the Godhead. For if the depths of such majesty could be searched out, faith would not be necessary, since human reason would comprehend everything. The bodily sense does not penetrate what is eternal and invisible; it does not apprehend incorporeal things, because it lies below them.

2. Imagination, which frequently exists in memory alone, judges every bodily form without matter; yet it does not apprehend what God is, since God has no bodily form derived from underlying matter.

Reason transcends this kind of representation as well. It considers through its own reflection both the senses and forms in their universality, yet it does not reach what exists in the individual natures of creatures—how much less can it search out what is incomprehensible in the Godhead?

Understanding, a higher eye in the soul, rises beyond the sphere of the whole universe and, at times, knowing that very nature of the Godhead in part, contemplates it. Hence the Apostle says: “We know in part and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, the partial will be abolished” (I Cor. XIII, 9).

But faith, which exists through love, although it is partial in its mode of possession, believes wholly, not partially, everything that is unseen, just as the Teacher of truth instructed and the Holy Spirit disclosed. It believes what understanding has not yet grasped. Therefore the righteous person lives not from understanding but from faith.

The higher embraces and judges the lower; the lower cannot in any way rise to the higher. The sense cannot accomplish anything apart from matter, just as imagination cannot function apart from forms—which the Greeks call *ideas*. [Note: [Col. 1408D] The edition reads “the form itself.”] The senses do not reach these forms for the sake of discernment, indeed they do not reach them at all. Nor does the *energia*—the active power—reach the standard of reason, which freely distinguishes each thing belonging to its own faculty without the coloring of imagination, although even it cannot yet behold the simple form of understanding that belongs to the Godhead.

Understanding therefore rises above all these faculties and distinguishes all the forms of reason and imagination. It also knows everything material and sensible that exists below it, yet it uses neither reason, imagination, nor the senses. With that purest eye of the mind, in a single act, it sees everything that lies beneath it.

But because it has not yet been thoroughly cleansed or clothed in complete incorruption, it must sometimes be purified by faith while we are on the way. Otherwise, as Isaiah confesses: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VII, 9).

Understanding is the reward of faith. Therefore we believe by faith what we do not yet understand and venerate it by works, so that by understanding we may grasp the whole of what is contained in faith.

Because God is Truth in this matter, understanding does not rightly dispute about faith, since faith believes what understanding and knowledge have not yet apprehended. It rests upon the rock, which is Christ, and unhesitatingly believes everything that the Holy Spirit has set forth in the Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments. The word of God, poured out by the power of the Holy Spirit into our ears, is sufficient; no one who is truly wise rightly judges it.

Therefore by faith alone we must fulfill what has been commanded, worshiping and venerating the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as he himself taught concerning himself—the one who alone knows himself, and into whom the angels themselves desire to look (I Pet. I, 12).

But because we cannot yet contemplate what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (I Cor. II, 9), let us believe in him in whom all these things exist. For he is the fountain of life, the unchangeable power, the unfailing light, the highest and everlasting good. How great is the abundance of their sweetness who fear him and believe in him with their whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength! [Note: [Col. 1409D] The edition reads “because of how great,” rather than “how great.”]

3. No one, therefore, understands all that God is except insofar as the Spirit reveals it to believers. As the Apostle Paul testifies: “God has revealed it to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among human beings knows what belongs to a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him?” (I Cor. II, 10).

See how well he reasons concerning the one who is ineffable and incomprehensible: even the spirit within a human being does not know what is in that human being who is beside us, and this spirit is shown to be what we are; yet it scarcely knows itself and does not apprehend what it itself is.

What, do you think, can human reason say about that nature which even angels do not apprehend? They contemplate him as he is, worship and love him; nevertheless, they neither doubt nor investigate how he is eternal without beginning and without end, or how the Father begot the Son while he never existed without the Son, or other matters of this kind that are ineffably spoken concerning him.

The truth, then, is what Paul says: “No one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God” (I Cor. II, 11). Therefore God’s nature—what he is, what kind he is, or how great he is—is known neither by sense, nor by any imagination, nor by human reason. But if someone has the Spirit who is from God, he knows the things that have been given to us by God (ibid., 12), so that we may believe in him and confess with heart and mouth that he is the one from whom, through whom, and in whom all visible things exist. [Note: [Col. 1409D] The published editions omit “and in whom are all visible things, in whom.”] Hoping in him, we desire to come to him, so that we may enjoy the eternal things more ardently and without end.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the faith of baptism, which must not be changed
1. The faith of baptism, by which those foreknown and predestined [Col. 1409D] for life are reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, is that faith which is commended to believers in love in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Lord says to the disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). This faith, so to speak, appeared perceptibly in Christ’s baptism when the Father thundered over him: “This is [Col. 1410A] my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 3:17).

[Note: [Col. 1409D] The edition reads *quod*, “that/because,” but *quando*, “when,” is better.]

And, so that the Father’s command might be fulfilled—he had forewarned us, “Hear him”—no one who reconsiders this faith ought to be received: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Since we have discussed this more fully in Matthew, we have set down only a few things here, because the subject is faith: so that not only may the Trinity of the entire majesty be declared most evidently intelligible, but also, although incomprehensible, may in some way be handled with the clearest light for understanding, as though distinguished by bodily senses. The Father, plainly, cries out to the Son with a voice; the same Son, truly made human in the flesh, is more fully proclaimed by that very Father; while the Holy Spirit is shown over [Col. 1410B] him in the form of a dove.

Moreover, through the very many things [Note: [Col. 1409D] The edition reads *plurimum* (“very greatly”); *plurima* (“very many things”) is better.] that John still did not know about Christ, he is taught by divine instruction, and the prophetic utterance is fulfilled: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of majesty has thundered; the Lord is over many waters” (Ps. 28:3). The Son, therefore, is proclaimed by the Father; he is proclaimed by the Holy Spirit; and he is also proclaimed by himself, when he reveals the Father concerning himself and testifies that he and the Father are one: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

What, then, can the mind, reborn through such a sacrament, retain any further element of doubt in the faith, when at one and the same moment the Father’s voice, descending to us, proclaims the Son visibly appearing in the waters, and the Holy Spirit above, in the form of a dove, teaches more clearly what ought to be understood about him?

[Note: [Col. 1409D] In the editions this passage is read somewhat differently: *Quid igitur ultra menti, tali renatae sacramento, dubitationis [Col. 1410D] momenti? Patris vox ad nos delapsa*—“What further force of doubt, then, is there for a mind reborn through such a sacrament? The Father’s voice has descended to us.”]

And if, indeed, “every word shall stand on the testimony of two or [Col. 1410C] three witnesses,” the testimony concerning himself of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit is rightly received with much greater firmness .

2. In this faith, then, we have been reborn. Why should we further reconsider the faith as though uncertain? The apostles have been commanded: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” When he said “in the name,” therefore, he showed that they are one, while [Note: [Col. 1410D] The edition reads *quia*, “because,” instead of *quod*, “that/which.”] he distinguished the Trinity with admirable clarity by three names sufficient for understanding. Yet he taught that these three are one name [Note: [Col. 1410D] The edition reads *nomine* (“by name”) instead of *nomen* (“name”)]; for although it is said, “Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Ps. 104:4), and also, “Seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7), nevertheless we ought rightly to [Col. 1410D] seek none other than the one God in three persons, in whose Trinitarian name we have been sealed. Under this faith, having been stripped of the world’s possessions, we entered the font naked.

In that font, whoever among us has been baptized in Christ Jesus [Note: [Col. 1410D] The edition omits *In Christo Jesu, in morte ipsius baptizati sumus*—“In Christ Jesus, we have been baptized into his death.”] has been baptized into his death: “For we have been buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. 6:4). Therefore we must no longer reconsider anything concerning the faith, but in every way preserve what we have believed [Note: [Col. 1410D] The edition reads *quae* (“the things which”) instead of *quod* (“what”)], and, by believing, have freely [Col. 1411A] received from God . We must believe absolutely that nothing else is to be believed; therefore it is not to be sought either, since we have believed that it has already been found. We seek nothing else, because he himself does not command us to seek anything else, since he is one; and we know [Note: [Col. 1411D] The edition reads *sumus* (“we are”), wrongly, instead of *scimus* (“we know”).] that, apart from this one thing, nothing else is necessary.

We embrace him because he is one; and, with the affection of a sure devotion, progressing, hoping, and loving in one and the same faith, we continually seek him because he is infinite, until [Note: [Col. 1411D] The edition reads *nunc* (“now”) instead of *donec* (“until”)], in an enigma and not yet in his visible form, we daily search out with the most ardent love the one whom [Note: [Col. 1411D] The edition reads *et quem* (“and whom”) instead of *quem* (“whom”).] we seek while holding him.

And when the enigmas of present things have been removed, we are also certain that no other God than the one and the same Trinity will appear to those who believe in him, just as we have now received him through faith. Through this [Col. 1411B] faith, therefore, the light of God’s face has been sealed upon us; and for that reason we must not look toward the infidelities of certain people or toward darkness and errors.

Relying, then, on the proof that future times are proclaimed as dangerous [Note: [Col. 1411D] The edition reads *praenuntiantur*, “are foretold,” instead of *pronuntiantur*, “are proclaimed.”], we desire, by warning in advance, to admonish certain people not to receive anything further [Note: [Col. 1411D] The editions add *nihil recipiendum*, “nothing is to be received.”] except what they received by believing in baptism, and that this—not something else—is what they must meanwhile seek. For the reasoning of seeking seems to consist only in three aspects of things: the object, the time, and the manner.

The object: so that we may consider what is to be sought.

The time: so that we may know when, lest perhaps we seek when we ought not, or fail to find sufficiently either something else or the very thing we are seeking. [Note: [Col. 1411D] In the editions this whole passage is given less clearly as follows: *Nec forte quando quaerendum non est, ne aut illud quod quaerimus, non satis inveniamus*—“Nor perhaps when one ought not to seek, lest we fail sufficiently to find even that which we seek.” The printed construction is retained.]

The manner: so that we may determine how far it is necessary to seek.

Therefore we must scrutinize [Col. 1411C] what Christ instituted, and hold fast to the one whom we rejoice to have found, because you could not have believed unless you had first found him. You sought in order to find [Note: [Col. 1411D] The edition reads *invenias*, “you may find,” instead of *invenires*, “you might find.”]; but you found in order to believe. In this faith, by believing, you fixed the whole process of seeking and finding, when you buried yourself with Christ in death through the tomb of the font, after the world had been stripped away [Note: [Col. 1411D] The edition reads *et spoliatus* (“and having been stripped”), rather than *exspoliato* (“after the world had been stripped”).]

But if you truly died, and your life has been hidden with God in heaven, why do you still argue about the faith with those who live for themselves and not for God, as though uncertain? Or why, when the persecutor rages, do you fear death, since you are already dead and are held with Christ in the tomb of the font, and you firmly believe that your life has been stored up in heaven? There is no doubt that if you take back your former life on earth, you have lost the new life [Col. 1411D] that you had hidden in heaven with Christ.

He has confined you within such a tomb, since he does not now want you henceforth to believe anything other than what he instituted. Therefore you too must certainly seek nothing else [Note: [Col. 1412D] *Profecto*, “certainly,” is absent from the editions.], nor, even when delivered over to tortures [Note: [Col. 1412D] The edition reads *adactus etsi invitus*, “driven, even if unwilling,” instead of *addictus, ac si invitus*, “delivered over, as if unwilling.”], confess anything else, as if unwillingly.

Finally, I judge it better to [Col. 1412A] remain in ignorance beneath the sacrament of baptism [Note: [Col. 1412D] The edition reads *manentem*, accusative singular “remaining,” instead of nominative *manens*, “remaining.”], lest you learn what you ought not, than, caught by some fraudulent curiosity, to be led beyond the captives [the supplied *extra captivos* is uncertain; *captivos* is accusative plural, “captives”] [Note: [Col. 1412D] The edition reads *captivus*, nominative singular, “as a captive,” instead of *captivos*.].

3. The one who knows Christ knows everything: “Your faith has saved you” (Mark 10:52). Therefore let the Christian remain within the font of faith from which he was reborn for salvation [Note: [Col. 1412D] The edition reads *ex quo*, “from which” in the masculine, rather than *ex qua*, “from which” in the feminine.]. And if he should hesitate about anything for a moment, let him touch Christ, still in the font, with the hand of faith—the font into which the Word, descending as flesh, was baptized for us.

Then, so that he may instruct us through the external ear, let him hear with the hearing of the inner ear the Father’s voice thundering from above: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). This voice, as though to convey something to him through a body [Note: [Col. 1412D] The edition reads *ejus*, “of him,” rather than *ad eum*, “to him.”], was indeed a real body, because it was perceptible to the ears. Therefore, since the Father resounded[Col. 1412B]  through the voice without being enclosed within it, he is rightly said in some way to have become perceptible to the ears, although he is incomprehensible [Note: [Col. 1412D] *Jure*, “rightly,” is absent from the edition.], just as the Holy Spirit is also shown to have appeared visibly through the form presented beneath him.

Nevertheless, according to the nature proper to him, since God the Trinity is rightly said to be wholly everywhere, he is not perceived as being in a place, because he is proved to be incorporeal, without place, and invisible. He is not bounded by sight, nor held by touch, nor heard through speech, nor sensed by movement.

Hence it is also said: “No one has ever seen God; but the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he himself will declare him to us” (John 1:18) [Note: [Col. 1412D] The edition reads *narravit*, “has declared,” rather than *narrabit*, “will declare.”]. This should not, however, be understood as though he ought to resound in our ears through sound; rather, because he is the Word and image [Col. 1412C] of the Father, when he makes himself known to our minds, he declares and reveals the Father manifestly through ineffable light, in accordance with his own testimony: “Whoever sees me sees my Father also” (John 14:9).

This vision is not grasped by bodily senses, but, as it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). The Father therefore proclaims the Son through the perceptible sound of a voice; and the Son, by showing himself visibly, since he is the Father’s Word, declares in himself none other than the one whose Son he is.

Moreover, the Holy Spirit, because [Note: [Col. 1412D] The edition reads *qui* (“who”) instead of *quia* (“because”).] he proceeds from the Father and the Son, is himself not divided in the nature of the substance of the majesty, but distinct in person; and, so that God the Trinity might be disclosed to human beings, he appeared in the middle in the form of a dove. Yet he is not thereby bounded by sight, just as the [Col. 1412D] Father is not here or elsewhere heard through speech, nor could he be sensed by movement when he walked in paradise.

Otherwise, whenever he showed himself to the fathers through an assumed form, he could be thought to have been perceptible, which it is absurd to believe. Rather, because he is invisible, he was seen as he willed—not as he is, but in whatever form he was pleased to appear. Here, moreover, he was heard differently, [Col. 1413A] not only by John, but elsewhere also by others inwardly; and differently by the crowd here or elsewhere, who in one place said that thunder had occurred (John 12:29).

Therefore it is not surprising if very many do not obey the preacher’s voice [Note: [Col. 1413D] The edition reads *voci … obediunt*, “obey … the voice,” with dative *voci* instead of accusative *vocem*. The ellipsis is in the printed note.], when it is proved that this voice also, although many heard it, benefited them nothing [Note: [Col. 1413D] The edition reads *cum et hanc vocem multis audientibus nihil profuisse probatur*—“when this voice too is proved to have benefited its many hearers nothing.”]. For it is God who gives increase within, without a voice. Concerning him blessed Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1413D] The edition omits *quod*, “that,” introducing the quotation]: “When he is thought to be absent, he is seen; and when he is present, he is not seen.” He did not say, “He is absent,” but “when he is thought to be absent.” For he is nowhere absent who fills heaven and earth and all things. He is not enclosed within small spaces or spread throughout great ones, but is wholly everywhere and contained by no place.

4. Whoever [Note: [Col. 1413D] The editions read *quivis credente mente intelligat, etsi distinctus*—“let anyone understand with a believing mind, although distinct”—omitting these words: *hic videt Deum, et cum absens [Col. 1414D] putatur, hic sane intelligit*—“this person sees God, and when he is thought absent, this person truly understands.”] understands this with a mind that rises beyond itself [Col. 1413B] sees God; and when he is thought to be absent, that person truly understands. Although God the Trinity appeared in baptism as distinct in persons, because he is inseparable he is wholly everywhere on account of the unity of his substance [Note: [Col. 1414D] The edition omits *fit*, “he becomes/is made.”].

Not indeed in a place, but wholly everywhere: the Father wholly in the Son, and the Son wholly in the Father, and the Holy Spirit wholly at once in the Father and the Son; and God remains coeternal. For whatever the Father is, this the Son and the Holy Spirit also are; and whatever the Son is, this the Father and the Holy Spirit are; likewise, whatever the Holy Spirit is, all this the Father and the Son are.

Yet the Father is one, the Son is another, and the Holy Spirit is another: another, I say, not another thing. For he who is the Father is not the Son or the Holy Spirit; and likewise he who is the Son is in no way the Father or the Holy Spirit; nor is the [Col. 1413C] same Spirit the Father or the Son.

Because God the Trinity desired to disclose this still more clearly to those who were inexperienced in the faith—those who did not yet know how to think of anything through the senses except corporeal things [Note: [Col. 1414D] The edition reads *temporalia*, “temporal things,” instead of *corporea*, “corporeal things.”]—he shone forth distinctly for their understanding in a threefold number of particular manifestations, so that those still infantile in faith might be drawn inward through these three senses, sight, hearing, and touch, and receive within themselves the first elements of faith.

Then, with the cooperation of the one who was perceived externally [Note: [Col. 1414D] The edition reads *quod*, “that which,” rather than *qui*, “the one who.”], perfect faith could thereafter be more fully nourished by the abundant breasts of the Scriptures. For those who were still merely natural could not yet fully grasp spiritual things. Therefore it was necessary that the tender infancy of believers receive faith through external sensation; and that the whole human being, returning inward from the sensation of the flesh and turning wholly toward God, should become spiritual by seeing invisible things through faith, and should move [Col. 1413D] upward through faith, nourished by the milk of doctrine, toward spiritual realities.

Hence very many of the saints progressed so far spiritually that, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things, they saw that these are better perceived by the mind than experienced through the bodily senses. For although sight or hearing is recorded in divine authority by many people, as in this passage, without any change in God himself, he was either seen through the body or certainly through [Col. 1414A] certain bodily images that God’s will chose, not nature’s formation. God made these things for whomever he wished, whenever he wished, and as he wished; yet his substance remained hidden within him, unchangeable, filling all things without any intervals of place or time, so that he is no less in a part than in the whole, nor greater in the whole than he is in a part.

Nevertheless, whenever he appeared as he wished in places and in time [Note: [Col. 1414D] The edition reads *apparuit*, “he appeared,” rather than *apparens*, “appearing,”] he did so in order to draw those who were themselves local and temporal toward belief in invisible things, so that they might set aside the things to which they were bound and which they saw daily being weakened by their own limitations.

Hence it is also certain, as we stated earlier, that in the font of baptism the whole divinity of the majesty in the Trinity poured itself in some way into bodily senses as [Col. 1414B] something perceptible , so that those reborn through faith might never thereafter receive another faith unto life than that through which each person is joined to God, and perish, deceived by bodily sense.

This font, indeed, has been sealed with the ring of faith; and therefore it must never admit any end. From its irrigating stream, the garden of delights—that is, the universal Church of God—flourishes green, sufficiently protected and enclosed on every side, because it rejoices that Christ within it was not only buried but also rose again.

In these first elements of faith the soul of every believer rests securely. In this faith it blossoms daily through works of virtue, and against every assault of affliction it sets up a shield of protection. Finally, surrounded by the strong rampart of excessive security, it confidently sings the words in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, [Col. 1414C] but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2) .

For it sleeps, lulled by certainty of its hope [Note: [Col. 1414D] The editions read *separata*, “separated,” but *soporata*, “lulled to sleep,” is better]; yet it remains awake with vigilant diligence, lest what has been sealed with the ring of faith be corrupted by fraud.

Therefore, as the apostle Paul testifies: “The one who approaches God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him” (Heb. 11:6). This, I say, is the complete and true faith: to believe that the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one omnipotent God, the avenger of all who despise him and the rewarder of the just. For his sake it is fitting confidently to avoid the evils he has forbidden and to do good with steadfast faith, working through love, all the way to the end of life.

## CHAPTER X. [Col. 1414D] On the power of faith 

1. Only the one who believes in God with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his strength—and not only believes but also loves him—knows the power of faith. Through this faith, the whole human being, who consists of soul and body, is promised immortality and true blessedness, not by human reasoning but by divine authority. Its power, therefore, is from God. Concerning this power [Col. 1415A] John testifies, saying: “But to all,” he says [Note: [Col. 1415D] The edition omits *inquit*, “he says.”], “who received him, he gave the power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

He immediately indicates what it means to receive him when he adds: “To those who believe in his name” (ibid.). Belief in his name is true faith, through which he gave us the power to become children of God. And if through it he gave us such power, there is no doubt that we are called and are children of God.

What, then, is there that faith cannot do, when it is certain that we have received so great a power? “We were born,” he says, “not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God” (ibid., 13). Through faith, therefore, we entered the font, although we were children of wrath; but we rose reborn from water and the Holy Spirit as children of God [Note: [Col. 1415D] The edition reads *surreximus*, “we rose,” rather than *exsurreximus*, “we rose up.”], because we first received God within us through faith.

[Col. 1415B] Therefore the Holy Spirit is God, and because we are born from him, we have certainly been born from God. But so that the weakness of our flesh, which we see and bear, would not despair of having risen to such excellence, it is immediately added: “The Word became flesh and dwelt in us” (John 1:14). This was said at least so that what seemed incredible might be persuaded from the opposite direction.

If the Son of God by nature, in his mercy, became the Son of man for the sake of the sons of men—for this is what “the Word became flesh and dwelt in us” means—how much more credible is it that, by nature sons of men and by the grace of God sons of God, we should dwell in God, having received power from the one from whom we were reborn?

In him alone, and from him alone, can we be blessed, having been made participants in his immortality, for whose sake the Son of God deigned to become a participant in [Col. 1415C] our immortality. For what is more difficult than this, when the power that is God and is from God can do all things?

Therefore, if faith is true and complete, no one knows how great the power of faith is except the one who lives from God and in God [Note: [Col. 1415D] The edition reads *nemo noverit*, “no one knows,” omitting *qui*, “who.”]. There is no doubt, then, that true faith can accomplish much with God.

By this same faith the holy men of earlier times, even without baptism, were able to do countless marvelous things. Recalling them, the apostle Paul says: “By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he received testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he still speaks” (Heb. 11:4).

See what faith could do in one and the same matter. God did not choose this sacrifice—or that one—more than the other, but the faith of the one offering it: “By faith [Col. 1415D] Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain.” By faith, not by substance, because whatever is without faith is sin (Rom. 14:23); and whatever is done with little faith is little before God, while what is done with great faith is great.

Hence he said to a certain woman: “O woman, great is your faith” (Matt. 15:28). And because it was great, hear how great a power it brought forth: “Let it be done for you as you wish.” However great or small the force with which anyone acts, it is not assessed before God beyond the measure of the faith that is offered [Note: [Col. 1415D] The edition reads subjunctive *offeratur*, “may be offered,” rather than indicative *offertur*, “is offered.”].

[Col. 1416A] 2. Therefore, with the Apostle, we must consider and count how many and how great things the earlier saints of God were able to do by faith, although they had not yet obtained the promise that we have now received in large part. Indeed, through faith they were able to do almost everything—or rather, as the Savior asks, we must believe that “all things are possible to the one who believes” (Mark 9:22).

Through faith they therefore performed many great wonders, which the apostle Paul enumerates: “The saints,” he says, “through faith conquered kingdoms, through faith practiced righteousness, and through faith obtained promises” (Heb. 11:32). Why say more? They did everything through faith, and therefore they were able to do such great things, because their faith remained true and unconquered.

And what could the apostles and holy martyrs not do through faith? They even wished, which is greater than all miracles, to despise themselves through [Col. 1416B] faith and die for Christ. Therefore they are called witnesses: in order to establish another, better, and perpetual life in Christ, they chose to depart from this fleeting and temporal life, having been subjected to harsh tortures [Note: [Col. 1416D] The edition reads *acribus*, “harsh,” agreeing with *cruciatibus*, “tortures,” instead of the printed *acris*.].

Likewise, the holy confessors, the holy virgins, and all the saints, filled with faith, did great and unspeakable things when they trampled underfoot both themselves and the present age, so that they might receive themselves immortal in blessed immortality [Note: [Col. 1416D] The edition reads *quando seipsos*, “when themselves,” omitting *et*, “also,” before *seipsos*.]. Unless they had believed Christ more than themselves, they would never have powerfully done such great things and patiently endured these sufferings.

Consider, therefore, O man, how much power the one possesses who gave his own people the ability to do such things. And if your faith is small, or nonexistent, implore faith so that it may be increased in you, because the faith that is in Christ can do all things.

Hence [Col. 1416C] Paul says: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4:13). For this reason God willed us not to examine ourselves by reasoning, but to believe in him through faith, and to know with certainty that the one who gave himself to us granted us the ability, through faith, to do all things in him.

Whenever we are unable, it is not because of weakness in the power he gave us, but because of the infidelity of sin through which we transgress, so that faith is made weaker. Therefore we must remember the throne of charity [Note: [Col. 1416D] The edition reads *solum*, “only,” rather than *solium*, “throne.”] from which we fell and do penance, so that we may powerfully fulfill through the love of Christ the former works of faith.

Otherwise, “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6), while through faith all things are possible to the believer in Christ [Note: [Col. 1416D] The edition reads *cum per fidem*, “since through faith,” rather than *cur*, “for why.”]. This is not so that one may perform miracles at an unsuitable time, but so that one may remain a son of God through adoption [Col. 1416D] after the end of time. This power is greater than anyone could hope for.

3. Therefore let faith come to our aid, since the reasoning of nature fails. And if in ourselves we are nothing, let us presume that we can do all things from him by believing, hoping, and loving. For just as it is power to be able to do all things in him, so it is great weakness to be able to do nothing or little from ourselves.

“But this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith” (1 John 5:4). Great, therefore, is the virtue of faith; great is its power. Nor is it without reason that through it we are [Col. 1417A] joined to God, and God is believed to dwell in us. If such power can come from God, because whatever our faith is, it is the substance of things hoped for—and the substance of things hoped for is God, while God is omnipotent—then divine majesty rightly granted to faith, which is from God and in which God is, the ability to do such great things, so that faith from God might be made firmer [Note: [Col. 1417D] The edition reads *persistit*, “persists,” rather than *praestitit*, “granted.”].

What, then, can we doubt about faith, when merely because we believed, the saints were able to do such great and unspeakable things [Note: [Col. 1418D] The edition reads *crediderunt*, “they believed,” rather than *credidimus*, “we believed.”], and we too can do them through faith? “This is the victory,” he says, “that conquers the world, our faith.”

It is just that faith should be able to do such things: through it we have believed what is not seen, so that the faithful may be more certain that the one in whom faith believes is supreme omnipotence and eternal power. The power of faith, therefore, is the manifestation of majesty.

[Col. 1417B] Faith has testimony from the works of miracles, since it can do nothing from itself but everything from the one by whom it is strengthened, in whom it believes. And the more it believes in the one who is greater, the more powerful it becomes. For one cannot believe more than the one in whom it is necessary to believe with one’s whole being.

Therefore, as I have said, faith cannot be retracted: it can do such great things that it conquers the world, and it has done still more through the saints, so that it has repeatedly displayed the works of the Godhead. But what is greater still, although they are dead, their faith continues daily to accomplish very numerous and extraordinary miracles, so that those who can do such things seem to live more than the living, because they live wholly in the one who can do all things.

O unwavering faith, which reaches such a victory that, even among those who have died and believed through you, you nevertheless remain vigorous in complete [Col. 1417C] omnipotence and perform works, so that you may be believed more certainly by the fearful and unbelieving. Thus nothing is truer than what you promise, nothing more powerful than the one from whom you can do such great things, and nothing happier than that you, victorious in tireless desires, lead your own and those who follow you daily with triumph to their destination.

You accomplish such things not only on earth; but, as an unconquered virgin penetrating the temples of heaven, you powerfully seize the kingdom of heaven with the weapons of your virtues. Those who fornicate apart from you you leave empty; without you we can do nothing, while through you all forces engage in battle and vices are trampled underfoot. Whoever does not believe in you will find nothing further by which he can accomplish anything belonging to life or virtue.

## CHAPTER XI. [Col. 1417D] On the righteousness of faith 

1. The righteousness of faith is that by which, through faith, we are made righteous from being ungodly, without any preceding merits of good works. By it we are freely justified without works, so that although we were children of wrath, by faith alone and through grace we may become children by adoption.

We are justified freely for this reason: even faith itself is not in us except through grace, and the justification of faith is also from grace. Hence David says: “His mercy shall go before me” (Ps. 53:1); and elsewhere he himself says: “Your mercy shall follow me” (Ps. 22:6). Otherwise, unless mercy first went before freely, no one would be faithful.

Freely, therefore, because faith is from grace. Then, when he says, “His mercy shall follow [Col. 1418A] me,” this means that Christ’s grace is granted so that each believer may remain faithful, so that the one who is righteous from faith may work through grace.

“For we reckon,” says the Apostle, “that a person is justified by faith without the works of the law” (Rom. 3:28). And shortly afterward, from Genesis: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4:3). “To the one who works,” he says, “the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt. But to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness” (ibid., 4–5).

See what faith can do: it believes in the one who is essentially righteous, so that, as he says, “the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ” may be “unto all and upon all who believe,” because one is “justified freely by his grace” (Rom. 3:22, 24). For all have sinned and [Col. 1418B] lack the glory of God .

The glory of God, therefore, is that he alone may appear righteous and powerful, from whom all are justified through faith in Jesus Christ. But we ought to ask what it means for a person to be justified without works through faith, since James says: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:26). How can it be made alive, so that the righteous person may live by faith, if it remains dead in itself beforehand?

We are therefore justified freely through faith, but not through any faith other than that which works through love. Since we are justified freely, I do not mean that no merits of faith preceded; rather, even the faith by which we would do something good was not in us. And so, while faith is poured into us without our merits, we are justified freely by faith without works.

But afterward it remains for this same [Col. 1418C] faith to persist in us through good and righteous works, so that it may be the faith that works through love, because “the righteous shall live by faith.” Otherwise, when it is dead without works, it demonstrates a dead person, so that the righteous no longer lives by faith, but believes and trembles with the demons.

2. True faith is therefore also grace, and for that reason it is never fruitless, nor does it accomplish anything without grace. The faith of Christ is given to us through the Holy Spirit by grace; by grace it is nourished; and by grace it is preserved so that it may persevere to the end. It accomplishes absolutely nothing without grace, because even faith itself, so that it may live, is freely inspired with good and righteous works.

Therefore it remains that “whoever boasts should boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17), because it depends “not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy” (Rom. 9:16). Otherwise, how can the [Col. 1418D] good that a person wills be attributed to the one who wills, or the goal toward which he runs to the one who runs, when he has neither the will nor the ability to run without the grace of the merciful God?

Do you not know, O man, that you received something already great and abundant when you began to will through God’s inspiration and to run through faith? Therefore do not boast as though you had not received it, nor applaud yourself as though from yourself you willed the good things you will or ran through faith toward the life to which you run. Rather, both willing and running already belong to the merciful God: so that, justified mercifully by grace through faith, you may not cease to will the good things that are unseen and to desire them; nor cease to run through faith toward God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, toward whom you were running, in whom are all things that are unseen and that you believe.

[Col. 1419A] Christ’s grace granted you the will [Note: [Col. 1419D] The edition reads *quidem*, “indeed,” rather than *quippe*, “indeed/for.”]; faith, by adhering to good works, showed you the way—which is Christ—and enabled you to run [Note: [Col. 1419D] *Monstravit*, “showed,” is preferable to the printed *ministravit*, “supplied.”].

Hence it is fitting to believe with all one’s heart, hope with all one’s soul, and love with all one’s strength. If you do not cease to will and to run until you arrive where you were going by willing and running by believing, then, because the omnipotent God is truthful and does not lie, you will certainly receive what you willed and, by seeing, enjoy what you believed.

Sometimes [Note: [Col. 1419D] The edition reads *interim*, “meanwhile,” instead of *interdum*, “sometimes.”], however, toil in asking; keep watch in seeking; persist in knocking, so that you do not fail. Ask by believing with the faith you received; seek by hoping for what you found; knock by loving the one to whom you entered.

For you are already living as a righteous person by faith [Note: [Col. 1419D] The edition reads *vivit*, “he lives,” rather than *vivis*, “you live.”]. Do not withdraw yourself from the life of faith, because “if you withdraw yourself, the divine Spirit,” he says, “will not please my [Col. 1419B] soul” [Note: [Col. 1419D] The edition reads *qui*, “who,” rather than *quia*, “because.”]. Beware, therefore, lest you be a child of withdrawal, but be a child of acquisition; for you have been bought and acquired by Christ’s blood.

Meanwhile, live as a righteous person by faith, presuming nothing about yourself. Let the faith of Christ, with grace cooperating, be enlivened by good and righteous works. Indeed, nothing that has been promised will be lacking [Note: [Col. 1420D] The edition reads *quidem*, “indeed,” rather than *quod*, “that.”], provided that you do not cease to will through grace and to run through faith.

This, I say, is the true righteousness of faith: not to presume upon merits, not to neglect Christ’s grace, and to attribute to him the good things you do. His grace has never been absent from anyone to whom faith, which exists through love, has been present, and through that faith the righteous person lives.

Therefore let everything we receive—the will and the ability to run, so that we may live as righteous people from God—belong to the merciful God. Concerning God’s promises, [Col. 1419C] let us give glory to God without hesitating through distrust, but strengthened by faith in all things, knowing most fully that whatever he has promised, he is powerful enough to do.

Let us also confess the good things of faith that we do, both in willing and in running: that without him we can do nothing, while through him the strengthened Apostle boasts that he can do all things. Thus we too may have glory not from ourselves, but before God .

3. For by these two we are justified: by willing through grace and by running through faith. For although there are some things that we will but cannot yet do, and others in which, by acting, we already run through faith by grace, both are nevertheless gifts of the Holy Spirit. In these, indeed, having peace with God, we are reconciled and justified freely through faith. For this reason God set forth a propitiation through faith in his blood, to demonstrate his righteousness (Rom. III, 25), so that he himself might be just and the one who justifies him who is of the faith of Jesus Christ. “To demonstrate,” he says, “his righteousness,” and not ours. Hence everything that we believe, and by which we are justified while living by faith, belongs wholly to him: truly, to the merciful God, and not to the one who runs, lest, by attributing anything to ourselves, we fall.

For Christ, as he himself says, is “the way, and the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). The way by which we run through faith; and whoever runs in it must himself walk as he walked. The truth into which we believe: by believing we come to know it, by knowing we love it; and by loving, we ask through faith, by asking we seek, and by seeking we knock. He is truly the life by which we are justified through faith, when we attribute it not to ourselves but to him from whom, justified by faith, we live. How, then, do we not live with the life [Note: [Col. 1420D] Edition: “of life”] when, hastening through faith toward the things that are not seen, we live wholly by faith? And therefore, if we are already just through faith, how can we doubt about life?

This, I say, is to believe in Christ, to be justified by faith, and to live according to him through righteous works. Concerning this faith the Savior says: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John XI, 26). Therefore, whoever is justified through faith as a just person, though previously dead as a sinner, lives because he believes in him who justifies the ungodly. And everyone who lives and believes in the things that are not seen, because they are eternal, undoubtedly lives the eternal life according to the inner person. Otherwise, how does he rightly believe, if the just person does not live by faith according to the eternal things?

Hence it is clear that faith is reckoned for righteousness not in the one who believes only in part, but in the one who truly believes with his whole being. This faith must be so great and of such a kind that it justifies the ungodly, so that he is no longer ungodly. This is sufficiently demonstrated in the case of the thief, whom Christ immediately carried from the cross into paradise as a righteous man [Note: [Col. 1420D] Edition: “carries”].

Abraham also, “because he believed, it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. IV, 3)—plainly because he believed with his whole being. For his faith had already preceded him in many affairs of his active life; at the end it was brought to completion in its several parts and gathered together in its entirety, by which he believed God wholly, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. It is by no means read in this way concerning the children of Israel, although they believed, as it is written, that they believed God and Moses his servant, and that this was reckoned to them as righteousness.

Thus, in Abraham, faith is gathered together as perfected from many parts, and ought to be reckoned as righteousness for each person, so that they may be children of Abraham. Such faith, then, and faith of such greatness, is according to the grace of Christ, so that the promise may be firm for believers through faith and not through the mind’s efficacy. That which is from grace truly justifies a person, so that he is righteous and has glory before God, whose grace enlightens him, lest any unrighteousness reign together with his faith.

Otherwise, what fellowship is there between light and darkness, or what participation between righteousness and iniquity (II Cor. VI, 14)? For if you rightly believe in Christ, you are shown to have been born of God; and whoever is born of God, as John testifies, does not sin (I John V, 18). But if he has sinned, it is evident that he does not believe perfectly. The sign, therefore, of true faith is that one does not sin; its certainty, however, is that he exercises the work of faith toward righteousness, so that he may have glory before God.

For faith is the beginning of justification before God, since it believes unto justification. And this faith, once it has been justified, like the root of a good tree after receiving rain, clings to the soil of the soul, so that branches may rise in it from Christ’s teaching and bear the fruits of works. For the root of righteousness does not come first from works; rather, the fruits of works grow from the root of righteousness, namely, from faith.

This is the root of righteousness that God accepts apart from works, provided that, remaining in that same righteousness, it produces the fruits of righteousness. This faith is not of just any kind, but wholly such as works through love: for example, mercy, kindness, gentleness, moderation, humility, patience, endurance, and the other riches of the virtues. Their fruit, together with its root, is reckoned as righteousness for every believer.
