Hence it is said of Abraham: “He believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” Nevertheless, this is according to grace and not according to debt, because, as the same Apostle says, “the grace of God is eternal life” (Rom. VI, 23). Therefore, if anyone thinks that he has faith without grace, let him consider that he has not yet obtained life, so as truly to live as a just person by faith, because in the grace of faith life is proved to be eternal.

For this reason the Apostle also says: “If I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIII, 2). Such faith, although it believes everything, has not received through grace the gift of love; therefore it does not work through love, so as to possess the eternal life by which the just person lives through faith. Otherwise, unless he lives by the life that is in Christ’s grace, how can anyone hasten toward eternity? [Note: [Col. 1421D] Edition: “who,” rather than “which.”]

Therefore, according to the Apostle, we must take the greatest care lest Christ’s grace remain empty in us. Without love it remains empty and profits us nothing, even if it removes mountains and drives out demons, because although faith may be complete in believing, the grace of love has not been perfected in action. And because grace is lacking, so that faith profits the believer nothing, eternal life is lacking to him, so that the just person may live by faith.

Hence we must pray with the apostles: “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke XVII, 5), so that it may be the faith that works through love in us, because “if anyone believes, even though he has died, he will live.” It is therefore evident that everyone who lives and believes in Christ will never die, wholly and completely, because he believes and is justified through the faith of God’s righteousness, concerning which the Prophet prays and says: “Lord, in your righteousness deliver me, and rescue me” (Ps. XXX, 2).

This righteousness of God, because it is from grace, is rightly called such; therefore the promise is held more firmly through faith, so that everyone who lives and believes will not die eternally. Otherwise, if someone believes but the just person does not yet live by faith, it profits him nothing unto life, because he is not yet subject to God’s righteousness.

Again, if someone has previously done whatever he may have done, but has been justified by this righteousness, he already lives the eternal life. Whoever has lived the eternal life will not die eternally, because what he lives is eternal, while he lives wholly in Christ, who is life, believing, hoping, and loving him with his whole being.

## CHAPTER XII. What the armor, or instruments, of faith are, by which it can accomplish so much

[Col. 1422A]

1. The armor, or instruments, of faith are the virtues to be practiced in life, by which faith is made alive through the Holy Spirit and strengthened in the inner person, so that it can withstand everything. This is that tower from the Gospel (Luke XIV, 28), which is built at the expense of the virtues, in which a thousand shields hang, together with all the armor of the strong. If someone wishes to erect it without these materials, it collapses, so that all who see him begin to mock him, because he began to build a tower of faith but was unable to finish it.

Therefore no one builds faith, so that it may reach as far as heaven and withstand everything, without the expense of the virtues. Its foundation, that it may be firm, is Christ, the strength of all the virtues [uncertain reading: loquatur]. Built with square stones through patience, endurance, and perseverance, it is brought to completion. It is secured by certain hope in heaven, lest it be shaken on earth amid the waves of temptations, like an anchor; and, as the Apostle testifies, we have this hope safely in heaven.

By love, the structure of the virtues is joined together between God and the human being or neighbor, and an indissoluble connection is cemented in a godlike manner, because love is the bond of perfection. In it the power of faith and the strength that it has from God fight with an extended hand, bearing the shield of good will, lest it be struck by the enemy; and from this it crowns itself in God.

Prudence, like an eye, observes with the utmost sharpness what things bring salvation and what adversities must be avoided. Counsel indicates how we may escape the former or preserve the latter. Justice clothes and covers faith like a breastplate, so that it may not be wounded. The sword of the Holy Spirit, which is the word of God, strikes the enemy forcefully.

Humility, for its part, the guardian of the virtues, binds together and arranges what we gather, lest the breeze and the wind of temptations scatter it here and there, so that, with Christ raising it up, the tower of faith may rise step by step. There obedience labors vigorously, if in any way it can please him who has proved himself through faith.

Gentleness, moderation, and kindness arrange the movements of the soul gently and pleasantly, lest they injure love in anything. Fear also pricks the conscience and brings the one running among the snares of temptations back to caution. But lest he be swallowed up by sorrows, the joy of the Spirit and the exultation of spiritual life gladden the mind, so that faith rejoices more in sufferings than in prosperity.

Wisdom and understanding illuminate it; it girds itself manfully with truth, so that it may be strong. Temperance, which is also called discernment, nourishes and governs all these instruments of the virtues like a mother, lest they grow weak [Note: [Col. 1422D] Edition: “lest it grow weak”], and lest lack of proportion dissolve the harmony and concord of the virtues.

2. Thus fortified with such weapons and the like, faith repels the enemy’s arrows, guards chastity, is adorned with purity, and grows rich and prosperous in every good thing. Hence it loves the poverty of the present life, while it longs for and seeks the eternal things that are believed.

It rejoices to possess only him in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, because he himself is the tower that is built from its foundation by the faith of Christ. Concerning this the prophet David says: “You have led me, because you have become my hope, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy” (Ps. LX, 4).

In this tower, faith, rooted and founded in the love of charity, stores all the instruments of the virtues. In it it treasures up for itself imperishable treasures, where thieves do not dig through or steal, where are all the eternal things that are not seen. Therefore, secure, it more wisely stores temporal possessions there, so as to receive them as eternal, as though it had spent them in this life. For it enjoys peace through Christ, already reconciled to God in the heavenly places, a peace that surpasses all understanding (Phil. IV, 7).

This peace guards the hearts and understanding of the faithful, lest the mind withdraw itself too far and be moved away from the faith, toward a place where it ought not to go. For wherever reason fails, or understanding falls short, faith grows, embraces us in its maternal bosom, and nourishes us until we reach the vision that we ardently hold in our minds through faith. Otherwise, whoever believes that he can comprehend everything about God by reason or understanding alone is greatly foolish.

3. For reason operates below faith, since wherever reason collapses, faith, divinely inspired, takes its place. For this reason many who trusted in human reason or in the art of eloquence, and who rashly wished to comprehend all the mysteries of the Godhead, withdrew farther from faith. Thus, while they attempted to exclude faith through reason, they became strangers to faith; and while they tried to circumscribe higher things by human senses, they spoke many things about faith without faith.

But true faith always rests securely in Christ. Although it knows very many things, it is enough for it to know Christ, and him crucified [Note: [Col. 1423D] The printed editions read “may know”]. Hence Paul also says: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II, 2).

In him, as in a tower of strength, faith is surrounded on every side by the virtues. With one and the same hand it builds the tower for the believer; with the other, through the equipment of its weapons, it overcomes wicked enemies and repels their ambushes, lest, deceived by false pleasures, it succumb.

4. Thus our holy fathers, ascending again from captivity as a figure of the whole Church, rebuild ruined Jerusalem with one hand; with the other, while enemies besiege them on every side, they fight bravely, imbued with the same faith divinely given (Ezra IV).

In this conflict faith also fights well with its own resources, so that it may always desire greater things. Hence it is rightly called magnificent, since it always seeks better things and forgets what lies behind it. Its strength is God, as he himself cries out: “Take courage; I have overcome the world” (John XVI, 33).

It is as though he plainly said: “It will not be by your strength, but by mine, that you will be victorious.” Therefore, if you fail and are driven back by temptations, look to my victory and implore my help, because your strength lies in my victory.

“Take courage,” he says, “not in yourselves but in my victory, because I have overcome the world.” Indeed, that I have conquered is an act of my power; and I have rightly granted this power also to faith. Only take courage.

Hence the Apostle also says: “This is the victory that conquers the world, our faith” (John V, 4). This faith is weakened unless it has confidence in Christ’s victory. Therefore we must believe with our whole heart what he promised: “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

Why, then, does he promise that he will be with us, unless once again so that he may fight and conquer in us? If faith is true, it is strengthened by such promises and the like, so that it does not fail when it is pressed. Otherwise, if it does not believe these things, the more it grows cold in trusting, the more it injures the strength of faith, which is Christ, by losing him.

For he does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, because he knows our strength. But whenever we are conquered, although through our own weakness, we are cast down by the fault of our will, having lost confidence, and therefore we fall.

For this reason perseverance in faith is necessary in all things, lest we surrender our hands to sin before divine power—which is with us—brings help. Yet he leaves us for a little while, so that we may be exercised in these things.

If we lose confidence, we fall more deeply into the temptation through which we slip; and while we look upon the darkness of sin, we lose the light of faith, in which a sure victory is promised to us. Therefore let magnificence flourish in faith, let confidence implore Christ’s help—for it is greatly necessary—and let perseverance burn until the end.

For it is most certain that Christ’s victory will never be absent from such great and such faith, because “whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 12). And if he delays, as the Prophet says, and is slow to grant what you desire, wait for it, because it will come and will not delay (Hebr. II, 3). Take care, therefore, not to lose endurance.

“Woe,” says the Prophet, “to those who have lost endurance and have turned into crooked ways” (Ecclus. II, 16). What, then, will they do when God begins to examine the consciences of each person?

Therefore do not abandon the faith [Note: [Col. 1424D] Edition: “do not become foolish”]; do not turn aside from the journey you have begun. Hurry toward the goal for which you were striving, and if you fall because of your frailty, rise again more quickly [Note: [Col. 1424D] Edition: “if you withdraw”]. Do not succumb to vices, but be unconquered in the mind of faith.

Let the enemy not hold back your steps as your soul hastens; let certain faith lead you to God. For you are not defeated until you lie down willingly; rather, you are still engaged in battle while you desire to conquer through faith [Note: [Col. 1424D] In the printed editions, “still” is absent].

No virtue therefore fights without faith, because “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV, 13). And therefore, whenever any weapon of faith has been broken, let the same faith take it up again; then faith itself will immediately recover strength, because it is the one that first brings the other virtues onto the field of battle.

It is faith that first seeks the field and, about to fight in the contest, advances fearlessly with arms extended and shoulders bare. It does not think of missiles or of the support of weapons; but, trusting in its courage, it kindles all the virtues of the soul for victory. Supported by them, it looks upon Christ standing above and crying out: “Take courage; I have overcome the world” (John XVI, 33).

Thus, though naked of human strength, it is always protected by God’s help [Note: [Col. 1425D] The printed editions read: “not improperly, itself”]. And, to speak more plainly, victory has never been lacking to anyone except the one whose great or such faith failed under the pressure of vices. Therefore we must always cry out: “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke XIV, 4).

## CHAPTER XIII. That each person has his own faith, although faith belongs to all

1. Although the Apostle says, “One faith, one body, one baptism” (Eph. IV, 5), nevertheless, as I said above, because of the difference among gifts, faith is considered special and personal in individuals. Thus, in one person it is reproved as small, while in another it is praised as great.

Yet it is rightly believed to be one and the same in all, through which we become one body in Christ [Note: [Col. 1425D] The printed editions omit “in Christ”], through which we are consecrated by one baptism, and in one hope of our calling there is one and only one faith by which we are reborn.

Nevertheless, because of the grace of gifts, faith is bestowed individually upon each person, and, according to the measure of his faith, as the Apostle Paul testifies, the other gifts of grace are granted. For faith is the initiator of all the virtues; therefore it is first given through the Holy Spirit, so that the remaining virtues may be distributed to individuals according to its measure.

Hence everywhere faith is either required first or given first. It is required when Martha is asked: “Do you believe this?” Then she says: “Certainly I believe, Lord, that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who has come into this world” (John XVI, 27). Immediately after her faith, Lazarus is raised.

And elsewhere, when a certain paralytic was being carried by four men, the evangelist says: “When Jesus saw their faith” (Matt. IX, 2), namely, the faith of those who carried him. This must be carefully considered, because whatever we do is weighed according to faith.

Hence the Lord, speaking about sacrifices in Leviticus, says: “The priest shall take a handful full of fine flour” (Lev. VI, 15). Thus the handful expresses faith, so that each person may offer God as much as faith contains.

The divine judge first examines inwardly and secretly the disposition of faith, and then evaluates the works that proceed from it. Works are performed openly, but faith is visible to God alone. Therefore the evangelist says: “When Jesus saw the faith of those who carried him.” For whatever is offered to God without right faith displeases him more, as is read concerning Cain: “God looked upon Cain and did not look upon his offerings” (Gen. IV, 5).

The reason why he did not look upon the offerings is clear: when he first looked upon Cain, he found in the intention of his heart that he was not offering with right faith. Therefore he rightly rejected his offerings, although they had been offered correctly. Hence Paul also says: “Because he was of the evil one” (I John III, 12)—that is, of an evil mind.

Therefore, before God, who examines the hearts of individuals, Cain received no praise as a reward. Hence Paul says: “Not the one who is circumcised outwardly, but the one who is a Jew inwardly” (Rom. II, 28); and concerning Abraham: “For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God” (Rom. IV, 2).

It is therefore clear from all this that knowing the hidden things of the heart belongs to God alone. He himself therefore foresees in each person the disposition of faith and the intention of the heart, so that each person may possess inwardly, before God alone, the glory that belongs to what God alone knows—namely, the glory that proceeds from faith. God alone observes the hidden things of faith and proves its quality and quantity.

Faith is not equal in everyone, although it is one. It is one because there is only one God; but it is not equal because faith is not perfect in everyone. Indeed, in one and the same person it is sometimes partial and sometimes perfect, so that he often possesses many things through faith, but the just person does not yet live in it.

“My just one,” he says, “lives by my faith.” Therefore whoever lives by the faith of Christ lives wholly for God, just as the one who said: “I live, yet no longer I; Christ lives in me” (Gal. II, 20).

Knowing this, the apostles said: “Lord, increase our faith.” For those who desire that their faith be increased already possess some faith, and from faith they ask to live wholly in faith.

2. Therefore let no one applaud himself as soon as he has believed something about God and done something through faith. Let him consider whether he already lives wholly by faith; then whether his faith has been rooted and founded in love, so that it may be the faith that works through love.

Otherwise, if he has, according to the Apostle, all faith so as to remove mountains but does not have love, it profits him nothing (I Cor. XIII, 2). Such faith is compared in the Gospel to a grain of mustard seed (Matt. XVII, 19). Even if it seems able to accomplish so much, it can indeed accomplish great things, because it has received great power from the great one: “He gave them power to become children of God” (John I, 12).

But those who merely remove mountains without love, drive out demons, and perform many works of power, although they have complete faith in believing, because they do not yet possess the inner organs of Christ’s love, degenerate from Christ. They have not yet received the full power of faith, so as to become children of God.

Nevertheless, faith is never so empty that its power is not conveyed everywhere in proportion to what kind and how great it is [Note: [Col. 1426D] The printed editions omit the words “its power is conveyed everywhere,” and continue: “when the inner organs of love are lacking to it, the power of adoption is also lacking,” and so forth]. When the inner organs of love are lacking to it, the power of adoption is also lacking, because every adoption and fatherhood are filled with the love of charity, and by love alone they are bound inwardly to one another.

Hence that faith which works through love must always be implored, so that, if faith is complete and true, it may be so in action and love as well as in believing, laboring in works of virtue, and possessing glory before God, before whom it always lies naked and open.

For faith is “the substance of things hoped for”; therefore it ought to contain within itself everything that is hoped for in the future. Otherwise, if it contains something else within itself, it is not Christ’s faith and is not the substance of things hoped for. For whatever is in Christ, we rightly hope for in its entirety if we rightly believe.

Therefore, as I said, we must always pray that we may believe rightly. And if anything in us is deficient in believing, we must implore with the apostles: “Lord, increase our faith,” until all things become possible for us who believe through Christ.

Through Christ, however, faith always exists and in him it abides; before him it unceasingly seeks and possesses glory, because all its glory is inward, while outwardly it devoutly despises everything that is done.

Inwardly it reads and prays; inwardly it works and loves; inwardly it gathers together its works of virtue. Inwardly, although it fights outwardly, it rests secure. Outwardly it fights, but inwardly it conquers. In the inward realm it obtains what it seeks; inwardly it carries away what it has obtained.

For this purpose it acts outwardly: so that it may draw everything inward to itself, where its confession is, and where all its beauty, holiness, and magnificence lie in its sanctification. It acts not only for itself, but also intervenes greatly for others who lack these things. By intervening, it very often becomes capable of granting what is requested [Note: [Col. 1427D] Edition: “makes capable of granting”].

Hence we read in the Gospel: “Let it be done for you as you wish” (Matt. XV, 28); and we often hear: “Your faith has saved you” (Mark X, 52). There is also this: “When Jesus saw the faith of those who carried him, he said to the paralytic: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you’” (Matt. IX, 2).

Behold, the Son of the Most High, through the faith of others, frees the sick man who had previously been a son of Gehenna [Note: [Col. 1427D] Edition: “who had previously been a son of Gehenna,” which is not very satisfactory; otherwise it ought to add “he frees the sick”]. Here the wonderful dispensation of faith is revealed: how much the faith of one person can accomplish, since it was able to obtain so much for another.

Hence also the Church of God, when children are brought to be reborn, whose faith—or rather whose reason or understanding—is nonexistent, so that they can believe, nevertheless believes that they are saved by the faith of others. And if you weigh the matter carefully, no salvation is granted without faith.

3. Yet, as I said, faith is small in some and great in others. For when the apostles were doubting, they were told: “Why are you fearful, you of little faith?” (Matt. VIII, 26) [Note: [Col. 1427D] Edition: “he says”]. But the centurion is praised because he found no such faith in Israel (ibid., 10).

Mary also is called blessed solely because she believed. For he says: “Blessed is she who believed; the things spoken to you by the angel will be fulfilled in you” (Luke I, 46). And it is no wonder if, in all who believe perfectly, the things rightly desired and sought through the love of faith are both fulfilled and granted.

Hence the Lord says: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed and say to this mountain, ‘Move from here and throw yourself into the sea,’ it will certainly happen” (Matt. XVII, 19).

Nevertheless, whether anyone understands this as spoken of any particular mountain or of any particular grain of mustard seed, no one who believes rightly ought to doubt that these things are as the Truth promised.

But faith is not possessed by everyone. For the Apostle also, among the other gifts of God and of the Holy Spirit, says: “To another faith is given in the same Spirit” (II Cor. XII). What do you think? Is it not also given to all those who have received either the word of knowledge or of wisdom, or the gift of healings, or prophecy, or kinds of tongues, and other things of this sort [Note: [Col. 1428D] Edition: “of this kind”], since all these things, according to the same Apostle, are distributed to each according to the measure of faith?

Certainly faith is first given to all who receive some grace of the Holy Spirit. But there are some who, just as others excel in wisdom, knowledge, the grace of healings, or prophecy, likewise excel in the virtue of faith, so that they are able to accomplish very much, although each person has his own faith.

In this faith, at the present time, some burn more fervently, fulfilling the precepts of an active life and trampling underfoot what is contrary to salvation. Others, however, meditate on heavenly things in such a way that they do not abandon earthly things.

If you question them, all alike confess that they believe in one God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. But the faith of all is not equal. Therefore the faith of our neighbor is assessed not merely from his speech but from his works, because to the degree that faith lives in him, he runs ardently toward the unseen things, either by willing what is good or by devoting himself to pious and righteous works.

It is more powerful for action to the degree that it is more devoted toward God, and it is stronger in resisting what is contrary to salvation to the degree that it is armed with the instruments of the other virtues and trusts in God.

And I do not say merely that one and the same faith is unequal in different people; it is not even always equal in one and the same person. One faith was in Peter when, being asked, “Who do you say that I am?” (Matt. XVI, 15), he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Another was in him when, questioned by a servant girl, he denied: “I do not know the man” (Matt. XXVI, 72).

But the Lord also said: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII, 32).

I think that when he had not yet been perfectly converted [Note: [Col. 1428D] Edition: “when he had not yet been converted perfectly,” but the manuscript reading is preferable], he was not yet fully faithful; yet, since his faith was granted that it might not fail, he certainly possessed some faith. Pressed by fear, he denied wrongly what inwardly, in his conscience, he secretly held. But such faith would also have perished inwardly unless mercy had quickly restored it by its gaze.

Afterward, having been converted, he confessed fearlessly even amid scourging and unto death. Thus the others also, while they still had to be strengthened, were not yet perfect in faith.

Therefore let no one applaud himself as perfectly faithful as soon as he has begun to believe, however slightly, until he feels Christ and the Holy Spirit dwelling in him through faith.

Hence the Apostle Paul says: “I bend my knees before the Father of my Lord Jesus Christ, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, strength to be strengthened through his Spirit in the inner person, and that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts; rooted and founded in love, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth, and to know the surpassing love of Christ, so that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God” (Eph. III, 14–19).

Behold: if you are faithful, you now know toward what you must strive, so that you may remain faithful. Hence also the Lord says in the Apocalypse of John to the Church: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you to eat from the tree of life” (Rev. II, 10).

A perfected faith, therefore, reaches unto death. Nothing soothing or harsh can resist it—not even death, which seems harsher than all things, until it apprehends the things that are not seen, to which no one ever comes except through death [Note: [Col. 1429D] Edition: “to which no one comes unless he comes through death”].

How rightly, then, faith does not fear even death! For if faith is the proof of things that are not seen, and hastens toward those things that it can comprehend only after death, how is it faith if it fears death?

And if the just person lives by faith, what sort of virtue is that which is the life of the just and gives life unto life, if it fears death [Note: [Col. 1429D] Edition: “which is the life of the just”]? The fear of death comes from the punishment of sin. Therefore the just person, already living by faith, ought not to fear, because just as Christ, who is life, destroyed death by death, so faith, the life of the just person, passes through death from death into life. Thus the just person now lives immortally—not by faith, but by the everlasting life that is now present in faith.

## CHAPTER XIV. That faith rightly concerns three times, and beyond them the eternal things
1. Indeed, faith believes no less in past things than in present and future things. “By faith,” says Paul, “we understand that the ages were ordered by the word of God, so that visible things came into being from invisible things” (Heb. 11:3). Whoever does not believe this is shown to be faithless. This is the faith taught by the divine Spirit through Moses, who says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1)—that is, all the creatures that exist in heaven and on earth. It therefore remains that faith believes in nothing other than the one God and in the things that come from the one God—namely, the Creator and creation.

For the Creator exists before every creation, above every creation, and beyond every creation. Before every creation, because he himself is without beginning, [Col. 1429D] and every creature comes from him. Above every creation, because he is more powerful and exalted, while creation exists entirely through him, by whom it is ruled and governed. Beyond every creation, because he is without end, whereas creation, coming to an end beneath him, truly and undoubtedly exists in order to be with him. Therefore nothing exists outside him; rather, he is before all things, above all things, and beyond all things.

Thus it is established that faith concerns the past, as well as the present and the future. It concerns the past when it believes what existed before the ages: the one God subsisting in three persons, from whom all things come. [Col. 1430A] It concerns the present when it understands that what now lies beyond the ages of this life is the one and same abiding God, through whom all things exist. It concerns the future when it does not doubt that what extends beyond the end of this age—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—will remain forever as one God in the Trinity, with whom all things exist.

And this, I say, is the height of riches in which faith believes. But because his ways are incomprehensible, faith remains, without any disputation or reconsideration, always whole and unshaken with Christ while we are on the way and the things believed are not yet seen. For we believe that he died, which is past; we believe that he now sits at the right hand of the Father, which is present; and we believe that he will come to judge the living and the dead, which is future.

But if someone asks a Christian what must be believed, then, although all things were rightly created by the one God, the nature of things must not be investigated in the manner of those whom the Greeks call “physicists.” One need not therefore fear going astray regarding the number of the elements, the movement, order, and eclipses of the stars, the shape of heaven, or the kinds and natures of animals. Nor should one think that anything harms Christian faith if we are ignorant of some matter concerning plants [Note: [Col. 1430D] The editions read “fruits.”], stones, springs, rivers, and mountains; or concerning the distances of places and times, the signs of impending storms, and other knowledge of such matters which they have discovered or claim that they will discover.

For they themselves have not found everything, although they have published some things by investigating through human conjecture, others by learning through historical experience, and still more by fabricating them according to their own opinion. It is enough for a Christian to understand that the causes of created things—whether heavenly or earthly, visible or invisible—exist solely through the goodness of God the Creator; that there is no nature which is not either God himself or from him; and that he is the Trinity: the Father, the Son begotten from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from both—one God, from whom all things were created. These things are not supremely, equally, or unchangeably good; nevertheless, each thing individually is good, and all things together are very good.

2. We therefore call that alone “faith” which the divine utterances have taught: faith concerning things that are not seen, not things that are entirely visible. And although in certain cases we give “faith” in the opposite sense, when we sometimes say without absurdity that we have seen and believed something, nevertheless the faith of our religion is never without hope and never without love; nor are hope or love ever without faith. Hence faith concerns invisible things, as does hope, of which the Apostle says: “Hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24).

Thus we already believe the things for which we still hope, and whatever we believe we certainly hope for; while hoping, we love. [Col. 1431A] Faith therefore embraces invisible things: God above all things, around all things, and within all things, wholly present everywhere and eternal. It also embraces every creature created by God the author. Separating creation from the Creator, faith believes, hopes in, and loves God alone for his own sake.

This, as I have said, is the faith of the Christian rule, which according to the Apostle “works through love.” Otherwise, unless you first believe, you have nothing to hope for or love, just as you have nothing to invoke. Faith is therefore trust in God—or rather, the substance which one ought to hope for and love for its own sake, because God is the supreme good.

“Faith,” he says, “is the substance of things hoped for,” because the measure of hope in us ought certainly to correspond to the measure of faith that works through love. Unless we hope for what is beyond us, we either appear to hope for something else [Col. 1431B] without the substance of hope or to love without it. Thus in prayer faith believes, while hope and love pray; but because they cannot exist without faith, faith also prays.

Otherwise we cannot pray for, invoke, hope for, or love invisible things in which we do not believe. Therefore great faith must be implored, [Note: [Col. 1431D] The edition lacks the words “so that there may also be great hope and love.”] so that there may also be great hope and love.

Although faith, hope, and love are moved through three times, as I have stated [Note: [Col. 1431D] The editions read “as I previously stated.”], they confess the eternal God, outside all time, as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Faith itself is affected by these times because it operates within time, so that each believer may reach the things that are always the same and eternal. This is not because the one in whom faith believes exists within time, but because the things that either were, are, or will be from him are entirely within time, until faith itself is brought to an end—faith which now believes, through pious works, the things carried out by the Lord.

Therefore, whoever you are, if you are not yet capable of believing the things that are not seen, at least believe through works. For visible things are invisibly brought into being by the craftsman through the word of power, so that from them you may grasp invisible things. “From the creation of the world, the invisible things are understood and perceived through the things that have been made.” Therefore visible things are governed by invisible things, and for that reason invisible things must always be sought through faith; once sought, they must be loved and enjoyed forever in devoted love.

We know with certainty that the things which are seen do not make themselves [Note: [Col. 1432D] The edition reads “make.”]; nevertheless, they have been made and are seen—not in the manner in which they are made, but in the fact that they altogether exist and have been made. The power, wisdom, and will of the Deity must therefore be believed, because whatever he willed or was able to do was present in his wisdom; for that reason he made nothing blameworthy. Just as he had no greater ability than will, nor a will greater than ability, so neither was his will or ability greater than his wisdom.

Thus everything is placed in his will, whose power nothing surpasses. The things that were made are held together by his power, and by his wisdom, in which they were made, they are governed. All these things together declare one God, since from diverse and contrary things there is one world. If it were not one, then the diverse and contrary things would never possess one harmony according to whose discretion and power the world is governed, nor would all things tend so harmoniously toward unity.

They disagree in nothing, so that they may form one. If there were many gods, as deceived paganism falsely claims, the elements of things so contrary to one another, and the diversity of natures and activities, would long ago have brought the age to an end—especially since, as they themselves imagine, those gods are diverse in character and contrary in power.

But now, while all things in the world together produce one benefit for humanity, and the manifold variety of things and times produces everywhere and in every age of the world one harmony, while individual things contribute abundance to human life, it is clear that there is one Almighty, according to whose will all these things occur and in whose wisdom they are prepared, so that they do not collapse away from one another but all together serve the needs of human life in harmony.

Although these things are visible, they are nevertheless moved inwardly and invisibly by the invisible God, so that through them the mind may return to him, from whom such great things are made without our eyes perceiving them. Therefore we walk by faith and not by sight, because we seek through faith the things that are not seen. The things that are seen we neither believe nor hope for, since by God’s gift we make use of them; but, still sighing, we seek the giver, that he who has given such great things that are seen may mercifully reveal himself to his own, whom we have not yet seen, so that he may be sufficient for us.

## CHAPTER XV. On the gift of grace and the perseverance of faith

1. Let no Christian therefore imagine that either the beginning or the perfection of faith is his own possession. Let him understand with complete certainty that faith is God’s gift, through which the other gifts are given. Otherwise, “who has given anything to him first, so that he should be repaid?” (Rom. 11:35).

Since, therefore, all things are from him, through him, and in him, the beginning of our faith is from him. Nor is it the case, as some wish, that everything else comes through him with this one exception. Rather, we are initiated into faith from him, and through him we receive increase, so that we may grow in faith; and in him we receive the gift of perseverance, so that we may remain in one and the same faith.

Hence the Apostle says: “It has been granted to you not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29). He thus indicates both things as God’s gifts, the beginning and the end, lest, if we say that we possess the beginning from ourselves, the increase of faith should already be the reward of our beginning and not the grace of the giver.

For who does not see that thinking comes first and believing afterward? No one believes anything unless he has first thought that it ought to be believed. Yet to believe is nothing other than to think with the assent of authority, and with greater certainty, about things that are not seen and that he himself has taught, without investigation. Although not everything that anyone thinks is believed, nevertheless whatever he believes, he thinks by believing, and by thinking he believes the things that pertain to the religion of Catholic faith or to devotion.

Hence the Apostle also says: “We are not competent to think anything as from ourselves; but our competence is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5). If we are not competent even to think, how much less are we competent to believe. Our true competence, by which we begin to believe, is therefore from God. And just as no one is sufficient for himself to begin, so no one possesses from himself any good work by which he may bring it to perfection. Our sufficiency for beginning and persevering is from God.

Whatever God has promised, he is powerful enough to accomplish. He therefore promised Abraham the faith of the nations, through which they would become his heirs. He powerfully brought this faith about among the nations, so that no flesh might boast before him [Note: [Col. 1433D] The edition omits “flesh.”], but might be saved by the grace that is in Christ Jesus. Otherwise grace is no longer grace unless it is freely given.

“What do you have,” then, “that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7). Suppose you imagine that you have faith from yourself. In that case you have something that you did not receive—especially since faith is rightly believed to be the beginning of all God’s gifts, as in the Apostle’s statement: “As God has apportioned to each a measure of faith” (Rom. 12:3).

But if faith is not from God, then the other things distributed according to the measure of faith are rewards of faith and not gifts. Such boasting is therefore evil, since we can possess nothing except by receiving it. Hence the Apostle says: “If you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?”

He does not cry out that faith was given to him so that he might be faithful, since “the remnant according to the election of grace is saved,” and not through works of merit. For it is God who works all things in all people (1 Cor. 12:6 [reference as printed: XXVI, 6]). If all things, then certainly faith also, through which the other gifts of virtue begin in us.

Therefore let no one applaud himself as possessing anything from himself except vices, lest he appear to boast in a human being. Rather, “let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31)—from whom, through whom, and in whom we possess not only the fact that we are faithful, but also the ability to remain in the same works of faith.

Finally, every good gift, which is the sacrament of faith, and every perfect gift—namely, the grace of remaining in the works of that same faith [Note: [Col. 1433D] The edition reads “of remaining in its works”]—is from above, descending from the Father of lights (Jas. 1:17). Let us therefore say with the Prophet: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. 113:9), because we can do nothing from ourselves except insofar as we have received it from God.

2. We have therefore received faith from God, if indeed we are already faithful, and for that reason we dare to call God our Father in heaven [Note: [Col. 1434D] The edition reads “Father from God.”]. “He gave,” says the Evangelist, “power to become children of God to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12). [Col. 1433D] This power is truly faith, through which we are adopted by God [Note: [Col. 1434D] The edition reads “by the Lord.”]; but it was given so that grace might be complete, not as a payment returned.

The Apostle says elsewhere: “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8:14). From this it must be noted that not only the faith or works of our religion, but the people themselves, insofar as they are sons, are led by the Spirit of God, lest they applaud themselves for works of merit.

Faith must therefore first be requested, since it is given in the same Spirit; then the works of faith must be increased through love; and finally that same faith must be preserved to the end.

If some virtue is lacking, the Apostle James teaches how we may obtain it. “If anyone,” he says, “lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach, and it will be given to him. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing” (Jas. 1:5–6).

Since all gifts of virtue must be requested from us in faith and are distributed according to the measure of faith, it is clear that faith itself is a great gift of God, although it was bestowed before we asked, because no one rightly believes against his will; yet the will itself to believe is prepared by the Lord.

To will and to accomplish are his gifts, so that no one may boast of himself but may entrust himself in all things to God’s mercy. For, according to that prophetic word of David, “His mercy will go before me” (Ps. 59:10); and elsewhere, when he himself prays, “His mercy will follow me” (Ps. 23:6). Thus we should presume on no one but him, since we possess nothing except from him.

“For it depends not on human willing or running, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16). Indeed, the fact that we now will and run is not some small matter but a great gift of God, according to the purpose of his will and not according to the merit of our will.

We did not choose him; he chose us, so that by believing we might choose him. He first produced faith in us, inspiring it, so that through that same faith we might receive the other good things that belong to him by asking, seeking, and knocking.

Therefore those whom he chose he did not find already chosen, but as vessels of wrath. He made them choose him by believing—those whom he foreknew and predestined before the foundation of the world in Christ “to be holy and blameless in his sight.” “In love,” he says, “he predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of his will, in which he graced us in his beloved Son” (Eph. 1:4–6).

Let no one therefore applaud himself as though anything came from himself, but let him attribute everything to God, who both foreknew and chose us—not because we were already chosen or holy through any merits present, past, or future, but through his mercy. We were vessels of wrath so that we might become holy through Christ, according to the good pleasure of his will and not according to the merit of our will. In his will he graced us, so that we have been saved by grace.

Hence the Apostle says: “You have been saved by grace through faith; and this,” he says, “is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God” (Eph. 2:8)—that is, we are saved by grace through faith.

Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent” (John 6:29). If the faith of believers is the work of God, then we rightly say that a person is justified by faith and not by works, so that from faith he may obtain the other gifts of virtue, in which we live righteously. According to grace, the promise may therefore be firm through faith, lest a person, entrusting himself more to his own weakness than to the firmness of God’s promise, should fall unawares.

But perhaps someone will say: “God’s will concerning me is uncertain to me, whether he wishes to save me by grace through faith” [Note: [Col. 1434D] The edition omits “to me.”]. What then? O man, is your own will concerning yourself certain to you? Do you not fear the saying: “Let the one who stands beware lest he fall”? (1 Cor. 10:12).

Your will concerning yourself is indeed uncertain to you. Why then do you not entrust yourself entirely to one who is firmer and more powerful than you, who has already freely given you something? For he not only granted you the ability to will and believe, although you would neither will nor believe unless he gave it; he also freely granted you the ability to run.

You must therefore trust in him more firmly, because it depends not on the one who wills or runs but on God who shows mercy. Do not lose such confidence. What we now will or run toward already belongs to him. Our faith must be entrusted to him from whom and through whom we believe. Hope and love must likewise be made firm in him and not in ourselves, because whatever we do is his gift: by his grace he first works in us through faith so that we may do these things rightly.

Know this with certainty: faith is the greatest gift of God [Note: [Col. 1435] The edition reads: “that believing is the greatest benefit of God; and one must not doubt as long as the will to believe and act remains, but must pray that this faith may exist,” and so forth.]. No one should doubt God’s mercy as long as there is a will to believe and to act, so that there may be that faith which works through love in good works, and which also works in us through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

[Col. 1435C]

## [ON HOPE]

## PROLOGUE TO THE BOOK ON HOPE

[Col. 1435]

Having dedicated to you, dearest friend, as a kind of introductory garment, the work on the matter of Christian faith, polished according to the insights of the Catholic Fathers, I shall now undertake, as I promised, a brief treatment of hope. Together with faith, its grace in Christ is so great that, through daily advances, it already securely possesses the eternal joys of heaven, penetrating to the secrets of heaven where Christ, having become High Priest for us, entered [Note: [Col. 1436B] The edition reads “penetrating,” singular.].

Concerning this possession of hope the Prophet sings: “The Lord is my hope” (Jer. 17:17). I considered it too little merely to write for you, who daily flourish with the flowering perfection of these virtues, a kind of marriage-contract document concerning each of them, as though you were worthy of so great a covenant, so that you might distinctly recognize with what things you are joined in the marriage of faith and what sort of patrimony you enjoy in hope through the perfected love of Christ’s promise.

For this reason, I ask that you graciously favor our prayers, so that in some way I may be able to explain adequately what the hope of Christians is.

*The prologue ends.*

## THE BOOK ON HOPE BEGINS

## CHAPTER I

God, then, is the hope of life and the communion of the mind, like an anchor amid the storms of the age, as the blessed and distinguished Apostle Paul says, exhorting us through the following comparison:

“By two unchangeable things,” he says, “in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have the strongest consolation, we who have fled for refuge to grasp the hope set before us. We have this hope as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, entering even into the interior of the veil, where Jesus, our forerunner, entered for us, having become High Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Heb. 6:18).

Our hope, then, which has been set before us, is a very strong and inviolable consolation, because it is impossible for God to lie—God who promised us the things for which we hope. We have this hope as an anchor.

He calls it an anchor according to the comparison with sailors. When they are carried about here and there amid the waves, they customarily cast out their anchor so that, fastened to the sea floor [Note: [Col. 1435D] The edition reads “to the ground.”], the safe and immovable ship may remain amid the storms of the tempest and not be driven by the force of the winds into places of shipwreck.

Thus our hope is anchored not in the floor of the sea but in Christ, who is the firmest rock. We have it as a safe and steadfast anchor, extending into the interior of heaven.

The comparison is remarkable: the ship is understood as the Church; the sea as the present age; the waves’ storms and tempests as the tribulations and persecutions of this age; and the force of the winds as hostile powers. Struck and driven by these, we cast out our hope like an anchor—not onto the sand of the sea but toward Christ—so that it may be fixed and made firm in him who is the firmest rock. We have it as a safe and most steadfast anchor of the soul.

The word “anchor” derives from the Greek *anchir*. *Anchir* is interpreted as “hand,” so that just as a hand gathers and constricts, the anchor appears to gather or constrict the sand. This is why it is so called. How aptly, then, our hope is called an anchor: whatever we bind through our action may be Christ, for whose love we even spend ourselves; and whatever we gather, let the mind be fixed in him, so that he himself may be our hope, as the Prophet sings: “The Lord has been my hope from my youth” (Ps. 71:5), so that we may not be torn away from him by any waves of temptation.

It is tied by the rope of faith and love, and these weave a threefold cord which, according to Solomon, is not easily broken (Eccl. 4:12). Through it the soul, joined to Christ, is made firm and is not severed by any delusions.

Nothing is more certain than what we hold in our hand. By the hand of hope, which is the safe anchor of the soul, Christ is held and bound. Concerning him the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I found him; I will hold him and will not let him go” (Song 3:4).

“I will hold him,” she says, with whatever hand—but surely with no hand other than the hand of hope, by which we sow as we go in faith and weep in longing. We sow in hope, just as everyone who plows has sown, wavering in nothing, because we hold him and remain in him; and whoever remains in him bears abundant fruit.

Hence the Apostle exhorts us: “Let us hold fast the hope set before us,” because all our hope has been set before us in Christ, whom God the Father set before us as an atonement [Col. 1437B] for our sins.

Let us therefore hold him—or rather, let us continually pray that we may be held by him whom we have as a safe anchor of the soul, by which we are bound so that we are not torn away by any mountains of winds, but, tied to him and running after him, remain immovable.

This hope is certainly inviolable. Even if for a while we sometimes lose confidence in ourselves, let us remain safe and firm in him by whose hand we are held and strengthened. He himself is our anchor, by which we are bound; and no one can take us away from it.

We hold it, and we are held; but it is greater to be held by Christ than to hold him, since we can hold him only as long as we are held by him [Note: [Col. 1437D] The edition reads “what we hold.”]. Nevertheless, it is necessary that we hold him in order to be held, so that we may not be torn apart by waves from either side.

Moreover, Christ is our hope, and through Christ we hope for whatever has been promised to us in him. We hope for nothing other than what has been given by him and in him to those who believe.

We rightly hope for the whole reality that is God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We also hope for the resurrection of the flesh, eternal life, and unending blessedness in Christ, because all these things have been given to us through him and from him.

All these things are first believed and therefore rightly hoped for. They are believed as realities; then they are hoped for through Christ because they have been given. This is our living hope, of which the Apostle says that he “regenerated us into a living hope” (1 Pet. 1:3). It is living and true, because Christ is life and truth.

Let us therefore remain in the same hope in which we were reborn, because we are in living hope [Note: [Col. 1437D] The edition adds: “Because we are in living hope and not yet in the reality.”] and not yet in the reality. Since we are not yet in the reality, we hope while awaiting the adoption of sons, which we have already received, possessed, and held in hope.

While holding it, we are secure, because we are already certain of the things given to us in Christ. Hence, when we pray, we say: “Our Father, who are in heaven.” Although we are not yet in the reality [Note: [Col. 1438D] The edition reads “rightly.”], we have already begun to be in hope whatever we shall be in the future.

For in hope, as the Apostle says, “he has already made us sit in the heavenly places” (Eph. 2:6); we have already risen together [Note: [Col. 1438D] The edition reads “we have already risen together.”] through baptism, just as we have also been buried with him through death.

Therefore we hold all these things as given to us through firm, true, and living hope. Holding this hope set before us, we are safe and secure, because we have it in Christ, in whom we believe all things.

He himself is the substance of things hoped for, which we have acquired through faith, although its realization is deferred. Therefore we await with devotion and patience the things that have already been given. He is the religious assent to a true future promise, the devoted expectation of the promised glory, the appointed possession of the saints, and the expectation of all future goods.

Regenerated in this living hope, we set our minds on the things above, where our life is kept hidden with Christ. Let us live there where we have been reborn. Christ is living and true hope, in whom we possess eternal things. Having been imbued and initiated with these things, let us hasten to enter the same glory of rest, into which we entered by being reborn—not through some ordinary promise, but through living hope.

## CHAPTER II. What the difference is between hope and faith

1. Although hope is related to faith and is close to believing, so that neither can stand without the other, nevertheless one must be distinguished from the other both in name and by a rational difference. Thus hope may be made firm by faith, and faith may continually be lifted by certain hope toward the eternal and unseen things.

Their first difference is this: nothing can rightly be hoped for unless it is rightly believed; nevertheless something can be believed that is not hoped for at all. For what believer does not believe in the punishments and torments of the wicked, yet does not hope for them, although he fears them entirely? Hope concerns good things alone, whereas fear concerns evil things.

Thus, although some have used “to hope” in place of “to fear,” hope properly always concerns good things, just as fear so often concerns evil things—even though the Prophet speaks of “holy fear enduring forever” (Ps. 19:9).

Finally, faith concerns evil things no less than good things, since both good and evil things are believed.

There is also a second difference between them: faith concerns past, present, and future things. It concerns past things in whatever we read in the holy Scriptures about the beginning of the world, and also in our complete belief that Christ died, which is past. It concerns present things when we profess to believe with true faith that he now sits at the right hand of the Father. It concerns future things when we proclaim without doubt, by believing, that he will come to judge the living and the dead, and that our flesh will rise again.

Hope, however, concerns future things alone, and good things. We hope for nothing except something future, even though faith continually occupies three times in believing. For although faith extends itself over three times in its act of believing, faith itself is present only [Col. 1439A]—just as, when we believe evil things, faith is always good whenever it believes rightly.

Otherwise, if faith is not present for someone, its having existed is of no benefit; this remains so until the vision of truth abolishes what is partial and what is in faith is found to be true. Thus, because it is true, faith is always good for the believer.

2. There is still another difference between them: hope is never without love, whereas faith is sometimes weighed down more by fear than lifted by love. Concerning this faith the Apostle James says: “The demons also believe and tremble” (Jas. 2:19); yet they neither hope nor love at all.

But the faith of Christians is that which works through love and is never found without hope and love. Thus they fear, while we who hope love; and if for a while we fear the punishment of sin, we fear in proportion as we hope less.

Therefore, whoever you are, stop sinning and receive judgment concerning your past deeds, so that by believing you may be able to hope. For just as hope is not without love, so the faith of Christians, if it is to be the faith that works through love, is not without charity.

Charity casts out fear, so that someone may hope more than fear. Therefore, in the present time, charity is never without hope, just as hope and charity are never without faith.

This is why faith, by believing, seeks things that are not seen and are eternal, while hope confidently asks to arrive at the reality which it has already received within itself as a gift and in which it is secure.

Then charity knocks tirelessly, and the two of them pray together that the door may be opened, that what is partial may be brought to an end, and that one may enjoy the realities that are perfect and eternal.

Hope and charity therefore pray, as I have said, and ask and knock; faith, however, believes and seeks what should be hoped for and loved. It does not seek in order to look for something else that may be hoped for or loved; rather, as I explained far above, because the unseen things are immeasurable, it seeks that these same things may be found ever more abundantly and perfectly through faith, so that they may be hoped for and loved more fully [Note: [Col. 1439D] The editions read “may be hoped for,” singular].

“For we walk by faith and not by sight,” and therefore faith also prays with them, since they cannot exist without it. Hence it is said: “How will they invoke him in whom they have not believed?” (Rom. 10:14). Nothing can be hoped for, certainly, that is not believed.

3. Moreover, faith concerns one’s own things no less than those of others. Each person believes that he once began to exist and was not eternal. He also believes many other things—not only concerning other human beings and matters pertaining to religion, but also concerning angels.

Hope, however, concerns only things belonging to the person who is shown to possess hope for them. Otherwise it should rather be called believing than hoping, unless there is a movement toward that same reality and it can happen to us.

We therefore believe things that sometimes do not come to us [Note: [Col. 1439D] The editions read “fit us.”], but we never rightly hope except for things granted through the benefit of merits and the grace of mercies, or [Col. 1440A] for things that can come to us through love [Note: [Col. 1440D] The edition reads “that is.”].

Furthermore, sometimes, by common usage, faith is spoken of regarding things that are seen; hope, however, concerns only things that are not seen, as the Apostle testifies. He himself defines faith as “the evidence of things not appearing.”

Nevertheless, when someone is said to have believed—that is, to have given his faith—not through words, things, or any chain of arguments, but through the evidence of present things, it does not seem so absurd that he should rightly be reproved in these words: “Then you saw and did not believe.”

Although this too may be a difference, we more properly call “the faith of Christians” that which the divine utterances have taught: faith concerning things that are not seen. In the same way, hope concerns those same things.

Hence the Apostle says: “Hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24).

When future good things are believed to be ours, they are nothing other than hoped for. Therefore the things that are unseen and eternal are first believed; when they are promised, they are hoped for; and when hoped for, they are loved, because they are supreme and everlasting [Note: [Col. 1440D] The edition reads “eternal.”].

Otherwise, according to Solomon: “Woe to those who have lost endurance”—that is, hope—“and have turned aside into crooked paths” (Eccl. 2:16). If they had not lost hope, they would not have turned aside toward precipices at the blows of the winds.

Nothing is more dangerous than despair. Therefore, whoever you are, do not let yourself be burdened by any weight of sins, dragged by any bonds of desire, or wearied by any delay in the fulfillment of promises.

If he delays, await him according to the Prophet. If you are being dragged down to the depths by the burdens of sins, recover confidence in hope, so that you may be able to fly toward the most merciful harbor of salvation, because Christ’s mercies have not yet come to an end.

And if you have fallen into the deep abyss of vices, firmly hope that, if you withdraw from them, he will mercifully free you from it. But if you are still dragged along, bound by them, the chain of hope, strengthened by love and faith, is stronger, provided that—even when you are willing to sin—you cease.

## CHAPTER III. On participation in faith and hope
1. It must certainly be understood that faith is the foundation of the other virtues and goes first out onto the field; hope, however, establishes the human being for reaching the things that are believed: faith gives the beginning of merits, while hope leads them to their summit; faith undertakes the beginning of believing, while hope daily contemplates the perfection of virtue; faith believes what is promised, while hope already sees what has been promised and embraces the inner regions of heaven, where Christ has entered. For by faith we walk, but by hope we have already arrived. Thus we are not yet blessed and undefiled [Note: [Col. 1440D] The printed editions read “thus therefore.”]; nevertheless, through that same hope, because we have been buried with Christ and have risen with him—who has made us sit in the heavenly places—we are already, in some sense, said to be on the way. Hope neither deceives nor is deceived, unless faith first withdraws. For hope is true if faith, having kept its covenant, has been fulfilled. Faith is the substance of things hoped for; when it is removed, hope is without substance, and therefore it is no longer hope when the capacity for hoping [Note: [Col. 1441D] The printed editions read *sperando* (“by hoping”) for *sperandi* (“of hoping”).] is lacking. Faith, namely, undisturbed, is always and everywhere the mother and nurse of hope [Note: [Col. 1441D] The printed editions read “and everywhere.”]. It is therefore evident that they cling to one another inseparably.

Hence, when the Apostle was speaking about Abraham, he said that “against hope he believed in hope” (Rom. 4:18). If he believed entirely in hope, then hope was again for him the way and the capacity for believing. From this it is clearly gathered that they provide one another with the substance of God’s promises, so that they may remain [Note: [Col. 1441D] The printed editions read: “so that, if they remain alternately.”].

It is remarkable that Abraham is said to have believed against hope in hope. If his hope was true, what could have come against the truth of hope? Indeed, since Genesis records that he had despaired of a son, perhaps the Apostle’s meaning is this [Note: [Col. 1441D] The printed edition reads *apostolo* (“to the Apostle”) for *apostoli* (“of the Apostle”).]: when he had believed, against the hope he had held concerning a servant [Note: [Col. 1441D] The printed edition omits *quam* (“which”).]—that the servant would be his heir—he changed the order and believed more fully and perfectly in hope of God’s promises, namely, that he, a hundred-year-old man, should receive as his heir a son from his barren and aged wife. Or perhaps it was because, believing with certainty that this very son would become a sacrifice and burnt offering, he hoped in God’s command, without hesitating through distrust; but, wholly dependent on God by unwavering faith and hope, he accepted with a pious and devoted heart whatever God commanded to be done.

For he hoped that the boy would live better with God by being offered to him than if he preserved him badly without God—the God who had given him existence when he did not yet exist. Against that expectation, nevertheless, he confidently believed in the hope he had heard: “This one shall not be your heir, but the one who comes forth from your loins shall be your heir.” And also: “Look up at the sky and count the stars, if you are able.” Then, he says: “So shall your offspring be” (Gen. 15:4–5). There is no doubt that he believed in this hope against that same hope by which, in offering his son as a sacrifice and burnt offering, he hoped that he would belong to God.

For he believed wholeheartedly in both directions: whatever he heard from God, he devotedly sought to fulfill, retracting nothing, doubting nothing, and finding fault with nothing in him. He did not examine the statement, “This one shall be your heir,” nor did he ask why God commanded him to kill [Note: [Col. 1442D] The printed edition reads “when he commanded him to kill him.”] the one whom, in his old age, he had received as his heir. He was wholly present to God, lived for God, and entrusted himself entirely to God in all things by faith, believing nothing about him except what was true and hoping nothing from him except what was salutary and beneficial to himself. This is undiscussed faith in God and certain hope in God, which all children must imitate completely: “For not those who are of the flesh, but those who are of faith, are sons of Abraham” (Gal. 3:7).

2. The children must preserve this faith and hope, steadfast and inviolate, so that they may become heirs; otherwise, how will they be capable of attaining what is not seen? For we have already been saved, as is also said concerning faith, that “through it we have been saved,” and: “Your faith has saved you.” Therefore, just as Abraham believed in hope against hope, so all who are his children through faith must themselves believe against hope in hope.

Consider each of the things that are believed: the resurrection of the dead, the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 1442D] The printed editions read “the heavenly kingdom.”], the adoption as children of God, and the blessed immortality of flesh and soul, insofar as human nature is concerned. Who could ever have hoped for such things, even if it had been permissible to believe that they existed? All these things appear to be against hope, insofar as we are concerned; but insofar as God’s power is concerned, they are rightly believed in hope, so that we may be children of Abraham.

Rightly, therefore, do we hope for such things following his example, since whatever God has promised, he is able to do [Note: [Col. 1442D] The printed editions read “and preserve.”], provided that true faith, together with unblemished hope and love, remains in us who have believed [Note: [Col. 1442D] The printed editions read “who believe.”]. Hence it is said of Abraham that “he did not grow weak in faith” (Rom. 4:19). This clearly demonstrates that there is such a thing [Note: [Col. 1442D] The printed editions read “at some time.”] as weakness of faith, just as there is health of faith. The Apostle therefore also admonishes us: “Rebuke them, so that they may be sound in faith” (Tit. 1:13).

Blessed, then, is the person whose faith does not grow weak, and whose certain hope against hope in the hope of life grows strong and bears fruit daily through faith. But one kind of hope rests solely and exclusively on God; this is the progress of Christians. Another is entangled in the various and uncertain persuasions of affairs, although these may be desired. Concerning the latter, the philosopher Seneca says to his Lucilius: “Hope is the name of an uncertain good.” Wretched, too, was the person who entrusted to such hope the one whom he was trying to call back from the world.

The hope of Christians, by contrast, is a certain and secure substance that neither deceives nor is deceived. Hence the Apostle says: “Hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:5). Immediately he gives the reason why it is not disappointed by any errors: “Because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.”

All these things, therefore, have been given through Christ to true and devout worshipers. Thus, contrary to the philosopher whom people at that time considered great, hope for Christians is not the name of an uncertain good, but something more certain than can be expressed. For the one who promised us such things is Truth itself and almighty. Therefore nothing uncertain remains in our hope concerning him, nothing doubtful—except that we are more certain about him than about ourselves. We are weak concerning ourselves, but strong concerning him. From this very weakness we are raised up by his mercy, so that, trusting and hoping, we may proceed toward him.

Therefore, as has been said, we hold nothing more certain than our hope, because it rests and reposes not in anyone else but in the one almighty God who does not lie. Faith, since it operates in the human being through the grace of Christ, often slips through human weakness. Hope, because it is wholly in God alone and is from God, is never diminished. Faith, indeed, performs two functions; hope relies only on God alone, whose promises the Lord says, “I do not change” [Note: [Col. 1443D] The printed editions read “I.”]. Therefore faith first fulfills both functions: it rightly understands, from God, whatever is believable, and carries out what he has promised concerning himself [Note: [Col. 1443D] The printed editions read “overcomes.”]. Since hope truly comes from God, it knows most fully that the truthful and almighty God, because he does not change his promises, will fulfill its desires.

3. Otherwise, cursed is the person who places his hope in a human being. He therefore presumes nothing upon a human being and, resting in the truth, produces nothing deceitful. If God delays any of his promises, hope waits devotedly, rests securely, and encourages in all things, while faith struggles and continually points out and displays the promises with its finger.

Hope is everywhere the undisturbed companion of that same faith. Their kinship is wondrous: hope always ardently seeks the things that are not seen and are eternal. Thus, while faith labors and sweats under earthly burdens, hope penetrates the heavens and displays the things that are everlasting.

This is why faith, our victory, conquers all things: it places its hope not in the flesh of its own arm but in God. For God is the hope of faith. Therefore, whenever we lack some grace, hope encourages us that nothing is lacking for the one who possesses God wholly. We are thus revived by confidence, so that everything we do, possess, and desire may be from God.

They therefore have one beginning, one middle, and one end. Neither accomplishes anything perfect without the other; and so we must pray that whatever we do in faith and hope may always be from God.

## CHAPTER IV. Why Hope Is So Called

1. As the truth of etymology demonstrates and the sayings of our ancestors confirm, hope (*spes*) is so called as though it were “a foot” (*est pes*), because it always has the effect of advancing toward those things that it confidently awaits with desire and patiently endures with distress of spirit.

Hence we also read: “Hope that is delayed afflicts the soul” (Prov. 13:12). This does not mean that hope does not proceed securely, with the steps of the virtues, toward what it longs for; rather, the mind burns more ardently while, through faith, it looks upon those things that it has already received in hope, although it has not yet grasped them in reality, and tastes through love what is delayed longer than it desires.

Therefore, continually inflamed with greater fervor [Note: [Col. 1443D] The printed editions read “is inflamed.”], it hastens in hope to reach them. If, God forbid, hope should fail it, it is submerged in violent despair; hence it is called “despair” (*desperatio*). For despair is so called because the foot needed for walking is absent from it on the way, which is Christ. Conversely, those for whom he himself is the way and hope are renewed daily by prosperous progress [Note: [Col. 1443D] The printed editions read “are renewed.”].

Concerning them the prophet Isaiah says: “But those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength; they will take up wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will fly and not faint” (Isa. 40:31). They will run with their feet, because a foot has been set for them on the straight way, so that despair may not steal upon them; and they will not grow weary, because they run securely on the way that is Christ [Note: [Col. 1443D] The printed editions read “they will run.”]; indeed, they are carried.

Hence the Lord says: “I will bear, and I will carry” (Jer. 22:59). Those whom he carries will certainly never faint, because they firmly hold in the hand of faith the hope set before them, which they have in heaven as a secure anchor for the soul. Therefore they proceed with certainty to the place where they rejoice that they have already arrived in hope.

Faith is fixed in Christ, while hope advances, so that by their alternating progress they may make the journey and lead the soul to the place where love, intoxicated [Note: [Col. 1443D] The printed editions read “inebriated.”], invites it. Hence he says: “They will renew their strength,” because the love of those who run ardently in faith and hope has become strong as death. But as soon as faith or hope fails anyone, that person grows lame and sluggish.

If both feet are absent, what progress in virtue can there be? Certainly, faith does not advance without hope, nor hope without faith; rather, they are set forth through each other’s steps and are made alive by one spirit of love. Otherwise, how does faith, even if it believes in God, hasten toward him without hope [Note: [Col. 1444D] The printed editions read “hasten.”], when it does not at all hope to reach him? Or how does hope walk [Note: [Col. 1444D] The printed editions read “walk.”] if it is not grounded in faith, which is the substance of things hoped for, and toward which it sighs daily with holy groans?

Hope therefore hastens toward those things that faith believes and love desires. Thus, as we said, the holy Fathers called hope “a foot,” because it is the foot of those who make progress in Christ [Note: [Col. 1444D] The printed editions read “because it is hope,” but “foot” is preferable.]. Conversely, for apostates and ungodly people, who lack the foot and the ability to walk, there is despair. Therefore they do not run except toward death, nor walk except toward punishments; they do not take up the wings of the virtues or renew their strength, but always seek the lowest things and set their minds on what belongs to the flesh.

2. But the righteous, trusting, sing with David: “My foot has stood on the straight way” (Ps. 25:12) [Note: [Col. 1444D] The printed editions add “in the direct way,” that is, “on the straight way,” which is a copyist’s gloss.]. If they should happen to fall—for “the righteous falls seven times a day” (Prov. 24:16)—they immediately recover their steadfastness and renew their strength in God, saying: “The Lord is my strength, my power, and my refuge.”

Isaiah strongly encourages this when he says: “Who among you has walked in darkness and has no light? Let him hope in the name of the Lord and rely upon his God” (Isa. 50:10). What could be said that is kinder or more merciful? If at some time you have walked, human being, in darkness and in carnal vices, he urges you not to abandon mercy in vain, but to hope again in God, so that he may be your foot for walking, and to rely upon your God, so that you may not be broken by any deceit of despair.

For if your former error has departed, as the same prophet acknowledges, you will have peace with your God.
