Therefore, turning to God, he says: “You will preserve peace, peace, because we have hoped in you” (Isa. 26:3). Then he adds: “Hope in the Lord through everlasting ages, in the Lord God, strong forever.” It is as though he plainly said: Since you have hoped in the Lord, hope not in transient things but through everlasting ages.

Now despise temporal things and desire the eternal, because the things that are seen are temporal, while the things that are not seen are eternal. But what does anyone hope for that he sees? Therefore, without any struggle of despair, hope in the Lord God, strong forever.

Hope not as carnal Israel does—always hoping for the goods of the present, although even these we can possess only from God [Note: [Col. 1445D] The printed editions read “not therefore can we possess them.”]—but let all our hope be directed toward the eternal goods of heaven. Then the things that do not hinder will be added, when we love only the things that are everlasting.

If we take excessive pleasure in temporal things of this kind, the foot is immediately weighed down, because we direct our attention less toward those things that are supreme and unfading. Let these temporal things be our provisions on the road of pilgrimage, but let the eternal things be our inheritance in our homeland.

Let us therefore run with the feet of faith, hope, and love. Let us walk without fainting [Note: [Col. 1445D] The printed editions read “without fainting on the journey; but meanwhile.”]; at times let us attain our anchor more exaltedly on winged flight, so that where Jesus, the high priest, has entered for us, we too may enter. Thus, where the Lord our hope is, there may we also be. Otherwise no place is safe.

Therefore David prays, saying: “Be for me a protecting God and a house of refuge” (Ps. 30:3). Blessed, then, indeed [Note: [Col. 1445D] The printed editions read “certainly blessed.”], and most certain is the progress of hope, which we have as a secure and firm anchor for the soul in heaven. Who, therefore, could despair of entering there, where we already rejoice in hope that we have entered?

Nothing is firmer, stronger, or more certain than the person who places his hope wholly and perfectly in the Lord, with all his heart, all his soul, and all his strength. We have therefore been established in hope, so that every good thing for us, in the present life and the future, may depend upon him and be accomplished, lest we fail to hope in him.

Hence David gratefully says: “In peace I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. 4:9). To make clearer why he comes so securely to sleep in peace, he immediately adds: “For you, Lord, have singularly established me in hope.” Established, then, in hope, as I have said, singularly in Christ, we proceed devoutly toward him, casting our seeds, like all cultivators of the fields. For, as the Apostle Paul says: “Everyone who plows or sows plows and sows in hope” (1 Cor. 9:10).

Let us believe our Creator, who promised the things that have already been given to us, and let us hope with all our innermost being, because we have been established for this purpose from him, in him, and through him: that we may grasp the things that are eternal [Note: [Col. 1445D] The printed editions omit “that.”].

## CHAPTER V. What Difference There Is between True and False Hope, and Whether Hope Can Be Said to Exist Except in God

1. We demonstrate from the divine utterances that true and false hope have the same substance as true and false faith. True faith concerning God consists in thinking rightly about everything and differing in nothing from his works. False faith, however, is not concerning him: it consists in believing what is unworthy, not adhering to the righteous works of faith, and trusting in some other evil.

Concerning this confidence Jeremiah says: “Cursed is the person who trusts in a human being, makes flesh his arm, and turns his heart away from the Lord” (Jer. 17:5). When he says “who trusts in a human being,” it is as though he said “who hopes,” because every confidence arises from hope, whether true or empty.

Let Ecclesiastes say what vanity is: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. 1:2). If, then, all those things that pass away and change are vanity, whoever places his hope or confidence in them has an empty hope, because he presumes upon vanity.

The Apostle also warns his hearers: “Do not hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Tim. 6:17). Their hope is certainly the hope of an uncertain good, as the one about whom we spoke above wished to express. David likewise says: “Do not hope in iniquity” (Ps. 62:10).

From this it is clear that hope is very commonly spoken of both true and empty things. Nevertheless, that hope [Note: [Col. 1446D] The printed editions read “that hope, then, is healthful.”] is proved to be healthful and true for Christians which, after the tribulations, poverty, and miseries of this life, produces patience; patience produces testing; and from that testing arises hope in Christ, which can never be wholly disappointed, because it is supported on every side by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

This is the true and indubitable substance of faith—the substance, I say, in expectation of which we live justly and devoutly. Hence the Apostle also says: “Let us live justly and devoutly, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the Lord” (Tit. 2:12–13).

2. But it must be asked how we are commanded to await the hope in which and with which we already live, reborn in Christ. Do we live justly and devoutly without hope, when nevertheless we do whatever good we do in hope? If we already have hope, how do we await what we possess? Or is the hope that exists at present miserable, while the hope that is in the future is awaited as blessed?

I would certainly not say this, because Christians have one hope, just as they have one faith. Therefore this hope with which we are sprinkled is itself the hope that we await [Note: [Col. 1446D] The printed editions omit “this.”], because from its brightness [Note: [Col. 1446D] The printed editions read “its love.”] it shines back into our hearts.

Just as heat never comes except from fire, and light never comes except from a source of light [Note: [Col. 1446D] The printed editions read “from light.”], so this hope with which we are suffused comes only from God. God is our hope, and therefore our hope is present and awaited. For although hope concerns both the future and what is absent, God is always present and everywhere, and our hope is always in him.

Until what has been promised comes to us, we await the blessed hope—namely, the immortality of flesh and soul—and the coming of the Lord, so that thereafter we may remain blessed with him and in him forever.

This, then, is true hope, which we possess as a secure and firm anchor. In possessing it, we await whatever is contained in it; and in awaiting it, we already possess, by gift, whatever has been promised to us in Christ. Therefore, at present we carry a blessed and everlasting hope concerning the future. We are commanded to live justly and devoutly while desiring and enduring it.

We must therefore watch carefully lest we lose endurance. The Apostle speaks of some people: “Woe to those who have lost endurance.” This endurance is continually refreshed amid various struggles by the sweetness of devout expectation, because hope supported by love is disappointed in nothing. For its sake all empty things are confidently despised and adversities are overcome.

Christian hope separates every human being from the worship of the gods, because “all the gods of the nations are vanity and demons.” It separates us from the things that are in the world, because all of them are empty. It separates us from errors and wicked persuasions, and it glories in the Lord alone and in his promises, to such an extent that it presumes nothing either upon itself or upon anyone else, lest it fall under the curse that says: “Cursed is everyone who makes flesh his strength and turns his heart away from the Lord.”

Indeed, hope enters wholly into the place where Jesus, the high priest, has entered for us, and, like an anchor, solidifies and strengthens the whole human being in Christ, so that the heart may be where it knows that the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are found.

Otherwise, if we are hoping in Christ only for this life, as the Apostle says, “we are more miserable than all human beings” (1 Cor. 15:19). When he says “only in this life,” he did not exclude it, as though we ought not to hope in him in this life [Note: [Col. 1447D] The printed editions read “that we ought not hope in him in this life.”]. Nevertheless, whatever we hope for at present [Note: [Col. 1447D] The printed editions read “whatever we hope for.”] must wholly be referred to the future, and we must first seek the things that are eternal.

Hence the Lord says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33). What things? Those that are necessary for the present life. They will indeed be added, because we struggle not for their sake but for the sake of those eternal things; and while hoping, we sow the seeds of life, directing our minds always toward them alone.

For, as the Apostle says: “Everyone who plows ought to plow in hope” (1 Cor. 9:10). Likewise, whoever does something good must certainly spend himself in hope of receiving it also [Note: [Col. 1447D] The printed editions omit “also,” reading “of receiving himself.”]. But the hope of farmers, because it concerns the present, ought to be in God, since he is the author and giver of all things, lest it prove to be foolish hope.

Concerning this, as the Apostle said [Note: [Col. 1447D] The printed editions omit “as he said.”], he declares that if we hope in Christ only for this life, we are more miserable than all human beings. Nevertheless, it is already a step toward going to God to refer even the good things of the present to him, from whom, although unworthy, we receive them [Note: [Col. 1447D] The printed editions read “from whom these things, although unworthy.”], so that through them we may be directed toward the things that are not seen.

Hence David speaks of the Jews: “He gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labors of the peoples.” Immediately he adds: “So that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law” (Ps. 105:44). Clearly, this was so that, made more secure by the hope already received, they might be more ardent in attaining the things that are eternal.

Therefore false hope is altogether that which, without God, rests in the uncertainty of riches, or in a human being, because he is flesh, or in anything else that is not at all. Firm and safe, however, is the hope that is only in God, hoping for the things that are not seen and are eternal.

3. Hope for receiving temporal things is not rightly directed toward the things that are seen [Note: [Col. 1447D] The printed editions omit “toward the things that are seen.”]; rather, it must be referred by intention toward the things that are not seen, and for their sake [Note: [Col. 1448D] The printed edition reads “for its sake.”] those temporal things must be sought as though on the way, with devout hope. Otherwise, to hope only for the present is a great misery [Note: [Col. 1448D] The printed editions read “to hope for everything.”].

If, then, everyone who plows ought to plow in hope, this very hope must presume that everything has been provided for us by God—not upon furrows or seeds, nor upon the ordering of time or the power of nature. From God we ought also to hope for temporal goods in the labors of the harvest, and we ought to refer what we hope for to the things that are eternal, so that we may reach them.

Hence the Psalmist also exhorts us, saying: “Hope in the Lord and do good” (Ps. 37:3). For we hope rightly for what has been promised when we fulfill what has been commanded, because “whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (Gal. 6:7).

Therefore the sole hope of Christians is this: that we hope from God for all the things that have been given to us, and sow in him the seeds of good works, which are promised to us a hundredfold. Thus hope itself, together with faith through love, continues to operate until the end amid prosperity and adversity.

Tested by these trials, it is in no way disappointed, because, with love poured into the heart, it is tirelessly lifted toward the things that are eternal. If someone has not yet ceased to sin and is not stirred to do what is commanded, he presumes in vain upon pardon or merit from God’s mercy.

Hope is not idle. Rather, from true faith in God and from the works of faith, it acquires for itself a rooted foundation [Note: [Col. 1448D] The printed editions read “substance.”]. This same faith, together with all the works of faith, is the substance of things hoped for. Therefore let each person test himself according to how much he does from faith and believes.

Rightly, then, one may hope from him only through faith—from him who has given the power to believe and to act through faith, and who causes us to be born as children of adoption. Otherwise it is presumption rather than hope if anyone hopes for more or for something other than what he rightly believes with the devotion of affection and carries out through the progress of piety.

What has been promised and given in Christ is believed; therefore it is rightly hoped for if faith, through love, has been fulfilled amid prosperity and adversity, with temporal things abandoned, so that it may bring back from God the result of its testing [Note: [Col. 1448D] The printed editions omit “from God the result.”].

By this testing, then, the person who, disputing with God, rejoiced in hope, confidently said: “I hope in you, Lord, that you do not stretch out your hand for my destruction” (Job 30:24) [Note: [Col. 1449D] The printed editions read “often saying.”]. It is as though he plainly said: “You stretch it out to scourge me, to test me, and to deliver me to death. But if I am plunged into the depths of hell, you will free me from there.”

See how great is this hope, and how it cannot be disappointed: it remains firm and solid, secure and devout, in God. It does not fear punishments or the place of hell, because there is nowhere that he who is able—the almighty God—is not present. Therefore the person whose hope is in him is proved to be altogether blessed even amid miseries.

David says: “Blessed is the one whose Lord is his God” (Ps. 144:15). Knowing this, blessed Job could not be miserable or disappointed in hell, because after his testing he believed that God was favorably disposed toward him everywhere; nor did he doubt that God had been present with him there.

It is plain that no Christian hope exists except the Most High God [Note: [Col. 1449D] The printed edition reads *nulla* (“no”) for *non ulla* (“not any”).], in whom are all things that are not seen. No one has ever truly held or now truly holds hope in anything else, however much it may be called hope, since such hope is altogether empty and false.

Knowing this, that holy woman exclaimed before the judge of her heart: “We have never had hope in another god” (Esth. 14:19). If she had, it would have been altogether empty, because “all the gods of the nations are demons.” The Lord alone, the truth of heaven, was her hope. From that hope all who rightly hope in him and persevere are blessed; therefore she gloried in him.

It is plainly clear that, although some hope may be spoken of here or there, it can be true only if it is from God [Note: [Col. 1449D] The printed editions add “to be.”]. True hope is never without confidence of reaching its goal. For without progress and the grace of attaining, it is no longer hope but ruinous despair.

Although true hope exists amid adversities, it is never without glory, even in tribulations—tribulations in which the Apostle Paul especially glories—and not only in them, but also in the hope of the glory of the children, which is never miserable.

True glory is always free from misery. Therefore the hope of glory cannot be miserable, since it is illuminated by glory. Let us therefore hold the hope of light, lest we be enveloped in darkness. Let us hasten toward the hope of immortality, so that we may be free from death.

Hope, then, concerns all those things that are not seen. Whoever preserves this hope, filled with good and righteous works, will enjoy all these goods without end and will be blessed even in death.

The hope of Christians is nourished so that it may grow strong daily by patience and by the consolation of the Holy Scriptures, as the Apostle Paul demonstrates when he says: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15:4).

Hope is therefore increased through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures, because from patience comes the testing that leads to perfection, from perfection in good works hope is entrusted to Christ, and through the consolation of the Scriptures it is made firm.

For this reason the Scriptures must be meditated upon, so that we may be consoled by them amid the various pressures of temptation; and patience must be preserved while we are wearied by our labors. Hence the Lord says: “By your patience you will possess your souls.”

Lofty, therefore, is the hope of glory, illuminated by all good things and growing feathers on the wings of the virtues, so that it may always lift the soul of its possessor to higher things.

## CHAPTER VI. On Despair

1. Nothing is worse at present than the evil of despair, because to despair is always to fall downward. Everyone who despairs acts either to lose the pardon freely granted by God or not to seek the pardon hoped for, although it has not yet been granted.

Therefore, whoever loves not to despair of this very thing and possesses that love because he loves it has no despair, but a step toward attainment. Whatever anyone hopes for, he loves; but as soon as he begins to despair of something, he also ceases to love it, because he declares that it does not belong to him.

What we love, we either possess or hope for. What is hoped for, we confidently believe belongs to us, and so we guard it with unwavering hope. Otherwise, to despair of God is to be alienated backward from him.

Therefore, blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is nothing other than despair and an unrepentant heart; and for this reason there is no forgiveness of sins wherever despair and impenitence of heart remain.

Hence it is not fitting to despair, lest one fail to attain, because despair is nothing other than acting so that hope may not reach its goal. To despair is to flee from hope, and whoever flees from hope apostatizes and withdraws from that very thing toward which he ought to have hastened by hope [Note: [Col. 1450D] The edition omits “thing,” substituting “and”; another printed reading has “toward hope.”].

It is necessary that the person who despairs, by alienating himself backward, never possess hope, just as one who continually fixes his gaze upon darkness never sees the light. For what does the person who looks toward darkness and persists in it [Note: [Col. 1450D] The printed edition reads “holding” for “looking toward.”] accomplish except ensuring that he does not see the light?

So also the person who despairs makes it impossible for anything good to happen to him. Therefore despair is nothing other than turning hope away from good things.

Let a person therefore lift his heart away from wickedness, because the more deeply he falls through despair, the farther he withdraws from the desired good.

2. Despair, however, arises from four causes: [Col. 1450D] namely, from lukewarmness or sluggishness; from love of temporal things or delight in pleasures; from the enormity of sins or crimes; and from contempt born of pride and the desire for self-determination. From lukewarmness or sluggishness it arises when the mind grows numb and God’s commandments are judged impossible—not because they are so burdensome, but because the mind, weighed down by miserable weakness, is unwilling to rise up, so that, through Christ’s grace, it might be able, with the Apostle, to do all things in him who strengthens our minds. Thus he does not acknowledge that Christ’s labor conquers all things, and becomes guilty, whether because, pressed down by evil torpor, he accuses nature [Col. 1451A]—[Note: The edition reads *malo*, “by evil,” instead of *male*, “badly” or “wrongly.”]—or because he judges that God has commanded burdensome and impossible things. It also arises from love of temporal things or delight in pleasures, when the mind rejoices as though blessed to take delight in these things—those concerning whom the peoples said, “whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity; whose sons are like newly planted shoots, and whose daughters are adorned like the likeness of a temple; whose storehouses are full, whose sheep are prolific, and whose oxen are exceedingly fat” (Ps. CXLIII, 8). Enticed by these things and intoxicated by various pleasures, the mind neither hopes for nor seeks eternal goods. [Note: The edition reads “acquires” instead of “seeks.”] It has therefore placed all its hope in these things and no longer looks toward anything else.

Next, despair arises from the enormity or excessiveness of crimes, because, with the devil deceiving him, a person judges his sins greater than God’s mercy [Col. 1451B]; sometimes, even though he presumes upon God’s power, he doubts his will. David, understanding this well, asks that mercy be shown to him not according to his sins, but according to God’s great mercy and according to the abundance of his compassions (Ps. L, 5), not reckoning his crimes to be as great as he knew God’s mercies to be. Another prophet likewise says: “I know that his compassions are many” (1 Chron. XXI, 13). It is therefore clear that there is no guilt which God’s mercy does not surpass, nor is there any number of offenses so great that the compassions are not more numerous—unless despair or impenitence of heart shuts the door.

Finally, from contempt arises the more dangerous despair in which all the angels of Satan are known to have fallen once and for all; through pride, they despise returning, even if they could. Hence Scripture says of the reprobate: “When the wicked has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3). Otherwise, if he had not plunged into despair through impenitence of heart, he would never have come into such a depth of evils that he would despise. This guilt is plainly more monstrous than all other guilt, and is remitted neither here nor in the future, because it closes the way to the Holy Spirit entering the soul, so that the soul may not receive forgiveness through his indulgence. And this is, as I said, to blaspheme against the Holy Spirit: to plunge into despair lest the heart return to repentance, and to relax [Note: The edition reads *reluctari*, “to resist,” instead of *relaxare*, “to relax” or “let go.”].

3. Therefore, although the crime is most monstrous, it is enough that, according to God’s great mercy, once repentance has been received, one should hope for forgiveness. [Note: In the editions, *recepta* is omitted, and the text reads again: “he should hope for forgiveness.”] If sins are innumerable, let him believe with certainty that mercy is more numerous still, lest either the greatness of the offense overwhelm us or its multiplicity engulf us. David, rightly considering this elsewhere, prays: “Let not the storm of water engulf me, nor let the deep swallow me up” (Ps. LXVIII, 16). For those whom despair has once swallowed, like demons it continually drags back to the depths, lest they return.

Hope, moreover, is a kind of progress, provided that it is not false; for false hope, just as it helps nothing, so true hope makes the one who hopes blessed. Great, therefore, is the security of the hope to which God’s promises—or rather, God himself in a special way—are present. Thus hope, according to the Hebrew truth in the Psalms, is called confidence or security, where it says: “For you, Lord, have made me dwell especially in security” (Ps. IV, 10). For it is great security for the soul to dwell under the help of the Most High and to abide under the protection of the God of heaven.

We have this safe hope within Christ’s inner veil, where Christ the high priest entered. For if you are a sinner, forgiveness reigns; if you are weak and sick, salvation; if you are dead through sins, life is given; and if you are in darkness, light shines all around. There is no place for despair where omnipotence is active—provided only that your soul is not pressed down [Note: The edition reads: “if neither the soul nor sluggishness should depress you.”] either by sluggishness, or enticed by transient goods, or engulfed by the enormity of crimes, or swallowed up by contempt. Once these things have been driven away, secure hope, safe in the refuge of the Most High, overcomes everything.

Hence all who hope in the Lord are already called blessed, even amid the miseries of this world. But those who hope do not sin, as the Psalmist sings: “All who hope in the Lord do not sin” (Ps. XXXIII, 23). It is clear from the Apostle’s words that charity never sins, because it never fails (1 Cor. XIII, 8); nor does hope, because it does everything in charity. There is therefore no hope that does not love and believe; and if it believes and loves, it does not sin. Hence the Truth also says: “Everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John XI, 26).

For all Christian hope proceeds from faith and charity. Take away faith, and there is nothing you can hope for, because faith concerns things that are unseen and eternal. If you hope for and love them because they are the highest good and eternal, you certainly believe both that they exist and that they pertain to you; you hope for them because they have been given and promised through faith. Hence God is said to dwell in us through faith, just as we are already in God through grace, in whom we have placed all our hope (Jer. XVII, 17). In another sense, just as God is called charity, so the Lord is also my hope.

4. But we must ask whether the very love by which God is loved is itself to be loved, and whether the faith by which God is believed is itself to be believed. Perhaps then we shall be able to understand whether hope itself is to be hoped for—the hope by which we hope for eternal things.

Concerning this hope the Apostle says: “He regenerated us unto a living hope” (1 Pet. I, 3), plainly because there is also a dead hope. And again he says: “Let us live justly and devoutly, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the Lord” (Tit. II, 13). From this it is evident that, although love is to be loved, not every love is to be loved, just as not everyone’s faith is to be believed. There is also a shameful love by which the mind often pursues things inferior to itself, and this is rightly called desire. So too there is false faith, which is called not faith but error.

Therefore, just as no love of a thing is to be loved except the love of that which cannot be absent when it is loved, and just as no faith whatsoever is to be believed except faith in that which is always the same and never changes, so hope is not to be hoped for with certainty except hope in that same reality which is already possessed when it is hoped for and which already makes those who hope in it blessed.

Concerning this hope the Prophet says: “Blessed are all who hope in you, Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII, 13). This is the blessed hope for which we wait, together with the coming of the Lord. But what does “we wait” mean except that, although we possess the same hope, we nevertheless hope for it, even though through it we are already blessed?

To love these things, therefore, is nothing other than to know them; nor is hoping or believing anything other than possessing them. Thus the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for.” If faith is the substance of things hoped for, it is certainly a sure and most firm reality, and hope must not waver. Otherwise, if faith deceives and the reality is emptied—if what was a phantom in faith is not found in reality, and what was loved in faith is not present—then loving is nothing other than desiring some thing for its own sake. When the phantom has failed, the reality that was believed or loved becomes indisputable misery. [Note: In the editions, *res* is omitted and *ea* is added: “the thing that is believed or loved becomes an indisputable misery.”]

Therefore faith in God must be established with the utmost certainty, so that the highest love may also grow strong. The disciples going to Emmaus expressed this well concerning the Lord: “We were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke XXIV, 21), plainly because they were hard-hearted in believing all that had been written about him; otherwise, if they had believed perfectly, they would also have hoped perseveringly. But when faith failed and hope withdrew, they said: “We were hoping.” When the Truth began to open himself to them from the Scriptures, faith immediately grew warm [Note: The edition reads “recovered” instead of “grew warm.”] and hope revived. Finally they said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the way?”

From this it is clear that neither of these is effective without the other; nor is either loved—or at least hoped for—if it is not possessed through faith. Otherwise, how could anyone be blessed in the present? True blessedness arises from the certainty of a reality of supreme goodness, which can never be absent while it is loved, hoped for, or believed in with complete faith.

5. Yet a person can possess what he neither loves, believes, nor hopes for, and therefore he is said to be blessed only falsely. For example, when the Prophet had counted the happiness of this world, he said: “They called the people blessed who possess these things” (Ps. CXLIII, 3). But lest you think that he immediately introduced true blessedness by excluding the false, he says: “Blessed is the people whose God is the Lord.”

With temporal things, therefore, hoping or believing is not the same as possessing, nor is loving the same as knowing; and therefore they are neither to be hoped for nor loved. Our hope and love must instead be directed toward him who cannot be taken away while he is hoped for or loved. Otherwise, if God is neither hoped for nor loved, no one can perfectly possess or know him. For who can know how good the highest good is if he does not enjoy it? If we do not love it, neither do we enjoy it; and therefore we do not possess what ought to be hoped for or loved, since we neither hope for nor love it.

Even though we can love what we do not possess, no one knows the blessed life while remaining miserable. For if it is to be loved as it is, then knowing it is possessing it, and possessing it is certainly hoping for it. Since these things are so, what else is it to live blessedly except to possess something eternal by knowing it?

Hence the Lord says to God the Father: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3). This is the eternal life of which it is rightly said, in accordance with faith, that it cannot be taken away from the one who hopes for or loves it. For everything hoped for as eternal is loved [Note: The editions omit: “and believed; but not everything that is believed is rightly loved.”] and believed; but not everything that is believed is rightly loved, because eternal punishment is not loved.

Nevertheless, there is a manner of speaking in the holy Scriptures whereby everything in which one believes is rightly hoped for [Note: The edition adds: “and loved.”] and loved. Consequently, we do not immediately hope for whatever is believed; but we do not believe in just anyone, since we ought to believe in no one other than God. We enjoy him and hope in him. For the most excellent of all things is that which God is. Therefore we cannot possess him except in that which is most excellent in us, namely, the mind. Whatever is possessed in the mind through believing is certainly also possessed through knowing.

What is known or believed, because it is the highest good, is rightly hoped for and loved. But no good is perfectly known unless it is perfectly loved, and before that it is not understood unless it is believed. For enjoyment of the highest good is charity. Faith is the beginning of all virtues and the way to the highest good; certain hope is their intermediate stage; and charity is the end of all commandments.

Yet the beginning does not exist without the end [Note: The editions omit: “although charity will be future without faith.”], even though charity will be future without faith, because when what is perfect has come, what is partial will be brought to nothing. Nor does their intermediate stage—namely, hope—exist without the beginning, faith, or without the end, perfect love. Thus we are given life by faith, carried upward by hope, and set aflame by charity.

Because by the things we believe we are carried by hope toward eternal things, among which we have placed hope like a secure anchor, the mind is moved by love of eternity so that it is always occupied with eternal things. Through these, finally, because they are eternal, the blessed mind lives.

Hence the Lord commands: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.” Since love is the mind’s appetite, and since—apart from its rational part, by which the mind understands—we see its other parts tending toward desire, when every appetite has been turned so that the whole mind is occupied in the love of God [Note: The editions read: “so that the whole mind may also be occupied in the love of God,” omitting “the whole.”], there will be great tranquility and peace in a person. He will desire to contemplate nothing other than what is loved and eternal.

In this way, too, the mind is affected by eternity through an indissoluble bond. Entirely intoxicated by it, the mind remains vigorous and is daily carried inwardly toward God by hope and by the force of love.

# CHAPTER VII. That for the present hope is not exercised very much without fear, nor fear raised to higher things without hope

1. The mind is therefore guided by the wings of these two virtues, as though by a double oar, while it is restrained by fear lest it deviate upward toward shipwreck. We are always lifted by hope toward better incentives to virtue, and, presuming upon what has been promised, we embrace them inwardly as though we had already obtained them; but necessarily we are pierced by fear, lest we slip here and there into vices. Thus we are restrained by fear and lifted up by hope.

Concerning this fear the Apostle Peter says: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. II, 12). And concerning hope the prophet Isaiah says: “In hope shall be your strength” (Isa. XXX, 15). It is therefore clear that we are strengthened by hope in the Lord and perform our works in good hope. Through fear we preserve both what has been done and what has been promised, as though stored or kept under a seal.

Hence the Prophet also sings: “The fear of the Lord is his treasure” (Isa. XXXIII, 6). Through these two means we are properly reduced to flour, so that, according to the Lord’s teaching [Note: The edition reads *doctrinam*, “teaching,” but *doctrina*, “teaching” as the subject, is better.], we may be kneaded into the unleavened bread of sincerity [Col. 1455C] and truth and become unleavened loaves.

For we are the Lord’s wheat because the grain has fallen into the earth; and by grace it is necessary that the upper and lower millstone, according to the most equitable right of the law, reduce us to flour. Concerning this millstone we read in the Book of Numbers: “You shall not accept the upper or lower millstone as a pledge” (Deut. XXIV, 6).

The upper and lower millstone by which the minds of the faithful are properly reduced to meal, becoming a new kneading, are not rightly accepted as a pledge when hope and fear are not removed from the preacher’s teaching. “You shall not accept” means, in effect, “you shall not take away.” Hence certain birds are called *accipitres*—hawks—because they take away. Concerning this word Paul says: “For you endure it if someone devours you, if someone takes from you” (2 Cor. XI, 20). As though he were saying: “You endure it if someone robs and takes away.”

From this it is plainly gathered that from the place of the pledge—that is, from the confession or conscience of some sin—the upper millstone, namely hope, must not be taken away, nor the lower one, which is the fear of love. Concerning this fear the Prophet sings: “The holy fear of the Lord endures forever and ever” (Ps. XVIII, 10).

These two virtues must therefore not be removed from the minds of individuals, because to the degree that hope carries the mind upward, fear must restrain below the heart that presumes wrongly [Note: The edition omits *male*, “wrongly,” although it is appropriate here]. They are so profitably joined to one another that neither can salutarily stand [Note: The edition reads *flare*, “to blow,” instead of *stare*, “to stand.”] without the other. For a person hopes in vain for mercy if he does not also fear the justice of the strict judge; and he fears justice dangerously if he does not firmly trust in the mercy of the giver.

The upper and lower millstone are therefore forbidden to be taken away from the place of the pledge, so that hope is never found without fear, nor fear without hope—not so that anyone, slipping away from hope, should remain in fear alone, or, deceived by presumption without fear, should perish in vain hope. For Christ’s mercy is not without justice, nor is justice without mercy. Therefore hope should temper the dread of fear, so that holy fear may guard the height of hope.

Concerning this fear the Prophet says: “Fear the Lord, all you his saints” (Ps. XXXIII, 10), and also: “The fear of the Lord is the confidence of strength.”

2. Great, therefore, is the confidence of fear, just as great is the glory of hope. Hope is the beginning of labor, whereas fear is the guardian of the reward. Thus a person acts confidently when his merits support him, striving more diligently by seeking better things so that each day he may become more worthy of such great hope.

For what athlete, if he despaired of the crown, would readily enter the stadium? Or if he sought it, would rightly be found a victor? Thus testing produces hope, and hope produces confidence. Therefore hope is not put to shame, although it is preserved thus far by holy fear, because faith, at its proper time, performs the works of love; in faith are preserved the riches of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge.

Hence what immediately follows is: “The fear of the Lord is his treasure.” Rich indeed is the treasure in which the riches of salvation shine and the resources of wisdom and knowledge gleam more gloriously. The treasure of these virtues is therefore preserved by fear and presumed upon through hope.

Hence the Apostle says: “He regenerated us in the hope of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. V, 2). Hope is always the attainment of rewards, or the glory of the one who desires. Fear, on the other hand, is a modesty suffused with holy love, lest one offend in any way against the reward to which one has been invited and which one intends in mind to please. This is not a penal feeling but a modest one, conquered by faith and by the love of true charity.

Otherwise, without fear the bond of love is scarcely, or never, preserved; just as without hope there is material for sluggishness or torpor. Hope, however, is an incentive to virtue. Everyone is therefore stirred toward what he desires, especially when he hopes, without any distrust, to receive that grace in full. Hence hope is never accompanied without joy, so that the manifestation of future blessedness may already be present in it.

Concerning this hope the Prophet promises, saying: “Let all who hope in you, Lord, rejoice” (Ps. V, 12). Otherwise, what blessedness is there in fear when it is handed over without hope? It is therefore rightly proclaimed without the joy of gladness, yet the Prophet calls the one who possesses it altogether blessed, because he is refreshed by the dew of gladness.

The same prophet says: “Let my heart rejoice, so that it may fear your name” (Ps. LXXXV, 11), and also: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord” (Ps. CXXVII, 1). Blessedness is therefore rightly promised in this fear, because through the grace of the Holy Spirit it is raised even to the hope of glory and is continually moved toward better things by these two virtues.

Thus, as I said, because we are the Lord’s grain of seed, we are reduced to powder by the millstones of these virtues and renewed by Christ’s teaching. Concerning this sacrifice we are commanded in Leviticus to take up a full handful, because the power of good works is not taken from us in greater measure than what is offered from faith. This, I say, is the flour that Sarah offered, and in which that woman from the Gospel stored and hid the leaven of Christ’s teaching according to the number of the Trinity.

3. Sometimes, although fear restrains and humbles the mind, at other times it strengthens and comforts it. Such is Solomon’s saying, which I mentioned above: “In the fear of the Lord is hope of strength.” For just as in the way of the world boldness produces strength and fear produces weakness, so in the way of God fear produces strength.

Hence Eliphaz, recounting the virtues of blessed Job, says: “Your fear is your strength, your patience and the perfection of your ways” (Job IV, 6). He joined strength to fear because, as has been said, strength of mind is generated from fear.

Our mind despises the terrors of temporal things more powerfully in proportion as it submits more truly, through strength, to their creator. Thus a mind rightly established in the fear of the Lord finds nothing outside him that it should fear, while it is raised inwardly above all things with confidence by a certain power [Note: The edition reads *pietate*, “devotion,” instead of *potestate*, “power.”].

The ascent of the virtues begins from fear [Note: The edition reads *quidam*, “a certain,” instead of *quidem*, “indeed”]. Then the mind is strengthened by courage; once strengthened, it patiently endures the evils of the present through the word [Note: The edition reads *praesertim*, “especially,” instead of *praesentium*, “of present things.”]. From this patience the perfection of God’s ways is undertaken, so that the mind may rise more firmly to hope. [Note: The edition reads “may rise again” instead of “may rise.”]

The Apostle accordingly testifies, saying that patience produces testing, and testing produces hope (Rom. V, 4). Through these stages, therefore, the mind, divinely invigorated, is certainly not put to shame, because the charity of God, poured out in the hearts of believers, accomplishes all these things.

Let it therefore be enough for the time being to have offered this preliminary account of the hope of our salvation. Let us bring to an end the little book that we have published in the hope that it may benefit the little ones, without bringing the hope itself to an end; so that in what follows, as your blessedness requested, we may take up charity with renewed strength and say something about it more ardently, though briefly—by the help of him who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one and true God, Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

[Col. 1457B]

# [On Charity]

## Prologue to the Book on Charity

[Col. 1457]

# [Col. 1457C] After a long interruption of my studies of Scripture, worn out by the prolonged shipwreck of caring for worldly affairs, although rustic, I at last devotedly return to the quiet that I love. I do so that what the sluggish activity of an indolent life had plunged into torpor, with the senses asleep, may be awakened and wiped clean by the charity of Christ, about which I desire to speak, lest my inactive diligence, enjoying for a little while a purified silence, should remain fruitless. [Note: The edition reads *tamen*, “nevertheless,” instead of *tandem*, “at last.”]

I have indeed dug the wells that the old man Abraham had dug. But because the Philistines are always eager to block them up, I must labor again with Isaac, having found living water in the wellspring of faith, so that we may be able to overcome the quarrels and calumnies of our enemies. Then I must dig out another well of hope more deeply, and thus overcome the disputes and enmities of all adversaries.

But because, after these tasks had at last been exhausted, through the Lord’s generosity we have tasted a little of the waters springing up into eternal life, it remains to dig out a third well, for which and against which no one can quarrel. This well is called breadth, concerning which the Psalmist says: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. CXVIII, 96), because it contains everything that is hidden and everything that is manifest [Note: The edition reads “everything that is possible” instead of “everything that is manifest.”].

Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, and that Ethiopian woman Zipporah were accustomed to come to these wells of water and draw from them. For they had rightly devoted these three most closely related sisters of the seven gifts to themselves in their minds with every act of love; drinking from them, they became intoxicated daily and were always found there.

Philosophers, too, wished to dig these same wells, which they called physics, ethics, and logic. But because they find water without Christ, they do not find living water. Solomon likewise composed three little books concerning these three virtues; in the third, how great are its breadth and depth is proved only by the embraces of the bridegroom and the kisses of the bride.

Concerning this well the Samaritan woman, asked about it, prophesies unknowingly that the well is exceedingly deep and that no one drinks from it unless Jesus gives him the water springing up into eternal life. It is indeed a deep fountain, to which no one ascends more deeply; therefore he must be invoked, without whom no one reaches that place to draw water.

These streams of the wells are by no means the broad waters that the seasoning of fables has made salty, but those that Jesus has opened to believers, saying: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII, 38).

This charity, about which we intend to speak [Note: The edition reads “about which we shall speak” instead of “about which we intend to speak”], may be called the commandment of commandments or the gift of all gifts, just as the Song of Songs is so called; for all commandments are fulfilled by this one, just as all the gifts of salvation are perfected by this one. Otherwise, whatever gift you may have without charity, it benefits you nothing.

*The prologue ends.*

# The Book on Charity Begins

## Chapter One. What Is Charity?

1. Let us ask John the Apostle, and he will tell what he drew from the fountain of Christ’s breast; for he says: “God is charity” (1 John IV, 16). Behold how brief a definition—and you have what charity is. Yet none of the philosophers penetrates it, because it is immeasurable and profound. For among them we read of several kinds of definition: for example, the *usialis* [essential] [Note: The edition reads *usiodis*; *usialis* is better, from the Greek οὐσία, “substance.”], which is substantial and is properly and truly called a definition; and a second, which in Greek is called *onomatica*, and may be termed a notion, because it conveys knowledge of the thing under inquiry from its operations.

But the Apostle openly proclaims that God is charity. This is not said relatively or merely by appellation, as certain things are said of the Lord, but substantially, as are truth, light, and the other things of which the Lord is predicated substantially. Hence we must ask whether God the Father is charity, or God the Son, or God the Holy Spirit, or God the Trinity itself together. Yet we must not confess that charity is God because it is God’s gift, but because charity is that substance which God is, just as are goodness, life, and the other things, as I said, which are said substantially of God.

For it is said to God: “You are my patience and my refuge” (Ps. LXX, 5), and many such things; likewise, “You are my hope and my mercy.” Yet we do not properly say, “You are my charity”; rather we must say, “God is charity,” as it has been said, “God is spirit.” Let whoever distinguishes this seek understanding from God, not reason from man. Yet although we say, “Wisdom, truth, life, or light is God,” and the like, all these are but one substance. Likewise, when we say that charity is God, it is the same as saying that God is life, light, wisdom, and the rest, because God the Trinity is a simple substance.

We rightly understand, therefore, that God the Father is charity, that God the Son likewise is charity, and that God the Holy Spirit is charity. [Note: The editions omit: “Just as God the Father is wisdom, and God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit.”] Just as God the Father is wisdom, and God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit, yet we do not therefore speak of three charities or three wisdoms, but of one wisdom and one charity; just as we confess one God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And just as the Son is properly called the Word of God and also the wisdom of God, so charity is most fittingly called the Holy Spirit; yet in such a way that the simple nature of God is not one thing in substance and another in charity, but charity itself is the substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, although the Holy Spirit is properly called charity.

John the Apostle likewise says: “Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God. And everyone who loves has been born of God; whoever does not love has not known God, because God is love” (1 John IV, 7). He makes clear that this same love is to be understood as the Holy Spirit, whom he said is from God, because the Holy Spirit is from God the Father and the Son. Yet the Son also is from God the Father; therefore this is indicated more openly where he says that we know that we remain in him and he in us because he has given us of his Spirit. And this is to remain in God: to remain in charity, because the Holy Spirit whom he gave us is love. And everyone who loves is from God, because the Holy Spirit [Note: The edition omits *sanctus*, “Holy.”], who is love, is God. Behold what charity is. Whoever remains in it is cheated by no enmities and no snares of calumny, but remains wholly from God and securely in God. [Note: The edition reads *ideo*, “therefore.”]

[Col. 1460C] 2. Therefore whoever has charity has the Holy Spirit in himself, because the Holy Spirit is charity; and such a person belongs to Christ, because he has the Spirit of Christ. Otherwise, if he does not have Christ’s Spirit, he has neither charity nor belongs to Christ, because he is without his Spirit. [Note: The edition reads *simul*, “at the same time”; *sine*, “without,” is much better.] Charity, therefore, which is God, is no small power. Hence it cannot be possessed except from him in whom it is, and in whom one must believe. John says: “We have known and believed the charity of God which he has in us” (1 John IV, 16). And what is “which he has in us,” unless it is that he has given us of his Spirit? [Note: The editor’s emendation *sancto*, “Holy,” for *suo*, “his,” is not so good.] Therefore, when the Spirit is given, Christ’s charity is poured out, as the Apostle Paul testifies: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” (Rom. V, 5).

Hence, when he came upon the Apostles, he appeared in the heat of fire, because charity makes those whom it fills burning and joins them to God. Therefore, if God the Father is charity and the Son is charity, the charity of the Father and the charity of the Son are one, not one person. Consequently, those who come together to God, who are perfect in charity, are rightly called one, in accordance with Truth’s assertion, and make their dwelling with him. For when such charity, which is God, is in anyone, that person loves nothing earthly, material, or corruptible, because it is contrary to the nature of charity to love anything corruptible—especially since he himself is the fountain of incorruption. For he alone has immortality, since God is charity, who alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light (1 John IV, 16; 1 Tim. VI, 16). What else is immortality believed to be but eternal life? God promises to give it to those who believe in him, the only true God, [Note: The edition omits *Deum*, “God.”] and in Jesus Christ his Son, whom he sent.

3. Therefore, before and above all things, this is said to be especially lovable and pleasing to God: that each person should love the Lord his God with his whole heart, whole soul, and all his strength, because God is charity, and the Son, who is from God, is charity. Hence God requires in us something like himself, so that through this charity which is in Christ Jesus, who is charity, we may be joined to him as if by a kindred affinity through the name of charity. Thus Paul, already joined to him, said: “Who shall separate us from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord?” (Rom. VIII, 35).

This charity makes one’s fellow human being a neighbour to oneself and to God, as Truth demonstrates in the Gospel (Luke X), saying to a certain proud man that a man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho fell among robbers. A priest and a Levite passed him by wounded and half-dead, but the Samaritan embraced him—the one who had shown him mercy—and declares that he was their neighbour [Note: The editions read *coram*, “before.”]; from the man’s own confession he makes it clear that he was neighbour. Hence he added: “Go, and do likewise” (ibid., 37), as though plainly saying: Whoever wishes to be a neighbour according to God, let him perform the works of charity, which are the bowels of compassion according to the inner person, so that they may remain one together in the Lord.

For that heavenly Jerusalem alone is made one body by charity; from it arise all kinship and everlasting fellowship. Hence, even now, let the soul be incorporated into the members of Christ and blaze with heavenly light. This is the fire which Jesus came to cast upon the earth, and what does he will but that it burn (Luke XII) and consume all the desires of carnal life? This indeed is the fire which came from heaven in the Old Testament and which the priest is commanded to keep continually fed, lest it be extinguished, because no burnt offering or sacrifice worthy of God is consumed by any other fire. But whoever offers strange fire, as happened to Nadab and Abihu, whom fire consumed (Num. III), will be punished with eternal death, because this fire is everlasting.

## Chapter II. Of what tongue charity is.

1. Therefore, “charity” is a Greek word, which in Latin is called *dilectio*, “love.” But in Greek *charity* expresses the force of its meaning better than *dilectio*, which derives its name from *diligere*, “to love” or “to value.” For we often love what we later judge should rather be condemned. It is indeed said that like loves like. Therefore, when we vicious people love vicious people—not because they are what they were created to be, but because they are vicious—is such love to be called charity, or does it come from God? Far from it. For everyone who loves is born of God. But the person who loves in this way certainly hates both himself first and the one whom he seems to love, since “everyone who loves iniquity hates his own soul.” Nevertheless, although it is hatred, it is called *dilectio* according to the etymology of the word; and therefore, as I said, this Latin expression does not everywhere adequately convey the force of *charity*, because charity is properly spoken of only when it comes from God, or is directed toward God, or is exercised for God’s sake. *Dilectio*, however, is sometimes approved even when it is hatred, just as, conversely, hatred is true love according to the understanding of the divine Scriptures: as in the saying, “He who hates his soul in this world” (John 12:25), and the other passages that are read in this connection.

But John speaks of no other love than that which comes from God and is God. Therefore he defines it absolutely and universally, saying: “Everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. He who does not love does not know God, because God is charity” (1 John 4:7–8). And this is the love of Christians: to love God, and in God, and for God’s sake. God is to be loved in himself and for himself, because he is the supreme good; but the members of Christ are to be loved in God, because they are members of him who is God—and therefore in God, because God, who is charity, poured into their hearts, makes them remain in God through the Spirit of adoption, so that they may rightly be called and truly be sons. Yet they are not to be loved as though they themselves were the supreme good, but because, in the supreme good, they are good sons, made good through the Holy Spirit, foreknown and predestined to remain in the Spirit of adoption.

All the rest are to be loved for God’s sake, because they were created good by the good God, although through their own fault they have become evil. *Dilectio* also seems to have been so called because it binds. For it binds two people to one another, since there can be no charity less than that which exists between two persons. It makes them of one mind in the household, so that many become “one heart and one soul.” Therefore it is rightly called “the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3:14). It also binds souls to God with the indissoluble bond of love, after he himself has first fastened them to himself with the cord of his love, so that they may remain in God.

Hence the Lord says: “Father, I will that they also may be one in us, as you and I are one” (John 17:22). Otherwise, how could that heavenly city of Jerusalem consist of such diverse people united in God, so that it could no longer be dissolved or corrupted by any deceitful contrivance, unless it were inwardly and outwardly so filled with the charity of Christ that it could not be submerged even amid the waves of the world? Hence it is said: “And he coated Noah’s ark with bitumen inside and outside” (Genesis 6). Unless it had been coated, it could not have been carried unharmed upon the waters. If, then, the Church is strengthened by God amid the blasts of the world so that it cannot be corrupted, how much more will this be true in the homeland, where there will no longer be any movement of storms?

For this reason David also sings (Psalm 147:12–14): “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem,” as though he were openly saying: “Because he has strengthened the bars of your gates, so that they can no longer be broken.” Then he added: “He has blessed your children within you; he has established peace within your borders.” For once the rejected and the children of curses have been excluded, all those who will be of one mind at the right hand of the blessed Father will be blessed. Their souls have already begun here to be one in Christ, so that there they may be gathered more fully into the unity of the Father.

2. Finally, unity is never divided; and therefore whatever is made firm by unity is held and bound by the strongest bond of love. Hence Holy Scripture, using what is almost the more honorable term, very commonly puts *charity* or *love* for affection or desire, although at times we also find love used of Christ, as in the Song concerning the bride: “Because I am sick with love” (Song of Songs 5:2). Likewise, in Proverbs concerning wisdom: “Love her, and she will preserve you” (Proverbs 2), and in various other passages. Nevertheless, where no occasion for a fall seems to be present, the name *love* is rightly inserted in the Holy Scriptures; but where the more exalted dignity of the name is commended, the term *charity* or *love* is used.

Even though it makes no difference in the divine utterances whether the love of God is called *amor*, *charity*, or *dilectio*, nevertheless the name *charity* is exalted to such a degree that God himself is called Charity. Hence John also says: “Beloved, let us love one another, because charity is from God, and everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. But he who does not love does not know God, because God is charity” (1 John 4:7–8).

Such a virtue therefore differs greatly from desire or ordinary love, concerning which the wise men of the world left written certain techniques by which love might be born or increased in the soul. But carnal people have certainly turned these into incentives to vicious and blameworthy love. For this reason Holy Scripture commends charity more gloriously, lest among us—where the more simple people there are, the more ignorant they often are—many should, because of this word, fall into love of carnal things, as did those who, because of what was said about the nature of love, fell headlong into carnal lapses and unchastity. This happened especially because they wished to demonstrate that the power of love was nothing other than a virtue capable of carrying souls from earthly things to the lofty heights of heaven, and that the highest blessedness could not be reached unless the soul were kindled by desire for love.

Certain people said much about the nature of love, but brought it forth only in shadowy form. They went astray because they did not grasp that God is charity. Therefore they did not know God, nor did they love him. But we, because we love, also know; and by knowing more fully, we love. Because we love, we rightly obey in all things, so that we even love our enemies. They are to be loved in such a way that we hate their vices, since they come from the good and are to be brought back to the good God, so that they may remain good.

[Column 1464A] 3. It is established, therefore, as I said, that the love by which *dilectio* is supported is sometimes understood in an evil sense; but among Christians it is understood only in a good sense. Whatever you love in God or for God’s sake, you must love as yourself. You must love and cherish God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole strength; for love and affection are the father’s inward bond with his son, the children’s outpouring toward their fathers, and also the bond of brotherhood. Otherwise, remove love, and what does a father have toward his son, or a son toward his father, or brothers toward one another?

Therefore, human being, love, because God is love. But why are you not loved by God, unless it is because you do not love? Otherwise, how can God, who is love, fail to love, since he himself is love? The prodigal son makes this clear. After he had wastefully consumed and lost his inheritance, at last, coming to himself, he called upon the father whom he had abandoned (Luke 15). And rightly so. Although by failing to love he had become degenerate, the father, remaining what he was, had not lost the inward affection of fatherhood; and that inward affection is charity.

Therefore God sent his Spirit, who is properly called Charity and proceeds from the Father and the Son into our hearts, so that through charity we might be incorporated into the body of Christ, and so that in the Father and the Son, together with the Holy Spirit, we might be one, just as they themselves are one in themselves. For the whole God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is one charity, one life, and one Deity. Therefore rightly, whoever loves—whoever has been given the ability to love—is born of God. And whoever remains in this love remains in God, and God in him (1 John 3).

## CHAPTER III. On Paul’s statement that charity is greater

1. For he says: “But now remain faith, hope, and charity, these three. But the greatest of these,” or, as our manuscripts have it, “The greatest among these is charity” (1 Corinthians 13:13). But blessed Augustine indicates that we ought to say, “The greatest of these.” For, he says, if one were to seem to say, “The greatest among these is charity,” one would appear to introduce another charity, as though it were a fourth thing, and, after counting the three—namely, faith, hope, and charity—place it above them.

Moreover, since the comparative sometimes governs the plural genitive, it seems better for it to sound with that same case. Thus, when we ask which of any three is first, wishing to recognize one of them as prior to the others, if we say, “Which is prior to them?” we seem to be asking about some fourth person who is prior to those three.

With this said, we must ask why the Apostle said, when these three remain here and all act together, and no one of them can be perfected without the others, that charity is greater than the other two—namely, than faith and hope at present, without which there is no charity. Charity is perhaps called greater because it believes all things and hopes all things, especially since I would not readily say at once that every faith possesses perfect charity. Hence the Apostle says: “If I have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:2).

Yet it seems to me that someone who lacks charity cannot possess all faith, so as to move mountains. Otherwise, how could anyone possess all mysteries and all knowledge, as the same Apostle says, unless he possessed charity—especially since John says: “Everyone who believes that Christ is Truth is born of God; and whoever is born of God does not sin” (1 John 5:1, 18)? From this it follows that the one who believes that Christ is the Truth is born of God; and whoever is born of God does not sin. But whoever sins does not believe, nor does he love, and he is subject to sin. It is therefore established that the one who sins does not love.

Charity consequently excludes the inclination to sin, just as it also casts out fear. Perfect charity belongs to complete faith, but faith is not always complete. Hence the apostles also said: “Lord, increase our faith”—that is, so that he might heal faith that was weak.

2. Faith, as charity’s forerunner, takes possession of the soul, because by believing each person begins to love; by believing, he possesses complete charity. Hence, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement, it remains that, just as charity believes all things, so perfect faith has at present all faith, because faith prepares the paths for true love.

Accordingly, all faith is present where perfect charity is present, because charity believes all things—that is, it makes one believe all things through faith—and enables such a soul to possess all faith, just as it possesses all hope, because charity hopes all things. Charity is therefore greater because it embraces everything through faith and hope.

Such charity fears nothing, but casts fear out. It endures all things and bears all things; and whoever bears all things does not fear even martyrdom, because the world has already been crucified to him, and he to the world, so that he does not fear the things that are in the world.

Charity is rightly also greater because it comprehends every kind of virtue required for life, just as a genus comprehends each of its species. It is constituted from all of them, just as all things subsist from it. The stability and perfection of all the virtues is therefore charity, because all things are rooted and founded in charity, so that it may remain acceptable to God and perfect.

Then, when the others have ceased, blessed charity will be more ardent. Faith and hope, for example, will have been emptied through the vision of Christ, because when that which is perfect has come, that which is partial will be emptied. Then charity alone will be greater than all the rest, even in relation to what exists at present, and it will shine more gloriously.

But in this valley of tears, because charity is from heaven, it remains like a stranger and is therefore rare. In the heavenly realms it wholly governs and reigns. Thus, when we have reached its proper home, charity will be all in all, because God is charity; and each person will reign in all things as one body with God, each the member of the other, blessed without end.

3. These, then, are the inward bonds of that city, its structure, and its life of everlasting glory. Therefore, if anyone wishes to live there, he must begin here through charity and work through it, because whatever is or is done without charity cannot profit that same life.

This is the more excellent way that the Apostle shows to the sons alone, and it is higher than all others. Hence he exhorts us more strongly, saying: “Pursue charity” (1 Corinthians 14:1), clearly because charity is greater than all the gifts of grace, since it is fulfilled from all of them, and each individual gift is made alive and grows from it so as to be beneficial.

For among the virtues there are beginnings, there are intermediate stages, and there are summits. Hence Wisdom, speaking of herself, says: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways” (Proverbs 8:22), so that from her those who wished to come to the Father might begin—that is, from Christ, the Wisdom of God the Father.

But the Apostle, when he was walking in the way that is Christ and following the God who called him toward the prize of the heavenly calling, was forgetting the things behind and stretching himself toward the things ahead, so that he might reach the heights. He had passed beyond the beginning of God’s ways, because he did not need an initial stage for undertaking the journey. Rather, walking along the way toward the truth, he was filled with charity, reached the goal, and remained in the way; through charity he had received adoption, becoming a son in the house with the Father, blessed without end.

From this it is clear that nothing in the way should hold us back, since even the Lord himself, insofar as he deigned to be our way, did not wish to hold us back. We must always pass onward, lest, weak as we are, we cling wrongly to temporal things, even though they were taken up and accomplished for our salvation. Rather, through them we should run eagerly toward the very one who liberated our nature by temporal things and placed it at the right hand of the Father.

This is what he himself says elsewhere: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, now we know him no longer” (2 Corinthians 5:16), because, stripped of the mortality and temporality of all things, God and man, the one Lord Jesus Christ, lives with the Father as the eternal God, remains, and reigns.

## CHAPTER IV. That charity is twofold

1. It is clear from all the places in the Scriptures, and throughout them all, that charity is one and the same yet twofold, namely, charity toward God and toward one’s neighbor; nor can either rightly exist without the other, since God, who is charity, commands that whoever loves God should also love his neighbor.

There is one love, but affection is moved by two commandments: we are to love God with our whole heart, with our whole soul, and with our whole strength, and our neighbor as ourselves, in God. We have this commandment also: that whoever loves God should love his brother.

If we say that we love God but hate even one brother, we are liars, and the truth—that is, God—is not in us, although we pretend to love him. For John says: “If you do not love the brother whom you see, how can you love God, whom you do not see?” (2 John 3).

The proof of love for God is therefore love of one’s neighbor, because love of one’s neighbor is the beginning of love for God. One’s neighbor must therefore be loved so that God may be loved in one’s neighbor, because all love of one’s neighbor, if it is just, is referred to God, in whom one’s neighbor is loved and for whose sake even an enemy is loved.

For this reason, in the Old Testament two tablets are said to have existed, written by the finger of God, because charity toward one’s neighbor and toward God is twofold, and through it the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured into our hearts. For the finger of God signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Thus Christ also, by the finger of God—that is, by the Holy Spirit—cast out demons. Accordingly, one and the same Spirit is at work in both the Old and the New Testaments, so that the charity of God and of one’s neighbor may fill the hearts of believers. In the former case it was written on tablets of stone, because that people bore a heart of stone; here it is written in the hearts of believers, where true love of God and of one’s neighbor is preserved.

Our Lord Jesus Christ gave this Spirit once while he still remained on earth, and once when he presided in heaven. For it is not openly shown to have been given in any other place than when it is received through his breathing upon them on earth, and afterward when it is manifested in various tongues as it comes from heaven.

Why, then, is it first given on earth and afterward sent from heaven to the disciples, unless because there are two commandments of charity—namely, love of God and love of one’s neighbor? Therefore it is first given on earth so that one’s neighbor may be loved, and afterward the same Spirit is given from heaven so that God may be loved. Thus, just as there is one Spirit and two givings, so there is one charity and two commandments.

## CHAPTER V. That there are four things to be loved

From the commandment of love we therefore understand that we ought to love four things. Yet three of these are referred to the love of God, because the command to love with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind invites all our thoughts, our whole life, and our entire understanding to God, so that a person may bring everything to God, from whom he has the very things he brings.

God does not permit any stream to be diverted away from him in such a way that the flow diminishes his love. When he says, “With your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with your whole strength” (Luke 10:27), he leaves no part of our life or of our love vacant. Rather, whatever else comes to be loved must necessarily be carried, as though by command, to the place toward which the whole impulse and fountain of love flows and runs.

Nevertheless, as I said, the complete love of Christ extends to four things: first, what is above us; second, what we are; third, what is beside us; fourth, what seems to be beneath us.

In the Scriptures no commandments from God are given concerning the second and the fourth, because however far anyone may stray from the truth, no one exists who does not in some way love himself and his own body. Although the fugitive soul has turned away from the unchangeable good, it nevertheless always acts so as to provide for itself and its body the things it loves. Therefore it cannot help loving itself and its body, although wrongly.

Whoever wishes to claim for himself what belongs properly to God alone loves himself wrongly, because such love is better called hatred than charity. Hence the Prophet says: “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6).

It therefore remains that God is to be loved with the whole self, as the supreme good. Whoever loves him keeps his commandments. Hence the Lord says: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (Job 14:15).

His commandments—indeed, the commandment of all commandments—are that we should love every neighbor as ourselves, because the whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments. Otherwise it would seem superfluous to command anyone to love himself and his body, since what we are according to the soul, and what is beneath us according to the body, belongs to us, and by an unshaken law we naturally love it. This law also seems to have been proclaimed to the beasts.

Scripture says: “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church.” Therefore it was necessary to command: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole mind” (Luke 10:27). Then: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” In these two commandments the whole law and the prophets are shown to depend.

For no commandment concerning things to be loved was given except these two, especially since love of God comes first, and the manner of that love is prescribed, so that all the rest flow into that one commandment.

Nothing, it seems, was said about love of ourselves. But when he says, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” he appears to have omitted nothing; rather, our own love is commended along with the commandment. Therefore the fullness of our love is that the soul should be loved in God for immortality and blessedness, and that our body should be prepared for health, incorruption, and immortality.

For just as the whole human being consists of soul and body, so love is complete when the neighbor’s body is loved as our own, and his soul according to God. Such love is an outpouring of the Holy Spirit, because, as the Apostle says, “the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5:5), so that our neighbor may be loved.

This charity always yearns upward, as though it were fire, because it comes from above. This visible fire also raises itself to the place from which it is said to have its substance and origin. In the same way, this fire of love, which Jesus came to cast upon the earth and wishes to burn, is always hastening toward the homeland. Those whom it has inflamed it desires to carry there, and it always desires to love the things that are above.

If it is love, it cannot fail to love the one from whom it comes and itself in the one in whom it exists. Accordingly, while it loves the one from whom it comes, it also loves itself, so that it may remain in the one in whom it exists.

Through this fountain the reborn soul passes into God, not through a change of substance but through the rebirth of its affection, so that it may love God with its whole self. But because it is sometimes hindered by the pleasures of the world, it says in the Song of Songs: “Draw me after you; we will run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song of Songs 1:3).

Nor does it wish to run after the one whom it loves alone, because it wishes the flesh also to pass with it into incorruption, as the Prophet sings: “My soul has thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh longs for you!” (Psalm 63:2).

When a person loves himself completely in God, he also loves his neighbor according to God. This is true and complete charity: to love God with one’s whole self, not for the sake of anything else but for his own sake, because he is the unchangeable and supreme good; then to love one’s neighbor in God and for God’s sake, so that our whole human being may thirst and long for God in every way.

## CHAPTER VI. Who is the neighbor whom we are commanded to love
