Every human being is understood to be our neighbor, whether because of the condition of nature, the effectiveness of action, or compassion shown through mercy. Nothing is more truly a neighbor than being what we are and willing what we wish for ourselves.

Therefore, wishing to explain to us what a neighbor is, the Lord, when someone asked him, “And who is my neighbor?” put forward this parable: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho” (Luke 10:29–30), and the other things that follow. Among other points, he shows that no one was more truly his neighbor than the one who cared for him and performed an act of mercy toward him, to such an extent that, when questioned, the man himself confessed this. The Lord then said to him: “Go, and you also do likewise” (Luke 10:37).

Therefore we ought to offer whatever, by wishing and acting, we can provide around our neighbor as an act of piety, so that he may in turn be our neighbor by acting likewise and freely performing a work of mercy toward us.

But no one does this freely who does it for God’s sake, because God first loved us so that we might love him. He gave us, through his Spirit—which is charity—the Holy Spirit, so that we too might be able to love.

If the kinship of the flesh possesses something of kinship, much more does the adoption of the children of God, which is wholly reborn from the spirit of love. It should also be noted that no one loves without the reward of recompense; for this reason no one loves gratuitously.

The name “neighbor” is relative, just as the names “father” and “brother” are, because no one is a neighbor except in relation to a neighbor, just as no one is a son or brother except in relation to a father or brother. Therefore, if that heavenly Father is rightly loved, then rightly also are neighbor and brother loved, and in that heavenly one we ourselves become heavenly.

No human being is therefore excluded from the mercy that we must show, since we are even commanded to love our enemies. “Love your enemies,” he says, “do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5:44).

Every human being is shown to be either our friend or our enemy. Therefore no one is excluded from the duty of piety, because love of one’s neighbor does no evil; indeed, it makes us outstanding in every good work. Hence charity is called the fullness of the law.

It is therefore clear that under this commandment, by which we are ordered to love our neighbors, the holy angels are also included, since they perform for us services of such great mercy as we can observe in the Holy Scriptures. For according to the Apostle, they are ministers placed in service for the sake of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation (Hebrews 1:14).

Therefore those who perform for us the greatest works of mercy are rightly counted as neighbors. For this reason our Lord also, because he wished to be our Samaritan, found us abandoned by robbers, lying half-dead. And because he provided the medicine of salvation, he became our neighbor by coming to us through the fact that he became flesh and dwelt among us.

Hence the Prophet also says: “As a neighbor and as our brother, so I was well pleased” (Psalm 35:14). Or, since the divine nature is more excellent and above us, the love of God is distinguished from the love of our neighbor. God alone, by his own goodness, provides us with the work of mercy, because he is the supreme good; but we love and show mercy to one another for his grace, so that we may be found in him, though we had been lost.

He acts so that we may enjoy the good that he himself is; but we love and have mercy on one another so that we may enjoy him, whom, because our sins demanded it, we had wrongly used against one another.

## CHAPTER VII. What is to be enjoyed and what is to be used

The holy Fathers have defined that some things are to be enjoyed, others are to be used, and others are both to be enjoyed and used.

Those things that are to be enjoyed are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the same Trinity, one and supreme reality, common to all who enjoy it, if indeed it should be called a reality and not the cause of all realities. This is especially so because no name is found that adequately corresponds to such excellence and majesty. Nevertheless, the Trinity is called one God: from whom all things are, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Each of these individually is God and a complete substance; together they are one God and one substance. This reality makes us blessed when we enjoy it.

We are helped, however, by the things that are to be used, as we strive toward blessedness. We must neither love nor cherish them at all, but use them so that we may reach and cling to that substance which makes us blessed.

Third among these are we ourselves, who both enjoy and use, placed between the two. Therefore we must beware lest we enjoy what is to be used, lest we be hindered on the way and fail to reach the homeland where God is to be enjoyed perfectly.

To enjoy is to cling to something through perfect love or affection for its own sake, and to love that same thing from the heart. To use, however, is to employ whatever comes into use for the sake of our necessity, in order to obtain what we love or cherish—provided, of course, that the thing in question ought to be loved. For we ought to love nothing for its own sake, but everything for God’s sake, because he is the supreme good, and our neighbor because he has been established by the supreme good.

Otherwise, improper use is more properly called abuse. Hence the Apostle says: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world” (James 4:4)—that is, whoever wishes to enjoy the things of the world and love them for their own sake—“will be constituted an enemy of God.”

These things are good for those who use them rightly; but for those who abuse them, they are truly found to be extremely destructive in pride.

For those who use them rightly, they are like provisions carried by someone who, while traveling, hastens to reach his homeland. Laden with food, he proceeds on his way; weighed down by it, he does not love it for its own sake, but by using it is able to reach the place toward which he is traveling, although he carries it unwillingly as he uses it.

Otherwise, whoever loves the things he uses by enjoying them is miserably enticed and drawn away from the good; he becomes sluggish on the way.

But if you pay attention, a person must not even enjoy himself, because he ought not to love himself for his own sake but for the sake of him whom he is to enjoy. Otherwise he does not turn himself toward God but, turned back toward himself, remains wretched in enjoying himself to his own ruin, because he lies not raised toward blessedness but cast down into misery.

Therefore, if a person, in a certain sense turned toward himself, must not enjoy even himself, how much less should he love anything else; rather, he should use it for necessity, so that he may reach the place from which the fountain of love flows.

For this reason let no human being, however good, flatter himself that he ought to be loved for his own sake. Rather, let all our love be referred to the Lord or for the Lord’s sake, so that in him we may love one another, in whom and from whom we are able to be blessed.

Otherwise, blessed Apostle Paul would not have said to Philemon, “I would enjoy you, brother, in the Lord” (Philemon 20). If he had not added “in the Lord,” he would have seemed to love him for his own sake. But the excellent teacher wishes to love him in the one, and to enjoy him in the one, in whom both of them could be blessed.

Therefore let us love God, not for the sake of anything else but for his own sake, because he is the supreme good, with our whole heart, our whole soul, and our whole mind. There is no reality that we ought to enjoy except him.

It follows that all our love should hurry toward the place where the supreme good is, and that we should enjoy those things through which we can be blessed, lest we abuse lawful things in pride and remain in misery amid them.

Therefore let us enjoy ourselves and our neighbors, but in him, so that, according to him and for his sake, we may love one another—not as we now are, but as we are believed to be destined to become. Thus, by improving ourselves each day on the way that is Christ, let us always cling to that supreme and unchangeable good.

All other things, however, we must neither enjoy but use. Their use must be referred to his grace, whom we love. This is the true rule of love: God is to be loved wholly and for his own sake, because nothing is better than he, and no good thing is found apart from him.

Then one’s neighbor is to be loved as oneself, with a human being loving according to God and for God’s sake.

No one is therefore found already perfect in every respect. Insofar as a person believes that he lives perfectly according to God, let him love himself in God, so that he may remain in him. But insofar as he is a sinner, let him love himself for God’s sake, so that he may reach perfection and grace, and so that the whole and complete human being may in some manner remain unchangeable and incorruptible.

For this purpose we must also love our neighbor. But since no one is so good in this life that he does not admit some evil, and no one is so evil that he does not possess some good, our neighbors are to be loved, in every case, in Christ, so that, stripped of their wickedness, all may reach him—foreknown and predestined through grace—and may be like the angels in heaven, enjoying the brightness of that place, blessed forever, and glorified in the praise of Christ.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the order of charity

We read in the Song of Songs of the bride rejoicing, where she says: “The king brought me into the wine cellar and ordered love within me” (Song 1:3). This is plainly a matter of great praise and a feeling of great love, when she says, “He ordered love within me.” Otherwise, unless love is ordered, it cannot be wholly true or perfect; for the person who lives justly and holily is the one who judges rightly about each thing according to what it is, and loves it as it ought to be loved, or uses it as it ought to be used.

That person has ordered love who either loves what ought to be loved, or does not love at all what ought not to be loved; who neither loves less what deserves greater love, nor more what is known to deserve less, but loves with the utmost equity what ought to be loved less or more. Such a person also strives not to think either too little or too much in loving those things which he ought to love with perfect equity [Note: Col. 1472D: the editions read, “ought” (decet).]. Thus, for example, no sinner, insofar as he is a sinner, is to be loved; but every human being, insofar as he is human, is to be loved for God’s sake. All the members of Christ, insofar as they are members, are to be loved in God, because they are members of Christ. God, however, because he is the supreme good, is to be loved wholly for his own sake.

Therefore, if God is to be loved more than any human being, each of us truly ought to love God more than himself—that is, more than his own soul—for whoever loves his soul more than God is not worthy of him. Thus the holy martyrs loved God more than themselves [Note: Col. 1473D: the editions read, “to love” (diligere)]; for that reason they laid down their mortal bodies and surrendered their souls, so that, according to God’s promise, they might find them in eternal life. In addition, one human being ought to be loved more than our body, because, according to the inner person, his soul is to be loved as our own soul is.

Nevertheless, everything is to be loved for God’s sake and in God more than the body, because the inner person can enjoy God with us, whereas the body cannot. The body lives through the soul, by which we enjoy God; therefore let us love the soul of our neighbor, according to the inner person, as our own, and his body unto incorruption, just as we love our own.

It is therefore clear that all are to be loved equally. But since we cannot benefit everyone [Note: Col. 1473D: the editions read, “but nevertheless, while [we cannot benefit] everyone”], we ought especially to care for those who, by the opportunity provided by place, time, or any other circumstance, are more closely joined to us, as though by lot. This bodily fire, too, touches with both heat and light those who are evidently nearer to it. But this fire of love embraces everyone in Christ or for Christ’s sake, whether present or absent: it groans on account of sinners, and remembers to praise God [Note: Col. 1473D: “God” is missing in the editions] on account of the saints, with whom and in whom it rejoices to share.

Then it invokes the Father together with them, saying: “Our Father, who art in heaven.” Who would not rejoice at so great an adoption? Who would not share in the joy of so great a brotherhood spread everywhere? Yet among all who enjoy God with us, we love some whom we ourselves assist; some from whom we receive assistance; some whose protection we need and whose needs we relieve [Note: Col. 1473D: the editions read, “and whose” (quorumque)]; and some to whom we ourselves contribute no benefit, nor expect any benefit from them for ourselves.

Nevertheless, we ought to love them all, so that they too may love with us, and may will, pray, and desire. Therefore all our love for one another must be directed toward that one end: that all may enjoy God, and enjoy one another in God, although at times we use our neighbors, just as they themselves use one another’s support.

We use their temporal assistance, but we enjoy them in the Lord according to the inner person, so that we may all be renewed in the knowledge of the Son of God and remade in the image of the glory of his brightness [Note: The editions read, “of his charity.”]. In these cups the bride, surely intoxicated, rejoices, saying: “The king brought me into the wine cellar” (Song 1:3).

These are the cups of Christ’s love, by which we are transformed into the form of the incorruptible God. For God is love, so that through love we may love, so to speak, that same love which is God—with all our heart, and with all our soul, and with all our strength. Then we are to love our neighbors as ourselves, doing to others what we wish done to us, and not inflicting on anyone what we do not wish done to ourselves.

This is ordered love; this is that perpetual fire which Jesus came to cast upon the earth and wishes to burn. This is the more excellent way which the Apostle points out, without which nothing prospers and against which nothing prevails; for it is an unconquerable strength of love, as strong as death. Everyone ought surely to nourish this love by fulfilling God’s commandments, so that everything we do may be increased by this fire in the presence of the divine majesty and become acceptable to God.

By these affections the reborn soul becomes a holocaust, presenting to God the body which is made alive by it [Note: The editions read, “by him”], a living, holy, pleasing sacrifice to God. Thus it becomes our reasonable service, assuredly because ordered love, first poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit, is continually inspired.

## CHAPTER IX. What the beginning of love is, and what its perfection is

No one, therefore, immediately becomes supreme; and for that reason we must seek the beginning of love, so that, with God inspiring us, we may be able to reach its perfection. Its work is nothing other than to love and, by loving, to fulfill Christ’s commandments.

Its beginning, however, starts from those things which are outward, although they are made alive inwardly [Note: Col. 1474D: the editions read, “although God gives life”]. For as the Apostle cries out: whoever possesses the substance of this world and closes the womb of mercy so as not to give to the needy is thought to possess not love, but not even the beginning of love. He says: “Whoever has the substance of this world and sees his brother suffering need, and closes his compassion against him, how is the love of God in him?” (1 John 3:17).

And thus he plainly says: How can one love inwardly who does not give what is outward? A closed womb does not allow compassion to flow toward one’s neighbor, while the person loves himself and transitory possessions more than his neighbor. How, then, can he give what he grieves to have taken away, when he does not give what he does not grieve to lose outwardly at all?

It is therefore clear that the beginning and evidence of love [Note: The editions read, “beginning”] is this: that we do not deny our neighbor what we can lose without pain and possess in excess. Then, whatever benefits we can provide, we should actively and dutifully provide. Otherwise, the love that appears to exist, while the womb of compassion remains inert and closed, is not love, since it denies a neighbor what it does not grieve to have taken away.

Let the womb of compassion therefore be opened, so that love may have a beginning, and let what belongs to this world at least not be denied to our neighbor, since all these things are known to have been given in common. Hence the Lord says: “If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke 16:12). What belongs to this world is alien to us, although it has been given for our use; therefore we ought not to deny our neighbors what has been given to all in common.

But if we deny outwardly what belongs to another, inwardly, with our compassion closed, we lose what belongs to us. Since we have said that the beginning of love consists in giving the substance of this world most generously to our neighbors, we must ask what the Apostle means when he says: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and deliver my body so that I may burn, but have not love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3).

Perhaps, then, someone can give his possessions to the poor without love, or deliver his body for some other undertaking [Note: The editions read, “for another”] so that he burns; but it is absolutely certain that without love it profits nothing. Moreover, as I have said, the work of love is to love; therefore whatever is done without love of God and neighbor profits nothing.

Love of neighbor preserves brotherhood; brotherhood, however, passes into adoption, and adoption makes us children of God through grace [Note: Col. 1475D: the editions read, “of one father of the household”]. Since we are brothers and children of one head of household [Note: The editions read, “of one father of the household”], the heavenly inheritance, by faith, and the substance of this world are common to us.

Thus we ought to give to our neighbors as to fellow heirs, and not deny each of them what belongs to them, because, according to the Apostle, we ought to owe nothing else than to love one another. Hence love “is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek what is its own” (1 Corinthians 13:5), since it recognizes the right of nature and the sharing of inheritance and grace.

Thus it eagerly strives to give to each person what belongs to this world as though it were a debt [Note: Col. 1475D: the editions read, “to give” (largiri)], because what belongs to this world is not ours; rather, those things that are eternal are known to belong properly to love. The things of this age are owed for use along the journey. But those things that lead to perpetuity and eternity, in which we are to enjoy blessedness, must be proclaimed and requested for our neighbors, because, by the Lord’s generosity, they have already become ours through grace.

Therefore, whether we provide material substance to our neighbor, perform an act of mercy, request good things for him, or proclaim heavenly things, the Apostle most generously commands: “We owe nothing else than to love one another.” Love alone is owed as a debt; we ought daily to pay it, so that by owing we may discharge it. But whatever we can give, let us not deny to our neighbors. Otherwise, whoever closes the womb of compassion toward a neighbor, and is thus known not even to possess the beginning of love, how can he give his soul for his friends, when he does not rejoice to share his possessions?

For as the Lord says: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his soul for his friends” (John 15:13). This, indeed, is the love that casts out all fear. Filled with this love, the saints were not at all afraid to die for Christ, and so they were also called friends of God.

But because all the commandments depend upon love [Note: Col. 1475D: the editions read, “depend” (pendent)], and the duties concerning God and neighbor are various, the order of the blessed is also various, and there are many dwelling places in the kingdom of heaven. Some possess the substance of the world and strive to give it generously to their neighbors [Note: Col. 1476D: the editions read, “to give” (largiri)]. Others, leaving everything behind, surrender not only their bodies but also their souls for God and their neighbors, and undertake everything they can for the common salvation, so completely that one man in the Old Testament wishes to be blotted out of the book of life for the sake of his brothers [Note: Col. 1476D: the editions read, “may wish” (optet)], while another in the New Testament rejoices to become accursed [Note: The editions read, “rejoices”].

It is therefore plainly evident that love will never fail, although what we say may seem difficult to the timid and unbelieving. But to those who are foreknown and predestined to be conformed to the image of the Son of God, everything seems easy: neither does the substance of the world occupy their minds, nor does any labor seem burdensome, because they are moved by the Spirit of God, from whom they have been reborn and called children of God [Note: The editions omit “are.”].

Let each person therefore at least possess the beginning of love, so that, moved by love of Christ, he may provide the goods of this age to his neighbors as provisions for the journey. Let him burn with faith and love, so that he may hear from the Lord: “What you did for one of these least ones, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40).

Let him hasten to perform the work of mercy and exhibit it through persistent deeds, since labor conquers all things, so that he may rejoice to help his neighbor in everything, and thereby, if circumstances should so determine, not fear to lay down his soul for his brothers and friends. In this way let that love be proved than which there is no greater among neighbors.

The gifts are various, the labor is various, and the order of merits is also various. Hence the Prophet says: “The queen stood, clothed in a garment of gold, surrounded by variety” (Psalm 44:10). But just as the person who lays down his soul for his friends is more blessed, so the person who closes the womb of compassion toward his neighbor so as not to help the needy is exceedingly wretched [Note: The editions read, “indeed”], for such a person remains in darkness and the shadow of death.

## CHAPTER X. How does God love us? So that he may enjoy us, or so that he may use us?

It is therefore clear from the divine mysteries of Scripture that God loves us greatly: he did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all. If he did not love us, when we were enemies, he would not have reconciled us to himself through the death of his Son, so that from enemies we might become not only friends but also children.

But if he enjoys our good once we have been adopted, he seems to be doing what no sane person would say, since all our good either comes from him or is himself. It is also clear from this that he needs the good of no one, because through him, from him, and in him not only our good exists, but also that of all the angels.

Therefore the Prophet turns to him and implores him, saying: “Preserve me, O Lord, for I have hoped in you. I said to the Lord: You are my God, for you have no need of my goods” (Psalm 15:1–2). It is as though he plainly said: For this reason I have placed all my hope in you, because you are the supreme good; otherwise, if you needed anyone’s good, you would not be God. But now, since you need none of my goods and are shown to need the good of no one else, I beseech you: preserve me, so that I may remain good.

It is therefore evident that God does not enjoy us, but uses us. Otherwise, if he neither enjoys nor uses us, it is not apparent how Truth loves us. Yet he does not use things as we use them, because we direct the things we use toward the end for which we may enjoy God’s goodness. God, however, directs our use toward his own goodness, because he makes good use of our evils; for he himself is supreme goodness, just as he is the supreme God and supreme love.

We too, insofar as we are from him, are truly good. Therefore, because he is just, we are not wicked with impunity. Thus God’s use of us, by which he uses us, is directed not toward his benefit but toward ours, and solely toward his goodness.

When we assist someone out of compassion, we do so for the benefit of the one for whom we feel compassion, and for our own reward when we show compassion. That reward is supreme: to enjoy God. Then, because we enjoy him, we ask to enjoy one another in him by loving one another. Otherwise, if we place our love only in ourselves, we remain on the way, because we have placed the hope of our blessedness in an angel or in a human being, however holy.

All our love must therefore be directed toward him from whom, through whom, and in whom alone we can be good. For neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth. Therefore, when you enjoy a human being in God, you enjoy God rather than the human being [Note: The editions read, “when you enjoy God with the human being.”].

You enjoy the one by whom you are made blessed, and you rejoice that through love you have reached the one in whom you had placed your hope.

Some say that one can enjoy something when one uses it with pleasure, since we carry that pleasure with us. But if we direct that same pleasure toward the supreme good, where we must remain, so that we may delight in it, this can no longer properly be called enjoyment, but use: the use by which we love one another, since our love is directed toward him to whom we rejoice to adhere wholly and in whom we have placed the end of our joy [Note: The editions omit “in” in “use by which we love one another.”].

Christ, the Word of the Father, is also called the beginning of the ways of God, so that all who wished to come to God might begin from him, since he is God. But as the Apostle says, “If we knew Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him” [cf. 2 Corinthians 5:16]. For according to the flesh he wished to offer himself as the way for those who were coming; it is fitting to pass beyond the beginning of the ways [Note: The editor added, “to which human beings…”], so that one may reach the life and truth in which the blessed remain.

Hence the Apostle, “forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead,” extends himself (Philippians 3:13), because he had already passed beyond the beginning of the ways of God and no longer needed the one from whom all who wish to come to life and truth and remain in Christ must begin and set out.

From this it follows that nothing in the way ought to hold us back, since even the Lord himself, insofar as he deigned to be our way, did not wish to keep us with him, but wished us to pass beyond, lest we cling weakly to temporal things, although he took them up and accomplished them for our salvation. Rather, let us run through those same things eagerly, as I have said, so that we may reach him who took the form of a servant and placed our nature at the right hand of the Father.

## CHAPTER XI. On nourishing love

Love must therefore be nourished, even if it is believed to have been given from heaven, because it is that perpetual fire. Accordingly, we read that in Leviticus the priest was commanded to nourish that heavenly fire every day. For it was not permitted to offer alien fire in the Lord’s sacrifice, lest the one who offered it perish, as Nadab and Abihu did. Instead, each morning and evening they placed wood upon it as fuel, so that it might be nourished and remain perpetually on the altar.

This is that fire which Jesus came to cast upon the earth and wishes to burn. Therefore we must ask by what nourishment love is fed—the love by which eternal things and one’s neighbor are loved, so that it may advance toward those things that always remain the same.

The love by which God and neighbor are loved is properly called charity, and it extends no further. But it is consummated and most purified when nothing else is loved. As we have said, this has also been called affection; but it is rightly ordered when God is loved more than the soul, so that a person would rather belong to God than to himself and directs every movement of his soul according to God’s will. Then he must subject the duties of the flesh to the judgment of his mind, so that he loves nothing other than God and his neighbor according to God’s will.

The poison of love, however, is desire for temporal things. Its nourishment, therefore, is the diminution of desire; its perfection is the absence of all desire, because desire alone is proclaimed to be the root of all evils.

Whoever wishes to nourish love should devote himself to reducing desires, fleeing the glory of the present life, and denying his own will. Desire is the love of obtaining or possessing the pleasures of the flesh and of the present life. The beginning of reducing it is to fear God, as it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110:10).

Once the soul has been initiated by these steps, it remains for it to reach wisdom, so that for the sake of eternal things it may despise everything that is thought good or evil in this world. Let no one despair concerning the promises and struggles of the saints.

Therefore, for the sake of pleasing God, let the soul do nothing except according to God. But since this journey of love involves so many dangers and difficulties, it is not now our purpose to discuss them; rather, we seek the beginnings by which love is nourished. It remains, then, that love of Christ should fully attend to the observance of his commandments, just as Truth himself says to his disciples: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14:15).

The observance of God’s commandments is therefore the fulfillment of love. But in this same love we walk by faith, from which we begin; otherwise, when faith grows weak, love languishes. Whenever the authority of the holy Scriptures wavers in the mind, faith falters; and when faith has fallen, each person immediately falls from love as well.

One cannot love what one does not believe to exist. Therefore the holy Scriptures must be searched more diligently and believed more fully, so that holy faith may grow and God’s commandments may be understood more abundantly.

Whoever thinks that he has understood the holy Scriptures, or any part of them, but does not, through that understanding [Note: The editions read, “through that understood matter”], build up faith and the twofold love of God and neighbor, has not understood them at all.

If, through the Scriptures of God themselves, he has already received faith and loves them, then by doing good he makes it possible also to hope that he will reach what he loves. Thus there are three things in which all knowledge and prophecy serve during this life. But faith will be succeeded by the vision of what was once believed [Note: The editions read, “hope”], which we shall see as it is; hope, however, will be succeeded by the blessedness itself to which we shall attain.

Love, however, will increase when these things pass away. For if we love by believing what we do not yet see, how much more will we love when we begin to see! And if by loving we hope for what we have not yet reached, how much more will we love when we have arrived!

The goods of the present life, just as they are desired when they are not possessed, immediately become wearisome once they are possessed. Heavenly and eternal things, on the contrary, are wearisome when they are not possessed, but when they are received they become the object of great desire. Sometimes, however, because through faith we believe them to be what they are, we already possess them in hope, since they have been given to us; and once possessed in this way, they are loved and tasted in advance.

For love of them, all the things of the present life—prosperity no less than adversity—are despised, provided only that those eternal things may be attained. Love therefore uses the instruments of all the virtues, and these are the pieces of wood placed as fuel for the Lord’s fire, so that it may be nourished on the altar.

That altar of the Lord is the Lord’s body, fully acceptable to God the Father, on which we offer all our vows, and on which they are consumed by the fire of love. Otherwise, whoever offers alien fire—that is, the desire of the flesh—will perish with Nadab and Abihu, because this fire is heavenly and comes from nowhere else; nor is it nourished anywhere except through the virtues and in Christ.

Morning and evening, therefore, wood is placed as fuel for holy love, so that it may burn continually on the altar, when the other virtues act through love. Otherwise it is extinguished, because love is never idle. When the virtues have been placed beneath it, it burns in Christ; and only then do all our vows, consumed by this fire, become acceptable to God.

“The end of the commandment,” says the Apostle, “is love from a pure heart and a good conscience” (1 Timothy 1:5). “From a pure heart,” he says, so that nothing may be loved except what ought to be loved; “and an unfeigned conscience,” so that hope may not be confounded by any shipwreck of error.

The understanding of all the Scriptures therefore refers to these three things, because whatever we read in the divine writings is contained in these three gifts, and the end of all the Scriptures is brought to completion in them. If it were not for the instruction of others, once these things had been fully attained, the holy Scripture would no longer be necessary.

Therefore, if love is to be nourished, friendship with the world and desire for the flesh must first be expelled. Then the wood of the virtues concerning God and neighbor must continually be placed beneath it, so that it may burn. For whoever does not first drive its poison out of himself possesses not the perfection of love, but not even its beginning.

## CHAPTER XII. On the distinction of love: whether there is a different love among those who preserve their first faith and those who return to penance after falling

1. Through Jeremiah the Lord plainly says to Jerusalem: “I remember you, taking pity on your youth and the love of your betrothal, when you followed me in the wilderness” (Jeremiah 2:2). And afterward: “Israel was holiness to the Lord, the firstfruits of his produce” (ibid., 3).

By these words he plainly indicates the more glorious love found in a persevering soul. The Lord, taking pity on its youth, remembers the love of its betrothal even when it has fallen. Virginal love is tender and sweet, especially in spiritual matters, where bridegroom and soul are joined by love alone.

The holy soul is compared with the firstfruits of the harvest consecrated to the Lord. Therefore the bridegroom loves virginity so tenderly that all who preserve it whole and undefiled follow the Lamb wherever he goes.

But of the soul that has fallen, Joel says: “Lament to me over the bride girded with sackcloth for the husband of her virginity” (Joel 1:8), grieving because she had fallen from such good merits, so that she incurred hatred, regarding the stumbling blocks of her sins as offenses.

The bridegroom therefore urges—or rather commands—that lamentation be poured out before him for her, or that the soul itself be mourned. Hence our translation has “mourn,” as though it meant: a virgin girded with sackcloth, mourning for the husband of her youth.

For Christ, the virginal bridegroom, had already withdrawn from her because of her evil deeds—he who said: “I will betroth you to myself in faith, in justice, and in mercy” (Hosea 2:19). But because she made void the first faith of her betrothal and regarded the blood of the covenant as polluted, she is commanded to mourn, girded with sackcloth, for the husband of her youth, because he has been taken away from her.

She is no longer soft and tender; therefore she ought to mourn, girded with sackcloth. Otherwise, if she had preserved the covenant of virginity, she would neither mourn nor have the bridegroom departed from her.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them; but the time will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast and mourn” (Mark 2:19).

The soul therefore has its joy and rejoicing as long as Christ is with it, because those are days of feasting, refreshment, and gladness. It has received an everlasting covenant from God and therefore overflows with delights; it enjoys the abundance of heavenly nourishment and is inebriated with the wine that gladdens the hearts of the saints.

But after it has lost the bridegroom through its own deeds, it is commanded to do penance in the sackcloth of its sins and to mourn itself [Note: The editions read, “itself”], because it lost its husband and the bridegroom rejected it on account of its foulness—he who had not only loved it freely but had also been crucified for it.

Thus, from the beginning, every soul dedicated the flower of its virginal life from Christ the fountain [Note: Col. 1481D: the editions incorrectly read, “the soul”; they read “enriched” (ditavit) for “dedicated” (dicavit)]. But when it turned aside toward the dishonors of this age, neglecting the pledge of its faith, it immediately lost the bridegroom of its virginity and mingled with the devil and its own wicked works, to whom it had previously renounced allegiance.

2. Yet the merciful Lord does not even then abandon the soul defiled by wicked crimes. Through Jeremiah he rebukes it, saying: “You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute; you refused to be ashamed. Therefore at least from now on call me: ‘You are my Father; you are the guide of my virginity’” (Jeremiah 3:3–4).

And he rightly says, “the guide of my virginity,” because as long as the soul wished to remain a virgin, preserving the covenant of love, it had Christ as its guide. After abandoning him, it began to walk along steep and broken paths and to fall into the depths.

Therefore, just as a woman despises her husband if she holds him in contempt, so the unhappy soul despised the Lord. For this reason the Lord recalls it through the prophet: “Will you be angry forever, or will you persevere to the end? Behold, you have spoken and done evil, and you were able” (Jeremiah 5:6).

Meanwhile the divine word uses many means to restrain the wretched soul from its crimes. But blessed are those who preserve their first love, lest they break the covenant of faith. Otherwise, if the first love were not more glorious because it was preserved from the beginning, the Holy Spirit would never have written through John in the Apocalypse to the angel of the church at Ephesus, among other things: “But I have this against you: you have abandoned your first love” (Revelation 2:4).

It is called “first” because it is either followed by another or because it is itself primordial and preeminent, when we are poured anew by the Holy Spirit in baptism. “Remember,” he says, “from where you have fallen, and do penance” (ibid., 5).

Indeed, no one rightly repents unless he first understands the excellence of the love and the grace he has lost, and the state to which he has come, so that he may bear the shame of his disgrace and turn again toward the things he has lost.

“Then do the former works,” he says. And what are the former works except those of love, by which one keeps all the commandments? These works are understood to be works of love—indeed, love itself. But because of the disgrace of the uncleanness [Note: The editions read, “of the heart”], they are called “works” merely by a change of name, although they are former works, so that there may be some distinction between those who remained and those who suffered shipwreck in the faith of Christ’s love.

Nevertheless, although many afterward love more greatly, glory is sometimes left unmentioned, and the beauty of appearance is also left unmentioned. We read only of Mary that many sins were forgiven her because she loved much (Luke 7:47). From this it is clear that love is, as it were, another baptism for souls.

And if the place from which we fell remains in the mind, why are we commanded to perform the former works unless it is so that through that love we may return to the things from which we previously fell?

### 3.

But there is a very great difference between the soul’s first love and its corrupted love, and that love—although it is itself one and the same love—which is restored after the soul’s fall. For the soul does not appear beautiful when it is darkened by its sins, even if it loves God greatly; since, as someone boldly said: “When I speak with God: although God can do all things, He cannot raise up again after her fall any virgin who has been corrupted. He can indeed free her from punishment, but He cannot crown one who has been corrupted.” This statement—[Note: [Col. 1482D] The Editor’s edition: “which statement indeed.”—] [Col. 1482B] is sufficiently terrifying if it should be proved true, especially since we read that Afra and very many others were crowned with martyrdom. Therefore this must either be understood only of the crown of virginity, or else read differently from the way our manuscripts have it, so that the meaning is that He cannot crown one who is uncorrupted. For the cause of what was done remains, even if a crown is granted on account of the great ardor of love afterward.

It is therefore written: “The virgin of Israel has fallen, and there is none to raise her up” (Amos I, 2). Yet this should not be understood to mean that there is no one, but rather as the expression of one grieving and imploring God’s help [Note: [Col. 1482D] The Editor adds: “he indicates.”]: no one but God can raise up again a prostitute, and He Himself was prevented from doing so by her who had fallen, because sins intervened, through His just judgment, although He could have done it by His power.

Otherwise, how is there joy in heaven, as the Lord testifies, “over one sinner doing penance more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance” (Luke XV, 7), if no one can return from ruin to glory? And if the Holy Spirit should so inflame with the fire of love the soul prostituted by any crimes that He makes its works of virtue more numerous or more excellent than those it would have made if divinely inspired, who is there who can judge that, where the grace of God so abounds—although sins previously abounded—the One who gave grace cannot repay its labor with a reward?

Nevertheless, the love of the laboring soul is not so beautiful, since it bears such confusion at the remembrance of its former bonds of love, now broken. Therefore, although it now burns more intensely in the soul with the ardor of love, it rightly [Note: [Col. 1482D] The Editor’s edition: “also grieves,” omitting “rightly.”] grieves [Col. 1482D] over the confusion of its guilt.

Thus the soul of anyone who rightly mourns itself appears filthy to itself because of guilt, although it now gives off a fragrance before God through forgiveness. On the one hand it burns before its Bridegroom with the love of affection, striving continually to satisfy Him through just and good works; on the other hand it is darkened by its own crimes. On the one hand it is rebaptized by its own tears; on the other it is darkened by the sight of its sins. On the one hand it shines with the grace of God sprinkled upon it and with the gifts of virtue. On the one hand it is sad because the scars of its wounds, or the cause of what it did, remain; on the other it is joyful because through love it has now returned to the embraces of its former husband.

It therefore rejoices more over forgiveness than it grieves over guilt. Having departed, it hastens toward immense joys, which it will one day attain when death has been swallowed up in victory. Sometimes, however, [Note: [Col. 1483D] In the printed editions “however” is absent.] as the prophet admonishes, it girds itself with sackcloth, covers itself with ashes, and laments bitterly because it has sinned against the Lord. Renewed each day by greater love, it is wounded in two ways.

Such love, then, because it is squalid and sprinkled with the bitterness of confusion, is called “second,” since it is not beautiful to behold, like Rachel, in whom the beginning of vision shines forth; rather, its eyes are bleary and darkened by the haze of sin. Yet because much has been forgiven it, it rightly loves more, and by loving bears more children than Rachel did. Thanks be to God, because each wife, though despised, is now compensated by fruitfulness for whatever is diminished in her beauty. [Note: [Col. 1483D] The printed edition has “despectus,” “despised,” less suitably.]

Therefore through Jeremiah also He exhorts her after her ruin: “At least from now on call me, ‘My husband’” (Jeremiah III, 4), although she had previously been rejected. And when Leah had borne her first child, she gloried that God had regarded her lowliness; then, because the Lord had seen that she was despised [Note: [Col. 1483D] The printed edition: “had seen.”]; and when she had borne a third child, she said: “Now my husband will be joined to me” (Genesis XXIX, 34), because she had borne him three sons.

You too, therefore, O soul, although you persist in laborious works, hasten to complete the number of virtues, so that your Bridegroom may be able to love you and be joined to you again—He who had previously despised you because of the ugliness of your crime—until a pure confession of love is born from you. Strive to be endowed with a good dowry, so that your Bridegroom may always be with you through love, and may compare you with the sister who remained beautiful to behold, so that whatever the stain of corruption disfigured in you, you may wholly repay through the offspring of virtue.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Apostle’s indication to the Corinthians of the supreme way, love

### 1.

“Still,” says the Apostle, after he had enumerated the gifts of the charisms, “I show you a more excellent way” (I Corinthians XII, 31). Then: “If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (I Corinthians XIII, 1–3).

He proposed three things: first, the tongues of angels and men, to indicate that whatever is uttered by the mouth without love profits the speaker nothing; but that, like brass or a cymbal struck by someone, those who speak in tongues without love profit themselves nothing and are empty within, without understanding.

Next comes prophecy, or those who excel in the gifts of knowledge, or who know mysteries: they already possess something within, but they are nothing, because although inflated by all these things, they lack inwardly the one thing that builds up—love. Furthermore, if they are helpful and distribute everything to the poor as food, and if they hand over their body without love so that it may burn, it profits nothing, because no sacrifice is acceptable to God unless it is consumed by the fire of love. God, therefore, is love, and whatever is offered without love is deprived of its reward [Note: [Col. 1484D] The printed edition: “is made void.”]

Thus the Apostle encompasses everything in these three things. For we do everything either with the mouth, the mind, or our actions. With the mouth, what is greater than speaking in the tongues of angels or of men? In the mind, what is more excellent than grasping prophecy, or knowing all mysteries, so that the mind may be called God’s fellow-initiate (*symmista Dei*) [Note: [Col. 1484D] The printed editions: “is called.”]? Then, if it excels in all knowledge and in all faith, so as to move mountains, what more outstanding thing can be proclaimed? Finally, in action, one who has distributed all his resources to the poor and burned his body in fire has nothing left to do beyond this.

When these things have been so magnified, love is rightly proclaimed as more excellent than they, without which nothing is acceptable to God, since love is the root of all good things and the bond of holy perfection. This is the clean way, which is certainly called holy, through which no outsider passes; only the righteous enter it. Therefore nothing is more excellent than it, since only the holy receive it and no outsider enters.

Otherwise, the sacrament of baptism is entered daily by bad people no less than by good people; all alike receive the Eucharist in the Church, possess prophecy, speak in tongues, know mysteries, excel in knowledge, perform signs of faith, and carry out many other things, transforming themselves into an angel of light [Note: [Col. 1484D] The printed editions: “transforming.”]. But love alone is received only by the good.

Therefore the Lord says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XII, 35). Take away love, then, and all the fruits of works are emptied at once, because love alone emptied Christ, so that He might take the form of a servant; and love alone, through adoption, again makes sons from servants.

The form of Christ’s discipleship and the recognition of Him is love. Whoever loses this form is alien from the body, because he is held fast by no bond of Christ, clothed with no beauty, adorned within by no loveliness. Therefore the name of Christ, like ointment poured out, shone forth through love, as we read in the Song of Songs; and for this reason the maidens love Him (Song of Songs I, 3), because our love alone renders a return to God’s love [Note: [Col. 1484D] The printed edition: “love in God.”], since He Himself first loved [Note: [Col. 1484D] The printed edition reads “Father” for “first.”] us, so that He might make us, who were children of wrath, His sons through adoption.

### 2.

For the whole perfection consists in love alone, because love admits no iniquity. Therefore no polluted person passes through it; but if someone once enters it, he is no longer polluted. Reborn in Christ, he is consecrated in His body. And in accordance with that word of Jeremiah, he has already found grace for himself, because the Lord appeared to him from afar and loved him with everlasting love; and what he has acquired is better than all the goods of life.

For it is like a watered garden, filled with every gift of blessings, and therefore in the Song of Songs it is gratefully sung by the Bridegroom: “A garden enclosed is my sister, a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain; your streams are a paradise” (Song of Songs IV, 12). See how well he is rebaptized who is nourished by love, in whose soul paradise now blooms.

You have, therefore, O soul, a fountain in which you may be reborn. And if you have made your first faith void, you nevertheless have a fountain sealed with the seal of Christ, in which no one who enters is an outsider. For I do not say that only Simon Magus, enveloped in the gall of bitterness, entered the baptismal fountain, but all the reprobate did so. Yet none of them entered that love from which no one who enters departs. They went out from the sacrament of the gift because they were not of us and were not reborn with us in love. [Note: [Col. 1485D] The printed edition: “namely.”] If they had been, they would certainly never have departed from it.

Therefore the blessed Apostle, seeing himself bound by the love of Christ, says: “Who will separate us from the love of God? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword?” (Romans VIII, 35). And to show the inseparable marriage of love, he says without hesitation: “For I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus” (ibid., 38–39).

Therefore whoever speaks so confidently has no doubt about love, because it is a garden enclosed and sealed, filled with every delight and every virtue. Indeed, it was easier for the enemy to rush into that place of the first paradise, from which he expelled Adam by his deceit, than to approach the fountain of love, to which no one can come unless he has been reborn from it.

Otherwise, even the devil, if he had entered into love, would no longer be an enemy but a fellow citizen of the saints and a member of God’s household. For love is with God—namely, with the Father—since God the Son, from God the Father, is love. Hence it is said: “With you is the fountain of life” (Psalm XXXV, 10), a fountain sealed, certainly, with the sign of the Father, since He is the image of God the Father.

From this fountain all draw the water of life, springing up freely into eternal life. No one, therefore, except Jesus Christ, gives this water, because the well is deep, the well of living waters. If anyone thirsts, let him come to Christ, and the eternal fountain will be given to him freely; but no one comes to receive it unless the Father has drawn him.

### 3.

From this it is clear that love is rightly called the more excellent way, which no one knows except the one who receives it, as I have said [Note: [Col. 1485D] The printed edition: “because.”]. The Samaritan woman in the Gospel mystically signifies this: “Lord, the well is deep, and you have nothing with which to draw” (John IV, 11).

Certainly she did not know with whom she was speaking, and she significantly indicates that the love of Christ is exceedingly deep: no one has anything with which to draw from it except the one who receives it. For love always tends toward God, from whom it derives its origin, and ardently looks toward one’s neighbor, with whom it knows how to share in creation and recreation.

Therefore, just as it is the highest virtue, so also is it the name; for we are never rightly commanded to love anything other than God and our neighbor through love. Although the word is often used improperly, love always excels in divine matters. For example, principally the name of God is in Him from whom all things, through whom all things, and in whom all things exist; and it declares the power and nature of the threefold majesty and unity.

Thus, in second place, human beings too are called gods by grace, those to whom the word of God came—called so by name, yet not falsely. In third place, the demons of the nations are called gods, not substantially or truly, nor by name through grace, but falsely, since Scripture says: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm XCV, 5).

So too love is first and principally a name belonging to God. For this reason we are commanded to love Him with our whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind, from whom we have the ability to love, since He Himself first loved [Note: [Col. 1486D] The printed edition: “the Father,” instead of “first.”] us. To love God is also to love eternal goods. Then, in second place, through that same love we are commanded to love our neighbor as ourselves. In third place, something else is falsely said to be loved under the title of love [Col. 1486C] [Note: [Col. 1486D] The printed edition: “to bind.”] when what should rather be called the desire for money, pleasure, or anything else is involved. [Note: [Col. 1486D] The printed edition: “because.”]

For God did not grant human beings the love of these things, but gave them their use. Thus every rational soul contains a movement of love; but the outcome of its reception varies, according as the mind tends toward the virtue of love. The affection of love itself was bestowed upon the rational soul through the kindness of the Creator, although at times it turns toward the love of money and the pursuit of greed, or toward the pursuit of empty glory, so that people become desirous of empty glory; or certainly toward a prostitute, so that they are found captive to lust and unchastity.

Likewise, while fornicating away from God, they pour themselves out still more perilously upon another power of so great a good and upon things like these. Even when they apply themselves to various arts, including those called liberal arts, they do not pursue the highest good while they entice themselves with these things, since the virtues of the mind are understood from that source from which they exist.

Therefore, to remove everything superstitious from the mind, the Lord says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength;” and then, “your neighbor as yourself.” “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matthew XXII, 37–40).

This is the deep and profound well of living waters; this is the fountain of life and the more excellent way, through which no polluted person passes. Whoever is reborn from it becomes a son by adoption, because the fountain of life flows within him, springing up into eternal life. This is the garden enclosed, the sealed fountain, in which the streams are a paradise.

From this source it already blooms in the minds of the saints, so that they may bear fruit for God, rooted and founded in love. Therefore whoever hastens toward life should continually desire that love be given to him, and should cultivate what has been given, so that his own love, by which he loves God and his neighbor, may daily refer itself more ardently to God, because God, who is love, refuses nothing to our love by which He Himself is loved.

Thus Paul says: “Love covers a multitude of sins” (I Peter IV, 8). And to speak more plainly: where love reigns, no sins have power, because love itself is the fountain of life and the cleansing of all crimes.

## CHAPTER XIV. On what is written: “But for me, to cling to God is good”

### 1.

Since we have said something about love, we ought to taste beforehand its goodness. The goodness of love, then, is the Trinity, and the Trinity itself is God, eternal love. This good alone and unique is such that to cling to it is to live, and so forth—to understand it is to taste it.

Therefore the Prophet says: “But for me, to cling to God is good, to place my hope in God” (Psalm LXXII, 28); and this is the good. In one and the same good he sometimes seems to distinguish goods for himself, because it is one thing to cling to God through the love of understanding and another to cling to Him through the desire of hope.

What is understood is certain and true; but not everything we believe is true, although I said above that in this pilgrimage faith is more excellent than understanding—not because it is more certain in itself, but because it has been established by truth. For a time it is more excellent, until what is partial is brought to an end. Then understanding alone will remain, through which we shall always be united and present.

But now whatever we understand less fully, we believe and hope for as we make our pilgrimage. Therefore we are already blessed through these two things: understanding and hoping. Through understanding we cling to God; through hoping we make our pilgrimage, because the rational soul understands God only partially. Whatever it understands of God is, insofar as it understands, joined to God and clings to Him.

For the soul understands that God is the supreme and unchangeable good, because He is always such and never undergoes any change. Therefore, since one who is changeable perceives himself to be so, it is good for him to cling to the unchangeable good, so that he may remain good from that source. But whatever he understands less fully, he must place all his hope in it until the eye of understanding is cleansed and evils are removed.

Through these two things the soul is already made blessed: through reality and through hope. Through reality, because it sees and knows God; through hope, because, like a secure anchor, it remains in the help of the Most High and under God’s protection.

Inflamed by these lights, the soul continually strives not to turn the eye of its mind away from the highest good. For whenever we look toward things grasped by the senses and toward bodily things, we are as though driven away from the light and wander in darkness. Yet we are not torn away from Him by hope; we remain, because God has become our portion, the portion of our heart, forever.

Otherwise, to withdraw from the fire of such love is to grow cold; to love something else is fornication. Therefore the Prophet says: “Behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish” (Psalm LXXII, 27). For to withdraw for a little while is one thing, and to distance oneself is another. To withdraw is to direct oneself elsewhere; to distance oneself is not only to desire earthly things, but also to seek them from demons or to love them as though they were the supreme good.

Yet although withdrawing from the focus of love is to grow weak, because hope is not severed amid the storms of the world, remaining under God’s protection is the safest anchor. But [Note: [Col. 1487D] The printed edition: “namely.”] the more lukewarmly we love [Note: [Col. 1487D] The printed editions omit: “the less we attend, and the less we attend.”], the less we attend; and the less we attend, the farther we are distanced. Therefore we must beware lest, as the mind becomes more distant, it commit fornication [Note: [Col. 1488D] The printed edition: “fornicate.”]: “You have destroyed,” he says, “all those who fornicate away from you” (Psalm LXXII, 27), because fornication is certainly contrary to chaste love.

### 2.

For the soul worthy of God seeks nothing other than God Himself from the Bridegroom whom it loves—not riches [Note: [Col. 1488D] The printed edition: “delights.”], honors, gold, estates, the pleasures of the world, or anything else that is in the world, because it loves only Him in whom it has everything and through whom, as it believes, all things were made.

Therefore let devoted chaste love always say: “But for me, to cling to God is good, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Psalm LXXII, 28). This, then, is the whole good, beyond which nothing greater is found. We shall cling to Him without weariness when we see Him face to face; but now, insofar as we can—for we cannot do so always—let us cling to Him through desire and cling to Him through understanding, lest perhaps we grow cold as we withdraw, or commit fornication by loving something else.

But because we cannot remain continuously in the ardor of love, since we cling less fully, let us place our hope in the Lord God by tasting Him in understanding, like a secure anchor in heaven. Place, I ask, your hope in the Lord, O soul, because as yet you do not cling to Him through presence, so that you may cling wholly to Him through the firmest hope.

You have the Most High as your refuge, placed in the help of God; remain under His protection. Raise yourself upward, because the weight of iniquity sits like a talent of lead, while the weight of love always breathes inwardly toward God like a flame.

Thus the flashing and upward-leaping impulses of love continually move the soul; but amid the secure yet wave-tossed airs of the world, fixed hope remains in God. For these are the things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love Him” (I Corinthians II, 9).

Love, therefore, and you will find them, because they have been prepared before the ages for those who love. Love alone will find through desire what hope already holds through the faith of love. Great, therefore, is the power of love, which embraces such things as eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and the human heart has not conceived; but they have been prepared from eternity for love.

That love which comes into the heart grasps all these things; having grasped them, it loves them. If the soul does not lose this love, it will enjoy without end the sweet embraces of its Bridegroom in blessedness.

### 3.

This work, Father, I have offered as devotedly as I could, since you once requested it, although occupied with many matters—not so that what I have said about these things should be sufficient [Col. 1490A], but so that your blessedness might still have something to present to beginners concerning these three virtues, without which no one is [Note: [Col. 1489A] The printed edition omits “is.”] a Christian.

Their fullness, then, completes the utterances of all the holy Scriptures. Whoever possesses them, written not with ink but by the Holy Spirit in the innermost heart, possesses on earth a complete understanding of spiritual things. On earth, certainly, because we are pilgrims; but according to the spiritual person we are renewed in heaven each day, bearing fruit through the knowledge of God.

Through the same giver and author of all good things and of these virtues, Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through immortal ages, and is blessed forever. Ame

[Col. 1489A]

## S. PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS, ABBOT OF CORBIE, ON THE PASSION OF THE HOLY RUFINUS AND VALERIUS

(According to Sirmond’s edition, *Works of Paschasius Radbertus*.)

[Col. 1489]

### [Col. 1489B] Radbertus, abbot of Corbie, to the Confessors of Christ

For the remembrance of the holy martyrs Rufinus and Valerius [Note: [Col. 1489C] XVIII Kalends of July, i.e. June 14].

When the feeling of supplication had brought us together, a little book concerning their contest was presented to us. Seeing that the sequence of its history had been corrupted, either because of its antiquity or because of the incompetence of its writer, I attempted, at the request of the inhabitants of that place, to transfer it into the form of a more polished style.

We believe this to be a religious service, worthy of the holy martyrs: since their teaching has shown us the path of life, their examples have trained us in the pursuit of virtue, and we are saved by their prayers and protected by their aid, we should also insert their victories into written memorials for the instruction of our frailty. We must not allow a benefit so useful and salutary to all who read devoutly to perish through the torpor of negligence.

For if a small fragment of a garment, or a little dust from a disintegrated body, obtained from the memorials of the saints, is believed to offer the faithful ineffable protection, who could worthily explain or even conceive how much material for salvation the lives and virtues of the saints provide to devout minds when they are recalled?

From them faith is strengthened, piety nourished, contempt for the world born, and desire for heavenly things generated. To say everything briefly, death is taken away and life is bestowed. Thus the Savior says: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live” (John XI).

Finally, the history of the saints is an incentive to holiness, a step toward advancement, and a gateway to heavenly contemplation—to resurrection from the dead and the perpetual good of immortality. Anyone who considers the matter wisely easily understands how much greater these things are than garments or the dust of bodies, even of saints.

Those things are corruptible; these are enduring. Those are earthly; these heavenly. Those are mortal; these eternal. In the former, the sentence of the first transgression is displayed; in the latter, the gifts of new freedom are confirmed. To say what is the case: the former supplied the honor and glory that these possess, while these suffered from the former a loss rather than receiving an increase.

The body that is subject to corruption weighs down the merit of dignity and wisdom; it does not raise it. Vices are friendly to flesh and blood, while virtues are opposed to them. Since this is so, does it not seem disgraceful that, while those things are clothed in golden cases and adorned with precious stones, these should be kept in a filthy and negligent manner?

This happens when they are either not established for the memory of posterity, or, having been violated by faults of sentences and words, are not restored to a form worthy of their dignity. It is not that the marks and astonishing deeds of the saints require verbal cosmetics or rhetorical ornaments, but their simple and natural expression should nevertheless shine with a distinct and honorable form, lest confused and harsh speech fail to instruct and instead offend the listener.

Moreover, just as a life of the saints carefully and suitably described expands their praises, so one treated negligently diminishes their glory, clouds the reputation of the Church, and conceals the victory of Christ.

In saying this we do not detract from the holy relics, since for all who venerate them devoutly they obtain forgiveness of sins, provide the aid of virtues, and confer the joys of immortality. Rather, as we look upon these things, may we desire both to hear the teaching and life of those whose memorials are contained in the holy ashes and to entrust what we have heard to the secret places of our hearts.

Thus, while we reverence their ashes with devoted service, may our mind continually contemplate their faces in a living likeness, so that our spirit, always joined to their spirit, may embrace as living those whom the world regards as dead. For those whom we encounter through memory, with whom we are joined through love, and to whom we speak through the vision of the heart are not rightly thought absent.

For this reason I do not consider that we deserve reproach, since we have labored to correct what was corrupted and restore what had grown old, seeking through these efforts to serve the usefulness of readers. We have not corrupted the truth of their deeds; rather, under our own expression we have woven together the history of the earlier writers.

If anyone rejects our edition, let him read the older one, if he prefers. It is enough for us that we have offered the devotion of our effort to the holy martyrs, cared for the advancement of those who believe in Christ, granted what was requested by those who asked, and not concealed the wondrous struggles endured for Christ.

As for the accusations of the ignorant, forged out of malice or envy, we ought to pass them by with deaf ears. But let us come to the narrative.

Under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian Augustus, a storm of persecution was raised against the churches of Christ. By now, indeed, the Gospel of truth had illumined the boundaries of the Roman world; by now the kingdom of heaven had been preached to almost all nations [Col. 1491C]; by now every tongue resounded with the praises of Christ, every nation celebrated them, and the prophecy had been fulfilled which says: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18). By now the Parthian had learned the path of the right road; by now the Ethiopian had changed his skin; by now Libya and Africa, wounded by the weapon of salvation, were receiving healing; the North had tempered its icy harshness with southern mildness; the West had extended the waning of its light toward the East; the warlike Gauls had beaten their swords into ploughshares and their spears into hoes. The Scythians no longer knew savagery, nor the Thracians brutality, having been tamed by the gentleness of sheep. Rome herself, the proud mistress of the world, had long rejoiced to submit her haughty neck to the humility of Christ; almost the whole world echoed with Christ’s glory, and the entire [Col. 1491D] world raised its eyes from the darkness of death toward the joys of the new light.

It was possible to see Israel drenched by the streams of the Jordan into the grace of renewal and, glorified through a second circumcision by Jesus, overthrowing the walls of Jericho at the sound of trumpets, burning Ai, assigning the city’s inhabitants to the uses of the tabernacle’s wood, and also destroying the city of letters—that is, the wisdom of the world—and possessing the whole region of the Canaanites after their kings had been conquered. Yet it would have been little that the Christian people protected their own rites and religion, unless they were also placed in charge of the affairs of the commonwealth for the sake of the sincerity of faith, the pursuit of virtue, and the practice of piety.

Thus soldiers of Christ occupied the imperial palaces, administered civic affairs, and managed the [Col. 1492A] governments of the provinces. Everywhere a sacred assembly could be seen shining in garments of holiness and with the insignia of uprightness; in the forum, in the streets, in the cities, and in the countryside, the praise of Christ resounded. Shrines were destroyed, images were shattered, sacred groves were burned; temples, however, were built for the heavenly King, altars were raised, crowds of peoples flocked to countless churches, hymns were celebrated with joy, and holy readings were recited with reverent fear of God.

Meanwhile the word of God was distributed by the leaders of the churches to every age, every sex, and every condition, according to the measure of each person’s understanding. Feast days were passed in the expectation of spiritual joy; the memories of the saints already resting in the heavenly dwelling were commemorated; the life of the citizens of heaven was practiced on earth, and, so to speak, earthly conduct had migrated into a heavenly form. What wonder was it, when heaven itself dwelt on earth? “The heavens,” he says, “declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18). I will say more: they no longer dwelt on earth but in heaven, of whom the Apostle says: “But your citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3). Therefore, having become heavens, human beings were in heavenly places; they had trampled earthly things underfoot, had climbed to what is above, and clung to what endures. They were both a source of terror and a marvel to all the nations round about.

For placed among those nations, they shone like lights in the world, so that the Holy Spirit could fittingly sing beforehand in praise of his Church: “How beautiful is my beloved, how comely! Beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army set in battle array” (Song of Songs 6:3, 9). Indeed, she was beautiful when she was adorned with holy conduct; comely when she was illumined by the insignia of virtues. Thus, in the honorable life of the people, she shone with lunar beauty; in the merits of her rulers, she gleamed with the splendor of the sun; and, through the most richly adorned modesty of the most careful religion, she struck all her adversaries with fear.

Thus the peoples of the nations, seized by such astonished admiration, were converted. Abandoning the worship of demons, they professed the service of divine religion; and, to be made participants in the heavenly kingdom, they eagerly sought the bath of the sacred font. For a very long time, therefore, the condition of the churches increased through prosperous advances, and their glory, rising above the earth and surpassing everything, seemed to be hastening toward heaven. No envy arose, no spite of the most wicked demon opposed them, since they were supported by the help of the heavenly right hand.

At that time, too, the people deserved well of God through the practice of piety and the observance of justice. But when, through great freedom and excessive indulgence, morals were corrupted and discipline was ruined—when one person envied another and one disparaged another; when they bit and attacked one another and stirred up civil battles against themselves; when they pierced the hearts of their neighbors with the arrows of their words; when rulers stirred up seditions and conflicts against rulers, and peoples against peoples; when pretense appeared on the face, deceit in the heart, and falsehood in speech; and when the heap of evils swelled in every particular—then divine Providence, perceiving the loss of discipline inflicted on its people through excessive peace and its own excessive gentleness, first began gradually to restrain those who were slipping. While the condition of the Church was still intact and its congregations remained, it temporarily allowed those who were in the army to be harassed only by the persecution of the pagans.

But when no understanding of this clemency was communicated to the peoples—in fact, when they believed that affairs were being conducted without divine Providence, as though they did not know God, and therefore persisted all the more in their wickedness—and when those who appeared to be leaders of the people, having become forgetful of the divine command, were inflamed against one another by quarrels, zeal, spite, pride, enmities, and hatreds, so that they believed themselves to possess tyranny rather than priesthood, forgetting Christian humility and sincerity, and celebrating the sacred mysteries [Col. 1493B] with profane minds, then at last, according to the words of the prophet Jeremiah (Lamentations 1 and following), “the Lord in his anger darkened the daughter of Zion; he cast down from heaven the glory of Israel, and did not remember his footstool in the day of his anger.”

And as he says again: “The Lord submerged all the beauty of Israel and destroyed all its walls; he overturned the covenant of his servant, profaned his sanctuary on the earth, destroyed him from purification, and cast his seat to the ground; he shortened the days of his time and covered him with confusion.” For he brought the glory of the Church, which shone like the stars of heaven in the night of this world, into disgrace and confusion. He did not consider in his heart that this people had once been beloved; that it had been redeemed by the blood of an immaculate Lamb; that it had been freed from Egypt through many signs and wonders (Exodus 1 and following); that it had been led across the dried-up waters of the Red Sea after the spiritual Pharaoh had been drowned; that it had heard the voice of the speaking God from heaven; that it had been fed with the bread of life; that it had been refreshed by the saving torrent of the Holy Spirit; and that it had been deemed worthy both to know and to receive the mysteries of eternal life. Remembering none of this, on the day of his fury the Most High cast down all the beauty of the sanctification of his people, so that what had previously been an honor became an insult, and what had formerly remained an object of veneration was given over to contempt.
