He removed the protection of the angels, destroyed the pastoral defense, gave the covenant of life to the nations to be profaned, and defiled all the beauty of religion with filth and abominations. And as glorious as it had previously been to all, so obscure and vile was it handed over to everyone [Col. 1493D]. Indeed, the temples of the living God were being destroyed from their very foundations; the sacred Scriptures were publicly burned in the streets; priests and leaders of the churches, stripped and bound, were dragged through the forums and streets and handed over to prisons. Strife was poured out upon the leaders, and they became a reproach to their neighbors, a mockery and derision to all the nations round about.

It was the nineteenth year of Diocletian’s reign, the month of March, the solemn day of Easter, as Eusebius’s history relates, when the emperor’s edicts were posted throughout the whole world, ordering that all the churches wherever they existed should be destroyed to the ground and that the sacred Scriptures should be burned in fire. Not long afterward, other edicts were also published, ordering that Christians, subjected to various punishments, should be forced to sacrifice.

Then the holy martyrs became a great spectacle both to angels and to human beings (1 Corinthians 4), as they were dragged to punishments by the cruelty of their persecutors and endured wondrous contests before all. Throughout all the cities, regions, and provinces, decrees of impiety were carried out, and new and carefully devised torments of every kind were inflicted on Christians. Some were shut up in prisons; some were beaten with whips; others, stretched upon the rack, were scraped with claws; they were sent into exile, subjected to wild beasts, suffocated in water, burned in fire, and struck down with swords. Nor did the impious hands of their persecutors spare even their dead bodies: they were either thrown out unburied to be torn apart by beasts and birds, or sunk into the waves and handed over to fish to devour, or reduced to ashes and scattered into the depths of the sea [Col. 1494B].

At this time, distinguished men, renowned for constancy in faith and holiness of conduct—Quintinus, Victoricus and Fuscianus, Rufinus and Valerius, Crispinus and Crispinianus, together with the other companions of their group, natives of the city of Rome—preached the word of life to the peoples of Belgica Secunda, who were still held fast by pagan superstition, and called them from the yoke of demons to the freedom of Christ. Marvelous in doctrine and illustrious in virtues, they illumined the Gauls like exceedingly joyful stars.

It is said that they entered the territories of Gaul with blessed Dionysius, who had been sent by blessed Clement, bishop of the Roman see, to warm the cold hearts of the pagans with the heat of faith; but the sequence of times contradicts this. For Saint Dionysius was crowned with martyrdom under Domitian Caesar, in the second year of his reign, whereas these men received the glory of immortality under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. This interval of time contains no fewer than two hundred and ten years—a number of years that denies to people of our age and of any other age not only the capacity to take part in so great a contest but even the possibility of living through the whole span bodily.

Therefore, as a plausible account demonstrates, he—that is, Dionysius—shone forth when the darkness of paganism still afflicted the Belgians with perpetual night, and, like the morning star, began to drive the shadows of unbelief from the minds of the faithless. These men, however, appeared like the brightest rays of the true sun when the serenity of light had already dispersed the shadows of night, yet the twilight of former unbelief still presented no perfect day of faith [Col. 1494D]. At the rising of their arrival, they promised the perfect light of belief and expelled the night of the whole of paganism.

Dionysius, therefore, with his companions, opened up the way of truth among certain peoples of Gaul through its first beginnings; these men taught them to walk along it with firm feet and steady steps. Nevertheless, it is no less meritorious to open the beginning of grace to minds still blind than to dedicate them to the fullness of perfection, since the rising of light inaugurates the whole integrity of brightness, and the summit of fullness always refers the beginning back to its source. Thus the rosy glow of dawn consecrates the brilliance of midday, and the dignity of this whiteness honors the illumination of its rising.

Otherwise, “Paul plants, Apollo waters, but God gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3). Let us not distinguish between merits, since we do not bestow the honors; let us not establish a dispute concerning crowns, since we do not know how to assess their contests. Let us leave judgment to him who made his martyrs conquer and gave crowns to those who triumphed.

Certainly, children should repay their fathers with dutiful veneration, and servants should strive to honor their patrons with reverent service. Let them contemplate the contests, not distinguish between them; marvel at the victories, not assess them; stand in awe of the crowns, not judge them.

When, therefore, savage barbarism venerated the ancient altars of demons with bloody hands—not with true religion but with impiety—and, in unanimous agreement and through a single superstition, looked up to numerous throngs of gods while the world was already growing old, and when no splendor of truth illumined the dark hearts of the Gauls, at last divine pity was moved. To drive away the darkness of death, it sent heralds of a new grace, through whom Belgica, laying aside its error, began to see the true light of faith.

From that point, gaining increases in salvation through daily advances, it continued to embrace worshipers of demons until the time of the aforementioned men, namely Quintinus, Rufinus, and Valerius, although it was adorned with the churches of Christ. But so that the holy martyrs might free the province from profane superstition, they set out from the city of Rome and went to Gaul—not from fear of the persecution that was then raging throughout the whole world, but inflamed by the zeal of charity, so that they might restore to the dignity of life those whom they had freed from the dominion of death.

For what would they avoid in one place when it thundered everywhere? Or what ensuing tortures would they fear, which they willingly endured for the love of Christ? They did not therefore enter the ferocity of the Gauls to flee bodily death; rather, so that they might hasten to Christ by the palm of martyrdom, they sought out the savagery of that fiercest people [Col. 1495C].

At this time Rictiovarus held the prefecture in Gaul. A man cruel in the ferocity of his spirit and more savage in the enormity of his impiety than the very laws of the emperors, he desired to satisfy the imperial decrees. Inflamed by the madness of his own frenzy, he began to conduct a most severe persecution against Christians, persuading them—now through threats, now through flatteries—to offer worship to the images; those who did not comply he killed by various kinds of torture.

For the servant of the demon, the arbiter of impiety, the fuel of vices, contended to bring down to the depths of Tartarus the souls hastening toward the palace of heaven and to subject once again to the yoke of demonic slavery those redeemed by Christ’s blood. He was, of course, an imitator of the devil, whose vessel he remained. The devil cast those established in the sublimity of paradise into a pit of tears; this man sought to thrust down from the fortress of virtue those who occupied it. The devil drove them from a springtime place of delight; this man attempted to turn them away from the kingdom of immortality.

Although they labored with a similar purpose and the same intention, they fought by different arts of deception. The devil, in order to deceive, girds himself as a flattering seducer through serpentine fraud; this man, in order to destroy, surrounded himself with deceit and violence. For the heap of savagery grew against innocence once it had been condemned; even religious service was demanded through tortures, although at first it had been urged by flattering favor. Yet the more difficult the contests sought by Christ’s soldiers, the more glorious a victory was prepared for them. The triumph of the conquerors rose higher precisely where the hostile hand fought with sharper savagery.

The executor of Satan, therefore, could rage against Christ’s army, but he could not overcome it; he was able to attack, but he withdrew defeated. After he had adorned many cities of Gaul with the rosy blood of martyrs, he came to the city of Rheims, where he killed many holy people through various punishments for their confession of Christ.

But after he had put to death, through the harshness of punishments, those whom he had found ennobled in that same place by the dignity of this name, he was stirred by the report of blessed martyr Quintinus: through signs of virtue and sublime preaching, he was turning many thousands of peoples away from the images and subjecting them to the religion of the true and ever-living God. Therefore, grieving exceedingly that the salvation of so many souls and the loss of demonic superstition were increasing, he departed from the city and made for the territory of the Viromandui.

For the book of the passion of the saints Rufinus and Valerius states that Quintinus was revered in that city in those days. The history of his own passion, however, indicates that he was first summoned by the prefect Rictiovarus in the city of Amiens and tortured with various punishments. When the prefect discovered the martyr of Christ’s unconquerable spirit, he sent him to Augusta Viromanduorum with his hands and neck bound in iron. After he had been brought there, he was subjected, while the same prefect raged, to the most dreadful [Col. 1496C] tortures; finally, he was beheaded and thrown into the river.

But where he was first heard is not ours to judge, since faith acknowledges that the place of burial was the place of his passion, and it does not seem contradictory if he first honored the city of Amiens not only with preaching but also with the title of glorious confession, and afterward, having gone to the Viromandui, stirred the ears of the impious prefect no less widely through the fame of his signs and the urgency of his preaching.

For when so great a martyr of Christ had been received into prison, although bound with iron, his tongue was not restrained from preaching. Rather, it was then that he preached him more steadfastly and more fervently: the one whose love inflamed him, so that he laughed amid whippings, rejoiced upon the racks, and danced for joy amid the plates being driven into him.

The prefect, therefore, leaving the city, turned aside to the royal palace at Rheims, which had been situated beside the River Vuidola. In that place the holy men Rufinus and Valerius were instructing a considerable community of believers through doctrine, excelling in conduct, and shining with virtues.

When information about them had been given to the prefect, he sent attendants and ordered them to be brought before him. When the martyrs of Christ learned this, they wished to hide themselves from the tyrant’s sight—not through fear of punishments, but through prudent deliberation and the teaching of humility.

For taught by heavenly instruction, which says, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matthew 10:28), they could not fear a temporal punishment, light and momentary affliction. They understood that by fearing present torments one does not escape punishments but earns them, and is not freed from the punishment of death but incurs the dangers of eternal condemnation.

Rather, they rejoiced to share in Christ’s sufferings through patience, so that they might become companions in his glory. Therefore, those who had been strengthened by faith, made certain by hope, and inflamed by charity did not seek a hiding place because they had been overcome by terror. Instead, attentive to the evangelical command that says, “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (ibid., 23), they avoided the boldness of rashness through the humility of prudence.

In the end, how many, abusing the presumption of rashness, believed that they would boldly seize the palm of victory, yet, exhausted by punishments, fell miserably from the stronghold of confession? But those who attributed nothing to their own strength and, trusting in the Lord, entered the field of combat under the banners of humility brought back a glorious victory over the enemy [Col. 1497B].

For Peter, the pillar of faith, while rashly presuming, was overthrown by the voice of a single little woman. But when he learned that the race does not belong to the swift nor victory to the strong, he corrected the boldness of rashness with the modest gentleness of humility. While he feared his own weakness, he became a victor—he who earlier, arrogating to himself what exceeded the merit of his condition, had been defeated.

For hope of victory must by no means be attributed to the confidence of an inconsiderate soldier, but to virtue. Its companions are always both hope in prosperity and caution in adversity. Therefore it is said in Proverbs: “Let your eyelids go before your steps” (Proverbs 4:25). By eyelids is understood the subtlety of discernment, by which every wise person ought to direct the path of his steps, lest, caught on the level ground of security, he fall through imprudence into the precipice of an abyss.

The soldiers of Christ, therefore, contemplating a higher counsel and desiring to withdraw from the face of the storm that was tossing the Church of God, sought the aid of concealment. Not far away there was a cave enclosed by a dense growth of thorns and brambles. The servants of Christ withdrew into it, wishing to remain hidden, so that they might either avoid the force of the persecution raging like thunder or, if heavenly dispensation commanded it, hasten from the workshop of virtues to the labor of the contest.

Meanwhile, while they awaited with anxious spirits the command of the heavenly Emperor, they devoted themselves to hymns and prayers. The cave became a church; the lair of beasts was converted into a house of prayer; the cavern sheltered those whom the palace drove away; the caves defended those whom the forum persecuted [Col. 1497D].

Thus we recall that formerly the prophets and the righteous of the earlier age sought caves and caverns of the earth as their protection—men whom cities had harassed, the royal court had driven out, and the world had despised. In the end, a cave received the patriarch Lot lest the fires of Sodom destroy him, and made him secure, buried in the earth, whom Zoar had shaken with fear (Genesis 19). The royal court decreed that Elijah should be killed, but a cave embraced him as he fled; and the one whom the city did not allow to live, the cave lifted up to the secret of divine conversation (1 Kings 19). In the mountains, in caves, and in hidden places of the earth, the sons of the prophets dwell—men whom populous cities, fortified castles, and broad villages assail with insults, pursue with hatred, and wear down with reproaches [Col. 1498A].

O human cruelty, propagated from the seed of sin! O savagery of souls, generated by the devil’s sowing! The lairs of wild animals receive those whom human dwellings reject. Among beasts are secure those for whom no safe place exists among human beings. Humans drive out the servants of the Most High, guardians of justice, lovers of peace, teachers of piety, and conquerors of iniquity; beasts receive them. Peoples attack them; wild animals revere them. Kings pursue them in order to kill them; beasts follow them in order to preserve them.

Yet those whom reason does not govern but fury drives, whom restraint does not control but lust engulfs, must be judged not human but beastlike, as Scripture says: “When man was in a position of honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Psalm 48:13).

While, therefore, the athletes of the eternal King dwelt in the hidden recesses of the earth, avoiding the tumult of crowds and the shouts of the court; while they inhabited the solitude of seclusion; while they embraced the quiet of heavenly contemplation; while, on the mind’s flight, they disregarded temporal things and pressed on toward eternal realities; while, nourished by heavenly sweetness, they despised the delights of the world and desired the presence of their King with burning prayers—the cruel tyrant’s guards at last found the servants of Christ, bound them in chains, and led them into the tyrant’s presence.

When they stood before his tribunal, he addressed them in these words:

“Rufinus and Valerius, what gods do you worship? Or the sacred rites of what religion do you venerate?”

The holy martyrs said:

“We worship one God, almighty, immutable, eternal, creator of all visible things; filling all things, ruling all things, containing all things. And we worship one Lord, Jesus Christ, restoring all things that are in heaven and all things that are on earth.

“But we do not venerate the gods who are images formed by human art, whose substance is wood or stone or shining metal—matter subject to corruption and vulnerability—to which art has given form and skill has bestowed beauty.

“Divine substance, however, derives its beginning not from elsewhere but from itself; it is not subject to time, since it has always existed before time. It suffers no diminution, remaining eternally in the fullness of itself; it knows no alteration; it is uniform, simple, steadfast, perfect, and perpetually subsisting. By its word the world and all the adornment of the world were made; by its Spirit every creature is established and governed. To him we offer daily a sacrifice of praise and the sacrifice of a contrite spirit.”

The prefect said:

“The unconquered emperors have decreed that, abandoning the superstition in which you worship a crucified and dead man, you should adore the almighty gods worshiped by the Roman commonwealth. It is impious to abandon the religion received from our ancestors, which advanced, governs, and protects the condition of the Roman Empire, and to pass, through the frivolity of the mind, to a novelty invented with childishness.”

The holy martyrs replied:

“We are not ashamed of the cross of Christ, which grants salvation to the world, nor do we deny that he endured bodily death, through which resurrection to life was given to us. But since you cast reproach upon the cross, consider this: when the Son of God was enduring the punishment of the wood, the sun fled, veiled in darkness; the earth trembled, and the rocks were split apart (Luke 23). The elements could not endure the gallows of the one whom they confessed to be their creator.

“You who revile him as dead, acknowledge that on the third day he returned into the air of light; after overcoming the author of death and despoiling the kingdom of hell, he ascended into heaven and brought back a triumph of joy before the presence of the Father, while the angels rejoiced (Luke 24).

“Thus, although God existed before the ages—for he is the Word of the Father through whom the ages were established—he mercifully chose to become human in order to free humanity. And to destroy the yoke of sin and the sting of death, obeying the command of the Father, he accepted by his own will the disgrace of the cross and the injury of death [Col. 1499B].

“To the wise of this world the cross of Christ is foolishness, but the wisdom of God made the wisdom of the world foolish (1 Corinthians 1). It taught that, by humbling himself even unto death, humility is the ascent by which one reaches heaven, and that patience is a virtue before which all the enemy’s power must yield.

“Nor was it fitting for a heavenly teacher to be armed except with the weapons of humility and patience, so that he might overthrow the devil’s pride through humility and trample down the boldness of presumption through the gravity of patience. In this way he taught those hastening toward the heavenly palace that the ancient enemy must be wounded with contrary arrows; that where pride had cast one down, humility must climb; and that where the mobility of fickleness had driven one away, the gravity of stability must return.

“The swelling of worldly philosophy does not grasp this discipline of divine reverence. It does not know how to humble itself in order to rise; it does not know how to become foolish—that is, to recognize its own foolishness—in order to grasp the rays of true philosophy. Therefore it laughs at the disgrace of the cross and criticizes submission to death in the Son of God, as though humility could be true unless it had exposed itself to contempt and degradation, or as though the fullness of patience could be shown unless the end of death revealed it. Human knowledge, which does not know such virtues, dreams.

“Eternal wisdom, however, teaches mortals how they may both see and climb the perfect stronghold of virtue. Therefore, as you charge, the Christian religion is not empty superstition but a doctrine of life, a teaching of salvation, and a worship of holiness.

“For this reason, to believers it is the glory of freedom to believe in the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ; to venerate his death as an act of piety is life from the dead.

“As for the gods whom your magnificence calls almighty, and whom the Roman commonwealth, deceived by wretched error, once worshiped, now that the truth from above has flashed forth, it is clear that most of it has been illumined. These gods do not exalt, govern, or preserve the power of the Roman world; indeed, they cannot even defend or help themselves.

“Finally, if you look at the statues placed in shrines, what divine power can they possess, when they have neither the gift of life nor any faculty of sensation? What help could they offer—not to a kingdom, cities, or peoples, but even to the smallest little animal, which does not possess as much power as we see in a worm or a bug [Col. 1500A]?

“These animals perceive that they are alive; those statues know nothing. These move back and forth of their own will; those cannot move unless they are either carried or pushed, since they possess no voluntary motion. These seek what is suitable for them and avoid what is contrary; those have no appetite, for insensibility deprives them of every feeling.

“Therefore those things that cannot perceive their own deficiency are unable to provide any help. Indeed, it is proved to be great madness for beings endowed with life and reason to hope for assistance from lifeless things.

“And if you choose to consider those whose images these are said to be, what virtue, what help, what divinity can they possess, when it is established that they were human beings and paid the debt of death? Nor were they human beings whom the honor of virtue and the distinction of a well-conducted life made illustrious, but men whom the dreadful deformity of vices stained with every infamy and disgrace.

“Finally, that greatest and best Jupiter, begotten by Saturn or Rhea and buried in Crete, demonstrates by his birth and death that he was not a god but a human being. To whom, then, could he grant salvation, when he could not drive death away from himself? Or to whom could he give the beginning of life, when he could not exist before he was born? Or how would that one protect the lives of others who, immediately after his birth, was secretly carried away to escape being killed and fled from his father’s jaws?

“If you say that poetic fictions should not be believed, your own reliable histories testify that he was concealed lest he be struck by his father’s sword. For Saturn, in order to hold the throne of the kingdom alone, had pledged to his brother that he would kill all the male children born to him; and this arrangement was preserved in the one who preceded Jupiter’s birth.

“Yet when Jupiter and Juno had been born as twins, Juno was presented to their father’s eyes, whereas Jupiter was taken away and carried to Crete to be brought up. What do all these things indicate except weakness and frailty? How, then, can a weak being provide the strength he does not possess, or how can one who is feeble give comfort, when he himself lacks assistance?

“But let us consider his life: how holy it was, how chaste, so that on that account he might rightly have deserved divine honors. Is he not found impious and impure from his earliest infancy? He deprived his father of the throne no less cruelly than violently; though young in age, he was great in wickedness; he could not endure the years of his decrepit old father, defeated his brothers and nephews, and seized sole control of the monarchy. He abstained from no disgraceful act.

“For he took his sister as his wife, and spared neither married women nor virgins, but defiled everything with fornications and adulteries. Nor did he preserve honor even for his own sex, but heaped the corruption of males upon his lust.

“Consider whether one who did such things is ‘greatest.’ Certainly he is not ‘best’—unless perhaps we have lost our senses, calling human beings who do such things wicked and depraved and judging them worthy of every punishment.

“Tullius charged Verres with adulteries: your Jupiter committed these same acts. He accused Publius Clodius of incest with his sister: for Jupiter the Best and Greatest, the same woman was both sister and wife.

“And what of his father Saturn? Is he not shown to have been mortal, since he fathered children through intercourse with a woman? Was he not a parricide, since he slaughtered his own children? Was he not devoted to vices, since in his desire to rule he had forgotten the very laws of nature? For, in order to hold power alone, after removing his brother, he struck a pact involving the blood of his children.

“Or is strength rightly attributed to that one who, after being defeated, lost his kingdom and hid himself in Latium to escape Jupiter’s anger? Thus he was an unhappy and pitiable god: deprived of his kingdom, driven from his home, he had nowhere to rest and survived as an exile in another’s hospitality.

“It is shameful even to mention Mars’ adulteries and bloodshed, for which crime of homicide he received a sentence of death but escaped punishment through the Athenians’ intercession.

“What of Juno’s abominable marriage bed? What of her feminine savagery toward her rivals should we mention?

“Or shall we, in the case of holy Venus, a public prostitute, remove divine honors from her? She earned the status of a heavenly deity for no other merits than that she first provided prostitutes with a model and established their law. If, then, a prostitute is a goddess, why is chastity praised in women? Why are adulteries condemned? Why is a prostitute subjected to infamy?

“Let true virtues be a reproach, since crimes and vices are proclaimed among the gods. But if this seems foolish, then those who are clearly exposed to vices are not gods.

“God, however, is the author of virtue and the lover of holiness, the fountain and origin of all goodness. Vices are opposed to virtue; uncleanness is incompatible with holiness; evil is manifestly hostile to goodness. By what logic, then, have vicious, impure, and wicked beings attained divinity, since no vice falls upon God?

“If criminals are to be worshiped as gods, then let adulterers not be punished, parricides not be condemned, thieves not be chastised, and prostitutes not be accused. In the end, whoever accuses, judges, and punishes those guilty of these and similar crimes demonstrates that the gods worshiped by the Roman commonwealth are worthy of punishment, not divine honor.

“Your philosophers teach that one ought to pursue virtue and wisdom. They say that human nature was adorned with reason by the supreme God for this purpose: that, guided by reason, human beings might regulate their life and conduct. They say that nothing else is the law by which crimes are condemned and virtues praised than the reason of nature, and that this alone makes human beings superior to beasts—if they are governed by understanding.

“Those who corrupt the law of nature and pursue the confusion of vices, they say, should be called not human beings but beasts, whose examples they embody.

“How, then, do they lavish upon those beings, as though they were heavenly, divine praises, when their disgraceful deeds are condemned by the laws? Therefore they are not divine beings who are convicted of being polluted by crimes; they are not omnipotent whom the corruption of their damaged nature proves to be weak.

“Nor do dead beings preserve the summit of Roman power, since, while alive, they were unable to preserve their own kingdoms.”

Seeing this madness, the poet exclaims:

O the cares of men! O how much vanity there is in human affairs! For what could be discovered to be more futile than assigning divine honors to criminals, neglecting the true God [Col. 1502A] and venerating images? This is not to uphold religion, but to defend superstition; not to follow piety, but to nourish impiety.

Seneca therefore rightly censures such worshipers:

> They venerate images of the gods, he says; they kneel before them in supplication, adore them, sit or stand beside them throughout the entire day, throw money before them, slaughter victims for them—and although they hold these things in such high regard, they despise the craftsmen who made them.

What could be said more clearly or openly to show that theirs is not religion but empty superstition? For what divinity do things possess that retain nothing living beyond their likeness? Or how can those things provide assistance to which the craftsman’s hand was unable to impart any rational sense? Or what power of virtue can things possess that have been assembled from fragile material?

There is therefore greater power in the one [Col. 1502B] who fashioned them. He made them when they did not exist; indeed, they would not have existed at all except through him, nor could they have been anything other than what their maker determined. Yet he could not give them everything that he himself possessed, since he could not impart to them either the reason or the life that he had.

But why have we brought forward this one philosopher, who laughs at the images of the gods, when nearly all your sages understood and wrote the same? Although they worshiped them—whether led to do so by custom or compelled by fear—they nevertheless understood and recorded in their writings for the memory of posterity that neither those images nor those whose likenesses they were said to be were gods, but men: born and dead. Yet the name of divinity was attributed to them solely because they had been exceedingly powerful kings. They transferred mortals from bestial savagery to human customs, not by divine power, but by human ingenuity. They bestowed upon them arts and many benefits, by which people might be encouraged toward an orderly life and the useful conduct of affairs.

The uneducated readily absorbed this error, believing that all powerful men were gods. From this the error passed down to later generations and entangled nearly all mortals, so that they venerated as gods those whom ignorant antiquity had consecrated. But God, wishing to free mortals from this lethargy, decreed that his Son should become incarnate, so that, placed among human beings as a man, he might recall them to the way of truth, so that, abandoning falsehood, they might know, venerate, and adore the true God.

For this reason, the doctrines we hold are not childish, [Col. 1502D] as you mock them, but divine. Human reason did not devise them; heavenly wisdom revealed them. To accept these teachings is to return from death to life. To hold fast to them is to live forever.

Therefore the error received from our fathers must not be preferred to the truth; rather, once the error has been condemned, the truth must be followed. For the farther paternal vices are propagated through their children, the more their deformity is accumulated by the very passage of time. Nor should the antiquity of false gods strengthen their authority, since no one doubts that falsehood must always be condemned.

Otherwise, if one asks about the antiquity of religion, it is evident that the worship of the one God—which began with the origin of the world—preceded the superstition of many gods, which began in the time of Jupiter and, after many generations of men, defiled the world. This can very easily be demonstrated from the divine Scriptures. But examine your own histories, and you will find that your Jupiter began to reign after his father Saturn, and that he did not receive the beginning of light before the world, or even together with the world, but many generations after their creation, when a multitude of mortals had already filled the earth.

Thus it is clear that he was not, as you proclaim, the discoverer of things and of human beings, but was himself merely one of the mortals, as your own writings testify. Nor was he eternal, since he began to reign on earth after many predecessors. He was truly a most arrogant man who was the first to claim divine honors for himself, though he was destined to rule only for a short time.

Therefore do not say that these men advanced, governed, and preserved the Roman state, since they were human beings, long ago reduced by the law of death to the dust from which they were taken—or else they were empty images, without reason, sensation, or life.

To this the prefect replied:

“For a long time our restraint has endured your speaking against the gods with insulting accusations. But if you do not obey the commands of the Augusti and render the gods the veneration that is their due, I will have you destroyed by various punishments.”

And he ordered their necks and hands to be weighed down with heavy bonds and that they be shut in prison, so that, bound by chains and oppressed by the weight, they might waste away. But the holy martyrs rejoiced that through suffering they were deemed worthy to become participants with Christ. Kindled by the fire of divine love, they transferred the body’s distress into the joy of the mind. Nor was divine favor absent from those who suffered on his behalf; rather, by pouring the gift of the Holy Spirit into their breasts, it transformed bodily weakness into the strength of courage.

Indeed, they bore the immense weight of the chains as though they were the lightest feathers. Everyone was astonished that their little bodies, worn down by fasting and vigils, could endure so great a mass of weight. They were therefore handed over to the prison that day, to be kept there through the following night. During that interval they did not lay down their hearts in grief or shrink in fear, but expanded them through the sweetness of the spirit into the love of Christ. They celebrated praises to the heavenly Father, offered hymns, gave thanks, and amid the filth of the prison meditated upon the joys of heaven.

Their limbs were bound with chains, but through the freedom of the Spirit they were joined to the heavenly hosts. They asked the supreme King to grant his athletes the fullness of faith, bestow the virtue of patience, give the palm of perseverance, and grant them the triumph of victory over the savagery of the enemy.

On the following day they were again brought before the tyrant’s tribunal. Thinking that they could more easily be overthrown by gifts, he began to address them in flattering language, as though moved by compassion:

“When I see that you are noble and prudent men, I am deeply grieved that such dignity should be squandered uselessly through madness. By abandoning the worship of the heavenly gods, you have abandoned the merit of holiness, the splendor of virtue, and the enjoyment of life; by pursuing the foolishness of old women, you have handed yourselves over to disgrace, infamy, and poverty.

“What wise man has ever despised splendid deeds of honor and voluntarily submitted to the shame of infamy? What noble man has ever scorned the glory of life and chosen to be abject and dishonored? Therefore return to the distinction of your homeland; return to the wisdom whose splendor illuminates you. Do not allow your minds, through a judgment once wrongly begun, to remain obstinately bound by the chains of perpetual error. As educated men trained in civilized moderation, readily turn your minds back toward what is honorable.

“Accept the ceremonies of your ancestors; show religious devotion to the sacred rites of the immortal gods. I will grant you many great gifts; I will raise you to the highest honors; I will exalt you with the most distinguished offices; I will commend you to the most invincible Augusti.”

To this the holy martyrs, neither softened nor deceived, but recognizing the fraud of the ancient enemy, replied:

“O deadly poison brought forth from the serpent’s mouth! O cup of death polished with Babylonian splendor! Thus long ago the devil deceived the inhabitants of paradise through the serpent; thus he deceived the human race through the beauty of the purple-clad prostitute.

“Indeed, while promising the inhabitants of blessed repose divine honors, he overthrew them, stripped them of the garment of immortality, and, casting them out from the delights of the most peaceful sweetness, brought them to the labors and miseries of a mutable existence. But the human race, while he persuaded it to pursue the prosperity of the present life and the glory of fragile power, he consigned to the prison of everlasting death.

“Nor, even now, has he forgotten his ancient fraud or ceased to weave the nets of deceitful capture, since he has taken up the sword of the judge’s tongue for battle on behalf of his own wickedness. In paradise he wielded the jaws of a brute animal as though they were a human tongue; here he has drawn the sword of a rational tongue, so that the clever enemy may stab those whom the wisdom of Christ has fortified beforehand with the blade of more subtle cunning.

“But he who was conquered by Christ’s power and pierced by the weapon of the cross seeks arms in vain against his soldiers. He prepares war to no purpose: he will receive not the palm of triumph but a fall in the outcome. The battle is now waged with Christ himself as its author, who proclaims to his soldiers: ‘Take courage; I have conquered the world’ (John 16:33).

“Therefore, standard-bearer of death, pay attention. In following Christ we have not abandoned the insignia of merit; we have seized it. We have not deserted the citadel of virtue; we have ascended it. We have not lost the joy of life; we have exchanged it.

“What rewards, then, do you exalt as arising from glorious deeds, when misfortune so often confounds them? What fame of mighty accomplishments do you proclaim, when a brief life swiftly consigns everything to oblivion? Or what joy of life do you boast of, when all the pleasures of the empty things you see slip away swiftly like a thin shadow?

“Did the splendid deeds of Pompey, commander of the whole world, help him when, worn out by the gravest fear of his proud conqueror, abandoned by his legions and stripped of his soldiers, he was beheaded as the prize of an enemy’s glory, and his nameless body earned only a makeshift burial in the sands? Or did fortune’s wheel sustain Caesar more favorably, who, after Gallic triumphs, after civil victories, and after the purple of imperial power, was pierced by many wounds and became a pleasing spectacle to his enemies in a cruel death?

“Where now, then, are the virtues of these men, which they produced throughout the Roman world with such great labor and utmost zeal? Where is the pomp of their riches, which they gathered from every region of the world after subduing peoples and nations? Where is the glory of their triumphs, by which they were lifted up and exalted? Since these things ended after so brief a course, they show how worthless they were—things that passed away with such speed.

“Therefore do not regard as great what is so small; do not believe to be stable what you see to be so empty; do not call joyful what you see to be so sad. For this reason we are warned not to love the world or the things that are in the world: they display appearance but conceal vanity; they pretend to power but hide weakness; they promise joy but produce sorrow.

“Therefore those who seem to possess these things are not happy, but miserable, because they embrace falsehoods in place of truths. For this reason we despise your gifts, reject your dignities, and regard your promises as nothing. For the servants of Christ, whatever the world considers exalted is contemptible; whatever it considers glorious is worthless; whatever it considers pleasing is accursed. They do not seek on earth the perishable riches for which incorruptible riches are prepared in heaven, since the world’s fleeting glory is not possession of the true good but material for vices.

“For whatever the world possesses as allurements is harmful to the flesh: the desire of the eyes and the pride of life. None of these things is from God the Father; they are from the devil (1 John 2). Therefore hold with complete certainty that no promise, no riches, no glory, no prosperity, and no adversity will be able to separate us from the love of Christ.”

At this the prefect grew angry and ordered them to be stretched upon the rack and beaten with leaden instruments. Amid whips and the most dreadful tortures, the holy martyrs rejoiced in hope of heavenly recompense, remembering that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in the saints” (Romans 8). They also remembered what the apostle James says to the faithful (James 1): “Consider it altogether joy, brothers, when you fall into various trials, knowing that tribulation produces patience, and patience produces a secure hope and faith, which the fruit of all good things will adorn.”

Drawing joy of mind from this, they gave thanks to the Lord and continually asked him to grant his servants strength and steadfastness to the end. When the tyrant saw that the saints persevered amid their torments and could not be overcome by scourging, he increased their punishments, multiplied their tortures, and did not cease to inflict whatever the malice of the devil could devise for their affliction.

When the structure of their limbs was broken apart by the excessive force of the punishments and a single wound covered the whole appearance of their bodies, their flesh fell away and their inward organs were exposed; nevertheless, strong in spirit, they remained steadfast in confessing Christ. It was utterly astonishing that limbs exhausted by hunger and thirst, weakened by fasts, and wearied by vigils could endure so many and such great tortures.

But in the very measure in which their bodily strength failed, they became stronger in the power of their minds; and in the measure in which the outward person was corrupted, the inward person received growth toward incorruptibility.

When he had seen that, after being tortured for a long time, they remained immovable in their confession of Christ, he ordered them shut up in prison again, until he might find tortures by which to compel them to perish. But the holy martyrs, placed in the darkness of the prison, lifted the vision of their minds toward the things above and gazed upon the unchanging and everlasting light that was denied them for a time.

Their bodies had indeed been torn by whips, seized by punishments, and wrenched apart by tortures; but their spirit, strong through faith, firm through hope, and fortified by love, meditated upon divine praises. Neither the horror of the prison nor the darkness of night could obscure the radiance of the heavenly light. Rather, the absence of bodily light and the dreadful ugliness of their dwelling passed into the majesty of their minds; and the darkness that had covered the sight of the body revealed the vision of the heart. For spiritual radiance is not kindled by the sun or blinded by night; rather, by the lamp of its own brightness it conquers the day and drives away the darkness of night, as the Prophet says of himself: “And night is illumination in my delights” (Psalm 138:11).

At last they relaxed their limbs in repose and, relieved by sleep, restored their weary bodies for the labor to come. Yet the mind was not overwhelmed by the heaviness of sleep; rather, kindled by divine fire, it was admitted into the mysteries of heavenly secrets. The bodily senses were closed to their physical functions, but opened to revelations from above.

Behold, as the light was already approaching, an angel of the Lord appeared, entering the prison’s enclosure. He filled the entire space of the cell with a great brilliance of light and said to them:

“Rufinus and Valerius, be steadfast, and with strong minds overcome all fear of punishment. It is near at hand that the Lord will receive you to himself with the palm of martyrdom and make you fellow heirs with the citizens of heaven, so that you may receive there the crowns already prepared for you by the Lord. I will now show them to you, that you may see them.”

After saying this, he placed upon their heads crowns that had descended from heaven. They shone with marvelous splendor, brighter than the radiance of the sun, and bloomed like emerald stones. In both qualities—their brilliance and their greenness—they signified the merit of those to whom they had been brought: they would remain green through the unfading perseverance of endurance and would shine through the purest beauty of virtues. Thus, endowed with divine gifts, they would be assured of the promises and, as in a mirror of life, behold in themselves both the palm of their victory and the insignia of their rewards.

When morning came, the prefect ordered them brought before him. After they had been led in, he saw that their faces were suffused with the beauty of a rosy flush and that the skin of their entire bodies shone with the whiteness of lilies. Nor was this surprising. The heavenly minister, commanded to adorn the martyrs’ heads with the insignia of ornament, had adorned the secrets of their minds and, as testimony to their future glory, illuminated even the outer limbs of their bodies.

A similar event is also reported of the protomartyr Stephen: standing in the council, full of the Holy Spirit, he shone with an angelic appearance. The radiance of divinity that had once filled Moses with such majesty that the people of Israel dared not look upon his face (Exodus 30) was illuminating the breasts of these men.

Earlier times were granted only one lawgiver shining with such grace; our age, however, has been granted many. For now we do not behold the forms of heavenly ministries through figures and shadows; with unveiled face we contemplate the glory of the Lord, transformed into the same image through the grace of the Holy Spirit. The weight of the greater glory therefore illumines not one person but many, so that it may be understood that what, because of the carnality of the old human being, was formerly received by only a small number has now been poured out for the communion of all through the renewal of the Spirit.

When the prefect saw the faces of the saints shining with marvelous majesty, he did not venerate the grace of divine power. Rather, filled with wickedness, he accused them of being magicians and sorcerers, claiming that they had thereby overcome the tortures inflicted upon them and refused to honor the gods.

O miserable blindness of the human mind, which is always darkened by the very light itself and turns the remedy of salvation into the destruction of a wound! Hence the Apostle’s saying: “For to some we are the odor of death unto death, but to others the odor of life unto life” (2 Corinthians 2:16). The same cause, according to the different qualities of those involved, brings salvation to one and destruction to another—not because the material of danger is different, but because those who receive it possess dissimilar dispositions. Thus a ray of the sun is judged suitable for healthy bodies but harmful to the sick.

This principle is illustrated in the present event: the tyrant is not instructed toward salvation by the heavenly miracle, but is driven toward an accumulation of greater evil. From the very source from which he ought to have received the light of faith, he heaps up the darkness of unbelief.

Thus enveloped in the shadow of impiety, he denounced the innocent and the pious as criminals and impious men. He declared that many would be punished with many great torments and put to a cruel death, lest through them the Christian religion grow stronger and the worship of the gods perish.

Then he ordered the officers to make them leave with their hands bound behind their backs, because he was hastening to a suitable place where they could be killed as a warning to others. They were led from that place for a distance of about seven thousand five hundred paces. When they arrived, they were beheaded beside the public road, on the bank of the River Vindol[a]. Thus drenched in the rosy crimson of their own blood, they returned their bodies to the earth and carried their blessed souls into heaven.

Not long afterward, when the persecution had ceased, they were taken up and transported with fitting honor, amid the singing of psalms and a great gathering of people, to their proper place. There they were committed to burial with pious veneration and fortified by a mound heaped over them—either so that they could not later be moved, or so that a notable memorial might be left for later generations. What an earlier age had provided for the most distinguished men by constructing tomb monuments, the devout people of the new age now provided for the holy martyrs.

Nor did that place receive the burial of the saints without divine providence: while alive, they had fed Christ’s flock there with the nourishment of the word and opened the door of life to many; there, therefore, they should also rest after death, so that those whom they had previously instructed by teaching and formed by their virtues might now be protected by their prayers and defended by their intercession.

They suffered on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July.

[Col. 1507C]

## Life of Saint Adalhard, Abbot of Corbie, by S. Paschasius Radbertus

(In Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum* of the Order of Saint Baud.

[Col. 1507]

### 1

It is the proper tribute of a work to imitate the most learned men, who, with devout affection of mind, mourned the deaths of their loved ones in Christ through acts of piety and, even in their mourning, followed them with wondrous [variant: many] praises. For, as blessed Ambrose said in his work concerning Valentinian:

> “Although writing about what you grieve is an increase of grief, nevertheless, in recalling the one whom we grieve to have lost, we often find consolation; and while, through writing, we direct and fix our mind upon him, he seems to us to come alive again in speech and to pour his whole substance into the marrow of our mind.”

It is, moreover, the task of posterity to commend their examples of virtue in writing, so that we may both discharge our debt of love toward those close to us and not deny their children the examples of the Fathers whom they ought to imitate.

We know, therefore, that they did not perish after death, but were more blessedly transformed, so that by dying they might reach the highest joys of everlasting happiness. For this reason they must not be wholly and completely erased from memory, especially such men, whose departure from this life did not bring an end to them through death, but changed them for the better.

Nor should we admit, in accordance with the madness of certain unbelievers, what Scripture says: “Our life is short and wearisome, and there is no relief at the end of a man, and no one has been known to return from the underworld” (Wisdom 2:1). Nor should we say that we were born from nothing and that after this we shall be as though we had never been.

Rather, it is true and must be professed without hesitation that Christ rose from the dead and conquered death by dying, so that likewise all who die in Christ may be found no longer dead, but alive and blessed in Christ. For God is the God of the living (Mark 12; Luke 20), not of the dead, since in him who lives all who are in him are found to be alive. Hence Scripture has become accustomed to call them “sleeping.”

### 2

For this reason, as I said, it is a most dutiful task to imitate holy men—namely, the aforementioned Ambrose, blessed Jerome, and the other sacred and exemplary men who composed eloquent epitaphs for their loved ones.

And even if I cannot attain to their standards of eloquence, know that I do not lack material for speaking. I desire to recall in writing the man whom nearly the whole world proclaims holy and admirable. Because we saw him and, although unworthy, enjoyed the love of his companionship, we cannot remain entirely silent, however unlearned we may be. Since we are denied the sight of him with our eyes, we may at least deserve to follow him through the service of the mind.

### 3

But when I begin to consider this, I am inwardly affected by two things that are sharply opposed: grief and joy. The Apostle forbids grieving over such a matter; yet the sudden desolation of all of us prevents not only my own rejoicing but that of us all. When the obligations of piety represented by both have been weighed, we ought rather to rejoice—and greatly to rejoice—in the hope of the eternal promise concerning so great a patron.

It is therefore beyond doubt that he has already passed through blessed struggles and now rests in Christ, destined to remain blessed without end. But because I am overcome by tears of love rather than by the cowardice of despair, I do not doubt that I may be excused—especially since the Apostle does not forbid weeping, except that we should not grieve concerning those who sleep as do the rest who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4).

It is one thing to grieve in despair; it is another to mourn and share in mourning because we have come here through the cause of sin, so that for a short time we scarcely seem to be anything at all. Therefore affection born of due piety ought undoubtedly to wash the burial of loved ones with tears—not the error of despair.

### 4

With such piety, although slow in the talents of my mind, I remember you, most beloved father Adalhard, glory of old age, embodiment of holiness, model of virtues. I remember you, I say, with such a bond of love that I can scarcely restrain myself amid the two conflicting obligations.

When I see that the Lord Jesus Christ wept over Lazarus, whom he loved, after he had died—and not only wept, but was troubled in spirit—I am compelled to weep greatly, deprived as I am of such a great heavenly oracle. Nature itself teaches that we ought not to forget those we love, but should commend them by whatever talents we possess, so that love may remain firm in the mind even after the sight of the flesh has been taken away, and so that the love once kindled in the mind may not die, but live more fully while the one we love lives better.

Therefore, dearest of my prayers, I scatter flowers over your tomb according to the custom of the people, wishing to adorn your funeral with the offices of letters, so that the fragrances of your virtues may not remain enclosed within the tomb but may waft far and wide as an example for generations to come.

I do not, as some do, think that boys should be stationed here and there around the tomb to sing your praises from memory and, like mournful songs, stir the hearts of their listeners to weeping and lamentation. Rather, I shall entrust the claims of truth to the faithfulness of writing, lest they be surrendered to the sluggish leisure of my mind. Thus refreshed by speaking with you, I shall remember you through the ages; nor will you be able to be torn from my mind unless I bring forth your name and praises.

My conscience assures me that whatever I say falls short of your praise. For this reason I am not at all ashamed to persuade myself to speak such things about you. Your present absence, therefore, while you remain with me, generates new emotions of tears; yet it also causes me to rejoice in your absence, because you have already happily reached the joys promised long ago.

### 5

Do not, I beg you, say to me as I weep: “You ought rather to rejoice over me than to mourn, most beloved son—especially since you know that I have escaped the world’s mockery and reached the fountain of eternal life. If you loved me, you would surely rejoice and share in my joy, because I now enjoy the robe of immortality and am satisfied by gazing upon the glory of majesty.”

I know, my Father, I know, I say, that, stripped of your fleshly garments, you now enjoy the heavenly vision. Yet I am overcome, suffused with devout love, and weep over your present absence, because everything I behold seems sad while I feel that you are absent and sigh for you.

And to use the words of Fortunatus:

> Just as a loving lamb, driven from its mother’s breast,  
> Wanders sadly and anxiously through the grassy fields:  
> Now it flees to the meadows, striking the air with its bleating;  
> Now it returns to the fold, for nothing pleases it without its mother.

Thus I represent myself in words concerning you, Father, in my absence from you. I wish, I say, that the day of your death had not dawned for me, [Col. 1510C] because no day could have been worse for my weakness, nor could any have risen more cruelly over all that belonged to you. As I consider what I should do and how I should act, bitter beneath my sorrow, I find no answer. As I said, the Apostle prevents me from grieving greatly; although I wish to weep much, I do not dare. Yet, though unwilling, I am persuaded to rejoice in the glory of your splendor.

For winter has already passed from you, my Father, and the rain has withdrawn. The wedding of the Lamb has therefore arrived; you enjoy the delights of paradise. Your voice has already sounded in my ears, and the voice of the turtledove has been heard, saying:

> “As we have heard, so have we seen, in the city of the Lord.”

We have indeed heard glorious things, but we see greater ones, in the city of the Lord of virtues—of virtues, therefore, and not of vices, because God founded it forever upon the foundation of perpetuity.

I clearly understand you singing such things, but I sigh in sorrow and groan anxiously, separated for so long from your companionship. And what is even more grievous, the world proclaims you a man of virtue, while we neither reach nor see you.

### 6

I know, therefore, that you do not wish to receive these praises, since you undoubtedly possess your praises already written in heaven. There you had entirely made your granary, and there your dwelling of mind always was.

Although what I offer you is small, I rejoice on your account, because you enjoy what you loved. I grieve for myself, because I lost you, torn from the breast, sooner than I wished. I rejoice because of you, but mourn for myself. Overcome, therefore, by your joys, I finally do not refuse to give thanks to God.

I give thanks because we had such a man as you. Yet I am overcome by affection because we lost you before you had taken us, your companions, into fellowship with the citizens of paradise. For this reason I beg you, my Father, look through the grates and, through the windows also, if the Lord grants it, behold your sons.

I know with what love you were endowed, with what faith you were firm, and with what hope you were long bound to the Lord as though by an anchor. I therefore hold most certainly that this threefold cord of yours is difficult—indeed, impossible—to undo.

You marvel not only at clouds and stars beneath your feet, but also at the high expanse of heaven, clothed in snowy whiteness. Therefore I ask you not to delay in showing mercy to the humble, whom you once urged toward such things on the field of combat.

Strong, my Father, was your love, like death. Therefore you were conquered by no enemy and overcome in no struggle. You courageously conquered the world’s pleasures; and therefore, we firmly believe, you are crowned with the glory of triumph.

Come, daughters of Jerusalem, and see the diadem with which our old man has been crowned in eternal solemnity! Consider the garments with which he has been gilded! See how, still young in strength, he conquered the wicked enemy; how, once a child, he trampled the world beneath his feet!

## Beginning of His Life

Adalhard is moved by the illicit marriage of his kinsman Charles.

### 7

Although he belonged to royal stock—[Note: namely, the son of Bernard, as Radbertus says below, no. 61. See the observations prefixed to the *Life*]—the grandson of the great King Pippin and cousin of the Emperor Charles, and although he had been educated in every worldly prudence during his training at the palace and appointed to study with the teachers alongside the ruler of the lands, he chose rather to be a friend of justice and truth than to consent to what was illicit, even when enticed by many flattering inducements.

It happened, therefore, that when the same Emperor Charles repudiated the daughter of Desiderius, king of the Italians, whom he had previously sought in marriage with the oaths even of certain Franks—[Note: The words of the monk of Saint Gall concerning this belong here, in Book II of *The Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 26. He says that after the death of his father Pippin, when the Lombards again harassed the Romans, Charles went to Italy, received their submission, and, to establish the peace, married the daughter of Desiderius, ruler of the Lombards, whom they call Ermengard. Not long afterward, because she was invalid and unable to bear children, he dismissed her on the judgment of the most holy priests.

“Nevertheless, while their father was still alive, Charles and Carloman had taken wives from the Frankish people, and they wished to repudiate them and take the daughters of Desiderius in their place, as is clear from a letter of Pope Stephen written to them, which is numbered 45 in the *Carolingian Codex*. Carloman died two years after his father, having already fathered children by Desiderius’ daughter. From this it becomes probable that both brothers, immediately after their father’s death, although already married, considered new marriages and, contrary to Stephen’s prohibition, obtained Desiderius’ daughters. Furthermore, after dismissing Desiderius’ daughter, Charles married Hildegard as a second wife, despite Adalhard’s opposition.”]

—it would have been easy to persuade the blessed old man, while he was still a palace trainee, to render some service of submission to the woman whom the king had taken while his former wife was alive. But he condemned such a marriage in every way and, a boy of blessed character, groaned that some of the Franks had become perjurers and that the king was using an illicit bed after rejecting his own wife without any fault on her part.

Inflamed by such great zeal, he chose, while still a boy, to leave the world rather than become involved in such affairs. Since he could not prevent his kinsman from acting contrary to what was right, he showed by his flight that he did not consent.

He is therefore believed to have been no less ready than John to die for justice: with equal determination he condemned the king’s illicit boldness and despised such a marriage. He did not consider the rights of kinship so as to give assent to the flesh, but placed first the laws of Christ, whose violation he could not endure.

Thus he preferred, with a free mind joined to Christ, to bear the disgrace of the cross, in order to confound every kind of strength, rather than, even if he were adopted into the kingdom, to become the king’s son.

## At Corbie, at the Age of Twenty, He Becomes a Monk
### 8. Despising the riches of Pharaoh’s kingdom, he finally came, as a monk, to enjoy God’s conversations, like Moses in the wilderness. For while he was still clothed in the garments of this world, he could not yet see the heavenly vision on the mountain; but, stripped of all these things and sanctified through God’s working grace, he became a disciple of the Savior. He had read: “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). [Col. 1512B] Nor was he unaware that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 19). Therefore he laid down the burdens of the little ass, so that he might more easily run along the narrow and constricted way of God’s commandments. Having laid these things aside, at Corbie—or rather, there, he sought Christ’s fountain—like that Davidic stag (Ps. 41). After he had remained there only a short while, he suddenly became, from a disciple of humility, a teacher of virtues; and he who the day before had seemed a servant was found to be the leader and guide of his fellow soldiers in Christ.

For you, good Jesus, had chosen for yourself a recruit and a boy. It was not he who chose you, but you who chose and preferred him, anticipated by your mercy. You chose him when he was nearly twenty years old, at the time when the unhappy age of humanity is especially fragile and very inclined to sin; at the time when, as you foretold, all your recruits who came out of the land of Egypt, from twenty years of age and upward, were enrolled by you in the book of life (Num. 1). Likewise, when Joshua again counted all those of this age and thereafter who were able to go forth to war (Josh. 8), they were reckoned into the heavenly company. These alone pitch their tents in the camp of the Lord; these alone go forth to battle.

Indeed, it is extraordinarily remarkable to conquer at the moment when one is being enticed by various allurements, and to triumph while being driven on by many inducements. Twenty is formed by five multiplied four times, or by four counted five times. When these numbers are thus combined, it is evident that those are readiest for battle who, in the age of the Old and New Testament, have grown old and have been educated by its wisdom. [Col. 1512D] Their strength, therefore, is especially well suited to warfare, and they must first be admonished to conquer themselves—especially since at that age the enemy, insofar as he operates through the flesh, employs greater arts of deception.

### He is appointed gardener.

[Col. 1513A]

### 9. Then, Christ, your boy in age but noble in mind, cast down the allurements of the world. Then he laid aside the weapons of King Saul, so that by you alone, the stone he carried in his heart, the great deceiver of souls might be struck down [or, according to another reading, he might strike him down]. Finally, he chose to carry you within his inmost heart: with you as his author, to fight against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. 6).

Why say more? Having entered the field of combat in this way, he reached the monastery [Note: [Col. 1513D] Adalhard is said in the fuller *Gallia Christiana* to have been admitted to the monastery of Corbie by Mordramnus. I would prefer to attribute this to Addo, his predecessor, who governed Corbie in the first year of Charlemagne’s reign, as is clear from a royal diploma granted to Addo. Addo was preceded by Leodgarius, also called Leudgarius or Leudharius, who is found signing the Synod of Attigny in the year 865 in Labbe’s edition of the Councils. He is the Leucharius who was abbot and ordered the writing of Saint Ambrose’s *Commentaries on Luke*.]: where, knocking according to his annual vow, he finally entered the gates of righteousness, through which only the righteous enter. Then he reached the gate fortified by virtue, which alone leads each of its followers to life.

For he entered the narrow and constricted way, which belongs to the few (Matt. 7), so that, with his mind enlarged, he might pursue the way of God’s commandments with the skill of the keenest art. And when he had long flourished wholly within monastic discipline, so that he seemed to belong more to heavenly than to earthly things, the fathers, moved by I know not what affection, appointed him gardener, apparently by royal command.

He rejoiced like a good athlete of Christ, and, as though amid the delights of paradise, he delighted inwardly in obedience. For he knew that the Lord had been buried in this very cave and had there appeared to Mary in the guise of a gardener (John 20). He knew that Christ had risen in that same place and that angelic visions had appeared there. Thus, digging up a treasure in the gardens of his soul, he anointed Jesus’ body with many kinds of perfume.

### He devotes himself to cultivating the soul.

[Col. 1513C] What do you suppose he said then, while performing such a service? If I am not mistaken, he said—if not with his voice, then at least in the affection of his mind; I mean, he said: “Let my beloved come into his garden, planted with virtue, and eat the fruits of his apples” (Song 5).

Thus there were various herbs of virtue in his soul; and for that reason he is undoubtedly said to have spoken the words, “Let him eat the fruits of his apples”—“his,” I say, because, if he bore anything good in his mind, he applauded not himself but the Lord’s grace. Others cultivate the outward labors of the fields rather than the virtues of the soul, being constrained to do so for obedience’s sake; but he, without neglecting such work, consecrated his soul, the garden of delights, to the Lord.

For he had done what he remembered being said to him: “Set me as a seal upon your heart” (Song 8:6). Fortified by this protection, he delighted more in inward conversation with the Lord than in the affairs of temporal things. Indeed, his beloved Christ had descended to visit the garden of his soul; he had descended to the bed of spices and fed there upon the delights of his virtues.

It is called a garden of delights, that is, paradise, because it signifies the human mind: for *Eden* is interpreted as “garden of delights.” Hence some have also called it flourishing. Christ therefore descended into it to gather the lilies of chastity [Col. 1514A] and to see whether the pomegranates had already blossomed.

### He shines through the sweetness of his speech.

### 10. As I have said, the soul of a good man is a garden full of delights and virtues, and thus ultimately another paradise. There myrrh—that is, the mortification of the members—is harvested [another reading: “is reaped”], together with the spices of the virtues. The rose, reddened with the blood of martyrdom, is gathered. The apples of the valleys shine, sprinkled with heavenly disciplines. Pomegranates sprout because of the fragrance of good works; besides this, there lies hidden within the blazing, holy ardor of the love of God.

Hence, brother, if you wish to consider the matter, our old man was wholly lovable and sweet; hence he was suited to every kind of pure speech. Did honey and milk not seem to flow from his tongue? He so poured himself forth in speech that he sometimes made certain people, as it were, drunk with holiness, while making all who were connected with him his friends through excessive sweetness. What else were his lips but a honeycomb dripping with honey? And, to speak more profoundly, what else but an organ of the Holy Spirit? Otherwise human wisdom could not have uttered what he spoke. His words, finally, flowed forth full of the gift of holiness and with a heavenly oracle.

### He avoids the company of his own people and withdraws to Cassino.

### 11. When he had thus long and extensively been moved by the Holy Spirit, he is said to have remembered the command given to Abraham, where Scripture says: “Go out from your land and from your kindred and from your father’s house, and come into the land that I shall show you” (Gen. 12:1).

When he had considered these words within himself, he began to meditate and say that he had not yet fulfilled this kind of command in deed. Although he had abandoned in mind the soil of his birth, he reckoned that he was still physically present in it. And although, in accordance with the Gospel command (Mark 10), he had already left father, mother, and kinsmen in order to be considered a disciple worthy of God, he was still greatly troubled because, although it was fitting to his rank, his relatives and acquaintances visited him more often than the quiet of his soul desired.

This resulted in his immediately slipping away in flight like another Elijah—not fleeing Jezebel, but fleeing the pleasure of the flesh. The stern soldier of Christ sought to escape so that, by fleeing himself, he might find himself more fully. Thus he who had recently been supported by many attentions of affection became a guest of pilgrimage, having, like Christ—which is an excellent kind of possession—not even a place where he could lay his head.

Therefore, fleeing himself in order to find himself, he reached Mount Cassino by the strength of the word, unwilling to know the cares of his homeland or to have praises about himself proclaimed by the wind of vainglory. He thought that he had acquired only this much: that, so long as he remained within the boundaries of his homeland, he was not yet separated from vices. And [Col. 1515A] so that he might not again be bound by the Devil’s new nets, he went beyond himself, proceeding to see whether he could somehow proclaim by a true account: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

### He is exposed by a hermit.

### 12. But when he came secretly to Cassino, which was thought to be the fountain and origin of all religious life, he was indeed received by the father [Note: [Col. 1515D] Presumably by Potho, if I am not mistaken, who governed Cassino for about six years from the year 771, having Theodemar as his successor. In the booklet *On the Translation of Saint Vitus*, another Adalhard is said to have withdrawn to Cassino with our Adalhard. I shall explain elsewhere why I regard this as suspect.] of the monastery; yet, by God’s arranging judgment, he was permitted to remain there only a short while.

For it is reported that immediately a certain hermit foretold to him, through the Spirit of God, who he was, where he came from, and for what reason he had arrived there. Then, shortly afterward, he foretold that messengers of the king would come, reclaim him, and restore him to his former position.

When he heard this, he was greatly disturbed that prosperity was not following his wishes. He immediately took the abbot of that place aside, told him everything about himself, and asked and implored him that, if there were any way he could escape, he would kindly agree, so that he might never again hear that man’s name, not even from afar.

### He is brought back to Gaul.

### 13. But God forestalled their plans. While they were delaying in devising a way out, he was suddenly forestalled by messengers who seized him and brought him back to his homeland.

What do you suppose? How bitter was his spirit, how mournful, because he was returning unwillingly to the borders of his homeland and the sweet fields of his native soil! Let our fellow monks hear this sort of man—those who rest sluggishly, smeared with the soot of shadows; let those hear who drag behind them herds of worldly people. Let them hear, I say, that it is not sufficiently safe to allow oneself to be softened by the affections of one’s own relatives.

Christ therefore does not know or acknowledge mother and brothers, in order to show us the true brotherhood of the mind: “Whoever,” he says, “does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. 12:50). Then he recalls the disciple from the duty of burial, so that he may not bury his father according to the due right of the flesh: “Let the dead bury their own dead, but you, follow me” (Matt. 8:22).

Our pious old man knew all this. Therefore he hastened to flee from the midst of his fellow citizens. For he remembered that Jesus performed no signs in his homeland and that a prophet is without honor except in his own country (Matt. 13). Stripped of the world’s honor, he therefore hastened to break out of the bonds of those he loved, so that he might truly claim for himself the honor of the mind and, to speak more profoundly, lead an angelic life on earth.

He seemed unable to become sufficiently poor in the midst of his relatives, who abounded in royal honor and shone with an abundance of riches. Therefore, breaking the bonds of a distinguished name, he wished to become poor without ambition, though formerly wealthy. But, an outstanding despiser of himself, he became more adorned through poverty, more renowned through flight, and more exalted through the lowliness of humility.

And, to use the words of blessed Jerome (Letter 2 to Nepotian), let some monks be richer than they were as laymen; let them possess under poor Christ the wealth they had not possessed under the rich and deceitful Devil, so that the Church may long for as rich those whom the world had previously held as beggars. Our Adalhard, however, trampling upon everything belonging to the world, conquered in appearance and crushed beneath his feet all that belongs to the world.

### He is chosen abbot. He shows himself an imitator of Augustine.

### 14. While he now sat quietly as a victor upon the lofty citadel of his mind, God’s providence appointed him once more to a new order of battle. Not long after his return, with the father of the monastery’s consent [Note: [Col. 1516D] This was Abbot Mordramnus, whose death is recorded on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July in the ancient list of the abbots of Corbie.], he was chosen—though not greatly unlike him—as another Augustine to succeed his predecessor while the latter was still alive, except that the former had been a bishop, whereas this man was appointed in the place of an abbot. Both, however, are found to have been perfect stewards of God.

He was a most distinguished imitator in his works, as though the attendant of the aforesaid father Augustine: very keen in intelligence, prompt in willingness, rich in eloquence, and sweet-flowing in speech. He affected his hearer with such benefit that you could scarcely believe his tongue to be anything other than the pen of the Holy Spirit. Tears commended his preaching, and groaning softened the hardness of the heart. A late rain of tears therefore flowed from him, so that minds might receive seed more abundantly for bearing fruit, and so that the heart of his hearers might be soothed by such a sense with the love of charity.

### Eulogy of Adalhard’s outstanding virtues.

[Col. 1516C]

### 15. His voice seemed full of the freshness of grace and stronger than every form of steadfastness. He himself, shining in bodily appearance, was believed to be full of the richness of the Holy Spirit. He was, in accordance with what Horace praises highly (*Satires* 2.7),

> Strong, and wholly smooth and rounded in himself.
