Strong, indeed, in faith, steadfastness, and virtue, so solid that he seemed to fear nothing and doubt nothing, even if the whole world, shattered by terror, were to collapse. Nevertheless, if he were ever driven by some storm of terror, sometimes he overcame it by hope, sometimes by reason; but worldly fear was never able to pierce him by raising itself against him.

He is said to have been smooth and rounded in himself—or rather, in God—because he was not only well fitted to himself in virtues and morals, but was also agreeable to everyone and most worthy of love, so that he was all things to all people and won almost everyone. He was noble in the flesh, but nobler in morals; full of God’s wisdom, but not idle in action; handsome in face, but more beautiful in faith and holiness; rich in ancestry, but richer in goodness, because he had been born as a shoot from the stock of heaven.

### His prudence and justice in the administration of Italy.

[Col. 1517A]

### 16. He was entirely clothed in the new man and, insofar as is permitted to mortals here below, renewed in the Lord within. His chariot was the four-horse team of the virtues; the wheels of that chariot were prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

He possessed such prudence that a fountain of counsel seemed to flow from his mind. He saw the past, present, and future together, so that he could foresee what ought to be done in each matter and what God’s counsel indicated should be pursued.

That he pursued justice is attested by France and by all the kingdoms of the earth, which were subject to his counsel; Italy above all, which had been committed to him so that he might instruct the kingdom and its young king Pippin [Note: [Col. 1517D] Pippin was baptized by Pope Hadrian and crowned king of the Lombards, or of Italy, in the year 781, according to Einhard. He died in the year 810 and was succeeded by his son Bernard, under whom Adalhard is also said to have administered Italy in the booklet *On the Translation of Saint Vitus*, below.] more honorably, usefully, justly, and prudently in the good order of the state and in the practice of religion.

There he earned such great praise that, as some are said to have declared, he was not a man but an angel, because of their love for his virtue. They acknowledge that he never considered anyone’s person in judgment, nor, according to the common proverb, was the wall of his mind broken by a golden fist. He alone, as they say, was able to cross unharmed the river of greedy Acheron and return from the Alps through the years without the danger of blindness.

Before him, the height of the proud trembled openly, while the humility of the gentle rejoiced. At his entrance he immediately removed all the tyrannical power that they had exercised over the people like unjust robbers, and they acted with as much boldness as their lord’s right permitted. Thus they had been devastating the whole land through an abominable power.

First, therefore, he restored peace to these people; then, as a pious judge, he restored to each person his rights. He possessed such great strength of wisdom that he used the word as the rod of a censor and judge, without delaying to assign to each person what was justly his. Thus he caused each person to fulfill his own duty and no one to usurp another’s right.

He was the treasurer of the poor, the patrimony of widows, the father of orphans, the consoler of the grieving, the arm of the weak, and indeed the scourge of the proud. Nevertheless, by a skillful disposition he removed everyone from the arrogance of mind, and he broke no one completely except one whom he saw to be beyond repentance.

### He is praised by Pope Leo III.

[Col. 1517D]

### 17. Thus, strong in virtue, gentle and meek, he reached the borders of the Romans, where Lord Leo, the apostolic bishop at that time, received him with such an intimate welcome that no Frank is known to have been received by him previously.

For this reason, one of our people reports that he said to him jokingly: “Frank, know this well: if I find you different from what I believe you to be, there will no longer be any need for another Frank to come here whom I ought to trust.”

This plainly shows how much weight that man possessed, since the loss of confidence in him would have proved the whole Frankish people unworthy of trust, and how great his steadfastness must have been.

### He writes to the Emperor Lothar.

[Col. 1518A]

### 18. His works, fulfilling his promises, reveal most fully how great he was; so do the letters that he recently sent to the emperor Lothar concerning the boundaries of good faith that must be maintained among human beings. Among other things, he writes as follows:

“What do you think, prince, if faith often possessed such force among bloodshed and the weapons of raging men, even among pagans, that each person entrusted himself to another’s sworn faith—how much force ought a pact promised in truth by a Christian to possess? I beg you, emperor, do not let anyone deceive you, because when faith is violated against anyone, it is not a human being, but God—my witness and truth—who is despised.”

From these words it is undoubtedly clear that it would have been easier for iron bonds to be broken than for the promises of this man’s faith to be contaminated—especially since nothing but a fountain of truth and remarkable simplicity shone throughout his heart. If you looked closely at him, you would find that his mind had been impressed with Christ’s seal; for that reason it could not be corrupted in any way.

### Adalhard emulates the virtues of others.

### 19. His mind was like a garden of paradise, enclosed by the wall of faith and planted with every kind of virtue. He imitated the humility of one man and the gentleness of another; he followed the frugal diet of a third and the moderate style of dress of another. He also possessed the patience of one and the meekness of another.

With frequent sighing he would say such a word of piety to me: “Upon whom shall I rest, unless upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

You know, good Jesus, why he repeated such words so diligently in the affection of his mind. He had all your commandments committed to his mind, distinctly and appropriately, to persuade himself toward holiness; and he discussed them with himself, keeping the sayings of your commandments before his eyes. In this way he considered the lives of all the saints in a single act of mental vision, continually turning over the examples of their virtues, so that from all of them he might gather one perfect man, filled with God and adorned by the service of religion.

### A comparison from Cicero.

### 20. Cicero, the king of Latin eloquence, writes in the second book of *On Rhetorical Invention* that, when the people of Croton were flourishing in wealth and were therefore counted among the blessed, they wished to enrich the temple of their religion with exceptional paintings. They summoned a certain Zeuxis, who seemed to surpass all other painters in talent, and hired him at a great price to paint for them an image of Helen, a marvelous work destined to endure through the ages.

He immediately asked them what beautiful maidens they had. They at once led the man to the gymnasium and showed him many boys endowed with great dignity. These boys had also brought home, with the highest praise, the most honorable victories from athletic contests.

As he greatly admired the forms and bodies of the boys and labored intensely over them, they said: “Their sisters are maidens among us. From these boys you may infer how great their dignity is.”

And he said: “Please bring them to me, so that, while I paint, I may transfer each of the most beautiful features from them onto the single image of the subject you have decided to request.”

They complied, and the painter selected five, whose appearance he judged to possess the form of beauty. For he did not think that everything he sought for loveliness could be found in a single body, because nature has polished nothing perfect in every respect within a single type—as though it would have nothing left to bestow on the others if it granted everything to one.

### Because of his great emulation of virtue, Adalhard rejoices in the names of Antony and Augustine.

[Col. 1519B]

### 21. So, too, did our old man enter the gymnasium of this life after he had been washed in the font of baptism and after his renunciation of the world. With what pure vision of mind did he see different people striving toward different ends? Some he saw sweating for worldly honors and the pleasures of the present life; others for luxury and the lust of the flesh; some pursuing justice; and others looking toward the life to come.

From among all those whom he could understand, however, he chose five maidens who continually adorn their lamps with the pious oil of charity and prepare to go out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. He imitated these with watchful mind, lest a thief should come by night and carry off someone sleeping.

He also heard from the athletic song of the saints how worthy of honor were their victories, and from all these he reformed in himself a single image of Christ. There, in the one God and man, Christ Jesus, he found everything beautiful and splendid belonging to eternal life, beyond what can be understood.

What nature forbade to be perfect in all the parts of the Church, grace granted, so that God might be all in all. Therefore he strove in every way and through everything, so that he might find Christ already in everything.

For this reason, according to what some report—such as the letters of Master Albinus [Note: [Col. 1519D] There exists Alcuin’s Letter 107, written to Antony, which Paschasius undoubtedly has in mind here. In it he urges Adalhard to secure the safety of Homer, or Angilbert, saying: “I wish through you to accomplish what I have recognized that I cannot accomplish through myself.” In this letter Alcuin mentions another letter written by him to Antony, which is not extant. Some think that Paschasius designates Adalhard by the names Arsenius and Jeremiah at the beginning of the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. But I shall demonstrate that Wala is meant, in the year 825, to which Wala’s Life must be referred.]—he was called Antony by some; by others, as stated above, Aurelius Augustine. He practiced one thing after the manner of Gregory and another after that of blessed Sylvester.

### His generosity toward the needy.

[Col. 1519D]

### 22. My conscience bears witness that I often wondered why he wished to borrow so much, in order to distribute it to the needy or spend it for the uses of his own people, until I examined the life of blessed Sylvester. In this he imitated Sylvester’s example, so that by continually borrowing he was always found poorer rather than richer.

He would often say to those associated with him: “Do you wish to know, I say, whether you seem stingy or generous? Know for certain that if you fear having given more than you ought, you are convicted of being stingy; but if you have given less than you should, that is certainly a sign of generosity. Therefore, my son, I warn you that, if you are negligent in this matter, you should rather appear guilty of giving more from our resources than of distributing too little.”

### By distributing his possessions generously, he often becomes needy.

### 23. The highest virtue knows that he so frequently gave with generosity that he himself and his people appeared to be in need. But then he was joyful, then he rejoiced and exulted in the Lord.

He would say: “Would that we might share, even in a small way, in the poverty of Christ!” Yet he never thought that he had been able to reach this condition, because Christ continually encouraged the fainthearted in him to learn to distribute their possessions generously and to trust in God’s generosity. Divine mercy anticipated him by supplying his needs.

Thus, when one day he had completely spent all the monastery’s supply of cheese porridge on guests, leaving nothing at all for the brothers, it happened that the cellarer, as though with a threatening voice and in a certain emotional state, said: “Father, I am amazed at what your expenditure of such a great quantity means. Look: you allow nothing to remain for the brothers to eat.”

Then he, being sweet in speech, smiled and said: “The Lord will provide.”

The other replied: “You always make such promises, but what you pour out so freely will not immediately be provided in this way.”

While these things were taking place, behold, two wagons arrived at the doors: one carrying some kind of fish, and the other full of cheeses. When the blessed Father heard this, he rejoiced for the brother and ordered him to appear at once.

“Look, brother,” he said, “you are proved wrong in what you feared; look, your foolish negligence is exposed.”

Then the other, simple in mind, seeing that he was being reproved by benefits, said: “Give, my Father, from now on; give as much as you wish. For I shall no longer say, ‘The Lord will not provide’; rather, I shall say plainly, ‘As much as you wish will be provided.’”

### By his example Adalhard rebukes the hard-hearted.

### 24. Such a great man could not, therefore, in prudent affection, have been unaware of what he was giving, to whom, and how much. Let this one fault, if you wish, be attributed to him: he used to say as follows:

“If I have so little available for giving that I do not possess enough to distribute to two needy people, so that only one of them may receive some assistance, it seems good to me to give the whole amount to the one to whom it more properly belongs, rather than give almost nothing to both or leave both entirely empty-handed.”

Thus he bestowed on one the double gift of benevolence and gave the other an expression of compassionate affection. See, hard-hearted people; see the bowels of compassion. Behold: although he could not give to everyone, he was nevertheless affected by the sorrows, poverty, and various misfortunes of all with a compassionate affection, as though they were his own.

### Adalhard was devoted to tears.

### 25. He was truly so great and so worthy that he could have asserted of himself, in a true account: “I am wounded by charity.” Unless he had been wounded by charity, he would not have mourned everyone’s misfortunes with continual lamentation as though they were his own.

Every day he wept—if not more often, then once or twice a day, namely morning and evening. This fire therefore burned perpetually within him, never failing on the altar of his soul; he was continually aflame with such a desire. There a sweet holocaust was made to the Lord; there victims were slaughtered, especially in the middle of the night, for he was constantly wakeful in prayer.

Then he burned away all the fat of the flesh and the allurements of desire in the fire of the flames. He offered to the Lord in sacrifice all his inward vital organs and his head together with his feet—that is, the beginning of life and the Lord’s end. For he first washed everything with tears, so that afterward all things might be burned more cleanly for the Lord.

I openly confess that I have never found a man in whom there was such a great fountain of tears and such great groaning. You would have thought that everything within him had dissolved into weeping and that his breast was being torn apart by deep sighs. It seemed as though thunder resounded within him while he struck himself with repeated blows, so that he might draw out more abundant showers of tears.

There is no doubt that we may rightly call them thunder, because you, good Jesus, were within him, watering the seeds of virtues with tears and washing the fruit of the full field you had blessed with a fountain of sprinkling.

### For what reason?

[Col. 1521C]

### 26. When I, insignificant as I am, once asked him about the nature of this lamentation and the grace of such abundant weeping, he replied:

“I weep, my son; I weep—not as though I ought to weep in order to humble myself, or so that I may behold the higher mysteries of heaven; but, I say, considering what I am, I mourn by weeping. I weep, not because I wished to weep in this way, but because I know that I ought to weep in this way; without doubt, I weep.”

O profound humility and lofty understanding of the man! You did not say these things because you knew yourself to be such, but so that you might invite me—whom perhaps you knew to be such—to weep at least later, and soften my stony breast by your tears. Otherwise, you wept because, having entered, as it were, within the Holy of Holies, you could not yet continually retain what you saw. For hope deferred afflicts the soul.

Thus, with the eye of your mind, you saw that heavenly homeland where choirs of hymn-singers celebrate God’s praises together. You enjoyed that blessed and happy harmony of heaven, where organs resound with an unfailing voice in the joy of jubilation; and, what is greater, you had already made your own soul a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit.

But when that same Spirit had flown somewhat higher, so that you sought him, you wept from excessive love, and you wept greatly, saying: “My soul melted when he spoke to me, for he spoke and departed; he departed so that the mind, eager to enjoy him, might burn more happily and, having found the flame, hold fast to the fire of charity more firmly.” [Col. 1522A]

That was why, my Father, in the hour of death the pious affection did not depart from your mouth, and you said: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:3).

For you already desired to enter the place of the wondrous tabernacle. The voice of exultation was already in your ears and confession in your mouth; the sound of one feasting was already being heard. In a certain way you were already among those whose dwelling is like that of all who rejoice.

As you wept over such things, they stood before your eyes; therefore you had wholly languished from love and said: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I am sick with love” (Song 5:8).

Let the devout reader know that, if he had separated himself for a little while from such things on account of some business, he hurried back at once as though he were returning from leaving holy places. Then, finding his whole self again, he was entirely present, as though on that day he had nothing else in his hands.

For immediately tears were present, immediately groaning, and every form of devotion. His soul instantly grew fresh again, while every bodily sense continually died to the world.

### How devout he was in the divine office.

### 27. If he entered the service of God—as he himself was accustomed to say with a joyful spirit—he immediately left all thoughts and concerns of temporal affairs outside the door, and entered wholly with himself, so that he might be wholly present to God and to himself.

If you had seen him, you would suddenly have observed him entering the more secret places of his mind and looking upon something with a reverent expression. He dipped the pen of his tongue into the fountain of the Holy Spirit, so that, purified, it might speak praises to God. During the praises themselves, perceiving I know not what musical sound, he sometimes wept most abundantly.

And why is this surprising? I heard it from a bishop who reported that, amid the crowds of the palace, while the king and his counselors were occupied with something else and the throng was making its customary uproar on every side, he often wept while sitting among them, as though he had come there to compete in weeping. Thus, while sitting there, he was secretly attending elsewhere upon the King of heaven.

### How he conducted himself outside the monastery.

### 28. If he was occupied here and there amid the dangers of the world on the Church’s business, he nevertheless did not abandon the practices of the rule. Instead of reading, he gave himself to tears, and in place of his other duties he served the Lord with the joy of his mind.

All his companions and traveling companions therefore knew that he did not wish to be approached continually. For this reason they walked at a distance from him, so that he might devote himself to God alone.

For the time had already come for him to worship the Father neither on the mountain nor in Jerusalem nor, so to speak, in any particular place, but in spirit and in truth. He had made his soul the temple of that same Spirit and the dwelling place of truth. Therefore, as it seemed to me, he was everywhere wholly with himself and wholly with God, and walked attentively with him.

### He recalls dissenters to peace.

### 29. For this reason he was always found cheerful, always gentle and joyful; for this reason he was regarded as so patient, so long-suffering, and so kind toward everyone. He was a son of peace and a chain of charity, so that brotherly hearts might cling to one another.

Spoletum and Beneventum know this. When they were continually striking one another with hostile swords, it happened that the blessed man traveled all the way there for this very purpose and entered Beneventum. While he was there, he restored such peace between them that, joined and allied with one another in peace, they remain united to this day through Christ.

Hence, not only among them but also among the Greeks and all the islands of the sea, he earned an extraordinary grace of love and a reputation for virtue. In this conflict he understood that both sides were Christians and brothers. He did not think that they could please God while being stained by such great slaughter and making booty of their own possessions, because, as the Apostle says: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and we know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” (1 John 3:15).

Therefore the pious Father placed himself between them and fully restored the peace of Christ that the Devil had violated. In such a task he appeared tireless and an outstanding champion of justice.

### Adalhard is exiled for the sake of truth and justice.

### 30. Adalhard is exiled for the sake of truth and justice

And so it happened that, when Emperor Charles [Note: Concerning a certain reliquary which Charles granted to Adalhard before his death, something must be said in the appendix to this Life.] had reached the end of his life and his son Louis Augustus had succeeded him in the kingdom, truth was once again, through the envy stirred up by the devil, harassed in him by its customary snares. This was nothing new, since truth is always found to have been an enemy among the wicked, and justice is torn apart by the accusations of fools.

For already the long-standing wickedness of perverse men, in accordance with Plato’s saying, was lamenting that states would be blessed and happy if lovers of wisdom governed them, or if their rulers happened to devote themselves to wisdom. Therefore, inflamed by deceit and envy, they devised how they might, as it were, remove Daniel from the king’s side [Mss., “make him”], so that, once justice no longer had a defender, the established order might be overthrown and iniquity, having destroyed its opponents by its own frauds, might recover a place from which to rule.

For you, God who see all souls, knew that you had implanted this plan in his heart: that he should yield to the commands of the king and the Church, which he had done only out of concern for the common good of all—namely, so that the liberty of the powerful, relieved from tyranny, might serve the Lord more earnestly, and so that praises might be rendered more devoutly to the Lord by right throughout all the churches.

But God, who always summons his own to higher things, wished to demonstrate more clearly what sort of man this one was and to show how great he was in adversity: so that he who had triumphed as so great a victor for God in prosperity might also triumph in adversity; and so that, since by the grace of God he had already acquired the seven Gospel beatitudes in life and conduct, he might fulfill by his deeds the eighth that remained. “Blessed,” says the Gospel, “are those who suffer persecution for justice, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10).

Thus the same man suffered from the haughtiness of the wicked and was falsely accused under the guise of humanity; yet, because of his love for justice and truth, he had kept nothing safe for himself except by surrendering himself to it in every way, even unto death. He had never concealed the truth through fear, nor had he ever allowed a place for falsehood. Rather, by the clemency of truth’s purity, he shielded the wretched who were especially harassed by the avarice and cruel incompetence of ignorant men.

Therefore, when the blindness of the wicked had woven the webs of spiders more craftily than carefully it had woven hunting nets, it refused to appear openly, lest perhaps the shamefulness of its depravity, when justice brought it back into view, should be displayed more hideously. Thus it came about that justice was punished in him without an accuser, without a confrontation, indeed without a hearing and without a judgment.

Driven from his present goods, stripped of his dignity, and disgraced in the opinion of the common people, he endured exile for the benefit of the commonwealth [Note: The reason for Adalhard’s exile is not clear. Certainly it was not the faction of Bernard, king of Italy, since that faction began in the third year of Adalhard’s exile; consequently he was not banished because he had been involved in it. Nor is he anywhere named among the accused in that conspiracy, although its principal authors are mentioned by Einhard, the author of the Life of Louis the Pious, and others. It seems certain that this exile was inflicted on Adalhard and his relatives for no other reason than that men endowed with power and intelligence were suspect to Louis—indeed a pious Augustus, but suspicious and fearful. This may be gathered from the Life of Louis himself, where the following is said of Wala in the first year of Louis’s reign: “Wala, who had held the highest position with Emperor Charles, was greatly feared, lest perhaps he might plot something sinister against the emperor.”]

But how blind and foolish was the cunning of the perverse! They were thinking of staining and sullying the reputation of the good and of virtue itself out of ambition for office—especially since the more unwilling they are to attain the glory by which they might be considered worthy of honor and a famous name, the more they are tormented by another’s glory.

But if God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom. 8:31.) Therefore they lied when they thought they could defile their honor and happiness, since they had carried the resources of their protection up to heaven. There, “neither thieves break through and steal” (Matt. 6:20). For no one possesses anything more precious than himself after God. Therefore, whoever guards himself by doing good must necessarily possess both himself and God entirely. No one can ever be deprived of the honor that belongs to him or of the value of his resources—than which nothing is richer—if he does not cast himself outside himself.

### Virtue is the most precious possession

31. The most precious kind of possession, therefore, is the glory of the virtues. Nothing is acquired with greater difficulty, nothing is received with greater sweetness in loving, and nothing is possessed with greater happiness.

Our old man had sought this treasure through labor; by seeking, he had found it more happily; and, once found, he carried it with him wherever he went and possessed it. Thus, the more he had been freed from worldly affairs, the more earnestly he devoted himself to his own possession; in this way he became richer everywhere and restored himself to heaven.

You already knew, shameless gain of greed, that the soldier of Christ was not held by your chains, nor was he obscured by your darkness. Rather, seated upon the lofty citadel of charity, he had subjected the world beneath his feet to the dominion of his generosity.

Therefore he went forth quite willingly—not wherever the zeal of the envious directed him, but wherever the Spirit of God led him—as though invited to a feast. Tell me, I ask you, wretched desire for the world: why are you swept away by empty joys? Why do you embrace external goods and momentary luxury instead of the delights of eternal life? Know that you can never make your own what the nature of things has made alien to you.

And if you seek to satisfy nature, know that what it requires is little. But if nothing can ever be enough for the luxury of desire, O wretched presumption of mortals and reckless desire, imitator of the virtues, why do you plunge yourself into such waves? Why do you anticipate the disasters of eternal death? Why do you rashly go beyond yourself, when, if you could be anything there, you would lose everything?

Behold, we know that you have always waged war against justice and truth. That is why you are still tormented by envy. First you stained the world with the murder of Abel by his brother; then, throughout all time, you slaughtered thousands of saints with the sword of iniquity; and, what is more criminal, you sold the Lord for the price of desire. Yet even now, while conquering, you are conquered, for you are already trampled beneath the feet of the saints.

Why do you not hear, unhappy one, the complaints of the saints crying beneath God’s altar against you: “Avenge, Lord, our blood!” (Rev. 6:10.) Perhaps you think that because you have not shed blood in this matter you will therefore be excused? I plainly confess that iniquity has deceived itself.

Do you hear the Lord saying: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Rom. 12:19)? But what you had devised unexpectedly—to exile our old man from the dwelling places of the earth—the Lord used for his crown. Thus, as is his custom, he turned your evil blindness into another’s good.

Behold, gold is again placed in the furnace; behold, it is tested by the fire of temptation; it is beaten and filed, so that at last it may shine more brightly as a beautiful vessel formed for honor.

Yet when someone observes the outcome of such events in the present, he may perhaps judge, in accordance with Virgil’s saying:

> “That no god cares for mortal affairs.”

For sometimes the just man perishes in his own justice: he is destroyed by the deceit of his accusers, while every wicked man claims for himself the praise of wisdom. Nevertheless, the outcome itself proved the end of both matters.

### Adalhard is banished to the island of Heri. On his other brothers and sisters

32. Meanwhile our old man, proven wise, was sent like one of the ignoble to the island of Heri. Sent there, he was deprived of every human honor [Note: Adalhard the younger, his foster-son and disciple, acted in the place of his excellent parent throughout the seven years during which Adalhard the elder was in exile; see below, no. 66], but in the meantime he was supported on every side by a heavenly rampart.

For a time that blessed chariot of kinship, joined together like that of Ezekiel, was broken apart, above whom Jesus, girt most fittingly with the breastplate of virtues, presided. There were five, therefore, born from the seed of one man. Of these, the Emperor Augustus, using three as trusted counselors, governed the Frankish empire with them, as though with a firmly established square, and administered the commonwealth, which they had greatly enlarged.

For concerning these horses Habakkuk had not inappropriately sung to the Lord, saying: “You mount upon your horses, and your riding is salvation” (Hab. 3:8). Their courses were unequal, but from the beginning their spirit was equal and carried them toward the palm of victory.

Afterward, with the Holy Spirit presiding over them, one purpose was brought to completion in them by unanimous consent. At first the horses seemed to run with different colors, united only in will; but finally, as blessed Jerome says, in this work they drew one yoke for the charioteer with equal necks and equal purpose, not waiting for the blows of the whip, but burning so ardently at the encouragements of Christ’s voice that they became teachers and leaders of the army of holiness.

Our old man was the eldest, most holy, already consecrated to the Lord in age and grace; more mature in counsel and superior to all in holiness. Next came Wala, the most illustrious of men, who later succeeded him as the outstanding Father of the monks; he clung closely to the king [al., “was closely attached”] and was raised to the highest dignity of prefecture [Note: Wala’s Life, written in two books, is found under the year 835]. In the senate he was more distinguished than all; in military affairs, stronger than all through his prudent spirit.

Such praise followed him in every matter of life that he was considered to possess far more power through love than all the pride and even tyranny of the others. For he was the guardian of justice and the ornament of honesty, and also the just oppressor of the oppressed.

### On his sisters Gundrada and Theodrada and his brother Bernarius

33. At his side stood their sister Gundrada, different in name but unquestionably equal in virtues, ever present to her brothers. She was indeed a maiden especially close to the king, the noblest of the noble. Amid the erotic passions of the palace and the beauty of young men, amid alluring pleasures and every enticement of lust, she alone, as we believe, deserved to carry away the palm of chastity and, as the saying goes, was able to pass unharmed through the impurities of the flesh.

She kept the scepter of chastity with her, since she believed that it would be far richer for her to preserve the integrity of her flesh than to violate the rosy flowers of chastity. Chastity is a virtue by which, as is proved, she deserved to be crowned happily, just as the most eloquent Tertullian says (On Chastity, ch. 1):

> “The flower of morals, the honor of the body, the beauty of the sex, the integrity of the blood, the fidelity of one’s lineage, the foundation of health, the pledge of every good disposition.”

And afterward:

> “Although rare,” he says, “and not easily perfected, and scarcely perpetual.”

This handmaid of Christ, therefore, amid every danger to chastity, chose to seek the field of battle and deserved to obtain the triumph of modesty.

The remaining two—namely our Bernarius and his sister Theodrada, devoted to God, who, having already yielded the fruit of marriage, had undertaken the second degree of chastity—sat at Jesus’ feet with Mary in the house. She governed the life of the consecrated women at Soissons; he adopted among us the form of Christ’s discipleship. Yet both hastened to run toward the one prize of the heavenly calling.

### On their unanimity and fraternal harmony

34. In this number of five I perceive a sweet musical sound, repeated and resounding in both parts, and I see their proportions singing together in a certain harmony.

If you first consider the men and then the two sisters, there will be a Greek diapente (the fifth) and a sesquialter proportion: for three exceed two by half of themselves. One, namely our blessed old man, sings among two and two; thus they produce the honey-sweet symphony of music and the form of the pyramid according to geometric discipline.

But what one does—that is, the old Adalhard—among the four, so that they may harmonize well, this same man, surpassing them, invites them to burn with love of the heavenly homeland like a square fire.

Otherwise, if you consider them as leaders in the affairs of the commonwealth, there will again be three devoted to public duties, like Martha, and two intent at Jesus’ feet solely on hearing the word. Thus our old father stands in the middle, walking as an intermediary between both ways of life, the active and the contemplative.

Finally, if you observe them carefully once more, three of them are those who win the triumph of continence, while two aim at a first chaste marriage. At last, however, both pairs draw the equal yoke of monastic discipline.

Thus they are proclaimed clothed in doubled garments in every respect, harmonious and concordant and swift [Bollandists, “of the same color”] in all things. I behold them, with Benjamin, each clothed among the five patriarchs in robes; but afterward I see them more gloriously adorned by our Jesus with a simple wedding garment. I also contemplate the talents entrusted to them, but I read that one reward has been set above them all.

### They are banished elsewhere

35. While they were thus eagerly contending for one another and on behalf of one another in all things, the wind of envy came and scattered them far from one another—especially those in whom the glory of the entire kingdom flourished—so that they might themselves be shown to be proven and might be strengthened by the virtues of those to whom they went.

At that time Corbie, long praised by the mouths of many, was mourning and weeping as it grieved to be deprived of so great a patron. For its consolation, by the Lord’s dispensation, it deserved to receive Wala, a most illustrious man among the other nobles it possessed, like a recruit of Christ. Later, after his brother’s death, it rejoiced to have him as its father in Christ’s place.

O providence of God, and prepared eyes extending throughout the whole earth, reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly! How incomprehensible are all your works and judgments, you who use human blindness according to an immeasurable plan of light! For a time you scourge the sons whom you intend to crown.

Therefore, almighty Father, this is why our Bernarius is sent back to Lérins [Note: Nevertheless, from the Life of Louis the Pious it may be gathered that Bernarius was exiled not to Lérins but to Fleury, or at least was taken from Lérins to the monastery at Fleury. The author says that Bernarius was summoned from the monastery of Saint Benedict and reconciled, and that he was restored with his brother Adalhard to the same place—namely, the monastery of Corbie.]; while your Wala, as I have said, is received at Corbie as a recruit.

Laying aside the military belt, so that he might wholly clothe himself in the desire for holiness, he undertook the first exercises of paradise, in order to complete in himself the measure of Christ.

Theodrada, like an innocent woman, is left at Soissons under her holy profession. The aforementioned Gundrada is sent to Saint Radegund, formerly queen [Col. 1528B], so that she might imitate the marks of her virtues, since she had shared with her, to some degree, a flourishing life amid the dangers of the palace. With her she prayed to God day and night and sometimes received consolation by entreating him for herself and her own.

### The holy man undertakes exile with a joyful spirit

36. When they withdrew from the palace as though dishonored, our old man went forth among them as though invited to a feast—strong in faith, cheerful in mind, and conscious of his purity. He gave thanks that he had been found worthy to suffer insult for the sake of truth (Acts 5).

Then, at one moment soothing his weeping brother with a kiss, at another comforting his sister with kind words and the encouragements of the saints, persuading his friends to show strength of mind, and displaying examples of virtue to the nobles of the palace, he demonstrated everywhere the remarkable steadfastness of his mind.

Thus, as is reported, two archbishops returned from him weeping. When the emperor Augustus asked them about him, they said:

“What do you think, O emperor? Do you wish to avenge yourself on this man by dishonoring him and exiling him to some part of the earth? We plainly confess that you could never have given him joy like this, by which his proven patience is now granted to him from heaven—especially since today he rejoices exceedingly that he is receiving back his former liberty in Christ.

“Know, therefore, that we have never seen him at any time more joyful or more cheerful. Supported by holy hope, he fears no encounter, however hostile, and no grief penetrates him here.”

When the emperor heard this, he was suffused with shame and regretted having done what he was now ashamed to prevent.

### He does not resent the emperor

37. But the pious servant of Christ said to those who were imputing this to Caesar as a crime:

“Do not, I ask you, my brothers, do not consider it as though what is happening to us lay within human power. For I confess that even if he chose something other than what has once been uttered by God, it could not be completely withdrawn unless it were first brought to completion by this deed. Nor can what has been ordained be fulfilled unless he himself consents.

“Therefore I warn you, dearest ones: recognize God in us, although he has chosen to fulfill his will through the hands of one whose agency I would not have desired. For, according to Job, when he has completed these things, many such things—and many more—stand ready for him (Job 23).

“Otherwise, when what has been determined has been fulfilled, we shall one day be recalled—not according to what lies in this man’s will, but according as he mercifully consents by his own nod.

“In the meantime, I ask you, spare the prince given to us by God. He is using not, in a certain sense, his own will, but that of our Lord, against whom we have sinned.

“Moreover, according to the word of blessed David, if the Lord is stirring him up against us, I beg you to pray earnestly that he may smell the sacrifice of our humility (1 Sam. 26) and receive his penitents in all things—yet in such a way that his will may be done.”

Behold how great and immovable was the patience that clung to him! What instruction, and what depth of compassion! Amid all these things, amid the voices of all who groaned and the words of their tears, he was himself their consoling mediator and persuader of virtue.

### Everyone laments as the holy man departs

38. For he was like a mirror of holiness and, amid all the claims of lamentation, an advocate for those who were bringing accusations. Tell me, I ask: who then, even with a heart of stone, would not weep? Who, even cut from flint, would not grieve? Or who, even with eyes of iron, could restrain himself from mourning?

Especially at that hour, when everyone cried out with one voice amid their weeping:

“Most evil blindness and wicked counsel, that the source of counsel should be carried away into exile! This will not be recovered, nor will any Frank be found who is so great and like him, a defender of charity and truth.

“We plainly confess: what a wicked fraud and cunning deception of poison! Behold how unjust a time is pressing upon us, while just and good men are dishonored and no one intervenes.

“What, then, do you think will become of us? Behold, they say, the restrainer of depravity is being removed; what place will justice have from now on? What soundness of counsel—especially since everyone seeks his own advantage?

“No one, therefore, takes thought for the commonwealth; each man takes thought most wickedly for himself. Counsel is sold for gifts, rewards follow, and they consider their own profits.”

### He spent seven years in exile on the island of Heri

39. Using these and similar voices of lamentation, they were compelled to make the hearts of all, one by one, groan with their tears.

They did not know that, by God’s hidden judgment, this had happened so that our old man would not see the evils as they occurred and the punishment of sin might meanwhile [Mss., “sometimes”] rage more freely against certain people.

Then, as though this alone were lacking to him—that which he had first desired—by the Lord’s dispensation he was driven from the human world. And we believe that he was nourished by heavenly sacraments, so that, since he had been forbidden merely to see the lands of earth, he might, following the example of John, become an investigator of the heavenly homeland.

What do you think? Could God have forgotten that he had previously delayed him from office in such a way against the will of his decree? But perhaps the long-desired wish is now granted to him so that, just as God had earlier wounded him through the labor of this office, he might afterward soothe him by granting him its exercise.

If even a stain of fine dust had soiled him amid the dangers of this world, accustomed as he was to the companionship of angels, he would wash it away in fountains of tears.

This is undoubtedly believed to have happened: for seven years—the number consecrated to this purpose—he was guided there by the holy Spirit, if somehow he might deserve to receive the sevenfold grace of that Spirit in its fullness.

Otherwise such a great and distinguished reputation for virtue would not have been conferred on him, unless divine judgment had arranged that he who was already famous throughout almost every region of Europe should also illuminate the farthest boundaries of Aquitaine, so that he who everywhere possessed power under the name of holiness might become still more renowned there, and afterward, supported everywhere by God’s help, might abound more richly in the rewards of his merits.

### On the great progress of the monks of Heri through the holy man

40. The holy brothers are suitable witnesses and trustworthy attestations of this matter. Among them, as they themselves confess, the blessed man appeared to have lived an angelic life for seven years.

The same man moved these brothers toward all that belongs to God with the sacred flame of devotion, for such was the power of charity in him that he could pour himself into everyone and establish them more firmly in God’s cause through his love.

For the highest power of God everywhere supported him through every harsh circumstance, the same power that had made the middle of the furnace breathe like a spirit of dew for the three young men. Therefore he was neither battered by storms nor struck by the force of winds.

He was founded upon the love of Christ. And, to speak with the Apostle (Rom. 8), what could separate him from the charity of Christ—tribulation, persecution, hunger, nakedness, or the sword? Indeed, to speak more plainly, neither death nor life, neither things present nor things to come, nor any creature could separate him from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus.

His feet were founded upon the rock, and therefore he could not be shaken.

### On their love and veneration for Adalhard

41. Recognizing this, the blessed men among whom he initially seemed to live under guard began to burn with great love for him and to venerate him exceedingly—not because of the honor of his royal kinship, but because of the beauty of his character, the lessons of his wisdom, and the sublimity of his virtues.

They honored him so greatly that even the Father of that place and the entire holy community venerated him with the service due to a father, conducted all their affairs according to his counsel, and obeyed him in everything, according to whatever he had once uttered with his mouth.

For you, incomprehensible Father God, were arranging all these things by your will, so that your devoted servant might at last obtain the long-desired leisure, and your devoted soldiers might be supported by his counsel.

### On his dwelling on the island of Heri

42. There he now enjoyed the perpetual Sabbath of heaven and tasted [al., “obtained”] how sweet the Lord is. I think there is no one who could fully express how immense were the praises and thanksgivings that resounded from his mouth there.

That dwelling was for him a happy habitation like paradise, from which the first man had been expelled through the envy of the serpent. The order of events is quite remarkable: the former, cast out from there, is covered with shame; the latter, as though brought back there at the serpent’s prompting, rejoices because he now enjoys angelic companionship.

Thus, as one of the most distinguished poets says (Virgil, Georgics 2), it was for him:

> “A very secure rest, and a life that knows not how to deceive,  
> Rich in varied resources, and leisure amid broad estates.”

And so he rejoiced exceedingly amid the soothing leisure of holiness, as though amid the pleasant places of a flower-bearing paradise. Nor is there doubt that, because of hatred for truth, he had been assigned to exile with blessed John, as venerable Bede the presbyter says (in a sermon on Saint John) [Note: Bede was called “the Venerable” by Paschasius Radbertus; at the same time Jonas also applies this title to him, as was stated in Bede’s eulogy under the year 735].

### How he advanced through exile

43. Indeed, it was possible to see everywhere the world’s wandering wheels and the armies of Babylon and Jerusalem clashing with one another, with weapons and flight alternately seized on either side.

Therefore, almighty Father God, your athlete mourned so greatly over the peril of this life as it passed away, and, overwhelmed by grief, groaned with immense lamentation, asking and begging especially that you spare the blindness of his enemies.

For the old father saw and foresaw that at this time the wretched life of the human race was being destroyed by pleasures; that Jezebel was calling herself a prophetess and deceiving the servants of God; that people were committing fornication and eating sacrifices offered to idols; that they were following the gluttony of the belly and being crowned by lust.

For, as I have said, it would seem monstrous if gluttony reigned without luxury, or luxury without gluttony.

Alas, how wretched is the condition of the belly, which, joined by affinity to such parts, is closed in at either end and clothed in the empty honor of an evil prosperity!

Therefore, although I use poetic speech, I warn you:

> “You who gather flowers and strawberries growing from the ground,  
> Flee from here, for a serpent lies hidden for these uses.”

Meanwhile our aforementioned old man did not cease to weep for those whom the desire to grow rich—or, as the manuscripts read, “to enrich others”—made like birds whom night illuminates and day blinds. Because they looked not to God’s ordering but to their own desires, they considered license or impunity for crimes to be entirely fortunate.

Yet through the enormity of their crimes, benefits were sometimes heaped upon the heavenly man, so greatly that he judged all his joy would come from having passed through temptation to the victory of the envious.

Therefore, wherever he turned, he advanced and continued to grow.

### On his patience in adversity

44. He rejoiced, therefore, that God’s will was being fulfilled in him, because he was being prepared to be wholly subject to God.

Among the other words of his patience, he used to say, when someone asked him about his exile, that he wished to imitate the example of the sheep in its simplicity and, like the hare, not to be concerned about changing places.

“For the sake of clothing others against the cold,” he said, “the sheep is stripped of its fleece without any jealous resentment, and from the remains of its own clothing another’s nakedness is warmed.

“Likewise, if there is in me some useful work of wisdom, I would wish anyone to receive it freely, without profit being gained by me. And so,” he added, “if I am driven here and there, like a hare pursued by the attack of one lying in wait, I neither leave with sorrow the place of rest in which I had long been firmly settled, nor hold with affection the place to which I am driven.

“Our citizenship is believed to be in heaven” (Phil. 3). Therefore we seek the things that are above, not those that are on earth (Col. 3). For we have died with Christ, and our life with him is hidden in heaven; when Christ, our life, appears, then we too shall appear with him in glory (ibid.).

With these and similar words he strengthened the minds of the brothers upon the rock that is Christ (1 Cor. 10), so that, since they seemed to have been placed outside the world amid the waves of the sea, they might be anchored more deeply in heaven by the hope that we possess like an anchor [Note: While Adalhard was exiled on that island, he ordered the Tripartite History to be copied, as it has survived up to the present among the manuscript codices of the Corbie Library preserved with us [lacuna]].

### At last he is restored to his honors

45. When he had thus been protected for seven years by the paternal battle-line of virtues, it happened, by the Lord’s consent, that the end of his exile arrived and that he was restored more gloriously to his proper honors.

I say “proper,” because they rightly belonged to him, and because he would illuminate the highest office of fatherhood by his merits. Otherwise, I said that he was to be restored to his honors because the honor proper to his merits and wisdom adorned him everywhere—not because he had lost anything by which he might be considered worthy of reverence, but because, deprived in the opinion of the common people of the office of honor, he was restored, as far as lay in them, by the pruning-hooks of dignities.

In truth, as the examined truth makes clear, he could not be dishonored, since heavenly grace illuminated him—especially since an honor not deserved rather disgraces the fool when he is made conspicuous in the highest offices than adorns him. His disgrace would have been less apparent if he had not been raised to lofty offices, where, as someone says, he protrudes like a swelling on the surface of the skin, so that he may appear an unworthy prelate.

But our old man was everywhere honored by all not so much with honors belonging to others as with the honors of his own merits; meanwhile everyone judged him worthy of honor.

Nevertheless, because dignity cannot make the wicked worthy of reverence, when it displays them to many it makes them more despised—indeed, the same dignity makes them unworthy. Our old man, on the other hand, was clearly endowed with such magnificent dignity that he deserved to be honored not only through the degrees of exalted office, but also because, supported by abundant counsel, he appeared exceedingly honorable even among strangers.

### They applaud and rejoice with him

46. When the appointed time had passed, he was at last recalled with the highest marks of respect, so that he might recover his former dignity [Note: Einhard and the author of the Life of Louis the Pious mention this restoration under the year 821, when it occurred]. Nearly everyone everywhere rejoiced and offered congratulations.

Voices of joy were therefore raised from every side even to heaven. The monasteries of monks rejoiced; the clergy of the churches resounded with delight; the joys of the common people smiled everywhere. There was a gathering of the people, as though, at a universal festival, he were being restored with the proclamation of heaven as a distinguished man.

### Only the men of Heri grieve

47. But the brothers with whom he had meanwhile lived, having heard the day of his return, began truly to grieve and to be sorrowful, while in a certain way also offering congratulations. Yet, because of their excessive love, they wept with great feeling and, even while weeping, could scarcely bring themselves to let him go.

Among them was Ragnardus, venerable for his virtue, who was afterward chosen abbot [Note: “Of the monastery of Heri” is omitted from the published lists of the abbots of Heri. He should be placed between Arnulf, who was abbot at that time, and Heriboldus, under whose abbacy the translation of the body of Saint Philibert took place. Its history will be related below [Col. 1534D]]. He burned with an exceptional spiritual fervor, weeping from the sorrow of his heart and yet, even while weeping, rejoicing.

He rejoiced because the lover of truth had recovered the place appointed by his merit; but he grieved deeply because he was being deprived of the presence of so great a man.

Thus it happened that, when the pious worshiper of God was about to depart from there, and all the brothers washed his footsteps and tracks with tears as they kissed them and bade him farewell, the aforementioned man of God withdrew into the house, into a chamber of tears, so that he would not see the one departing—the man whom he wished to remain with him more than himself and for whom he would undoubtedly have been ready even to die.

But when the old man had searched for him for a long time, he was found weeping and lamenting in a certain dark place and drawing many sighs. When he was summoned to bid farewell to the old man, he refused to come out and begged the messengers not to expose him there as he wept.

When the holy man’s charity heard this, he returned from the ship, so that he would not leave without embracing the brother whom he knew to be holy.

When the holy old man came to him, Ragnardus began to cry out loudly and say:

“Why have you come here, blessed Father? Or why have you now wished to show yourself to me? I call God to witness that I would rather bury you here dead than have you leave me here alive.”

Then all the brothers and servants followed him with loud weeping. At last the sails were raised and the oars were driven forward. Everyone groaned and waited on the shore as long as they could see him. One spirit of love burned within them, and therefore they could not contain themselves.

### The holy man spares the emperor

48. His bodily sight had been released, though not the sight of his heart, and his body had been weakened by prolonged emaciation. At last he reached the palace, where everyone received him with elaborate honor. They considered how the royal majesty might make amends to him, for they feared that they would incur danger because of the injury done to so great a man.

Then the blessed old man, seeing them occupied with such thoughts in shame of heart, came forward into their midst and soothed the king’s embarrassed mind with gentle words. He persuaded him not to retain any resentment in his heart concerning what had happened, but to attribute everything to God’s judgment.

### He is restored to his monastery

49. Meanwhile, compelled by that same prince, he was forced to resume his monastery of holy life at the request of his sons, so that they might at least in some manner deserve to receive him.

When he arrived among them, long desired, so that he might be embraced in their pious arms, the fever that is hostile to health was afflicting him, so that two emotions wounded the hearts of each one.

In every individual there struggled the sorrow of compassion and the fervor of joy, because they saw the limbs of their most beloved man being cruelly torn apart, for whom they would willingly have endured even the loss of life, however brave they might be.

Now the greatness of their joy prevailed over all; now the outpouring of tears. Together they raised mixed praises of joy even to heaven, so that no one could doubt that the Lord had come there in him. They all rejoiced at receiving him in this way, and he addressed them all kindly.

### He is recalled to the palace
### 50. He returns to the palace

But after he had rested there sweetly for a short while, refreshed by the service of charity, he was summoned again by Augustus with even greater honor, and returned to the palace. When he had entered, he seemed—as someone has said—to be illumined by the rays of virtue: “When Titan comes, the stars wither.” At once the folly that had been concealed beneath a cloak of darkness was exposed, and immense astonishment arose that the senate of the people had been led into such absurdity. When they discovered that they had been thoroughly deceived by envy [another reading: “that they had been deceived”], they annulled almost everything that during this period they had, as it seemed to them, devised with ingenuity.

Thus the cruel captivity of many was ended, especially of those who derived power from royal descent. In one person, therefore, liberty was restored to all, wherever they were being held, except those whom death had previously deprived of life. Then the tonsure imposed on certain men because of the savagery of the madness passed into a crown, and they freely gave to God what shortly before they had unwillingly received, as though to their disgrace.

### The Emperor publicly performs penance with others

### 51.

What more need be said? The glorious emperor himself, undertaking public penance for some of his offenses [Note: This occurred at the assembly held at Attigny, where, according to Einhard’s testimony, he made a public confession and performed penance for what had been done against Bernhard, the son of his brother Pippin, and also concerning Abbot Adalhard and his brother Wala. Read the Life of Louis the Pious for that year, namely 822, and Agobard’s book On the Dispensation, where it is reported that the venerable old man Adalhard exalted Louis with praises because of the measures enacted at that assembly. In the following year Adalhard again assembled with others at the palace of Compiègne at the emperor’s command, according to Agobard himself], became the most humble of all—he who, as though through royal arrogance, had been his own worst persuader—so that the eyes of those whom his offense had wounded might be healed by royal satisfaction. For it is clearly and unquestionably evident that all regarded what he willed and looked to what he did not will. But unless the champion of truth had returned, it would by no means meanwhile have become apparent by what lethargic spirit they were oppressed. Therefore mature old age, by persuasion, sought to heal the wound of their blindness with the salutary antidote of Christ.

### The condition of the kingdom is reformed

### 52.

After this he labored so that the virtue of justice and the virtue of wisdom might recover their seats, so that each person might preserve the charge entrusted to him and grant to each his proper rights. Moreover, in accordance with the Apostle, he suppressed everywhere as a plague innovations in speech and rash presumption (1 Tim. 6). Whatever, therefore, he did not find in the law of charity he judged hostile to God and rejected as poison.

When through these and similar commendations he had shone more brightly, like gold tested by fire, he became ten times more honored by everyone, so that his praise resounded splendidly from every mouth. He was embraced by the hands of all and was revered by all as a father. To the teachers of the churches [Note: This is demonstrated especially by the Consultation and Supplication of Agobard, presented to the holy fathers Adalhard, Wala, and Helisachar, concerning the baptism of Jewish slaves], he was like a son in humility, but in counsel and prudence like a renowned supporter.

As he labored tirelessly so that all might be found perfect and worthy of God, a new order of the Franks finally seemed to be born, and the dawn of justice to rise as from the east. For the sea spread by madness had already grown calm in part, and, as Virgil says, the breezes had fallen amid murmuring whirlwinds (Eclogue 9). The virgin of desire had returned, as the same poet says—if it is permissible to alter the expression slightly—and the reign of Saturn had returned [another reading: “the reign of tyranny”], because a generation of good understanding had now shone forth as though in the high heavens (Eclogue 4).

### Adalhard unwillingly retains the office of abbot

### 53.

When all around him had thus far been illumined by the pursuit of satisfaction, and his own people were enjoying the highest leisure with him, he finally wished to free himself from these cares, so that he might be attentive to himself and to God. But the holy brothers by no means allowed this, although he offered them many excuses based on his old age. For the more mature he was in years, the more beneficial he seemed to those striving toward the heights of virtue—especially since, through the vigor of the Holy Spirit and the freshness of his still-unexhausted flesh, he remained sufficiently vigorous, taking care to weary himself with labors and the duties of vigils, even beyond what the endurance of young men could bear.

### Cheerful in appearance, he is harsh only toward himself

### 54.

For who was ever as fervent as he was? Or who seemed a harsher judge of another than he was of himself? I plainly confess that he never had need of correction except because he was too severe toward himself. Thus, when his brothers and sons often rebuked him publicly, asking why he was so hostile to himself when he was regarded as so discerning by everyone, he would say, in order to soothe their wounded spirits:

“I shall take care of myself, and I shall provide fully for your servant, so that he may not perish from hunger or labor.”

But after this had been accomplished, by concealing himself for a little while [another reading: “gradually”], he soon resumed hunger and the duties of labor, so that scarcely could youthful limbs endure the austerities and vigils with which he afflicted himself. Nevertheless, he was always full of the freshness of health, always sufficiently ruddy despite his disciplined leanness, handsome in face and pleasing in appearance. Nor did sluggish anger wrinkle his face and forehead; rather, mature cheerfulness composed his entire appearance, making him dignified and fitting. Holy gray hair adorned him with snowy whiteness; and, like a lily above rose-colored garments, the hair of his head gleamed here and there upon his skin, like the raised leaves of palms. Thus, as it is written in the Song of Songs, our old man was “white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands” (Song 5), so that in him human nature might be reproached for being corrupted by vices before it reaches maturity.

### He is praised for his qualities

### 55.

And even if I wished for a while to praise the bodily clay of him, so greatly worn down yet radiant, whatever effort I expend would be slight; for that which shone more beautifully in him was that, adorned with the splendor of virtues, he gleamed like a lily among rose-colored hues, filled with Christ. There is no doubt that “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40); but the virtue of Christ, which always flourished in him, remains forever.

Furthermore, if I wished to describe from childhood the figure of his nobility, which in Greek is called χαρακτηρισμός (*charaktērismos*), I would be ineffective. For even if his person were considered according to the eloquence of rhetorical art, and could be shown worthy of praise, that which was far more excellent in him would take precedence: he had wholly passed from flesh into spirit.

According to the aforementioned expertise of the art, a person has many attributes by which he may best be recognized. The quality of a perfect man is considered, according to the orators, by his name, homeland, lineage, rank, fortune, body, education, character, way of life; by whether he administers his affairs well; by what domestic custom governs him; by the disposition of his mind, his skill, condition, bearing, countenance, gait, speech, and feeling.

When such matters and others like them are considered concerning him, it is pleasing to see whether our bright old man flourished with as many praises of virtue as there are distinguished topics of praise proclaimed by this art.

### Concerning his name, nation, lineage, and fortune

### 56.

Of these categories, it is rightly asked first concerning his name: was he wise? But if he was instructed more by heavenly teaching than by the eloquence of an art, how could he not have been wise? Wisdom is knowledge of human and divine matters joined with the practice of living well. Hence there is no doubt that he may rightly be called a true philosopher, or at least a wise man, insofar as is permitted: he prudently pursued what belonged to God through the grace of God, and diligently administered what belonged to human beings.

Devoting all the effort of his life to these two commandments, he himself was wholly expended in them.

By nation, as is clear to everyone, he was a Frank of the highest lineage. But, reborn in Christ, where he lived in spirit, he shone forth to all as wholly heavenly by nation. Thus his homeland too, although he was born here in the flesh, was undoubtedly that heavenly Jerusalem, according to the Apostle (Heb. 12), through him who has already made us sit in the heavenly places in hope.

By lineage he was the noblest of the noble Franks, descended, as I said shortly before, from an illustrious family; but ultimately, through Christ’s homeland, he was adopted by God as a son. Although he seemed great in royal dignity, he became greater through the sublimity of everlasting life.

What fortune had enriched him is shown by his life, in that he abandoned everything; and, in accordance with the saying, though poor in narrow circumstances, he reigned by possessing God. For this reason, as we believe and hope, now that he has been placed over many things, the joys of life serve him.

### His appearance also shines forth

### 57.

How handsome he was in body is also revealed by the excellence of his character. To him may not improperly be applied the passage from the Song of Songs (Song 5:11 and following):

“His head is the finest gold”; his hair was like the raised leaves of palms, because he strove daily to ascend upward to God.

“His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed in milk”: for his simple gaze was wholly intent upon the teaching of Christ, from which we, like little children, were nourished with milk; nor was it mixed with the gall of desires, but washed in true innocence of mind.

“His cheeks are like beds of spices, planted by perfumers,” namely, adorned by holy teachers with herbs bearing every flower of doctrine and virtue.

“His hands are rounded,” expressing the form of holiness and swiftly applying themselves to every good through spherical movement; “full of hyacinths,” shining with the appearance of heaven as they stored up treasures in heaven, and filled with many gifts.

“His belly is ivory,” marked out with ranks of virtues.

“His throat is most sweet,” because of the honeycomb of eloquence; and he was wholly desirable through the commendability of his character and his exceptional charity.

Therefore we seek you, Father, while you feed among the lilies; we seek him whom our soul loves (Song 6). In our bed, through the nights, we seek you with tears. Let your voice sound, I beg, in our ears; for your voice is sweet and your face beautiful. We cannot fail to love you as a father, whom we believe will be present for our sake.

### Concerning his wisdom and character

### 58.

If the question concerns his education, he was learned—another Moses—in all the wisdom of the present life, like one of the sons of a king. Then he was led to Sinai, where the presence of the Lord himself is revealed, and entered there to enjoy continual familiarity with him.

His character is attested by his life, which breathes the highest marks of merit and is praised with the greatest commendations. His way of life—for philosophers define it as the exercise of the enjoyment of a perfected work, by which one reaches rest—was the Lord whom he had loved, whom he had cherished, whom he continually desired.

The stages of these virtues are as follows. Among them the first is the disposition of the mind. This disposition is a change of mind or body caused by some circumstance. From being thus affected, it turns itself toward earnest endeavor in order to obtain the desired result. “Earnest endeavor,” I say, is a constant and vehement occupation of the mind with some matter, accompanied by great desire.

After the habit of the acquired thing has been assumed, we attain fully what is perfect. Concerning this it is written: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your holy ones rejoice” (Ps. 131:9). Blessed indeed is the garment of virtue with which each person is clothed, and he guards his garments so that he may not walk naked.

The one clothed in the wedding garment is not cast outside (Matt. 22). If our first parent had finally preserved it in paradise, he would never have been found naked with his eyes opened (Gen. 3). Hence, as it is written, when he descended, thieves stripped him, inflicted wounds, and departed (Luke 10).

But our flourishing old man, clothed again in such a garment, we now believe hears this promise: “He will walk with me in white,” Christ says to him, “because he is worthy, and I will not blot out his name from the book of life” (Rev. 3). While clothed in such a garment, this outstanding father exercised himself greatly so that, as the nourishment of his way of life, he might enjoy Christ, whom he had put on.

### Concerning his proper administration: he establishes a hospice

### 59.

It remains, in accordance with the discipline mentioned above, to inquire how he administered his affairs. What shall I say about how he administered his affairs, when he did not even retain himself for himself? For he had done what he heard from the Lord:

“If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

After fulfilling this, how he administered the property of his church is attested by suitable witnesses, the holy brothers, whose counsel and service he used. Through them he arranged everything so that there would be enough for everyone, that no one would have an excessive surplus, and that nothing would perish uselessly; rather, everything would be distributed more humanely to the praise of God.

He provided the brothers with what was beneficial for the present life and cut away whatever was harmful or superfluous. He supplied abundant provisions to all guests and preserved his household sufficiently unharmed from the yoke of servitude.

Indeed, throughout the individual villages he appointed widows of this household who had been left destitute, as well as unmarried men, and continually supplied them with stipends. He had also established in those same places, as though a hospice, suitable provision for orphans, the weak, and guests, so that all might possess the property of the church as though it were their own patrimony.

I call God as my witness that he himself often appointed the ministers of this service like a physician, so that they too might devise skillfully how to prepare something for them to eat, and so that their health would not fail through such foods.

He was so generous to the king and to the rich among our people that, through him, God—the giver of all—might be glorified in everything. He judged it much more blessed to give than to receive, and always sought, insofar as it depended on him, to walk midway between poverty and riches for the sake of others, so that those who had might be instructed to be as though they did not have.

He had also judged it right that all the servants of this church should regard him as a father, yet should not doubt that he was their Lord even when they were proud. Moreover, he was so zealous a supporter and instructor of their virtues that he became, though discerning, an exceedingly harsh persecutor of their vices.

### Concerning his domestic practice

### 60.

Now, according to what standard of custom he was accustomed to live, the measure of the holy oracle knows: in it were the hidden manna and the golden urn, the golden altar of incense, and Aaron’s rod that had blossomed. It had twenty cubits [manuscripts: “twenty cubits’”] in length, twenty in breadth, and twenty in height (Lev. 16; Num. 16), so that, completed on every side by a double denarius, it might be supported by the perpetual square of love of God and neighbor.

There is no doubt that the Lord was his foundation. Beneath what measure he was designated, only divine contemplation knows what our old man practiced according to his domestic custom.

### Concerning his disposition, skill, and condition

### 61.

In disposition he was so attracted by the incentives of every good thing that he burned with the service of charity toward the fraternal heart. Next, the skill in which he had been trained is evident, because he was found fruitful in the counsel of learning. He was, as they say, an observer with a thousand eyes of prudence, a most eloquent disputant concerning virtues, and so holy an instructor of the liberal arts that one might verify in him the saying of blessed Antony: “Sense discovered art,” and “he who is sound in sense has no need of art.”

What more should I say about his condition? As I said above, he shone forth illustrious from royal offspring. Nor should I say anything further about the other condition—whether he was, as they call it, natural-born, adopted, or disowned—for it is acknowledged both that he was the son of Bernhard, brother of the great King Pippin, and that he was adopted as a son by God.

### The holy man excels in countenance and dress

### 62.

What sort of dress he wore has been established by what I said shortly before: Christ is shown to have been his long tunic. As for the character of his clothing, it scarcely appears to have been sufficient even for a monastic garment; it protected his limbs chiefly against the cold rather than contributing anything to dignity.

Some, jokingly, called it “a coat of mail against the cold,” because it was made of skins and, like a breastplate around the entrails, provided warmth. In appearance he was pleasing and resembled the stature of a palm tree, because he was beautiful to look upon and dignified, as though nourished by the delights of paradise.

“How beautiful are his steps, and how lovely his feet for announcing the gospel” (Rom. 10)! For [he was] swifter than does in his feet, and more adorned in footwear [than] a prince’s daughter—

### His eloquence as well

### 63.

How eloquent his speech was, how full of meaning, how sweetly it flowed to the ear! His letters addressed to many still exist, and all who heard him testify that they had never heard anyone speak more abundantly or expressively.

In voice he soothed the ear more melodiously than a swan; and the melody of his speech was sweeter to the palate of the heart than honey. All his narration was exceedingly clear, concise, and lucid—a kind of diction that orators praise with the highest commendations—retaining nothing muddled [the reading *fecilentum* is uncertain] or obscure in its meaning.

Rather, proceeding with a plain step in its clauses, his honey-flowing meaning was enclosed by a very rich conclusion. The sound of his assertions was an exposition of his words, so that the proper meaning of the words was shaped by his voice and the qualities of each part restored to their respective senses.

All the members of his narration were distinguished by sections, making them very easy to retain and extremely effective for persuading or dissuading. He always encouraged his hearers more eagerly to pay attention, made them hotter than fire in their desire, dispersed their sluggishness, and stirred the inactive to action.

If such eloquence had been granted to me, I would complete what I have attempted more brilliantly.
