But now, ignorance deserves excuse and intention deserves pardon—especially since no one’s style would be better suited to this task than that of the man whose life excels and whose speech likewise surpasses all others. Since, however, the wave of my talent denies me this, it will be evident that I have at least fulfilled the obligations of charity by wishing to do so.

### Concerning his feeling

### 64.

It remains now to make known what his feeling was like. But by what skill of art shall I reveal the disposition of his mind, when in every affair of life he was moved by one constant ardor of spirit?

Always desiring to depart and be with Christ (Phil. 1), he wearied himself with labors. Although he confessed otherwise, he inwardly understood that remaining in the flesh was necessary for our sake. Therefore, with all the strength of his life, he strove to benefit everyone, occupied—as I may say—with a thousand tasks of charity.

Above all, he was the counsel of the entire homeland and the father of all in need. With mouth and hands, and with every resource at his disposal, he was, for the freedom of Christ, the servant of all.

### The beginnings of Saxon Corbie

### 65.

While he was always inflamed with ardor, he reached the borders of Saxony, where a very small cell had already begun to be built by a holy man, his namesake Adalhard, at the expense of this monastery. The blessed man had been his fostered and familiar son and had acted as his representative in that place while Adalhard himself was held in exile on the island of Héro, a citizen of the world and of paradise.

When the most holy father and old man saw that the work begun was an act of piety, he approached the king and asked him to grant him a place for building, because the location where it had been situated was not considered useful or suitable.

When the emperor Augustus heard this, he rejoiced greatly and wished to grant him many things, except that Adalhard himself restrained him—he never allowed anyone to give him as much as he wished, but only as much as Adalhard himself judged, even if it were little—always practicing the Apostle’s saying that it is more blessed to give than to receive.

After receiving permission from the king to build it wherever he wished, he chose a very pleasant place and one highly suitable for monks to inhabit. There the king later bestowed many benefits for the love of almighty God.

### The location and shape of the place

### 66.

The place lies for those traveling toward the rising sun from the spring of the Father [Note: That is, Paderborn, says Bollandus, which signifies “the source of the river Pader”], above the bank of the Weser, situated on the level ground of a valley in the shape of the letter Δ. To the east it has the aforementioned riverbed and a mountain extending along the river before it.

From the south another mountain emerges from the river and bends toward the west; from the north another proceeds in the opposite direction with an equal arrangement, until, giving one another a road through the middle, they join together. Thus a valley is formed in the middle, expressing, as I remember, the shape of Δ in this manner.

Nor is this without reason. For the teacher of truth, instructed by divine direction, chose such a place: one that would nourish the disciples of Christ, describe them by its character, and mark them by its situation.

### An explanation of the mystical arrangement of the abbey of Corbie

### 67.

Among all geometrical figures, nothing more complete or perfect than the triangle is found. In arithmetic this number alone is the beginning of all breadth and surface; in geometry this is found more plainly. Whoever carefully examines this figure will find nothing more marvelous in these arts, nor is anything greater or better proclaimed in our discipline than the Trinity, the true God.

Thus nothing formed without this number is indicated to be perfect—namely, nothing without a beginning, an end, and the middle between beginning and end. This figure is, as I said, the principle of breadth, because all other surfaces are resolved into it. But because it is subject to no principles and took its beginning from no breadth other than itself, it is resolved into itself.

If it is raised upward in the manner shown, it signifies that those who dwell there ought to burn with the fire of charity. That it is the beginning of breadth shows that the broad commandment of God can be fulfilled only by a heart that has been enlarged. That it resolves all surfaces into itself clearly signifies that all the remaining virtues are perfected by its breadth. Charity itself is perfected only by worshiping the Trinity in unity, so that true perfection may hold indivisible unity in these three.

Let this much suffice concerning what I have said, so that I might show how prudent and wise he was, and with how great a fire of charity he burned—he who prepared for his disciples such a great and excellent place to inhabit, watered with streams, as though it were Lower Egypt and another paradise of the Lord, for those coming from the spring of the Father toward the rising sun.

Truly I said “from the spring of the Father,” because those reborn in Christ are believed from there to pass not only toward the rising sun but even beyond the sun. The blessed father called this place Corbie after the other one, so that it might be a sign for posterity of the place from which the earlier foundation had originated.

### Adalhard exhorts his people to pursue poverty

### 68.

Who, my dearest Father, could sufficiently recount your provident teaching in all things? I frankly confess that whenever I remember you completely, I am astonished at how provident you were in everything.

I remember your teachings by which you nourished and instructed them, tender ones, in faith and charity, placing hope between them; in character and every teaching of life; and also in how they ought to receive things offered to them by anyone, while you carried out these matters with them amid the burdens of administration.

In all things you urged them not to be desirous of earthly possessions, nor to wish to accept anything by which others would be burdened. If they were heirs of the benefactor’s property, they were to consider carefully lest they themselves—whose inheritance it was—should later become needy.

This was his careful and pious concern in all places over which he presided: that he should accept nothing dishonorable and that no one, as though out of compassion, should later be oppressed by regret. For he said that many, not only governors of churches but also those living there for God—who seemed to have renounced the world—were deceived for this reason: they abounded in excessive possessions to such an extent that they were compelled to serve the world again, though they ought to have been dead to it.

“What benefit,” he said, “can there be in stripping future heirs of their own possessions and then subjecting them again to worldly business? It is clear that at the present time we serve the commonwealth for this reason: because, weakened by our desires, it is plainly unable to subsist by itself. Thus we wretched people, who ought to have been free in Christ, have become, even against our will, slaves of the most shameful servitude.

“Therefore, having seized the opportunity, as though in God’s cause we carry the world’s military burden, although the Apostle says: ‘No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs’ (2 Tim. 2:4). For we are not blamed because we retain only what is necessary, but because we possess what is superfluous—as they themselves say. From the very source from which we miserable people wish to be broad in possession, we become narrow in every good work.

“Therefore, little sons, be content with the poverty of Christ, without which no one is rich. Know that the poor in spirit are blessed, for the kingdom of heaven is promised to them (Matt. 5). Therefore, my brothers, do not lose the eternal possession by pursuing greed as though it were an act of ownership.

“Be, then, what the eternal calling of Christ wished you to be, so that, by sharing in the poverty of Christ, you may deserve to be rich with him without end.”

### He rejoices over the establishment of New Corbie

### 69.

As he strengthened and confirmed them daily with these and similar teachings, there was being built there, by God’s agency, not only the foundation of a monastery but also of a heavenly homeland.

What do you think—how great was the joy then moving his mind, how great the gladness, when the love of almighty God burned so fiercely in them that the whole region blessed God through them?

I confess that, when he sometimes returned to us, he could scarcely contain himself because of his devout love and spiritual joy. He rejoiced and exulted here and there because Christ was glorified through him in many people.

While watering and feeding us with heavenly nourishment, and planting and propagating them in Christ, he labored so that they might bear abundant fruit for God. In everything he showed himself to act as Christ’s representative, even surpassing all others in the form of humility.

### Concerning the seven stages of perfection

### 70.

Thus he was continually moved by one spirit of jubilation and desired the stage of entrance. According to blessed Augustine, in the book where he speaks about the quantity of the soul, entrance is one of the seven virtues and the sixth stage of perfection.

The fifth of these stages is tranquility; the sixth, entrance; the seventh, contemplation. They may be expressed most suitably in the following way: entrance into oneself, when any soul enters into and dwells with itself; entrance toward God, when, desiring him ardently each day, it enters into him, saying:

“My soul thirsted for the strong and living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:3).

And entrance with God, when, already contemplating him continually in clear light, the soul clings to him—him upon whom even the angels desire to look.

Our old man rejoices that he has now reached this state, gives thanks that he has deserved it, and embraces the conviction that he has attained it with the highest eagerness of spirit.

### Concerning Adalhard’s charity toward his people

### 71.

What else, therefore, shall I say but the words of Elisha: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and the charioteer of its virtues!” (2 Kings 2). Behold how suddenly you leave us desolate! Therefore we seek you with a tearful voice and search for your honey-sweet character each morning in our inmost hearts. The pupil of our eye is never silent or consoled except when it promises itself that you are more fully present for our sake.

We remember at what breasts you nursed us, with what abundance we enjoyed the oracle of God in you, on what great oarings of wings we were carried, and how we were nourished by the entrails of charity. Thus, even if we were made of stone, your prayer of compassion would soften us.

For you had become everything to all of us, so that you might win us for Christ. If you turned to the particular concern of some individual, you gave one counsel for life in a moment; at another time you soothed another with kisses. You clasped one person’s hand and touched another’s heart with marvelous affection. Thus you were one for everyone and wholly present to each individual.

### He kept them written on a tablet and often met with each one

### 72.

Although you always held the names of the brothers written within the heart of your holy concern, a carefully written list of their exact number was almost never absent from your hand. Thus you diligently examined them all and anxiously considered the character of each one.

You already disputed with yourself in judgment concerning each individual, lest you later suffer loss concerning the sheep entrusted to you. You knew well what was useful for each person, and therefore offered each one what suited his salvation.

Your discernment departed in no way, insofar as it is permissible to say so, from its purpose: it was ready to fulfill what was suitable for each individual, yet generally appropriate for all. You scarcely left anyone during the week without speaking with him in the affection of familiarity; and, except for some cause of impossibility, you instructed no one whom you did not address generally each day. You provided health-giving things to everyone and, as we believe, denied no one what was necessary.

Therefore, daughters of Jerusalem—as I am compelled to say—weep for this old man of ours and take up lamentation. Weep for the man who clothed us above with the scarlet of charity, woven throughout with delights, and who supplied the adornments of virtues for our service.

Put on sackcloth and mourn bitterly, because he who consoled and cherished us like a nurse in her bosom has been taken away and departed. Therefore my soul shall weep bitterly, and there shall be tears upon my cheeks for as long as I do not behold him whom my soul loves.

Do you think, Father, that the time will come for me when, in some manner or other, I may be permitted to see the face and appearance of your countenance?

### He leaves behind an immense longing for himself

### 73.

But what shall we do now, my soul, in the time that follows? Behold, until now we have moved, as it were, among rose-covered fields, and have looked upon the pleasant places of virtue, abundantly bedewed from the fountain of the Holy Spirit.

Now, however, we must reveal the end of his death: the death he had is to be glorified, his loss is to be mourned, and his arrival among the joys of the blessed is to be celebrated with congratulations.

But the more pleasantly we dwell upon what is loved, the more grievous it is to endure his absence, whom we always perceive as present. Therefore, as though everything were sprinkled with mist, all that we behold is sorrowful. Our eyes grow dim, we are covered with sobs, our fingers tremble, our heads whirl, tears pour forth, and, in addition, there is a certain desire to weep born of devoted love.

Thus, whenever we fashion these words at greater length for consolation, we are moved by love more ardently, and by loving are pressed more heavily by grief. Therefore, my dearest Father, I shall pass more quickly over the pages of your death, for a violent languor overwhelms me when I linger there too long.

Meanwhile, the capacity for mourning trickles forth here; but shortly afterward we shall be consoled by your arrival, where you now rejoice in gladness.

Therefore, we ask you, before the pen begins to strike the hour of your departure: return, O Shunamite, return, I say, for a little while, so that we may look upon you. The pen will thereby recover the breath of its speech, and we shall pass more lightly through the bitter course of reading.

Return, return, my dearest one. And what shall we see in you except how you have been arranged like the ranks of an army? Turn toward us at least once, we ask, so that we may see what kind of man you formerly were among us and how great you now are.

Behold, you have ascended—we know it—through the wilderness, like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible in God, like an army arranged in battle.

### Near death, he speaks to his people and asks their forgiveness

### 74.

What, then, could appear more terrible to human eyes than the appearance of your face at that hour when you granted us forgiveness?

For when we asked you, Father, you had ordered us all to sit upon the ground, so that you might behold all your people completely and we might look upon you with raised eyes. I confess that I had never heard anything more orderly granted by a teacher, nor had I ever seen anything more ardent or terrifying than what was in your eyes.

Thus, laying out the meaning more closely, you spoke at length to everyone:

“Behold, I am coming to give an account for the sheep entrusted to me. But you, my flock committed to me, who are about to receive judgment concerning your obedience and disobedience, attend carefully: I, the same man who now stand before you, shall be present with you in the dread judgment, and I shall present what profit I have made from the money of the talents, or how I have spent it.

“Meanwhile, however, if there is anything in which I have offended against you, knowingly or unknowingly, willingly or unwillingly, forgive me, as I, in accordance with what is fitting, release whatever is mine to forgive in Christ’s place.”

### He places his hope in the Lord
75. Having thus set forth these matters, he withdrew, full of spiritual fervor, as though he were already destined to be the judge in his own case, preparing himself as if he were then about to fight against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places and give an account of his stewardship [Col. 1545D]. Although he had always conducted himself as though at the point of death, he was then arranging the sharpness of his mind more carefully, as though he were about to go against legions, if perhaps he might escape the deceits of this life without hindrance. But because the pursuer is said to surpass his tenfold force by twenty thousand, he always prayed to the Lord for the things that make for peace.

“Lord,” he said, “place me beside you, and then let every hand fight against me; otherwise I shall not escape the troops of the wicked, because you alone have been found free among the dead. For the exactor comes to you, and in you he finds nothing that belongs to him. Therefore make me cling more firmly to you, so that through you I too may be found free from every evil in your body.”

He examines his conduct with the elders; he sets forth his faith.

[Col. 1546A]

76. Examining himself completely in this way, he still found in himself various things, as though they had not yet been exhausted, and ordered that he explain them before certain brothers—one of whom, though unworthy, was I—asking whether he feared that he would rightly come to judgment on account of them. Having heard these matters, we examined them according to divine Scripture and judged that they did not pertain to him, although he himself had long and deeply mourned them as his own. What do you think—how subtly he debated the remaining [or, in the alternative reading, all] matters with himself? How severe he was toward himself, punishing himself even for the faults of others as though they were his own!

Meanwhile, warning and instructing each person about each matter, he said that after his death they should agree among themselves in peace, chastely and rightly according to God, concerning the elections. [Col. 1546B] He also set forth his faith before some of us, and almost the whole teaching that he had taught, so that by this means he might commend it more firmly to our hearts.

Hence we are drenched with such sorrow in his absence; yet from another direction [al., “from this point”] we rejoice, because such things are remembered about a father. From one side we are moved to this, from another drawn toward that. We mourn in him the maturity of his character, the firmness of his faith, the solidity of his hope, the complete foundation of his charity, his most profound Christlike humility, and his richest generosity in all things. I do not, as I say, mourn miserable Jerusalem as the Savior did; rather, I weep because in the death of one man all the virtues seem likewise to have fallen—not because he who has departed is lacking to us, but because we have ceased to see such a man, whom we can scarcely, or never, remember without tears.

The author grieves that so beloved a head must be lifted up.—How eloquent the holy man was.

[Col. 1546C]

77. Who will remember him with dry eyes, in whom almost all the glory of goodness has been taken away? Or who would not grieve that the protection of all Europe has suddenly perished? Who could recite the brilliance of his letters and his eloquence without inward unease? If you had heard him speaking publicly, his speech flowed sweetly; but if he spoke in that barbarous language which they call German, he excelled in clarity of expression. And if he spoke Latin, then, because of the eager sweetness of his speech, breath itself seemed unable to go farther.

Therefore, all of you dearest to me, who know what good the presence of so great a man possesses, and who pass along the way, [Col. 1546D] attend and see whether there is any sorrow like the sorrow of us all. See, then, how suddenly the Lord has harvested us, and we have become squalid, our beauty having been taken away. Blight has seized us, because our rosy beauty has been turned into ashes.

Three days before Christ’s Nativity Adalhard is seized by fever; nevertheless, each day he hears Mass and receives Communion.

78. The old Simeon had therefore prepared himself to meet the Savior’s birthday with lamps lit, and joyfully to receive in his arms the King of kings, the Lord Jesus Christ, coming forth from his chamber. But three days before the Lord’s Nativity a very severe fever seized him while, according to custom, he was weeping in the basilica in the middle of the night [Col. 1547A]. Remaining at the vigils in this condition, he consecrated to the Lord in his heart a sacrifice of jubilation together with the brothers. And the higher the choirs sang, as many witnesses attest, the more he wept amid his rejoicing. Thus he continued on until the praises of Matins, and, no less feverish with love for Christ, he grew weak, as it is written in the Song of Songs: “Sustain me with flowers, surround me with apples, because I languish with love” (Song of Songs 2:5).

Although each day he was pressed by ever greater pains, he did not relax his spirit, always intent upon God. He therefore arranged everything with such foresight as though he suffered no bodily evil, establishing and ordering the several workshops in such a way that his end would find nothing unfinished—especially so that the holy day might be celebrated with fitting honors.

After this had been accomplished, he began to be pressed more violently by the fevers. [Col. 1547B] Nevertheless, each day he came to the oratory [Note: [Col. 1547D] This oratory still stood within the memory of our fathers in the area that is now empty beside the town walls, between the garden and the inflow of the river Corbei into the town.] of blessed Martin, whom he had always loved abundantly in life. There, hearing Masses, he received Holy Communion until the final day of life led him out of the darkness of this night.

When Bishop Hildemann arrives, the holy Father rejoices greatly.

79. Meanwhile the blessed man Hildemann, the bishop whom he himself had raised as a monk and whom, with the king’s permission, he had exalted to the distinguished honor of bishop of Beauvais, heard that the holy Father was ill. [Note: [Col. 1547D] Saint Hildemann will be discussed below under the year 842.] He came immediately and kept continual watch before him until he brought his life to its end; and he buried him with his own hands together with all the brothers.

When he arrived, the holy Father rejoiced and was glad with the greatest liveliness, scarcely able to contain himself because of the excess of his exultant joy. For he gave immense thanks to God that He consoled him by Hildemann’s arrival, and he said:

“God, founder and ruler of all things, I give you thanks, because I have not been deprived of my desire.”

He awaits death with a serene countenance.

80. Meanwhile, when the same holy bishop had begun to ask us whether he ought to be anointed with the oil of blessing, as was decreed by the blessed Apostle (James 5), we asked him whether he wished it, although we knew beyond doubt that he was not held by the burdens of sins. [Note: [Col. 1574D] From this it is clear that Radbert’s conviction, and therefore that of the faithful of his time, was that the anointing of the sick was principally effective for cleansing away the burdens of sins. It is also clear from Adalhard’s reply that he did not request this sacrament for the sake of health—which is also an effect and secondary purpose of the sacrament—as was stated in the Preface to the first age.]

When he heard this, he raised his eyes to heaven and earnestly begged that it be done. What do you think the holy mind was doing then? With how many tears was it filled! [Col. 1547D] His eyes were fixed upon God, while his hands were extended toward heaven. Inviting the Holy Spirit, he said:

“Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace according to your word, because I have received all the sacramental mysteries of yours. And now what remains except that I come to you? Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will; only let your will be done.”

For a long time he had thirsted to come to the fountain. Hence, also in an almost playful voice, yet full of the gravity of faith, he often said:

“From here I shall go, and I shall come to my God. Gladly, I say, I shall come; gladly I shall die; and gladly I shall pass through the great pits of this life, because I am destined to reach everlasting joys, long promised to me.”

He says that he saw Christ.

81. With these and similar sayings the soldier of Christ diligently armed himself until he entered “the place of the tent of the marvelous, amid the voice of confession and praise,” where an army of a multitude celebrating a festival was also found. There, it is believed, our old man, rejoicing, began to sing:

“The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Romans 13:12).

While, still feverish in the flesh on each day, he commended himself to God with immense praises in this way, it happened suddenly that the holy bishop entered to him while he was alone by himself. Immediately he cried out to him:

“Run quickly, O bishop, I command you, and kiss the feet of my Lord Jesus Christ, for behold, he is present.”

When the bishop heard this, he trembled greatly, because he had no idea where he should go or what he should do. But after saying this, Adalhard withdrew silently and rested.

Then, after the eighth day of Christ’s Nativity had been completed, he began more eagerly to insist that, now that the days had been celebrated, he might depart from here, if somehow he might at last reach that festival which night does not interrupt and illness cannot corrupt.

When part of the middle of the night had passed, he began in this manner and said to the brothers:

“O sons, always most dear to me in the Lord, know that today I shall go from here. For it has already been granted to me to depart from here and to see—may it happen—and to appear before the sight of my Redeemer. The course of my struggle has therefore now ended, and it remains entirely unknown to me what I shall receive as the reward of my calling.”

Yet we believe, Father, that you received what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (otherwise the labor of faith is empty), especially since you could truthfully have said with the Apostle:

“I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the righteous Judge will give me on that day” (2 Timothy 4:7–8).

He dies after speaking at Matins, strengthened by the viaticum.

82. When morning had come, the same blessed Father summoned some of our number and began urging them to anticipate Matins more quickly. After these words, his heavenly tongue fell silent in the praise of Christ.

Then, when all the holy brothers had assembled together, he received Holy Communion at about the first hour of the day. They began to commend him to the Lord with hymnic praises, and continued in his funeral rites until the ninth hour of the day. Then he too [or, in the alternative reading, thereafter], at the same hour when Christ on the cross [Col. 1549A] gave up his spirit, gave up his spirit. [Note: [Col. 1549D] Namely, on the fourth day before the Nones of January, and indeed at the beginning of the year 826. I infer this year from the Chronicle of New Corbie, over which he presided for four years beginning in 822; also from a Saxon manuscript chronicle, in which his death is placed in the year 825 according to the old reckoning, in these words: “Saint Adelhard, abbot of Corbie, died, and Warinus succeeded him”; and finally from the Life of Saint Anscharius, who, after Adalhard’s death, was sent to Denmark by Wala, his successor as abbot. From these facts it is understood that Adalhard came close to his eightieth year, as is read in the following Eclogue, since he became a monk at the age of twenty, not before the year of Christ 770, according to the observations recorded above in the Martyrology of Nevelon, a Corbie monk who lived in the twelfth century. There these words are read: “On the fourth day before the Nones of January, at the monastery of Corbie, the feast of Saint Adalard, confessor and abbot, to whom Christ appeared at the moment of death. Wala and Uvarinus, his successors in both Corbies.”]

This was given as a sign that the one whose cross he had borne in life and whom he had followed would likewise follow his footsteps at the moment of death, until he reached the one whom he had sought, desired, and long longed for with his whole heart.

What do you think the mourning of all was at that hour, and how extraordinary were the laments of the monks! The voice of the singers rose upward as one voice on high, while the weeping of all below tore apart the breast of each person. For, as it has been said elsewhere, it was pious both to rejoice with so great a man and to weep at his departure.

Who would not have wept, even if he had been born from stone, at that hour when the renowned shepherd of God, departing from here, sought the heavens? For he was the one, good Jesus, whom alone among all I found to be an abbot; he was the one among all whom I found seeking another’s good more than his own. As a mother loves her only son, so he loved each of them most tenderly, and he invited them to attain what was more solid.

The author mourns his death.

83. Therefore, I ask you, men, attend and see: all you peoples, see the mother Corbie—which is a hive of monks—weeping, I say, and saying:

“My magnificent one has been taken away from me, and among all my beloved ones there is no one to console me. For the Lord has fulfilled his fury against me and has done what he had conceived. He has therefore fulfilled what he had commanded from ancient days: ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall go’ (Genesis 3). Therefore my dearest one has departed from me and withdrawn.

“Israel’s virgin has therefore returned to her cities and thereafter walks gloriously upon the waters of eternal redemption. For he was the one who was dearest to me among my vows; he was the one who converted my soul and guarded my life; he was the one who, rising at the beginning of the vigils for us, poured out his heart like water before the sight of the Lord. But now the Lord has left us desolate for a little while on his account, worn down by sorrow.

“Therefore we place our mouths in the dust, hoping in the Lord’s mercies, if perhaps there is hope that we may reach the place where our pious Patron is believed already to have arrived. Until this happens, until the desired day comes, let my tongue cling to my jaws if I do not remember you, Father Adalhard; if I do not place you at the beginning of my recollections. Otherwise, let my right hand forget me unless I proclaim your name and praises.

“I believe, dearest of my beloved ones, that maternal love could perish sooner than we could cease loving you. For even if she forgets her own children, we shall never forget you. As long as the ages endure and night takes its turn with day, the fame of your most holy life will always be proclaimed, and we shall never be free from praising you.

“But you, we ask, draw us after you from here; let us run after the fragrance of your ointments, for your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments. The upright love you; therefore we seek you until we reach the place where you feed and where you lie down, for we know that it is at midday.”

A passing remark on Orpheus’ descent to the underworld.

84. We do not therefore, according to what the myths report that the Thracian [Treicius] prophet did, lament the death of a spouse in the underworld; rather, we raise the Father’s name above the stars, since we confess that you have solemnly ascended there.

Therefore, although that man was fortunate who, in fiction, was able to see the shining source of the good, and fortunate who was able to loosen the bonds of heavy earth, we are more fortunate, who can direct such and so holy vows to you, our father.

For it is imagined that the prophet mentioned above, weeping for his wife in mournful melodies, made the forests run after him and the rivers stand motionless. He joined the fearless flank of a stag to savage lions, and the hare no longer feared the dog made gentle by his song. When his passion burned with the innermost heat of his body, and all that he had subdued could not even then soothe his mind, he went to the gods above, seeking his wife. When he did not find her, he entered the dwellings below, tempering soothing songs on sounding strings and drawing upon whatever he had drunk from the distinguished springs of the Muses.

At his songs the goddess of the shades, taking pity, said:

“At last, judge, we are overcome; and therefore we grant the wife to the man, purchased by song.”

What grief do you think he expressed then, according to the poetic account? What dirges did love, redoubled, stir? With what prayers did he plead for pardon, when the underworld had marveled at his new songs and the goddesses who avenge crimes, now sorrowful, were wet with tears?

Honors rendered to the dead Adalhard.

85. But, dearest Father, we introduce these things not because we are unaware that no one has returned from the underworld without Christ, but because we wish to disclose what good there is in love. Love is its own greatest law; therefore, by imitation, we seek you as though through a law, because your whole life was a law of life, so that we may deserve to reach you—or rather, to reach you because you have reached Christ, and we believe and desire that you have arrived there.

We pray that God, moved by our prayers, may hear us and that you may be granted to us—or rather, that we may be granted to you—because we ask that you have been given to paradise. For we believe that there you are already crowned from the head of Amana, from the summit of Sanir, from the lairs of lions, and from the mountains of leopards. You have conquered all these things in triumph. Therefore you have become sweet amid the delights of paradise and beautiful, and there is no blemish in you.

You are embraced by Christ’s right hand, and press his left beneath your head, sleeping in the sleep of peace. Therefore you have become before him as one who has found peace. Your bed, then, because you dwell in Christ’s peace, is flowering according to the quality of your merit; the beams of your house are cedar, and its ceiling is cypress.

And we, most loving Father, rejoice and congratulate you according to our understanding, because, when the house was overturned, the drachma that had been lost was found in you. It had been lost, surrounded by the darkness of night, but with lamps lit it is more happily found again in you.

Therefore, for the time being, when we are unable to do anything else, we sit weeping around the borders of your tomb and scatter upon it the flowers of our prayers. We read above it that good name which you acquired better than great riches. Some of us gather pale violets and shining lilies for you; others narcissus [Col. 1551B] and flowering roses. Others scatter sweet-smelling thyme; these adorn it with colocasia and soft blueberries. Some mingle sweet fragrances; others water it with salty springs of tears. And I weave over it a mantle of letters, so that your holy name may be preserved for future ages.

I do not weave it, however, with the embroidered artifice of eloquence; rather, I wrap it in a clean linen cloth through the work of purity. But if anyone wishes to know this man more fully—how powerfully he conquered the world by faith—let him read where a new name and the name of the new city Jerusalem are inscribed for him. And when he understands with what ornaments the city shines, let him attribute all of this to him, because there he is believed to have somehow been made by God both the city itself and the possessor of that city.

Wala, his brother, succeeds him.

[Col. 1551C]

86. Therefore rejoice and be glad, virgin of the faith, blessed Corbie, so called from ancient times, because you deserved to enjoy and possess in Christ such a patron. I ask you, renowned mother of religion, embrace this man whom you trained, while he was a recruit, in heavenly conduct with sobriety and discretion; and imitate him, who later enlarged you with many honors.

Why, then, are you consumed with sorrow, virgin and daughter of the Most High God, as though you had no counselor? Behold, he has left you his brother as heir, who will still sweat through many labors on your behalf.

Wipe away your tears, I ask, because you too will send this old man from your midst to meet him, when all the regions of the earth have sent their most distinguished men. Moreover, when the neighboring monasteries have given their own—namely, Vedastus of Arras, and the most holy Richarius of Centula, and men renowned for religion from all around—you too perhaps will give, with no unequal vow, a man most worthy of God.

Nor will you then be unfruitful, when among the others you also bring forth this man for the Lord from the dust of the earth. Rather, rejoicing and glad, you will come, bringing at least a few sheaves. Therefore take courage and act with greater strength until Amalek meets you on the way, because another Joshua, already your leader and guide, fights beside you with courage in the battle line.

[Col. 1552A] Therefore support this man, already fighting at the head among many; look also upon him on the mountain, now stretching his hands to the heights before the Lord. This one fights; that one prays. This one presses the enemy; that one conquers.

For he is, dearest mother to me, a lover of the brothers and of the people of Israel. He is the one who prays greatly for his own, perpetual in charity. He is the one who, as I believe, will be a constant intercessor for the citizens.

Therefore, Lord, in accordance with the words of blessed Ambrose, since no one has anything that he would bestow on others more than what he desires for himself, do not separate us after death from him whom we experienced as most dear in this life. Rather, make us be with him where you are, so that in this way we may enjoy his perpetual vision with you in Christ, whom because of you we loved exceedingly as most dear in this life, and who now lies buried in the peace of Christ.

Epitaph of Adalhard.

[Col. 1552B]

87. The limbs of the dearest old man were decently buried in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, beneath the roof, midway among the four central supports of that same church [Note: [Col. 1551D] Commonly called “cintres,” that is, the arches supporting the vault, as was explained in the first part of the second age. Which four abbots of French Corbie were those among whom Adalhard was buried is not established.], covered by a polished stone. Upon it the following, engraved in eight verses and worthy of being read as a work of musical poetry, is inscribed:

> Here lies the distinguished abbot, venerable for his merits,  
> Our Adalhard, an old man worthy of honor.  
> Of royal lineage, by right a citizen of paradise,  
> A man upright in charity, in conduct and in faith.  
> As you recall him beneath the tomb, whoever you are, traveler,  
> See what you are and what you will be, since death snatches all things.  
> For after the Lord’s octave, released from the flesh here,  
> He joyfully sought the stars on the following day.

He lies midway among the four abbots of Corbie.

[Col. 1552C]

88. Four venerable men were also buried there all around him, men whom the Lord had raised up in the same office of service. I do not think this occurred by chance, but so that those whose one warfare in Christ had been to carry the cross after Jesus more nobly in the same place might have one place of burial, which would adhere there all the more significantly in the likeness of that same cross.

Our old man is seen in the middle of them. Above him the signals are sounded at the hours of the divine office. [Note: [Col. 1552D] Indeed, before the lower step of the screen, as Saint Gerard notes in the Preface to his Book of Miracles—that is, at the screens separating the presbytery from the choir of the church.] This makes clear what is believed to have taken place: that his tongue had been the cymbal of the Holy Spirit and an invitation to the office of divine work dedicated there.

Hence the eight verses are entitled in accordance with the fact that he died after the Lord’s octave, so that it might be shown that, having completed his work to which he had formerly invited everyone, he happily reached the Lord’s octave, with no letter-number diminished.

[ECLOGUE OF TWO HOLY WOMEN.]

What follows is the ECLOGUE OF TWO HOLY WOMEN, brought together in one lament of affection. It is said that he had nurtured one of them as though she were, in Christ’s place, one Church joined to him in marriage—namely, Corbie in Gaul—and that he had wondrously begotten the other from her, according to monastic discipline and with careful balance—namely, Corbie in Saxony. It is also stated that one of them was called Galathea because of the brightness of her face, while the other was consecrated under the name of Phyllis because of the love of charity.

GALATHEA.

> Weep, I ask, men; weep piously with me for the Father,  
> And let every more advanced age implore pardon.  
> Scatter tears upon the ground; furnish the fields with flowers:  
> Let everything here sweat with tears at the Father’s watch.  
> Let the heart disclose its groans through the office of the tongue,  
> So that even the stars may resound everywhere with the same lament.  
> Let rustic, Roman, and Latin tongues celebrate together,  
> And let the Saxon—who [alternative readings: “and” or “also”] likewise laments—say instead of song:

> “Turn all of you here,” the greatest singer sang;  
> “Prepare a tomb, and add a song above the tomb;  
> Gather the blessed limbs of the old man into a renowned resting place,  
> He who strove to open for us the warm veins.

> “At his funeral let the clergy, their throng mingled,  
> Recite divine poems with alternating voices.  
> Let the shepherds proclaim in verse what the great man was:  
> ‘The keeper of a beautiful flock, himself more beautiful still.’

> “And let the common people answer in turn:

> “‘Benevolent God our creator,  
> Grant pardon to your servant; we pray and ask for the kingdoms of paradise.  
> Have mercy on the old man; have mercy on your own.  
> You know at last how worthy he was of mercy.’

> “From here let the love of the heart, grief, and groaning resound;  
> From here let children and old men behold his virtue and name.”

PHILIS.

> Who, I ask, would not mourn a man raised above the stars,  
> Reduced to ashes, or enclosed beneath hard marble?  
> His fame for virtues flies throughout the whole world;  
> Yet his imperial lineage is food for worms.  
> Alas, what can we wretched people, placed beneath death, do for him?  
> We weep and groan, but we cannot call him back.  
> He has been called away and is absent, yet he does not hear his lovers.  
> Breasts are burst, entrails are torn by grief;  
> He neither hears the tears nor the dirges of the sorrowful.  
> And because we are tormented and torn within our hearts by tumult,  
> Grief is present to our minds, but most deaf death does not care.

> We preserve for him a dusty clod from his body;  
> But he, renowned, carried in a joyful choir, rejoices among the stars.  
> Therefore, by the man’s virtue, I would have boys and girls  
> Mourn with pious hearts and draw forth salty springs,  
> So that, because sorrowful origin has given us all what we suffer,  
> And because this is one nature inherited from our ancestors,  
> There may also be one compassion of mind among all;  
> Let the tears of sadness strike heaven together.  
> Let the single weeping of the monks flow from every mouth.

GALATHEA.

> I ask that Corbie bury the old man, the elder, in the tomb.  
> But I, the younger, soon deprived of such a patron,  
> Will utter a groan in alternating voices instead of song.  
> You, as a happy mother, who long ago bore me from one man and formerly called me by your own name, speak.  
> O beautiful one, you will now be another [the reading is uncertain] to me for ever—  
> You whom that blessed man founded three times with rejoicing hands,  
> Giving many saving oracles in his words.  
> For when the savage power of the demon raged with its wickedness,  
> And the worship of the shrine had defiled the whole land,  
> He overturned the altars of cattle and consecrated sheepfolds to Christ.  
> Then, cutting out the grove at its root and removing it far away,  
> He established holy monasteries filled with monks.

PHILIS.

> O exceedingly happy one, though richly endowed with divine gifts! What sorrows I am compelled to undergo!  
> When you seemed first to have earned at Amiens  
> The task of presiding over the flock of Corbie, most holy shepherd,  
> The Saxon land also came to know you as Father,  
> So that you might return to God the talents entrusted to you, doubled.

> But you, faithless death, do not know how to spare your poisons  
> For him [the printed reading is “Ulii,” perhaps *illi*] or for us; nor do you care for gifts—the printed text, corruptly, continues: *munera cura. munera curas* (“care for gifts, you care for gifts”).  
> You do not know how to love men; you do not know how to preserve patrons.  
> You remain for all as the one irrevocable fate of an hour,  
> By which you snatched the blessed man from us by a death described with the uncertain printed reading *stimplo*,  
> Whom all together with complaining voices  
> We mourn, groan, weep, shed tears, and love.  
> But wretched one, you do not know how to show mercy to the wretched in their misery.  
> Alas! Behold, envious one, you drag everyone with you,  
> So that you swallow up everything we have scarcely lived until now.

GALATHEA.

Then our most humble and venerable sister said:

> “O how gentle and gracious the master was in speech;  
> Why have you left us so suddenly, when we are so very tender?  
> You die, indeed, forever happy.  
> But I, a fierce virgin, bloodied by many wars,  
> Am drenched after you by a rain-bearing fountain of tears,  
> And beneath an immense groaning I beat my guilty breast.  
> From here I wash my spotted face with salty drops,  
> Although I am dark and dusky with my own stains and poisons,  
> So that, sprinkled upon my snowy face with the color of roses,  
> I may grow yellow, shine, give fragrance, and become moist all at once.  
> And, exceedingly happy in your time, I shall mourn,  
> As long as the final mournful part of life remains.”

PHILIS.

Then the mother said, she from whose name I am called:

> “You will never overcome me with tears or weeping,  
> Nor with light songs resounding, nor with vows spread forth.  
> Therefore I would have you mingle honey, while I adorn with flowers.  
> You too gather pale violets, while I gather lilies,  
> And scatter over the tomb the sweetest herbs,  
> Since he was worthy of these gifts,  
> He who himself bestowed many delights upon us  
> And painted you entirely with the rosy blood of Christ.

> “Thus Isaiah the prophet once foretold.

> “From here holy trees of beauty come to you, clapping their hands;  
> The myrtle, the fir, and the pine rejoice there;  
> The vine and shining grape, too, and the olive grows fat.  
> And as a paradise and garden of delights,  
> You are nourished by waters flowing down from heaven’s summit.  
> You who had been a sterile region, a descent to hell,  
> Now stand open as the gate of heaven or the doorway of life.  
> Nor can the former faithlessness of death equal  
> The swift course in which you now glory.  
> Now your lofty head touches the stars of heaven,  
> And you shine exceedingly throughout the world in your radiance,  
> So that no former nurse of monks  
> Could be more fertile beneath the four-sided hinge of heaven.

> “Therefore, sister, I ask you to make lament instead of song  
> For the Father, who had scarcely completed eighty years.” [Note: [Col. 1555C] Adalhard did not live a full eighty years, since he became a monk at the age of twenty at the beginning of Charlemagne’s reign, not before the year 770; therefore he barely reached seventy-eight years of age.]

> “And perhaps your breasts had not yet flowed with milk;  
> When suddenly the jar of the fountain perished or was shattered—  
> He full of the counsel of his homeland and the wisdom of Christ.”

GALATHEA.

“Ah! Mother supported by God,” the daughter then said,

> “Why do you wish to renew such great sorrows by recounting them?  
> Or to recall the day than which none was more savage,  
> Nor has been, nor can be, nor will be in the future?  
> That day, when our patron perished, took away from us  
> All the beauty of life, cutting short the vows of virtue.  
> Alas! How miserable we are, who live without him!  
> We who have been cast down into an exceedingly evil lot,  
> Because, placed together, we were unable to go to heaven,  
> Although I judged it better to die with him than to live.”

PHILLIS.

> Therefore, peoples of Christ whom the water has washed,  
> Bring forth liquid streams from the depths of your breasts;  
> Let us mourn my virginal husband, taken by fate,  
> Prudent, sober, chaste, filled with charity,  
> Gentle, humble, and also just and kind;  
> Noble in character, so that no one was wiser than he.  
> In whose speech Christ’s wisdom shone.  
> A fountain stood open, leaping forth; the teaching of life likewise leapt forth.  
> Distinguished in conduct, full of the teaching of virtues;  
> Gentle, peaceful, merciful, and exceedingly modest.  
> These, recognize, were the possessions of his rightful domain;  
> These are the bridal gifts of my dowry, each exhaling its fragrance.  
> Hence blessed love grows so greatly for him in me  
> As spring truly increases new flowers from the earth.  
> But for that very reason grief grows greater in my mouth,  
> Because an insatiable ardor burns too fiercely in it [that love],  
> And because from now on there is no remedy for my sorrow  
> Unless I am at least permitted to compose his holy name.

GALATHEA.

To this the exceedingly happy Galathea confesses:

> “Begin now to set aside such anxious complaints.  
> For perhaps the Muses marvel at such a funeral  
> And have left you, your songs and melody stunned.  
> Everything, even the stones, groaned together with your dirges.  
> O,” she said, “if then that return of love should come,  
> What floods of tears we are compelled to pour out for him,  
> So that at last we may be renewed by drinking in his sweetness!  
> At times, hand in hand, let us go toward the citadel,  
> Toward the chambers of the kingdom, where he has long been calling us.  
> There let us feed in the everlasting fields of heaven,  
> Where the blessed old Menalcas deserved to enter,  
> He who led our loves with him so far.”

PHILLIS.

> “And he draws sighs after him from our very fibers.  
> For there the rights of our desire must come together,  
> Although the tomb lies sadly midway along our path.  
> But if we knock persistently and seek, I say,  
> There is no doubt that after the ashes we shall come to the city  
> Where piety, goodness, peace, light, and wealth reign;  
> Where the fruits of joy, rest, and gladness shine;  
> Where every good thing gleams and sweet concord soothes;  
> Where glory, praise, and honor flow from one fountain;  
> Where eternal life rejoices and the pastures of virtues bloom;  
> Where angelic sheep rejoice and heavenly rewards flourish,  
> Finally made firm by everlasting gifts.

> “There God is always present, and rich things are opened.  
> Among the companies of the apostles and patriarchs  
> A fragrance breathes, sweeter than all herbs.  
> With the martyr choir shining, moss-covered camps open,  
> And the prophets exhale sweetness from what they have drunk.  
> The white companies grow golden with virgin flowers.  
> All things celebrate pious joys there everywhere,  
> And all resound, singing with one heart,  
> Each person uttering such honey-sweet songs.”

GALATHEA.

“Stop, sister; say no more,” Mother Galathea said.

> “Perhaps we shall sing these things better when, rejoicing,  
> Paradise too shall be green for us by our lot.  
> Until then, pluck the flowers and lilies of the fields,  
> Until they smile amid the joys of alleluias.*  
> Scatter violets along the road, fields with flowers of virtue;  
> Paint the path with roses; strew lilies through the streets.”

[Col. 1557]

EPITAPH OF ARSENIUS, OR THE LIFE OF THE VENERABLE WALA, ABBOT OF CORBIE IN GAUL, WRITTEN BY PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS IN TWO BOOKS, IN DIALOGUE FORM.

(In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. V, p. 453, from a very ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs.)

[Col. 1557]

PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS.

Where the work was found. Who Arsenius was.

[Col. 1557A]

1. I found this excellent work on the deeds of Wala, abbot—whom others call Walon or Walach—in a manuscript of the Paris monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs. This codex had formerly belonged to the library of Saint-Arnulf at Crépy. The form of the writing readily persuades me that the parchment codex was written in the age of Paschasius Radbertus. I inferred that it was his autograph, or at least a primary copy reviewed and corrected in his own hand, because at the beginning the corrector added *legi* (“I have read it”); moreover, no other copy survives in the Corbie library.

This work is entitled *Epitaphium Arsenii*. On seeing the title and eagerly reading through the manuscript, I supposed that it concerned Adalhard, abbot, whom learned men had inferred from Paschasius Radbertus’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* to have at some time been called Arsenius. But after reading the entire epitaph more carefully, I noticed that Arsenius is Wala, Adalhard’s brother and successor in the government of Corbie; and that Adalhard is here called Antonius [Col. 1557B], just as Paschasius reports that he was called in Adalhard’s *Life*.

Nevertheless, I understand that the name Arsenius was attached to Adalhard through an old error, from a Corbie manuscript of Paschasius’s *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. There, after the words that stand at the beginning of the printed editions:

> “He knows, therefore—and I do not doubt that your experientially acquired skill in the disciplines knows it—that our Arsenius, whom our own age has now brought forth for us as another Jeremiah after that one, entrusted you to me in the matter of faith. For this reason I took care, without weariness, to snatch you from among the waves from your earliest youth; but I confess that I did not run in vain,”

the following words occur in the Corbie manuscript:

> “But the aforesaid Father, namely Adelhard, as is customary among those who favor justice, bears exile for the sake of the faith—if I may use the Comic poet’s expression, because, knowing the truth and being full of cracks, he refused to remain silent. Hence we are still uncertain what God’s providence may further wish concerning him, whom we now see being driven on every side by divine promises of future merits. Yet you have not followed youthful impulses [Col. 1557C].”

And so forth, as in the printed editions. Although this addition is Paschasius’s, the words “namely Adelhard” were certainly inserted by some interpolator, who supposed that Adalhard’s exile was being discussed, whereas the subject is the exile of Wala the abbot, whom Paschasius throughout these books calls Arsenius and Jeremiah.

### Why this history is obscure

2. It is therefore established that this work concerns the deeds of Wala the abbot. When Paschasius was writing his history, Wala’s rivals and adversaries—powerful men—were still alive. He consequently thought it best to veil the entire history under fictitious names, lest the conduct of his rivals provoke resentment [Col. 1558A].

And indeed, since this *Life* consists of two books—of which the first treats Wala’s deeds before the deposition of Louis the Pious, while the second deals with the deposition itself—the subject was difficult to handle, whether under Louis the Pious, during whose reign the first book was written, or under Charles the Bald, Louis’s son, during whose reign the second was composed. Hence Paschasius everywhere uses fictitious names, so that to the uninitiated he might appear to present an enigma rather than a history.

### Key to the history

3. Therefore, for the benefit of those less familiar with historical matters, I provide here a key to the history, explaining the proper names by which the secrets of the entire affair are disclosed.

Wala is called **Arsenius**; Adalhard, **Antonius**; Louis the Pious, **Justinian**; the empress Judith, Louis’s wife, **Justina**; the emperor Lothair, Louis’s son, **Honorius**; Louis’s other son, king of Bavaria, **Gratian**; his son Pippin, king of Aquitaine, **Melanius**; Bernard, duke of Septimania and chamberlain of the palace, **Naso** and **Amisarius**.

There is also another person, called **Phasur** in Book II, chapter 16; but I have been unable to determine who he is. Might he perhaps be Ruadbern or Rodbern, who brought Judith back from Italy and was praised for that reason in a poem by Walahfrid Strabo—the man who later became chamberlain of Charles the Bald—on the basis of Audradus’s revelation?

### When this history was written

4. The first book of this history was published by Paschasius immediately after the death of Wala the abbot, before the year 840—that is, while Louis the Emperor was still alive. The second was published after Paschasius had resigned the governance of the monastery of Corbie, which occurred in 851, as has been demonstrated in his *Eulogy*.

Since the later book is entirely occupied with explaining the disturbances that arose during the two periods of Louis the Emperor’s troubles, Paschasius appears to have deferred committing them to writing [Col. 1558C], lest the dangerous and contentious matter inflame the supporters of either side.

### Paschasius is affirmed as the author

5. No one who reads this work will deny that its author is Paschasius Radbertus, who is himself one of the interlocutors. Yet no one will read it without gaining much, whether from its outstanding examples of virtue or from the remarkable historical events reported here in great number. Indeed, in my judgment there is scarcely any history of the deeds of the saints in which more facts worthy of knowledge are related.

I do not know whether this work was seen by Jacobus Baro, the chronicler and Corbie monk who stopped writing in the previous century. For, speaking of Wala, he says:

> “The blessed Radbertus Paschasius composed his Life together with the Life of the blessed Adalhard, abbot.”

That chronicler makes many errors concerning ancient matters, though he is more reliable regarding recent events.

It was necessary to preface the history of Wala at such length, both to illuminate a hitherto unknown work and to commend the kindness of the Reverend Father, prior of the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, who most courteously allowed me to use this excellent manuscript.

### Wala defended against slanders

6. In the second book Paschasius is wholly occupied with defending Wala the abbot against the slanders of his adversaries, who accused him of violating his loyalty to Louis the Emperor. There were approximately three principal charges.

The first was that a monk had entangled himself in the civil affairs of the state; the second, that he had advised Louis the Emperor to repudiate the empress Judith; the third, that he had taken part in Louis’s deposition [Col. 1559B].

Paschasius answers the first objection in Book II, chapter 15. Wala, he explains, possessed such dignity and authority at court that, although before becoming a monk he had been among the leading men of the palace, after becoming a monk and abbot he was appointed by the emperor as counselor of the entire empire. The same emperor had previously ordered him to be tutor to his son Lothair, as we learn from Book I, chapter 25.

The monuments of that period, especially those of Agobard, bishop of Lyon, show how great his authority was. Agobard’s *Consultation and Petition to the Nobles of the Palace concerning the Baptism of Jewish Slaves* was addressed to the most blessed lords and fathers, the holy men Adalhard, Wala, and Helisachar. His letter against the impious decree concerning the baptism of Jewish slaves was directed to “the most holy lords, the most blessed and illustrious men, Hilduin, overseer of the sacred palace, and Wala the abbot.” Agobard calls them the chief and almost the only helpers of the most Christian emperor in the way of God.

For this reason, he says, one of them—Hilduin—was always present at the palace, while the other—Wala—was frequently there, so that by their most prudent suggestions they might exhort and assist the emperor in works of piety [Col. 1559C].

Wala was employed in such affairs above all because Louis the Emperor wished it; Wala was also his kinsman.

Paschasius satisfies the second accusation in Book II, chapter 8, and the following chapters. He answers the third in chapter 18 and elsewhere, where he proves that Wala always resisted Louis’s deposition and, when he understood at last that he could achieve nothing, withdrew to Italy from the factionaries.

Yet because it is difficult in such disturbances to keep one’s conduct so measured that no fault is committed—or at least that the opposing party is not provoked—an assembly of Frankish nobles was summoned by Emperor Louis at Aachen in the year 835, as we read in his *Life*:

> “So that the means of mutual reconciliation between themselves and him might be investigated. When the aforesaid matter had been debated and brought to its conclusion, the emperor, together with his wife, first wished to be reconciled with Wala himself, dismissing with great cheerfulness and kindness of heart whatever offenses he had committed against them. Through him and the other envoys sent to his son Lothair, he ordered him to come as quickly as possible; if he did so, he should know that this would be most advantageous for his future. They returned and reported the matter to the son. But before the emperor’s command could be carried out, illness and fever intervened: it took Wala from this human life, while it threw Lothair onto his sickbed and caused him to languish for a very long time.”

Paschasius does not mention this reconciliation between the emperor and Wala, although he was present at most of Wala’s deeds.

### The year and day of Wala’s death

7. The same author of Louis’s *Life* again discusses Wala’s death under the year mentioned above:

> “At that time it is pitiful to relate how great a mortal pestilence invaded the people who had followed Lothair. Within a short time, that is, from the Kalends of September until the Mass of Saint Martin, these leading men departed this life: Jesse, [Col. 1560B] formerly bishop of Amiens; Elias, bishop of Troyes; Wala, abbot of the monastery of Corbie,” and so forth.

It is therefore clear that Wala departed this life in the year 835, though Paschasius does not record the day. In the very ancient register of the abbots of the monastery of Corbie, compiled approximately seven hundred years ago, Wala the abbot is said to have died on the second day before the Ides of September; and in the Corbie chronicler cited above, on the twelfth day of September—which amounts to the same date.

Yet in the *Register of Meals* of the same monastery, likewise written in the ninth century, the following is recorded concerning Wala:

> “On the day before the Kalends of September Wala the abbot died. His commemoration is to be made from Busco.”

And lest anyone think that an error has entered this passage, the death of Abbot Isaac is added immediately afterward as having occurred on the fifth day before the Ides of the same month. Wala therefore died before that date. Accordingly, the catalogue of abbots found in the same manuscript seems to require correction; the chronicler, who was misled by that catalogue, must likewise be corrected.

It makes no difference that in the *Life of Louis the Pious* Wala is said to have died with the others “from the Kalends of September,” for this can rightly be explained as referring to the proclamation of the Kalends, which takes place from 14 August onward. In the same way Saint Benedict used “the Kalends of October” in chapter 48 of his Rule, according to the note of our Menard in chapter 55 of the *Concordia*.

At the end of the second book Paschasius reports certain signs of Wala’s sanctity approved from heaven. They are not, however, of such a kind that the ancients absolutely called him a saint or blessed—not even Paschasius himself, nor the monks of Bobbio, among whom he was buried. I have therefore thought it preferable to call him venerable.

In the aforementioned *Register of Meals* it is prescribed that on the day of Wala’s death a provision for the brothers is to be made from Busco (Bus), an exempt provostship of Corbie near Mont-Desir.

8. Finally, I point out that the second book of this *Life* is far superior to the first, in which Paschasius sometimes appears to insert dialogues that are unnecessary.

# BOOK ONE

**Interlocutors:** Paschasius, Adeodatus, Severus, Chremes, and Allabigus, monks of Corbie.

## INTRODUCTION

### PASCHASIUS

Often, brother Severus, I silently and at length wonder what new thing has happened to our Adeodatus. After the threshold of such great mourning has been crossed, he once again, as I think at your urging, commands us to renew those unspeakable sorrows of which Maro speaks, and asks that we paint for future ages, after the manner of Zeuxis, an image of our Arsenius’s character [Col. 1560D].

He does not sufficiently consider that I am a clumsy painter, and that I am ashamed to display the portrait of so great a man, glorious in the flowers of his virtues, in the mirror of literature for posterity, lest I appear still more disgraceful. Yet it is some consolation that, although I am confused on many grounds, I am illuminated by the merits of his virtues—even though I cannot find any suitable beginning for these things.

Where shall I begin to tell what I partly saw with my own eyes, partly received with my ears, and understood more fully in my mind?

### SEVERUS

It is indeed astonishing that you wonder, man—[the text has *thr*]—if you are ashamed to reveal the image of one made beautiful by the goodness of his character, whose imitator you ought to have been and whose fatherly features, as they say, you ought to have reproduced. I too am bound by the same wishes through the affection of discipleship, especially since nothing is more timid or more cowardly than to grieve without feeling grief, or to lack the courage to lament the miseries by which one is oppressed.

### PASCHASIUS

I shall strive, act, and attempt what you urge, Severus, since no one who grieves and knows how to lament can fail to do so, and no one amid torments fails to dare to sigh [Col. 1561B]. I would sooner leave my soul from my body than cease to love him and fail to commend him in prayer to those for whom it may be beneficial.

### ADEODATUS

It is best, when someone has departed from the body, to recall in the mind whatever virtues belonged to him, so that what seemed to have perished in him may revive in us. Virtues are always flourishing and green for their reward; they do not die in anyone unless they are destroyed by vice, even though they may ever be capable of being destroyed or weakened.

Faith gives us confidence, and hope gives us consolation, when concerning someone whom you knew to be good you presume that he has died in God, and when you pursue and love him through the obligations of charity in your prayers. Otherwise, are we to be regarded as mere down, lifted up by the wind? Far be it from us.

But when such people have gone before us, we ought to believe that these things are present more fully in him who said: “Everyone who believes in me will never die” (John 11:26). For this reason they should not be mourned as though dead, but commended in our prayers as patrons [Col. 1561C].

### PASCHASIUS

Let us leave this aside, my brother and son. May the gift of the Holy Spirit make us worthy of these gifts, he who adorned him with such flourishing flowers of virtue. But I fear that, while I try to please you, I may offend many.

Do you not know, Severus, that our most unhappy age has produced for us another Jeremiah after that one? You yourself have often heard, as I recall, this Arsenius proclaim with flowing tears:

> “Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife, a man of discord throughout the whole earth!”

You command me to bury upon his tomb the mourning brought about by time—to sprinkle the epitaph, as the ancients did, with tears—and now you wish the devastation of the conflagration to be stirred from its ashes after the quarrels of discord have fallen silent.

Do you not see, Severus, that even now throughout the whole earth everything is blazing with the flames of desire and that ravenous envy is laying waste to all things?

### SEVERUS

I see it plainly, since, in accordance with the Apocalypse, “a great mountain burning before our eyes was cast into the sea” of this wicked age, as our sins increased; and “a great star burning like a torch” (Revelation 8) traverses the world and reduces the minds of individuals to ash.

Against these men Arsenius, bearing the peace of Christ, preferred to extinguish their flames [Col. 1562A]. But, because their sins demanded it, the bitterness of wormwood overcame the sweetness of so great a man on every side, so that he could not prevail against the wicked wills of the people.

### PASCHASIUS

As I understand, by Hercules, you have no doubt about this man’s conscience. But, recalled by your words to me, I shall relate what I saw in a vision before these events occurred.

I saw from a distance something like a mountain piled up from a mass of timber, almost reaching the clouds and set ablaze with fires. Before it stood someone—I do not know who—tall in stature, who was trying, as though to make the flames burn more and more intensely, to strike down all the already-burned material with a rod. I could not discern the end of that conflagration.

I judge that these things signified matters of this kind.

### SEVERUS

As I see it, our Adeodatus has sought to utter dirges, whereas you, on the contrary, wish to provoke laughter. Otherwise, if you had not been asleep, you would certainly not have confirmed by doubtful dream-phantasies what I said and what you yourself see.

But now I wish you to wake up and attend to what we ask.

### ADEODATUS

You frequently employ, Severus, the sharpness of Chrysippus, and even playfully [perhaps *jocos*] repel distinguished speech with the blade of your eloquence. I ask you not to act too severely, in accordance with the omen of your name; rather, act with us, so that we may shape an image of the father with a moderate pen.

### SEVERUS

I accept your advice. But I think the image of his character will not be fully formed from the face of one man alone: he displayed in his actions the integrity of many illustrious men [Col. 1562C].

It often seemed to me that he possessed a mixture of the character of the earlier Arsenius; at other times he assumed the person of Father Benedict; and sometimes, as I have already mentioned, he performed the office of Jeremiah, pressing forward more sharply with an adamantine forehead [sic], although he was gentle in spirit and the mildest of men.

### PASCHASIUS

You plainly show that, while he lived, you painted him in your mind with the brush of piety, which, according to the Apostle, is useful for all things. Yet if I wished to pursue [variant: *prosequi*] these matters, scarcely anyone—or only a rare person—would believe them.

### ADEODATUS

Who has ever demanded witnesses under oath from a historian? Yet if necessary, there are more good men than not who will give the right hand of an oath to your assertions. It would be unworthy of a friend of truth to evade this and timidly remain silent when people ask for something concerning the truth [Col. 1562D].

### PASCHASIUS

Have you not read that effort is ineffective [variant: *inefficax*] when applied to a matter that lacks an effect? You know all too well how often truth is trampled and driven from its seat. Therefore, even if I should prove that no one in our time has borne the form of Father Benedict—and even if that sun which sees all things were to testify—whoever hears it will consider it false, although the truth remains secure.

### ADEODATUS

I do not believe that a matter lacks effect if it bears the fruit of love and piety. It is therefore not absurd, even if the envious become deaf, to relax for a little while the affection of love, which is well nourished by tears, soothed by weeping, and fixed in contemplation upon the one whom you love, becoming green again; and to sprinkle the tomb of so great a Father at least with the flowers of lamentation [Col. 1563A].

### PASCHASIUS

You speak truly, and you urge us with sufficient devotion to escort the holy sacrifice of God, pleasing to God, with tears to the palace of heaven—not because we possessed him as such, but because we have lost him as such, and, burdened by our sins along with him, have not yet been able to accompany him.

But if that ancient proverb were true, that misery alone is free from envy, we would freely pursue him in our prayers. As it is, I know that amid our miserable tears there will be much envy on the part of certain people, who will thrust out their arms in reproach, especially if they notice the story concerning whom the narrative is being woven [Col. 1563B].

### SEVERUS

This is what I observed earlier. You seem to me to be suffering from a kind of lethargy [*litargo*; variant *lethargum*]. Did you not say that you would paint an image of his character and weave, as it were, the history of an event [printed *rei gestam*; read *rei gestae*]? Yet now you bring us a fable.

### ADEODATUS

It is strange, Severus, that you always use such familiar sharpnesses of language. It seems to me that he said “fable” not to you, but to those for whom everything supported by truth is a fable and a game. You read the history of this matter in your own conscience. Therefore, for you it is not a fable but [Col. 1563C] the truth that is revealed.

### PASCHASIUS

You act rightly, Adeodatus, if you favor the prayers with which you weary the man. But what will strangers do when we are accused by someone who knows? Have you not read what a recent pagan theme produced [Note: In the manuscript, *tema*. I confess that I do not know who that Drusilla was, or whether the name is fictitious.]: that someone saw Drusilla going up into heaven?

Perhaps the same person will say that he saw Arsenius making his journey into heaven. Therefore, if you do not trust yourselves, ask him whether he wishes to or not, and he will perhaps show that he has seen what is happening in heaven—for we do not believe in divine things.

If you question him, he will tell the story even to one person; before many people, I think, he will never say a word. For ever since he swore in the Senate that he had seen that same woman ascend into heaven—and no one believed him for so good a report—he has affirmed in carefully composed words that he will tell no one whatever he may see, even if he should see a man murdered in the forum [Col. 1563D].

### ADEODATUS

I perceive what you are suggesting, somewhat more timidly than is appropriate. Do you think that you can relate anything that will please everyone and that everyone will believe?

What, then, is clearer or more blessed than that message—and, what is greater, what is truer—that Christ, victorious over the underworld, went with his flesh to heaven; that he opened a way for all who wish to go there; that he kept the gates open; that he remitted sins; that he granted grace; and that he gave the ability to go there through faith [Col. 1564A]?

Yet why is it that some do not believe, many contradict it by their deeds, and few come, when so many miracles shine forth, so many examples of patriarchs converge, and the proclamations of the prophets point out what happened as though with a finger; when the elements perceive it, and the angels obey and proclaim it?

All the apostles are witnesses to these promises and declarations of deeds; the martyrs of Christ are witnesses as well; and so are innumerable confessors and virgins, whose faith is attested by miracles through their merits.

When so many proclamations and witnesses concerning such a good message are disregarded, you have no reason to complain if many have not believed the proclamation of their salvation and if there are people who hold sufficiently good opinions about him.

### PASCHASIUS

Solomon’s saying is true: “Iron is sharpened by iron” (Proverbs 27:17). So you too, my brother, often sharpen the friends whom you love, so that they may make progress through being loved.

I therefore follow devotedly wherever you lead me. Yet take care that, where there is no benefit, inquiry may cease for the sake of salvation.

# CHAPTER ONE

### ADEODATUS

I ask you to unfold the mixture of qualities from which the inner man is formed intact, since his face and family were almost universally known; or explain with whom he should be compared, as Severus has mentioned.

### PASCHASIUS

Certainly, from boyhood, through military service and rank, he increased the glory of the earlier Arsenius [Col. 1564C]. For he was a cousin of the greatest Emperor and dearer to him than anyone else. He was truthful in speech—as is said of that man [Note: This concerns Saint Sebastian, in whose *Acts* these words are read: “For he was a man of complete prudence, truthful in speech, just in judgment, provident in counsel, faithful in what was entrusted to him.” What Paschasius adds—“whose ashes, recently brought among us, shone with such great miracles”—is therefore to be understood of his translation to Gaul, that is, to the monastery of Saint-Médard at Soissons, in which city Paschasius had been educated from childhood.]—whose ashes, recently brought among us, shone with such great miracles; he was just in judgment, provident in counsel, and supremely faithful in what was entrusted to him.

In the senate he surpassed everyone in intelligence. If he were questioned about any matter of business, whatever could best be said or discovered flowed immediately, without delay, from the fountain of his counsel.
