Even then he possessed supreme virtue and authority enlarged by many circumstances. Goodness and nobility of character and family commended him. He was distinguished by wisdom, so that he excelled in divine matters as he surpassed others in all human affairs.

He also possessed an eloquence in both languages—by which wisdom is usually aided—and an abundance of speech sufficiently restrained for persuading people of whatever he wished [Col. 1564D]. Because he shone with such qualities, he was loved by everyone.

### ADEODATUS

Although he was such a man, I should like you to explain why he so frequently lamented that he had been born “a man of strife and a man of discord,” especially since, as you say, he was loved by everyone.

### PASCHASIUS

I admit that zeal for religion grew in him, and that his virtue increased through grace. At that time he did not yet know the injuries inflicted upon the state, whose growth he was glad to see. Therefore, in accordance with Jeremiah, he devoted himself more to the firmest alliances among the nobles and the holiest friendships among the people than to lamenting the sins and injuries to the state, which had not yet grown so great.

Do you not know, Adeodatus, that a good man takes thought not only for himself but also for his country and his fellow citizens? You know Scipio as well, and the other men of that age who, on account of the greatest services and the many benefits of virtue they rendered to their country, endured hatred and various dangers of death.

# CHAPTER TWO

### ADEODATUS

Alas that the more numerous part seeks the depths! If only I did not know such things among the religious men of our age! I now ask how he came to the monastic discipline.

### PASCHASIUS

The glory of the world is never without envy, nor prosperity without the danger of some adversity. But a good man uses both sides for salvation.

Thus, when Arsenius was being struck by the plots of certain people and saw the shamelessness of violent men occupying undeserved positions, he found the time he had previously vowed to God in his mind and longed for. He saw that cunning, eloquent men held positions, and that the lowliest people, with a “marsa” hand [sic; reading uncertain], were overthrowing those most famous and most beloved by the people.

When he saw such men acting against the wise by power rather than reason, and being superior and, in the judgment of the crowd, most worthy, he foretold that many troubles and many shipwrecks would come upon the people.

Then, although many opposed him, he laid aside the world and its allurements without regret, insofar as he had held them without love. Since he was inflamed by divine love, he left everything and sought a monastery [Note: Namely, the monastery of Corbie in Gaul, as is clear from Paschasius himself in the *Life of Saint Adalhard* above. This occurred after the year 814, when Louis the Emperor sent Wala, together with Warnarius, Lantbert, and Ingobert, to Aachen to remedy the scandal in the royal family, according to the *Life of Louis the Pious*. I infer from this that Louis the Emperor was the author of his withdrawal, because at the Synod of Attigny in 822 he performed penance for what had been done concerning Adalhard the abbot and his brother Walachus, as Einhard testifies.] of monastic discipline, so that he might be governed not by his own laws but by the laws of Christ and by the divine Spirit.

For he had read that “those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8:14). Therefore, eagerly, he preferred in everything not himself but Christ.

Ask Severus how he conducted himself there. Until now, while I have been concerned to hear you, I have borne more lightly what I endure. But now, as soon as I have touched upon the man whom I had seen and possessed, I have found new and renewed sorrows that I thought had passed away.

For this reason I shall be silent for a little while, until my eyes find a fountain of tears and draw out water, because my comforter has gone far from me, turning my soul [Col. 1565D].

He has gone far away because he withdrew from here to God, worn out by the great burden of miseries endured for the people and for the religion of Christ. No one among us is unaware of how many bites tore him when he was ready to die.

They acted as though they were saying to him what Jeremiah says: “Come, let us strike him with the tongue, and let us pay no attention to all his words” (Jeremiah 8:18).

Oppressed by the weariness of such and so many things, he sometimes sought a place to remain [Note: I think this is said by anticipation of the monastery of Bobbio, where the author testifies at the end of Book II that Wala died], in the help of the Most High and under the protection of the God of heaven, where none of his enemies could approach him violently.

But while he took thought for himself, he left us, for a time, desolate and full of sorrow. Therefore my inward parts have been greatly disturbed, my liver has been poured out upon the earth because of the absence of so great a Father, and through my tears I cannot look upon the image of his character.

But I shall weep and continue to weep until my eyes waste away, so that at least in this way I may console my own miseries, since I have suddenly lost such a consoler of the soul.

### SEVERUS

I beg you to rest for a little from weeping, lest your inward parts again be stirred by fresh tears and we be unable to set down what we know.

Before darkness covers your eyes, let the image of his character be painted in its more beautiful colors. Then, at last, the full remembrance of his radiant face will open the hot springs of tears. In that jubilation, with him looking down from above, we shall shed tears—here rejoicing, there grieving; here sorrowful, there glad; here deprived, there carried upward.

For although it is a matter of sorrow that we have lost him, it ought to be a matter of joy that we have sent such a man ahead as an intercessor to the palace of heaven.

Do you not know that Jeremiah, whose type this man bears, though the people had sunk him into a sufficiently muddy pit, was finally lifted up to the stars and prays greatly? If that man poured out unceasing prayers to God for those for whom, while he lived, he had been forbidden to offer prayer and praise, what do you think this man will do for those whom, as dear sons, he left so suddenly in desolation?

For we read this said of Jeremiah:

> “This is the lover of the brothers, Jeremiah, the prophet of God; this is the man who prays much for the people and for the whole holy city of Jerusalem.”

If that man, though forbidden, takes up praise and prayer for the city and the people whom he once lamented so bitterly while alive, for whom he composed dirges and established laments, what will this man do for his own people, whom he loved?

I admit that he will be an intercessor not only for us, but also, like Jeremiah, for those whom he endured as enemies. For the rebukes of both men, so severe against the people, arose not from hatred but from love.

Although these people may believe this less readily, we who knew him cannot doubt that the promises of Christ will not be denied to one who endured such great struggles for the truth.

If faith could be purchased at a price, we would pay whatever was necessary so that they would cease pursuing with hatred the man whom charity nourished, justice advanced, and piety adorned.

Therefore I urge them to be silent and stop cursing, lest they reveal their own evil deeds. For they ought to imitate—more than their own perverse faith—the cunning and faithlessness of this man, as they accuse him of possessing [Col. 1566D].

### PASCHASIUS

You attack sharply, brother Severus. Take care to observe Terence’s maxim: “Nothing in excess.” For all whose conscience is less secure are, somehow, more suspicious; they take everything as an insult, and because of their own deeds they always think that they are being blamed.

# CHAPTER THREE

### ADEODATUS

I think that if you show what true faith toward one’s neighbor is, and what sort of faith is to be kept toward lords to whom it is promised, each of us will be able to see more clearly and judge his own conscience. For this charge is brought against him: that he did not keep the faith owed to the Emperor [Col. 1567B].

### PASCHASIUS

You urge us very well to make clear how many adulterate true faith and corrupt it, being ignorant of what they promise.

The faith of Christians, according to the Apostle, is that which works through love. Remove love, and faith is abolished [*abolitur*; variant *aboletur*], because love circumscribes all the rights of faith.

Moreover, love of Christ and of one’s neighbor admits no sin, at least not with consent. It is therefore clear that anyone who loves or consents to what is unjust wickedly hates his own soul, as well as the person to whose iniquity he gives favorable consent.

From this it follows plainly that faith ought not to mean that one should seek whatever one wishes, so as to rise up in accordance with the will even of an earthly lord against God’s commands; otherwise, by consenting to evil, one would lose the faith that works through love in one’s neighbor.

Rather, one must provide what belongs to love and, through faith, fulfill with greater constancy and care whatever concerns the salvation of one’s neighbor.

Otherwise Herod and his accomplices would have been free from guilt because they were bound by an oath—if faith prescribed that whatever one wished should be done and whatever one promised should be fulfilled.

Therefore one must first take care not to promise anything rashly under oath; then, if one has made a vow, one must avoid advancing toward worse things.

“For we ought to owe nothing,” says the Apostle (Romans 13:8), “except to love one another.” Therefore each person should fulfill what he owes by paying it, and by fulfilling it should owe it: namely, the faith that works through love.

Otherwise faith is not faith, because it does not arise from love of God and of one’s neighbor, but is an earthly adjuration, a carnal and diabolical bond [Col. 1567D].

No one therefore keeps faith well where God is despised and the salvation of one’s neighbor in the future life is neglected.

### ADEODATUS

Alas, how miserable are the ages of our time, in which willing always comes first [printed *tantum*; read *tam*]! Then each person marshals whatever he understands and can do in order to bring his desire to completion, even when the desire is perverse—especially when it would first be necessary to understand what one ought to will, then to will what one understands, and finally to do, with good will, what one is able to do.

Now the minds of all give birth to monsters, since what ought to follow goes first, while the head, which ought to precede, follows everywhere instead. In the middle, power swells playfully on every side, and consequently what the Comic poet says comes true for everyone:

> “I want, I do not want; I do not want, I want.”

Each person suffers from an exceedingly unhappy and childish confusion.

### PASCHASIUS

For this reason, about two years ago, when I was speaking to one of the leading senators and urging him to correct himself, I overcame him by reason and by divine judgments. He then said to me:

> “Do you hear me? Those things you describe, although divine, had a place and force for the conduct of life in the age in which we were born and at the time when we were born. But in this age in which we now live, you should know that they contain no usefulness or reason.”

With these words we departed: he laboring after his own will, while I rested from my own ability.

### ADEODATUS

This matter seems not merely to be blindness, my Paschasius, but a remarkable madness of mind. A person perceives where he is and what he is doing; yet he remembers where he has been and how uncertainly he is going forward, and still cannot return—or even wish to return—to what he was. Instead, by acting insensibly, he follows his own will, lest he who once was so return to himself.

### SEVERUS

Who, I ask, can be more deficient [printed *deficisci*; read *deficere*] in understanding than someone who does not perceive himself and does not hear what he himself says? But perhaps, as I think, you suppose that, by making such clear attacks, even your own raging silences cannot hear. For that reason you do not fear speaking such things freely.

### PASCHASIUS
We are speaking of what faith toward one’s neighbors ought to be, and what form it ought to preserve. For that reason I thought it should by no means be left unmentioned; for, as you know, our Arsenius truly possessed, displayed, and preserved this faith—faith which works with love, is supported by truth in all things, and strengthened by justice. It was not a faith that deceitfully misleads through flatteries or exalts whatever vices each person happens to favor. Rather, in every affair and word, in every matter and agreement, he searched to discover whether the truth, which was his friend, was present; and, as though examining each matter from the fingernail outward, he investigated the causes of affairs and transactions, lest falsehood might have cut a fissure somewhere. Then, so that the several parts of faith might proclaim the harmony of justice in a single concert, he set everything before his eyes, and commended it daily to the Lord in prayer, so that love might direct everything inwardly.

## CHAPTER IV

### ADEODATUS

[Col. 1568D]

I am astonished how, amid the various and innumerable occupations of affairs, as I hear, he could devote himself so intently to God, and remain present to himself wherever he was; especially since, whenever we wish to devote ourselves to God, we are drawn away, and when we seek ourselves, we can scarcely find ourselves.

### PASCHASIUS

I admit, my dearest Adeodatus, that he was always with himself and with God everywhere. For, as the saying goes, he did not surrender himself to affairs but entrusted himself to them; and, while managing his thoughts amid the crowds of people, he always carried something salutary in his mind. And, so that the faithless may believe, I testify that I never saw anyone who was so present to himself everywhere and who walked about so watchfully; so that he scarcely, or never, allowed himself to be drawn away, although he was occupied with countless and very weighty matters.

At meals, whether he himself entertained guests or some great person invited him, I was never able to observe him taking food with such moderation over a sustained period that many would have regarded the refreshment of a meal as the height of abstinence and frugality of diet, if they had been able to attain such abstinence at least in Lent. Unhappy me, who am now deprived of his sight and am not ashamed to do before many what I then feared to do before him! For I knew that he would not spare me if I admitted anything immoderately. You should ask Severus about these matters, since he too [Col. 1569B] often endured this discipline with me.

### SEVERUS

I understand well enough what you are getting at: perhaps it will someday become clear that I had extended my hand to my mouth rather too eagerly. We often had to endure together the rebuke which he brought upon us on that account, and even today our consciences are scourged by his very frequent rebuke.

Yet concerning what you say, the fathers, brothers, and fellow disciples are witnesses. They know that, like a farmer hoeing, he immediately brought the word and sentence of correction as a hoe at the very beginning of sin, so that Christ’s harvest might spring up more abundantly. For he did not act like certain people who deliberate until offenses have grown large; rather, in each case he killed the origin of sin at once with the sword of the word.

How, then, could he negligently spare his own, when he yielded nowhere and never to those of higher rank unless he was giving admonition? He had made Solomon’s sentence his own: “The words of the wise are like goads and nails driven deep.” For with the point of his word he fastened down the growth of vices and more firmly established on high the beginnings of virtues.

Exceedingly fortunate and blessed was the man who, occupied with such great and alternating courses of affairs, remained one and the same, a continuous and outstanding censor of himself; who, even in such a lofty retreat, devoted himself to study, to God, and to love. This, therefore, was his business and the purpose of his business; this his leisure and his labor; these his fasts and vigils; this his care and perpetual concern of mind: that he never cease what he had once begun in the service of Christ.

Hence it shone forth most clearly to others that he was always so great and the same toward himself, God, and his neighbors; he was more severe toward no one than toward himself, and judged no one more than himself.

## CHAPTER V

### PASCHASIUS

I consider, brother, and recall what you are saying; but the place has not yet come—[Note: Something seems to be missing here, and therefore I omit it, or something similar.]—although unwillingly, the matters you propose. Nevertheless, I admit that I once asked him why he was so severe toward himself and, when alone, walked about so sad.

To this he replied: “You should know that I am with myself, and that I decide what is within me. For this reason I do not yet rejoice in any joys except those of hope alone.”

Let our people, then, consider this man who gnaw at him and accuse him on the basis of others’ faults—this man who examined himself so strictly. Do they think that, contrary to the Apostle, he will now be judged banished from the council of the just by the Lord? Rather, planted in Christ, to whom he clung in life, he joyfully sings: “You have delivered me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word” (Psalm 90:3).

But while he was being emptied of such and so many evils, he left us miserable. May they forgive us, then, if we slip more secretly into tears in our retreat, we who earlier restrained ourselves lest we seem to mourn one whom the wicked hated without cause. Now, however, when they have at last fallen silent, we shall relax our lamentation, since weeping and tears are the nourishment of longing, while longing is the pleasant remembrance of one who has been lost. For although harsh death terrifies us, the memory of a beloved name delights us.

Thus someone has said that the death of friends possesses a certain pleasure, and that their memory is sweet, like fruits that seem at once pleasantly sharp. When, therefore, an interval presents itself, the pure delight of hope returns to us, because we love those whom we possessed as though we too were suddenly going to depart from here, and we have lost them as though we still possessed them.

Glorious, blessed, and sweet is this hope. Therefore, my father Arsenius, we rejoice on your account and console ourselves, because we presume that you have reached the blessedness of hope, and we believe that through your merits we too are helped toward that place—though for the moment sorrowful here, yet rejoicing, since a happier outcome awaits you than an end awaits us, unless your departure comes first.

Perhaps it would have been better for you to go, so that Christ’s consolation might come, so that, leaving everything behind, we might swiftly be with you in mind, and so that, through unwearied prayers, our ability to obtain pardon might receive strength and our spirit might receive confidence to arrive there.

Therefore, my Father, we are not miserable because of you but blessed: for your presence in spirit is not lacking to us, nor is the shepherd’s care diminished; rather, grace is increased. For what is death except sleep? We can establish this from many passages of Scripture. If, during the quiet of night, while still attached to bodily bonds, souls shut up as though in the prison of their limbs can perceive higher things and all that is distinguished by its own images, how much more, stripped of every stain of corruption, do they behold them—as one of the saints says—with an already pure and ethereal sense?

Thus we are confident that you, Father, are more present to us than, during the use of this life, we were able to have the opportunity of seeing one another. For, as we believe, your sweet absence is present to us everywhere, whereas then your presence could not be wholly so; just as now your very presence is absent in an unpleasant way, because you are believed to exist in the one to whom all things are open and present.

Great, therefore, is the power and ineffable virtue by which neither death nor time can tear away those whom that one and same majesty of God has blessed. Hence, my Father, you are believed rather to live for us now, since you live better for yourself.

The tears are already becoming sweet, and weeping more pleasant, because although death is hated, your love is life for us. For death, having been drained, has been absorbed into life; therefore you live, Father, and live blessedly.

We ask you to be present to us, you who live better with him in whom all things live and in whom we move and exist. The promises of this hope cool the ardor of our spirit; our affection, released, also gradually evaporates.

I ask that the image of your spirit may fly to us continually and pour over us sweet visions of true sleep, if it is permissible to say so, so that you may be wholly present, though we are deprived of the sight of your bodily form alone. For your daily presence arouses constant remembrance, and affection reproduces your image; when these are brought before us, they renew our grief.

Therefore, my Father, be present to us at times, and we embrace you in mind and spirit. We kiss you again and again, address you, and clasp you.

Utterly unhappy am I, who heard the final admonitions of your words from so far away. For you said—as our Chremes reported to me, and said in these words: “So, my son, act: if in any way you can, put whatever good you know into practice, lest you be found lesser than yourself.”

These were your final words to me, my Father; these were the commands of your judgment. You were not concerned that I should know what is perfect—for I did not know it—but that, by knowing, I should make progress.

To you, unaware of what was soon to happen, something that cannot be passed over, I had replied—more truly than jokingly—that three things do not continuously exist together in a human being: namely, knowing, willing, and being able. For many things that we know to be good, under the pressure of sins we sometimes do not will; and if willing is already present, we sometimes do not have the ability.

God alone is such that his knowledge is neither greater than his will nor his will greater than his power; rather, whatever he knows, he wills and can do. Therefore he accomplishes all things in his wisdom. Human beings, however, have none of these things without the grace of Christ.

And so I ask you: renew us by your prayers and assist us with your petitions. For a teacher’s admonition is perfect if he helps by his prayers those whom he has admonished. This is the duty that belongs to your praise: you were in no respect deficient, provided that, after announcing God’s will to your own people as far as possible, you commend them through prayer and merits, so that those who through you were permitted to know what is expedient may receive from God the will and ability to do what pleases him.

## CHAPTER VI

### ADEODATUS

I should like you to go back further, to the early training of so great a man, since we believe that the merits of such perfection grew together with him. True virtues do not arise without innocence; innocence, in turn, is made firm by the effectiveness of the virtues. Moreover, firmness is strengthened by the long habit of good works as merits increase.

In a fitting alternation in the perfect man, simplicity should correspond to prudence, and prudence should reinforce simplicity, so that what is in flower may produce fruit, and the flowers may first promise the fruit of good hope. A flower may sometimes fall without fruit; fruit, however, does not spring up without a flower.

Therefore I should like you first to unfold the flowers, so that sweeter fruit may abound, since, although fruit is useful, the flower of tender life gives off a more beautiful fragrance. Hence, even if this man flowered before, the fuller virtue of his flowering came through the grace of Christ.

### PASCHASIUS

[Col. 1572A]

You ask, Adeodatus—you ask perhaps about the time when I was not present. Yet, because he shone as a man known from the womb, I have learned many things worthy of the most enduring remembrance from reliable reports.

From childhood he was assigned, during his early service at the palace, to liberal studies, possessing nobility of conduct and uprightness of understanding. Augustus, recognizing the power of his ability—although he was his cousin, the son of his paternal uncle—decided, not by chance but by divine dispensation, to humble him at someone’s instigation and reduce him among the lowest, so that his tender age might be tested in the furnace of trial like gold. In this way, while still young, he would learn to endure adversity bravely no less than prosperity with equanimity.

For it is written: “As the furnace tests gold, so temptation tests the righteous” (Wisdom 3:6). And so the testimony of his justice was already shining forth, so that greater grace might be bestowed.

After being worn down for a long time in the kiln of humility, he became conspicuously gentle. Entrusted to some nobleman under a free custody, upright and capable, his reputation grew daily, and the praises of his life and renown were heaped up.

Who, then, would not recognize that he was already being tested by a divine apprenticeship, when, though no faults of wrongdoing existed, he was so oppressed by a neighbor—innocent and just—as though he were guilty and alien to the nature of Augustus?

Some report that, at that time, while he was traveling sadly and driving oxen with a wagon, he encountered a certain peasant, girded with a belt and armed. Arsenius said to him: “Would you, poor man, lay down the arms you are carrying and take up these with which I am encumbered?”

After these words, the traveler, scarcely believing what he heard, finally deprived himself of his own arms without loss and carried away the unexpected gifts.

Then our Arsenius said: “The lowly things suit me better with a wagon, since I am not now engaged in the warfare of this world but in the business of common life.”

What, then, brothers, was he saying except what David said by his example: “I shall become still more lowly, and I shall be humble in my own eyes” (2 Samuel 6:22)? Especially since, the more unworthy someone appears to himself for God’s sake, the more acceptable he becomes to God; and when he regards himself as great and self-sufficient, he is, as we read, considered little.

What more is there to say? After these things had been completed, divine power soon advanced him through many honors, and he became more acceptable to everyone the more upright he was. He was restored to the palace and elevated in favor.

As he progressed and grew daily, Augustus appointed him steward of the entire household, and he was everywhere revered as second after Caesar, so that one might have thought another Joseph was moving the scepters of the kingdom.

[Note: This is why, when Bernard, son of Pippin and his own nephew, was sent to Italy, Charles ordered Walo, the son of his paternal uncle Bernard, to remain with him until the outcome of events should bring security to our people, as Einhard says under the year 812. The author of the Life of Louis the Pious, under the year 814, says: “Wala, who held a position of the highest rank with Emperor Charles, was greatly feared, lest he might be plotting some evil against the emperor. Nevertheless, he came to him very quickly and, submitting himself to his will with the deepest humility, commended and subjected himself to him according to Frankish custom.”]

He was on everyone’s lips and pre-eminent in every matter, especially as an exactor of justice. Through his diligence, civil law was administered to the good without evasion; and his presence terrified the guilty no less than it soothed the pious.

A senator, so to speak, among senators, already more effective than all those holding confidential office, because he wanted nothing except what he could know to be most excellent: provident everywhere, ready everywhere, and devoted and energetic everywhere. No one dared indicate in his presence that he wanted anything other than what was just.

Before him, the right of citizens never became a commodity; rather, acting generously in all things, he appeared voluntarily to those who sought him. Sometimes, therefore, he was sent specifically to deal with matters that properly belonged to Augustus.

Thus, after he had already assumed a military command, he is said to have led an army against the enemy in Caesar’s place with great distinction.

[Note: Namely, against the Abitrices; below, chapter 11, I believe this name refers to the Abotrites. After peace was made between Charlemagne and Hemming, king of the Danes, in the year 811, six of the Frankish nobles signed the treaty of concord. The first named is Walah, son of Bernard; afterward come the others, all counts, as Einhard writes in his Annals. At that time the names “dukes” and “counts” were used almost interchangeably. Add that Wala had been married, as is shown by Book II, chapter 8.]

The ferocity of barbarian peoples, subdued by his acts of kindness, loved him exceedingly, as you know; and, once he had become a monk, they often flocked to him with devotion.

## CHAPTER VII

### SEVERUS

[Col. 1573B]

We often discussed what it was that made him love those same peoples, and why he would so eagerly go to them, frequently setting aside the leading men of our Order, and devote himself to them completely and tirelessly. But the reason is easily understood: he did these things out of an affection for piety, so that he might provoke them by his example and instruct them in honorable conduct, since they had only recently come to the faith of Christ.

### PASCHASIUS

That is so, my Severus. For this reason he was more acceptable and, as I myself often observed, dearer to them than anyone else.

Perhaps you remember when we went there together with our Antonius on account of the new monastery.

[Note: That is, New Corbie, which monastery the abbot Antonius, or Adalhard, visited in the year 822 in order to put the finishing touch to the work already begun.]

There I observed how highly he was regarded and how important he was. If I may put it so, had he descended from heaven, he would have been revered even more than he once had been in the palace, although he was now a monk.

When we came to certain people who did not recognize him in his changed clothing, they were ravaging the fields of their own people in a hostile manner and laying waste to the neighboring lands. Our Antonius, being kindly disposed, wished to correct them by his gentleness, but he was not heeded.

Then he presented Arsenius to them and had him address them, so that they might restrain themselves from such acts. When they heard this, they began to look at him more attentively, wondering whether he was the man we claimed. Although many of us tried to persuade them, they scarcely believed it, because they could not imagine that so distinguished and powerful a man had come to such humility and degradation.

One of them said to him: “Are you the man whom our famous world celebrates so widely?”

He replied: “I am.”

Then, I admit, another said: “You are not even worth the very least part of his finger, much less worthy to be called such a great man.”

After these words, we all smiled slightly and departed.

### ADEODATUS

I wish you would proceed more seriously. I do not see what benefit there is in such matters, in which the world’s grandeur is praised, especially since death will also obliterate whatever pleasures there may have been. Do you not know that the person who cultivates the world loses what is precious? For what else is it to revisit the pomp of the world than to deny the faith of Christ?

### PASCHASIUS

I think exactly so. Yet good men, although they seem to engage in worldly things, preserve a directed mind and do not allow themselves to be summoned away toward all external matters, even if everything resounds outside and is supported by great commotion.

What, then, do you think is more difficult: to use purple and vessels made of gold and silver as though they were earthenware, or to use sackcloth and not be moved? Is it possible to use those same humble things as though they were most precious, without being affected by poverty?

### ADEODATUS

I would call a man capable of both things one of great virtue. But such a person is scarcely, or rarely, found: one whom elevation does not cast down, whom lowliness does not move, whom the height of wealth and honor does not exalt, whom poverty does not affect, and whom the business of varied affairs does not exhaust.

### PASCHASIUS

Yes, Adeodatus, that is so. But true virtue exists in both conditions when a good and devoted mind expresses it: when neither desire nor greed nourishes the spirit, but generosity ennobles one’s conduct and uprightness commends one’s life. Virtues do not quarrel; vices do not oppress; one passion of the emotions does not harass another; external circumstances do not destroy what is within.

Otherwise, even in the desert, what benefit is there in the harshness and silence of the whole region if corrupt passions rage within and vices alter the mind? Therefore true and peaceful rest is that which reason orders everywhere and the serenity of religion commends.

For this reason, as we have learned, certain people who withdraw from the world still remain amid its waves, because they have not proved that they have departed from it in mind. Others, however, whose early training in virtue took place amid military affairs, later come to the service of Christ purer and clearer-sighted than if they had been inexperienced.

### ADEODATUS

Yet there must be experience of virtue in these men, on account of which they are judged distinguished; for even pagans were considered capable and upright among their own people, and some are said, according to popular estimation, to have been admitted among the gods.

### PASCHASIUS

You seem to me, in everything we discuss, uncertain and infected, as it were, with a plebeian coloring, unable thereafter to receive any other movement of the mind—especially since varied rumor infects minds with a variety of distortions.

Perhaps you too have been so infected by the slanders of many that you can no longer accept another judgment about this man, whom many so tear apart and the ignorance of the crowd gnaws away at.

### ADEODATUS

[Col. 1575A]

Do you not remember Cato’s saying, that many people say many things, and therefore trust is rare? Nevertheless, concerning this man I have, I admit, the best possible faith. I clung to him at the end of his life; I came to know him, though late, and loved him greatly, adorned as he was with virtues.

But faith should not easily be given concerning everything. Hence the Apostles too are said to have believed slowly, lest their faith appear rash. We too, therefore, ought to do nothing precipitately or thoughtlessly. We must neither be so infected by the impression made by the crowd or by anyone else that we become unable to accept what is better, nor, so to speak, be softened like wax, receiving upon our surface the impressions of every seal.

Each person’s image must therefore be tested, and his faith tested as well, so that once you have tested something thoroughly, you do not judge it again.

### PASCHASIUS

You admit this correctly. But I want you to consider how upright men lived amid the highest honors of the world and how capable men soon passed from military service to the grace of Christ.

I shall say nothing, then, of David, whom neither royal dignity nor abundant possessions enticed, nor the occupation of affairs turned away from the gift of grace. I shall say nothing of all the others who, adorned with the flowers of virtue at the summit of greatness, are said to have pleased God and to have shone with many sacred mysteries.

I shall come to our own men, whom the Church of Christ received from the world’s military service as glorious bishops. I speak of Ambrose, who immediately gained the episcopal chair from the prefecture; and of Hilary, whom Gaul celebrates as an outstanding teacher.

Such men, and men of this kind, the world has often raised up from itself through the grace of Christ. Therefore there is no doubt that divine providence established this man, too, adorned with the jewels of virtue amid the insignia of senatorial dignity, and that mercy refined him, so that, transformed from so lofty a position, he might become a vessel of honor in the monastic life.

## CHAPTER VIII

### SEVERUS

[Col. 1575D]

It has long been my expectation to hear what doubts you wish to raise about a man whom—as I must confess—we knew more deeply than we knew ourselves, to whose inner life we were privy, whom we do not doubt to have been a follower of justice and truth, and in whom we trusted more than in ourselves.

Perhaps, then, like certain philosophers, we hold everything doubtful and philosophize that nothing certain can be grasped. Otherwise, ask our Chremes, or this Allabigus, whose trumpet blast might perhaps even persuade the deaf that he lived, while still in the world, more distinguished than all the others in honorable conduct and virtue.

### CHREMES

Almost no one is unaware of this, because he was unknown to scarcely anyone; but envy denies what conscience approves in many.

From this it is perfectly clear that, although he may have given offense, he was nevertheless superior to all the leading men of our age, even in the eyes of his rivals; and, if he did not please them, he was nevertheless called good by everyone.

In the world he was a generous giver of alms and such a liberal distributor of tithes that you would have judged him to be distributing not his own possessions but things entrusted to him for this purpose. After the annual tithe, he continually devoted a daily portion to the poor of Christ, both from every income and provision for sustenance and from the various expenses of gifts. He reckoned this as his inheritance, this as the price of his profit, this as the merchandise of his justice.

But, as I see, our Allabigus is becoming angry, as though rebuked; perhaps for that reason he sometimes rubs his bare hand and does not think well of what you are proposing.

Then he said:

“Why, then, are you sowing jests in a playful manner? And if I seem bald to you, why do you despise Elisha? Do you not know, Chremes, that many winds have blown upon me? Perhaps, then, I acquired these things by swearing on this head.

But now, since they do not believe me, I have found something new, after Terence, by which to pursue those who wish to be first of all but are not. When they laugh, I smile back; I admire their talents; whatever they say, I praise it; and if they deny something, I praise them. Whatever someone denies, I deny; whatever they affirm, I affirm.

Then I commanded myself to flatter everyone, because that is now a very profitable business. Nevertheless, I shall at least show a little faith, since I am fully conscious of how well I know this man, and I shall invent nothing false, because I find no one dearer to my heart.

In his own time he was more acceptable to everyone, although the monstrous final age of this world foolishly and wickedly hated him and pursued him with lies.

Yet I ask you not to think me so sluggish, ungrateful, inhuman, or foolish that the habit of so great a man, his close companionship in life, love, and shame at forgetting him do not move and admonish me to keep faith with the man with whom I endured many things, from whom I learned more, and through whom I came to know the very best virtues even while still in the world—on account of whose love I first left the world after God.

Therefore, if any of you has opposed me with something from the horn, let him hear the trumpet of truth. For although the envious may grow deaf, this Arsenius was a true athlete of Christ. And although, being unskilled in speech, I may be unable to enumerate many things, I do not blush to mourn before others whenever I bring them back to mind, so that in this way at least I may cool the full misery of our sorrows.

For although I think we should rejoice that we possessed such a man, we must also weep sufficiently because, having always lived with him, we were absent from him at the end. Perhaps, if we had been with him, we would have received more of his spirit.

Have you not read what Elijah said to his own Elisha when Elisha asked that a double portion of his spirit might be in him? ‘If you see me when I am taken away,’ he said, ‘what you ask will be granted’ (2 Kings 2:11).

So too, brothers, if we had been with him when he departed from here to heaven, perhaps he would have poured out upon us some pledge of his spirit. But now how miserable we are, since we were not even permitted to know the hour of his departure, while we thought he was still alive!”

### PASCHASIUS

As I hear it, this shaven man who seemed an ignoramus has suddenly become a philosopher of lamentation, and there is no doubt that he has been inspired by the spirit of the man whom we mourn.

Otherwise, if he had not been touched by that spirit, how could he have anticipated such things before the son came there, when the time for lamentation with his innermost being poured out would come? For he is not the flatterer of falsehood, as he pretended, but, as I perceive, a denouncer and herald of truth.

Someone may think little of what he hears, especially since I have no friend today before whom I would dare reveal all my secrets, although this man exposes even our secrets to our enemies. For sometimes dignity prevents disclosure before one person; before another, shame at the foolishness of the deed restrains us, lest we seem faithless or insolent.

Therefore it is our task to understand when and wherever circumstances require us to flatter or obey, and, concerning this man, somehow even to remain silent. Since we could neither deliberate beforehand about the death of so great a man nor foresee it, we must now deliberate beforehand about what we shall say, and to whom, and when.

Our spirit had been sufficiently afraid to think of something like this about him beforehand—something whose occurrence we would eventually mourn. It was not that we were ignorant of the human condition; rather, a certain habit of wishing had clouded our sense of our common fragility, so that we knew how to think of him only in favorable terms.

Thus, when long ago I had been sent by Augustus on the business you know about, before I reached Agrippina on my return, I learned that the man whom we now mourn had received exile as his reward. Several of us monks were taking our meal together, and a reading from the prophet Isaiah was being given, where it says: “Egyptians will rise against Egyptians, and Egypt will be torn apart within itself” (Isaiah 19:2).

Then I groaned; then, as though flooded and drenched by a downpour of tears, I withered, torn apart by grief, so that everyone was astonished. Some asked what had happened; others thought that I was conscious of some guilt of his. Yet none of them, who seemed excellent comforters, has ever been to me what he was yesterday.

Nevertheless, I admit that at that very hour everything that later happened came into my mind. Therefore there is no doubt that the divine Spirit fills all things everywhere, including even those things that it does not possess.

### SEVERUS

I shall speak of what is in my mind; you decide. While he was alone, while there was no other hope, while ability remained strong, many people favored him and awarded him the palm. But after the situation was reversed, those very people about whom you are asking were themselves reversed.

I would not say that such things happened merely by chance, since both the reading and the tears together revealed that our Egypt would be torn apart within itself. Perhaps even then the belly of our innermost being was lamenting, like a cithara, against the abominable things that were to come.

## CHAPTER IX

### ADEODATUS

When various affairs arise, the style of conversation becomes confused; the order of speech is not preserved, and the abundant stream of weeping is not drawn from the breast’s spring. I want you, therefore, to open for us the spring that is warm and to indicate what sort of man he was and how great when he came to the monastic life.

For although virtues are beautiful beneath a hidden cloak, and although it is beautiful for them to flourish amid the enticements of the world, they become more beautiful in the school of virtue, where, once vices have been cut away, the field is fragrant with the perfumes of fellow soldiers, and all meditate only upon what belongs to God and what is holy.

### PASCHASIUS

If you ask, Adeodatus, what sort of man he was when he came, I admit that he was such as that poet of yours, Virgil Maro, describes: “entirely smooth and rounded.” Although this verse is highly praised in your Virgil, it is read as much older in Horace, who, speaking of the wise man, says that he is strong and “entirely smooth and rounded in himself.”

From this it is perfectly clear—as in very many other passages—that your Maro, clever in talent, carried off praise from the opinions of others and, from many fragments of philosophers, made a banquet of vanity, at least for boys, like a beggar.

But our man shone more laudably than he, immediately illuminated by the grace of Christ after leaving the world. He came strong in God and smooth—or rounded, as they say—for nothing is more rounded in every respect from a point than when virtues accord with reason and with God.

Does virtue not rightly seem to you to be a kind of equality of life, everywhere corresponding to reason? And if one thing in life differs from another, does it not, if I am not mistaken, give greater offense—as that distinguished writer says—than if some part of a circle were separated from the other parts by a greater or smaller interval?

That, then, is true virtue and reason: they make life perfect. Life is perfect everywhere if it accords with truth and equals the virtues. Therefore a person is rightly judged capable and upright in life if he lives so well and honorably that he appears to live according to God through the virtues.

Yet scarcely anyone believes such things about this man, because he is everywhere slaughtered by hatred and envy. For that reason I think he should be praised more sparingly where truth is strangled by insults and envy destroys justice.

### SEVERUS

If you were living in the time of persecution, would you claim that you knew nothing at all about Christ? Or would you at least remain silent? Now, however, I ask you, set fear aside; you will not again swear anything here merely because someone demands it.

Otherwise say this: “If I harm what I love, I shall harm it without end.” For I have enough love from what I once drank in concerning him, and I can receive nothing else.

Therefore, if what has been seen does not suffice, let us ourselves also take up the weapons of virtue. For if I do not cease to praise God worthily for such and so great things, I shall be happier, although I myself am lesser than his admonitions and conduct.

### PASCHASIUS

We are undertaking great things, brother Adeodatus, but virtue is never anything except arduous. Let us therefore tell, as it is said, a story known throughout the whole world.

For, as you say, little virtue is shown by keeping silent about matters, just as, conversely, it is a serious fault to speak what ought to be kept silent—although in many cases it may have been useful to conceal what ought to be revealed, and to reveal what ought to be kept silent.

Our Arsenius came to the monastic life already almost perfect, although he is believed ultimately to have grown greater and better, since no one is unable to make progress in virtue during this life.

He came, as your aforementioned poet says, already:

> A good and wise man, such as Apollo, consulted,  
> Could scarcely find one among thousands of all mankind:

He examined himself as his own judge, completely and to the fingernail. I admit that I have never seen anyone who examined himself like this man—not merely daily, but continually probing the innermost parts of his own actions, as thoroughly as no most diligent judge investigates the affairs of another.

### ADEODATUS

I ask you: if he came already smooth and rounded, how could he later become greater and better than himself? Can anything be more rounded than what is round? And if it can, then what was round was not wholly round, so that, from the immovable point—that is, through the work of divinity—the circle of virtues might be formed.

### PASCHASIUS
[Col. 1579B] As far as the form required by the discipline of geometry is concerned, what you say seems to be the case. But if we speak of virtues, since they are always moved with perfect equality on every side within the sphere, with Christ inwardly giving them their measure, their beginning is initiated here, in accordance with the form; but there, where the city of virtues is, it reaches completion. Hence, in comparison with God, just as no one is good, so no one is perfect; and just as no one is perfect, so no one is smooth or round. Yet a human being is called both good and perfect; and if perfect, certainly smooth, because he is conformed to Christ, in whose circuit the rainbow is said to be found (Rev. 4:3), from which the whole perfection of the virtues is signified.

Moreover, no one makes progress toward these things who does not discover himself every day to be greater and better. Hence also the prophet says: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has set ascents in his heart” [Col. 1579C] (Ps. 83:6). What it means to set ascents he adds by explaining each one: “And they will go,” he says, “from virtue to virtue.” Thus the form of all the virtues, through the particular love proper to each, produces the soul’s measure or quality. It is therefore established that the soul grows through virtues, but through vices diminishes and tends toward non-being.

This man of ours, then, advanced every day from virtue to virtues, and likewise from being toward greater being; and just as he advanced toward what was greater and better, so, although he was already smooth through his virtues, he was continually shaped by Christ’s hand so that he might become more perfectly formed and round. But what sort and size of man he already was when he laid aside his worldly service is witnessed by the present Father and the brothers, who, attentive and vigilant enough, examined him by many tests of probation [Col. 1579D] and disciplines of careful training while, as a novice, he knocked at the door of monastic observance.

They bear witness that he was tested like gold in a furnace amid every harsh and bitter rebuke, so much so that, although he was still a recruit, he was already regarded as a perfect soldier of Christ. The Spirit of God was in him; and therefore, as the story goes, he was broken by no darts of annoyance, but every day emerged more thoroughly tested than before.

How true, then, is the Apostle’s statement that “all things work together for good for those who are called saints according to the purpose” (Rom. 8:28). For even the things inflicted upon him as evils certainly became gains for him. He sang with the prophet to the Lord: “Because of the words of your lips I have kept to difficult ways” (Ps. 16:4). I confess that what seems hard to many was light to him; for he was a monk.

## CHAPTER X

### ADEODATUS

[Col. 1580A]

What praise is it to declare him a monk? Are not we, and very many others, also reckoned monks by name?

### PASCHASIUS

Indeed, we are reckoned so only by name, but are found false in practice. Hence one of the Fathers, looking carefully at himself, said: “Woe is me, for I bear the false name of monk.” If you consider the matter diligently, monks are rarely found.

But this man of ours was one among thousands, the one man pointed out by the finger. Do you not remember how the eyes of all who came to us were drawn toward him? At once they looked at him among all the others, and, as though fixed upon a light, sought him out and desired to speak only with him. Even though he had been last from the beginning, he was honored by all above everyone else.

No one, as commonly happens even before the Father, wished to be found blameworthy before him, even in some trivial matter. His gravity and upright conduct illumined everyone; and therefore each person, with a modest mind, lowered his face before him. One might more readily commit something blameworthy in the presence of the sun than in his presence.

But now how wretchedly we live without him, enticed by the many practices of seduction! We are all made worse by license; whenever it enters someone’s mind, it frequently causes him to lose the reins of gravity. So ask Severus, if you wish to learn anything about him.

### SEVERUS

Brothers, brothers, what can I say, or where can I find an abundance of words, when nothing of him remains in me except the ability to weep and lament? It was good for me when, while I bore the yoke of my youth with him, I remained before him almost like a solitary and kept silent—more so than now, when the license to speak has been relaxed. I think that I then had greater freedom from blame in matters which I feared I might commit.

Through habit I suffer what is now almost universal among human beings: I see and judge another’s faults better than my own. For that reason I often commit dishonorable acts, especially because I frequently associate with those who know neither what is right, nor what is good, nor what is fair. They neither care for nor discern what is better or worse, beneficial or harmful. Nothing pleases them except what they desire; they acknowledge as knowledge nothing except what they want, even when reality does not permit them to be what they wish.

Moreover, we award the palm to, and magnificently exalt, anyone who possesses such force, power, and efficacy [Col. 1580D] in deceiving that he can establish falsehoods in place of truths and judge the wicked to be the best. For this reason, now is not the time to proclaim anything praiseworthy about him. Yet, since everyone knows him, even if they hate and envy him, much eloquence is not needed for his praise, since each person declares him more religious than all others of our time and more perfect.

For he was a disciple of monastic discipline in every respect, serving for a long time under a Rule or an Abbot. I say “disciple” because in everything he showed himself submissive and humble, rejoicing more in being subject than in presiding; yet he took care to be useful both under the yoke of a master and afterward as a superior.

Thus he is finally found to be a perfect Father and master, because he is approved as a more perfect disciple and son than the others—a kind of person you will find extremely rare, since individuals generally rejoice more in presiding than in being subject and useful. Otherwise there would not be such a scarcity of perfect superiors, nor such great difficulty in making progress; for many, although they preside, scarcely desire to benefit a few and harm many.

How great he was under the discipline of obedience is praised by many voices. Hence the following event: while he was still a novice, when the riverbed was swollen, it was ordered, as usual, that the brothers should go in and cut down the rising vegetation so that the river would not overflow further. Then he began exhorting the others to go inside wearing only their tunics, so that they might work more effectively. At these words, several entered with him.

After they had suffered intense cold, word was brought to the Father at the monastery. At his command they were immediately taken out and disciplined, so that they would not dare such things again. It is therefore clear that, through the fervor of a good love—if it is permissible to put it that way—an excess amounting to fault often occurs, when the mind deliberates less because it is compelled by the love of charity, although the Apostle Paul says: “Charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13:18).

We read that such things often happened to Peter as well, when he considered too little what he was expressing with his mouth. Yet this excess, if I may confess it thus, is not a mark of love but of ignorance; hence its flame is cleansed more lightly.

Did you not see what sort and size of man he was when he presided over our hospitality? How humble, how devoted! Which nobleman have you ever seen constantly seeking such lowly tasks, enduring such harsh things, and carefully handling such repulsive and foul objects? I do not mean merely the lowly footwear of guests, but the wounds of the poor and their foul clothing. Sometimes he washed them as though carrying aromas. He tirelessly endured all their needs without growing weary.

O good Lord Jesus, how tireless you made him for every duty of love! How vigorous, effective, and devoted! He labored at his frequent ministry with such attentiveness that during the day he placed the care of the poor, guests, and sick above all things and before everything else. At night, after completing a very brief period of sleep, he lay prostrate on the ground before the holy altars with Mary, no less tirelessly before the brothers’ vigils than after them, at the feet of the Lord Jesus.

You know, Lord Christ, with what rain of tears he watered the ground, asking you, sighing for you, seeking you, knocking at you, so that you might open to him the door of your mercy [Col. 1581D]—that you might also open what you had hitherto closed to him, and receive him where in your clemency you had opened it to him. Once these doors had been opened, as we believe, he then entered by knocking in faith; now, enjoying their contents, he embraces them in the love of charity.

He could say with the Prophet: “My eyes have failed at your word, saying: When will you comfort me?” (Ps. 118:82). I therefore confess that I have often seen places damp with the showers of his tears and observed eyes almost consumed by weeping.

You too, I think, saw him frequently worn down by the anguish of vigils; you saw him wet with tears; you saw him oppressed by groans; surely you saw him thinned by wasting, his skin clinging to his bones through his frugal diet, and his face wasting away beneath the labors of his life [Col. 1582A].

For he practiced both lives in their proper times: the active life by day and the contemplative life by night. Sprinkled on both sides with their flowers, he knew, with Mary, although he was often with Martha, that “one thing is necessary.” Therefore he continually strengthened each activity toward that one thing: there he breathed toward it with sighs, here he drove himself toward it through the duty of love. By day he labored to pour the sweat of his body over the field of his body, and by night his tears.

You would have seen him in the morning covered as though with purple dew and sprinkled with showers of tears. If you wish to know the truth more fully, ask Severus, who always strove and was able to keep vigil more than I did, and therefore knew more thoroughly about all these things.

### SEVERUS

[Col. 1582B]

Although you say these things about me falsely, I nevertheless learned much about him, however imperfectly, which ought rightly to be praised. Do you not remember with what cold he sang to the Lord? He scarcely ever withdrew from the holy altars during the nights, except once to go to bed.

If you had asked him whether he wished to spend the night awake in singing, asking, seeking, knocking, and overcoming the night with groans and tears, he would have answered with that saying of Cato: “Whether I want to or do not want to; whether I can or cannot; nevertheless I am glad to keep watch for this reason: ‘Blessed are those who watch at my doors, for if they seek me at dawn, they will find me’” (Prov. 8:34).

Otherwise, unless it were for the blessedness of perfect labor, he would never have endured such and such great duties of vigil. Especially, no one could fail in the morning to see the dewy pavements of the ground [Col. 1582C] on which he had served the Lord during the night.

O what a time that was! You would have seen all the others roused on successive nights as though at the crowing of a single cock, and groans sounding deeply here and there.

But now, the more deeply we sleep, the more dead we live; for while we serve sleep, although we live, we are dead.

## CHAPTER XI

### PASCHASIUS

You speak only about his vigils. But either you do not remember what sort and size of man he was in the rest of his life, or else you dare not reveal what you reproach me for concealing.

### SEVERUS

I certainly dare, but one must not speak recklessly about anyone.

### PASCHASIUS

[Col. 1582D]

Take care, brother, lest you incur the censure of the comic poets; for, as they say, no one is free, no one obedient, no one able to handle the truth correctly, no one able to know anyone, nor to be known by anyone wherever life is not lived rightly.

Perhaps, therefore, you do not wish to show how highly you valued him, nor did he dare to believe that what is fitting for a father was due from you to him. If these things were so, perhaps you could never remain silent about him, even if you wished to.

### SEVERUS

I certainly desire to display in him the things that belong to virtue, since I believed him to be greater than myself. For he himself retained nothing about himself that I did not know. He poured himself out completely, so that he might form in me the features of a father.

He did not spare himself time or look back, but committed his whole self to God and transferred himself to the things that are unseen. Hence it became clear, whenever he heated the brothers’ winter dwelling in another’s stead, with how much more nobly he shone in virtues, and amid how many bright fumes of bitter trials he glowed, blackened more densely than pitch [Col. 1583A].

He was so consumed by that fire and the furnace’s blaze that you would have seen him no longer clothed in flesh, but animated by the spirit of a kind of sooty image.

### PASCHASIUS

I remember and recall it well, for the Lord tested him like gold in a furnace, so that at last he might receive him as a kind of burnt offering. He willingly exhausted himself through labors, desiring more to endure the world’s evils for God than whatever things are pleasant.

He afflicted himself with fasts and restrained himself through frugal nourishment. He also cared for everyone and was burdened by deep concern for the brothers. He diligently served guests and sick brothers. When several, out of reverence for him, had shrunk from accepting his service, he would often say:

“Hey, you! Why do you want to empty my office and take away the obedience entrusted to me?”

At that voice, whoever presented himself to be handled by his hands immediately became compliant. Hence, day by day, fame carried him farther and farther through everyone’s ears and commended him as worthy of praise.

What more need be said? After Antonius died, he was soon installed in his place as an eminent Father [Note: [Col. 1583D] Wala succeeded Adalhard in the year 826, as was said above in the Life of Saint Adalhard. This Wala was the one who persuaded Louis Augustus to send Anscharius to the northern peoples.].

On account of this election, I myself was sent by the brothers and soon obtained from Augustus what many had long desired. He had previously gone to visit our brothers, in order to conceal himself, and to cultivate that second [Note: [Col. 1583D] That is, Saxon Corbie, among whose monks living there under Abbot Adalhard Wala is numbered in the Corbie Chronicle preserved by Meibomius.] which is itself the mother by its name, and which is also the mother herself, but another; another, yet itself.

When he was recalled from there, our election soon seized him. Concerning his abstinence in life and the severity of his discipline, certain nobles—so I understood—then urged me, at Augustus’s command, saying that we could not endure him or imitate the pattern of his life.

To this I replied almost laughing: “Do you not know, hey you, who we are? Surely we do not monstrously wish, as some are accustomed to do, to choose the tail instead of the head? What do you think—if he were as great as some of the more excellent saints, would that change anything? Since we cannot keep pace with him, should we prefer one who walks behind rather than one who goes before?”

Then, smiling slightly, he reported these words to Augustus, as I believe. Once they had been spoken, I obtained everything I wanted, and exactly as I wanted it. Compelled by him, he obeyed the wishes of our community, though unwillingly—the same man who had previously evaded the office of superior for as long as he could.

### ADEODATUS

I fear that those who bark against such a man may perhaps feel that the one of whom you proposed to speak enigmatically is being praised too openly [Col. 1584A].

### PASCHASIUS

We are saying nothing offensive or unknown. Therefore, although the title is shadowed, the outlines of his deeds reveal him, just as painters do who know how to paint well and often portray faces in such a way that they speak without letters or voice.

But since I have not yet put my lips to such matters, and keep them stored beneath silence, that day will come, I believe, when I may openly recount his deeds and explain more clearly the things that are most excellent in him.

For the present [printed: interim], however, as you advise, since one must not go to excess in anything, it is better to speak cautiously and lament more fully that we live without him, when I would have considered it better to die with him. For his death has been transferred into life [Col. 1584B]—perhaps before the time we desired—lest wickedness change his heart. If this is not so, ponder the matter carefully.

### ADEODATUS

I truly believe and ponder it, because the truthful voice says: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live” (John 12:44). This man believed not superficially but wholly, with love, since the only faith by which one lives is that which works through love. And because he thus lived and believed in the one who gives life to the dead, he will not die forever.

### PASCHASIUS

Faith supplies this to you also, because you believe in this way. How much more should we believe that one who exudes the fragrance of such great works of virtue now receives imperishable fruits?

From the day of his profession he carried the mortification of Christ in his body [Col. 1584C]. Thereafter, when he had been elected Father, he advanced everywhere as though carrying Christ’s standard into battle, the first to take the field against the most savage enemies.

When his service was changed, the soldier too was changed. He who had first borne arms against the Abotrites [Note: [Col. 1584D] The Abotrites, northern peoples living beyond the Elbe near the island of Rügen, whom Charlemagne is said to have subjected to himself in the Life of Louis the Pious under the year 815.]—an untamed people—is finally praised more gloriously for having borne the standards of the virtues against the monsters of vice.

Thus he now carries the palm as his reward, having formerly despised the honors of the world for the sake of religion.

## CHAPTER XII

### ADEODATUS

We know all this; but I would like you to explain how he conducted himself under our Antonius, especially for the sake of our brothers living in Saxony, whose lineage he shared [Col. 1584D] [Note: Paschasius says the same below, in chapter 13. See the preliminary Observations on the Life of Saint Adalhard above.], so that they may fully know what sort of founders of their faith they possessed.

### PASCHASIUS

If I begin to recount this, I do not know where to begin, where first to turn, or where to proceed, because their life and actions were so inseparable that, after coming to know them, you cannot discover what one of them did without the other.

Even if some particular task was proper to one, or differed according to strength, time, or office, their common vow and single will nevertheless remained one. You would see them, as though under one yoke, drawing the plow of the Lord’s agriculture with equal composure and supporting one another’s burdens.

If it happened that they were separated for a while because of place or time, you would see one of them seek the other with groaning and longing, as an ox seeks an ox; for neither considered himself wholly present when the other was absent. Indeed, each was more with the other in affection than with himself wherever the other might be.

Just as an ox often bears witness through frequent lowing to the loving affection of the other if the one with whom it was accustomed to draw the plow at its side should be absent, so they groaned anxiously to one another out of longing, considering what the other might be doing, until they restored one another to one another.

Although one of them was older in age and the other quite young, their longing was equal. Although this one was stronger in body and the other loftier in the ardor of charity, their intention, purpose, and will were nevertheless one.

This one was sharper in perception, but our old man was broader in counsel and charity. This one was more fervent, as though on behalf of justice, but the other more mature in deliberation and deeper in foresight. Thus the younger would answer each matter more sharply on the spur of the moment, while the elder considered at greater length, both what would be beneficial in the present and whatever might happen afterward.

Although they were brothers in the flesh and most closely united in faith and will, they nevertheless appeared different in character in this respect: the elder represented in himself an excellent father to everyone, while the younger represented a disciple of monastic discipline and a most beloved son in every form of submission.

### SEVERUS

No one doubts these things, since, as everyone acknowledges, they were unique in holiness and religion among the entire royal lineage and most devoted to goodness. It is therefore no wonder that they strengthened one another through their virtues, since they also offered themselves as examples for others to imitate.

But although our Antonius now seemed weakened by old age and worn out by labors and cares, he was nevertheless greater in charity. This younger man always warmed his side through the zeal of a pious devotion and humbly fulfilled the duties of government on his behalf.

You would see him provide everything for him as for a son; show him reverence as a junior; serve him as a servant; show diligence as a most beloved brother; and at times offer tender affection as a father. He also received his authoritative counsel with complete humility as an elder. He possessed such patience in all things that no injury caused by annoyance could move him.

### PASCHASIUS

You remember well, brother, so well that, on account of one relationship, you seem to enumerate for us the duties of many relationships, so that in one and the same man we may grieve that we have lost not one person but several.

Especially when necessity compels us to remember what we lost both in this man and now in Antonius, whose brotherly brilliance [reading: charity] and the pleasantness of whose life shone and gleamed not only for us but throughout the whole empire of the kingdom, as though you could see two lights of heaven shining everywhere.

This one shone less, if I may put it so, and the other more, because the one was a father and the other a son; the one an older elder, the other perhaps sharper in the agility of his character, just as he was younger in age.

There was no flattery in them, but on both sides an expressed affection, and no disagreement between them. You could not find anything to add to the likeness of their purpose, because one spirit was in them, one faith, one harmony of peace, and true religious holiness in all things.

Therefore you would find among them nothing except the whole range of things belonging to charity and piety. You would not discover them exchanging roles, nor would you recognize either of them wishing anything other than what the other wished.

Their beauty of character consisted in this: if one surpassed the other in some virtue, you nevertheless perceived in them a single harmony of uprightness and one balance of virtue. What was proper to one in them was so present that you would judge it common to both, so much so that one could truly be called half of the other, while the other was regarded as the younger man’s completeness.

This is why, beloved, they planted such united and devoted shoots of a new planting in Saxony and, with the Lord’s favor, built monasteries for both sexes from the foundations [Note: [Col. 1585D] For men, the new Corbie; for virgins, Herford. Concerning both, see the history of the translation of Saint Vitus.]

## CHAPTER XIII

### ADEODATUS

[Col. 1586C]

I wonder why you wish to make them equal, since it was not this man but Antonius, because he was the pastor of this place and possessed the means, who built those monasteries. This man, however, was as though one among many, although more acceptable in grace, deeper in counsel, first in willingness, greater in assistance, and more earnest in his vow.

Therefore, although they always loved each other greatly and each wished the other’s labor to be his reward, the recompense for the work is rightly assigned to the one through whose labor the deeds accomplished are dedicated; for although neither ever had the will to undertake what was pious and holy without the other, the merit is nevertheless rightly assigned to the one who possessed the power to act, even though the labor was common.

### PASCHASIUS

[Col. 1586D]

As far as external human judgment is concerned, so public opinion often celebrates praises among the people. But the divine Judge inwardly distinguishes the grace he gave to each person, and afterward the labor each person expended after receiving grace.

The will of these two, however, was one, and each of their wills depended upon the other’s. Once the word had come forth from the mouth, it became clear to everyone that this plan had first been divinely inspired in this man, on the occasion of certain people of his own race [Note: [Col. 1586D] That is, Saxon, as above in chapter 12.] who came to us for the sake of conversion and handed over their possessions to us so that a monastery might be built.

Since this man was fervent in love for God and holy religion, for his relatives of the same race and for his homeland, he began to persuade the excellent Abbot, his namesake [Note: [Col. 1587] Namely, the younger Adalhard, who governed the monastery of Corbie in place of the exiled elder Adalhard.], more insistently and with repeated appeals, to undertake the labor of this work and provide the expenses. For he was already then the man in whom the domestic care and concern of our monastery rested, while its public repose was maintained.

When that Father heard these things, he made the vow and will of our Arsenius his own. Thus the work of virtue began and prospered for a time, until the old Antonius returned from exile and was restored to favor.

When he returned, this man’s will immediately became the old man’s will, so that you would see the son, in this matter of grace, beget an outstanding father. His repeated exhortation in this matter made the intention of the two one and their will one, for God had given them one desire and one aversion. They had already been undivided in all other matters as well, since neither wished to live without the other; their feeling of mind, desire, and concern for holy religion were one.

Therefore let the prudence of the sons consider—especially those whom their faith jointly begot and whom charity dedicated to the Lord in this work—whether a greater reward should belong to anyone than to the man who first, after God, caused the others to desire this through his repeated exhortation, and then compelled them to complete it.

By his powerful assistance he carried the work forward more than on his own shoulders, strengthened it through more careful counsel, and, with the emperor, the most eminent men of the entire kingdom, and everyone else whom he could reach, pursued this matter with every ingenuity, skill, and effort so that the labor might be completed [Col. 1587C], while he encouraged the work that had been begun.

## CHAPTER XIV

### SEVERUS

This is not hidden from us, since we perceived all these things very clearly and saw with our own eyes what he did. Several people even cried out that he was plundering all the goods of our monastery merely to enrich those places at our expense.

Yet this is part of his praise: without offending good men, he enriched those places with every kind of good and filled them with resources, while nevertheless not greatly diminishing our own.

He governed his brother’s household and already demonstrated in himself the office of abbot that he was destined to hold. Within, he provided the support and form of holy religion; outside, he provided a shield of defense, protection, and the adornment of complete uprightness.

Moreover, as I said, while he was already then sharing the care of the monastery with the Father, he was like an arbiter in counsel and an arranger of affairs, concerned for everyone. He was also a careful provider for souls, laboring so that our holy old man would not displease God in anything and so that he might please him in all things.

He was a dispeller of sorrow and the staff of the most holy elder’s old age, as well as the stimulus to virtue for all of us. The holy old man rejoiced greatly in him and congratulated himself on him as a renewal of the vigor of grace; and he himself illumined the younger man with his holy admonitions and virtues.

Thus you would see them refreshed by one another and making progress in all things [Col. 1588A]. Perhaps Paschasius knows these matters better: what they did, both within and outside, and how they did it. He was their close companion in everything, almost a third person among them in every undertaking.

## CHAPTER XV

### PASCHASIUS

I do not deny what you assert, especially how they built monasteries for both sexes among that people, with what devotion and fervor of charity, and with what humility and sublimity of virtues. In themselves they displayed the form of holy religion and examples of perfection, so that disciples following them under monastic discipline in succeeding ages might have in them things to imitate.

For, as the Lord, the teacher of truth, says: “Every disciple will be perfect if he is like his teacher” (Luke 6:40).
