Therefore these men truly became imitators of Christ, so that a future flock, securely placed upon the foundation, might be built in the Lord. Otherwise the summit might be raised without the squaring of virtues and the firmness of faith, or foundations might be laid without the summit of supreme perfection.

Because they made themselves worthy of imitation, they must truly be followed above all others, and their admonitions and examples must be preserved, lest what has been well established in the foundation totter badly at the summit, or what has been most excellently cast into the seed sprout worse in the shoot.

Then let our common lament be for our lost fathers, since our gain was common: we lived with them under such great discipline. When their duties are recalled and their virtues reviewed, the mind cannot remain unaffected. Yet in that very affection of mind and sorrow we are refreshed, and our love is renewed—especially those of us who saw them.

Moreover, for me, who was with them when they began these same works, their absence always appears present, as though I were turning my head backward: when they walked along the road, when they were in a place, when they arranged each detail, when they were in council and conversed with one another; when I drank in their grace with my eyes, perceived with my ears the speeches they proposed, and received the words they uttered.

If it is now a joy of mind for me to look back upon these things, what do you think, beloved, was the grace then, the joy, the blessedness of those times, when I saw them meditating on such great and such excellent things [Col. 1588D]?

I confess that I cannot recount how greatly I admired their virtues in silence within myself, nor how much I congratulated myself that the Lord had given me such patrons, in whose company I was, though unworthy, a third.

Not by merit, grace, or the honor of any dignity, but by their condescension, I was present merely as a spectator and auditor, counted among them. Nevertheless, clinging to them with sufficient modesty, I did not despair of possessing at least the efficacy of simplicity and innocence.

When I observed their prudence, I greatly admired in them the simplicity of a dove; and if I looked toward their simplicity, I found almost no spirit of prudence in myself worthy of admiration [reading: prudence].

They always joined this simplicity to marvelous virtues, and prudently matched in their examples what they said in words. What both had previously been scarcely able to accomplish, one of them would then complete alone. And if one sometimes did something without the other, you would nevertheless see both of them there, as though by their custom of acting together.

Although one of them occasionally presented an uncovered side, he nevertheless displayed the other’s affection beforehand in his character and office. Thus you would marvel at the one concern of their minds, one holy and irrefragable grace; though not one body, one strength of mind, one purpose, and one modesty of reflection.

When they stretched measuring lines by hand, measured with a reed, and laid out both sites [Col. 1589B], marking the places where each feature was to be made, it seemed that they were measuring a building according to the structure described by Ezekiel (40:2), sloping toward the south, so that they might place its foundation and summit in heaven.

When they raised their steps together, they lifted their faces and eyes there, so that you might judge them to be entrusting to God in heaven whatever they planned to accomplish on earth, and placing there the *katabula*—the foundation-bases or supports, the precise sense being uncertain—where scarcely the summits of others rise.

### ADEODATUS

As I see it, after the manner of the Apostle Thomas, these men were laying the foundations of places and the structures of houses that would never grow old; they were building workshops and raising summits that would never collapse.

Otherwise, I do not believe they would have attempted such things in so distant a region unless, because the new light of Christ had recently shone upon that people [Col. 1589C] through the Holy Spirit, it had seemed good to them to establish heavenly buildings among them on earth, so that they too might say in the spirit with John:

“We saw a new Jerusalem happily descending from heaven in our own places, adorned in both sexes with its jewels.”

Thus everyone proclaims them throughout those same regions, so that no one may hesitate to say that in that people there are divine camps, dedicated to the Lord together with their twin offspring.

## CHAPTER XVI

### SEVERUS

Although all these things are as you assert, I would nevertheless like to know what more our Arsenius did in that undertaking than any one of us who were fellow-workers with the holy elder [Col. 1589D], especially since at that time he possessed no power or opportunity to do more than his other fellow soldiers.

Therefore we must take care not to attribute more to him than is appropriate, for the truth itself stands as it is. Perhaps, then, as was said above, such a great desire was divinely breathed into him; afterward, however, he shared with his other brothers a common will, a common ability—or inability—and common action, while obeying in each particular.

### PASCHASIUS
First, as you assert, he had this distinction of merit in the undertaking: that he himself conceived it in his mind before everyone else; then, once the matter became clear, he did more in this respect because he desired it more than anyone else. His own prior will generated, stirred up, and nourished everyone’s will in this undertaking, through his prayers and constant exhortations, together with prudent counsel. Thus, although in Antonius there was the power and outstanding wisdom to carry it through, as well as great strength to complete it, in this man there appears, in a certain way, a more excellent grace, although the grace was shared by both; for whatever Antonius did or desired began entirely with this man, together with God’s grace, and was nourished by him.

And not only what Antonius desired and did, but also whatever the others contributed through their support—for example, the exceedingly pleasant, wealthy, and fertile site on which the monastery is shown to have been founded, together with everything by which that place is surrounded on every side. Therefore, none of us is unaware whose inheritance it was—an inheritance that he would never have yielded to anyone else in his lifetime, not even, if I may say so, to a king—unless he had been compelled by this man’s divine exhortations. He could refuse him nothing, since from early youth he had been dear and intimate with him above all others. Moved, then, by this man’s prayers and counsel, and willingly persuaded by his urging, he gave to God whatever he possessed on earth that was dearest to him.

[Note: Gerard, in the Life of Saint Adalhard, writes that this place was granted by the parents of Theodradus [Col. 1590D], the Saxon who became a monk at Corbie in Gaul.]

Thus this grace is rightly attributed to him: he both chose for this undertaking a place once selected by the Lord and suited to it, and was able to obtain it—for I do not know whether any other mortal could have done so. In that same people he was greatly loved and exceedingly famous. This became clear when Antonius came to a certain assembly [Col. 1590C] not far from that place, where a crowd of them had gathered because of the two men.

When we had been received by them with reverence, they all began to turn their faces toward our Arsenius and, out of their immense love and admiration, to surround him more closely—so much so that, out of joy and longing, they were drawing him away from us. None of them was looking at Antonius, although he held the authority; we were supporting him on either side and, packed closely around him, were honoring him as best we could, like a lord. Yet none of them paid attention either to us or to him, or considered who he was.

Then Antonius, rejoicing in his humility because they had excluded us all, and exulting in the brothers’ reception of Arsenius, turned to me with a smile and said: “Brother, we can certainly leave here, since no one here cares about either of us or notices that we amount to anything.” And so, taking two of them and leaving everyone else behind, we returned happily and joyfully to the place already mentioned, as though we were alone.

I have said this so that the nobility of the sons may know what sort of founders they had: men who thought humbly of themselves in everything and, unlike others, were not moved by any of the world’s favor. Therefore, neither was the one confounded by shame, nor did the other become insolent through honor. The reception and fame of the one among the people were the joy and exultation of the other—not merely because he was agreeable and loved by everyone, but because he was worthy of love and acceptance, so that, according to God, he might prosper well in all things.

As for humility, I do not know who was more exalted in it, unless someone should wish to discover this from their deeds. Although both were distinguished according to worldly rank, they nevertheless competed with each other to see which of them would be found the humbler.

That is why Antonius, although he was father and lord, modestly showed his son and younger brother such reverence—so much, I do not know whether anyone would wish or be able to show as much to an equal. Conversely, who could adequately describe the care this man took not to be surpassed by anyone in service, in reverence for the honor due, in care and solicitude, in every service of dutiful servitude, in speech and dress, and even in his manner of walking? No one could imitate him.

Moreover, as an example to others, I shall reveal one instance among many of the abasement they showed toward themselves. This man, who was more sparing than everyone else even with the most humble food, also wished to be content with the customs of his homeland. He said that it was not fitting for a monk to wear more elegant clothing or to eat finer food than the fellow provincials among whom he lived, since he ought to be content with what was humbler according to the custom of the province in which he lived.

[Variant: “in which they live” / “in which he lives.”]

He therefore ordered shoes to be made for himself according to the custom of his homeland, called *Ruhilingos*, and wished to wear them, unless the Father had forbidden this for reasons of discretion.

But I am astonished that he wished to be so discerning in this matter, when in his own case—if it is permissible to say so—he may be judged superstitious. For at that time, while traveling, he allowed no arrangements to be made for him at night, as travelers usually do, by which we might be protected from the rain. Nor did he permit any tent to be obtained for him, day or night. Instead, we rested stretched out upon the ground, and, as a certain poet sings, the health-giving grass gave us sleep.

The blessed Father did, however, provide both for himself and for me with exceptionally deep and ample furrows in the field—such as are commonly found in that land. He ordered me to spread our bed there; their sides, enclosing us on either side, provided beautiful supports, while a horse saddle placed in the middle offered one “Alps” as a pillow for me and another for him. We had nothing else there except what we had above and below us during the day. This was the entire softness of our bed, and a sufficiently honorable display.

## SEVERUS

[Col. 1591D]

Nor does this seem superstitious, as you think, especially since Jacob, when he went through great hardship to obtain a wife, is said to have had nothing but a stone beneath his head on the journey and to have carried no comforts with him except a staff. What wonder, then, if this man, while going to betroth a virgin to Christ the Lord and present her as a chaste wife to one man, was supported by no honors and adorned with no display, since he had to demonstrate fully, both in himself and in us, everything he wished the bride whom he was leading to Christ to preserve? He wished her always to pursue most earnestly the most holy poverty rather than the world’s luxuries and to embrace the hard and rough paths by which one goes entirely to Christ.

For we know that the holy Father made himself worthy of imitation not only in this undertaking, but also in everything by which the religion of Christ is commended. Perhaps you say these things because so few people display anything of this kind in themselves, since everyone pursues the pomp of the world. Yet on the occasion of the journey you have mentioned, this man showed his sons even greater examples of virtue.

## CHAPTER XVII

### PASCHASIUS

What if I now turn my attention entirely to recounting their services and reviewing their virtues? The recollection itself, as I perceive, will renew our sorrows, whose memory is a delight to the mind and an incentive to virtue. Therefore, remembering them is a source of sweetness, since their holy memory is more pleasant and more joyful in the mind than any present enjoyment of luxury. Indeed, in the present age, rightly speaking, no joy exists without sorrow, no sweetness without bitterness, no dignity without confusion, and no gladness of mind without sadness.

For everywhere there is mourning, everywhere pain and groaning, since everywhere evil is heard—not merely every day, but every hour—and nothing but confusion is announced.

These two men, although evils were already multiplying, could not leave us entirely sorrowful, because they were men of virtue. They consoled us with their words, instructed us by their examples, strengthened us with their counsels, and nourished us with pious disciplines.

Therefore they still remain with us today and will always remain, if we are true imitators of them and lovers of virtue. If we truly love these virtues, we have already begun not to be here, but to live as exiles—at least in desire, by which our better portion exists. For we are never wholly in ourselves if we truly loved them; rather, we are in them, because they were the head in whom the greater part of us was contained.

And because both of them live in Christ, we ought for that reason to make our devout pilgrimage there more earnestly—to the place in which the fullness of all things and the portion of each individual are found. Hence their memory is more delightful than all riches and more welcome than any present good, since there is the whole fruit of our people.

Before they went there, they transplanted all their possessions to that place, so that they might raise us upward, us whom they were nourishing as little ones in Christ. How much more ought the sons whom they begot for this purpose to dwell there, so that they might blossom like lilies in the heavenly places and grow like the cedars of Lebanon on the heights?

## CHAPTER XVIII

### SEVERUS

As I hear it, Rome was built in one way by two brothers, while our new foundation, named after us, was built in another. The former was built carnally on earth, the latter spiritually, so that it might be extended in heaven. The former was built to subdue nations under its rule, the latter to draw its own people out of the world. The former was built to increase in possessions and grow rich in material abundance, whereas the latter, rich through blessed poverty, was to have its foundation in heaven.

That one therefore began to be built in blood and grew through warfare and bloodshed; this one was built so that it might love the poverty of the present life in the spirit and become rich in heavenly things.

### PASCHASIUS

As I see, you are acting according to your custom: you blame others severely before correcting them. Perhaps you are considering those whom these two brothers planted unanimously, so that they might grow and be extended in heaven. It already seems to you that they are acting contrary to their precepts and institutions and to their sufficiently prudent warnings: growing in possessions, overflowing with luxuries, and expanding through the honors and pomps of the world.

Otherwise, I think it would have been pointless to mention the two buildings, except that the former was built on earth in blood, while this one, dedicated to the Lord by these men, is being constructed according to what Ezekiel describes, as though it were a building sloping toward the south.

It has the same measurements, upon the same foundations, with the same width and length, the same number of gates, and the same windows; it has no other increase in the magnitude of its possessions.

When these two outstanding men were laying the foundations among the nations to the north of the city, together with their towers and fortifications, they earnestly urged three things above all: that the brothers should not rejoice in becoming excessively rich in possessions or seek the riches of the world by setting their hearts upon them, but should flee luxuries and pleasures as though they were poisons.

Finally, they warned them not to take pleasure in honors or pomp, as though these were offered for the sake of religion, lest they should become completely puffed up and perish in vain. We see that many well-founded churches in Gaul have perished in this way, having abandoned religion.

Therefore, instructed by many examples, these men warned their sons in advance not to overflow with human possessions, for whose sake they might serve the world, but to be poor in spirit, humble and meek, gentle and merciful, and always hungering for righteousness in all things. Thus everyone would wish them well because of the purity of their hearts; people would wish them prosperity and, rather than envying them because of their possessions and good fortune, would not oppress them with worldly servitude.

Even now, by God’s favor, everyone speaks good things about them and thinks well of them. They are still illustrious in virtues and admirable for the goodness of their lives, because their fragrance still spreads among them, their virtues flourish, their praises are proclaimed, religion is magnified, and their outstanding nobility is preached. Their blessing still flourishes in them, the most ample dignity of their life is commended, the abundant fruit of their merits increases, and splendid grace springs up and is exalted.

## CHAPTER XIX

### SEVERUS

Whatever their exceedingly great reputation for virtue celebrates everywhere would be praiseworthy, brothers, if they had not first formally alienated from our monastery the possessions entrusted to it, together with everything in those regions that had been bestowed upon us, from the lawful property of this monastery—which is highly remarkable—and had wished to make those possessions their own property personally.

This is especially remarkable since scarcely anyone who presides over a place fails to wish to enrich it with possessions more and more, so that he may be able to dominate and expand it further, under the guise of religion and with the pomp of power.

These men, however, acted in the opposite way. Not only did they refuse, although they could have done so, to enrich with possessions the place over which they presided; they also disposed of what had been entrusted to them and reduced it to the free use of the brothers, so that it would not belong to us.

### PASCHASIUS

What they taught in words, then, they did in order to confirm through examples. They warned us and the others not to accept unnecessary possessions or seek an abundance of resources under the guise of God’s religion. Rather, we should set a limit to the possessions and property of the Church, lest we extend a finger beyond it, as the prophet warns, or join field to field as far as the boundary of the place, without end to our covetousness.

[Note: Paschasius recalls these same admonitions of Adalhard for New Corbie in the Life of Adalhard above.]

But lest this freedom of action seem unjust to you, know that it is more fruitful and honorable—and therefore more just and useful—for these possessions to serve the Lord freely, directly, in the uses of the monastery, than for us to dominate them very inappropriately and superfluously by hereditary right. For wherever an inheritance is shown to serve the Lord or his Church, it is expended with sufficient religious devotion and charity in the uses of his servants.

Thus the gift of grace is greatly enriched when, from one root of perfect love, two monasteries of monastic discipline are multiplied.

## CHAPTER XX

### ADEODATUS

It is enough that up to this point you have discussed both men equally, since their virtue in action and their intention of mind were one. But because we have decided to pursue Arsenius in this work with lamentation—and because he labored even more in these matters—he alone should be commended with tears. For if he had not departed from here so quickly, perhaps he would have made the brothers of whom we speak citizens of heaven, since in everything he displayed contempt for the world before them.

He would certainly also have taught them to despise themselves for the sake of faith, just as he himself had first despised himself. He would therefore have brought everyone’s hearts together into one through the grace of charity, so that no one would extend himself beyond the norm and measure of monastic discipline toward the things that are outside.

This is sufficiently shown by the superior [Note: I think he means Warinus, Adalhard’s successor in the governance of New Corbie for thirty years; the author appears to attribute arrogance and swelling pride to him, although Warinus is highly commended in the little book on the translation of Saint Vitus.], whom they had preferred to preside there when he returned, if he had not, being expelled again so quickly, gone to Italy.

For we learned with certainty that he would by no means have presided there again until he had learned to think humbly of himself, not to be puffed up by his lineage, not to embrace luxuries, not to indulge in the frivolities and vanities of the world, and not to pursue worldly things.

You would certainly have seen, here and there, buildings of the heavenly homeland rising according to the pattern of that city which I mentioned above—a city that always inclines toward the south, is measured by heavenly dimensions, and does not expand in the world according to human standards. You would have seen towers and fortifications of faith being humbly raised there even to the heavens, every kind of virtue arising, and the place expanding not through the pomp of pride in possessions.

Nevertheless, although I confess this, his fragrance still spreads there today; virtues flourish, instruction in morals prevails, the nobility of his way of life remains, his gravity is admired, charity is praised, and the excellence of discipline is proclaimed in everything. Thus the fame of the mother is everywhere announced as exceedingly glorious because of the fruitfulness of the daughter, and abundance, spreading in every direction, increases throughout all her offspring.

These, then, brothers, are the praises of our Arsenius; these are the benefits of his work and the marks of his virtues. As long as the ages endure and the religion of the Churches remains, his praises and the fame of his good life will never cease from human lips.

Nor is this without reason, since the fruit will overflow in multiplied seed: the praise of the sower increases again in the harvest, and the harvest is multiplied through the years into many more.

Thus the sentence of the true God is confirmed, in which he says: “Everyone who has left everything that he possesses for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matthew 19:29).

This man therefore left many things but acquired greater things in the world, since, by loving the Church, he made all the Church’s resources his own. He left innumerable things, since he utterly trampled down himself and every desire of the present life. He left everything when he humbled himself so completely that we saw him daily wearied by labors, tormented by innumerable vigils, and unceasingly mortifying his body with fasts and abstinence.

You could see in him, with the prophet David, his skin cleaving to his bones and the strength of his flesh continually wasting away from excessive hunger. Thus, clothed in the poverty of Christ, he rightly shone forth as fortunate and blessed: for the sake of religion he despised the honors he had held in the world.

But how vigorous he was in works directed toward virtue is witnessed by Severus, who did much with him so that their brothers might advance through his example.

## CHAPTER XXI

### SEVERUS

I bind my word to you by this condition: I shall withhold many more things that I know about him and preserve his memory properly, so that, when the time comes, once the fires of enmity have been extinguished, I may explain them openly to those who wish to hear. For if someone now openly tells anything false, empty, or fabricated about him, it is more pleasing to them.

Therefore, as this Allabigus admits, I was the first to discover this path: since there is a kind of people who wish to be first in everything, although they are not, I pursue such people and compare myself with them, so that they may laugh and I may voluntarily smile back at them. For now there is no opportunity to speak of good things, since such people think that they are being diminished when they hear others praised.

### PASCHASIUS

Good Jesus! What does one person owe another, when this man has lost his virtue together with his possessions and does not dare to speak what he knows? Perhaps, then, all his acquaintances, friends, and fellow soldiers have abandoned him so completely that no one dares to speak about him.

### ADEODATUS

What I hear is frightening, Paschasius: that, because of the favor shown to wicked people, good men do not dare to pursue what is good. Therefore, I wish you to recover your strength; make yourself bold. If possible, recall Severus, so that he may not be too fearful and, deceived by vain hope, consume the good things he has learned.

### SEVERUS

Shall I then stop praising this man, whom I desire day and night, upon whom I meditate, whom I admire, whose phantom I even find refreshing to see with my eyes? When I recall him, I burn more fiercely with love; when I commend him, I share in the truth. Shall I cease praising him among the good, when he is proved worthy of praise even among those whose hatred infects them?

For he bears the palm of praise, even though these men contradict him, like holy Jeremiah, who speaks of those who utter falsehoods from their hearts against him. For, once he had become superior—as is attested not only by the whole congregation of the monastery over which he presided, but also by the familiar knowledge of many monks—he was, without exception, the lord of those who were subject to correction and the abbot of us all.

He was an abbot because he was the father of everyone, bearing toward each person a heart filled with the dew of Christ’s charity and displaying an attitude of pious affection. He was a lord because he indulgently allowed no one to behave wantonly, as those who take pastoral care lightly are accustomed to do; rather, he surpassed everyone in the inspection of their morals and lives.

Yet he drew even the most remote by his exhortations and lifted and carried those who were bearing fruit with Christ upon the shoulders of his virtues. He left no one lukewarm whom he did not warm with his encouragements; no one whom he did not season with the salt of wisdom; and no one whom he did not treat with the sharp teachings of correction, if the condition of the illness permitted it, with Christ’s grace cooperating.

Nevertheless, he diligently performed the duties of a physician suited to healing the wounds of sin. In persuading people toward virtue, he offered examples from his life no less than he showed diligence in instruction, whether at a convenient or inconvenient time. In everything he maintained one charity and one discipline, neglecting and disregarding nothing that seemed capable of benefiting the salvation of the souls entrusted to him.

But now I would like Paschasius to continue, since he always pursued him more through agreement in counsel than through examples of action—although he now calls me a flatterer, because I was everywhere his constant companion.

### PASCHASIUS

I have never seen a man more cunning than you. Did you not just confess this yourself, and now evade the very things you were applauding as worthy of being consulted? Nevertheless, so that I may not remain silent about what many know: I have seen no one like him for governance, no one who possessed such energetic virtue and who everywhere remained so indefatigable in the care of holy solicitude. Whether absent or present, he kept such close attention to the flock entrusted to him that he thought of almost nothing else except how he would render an account for each person before Christ’s tribunal.

Therefore, he very often warned everyone generally, and many individually, with no less force, about the will of free choice and the authority over one’s own body according to the profession of monastic discipline, so that none of us would follow his own will.

“Otherwise,” he used to say, “how shall I render an account for anyone unless he leaves with me the authority over his own body and the will of his own free choice? But if he retains himself under his own authority or will, let him know that he will have to render an account—not only for his own deeds of word, thought, or action, but also because, contrary to the profession of monastic law, he retained himself under the authority of his own power or the will of his heart.

“I shall indeed be free to the extent that the authority due to me remains ungranted and the will of his own choice is not yielded to me. Nevertheless, whatever I can do I shall add in charity, so that I may be found free of responsibility concerning authority and will, lest I be deceived either by a merely nominal authority or by the will to pursue my own course.”

Good Jesus, with what care and unceasing solicitude for the sheep and for souls he was concerned—now instructing everyone generally, now warning individuals particularly; restraining one with threats, soothing another with the blandishments of teaching; recalling this one, in accordance with what the Prophet says, “I will restrain you with my praise” (Isaiah 48:9), as though by flattering praise; restraining another with reproaches. Yet he always stirred everyone by his own example.

His words, as I said, were like nails driven deep. And although he presented them to everyone in the assembly, each person seemed to be addressed more particularly. He left nothing untouched and nothing unexamined in the whole structure of the Rule. If he found anything that everyone was doing inadequately, he brought it forward with exhortations before many people and urged them not to neglect the divine commands, even when the matter might seem insignificant.

If anyone among them failed to comply after transgressing any of the words of the holy Rule, he rebuked him either publicly or more privately and seasoned him with the salt of instruction. He disregarded nothing. Holding the salvation of souls before and above everything, he judged even the smallest matters to be of the greatest importance.

Thus every word of his was seasoned with salt. For this reason he either treated wounds, lest the flock perish through diseased actions, or, guarding the health of souls, implanted virtue in their minds. His assigned sheep might always lie down in green pastures beside springs of water and grow fatter there in abundance. He also induced them by material benefits to keep the law of the Rule and seek Christ’s commandments.

### SEVERUS

Someone says [Note: Terence, *The Brothers*, Act IV, scene 4] that never has anyone lived with his affairs so well ordered that circumstances, age, and experience do not always bring him something new and warn him that what he thinks he knows, he does not know, and that what he had considered primary he rejects through experience. This has now happened to us, to our great sorrow.

For we have almost lost the hard life that we once lived with him, now that the period has nearly run its course. Therefore, we now judge the matter according to ease and think that nothing is better for a person, in accordance with the proverbs of Solomon, than to overflow with luxuries and enjoy the fruits of his own labors.

This is now very easy to understand, when someone always conducts his life in idleness and banquets, is gentle and indulgent toward himself in luxurious pleasure, dares to offend no guilty person for the sake of truth, is not accustomed to contradict anyone, smiles at everyone, and rebukes no one; when he lives for himself and spends money on himself. And behold, everyone blesses, loves, and glorifies him.

But people are accustomed to mark us out as uncultivated, savage, gloomy, fierce, grasping, and slanderers of others. Thus, while we strive to satisfy such people, we wear out our lives and our years in pursuit, and sometimes receive hatred from them as the fruit of our labor, while they enjoy their own advantages. Others love and cherish them, while they avoid us and wish that such people may continue to live.

[Note: From these and other statements I infer that Severus was an abbot—perhaps Heddon, who governed Corbie after Wala.]

They entrust their own counsels to those men and commend their vows to them; but they await our death and promise themselves that they will be free if we cease to blame these things and can rebuke them in no duty.

Therefore, if we wish to praise this man, they think that they themselves are being criticized.

## CHAPTER XXII

### PASCHASIUS

Come, come, let us now try the opposite: let us see whether we can say something gently or act kindly. If not, let us seek to be loved again by our own people. Let us try to soften them by commending to posterity what deserves praise, and by giving, serving, exhorting, and loving, so that they may love what is good even if they cannot or do not wish to imitate it, and may not despise the truths we set before them.

Do you not remember what our Arsenius did when one of our men, envious of another’s appointment as superior, was swelling with pride because he saw himself covered with a very humble winter cloak while the other had been preferred?

### SEVERUS

I remember it clearly and recall it well, since he immediately found an antidote for the man’s advantage. He put on an especially fine cloak of excellent fabric. After three days, when the other man’s swelling pride had already subsided, the Father met him, rushed to embrace his neck, and kissed him repeatedly. Then, removing his own cloak, he put it on the brother and clothed him in it. The brother, soothed by these kindnesses, withdrew cheerful and restored.

The Father then gloried in himself and rejoiced in the other, because he had found such a remedy for the wound—one by which his own merit was increased and the other’s health was restored.

Wearing that garment for many days, he confronted our pride: we are sometimes elated by more precious clothing, when it would be fitting for us to be humbled by it. He imitated the supreme master of the household, who went out first to meet his returning son and had him clothed in the finest robe, so that charity might invite to love the one whom luxury had driven into exile.

Behold, in one and the same action we saw three things: the brother’s cure, the Father’s increase, and an example of religious conduct for all of us.

But since we are not such people, we ought to groan deeply, because while we delight in more refined possessions, we are even despised by secular people. They know, indeed, what we ought to have been.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### ADEODATUS

[Col. 1599A]

I am astonished that, although he possessed such great charity and holiness, some people insist that he was severe or harsh, as though they were cutting off the edge of a strip from the border of his cloak—especially since they raise him up with many praises for the other virtues of his life.

### PASCHASIUS

Please do not be astonished that you recognize this from the Gospel. The lazy servant calls his master harsh—not because he is harsh, but because the lazy servant, paralyzed by the faults that demand correction from him, strives to defame his master.

Let such people return to their conscience, lest, while proclaiming this man harsh, they increase their own more grievous blows and heap vengeance upon themselves. For even though the Lord is said to gather where he has not scattered and to demand with interest where he has not sown, what do you think made him appear severe, when he is proved to have been pious and gentle, except the laziness of those who were sluggish?

They therefore prove themselves lazy because they do not wish to follow him, and they call harsh the man who scarcely restrained their vices gently and summoned them to virtue by his example. Otherwise, if he seems harsh, harsher will be the punishments of the deceiver, since he blamed nothing but vices and cultivated virtues, lest he return empty the talent entrusted to him.

If Jeremiah were in charge of such people, there is no doubt that he would be condemned as harsher, since the Lord had made his forehead harder than their foreheads. Luxury always judges men of virtue to be harsh and uncultivated.

Nevertheless, this man was kind and pious. He indulged others more than he ever indulged himself, but he either restrained vices or cut them out completely at their beginning. Therefore, if he was harsh, he was harsh toward those who were turned neither from their efforts by punishments nor softened by rewards—those whose hearts had become numb, so that they felt neither his pious admonitions nor those of Christ, since sometimes fear benefits certain people more than love.

Hence it is also written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110). For this reason Arsenius acted now with threats, now with blows, now with material benefits, and now with gentle exhortations, so that he might make us sons adopted by Christ. With every kind of skill and prudence he cared for each person, lest anyone, deceived by the devil’s cunning, should perish.

Did you not see what he did with that brother who, in his folly, wanted to depart because he was unwilling to endure what his own faults had brought upon him?

## CHAPTER XXIV

### SEVERUS

[Col. 1599D]

We certainly saw it and took part in it. To prevent him from leaving in such a state of agitation, we placed soldiers at the gate to frighten him. Compelled by fear, he turned back inside and fell prostrate at the Father’s feet, drenched in tears.

### PASCHASIUS

I am truly glad that you remember it, and I rejoice greatly, because the man of whom we are speaking, maintaining the moderation of a more perfect life, thereby advanced greatly, as I believe, toward virtue.

Good Jesus, what joy there was then! It was as though you had seen the prodigal son returning and the father rejoicing. He wept from joy, and the son, now softened, wept as well. When I saw them both weeping so intensely, I too was deeply moved and mingled many tears with theirs, giving thanks to God, as though we were receiving him back from the dead.

Such was the Father’s severity, such were the inward workings of his rigor, such his will, and such his affection. But how wretched we are now, when freedom to sin is granted to us! For if at that time no one sinned with impunity, and yet relapses still occurred, how much more is this the case now that we flatter our own evils.

## CHAPTER XXV

### ADEODATUS

As I see it, this man possessed perfect charity: he loved his own as Christ loved, and he required in deeds what is found in the divine disciplines. Yet they say that he was not sufficiently accommodating; for that reason he was loved less in return and visited less often by many.

### PASCHASIUS

I admit that I often said these words to him, although I knew that he had become almost everything to almost everyone. But he answered—not, as some do, by way of excuse, but indeed humbly—that he did not have a breadth of heart as great as the sand of the sea, so as to be able to do everything. Then he said: “To whom do you wish me to conform myself? To the idle or the vicious? To the babblers and jesters? Have you not read what the Apostle cries: ‘Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed in the newness of your mind’ (Rom. XII, 2)?”

By such and similar examples, with unceasing effort, he raised himself more highly toward the virtues, lest frivolity dissolve that seriousness of mind which he inwardly offered to the Lord of charity. I wonder, brother and son, why those devoted to wantonness and pleasures wish the more perfect to conform themselves to them, when they themselves ought rather to pass over to the form of virtue. Otherwise they will not be children of adoption unless, being foreknown and predestined, they become conformed to the image of the Son of God.

Foreknown and predestined to this form, our Arsenius therefore did not greatly adapt himself to childish games, although he would sometimes stand upon a high rock, *rari nantes* (“scattered swimmers”).

[Note: Thus it is read in the manuscript codex. The author appears to allude to the Virgilian expression, made into one word from two:]

[Col. 1600D] “[They] appear, few swimmers, in the vast whirlpool.” He urged the boys, with his playful remarks, to come nearer to him on the shore. Although he said little that was capable of provoking laughter, he nevertheless conducted himself with gravity, lest disciplined virtue be dissolved; rather, like a nursing infant stripped of its rattles, nourished at its father’s breast, he urged it to seek greater perfection. Yet none of them trusted his own laughing face in his presence unless he restored himself to gravity, because, as Job says: “Even when he laughed at them, they did not believe him” (Job 29:24). For although he relaxed the gravity of his speech, the brightness of his face did not fall to the ground; he acted with wit so that those conversing with him might be stirred to the pursuit of virtue.

Moreover, when they heard him, they awaited his judgment and remained attentive and silent for his counsel. Although Job was far inferior in virtues, nevertheless the ear that heard him called him blessed, and the eye that saw him bore witness that he had delivered the poor man crying out, and the orphan who had no helper. For the blessing of the perishing came upon him, since from childhood he had plainly been clothed in justice as in a garment. Hence he also investigated most diligently a case that he did not know.

Therefore, since he had been the tutor of Augustus Caesar [Note: [Col. 1601D] Namely, of Lothair, son of the emperor Louis, concerning whom see the Annals of Einhard under the year 822. Louis sent his son Lothair to Italy, together with Wala, a monk and his kinsman—that is, the brother of Abbot Adalhard—and Gerung, master of the doorkeepers. He sent them so that Lothair might make use of their counsel both in household affairs and in matters pertaining to the welfare of the kingdom. This is relevant to what Amalarius records in the preface to his Antiphonary concerning the embassy of Abbot Wala to Rome, from which he brought the books of the Roman Antiphonary back to Francia, that is, to his own monastery.] beyond the Pennine Alps, let us ask Chremes what he accomplished in judicial matters and in the administration of affairs and the discipline of justice.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### CHREMES

I fear to praise the man, lest I be thought to do so more from flattery than from what I have received from him, and to be currying favour. Nevertheless, lest I remain altogether silent about what a great and diligent investigator of truth he was, how energetic in judgment, how courageous against the highest judges when they acted unjustly, and how effective by his intelligence against those corrupted by gifts, I shall disclose one example among many. By this deed I learned of nothing more unjust in those times.

A certain noble widow entrusted herself and her property to a judicial official, as though to a defender; by a deed of transfer in her will she assigned him almost half of her possessions, so that the rest might remain secure for her. But he soon craftily seized everything in the same will and brought forward witnesses. Thus, when the woman mentioned above wished to return to her own property and make use of it, they appeared to prevent her from entering it, as though she had handed everything over to her defender. And, as they say jokingly, he defended everything well who left nothing to the possessor.

Then the unhappy widow, deprived of her own possessions, approached the emperor. He entrusted her, by sacred letters, to one of the bishops together with the other judges of the region, so that they might investigate her case carefully and render a just judgment. But because each person had turned aside after his own greed, the widow’s case did not gain entry to them. Therefore, fabricating a lie for themselves, they applauded one another together with the witnesses, so that the people would not understand such things, and all of them, even the priests of Christ, might practice deceit.

When these things had been done, and the woman had already been driven away from her property, that defender received word from the leading men of the people that no further dispute over any of these possessions should arise. Nevertheless, after being afflicted by many evils and the anguish of hardships, she at last, exhausted by the long journey over the rugged mountain ridges of the Alps, returned to Gaul and began to assail the king with her tears.

Then the king, moved by such great cries of misery, entrusted her to our Arsenius, who at that time was being sent together with the emperor’s son for the instruction and administration of the kingdom, as one especially trusted and close to him. Arsenius sent her ahead and ordered her to return to her own property until he himself should arrive in the country, so that she might then appear before him together with her witnesses.

When this was heard, all Italy trembled and turned to the crafty arguments of its fraud. It began to devise an ambush against the woman’s life, because it saw that the man was coming whom it did not think could be corrupted by gifts. By these weapons he was accustomed to break everyone’s minds and lure them into the embraces of their desires, since almost all follow rewards and love gifts.

But when they could accomplish nothing toward wickedness against this man, they turned to fraud by means of an iniquitous deed. When he had ordered the defender to restore at least some portion of the possessions that he had unjustly stolen by deceit, the man, knowing that he was surrounded, secretly sent three of his men along a road to kill her. But since three persons were involved in the matter, this seemed insufficiently safe for preserving silence. He added crime to crime, lest, if they were questioned, they should reveal the deed. Separating them far from one another, he ordered one of them to kill the other two, so that no one would remain on the face of the earth to disclose the innocent blood that had been shed through deceit. The wretched man cared little what the divine judge might think, so long as he escaped human judgment.

But our Arsenius, inflamed with zeal for God, employed many devices lest what was hidden should remain concealed, since it was certain that the matter had become manifest, although it could not be established by judgment or witnesses who had committed it. Nevertheless, one of them was eventually found buried in a subterranean cave belonging to someone; from this an incongruous inference arose. The man in whose cave he was found was indeed held guilty, while the other was accused on suspicion that the deed had been done at his instigation; yet neither could be convicted by anyone.

What grief, do you think, was then in Arsenius’ heart, and what groaning? You saw, Lord Jesus, how many prayers and how many tears he poured out before you—the one who had once heard the blood of righteous Abel crying from the earth—so that you might also reveal by whom the blood of these men had been shed.

Against him all Auxonia, together with its senators, corrupted by gifts, struggled and acted so that the guilty man, who was a notorious robber and murderer to everyone, would not be found by anyone. But you, God, who search hearts and minds, knew everything; nevertheless, you afflicted your champion with great zeal and did not show him what was evident to many, but only to his accomplices. Almost everyone, down to the last man, was striving to prevent the guilty person from being found, because in the sight of you, God, many had already become guilty through one man.

With how many insults the wicked then tore at your soldier, and with how many slanders they gnawed at him, as though he alone before all others were unbelieving, he alone the persecutor of the innocent contrary to law! They therefore produced the law who did not fear violating justice. But innocent blood cried from the earth; and the slain, now received among the dead, were already declaring that they had unjustly shed it.

Why say more? All the nobles of the palace acted now through laws, now through witnesses, now through many ingenious arguments, so that he might release the same guilty man as though he were innocent. At times they also wearied him with entreaties. But he was deceived by no trickery and broken by no reproaches; unconquered, he did whatever he could, if somehow at last the truth might be revealed.

Finally, when they saw his steadfastness, they decided that unless he accepted a judgment concerning the man, they would do nothing further in the dispute, although the law was clear in part. The people applauded, as though Christ’s soldier were unwilling even to accept a judgment.

When he heard this, he took up his customary weapons again and imposed a fast upon himself and upon us who were with him, lest, as often happens, some fraud of the enemy should prevail in that very judgment. We therefore spent the entire night in vigil and prayer, asking that the Lord first expose the perpetrator of so great a crime.

When morning came, trusting in God’s mercy, we proceeded as though to a spectacle, where the entire people had already gathered. There was then much insulting by the powerful, so much so that several bishops were drawn into this harassment, because the cause of so great a crisis did not gain entry to them.

Then the true champion of Christ began to press them to prepare the judgment. Standing among them with hands outstretched, he poured out prayers to God with tears, lest such great folly in judgment stain even the upright with its blemishes. As soon as these prayers had been poured forth, they rose from his cheek and pierced heaven; and because the gift had overturned the tribunal of human judgment, the tears stood before the throne of Christ’s grace, while innocent blood cried out from the earth together with them.

Indeed, the inward judge, as though once again rebuking Cain’s ancient conscience, compelled the man to confess what had been badly concealed in secret. He immediately fell trembling and groaning at Arsenius’ feet, because the divine judge was punishing his wretched conscience within.

Struck by a new fear, he began also to denounce all those whose protection he had used in daring this deed. He declared that nothing at all remained to him of everything he had possessed, save the ground on which he stood, especially since he had transferred it all to those standing around him. Thus those men, blinded, had perverted the judgment, to such a degree that they afflicted Arsenius with their hatred and harassed him with plots. But now, convicted by divine judgment, they all departed in confusion, and the wretched man was mercifully restored to repentance.

### PASCHASIUS

A most unhappy age, when, if someone wishes or judges something good, no one is prepared to obey; rather, each person attends to his own will and not to God’s. All love gifts and pursue rewards; all alike have the same devotion and the same stubbornness. They seem to look toward wickedness as though engaged in one and the same game—if indeed this sort of thing can be called a game.

Perhaps for this reason they place little faith in what is said, because they judge our Arsenius by their own pursuits, as though no one could be anything other than what they themselves are. Among them there is no truth, because it has fallen in the streets, and equity could not enter. Thus the widow’s blood did not gain entry to them; but because it was innocent, it lay exposed to plunder.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### SEVERUS

What is it that moves Chremes so greatly concerning these affairs, when, even while he lived among us, he almost every day drew out into public view the secrets of judgments by conjecturing about the hidden chambers of hearts, so that scarcely anyone dared to conceal his secrets from him? Yet, after investigating the acts of their offenses, he immediately applied Christ’s gentlest medicine to the sick.

### CHREMES

It is indeed as you recall. But here many were present who investigated such matters with him for the sake of salvation; there, however, no one or scarcely anyone was found who would not corrupt truth or justice—indeed, who would not take up arms against the man who refused to defend wicked crimes.

Thus, on another occasion, a certain man had fraudulently brought forward the testament of another’s inheritance. He produced witnesses and secretly placed the document in a sword sheath; then he deceitfully returned it to the person bringing the suit. The latter, unaware of what he was receiving, soon set it aside there by chance and asked for the page of his inheritance again, so that he might return it.

But the other man, on the contrary, acted with his witnesses, claiming that he had returned to him all the documents belonging to his rights. Since an oath is the conclusion of every dispute, and they swore to this, the wretched man had nothing that he could claim again. Nevertheless, when he came before the court, he stated in plaintive tones what had happened.

Then our Arsenius, smiling slightly, ordered the accused to come forward, as though he were already aware of the sequence of so great a crime.

“Wretched man,” he said, “how did you devise so great and such a cunning trick of this kind?”

When the other saw that he had apparently been detected, he fell at his feet and disclosed what had been hidden.

### ADEODATUS

As I see it, Solomon’s wisdom was present in this man, and therefore he was so discerning in investigating secret affairs.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### PASCHASIUS

What Parmenus says often happens [Note: [Col. 1603] In Terence, at the end of the *Hecyra*]: that any thoughtless person sometimes unknowingly does more good than he ever does knowingly.

But our man never acted thoughtlessly in relation to his profession. He often seized hidden things in the nets of his conjectures, as we ourselves also frequently see in the offenses of certain brothers. From the beginning, sinners always approach the shadows and eagerly seek to escape notice, lest what is evident to the divine gaze should appear to those who accuse them.

But since, after entering Italy long ago, we have been exiled beyond the Pennine [sic] Alps—where we saw Saturn’s golden reign and its wicked arts, and where the Ausonian soil reigns and plays the harlot in every way in which the world does so—let us at last return to Gaul, with almost all things corrected and with Eugenius, a most holy man, appointed bishop of the apostolic see. It is said that many labored at his ordination so that through him the things long corrupted by the negligence of many might thereafter be corrected.

## CHAPTER XXIX

### ADEODATUS

Perhaps, then, Paschasius, you are sharply blaming, no less covertly than cleverly or ingeniously, the man whom you had resolved to praise—as though you had seen the little gifts he brought to the brothers, almost every kind of wealth or ornament in which the world delights. Indeed, we all testify together that none of us had seen gifts of such a kind or such magnitude.

### PASCHASIUS

I would never have believed you so suspicious and so quarrelsome [reading uncertain: perhaps *morosus*, “peevish”], to such a degree that you would turn things sincerely spoken by me into an occasion for slander. Perhaps you are disturbed about these matters in the manner of certain people, from whom you derive your judgment of another.

Nevertheless, no one who judges rightly concerning his neighbor’s conscience could doubt that all those things were blessings—that is, gifts—of chaste affection, or the services of great men offered out of the reverence owed to him, since he was administrator of the kingdom and the emperor’s tutor.

With what conscience he was secure before all of us, he said:

“All these things that you see you may receive with as much security and without any danger as I, without any charge of desire or loss to anyone, have freely accepted before God and you, since they were offered for the honorable purpose of acceptance and for the honor of the emperor and your advantage. Otherwise, no one unjustly acquired or lost anything on their account, nor did anyone grieve over what was received or given. Rather, as is true, when I did not wish to accept them, many begged that they be brought to you as alms.

“Therefore, once these things have been received in this manner, it is evident that I did not speak of them as you suppose, but that I was noting the delights of the homeland and the kingdom. For I knew this man to be so generous and so contemptuous of the world in all things that, in accordance with the Lord’s word, he had abandoned himself.

“Therefore, the man who abandoned himself so perfectly, as everyone was permitted to know—what could he acquire for himself, not merely unjustly or greedily, but even licitly? Rather, as I have admitted and as the matter made clear to us, he accepted these things chiefly lest those who wished to give them should be offended and injured when he refused, or lest we should slander him, hearing that he had despised what was being sent to us, if he returned empty-handed at our expense.”

### ADEODATUS

I am pleased that I charged you with blaming him because there had been talk of the things he had brought, so that everyone may understand how generous he was, how alien to the world, and how dead to the world: neither in return for all these things did he seek favour from us, nor for any other benefits from outsiders, even dishonestly; rather, always conscious that he pleased God, he strove to do so in all things.

### PASCHASIUS

It is as you say, my brother. Indeed, some of our own people did not understand at the time that these things had been given to him as gifts, but thought that they had been sent to us by very many great men, or by the supreme Pontiff of the apostolic see, who had bestowed very many things upon him.

Thus it happened one day that, when one of the brothers was praising him for such deeds and things of this kind, another is said to have replied:

“Why do you praise him in this way? Were not the things he brought sent to us?”

When he had said this, we all laughed.

Then another said: “Perhaps it is fitting that such great and numerous things should be sent to you.”

“What a wretched human condition,” I said, “which is so dull, envious, or ungrateful! Otherwise, if he had not been laboring under some burden, he would never have confessed so.”

Nevertheless, it is clear that our Arsenius was at that time so loved and renowned that no one in the kingdom equaled him. For this reason he was gratified by such gifts and so many of them, to such a degree that, unwilling though he was, he was compelled to accept them freely, lest the affection of love be wounded.

Let others do what they can; let them plot and threaten as much as they can; let them sell justice for gifts; let them rage with fraud or deceit, and make everything available for sale to everyone. Yet none of them received gifts so numerous or so distinguished as those that were offered freely to this man alone, out of love and reverence.

Since we have now turned our writing back toward Gaul, let us bring the book to an end. For the matters that must be pursued thereafter with groaning are so dreadful and so monstrous that scarcely anyone—or perhaps no one—can comprehend them mentally, because they are exceedingly terrifying and confused. When the pen reaches them, I do not know whether the letters can be formed through tears, even if the writer of those things should possess a heart of stone, lest they be washed away by weeping—much less whether the order and structure of the narrative can be formed.

For the present [*interim*; printed *interdum*, “sometimes”], let us console ourselves with the joy of conscience, because we knew and possessed such a great man, one concerning whom we do not fear to rejoice in the Lord. And we must take care not to be broken by any slanders, because in the present age many even of the more honorable speak against the good, so that no one can emerge untouched.

## BOOK TWO

**Interlocutors:** PASCHASIUS, ADEODATUS, THEOPHRASTUS

[Col. 1605]

## INTRODUCTION

### ADEODATUS

[Col. 1605D]

After innumerable internal cares of office, after immense external causes of occupation, after the varied events of affairs and business and the losses of life, after the long fatigue and continual movement of diverse journeys here and there, after the unceasing pressures of everyone—at last, by the dispensation of divine judgment, everything having been abandoned because rest and freedom of spirit have been restored to you, Paschasius, you ought to remember what we once left unfinished, so that at some time hereafter we may complete the form of the father’s epitaph, which we began long ago to commend in writing. Otherwise, it would have been more honorable not to begin than not to complete what was begun.

### PASCHASIUS

I confess that it is so, my brother. But after the deaf silences of life and after abandoning literary studies, I fear returning to what either forgetfulness has carried away or the fickleness of character now disdains to hear. Moreover, even if there were time to speak of such things, especially now I have no eloquence of writing—although I once possessed some.

Nevertheless, lest what we began come to nothing, to the shame of our enemies and the example of the lazy, I shall attempt what you urge and begin, although the lamentations over the deeds that remain are inexhaustible.

But since Severus has meanwhile entered upon the happy way of all the earth, and Chremes has already departed amid our troubles [Note: [Col. 1607D] That is, amid the disturbances that occurred to Abbot Paschasius in the monastery of Corbie, concerning which we spoke above in Paschasius’ *Eulogy*], it is necessary for us to choose one of those who, in the manner of the holy Fathers, lived with him and with us. Through him, truth may be better commended, as though under three witnesses, and our lament may not be found discrepant either in character or in number.

Therefore, brother, since it was your part to begin again what we started, let it also be yours to choose a companion for this portion.

### ADEODATUS

Although I am less suitable for making a judgment because of my predisposition—for I am devoted to your commands—I do not reject what you demand. We are not properly seeking a philosopher for lamentation, but one of them whose memory of pious recollection or whose affection may stir us to tears. Therefore, if it seems good to you, although he is smooth-faced, let us choose Theophrastus from among them all.

### THEOPHRASTUS

I would never have imagined, then, that you wished to sow jokes as a game or pursue childish things.

### PASCHASIUS

Do not wonder, brother, if Adeodatus chose you, smooth-faced, for this task, since he did not spare me, decrepit and long buried beneath such studies. For the upright and lovers of a good conscience ought especially to commend laments and truth to those who hear them. Therefore, the two of us, long afflicted in many ways, can now disclose our tears suitably to our sons and friends.

## CHAPTER I

### ADEODATUS

But before we come to the lament, I ask you to show us the beginning of so great a crisis, because no sane person can believe that these things occurred among the people without offense against God.

### PASCHASIUS

What you say is true, by Hercules. But it is not yet permitted to disclose everything to everyone, especially to those who hate truth and delight in crimes. Nevertheless, even if they do not approve of what is good, truth must not always be concealed, because the man of whom we speak freely spoke the word of truth even to those who reproached him for it.

It therefore happened that, before these evils of the whole empire became evident, and while various calamities and scourges were increasing among the people day by day through God’s just judgment, the emperor, together with his senators and the leading men of the land, began to ask what it was that the divine majesty, having been offended, was revealing to the people through so many such signs over so long a time. For already, as Scripture bears witness (Isa. 28:19), “only affliction gave understanding to the hearing.”

Then it was ordered that each person should investigate the matter more carefully until another assembly [Note: [Col. 1608D] I read that this assembly was held in the year 829 in a letter of Louis Augustus prefixed to the Sixth Council of Paris]: what it was by which God had been offended, and by what works he might be appeased.

When these orders had been issued, our Arsenius immediately set before their eyes the wretched condition of the world, the divine laws, and likewise the decrees of the Fathers. In them he at once perceived in how many ways the churches of Christ had been corrupted and by what kinds of works of the flesh the whole people had been polluted.

For this reason he produced a small memorandum for himself, for the sake of memory, in which he set down in writing all the vices of this kingdom with precision, and did so so carefully that none of his adversaries could deny that all these things were indeed so.

Returning from there to the court, he presented everything individually before the emperor and before all the bishops and senators of the churches. He set out the duties of the various orders, the evils that were increasing, and showed that everything had been corrupted or perverted.

### THEOPHRASTUS

I am utterly astonished that, although we are provoked by such great examples of his, none of us dares to recount the truth about him fully to posterity, even though one may dare to expose the sins of the people, accumulated over a very long time—disasters, pestilences, famines, irregularities of the seasons, and even the terrors of visions.

Indeed, these evils were preceded by the earlier deceptive invention of powders, under which there was such great affliction and such a prodigy of falsehood that it was made clear to the prudent that the whole world had been handed over into the enemy’s power for testing.

From this it is evident that, because of such causes and things of this kind, the sins of the kingdom—which have not yet reached their completion—are daily heaped up for the worse. Thus what we have found to have happened in many places remains: it is being destroyed. We must fear lest what we read has already been done among many peoples should also happen among us.

I would certainly not say that it was without cause that the miracles of the saints who had long rested in Christ recently shone forth—so many and such great miracles performed at one time at the relics of the saints as had never been heard of in the world. For, as though at cockcrow, the saints, carried here and there throughout this kingdom, aroused one another as if for a concert of song.

This was meant to show that our infidelity required it, in accordance with the Apostle, because signs, as he himself most truly testifies, are given not to the faithful but to unbelievers—so that, if somehow we might at last awaken and rise from the darkness of our blindness to the true light, which is Christ.

### ADEODATUS

Perhaps, then, if he had first been summoned to this colloquy of lamentation, he would have exposed us as a traitor, unable to restrain his spirit while speaking. Therefore, although what he touches upon is true, he does not wait to speak of it in its proper place.

### THEOPHRASTUS

The things I proposed are more rightly brought forward in another place, because the evils that had grown piecemeal are first struck in this present time. For this empire has grown through prosperous successes up to the present, as though it had reached the perfect age of fullness. But the vices committed piecemeal amid prosperity, as usually happens, had accumulated and grown old; by God’s just judgment they are exposed no less by scourges than by new miracles of virtue.

Therefore, if I am not mistaken, these matters must be marked and lamented here, so that, if not for us, at least for posterity, they may become an example for correction.

## CHAPTER II

### PASCHASIUS

We cannot deny that it is so. Nevertheless, we must not omit what our Arsenius then proposed before all the leading men, including the highest. For these and similar matters had driven him to show all, on divine authority, as though he were a second Jeremiah, in what ways they had all offended God. He steadfastly admonished them, in the duty of charity, to destroy, scatter, and uproot the evils they had committed, but thereafter to build and plant the good things they had neglected.

“In the meantime,” he said, “you know by what orders Christ’s Church is constituted. For it is certain that, according to the duties of each person, the order of discipline and the condition of the commonwealth must be sought. First, therefore, divine matters within must be considered, and then human matters without, because without doubt the condition of the whole Church is administered through these two orders.

“Let the emperor and king be devoted to his own office. Let him not undertake the affairs of another, but only those proper to his own jurisdiction; nor let him neglect them, because for all these things the Lord will bring him to judgment.

“Let the bishop and the ministers of the churches attend more specifically to the things that belong to God.

“Then let the king appoint as rulers in the kingdom men of the kind whom the Lord commands to be sought carefully in the law, men in whom the king may remain secure and for whom he may be secure—men whom he knows to be upright and suitable for ruling God’s holy people, not according to his own desires, appointing those who favor him, but those who hate greed and love God and justice.

“His office, in fact, is always to arrange what is right and just and to correct what has been corrupted. Otherwise, O king, unless you preserve what has been commanded, a stronger punishment awaits you, and, if God turns away, one destruction awaits all in you.

“Therefore take care to neglect nothing, because in you alone, according to Solomon (Wis. 6:26), lies the stability of the whole kingdom. In divine matters, however, do not intrude beyond what is expedient.”

### ADEODATUS

As I understand it, you rightly called him a second Jeremiah, on account of his steadfastness in faith and the hardness of his brow, since he so boldly reproached the emperor for having neglected, because of luxurious idleness and the worst customs of kings, the duties of his office, being preoccupied with empty affairs.

### PASCHASIUS

What was said then was more severe, and I shall disclose a little of it. For he said to the emperor:

“Most reverend Emperor Augustus, I should like you to tell us: why is it that, often leaving your own duties behind, you devote yourself so greatly to divine matters? Or what is it that you give when you bestow the honors of the churches—or rather, as I understand, the burdens that you distribute?

“If these possessions have been lawfully consecrated to the Lord as alms, they belong to his churches, because they have been lawfully given to his poor and to those who serve him in a special way. But if you think that you have authority to give blessings and the Holy Spirit, which God’s chosen will thereafter worthily receive from the Lord and from the sacred consecrated bishops, know that what you presume lies outside your office.

“Otherwise, if, by the authority of the holy Fathers, what you do is to be done more cautiously according to God, and what you distribute is to be made more fruitful, the manner must be regulated together with the clergy, the people of God, and the holy bishops. This is so lest you choose what belongs to yourself and usurp divine things for yourself, or lest the crowd or some individual confuse so great a grace in any way. For in these matters only divine concerns and the means of our salvation are to be considered.

“Therefore there is almost the same principle in the possessions of the churches, because their resources are nothing other than the prices of sins, the vows of the faithful, and the patrimonies of the poor. Whatever has once been lawfully consecrated to God should therefore be freely assigned, through his soldiers and the poor, to the uses of his service.

“Let the king have the commonwealth freely at his disposal for the administration of his military service; and let Christ also have the possessions of the churches, as another commonwealth, entrusted to his faithful ministers for the use of all who are needy and serve him.

“Let this be the king’s duty: to entrust them to men who will distribute faithfully and provide wisely, so that all may glorify God and rejoice in Christ, no less because of the promises of future things than because of the consolations of the present.

“Otherwise, as the Apostle says, those who seize what belongs to others will not possess the eternal kingdom. How much more, then, will those who defraud God and the churches of what belongs to them—things with which sacrileges [perhaps *sacrilegis*, ‘sacrilegious persons’] are joined—not possess it? [Read *defraudant*, ‘defraud,’ for printed *defraudantur*].”

### THEOPHRASTUS

If it is as he asserted, and if God exercises any providence concerning these matters, I do not know which of our princes can be saved, since nothing is so sweet [sic] to them as the estates of the churches, and nothing so pleasing, as it is written: “Stolen bread is sweet, and stolen water is sweeter” (Prov. 9:17).

### PASCHASIUS

It is true, my brother. For this reason God’s anger has been poured out upon our princes, who cause them to wander in a trackless place rather than on the road, while secular men improperly intrude themselves into the seizure of divine things.

The priests of Christ and the ministers of the altar, together with divine matters, cast themselves outward from their inner concerns, and—what is worse—they now transfer them without shame, although they read that “no one serving as a soldier for God involves himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2:4).

From this arise the worst presumption and confusion; from this, the devouring flame of desire; from this, the emptying of virtues and the fuel of sin. Either the ministers of Christ, enticed by their possessions lest they lose them, are expelled [perhaps: impelled] toward things that are not expedient for them, or secular men, inflamed by the heat of their desires, seize what belongs to God as though protected by royal authority and, with reckless right, rise up against God.

When all this had been fully explained before the king, before the bishops of Christ, and before the leading men of the land, none of them denied it.

### ADEODATUS

I wonder what could be denied when everything is open to all and scarcely anyone contradicts it. Indeed, provoked against one another, they make everything worse on every side and turn it toward the worst uses.

## CHAPTER III

### PASCHASIUS
## PASCHASIUS

Alas! How such madness grows daily at the present time, so that, on account of such deeds and words, everyone turns increasingly toward what is worse rather than toward an increase of correction. Therefore all then began—especially the ecclesiastical men—to ask and protest how otherwise the dignity and honor of the churches could stand, as though they had not read the decrees of the holy Fathers.

Then our Arsenius said:

“Consider what things are contrary to divine authority, so that they may be corrected by the authority of God himself. For in your hands are rights no less human than divine.”

Then the secular men said:

“Even if all this is so, the commonwealth, weakened by many causes, cannot suffice by itself. We must deal with ecclesiastical resources and with the soldiers, and we must be supported by the contribution of those resources. Therefore, tell us,” they said, “what you are planning.”

But he replied:

“I wonder what you are asking. Behold, as has often been shown, our king lays claim to many of the resources of the churches for his own uses and those of his people. But there are very many anathemas of the holy Fathers, issued with divine authority—as you know, since they have often been reread in your presence—which utterly condemn the seizure of church property by force or power, whoever the judge may be. Therefore, I ask you to consider this: if one of the faithful has brought his offerings to God upon the altar, whether little or much, and then someone comes rashly and by force or theft carries off what has been offered or consecrated, I ask you to judge what kind of offense such an act is.”

They all at once decreed that it was sacrilege, as though they had been inwardly touched by some new oracle.

Then he said:

“Let no one deceive you, most illustrious Augustus: for it is exceedingly dangerous violently to plunder things once faithfully dedicated to God for the uses of the poor and the servants of God, and afterward to divert them to secular uses against divine authority. And if, according to the judgment of Truth, ‘whatever these holy pontiffs bind on earth will be bound also in heaven,’ then those many anathemas of the holy Fathers that are read in the sacred canons as having been issued against such acts are to be feared. For, in my estimation, the authority of those who now reign with God is no less effective.

“Therefore, as you say, if the commonwealth cannot survive without contributions from church property, a method and an order must be sought with the utmost reverence and religious devotion to Christianity: namely, whether you and your people ought to receive something from the churches for their defense rather than for plunder, lest such presumption proceed under the curses and execrations of the holy Fathers.
