“Moreover, if these holy pontiffs are to provide anything for military purposes, let them provide it in this way; and let this be done reasonably in every matter, so that they themselves are not compelled to rush into secular affairs and irreligiously serve the pageants of the world, which they have renounced. For, as I said according to the Apostle, no one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business. Otherwise, if any one of them does so, he is not a true Christian, because he still serves the pageants and works of the devil.”

After he had said this, they began to ask what the “pageants” were. But he replied:

“It is for you to decide this, and to show yourselves more evangelical men than those who long for the things in which the world reigns and glories.”

## CHAPTER IV

### THEOPHRASTUS

“This, as I still hear today, is what some slander him for: that he wanted the property of the churches to be divided, and that only as much should remain with the churches as was fully sufficient for them; while the rest should serve the secular army.”

### PASCHASIUS

“That is by no means so, as you wrongly think, just as many thought at that time. For he determined or indicated nothing rashly concerning this matter. He merely urged that whatever had to be done should be done in such a way that neither side would sin against God for the sake of earthly possessions.

“Accordingly, when various bishops tested him by asking what he wanted to come of it, no one could discover anything other than what he had said publicly to everyone before Augustus.

“Meanwhile, while these matters were being discussed, he pointed out and enumerated the dangers of the monasteries, since even at that time some were held by laymen. Although today far fewer are found that are governed according to their proper order, nearly all have been occupied or corrupted for worldly uses and pursuits as a punishment for sin. For although the king had initially begun well concerning these matters, in the end, as evils multiplied, they were overrun by secular men.

“He also repeatedly and strongly condemned the fact that bishoprics were not properly bestowed according to canonical authority, and that the election was not being observed.

“When all these matters had thus been exposed on every side, and none of them could deny that the ecclesiastical order was corrupt in every respect, they devised the holding of synods in three places [Note: Rather, in four places—namely, in the city of Mainz, in the city of Paris, at Lyons, and at Toulouse, as is stated in the letter of Louis cited immediately below], in which they might investigate the matter more carefully—not because, as the outcome demonstrated, they wanted to reform such things, but so that they might occasionally support the king. For even then they were devising the human schemes that later became evident; and therefore divine matters were attended to less.”

## CHAPTER V

### ADEODATUS

“I am surprised that, when his words are being recalled, he is absent, though we did not wonder at him when he was present. Since he was so humble—so humble that no one appeared humbler, and no one more dead to the world—how is it that, among the highest ranks of the churches, namely the bishops and senators, he spoke in the senate before Augustus with such deliberation and firmness?”

### PASCHASIUS

“You do not fail to know, brother, what sort of man he was: one whom neither the terror of threats, nor the force of circumstances, nor hope of present things, nor fear of future things, nor promises of resources, nor threatened kinds of punishment, nor any authority could recall from the love of Christ, from devotion to his country and people, from love of the churches, or from loyalty to the emperor.

“Therefore he spoke such things, and many more, steadfastly, like another Jeremiah. In particular, he strongly denounced the clerical soldiery at the palace, whom the common people call chaplains, because it is no ecclesiastical order. They serve for no other reason than the honors of churches, worldly gain and profit, without any proof of qualification for teaching, and the ambitions of the world. [Note: Walahfrid Strabo attacks court clerics of this kind in his poem on Wettin’s dream, above at the year 824. Hence Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, writes in Letter 25: “Moreover, a report circulates among us that the clerics of the palace seek and request lordship over various monasteries; they have no other concern than to satisfy their greed by oppressing the servants of God.” Compare the Life of Benedict, abbot of Aniane, no. 54, above.] Their life is therefore neither under the rule of monks nor canonically subject to a bishop, especially since the churches have no other forms of training than under these two orders.

“For he used to say that every man ought to be either a canon, or a layman, or a monk. If he was none of these, he was shown to be under no order, because such men appeared to be without a head.

“Although this heresy has claimed that name for itself elsewhere, nevertheless, as he himself acknowledged, no worse disease of the churches could be found in that age: a disease which, from the time it began, corrupted all their rights. It did so to such an extent—and many of them were vicious—that nearly all the monasteries of monks, canons, and women were occupied by laymen and everything was corrupted.

“For these reasons, since he had foreseen what was to come, he never hesitated to speak a judgment worthy of the condition of the kingdom, the safety of the people, the stability of the churches, and the observance of peace, even if it displeased anyone.”

## CHAPTER VI

### ADEODATUS

“As far as can be understood, those who were then present were not counselors or guardians of their country, but robbers. The darkness of the present blinded their narrow minds; a perverse humility filled them with darkness; desire stained them with filth—so greatly that they could neither understand nor contemplate, grasp nor endure the very name of the consulship, the splendor of that honor, or the greatness of so vast an empire.

“Therefore they must be called not counselors but traders and sellers of so great a dignity, and disturbers of the churches. They not only failed to deliberate when this man warned them, but evaded, overturned, and betrayed one another, so that neither might such things be corrected nor even the worse things that threatened be resisted, although they could have done so.

“And therefore, as Paschasius lamented shortly above, such things happened not undeservedly—or rather, because they refused to receive the spirit of truth for correction, they received the spirit of error for their ruin. Hence it is that even today none of the princes can explain the ways of the commonwealth toward justice.”

### PASCHASIUS

“Nor is it undeserved, because they refused to stand for God and did not seek first the things that are God’s, in order to correct what had already been corrupted. If God, withdrawing from them, has caused the counsel of the country to perish, faith to vanish, peace to flee, and the prosperity of every undertaking to lie hopeless today, this is no wonder.

“Now scarcely anyone shows loyalty to kings; no one gives sound counsel for the country or its citizens; no one extends due charity to allies and friends. Judges do nothing except what can be bought. The people do not support the imperial offices. The authority of the prelates has no force, because imperial and royal authority has perished. The commonwealth and the churches are utterly impoverished, because plunderers seize their goods. All the most eloquent have been made mute, because the power to act and speak has been emptied out.

“For in these respects nothing greater or more ingenious has ever been known; yet the ability and knowledge to act are worn out in pursuit of each individual’s will.

“Therefore, as I believe, because at that time they did not listen to this man’s voice—or rather, to God’s—their entire prosperity has been turned into its opposite, their strength has been broken, counsel has fled, and, as the prophet says, all wisdom has been swallowed up.

“He himself, foreseeing what was to come, warned them of this after these matters had been set forth in the same assembly. Soon afterward he was seized by a severe illness, which physicians call lientery, so that power might be perfected in weakness. From that time onward he was silent, until God’s judgment seized us and the sins that had already been completed became evident in deed—to such an extent that what we now do are no longer merely sins, but the punishment of sin.”

## CHAPTER VII

### THEOPHRASTUS

“Why such things happened is now clearer than daylight. But it is rightly asked where they began, since we believe that it happened by a just judgment that their hearts were hardened, so that they would not listen when their sins demanded it; and that afterward divine vengeance might justly rage more fiercely against us sinners.”

### PASCHASIUS

“O that day, which brought almost eternal darkness and calamity upon this world; which tore apart and divided piecemeal the peaceful and united empire; violated kinships; tore apart blood relatives [Note: The manuscript reads *dirempsit* (‘tore apart’) in place of *diremit* (‘separated’), just as Alcuin writes *empserat* for *emerat* in epigram 163]; produced enmities everywhere; scattered fellow citizens; exterminated faith; destroyed charity; violated the churches as well; and corrupted everything!

“Hence civil wars—and, so to speak, wars worse than civil—arise daily. Almost the entire army of the country is slaughtered here and there. Provinces, districts, and cities are everywhere laid waste. If any survivors remain, powerless everywhere, they either flee or are cut down by the sword. From all sides come the incursions of pagans and enemies; and, as the entire populace is struck down, countless villages and cities are burned.

“Alas, miserable day, followed by an even more wretched night! But no day was more wretched than that when the criminal was called Naso by the Spaniards [Note: This was Bernard, prefect of the Spanish March and count of Septimania and Toulouse, son of Count or Duke William. Thegan, in his *Book of the Deeds of Louis*, chapter 38, states that Duke Bernard cleared himself of the accusation of adultery after no one was found who had dared to impose that charge upon him with arms. Nevertheless, Nithardus testifies in Books I and II—despite his devotion to Charles—that Bernard abused the commonwealth recklessly and utterly overturned it] by the Spaniards—that Amisarius who abandoned everything honorable in which he had been trained [Note: That is, educated and instructed by his excellent father William]—and foolishly plunged himself into every mire and whirlpool.

“For as soon as he arrived, like a savage boar he overturned the palace, destroyed its counsel, and scattered every principle of reason. He expelled and crushed all counselors, both divine and human; occupied the bedchamber; and, in a factional manner, so that it seemed like a conspiracy, invaded everything more openly. He was so blind that he could put nothing before what he himself had discovered. He set divine things aside, plunged into human affairs by right and wrong alike, suddenly uprooted and defiled everything, and emptied the royal dignity.

“He broke treaties, confused order, and changed everything so that no condition remained. He turned day into night and again changed night into day. He disowned sons from their father and the father from his sons. Thus his tyranny advanced until it surpassed all others and left nothing intact.

“Those who had possessed due honors lost them. The very best men—men of the highest rank, nobility, and worth—who had not yet improperly attained whatever positions they held, had lost the authority to act [reading: *amiserant*, ‘had lost’]. For at that time no one had an easier way to retain and acquire honors, or to obtain whatever he desired or coveted, than to follow the path preferred by the tyrant Naso.

“Meanwhile, feminine power had broken all the bones of virtue. Therefore, foolish, without eyes or understanding, he had plunged into everything. The confusion of the entire empire was already in motion, so that no one could acquire power, no one honor, no one resources without crime or without the costly condemnation of others.

“This is indeed the fruit of faithlessness and discord. Therefore it is always most prudent to sow the seeds of prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance, so that you may reap a hundredfold fruit for your labor, rather than the schemes of desires and vices, from which judgment is reaped and the vengeance of destruction grows.

“O day, that day of darkness and gloom! O accursed day, when such a policy began! And this is the hour of God’s fury, the hour of our retribution in punishment, when the eyes of all were opened with Balaam the diviner; when we all fell, and the rod of God’s fury awoke; when every right of the laws was violated.”

## CHAPTER VIII

### ADEODATUS

“Alas for the crime! How suddenly such enormous and dreadful losses grew in the kingdom, although sins accumulated piecemeal had demanded it. Therefore we ask what it was that caused Arsenius to plunge himself again into such bitter and destructive dangers. Perhaps he could not foresee what end those things would have which he wished to confront. We ask you to explain this.”

### PASCHASIUS

“Indeed, brother, he saw the countless and immense evils that arose daily, but he could not foresee what was going to happen. He wished, insofar as he could, to confront and resist them—for the faith of the kingdom and the king, for the love of his country and people, for the religion of the churches and the safety of the citizens. All these were dearer to him than his own life.

“But because these things had not been rejected and resisted at the beginning, they prevailed with impunity, as sins demanded, to the destruction of all, so that no one remained strong and wise enough to oppose them.

“When the same man had recovered from his illness, he began to hear everywhere of disgraceful and most obscene things, shameful and dishonorable—not ordinary things, but things such as had never been heard of in our age. At this, all his inward parts were immediately stirred by compassionate feeling, because what had once been a theater of honor had become a palace in which such a quantity of renewed magical illusions had burst forth that no one now believed such things existed anywhere in the world.

“He could not restrain himself from tears because of grief and love, since good, eminent, and most truthful men reported these matters to him day and night. For the more he had loved the Church of Christ and Augustus, together with the people and his offspring, the more deeply he was afflicted with sorrow.

“Even the leading men of the palace, from both orders, came and asserted that everything was so—or rather, worse than it was commonly said to be.

“Then he himself chose to come there by whatever means he could, if perhaps he might help through his skillful arguments or counsels and turn back that fury before it disturbed and overturned everything.

“When he arrived, he did whatever he could. He spoke with Augustus and with the nobles about what he had understood, and warned them, concerning the things that were being done, of what he had perceived.

“He also addressed that most factious beast faithfully, with every service of friendship, since previously his father and Arsenius himself had been very close friends to him. Nor was this without reason, since he had once married his wife, the sister of that man, the daughter of a most noble and magnificent man [Note: From this we infer two things: first, that Wala had been bound by marriage before entering the monastic life; second, that his wife was Bernard’s sister, the daughter of Count William—either Helinbruga or Gerberga. Gerberga later became a nun and, according to Thegan, was shut in a barrel at Chalon and thrown into the river Saône at Lothair’s command as a sorceress].

“From childhood, therefore, he had shown him a father’s tender affection, care, and concern in everything—more even than if he had been his father.

“But when he saw that the man was already blind in mind, alienated, and rushing headlong, he said everything he could. Although the man, already savage in his behavior and intoxicated by the gall of his desires, refused to listen, Arsenius saw that he could accomplish nothing. Having considered everything, he returned to the monastery in sorrow and lamentation, without result.

“Soon afterward, the rulers and leading men of the palace, already expelled and cast down, followed him, weeping and mourning because all the rights of the entire empire were being violated by one shameless man; the best men were being driven out; and strong and renowned men everywhere were being oppressed—not by the strength of that defiler, but by deceit and the most evil fraud.

“Each messenger reported things worse than the worst. Everyone streamed from every side to Arsenius and sought counsel from him as from a fountain.

“But he, mourning and grieving, was entirely suspended in spirit toward God, fearful lest God might somehow help him in such dangers. He urged each of them individually to endure and await God’s judgment. Then he advised each to return to the palace, observe and understand what was happening, persuade others toward better and salutary measures, and strive with whatever effort they could to oppose such great disturbances.

“When they did this, the highest were repelled, the eminent were cast down, the wicked were gathered together, the most worthless were honored, and criminals were brought in.

“Then, having learned these things, they reported to Arsenius the evils in the world—evils scarcely ever heard of—that everything in so glorious an empire had suddenly been changed.

“The palace became a brothel, where fornication ruled and an adulterer reigned. Crimes were heaped up. Abominable and magical practices of every kind were sought—so many that I had never believed any such things remained in the world. Nothing was omitted from the sum of all evils; everything was reported everywhere.

“Nevertheless, this serious and cautious man was not even then moved except to tears, until their faction was exposed and confirmed by the very men who were fully aware of such wicked counsels: namely, that the same tyrant wished secretly to kill Augustus by some means, so that he might appear to have died suddenly from his illness; and afterward to kill his sons, together with the best princes of the kingdom, whoever he might first be able to seize by deceit.

“When the most serious and truthful men reported that these things were undoubtedly so, he was struck by overwhelming sorrow. He sent again and again suitable persons, members of holy religion and men of proven character, to come secretly and remain for a time within the palace among certain people who were in some way involved in the same counsels, until they could investigate more carefully what was true.

“Soon they discovered that everything had been conducted secretly just as it had been reported: how, when, and in what manner the tyrant had decided that what he was plotting should be done. They also reported with certainty that those who were privy to this plan had already issued such orders.

“Then, together with the highest counselors and certain holy bishops, as well as the chief officials of the palace, he began to ask, in the faith of Christ, what he ought to do so that such things might not be accomplished to the overthrow of the entire empire.

“Then all, with one voice, weeping and wailing—the great and the highest, together with all the servants of God who were present—firmly said [supplied: ‘said’] that no one could be faithful to God and to his holy Church if, being able to help in such dangers, he did not do so.

“Thus, after many urged him, and having accepted their counsel, together with the most distinguished and renowned men he committed himself to the cause of Christ’s faith, the condition of the empire, the peace of the churches, the love of the king and kingdom, and the safety of his sons. Set aflame by zeal for God, he acted so that the adversary’s fraud would not prevail, the dignity of the country would be preserved, and the safety of the citizens would remain, even at great risk. For the sake of justice and faith, devoted to the liberty of all, he offered his own safety.

“Otherwise, if he had wished to take the side of the faction, he would have been more acceptable to everyone and held in greater honor by all.

“But since he was strong in spirit, distinguished in holiness, clothed in justice, strengthened by faith, grounded in charity, and armed with the weapons of virtue, he chose rather to die than to endure such a crime and such a most cruel offense—one that, if they consented to it, would bring ruin, destruction, and eternal damnation upon all.

“Therefore he began to fear nothing for himself, provided only that he could anticipate the Christian princes, the prelates of the churches, and the entire people, and free everyone from so atrocious a danger of death, since one destruction threatened all good men.”

### ADEODATUS

“We ought to have lamented one thing, but what has happened compels us to lament matters far worse, because they are much more bitter and cruel than what we proposed to mourn. Therefore they must be recounted again with a grieving heart.

“For he is not so much to be mourned as these things are continually to be lamented, so that God’s anger may be turned away from us. Nevertheless, what we grieve over must be commended with tears, lest our own man be entangled in any accusations of his adversaries. Even if we had the ability to plead, we cannot answer every charge made against each point.

“Therefore let us seek the grace of compassion rather than sometimes introduce complaints of reproach. Let us offer the pains of our hearts rather than undertake the role of defending him with our own skill.

“Then, if we have acted with excessive sharpness or more freely than we ought, and if they wish it, we ask only that they forgive as much ignorance or intemperance as they think ought to be allowed to pious grief or justice.

“For no greater pain can exist than ours, in which so great a Father is mourned as having suddenly been taken away and as being torn apart by so many evil slanders and hatreds—he who was worthy of much love and is daily persecuted.

“In him and with him we lament together the destruction of the country, the overthrow of the churches, the calamities of the poor, the oppression of the rich, the incursions of barbarians, the slaughter of the people, the wars of the arrogant, the plots of all, and—most atrocious of all—the destruction of souls. For when he was despised and not heard, all these things occurred.

“Therefore I ask you not to falter, even when attacked with threats and provoked by blasphemies. And let no one say that in laments such things should not be heaped up or repeated. Let him know that they should be repeated nowhere more than here, especially when such evils multiply, when truth is persecuted with hatred, and when justice is defeated.

“Thus the prophet Jeremiah, after rebukes, persecutions, and assaults, turned to lamentation and bitterly mourned everything that had happened on account of sins.”

## CHAPTER IX

### PASCHASIUS

“You exhort us well, brother—if only the things were not so numerous that we cannot sufficiently recall or even contemplate them. I do not speak of what happened long ago, but only of what has occurred since this impure and impious enemy of every religion confused, disturbed, and perverted everything: mingling all honorable things with obscene ones and religious things with vanities.

“It has reached such a point that neither mind, tongue, nor voice is capable of recounting the schemes begun by this most senseless man, surrounded as he was by a cesspool of every crime.

“For he thought that he could seize control of everything through diabolical magic; overcome it not by counsel but by omens; and forestall it through auguries. He had so deceived the most sacred Augustus with his illusions that he drove away everyone whom either he himself or his great father the emperor had trained, excluding them from private access, conversation, intimacy and counsel, loyalty, honors, and every association of their former life.

“This man, frenzied and the author of crime, fortified by royal power, showed himself to be the punishment of past crimes and the increase of evil. Hence it happened that no one in the kingdom could do anything except what he wanted or commanded.

“Everyone was thus oppressed, as though by a sign of God’s fury, so that no one dared resist or oppose him. The power and will of the pious emperor were, as though innocently, joined to the most filthy man. This was done as a lasting memorial of disgrace.

“For when the plans long since begun and devised were now being initiated, and the king and queen set out under the leadership of that most savage beast, Augustus went like an innocent lamb to sacrifice. The great and merciful emperor went to his death, deceived by the very person against whom Solomon had warned him to beware—or rather, delivered into the traps of that pimp—since he was preserved for no other reason than that the right of imperial power might be seized through his authority and the enemy’s fraud spread to everyone.

“No one, therefore, believes or reflects upon what was done—what acts were carried out, in what manner, or how great they were. Consequently, no one understands why or how they happened, or who were the authors of the evil and who were the good.

“Therefore everyone, ignorant and wicked, blames Arsenius as though he were the instigator of the evils.

“Meanwhile, while these things were being done, the emperor, like an innocent lamb going to sacrifice, had set out from his place and was unknowingly going to his death. Then the hand of the Lord came upon the entire people. They all came together, as though compelled by God, for the faith of the king and kingdom, for the safety of the people and country, for the stability of the empire, and for the succession of his sons.

“For everyone had heard, and each had learned from his own place, that one destruction had been prepared for them all.

“When they were together, as though summoned by God, each reported the evils he had heard—some those they had seen and learned of, or in which they had taken part. When these reports had been exposed on every side, it became perfectly clear that one destruction and death threatened Augustus and his sons, together with all the princes.

“Melanius, the son of the most pious Caesar, had also come with them and was in danger—the king together with all his people—because a journey had been undertaken against him without his father’s knowledge, so that he might be killed first, before his father.

“Then, while everyone was uncertain what they should do about these matters and was overcome with grief, Gratianus flew in from the outer guards. He had long been detained under oath and had endured those circumstances with his father at that time. In his own voice he reported what had been said, what had been done, and what he had learned was going to happen.

“For he had remained there a long time and now saw nothing other than death threatening him. Having fled to them, he recounted everything he had learned while detained inside.

“At this point no doubt remained among them concerning the adultery, the magical illusions of sorcerers, or the divinations. Through him they heard of things so great and of such a kind as were believed no longer to exist anywhere—things that had then gathered at the palace from every part of the world, as though Antichrist had appeared with his magic.

“Finally, he declared the plot for the murder of his father and the overthrow of the entire empire: how it had been arranged through omens, auguries, counsels, plots, and every kind of evil art.

“Then all these nobles and the two sons, Melanius and Gratianus, who were present, decided that they ought rather to die than continue to consent to this: that one criminal, disgraceful man and author of every evil should be an insult, ruin, and everlasting reproach to them all.

“Arsenius, grieving and sorrowful in the fear of God, agreed at that time to this counsel and decision, because he could find no other means of escape. His purpose was not to deprive Augustus of the empire, nor to treat him dishonorably in any way or by anyone, insofar as the outcome of the affair permitted, but to drive out the enemy together with his accomplices and prevent the adultery, which was already public, from remaining hidden any longer, to the confusion of all.

“The sorceresses gathered there, the diviners, interpreters, and mutes, as well as dreamers, those who consulted entrails, and many others trained in evil arts, were to be expelled from the sacred palace. Their prophecies of that abominable art were so numerous and so powerful that they drew many into error. It seemed that all the inventions of diabolical art had sprouted anew in the world.

“This was all being done through fraud or deceit around Augustus, so that he could not perceive at all what was happening day after day. Otherwise, if he had not been forestalled by evil arts, it could never have happened that he would neither hear nor believe his most faithful counselors and holiest prelates when they told him such things—men whom he had once always kept in his council.

“For he received no one else into his confidence except those whom Justina wished. Nor was he able to hear, love, or agree with anyone else, so long as these things continued, except those whom she commended to him as trustworthy. And what is more astonishing, as they say, he would not even desire anything except what she desired.

“Then one of the bishops, while all the prelates of Christ, the senate of the entire empire, and the whole people stood before him and were already reproving him with steadfast faith on account of these things, said:

“‘I know that, although such great matters are being reported, you have until now been badly deceived by these arts and have assented to them. When you have been stripped of the things with which you are clothed, you will recover yourself and become the excellent emperor you always were before.’”

### ADEODATUS

“As far as I can see, no such deed is recorded in history: that a people acted in this way for a prince against a prince. I think it was either the excessive affection of the senators and prelates for Augustus and his offspring, once the reasons had become clear, that caused them to raise him reverently back up into the kingdom; or else blind recklessness caused them to presume such things without any established grounds other than the people’s judgment, the offenses of certain persons concerning adultery, sorcerers, and various other matters.

“Therefore it does not seem to me that, on such grounds, the entire ecclesiastical religion and the whole order of the people ought to rise up and be stirred in this way against Caesar—unless perhaps something else lies hidden which appears more serious.

“We ask this because you were present at that same assembly and affair. Explain it somewhat more clearly, so that our Arsenius may appear more excusable.”

## CHAPTER X

### PASCHASIUS
Yet, as you say, I was present at that same assembly, when all the princes, gathered together peacefully—as far as we were then able to understand—argued these matters against the emperor; I do not deny it. But I am altogether unable to retain everything that was said or answered. Nor is it therefore surprising, since you too do not recall what I listed a little earlier in brief. Otherwise, if you were not forgetful, you would certainly be a slanderer: you would never have considered insignificant the matters I reported as grievous, since nothing more wicked could have occurred if the nobles of the kingdom and the sons already created kings had permitted what I listed to take place.

Accordingly, in that assembly the king gave thanks to the people for these actions, although he concealed something else in his heart:

> “You have done,” he said, “things such as no people have ever been seen to do. For I too was the first to admit and do things such as no king before me is found to have done. And therefore,” he said, “I give thanks to almighty God, who has brought so grave an evil to so peaceful an end. Henceforth, I declare that I shall do nothing of this kind, nothing without your counsel. For just as the empire was formerly ordered and constituted by me together with you, so I decide and wish that it remain. As for this woman whom you have condemned, since vengeance upon her belongs to me, I grant her life according to the common laws, as you demand—provided, however, that she thereafter live under the sacred veil [Note: *The Life of Louis the Pious*, under the year 830, when these events occurred: “But when the emperor discovered that their conspiracy against himself, his wife, and Bernard had been most obstinately and fatally armed, he allowed Bernard to entrust himself to flight; he ordered his wife to remain at Laon in the monastery of Saint Mary, while he himself went to Compiègne. The author adds that Judith was afterward compelled by Warinus and Lambert either to take the veil herself and persuade the emperor to cut his hair. After she had secretly spoken with the emperor, and he had allowed her to escape death, she placed the veil upon her head; but concerning her tonsure the emperor requested time for deliberation. Compare the *Annals of Saint-Bertin*, in which Judith is said to have been sent to the monastery of Saint Radegund at Poitiers, and Bernard to have fled to Barcelona.] and perform penance.”

When these matters had thus been settled peacefully in the same assembly, the glorious emperor was lifted back onto the throne and raised up with acclamations. The entire people then became, if that were possible, even more faithful to him than before. Such, indeed, is Arsenius’s disloyalty—so those who do not know the facts falsely suppose—although by his wise counsel he forestalled the tyrant before he could accomplish what he was plotting: to kill the emperor, destroy all his offspring, and take the wife whom he had dishonorably polluted. If he were allowed to do so, he would seize the empire with her and either kill all the elders of the realm or cruelly subjugate them in oppression; or else he would cross over with her to Spain.

For this reason Arsenius exposed himself to danger and freed everyone from the evil of so great a crime. He therefore did nothing against the emperor, although the ignorant and malicious think otherwise; rather, he acted for the emperor and the empire, for his country and all the elders, for faith and zeal for God, for the Christian religion and the safety of the citizens. Accordingly, in consequence of this act, all the laws—divine as well as human—were shortly afterward annulled. An excessive fraud was concealed, as though under the appearance of faith and the royal will.

This is why even today many err concerning him, calling good evil and calling good what everyone then rejected as evil. From that evil countless evils have arisen, and more atrocious evils arise every day. At that time, however, everyone praised and exalted him everywhere as the liberator of all, especially when Caesar Augustus Honorius, summoned from Italy [Note: That is, around the month of May, according to the already-cited *Life of Louis*, which you should consult and compare with this history], arrived. Justinian had once made him his partner in the empire and successor to the entire monarchy, with the will and consent of all. He was attempting to expel and overthrow him together with his father [Note: *Col. 1622D*] and his other brothers, the kings. At his arrival many things were exposed, and matters that had been spoken of were brought to light.

Because the brother of that madwoman [Note: Heribert, namely, concerning whom the *Life of Louis the Pious*, under the aforementioned year, says: “Heribert, Bernard’s brother, was punished by the loss of his eyes, contrary to the emperor’s will; Odo, his cousin, was deprived of his arms and carried into exile as one conscious of and a supporter of the acclamations made on behalf of Bernard and the queen. Read Nithard’s book and the *Annals of Saint-Bertin*.], having been convicted and confessed that he had consented, was blinded in the same assembly by public judgment, though his life was mercifully spared.

But because none of the things being done came from Justinian’s heart or mind—for he was being incited and flattered by enemies of true faith and justice—and because he was again overcome by feminine influence, he was persuaded that many dishonorable actions had been committed against him, not for the sake of faith, and that he could not thereafter rule well unless he avenged himself upon them; and, further, that he must recover the wife taken from him after the veil had been imposed.

A deeply embedded wound in the heart was at times concealed; accomplices were again increased, so that the empire might be overthrown. Honorius, who had long been his father’s partner and had been made emperor by all, was removed from power and expelled from the partnership. The oaths sworn to him [Col. 1623B] were violated by paternal authority.

The good and illustrious men who had earlier fought for the faith, driven out the tyrant, expelled adultery and every disgrace from the imperial court, saved the country and the people, and—as we have said—freed the emperor and his sons; who, after these deeds by which they had restored him to the imperial throne, submitted themselves, together with the son’s partnership, in fidelity to the father, having acted for the faith, so that nothing but faith and truth appeared in them—all these men were likewise targeted.

When evil men laid traps, an opportunity and a place were chosen. All who had previously kept faith with him were scattered. The senate was sent into exile, and all the magnates and formerly most beloved and foremost men of the palace were condemned. Among them our Arsenius too was seized; nevertheless, at the emperor’s command, he was exiled by the office of the bishops, as though with the greatest honor.

He was then shut away and carried to a very distant region of the earth, into a lofty and exceedingly narrow cavern [Note: This was at Lake Leman. Below, in chapter 12, Wala’s exile is mentioned in the book *On the Translation of Saint Vitus*, also below, and in Nithard, book I of his history. In the *Life of Louis Augustus* it is merely said that the abbot Wala was ordered to return to the monastery of Corbie and live there according to the rule.], where no access was possible except, by God’s judgment, an angelic one.

Not long afterward, when I had come there, sent by the emperor concerning ecclesiastical and monastic affairs, I climbed up to visit him—though not without danger, for his consolation. There, amid very abundant tears, alternately tears of joy and sorrow, we spent a joyful, though mournful, day together: joyful because of our mutual sight and our clear conscience, since there was no guilt of wrongdoing in him; mournful because, in return for the benefit of such great virtue, he had suffered exile and hatred, prison custody, and the injury of dreadful calamity.

While I was with him, amid sweet and bitter words, I wished to persuade him to confess that he had exceeded himself in something and thereafter to agree in everything with whatever the emperor desired. I thought that perhaps, together with certain friends, I could act so that he might be restored to favor—something the emperor also greatly desired, if only Arsenius would consent to him.

To this he replied:

> “I marvel at you,” he said, “if you doubt my conscience in anything, since I am no more conscious than you are of any guilt in those matters for which I am blamed. Therefore you ought rather to have persuaded me to strive more fully for justice than to grow even slightly lukewarm, or to agree to or confess anything against the truth or against what is honorable.”

Then I said:

> “I do not doubt it at all. Nor would I wish to obtain anything more from you in this matter than a word acknowledging excess and an expression of consent, because through these two things I believe that I and my friends could obtain not only pardon for the offenses but also greater favor, proper and greater honors, and, in addition, whatever you might wish concerning him and from him.”

Then, with a slight mocking smile, he said:

> “Do you perhaps think that you have him and all who favor him in your power? Do you not fear God’s judgments? What if I falsely pronounce against myself a sentence of confession and the lie of guilt, abandoning the justice of true faith and purity of heart? It may therefore happen that, by divine judgment, the sentence is turned against you, contrary to what you suppose. If, for the sake of anyone’s favor, honors, fear, or goodwill, I abandon the truth and say something false against myself, and, when this is discovered by God’s just judgment, I am condemned by my own mouth and receive the sentence of death—while you urge me to avoid lesser dangers and seek honors or favor—beware lest I incur more cruel ones. While you urge me to flee temporal injuries or seek honors, I may, through an ineffable dispensation of judgment, acquire condemnation to eternal death. Therefore, brother, let us stand on the road of truth upon which we have entered, and let us have hope, because these things admit us to eternal life, which is Christ.”

At these words I was confounded and fell silent.

It is certain that his conscience was concerned with nothing except God and for God: with regard to the emperor and his sons, his country and the churches, the nobles and magnates, religion and the salvation of the people. For he sought nothing of his own, but only the things of Christ.

Therefore he is mistaken who supposes that Arsenius was brought into danger of exile or death because he knowingly or willingly did anything wrong in these matters: because he injured his country, violated the majesty of the empire, dishonored the emperor and his sons (*exinhonoraverit*, sic), corrupted faith, or disturbed peace. Good and prudent men do not accuse him of failing to love ecclesiastical rights, the king’s glory, or the greatness of the empire; rather, they accuse him because, by loving these things too greatly, he committed some offense.

For this reason he is rightly not summoned as guilty of malice in all these matters, but as guilty of virtue, since blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice. He is rightly called a new man of virtue, because he extinguished the destructive madness and fury of fraud and deceit; freed the emperor from death, his sons from destruction, and the kingdom and empire from the invasion of a tyrant.

From the palace of the sacred empire he drove out every abomination, expelled adultery, condemned persons practicing sorcery, and restored honor. He restored the father to his sons and the sons to their father. He did not permit the monarchy at that time to be divided into factions, and he forbade the violation of the oaths sworn to the emperor’s son.

He wished to preserve every good thing and cast down and crush evil, so that all might live a safe and peaceful life according to God; so that the election solemnly made by the father and by all in favor of the son, and the imperial consecration confirmed by the authority of the apostolic see, might remain unshaken—for the concord of peace, the stability of the monarchy, the glory of the principate, and the honor and glory of the Christian religion, which by now is almost everywhere trampled underfoot, afflicted, and held captive by the faithless and the enemies of so great a name.

He wished, through the vigilance of his counsel, to ensure that so glorious and Christian an empire not be divided into factions, since, according to the Savior’s saying, “Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated” (Matthew 12:25). We all lament and mourn that this has happened today, at every moment.

He wished the oaths, as we have said, which had been sworn to Honorius [Note: Louis Augustus declared Lothar his partner in the empire in the year 817 and arranged for this to be confirmed at Rome by Paschal in the year 823, with the customary oaths sworn to the new emperor. Consult the book *On the Life of Louis the Pious*, Einhard, and others], and the faith that had been pledged, to be preserved intact, lest the entire people be stained by such great perjuries.

He wished the unity and dignity of the whole empire to remain, for the defense of the country and the liberation of the churches, for the integrity of its possessions and the administration of the churches’ resources. But now, as we see, everything has been altered or thrown into confusion.

Let every enemy, therefore, take notice and understand with what splendid virtues Arsenius is adorned and by how many testimonies he is commended for justice. It is not the good and upright who tear him apart or defame him, but the guilty and malicious, or the ignorant deceived by rumors, who pursue him with hatred. His honorable and most distinguished deeds commend him everywhere, and his life bears witness to them.

Those who wish to disparage his life and diminish his praises thereby accuse themselves: either they lack understanding, or they have been unwilling to contend for virtue, becoming flatterers so that the things we lament might not come to pass. Otherwise, to seek glory and honors without labor and virtue is vanity.

Let our Arsenius therefore have praise, because, together with the grace of Christ, he won the honors of eternal life. Let him possess fame and acclaim, because, after dishonor and exile, life and immortality have now been granted him.

## ADEODATUS

I am sufficiently astonished and cannot cease to marvel at a man raised up by such great and manifest praises, praised by the mouth of everyone, concerning whom the whole Church and the whole people bear witness that he always drove away by his counsel the evils that then prevailed and increased; that he preserved the king’s glory, the empire, and the sons; and that he wished to oppose such great evils before they arose—evils under which the whole Church, the whole people, every age, and every order now suffer and mourn.

What is the reason that they refuse to perceive and understand this, especially when they themselves are afflicted by the same evils, yet refuse to observe or recognize where and from whom these things arose, by whom they were produced, or by whom they were nourished and propagated? For if his counsel had been heard, what benefited everyone and would please everyone today would have resulted.

But lest an opponent of evil prevail by counsel against the plots of malicious men, against the wickedness of the unjust, indeed against the emperor himself—who, as is daily evident, fought against his sons, against the empire, against his country, and against the safety of the people with whatever power, honors, intelligence, skill, weapons, and multitude of soldiers he could muster—Arsenius is expelled, cast down, delivered over to exile, and confined, as you say, in a lofty cavern, so that he could no longer offer any mortal counsel of salvation, counsel that might oppose the worst will.

For wisdom or counsel did not precede, so that a good will might be guided toward prosperity and safety. Rather, the intention of an evil will went before, and cunning, intelligence, and unjust power were employed so that the cruelty once resolved upon and the will already begun might not be broken.

## CHAPTER XI

### PASCHASIUS

You perceive, brother, where the devouring flame of the conflagration leads. For unless the mind had been badly deceived by various illusions, and power inflamed while an unyielding will was preserved, and unless the faith of the faithful had remained humble and devoted with all reverence, he could never have acted so destructively against his own safety and that of everyone else, partly by persuasion and partly by power and ingenuity.

But because their faith was undefiled and uncontaminated, those who were good, deceived by excessive reverence, did not wish at first to oppose him injuriously. For that reason they incurred the danger of condemnation, and almost everyone’s ruin became one and the same.

Thus, again and again, while he was in the same cavern, he greatly rejoiced for himself that he was suffering injury for the sake of justice; but he grieved over the dangers that he already saw approaching. He grieved because good and excellent men were being attacked; because wholly innocent and faithful men were being oppressed and dishonored and handed over to exiles, prisons, and various hardships of injury.

Although this man was living almost among the clouds—elevated as far as is permitted to mortals—and was leading an angelic life, his custody did not seem sufficiently safe to the emperor, his followers, and the supporters of Justina, who had returned to the marriage, because of Honorius, who was himself staying in those regions after being rejected from partnership in the empire.

They feared that he might give counsel of salvation to Honorius or to the leading men, by which iniquity would be broken and the cruelty begun against the virtues would cease. Therefore he was quickly brought down from the lofty cavern and transported to Herus [Note: This island is mentioned in the *Life of Saint Adalhard*, who lived there in exile for seven years; it will also be discussed below, where the translation of the body of Saint Philibert is treated], an island in the Ocean, the last of all lands, so that, like blessed John, he might see only divine things and be unable, through human understanding, to touch upon human affairs or offer words of restoration to anyone.

### THEOPHRASTUS

As far as I can conceive in my mind, the calamity inflicted upon the man and his exile without law, without judgment, without guilt—but rather for faith, defense, and justice—is not punishment for sin but a proclamation of praise. It did not diminish the glory of his most illustrious name; it actually enhanced it and spread his honorable reputation everywhere.

For if anyone should go there today where he was, he will sense the fragrance of the virtues he left behind, since his entire life was full of gravity, full of good works, and full of religion. Thus the hardship or tribulation of time extended praise of him everywhere, for everlasting remembrance.

Although it is more desirable to complete the course of life without pain or injury, nevertheless, for the glory of immortality and the reward of eternal recompense, the labor of pious struggle, which has no end, brings greater reward than luxurious rest.

Therefore he was always strong and steadfast in every excellent purpose and pious labor, always gentle and patient, prepared with complete devotion to receive whatever divine virtue might decree. He did not regard exile as exile, wherever he might be, because he was with God; rather, he regarded it as his country.

Thus in every place he was, with the Apostle, a good odor to God. For that reason the fame and glory of his holy name were carried here and there.

### PASCHASIUS

It is as you say. Therefore he may not be called an exile, but rather those who compelled him to live in exile. For wherever they were, they were exiled from themselves, from understanding, and from counsel, since by their crimes they made every country devoid of citizens and excellent men, and like an exile.

What does the name “exile” itself mean? Certainly, the punishment of calamity and disgrace. When, then, is it disgraceful? Truly, when it is the punishment of sin. It is also the opinion of men that this is so when someone is condemned unjustly.

But in this case he did not bear the name of exile because of his own sin, but by an unjust decree, while God acted justly. No one could be so insane as to say that it was sinful to act with wise counsel for the faith, for the life of the emperor, for his sons and the empire, for the safety of the people and the salvation of the country, for justice and the laws of the emperors, for the stability and unity of the kingdom and the concord of peace, for the removal of vices and abominations, against adultery—which is the final evil—and against the dishonor of the whole empire.

Thus no one could be so mad, insane, or ignorant as to consider happy or sensible those who praise such actions, performed against conscience and against the safety of all, while blaming this man. As though all those who, struggling for justice, endured such triumphs of injury had not been happy! From the company of all these he was chosen in his own time, so that for outstanding and countless benefits he might receive the honors of insults.

Hence, in a new manner, he was magnificently honored by being led into exile at Herus, with the conscience of those who supplied such counsels bearing witness to the fact. For the innocent and excellent man was harassed in this way for no other reason than that he might not oppose evil efforts with good counsel.

Thus they did what all the faithless of old practiced against the saints. Therefore he too endured similar things, suffering with them so that he might reign with them.

## ADEODATUS

O monstrous and wicked intention! Who has ever heard of someone hating those by whose counsel and foresight he had been preserved for life, and whose faith and assistance had saved him and his possessions? Or who has ever been so wise as to love those whose agreement they sought, when those men were enemies of himself and his people, and whose insults, through their wickedness, had defiled all his honor with filth?

Alas, what unprecedented madness of obscenity, where every entrance to vice is opened! When Justina, though polluted, is received, the pollution is not corrected, nor is room given to fear so that it might be corrected.

Therefore traps are prepared for this man, and he is moved from place to place, because everywhere virtues displease vices and are not considered safe enough by vicious men so long as they are believed to exist somewhere.

Thus a man of virtue, a lover of chastity, and a defender of justice is expelled here and there without witnesses: for his virtue was public, without judgment, without crime, without a hearing, and without wrongdoing.

Therefore I would like you to disclose what he did after being transported to Herus, the last island of the earth.

## CHAPTER XII

### PASCHASIUS

I openly acknowledge that he did there what aromatic spices usually do, and what he had done in the aforementioned cavern—except that there he saw the sky and the Pennine Alps, as well as Lake Leman, whereas here he saw only the sea and the sky. Here and there he meditated upon God in his mind, always carrying himself with himself as present to himself.

According to David, he saw the wondrous swellings of the sea; in the heights of his mind he saw the Lord. He therefore contemplated the wheels and revolutions by which the world is turned, while he rejoiced that he himself had been firmly established on solid ground. He greatly rejoiced, as though placed in a paradise of delights because of its immense beauty, since he had escaped from the depth of iniquity, where the rivers of those who contend against one another continually raise their waves up to heaven under the impulse of demons, yet do not cover the earth.

Just as no one can count those waves and swellings, so no one can comprehend the power of the divine dispensation. Therefore let every faithful person hear, with Arsenius, the voice of the Lord saying to the sea and to the world:

> “Thus far you shall come, and here you shall break your swelling waves.”

Otherwise, unless he had been strengthened by these promises and founded upon the firm rock, he would not have remained so immovable and unshaken amid so many whirlwinds of injuries, collisions, and crashes of temptations.

There, for a short time—alas for the wickedness!—although he was with blessed John and inferior to him, he was permitted with exultation and gladness of heart to contemplate divine mysteries. Yet, for as long as he was refreshed by the delight of eternal contemplation, he left a good example to his brothers and a reputation for holy religion to those who came after.

And because what is more feared is never thought sufficiently secure, he is not permitted to remain confined even here, outside the land, as though outside the world. For John too was feared while confined in prison.

Thus Justina, having now given birth and returned to the marriage after trampling upon the veil, asked where he was—the man whom, as I suppose, she would have wished to live nowhere. But the devil, envious of every good thing, begrudged him longer enjoyment of such delights of virtue. For there was nowhere in this mortal life where he could be more pleased. Therefore he is removed from so delightful a place of joy.

## CHAPTER XIII

### ADEODATUS

Please disclose to us what happened, since no safer or more remote place can now be found, and yet he is expelled from the place where no human access seemed possible except by a long voyage across the sea. It is also certain that Antony [Note: That is, Adalhard, Wala’s brother, as was said above in his Life] was once placed there because of the strictest custody.

This man, too, was greatly loved by everyone, although for a long time he had already been loved because of his own good deeds and benefits. Antony certainly left there many deposits of virtue, commended his merits to God, and carried the fragrance of virtue with him everywhere.

### PASCHASIUS

You ask what the occasion was. I have already shown that it was like the occasion John had in prison, when he was struck by the sword. At that time King Melanius was related to them in those regions, and they had decided to lay hands upon him. It was therefore arranged that he should not be aided by counsel, since he himself was blinded by many acts of sin.

On this pretext, although he was honored because his merits were revered and his counsels feared, he was lifted up with injury from exile and conveyed most ceremoniously, like fragrant incense, through the middle of Gaul to Germany.

He always carried his country with him everywhere, because everywhere he was known, everywhere loved, and everywhere loved more dearly in proportion to his innocence. Having by now passed through his trials, he feared no force and no power, although he had not yet satisfied the minds of his adversaries or appeased the hatred of the wicked. For the time being, however, he had sated the faithlessness and crime of the traitors—not completely, because his will resisted what they wanted.

Therefore they were afraid that he might aid good counsels and that their fraud would be exposed and perish. For they were not enemies to him as one who had already been expelled, but to the virtues that, with God’s help protecting him, he could not lose anywhere.

What more can I say? He left behind a hive of monks made fruitful with virtue. And behold, when he was brought again with joy to Germany, a choir of monks received him [Note: Perhaps the monastery of Fulda? As far as I know, there is no record of this among the ancient writers]; and, under the leadership of bishops, he was again restored to the same place and abbacy, though dishonorably, in a certain sense honorably.

### THEOPHRASTUS

O our wretched times! O the plots of our foolish disagreements, which have brought so peaceful a kingdom to such a degree of civil frenzy! Yet blessed is the man whose reputation for virtue is spread everywhere.

I think there is no region, no soil of our lands—not even of the most remote; no sea, no islands, no shores; no place, house, or city in which the praises of this man do not exist and in which the traces of his chaste counsel do not remain impressed. He offered these things to all with incredible gravity, virtue, steadfastness, and purity of heart.

For there was in him integrity of mind, holy religion, diligence in affairs, and moderation of virtues, by which his authority was greatly commended. Therefore, wherever he was, he was revered and regarded as an outstanding patron, because even in the consciences of those who, as far as lay in their power, condemned him to exile, he was venerable for the merit of his life and virtue.

But exile was not exile for him at all; rather, it was an increase of merits. For, as the Psalm sings, “Going forth, he went from place to place, bearing his seeds” (Psalm 125:6).

Everywhere he had the confessors of Christ as intercessors. Everywhere he found in them examples supplied by God for his encouragement. Everywhere he himself left behind a testimony, and he had with him the company of monks among whom he had lived. Their prayers commended him, their consolations sustained him, and their solemn offices soothed him. He instructed them by his examples, encouraged them by his words, and fortified them by his counsels.

Therefore even today he is greatly loved in those same places, wherever he was. He is continually praised and commended, even by those who never saw him, so that his fame and praises may always flourish.

## CHAPTER XIV

### PASCHASIUS

Nevertheless, in the same monastery to which he had been brought, he was again not permitted to remain for long, lest perhaps he become involved in counsel or conversation with Gratianus in those regions. For he remained everywhere the same, and once he had resolved, according to God, what he ought to desire, he held to it tirelessly, lest the strength of his spirit be broken by any injuries of hardship.

What more can I say? He was returned to his own monastery, deprived of the same honors, because he was revered everywhere, lest he have an opportunity to act against a will that had once been implanted in him.

For this reason, when he returned, we were filled no less with sorrow than with joy: sorrowful because he was deprived of his office, but joyful because we had at least been deemed worthy to see him and were permitted to have him with us.

His great humility and submission while he was there, his devotion and readiness for everything, will, I think, not be erased from memory. For shortly afterward, although he had been wearied by many burdens of injuries, papal envoys arrived [Note: This occurred in the year 833, when Pope Gregory IV came to Gaul to restore peace. From this it is inferred that Wala suffered exile from the year 830 until approximately the time when he had already been recalled. Certainly Nithard, in book I, writes that Wala was recalled in that very year, together with Elizachar, abbot of Centula, Matfrid, and the others who had been confined in exile], along with the kings’ sons and nobles, all of whom had come together with that most holy man for the sake of peace and unity, for the father’s pardon and reconciliation, so that they might obtain forgiveness by the authority of the Pontiff and the empire might be saved.

They brought letters heavily charged with every kind of divine authority and ordered him, with every adjuration, to come to meet the supreme bishop in assistance, although he had already suffered much on their behalf. If he were unwilling, the emperors ordered them to bring him away by force, but with every honor and reverence.

When we all heard this, we were greatly afraid, especially because our entire monastery was occupied by soldiers. At first, however, we did not know what they intended. We were therefore very frightened and asked what was happening. Then they disclosed the truth of the matter, but he himself refused to go with them.

They attacked us, saying that if they could not otherwise accomplish it, they would have to take him away by force. At these words we were all deeply afflicted with sorrow and terror, since great danger threatened both us and him, whether we did what they asked or refused to do so. We were already excessively saddened by the many dangers he had endured, and, because he had previously accomplished nothing by them, we were afraid lest he be forced to undergo them again.

The authority of the supreme pontiff was displayed before us and read aloud: it was for peace, for the reconciliation of father and sons, princes and nobles, for the condition of the churches, for the unification of the people, and for the salvation of the entire empire.

There were also others on behalf of the sons, asking him for their sake to come to their aid with his counsels. He had already suffered much for them, and they begged him not to abandon them at the end of their danger.

They also announced the divine power that had leveled the precipitous road across the Pennine Alps before the holy apostolic man. The road had been blocked by many obstacles so that no army from those regions might cross over here again, but, as was reported, it had opened of its own accord for them.

When these and countless other matters had been presented, we began to urge him to obey the supreme pontiff of God for the sake of peace, even if it should happen that he died with him. “There is,” we said, “great authority by which you are summoned; there is also great necessity and justice for which you are summoned. Nor is the obedience under which it is fitting for a man so devoted to God to obey such a great pontiff, together with all the other holy faithful of God, any less binding.”

## CHAPTER XV

### ADEODATUS

This is what many people criticize, as though he ought not to have concerned himself further with these matters or involved himself in such affairs. Yet the grace of the Holy Spirit prescribes no authority belonging to any rule; rather, the providence of Christ arranges all things, and each person advances in his several duties, to the extent and in the manner appropriate to each.

One must consider what each person does, and how and where he does it. For, as is read in that same Rule, the enclosure of the monastery is an instrument of virtues and good works, by which everything may be completed more diligently and according to the rule.

For this reason, since someone who is not permitted to do anything without the abbot’s command must consider whether he was permitted, without transgression, to rush into matters so great and uncertain, it is exceedingly dangerous for anyone to abandon his own purpose and thoughtlessly involve himself in matters that are neither expedient nor suited to his office [Note: See chapter 4 of the Rule of Saint Benedict].

### PASCHASIUS
The following is the statement of many—but of those who do not consider what dignity or rank this man possessed. For after he had been elected pastor by everyone and, as we believe, had accepted from God the office to which he had been called as ruler, he was appointed, together with the other chosen men, counsellor of the whole empire, and was placed before the rest in faith and counsel. Indeed, he had already held this precedence even before he was elected, because on account of his lineage, the merit of his life, and the education he had received from almost the beginning of his youth among the senate and the wise men of the kingdom; because of the power of his mind and the nobility of his understanding, he was listened to very attentively by everyone and revered by each individual.

Therefore, since he was already a prelate, he was appointed senator together with the other pastors of the churches, and with all the other senators of the palace or kingdom, so that he might give counsel on every matter. It does not seem to me that he could, without endangering himself, have neglected first to offer counsel concerning the matters we have enumerated, in which the destruction of everyone was plainly impending. Otherwise, there was no monk greater or holier than John, who was therefore beheaded; none more acceptable than Elijah; none more religious than Elisha, or than the other holy men and prophets who manfully resisted kings and contended for justice even unto death. For this reason Zechariah was slain, Isaiah was sawn in two, and Jeremiah was cast into a pit; but this man, far inferior to them, was raised up in a most exalted cave.

Anyone who says, therefore, that he ought not to have stood for justice or contended for the faith against so many and such great evils that brought death; or that, since arms were not permitted, he ought at least not to have resisted by counsel, exhortation, and persuasion—such a person is mistaken. These evils soon became manifest to everyone, and thereafter became greater and more atrocious than our pen, as it flows onward, either wishes or is able to recount. Whoever pretends not to know what and how great they were, or how utterly wicked were the things that arose from them and still endure, is altogether either foolish or mad. Therefore, no sane person who wishes to defame this man would say that he wanted, by his wise counsel, to oppose such things.

**THEOPHRASTUS**

I was exceedingly astonished, and many are astonished, that in support of so great an empire, and of so great a dignity of kingdom and churches, so few prelates or senators of strong and courageous spirit were found who dared to expose themselves and their own safety to danger for the welfare of the entire empire and for the common good.

In our own time, each of us should rather marvel if he sees a good and courageous man than if he sees someone timid, or someone who consults for himself rather than for the commonwealth—for the commonwealth is either nonexistent or extremely small. Thus there is no one either for the churches or for the people who dares, or who is able, to correct what has been corrupted or perverted.

To omit recalling the case of each individual, we can see at a glance those who, with the counsel and assistance of all good men at that time, restored the afflicted, overthrown, and dishonoured dignity of the king and the churches, and freed it from domestic brigandage; and then see those same men mournful, dishonoured, declared faithless, and condemned—by death, disgrace, imprisonment, and exile. Meanwhile, those who violated, harassed, disturbed, and overthrew all things divine and human by their plunder were not only exultant and joyful, most courageous and excellent [or: most fruitful], honoured with honours and covered with glory; they also plotted ambushes and dangers against distinguished, wise, and honourably zealous men, and so feared nothing for themselves.

Although that affair contains many disgraceful and detestable features, nothing is more abhorrent than this: dangers of death and calamities of deposition are now inflicted not merely by brigands and plunderers, by the utterly criminal—men worn down by poverty or ruined by their own wickedness—but also by the very best men who once existed, by men distinguished for the authority of religion, and by men exalted through the nobility of their flesh. From these men, too, plunder and oppression proceed. Now scarcely anyone leads soldiers behind him on the strength of his own lawful pay; they are led by plunder and violence. That utterly filthy Naso was the first to teach this, and he lived to the end as a public robber.

[Note: [Col. 1633D] The Annals of Bertin assign Bernard’s end and killing to the year 844. Hence it is clear that this second book was written long after that time.]

Now, the more these men are surrounded by brigands, the more powerful they become, so that no one may oppose their plundering. Yet although military forces are increased on their behalf, none of them seems to possess strength except for civil destruction. It is therefore no wonder that this man, summoned by the supreme bishop, opposed such people. He had first wished, with Moses, to be blotted out of the book of life for the people of God, for Augustus and his sons; and likewise, with Paul, to become accursed for the sake of his brothers and the churches.

**ADEODATUS**

It is no wonder, then, if, worn out by so many exiles and stained by so many disgraces, he resisted at first. For, as we saw and learned, unless all of us had forcibly compelled him, and unless the authority of the supreme pontiff had pressed him so heavily, he would never again have consented to anything of this kind.

But now, urged by his brothers, summoned by the supreme pontiff with solemn adjurations, and entreated by the sons of Augustus, the kings; entreated also by the people and prelates with whom he had formerly been involved in the original cause of this affair, he finally judged—compelled by the need for concord and peace—that he should come there and obey the supreme bishop, joining himself to the man who had undertaken so great a labour for the whole people of God, if perhaps he might restore peace with him in the kingdom and remove the disagreements.

There is therefore no ground for reproaching him. Indeed, the greater blame would have been his if he had abandoned the command of so great an authority because of the danger threatening his present life. For it is more praiseworthy to die well, or to face danger with good and excellent men, than to live wickedly or to consent with the worst of men. One thing is the punishment of judgment; another is the increase of sin.

Thus he did not again deliver himself to danger thoughtlessly, as some say, or contrary to the purpose of true religion. Rather, he offered himself with the greatest devotion and in a praiseworthy manner, standing between both parties, if he might be received equally by all. Nor could he be deterred by his own dangers, since he had so often exposed himself on behalf of others.

From this point let us proceed with Paschasius, who remained constantly his companion. No danger to his present life could deter him from following the man whom he had loved in Christ and whom he had resolved to imitate. He had also wished to die with him, in good conscience concerning him, for the faith of Christ, if the time of danger should come.

**CHAPTER XVI**

**PASCHASIUS**

I plainly confess that, whatever feeling prompts you to say what you are saying, it is exactly as you say. The journey we undertook is sufficient proof: we travelled amid the clashes and ambushes of those who lay in wait for us, amid legions running here and there against us. Until we reached the Augusti, the kings, and the holy pontiff himself, we proceeded continually in the greatest danger, with fear and trembling, fearing that we might not be permitted to reach our destination.

For, if this had been discovered, a stricter guard would have received us than had formerly been imposed upon him. At that time Justina was with Augustus. She was turning once again the sceptres of the whole monarchy, stirring up the waves and seas, driving the winds, and turning the hearts of men toward whatever she wished. Since they had expelled from her service the one most disgraceful man whom we mentioned—namely Naso or Bernard, who withdrew to Septimania, as Nithard records in Book I, although in the year 834 he attempted to return to his former rank by expelling the monk Guntbald, who, after labouring greatly for the restoration of Louis Augustus, wished to be second in the empire. He was a monk of the monastery of Saint Medard, as is understood from Nithard—other utterly criminal men served her.

Since we could not avoid them except by passing through the midst of their cohorts, we nevertheless arrived safely, with God protecting us. When we had reached the place, the kings, princes, and the entire people received us with overwhelming joy.

Then, when we were brought before the most holy pontiff, he received us with great eagerness and considerable reverence. He himself was troubled in spirit by the things he had encountered—things he could never previously have believed possible. Yet he was terrified—something greatly to be lamented—by Augustus and all his followers, even by the bishops who, on the day before our arrival, had given him their right hands and promised that they would be united in resisting those who stood on the opposite side, namely the royal sons, the princes, and the people. Moreover, they were taking counsel together and insisting, alas, that they ought to depose the apostolic bishop because he had come without being summoned.

[Note: Elsewhere, if I am not mistaken, there is no mention of this threat. The author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* indeed reports that the bishops, whom the pontiff threatened with excommunication if they were disobedient to the will of the emperor and his sons, replied that if he came intending to excommunicate them, he would depart excommunicated. Gregory himself, in the letter to the aforementioned bishops published among the letters of Agobard, complains that they had said that, unless the pontiff came according to their will, they would not allow their churches to remain in agreement with him but would oppose him so completely that, as he says, he would be permitted neither to act nor to arrange anything in their dioceses, nor to excommunicate anyone while they resisted him. But there is no complaint concerning a threat of deposition.]

Phasur and the others who shared Justina’s views were there. When the pontiff heard this, he was greatly astonished and afraid. Therefore we gave him certain writings supported by the authority of the holy Fathers and composed by his predecessors, writings that no one could contradict. They showed that it belonged to his power—indeed to the power of God and blessed Peter the apostle—and to his authority to go and send to all nations for the faith of Christ and the peace of the churches, for the preaching of the Gospel and the assertion of the truth. In him was the whole pre-eminent authority and living power of blessed Peter, by whom all must be judged, while he himself must be judged by no one. When the pontiff received these writings, he accepted them gratefully and was greatly strengthened.

**THEOPHRASTUS**

Alas, what must Augustus have been like at that time, and what must Justina have been like, who then turned everything according to her own will? And what must the princes have been like, when such men were found among Christ’s prelates, so that, just as the former rose up in human matters, the latter rose up in divine ones?

Like the false prophets of old, they scattered the people with their horns toward every wind and rose up against the head of the whole Church of Christ, so that he might not bring peace between father and sons, between Augustus and the princes; so that those who had been scattered, exiled, and unjustly dishonoured might not be reconciled; so that peace might not be restored to the churches; and so that the arrangements of earlier times and the kingdoms divided among the sons might not remain firm and undisturbed.

These things happened because Justina inflamed their zeal in this way.
