They did not offer the prince counsel from their hearts or minds; rather, by flattering and fawning for the sake of favour, they trampled truth, justice, peace, and concord underfoot and resisted with all their strength those who seemed to be contending on behalf of these things.

Yet what justice the sons and the people possessed, since on both sides they opposed one another, while the father plotted against the sons and the sons seemed to have risen up against the Father, so that all were enemies—because you were present, we ask you to explain to us.

**CHAPTER XVII**

**PASCHASIUS**

It is clear that the parts of justice are many. One kind is the justice of the kingdom of God, another that of an earthly kingdom; one exists between parents and relatives, another between outsiders and strangers. Indeed, as there are laws and customs among the nations, so many kinds may be said to exist according to the usage of justice.

Therefore the measure of justice in this matter must be gathered no less from the law of God than from the law of one’s country, and also from the law of nature. For just as it is written, “Children, obey or show deference to your parents,” so too it says, “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger.” If both duties had been carefully observed, so great an evil would not have increased.

Yet, so that the matters I have proposed may become clear, the *Capitula* must be recalled.

[Note: If I am not mistaken, no one has so far reported these *Capitula*.]

Augustus the father addressed these *Capitula* to his sons, as if presenting a complaint, in order to declare what he demanded from them.

First, he reminded them that they were his sons and that he himself had begotten them with God as author.

To this they replied:

“We give thanks to almighty God,” they said, “who has granted you to remember such things about us—for they are true—and not only to remember them but also to command them. For we, most excellent of the Augusti, possess nothing dearer in life after God than you, our most sacred father. We possess nothing more glorious than that we are considered and are your sons; nothing richer, nothing more abundant, nothing more magnificent for us in honour, excellence, and dignity, in the praise of your name and the splendour of glory.

“Therefore, most glorious lord, we have come humble and devoted, submissive and subject, as is fitting. May your piety and gentleness deign only to remember concerning us that we not be condemned unjustly, disowned without a crime, or disinherited without fault. For we are not rising up against you, as those who seek our destruction say and accuse us of doing. Rather, we ask suppliantly for pardon, indulgence, and mercy.”

Then, in another chapter, he said:

“Remember also that you are my vassals and that you have confirmed your loyalty to me by oath.”

To this they again replied:

“We remember well that this is as you have commanded. For by nature, by our promises, and by every true oath of loyalty, we are indeed faithful. Therefore, just as we have never abandoned service in your army, so, as long as the spirit remains in us, we shall never become deserters. Your glory, honour, and prosperity are dearer to us than our own lives.

“And so we have not come against you; rather, we are prepared for everything on your behalf, provided only that we may obtain your former grace and mercy. Nor have we brought with us these men who are here with us against you. Since, as he had taught us, we did not dare to come simply and unguarded, we brought them because of those who lie in wait for us, wishing to destroy us and overturn the empire of your glory. They are also trying to disturb and corrupt your most serene, pious, and gentle spirit—which by nature is filled with every excellence of the highest nobility and illumined by the grace of Christ—against us and against all the faithful, and to change it into the bitterness of an alien nature. For in former times they did nothing other than attempt to destroy you as well.

“Against these men we have come to your clemency so that they may be exposed and so that the throne and majesty of your empire may be confirmed more gloriously as their crimes become clear. We ourselves seek reconciliation and pardon, since, as far as it has been in our power, we have never willingly incurred any guilt.”

He added:

“You ought to know,” he said, “that for a long time I have most devotedly undertaken the defence of the apostolic see, although you now unjustly claim against me that you may exclude me from this office, which, as long as I live, I cannot abandon.”

Then Honorius, together with his brothers, said:

“Let your sublimity consider, and deign to remember, that your most excellent providence in Christ likewise caused me to undertake this care, and especially the defence of that see and of the other churches, when your majesty, together with the will of the people, appointed me a partner of the whole empire in every power and honour, in every document and coinage, and in every arrangement, while preserving your honour and providence.

“Indeed, your imperial excellence graciously sent me to that same see to confirm in me whatever your pious dignity had decreed, so that I might be its associate and partner not less in sanctification than in power and name. Therefore, since before the holy altar and before the sacred body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, I received from the supreme pontiff—with your consent and will—the blessing, honour, and name of the imperial office, and moreover the diadems for my head and the sword for the defence of that Church and of your empire, no one with you more than I wishes or ought to defend it.”

[Note: Agobard, bishop of Lyon, in his mournful letter to Louis Augustus, writes: “In the course of time, whenever imperial letters were sent for any reason or to any destination, they contained the names of both emperors. Later, however, when the will changed, the arrangements were overturned and his name was omitted from the letters.”]

“And because I have heard that many are plotting against him, I wish it to be clear to everyone that no one will harm him without me. I brought him as the vicar of blessed Peter, for peace and concord, to reconcile your most serene piety.”

The glorious Caesar again commanded that it was not right for them to prevent the apostolic bishop from coming to him or to block the roads by which he might come.

To this Honorius replied:

“Most serene lord, we have by no means blocked his routes of approach. Rather, with God’s help, we opened them, although by your command they had been obstructed among the Alpine passes and steep precipices, so that no mortal could freely cross until they had been levelled by God’s power and our labour. Thus I can say with the prophet that crooked places were made straight and rough ways level.

“For this purpose we compelled him to undertake this labour, so that he might come to you as the supreme intercessor in the place of blessed Peter, whose power lives in him and whose authority is pre-eminent. Therefore we do not, as we are accused, prevent him; rather, we present him with the utmost devotion. We humbly beseech him in the cause of God and of ourselves.”

Again Augustus said:

“You are acting unjustly by keeping our sons, your brothers, with you and making them rise up against me.”

“Far from it, far from it,” Honorius replied, “my lord. Since they had been driven away and rejected, and expelled far off by persecutions, I resolved to bring them back to your clemency. I suppliantly ask that your holy fatherhood deign to remember that we are your sons, and that your majesty not deign to disown or destroy us without fault. Rather, let the affection of the flesh move the entrails of your piety, together with justice—not less the justice of the law of nature than that of the law of God—and deign to have mercy on us.”

Finally he said:

“You have also unjustly received our vassals and keep them with you.”

Honorius replied:

“Let your blessedness know that this is not so. When they too had been scattered and driven away, or detained in custody and exile, they fled to us and to this blessed bishop, so that he might intercede for them with your most serene clemency. Let them not be condemned unjustly, since they stood for your faith and justice, lest the fraud and deceit of the most criminal men should prevail.

“This is what I have always heard in your sacred council and in the senate of illustrious men; this is what I have always recognized in your deeds; this is what I have heard from you; this is what we read in the deeds of the ancients: that strong, distinguished, and deserving men ought to be honoured and glorified rather than driven away—men who prudently restrained the assaults and attempts of wicked people, who resisted the audacity of conspirators by authority, faith, constancy, greatness of spirit, and counsel.

“I mean those men who, through their own fickleness and ruin, have defiled your empire with every kind of wickedness. Since these men exposed and drove them away, they ought to be honoured and glorified rather than accused by the most pestilential of men. For they themselves were first nurtured in your disciplines, instructed by your counsels, elevated by your dignity, and distinguished by honours; they were always regarded as the foremost and most eminent men of the palace.

“Therefore we judged that we should bring them back to your most merciful piety and present them to your sight. We ought not, therefore, to incur offence if we restore and reconcile to your favour those whom the fraud of factional men destroyed.”

This, then, is the exchange of accusations between the two sides; these are their mutual complaints; this is the father’s proposal and the sons’ reply.

Since they could not even then obtain any consent to pardon, the holy and supreme pontiff, the vicar of blessed Peter, was sent as intercessor. When he arrived, he was received with no honour appropriate to his rank.

[Note: Hincmar, bishop of Reims, writes in Letter 41 to Hadrian II: “And how Gregory, having been secretly taken away, came into Francia with Lothair, against the opposition of his father; and how peace afterwards existed in Francia as it had not before, and how the pope himself did not return to Rome with such honour as was fitting and as his predecessors had received.” Yet Thegan testifies in chapter 42 that gifts were exchanged between the parties. Read Agobard’s letter concerning the comparison of the two regimes. The place where Louis met with his sons was called the Field of Lies, between Argentaria and Basel, according to Thegan.]

Nevertheless, after giving his blessing according to his custom, he stated the purpose for which he had come.

The emperor said to him:

“We do not receive you, holy pontiff, according to the custom of the ancient kings—with hymns and praises and with the other honours due to your dignity and religion—because you have not come in the manner in which your predecessors were accustomed to come when summoned to our predecessors.”

He replied:

“Know that we have come properly, for we have come for the peace and concord which the author of our salvation left to us, and which has been entrusted to me to preach and proclaim to all. Therefore, emperor, if you receive us and the peace of Christ worthily, that peace will rest in you and also in your kingdom. But if not, the peace of Christ will return to us, as you have read in the Gospel, and will remain with us.”

**THEOPHRASTUS**

Alas, what had happened that so religious and devoted an emperor, more so than all those who had preceded him, acted so foolishly and thoughtlessly, giving honour neither to God nor to blessed Peter the apostle?

It was an evil and utterly disastrous obstinacy of mind and hardness of heart; and a woman’s persuasion—the same persuasion that first deceived our ancestor—which, as we recognize with grief, deceived him as well. We therefore lament that a man of such authority and holiness was pressed down by such dense darkness and did not remember what the Truth says: “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever hears you hears me” (Matthew 10:40).

Alas, what and how great was the fascination and blindness of mind that deceived so great and distinguished a man amid so many temptations and dangers, amid so many scandals, so that he could never be recalled to his senses and could not be healed by any counsel of the Holy Scriptures.

He was seen daily to meditate on the law of God, yet with a hardened heart he withdrew so far from the law of true love. Otherwise, he would never have so stubbornly provoked his sons to anger against the commandment, nor so frequently and cruelly pursued them, disowned and attacked with the hostile sword, when they wished him no evil except that the arrangements which he himself and the whole people had first established and confirmed by oath should remain unshaken.

If he had loved or governed either the people or the Church of Christ entrusted to him by God—or at least the commonwealth—he would never, for the will or persuasion of one woman, have permitted such great evils to befall the kingdom: evils that perhaps will never cease, either through human ingenuity, virtue, counsel, or the power of anyone.

Meanwhile, because we grieve deeply, tell us what the supreme pontiff accomplished with him, or what he obtained.

**CHAPTER XVIII**

**PASCHASIUS**

As you have often read, ambassadors who failed to obtain peace returned from the place to which they had been sent. So this man also returned without success, without honour, and without fruit for so great a labour.

Nevertheless, after the day on which he returned, during the following night, the hand of the Lord came upon the entire people by God’s just judgment. The minds of individuals were changed, and everyone was shaken and terrified by fear of God.

That same night they abandoned Augustus without anyone’s persuasion or exhortation, as far as I could discover.

[Note: Thegan, however, says that this was done by common counsel; and the author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* says that the people drifted over to Louis’s sons partly through gifts, partly through promises and threats.]

All of them, from the least to the greatest, went to Honorius, joined themselves to his camp, and appeared in the morning with their tents fixed around him. Thus each person on the side of the sons and the pontiff said, “Manu!”—which is interpreted, “What is this?”

[Note: Read *Manhu*. This was the cry of the sons of Israel when they first saw the manna, Exodus 16:15.]

For it was altogether a great wonder to everyone, who knew nothing of what had happened. The day before, they had been so strong and steadfast, trusting in their numbers, in everyone’s promises, in the counsel of the pontiffs and senators, in paternal authority, and in numerous assurances. Yet they were found so changeable and weak that, without consulting anyone or considering anything, they abandoned Caesar alone with his Justina and flew throughout the entire night to the son against whom they had come and against whom they had taken their stand, like chicks gathering beneath their mother’s wings. In the morning they had set up their camp, and one people appeared.

We therefore went very early to the same pontiff because of the miracle that had occurred. And behold, in the midst of us one of the Romans cried out in a singing voice:

“The right hand of the Lord has shown strength,”

and the other words that follow.

Then that holy man and all who had gathered judged that so illustrious and glorious an empire had fallen from the hand of the father, and that Augustus Honorius, who was the heir and had been made his associate and advanced by his father and by all, should raise it up and receive it. Otherwise, they all said, if he did not do so, they would unanimously choose someone who would bring them aid and defence.

After these words Honorius consented and assumed the whole monarchy of the empire, taking his father with him—though I do not know by what judgment.

When I saw this, I addressed Arsenius concerning it and said that it seemed wrong to me for so sudden an event to alter so great an empire without more extensive counsel and more careful planning: he had been made an associate in good faith, so that shortly thereafter, by the fall of his father, he might claim the whole monarchy for himself.

He replied:

“It was our task to come here, to labour with good will for everyone, and to offer counsel for peace, calming the civil war that threatened. But now, just as no one listens to us, so no one pays attention to what we have learned. For, as you have read, everyone either fears, desires, rejoices, or grieves.

“They fear what happened earlier, lest what has now been done be avenged again. They desire—every one of them, while the opportunity remains—to reach as quickly as possible what they already possessed, or to acquire what they did not yet possess.

“They rejoice greedily and exultantly over these honours, because everyone seeks his own interests and few seek the things of God and what is useful. The rest, therefore, grieve because they fear losing what they have. It was through the boldness or counsels of these men that Caesar Augustus acted thus against his sons.”

**CHAPTER XIX**

**ADEODATUS**

As I understand it, these men were more like kites than consuls. They thought of nothing except deciding matters concerning their own honours, each considering how much more he might seize for himself. Yet, since the empire had fallen from the father’s hand, they ought already to have reflected and investigated with that same pontiff, together with Honorius and his brothers, why it had fallen. Then they should have corrected, strengthened, and firmly established everything together, so that thereafter it might remain united and unshaken.

The foremost and highest men ought to have watched over the matter with great foresight and much counsel, lest the commonwealth and the condition of the whole empire, once collapsed, should perish again through discord. For among distinguished and powerful men, discord usually has no other outcome than either universal destruction or the domination of the victor, together with the restoration of the kingdom’s unity, peace, and concord.

But because this man was not firmly established on the throne with prudent counsel, and because the victor did not hold his dominion with God—for the father had fallen by God’s judgment—and because peace was not fully restored while each person sought his own interests, the kingdom again perished in the son’s hand and slipped away. Thus, while neither of them sincerely walked before God, it remains to this day shaken and divided.

A hidden hatred also remains between the brothers, together with a deep wound implanted in their breasts and branded upon the minds of the greatest men. On their account the commonwealth continually tends toward worse things and collapses. Opportunities are sought, and each person awaits his moment, because the authority of the kings—which is fitting and necessary for government—has fallen, while the agreement of all is regarded as torn apart and broken.

Judgments and sound counsels have perished. The votes of men are heaped up, but, weakened in strength, they accomplish nothing, to such an extent that scarcely a man is found who will oppose himself for the safety of his country or offer himself to danger for his fellow citizens.

Therefore, according to the sentence of the Truth, the divided kingdom is daily laid waste and corrupted, because where there is no governor, the people fall. Yet each side has lost God as its governor, since amid their dangers they sought him with a feigned heart.

Thus, one day, when the foremost men and consuls of the palace were meeting and watching together in secret, they divided the whole empire among themselves with Augustus the son. They paid no attention to the precedence of parents, to the equality of the great, to the great number of nobles, to the former faithful men who had deserved well, or to the dignity of the churches—which is the most important thing—or to reverence for God from the heart.

When this had suddenly been done, Arsenius arrived. Those men, confused because they were conscious of what they had done, offered him the lots of the distribution, in case there was anything that might displease him.

Then, being shrewd in his replies, he said:

“Everything has been well arranged, except that you have left nothing of its own to God, nor have you established anything that might please good men.”

After he had said this, he began to grieve more and more, because he was now scarcely listened to at all, having been overcome by the greed of the blind. As a result, at every moment royal power was weakened and rather perished than increased.

Crimes multiplied, discord was again inflamed, quarrels were stirred up, and ambushes were nourished. Augustus the father was revived by the exhortations of many, who insisted that he ought to be restored to the throne of the empire.

On every side seditions were stirred up and dangers increased, to such an extent that there was no house, city, municipality, village, or province in which discord did not continue to reign.

At that time, however, the dangers grew still greater in turn, until Augustus the father was raised again to the seat of the kingdom and the son was driven out.

**CHAPTER XX**

**PASCHASIUS**
He was therefore not expelled, as you assert, nor did he act so foolishly as you lament; for he upheld and preserved the kingdom and empire that had fallen, together with his father Augustus. He committed no offense in it except what the entire senate and people compelled him to do, in depriving him of power and subjecting him to the judgment of the bishops, who reduced him to penance. Our Arsenius, together with God’s grace, moderated all these matters, lest either party act toward the other more cruelly than nature allowed, or more wickedly in so great a crisis.

But when the devouring flame of discord raged more fiercely, and the father Augustus would not willingly yield in anything or soften, Arsenius, lest parricide should result, acted on his holy counsel so that Augustus the son, leaving his father once more on the imperial throne, sought pardon and departed freely with all his supporters, because the wrath of God had boiled over and been poured out upon the whole people on every side. For, according to Job (2:6), “the tents of robbers abounded” on both sides, and they provoked God boldly enough by their wicked deeds. And therefore Arsenius’s counsels now accomplished less. For everywhere the doors of desire stood open, and cupidity had burst into flame.

Thus he chose suspension—withdrawal from their midst—because although God had placed everything in their hands, no one sought God from the heart, with whom are wisdom and strength; he possesses counsel and understanding. Hence it is plainly established that when the almighty God destroys someone, no one can rebuild him; when he shuts someone in, no one can open. And therefore, because he was alternately destroying those whom he had raised up and raising again those whom he had shut in, Arsenius preferred to depart freely rather than remain among them as a servant of sin.

He was already considering, stunned, that human strength and ingenuity were nothing, and that wisdom rightly seemed more like folly. For, as Scripture testifies (Job 12:16), “he knows both the deceiver and the one deceived.” Therefore, when he saw various deceits and frauds clashing on every side, he arranged that the son should yield to the father and depart unharmed with his army, while the father remained in power with those who wished to remain with him. Thus all were to understand that he alone is the omnipotent king who brings counselors to a foolish end and judges to bewilderment; who loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord—which we plainly saw happen in this case.

But because neither party had sought God wholly and worthily, they were changed in turn through alternating reversals, and the people were scourged, so that all might understand that he is the God who brings priests to dishonor and overthrows nobles. Otherwise such great distress and confusion of all things would never have arisen except from their sins. For the speech of the truthful had been changed, and the teaching of the elders had been taken away.

Therefore this man alone could no longer stand against everyone, except to the extent that he acted as he did, lest the outcome of events then deteriorate into something worse, as many on every side were urging. For contention and contempt had been poured out upon the rulers. But what was then prevented—we grieve to say—we later saw happen, lest civil war arise among them. Nevertheless, our man would have preferred to die rather than assent to or participate in anything of that sort.

For this reason the son persuaded him to depart with all his followers, so that the father might take possession of the empire, which had formerly been badly administered. Since God, who changes the hearts of the rulers of the earth and deceives them so that they wander uselessly along an impassable road, had hardened his heart and committed the whole matter to his judgment, nothing more wicked would arise between them.

It was then a sorrowful sight to behold, as their sins demanded, what Job says: “They will grope as in darkness and not in light, and he will make them stagger like drunken men” (Job 12:25). For he alone exists whose purpose no one can turn aside; he will do whatever he wishes according to his just judgment.

Our man, therefore, considering these judgments and the events that had occurred—events that grew worse and increased daily—foresaw, though late, what was to come, and what we now see fulfilled on every side. Hence he chose to flee rather than remain with either of them. For the father wanted, as I myself witnessed, to retain him with himself at that time with great insistence and every mark of honor and reverence—even if he wished to require an oath and pledge of loyalty from his followers—and then Augustus the son wished to take him away with him.

Yet he listened to neither of them; indeed, he resisted both firmly, departed from both, and entered Italy with winged steps. He took refuge within the monastery of Saint Columbanus—namely, [the monastery] at Bobbio.

**Note:** [Col. 1643D] This was evidently the monastery at Bobbio, whose incomplete catalogue of abbots survives in Ughelli’s *Italia sacra*, with Wala omitted, since he governed the place for less than a full year; and with Ebo, archbishop of Reims, to whom this abbey was entrusted, as Frodoard testifies in Book II, chapter 20 of his *History of Reims*.

Since that monastery, like all the others, was in danger of being overrun by plunderers, he accepted it for governance at the brothers’ own request; and for as long as he lived, he governed it nobly and peacefully.

## CHAPTER XXI

### THEOPHRASTUS

This is why many attempt to criticize him: because he abandoned the place in which he had professed and been elected, and seized another by whatever means, as though led by ambition. Perhaps, then, it would have been more religious either for him to remain in his own monastery and do peacefully what, as you admitted shortly before, he could have done; or to remain in the same place without the burden of governance. In the one case, there would have been fulfillment of his vow; in the other, the praiseworthy exercise of humility.

### PASCHASIUS

Perhaps you have not read the *Life and Deeds of that blessed Columbanus*. Expelled from Luxeuil through the jealousy of a certain woman, he rebuilt this place again and governed many brothers there commendably until the end of his life.

**Note:** [Col. 1643D] Namely, Brunhild, queen of the Franks, as is clear from the *Acts of Saint Columbanus*.

For he ought not to have hidden the talent entrusted to him in the ground, but to have distributed it among the brothers, as we read that blessed Benedict and very many others did.

It therefore appears that he defended it from enemies no less effectively, governed it most religiously under the holy Rule, and diligently increased it, having begun in that same profession as in the first. Since he did not believe that he could live peacefully in his own monastery or make progress in the office of governance, I think no person of sound mind would criticize him for withdrawing, under the same religious observance, to a place of quiet and great usefulness to the brothers, where he could benefit many.

I do not know whether he could have saved himself with us amid so many dangers, where faith is now nowhere, or scarcely anywhere, found—especially among those who desire, or appear, to be supreme. Among such people, to despise worldly honors for the sake of religion is considered cowardice.

## CHAPTER XXII

### ADEODATUS

We know all these things and how he conducted himself among them. And if despising honors is a crime, loving Christ’s poverty is judged imprudence. But since earlier we grieved over what Paschasius has recounted as having happened; since we lamented the crises of events and their varied outcomes, recounted the temptations, and, mourning, enumerated the various affairs of the causes involved; it now remains for us to turn our attention to the end and to his death.

We were not present, nor did we scatter tears like flowers at his vigils or around his tomb. At least, though absent and far away, let us commend him to the Lord in our prayers; and since we do not know the day of his burial—or the anniversary of that day—let us commemorate it for as long as life remains to us.

That day is surely, in our minds, a representation of future rest. In it lives the one who is thought to be dead; and commendation of his memory declares that the day of death is better, when he entered everlasting life, than the day of his birth, when he began to live and at once became subject to death.

### PASCHASIUS

You rightly encourage us, brother, by commanding us to approach and recount his death in such a way that you teach us not to mourn it. For just as through one person’s sin death passed to all human beings, so through one person resurrection is granted, and all who die piously live blessedly with him.

Therefore, because we cannot avoid the author of our race, we cannot escape the author of death. And if we do not escape him, neither can we avoid what is common to all. It is improper, then, for us to despair of the life that is in Christ, since he alone is the author of life and resurrection.

Thus, just as death came through one, so we must most truly believe that life also comes through one, Jesus Christ—not life of any kind, but blessed and eternal life. Therefore, beloved, the day of the death of our father is rather a day of life than of death, since through death he entered this everlasting life.

We ought therefore to take comfort rather than mourn, because this death is the lot of all; nor should we regard as harsh whatever belongs to everyone. It is not to be mourned, first because it is common and owed to all; then because it releases us from all the troubles of the world; finally because it is like sleep, since it frees us from the labors and cares of this world and grants rest after the miseries and pains of the present life.

Accordingly, this annual day rightly strengthens our faith, gives us hope of arriving, and pours back into us the charity of love. Whom does the grace of resurrection fail to console? Whom does hope not lift up, and confidence of attaining not strengthen? Whom does charity not kindle, and whom does such great inner love not enliven—love that is born only from the Holy Spirit?

Although, therefore, we have hitherto lamented the various accidents and labors of misery, it remains now to direct our minds there and behold that day on which God lives, and to turn our attention after him. For that day, though one and unique, is better in the courts of the Lord than thousands elsewhere.

We must not, however, fix all our senses upon the Father, lest sorrow again creep in because he is absent. Yet we should not be exiles from such great devotion and grace toward the one we love. We ought to dwell with him in our minds where such great joys are proclaimed—joys to which he came when invited, and into which he himself entered with gladness.

### THEOPHRASTUS

What, then, do you mean by saying that he came when invited? Were not all invited who received baptismal regeneration through faith? All have been called to the same immortality. It is therefore absurd to mourn this man as though he were dead.

It is also foolish to grieve in a special way over what you know has been prescribed for everyone, since this is to raise the mind above its condition, refuse the common law of death, reject fellowship with nature, and fail to recognize the measure of the flesh.

But if, as you say, he came when invited to this destiny so that he might willingly receive it, you are describing the case of a just debtor who voluntarily comes to meet what he owes, prepared to repay his debt.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### PASCHASIUS

I certainly did not say without reason that he came when invited. For I heard from a holy bishop who related it that, before the day of his death approached, he was called and invited in a vision not only once but twice, as though he were about to complete his mission before the presence of the eternal King and receive a reward for his labors.

Thus our Arsenius told him, even before he contracted the fever of death, that he would shortly depart from here through death.

**Note:** [Col. 1645D] The author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* calls it a *lues*, evidently to signify that it raged among many. He plainly calls it a fever when speaking of Wala and Lothair, whom this fever, bringing him down to his sickbed, made ill for a long time. Paschasius bears the same witness concerning Lothair a little below.

As the bishop mentioned above was able to understand, he thereafter lived more joyful in hope and did not suffer long from the fever. Once seized by it, he was more concerned for the emperor Augustus, with whom he was then staying, than for himself, lest the emperor, being afflicted by fevers, should seize the occasion to omit what he had recently promised his father.

In this it is evident that he remained unconquered in faith and devoted in charity, comforted by the hope of his calling. Bound to Christ by this threefold cord, he safely returned his soul to heaven.

**Note:** [Col. 1645D] The often-praised author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* states that Wala died in the year 835. I quoted this author’s words above in the preliminary observations, where the day of Wala’s death was discussed.

His little body was received into the earth in the basilica where blessed Columbanus rests. I do not think it happened without purpose that one house and one neighboring burial place should encompass and commend those whom one religion had held, whom nearly the same trial had expelled from their own seats as exiles, and driven into Italy.

There were two queens of no different wickedness who did this—not at the same time, but joined and associated under one impious crime. Because of a similar jealousy they could not bear holy men to rebuke their similarly wicked conduct sufficiently, or to oppose them in any matter. Therefore, by deceit and fraud, plotting against them, they forced them to leave the monasteries over which they presided and go to Italy.

**Note:** [Col. 1646D] That is, to Auxonia, or Italy, where both lived in the same place, although their reasons differed.

Thus those whose life together had been shared, though their circumstances differed somewhat; whose religion and flight from the plots of two women had been one; also had one repose after labor and one rest in burial.

The one was a holy confessor of Christ, approved by his virtues; the other, as his follower, was supported by his merits, commended by praise, and aided by prayers.

Nor do I believe that it happened without God’s providence. They had exposed themselves to danger for faith, zeal for God, religion, equity of judgment, and the pursuit of virtue; and in one place they reached the end of their labor.

It is therefore beyond doubt that the distinguished Father rests, clad in the garment of a confessor, with God’s holy confessor in eternal rest. He, too, had been expelled from his monastery as an exile, driven from his homeland and from the office of governance, by an example like that of the other. Thus, since their trial was one, may one consolation of rest refresh them in eternity according to the quality of their merits, and may the reciprocal proportion of justice adorn them in heaven.

Because of so great a hope, then, we ought to console one another rather than grieve. The sorrow of such great mourning has been eased not only by confidence in his blessedness, but also obliterated by time, overcome by reason, and long ago softened by prudence.

Although we rightly mourned when we lamented his various afflictions, counted his manifold trials, and explained his misfortunes, we should now rejoice with him, be refreshed by joy instead of mourning, be restored by the gladness of good hope instead of sorrow, and inwardly clothe ourselves with exultation instead of sadness, because we know for certain that the distinguished Father survives his body.

Although he was absent from us when he died, he is nevertheless present, because he lives blessedly in the one who is everywhere. His soul, released from the barriers of its bodily senses, now sees with an unimpeded gaze what, while situated in the body, it could not see.

If, while sleeping, the soul raises itself to higher things, as though buried in the body, and sometimes announces to the body visions of absent or even heavenly realities, how much more does it do so when freed from the troubles of the world and living wholly in the Lord, who lives everywhere and fills and governs all things everywhere?

Our Father has not journeyed far away anywhere except to the one in whom and for whom he lived, who is everywhere in himself and lives everywhere. For he died daily with the Apostle in order to live more perfectly for God. As the philosophers say, “the life of a wise man is meditation on death.”

He meditated on reaching what is perfect, when the eternal vision would appear to the beholder with unveiled face—not partially, nor in a riddle or shadow, but in truth, as it is. This could not happen in the present, because, according to the Apostle, “at present we know in part and prophesy in part.”

But when what is perfect in that life has come to us, what is partial will be abolished, and what is now partial will then be perfect (1 Corinthians 13:9).

No one would hasten toward the end, trusting in the Lord, unless he were fleeing the afflictions of this life, for which David laments, saying to God: “Behold, you have set my old days before you, and my substance is as nothing before you; nevertheless every living person is altogether vanity” (Psalm 38:6).

Therefore this man, brothers, after he had understood and learned these things, never delayed fleeing his own will. He did not wish to be disturbed vainly in the world, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches. He hoped in the living God, to whom he attained.

Thus, when he tasted the death of the body, he found life, because he did not undergo the first death of the soul.

Death is spoken of in three ways: first, when we die to sin and live to God; second, when we sin unto death, of which it is said, “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:4); third, the departure from this life, through which Christ also died, and through which everyone who has tasted this life will die, so that he may no longer be able to sin.

Thus one death is called spiritual, another natural, and a third penal. Yet the death now called natural, although it may appear penal to some, was not given by the Lord as a punishment, as those who have written books on the goodness of death maintain; rather, they say that it was given as a remedy, because one thing was prescribed for Adam as punishment and another as a remedy.

As punishment, it is said: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife more than to me, and ate from what I had commanded you not to eat, cursed is the earth in your work,” and so forth, “until you return to the earth from which you were taken” (Genesis 3:17).

These are the forms of punishment: the earth is cursed, and thorns and thistles spring forth in his labors. The thorns and thistles choke the word of life; they also generate cares and anxieties by which the food that comes from heaven is killed and excluded—the food by which every person who lives for God is nourished—and death is enclosed, by which the soul lives under punishment.

Therefore this death was given by the merciful Lord as a remedy, as though it were the end of evils. For this reason it is not said to Adam, “Because you listened to the voice of your wife, you shall return to the earth.” Had this been said, it would have been a penal sentence, as is the statement, “Cursed is the earth in your work,” and the rest.

You therefore have the death of the soul, namely sin; you have the punishment that is rightly called true death; and you have the death that is rather the end and remedy of our punishments, by which the course of this life is cut short for a time.

Thus this death, by which Abraham died and by which our Father died, by which we all die, is not only not an evil but is even a good. For this reason blessed Ambrose also published a highly necessary book *On the Good of Death*.

Therefore, if we mourned at the death of so great a Father, and lamented the various sorrows of events and his many labors, let us rejoice with him, because for him to live was Christ and to die was gain.

Let us die with him, so that we may live with him in Christ. Let us learn through daily practice to die to the world, so that we may be separated from the flesh and live, through meditation, as though in heaven. Let us sometimes take on the likeness of death, lest the punishment of death overtake us, so that through the good of death we may reach eternal life, in which there will no longer be death or mourning.

Let us die the death of the righteous, so that we may live with them. Let us also die the death of this great Father, because, as we believe, he now lives blessedly, so that we too may be able to live with him—something for which he always prayed and taught.

Let us offer within ourselves the vows of that Father, because he vowed and offered us to God as a sacrifice, especially our brothers, a new offering for sacrifice, whom he dedicated to the Lord. Not only those whom he himself instructed and gathered, but also all who will in the future be there for the same instruction that he dedicated to the Lord.

He did not live only for himself and God; he lived for all of us as an example and instruction, so that he might teach us to live for God. Therefore his life benefited us, while for him, with the Apostle, to die was gain.

Let us therefore humbly entreat that Christ, who offers the vows of the saints to God the Father, may himself bestow upon us, for the increase of his merits, gifts that may be offered more abundantly to God the Father as an accumulation of his reward for him. May our offering and his offering within us, through Christ, be accepted as an everlasting sacrifice, so that those whose profession in the sacrament of holy confession was one may also share together in the eternal reward in joy.

## CHAPTER XXIV

That he himself was carried to the joys of eternal life by angelic hands, we learned fully from the venerable account of Queen Ermengard. She often said, with pious remembrance, that at the departure and hour of death of so great a man she had sent messengers throughout various parts of Italy, so that individual holy men might commend his soul to the Lord in their prayers.

Among these arrangements, she also sent to her own highly distinguished monastery, situated within the walls of the city of Brescia.

**Note:** [Col. 1649C] Thus the ancients wrote, for example Riculf, bishop of Soissons, in chapter 19 of his *Constitution*, following Gregory the Great. We call it Brescia. The monastery of Saint Savior and Saint Julia at Brescia was already famous at that time. It had been built by Ansa, wife of Desiderius, king of the Lombards. Lothair Augustus wished it to be entrusted to his wife Ermengard and, after her death, to their daughter Gisela, issuing a diploma that survives in volume II of the *Casinensian Bullary*, p. 24. On p. 33 there is another document of the emperor Louis II concerning the anniversary of his sister Gisela, abbess of the same place. In the same monastery, Engilberga, the wife of Louis himself, became a nun after her husband’s death.

The monastery was about forty miles from Ticinum, and a multitude of nuns served the Lord there. The queen likewise commanded and earnestly implored them to commend the blessed soul of the man of God to Christ God in their prayers.

When the messengers sent for this purpose arrived at that town, they found these servants of Christ already discussing the death of the man mentioned above and speaking to one another as though they knew beforehand the hour and time of his departure.

When they had reread the sacred letter that the queen had sent, they found that everything concerning him had occurred as it had been disclosed to them by the angels. For among them were two most holy virgins who testified that all these things had been revealed to them as they had predicted, because they had heard angelic choirs carrying the blessed man’s soul into heaven, as though through that very place.

At his funeral, among other things, they sang the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise you, God; we confess you as Lord”—in alternating voices according to ecclesiastical custom. By their harmony they commended the funeral of the blessed man to the merciful Lord.

When only the two of them had continued these praises for a long time, they eventually summoned all the others so that they too might hear them. But none of the others was granted this, except those two alone, so that they might serve as witnesses to the truth.

While they were speaking in this way, the sacred letter that the aforesaid messengers had brought was reread, and they found that he had died at the same hour and on the same day on which the angels had carried him away with praises.

It is therefore clear that what Scripture testifies is true: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life” (James 1:12). And so that these matters might be made manifest, it was reported to the queen with complete truthfulness that only the two women had heard these and other such ineffable things.

But perhaps some incredulous slanderer will say that a man exposed to such temptations and battered by such pressures did not deserve these things—especially since Christ himself is the judge, who exposed and tested him, and, once he had been tested, rewarded him, as we believe, just as he promised in the Gospel, saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matthew 25:21).

Make what I say false, then, although the things recounted earlier about him are true [lacuna]. Therefore, by his own and just [lacuna], he received from God the rewards of eternal life [lacuna]; for this reason, the Gospel says (Matthew 20:13): “Friend, I am not doing you an injustice [lacuna]. I give freely. Did you not also agree with me for the denarius of eternal life? Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish? For I repay no one with a reward except freely, because I am good. Or is your eye evil because I give freely [lacuna] to no one except because [lacuna] from his work for God.”

Let us therefore, brothers, give thanks freely to God, who granted these things to him and promised himself to us, for having bestowed such gifts upon him [lacuna].

**Note:** [Col. 1649C] These few words, marked by dots and omitted here, have completely worn away and fallen out; they are certainly not of great importance. At the end only one line is missing, at which *Wala’s Epitaph* ends. For Paschasius Radbertus entitled his two preceding books on Wala’s deeds, as I warned at the beginning, *Wala’s Epitaph*, in the same manner in which Ursus, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and an author of that period, calls Basil the Great’s *Epitaph* the funeral oration that Gregory of Nazianzus wrote about him. The passage occurs in Ursus’s preface to the *Life of Basil*, attributed to Amphilochius, in these words: “It should certainly be noted that when some read in these deeds what Saint Amphilochius wrote, they suppose it to differ from what Saint Gregory of Nazianzus records in the *Epitaph* of this great man.” Rosweidus comments on the passage as follows: “Basil’s *Epitaph*, or funeral oration, written by Gregory of Nazianzus, is found in volume I of Gregory of Nazianzus’s works, Oration 20. He also composed another *Epitaph*, or funeral poem, about the same man,” and so forth. Thus Radbertus calls his own laudatory work about Wala *Wala’s Epitaph*, which he undertook immediately after Wala’s death in place of a funeral oration.

[Col. 1661]

# INDEX TO THE DOGMATIC OPUSCULA OF PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS

Namely, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, the *Letter to Frudegard*, the *Book on the Virgin’s Childbirth*, and the treatise *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*. (The reader is referred back to our columns.)

[Col. 1661]

B

The faith of baptism must not be altered, 1409. Our good is either from God, or God himself is our good, 1476.

C

To think carnally about the Eucharist is not to think rightly, 1356. The flesh that gives life in the Eucharist is not human flesh, which in no way gives life, 1356. The flesh received in the Eucharist is itself the flesh that hung upon the cross, 1351. Charity is one, but there are two commandments of charity, 1467. Although charity is believed to have been given from heaven, it must nevertheless be nourished, because this fire ought to be perpetual, 1478. Charity is the fountain of life and the cleansing of all sins; where it reigns, offenses have no power, 1487. It is, as it were, another baptism of souls, 1482. It fills people, makes them ardent, and unites them to God, 1460. If it is absent from the heart, whatever is uttered by the mouth benefits the speaker nothing, 1483. Charity alone is perceived only by the good, 1484. Charity is the bond of holy perfection and the root of all good things, 1484. Virginal charity is tender and sweet in spiritual matters, where the Bridegroom and the soul are joined in covenant, 1480. A soul rich in charity is like a watered garden, filled with all the gifts of graces, 1485. He has ordered charity who loves what ought to be loved: nevertheless, he must not love what is lesser more, nor what is greater less than it ought to be loved, 1472. No one knows charity except the one who has received it, 1485. The good of charity is the Triune God, and the Trinity itself is the God who is eternal charity, 1487. The nourishment of charity is diminished desire, 1478. The work of charity is to love and, by loving, to fulfill Christ’s commandments, 1474. Let each person perform works of charity according to God, if he wishes to be a neighbor, 1461. Desire for temporal things is the poison of charity, 1478. Christ’s birth and incarnation, no less than his passion, are the mystery and sacrament of salvation, 1360. To assert that Christ was born from corruption is impious; for if he were from corruption, he would already have been born under a curse, 1369. From the moment he was conceived, Christ was human, yet always the same one who had previously been God, 1382. Christ was not born according to the law of nature, since he was not brought forth according to nature’s customary process, 1368. Christ conquered death by dying, so that those who die in Christ might be found no longer dead but living and blessed in Christ, 1508. Heavenly and eternal things, when they are not possessed, are objects of disdain, but when they are received, they are greatly desired, 1479. The Eucharistic supper is that same supper which the apostles themselves ate and drank, 1359. The counsel indicates what things contrary to salvation we should avoid, 1422. We receive in the Eucharist the body and blood that were handed over for the remission of sins; therefore we receive Christ himself, without whom no remission takes place, 1358. One must by no means believe in someone in whom it is not permissible to hope, 1404. For those who believe in God there is a great abundance of sweetness, 1409. To believe without understanding is far better than to understand badly and be subject to errors, 1407. The things spoken divinely about God are credible; they are understood only after they have first been believed, 1405. There are three kinds of credible things, 1404. He believes in God who worships him with hope and charity, 1403.

D

The love of God is not preserved wholly if faith is denied to one’s neighbor, 1404. Everything we believe, and by which we who live by faith are justified, belongs to God’s mercy, [Col. 1662] 1419. The nature of God, which not even the angels grasp, is all the more inaccessible to human beings, 1409. Many, rashly wishing to comprehend the secrets of the Godhead, have withdrawn farther from the faith, 1423. Nothing is better than God, nor is anything good found apart from him, 1472. One must believe without any doubt in God, who is truth, when he speaks, 1399. To believe God in the heart unto righteousness is to stand by faith in the substance of God, 1397. God cannot in any way be taken away from humanity [reading uncertain: *tolli*]; for he is higher than we are, is not subject to our senses, and, because he is immense, requires immense faith by which he may be grasped, 1394. God is neither lesser in a part than in the whole, nor greater in the whole than in a part, 1414. Truth is not accidental but essential, 1399. Because he is just, we sinners do not go unpunished, 1477. God is wholly everywhere and is contained by no place, 1413. The one God is to be sought in three persons, 1410. God is the way by which we run in faith, the truth in which we believe, and the life by which we are justified through faith, 1419 ff. To despair is to become alienated backward from God, 1450. Despair arises from four causes, 1450. Once despair has been removed, God’s mercy is greater than any number of crimes, 1451. Nothing is worse than the evil of despair, 1450. Christ’s love extends to four things, 1467. Our love must be referred to him from whom, through whom, and in whom alone we are able to be good, 1477. Love is rightly ordered when we prefer to belong to God rather than to ourselves, 1478. The love of one who wishes to claim for himself what properly belongs to God is called not charity but hatred, 1468. Love alone will find through desire what hope already holds through the faith of love, 1489. Love of neighbor is evidence of love of God, 1467. One must love one’s neighbor so that God may be loved in one’s neighbor, 1467. A person who loves himself wholly in God also loves his neighbor according to God, 1469. Christ offered two cups to the disciples: in one he wished to express his passion, and in the other to prefigure the passion of his faithful, 1359. The distinction between that figurative Passover in which the lamb was sacrificed and this Passover, celebrated according to the order of Melchizedek in bread and wine, 1359. The two cups are to be understood as the two Testaments: one belonging to the lamb, the other to the mystery of the body, 1360.

E

The Eucharist produces life in those who approach worthily, but judgment of condemnation in those who receive it unworthily, 1356. The Eucharist contains not merely a certain power of Christ’s flesh but Christ’s actual flesh, 1357. The Eucharist presents not a shadow or figure of Christ’s body but the body itself, 1367.

F

No one is faithful unless mercy first comes freely before him, 1417. God is grasped by faith; once grasped, he is preserved and held in our hearts, 1394. The devout person hastens ardently by faith from what is perceived by the intellect to what he does not yet understand, 1398. When faith is emptied out, the substance of faith remains—namely, unchanging truth, to be enjoyed in vision, 1396. Knowing God by faith benefits salvation nothing if one denies him in conduct and deeds, 1400. When faith, which works through love, is removed, a person is no longer counted righteous but dead among the ungodly, 1398. Christ is the foundation of faith, 1422. Only the one who both believes in God and loves him with his whole heart knows the power of faith, 1414. No one knows how great the power of faith is unless he lives from God and in God, 1415. The other charismatic gifts are granted to each person according to the measure of faith, 1425. God first creates faith in us before inspiring us, 1434. We owe our neighbor no other faith than that which works through love, 1402. We know that faith exists in another from the fruits that faith ordinarily produces through love, [Col. 1663] 1398. The faith that we wish our neighbor to preserve toward us—we must preserve toward him, both in kind and in equal measure, 1401. The more you grow cold through trusting, the more you lose the strength of faith, 1424. Faith must be given to God, who does not lie, 1351. It must be given to one’s neighbor, on account of charity, even if the truth does not shine forth, provided that falsehood is not apparent, 1402. Faith is the initiator of the other virtues, 1389. It concerns past things, as well as present and future things, 1429. Faith is that by which we truly believe and confess, even if we do not yet understand, 1399. Faith that works through love makes us righteous, 1418. Faith is superior to understanding, 1487. False faith presents false hope; therefore it is called not faith but error, just as it is called not hope but delusion, 1393. Faith is the substance of things hoped for because it contains within itself all those things that are not seen, 1394. Faith is complete when one believes in God with one’s whole heart and keeps all his commandments, 1400. Faith is the origin of righteousness, the head of holiness, the beginning of devotion, and the foundation of religion, 1391. Faith rejoices more in sufferings than in prosperity, 1422. Faith is God’s greatest gift, 1436. Faith is weakened unless it has confidence in Christ’s victory, 1424. Faith is bare of human strength; victory has never failed anyone except the person whose such faith has failed, 1425. Faith must depend wholly upon God and remain in God, 1392. Faith in one’s neighbor is rare, because many people say many things, 1401. The faith by which one believes must be distinguished from the things that are believed, 1397. Although faith belongs to everyone, it is proper to each person individually, 1425. Wherever reason or understanding fails, faith grows, 1423. Right faith is truer than vision: we are sometimes deceived by sight, never by faith, 1395. Faith is reckoned as righteousness not for the person who believes only in part, but for the one who believes wholly, 1420. There is a special and particular faith in individuals because of the difference among gifts, 1425. Faith works so wonderfully in some of the dead that they seem to live, though dead, more than the living do, 1417. Faith can do everything through the one by whom it is strengthened, in whom it believes, 1417. Faith contains within itself everything that is hoped for in the future, 1427. Faith is that tower built at the expense of the virtues, 1422. Faith is one, certainly, but not equal in everyone, 1426. True faith is also grace; therefore it is never unfruitful, nor does anything operate without it, 1418. True faith rests securely in Christ, 1423. Faith exercises the virtues and completes the charisms of the sacraments, 1391. Our strength is in Christ, who conquered the world, 1424. Charity is the enjoyment of the highest good, 1454.

G

Grace gives us the will; faith supplies the running along the way by clinging to good works, 1419. All our deeds, whatever their character, are weighed according to faith, 1425.

H

The understanding of the theological virtues is inaccessible to every human being unless it is breathed into him by the Holy Spirit, 1389. Whatever a person has promised in faith to the Creator, he must preserve even unto death, 1399. A person who trusts more in his own weakness than in the firmness of God’s promise soon falls, 1434.

I

Our sufficiency both for beginning and persevering comes from God, 1443. Infidelity drove us from the tree of life; fidelity must bring us back, 1392. At the very hour of the sacrifice, heaven is opened at the priest’s voice, 1355. The beginning of justification before God is faith, 1420.

J

Justification depends upon these two things: willing through grace, namely, and running through faith, 1419. The true righteousness of faith is not to presume upon merits, 1419. Righteousness puts on faith as a breastplate, so that it may not be wounded, 1422. The root of righteousness is not first from works; rather, the fruits of works grow from the root of righteousness [the printed *rudicae* is apparently corrupt], 1421. The righteous person judges each matter according to what it is; he loves things as they ought to be loved and uses them as they ought to be used, 1472.

M

The gifts of merits are varied, labor is varied, and order is varied, 1476. Christ’s mercy, just as it is not without justice, so justice too is not without mercy, 1456. Meekness, modesty, and kindness gently and pleasantly compose the movements of the soul, 1422.

N

An inferior nature neither grasps nor understands the cause and reason of a superior and immeasurable nature, 1358. No one is saved without faith, hope, and charity; no one is rightly considered a Christian, 1393. No one comes to Christ—that is, to charity—unless the Father first draws him, 1485. No one is perfectly faithful until he senses through faith that Christ and the Holy Spirit dwell within him, 1428. No one can do anything from himself except insofar as he has received it from God, 1433. No one possesses anything from himself except vices, 1433. No one repents rightly unless he first understands the excellence of charity and the grace that he has lost, 1481. No one is sufficient for himself either to begin any good work or to bring it to completion, 1433. No one is so evil in this life that he does not admit some good, nor so good that he does not admit some evil, 1472. No nature can be found that is not either God himself or from him, 1430. No one clings to God without faith, 1389.

O

Obedience unto death belonged not to Christ’s divinity but to his humanity, in which he assumed our duties and names, 1360.

P

Peace exists in the person whose whole mind is turned toward the love of God, 1455. A sinful person has only imperfect faith, 1420. God gave human beings the use of money, not love of money, 1486. The summit of perfection consists in love alone, because charity admits no iniquity, 1484. We believe Peter, Paul, the angels, the saints, and every creature; in God alone we believe, 1403. To please God, let us do nothing except according to God, 1478. The soul of one who repents rightly is foul to itself through guilt, but already fragrant to God through forgiveness, 1482. Testing produces hope, and hope produces confidence, 1456. The commandments are to be fulfilled by faith alone, 1409. Every human being is understood as our neighbor, 1469. Prudence, like a sharp eye, contemplates what belongs to salvation and what is contrary to salvation, 1422. The childbirth of the Virgin, through whom so great a blessing blossomed and grace flowed forth, was not subject to pains, 1373. To venerate the most holy childbirth of the Virgin in mind and heart is a grace of the divine gift, 1367.

R

Heavenly and divine reason is not subject to human senses, 1353. There is nothing that we ought to enjoy except God, 1471. Some things are to be enjoyed, others used, and still others both enjoyed and used, 1470. Nothing concerning the faith is to be retracted; rather, what we believe must be guarded in every way, 1410.

S

No sacrifice is acceptable to God unless it is consumed by the fire of charity, 1484. The salvation of the human race, and the effectiveness of the other virtues, depend upon the theological virtues and upon these virtues themselves, 1389. Through faith the saints were able to do everything, even to die for Christ, 1416. The saints confer very many benefits upon those who piously venerate them, 1491. Knowledge of the things that divine power accomplishes in the mysteries lies in faith; reason lies in God who acts, 1358. Whoever reads the Scriptures but does not build from them faith and genuine love of God and neighbor has not understood them, 1479. The wholly bodily sense does not penetrate to eternal things, since it lies below them, 1408. It is absurd to hope except in God, 1404. What is known and believed is rightly hoped for and loved because it is the highest good, 1454. By the hand of hope, which is the anchor of the soul, Christ is held and fastened by us, 1437. As long as we hold hope set before us, we are safe and secure, 1438. Faith makes hope solid; hope lifts faith toward those eternal things that are not seen, 1438. Hope is increased by patience and the consolation of the Scriptures, 1449. Hope raises us toward better incentives to virtue, 1455. Hope and faith must be distinguished by a rational difference, just as they are distinguished by their names, 1438. Hope is our strongest and inviolable consolation, 1435. Our hope must be placed in God because he is the highest good, 1477. Our hope is anchored not in the seabed but in Christ, who is the firmest rock, 1435. If hope is false, it benefits the one who hopes nothing; if true, it makes him blessed, 1451. Spiritual things are better seen by the mind than perceived through bodily sensation, 1413.

T

Fear, although it sometimes restrains and humbles the mind, at other times strengthens and comforts it, 1457. The tower that faith builds is God himself; in this tower it stores up unfading treasures, rooted in the love of charity, [Col. 1665] 1423.

V

To will and to run are given to us by God according to the purpose of his will, not according to the merit of our will, 1434. The word of almighty God is effective for everything he wills, 1359. The word of God is the sword of the Holy Spirit, 1422. God can indeed raise up any corrupted virgin after her fall, but he cannot crown her, 1182. The virginity of Blessed Mary is the glory of all the Churches, and especially the honor of religious women and the model of virtue, 1367. When she gave birth, the Virgin Mary was as far removed from groaning and pains as she was from guilt, 1374. The Virgin Mary did not give birth to the Lord according to natural law, 1383. The virtue of good works is received to the extent that it is offered from faith, 1457. The virtues of the soul are understood through the one from whom they come, 1486. The virtues are food for the Lord’s fire, 1479. The vision of God is not apprehended by bodily senses, 1412. If you wish to come to God, begin with Christ, who is called the beginning of God’s ways, 1477.

[Col. 1665]
